# BOOK THREE

...some who, though they were previously of no reputation, after they enjoyed his intimacy, shortly emerged as the highest of all those among whom they had previously been the lowest. **SOCRATES:** Do you know what kind of thing this is, O son of Demodocus? **THEAGES:** I know, by Jupiter! <note>original: "per Iovem"</note> And if you are willing, I shall become such as they were. **SOCRATES:** Not so, O best of men; but this has escaped you, what kind of thing <margin>Something concerning the spirit of Socrates.</margin> <margin><insert>The spirit of Socrates</insert></margin> it is. I shall tell you. There is present with me, by a certain divine fate, a certain spirit <note>original: "demonium." Socrates refers to his 'daimonion,' a divine inner voice or sign.</note> that has followed me from earliest childhood. For this is a voice which, when it occurs, always signifies a dissuasion from the thing I am about to do; it never, however, urges me on. And if any of my friends communicates anything to me, and the voice appears, it dissuades him and does not permit him to do it. Of which matter I shall give you witnesses. You know Charmides, the good man and son of Glaucon; he once communicated with me when he was about to practice in the stadium at Nemea. And immediately as he began to say that he was going to practice, the voice appeared, and I prohibited him, explaining to him how the voice of the spirit had appeared, warning him not to practice. Then he said: "Perhaps it signifies that I shall not emerge as the victor. But even if I am not to obtain victory, yet by practicing at this time, I shall make some progress." And having spoken thus, he went away to compete. It is worthwhile, therefore, to inquire what happened to him from this contest. Or if you wish, ask Clitomachus, the brother of Timarchus, what Timarchus said to him when he was almost about to die—he himself and Euathlus the runner, who received him as he fled—he will relate to you what he said then. **THEAGES:** What was it? **SOCRATES:** "O Clitomachus," he said, "I come now to die because I was unwilling to obey Socrates." And why should I mention what Timarchus said when he rose from the banquet—Timarchus and Philemon, son of Philemonides, being about to kill Nicias son of Hiroscamander? For they alone were conscious of the ambush. Timarchus said to me: "What do you say, O Socrates? You all drink; but I must go out elsewhere, but I will return a little later if the opportunity arises." Then the voice came to me. "Therefore do not rise," I said, reporting the usual sign given to me by the spirit. He stayed. Then, having waited a little while, he burned again with the desire of going, saying, "I am going now, Socrates." And because I heard the voice again, I restrained him once more; until the third time, desiring to hide from me secretly, when I had turned my mind elsewhere, he stole away. And having set out thus, he performed those deeds by which he fell into death. Whence he had said these same things to his brother, as I now say to you, that he was coming to die because he had been unwilling to believe me. You will hear, moreover, from those who are in Sicily, what I predicted concerning the conflict of the army. And past events may be heard from those who knew them. But we can even now test the sign of the spirit to see if it says anything. For Neon, son of Calus, has gone out on an expedition. The sign appeared to me; he sets out now with Thrasylus to wage war against Ephesus and Ionia. I, however, think he will either be killed or fall into something of that sort; and I fear greatly for the rest of the business. I have told you all these things for this reason: because this power of the spirit is all-powerful in the intimacies of those who associate with me. For it opposes many, nor is it permitted to bring help to those who have a habit of being with me against the spirit's will, wherefore it is impossible for me to live with them. But it does not prohibit me from clinging to many, yet they are not helped at all by our association. Those, however, whom the spirit favors in the intimacy itself, these are the ones of whom you yourself have perceived: for they make progress in a short time. But some of them have this benefit firm and durable; most, however, as long as they are with me, are wonderfully powerful. But when they depart from me, they differ not at all from others. This once <margin>To Aristides, son of Lysimachus.</margin> happened to Aristides, son of Lysimachus. For staying with me, he progressed much in a short time; but afterward he set out for military service. Returning then, he found Thucydides, son of Melesias, with me; this Thucydides had appeared as my adversary in certain discourses the day before. When Aristides had greeted me and spoken certain things besides, he said, "O Socrates, I hear Thucydides boasting and even contending with you in certain matters, as if he were something." "It is as you say," I replied. Then he said, "Does he not remember, before he adhered to you, that he was like a slave? <note>original: "mancipium." Implying he lacked intellectual freedom or skill.</note>" "It does not seem so, by the gods," I said. "But I," he said, "am ridiculous." "Why most of all?" I asked. "Because before I went away from here, I dared to dispute with anyone; nor did I seem inferior to anyone in debating, so that I boldly approached gatherings of the most excellent men. But now, on the contrary, I flee from whoever I understand to be learned: I am so led away by shame on account of my ignorance." "Did the power itself leave you suddenly," I asked, "or little by little?" "Little by little," he said. "But when it came upon you, did something happen to you while learning from me, or otherwise?" "I will tell you, O Socrates: a thing incredible, yet true. I never learned anything from you, as you yourself know, but I made progress whenever I was with you; even if I were only in the same house, though not in the same part of the house; yet more so whenever I was in the same part. And I seemed to myself to progress much more when, being in the same part, I looked at you saying something, than when I looked at another. But I progressed by far the most when, sitting near you, I touched you. But now all that habit has flowed away." Such, therefore, O Theages, is our association. For if it is pleasing to God, you will progress very much and in a short time; if otherwise, not at all. See therefore if it might not be safer for you to be instructed by one of those who themselves hold in their own power the utility by which they benefit men, rather than to attain it from me by a certain fortune. **THEAGES:** It seems to me, Socrates, that we should do this: let us test that spirit by our association. If it nods to us, all will be well; if not, we will consult together what must be done: whether we should adhere to someone else, or try to appease this divine thing that is implanted in you by prayers and sacrifices and any other way that the prophets may set forth. **DEMODOCUS:** Do not resist this youth in these things, O Socrates; for Theages speaks well. **SOCRATES:** But if it seems necessary to act thus, let us act thus.

<meta>This page begins the translation of Plato's "Meno," specifically the introductory "Argumentum" (summary/analysis) by the Renaissance scholar Marsilio Ficino, followed by the opening of the dialogue itself. Ficino’s introduction provides a philosophical framework for understanding the text before the reader encounters the conversation between Socrates and Meno.</meta>

# MENO, OR ON VIRTUE. PAGE VI.

## Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for the Meno, On Virtue.

<margin>The three duties of dialogues.</margin>
There are four kinds of argumentation which Plato uses—example, induction, reasoning, and the enthymeme <note>A syllogism or logical argument where one premise is implied rather than stated.</note>—and the manner in which they are formed is sufficiently declared in the compendium of Alcinous, which we have also translated. There we also find three species of Platonic dialogues, and which argumentations he is accustomed to use in each species of dialogue. For a dialogue either only inquires and refutes the false, or it only explains and teaches the true, or it is engaged in both. The first is "inquisitive and contentious." The second is "expository." The last is called "mixed." Now, although the *Meno* is mixed, it nevertheless for the most part contends and refutes; and it touches upon all forms of argumentation. Thus, unless one collects the meanings from other dialogues of Plato—which pertain more to exposition than to dispute—and adds them to this *Meno*, it would be difficult to elicit the sum of this disputation. This sum, however, is to inquire into what virtue is and how it is present in us. Socrates achieves this while he refutes four definitions of virtue from Meno, Aristippus, Gorgias, and Prodicus; and he retracts his own definition, introduced after those, with twin objections. Indeed, truth shines forth from the redargution <note>The act of refuting or disproving.</note> of falsehood. Now, the virtue of a human is an affection or habit of the soul, by which its natural power exercises its own work in the best way; this definition is handed down in the books on the Republic. The work of any power is then best exercised when it is directed toward its end. That which contributes to the end is called "useful." Rightly, therefore, in this disputation, the common duty of virtue is handed down as being this: to make both our actions and those things which we use in acting useful. Therefore, that definition accords with this dialogue and is common to all virtues. Truly, there are many species of virtues, according to the diversity of the powers of the soul and its acts, in which, however, that one common account of virtue which has been mentioned is always perceived. <margin>The cognitive powers of the soul.</margin> The first power of the soul is the Mind, whose act is the perpetual contemplation of truth. The second is Reason, whose act is the investigation of truth. The third is Phantasy <note>The faculty of imagination or mental representation.</note>, whose act is the collection of those things which the senses, its messengers, offer up; through which it performs its discourse. <margin>The appetitive powers.</margin> And these are the powers of the soul which are called "cognitive." There remain three others, which they call "appetitive": Will, the power of Anger <note>original: "irascendi vis," the spirited or courageous part of the soul.</note>, and Desire. The act of the Will is to long for what the Mind and Reason offer. The act of the Irascible <note>The spirited part of the soul.</note> is to attack what Reason and Phantasy propose. <margin>Two vigors.</margin> The act of the Concupiscible <note>The desiring part of the soul.</note> is to adopt what Phantasy and the senses present. Beyond these six, two others are subject: the vigor of moving and of nourishing, but these, along with the higher powers, communicate either nothing or very little in the matter of virtue. The affection of the mind which perfects contemplation is Wisdom; that which perfects the investigation of reason is Science <note>Knowledge/Systematic study.</note> and Prudence. Science concerns the investigation of those things which nature makes; Prudence concerns consultation in those things which we ourselves do. That which perfects the discourse of Phantasy is Right Opinion, which some call sagacity. Justice and Liberality govern the Will. Fortitude and its followers govern the Irascible. Continence and Temperance together govern the Concupiscible. It is common to all these that each of them is an affection perfecting the act of a natural power, while it renders it decorous and useful for attaining the ultimate end. Truly, the various virtues are held in different ways. Wisdom, indeed, is by nature: for it is the eternal embrace of all reasons in the mind, and the perpetual intuition of truth. Science is acquired through the doctrine of philosophy, which Reminiscence <note>The Platonic theory that learning is actually "remembering" knowledge the soul had before birth.</note> provides; while Reason, which once cast away its wings, recovers them again by remembering as it turns back toward the Mind. Prudence comes through doctrine and simultaneously through long experience of things. Right Opinion comes from examples, authority, induction, or by chance. Justice, Fortitude, Temperance, and the other moral virtues are perfected by the laws of Prudence and Right Opinion and by legitimate exercise. Whence Plato placed these two principles of the moral virtues: Prudence and Right Opinion. For this reason, Prudence frequently usurps the name of the whole moral virtue in Plato's writings. There is also a certain virtue pertaining to Right Opinion: by which legitimate princes and citizens, honest in action yet lacking in contemplation, care for the public good; this they name "civil skill." And Plato disputes, both in the *Theages* and in the present *Meno*, that this faculty is given to civil men in no other way than by divine chance. By this summary, therefore, one may gather the mind of Plato in the *Meno*; and with this sort of distinction having been premised, one will reject contradictions and avoid objections. Truly, I did not think it right to treat that disputation concerning reminiscence and geometric figures in this argument, because it was inserted not as the principal matter, but as an accessory. For an "Argument" requires the sum and the head of the matter. Indeed, to discuss every single point is the duty not of an argument, but rather of a commentary.

# MENO, OR ON VIRTUE.
## MENO. SOCRATES. A BOY. ANYTUS.

<margin>Socrates' evasion of answering, so that he might reach the point of questioning.</margin>
**MENO.** Can you show me, Socrates, whether virtue is acquired by teaching, or rather by practice? Or perhaps it is obtained by men neither by teaching nor by use, but is in men by nature itself, or in some other way? **SOCRATES.** Hitherto, O Meno, the Thessalian people have been held illustrious among the Greeks, both for their equestrian skill and also for their riches. Wherefore Gorgias has so accustomed you, that

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>Gorgias allowed anyone to ask whatever they wished.</margin>
...you should answer those who question you fearlessly and with a high spirit, as becomes those who possess knowledge. For indeed, he [Gorgias] himself allowed any of the Greeks to ask whatever they wished, and he responded to each one. To us, O friend Meno, the opposite has happened: it is as if our wisdom has somehow dried up, and seems to have diverted from these places toward you. Therefore, if you should attempt to question any of our people in this manner, there will be no one who will not answer you with a smile: "O guest, perhaps I seem to you to be some blessed person, since you think I know whether virtue comes to men through instruction or some other means. But I am so far from this knowledge that I do not even understand what virtue itself is." And yet I myself, O Meno, am affected in this way: I am situated in nearly the same poverty of mind as my fellow citizens, and I accuse myself of being utterly ignorant of what virtue is. Since I do not know what it is, how could I know what *sort* of thing it is? Does it seem possible to you that someone who does not know at all who Meno is, could know whether he is good, or wealthy, or noble, or the opposite? 
**MENO:** Not at all, in my view. But truly, O Socrates, do you really not know what virtue is? Shall we report this about you back in our homeland? 
**SOCRATES:** Not only that, I ask, my friend, should you proclaim at home, but also that I have never yet, as it seems to me, met anyone who did know it. 
**MENO:** Did you not even meet Gorgias when he was staying here? 
**SOCRATES:** I did indeed. 
**MENO:** And did he seem to you to be ignorant of these things? 
**SOCRATES:** I do not quite remember, O Meno; therefore, I cannot report at present what I thought then. But perhaps he does know, and you hold onto what he taught; therefore, if it pleases you, you yourself tell me. For you perhaps agree with him? 
**MENO:** I certainly do. 
**SOCRATES:** Let us then leave him out of it, since he is absent. But you yourself, O Meno, tell me, I beseech you by the gods: what do you think virtue is? # MENO, OR ON VIRTUE. FOLIO VII.

...you think, if we add "justly" to the acquisition. But "unjustly," certainly not. MENO: I certainly think so. For justice is virtue. SOCRATES: Is it *virtue*, O Meno, or *a* virtue? <note>Socrates is distinguishing between the essence of Virtue itself and specific examples of it.</note> MENO: What do you mean by that? SOCRATES: Just as I would say of anything else; for instance, regarding roundness, I would say it is *a* shape, not simply *the* shape; and I would speak this way because there are other shapes besides roundness. Just as I would have answered you if you had asked me about other shapes, so you must tell me what the other virtues are. MENO: Courage, temperance, wisdom, magnificence, and very many others. SOCRATES: Again we have fallen into the same trap. # BOOK FOUR

<margin>Gorgias allowed anyone to ask whatever they wished.</margin>
...you should answer those questioning you fearlessly and with a high spirit, as befits those who possess knowledge. For indeed, <note>Gorgias of Leontini, a famous Sophist and rhetorician.</note> Gorgias himself allowed any of the Greeks to ask whatever they wished, and he responded to each one. To us, O friend Meno, the opposite has happened: it is as if our wisdom has somehow dried up, and it seems to have departed from these lands to yours. Therefore, if you should try to question any of our people in this manner, there will be no one who will not answer you with a smile: "O stranger, perhaps I seem to you to be some blessed person, since you think I know whether virtue comes to men through teaching or by some other means. But I am so far from this knowledge that I do not even understand what virtue itself is." And I myself, O Meno, am affected in this way: I am placed in nearly the same poverty of mind as my fellow citizens, and I accuse myself of being utterly ignorant of what virtue is. Since I do not know what it is, how could I know what sort of thing it is? Does it seem possible to you that someone who does not know at all who Meno is, could know whether he is good, or wealthy, or noble, or the opposite? 

ME. Not at all, in my view. But truly, O Socrates, do you really not know what virtue is? 

SO. Shall we report these things about you in your homeland? 

SO. I ask that you do not only proclaim this at home, my friend, but also that I have never yet, as it seems to me, met anyone who did know it. 

ME. Did you then never meet Gorgias when he was staying here? 

SO. I did indeed. 

ME. And did he seem to you to be ignorant of these things? 

SO. I do not remember well enough, O Meno; therefore I cannot report at present what I thought then. But perhaps he did know, and you hold onto what he taught; therefore, if it pleases you, speak yourself. For perhaps you agree with him.

# BOOK FOUR

and from this response you might also easily define what flavor is, what voice is, what odor is, and many other things of this sort. ME. Entirely so. SO. And yet, O Meno, that response is "tragic" <note>original: "tragica" — likely referring to a grand or poetic style of speech associated with Gorgias, rather than a sad one</note>, and therefore it pleases you more than the definition of figure. ME. It truly does. SO. But for my part, O son of Alexidemus, I am not at all persuaded; for <margin>That [former definition] is better and closer to the analytical method.</margin> the former is better, and perhaps even that one will not please you, as I think, unless you object to us now as you did yesterday, saying that you will depart before the mysteries are completed; but stay, and be initiated here into the mysteries. ME. But I would stay a long time, O Socrates, if you would tell many such things. SO. I will certainly omit nothing, but will speak such things for both your sake and mine. I fear, however, that I may be less able to say many things of this kind. But come now, gird yourself to keep your promises to us: and express to us in common what virtue is: and do not, as you have done until now, break one thing into many pieces—as the wits say, mocking those who always split something into many parts—but leaving it whole and sound, tell me at last what virtue is. You have received examples of speaking from me. <margin>Third definition of virtue.</margin> ME. It seems to me, O Socrates, that virtue is, as the poet says, "to rejoice in honorable things and to be able [to achieve them]." And I call this very thing virtue: <margin>Fourth definition.</margin> to desire honorable things and to be able to attain them. SO. Do you say that one who desires honorable things desires good things? ME. Entirely. SO. Do you speak as if there are some who desire good things, and others who desire evil things? ME. Indeed. SO. Do not all men then, O best of men, seem to you to seek good things? ME. Not to me. SO. Some then seek evil? ME. Yes. SO. Do you say this as if they think the things that are evil are good? Or even knowing that they are evil, do they nevertheless desire them? ME. I say both. SO. Do you think anyone, knowing evils for what they are, nevertheless seeks them? ME. I believe so. SO. What do you say this man longs for? That these things be present to him? ME. To be present, certainly; for what else would he wish? SO. Does he who desires evils, knowing them to be evil, think they help him when they are present? Or rather that each one harms him by its presence? ME. There are certainly those who think evils are beneficial; nor are there lacking those who know they are harmful. <margin>Refutation of the fourth definition.</margin> SO. Do they seem to you to know evils for what they are, who think evils benefit anyone? ME. Certainly that does not seem so to me. SO. From these things, therefore, it is clear that those men do not seek evils who do not know them; but rather those things which they thought were good, though they are actually evil. Therefore, being ignorant of them and thinking them good, it is clear they desire good things instead. Is it not so? ME. So they seem to be. SO. But truly, those who affect evils, as you say, and think they harm whoever they happen to, do they not know that they will be harmed by their presence? ME. It follows necessarily. SO. But do they not think those who are harmed are miserable, insofar as they are harmed? ME. This also is necessary. SO. And are not the miserable unhappy? ME. I suppose so. SO. Is there anyone who wants to be miserable and unhappy? ME. It does not seem so. SO. No one, therefore, wants evils, if indeed he does not want to be such a person. For what else is it to be miserable, than to desire evils and to fall into them? ME. You speak the truth, O Socrates; for no one wants evils. SO. Did you not say a little while ago that virtue is to want good things and to be able [to get them]? ME. I did indeed. SO. Does it not follow from what has been said: that the will itself is present in everyone, and by this reasoning no one is better than another? ME. It appears so. SO. Therefore, if indeed one man is better than another, and it is not according to the will itself, it follows that he is better according to the power itself. ME. It follows. SO. According to your reasoning, then, this is virtue: the power of acquiring good things. ME. It seems to be exactly as you now take it. SO. Let us observe hereafter whether you say this truly or not; for perhaps you speak well. You say that to be able to claim good things is virtue? ME. That very thing. SO. And do you not call these things "good," such as health, riches, and possessing much gold and silver, and furthermore holding honors and offices in the republic? Do you call anything else good besides these? ME. Not at all; but I say all such things are good. <margin>Those things which are between evil and good are not good unless a part of virtue is present.</margin> SO. Well then, to acquire gold and silver is virtue, as says Meno, the ancestral guest of the Great King. But do you add to this gain, O Meno, "justly and holily," or does it make no difference, so that even if one possesses these things unjustly, you nevertheless call such gain virtue? ME. By no means, O Socrates; but vice. SO. Entirely, therefore, as it seems, there is need for the presence of justice, or temperance, or holiness, or another virtue in this possession. Otherwise it will not be virtue, even if one claims good things for himself. ME. For how could virtue exist without these? SO. But is not the failure to acquire gold and silver, when it is not just, whether for oneself or another—is not this very lack also virtue? ME. It seems so. SO. No more, therefore, will the abundance of these goods be virtue than the lack of them. But as it seems, whatever is done with justice is virtue; but what is done without it and its like is wickedness. ME. What you say seems to me to be necessary. SO. Did we not say a little while ago that each of these is a part of virtue: justice and temperance and other such things? ME. We clearly said so. SO. Is it thus, O Meno, that you mock me? ME. To what end is this, O Socrates? SO. Because when I had prayed you not to break virtue into pieces any further, and had given examples of how to respond, you neglected it, saying that virtue is the ability to acquire good things with justice; yet you confessed justice to be a part of virtue. ME. It is so. SO. Does it not follow from these things which you have now conceded, that virtue is to do whatever is done with a part of virtue? For you confess justice and each of these things to be particles of virtue. ME. What then? SO. Because when I asked you to show virtue itself as a whole, what it is, you explained it in no way; but you said every action, whatever is done with a part of virtue, is virtue—as if you had already told me in summary what the whole of virtue is, and I would now understand it if you divided it into particles. Therefore the same question arises for you again, O Meno: what is virtue? If indeed every action done with a part of virtue is virtue. For that is what is said when every action with justice is defined as virtue. Do you not see that the same question is needed again? Or do you think anyone knows a certain part of virtue, who does not know the nature of the whole? ME. No.

# MENO, OR ON VIRTUE. FOLIO VIII.

It seems so. **SOCRATES:** If you remember what I answered you in the previous parts regarding "figure" <note>Socrates refers to an earlier part of the dialogue where they defined geometric shapes to establish a method for definitions</note>, we both rejected that kind of answer which relies on things that need further proof and are not yet settled as certain. **MENO:** And we were right to reject it. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, my best of men, do not think that while the question is "what is virtue itself, universal and whole," you will make it clear to those asking by answering according to its parts. Do not think you can explain anything else by answering in that same way; rather, the same question will be needed again: "What is this virtue" which you assume when you say these things? Do I seem to be saying anything to you? **MENO:** To me, at least, you seem to speak rightly. **SOCRATES:** Answer then again from the beginning: what do you and that friend of yours <note>Referring to Gorgias, Meno's teacher</note> assert virtue to be?

<margin>A relaxation of the debate from Socrates' usual manner of disputing.</margin>
**MENO:** I had heard indeed, O Socrates, before I spoke with you, that your only work is to doubt and to cast the thorns of doubt into others. And now indeed, as it seems to me, you disturb me with charms and sorceries and incantations, so that I am full of uncertainty. And you seem to me entirely (if it is proper to bite you a little in jest) to be most like, both in form and in all other ways, to that very flat sea fish which is called the *torpedo* <note>The electric ray or numb-fish</note>. For that fish makes anyone who approaches and touches it go numb. And you too now make me numb. For in truth, I am numb in both soul and mouth, and I hesitate, finding nothing to answer you—even though I have already disputed a thousand times about virtue before many people, and, as it seemed to me, very well. But at present, I am not able to say in any way what virtue itself is. Therefore, I think you have looked out for yourself cautiously by never traveling elsewhere. For if you did these things as a stranger in a foreign city, acting like a sorcerer and a magician, you might perhaps be led to execution. **SOCRATES:** You are clever, O Meno, and you almost deceived me just now. **MENO:** Why is that, O Socrates? **SOCRATES:** I realized for what reason you depicted me with such a comparison; for what other reason than that I might depict you in return? For handsome men, when they are portrayed, are usually delighted. Indeed, it is fitting, for the images of the beautiful are beautiful. But I shall not portray your person at all. Indeed, if that numb fish is itself numb while making others numb, then I am very like it; but if not, then not at all. For I do not make others waver while being fertile with answers myself; rather, being the most doubting of all men, I make others doubt as well. For at present, I certainly do not know what virtue is; you, however, perhaps knew before you met me, but now you are like one who does not know. Nevertheless, I have resolved to discuss this with you and to investigate what virtue might be.

<margin>Meno's uncertainty regarding the inquiry into what he does not know.</margin>
**MENO:** But by what path will you investigate this, O Socrates, which you do not know at all what it is? What sort of thing will you set before yourself as the object of your inquiry when you do not know it? Or even if you should stumble upon it, by what sign will you recognize that it is the thing you did not know? **SOCRATES:** I understand what you mean, O Meno. But do you not see what a litigious argument you have brought into our midst? Namely, that a man seeks neither what he knows nor what he does not know. For if he knows it, there is no need for inquiry. But neither does he investigate what he does not know, for he does not know what he should seek. **MENO:** Do you not think, O Socrates, that this reasoning is rightly introduced? **SOCRATES:** Not at all. **MENO:** Can you say why it does not please you? **SOCRATES:** I can. For I have heard it at some time from men and women skilled in divine matters. **MENO:** What is their speech? **SOCRATES:** True, as it seems to me, and excellent. **MENO:** Who is it, I say, and who are the witnesses? **SOCRATES:** Those who assert this are religious men and also religious women, who have made it their care to be able to give an account of the things they profess. Besides these, Pindar and whoever among the poets are divine say such things. Consider, I pray, whether they seem true to you. For they say that the soul of man is immortal; and that it sometimes departs, which they call dying, and then returns again, but never perishes. For which reason they warn us to lead life as holily as possible.

<margin>The opinion of Pindar and the divine poets concerning the immortality of souls.</margin>
For whoever has already paid the penalty to Proserpina <note>Persephone, queen of the underworld</note> for ancient misery, to those she returns the soul again to the upper sun in the ninth year, until they emerge as kings outstanding in glory, speed, and wisdom. For the rest of time, they are called holy heroes among men. Since, therefore, the soul is immortal and has returned many times into this life, and has seen very often both the things in this life and the things in the other life, and has perceived all things, there is nothing at all remaining that it has not learned. For which reason it is no wonder if it can remember those things which pertain to virtue and to other things, since it knew them once before. For since all nature is akin and in harmony with itself, and the soul has learned all things, nothing prevents a man who remembers one single thing—which they call "learning"—from recovering all the rest, if he is brave enough not to grow weary in seeking. Therefore, seeking and learning is remembrance <note>original: *reminiscentia*</note>. For this reason, one should by no means believe that litigious argument; for it would make us lazy in a way. That argument also wonderfully pleases softer men. But our reasoning makes us diligent investigators of things; relying on this as true, I desire to search out with you what virtue is.

<margin>What learning is according to them. What remembrance is.</margin>
**MENO:** Indeed, O Socrates, but do you assert absolutely that we do not learn? That what we call learning is remembrance? Can you teach me that this is so? **SOCRATES:** I said before, O Meno, that you are clever. And now you ask whether I can "teach" you, when I have just asserted that there is no teaching but only remembrance—so that I might immediately be seen to contradict myself. **MENO:** By Jove, O Socrates, I did not say this with that intent, but rather I spoke that way out of habit. But if you can show it to me by any means, show it, I beseech you. **SOCRATES:** It is by no means easy, yet I will try to explain it for your sake. But call here to me one of those who follow you, so that we may try this demonstration on him. **MENO:** Gladly. Hey you, come here. **SOCRATES:** Is he Greek? And does he speak Greek? **MENO:** He is Greek, and was born and raised in my house. **SOCRATES:** Pay attention then, whether he remembers or whether I teach him. **MENO:** I shall certainly pay attention.

SOCRATES: Come now, boy, do you recognize that this square space is such a thing? BOY: I do indeed. SOCRATES: Does a square have all these four lines equal? BOY: It does. SOCRATES: And does it not also have these lines that are drawn through the middle equal? <note>Referring to the bisecting lines of a square.</note> BOY: Those too. SOCRATES: Can such a space be both larger and smaller? BOY: It can. SOCRATES: If, therefore, this side were two feet, and this one also two, how many feet would the whole itself be? SOCRATES: But since the other side is also two feet, is it anything other than twice two feet? BOY: That is it exactly. SOCRATES: So it becomes twice two feet. BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: And how many are twice two feet? Calculate it. BOY: Four. SOCRATES: Could there not be another space double this one, having all its lines equal in the same way as you see this one has? BOY: Certainly. SOCRATES: How many feet will it be? BOY: Eight. SOCRATES: Come now, try to tell me, how long is each line of that square? In this state of uncertainty, he will search along with me, while I teach him nothing, but rather only ask him questions. Observe <note>original: "Obserua obsecro diligenter"</note> carefully, I pray, whether I ever seem to be teaching and explaining anything to him, rather than simply inquiring into his own individual opinions. SOCRATES: Indeed. And can we add another equal to it? BOY: We can. SOCRATES: And a third, equal to each of these? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: And can we fill in the one in the corner? BOY: Certainly. SOCRATES: Would these then result in four equal spaces? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore, how many times larger is this whole space than that first one? BOY: Four times. SOCRATES: But we needed to produce a double space <note>an 8-foot square</note>, do you remember? BOY: Very much so. SOCRATES: Does not this line, stretched from corner to corner, divide each space in two? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore, are there four of these equal lines enclosing this space? BOY: There are. SOCRATES: Consider then, how large is that space? BOY: I do not understand. SOCRATES: Since there are four of these lines, does each line cut each square in half on the inside? BOY: It does. SOCRATES: How many such halves are in this interior space? BOY: Four. SOCRATES: And how many in that first one? BOY: Two. SOCRATES: And what is the ratio of four to two? BOY: Double. SOCRATES: So how many feet does this space become? BOY: Eight. SOCRATES: From which line specifically? BOY: From this one. SOCRATES: From that one which is four feet long, drawn from corner to corner? BOY: Yes. SOCRATES: The experts <term>sophistae</term> <note>Socrates refers to "sophists" or "wise men" here as the source of technical terms.</note> call this the **diagonal** <note>original: "diametrum"</note>; and if its name is the diagonal, then from the diagonal, as you say, O Boy, a double space is born. BOY: Exactly, O Socrates. SOCRATES: What do you think, Meno? Did he ever answer from any opinion other than his own? MENO: Never; always from his own. SOCRATES: And yet he did not know, as we confessed a moment ago. MENO: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, these opinions were already in him. MENO: They were. SOCRATES: So, in one who is ignorant, true opinions about the things he does not know are actually present. MENO: It appears so. SOCRATES: And now these opinions have been stirred up in him as if in a dream. If someone were to ask him these same things often and in many ways, you know for certain that he would eventually know them as perfectly as anyone else. MENO: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore, will he not know these things by himself, with no one teaching him at all, but only asking questions, thus recovering the knowledge from within himself? MENO: That is so. SOCRATES: But to recover knowledge within oneself—is that not what we call **recollecting**? MENO: Precisely. SOCRATES: Now, the knowledge he has now, he either acquired at some time or always possessed. MENO: True. SOCRATES: And if he always had it, he was always a knower. If he acquired it, it was certainly not in this life, for no one taught him geometry—especially since he will do the same with all other parts of geometry and all other disciplines. Is there anyone who taught him all this? It is likely you would know him, especially since he was born and raised in your house. MENO: I know for certain that no one has taught him. SOCRATES: But does he have these opinions? MENO: It appears necessary, Socrates. SOCRATES: But if he did not acquire them in this present life, it is clear he possessed and learned them at some other time. MENO: It appears so. SOCRATES: And was that not the time before he was a human being? MENO: That very time. SOCRATES: Therefore, if there is a time when he is not a human, and yet true opinions are in him—which, when awakened by questioning, become knowledge—then surely his soul has known these things for all time. For through all time, he either is or is not a human. MENO: It seems so.

<margin>It is demonstrated that the soul is immortal.</margin>
SOCRATES: Therefore, if the truth of all things is always in the soul, is the soul not immortal? Wherefore, you ought to be bold and full of great hope; what we do not know at present—that is, what we do not remember—we must strive to recollect. MENO: You seem to speak well, Socrates, though I know not how. SOCRATES: I think so too, Meno. I would not assert the rest of the argument too strongly. But this I would fight for to the end, in both word and deed: that we are better, more capable, and less lazy if we believe we must search for what we do not know, rather than if we thought that what we do not know can neither be sought nor found. MENO: In this too, you seem to speak rightly, Socrates. SOCRATES: Since we have agreed that it is permitted to search for the unknown, shall we investigate together what **virtue** is? MENO: By all means. However, it would be more pleasing to me to hear first what I asked at the beginning of our discussion: whether virtue is something to be pursued as if it can be perceived through teaching, or whether it is in us by nature, or comes to men in some other way. SOCRATES: But Meno, if I had command over you as I do over myself, we would not investigate whether virtue is taught or not until we had first searched for what it is. But since you do not even attempt to master yourself (so that you may live as a free man) and yet you entreat me to answer at your whim, I will yield to you. It seems we must consider the quality of a thing when we do not yet know what the thing is. However, turn aside a little from your purpose: allow us to consider from a **hypothesis** <note>original: "ex suppositione"</note> whether virtue is possessed by teaching or some other way. I speak of a "hypothesis" in the way geometers often discuss things; for example, if someone asks them whether a particular triangle <note>original: "trigonus"</note> can be inscribed in this circle.

<margin>In what way it is permitted to dispute about the quality of a thing when it is not yet known what it is. This triangular space. This theorem is discussed in Book 4 of Euclid, second proposition.</margin>

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram containing a horizontal line and a triangle formed by lines extending to the circle's edge, illustrating a mathematical hypothesis about area and inscribed shapes.</image-desc>

If this space is such that, when applied to its given line, it falls short by a space equal to the area applied, I think one thing will follow; and another if it cannot. Therefore, I have decided to dispute by hypothesis about what happens regarding its production into the circle: whether it is possible or not. So it is with us regarding virtue: since we know neither what it is nor what kind of thing it is, let us search by assuming this: whether it can be taught in this manner, if virtue is...

# BOOK FOUR

->**Socrates and Meno**<-

<margin>Whether virtue is acquired by teaching, and when: and first it is shown to be acquired insofar as it is made into knowledge, and does not consist in nature.</margin>
Can any of those things which concern the soul be taught, or not? In the first place, if it is something other than knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note>, can it be taught or not—or rather, as we just said, be recalled to memory? Let it make no difference to us which name we use. But can it be taught? Is it not manifest to all that a human teaches nothing except knowledge? MENO: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: But if virtue is a kind of knowledge, it is received by teaching? MENO: Why not? SOCRATES: This, therefore, is settled quickly: for if it is of such a kind, it is taught; but if otherwise, not at all. MENO: Exactly. SOCRATES: After this, I think we must investigate whether virtue is knowledge, or something else. MENO: I also think that must be asked. SOCRATES: Do we say that virtue is anything other than a good? And does this position remain stable for us, namely that virtue is a good? MENO: Strongly so. SOCRATES: Indeed, if there is some good separate from knowledge, then perhaps virtue will not be knowledge; but if there is no good that knowledge does not encompass, then in suspecting that virtue is knowledge, we shall surely suspect rightly. MENO: These things are true. SOCRATES: Furthermore, we are good by virtue? MENO: We are. SOCRATES: And if good, then useful: for all good things are useful. MENO: It is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, virtue is also something useful. MENO: From those things we have admitted, it necessarily follows. SOCRATES: Let us consider again in individual cases what kind of things benefit us: are health and strength, beauty and riches, and other such things said to be beneficial? MENO: Yes. SOCRATES: Yet we admit these same things sometimes cause harm. Or do you feel otherwise? MENO: I certainly feel so. SOCRATES: See then what leader makes these things harmful or beneficial. Is it not when right use <note>original: "rectus usus"</note> presides that they help, but on the contrary, they harm? MENO: Exactly. SOCRATES: Furthermore, let us consider the things concerning the soul. You call something Temperance, and Justice, and Fortitude, and Teachability, and Memory, and Magnificence, and other such things? MENO: Indeed. SOCRATES: Observe, I pray, which of these do not seem to be knowledge at all, but something else besides knowledge: do they not sometimes help and sometimes hurt? For instance, fortitude apart from prudence <note>original: "prudentia"</note>: is fortitude anything other than a certain boldness? When a man is bold with reason, it helps; when without reason, it hurts. MENO: It is so. SOCRATES: Temperance also and teachability in the same way: when perceived and seasoned with reason, they are an advantage; but otherwise, a detriment. MENO: Very much so.

<margin>The merits of prudence and imprudence.</margin>
SOCRATES: To speak summarily then, all the impulses of the soul and all its inclinations tend toward happiness <note>original: "beatitudinem"</note> under the leadership of prudence, but toward the contrary under imprudence. MENO: It seems so. SOCRATES: Therefore, if virtue is one of those things that exist in the soul, and is necessarily useful, it must be this prudence: since all things concerning the soul are not in themselves either beneficial or harmful, but by the addition of prudence or imprudence, they immediately become either useful or harmful. By this reasoning, since virtue is the most beneficial of all, it is concluded to be a kind of prudence. MENO: It certainly seems so to me. SOCRATES: Furthermore, in the other things we were just mentioning: that wealth and the like are sometimes useful and sometimes harmful—just as prudence, presiding over the other powers and duties of the soul, makes them useful, while imprudence does the opposite, so also the soul, using and leading these things rightly, makes them good, but not rightly, makes them evil. MENO: Exactly. SOCRATES: But the prudent soul leads rightly; the imprudent one wanders. MENO: These things are true. SOCRATES: Wherefore it must be asserted altogether that all other human affairs are referred to the soul, and those in the soul to prudence, if they are to be good; and by that reasoning, prudence itself will be the beneficial thing, and we have already said that virtue is beneficial.

<margin>Prudence is either the whole of virtue or a part of virtue.</margin>
MENO: Entirely. SOCRATES: Therefore, do we admit that prudence is virtue, either as a whole or as some part? MENO: All these things seem to me to be said rightly. SOCRATES: If these things are so, will men not be good by nature? MENO: It does not seem so to me. SOCRATES: Moreover, this would happen if they became good by nature: there would surely be those among us who could recognize our sons who were good by nature, and we, selecting them by their evidence, would preserve them in a certain citadel, sealing them up much more than gold so they would not be corrupted; but after they grew up, they would be useful citizens in the republic. MENO: That is consistent, O Socrates. SOCRATES: But since they are by no means good by nature, is it perhaps by discipline <note>original: "disciplina"</note>? MENO: That appears necessary. And according to our position, it follows that if virtue is knowledge, it is received by teaching. SOCRATES: Perhaps, by Jove! Yet I fear lest we have admitted that too rashly. MENO: In the previous points, it clearly seemed to be said rightly. SOCRATES: But it ought to seem so not only in the past, but also in the present and future time, if there is to be anything sound in it. MENO: What is the impediment? Looking at what in particular do you suspect and doubt that virtue might not be knowledge? SOCRATES: I will tell you, O Meno. That virtue can be taught, if indeed it is knowledge, I do not at all reject as if it were incorrectly stated; but as to whether it is knowledge, see if I doubt with justice. Come, answer me this: if anything can be taught—I speak not only of virtue, but of any other thing—is it not necessary that there be some teachers and students of it? MENO: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: But on the contrary, if there are neither teachers nor listeners of a thing, if we should conjecture that it cannot be taught, would we not conjecture probably? MENO: It is so; but do you think there are no teachers of virtue? SOCRATES: Often indeed have I investigated whether there were any masters of this with all zeal, and I never found any, even though I sought it together with many others, and those who seemed to be skilled in this faculty.

<margin>It is shown that there are no teachers for the handing down of virtue.</margin>
And now indeed opportunely, O Meno, this man has sat down next to us: let us make him a participant in this inquiry. And we shall rightly employ him as a partner: for he was born of a wealthy and wise father, Anthemion, who surely became opulent not by some chance or by anyone's bounty—as recently the Theban Ismenias obtained the money of Polycrates—but gained it by his own prudence and vigilance. Furthermore, he is neither a proud citizen nor inflated or difficult, but has stood out as a modest, upright, and easy-going man. Then, he educated this man well and at great expense, to which the whole Athenian people are witness, who even elect him to the highest magistracies. It is right to investigate together with such men whether there are any masters of virtue, and who they are. Therefore come, O Anytus, join me and your guest Meno in seeking who the teachers of this thing are, and consider it in this way: if we wanted this Meno to become an excellent physician, to which teachers would we especially lead him? Would it not be to the physicians...

However, he begins to doubt if virtue can be taught, noting the apparent lack of professional teachers, and invites Anytus to join the discussion.</summary>

# MENO, OR ON VIRTUE. FOLIO 10.

**SOCRATES.** Certainly. **ANYTUS.** Exactly. **SOCRATES.** And if we wanted someone to become an excellent cobbler, would we not send them to the cobblers? **ANYTUS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And in other matters in the same way? **ANYTUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** So tell me again about physicians; when we said a man must be sent to the physicians if we want him to be a physician, did we not mean this: that he ought to be placed specifically with those who profess that art and openly take a fee for it from their pupils? Must we not take this into account if we are to place him wisely? **ANYTUS.** That is so. **SOCRATES.** And regarding the sound of flute-players, and all other things, we must judge similarly. For it would be no small folly, while we were eager for someone to become a flute-player, to be unwilling to commend him to those who promise this skill and receive a fee, but instead to impose this burden on those who neither claim to be teachers nor have any pupil in this art in which we desire the one we are sending to be instructed. Would that not be far from reason? **ANYTUS.** By Jupiter <note>original: "Per Iovem"; a common oath in Latin translations of Greek texts</note>, it would not only be without reason, but even a kind of madness. **SOCRATES.** You speak well. Now, therefore, you may deliberate together with me about this guest of yours, Meno. For he, O Anytus, told me long ago that he desires this wisdom and virtue by which men rightly govern states and households, and educate their own children as well as possible, and know how to both receive and dismiss citizens and guests as befits a good man. Consider, then, to whom it is most proper to send him for the sake of acquiring this virtue. Or is it clear from what we have just said that he should be committed to those who promise to teach such things, and who always offer themselves openly to any of the Greeks wishing to learn, taking a prescribed price for this instruction? **ANYTUS.** And who do you mean, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** You know yourself, in a way, that these are the ones who are publicly called Sophists <note>The Sophists were itinerant professional teachers in ancient Greece who charged fees for instruction in rhetoric and virtue.</note>. **ANYTUS.** By Hercules! <note>original: "Hercle"</note>
<margin>The Sophists are criticized, and the discussion is relaxed again.</margin>
Hush, I pray you, Socrates! May no relative, or familiar friend, or citizen, or guest of mine fall into such madness as to be ruined by clinging to those men. For the company of those who follow them is a manifest plague. **SOCRATES.** Why do you say so, Anytus? Are those who alone of all mankind profess to benefit men so much worse than others that they not only do not help (as others do) with what is entrusted to them, but on the contrary, they corrupt it? And for this, they demand a fee publicly? Truly, I do not see by what reasoning I should believe you. For I knew one man, Protagoras, who accumulated more money from this wisdom than even that famous Phidias, whose works are so clear and beautiful, or ten other sculptors combined. **ANYTUS.** But it would be absurd if those who sew old shoes and mend clothes could not remain hidden for thirty days if they returned them in worse condition than they received them. **SOCRATES.** Otherwise, if they did such things, they would soon perish of hunger. But
<margin>Protagoras taught for more than forty years.</margin>
Protagoras deceived all of Greece for more than forty years while perverting his associates and returning them in worse condition than he had received them. For I believe he departed this life nearly seventy years old, having spent forty years in this art. And through all that time, even to this day, he remained famous. And not Protagoras alone, but many others too, some before him and some even now living. Shall we say, according to your speech, that they knowingly deceive and harm the youth, or that they are unaware of it themselves, and are thus insane—though they are judged by some to be the wisest of all? **ANYTUS.** They are far from being called insane, Socrates; rather, it is the young men who give them money who are so. And even worse than these are those to whom the care of the youth belongs, if they commit them to such men. Most insane of all are the city-states that receive them and do not expel them, whether a stranger or a citizen attempts this work. **SOCRATES.** Has any of the Sophists ever done you a wrong, Anytus, that you are so angry with them? **ANYTUS.** I have never had any dealings with any of them, nor would I permit any of my people to use them. **SOCRATES.** Then you have never experienced their manners. **ANYTUS.** Nor may I! **SOCRATES.** By what reasoning then will you distinguish whether a thing be good or evil, of which you have made no trial? **ANYTUS.** I know clearly what sort they are, whether I have tried them or not. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps you are a prophet, Anytus; for I would greatly wonder how you knew this by any other reason from what you have just said. But we are not seeking those to whom Meno might go and be corrupted—let those be the Sophists, if you wish. But help your father's friend: show him to which of those who inhabit so great a city he should cling to obtain the virtue we described. **ANYTUS.** Why do you not point them out yourself? **SOCRATES.** I have already brought forward those whom I thought were teachers; but according to your reasoning, I have accomplished nothing at all. And perhaps you speak the truth. Therefore, you also now fulfill your part of this duty. Point out to which of the Athenians he should go. Name anyone you like. **ANYTUS.** Why is there a need to hear the name of one man? Whichever of the good and famous Athenians he happens upon, he will become better through that man's company—provided he obeys—than through the company of the Sophists. **SOCRATES.** But did these excellent and good men become such of themselves with no one instructing them, and can they nevertheless teach others, though they themselves learned from no one? **ANYTUS.** I believe they learned from the elder men who were excellent and good. Do you not think many distinguished and excellent men have existed in this city? **SOCRATES.** To me indeed, Anytus, there seem to be men here skilled in civil administration, and that there were no fewer in the past. But were they suitable teachers of their own virtue? For this is what is now being discussed: not whether there are or were good men here, but whether virtue can be taught; and because of this, whether good men (either past or present) knew how to hand down to another the virtue with which they were endowed, or whether perhaps virtue can neither be handed down to another nor received. That, I say, is what Meno and I have been seeking for a long time. Consider it thus from your own speech: Do you not admit that Themistocles was a good man? **ANYTUS.** Most of all. **SOCRATES.** And that Themistocles was a good teacher of his own virtue, if any other man was a master of virtue? **ANYTUS.** I suppose so, provided he wished to be. **SOCRATES.** Do you think he did not wish others to become good too, especially his own son? Or do you think he envied his son and deliberately did not communicate his own virtue? Have you not heard that Themistocles made his son Cleophantus so vigorous in horsemanship that he could stand upright on a horse...

I believe he did; but I suspect that virtue cannot be taught. And lest you think only a few ignoble Athenians fail in this, observe again that Thucydides <note>Not the historian, but Thucydides son of Melesias, a political rival of Pericles.</note> raised two sons, Melesias and Stephanus, whom he taught diligently in other matters, especially wrestling, so that they surpassed the rest of the Athenians. It is unthinkable that he would spend a fortune to make his sons skilled in wrestling, yet would not want them to attain virtue—which he could have passed on for free—if only it could be taught. Or was Thucydides perhaps a man of no account? Did he not have many friends, both citizens and allies? On the contrary, he was from a noble family and held great authority among his fellow citizens and all the Greeks. Therefore, if goodness could be acquired through teaching, he would have found someone, either a citizen or a foreigner, to make his sons good, even if he himself lacked the leisure due to the affairs of the Republic. But see, my friend Anytus, whether virtue can perhaps not be taught at all. ANYTUS. O Socrates, you seem to me to disparage men more freely than is proper. I advise you, if you are willing to listen: take care of yourself. 

<margin>In Athens, it was dangerous to wrong anyone.</margin>
Perhaps in another city it is easy to affect citizens with either injury or benefit, but in this one it is exceedingly grave and dangerous; I do not think this escapes your notice. SOCRATES. O Meno, Anytus seems to be angry with me, and I am not surprised. For first, he thinks I am disparaging these great men, and second, he considers himself to be one of them. But if he ever learns what it truly means to "speak ill" of men, he will cease to be angry; for now, he is ignorant of it. But tell me yourself: are there famous and good men among us? MENO. Certainly there are. SOCRATES. Are they willing to present themselves as teachers to the youth? Do they profess this, or even admit that virtue can be taught? MENO. No, by Jove, Socrates! Sometimes you hear them say virtue can be taught, and other times they say it cannot. SOCRATES. Shall we call those men "masters" of a subject when they cannot even agree on this point? MENO. Not at all, it seems to me, Socrates. SOCRATES. Well then, do you think the Sophists <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece who charged fees for instruction in rhetoric and virtue.</note> are teachers of virtue, since they alone proclaim it? I do not know what to say, Socrates. The same thing happens to me as to most people: sometimes I think they are teachers, and other times I deny it. SOCRATES. But if you cling to the wicked, you will surely lose the mind you have.* Do you see how here he speaks as if virtue can be taught? MENO. It appears so. SOCRATES. Do you know of any other subject where those who profess to be teachers are not only unable to teach others, but are said not even to know it themselves? # MENO, OR ON VIRTUE

[FO. XXI.]

Looking back at our previous inquiry, it escaped our notice in a ridiculous way that it is not only under the guidance of **knowledge** <note>original: *scientia*</note> that affairs proceed rightly and well; or perhaps it eluded us by what means good men are made. **MENO.** What do you mean by that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Thus: we rightly confessed that good men must be useful, since the matter could never be otherwise, could it? **MENO.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** And we also rightly agreed among ourselves that they will be useful if they are in charge of conducting affairs rightly. **MENO.** Rightly so. **SOCRATES.** But it seems we did not rightly assert that no one can lead rightly unless they are **prudent** <note>meaning possessing practical wisdom or *phronesis*</note>. **MENO.** How do you say that is right? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you. If someone knows the way to Larissa <note>A city in Greece; Socrates uses this as a practical example of navigation</note>, or wherever else he might travel, and leads others there, will he not lead them rightly and well? **MENO.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** But what if someone has a **right opinion** <note>original: *recte opinatur*</note> as to which path leads to Larissa, though he has never traveled it nor known it for certain? Would he not also lead rightly? **MENO.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And as long as he holds a right opinion about things of which the other has knowledge, he will be no worse a leader—thinking the truth without knowing it—than the one who actually knows those things? **MENO.** Certainly not.

<margin>Right opinion is devised, which is also called true opinion. It shows the agreement between right opinion and knowledge. The difference between right opinion and knowledge.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, **true opinion** is no less effective for right action than prudence. And this is what we overlooked in our consideration of virtue earlier: when we claimed that prudence alone was the guide for acting rightly. But this other thing was true opinion. **MENO.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, does right opinion contribute any less than knowledge? **MENO.** In this way it contributes less, Socrates: because he who has knowledge always succeeds, whereas he who has right opinion sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails. **SOCRATES.** What are you saying? Does not he who proceeds with right opinion always achieve his goal, so long as he opines rightly? **MENO.** That appears necessary. Therefore, I wonder why, since this is so, knowledge is held to be so much more excellent than right opinion, and I doubt why each of them is a distinct thing. **SOCRATES.** Do you know why you wonder at this, or shall I tell you? **MENO.** Tell me, by all means. **SOCRATES.** Because you have never considered the **statues of Daedalus** <note>In Greek myth, Daedalus built statues so lifelike they would run away if not tied down</note>; perhaps they do not exist among you. **MENO.** To what purpose do you say this? **SOCRATES.** Because if these are not tied down, they depart and flee; but if tied, they remain. **MENO.** What of it? **SOCRATES.** Among his works, one that is loose is not of much value, like a runaway slave, for it does not stay. But one that is tied is worthy of admiration, for they are very beautiful works. For the sake of what do I say this? For the sake of **true opinions**. For these, as long as they stay, are beautiful works and accomplish all good things.

<margin>Right opinion is recollection.</margin>

However, they are unwilling to stay for long, but flee from a man’s soul; therefore they are not of much value until someone ties them down by **reasoning out the cause** <note>original: *ratiocinatione a causis*</note>. And this, my friend Meno, is **recollection** <note>original: *reminiscentia*; the Platonic idea that learning is recovering innate knowledge</note>, as we agreed between us above. After they are tied down, they first become knowledge, and then they become lasting. For this reason, knowledge is more excellent than right opinion, and differs from it by this certain bond. **MENO.** By Jove, Socrates, that is a fitting comparison! **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, I speak not as one who knows, but as one who conjectures. But that true opinion and knowledge are two different things, I seem to myself to have concluded clearly. And if I were to claim to know anything else—and I would say I know few things—this is one thing I would count among those I know. **MENO.** You speak rightly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** What then? Is this not also right: that true opinion, guiding any work, achieves it no worse than knowledge? **MENO.** This also is true. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, true opinion is nothing worse than knowledge, nor less useful for actions; nor is the man who has true opinion inferior to the one gifted with knowledge. **MENO.** That is so. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, we agreed that a good man is useful. **MENO.** We agreed. **SOCRATES.** If, therefore, men were good and useful to cities not through knowledge alone—if they were found at all—but also because of right opinion; and since neither of these is in men by nature (neither knowledge nor true opinion), nor are these acquired <insert>by nature</insert>—does it seem that any of these are present by nature? **MENO.** Not to me. **SOCRATES.** Since they are not present by nature, then good men will not be good by nature either? **MENO.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Since it is not by nature, we were considering whether it comes by teaching? **MENO.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And it seemed it could be taught if virtue were prudence? **MENO.** It did. **SOCRATES.** And if it could be taught, it would also be prudence? **MENO.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** And if there were teachers, it could be taught; if not, not at all? **MENO.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** And we denied by common consent that there are teachers of it? **MENO.** We denied it. **SOCRATES.** We concluded, therefore, that it is neither taught, nor is it prudence? **MENO.** We concluded that.

<margin>Two things lead rightly: true opinion and knowledge.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** Moreover, we conceded that it is a good thing. **MENO.** We conceded it. **SOCRATES.** And that which leads rightly is good and useful. **MENO.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Finally, only these two things lead rightly: true opinion and knowledge; a man gifted with these is said to lead rightly. For things that happen by chance are not governed by human command; but in those things where a man is a guide to the right, these two are the guides: true opinion and knowledge. **MENO.** It seems the same to me. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, since virtue cannot be perceived through teaching, it is by no means knowledge. **MENO.** It does not appear so. **SOCRATES.** Since there are two good and useful things, one of them is excluded: knowledge will not be the guide in civil action. **MENO.** Not as it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is not by a certain wisdom, nor as wise men, that those who govern the republic administer it—men such as those in the time of Themistocles, and those whom Anytus <note>One of Socrates' accusers; a politician present during this dialogue</note> mentioned a moment ago. Hence, they cannot make others such as they are themselves, because they are not such through any knowledge. **MENO.** It seems to be as you say, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** If not by knowledge, it remains that civil men govern cities using **right opinion**, being no differently situated regarding prudence than soothsayers and those seized by **divine frenzy** <note>original: *divino furore*; a state of inspiration rather than rational understanding</note>. For these people announce many true things, yet they understand nothing of what they speak. **MENO.** So it seems to be. **SOCRATES.**

<margin>He who is a good man is called divine.</margin>

Is it not right then, Meno, to call such men "divine," who, though not using their minds, nevertheless accomplish many great things in both word and deed? **MENO.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we shall rightly call divine those whom we just mentioned—soothsayers, the inspired, and all poetic men; and we shall consider civil men no less divine than the rest, being breathed upon by the divine power and possessed by God, whenever they direct the republic, saying many and great things which they do not understand. **MENO.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Women also, Meno, call good men "divine." And the Spartans, whenever they wish to commend a certain good man, say, "This is a divine man." **MENO.** And they seem to speak rightly, Socrates—though perhaps Anytus here is offended by you saying such things. **SOCRATES.** I do not care at all...

<summary>Socrates argues that "right opinion" is as effective as knowledge for practical action, but lacks the stability of knowledge because it is not "tied down" by an understanding of causes. He concludes that great statesmen govern by divine inspiration or right opinion rather than teachable knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Meno, virtue, knowledge, right opinion, Daedalus, Larissa, Anytus, republic, divine inspiration, recollection</keywords>

# BOOK FIVE
<meta>catchword: e</meta>

<margin>Virtue is one in itself</margin>
Virtue is one: we shall discuss this with you, O Meno, at another time. If we have investigated correctly in this entire dispute, virtue will certainly come to us neither by teaching nor by nature; rather, it will flow by divine providence, without the use of the intellect, into the one who has been allotted it—unless, perhaps, there should exist someone among statesmen of such a kind that he could also make another person a statesman. For if such a man existed, he would be among the living as Homer says Tiresias was among the dead, saying: "He alone excels in wisdom among those in the underworld; the rest flit about as shadows." <note>original: "Sapiētia præstat solus iis, qui apud inferos: ceteri vero vmbræ volitāt." A quote from the Odyssey regarding the blind prophet Tiresias.</note> Similarly, such a citizen would stand in relation to others as a reality among shadows. For he would be a true thing in respect to virtue. MENO: You seem to me to speak excellently, O Socrates. SOCRATES: From this reasoning then, O Meno, it appears that divine virtue is present in whomever it is present by divine providence. However, we shall only then comprehend the clear truth about this when, before asking in what way virtue is present, we first attempt to investigate what virtue is in and of itself. But now it is time for me to go elsewhere. As for you, persuade your guest Anytus <note>Anytus was one of the historical accusers of Socrates; the text suggests that softening his heart might save Socrates and benefit Athens.</note> of what you have been persuaded, so that he may be gentler. For if you persuade him of this, you will also benefit the Athenians.

<margin>Marsilio's Argument on the First Alcibiades, or on the Nature of Man.</margin>
### Marsilio's Argument on the First Alcibiades, or on the Nature of Man.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' containing intricate foliate and floral scrolls.</image-desc>
The most brilliant book of our Plato, which is titled *First Alcibiades*, is more beautiful than Alcibiades himself and dearer than all gold; it teaches what man is and what his duty is. Now, man is a rational soul, the chief of the mind, making use of a body. From this definition, his duty is drawn and distributed in three ways. For as he is a rational soul, he reflects upon himself in a certain circle of reasoning by observing himself. As he is the chief of the mind, he flows back into the divine mind like a stream into its source. As he is one using a body, he applies himself to governing human affairs. Therefore, the perfect and absolute duty of man is, first, to observe his own nature; then, from that nature as if from an image and effect, to turn toward the divine mind, which is its model and cause. Once the human soul is illuminated by this, it understands the Good itself, the Useful itself, the Beautiful itself, and the Just itself, and perfectly comprehends these things within its own being. From this, it knows what is good and what is useful for other men with whom it lives or whom it rules. And when it has recognized the absolute Good and the good of others, it must then approach the care of itself and of every other person according to the norm of the knowledge of the Good. There is a need for the study of philosophy—moral, mathematical, and theological—so that the soul may return to itself and to the mind that is its cause. Indeed, moral and mathematical discipline restores the soul, which was immersed in the body, back to itself; theology seizes it above itself and lifts it outside of itself into God. The knowledge of the divine mind and the Ideas is called Wisdom. The knowledge of oneself, and the joining of one's own goods and the useful flowing from the intuition of the divine mind, is called Prudence. Truly, as Prudence understands the Good, it refers human actions, both public and private, to the best end. As it understands the Useful, it directs the convenient means and proper ways by which it may reach that end. As it understands the Beautiful, it establishes what order and what measure should be preserved in this progress, as if on a journey. As it understands the Just, it prescribes the distinction of individual works, the observance of the imposed order, the punishment for transgression, and the reward for those observing the law of this journey. Thus, from philosophy one approaches Wisdom, and from Wisdom to Prudence; Prudence, the mistress of life, provides the discipline for one's private affairs and for the state. Man governs through Prudence; however, the home and the city preserve public friendship and justice. I call "public friendship" that union by which all gather freely under the same law and ruler and look toward the same end. I name "public justice" the lawful distinction by which individuals, though under the same ruler and toward the same end (that is, the public good), nevertheless proceed by different paths; they preserve the various distributions of duties assigned by nature and laws according to the nature and dignity of each, and they perform their own proper office without usurping that of another. In this dialogue, there are two theological expressions: "the thing itself" 

<margin>The thing itself: each individual thing.</margin>
and "each individual thing." <note>original: "Ipsum idē, ipm, & ipsum vnūquodq." Ficino is discussing Platonic terminology for the Soul as an Idea versus the soul in a body.</note> Regarding man, the former signifies the soul as an Idea; the latter signifies the soul in the body. But concerning these, I will write more extensively in the commentaries which I have now begun to write on these ten dialogues of Plato.

---

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue in which Alcibiades is introduced, a most beautiful youth of the Greeks, noble and wealthy, having the talent and hope for great deeds: so that it might be shown that the nature of man does not consist in these parts.</margin>
### THE FIRST ALCIBIADES, OR ON THE NATURE OF MAN. SOCRATES. ALCIBIADES.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'S' depicting a landscape with figures in classical or Renaissance attire, with architectural structures in the background.</image-desc>
Son of Clinias, I think you wonder why, although I was the first of all to begin loving you, and while others have ceased to love you, I alone persevere in my benevolence; and while your other friends have been daily troublesome to you with their frequent company, I have not even greeted you for so many years. The cause of this matter was not anything human, but a certain opposing divine spirit <note>original: "dæmoniū." Referring to Socrates' famous 'daimon' or inner voice.</note>, the power of which you will hear about in what follows. But now, since it no longer opposes me, I have come here in this way. I hope, moreover, that it will not oppose us in the future. In the time before this, I was observing how you conducted yourself toward your friends. Although they were many and proud, there was none among them who did not leave having been surpassed by your arrogance. I will explain the reason why you despised them. For you say that you lack nothing from other men, since those things are in you: they are so excellent that you need no one for the goods of either body or soul. You think that you especially excel in a tall and handsome physical stature. And that is evident to everyone. Furthermore, you boast that you are born of the most noble race compared to others in this city, the greatest of the Greek cities; on your father's side, you have many friends and relatives who are the best of men, who can supply you with everything when there is need. On your mother's side, they are neither inferior to these nor fewer in number.

<margin>Athens, the greatest of the Greek cities.</margin>
But you think Pericles, the son of Xanthippus, brings you much greater authority for conducting affairs than all these; your father left him as a guardian for you and your brother. He is able to do whatever he wishes, not only in this city, but in all Greece; and...
