# ALCIBIADES, OR ON THE NATURE OF MAN. FOLIO 12.

among many and broad races of barbarians. I might also add your most ample riches, did I not know that you boast of these least of all. Because of all these things, elated by pride, you have put all your companions to flight with your haughtiness. And they, being your inferiors, yielded to you. Nor indeed did these things escape your notice. Wherefore it does not escape me either that you wonder in what spirit I have persevered in my benevolence, or what hope I have conceived regarding you, that while others left you, I alone of all remained.

**ALCIBIADES.** But perhaps you do not know, O Socrates, that you have anticipated me by just a little. For it had come into my mind that I should approach you first and ask these very same things: What is it you want? With what hope do you trouble me, so that wherever I am, you are always most observantly present? For in truth, I wonder what your plan is, and I would gladly hear it.

<margin>He wins over your goodwill and attention for himself.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** You shall hear this from me then, as is fitting, as soon as possible, if indeed you desire to know what I am thinking, as you say. For I shall relate it as if to one waiting and ready to listen.

**ALCIBIADES.** And most certainly so; only speak.

**SOCRATES.** Look then; for it ought not to seem strange if, just as I was slow to begin, so I am slow to finish.

**ALCIBIADES.** O best of men, speak now, for I am listening.

**SOCRATES.** I must indeed speak. It is a difficult thing to enter into friendship and intimacy with one who has surpassed all his other friends. Yet I must dare to express my mind. Truly, O Alcibiades, if I had known you to be content with those things we recounted above, and to have enslaved your life to them, I believe I would have laid aside my benevolence toward you long ago. But now I shall reveal certain other thoughts you have about yourself, so that you may understand for what reason, once I set my mind upon you, I never stopped. You seem to me, indeed, as if some god were to say to you, "O Alcibiades, do you wish to live possessing only those things you have now? Or would you rather choose death immediately unless it were permitted to attain greater things?" But I shall reveal the hope by which you now lead your life. You think that if you soon ascend to the assembly of the Athenian people—which you expect will happen in a few days—you will demonstrate to the Athenians that you are worthy of greater honor than either Pericles is, or any other of those who flourished in former ages. And if you show this, you will have the greatest authority among your citizens. And if you are most powerful in this city, you will also be the most famous of all the Greeks, and even of the Barbarians who inhabit the same region as the Greeks. And if that same god granted you the empire of Europe, but forbade you to cross into Asia and lead affairs there, it seems to me you would not yet choose to spend your life with these things alone, unless you could propagate your name and power, so to speak, through all races of men. And I believe you consider no one worthy of memory except Cyrus and Xerxes. That you are nourished by such a hope, I do not merely guess, but I know for certain. Perhaps you too will confess, being conscious of your own mind, that I have spoken the truth.

<margin>From the person speaking.</margin>
**ALCIBIADES.** What do these things, O Socrates, have to do with that reason you wished to assign for why you have not yet deserted me?

**SOCRATES.** I will tell you, O son of Clinias and Dinomache <note>Alcibiades' parents; Dinomache was of the noble Alcmaeonid family</note>. You cannot lead these thoughts of yours to their desired end without me; so much do I trust in my power over you and your affairs. For this reason, I believe the god himself did not permit me to converse with you in the past; and I waited until he permitted it. For just as you hope to show your city that you are worthy of every honor in its eyes, and having demonstrated these things, that nothing remains so great that you cannot immediately accomplish it, so I also trust that I have great power with you as soon as I see that I am more worthy than all others—neither a guardian, nor a kinsman, nor anyone else except me alone, with God's favor, will hand over to you that power which you desire. Therefore, as long as you were younger and had not yet come into such great hope, in my opinion, the god prohibited me from disputing with you, lest I contend in vain. But now he has impelled me. Now, therefore, you shall hear.

**ALCIBIADES.** You seem much more wonderful to me now, O Socrates, since you began to speak with me, than when you followed me in silence; although even then you seemed such a man by your very appearance. If, therefore, you have known best, as it seems, whether I was revolving these things in my mind or not, even if I have expressed them less in words, there will be no further trouble in persuading you; let it be so. If, then, I intend this most of all, how I may attain it through you, and if these things cannot be perfected without you, can you say how?

**SOCRATES.** Do you ask whether I am about to begin a long speech, such as you are accustomed to hearing? That is not my manner. Nevertheless, I can show you, as I believe, that these things are so, provided you are willing to comply with me in this one thing alone.

**ALCIBIADES.** Unless you demand something difficult, I agree.

**SOCRATES.** Does it seem difficult to you to answer what is asked?

**ALCIBIADES.** Not at all.

**SOCRATES.** Answer then.

**ALCIBIADES.** Ask.

**SOCRATES.** Shall I ask you as one thinking those things which I said you were thinking?

**ALCIBIADES.** Let it be so, if you please, so that I may finally see what you bring.

**SOCRATES.** Come then; you certainly intend, as I said above, to go soon to the Athenian people to give counsel. If, therefore, as you were about to go to the assembly, I met you and said: "O Alcibiades, since the Athenians have decided to deliberate about something, have you also stood up to deliberate? Is it concerning those things which you know better than they?" What would you answer to this?

**ALCIBIADES.** I would certainly answer: concerning those things which I know better.

**SOCRATES.** Are you then a good counselor concerning those things which you know?

**ALCIBIADES.** Why not?

<margin>We know in two ways: either by discovering or by learning. Alcibiades refused to play the flutes.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Do you not know only those things which you have learned from others, or discovered yourself?

**ALCIBIADES.** What others could there be?

**SOCRATES.** Is there anything that you ever learned or discovered when you were unwilling to discover or learn?

**ALCIBIADES.** There is not.

**SOCRATES.** Did you ever wish to inquire into or learn those things which you thought you already knew?

**ALCIBIADES.** Never.

**SOCRATES.** Of the things you now know, was there once a time when you thought you were ignorant of them?

**ALCIBIADES.** Necessarily so.

**SOCRATES.** And the things you learned, I myself almost know; if anything has escaped me, tell me. For you learned, as I remember, letters, how to play the lyre <note>original: "citharam"</note>, and wrestling <note>original: "palestram"</note>; for you refused to play the flutes <note>Alcibiades famously rejected the flute because it distorted the face</note>. These are the things of which you have knowledge, unless perhaps you learned something in secret; but I think you did not leave the house by night or day without us knowing.

**ALCIBIADES.** I have heard no teachers other than these three.

**SOCRATES.** Whenever the Athenians consult about letters, how they ought to be written, will you come forward to give advice?

**ALCIBIADES.** No, by Jove.

**SOCRATES.** What about when they consult on playing the lyre?

**ALCIBIADES.** In no way.

**SOCRATES.** Nor are they accustomed to debate about wrestling in the assembly.

**ALCIBIADES.** Not at all.

**SOCRATES.** When, then, and concerning what matter are they consulting? For it is not when they consult about buildings.

**ALCIBIADES.** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES.** For a builder would give better counsel than you.

**ALCIBIADES.** True.

**SOCRATES.** Nor when they debate about prophecy.

**ALCIBIADES.** Not at all.

# BOOK FIVE

**SOCRATES:** For a prophet knows these things better than you.
**ALCIBIADES:** Better, indeed.
**SOCRATES:** Whether he be small or great, handsome or deformed, noble or low-born.
**ALCIBIADES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** For it is the duty of a man of knowledge, not a man of wealth, to give counsel on each matter.
**ALCIBIADES:** Why not!
**SOCRATES:** And therefore, whether the one who advises be rich or poor, it will make no difference to the Athenians when they deliberate on how the citizens may be healthy; rather, they will seek only that the counselor be a physician.
**ALCIBIADES:** And rightly so.
**SOCRATES:** When, therefore, and in what cause will you be a suitable counselor?
**ALCIBIADES:** When they deliberate concerning public affairs.
**SOCRATES:** What, when they ask about naval matters, what kind of ships ought to be built?
**ALCIBIADES:** No, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** For you do not know how to construct ships. Is this the reason, or is it something else?
**ALCIBIADES:** Nothing else.
**SOCRATES:** But then, concerning which of their affairs were you speaking?
**ALCIBIADES:** When it is about war, O Socrates, or peace, or some other business of the city.
**SOCRATES:** Do you mean when they debate with whom peace should be negotiated, and against whom war should be waged, and in what manner?
**ALCIBIADES:** Precisely.
**SOCRATES:** And it is necessary to declare these things to those for whom it is advantageous?
**ALCIBIADES:** To these very ones.
**SOCRATES:** And then at the time when it is better?
**ALCIBIADES:** Entirely.
**SOCRATES:** And for as long as it remains better?
**ALCIBIADES:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** If, therefore, the Athenians were asking against whom they should contend in the wrestling school or in boxing, and how, would you advise them better than the master of the gymnasium?
**ALCIBIADES:** The master of the gymnasium would be better.
**SOCRATES:** Can you say what that man looks toward when he advises with whom they should wrestle in the gymnasium or not, and when, and in what manner? I mean something like this: must they not contend with those for whom it is advantageous?
**ALCIBIADES:** With those, certainly.
**SOCRATES:** And as much as is better?
**ALCIBIADES:** And as much as is better.
**SOCRATES:** And then, when it is better?
**ALCIBIADES:** Exactly.
**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, a singer must strike the lyre and dance according to the pattern of the song itself.
**ALCIBIADES:** He must.
**SOCRATES:** Is it not then when it is better?
**ALCIBIADES:** Then, certainly.
**SOCRATES:** And as much as is better?
**ALCIBIADES:** I admit it.

<margin>What is "better" in every study or matter: it is that which is rightly disposed through all things.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** What then, since you have named the "better" itself in both cases—both in the striking of the lyre according to the song, and in the gymnasium—what do you call that which is "better" in the right sound for singing? Just as I call that in the gymnasium "gymnastic." What do you call that other thing?
**ALCIBIADES:** I do not understand.
**SOCRATES:** But try to imitate me. I indeed answer that the "better" itself is that which is rightly disposed through all things. Now, that which is done according to art is rightly disposed, is it not?
**ALCIBIADES:** That is it.
**SOCRATES:** Is the art not gymnastic?
**ALCIBIADES:** Why not!
**SOCRATES:** That which is better in the gymnasium, I called gymnastic.
**ALCIBIADES:** You did indeed.
**SOCRATES:** Was it not right?
**ALCIBIADES:** It seems so to me.
**SOCRATES:** Come then, you too; for it becomes you also to discourse rightly. Tell me first, what is the art to which it belongs to sing, play, and dance rightly? What is this whole art called? Can you not yet express it?
**ALCIBIADES:** Not yet.
**SOCRATES:** But strive thus: who are the goddesses of this art?
**ALCIBIADES:** Do you mean the Muses, O Socrates?
**SOCRATES:** I do indeed. Look now, what name does that art obtain from them?
**ALCIBIADES:** You seem to me to be speaking of music.
**SOCRATES:** I am indeed. What is it, then, that is performed rightly according to this? Just as in that other art I named "gymnastic" for you as that which was done rightly according to art. In this one, in the same way, what do you say it is, and how is it done?
**ALCIBIADES:** It seems to me to be "musical" and "musically."
**SOCRATES:** You speak well. Come now, what do you call that which is "better" in war, and that which is "better" in peace? Just as you spoke in the previous cases of the "better" in each: in one that which is more musical, and in the other that which is more gymnastic. Try similarly to pronounce the "better" itself in these matters.
**ALCIBIADES:** I have nothing to say.
**SOCRATES:** But truly it is a disgrace if someone should bring you food and ask which is better, and when, and how much, and you could answer that it is the "healthier" choice—even if you do not profess to be a physician—but in that matter in which you boast of being skilled, and rise up as an educated man to give counsel, you are at a loss for an answer when asked what is "better." Is this not, I say, a disgrace?
**ALCIBIADES:** Most disgraceful.
**SOCRATES:** Consider then, and try to show us toward what the "better" itself tends in making peace, and with whom it ought to be made, and also in war, against whom it ought to be waged!
**ALCIBIADES:** Even if I search, I am unable to find it.
**SOCRATES:** Have you noticed when we wage war, what it is that we accuse, and what we call that by which we are incited to war?
**ALCIBIADES:** I have noticed indeed that we are called to arms when we have been deceived, or coerced, or deprived of something.
**SOCRATES:** Come, tell me how suffering those things in this way or that way differs?
**ALCIBIADES:** When you say "this way or that way," do you mean the same as if you said "justly or unjustly"?
**SOCRATES:** Exactly.
**ALCIBIADES:** It differs entirely and according to the wrong done.
**SOCRATES:** Against whom will you urge the Athenians to go to war? Against those who inflict injury, or those acting justly?
**ALCIBIADES:** That is a hard question you ask; for even if someone thought that even just men ought to be oppressed, he would not confess it to you.
**SOCRATES:** For this is not lawful, as it seems.
**ALCIBIADES:** Not at all.
**SOCRATES:** Nor does it appear good. In these matters, therefore, you would speak concerning that which is just.
**ALCIBIADES:** It is necessary.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, in waging war or not waging it, and with whom one ought or ought not, and when one ought or ought not, is the "better" anything other than that which is "more just"?
**ALCIBIADES:** It seems so.
**SOCRATES:** Is it then, O friend Alcibiades, that this escapes you: that you are ignorant of this? Or if, without my knowledge, you have gone to a teacher from whom you learned to judge what is more just and what is more un-

<margin>He discerns who finds; he finds who seeks; he seeks who thinks he is ignorant.</margin>

-just? Come, show me this man, so that you may present me to him as a disciple and a guest.
**ALCIBIADES:** You are mocking me, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** No, by the God who is a friend to me and you—whom I would least of all deceive with an oath—but if you have one, say who he is.
**ALCIBIADES:** What if I do not have one? Do you not think I could otherwise discern just and unjust things?
**SOCRATES:** Yes, if indeed you found it out.
**ALCIBIADES:** Do you not think I have found it?
**SOCRATES:** Certainly, if you have sought it.
**ALCIBIADES:** Then you do not believe I have sought it?
**SOCRATES:** I would believe it, if only you had thought you were ignorant of it.
**ALCIBIADES:** Was there not a time when I was in that state?
**SOCRATES:** You speak well; but can you assign to us that time, when you did not think you had knowledge of just and unjust things? Come, did you seek those things last year and not think you knew them, or did you think you knew? Answer truly, so that the discussions do not proceed in vain.
**ALCIBIADES:** I thought I knew.
**SOCRATES:** And in the third year before that time, and the fourth, and the fifth, was it not the same way?
**ALCIBIADES:** The same.
**SOCRATES:** And before these times, were you not a boy?
**ALCIBIADES:** I was.
**SOCRATES:** Then I know surely that you thought you knew.
**ALCIBIADES:** How do you know?

# ALCIBIADES, OR ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

## FO. XIII. (13)

...and you exercised yourself in other boyish studies, as if you had the least doubt about what is just and unjust; instead, you spoke boldly about whichever boy the conversation fell upon, saying he was wicked and unjust, and acted unjustly. Do I speak the truth? ALCIBIADES: What was I supposed to do when someone treated me with injustice? SOCRATES: If it happened that you were ignorant of whether he was committing an injustice or not, would you then ask what you ought to do? ALCIBIADES: By Jove, I was certainly not ignorant; I clearly understood that an injustice was being done to me. SOCRATES: Therefore, you thought even while you were a boy that you knew the just and the unjust. ALCIBIADES: And I did indeed know. SOCRATES: At what time did you discover it? For it was not at that time when you believed you already knew it. ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: When, then, did you think you were ignorant of these things? Consider it, for you will not find such a time. ALCIBIADES: By Jove, O Socrates, I do not know what to say. SOCRATES: You do not, therefore, know these things through discovery. ALCIBIADES: It seems not. SOCRATES: But a little while ago you said you had not received them through instruction either. If you have neither discovered nor learned them, in what way and from where do you know them? ALCIBIADES: Perhaps I did not answer correctly when I asserted that I knew through discovery. The truth of the matter was this: I learned them myself, I suppose, just as others do. SOCRATES: We are sliding back into the same problem: tell us from whom you learned. ALCIBIADES: From the common people <note>original: "A vulgo"</note>. SOCRATES: You are not resorting to proven teachers when you refer yourself to the common people. ALCIBIADES: Are they not sufficient for teaching these things? Can they not even teach things pertaining to games of dice <term>talares ludos: games played with knucklebones or dice</term>, even if these are of less value than justice? Do you not think so too? SOCRATES: I think so. ALCIBIADES: Then can they not hand down certain smaller things, and even some greater ones? SOCRATES: I suppose so. ALCIBIADES: Indeed, they can teach many things better than a dice game. SOCRATES: What are those? ALCIBIADES: Such as speaking Greek. For I learned from them, and I had no teacher other than those whom you said were hardly proven masters. SOCRATES: O noble youth, for this specific thing the common people are indeed suitable teachers, and they are rightly praised in this instruction. ALCIBIADES: Why? SOCRATES: Because they possess what it becomes good teachers to have. ALCIBIADES: What is that? SOCRATES: Do you not know that those who are going to teach something must understand it before they teach it? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: And those who understand must agree with one another <margin>What ought to be in good teachers.</margin> and not differ? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: In those things where they disagree, would you assert that they know them? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: How then could they be good masters of these things? ALCIBIADES: In no way. SOCRATES: Do you see whether they seem to disagree with you if you ever ask what is a stone and what is wood? Do they not all point to the same thing when they want to take up wood or stone? And in the same way in all such matters? ALCIBIADES: I understand roughly that you are saying something similar about the Greek language, are you not? SOCRATES: I am indeed. And therefore, in these matters, do not cities agree with one another, as we said, both privately and publicly, and they do not doubt—this one calling it this, and that one calling it something else? ALCIBIADES: They do not doubt. SOCRATES: Rightly, then, they would be suitable teachers of these things. ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, if you wished to turn out learned in these matters, we would rightly send you <margin>He who wishes to learn a language should be sent among the multitude; for the people are the master of language.</margin> to the instruction of the multitude. ALCIBIADES: Entirely. SOCRATES: But if we wanted to know not only who are men and who are horses, but also which of them are most capable in a race and which are not, could the common people ever instruct us? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: This will be sufficient proof for you that the common people do not know all things, nor are they fit teachers of them, since they by no means agree among themselves about them. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: If we desire to understand not only who are men, but who are healthy or sick, will the multitude ever teach us? ALCIBIADES: No. SOCRATES: You will easily notice that the multitude cannot teach these things <margin>That the common people do not know how to teach.</margin> if you consider their discordant opinions. ALCIBIADES: Truly. SOCRATES: But concerning just men and things, does the multitude agree with itself and with others? ALCIBIADES: Not at all, by Jove, O Socrates. SOCRATES: But in these things they disagree greatly? ALCIBIADES: Most greatly. SOCRATES: I suppose you have never seen nor heard of men disagreeing so much about the healthy and the sick that they waged war over them and killed one another. ALCIBIADES: Never. SOCRATES: But concerning the just and the unjust, how bitterly they disagree! Even if you have not seen it yourself, I suppose you have heard of it from many others, and especially from Homer in the *Odyssey* and the *Iliad*. ALCIBIADES: Entirely, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Are not all these <margin>The *Iliad* and *Odyssey* are about the distinction between the just and the unjust.</margin> poems about the distinction between the just and the unjust? ALCIBIADES: They are. SOCRATES: And the battles and deaths between the Achaeans and Trojans were surely because of this same disagreement; and by the same reasoning between the suitors of Penelope and Ulysses. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: And I think that between the Athenians, Spartans, and Boeotians—who perished first at Tanagra and then at Coronea, where your father Clinias also met his end—no other matter than the difference between the just and the unjust caused such a very bitter fight to break out. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Shall we say then that those people knew the things about which they contended so bitterly, so that in arguing about the just and the unjust they underwent all extremities? ALCIBIADES: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: Do you not refer yourself to those teachers whom you yourself admit are ignorant? ALCIBIADES: I seem to. SOCRATES: In what way is it consistent for you to know the just and the unjust, in which you wander so much, since you seem neither to have learned from anyone nor to have discovered them by yourself? ALCIBIADES: From what you say, it is not consistent. SOCRATES: Do you see again, Alcibiades, that you have not said this correctly? ALCIBIADES: What? SOCRATES: That you said I was saying these things. ALCIBIADES: What? Do you not say yourself that I am ignorant concerning the just and the unjust? SOCRATES: Not at all. ALCIBIADES: Is it I, then? SOCRATES: You, I say. ALCIBIADES: In what way? SOCRATES: You will understand it thus: if I ask you whether one or two is more, will you not answer two? ALCIBIADES: Two. SOCRATES: By how much? ALCIBIADES: By one. SOCRATES: Which of us will be the one who says two is more than one by one? ALCIBIADES: I. SOCRATES: Was I not the one questioning, and you the one answering? ALCIBIADES: Yes. SOCRATES: Concerning these things, then, which of us seems to be speaking? I who am questioning, or you who are answering? ALCIBIADES: I. SOCRATES: What if I ask how many letters are in "Socrates," and you answer, which of us will be the one who speaks? ALCIBIADES: I. SOCRATES: Come, say in one word: whenever a question and answer occurs, who is the one who speaks: the questioner or the respondent? ALCIBIADES: The respondent, it seems to me, O Socrates. SOCRATES: In the previous parts, I always questioned. ALCIBIADES: Always. SOCRATES: And you answered. ALCIBIADES: I answered. SOCRATES: Therefore, as for what has been said so far, which...

<summary>Socrates leads Alcibiades to realize that the common people are unreliable teachers of justice because they disagree and go to war over it, unlike their agreement on simple facts like language or objects. Socrates also demonstrates that it is the respondent, not the questioner, who makes the assertions in their dialogue.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE

...said of us! ALCIBIADES: From what has been conceded, I seem to have been the one who said it. SOCRATES: Was it not said that Alcibiades, the noble son of Clinias, being ignorant of just and unjust things, thought he knew them, and was about to ascend to the assembly of the Athenians to advise them on things he did not know? ALCIBIADES: It was. SOCRATES: That line of Euripides <note>A reference to Euripides' play *Hippolytus*: "You hear this from yourself, not me."</note> now occurs to us, O Alcibiades. For you seem to have heard those things from yourself, not from me. Nor did I say these things, but you did; you accuse me in vain. And indeed you speak well. For you have resolved, O best of men, to undertake a certain madness: to teach those things which you neither know nor have cared to learn. ALCIBIADES: I think, O Socrates, that the Athenians and other Greeks rarely inquire into what is more just or what is more unjust. For they think such things are obvious. Therefore, omitting these, they inquire into what is advantageous for those acting. For I do not think the just and the useful are the same. Indeed, injustice has profited many who act unjustly, while on the contrary, justice itself has not helped others who act justly. SOCRATES: Therefore, some things will be just, and others will be beneficial. But do you think you know what things are useful to men, and for what reason? ALCIBIADES: And what prevents it, Socrates? Unless you ask again from whom I learned it, or how I found it out myself. SOCRATES: You are acting now as if, should you say something incorrectly and it could be shown by the same reasoning as before, you nevertheless think some new things ought to be heard, and new demonstrations brought forward, as if the previous ones were worn out and broken like the equipment and clothes used on a stage—which you would no longer wear unless someone brought something else pure and unspotted. But I, setting aside the preludes of your speech, will nonetheless ask: from where did you learn what is useful, and who was the teacher? And I will seek all the rest as before with a single question. Yet I think you will return to the same point: you will not be able to show by what reasoning you learned the useful, whether by instruction or by discovery. But since you are so devoted to luxuries that you do not seem likely to taste the same discourse gladly, I let this go: whether you know or not what is useful or useless to the Athenians. But why do you not demonstrate whether the just and the useful are the same, or different—either by questioning me yourself, as I did you, or if you prefer, by running through the argument by yourself in your own speech? ALCIBIADES: I do not know, O Socrates, if I would be able to dispute against you. SOCRATES: But, my good man, imagine me to be the assembly and the people for the present: must you not persuade each one there? ALCIBIADES: I must. SOCRATES: Is it not the mark of the same person to be able to demonstrate something to one person privately, and also to many together regarding what he knows? Just as a grammarian <note>term: *grammaticus* - a teacher of letters and literature</note> instructs one and many alike in letters; and in the same way, who can show numbers to one and to many? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And this person is the arithmetician. ALCIBIADES: He is. SOCRATES: And you, therefore, can persuade one person of the same things you can persuade many. ALCIBIADES: It is likely. SOCRATES: And these are clearly the things which you know. ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: The only difference between the rhetorician who speaks before the people and the one in this kind of gathering is that the former persuades everyone at once, while the latter persuades individuals separately. ALCIBIADES: So it seems. SOCRATES: Come then, since it appears to be the mark of the same person to show things to many and to one, practice now before me and strive to show me that the just is sometimes not beneficial. ALCIBIADES: You are being insulting, Socrates. SOCRATES: Now I am going to demonstrate to you, by way of "insult," the opposite of those things which you do not want from me. ALCIBIADES: Speak. SOCRATES: Just answer what is asked. ALCIBIADES: Not at all, but you say it yourself. SOCRATES: Do you not want to be persuaded as much as possible? ALCIBIADES: Entirely. SOCRATES: If you yourself say that these things are so, will you not be most persuaded? ALCIBIADES: It seems so to me. SOCRATES: Answer then; for unless you hear from yourself that all just things are useful, you will not believe another saying it. ALCIBIADES: No; but I must answer now, for I think it will do no harm. SOCRATES: You are a prophet indeed; tell the truth: do you assert that some just things are beneficial and some are not? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: And what of these: are some beautiful <note>The Greek concept of *kalon* implies both physical beauty and moral nobility.</note> and some the opposite? ALCIBIADES: How do you ask this? SOCRATES: Whether anyone ever seemed to you to do things that were shameful, but nevertheless just? ALCIBIADES: Never to me. SOCRATES: Therefore all just things are also beautiful. ALCIBIADES: So it is. SOCRATES: Again, are all beautiful things good, or are some good and some bad? ALCIBIADES: I think, Socrates, that some beautiful things are bad. SOCRATES: And some shameful things are good? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Do you mean something like this: as if some, while wanting to bring help to a friend or relative in battle, died from wounds; while those who did not provide the due help departed from there unharmed? ALCIBIADES: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Do you not call help of this kind beautiful, where one tries to save those whom he ought? And that is courage? ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: But you call it bad on account of the deaths and wounds? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: Is courage not one thing, and death another? ALCIBIADES: Another. SOCRATES: Therefore, to bring help to friends is not beautiful and bad according to the same thing. ALCIBIADES: It does not seem so. SOCRATES: See then whether, by the same reasoning that it is beautiful, it is also good. As in these cases: you concede that to bring help is beautiful according to courage; but is courage itself good or bad? Consider it this way: which would you choose to have, good things or bad things? ALCIBIADES: Good things. SOCRATES: Would you not desire the greatest goods most, and least of all wish to be deprived of them? ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: What do you say of courage? At what price would you trade it? ALCIBIADES: I would not even want to live if I were a coward. SOCRATES: Does cowardice seem to you to be the extreme evil? ALCIBIADES: To me, yes. SOCRATES: Equal to death, it seems. ALCIBIADES: Equal. SOCRATES: Life and courage are the opposites of death and cowardice? ALCIBIADES: They are. SOCRATES: And you would most desire these to be present to you, and those least? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Is it not because you think these are the best and those the worst? ALCIBIADES: Very much so. SOCRATES: Therefore, to bring help to friends in battle: you called it beautiful according to the good—that is, the action of courage. ALCIBIADES: I certainly seem to. SOCRATES: But according to the action, it is bad—that is, the evil of death. ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Is it not fitting to name each action thus:

<margin>Insofar as it brings good, it is beautiful; insofar as it brings evil, it is shameful.</margin>

if you call it bad insofar as it brings evil, conversely, it is proper to call it good insofar as it brings good. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: And is it not also beautiful insofar as it is good, and shameful insofar as it is bad? ALCIBIADES: Very much so. SOCRATES: When you say, therefore, that help in war is beautiful but bad, it is the same as if you had said it is good...

<summary>Socrates leads Alcibiades through a dialectic argument to prove that the "just" is always "useful" by connecting the concepts of the beautiful, the good, and courage. He challenges Alcibiades' assumption that a noble act (like dying for a friend) can be "beautiful" yet "bad."</summary>

# ALCIBIADES I, OR ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

...yet it is an evil. ALCIBIADES. You seem to me to speak the truth, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Therefore, nothing is beautiful insofar as it is beautiful and evil; nor is anything base insofar as it is base and good. ALCIBIADES. It does not seem so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, consider it in this way: whoever acts beautifully, does he not act well? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. And those acting well, are they not happy? ALCIBIADES. Why not?
<margin>They are happy because of the possession of good things.</margin>
SOCRATES. Are they not happy because of the possession of good things? ALCIBIADES. Most certainly. SOCRATES. And are these things acquired from the fact that they act beautifully and well? ALCIBIADES. Surely. SOCRATES. Therefore, to act well is a good. ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. And is not a beautiful action a good one? ALCIBIADES. Surely. SOCRATES. Thus, the beautiful and the good appear to us again as the same thing. ALCIBIADES. They appear so. SOCRATES. Therefore, whatever we find to be beautiful, we shall also find to be good by this reasoning. ALCIBIADES. It must be so. SOCRATES. Do good things benefit us or not? ALCIBIADES. They benefit us. SOCRATES. Do you remember what we confessed above regarding just things? ALCIBIADES. I believe we said those acting justly must necessarily do beautiful things. SOCRATES. And those doing beautiful things, do they not also do good things? ALCIBIADES. Yes. SOCRATES. And do good things profit us? ALCIBIADES. Entirely. SOCRATES. Therefore, O Alcibiades, just things are useful. ALCIBIADES. It seems so. SOCRATES. Did you not say these things yourself, while I only asked the questions? ALCIBIADES. It appears so. SOCRATES. If someone were to stand up before the Athenians or the Peparethians <note>A small island in the Aegean</note> thinking he could distinguish just and unjust things, and said he knew that just things are sometimes evil, would you not laugh at him, since you yourself assert that the same things are both just and useful? ALCIBIADES. By the gods, O Socrates, I do not know what to say; I seem to be in an absurd state. For now one thing seems true to me when you question me, and now another. SOCRATES. Do you not know, my friend, what this affection is? ALCIBIADES. I do not know. SOCRATES. If someone asked you whether you had two or three eyes, or two or four hands, or something of this sort, do you think you would answer now one thing and now another, or always the same? ALCIBIADES. Although I am now wary of myself, I think I would answer the same. SOCRATES. And is the cause of this not because you know the answer? ALCIBIADES. I think so. SOCRATES. Therefore, concerning things about which you unwillingly give contrary answers, it is clear that you are ignorant of them. ALCIBIADES. That is consistent. SOCRATES. Do you not confess that you have erred in answering about the just and unjust, the beautiful and the base, the good and the evil, the useful and the useless? And is it not manifest that you erred for this reason: because you were ignorant? ALCIBIADES. It seems so to me. SOCRATES. Is it then the case that when someone is ignorant of something, his mind must necessarily err regarding it? ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. Do you know by what means you might ascend into heaven? ALCIBIADES. Not at all, certainly. SOCRATES. Does your opinion wander concerning this? ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Do you know the cause of this? Or do you prefer that I tell you? ALCIBIADES. Tell me. SOCRATES. Because since you do not know, you do not *think* you know. ALCIBIADES. How do you say that again? SOCRATES. Look at it with me: those things which you do not know, and you recognize that you do not know them, do you stumble in them? Just as you know that you do not know how to prepare gourmet meals? ALCIBIADES. Entirely. SOCRATES. Do you have an opinion on how they should be prepared and thus err? Or do you rather yield to the one who knows? ALCIBIADES. In that way. SOCRATES. What if you were sailing? Would you have an opinion and wander about whether the rudder should be turned inward or outward? And being ignorant, would you go astray? Or would you rather yield to the pilot and remain quiet? ALCIBIADES. To the pilot. SOCRATES. Therefore, you do not err in those things you do not know, if you know that you do not know them. ALCIBIADES. It does not seem so. SOCRATES. Do you perceive that errors in actions are due to this ignorance: that he who does not know thinks he knows? ALCIBIADES. How do you say that? SOCRATES. We undertake to act when we think we know what we are doing. ALCIBIADES. It is so. SOCRATES. But if any are conscious of their ignorance, they commit themselves to others. ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. Therefore, among the ignorant, these alone live their lives without fault, because they trust themselves to the care of others. ALCIBIADES. Indeed. SOCRATES. Who then are those who sin? For it is not those who know. ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Since neither those who know, nor those among the ignorant who are conscious of their ignorance err, who else remains but those who, while they do not know, think they know? ALCIBIADES. None other but these. SOCRATES. This ignorance, therefore, is the cause of evils and is a blameworthy lack of knowledge. ALCIBIADES. Truly. SOCRATES. And when it concerns the greatest things, then it is the worst and most shameful. ALCIBIADES. Most especially. SOCRATES. Can you name anything greater than the just, the good, and the useful? ALCIBIADES. Not at all. SOCRATES. Do you not assert that you have erred regarding these? ALCIBIADES. I do. SOCRATES. And if you err, is it not clear from what was said above that you are not only ignorant in the greatest matters, but also that while being ignorant, you think you know? ALCIBIADES. I seem to be. SOCRATES. Alas, O Alcibiades! What a disease you are pressed by! I shudder to name it. Nevertheless, since we are alone, it must be said. For you are involved in the most shameful ignorance, O best of men, as you yourself prove by your own speech. For this reason, you rush into civil affairs before you are skilled in governing. And this disease has not held you alone, but also all those who administer this republic, except for a very few, and perhaps except for your guardian, Pericles. ALCIBIADES. It is said, O Socrates, that Pericles did not become wise by chance, but because he had familiar dealings with many wise men, Pythoclides in the first place, and Anaxagoras; and even now, at such a great age, he associates with Damon for the sake of wisdom. SOCRATES. Have you ever seen a wise man who, in that matter in which he himself is wise, could not make another man wise? Just as the one who instructed you in letters was himself wise and rendered you equally wise; and in the same way, he could have instructed anyone else. ALCIBIADES. Indeed. SOCRATES. And you too, having been taught by him, will be able to instruct another. ALCIBIADES. I will. SOCRATES. Similarly the cithara-player and the master of the gymnasium. ALCIBIADES. Entirely. SOCRATES. This, therefore, is the best conjecture: that someone knows something when they can show another person who has been taught by them. ALCIBIADES. It seems so to me.
<margin>The best conjecture of one who knows.</margin>
SOCRATES. Can you name anyone who was made wise by Pericles, beginning with his sons? ALCIBIADES. What if Pericles' sons were born dull-witted? SOCRATES. But what about your brother, Clinias? ALCIBIADES. Why do you bring up Clinias, a man who is insane? SOCRATES. Since Clinias is indeed mad and the sons of Pericles were born dull, what cause shall we ascribe to you, for which he neglects you when you are as you are? ALCIBIADES. I myself, as I think, am at fault, since I did not apply myself to him. SOCRATES. But tell me of other Athenians or guests, which servant or freeman he made wiser by his company, just as I can show you that Pythodorus son of Isolochus and Callias son of Calliades became worthy and wise men through the familiarity of Zeno <note>original: "Xenonis"</note>, to whom each gave a hundred minae. ALCIBIADES. By Jove, I have no one to name. SOCRATES. So be it. What then do you think of yourself? Whether you will remain as you are now in the future, or be cured in some way? ALCIBIADES. There is need of common counsel, O Socrates. For indeed I understand your words and I agree with them.

<summary>Socrates leads Alcibiades to realize that his contradictory answers stem from "double ignorance"—thinking he knows about justice and politics when he does not. They conclude that a true expert must be able to teach others, a standard Pericles seemingly failed to meet with his own family.</summary>

# BOOK FIVE

For those who govern the state, except for a very few, seem to me to be unlearned. SOCRATES: What then? ALCIBIADES: If they were experts, it would be necessary for one approaching politics to compete with them on equal terms: only after he had learned and exercised himself should he then finally go forth as if against trained athletes. But now, since even these unlearned men have entered into public affairs, why do I need exercise? Why the study of discipline? For I know that I shall far surpass these men by my natural gifts. SOCRATES: Good heavens, what a thing you have said, my best of men! How unworthy of your character and the other qualities you possess. ALCIBIADES: To what end do you say this, Socrates? SOCRATES: For I take it heavily on account of the mutual goodwill between us. ALCIBIADES: What exactly? SOCRATES: That you should think it a worthy contest for you to be against the men who are here. ALCIBIADES: Against whom then? SOCRATES: Is it not fitting that a man who thinks so highly of himself should seek a greater challenge? ALCIBIADES: What do you mean? Is my contest not against these men? SOCRATES: If you intended to steer a fighting trireme <note>A Greek warship with three banks of oars</note>, would it be enough for you to excel your fellow sailors in steering? Or would you think that while this is necessary, you should look instead toward your strenuous adversaries? You should not do as you are doing now—looking at your own supporters, whom you ought to excel so much that you do not even think of fighting against them, but rather, holding them of little account, use them as assistants against external enemies, if indeed you truly wish to perform some noble deed worthy of yourself and your state. ALCIBIADES: Indeed, I do think of that. SOCRATES: Is it worthy that you should think it enough if you are the most excellent of your own soldiers? Should you not rather look toward the leaders of the enemy, considering by what means you might excel them, always watching them and fortifying yourself against them? ALCIBIADES: Of whom do you speak, Socrates? SOCRATES: Do you not know that our city is at war on all sides with the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> and the great King of the Persians? ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Since you have it in mind to become the leader of this city, will you not judge correctly if you think that you will undergo a contest against the kings of the Lacedaemonians and the Persians? ALCIBIADES: You seem to speak the truth. SOCRATES: No, my good man; it is fitting for you to look at Midias the quail-breeder and others of that sort, who attempt to handle civil affairs while still possessing the souls of slaves, as women would say:

<margin>To have hair in one's soul: this seems to be a proverb derived from a dirty piece of cheese or bread, applied to a rustic, unlearned, and barbarian soul.</margin>

having hair in their souls because of their rustic ignorance, not yet casting those things aside but still smelling of barbarism; and being so affected, they come forward to flatter the city, not to rule it. It is toward these men, I say, that you think it fitting to look; and so you neglect yourself, neither learning whatever pertains to erudition—though you are about to enter such a great contest—nor exercising yourself in what is necessary, nor preparing what must be prepared; and thus, you take up the administration of civil institutions. ALCIBIADES: O Socrates, you seem to me to speak the truth. However, I think the leaders of the Lacedaemonians and the kings of the Persians differ in no way from others. SOCRATES: But, my best of men, consider, I pray: what sort of opinion is this of yours? ALCIBIADES: In what regard? SOCRATES: Do you think you would take care of yourself more diligently if you feared them and judged them powerful? Or if you feared them not at all? ALCIBIADES: If I judged them powerful. SOCRATES: Do you think that taking care of yourself can harm you in any way? ALCIBIADES: In no way; on the contrary, it helps the most. SOCRATES: This opinion of yours contains this one great evil in particular. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: And secondly, that it is false; observe this from the probabilities. ALCIBIADES: How? SOCRATES: Whether it is likely that better natures are found in a noble lineage than in an ignoble one? ALCIBIADES: It is manifest that they are in the noble.

<margin>It is likely that better natures exist in a noble lineage than in an ignoble one.</margin>

SOCRATES: And do not the well-born, if they are also well-nourished, finally reach virtue in this way? ALCIBIADES: It is necessary. SOCRATES: Let us therefore consider our affairs by comparing them to theirs: first, whether the kings of the Lacedaemonians and Persians seem to be sprung from a more ignoble race than we are. Or are we ignorant that they trace their descent from Hercules, and the others from Achæmenes? And the origin of both Hercules and Achæmenes is traced back to Perseus, the son of Jupiter <note>Latin: Iovis; the Greek god Zeus</note>. ALCIBIADES: And our lineage, Socrates, goes to Eurysaces, and from Eurysaces to Jupiter. SOCRATES: And yet our lineage, noble Alcibiades, also goes to Daedalus; and Daedalus to Vulcan, the son of Jupiter. But the ancestors of those men, beginning from these, are kings from kings all the way to Jupiter. The former are kings of Argos and Lacedaemon; the latter are always kings of Persia, and often, as now, of Asia. But we and our ancestors were private citizens. If you had to show the progenitors and the fatherland of Eurysaces—Salamis—or even of the earlier Aeacus—Aegina—to Artaxerxes the son of Xerxes, what laughter do you think you would bring upon yourself! But see to it that we are not inferior to them in the dignity of our race and also in our education.

<margin>The education of the Persian kings.</margin>

Have you ever heard how great is the dignity of the Lacedaemonian kings? Their wives are publicly watched by the Ephors <gloss>that is, the overseers</gloss>, so that, as far as possible, a king is not born from any other than the race of the Heraclidae <note>Descendants of Hercules</note>. But the King of the Persians so excels that no one suspects the king was born from anyone other than the king himself. Therefore, the king's wife is guarded by nothing other than fear. After the first-born who succeeds to the kingdom is born, first all who are under the kingdom celebrate that day; and so thereafter, every year, all of Asia honors the king's birthday with sacrifices and feasts. But when one of us is born, not even the neighbors notice much, as the comic poet says, O Alcibiades. Next, the boy is nurtured, not by just any nurse, but by eunuchs who seem the best of those around the king; to whom other things regarding the care of the boy are entrusted, and especially that they make the child as beautiful as possible, shaping and straightening his limbs. And doing these things, they are held in great honor. When the boys have completed their seventh year of age, they go to masters of the equestrian art; then they proceed to the hunt. In the fourteenth year, those whom they call the royal pedagogues take up the boy. These are four men chosen from all the Persians, the most distinguished of their age: the wisest, the most just, the most temperate, and the bravest.

<margin>The magic of Zoroaster is the worship of the gods.</margin>

The first of these teaches the magic of Zoroaster, the son of Oromasius—which is the worship of the gods. And the same man teaches the royal institutions. The second admonishes him to be truthful in all his life. The third ensures he is not overcome by any desire, so that he may be accustomed to living freely; and truly a king, ruling first over the things within himself, and serving no one. The fourth, finally, renders him fearless and intrepid, lest by fearing anything he should become a slave. But for you, Alcibiades, Pericles appointed as a pedagogue Zopyrus the Thracian, the most useless of all his slaves due to old age. I would tell you the rest of their education, etc.

<summary>Socrates humbles Alcibiades' political ambitions by comparing his meager upbringing and local rivals to the superior lineage, wealth, and rigorous education of the Spartan and Persian kings. The text emphasizes that true leadership requires self-discipline and specialized training rather than mere natural talent.</summary>

# ALCIBIADES I, OR ON THE NATURE OF MAN. FOLIO 15.

...the education of your adversaries: unless I feared being too long-winded. Furthermore, these points are sufficient to show the rest which follow from them. But as for you, no one—not even your kinsmen, so to speak—cares about your birth, upbringing, or education, unless perhaps your friends take an interest. If, however, you wish to consider the wealth, the luxury, the ornate style of clothing, the scent of ointments, the crowd of attending servants, and the other refinements of the Persians, you will blush for your own sake, realizing how much inferior you are to them.

<margin>Praises of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note></margin>
On the other hand, if you wish to look at the temperance of the Lacedaemonians, their modesty, ease, gentleness, magnanimity, moderation, orderliness, bravery, constancy, endurance, their desire for victory, and their love of glory, you will judge yourself a mere child in all these things. If, again, you attribute something to wealth and think there is something in it, let us not pass this over in silence. If you only realize where you stand and look upon the riches of the Lacedaemonians, you will surely recognize that we are far surpassed by them. For whatever lands they possess, either of their own or of Messenia, no one would doubt that they exceed ours in size and fertility, and in the multitude of slaves (both others and the Helots), and furthermore in horses and the abundance of other livestock which Messenia produces. But I omit all these things for the present. Truly, there is such a great abundance of gold and silver among the Lacedaemonians as not even the rest of Greece combined possesses. For many centuries now, it has flowed there from all of Greece and often even from the barbarians, but it never flows out.

<margin>Aesop's fable.</margin>
But in truth, just as the fox said to the lion in Aesop regarding the tracks of the beasts, so too the tracks of money entering Lacedaemon are seen worn into the dust, but those leaving are nowhere to be seen. From this, one may conjecture that the Lacedaemonians are the wealthiest of all the Greeks in gold and silver. Furthermore, their king is the richest of all. For the greatest part of these things comes to him. Moreover, a very large tribute is paid to the king. And while the affairs of the Lacedaemonians are grand compared to the rest of the Greeks, they are narrow compared to the Persians and the kings of the Persians.

Indeed, a certain grave man, one of those who had traveled to the King of the Persians, reported to us that he once traveled for nearly a whole day through a wide and fertile province which the inhabitants call the "Queen's Girdle."

<margin>Calyptra <note>A veil or head-covering</note></margin>
<margin>Provinces named after the ornaments of the Queen's limbs.</margin>
There was also another called the *Calyptra* (that is, a woman's head ornament); and thus many other beautiful and fertile regions are assigned to the Queen's adornment, and names are imposed on individual places from individual ornaments. Therefore, I think if someone were to tell Amestris, the wife of Xerxes and mother of the king, that the son of Dinomache intended to fight with her son—when Dinomache's finery is worth perhaps fifty minae, while her son has less than three hundred *plethra* <note>A unit of land measurement</note> of land in Erchia—she would wonder what Alcibiades relies on to dare to fight with Artaxerxes. I believe she would think this man attempts it relying on nothing else but diligence and wisdom; for these alone are considered worthy of esteem among the Greeks. But if she heard that this Alcibiades was entering such a contest—firstly, not yet twenty years old; secondly, entirely unlearned; and thirdly, not obeying his friend who says he must first learn and practice before attacking such a king—I think she would be moved by wonder and ask what it is this youth trusts in. If we replied that you trust in beauty, height, nobility, wealth, and spirit, O Alcibiades, they would think us insane, seeing all these things are superior among their own people. In the same way, Lampido, daughter of Leotychides, wife of Archidamus, and mother of Agis (all of whom were kings), would wonder, knowing what things she has around her, that a man so poorly equipped would not hesitate to declare war on her son. And yet, does it not seem shameful if the women of our enemies have a more correct opinion of us than we do of ourselves, regarding how we ought to prepare ourselves against them? Therefore, O my blessed friend, obey the epigram at Delphi: *Know Thyself*. For these are our adversaries, whom you yourself were considering, and whom we can surpass by no other means than industry and art. If you are inferior in these, you will also lack glory among the Greeks and barbarians, which you seem to desire so ardently that no one ever craved anything more passionately.

ALCIBIADES: What care then do you think should be applied, O Socrates? Can you show me? For you seem to me to have spoken the truth beyond what can be said.
SOCRATES: I can indeed, but there is need of common counsel as to how we may become as good as possible. For I say that not only you, but I also, stand in need of education. For there is only one thing in which I differ from you.
ALCIBIADES: What is that?
SOCRATES: My guardian is better and wiser than yours, Pericles.
ALCIBIADES: Who is this, O Socrates?
SOCRATES: God, O Alcibiades, who forbade me to discourse with you before this day; trusting in Him, I tell you that you will achieve fame through no one else but through me.
ALCIBIADES: You are joking, O Socrates.
SOCRATES: Perhaps, yet I speak the truth, for we both need care; indeed, all men do, but we most of all.
ALCIBIADES: That I am in need, you do not lie at all.
SOCRATES: Nor that I am myself.
ALCIBIADES: What then is to be done?
SOCRATES: We must neither hesitate nor indulge in softness, O friend.
ALCIBIADES: Certainly.
SOCRATES: In what capacity?
ALCIBIADES: In that, clearly, of good men.
SOCRATES: Good in what matter?
ALCIBIADES: In managing affairs.

<margin>In what affairs.</margin>
SOCRATES: In which ones? In the business of horsemanship?
ALCIBIADES: No.
SOCRATES: For we would go to the horsemen for that.
ALCIBIADES: Surely.
SOCRATES: Did you mean in the steering of a ship?
ALCIBIADES: Not at all.
SOCRATES: For we would go to the sailors.
ALCIBIADES: We would.
SOCRATES: In what business then, and in the duty of what men?
ALCIBIADES: In those things which the famous and good men of Athens manage.
SOCRATES: Do you call the famous and good "prudent" or "imprudent"?
ALCIBIADES: Prudent.

<margin>In whatever one is prudent, in that same thing he is good.</margin>
SOCRATES: In whatever a person is prudent, is he good in that same thing?
ALCIBIADES: Certainly.
SOCRATES: And the imprudent is bad?
ALCIBIADES: Bad.
SOCRATES: Is a shoemaker prudent in the work of shoes?
ALCIBIADES: Entirely.
SOCRATES: Therefore he is good at this?
ALCIBIADES: Good.
SOCRATES: But what about making clothes? Is this cobbler not imprudent there?
ALCIBIADES: Yes.
SOCRATES: Therefore he is bad at this?
ALCIBIADES: Yes.
SOCRATES: Therefore, according to this reasoning, the same man will be both good and bad.
ALCIBIADES: It seems so.
SOCRATES: Do you say that good men are also bad?
ALCIBIADES: ...

# BOOK FIVE

Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Whom then do you call the "good"? **ALCIBIADES:** Those who are capable of leading in the city. **SO:** But surely not leading horses? **AL:** Certainly not. **SO:** But men? **AL:** Men. **SO:** Not sick men, surely? **AL:** No. **SO:** Or perhaps those at sea? **AL:** I do not mean those. **SO:** Harvesters then? **AL:** Nor those. **SO:** Those doing something, or doing nothing? **AL:** Those doing something. **SO:** What then are they doing? Declare that to me. **AL:** I mean those conducting commerce and dealing with one another, just as we live our lives in cities. **SO:** Do you say they rule over men who make use of men? **AL:** I do. **SO:** Like pilots who make use of rowers? **AL:** No. **SO:** For that is the virtue of the pilot’s faculty. **AL:** It is. **SO:** Perhaps you meant ruling over flute-players, who lead those who sing and make use of dancers? **AL:** Not those either. **SO:** For that belongs to the faculty of the choral master! **AL:** Entirely. **SO:** What then do you call being able to rule over men who make use of men? **AL:** To preside over men communicating with one another in the administration of the republic and in commerce. **SO:** What art is this? Just as if I were to ask you again, what faculty makes us know how to preside over those communicating in navigation? **AL:** The pilot's art. **SO:** And for those communicating in song, as was said just now, what science teaches how to preside? **AL:** That which you just mentioned, the discipline of the chorus. **SO:** But for those communicating in the republic, what do you call this science? **AL:** Good counsel, O Socrates. **SO:** Does the pilot seem to you to lack counsel? **AL:** Not at all. **SO:** Is it itself also "good counsel"? **AL:** It certainly seems so to me. **SO:** For the safety of those sailing. **AL:** You speak rightly. **SO:** But what do you call "good counsel," and toward what does it look? **AL:** Toward the better institution of the city and its safety. **SO:** By what thing being present or absent is it better disposed and preserved? Just as if you asked me, by what being present or absent do bodies fare well: I would answer by health being present and disease removed. Do you think the same? **AL:** The same. **SO:** And if you asked the same about the eyes, I would answer by the same reasoning: blindness being driven out and sight applied. And that ears are cured by deafness being put to flight and hearing brought in? **AL:** Correct. **SO:** But the city—by what being removed or what being applied does it become better and better instituted? **AL:** It seems to me, O Socrates, when there is friendship among the citizens, and hatred and sedition are absent. **SO:** Do you call friendship "agreement" <note>original: *consensio*</note> or "disagreement"? **AL:** Agreement. **SO:** Through what art do cities agree regarding numbers? **AL:** Through arithmetic. **SO:** And private individuals, is it not through the same? **AL:** Certainly. **SO:** And each person with himself? **AL:** Surely. **SO:** Through what art does each agree with himself about the span and the cubit <note>Ancient units of measurement</note>, which of them is greater? Is it not through the skill of measuring? **AL:** Why not? **SO:** And do not private individuals and cities likewise agree? **AL:** Indeed. **SO:** And about weights in the same way? **AL:** I agree. **SO:** This agreement, then, which you spoke of—what is it? About what? What art provides it? For that agreement is such that it exists in the republic and in every private individual toward himself and others. **AL:** It is likely. **SO:** What is it then? Do not be loath to answer, but tell it promptly. **AL:** I truly think it is the friendship and agreement by which a father and mother agree in loving their son, and brother with brother, and wife with husband. **SO:** Do you think, O Alcibiades, that a husband agrees with his wife about wool-working—the unskilled with the skilled? **AL:** Not at all. **SO:** Nor should he; for this is a woman’s discipline. **AL:** Truly. **SO:** But will a woman agree with a man about military work? Since she has by no means learned it. **AL:** Not at all. **SO:** For you would say that is manly. **AL:** Indeed. **SO:** There are therefore certain disciplines of women and certain of men, according to your speech. **AL:** Why not? **SO:** In these things, therefore, there is no agreement between women and men. **AL:** None. **SO:** Nor therefore friendship, if indeed friendship is a certain agreement. **AL:** It does not seem so. **SO:** And therefore, insofar as women perform their own duties, they are not loved by men. **AL:** It does not appear so. **SO:** Nor men by women, while they handle manly things. **AL:** No. **SO:** Then cities are not best instituted when individuals apply themselves to their own works? **AL:** Yet I think so, O Socrates. **SO:** How can you say this when friendship is removed, which we confessed makes cities well-constituted when present, and otherwise when absent? **AL:** But it seems to me that friendship exists among men for this very reason: because each performs his own duty. **SO:** You were not saying that a moment ago; but now how do you say again that friendship arises when agreement is applied? Can agreement exist about these things in which some are skilled and others unskilled? **AL:** It cannot happen. **SO:** Do they do just or unjust things when individuals perform what pertains to them? **AL:** Just things, perfectly. **SO:** Therefore, when citizens act justly in the city, there is no friendship? **AL:** This likewise seems necessary, O Socrates. **SO:** What then do you call friendship or agreement, about which we ought to be wise and good counselors in order to be good men? For I cannot perceive what it is or in whom it exists; since from your speech it seems sometimes to be in the same people, and sometimes to be absent from them. **AL:** By the gods, O Socrates, I do not understand what I am saying myself; I seem to have been hidden from myself for a long time, being in a most shameful state.

<margin>What it is for each to care for himself. For he proceeds from here to teach what the nature of man is, since he has shown up to this point what it is not and in whom it is not.</margin>
**SO:** It is right to be confident. For if you had only noticed this at fifty years old, it would be truly difficult to care for yourself; but now you are at that age in which it is right to notice it. **AL:** What then must one do who notices this? **SO:** Answer the things I shall ask you, Alcibiades. If you do this, and God wills it—if any faith is to be placed in my prophecies—you and I together shall fare better. **AL:** It shall be so, as far as it pertains to me answering. **SO:** Come then, what is it to "care for oneself," lest we often be hidden from ourselves, not caring for ourselves while we think we are doing so? And when does a man do this? Does he have care for himself as often as he has care for his belongings? **AL:** It seems so to me. **SO:** What? Does one care for his feet when he cares for the things that belong to the feet? **AL:** I do not understand. **SO:** Do you say there is something belonging to the hand, just as a ring is? **AL:** I do indeed. **SO:** Do you think the ring belongs to any other member than the finger? **AL:** Not at all. **SO:** And the shoe to the foot in the same way? **AL:** Yes.

<summary>Socrates leads Alcibiades to admit his ignorance regarding the nature of "good counsel" and "friendship" within a state. The dialogue shifts toward the philosophical necessity of "caring for oneself" as the foundation for leadership.</summary>

# ALCIBIADES ON THE NATURE OF MAN. PAGE XVI.

# ALCIBIADES ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

**SOCRATES.** When we take care of our shoes, do we then take care of our feet? **ALCIBIADES.** I do not quite follow you, Socrates. **SO.** What then, Alcibiades, do you call the right care of anything? **AL.** I do. **SO.** Is it not when something is made better? Do you then say that is its right care? **AL.** I do. **SO.** Which art makes shoes better? **AL.** Shoemaking <note>original: "Cerdonica"</note>. **SO.** By shoemaking, therefore, we take care of shoes? **AL.** By that very art. **SO.** Do we also take care of the feet by shoemaking? Or rather by that art by which we make the feet better? **AL.** By that one. **SO.** And are the feet not made better by the same art as the rest of the body? **AL.** It seems so. **SO.** Is this not gymnastics? **AL.** Most certainly. **SO.** Therefore, by gymnastics we care for the feet, but by shoemaking we care for those things which belong to the feet. **AL.** Exactly. **SO.** And by gymnastics we care for the hands, but by the art of ring-making <note>original: "annularia"</note> we care for those things which belong to the hands. **AL.** That is so. **SO.** And by gymnastics we care for the body, but by weaving and other skills we care for those things which belong to the body. **AL.** Entirely. **SO.** Therefore, do we care for the thing itself by one art, and for the things belonging to it by another? **AL.** It appears so. **SO.** Therefore, when a person cares for his own things, he does not then care for himself. **AL.** By no means. **SO.** For it seems the art that cares for us is not the same as the one that cares for our things. **AL.** It does not appear to be. **SO.** Come then, by what art can we care for ourselves? **AL.** I have nothing to say. **SO.** But this much we have agreed upon: that we do not care for ourselves by that art which makes some of our belongings better, but by that which leads ourselves to a better state <note>original: "ad meliorem frugem" - literally "to better fruit/worth"</note>. **AL.** You speak the truth. **SO.** Could we ever know which art makes a shoe better if we did not know the shoe itself? **AL.** It would be impossible. **SO.** Nor could we know what makes a ring better if we were ignorant of the ring. **AL.** True. **SO.** Shall we ever know by what art we ourselves might become better, so long as we are ignorant of ourselves? **AL.** Never. **SO.** Is it an easy thing to know oneself, and was he a fool who inscribed that at the temple of Apollo, or is it rather something difficult and not a task for every man? **AL.** To me indeed, Socrates, it has sometimes seemed easy and the duty of anyone, but at other times the most difficult of all things. **SO.** But whether it be easy, Alcibiades, or difficult, for us it stands thus: that if we understand it, we shall also understand by what method we are to be cared for. But if we are ignorant, we shall not. **AL.** It is as you say. **SO.** Come, how shall we find that "self-same" thing? For perhaps in this way we might find what we ourselves are. But while ignorant of this, we never shall. **AL.** You speak rightly. **SO.** Attend then, by God: with whom are you disputing? Is it not with me? **AL.** With you. **SO.** And am I not disputing with you? **AL.** And you with me. **SO.** It is Socrates, therefore, who disputes. **AL.** It is. **SO.** And Alcibiades who listens. **AL.** So it is. **SO.** Does Socrates not dispute by means of speech or reason? **AL.** Why not? **SO.** And do you call disputing and using speech or reason the same thing in a certain way? **AL.** The same. **SO.** But is not the one who uses a thing
<margin>
The one who uses is different from that which is used.
</margin>
different from that which he uses? **AL.** How do you mean? **SO.** Just as a shoemaker cuts with a circular and semi-circular tool and other instruments. **AL.** It is as you say. **SO.** Is not the one who cuts and uses the tools one thing, and the tools which he uses another? **AL.** Why not? **SO.** Likewise, is the lyre-player one thing, and the plectrum with which he strikes the lyre another? **AL.** Another. **SO.** This is what I was asking just now: whether the user and that which he uses always appear to be different things. **AL.** They appear so. **SO.** Do we say the shoemaker cuts with instruments only, or also with his hands? **AL.** With his hands also. **SO.** Therefore he uses these as well. **AL.** He uses them. **SO.** And does he not also use his eyes when cutting leather? **AL.** Entirely. **SO.** And we have conceded that the user is something different from the things he uses. **AL.** We have. **SO.** The shoemaker and the lyre-player, therefore, are something other than the eyes and hands they use. **AL.** It appears so. **SO.** Does not
<margin>
Man is something other than his body.
</margin>
man use his whole body? **AL.** Completely. **SO.** The user is certainly different from that which he uses. **AL.** So it is. **SO.** Man, therefore, is something other than his own body. **AL.** It seems so. **SO.** What then is man? **AL.** I do not know. **SO.** You know he is that which uses the body. **AL.** I know. **SO.** Does anything else use the body but the soul? **AL.** Nothing else. **SO.** Does it not rule? **AL.** It rules. **SO.** Furthermore, I think no one would estimate this otherwise. **AL.** Why not? **SO.** Unless man be one of three things. **AL.** Which three? **SO.** Either the soul, or the body, or the whole composed of both. **AL.** Why not? **SO.** But we have confessed that man is that which rules the body. **AL.** We have. **SO.** What then is man? Does the body rule itself? **AL.** In no way. **SO.** For we said it was subject to it. **AL.** Certainly. **SO.** Therefore, this is not what we are seeking. **AL.** It seems not. **SO.** But perhaps both together rule the body, and that is man. **AL.** Perhaps. **SO.** On the contrary, least of all; for if one of them does not rule,
<margin>
That man is nothing other than the soul.
</margin>
there is no conjecture that both rule together. **AL.** You speak rightly. **SO.** Since, therefore, neither the body nor the two together is man, it remains, I think, either that man is nothing at all, or if he is something, he is nothing other than the soul. **AL.** Entirely. **SO.** Do you still need it to be shown more clearly to you that the soul is man? **AL.** No, by Jove, for these arguments seem sufficient to me. **SO.** And if these things have not been discussed in their entirety, they are nevertheless sufficiently introduced for the present. For we shall only comprehend it fully when we have found that which we just now passed over because it required a broader speculation. **AL.** What is that? **SO.** That which was said a little while ago: that we must first consider the "self-same" <note>original: "ipsum idem" - referring to the abstract concept of the Self</note>, but now instead of the "self-same" itself, we have considered each thing as it is. And that perhaps will suffice. For we could say nothing in ourselves is more primary than the soul. **AL.** Certainly not. **SO.** Is it not fitting to think so, that you and I are conversing with each other, soul to soul, using words? **AL.** Most especially. **SO.** This, therefore, was what we were saying a little while ago: that Socrates disputes with Alcibiades using speech, not directed at your person <note>meaning your physical appearance</note> as it appears, but directing words to Alcibiades: and this is the soul. **AL.** It certainly seems so to me. **SO.** Therefore, he who commands "Know thyself" commands us to know the soul. **AL.** It seems so. **SO.** Whoever, therefore, knows the body, knows his own things but not himself. **AL.** So it is. **SO.** And therefore no physician, insofar as he is a physician, nor any trainer, insofar as he is a trainer, knows himself. **AL.** Not as it seems. **SO.** Much less do farmers and other craftsmen know themselves; for they consider neither themselves nor their own things, but things even more remote according to their arts. For they attend to those things by which the body is cared for. **AL.** You speak the truth. **SO.** Wherefore, if wisdom <note>original: "prudentia"</note> is to know oneself, none of these is wise according to his art. **AL.** Not as it seems. **SO.** For this reason, these are seen as mechanical arts, and not the disciplines of a good man. **AL.** Entirely. **SO.** Again, does not whoever takes care of the body take care of his own things, but not himself? **AL.** It appears so. **SO.** But he who cares for money cares neither for himself nor his own things, but for things far removed from his own. **AL.** It seems so. **SO.** Therefore...

<summary>Socrates leads Alcibiades to the conclusion that the "self" is the soul, distinguishing the person from the body they inhabit and the tools they use. He argues that true self-knowledge and care pertain to the soul, while arts like medicine or shoemaking only care for the body or its accessories.</summary>
