...indulges his own interests who accumulates money. **ALCIBIADES.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, whoever has ever loved the body of Alcibiades did not love Alcibiades himself, but rather those things which belonged to Alcibiades. **AL.** You speak the truth. **SO.** But he who truly loves you, loves your soul. **AL.** That seems to follow necessarily from your reasoning. **SO.** Is it not true that the lover of your body, as soon as your outward beauty begins to fade, departs and abandons you? **AL.** It appears so. **SO.** But he who loves your soul never leaves, until you reach a better harvest <note>i.e., spiritual or intellectual maturity</note>. **AL.** That is consistent. **SO.** For this reason, I do not abandon you at all; rather, I persevere in friendship while others depart as your body ages. **AL.** Oh, how well you do, my Socrates; I pray you do not abandon me in the future. **SO.** Then strive to become as beautiful as possible. **AL.** I shall try. **SO.** This is how your situation stands: there never was, nor is there now, I believe, any lover of Alcibiades, son of Clinias, except for one, and a lovable one at that—Socrates, son of Sophroniscus and Phaenarete. **AL.** You speak the truth. **SO.** Did I not say that I had anticipated you somewhat when I came to greet you? For you had determined that you would meet and question me first, asking why I alone have not left you. **AL.** That was indeed the case. **SO.** This is undoubtedly the cause: because I alone was a lover of *you*; the others were lovers of *yours* <note>meaning your physical traits or wealth</note>. These others slip away with time. But you are now blooming for the first time; and henceforth, unless you are corrupted by the Athenian people and become more base, I shall never leave you. For I fear this greatly: that by becoming a lover of the people, you might be corrupted by us. For many noble men among the Athenians have suffered this. For the people of great-hearted Erechtheus <note>A legendary king of Athens; here referring to the Athenian citizenry</note> wear a mask; but one must behold them stripped bare. Therefore, apply this caution of which I speak. **AL.** What caution? **SO.** Strip that mask off first, oh blessed one, and learn whatever must be known before you handle civil affairs; so that you may approach the republic carrying a protective "alexipharmacum"—that is, a medicine that wards off evil—lest you ever suffer any adversity. **AL.** You seem to speak well to me, Socrates; but try now to explain to us by what means we may care for ourselves. **SO.** Has this not been sufficiently defined by us in the preceding parts? For we concluded above what we appropriately are. We were afraid lest, being deceived in this, we might perhaps remain hidden from ourselves, taking care of something else and not our own selves. **AL.** It is as you say. **SO.** Then it was conceded that care must be had for the soul, and one must always look back toward it. **AL.** That is manifest. **SO.** But the care of bodies and money should be left to others. **AL.** Why not? **SO.** By what means, then, might we know this clearly? For once this is understood, we shall also understand ourselves. Or have we perhaps not yet understood the Delphic inscription itself, which gives right counsel, and which we mentioned above? 
<margin>
Explanation of the Delphic inscription: "Know thyself."
</margin>
**AL.** What do you mean by that, Socrates? **SO.** I will tell you what I suspect this inscription counsels us; it seems its example cannot be found just anywhere, but only in sight. **AL.** How do you mean that? **SO.** Consider this yourself: if the inscription had counseled our eye as if it were a man, saying "See yourself," how would we think it had advised us? Would it not be to look into that in which the eye, by gazing, would see itself? **AL.** Certainly. **SO.** Let us consider, then, what we might look into most effectively so that we might see both it and ourselves at the same time. **AL.** Into mirrors and other such things. **SO.** You speak correctly, but is there not something of this kind in the eye with which we see? **AL.** Very much so. **SO.** Have you not noticed that the face of a man looking into an eye shines back in the vision of the one opposite, as if in a mirror, which we call the "pupil"—being an image of the one looking in? **AL.** I have noticed. **SO.** An eye, therefore, only sees itself when it looks into an eye, and specifically into that part which is the best part of the eye, and by which the eye itself sees. **AL.** It appears so. **SO.** But if it looks at any other part of the man, or at anything else at all except that which this is like, it will by no means perceive itself. **AL.** True. **SO.** Therefore, the eye, when it is to see itself, must look into an eye, and into that place of the eye in which the virtue <note>or "power/excellence"</note> of the eye resides. That is the sight and the sharp point of the pupil. **AL.** So it is. **SO.** In the same way, my friend Alcibiades, if the soul wants to know itself, it must look into a soul, and especially into that place of the soul in which the virtue of the soul resides—wisdom—and into another thing which this is like. **AL.** So it seems to me, Socrates. **SO.** Can we find anything in the soul more divine than that which deals with intelligence and wisdom? **AL.** By no means. **SO.** Therefore, that part of the soul is like the divine; 
<margin>
Like the gods.
</margin>
and indeed, anyone looking into it and seeing all that is divine—namely God and wisdom—will thus thoroughly know himself. **AL.** It appears so. **SO.** And we concede that to know oneself is prudence <note>Latin: *prudentia*, often used for the Greek *sophrosyne* or self-knowledge/temperance</note>. **AL.** Entirely. **SO.** But if we neither knew ourselves nor were prudent, could we know our own things, whether they be evil or good? **AL.** How could this be possible, Socrates? **SO.** Does it perhaps seem impossible to you for someone who does not know Alcibiades to nevertheless know the things that belong to Alcibiades, insofar as they belong to Alcibiades? **AL.** Impossible, by Jove! **SO.** Nor can we know our own things as our own, unless we first know ourselves? **AL.** In no way. **SO.** If we are ignorant of our own selves, we will not understand those things which belong to our affairs? **AL.** It seems not. **SO.** Therefore, we did not agree correctly before when we asserted that some people, though ignorant of themselves, could nevertheless distinguish their own affairs. For it seems the duty of one and the same art to distinguish all these things: oneself, one's own things, and the things belonging to one's affairs. **AL.** It seems so. **SO.** But he who is ignorant of his own things is also ignorant of the things of others. **AL.** Why not? **SO.** Therefore, if he is ignorant of others' things, will he not also be ignorant of the things of the city? **AL.** It must be so. **SO.** Such a man, then, could never be a statesman. **AL.** Certainly not. **SO.** Nor even a manager of a household. **AL.** Nor that. **SO.** Nor will he understand what he is doing. **AL.** Not at all. **SO.** And being ignorant, will he not err? **AL.** Greatly. **SO.** And he who errs, does he not act badly both privately and publicly? **AL.** Why not? **SO.** And acting badly, is he not miserable? **AL.** Most certainly. 
<margin>
No one is happy unless wise. The wicked are miserable.
</margin>
**SO.** And also those with whom he does these things? **AL.** They also. **SO.** Therefore, no one can be happy unless he is wise and good. **AL.** No one. **SO.** It follows that wicked men are miserable. **AL.** Exactly. **SO.** Therefore, it is not the one who becomes rich, but the one who is prudent, who avoids misery. **AL.** It seems so. **SO.** For which reason, neither with walls, nor with ships and triremes and dockyards, oh Alcibiades, nor with a multitude or greatness without virtue...

He concludes that without this self-knowledge and virtue, one cannot successfully manage personal or state affairs and will inevitably be miserable.</summary>

the city does not need [power] for happiness. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: If you are to govern the city rightly, the citizens must be imbued with virtue. ALCIBIADES: Why not? SOCRATES: Can anyone give to others what he does not have himself? ALCIBIADES: But how could he? SOCRATES: Therefore, he who is to command not only himself and his own, but also the republic and those things pertaining to it, must first be adorned with virtue himself! ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, neither sovereign power nor the license to do whatever one pleases should be acquired for yourself or the republic, but rather justice and prudence <note>Latin: *prudentia*, often meaning practical wisdom or foresight</note>. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: By acting justly and prudently, both you and your republic will perform a work pleasing to God. ALCIBIADES: That is fitting. SOCRATES: And as we said before, you will act by looking into the divine splendor. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Indeed, by looking there, you will clearly discern yourselves and your own goods. ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Will you not then act rightly and well? ALCIBIADES: We shall. SOCRATES: Truly, I am prepared to guarantee that if you live in this way, you will be happy. ALCIBIADES: A reliable guarantor, certainly. SOCRATES: On the contrary, if you live unjustly, looking away into the darkness devoid of divinity, you will perform works similar to those [darknesses], as is consistent, being utterly ignorant of yourselves. ALCIBIADES: It seems so. SOCRATES: For to whom, my friend Alcibiades, is power present to do whatever he pleases, yet he is deprived of mind <note>i.e., lacking reason or sanity</note>: what is likely to happen to him, whether he be a private citizen or a republic? Just as if a sick man had free license to ignore the reasoning of a doctor, but exercised a sort of tyranny so that no one could deter him, what would happen to him? Is it not likely his body would be ruined? ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: What if, on a ship, someone had all license to do whatever seemed best, yet lacked mind and skill in steering; do you see what would happen to him and his companions? ALCIBIADES: I suppose he would destroy both himself and his companions. SOCRATES: Does it not then happen to every republic, and every empire and dominion where virtue is lacking, that it fares badly? ALCIBIADES: It must be so. SOCRATES: Therefore, most excellent Alcibiades, it is not tyranny that must be prepared for ourselves or the republic, but virtue, if only we wish to be happy. ALCIBIADES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Furthermore, before virtue is present, it is better for a man—not just a boy—to be ruled by a better person than to rule. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Is not that which is better also more beautiful? ALCIBIADES: It is so. SOCRATES: And what is more beautiful, more fitting? ALCIBIADES: Why not! SOCRATES: It is fitting, therefore, for the evil man to serve; for it is better. ALCIBIADES: It is fitting. SOCRATES: Therefore, depravity is servile. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: But virtue is free <note>Latin: *liberalis*, meaning both "noble" and "befitting a free man"</note>. ALCIBIADES: It is so. SOCRATES: Must not slavery be fled, my friend? ALCIBIADES: Most greatly indeed, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Do you perceive how you stand now: whether freely or the opposite? ALCIBIADES: I do indeed, and it seems to me I feel this deeply. SOCRATES: Do you know how you can flee that which now occupies you? Do not note this in a famous man <note>Socrates likely refers to Alcibiades' own high status</note>. ALCIBIADES: I do know. SOCRATES: How then? ALCIBIADES: If you wish it, O Socrates. SOCRATES: You do not speak rightly, Alcibiades. ALCIBIADES: But how should I speak? SOCRATES: If God wills it. ALCIBIADES: I say it indeed: and I add this besides: that we shall risk exchanging roles; I putting on yours, and you mine. For it cannot be otherwise than that I shall follow you hereafter, and you shall be led by me. SOCRATES: O noble youth, my love for you is then no different from a stork, if after it has cherished a winged love near you as if in a nest, it is nourished by it in turn. ALCIBIADES: Truly, so it is, and I shall begin from here to meditate on justice. SOCRATES: O how I wish you would persevere. But I fear, distrusting your nature and seeing the strength of this city, lest it overcome both me and you together.

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino of Florence on the Second Alcibiades, or on Prayer.

<image-desc>A large historiated initial 'Q' showing a floral or foliate design within a square frame.</image-desc>

Since the Second Alcibiades is truly a most holy book inscribed "On Prayer," we must summarize what a vow <note>Latin: *votum*, meaning both a vow and a prayerful request</note> is, what should be sought in a vow, and when, and how.
<margin>Definition of a vow</margin>
This definition is taken partly from Orpheus and partly from Plato. A vow is an ardent affection of a chaste mind dedicated to God, desiring what appears to be good. To this affection, Zoroaster and Orpheus applied incenses and characters <note>mystical symbols</note> whenever prayers were directed to secondary deities. Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> and Plato, when they venerated the majesty of the supreme deity, removed all external ceremonies, leaving only the pure fragrance of the soul. But concerning all these things, we speak more diligently in our commentaries. In a vow, Plato wishes for the "good" to be sought; and this is evident because he approves this petition by the testimony of the poets
<margin>What a vow is.</margin>
<margin>What should be sought in a vow.</margin>
and the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>; and he thinks it is safe for both the prudent and the imprudent; and that a vow of this kind can be made by anyone and at any time. But the petition for a certain and specific good is only to be made when one has attained prudence; otherwise, it is dangerous. Here he discusses much concerning prudence; which you, O Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici, Ficino's patron</note>, most prudent of all men, should read diligently, so that you may recognize exactly how much he values prudence. Therefore, a universal prayer, by which only the "good" is sought, can always be made; but a specific one, by which something certain that seems good is desired, should only be made when one knows what ought to be asked. One will know this when he understands what is good and what is evil. He will understand this when he has learned from the Mind. He will learn when he turns himself toward it. He will turn when he has purged the soul and expelled the darkness. He will purge it when he has given himself over to legitimate philosophy. He will give himself when he recognizes his own ignorance. Therefore, "Know Thyself" was inscribed on the temple of Apollo, lest anyone should approach the orator <note>the god/oracle</note> rashly.
<margin>Know thyself.</margin>
In what order one should pray in a specific prayer, Mercury in his orations, and Orpheus in his hymns, and Pythagoras in his Golden Verses have taught, whose rites we shall explain elsewhere. Then Plato, imitating these theologians, introduces Socrates praying thus in the book *On Beauty* <note>The Phaedrus</note>: "O friend Pan and other deities, grant, I beseech you,
<margin>The prayer of Socrates to the Gods.</margin>
that I may become beautiful within: and that whatever lies outside me may be friendly to those things within. May I consider the wise man alone to be rich. And grant me only as much gold as no one but a temperate man can bear or carry." What does Socrates seek? The Good. What good? Wisdom: that is, the knowledge of divine truth, which God alone can give.

# BOOK SIX

Only a beautiful soul—that is, one that is temperate, pure, and bright—is able to receive [wisdom]. What does it demand first of all? That one makes oneself worthy of wisdom. For it is surely the part of a reckless man to seek some gift of which he is unworthy. Who is worthy of divine wisdom? He who is prepared to bear its light. Who is prepared? He who, first through continence, then through temperance, and finally through holiness—that is, civil and <term>purgatorial virtue</term><note>Virtues that "purge" or cleanse the soul from bodily distractions to prepare it for contemplation.</note>—has so expiated his mind that he emerges beautiful, which is to say entirely pure and shining. He will then desire <term>exemplary virtue</term><note>The divine patterns or "Ideas" of virtue existing in the mind of God.</note>—namely, divine wisdom alone—as the treasury of all riches. Therefore, Socrates prays to God, the father of all, and his ministers to breathe favorably upon him, so that by their kind and propitious favor he may emerge purified. As for bodily and external things, he passes over them lightly, choosing to hold them only insofar as they do not hinder the tranquil purity of the soul. Then, having acquired this beauty, he prays that he might consider wisdom alone—that is, the knowledge of God—to be all wealth and sufficiency, and thirst for it alone. Finally, being prepared through the aforementioned steps, he asks for this glowing gold of divine wisdom. Yet he does so neither proudly nor slackly. For intemperate men obtain the smallest knowledge of truth; God embraces the highest and infinite truth in himself; but the temperate man attains a great and ample portion. He asked, therefore, for as much of this gold as a temperate man alone is able to carry. This, I believe, is the "refined gold" which John commanded to be bought in the Apocalypse <note>original: "aurū ignitū... Ioan. in Apocalypsí"; a reference to Revelation 3:18.</note>.

->ALCIBIADES II, OR ON PRAYER. SOCRATES AND ALCIBIADES.<-

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative initial Q showing the philosopher Socrates seated and instructing the young nobleman Alcibiades, with a view of the countryside through a window.</image-desc>
SOCRATES: Where are you going to pray, O Alcibiades? ALCIBIADES: To the temple, Socrates.
SOCRATES: You seem to carry a certain sadness about you, and you fix your eyes on the ground as if you are meditating on something. ALCIBIADES: But what need is there for meditation on these matters, Socrates? SOCRATES: The greatest need, it seems to me. For tell me, I beseech you by Jupiter: do you not think the gods sometimes grant what we pray for—both privately and publicly—and sometimes not at all? Do they not nod "yes" to some and the opposite to others? ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Does it not seem to you, then, that there is need for great foresight, lest a man unknowingly asks for great evils while believing he is asking for good things? And the gods might be in such a mood as to grant his requests—just as they say Oedipus prayed to God that his sons should divide their kingdom with the sword. Though he could have asked for release from his present evils, he called down others instead. Thus those things came to pass, and from them many other grave troubles followed, which there is no need to recount one by one. ALCIBIADES: But you have brought up a madman as an example. For what man of sound mind, do you think, would dare to pray for such things? SOCRATES: Is not being "insane" the opposite of being "prudent"? ALCIBIADES: Precisely.

<margin>Plato denies there is a middle ground between the healthy and the sick.</margin>
SOCRATES: Now, do some men seem to you to be unwise and others prudent? ALCIBIADES: They certainly do. SOCRATES: Come then, let us consider who these people are. We have already agreed that some are unwise, some are prudent, and some are insane. ALCIBIADES: Agreed. SOCRATES: Furthermore, some people are in good health. ALCIBIADES: They are. SOCRATES: And others are sick. ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Therefore, they are not the same. ALCIBIADES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Are there some who suffer neither of these states? ALCIBIADES: Not at all. SOCRATES: For a man must necessarily be either sick or not sick. ALCIBIADES: So it seems. SOCRATES: Do you judge the same regarding prudence and lack of prudence? ALCIBIADES:

<margin>There is no middle ground between the prudent and the imprudent.</margin>
What do you mean? SOCRATES: Do you think a man must be either prudent or imprudent? Or is there some third middle state, by which a man is neither prudent nor imprudent? ALCIBIADES: Nothing of the sort. SOCRATES: Therefore, he must necessarily experience one of the two. ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Do you remember admitting that insanity is the opposite of prudence? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: And also that there is no middle state that makes a man neither prudent nor imprudent? ALCIBIADES: I agreed to that. SOCRATES: Furthermore, how can two different things be the opposite of the same single thing? ALCIBIADES: They cannot. SOCRATES: Therefore, lack of prudence and insanity seem to be the same thing. ALCIBIADES: They do.

<margin>One thing cannot have two opposites; but if two things were previously called opposites, those two are the same.</margin>
SOCRATES: If, therefore, we say that all imprudent people are insane, we shall be speaking correctly; and among your peers, as well as those older than you, whoever is imprudent is insane. Do you not think there are very few prudent people in this city, and many imprudent ones—whom you call insane? ALCIBIADES: I do. SOCRATES: Do you think we would be safe living among these insane people, and that we would not be bitten or beaten by them, or suffer what madmen usually do, if they had not been punished long ago? But look, my friend, lest the matter be otherwise. ALCIBIADES: How so, Socrates? For it appears it is not as I had thought. SOCRATES: Certainly not as it seems to me; but we must think of it this way. ALCIBIADES: How do you say? SOCRATES: I will tell you. We assume some people are sick, do we not? ALCIBIADES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Do you think it necessary that every sick person must suffer specifically from gout, or fever, or inflammation of the eyes? Or can they be afflicted by other diseases, since there are many species of disease besides these? ALCIBIADES: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Does every eye inflammation seem to be a disease to you? ALCIBIADES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And is every disease also an eye inflammation? ALCIBIADES: Not to me; yet I do not know what to say. SOCRATES: If you pay attention to what I say, and we investigate together, we shall likely find what we seek. ALCIBIADES: I am paying as much attention as I can. SOCRATES: Is it not agreed between us that every eye inflammation is a disease, but not every disease is an eye inflammation? ALCIBIADES: Agreed. SOCRATES: And we seem to have agreed correctly. For all those with fever are sick, but not everyone who is sick has a fever, or is afflicted by gout or eye inflammation. But everything of this sort is commonly called "disease." Now, doctors say the treatment for these differs; they are not all similar, nor are they treated similarly; rather, they are all diseases according to their own specific nature. Just as we assume there are certain "craftsmen," do we not? ALCIBIADES: Precisely. SOCRATES: And cobblers, and smiths, and sculptors, and many others whom there is no need to list individually; they have distinct occupations, and all are indeed craftsmen, yet they are not all smiths, nor all tanners, nor all sculptors; but all are craftsmen generally. ALCIBIADES: That is so. SOCRATES: By the same reasoning, they divide "imprudence" greatly among themselves: and those who have the greater...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Alcibiades regarding the nature of prayer and the danger of human ignorance. Socrates is currently categorizing different types of "imprudence" or lack of wisdom.</meta>

# ALCIBIADES II, OR ON PRAYER

<margin>There are many kinds of imprudence.</margin>
...they are assigned a share of imprudence: those who are raving and mad are called "insane"; those who are somewhat less so are called "dull" or "thunderstruck." Those who wish to signify the same things with more honorable terms call them partly "high-spirited," partly "inept"; some call them "not bad," "innocent," "inexperienced," or "stupid." You will find many other names as well, by all of which imprudence is signified. However, they differ—as it appeared they differed in the previous points—just as art differs from art, and disease from disease. How does it seem to you? ALCIBIADES: I agree. SOCRATES: But to return to where we digressed: the purpose at the beginning of the discussion was to judge who were prudent and who were imprudent. We agreed that there are such people, did we not? ALCIBIADES: We agreed. SOCRATES: Do you consider those who know what should be done and said to be prudent? ALCIBIADES: Indeed. SOCRATES: And those who see neither are imprudent? ALCIBIADES: Those very ones. SOCRATES: Do not those who are ignorant of both these things remain hidden from themselves, both in acting and in speaking what they ought not? ALCIBIADES: It appears so. SOCRATES: From among these men, O Alcibiades, I said Oedipus was one. <note>Oedipus is the classic example of one who acts in ignorance of his own situation, killing his father and marrying his mother.</note> You will also find in our times many who are not driven by sudden impulse, as he was, nor thinking they desire evils for themselves, but rather goods. For he, just as he did not desire [evil], so he did not think [he was doing it]. But there are some who suffer the opposite of these. I think that if the god to whom you are going to pray should present himself to your eyes before you consecrated anything, and should ask you if it would be enough for you to obtain the tyranny over the Athenians—and if you thought this a small thing, he would add that of all the Greeks; and if he saw that you were not satisfied even with these unless he added all of Europe; and if he felt that even that would not suffice you unless on that same day everyone knew that Alcibiades, son of Clinias, was tyrant—and if he therefore granted you all these things, I think, I say, that you would return from him with great joy, as if you had successfully obtained the greatest goods. ALCIBIADES: I think so, Socrates, and so would anyone else who happened to obtain the same.

<margin>The prudent are those skilled in what to do and say.</margin>
<margin>The quality of the request is discussed.</margin>
SOCRATES: However, you would not choose to have the tyranny of all the Greeks and even the barbarians if it meant the loss of your soul. ALCIBIADES: Not as I think, since I would be able to make no use of it. SOCRATES: What if you could use it, but use it badly and with harm? Not even then? ALCIBIADES: Certainly not.

<margin>It is not safe to blindly accept what is offered, or to blindly desire the outcomes of Tyrants.</margin>
SOCRATES: You see, therefore, that it is not safe either to blindly accept what is offered or to pray for it, if one is to undergo misfortunes because of it, or lose one's life immediately. We could mention many who, when they had sought tyranny and contended with burning zeal for its attainment—as if they were to obtain some good—perished, circumvented by snares because of that very tyranny. I think you have also heard of some things done yesterday and very recently: how someone, thirsting for such delights no less than he, killed Archelaus, the tyrant of the Macedonians and a lover of such delights, <note>Archelaus was assassinated in 399 BCE by his lover/page, Craterus, who sought the throne.</note> so that he might soon be a tyrant and happy. But when he had held the tyranny for three or four days, he in turn perished, overwhelmed by others in an ambush. But to mention things we have not perceived by hearsay, but have seen ourselves being present: you see, moreover, which of our citizens, having sought and obtained the command of the army, are partly wandering as exiles even in these times, and partly have been condemned to death. And if some, perhaps, seemed to have acted vigorously in extreme dangers and fears, not only in the army itself but even after they returned to the city, they were affected by no less calumny from plotting citizens than from soldiers; so that most of them finally wished they had lived as private citizens rather than in public office. Therefore, if dangers and labors of this kind brought us any utility, certainly this zeal would have some reason. But now the matter stands far otherwise. You will find, moreover, in the same way, some men who pray for sons with vows; but when they have obtained sons, they fall into the greatest calamities and sorrows. For many, since their children persist in being wicked throughout their whole age, finish their entire life in mourning. Those who have obtained honest sons but lose them by some adverse chance are no less miserable than the former; so that they would utterly choose never to have fathered sons. And although these and many other such things are manifest, one would rarely find anyone who would either abstain from what is given or, if he were to obtain it by praying, would omit the vow. Very many would depart neither from an acquired tyranny, nor from an obtained prefecture, nor from countless other things which, when they possess them, hurt rather than help; instead, they would rather pray that those things be granted to them if they are ever absent. Sometimes, after a short time, they condemn their past vows, recurring to the opposites. Wherefore I truly fear lest men blindly accuse the gods, as if evils were brought by them; but they themselves, whether by a certain perversity or by folly, prepare for themselves sorrows sharper than death.

<margin>The poet's worthy request.</margin>
Therefore, that poet seems prudent to me who, having experienced unwise friends and seeing them both doing and praying for things that were least conducive to them—though they seemed useful to them—spoke thus in prayer: "King Jupiter, grant us the best things whether we pray for them or not; but command that evil things be absent even from those who ask for them." <note>This is a famous anonymous prayer often attributed to a poet, cited by Plato to show that God knows better than humans what is good for them.</note> Therefore, the poet seems to me to speak rightly and cautiously; but you, if you have anything in your mind to bring against these things, do not be silent. ALCIBIADES: It is difficult, O Socrates, to contradict things that have been well said.

<margin>Ignorance</margin>
But I am thinking how great an evil ignorance is for men, since because of it, it is hidden from us when we do something badly; and what is worst, because of it we sometimes pray for the worst things for ourselves, which indeed no one would think. But anyone would think this: that he is able to ask for the best, not the worst, for himself. For this would truly be like a certain curse, not a vow.

<margin>On the goodness and malice of ignorance.</margin>
SOCRATES: But perhaps, O best of men, someone wiser than you and me might say that we do not speak quite correctly when we thus blindly blame ignorance, unless we add this: what kind of ignorance it is, and of what things. For to some people in a certain state, ignorance is perhaps a good, just as to others it is an evil. ALCIBIADES: What are you saying! Is there anything which it is sometimes better for someone, in whatever state he may be, to be ignorant of than to know? SOCRATES: It certainly seems so to me, though not to you. ALCIBIADES: No, by Jupiter. SOCRATES: Truly, I will not judge that you would wish to have committed against your mother what they say Orestes and Alcmaeon and whoever were such committed. <note>Orestes and Alcmaeon are mythological figures who killed their mothers to avenge their fathers.</note> ALCIBIADES: Speak words of good omen, by Jupiter, O Socrates! SOCRATES: It is not fitting, O Alcibiades, for him who says he would not wish you to have done those things to be told to speak words of good omen, but rather if someone were to say the opposite. Since a deed so horrible seems to you that it ought not even be easily pronounced, do you think Orestes, if he had been prudent and had known what was good for him, would have [dared] so great a crime...

He concludes by suggesting that in some cases, ignorance of how to commit a crime might actually be a "good" compared to the knowledge of how to do evil.</summary>

# BOOK SIX

<warning>Significant bleed-through/ghosting from the reverse page is visible at the top and in various margins.</warning>

<margin>What kind of ignorance is evil.</margin>
...would he have dared to do it? ALCIBIADES. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Nor any other man, I think. ALCIBIADES. None. SOCRATES. It seems, therefore, that ignorance of the best—and to be ignorant of what is best—is an evil. ALCIBIADES. It certainly seems so to me. SOCRATES. And does it not seem so to them, and to everyone else? ALCIBIADES. I admit it. SOCRATES. Let us consider this further: what would happen if you also possessed a certain ignorance, by which you did not recognize Pericles <note>Pericles was a prominent Greek statesman and Alcibiades' guardian</note>, while believing it was better to kill Pericles, your guardian and friend? Suppose you took a sword and hurried to his doors, asking if he were within, wishing to kill only him and no one else; and the servants answered that he was inside. Now, I do not say that you actually desire such a thing; but does it not seem to you—since nothing prevents a man who is ignorant of what is best from having a certain opinion—that you might judge what is worst to be sometimes the best? Does it not seem so to you? ALCIBIADES. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Therefore, if you entered the house and, seeing him, thought he was someone else, would you kill him? ALCIBIADES. No, by Jove! <note>original: "per Iovem" - a common oath in Latin translations of Greek texts</note> So it seems to me. SOCRATES. For you would not kill just anyone chance offered, but the one you had determined upon, would you not? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. And if you attacked frequently, but always failed to recognize Pericles, would you ever fall upon him? ALCIBIADES. Never. SOCRATES. And do you think Orestes <note>The mythological figure who killed his mother Clytemnestra</note> would ever have laid hands on his mother if he had not recognized her? ALCIBIADES. I do not think so. SOCRATES. For he did not intend to kill just any woman he met, but specifically his mother. ALCIBIADES. These things are true. SOCRATES. Therefore, for men affected in this way and involved in such opinions, it is better to be ignorant of such things. ALCIBIADES. It seems so. SOCRATES. Do you see now how a certain ignorance is a kind of good for men in a certain state, and not an evil as it seemed to you before? ALCIBIADES. It is apparent.

<margin>Certain paradoxes. The possession of sciences is harmful without the knowledge of the best.</margin>
SOCRATES. Furthermore, if you wish to discuss what will next be brought forward—which is wonderful to say—perhaps it will seem probable to you. ALCIBIADES. What is that, O Socrates? SOCRATES. It truly seems that the possession of all other sciences <note>term: "sciences" (scientiarum) here refers to technical skills or branches of knowledge</note>—unless one has acquired the knowledge of the best—rarely profits, and usually harms the one who is endowed with such sciences. Consider it this way: Does it not seem necessary to you that when we are about to do or say something, we must first either think we know, or truly know, what we ought to do and speak so readily? ALCIBIADES. It clearly seems so to me. SOCRATES. Do not the orators, as soon as they know how to give counsel, or at least think they know, give us counsel everywhere? Some concerning war and peace, others about building walls or preparing and fortifying harbors; and to speak briefly, whatever the city itself does against another city or within itself, is it not accomplished by the counsel of orators? ALCIBIADES. You tell the truth. SOCRATES. See also what follows, if possible. Do you call some men prudent and others imprudent? ALCIBIADES. I do. SOCRATES. And many indeed imprudent, but few prudent? ALCIBIADES. Certainly. SOCRATES. Do you not name them both by looking toward something? ALCIBIADES. Indeed. SOCRATES. Would you call a man prudent who knows how to give such counsel, unless he knows how to teach whether it is better, and *what* is better? ALCIBIADES. Not at all. SOCRATES. Nor, I think, whoever knows how to fight, yet is ignorant of when and for how long it is better. ALCIBIADES. That is so. SOCRATES. Nor if someone knows how to kill another, and despoil them of money, and make them an exile from their country, unless he also knows when and for whom it is better. ALCIBIADES. By no means.

<margin>Who ought to be called prudent.</margin>
SOCRATES. Whoever, therefore, knows any of these things, provided that the knowledge of the best is also present—which is the same as the "useful" science—this man perhaps you will call prudent. ALCIBIADES. This very man. SOCRATES. And we shall say that the prudent man is a sufficient counselor for himself and his country; but the imprudent man is the opposite. How does it seem to you? ALCIBIADES. The same. SOCRATES. But what if someone knows how to ride, or shoot arrows, or practice wrestling, or boxing, or any other contest, or any other of those things we know in part: by what name do you call him who understands what is better in the art? Is he not a horseman according to the equestrian art, a boxer according to the boxing art, a flute-player according to the flute-playing art, and in others the same way? Or otherwise? ALCIBIADES. Thus, certainly. SOCRATES. Does it seem to you that he who understands any of these things should be called a prudent man, or is he still far from it? ALCIBIADES. Far further. SOCRATES. What kind of city, then, will you think that is, which consists of skilled archers, and flute-players, and athletes, and other craftsmen, and where those skilled in the military art and those ready for killing are admitted, as well as those puffed up by the administration of civil affairs—but the knowledge of the best is lacking, which knows when and toward whom it is better to use each of those skills? ALCIBIADES. An ignoble one, O Socrates. SOCRATES. You would say this most of all, I think, if you saw each of them being ambitious and taking many parts of the republic for himself so that he might be most powerful—most powerful, I say, in that which is best according to the art itself, but wandering far from what is best for himself and the republic, because he has trusted in opinion without mind <note>term: "opinion without mind" (opinioni sine mente) refers to belief without rational understanding or moral purpose</note>. Since these things are so, would we not rightly call this city full of the greatest tumult and iniquity? ALCIBIADES. Rightly, by Jove! SOCRATES. Did it not seem necessary to us first to think we know, or truly to know, that which we are about to do or say? ALCIBIADES. It did. SOCRATES. If someone does what he knows or thinks he knows, but adds the knowledge of the best, does it not follow that he acts usefully for himself and for the republic? ALCIBIADES. Why not? SOCRATES. But on the contrary, [without it] he acts neither for the city nor for himself. ALCIBIADES. It is so. SOCRATES. And how does it seem to you now: thus, or otherwise? ALCIBIADES. Not otherwise. SOCRATES. Did you say you call many imprudent, and fewer prudent? ALCIBIADES. I did. SOCRATES. Did we not say again that the many wander from that which is best, since they mostly consent to opinion without mind? ALCIBIADES. We clearly said so. SOCRATES. It is therefore profitable for many neither to know anything, nor to think they know; for they will be more ready to perform those things which they either know or think they know. But in acting, they will harm themselves more often than they help. ALCIBIADES. You speak the most true things. SOCRATES. When, therefore, I said that all other sciences—if the knowledge of the best be absent—harm rather than profit the possessor, did I seem to you then to speak rightly? ALCIBIADES. If not then, at least now, O Socrates. SOCRATES. It is necessary, therefore, for a city and a soul that is to live rightly to embrace this science without doubt, just as the sick man seeks the physician, and he who wishes to sail prosperously seeks the pilot. For the more the soul, without this science, occupies itself with riches or bodily strength or any such thing, the greater the sins that must be committed from them. But he who is adorned with many and various arts and sciences, yet becomes a stranger to this science, being led by each of the others—will he not deservedly be tossed about by a great storm? For indeed, wandering on the sea without a pilot, he is destined to perish in a short time.

# ALCIBIADES II, OR ON PRAYER
<note>Folio number 19 is handwritten in the top right corner.</note>

<margin>
Poets speak through riddles.
Poetry is full of riddles.
Homer is most divine.
</margin>
...certainly that verse of the poet seems to apply to him, in which he says by way of reproach: *He knew many things, but he knew them all badly.* <note>original: "Multa quidem nouerat: sed male nouerat omnia." This refers to the pseudo-Homeric comic poem *Margites*.</note> **ALCIBIADES.** But truly, that saying of the poet does not seem to me to fit our purpose at all. **SOCRATES.** On the contrary, it fits perfectly; for both he and almost all other poets speak through riddles. For the whole nature of poetry itself is full of riddles, and not just anyone can discern them. Added to this is its nature: that if it resides in an envious man who is unwilling to reveal his thoughts to others, it is a wonder how difficult it is to know what the poet intended. For you should not think that Homer, the most divine and wisest poet, was ignorant of the fact that it is impossible to know something "badly"; for he is the one who says that Margites knew many things, but knew them all "badly." But he hides the meaning in a riddle, as I believe, putting "badly" in place of "evil," and "to know" for "to have knowledge of." Hence a certain composition is formed outside the measure of the verse, but what he means is this: *He indeed knew many things, but it was an evil for him to know all these things.* It is clear, therefore, that if it was an evil for him to know many things, he himself was also evil—if any faith is to be placed in the arguments stated above. **ALCIBIADES.** It certainly seems so to me, O Socrates. For what words should I ever believe, if I do not believe these? **SOCRATES.** And indeed it seems right to you, and to me again in the same way. But come, by Jove: do you see how great and of what sort the ambiguity is in this? You seem to be entangled in it yourself. For tossed up and down, you never truly stand firm; but what you once asserted, you now condemn. If by chance the god whom you are approaching to pray to, presenting himself before your eyes before you make your vow, should ask you: whether it would be enough for you to have any of those things mentioned at the beginning, or if he should grant you the license to ask for whatever you please—what then would you think it opportune to do: to accept what the god offered, or to ask for yourself? **ALCIBIADES.** By the gods, O Socrates, I do not know what I should answer; but it seems to me a thing of madness to pray for something rashly, and one must consider diligently lest he be unaware of himself, seeking evils when he thinks he is praying for good things—and a little later, as you were saying, he might shift to contrary vows. **SOCRATES.** Is not the poet more prudent than we, whom we mentioned at the beginning of the discussion, who prayed that evils be kept away even from those who ask for them? **ALCIBIADES.** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> also, O Alcibiades—whether imitating this poet or noticing it for themselves—keep the same vow both privately and publicly: praying to the gods to grant them "beautiful things along with good things," and no one would hear them pray for more than that. Yet up to these times, they are no less happy than other men. If, however, anything has ever succeeded less prosperously for them, it is not their prayer that is the cause; since it is in the power of the gods, I believe, to grant what we pray for or the opposite. I wish, moreover, to relate another thing to you, which I once heard from certain elders. For they said it happened that whenever the Athenians waged war with the Lacedaemonians, they were unfortunate both by land and by sea, and never returned as victors. The Athenians, troubled by this matter and having no devices by which to avoid such great calamity, decreed to consult Hammon <note>The Oracle of Ammon in Libya</note> as to why the gods granted victory to the Lacedaemonians rather than to the Athenians, since they [the Athenians] offered both more and more fitting sacrifices than the rest of the Greeks, and adorned the temples with statues and gifts as no one else did, and celebrated the most expensive and beautiful processions every year, and in all expenditure pertaining to the divine, they were more magnificent than all the Greeks; while the Lacedaemonians had no care for these things, being so stingy regarding divine worship that they sacrificed mutilated animals everywhere, and were far more sparing in all other ceremonies than the Athenians, even though they do not surpass us in the amount of their money. After the messenger had said these things, asking how they might be delivered from the present calamity, the prophet did not answer much. For the god did not permit it. But calling the messenger of the Athenians, he spoke in this manner:

<margin>
The prophet answered on behalf of the god Hammon.
</margin>
"Thus says Hammon: the blessing of the Lacedaemonians is more pleasing to him than all the sacred rites of the rest of the Greeks." And he answered them no more than this. Now, it seems to me that the god meant no other "blessing" than their prayer; for it differs greatly from the others. For the rest of the Greeks, some sacrificing oxen with gilded horns, others adorning temples with excellent gifts, ask for whatever occurs to them, whether good or evil. But the gods, when they hear them praying, do not accept their most wealthy processions and sacrifices. Therefore, it seems to me that it must be diligently considered what should be said and what should not be said. You will find other similar things in Homer. For he says that the Trojans, when they were building a suburban structure, dedicated precious sacrifices of oxen to the immortal gods. And a sweet scent was carried from the shore by the winds all the way to heaven; but the blessed gods did not eat of it at all, because Ilion <note>Troy</note> and Priam and Priam's people were hateful to them. Therefore, it did nothing for the Trojans, since they had the gods against them, to rashly offer sacred rites and gifts to them. For the nature of God is not such that he is led by gifts like a wicked moneylender.

<margin>
The nature of God toward gifts.
Because with gods and men, justice and prudence are honored.
Who are the prudent and the just.
"High-mindedness" is the most honorable name for foolishness.
</margin>
But we are too delirious if we ever think ourselves more acceptable to God than the Lacedaemonians on account of our gifts. For it would be a grave thing if God looked to our gifts and sacrifices rather than to the soul, whether it be just and holy. To which soul indeed I believe God pays much more attention than to great expenses, processions, and sacrifices—which nothing prevents even a man who has sinned much against God and men, whether a private citizen or a state, from performing every year. But God, being incorruptible by gifts, scorns all these things, as he himself and his prophet foretold. From which it is clear that both with God and with men of sound mind, justice and prudence are especially honored. Now, those are prudent and just who know what is fitting to do and say toward God and men. I desire, however, to hear from you what you yourself think of these things. **ALCIBIADES.** To me indeed, O Socrates, it seems no different than it does to you and to the god; for it would not be right for me to disagree with God. **SOCRATES.** Do you remember saying that you were in great doubt and danger, lest you be unaware of yourself when you prayed for evils instead of goods? **ALCIBIADES.** I remember. **SOCRATES.** Do you see then that it is not safe enough for you to proceed to prayer, lest perhaps God, hearing you praying, should refuse those sacrifices of yours, and you should bring back something else by chance? Therefore, it seems to me worthwhile to keep quiet. For because of their "high-mindedness"—which is the most honorable name of all for those by which foolishness is signified—I do not think you wish to use the prayer of the Lacedaemonians. Therefore, it is necessary to wait until one learns how...

<summary>Socrates explains to Alcibiades that God values a just and prudent soul over expensive sacrifices, citing the Lacedaemonians' simple but effective prayers as superior to the Athenians' lavish rituals. He warns Alcibiades that praying without wisdom is dangerous, as one might accidentally ask for their own ruin.</summary>

SOCRATES. It is he who cares for you. But it seems to me—just as Homer says Minerva <note>Athena</note> removed the mist from the eyes of Diomedes so that he might distinguish god from man—that it is first necessary to remove from your soul the darkness which now surrounds it; then to bring near those things through which you may discern what is good or what is evil; for now you seem unable to do so. So do I take this crowning by you as an omen. For I seem to myself to be tossed in no less a storm than Creon; for I desire to excel all your friends.

## Argument by Marsilius Ficinus on the Minos of Plato, or on Law.

<margin>What law is.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'M' featuring floral and scroll motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>Minos inquires concerning law: let us briefly understand what law is in general, how many species it has, and from whence it originates. If anyone diligently observes the words of Plato in this book on law, and in the books of *The Laws*, as well as *The Republic*, he will define law with this universal definition: Law is the true method of governing, which directs the governed through convenient means toward the best end, establishing punishment for the transgressor and reward for the obedient. From this it follows that when institutions are not based on truth, nor proceed by a straight path toward the best, they are by no means laws, but rather decrees, edicts, or institutes. For from "law" comes "legitimate," from "legitimate" comes "just," and from "just" is often named a "good, right, and true work"; therefore, it is necessary that a true law be good. It also follows that law is eternal and utterly immutable, and the same among all nations regarding the same things, provided it is true. For that which changes with times, places, and opinions is <margin>Four species of law.</margin> not called law, but an institution. Furthermore, as gathered from the *Timaeus*, *Phaedrus*, and *Gorgias*, there are four species of law. First, the divine, which Plato calls Providence. Second, the celestial, which he calls Fate. Third, the moving, which he calls Nature. Fourth, the human, which he calls natural Prudence. The first is in the divine mind, which Orpheus and Plato wish to be the law of Saturn. The second is in the higher part of the World Soul, which they call the law of Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. The third is in the moving and lower power of that soul, which they call the law of the first Venus. The last is in the mind of man, which they call the law of the second Venus. The first flows from the Supreme Good, which is above the mind. The second from the mind and the Supreme Good. The third from the Supreme Good, the mind, and the universal soul. The fourth likewise from the Supreme Good, the mind, and the soul. All, however, reflect back again toward the Good itself. The first is in Ideas, around the Supreme Good, above reasons. The second is in reasons, around Ideas, above seeds. The third is in seeds, around reasons, above forms. The fourth is in notions, around reasons, above acts and arts, which he calls the "Royal Law," the imitator of the supreme King. From whence law proceeds is elicited from what has been said. All flow from the very principle of things, but in various ways, as has been stated. For this reason, all illustrious founders of laws referred the invention of laws to God, but through different names and intermediaries. Zoroaster, giving laws to the Bactrians and Persians, referred them to Oromasis <note>Ahura Mazda</note>. Trismegistus to the Egyptians, to Mercury <note>Thoth</note>. Moses to the Jews, most rightly to the Father of all nature, God. Minos to the Cretans, to Jove. Charondas to the Carthaginians, to Saturn. Lycurgus to the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, to Apollo. Draco and Solon to the Athenians, to Minerva. Pompilius to the Romans, to Egeria. Mahomet to the Arabs, to Gabriel. Zamolxis to the Scythians, to Vesta. Our Plato, to the Magnesians and Sicilians, to Jove and Apollo. To the Arcadians, however, and the Thebans and Cyrenaics requesting laws, he refused.

## MINOS, OR ON LAW. SOCRATES. MINOS. SOCRATES.

<margin>When we are asked simply, it is not right to doubt that which is a part of the whole.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' featuring floral and scroll motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>WHAT exactly is Law among us? MINOS. About which law do you ask? SOCRATES. Is there any difference by which one law differs from another law insofar as it is law? Pay close attention to what I am asking! For I ask just as if I had asked: "What is gold?" and if you, in the same way, were to ask about which gold I am inquiring, I would judge that you were not questioning correctly. For gold does not differ from gold insofar as it is gold, nor does a stone differ from a stone insofar as it is a stone; in the same way, law does not differ from law, but all are the same. For each of them is law in a similar way, not one more and another less. Therefore, I ask generally about this whole: "What is law?" If you have the answer ready now, explain. MINOS. And what else, O Socrates, would law be but the things established by law? SOCRATES. <margin>He gathers the definition through a comparison made to other things.</margin> Does speech seem to you to be the things said in speech? Or sight the things seen? Or hearing the things heard? Or is speech one thing and the things pronounced another; sight one thing and the things seen another; and hearing likewise different from the things heard; and thus law one thing, and the things commanded by law another? Does it seem so to you, or otherwise? MINOS. So it seems, certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, law is not the things perceived by law. MINOS. It does not seem so. SOCRATES. What then law might be, let us consider in this way. If someone should inquire about those things we just mentioned, saying: "Since you assert that things seen are perceived by sight, what is sight?"

# MINOS, OR ON LAW. FOLIO 20.
### c.iiii.

to the things through which they are perceived, we would certainly answer that it is a sense of this kind which declares colors through the eyes; and to one asking about hearing, the sense which draws in the voice through the ears. In the same way, if he asks—since a legal matter is established by law—what is the law by which these legal matters come to be? Is it some sense or a declaration? Just as things which people learn are grasped by the declaration of knowledge, and are found by the showing of discovery, just as healthy and harmful things are shown by medicine; but the things which the gods think, as the prophets say, are known by the faculty of divination.

<margin>What prophecy is.</margin>
For is not prophecy the discovery of such things? MI. Entirely. SO. Which of these do we chiefly presume law to be: these institutions and decrees? MI. So it seems to me. For what else would anyone say law is? From which it appears that the whole of what you were asking is this: the law of the city is an institution.

<margin>Another false definition of law: and its refutation.</margin>
SO. Do you call the opinion of the city "law"? MI. I do indeed. SO. And perhaps you speak rightly, but perhaps we will understand it better in this way. Do you call some people wise? MI. I do. SO. Are not the wise made wise by wisdom? MI. Yes. SO. And the just made just by justice? MI. Entirely. SO. Therefore, are the law-abiding made law-abiding by law? MI. Certainly. SO. And the lawless made lawless by lawlessness? MI. Surely. SO. But are the law-abiding just? MI. Yes. SO. And the lawless unjust? MI. Yes. SO. Is not law and justice something most beautiful? MI. It is so. SO. And is not injustice and lawlessness most foul? MI. Most foul. SO. And does the former preserve cities and all other things, while the latter perverts and destroys them? MI. Yes. SO. Therefore, one ought to think of law as something beautiful, and seek it as something good. MI. Why not? SO. And did we not say that the institution of the city is law? MI. We did. SO. Are not some decrees good, and some even bad? MI. They certainly are. SO. Yet law was not bad. MI. Certainly not. SO. Therefore, it must not be asserted so simply that the law of the city is an institution. MI. It does not seem so to me at all. SO. For it is not fitting for an unjust constitution to be law. MI. No.

<margin>Law is a certain opinion.</margin>
SO. Nevertheless, law also seems to me to be a certain opinion; and since it is by no means a wicked opinion, is it not clear—if indeed it is an opinion—that it is a good opinion? MI. It is agreed. SO. And a good opinion, is it not a true opinion? MI. It is. SO. And is not a true opinion the discovery of reality <note>original: "veritatis inventio" - literally "the discovery of truth."</note>? MI. Certainly. SO. Law, therefore, is the discovery of reality. Or do we not always use the same laws regarding the same things, once the truth of things has been found? SO. Nevertheless, law wishes to be the discovery of reality. But if men use laws that are not the same, it seems they are not always able to find the reality which the law seeks. But come, let us see if it may appear more clearly to us from this: whether we live by the same laws always or different ones at different times, and whether all men use the same or some use one and others another. MI. Indeed, that is not difficult to know, O Socrates: that they do not always live by the same laws, nor do some always live like others. For our laws do not permit men to be sacrificed;

<margin>Among the Carthaginians it is considered just to sacrifice sons.</margin>
but among the Carthaginians it is held just and holy, so much so that some of them sacrifice their sons to Saturn, as you yourself have perhaps heard. And it is not only barbarian men who follow laws different from ours, but even those who inhabit Lycia; and the successors of Athamas, what kind of sacrifices they offer, even though they are Greeks. You have also heard what kind of laws we once observed regarding funerals, slaughtering victims before the corpse was carried out, and calling those who would carry the urns.

<margin>Ceremonies regarding the deceased.</margin>
And those who were older than these even buried the dead at home; of which things we observe nothing at all in these times. We could, moreover, cite innumerable examples of this. For a wide province lies open to show that neither do we always live by the same laws as ourselves, nor do men live by the same laws as one another. SO. It is no wonder, O best of men, if you speak correctly, but it escaped my notice. But as long as you narrate what seems right to you in a long speech, and I do the same in turn, we shall never, I think, agree. But if a common discussion is proposed, perhaps we shall reach an accord. Therefore, if you wish, question me yourself, and consider it together with me; or if you prefer to answer, then answer. MI. I am willing indeed, O Socrates, to answer whatever you please. SO. Come then: do you think just things are unjust, and unjust things just? Or rather that just things are just, and unjust things are only unjust? MI. Indeed, that whatever things are just are just, and whatever are unjust are unjust. SO. And is it not thought so everywhere among nations, just as it is here? MI. Yes. SO. And among the Persians, is it not so? MI. Among the Persians too. SO. And is it not always so? MI. Always. SO. Are things that weigh more judged heavier here, and those that weigh less lighter, or the opposite? MI. No, rather those drawing more are heavier, and those drawing less are lighter. SO. And is it the same in Lycia and Carthage? MI. The same. SO. Beautiful things, it seems, are everywhere thought beautiful, and ugly things the opposite, ugly; not beautiful things ugly, or ugly things beautiful. MI. It is so. SO. Is it not generally true through all things: that things which are true are judged to be, and those which are not true are not, both among us and among all men? MI. It seems so. SO. Therefore, whoever wanders from the truth also wanders from the law. MI. According to your reasoning, O Socrates, the same legal things seem to be always the same both among us and among others. But when I notice us changing laws up and down without end every day, I cannot give you my credit. SO. Perhaps you do not perceive that these things, though transposed, remain the same. But look at it with me in this way. Have you ever come across a book about the cure of diseases? MI. I have. SO. Do you know to what art that book belongs? MI. I know it belongs to medicine. SO. Do you call those who know these things doctors? MI. I do. SO. Do those who know establish the same things about the same matters, or do different people establish different things? MI. The same. SO. Do the Greeks alone agree with Greeks, or do even the barbarians agree both with themselves and with the Greeks about the things they know? MI. It is absolutely necessary for Greeks and Barbarians to judge the same things about what they know. SO. You have answered well; but is it not also always so? MI. Always. SO. Do not doctors write down what they judge to be true regarding health? MI. Indeed. SO. Therefore, the writings of doctors are the laws of doctors? MI. They are. SO. And the geometric writings are the laws of geometers? MI. Certainly. SO. Whose are the writings and constitutions regarding the cultivation of gardens? MI. The gardeners'. SO.

<margin>All perceptions of the arts are laws.</margin>
Therefore these are the laws of gardening? MI. Yes. SO. Of those who know how to be in charge of gardens? MI. Why not?

<summary>Socrates leads Minos to the conclusion that true law is not merely a city's decree, but the "discovery of reality," comparing it to the universal principles found in medicine and geometry.</summary>

# BOOK SIX

**SOCRATES.** But gardeners know this. **MINOS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And by whom are the writings and instructions on the seasoning of meats composed? **MINOS.** By cooks. **SOCRATES.** These laws, then, belong to cooks. **MINOS.** They do. **SOCRATES.** To those, evidently, who are skillfully knowledgeable in preparing meats. **MINOS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Do they know these things, as they say, the cooks? **MINOS.** They know them. **SOCRATES.** Come then, tell me: by whom are the writings and instructions on the government of a city composed? Is it not by those who are skilled in administering the republic? **MINOS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** Do any others besides civil and royal men know this? **MINOS.** Only they. **SOCRATES.** These, then, are civil writings, which royal men and good men call decrees. **MINOS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Those who know do not establish one thing and then another regarding the same matters. **MINOS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, legitimate things are not one thing at one time and another at another. **MINOS.** Not at all.

<margin>Those who waver and change do not know.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** If we see some people differing and changing, shall we say they know, or are ignorant? **MINOS.** That they are ignorant. **SOCRATES.** And is not that which is right in each case to be called "legitimate" in each case? Just as what is done according to the reason of a doctor, or a cook, or a gardener, is the "law" <note>Latin: *legitimum*</note> in those fields? **MINOS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** On the contrary, however, that which is not at all right should no longer be called legitimate. **MINOS.** No longer. **SOCRATES.** It becomes, therefore, illegitimate. **MINOS.** It must be so.

<margin>What the royal law is.</margin>
<margin>Law is the discovery of truth.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** For which reason, in constitutions concerning the just and the unjust, and concerning the order of the city and the method of governing, whatever is right is the "royal law." But what is not right is by no means a royal law, because it seems that knowledge is lacking; for indeed it is illegitimate. **MINOS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** We have rightly confessed, then, that law is the discovery of truth. **MINOS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, let us consider this as well: who is skilled in scattering seeds into the earth? **MINOS.** The farmer. **SOCRATES.** He, surely, distributes the appropriate seeds to each soil. **MINOS.** Truly. **SOCRATES.** The farmer, therefore, is a good legislator in these matters; and his laws and distributions for these things are right. **MINOS.** True. **SOCRATES.** Who is a good law-giver in the striking of notes for harmony, and imparts them according to worth, and whose laws are right? **MINOS.** The flute-player and the lyre-player do these things. **SOCRATES.** He who is most "lawful" in these things is therefore the greatest flute-player. **MINOS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Who can best adapt nourishment to bodies? Is it not he who knows how to apply what is suitable to each? **MINOS.** That very person. **SOCRATES.** His partitions and instructions are best, and whoever is most "lawful" regarding these is the best law-giver. **MINOS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Who is he? **MINOS.** The physical trainer <term>Paedotriba: a teacher of gymnastics and physical excellence</term>. **SOCRATES.** He knows how to feed the multitude of human bodies. **MINOS.** Truly. **SOCRATES.** But for him who knows how to feed a flock of cattle, what is his name? **MINOS.** A shepherd. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the laws of the shepherd are best for sheep. **MINOS.** Best. **SOCRATES.** And the cowherd's for cows. **MINOS.** Also.

<margin>The King's laws are best for the souls of men.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** But whose laws are most especially best for the souls of men? Are they not the King's? **MINOS.** The King's. **SOCRATES.** You say well. But can you recall: who among the men of old stood out as the best law-giver regarding the blowing of flutes? Perhaps you do not hold it in mind; do you wish me to remind you? **MINOS.** Very much so.

<margin>Marsyas first imposed laws upon the flutes.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Marsyas and his disciple, Olympus the Phrygian. **MINOS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** The flute-harmonies of these men are indeed most divine; they alone stir the listeners, and show who most especially stands in need of the gods; and they alone have endured to this day as being divine. **MINOS.** These things are true.

<margin>Who were the first law-givers among the Greeks.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** But who among the ancient kings is said to have been the best law-giver? Whose institutions still exist as if divine? **MINOS.** I do not recall at all. **SOCRATES.** Do you not know which of the Greek nations use the most ancient laws? **MINOS.** Perhaps you mean the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> and Lycurgus, the law-giver of the Lacedaemonians. **SOCRATES.** But these institutions have perhaps not yet filled three hundred years or a little more; and do you know from where they obtained the better parts of them? **MINOS.** They say from Crete. **SOCRATES.** Those people, then, among all the Greeks, live by the most ancient laws. **MINOS.** True.

<margin>Concerning Rhadamanthus and Minos.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** Do you know who were the most excellent kings among them? Namely, Minos and Rhadamanthus, the sons of Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> and Europa, whose laws these are. **MINOS.** They say, O Socrates, that Rhadamanthus was a just man, but that Minos was rustic, harsh, and unjust. **SOCRATES.** O best of men, you are repeating an Attic and tragic fable. **MINOS.** Is this not what is circulated about Minos? **SOCRATES.** Yet Homer and Hesiod do not testify to those things; and they are far more reliable witnesses than all the tragic poets, by whose testimony you speak such things. **MINOS.** And what do they hand down concerning Minos?

<margin>One must be careful both in praising and in accusing any man.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** I will tell you, lest you, like many others, speak profanities. For nothing is more profane than this. Indeed, first, we must take care lest we sin in any word or deed; and secondly, lest we sin against divine men. Rather, it is fitting to take diligent care whenever you are about to praise or blame a man, lest you go astray. And for this reason, we must primarily take care to distinguish between good and bad men. For God is exceedingly indignant whenever anyone blames one who is like Him, or approves one who is unlike Him.

<margin>A good man is like God.</margin>
<margin>A good man is the most sacred of all things.</margin>
For a good man is like God. Do not think that stones and wood and birds and serpents are sacred, but men are not. On the contrary, a good man is the most sacred of all things; conversely, a bad man is the most profane. And now I will relate for what reason Homer and Hesiod extol Minos himself, so that you, a man born of man, may no longer speak rashly against a hero who is the son of Jupiter. For Homer, when he made mention of Crete, that it was very populous and had ninety cities in it, said: "Among them is Knossos, a great city in which Minos reigned, having conversed for nine years with great Jupiter."

<margin>Crete inhabited by ninety cities.</margin>
So great is this praise of Homer for Minos, explained in few words, that he never extolled any of the heroes with equal praise. For that Jupiter is a "sophist" <note>here meaning a teacher of wisdom</note> and that art is most noble, I have often told you elsewhere, but it is made most clear in this place. For he says Minos conversed with Jupiter for nine years, accustomed to go for the sake of his instruction, as if Jupiter were a sophist. That he was educated by Jupiter with such a great gift is a marvelous praise, which Homer bestowed on no other hero. Furthermore, in the *Odyssey*, he introduced Minos judging the souls of the dead, holding a golden scepter. But he does not introduce Rhadamanthus judging or conversing with Jupiter, either here or elsewhere. Therefore, I assert that Minos was honored by Homer above all others. For since he is the son of Jupiter, the fact that he was educated by him alone is not an excess of praise. Indeed, that verse signifies this: "Minos reigned for nine years, the companion of great Jupiter." Namely, that Minos met with Jupiter for nine years in discourse. For discourses are dear; and he is most dear who meets in discourse. Thus Minos entered the cave of Jupiter for nine years to be instructed. Whence and...

# MINOS, OR ON LAW PAGE 21

[Socrates continues:] ...he spoke and taught others those things which he had received from Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> every nine years. Yet there are those who interpret this differently and perversely: calling him a drinking companion, a glutton, and a playfellow of Jove. But we can infer that they do not interpret correctly based on this: that no Greeks or Barbarians <note>Non-Greeks</note> abstain from symposia (that is, drinking parties) and such games except the Cretans and the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, who learned it from the Cretans. Furthermore, in Crete, among the other laws of Minos himself, this one stands out: *Do not drink with one another to the point of drunkenness.* It is certain, moreover, that he commanded his citizens to observe what he judged to be honorable. Nor is Minos portrayed as a wicked man; otherwise, he would have done one thing himself while commanding another to be done. But that custom was, as I said, a conference of words for the sake of discipline, and he established laws of this kind for his citizens, through the observation of which Crete has been happy for all time, as has Lacedaemon since it began to use those laws as if they were divine.

<margin>Rhadamanthus was a skilled judge, not a founder of law.</margin>
<margin>Cretan laws</margin>
Rhadamanthus was indeed a good man, for he had been instructed by Minos; yet he did not learn the entire royal discipline, but only how to serve the king in judgments. Whence he was called a "skilled judge." Minos used him plainly as a guardian of the laws throughout the city, but for the rest of Crete, he used Talos as guardian. For Talos surveyed all the villages three times a year to observe their laws, carrying around the laws engraved on bronze tablets. From this, they were called "brazen." Hesiod, moreover, brought a certain lineage to Minos himself. For when he made mention of that name, he said: *He who excelled among mortal kings and ruled over many nations, holding the scepter of Jove, with which he governed cities.* Here again, he calls the "scepter of Jove" nothing other than the teaching of Jove, by which he moderated all of Crete. 

**MINOS:** For what reason then, O Socrates, has this rumor spread among men that Minos himself was a rude and harsh man? 

**SOCRATES:** For the same reason that you, O best of men, and every other person who cares for reputation, ought to take diligent care—if you are wise—not to have any poetic man as an enemy. For poets have the greatest power in both directions: both for praising and for disparaging. In this matter, Minos surely erred when he took revenge on us for bringing war to this city; for it is filled with many wise men, and especially with poets of every kind, and particularly tragic poets.

<margin>Tragedy is a very ancient invention of Athens.</margin>
Tragedy is indeed very ancient here; it did not take its beginning from Thespis or Phrynichus as many think, but if you wish to investigate, you will find tragedy to be a much older invention of this city. 

<margin>The property of tragedy.</margin>
This genre, out of all poetry, vehemently delights the people and attracts listeners; in it, we took our revenge by bringing Minos onto the stage. But also for this reason, he forced us to pay those tributes. In this, therefore, Minos erred when he provoked us; from which it happened, as you yourself ask, that he became infamous. Since he was a good and law-abiding man, as we said above, and an excellent shepherd of the people, his laws are proof of it, which remain immutable as having been found through the true governance of the state. 

**MINOS:** You seem to have brought forth a likely argument, O Socrates. 

**SOCRATES:** Does it not seem to you then, if I speak the truth, that the Cretans, the citizens of Minos and Rhadamanthus, use the most ancient laws? 

**MINOS:** It seems so indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** These men, therefore, were the most excellent givers of all ancient laws and shepherds of men, just as Homer calls the leader of an army the "shepherd of the people." 

**MINOS:** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** Come then, by Jove the friend, if someone should ask us: a founder of laws regarding the health of the body, what does he apply to the body so that it maintains good health? We would surely answer correctly and briefly: nourishment and exercise, sometimes intensifying and sometimes relaxing, and thus composing the body. 

**MINOS:** Correct. 

**SOCRATES:** If after this he should ask again: the giver of laws pertaining to the soul and its best shepherd, what does he apply to it to make it better? What shall we especially answer him, so that we may be less ashamed of ourselves and our age? 

**MINOS:** I do not know what to say. 

**SOCRATES:** But it is a very shameful thing for both of us to seem to know what things are good or evil for others, while being ignorant of what is so for ourselves. 

**The End of Minos, or On Law.**
