## THE ARGUMENT of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine on Euthyphro, or On Holiness.

<image-desc>A historiated decorative drop-cap initial 'E' depicting a figure seated in an architectural interior with a book, possibly representing Socrates or a philosopher.</image-desc>
The *Euthyphro* is entirely engaged in refutation. Because of this, some Platonists have called this book "litigious," just like the *Euthydemus* and *Hippias*. But in truth, while Socrates refutes the false opinions of Euthyphro concerning holiness, he marks the tracks for those hunting the truth. In this book, and also in the *Gorgias*, Plato calls holiness that part of justice which renders to God His due. It renders to God His due when it returns to God those things which it received from God without a mediator. For the body—as Plato disputes in the book *On Nature*—we received from the four elements; the natural complexion of the species from the celestial spheres; the parts of the soul which are drawn by affections from demons <note>daemons/spirits</note> and the souls of the stars and spheres. But reason and mind, the image of our Parent, we received from the Creator of the whole world Himself, without any ministry of the heaven-dwellers or demons.

<margin>Piety. What holiness is. Religion. The indissoluble cord.</margin>
This, therefore, was of God; this must be returned to God; and this retribution is called holiness. Piety precedes it; religion follows it. For piety is the recognition of God the Parent. Holiness is the recognition and retribution to God of that which is God's. Religion is the indissoluble binding with God Himself through constant meditation and just works of that which has been returned to God. Thus that wise man rightly said: *a threefold cord is difficult to break* <note>Ecclesiastes 4:12</note>; a cord, I say, woven from piety, holiness, and religion. Piety excites holiness. Holiness confirms and sanctions piety. Holiness also moves religion. Religion binds holiness. For first, there is need of this—either by instinct, inspiration, or admonition—that we think of our God as our Parent with undoubting faith, which he willed to be piety. When someone has begun these things, he soon fixes every intention of mind and reason on knowing and loving God. And this frequent intuition in knowing and loving divinity is how Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius" (Hermes Trismegistus)</note> also defines holiness. From this flaming intention toward God and ardor of mind, it happens that we meditate upon and practice all the works, institutions, and commands of God; and with constant study, we "re-read" <note>original: "relegamus," a play on the etymology of "religio"</note> whatever pertains to His veneration. On account of which, by re-reading and binding ourselves, we are "religious" to God. With this definition and distinction having been sent ahead, those things which are said about holiness in the *Euthyphro* or elsewhere by Plato...

--- Page 62 ---
<meta>This page begins the translation of Plato's Euthyphro, following introductory philosophical remarks on the nature of holiness. The dialogue begins with Socrates meeting Euthyphro near the court of the King Archon.</meta>

# BOOK EIGHT

...are made clear. And when it is said that the holy is what is loved by God, it is true: but because it is holy, it is loved by God, not because it is loved is it holy. <note>This refers to the famous "Euthyphro Dilemma": is something good because God loves it, or does God love it because it is inherently good?</note> And because it is loved, it is a "beloved thing," yet it is not loved because it is a "beloved thing": since the holy and the beloved are not altogether the same. For the essence of holiness does not consist in the mere fact of being loved, but rather consists in retribution and devotion itself. Furthermore, when it is said, "Holiness is the ministering care of God," that is also truly said. But for what work of God is it a minister? For the conversion of the soul. For the work of God is to create, to convert, to purify, to enlighten, and to perfect. When God first begins to convert the soul to himself by the instinct of piety through inspiration: that very assent, by which the soul itself freely restores itself to the converting God, is called holiness: which is indeed the minister of God for the completion of conversion. Finally, it is added: Holiness is the science of vowing and sacrificing to God. This pertains especially to religion: which, as we have said, accompanies holiness. By vowing, one asks; by sacrificing, one gives. What does one ask from God? Oneself. What does one give to God? Oneself. It was the same thing which is in the divine mind that he seeks; which Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes</note> sought from Periander. Moreover, he gives his own nature as a participant in the Idea.

### PLATO’S EUTHYPHRO, OR ON HOLINESS. EUTHYPHRO. SOCRATES.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' at the beginning of the dialogue. The letter is set within a square frame featuring a pastoral landscape with trees and a building in the background.</image-desc>

<margin>Occasion of the dialogue.</margin>
**EUTHYPHRO.** What news has happened, O Socrates, that you have left your exercises in the Lyceum <note>A gymnasium and public meeting place in Athens</note> and are now loitering here around the King’s Porch? <note>The office of the King Archon, who handled religious legal matters</note> For surely you do not have a case before the King, as I do. **SOCRATES.** The Athenians, Euthyphro, do not call this a "case," but an indictment. **EUT.** What are you saying? Has someone indicted you? For I would never think that you had indicted another. **SOC.** Certainly not. **EUT.** But someone else has indicted you? **SOC.** Exactly. **EUT.** Who is he? **SOC.** I do not even know the man very well myself, Euthyphro. For he seems to be young and unknown; but they call him, I believe, Meletus, from the Pitthean district—if you know a Pitthean Meletus with long, straight hair, a hooked and eagle-like nose, and a thin beard. **EUT.** I do not know him, Socrates. But what charge has he brought against you? **SOC.** One that is not ignoble, it seems to me. For it is no small thing for a young man to have knowledge of such a great matter. He says he knows how the young men are being corrupted, and who those are that corrupt them. He appears to be a wise man, and having observed my ignorance, he accuses me before the city as if before a mother, for destroying his peers. Indeed, he seems to me to be the only one who knows how to begin correctly in politics. For the care of the young should be the first priority, so that they may become the best possible men; just as it is fitting for a good farmer to care for the tender plants first, and afterwards to look after the others. And so Meletus perhaps is first weeding us out, as he says, who corrupt the sprouts of youth; after this, by applying care to the elders as well, he will be the cause of many and great goods for the city—as is likely to happen for one who has made such a beginning. **EUT.** I would hope so, Socrates, but I fear the opposite may happen. Truly, he seems to me to be starting by attacking the very heart <note>original: "a vesta" - referring to Vesta/Hestia, the goddess of the hearth</note> of the city when he attempts to do you wrong. Tell me, what does he say you are doing to infect the youth? **SOC.** Absurd things to hear, O wonderful man! For he says I am a maker of gods; and he has indicted me for the sake of the gods, as he says, for introducing new gods and not believing in the old ones. **EUT.** I understand, Socrates; it is because you say that your "divine sign" <note>The *daimonion*, an inner voice Socrates claimed warned him against certain actions</note> occurs to you from time to time. Therefore, he has written this indictment against you as one who innovates in divine matters, and he comes to court to slander you, knowing that such things are easily misrepresented to the common people. Me too, when I speak in the assembly about divine things and predict the future, they laugh at me as if I were insane; although I have never predicted anything that was not true. They envy all of us of this sort; but we must not care about them, but proceed in the same way. **SOC.** O friend Euthyphro, to be laughed at is perhaps of no consequence. For it seems to me the Athenians do not care much if they think someone is clever, provided he does not teach his wisdom to others. But when they feel someone is imbuing others with his own skill, they become angry, whether out of envy, as you say, or for some other reason. How they are now disposed toward me, I do not care to test. For perhaps you seem to show yourself rarely to others and are unwilling to propagate your wisdom. But I fear that because of my humanity and love for the human race, I am hated by them. For I offer myself to everyone everywhere, not only without pay, but even gladly offering my own resources if anyone wishes to hear me. If, therefore, as I was just saying, they were going to laugh at me as you say they do at you, it would not be unpleasant to be dragged into court by jokers and laughers. But if they are in earnest, how it will end is hidden from everyone except you prophets. **EUT.** Perhaps it will be nothing, Socrates; you will fight your case with your own strength, and I think I shall fight mine. **SOC.** Do you have a case then? Are you the defendant or the prosecutor? **EUT.** I am prosecuting. **SOC.** Whom? **EUT.** One whom I seem mad to be pursuing. **SOC.** Why? Are you pursuing someone who has wings? **EUT.** He is far from flying, as he is already quite old. **SOC.** Who is he? **EUT.** My father. **SOC.** Your own father, my good man? **EUT.** Exactly. **SOC.** What is the accusation, and what is the trial about? **EUT.** Murder, Socrates. **SOC.** By Hercules! <note>An exclamation of surprise</note> Perhaps, Euthyphro, many are ignorant of how this can be done rightly. For I do not think it is the work of just anyone to do this correctly, but of someone far advanced in wisdom. **EUT.** Far advanced, by Jove! <note>By Zeus</note> **SOC.** Was it one of your relatives who was killed by your father? Or is that clear? For you would not accuse your father of murder for the sake of a stranger. **EUT.** It is ridiculous, Socrates, if you think it makes any difference whether the person killed was a relative or a stranger; and that this alone should not be observed: whether he who killed did so justly or not. If justly, let it go; but if unjustly, he must be prosecuted, even if the killer is a member of one's own household. For the pollution is the same if you knowingly associate with such a man...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Euthyphro outside the courthouse. Euthyphro has just explained that he is prosecuting his own father for the death of a laborer.</meta>

# EUTHYPHRO, OR ON HOLINESS. PAGE 22.

I would have approached him, nor would I have purified myself and him through a trial, even though he was a client and a servant of mine. For while I was engaged in farming in Naxos, he served us for wages; but having been provoked to anger by another of our household servants, he immediately slit his throat. Wherefore my father, having bound his hands and feet, cast him into a pit. And he sent a man here to ask a legal interpreter <note>original: "iuris interprete," referring to the *exegetai*, religious officials who interpreted sacred law</note> what ought to be done. Meanwhile, he neglected that bound man as a murderer, as if it mattered nothing at all if he should perhaps perish. Which is exactly what happened: for before the messenger himself could return from the interpreter, he died of hunger, cold, and his bonds. For this reason, my father and the rest of my relatives are indignant that, on account of a murderer's death, I accuse my father of homicide—who, as they themselves say, did not kill him, or even if he had killed him, one should not care about the death of a murderer. For they say it is impious <note>original: "prophanum"</note> for a son to take legal action against his father; judging poorly, O Socrates, how the divine law stands regarding what is holy or impious. **SOCRATES.** Do you, by Jove <note>original: "per iovem," translating the Greek "by Zeus"</note>, O Euthyphro, presume to know so sincerely how divine, holy, and impious matters stand, so that with things having happened as you say, you do not fear that in accusing your father of murder, you might be committing something impious yourself? **EUTHYPHRO.** My study would be of no use to me, O Socrates, nor would Euthyphro excel other men in any way, if I did not clearly discern such things. **SOCRATES.** O admirable Euthyphro, it is best that I become your disciple; and in the dispute I have with Meletus <note>The man who accused Socrates of impiety</note>, I shall primarily object with this: that I have hitherto professed the knowledge of divine things; but now, after he has said that I fashion new gods by my own vain opinion, I have become your disciple. If therefore, O Meletus, I should say you think Euthyphro feels correctly in these matters, then think the same of me, and do not condemn me. If not, summon that teacher of mine to judgment before me, as a man corrupting the elderly—namely me and his own father: me by teaching, and him by correcting and punishing. But if he will not obey me, and does not drop the lawsuit or substitute you for me, I will nevertheless force him to say these very things in court, to which I previously challenged him. **EUTHYPHRO.** Yes, by Jove, O Socrates! For if he should attempt to accuse me, I would find, I think, where he is weak and infirm; and the discussion in court would be about him long before it was about me. **SOCRATES.** And I, considering these things, my sweet friend, desire to be your disciple: since I know that while others, and this Meletus, do not even seem to see you, he has inspected me so sharply and easily that he has accused me of impiety. Now therefore, by Jove, tell me what you asserted you clearly know: what you would have holiness to be, and what unholiness, both concerning murder and all other things. Is not the holy itself the same in every action? And again, is not the impious the opposite of all that is holy, yet always like itself, having one single form <note>original: "ideā," referring to the Platonic Idea or Essence</note> according to which it is impious, whatever is to be impious? **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely so, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Tell me then, what do you call holy, and what impious?

<margin>The first definition of the holy, rendered from a single holy act.</margin>
**EUTHYPHRO.** I call holy exactly what I am doing now: to bring to justice the one who acts unjustly, whether regarding murder, or sacrilege, or anything else of this kind, whether it be father, or mother, or whoever else has sinned. To do otherwise is impious. Indeed, see, I pray, O Socrates, what a strong proof of the law I shall offer you—which is just as I have told others—teaching that things are done rightly only when we do not spare any sinner, whoever he may be. For all men confess that Jove himself is the best and most just of all the gods; yet they say he bound his own father because he had devoured his children without right. They further assert that he castrated his father for similar reasons. Yet they are angry with me because I prosecute a parent liable for injustice. And so these men think contrary things to themselves, both concerning the gods and concerning me. **SOCRATES.** But this is the very reason, O Euthyphro, that I am being accused. I do not have a sufficient answer. For whenever someone said such things about the gods, I bore it with difficulty; for which reason, it seems, they say I sin. But now, if these things seem so to you, who are an expert in these matters, it is necessary that we also agree. For what else could we say, we who profess to understand nothing of these things? But by Jove the Friend, tell me, do you yourself think these things actually happened? **EUTHYPHRO.** And even more wonderful things, O Socrates, which are hidden from many. **SOCRATES.** Do you then believe that a war is waged among the gods, with enmities and battles and many other things, which are recorded by the poets and skilled writers? From which also our sacred rites are full of variety, and in the great Panathenaea <note>A major festival in Athens</note> a robe embroidered with these scenes is hung in the citadel. Shall we confess these things to be true, O Euthyphro? **EUTHYPHRO.** Not these alone, O Socrates, but as I said a little while ago, I can explain many other things about divine matters if you wish; which when you hear, I know you will be greatly amazed.

<margin>Refutation of the given definition.</margin>
**SOCRATES.** I would not wonder; but you shall relate those things hereafter with greater leisure. For the present, strive to explain more clearly what I just asked. For you did not sufficiently teach me before, my friend, when I asked what holiness was; instead, you said that the holy was what you were doing now, while accusing your father of murder. **EUTHYPHRO.** And I spoke the truth, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps. But are there not many other things, O Euthyphro, that you call holy? **EUTHYPHRO.** There are indeed. **SOCRATES.** Remember then, that I did not ask this of you: that you show me one or two of many holy things, but that very form <note>original: "speciē"</note> by which all holy things are holy. For you said that all holy things are holy by one idea, and again those that are impious are impious by one idea. **EUTHYPHRO.** I did. **SOCRATES.** Demonstrate to me what this very idea is, so that looking upon it and using it as a sort of model <note>original: "exemplari"</note>, I may say that whatever you or anyone else does of such a kind is holy, and what is unlike it, I may deny. **EUTHYPHRO.** If you wish it so, O Socrates, I shall say it. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, I do wish it.

<margin>The second definition of the holy, rendered from the "passion" (effect) of the holy, but in an absolute sense: <insert>Holy and Impious</insert></margin>
**EUTHYPHRO.** That which is dear to the gods is holy; but that which is not dear is impious. **SOCRATES.** Most beautifully, O Euthyphro! You have finally answered just as I was asking you to answer. Whether you have answered truly, however, I do not yet know; but you will clearly show us that these things are true. **EUTHYPHRO.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Come then, let us consider what we are saying. A deed dear to God is holy, and a man dear to God is holy; but a deed hateful to God is impious, and a man hateful to God is called impious. But the holy and the impious are not the same, but entirely contrary. Is it not so? **EUTHYPHRO.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Do these things seem well said? **EUTHYPHRO.** So I believe.

<summary>Euthyphro attempts to define holiness by his own actions against his father, citing myths of Zeus as justification. Socrates rejects this specific example, leading Euthyphro to his second definition: that holiness is what is pleasing to the gods.</summary>

# EUTHYPHRO, OR ON HOLINESS. PAGE 23.
<meta>catchword: So</meta>

I think it is said. SOCRATES: Perhaps, my good man, we shall understand it better this way. For consider it thus: Is the holy loved by the gods because it is holy, or is it holy because it is loved by the gods? <note>This is the famous "Euthyphro Dilemma": does God command things because they are good, or are they good simply because God commands them?</note> EUTHYPHRO: I do not understand what you are saying, Socrates. SOCRATES: I will try to explain more clearly. We speak of a thing being "carried" and "carrying," "led" and "leading," "seen" and "seeing," and all such things. Do you understand that these are different, and in what way they differ? EUTHYPHRO: I think I understand. SOCRATES: And is there not something that is "loved," and something different from it which is "loving"?

<margin>Is there not something loved?</margin>
EUTHYPHRO: Why not? SOCRATES: Tell me then, is the thing carried "carried" because it is being carried, or for some other reason? EUTHYPHRO: Not at all, but for that very reason. SOCRATES: And the thing led likewise because it is being led? And the thing seen because it is being seen? EUTHYPHRO: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, it is not because it is a "seen thing" that it is seen, but on the contrary, because it is seen, it is a "seen thing." Nor is it because it is a "led thing" that it is led, but because it is led, it is "led." Nor because it is a "carried thing" is it carried, but because it is carried, it is "carried." Is it not clear, Euthyphro, what I mean to imply? I mean this: if something becomes or is affected by something, it is not because it is a "finished thing" that it becomes, but because it becomes, it is "finished"; nor because it is an "affected thing" is it affected, but because it is affected, it is "affected." Do you admit this? EUTHYPHRO: I do indeed. SOCRATES: And is not the "loved thing" either something becoming or something being affected by another? EUTHYPHRO: Entirely so. SOCRATES: This, therefore, holds in the same way as the previous examples: it is not because it is a "loved thing" that it is loved by those who love it, but because it is loved, it is a "loved thing."

<margin>The reasoning of Lily <unclear>...</unclear></margin>
EUTHYPHRO: Necessarily. SOCRATES: What then do we say about the holy, Euthyphro? Is it loved by all the gods, as your argument asserts? EUTHYPHRO: Yes. SOCRATES: Is it because it is holy, or for some other reason? EUTHYPHRO: For this very reason. SOCRATES: Therefore, because it is holy, it is loved; it is not holy because it is loved? EUTHYPHRO: So it seems. SOCRATES: Yet because it is loved by the gods, it is a "loved thing" and "dear to the gods"? EUTHYPHRO: What prevents it? SOCRATES: Then "dear to the god" is not the same as "holy," Euthyphro, nor is "holy" the same as "dear to the god," as you say; but the one is different from the other. EUTHYPHRO: In what way, Socrates? SOCRATES: Because we agree that the holy is loved for this reason: because it is holy; but it is not holy because it is loved. Is that not so? EUTHYPHRO: Certainly. SOCRATES: But the "loved-by-god" thing, by the very fact that it is loved by god, is "loved-by-god"; it is not loved because it is a "loved-by-god" thing. EUTHYPHRO: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: But if "loved-by-god" and "holy" were the same thing, then if the holy were loved because it is holy, the "loved-by-god" would also be loved because it is "loved-by-god." Or if the "loved-by-god" were "loved-by-god" because it was loved by god, then the holy would be holy because it was loved. But now you see that they are the opposite, as they are entirely different from one another. For the one (the loved-by-god) is such as to be loved because it is loved; but the other (the holy) is loved because it is such as to be loved. You seem, Euthyphro, when asked what the holy is, to be unwilling to show its essence, but rather to assign a certain "affection" <note>original: "passionem" - here meaning a quality or attribute rather than the core definition.</note> which this holy thing has received—namely, being loved by all the gods. But what it actually *is*, you have not yet explained to us. So if it pleases you, do not hide it from me, but define again from the beginning: what is the holy itself, whether it is loved by god or undergoes anything else? For we will not disagree about this. But tell me promptly now: what is holy, and what is profane? EUTHYPHRO: But Socrates, I do not find how to express to you what I am thinking. For whatever we propose always flows away from us and refuses to stay where we place it.

<margin>The works of Daedalus.</margin>
SOCRATES: Your words, Euthyphro, seem to be the works of our ancestor Daedalus. <note>Daedalus was a mythical inventor whose statues were said to be so lifelike they would walk away if not tied down.</note> If I had said and proposed them, perhaps you would have mocked me, saying that my verbal inventions run away and refuse to stay put because of my kinship to him. But now, since these are your own suppositions, we need some other joke; for they refuse to stay put for you, as you yourself see. EUTHYPHRO: On the contrary, Socrates, it seems to me that what has been said admits of that same joke. For I am not the cause of them circling around; you seem to me to be the Daedalus himself. For as far as I am concerned, they would have stayed still. SOCRATES: I seem then, my friend, to be more skilled in this art than he was, in that he only made his own works unstable, but I, it appears, do so to the works of others as well as my own. And this is the most beautiful part of my art: that I am wise against my will. For I would rather have my arguments remain immobile and fixed than to possess the wisdom of Daedalus along with the riches of Tantalus. <note>Tantalus was a wealthy king in myth, famous for his eternal punishment and his great riches.</note> But since you seem to be shrinking from the labor like a pampered man, I will strive with you to show the way, so that you may instruct me about the holy itself; do not give up in the middle of the talk. See now if it seems necessary to you that everything holy is just. EUTHYPHRO: It does indeed. SOCRATES: Is then everything just also holy? Or is everything holy just, while the just is not all holy, but partly holy and partly something else? EUTHYPHRO: I do not follow what is being said, Socrates. SOCRATES: And yet you are no less younger than I than you are wiser; but as I said, you are pampered by the abundance of your wisdom. But, blessed man, rouse your strength and exert yourself. For what I was saying is not difficult to grasp.

<margin>He critiques this: where there is fear, there is also shame.</margin>
For I say the opposite of what the poet sang in these words: "Of Jove the creator, who begot all these things, he is unwilling to speak; for where there is fear, there is also shame." I disagree with the poet on this. Do you want me to tell you where I differ? EUTHYPHRO: Very much. SOCRATES: It does not seem to me that wherever there is fear, there is also shame. For many, I think, fear poverty and disease and other such things, yet they feel no shame in them. Does it not seem so to you? EUTHYPHRO: It does. SOCRATES: But wherever there is shame, there is also fear. For whoever feels shame and blushes, dreads the reputation of wickedness. EUTHYPHRO: He dreads it certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, it is not right to say "where there is fear, there is shame," but rather "where there is shame, there is fear." Yet it is not the other way around: that wherever there is fear, there is also shame. For I believe the nature of fear is broader than that of shame. Just as shame is a part of fear, so the odd is a part of number. Therefore, it is not the case that wherever there is number, there is an odd number, but where there is an odd number, there is also a number. Do you follow? EUTHYPHRO: Perfectly. SOCRATES: This is what I was asking before: whether where there is justice, there is also holiness; or rather where there is holiness, there is justice. For where there is justice, there is not always holiness, since holiness is a part of justice. So...

...or do we say otherwise? EUTHYPHRO. Certainly, it seems to be well said. SOCRATES. Look then at what follows: if the holy is a part of the just, we must find out, as it appears, what kind of part of the just the holy is. If you were asking me now about one of the things mentioned before—for instance, what kind of part of number is the "even," and what kind of number it is—I would surely answer: that which is not scalene <note>original: "scalenus," meaning unequal-sided</note> but isosceles, that is, not unequal-sided but equilateral. Does it not seem so to you? EUTHYPHRO. To me, certainly. SOCRATES. Try then to teach me in the same way what kind of part of the just the holy is, so that I may immediately tell Meletus <note>The man who accused Socrates of impiety</note> not to accuse us further of injustice and impiety, since we have learned sufficiently from you what things are pious and holy, and what are the opposite. EUTHYPHRO. That part of the just, O Socrates, which is concerned with the care of the gods, I reckon to be the holy and the pious; while that which pertains to the care of men is the remaining part of justice. SOCRATES. You seem to me to speak well, O Euthyphro, 
<margin>The definition of the holy begins to appear.</margin>
but there is one small thing I require further. For I do not yet understand this "care" you speak of. Surely you do not mean that this care is like the cares directed toward other things. For instance, we say: not just anyone knows how to care for horses, but the horseman. Is it not so? EUTHYPHRO. Exactly. SOCRATES. For the horseman’s skill is the care of horses. EUTHYPHRO. Yes. SOCRATES. And the hunter’s skill is the care of dogs, and the herdsman’s is the care of cattle. EUTHYPHRO. Entirely. SOCRATES. But holiness and piety are the care of the gods: is this what you assert, Euthyphro? EUTHYPHRO. I do. SOCRATES. Does not all care intend the same thing: to bring some kind of good and utility to that which is cared for? Just as horses are helped by the horseman’s diligence and become better. Does it not seem so? EUTHYPHRO. To me, clearly. SOCRATES. And dogs by the hunter’s skill, and cattle by the herdsman’s, and all other things likewise. Do you think care tends toward the harm of that which is cared for? EUTHYPHRO. No, by Jupiter! SOCRATES. But toward utility? EUTHYPHRO. Why not? SOCRATES. Since holiness is the care of the gods, does it benefit the gods and make them better? Would you concede that whenever you perform a holy act, you make one of the gods better? EUTHYPHRO. Never, by Jupiter! SOCRATES. Nor do I think you mean that, Euthyphro; far be such a suspicion from me. That is why I asked what kind of "care of the gods" you meant, not believing you meant something of that sort. EUTHYPHRO. And rightly so, Socrates; for I do not assert such a thing. SOCRATES. Come then, what kind of care of the gods will holiness be? EUTHYPHRO. That by which 
<margin>All care intends this: that it brings some kind of good and utility to that which is cared for.</margin>
servants care for their masters. SOCRATES. I understand. This care would be, it seems, a certain service to the gods. EUTHYPHRO. Exactly. SOCRATES. Can you say what the service of physicians—the "ministering care" of doctors—provides? Is it not health? EUTHYPHRO. To that very thing. SOCRATES. And the ministering skill of those who build ships, what does it serve? EUTHYPHRO. The construction of a ship. SOCRATES. And that of house-builders, is it not for the construction of a house? EUTHYPHRO. Indeed. SOCRATES. Tell me then, best of men: that ministering care of the gods, toward the completion of what work does it serve the gods? It is clear that you know, since you affirmed that you know divine things above all others. EUTHYPHRO. And I speak the truth, Socrates. SOCRATES. Tell me then, by Jupiter, what is this wonderful work which the gods accomplish with us as their ministers? EUTHYPHRO. Many and beautiful things, Socrates. SOCRATES. 
<margin>The chief work of a general in battle is to conquer.</margin>
Trained generals also accomplish many and beautiful things, my friend, but you would say their chief work is to conquer in battle, would you not? EUTHYPHRO. Why not? SOCRATES. And farmers, I think, accomplish many and beautiful things, yet the sum of them is to gather food from the earth. EUTHYPHRO. Exactly. SOCRATES. Of the many and beautiful deeds the gods perform, what is the sum? EUTHYPHRO. I said a little while ago, Socrates, that it is a long task to comprehend all these things perfectly. But I tell you simply this: if someone knows how to speak and do things pleasing to the gods, by praying and sacrificing, these are holy things; and these 
<margin>The chief work of farmers.</margin>
duties preserve both private houses and cities. The opposite are impious, and they overturn and destroy everything. SOCRATES. You could have explained the sum of what I asked in much fewer words, Euthyphro, if you had wished. But you seem not at all ready or willing to approach teaching me; and now, just as you were on the verge of it, you turned away. If you had answered, I might have learned holiness from you. But now—for the questioner must follow the questioned wherever he leads—what do you say again that the holy and holiness are? Is it not a certain science of praying and 
<margin>Another definition of the holy.</margin>
sacrificing? EUTHYPHRO. It is. SOCRATES. Is not sacrificing the offering of gifts to the gods? And is not praying the asking of things from the gods? EUTHYPHRO. 
<margin>What it is to sacrifice.</margin>
Very much so, Socrates. SOCRATES. Therefore, holiness will be the science of giving to the gods and asking from them, according to this reasoning. EUTHYPHRO. 
<margin>What it is to pray.</margin>
You have understood what I was saying very well, Socrates. SOCRATES. I am greedy for your wisdom, my friend; I apply my mind so that your words are not poured out in vain. But tell me, I pray, what is this service toward the gods? Do you say it is to ask something from them and give to them? EUTHYPHRO. Certainly. SOCRATES. To ask rightly from them, is it not to ask for those things we need? And to give rightly, is it to offer them those things they require? For it would not be skillful to bestow on someone things they do not need. EUTHYPHRO. You speak the truth, Socrates. SOCRATES. Holiness, then, Euthyphro, will be a kind of mutual commerce <note>original: "mercatura," meaning trade or business</note> between gods and men. EUTHYPHRO. Commerce, if you like to call it that. SOCRATES. But nothing pleases me unless it is true. Tell me then: what utility do the gods get from our gifts? For what they give to everyone is plain to see. Nothing is good for us that they do not provide; but what do they receive from us that benefits them? Or are we so much more successful in this commerce that while we receive all good things from them, they report no good from us? EUTHYPHRO. Do you think, Socrates, that the gods are helped in any part by what they receive from us? SOCRATES. But what then are these gifts of ours offered to the gods? EUTHYPHRO. 
<margin>The same as before.</margin>
What else do you think than honor, veneration, and, as I just said, gratitude? SOCRATES. Therefore, Euthyphro, the holy is something grateful, but not useful or pleasing to the gods? EUTHYPHRO. I reckon it is, above all things, pleasing. SOCRATES. This then is the holy again: that which is pleasing to the gods. EUTHYPHRO. Most certainly. SOCRATES. And you wonder, when you say these things, that your arguments do not stand still but rather seem to waver? You blame me as if I were Daedalus <note>The mythical inventor whose statues were said to move on their own</note> making them totter, when you yourself are far more skillful than Daedalus, making your words revolve in a circle. Do you not perceive that they flow back to the same point? Do you remember that earlier the "holy" and the "dear to God" appeared not to be the same, but different from each other? EUTHYPHRO. I remember. SOCRATES. But now do you not notice that you are saying the holy is what is pleasing to the gods? And this is nothing other than what is dear to God...

# ARGUMENT FOR THE PARMENIDES. FOLIO XXIII.

Or not? EUTHYPHRO. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Therefore, either we did not grant it correctly then, or if we were correct then, we would not be judging correctly now.
EUTHYPHRO. So it seems. SOCRATES. Therefore, we must examine again from the beginning what is holy. For I will not, of my own will and gladly, shrink from standing my ground until I learn it. But do not despise me; rather, apply your mind fully and now, as much as possible, express the truth. For you know it, if any man does. Nor should you be let go, like Proteus <note>A shape-shifting sea god in Greek mythology who would only reveal the truth if held fast.</note>, until you have spoken. For unless you clearly knew the holy and the profane, you would never have decided to pursue an old man and your father as a defendant for death for the sake of some laborer; instead, you would have feared the gods, lest perhaps you were undertaking this incorrectly, and you would have blushed in the sight of men. But now I know that you clearly believe you know the holy and the profane. Speak then, O best Euthyphro, and do not hide from us what you think it is. EUTHYPHRO. Another time, O Socrates; for now I am hurrying elsewhere. It is time for me to go. SOCRATES. What are you doing, my friend! By leaving, you have cast me down from a great hope: the hope I had of learning from you what is holy and what is not holy, and thus escaping free from Meletus's accusation <note>The legal charges brought against Socrates for impiety.</note>, by showing him that I had obtained wisdom in divine matters from Euthyphro, and that I would no longer, out of my own unrefined opinion, introduce anything new concerning the divine, but would live the rest of my time much better.

->centered The End of the Euthyphro.<-

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine for the Parmenides, or concerning the one principle of all things, or concerning the Ideas.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' containing scrolling foliate designs and a central face or mask.</image-desc>
Since Plato has scattered the seeds of all wisdom throughout all his dialogues, he collected all the institutes of moral philosophy in the books on the Republic; he embraced the whole science of natural things in the *Timaeus*, and the universal theology in the *Parmenides*. And while in others he has surpassed all other philosophers by a long interval, in this one at last he seems to have surpassed himself, and to have brought forth this celestial work divinely from the inner sanctuaries of the divine mind and the innermost shrine of philosophy. Whoever approaches its sacred reading should first prepare himself with sobriety of soul and freedom of mind before he dares to touch the mysteries of this celestial work. For here the divine Plato disputes most subtly concerning the One itself, how the One itself is the principle of all things, above all things, and all things are from it. In what way it is outside all things, and in all things: and all things are from it, through it, and toward it. But he ascends by degrees to the understanding of this One, which is above essence. For the One is found in a threefold order. In those things which flow and are subject to the senses, and are called "sensibles." Also in those things which are always the same and are called "intelligibles," to be perceived no longer by the senses, but by the mind alone. Nor is it only in these, but truly also above sense and sensibles, and above intellect and intelligibles, the One itself exists. Wherefore in this dialogue, Zeno of Elea, first the disciple of Parmenides the Pythagorean, proves that there is a "one" in sensible things, showing that if these were many, in no way participating in the nature of the one, many errors would follow. Then Socrates, not indeed opposing Zeno, but raising him higher, leads him to the consideration of the One and of Unity, which are in intelligible things, lest he linger in this "one" which is in sensible things. From this, therefore, they arrive at investigating the Ideas, in which the unities of things consist. Finally, the elder Parmenides himself, by no means contradicting Socrates but completing his begun contemplation, explains the entire reasoning of the Ideas. Here he introduces four questions concerning the Ideas. First, whether they exist. Second, of what things there are ideas, and of what there are not. Third, what kind they are, or what power they have. Fourth, how they are participated in by those things which are below them. From here he now ascends to the One which exists above intelligibles and ideas, and brings forward nine suppositions concerning it: 
<margin>Nine suppositions concerning the One.</margin>
five if the One is; four if the One is not: inquiring what follows in either case. These suppositions are drawn from a threefold partition of the One and a twofold partition of its "not-being." For the One is found to be threefold: above being, in being, and after being. "Not-being" itself is subjected to a twin consideration: either it is in no way, or it is partly being and partly not being what is thought. Thus the first supposition treats, if the One exists above being, what follows concerning it toward itself and toward other things. The second, if the One is with being, how it relates to itself and to others. The third, if the One is placed under being: what happens to it toward itself and others. The fourth, if the One consists above being, how other things relate both to themselves and to the One. The fifth, if that One is which is located with being, what happens to others toward themselves and toward it. The sixth, if the One is not, so that it partly is and partly is not, by what reason it relates to itself and to others. The seventh, if the One is not so that 
<margin>Here one other supposition seems to be missing which says: if the One is placed under being, how other things relate both to themselves and to the One.</margin>
it is in no way, in what way it relates to itself and to others. The eighth, if the One is not so that it partly is and partly is not, what happens to others toward themselves and toward it. The ninth, if the One is not so that it is in no way, what others finally suffer toward themselves and toward it. In all these, Parmenides generally intends to assert this most of all: that the One is the principle of all things, and with it positioned, all things are positioned; but with it removed, they are destroyed. Thus, in the first five suppositions, he hands down five grades of things with the One positioned in the order of things. In the four following, he inquires how many absurdities, how many errors, and how many evils follow if the One itself is removed. The first of the five superior ones 
<margin>This word "One."</margin>
discusses the supreme One: God: how he creates and disposes the orders of the following gods. The second concerns the individual orders of gods, in what way they proceed from God himself. The third concerns divine souls. The fourth concerns those things which 
<margin>This word "other" and "others."</margin>
occur around matter: how they are produced by superior causes. The fifth concerns prime matter, how by its own nature it is devoid of forms and depends on the first One. Furthermore, it should be noted that in this dialogue, when "the One" is said, in the manner of the Pythagoreans, anything signifying a substance entirely free from matter can be meant: such as God, mind, or soul. But when "the other" and "others" are said, it is permitted to understand both matter and those things which occur in matter. These things having been premised and observed, let us come to the dialogue itself.

# BOOK NINE

<margin>Occasion of the dialogue.</margin>

When we had set out from our home in Clazomenae <note>A Greek city in Ionia, modern-day Turkey</note> for Athens, we happened upon Adeimantus and Glaucon near the marketplace. Adeimantus took me by the hand and said, "Greetings, O Cephalus! If there is anything you need that is within our power, you have only to ask." I replied, "In fact, I have come for the very purpose of seeking your assistance." "Then explain," he said, "what it is you need." I then asked, "What was the name of your half-brother? I do not quite remember it, for he was nearly a boy when I last came here from Clazomenae, and a long interval of time has passed since then. I believe his father’s name was Pyrilampes." "Exactly," he said, "and his own name is Antiphon. But what is it specifically you are looking for?" I answered, "These fellow citizens of mine are ardent lovers of wisdom. They have heard that this Antiphon was for a long time an intimate associate of Pythodorus, the companion of Zeno, and that having frequently heard from Pythodorus the arguments which Socrates, Zeno, and Parmenides once debated among themselves, he retains them in his memory." "What you say is true," he replied. "It is those arguments, then, that we desire to hear." "That is not difficult," he said, "for while he was a youth, he practiced them diligently. Now, however, following after his grandfather of the same name, he spends most of his time occupied with equestrian matters. But if it is necessary, let us go to him; he recently left here for home, and he lives nearby in Melita."

When this was said, we went there and found Antiphon at home, handing over a certain bridle to a smith to be fitted. After he had finished with the man and my brothers explained the reason for our visit, he recognized me from my previous stay and greeted me warmly. When we begged him to recount that disputation, he at first refused, for he said it was no small labor; eventually, however, he set it forth.

Antiphon said that Pythodorus related how Zeno and Parmenides once came to the great festival of the Panathenaea. Parmenides was already an old man, grey-haired but of a noble appearance, being roughly sixty-five years of age. Zeno was nearly forty, tall and of a graceful figure, and was said to be the intimate of Parmenides. He said they were staying at the house of Pythodorus outside the walls in the Ceramicus <note>The "Potters' Quarter" of Athens</note>. Socrates had come there, along with many others, desiring to hear the writings of Zeno, for they had then been brought to that city for the first time. Socrates was at that time quite young. Zeno himself was reading to them, as Parmenides happened to be out of the house. Pythodorus said that very little of the reading remained when he himself entered the house along with Parmenides and Aristotle (the one who was later one of the Thirty Tyrants). Thus, they heard only the few parts that remained to be read, though Pythodorus had heard the whole thing from Zeno previously.

When he had heard these things, he said that Socrates asked that the first hypothesis of the first discourse be read again. When it was read, he immediately asked: "How do you mean this, O Zeno? That if the things that exist are 'many,' they must be both like and unlike? But this is impossible, for neither can the unlike be like, nor the like be unlike. Is that not what you are saying?" Zeno replied that it was indeed. "Then if it is impossible for the unlike to be like and the like to be unlike, is it also impossible for there to be 'many'? For if there were many, these impossibilities would result. Is this the intent of your discourses: to assert nothing other than that 'the many' do not exist? And do you consider each of your arguments to be a proof of this, thinking you have provided as many proofs that the many do not exist as you have written arguments? Is that what you mean, or do I not perceive it correctly?" "On the contrary," Zeno replied, "you have understood perfectly what these writings intend."

Socrates then said, "I see, O Parmenides, that Zeno here wishes to be joined to you not only in friendship, but also by his compositions. For in a way he has written the same thing as you, but by a certain variation he tries to deceive us into thinking he is saying something else. For you, in your poems, say that the All is One, and you provide beautiful arguments for this. He, on the other hand, says there are not 'many,' and he offers many powerful proofs of his own. Thus, while one says 'One' and the other says 'not many,' and each speaks in such a way that they seem not to be saying the same thing—even though they say nearly the same—it seems to us that these things are spoken above our heads."

"It is so, O Socrates," Zeno said. "Yet you have not entirely perceived the truth of these writings, though you track and investigate the words as well as Laconian hounds. But first, this escaped you: these writings do not boast of being written for the reason you think—to hide something from men as if achieving some grand feat."

<margin>
Written works were suppressed and only published with deliberation.
</margin>

"But you have touched upon something that happened by chance. The truth is, these books were composed in my youth, and someone stole them and published them before I could decide whether they should be brought to light or not. Therefore, it escaped you, Socrates, that you think it was written from elderly ambition rather than youthful contention. Nevertheless, as I said, you did not guess poorly." "I accept that," said Socrates, "and I believe it is as you say."

->Concerning the Ideas.<-

"But answer me this: do you not think there exists, in and of itself, a certain Form <note>The Platonic 'Idea' or 'Form'</note> of Likeness? And another Form contrary to it, of Unlikeness? And that you and I, and these things we call 'many,' participate in these two? And that whatever participates in Likeness becomes like to the extent that it participates? And those in Unlikeness become unlike? If all things participate in both contraries, and because they are participants in both, they are both like and unlike themselves, what is the wonder in that? If one were to say that Likeness itself becomes unlike, or Unlikeness itself becomes like, that would be a marvel..."

as I think it would be. But if someone were to assert that things which participate in both <note>original: "in utrisque"</note> experience both, it would seem to me, O Zeno, to be nothing to wonder at. Nor would I marvel if someone said all things are one, because they participate in the one; and these same things are again many, because they also participate in multitude. But if he should assert that the One itself is many, or that Multitude itself is one, and should show that these **Genera** <note>General classes or kinds</note> and **Species** <note>Specific forms or types</note> receive these contraries within themselves, that would indeed be worthy of admiration. For if someone demonstrates that I am both one and many, why is that a marvel? Since, wishing to assert that I am many, he might say that my right side is one thing, my left another; some parts are in front, others behind; and finally some are above and others below; for I am, as I think, a participant in multitude. And when he wishes to show that I am one, he might say that of the seven of us here, I am one man, a participant in the unit; likewise, there is nothing to wonder at. Therefore, he affirms both. If, then, someone should attempt to demonstrate that such things as stones and wood and other things of this sort are both one and many, we shall admit that he has shown them to be one and many; yet he has not shown the One to be many, nor the Many to be one, nor has he proclaimed anything marvelous, but only what we would all confess. But if someone, as I said a moment ago, were first to distinguish the **Species** themselves according to themselves and separately—such as Likeness, Unlikeness, Multitude, the One, Rest, Motion, and other such things—and then assert that these can be mixed and separated among themselves, I would be utterly amazed, O Zeno. And although I think those things you have written have been handled as befits a brave man, I would marvel and rejoice much more if someone could more clearly explain this same question, which is deeply entangled in the **Species** themselves, just as it has been set forth in the things we see, so also in those things which are grasped by **Reason** <note>original: "ratione comprehendunt"</note>.

While Socrates was saying these things, Pythodorus said he thought that Parmenides and Zeno were annoyed with Socrates at each point; but they listened with the greatest attention, and frequently looking at one another, they smiled, as if admiring Socrates. When Socrates had finished speaking, Parmenides said: "O Socrates, how worthy of admiration you are for the impulse with which you approach arguments so readily."

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'V' featuring floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc> "But tell me, I pray. "Oftentimes," said Socrates, "I have been turned about in this ambiguity: whether one should speak of these in the same way as the more noble things, or otherwise." "Have you also doubted about these things, O Socrates, which someone might perhaps think ridiculous—such as hair, or mud, or filth, and other most ignoble and vile things? Do you hesitate whether a separate **Species** of each of these must be placed, existing as something different from those things we handle, or not?" "By no means," said Socrates, "but these things which we see, these they are; to think there is a certain **Species** of them would perhaps be too ridiculous. Sometimes this thought has disturbed me, lest there be something of the same kind concerning all things; but after I have stood there for a little while, I flee from it, fearing lest I might perish, having sunk into a deep pit of nonsense. Returning from there to those things which we previously said have **Species**, I occupy myself with them." "You are still young, O Socrates," said Parmenides, "and philosophy has not yet taken hold of you. But it will take hold of you, in my opinion, when you neglect none of these things; but now, because of your age, you still look to the opinions of men."

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' featuring floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc> "But tell me this. Does it seem to you, as you were saying, that certain **Species** exist, and that those things which participate in them receive their names from them—as for instance, those participating in Likeness are called 'like,' those in Greatness 'great,' and those in Beauty and Justice are called 'beautiful' and 'just'?" "Very much so," said Socrates. "Does not whatever participates in a **Species** receive either the whole **Species** or a part of it? Or is there some other mode of participation besides these?" "And what other could there be?" Socrates said. "Does it seem to you, then, that the whole **Species**, being one, is in each of the many? Or how?" "What prevents it from being one?" "Therefore, one and the same thing will be whole and one at the same time in many separate things; and thus it will exist separately from itself." "Not at all," said Socrates. "For just as one day is present everywhere at once, yet it is not separated from itself; so nothing prevents any **Species** from being one and the same in many things at once, without being separated from itself." "Beautifully, O Socrates, you show one and the same thing in many at once, as if you were to spread a veil over many men and say that one whole thing is over many. Is that not the sort of thing you mean?" "Perhaps." "Then will the whole veil be over each man, or will one part of it be over one, and another over another?" "A part." "Therefore, O Socrates, the **Species** will be divisible; and those things which participate in them will take a part; and the whole will no longer be in each, but a part of each will be one." "So it appears." "Will you then, O Socrates, wish to divide the one **Species** in reality, and yet have it still be one?" "In no way." "Consider then: if you divide Greatness itself, and each of the many great things is great by a part of Greatness smaller than Greatness itself, will that not seem far from reason?" "Absolutely." "What then? If each thing participates in a part of Equality, will it have something which, being smaller than Equality itself, makes that which has it equal to something?" "Impossible." "And if any of us has a part of the Small, the Small itself will be greater than that part, since it is a part of it; and thus the Small itself will be greater. # BOOK NINE

Socrates said: "The rest will participate in the forms; since they can grasp them neither according to the whole nor according to the parts! By Jove, this seems no light matter to determine." Regarding what you say: "What then? I think you posit each single form from this: when several things seem large to you, perhaps one single idea appears to you as you look across them all; whence you think the 'Large' itself is one." You speak the truth. "What if you look at the 'Large' itself and the other large things in the soul in the same way across all of them? Will not a certain single 'Large' appear again, by which all these must necessarily appear large?" It appears so. "Therefore, another species of magnitude will shine forth again beyond magnitude itself and those things participating in magnitude; and in all of these, another again, by which all are large; and no longer will each species be one, but rather infinite in number." 

"But perhaps," said Socrates, "each of these forms is a certain notion; and cannot exist anywhere except in minds. For thus each would be one, and the consequences just mentioned would no longer happen." "What then?" he said. "Is each notion one? But a notion of nothing? That is impossible. But of something?" Of something, certainly. "Of something existing or not existing?" Existing. "Is it not of some one thing, which that notion understands as following through all things, being a single idea?" Entirely. "Furthermore, will not this which is understood to be one, always the same in all things, be a form?" This also seems necessary. 

"What then?" said Parmenides. "Is it not necessary, since other things participate in forms, that each consists of notions, and all things think? Or, though they are notions, do they yet think nothing?" "But that," he said, "does not make sense; rather, it seems to me most likely that these forms stand in nature as patterns <note>original: "exemplaria"</note>, while other things are made like them and are likenesses; and these participate in the forms in no other way than by being made like them." 

"If therefore anything is like the form, as you say, is it possible for the form itself not to be like that which has been made like it, insofar as it has been made like it? Or can it be thought that the like is not like unto its like?" Certainly not. "But must not the like necessarily participate in one and the same form as that which it resembles?" It must. "But that by which the likes, through participation, become like—will that not be the form itself?" Absolutely. "Therefore, nothing can be like the form, nor the form like another. For beyond the form itself, another form would always emerge; and if that were like anything, another again. And this progression will never cease: a new form will always occur if the form becomes like the participant." You speak most truly. "Therefore, other things do not participate in forms through likeness; but some other mode of participation must be sought." It appears so. 

"Do you see, O Socrates, how great an ambiguity follows if one distinguishes the forms as being themselves according to themselves?" "Very much so," he said. "Know, moreover, that you do not yet, so to speak, comprehend how great the difficulty is, if you always posit one form for each existing thing by distinguishing it." "How so?" he said. "There are many other reasons, but this is the greatest: if someone should assert that those forms cannot be known, being such as we say forms ought to be. Someone saying these things could not be refuted unless the doubter were experienced in many things and ingenious, and willing to follow the demonstrator through many things in a long sequence. Nevertheless, he could not be persuaded, for he will force the conclusion that they are unknown." 

"Why, O Parmenides?" said Socrates. "Because, O Socrates, I think both you and anyone else who posits a certain essence of each thing existing itself according to itself, would concede that no form exists in us." "For in what way," said Socrates, "would it exist itself according to itself?" You speak rightly. "Therefore, do not all those ideas which look to one another have their essence in relation to themselves, and not toward those things which are around us—whether one calls them likenesses or whatever else—by participating in which we are named as individual things? Those things around us, being equivocal to them, are likewise in relation to themselves and not to the forms; and they are named after themselves and not after those forms." 

"How do you mean?" said Socrates. "Just as if one of us is a master or a servant of someone, he is not a servant of the 'Master' itself which is a master, nor is the one called master a master of the 'Servant' itself which is a servant; but both of these are as a human being. But Mastery itself is what it is of Servitude itself; and again, Servitude itself is in the same way servitude of Mastery itself. Neither do the things in us refer to those, nor do those which are there refer to us; but as I said, they are of themselves and in relation to themselves, and the things here are similarly in relation to themselves." <margin>Knowledge is the truth of being and of that which is.</margin> "Do you understand what I say?" "I understand entirely." "Is not knowledge itself, which is knowledge, the knowledge of that 'Truth' itself which is?" "Entirely so." "And again, each of the knowledges, which is what it is, is a knowledge of some of the things that exist. Is it not?" "Certainly." "But our knowledge—will it not be the knowledge of the truth that is around us? And again, each of our knowledges, the knowledge of each of the things around us?" "It is necessary." "However, you agree that we neither have the forms themselves, nor can they be around us?" "Certainly not." "Do the kinds of knowledge themselves know those things which are individuals?" "Certainly." "Which form we do not have." "Certainly not." "Therefore, no form is known by us, since we are not at all participants in knowledge itself." "It does not appear so." "Therefore, the 'Beautiful' itself and the 'Good' itself are unknown to us," <margin>The Beautiful itself and the Good itself are unknown to us.</margin> "and finally all things which we suppose to be ideas." "It seems so." 

"Consider this also, which is even more serious." "What is that?" "Would you not confess that if there is a certain genus of knowledge itself, it is much more excellent than this knowledge of ours? And the same for beauty itself and the rest?" "Indeed." "If anything else participates in knowledge itself, would you not say that none but God has the supreme knowledge?" "It is necessary." "Will God, having embraced knowledge itself, be able to know these things of ours?" "Why not?" "Because," said Parmenides, "we have confessed, O Socrates, that those forms do not have the power they have toward our things, nor do our things have power toward the heavenly ones; but each refers to itself." "We clearly agreed." "Therefore, if the supreme mastery itself is with God, and the supreme knowledge itself, never will mastery itself rule us, nor will knowledge itself know us or anything of ours; but we similarly do not rule the gods—"

# ON THE ONE PRINCIPLE OF ALL THINGS AND ON THE IDEAS. FOLIO XXVI.

## d ii

...we shall [not] rule by our authority, nor shall we perceive anything divine by our knowledge. And by that same reasoning, they <note>The gods</note> will neither be our masters, nor, being gods, will they pay attention to human affairs. But would not this discourse seem truly marvelous, he asked, if someone were to deprive God of knowledge? These things, O Socrates, said Parmenides, and many others besides these, must necessarily happen to the Forms <note>original: "speciebus," referring to the Platonic Ideas</note> if indeed these are the Ideas of things, and if someone defines each Form as something existing in itself. 

From this, whoever hears these things wavers and doubts whether perhaps the Ideas are nothing at all, or if they do exist, he thinks it necessary that they be unknown to human nature; so much so, that he who says these things seems to be making a valid point. And as I said a little while ago, it is a wonder how incredible it is: and it belongs to a man of great talent to be able to perceive that there is a certain genus for each thing, and an essence according to itself. Furthermore, it is the task of an even more wonderful man to be able to teach these things to others after he has found them, discerning all things sufficiently. 

I agree, O Parmenides, said Socrates; for what you say harmonizes wonderfully with my mind. Nevertheless, said Parmenides, if someone, moved by the aforementioned reasons, should take away the Forms of existing things and not distinguish the specific Form of each one, he will have nowhere to turn his intellect, since he has not allowed that the Idea of each existing thing always exists as the same; and in this way, he will utterly destroy the faculty of discourse. You also seem to me to have perceived such a reason especially. 

You speak the truth. What then will you do regarding philosophy? Where will you turn if these things are unknown? I do not seem to discern that at present. You are attempting to define what is beautiful, just, good, and any of the other Forms, O Socrates, before you have been sufficiently exercised. For I noticed this some time ago, hearing you here disputing together with this Aristotle <note>Not the famous philosopher, but a member of the Thirty Tyrants who was a youth at the time of this fictionalized dialogue</note>. Truly, believe me, that impulse of yours is beautiful and divine, by which you fly toward reasons. 

But collect yourself, and exercise yourself more diligently in that faculty which seems to be useless and is called "idle chatter" or "garrulity" by the many, while you are young; otherwise, the truth will flee from you. What is the method of this exercise, Parmenides? It is that, he said, which you heard from Zeno. But I also wondered at that statement of yours to him, when you said that one ought not to let thought stop at those things which are perceived by the eyes and their error, but to ascend to those things which one might best comprehend by reason and which one considers to be Forms. Nor does it seem difficult in this way to explain similarities and dissimilarities, and the other things that belong to existing things. 

And you have spoken well. But besides this, it must also be observed that you should not only suppose "if something is" and then consider what follows from that supposition, but also suppose "if that same thing is not," if you wish to be more perfectly exercised. How do you mean that? For example, if you wish to consider regarding that supposition which Zeno brought forward: "if many things exist," what will happen to the many themselves in relation to themselves and to the One, and to the One in relation to itself and to the many. And again, "if many things do not exist," it must again be considered what happens to the One and to the many, both toward themselves and toward each other. 

And again, if one should suppose that "Likeness" exists, or does not exist: what would chiefly happen from either supposition, both to those things which were supposed and to all other things, in relation to themselves and to each other. The same reasoning applies to Unlikeness, to motion, rest, generation, corruption, being, and non-being; and to embrace it in one word: concerning whatever is supposed either to be or not to be, or to undergo any other property, one must consider what follows from the supposition in relation to itself and to any of the others you choose—to several, and to all things likewise—and again how other things relate to themselves and to whatever else you assume, whether you posit it as existing or as non-existing; if indeed, being absolutely exercised, you intend to look deeply into the truth. 

You bring up an arduous task, he said, and I do not entirely understand you. But why do you not yourself suppose something, running through it in that manner, so that I may understand more clearly? You impose a great burden on an old man, O Socrates. Then Socrates said: Why do you not yourself, O Zeno, discuss this matter? To which Zeno, smiling, replied: Let us pray to Parmenides himself, O Socrates; for what he says is no light matter. Do you not see how great a business it is that you command? If we were more numerous, it would certainly not be fitting to ask this. 

For it is unseemly to treat such things in the sight of many, and especially for an old man. For many are ignorant that without this discourse and wandering through all things, it is impossible for the mind to become master of the truth. I therefore, O Parmenides, pray along with Socrates that I also may be allowed to hear these things after so much time has passed. When Zeno had said these things, Antiphon related that Pythodorus said: he also, and Aristotle, and all the others besought Parmenides to demonstrate what he had said, and not to do otherwise. 

Then at last Parmenides said: It is necessary to obey; and I seem to fall into a state similar to that of the horse of Ibycus. To which horse—an elderly athlete about to enter a chariot contest and fearing the outcome because of his experience—Ibycus himself, comparing himself, looked and <margin>The horse of Ibycus.</margin> said: "And I myself, now an old man, am forced to return to loves." By the same reasoning, I seem to myself to tremble greatly when I think how I, now great in age, can swim across such a deep sea of discourse. 

Yet I must comply, since Zeno himself asks; for we are the same. Where then shall we begin? Or what shall we suppose first? Since we have entered into this game of business, do you want me to start first from my own supposition, supposing concerning the One itself: whether the One is, or is not, what happens? By all means, said Zeno. Who then will answer me? The youngest? For he will provide less trouble, and will answer what he himself thinks; thus his response will tire me less. I am ready, O Parmenides, said Aristotle. For you mean me when you command the youngest to answer. But come: ask me as you please, as I shall answer most willingly.

Despite his age, Parmenides agrees to demonstrate this "sea of discourse" using his own theory of the One, with the young Aristotle as his respondent.</summary>

# ON THE ONE.

<margin>
The first supposition: "if the One is." It must be understood as "if unity exists." For the word "is" is added for the sake of <unclear>the expression</unclear>. And the first argument is from the contrary.
</margin>

Come then, if the One is, the One itself will certainly not be many. But how? Therefore, it must neither be a part of anything, nor must it be a whole. Why so? A part is surely a part of a whole. It is. What then? Is not a whole that from which no part is missing? Exactly. In both cases, therefore, the One itself would be composed of parts: both existing as a whole and having parts. It must be so. In both cases, again, the One itself would be many rather than one. True. But it must not be many; rather, it must exist as the One itself. It must indeed. Therefore, it will neither be a whole nor will it have parts, if the One itself is to be one. Certainly not. If it has no part, it will have neither a beginning, nor an end, nor a middle; for these would be parts of it. Correct. Furthermore, the beginning and the end are the limits of anything. Why not? Therefore, the One itself is infinite, since it lacks a beginning and an end. Infinite. Therefore, it is also without shape; for it partakes neither

<margin>
What is round. What is straight.
</margin>

of the round nor of the straight. Why? Furthermore, the round is that whose extremities are everywhere equally distant from the center. Precisely. And the straight is that whose middle is directly in front of both extremities. So it is. Would not the One itself have parts and be many if it partook of a straight or circular shape? Entirely so. Therefore, it is neither straight nor round, since it has no parts. Right. Furthermore, being such as it is, it is nowhere; for it can be neither in another nor in itself. Why so? If it were in another, it would be enclosed in a circle by that in which it was, and would be touched by it in many places and by many parts. But since the One is indivisible <note>original: "impartibile"</note> and devoid of roundness, it is impossible for it to be touched in many ways by a circle. Impossible. But if it were in itself, it would contain itself; being nothing other than itself, if indeed it were in itself. For nothing can be in anything without being

Therefore, the One itself is nowhere, since it is neither in another nor in itself. Nowhere. Consider, I pray, whether that which is of this sort can either stand still or move. Why not? Because

For part of it is already in that which it undergoes, and part is simultaneously outside. But that which consists of no parts can never be as a whole within something and as a whole simultaneously absent. True. Therefore, the One itself seems neither to stand still nor to move. It does not appear so. Likewise, it is the same neither as another nor as itself; and again, it is different neither from itself nor from another. Why so? If it were different from itself, it would be different from the One, and would not be one. True. And if it were the same as another, it would be that other, and not itself. Therefore, it would no longer be the One itself, but something other than the One. So it is. Therefore, it should never be said to be the same as another or different from itself. Never, clearly. But neither can it be different from another as long as it is one. For it does not befit the One to be different from anything; that belongs only to that which is "other" than another. But it fits no other. Correct. Therefore, from the fact that it is one, it will not be different. Or what do you think? Not at all. Because unless it were this, it would not be by itself; if not by itself, then not itself. But itself, being in no way different, is different from nothing. Right. Yet it will not be the same as itself. Why not? The nature of the One itself is not the same as the nature of "the same" <note>the concept of Identity</note>. Why?

The nature of the One is different from the nature of the Same.

It is impossible, therefore, for the One itself to be either different from another or the same as itself. Impossible.
