# PARMENIDES, OR ON THE ONE AS THE UNIVERSAL PRINCIPLE AND ON IDEAS. FOLIO XXVII.

It appeared from what was said before that the "same" is naturally distinct from the "one." It certainly appeared so. However, if the "one" itself receives anything besides that which is "one," it suffers being more than one. But that is impossible. Yes. For this reason, the "one" itself never allows itself to be the "same" as either itself or another. It does not seem so. Therefore, it cannot be "similar" either to itself or to another. So it appears. Nevertheless, it does not sustain being "other" any more than that; for then it would happen to be more than one. More indeed. That which becomes "other" than itself or another also becomes "dissimilar" to itself or to another; since that which receives being the "same" becomes "similar." Correct. Whence the "one" itself, since it has in no way received the "other," will never become "dissimilar" either to itself or to another. Never indeed. For which reason the "one" itself is neither "similar" nor "dissimilar" to itself or to another. No, so it seems. 

<margin>Each equal</margin>Besides these things, since it is of such a nature, it is neither "equal" nor "unequal" to anything, whether to itself or to another. Why so? Because that which is "equal" is of the same measures as that to which it is said to be equal. So it is. That which is "greater" or "lesser," in relation to those things with which it is commensurable, has more measures than the smaller and fewer than the larger. Certainly. But to those with which it is incommensurable, it will be of smaller measures in one respect and larger in another. Why not? Is it not impossible that that which in no way participates in the "same" should obtain either the same measures or anything else that is the same? Impossible. Therefore it will be equal neither to itself nor to another, since it does not use the same measures. Not at all, as it appears. Furthermore, if it were circumscribed by more or fewer measures, it would consist of as many parts as there are measures; and again it would no longer be "one," but rather as many as there are measures. Right. But if it were of one measure, it would become equal to that measure. Yet it appeared impossible for the "one" itself to be equal to anything. It certainly appeared so. Therefore, since it participates neither in one measure, nor in many, nor even in few, nor in any way in the "same," it will never be equal to itself, as it seems, nor to another; nor furthermore will it be greater or less than itself or another. It is exactly so. 

Or perhaps the "one" itself appears to be "older" or "younger" than something, or even of the "same age"? What prevents it? This indeed: since if it shares the same age with itself or with another, it will participate in equality and similarity of time. It was shown, however, that neither equality nor similarity can be present in the "one" itself. It was indeed shown. Did we not also say that it exists without partaking in inequality or dissimilarity? Most certainly. In what way, then, can that which is of such a nature be older or younger than anything, or equal in age to any? In no way. Therefore the "one" itself will not be younger, nor older, nor equal in age either to itself or to another. It does not appear so. Likewise, the "one" itself, being such, will never even be in any time. For it is necessary that whatever is in time should always become older than itself. Necessary. And that which is older is always older than something younger. Why not? Therefore, that which becomes older than itself also becomes younger than itself at the same time, if indeed it must exist in some sense. How do you say? In this way: one opposite does not need to "become" anything to the other when the other opposite already exists; but when this one already exists, the other has already passed; and in the future, it will be. While one opposite is "becoming," the other opposite has neither passed, nor will be, nor is: but is "becoming," and cannot be otherwise. Necessary. But "older" is an opposite to "younger," and to no other at all. It is. That which becomes older than itself, therefore, must also become younger than itself. It seems so. Furthermore, it does not become older or younger than itself for a longer or shorter time, but always becomes, and is, and was, and will be, for a time equal to itself. These things are also necessary. It seems necessary, therefore, that whatever is in time, and participates in such a thing, shares the same age with itself, and becomes older and younger than itself at the same time. It appears so. But none of these passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to "attributes" or "undergoing a state."</note> happen to the "one" itself. None. Therefore it participates in no time, nor is it in any time. Not indeed, as reason dictates. 

<margin>The words "is," "was," "will be," "becomes," "will become," "has been done," signify time. In the word "is," there is not only the thing itself, but also essence. Being is denied of the One. Of a non-entity there is nothing, and in a non-entity there is nothing.</margin>What then? Do not "it was," "it has been," "it was becoming," seem to signify participation in past time? Quite so. And "it will be," "it will become," "it will have been done," do they not designate the future to us? The future. And "is" and "becomes" are marks of the present time. Entirely so. If therefore the "one" itself participates in no time at all, it neither "was" ever, nor "becomes," nor "is," nor "will become," nor "will have been done," nor "will be." These things are most true. Can anything participate in essence <note>original: "essentia"</note> otherwise than according to one of these? Not otherwise. In no way, therefore, is the "one" itself. It does not appear so at all. It is not, therefore, in such a way that it "is" one; for it would then be a being and a participant in essence; rather, as it seems, the "one" itself is neither "one" nor "is," if this reasoning is to be believed. It appears so. But for that which "is not," is there anything either for it or of it? How could there be? Therefore it has no name, no discourse, no knowledge, no sense, no opinion. It does not seem so. Wherefore it is neither named, nor spoken of, nor thought of in opinion, nor known, nor is it perceived by any of those things which are. It certainly does not seem so. Or is it possible for these things to be so concerning the "one" itself? Not, as it seems to me.

I certainly wish it. If the "one" is, did we not confess what things happen concerning it, and of what sort they ought to be? Indeed. Meditate again from the beginning: if the "one" is, is it possible for it to be, but in no way participate in essence? Impossible. But the essence of the "one" will not be the same as the "one" itself. Otherwise, if it were the same, it would not be the essence of that thing, nor would the "one" itself have participated in it; but as often as "one is" was uttered, it would signify something similar, as if we said "one, one." This: If "it is" is said of the one being, and "one" is said of the being one; and essence and one are the same; since the "one" we supposed exists, is it not necessary that the whole itself is "one being," and its parts exist as both "one" and "being"? <margin>Because "one" concerning essence is also many.</margin>

Whenever I say "essence" and "one," do I not say "both"? You do. And if I say "essence and the other" or "the other and the one," do I not in each case say "both"? Exactly. Therefore, the "one" itself, distributed by essence, is an infinite multitude. It is clear. Not only, therefore, is the "one being" many, but the "one" itself, distributed by essence, must be many. # PARMENIDES, OR ON THE ONE, THE PRINCIPLE, AND ON IDEAS.

<margin>
The One is both one and many, a whole and parts, finite and infinite. Every whole has a beginning, middle, and end.
</margin>

...then the whole will be one. Do not the parts comprise the whole? They do. That which comprises, however, is a limit. It is. Therefore, the one being is, in a certain way, both one and many, a whole and parts, as well as finite and infinite in multitude. It appears so. Since it is limited, does it not also have extremities? It must. Furthermore, if it is a whole, will it not have a beginning, a middle, and an end? Can any whole be found without these three? And if any of them were distant from that which is one, would the whole still exist? Not at all. For this reason, the one has a beginning, a middle, and an end. It has. The middle, indeed, is at an equal distance from the extremities on all sides; for otherwise, it would not be the middle. Certainly not. Furthermore, since the one is such, it partakes of some figure, whether straight, or round, or some other composed of both. Without a doubt, it partakes. Moreover, if it is of this sort, it will be both in itself and in another. In what way? Any part is in the whole, and none is entirely outside the whole. Granted. Are the individual parts enclosed by the whole? Yes. But the one exists as all its own parts; it is neither more nor less than the sum of them. So it is. And is not the whole also one? Why not? If all the parts are enclosed by the whole, and the one is all of them and the whole itself, and the individual parts are contained by the whole, then the one will be contained by the one; and thus the one itself will now be in itself. So it seems. Yet, the whole is by no means in the parts—neither in all of them, nor in any one. For if it were in all, it would necessarily be in one; for if it were not in some one part, it could not be in all. But if this one consists of all the parts, and

<margin>
How it is understood that the one is contained by the one and by itself.
</margin>

the whole is in it, and not in one part, how can the one be in all of them? In no way. But it is no more in some of the parts. For if it were in some, the greater would be in the lesser, which is impossible. Impossible. If it were nowhere, would it not be nothing at all? And yet, since it is a whole and is not in itself, it remains that it exists in another. Entirely so.

That which is nowhere is nothing at all.

How everything stands and moves.

follow that it both stands still and is moved? Why so? It stands still, surely, because it remains in itself. For being inherent in the one, and not departing from it, it is in the same—that is, in itself. It is indeed. But that which is always in the same must always stand still. It must. On the other hand, that which is always in another must necessarily never be in the same; and if it is never in the same, it never stands still. That which does not stand still must be moved. So it is. It is necessary, therefore, that the one, since it is always in itself and in another, always both stands still and is moved. It seems so. Furthermore, it must be the same as itself, and other than itself; and likewise, in relation to other things, it must be both the same and other—if indeed what was said above applies to it. By what reasoning? Everything stands in relation to the universe in this way: it is either the same or other. If it is not the same or other, it will be a part of that to which it is related, or it will be as a whole to a part. That is clear. Is the one itself a part of itself? By no means. Therefore, it will not be a whole in relation to itself as if it were a part of itself. For that is not possible. Or is the one perhaps other than the one? Not at all. Therefore, it is not other than itself. Certainly not. If it is neither other, nor a whole, nor a part in relation to itself, what else remains but that it is the same as itself? That very thing. But what of this? That which is elsewhere than itself, while existing in the same as itself—is it not forced to become other than itself, if indeed it exists elsewhere than itself? So it seems to me. It was clearly shown that the one is of this kind: namely, that it is in itself and in another. It was indeed shown. From this, therefore, it is established that the one is other than itself. It seems so. But if something is other than something, is it not "other" by means of the <term>Other</term> <note>original: "alterum"; referring to the Platonic Form of Difference or Alterity</note>? Necessarily. Are not those things which are not one "other" than the one, and the one "other" than those which are not one? Why not? Therefore, the one will appear other than all other things. Other. Consider further: are not the "Other" itself and the "Same" itself opposites to each other? Why not? Will the Same ever be willing to exist in the Other, or the Other in the Same? Never. Therefore, if the Other is never in the Same, there is nothing among existing things in which the Other is for any amount of time. For if it were in something for any time, during that time the Other would be in the Same. Would it not? Since it is never in the Same, the Other will never be in any of the things that exist. You speak the truth. Therefore, the Other will be neither in those things which are not one, nor in the one. Certainly not. It follows that the one cannot be other than those things which are not one, nor those things which are not one be other than the one, by means of the Other itself. It clearly follows. Unless they participate in the Other, they cannot be other than one another by their own nature. But how? If they are other neither by themselves nor by the Other, they can in no way be other than each other. In no way. Furthermore, those things which are not one do not participate in the one at all, for then they would not be "not one," but in some way one. But for this reason, because they are not one, they are not even a number. Otherwise, they would not be entirely devoid of the one, if they possessed any number. Certainly not. But are those things which are not one parts of the one? Or is it in this way perhaps that they participate in the one? They participate. If, therefore, this is entirely one, and those are not one, the one will not be a part of those which are not one, nor a whole to them as if they were parts; nor again are those which are not one parts of the one, nor wholes as if the one were a part. Certainly not. But we have asserted that things which are neither wholes, nor parts, nor other than each other, must be the same as each other. We have. Do we therefore admit that the one, when it stands in such a relation to those things which are not one, is the same as them? We admit it. Therefore, the one, as it seems, is something other than other things and itself, and again the same as itself and them. So reason persuades. Is it not also similar and dissimilar to itself and others? Perhaps. Since it was shown to be other than others, the others will also be other than it. What prevents it? Is it not other than others in the same way that others are other than it—neither more nor less? Why not? If neither more nor less, it remains that it is similarly so. Similarly. Furthermore, if it happens to the one that it is other than others in the same way that others are other than it, from this it follows...

# BOOK NINE

...so that the same condition applies to the one as to the others. What do you say: does not each name have its own meaning? It does. And do you pronounce the same name either many times or once? Indeed. When you utter it once, do you call upon that which the name belongs to; and when many times, do you not? Or rather, whether you pronounce the same name once or often, is it not necessary that you always mean the same thing? Always the same. Is not "the other" <note>Latin: *alterum*</note> also a name imposed to signify something specific? It is. Therefore, as often as you utter this name, whether once or many times, you refer to nothing else, nor do you name anything other than that which this name belongs to. Necessarily. Therefore, when we say that the one is "other" than the others, and those others are "other" than the one, by pronouncing this name "other" twice, we never introduce it to signify anything else than the nature to which the name properly belongs. Entirely so. If, then, the one is other than the others, and the others are other than the one, by experiencing that same "otherness" which is in the others—according to that, and not according to something else—the one is other than the others; and whatever experiences the same thing is "similar" <note>Latin: *simile*</note>, is it not? Rather, it is so according to that. But in that the one has the property of being other than the others, according to this same point, anything is similar to anything else; for everything is other than everything else. So it seems. Is not "similar" the contrary to "dissimilar"? It certainly is. And is not "the other" the contrary to "the same"? That too. However, it was also shown that the one is "the same" as the others. It was clearly shown. But to be "the same" as the others is a contrary state to being "other" than the others. Very much so. Yet insofar as it was "other," it appeared "similar." From this. Therefore, insofar as it is "the same," it will be "dissimilar" according to the state contrary to that state which made it similar. For did not "otherness" make it similar? Precisely. Therefore, "sameness" will render it dissimilar; otherwise, it would not be the contrary of "otherness." It appears so. From these points, it is concluded that the one is both similar and dissimilar to the others: insofar as it is other, it is similar; insofar as it is the same, it is dissimilar. It seems to have such a logic. And it has this one too. Which? That insofar as it has experienced "sameness," it has not experienced something foreign. If it has not experienced something foreign, it is not dissimilar; if not dissimilar, it remains that it is similar. But if it has taken on something else, it is foreign; if foreign, it would be dissimilar. You speak truly. Therefore, because the one is both the same as the others and other than them, according to both of these and according to each of them, it will be both similar and dissimilar to the others. Most certainly. And will it not be the same way in relation to itself? Since it appeared both other than itself and the same as itself, will it not appear, according to both and each, equally similar and dissimilar? Very much so.

Consider further, I pray, in what way the one stands regarding touching or not touching itself and the others. I am considering it. It was established that the one itself is in itself as a whole. Correct. And is not the one also in the others? It is. Insofar as it is in the others, it touches the others; but insofar as it is in itself, it is prevented from touching the others, but touches itself, since it is in itself. It appears so. By this reasoning, the one touches both itself and the others. It touches them. But what about this? Must not whatever is going to touch something lie near that which it is to touch, and occupy that position which follows the position of the first thing? This is necessary. Therefore, if the one is to touch itself, it must exist immediately after itself, occupying the seat next to the place in which it is. It must entirely. If the one were two, would it not do this and exist in two places at once? But as long as it is one, it cannot. It is as you say. Therefore, the same necessity ensures that the one is not two, and does not touch itself. The same. But it will no more touch the others. Why? Because we said that whatever is to touch something must be placed separately, next to that which is to be touched, with no third intermediate between them. True. Therefore, at least two things must be present whenever there is to be a touch. There must. But if a third medium intervenes between two terms, there will be three things in order, but only two touches. Precisely. And so, whenever one thing is added, one touch is also added. From this, it happens that the touches themselves are exceeded by the multitude of numbers by one. For by as much as the first two exceeded the touches themselves (so that there were more in number than there were touches), by that much the total number thereafter exceeds the total touches. For thereafter, one is added to the number and one touch is added to the touches. Right. Therefore, however many things there are in number, there are always just as many touches, minus one. You speak the truth. Thus, if there were only the one, and not even two, there would be no touch. In what way? We said that the things which are "other" than the one are neither the one, nor do they participate in the one, as long as they are "others." We said that. From this, it is settled that there is no "one" number in the others, since the one is not present in them. Indeed, how could that happen? Whence the others are neither one, nor two, nor designated by any other number. Certainly not. Therefore, the one itself is only one, and there are not two. Not, as it appears. And if there are not two, there will be no touch. None. Therefore, neither does the one touch the others, nor the others the one, since no touch exists. Not at all. For all these reasons, the one touches itself and the others, and equally does not touch them. So it seems.

Is it, moreover, both equal and unequal, both to itself and to the others? But in what way? If the one were greater or smaller than the others, or the others again greater or smaller than it, they would not be so—the one from being one, and the others from being others—greater or smaller than each other from their own essences; but if, besides their own natures, both had "equality" <note>Latin: *aequalitatem*</note> in addition, they would be equal to each other. If these had "greatness" <note>Latin: *magnitudinem*</note> and those "smallness" <note>Latin: *paruitatem*</note>, or the one had greatness and the others smallness, whichever species greatness was present in would be the greater; whichever smallness was in would be the smaller. Necessarily. Are there not two such species, Greatness and Smallness? For if they did not exist, they would never be contrary to each other, nor be present in things. It is as you say. Therefore, if smallness happens to the one, or to the whole...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue from the previous section, specifically focusing on the relationship between "The One" and the concepts of size (greatness and smallness), number, and time. # PARMENIDES, OR ON THE ONE AS THE PRINCIPLE OF ALL THINGS, AND ON IDEAS. FOLIO XXIX.

<note>This heading identifies the text as part of the *Parmenides*, a notoriously difficult Platonic dialogue about the nature of unity and being.</note>

...resides in the whole or in some part. **It is necessary.** If it resides in the whole, it will either be amplified within through an equal extension across the entire one, or it will be encompassed by external limits. **Clearly.** Indeed, smallness infused equally into the one will undoubtedly be equal to the one; but if it encompasses it, it will be greater. **Why not?** Is it possible for smallness to be equal to or larger than anything, and thus produce the effects of greatness and equality, thereby ceasing from its own function? <note>The "function" of smallness is to make things smaller; if it makes them larger, it contradicts its own nature.</note> **Undoubtedly impossible.** Whence he concludes that smallness cannot be in the whole one. It remains, perhaps, that it is in a part. **It remains.** Yet not in the whole part; for it would produce the same effects against the part as it had against the whole; namely, it would always be equal to or greater than that very part in which it resides. **It follows necessarily.** Therefore, smallness will never adhere to any thing, since it adheres neither to the part nor to the whole. From which it follows that nothing will be small except smallness itself. **So it seems.** But neither will greatness be present. For anything else besides greatness itself would be greater—namely, that in which greatness resides. Nevertheless, nothing is small, which indeed ought to be exceeded by the great, if anything becomes great. For in what way will you find anything small if smallness resides in nothing? **You speak the truth.** Furthermore, greatness itself will be greater than nothing other than smallness; nor will smallness itself be smaller than anything other than greatness itself. **Than nothing.** Wherefore other things besides the One will be neither greater nor smaller than the One, since they are devoid of greatness and smallness. Nor will these two <note>Greatness and smallness</note> have any power against the One itself by which they might exceed it or be exceeded by it; rather, they will produce this effect between themselves. Nor indeed will the One itself be greater or smaller than these two, or any other things whatsoever, inasmuch as it is devoid of both greatness and smallness. **So it appears.** And therefore, since the One is neither greater nor smaller than other things, it will neither surpass others nor be surpassed by others. **Without a doubt.** Does it not necessarily follow that what neither surpasses nor is surpassed must be in an equal state? And if in an equal state, that it is equal? **Indeed.** Furthermore, if the One relates to itself as being devoid of both greatness and smallness, it would neither exceed itself nor be exceeded by itself; but being in an equal state, it would always be equal to itself. **Most certainly.** Thus the One is equal to itself and to others. **So it seems.** Nevertheless, since the One is in itself, it circles itself from the outside; and thus, embracing itself, it stands out as larger than itself; and since it is also contained, it is narrower; whereby it happens that the One is both greater and smaller than itself. **It so happens.** Is this not also necessary, that nothing is found besides the One and "others"? **Necessary.** Likewise, whatever exists, must it not always be somewhere? **It must.** Furthermore, that which is in something: is it not always the smaller in the larger? For otherwise one thing would not be in another. **It is as you say.** But since there is nothing besides the One and others, and it is necessary for these to be in something: is it not necessary that these be in each other in turn? The others in the One, and the One in the others; or else exist nowhere at all? **It is established.** Because, therefore, the One is in the others, for that reason the others are greater than the One, inasmuch as they contain the One; but the One is smaller than the others, because it is contained. But because the others are in the One, the One is greater than the others for the same reason, and those others are smaller. **It seems so.** The One, therefore, is equal, greater, and smaller than itself and others. **It appears so.** And yet, if it is greater, smaller, and equal, it will be of equal, more, and fewer measures in relation to itself and to others; and if of measures, then also of parts. **What prevents it?** Having, therefore, the same measures, and more, and fewer, it will also be more and less in number, both in relation to itself and to the rest; and also equal to itself and others for the same reasons. **In what way?** Those things than which it is greater, it has more measures than they; and as many measures, so many parts; and those than which it is smaller, in the same way; or those to which it is equal, likewise. **It is so.** Is it not, since it is greater, smaller, and equal to itself, that it participates in equal, more, and fewer measures in relation to itself; and since in measures, also in parts? **Why not?** And having parts equal to itself, it will be equal to itself in multitude; but having more, it will be more; and finally, having fewer, it will be less in number than itself? **It seems so.** And will the One not relate to others in a similar way? Because it appears greater than them, it must be more in number than they; but because it is smaller in size, it is also smaller in number; and finally, because it is equal in size, it must also be equal in number. **It happens necessarily.** By this reasoning again, the One will be equal, more, and less according to number in relation to itself and the others. **It will indeed.** Does the One not also participate in time, and is it not, and does it not become, younger and older than itself and others at the same time? And again, on the contrary, neither younger nor older than itself or others while it participates in time? **But how can that be?** To "be" certainly belongs to it, if indeed it is the One. **It belongs.** 

<margin>What the word "to be" [data esse] means.</margin> 

But what else is "to be" itself than the participation of essence with the present time? Just as "it was" is the communication of its essence with the past, and "it will be" with the future? **That is it exactly.** Therefore, if it participates in "being" itself, it must also be a participant in time. **Certainly.** Is it not of flowing time? **Surely.** Therefore, it always becomes older than itself, if indeed it runs according to time. **Necessary.** Do we remember that what becomes older always becomes older than that which is becoming younger? **We remember.** Therefore, since the One becomes older than itself, does it not become both younger and older than itself while it becomes older? **It is necessary.** It becomes, therefore, in this manner, younger and older than itself. **It does.** But is it not "older" then, when it reaches the "now" of present time, which is the middle between "was" and "will be"? For in running from the preceding to the succeeding, it does not skip over the "now" itself. **Certainly not.** Does it not then cease becoming older as soon as it touches the present? And then it does not "become," but "is" already older? For that which proceeds from the present itself is by no means grasped. For that which proceeds is so situated that it touches both the present and the future: leaving the present, and apprehending the future, falling as a medium between the two, the present and the future. **True.** But if it is necessary that whatever "becomes" cannot bypass the present itself: as soon as it has reached it, it ceases to become, and is then already that which it was becoming. **It appears so.** The One, therefore, when it has become older...

the present catches up to it, it ceases becoming, and is now older. Entirely so. And is it not older than that which was becoming older? It was becoming older than itself. Yes. But that which is older is older than something younger. Therefore, the One is younger than itself at the moment when, having become older, it catches up to the present. Necessarily. Furthermore, the present is always with the One throughout its entire being; for it is always "present" as long as it exists. Why should it not be? Therefore, the One always is and becomes both younger and older than itself. So it seems. Moreover, is it for a longer or shorter time than itself, or rather an equal time? Equal. When it exists or becomes for an equal time, it maintains the same age. What prevents it? But when it fulfills the same age, it is neither older nor younger. Not at all. Therefore, since the One both is and becomes for a time equal to itself, it neither is nor becomes older or younger than itself. It certainly does not seem so to me. But how does it stand in relation to other things? I do not know what to say. You can say this much: that things other than the One, if indeed they are "others" and not "the other," are more than one. For if they were "the other," they would be one. But since they are others, they are more than one and possess a multitude. They certainly do. But a multitude possesses a larger number than one. Certainly. What then? Of those things that pertain to number, which shall we say come into being first: those that are more, or those that are fewer? Those that are fewer. Therefore, that which is the fewest is first. And is that not the One? Indeed. The One, therefore, was the first made of all things that possess number; and all other things possess number, since they are "others" and not "another." They certainly do. But that which was made first existed earlier, and the others later. Those made later are younger than that which was made before. And so, in this way, the others are younger than the One, and the One is more ancient than them. Certainly. But what about this? Can the One be made contrary to its own nature? Or is that rather impossible? Impossible. Yet it appeared that the One has parts; and if it has parts, it also has a beginning, a middle, and an end. Clearly. Does not the beginning come into being first of all—both of the One and of each of the others—and after the beginning, all the rest until the end? Why not? Do we admit that all these remaining things are parts of the whole and of the One? And that the One itself was made as a whole and a unit only together with the end? We admit it. The end, I think, is made last; and at the same time, the One is completed according to its nature. For this reason, if it is necessary that the One is not made contrary to its nature, then being completed at the same time as the end, it is by right of its nature perfected last of all. Thus, the One is younger than the others, and the others are more ancient than the One. So it seems to me again. But what! A beginning or any other part, whether of the One or of any other thing—if it is a part and not parts—is it not "one," since it exists as a part? That is necessary. From this it follows that the One comes into being simultaneously with the first part made, and simultaneously with the second, and is never absent from any of the others that come into being, until, running through to the very last, it becomes a whole One—excluded from generation neither by the first, nor the middle, nor the last, nor any other at all. True. Therefore, the One is of the same age as all the others. Wherefore, if the One itself was not born contrary to its nature, it is neither earlier nor later than the others, but rather was made at the same time. And so, according to this reasoning, the One is neither older nor younger than the others, nor the others than the One; but according to the previous reasoning, the One is both older and younger than all the others, and conversely, all the others than the One. It would be entirely so. This, then, is how it stands, and such is the result. But what do you think of the statement that the One becomes older and younger than the others, and the others than the One, and also that it becomes neither younger nor older? Does it stand in the same relation regarding "becoming" as we said it did regarding "being," or otherwise? I do not know what to say. I will say only this: if one thing is more ancient than another, it cannot become more ancient than it was before by any greater interval of age; nor can that which is younger become younger in the future. For equals added to unequals—whether to time or to anything else—always make them differ by the same interval as before. Nothing prevents it. Therefore, that which exists cannot become either more ancient or younger than the One, since the same distance of age always intervenes; rather, it is and was older, and the other younger, but it by no means "becomes" so. It is as you say. Thus, the One never becomes either younger or older than the other things that exist. Never. But look hereafter whether they become younger and older in some other way. In what way? In this way, I say. Was it not established that the One is more ancient than the others, and the others than the One? What then? Since the One is older than the others, it has existed for a longer time than they. Indeed. Pay attention.

| **Three-cubit line.** <note>original: *Linea tricubitalis*. A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm.</note> | **Cubit added.** |

For if you add an equal cubit to a three-cubit line (as the longer) and to a two-cubit line (as the shorter), you will make a four-cubit line with the former and a three-cubit line with the latter. But the four-cubit line exceeds the three-cubit line by a smaller fraction than the three-cubit line exceeds the two-cubit line. For the three-cubit line exceeds the two-cubit line by half of the two-cubit line; but the four-cubit line exceeds the three-cubit line by a third part of the three-cubit line, which is a smaller fraction than a half. The same is found in other additions where longer things exceed shorter ones; the same ratios derived from the longer ones produce the same result. Just as three exceeds two by one-third <note>The translator likely means the difference (1) is 1/3 of the new total (3), or is comparing the ratios of growth.</note>, and four exceeds three by one-fourth, which is less than a third.

# PARMENIDES, OR ON THE ONE AS THE UNIVERSAL PRINCIPLE AND ON IDEAS. FOLIO XXX.

Consider again: if we add an equal amount of time to a longer and a shorter period, does the longer then differ from the shorter by an equal fraction, or a smaller one? By a smaller one. Therefore, the One will not exceed others by as great an interval of age as it did before; rather, having received an equal amount of time as the others, it will always differ from them by a smaller proportion of age than before. Is it not so? Certainly. And if something exceeds another by less age than before, does it not become younger than before in relation to those things compared to which it was older? Younger, without a doubt. If that becomes younger, will not those others become older than before in relation to the One? Entirely so. That which was becoming younger before, therefore, becomes older in relation to that which was becoming [older] before and was more ancient. Yet it is never actually "more ancient"; rather, it is always *becoming* more ancient than the other. The latter, moreover, grows younger, while the former grows older; conversely, that which is older is similarly made younger than the younger. For since these tend in opposite directions, they become opposites to one another: the younger becomes older than the older, and the older becomes younger than the younger. But they cannot have *become* so [already]. For if they had already become so, they would no longer be becoming, but would already be. As it is, they are becoming both younger and older than one another. The One becomes younger than the others because it appeared to be older and to have been brought into being first. The others become older than the One because they were brought into being later. By the same logic, the others stand in a similar relation to the One, since they appeared to have been brought into being earlier and prior to it. The same seems true to me as well. Is it not by this reasoning that neither becomes younger or older than the other, insofar as they differ from one another by an equal number? Just as the One would not become older or younger than the others, nor the others than the One? But by the reason that the prior must always differ from the posterior (and vice versa) by a certain part, it is necessary that they become older and younger than each other—both the others in relation to the One, and the One in relation to the others. Most certainly. For all these reasons, therefore, the One is and becomes both older and younger than itself and others; and again, it neither is nor ever becomes younger or older than itself or others. Exactly. Since the One is the principle of time, and can become older and younger, is it not also necessary that it participates in the past, the present, and the future, since it participates in time? It follows necessarily. Therefore, the One was, and is, and will be; and it was becoming, and is becoming, and will become. Why not? There would also be something belonging to it and of it; there was, and is, and will be. Most certainly. And therefore, there would be knowledge, opinion, and perception of it, since we ourselves are presently treating all these matters concerning it. You speak rightly. Likewise, a name and a definition <note>original: "sermo," often translated as "discourse" or "account"</note> belong to it; it is named and spoken of. And whatever such things are found regarding other entities, they also exist regarding the One. That is exactly how the matter stands.

<margin>The third supposition: that is, if the One is not, it does not participate in existence <note>original: "sub esse"</note></margin>
But now, for the third time, let us discuss it again. If the One is as we have described above—is it not necessary, since it is both one and many, and again neither one nor many, and a participant in time—that because it is "one," it participates in essence <note>meaning "being" or "substance"</note> at some time; but because it "is not," it does not participate at another time? This is necessary. Is it possible that while it participates, it then participates not at all? Or when it does not participate, that it then participates? Impossible. Therefore, it is a participant at one time, and at another time it is without a share. For only in this way can it be both a participant and non-participant in the same thing. Correct. Is there not a time when it receives being, and when it loses being? Or how can it be that it sometimes has it, and sometimes does not, unless it at one time acquires it and at another loses it? Not otherwise. To receive essence—do you not call this "becoming"? I do. And to be deprived of essence, is that not "to be destroyed"? Most certainly. The One, therefore, as it seems, by taking up and laying down essence, comes into being and passes away. Necessarily. And since it becomes both one and many, being generated and failing, does it not cease to be many when it becomes one, and cease to be one when it becomes many? Greatly so. And when it becomes one and many, must it not be dispersed and gathered together? It must. Also, whenever it becomes unlike and like, must it not be assimilated and, so to speak, "dis-assimilated"? Indeed. And when it becomes greater, smaller, and equal, must it not increase, decrease, and be equalized? So it is. But whenever it passes from motion into rest, or from rest into motion, this must not happen in a single [stretch of] time. For what reason? Because after it has first stood still, it is moved afterward; and having been moved before, it then comes to a halt. For it cannot undergo these things without a change <note>original: "transmutatione"</note>. It cannot. But there is no time in which a thing can be in such a state that it neither stands still nor moves. None. Nevertheless, it does not pass over without a change. That would not be consistent. When, then, does it pass over? For it does not pass over while it stands still, nor while it moves, nor while it is in time. Certainly not.

<margin>The "moment" and the "instant" are found. The moment is a middle nature between motion and rest.</margin>
Is there not this marvelous thing in which it then exists when it passes over? What is that? The indivisible "moment" <note>original: "momentum," referring to the Greek *exaiphnēs* or the "sudden"</note>, I say; for this moment signifies a certain thing from which the transition to either state is made. For it does not pass over from a state of rest while it is resting, nor from motion while it is moving. But this momentary nature itself is wonderful: it is placed as a middle between motion and rest; it is in no time at all; and into this and out of this, that which was moved passes into a state of rest, and that which was resting passes into motion. It appears so. Thus the One, if indeed it stands still and moves, undoubtedly passes into both states. For only in this way does it do both. But in passing, it passes in an indivisible moment. And when it migrates, it is in no time; it neither stands still then, nor moves. Not at all. Does it not stand in the same relation to other changes: when it migrates from being itself into destruction, or from non-being into becoming? It then becomes a middle between certain motions and states; it neither is then, nor is it not; it neither becomes nor is destroyed. So it seems. By the same reasoning, when migrating from one into many, and from many into one, it is neither one nor many; it is neither gathered together nor dispersed. And migrating from like to unlike, and again from unlike to like, it is neither like nor unlike; neither assimilated nor, so to speak, dis-assimilated. And from small into great, and into the equal itself, and vice versa...

<summary>This page explores the temporal paradoxes of "The One," arguing that it must exist in a state of constant transition (the "moment") to move between opposite states like motion and rest or being and non-being.</summary>

# BOOK NINE.

passing through: not small: not large: not increasing: not decreasing: not equalizing. It is not seen.
All these things, therefore, if the One exists, it experiences. Why not?

---

<margin>Fourth supposition.</margin>
Must we not consider what the others <note>The "others" (Latin: *alia*) refers to everything that is not the "One."</note> besides the One experience, if the One exists? We must. Do we say that if the One exists, the things other than the One must experience something? We do. Is it not because they are other than the One that they are not the One? Otherwise, they would not be other than the One. Correct. Yet they are not entirely deprived of the One, but in a certain way they participate in the One. By what reasoning? Because the things other than the One, by the fact that they consist of parts, are other than the One; for unless they had parts, they would be entirely one. Right. Moreover, we have asserted that the parts belong to that which is a whole. We have clearly asserted it. And yet the whole itself must be one made of many, of which the parts 
<margin>A part is not of the many but of the whole</margin>
are what are called parts. For any of the parts is not a part of the many, but exists as a part of the whole. But how is this? If it were a part of the many among which it existed, it would be in some way a part of itself—which is impossible—and a part of each of the others. For if it is not a part of the one whole, but of all the others, it will be a part of each one. And thus it will not be a part of each one <note>The logic here is that a part cannot belong to a collective "many" without belonging to a unified "whole."</note>. But not being a part of each, it will be a part of none of the many. And if it is a part of none of all these things, it is impossible for it to be anything at all. That is clear. Therefore, whatever is a part is not a part of the many nor of all, but of a certain single idea and a certain single thing which we call a "whole," made one and perfect out of all. It is a part of this, I say, whatever part it may be. Entirely so. If, therefore, the others have parts, they participate in the whole and in the One. Most certainly. Whence it is necessary that the others themselves, being different from the One, are one perfect whole containing parts. Necessary. Furthermore, the same reasoning applies to each individual part. For it must participate in this One. For if each of them is a part, this very expression "each one" signifies "one" in some way. For it signifies something distinct from the others and existing by itself, if indeed it is to be "each one." Right. But it will be a participant in the One if it is something other than the One; otherwise, it would not participate, but would be the One itself. But indeed, nothing can be one except the One itself. It is necessary for both the whole and the part to participate in the One. For the whole itself will be one, of which the individual parts are parts; and each part will be one part of the whole, whatever part of the whole it may be. So it is. Is it not then the case that since they are other than the One, all things that participate do so by the One? Why not? But the things other than the One are in some way "many." For if they were neither one nor more than one, they would be nothing at all. Nothing indeed. But since they are more than one, being participants in a single part and a single whole, is it not necessary that the things participating in the One are infinite in multitude? In what way? Clearly this: they are something other than the One, and they do not yet participate in the One at the moment they first begin to participate in it. Certainly. Are they not multitudes in which the One is not present? Multitudes, certainly. Because if we wish to extract by the intellect the smallest possible thing from them, will it not be necessary that the thing extracted—since it lacks the One—is a multitude and not one? Necessary. Does it not seem to you that by always considering the nature of that other species <note>The "other species" refers to the nature of "the many" or "the other" when viewed apart from the unifying principle of the One.</note> in itself, however much you look, it will always appear infinite in multitude? Very much so. Nevertheless, after each part has become one, the parts now have a limit <term>terminus: a boundary or limit that defines a thing's form</term> in relation to each other and to the whole, and the whole in relation to the parts. Quite so. Thus, for the things other than the One, it happens that from the One itself and from themselves—now communicating in the One—something else arises in them which provides a limit to each other; whereas their own nature, according to itself, is infinity. It is manifest. In this way, then, the things other than the One are both wholes and parts: they are both infinite and they participate in a certain limit. Entirely. Are they not, moreover, both similar and dissimilar to each other and to themselves? Why? Insofar as they are all infinite according to their own nature, they all experience the same thing in this regard. They do. Likewise, insofar as they all participate in a limit, they all experience the same thing in this regard as well. Why not? Yet, insofar as it happens that they are both finite and infinite at the same time—which are contrary states <term>passiones: "passions" or "affections," meaning the properties or conditions a thing undergoes</term>—they are as dissimilar as possible. Exceedingly so. Therefore, according to either condition, they will be similar to themselves and to each other. But according to both conditions together, they will be most contrary and dissimilar. It is established. Thus, the others will be the same as themselves and each other, and both similar and dissimilar. They will be. And we shall easily find that those things which are other than the One are the same and different from each other, both in motion and at rest, and undergoing all other contrary conditions, since they have already undergone the aforementioned conditions. You speak rightly.

---

<margin>Fifth supposition.</margin>
Should we not, moreover, if we pass over these things as clear, consider again: if the One exists, will the things other than the One also behave in this way? Or only in this way? Entirely. Must we then start again from the beginning: if the One exists, what must the others experience? We must. Will not the One be separate from the others, and the others separate from the One? Why? Because there is nothing else besides these which is different from the One and different from the others. All things are essentially encompassed when "the One" and "the others" are mentioned. All things. Therefore, nothing remains besides these in which both the One and the others might reside as if in the same seat. Nothing at all. Never, therefore, do the One and the others coincide in the same thing. Never. They are therefore separate. Separate. Moreover, it was said that the One itself truly has no parts. But how could it have them? Therefore, neither the One as a whole will be in the others, nor will its parts be in them, since it is separate from the others and consists of no parts. So it is. In no way, therefore, will the others participate in the One, since they take neither the whole of it nor a part. In no way, it seems. And for that reason, the others [are] in no way...

<summary>This page explores the relationship between "the One" and "the others," arguing that for anything to exist as a whole or a part, it must participate in the principle of Unity. It concludes that without the One, the "others" would be an infinite, formless multitude, but through participation, they acquire limits and properties.</summary>

# PARMENIDES, OR CONCERNING THE ONE AS THE UNIVERSAL PRINCIPLE AND CONCERNING IDEAS.

...are one: nor do they have any unity within themselves. **By no means.** Therefore, the "others" are neither many nor one. For if they were many, each of them, being a part of a whole, would be one. But now, being neither one, nor many, nor a whole, nor parts, the others are nothing, since they participate in the One in no way. **Correct.** Wherefore they are neither two, nor three, nor does any "one" exist in them, since they are utterly deprived of the One. **So it is.** Thus, the others are neither like, nor unlike, nor the same as the One: nor does likeness or unlikeness exist in them. For if they were like and unlike, by the very fact of having likeness and unlikeness within themselves, they would contain within themselves two contrary forms <note>original: "species"</note> just as much as the One itself. **It appears so.** But it is impossible for things that participate in nothing to receive two certain things within themselves. **Certainly not.** Therefore, they are neither like, nor even unlike: nor both together; for if they were like or unlike, they would participate in one or another form: and if both, in two certain contrary forms, but these have been shown to be impossible. **You speak the truth.** Therefore they are not the same, nor other, nor moved, nor at rest, nor arising, nor perishing, nor greater, nor smaller, nor equal, nor finally have they obtained anything of this kind. For if they received any such thing, they would participate in one, and two, and three, and in the even and the odd: participation in which is forbidden to them, as they utterly lack the One. **These things are most true.** For these reasons, therefore, if the One is, the One is all things, and it is nothing, both in relation to itself and to others in the same way. **The matter stands entirely thus.**

---

<margin>The sixth supposition.</margin>
**But** indeed, if the One is not, must we not consider what follows after this? **We must.** What then is this supposition: "if the One is not"? Does it differ in any way from this: "if the Not-One is not"? **It differs indeed.** Does it only differ? Or is this—"if the Not-One is not"—entirely contrary to that—"if the One is not"? <margin>A negative from an infinite subject is the contrary of a negative from a finite subject.</margin> **Entirely contrary.** But what if someone should say: "if greatness is not," or "smallness is not," or anything else of this kind, would he not demonstrate in each case that he expresses "non-being" as something distinct? **Entirely.** Does he not then now declare that he calls "non-being" something other than the rest when he says, "if the One is not": and do we understand what he says? **We understand.** First, therefore, he expresses something that can be known: then something different from the others, when he says "the One," whether he adds "to be" or "not to be" to it; nevertheless, he knows what he says is "not to be," and that it is something different from the others, does he not? **Necessarily.** In this manner, therefore, it must be said from the beginning: if the One is not, what must it be? In the first place, therefore, this must happen to it, as it seems: namely, that there is some knowledge of it: or else we understand nothing of what we say when we utter "if the One is not." **You speak the truth.** And is it not also the case that "others" are different from it, or is it not predicated as different from the others? **Most certainly.** Therefore, diversity <note>or "difference"</note> also belongs to it besides knowledge. For he does not speak of the diversity of others when he calls the One different from the others, but of its own diversity. **It appears so.** Furthermore, he says this "non-being" participates in "that," and "of something," and "this," and "to this," and "of these," and all things of this sort. For he would not speak of "the One," nor of "others" from it, nor would anything belong to it, nor would he name anything of it, unless it were a participant in "something" and other such things. **Right.** However, for the One to "be" unless it exists is impossible. But nothing prevents it from participating in many things. **True.** It is necessary: if indeed that "One" itself, and no other, is not. But if neither "the One" nor "that" is, nor will it even be, but the discourse is about some "certain thing," then nothing ought to be pronounced. But if "that One" specifically, and not another, is presupposed, it must be said to participate in "not being" itself, and in many other things. **And most especially.** Wherefore unlikeness belongs to it in relation to others. For since the others are different from the One, they must be foreign to it. **They must.** And are not foreign things alienated? **Why not?** And are not alienated things unlike? **Plainly unlike.** And if they are unlike the One, they will be unlike an unlike thing. **Plainly.** Therefore, unlikeness will also be present in the One, according to which the others are unlike it. **It seems so.** And if unlikeness to others belongs to it, will not likeness to itself be appropriate? **In what way?** If unlikeness to the One were in the One, the discourse would surely not be about such a thing as the One: nor would the supposition be about the One, but about some other thing. **Exactly.** Nor indeed would it be fitting. For this reason, it is necessary for likeness to itself to be present in the One. **It must.** Likewise, it is not equal to others. For if it were equal, it would already surely "be": and it would exist as similar to them according to equality. Both of these, however, are impossible, since the One is not at all. **Impossible.** But since it is not equal to the rest, is it not also necessary that the others are by no means equal to it? **Necessary.** And those things which are not equal, are they unequal? **Unequal.** And are unequal things unequal to some unequal thing? **Certainly.** Whence the One also appears to be a participant in inequality, according to which the others are unequal to it. **A participant indeed.** Furthermore, greatness and smallness pertain to inequality. **They pertain.** And therefore greatness and smallness belong to such a "One." **It seems so.** Again, greatness and smallness are always distant from each other. **They are distant.** And therefore a certain middle always intervenes. **Certainly.** Do you find any other middle between these except equality? **None.** It is established, therefore, that equality, greatness, and smallness seem to happen to the One while it is not. **They seem so.** Besides these, it must also participate in essence <note>original: "essentia"</note> in some way. **But how?** It must have itself in the way we have said; for unless it were so, we would by no means be speaking the truth when we confess the One is not. But if we speak the truth, it is manifest that we are uttering things that "are," is it not? **It is so.** And when we say that we speak the truth, it is necessary that we profess to assert things that "are." **Necessary.** <margin>If a thing exists, the speech from it is true: if the speech made from the thing is true, the thing is also true.</margin> Therefore, the One is, as it seems, a "non-being." For if it were not "non-being," but should yield some part of its being to this—that it is not—it would immediately be "non-being." **Entirely so.** It must therefore have "being non-being" as a bond of its "not being," if it ought not to be: just as "being" itself has "not being non-being" as a bond of its own being, so that it may be allowed to "be" perfectly again. For thus "being" itself will most truly be: and "non-being" itself will most truly not be, if "being" itself participates in the essence of being "being," and not...

<summary>This page concludes the first series of deductions regarding the One and begins the "Sixth Supposition," exploring the paradoxical properties of the One if it is assumed not to exist. It argues that even a non-existent One must possess certain attributes like difference, unlikeness, and a form of "being non-existent" to be a subject of discourse.</summary>

# BOOK NINE

<note>original: "LIBER NONVS"</note>

...the essence of being is non-being, if it must exist at all; but non-being itself does not participate in the essence of *not* being non-being, but rather in the essence of *not* being being: if indeed non-being is to be seen as such entirely. These things are most true. Therefore, since being is a participant in non-being, and non-being is a participant in being itself, is it not necessary for each one, since it is not, to participate in being itself, so that it may truly not be? It is necessary. Essence, therefore, appears to be present in the One if it is not. It appears so. And non-essence again: if it is not at all. Why not? Can anything, which is said to be affected in a certain way, be said to be so and not to be so, when it has not yet been changed from a state of this kind? It cannot. Whatever, therefore, is so and is not so, undergoes a certain change. It undergoes it. But shall we call change a motion <note>original: "motum"</note>, or something else? Motion. And did not the One appear as both being and non-being? It appeared so. Therefore, it is both so and not so. It appears so. Therefore, the non-existent One appears to be moved, since it receives a change from being itself into non-being. It is clear. But indeed, if it is nowhere in the nature of things: since it is not, it certainly cannot migrate from one place to another. For how could it? Therefore, it does not move by passing through. Not at all. Nor yet will it revolve in the same place. For that very "same" <note>the concept of identity or fixed location</note> it nowhere touches. For "the same" is being; but it is impossible for non-being to be in any of those things which exist. It is certainly impossible. Therefore, the One, since it is not, could never revolve in that in which it is not at all. Never. Nor is the One altered from itself, whether it exists or does not exist. For the discourse would no longer be about the One if it were altered from itself, but about something other than the One. Correct. If it is neither altered, nor revolves in the same place, nor moves forward, how shall it be moved? In no way. But that which cannot be moved must necessarily be at rest; and that which rests must stand still. Necessary. Therefore, if the One is not: it stands still and is moved. It appears so. Furthermore, if it is moved, it must undoubtedly be changed; for insofar as something is moved, it is no longer in the same state as before, but in another. Clearly. Therefore, while the One is moved, it is also altered. Certainly. Yet, being in no way moved, it is in no way altered. In no way at all. Therefore, the One which is not: insofar as it is moved, it is undoubtedly altered; but insofar as it is not moved, it is not altered at all. Not at all. And thus the One, if it does not exist, is altered and also not altered. It is established. That which is altered: must it not become other than before, and cast off its former state? And that which is not altered: must it neither become nor perish? It follows necessarily. Whence the One which is not: because it is altered, it is created and perishes; but because it is not altered, it neither becomes nor perishes. And so it both becomes and perishes alike. And again, it neither becomes nor perishes. So it is.

<margin>
The seventh supposition.
What "non-being" signifies.
Non-being simply cannot exist, nor touch essence.
</margin>
Now let us return again to the beginning, to see clearly whether these things appear hereafter as they have until now, or otherwise. This is worthwhile. Have we not already discussed what happens concerning the One if it is not at all? We have. But as often as we utter "non-being," does it signify anything else to us than the absence of essence from that which we pronounce not to be? Nothing else. When we say something is not, do we understand it in some way not to be, and in some way to be? Or rather, does this very phrase, "it is not," whenever it is pronounced, simply signify that it is in no way whatever; and since it is not, it is in no part capable of essence? It signifies that absolutely. Therefore, non-being itself cannot be, nor can it touch essence in any other way. Not at all. But are becoming and perishing anything other than the former receiving essence, and the latter losing it? Nothing else. Therefore, that to which no part of this can belong: it never either receives it or loses it. Never. Therefore, since the One is in no way, it is not fitting for it to be born, nor to be cast away, nor in any way to receive essence. It is proper. Thus the One itself does not perish since it is not, nor does it become, as it is in no part capable of essence. It does not appear so. Nor again is it in any way altered; for then it would both become and perish, if it could suffer this. True. If it is not altered, is it not also necessary that it be in no way moved? Necessary. Yet we shall not assert that what in no way is stands still anywhere; for that which stands must always be in some "same" thing. Why not? Thus we shall plainly confess that it, since it is not, never either stands or moves. Never. Furthermore, nothing of those things which exist is present to it. For then it would participate in essence, as it would be a participant in something existing. It is manifest. Therefore, neither greatness, nor smallness, nor equality happens to it. Certainly not. But no more will likeness or diversity be present to it, either toward other things or toward itself. It appears not at all. And can other things be in any way to it, since nothing at all can be to it? It is not permitted. Wherefore other things are not like it, nor unlike it, nor the same, nor other. Certainly not. Or will that which is "of it," or "to it," or "something," or "this," or "of this," or "of another," or "to another," or "once," or "hereafter," or "now," or knowledge, or opinion, or sense, or speech, or a name, or any other of those things which exist, exist concerning that which is not at all? Not at all. By these reasons, therefore, if the One is not, it is in no way whatever. It certainly does not seem to be in any way whatever.

<margin>
The eighth supposition.
</margin>
It must be discussed again: if the One is not, what must the things other than the One suffer? It must be discussed. First, therefore, those other things must exist; for unless they were "others," there would be no discussion about "other" things. So it is. And if the talk is of others, the others are surely different. Do you not call "other" and "different" the same thing? I do. Do we not say that the different is different from another different thing, and the other is other than another? Certainly. Therefore, if there are to be others to these others, there will be something by which they are others. Necessary. What then will that especially be? They will not be others from the One, since that is not at all. Certainly not. Therefore, they are others to each other. For that alone remains, otherwise they are from nothing...

<summary>This page explores the logical paradoxes of the "Non-Existent One," arguing that if the One does not exist, it must simultaneously undergo change and remain still, while also concluding that absolute non-being cannot participate in any qualities like size, likeness, or time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translation of a Latin edition of Plato's Parmenides, specifically the concluding arguments regarding the "One" and the "Others," before transitioning into Marsilio Ficino's introduction to the Philebus.</meta>

FO. XXXII.

# ARGUMENT ON THE PHILEBUS

others will be. Correct. Therefore, according to the multitudes, each is different from the other. For indeed, according to the "one," they cannot be, if the one does not exist. But any heap of them, as it seems, exists as an infinite multitude. And if someone suspects what appears to be the smallest <note>referring to a point or atom</note>, like a dream within a dream, suddenly instead of what had seemed to be one, a multitude occurs; and instead of what had appeared smallest, it now appears very great compared to those parts selected and discerned from it, most rightly. In such heaps, I say, things will be diverse from one another besides the one, if, the one not existing, others exist. Most certainly. Will there not be many heaps? Each of which will seem to be one at first glance, yet none will be one, since the one itself is not at all? Certainly. Likewise, some number of them will seem to be present, if indeed each is one, even though they are many. Very much so. Furthermore, even and odd will falsely appear, with the one being entirely absent. Falsely. Moreover, that which first appears small in them, as was said, immediately shows itself as very great and very numerous in relation to the individual small parts, which are also many. What prevents it? Each equal heap will also seem to be many and small heaps. For it would not clearly seem to have passed from the greater to the lesser, unless it first seemed to have come to the middle; but this will be a certain phantom of equality. It is likely. Does it not have a limit toward another heap, but toward itself it has neither beginning, nor middle, nor end? For what reason? Because whenever the intellect contemplates any of these, another beginning always occurs before the beginning, and after the end, another end always follows; likewise in the middle, there are always other things more internal than the middle, and always smaller, because not even one thing can be grasped in these, since the one is not at all. You speak most truly. Finally, I think it must necessarily be torn apart as something dispersed, whatever the intellect assumes. For a heap is always grasped as being of one. Without a doubt. Does not such a thing appear as one to someone looking from a distance and dimly? Necessarily. But to one understanding closely and sharply, is not each thing infinite in multitude, since it is deserted by the non-existent one? This is necessary above all else. In this way, therefore, all other things must appear infinite, and having a limit, and one and many, if not the one, but others besides the one exist. It must be so. Will they not also appear similar and dissimilar? But how? For since all things appear as one to someone looking from a distance like a sketch, they will seem to communicate in some same thing and be similar. Entirely. But to one approaching closer, they appear many and different, and by the very phantom of diversity, different from themselves and dissimilar. So it happens. It is necessary, then, for those heaps to appear both similar and dissimilar, both to themselves and to each other. And most especially. Will they not also be the same and different from each other, both touching themselves and separate from themselves, agitated by all motions and staying everywhere, rising and setting, and neither and all such things—which indeed would be easy for us to run through, if many existed while the one did not? You tell the truest things.

<margin>Ninth supposition.</margin>
Returning now again to the beginning, let us declare, if the one is not, what will happen to the others besides the one. Let us declare. In the beginning, therefore, the others will not be the one. For how could they? Nor yet will they be many. For in those things which are many, the one is also present. For if none of them is one, all are nothing; wherefore they are not even many. You speak the truth. Since, therefore, the one is not in the others, they are neither many nor one. Clearly not. Nor do they even appear to be one or many. Why so? Because the others have no commerce at all with those things which are not; nor does anything from those things which are not at all pertain to any of the others. For no part is present to those things which are not. True. Therefore, neither an opinion of that which is not at all, nor a phantom is in the rest, nor in any way is that which is not conceived by the others in opinion. Certainly not. Wherefore if the one is not, nothing of the others is conceived by opinion to be either one or many. For it is entirely impossible to opine "many" without the "one." Exceedingly impossible. Therefore if the one is not, the others neither are, nor are they thought by opinion to be one or many. They do not seem so. Whence they are neither similar nor dissimilar. No. Nor yet the same, or different, nor touching, nor separate; nor the rest of the things we narrated in the previous sections as appearing to look toward the others themselves, do they now look toward the others, or seem to look toward them, if the one is not at all. True. Shall we not say rightly, to speak summarily: if the one is not, nothing is? Most especially. Let this be said by us, and that besides: that as it seems, whether the one is or is not, both itself and also the others, in relation to themselves and to each other, all things entirely are and are not, and moreover appear and do not appear. These things are indeed most true.

---

### Argument of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine on the Philebus, a book of Plato: or on the Supreme Good.

<margin>The supreme good of the soul.</margin>
<margin>What is ambrosia; what is nectar.</margin>
<margin>The supreme good in the mixture of wisdom and pleasure.</margin>
The purpose of this book is to discourse on the supreme good of the soul. This supreme good is spoken of with a certain condition, since the supreme good of all things is called the absolute principle. Concerning this good which is "with condition," he disputes in this book; concerning that which is absolute, he disputes in the *Parmenides*. From this absolute, however, this [other good] flows, just as a certain light depends on the very source of all light. Wherefore in the *Phaedo* and *Theaetetus* it was said by Plato that the supreme good of the soul is the likeness of God. But nothing becomes like the sun except by a certain infusion of its own light. Whence the good of the soul will also be the complete attainment of the divine light. That light descends first into the mind, then into the will. In the mind is truth; in the will is joy. In the mind it is named "ambrosia" by Plato here and in the *Phaedrus*; in the will it is named "nectar." Therefore, he placed the supreme good of man in the mixture of wisdom and pleasure. But before this, he denied that blessedness could consist in the account of either wisdom or pleasure alone, because the triple condition of the supreme good was found in neither...
