<meta>This page continues the introductory commentary and begins the translation of Plato's "Philebus," a dialogue concerning the nature of the "Highest Good" (Summum Bonum). The previous section likely established the context of the debate between pleasure and wisdom.</meta>

<page-num>XXII</page-num>
<header>BOOK TEN</header>

<margin>Three conditions of the highest good.</margin>
...perish. This [the Good] is such that it must be perfectly complete, sufficient, and desirable. It is **perfect** because it lacks nothing in itself. It is **sufficient** because nothing is missing for the one who possesses it. It is **desirable** because whatever can be longed for exists within it and from it. Therefore, because it is perfect, it is sufficient; because it is sufficient, it is desirable. Truly, because it is enough for itself, it suffices for another; because it suffices for another, it is desired by another. It is demonstrated that these qualities belong neither to wisdom alone, nor to pleasure alone, but to a certain mixture of both. Here, they speak at length about the genus, origin, and nature of pleasure and wisdom; about the infinite and the limit; about the composite and the principle of composition. And finally, it concludes that the **highest and absolute good in nature is the measure of all things**; this is the principle of all nature. However, the highest good of the mind and soul is the possession of that first principle, which belongs to the mixture of wisdom and pleasure through truth, proportion, and beauty. For this reason, in the first rank of goods, **measure** is placed; in the second, **truth, proportion, and beauty**; in the third, **mind and wisdom**; in the fourth, **science, art, and right opinion**; in the fifth, **temperate pleasure**. A man is called blessed who has attained the wisdom of divine things and the skill in human affairs consisting of a certain science, art, and right opinion; he exults entirely in the joy of contemplation, and commits himself to the pleasures of the senses only insofar as wisdom, science, and joy receive no hindrance therefrom. The introduction to the dialogue is as follows: When Socrates and Philebus had exchanged many arguments back and forth concerning the highest good, and Philebus, now weary of disputing, congratulated Protarchus who had recently arrived, he agreed that Protarchus should take up his role in the debate. Protarchus, being a youth, immediately consented. Turning to him, Socrates says: "Consider what a guardianship you are undertaking, and do not hasten rashly into the dispute. Rather, hear the opinion of both sides first, and accept for defense that which appears more probable to you as you examine it with right reason." But now let us come to the dialogue.

## PLATO’S PHILEBUS, OR ON THE HIGHEST GOOD.
### SOCRATES. PROTARCHUS. PHILEBUS.

<margin>The highest and absolute good in nature is the measure of all things.</margin>
<margin>The five ranks of goods.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative floriated initial "V" at the start of the word "See".</image-desc>
**SO.** See, O Protarchus, what sort of discourse you are now about to receive from Philebus, and against which point of view—one that may not harmonize with your own reason—you are to fight. Shall we briefly summarize both opinions? **PRO.** I certainly wish to. **SO.** Philebus says that for all living beings, the good is joy, pleasure, delight, and everything else of this kind. Our contention against him, however, is that these things are not the Good itself; rather, to be wise, to understand, to remember, and things related to these—such as right opinion and the discourse of true reason—are better and more powerful than pleasure for all who are capable of them; and the attainment of these is the most useful of all things, both for the present and the future. Have we both spoken in this manner, O Philebus? **PHI.** Most certainly. **SO.** Do you, O Protarchus, take up this dispute that is now offered to you? **PRO.** It is necessary that I take it up. **SO.** Philebus is indeed now weary of speaking; yet it is necessary to define with all zeal what is true in these matters. **PRO.** It is necessary indeed. **SO.** Come then, let us affirm this in addition. **PRO.** What is that? **SO.** That each of us will try to demonstrate a certain habit and disposition of the soul <note>Latin: "habitū quēdā & affectionē animi"</note> which is able to provide a blessed life to all men. Is it not so? **PRO.** Certainly. **SO.** And you, surely, will demonstrate the habit and disposition of rejoicing; we, however, that of being wise. **PRO.** So it is. **SO.** But if some other habit should appear more excellent than these, and should seem more closely related to pleasure, we shall both be surpassed by such a life, provided it be stable and firmly held; and pleasure shall surpass wisdom. **PRO.** Indeed. **SO.** But if it be closer to wisdom, then wisdom shall surely conquer pleasure, and pleasure, on the contrary, shall yield. Do you concede these points? **PRO.** To me, they seem necessary to concede. **SO.** But how do they seem to Philebus? **PHI.** To me, pleasure certainly seems to excel, and always will. But you yourself shall decide, O Protarchus. **PRO.** Since you have now yielded the duty of the dispute to us, Philebus, you no longer have the power to agree or disagree with Socrates. **PHI.** You speak the truth. **SO.** But now, for the sake of purification, let me first invoke and call to witness the goddess herself. **PRO.** And we also shall be witnesses that you have said these things. But hereafter, O Socrates, with Philebus's consent, let us try to resolve the matter in whatever way you wish.

<margin>Venus is most truly called Pleasure.</margin>
<margin>Reverence toward the gods.</margin>
<margin>Many modes of delighting.</margin>
**SO.** Let us begin, then, starting from the goddess herself, whom Philebus here says is called Venus <note>original: "Venerē"</note>, but whose truest name is Pleasure <note>original: "voluptas"</note>. **PRO.** Quite right. **SO.** For me, reverence toward the names of the gods is always not a human dread, but surpasses the greatest fear. And now, I call her Venus just as it is pleasing to them; but I know that pleasure is a varied thing. Starting from it, as I said, we ought to investigate what nature it has. For as far as hearing is concerned, it simply seeks one thing; yet it takes on forms that are quite varied and in some way unlike one another. Pay attention: for we say that an intemperate man takes delight; likewise, a temperate man takes delight in temperance itself; a foolish man takes delight in foolish opinions and is full of vain hope on all sides; and a wise man takes delight in wisdom. If anyone should deny that these pleasures are unlike, he would rightly be seen as a fool. **PRO.** These, O Socrates, proceed from contrary things, yet they are not contrary to each other; for how could pleasure not be most similar to itself in all things where it is pleasure? **SO.** Indeed, O blessed one, color does not differ from color insofar as each one is a color. Yet we all know that black, besides being different from white, is even its contrary. Furthermore, figure relates to figure in the same way: in genus, the whole is one; but the parts of this genus are partly far different from each other, and partly even contrary; and we shall find many other such things. Therefore, do not trust this reasoning which makes individual contraries into one. For I fear lest perhaps some pleasures are contrary to each other...

# PHILEBUS, OR ON THE HIGHEST GOOD.
## FOLIO XXXIII.

...let us find the differences. PROTARCHUS: Perhaps, but how will this obstruct our argument? SOCRATES: We say it obstructs it because you call things that are themselves dissimilar by one and the same name. For you claim all pleasant things are good; now, no argument prevents pleasant things from being pleasant. However, since many of them are bad and some are good, as we said, you nevertheless call them all "good." And you will be forced to confess they are dissimilar to one another if someone compels you. What, then, is found identically in common across all pleasures, both bad and good, for the sake of which you call them all "good"? PROTARCHUS: What are you saying, Socrates! Do you think anyone, having established that pleasure itself is the good, would then concede to you that some are good and others are bad? SOCRATES: Nevertheless, you will admit that many are dissimilar, and most are even contrary to one another. PROTARCHUS: Not at all, insofar as they are pleasures. SOCRATES: We are sliding back into the same point, Protarchus. We shall be saying that pleasure differs in no way from pleasure, but that all are similar to one another. And the examples brought forward a little while ago will move us not at all; we shall contend just like those who are unskilled and rude in disputations. PROTARCHUS: In what way do you mean? SOCRATES: That if I, imitating you and resisting, should dare to say that the most dissimilar thing of all is the most similar to the most dissimilar, I could assert the same things as you. Whence we shall appear ruder than is proper, and our argument will fail and slip away. Let us therefore recall and retract it; for perhaps by taking turns and returning, as it were, to the same handles <note>original: "ansas" - a metaphor for points of an argument one can grasp</note>, we shall agree in some way. PROTARCHUS: Tell me how? SOCRATES: Suppose I am questioned again by you, Protarchus. PROTARCHUS: About what? SOCRATES: Wisdom, knowledge, mind: and whatever I, establishing them from the beginning, called "good"—when asked what the good itself is, will they not suffer the same fate as your argument? PROTARCHUS: In what way? SOCRATES: For all the sciences will appear to be many, and some of them dissimilar to one another. And if they are even contrary, would I be worthy of the present dispute if, fearing this very thing, I said no science was dissimilar to another science? Thus, finally, our discourse would vanish like a fable, and we would be saved only by a certain rudeness. But it is not at all becoming to act thus; rather, the preservation of the argument must be considered. Therefore, it pleases me equally in your speech and in mine: let it be that pleasures appear many and dissimilar, and furthermore that sciences are many and different. Therefore, by no means hiding the difference between my good and yours, Protarchus, but rather bringing it into the light, let us dare to discuss it: if in some way it is signified through refutation whether it is proper to call pleasure itself the good, or wisdom, or some third thing besides these. For now we ought by no means to contend so that what I propose or what you propose should win, but so that we may favor that which is most true. PROTARCHUS: So it ought to be. SOCRATES: Let us also affirm this much more in your confession. PROTARCHUS: What is that? SOCRATES: That which fatigues all men, both the willing and the unwilling, some especially and at times. PROTARCHUS: Speak more plainly. SOCRATES: The discourse which has now occurred is wonderful in its nature: that Many are One, and One is Many—wonderful to say. And it is easy to raise doubts against him who posits either one. PROTARCHUS: Do you mean when someone asserts that I, for example, Protarchus, am one born by nature, and then predicates of me again that I am many and contrary things: great, small, heavy, light, and the same man many other things? SOCRATES: You, Protarchus, are introducing those wonders concerning the One and the Many which are common knowledge and, so to speak, already conceded by everyone; these should not be attempted, as they are childish and easy to know, and would be the greatest obstacles to future disputation if one admitted them. Nor should these be considered wonders: when someone, dividing the members and parts of anything by reason, confesses that all these are that One, and then refutes such things, laughing as if he were forcing one to confess monsters—that the One is many and infinite, and the many are One. PROTARCHUS: But what other things do you mean, Socrates, which are not yet conceded or common knowledge regarding this same discourse? SOCRATES: When someone, my boy, posits the One itself as nothing from those things which are born and perish (as we said a little while ago), then it is conceded that such a One ought by no means to be refuted. But when one tries to affirm one Man, one Ox, one Beauty, and one Good, then indeed in these unities and things of this sort, anxious study becomes ambiguity with division. PROTARCHUS: In what way? SOCRATES: First, indeed, whether it should be admitted <margin>First doubt concerning unity.</margin> that there are certain unities of this kind truly existing. Secondly, how each of them is to be thought <margin>Second doubt.</margin> to be always one and the same, admitting neither birth nor destruction, and most firm in its unity. Finally, whether <margin>Third doubt.</margin> it must be placed in things generated and infinite, either dispersed and made many out of one, or itself as a whole apart from itself—which indeed would seem the most impossible of all, that one and the same thing should become many in many things at once. It is not those things, therefore, Protarchus, but these concerning the One and the Many which, when poorly understood, are the cause of all difficulty and failure; but when well examined, they are the cause of ease and fluency. PROTARCHUS: We ought, Socrates, to discuss this first at present, as I also confess; and consider that all these men concede such things to you. Perhaps we shall begin now, since a great and varied battle exists in these doubts; from here, then? We say that the same One and <margin>Proverb: Do not move an evil that lies well. <note>Equivalent to "let sleeping dogs lie."</note></margin> Many are made by reasons and discourses, always running about everywhere through every single thing they say, both now and of old. And this neither began now, nor will it ever end; but it is, as it seems to me, this immortal and never-failing passion for reasons and discourses implanted in us. As soon as some youth has tasted it, he congratulates himself as if he had found a certain treasure of wisdom, and full of pleasure he exults and raves; he promptly tries every dispute and runs through the discourse in every direction: now turning it to one side and mixing it into one, then unfolding it again and distributing it into many; where indeed he first casts himself into doubt and difficulty...

# BOOK TEN

...especially casts down, then whoever is nearest, whether younger, older, or an equal, sparing neither father nor mother, nor any of the listeners, and indeed hardly sparing other living creatures, let alone men, provided he can find an interpreter. PROTARCHUS. Do you not see, Socrates, that all of us standing here are young men? Are you not afraid that we might make an assault upon you along with Philebus, if you rebuke us in such a way? Nevertheless: for we understand what you are saying; if there is any method, if there is any device to kindly cast out this confusion from the discussion in some way, and to find a more convenient path into reason and discourse, meditate on it yourself: we will truly follow you to the best of our strength. For the present discourse, Socrates, is no small matter.

<margin>A more beautiful way, a gift of the gods which Plato always loved.</margin>
SOCRATES. Certainly not, boys—for that is what Philebus called you. Yet there is no more beautiful way, nor can there be, than that which I have always loved. But it, often fleeing from me, has left me deserted and helpless. PROTARCHUS. What way is that? Just tell us. SOCRATES. It is not too difficult to declare, but truly most difficult to use. For whatever things have been discovered by art have come forth into the light for men through this: observe, I pray, what I am saying.

<margin>The ancients were both better than us and closer to the gods.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. Just say it. SOCRATES. A gift of the gods to men, as it seems to me, descended through a certain Prometheus along with a most brilliant fire. For the ancients, who were better than us and closer to the gods, handed down these oracles to us: that since all things which are said to exist forever consist of the One and the Many, and have Limit and Infinity <note>original: "terminum & infinitum"</note> innate within them, it behooves us, with things being so, to always search by positing one single Idea <term>Idea: a universal form or category</term> concerning anything generally, for we shall find it implanted there. If we comprehend this, after the one, we must examine if there are somehow two; if that is not apparent, then three, or some other number; and to divide each of those things which are "one" again in the same manner until one knows not only that the original "one" is many and infinite, but also exactly how many it is. One should not apply the idea of the Infinite to the multitude until one perceives every number falling between the Infinite and the One in the middle.

<margin>At this point, he who is able to know: since knowledge is posited as a virtue, and virtue is in the middle ground, knowledge also exists in a certain middle ground, that is, between the limit and the infinite.</margin>
Then at last, let each "one" of all the things passing into the infinite be dismissed. The gods, therefore, as we have said, granted us the ability to investigate, learn, and teach one another in this way. But the wise men among men who exist now introduce the "one" and the "many" however it happens, faster or slower than is proper; and after the "one," they immediately jump to the infinite, but the middle terms escape them. By these things, the method of disputation is distinguished into both the dialectical <term>dialectica: logical investigation of truth</term> and the litigious <term>litigiosa: arguing for the sake of winning</term>.

<margin>One must proceed all the way to the most specific things.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. Some of what you have said, Socrates, I seem to understand; other parts I desire to hear more clearly. SOCRATES. This is clearly evident in letters <note>i.e., the alphabet</note>, Protarchus, as we have said. Therefore, take this example from those things you have learned. PROTARCHUS. In what way? SOCRATES. The voice which breaks out of the mouth for us is one; and again, voices are infinite in number, both for everyone and for each individual. PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Yet we are made wise by neither of these: neither because we know its infinity, nor again because we know its unity; but because we grasp how many they are, and of what kind, this is what makes each of us a grammarian.

<margin>For all dialectical and litigious disputation, and whatever else can be understood, is concerned with the middle terms, that is, the species.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. You speak most truly. SOCRATES. The same thing also makes a man a musician. PROTARCHUS. By what reasoning? SOCRATES. In a certain way, the voice in this art is also one. PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Likewise, two things must be posited: the low and the high, and a third, the middle tone; is it not so? PROTARCHUS. It is. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, you will not yet be a wise musician if you know only these; and if you are ignorant of those other things, so to speak, you will be of no account in music. PROTARCHUS. Of none.

<margin>By this reasoning, Aristotle also forced voices into ten categories.</margin>
SOCRATES. But after you have received, my friend, how many intervals of the voice there are in number between the low and the high, and of what kind they are, as well as the limits of the intervals, and however many compositions arise from these—which our ancestors, observing them, handed down to us their followers to call "harmonies" of this kind. Furthermore, in the movements and gestures of the body, they showed other such things to exist, which they ordered to be called rhythms and measures when measured by numbers. Think, moreover, that we ought to consider in the same way every thing that is "one" and "many"; for when you grasp these things thus, you then become wise. And when you comprehend any other thing in this way, you will again be made wise regarding it.

<margin>Wisdom is concerned with the finite, that is, the middle terms.</margin>
<margin>There is no reason/logic regarding the infinite.</margin>
But the infinite multitude of individual things in each case leaves you unskilled in wisdom, reason, and number, as you are looking toward no number of anything at any time. PROTARCHUS. Socrates seems to me to have spoken these things excellently, Philebus. PHILEBUS. To me as well, but what does this speech have to do with the matter? What does it mean? SOCRATES. That Philebus of yours has asked rightly, Protarchus. PROTARCHUS. Entirely. Answer him then. SOCRATES. I will do what you want, when I have disputed about these same things for a little while longer. For just as if someone takes a certain "one," he ought not, as we said, immediately descend into the nature of the infinite, but into some number; so conversely, if someone is forced to take the infinite first, he should not go immediately to the "one," but should aim for a certain number which has some multitude, and finally end in the "one" from all of them. What we have just said can be seen again in the example of letters.

<margin>Theuth, a divine man among the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>Concerning the species of letters.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. How? SOCRATES. After he thought upon the infinite voice—whether it was some god or a divine man, such as Theuth is said to have been among the Egyptians—he first considered the vowel letters in that infinity of voice, which are not one but several; and again others which were participants not of voice, but of sound <note>original: "phthongi"</note>. And he similarly defined a certain number of these. Then he distinguished a third species of letters, those which we now call mutes; finally, he separated the liquids and the mutes down to each individual one, and the vowels and the middle ones in the same way, until, grasping their number, he called each and all of them an "element." And since he saw that no one could perceive the "one" itself by itself apart from the rest, he devised a bond of this kind: that being one, and making all these one in a certain way, he established one art over them called "grammar." PHILEBUS. I have comprehended these things more clearly than the previous ones when compared to each other, Protarchus. Yet I still desire the same thing now as I did earlier in this disputation. SOCRATES. Do you ask this, Philebus: namely, what these things contribute to our discourse? PHILEBUS. Yes, that is what Protarchus and I have been seeking for a long time. SOCRATES. Is it not this...

# PHILEBUS, OR ON THE HIGHEST GOOD. FOLIO 34.

...attained, you are asking again, as you did before. PHILEBUS: In what way? SOCRATES: Did a dispute not arise between us from the very beginning concerning wisdom and pleasure, as to which of these should be chosen? PROTARCHUS: Indeed it did. SOCRATES: And we said that each of them was a single thing. PROTARCHUS: We certainly did. SOCRATES: This is exactly what the previous discourse requires: in what way each of these is both one and many; and how it does not immediately become infinite, but rather how each thing receives a certain number before it is stretched out into the infinite. PROTARCHUS: Socrates, you have led us, I know not how, by a certain circular path into no small question, O Philebus. Therefore, come: consider which of us should respond to the present interrogation. For perhaps it is ridiculous that I, the successor to this whole dispute, should command this very thing of you again, simply because I am unable to answer it now. Yet it would be much more ridiculous if neither of us were able. Meditate, therefore, on what we should do. For Socrates seems to me to be seeking the species <note>types or categories</note> of pleasure from us now: whether they exist or not, how many there are, and of what sort they are; and to inquire similarly concerning wisdom. SOCRATES: You speak the truth, O son of Callias: for unless we can observe that which is similar, the same, and the contrary regarding any single thing—as the preceding speech showed—none of us will ever be of any value in anything. PROTARCHUS: So it truly seems to be the case, Socrates.

<margin>It seems to be a "second voyage" not to be hidden from oneself.</margin>
But it is a noble thing for a temperate man to discern all things. Indeed, a "second voyage" <note>A Greek idiom (deuteros plous) meaning the next best way when the primary way fails; here, a more cautious or secondary path of inquiry.</note> seems to be to not remain hidden from oneself; I shall explain why I have said these things now. You yourself, Socrates, were the author of this gathering for us, and you offered yourself to investigate what is best among human affairs. For when Philebus asserted that pleasure, delight, joy, and others of this kind were the best things for men, you immediately contradicted him, saying that those things he mentioned were not the best, but rather those which we often bring back to memory of our own accord when acting rightly, so that both may be examined by repeated memory. You say, however—as it seems—that what must be rightly called the "Good," being more excellent than pleasure, is mind, knowledge, intelligence, art, and others of this sort, which we ought to take up rather than those others. Since, therefore, both of these had been spoken of with a certain ambiguity, we threatened you with a joke that we would not let you go until a sufficient end was imposed on this controversy by a certain determination. You indeed conceded, and offered yourself to us to carry this out. But we say, as children are accustomed to: "there is no taking back of things rightly given." <note>A common ancient proverb similar to "no Indian giving."</note> Apply, therefore, this manner of disputing to those things which have been said. SOCRATES: Which do you mean? PROTARCHUS: Why do you throw in the thorns of doubt and ask those things for which we could not give you a sufficient answer at present?

<margin>Neither pleasure nor wisdom is the highest good, but a third thing.</margin>
For we ought not to think that the end of this dispute is the ambiguity of us all. And if we are less capable of it, you must act, for you promised. Therefore, consult on these matters: whether the species of pleasure and wisdom are to be distinguished, or rather dismissed, or whether you can and wish to open up in some other way what is now doubted between us. SOCRATES: It is not fitting for me to fear that anything will be difficult now, since you have spoken these things in such a way. For by saying "if I wish," all fear is utterly put to flight; moreover, it seems that some one of the gods has supplied us with a certain memory for these things. PROTARCHUS: In what way, and the memory of what? SOCRATES: Since formerly, whether dreaming or awake, I heard certain arguments, I am now thinking about pleasure and wisdom—that neither of these is the Good, but some third thing, which is different from both and better than both. And if this should now be clearly evident to us, pleasure will be far from victory; for the Good would by no means be the same as it. Is it so? Or otherwise? PROTARCHUS: Certainly so. SOCRATES: Therefore, in my opinion, we shall no longer need the species of pleasure for division, which will become clearer in what follows. PROTARCHUS: You speak excellently; proceed thus, I pray. SOCRATES: Let us first affirm a few small things.

<margin>
The condition and lot of the Good is threefold: that it be perfect, sufficient, and desirable.
</margin>
PROTARCHUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: Regarding the lot of the Good itself: is it necessary that it be perfect, or not perfect? PROTARCHUS: Of all things, O Socrates, it is the most perfect. SOCRATES: What then: is the Good itself sufficient? PROTARCHUS: Why not? And in this very thing it must differ from all things that exist and excel them all. SOCRATES: This also, I think, is most necessary to assert of it: that every knowing being hunts for it and desires to apprehend it, wishing to possess it in itself and other things around it, and cares for nothing else except those things which are perfected together with good things. PROTARCHUS: It is not possible to fight against these things. SOCRATES: Let us consider, therefore, and judge the life of pleasure and the life of wisdom, looking at them separately. PROTARCHUS: How do you mean? SOCRATES: Let there be no wisdom in the life of pleasure, and no pleasure in the life of wisdom. For if either of these is the Good, it ought to need nothing further; but if it should appear lacking, it is no longer truly the Good for us. PROTARCHUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Do we wish to make a trial of this in you? PROTARCHUS: By all means. SOCRATES: Answer then. PROTARCHUS: Speak, please. SOCRATES: Would you wish, O Protarchus, to live your whole life enjoying the highest pleasures? PROTARCHUS: Why would I not wish it? SOCRATES: Would you think you needed anything else besides, if you enjoyed the perfect possession of these? PROTARCHUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: Consider then: would you not need wisdom itself, and intelligence, and proper reasoning, and others related to these, or the sight of any thing? PROTARCHUS: And why? I would have all things if I enjoyed pleasure. SOCRATES: And living thus, would you abound in the chief pleasures throughout your whole life? PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: If you were utterly lacking in mind, memory, knowledge, and true opinion, first of all, you would necessarily be ignorant of this very thing—whether you were rejoicing or not—since you would be void of all wisdom. PROTARCHUS: Necessarily. SOCRATES: And since you would be deprived of memory, you would surely not remember that you had ever been delighted; no memory of a pleasure happening suddenly would remain. And being bereft of true opinion, while you were rejoicing, you would not think you were rejoicing at all. Being also deprived of reason, you would not be able to reason that you would obtain any pleasure in the future. You would lead the life not of a human, but of a certain lung-fish <note>original: "pleumonis"</note>, that is, similar to a sea sponge or a sea oyster. Are these things true? Or can we think otherwise?

# BOOK TEN

<margin>Which of the three lives is best.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. And how could it be otherwise? SOCRATES. Is a life of this sort <note>referring to a life of pure pleasure without intellect</note> to be sought by us? PRO. The present argument, O Socrates, has rendered me mute. SO. Let us not stop here, I beseech you; but now, bringing the life of the mind into our midst, let us consider it further. PRO. What kind of life do you mean? SO. Whether someone would choose to live in such a way that he possessed all wisdom, mind, knowledge, and memory of all things, but enjoyed absolutely no pleasure, nor on the other hand was affected by any pain—but lived entirely without any such affection? PRO. Neither of these lives, O Socrates, seems to me or to anyone else, I think, to be chooseworthy. SO. What then, O Protarchus, of a life mixed from both, coming together into one and made common? PRO. You mean a life of pleasure combined with wisdom and mind? SO. That is exactly what I mean. PRO. Everyone would surely choose this life rather than either of the former two; not just one person choosing it and another not, but all would seek it equally. SO. Do we see, then, what follows from this? PRO. Certainly; that of the three lives proposed, two are neither sufficient nor desirable for either men or other living creatures. SO. Is it not already clear concerning these that neither of them possesses the "Good" itself? For if it did, it would be perfect and sufficient, and would be sought after by all plants and animals that were able to live that way forever. But if any of us chooses otherwise, he chooses against the nature of what is truly to be desired, and does so not willingly, but out of ignorance or some unhappy necessity. PRO. This seems to be the case. SO. It seems, then, that enough has been said to show that Philebus's "Goddess" <note>Aphrodite, representing Pleasure</note> is not to be considered the same as the Good itself. PHILEBUS. But neither is your "Mind," O Socrates; for it suffers from the same objections. SO. Perhaps mine does, O Philebus; but I do not think the true and divine Mind is so, but rather that it stands differently. Therefore, I have no doubt that we must award the palm and the victory to the "Common Life" <note>the mixed life of pleasure and intellect</note> over the life of Mind alone. But it remains to be judged to which of the two we should grant the second place. For perhaps one of us will contend that Mind is the cause of this common life, and the other that Pleasure is; and thus the Good itself would be neither of these, though perhaps one might judge one of them to be the cause of it. On this point, therefore, I would especially contend against Philebus: that in this mixed life, whatever it is that makes it desirable and good, Mind is more akin and similar to it than Pleasure. And by this reasoning, Pleasure would hold neither the first nor even the second place; indeed, it would be far from the third, if any credit is now to be given to my mind. PRO. And so, O Socrates, Pleasure seems to have been struck down and prostrated by your arguments; for she has fallen from the hope of victory. Regarding Mind, however, it must be said that it would not be wise to claim victory for itself, as it would suffer the same fate. Pleasure, perhaps deprived of the second place, will now be utterly despised by her lovers; for she will no longer appear as beautiful as before. SO. What then? Is it not better to let her go, and not afflict her with further exquisite examination and refutation? PRO. You say nothing, O Socrates! SO. Is it because I suggested something impossible—that Pleasure could be "afflicted"? PRO. Not only for that, but because you ignore that none of us will let you go until you have reached the end of this reasoning. SO. Good heavens, Protarchus! The discourse that follows is very long, and by no means easy. For it is clear that we need other weapons besides the previous arguments if one is to secure the second prize for Mind. Perhaps these, too, are like stings. Is it not necessary? PRO. Why not? SO. Let us then set down a beginning for this, striving to grasp it cautiously and distinctly. PRO. What kind of beginning do you mean? SO. Let us distinguish all things that now exist in the universe into two parts—or rather, if you wish, into three. PRO. In what way? SO. Let us take some of the things we have just mentioned. PRO. Which ones? SO. We were saying that God has revealed that among existing things, there is the **Infinite** <note>Latin: *infinitum*; Greek: *apeiron*</note> and the **Limit** <note>Latin: *terminum*; Greek: *peras*</note>. PRO. Entirely so. SO. Let us posit these two as species; and the third as that which is one thing mixed from both. Yet I seem ridiculous as I strive to divide and enumerate sufficiently according to species. PRO. What are you saying, my good man? SO. It is clear that a fourth genus is still needed. PRO. Which one? SO. Consider the **Cause** of the mixture of those others. Set that down as the fourth besides those three. PRO. And will you not also need a fifth, something that discerns or separates? SO. Perhaps, but not at present, I think. But if it should be needed, you will forgive me as I pursue a "fifth life." PRO. What is to stop you? SO. First, then, selecting three out of the four, and two out of the three, let us consider how each of the two is many, divided and dispersed. And bringing them back into one, let us strive to think how each is both one and many. PRO. If you say this more plainly, perhaps I will follow. SO. I mean the two that were proposed: the **Finite** and the **Infinite**. I will try to show how the Infinite is in a certain way "many"; as for the Finite, let that be deferred for later. PRO. Let it be deferred. SO. Pay attention then: for what I bid you consider is difficult and highly debatable. Yet take note. First, consider the **Hotter** and the **Colder**: whether you can find any limit in them.

<margin>That the Infinite is many.</margin>
Or rather, do the "More" and the "Less," as long as they are in these kinds, reject a limit? For if a limit were applied, they themselves would cease to be. PRO. You speak the truth. SO. Yet we always say that in the hotter and colder there is a "more" and a "less." PRO. Very much so. SO. Therefore, this reasoning always shows us that a limit is absent from them, and being without an end <note>Latin: *sine fine*, a play on "infinite"</note>, they become entirely infinite. PRO. Most vehemently, Socrates. SO. Well done, friend Protarchus, you have noticed it! Now, this very word "vehemently" which you just pronounced, and also its opposite "mildly," have the same power as "more" and "less."

<margin>The "More" and "Less" reject limit and quantity.</margin>
For wherever they are present, they do not allow each thing to be a specific quantity; but always introducing a "more" to the "milder" and a "milder" to the "more" in all actions, they produce a "more and less," while always obscuring definite quantity. For if they were to destroy quantity and the measured state, and in its place the "more vehement" and "milder" were to take its seat...

<summary>Socrates leads Protarchus to conclude that neither a life of pure pleasure nor pure intellect is sufficient, proposing instead a "mixed life." He then begins a metaphysical classification of all existence into the Infinite, the Limit, the Mixture, and the Cause.</summary>

# PHILEBUS, OR ON THE HIGHEST GOOD. FOLIO XXXV.

and allow them to occupy less space, these very things will suddenly be driven from their seat. For the "more hot" and "more cold" would no longer remain if they took on a definite quantity. Indeed, they will flee and no longer stand firm—the "more hot" and "more cold" themselves—wherever a fixed quantity reigns, for their progression ceases. For this reason, it is established that the hotter and colder are **infinite** <note>original: *infinita*; here meaning "without limit" or "indefinite" rather than "eternal"</note>. PROTARCHUS: So it appears, Socrates; yet as you said yourself, these things are not easily grasped. Perhaps if they are repeated again later, they will show the questioner and respondent alike to be in agreement. SOCRATES: Well said; and so we must act according to our strength. But look first:

<margin>The sign of an infinite nature.</margin>
should I set this as the sign of an infinite nature, so that we do not prolong our discourse too much by running through every single instance? PROTARCHUS: What do you mean? SOCRATES:

<margin>Things in the genus of the infinite.</margin>
Whatever admits of "more" and "less," of "vehement" and "gentle," of "too much," and things of this sort, must all be reduced into the single genus of the **infinite**. Just as we said before: asserting that all things which are divided and dispersed must be collected into one, and signified according to one power and one certain nature. Do you remember? PROTARCHUS: I remember. SOCRATES:

<margin>Things in the genus of the finite.</margin>
But those things which do not admit such variations, but rather their opposites—first the equal itself and equality, then after the equal, the double, and every proportion that demonstrates number to number or measure to measure—all these, I say, we should rightly refer to the genus of the **finite** <note>original: *finiti*; meaning "the limit" or "the bounded"</note>. What do you say to this? PROTARCHUS: Most excellently put, Socrates. SOCRATES: Come then, what idea shall we say is produced from the mixture of both? PROTARCHUS: You will tell me that, I think. SOCRATES: Rather, a God will—if only some god hears my prayers. PROTARCHUS: Pray then, and observe. SOCRATES: I am observing. And it seems to me that one of the gods has now breathed upon us in friendship. PROTARCHUS: Why do you say that? What conjecture do you use? SOCRATES: I will speak plainly; stand by with attentive ears. PROTARCHUS: Speak then. SOCRATES: Were we not just now speaking of a "more hot" and "more cold"? PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Add to these the "drier" and "moister," the "more" and "fewer," the "faster" and "slower," the "greater" and "smaller." And finally, all those things which we previously reduced to a single nature that admits of more or less. PROTARCHUS: Do you mean the nature of the infinite? SOCRATES: That very one. Mix it hereafter with the offspring of the **limit**. PROTARCHUS: Which offspring? SOCRATES: The offspring of the limit, which indeed it behooved us to collect into one just as we did with the infinite; though we have not yet collected it. But perhaps now the same will happen: for when these two are reconciled, that third condition will be revealed. PROTARCHUS: What do you mean, and how? SOCRATES: The offspring of the equal and the double, and whatever puts to flight mutual difference and contrariety; by making things commensurate and harmonious, it effects **number**. PROTARCHUS: I understand; for you seem to me to be saying that if these are mixed, certain "generations" <note>meaning "products" or "results"</note> will result from each of them. SOCRATES: And I seem to be right. PROTARCHUS: Speak then.

<margin>The right joining of these, i.e., of the equal or double or others.</margin>
SOCRATES: In diseases, did not the right communion of these generate the nature of **health**? PROTARCHUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And in the high and the low, the fast and the slow—though they are infinite—did not this limit bring them forth and provide the perfection of **music**? PROTARCHUS: Splendidly. SOCRATES: Furthermore, in the case of bitter cold and stifling heat, it took away that which is called "too much" and "too little" and "infinite," and applied the measured and the commensurate. PROTARCHUS: Why not? SOCRATES: From these, the seasons of the year and all beautiful things have flowed, the infinite and the finite coming together. PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: And I omit countless other things—such as beauty and strength along with health.

<margin>Disease exists in the exceeding or ceasing of hot, cold, moist, and dry. But if you speak of proportion, it is health.</margin>
In souls also, there are many and noble things: for this Goddess <note>referring to the divine principle of Order or Limit</note>, observing that wantonness and all wickedness lack any limit of pleasures and fulfillment, applied **law** and **order**, in which the limit dwells. You say, Philebus, that the soul is thus tainted and destroyed; I, on the contrary, say it is preserved. But to you, Protarchus, how does it seem? PROTARCHUS: These things are entirely according to my own opinion. SOCRATES: Have I not now presented these three, provided you understand them? PROTARCHUS: I believe I grasp them. One you assert is the **infinite**. The second is the **limit** in things that exist. But the third—what you mean by that, I do not quite hold. SOCRATES: The abundance of the generation of this third thing has amazed you, O wonderful man. The infinite also contained many genera, yet they appeared as one because they were marked by the genus of "more and less." PROTARCHUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: However, the limit did not contain many, nor did we have any difficulty admitting that it was one by nature. PROTARCHUS: How could we? SOCRATES: In no way. But know that by the **third**, I mean this one thing: whatever is born from these two—namely, a **generation into essence** <note>original: *generationem in essentiam*; the coming-into-being of a stable reality</note> from the measures established together with the limit. PROTARCHUS: I understand. SOCRATES: But what the **fourth genus** is, besides these three, remains to be discussed. This is a common inquiry. See now if it seems necessary to you: that whatever is generated is generated through some **cause**. PROTARCHUS: To me, plainly. For how could it happen without one? SOCRATES: And the nature of the "maker" differs from the "cause" in name only; the maker and the cause may rightly be called one. PROTARCHUS: Rightly. SOCRATES: Furthermore, the "thing made" and the "thing generated" will differ only in name. PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: The nature which is the maker always precedes and leads; but that which is made and generated by it follows. PROTARCHUS: Exactly. SOCRATES: Therefore, the cause is not the same as that which serves the cause for generation. PROTARCHUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Did not the things generated, and those from which they are generated, provide us with three genera? PROTARCHUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: And the craftsman of all these we set as the fourth, and call it the **cause**, as it has been shown to be something different from the others. PROTARCHUS: We set it so without doubt. SOCRATES: Now it is proper, since the four are distinct, to enumerate them one by one for the sake of memory. PROTARCHUS: By all means. SOCRATES: First, then, I call the **infinite**; second, the **limit**; third, the **essence** mixed and generated from these. The last is the **cause** of the mixture and generation. If I call this the fourth, would I err? PROTARCHUS: In no way. SOCRATES: Come then, what was our discourse, and what were we seeking most when we came to this? Was it not this...

<summary>Socrates defines four fundamental categories of existence: the Infinite (indefinite qualities), the Limit (mathematical proportion), the Mixture (the resulting reality like health or music), and the Cause (the creative force). This framework is used to analyze the nature of pleasure and the good life.</summary>

# BOOK TEN

<margin>That which is generated is not mixed from just any two things, but consists of two: the infinite and the limit.</margin>
<margin>That pleasure and pain belong to the class of infinites.</margin>
<margin>Neither is pleasure the whole good, nor pain the whole evil.</margin>

We were seeking, of course, to whom the second prize of victory should be granted: to pleasure, or rather to wisdom? Was it not so? PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: After we have distinguished these things in this manner, will we not better judge to whom the first and to whom the second palm of victory should be given, based on those things which came into the contest above? PROTARCHUS: Perhaps. SOCRATES: We have surely established that the victorious life is one mixed from pleasure and wisdom. PROTARCHUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: We see, in a way, what kind of life this is and to what class it belongs. PROTARCHUS: We see it. SOCRATES: It is surely a part of the third class <note>The "Mixture" of the Limit and the Infinite</note>. For that mixture is not just from any two things, but from all infinites bound by a limit. Therefore, this victorious life will rightly be a part of that class. PROTARCHUS: Quite rightly. SOCRATES: Come now, sweet Philebus, to which of the aforementioned classes will your "simple" life <note>The life of pure pleasure without intellect</note> be rightly thought to belong? Answer this before it is explained. PHILEBUS: Just speak. SOCRATES: Do pleasure and pain have a limit, or are they rather of that class which admits of "more" and "less"? PHILEBUS: They are of those that admit of "more," Socrates; for pleasure would not be the "whole good" unless it were by its own nature infinite in multitude and in the degree of "more." SOCRATES: But neither is pain, Philebus, the "whole evil"; wherefore we must now consider something other than the nature of the infinite which provides pleasures with some portion of the good. Truly, your life is made of those indeterminate things. But as for wisdom, knowledge, and mind—to which of the aforementioned classes, Protarchus and Philebus, shall we refer them without sinning against piety? For no small danger seems to loom over us, whether we treat what was just asked correctly or incorrectly. PHILEBUS: You are extolling your own God, Socrates. SOCRATES: And you, my friend, your Goddess <note>Referring to Aphrodite/Pleasure</note>. But we must return to what was asked. PROTARCHUS: Socrates speaks well, Philebus. Therefore, we must trust him. PHILEBUS: Did you not promise, Protarchus, that you would speak for me? PROTARCHUS: Certainly. But now I hesitate and fear; and I beseech you, Socrates, to be present with us like a prophet, lest we, wandering away from the contestant, sing out of tune. PHILEBUS: You must have faith, Protarchus; for you command nothing difficult. SOCRATES: Indeed, truly extolling God as Philebus says, I have disturbed you in jest by asking of what class mind and knowledge are. PROTARCHUS: Very much so, Socrates.

<margin>The Intellect is the king of heaven and earth.</margin>

SOCRATES: It is easy, however: for all the wise, extolling themselves, agree that the Intellect is the king of heaven and earth; and perhaps they speak correctly. If you wish, we will examine this class more extensively. PROTARCHUS: Speak as you judge best, Socrates, fearing nothing of prolixity, for you will not be troublesome. SOCRATES: You speak excellently; let us therefore begin by asking this. PROTARCHUS: From where? SOCRATES: Whether, Protarchus, we should say that this universe is driven by some irrational, reckless, and fortuitous power? Or on the contrary, as our ancestors felt, that it is governed by a certain order of mind and wonderful wisdom? PROTARCHUS: There is no comparison. For what you just said, Socrates, seems to me profane; but to confess that all these things are adorned by Mind—a sentiment worthy of the sight of the world, the sun, the moon, and the other stars, and finally the whole celestial circuit—I would never speak otherwise of them, nor dare to feel otherwise. SOCRATES: Do you wish, therefore, that we also confirm what was asserted by the ancients: namely, that these things are so? And not only should we think that other things cannot be brought forward without danger, but also undergo the danger of reproach along with them, if some harsh and vehement man should contend that these things are not so, but are carried along without order? PROTARCHUS: Why should I not wish it? SOCRATES: Come then, contemplate what follows. PROTARCHUS: Speak now. SOCRATES: We see that those things which concern the bodies of living beings—fire, water, breath <note>original: "spiritum"</note>, and earth—are present in the composition like tossing waves, as they say. PROTARCHUS: Very much so; for in these discussions we truly toss about because of ambiguity.

<margin>On the vileness of the elements in us.</margin>

SOCRATES: Therefore, take this concerning each of those things which are around us. PROTARCHUS: What is that? SOCRATES: That each of these in us is small and vile, and in no way sincere or whole, nor bearing a power worthy of its nature. Observing this in one, think the same of all the rest. For instance, there is fire in us, and there is also fire in the universe. PROTARCHUS: There is. SOCRATES: Is not this fire of ours small, weak, and vile? But that which is proper to the universe is wonderful in quantity and beauty, and in every power that pertains to fire? PROTARCHUS: You speak the absolute truth. SOCRATES: And is it so: is the fire of the whole world nourished and drawn from our fire, or on the contrary, is mine, and yours, and that of all other living things drawn from it? PROTARCHUS: These things are not worthy of an answer <note>meaning the answer is too obvious</note>. SOCRATES: Correct; you would say the same also of the earth of animals and of the world, and of all the other things we asked about above. PROTARCHUS: Who, answering otherwise, would be esteemed of sound mind? SOCRATES: No one, perhaps; but now to the rest. Looking at all these things just mentioned composed into one, we call it a "body." PROTARCHUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Take the same also concerning this which we call the "world" <note>original: "mundum"</note>. By the same reasoning, it is a body, composed of the same things. PROTARCHUS: You speak correctly. SOCRATES: Is our body entirely from this body, or on the contrary, is it [the world] nourished from ours, and does it receive and have whatever we mentioned a little while ago? PROTARCHUS: This also, Socrates, ought not to fall into question. SOCRATES: What of this? Ought it or not? PROTARCHUS: Say what it is. SOCRATES: Shall we confess that our body has a soul? PROTARCHUS: It is established. SOCRATES: From where, friend Protarchus, did it receive it, unless the body of the world—which contains the same things as ours and even more excellent things—has a soul? PROTARCHUS: From nowhere else. SOCRATES: For it is not to be thought, Protarchus, that those four—the Limit, the Infinite, the Mixture, and the class of Cause which is the fourth among them—which provide soul and body to those things in us, while it imprints a shadow and prepares remedies for the failing body, and establishes and restores other things in others, is called all and perfect wisdom; while these same things exist in the whole heaven and its greater parts, and moreover exist purer and more excellent.

<summary>Socrates argues that just as the human body is a small, "vile" reflection of the vast elements of the universe, the human mind and soul must also be derived from a greater, divine Mind that governs the cosmos. He concludes that the universe is not ruled by chance but by a supreme Intellect, which belongs to the category of "Cause."</summary>

yet in those things, the nature of the most noble and precious is least found. PRO. That would certainly have no reason in it. SO. PRO. What then shall we remember? SO. It is necessary hereafter to observe in which of these two each consists, and through what affection it occurs, whenever it occurs. That common genus, friend Socrates—repeat, I pray, what you mean by it among those things distinguished above. SO. I shall do so, O wonderful man, to the best of my strength. PRO. You say well. SO. Let us understand the "Common" to be that which we numbered third out of the four. PRO. Do you mean that which you placed after the Infinite and the Finite, in which you placed health and harmony, as I believe? SO. You speak rightly; but now apply your mind most especially to what is to be said. PRO. Speak now. SO. I say that when **Harmony** is dissolved in living beings, the dissolution of nature and the generation of **Pains** occur at that time. PRO. That is consistent. SO. Conversely, when harmony is tempered and restored to its own nature, it must be said that **Pleasure** is created—if indeed the greatest matters are to be concluded in few words. PRO. I think indeed that you speak rightly, O Socrates, yet we must strive to express the same more clearly. SO. Are not common and well-known things easy to recognize? PRO. What are those? SO. **Hunger** is indeed a dissolution and a distress. PRO. It is. SO. But **Eating** is a replenishment and a pleasure? PRO. Yes. SO. **Thirst** again is a corruption, a dissolution, and a pain. But the power of moisture restoring what has been dried out is pleasure. Furthermore, an unnatural separation and dissolution caused by heat is distress. But restoration according to nature and cooling is pleasure. PRO. Entirely. SO. Also, the thickening of moisture against the animal's nature caused by cold is pain. Conversely, when the moisture thaws and returns to its own nature, that return is pleasure. And in summary, consider whether this speech seems fair to you. Whenever
<margin>When pain and pleasure are born in all things.</margin>
the animated species—born, as we said, from the Infinite and the Limit according to nature—is corrupted, such corruption is **Pain**. But when these flow back into their own essence, we call this return **Pleasure**. PRO. Let it be so. For this seems to me very likely. SO. Let us therefore place this as one species of pleasure and pain in both these affections. PRO. Let it be placed. SO. Place next the **Expectation** of these affections in the soul. An expectation, I say, which precedes the pleasurable, hoping and rejoicing and sweet; but that which is distressing, fearful and mournful. PRO. There is therefore this other species of pleasure and pain, apart from the body, proceeding from the expectation of the soul alone. SO. You have understood rightly: In these, as my opinion goes, both existing pure and unmixed—namely pleasure and pain—we shall clearly discern whether the whole genus of pleasure is to be loved, or whether this should rather be attributed to some other of the aforementioned things; while to pleasure and pain, as to hot and cold and other such things, it belongs that they are sometimes to be loved, and at other times not to be loved, as they are by no means "goods" in themselves, but sometimes, by receiving a certain quality, they follow the nature of the Good. PRO. You say rightly that he who scrutinizes such things must proceed thus. SO. First, therefore, let us look at this: if it is true what I was saying, that pain follows the destruction of those things and pleasure follows their restoration; when they are neither being destroyed nor restored, what state should we then chiefly attribute to living beings? Answer me with an intent mind: does it seem necessary to you that any animal at that very time neither rejoices nor is pained? PRO. It is certainly necessary.
<margin>The middle state of pleasure and pain.</margin>
SO. There is therefore this **Third State** besides the affection of mourning and rejoicing. PRO. There is indeed. SO. Come then, try to remember this. For whether we remember it or not matters greatly for judging pleasure; let us, however, touch upon something briefly concerning it if you wish. PRO. Speak then: what is it? SO. Nothing prevents him who chooses the life of **Contemplation** from living in this way. PRO. You mean apart from joy and distress? SO. It was said in the comparison of each life that the man devoted to contemplation does not in any part either rejoice or feel pain.

e,iiii.

<margin>The contemplative life, being neither with joy nor with sadness, is most divine.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. It is altogether as you say. SOCRATES. Is this not fitting for him <note>referring to the divine or the intellect</note>? And perhaps it would be no wonder if this life were the most divine of all others. PRO. Is it then absurd for the gods to rejoice, or on the contrary, to be saddened? SO. Entirely absurd;

<margin>It is absurd for the gods to either rejoice or be saddened.</margin>
for both are unseemly for them. But let us investigate this next: whether it contributes anything to this discussion; and we shall assign it to the Mind for the second prize of victory, if we cannot assign it the first. PRO. You speak rightly. SO. And yet another species of pleasures, which we have assigned as proper to the soul, consists in memory. PRO. In what way? SO. First, it seems we must understand what memory is; or rather, before that, what sensation is, if we wish to elucidate these things more clearly. PRO. How do you mean? SO. Suppose that of all the experiences <note>original: "passionibus," referring to things acted upon the body</note> of the body, some are extinguished in the body before they flow through to the soul, leaving it free from the experience; others are diffused through both and bring about a certain kind of concussion, as much proper to each as common to both equally. PRO. Let it be so supposed. SO. And if we say that the experiences not propagated through both remain hidden from the soul, while those flowing through both become known to the soul, shall we be speaking correctly? PRO. Certainly. SO. Therefore, do not think that I mean this "remaining hidden" is in any way the generation of forgetfulness; for forgetfulness is the exit of memory. But in those things just mentioned, memory did not yet exist. It is absurd to say there is a loss of that which neither is nor was. PRO. Absurd. SO. Change the names then, at least. PRO. How? SO. Instead of saying it is "hidden from the soul" when it exists without the disturbance of bodily passion: what you now seem to call forgetfulness, call rather "insensation" <note>original: "insensationem," a lack of sensory perception</note>, if I may put it that way. PRO. I follow you. SO. But the movement produced in the common experience of body and soul, if you call it sensation, you will not name it out of place. PRO. You speak the truth. SO. Do we not now perceive

<margin>Memory is the preservation of sensation.</margin>
what we wish to be called sensation? PRO. We perceive it. SO. Furthermore, in my opinion, one will rightly call the preservation of sensation "memory." PRO. Quite rightly. SO. And do we admit that recollection differs from memory, or not? PRO. Perhaps. SO. Is it not chiefly in this? PRO. In what? SO. Whenever the soul, by itself and without the body, resumes and notices those things it once experienced with the body: then we assert that it remembers, do we not? PRO. Very much so. SO. Moreover, when it has suffered a loss of memory, and then—either by sensation or by the instruction of learning—it recalls that memory again within itself, it is thought to recollect. And these things we now call memories and recollections. PRO. You speak well. SO. But for the sake of what have all these things been said?

<margin>Experience belongs to the body, but desire does not belong to the body.</margin>
PRO. What indeed? SO. So that we may grasp the pleasure of the soul without the body as greatly and clearly as possible, and likewise desire; for through these things both seem to be declared. PRO. Let us proceed now to the rest, Socrates. SO. It is fitting to consider many things while investigating the origin of pleasure and its every form. And now indeed we must first see what desire is, and from where it is born. PRO. Let us see now, I pray; for we shall lose nothing. SO. On the contrary, O Protarchus, when we find what we were just seeking, we shall lose something: namely, our doubt. PRO. How beautifully you have returned the favor! But let us now explain what follows. SO. Did we not say that hunger and thirst, and many such things, are certain desires? PRO. Greatly so. SO. Looking at what same thing do we call such diverse things by one name? PRO. By Jove, it is not easy to say, Socrates, yet it must be said. SO. Let us begin again from the same things. PRO. Which ones? SO. Do we say someone thirsts? PRO. We do. SO. And this is to be emptied out. PRO. Why not? SO. And is thirst a desire?

<margin>To thirst is not of the body, but of the dried-out state of the body.</margin>
PRO. It is. SO. Of a drink? PRO. Of a drink. SO. Or rather, of the replenishment of drink? PRO. Of this, certainly. SO. He who is empty and exhausted, therefore, seeks the opposites of those things he suffers. For since he is empty, he desires to be filled. PRO. It is altogether manifest. SO. What then! Can he who is first exhausted reach its replenishment either by sensation or by a certain memory—a thing which he is not suffering in the present time, nor has ever suffered? PRO. In no way. SO. But we admit that he who desires, seeks something. PRO. Why not! SO. Therefore, he does not desire what he suffers. For he thirsts, and thirst is a lack; yet he affects replenishment. PRO. So it is. SO. Something of him, therefore, reaches the fulfillment of what he desires. PRO. Necessarily. SO. The body indeed cannot, for it is exhausted. PRO. Certainly. SO. It remains that the soul attains the replenishment through memory. PRO. It is clear. SO. For by what else would it attain it? PRO. By almost nothing else. SO. Do we notice what is achieved for us from these reasons? PRO. What is that? SO. This reasoning dictates that desire is not of the body. PRO. In what way? SO. Because it always shows the effort of every living being to be contrary to its bodily experiences. PRO. Entirely. SO. But the impulse drawing toward the contrary of the experiences implies a memory contrary to those experiences. PRO. Altogether. SO. Therefore, the reasoning, by showing that memory leads toward the thing desired, has explained that every impulse and desire, and the ruling principle of every living thing, belongs to the soul. PRO. Quite rightly. SO. This reasoning, therefore, does not admit that our body thirsts or hungers, or suffers anything of that kind. PRO. You speak the truth. SO. Furthermore, we shall consider this concerning these matters: that this reasoning seems to want to demonstrate a certain type of life in these things. PRO. In what things, and of what life do you speak? SO. In filling and emptying, I say: and in all things that pertain to the safety or destruction of living beings; and if any of us, being in either state, is afflicted, then he rejoices according to the changes. PRO. So it is. SO. What if he remains in the middle of these? PRO. How in the middle? SO. Because of the experience, he is indeed saddened; but he remembers past pleasures. The sadness ceases, yet he is not yet filled: what then should be said? Is he not in a middle state of experience? PRO. It should be said. SO. Is he altogether grieving, or on the contrary, rejoicing? PRO. Not rejoicing, by Jove, but rather affected by a double sadness: according to the body in its experience, and according to the soul in the heat of expectation. SO. How, Protarchus, did you say the grief was double? Is it not...

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus analyze the nature of sensation, memory, and desire, concluding that desire is a function of the soul's memory rather than a purely bodily impulse. They establish that while the body experiences lack, the soul uses memory to seek the opposite state (replenishment).</summary>

...empty, does someone sometimes hope for a certain replenishment, and at other times, conversely, despair of it? PROTARCHUS. Very much so. SOCRATES. Now, while he hopes to attain it, does he not seem to rejoice in the very memory of it, even while he is empty and suffering at that same time?
PROTARCHUS. Necessarily. SOCRATES. Then at that time, both man and the rest of the animals feel joy and sorrow simultaneously. PROTARCHUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. But when someone who is empty entirely despairs of replenishment, does not a double passion regarding pains then arise, which you, looking at it just a moment ago, thought was simply double? PROTARCHUS. These things are true. SOCRATES. Let us use this discussion of such passions for a certain purpose. PROTARCHUS. To what purpose do you mean? SOCRATES. In what way, then, O Protarchus, can fears be true or false? Or expectations true or not true? Or opinions true or false? PROTARCHUS. I would consider opinions to be so, but these others not at all. SOCRATES. What do you say? We seem to be starting a discussion that is not brief. PROTARCHUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. But we must consider if it is appropriate for the sons of that famous man <note>Likely a reference to Philebus or the lineage of the argument</note> to be making such claims. PROTARCHUS. Perhaps so. SOCRATES. Therefore, everything superfluous and whatever is beside the point must be dismissed. PROTARCHUS. Correct. SOCRATES. Tell me then: a continuous wonder always holds me regarding these questions we have now introduced. PROTARCHUS. In what way do you mean? SOCRATES. Are there not some among the number of pleasures that are false, and others true? PROTARCHUS. How can that be? SOCRATES. Then, according to you, one is never said to truly or falsely rejoice or be sad; nor would anyone find among the frantic and the insane someone who seems to rejoice when he does not rejoice, or to grieve when he does not grieve. PROTARCHUS. We all admit, O Socrates, that all these things are so. SOCRATES. But is this correct, or should we perhaps deliberate whether these things are said rightly or not? PROTARCHUS. We should deliberate, in my opinion. SOCRATES. Let us distinguish more clearly, then, what was just said about pleasure and opinion. Is there such a thing among men as "to opine"? PROTARCHUS. There is. SOCRATES. And "to rejoice"? PROTARCHUS. And to rejoice. SOCRATES. And is there not also something conceived by opinion? PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. And that in which the one rejoicing finds joy? PROTARCHUS. That too. SOCRATES. He who opines, whether he opines rightly or not rightly, does not lose the fact that he is truly opining. PROTARCHUS. How could he? SOCRATES. So too, he who rejoices, whether he rejoices rightly or not, does not lose the fact that he is truly rejoicing. PROTARCHUS. Indeed, these things are so. SOCRATES. In what way, then, is opinion true and false, while pleasure is only true, when both "to opine truly" and "to rejoice" have been accepted as similar? PROTARCHUS. This must be considered. SOCRATES. Is it not because truth and falsehood are inherent in opinions? And opinion is not made such solely because of these, but rather what kind of opinion each is? Is this what you say we must consider? PROTARCHUS. Yes. SOCRATES. Furthermore, we must investigate whether pleasure and pain remain only what they are, or whether they are made to be of a certain quality. PROTARCHUS. That is clear. SOCRATES. But it is not at all difficult to see that they become of a certain quality. We granted long ago that pleasures and pains become great and small, intense and mild. PROTARCHUS. We granted it. SOCRATES. And if depravity is added to these, we shall confess that a depraved opinion and likewise a depraved pleasure is produced. PROTARCHUS. What prevents it? SOCRATES. What if rectitude or the opposite of rectitude is applied to either of these? Shall we not call it a "right opinion"—which undergoes rectitude—and a "right pleasure" similarly? PROTARCHUS. It follows necessarily. SOCRATES. And if what one grasps by opinion is deceptive, shall we not call the opinion false rather than right? PROTARCHUS. Indeed. SOCRATES. Likewise, if we perceive that we wander astray in pleasure or pain regarding that in which we rejoice or are distressed, shall we call it a right or good pleasure, or honor it with some noble name? PROTARCHUS. But that cannot happen, if indeed the pleasure itself is at fault. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, pleasure often arises in us from a false opinion. PROTARCHUS. Without a doubt. Yet, O Socrates, we call the opinion of that sort false; but no one would ever call the pleasure itself false. SOCRATES. You defend the account of pleasure too promptly, O Protarchus, in the present moment. PROTARCHUS. Not at all; I only speak what I hear. SOCRATES. Is there no difference for us, my friend, between the pleasure that proceeds from right opinion and knowledge, and that which follows false opinion and ignorance? PROTARCHUS. It is likely that they differ by no small interval. SOCRATES. But let us come to examine this very distance. PROTARCHUS. Lead on wherever you please. SOCRATES. Behold, I lead you this way. PROTARCHUS. Which way? SOCRATES. Some opinion is true, and some is false. PROTARCHUS. It is. SOCRATES. Pleasure and pain often follow these. PROTARCHUS. They follow. SOCRATES. Does not opinion arise in us from sense and memory? And does it not happen that I deliberate by opinion at my will? PROTARCHUS. Especially so. SOCRATES. Must we not think that we stand thus regarding these things? PROTARCHUS. In what way? SOCRATES. Do you not confess that sometimes a man, seeing something from a distance confusedly, wishes to discern the objects more clearly? PROTARCHUS. I do confess it. SOCRATES. He will therefore ask himself in a certain way. PROTARCHUS. How so? SOCRATES. "What is that which appears over there next to the rock under the tree?" Does he not seem to say these things to himself when he looks at such things as have appeared to him at some time? PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Then, as if answering himself, he says, "That is a man," having attained the truth, as it were. <margin>Opinion is formed here from sense and memory.</margin> PROTARCHUS. Exactly. SOCRATES. Again, perhaps changing his mind, he asserts it is some work made by shepherds. PROTARCHUS. Very much so. SOCRATES. And if someone were present with him, he would pour out into speech what he had turned over in his mind, saying the same things to the one present. And what we previously called "opinion" would then become "speech." PROTARCHUS. Manifestly. SOCRATES. But if he is alone, repeating this same thing to himself, he proceeds within himself, sometimes keeping it for a long time. <margin>The soul is like a book and a blank tablet on which nothing is yet depicted.</margin> PROTARCHUS. Entirely. SOCRATES. What then? Do you feel the same as I do in these matters? PROTARCHUS. What is that? SOCRATES. It seems to me then that a man's soul is like a certain book. PROTARCHUS. By what reasoning? SOCRATES. Memory, coinciding with the senses in the same thing, and those passions which are around these things, seem to me to write certain words in the soul in a certain way. And when they write true things, a true opinion of this kind...

The painter: who, following the scribe, paints images of the spoken words in the soul. PRO. How and when should we say he performs this? SO. When someone, having withdrawn from sight or another sense the things spoken and perceived by opinion, somehow contemplates within himself the images of those spoken and perceived things—does this not happen within us? He concludes that there are true and false pleasures and pains.

according to this reasoning, certain false pleasures in the souls of men—imitations of the true, or rather ridiculous ones—and pains in the same manner. PRO. They exist in both. SO. Was it not possible to form opinions about things that neither were, nor are, nor will be? PRO. It was. SO. And these were the things that then produced false opinion and the act of opining falsely. Was it not so? PRO. It was. SO. Must we not grant in those cases a certain state corresponding to pleasures and pains? PRO. In what way? SO. Because it was possible for someone to truly rejoice, in whatever way or however randomly he exults, yet not in things that are or were, and often even to rejoice in things that will never happen. Gather what follows from these things. PRO. Tell me. SO. Whenever those things concur, pleasures and pains also meet, as do the perceptions of them, which are contrary—as has just now become clear. PRO. It appears so. SO. Is this also agreed upon between us? PRO. What? SO. That both pleasure and pain can be experienced to a greater or lesser degree, and are referred to the genus of the "infinite" <note>original: "infiniti," referring to the Pythagorean/Platonic concept of the Indeterminate or Unlimited</note>. Is it not our purpose in this judgment to distinguish everywhere which of these is greater, which is smaller, which is more intense, and which is more internal—pleasure compared to pain, pain to pain, and again pleasure to pleasure? PRO. These things are indeed so, and that is the purpose of our judgment. SO. What then? In the case of sight, does looking at magnitudes from a distance or from nearby obscure the truth and compel one to form false opinions? And does the same not happen in the case of pains and pleasures? PRO. Much more so, Socrates. SO. That is certainly the opposite of what was told a little while ago. PRO. What do you mean? SO. For then, these opinions, having been made false or true, previously filled the pains and pleasures with their own passion. PRO. You speak the truth. SO. But now, because they are seen to shift here and there from a distance or from nearby, and are compared to one another, the pleasures seem greater and more vehement when compared to pains, and the pains conversely when compared to pleasures. PRO. Such things must necessarily happen for those reasons. SO. And if, by as much as each appears greater or smaller...
