# PHILEBUS, OR ON THE HIGHEST GOOD. FOLIO XXXVIII.

<margin>
Great changes bring pleasures and pains; small ones do not.
The threefold life: pleasant, sad, or neutral.
</margin>

¶ ...appear to be what they truly are: you would take away just as much yourself. Is it not so, that since both appear to be something, yet are not, you would say they do not appear correctly? Nor would you ever dare to assert that such portions of pleasure or pain are right or true? PRO. That is so. SO. After this, then, let us look into whether, by this reasoning, we might bring to light false pleasures and pains much more than those which both appear in living beings and exist. PRO. What kind do you mean, and in what way? SO. It has been said many times: that when the nature of anything is corrupted by combinations or separations, by fillings or emptyings, or by certain increases or decreases, then pains, distresses, tortures, and others of that kind arise. PRO. This has indeed been said often. SO. But when they are restored to their own nature, we have established that such restoration is pleasure for us. PRO. Correct. SO. But what about when none of these things happen regarding our body? PRO. But when does that occur, Socrates? SO. That question of yours, Protarchus, is not to the point. PRO. Why so? SO. Because nothing prevents me from asking again what I asked before. PRO. What was that? SO. If such a thing does not happen, Protarchus, I say: what must necessarily happen to us as a result? PRO. Do you mean, for instance, when the body is moved in neither direction <note>i.e., neither toward pain/corruption nor toward pleasure/restoration</note>? SO. Exactly that. PRO. It is clear, Socrates, that neither pleasure nor pain is perceived at that very time. SO. You have answered quite rightly. But I think you perceive this: that one of these things must always happen to us, as the wise men <note>likely referring to Heraclitus and his followers</note> hand down; for they say all things are constantly flowing up and down. PRO. They do say that, and they do not seem to speak poorly. SO. For how could they speak poorly, since they were not bad men? But I wish to avoid the looming argument; I intend to flee this way, and you flee along with me. PRO. Tell me, which way? SO. Let us say to them that these things are so. But you answer: Does a living being always feel whatever it suffers <note>original: "patitur" - experiences or undergoes</note> while suffering it? And while we are growing, does it escape our notice, or when we suffer anything else of this kind? Or is it entirely the opposite: for almost all such things escape us? PRO. Entirely the opposite. SO. Therefore, what we just said was not correctly stated by us—that changes made up or down bring pleasures and pains. PRO. Why not? SO. It can be said more correctly and safely in this way. PRO. How? SO. That great changes bring pleasures and pains, but moderate and small ones do not at all. PRO. It is said more correctly in that way than the other, Socrates. SO. Indeed, if these things are so, the life described earlier will soon return. PRO. Which one? SO. The one we placed as being without sorrow and without joy. PRO. You speak the truth. SO. From these, let us establish a threefold life: the pleasant, the sad, and the neutral. Or do you feel otherwise? PRO. Not otherwise than that: namely, that there is a threefold life. SO. Therefore, not to feel pain will not be the same thing as to feel joy. PRO. Not at all. SO. Whenever you hear, then, that it is the sweetest of all things to pass one's whole life without sorrow, what do you think the person saying that means for himself? PRO. He seems to me to mean that "sweet" is this very thing: not to feel pain. SO. Set up three things as you please; and to use more beautiful names, call one gold, the other silver, and the remaining one neither. PRO. Let them be set. SO. That which is neither of these: can it become either of them? Either silver or gold? PRO. It cannot. SO. Therefore, if the middle life is ever called or thought to be pleasant or sad, it is by no means correctly thought or spoken of. PRO. Certainly. SO. And yet, my friend, we perceive that some people speak and think this way. PRO. Very much so. SO. Do they then think they are rejoicing at the time when they are not grieving? PRO. They do say so. SO. Do they not then think they are rejoicing? For they would not pronounce it otherwise. PRO. It appears so. SO. They think falsely about joy, since the nature of joy and of painlessness are different. PRO. Different indeed. SO. Which shall we choose? That these three states are among us, as just now, or only two: pain as an evil to men, and the absence of sadness, being a good from this very fact, is named "sweet"? PRO. How that might be, Socrates, let us ask ourselves; for I do not understand. SO. Truly, Protarchus, you do not understand the adversaries of this Philebus. PRO. Whom do you mean? SO. Those who are said to be especially skilled in the nature of things, who do away with pleasures entirely. PRO. What then? SO. They call all those things "escapes from pain" which the followers of Philebus call "pleasures." PRO. Do you advise us to believe these men, Socrates? SO. Not at all; but let us use them as certain prophets who speak not by art, but by a certain indignation of a not ignoble nature; they utterly abhor the feeling of pleasure from the beginning, and wish for nothing in it to be pure—so much so that they call its very allurements a kind of wicked entanglement rather than pleasure. Use them, then, for this purpose, considering also the other things they most passionately attack. After this, however, accept which pleasures I consider to be true, so that by considering the force of pleasure from both their arguments, we may finally prepare ourselves to judge. PRO. You speak rightly. SO. Let us then follow in the footsteps of their indignation, as if following defenders. I think they mean something like this, beginning from a higher and further point: that if we wish to know the nature of any species—for instance, the nature of "hard"—would we know it best by looking at the hardest things, or at things only slightly hard? You must answer these indignant questions, Protarchus, just as I do. PRO. I must indeed; and I answer them that we must look toward the greatest magnitudes. SO. If we wish to know what nature the genus of pleasure has, we must look not at small pleasures far removed from the peak, but at those which are called the highest and most vehement. PRO. Anyone would grant you that now. SO. Are not those which are the greatest pleasures, as we have often said, placed most readily before the others—namely, those concerning the body? PRO. Why not? SO. Are they found to be more vehement in those who are sick than in those who are healthy? Let us be careful, I pray, lest by answering rashly we fall into error... <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "aegris" (the sick) indicates the start of the next page.</note>

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus discuss the "threefold life" (pleasure, pain, and a neutral state), arguing that the mere absence of pain is often falsely labeled as pleasure. Socrates introduces the views of "pleasure-haters" who see all pleasure as a mere escape from pain, suggesting they examine the most intense physical pleasures to find the truth.</summary>

# BOOK TEN

**SOCRATES:** In what way? **PROTARCHUS:** Perhaps we should admit it is so in those who are in good health. **SOCRATES:** It is likely. **PROTARCHUS:** Do not those pleasures exceed all others greatly where burning desires are present? **SOCRATES:** That is true. **PROTARCHUS:** Do not men afflicted with fevers and similar diseases suffer both intense thirst and cold? And whatever they are accustomed to suffer in the body, they suffer much more than others; whereby it happens that they have greater needs, and in filling those needs, they are more vehemently delighted. Or shall we deny this is true? **PROTARCHUS:** It appears entirely as has been said.

<margin>The opinion of some regarding immense pleasure.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** What then? Shall we seem to think correctly if we assert that if anyone wishes to see the greatest pleasures, he should look not to health, but to disease? And see that you do not think I ask this with the intent of seeing whether the sick are soothed by more delights than the healthy; rather, consider that I am asking where the magnitude and vehemence of pleasure occurs. For we said before that we must investigate what its nature consists of, or what those say who asserted that it does not exist at all. **PROTARCHUS:** I follow almost everything you say. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps you will show no less, O Protarchus. Answer now: In lust and wantonness, do you see—I do not say more—but more vehement and more intensely great pleasures than in a temperate life? Speak, I pray, applying your mind. **PROTARCHUS:** I perceive what you mean, and I see a very great excess. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, the proverb "nothing in excess" <note>original: *nihil nimis*, the Latin translation of the Greek *meden agan*</note> always restrains the temperate, and they obey it. But the heat of pleasure, seizing intemperate and dissolute men even unto madness, compels them to exult with immoderate cries. **PROTARCHUS:** You speak rightly. **SOCRATES:** And if this is true, it is clear that in a certain depravity of both soul and body, rather than in virtue, vehement pleasures and vehement torments consist. **PROTARCHUS:** It is certainly clear. **SOCRATES:** Should we not elicit some from the many, investigating by what reason they ought to be called "great"? **PROTARCHUS:** It is necessary. **SOCRATES:** Observe, therefore, what the pleasures of such diseases are like. **PROTARCHUS:** Of what kind? **SOCRATES:** The pleasures of the deformed <note>likely referring to "shameful" or "unseemly" pleasures</note>, which those whom we called "indignant" utterly shudder at. **PROTARCHUS:** What kind, I say? **SOCRATES:** Such as in the remedy for the itch <note>original: *scabiei*, referring to skin irritations or scabies</note> which is done by scratching, and others of this sort; needing no other medicine, this passion—by the immortal gods!—shall we call it pleasure or rather pain? **PROTARCHUS:** This seems to be a certain evil mixture, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Yet we did not fall into this discourse for the sake of Philebus. But because unless these pleasures, and those which follow them, are inspected, we shall almost never be able to judge what is now sought. Must we not proceed to their relatives? **PROTARCHUS:** Do you mean those which share in a mixture?

<margin>Mixtures of pleasure and pain in the body.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** These very ones. There are, therefore, mixtures of the body itself in bodies, and of the soul in the soul. And we shall find the pains of the soul mixed with the pleasures of the body; and that commixture of both is sometimes called pleasure, and sometimes pain. **PROTARCHUS:** In what way?

**SOCRATES:** As for example, when someone in the state of restoration or corruption suffers opposites at the same time: being cold he often grows warm, and being warm he sometimes cools; seeking, as I think, to attain the one and cast off the other. What is said of both—sweet mixed with bitter—standing with the difficulty of rejection, produces distress and then a wild encounter. **PROTARCHUS:** What is said at present is especially true. **SOCRATES:** Are not some of these mixtures composed equally from both sides, and some from one or the other exceeding? **PROTARCHUS:** Nothing prevents it. **SOCRATES:** Speak then of the number of those which contain more pain than delight: those are the ones that follow the itch and the ticklings; when that which is within boils and swells, and one does not reach it by scratching or rubbing, but only spreads what is around the skin. Then indeed, bringing those parts to the fire, and often changing them into the opposite by a certain ambiguity, they produce inestimable pleasures; sometimes, on the contrary, they show pleasures mixed with the troubles of the exterior to the interior parts, in whichever direction the inclination occurs, because they spread the mixed things by violence or confound the dispersed, and at the same time bring pains to the pleasures. **PROTARCHUS:** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES:** Again, when a fuller pleasure is mixed according to all such things, then a portion of pain woven in tickles and affects one with a certain light sadness? And again, the more abundant part of pleasure poured in provokes, and sometimes compels one to leap up, and produces all kinds of colors, all kinds of figures, all kinds of breaths with every incitement, and exclamations with insanity? **PROTARCHUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** It forces him, moreover, O friend, to exclaim about himself, or then another to exclaim, that soothed by these pleasures and melting away, he almost dies; and the more intemperate and imprudent one is, the more he pursues pleasures of this kind. And he proclaims these, moreover, as the highest delights; and he who softens his whole life with these delights, he considers most blessed. **PROTARCHUS:** You have collected all the things that come into the estimation of the many, O Socrates.

<margin>Mixtures of pleasure and pain of the soul in the soul.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** Concerning the pleasures, O Protarchus, which are mixed in the common passions of the body from without or within, it has been said. But concerning those which are mixed in the soul, certain opposites are cast toward the body: namely, pleasure with pain, and pain with pleasure, running together into one mixture. And we ran through these in the previous parts: that when one is emptied, he desires replenishment; and hoping, he rejoices, but being exhausted, he is distressed. At that time we did not confirm these things with testimonies; but now we say that when the soul differs from the body in all those things whose multitude is not sufficiently grasped, one mixture of pain and pleasure emerges. **PROTARCHUS:** You seem to speak quite rightly.

<margin>Pleasures of the soul in the soul.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** One more encounter of pain and pleasure remains. **PROTARCHUS:** Which one? **SOCRATES:** That which we said the soul often receives within itself. **PROTARCHUS:** By what reason do we assert this? **SOCRATES:** Anger, fear, desire, lamentation, love, emulation, envy...

They explore the physical and psychological overlap of pleasure and pain, using examples like the relief of an itch or the frenzy of lust.</summary>

# BOOK TEN

The mixture itself can be more easily shown in loves, fears, and others. You will recognize this from your own experience; and keeping what has been said in mind, let me go: do not force me to descend into those things one by one in order, which would lead to a long-winded dispute. But take this simply: both the soul without the body, and the body without the soul, as well as the mutual meeting of both, have a shared involvement in all disturbances of pleasure and pain. Tell me then: will you let me go, or keep me until late at night? For I think if I say a few more things, you will release me. Indeed, I promise you the full discourse on all these matters tomorrow; but for the present, I desire to proceed to the judgment that Philebus established. PROTARCHUS. You speak excellently, Socrates; therefore, relate what remains in whatever way pleases you. SOCRATES. According to nature, after mixed pleasures, we shall arrive by a certain necessity at those that are in some way pure.

<margin>Concerning pure pleasures.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. Quite right. SOCRATES. I will endeavor to signify them to us by way of distinction. I do not entirely agree with those who say all pleasures are merely the cessation of pains. However, as I said, I use them as witnesses to show that many things *seem* to be pleasures when they are not; and also against those which, though they appear great and numerous, are nevertheless mixed with sadness: they are occupied with the cessation of great pains concerning the deficiencies of the body and soul.

<margin>Which are true pleasures.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. Which pleasures then, Socrates, should one rightly judge to be true? SOCRATES. Those which consist of beautiful colors and shapes, and most scents, and harmonies; and whatever things have hidden needs <note>original: "indigentiãs... occultas" - referring to desires we aren't consciously pained by until they are satisfied</note> of the senses without distress. They exhibit fulfillments that are manifest, sweet, and free from sadness. PROTARCHUS. By what reasoning, Socrates, do we say these things? SOCRATES. Certainly, what I speak of is not immediately clear; nevertheless, I must try to explain. For I speak of the beauty of shapes—not as most people perhaps understand them, such as those of animals or certain paintings—but I mean something straight and circular, and from these, the things made by lathes: planes and solids, and those constructed with <term>canons</term> <note>original: "canonibus" - here meaning rulers or measuring rods</note>, that is, rules and squares, if you follow me. For I say these are not beautiful in relation to something else, as other things are, but are always beautiful by their own nature, having their own pleasures in no way associated with the delights of movement; and likewise, that colors are beautiful and pleasing for the same reason. But do we understand? Or what remains? PROTARCHUS. I am striving, Socrates; but you also strive to explain more clearly. SOCRATES. I say further that the delights of sounds are clearly sweet and pure, containing one entirely pure melody, compared to nothing else, but beautiful by nature and bringing innate pleasures.

<margin>The class of pleasures following scents: less divine.</margin>
PROTARCHUS. This also is true. SOCRATES. However, the class of pleasures following scents is less divine; but because they do not mix pains with their necessary functions, and wherever and in whomever this happens to be present, I place this as a total benefit to them. And so, understand now that we have gathered two species of pleasures. PROTARCHUS. I understand.

<margin>The pleasures of the sciences are twofold.</margin>
SOCRATES. Here let us also add the pleasures of the <term>sciences</term> <note>original: "disciplinarũ" - refers to learning, studies, or branches of knowledge</note>, if indeed these do not seem to contain the act of learning, nor to bring pains from the beginning because of the greed for knowledge. PROTARCHUS. I agree. SOCRATES. But what if someone imbued with doctrine then forgets it—do you not see that a certain sadness follows? PROTARCHUS. Not by nature, certainly, but by a certain reflection on the experience, when one is saddened because of the lack created by the loss. SOCRATES. But, my blessed friend, we are at present treating the experiences of nature, not of opinion. PROTARCHUS. You assert truly that the forgetting of doctrine happens without natural sadness. SOCRATES. We must confess, then, that the pleasures of the sciences are free from pain, and belong not to many men, but to very few. PROTARCHUS. It must be confessed, without a doubt. SOCRATES. After we have separated pure pleasures from the impure, we must now add immoderation to the vehement pleasures, and moderation to the calmer ones. And those which admit of the "more" and "less"—the intense, the relaxed, the great, the small, the rare, the frequent—it is proper to refer to the genus of the "infinite" <note>original: "infiniti gen⁹" - the Pythagorean/Platonic concept of the Indefinite or Unlimited</note> which runs through the soul and body according to more or less; but those which do not admit these are rather to be referred to the commensurate genus. PROTARCHUS. You speak rightly, Socrates. SOCRATES. After this, one thing further must be established regarding pleasures. PROTARCHUS. What is that? SOCRATES. Whether we should say that what contributes to truth is the pure and sincere itself, or the vehement, the much, the great, and the sufficient. PROTARCHUS. What do you mean by asking these things, Socrates? SOCRATES. I would wish to omit nothing, Protarchus, in this very debate between pleasure and knowledge. Since a certain portion of each of them is pure and a certain portion impure, so that each pure part coming into judgment may offer itself open and ready for me, and you, and all these others to judge. PROTARCHUS. Skillfully put. SOCRATES. Come then, let us think about all the things we call pure genera in this way, bringing one of them forward first into our midst. PROTARCHUS. Which shall we pick out? SOCRATES. White, if you wish. Let us first consider the genus. PROTARCHUS. I am willing. SOCRATES. In what way then is there whiteness, and what will its purity be? Whether it is that which is greatest and most abundant, or that which is so sincere that no other color is in it? PROTARCHUS. It is clearly established that it is that which is especially sincere. SOCRATES. Well said; shall we not affirm, Protarchus, that this is the truest and most beautiful of all whites, and not that which is most abundant or greatest? PROTARCHUS. Correct. SOCRATES. If therefore we say that a small but pure white is whiter, more beautiful, and truer than a mixed and large amount of white, shall we be entirely correct? PROTARCHUS. Correct, without a doubt. SOCRATES. Shall we need many more such examples to judge pleasure? Or will it suffice to know here that any pleasure, whether small or great, few or many, provided it is removed from pain, is sweeter, truer, and finally more beautiful? PROTARCHUS. That single example is enough. SOCRATES. But what about this? Have we heard that pleasure is always a "becoming" <note>original: "generationẽ" - the process of coming-into-being</note>,

# PHILEBUS, OR ON THE HIGHEST GOOD

...than itself: the other always seeking something else. PROTARCHUS: By what reasoning? And what are these things you speak of? SOCRATES: The one is, by its own nature, most worthy of veneration; the other, however, is deficient. PROTARCHUS: Express this more clearly. SOCRATES: We have seen through wisdom certain beautiful and good objects in number, and furthermore, those who excessively desired them. PROTARCHUS: We have seen them. SOCRATES: Since these two exist, look for two other similar things, so that in everything we discuss, there is a third to the other two. PROTARCHUS: I beg you, Socrates, set forth what you mean even more clearly. SOCRATES: It is nothing complex, O Protarchus, we are merely playing. PROTARCHUS: I have barely grasped it at last, despite the frequent repetition. SOCRATES: Perhaps as the discussion proceeds, we will comprehend it more clearly. PROTARCHUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Let us take up these two again. PROTARCHUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: One indeed is "becoming" <note>original: *generationem*; the process of coming-into-being</note>, the other is "being" <note>original: *essentiam*; true essence or stable reality</note>. PROTARCHUS: I accept these two from you: being and becoming. SOCRATES: Correct. Now, which of these do we say is for the sake of the other? Is becoming for the sake of being, or is being—insofar as it is called being, that is, according to that which exists—for the sake of becoming? Do you perceive this? PROTARCHUS: I seem to; but by the gods, why do you ask me! SOCRATES: I am asking something of this sort, O Protarchus: is the building of ships done for the sake of the ship? Or is the ship for the sake of the building of ships? And I say the same of all such things. PROTARCHUS: Why do you not answer yourself, Socrates? SOCRATES: Nothing prevents it; however, you should join in. PROTARCHUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: I say that for the sake of "becoming," all drugs, tools, and all matter are applied to all things; but each individual process of becoming is for the sake of an individual being; and finally, the whole of becoming is for the sake of the whole of being.

<margin>That pleasure is not the Good.</margin>
SOCRATES: Quite clearly. And will not pleasure, if indeed it is a "becoming," necessarily exist for the sake of some "being"? PROTARCHUS: Why not?

<margin>That for whose sake a thing is done is the Good.</margin>
SOCRATES: That which is such that things are done for its sake—while it is never done for the sake of another—is perhaps placed in the category of the Good; but that which is for the sake of another should perhaps, O best of men, be reduced to another category. PROTARCHUS: That is entirely necessary. SOCRATES: Therefore, if pleasure is a "becoming," we shall rightly refer it to a lot other than that of the Good. PROTARCHUS: Rightly indeed.

<margin>The absurdity of saying pleasure alone is the Good.</margin>
SOCRATES: Is it not as I predicted at the start of this dispute: thanks must be given to the one who says that pleasure is a "becoming," but that no "being" of pleasure exists? For it is clear that such a person would utterly mock anyone who proclaims pleasure to be the Good. PROTARCHUS: Greatly so. SOCRATES: Furthermore, this same man will laugh at and despise those who are too zealously devoted to "becoming." PROTARCHUS: In what way, and what kind of people do you mean? SOCRATES: Those who, while quenching hunger and thirst, or anything else which "becoming" cures and settles, rejoice in the becoming itself as if it were the Good; and they say they would not choose to live at all unless they were thirsty and hungry, and affected by the other things that follow these. PROTARCHUS: They certainly seem to. SOCRATES: But we all admit that the opposite of "becoming" is "destruction." PROTARCHUS: Necessarily. SOCRATES: Whoever seeks these things chooses corruption and becoming, rather than that third life which we proposed: a life void of both joy and sadness, but consisting of the purest possible intelligence. PROTARCHUS: Whoever asserts that pleasure is our Good, Socrates, will be far from reason.

<margin>On the purity of the sciences.</margin>
SOCRATES: Very far indeed; since it is possible to show it by this further reasoning. PROTARCHUS: Which one? SOCRATES: For why would it not be absurd if nothing were good or beautiful either in the body or in anything else except the soul—and yet in the soul, one called only pleasure "good"? And what of courage, temperance, intelligence, and all other goods? Is the soul not their source? Not at all! And furthermore, to assert that a man devoid of pleasure but affected by pain is "evil" while he suffers, even if he is the best of all men; and conversely, to say that he who is soothed by pleasures is more excellent in virtue the more he exults. PROTARCHUS: All these things, O Socrates, are more absurd than can be said. SOCRATES: Lest we seem to pursue the examination of all pleasure while neglecting mind and science, come now, if there is any "filth" <note>impurities or inaccuracies</note> attached to them, let us shake it off. Until, finally penetrating to their purest nature and inspecting it, we can use the truest parts of both these and pleasure for our judgment. PROTARCHUS: Skillfully put. SOCRATES: Does not science show us one thing regarding doctrine, and another regarding education or nourishment? PROTARCHUS: It is so.

<margin>The most powerful elements in the arts.</margin>
SOCRATES: Let us first investigate those faculties which use the hands: whether in them there is something more according to science and something less; and whether we should consider one part purest and another part more impure. PROTARCHUS: That is certainly fitting. SOCRATES: We must distinguish the principal parts from each. PROTARCHUS: Which ones, and in what way? SOCRATES: For instance, if one were to separate from all arts the skill of counting, measuring, and weighing, what remained of each would be, so to speak, a worthless thing. PROTARCHUS: Worthless indeed. SOCRATES: For the remainder would proceed by a kind of imagination and the experience of the senses and practice; and by conjectures, which most people call "arts," having gained power through care and labor. PROTARCHUS: You bring up entirely necessary points.

<margin>Music uses guesswork and is without measure.</margin>
SOCRATES: Is it not so where music is full of these things, it tunes harmony first not by measure, but rather by the conjecture of diligence? And its entire faculty of playing seeks the measure of each string by the conjecture of its movement, so that it has much obscurity mixed in, and very little stability! PROTARCHUS: Most true.

<margin>The weakness of medicine, agriculture, pilotage, and military art.</margin>
SOCRATES: Furthermore, we shall find that medicine, agriculture, pilotage, and the military art are similarly established. PROTARCHUS: Very much so.

<margin>The nobility of architecture.</margin>
SOCRATES: But architecture uses many measures and instruments; because it uses them more frequently, it is rendered the most clear and the most technical among many faculties. PROTARCHUS: In what way? SOCRATES: In the construction of ships and houses, and many other things pertaining to the craft of woodworking, it uses the rule, the lathe, the compass, the line, the plumb-line, and also an instrument suitable for straightening wood. PROTARCHUS: You speak very rightly, O Socrates.

<margin>Arts in a double order.</margin>
SOCRATES: Let us therefore place those which are called arts into two ranks: music, which in its works follows after those with less clarity; and architecture...

<summary>Socrates and Protarchus distinguish between "becoming" (process) and "being" (the end goal), concluding that pleasure is a process and therefore cannot be the ultimate Good. They then begin to rank the arts and sciences based on their precision, noting that fields like music rely on guesswork while architecture relies on precise measurement.</summary>

<margin>Proverb: Things which are beautiful are to be repeated twice and thrice.</margin>
"Things which are beautiful are to be repeated twice and thrice." <note>A common Greek proverb suggesting that good arguments or beautiful things bear repeating.</note> PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. By Jove, I think the previous statements were made thus. PROTARCHUS. How? SOCRATES. Philebus says that pleasure is the right goal for all living creatures, and that everyone ought to strive toward it; and that this is the "Good" itself for all beings; moreover, that these two names, "Good" and "Pleasant," belong to the same nature. Socrates, however, says first that this is not the case at all; and just as there are two names, "Good" and "Pleasant," so there are also two different natures. Furthermore, that wisdom participates more in the Good than pleasure does. Are these not the things, O Protarchus, that were being said? PROTARCHUS. Exactly. SOCRATES. This also was then, and is now, worthy of agreement. PROTARCHUS. What sort of thing? SOCRATES. That the nature of the Good itself differs from others chiefly in this. PROTARCHUS. In what way? 
<margin>In what the nature of the good differs from others.</margin>
SOCRATES. To whichever of living beings this is present, always and entirely and everywhere, it lacks nothing else and contains perfect sufficiency. Is that not so? PROTARCHUS. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Did we not attempt by reason itself to place each one separately from the other—that is, pleasure apart from wisdom and vice versa—to look into the life of each? PROTARCHUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Did either of these then seem to us to be sufficient? PROTARCHUS. And how could it have seemed so! SOCRATES. Because if by chance some error was made then, let someone now at least resume and assert more correctly: placing memory, knowledge, wisdom, and true opinion in the same category <note>original: "ideæ"</note>, and considering whether anyone would choose for himself or another either to be or to become anything at all without these—much less choose pleasure, whether the greatest or most vehement, without them. For if deprived of these, he will neither truly think he is enjoying himself, nor know in what condition he is affected, nor preserve a memory of the feeling itself through any length of time. You might say the same of wisdom: whether anyone would prefer to attain wisdom far removed from even the slightest pleasure rather than with certain pleasures, or all pleasures without wisdom rather than with some wisdom. PROTARCHUS. No one, Socrates. Truly, there is no need to repeat these things so many times now. SOCRATES. Therefore, neither of these is perfect, universally desirable, or the absolute Good. PROTARCHUS. Neither. SOCRATES. Either, then, we must grasp the Good itself clearly, or some image of it, so that, as we said, we may see to which the "second prize" <note>original: "secundæ sortes"</note> should chiefly be awarded. PROTARCHUS. You speak very skillfully. SOCRATES. Have we not entered upon a certain path toward the Good itself? PROTARCHUS. Which one? SOCRATES. If someone seeking a certain man first learns the house where he lives, he will surely have a great aid toward finding him. PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. So also the present and previous reasoning warned us not to seek the Good itself in the simple life, but in the mixed life. PROTARCHUS. Entirely. SOCRATES. Yet there is a more certain hope that we will find what we seek in that which is beautifully mixed than in its opposite. PROTARCHUS. More certain indeed. SOCRATES. Let us mix them then, O Protarchus, first vowing to the gods—whether Dionysus or 
<margin>The mixture is dedicated to Dionysus and Vulcan.</margin>
Vulcan, or whichever of the gods has been allotted the office of mixing. PROTARCHUS. It must be done exactly so. SOCRATES. And yet, as if we were mixing wine, certain springs stand before us. One can compare the spring of pleasure to honey. But the spring of wisdom, sober and without the force of wine, to a certain sharp and most healthful water. Let us strive to blend these liquids together as beautifully as possible. PROTARCHUS. We must certainly strive. SOCRATES. Come, tell me first: if we mix all pleasure with all wisdom, will we have joined them beautifully? PROTARCHUS. Perhaps. SOCRATES. But it is not at all safe. However, I trust I shall now declare a way we may mix them more securely. PROTARCHUS. Tell me how. SOCRATES. Was it not clear in the previous parts that one pleasure is different from another, and again one science from another, and that some science is more pure? PROTARCHUS. It was quite clear. SOCRATES. Science also differs from science: one indeed concerns those things which are born and perish, the other concerns those things which neither become nor pass away, but are always the same in the same way. And looking toward truth itself, we think the latter is truer. PROTARCHUS. Quite right. SOCRATES. If we connect the truest portions of each together, will the mixture of these be sufficient to provide us with the most desirable life? Or will we need something else of another sort besides? PROTARCHUS. It seems to me we should do so. SOCRATES. Let there be for us, then, a certain wise man who knows what justice itself is, and has reason as a companion to his understanding, and likewise knows all other things that exist. PROTARCHUS. Let it be so. SOCRATES. Will this man be endowed with sufficient knowledge if he holds the ratio of the divine circle and sphere itself, but is entirely ignorant of this human sphere and these circles, even while using the canons—that is, the rules—and circles in architecture and similar works? PROTARCHUS. Our knowledge will be ridiculous, O Socrates, if it is occupied only with divine things. SOCRATES. What do you say? Must we also insert and mix in the impure and unstable art of the false rule and circle? PROTARCHUS. This is necessary, if any of us is even to find the way that leads home. SOCRATES. And what about music, which we said a little while ago was based on conjecture and imitation...

...to be far from full purity? SOCRATES: That is also necessary, if indeed our life is to be any kind of life at all. PROTARCHUS: Do you wish then, like a doorkeeper pushed and forced by a crowd, that I should now throw open the doors and allow all the sciences to flow together and be mingled, the pure with the inferior? SOCRATES: It is nothing new, O Protarchus, for someone to be harmed by other sciences when they possess the primary ones. <note>original: "Haud nouū o Socrates lędi aliquē a sciētiis aliis: q̄ primas habent." PROTARCHUS: Let them be sent in altogether. SOCRATES: Now it seems we must go back to the fountain of pleasures. For when we thought to mix them, the true portions were by no means brought out to us first; rather, you should know that for the sake of the love of the whole, they all run together into the same place before we have permitted the pleasures. PROTARCHUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: But time now presses us to consult about the pleasures: whether all should be heaped together, or whether only the primary and true ones should be admitted. PROTARCHUS: It makes a great difference for security to admit the primary and true ones. SOCRATES: Let the commerce of these be admitted then. But what next? If any are necessary, just as in the other case, should these also be received into the mixture? PROTARCHUS: What prevents it? SOCRATES: Let us therefore receive the necessary ones in whatever way. If, just as it was established that knowing all arts is harmless and useful in life, it should now be established concerning pleasures—namely, that enjoying them all is harmless and useful—perhaps they should all be mixed for everyone. What do you say to this? PROTARCHUS: How shall we speak of these? What shall we do? SOCRATES: We should not ask such a thing of ourselves, Protarchus, but of the pleasures and sciences themselves. PROTARCHUS: How so? SOCRATES: "O dear ones, whether you should be called pleasures or by some other name: do you choose to dwell with all wisdom, or to be apart from wisdom?" I think they would necessarily answer this. PROTARCHUS: What? SOCRATES: That, as was said before, it is neither very possible nor useful for one genus to be entirely apart from the other. "We think the best of all genera for us would be that genus itself in which both all other things and also our individual powers are perfectly known." PROTARCHUS: And we shall rightly confess that they have answered deservedly. SOCRATES: It remains, then, to ask Mind and Wisdom in turn: since we say they lack pleasures in the mixture itself, what kind of pleasures do they especially need? PROTARCHUS: Deservedly so. SOCRATES: Our interrogation hereafter will be such: "Whether, besides those true pleasures, the commerce of the most vehement and immense pleasures is agreeable to you?" Perhaps they will answer thus: "Such pleasures are not agreeable to us, O Socrates. For these offer us innumerable impediments. Indeed, furious pleasures disturb the souls in which we dwell, and do not permit us to grow; and for the most part, they entirely corrupt our progeny by bringing in forgetfulness through negligence. But as for the other true and pure pleasures which you yourself described, consider them almost domestic to us. And besides those, include those which are taken with health, temperance, and the other virtues. For these, which are the handmaidens of virtue as if of some god, we gladly admit. But those which join with madness and other wickedness, it is absurd to mix with the mind—at least for one who wishes to discern the most beautiful and harmonious mixture and temperament, and in it to learn thoroughly what is good by its own nature in man and the universe, or what idea of it we must divine to exist." Shall we not say that Mind has answered wisely and as if master of itself, both concerning itself and memory and right opinion? PROTARCHUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And yet this is also necessary, nor could it ever be otherwise. PROTARCHUS: What is that? SOCRATES: That to which we do not mix truth, that thing would never become true nor have been made so. PROTARCHUS: For how could it? SOCRATES: In no way. But if anything further is lacking to this mixture, you yourself and Philebus say so. For to me, this discourse seems to have been settled like a certain incorporeal world that will beautifully rule over an animated body. PROTARCHUS: Know, O Socrates, that the same seems so to me. SOCRATES: If we say that we have recently entered the vestibule of the Good itself and of such a habitation, would we perhaps be professing rightly in some way? PROTARCHUS: It certainly seems so to me. SOCRATES: What in such a mixture seems to us most precious, and especially the cause why this constitution is most pleasing to all? For if we know that, we shall then dispute whether it stands more closely and properly in the universe to pleasure or to mind. PROTARCHUS: Wisely put. For that will contribute most to the judgment proposed to us. SOCRATES: And yet it is by no means difficult to find the cause why any mixture is to be valued either very much or very little. PROTARCHUS: In what way do you mean? SOCRATES: No one is ignorant of this. PROTARCHUS: What is it then? SOCRATES: That any mixture, of whatever kind, that does not participate in the nature of measure and commensurability, necessarily destroys its ingredients and, moreover, itself. For this is not a temperament, but a certain intemperate, scattered, and haphazard collision that usually happens to us. PROTARCHUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Now indeed, the power of the Good itself, transferring itself into the nature of the Beautiful, escapes our notice. For measure and commensurability are clearly beauty and virtue everywhere. PROTARCHUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: Furthermore, we said that truth is mixed with them in the temperament itself. PROTARCHUS: Altogether. SOCRATES: Because if we cannot embrace the Good itself in one idea, let us at least grasp it with three: Beauty, Commensurability, and Truth; and let us say that this whole, as if one, is the cause of those things which are in the mixture; and because of this, as something good, the mixture becomes good. PROTARCHUS: Most rightly. SOCRATES: Who then, O Protarchus, would now be a fit judge of pleasure and wisdom: which of these happens to be more closely related and more excellent toward the best, both among men and among gods? PROTARCHUS: It is clear indeed; yet it is better to run through it by reason as well. SOCRATES: Let us therefore judge concerning pleasure and wisdom according to each of these three. For we must see to which of the three we may bring each as more closely related. PROTARCHUS: Do you speak of Beauty, Truth, and Measure? SOCRATES: Certainly. First, then, take Truth, Protarchus; and having taken it, look now to the three: Mind, Truth, and Pleasure; and after you have considered it long and maturely, answer yourself: whether pleasure or mind is more [near] to truth—

# PHILEBUS, OR ON THE HIGHEST GOOD. FOLIO 42.
f.ii.
<meta>Catchword: f.ii.</meta>

<margin>The Mind is either truth itself or most similar to it.</margin>
...closer. PROTARCHUS. Why is there a need for long meditation? There is, I think, a very great difference. For pleasure is the most reckless of all things; it is said of the pleasures of love—which are esteemed the greatest of all—that the gods utterly forgive those who break their oaths <note>original: "peierantibus"</note>, as if they were children, possessed of no understanding. But the Mind is either the same thing as truth, or certainly the most similar to it and the truest of all. SOCRATES. Does it then remain to consider that measure and moderation: whether pleasure or wisdom is more capable of containing it? PROTARCHUS. That which you now bring up is also very easy to determine. I believe indeed that nothing can be found more immoderate than pleasure and its exultation; and on the contrary, nothing more moderate than mind and knowledge. SOCRATES. Excellent. But answer a third question as well. Is the Mind more a participant in beauty, or is pleasure itself? Which is more beautiful: the mind or pleasure, or the opposite? PROTARCHUS. As for the Mind and wisdom, Socrates, no one has ever—either truly or falsely—seen them as ugly, or in any way imagined them to have been so, to be so now, or to be so in the future. SOCRATES. Correct. PROTARCHUS. But if we observe someone pursuing the greatest pleasures, we blush at how ridiculous or obscene they are; we hide them, granting such things to the shadows of night as if they were unworthy of the sight of the light of day. SOCRATES. Therefore, O Protarchus, declare to all, both through messengers and with your own present voice: that the possession of pleasure is neither the first nor the second good. But the first must be thought to belong to measure, the moderate, the opportune, and all such things which have claimed an eternal voice of approval. PROTARCHUS. That appears to be the case from what has just been said. SOCRATES. The second then concerns the commensurate, the beautiful, the perfect, the sufficient, and all that are of this order. PROTARCHUS. So it seems. SOCRATES. The third, as I myself prophesy, if you place the mind and wisdom there, you will not wander far from the truth. PROTARCHUS. Perhaps. SOCRATES. The fourth were those things we set down as belonging to the soul itself: the sciences, the arts, and right opinions. These follow immediately after those three because they are more closely related to the good than pleasure is. PROTARCHUS. Possibly. SOCRATES. In the fifth place, put those pleasures which we defined as being free from pain: naming them the pure sciences of the soul itself, following the senses. PROTARCHUS. Perhaps. SOCRATES. "In the sixth generation," says Orpheus, "finish the adornment of the song." Our discourse also seems to finish at the sixth judgment. From here, nothing else remains for us except to add a head to what has been said. PROTARCHUS. It is certainly fitting. SOCRATES. Now, dedicating this same discourse for the third time to the Savior <note>A traditional Greek formula for concluding a toast or a task</note>, let us briefly touch upon it. PROTARCHUS. In what way? SOCRATES. Philebus said that every pleasure is entirely the good itself for us. PROTARCHUS. You seem, Socrates, to have just called for the third time to repeat the discourse itself. SOCRATES. This very thing. Let us hear what follows. Indeed, considering what I just recounted and bearing heavily against the discourse of Philebus and countless others, I said that the mind is by far better and more powerful than pleasure for the life of men. PROTARCHUS. These things were said. SOCRATES. Suspecting, however, that there were many other things, I added that if something appeared superior to both of these, I would fight on behalf of the mind against pleasure for the second place; thus pleasure would be stripped even of the second honors. PROTARCHUS. You said this as well. SOCRATES. Furthermore, when I said that the good itself is the most sufficient of all, it was established that neither of these two was sufficient. PROTARCHUS. You tell the truth. SOCRATES. And when in this discourse mind and pleasure were seen to lack the power of sufficiency and perfection, it appeared that neither was the good itself. PROTARCHUS. Quite right. SOCRATES. Moreover, since a certain third thing was established to be better than both, the mind certainly appeared, by a long interval, closer to the superior and surpassing Idea than pleasure did. PROTARCHUS. Why not? SOCRATES. Therefore, will not the power of pleasure obtain the fifth rank, according to the sentence which the present judgment has brought forth? PROTARCHUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. Yet oxen, horses, and all wild beasts would give the first place to pleasure, because they are enslaved to its allurements. Many people, trusting in them—no differently than diviners trust in birds—judge pleasures to be the most powerful of all for living well; they bring the loves of beasts as wealthier witnesses than the loves of those who prophesy by the reason of the philosophical muse. PROTARCHUS. We all confess, O Socrates, that you have told the absolute truth. SOCRATES. Do you not then dismiss me now? PROTARCHUS. A small thing still remains, O Socrates. You must not, as if already exhausted, stop before we do; I will bring back to your memory those things that remain.

<margin>Pleasure is most immoderate; mind and knowledge are most moderate.</margin>
<margin>No one sees the Mind as ugly.</margin>
<margin>We blush seeing someone pursuing pleasures.</margin>
<margin>First good. Second. Third. Fourth. Fifth. Sixth.</margin>

->THE END OF PHILEBUS.<-

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine on the Hippias, or on the Beautiful or the Honorable, to Piero de' Medici, Father of the Fatherland.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial "E" featuring a classical figure (possibly a scholar or deity) seated within the letter's architecture.</image-desc>

**H**e <note>Plato</note> disputes concerning the beautiful in the *Phaedrus*, the *Symposium*, and the *Hippias*. In the *Hippias*, because Socrates acts against Hippias the Sophist—who, although he was ignorant, thought he knew—and because ignorance renders the soul unteachable, he does not sufficiently teach what the beautiful is. Instead, he shows what it is not and refutes false opinions. He calls him a "Sophist" who strives to seem wise rather than to be so, for the sake of money and honor. That Hippias is such a man is declared in the prologue and at the end of the poem. Taking the occasion from a certain speech of Hippias which discussed beautiful duties, Socrates asks what is the beautiful itself, through which all other things become beautiful. For it is necessary to refer particulars to the universal that is in particulars, and the universal that is in particulars to that which is above individual things: the Universal. For individual beautiful men are made beautiful through a certain form common to individuals; but the common form is derived from a divine species as if from a...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical analysis of Plato's dialogue "Greater Hippias," focusing on the definition of beauty and the transition from sensory perception to intellectual understanding.</meta>

# BOOK ELEVEN

The character is imprinted with a seal, since every multitude is reduced to the one which is in the multitude: and the one which is in the multitude is reduced to the one which is above the multitude. Therefore, since there are many beautiful things, it is necessary that each one be beautiful through a beauty common to all and implanted in all: and that the beauty which is in all, just as it exists in another and not in itself, so it depends on another and not on itself. Each of the individual beautiful things Plato calls "this beautiful thing"; the form in all things he calls "beauty"; the species and Idea above all things he calls "the Beautiful itself." <note>Plato distinguishes between a beautiful object, the quality of beauty shared by objects, and the transcendent Idea of Beauty.</note> The first is reached by sense and opinion. The second is thought by reason. The third is intuited by the mind. When Hippias is questioned, he defines it three times according to sense and opinion. After these are refuted, Socrates also defines it three times. Twice indeed according to reason. Finally, according to the mind. For the Sophist <note>Hippias was a Sophist, a paid teacher of rhetoric often criticized by Socrates for valuing persuasion over truth.</note> proceeds by sense and opinion; the philosopher rather by reason and the mind. First, Hippias answers that a beautiful maiden is the Beautiful itself. That this is false is established by this: since not all things that are beautiful become beautiful through a maiden. And a maiden, if compared with beasts, appears beautiful; if with gods, she appears deformed. Therefore, she seems no more beautiful than ugly. Then Hippias answers with something else similarly from individual beautiful things, not a common one. Namely, that gold is the Beautiful itself, by which all things become beautiful. Socrates rejects this for the reason that gold, to whatever things it is suited, makes those things beautiful. But it deforms others. Therefore, it does not make things simply beautiful, but only when they are fitting. Wherefore it adorns a thing no more by its own reason than by the reason of another. Nor is gold the only thing by which all things are adorned: but silver also and ivory, and others of this kind. In the third place, he brings in something else which is also specific rather than common: he says it is beautiful for a body to be in good health, to be wealthy and honored, to die an old man, to be buried by one's sons, and to bury one's parents. It is clear this is false, because it does not make all things besides man beautiful by this very fact. Furthermore, this is perhaps beautiful among men; among the gods and the sons of gods, it is ugly, where parents do not die. Having refuted these things which Hippias brought forward concerning individual corporeal things through sense and opinion, Socrates, now tending toward higher things, brings in not what sense offers to opinion, but what reason offers to opinion. For first, he says the "becoming" <note>original: "decorum" - that which is fitting or appropriate</note> is the beautiful. This indeed is more incorporeal and common to more things. Yet he refutes it by this division: the becoming either makes things only *seem* beautiful, or it provides both their seeming and their being. If the first: a certain deception exists concerning the beautiful, and the becoming exists rather than the Beautiful itself. For true beauty makes things be beautiful, just as true greatness makes things great, even if they are not seen. If you say the second, you speak falsely. For if the Beautiful itself, as often as it grants things to *be* beautiful, were likewise to grant them to *seem* so, then whatever things are beautiful would appear so to all just as they are. That this is false, the contentions and controversies about beautiful things show us. Secondly, he brings in something else which reason offers to opinion. He calls the "useful" <note>original: "utile"</note> the beautiful. Utility is something incorporeal and common to many. Nor is it a wonder that thought is deceived concerning the becoming and the useful. For the former involves the order of part to part, and of parts to the whole; the latter involves the order of some whole to another whole; and order truly seems to represent beauty. Therefore, one easily accepts the becoming or the useful for the beautiful. That the becoming is not the beautiful was established; that the useful is not, he shows thus. The useful is that which has power to do something. Therefore, power and utility are the same. Because whatever we do, we do by a certain power; but we mostly do evil things; therefore power and utility mostly bring about evil; but the beautiful is never the cause of evil. Therefore, not just any utility is the beautiful. But at least that which contributes to the good, someone will answer; against whom he argues thus. That which tends toward the good is the "conducive." The conducive produces the good; that which produces something is different from that which it produces; wherefore the conducive is one thing, the good another. The conducive and the beautiful are the same. Therefore, the beautiful and the good are different. Thus neither is the beautiful the good, nor the good the beautiful; which is utterly absurd. Finally, the errors of sense, opinion, and thought having been convicted, the mind dictates to reason: that the beautiful is a certain grace which moves and allures the soul through the mind, sight, and hearing. This is surely elicited partly from the end of this dialogue, and partly from Plato's *Phaedrus* and *Symposium*. By what reason

<margin>What is the beautiful</margin>
this grace is present, and by what name it should be called, Socrates inquires; yet he does not declare it to the ambitious Sophist, though he revealed it to Phaedrus and to Agathon, who, although they were ignorant, were teachable because they acknowledged their own ignorance. Grace is indeed beauty: not by reason of sense, because it would not suit the mind, and would belong to the other senses equally as to hearing and sight. Not by reason of the mind, because it would escape the eyes and ears. Nor even by reason of pleasure, because this is found not only in hearing and sight, but in all senses. Not by reason of hearing alone, for it would not be congruent with the mind and sight. Not by reason of sight, for it would be lacking to hearing and the mind. Not by reason of hearing and sight together, because beauty would be in sight and hearing joined as one. But in each of them acting separately from the other, there would be no beauty. We wish, however, that grace to be perceived commonly by the three powers of the soul, and commonly by their three objects. Wherefore he adds that the pleasures of the mind, sight, and hearing are beautiful because they are the most harmless and best of all pleasures. If you understand "best" as the same as "conducive," the previous ambiguity will return. The conducive produces the good; therefore it is the cause of the good. Cause and effect are different. Therefore the conducive is one thing, the good another. From which it follows that the beautiful is one thing and the good another. Therefore neither is the beautiful the good, nor the good the beautiful. But if you explain "best" as harmless, easy, spiritual, shining, and vital (so to speak), you will be made a master of the truth. For beauty is nothing other than the splendor of the highest good, shining in those things which are perceived by the eyes, ears, and mind, and through those things converting the sight, hearing, and mind to the good itself. From which it happens that beauty exists as a certain circle of divine light flowing from the good, residing in the good, and eternally reflected through the good and toward the good. Socrates revealed this mystery, which he claimed to have learned from the Sibyl Diotima, not to the sophists but to his disciples. What is the good itself, the one principle of all things, pure act?

<summary>This page analyzes the philosophical definitions of beauty presented in Plato's dialogues, refuting the Sophist Hippias's materialistic definitions in favor of a spiritual "circle of divine light." It concludes that beauty is the splendor of the Good that draws the soul back toward its divine source.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Hippias, beauty, the becoming, utility, the good, Diotima, grace, mind, reason, sense</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the Neoplatonic commentary by Marsilio Ficino on the nature of Beauty before transitioning into the formal translation of Plato's "Greater Hippias."</meta>

# THE GREATER HIPPIAS, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL. FOLIO 44.
<sig>f.iiii.</sig>

...act, giving life to all things that follow: what is the Beautiful itself? It is a life-giving act flowing from the primary source of all goods. First, it infinitely adorns the Mind <note>Latin: *Mentem*; referring to the Divine Intellect</note> with the divine order of Ideas. Next, it fills the following deities and minds with a series of rational principles. Thirdly, it ornaments Souls with numerous discursive movements. Fourthly, it clothes Natures with seeds; and fifthly, it clothes matter with forms. The Sun certainly creates visible bodies and seeing eyes. Into the eyes, so that they may see, it pours a lucid spirit. Bodies, so that they may be seen, it paints with colors. Yet neither the ray proper to the eyes, nor the colors proper to the bodies, are sufficient to perfect vision unless the one light itself—which is above the many and from which the many proper lights are distributed to eyes and bodies—arrives, illuminates, excites, and strengthens them. In the same way, that primary act itself (that is, God) has bestowed a species and an act upon individual things by producing them. This act, when received in a passive subject, is weak and powerless for the execution of its work. But the perpetual and invisible light of the divine Sun always stands by all things: it cherishes, gives life, excites, completes, and strengthens. Concerning this, Orpheus divinely said: *Cherishing all things and carrying himself above all.* <note>Ficino quotes a Latin translation of an Orphic fragment.</note> Insofar as he is the act of all things and strengthens them, he is called "the Good"; insofar as he gives life, softens, soothes, and excites, he is called "the Beautiful." In the objects that must be known, Beauty allures those three powers of the cognizing soul. As the power in the knower applies itself to the known, it is called "Truth." Insofar as he is the Good, he creates, rules, and completes. Insofar as he is the Beautiful, he illuminates and infuses grace. However, all things must be prepared to receive the grace of the divine splendor. Bodies, indeed, by proportion (which consists of order, measure, and species). Voices by harmony (which is composed of numbers and intervals). Duties by the rectitude of character toward a good end. Disciplines by order toward a true object. The Soul by purity through turning away from lower things and turning toward the higher. The Mind by an eternal intuition into the Good itself. Through all these steps, the ray of divine beauty penetrates. In the body, it shines in numerical equality, subject to place and motion. In voices, it shines in Harmony, outside of a fixed place but dispersed in motion. In duties, disciplines, and the soul, it exists in motion but consists of vital reason. In the mind, it is above motion, shimmering in the eternal series of Ideas. In the Good itself, it is pure act, bringing life and grace to all. I pray, Peter de' Medici, most illustrious of men, that you read these things with your usual diligence. For you will thoroughly recognize the wonderful beauty of your own mind, and you will notice how closely you approach the Beautiful itself, which is discussed here.

### PLATO’S GREATER HIPPIAS, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL, TRANSLATED FROM GREEK INTO LATIN BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE, FOR PETER DE' MEDICI, FATHER OF THE COUNTRY.

#### SOCRATES. HIPPIAS.

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue, with a provocation and testing toward the Sophist, in which the wordiness, boasting, and audacity of the Sophist are revealed.</margin>

SOCRATES: Hippias, the wise and the beautiful, how rarely you come to Athens! HIPPIAS: I am not given leisure, Socrates. For whenever the citizens of Elis have something to negotiate with foreign nations, they commit the embassies to me above all others, judging me to be a fit messenger and an evaluator of what is said in various cities. Therefore, I have often gone as an ambassador to other cities, and most frequently to Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> regarding the greatest matters. This is why I frequent these places less often than you asked. SOCRATES: This is certainly the mark of a wise and perfect man, Hippias. Privately, you are able to benefit many young men from whom you receive money, giving them more than you receive. And again, publicly, you serve your fatherland as is fitting for one who should not be looked down upon by the common people, but held in the highest esteem. But, Hippias, what was the reason that those ancient men who attained the name of "the Wise"—Pittacus, Bias, and those around the time of Thales of Miletus, and those following down to Anaxagoras—all or most of them abstained from civil actions? HIPPIAS: What else do you think held them back, Socrates, but a weakness of intellect, since they could not prudently administer both private and public affairs? SOCRATES: Just as other arts have received growth over time, so that the craftsmen of our time far excel those of the past, should we say that your faculty—namely the study of the Sophists—has grown for the better, and that the ancient students of wisdom would appear quite worthless if compared to you? HIPPIAS: You speak quite rightly. SOCRATES: Therefore, if Bias were to rise back to life today, he would be laughed at by us; just as sculptors say that if Daedalus <note>The mythical inventor and craftsman</note> were to return to life and manufacture such things as those from which he once gained glory, he would be ridiculous. HIPPIAS: It is just as you say, Socrates. Nevertheless, I am accustomed to always prefer the ancients over the moderns, so that I might avoid the envy of the living and the indignation of the dead. SOCRATES: You seem to me, Hippias, to both think and speak excellently. I too can testify that you speak the truth. For in reality, your faculty has increased and has taken on the power to administer public affairs along with private ones. Indeed, Gorgias of Leontini, the sophist, came here as an ambassador for his country, as he was the most outstanding of all the Leontines in the governance of civil affairs. There, he was judged to have spoken excellently to the people. Then, disputing privately and spending time with the youth, he accumulated much money in this city. Furthermore, if you wish to hear, our friend Prodicus has also often...

<margin>Regarding Prodicus.</margin> He has often served in public offices; for instance, recently coming from the island of Chios, when he spoke publicly in the assembly, he was highly approved. In private discussion, by educating young men, he has earned countless sums of money. However, among those ancient thinkers, none ever thought it worthy to seek a reward of silver, or to show off their own wisdom in a gathering of diverse men; they were so simple and unenergetic, and the sheer amount of silver to be made was hidden from them. But each of those whom I just mentioned accumulated more silver through their wisdom than any other craftsman from any art whatsoever. And Protagoras did the same before them. HIPPIAS: You know nothing extraordinary in this matter, O Socrates. For if you saw

<margin>Protagoras before Gorgias and Prodicus.</margin> how much silver I have earned, you would be stunned. I will pass over other things. But once, having set out for Sicily while Protagoras was living there—and he was held in the highest honor, being much older than I—in a short time I collected more than one hundred and fifty minas <note>A mina was a unit of currency; 150 minas was an enormous fortune, roughly 15,000 drachmas.</note>; and from one tiny region called Inyca, more than twenty. When I returned home, I gave it to my father, which both he and the rest of the citizens greatly admired. Indeed, I reckon that I have gathered more money than almost any two other sophists you please put together. SOCRATES: O, what a magnificent thing! This is the greatest proof, Hippias, of how much you and the other wise men of this age surpass the ancients. For first, how great the ignorance of Anaxagoras seems to have been! The opposite happened to him compared to you. For he is said to have

<margin>Anaxagoras squandered a large patrimony to practice philosophy.</margin> neglected and squandered a large inheritance; so foolishly did he practice philosophy. And they hand down other such stories about the rest of the wise men of those times. Therefore, you seem to have brought forth this excellent conclusion: that our wise men excel their predecessors. Many agree on this: that a wise man ought, first and foremost, to be wise for himself. The sum of this "wisdom" is that the most silver be acquired. But enough of these things. Tell me this: since you have visited many cities, where exactly did you earn the most? Was it at Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>, where you have gone most frequently? HIPPIAS: Not by Jupiter <note>original: "per Iovem"</note>, O Socrates. SOCRATES: What are you saying? Was it the least? HIPPIAS: On the contrary, nothing at all, ever. SOCRATES: What you say is a marvel, O Hippias, and wonderful to tell. Answer me this: can your wisdom make those who spend time with you and learn from you better in virtue, or not? HIPPIAS: Very much so. SOCRATES: Were you able to make the sons of the citizens of Inyca better, but the sons of the Spartans not at all? HIPPIAS: Far from it. SOCRATES: Or perhaps the Sicilians strive to become better, while the Lacedaemonians neglect it? HIPPIAS: No, the Lacedaemonians desire the same. SOCRATES: Did they lack your company because of a lack of money? HIPPIAS: Not at all; for they are wealthy. SOCRATES: Since they desired wisdom and had the means, and you were able to fulfill their wishes, why did you not return from there extremely wealthy? Or perhaps the Lacedaemonians themselves educate their sons better than you do? Shall we say that? Do you agree? HIPPIAS: In no way. SOCRATES: Were you unable to persuade the young men at Lacedaemon that they would make more progress toward virtue by sticking with you than if they lived with their own people? Or could you not induce the parents to entrust their sons to you rather than to their own care, if indeed they cared for their sons? For they were not so envious of their sons that they did not want them to turn out the best. HIPPIAS: I certainly do not think they were envious. SOCRATES: Is Lacedaemon not established with good laws? HIPPIAS: With very good ones. SOCRATES: In such governments, virtue is honored most of all. HIPPIAS: Most certainly. SOCRATES: And you know best of all men how to pass this virtue on to others. HIPPIAS: Absolutely, Socrates. SOCRATES: He who can teach horsemanship excellently—would he not be more honored and earn the most in Thessaly than in the rest of Greece? And similarly elsewhere, wherever this art is held in high value? HIPPIAS: That is consistent. SOCRATES: Therefore, if one is able to instruct young men in the most noble precepts of virtue, why is he not highly honored in Lacedaemon, and why does he not accumulate countless riches there, and similarly in any city of the Greeks where virtue is valued most? But perhaps, Hippias, we ought to believe those things happen more in Sicily and Inyca. If you command it, it must be believed. HIPPIAS: It is not the ancestral custom, O Socrates, for the Lacedaemonians to change their laws, nor to educate their sons contrary to custom. SOCRATES: What are you saying? Is it not the ancestral way of Lacedaemon to act rightly, but rather to go astray? HIPPIAS: I would never assert that. SOCRATES: Would they not act rightly if they educated their youth better, rather than worse? HIPPIAS: Rightly; but their law does not admit foreign disciplines. Otherwise, if anyone else had ever earned money there for the sake of teaching, know that I would have earned the most. They are delighted when they hear me and they praise me; but as I was saying, their law forbids foreign things. SOCRATES: Do you call law a destruction of the state, Hippias, or its salvation? HIPPIAS: In my opinion, law is established for the sake of utility; sometimes, however, it is harmful if it is poorly laid down. SOCRATES: Do not lawgivers establish law as a certain maximum good for the city? And if the law is removed, can we not live in the city without injustice? HIPPIAS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, whenever those who strive to make laws miss the "good," they depart from what is lawful and from the law. What do you say to this? HIPPIAS: By exact reasoning, that is how it is, Socrates. However, men are not accustomed to naming it so. SOCRATES: Which men, Hippias? Those who know, or those who are ignorant? HIPPIAS: The common people. SOCRATES: Are those who know the truth the "common people"? HIPPIAS: Not at all. SOCRATES: But truly, those who are wise judge that what is more useful is more "lawful" than what is useless, for all men in reality. Do you not admit this? HIPPIAS: I admit it is so in reality. SOCRATES: And is it not as the knowledgeable think? HIPPIAS: Exactly. SOCRATES: But it is better, as you say, for the Lacedaemonians to be imbued with your discipline, even if it is foreign, rather than their ancestral one. HIPPIAS: And I speak the truth. SOCRATES: Furthermore, do you say that whatever things are more useful are more lawful? HIPPIAS: I did say that. SOCRATES: Therefore, according to your reasoning, it is more in accordance with the law for the sons of the Lacedaemonians to be taught by Hippias than by their parents.

...since you would truly benefit them more than those others. HIPPIAS: I would benefit them without a doubt, Socrates. SOCRATES: The Spartans <note>original: "Lacedęmonii"</note> act against the law, then, when they do not entrust their sons to you to be educated in exchange for the gold you are offered. HIPPIAS: I certainly agree; you seem to be speaking on my behalf. Therefore, it is not fitting for me to contradict you. SOCRATES: We find that the Spartans are lacking in good laws, even in the most important matters, although they seem to use better laws than the rest of the Greeks. SOCRATES: Does a discourse on geometry delight them? HIPPIAS: Least of all; for very few of them, so to speak, know how to count. SOCRATES: They are far, then, from listening willingly to reasonings and calculations. HIPPIAS: Very far, by Jove! HIPPIAS: They listen attentively to the lineage of heroes and men, the foundations of ancient cities, and in short, the whole history of antiquity. For this reason, I have been forced to learn and practice all things of this kind for their sake. SOCRATES: How well it has gone for you, O Hippias, that the Spartans do not find it troublesome if someone were to recount our leaders starting from Solon! Otherwise, you would have had to exhaust yourself learning their names. HIPPIAS: Why exhaust myself, Socrates? Hearing fifty names once, I can repeat them from memory. SOCRATES: You speak well; but I had not noticed that you possess such a powerful memory. Therefore, I now understand that the Spartans rightly delight in you as a man skilled in many things; they use you just as children use old women for the pleasure of storytelling. HIPPIAS: By Jove, Socrates, I was recently an object of admiration there while discussing the beautiful studies in which a young man should be instructed. For there exists a certain brilliant speech composed by me, which is especially powerful in its elegance of words; the form and beginning of the speech is of this kind: after Troy was captured, Neoptolemus asked Nestor what are the most beautiful studies which a young man, by applying himself, might become an illustrious man. In response, Nestor recounts many beautiful precepts. I delivered this speech there, and I am going to deliver it here also on the third day from now in Phidostratus's school, and moreover many other things worthy of hearing. For Eudicus, the son of Apimantus, asked me. Therefore, see to it that you also are present, and bring others with you who know how to judge what is said by listening. SOCRATES: These things shall be done if God wills, Hippias. But for the present, answer a brief thing about this very matter; for you have reminded me opportunely. For recently, O best of men, when in a certain conversation I was praising some things as beautiful and disparaging others as ugly <note>original: "turpia," meaning shameful or base</note>, someone brought this doubt into our midst, questioning me very contentiously thus: "From where, O Socrates, do you know what is beautiful or ugly? Can you define what the beautiful is?" But I, on account of my ignorance, hesitated, nor did I have a suitable answer; and leaving the gathering of men, I was angry with myself and vehemently blamed my own rudeness. I threatened that as soon as I should meet one of you who profess wisdom, I would try to hear and learn it, and having diligently prepared, I would return to the one who had asked, so that I might fight again on the same matter. Therefore, you have now come most opportunely, as I was saying. Teach me, I beseech you, what the beautiful itself is. Try, I say, most diligently to open up the whole matter in answering, lest I be mocked again for being refuted. For you know it clearly, and it is a small thing among the many things you are skilled in. HIPPIAS: A small thing, by Jove, Socrates, and of no value, so to speak. SOCRATES: I shall learn it easily then, and no one will refute me further. HIPPIAS: Certainly no one. For my study would be worthless and unrefined otherwise. SOCRATES: By Juno, you speak well, Hippias, if we can catch that man. If it makes no difference to you, I wish to repeat them, so that I may learn more vehemently and firmly. HIPPIAS: Repeat as you please; for as I was just saying, it is not a difficult question; but I could teach you to answer more difficult things, so that no one could refute you. If you had shown him your speech about beautiful duties, as soon as you had finished speaking, he would have asked about nothing else before asking about the beautiful. HIPPIAS: By justice, certainly. SOCRATES: And is not this justice itself something? HIPPIAS: Entirely. SOCRATES: And are not all who are wise, wise by wisdom? And similarly, are not all good things good by the good? HIPPIAS: What prevents it? SOCRATES: But wisdom and the good must exist in themselves. HIPPIAS: By the beautiful, certainly. SOCRATES: Is there, therefore, the beautiful itself? HIPPIAS: It exists, without a doubt. SOCRATES: Here he will immediately ask: "Tell me, guest, what is this beautiful itself?" HIPPIAS: Does he who asks these things need to hear what is beautiful? SOCRATES: It does not seem so to me; but the beautiful itself is something else. HIPPIAS: How will this differ from that? SOCRATES: Does it seem like nothing to you? HIPPIAS: Nothing, certainly; for it does not differ. SOCRATES: But it is clear that you know better. Consider, however: he does not ask what thing is beautiful, but what is the beautiful itself. If I answer this, then, will the question have been answered correctly, and I shall not be refuted? SOCRATES: Then he will interject: Is it fitting for that beautiful pot we spoke of before, full of good legumes, to have a golden ladle added to it, or one made of fig-wood? HIPPIAS: By Hercules! What kind of man are you describing? Why do you not utter his name? SOCRATES: You would hardly recognize the man, even if you heard the name. HIPPIAS: Nevertheless, I recognize even now that he is unlearned. SOCRATES: He is excessively curious, O Hippias. But what shall we say? Which of the two ladles is more suitable for the legumes and the pot: the wooden one or the golden one? For the wooden one provides a sweeter aroma, and it will not strike and break the pot, spilling the legumes; nor will it extinguish the fire with water; nor will it deprive the men who are about to eat of their precious meal. The golden ladle, however, would do the opposite. For which reason, the fig-wood seems to me more fitting than the golden, unless you contradict me. HIPPIAS: It is indeed more fitting; I would certainly not dispute with a man who asks such things. SOCRATES: Rightly so, my friend.
