Therefore, this is affected in the same way as those previous things, namely the maiden and the pot; and even more ridiculously, it is beautiful for some and not at all for others. Wherefore he will rebuke me thus: "Can you still not today, O Socrates, express what the beautiful itself is, about which we are inquiring?" And he will justly scold me so long as I give you such answers. Such is the general nature of our dispute. Sometimes, however, as if pitying my lack of skill and ignorance, he himself comes to my aid, asking: whether such a thing seems to me to be the beautiful itself, or whatever else is being disputed. **HIPPIAS.** How do you mean that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** I shall tell you. "O blessed Socrates," he says, "stop answering such things in this way; for they are inept and easily refuted. But take note: whether the beautiful itself might appear to be such a thing as we touched upon above, when we said that gold is beautiful for those things for which it is **fitting** <note>original: "decens"</note>, but conversely, not for those for which it is not. And all other things, for which the fitting itself and its nature are suitable, become beautiful. See then whether this **fitting** is the beautiful itself." Now, I have been accustomed to concede such things here and there, for I find nothing to object to. But does it seem to you that the fitting is the beautiful itself? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely so, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Let us take care lest we be deceived in some way. **HIPPIAS.** We must certainly take care. **SOCRATES.** See then, do we call the "fitting" that which, when it arrives, makes individual things **appear** beautiful, or that which **makes** them so, or neither of these? **HIPPIAS.** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** Is it that which makes things appear beautiful, just as if someone who is ugly were to be adorned with fitting clothing and shoes, he would appear more beautiful? If the fitting makes those things in which it is present appear more beautiful than they are, would not the fitting be a kind of deception concerning the beautiful? And would this not be what we are seeking, Hippias? For we were seeking that by which all beautiful things are beautiful, just as all great things are great by an excess. For by this all things are great; and even if they are not seen, yet if they exceed, they must be great. So also we sought the beautiful, by which all things are beautiful, whether they appear so or not: what might that be? The fitting is certainly not it; for it makes things appear more beautiful than they are, insofar as it is fitting, as you yourself were saying; but it does not allow them to be seen as they truly are. But that which makes them **be** beautiful, as I was saying a moment ago, whether they appear so or not—that is what must be stated: for this is surely what he seeks, if he seeks the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** But the fitting, Socrates, when it is present, makes things both **be** and **appear** beautiful. **SOCRATES.** Therefore it is impossible for things that are truly beautiful not to be seen as beautiful, as long as that which makes them be seen is present. **HIPPIAS.** Impossible. **SOCRATES.** Shall we confess this, Hippias: that all truly beautiful institutions and pursuits are also thought to be beautiful by everyone? Or on the contrary, are they unknown, so much so that men fight most bitterly over them both privately and publicly? **HIPPIAS.** I think they are rather unknown, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Yet they would not be unknown if they appeared beautiful just as they are beautiful. And they would appear so if the fitting were the beautiful, and compelled things not only to be, but also to appear beautiful. Wherefore, if the fitting is that which makes things be beautiful, it is the beautiful we seek; yet it is not that which compels them to appear so. But if the fitting only makes them appear so, it is by no means the beautiful itself which we seek, for that compels them to **be**. To appear and to be at the same time: the fitting can make neither the beautiful nor anything else do that. Let us choose now, whether we think the fitting is that which makes things appear beautiful, or that which makes them be so. **HIPPIAS.** I think it is that which makes them appear so, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Good heavens! How far the knowledge of the beautiful itself has fled from us, Hippias, since the fitting has appeared to be something other than the beautiful itself. **HIPPIAS.** By Jove, Socrates, to me this is quite absurd. **SOCRATES.** But, my friend, let us not give up yet; for I have not cast away all hope of finding what the beautiful is. **HIPPIAS.** There is every reason to hope, Socrates; for it is not difficult to find. Indeed, I am sure that if I were to withdraw into solitude for a little while, I could explain it to you more exactly than can be expressed, so that you would require nothing further. **SOCRATES.** Alas, do not say that in a loud voice, Hippias, lest it become indignant and flee further from us; do you not see how much it has exhausted us so far! But I say nothing. For when you are alone, you will find it easily, I think. But come, by the gods, find it while I am present; and if you wish, as we have done so far, so hereafter: search for it together with me. If we find it, it will be well. If not, I shall be content with my lot. But you, after you have departed, will find it easily. Yet if we find it now, I shall no longer be a nuisance to you, demanding what you have thought out by yourself. For the present, consider whether this seems to be the beautiful to you. Attend, I pray, diligently, lest I be delirious. Let this be the beautiful: **that which is useful.** <note>This marks the transition to the next proposed definition.</note> I make a conjecture of this matter chiefly from this: eyes are beautiful, not those which are incapable of seeing, but those which are capable and **useful** for seeing. **HIPPIAS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And we say the whole body is beautiful in the same way: one for running, another for wrestling. Likewise all animals: as a beautiful horse, or cock, or quail; and all equipment and vehicles, both for land and sea, ships and triremes; also all instruments pertaining both to music and to other arts; likewise, if you wish, pursuits and laws—we call each of these beautiful in almost the same way: looking, of course, to the condition under which each was born, or made, or placed; and that which is useful, and in what way it is useful, and for what it is useful, and when it is useful, we call beautiful; but that which is useless in these respects, we call base. Does it not seem the same to you, Hippias? **HIPPIAS.** It does indeed. **SOCRATES.** We say rightly then, above all else, that the **useful** itself is the beautiful. **HIPPIAS.** Very rightly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Is not that which can effect something useful for that which it is capable of? And the incapable, on the contrary, useless? **HIPPIAS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Therefore **power** <note>original: "potentia"</note> is beautiful, and lack of power is base. **HIPPIAS.** Most certainly; for all other things testify to us that it is so, and especially political matters. Since in one's city and republic, to be powerful is the most beautiful of all things, but to be powerless is base.

...most [shameful]. **SOCRATES:** You speak excellently. This power, and these useful things which lead to the execution of evil: shall we call them beautiful, or far otherwise? **HIPPIAS:** They are far from beautiful, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it seems to us that the "powerful" and the "useful" are not the beautiful itself. **HIPPIAS:** On the contrary: provided that it is able to do good, and contributes to that end. **SOCRATES:** That idea is therefore rejected: that the powerful and useful is simply the beautiful. But was this it, Hippias, at which our mind was aiming? Namely, that the powerful and useful *for the purpose of achieving good* is the beautiful. **HIPPIAS:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** This is the "conducive," is it not? **HIPPIAS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Thus, beautiful bodies, beautiful legal institutions, wisdom, and the other things we mentioned just now, are all beautiful because they are conducive to something. **HIPPIAS:** It is agreed. **SOCRATES:** It seems to us, then, that the conducive itself is the beautiful. 
<margin>Whether the conducive is the genus of the beautiful</margin>
**HIPPIAS:** Most of all. **SOCRATES:** And yet, the conducive is that which produces good. **HIPPIAS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** But that which produces is nothing other than a cause. **HIPPIAS:** Nothing else. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the beautiful is the cause of the good. **HIPPIAS:** It is indeed. **SOCRATES:** But the cause is one thing, and that for the sake of which the cause exists is another. For the cause cannot be the cause of the cause itself. This can be best inferred from this: was it not established that the cause is the producer? **HIPPIAS:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** And by the producer, the effect is made; the effect is not the producer. **HIPPIAS:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** The producer is one thing, the effect another. **HIPPIAS:** Another, certainly. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the cause is not the cause of itself, but of that which is produced by it. **HIPPIAS:** So it is. **SOCRATES:** Thus, if the beautiful is the cause of the good, the good is made by the beautiful. And for this reason, it seems, we desire prudence and all other beautiful things: because the work that is born from them—that is, the good—is desirable. Whence, through what we have found, the beautiful seems to have the status of a father to the good. **HIPPIAS:** Entirely so. You speak excellently. **SOCRATES:** And is this also excellent: that the father is not the son, nor is the son, in turn, the father? **HIPPIAS:** That too. **SOCRATES:** For indeed, the cause is not the effect, nor the effect the cause. **HIPPIAS:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** By Jove, my best of men, then neither is the beautiful the good, nor is the good the beautiful. Or does it seem possible to you, from what has been said? **HIPPIAS:** Not to me, by Jove. **SOCRATES:** Does this please us? Are we willing to assert that the beautiful is not the good, nor the good the beautiful? **HIPPIAS:** No, by Jove, it does not please me. **SOCRATES:** By Jove, Hippias, it pleases me least of all, based on what has been said. **HIPPIAS:** So it truly seems. **SOCRATES:** No longer, then, does that argument seem as excellent as before—the one asserting that the beautiful is the conducive, the useful, and the powerful for producing some good. Rather, if possible, it is to be judged more absurd than those earlier ones, in which we called a maiden and the other individual things we mentioned "the beautiful itself." **HIPPIAS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, Hippias, I know not where to turn; for I hesitate and am in doubt. But do you perhaps have something? **HIPPIAS:** Not at the moment; but as I said before, if I reflect by myself, I know for certain I shall see something. **SOCRATES:** But I think, because of my burning greed for understanding, I shall by no means tolerate your delay. But look, now something else has come into my mind. Attend, I pray, 
<margin>Beauty touching upon delight</margin>
to whether that which delights us—I am not speaking of just any pleasure, but that which comes through sight and hearing—whether such a thing should be called beautiful. For how can I resist? Since beautiful men, and various decorations, paintings, and beautiful sculptures delight us when we look at them? Beautiful songs also, and voices, and all music, and speeches, and storytelling affect us similarly? Therefore, if we were to answer that bold and persistent man <note>Socrates refers to his "harsh critic," who is actually his own conscience or alter-ego.</note> that the beautiful is that which delights through sight and hearing, would we not repress his boldness? What do you think? **HIPPIAS:** Now, Socrates, it seems to me that "what the beautiful itself is" has been skillfully stated. **SOCRATES:** But what of it? Shall we say that beautiful pursuits and laws are beautiful because they are pleasant through sight and hearing, or are they contained in some other category? **HIPPIAS:** These things perhaps escape the notice of men, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** By the dog, Hippias! <note>original: "Per canem" - a common Socratic oath.</note> Not him—the one whom I would fear most of all if I were to pretend to talk nonsense or say something when I was saying nothing. **HIPPIAS:** Who do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Socrates, the son of Sophroniscus; who would no more allow me to judge these things easily without discussion than he would allow me to think I know what I do not know. **HIPPIAS:** But to me also, now that you have said it, that which pertains to laws seems to be something else. **SOCRATES:** Rest a little, Hippias. For we seem to have fallen into the same ambiguity regarding the beautiful as we did a moment ago, while we thought we held something certain. **HIPPIAS:** How do you say that, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** I will say what it seems to me, so that I may see if I speak any truth. These things which pertain to pursuits and laws might not seem to exist outside the senses of seeing and hearing. But let us sustain this argument which asserts: that which is pleasing to these senses is beautiful; and let us not bring the laws into the middle yet. But if someone should ask us—either the man I mentioned or anyone else—in this manner: "What, Hippias and Socrates? Do you judge only that pleasure which is perceived by two senses to be beautiful, but you do not say that those things which flood the other senses with sweetness—foods, drinks, the acts of Venus <note>Sexual pleasures.</note>, and other such things—are beautiful?"

<summary>Socrates and Hippias reject the idea that the beautiful is the "conducive" because that would make the beautiful the cause of the good, and thus distinct from it. They then propose a new definition: that the beautiful is pleasure derived specifically from sight and hearing.</summary>

# BOOK ELEVEN

Or perhaps these are not sweet? Or do you place no pleasure in the senses other than in hearing and seeing? What, I ask, O Hippias, shall we answer? HIPPIAS. We will agree that great pleasures are also present in the other senses. SOCRATES. But he <note>Socrates refers to his "harsh" imaginary interlocutor who cross-examines them.</note> will say: for what reason, since these are no less pleasures than the others, do you deprive them of the title of "the beautiful"? Why will we answer? There is no one who would not laugh at us if we said that eating is not sweet, but "beautiful"; or that a fragrant odor is not sweet, but "beautiful." Regarding the acts of Venus <note>original: "Veneris... motus" - a reference to sexual intercourse</note>, everyone would agree it is something most sweet; but if one partakes in this, it must be done so that it is hidden, as if it were most base to be seen. When we have said these things, Hippias, he will perhaps answer: "I understand indeed that for a long time shame has hindered you from calling pleasures of this sort 'beautiful,' because they do not seem so to men. But I was not seeking that which *seems* beautiful to the crowd, but that which *is* beautiful itself." But we shall repeat to him that the beautiful is what we have already proposed: namely, that part of the pleasurable which charms through the eyes and ears. But you, Hippias, where will you turn? Or shall we perhaps bring forward something else? HIPPIAS. Nothing else besides this, O Socrates, should be answered. SOCRATES. "Excellently said," he will interject. "If, therefore, only that which comes as a delight through sight and hearing is beautiful, then that which delights through another sense is not beautiful at all. Shall we confess this?" HIPPIAS. We shall confess it. SOCRATES. He will then ask again: "Is that which is pleasant through sight, pleasant through both sight and hearing? And is that which is pleasant through hearing, pleasant through both hearing and sight as well?" To this we say: in no way can that which is through one be through both, for that is what you seem to be asking us. But we said that each of these two pleasures is beautiful in itself, and similarly both together; should we not answer thus? HIPPIAS. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Then he: "Does a pleasure differ from a pleasure in the very fact that it is a pleasure? I am not asking whether one pleasure is greater or smaller than another, or more or less; but whether, out of many pleasures, one differs from another in this very respect: that this one is a pleasure, and that one is not." We will say it does not seem so to us. HIPPIAS. Clearly not. SOCRATES. Here he will interject: "For no other reason than because they are pleasures, you have chosen these pleasures above all others from the whole number, seeing something such in both of them—namely, that they have a certain nature differing from the others—looking toward which you assert they are beautiful? For the pleasure of sight is not beautiful because it happens through sight. For if that were the cause of its beauty, the pleasure that happens through hearing would in no way be beautiful, since it is by no means produced through sight." Shall we confess that he speaks the truth? HIPPIAS. We shall certainly confess it. SOCRATES. "Nor again is the pleasure of hearing beautiful because it happens through hearing; otherwise, that which is perceived through sight would not be beautiful, since it is not the same as that which is produced through hearing." Shall we admit, O Hippias, that the man who says these things speaks the truth? HIPPIAS. Truly, the truth. SOCRATES. "Nevertheless, both," he will say, "are beautiful, as you say." Do we say so? HIPPIAS. We certainly do. SOCRATES. They have, therefore, something common and identical which makes them beautiful; something which is present in both commonly, and in each individually. For otherwise, both would not be beautiful, nor would each one be. Come, answer me as if to him. HIPPIAS. I answer that it seems to me as you say. SOCRATES. For if these pleasures both underwent something that neither of them experienced individually, they would never be beautiful by such an experience. HIPPIAS. So it is, O Socrates. For how could it happen that both suffer what neither of them suffers? SOCRATES. It does not seem possible to you? HIPPIAS. Indeed, I would be utterly unskilled in both these matters and in such ways of speaking. SOCRATES. Pleasantly said, O Hippias; yet I perhaps run the risk of appearing to see something which cannot possibly be as you say. But I see nothing. HIPPIAS. You do not run a risk, O Socrates, but you are being too dismissive. SOCRATES. Indeed, many things of this kind come into my mind to which I do not give credit, because they are not approved by you—you who have accumulated more money through the study of wisdom than the rest of our time. But I, O friend, as one who has never gained anything, wonder if perhaps you are joking with me and deluding me on purpose, so many things seem to occur to me. HIPPIAS. No one will understand better than you, Socrates, whether I am joking or not, if you begin to bring forward these things that occur to you; for you will seem to say nothing, since you will never find something that neither I suffer, nor you, but that we both suffer together. SOCRATES. How do you mean, Hippias? Perhaps you are saying something that I do not quite understand. But listen to me, I will explain what I feel more clearly. It seems to me that it does not happen that I am <note>Socrates is beginning a logical puzzle about properties held by a pair but not by individuals, such as the number "two".</note>, nor am I, nor are you similarly, able to suffer this both together. Likewise, other things which we both suffer, neither of us exists as. HIPPIAS. You seem to be bringing forth monsters again, O Socrates, and certainly more so than a little while ago. Just listen. If we were both just, would we not also be so individually? Or if both were unjust, would not each be? Or if both were healthy, would not each be? And if each of us labors in something, or is wounded, or struck, or suffers anything else, do we not both suffer the same? Furthermore, if we were both made of gold, or silver, or ivory; and even if you wish, noble, or wise, or honored, or old, or young, or anything else human: would it not be entirely necessary for each of us to be that thing? SOCRATES. Entirely so. HIPPIAS. But you, O Socrates, do not consider things as wholes; nor do those with whom you are accustomed to dispute. You immediately strike at "the beautiful" and whatever else is to be discussed, and you divide each thing by debating; and therefore, great and universal bodies, having obtained a continuous essence from nature, escape you. And now the truth flees you to such an extent that you think there is some experience or essence which concerns both together, but not the individuals; and conversely, what is in the individuals is not in both. So irrational, reckless, inept, and foolish are you. SOCRATES. Such are our affairs, Hippias; not as one would wish, but as the worn proverb goes:

<margin>

If not what you desire, then desire what you can do.
</margin>

# HIPPIAS MAJOR, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL.

...but such as they are able to be. But you yourself always help us by reminding us. Indeed, before you reminded us of these things, how foolishly we were affected: I shall reveal this to you even more clearly if I report what I felt about these matters. Shall I speak? **HIPPIAS:** You will be reporting to one who knows, Socrates; for I know the condition of all those who occupy themselves in disputation. Nevertheless, if you desire, tell the story. **SOCRATES:** I do indeed desire it. For truly, we were so ignorant before you said these things, that we thought of me and you that each of us is one, but yet that we are not both that which each of us is. For we are not one, but two. We were that foolish. But now we have learned from you that if we are both two, it is necessary that each of us is likewise two; and if each is one, then both are equally one. For it is impossible, according to Hippias, for it to be otherwise by the universal and continuous logic of essence <note>original: "essentiæ ratione"</note>. But that which both were, the individuals were the same; and conversely, what the individuals were, both were equally. Now therefore, persuaded by you, I sit here; yet first, O Hippias, remind me of this: Are you and I one? Or are you two and I two? **HIPPIAS:** What are you saying, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** These very things I am saying. For I fear to speak openly before you, for you are angry with me and the crowd when you seem to yourself to be saying something <note>Socrates is playfully mocking Hippias's vanity and his insistence that properties must be shared by the whole and the parts</note>. But tell me at the same time: is not each of us one, and has not each experienced being one? **HIPPIAS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And if one, then also odd <note>In Greek mathematics, the number one is the source of odd numbers</note>. Or do you not consider one to be odd? **HIPPIAS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And since we are both two, are we both odd? **HIPPIAS:** By no means. **SOCRATES:** But are we both even? **HIPPIAS:** Even. **SOCRATES:** Because we are both even, does it follow that each of us is also even? **HIPPIAS:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is not entirely necessary, as you were just saying, that whatever both are, the individuals are, and whatever the individuals are, both are. **HIPPIAS:** Not in things of this sort, but in those which I recounted above. **SOCRATES:** That is enough for me, Hippias. For those things suffice since some things seem to be one way, and others another. I said indeed, if you remember where this talk began, that pleasures through sight and through hearing are beautiful, not because of that which either of them has (but both by no means), or what both have (but the individuals not at all); but rather because of that which both and each possess. And for that reason, I judged both and each to be beautiful. And you agreed. And I, for this reason, through that very essence which follows both, judged both to be beautiful, if indeed they are beautiful; but by that which leaves out one or the other, not at all. And now I think the same. But tell me as if from the beginning: if the pleasure which comes through sight and that which comes through hearing are both and individually beautiful, does not that which makes them beautiful follow both and each? **HIPPIAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Is it because they are individually and collectively pleasures that they are beautiful? Or by this reasoning would other pleasures be no less beautiful? For it was established that they were no less pleasures. Do you remember? **HIPPIAS:** I remember. **SOCRATES:** But because they occur through sight and hearing, for that reason it was said they are beautiful. See if I speak the truth. For as I remember, we said: the beautiful is that which is pleasant, not indeed through any senses whatsoever, but only through sight and hearing. **HIPPIAS:** Exactly so. **SOCRATES:** Does not this quality <note>original: "passio," here meaning a shared property or attribute</note> follow both, but the individuals not at all? For each of them, as we said above, is not through both; but both are indeed through both, the individuals not at all. Is it so? **HIPPIAS:** It is. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, they are not beautiful by that which does not follow the individuals. For that which is said of both does not follow the individuals. Wherefore it is permitted to call both of those beautiful according to the hypothesis, but the individuals by no means. Or do we say otherwise? Is this not necessary? **HIPPIAS:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** Should we say then that both are beautiful, but the individuals are not? **HIPPIAS:** What prevents it? **SOCRATES:** This, my friend, seems to stand in my way: that certain things are judged to be present in others in such a way that if they are present in both, they are present in each; and conversely, if in each, then in both. Such were the things you recounted. **HIPPIAS:** They certainly were. **SOCRATES:** But those I reported were not; in which number was that which is called "both" and that which is called "each." Is it not so? **HIPPIAS:** It is. **SOCRATES:** Which of these seems to you, O Hippias, to be the "beautiful"? Is it like the things you set forth? As if I am robust and you are, then both are robust. Likewise if I am just and you are, then both are; and conversely, if both are, then each is. Or does nothing prevent it from happening as it does in even and odd numbers? Where both are sometimes even, but the individuals are odd; and sometimes both are even, and the individuals are sometimes such that they cannot be expressed <note>likely referring to irrational numbers or specific mathematical ratios</note>, while both can be, and sometimes they cannot. And many other things of this kind which I said occurred to me. In which group do you place the beautiful? Does it appear to you as it does to me? For it seems too absurd to me that we should both be beautiful but not individually. Or conversely, individually beautiful but not both; or any other such thing. Do you choose as I do? Or rather in that other way? **HIPPIAS:** In that way, certainly. **SOCRATES:** You do well, Hippias, so that we may free ourselves from a long inquiry. For if the beautiful is from these things, then that which delights through sight and hearing will no longer be the beautiful. For it makes both beautiful, but the individuals not at all. But this is impossible, as we have agreed. **HIPPIAS:** We have agreed, certainly. **SOCRATES:** It is impossible, therefore, that the pleasant through sight and hearing is the beautiful. For if that were the beautiful, something impossible would follow. **HIPPIAS:** These things are true. **SOCRATES:** Here that quarrelsome fellow <note>Socrates's imaginary critic, often interpreted as his own conscience or "daimon"</note> will say: "Explain again from the beginning, since this has failed you: what do you say this 'beautiful' is, which is in both pleasures, because of which you call them beautiful, honoring them above the rest?" It seems necessary to me, O Hippias, that we answer that they are harmless beyond other pleasures and the best, both together and individually. Or do you have something else by which they differ from others? **HIPPIAS:** Nothing; for in truth they are the best. **SOCRATES:** Then he will say: "Is this then what you say the beautiful is: beneficial pleasure?" I shall answer that it seems so; and you? **HIPPIAS:** I also. **SOCRATES:** And he will say to this: "Is not the beneficial that which produces good? But it is established that the producer and the thing produced are different, whence we fall back into the same problem." For neither would the good be beautiful, nor the beautiful good, if indeed each of them were something else. We shall answer him immediately that it is so, if we are wise. For it is a sin not to agree with one who speaks rightly.

# BOOK TWELVE

<margin>Another false definition of the beautiful.</margin>HIPPIAS: What else do you think all these things are, Socrates, but mere scrapings and clippings of speech—as I said before—broken down into the smallest bits? But this is what is truly beautiful and worth much: to be able, by delivering a fine speech in a court of law, or a council, or any other public gathering where words are spoken, to persuade the listeners and carry away not some small prize, but the greatest of all: the safety of oneself, one's property, and one's friends. One ought to embrace these things, letting go of these petty little questions, lest you seem to be a fool while you deal in delusions and trifles, as you are doing now. SOCRATES: O friend Hippias, you are indeed blessed, for you know what things a man ought to study, and you yourself have studied them abundantly, as you claim. But as for me, a certain strange fortune holds me back; for I am always wandering and in a state of begging. Whenever I show my poverty to you wise men, I am rebuked by you in turn with words. For you constantly reproach me with the same things you just said: that I deal in stupid, thin, and worthless matters. Finally, when I am persuaded by you and I repeat the same things you do—that it is best to speak elegantly in court or any other assembly and to achieve one's desire—certain others of our people, and especially that man who always refutes me, severely scold me. That man is very close to me in kin and lives in the same house with me. Therefore, as soon as I enter the house and he hears me saying such things, he asks if I am not ashamed to dare to dispute about beautiful works, when I have been so clearly refuted concerning the beautiful, since I do not know what the beautiful itself is. For he says: "By what means will you understand which speech is beautifully composed and which is not, or any other beautiful or base action, while you are ignorant of what the beautiful itself is? And since you are in such a state, do you think it is better for you to live than to die?" Thus it happens to me, as I was saying, that I hear ill both from you and from him. But perhaps it is worthwhile to endure all these things; for it is not absurd if I have gained something from it. Indeed, Hippias, I have profited so much from the company of both of you that I seem to finally understand that proverb which says: *Beautiful things are difficult.* <note>original: "Pulchra difficilia esse"</note>

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino of Florence on Plato’s Lysis, or on Friendship, addressed to Piero de' Medici, Father of the Fatherland.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a landscape with a tree and a bird.</image-desc>Where Socrates disputes with the sophists and their followers, he refutes false opinions and signifies truths rather than teaching them directly. For sharp minds, once false things are refuted, hunt for the truth from a small trail. This is evident in the *Euthydemus*, *Protagoras*, *Meno*, *Hippias*, *Euthyphro*, and *Lysis*. However, where he holds discourse with his own disciples and students, he demonstrates and teaches, which is understood from many of his dialogues. In the *Lysis*, therefore, since he disputes about friendship among the disciples of the sophists, Socrates strives more to confute false ideas than to show true ones. But what Plato’s opinion is regarding friendship and love can be gathered from this book, but fully grasped from the books of the *Laws* and many others. He wishes friendship to be an honorable and perpetual communion of the will. The end <note>The "goal" or "purpose"</note> of this is one life. Its principle <note>The "origin" or "starting point"</note> is kinship. Its medium, however, is love. By calling it "honorable," he excludes the companionship of wicked men and the encounters of the lewd. By "perpetual," he warns that the lighthearted goodwill of youths, even if honorable, should not yet be called friendship. By "will," he signifies that a mere similarity of opinion or some art is not sufficient to perfect friendship. By "communion," he indicates a reciprocity of goodwill. The end of this is that from two souls, one is made by will; from one will, one life; and finally from one life, the enjoyment of one and the same idea of the divine. The principle by which the desire for this communion is excited is kinship. Kinship signifies a correspondence in the Idea, the star, the guiding spirit <note>original: "genio"</note>, and a certain affection of the soul and body. For those who hang from one thing strive to return to the One, through the One, and toward the One. Love exists as the medium and, as it were, a path to friendship. Since love is the desire for the beautiful, and friendship is both led by and named after love, it is necessary that those who are to be friends be beautiful. I say "beautiful" those whose souls are beautiful. For man is the soul; the body of man is an instrument; and whoever loves a beautiful body loves not the man, but those things which belong to the man. Therefore, whenever that kinship is present and the beauty of souls concurs, perfect friendship is born. If the form of the body is joined to this beauty of souls, they begin to love more quickly and attain the habit of friendship in a short time. This happened in the mutual goodwill of Plato and Dion. But if the form of the body is joined with a deformity of the soul, there arises a desire not for honorable communion, but for base encounter. From this, not friendship, but rather petulance first, and then discord proceeds. Therefore, if kinship is lacking, they are never friends. If kinship is present but all beauty is lacking, they are sometimes well-wishers rather than friends. But if the beauty of the body, not the soul, is joined to kinship, the heat of obscene encounter arises instead of the desire for friendship. When one is beautiful in soul and the other is base, that kinship produces a desire for admonition and rebuke. But if the soul of one is beautiful and the other is neither beautiful nor base, the will to teach and learn from one another comes from kinship. Finally, from that rebuke and this teaching, friendship is born. This is shown by the love of Socrates for Phaedrus and Alcibiades. But truly, kinship having found beauty on both sides quickly procreates an indissoluble friendship. This consisted in the goodwill of Plato and Aster. And this, as gathered from many sources, is the opinion of our Plato on friendship. In this dialogue, however, he first rebukes those who abuse love and serve base lust under the appearance of friendship. Then those who from only...

<meta>This page continues the introductory argument or summary (argumentum) for Plato's dialogue "Lysis," which explores the nature of friendship. The previous page likely introduced the setting and the initial encounter between Socrates and the youths.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE LYSIS. FOLIO 48.

He advises those who, because of the beauty of their bodies, think themselves worthy of being loved. Third, he refutes those who held less truthful views concerning friendship. Finally, he points out a certain path for sagacious minds to hunt down friendship. The individual parts are clear to those reading them in their proper places. For while Socrates mocks Hippothales and Ctesippus with irony and jokes because they were captured by a base love, he signifies <note>original: "significat" - here meaning he indicates a deeper philosophical point through his humor</note> something more. And while he instructs the youths in morality in their presence, he advises lovers: in what manner one ought to love, and how they should live together.

When he had finished instructing the lovers, he moves to the second part of the dialogue, aimed at instructing the beloved. There, through a long series of introductions, he teaches that it is not by the fleeting beauty of this little body, but by the true beauty of the soul—namely, wisdom and prudence—that it is fitting to catch friends.

In the third place, he offers a refutation: first of the opinion of Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawmaker and poet</note>, who says that those who are loved are friends, even though they often hate those who love them. He adds also that it is not merely those who love who are friends, because they often hold in hatred those whom they love. Here he concludes that reciprocal goodwill must be called friendship.

Next, he censures Empedocles <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that "like attracts like"</note>, who wished any simple similarity to be sufficient for friendship. That this is false is shown by the similarity of many arts, which more often produces envy and hatred than friendship. After this comes the opinion of Hesiod and Heraclitus, that "dissimilars" <note>opposites</note> are friends. That this is false is evident from the fact that since hatred and love are dissimilar, they are not friends; nor are a just man and an unjust man; and so on for others. For if something at some time seems to desire its dissimilar—as that which is dry desires moisture, or that which is cold desires heat—it must be said that it does not love its contrary, but seeks the restoration of itself from the contrary. For that which is burned by excessive heat beyond its nature is reduced to its natural temperament through cold. Therefore, it does not love the cold, but the temperament achieved through the cold. The same judgment applies to other contraries.

Having refuted these, Socrates introduces a certain opinion as his own, speaking almost like a prophet. Here he divides the affections of the soul into three parts: the good of the soul, the evil, and the neutral. He argues that the evil can never be a friend to the good because of their diversity. The evil is harmed by the evil because of injustice. Therefore, neither are these friends to each other. It is also impossible for the neutral to love the evil, for since evil is harmful, it is always held in hatred by its very nature. It remains that friendship exists between the good and the good, and between the neutral and the good. The former consists in joy; the latter in desire. From these, two species of friendship have arisen.

But certain objections arise which seem to disturb this, which Socrates brings forward openly, while he hints at the solutions secretly. First, because the good is similar to the good, and it was said against Empedocles that "likes" are not friends. Here it must be understood: it was not said that likes can in no way become friends; rather, it was denied that *any* simple similarity is sufficient to create friendship. Likewise, when he objects secondly: the good man is self-sufficient, therefore he does not desire another, hence he does not love, and thus is not a friend to the good. It must be explained that this absurdity does not follow from Plato's mind, but from the sayings of Empedocles and Heraclitus, in which they do not distinguish the desire of love from friendship. Therefore, it would be necessary for a perpetual craving to exist alongside friendship.

Plato, however, wants friendship to be a certain habit <term>habit - a stable disposition or state of character</term> contracted from long-lasting love. Thus, love is friendship in its beginning, but friendship is an "inveterate" <note>long-established</note> love, in which much more pleasure remains than desire. From this it follows that he who had desired is now delighted. Therefore, the habit of friendship does not necessarily require the burning desire for one who is present, but requires delight. Thus, if a good man desires a good man less <note>because he is self-sufficient</note>, he nevertheless does not rejoice in the good man any less; which is of the greatest value for maintaining the reason of friendship. And this is one species of friendship: namely, between the good and the good, established in joy rather than in desire.

There is also another species which includes more desire than pleasure, arising between the neutral and the good. The reason why this happens, for whose sake, and because of what, is clear enough in the text. He describes it first as an opinion suggests, then gradually amends it. For when he had said that the neutral loves the good friend because of the evil enemy, for the sake of the friendship of the good, he immediately corrects the statement by objecting to it. Here he first teaches: all friendships directed toward men are imperfect, and are images of the friendship which looks toward the first Good itself and the Author of all things <note>God</note>, who is loved first and is the cause for all these things being loved. And whoever loves anything holds that "First" as the end <note>goal</note> of love. For from the first Good, goodness is in all things; from the first Beauty, grace is present in each; for goodness draws us, and beauty allures us. Therefore, it is not those inferior things that move us, but that "First" within them draws and allures. Thus, we love that "First" in them and through them, not the things themselves. In this, the piety of our Plato toward God and his supreme religion shines forth wonderfully.

He shows, moreover, that we are not always friends for the sake of another. For we do not desire the first Good for the sake of another good. Likewise, you would not desire the good because of evil. For even if all evil were removed from the nature of things, the good would remain pleasing by its own nature; and the appetite in that which is "less good" would be drawn toward achieving the "greater good." For it is not evil that excites the appetite for the highest Good, but the lack <note>original: "egestas" - poverty or need</note> of the "less good" itself turns toward its own fulfillment in the highest Good; which indeed should not be called an evil—because evil never leads to good, nor a contrary to a contrary—but rather the beginning of good.

Having brought these points for amendment, he introduces a certain principle for investigating friendship more perfectly: for he says that kinship and the suitability of nature produce friendship, about which we said enough at the beginning. Finally, he bites at those youths and adolescents because they are ignorant of what is deservedly to be loved, what true friendship is, and in what way it may be joined honestly and stably; and before they learn these things, they strive to enter into friendship rashly, shamelessly, and petulantly. But lest he make them hostile to him, he signified these things secretly, and rebuked himself along with them. This is enough concerning the argument. Let us come to the Lysis.

-> THE END OF THE ARGUMENT FOR THE LYSIS. <-

WHEN I was walking from the Academy toward the Lyceum <note>The Academy and Lyceum were the two most famous gymnasia/schools in ancient Athens.</note> by the very outskirts of the city, I drew near to the Pylis, where the fountain of Panops is located. There I encountered Hippothales, the son of Hieronymus, and Ctesippus of Paeania, and other youths with them. When Hippothales saw me coming, he said, "O Socrates, where are you going and from where have you come?" I replied, "From the Academy toward the Lyceum." Then he said, "Come here to us, and do not go any further." "To what place should I come," I asked, "and with which of you do you wish me to be?" He pointed to a certain enclosed gymnasium across from the walls with an open door and said, "We want you to stay here; here we and many others—and indeed honorable ones—exercise ourselves." SOCRATES: "In what specifically does this exercise of yours consist?" HIPPOTHALES: "In the wrestling school <term>palaestra: a site for wrestling and physical education</term> which was recently established, but mostly in conversations, which we would gladly share with you under this roof." SOCRATES: "You do well. But who is the teacher there?" HIPPOTHALES: "Your companion <margin>Miccus, a companion of Socrates.</margin> and admirer, Miccus." SOCRATES: "By Jove, he is no ignorant man, but a skilled teacher of wisdom <term>sophista: here used in the sense of a professional educator</term>." HIPPOTHALES: "Do you wish to follow me inside, so that you may see those who are there?" SOCRATES: "I would first gladly hear what I am entering into, and who is the most honorable person present." HIPPOTHALES: "One person seems so to one, Socrates, and another to another." SOCRATES: "But to you, Hippothales, who is the most honorable? Tell me, I pray." But when he was asked, he remained silent. Then I said, "O Hippothales, son of Hieronymus, there is no need for you to reveal whether you love someone or not. For I know how vehemently you are accustomed to love those who are most honorable. In other matters I am dull and useless, but this one gift has been given to me by God: that at first sight I can recognize those who are in love." <note>original: "amicos agnoscam" - here Socrates refers to recognizing lovers/friends.</note> To this he answered nothing. But Ctesippus said, "How polite you are, Hippothales, that you do not wish to tell Socrates the name of your friend! For if he stays with you for a little while, he will hear you speaking of him constantly. He has already filled our ears, O Socrates, with the name of Lysis. We only rest after he has been drinking; and even when we are woken from sleep, we immediately seem to hear the name of Lysis. And the things he says in prose are fit and elegant enough, yet they are less intense. But whenever he strives to use and pour out our poems and writings, he acts more vehemently; and what is more serious, he sings daily to his friends in a very loud voice, which we must endure. But just now, when asked by you, he fell silent." I said, "This Lysis seems to be a youth; for hearing his name, I did not recognize it." Then he replied, "They rarely speak his name; but he is identified by his father's name, as he is a very noble man. He is still a youth himself; for I am persuaded that you are far from being ignorant of his appearance, for he is endowed with such an honorable nature that he could be known to everyone by that alone." "Whose son is he?" I asked, "tell me, I pray." "The eldest son of Democrates of Aexone," he said. Then I said, "Behold, O Hippothales, what a noble and constant affection you have found! Come, show me also what you show to these others, so that I may see whether you know what a friend ought to say about his friends to himself and to others." HIPPOTHALES: "What do you weigh from these things they are saying, Socrates?" SOCRATES: "Do you deny that you love the one he mentioned?" HIPPOTHALES: "By no means; but I say I compose or write nothing about them." To this Ctesippus said, "He is not of sound mind; he raves and is insane." SOCRATES: "O Hippothales, I do not care much to hear poems or even songs, if you have composed any for your friends; but I desire to understand with what mind you are toward them." HIPPOTHALES: "Ctesippus here will tell you. For he knows and remembers, since, as he says himself, he is beaten down by hearing it from me every day." CTESIPPUS: "And most certainly, by the gods! For it is ridiculous that while he loves him above all others, he can offer nothing from his own wit that even any boy could not do. For the same things that the whole city proclaims about Democrates and Lysis's grandfather and all their ancestors, he also carries around: their wealth, their many horses, their victories at the Pythian, Isthmian, and Nemean games with four-horse chariots and single horses, and even things more ancient than these. For lately he recounted to us in a certain poem a story of hospitality and feasting, in which one of Lysis's ancestors once received Hercules because of their kinship; for he too was born from Jove and the daughter of a certain prince of the people—things that even old women sing. And many other such things, O Socrates. These are the things he forces us to hear by narrating and singing." SOCRATES: "O ridiculous Hippothales, before you have conquered, you fashion and chant a song of praise for yourself." HIPPOTHALES: "I do not proclaim these things for myself, Socrates." SOCRATES: "Not as you think." HIPPOTHALES: "Why do you say that?" SOCRATES: "Most of all, these odes redound upon you alone. For if you win such a friend, such praises will be an ornament to you, as if to a certain victor, when you have obtained such a friend. But if he eludes you, the <margin>A precept in acquiring friends.</margin> greater the praises you have attributed to him, the greater and more ridiculous you will be judged for being deprived of such goods. Whoever, therefore, is wise in acquiring friends, does not praise any of them until he has secured their familiarity, for he fears the future. For most people, when they feel themselves being praised and extolled, swell with pride. Does it not seem so to you?" HIPPOTHALES: "It does to me." SOCRATES: "And the more proud they become, the more difficult they are to capture?" HIPPOTHALES: "It is likely." SOCRATES: "What kind of hunter would that man seem to be to you, if he drove the wild beasts away in such a way that they became both safer and more difficult to catch in the future?" HIPPOTHALES: "An unskilled one, obviously." SOCRATES: "And yet, to not soothe men with speeches and songs, but rather to provoke them, is a labor quite foreign to the Muses." HIPPOTHALES: "It seems so." SOCRATES: "See then, O Hippothales, lest by all these things you make yourself liable...

For he is exceptionally eager to listen. Entering, we found the sacred ceremonies nearly finished; the youths, dressed in their finery, were playing with pebbles and dice. Some were playing outside in the vestibule; others in a corner of the gymnasium were practicing "odds or evens," drawing pebbles out of certain baskets. Others stood around watching them, among whom was Lysis. He stood among the youths wearing a garland, surpassing all in his natural character; he was thought to be not only beautiful, but also honorable and good. We, for our part, sat down opposite them where there was a quiet place and began to converse with one another. Lysis turned and frequently cast his eyes toward us, as if he desired to come closer, but he was afraid to approach alone. Meanwhile, Menexenus entered from the courtyard while playing, and seeing me and Ctesippus, came to sit with us. When Lysis saw him, he followed and sat down next to him. Others arrived as well. Hippothales, when he saw many had gathered, desiring to remain hidden, withdrew to a place where he thought he could not be seen by Lysis, lest he might be bothersome to him; and standing there, he listened.

I, looking at Menexenus, said, "O son of Demophon, which of you is the elder?" "We are in dispute," he replied. To which I added: "Do you also dispute which is of more noble birth?" "That too." "And also which is more handsome?" They both smiled. "Which of you is richer, I shall certainly not ask. For you are friends, are you not?" "Very much so," they replied. "And among friends, all things are held in common. Therefore, in this you do not differ at all, if indeed you speak truly about friendship." They agreed. But when I wished to inquire which was more just and wiser, someone interrupted us and summoned Menexenus, saying he was called by the master of the gymnasium. He seemed to me to be a priest of the sacred rites. He departed, therefore, and I questioned Lysis.

"Tell me, O Lysis, do your father and mother love you dearly?" LYS. Very much. SOC. And do they not desire you to be most happy? LYS. How could they not? SOC. Does a man seem happy to you if he is a slave, and is permitted to do nothing that he desires? LYS. Not by Jove. SOC. Therefore, if your father and mother love you and wish you to become happy, they will take every care and diligence that you live happily. LYS. What prevents it? SOC. Will they then permit you to do whatever you please, and not oppose your desires? LYS. By Jove, O Socrates, they hinder me in many things! SOC. How can you say this? While they wish for you to be happy, do they hinder you from obtaining your wish? Answer me this: if you desired to be carried in one of your father's chariots, taking the reins when he competes, would he permit it? LYS. Not at all. SOC. Whom then would he permit? LYS. There is a certain charioteer hired by my father for a wage. SOC. What do you say? Your parents would grant a mercenary the free management of the horses rather than you, and pay money besides for this work? LYS. Why not? SOC. But would they permit you to drive the mule team and strike them with the thongs? LYS. Why would they permit me? SOC. Is no one allowed to whip them? LYS. Certainly, the muleteer. SOC. A slave or a free man? LYS. A slave. SOC. They value a slave more than you, their son, and grant him more freedom of action. Furthermore, answer me this: do they permit you to rule yourself, or not? LYS. Not in any way. SOC. Who rules you? LYS. A tutor <term>paedagogus: a slave tasked with supervising a child</term>. SOC. Is he a slave? LYS. Our slave. SOC. How burdensome it is, for a free man to be subject to a slave! But in what actions does this tutor command you? LYS. While he leads me to my teachers. SOC. And do these teachers also command you? LYS. Entirely. SOC. Your father, then, has willingly placed many masters and rulers over you. But when you return home to your mother, does she let you do whatever you like so that you may be happy—perhaps with the wool-working or the loom when she weaves? Does she let you touch the sword, the shears, the shuttle, or the comb, or other instruments of wool-working? LYS. She would not only forbid it, but would strike me if I dared to touch them. SOC. By God! Have you done some injury to your father or mother? LYS. None at all. SOC. For what reason, then, do they refuse to let you be happy and dispose of things according to your own judgment, but instead educate you daily so that you are always serving someone, and, to put it briefly, do nothing according to your own will? Thus it happens that such great wealth seems to benefit you not at all, since anyone else manages it more than you. And what is more, not even your noble body is yours to rule, since another feeds and tends it; you, O Lysis, have no command, nor do you achieve any of your desires. LYS. It is because I am not yet of age, O Socrates. SOC. See that this is not the least of what hinders you, O son of Democrates. For I believe your father and mother do grant you some things, and do not wait for a more advanced age; for instance, whenever they want something read or written for them. For they entrust these things to you above the other servants. LYS. Very much so. SOC. In these matters, you are permitted in both writing and reading to observe whatever order of letters you wish. And when you take up the lyre, your parents do not prevent you, I suppose, from tightening or loosening any of the strings, or plucking them with the plectrum. LYS. Certainly not. SOC. What is the reason, O Lysis, that they permit you in these things,

both Greeks and Barbarians, both men and women; and in these matters we shall act according to our own judgment, nor will anyone willingly stand in our way. But those things which we do not know, no one will permit us to do as we please; instead, everyone will resist us to the best of their power—not only strangers, but even our parents and what is even closer to us: we ourselves shall not belong to ourselves, but shall be servants to others. Shall we be friends to any man, or will anyone love us in those matters in which we are useless? LY. Never. SO. Therefore, neither your father nor anyone else loves another insofar as he is useless. LY. It seems not. SO. If, therefore, you turn out to be wise, everyone will be your friend and intimate. For you will be useful and good. If not, no one else, nor your parents, nor your kinsmen will be your friends. Can anyone be proud and boastful in those things in which he is not yet wise? LY. How could that be? SO. When I had heard these things, I turned my eyes toward Hippothales, and I was very close to saying: "O Hippothales, this is the way one should dispute with youths: by correcting and humbling them, not by flattering and puffing them up as you do." From my earliest childhood, I have had a certain desire for one particular possession, just as others have. For instance, one man desires horses, another dogs, another gold, another honors. I set little value on these things; they do not move me much. But I burn with the desire to acquire friends. Therefore, I would rather have a good friend than the most precious quail or cock; and, by Jove, rather than a horse or a dog; and, by the faith of the gods <note>original: "mediuſfidius"</note>, I would rather choose a best friend than obtain the gold of Darius, or even capture Darius himself. The lover of the beloved, or the beloved of the lover? Or does it make no difference? ME. It seems to me to make no difference. SO. What do you say? **Socrates:** Furthermore, can there not be found a certain lover whose beloved does not respond in turn with love? **Menexenus:** There can. **Socrates:** And does it not often happen that the lover is even hated? This sometimes happens to lovers in regard to those they love. For lovers, though they love most ardently, are sometimes not loved back at all; indeed, they are quite often even hated. Do I not seem to you to speak the truth? **Menexenus:** Most true. **Socrates:** In these cases, does not one party love, while the other is loved? **Menexenus:** Certainly. **Socrates:** Which of them, then, is the friend of the other? Is the lover the friend of the beloved, whether he is loved in return or hated? Or is the beloved the friend of the lover? Or is neither the friend of the other, unless both love each other in turn? **Menexenus:** So it seems to be the case. **Socrates:** Therefore, we now think differently than we did before. For then it seemed that if only one party loved, both were friends; but now, on the contrary, unless each loves the other, we must say neither is a friend. **Menexenus:** So it appears. **Socrates:** Nothing, therefore, is a friend to that which loves it, if it is not loved in return. **Menexenus:** It does not seem so. **Socrates:** Therefore, men are not "friends of horses" if the horses do not love them back; nor are they "friends of quails," nor of dogs, nor of wine, nor of exercise, nor "friends of wisdom" <note>original: "sapientiae" — the literal root of the word "philosopher"</note> unless wisdom loves them in return. For individuals love these things, yet these things are not "friends." Therefore, that poet lies who says: *Happy is he who has boys as friends, and horses, and hunting dogs, and a guest from a foreign land.* **Menexenus:** It does not seem so to me. **Socrates:** Does he seem to you to speak the truth? **Menexenus:** The truth. **Socrates:** Therefore, the beloved is a friend to the lover, as it appears, O Menexenus, whether the beloved loves or hates; just as very young children sometimes do not love at all, and sometimes even hate, when they are punished by their parents. Yet even then, while they vehemently hate, they are most dear to their parents. **Menexenus:** I agree. **Socrates:** Therefore, it is not the lover who is the friend according to this reasoning, but the beloved. **Menexenus:** It seems so. **Socrates:** And the one who is hated is the enemy, not the one who hates. **Menexenus:** That appears to be the case. **Socrates:** Thus, many are loved by their enemies and hated by their friends; they are friends to their enemies and enemies to their friends—if the beloved rather than the lover is the friend. But what an absurdity this would be, O sweet friend! Indeed, it is impossible for a friend to be an enemy, or an enemy to be a friend. **Menexenus:** You seem to speak the truth, O Socrates. **Socrates:** And if this can in no way happen, it remains that the lover is the friend of the beloved. **Menexenus:** It appears so. **Socrates:** Similarly, that which hates is the enemy of that which it hates. **Menexenus:** It must be so. **Socrates:** We are now forced to concede the same things we did before: that often a friend is something that is not a friend, and often even an enemy—whenever one loves someone who does not love them or who even dislikes them. Sometimes one will be the enemy of someone who is not an enemy, or even a friend—when one hates someone who does not dislike them, or who even loves them. **Menexenus:** So it seems. **Socrates:** What then shall we say, if neither the lovers are friends, nor the beloved, nor both lovers and beloved together? Shall we say there are some others besides these who have been friends? **Menexenus:** By Jove, O Socrates, I do not find what to answer. **Socrates:** See, O Menexenus, lest perhaps we have searched incorrectly in our previous points. Then Lysis said: "That is how it seems to me, O Socrates." And having spoken thus, he blushed. For it seemed to me that what he said escaped him against his will, because he was watching so attentively. For while he was listening, he seemed to be quite caught up in it. I, therefore, wishing Menexenus to rest, and being greatly delighted by the other's love of wisdom <note>original: "philosophia"</note>, addressed Lysis thus: "O Lysis, you seem to me to speak the truth; for if we had considered correctly, we would not have wandered so far. Therefore, let us not proceed further by this path. For this consideration seems to me like a difficult and rough road. But the journey we have now begun should be continued with the help of the poets. For they are to us like fathers and guides of wisdom. They certainly do not speak badly when they advise us who are friends. Moreover, they claim that friends are made by the guidance of a reconciling God. For they say: *God always leads like to like, and makes them known.* Have you not yourself encountered these words?" **Lysis:** I have. **Socrates:** Perhaps you have also read the writings of the wise, in which they affirm these same things: that like is always necessarily a friend to like. And this is the opinion of those who treat of nature and the universe. **Lysis:** You speak the truth. **Socrates:** Do they speak well? **Lysis:** Perhaps. **Socrates:** Perhaps it is true in part; perhaps even in total. But we do not yet understand it. For it seems to us that the more a wicked man adheres to a wicked man, and the more frequently he associates with him, the more he becomes an enemy. For he inflicts injury; and it cannot be that the one who injures and the one who receives the injury are friends. Is it not so? **Lysis:** Entirely so. **Socrates:** By this reasoning, half of that saying will be false, if indeed the wicked are alike. **Lysis:** Certainly. **Socrates:** But they seem to me to say that the good are alike to one another and are friends; but the wicked, as is often said of them, are never like even themselves, nor like each other, but are entirely disturbed and unstable. He who disagrees with himself can in no way agree with another, nor can he be a friend to anyone. Do you not think the same? **Lysis:** Indeed. **Socrates:** This, therefore, as my opinion goes, O friend, is what they mean when they say like is friend to like: that only the good man is a friend to the good man; but the bad man is never truly a friend to either the good or the bad. Do you agree? **Lysis:** I assent. **Socrates:** We have now found who are friends. For reason dictates that those who are good exist as friends. **Lysis:** It is established. **Socrates:** I think the same. But there is something that disturbs me. And see, I pray, what I suspect. In what way is like a friend to like, insofar as he is like? And is such a person useful to such a person? Indeed, let us consider it thus. What benefit or harm can any like thing bring to any other like thing, which it could not do for itself? Or what can it experience from the other that it could not experience from itself? Since these things are such that they do not help each other in any way, how can they be sought by one another? **Lysis:** In no way. **Socrates:** That which is not sought, how can it be a friend? **Lysis:** In no way. **Socrates:** Or perhaps like is not a friend to like insofar as he is like? But the good man is a friend to the good man insofar as he is good, not insofar as he is like? **Lysis:** Perhaps. **Socrates:** What then? Is not the good man, insofar as he is good, to that extent sufficient unto himself? **Lysis:** Yes. **Socrates:** He who is sufficient unto himself, by that very sufficiency, lacks nothing at all. **Lysis:** What prevents it? **Socrates:** He who lacks nothing, seeks nothing. **Lysis:** Nothing indeed. **Socrates:** If he does not seek, he does not love. **Lysis:** No. **Socrates:** He who does not love is not a friend. **Lysis:** It does not seem so. **Socrates:** How then will the good be friends to the good, who neither desire each other when absent—since they live sufficiently with themselves—nor need each other when present? By what reason can such men value each other highly? **Lysis:** By none. **Socrates:** They will never be friends, who do not [value] each other...

# TWELFTH BOOK.

...is of great value. **LYSIS.** Never. **SOCRATES.** Consider now, O Lysis, where we have fallen, and whether we have been altogether deceived. **LYSIS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** I once heard from someone—and I even remember it now in your presence—that like is the enemy of like, and the good are most hostile to the good. He also used the testimony of Hesiod <note>A Greek poet (c. 700 BC); the reference is to his work *Works and Days*.</note>, who says that "potter envies potter, singer envies singer, and physician envies physician." And in other matters he asserted it was similarly necessary: that similar things abound in envy, emulation, and contention toward one another, while dissimilar things are joined in friendship. Furthermore, he said the poor man becomes a friend to the rich out of necessity, and the weak to the strong for the sake of help, and the sick man to the physician in the same way. The ignorant man also desires and loves the expert. He added, moreover, certain more sublime things: that it is far from the case that like is a friend to like; but on the contrary, that which is most opposite is most friendly to its opposite. For each thing desires not its like, but its opposite: thus the dry desires the moist, the cold desires the hot, the bitter the sweet, the sharp the blunt, the empty desires fullness, the full emptiness, and other things likewise. For the opposite provides nourishment to its opposite. But like is not at all nourished by like. Indeed, he who taught such things seemed to be a most eloquent and elegant man. For he spoke well. But how does it seem to you? **MENEXENUS.** It seems correct, as it appears at first glance. **SOCRATES.** Shall we say then that the opposite is most friendly to its opposite? **MENEXENUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Let it be so, O Menexenus. But I ask you, is this not strange and foreign? Immediately those "wise men" <note>Socrates often uses "wise men" (sophists) sarcastically to refer to professional debaters.</note> will rise up against us of their own accord, those who excel in the eloquence of refutation; and they will ask us: is not hatred the greatest opposite of friendship? What shall we answer them most especially? Shall we not be forced to admit they speak the truth? **MENEXENUS.** We shall be forced. **SOCRATES.** Will they then say the enemy is a friend to the friend? Or the friend a friend to the enemy? **MENEXENUS.** Neither. **SOCRATES.** Nor the just to the unjust, or the temperate to the intemperate? Or the good to the bad? **MENEXENUS.** It does not seem so to me. **SOCRATES.** And yet, if a thing is a friend to something according to opposition, these things ought to be friendly. **MENEXENUS.** They certainly ought. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, neither is like a friend to like, nor opposite to opposite. **MENEXENUS.** It does not seem so. **SOCRATES.** Come, let us observe this also, lest it escape us even more, that in truth nothing of these things we have mentioned is a friend; but that which is neither good nor evil sometimes becomes a friend of the good. **MENEXENUS.** What are you saying? **SOCRATES.** I myself do not know, by Jove! <note>original: "per Iovem" - a common oath to Zeus/Jupiter.</note> For I waver because of the ambiguity of the form. And it seems, as the old proverb has it, that "the beautiful is a friend." For it appears to be something soft, smooth, and sleek; and therefore it perhaps easily glides into us: it creeps and penetrates as if it were something slippery and smooth. For I say that the good itself is beautiful. Do you not also? **MENEXENUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, I offer this to you as a divination: that the friend of the good and the beautiful is that which is neither good nor evil. Hear why I prophesy this. It seems to me there are three kinds. One good, another evil. The last, that which is neither good nor evil; what about you? **MENEXENUS.** To me also. **SOCRATES.** Neither is good a friend to good, nor evil to evil, nor good to evil, as the previous reasoning forbids. It remains that if anything is a friend to something: that which is neither good nor evil becomes a friend either to the good, or to something such as itself. For nothing will be a friend to evil. **MENEXENUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Nor yet like to like, as we showed a little while ago. **MENEXENUS.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, that which is neither good nor evil will not be a friend to that which is also such as itself. **MENEXENUS.** It does not seem so. **SOCRATES.** Only that which is neither good nor evil, therefore, can become a friend to the good alone. **MENEXENUS.** It seems necessary to follow. **SOCRATES.** Was this just now set forth correctly by us, O boys? If we consider a healthy body, it does not need the art of medicine; nor does it need any help at all, for it is in a sufficient state. Hence no one who is healthy is a friend to the physician for the sake of health itself. **MENEXENUS.** No one. **SOCRATES.** But the sick man is, I think, because of the disease itself. **MENEXENUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Disease is indeed an evil; but the skill of medicine is a certain good and useful thing. **MENEXENUS.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** The body, in that it is a body, is neither good nor evil. **MENEXENUS.** True. **SOCRATES.** But the body is compelled by disease to seek and love a remedy. **MENEXENUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** It follows that what is neither good nor evil becomes a friend of the good because of the presence of evil. **MENEXENUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** But it is established that this happens before that thing becomes evil because of the presence of evil. For that which is evil has not been made in the place of the good which it desires, or of which it is a friend. For we showed it was impossible for evil to be a friend to the good. **MENEXENUS.** Impossible, without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Pay attention, I pray, to what I say. For I assert that some things become such as that which is present to them, and some do not; just as if someone wished to dye something with a certain color, the infection of the color would be present in some way to the thing colored. **MENEXENUS.** It would be present. **SOCRATES.** Is not the colored thing then also such as it is accustomed to be? **MENEXENUS.** I do not understand. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps you will understand it this way: if someone should stain your hair, which is blond, with white lead <note>A toxic white pigment used in antiquity as a cosmetic.</note>, would it become white? Or would it rather appear so? **MENEXENUS.** It would appear so. **SOCRATES.** Yet whiteness would be present to it. **MENEXENUS.** It would be present. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, it would be no more white for all that; and though the brightness is present, it would be neither white nor black. **MENEXENUS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** But when they grow white from old age, then, O friends, they become such as that which has come upon them: white by the presence of the white color. **MENEXENUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** This is what I had asked: whether everything to which such a thing is present immediately turns out to be such itself; or rather, if it is present in a certain way, it becomes such, but otherwise not at all. **MENEXENUS.** In this way. **SOCRATES.** By the same reasoning, that which is neither good nor evil, when evil is present, is not yet evil, though sometimes it becomes evil. **MENEXENUS.** Altogether. **SOCRATES.** When it is not yet evil though evil is present, this presence compels it to desire the good; but the presence which makes it evil rejects both the desire for the good and friendship. For it is no longer "neither," but evil. But an evil friend cannot be for the good, nor a good for the evil. **MENEXENUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** For this reason, the wise should be said to no longer practice philosophy, whether they be gods or men; nor those who are so corrupted by ignorance that they have been made wicked. For no one who is evil and utterly ignorant practices philosophy. There remain, therefore, those to whom this evil—namely ignorance—is present, but who are not yet entirely unlearned or ignorant of what they are; rather, they acknowledge their own ignorance, because of which awareness they practice philosophy—that is, they love wisdom—being not yet good or evil. For those who are evil by no means practice philosophy, nor do those who are good. For neither did opposite appear to us as a friend to opposite, nor like to like, as shown above. Do you remember? **MENEXENUS AND LYSIS.** We certainly remember. **SOCRATES.** Altogether...

<summary>Socrates explores the paradoxes of friendship, arguing that friendship exists between the "neutral" (neither good nor evil) and the "good" due to the presence of evil, such as a sick man seeking a doctor. He concludes that philosophy is practiced only by those who recognize their own ignorance, as neither the perfectly wise nor the utterly ignorant seek wisdom.</summary>
