<meta>This page continues the Socratic dialogue "Lysis" (On Friendship). Socrates is speaking with the youths Lysis and Menexenus, attempting to define the true nature of a "friend" or "dear thing."</meta>

# LYSIS, OR ON FRIENDSHIP. FOLIO 51.

O Lysis and Menexenus, we have discovered what a friend is and what is not. For we concluded above, regarding both the soul and the body, that that which is neither good nor evil becomes a friend of the good because of the presence of evil. They both agreed to all these things. And I was greatly rejoiced, like a hunter who had finally caught the prey he had been tracking. Then, I know not how, a certain strange and absurd suspicion arose in me, as if the things we had agreed upon were not entirely true. And immediately troubled, I said: "Good heavens, Lysis and Menexenus, we seem to have been having a dream." 

**MENEXENUS:** "Why is that?" 

**SOCRATES:** "I fear that, like men who are proud and vain, we have fallen into false arguments concerning the friend." 

**MENEXENUS:** "By what reasoning?" 

**SOCRATES:** "Clearly by this: Is a friend a friend to someone, or not?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Necessarily so." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is it for the sake of no one and because of nothing, or for the sake of someone and because of something?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Certainly for the sake of someone and because of something." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is that thing for whose sake a friend is a friend to someone itself a 'dear thing' <note>original: "amica"; Socrates is exploring whether we love things for themselves or as tools to reach a higher goal</note>? Or perhaps is it neither dear nor even hateful?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "I do not quite understand." 

**SOCRATES:** "That is likely. But in this way, both you and he, I think, will understand better. Did we say that a sick man is a friend to the physician?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "We did." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is he not a friend to the physician because of disease, and for the sake of health?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Yes." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is disease an evil?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Of course." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is health a good, an evil, or neither?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "A good." 

**SOCRATES:** "We said before that the body, since it is neither good nor evil, is a friend to medicine because of the evil of disease; but it gains the friendship of medicine for the sake of health, which is a good." 

**MENEXENUS:** "Exactly." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is health a friend <note>meaning "a dear/desired thing"</note> or not a friend?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "A friend." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is disease an enemy?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Entirely." 

**SOCRATES:** "Therefore, that which is neither good nor evil is a friend of the good because of the evil and the enemy, and for the sake of the good and the friend." 

**MENEXENUS:** "That is clear." 

**SOCRATES:** "Therefore, a friend is a friend for the sake of a friend because of an enemy." 

**MENEXENUS:** "I suppose so." 

**SOCRATES:** "Come now, boys; since we have reached this point in the debate, let us, I pray, attend diligently lest we be deceived. First, that a friend has become a friend of a friend seems like 'like being a friend to like,' which we established earlier was impossible—I will pass over that for now. But let us consider this further, lest our present opinion deceive us. We said medicine is a friend for the sake of health." 

**MENEXENUS:** "We affirmed it." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is health not also a friend?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Very much so." 

**SOCRATES:** "If it is a friend, it is a friend for the sake of something." 

**MENEXENUS:** "It is." 

**SOCRATES:** "Namely, for the sake of a friend, if our previous concessions hold." 

**MENEXENUS:** "And a friend." 

**SOCRATES:** "Will that again be a friend for the sake of another friend?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Certainly." 

**SOCRATES:** "It is necessary that by this progress we arrive at a certain First Principle <note>original: "principium quoddam"; the 'First Dear Thing' or 'Proton Philon'</note> which is no longer referred back to another friend, but is that which is the Primary Friend, toward which all things we call 'dear' look." 

**MENEXENUS:** "It is necessary." 

**SOCRATES:** "This is what I was saying must be considered: lest all those other things which we said were dear for the sake of that one deceive us like mere phantoms of it; while that first thing is the truly dear friend. Let us consider it in this way. Whatever someone values highly—for instance, a father his son—he prefers above other things. And because he values his son so much, he also values certain other things because of him. For example, if he realizes his son has drunk hemlock <note>a common poison in ancient Greece</note>, he will value wine highly, provided he thinks it will cure the poison." 

**MENEXENUS:** "Very much so." 

**SOCRATES:** "And also the jar in which the wine is kept?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Certainly." 

**SOCRATES:** "Does he then value a clay cup or three measures of wine more than his son? Or is it rather this way: all this effort does not look to those things which are prepared for the sake of another, but returns to that for whose sake the rest were sought? It is not true, as we often say, that we value silver and gold highly. For all our intention and valuation belongs to that one thing for which these are prepared." 

**MENEXENUS:** "That is agreed." 

**SOCRATES:** "The same reasoning applies to the friend. For whatever things we said were dear to us for the sake of some friend, we have named with an improper term. It appears that the true friend is that toward which all these so-called friendships tend." 

**MENEXENUS:** "So it seems." 

<margin>A friend is not a friend for the sake of any other friend.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** "Therefore, the true friend is not a friend for the sake of any other friend." 

**MENEXENUS:** "True." 

**SOCRATES:** "Let us set aside, then, the idea that a friend is a friend because of some other friend. But is the good not a friend?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "I think so." 

**SOCRATES:** "Does one love the good because of evil? Is this how it stands? If of the three things we mentioned—good, evil, and the neutral—two are taken, and evil departs and touches nothing (neither body, nor soul, nor anything else we said was in itself neither good nor evil), would the good then be entirely useless to us? For if nothing further harmed us, we would have no need of any benefit from the good. And thus it would be clear to us then that we sought and loved the good because of evil, as if the good were a remedy for evil, and evil were the disease. When there is no disease, we need no medicine. Is the good so constituted by nature that it is loved by us—who are in the middle between good and evil—only because of evil? Does it contribute nothing by its own nature?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "So it seems." 

**SOCRATES:** "Therefore, that friend in which all other things (which were called dear for the sake of another) ended, is in a very different state than they are. For those were called dear for the sake of a friend. But that which is truly a friend appeared to us to be so because of an enemy. If the enemy were gone, it would no longer be a friend to us." 

**MENEXENUS:** "Not as the present reasoning persuades me." 

**SOCRATES:** "If evil were rooted out, would no hunger or thirst remain, or anything of that kind? Or perhaps some hunger would remain, since men and other animals would still exist, yet it would not be harmful; and thirst and other desires would remain, but not be evil, once evil was entirely rooted out? Or is this perhaps a ridiculous question: what would then remain and what would not?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Who knows?" 

**SOCRATES:** "This at least we know: that it happens now that a hungry person is harmed, and it also happens that he is helped." 

**MENEXENUS:** "Both." 

**SOCRATES:** "And does it not happen that one who is thirsty, or desiring anything else of this kind, sometimes desires usefully, sometimes harmfully, and sometimes in neither way?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Very much so." 

**SOCRATES:** "If evils perish, will those things which are not evil perish with them?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "By no means." 

**SOCRATES:** "There will be, therefore, desires that are neither good nor evil, even if evils have been destroyed." 

**MENEXENUS:** "It is likely." 

**SOCRATES:** "Is it possible that he who desires something and burns for it does not love that very thing?" 

**MENEXENUS:** "Not as it seems to me." 

**SOCRATES:** "For this reason, even if evils are destroyed, it seems that frie[ndship]... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "amicus" or "amicitia" at the end of the page</note>

<summary>Socrates argues that we often call things "dear" only because they lead to something else, eventually leading to a "Primary Friend" or "First Dear Thing." He questions whether we only love the good as a remedy for evil, suggesting that if evil were abolished, our need for the "good" might vanish, though neutral desires would remain.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Lysis, Menexenus, friendship, First Dear Thing, Proton Philon, good and evil, medicine and health, desire</keywords>

# ARGUMENT ON THE THEAETETUS.

...some causes will remain. ME. So it is. SO. But if evil were the cause of one being a friend to another, then if evil were removed, nothing would be a friend. For if the cause is removed, its effect cannot remain. ME. You speak rightly. SO. Did we not agree above among ourselves that a friend loves something, and because of something; and that because of evil, that which is neither evil nor good loves the good itself? ME. We agreed. SO. But at present, a different cause for mutual loving appears. ME. So it seems. SO. Is it not as we were just saying, that desire is the cause of friendship? And that 
<margin>Whether desire is the cause of friendship. That which it seeks, it seeks because it is in need.</margin>
which it desires is the "friend" at the moment when it desires it? And that what we said above about being a friend is a sort of shadow, like a fiction drawn out too far? ME. It appears so. SO. Truly, that which seeks, seeks that which it lacks. ME. Exactly. SO. Therefore, the "friend" is in need of that which it lacks. ME. So I think. SO. Anything lacks that of which it has been deprived. ME. What prevents that? SO. Therefore, Menexenus and Lysis, it seems that love, friendship, and desire exist for that which is one's own and kindred. ME. & LY. We concede this. SO. Therefore, if you two are friends to each other, you are by nature somehow related. ME. & LY. Most certainly. SO. And whoever else desires another, O boys, or loves them: he desires and prizes and loves them for this reason—that he is kindred to them, either according to the soul, or the soul's habits, or character, or appearance. Otherwise, he would never prize them. Menexenus plainly agreed. Lysis was silent. But I said: it is necessary that we love what is by nature our own. ME. It seems so. SO. Therefore, it is necessary that a legitimate and least-pretending lover be loved in return by his beloveds. To this, Lysis and Menexenus finally nodded, though with difficulty. Hippothales, however, jumping for joy, turned all sorts of colors. But wanting to discuss the speech more diligently, I added this: If "one's own" and "the similar" are different, we have already said, O Lysis and Menexenus, what a friend is; but if "the similar" and "one's own" are the same, it is not easy to reject the previous argument <note>original: "sermonem superiorem"</note> that the similar is useless to the similar insofar as it is similar—and the useless can in no way be a friend. Do you wish then, since we have become as if drunk from arguing, that we admit "one's own" is one thing and "the similar" is another? ME. We certainly do. SO. Shall we set down the Good as being "one's own" to everyone, and the Evil as "alien"? Or Evil as "own" to evil, Good to good, and to the neutral, the neutral? ME. & LY. Each of these seems to us to be "own" to each. SO. Again, O boys, we have fallen into those same arguments about friendship which we refuted at the beginning. For the unjust will be no less a friend to the unjust, and the bad to the bad, than the good to the good. ME. So it seems. SO. What further? If we say the Good and "one's own" are the same, is not only the good a friend to the good? ME. Entirely. SO. But we thought that this, too, was refuted by us a long time ago. Do you remember? ME. Very well. SO. To what argument then shall we turn next? To none, evidently. It is worthwhile then, like wise men in the courts, to summarize by enumerating what has been said. For if neither the lovers, nor the beloved, nor the similar, nor the dissimilar, nor the good, nor "one's own," nor any of the others we listed—which I cannot remember because of their multitude—if, I say, none of these is a "friend," I truly have nothing more to offer. When I had said this, I thought to call upon some of the elders; but immediately, like certain spirits <note>original: "daemones"</note>, the tutors of both Lysis and Menexenus, along with their brothers, ordered them to return home. For the evening star had come. At first, we and the others standing around tried to drive the tutors away. But when they paid us no mind and, muttering in their barbarian way, took it badly and called the boys more frequently, we were overcome by their persistence and broke up the gathering. Indeed, they were leaning on the Hermae—that is, certain square stones—and were pressing us importunately. Afterward, as they were leaving, I turned to Menexenus and Lysis and briefly said: At present, we seem to have turned out ridiculous and foolish, both myself, an old man, and you boys. For these people leaving will mock us, because we think we are each other's friends—for I count myself among you—yet we have not yet been able to find out what a friend is.

-> THE END OF LYSIS. <-

### To Peter de' Medici, Father of the Fatherland.

Theaetetus, however, answers that knowledge is geometry, arithmetic, and the other

disciplines of this kind, and individual arts. Socrates rejects this response as being less than suitable to the question. Because when he was asked what knowledge *is*, he enumerated not what it is, but *how many* knowledges there are: and he explained what things they are knowledges *of*. For he who says "arithmetic" does not say knowledge itself, but the knowledge of numbering; and he who says "geometry" says the knowledge of measuring. Furthermore, the response is ridiculous because it explains through the unknown. For no one can know that this is the knowledge of numbers or figures unless he knows what "knowledge" is. Moreover, the response is superfluous. For while he could have embraced the definition <note>original: "rationem"</note> of knowledge itself in a few words, he enters upon an infinite journey by

For Protagoras thinks that "Man is the measure of all things": of existing things that they are, and of non-existing things that they are not; and that things are to each person such as they appear to each. For such as each thing is, such is it sensed. Such as they are sensed, such they appear to the "phantasia"—that is, the internal sense. By which he wishes to effect that sensation is knowledge. # ARGUMENT FOR THE THEAETETUS. FOLIO 52.
g.iiii.

Indeed, Thales of Miletus, Homer, Epicharmus, Empedocles, Heraclitus, and Protagoras all agreed on this point. For when Thales says that water is the principle of all things, and Homer says that Oceanus is the father of all and Tethys the mother, they all show that everything is in a state of flux <note>The Greek concept of *panta rhei* or "everything flows."</note>. These others whom we have mentioned, following their lead, said that nothing ever *is*, but that each thing is always *becoming*. Hence, nothing is absolutely such-and-such in itself rather than something else; but through motion, mixture, and the relation of one thing to another, it becomes and appears such-and-such to one person, and something else to another. They believe it is established that all things are in motion because all things are produced by motion; moreover, they infer that all things come from motion because that by which a thing is made also preserves it. Both those things pertaining to the soul and those pertaining to the body are preserved by motion and exercise, but perish through leisure and sluggishness. Therefore, all things come from motion. Furthermore, as long as the spheres of the heavens are moved, the four elements are mixed. Insofar as these are mixed, they beget the lower things; and after they are begotten, they are preserved by exercise. Thus, motion effects all these things. They add that generation comes from heat, and heat comes from the motion of the sun or the collision of bodies.

But because nothing is any one thing according to itself, they introduce this example: whiteness, or any color, is neither the sight of the eyes nor the motion of bodies; rather, a certain intermediate result arises from the sight and the motion—that is, a specific "passion" <note>In the sense of a passive experience or sensation.</note> around the eyes. And from the different disposition of the one looking, and the various modes of gazing, different colors are seen and come to be, sometimes one way and sometimes another. Furthermore, the varying motion of rays striking bodies and hitting the eyes offers diverse and multiform images. Indeed, the same thing often appears as a different color to different men and animals, and it is so; often it even appears different to the same person regarding the same object, not at the same time but at another, due to the mutation of nature itself. They think, therefore, that whatever exists is motion.

Now, there are two species of motion: one in acting, the other in suffering <note>Active and passive motion.</note>. By the mixing of these motions, they say all things are fashioned. The outcomes are twin in appearance but infinite in number: namely, the sensible object and the sense; the sense is always present and meeting with the sensible. For as often as some power of sensing and something consonant with it cohere together, two things arise from their concurrence: regarding the object, a sensible quality—color, taste, smell, and others of this kind; regarding the power of the soul, a sense. When these are disjointed, those things do not happen. Thus it happens that of those things offered to the five senses, nothing is such-and-such by its own nature; but by meeting with the sense, it becomes one thing at one time and another at another. For nothing is acting or suffering according to itself, but each is so in their mutual encounter. Therefore, nothing is any one thing by itself, but it always becomes in relation to something else and for someone; it never *is*, but truly becomes and flows forever.

<margin>
Socrates' refutation of the aforementioned.
</margin>

But Socrates refutes these points by noting that those who are drunk, those suffering from frenzy, the insane, and the sleeping when they dream—as well as those who have their senses corrupted by some other disease—affirm that they sense and think truly, even though all their visions are said to be false. From this it follows that not all things seen are true. They fall into the same doubt regarding whatever we are said to sense while awake and sober. For we give almost equal time to sleep and wakefulness in turn. Therefore, it is doubtful whether these or those are rather dreams and false.

<margin>
Protagoras' response to Socrates.
</margin>

But those who wish to think that all appearances are true would respond thus: that the various affections of the acting or suffering agents produce different results, and the objects sensed act according to the affection of the sufferer's sense. This affection is one thing in the waking person and another in the sleeper, the sick, or the healthy. For this reason, different judgments arise, yet all are true, because all things are to each person such as they are judged to be. For one must remember what was said above: that nothing is absolutely one thing by its nature, but whatever a thing is, it is in relation to another, for another, and of another. Rather, whatever becomes is something, but nothing truly *is*. Thus these things harmonize with each other: according to Homer and Heraclitus, all things flow; according to Protagoras, man is the measure of all things; according to Theaetetus, knowledge is sense-perception.

<margin>
Another refutation by Socrates.
</margin>

Against them, Socrates argues thus: If knowledge is sense-perception, then brute animals, which prevail in the senses more than man, will excel in knowledge. Likewise, if whatever is seen is true, then the thoughts of any man are equally right; no one is wiser than another, nor is God wiser than man. Added to this is that the faculty of teaching, disputing, and refuting would be vain, since those who judge truly about individual things would need to learn nothing; nor should those things which each person possesses be questioned, nor should anything be refuted, since indeed any thoughts are true.

Furthermore, if sensing and knowing are the same—as seeing and hearing—when unlearned boys first look at letters, they see them; therefore they know them. Or if they are said not to know them, let it also be said they do not see them. And when we first hear foreigners pronouncing their own language, not yet being skilled in that tongue, we shall affirm that just as we hear, so we know what they utter. But if anyone denies understanding, let him similarly deny hearing.

<margin>
Protagoras' second response.
</margin>

Protagoras will respond to this last point: that we know what we see or hear, and what we are ignorant of, we do not even sense. For instance, boys see the shape, the position of parts, and the color in letters, and seeing them, they know them. Those hearing foreign voices know the sharp and the grave sounds as they hear them; but they are entirely ignorant of the meanings of the letters and voices, which they do not sense.

<margin>
Against Protagoras.
</margin>

Against him, it is inferred thus: From this, O Protagoras, it follows that when they know the meanings, they know by something other than sense. Therefore, knowledge is something other than sense. Likewise, if to see is to know, then not to see will be not to know. But what someone has seen, learned, and remembered, he knows. Yet often he does not see it; therefore he also does not know it. Wherefore the same person both knows and does not know at the same time. Furthermore, if you see something with one eye and discern nothing with the other closed, you see and do not see that thing equally. Wherefore some litigious person might say: "If to see is to know, and not to see is not to know, you know and do not know the same thing at once." Add that when you perceive something from afar and confusedly, you indeed see it, yet you do not know it since you doubt. Therefore, knowledge is not sense-perception.

<margin>
Protagoras' response.
</margin>

Protagoras would perhaps respond by first distinguishing between memory and knowledge. For when someone first experiences something by sensing, he begins to hold it by memory; then, even when not experiencing it, he remembers. When he senses and experiences the same thing again, he recollects. In the first case, he knows by act, not by habit <note>original: "actu non habitu" — referring to active use versus stored potential.</note>; in the second, by habit, not by act; in the third, by both act and habit together. Therefore, he sometimes both knows and does not know, yet these are not contrary. For he does not ignore it in the same way that he knows it. Therefore, when he does not see, he nevertheless remembers; he knows by habit, but does not know by act. These are not contraries. And when it is said by Socrates that one person is wiser than another, Protagoras responds that some are not to be called wise and others foolish because some think true things and others false. For each person thinks those things which he experiences; he experiences those things by which he is moved; he is moved by those things which act; those things act which exist; and those which exist are true. From this he concludes that everyone thinks true things; yet he asserts that not all think good and becoming things. The wise are those who...

# ARGUMENT OF THE THEAETETUS

Those who are well-disposed accept whatever is offered as good; they think things are good for them, and as they think, so they are. But the foolish, being ill-disposed, judge things to be bad, and so they are bad for them. Against the claim that "everyone opines the truth," Socrates argues as follows: It happens in all of life and in individual skills that we believe ourselves to judge truly in some matters, while in others we defer to others—for everyone excels in some particular skill and yields to another in an unfamiliar art. Either this estimation is true, or it is false. In either case, it is not true that all men think truly. For if that estimation is true, then it will be true that some people judge truly in many things where we ourselves opine falsely. Therefore, not everyone opines the truth. But if the estimation is false, then in this at least we are often deceived; wherefore not every opinion is true. Furthermore, it often happens that what one person thinks is true is abhorred by the opinion of everyone else. Those things will therefore seem true to him, but false to others. They will thus be false more often than true, in proportion to the greater number of people who think them false rather than true. Therefore, that individual is not the measure of things, but others are. Wherefore he was not the measure of all things. Likewise, Protagoras’s opinion—that every opinion is true—is a paradox and contrary to almost everyone’s opinion; for almost the entire human race deems some opinions to be false. If every opinion is true, then this universal judgment <note>i.e., the judgment that some opinions are false</note> is also true; therefore, as they think it is false, so indeed is the position of Protagoras himself, which says every opinion is true. For by saying this, it concedes that it is itself false. And if he should say that those who abhor his words think falsely, the same thing follows from this: namely, that not every opinion is true. Furthermore, he who is ignorant cannot be the measure of that which he does not know. He who doubts is ignorant. All men doubt; therefore they are ignorant of many things. Thus, not all men are the measure of all things. And when it is said that things are such as they appear to each individual, this is an error. For those things which appear healthy or harmful to the body to those ignorant of the medical art are not always so; often their opinion deceives them. And those things which citizens, in deliberating, decree to be useful or harmful in the administration of the state are not always so for the state. For many things which they hoped would be beneficial are harmful, and things they thought would be harmful are beneficial. But if the healthy and the useful themselves do not consist solely in the opinion and custom of men, but have some nature beyond their substance, much more so do the honorable and the good. For the good is the principle and the end of useful things. Therefore, neither in those things which pertain to the care of the body, nor in those which pertain to the soul and the government of the state, are things such as they appear to each individual. Indeed, if whatever appeared were so, then whenever someone predicted the future, he would foresee it with too much truth. Which is false. For rarely do future events turn out as they are thought. And if someone judges concerning the future, it is not just anyone who does so, but the expert in those things which pertain to his art. For a physician foresees a future fever better than a musician, and a musician foresees a future harmony better than a physician. Finally, having refuted these points, Socrates, taking the opportunity from the freedom or servitude of speaking, disputes concerning the freedom of those practicing philosophy and the servitude of citizens and rhetoricians: what the life of each is like, and that the end <term>finis: the ultimate goal or purpose</term> of the philosopher is to ascend from human evils to celestial goods. He speaks of the rewards of those who seek heavenly things and the punishments of those who gape at earthly things. This digression being finished, he returns to the proposed question. Its foundation was the opinion of Heraclitus that all things are in motion. Against <margin>Plato approves of Parmenides saying that all things are one and immobile.</margin> this, Parmenides, Melissus, and Zeno the Eleatic held the opposite view. For they posited that the All is one and immobile. Plato explains and approves their dogma in the book *On the One Principle of All Things*, which we have translated. But against Heraclitus and Protagoras, he begins to argue from the division of motion. There are two kinds of motion. One is motion according to place; the other according to the nature of the thing. The former is called local motion <note>Latin: *latio*</note>, the latter alteration. There are two species of local motion: transit and circulation. For <margin>The distinction of motions.</margin> transit occurs from place to place, while circulation occurs around one and the same place. But motion in the very nature of the moved thing is effected either according to substance, or concerning quantity or quality. If it is according to substance toward being itself, it is called generation; if toward non-being, corruption. According to quantity, it is called increase toward the greater, and decrease toward the lesser. Motion from quality to quality is named affection <note>or "alteration of state"</note>. It then receives various names from various qualities. For that which pertains to heat is heating; to cold, cooling; to color, coloring; and similarly for the rest. This distinction having been premised, Socrates asks: if all things are in motion, do individual things move by both those kinds of motion, or do many move by one and others by both? If many move by only one, it follows that they are no more moving than standing still. For if they move in one way, they also rest in another way. But the opinion of those men <note>the Heracliteans</note> does not intend this; rather, that all things move entirely without any standing still, whereby they are agitated by all motions. Therefore, while things are carried from place to place, they meanwhile pass continually from one affection to another: as from heat to cold, whiteness to blackness, or the reverse. It is asked whether they remain for any time under one of these forms, or not. If they remain, it follows that not all rest has been expelled. If they do not remain, then while they pronounce something to be "hot" or "white," it ceases to be hot or white. Indeed, before the pronunciation is finished, the form ceases to be. Whence nothing is ever truly pronounced or perceived; nor should that be predicated as "hot" more than "not hot," or "white" more than "not white," since it consists in nothing, and both becomes and does not become equally while it is being uttered. For which reason the forms of things are unknown to us. The same must be said of sense. For neither does sight remain for a moment in seeing, nor hearing in hearing. Wherefore it happens that we no more see or hear than we do not see and do not hear, even while we profess to see and hear. From which it follows that if the senses are removed, the truth of the senses is also removed; which being removed, it can in no way be said that sense is knowledge. He adds also another reason, for the understanding of which one must note: that Plato attributes no cognition to the body, just as he attributes to it no life. That which lives, feels; the soul lives, and the soul feels. In the body, however, there is neither life nor sense, but the works of life and sense are manifested. Therefore, what others call the "five senses," he prefers to call the "five organs of sense"; he thinks that nothing feels with these instruments, but that through these as if through channels, individual things are felt by a certain single power of the soul, which he calls the "common sense." Into this, from all sides and from the individual organs of the body—as lines from the circumference to the center of a circle—various passions flow: colors through the eyes, sounds through the ears, odors through the nostrils, tastes through the tongue, and finally through the whole body...

<summary>This page outlines Socrates' refutation of Protagoras's relativism and Heraclitus's theory of constant flux, arguing that if everything is always changing, knowledge and language become impossible. It also introduces the Platonic view that the soul, not the body, is the true seat of sensation and cognition.</summary>
<keywords>Protagoras, Heraclitus, Parmenides, relativism, universal flux, common sense, theory of motion, epistemology, soul vs body, Plato</keywords>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE THEAETETUS.
## FO. LIII.
### g v.

It is evident that the body perceives heat, cold, moisture, dryness, weight, lightness, softness, hardness, smoothness, roughness, thinness, density, sharpness, and likewise bluntness, not through many powers, but through a single power of the soul. For by perceiving color, we say it is not a voice; and by perceiving flavor, we pronounce it not to be an odor. One thing cannot be distinguished from another unless the soul knows both. No organ extends to the same things as another organ; or if it does, not in the same manner. Therefore, the distinction between those things which are sensed is not in the organs, but in a certain single power of the soul perceiving individual things and simultaneously distinguishing individuals from one another. Since the soul itself can do all these things alone—which even the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> do not deny—what need is there for many senses? This sense, which they call the <term>common sense</term><note>The faculty that integrates data from the five individual senses into a single experience.</note>, is present in all animals immediately at birth. 

Beyond this is another power, which he names <term>phantasia</term><note>Imagination or appearance.</note>, opinion, and thought. Its duty is to judge those things which the common sense perceived through the five organs, not only regarding their quality, but what they *are*: that each of them is the same as itself, different from another, one separately, or joined together as two or three; likewise similar and dissimilar, good or bad, beautiful or ugly, useful or harmful; and to run from one to another by reasoning, to apply one thing to another, and to compare past and future with the present. Thus, by this power, we judge essence, unity, number, sameness, difference, similarity, dissimilarity, the beautiful, the ugly, the good, the bad, the useful, and the useless. Since this judgment is not present immediately at birth, but a long time after, and not in all animals but only in some, it is clear that we perceive these things by some other power besides the common sense. This he calls perfected phantasia and opinion. 

Yet this itself is not sufficient. For it judges all these things in a certain proper and particular way, under a certain time, place, and condition. We know, however, that we also judge concerning these same things in a generic and universal way—not just that this man here or there is useful now, but what humanity itself always is, and what utility itself is everywhere. Therefore, there is need for another power which, perceiving the universal reasons of things, discourses from one to another and argues by discoursing. No one doubts that this happens in us when we weave <term>syllogisms</term><note>Logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>. This we call universal reason or thought, while we may call opinion itself particular thought. 

Finally, the **Mind** <note>Latin: *mens*; the highest intellectual faculty.</note> approaches this: which perceives all the reasons of things not by discourse, but by a simple and stable intuition. For above motion and time, there must be stability and eternity. Motion and time are in reason; in the mind there is stability and eternity. For it does not learn one thing after another, but holds all things at once. Above the mind is the very unity of the soul, the character of the **Highest Good**, by which it is joined not to the reasons and ideas of things, but to the first principle of all things, which is the **One** itself. 

Since all the powers of the soul involved in cognition have been enumerated, and knowledge consists in cognition, we must see in which power knowledge chiefly resides. It does not suit **Sense**, as has been established by many reasons, and especially this: because that common sense does not judge the essences of things, but perceives only certain passions of bodies. Whoever is ignorant of essence is ignorant of truth. He who is devoid of truth is far removed from knowledge. Therefore, knowledge is not in sense, where the soul perceives not through itself but through the body, and is therefore often deceived. 

But perhaps it consists in phantasia and opinion, where we now perceive essences, and the soul judges by itself without the service of the body. And this opinion pleases <term>Theaetetus</term><note>The young mathematician who is the title character of the dialogue.</note> in a famous passage: that knowledge is opinion—not just any opinion, but **true opinion**. False opinion, however, is ignorance. But when Theaetetus had distinguished opinion into two types, true and false, <term>Socrates</term> immediately asked how false opinion could exist. He supposes one thing: that whoever opines, opines either those things which he knows or those which he does not know. Whence he reasons in this manner: He who opines false things never opines falsely from the fact that he thinks some things which he knows are certain other things which he also knows. For he who knows both never takes one for the other. Nor does he take things he does not know for other things he does not know. For he judges nothing concerning those things which have never come into his thought. Nor does he think that what he knows is that which he never knew, or conversely that what he does not know is that which he knows. For who would take the known for the unknown, or the unknown for the known? In these ways, therefore, it seems no one can opine falsely. 

But perhaps men opine falsely in some other way: when they opine things which are not. From which false opinion will be to opine things that do not exist. But neither can that happen. For whoever sees, sees some one thing; he who sees some one thing, sees something existing; but he who sees what is non-existent sees not even one thing. He who sees not one thing, sees nothing; he who sees nothing does not even see. Therefore, either he does not see, or he sees that which is. We can affirm the same regarding hearing and the other senses. Wherefore, since opinion follows sense, whoever opines, opines some one thing; he who opines some one thing, opines something existing. Therefore, he opines that which is. But he who opines what is non-existent opines not even one thing. If not one thing, then nothing. If he opines nothing, he does not even opine. Thus, either he does not opine at all, or he opines that which is. Therefore, in this way too, no one will opine falsely by opining things which are not. 

There remains another way in which a substitution occurs, so that we take one thing for another: such as the ugly for the beautiful, or the useless for the useful, which Socrates refutes thus: To opine is to speak with oneself, while we interrogate ourselves, answer, affirm, and deny. Nor is this internal speech inferior to external speech. In external speech, no one ever says that what is ugly is beautiful, or that a man is an ox, or that the even is odd, or anything of this sort. Therefore, much less will he conclude in thinking that one of these is the other. For either he knows both, or only one. If both, he would never mistake them. If one, not even then, for he would never take what he knows for that which has not yet come into his thought. Thus it seems it has not yet been discovered how false opinion exists in us. 

Yet here Plato, as also in the *Philebus*, *Sophist*, and *Meno*, uses six names pertaining to the same power of the soul to signify its six duties. For when, after the common sense, the same soul perceives what the common sense apprehended, by its opining power, that first perception is called **imagination**. As it preserves what is apprehended, it is called **memory**. As it resumes within itself what it has stored, it is **reminiscence**. And when, in resuming, it discourses from one thing to another by a certain reasoning, it is **thought**. After the discourse is finished and it affirms or denies something, it is **opinion**. But indeed, when the soul, refashioning by thought the things perceived through sense and memory, looks back at them as if at those things from which they flowed—and thinks that what are images are true things—Plato calls this a certain picturing and **phantasia**.

<margin>
Phantasia, opinion, and thought are a power beyond the common sense according to Plato.
</margin>

<summary>This page outlines the Platonic hierarchy of cognition, distinguishing between basic sensory perception, the "common sense," and higher faculties like opinion, reason, and the intuitive Mind. It specifically explores the logical difficulty of defining "false opinion" as presented in the Theaetetus dialogue.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Argument of the Theaetetus," a summary and philosophical commentary on Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of knowledge. It follows the previous discussion on the "wax tablet" metaphor for memory.</meta>

# ARGUMENT OF THE THEAETETUS.

And when he introduces the waxen image, he by no means understands the nature of the physical brain. For he did not say the waxen image was in the body, but in the soul. Since, however, there is nothing corporeal in that which is incorporeal, these things must be understood through a certain metaphor and a similarity of functions, rather than literally as the words sound. He does not wish the images of things to be fixed in the body, nor to be molded in the soul by external objects; rather, he suggests that the soul either possesses them from its own nature, or, taking the opportunity from external movements and the passions of the body, it conceives forms and reasons within itself by its own power. Whoever doubts these things should read the commentaries of Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who interpreted Plato's works spiritually.</note>, that supreme interpreter.

Having explained these things, we must return to the modes of false opinion. Socrates introduces many and rejects many; and in order to restrain the pride of the sophists, he frequently refutes, again and again, those things which they have conceded. Finally, we must gather from Plato’s mind: that when a certain sensible object first meets us, and by its meeting produces sensation in us, and from sensation comes memory; and then later the same object presents itself to us again; we combine the preceding memory with the following sensation. In these instances we then say "Socrates," "horse," "fire," and other such things. And this is what some call "opinion"—our act of combining a preceding memory with a recent sensation. 

<margin>
The forms that are in the soul are not the same as those outside it.
</margin>

Whenever these things that are gathered together harmonize with each other, a true opinion exists; if they disagree, it is a false opinion. For if someone, while keeping the appearance of Socrates in his memory, should encounter Plato himself and think, because of a certain similarity, that he is meeting Socrates again—subsequently drawing the sensation of Plato as if from Socrates and fitting it to the memory of Socrates—a false opinion results. And in this way, false opinion arises from the comparison of sensation to thought. 

<margin>
What is true and what is false opinion.
</margin>

It also happens in another way: by the comparison and exchange of one thought for another thought. For someone can, by thinking, exchange the species of certain numbers that lie hidden in the memory, even without a present sensation, so that he takes 12 for 11, or conversely 11 for 12. But a certain doubt arises. For whoever preserves the species <note>In this context, "species" refers to the mental "form" or "concept" of a thing.</note> knows those things of which he has the species. Therefore, he knows these numbers. But if he exchanges them, he is ignorant of them. Therefore, he both knows and is ignorant of the same thing at the same time. 

<margin>
Two types of false opinion.
</margin>

The answer must be: it is not absurd for one who knows in one way to be ignorant in another. For he knows by habit <note>original: "habitu" — meaning he possesses the knowledge as a latent skill or state.</note>, but is ignorant in the actual moment of performance. Therefore, with these obstacles removed, two types of false opinion have been found and explained just above. 

Another doubt arises. Because if someone, while possessing the distinct sciences <note>original: "scientias" — here meaning "branches of knowledge" or "certain understandings."</note> of certain things, should form a false opinion by exchanging them and taking one for the other, he seems to be ignorant of the very thing of which he has knowledge; and what is worse, he is ignorant through knowledge itself, not through ignorance—since knowledge itself would be the cause of the exchange, and the exchange the cause of the ignorance. If this is so, since knowledge makes us ignorant, nothing prevents ignorance from making us know. 

Theaetetus responds to this by saying that a form of "un-knowledge" <note>original: "inscitiae" — lack of knowledge or ignorance.</note> should be placed in the soul just like a form of knowledge; and that he who takes one for the other is deceived, and thus is ignorant through ignorance rather than through knowledge. This response is by no means sufficient: for in the same way as above, one will ask: if he exchanges these forms with each other, does he know both? Or is he ignorant of both? Or does he know one and remain ignorant of the other? From this, the previous controversy will return. Likewise, if a form must be posited by which knowledge knows, and one by which ignorance knows, then other forms must be posited by which *these* forms are known, and others again by which *those* are known; and so we shall proceed into infinity. 

Therefore, it is not so; a different answer must be given. For it should have been said, as Socrates touched upon above: that the notions of the right things are not the causes of the exchange, but rather a confusion of notions, long-term negligence, or an external similarity that has not been exactly examined. Therefore, we seem to be ignorant not through knowledge, but rather through confusion, negligence, and deception. However, these things cannot be absolutely judged until it has been declared what knowledge is. For we distinguish darkness by light, silence by a sound <note>original: "fontem" — literally "source" or "spring," here likely implying the source of sound.</note>, evil by good, and the false by the true. Therefore, before defining what knowledge is, it seems that false opinion must be explained if we desire to comprehend it perfectly. 

Hence, Theaetetus asserts that knowledge is "true opinion." Socrates refutes this by the fact that the faculty of oratory persuades but does not teach. He who persuades induces an opinion—and a true opinion when he reports true things—yet it is not knowledge. For concerning those things which are always in motion and are sometimes one way and sometimes another, there is never certain knowledge. Such are human affairs, which orators deal with, especially since they often induce their listeners to believe things about which they themselves are in doubt and at which they were never present. 

After this, Theaetetus adds the definition of Leucippus and Theodorus of Cyrene: "Knowledge is true opinion with an account" <note>original: "cum ratione" — with a rational explanation or definition.</note>. And therefore, those things which have an account can be known; those which lack an account cannot. And Prodicus of Chios, imitating Leucippus, asserted that the elements of things, because they are simple and therefore without an account, are unknown; but composite things, since they can have an account, are known. By "account" <note>original: "rationem"</note> they understand a definition and a certain speech declaring the substance and property of a thing. Because this includes several things—the subject, the predicate, and sometimes even the copula (that is, the verb) and nouns—it signifies something composite. But the element is simple, and therefore devoid of an account, and is left unknown. 

Socrates refutes these two statements. First, he refutes the latter one, which says: "Elements, because they are simple, are unknown; things made from them, because they are composite, are known." Then he refutes the former: "That knowledge is true opinion with an account." And for the sake of explanation, he takes letters for elements and a syllable for a composite. But what he teaches about these, he wants to be understood about all things. 

The first reason against them is this: just as composites depend on elements, so the cognition of composites is perfected by the cognition of elements. For they cannot be known without the cause that was their origin. Therefore, it is impossible to know composites if the elements are unknown. Likewise, take a certain composite: for example, "So," the first syllable of the name Socrates. Is this syllable both elements? Or is it a single form born from the elements coming together? If it is both, then whoever knows this syllable "So" knows both elements. And if asked what "So" is, he will answer "S" and "O." And if he is ignorant of "S" and "O," he will never know "So." For he who does not know each one, does not know both. It is therefore impossible to know composites if the elements are unknown. But perhaps someone will say that the syllable, and every such form, is not the elements, but exists as a single thing besides them. Socrates asks him this: whether this form, and the syl—

It uses the analogy of letters and syllables to argue that one cannot know a complex whole without first knowing its simple elements.</summary>

# ARGUMENT OF THE THEAETETUS. FOLIO 54.

<meta>Catchword: recollection</meta>

whether a syllable has parts or not. If it has, it is a certain "whole" and "all." But "whole" and "all" are nothing other than all the parts, as is evident in numbers. For a whole number is nothing other than all the units it contains; and thus this form <note>Latin: *species*, referring to the unified concept of the syllable</note> will consist of parts, and the parts will exist by the very fact that they belong to the whole. Therefore, just as the form is known, so too are the elements known. For if one knows the form, he knows the "whole" and the "all." If he knows the whole and the all, he knows that none of its parts are missing. Therefore, he knows that it has individual parts; thus, he knows each one. If he were ignorant of these, he could not know whether they were all present or not. It is impossible, therefore, to know the form if the elements are unknown. 

But if someone should say that the form itself is a single thing having no parts, because the elements of which it consists are not its "parts," it follows that it must be simple and indivisible. For which reason, just as the element was said to be unknown because it is simple, so the form itself would be said to be unknown because it is simple. Therefore, it can in no way happen that forms made from elements are known while the elements themselves are unknown. This is also clearly evident from the fact that in every individual art, the foundation for understanding that art is to comprehend the elements of the things with which the art deals. Otherwise, all labor is in vain. 

Finally, having refuted this, Socrates now begins to repel the main part of the proposition where it was said: **Knowledge is true opinion with an account** <note>Latin: *ratio*, often translated as "logos" or "reasoned explanation"</note>. For three things can be signified by the name of "account": either speech, or a discourse through the elements of a thing, or a definition. If the first, every opinion will be knowledge. For whether we opine truly or falsely, we are able to express what we feel in speech; therefore, even he who opines falsely will opine with an "account." If the second: whenever someone discourses through the elements, he would be said to "know." But that is false for this reason: because in discoursing, one can transpose the elements and pervert the order, referring the element of one thing to another, and applying the element of one to another. He who confuses these things cannot be said to "know." 

If he understands the third—that is, definition—and calls knowledge "true opinion with a definition," we argue against him thus: A definition is the interpretation of a difference. Therefore, whoever defines assigns a specific difference alongside the common features of the thing. But does he who opines truly of Socrates and Theaetetus perceive the differences of Socrates and Theaetetus in his opining, or not? If he does not perceive them, he does not even opine truly; for I would never truly distinguish one from the other unless I discerned the differences of each. Therefore, by the very fact that he opines truly, he is skilled in the differences. For which reason there is no need to add an "account"—that is, the notion of the difference—to true opinion. 

But perhaps someone might say that a certain sense and imagination of the difference is included in the opinion itself, rather than a certain understanding of the natural difference; and therefore, the "understanding of the difference" must be added to the definition of knowledge. Against this, Socrates argues thus: A definition is surely absurd by which the same thing is described by the same thing. When we say knowledge is true opinion with an account (that is, with the understanding of the difference), we define knowledge by knowledge. For the "understanding of a difference" is the "knowledge of a difference." Whence knowledge will be true opinion with the *knowledge* of the difference—which is a ridiculous thing to say. 

From all these points, the false definitions of the Sophists have now been refuted. The first, which said knowledge is the individual faculties that are learned; the second, that knowledge is sense-perception; the third, that knowledge is true opinion; the fourth, that knowledge is true <margin>Seven definitions of knowledge rendered by the sophists.</margin> opinion with the utterance of speech; the fifth, true opinion with a discourse through the elements; the sixth, true opinion with the imagination of the difference; the seventh, true opinion with the knowledge of the difference. 

These having finally been refuted, we must see what Plato teaches. Following the Pythagoreans Brontinus and Archytas in nearly the sixth book of the *Republic*, he posits two genera of things: namely, the **intelligible** and the **sensible**. The former is stable and incorporeal; the latter is mobile and corporeal. He calls the way to knowing the former "reason" <note>Latin: *ratio*</note>; the way to the latter "sense." The common notion of the former he calls "understanding" <note>Latin: *intelligentia*</note>; of the latter, "opinion." But he divides both genera in two. For he wants there to be a primary and secondary intelligible: in the first are contained the **Ideas** (that is, the forms and notions of the Divine Mind), and other minds and souls; in the second, numbers and figures. For although numbers and figures are incorporeal, yet because they admit of some division, they are not to be esteemed with the same dignity as indivisible substances. The cognition of the former he calls "intellect" <note>Latin: *intellectus*</note> by its proper name; the thought of the latter he calls "intellectual." 

He also divides the sensible by an equal division into primary and secondary. In the first, he places all corporeal bodies. In the second, shadows and images of bodies, whether they appear in water or in mirrors. And he considers these to stand in relation to bodies as mathematical things stand to divine things. The perception of bodies he properly names "belief" <note>Latin: *credulitas*</note>; of shadows, "imagination." Furthermore, he denies that there is knowledge concerning the shadows of bodies, or bodies, or mathematics; but he locates it in the intellect of divine things alone. This he also signified in this dialogue at the beginning, when he proposed that knowledge and wisdom are the same. For he testifies everywhere that wisdom is the contemplation of divine things. 

How the intellect itself (that is, knowledge) differs from opinion, he shows in the book *On Nature* <note>Referring to the *Timaeus*</note> with these words: "If intellect and true opinion are two things, it is necessary that the Ideas be comprehended by themselves through the intellect rather than the sense. But if, as it seems to some, true opinion differs not at all from intellect, all things which we perceive as corporeal must be held as certain. But I think two things must be said, because both are distant by a great difference: for doctrine <note>teaching</note> insinuates one into us, while the assumption of persuasion brings the other. One is always with true reason; the other is without any reason. One of them is not transferable by any reason; the other is nodding and uncertain. What then? Every man is a participant in right opinion; but intellect is the property of God, and of very few chosen men!" He testifies to almost the same things in the *Meno* and the *Philebus*. 

What then is knowledge? The comprehension of divine things by certain reason. This is in the intellect, first and always. In the reason, second, and not always. For since reason is the medium between intellect and opinion, as often as it is extended to lower things, it is filled with the errors of opinion and ceases to think on the divine. But when it is turned back to the Mind, its leader, it drinks in the cognition of divine things. This, Plato calls "wisdom" by its proper name in the Mind, and "recollection" <note>Latin: *reminiscentia*</note> in the reason. And therefore, concerning the "obstetric faculty" <note>The Socratic method of "midwifery"</note> through which we recollect, in this dialogue...

# PLATO’S THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE, TRANSLATED FROM GREEK INTO LATIN BY MARSILIO FICINO FOR PIERO DE' MEDICI, FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND.

### EUCLIDES. TERPSIO. SOCRATES. THEODORUS. THEAETETUS.

<margin>EUCL.</margin>
O Terpsio, did you come from the country just now, or some time ago? TER. Some time ago, and I looked for you in the forum; and I wondered that I was nowhere able to find you. EU. I was not in the city. TER. But where? EU. When I had gone down to the port, I came upon Theaetetus, who was being carried to Athens from the camp at Corinth. TER. Alive or dead? EU. Half-alive. For he has been afflicted by certain wounds; and what is worse, he has also been wasted by a long-lasting disease in the camp. TER. Not dysentery? EU. That very one. TER. Oh, what a man you describe placed in such danger. EU. A truly noble and excellent man, O Terpsio, for a little while ago I heard some people who were extolling him with wonderful praises regarding military matters. Nor should that seem a wonder; indeed, it would be far more a wonder if it were otherwise. TER. Why did he not turn aside to Megara? EU. He was hurrying home. For I both advised and entreated him, but he refused. Moreover, while accompanying him, as I was departing from him, I remembered Socrates, and wondered how divinely he prophesied on many other occasions, and especially about this man. For a few days before he departed from life, he met Theaetetus, who was still a young youth; and he both approved of and wondered at his natural talent. Then, when I went to Athens, he related to me each of the arguments of that discussion, which were most worthy of being heard, and added besides that he would altogether be an outstanding man if he grew up. And he seems to have predicted too truly. TER. Certainly. But what were the speeches? Can you relate them now? EU. Not by words, by Jove! But by letters. For having returned home, I immediately sketched them out in commentaries; then, by remembering better, I wrote them more extensively. And as often as I went to Athens, if anything had slipped my mind, I would question Socrates; and returning here, I would correct it. Thus it happened that almost that entire discussion has been written down. TER. You speak the truth. For I heard these things from you long ago; and desiring to know them, I have often come here seeking you. What then hinders us now from running through it? Truly, I have need of rest, for coming from the fields, I am exhausted. EU. I also accompanied Theaetetus as far as Erineum. For which reason I would very gladly rest. Let us go then. For while we are sitting, a boy shall read it through. TER. Very well. EU. This, O Terpsio, is the book: not composed as if Socrates were relating it to me, as he actually did relate it; but as if he were disputing in person with those with whom he told me he had disputed. He said these were the geometer Theodorus and Theaetetus. So that it would not be troublesome if "I said" and "he said" were too often interposed, I have introduced Socrates himself disputing with them, having avoided those phrases. TER. Skillfully done, Euclides. Hey you, take the book and read. SOC. If I cared for the Cyrenians above others, O Theodorus, I would especially inquire of you regarding what concerns them, if any youths there were ardently applying themselves to the study of geometry or some other philosophy. But now I love our own more than those; and I rather desire to understand which of our youths seem likely to turn out as honorable men. I always explore these things myself to the best of my strength, and I often inquire of others to whom I see the youths flocking. Not a few follow you, and rightly so. For you seem worthy of a crowd for the sake of other things, and especially geometry. If therefore you have found anyone worthy of mention, I would gladly hear it. THEO. Indeed, Socrates, it is fitting both for me to relate and for you to listen to what sort of youth I have found among your citizens. If he were handsome, I would fear to praise him, lest I might perhaps seem to someone to be captured by love for him. But now, do not be angry with me nor disturbed: for he is not beautiful. He is similar to you, with a snub nose and prominent eyes; although he exceeds the limit in these things less than you do. I speak freely with you. Know first that I have found no youth yet, although I have been involved with many, gifted with such a wonderful happiness of nature. It is very difficult to find a man who is at once talented and, above others, gentle and manly. Indeed, I do not think there ever was one; I see it is necessary that they are so constituted by nature. For others who are sharp and sagacious like this one, and have good memories and are teachable, are for the most part headlong into anger and impulse; they are burned and carried away like ships without anchors; and they turn out furious rather than brave. But those who are heavy, when they apply themselves to disciplines, are often sluggish, numb, and forgetful. But this one proceeds to disciplines and questions so gently, freely, sweetly, and readily, with the greatest mildness, that it seems like the smooth and sweet flow of a silent stream of oil; and it is a wonder that such a great genius carries out these things so maturely. SOC. You bring excellent news. But whose son among our citizens is he? THEO. I heard his name, but it has slipped from memory. But he is the middle one of those who were coming toward us a little while ago in the street that is outside the walls. He and some of his companions have been rubbing themselves with oil; now, the game being finished, he seems to be coming here. See whether you recognize him or not. SOC. I do recognize him. He is the son of Euphronius of Sunium: a man, O friend, undoubtedly such as you have described the son; most esteemed among all, who left a large patrimony. But

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE. FOLIO 55.

I have not heard the boy's name. THEODORUS: Theatetus is his name, O Socrates; however, his guardians seem to have squandered his inheritance. Nevertheless, he excels wonderfully in generosity. SOCRATES: You describe a noble man; bid him come here and sit with us. THEODORUS: Let it be so. O Theatetus, come here to Socrates. SOCRATES: Come, I pray you, Theatetus, so that I may observe myself: what sort of face I carry. For Theodorus says that I am like you in countenance. Now, if he brought a lyre with the strings of both of us tuned, would we immediately believe him? Or would we first inquire whether he were a musician? THEATETUS: We would inquire. SOCRATES: And if we found him to be such, we would certainly believe him; but if he were unskilled in music, not at all? THEATETUS: That is so. SOCRATES: Now, therefore, if the similarity of our faces is of concern to us, we must see whether he who says so is a painter or not. THEATETUS: So it seems. SOCRATES: Is Theodorus a painter? THEATETUS: I have not noticed. SOCRATES: But is he a geometer? THEATETUS: Most certainly, O Socrates. SOCRATES: And also an astronomer, a logician <note>original: "dialecticus"</note>, a musician, and skilled in the other disciplines? THEATETUS: So it seems to me. <margin>Faith is not to be placed in one who does not know what he praises or blames.</margin> SOCRATES: Therefore, when he declares us to be similar in some part of the body, praising or blaming it in a way, not much faith should be placed in him. THEATETUS: Not as it appears. SOCRATES: But if he should praise someone for the virtue and wisdom of the mind, would it not be fitting for the listener to consider the one praised, and for the praised one to show himself? THEATETUS: Entirely so, O Socrates. SOCRATES: See then, O friend Theatetus: it is in your interest to show yourself, and mine to consider you. Know that although Theodorus has praised many to me, both strangers and citizens, he has extolled no one with greater praise than you. THEATETUS: That would be well, O Socrates, but see that he did not say it in jest. SOCRATES: This is not the custom of Theodorus. But do not refuse what has been granted; you might suggest he acts in jest so as not to be forced to testify. It is not easy to refute his opinion; but persist boldly in what has been granted. THEATETUS: It must be done, if it seems so to you. SOCRATES: Tell me then. Do you learn some geometry from Theodorus? THEATETUS: I do. SOCRATES: And those things which pertain to astronomy, harmony, and logic—do you learn them? THEATETUS: I certainly strive to. SOCRATES: I also, O boy, learn from him and from others whom I think understand something of these things. And although I hold myself moderately in other matters regarding these, I have a certain small doubt which must be investigated with you and these others. Therefore, I pray you answer me: is not learning becoming wiser in that which one learns? THEATETUS: That very thing. SOCRATES: And are the wise <margin>Whether wisdom and knowledge are the same.</margin> wise by wisdom? THEATETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Does this differ in any way from knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note>? THEATETUS: In what way? SOCRATES: Namely, are they wise in the same things in which they are knowing? THEATETUS: What prevents it? SOCRATES: Is wisdom and knowledge therefore the same? THEATETUS: The same. SOCRATES: This is that which I doubt; I cannot conclude within myself what knowledge is. Have we anything to say to these things? What do you assert it to is? Which of us will show it first? Whoever errs shall sit as an "ass," as boys playing in a circle say; but he who proves true shall rule over us and command whatever he wishes to be answered. Why are you silent? For I do not intend, O Theodorus, to use any rudeness out of a love for words. <margin>It is the mark of a rustic not to laugh.</margin> For I desire to lead you into a discussion and for us to become mutual friends and interlocutors. THEODORUS: This would not be at all rude, O Socrates. Rather, bid one of these boys to answer you. For this manner of disputing is unusual to me, and my age prevents me from becoming accustomed to it now; but these things are more fitting for them, and they will profit far more. In truth, youth profits in all things. <margin>Youth profits in all things.</margin> And as you have begun, do not let Theatetus go, but question him. SOCRATES: You hear, O Theatetus, what Theodorus says; whom, I think, you will gladly obey. For it is not right for a youth to be less than obedient to a wise man in matters of this kind. Therefore, answer ingenuously: what do you think knowledge is? THEATETUS: I must obey, O Socrates, since you both command it. For if I err in anything, you will correct me. SOCRATES: We shall do so, without doubt, if we are able. <margin>The first definition of knowledge.</margin> THEATETUS: It seems to me that knowledge consists of those things which one can learn from Theodorus: geometry and the others you enumerated above; furthermore, the crafts of cobblers and other artisans—all and each of these are nothing other than types of knowledge. SOCRATES: Nobly and magnificently, O friend! When asked for one thing, you have given many and various things instead of one. THEATETUS: Why do you say that, O Socrates? SOCRATES: Perhaps I say nothing; yet I will reveal what I think. Whenever you say "the craft of cobbling," do you say anything other than the knowledge of making shoes? THEATETUS: Nothing else. SOCRATES: What then, when you say "carpentry," that is, the builder's art—is it anything other than the knowledge of wooden works? THEATETUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: In both, therefore, you declare that of which each is a knowledge. THEATETUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: But our question was not this: of what things are there knowledges, or how many are there. For we were not seeking to count them, but to know what knowledge itself is. Or do I say nothing? THEATETUS: On the contrary, you are right. SOCRATES: Consider this also: if someone asked us about one of these cheap and common things, such as clay—what it is—and we answered him: the clay of those who make pots, the clay of those who make ovens or lanterns, the clay of those who mold bricks; would we not appear ridiculous? THEATETUS: Perhaps. SOCRATES: First, we would be judging falsely, thinking that the questioner understands us whenever we answer "the clay of those who mold figures of boys" or other such things. Secondly, do you think anyone will know the name of a specific thing unless he recognizes what that thing is? THEATETUS: By no means. SOCRATES: Therefore, he will not know the knowledge of shoes who does not know what knowledge is at all. <margin>When the simple is unknown, the specific is unknown.</margin> THEATETUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: He will also be ignorant of cobbling, whoever is ignorant of knowledge, and any other art. THEATETUS: That is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, the answer is absurd if someone, when asked what knowledge is, responds with the name of some art. For he answers what the knowledge is *of*, when he was not asked about that. THEATETUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: Furthermore, when it is possible to answer simply and briefly, he wanders through an immense circuit. Just as in the question about clay: a light and simple answer can be brought forward—that clay is earth mixed with moisture. But whose clay it is should be omitted. THEATETUS: It easily seems so now, O Socrates. For you seem to seek what recently came to mind for me and for this Socrates here, who is similar to you in name, while we were disputing. SOCRATES: What was that, O Theatetus? THEATETUS: Theodorus here...

# BOOK THIRTEEN.

...wrote concerning the powers <note>original: "viribus," here referring to mathematical roots or magnitudes</note> of three-foot and five-foot lengths, which are not commensurable in length with a one-foot magnitude. And proceeding in the same way, selecting each one up to the magnitude of seventeen feet, he finally stopped there. It occurred to us, then, since these powers appeared to be infinite in multitude, to try to collect them into one category by which we might name them all. **SOCRATES:** Was such a thing discovered? **THEAETETUS:** It seems so to me; consider it yourself as well. **SOCRATES:** Speak. **THEAETETUS:** We divided all number into two parts. One which can be produced by multiplying equal by equal: which we compared to a square figure, calling it "square" and "equilateral." **SOCRATES:** Excellent. **THEAETETUS:** And that which is between those such as three and five, and every number which cannot be produced by equal times equal, but is produced either by a larger number taken fewer times or a smaller number taken more times, and always contains a larger and smaller side: we compared this to an oblong figure <note>literally "a figure with one side longer"</note> and called it an oblong number. **SOCRATES:** Splendid, what then? **THEAETETUS:** All lines which square an equilateral and plane number, we defined according to length; but those which square the oblong, we defined according to their powers: as being in no way commensurable with the former in length, but commensurable in the planes they are able to form. And concerning solids, there was another similar classification. **SOCRATES:** Best of all, boys! Therefore Theodorus shall by no means be found guilty of false testimony. **THEAETETUS:** Indeed, Socrates, regarding the question you ask about knowledge, I am not able to answer as I did concerning length and power, although you seem to me to be seeking something of that sort. Thus it happens that Theodorus appears a liar in turn. **SOCRATES:** What? If he had praised you for speed in running, saying he had seen no youth more ready for the race, and then in running you were beaten by an adult and a very swift man, would you think he had praised you any less truly? **THEAETETUS:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** But do you consider knowledge, as I was saying just now, a "light" discovery, or rather a heavy and supreme one? **THEAETETUS:** By highest Jove, I think it is something great. **SOCRATES:** Have confidence in your powers, and do not undervalue the testimony of Theodorus. Strive with all reason and zeal, as in other things, so also concerning knowledge itself, to assign a definition of what it is. **THEAETETUS:** For the sake of striving, Socrates, we shall do this. **SOCRATES:** Come then, be of good heart, for you have just explained it excellently. Try to imitate that answer concerning the powers: just as you grasped many of them in one species, so also embrace many knowledges in one definition. **THEAETETUS:** Know, Socrates, that I have often attempted to consider this when I heard your questions being circulated. But I cannot persuade myself that I am fit for this, or that I have enough [ability], nor have I heard another disputing as you prescribe; yet I do not desist from the inquiry. **SOCRATES:** You are in pain, my friend Theaetetus, as if you were just about to give birth; because of this you are not empty, but pregnant. **THEAETETUS:** I do not know, Socrates; I am expressing what I have suffered. **SOCRATES:** O ridiculous man! Have you not heard that I am the son of a midwife, the very noble, sharp, and grim Phanarete? **THEAETETUS:** I have indeed heard it. **SOCRATES:** And have you heard that I also practice the same art? **THEAETETUS:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Know that it is so; but do not accuse me before others. For it has remained hidden from all until now that I am endowed with this art; and as if I were ignorant, they do not proclaim this about me. But that I am "absurd" and lead men into ambiguity—have you heard this? **THEAETETUS:** Exactly that. **SOCRATES:** Do you wish me to assign the cause of this to you? **THEAETETUS:** Why should I not? **SOCRATES:**

<margin>The sides of this square are between three and five: and with them they are incommensurable in length. But the products are commensurable. For their product is equal to a square, as is evident.</margin>

For you know that none of them helps those in labor as long as she herself conceives and bears children; but only when she is already past childbearing. **THEAETETUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** They say Diana is the cause of this: who, since she is sterile, took up the protection of births. She forbade sterile women from becoming midwives, because human nature is too weak for the arts of those things which it has never experienced. But to those who are prohibited by old age from conceiving, she granted this, honoring her own likeness. **THEAETETUS:** That is likely. **SOCRATES:** Is it not also probable and necessary that those who are pregnant, and those who are not, are more sharply noticed by midwives than by others? **THEAETETUS:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Moreover, by medicines and incantations, midwives are able to rouse or soften the pains of labor, and to help those laboring with difficulty, and to bring forth the fetus; and if it should perhaps seem untimely, to dull the pain and push it back. **THEAETETUS:** You tell the truth. **SOCRATES:** Have you also heard this about them: that as matchmakers they are most fit in arranging marriages, since they know best which woman should be joined to which man for the procreation of noble offspring? **THEAETETUS:** I did not know that well. **SOCRATES:** You should know they glory in this no less than in the cutting of the umbilical cord itself. Do you think it is the duty of the same or a different art to cultivate and collect the fruits of the earth, and again to distinguish what plant or what seed should be cast into which soil? **THEAETETUS:** Of the same. **SOCRATES:** But in women, my friend, do you think this is one faculty and that another? **THEAETETUS:** It is certainly not likely. **SOCRATES:** Certainly not.
