# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE. FOLIO 56.

<margin>The obstetric art of Socrates.</margin>
If it were possible, the greatest and most noble task of a midwife would be to discern the true from the false. But what do you think? THEAETETUS: Exactly the same. SOCRATES: My art indeed possesses everything that pertains to the diligence of their midwifery. But it excels in this: that it assists men, not women, in labor, and it examines the births of souls, not of bodies. Most importantly, this power resides in my art: to be able to examine delicately whether the young man’s thought is bringing forth a mere phantom and falsehood, or something fruitful and true. Furthermore, the same thing happens to me as to the midwives: I am sterile and empty of wisdom. And as for what many have objected against me—that I question everyone but never answer myself, because I have nothing wise to offer as an answer—they object quite truly. This is surely the cause: God compels me to assist those in labor, but has forbidden me to procreate. Therefore, I am not at all wise, nor does any birth of my own mind exist as my offspring. However, those who associate with me appear at first to be ignorant; but later, through my company, those whom God himself favors improve in a wonderful way, as it seems to themselves and to others. Yet this is certain: they never learn anything from me; rather, they themselves, possessing many excellent things within them, find them. God and I are surely the cause of this midwifery, as can best be conjectured here. For many, being ignorant of this in the past and considering themselves the cause, despised me—perhaps persuaded by others—and departed from me sooner than was proper. Once they left, due to bad company, they suffered miscarriages of the ideas remaining within them. Moreover, those things which I had delivered through my midwifery from the depths of their souls, they lost entirely by nourishing them poorly, because they preferred falsehoods and phantoms over the truth. Finally, they appeared to have become ignorant both to themselves and to others, as they deserved. One of their number was Aristides, the son of Lysimachus, and many others. But when they return to me, needing my company again and desiring it wonderfully, my <term>daemon</term> <note>Socrates' "divine sign" or inner voice that warned him against certain actions.</note> forbids me to associate with some, while it permits it with others, who then improve greatly once more. Indeed, my companions suffer the same as women in labor. For they are tormented and filled with difficulty day and night, much more than those women. My art is able both to stir up and to soothe this sting. And this is how their affairs stand. Sometimes, O Theaetetus, noticing those who are not "pregnant" and do not need my help, I gladly join them in marriage to others; and, if I may speak with God's guidance, I predict quite sharply with whom they might best flourish. Many of these I have handed over to Prodicus, and many also to other sophists and divine men. I have recounted all these things at length, my best friend, for this reason: I suspected that you were heavy with some inner concept, as you yourself think. Therefore, commit yourself to me as to the son of a midwife, and one who is himself highly skilled in the obstetric faculty, and strive with all your might to answer what I inquire. And if, while I am examining what you have said, I should refute and cast it aside as appearing to be a phantom rather than the truth, I pray you do not be angry, just as women having their first birth feel toward their children. Many, O wonderful youth, have already been so affected toward me that they were ready to attack me with their teeth if I took away some nonsense from them; they did not think I did this out of benevolence, for it escaped them that no god is malevolent toward men. Nor do I do any such thing out of malevolence. It seems clearly forbidden to me to admit the false and to reject the true. Therefore, Theaetetus, try again from the beginning to explain what knowledge is, as far as you are able; but never say you are unable. For if God wills it and helps you, you will be capable. THEAETETUS: Since you command it so, Socrates, it would be shameful if one did not bring forth his opinion. It seems to me that what someone knows, he perceives by what he knows; and as it now appears, knowledge is nothing other than sensation. SOCRATES: You have answered nobly, my boy. For that is how one must express what he thinks. But let us consider this together: whether this "offspring" is solid or empty. You say that sensation is knowledge? THEAETETUS: I do. SOCRATES: You seem to have brought forth a definition of knowledge that is not to be despised, but it is the same one that Protagoras introduced, though in another way. For he says that man is the measure of all things: of those that exist, that they are; and of those that do not exist, that they are not. Have you ever read it? THEAETETUS: I have read it many times. SOCRATES: Does he not say it this way: as individual things appear to me, so they are to me; and as they appear to you, so they are to you—since we are both men? THEAETETUS: He certainly says that. SOCRATES: And yet it is probable that a wise man is by no means talking nonsense. Let us follow this up. Does it not often happen that when the same wind is blowing, one of us feels cold and the other does not? And one barely feels it, while the other feels it intensely? THEAETETUS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Shall we then say the wind itself is cold in itself, or not cold? Or shall we believe Protagoras, that it is cold to the one who feels cold, and not to the one who does not? THEAETETUS: So it seems. SOCRATES: Does it not appear so to both? THEAETETUS: It does. SOCRATES: But "to appear" is "to sense"? THEAETETUS: It is. SOCRATES: Therefore, appearance and sensation are the same in matters of heat and other such things. For as each person senses things, so they appear to be to each. THEAETETUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: Sensation, therefore, is always of a thing that exists, and it is true, since it is knowledge. THEAETETUS: That appears to be the case. SOCRATES: Was not Protagoras exceptionally wise by the power of the Graces? And did he not signal this to us, the crowd, in riddles, while explaining the truth to his disciples in secret? THEAETETUS: In what way do you mean that, Socrates? SOCRATES: I will tell you, and it is no small thing: that nothing is one certain thing in itself; nor can you rightly name a thing as "this" or "of such a kind" from itself. For if you call it great, it also appears small; and if heavy, it appears light. The same reasoning applies to the rest, as if nothing were one, or anything, or of any quality. But from motion, movement, and mutual mixture, all things are made which we say "exist," though we name them incorrectly. For nothing ever *is*, but is always *becoming*. And in this, all the wise men in order, except for Parmenides, have agreed: Protagoras, Heraclitus, Empedocles, and the greatest of the poets in both kinds of poetry: Epicharmus in comedy, and Homer in tragedy. For when Homer called the Ocean the father of the gods and Tethys their mother, he proclaimed that all things are born from flux and motion. Does he not seem to mean that? THEAETETUS:

<margin>Fire is created from motion and friction.</margin> To me indeed. **SOCRATES:** Who then would dare to fight against such a great army, and its leader Homer, without appearing ridiculous? **THEAETETUS:** It is a difficult thing, O Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Difficult without a doubt, Theaetetus, especially since these arguments can serve this discourse by showing that motion <note>original: "motu"</note> provides the appearance of being and becoming, while rest <note>original: "stare"</note> causes non-existence and destruction. For fire and heat, which beget and govern all other things, are themselves produced by motion and friction: and this is motion. Is this not the origin of fire? **THEAETETUS:** Certainly it is. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, the race of living animals is born from these same things. **THEAETETUS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** What about the condition of bodies? Is it not corrupted by ease and sluggishness, but preserved by exercise and motion? **THEAETETUS:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** And does not the condition of the soul acquire learning through discipline and meditation—which are motions—and thus preserve and perfect its knowledge? Whereas through ease, that is, negligence and sloth, it learns nothing at all, and if it has learned anything, it forgets it. **THEAETETUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, motion is a good thing for both the soul and the body, while rest is the opposite. **THEAETETUS:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Moreover, regarding those states called fair weather and calms, I assert this: that still waters putrefy and perish, while others are preserved; and to these I will add the testimony of the Colophonian <note>referring to Homer</note>, namely the "golden chain," by which Homer means nothing other than the Sun. For as long as the circuit of the sun continues, all things among both gods and men exist and are preserved. But if this were to stand still as if bound, all things would immediately be dissolved, and it would happen as they say: the world would be turned upside down. **THEAETETUS:** To me also, O Socrates, you seem to speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Receive also this regarding the eyes: first, that the color we call "white" is not something existing outside your eyes, nor in your eyes, nor should you attribute a fixed place to it. For then it would be in a fixed order and remain there, and would no longer be in a state of becoming. **THEAETETUS:** But how? **SOCRATES:** Let us follow the previous discourse, positing nothing as being one thing in itself; and thus black and white and every other color appear to us as generated by the application of the eyes to a corresponding motion. And that which we call by the name of color will be neither the thing applying itself nor the thing applied, but a certain intermediate effect peculiar to each. Or would you maintain that whatever color appears to you, the same appears to every other animal? **THEAETETUS:** No, by Jove! **SOCRATES:** What about another man and yourself? Does everything appear the same to both? Or rather, does it not even appear the same to yourself, because you are never exactly the same as yourself? **THEAETETUS:** I think the latter is more likely. **SOCRATES:** If that by which we measure, or that which we touch, were "large" or "white" or "hot" in itself, it would never become something else when encountering another thing, if it remained unchanged. For if the thing measured or perceived were any of these in itself, it would not become something else when another thing approached it, without undergoing change itself. For at present, my friend, we are easily forced to say certain wonderful and ridiculous things, as Protagoras himself and everyone else of his opinion would admit. **THEAETETUS:** In what way, and what kind of things do you mean? **SOCRATES:** Take a brief example and you will understand what I want. If you place six dice next to four, we say the first six are more than the four, exceeding them by half. Whence the proportion is named "one and a half." But if you place them next to twelve, they are fewer by half. This cannot be said otherwise. Or can you? **THEAETETUS:** In no way. **SOCRATES:** What then: if Protagoras or someone else asked you, "Theaetetus, can anything become larger or more in any other way than by being increased?" what would you answer? **THEAETETUS:** If I offer what I truly think, O Socrates, I would say it is impossible. But if I look back at our previous position, I might say it is possible, lest I contradict myself. **SOCRATES:** Well said, and divinely, by Juno, my friend! Therefore, if you answer that it is possible, that saying of Euripides will happen: our tongue will be unrefuted, but our mind will be refuted. **THEAETETUS:** Certainly so. **SOCRATES:** If you and I were eloquent and wise, after all the thoughts of the mind had been discussed, we would then, testing our eloquence and subtlety, compete with one another like Sophists with little traps, clashing words against words. But now, being unrefined, we wish first to contemplate these things in themselves, to see what our thoughts are, and whether they agree or disagree with one another. **THEAETETUS:** I would very much like that. **SOCRATES:** And I no less. But since we are so disposed, let us calmly, as people at leisure, examine again—not being angry with one another, but truly examining ourselves—what these appearances and "phantasms" <note>mental images or perceptions</note> within us are. Considering these first, we shall say, I think, that nothing ever becomes greater or smaller, either in bulk or number, as long as it remains equal to itself. Is it not so? **THEAETETUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Secondly, that to which nothing is added or subtracted, this never increases nor decreases, but always remains equal. **THEAETETUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Thirdly, we shall say: that which was not before, and is afterwards, cannot be unless it becomes and has been made. **THEAETETUS:** So it certainly seems. **SOCRATES:** These three concessions fight against each other in our minds when we speak of those dice, or when we admit that I, an old man, while remaining the same size, neither increased nor diminished in any part, am now larger than you, a youth, but later will be smaller—not because my bulk was taken away, but because yours increased. For I am later what I was not before, yet without having "become" so; for it is impossible to have been made without "becoming." Yet losing no bulk, I have never become smaller. And infinite other things of this kind happen if we admit these points. Tell me, O Theaetetus, for you seem to me not unskilled in these matters. **THEAETETUS:** By the gods, O Socrates, I wonder greatly what these things are; and sometimes, while looking at them, I am overwhelmed by darkness. **SOCRATES:** Theodorus, my friend, seems to have guessed your nature not badly. For this feeling of wonder <note>original: "admiratio"</note> is especially characteristic of a philosopher. For there is no other beginning of philosophy than this. And he who said that Iris <note>the messenger of the gods/the rainbow</note> was the daughter of Thaumas <note>whose name means "Wonder"</note> did not absurdly explain her origin. But do you perceive why these things are as they are according to the followers of Protagoras, or not? **THEAETETUS:** Not yet, it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** Will you be grateful to me then if I reveal to you the hidden truth of the understanding of this man, or rather, of these most excellent men? **THEAETETUS:** Why should I not? And a great gratitude indeed. **SOCRATES:** Look around now, and at the same time be carefully on guard, lest any profane person hear these things. For the profane are those who think nothing exists except what they can hold in their hands, but actions and generations...

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE. FOLIO 57.
h

<margin>The opinion of those who say nothing is invisible.</margin>
...and they do not at all accept the invisible universe as part of essence. THEAETETUS: You describe men who are exceedingly hard and stubborn, Socrates. SOCRATES: These, my boy, are quite estranged from the Muses. But there are others who are more refined, whose mysteries I am about to narrate to you. The principle follows from which the things we just spoke of flow. This is their principle: that the universe is motion, and besides motion, there is nothing. Of motion, however, there are two species, both infinite in multitude: one has the power of acting, the other of being acted upon <note>original: "in agendo, altera in patiendo" - referring to active and passive forces</note>. From the mutual meeting and collision of these, effects arise that are infinite in number but twin in species: namely, the sensible object and the sense, which is always produced and meets with the sensible. These are the names of the senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and the touch of cold and heat. These are followed by pleasures, pains, desires, and fears, and countless other affections, some without names, though many are named. Furthermore, the sensible genus is kindred to each of the senses. To all kinds of visions, all kinds of colors are kindred; to the ears, likewise, voices; and to the other senses, other kindred sensible things are similarly present. What then, Theaetetus, does this discourse have to do with what went before? Do you notice? THEAETETUS: Not very much, Socrates. SOCRATES: See whether a discourse of this kind leads to this conclusion. For it means that all these things, as we said, are in motion; and in these motions, there is speed or slowness, insofar as slowness is in the thing itself and moves toward what is near, and thus generates. But the things thus generated become swifter. For they are carried along, and their nature consists in the movement of that motion. Therefore, when the eye and something commensurate with it meet, they generate whiteness and its kindred sense, which would never have been born unless one of them had come toward the other. Then indeed, in the midst of the motion, vision from the eyes and whiteness from that which co-creates the color meet; the eye is filled with vision and sees, and it becomes not vision, but a seeing eye. That which co-creates the color is filled with whiteness and becomes not whiteness, but a white thing—whether it be wood or stone or whatever else happens to be colored with such a color. The same must be judged of other things, such as heat and hardness, and all others. We disputed earlier that none of these is any one thing by its own nature, but all things come to be in their mutual meeting and are of all kinds because of motion. For we cannot firmly understand, as they say, that either the agent or the patient <note>The "actor" and the "receiver" of an action</note> is any one thing by itself. For the agent is nothing before it meets the patient, nor the patient before it meets the agent. Then, by clinging to one another, the agent or patient flashes forth. From all this follows what we said from the beginning: that nothing is one according to itself, but is always becoming for someone; "being" itself must be excluded from everywhere, although we were often forced in our previous discussion by habit and ignorance to use that word "being." Nevertheless, as the discourse of the wise dictates, one should in no way predicate that something belongs to someone, or to me, or "this" or "that," or any other name that signifies existence; rather, according to nature, one should speak of things as they act, become, perish, and change. For if anyone makes a stand in speech that something "is," he will easily be refuted. It is necessary to speak this way both of individuals and of things collected together—in which collection they place "man," "stone," and every animal and species. Do these things seem pleasant to you, Theaetetus, and will you taste them as if they please you? THEAETETUS: I do not know, Socrates, and I am even uncertain about you, whether you relate these things as being in harmony with your own mind, or whether you are testing me. SOCRATES: You do not remember, my friend, that I know none of these things, nor do I claim any such things as my own; for I am sterile <note>Socrates famously compared himself to a midwife who is past childbearing age but helps others give birth to ideas</note>. But I move and exercise you in the manner of a midwife, and for this sake, I enchant you and offer you the delicacies of the wise to taste until I bring your opinion into the light. When it has finally been brought forth, then for the first time I will examine whether it be vain and sterile, or fruitful and solid. Boldly, therefore, and constantly, well and manfully, bring forth your opinion on these things I shall ask you. THEAETETUS: Ask then. SOCRATES: Tell me then if it pleases you that nothing "is," but that the good and the beautiful and all those things we enumerated a moment ago are always "becoming." THEAETETUS: While I hear you discussing it, they seem wonderfully probable and must be admitted. SOCRATES: Let us not omit what remains. For it remains to speak of dreams and diseases, and especially of madness, and of those who are said to hear or see in a distorted way, or to perceive otherwise obliquely. For you know that in all these cases, the discourse we related above is refuted without any controversy, since the senses in them are utterly deceived. And so far is it from being the case that all things are as they appear to someone, that on the contrary, none of the things that appear actually exist. THEAETETUS: You speak the truth, Socrates. SOCRATES: Where then, my boy, will he flee who affirmed that sense is knowledge, and that what appears to each person is for that person exactly as it seems? THEAETETUS: I am ashamed to speak further, Socrates. For I have nothing to bring forward. For what I had proposed, you have utterly subverted by frightening me. Indeed, I could never deny that those who are mad or dreaming think falsely, since some of them think they are gods, and others believe they are flying like birds. SOCRATES: Do you see what sort of ambiguity follows concerning true things and dreams? THEAETETUS: What sort? SOCRATES: That which I think you have often heard: whenever it is asked by what conjecture it can best be shown whether we are all sleeping and dreaming each thing we think, or whether we are awake and truly interacting with one another. THEAETETUS: Truly, Socrates, it is doubtful by what conjecture one might discern it. For all things seem to follow the same pattern in turn. For nothing prevents us from seeming to converse as if dreaming the very things we just discussed. And when in sleep we think we are relating dreams, these are wonderfully similar to those. SOCRATES: You see now how easily controversy arises, since it is doubted whether things seen are dreams or true things. Moreover, since an equal time is given to sleep as to waking, in both the soul contends to assert present opinions as true. Therefore, for a time we say these are true, and for an equal time those; and we affirm both similarly. THEAETETUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: The same reasoning applies to diseases and madness, except that the time is unequal. THEAETETUS: Quite right. SOCRATES: Is truth determined by the length or shortness of time? THEAETETUS: That would be quite ridiculous. SOCRATES: Can you show by any other argument which of these opinions are true? THEAETETUS: Not as it seems to me...

# BOOK THIRTEEN

<margin>
The opinion concerning those things which are perceived.
</margin>

Socrates: Listen then to me regarding what those who wish to maintain that appearances are always true might respond. For I think they would ask you this, O Theaetetus: if something is entirely "other" than something else, will it in any way have the same power as that other? Let us not assume that it is partly the same and partly other, but that it is completely different. THEAETETUS: It can have nothing the same, either in terms of power or anything else whatsoever, when it is entirely other. SOCRATES: Must we not also consider such a thing to be "dissimilar"? THEAETETUS: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: If, therefore, something becomes similar or dissimilar to itself or to another, we shall admit that insofar as it becomes similar, it becomes the "same," and insofar as it becomes dissimilar, it becomes "other." THEAETETUS: That follows necessarily. SOCRATES: Did we not grant above that there are many—indeed, innumerable—active and passive factors? THEAETETUS: We did. SOCRATES: And furthermore, that one thing mixed with another and then another will generate not the same results, but different ones? THEAETETUS: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Let us speak then of me and you and others according to the same logic: for instance, Socrates in good health and Socrates when ill. <note>Socrates uses himself as an example to show how the "perceiver" changes state just as much as the "perceived" object.</note> SOCRATES: Then, a certain result is produced by Socrates in such a state and a draft of wine: regarding the tongue, a sensation of bitterness; regarding the wine, a bitterness is created and set in motion—and this produces not "bitterness" itself, but something "bitter"; and for me, not "sensation" itself, but a "perceiving being." THEAETETUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And I shall never be anything else while perceiving thus, for a sensation of one thing belongs to one specific state, and it makes the perceiver different and of a different quality. Nor will you, in encountering something else, ever become the same by generating the same result. For by generating something else from something else, you will become different and altered. THEAETETUS: These things are true. SOCRATES: I shall not become such a thing for myself, nor will that object become such a thing for itself. THEAETETUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: It is necessary, however, that I become a perceiver of *something* when I become "perceiving." For it is impossible to be "perceiving" and yet perceive nothing; and that object must also necessarily become something to someone whenever it renders itself sweet or bitter or anything of this sort. For "sweet" cannot become sweet to no one. THEAETETUS: That is entirely the case. SOCRATES: It remains then, I think, that whether we "are" or "become," we are or become in relation to one another, since necessity itself binds our essence together. It binds it, I say, neither to any other thing nor to ourselves; it follows, therefore, that we are bound to each other. Therefore, whether someone says a thing "is" or "becomes," it must be understood as: it is or becomes *for* someone, or *of* someone, or *in relation to* something. But that anything should "be" or "become" itself in and of itself—this neither should one profess oneself, nor allow another to assert, as the preceding argument warns. THEAETETUS: That is perfectly so, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Since, then, that which acts upon me is for me and not for another, do I not also perceive it myself, and no one else? THEAETETUS: How could it be otherwise? SOCRATES: Therefore, my perception is true to me; for it always belongs to my own essence. And I, according to Protagoras, am the judge both of those things which are, that they are to me, and of those things which are not, that they are not. <note>original: "homo mensura" - the famous Protagorean doctrine that "Man is the measure of all things."</note> THEAETETUS: So it seems. SOCRATES: What then stands in the way of my being "knowing," just as I am "perceiving," since I am neither deceived nor do I stumble in thought concerning those things which either are or become? THEAETETUS: Nothing at all. SOCRATES: You were saying excellently, then, that knowledge is nothing other than perception. These ideas indeed converge into the same point: according to Homer and Heraclitus and all that tribe, that all things flow like a river; according to Protagoras, that most wise man, that man is the measure of all things; and finally, according to Theaetetus, given the premises above, that knowledge is perception. Shall we say then, O Theaetetus, that this opinion is, as it were, your newborn child, recently brought forth by you, but delivered into the light by my "midwifery"? <note>Socrates famously compared his method of questioning to midwifery (maieutics), helping others give birth to their own ideas.</note> What do you say? THEAETETUS: It must be so, O Socrates. SOCRATES: This child, such as it is, we have at last with difficulty brought forth. After the birth, however, as is the custom on the fifth day from its birth, we must perform the purification ceremony by carrying it in a circle, <note>original: "amphidromia" - a Greek ritual where a newborn was carried around the hearth.</note> taking care lest it deceive us—if perhaps it is not worthy of being reared, but is empty and false. Do you think your offspring must be nourished at all costs and not cast away? Or if you see your firstborn rejected, will you not take it hard to have it removed? THEODORUS: Theaetetus will bear it, Socrates. For he is not ill-tempered. But tell me, by the gods, is the matter not so? SOCRATES: You are fond of discussion and a good man, O Theodorus, for you think I am a sort of bag full of arguments, and that I can easily pull them out to say that these things are not so. But you do not notice what actually happens: that no argument ever flows from me, but always from the one who is disputing with me. I myself know nothing except one small thing: how to receive an argument from a wise man in a fitting manner. And now I shall try to speak from this man's ideas, not from my own. THEODORUS: You speak more rightly, Socrates. Therefore, please do so. SOCRATES: Do you know, Theodorus, what I admire most in the sayings of your friend Protagoras? THEODORUS: What is it? SOCRATES: The rest pleased me well enough, where he proved that what seems to each person exists for that person. However, I was amazed at the beginning of his discourse, which he writes in the introduction to his book *On Truth*. He did not say that a pig or a "monstrous dog" or any other marvelous thing among those that perceive is the "measure of all things." Had he done so, he would have begun to speak quite magnificently and with greater pride and contempt, showing that while we admire him as a god for his wisdom, he himself is no wiser than a tadpole, <note>original: "rana Gyrina" - a tadpole.</note> let alone any other man. Or shall we say otherwise, Theodorus? If that which each man opines through perception is true for him—and no one can judge another's experience better than he, nor can anyone discern another's opinion more aptly than the person himself to see if it be true or false—but as often...

<margin>
Socrates professes that he knows nothing.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus conclude that if knowledge is perception, then every individual is the sole judge of their own truth. Socrates then begins a satirical critique of Protagoras, questioning why a human should be the "measure of all things" rather than a pig or a tadpole if all perception is equally valid.</summary>

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE
## h ii
<meta>Catchword: con</meta>

Now we have discovered that each person forms their own opinions; and if these are all right and true, why, my friend, did Protagoras himself stand out as so wise that he was considered worthy to be a teacher of others for a very large fee? And why are we considered more ignorant—his disciples, as it were—when each person is the measure of their own wisdom? How Protagoras must be talking nonsense in these matters! My own pursuit of the <term>midwifery of the mind</term><note>original: "obstetriciae facultatis"; Socrates famously compared his method of questioning to midwifery, helping others give birth to their own ideas.</note> will be equally ridiculous! Indeed, the entire duty of debating would be empty. For those efforts of discussing and refuting one another's fantasies and opinions, if they are all correct, will be nothing other than manifest madness, if Protagoras's book is true and he is not joking in secret.

**THEODORUS.** Socrates, since I am a friend, as you were just saying, I would never allow Protagoras to be refuted by my concession, nor would I want to fight against you contrary to my own judgment. Come then, go over everything again with Theaetetus. Indeed, he has seemed to follow you quite aptly and diligently so far.

**SOCRATES.** If you had gone to Sparta, Theodorus, and saw others at the wrestling school exercising with naked bodies, would you not think it worthwhile to compare your own appearance with theirs, stripping your own limbs in public?

**THEODORUS.** Truly, what do you think! If they would permit me, just as I hope you will permit me now: that I should only watch, and not be dragged into the gymnasium, being a man of tough skin by now, while they might more willingly wrestle with someone younger and softer!

**SOCRATES.** Yet if that is pleasing to you, O Theodorus, it is not troublesome to me, as the <margin>Proverb: If it is pleasing to you, it is not troublesome to me.</margin> well-worn proverb goes. Let us therefore approach the wise Theaetetus again. Tell me, I pray, Theaetetus, first regarding what we just ran through: will you not also wonder if you suddenly appear no less wise than any other man or even the gods? Or do you think that Protagorean "measure" was introduced less for the gods than for men?

**THEAETETUS.** Not at all; and I wonder greatly at what you ask. For while we were explaining above how whatever seems to each person is true for that person, it seemed to be said quite skillfully; but now, a contrary opinion immediately comes to mind.

**SOCRATES.** You are still young, my friend, even a boy; and therefore you are easily persuaded by a public speech. For to these things Protagoras, or any other follower of his, will say: "O noble boys and men, gather for the assembly; bring the gods into the midst, about whom I have decided neither to speak nor write as to whether they exist or not; and say these things which many listeners would admit: how grave it would be if any man did not far surpass any brute animal in wisdom." But bring no demonstration or necessity; use only a reasoning of probability. If Theodorus or any other geometer wished to use such reasoning in geometric disputes, he would be valued at nothing at all. Consider therefore, both you and Theodorus, whether you accept such great matters confirmed by probable reasoning.

**THEAETETUS.** You would be speaking unjustly, Socrates, and so would we; but now we must consider it in another way, as you and Theodorus agree.

**THEODORUS.** In another way, certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Let us both think on this: whether knowledge and sense-perception are the same, or something different. For the whole previous discourse tended toward this, and for its sake we touched upon many and wonderful things.

**THEAETETUS.** That is entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Shall we confess that whatever we perceive by seeing or hearing, we also know? For example, shall we say that we do not hear the voice of foreigners before we have learned it when they speak? Or do we hear and know it at the same time? And if we are entirely ignorant of letters when we look at their arrangement, shall we deny that we see them? Or shall we assert that we also know them if only we have seen them?

**THEAETETUS.** That very thing which we perceive and hear in these cases, Socrates, we will further affirm that we know: of the former, we inspect and likewise know their shape and color; of the latter, we hear and likewise know the high and low pitch of the voice. But what grammarians and interpreters teach about these things, we neither perceive by seeing and hearing, nor do we know them.

**SOCRATES.** Excellent, O Theaetetus; I should not argue with you on these points so that you may progress more. But look at another thing that is added to these: how it might be repelled and avoided.

**THEAETETUS.** What is that?

**SOCRATES.** This indeed: if someone should ask whether it is possible that what someone once knew and still holds in memory and preserves fixed, they nevertheless do not know that very thing. I am drawing this out into a long speech, desiring to ask whether someone who retains in memory what they learned might not know it.

**THEAETETUS.** How could this happen, Socrates? What you say would be a monster!

**SOCRATES.** Take heed, I pray, lest I myself am also raving. Do you not say that seeing is perceiving, and vision is sense-perception?

**THEAETETUS.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** Does not he who sees something know that which he sees, as the present discourse proposes?

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Do you call memory something?

**THEAETETUS.** I do indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Is it of something, or of nothing?

**THEAETETUS.** Of something, certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Is it not of those things which one has learned and perceived?

**THEAETETUS.** Of those, surely.

**SOCRATES.** What a person has seen, they sometimes remember?

**THEAETETUS.** They remember.

**SOCRATES.** Do they also remember when they close their eyes? Or when they do something of this sort, do they first forget?

**THEAETETUS.** That would be an absurd thing to say, Socrates. Yet anyone who wants to preserve the previous argument is forced to admit it; otherwise, not at all.

**SOCRATES.** By Jove, I also suspect so; but I do not yet sufficiently understand.

**THEAETETUS.** Tell me how.

**SOCRATES.** This indeed: he who sees knows that which he sees, as we have confessed; for we agreed that vision, sense-perception, and knowledge are the same.

**THEAETETUS.** We agreed.

**SOCRATES.** But he who saw, and therefore knows, remembers what he saw even with closed eyes, and does not then see anything.

**THEAETETUS.** So it happens.

**SOCRATES.** But not to see is not to know, if indeed to see was to know.

**THEAETETUS.** True.

**SOCRATES.** It happens, therefore, that what someone once knew, they do not know even while they remember it, if they do not see it. Which, if it happened, we predicted would be a kind of monster.

**THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES.** It seems, therefore, that something impossible happens if one posits that knowledge and sense-perception are the same.

**THEAETETUS.** So it appears.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must confess they are different.

**THEAETETUS.** It seems so.

**SOCRATES.** Wherefore we must seek again from the beginning what knowledge is. But what are we doing, Theaetetus?

**THEAETETUS.** About what do you ask?

**SOCRATES.** We seem to me like a lazy rooster, crowing and backing away from the dispute before we have conquered.

**THEAETETUS.** How so?

**SOCRATES.** We seem to have reached an agreement based on the contradictions of terms; and having dealt with such a thing, we search for words and stop at them. And although we profess to be philosophers and not mere competitors, we are doing the same thing as those sharp men do in secret.

**THEAETETUS.** I do not yet understand what you mean.

**SOCRATES.** I will try to explain what I feel in these matters...

<summary>Socrates challenges the Protagorean idea that knowledge is merely sense-perception by demonstrating a logical contradiction: if seeing is knowing, then a person who remembers something with their eyes closed would simultaneously know it (via memory) and not know it (via lack of sight).</summary>

# BOOK THIRTEEN

<note>original: LIBER TERTIVSDECIMVS. Note that in this edition, the dialogue is divided into "books" rather than the modern Stephanus pagination.</note>

...we asked whether it is possible for someone who has learned and remembers something not to know it. By showing that one who has seen something can remember it even with eyes closed, yet does not see it, we demonstrated that he would simultaneously be "not knowing" and "remembering"—which is utterly impossible. And so the Protagorean fable has completely vanished, and yours along with it, which sang that sensation and knowledge were the same thing. THEAETETUS: That is certain. SOCRATES: Not at all so, I think, my friend, if the father of that other fable were still alive; he would defend it most vigorously. But now we are pursuing an orphan and stripping it bare. Even the guardians whom Protagoras left behind—one of whom is Theodorus here—refuse to come to its aid. However, for the sake of justice, we shall attempt to support it ourselves. THEODORUS: It is not I, Socrates, but rather Callias son of Hipponicus who is the guardian of Protagoras's affairs. We have indeed suddenly turned away from mere words toward geometry. Nevertheless, we shall be grateful to you if you bring him aid. SOCRATES: You speak skillfully, Theodorus. Pay attention, then, to the way in which I shall help. If one does not pay attention to the force of words—by which we are usually accustomed to affirm or deny anything—he will be forced to admit even more absurd things than before. Shall I tell you how? To you, or to Theaetetus? THEODORUS: To both in common. But let the younger one answer, for if he is refuted, he will be less blamed. SOCRATES: I speak of a difficult question of this sort: is it possible that he who knows something, should be ignorant of that which he knows? THEODORUS: What shall we answer, Theaetetus? THEAETETUS: I think it is impossible. SOCRATES: Not at all, if you were to posit that seeing is knowing. 

<margin>The proverb: "trapped in a well."</margin>

For what will you do with an inescapable question, being "trapped in a well" as they say, if an intrepid man asks you, covering one of your eyes with his hand, whether you see your garment with the covered eye? THEAETETUS: I would say not with that one, but with the other. SOCRATES: Do you not then simultaneously see and not see the same thing? THEAETETUS: In a certain way, yes. SOCRATES: He will not say "I ask or command 'in what way,'" but rather "whether that which you know is the same as that which you do not know." In the present case, you seem to see what you do not see; and you have previously confessed that seeing is knowing, and not seeing is not knowing. Consider what he might conclude against you from these points. THEAETETUS: Plainly the opposite of what I had proposed. SOCRATES: Perhaps many more such things would have happened to you, O wonderful boy, if someone had asked you whether it is possible to know sharply or dully, to know from close up but not at all from a distance, or to know the same thing intensely and weakly, and many other such things. A "shield-bearing" man <note>A metaphor for a professional debater or mercenary of logic.</note> hired for pay, seeking these things in speech, would have ambushed you when you equated knowledge and sensation; he would have attacked your hearing, smell, and other senses in order, and with too much zeal and diligence would have refuted you. Catching you, he would not have let you go until you, having admired his exquisite wisdom, were bound by him. Once captured and bound, you would have redeemed yourself for as much money as you and he had agreed upon. What reason, then, will Protagoras assign for defending his opinions? Perhaps you would ask this. Must we try something else? THEAETETUS: Most certainly. SOCRATES: All these things which we say in bringing him aid, he himself, I think, would also admit, while looking down on us utterly and objecting: "This good Socrates, when he had asked a boy whether anyone can simultaneously remember and be ignorant of the same thing, and the boy in terror denied it, showed me to be ridiculous in dispute because the boy could not see through the matter. But the reality, O most cowardly Socrates, is this: whenever you consider any of my views through questioning, if the person questioned answers the same things I would answer and is refuted, then consider me refuted as well. But if he answers differently, then only he who answered is refuted. To begin with, do you think anyone will grant you that memory is present to someone when he no longer experiences those things he once experienced? And that the experience itself is the same as it was when it was occurring? Far from it. Or do you think he will fear to admit that it is possible for someone to know and not know the same thing at once? Or if he lacks the courage for that, do you hope he will grant that a person who has become dissimilar is the same as he was before he became dissimilar? Or rather that this person is 'someone,' but not 'these,' and that these become infinite in number if dissimilarity occurs—provided we must avoid mutual word-hunting? But, O blessed man, attack what I say more generously: refute me if you can by showing that sensation does not become private to each of us; or even if it is private, that what appears does not 'become' for that person alone to whom it appears. 

<margin>For Protagoras.</margin>

When you tell stories of pigs and monstrous dogs, you not only imitate a beast yourself, but you also persuade others to do the same to my writings. You do not act rightly. For I assert that the truth is as I have written: that each of us is the measure of those things which are and those which are not. But one man differs greatly from another in this very respect: that some things are and appear one way to one man, and another way to another. I by no means deny that wisdom and the wise man exist. On the contrary, I call that man wise who, by changing the condition of the person to whom things seem and are 'bad,' makes things appear and be 'good' for him. Do not pursue my speech merely in words, but learn more clearly what I mean: recall to memory what was said above—that to a sick man the things he tastes appear bitter, and they are so; to a healthy man they are the opposite, and they appear so. One must not assert that either of these is wiser because of this—for that cannot be—nor should it be proclaimed that the sick man is ignorant because he thinks these things, or the healthy man wise because he thinks differently. Rather, one must be changed into the other state, for the other state is better. Similarly, in education, one must be changed from one state to a better one. But the physician transforms by medicines, the <term>sophist</term> <note>A professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy in Ancient Greece.</note> by speeches. For no one makes a person who thinks falsely think truly afterward—since no one can think things that are not, nor anything other than what he experiences, and these are always true. However, one can make a person who, through a depraved state of soul, thinks things related to that state, then think different things with a healthy mind. These latter things most people, out of ignorance, call 'true appearances.' I, however, call some things better than others, but by no means truer. Furthermore, my friend Socrates, I do not call the wise 'frogs'; rather, I call them physicians in respect to bodies, and farmers in respect to plants. I say that these men, whenever a plant is 'sick' with depraved sensations, instill good, healthy, and true sensations into them; likewise, wise and good orators make good things seem just to cities instead of bad things. For whatever things seem just and honorable to any city, these are indeed just for it..."

<summary>Socrates presents a defense of Protagoras's "Man is the Measure" doctrine, arguing that while all perceptions are equally true to the perceiver, a "wise man" (like a doctor or sophist) can shift a person's state so that "better" things appear to them.</summary>

# THEAETETUS OR ON KNOWLEDGE.

...such things as long as he thinks them so; but the wise man, in place of each of these bad things, causes good things both to be judged and to be real. By the same reasoning, the sophist who is able to educate those who are learning in this way is wise, and is considered worthy of a large reward by his listeners. And so some are wiser than others; yet no one thinks falsely; and you, whether you wish it or not, must admit this very thing, since you are the "measure of things." For this argument is preserved in these points. If you can oppose it again from the beginning in any way, do so, bringing it back to a contrary reasoning. Or if you wish to do it by questioning, proceed by questioning. For this is not to be avoided, but most of all to be followed by those who are of sound mind. Yet do it in this way: do not be unjust in your questioning. It is surely absurd for a man who professes to meditate especially on virtue to be constantly unjust in his speech. Now, to act unjustly in these matters is when someone does not distinguish between competing in a contest <note>original: "certans," referring to eristic or debating for victory</note> and engaging in a discussion; in the former contest, of course, one plays and deceives as much as possible; but in the latter discussion, one acts seriously and corrects the person debating, pointing out to him only those fallacies which he himself has stumbled upon from his own past discussions. If you do this, those who associate with you will blame themselves, not you, for their own confusion and lack of progress; they will follow and love you immediately, but they will hate themselves and flee from themselves toward philosophy, so that, having become different people, they may lay aside their former habits. But if you do the opposite, as many others do, the opposite will happen to you: instead of philosophers, you will make your associates enemies of this study when they grow older. 

If, therefore, you follow my advice—as was also said above—you will consider, not with a hostile or contentious spirit but sitting with us with a favorable mind, how we say all things are in motion, and what seems to each person to be, both privately and publicly. From these things you will inquire whether knowledge and perception are the same or different. And do not argue from the common use of words and names, as many do, dragging them wherever they please and casting various small doubts <note>original: "scrupulos," literally small sharp stones that hinder a traveler</note>. These things, O Theodorus, I have attempted in defense of your friend to the best of my ability—small things from a small man. For if he were alive himself, he would fight more strongly and magnificently for his own cause.

**THEODORUS.** You are joking, O Socrates, for you have fought bravely for him.

**SOCRATES.** You speak rightly, my friend. But tell me: did you notice just now when Protagoras rebuked us, saying that by debating with a boy we were fighting against his writings out of a boyish fear? And when he exhorted us to a refinement of speech, did he not then command that honesty especially, and the "measure" itself of all things, be treated seriously in his words?

**THEODORUS.** How could I not have noticed, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** What then? Do you bid us obey him?

**THEODORUS.** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Do you see that all these except you are boys? Therefore, if we believe him, it is necessary for me and you together to examine his argument seriously by questioning and answering in turn, so that he does not accuse us again of mocking his words by playing with boys.

**THEODORUS.** What prevents Theaetetus from following you in your investigation better than many bearded men?

**SOCRATES.** Yet not better than you, O Theodorus. Do not think it right that I should bring every aid to your deceased friend while you bring none. But follow me, I pray, for a little while, until we find at least this: whether it is fitting for you to be the "measure" in geometric figures, or whether all are equally as skilled as you in astronomy and the other arts in which you are rightly seen to excel.

**THEODORUS.** It is difficult, O Socrates, for one sitting near you not to answer when asked. I was surely raving a little while ago when I said you would allow me not to gird myself for the fight, and that you would not compel me in the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> fashion. But now you seem to lean more toward Sciron <note>A mythical bandit who forced travelers to wash his feet before kicking them off a cliff</note>. For the Lacedaemonians bid one to strip or depart. But you seem to imitate Antaeus <note>A giant who forced travelers to wrestle him to the death</note>. For you do not let go of one who encounters you until you have forced him to strip and wrestle with you.

**SOCRATES.** You have found a fitting comparison for my disease, Theodorus. Yet I am more robust than they. Countless Heracleses and Theseuses, strong in speaking, have already encountered me; yet I do not desist any the more, so much has a vehement love of this exercise invaded me. Therefore, do not grudge me this, so that by exercising with me, you may help both yourself and me.

**THEODORUS.** I resist no longer; lead where you please. This whole "fated necessity" which you bring into these matters must be endured by the one bound to it. Yet I will not commit myself to you beyond what you have proposed.

**SOCRATES.** That will be enough. But watch this for me: that we do not secretly slip into a boyish way of speaking, and for that reason someone mocks us again.

**THEODORUS.** I shall certainly try with all my might.

**SOCRATES.** Let us first take up again what we touched upon above: whether or not we rightly disapproved of his argument when he proposed that each person is sufficient to himself for wisdom. Furthermore, Protagoras conceded to us that many differ among themselves in being better or worse—those whom he would call wise. Did he not?

**THEODORUS.** He conceded it.

**SOCRATES.** For if he were present and had conceded it himself, rather than us admitting it in his favor, it would not be necessary to confirm the same things by repeating them. But now perhaps someone might think we are not sufficiently qualified supporters of his affairs. Therefore, it is better to concede clearly how the matter stands. For it makes no small difference whether it is this way or otherwise.

**THEODORUS.** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, let us take the confession as briefly as possible, not from others, but from his own argument.

**THEODORUS.** How?

**SOCRATES.** Thus: He said that what seems to each person, is to that person to whom it seems.

**THEODORUS.** He certainly said that.

**SOCRATES.** Do we not also, O Protagoras, speak of the opinions of a man—indeed of all men—and do we not assert that there is no one who does not think himself wiser than others in some things, and others wiser than himself in other things? In the greatest dangers, whenever they are in camps, or in sickness, or tossed on the sea, do they not look to the leaders in each case as gods, as their saviors, because they excel others in nothing but knowledge? And in all human affairs, do they not seek teachers and leaders for themselves and other living things and works—those who commonly estimate themselves sufficient both to teach and to command? In all these things, what else shall we say but that men think there is both wisdom and ignorance among themselves?

**THEODORUS.** Nothing else.

**SOCRATES.** Do they not consider wisdom to be true thought, and ignorance to be false opinion?

**THEODORUS.** Of course!

**SOCRATES.** Where then, O Protagoras, shall we turn the argument? Shall we say that men always have true opinions? Or sometimes true, and sometimes false? From both it follows that they do not always have true opinions, but both kinds. Pay attention, Theodorus, whether anyone from Protagoras's [school]...

followers: or perhaps you wish to fight about this very point: that there is no one who does not think someone else holds false opinions and is ignorant. THEODORUS. That is incredible, Socrates. SOCRATES. And yet the argument falls into this necessity: that it proclaims man the measure of all things. THEODORUS. In what way? SOCRATES. Whenever you judge something within yourself and then declare your opinion to me, let it be true for you according to that argument; but are we not able to become judges of your judgment? Or do we always judge that you hold true opinions? On the contrary, do not countless men fight with you every day, holding opposite opinions to yours and thinking that you judge and believe falsely? THEODORUS. By Jove, Socrates, there are very many indeed, as **Homer** says, who provide me with trouble among men. SOCRATES. What then? Shall we say that you then hold true opinions for yourself, but false ones for the many? THEODORUS. It seems to follow necessarily from what has been said. SOCRATES. What about Protagoras himself? Is it not necessary that if he himself did not think man was the measure, nor did the many (as indeed they do not), then this "Truth" which he wrote would be true for no one? But if he himself thought so, but the multitude does not agree, know first that by as much as those to whom it does not seem true outnumber those to whom it does, by so much more it *is not* than it *is*. THEODORUS. It must be so, if indeed according to individual opinions it both will be and will not be. SOCRATES. Then it has this most excellent point: He, concerning his own opinion, grants in a certain way that the sentiment of those who disagree—by which they believe he is lying—is true, since he admits that everyone opines the truth. THEODORUS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. Does he not admit his own opinion is false, if he grants that the judgment of those who think he opines falsely is true? THEODORUS. Necessarily. SOCRATES. But the others do not at all concede that they themselves are lying. THEODORUS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. But he, in turn, admits this opinion also to be true based on what he wrote. THEODORUS. It is clear. SOCRATES. Therefore, from all that has come from Protagoras, it will be disputed what he would most concede. When he grants to someone contradicting him that they opine the truth, then indeed Protagoras himself will confess that neither a dog nor any random man is the measure, either of all things or even of a single thing which he has not learned. Is it not so? THEODORUS. It is certainly so. SOCRATES. Since, therefore, it is doubted by all, Protagoras's "Truth" will be true to no one—not to others, nor even to himself. THEODORUS. We are trampling my friend <note>Referring to Protagoras, who was a friend of Theodorus</note> quite heavily, Socrates. SOCRATES. Is it unknown to you, friend, whether we have trampled him rightly? It is likely that he, being older, was also wiser than us. If he suddenly rose up and attacked us, he would likely refute me for talking nonsense in many respects, and you for agreeing, and then he would immediately vanish. Nevertheless, we must use ourselves as we are, such as we are, and always express the things that seem true to us. And now shall we say that anyone would concede this very thing: namely, that one person is wiser or more ignorant than another? THEODORUS. It seems so to me. SOCRATES. Shall we say the argument stands most firmly in this, which we wrote down while favoring Protagoras: that many things are indeed such as they seem to each person—hot, dry, sweet, and others of this kind? But if he will confess that in certain things one person differs from another, such as regarding things healthy or harmful, he will surely assert that not every little woman, child, or beast is sufficient to cure itself through knowledge of health. Rather, in this especially, if in anything, they differ. THEODORUS. The same seems true to me. SOCRATES. Furthermore, in matters of the state—honorable and shameful, just and unjust, holy and unholy—whatever each city thinks and establishes as law for itself, will those things truly be so for each? And in these matters, is no private citizen wiser than another, nor city than city? But truly, in that which they establish as useful or useless to the republic, if in anything, I say they will confess that they differ here especially: one counselor from another, and one republic from another, in finding the truth. Nor will he ever dare to admit this: that whatever a city institutes thinking it beneficial to itself, those things will always be advantageous to it. But I say to you, regarding the just and unjust, holy and profane, they wish to affirm that none of these things has any substance by its own nature; but by common opinion it then becomes true when it seems so, and for as long as it seems so. And whoever does not entirely embrace the argument of Protagoras, they introduce wisdom in some such way. But for us, O Theodorus, a larger argument looms out of a narrower one. THEODORUS. Are we not at leisure, Socrates? SOCRATES. We seem to be. THEODORUS. For what reason do you say this? SOCRATES. Those who have been rolled about in the courts and the forum from their youth seem, compared to those who have been brought up in philosophy and such studies, as slaves compared to free men. THEODORUS. In what way? SOCRATES. From the fact that for the latter, as you were saying, leisure is always present;

<meta>This page continues the famous "digression" in Plato's Theaetetus, where Socrates contrasts the worldly lawyer or politician with the true philosopher. The previous page likely established the setting of the court and the constraints of time (the water-clock) on legal speech.</meta>

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE. FOL. 60.

...let us return to the point; for you were saying quite rightly that in the choir of philosophers we are not the servants of our speeches, but rather our speeches are our servants, and each of them waits to be finished by us whenever it seems good to us. For neither a judge nor a spectator—as is the case with the poets—presides over us as a censor or master.

**SOCRATES:** Let us speak then, since it pleases you, about those who are the leaders in this field. For why should we speak of those who misuse the study of philosophy? These men, from their youth onwards, first of all do not even know the way to the marketplace <note>The *forum* or *agora*, the center of public and legal life.</note>; they know nothing of the courtroom, the council-chamber, or any other public assembly of the city. As for the laws and decrees, whether spoken or written, they neither see nor hear them. They do not even dream of the political clubs, the gatherings for office-seekers, the banquets, or the rowdy parties. Furthermore, whether someone in the city is of good or bad birth, or if some evil has been inherited from one's ancestors—whether male or female—it escapes the philosopher's notice more than (as the saying goes) the grains of sand in the sea. <margin>The proverb: "The number of the sands of the sea escapes me."</margin> And he does not even know that he does not know these things. For he does not abstain from them for the sake of common glory; rather, in reality, only his body dwells and moves in the city, while his mind, considering all these things of little or no value, flies everywhere—as Pindar says—measuring what is beneath the earth and on the plains, and transcending the heavens through astronomy, scrutinizing the entire nature of all things that pertain to the universe, but never applying itself to the things that are close at hand.

**THEODORUS:** In what sense do you say this, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** Just as it is told of Thales <note>Thales of Miletus, often called the first Greek philosopher.</note>, who, while looking up at the heavens and intent upon the stars, fell into a pit. A certain clever Thracian maidservant is said to have mocked him, saying that he strove to see what was in the heavens but did not see what was right before him and at his feet. <margin>Thales fell into a pit while looking at the sky.</margin> The same reproach can be cast upon all who occupy themselves with philosophy. For it escapes the philosopher's notice not only what his neighbor is doing, but almost whether he is a human being or some other creature. But as to what a human being is, and what action or passion is proper to such a nature, he searches this out with great effort. Do you understand, Theodorus, or not?

**THEODORUS:** I certainly understand, and I approve of what you say.

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, my friend, as we said before, whenever such a man is forced to discuss things at his feet or before his eyes—whether privately with someone or publicly in a court of law or elsewhere—he provokes laughter, not only from Thracian girls but from the rest of the crowd. Because of his inexperience in these matters, he falls into pits and many ambiguities. There, a certain absurd clumsiness brands him with the mark of ignorance. For when someone must be insulted, he has nothing to bring up as a reproach, being ignorant of people's private evils; since he never noticed the specific flaws of individuals, he appears ridiculous as if he were witless. Also, in the praising and extolling of men, since he does not pretend or hide anything but laughs openly, he seems to be a fool. For when he hears a tyrant or a king being praised, he thinks he is hearing some swineherd, shepherd, or cowherd being extolled for getting a lot of milk; <margin>That tyrants are like shepherds.</margin> however, he considers that kings and tyrants tend and "milk" a more difficult and treacherous animal. He thinks such a man must become rustic and unrefined due to his occupation, no less than a shepherd—enclosed by the city walls just as a shepherd is by a mountain fold. Furthermore, when he hears of someone possessing ten thousand acres of land or more as if it were something great, he thinks he is hearing of a very small thing, as he is accustomed to looking at the whole world. <margin>Hence the saying: "There is no king who does not come from the lowly, nor any lowly man who does not trace his origin to a king."</margin> Whenever someone recounts their noble lineage, being able to list seven wealthy ancestors, he considers such praise to be the mark of a dull mind that thinks of nothing great due to ignorance; it is as if they cannot look at the nature of the whole world and see that every one of us has had countless ancestors and forefathers, among whom have been thousands of rich and poor, kings and slaves, barbarians and Greeks. Even when someone counts twenty-five ancestors and traces their origin back to Hercules, son of Amphitryon, the philosopher laughs at him for being unable to calculate further back—to see that the twenty-fifth ancestor of Hercules was simply whatever person chance made him—and for being unable to shake off the vanity of a foolish mind. In all these things, the philosopher is laughed at by the common people; partly because he appears proud and disdainful, and partly because he is ignorant and hesitant regarding what is right in front of him.

**THEODORUS:** You have described the situation exactly as it happens, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** But, my friend, when the philosopher draws someone upward, and that person is willing to leave behind the discussion of "how I have wronged you or you me" and ascends to the contemplation of justice and injustice themselves—what each is and how they differ from all other things—or leaves behind the question of whether a king is happy because he possesses much gold to contemplate kingship itself and human happiness and misery—what they are and how it fits human nature to seek the one and flee the other—when, I say, that sharp, litigious lawyer is required to give an account of these things, then he in turn pays the penalty to the philosopher. <margin>See that he is a "barbarian" who speaks in a distorted and clumsy way.</margin> He suffers from vertigo, looking down from a high vantage point with blurred eyes; being unaccustomed to looking from above, he is troubled, stammers, and speaks like a barbarian. This does not provoke laughter in Thracian maids or the uneducated (for they do not perceive it), but rather in all those who have been brought up in freedom and not in a slavish life. This, Theodorus, is the condition of each. One is the man brought up in liberty and leisure, whom you call a philosopher. Though he may truly be blamed, he only appears foolish and inept whenever he performs "slavish" tasks—such as not knowing how to pack a bundle of bedding, season a dish, or craft flattering words of adulation. The other is the condition of the man who can perform all these services quickly and expertly, but does not know how to wear the cloak of a free man becomingly. Furthermore, he is entirely ignorant of how to sing the true life of the gods and of blessed men in the proper harmony of speech.

**THEODORUS:** If you could persuade other men of what you say, Socrates, as you persuade me, there would be more peace and fewer evils among men.

**SOCRATES:** But it is impossible, Theodorus, for evils to be entirely rooted out. For it is necessary that there always be something opposite to the good. <margin>It is impossible for evils to be entirely rooted out. Which evils are in the lower regions.</margin> These evils cannot have a place among the gods, but they haunt mortal nature and this lower region...

they necessarily go around. Wherefore we must strive to flee from here to there as quickly as possible. Now, flight consists in becoming as like to God as is within our power; and to become like God is to become just and holy, together with wisdom. But, O best of men, it is not easy to persuade people of this: that virtue is to be followed and vice shunned, not for the reason the common crowd thinks—namely, so that you do not seem wicked and that you appear good. These things, in my view, are the trifles of old women <note>original: "anicularum nugae"</note>. But let us state what is true in this way: God is never and in no way unjust, but is most perfectly just; he encompasses the full power of justice, and nothing is more like him than a man who is as just as possible. Around this is centered the true industry and strength of a man, as well as his laziness and weakness. Indeed, the knowledge of these things is true virtue and wisdom; whereas ignorance of them is, conversely, manifest unskillfulness and wickedness. Other perceived abilities and "wisdoms" seen in civil magistrates are actually troublesome, and in the mechanical arts, they are merely menial. Therefore, if someone has done something unjustly, or has spoken or committed something profane, it is better by no means to concede that he is powerful or fertile in his cleverness. For men of this sort exult in their disgrace; 

<margin>The proverb "an inert weight" carries weight.</margin> 

they think they hear that they are by no means abject and empty little men—mere "inert weights" <note>original: "pondus iners," a reference to Horace or similar classical idioms for useless people</note> as the saying goes—but rather men of such character that they can flourish safely in the Republic. Therefore, the truth must be expressed: that they are all the more the sort of people they think they are not, precisely because they do not think they are. For they are ignorant of the penalty of injustice, which is the thing one should least of all be ignorant of. For it is not what they perhaps imagine—beatings and killings, which those who have done nothing unjust often suffer, and which the unjust often avoid—but rather a penalty that cannot be escaped. THEODORUS: Which one do you mean? SOCRATES: Since in the order of things, my friend, there are two patterns—one divine and most blessed, the other devoid of God and most miserable—they do not see that this is the case. Occupied by extreme folly and madness, they secretly become like the latter through their iniquitous actions, and unlike the former. They pay the penalty for this crime by leading a life suited to that which they have become like. Indeed, if I were to say that unless they cease from their wickedness, that place free of evils will not receive them after they have finished this life, but that here they will always bear the likeness of their own life, evil men dwelling together with the evil—they, as clever and malicious men, will say they are hearing mere ravings. THEODORUS: And very much so, Socrates. SOCRATES: I know it well, my friend. One thing at least happens to them: if ever they are required to give and receive an account in private of the things they disparage, and they wish to endure the delay of manly disputation and not flee like cowards, then at last—and this is the absurd part—they are by no means pleased with themselves in what they say, and their rhetoric utterly vanishes, so that they seem to differ in no way from children. But let us put an end to these matters, since they are outside our purpose. Otherwise, the great amount of material flowing in from all sides will overwhelm the discourse we originally began. Let us return to the previous points, if you agree. THEODORUS: To me, Socrates, those things were not at all unpleasant to hear. For men of this age easily follow such things. Nevertheless, if it pleases you, let us return to where we left off. SOCRATES: We had reached the point in the dispute where we said that those who place all essence in motion—and hold that whatever "seems" to each person actually "is" for that person—would assert this most vehemently in other matters, and somewhat in matters of justice: that whatever a city establishes as appearing just to itself, these things are just for it as long as the statutes remain. But perhaps no one would be so bold as to contend the same regarding "good" and "useful" things: namely, that whatever a city establishes as appearing useful to itself, these things are beneficial to it for as long as they are decreed—unless perhaps one speaks only of the *name* "useful"; but that would be a joke, a mere sophistry <term>captiosum: a deceptive or fallacious argument</term> regarding what we intend. THEODORUS: Undoubtedly. SOCRATES: Therefore, it should not be said in that way. Rather, whatever the city names as such, it looks toward that goal in establishing laws; and it establishes individual laws as being as useful to itself as it thinks and is able. Does it intend anything else in passing laws? THEODORUS: Nothing else. SOCRATES: Does it always achieve its wish? Or does opinion often deceive it? THEODORUS: I believe it is often deceived. SOCRATES: Furthermore, anyone will more readily admit these same things if one asks about every species in which the "useful" consists. It also pertains, in a way, to future time. For whenever we establish laws, we establish them as being profitable for the future, which we might more rightly call "the future." THEODORUS: Exactly. SOCRATES: Come then, let us ask Protagoras or any other follower of his: "You assert, O Protagoras, that man is the measure of all things: of white things, heavy things, light things, and each of such things. For since he contains the power of judging them in himself, and judges them to be such as he experiences them, he judges things that are true for himself and which exist. Is it not so?" THEODORUS: Plainly so. SOCRATES: "But Protagoras, shall we say he also has the power of judging things in the future? And do things turn out for the one who expects them just as he thinks they will be? When someone unskilled in medicine thinks he is going to fall into a fever and become hot, but the doctor thinks the opposite, whose opinion do we consider will be true? Or both? Will it be neither hot nor a fever for the doctor, but both for the patient?" THEODORUS: That would be ridiculous. SOCRATES: "Furthermore, regarding whether a wine will be sweet or harsh, the opinion of the farmer prevails over that of the lyre-player." THEODORUS: Why wouldn't it? SOCRATES: "Nor does a gymnastics master judge better than a musician about what will be harmonious or discordant, even if it later seems harmonious to the gymnastics master himself." THEODORUS: By no means. SOCRATES: "And when a table is prepared and a feast is to be offered, and something is to be predicted about the future sweetness of the dishes, is not the cook's opinion better than that of any unskilled person? We do not fight over what *is* or *was* sweet to each person, but rather over what *ought to seem* to be so to each in the future. Is each person a fit judge for himself? Or would you, Protagoras, foresee more rightly than any unlearned man what is likely to be persuasive to individuals in a future judgment?" THEODORUS: In this very thing especially, Socrates, Protagoras professed to excel all others. SOCRATES: O wretched man! No one would have followed him for the money he offered, unless he had persuaded his associates that neither a seer nor anyone else could foresee what will be probable and seem to be in the future better than he himself.
