# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE, FOLIO 61.

...with foretelling? THEODORUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: And do not the positions of laws and their utility look toward the future? And would anyone not admit without controversy that the constitution of a republic often wanders away from what is actually useful? THEODORUS: Greatly so. SOCRATES: Let enough now be said against your teacher <note>Protagoras</note>: for he is forced to admit that one man exists who is wiser than another, and that such a man is the "measure." But as for me, even if I am unskilled in knowledge, nothing forces me to become a measure, as his recent discourse urged—namely, that whether I wished it or not, I was such a measure. THEODORUS: From that point, O Socrates, his discourse seems most convicted; and from this as well: that it makes the opinions of others valid, yet these very opinions openly reject his own words, deeming them false. SOCRATES: In many ways besides, O Theodorus, one may catch this: that not every opinion of every person is true. But concerning the present passion <note>original: "passionem," referring here to immediate sensory experience or "feeling"</note> of each person, from which the senses and the opinions according to them are born, it is more difficult to catch that these senses and opinions are not true. But perhaps I say nothing. For if they have attained [truth], they cannot be convicted; and those who assert that they are certainties and forms of knowledge might perhaps not be wandering. And therefore Theaetetus here said, not without reason, that sense-perception and knowledge are the same. Wherefore we must approach closer, as the Protagorean discourse instructed, and examine this "agitated essence" <note>The theory that everything is in constant flux</note> by striking it, to see if it gives off a whole or a cracked sound. Certainly, a battle of no small scale and among no few people has arisen over it. THEODORUS: It is indeed far from being a cheap contest; for it has been spread everywhere through Ionia. Indeed, the followers of Heraclitus support this discourse with the utmost zeal. SOCRATES: Therefore, O friend Theodorus, these things must be inspected from their origins, just as they propose. THEODORUS: Entirely so. For, O Socrates, concerning these Heracliteans—or as you say, Homerics, and even those more ancient—it is thought by the experts of Ephesus that they speak as if driven by a goad or a frenzy. For they are aptly carried along in their writings. But delay or waiting in speech and questions, and quietness between responding and questioning, is less present in them than nothing at all. Rather, it exceeds even "nothing" in how little rest is in them; but if you ask any of them about something, they shoot at you as if drawing obscure little words from a quiver. And if you seek the reason for this, they strike you with some other new naming; you will never accomplish anything with any of them, nor they with each other. And they take the most observant care of this one thing: that they permit nothing stable to exist either in speech or in their own souls, thinking, as it seems to me, that stability itself is [the enemy]; and they pursue it with all their strength and violently expel it from everywhere. SOCRATES: Perhaps, O Theodorus, you have seen these men in battle, but never in peace. For they are not your friends. But I suppose they say such things to their disciples in leisure, whom they wish to make like themselves. THEODORUS: What disciples, O blessed man? For among those people, one does not become the disciple of another; but they spring up spontaneously, wherever each of them happens to be seized by frenzy. And one thinks the other knows nothing. From these, therefore, as I was just saying, you will never receive a rational account, whether they are willing or unwilling. But we must consider it as if we had received a formal proposition. SOCRATES: You speak skillfully. Indeed, we have received another proposition from the ancients who hid it from the common folk in poetry: that the origin of all other things is Oceanus and Tethys, a flow, and nothing stands still. But from the more recent, as if they were wiser, it is demonstrated openly so that even their cobblers <note>original: "cerdones," meaning low-level craftsmen</note> might perceive their wisdom by listening, and might cease to foolishly think that things partly stand still and partly move; and learning that all things move, they might venerate them. But, O Theodorus, the opinion of certain others almost escaped me, who showed the opposite of these. Namely, that the "Universe" is the fitting name for this existing immobile thing; and whatever else the followers of Melissus and Parmenides asserted in opposition to all these: that all things are One, and that this One itself stands within itself, having no place at all in which it might move. What shall we say of all these, O friend? For having progressed gradually, we have secretly escaped into the middle of both. And if we go away without fighting for either side, we shall pay the penalty like those who play "on the line" in the wrestling schools, when they are caught by both sides and pulled in opposite directions. It seems, therefore, we must first deal with those whom we first approached, the "flowing" ones. And if they seem to say anything probable, we shall pull ourselves along with them and flee the others. But if those who posit a stable universe bring forth truer things, we shall flee to them from those who move even the immobile. But if neither side appears to bring us anything likely, we shall turn out to be quite ridiculous: thinking that we, cheap little men, know something great, while disparaging those ancient and wise men. See then, O Theodorus, whether it is better or not to undergo such a danger. THEODORUS: It must by no means be allowed, O Socrates, that we do not discuss what truth or what falsehood the senses of both sides hold. SOCRATES: It must be discussed now, since you also approve of it. It seems to me that the beginning of this disputation should be taken from motion: namely, by what motion they say all things are moved. What I wish to say is this: whether they introduce one species of motion, or, as it seems to me, two species. Nor do I wish this to seem so to me alone, but to you also, so that we may both suffer together whatever must be suffered. Tell me then: do you say a thing is "moved" when it changes place from place, or turns in the same spot? THEODORUS: I do. SOCRATES: Therefore, let this be one species. But when something remaining in the same place grows old, or becomes black from white, or hard from soft, or is changed by some other alteration: shall we not rightly call this a second species of motion? THEODORUS: Rightly. SOCRATES: From these it is necessary that twin species of motion exist: namely, alteration and local motion. THEODORUS: Correct. SOCRATES: This distinction having been made, let us now go to those who want all things to be moved, and let us interrogate them in this way: Do you admit that anything is moved in both ways, both altered and carried along? Or that some things move in both ways and some in only one? THEODORUS: Indeed, I have nothing to offer. SOCRATES: I think, however, they will say in both ways. Otherwise, O friend, things will seem to them to be both agitated and consistent at the same time; certainly, they will appear so, nor [will they be] more moved...

<margin>
The habit of the Heracliteans in disputing.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates and Theodorus examine the Heraclitean theory of universal flux versus the Eleatic theory of a stable, unified universe. Socrates distinguishes between two types of motion—change of place and internal alteration—to test the validity of the "everything moves" argument.</summary>

# THIRTEENTH BOOK

<margin>Nothing is one thing in and of itself.</margin>
...it will be permitted to assert that all things stand still. THEODORUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Since these things must be moved, and the absence of motion belongs to nothing, then all things are surely always moved by every kind of motion. THEODORUS: That follows necessarily. SOCRATES: Consider this then from their sayings: namely, the generation of heat, or whiteness, or anything else. Did we not say they think each of these is carried along simultaneously with sensation between the "acting" and the "undergoing" <note>Latin: *agens & patiens*, the active and passive elements of perception</note>? And that the "undergoing" element becomes a perceived thing but not the sensation itself, while the "acting" element becomes a producer of something, yet not a quality? Perhaps "quality" <note>Latin: *qualitas*; Socrates notes this is a technical philosophical term</note> seems a foreign word to you, and you do not grasp it spoken of in a general sense; listen then to the parts. For the "acting" element is neither heat nor whiteness, but rather "the hot" and "the white," and others in the same manner. Do you remember we said above that nothing is one thing according to itself, nor moreover is there an "acting" or "undergoing" element, but from both meeting each other in turn, sensations and sensible things emanate, making some things to be of a certain quality, and others to perceive? THEODORUS: How could I not remember! SOCRATES: Shall we pass over the rest of what they say, or is it otherwise? Let us search more diligently for the sake of what is being disputed. All things move and flow, as you say. Is it not so? THEODORUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: And are they not carried along and altered simultaneously by both those motions we distinguished? THEODORUS: Why not, if it is necessary for them to be perfectly moved? SOCRATES: If therefore they were only carried along, and yet not altered, could we say what kind of things flow as they are carried, or how should we say it? THEODORUS: In this way. SOCRATES: But since it does not remain so that the "white" which flows remains white, but is changed—so that there is a flux of this very whiteness and a transition into another color, lest it be found to remain in any way—can we ever pronounce any color so as to name it correctly? THEODORUS: But how, O Socrates? Either in this or in any other case, can it be done if it continually escapes while we are speaking, seeing as it always flows? SOCRATES: What further should be said of any sense, such as seeing or hearing? Does it ever remain in vision or hearing? THEODORUS: Not at all, since all things are moved. SOCRATES: Therefore, one should no more say "to see" anything than "not to see," nor use any other sense more than not to use it, since all things are utterly transformed. THEODORUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: And yet sensation itself is knowledge <note>Latin: *scientia*, translating the Greek *episteme*</note>, as I and Theaetetus said. THEODORUS: It was so said. SOCRATES: Therefore, we have answered what knowledge is no more than what it is not. THEODORUS: So it certainly seems. SOCRATES: We would therefore appropriately amend that answer if we contended to demonstrate that all things are moved, so that the answer might seem right. But this, as it seems, has appeared: that if all things are moved, any answer about whatever one might respond is equally right—whether one responds that it is "so" or "not so." Or if you prefer, we should say "becoming" so as not to make their speech stand still. THEODORUS: You speak rightly. SOCRATES: Except in this, O Theodorus, that I said "so" and "not so"; but one ought not even to say "this" or "so." For it would no longer be moved "so," nor again "not so." For this is not motion; but another name must be imposed by those who hold such views, since now they have no words for their hypothesis, unless perhaps this expression: "not in any way" <note>Latin: *nō, quōcunq̄ hŕe videant̄*, an attempt to capture the radical instability of the flux doctrine</note>, however they may seem to be, which fits them best when spoken infinitely. THEODORUS: That expression is very suitable for them. SOCRATES: Now, O Theodorus, we have settled what pertains to your friend <note>Referring to Protagoras</note>, yet we have not yet granted him that every man is the measure of all things, unless he be a wise man. Moreover, we will not grant that knowledge is sensation according to that reasoning which predicts all things are moved—unless perhaps Theaetetus here persuades us otherwise. THEODORUS: You have spoken best, O Socrates. For these things being finished, it is right that I also be released from these matters, as was agreed between us. THEAETETUS: Since the dispute against Protagoras has reached an end, do not stop, I pray, Theodorus, before you and Socrates run through those who moreover wished that all things stand still, just as you proposed a little while ago. THEODORUS: Since you are young, O Theaetetus, you teach your elders to do wrong while you exhort us to transgress our agreements. But prepare yourself so that you may give an account to Socrates for the rest, if he wishes. THEAETETUS: I would most gladly hear those things of which I speak. THEODORUS: You "provoke a knight into the field" <note>A proverbial expression for challenging someone to their specialty</note> when you call Socrates to dispute. Ask, therefore, and you shall hear. SOCRATES: I seem indeed, O Theodorus, unlikely to obey Theaetetus in what he commands. THEODORUS: What stands in the way of your complying? SOCRATES: Although I fear Melissus and the others who say the universe is one and standing still, lest we seem burdensome in harassing them, I fear them less than I fear the one Parmenides. For Parmenides, to use Homeric words, seems to me "venerable and awesome." I spoke once with that man when he was very old and I was still quite a youth; he seemed to me to possess a profound and altogether noble wisdom. I dread, therefore, lest we understand neither his words nor his voice, and much more that what he implies in his words may lie hidden from us. And what is greatest: that for the sake of which our dispute began—inquiring what knowledge is—might be left unexamined if we indulge in a boldness of words. Especially since that most ample question we just introduced, if treated outside our purpose and as a digression, would suffer too much; and if it were perfected more broadly and exactly, it would hinder the investigation of knowledge itself. Neither is fitting; rather, we must bring Theaetetus's "offspring" concerning knowledge into the light by the midwife's art and examine it diligently. THEAETETUS: If it seems so, it must be done so. SOCRATES: Consider this further, Theaetetus, regarding the above. You answered that sensation is knowledge, did you not? THEAETETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: If someone asked by what a man sees white and black, or by what he hears sharp and deep sounds, you would answer, I think, with eyes and ears. THEAETETUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: As in common names and words, it is often the mark of a noble mind not to inquire with exact curiosity, while the contrary is illiberal; yet sometimes it is necessary, as we are compelled to examine at present, in what respect your answer is less than right. Attend to which answer is more correct: whether that which says "that by which we see is the eyes," or that which says "through which we see." Likewise, "by which we hear is the ears," or "through which we hear." THEAETETUS: It seems to me, O Socrates, that we should answer "through which" we perceive each thing, rather than "by which." SOCRATES: It would be absurd indeed, O boy, if many senses were in us as if in "wooden horses" <note>A reference to the Trojan Horse; Socrates argues for a unified soul rather than a collection of disconnected senses</note>, and all these did not tend toward one thing—whether an idea, or a soul, or whatever it should be called—which perceives through these as through instruments...

<margin>In this place Plato seems to agree with Parmenides.</margin>

<summary>Socrates and his interlocutors conclude their critique of the Heraclitean "universal flux" theory, arguing it makes language and knowledge impossible. Socrates then prepares to examine the opposite view—that the universe is unmoving—while shifting the focus to how the soul perceives "through" the senses rather than the senses perceiving on their own.</summary>

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE. FOL. LXII.

we perceive things that are subject to the senses. THEAETETUS. That seems more likely to me than the other way. SOCRATES. For this reason, I am investigating these things with you diligently, so that we may see whether it is through one and the same thing within us that we perceive white and black through the eyes, and certain other things through other organs; and whether, if asked, you could refer each of these to the body. It is perhaps better for you to answer each point yourself than for me to grow weary by acting on your behalf. Tell me then: those things through which you feel heat and dryness, lightness and sweetness—do you not assign them to individual organs of the body, or to something else? THEAETETUS. To nothing else. SOCRATES. Will you not also admit that what you feel through one power, you cannot feel through another? For instance, what you feel through hearing, you cannot feel through sight; and conversely, what you feel through sight, you cannot feel through hearing? THEAETETUS. Why should I not admit it? SOCRATES. If, therefore, you think something about both of them, you certainly do not perceive it through one organ, nor through the other, regarding both. THEAETETUS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Concerning sound and color together, you first think this: that they both *are*. THEAETETUS. I do. SOCRATES. Likewise, that each is different from the other, and the same as itself. THEAETETUS. That as well. SOCRATES. And that both together are two, but each is one. THEAETETUS. That too. SOCRATES. Can you moreover judge whether they are similar or dissimilar to each other? THEAETETUS. Perhaps. SOCRATES. Through what, above all, do you form these thoughts about them? It is not through hearing, nor through sight; nothing common to both can be received through those. Furthermore, we may conjecture from what we are saying: if it were possible to judge concerning both whether they are false or not, you could undoubtedly declare by what means you judged; and it is clear that this is neither sight nor hearing, but something else. THEAETETUS. Why should the power of the tongue not effect this? SOCRATES. You speak cleverly. But that power—through what does it show you what is common to each, or what is above each, by which you denote "being" and "non-being," which we were asking about just now? What kind of organs will you assign to all these, through which that which feels in us perceives each thing? THEAETETUS. You mean "essence" <note>original: *essentia*, referring to the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note> and "non-being," similarity and dissimilarity, as well as "the same" and "the other," and also "one" and any other number applied to them. For it is clear you are asking through what bodily instruments the soul perceives "even" and "odd" and the things that follow. SOCRATES. You follow me excellently, O Theaetetus; these are the very things I am asking. THEAETETUS. By Jove, Socrates, I do not know what to say, except that I think there is no such specific organ for these as there is for those; rather, the soul itself, through itself, judges the commonality in all things. SOCRATES. You are beautiful, O Theaetetus, and not, as Theodorus said, ugly. For he who speaks beautifully is beautiful and good. Moreover, you have done me a great favor. For you have freed me from a very long and heavy dispute, since it seems to you that the soul observes some things through itself, and apprehends others through the powers of the body. This was indeed my own opinion. I desired that you also be persuaded of the same. THEAETETUS. I am certainly persuaded. SOCRATES. In which class do you place "essence"? For this follows upon all things. THEAETETUS. Among those things which the soul itself aims at and attains by itself. SOCRATES. And what of the similar and dissimilar, the same and the other? THEAETETUS. These also. SOCRATES. What of the beautiful and the ugly, the good and the evil? THEAETETUS. These also seem to me to consider essence in relation to one another above all, calculating and comparing within itself the past and the present in relation to the future. SOCRATES. Note this as well: it will feel the hardness of a hard thing through touch, and the softness of a soft thing in a similar way. THEAETETUS. Yes. SOCRATES. But their essence, and what they are, and their mutual contrariety, and the essence of that very contrariety, the soul itself, revolving and comparing them with one another, strives to discern. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Is it not the case that for humans and beasts, as soon as they are born, a certain natural faculty is present, by which they feel the sensations <note>original: *passiones*, meaning "undergoings" or raw sensory inputs</note> flowing through the body into the soul? But reasoning <note>original: *ratiocinatio*</note> and the comparison of these things regarding their essence and utility—this arrives only with difficulty, after long periods of time, through frequent study and discipline, for those to whom it comes at all. THEAETETUS. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Now, can we grasp truth where we do not grasp essence? THEAETETUS. Not at all. SOCRATES. But if someone lacks the truth of a thing, can he have any knowledge of it? THEAETETUS. How could that be possible? SOCRATES. Therefore, knowledge is by no means in the sensations, but it seems to be in the reasoning that revolves around them. For we can touch upon essence and truth through the latter, but by no means through the former. THEAETETUS. That is certain. SOCRATES. Now, do you call that and this the same, when they differ by such a great distance? THEAETETUS. It would hardly be right. SOCRATES. What name do you attribute to those things—to see, to hear, to smell, to taste, to be warmed, and to be cooled? Is it not "to sense"? THEAETETUS. That very thing; what else? SOCRATES. You call this whole category "sensation," then? THEAETETUS. Necessarily. SOCRATES. We have denied that the perception of truth belongs to this, since it does not perceive essence. THEAETETUS. So it is. SOCRATES. Therefore, it will not be a part of knowledge either. THEAETETUS. No. SOCRATES. From this it follows, O Theaetetus, that knowledge and sensation will never be the same. THEAETETUS. Never at all. SOCRATES. In these things it has become clearly evident that sensation is one thing and knowledge is another. But we did not begin to argue for the sake of finding what knowledge is *not*, but rather what it *is*. We have proceeded this far in the dispute as to judge that knowledge is in no way to be sought in sensation, but rather in that name which the soul receives when it, by itself, is occupied and acts concerning those things which *are*. THEAETETUS. But this, O Socrates, as I myself think, is called "opining" <note>original: *opinari*, the act of forming an opinion or belief</note>. SOCRATES. You think rightly, my friend. And now observe, having erased all the previous things from your soul, whether you see anything more, now that you have been brought this far. Explain again what knowledge might be. THEAETETUS. To say that any opinion whatsoever is knowledge, O Socrates, is impossible, since there is also such a thing as false opinion. But it appears that **true opinion** is knowledge. Let that be my answer for now. If, as the discussion continues, something else appears, we shall try to bring that forward. SOCRATES. Well done, Theaetetus; it is right to argue with such a ready mind, and not to hesitate as you did at first. For if we do this, one of two things will happen: either we shall find what we seek, or at least we shall think we know less of what we are ignorant of. That will be no small gain. And now, what do you say? Since there are two species of opinion—one true and the other false—do you define true opinion as knowledge? THEAETETUS. I do. For so it seems to me at present. SOCRATES. Should we then treat opinion from the beginning? THEAETETUS. What do you mean? SOCRATES. It disturbs me now and often at other times, so that I am in great ambiguity both toward myself and toward others: I cannot explain...

# BOOK THIRTEEN

<note>original: "LIBER TERTIUSDECIMUS" - This likely refers to a specific division in a Renaissance edition of Plato's *Theaetetus*.</note>

...considering what this affection in us is, and in what way it comes about. THEAETETUS: Which one? SOCRATES: That a person thinks falsely. I am even now in doubt about this: should we let it go, or consider it differently than we did above? THEAETETUS: Why not, Socrates, if you think it in any way fitting? For you and Theodorus said very well in the previous discussion regarding leisure, that nothing in such matters is pressing. SOCRATES: You have reminded me opportunely; for perhaps it will not be beside the point to run over the track again. For it is better to determine a small amount well, than a great deal insufficiently. THEAETETUS: It is better indeed. SOCRATES: How then, and what do we say? Do we say that false opinion is common, and that one of us thinks falsely and another truly, as if these things were so by nature? THEAETETUS: We say so without doubt. SOCRATES: Does this not apply to us concerning all things as well as individual things? Namely, to know or to be ignorant? For learning and forgetting—as they are intermediaries between these—I will remain silent about for the present, since they contribute nothing to our purpose. THEAETETUS: Nothing else remains, Socrates, besides knowing or being ignorant concerning each thing. SOCRATES: Is it not therefore necessary for one who thinks, to think of those things which he knows something about, or does not know? THEAETETUS: It is necessary. SOCRATES: Furthermore, it is impossible for one who knows to be ignorant of the same thing, or for one who is ignorant to know it. THEAETETUS: How could it be otherwise? SOCRATES:

<margin>It is better to determine a small amount well than a great deal insufficiently.</margin>
<margin>Knowing and being ignorant concerning all and individual things.</margin>

> Those things he knows: to think they are: those things he knows.
> Those things he does not know: to think they are: those things he does not know.
> Those things he knows: to think they are: those things he does not know.
> Those things he does not know: to think they are: those things he knows.

Does he ever think falsely of what he knows, thinking those things are not what they are, but some other things he also knows; and knowing both, is he again ignorant of both? THEAETETUS: But this cannot happen, Socrates. SOCRATES: Or perhaps those things he does not know, he thinks are certain other things which he does not know? And he who knows neither Theaetetus nor Socrates, can he ever think that Socrates is Theaetetus, or conversely that Theaetetus is Socrates? THEAETETUS: Never. SOCRATES: Nor yet does one think that things he knows are things he does not know; nor again that things he does not know are things he knows. For that would be a marvel. In what way then will anyone think falsely? For it is not permitted to think besides these things, since we either know or are ignorant of all things. But in these, it seems no one can think falsely in any way. THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Or perhaps we should not consider what we seek by proceeding according to "knowing and not knowing," but according to "being and not being"? THEAETETUS: How do you mean? SOCRATES: Lest it be simple: that he who thinks non-existent things <note>original: "non existentia" - things that do not exist</note> about anything cannot help but think falsely, however else he might devise it. THEAETETUS: That also is fitting, Socrates. SOCRATES: How then, and what shall we answer, Theaetetus, if someone asks us: is it possible for anyone to do what is said—namely, that a man thinks that which is not, whether concerning some of those things which are, or concerning the thing itself? To this we will both answer: that it is so when someone does not think the truth while thinking. Or in what other way? THEAETETUS: Certainly so. SOCRATES: Does such a thing happen elsewhere? THEAETETUS: What do you mean? SOCRATES: Can someone see something, yet see nothing? THEAETETUS: It can in no way happen. SOCRATES: But truly, if he sees some one thing, he sees something of existing things. Or do you think "one" can be among those things which are not? THEAETETUS: Not at all. SOCRATES: Therefore, he who sees some one thing, sees something that exists. THEAETETUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: And he who hears something, hears some one thing, and hears an existing thing. THEAETETUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: Likewise, he who touches something, touches some one thing, and an existing thing besides, if indeed it is one. THEAETETUS: That also. SOCRATES: And he who thinks, does he not think some one thing? THEAETETUS: It must be so. SOCRATES: And he who thinks some one thing, does he not think an existing thing? THEAETETUS: I agree. SOCRATES: Therefore, he who thinks a non-existing thing, thinks nothing. THEAETETUS: It seems not. SOCRATES: But he who thinks nothing, does not think at all. THEAETETUS: That is certain. SOCRATES: It is therefore impossible to think that which is not, whether concerning any of the things which are, or concerning the thing itself. THEAETETUS: It seems impossible. SOCRATES: Thinking falsely is therefore something other than thinking things which are not. THEAETETUS: It appears to be something else. SOCRATES: Neither in this way, then, nor as we considered a little while ago, does false opinion exist in us. THEAETETUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: But perhaps we call it this in the following manner. THEAETETUS: In what way? SOCRATES: We call "false opinion" a certain "other-opinion" <note>original: "alienam opinionem" - thinking one thing is another</note>: when someone says that one of the things which are is another of the things which are, by exchanging them in thought. For in this way he always thinks of something that exists, but he thinks of one thing in place of another; and since he misses the mark of what he was thinking, he is rightly said to think falsely. THEAETETUS: Now you seem to have spoken rightly. For whenever someone thinks the ugly is beautiful, or conversely the beautiful is ugly, then he truly thinks falsely. SOCRATES: Do you despise me, my Theaetetus, and have no fear? THEAETETUS: Why is that? SOCRATES: I do not think I seem to you to have explained what is truly false; having been asked whether it is possible for the swift to become slow, or the light heavy, or any other contrary to become its own contrary, not according to its own nature but according to the nature of its contrary. Lest you venture this in vain or rashly, I let it go; and it pleases you, as you say, that thinking falsely is the same as "other-thinking." THEAETETUS: To me it does. SOCRATES: Is it therefore, as you think, to place one thing as another in thought, and not as itself? THEAETETUS: It is indeed. SOCRATES: When the thought does this, is it not necessary for it to think either both or one of them? THEAETETUS: Entirely necessary. SOCRATES: Either simultaneously or alternately? THEAETETUS: That also. SOCRATES: But do you call "thinking" the same thing as I do? THEAETETUS: What do you call it? SOCRATES: The discourse which the soul itself rolls around within itself concerning the things it considers. I declare this to you as one who does not know much. For this is how it appears to me: that in thinking, the soul does nothing other than converse with itself: questioning, answering, affirming, and denying. But when it has defined something—whether noticing it slowly or quickly—and asserts it and no longer wavers, this we call "opinion." Therefore, I call "to think" to speak, and "opinion" a discourse, not to another nor with the voice, but in silence and to oneself. But what do you feel? THEAETETUS: The same. SOCRATES: Therefore, when someone thinks one thing is another, then, as it seems, he says to himself that one thing is the other. THEAETETUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Remember, I pray, if you have ever said to yourself that the beautiful is altogether ugly, or the unjust is just; indeed, consider the sum of all things: whether you have ever tried to persuade yourself that one thing is most certainly another; or on the contrary, have you ever dared even in dreams to say to yourself that even things are altogether uneven, or anything else of this kind?

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE.

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly never. **SOCRATES.** Do you think anyone else, whether wise or foolish, would ever dare to seriously persuade themselves—either in thought or speech—that an ox is necessarily a horse, or that two are one? **THEAETETUS.** By Jupiter, not at all. **SOCRATES.** If thinking is the soul's conversation with itself, then no one who considers both things and grasps them with the mind would ever say or think that one is the other. Let us set aside the phrase "the other" if you like; my point is this: no one thinks that the base is beautiful, or anything else of that kind. **THEAETETUS.** I set it aside, Socrates; I agree with what you say. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is impossible for one who thinks of both to think that one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** That is clear. **SOCRATES.** But neither will he who thinks of only one, and not the other at all, ever think that one is the other. **THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth; for he would be forced to grasp even that which he is not thinking of. **SOCRATES.** Thus, neither he who thinks of both, nor he who thinks of only one, can hold a "false opinion" by mistaking one thing for another. Therefore, whoever defines false opinion as "thinking one thing is another" <note>original: "aliena opinari"</note> achieves nothing. It is clear that false opinion does not exist in us in this way, nor according to our previous arguments. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** And yet, O Theaetetus, if it appears that this does not exist, we shall be forced to admit many absurdities. **THEAETETUS.** Such as? **SOCRATES.** I will not tell you until I have tried to consider it from every angle. For I would be ashamed for us—while we are still in doubt—to be forced to admit the things I am saying. But if we escape these difficulties and become free, then we shall speak of others suffering such things, being ourselves entirely removed from such error. But if we fail entirely, then, humbled like those who are seasick and tossed by waves, we shall allow the argument to trample us or lead us wherever it wishes. So, listen to what I have found in my search. **THEAETETUS.** Speak then. **SOCRATES.** I will not admit we were right to agree that it is impossible for someone to think that things they know are things they do not know, and thus be deceived. Rather, it can happen in a certain way. **THEAETETUS.** Do you mean what I suspected when we said such a thing? That sometimes I, knowing Socrates, but seeing someone else at a distance whom I do not know, might think that person is the Socrates I know? For it happens as you say. **SOCRATES.** Did we not already reject that, because it resulted in us not knowing the very things we know? **THEAETETUS.** Exactly. **SOCRATES.** Let us not proceed that way then, but let us propose it in this manner. Perhaps someone will agree with us, or perhaps they will oppose us. But let us attend to that which is necessary to examine this all-turning argument. See if I am saying anything sensible: can one who was previously ignorant of something later learn it? **THEAETETUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** And then another thing, and another? **THEAETETUS.** What is to stop it? **SOCRATES.** Imagine, for the sake of example, that there is a wax tablet in our souls: in one person it is larger, in another smaller; in this one of purer wax, in that one dirtier or harder; in some softer, and in some of a tempered quality. **THEAETETUS.** I imagine it. **SOCRATES.** Let us say this is the gift of Memory, the mother of the Muses <margin>Memory is the mother of the Muses.</margin>; and that whatever we wish to remember of what we see, hear, or think ourselves, we press into this wax through our senses and intellects, as if we were leaving the impression of a signet ring. Whatever is imprinted, we remember and know as long as the image remains; but when it is erased or cannot be imprinted, we forget and do not know. **THEAETETUS.** Let it be so. **SOCRATES.** Now, consider whether one who knows those things, but considers something he sees or hears, might hold a false opinion in this way. **THEAETETUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** By thinking that things he knows are sometimes other things he knows, and sometimes things he does not know. We were wrong to agree earlier that this was impossible. **THEAETETUS.**

---

-> REGARDING KNOWLEDGE WITHOUT PERCEPTION <-

> To know: what he knows.
> To know: what he does not know.
> Not to know: what he does not know.
> Not to know: what he knows.

-> REGARDING PERCEPTION ALONE <-

> To perceive: what he perceives.
> To perceive: what he does not perceive.
> Not to perceive: what he does not perceive.
> Not to perceive: what he perceives.

-> REGARDING BOTH JOINED TOGETHER <-

> To know and perceive: what he knows and perceives.
> To know and perceive: what he knows and does not perceive.
> To know and perceive: what he perceives and does not know.
> Not to know and not to perceive: what he does not know and does not perceive.
> Not to know and not to perceive: what he knows and perceives.
> Not to know and not to perceive: what he does not perceive and knows.

---

-> There are also other combinations: because they can easily be formed from these, they have been left out. <-

<summary>Socrates introduces the famous "wax tablet" metaphor to explain how memory works and how false opinions might arise from a mismatch between stored knowledge and new perceptions. He categorizes the different ways knowledge and perception can interact or fail to interact.</summary>
<keywords>wax tablet metaphor, memory, false opinion, perception, Socrates, Theaetetus, epistemology</keywords>

# BOOK THIRTEEN

->Now, or in what way do you mean?<- **SOCRATES**: We must speak of them in this way, by distinguishing them from the beginning: that which someone knows, and of which he preserves a memorial in his mind but does not currently perceive, he cannot think to be some other thing which he also knows and of which he preserves an image, but does not perceive. Or again, to think that what he knows is that which he does not know; or that of which he preserves no image, and what he does not know, to be moreover that which he does not know; and what he does not know, to be that which he knows. Or what he perceives, to be some other thing of those which he perceives; or what he perceives, to be something he does not perceive at all; or what he does not perceive, to be one of those things he does not perceive. Or what he does not perceive, to be one of those things he does perceive. Much less can he think that what he knows and perceives, and for which he preserves an image according to the sense, is some other thing which he also knows and perceives and preserves in the same way; or that what he knows and perceives and retains correctly, to think it is what he knows. Or that what he knows and perceives and similarly retains, is that which he perceives. Or that what he neither knows nor perceives, is that which he neither knows nor perceives. Or that what he neither knows nor perceives, is that which he does not know at all. Or that what he neither knows nor perceives, is that which he does not perceive at all. All these cases are such that no one can hold a false opinion in them by any reasoning. It remains, therefore, that it happens in certain cases of this kind, if indeed it happens anywhere at all. **THEÆTETUS**: In which cases? Let me see, I pray, if I may understand better from the examples themselves. For at present I do not follow: how, in things which someone knows, he might think them to be certain other things which he both knows and perceives; or which he does not know, yet perceives; or which he knows and perceives, to be those which he both knows and perceives. Therefore, I am now failing much more than before. **SOCRATES**: Come then, listen again in this way. You certainly recognize **Theodorus** and hold his likeness in your memory, and similarly **Theætetus**. Sometimes I see them; sometimes I do not see them. And sometimes I touch them; at other times not at all. In the same way, I both hear them and apprehend them by other senses. Often, I perceive you by no sense at all, but within myself I know and remember you nonetheless. **THEÆTETUS**: Exactly. **SOCRATES**: Note this first, then, from those things I am about to set forth: that one can not perceive what he knows, and he can also perceive it. **THEÆTETUS**: That is so. **SOCRATES**: And is it not also true that what he does not know, he often does not perceive, and often he only perceives it? **THEÆTETUS**: Let it be so. **SOCRATES**: See if you follow better now: **Socrates**, while he recognizes **Theodorus** and **Theætetus**, but sees neither, nor perceives them by any other sense, would never think within himself that **Theætetus** is **Theodorus**. What do you say to this? **THEÆTETUS**: These things are true. **SOCRATES**: This was surely the first of the things I was saying. **THEÆTETUS**: It was. **SOCRATES**: The second was this: that while I recognize one of us and am ignorant of the other, and perceive neither, I never think him whom I know to be him whom I do not know. **THEÆTETUS**: Correct. **SOCRATES**: And this third thing: while I know neither and perceive neither, I never judge him whom I do not know to be some other whom I also do not know. And so on, imagine all the aforementioned cases repeated similarly, in which I will never have a false opinion about you and **Theodorus**, neither knowing nor being ignorant of both, nor knowing one while being ignorant of the other. The same reasoning applies to the senses. **THEÆTETUS**: I follow indeed. **SOCRATES**: It remains, therefore, that false opinion occurs in this: when, knowing you and **Theodorus**, and preserving in that **waxen image** <note>The "wax tablet" (cera) is a famous Platonic metaphor for memory.</note> the figures of both from a long time—just like the imprints of rings—and not seeing both sharply, I fail in assigning the proper mark of each to its proper vision, so as to fit it into its footprint that recognition may occur. Instead, I wander, and like those who err by putting on the wrong shoes, I switch them; and I transfer the vision of each to the other's likeness. I suffer something similar to those things which result in mirrors crosswise, when the right side of the view is changed to the left. And thus I am deceived, and a "foreign opinion" is born, which is what is called holding a false opinion. **THEÆTETUS**: Oh indeed, **Socrates**, such an experience of opinion is exactly as you have wonderfully described it. **SOCRATES**: Furthermore, when knowing both, I perceive one in addition, but the other not at all, yet I have the knowledge of the other not according to the sense—which is what I said above, and you did not understand me. **THEÆTETUS**: Certainly not. **SOCRATES**: Yet I was saying this: that he who recognizes the other and perceives him, and has the knowledge of him according to the sense, will never think him to be some other whom he also recognizes and perceives, or whose knowledge he does not have according to the sense. Was this not it? **THEÆTETUS**: Indeed. **SOCRATES**: It was somewhat passed over, what is now being said, when we asserted in the previous parts that false opinion happens whenever someone, knowing and seeing both, or perceiving them by some other sense, and holding the imprints of both, does not have each according to its own proper sense. Rather, like an unskilled archer, he wanders far from the mark—which indeed has been called a lie. **THEÆTETUS**: And not without reason. **SOCRATES**: And when the sense of one of the imprints is present, but not the other, and he ascribes the sense of the absent one to the one present, this thought is entirely deceived. To speak briefly: regarding those things which one has never either known or perceived, he cannot be deceived or lie or have a false opinion, if what we are now saying is true. But in those things which we know and perceive, in those very things true or false opinion turns. When it brings together and shapes the proper likenesses with a direct gaze and effort, it is true. But when it is crosswise and oblique, it is false. **THEÆTETUS**: Have these things not been excellently said, **Socrates**? **SOCRATES**: When you have heard this, you will assert it even more vehemently. Furthermore, to have true opinions is beautiful, but to lie is shameful. **THEÆTETUS**: Why not? **SOCRATES**: They say these things happen mostly from this: when the **waxen image** in someone's soul is deep and abundant, smooth and moderately worked, those things which flow in through the senses are engraved into this—

<margin>
In whom there is no false opinion, and in whom there seems to be.
</margin>

<margin>
What **Homer** called the "heart" of the soul.
</margin>

<margin>
Those who are mindful and sharp.
</margin>

<margin>
Those who are forgetful.
</margin>

<margin>
Those who are quick and those who are slow to perceive.
</margin>

—which **Homer** called the "heart" <note>original: "cor"</note> of the soul, implying this likeness to wax <note>original: "cerae"</note>. Because the imprints are pure and set deeply, they become long-lasting. And first, men so constituted are teachable and sharp; then they are also mindful; finally, they do not switch the likenesses of the senses. From this, they undoubtedly think true things, for since the imprints are in a clear and ample region, they quickly distribute each into its own proper image. These things are called existing and true, and such men are said to be wise. Does it not seem the same to you? **THEÆTETUS**: In a wonderful way. **SOCRATES**: Therefore, when someone's "heart" is thick—which the most wise poet praised—or when it is muddy and not from purified wax, or too soft, or hard, it does not hold itself well at all. For wax that is too soft makes people quick to perceive, but also forgetful. Hard wax, on the contrary, makes them remember for a long time, but they are inept and slow at perceiving. And those who have a thick and rough or stony...

He further distinguishes how the quality of the "wax" (the soul's capacity) affects intelligence, memory, and the ability to form true opinions.</summary>

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE.

...contains earthy or drossy matter, it holds obscure images. These are also obscure and hard: for there is no depth present. Others are obscure and softer: for they easily vanish due to confusion. But if, besides these, they are crowded together 
<margin>Those prone to false opinion.</margin>

and hear them so: and often, by thinking one thing instead of another, they conceive a deception; and these, being deceived, are called liars and ignorant. THEAETETUS. You speak most correctly, Socrates. SOCRATES. It must be admitted then that false opinions exist in men. THEAETETUS. Strongly so. SOCRATES. And true ones as well. THEAETETUS. And true ones. SOCRATES. Now indeed we must consider it well established that there are two kinds of opinion. THEAETETUS. Greatly so. SOCRATES. Truly, Theaetetus, a talkative man seems to be quite troublesome and annoying. THEAETETUS. To what end is this? SOCRATES. Because I am annoyed by my own lack of skill, which is like a kind of talkativeness. For what other name could one give it, when someone, due to a slowness of wit, turns arguments upside down and back again, since he cannot be persuaded; and being so dull, is entirely unable to unravel any disputation or escape from doubts? THEAETETUS. But why are you annoyed? SOCRATES. I am not only distressed: but I also doubted what I should answer if someone asked: "O Socrates, have you now found that false opinion consists not in the senses relative to each other, nor in thoughts, but in the meeting of sense with thought?" And I would admit it, I think, boastfully, as if I had found something extraordinary. THEAETETUS. It seems to me, Socrates, that what has now been shown is not at all shameful. SOCRATES. To this he might add: "Do you say that a man whom we only think of, but by no means see, we might ever think to be a horse? Which in the present we neither see nor touch, but only think of, and perceive nothing else about him?" I will admit, I think, that I say this. THEAETETUS. And rightly so. SOCRATES. Then he will say: "Therefore, one who thinks only of eleven, according to this reasoning, will never think it is twelve, which he also only thinks of." What to this? THEAETETUS. I will answer that someone seeing or touching eleven things might think they were twelve; but those which he holds only in thought, he would never judge similarly. SOCRATES. What further? Do you think anyone considers with himself five and seven—I do not mean five and seven men, nor anything else of that kind, but the very numbers five and seven which we said were impressions there in the wax—and that no one can have a false opinion about them? THEAETETUS. I think so. SOCRATES. If someone considers these, searching within themselves how many they are, will not some judge them to be eleven, and others twelve? Or will everyone say and think they are twelve? THEAETETUS. No, by Jove! Indeed, many say eleven; and if someone asks about a larger number, he errs even more. For I think you are speaking of all numbers. SOCRATES. You think rightly. Consider then, whether this also happens: that is, that someone thinks the very twelve which are in the impression are eleven? THEAETETUS. It seems so. SOCRATES. Does this not return to the previous problem? For he who suffers this, judges that which he knows to be something else which he likewise knows: which we rejected above as impossible. And from this very thing we are forced to admit that false opinion does not exist, lest one and the same person be forced to know and not know the same things at the same time. THEAETETUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. From these things it is now clear that false opinion must be defined otherwise than as the exchange of thought for sensation. For if it were so, we would never be deceived in our thoughts themselves. Now, however, either there is no false opinion, or if there is, it is possible for what one knows to be simultaneously unknown. Which do you prefer? THEAETETUS. You have proposed an ambiguous choice, Socrates. SOCRATES. Reason seems to forbid admitting both. Nevertheless, we must dare everything. What if we dare to set aside our shame? THEAETETUS. In what way? SOCRATES. If we wish to explain what "to know" itself is. THEAETETUS. Why is this shameless? SOCRATES. You seem not to have noticed enough that our whole discourse from the beginning has been an investigation of knowledge, as if we were ignorant of what it is. THEAETETUS. I understand. SOCRATES. Is it not the mark of a shameless mind, while being ignorant of knowledge, to show what "to know" is? But, O Theaetetus, for a long time we have wandered far from the purity of disputation. For a thousand times we have said these things: "We recognize," "we do not recognize," "we know" and "we do not know," as if we understood one another; but meanwhile we were ignorant of knowledge. Therefore, even now if it pleases you, let us use those terms: namely "to be ignorant" and "to understand," as it is convenient to use them, even if we are devoid of knowledge. THEAETETUS. But in what way, Socrates, could you dispute if these were taken away? SOCRATES. In no way, while I remain as I am; yet I could in some way, if I were a contentious man. And if such a person were present now, he would profess to abstain from these terms, and would vehemently deter us from those things which I am telling. But since we are simple and slow, do you wish that I dare to set forth what "to know" itself is like? For it seems to me to be worthwhile. THEAETETUS. Dare, by Jove! For we will give you pardon for using these terms. SOCRATES. Have you heard what they now say "to know" is? THEAETETUS. Perhaps, but I do not remember at present. SOCRATES. They call it "having knowledge," that is, to use it. THEAETETUS. So it is. SOCRATES. 
<margin>It is one thing to have knowledge; another to use and possess it.</margin>
But we, changing it a little, shall say "to possess knowledge." You will ask, perhaps, how this differs from the other; perhaps not at all. But what seems right to me, examine with me after you have heard it. THEAETETUS. If only I can. SOCRATES. To possess does not seem to be the same as to have: just as if someone, having bought a garment and keeping it, and being able to use it at his pleasure, does not wear it; we would say he certainly does not "have" it, but he does "possess" it. THEAETETUS. And rightly so. SOCRATES. See further whether it can happen that he who possesses knowledge does not have it: just as if someone, having hunted wild birds, either doves or any others, feeds them in an aviary <note>original: "aviario"</note> built at home: in a certain way he will say he always "has" them, because he possesses them; in another way he does not "have" them, but he has mastery over them; and since he has enclosed them in a domestic circuit, he can take them whenever he wishes, and have whichever he wants at his will, and let them go again. THEAETETUS. It is so. SOCRATES. Again, just as we previously fashioned a certain waxen figment in the soul, so now let us fabricate in every soul a certain aviary of all kinds of birds. Some of these fly about separately from others in distinct flocks; others together...

# BOOK THIRTEEN

...only a few, or some alone, or scattered everywhere wherever they happen to fly. THEAETETUS: Let it be so; what then comes next? SOCRATES: I would say that in children this cage is empty; and let us understand the birds to be branches of knowledge <note>Latin: *scientias*</note>. When someone acquires a branch of knowledge, he shuts it up in this enclosure. We say he has "found" or "learned" the thing itself which is the object of that knowledge, and that this is what "knowing" is. THEAETETUS: Agreed. SOCRATES: Then, consider what names we must use for the act of wanting to hunt for a specific piece of knowledge again, to catch it, hold it, and let it go again. Are they the same names as before when they were merely being acquired, or different ones? Perhaps you will understand me more clearly from this: Do you call arithmetic an art? THEAETETUS: I do. SOCRATES: Suppose this to be a hunt for the knowledge of all even and odd numbers. THEAETETUS: I suppose it. SOCRATES: By this art, the arithmetician has the knowledge of numbers subject to him like certain slaves <note>Latin: *mancipia*</note>, and he hands them over to others. THEAETETUS: Exactly. SOCRATES: And of the one who hands them over, we say he "teaches," while the one who receives "learns"; and the one who has them in his possession in that cage, we say he "knows." THEAETETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Now pay close attention to what follows. A perfect arithmetician knows all numbers in his mind; for the knowledge of all numbers is present in his soul. THEAETETUS: Nothing prevents that. SOCRATES: Does such a man not sometimes count, either internally to himself or externally, things that consist of numbers? THEAETETUS: Why not? SOCRATES: But we shall posit that "counting" is nothing other than considering how great any number is. THEAETETUS: Nothing else, surely. SOCRATES: Therefore, he who we confessed knows every number seems to be considering what he already knows as if he did not know it. Do you hear these ambiguities? THEAETETUS: Indeed I do. SOCRATES: Since we compared the possession of the dovecote <note>The "Aviary" metaphor for memory</note> to the hunt, we shall say the hunt is twofold: one before acquisition for the sake of possessing, and another after one has acquired and possessed it, for the sake of catching and holding in the hand those very things which he has long possessed. And so, those things whose knowledge he previously gained by learning, or which he knew before, he can "learn" again by taking up the knowledge of each and bringing into the light things that were hidden. THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: That is why I was asking a moment ago what names we should use when we speak of these things: for instance, when an arithmetician is about to count, or a grammarian is about to read. For then, though he knows, he attempts to "learn" again from himself what he already knows. THEAETETUS: But that is absurd, Socrates. SOCRATES: Or should we say he does *not* know how to count or read them, even though we have already granted him the understanding of all letters and numbers? THEAETETUS: That is also absurd. SOCRATES: Do you want me to tell you, then? We do not care what names anyone uses for "knowing" and "learning." But since we have determined that possessing knowledge is one thing, and "having" <note>In the sense of active use</note> what one possesses is another, we say it is impossible for someone not to possess what he possesses. Therefore, it never happens that someone does not know what he knows. Yet, a false opinion can be taken up concerning that very thing. For it can happen that we take the knowledge of one thing for the knowledge of another; as when one of us, hunting for one of the internal pieces of knowledge, is deceived and seizes another flying past. Just as when one thinks eleven is twelve, he takes the knowledge of eleven in place of the knowledge of twelve—since both remain within—taking, as it were, a wood-pigeon for a dove. THEAETETUS: That is indeed likely. SOCRATES: But when he catches the one he is aiming for, then he is said to be free of falsehood and to think truly. In this way, both true and false opinion exist, and none of the things that troubled us above will be an obstacle. Perhaps you agree with me; or what will you do? THEAETETUS: I agree. SOCRATES: Now we have escaped that dilemma by which men were forced to say they do not know what they know. For it does not happen that we do not possess what we possess, whether we are mistaken or judge truly. However, something else more serious occurs to me. THEAETETUS: What is that? SOCRATES: If the exchange of knowledges becomes a false opinion. THEAETETUS: How so? SOCRATES: Is it not utterly absurd that he who has the knowledge of a thing should be ignorant of that very thing—not through ignorance, but by his own knowledge of it? Then, that he should think this thing is another thing, and this other thing is that! How irrational it is that, while knowledge is present, the soul should recognize nothing and be ignorant of everything! Indeed, by this logic, nothing prevents present ignorance from making us know something, or blindness from making us see—if knowledge can make someone ignorant. THEAETETUS: Perhaps, Socrates, we did not introduce the terms correctly when we placed only "knowledges" in the soul. We ought to have introduced "ignorances" <note>Latin: *inscitias*</note> flying about in the soul together with knowledges; and the man hunting sometimes catches a knowledge, and other times an ignorance about the same thing; and when he hits upon a knowledge, he opines truly, but with ignorance, falsely. SOCRATES: I could not easily refrain from praising you, Theaetetus; yet consider again what you have said. Let it be as you say. He who falls into ignorance will opine falsely, as you say; will he not? THEAETETUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Yet he will not think he opines falsely. THEAETETUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: But rather truly; and he will be affected as if he knows those things in which he errs. THEAETETUS: Why not? SOCRATES: And therefore, he will think he has caught a knowledge in his hunting, not an ignorance. THEAETETUS: That is clear. SOCRATES: Now, by a long circuit, we have fallen back into our first doubt. For that contentious refuter will say with a smile: "O good men, does someone who knows both—knowledge and ignorance—think that one which he knows is the other which he also knows? Or knowing neither, does he think the one he does not know is the other which he also does not know? Or knowing one but not the other, does he think the one he knows is the one he does not know?" Or will you tell me again that there are "knowledges of knowledges and ignorances," which the owner keeps in some other ridiculous cages or waxen figments, knowing them as long as he possesses them, even if he does not have them at hand? And so you will be forced to revolve in an infinite circle around the same point, achieving nothing. What do you say to this, Theaetetus? THEAETETUS: By Jove, Socrates, I do not know what to answer. SOCRATES: Does not reason admonish us, Theaetetus, that we did not correctly investigate false opinion before investigating knowledge, and left knowledge undiscussed? It is impossible to know these things before knowledge has been sufficiently defined! THEAETETUS: It is necessary, Socrates, to assert what you say at present. SOCRATES: What then? Shall we discuss knowledge again from the beginning? For we are not yet tired of speaking. THEAETETUS: Certainly not; if you yourself are not...

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE.

thin. **SOCRATES.** Come then, in what way can we define these things so that we least contradict ourselves? **THEAETETUS.** Just as we contended above, for I have nothing else to offer. **SOCRATES.** How above? **THEAETETUS.** I wished to say that knowledge is true opinion; for to have a true opinion is far from error, and all things that proceed from true opinion are decorous and good. **SOCRATES.** He who leads the way across a river for those following, when they ask how deep the water is, says "it will show itself." So if we enter into the search, perhaps the very obstacle we seek will reveal itself; but if we remain still, nothing will be clear. **THEAETETUS.** You speak well; let us go now to seek it. **SOCRATES.** Is this not a matter for a brief investigation? For the whole of art <note>original: *Ars*; here referring to the craft of rhetoric</note> is proof to us that knowledge is by no means this. **THEAETETUS.** By what reason? What faculty? **SOCRATES.** That of those who are wise above others: whom they call orators and lawyers. For these men persuade by their art, they do not teach. They lead the listeners to hold the opinions they themselves desire. Or do you think any are so powerful in teaching that, when no witnesses were present for robberies or other injuries, they can nevertheless teach the truth of the crimes committed in the short time the water-clock allows? <note>The "water" refers to the *clepsydra*, the water-clock used to time speeches in Athenian courts.</note> **THEAETETUS.** I do not think they teach at all, but rather persuade. **SOCRATES.** And do you not assert that to persuade is the same as to lead into an opinion? **THEAETETUS.** Exactly the same. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, when judges are justly persuaded concerning things which only he who saw them knows—and no other—then, judging those things from hearsay and having obtained a true opinion without knowledge, they judge rightly in the matters they were persuaded of, provided they judge well? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Yet if true opinion, judgment, and knowledge were the same thing, my friend, that excellent judge would never judge rightly without knowledge. But now it seems each is something different. **THEAETETUS.** I once heard something from someone about knowledge which I had forgotten, but now I remember. He said that true opinion with a reason <note>original: *ratio*; translating the Greek *logos*</note> is knowledge, but that which is without reason is outside of knowledge; and things which lack a reason cannot be known, but those which have a reason can be known. **SOCRATES.** You speak excellently. But tell me how he distinguished these very things—what can be known and what cannot—so that we may see if you and I have received it in the same way. **THEAETETUS.** I do not know if I shall find it, but perhaps if another explains it, I might follow. **SOCRATES.** Hear then a dream for a dream. I also seem to have heard from certain people that the primary elements <note>original: *elementa*; the basic building blocks of matter or language</note> from which we and other things are composed have no "account" <note>original: *orationem*; a definition or explanation</note>. For each of them can only be named by itself; one cannot predicate anything else of it, neither that it *is* nor that it *is not*. For already "being" or "non-being" would be added to it. But one ought to add nothing, if one is to speak of that thing alone. Indeed, they do not want "itself," or "that," or "each," or "alone," or "this," or other such things to be applied. For these things run around and are assigned to everything, being something other than the thing to which they are added. But it would be necessary, if the thing itself could be spoken of and had its own proper account, to speak of it apart from all others. Now, however, it is impossible for any of the primary elements to be expressed in a discourse; for it has nothing else but a name, and only has a name. But those things composed of them, just as the things themselves are woven together, so their names, when woven together, become an account. For the weaving together of names is the substance of discourse. Wherefore the elements are without account or reason, and are unknown, though they are perceivable by the senses; but the syllables are both known and can be spoken of, and can be grasped by true opinion. Therefore, when someone acquires a true opinion of something without a reason, they say his soul perceives the truth about it, but does not know it. For he who cannot give and receive a reason is ignorant of that thing. But when he attains a reason, he is able to know all these things and attains perfect knowledge. Did you hear it this way in your dream, or otherwise? **THEAETETUS.** Entirely in this way. **SOCRATES.** Does this please you? And in this way do you assert that true opinion together with a reason is knowledge? **THEAETETUS.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Is it so, Theaetetus, that we have today grasped that which many wise men sought for a long time and grew old before they found? **THEAETETUS.** To me at least, Socrates, what has just been said seems well said. **SOCRATES.** And rightly so: for what knowledge could ever exist without reason and right opinion? Yet one thing among the things said displeases me. **THEAETETUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** That which seemed to be said most magnificently: that the elements are unknown, but the class of syllables is known. **THEAETETUS.** Is that not right? **SOCRATES.** We must certainly look into it. For we have as hostages of the argument the very examples which he used when he said all these things. **THEAETETUS.** Which ones? **SOCRATES.** The elements of letters and syllables. Or do you think the one who said what we are recounting was looking at anything else? **THEAETETUS.** No, certainly not at other things, but at these specifically. **SOCRATES.** Let us then review and examine them, or rather examine ourselves: did we not learn letters in this way? Answer this first: do syllables not have an account or definition, while elements have none? **THEAETETUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** It seems so to me as well. If someone should ask about the first syllable of "Socrates," saying, "Theaetetus, tell me, what is 'So'?" What would you most likely answer? **THEAETETUS.** That it is 'S' and 'o'. **SOCRATES.** You have, then, this account of the syllable. **THEAETETUS.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Come, tell me further the account of 'S' itself. **THEAETETUS.** But how can anyone state the elements of an element? For 'S' itself, Socrates, is a certain sound of the mute letters, a kind of hissing of the tongue; but for 'B', there is neither voice nor sound, as is the case with most elements. Wherefore they say quite rightly that they are without reason, of which only those seven <note>The seven vowels of the Greek alphabet</note> have a voice, but no reason at all. **SOCRATES.** This, then, my friend, is what we have asserted concerning knowledge. **THEAETETUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** But when we said the element is unknown and the syllable is known, were we right? **THEAETETUS.** It is probable. **SOCRATES.** Do we say the syllable is both elements, or if there are more than two, all of them? Or rather a single idea born from their composition? **THEAETETUS.** I think we mean all of them. **SOCRATES.** Look then at the two, 'S' and 'o'. If both are the first syllable of my name, whoever knows the syllable knows both. **THEAETETUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Therefore, he knows 'S' and 'o'. **THEAETETUS.** Clearly. **SOCRATES.** What then, if he is ignorant of each, will he know both? **THEAETETUS.** That would be absurd and contrary to reason. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, if it is necessary to know each, since he would know both, it follows that it is necessary for him to know the elements beforehand if he is ever to know the syllable; and so our beautiful argument will escape us. **THEAETETUS.**

<margin>
Oratory and lawyering are not knowledge.
</margin>

<margin>
Primary elements have neither discourse nor reason. And that which is primary, nothing ought to be added to it.
</margin>

<margin>
The weaving together of names is the substance of discourse.
</margin>

<margin>
Concerning the elements of letters and syllables.
</margin>

# BOOK THIRTEEN

And repeat it often, lest we do not guard it well. Perhaps it was necessary to define the syllable not as the elements themselves, but as a certain single form constituted from them, which has a single "idea" <note>original: *ideam*; here meaning a unified form or essence</note> of itself and differs from the elements. SO. Exactly so; and perhaps it is better this way than the other. Therefore, we must consider this diligently, for it is not fitting that such a great and noble argument be abandoned through lazy speech. THE. Certainly not. SO. Let the syllable be, then, as we were just saying: a single form <note>original: *idea*</note> produced from the individual combined elements, both in letters and in all other things. THE. Entirely so. SO. Must it not be that it has no parts? THE. Why so? SO. Because wherever there are parts, the whole must necessarily be all those parts. Or do you call the "whole" a certain single form made from parts, yet differing from all those parts? THE.

<margin>Whether the "all" and the "whole" are the same.</margin>
Indeed I do. SO. But do you call the "all" and the "whole" the same, or do you say they differ? THE. Since I have no certainty, yet because you bid me answer promptly, I will venture to answer that they differ. SO. Your promptness, O Theaetetus, is correct. But whether the answer itself is correct, we must consider. THE. Indeed. SO. Do not the "whole" and the "all" differ according to the present argument? THE. Certainly. SO. What then? Do "all things" and "the all" differ in any way? For example, when we say: one, two, three,

<margin>Whether "all things" and "the all" are the same.</margin>
four, five, six; or twice three; or three times two; or four and two; or three, two, and one. In all these, do we speak of the same thing, or something else? THE. Entirely the same. SO. Is it anything other than six? THE. Nothing else. SO. In each way of speaking, do we not find "all six"? THE. Yes. SO. Again, do we not say "one certain thing" when we say "all"? THE. It is necessary. SO. Is it anything other than six? THE. Nothing else. SO. Therefore, in those things which consist of number, we say that "the all" and "all the parts" are the same. THE. So it appears. SO. Let us speak of them in this way: the number of an acre and the acre itself are the same, are they not? THE. The same. SO. And the number of a furlong <note>original: *stadii*</note> and the furlong likewise? THE. That too. SO. Also the number of an army and the army itself, and other things of this kind in the same manner. For the entire number existing is the "all" of each of those things. THE. Truly. SO. But is the number of the individual units anything other than the parts? THE. Not at all. SO. Therefore, whatever things have parts consist of parts. THE. It appears so. SO. But it is granted that "all the parts" are the "whole," since the entire number is the "all." THE. That is so. SO. Thus the "whole" does not consist of parts <note>Socrates is testing a paradox here: if the whole is the same as the "all," then it is just the sum of parts, not a new thing</note>; for it would be the "all" if it were all the parts. THE. It does not seem so. SO. Is a part what it is of anything other than a whole? THE. Of the "all" itself. SO. You fight vigorously, Theaetetus. Is not the "all" itself "all" because nothing is missing? THE. Necessarily. SO. And is not the "whole" also "whole" by the same reasoning, because nothing is absent? But that to which nothing is lacking is neither a "whole" nor is it the "all" itself by itself. THE. It seems to me now that the "whole" and the "all" do not differ at all. SO. Did we not say that where there are parts, the "whole" and the "all" are all the parts? THE. Clearly. SO. Again, as we attempted a moment ago: if the syllable is not the elements, must it not be that it does not have the elements as its parts? Or if it is the same as them, it must be just as knowable as they are. THE. Certainly. SO. Lest this should happen, we posited that the syllable was something other than the elements. THE. Other. SO. But what if the elements are not parts of the syllable? Can you name any other things which are parts of the syllable, yet are not its elements? THE. I would never call things "parts" that are not elements. It would be ridiculous to pass over the elements and seek other things. SO. Entirely, therefore, according to this reasoning, O Theaetetus, the syllable appears to be a single, indivisible form <note>original: *impartibilis idea*</note>. THE. It seems so indeed. SO. Do you remember, friend, that we admitted in the earlier parts that there was no "account" or "reasoning" <note>original: *ratio*; translating the Greek *logos*</note> for the primary things from which others are composed, because each thing existed as a simple unit in itself? And that "being" could not be predicated of it, nor "this," nor "that," as if these were foreign and alien to it? And we said this very cause prevents it from being described and known? THE. I remember. SO. Is there any other cause besides this which makes a thing uniform and indivisible? For I see no other. THE. There seems to be none. SO. Does not the syllable fall into the same category as that, since it is a single species and has no parts, but is a single form? THE. Very much so. SO. If, therefore, the syllable is many elements, and a certain whole, and those are its parts, then the syllables and elements can be known and described in the same way, since it was established that all the parts are the same as the whole. THE. Especially so. SO. But if it is a certain single and simple thing, the syllable is just as devoid of definition and knowledge as the element. For the same cause will make them both so. THE. I cannot say otherwise. SO. Therefore, let us not accept the argument of anyone who says that the syllable can be spoken of and known, but the elements cannot. THE. Certainly not, if we believe this reasoning. SO. What if someone said the opposite? Would you not rather concede to those things of which you were conscious in your own first lessons in letters? THE. What are those? SO. That you strove to learn nothing else than to discern the elements with your eyes and ears, and to note each one by itself, so that their position in speech or writing would not confuse you. THE. You tell the truth. SO. And to have learned the art of the lute-player <note>original: *citharistam*</note>—what else is it than to distinguish each tone of every string? For anyone would call these the "elements" of music. THE. Nothing else. SO. Since, therefore, we have become experienced in elements and syllables, and we wish to make a conjecture from these to other things, we shall certainly assert that the category of elements

<margin>The category of elements contains a clearer understanding than the syllable.</margin>
contains a clearer and more fundamental understanding than the syllable, for the absolute perception of individual disciplines. And if anyone says the syllable is known but the element is by nature unknown, we shall think he is joking, whether he means to or not. THE. Most certainly. SO. Moreover, other demonstrations of the same thing would be open to us; but let us not, for the sake of these, abandon our inquiry into the proposal: namely, what is to be judged concerning the statement that "perfect knowledge is right opinion combined with an account <note>original: *ratione*; *logos*</note>." THE. We must inquire by all means. SO. Come then, tell me what "account" signifies to us. For it seems to me to signify

<margin>What "account" and "speech" signify.</margin>
one of three things. THE. Which ones? SO. I think the first is to express one's thought with the voice through words and names, showing one's own opinion in the voice just as in a mirror or in water. Does not speech <note>original: *sermo*</note> seem to be something of this sort to you? THE. To me, yes. SO. We say that he who does this "speaks." Does he not...

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus debate whether a "syllable" (a compound) is merely the sum of its "elements" (parts) or a unique, indivisible form. They conclude that if elements are unknowable, then syllables must be too, ultimately arguing that understanding the basic elements is more fundamental to knowledge.</summary>
