<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Theaetetus regarding the definition of knowledge (scientia). It follows the discussion of whether true opinion combined with a rational explanation (ratio) constitutes knowledge.</meta>

# THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE

-> i ii <-

Anyone can do this: namely, to show more or less slowly what they think about individual things, unless perhaps they are naturally mute or deaf. And so, whoever holds a right opinion on something seems to hold that opinion with a rational account. Thus, a right opinion will never exist without knowledge. 

**THEAETETUS.** These things are true. 

**SOCRATES.** Let us not, therefore, easily condemn the man who affirmed that knowledge is what we just said <note>The definition of knowledge as "true opinion with a rational account."</note>, as if he were saying nothing. For perhaps he did not mean that, but rather that when asked what each thing is, one can respond to the questioner through its elements. 

**THEAETETUS.** What do you mean by that, Socrates? 

**SOCRATES.** Just as Hesiod says of a wagon: "A wagon consists of a hundred pieces of wood." I could never list them all, nor could you, I think. But it would be enough for us if, when asked "What is a wagon?", we could answer: wheels, axle, body, rails, and yoke. 

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES.** But that man might think that we—as if asked about your name and responding syllable by syllable—were to be laughed at. We would be holding a right opinion and saying what we say, yet thinking we are grammarians <note>In this context, "grammarian" refers to a master of letters and language.</note> and possessing the rational account of the name "Theaetetus" in a grammatical way. But this is not speaking according to knowledge until one determines each thing through its elements along with true opinion, as was said above. 

**THEAETETUS.** It was certainly said. 

**SOCRATES.** So it is that we have a right opinion about the wagon. But he who can run through those hundred parts, grasping the essence of the wagon itself, has also comprehended the rational account along with true opinion. In place of a mere "opinant," he has emerged as a craftsman and a possessor of knowledge regarding the essence of the wagon, determining the whole through its elements. 

**THEAETETUS.** Does this not seem right to you, Socrates? 

**SOCRATES.** If it seems right to you, my friend, and you accept that a discourse through elements concerning each thing is a "rational account," while a process through syllables—or according to some greater unit—is devoid of the act of speech <note>original: "orationis expertem"</note>, tell me this, so we may consider it more diligently. 

**THEAETETUS.** I accept it, and very much so. 

**SOCRATES.** Do you think anyone is a "knower" of anything when the one and the same thing seems to him at one time to belong to one thing, and at another time to another? Or when he opines now this and now that about the one and the same thing? 

**THEAETETUS.** Not by Jove! 

**SOCRATES.** Has it escaped your memory that in learning your letters, you and others did these very things? 

**THEAETETUS.** Do you mean we were accustomed to opine now this letter and now that for the same syllable? Or to refer the same letter sometimes to its proper syllable and sometimes to a foreign one? 

**SOCRATES.** That is what I mean. 

**THEAETETUS.** I have not forgotten; nor do I think those who are so affected have knowledge. 

**SOCRATES.** What then? If someone at that time, writing "Theaetetus," thinks he should write "Th" and "e," and writes them; and again, wanting to write "Theodorus," thinks he should write "Th" and "e," and writes them—shall we say he "knows" the first syllable of your names? 

**THEAETETUS.** We agreed just a moment ago that one who is so instructed does not yet know. 

**SOCRATES.** What prevents someone from suffering this same thing regarding the second, third, and fourth syllables? 

**THEAETETUS.** Nothing at all. 

**SOCRATES.** Will he then, having the discourse through the elements, write "Theaetetus" with right opinion when he writes it in its proper order? 

**THEAETETUS.** Without a doubt. 

**SOCRATES.** Is he not still ignorant, but holding a right opinion, as we said? 

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** And he has the "rational account" along with right opinion, for he has the discourse through the elements as he wrote, which we agreed was the "account" <note>original: "orationem"</note>. 

**THEAETETUS.** True. 

**SOCRATES.** There is, therefore, my friend, a certain right opinion with a rational account which it is not yet proper to call "knowledge." 

**THEAETETUS.** So it appears. 

<margin>There is a certain right opinion with a rational account which is not knowledge.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** We have stumbled upon a dream, it seems, while we consider ourselves to have the truest account of knowledge. 

**THEAETETUS.** But we should not find fault yet. For perhaps one should not define the "account" or "rationality" itself in that way, but should choose the remaining of the three species—one of which we said he would choose who asserted that knowledge is right opinion with a rational account. 

**SOCRATES.** You have reminded me opportunely. For one species still remains. 

<margin>Three species of rational account.</margin>

The first was the image of thought in the voice; the second was the process through the elements to the whole. 

**THEAETETUS.** What do you say the third is? 

**SOCRATES.** That which most people would admit: namely, being able to assign a certain sign by which the thing under discussion differs from all others. 

**THEAETETUS.** What such account can you assign to me, or of what thing? 

**SOCRATES.** As for example, concerning the sun: if you wish, I think you can sufficiently grasp that it surpasses in light all things that revolve in the heavens around the earth. 

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES.** Grasp why this was said. It is what we were just relating: if you grasp the difference of each thing, by which it is distinct from others, you will have grasped the "definition" <note>original: "definitionem"</note> as some teach it. 

<margin>Certain things concerning definition.</margin>

But as long as you touch upon something common, you will have the commonality of those things. 

**THEAETETUS.** I understand; and I think it right that something of this sort be called a "rational account." 

**SOCRATES.** But he who, along with right opinion, grasps the difference by which each thing is separated from every other, will then know that very thing which he previously only opined. 

**THEAETETUS.** That is consistent. 

**SOCRATES.** Now at last, O Theaetetus, since I have come closer to this as if to a sort of sketch, I perceive that I understand nothing at all in these matters. As long as I was looking from a distance, it seemed to me that something was being said. 

**THEAETETUS.** Why so? 

<margin>The difference between knowing and opining.</margin>

**SOCRATES.** I will tell you if I can. Having a right opinion about you, if I furthermore grasp your definition, I know you; otherwise, I merely opine. 

**THEAETETUS.** That is so. 

**SOCRATES.** But the definition was the interpretation of your difference. 

**THEAETETUS.** It certainly was. 

**SOCRATES.** When, therefore, I was only opining, I perceived in my thought none of those things by which you are distinct from others. 

**THEAETETUS.** Nothing, it seems. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, I was attending to certain common things, of which you have nothing more than anyone else. 

**THEAETETUS.** That necessarily follows. 

**SOCRATES.** Tell me, by Jove: how then was I opining you rather than anyone else? Suppose me thinking thus: "Theaetetus is he who is a man, and has a nose, and a mouth, and eyes, and other members similarly." Does this thought make me notice Theaetetus rather than Theodorus, or the lowliest of men? 

**THEAETETUS.** How could it? 

**SOCRATES.** But if I think of him not only as having a nose and eyes, but also a snub nose and prominent eyes, I will no more opine you than myself, or others who are such. 

**THEAETETUS.** Quite so. 

**SOCRATES.** But I think I will not opine Theaetetus until this snub-nosed shape—distinct from all other snub shapes I have seen—is impressed upon me by some mark proper to him...

<summary>Socrates and Theaetetus examine the third definition of "rational account" as the ability to identify the unique difference that distinguishes a thing from everything else. Socrates argues that even this fails to fully define knowledge, as one must already have a "right opinion" of those unique characteristics to identify the person at all.</summary>
<keywords>Theaetetus, Socrates, knowledge, opinion, rational account, definition, elements, syllables, unique difference, snub-nosed</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the dialogue of the Theaetetus and begins Marsilio Ficino’s introduction to the Ion. The catchword "tur" from the previous page connects to the first word "infitam" (likely part of "infinitam" or a similar construction in the original manuscript flow).</meta>

# BOOK FOURTEEN

<note>original: "infitam mihi distinguam"</note> I shall distinguish what is implanted in me: and other things similarly: from which you might recognize me. And if I then show you yourself, you will remember me: and you will cause yourself to have a correct opinion. THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Therefore, concerning the <term>proper difference</term> <note>The specific quality that distinguishes one thing from all others.</note>, a correct opinion revolves around each thing. THEAETETUS: It appears so. SOCRATES: What further thing will it be, then, to assume a definition along with a correct opinion? For if one says to simultaneously hold an opinion on the principle by which it is distinguished from others, the precept will be ridiculous. THEAETETUS: How so? SOCRATES: We consider those things of which we have a correct opinion insofar as they differ from others. And so your speech is in a way like a whip, or like a sort of turning of a staff or anything similar, as the proverb says; it would say nothing to either of us regarding this precept. For one would rightly call it a "blind man's precept." Since to command that we take up what we already have, in order to learn those things which we already opine, seems to be the mandate of a blind man. THEAETETUS: Come, tell me what you were just seeking? SOCRATES: If, O boy, to "receive a rational account" means to "know," and not merely to "opine the difference," then a rational account would be a sweet thing indeed, the most beautiful of all things pertaining to knowledge. For to receive knowledge is to know. THEAETETUS: It certainly is. SOCRATES: Therefore, being asked what knowledge is, one answers that it is correct opinion with the knowledge of the difference. For according to him, this would be the assumption of a rational account. THEAETETUS: So it seems. SOCRATES: It is altogether foolish, when we are seeking knowledge, to say it is correct opinion with knowledge—whether it be knowledge of the difference or of anything else. Therefore, neither sensation, O Theaetetus, nor true opinion, nor a rational account assumed with true opinion, is knowledge. THEAETETUS: Not as it seems. SOCRATES: Does any other offspring <note>Socrates famously compared his method to midwifery, helping others "give birth" to ideas.</note> regarding knowledge remain in us, my friend? Or have we now given birth to everything? THEAETETUS: By Jove, I have brought forth more through your leading than I had within myself. SOCRATES: Has not this midwifing art of ours shown that all these things were born empty and unworthy of upbringing? THEAETETUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: If, therefore, you should later strive to become full and fertile with other ideas, and you become pregnant, you will be full of better things because of the present discussion. And if perhaps you remain empty and sterile, you will certainly be less troublesome to your associates, and gentler through your <term>temperance</term> <note>Sophrosyne: self-control and self-knowledge.</note>: for you will not think you know what you do not know. My art can do this much, and nothing more. Nor do I know those things which many others—whoever are and have been great and wonderful men—know. But I and my mother were allotted this midwifing faculty by God: she indeed concerning women, but I concerning noble and honest youths. But now I must go to the King’s Porch; for Meletus has called me into judgment <note>A reference to the legal charges that led to Socrates' trial and death.</note>. Tomorrow at dawn, O Theodorus, we shall return here.

->THE END OF THE THEAETETUS, OR ON KNOWLEDGE.<-

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino the Florentine on Plato’s Ion, or on Poetic Frenzy, to Lorenzo de' Medici, a Magnanimous Man.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc> Our Plato, most excellent Lorenzo, defines <term>frenzy</term> <note>original: "furore"; refers to divine inspiration or "madness" rather than anger.</note> in the *Phaedrus* as an alienation of the mind. He hands down two kinds of alienation. One from human diseases. The other proceeding from God. The former he calls "insanity"; the latter he calls "divine frenzy." Insanity casts a man down below the human species and in a way renders a brute out of a man. Divine frenzy raises him above human nature and he passes into God. Moreover, divine frenzy is an illumination of the rational soul, through which God draws back the soul—which had fallen from the heights to the depths—from the depths back to the heights. The fall of the soul from the very One, the principle of all things, to bodies, is effected through four steps: through Mind, Reason, Opinion, and Nature. For since in the whole order of things there exist six steps—of which the highest holds the One itself, the lowest the body, while the middle are the four we mentioned—it is necessary that whatever falls from the first to the last must fall through the four middle steps. The One itself is the limit of all things, the measure of infinity, and devoid of multitude. Mind is indeed a multitude, but stable and eternal. Reason is a mobile multitude, but finite. Opinion is an infinite mobile multitude, but united in substance and points. Nature is similar, except that it is diffused through the points of the body. The body, however, is an infinite multitude, subject to motion, and divided in substance, points, and moments. Our soul regards all these: through these it descended, and through these it also ascends. For as it is produced from the One itself, which is the principle of all, it has been allotted a certain unity which unites its whole essence, powers, and actions; from which, and toward which, the other things in the soul are related, just as lines are from and toward the center of a circle. It unites not only the parts of the soul to each other and to the whole soul, but the whole soul to the One itself, the cause of all things. But as it depends on the Divine Mind, it contemplates the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect forms of things in Platonic philosophy.</note> of all things through the Mind in a stable act. As it regards itself, it thinks the universal reasons of things and discourses by reason from principles to conclusions. As it regards the body, it conceives the particular forms of mobile things by opinion and runs through them. As it works upon matter, it uses nature as an instrument by which it unites, moves, and forms matter; from which proceed generations, growth, and their opposites. You see, therefore, how it falls from the One, which is above eternity, into eternal multitude; from eternity into time; from time into place and matter. Wherefore, just as it descends through four steps, it must necessarily ascend through four. Moreover, divine frenzy is that which turns it back toward the things above, as stands in its definition. Therefore, four species of divine frenzy exist: first, poetic frenzy; second, the mystery-rite; third, divination; fourth, the affection of love. Poetry is from the Muses; mystery from Dionysus; divination from Apollo; and love from Venus. For the soul cannot return to the One unless it itself is made one. But having become many, it has fallen into the body, distributed into various operations, and looking toward individual things. From this, its superior parts almost fall asleep, while the inferior parts dominate the others. The former are affected by torpor, the latter by perturbation; the whole soul is filled with discord and lack of harmony. Therefore, there is need first of all for poetic frenzy, which through musical tones may arouse what is torpid, and through harmonic sweetness may [calm] what is tur... <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "tur" likely begins "turbantur" (disturbed).</note>

It then transitions into Marsilio Ficino's Neoplatonic introduction to Plato's Ion, explaining the "divine frenzy" and the soul's descent and ascent through the levels of reality.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the "Argument" or introductory summary to Plato's dialogue *Ion*, translated and commented upon by Marsilio Ficino. It establishes the Neoplatonic framework of the "four divine madnesses."</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE ION.

<note>original: "Argumentum in Ionem"</note>

...be soothed; finally, through the harmony of diverse things, let it drive away clashing discord and temper the various parts of the soul. Nor is this enough. For a multitude still remains in the soul. Therefore, a mystery is added which, through purifications and sacrifices and the entire worship of the gods, directs the intention of all the parts toward the mind, by which God is worshipped. Whence, since the individual parts of the soul have been reduced to a single mind, the soul has now become a certain whole "one" out of many. But thirdly, there is still need for a madness <note>Ficino uses "furor" to mean a divine frenzy or inspired state, not anger.</note> which may lead the mind back to unity itself, the head of the soul. Apollo effects this through prophecy. For when the soul rises above the mind into unity, it foretells future things. Finally, when the soul has been made one—the "one," I say, which exists in the very essence of the soul—it remains that it be immediately turned into the One which is above essence. Celestial Venus herself fulfills this through love, that is, the desire for divine beauty and the ardor for the Good.

Thus, the first madness tempers the unharmonious and discordant; the second makes a tempered whole out of the parts; the third makes a whole above the parts; the fourth leads into the One which is above essence and the whole. The first distinguishes the "good horse" (that is, reason and opinion) from the "bad horse" (that is, confused imagination and nature). <note>A reference to the chariot allegory in Plato's *Phaedrus*.</note> The second subjects the bad horse to the good, and the good to the charioteer (that is, the mind). The third directs the charioteer toward his own head (the apex of the unity of the mind). The last turns the head of the charioteer toward the Head of all things. There the charioteer is blessed, and standing his horses at the manger (that is, divine beauty), he sets before them ambrosia and nectar to drink (that is, the vision of beauty and the joy from that vision). These are the works of the four madnesses, about which Plato disputes generally in the *Phaedrus*: specifically about the last madness (love) in the *Symposium*; and about the first (poetic madness) in the present dialogue, which is titled *Ion*.

In the *Phaedrus*, he defines it thus: Poetic madness is a certain possession by the Muses, which, having obtained a tender and insuperable soul, awakens and rouses it through songs and other poetry for the instruction of the human race. "Possession" signifies the rapture of the soul and its conversion into the powers of the Muses. He calls it "tender," meaning agile and formable by the Muses; for unless it be prepared, they do not possess it. "Insuperable," because after it has been seized, it overcomes all things, and can be neither stained nor overcome by any inferior things. It "awakens" the body from sleep to the vigilance of the mind; from the darkness of ignorance to light; from death to life; from Lethean forgetfulness <note>Lethe was the river of forgetfulness in the underworld.</note> it recalls it to the remembrance of divine things. It "rouses," stimulates, and inflames it to express in songs those things which it contemplates and foretells. After the definition, he adds that he who approaches the gates of poetry without the madness of the Muses is himself empty, as is his poetry; as if poetry were of such great value that it cannot be acquired without the highest favor of God.

He delivers these same things in the *Ion*: both whence this madness comes and through how many steps it descends. Moreover, Plato says in the fourth book of the *Laws* that God, fortune, and art govern all human affairs. From which it follows that poetry is either a gift of God, or a chance of fortune, or a work of art. Socrates inquires with Ion the rhapsode which of these is most true.

<margin>What a rhapsode is.</margin>

A rhapsode in this book signifies a reciter, interpreter, and singer of poems. Ion interpreted the poems of Homer and sang to the lyre before the people; and he was so affected that he would explain no other poet besides Homer, even if they related the same things with the same facility as Homer. Moreover, he explained everything of Homer’s quickly. Whence he argued thus: Either Ion brings forth what Homer writes by chance, or by art, or by divine inspiration. Not by chance, because he would interpret not all things, but only a few, and without continuation or order. Not by art, because whoever possesses an entire art judges whatever is subject to that art. But the poems of Hesiod and others are subject to the same poetic study as those of Homer, especially those treating the same subjects; yet Ion does not perceive them, though he explains Homer perfectly. Therefore, he does not judge by art. It remains that it is by divine inspiration. From which it is clear that Ion, the interpreter of the poet, and many others who are similarly affected, interpret another's poetry by divine instinct. For if human genius is not sufficient to receive poetry already delivered, much less will it suffice for its invention. Therefore, neither Homer nor any other true poet attained poetry without celestial inspiration.

Socrates shows this here in other ways. First, thus: Poets deliver all arts and sciences. But it is impossible to have learned all these by human study, since it is difficult to perceive even one in part. Therefore, they bring them forth not by human art, but by a certain divine infusion. The proof of this is that many prophets, after the impetus of the madness has subsided, do not sufficiently understand what they have written, even though they treated individual arts correctly while in the madness—which the individual craftsmen of those arts judge by reading them. Furthermore, we often see a crude and inept man suddenly turn out to be a good poet and sing something magnificent and divine. To achieve great things in a moment is not the mark of human genius, but of one divinely inspired. In this matter, God clearly shows that this intelligence is infused by His will. And to demonstrate that it is so, He often seizes certain inept men rather than the polished, and the insane rather than the prudent; lest, if He used sharp and prudent men for these things, it might be thought that they were done by human subtlety and industry.

Since, therefore, poetry is not from fortune nor from art, it is granted by God and the Muses. When he says "God," he means Apollo; when "Muses," the souls of the spheres of the world. Jupiter is indeed the mind of God. From this comes Apollo, the mind of the soul of the world and the soul of the whole world; and the souls of the eight celestial spheres, which nine souls are called the nine Muses. Because while they move the heavens harmoniously, they produce musical melody; which, distributed into nine sounds—namely, the tones of the eight spheres and the one harmony of all—produces the nine sirens singing to God. Therefore, from Jupiter come Apollo and the Muses; from Apollo (that is, the mind of the soul of the world), the choir of Muses is led, because that mind, just as it is illuminated by Jupiter, so it illuminates the souls of the world and the spheres. Moreover, the steps by which that madness descends are these: Jupiter seizes Apollo. Apollo illuminates the Muses. The Muses awaken and rouse the tender and insuperable souls of the prophets. The inspired prophets inspire their interpreters. The interpreters, moreover, move the listeners. But by different Muses, different souls are seized.

<summary>This page introduces Plato's Ion by explaining the four types of divine inspiration (poetic, religious, prophetic, and amorous) and argues that true poetry is a gift from God rather than a learned skill.</summary>

# BOOK FIFTEEN

...because other souls have been attributed to the other spheres and stars, as [Plato] relates in the *Timaeus* <note>A Socratic dialogue by Plato concerning the nature of the physical world and human beings</note>. The Muse **Calliope** is the voice resulting from the voices of all the spheres. **Urania**, named for her dignity, belongs to the starry sky. **Polymnia** belongs to Saturn because of the memory of ancient things which Saturn exhibits, and his dry and cold complexion. **Terpsichore** is Jupiter, for he is a bringer of health to the chorus of men. **Clio** belongs to Mars, because of the desire for glory. **Melpomene** belongs to the Sun, because he is the tempering force of the whole world. **Erato** belongs to Venus because of love. **Euterpe** belongs to Mercury because of honest delight in serious matters. **Thalia** belongs to the Moon because of the greenness <note>vitality/growth</note> provided to things by her moisture. Likewise, **Apollo** is the soul of the Sun; his lyre is the body of the Sun; its four strings are his four motions: the annual, the monthly, the daily, and the oblique. There are four voices: the highest, the lowest, and the Dorian; there are four triplicities of the signs <note>Zodiac signs grouped by elements</note>, from which the four qualities of the seasons are produced. Indeed, Calliope inspired **Orpheus**. Urania inspired **Musaeus**. Clio inspired **Homer**. Polymnia inspired **Pindar**. Erato inspired **Sappho**. Melpomene inspired **Thamyris**. Terpsichore inspired **Hesiod**. Thalia inspired **Virgil** <note>original: "Maronem"</note>. Euterpe inspired **Ovid** <note>original: "Nasonem"</note>. The same spirit seized **Linus**, and the same **Phoebus** <note>Apollo</note> even now agitates you, O best **Lorenzo**—Phoebus, I say, who gave the prophecy to your grandfather **Cosimo**, the bow and medicines to your father **Piero**, and finally to you, the lyre and songs.

### THE *ION* OF PLATO, OR ON POETIC MADNESS, TRANSLATED FROM THE GREEK LANGUAGE INTO LATIN BY MARSILIO FICINO FOR THE MAGNANIMOUS LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

-> SOCRATES, ION. SOCRATES: <-

<margin>Homer is the best and most divine of all poets.</margin>
I bid **Ion** greetings. From where have you come to us? Do you come from Ephesus? **ION.** Not at all, Socrates, but from Epidaurus, from the festival of Asclepius. **SOCRATES.** Did the Epidaurians establish a contest for the rhapsodes <note>term: rhapsode; a professional performer of epic poetry in Ancient Greece</note>—that is, those who recite poems—not only in these but also in every other kind of music? **SOCRATES.** Compete with us then. **ION.** Why should I compete with you? We have already carried off the first prizes, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Well said. Come, let us pursue victory in the celebration of Pallas <note>Athena</note>. **ION.** These things shall happen if God wills it. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, O Ion, I have always highly valued your art. For it is worth much that it suits your art to adorn the body and appear as beautiful as possible; and that it is necessary to be conversant with many good poets, and especially with **Homer**, the best and most divine of all poets—not only to learn his verses, but also his meanings. For no one could ever become a rhapsode unless he understood what was said by the poet. For the rhapsode ought to interpret the mind of the poet to the listeners; but it is impossible for him to do this if he is ignorant of the poet's meaning. Therefore, all these things seem worthy of high regard. **ION.** You speak the truth, Socrates; and in this I have labored greatly. I profess that I can explain Homer more brilliantly than anyone else: so that neither Metrodorus of Lampsacus, nor Stesimbrotus of Thasos, nor Glaucon, nor any of the ancients could ever explain as many or as brilliant meanings of Homer as I can. **SOCRATES.** Rightly so, Ion. It is clear that no envy will prevent you from opening these things to me. **ION.** It is worth hearing how vehemently I have extolled Homer by adorning him. For which reason I judge myself worthy to be decorated with a golden crown by those who are students of Homer. **SOCRATES.** I shall certainly find leisure to hear you at some time; but for now, answer me this one thing: are you skilled only regarding Homer, or also regarding **Hesiod** and **Archilochus**? **ION.** Only regarding Homer. For that seems sufficient to me. **SOCRATES.** Are there not some things about which Homer and Hesiod report the same? **ION.** I believe there are many. **SOCRATES.** Would you explain those things which Homer says better, or those which Hesiod says? **ION.** Equally regarding both, Socrates, in those matters where they report the same. **SOCRATES.** But what about those things in which they do not say the same? For instance, both Homer and Hesiod speak about prophecy. **ION.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And in what these poets agree or disagree when they speak of prophecy, would you explain it better than some skilled prophet? **ION.** The prophet would explain it better. **SOCRATES.** But if you were a prophet, could you not explain not only those things in which they agree, but also those in which they disagree? **ION.** It is evident. **SOCRATES.** What then: are you powerful and eloquent only regarding Homer, but not at all regarding Hesiod and other poets? Does Homer <margin>What things are explained in all of Homer's poetry</margin> deal with different subjects than those which other poets treat? Has he not narrated many things pertaining to war, and to the customs of good and bad men toward one another, both private citizens and craftsmen? And has he not sung of the gods, how they act toward one another and deal with men; and of celestial passions and movements, and likewise of those things which are in the underworld, and the genealogies of heroes? Does not all of Homer's poetry revolve around these things? **ION.** You speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Do not the other poets sing of the same things? **ION.** Certainly the same, but not in the same way as Homer. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps worse? **ION.** Much worse. **SOCRATES.** Therefore Homer is better? **ION.** Better, certainly. **SOCRATES.** O Ion, you charming head: when many speak about numbers, and one of them speaks correctly, can someone not recognize the one speaking well in that matter? **ION.** He can. **SOCRATES.** Is it the same person who recognizes the one speaking poorly, or someone else? **ION.** The same person. **SOCRATES.** Is this not the one who is endowed with the art of arithmetic? **ION.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** When many speak about foods, which ones are healthy, and someone speaks correctly on that matter, will one person notice the one speaking well, and another notice the one speaking poorly? Or one and the same? **ION.** The same, without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Who is this? What is his name? **ION.** A physician. **SOCRATES.** Is it not...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and the rhapsode Ion regarding the nature of poetic inspiration. Socrates is arguing that Ion's skill is not a learned art (techne) but a divine gift.</meta>

# ION, OR ON POETIC FRENZY
## FOLIO LXVIII.
iiii
<meta>catchword: hymn</meta>

...we say in summary, when many people speak on the same subject, will not one and the same person distinguish between the one who speaks poorly and the one who speaks well? And unless he recognizes the one who errs on that subject, will he ever recognize the one who perceives it correctly? ION: Certainly. SOCRATES: And is he not himself equally skilled in both cases? ION: Entirely so. SOCRATES: You assert that Homer and other poets, among whose number are Hesiod and Archilochus <note>Hesiod and Archilochus were famous early Greek poets; Hesiod for didactic verse and Archilochus for iambic satire.</note>, report the same things—yet not in the same way, but Homer better? ION: And I speak the truth. SOCRATES: If you recognize the one who speaks well, you understand those who speak poorly, in that they err. ION: That is consistent. SOCRATES: If therefore we say, O best of men, that Ion is similarly skilled and powerful regarding Homer and other poets, we shall by no means be in error; since he himself confesses that the same judge is fit to evaluate those who are occupied with the same subject, and that almost all poets fashion the same things. ION: For what reason then, O Socrates, when someone discourses on another poet, do I neither pay attention nor am I able to contribute or compare anything worthy of esteem—but I immediately yawn and grow sluggish? Yet as soon as someone mentions Homer, I am instantly awakened and pay attention, and the faculty of speaking seems to supply itself to me? SOCRATES: It is by no means difficult, my friend, to guess the cause of this. For it is clear that you do not speak skillfully about Homer by art or science. For if it were by art, you would be able to speak similarly of all other poets, for poetry is surely a whole, is it not? ION: It certainly is. SOCRATES: Is it not true that after someone has acquired any other whole art, he judges equally regarding all things that fall under that art? Indeed, the method of consideration is the same for all arts. Do you wish for me to explain to you the reasoning by which I say this? ION: I desire it, by Jove, O Socrates. For as often as I hear you wise men, I am immediately affected by a certain wonderful joy. SOCRATES: I wish, O Ion, that you were speaking the truth. But you rhapsodes and actors are the "wise" ones, and those whose poems you sing; I, however, speak nothing but the truth, as befits a man of "plain wit" <note>original: "pinguis minervae hominem" - a Latin idiom for a person of plain, blunt common sense rather than subtle learning.</note>. For look at how slight and easy to know is that which I was asking about just now. Anyone can perceive what I was relating: namely, that things must be considered in the same way if one has acquired a whole art for oneself. For example: Is not the art of painting a certain whole? ION: It is. SOCRATES: Have there not been, and are there not now, many painters, some good and some bad? ION: Certainly. SOCRATES: Have you ever seen anyone who is able to sufficiently demonstrate both the things which Polygnotus son of Aglaophon <note>A famous 5th-century BC Greek painter.</note> painted correctly and those he did not, but is unable to do so for other painters? And if someone shows the work of other painters, he falls asleep, and no faculty for speaking or conjecturing is available to him; but when a judgment must be made concerning Polygnotus, or any other single painter, he wakes up, pays attention, and has the faculty of speech? ION: Not by Jove. SOCRATES: What about in the craft of statuary? Have you seen anyone who is able to explain the things which Daedalus son of Metion, or Epeius son of Panopeus, or Theodorus of Samos, or any other maker of statues has well-contrived, but in the works of other sculptors he grows sluggish and falls silent? ION: By Jove, I have never found such a man. SOCRATES: And yet, I think, neither in the blowing of flutes, nor in the plucking of the cithara, nor in singing to the cithara, nor in rhapsody have you ever looked upon a man who can explain the works of Olympus, or Thamyris, or Orpheus, or Phemius the rhapsode of Ithaca, but fails in the works of Ion of Ephesus, and can neither perceive nor compare what he modulates well and what he does poorly. ION: I have nothing to say to contradict you in this; but nevertheless I am conscious within myself that I report the most beautiful things about Homer beyond all other men, and that a wealth of speaking does not fail me. And all others praise me in this matter, but in other poets they do not. See then what this might be. SOCRATES: I see it, Ion; and I will begin to reveal to you what it seems to me to be. That you speak well of Homer is not provided to you by art, as I was just saying; but it is a **divine power** that moves you, just as in the stone which Euripides named the Magnet, but which some call the Heraclean stone.

<margin>
Concerning the stone called the magnet, also the Heraclean stone.
</margin>

This stone not only attracts iron rings, but also infuses a power into the rings themselves, by which they can do this same thing: and just like the stone, they attract other rings. Whence a long chain of iron and rings often hangs together; and for all of these, the power of attraction comes from that stone. In the same way, the Muse herself incites poets by divine instinct; and the poets, having been incited, seize others with their frenzy. Therefore, from all these, the series itself is woven together. Thus all the distinguished poets of songs sing all those famous poems not by art, but by divine inspiration; and just as the Corybantes <note>Priests of Cybele who performed ecstatic, frenzied dances.</note> do not dance with a sane mind, so the excellent modulators of songs do not fashion these chants with a sane mind; but when they rise into harmony and rhythm, they are possessed and become like Bacchants; just as the Bacchic women, with an insane mind, draw honey and milk from the rivers, but are unable to draw them with a sane mind. And the soul of those who fashion the songs produces that which they themselves report. For the poets tell us that, drawing from the fountains where honey gushes forth, and plucking from the gardens and hills of the Muses, they bring songs to us, just as bees bring honey from flowers; and they assert that they fly like bees. In which matter they speak the truth. For the poet is a **light, volatile, and sacred thing**; nor can he sing poetically before he is full of the god, and placed outside himself, and alienated from his mind. For as long as anyone is master of his mind, he can neither fashion songs nor give oracles. It is as if poets do not sing these famous things you report about Homer by art, but by chance each one is able to do that correctly to which the Muse has incited him. This one sings dithyrambs; this one praises someone; that one sings dance-songs and choruses; another epic poems; another iambics. In other things, each of them is unskilled and inept. For they say these things not by art but by divine power. For if they knew how to speak correctly about one of these by art, they would be able to do the same for all the others. For this reason, God, taking away their mind, uses them as his ministers, and as messengers of oracles and divine prophets, so that we who hear may perceive that it is not they who report such worthy things—since they are least in control of their own minds—but that God speaks these things and cries them out to us through them. A most evident proof of this matter can be Tynichus of Chalcis, who previously had composed no poem worthy of memory, yet wrote a hymn...

Praise of poets.

### THE BOOK OF PLATO, OR ON POETIC FRENZY, TRANSLATED FROM THE GREEK LANGUAGE INTO LATIN BY MARSILIO FICINO FOR THE MAGNANIMOUS LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

-> SOCRATES AND ION. <-

<margin>Homer is the best and most divine of all poets.</margin>
**SOCRATES:** I bid Ion greetings. From where have you come to us? Do you come from Ephesus? **ION:** Not at all, Socrates, but from Epidaurus, from the festival of Asclepius. **SOCRATES:** Did the Epidaurians establish a contest for the rhapsodes <note>performers who recited epic poetry</note>—that is, those who recite poems—in honor of the god? And was it only in this, or in other kinds of music as well? **ION:** In all kinds. **SOCRATES:** Did you compete then? **ION:** Indeed, and we carried off the first prizes, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** You speak well. Come, let us see if we may achieve victory in the celebration of Pallas <note>Athena</note>. **ION:** These things shall be, if God wills it. **SOCRATES:** Truly, Ion, I have always highly valued your art. For it is worth much that it suits your art to adorn the body and appear as beautiful as possible; and that it is necessary to be conversant with many good poets, and especially with **Homer**, the best and most divine of all poets—not only to learn his verses, but also his meanings. For no one could ever become a rhapsode unless he understood what was said by the poet. For the rhapsode ought to interpret the mind of the poet to the listeners; but it is impossible for him to do this if he is ignorant of the poet's meaning. Therefore, all these things seem worthy of high esteem. **ION:** You speak the truth, Socrates; and in this I have labored greatly. I profess that I can explain the meanings of Homer more brilliantly than anyone else; so that neither Metrodorus of Lampsacus, nor Stesimbrotus of Thasos, nor Glaucon, nor any of the ancients could ever explain as many or as excellent meanings of Homer as I can. **SOCRATES:** Rightly said, Ion. It is clear that no envy will prevent you from opening these things to me. **ION:** It is worth hearing how vehemently I have extolled Homer by adorning him. For which reason I judge myself worthy to be decorated with a golden crown by those who are students of Homer. **SOCRATES:** I shall certainly find leisure to hear you at some time; but for now, answer me this one thing: are you skilled only in Homer, or also in **Hesiod** and **Archilochus**? **ION:** Only in Homer. For that seems sufficient to me. **SOCRATES:** Are there not some things about which Homer and Hesiod report the same? **ION:** I believe there are many. **SOCRATES:** Would you explain those things which Homer says better than those which Hesiod explains? **ION:** Equally well for both, Socrates, in those matters where they report the same. **SOCRATES:** What about those things in which they do not say the same? For instance, both Homer and Hesiod speak about divination. **ION:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** And in those things where these poets agree or disagree when they speak of divination, would you explain them better than a skilled diviner <note>prophet/seer</note> would? **ION:** A diviner would explain them better. **SOCRATES:** But if you were a diviner, would you not be able to explain not only those things in which they agree, but also those in which they differ? **ION:** It is evident I would. **SOCRATES:** What then: are you powerful and eloquent regarding Homer, but not at all regarding Hesiod and other poets? Does Homer deal with different subjects than those which other poets treat? Did he not narrate many things pertaining to war, and to the mutual customs of the good and the bad, of private citizens and craftsmen? And did he not sing of the gods, how they interact with each other and with men, and of celestial passions and movements, as well as things in the underworld and the genealogies of gods and heroes? Does not all of Homer's poetry revolve around these things? **ION:** You speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Do not the other poets sing of the same things? **ION:** Certainly the same, but not in the same way as Homer. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps worse? **ION:** Much worse. **SOCRATES:** Therefore Homer is better? **ION:** Better, certainly. **SOCRATES:** O charming Ion: when many speak about numbers, and one of them speaks correctly, cannot someone recognize the one who speaks well in that matter? **ION:** He can. **SOCRATES:** Is it the same person who recognizes the one speaking poorly, or someone else? **ION:** The same person. **SOCRATES:** And is this not the one who is endowed with the art of arithmetic? **ION:** Indeed. **SOCRATES:** When many speak about foods, which ones are healthy, and someone speaks correctly on that matter, will one person notice the one speaking well, and another notice the one speaking poorly? Or is it one and the same person? **ION:** The same, without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Who is this? What is his name? **ION:** A physician. **SOCRATES:** Is it not...

# ION, OR ON POETIC FRENZY. FOLIO LXVIII.

...we say in short, when many people speak on the same subject, that one and the same person will distinguish both the one who speaks poorly and the one who speaks well? Or if he does not recognize the one who errs in that same matter, will he ever recognize the one who perceives it correctly? ION: Certainly. SOCRATES: And is not that same man skilled in both? ION: Entirely. SOCRATES: Do you assert that Homer and other poets, among whose number are Hesiod and Archilochus <note>Hesiod and Archilochus were famous early Greek poets; Hesiod for didactic epics and Archilochus for iambic satire.</note>, report the same things? Yet not in the same way, but that Homer speaks better? ION: And I speak the truth in saying so. SOCRATES: If you recognize the one who speaks well, you must understand that those who speak poorly are in error. ION: That follows. SOCRATES: If therefore we say, O best of men, that Ion is similarly skilled and powerful regarding Homer and other poets, we shall by no means be in error; since he himself confesses that the same judge is fit to evaluate those who are engaged in the same subject; and indeed almost all poets fashion the same things. ION: Why is it then, O Socrates, that when someone discusses another poet, I neither pay attention nor am I able to contribute or compare anything worthy of esteem—but I immediately yawn and grow sluggish? Yet as soon as someone makes mention of Homer, I am instantly awakened and pay attention, and the faculty of speaking seems to supply itself to me? SOCRATES: It is by no means difficult, my friend, to guess the cause of this. For it is evident that you do not speak skillfully about Homer by art or science. For if it were by art, you would be able to speak similarly of all other poets. For is not poetry a whole? ION: It certainly is. SOCRATES: And is it not true that after someone has acquired any other whole art, he judges equally regarding all things that fall under that art? Indeed, the method of consideration is the same for all arts. Do you wish for me to explain the reason why I say this? ION: I desire it, by Jove, O Socrates. For as often as I hear you wise men, I am immediately affected by a certain wonderful joy. SOCRATES: I wish, O Ion, that you were speaking the truth. But you rhapsodes and actors are the "wise" ones, along with those whose poems you chant; I, however, speak nothing but the truth, as befits a man of "thick Minerva" <note>original: "pinguis mineruæ hominē" — a Latin idiom for a man of plain, blunt common sense without refined artifice.</note>. For look at the matter I was asking about just now, how slight it is and easy to know. Anyone can perceive what I was saying: namely, that in the same way, individual things must be considered if one has acquired a whole art for oneself. For example: Is not the art of painting a certain whole? ION: It is. SOCRATES: And are there not, and have there not been, many painters, some good and some bad? ION: Certainly. SOCRATES: Have you ever seen anyone who is able to sufficiently demonstrate the things which Polygnotus son of Aglaophon <note>A famous 5th-century BC Greek painter.</note> painted correctly, and those he did not, but is unable to do so for other painters? And if someone shows the work of other painters, he falls asleep, and no faculty for saying or guessing anything is available to him; but when a judgment must be made about Polygnotus, or any other single painter, he wakes up, pays attention, and has the faculty of speech? ION: Not by Jove. SOCRATES: What about in the craft of statuary? Have you seen anyone who is able to explain the things which Daedalus son of Metion, or Epius son of Panopeus, or Theodorus of Samos, or any other sculptor has well-contrived, but in the works of other sculptors he grows sluggish and falls silent? ION: By Jove, I have never found such a man. SOCRATES: And yet, neither in the blowing of flutes, I think, nor in the striking of the lyre, nor in singing to the lyre, nor in rhapsody have you seen a man who can interpret the works of Olympus, or Thamyris, or Orpheus, or Phemius the rhapsode of Ithaca, but fails in the works of Ion of Ephesus, and can neither perceive nor compare what is modulated well and what is not. ION: I have no way to contradict you in this; but nevertheless I am conscious within myself that I report the most beautiful things about Homer beyond all other men, and that I do not lack an abundance of speech. And all others praise me in this matter, but in other matters they do not. See then what this might be. SOCRATES: I see it, Ion; and I will begin to open to you what it seems to me to be. That you speak well of Homer is not an art present in you, as I was just saying; but it is a divine power that moves you, just as in the stone which Euripides named the Magnet, but which some call the Heraclean stone.

<margin>Concerning the stone called the Magnet, also the Heraclean stone.</margin>
This stone not only attracts iron rings, but also infuses a power into the rings themselves, by which they can do this same thing: and just like the stone, they attract other rings. Whence a long chain of iron and rings often hangs together; and for all of these, the power is drawn from that stone. So the Muse herself incites poets by divine instinct; and the poets, having been incited, seize others with frenzy. Therefore, from all these, the series itself is woven together. Thus all the famous poets of songs sing all those distinguished poems not by art, but by divine inspiration; and just as the Corybantes <note>Priests of Cybele known for ecstatic, frenzied dancing.</note> do not dance with a sane mind, so the excellent modulators of songs do not fashion these chants with a sane mind; but when they rise into harmony and rhythm, they are occupied and become like Bacchants; just as the Bacchic women, not being of sane mind, draw honey and milk from the rivers, but cannot draw them when they are of sane mind. And the soul of those who fashion the songs works this, as they themselves report. For the poets tell us that, drawing from the fountains where honey gushes, and plucking from the gardens and hills of the Muses, they bring the songs to us, just as bees bring honey from flowers; and they assert that they fly like bees.

<margin>The place of poets.</margin>
<margin>The Corybantes are of insane mind.</margin>
In which matter they speak the truth. For the poet is a light, volatile, and sacred thing; nor can he sing poetry before he is full of the god, and placed outside himself, and alienated from his mind. For as long as anyone is master of his mind, he can neither fashion songs nor give oracles. It is as if poets do not sing these famous things by art—the things you report about Homer—but by chance and divine power each one is able to do correctly that which the Muse has incited him to. This one sings dithyrambs; this one praises someone; that one sings dance-songs and choruses; another epic poems; another iambics. But in other things, each of them is unskilled and inept. For they do not say these things by art but by divine power. For if they knew how to speak correctly about one of these by art, they would be able to do the same for all the others. For this reason, God, taking away their mind, uses them as his ministers, and as messengers of oracles and divine prophets, so that we who hear may perceive that it is not they who report such worthy things, since they are least in control of their own minds; but that God is speaking these things, and through them, he is calling out to us. An most evident proof of this matter can be Tynnichus of Chalcis, who previously had composed no poem worthy of memory, but [composed] a hymn...

<margin>The poet is a light, volatile, and sacred thing.</margin>

# BOOK FOURTEEN

<margin>
Poets are the interpreters of the gods.
</margin>

...but as for the song to Apollo which everyone sings—perhaps the most beautiful of all songs—he is said to have discovered it through the inspiration of the Muses. In this, the god seems to have shown us most clearly that we should not doubt that these excellent poems are divine works of the gods rather than human works of men. For poets are nothing other than the interpreters of the gods, provided they are seized by a divine frenzy <note>original: "furore"; referring to the Platonic concept of 'divine madness' or poetic inspiration</note>, regardless of which deity possesses them. Indeed, the god intended to demonstrate this by purposely singing the most beautiful melody through the most unskilled poet. Do I not seem to be telling you the truth? ION: To me, certainly. You touch my soul with these words, Socrates, and you affect me; for it seems to me that by some divine fate, distinguished poets interpret these things for us from the gods. SOCRATES: Do you rhapsodes <note>A professional performer or reciter of epic poetry</note> not interpret the writings of the poets? ION: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Are you not, then, interpreters of interpreters? ION: We are. SOCRATES: Pay attention to what I want, and answer me this, Ion; do not hide from me that which I shall ask you. When you recite verses aptly and leave the spectators struck with amazement—whether you are singing of Ulysses leaping onto the threshold of his home and revealing himself to the suitors, pouring out his arrows before his feet; or of Achilles rushing at Hector; or when you utter something piteous and lamentable concerning Andromache, or Hecuba, or Priam—are you then in your right mind? Or are you alienated from your mind? And is your soul, inspired by the deeds you recount, convinced it is present there, whether the events take place in Ithaca or at Troy, or wherever the verses carry you? ION: You have brought me a very clear observation, Socrates. I will not hide it from you as I recount this. For whenever I say anything piteous, my eyes are sprinkled with tears. When I say something terrifying or vehement, my hair stands on end from terror and my heart leaps. SOCRATES: Shall we say then that a man is in his right mind who, at sacrifices and festivals, adorned in beautiful clothing and golden crowns, weeps when he has lost none of these things? Or who feels fear while standing among enemies, more than he usually would when he is situated among many friends, where no one strips him or does him any injury? ION: No, by Jove, Socrates, if we wish to confess the truth. SOCRATES: Have you noticed that the multitude of spectators is moved by these same things you perform? ION: I have indeed seen it often; I look down from the platform itself and see them weeping, staring intensely, and stunned by the things being narrated. And I must pay great attention to them. For if I move them to tears, I myself shall receive money and laugh; but if I move them to laughter, I myself shall lose money and weep. SOCRATES: Do you see then that the spectator is the last of the rings—those which I said receive power from one another under the magnet stone? <note>Socrates uses the metaphor of a magnet to show how divine inspiration flows from the Muse to the poet, then to the rhapsode, and finally to the audience.</note> You, the reciter and actor, are the middle; the first is the poet himself; but God, through all of these, draws the souls of men wherever He wishes, while He suspends and transmits the power from one to another. From this, as if from that stone, a long series hangs, where those who dance in the chorus, and the teachers and disciples, are linked step by step at the side; the rings of this chain are suspended from the Muse. One poet is suspended from one Muse, another from another. We call this being "possessed," which is indeed very close to it. For he is held by these first rings, which are the poets; others in turn are seized by others and become divine: some by Orpheus, others by Musaeus, and many are possessed and held by Homer—of whom you, Ion, are one. You are seized by a frenzy from Homer. And if anyone sings the works of another poet, you fall asleep and lack the faculty of speaking. But if anyone chants a melody of this poet [Homer], you are immediately awakened, your soul leaps, and your faculty of speaking suffices. For it is not by art or science, but by a certain divine fate and possession of the mind that you recount what you say about Homer. And just as the Corybantes <note>Priests of Cybele known for ecstatic dancing and music</note> are only acutely sensitive to that melody which belongs to the god by whom they are possessed—and they abound in words and gestures fitting to that harmony, while they ignore others—so you, Ion, when someone mentions Homer, you are eloquent in speaking; but in other matters, you lack the capacity. This is the cause of what you were asking: why you are so fluent regarding Homer but fail regarding others. It is because you are a vehement praiser of Homer not by art, but by divine fate. ION: You speak rightly, Socrates. Yet I would be surprised if you could argue so sharply as to persuade me entirely that I celebrate Homer's praises while being "moon-struck" <note>original: "lymphatum"; meaning distracted, frantic, or possessed</note> and raving. For I do not think I would seem like a madman to you if you heard me speaking about Homer. SOCRATES: Indeed, I wish to hear you; but not before you answer me which of the things Homer deals with are those he deals with best. For he does not deal with all things. ION: You know well, Socrates, that there is nothing he does not deal with. SOCRATES: Yet he does not treat well those things which you are ignorant of, but which Homer writes about. ION: What are those things which Homer narrates but I do not know? SOCRATES: Does he not frequently explain many things about the arts? For instance, about the discipline of chariot-driving. If I remember the verses, I will recite them to you. ION: But I will recite them; for I remember. SOCRATES: Tell me what Nestor commands his son Antilochus when he advises him to turn the horses cautiously while running in the equestrian race established in honor of Patroclus. ION: *Lean a little to the left, and urge the right horse with lashes and threats, while also loosening the reins with your hands. When you reach the turning post, let the left horse be turned inward, until the edge of the axle-hub seems to reach the very limit; but avoid the middle stone.* <note>A translation of Homer's Iliad, Book 23</note> SOCRATES: These are sufficient, Ion. Whether Homer speaks rightly or otherwise in these verses, who would perceive it better: a physician or a charioteer? ION: A charioteer, without a doubt. SOCRATES: Is this judgment made by art, or by something else? ION: By nothing other than art. SOCRATES: Has not God granted to each art the faculty of judging a certain specific work? For we shall not perceive through the medical art those things which we know through the art of steering a ship. ION: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Nor shall we observe through architecture those things we see through medicine. ION: Surely not. SOCRATES: Is it not similarly so in all arts, that what we comprehend by one specific art, we least comprehend by another—

# BOOK FOURTEEN

<note>The dialogue continues with Socrates questioning Ion, a professional reciter of poetry (rhapsode), on whether his skill is a technical art or divine inspiration.</note>

...tes. SOCRATES: Is it not true that he who is the best commander of an army is also a good reciter? ION: Not at all. SOCRATES: But do you admit this: that whoever is a good reciter is also a good commander? ION: Very much so. SOCRATES: Are you not the best reciter among the Greeks? ION: Clearly, O Socrates. SOCRATES: And are you also the best commander among the Greeks? ION: Certainly, O Socrates, for I have learned these things from the writings of Homer. SOCRATES: Why then, by the gods, since you are the best army leader of all the Greeks as well as the best reciter, do you go about performing poems but never lead a military force? Do you think a reciter decorated with a golden crown is of great use to the Greeks, but a commander is of no use at all? ION: O Socrates, our city <note>Ephesus</note> is subject to yours and governed by you; therefore it does not need a commander. Your state and that of the Spartans would never choose me as a leader of the army, for you believe yourselves to be suitable leaders. SOCRATES: O excellent Ion, do you not know Apollodorus of Cyzicus? ION: Which Apollodorus? SOCRATES: That man, of course, whom the Athenians often chose as commander even though he was a foreign guest; and Phanosthenes of Andros; and Heraclides of Clazomenae. This city, though they were foreigners, appointed them to the praetorship and other magistracies because they showed themselves to be outstanding men. Will the city then not choose Ion of Ephesus as a commander and affect him with honor, if he is seen to excel in virtue? What of it? Are you Ephesians not Athenians by ancient origin, and is Ephesus inferior to any city? But you, O Ion, if you speak the truth and are able to praise Homer by knowledge and art, you do me an injustice. For after professing to know many beautiful things about Homer and promising to show them to me, you now deceive me; you are far from showing them, since you are unwilling to reveal what those things are in which you are skilled, nor what faculty you are equipped with, despite my long entreaty. Instead, you turn like a shifting Proteus <note>A sea-god capable of changing shapes</note>, twisting up and down, until finally, escaping me, you emerge as a commander—all so you don't have to show me how your skill regarding the wisdom of Homer works. For if this skill is in you by art, as I just said, and you deceive me after promising to explain it, you are certainly unjust. But if you lack the art and are instead snatched up by Homer through a certain divine fate, and though you understand nothing, you say many beautiful things about this poet (as I judged of you), then you do no injustice. Choose which you prefer: to be called an unjust man, or rather a divine one. ION: There is a great difference, O Socrates; it is much more beautiful to be judged divine. SOCRATES: This more beautiful thing, then, is what you have with us, O Ion: that you are a divine rather than an artistic praiser of Homer.

-> Preface to Plato’s Sophist according to Proclus, translated by Marsilio Ficino. <-

<margin>Properties of the sublunary craftsman.</margin>
Plato calls the "Sophist" not only a certain type of man, but also Love, Pluto, and Jove; and he says the sophistic art is most noble. From this we understand that this dialogue regards a more noble subject than it appears. For it is the intention, according to the great Iamblichus, to treat the "sublunary craftsman" <note>The 'demiurge' or force shaping the world below the moon</note>. For he is a maker of idols, a purifier of souls, always separating them from contrary reasonings; a transmutator; and a mercenary hunter of wealthy youths. While he receives souls full of reasonings coming from above, he receives a reward from them: the very fabric of the souls, which is made according to the reckoning of mortals. He occupies himself with that which "is not," because he brings into being things that are in matter. And he loves what is truly false—that is, matter. Yet at the same time, he looks toward that which truly "is." He is also "many-headed," since he has claimed for himself many vital essences through which he disposes the variety of generation. He is also a magician of generation, while he soothes and allures souls with natural reasonings, so that they are moved away from generation only with difficulty. Indeed, both Love is called a magician and Nature a sorceress by some, because of the reciprocal attractions and enticements that proceed according to nature. Now, therefore, he wishes to declare the sophist in every way. For the philosopher is a sophist, since he imitates the celestial craftsman and the craftsman of generation. And the distributive faculty imitates the progress of things from the One; and the craftsman of generation imitates the celestial craftsman, wherefore he is a sophist. And even man himself is a sophist, because he is called a sophist for imitating great things. And for that reason, he called the sophist "many-headed." The Eleatic Guest represents the father of craftsmen, super-celestial and absolute. The listeners, however, represent the intelligences of the craftsman—the one of Jove, the other of the angelic nature, acting as an interpreter and geometer. And since the craftsmanship, beginning from the thing inspected, ends in perfection, that Guest deals first with Theodorus, then by conversion with Socrates himself. Thus far Proclus. Next, Marsilio’s notes. AFTER the *Theaetetus* concerning knowledge, the *Sophist* must be read concerning "Being" itself, which is the object of knowledge. While "Being" is discussed here (the concern of the philosopher), "Non-being" is treated meanwhile, toward which the sophist declines. According to Pythagoras and Plato, *sophos*—that is, "wise"—is God alone. The philosopher, however, is the true imitator of God. The sophist is the ambitious and deceptive rival of the philosopher. Plato brings forward six definitions of the sophist. Because a definition cannot be had without division (through which those things that do not belong to the thing being defined are separated, and its genus is divided by differences, from which finally the species is composed and defined), Plato, intending to define the sophist, first devises the most exact partitions. He warns that no one can discern the hidden nature of any thing unless they separate it entirely from foreign qualities...

<margin>Love the magician and nature the sorceress.</margin>

<margin>According to Pythagoras and Plato, God alone is wise. Who is the philosopher.</margin>

# FOLIO 70.
## THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING.

<note>This introductory paragraph by Ficino summarizes the dialogue's metaphysical arguments.</note>
...has separated from you. Accordingly, he brings forth descriptions of being and non-being to the best of his ability, and subjects being—just as in the *Parmenides*—to the One. He counts five genera <note>technical term: *genera*, the "Great Kinds" of being</note> of being: essence, identity, and difference, rest, and motion. He teaches that true essence belongs to incorporeal things, while imaginary essence belongs to corporeal ones. Furthermore, he greatly detests those who deny the existence of the incorporeal, as well as those who think either that all things are in motion alone, or that all things remain only at rest. Likewise, he disputes concerning science and opinion, and true or false speech, and concerning the verb and the noun, insofar as it is seen to pertain to the disputation of being itself. Finally, after he has disputed concerning the sophist and the philosopher together, he concludes the book with a certain divine sentiment: namely, that natural things are the works of God. Indeed, he had proved that all works of nature proceed from a certain divine wisdom infused into the world. But shadowy and fallacious things, he says, are demonic deceptions. In the same place, he says that the sophist is hidden from us as if enveloped in the darkness of non-being (that is, the false), and that the philosopher is likewise hidden, but for another reason: because, namely, being surrounded on all sides by the splendor of being itself (that is, divine truth), he utterly surpasses the intuition of common minds.

<margin>Being under the One and the five genera of being.</margin>
<margin>Natural things are the works of God.</margin>

### PLATO’S SOPHIST, OR ON THAT WHICH IS, OR BEING, TRANSLATED FROM GREEK BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI, THE MAGNANIMOUS MAN.

### THEODORUS. THEAETETUS. SOCRATES. THE VISITOR FROM ELEA, WHO PERHAPS IS MELISSUS. THEODORUS.

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue.</margin>
<margin>God dwells among modest men.</margin>
We have come, O Socrates, at an opportune time, just as we agreed among ourselves yesterday; and we bring this guest here with us, who is from Elea, of the circle of Parmenides and Zeno: a man especially studious of wisdom. SOCRATES. Perhaps, O Theodorus, while you believe you are bringing a guest with you, you are bringing a certain god. For Homer says that, among other gods, the god of hospitality especially dwells among men who participate in just modesty, to look upon the insults and injuries of men. Perhaps even here one of those from above has followed you, to examine and correct us who wander from the paths of disputation. And he himself is a god of refutation. THEODORUS. This is not the manner, O Socrates, of this guest. He is more modest than those who are devoted to controversies. To me, he seems to be no god among men, but someone divine. Indeed, I call all philosophers divine. SOCRATES. And rightly so, my friend. Yet the race of philosophers is not much easier to discern, so to speak, than that of the gods. For all those who philosophize not falsely but truly, appear in many forms because of the ignorance of others, while they travel through cities and look down upon the life of those below as if from a high watchtower. And these are esteemed as nothing by some, while by others they are honored in the highest degree. And sometimes they appear as statesmen, at other times as sophists, and occasionally, in the opinion of some, they are held to be altogether insane. Therefore, I desire to inquire of this guest, if it should be pleasing to him, what his associates in Elea think of these, what they say they are, and how they name them. THEODORUS. Which things are those? SOCRATES. The sophist, I say, the statesman, and the philosopher. THEODORUS. What specifically, and of what sort, is the doubt that has arisen concerning these, or what do you think should be sought? SOCRATES. This: whether they wish all these to be one, or two. Or whether, just as there are three names, they have also distinguished three genera, assigning individual names to individual genera. THEODORUS. No envy, I think, will prevent him from explaining these things to you. But what do you say, guest? VISITOR. What you say also: there is certainly no envy; nor is it difficult to say that they thought there were three. But to distinguish them individually, and to define what each one is, is neither a small task nor an easy one. THEODORUS. You have happened, O Socrates, upon the very same question which we also, before we came here, asked of him; and he answered us then the same things he now answers you: that he had indeed heard it, and remembered it. SOCRATES. In that which we first asked, therefore, you ought to gratify us, O guest. But first declare this to us: whether you are accustomed to explain what you wish to bring forward by yourself in a continuous speech, or rather by questioning, in the manner Parmenides used to follow? Whom I, as a youth, once heard disputing in that way when he was quite an old man, bringing forth most beautiful arguments. VISITOR. If one responds easily and aptly, it is easier to discourse with another by questioning; but if not, it is easier for each to dispute by himself. SOCRATES. You may therefore choose whichever of these you wish. For all will most willingly comply. I indeed advise you to choose some young man, either this Theaetetus, or any other who seems more fit to you. VISITOR. A certain shame and modesty holds me back, O Socrates, since I am speaking with you for the first time, not to return word for word in turn, but to begin a long discourse, whether alone by myself or with another responding for the sake of demonstration. For no one should trust that what has just been asked can be explained lightly. For it requires a long disputation. On the other hand, if I do not comply with you, and especially with these men, when you have asked so modestly, it seems to me it would be something boorish and foreign to the gentleness of a guest. Especially since I shall have this Theaetetus as a companion in disputation, based on what I was saying and what you just ordered. THEAETETUS. Certainly so, O guest...

<margin>Parmenides used to dispute by questioning.</margin>
