# FIFTEENTH BOOK

<margin>Knowledge of a thing with its underlying reasons excels over knowing the name alone.</margin>
As Socrates says, you will gratify everyone. GUEST: There is nothing further to be said against these things, Theaetetus. From here on, I must deal with you. If by chance the length of this discourse becomes tedious to you and you grow weary from the labor, I pray you, do not blame me, but these companions of yours who are the cause of it. THEAETETUS: I do not think anything will be troublesome; for if I happen to become exhausted, we shall call upon this Socrates <note>Referring to "Socrates the Younger," a student often distinguished from the famous philosopher</note>, who is similar to Socrates in name, but to me a partner and equal in exercise, who is accustomed to carrying out many laborious tasks with me. GUEST: You speak well; and concerning these matters, you will deliberate with yourself as the talk proceeds. But now you must consider with me in common: we should begin, it seems to me, with the Sophist himself, and first define what he is. For at present, you and I have only this common name in hand. As for the thing itself which is designated by the name, perhaps each of us conceives of it differently. It is better in every case to perceive the thing itself through its reasons <note>original: "cum rationibus" — meaning with a logical definition or structural understanding</note> than to know the name alone without a reason. Indeed, this genus of the "Sophist" which we are now seeking is not easily defined. It is a common opinion of all that if one wishes to handle great matters correctly, one ought to consider them first in certain smaller and easier things before the greatest. Since I believe the genus of the Sophist is difficult to grasp, I advise us, O Theaetetus—

<margin>An ancient opinion regarding the knowledge of great things.</margin>
—that we first practice that method of inquiry on something else that is easier. Unless, perhaps, you can show a more convenient way. THEAETETUS: I have no more convenient way. GUEST: Do you wish for us to bring forward something small and cheap as an example for the greater thing itself? THEAETETUS: I do. GUEST: Should we not propose something well-known and slight, which nevertheless contributes to the understanding of greater things? Such as the fisherman. For that is a light and slight thing. THEAETETUS: Certainly. GUEST: Yet it seems to have a path and a logic suited to the matter we are discussing. THEAETETUS: That would be excellent. GUEST: Come then, let us begin from here.

<margin>A transition must be made to easier things so that what is sought may be known.</margin>
Tell me whether we should place him as a man of art <note>A skilled professional</note>, or as one unskilled in art, but a participant in some other power. THEAETETUS: By no means unskilled in art. GUEST: There are roughly two species of all arts. THEAETETUS: Which? GUEST: Agriculture, and the care of any mortal body, and every faculty concerned with any composite thing fashioned or turned, which is commonly called "equipment," and that which imitates these; I say this entire faculty of this kind ought to be called by one common name. THEAETETUS: In what way? And by what name? GUEST: Whenever someone brings into being that which was not before, we say that he who acts "makes," and that which is acted upon "is made." THEAETETUS: Correct. GUEST: All the things we just recounted have power toward this end. THEAETETUS: They certainly do. GUEST: Let us therefore name them, in summary, the "productive faculty." THEAETETUS: So be it. GUEST: But all species of learning and knowledge, and that which is skill in gain, competition, and hunting, should be called in summary the "art of acquisition"; since none of these manufactures anything, but rather acquires things that are and have been—partly taking them by words and actions, and partly not yielding to those who would take them. THEAETETUS: That is fitting. GUEST: Since every art is engaged either in acquiring or in producing, in which genus shall we place the skill of fishing? THEAETETUS: In that which acquires, obviously. GUEST: Are there not two species of that which acquires? One is exchange between willing parties, by gift, purchase, or wage. The other is taking possession <note>original: "mancipatio" — a legal term for formal transfer or seizure</note> made either by deed or by word. THEAETETUS: From what has been said, it is clear that this is so. GUEST: Taking possession is twofold. THEAETETUS: In what way? GUEST: One is open, which takes by contending. The other is hidden, which takes by hunting. THEAETETUS: So it is. GUEST: It is also fitting to divide hunting in two. THEAETETUS: How in two? GUEST: It hunts either a thing without a soul, or a thing with a soul. THEAETETUS: Why not? If indeed both these exist. GUEST: They certainly do. And we should dismiss what pertains to the inanimate—except for certain parts of the power of swimming and other such small things—and call the capture of the animate "the hunting of animals." THEAETETUS: Let it be so. GUEST: There are deservedly two species of such hunting: one is the hunting of land animals, distinguished by various species and names. The other is the hunting of agile creatures, which is called the hunting of those that swim. THEAETETUS: Entirely so. GUEST: Of the agile ones, some wander through the air by wings, others through the water. THEAETETUS: Certainly. GUEST: The hunting of flying things is called fowling. THEAETETUS: Without a doubt. GUEST: And that of aquatic things is, roughly and in summary, fishing. THEAETETUS: Entirely. GUEST: Do we not divide fishing into two greatest members? THEAETETUS: Which are those? GUEST: For we fish either with enclosures or by striking. THEAETETUS: How do you distinguish the two? GUEST: Whatever hems something in for the sake of restraining it by grasping is called an enclosure. THEAETETUS: Exactly. GUEST: Will you call baskets, nets, snares, drags, and other such things anything other than enclosures? THEAETETUS: Not otherwise. GUEST: This, then, and other similar modes of hunting which accomplish their end by hemming in, is a certain species of fishing. THEAETETUS: It is. GUEST: There exists another species which captures with hooks and spears. THEAETETUS: It is fitting to call this "striking fishing" commonly; unless you perhaps bring forward something more beautiful, I do not care for the name; this is sufficient. GUEST: Some do this at night by the light of fire; for which reason it is called "fire-bearing fishing." THEAETETUS: Exactly. GUEST: Others do it by day, carrying a hook at the end of a rod and using tridents. Whence all this fishing is called "hooked and twisted." THEAETETUS: It is agreed. GUEST: He who strikes while fishing with a certain barbed instrument and thrusts the trident from the upper part to the lower is said to use "trident and spear fishing." THEAETETUS: So they say. GUEST: There remains another species. THEAETETUS: Which one? GUEST: A certain striking made with a hook, contrary to the one above, not in just any part of the fish but in the head and mouth only, pulling back from the lower part to the upper with rods and reeds. What shall we say is the best name for this, O Theaetetus? THEAETETUS: We seem to have now completed what we proposed to seek out above. GUEST: Now, therefore, you and I have not only established the name of fishing by common opinion, but we have also received a sufficient definition of the thing itself. Furthermore, half of the whole art was in the division: that which is engaged in acquiring; of this, that which captures and takes possession; of this, hunting; of hunting, the prey of animals; of which, the capture of agile animals; of the agile—

<margin>The first transition from the Sophist to the fisherman. The division of all arts.</margin>

<margin>Here one may see Plato's art of defining by division.</margin>

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus begin their search for a definition of the "Sophist" by first practicing the method of logical division on a simpler subject: the fisherman. They categorize fishing as an art of acquisition, specifically a form of hunting agile aquatic animals by striking.</summary>

# THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING
## FOLIO LXXI.

<meta>Catchword: hunter</meta>

...universally called fishing: of the fishing arts, that which strikes and beats is "striking-fishing"; that which is done with a hook is "hook-fishing." Finally, the kind of striking that is done from below upwards, pulling back, and which takes its name from that action, is called "pulling-back" or "angling-fishing." 

**THEAETETUS.** This has been shown abundantly. 

**STRANGER.** <note>original: "HO." for Hospes (Guest/Stranger)</note> And yet, following this example, we have determined to find out what a "sophist" is. 

**THEAETETUS.** Exactly. 

**STRANGER.** And this was the first thing asked: whether we should place the one who fishes with a hook as a complete amateur, or as a participant in some art. 

**THEAETETUS.** That is so. 

**STRANGER.** And now indeed, shall we call the sophist an amateur or a skilled man? 

**THEAETETUS.** By no means an amateur. I understand indeed that it is not proper for one so named to be unskilled, but rather equipped with a certain art. 

**STRANGER.** By what art then? Shall we remain ignorant of the mutual kinship between these two? 

**THEAETETUS.** Between which two? 

**STRANGER.** Between the angler and the sophist. 

**THEAETETUS.** In what way? 

**STRANGER.** Both seem to me to be certain kinds of hunters. 

**THEAETETUS.** What prey does this second one pursue? For we have already spoken of the first. 

**STRANGER.** We divided all prey into two parts: the swimming and the walking. 

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly. 

**STRANGER.** And we followed the hunting that pursues swimming and aquatic creatures; but we passed over the hunting of walking creatures, noting that it was manifold. 

**THEAETETUS.** Without a doubt. 

**STRANGER.** Thus far, the angler and the sophist both proceed equally from the art of hunting. 

**THEAETETUS.** They certainly seem to. 

**STRANGER.** From the hunting of animals, some descend into the sea, rivers, and lakes, and hunt the animals therein. 

**THEAETETUS.** Why not? 

**STRANGER.** But others go onto the lands and rivers, as if into certain meadows, abundant in youth and wealth, to capture the animals therein. 

**THEAETETUS.** In what manner? 

**STRANGER.** Of the hunting that takes place on land, there are two main parts. 

**THEAETETUS.** What is each like? 

**STRANGER.** One is of domestic animals, the other of wild ones. 

**THEAETETUS.** Is there any hunting of domestic animals? 

**STRANGER.** Suppose I say it as I please: either man is a domestic animal, or no animal is domestic; or some other animal is tame and man is a wild animal; or man is indeed tame, but there is no hunting of man. Determine for the present which of these sounds more consistent to you. 

**THEAETETUS.** I think, Stranger, that man is both a tame and a huntable animal. 

**STRANGER.** Furthermore, we establish a twofold hunting of domestic creatures. 

**THEAETETUS.** By what reasoning? 

**STRANGER.** That which compels by demonstration, and that which reduces to slavery; furthermore, tyranny and military captivity—all these violent things we commonly call hunting. 

**THEAETETUS.** Excellent. 

**STRANGER.** But that which is done by judging, or speech-making, or associating, we call collectively the "art of persuasion." 

**THEAETETUS.** Correct. 

**STRANGER.** Of this, there are two kinds. 

**THEAETETUS.** Which ones? 

**STRANGER.** Public and private. 

**THEAETETUS.** Both species exist. 

**STRANGER.** Again, the hunting of private persuasion is done either for pay or for gifts. 

**THEAETETUS.** I do not understand. 

**STRANGER.** You seem never to have considered the hunting of lovers. 

**THEAETETUS.** In what regard? 

**STRANGER.** Because they even bestow gifts upon those they have captured. 

**THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth. 

**STRANGER.** Let this, then, be the species of the "art of love." 

**THEAETETUS.** So be it. 

**STRANGER.** But that which is done for pay, and is concerned with favor and prepares the allurements of pleasure so that it may receive sustenance for pay alone—this we call "adulation," an art that devises pleasures. 

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly. 

**STRANGER.** Or it professes to associate for the sake of showing virtue, and demands money for pay: and that genus seems to require another name. 

**THEAETETUS.** Why not? 

**STRANGER.** <margin>First definition of the sophist.</margin> What name? Try to express it. 

**THEAETETUS.** It is clearly evident. For we seem to have found the Sophist now, and I think this name fits him best. 

**STRANGER.** As gathered from this dispute, it is clear, O Theaetetus, that the sophistical faculty should be called an art concerned with associating and acquiring; it is a hunting of walking, land-dwelling, and domestic animals: namely, the private capture of men for a wage of money, and the ensnaring of wealthy and noble youths by the reputation of virtue and learning. 

**THEAETETUS.** It must be said exactly so. 

**STRANGER.** Furthermore, let us consider it in this way. For what is now sought is not a participant in a simple art, but a varied one. Indeed, from those things we said above, one may conjecture through a certain image that he is not of this genus we mentioned, but of another. 

**THEAETETUS.** Of which, then? 

**STRANGER.** Of the art concerned with acquiring, two species were related: hunting and commerce. 

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly. 

**STRANGER.** Of commerce there are two species: one consists in giving, the other in buying and selling. 

**THEAETETUS.** So it is indeed. 

**STRANGER.** Again, we divide that which pertains to buying and selling into two parts. 

**THEAETETUS.** In what way? 

**STRANGER.** He who makes his own works for sale is called a "seller of his own"; he who sells the works of others is an "exchanger." 

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely so. 

**STRANGER.** Exchange is either performed between citizens of the same city, which we call "retail trade," or between citizens and foreigners by buying and selling things moved from one city to another, which we call "merchandising." 

**THEAETETUS.** Why not? 

**STRANGER.** Merchandising, moreover, is twofold: one looks to the nourishment of the body; the other to the learning of the soul, and it exchanges instruction for coins. 

**THEAETETUS.** How do you mean? 

**STRANGER.** Perhaps we are ignorant of what pertains to the soul. For we recognize what pertains to the body. 

**THEAETETUS.** Indeed. 

**STRANGER.** <margin>The merchandising of disciplines.</margin> We call him a merchant no less than the one selling food for the body, who buys music in one place by learning it and sells it in another by teaching it; and likewise with literature, and stage-craft, and other disciplines of the soul, both serious and playful. 

**THEAETETUS.** You speak the truth. 

**STRANGER.** Will you not likewise call him a merchant who travels through various cities to exchange disciplines for coins? 

**THEAETETUS.** Certainly, likewise. 

**STRANGER.** One part of this kind of merchandising is called "demonstrative"; the other part is "ridiculous," yet since it is a selling of disciplines, it must be called by some similar name of selling. 

**THEAETETUS.** Entirely. 

**STRANGER.** But he who sells other faculties must be called by one name, and he who sells the precepts of virtues by another. 

**THEAETETUS.** Nothing prevents it. 

**STRANGER.** It is fitting to name him who sells other faculties a "seller of arts"; but that man who hands over morals for pay, by what name will you call him? Can anyone rightly name him anything other than what we now seek, the "Sophist"? 

**THEAETETUS.** Not otherwise, indeed. 

**STRANGER.** Now therefore let us conclude, gathering in this manner: that in the second <margin>Second definition of the sophist</margin> inquiry, the sophist appeared to us as an acquirer of this sort: namely, an exchanger, a buyer, and a seller: a merchant, to be precise, who sells the disciplines of the soul, pertaining especially to the discourses and institutions of the virtues.

<summary>This page features a Platonic dialogue defining the "Sophist" through two distinct logical divisions: first as a "hunter" of wealthy young men, and second as a "merchant" who sells intellectual and moral instruction for profit.</summary>
<keywords>Sophist, hunting, commerce, education, virtue, Plato, Theaetetus, logic, division, merchandising of the soul</keywords>

# BOOK FIFTEEN

THEAETETUS: Certainly.
STRANGER: <note>The speaker "HO." refers to the *Hospes* or Stranger from Elea.</note> I suspect you will call this man a "sophist" for a third time, for he remains in the same city and partly buys, and partly devises his own subjects of study, intending to sell them to make a living.
THEAETETUS: Nothing prevents it.
STRANGER: You will therefore give the name "sophist" to the one who is engaged in acquisition and exchange—that is, he both buys and sells, acting as a retailer of either his own inventions or those of others, provided he sells things concerning the pursuit of virtue.

<margin>Third definition of the sophist.</margin>

THEAETETUS: It is necessary to agree, since the reasoning demands it.
STRANGER: Let us look again to see whether the kind of person we are currently seeking is similar to something else.
THEAETETUS: To what?
STRANGER: Within that art which pertains to acquisition, there was a certain part called the "faculty of competition."
THEAETETUS: There certainly was.
STRANGER: It would not be out of place, then, to divide that into two parts.
THEAETETUS: Into what parts will you divide it?
STRANGER: One part is fighting, and the other is resisting.
THEAETETUS: True.
STRANGER: When the fight is body against body, it is appropriately called "violence."
THEAETETUS: Appropriately.
STRANGER: But that which is committed with words against words is called "disputation." <note>original: *ambiguitas*</note>
THEAETETUS: Certainly.
STRANGER: There are two species of disputation.
THEAETETUS: Which ones?
STRANGER: When one competes publicly in a continuous speech concerning what is just or unjust, it is named "forensic controversy."
THEAETETUS: That is so.
STRANGER: But when one contends privately through short little arguments in a process of questioning and answering, we are accustomed to call it "contradiction."
THEAETETUS: Quite so.
STRANGER: Furthermore, the kind of contradiction that happens randomly in business dealings is done without art, and should be set aside as its own species. For reason distinguishes it from the others, yet it has received no specific name from the ancients, nor will it receive one from us now; for it is not fitting.
THEAETETUS: Without a doubt.
STRANGER: For it is split into various and tiny matters. But the kind that proceeds by art, and disputes generally about the just and unjust and other things, is usually called "litigation." <note>original: *litigium*</note>
THEAETETUS: Plainly.
STRANGER: Litigation is twofold: one kind wastes one's inheritance, the other accumulates money.
THEAETETUS: Entirely so.
STRANGER: Let us try to find what name should be assigned to each.
THEAETETUS: We must.
STRANGER: Whoever delights in the study of this sort of contention, neglects his own affairs, and composes words that are pleasant to his listeners—always hunting for little questions—should be called, in my opinion, nothing other than a "trifler" or a "chatterbox."
THEAETETUS: Quite so.
STRANGER: But now, you take your turn and tell me: what should we call the one who applies himself to accumulating money from private litigations?
THEAETETUS: Anyone who wishes to answer without error will call him this marvelous "sophist" whom we are seeking.

<margin>Fourth definition of the sophist. A proverb: "not to be caught with one hand."</margin>

STRANGER: He offers himself to us now for the fourth time.
STRANGER: Reason now shows that the sophist is nothing other than a contentious person who uses contradictions for the sake of profit, competing in fighting, and being more studious of gain than anything else.
THEAETETUS: That is entirely it.
STRANGER: You see the truth of the saying that this is a "variegated animal"—and as the proverb goes, he is "not to be caught with only one hand." <note>A Greek proverb meaning something is slippery or difficult to grasp; one must use both hands to hold it.</note> Must we then use both?
THEAETETUS: It is necessary.
STRANGER: Therefore, we must act with all our strength and follow his tracks in this way. Tell me, do we have any names for "servant-like" tasks?
THEAETETUS: Many. But which of the many are you asking about?
STRANGER: Such things as when we say to strain, to distribute, to cook food, or to separate.
THEAETETUS: Why not?
STRANGER: To card wool, and also to draw it out, to weave with a comb—we find many other such things in the arts, do we not?
THEAETETUS: What do you intend to show by bringing in these examples and asking about all of them?
STRANGER: All the things we have mentioned pertain, in a way, to "discerning" or "distinguishing."
THEAETETUS: Indeed.
STRANGER: In my opinion, since one art is involved in all these things, we shall call it by one name.
THEAETETUS: What name?
STRANGER: Let us call it the "discerning art." <note>original: *discretiuum*</note>
THEAETETUS: So be it.
STRANGER: Look again: can we find two species of this?
THEAETETUS: You are imposing a consideration that seems to me to require a quick and brief look.
STRANGER: Truly, in these "discernments" we mentioned, we were partly separating the worse from the better, and partly like from like. For that seems to be roughly what was said. I do not have a specific name for the latter; but for the former, which leaves behind what is better and cuts away what is worse, I do have a name.
THEAETETUS: What is it?
STRANGER: All such discernment, as I conclude, is commonly named "purification." <note>original: *purgatio*</note>
THEAETETUS: That is clear.
STRANGER: And will not everyone recognize that there are two species of purification?
THEAETETUS: Perhaps, if one thinks about it for a while; for I do not know at the moment.
STRANGER: Nevertheless, it is fitting to embrace many species of bodily purifications under one name.
THEAETETUS: Which ones do you mean, and by what name?
STRANGER: The purification of a living body from within, performed through gymnastics and medicine; and that which cleanses from without by baths (which is a lowly thing to say). Likewise, that which cleanses inanimate bodies by the service of fullers <note>People who clean and thicken cloth.</note> through wiping and coloring; and the whole care of decorating the body—these all receive various and lowly names individually.
THEAETETUS: Indeed.
STRANGER: Entirely so, O Theaetetus. But the progress of reasoning cares no more or less for one than the other, whether the purification is applied by sponges and poultices or by medicines that purify and help more. For in order to achieve an understanding of all arts, it honors each individual art equally by investigating what is related or unrelated, and it does not consider some more ridiculous than others based on their similarity. Furthermore, it does not think it any more honorable to practice the work of hunting through military discipline than through any other very lowly work. And now, as you were asking, by what name shall we encompass all the faculties that strive to purify a body, whether living or inanimate? It will matter nothing to the present dispute what name is found that seems more decent, provided it is distinct from the purifications of the soul, and includes all those that purify the body. Furthermore, the goal now is to separate purification from all other things, if we look at where the argument is heading.
THEAETETUS: I have noticed, and I admit there are two species of purification: the purification of the soul being different from the purification of the body.
STRANGER: You speak excellently. And follow me in this further: try to divide what I am about to say into two parts again.
THEAETETUS: Wherever you lead, I will try to share the path with you.
STRANGER: Do we say that "wickedness" <note>original: *prauitas*</note> in the soul is something different from "virtue"?
THEAETETUS: Certainly different.
STRANGER: And indeed, we said that purification is nothing other than cutting away what is wicked and keeping the rest.
THEAETETUS: We said that, without a doubt.
STRANGER: If, therefore, we find any removal of wickedness regarding the soul, [it is] pure...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous folio regarding the definition of the Sophist and the nature of purification. The speakers are the Stranger (HO. for Hospes) and Theaetetus (THE.).</meta>

# THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING

...we must call this "purgation" <note>original: *purgationem*; a cleansing or clearing away of filth</note>. 
**THEAETETUS.** Certainly. 
**STRANGER.** Two species of wickedness are posited in the soul. 
**THEAETETUS.** Which ones? 
**STRANGER.** One is like a bodily disease; the other is like deformity <note>original: *turpitudinis*; literally "baseness" or "ugliness"</note>. 
**THEAETETUS.** I do not quite understand. 
**STRANGER.** Perhaps you do not consider "disease" and "sedition" <note>original: *seditionem*; internal strife or factionalism</note> to be the same thing? 
**THEAETETUS.** Again, I do not know how to answer this. 
**STRANGER.** Do you think sedition is anything other than the corruption of a natural kinship, arising from some sort of discord? 
**THEAETETUS.** Nothing else. 
**STRANGER.** And is deformity anything other than the lack of proportion resulting from the dissonance of things that are naturally related? 
**THEAETETUS.** Exactly that. 
**STRANGER.** What then? Do we not see in those whose souls are depraved that opinions disagree with desires, anger with pleasures, and reason with pains? 
**THEAETETUS.** Very much so. 
**STRANGER.** And yet all these things are naturally related. 
**THEAETETUS.** That is clear. 
**STRANGER.** It is fitting, then, to call wickedness of the soul "sedition" and "disease." 
**THEAETETUS.** Correct. 
**STRANGER.** If we see things that, having a certain goal set before them, wander and miss the mark in every movement as they strive to reach it, shall we say they err through some mutual harmony and common agreement, or through contrary causes? 
**THEAETETUS.** Clearly through dissonance and lack of measure. 
**STRANGER.** And yet we know that no soul is willingly ignorant of anything. 
**THEAETETUS.** Plainly. 
**STRANGER.** Ignorance is indeed a certain madness of the soul, which, while it strives for truth, <margin>What ignorance is</margin> wanders away from understanding itself. 
**THEAETETUS.** Entirely. 
**STRANGER.** It is fitting, then, to call an ignorant soul <margin>The nature of the ignorant soul</margin> out of tune and deformed. 
**THEAETETUS.** So it seems. 
**STRANGER.** There are, therefore, these two types of evils in the soul. One is commonly called "wickedness," which is undoubtedly a disease of the soul. 
**THEAETETUS.** It is so. 
**STRANGER.** The other they call "ignorance," but they are unwilling to confess that this is a "wickedness" of the soul. 
**THEAETETUS.** It must be entirely conceded—though you doubted me when I said it just now—that two types of wickedness exist in the soul: we should consider cowardice, intemperance, and injustice, and all other such things, as a "disease"; but the vast and varied state of ignorance must be called "deformity." 
**STRANGER.** But regarding the body, are there not two arts found for these two evils? 
**THEAETETUS.** Which ones? 
**STRANGER.** Against deformity, gymnastics; against disease, the skill of medicine. 
**THEAETETUS.** It appears so. 
**STRANGER.** And against insolence, injustice, and cowardice, is not the most suitable of all arts the corrective and punitive power of judicial censure? 
**THEAETETUS.** That is likely, as far as human opinion goes. 
**STRANGER.** But against universal ignorance, what remedy is found other than instruction <note>original: *doctrinam*; teaching or education</note>? 
**THEAETETUS.** None. 
**STRANGER.** Now, should we say there is only one simple kind of instruction, or several types? Indeed, observe that there are two primary types. 
**THEAETETUS.** I am observing. 
**STRANGER.** It seems to me we shall find it most quickly this way. 
**THEAETETUS.** How? 
**STRANGER.** If we consider that ignorance is twofold, it follows that it requires a twofold method of teaching, so that each method may be applied to each type of ignorance. 
**THEAETETUS.** Is what we are seeking now clear to you? 
**STRANGER.** I see one great and burdensome part of ignorance, outweighing all its other parts. 
**THEAETETUS.** Which one? 
**STRANGER.** This: when someone thinks they know those things which they do not know. From this, surely, proceed all the false opinions that deceive us. 
**THEAETETUS.** It is so. 
**STRANGER.** And yet I think the name "lack of skill" <note>original: *inscitia*; a specific type of ignorance where one is unaware of their own lack of knowledge</note> fits this part of ignorance alone. 
**THEAETETUS.** Precisely. 
**STRANGER.** What then do you think we should call the part of instruction by which we are freed from this ignorance? 
**THEAETETUS.** I suppose the other part is called "instruction in the arts," but this part is called "discipline" <note>original: *disciplinam*; here referring to education or "upbringing"</note>. 
**STRANGER.** It is called so by almost all Greeks. But we must further consider whether this is a single whole, or whether it has some division worthy of a name. 
**THEAETETUS.** It must certainly be considered. 
**STRANGER.** It seems to me that this also admits of a division. 
**THEAETETUS.** By what reasoning? 
**STRANGER.** Of that faculty which teaches by speech, one part seems harsher, and another gentler. 
**THEAETETUS.** How do we describe each? 
**STRANGER.** One is the old ancestral way, which they used to use especially toward their sons—and many still use it whenever they do wrong—sometimes rebuking them harshly, sometimes advising them more mildly. We can call this whole approach "admonition." 
**THEAETETUS.** It is so. 
**STRANGER.** On the other hand, some, having reasoned within themselves, have concluded that all lack of skill is involuntary, and that no one who believes they already know a thing will ever try to learn it; thus, the "admonitory" form of discipline achieves hardly anything despite much labor. 
**THEAETETUS.** They think rightly. 
**STRANGER.** Therefore, they proceed by another path to uproot this kind of opinion. 
**THEAETETUS.** By what path? 
**STRANGER.** They examine and question a person on those matters which he thinks he understands best and expresses most clearly, while in fact he says nothing true. Then they easily dismantle the opinions of those who wander; collecting them by reasoning, they bring them together and show that these opinions are contrary to themselves, regarding the same things, in the same respects, and according to the same principles. Those who see this become angry with themselves and grow gentle toward others. In this way, they cast off great and stubborn opinions. This liberation is the most pleasant of all to hear, and truly the most stable. For indeed, my dear boy, those who undertake to purge these people think no differently than physicians who treat bodies. For physicians teach that the body cannot be nourished by healthy food until the impediments are driven out. Similarly, these teachers believe the soul cannot benefit from excellent doctrines until the one who errs is refuted and made to feel shame; and once the impediments to learning—namely, false opinions—are repelled, he emerges pure, no longer thinking he knows what he does not know. 
**THEAETETUS.** This is the best and most modest state of all. 
**STRANGER.** For these reasons, Theaetetus, we must say that the greatest and most principal purgation is "refutation" <note>original: *redargutionem*; the Socratic method of elenchus</note>. He who has not been refuted, even if he be a Great King, is impure in the greatest matters; he remains unlearned and base in those things in which he who is to be truly happy ought to be most pure and beautiful. 
**THEAETETUS.** That is entirely true. 
**STRANGER.** Whom shall we say uses this art? I fear to say "the Sophists." 
**THEAETETUS.** Why? 
**STRANGER.** Lest we grant them more honor than is fitting. 
**THEAETETUS.** Nevertheless, what has just been said seems to describe someone of that sort...

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus discuss the "purgation" of the soul, distinguishing between moral vice (disease) and ignorance (deformity). They conclude that the most effective teaching method is refutation, which shames the student out of their false belief in their own knowledge.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Sophist, Theaetetus, purgation, ignorance, discipline, refutation, Socratic method, vice, education</keywords>

STRANGER: And you are rightly in doubt, since it is likely that the Sophist himself is altogether in doubt as to which way he might escape our reasoning. THEAETETUS: You speak excellently. STRANGER: First, while standing, let us breathe a little, and let us reason with ourselves while recovering. STRANGER: In the second, a kind of merchant of the soul's teachings. THEAETETUS: Entirely so. STRANGER: In the third, a petty retailer of these same things. THEAETETUS: And that too. In the fourth, a seller of his own invented teachings. STRANGER: You have recalled it very well. I myself will bring back the fifth: a certain competitor in arguments, and an overly skillful litigator. THEAETETUS: So it was established. On account of which, one calls him who seems imbued with various sciences by many names instead of one. THEAETETUS: So it appears to be established by nature in some way. STRANGER: Lest the same thing happen to us because of sluggishness in this investigation, let us first repeat one of the things said about the Sophist. STRANGER: What about those things which are seen by the eyes—the heaven, the earth, and those things contained within them? THEAETETUS: Most certainly. THEAETETUS: Altogether so. STRANGER: What about laws and the republic? Do they not profess to make men contentious in these as well? THEAETETUS: No one, so to speak, would dispute with them unless they promised this. THEAETETUS: You seem to me to be speaking of what Protagoras wrote about wrestling and the other arts. <note>Protagoras was a famous Sophist known for the "Man is the measure of all things" doctrine.</note> STRANGER: And about many others, O blessed one. But is not the art of contradicting itself, in short, a faculty that can bring all things into controversy? <margin>The art of contradicting can bring all things into controversy. No one can know all things.</margin> THEAETETUS: It seems to omit almost nothing. STRANGER: But by the gods, O boy, do you think this is possible? STRANGER: What then would seem wonderful in the power of the Sophists? THEAETETUS: Regarding what especially? STRANGER: Namely, how they could ever persuade the young that they are the wisest of all in every single thing. THEAETETUS: And no one would desire to be instructed by them for a large sum of money. STRANGER: But now they do desire it. THEAETETUS: And vehemently so. STRANGER: I think they seem to know those things in which they oppose others very well. THEAETETUS: Why not? STRANGER: But they resist in all things. Do they not? THEAETETUS: Without a doubt. STRANGER: Therefore, they seem to their disciples to be wise in all things. THEAETETUS: Why not? STRANGER: And yet they are not. For it is established that this is impossible. THEAETETUS: Impossible indeed. STRANGER: Therefore, the Sophist has appeared to us to have an *opinion* about all things rather than true *science* <note>original: "scientia" (knowledge/understanding)</note>. THEAETETUS: Entirely. And what you just said, you seem to have said very rightly. STRANGER: Let us therefore set forth some clear example of these things. THEAETETUS: What kind? STRANGER: This one. But attend diligently and answer aptly. THEAETETUS: What kind, I say? STRANGER: You are immediately ignorant of the beginning of this speech. For you do not understand what this word, "all," signifies. THEAETETUS: Certainly not. STRANGER: I say that in the number of all things are you and I, and also other animals and trees. THEAETETUS: How do you mean? # THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING. FOLIO 73.
k

<margin>He makes all things through imitation.</margin>
of the heavens and the gods and all other things; and since he fashions each thing quickly, he sells each for a small price. THEAETETUS. You are describing a kind of game. STRANGER. What indeed? Must we not say that he is joking who claims to know all things, and professes to teach another all things for a small fee and in a short time? THEAETETUS. Entirely so. STRANGER. Do you have any species of play more skillful and pleasant than imitation? THEAETETUS. None. You have described a vast species, encompassing all things in one, and a manifold one at that. STRANGER. Do we not understand that he who promises to do all things by a single art—like a painter fashioning <term>equivocal images</term><note>original: "aequiuoca rerū simulacra" - images that share a name with the real thing but differ in essence</note> of things—can deceive foolish children? While he shows his paintings from a distance to those looking on, he acts as if he could accomplish whatever he wishes. THEAETETUS. What prevents it? 

<margin>There is an art in speech similar to that of painters.</margin>
STRANGER. Do we not think there is another such art concerning speech? By which seducers, using certain juggleries as it were, are able to deceive young men who are still far from the truth of things, by instilling certain likely images into their ears in place of true things: so much so that they seem to speak the truth, and to be the wisest of all men in all matters? THEAETETUS. Nothing prevents there being another such art of this kind. STRANGER. It is necessary, O Theaetetus, that many of those who have heard these things, when they have grown up and considered the things themselves at close hand, being forced by certain experiences to touch things clearly, will cast away their former opinions; and they will change so much that what seemed great will appear small, and what seemed easy will appear difficult: and the individual <term>phantasms</term><note>mental images or illusions</note> conceived in speech will be forced into their opposites by the progress of actions. THEAETETUS. So it seems to me, as far as the judgment of my current age reaches. For I think I am still among the number of those who are far from the truth. STRANGER. But we who are present will try to bring you aid. And now let us strive to apply intelligence as closely as possible without formal doctrines. Tell me first about the Sophist: is it agreed between us that he is a kind of juggler, an imitator of true things? Or do we still suspect that he might have true knowledge of those things about which he seems able to contradict others? THEAETETUS. Who could suspect further, Stranger? It is already clear from what has been said that he is among those who excel in a single discipline. STRANGER. Therefore he must be called a juggler and an imitator. THEAETETUS. Without a doubt. 

<margin>The seventh definition of the Sophist.</margin>
STRANGER. Next, we must take care not to let this prey escape, for we have almost caught the Sophist in our reasoning as if in a net. Therefore, he shall by no means escape this at least. THEAETETUS. What is that? STRANGER. That he is clearly one of those who deceive by hallucinations and juggleries. THEAETETUS. I think the same. STRANGER. It has been shown that we must first divide the <term>imaginary art</term><note>the art of making likenesses</note>—that is, the maker of images—and when we have entered it, if the Sophist awaits us there, we should seize him as commanded by the royal discourse and show our prey. But if he hides by slipping into the sub-parts of the art of imitation, he must be pursued: and the part in which he hides must be divided and opened up until he is entirely captured. For neither he, nor any other kind of person, will escape him who is able to search through all things one by one. THEAETETUS. You advise well; and so it must be done. STRANGER. According to the previous method of division, I now seem to see two species of imitation. But I am uncertain in which species to place the <term>Idea</term><note>the essential form or definition</note> we are seeking. And you? THEAETETUS. First distinguish and declare these two species. STRANGER. I see one art of <term>likeness-making</term><note>original: "assimilandi artē" - the art of making an accurate copy</note>: whose work is to produce an emulating image according to the proportions of the model in length, width, and depth, and with the appropriate colors. THEAETETUS. Do not all who imitate something do this to the best of their power? STRANGER. Do not all who fashion or paint some great work do this? For if they gave the true proportions of beautiful things to their images, the upper parts would appear smaller than is fitting, and the lower parts larger, because the former are seen by us from a distance and the latter from nearby. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. STRANGER. Therefore, artists, having dismissed the truth, do not accommodate to the images those proportions which truly exist, but those which *seem* beautiful. THEAETETUS. Exactly. STRANGER. Must not this species then be called "likeness-making"? THEAETETUS. Certainly. STRANGER. Therefore, we shall call that part of geometry which deals with these things "likeness-making," as we said above. THEAETETUS. Just so. STRANGER. What then shall we call that which *appears* similar to the beautiful, but which, if seen from a position where one could view it sufficiently, would not be similar to the beautiful? Since it appears to be so, but is not actually similar, should it not be called a <term>phantasm</term>? THEAETETUS. Indeed. STRANGER. This part is a whole genus of imitation, following painting. THEAETETUS. Surely. STRANGER. And the art which fashions a phantasm rather than a true image, we think should rightly be called "phantastic." THEAETETUS. It is fitting. STRANGER. These, then, are the two species of the imaginary faculty I proposed: one which produces likenesses, the other which produces phantasms. THEAETETUS. Correct. STRANGER. And that is what I was doubting: in which species the Sophist should be placed; I do not yet recognize it clearly. Truly, this man is marvelous and difficult to know, since even now he has very cleverly turned away and retreated into the hiding places of an obscure species. THEAETETUS. So it seems. 

<margin>A marvelous doubt concerning non-being.</margin>
STRANGER. Will you recognize him if you merely agree with me? Or has a certain impulse from this discourse led you to confess suddenly out of habit? THEAETETUS. To what end is this? STRANGER. We have fallen into a truly difficult consideration. For it is always a matter of great doubt, both in the past and the present, what is meant by this: that something "appears" and "seems" to be, but "is" not at all. And that someone speaks certain things, which are nevertheless not true. It is indeed a marvel, Theaetetus, if he does not contradict himself—he who asserts that it actually happens that one speaks and thinks false things. THEAETETUS. Why? STRANGER. Because such a speech admits that "that which is not" *is*. For a falsehood could not otherwise come to be. 

<margin>The opinion of Parmenides concerning that which is not.</margin>
But the great Parmenides, O boy, while we were still boys, preached this constantly from the beginning. For he jokes thus in his poems: "Never," he says, "and in no way are those things which are not; but you, seeking by this path, restrain your mind." From that witness...

<column-break/>

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus define the Sophist as a "juggler" or creator of "phantasms"—illusions that appear true from a distance but lack the actual proportions of truth. This leads to a profound philosophical problem: how can one speak of "that which is not" without contradicting the logic of Parmenides?</summary>

...testimony is offered: and a discourse of this kind, if it be examined even moderately, will lay the matter open. Come then, let us look into this first, if it pleases you. THEAETETUS: It makes no difference to me; see to it yourself. Wherever you think it best to go, proceed, and lead me. HOST: That is exactly how we must act. HOST: Nor should this be conceded: that such a man says "something," but not "one thing"—that is, to say nothing. THEAETETUS: And yet, he who attempts to utter "non-being" should not even be said to speak. From this, the discourse would reach the extreme of doubt. HOST: Do not say this is the greatest doubt yet. THEAETETUS: Tell me how you say that, I pray, and do not be reluctant. HOST: To that which *is*, some other thing of those which *are* can be joined. THEAETETUS: Nothing prevents it. HOST: But to that which *is not*, shall we say that anything from those things which *are* can ever be present? THEAETETUS: Not at all. 

<margin>
The greatest and first doubt concerning non-being.
</margin>

HOST: Do we place the whole genus of numbers in the order of those things which *are*? THEAETETUS: Certainly, if anything else is to be placed there. HOST: Therefore, we should apply neither a multitude of numbers nor "one" to non-being. THEAETETUS: We would not be applying them correctly, as reason shows us. HOST: In what way, then, could anyone utter with his mouth or comprehend in thought "those things which are not," or "non-being" apart from number? THEAETETUS: By what reasoning? HOST: Whenever we say "non-beings," do we not attempt to apply a multitude of number? THEAETETUS: To both. HOST: And whenever we say "non-being," do we not apply "one"? THEAETETUS: That is manifest. HOST: Indeed, we said it was neither just nor right for anyone to dare to join "being" to "non-being." THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. HOST: Do you notice that non-being according to itself can neither be uttered, nor correctly spoken, nor thought; but it exists as unthinkable, ineffable, and irrational? <note>The Host argues that even calling non-being "it" or "nothing" gives it a singular "being" it shouldn't have.</note> THEAETETUS: Entirely. 

<margin>
Non-being is unthinkable and ineffable.
</margin>

HOST: Did I not lie a little while ago when I said I would bring in the greatest doubt concerning it? THEAETETUS: Can we bring in another even greater than that? HOST: What indeed, O wonderful youth? Do you not see from what has been said that non-being overwhelms the one who refutes it with such darkness that as soon as he attempts a refutation, he is forced to contradict himself? THEAETETUS: Speak more clearly. HOST: There is no need to look for anything clearer in me. Indeed, when I had supposed that non-being was a participant in neither the one nor the many, yet both a little while ago and even now I uttered it as "one" while I was pronouncing "this very non-being." Do you perceive it? THEAETETUS: I perceive it. HOST: Furthermore, I said above that it was inexplicable, ineffable, and irrational. Do you hold that? THEAETETUS: Plainly. HOST: Was I not, while attempting to predicate "to be" of it, uttering things contrary to what I said before? THEAETETUS: It seems so. HOST: When I attributed "this" to it, did I not speak as if of one thing? THEAETETUS: Without a doubt. HOST: Moreover, while I was calling it "irrational," "inexplicable," and "ineffable," I was pronouncing it singularly, just as if I were making words about "one" thing. THEAETETUS: Why not? HOST: We said surely that if anyone wished to speak correctly, he ought to determine it neither as one nor as many, nor call it "it" at all. For by such a naming, it would be placed in a certain single species. THEAETETUS: Exactly. HOST: What further shall be said of me, then? For both before and now, he will find that I have succumbed in this battle against non-being; with me, speaking of non-being, no correct speech is found. But let us now consider you, if it pleases. THEAETETUS: What do you say? HOST: Come, try well and generously—for you are young—and with all attention of mind, to utter a correct discourse about non-being, applying to it neither essence, nor "one," nor a multitude of number. THEAETETUS: I would be rash if I attempted the same battle in which you succumbed. HOST: Therefore, if you wish, let us pass over you and me; and until we find someone capable of correct speech, let us say in the meantime that the Sophist has hidden himself quite craftily above all others in obscure hiding places. THEAETETUS: Most certainly. HOST: Nevertheless, if we assert that the Sophist is powerful in a certain "phantastic" art <note>The art of making appearances or illusions.</note>, he will easily find an occasion against us from this use of speaking and turn our words to the contrary. For while we call him the author of "images" <note>original: "simulacrorum"</note>, he will ask what we mean by an "image" especially. We must think immediately, Theaetetus, how we should answer the Sophist when he questions us so. THEAETETUS: We will say, of course, that images are those things which are offered in water and mirrors; also painted and sculpted things, and others of this kind. 

<margin>
False definition of an image.
</margin>

HOST: You seem, Theaetetus, never to have seen a Sophist. THEAETETUS: Why? HOST: He will seem to speak with you either with closed eyes or without eyes at all. THEAETETUS: By what reason? HOST: He will laugh at you when you answer by means of figures and mirrors, as if you were speaking with one who sees; he will pretend to be entirely ignorant of water, mirrors, and sight, and will inquire only about this. THEAETETUS: About what? HOST: About that, I say, which is common to all these things you have mentioned; and because it is as if "one in many," you have called it by one name: "image" <note>original: "simulacrum"</note>.

# THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING. FOLIO LXXIIII.
## k ii

Proceed then with certainty: do not yield through laziness, but respond generously. THEAETETUS: What else, Stranger, should we call an image <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> except that which in some way approaches the likeness of the truth, yet is something else of that kind? STRANGER: When you say "something else of that kind," do you mean it to be understood as true, or as something else? THEAETETUS: Not true by any means, but a likeness. STRANGER: Do you call that which is "truly being" <note>original: "vere ens"</note> the "true"? THEAETETUS: Exactly that. STRANGER: And is not the "not-true" the opposite of the true? THEAETETUS: What prevents it? STRANGER: If, therefore, you deny that what you call a likeness is "true," you also deny that it "is" <note>original: "ens," meaning it lacks real existence</note>. Yet it exists in some way. THEAETETUS: In what way? STRANGER: You admit that it exists, but does not *truly* exist. THEAETETUS: Certainly not as a true being, but as a true image. STRANGER: Therefore, that which we say is truly an image is not truly a being; and that which is not truly a being, truly is. THEAETETUS: It seems that "non-being" is entangled with "being" in marvelous ways. STRANGER: Why should it not seem marvelous? Do you see how cleverly this many-headed Sophist has now forced us, against our will, to admit through this alternation that non-being in some way exists? THEAETETUS: Who could fail to see it? STRANGER: By what reasoning shall we define his art so that we remain consistent? THEAETETUS: Why do you speak as if you are greatly afraid? STRANGER: When we assert that he deceives us regarding appearances <note>original: "phantasma"</note>, and we name his art the "craft of deceiving," do we then say that our soul holds false opinions, ensnared by his little traps? Or do we judge otherwise? THEAETETUS: Not otherwise, certainly. STRANGER: Is a false opinion the opposite of opining those things which are? THEAETETUS: Opposite. STRANGER: Do you say, then, that false opinion is opining things that are not? THEAETETUS: I do. STRANGER: Does it think that things which are not, do not exist? Or that things which in no way exist, in some way do exist? THEAETETUS: If anyone ever lies in their opining in any way, it is necessary that they judge things which are not, to be in some way. STRANGER: And will they not also think that things which entirely are, in no way exist? THEAETETUS: That also. STRANGER: And is this similarly false? THEAETETUS: It is. STRANGER: Furthermore, a lying speech will be judged by the same reasoning: namely, one that pronounces that things which are not, are; and conversely, that things which are, are not? THEAETETUS: In no other way can a lie be made. STRANGER: Scarcely otherwise. Yet the Sophist will not admit these things. How could a man in his right mind admit them, when it was established earlier that those things <note>referring to non-being</note> can neither be spoken, nor uttered, nor described, nor thought? Do we understand what is being said, Theaetetus? THEAETETUS: Why should we not understand? He will object to us that our own speech contradicts itself, since we now place "non-being" in opinion and in speech. Whence he will say we are often forced to attach "being" to "non-being," which we previously agreed could not be done. STRANGER: You have recalled it correctly. But we must now consult on what we ought to do about the Sophist. For if we attempt to define him by placing him in the art of jugglers and liars, many objections and doubts arise. THEAETETUS: That is clear. STRANGER: We have so far pursued only a tiny portion of those parts, out of innumerable ones, so to speak. THEAETETUS: If these things are so, it is impossible to catch the Sophist. STRANGER: What then? Shall we desist from the investigation because of weakness? THEAETETUS: I think we should by no means desist, if there is any way we might be able to capture this man. STRANGER: You will grant me pardon then: and as you were just saying, you will consider it satisfactory if we make even a little progress in so arduous a quest. THEAETETUS: I will grant it, and gladly. STRANGER: I ask this of you above all. THEAETETUS: What is it? STRANGER: That you do not judge me to be becoming a kind of parricide <note>The "killing" of a father's ideas</note>. THEAETETUS: To what end <margin>A dispute against Parmenides</margin> is this? STRANGER: For the sake of our resistance, it will be necessary to examine the speech of father Parmenides, and to force "non-being" to be in some way, and "being" in turn, in some way, not to be. THEAETETUS: It seems this must be fought out in our speeches. STRANGER: Even a blind man, as they say, could see that; for unless these things are refuted or conceded, no one will be able to speak of false speeches, or opinion, or likenesses, or images, or imitations, or appearances, or of those arts which deal with these things, without moving the listeners to laughter, while he is forced to utter contradictions to himself. THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. STRANGER: Because of this, we must dare to press against the paternal speech, or abandon it entirely if we are held back by any laziness or shame. THEAETETUS: But nothing shall prevent us from doing so. STRANGER: I ask a third thing of you, also a small matter. THEAETETUS: Speak, please. STRANGER: I said a little while ago that I am always exhausted by the refutation of such things. THEAETETUS: You did indeed. STRANGER: I fear that because of what I have said, I may seem mad to you, turning myself up and down immediately. For your sake, we will attempt the refutation of that speech, if by chance we may refute it. THEAETETUS: For this reason, then, gird yourself for the fight with a brave heart. For in my judgment, you will not be said to have done wrong if you undertake his refutation. STRANGER: Where shall we most conveniently begin this dispute full of danger? I think, O boy, we must necessarily go by this path. THEAETETUS: Which one? STRANGER: That we first discuss those things which seem easier, lest, deterred by the difficulty of the matters, we immediately desist from what we have begun; but so that we may easily proceed by debating with common consent, as if we could judge these things lightly and well. THEAETETUS: Express what you feel more plainly. STRANGER: Parmenides seems to have pursued these things with an easy discourse, as has whoever else ever dared to determine how many and of what kind beings are. THEAETETUS: In what way? STRANGER: Each one seems to have told us a story as if we were children. One says that there are three things which exist: some of which <margin>Opinions regarding the number of beings</margin> at times fight with each other, but sometimes, having been reconciled, they come together into one and give birth, and provide nourishment to their offspring. Another, however, posited two: the moist and the dry, or the hot and the cold; and he joined them together and set them free. But the Eleatic doctrine among us, taking its origin from Xenophanes, or even from those more ancient, posits that all things which are said to be are "One," and discusses this in the manner of a myth. But certain Ionian and Sicilian muses, later than these, thought it best to entwine both of these in turn: so that being is both "many" and "one," held together by discord and concord. For that which differs always comes together, as the more vehement muses sing. But the gentler muses allowed that these things are always so. And this universe is in turn now one...

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus discuss the paradox of "non-being" and the necessity of challenging the philosopher Parmenides' doctrine that "non-being" cannot exist, in order to define the Sophist's art of deception. The Stranger begins reviewing historical theories on the number and nature of "beings" (the One, the Many, etc.).</summary>

GUEST: That they have looked down upon us far too much. For each of them pursues his own work, with no care given to us, whether we follow along or not. THEAETETUS: In what way do you mean? GUEST: Whenever one of them says that what is, or was, or shall be, is many, or one, or two, and that the hot is mixed with the cold, introducing certain separations and combinations—what, by the gods, Theaetetus, do you suppose is signified by these things? I, for my part, while I was younger, whenever someone brought up this very "non-being" about which we are now uncertain, I was confident that I understood it exactly. But now we must think about the greatest, the foremost, and the first. THEAETETUS: What do you mean? Do you think we should first inquire about "being," what those who announce it chiefly intend to signify? GUEST: You have understood clearly, Theaetetus. I say indeed that we ought to dispute in such a way as if they were present, and thus to question them: "O you, whoever you are that assert that hot and cold, or any two such things, are all that exists, what do you mean exists in both of them, whenever you predicate that both and each 'are'? What should this very 'being' be understood by us to be when you utter it? Is it some third thing besides those two? For if it is so, three kinds must now be placed according to you, not just two. But if you call one of the two 'being' itself, you will not be saying that both are in a similar way. For both would then be one, not two." THEAETETUS: You speak the truth. GUEST: Do you wish to call both of them "being"? THEAETETUS: Perhaps. GUEST: But we shall say to them, "O friends, in this way too you would be affirming these two to be one." THEAETETUS: You conclude rightly. GUEST: Since, therefore, we are at a loss in this, at least declare to us sufficiently what you mean to signify by this name "being" when you pronounce it. For it is clear that you have known for a long time; we, however, thought we knew until now, but now we hesitate. Therefore, teach us this first of all, lest while we think we are learning what you hand down, an opinion deceives us. If we demand these things both from them and from others who posit that the whole itself is more than one, shall we be in error? THEAETETUS: Not at all. GUEST: What about those who teach that the whole is one? Must we not inquire with all our strength what they call "being" itself? THEAETETUS: Why not? GUEST: Let them answer these things then: "Do you say that the one alone is?" "We say so," they will answer. Will they not? THEAETETUS: Yes. GUEST: Do you call something "being"? THEAETETUS: Certainly. GUEST: Is it the same as "the one," using two names for the same thing? Or is it something else? THEAETETUS: What will they answer to these things, Guest? GUEST: It is clear, O Theaetetus, that he who has supposed this will not easily answer these and other such objections. THEAETETUS: For what reason? GUEST: To confess two names when only one is posited is absurd. THEAETETUS: Why not? GUEST: Furthermore, it is rash to admit, when someone says so, that a name is anything. THEAETETUS: In what way? GUEST: He who posits a name as different from the thing introduces two things. THEAETETUS: That is clear. GUEST: Moreover, if he concedes the name is the same as the thing, he is forced to confess either that it is the name of nothing, or if it is the name of something, that it is the name of a name, and of nothing else. THEAETETUS: So it is. GUEST: And the one is only the being of one; and this being of a name is the one being itself. THEAETETUS: It must be so. GUEST: What further? Will they say the "whole" is different from the "one being," or the same? THEAETETUS: Why would they not say it is the same? For he says so. GUEST: If therefore it is a whole, as Parmenides says, "like the mass of a sphere equal on all sides, from the center to the circumference everywhere equally distant; for nothing is either greater or more powerful than it," it is necessary for being itself, because of such a circumference, to have a middle and extremes; and therefore to consist of parts. THEAETETUS: So it must be. GUEST: And yet nothing prevents that which is divided into parts from admitting the quality of the one in all its parts; and in this way both "all being" and the "whole" exist as one. THEAETETUS: Nothing at all. GUEST: But that which suffers these things <note>i.e., having parts</note>, is it not impossible for it to be the "one itself"? THEAETETUS: Why? GUEST: Because according to true reason, that which is truly one must be posited as altogether indivisible. THEAETETUS: It certainly must. GUEST: But that which is such that it is constructed from many parts will not harmonize at all with that definition. THEAETETUS: I understand. GUEST: Will the whole itself, receiving the quality of the one, thus be both one and a whole? Or shall we say that the one-whole does not exist at all? THEAETETUS: You have proposed an ambiguous choice. GUEST: You speak the truth; since being admits to being one, why will being and the one not appear as the same, and all things be more than one? THEAETETUS: Certainly. GUEST: Because if being is not a whole, by the fact that it has received that quality, yet the whole itself exists, being is made lacking in itself. THEAETETUS: Very much so. GUEST: Indeed, according to this argument, when it is deprived of itself, being itself will be non-being. THEAETETUS: It follows. GUEST: And so again all things will exist as more than one, since both being and the whole have obtained a proper nature separate from the other. THEAETETUS: Indeed. GUEST: And if the whole does not exist at all, these same things happen to being; and besides the fact that it happens not to be, it also happens that being was never even brought into existence. THEAETETUS: Why? GUEST: Whatever is brought into existence is always brought into existence as a whole. <margin>Always that which is made is made as a whole.</margin> Therefore, he who does not place the "one" or the "whole" in the order of things that are, ought not to call it either essence or generation as if it existed. THEAETETUS: It seems to be entirely so. GUEST: Furthermore, that which is not a whole cannot be a quantity in any way. For insofar as it is a quantity, to that extent it is also a whole. THEAETETUS: Exactly. GUEST: Innumerable other doubts besides these rise up against him, whoever posits being as either one alone, or as some two things. THEAETETUS: The things we have just shown testify to this. For one doubt always arises more serious than the last against what was said. GUEST: The discourses of those who discuss being and non-being exactly are not...

# THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING. FOLIO 75.

as we have related. However, let these things suffice. But let us bring forward again those who treat the matter differently, so that from all of these we may understand that it is no easier to define what **being** is than what **non-being** is. THE. Certainly, these too must be approached. HO. <note>The "HO." refers to the *Hospes* or Stranger from Elea, the lead speaker.</note> There appears to be among them a kind of battle of the giants because of the controversy in which they contend with one another concerning **essence**. THE. In what way? HO. Some of them drag all things down from heaven and the invisible region to the earth with their very hands, seizing rocks and oaks. For since they touch all such things, they affirm that only that exists which can be perceived and touched in any way; they hand down the same definition for **body** and **essence**. But whatever is said to exist without a body, they despise, refusing to hear anything else. THE. I know well the men you speak of. For I have encountered many such. HO. Their adversaries, however, quite cautiously and piously fight from above, from an invisible seat, on behalf of an invisible essence; they compel certain **intelligible** <note>original: *intelligibiles* — things grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note> and incorporeal **forms** to exist as true essence. But the bodies of the former, and that which they call "truth," they break into small pieces in their arguments; and they name **generation** <note>original: *generationem* — the realm of becoming or change</note> as a flowing substitute for essence. From this, a huge and inextricable fight has always existed between both sides concerning these things. THE. You tell the truth. HO. Let us now demand from both, one by one, the account of essence which they propose. THE. How shall we demand it? HO. From those who place essence in the forms, it is easier, for they are gentler. But from those who drag everything by force to bodies, it is harder—perhaps even impossible. But it seems we must deal with them in this way. THE. In what way? HO. It would be better to make them better in their character, if it were possible. But if that cannot be done, effort must be given so that we may at least make them so in speech, assuming they would answer more modestly and correctly than they do now. For what is conceded by better men is firmer and more powerful than what is conceded by worse men. We, however, do not care for that, but seek the **truth**. THE. Rightly so. HO. Bid those who have been made "better" to answer you immediately, and interpret what they say. THE. Let it be done. HO. Do they assert that what they call a "mortal animal" is something? THE. Why would they not? HO. Do they not call this an animated body? THE. Strongly so. HO. While they maintain this, do they intend for the **soul** to be something? THE. Yes. HO. Do they judge one soul to be just and another unjust; one wise and another foolish? THE. Certainly. HO. And is it not by the habit and presence of justice and other such things that such a soul becomes so, and by their opposites, the opposite? THE. They admit these things too. HO. Will they grant that what can be present to or absent from something is "something"? THE. They certainly grant it. HO. Since, therefore, justice and wisdom and any virtue are something, as well as the opposite of each virtue, and furthermore the soul in which these things happen—do they think each of these can be seen and touched, or not? THE. They think almost none of these can be seen. HO. Do they think any of these have a body? THE. They do not answer these things simply; rather, they say the soul has some kind of body, but as for wisdom and the other things you asked about, they do not yet dare to assert either that they are nothing or that they are bodies. HO. Without a doubt, Theaetetus, these men have turned out better for us; for whoever among them are "Spartans" <note>original: *Spartae* — likely referring to the "Sown Men" of myth, i.e., the crude materialists</note> and indigenous would not shrink from asserting neither of these; rather, they would contend that whatever cannot be squeezed in a fist is absolutely nothing. THE. You have described almost exactly what they feel. HO. Let us inquire of them again. For if they concede that even the smallest thing is incorporeal, it is enough. We seek for them to express that which is implanted in both incorporeal and corporeal things alike, by reason of which they say both "are." THE. An answer might perhaps fail them if such a thing happened to them. HO. See whether, if we propose it, they will admit that **being** is something of this sort. THE. What is it? Declare it. For perhaps we will understand. HO. I say that whatever has obtained any **power** <note>original: *potentiam* — capacity or force</note> whatsoever, either to act upon another or to suffer <note>original: *patiendum* — to be acted upon</note> from another, even in the smallest degree from the most trivial thing, and even if only once—anything of that sort truly "is." And I define **being** by this definition: that it is nothing other than **power**. THE. Indeed, since they have nothing better than this at present, they accept it. HO. Good; perhaps later it will seem to us and to them that we must speak otherwise. But let this remain admitted and settled for now. THE. It remains so. HO. Let us now descend to the "friends of the forms." You, then, interpret their sense for us. THE. It shall be done. HO. Do you say that **essence** is one thing and **generation** another, separating one from the other? THE. Without controversy. HO. And that through the body and through the senses we communicate with generation, but through the soul and through reason we communicate with true essence—which you assert always stays the same and in the same manner, while generation appears differently at different times? THE. We assert this. HO. This "communication," O best of men, what do you say it is in both? Is it that which we introduced a little while ago? THE. What was that? HO. A "suffering" or an "action" arising from a certain power, from those things which come together with one another. Perhaps, O Theaetetus, you do not quite grasp their answer to this, but my long acquaintance with them helps me to perceive it. THE. What then do they answer? HO. They do not grant us what was said above against the "earth-born" men concerning essence. THE. What was that? HO. I placed this as a sufficient definition of beings: namely, whenever any power of acting or suffering, even the smallest, is present. THE. That very one. HO. To this they say that generation participates in the power of acting or suffering, but no such power is suitable for essence. THE. Is there not something in what they say? HO. To this we must object: we desire to hear more clearly from them whether they agree that the soul **knows** and that essence **is known**. THE. They certainly affirm it. HO. Do you call "knowing" or "being known" an action or a suffering, or both? Or do you wish for neither of these to participate in the other? It is clear that they would say neither in the other. Otherwise, they would now admit the opposite of what they conceded above. THE. I understand. HO. If indeed knowing were to act upon something, then being known would be to suffer; thus essence, by this reasoning, would "suffer" <note>i.e., be changed or affected by the act of being known</note>...

Therefore, you think of Being itself as some third thing: and as if motion and rest were contained under it, you grasp both: and looking back at their communion in essence, you thus name them both as "being." THEAETETUS. We truly seem to be prophesying some third thing, Being itself, when we say that motion and rest "are." STRANGER. For this reason, Being itself is not both of those—motion and rest—but something else besides them. THEAETETUS. It appears so. STRANGER. Therefore, Being by its own nature neither stands still entirely, nor moves. THEAETETUS. It must be said almost so. STRANGER. Let us therefore pursue the discourse as decently as we can concerning both equally. THEAETETUS. Wisely said. STRANGER. Let us say plainly in what way we call this same thing by many names. THEAETETUS. Bring forward an example of this. STRANGER. Calling a man "one," we name him with many surnames when we attribute to him colors, figures, magnitudes, virtues, and vices; in all of which and many others we say he is not only a "man," but also "good" and many other things: and we act similarly in other cases. For setting down any one thing, we then call it many things by many names. THEAETETUS. You tell the truth. STRANGER. Whence, as I think, we have given an occasion for contradiction to young men and to old men of slow wit. For anyone can immediately object: that it is impossible for many to be one, and one to be many. Therefore they exult while they do not allow a man to be called "good," but rather "good" to be "good," and "man" to be "man." You have often encountered, I think, Theaetetus, men who study such quibbles: often even elders, who because of a lack of wisdom, admire these things: and as if they had found something magnificent, they boast recklessly. THEAETETUS. Very much so. STRANGER. So that the discourse may encompass all who have ever spoken anything concerning essence, let the things we shall next submit by questioning be understood as spoken both against these and against the others we mentioned above. THEAETETUS. What are those? STRANGER. Whether we shall join essence neither with
<margin>Whether there is no mixing of things, or a mixing of all, or of some and not others.</margin>
motion nor rest: nor anything else with any other: but as if things were unable to communicate with each other, we shall entirely separate them in our discourses. Or shall we gather all things into the same, as if individual things could be mixed?

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus explore the paradox of "Being," concluding that it must encompass both motion and rest yet remains a distinct "third" concept that is difficult to define. They begin to examine how different properties can be attributed to a single subject and whether all things can be "mixed" or combined in discourse.</summary>

# THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING. FOLIO 76.
