Or will it be permitted in some cases, and in others not at all? Which of these options, Theaetetus, do we think they will choose? THEAETETUS: I do not know how to answer for them. Why did you not investigate what follows from each by answering one by one? STRANGER: You advise me well. Let us suppose then, if you will, that they say first that nothing at all has any communion <note>original: *communionem*; the Greek *koinōnia*, meaning participation or sharing between forms</note> with anything else. Would not motion and rest in no way participate in essence? THEAETETUS: In no way, certainly. STRANGER: But will either of them exist if neither participates in essence? THEAETETUS: It will not. STRANGER: Immediately, by this confession, all things are overturned, as it seems: both the dogmas of those who say all things move, and those who wish all things to stand still as one. And also those who, according to the forms, always think that the things which are exist in the same way and according to the same conditions. For they all add "to be" to their descriptions: some saying things truly move, others that they truly stand still. THEAETETUS: That is exactly so. STRANGER: Also, those who sometimes compose all things and sometimes divide them—whether they divide into one and from one into infinite parts, or into finite elements and compose from these—similarly, whether they suppose this happens alternately or always: in all these cases, I say, they say nothing true, since there is no mixing of things. THEAETETUS: Correct. STRANGER: Furthermore, we ourselves would carry out our discourse most absurdly if we permitted no thing to be called by another name through the communion of another's property. THEAETETUS: How so? STRANGER: They are forced to use "being" regarding each thing in a certain way, and "separately," and "other," and "according to itself," and innumerable other terms. Since they cannot abstain from these nor keep them from interfering in their speech, they need no refutation from others; but, as the saying goes, they have an enemy and adversary at home <margin>Proverb: They have an enemy at home.</margin> who cries out from within, like the absurd Eurycles <note>A famous Athenian ventriloquist; the Stranger suggests these thinkers carry a contradicting voice inside themselves.</note>, whom they carry around with them. THEAETETUS: What you say is true and a fitting comparison. STRANGER: But what if we say all things have the power of mutual communion? This, surely, I can refute myself. THEAETETUS: By what reasoning? STRANGER: Because then motion itself would be entirely at rest, and rest would be in motion, if they were mixed with one another. But it is by the highest necessity impossible for motion to stand still, or for rest to move. THEAETETUS: Why not? STRANGER: Therefore, only the third option remains. THEAETETUS: Indeed. STRANGER: For one of these is necessary: either all things mix, or none do, or some mix and others do not. THEAETETUS: Entirely necessary. STRANGER: The first two certainly cannot be found to be true. THEAETETUS: Certainly not. STRANGER: It follows that whoever wishes to answer correctly must propose the remaining of the three. THEAETETUS: Exactly. STRANGER: Since some things are willing to unite and others are not, it happens to things much as it does to letters. For some letters are coupled with each other, and some are not. THEAETETUS: That is clear. STRANGER: Indeed, the series of vowels is extended through the others like a kind of bond, without which no other letters can be bound together. THEAETETUS: Very much so. STRANGER: Does everyone understand which letters agree with which? Or is art <note>original: *arte*; here meaning a technical skill or science</note> needed to do it correctly? THEAETETUS: Art. STRANGER: Which one? THEAETETUS: Grammar. STRANGER: Is it not the same regarding the sounds of low and high pitches? For he who discerns by art which voices are consonant or dissonant is a musician; but he who is ignorant is unskilled in music. THEAETETUS: It is so. STRANGER: And in other arts and the lack of arts, we shall find other such things. THEAETETUS: That is manifest. STRANGER: Since we have said that the kinds of things have mutual communion in the same way, must not a certain science guide the discourse? Whoever is to show correctly which kinds agree with which, or are dissonant, must also know through all things if they agree so that they can be mixed: and again in divisions, if through all things one form is the cause of the division? THEAETETUS: Science is certainly needed, and perhaps the greatest of all. STRANGER: What then shall we call this, Theaetetus? Have we perhaps secretly stumbled upon the science of free men? It seems that while we were seeking the Sophist, we have found the Philosopher first. THEAETETUS: How so? STRANGER: To divide by kinds, and neither to believe the same form to be another, nor another to be the same—shall we not say this is the office of Dialectic? THEAETETUS: We shall certainly say so. STRANGER: Whoever can do this perceives acutely one idea extended everywhere through many, each being placed separately; and many others embraced from the outside under one; and again one idea coupled into one through all those which are many; and many forms distinct on every side. This is to know how to discern by kind in what way individual things can communicate in turn, and in what way they cannot. THEAETETUS: Entirely. STRANGER: But truly, you will grant the work of dialectic to no other, I think, than to one who philosophizes purely and legitimately. THEAETETUS: How could it be given to another? STRANGER: We shall find the philosopher in such a place both now and in the future, if we seek him; though he too is not easily seen here. But the Sophist and the Philosopher escape the sight of the eyes for different reasons. <margin>How the philosopher and sophist hide.</margin> THEAETETUS: How? STRANGER: The Sophist, I say, because he runs away into the darkness of non-being; and by long habit he is covered by that darkness, therefore he is discerned with the greatest difficulty. THEAETETUS: So it is. STRANGER: But the philosopher, always clinging by reasoning to the idea of being itself, is not easily seen because of the brightness of that region. For the eyes of ordinary souls cannot endure the rays of divinity. <margin>The eyes of ordinary souls cannot endure the rays of divinity.</margin> THEAETETUS: It is likely that these things are no less true than the others. STRANGER: We shall treat this more clearly elsewhere, if it is willed. But the Sophist must not be dismissed before he is sufficiently known by us. THEAETETUS: Excellent. STRANGER: Since, therefore, it is agreed between us that some of the kinds meet each other, and some entirely disagree—and some indeed with a few, others with many, and some even cohere through all things with all—let us follow the reasoning of this discourse in this manner. I say not of all forms, lest we be confounded by the multitude: but choosing some of the greatest, let us first see what kind each is, then what mutual communion they have; so that if we cannot grasp being and non-being with a perfectly clear notion, at least we may not lack a suitable way of disputing about them, as far as the condition of this investigation allows. For if we say that non-being is truly non-being, as if imagining it, we might perhaps be innocent...

...we shall escape. THEAETETUS: That is certainly fitting. STRANGER: Indeed, the greatest of all the kinds which we were just now recounting are **Being** itself, and **Rest**, and **Motion**. THEAETETUS: Very much so. STRANGER: And we said these two <note>Rest and Motion</note> cannot be mixed with each other. THEAETETUS: Certainly. STRANGER: But **Being** is mixed with both; for both, in a certain way, *are*. THEAETETUS: Nothing prevents that. STRANGER: It follows then that these are three. THEAETETUS: It follows. STRANGER: Now, is not each one of these something *other* than the remaining two, and the *same* as itself? THEAETETUS: It is. STRANGER: But what do we mean now by this "Same" and "Other"? Are they two other kinds, different from the three mentioned above, but always necessarily linked to them—so that we must think of five kinds? Or are we unknowingly calling one of those three "Same" or "Other"? THEAETETUS: Perhaps. STRANGER: But truly, **Motion** and **Rest** are neither the "Other" nor the "Same." THEAETETUS: For what reason? STRANGER: Because whatever we call both Motion and Rest in common, that cannot be either one of those two. THEAETETUS: Why? STRANGER: Because then Motion would rest, and Rest likewise would move. For regarding both, whichever of those two <note>Same or Other</note> were applied to them, it would force the one to cross over into the opposite of its own nature, as it would participate in its contrary. THEAETETUS: Exactly. STRANGER: Yet both participate in the "Same" and the "Other." THEAETETUS: Indeed. STRANGER: Let us not say, then, that Motion is either the "Same" or the "Other," nor Rest likewise. THEAETETUS: Certainly not. STRANGER: But should we think of **Being** and the **Same** as being one and the same thing? THEAETETUS: Perhaps. STRANGER: But if Being and the Same differ in no way from each other, then whenever we say that Motion and Rest both *are*, we would be calling them both the "Same." But this is impossible. Therefore, the Same and Being cannot be one. THEAETETUS: That is almost exactly what must be said. STRANGER: Let us then place the **Same** as a fourth species besides the three above. THEAETETUS: Let us do so. STRANGER: And must we place the **Other** in the fifth place? Or should we think of this and Being as two names signifying one thing? THEAETETUS: Perhaps. STRANGER: I think, however, you will grant that of the things that exist, some are themselves according to themselves <note>absolute</note>, while others are referred to something else <note>relative</note>. THEAETETUS: Why not? STRANGER: And the "Other" is always relative to another, is it not? THEAETETUS: Always. STRANGER: This would not be so unless the "Other" and "Being" differed greatly from each other. If the "Other" participated in both species as Being does, there would be something among those things that are "other" which would not be "other" in relation to another. But now, whatever is truly "other," it follows by necessity that it is "other" by virtue of what it is. THEAETETUS: It is as you say. STRANGER: It is fitting, then, to place the nature of the **Other** as a fifth species among those we have joined together. THEAETETUS: Truly. STRANGER: And we must say that this nature runs through all of them; for each one is "other" than the rest, not through its own nature, but because it participates in the idea of the "Other." THEAETETUS: Indeed. STRANGER: Thus let us speak of the five, repeating them one by one. THEAETETUS: How? STRANGER: First, that Motion is altogether something other than Rest. Is it to be asserted thus, or otherwise? THEAETETUS: Exactly thus. STRANGER: Therefore, it is not Rest. THEAETETUS: By no means. STRANGER: But it *is*, because it participates in Being. THEAETETUS: It is. STRANGER: Again, Motion is other than the "Same." THEAETETUS: Almost. STRANGER: Therefore, it is not the "Same." THEAETETUS: Certainly not. STRANGER: Yet it is the "Same" in a certain way because of participation. For all things participate in the Same. THEAETETUS: Most certainly. STRANGER: It must be conceded then, without controversy, that Motion is both the "Same" and "not the Same." For we do not pronounce both in the same sense; it is the "Same" because it participates in the Same in relation to itself. But it is "not the Same" because it also receives the "Other," by which it is separated from the Same; thus it is not that, but something else. Wherefore it is rightly called "not the Same" again. THEAETETUS: Rightly, without a doubt. STRANGER: Furthermore, if in some way Motion were to admit of Rest, it would not be absurd to call Motion "stable." THEAETETUS: Correct—provided we have conceded that some of the kinds are willing to communicate with each other, and some not at all. STRANGER: But we arrived at the demonstration of this earlier than the refutation of the present points: namely, that this is how nature holds itself. THEAETETUS: Why not? STRANGER: Let us say again that Motion is other than the "Other" itself, just as it was something other than the "Same" and "Rest." THEAETETUS: It is necessary. STRANGER: It is, therefore, in this sense, both "other" in a certain way and "not other." THEAETETUS: True. STRANGER: What then follows? Shall we say the "Other" is other than the three, but not different from the fourth, when we have confessed there are five, of which we proposed to consider one? THEAETETUS: But how? For we cannot introduce a smaller number of them than was established above. STRANGER: Therefore, fearing nothing, we shall assert that Motion is something other than Being. THEAETETUS: We shall assert it immediately. STRANGER: Therefore, Motion truly exists as "not-being," and also as "being," since it participates in Being. THEAETETUS: That is indeed manifest. STRANGER: It follows, therefore, that "not-being" exists in Motion and in all other kinds. For in each one, the nature of the "Other," while it makes each thing "other" than Being itself, makes each thing "not-being." And so we shall predicate that all things are similarly "not-beings" for this reason; and because they participate in Being, we shall say again that they *are*, and we shall call them "beings." THEAETETUS: It appears so. STRANGER: Therefore, regarding any species, Being is one, but "not-being" is infinite in multitude. THEAETETUS: So it seems. STRANGER: And must we not say that Being itself is other than each of the others? THEAETETUS: It is necessary. STRANGER: Therefore, Being *is not* as many things as there are other things; for since it is not those things, it is itself one, but it is not the others, which are infinite in number. THEAETETUS: That is almost exactly what must be said. STRANGER: These things should not disturb us, since the nature of the kinds has a mutual communion. If anyone does not accept this, he should know that once the previous points are granted, these must be conceded as well. THEAETETUS: You speak justly. STRANGER: Let us look at this also. THEAETETUS: What is it? STRANGER: Whenever we say "not-being," as it seems, we are by no means speaking of the *contrary* of Being, but only of something *other*. THEAETETUS: How so? STRANGER: Just as when we say "not large," we do not signify "small" any more than we signify "equal" by that word. THEAETETUS: That is so. STRANGER: Therefore, we shall not admit that a contrary is signified when a negation is spoken; we shall only affirm that the "not" signifies something of the number of "others" when it precedes names—or rather, whenever it precedes the things themselves about which the names following the negations are pronounced. THEAETETUS: That is entirely so. STRANGER: Furthermore, if it seems good to you, let us meditate on this. THEAETETUS: What is that? STRANGER: The nature of the "Other" itself appears to be divided in the same way as knowledge. THEAETETUS: Come, tell me how. STRANGER: It is one, and that part...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from the previous folio, focusing on the ontological status of "non-being" (the non-existent) as a distinct category or "form" in Platonic philosophy. The Stranger (Hospes) and Theaetetus are refining the definition of the Sophist by examining how things can "not be" something else.</meta>

# THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING

resides in something, and being determined individually, it has obtained its own proper name: for which reason there are said to be many arts and sciences. THEAETETUS. Exactly. STRANGER. And do not the parts of the nature of the "Other" itself, which is one, suffer the same thing as the parts of science? THEAETETUS. Perhaps. But explain by what reasoning. STRANGER. Is there some part of the "Other" opposed to the Beautiful itself? THEAETETUS. There is. STRANGER. Shall we say this part is nameless? Or rather that it has a name? THEAETETUS. That it has a name. STRANGER. For that which we pronounce "not-beautiful" everywhere, this is "other" than nothing else than the nature of the Beautiful. Come then, answer this. THEAETETUS. To what shall I answer? STRANGER. Since something is determined in a certain part of beings, and is again opposed to some being, and it happens thus to be called "not-beautiful," it follows that the "not-beautiful" is something: since it is that to which it is opposed. THEAETETUS. Quite right. STRANGER. Does it not follow from this discourse that the Beautiful is to be placed more in the number of beings, and the "not-beautiful" less? THEAETETUS. Not at all. STRANGER. Similarly, therefore, the "not-great" must be said to exist just as much as the "great." THEAETETUS. Similarly. STRANGER. Furthermore, the "not-just" must be asserted to exist on equal terms with the "just." THEAETETUS. Without a doubt. STRANGER. And the reasoning will be the same concerning the rest: since the nature of the "Other" itself has appeared to be from the genus of beings. And since that exists, it is necessary that its parts no less exist. THEAETETUS. What prevents it?

<margin>It is proved that non-being exists.</margin>

STRANGER. The opposition itself which exists between a part of the nature of the "Other" and a part of Being: is no less, if it is permitted to say so, an essence than Being itself; nor does it signify the contrary of that, but only something "other." THEAETETUS. Clearly. STRANGER. What then shall we call it? THEAETETUS. It is certainly established that this is the very "non-being" sought by us for the sake of the Sophist. STRANGER. Or as you were saying, does it leave behind the essence of none of the others? And must one now boldly say that non-being firmly has its own nature: just as the great was great, and the beautiful was beautiful, and also the not-great and the not-beautiful? And in the same way, was not-being according to the same [logic] and is not-being one species numbered among many other beings? Do we doubt further concerning this, Theaetetus? THEAETETUS. Not at all.

<margin>That non-being firmly holds its own nature.</margin>

STRANGER. Do you notice how far we have diverted from the mind of Parmenides? <note>Parmenides was a pre-Socratic philosopher who famously argued that "non-being" is unthinkable and impossible.</note> THEAETETUS. Why so? STRANGER. We have transgressed his limits: while we have considered and shown further than he established. THEAETETUS. In what way? STRANGER. Because he says: "Never, nowhere, in no way are non-beings. But you, seeking, restrain your mind from this progress." These are his words. But we have not only shown that non-beings exist, but we have demonstrated what the species of non-being is. For when we showed the nature of the "Other" itself to exist, and to be divided and dispersed through all beings mutually, then we asserted that the part of it opposed to that which is the "being" of each thing, is itself truly "non-being." THEAETETUS. You seem to me, O Stranger, to have spoken the absolute truth.

<margin>The verses of Parmenides.</margin>

STRANGER. Let no one therefore say that, after we have shown non-being to be the contrary of being, we dare to say that it exists. For we have long since passed over whether it is truly a contrary or not. But that which we have now said to be non-being, he who believes less must either disprove; or if he cannot disprove it, he must believe it until he can contradict it: namely, that the genera are mixed with one another, and Being and the "Other" <note>original: "alterum"</note>—by penetrating through each other and through all other things—mutually capture themselves, while the "Other" participates in Being. For it exists because of participation of this kind: yet it is not that very thing in which it participates, but something else. Since, however, it is other than Being itself, it follows necessarily that it is said to be non-being. Being also, from the fact that it is a participant in the "Other," must be called something other than the other genera. And since it is other than all the rest, it exists neither as one certain thing from them, nor as all of them: but only as that which it is. Wherefore Being, without doubt, in many things is not many things. And other things also, both universal and singular, in many ways "are," and in many ways "are not." THEAETETUS. You tell the truth.

<margin>He who does not believe the position ought to prove things; he who cannot disprove it ought to believe.</margin>

STRANGER. If anyone does not grant faith to these contrary conversions, he ought to think how to bring forward better things than these. But if someone has found something arduous, he glories in it, drawing discourses now to these, now to other things; he has devised things hardly worthy of much study, as these discourses testify. For this is neither something extraordinary, nor difficult to find. But that which is arduous and noble is this. THEAETETUS. What? STRANGER. That which was also said above: that, omitting these things as trivial, one might be able to follow by refuting individually, whenever someone says that what is "other" is the "same," or what is the "same" is "other," so that each suffers this through its own proper reason. So that he might be able to show again that what is the same is in some way other; or the other is the same; the great also small, and the like unlike. And thus he might always be able to easily bring forth contraries in discourse. Nor indeed is any refutation so true; and since some "being" has recently been perceived, it is new. THEAETETUS. Entirely so. STRANGER. Moreover, O best of youths, to sever everything from everything is both unharmonious and the mark of a man entirely unskilled in music and philosophy. THEAETETUS. Why? STRANGER. All speech is utterly destroyed if each thing is segregated from all others. For speech consists because of the mutual coupling of species. THEAETETUS. It is so. STRANGER. Notice, I pray, how opportunely we have now compelled those fighters to permit one of the classes to be mixed with the other. THEAETETUS. To what end especially? STRANGER. To this: that speech <note>original: "oratio," referring to 'logos' or discourse</note> might be one certain thing from the genera. For if we were deprived of this, we would for the most part lack philosophy. It is necessary, moreover, in the present to define by common consent what speech is. For if it were entirely removed from our midst, we could speak of nothing. It would be removed, however, if it were granted that there is no mixture of things. THEAETETUS. That is indeed right. But for what reason speech must now be defined, I do not understand. STRANGER. But perhaps in this way you will perceive it. THEAETETUS. How? STRANGER. Non-being was established as one certain genus existing from the others, diffused through all things that are. THEAETETUS. It was established. STRANGER. We must consider therefore next whether it mixes with opinion and speech. THEAETETUS. Why? STRANGER. Because if it is in no way mixed with these, it is necessary that all things are true; but if it is mixed, false opinion and false speech arise.

<summary>The Stranger argues that "non-being" is not the opposite of being, but rather the "Other," existing as a valid category through its participation in Being. This ontological mixing is presented as the necessary foundation for the possibility of speech, philosophy, and falsehood.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Sophist, non-being, Parmenides, participation, theory of forms, dialectic, philosophy of language, ontology</keywords>

<meta>Continuing the dialogue between the Stranger (Hospes) and Theaetetus regarding the nature of the Sophist and the possibility of falsehood.</meta>

# BOOK FIFTEEN

To speak of and to think of non-beings—this is precisely what is false, occurring in both speech and thought. THEAETETUS: That is so.
<margin>From non-being comes falsehood; from falsehood, deception; from deception, a filling up of fantasies.</margin>
STRANGER: But since there is falsehood, deception follows. THEAETETUS: Immediately. STRANGER: Once deception has arisen, it is necessary that everything be filled with likenesses, images, and fantasy. THEAETETUS: Nothing stands against that. STRANGER: We were saying that the Sophist had fled from here while he refused to admit that falsehood exists in any way: because no one thinks or pronounces "non-being," since non-being is in no part a participant in essence. THEAETETUS: So it was said. STRANGER: But now, this non-being has appeared to us as a participant in being. Therefore, he will no longer fight in this manner. But perhaps he will say that some species participate in non-being, and some not at all; that speech and opinion are among those that do not participate; and therefore
<margin>The power of fantasy is the mistress of likenesses.</margin>
he will contend that the "fantastic" faculty—the mistress of likenesses in which we placed him—exists nowhere, since opinion and speech do not participate in non-being in any way. Or he will say that nothing is false since no such communion is found. Wherefore, we must first investigate what speech, opinion, and fantasy are, so that once these are declared, we may perceive their communion with non-being. Having inspected this, we may show that something is false; and once we have shown this, we may bind the Sophist in it if he is guilty. Otherwise, releasing him, we shall seek him in some other genus. THEAETETUS: It seems entirely true, Stranger, what we predicted about the Sophist from the beginning: namely, that he would be difficult to catch. For he is hedged in by many obstacles; nor can anyone reach him unless they first remove the obstacle he first threw down. And now, indeed, we have barely escaped that objection by which he inferred that non-being exists in no way. Immediately, however, another has been brought in. Whence it is necessary to show falsehood regarding speech and opinion; and perhaps after this another, and another after that; and no end is found. STRANGER: Whoever is able to make even a little progress after an attack, Theaetetus, ought to pursue it with a brave heart. For he who hesitates in these matters will never be bold in others. For he who in these things either
<margin>Proverb: He will never take the city.</margin>
accomplishes nothing or is driven back, will never, as the proverb goes, "take the city." But now that we have shattered this huge obstacle, the remaining things are smaller and lighter. THEAETETUS: You speak excellently. STRANGER: Let us therefore first take up speech or opinion, so that we may show more clearly whether non-being
<margin>On speech and opinion.</margin>
touches these, or whether both are entirely true, and neither is false. THEAETETUS: Very good. STRANGER: Come, just as we spoke regarding species and letters, let us likewise think again regarding names. For it seems that what is now sought behaves in this way. THEAETETUS: What specifically do you want to be understood about names? STRANGER: Whether they all fit together, or none, or whether some harmonize and others are dissonant. THEAETETUS: It is clear that some fit together,
<margin>Which voices are congruent; which are not.</margin>
and some do not at all. STRANGER: Perhaps you mean something like this: that those said in sequence which express something, fit together; but those which, when continued, signify nothing, do not agree. THEAETETUS: How, or what were you saying? STRANGER: What I thought you understood and admitted. For there are two genera of declarations which are made by the voice regarding essence. THEAETETUS: In what way? STRANGER: One genus of names, and another of verbs. THEAETETUS:
<margin>Which voice is a verb; which a name.</margin>
Tell me both. STRANGER: The declaration which signifies actions, we call a **verb**. THEAETETUS: Indeed. STRANGER: But the vocal sign imposed upon those who perform the actions, we call a **name**. THEAETETUS: Exactly. STRANGER: Speech is never produced from names alone placed one after another; nor again from verbs pronounced in sequence without names. THEAETETUS: I have not learned this. STRANGER: It is certain that you were nodding just now while your mind was elsewhere; for this is exactly what I wanted to say: that if these are pronounced only in such a sequence, they do not make speech. THEAETETUS: How? STRANGER: For example: "walks," "runs," "sleeps," and whatever other verbs signify actions; if someone joins them all together, he makes speech no more for it. THEAETETUS: That is so. STRANGER: And again, when he says: "lion," "stag," "horse," and other names which signify the agents themselves, no speech is yet composed by this continuation. For the things uttered do not show an action, or an impediment to action, or the essence of a thing—whether existing or non-existing—until verbs are mixed with names. Then, for the first time, they agree; and immediately speech is made. This first complexity of these elements is the first speech, even if it is very short. THEAETETUS: How do you mean? STRANGER: When someone says, "Man learns," do you say this is the first and shortest speech? THEAETETUS: I do. STRANGER: Then indeed he declares something about
<margin>The first and shortest speech: "Man learns." He speaks, who joins a name with a verb.</margin>
those things which are, or are becoming, or have been, or will be. He does not only name, but he accomplishes something, coupling verbs with names. And therefore we say he does not merely name, but speaks; and by such a context of names, we have enunciated speech. THEAETETUS: Correct. STRANGER: Truly, just as other things harmonize with each other as we said above, and some are dissonant, so also some signs of the voice by no means agree, while some by their agreement forge speech. THEAETETUS: Exactly. STRANGER: Take this brief point as well. THEAETETUS: What is it? STRANGER: It is necessary that speech, whenever it occurs, be the speech *of someone*; for it is
<margin>Speech must belong to someone.</margin>
impossible for it to be the speech of no one. THEAETETUS: So it seems. STRANGER: And must it not also be of a certain quality? THEAETETUS: It must indeed. STRANGER: Let us observe carefully, I pray. THEAETETUS: It is proper. STRANGER: I shall bring a speech to you, joining a thing with an action through a name and a verb; you tell me of whom or what the speech is. THEAETETUS: I shall do as well as I can. STRANGER: "Theaetetus sits." Is that speech long? THEAETETUS: No, it is moderate. STRANGER: It is your turn now to say about whom and whose speech it is. THEAETETUS: About me, obviously, and it is mine. STRANGER: And this one? THEAETETUS: Which one? STRANGER: "This Theaetetus, with whom I am now disputing, flies." THEAETETUS: No one would say otherwise of this one either, except that it is about me and is mine. STRANGER: We said that every speech must be of a certain quality. THEAETETUS: We did. STRANGER: One true, the other false. The true one predicates things that are, as they are, about you. THEAETETUS: Certainly. STRANGER: But the false one predicates things other than those that are.

<summary>The Stranger and Theaetetus define the basic structure of a sentence (speech) as the combination of a name and a verb. They establish that speech must be about something and can be either true or false depending on whether it describes reality as it is.</summary>

# THE SOPHIST, OR ON BEING

**THE.** Certainly. **HO.** Therefore, he asserts that things which are not, exist as if they were. **THE.** Almost exactly so. **HO.** In truth, we previously said that there are many other things that "are" concerning you, since many things "are" around each individual thing, and many things "are not." **THE.** Entirely so. **HO.** First, it is necessary that the statement I just made about you is, according to the definition of a statement, one of the shortest possible. **THE.** So we have agreed. **HO.** Next, tell me: must it not be about someone? **THE.** It must be about someone. **HO.** If it is not about you, it is much less about anyone else. **THE.** That is clear. **HO.** If it is about no one, it is not a statement at all. For it has been shown that it is impossible for something to be a statement and yet be the statement of no one. **THE.** Cleverly put. **HO.** Therefore, whenever things are predicated of you as if they were true, but they are not, such a composition of verbs and nouns is undoubtedly a false statement. **THE.** You speak very truly. **HO.** But what shall we say of thought, opinion, and phantasy <note>original: "phantasia"; here meaning mental imagery or appearance</note>? Is it not now clear that all these kinds produce both truth and falsehood in our souls? **THE.** By what reasoning? **HO.** You will understand easily if you first grasp what each of these is, and how they differ from one another. **THE.** Let it be granted. **HO.** Are not thought and speech the same, except that thought is called that internal conversation within the soul itself, carried out without the sound of the voice? **THE.** Exactly. **HO.** But the outward flow of that speech through the mouth is called a statement. **THE.** True. **HO.** And we notice this same thing present in a statement. **THE.** What? **HO.** Affirmation and negation, I mean. **THE.** Certainly. **HO.** When this occurs in the soul through thought in silence, can it be called by any name other than opinion? **THE.** Not at all. **HO.** What then? When such an experience happens not through thought alone but through sensation, can it be named anything other than phantasy? **THE.** Not otherwise. **HO.** Since it has appeared that a statement is partly true and partly false, and thought is the soul's internal conversation, and opinion is the conclusion of thought, and that which is called phantasy is a mixture of sensation and opinion: it seems necessary that thoughts and opinions are partly true and partly false, since they are kindred to statements. **THE.** Nothing stands against it. **HO.** Do you notice that we have found false statement and false thought more easily than we expected? We were truly afraid that in seeking these things, we were undertaking a useless and inexplicable task. **THE.** I notice it. **HO.** Therefore, let us not fear what remains. But since these things have been revealed, let us resume those previous divisions according to their kinds. **THE.** Which ones? **HO.** We divided the "image-making art" into two: the "likeness-making" <note>original: "assimilatricem"; the art of making true likenesses</note> and the "phantastic" <note>the art of making deceptive appearances</note>. **THE.** So we did. **HO.** But we were uncertain in which of the two arts we should place the Sophist. **THE.** Indeed. **HO.** After this uncertainty, a deeper darkness suddenly emerged, when a doubt was raised by everyone that neither an image, nor a likeness, nor a phantom exists at all, because falsehood exists in no way, nowhere, and never. **THE.** You tell the truth. **HO.** But now, since false statement and false opinion have appeared, it is possible for there to be certain imitations of true things, and from this condition, the art of deceiving may flow. **THE.** Certainly possible. **HO.** Furthermore, it was conceded that the Sophist is occupied with these things. **THE.** It was. **HO.** Let us strive again to divide the proposed genus in two, always proceeding to the right-hand part of the division; and whatever the Sophist shares in common, let us look around so that, having cut away all commonalities, we may behold his own proper seat and form, and show it to those who by nature approach the progress of such learning. **THE.** Well said. **HO.** Did we not at the beginning introduce the art of "making" as one part, and "acquiring" as the other? **THE.** Certainly. **HO.** Having later divided the art of acquiring, we placed the Sophist under it, in hunting, combat, trade, and such species. **THE.** That is exactly how it was done. **HO.** But now, since the art of making also encompasses the Sophist, it is clear first of all that this art must be divided in two. For imitation is a kind of making—namely, of images, not of true things, as we said before. **THE.** Without a doubt. **HO.** Therefore, let there first be two parts of the productive faculty. **THE.** Which? **HO.** The divine and the human. **THE.** I do not yet understand. **HO.** If we remember what was said above, we defined the productive faculty as a certain power that is the cause of things coming into being which did not exist before. **THE.** We remember. **HO.** All mortal animals, plants, whatever grows from seeds or roots in the earth, and whatever inanimate things exist in the earth, whether they can be liquefied or not—shall we say they are fashioned by any other maker than God, coming to be after they previously were not? Or shall we follow the doctrine and speech of the many? **THE.** Which many? **HO.** Those who say that these things are produced by nature itself from some fortuitous cause, acting without a mind; or rather with reason and divine knowledge granted by God himself. **THE.** Perhaps because of my age, I fluctuate between one opinion and the other. But at present, looking to you and thinking that you believe all these things are produced by God, I hold that same view myself. **THE.** Very rightly, Theaetetus. And if we thought you would think otherwise in the future, we would now use reason along with a certain necessary persuasion to make you believe us. But since I know your nature is such that, even without our demonstration, you will proceed of your own accord toward those things to which you say you are now drawn, I will let it pass. For such a dispute would be superfluous. I will posit that those things said to be produced by nature are made by divine art; but those things composed by men from these materials are human; and by this reasoning, there are two genera of the productive faculty: namely, the human and the divine. **THE.** Excellent. **HO.** Since there are two arts, divide each again in two. **THE.** How? **HO.** Just as the entire productive art was divided by width, let it now be divided by length; and thus four parts are made: two human in relation to us, and two divine in relation to the Gods. **THE.** Certainly. **HO.** From these, divided again in another way, one part of each partition is productive of things; the remaining parts are called "imaginary" <note>image-making</note>. Whence the faculty of making is again divided in two. **THE.** Tell me again how each is divided. **HO.** We know that humans and other animals, and the elements from which they are produced—fire and water—are the kindred works of God. **THE.** Certainly. **HO.** After these follow the images of these things, produced by a certain demonic <note>original: "daemonica"; here meaning supernatural or divine, not necessarily evil</note> contrivance. **THE.** Of what sort? **HO.** Phanta...

# BOOK FIFTEEN.

...phantasms that occur to those sleeping; or those seen by day without artifice, such as a shadow when darkness is mixed with fire; or a double image when a light, both internal and external, meets upon clear and smooth surfaces and, by providing a sensation contrary to usual vision, creates a specific form. There are, therefore, these two works of divine creation: namely, individual things themselves, and the subsequent images of those individual things. Human art also, through architecture, builds a house, and through painting, creates an image of a house—like a kind of human dream made for those who are awake. THE<note>Theaetetus</note>: No doubt. HO<note>The Stranger/Host</note>: In other things as well, by dividing into two, we find twin works of our creative action. For we make the thing itself by a primary faculty, but the image by an imaginary one. THE: I understand clearly now; and I set down two types of the creative faculty. First, I divide it into divine and human; then into the creation of things themselves or their images. HO: Let us remember, I pray, that we said there must be two kinds of the imaginary faculty: the "assimilative" <note>likeness-making</note> and the "fantastic" <note>appearance-making</note>—if indeed something truly false, and a false thing among those that exist, is to be found. THE: It was certainly said. HO: Has it not been established? And therefore shall we now count these two types without controversy? THE: Certainly. HO: The "fantastic" must therefore be cut into two again. THE: In what way? HO: One made through instruments; the other where the creator of the phantasm presents himself as the instrument. THE: How do you mean? HO: Whenever someone, using your shape, renders his own body similar to yours, or his voice to your voice; this imitation is called "fantastic." THE: Indeed. HO: Calling this the "imitative" part, let us distribute it thus: and let us pass over all the rest as if we were now eager for rest, and let us grant to another to collect it into one and assign it a fitting name. THE: Let the power be distributed, and let this be dismissed. HO: This, moreover, O Theaetetus, must be considered double. For what reason, observe. THE: Tell me. HO: Of those who imitate, some do this knowing what they imitate; others, however, do so in ignorance. Shall we place any greater discrepancy and division than that between ignorance and knowledge? THE: None. HO: Was not the imitation we just mentioned that of those who know? For he who knows you imitates your shape. THE: That very one. HO: But what should be said of the shape of justice and of virtue as a whole? Do not many, while they are ignorant but think they know, strive in both words and deeds so that it appears to be in them, imitating that which seems so to them? THE: Very many indeed. HO: Does hope fail them so that, just as they are not just, they do not even appear so? Or the opposite? THE: The opposite. HO: Shall we call this imitator different from the former one—the ignorant from the knowing? THE: We shall clearly. HO: Will they derive a single name proper to both? Or is it perhaps difficult because some ancient cause of dividing genera into species was unknown to our predecessors, so that no one contended to divide them, and therefore they are necessarily poor in names? And if it may seem a bit bold to say, yet for the sake of declaration and distinction, let us name that imitation which accompanies opinion "opinable imitation"; but that which accompanies science, a certain "historical and knowing imitation." THE: So be it. HO: We must use only one of these names. For we placed the Sophist in the genus of imitators, but not in the genus of those who know. THE: That is so. HO: Let us therefore examine this "opinionated" imitator like iron, to see if he is solid and simple, or the opposite. THE: Let us examine him. HO: He is certainly very manifold. For one kind of Sophist is foolish and silly, thinking he knows what he only opines. But the other figure, because of his varied revolution in speeches, certainly carries much suspicion and fear lest he be ignorant of those things which he pretends to know before others. THE: He is entirely of both kinds, as you have narrated. HO: Shall we not therefore set down one as a simple imitator and the other as an ironic imitator? THE: It is consistent. HO: Of this latter, do we say there is one genus or two? THE: You see to it. HO: I am thinking, and two offer themselves to me as I think. One indeed uses irony publicly with a long speech before the people; the other privately, with certain small quibbles, forces the one disputing with him to contradict himself in his own speeches. THE: You speak very rightly. HO: What shall we name that former one? Civil or popular? THE: Popular. HO: And the other, "Sophon"—that is, wise—or "Sophistic"? THE: It is not permitted to call him wise, since we have established him as ignorant. But because he imitates the wise man, he shall receive a certain name similar to that. And at last I understand: it is fitting that this very man be called, entirely and truly, the Sophist. HO: Shall we not, as before, now bind his name together, folding it from the end back to the beginning? THE: Entirely. HO: He will finally be truly defined as a Sophist who asserts that this is his generation and lineage. The Sophist, I say, is he who in speeches forces the one disputing to contradict himself; who is a part of the ironic, coming from the opinionated imitator, proceeding likewise from the fantastic genus of the imaginary faculty: the determined progeny not of divine, but of human creation; and from the number of those who, with words as if with certain spells, deceive their listeners in a wonderful manner. THE: It must be said exactly so.

# PREFACE TO THE CIVIL STATE.

<note>original: "ARGVMENTVM IN CIVILEM"</note>

—and from the royal faith of the kings of faiths, and from the empire of the world, he might now be named a leader born for the world; indeed, men, by changing the letters <note>A wordplay on the name "Federicus" and "Fide regit" (he rules by faith)</note>, would call and declare Federico of Urbino to be the Duke. All the deities assented to Jove, except for Juno. For Juno alone, the ambitious queen of the thicker air, has until now envied the celestial kingdom on earth. But Pallas <note>Athena</note> and Mercury, with the others favoring and with Truth as a witness, long ago most willingly bestowed the crown and royal scepter upon the same man to whom Jupiter did. Since the Academy everywhere worships and follows Pallas and Mercury, it also most happily grants the kingdom and monarchy of the whole world—such as the divine Plato describes—to Federico, Duke of Urbino, both by the judgment of Jove and by the most well-deserved testimony of Truth.

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino on Plato’s Book Concerning Kingship, or the Statesman.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a crescent moon and stars within a circular frame, set against a floral background.</image-desc>Since God and nature produce man for the sake of acting, He certainly produces him so that he may act. Let him act for the sake of divine things. Just as there is one end for the sake of which nature creates the thumb, another for the sake of which it creates the hand or foot, and yet another toward which it creates the whole man: so there is one end toward which it directs the individual man, another toward which it directs the family, and likewise another toward which it directs the city and the kingdom. And finally, that end must be considered the best for the sake of which God created the entire human race. Let no one think that while there is a certain end for every particular group, there is none for the whole; or that while order exists in the parts of human life, there is nonetheless confusion in the universal kind of life; or finally, that while the parts have a union among themselves for the intent of a single end, the whole itself is dispersed. For this reason, it is necessary that there be a certain end for the human race, and that it consist in a certain action concerning perfection, through which it may both imitate higher things according to its strength and diligently govern lower things. Let science indeed investigate natural things; let prudence dispose human affairs; and let it worship and venerate divine things through piety. Therefore, an end of this kind requires a twin life: established similarly in action and in contemplation, yet in such a way that action is instituted for the sake of contemplation as something more divine. 

Furthermore, the absolute perfection of both lives requires so many and such varied supports that it cannot be fulfilled by a few, nor even by many men, but only by the whole human race together. It is impossible, however, for such diverse powers to be led through such diverse means to one common end for all, unless they are led by one person through a single law leading everyone equally into one. Just as craftsmen and assistants, differing greatly among themselves in kind and character, bringing together very diverse materials into one form of a building, will never conveniently assemble and construct it opportunely unless they are ruled by one single law of one architect. Wherefore, not without cause, when Plato sought the king as the monarch of the world, he first brought the architect into the midst; and he finally distinguished science into three kinds. The first of these is occupied in knowing, the second in acting, and the third in making. In the first he placed arithmetic and geometry; in the second, the architect; in the third, the craftsman and assistant. He proved that the faculty of the architect should be placed in the middle between pure speculation and pure service; yet it participates more in speculation than in service, for it does not only judge in the manner of geometers, but also commands those who make things and is always present at the workmanship. He wishes the king to be of such a sort: namely, one who judges truths in the manner of those who contemplate, and who mandates laws to be carried out—not someone else's laws, but his own. 

Accordingly, Plato, using a most exact division which is necessary for the definition of the science, names the king—in the Homeric fashion—the shepherd and caretaker of the human race. He designates that there ought to be one shepherd of the entire human race as if of one sheepfold, where he says that God was once the shepherd of the human race, under whom that golden age of Saturn existed. He also judges that the king should be called the pilot <note>or Governor</note> of human life, as if of a ship. He signifies, moreover, that the empire of all must be brought into one, so that human governance may be as similar as possible to the divine; for indeed, God is the one ruler of the whole world. This he confirms briefly by these reasons: First, if you subject the three parts of the world—Asia, Africa, and Europe—distributed to three kings, it will very easily happen that either one will wage war against two, or two against one at some time; or at least they will be forced to dispute concerning borders or some other matter. Therefore, either the judgment of the suit must be referred to one of the three, or to a certain fourth judge appointed besides the three. By whatever reason that is finally done, it will be necessary for the judge—if his sentence is to be obeyed—to have empire over those among whom he judges. Otherwise, the judgment will be of no moment, and he will judge in vain, which might seem to be dissolved by kings who are either more powerful or at least equally so. 

Therefore, there must be one king as the judge of all, to be venerated by all without a doubt. Furthermore, the king ought to be an exemplar of virtues to his subjects. He will be such especially if he is one above all, upon whom everyone casts their eyes. If he possesses the whole world, he will neither affect the kingdom of another nor envy others. These two things—namely, greed and envy—are the primary causes of robberies and wars; and since his own things are most dear to each, he will most greatly love all as his own; he will love all nations equally and care for them equally. He will desire peace above all; he will crave tranquility and an abundance of all goods, such as appeared as a certain shadow of monarchy during the reign of Octavian <note>Augustus Caesar</note>. The subjects will live most justly, since no path of flight lies open anywhere to the unjust under a Monarch; and though they live with the least license for sinning, they will nonetheless live in the highest liberty: not serving tyrants, or a few powerful men, or madness...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino argues for a universal monarchy, comparing the King to an architect or a shepherd, asserting that a single world ruler ensures peace and mirrors divine order.</summary>
<keywords>Monarchy, Plato, Federico da Montefeltro, political philosophy, universal peace, Augustus Caesar, Golden Age of Saturn, divine governance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical introduction to Plato’s "Politicus" (The Statesman), likely authored by the translator Marsilio Ficino. It discusses the nature of the ideal ruler and the allegorical "Age of Saturn."</meta>

# SIXTEENTH BOOK
# 211

not by the rages of a subject people, but by a wise, just, and pious king, thus led toward the common good just as sailors are led to port by the prudence of a just helmsman. In this matter, those who are ruled consult their own interests by obeying the king; and the king himself will live not so much for himself as for all those committed to his care by God. For right governance, as is debated in the books *On the Republic* <note>Plato's *Republic*</note>, establishes the ruler for the sake of those who are ruled, not the ruled for the sake of the ruler. Furthermore, he compares the king to a doctor: warning that, in the manner of doctors, he should impose laws and bring salutary remedies both opportunely and, if necessary, unopportunely, both to those who are willing and sometimes to those who are unwilling. Indeed, he more often calls such a governor and curator a "civil man" <note>original: *civilem virum*; referring to the title *Politicus*</note> than a king, signifying that he ought to be so human and, if possible, mild, that he appears to be a fellow citizen among citizens, superior in prudence, justice, and care rather than by any other excess. But if anyone, by some very great interval, manifestly surpasses all others in prudence and justice, he judges without controversy that this man—even if he lives as a private citizen—is the king of all created by God. If, however, among some men there is very little difference in these respects, they should be reduced as it were to one, and royal authority granted to them. But to a multitude, by no means; for a multitude worthy of such great authority can nowhere be found. 

As can be gathered from his other books, he wishes royal authority to be handed down by the elders and the most proven men: whose senate would then be the colleague of the king, as in a republic of the best men <note>an aristocracy</note>. Moreover, the king should establish laws together with the senate. These laws may not be transgressed by any private person, nor changed by the common people. It should, however, be permitted to the king and the senate together, according to the opportunity of the time and as far as is expedient, to accommodate them with diligent equity to the things themselves and the times: and to change them if necessary. In his letters, he deems the king himself to be held sacred, and to be appointed in the manner of the Egyptian priests as a presiding officer of sacred rites and mysteries: and as one who is sacred and free from contamination, he does not permit him to be present in judgments where slaughter, exile, or imprisonment are discussed. 

Therefore, in this very book, he proves that such royal dignity is the best of all forms of governance, as we have said: but the worst is tyranny, which commands neither by law nor by a legitimate mind, but rather by impulse and lust. In the second place, he praises the "best men" <note>aristocracy</note>, and likewise censures the "power of the few" <note>oligarchy</note>. In the third place, he praises the governance of the many, namely the popular form <note>democracy</note>, if they govern by law: and likewise censures it, if not by law. After this, he debates what the royal duty is: namely, to provide whatever is necessary for the human race, and especially for living well and blessedly. He should prudently judge how many and what kind of arts contribute to this very end, whether in peace or in war, whether in speaking or in acting, either publicly or privately: and he, together with the senate, should have supreme command over all. 

But above all, he should compose the souls of all with a certain most decent mixture of fortitude and temperance, imitating musicians, who, rightly mixing high notes with low, modulate the sweetest harmonies. For he demonstrates—and indeed divinely—that it is not safe to strain souls too far toward fortitude, as if into a sharp pitch; or to relax them too much toward temperance, as if into a deep pitch. For from the former, they eventually emerge as wild; from the latter, as effeminate. And those citizens attack their country like enemies; while these others defend neither themselves nor their country from enemies. Wherefore he deems it best that a consonance of characters be forged everywhere from a graceful coupling of both virtues. 

But let enough be said thus far concerning the order of the book. As for what he debates regarding the motion of the spheres, providence, and fate, we have sufficiently explained these in our *Theology* <note>Ficino's *Platonic Theology*</note>. In these matters, he certainly teaches us allegorically that we have no true and legitimate king except either in heaven itself, or on earth him whom the King of Heaven himself has appointed for us as a shepherd: a shepherd, I say, not in name alone, but one who represents the King of Heaven himself to the best of his ability by the faith and likeness of his life. 

He also commemorates two kingdoms, namely of Jove <note>Jupiter</note> and of Saturn: and he places the kingdom of Saturn before the kingdom of Jove as being more happy. For under Jove, human action and life are signified; but under Saturn, the contemplation of divine things. For Saturn, called *Cronos* in the Greek name, as Plato teaches in the *Cratylus*, encompasses the inviolable purity and integrity of the mind. When he says that men live blessedly while Saturn is reigning, he shows that the human race will be blessed when a certain divine mind reigns, which establishes actions for the sake of contemplation. 

I shall soon make an end to this argument, if I first bring forward a brief allegory of this mystery. For he says that the present circuit of the world from East to West is Jovian and fated. But there will one day be another opposite to this under Saturn, from West back to East. In which men will be born spontaneously: and will proceed from old age into youth: and nourishment will be supplied to them freely from the earth under a perpetual spring according to their wish. I judge that he calls the soul of the world "Jove": by whose fatal law this manifest order of the manifest world is disposed. Furthermore, he wishes the life of souls in elemental bodies to be Jovian, or devoted to the senses and action. But Saturn is the supreme intellect among the angels, by whose rays souls are illustrated beyond the angels, and are kindled: and are continually raised to the intellectual life according to their powers: whenever they turn to such a life, they are said to live under the reign of Saturn, insofar as they live by intelligence. Therefore, in that life, they are said to be regenerated spontaneously because they are reformed for the better by their own choice. Again, they grow young from day to day—that is, from day to day (if indeed days are numbered there) they flourish more and more. This is what the Apostle Paul meant: *The inner man is renewed from day to day.* Finally, nourishment is supplied to them in abundance under a perpetual spring: because they enjoy the wonderful spectacles of truth itself, not through the senses and laborious discipline, but through an inward light, and with the greatest tranquility and pleasure of life.

# ON THE STATESMAN OR ON KINGSHIP. SOCRATES, THEODORUS, STRANGER, SOCRATES JUNIOR.

**SOCRATES.** I owe you a great debt of gratitude, Theodorus, for having introduced me to both Theaetetus and this Stranger from Elea <note>The "Stranger" (Hospes) is a philosopher from the school of Parmenides in Elea.</note>. **THEODORUS.** You will perhaps owe me a triple debt, Socrates, after they have defined for you the Statesman and the Philosopher. **SOCRATES.** Is that so, Theodorus? Shall we say this is the case, having heard it from one who excels in geometry and calculations? **THEODORUS.** In what way, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Because you have evidently placed an equal value on each of these men; yet in honor they stand further apart than can be expressed by your mathematical proportions. **THEODORUS.** Well and justly spoken, Socrates, by our god Hammon <note>An Egyptian deity often identified with Zeus/Jupiter; Theodorus, being from Cyrene in Libya, swears by this local god.</note>; you have quite memorably rebuked my error in calculation. Therefore, I shall come to you for such matters hereafter. But you, Stranger, do not be reluctant to gratify us; rather, choose whether you wish to describe the Statesman or the Philosopher first, and then describe the one chosen. **STRANGER.** It must be done as you command, Theodorus; since we have once begun, we must not stop until we reach the finish line. But what should be done regarding young Theaetetus here? **THEODORUS.** In what regard? **STRANGER.** Shall we let him rest now? And in his place, shall we take this Socrates <note>Socrates Junior, a student, not the elder Socrates.</note> as his partner in the exercise? What do you advise? **THEODORUS.** Take Socrates. For since they are both young, they will easily bear all labors, especially with a break in between. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, Stranger, both seem to be related to me in a way. You judge Theaetetus to be like me in the features of his face. As for this Socrates, since his name is the same as mine, it provides us a certain mutual kinship. It is proper for us, being similar by a certain nature, to recognize one another through conversation. I met with Theaetetus yesterday in dispute, and today I have heard him responding to this Stranger. But with Socrates, neither has yet occurred. It is necessary to examine him as well. Let him respond to you now; he can respond to me another time. **STRANGER.** So we shall do, Socrates. Do you hear, Socrates? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** I hear. **STRANGER.** Do you agree with him? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** I agree. **STRANGER.** As far as you are concerned, then, nothing prevents us from discussing. And it is even less fitting for me to be an obstacle to this dispute. Indeed, after the Sophist himself, it seems necessary that we investigate the Statesman. Respond then: is it proper to place this man in the number of those who are called "knowers" <note>Those possessing *scientia* or systematic knowledge.</note>? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** It is proper. **STRANGER.** Therefore, we must divide the sciences, just as we did when seeking the Sophist. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Perhaps. **STRANGER.** Yet the method of dividing is not the same. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** No. **STRANGER.** But another. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Another. **STRANGER.** Where then shall we find the path to the science of the statesman? For it must be found: and having set it apart from all others, we must fix one "idea" <note>The Platonic *Idea* or Form.</note> upon it, and another single "species" upon the others; and we must think as if all sciences were enclosed within two species. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** It is your task now, Stranger, to do this. Not mine at all. **STRANGER.** Indeed, it is yours too, once it has been made clear. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** You speak wisely. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, arithmetic and several others very similar to it are free from action; they provide only knowledge. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** That is certainly how it must be said. **STRANGER.** But those which pertain to architecture and manual labor possess a science innate to actions; they complete bodies produced by them which did not exist before. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** It is clear. **STRANGER.** Divide all sciences thus. One as active; the other as only knowing names <note>Theoretical or speculative knowledge.</note>. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Let there be two species of science, though all science is one. **STRANGER.** Do we wish the Statesman, the King, the Master, and the Head of the Household to be the same? Or do we place as many arts in these as there are names? Rather, follow me in this division. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Which one? **STRANGER.** This one, I say. If some private citizen is able to sufficiently advise a public physician, is it not necessary that he be called by the name of the same art as the one he advises? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Certainly. **STRANGER.** What then? If some private citizen can admonish and instruct the king of a city, will he not be said to possess that science which the ruler ought to have? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** He will. **STRANGER.** But the science of a true king is the royal discipline. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** It is. **STRANGER.** Whoever is endowed with it, whether he performs a public duty or lives as a private citizen, will rightly be called "royal" according to this skill. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Rightly. **STRANGER.** Truly, the head of a household and a master are the same. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** The same indeed. **STRANGER.** Does it matter for the sake of ruling whether a city is large or small? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Not at all. **STRANGER.** Therefore, the science of all these is one, which is what we were inquiring about just now: whether one calls this discipline royal, or political, or domestic, let us think it makes no difference. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** None. **STRANGER.** This at least is doubtful to no one: that every king can do very little with his hands or the rest of his limbs for the safety of the kingdom, but very much by intelligence and strength of mind. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** It is established. **STRANGER.** Do you wish then that we say the king is closer to speculative science than to active science or manual labor? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** I certainly do. **STRANGER.** We shall therefore put together the science of the state and the statesman, and the royal science and the king, as one and the same. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Clearly. **STRANGER.** And we shall proceed in order to the following things, especially if we distinguish speculative science. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Entirely. **STRANGER.** Attend, I pray: do we see any division in this? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Tell me, of what kind? **STRANGER.** Of this kind, I say. There exists a certain faculty of calculation. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** There exists. **STRANGER.** That, I believe, is of the number of those which are engaged in speculation. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** Certainly of that number. **STRANGER.** The faculty of calculation will surely know the difference between numbers. Do we attribute any other work to it than to discern and judge what is known? **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** What else? **STRANGER.** For no architect uses manual labor, but presides over those who use it. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.** That is so: since he applies judgment, not manual service. **SOCRATES JUNIOR.**

<margin>
Mathematics is free from action: possessing knowledge alone.
One part of science is active: the other is knowing.
The statesman, king, master, and head of household are the same.
Who is the "royal" man.

# BOOK SIXTEEN

That too is true. **GUEST:** Rightly, therefore, he must be said to participate in the science of contemplation <note>original: "speculandi scientię"; referring to theoretical rather than practical knowledge</note>. **SOCRATES:** Most certainly. **GUEST:** This, as I judge, pertains to this judge: that he does not hand over the workmanship like a calculator, but applies himself assiduously; and he mandates and ordains to individual workers their own proper work, until they have finished what was commanded. **SOCRATES:** Correct. **GUEST:** Are not all these sciences contemplative, as are all those that follow the science of calculation? But do these two types, judgment and command, differ from one another? **SOCRATES:** They appear to. **GUEST:** Wherefore, if we distribute all contemplation into two, and assign one part to judgment and the other to command, we shall perhaps think we have distributed them rightly. **SOCRATES:** Rightly indeed, as my opinion goes. **GUEST:** Those who treat something in common think themselves mutually satisfied if they ever agree. **SOCRATES:** Why not? **GUEST:** As long, therefore, as we are in accord in this, the opinions of others are to be disregarded. **SOCRATES:** Entirely. **GUEST:** Come then, in which of these arts is it fitting to place the royal man? In the judicial, as a kind of spectator? Or rather in the commanding art, as a master? **SOCRATES:** In this latter one, rather. **GUEST:** We must see, moreover, if the commanding art admits any distinction. And so it seems to me. By as much as a shopkeeper differs from one who sells his own work, so a king differs from a herald. **SOCRATES:** In what way? **GUEST:** Shopkeepers, receiving the works of others previously sold, sell them again themselves. **SOCRATES:** True. **GUEST:** Not otherwise does a herald, having the opinion of another mandated to him, mandate it himself to others. **SOCRATES:** So it is. **GUEST:** Shall we then mix the royal faculty with the commanding, the preceptive, the prophetic, and the heraldic, and <margin>Commanding faculties.</margin> many other arts of the same kind, because they command all? Or would you rather, according to the previous comparison, devise a name also through some comparison? Since indeed the genus of those who command their own things is almost <margin>In which genus the Royal is found.</margin> without a name; and so let us divide these: so that we place the royal genus in the number of those who mandate their own things, omitting all others, upon which anyone else may impose names as he pleases; for our discourse was instituted for the sake of the prince, not the subject. **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **GUEST:** After this has been sufficiently distinguished from those by diversity, it must again be divided into its property, if only we find any yielding partition in it. **SOCRATES:** Very much so. **GUEST:** And it seems it can be found. Follow me, then, in dividing. **SOCRATES:** Where shall I follow? **GUEST:** Whoever presides by commanding, commands for the sake of some generation <note>meaning the production or bringing-forth of something</note>. **SOCRATES:** Without a doubt. **GUEST:** For it is not very difficult to divide all generated things in two ways. **SOCRATES:** By what reason? **GUEST:** Part are animate, part are inanimate. **SOCRATES:** It is established. **GUEST:** If we wish to cut the commanding part of the contemplative faculty into these members, let us cut it. **SOCRATES:** Into what? **GUEST:** Let one part of it be placed in the generation of the inanimate; the other part in the generation of the animate. And thus the whole will be cut in two. **SOCRATES:** Indeed. **GUEST:** Let us dismiss one part; taking up the other: and let us divide that whole again into two. **SOCRATES:** Which of those do you think should be taken up? **GUEST:** That which commands concerning animals. For royal majesty does not preside over the inanimate like architecture, but more nobly over living things; and its power is occupied with these. **SOCRATES:** Excellent. **GUEST:** Concerning the generation and nutrition of animals, a double care is found. One of a single animal. The other of the whole herd. **SOCRATES:** Rightly. **GUEST:** But the civil man does not undertake a private care, like a plowman who drives an ox, or a groom who saddles a horse; but he acts in the place of him who feeds horses or oxen. **SOCRATES:** What has now been said seems to be true. **GUEST:** Whether from the nutrition of animals do we call that which feeds them in herds "herd-nutrition," or "common nutrition"? **SOCRATES:** Both occur in speaking. **GUEST:** You have answered excellently, Socrates; and if you avoid curiosity over words, you will turn out <margin>Curiosity over words is to be avoided.</margin> much wiser in your old age. Therefore, for the present, it must be done as you bid. But do you not see in what way showing herd-nutrition to be twofold makes it so that what will be investigated in doubles for that which is now proposed, is sought again in halves? **SOCRATES:** I will certainly strive; and it already seems to me that <margin>The genus is the double of two species: the species is the half.</margin> one is the common guardianship of men, the other of brutes. **GUEST:** You have distinguished altogether and bravely. Yet we must beware with all our strength lest this happen to us hereafter. **SOCRATES:** What do you warn us to beware of? **GUEST:** That we do not separate one tiny particle against many and large ones; nor take it without a species; but let that part have a species at the same time. For it is a most beautiful thing to discern what is sought from others immediately, if only <margin>A warning in making the division.</margin> it be done rightly: just as you yourself a little while ago, judging about dividing: yet you hastened to divide, turning your speech toward men. But it is not quite safely friendly to arrive at something extreme and thin. <margin>Precepts for making a division.</margin> It is better to proceed through the middle by partitioning. For thus we find ideas more easily and better. This, moreover, refers entirely to those things which are sought. **SOCRATES:** By what reason do you say this, Guest? **GUEST:** I must try, on account of the benevolence of your nature, to explain more clearly. At present, it is impossible to declare what is proposed through these things so that nothing is missing. But for the sake of declaring it, it seems it should be extended a little further. **SOCRATES:** What, finally, do you find fault with in our partition? **GUEST:** Something like this: if someone, contending to cut the human race into two, should partition it just as many of those who live here partition it. These, forsooth, separate the Greek race as one from all others. For all others, who are innumerable and bound by no communion of life or speech among themselves, they designate by the name "barbarian": and because of this appellation, they think this whole is also one genus. It would be similar, moreover, if someone wishing to divide number into two, should take ten thousand separately from the others as one species; and then, imposing one name on the rest, should set them down as one genus. But a division would be made more rightly and more by species and by two members, if one were to divide number by even and odd; or the human race by male and female: but should only then segregate the Lydians and Phrygians or certain others from all others, when both the hope and the faculty of finding the genus and the part of both differing from each other failed him. **SOCRATES:** You speak skillfully, Guest. But show by what reason that could be more clearly understood, that a part and a genus are not the same, but different. **GUEST:** O best of men, Socrates,

<summary>The Guest and Socrates use the method of logical division to define the "Statesman," distinguishing the art of command from judgment and narrowing it down to the collective care of human beings rather than animals or inanimate objects. The Guest warns against "unscientific" divisions, such as the arbitrary distinction between Greeks and Barbarians, advocating for divisions based on natural species.</summary>
