# THE STATESMAN, OR ON KINGSHIP
## FOLIO LXXXI.
### l

<margin>What is the difference between a part and a species.</margin>
What you ask is no light matter. We have already wandered further from our original purpose than is fitting for a logical discussion. Now, as is proper, let the discourse return to the point from which it departed. At another time, when we have leisure, we will follow these tracks as if on a detour. However, O Socrates, you must be carefully on your guard against this: do not ever think you have heard me say that these are distinguished appropriately. **SOCRATES:** What do you mean? **STRANGER:** That a "part" and a "species" <note>original: *species*, often translated as "class" or "form" in Platonic logic</note> are the same thing. **SOCRATES:** Why so? **STRANGER:** Whatever is a *species* of something must necessarily also be a *part* of that same thing of which it is called a species. However, it is not necessary for a *part* to be a *species*. Always report me as saying it this way rather than the other, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** It shall be done as you command. **STRANGER:** Now then, tell me. **SOCRATES:** What? **STRANGER:** This point from which we digressed. I believe we have wandered this far because, when you were asked how the nourishment of the herd should be divided, you suddenly answered too broadly, saying there are two kinds of living creatures: one of humans, and the other of all beasts together. **SOCRATES:** That is true. **STRANGER:** Then indeed you seemed to me to have cut off one part and thought the entire remaining group of animals should be placed together because you could call them all by one common name, "beasts." **SOCRATES:** That is how it happened. **STRANGER:** This, my brave Socrates, is just as if some other animal—say, a crane, or some such creature—were a sharer of intelligence and named things as you do: it might set "cranes" as one distinct race, and then group all other creatures, including humans, into one other single kind, calling itself the "rational race" and all others "beasts." Therefore, let us try to avoid all such errors. **SOCRATES:** By what path? **STRANGER:** Let us not divide the whole race of animals at once, so that we may err less in these matters. For it is not right. We erred in that way just now. **SOCRATES:** How? **STRANGER:** That part of contemplative science which looks toward commanding was established as belonging to the kind that cares for animals—specifically, herding animals. Was it not so? **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** Therefore, at that point, the whole animal kingdom was distinguished into the wild and the tame. For those whose nature is such that they can be tamed are called domestic; the rest are wild. **SOCRATES:** Excellent. **STRANGER:** Now, the science we seek is among the domestic ones, and it was to be sought regarding the social kind of animals. **SOCRATES:** Indeed. **STRANGER:** Therefore, let us not divide by looking at everything at once, nor let us hurry too much in our partitioning so that we might suddenly grasp the "civil science" <note>The art of politics or statesmanship</note>. For excessive haste has caused that which is said in the proverb to happen to us now. **SOCRATES:** What is that? **STRANGER:** That when we have hurried too much in the division, we finish more slowly. **SOCRATES:** And the Stranger has rightly said so. **STRANGER:** So much for that. But let us again divide the common nourishment of animals from the beginning. For perhaps the discourse itself, led step by step to its end, will demonstrate more clearly what you so vehemently desire. Answer this. **SOCRATES:** To what shall I answer? **STRANGER:** Perhaps you have heard this from many people—for I do not think you have been present among those who tame fish in the Nile or in the royal lakes. But perhaps you have seen what happens at fountains. **SOCRATES:** I have seen these things myself, and heard the others from many. **STRANGER:** Furthermore, you have heard and believe that some people breed flocks of geese and cranes, even if you have never spent time in the fields of Thessaly. **SOCRATES:** Without a doubt. **STRANGER:** I asked you these things because the common care of animals seems to be partly of aquatic creatures and partly of land creatures. **SOCRATES:** It is indeed. **STRANGER:** Do you agree that the care of the herd should be distinguished in two ways, so that it nourishes partly wet and partly dry animals? **SOCRATES:** I certainly agree. **STRANGER:** No one will ask which of these the royal care looks toward, for it is doubtful to no one. **SOCRATES:** To no one. **STRANGER:** For everyone will distinguish the nourishment of the dry animals especially. **SOCRATES:** Into what members? **STRANGER:** Into the care of those that fly or those that walk. **SOCRATES:** That is the truth. **STRANGER:** And that the civil faculty <note>The skill of the statesman</note> is concerned only with those that walk, even the most foolish person, so to speak, would notice. **SOCRATES:** Without controversy. **STRANGER:** Furthermore, we ought to divide the nourishment of the walking kind into two, like an even number. **SOCRATES:** It is clear. **STRANGER:** Now, two paths seem able to lead us toward where our discourse tends. One is a short-cut, which separates a small portion from a large one. The other is a longer circuit, which observes that rule mentioned before: that the division should be made through the middle. We may enter whichever we wish. **SOCRATES:** Is it not possible to go by both? **STRANGER:** Not at the same time, O wonderful youth! But it is possible at different times. **SOCRATES:** I choose both, then—one after the other. **STRANGER:** That is easy, since what remains is small. Truly, in the beginning or middle of the journey, this would have been a hard rule for us. But now, since it seems best, let us first enter the longer way. For since we are fresh, we will complete the long journey more easily. Look at this distinction. **SOCRATES:** Just say it. **STRANGER:** Those that walk, and are tame, and gather in herds, are divided into two parts according to nature. **SOCRATES:** Into what parts? **STRANGER:** Some are armed with horns; others lack them. **SOCRATES:** That is apparent. **STRANGER:** Dividing the care of walking animals, describe the condition of each part in words. For if you wish to name them, you will complicate the matter too much. **SOCRATES:** How then do you think we should speak? **STRANGER:** Since the care of walking animals is distinguished in two ways, one part is located in the horned part of the herd, and the other is left in the hornless <note>original: *mutilata*, literally "maimed" or "mutilated," used here for animals naturally without horns</note> part. **SOCRATES:** This has been thoroughly stated; for they have been shown sufficiently. **STRANGER:** It is clear that the king is the shepherd of a certain hornless herd. **SOCRATES:** It is certainly clear. **STRANGER:** Therefore, breaking this down, let us try to show what is moved. **SOCRATES:** By all means. **STRANGER:** Does it please you to divide it into a part with solid hooves and a part with cloven hooves? Or rather into specific and common generation? Do you understand? **SOCRATES:** What? **STRANGER:** That the species of horses and donkeys breed promiscuously with each other. **SOCRATES:** Certainly. **STRANGER:** But the remaining domestic and social animals breed only within their own species without foreign mixing...

<margin>Proverb: To finish more slowly by hurrying too much. Fish being tamed near the Nile.</margin>

# BOOK SIXTEEN

<margin>Promiscuous generation and simple generation.</margin>
...they procreate. SO. That is clear to everyone. HO. Does civil discipline, then, care for animals of promiscuous generation <note>original: "promiscue generationis," referring to animals that interbreed freely</note>, or those of simple generation? SO. Of the unmixed and simple kind, without a doubt. HO. Just as we have preserved this nature of living beings in the previous sections up to this point, we ought to cut it into two parts. SO. That is proper. HO. Indeed, we have already distinguished almost all domestic animals of a sociable nature—which they call tame—except for two kinds. Furthermore, it is not fitting to count our own kind among the gregarious cattle. SO. Certainly not, but in what way? HO. This, I say, must be distinguished into two, just as it is fitting to distinguish you and Theaetetus, since you are both well-versed in geometry: namely, by the diagonal, and again by the diagonal of the diagonal. SO.

<image-desc>A logical diagram consisting of a square divided into four sections by a diagonal line and a horizontal line. The top section is labeled "DIAGONAL", the middle section "BIPED", and the bottom section "QUADRUPED". Along the diagonal line, the words "OF THE DIAGONAL" and "GONAL" are written.</image-desc>

Why do you say that? HO. Is the condition of the human race for the progress of nature established in any other way than as a biped in potentiality, like a diagonal? <note>A mathematical metaphor: the diagonal of a square of side 1 is the square root of 2; the Stranger is using geometric ratios to classify humans as "two-footed" creatures.</note> SO. Not otherwise. HO. The condition of the remaining kind is again, according to potentiality, the diagonal of our potentiality, since it is constituted with twice two feet <note>i.e., four feet</note>. SO. Nothing prevents it from being so. And I almost understand now what you wish to show. HO. Do we see, O Socrates, what a ridiculous thing happened to us in the previous division? SO. What was that? HO. The human race was mixed together and running alongside the most noble and easiest race of all <note>likely a reference to pigs or similar livestock in the previous logical division</note>. SO. I see it, and clearly, what follows. HO. Is it not fitting that those which are slowest arrive last? SO. That is consistent. HO. But we did not notice this at all: that the King would appear even more ridiculous running along with the herd, performing his course with the one who, of all men, is best trained for the ease of life. SO. Entirely so. HO. Now it is clearly evident, O Socrates, what was said in the inquiry of the Sophist. SO. What was that? HO. That in this kind of progression of speech, he cared nothing for the pure more than the impure, and did not at all despise the shorter before the longer; but he always accomplishes that which is most true. SO. So it seems. HO. After this, do not get ahead of me by asking for a shorter way to the definition of the King; I shall enter first. SO. By all means. HO. I say, therefore, it was necessary above to distribute the walking animal into biped and quadruped; but since man was then left grouped only with the winged kind, we should again divide the biped genus itself into the naked animal and the feathered one. Then, with this distinction added, and the art that nourishes and preserves men being shown, we may now place the civil and royal man over it like a charioteer, giving him the reins and the rudders of the city, as if this knowledge were his own. SO. You have returned the discourse to me most excellently, and as if it were a debt, with the digression itself serving as interest and being fully paid. HO. Come then, let us collect the discourse on the name of the civil art from the beginning to the end. SO. Certainly. HO. Of that science which is engaged in contemplation, one part was the skill of commanding; a part of this was that faculty which commands by itself and its own authority; a not insignificant member of this was the nourishing of animals; of this, again, the feeding of the herd; by which the feeding of walking animals is divided. From that, the species was selected which pastures animals lacking horns. Furthermore, it is necessary to fold a triple part of this—not at all a small one—if anyone wishes to encompass it in one name, calling it the science of generation concerning the mixed care of the shepherd. The portion of this in the biped herd that feeds only men is that very imperial faculty we seek, which we name both royal and civil. SO. Exactly. HO. Has it really been done by us as I say, O Socrates? SO. Regarding what? HO. Whether what we proposed has been sufficiently finished? Or has this been mostly overlooked in the question: that we have described it in a certain way, yet not yet fully defined it? SO. Why do you say that? HO. I will try to explain more plainly what I feel. SO. Speak now. HO. Since it is established that there are many faculties of shepherds, one certain one of those, and of the care of one herd, seemed to be civil discipline itself. SO. Indeed. HO. We showed that this was the common nutrition not of horses nor of other brutes, but of men only. SO. That too. HO. Let us see, then, the proper difference of the shepherd-kings. SO. What difference? HO. If someone by chance, having the name of another art, should claim for himself the common nutrition of the herd, what should be said? SO. In what way do you mean? HO. Just as if merchants, farmers, and cooks, and moreover gymnasts and doctors, should rise up against the shepherds whom we have called "politicians," and assert that they themselves are the shepherds of men; since they themselves supply food not only to the common people, but even to kings and magistrates. SO. Would they not be speaking the truth? HO. Perhaps. And let us consider this. But we know this: that no one would contend with a cowherd about these things; but he himself is without controversy the shepherd of the herd who cares for the oxen; he is the doctor; he is the author of their matings, and the helper and nurturer of every birth. Furthermore, no one delights, draws, and soothes the herd better with jests and music—as much as their nature is capable of—handling music for his herd with instruments and voice. And the same reasoning applies to other shepherds. Is it not so? SO. Very much so. HO. In what way, then, does that discourse about the king seem right and whole, when we posit him as that shepherd and nurturer of the human herd, separating him alone from the others, when many others contend for this very thing? SO. In no way. HO. Did we not rightly doubt a little while ago, when we suspected that we might only be bringing in a certain figure of a king, yet not yet perfectly defining the statesman himself, unless we first [distinguish] those who entangle themselves with him, and...

The condition of divine things.</margin> but the nature of the body is not capable of this order. Furthermore, all that which we have called the heaven and the world has received many and happy gifts from its progenitor; yet because it participates in a body, it could not be entirely free from any change. <margin>That which participates in a body is not free from change.</margin> Nevertheless, as far as is possible, it is moved in the same place, according to the same things, and by one motion. Therefore it has obtained a circuit, in which there is the least possible variation of its agitation. From all these things it must be said that the world neither turns itself always, nor is it always reflected by God himself in a double and contrary circuit; nor again do two gods with contrary opinions turn it. SO. Those things seem very plausible. HO. Reasoning from these things which have been said, let us consider that event which we said was the cause of all wonders. And it is of this sort. SO. Of what sort? HO. That the machine of the whole world is revolved sometimes as it is now, and sometimes in the opposite direction. SO. In what way? HO. This change must be considered the greatest and most extreme of all celestial alternations. SO. It seems so. HO. Wherefore it is consistent that then the greatest changes occur concerning us who live within the world. SO. That also is likely. HO. Nor indeed is it hidden from us that the nature of living creatures tolerates great, many, and all kinds of changes with pain and difficulty. SO. It is certain. HO. In the beginning, in whatever age any animal has been established, it ceases to proceed in that same age; nor does any of the mortals become older further; but it passes into a contrary form: and puts on a younger and softer habit; the gray hairs of the elders grow black; and those whose cheeks were bearded before, now with the beard laid aside, are restored to their former appearance. <margin>Old men return to the nature of children.</margin> The bodies of youths also, with their hair fallen, become soft, and gradually decreasing through individual days and nights, they return to the nature of a child; and in these, both souls and bodies undergo the habit of children; finally, wasting away, they fail and perish. Furthermore, the corpses of those who suddenly fell by the change of the celestial turning suffer the same thing, and by a similar regression, they rot secretly and in a short time. SO. But was the life which you say existed under the reign of Saturn <note>The Roman name for Cronus; in mythology, his reign was a "Golden Age" of plenty.</note> under those former celestial revolutions, or under these current ones? For it is certain that a change in the sun and the other stars occurs in both types of rotations. **THE GUEST:** <note>Original: "HO." for Hospes, the Stranger/Guest in Plato's Statesman.</note> You have followed the argument very well. As for your question—that all things were born for men of their own accord—that by no means fits the present revolution, but rather belonged to the previous one. In that time, God stood as the primary prince and caretaker of the entire circuit; just as now, through various regions of the world,

<margin>The life of men under Saturn.</margin>

the individual parts of the world are distributed by presiding gods. The genera of animals were also allotted to divine spirits <note>Original: "demones," referring to intermediary spirits or guardians, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note> as divine shepherds, each of whom was sufficient to provide all things for the individuals over whom he presided. For this reason, nothing was wild; all rapacity and greed were far away; war and sedition were entirely absent; moreover, the other features that followed the condition of those times are innumerable. As for what is said about the ease of sustenance and the freedom of life, it was said because God himself fed them: he was their shepherd and guardian, just as men now (whose nature is more divine) are the shepherds of brute beasts. While God was the guardian, there were no constitutions of states, nor marriages of males and females for the procreation of children. For all were revived out of the earth, unmindful of past things. All such things were absent. Indeed, trees and the fertile soil provided them with fruits, apples, and grain in abundance of their own accord, without the labor of agriculture. Furthermore, they fed naked, unencumbered, and wandering for the most part. For the climate was harmless to them, and soft beds were prepared everywhere from the many grasses sprouting from the earth. You hear, O Socrates, the life of men living under Saturn; but this present life, which they say belongs to Jupiter, you have experienced yourself. Are you willing and able to judge which of the two is the happier? **SOCRATES:** Not at all. **THE GUEST:** Do you wish then that I should judge it for you in some way? **SOCRATES:** Most certainly. **THE GUEST:** If the former foster-children of Saturn, in such great leisure and freedom of life, and having the power to converse not only among themselves but also with the beasts, used all these things for philosophy—living among themselves and with the beasts, and inquiring from every nature that has some power of perception different from others to acquire wisdom—it can easily be judged that they surpassed us in living blessedly by a vast interval. But if, being filled to satiety with feasts and drinks, they shared such fables among themselves and with the beasts as are now reported of them, this too, in my opinion, would be very easy to judge. But let us omit these things until some suitable messenger appears to tell us whether those men devoted their efforts to science and conversation. But the reason why we entered upon this fable must now be told, so that we may join what follows with what went before. When the time of all those things was fulfilled, and it was necessary for a change of the circuit to occur—the earthly race being entirely consumed, since every soul had fulfilled all its generations and each had cast as many seeds into the earth as were mandated for it—then the Governor of the universe, as if letting go of the reins of the rudders, returned to his own place of observation. Fate and innate desire then revolved the world again. Moreover, all the gods who were colleagues of the supreme spirit, presiding over individual regions, noticing what had happened, deserted their parts of the world. The world then, recoiling with a contrary motion of beginning and end, shaking its interior with a huge earthquake, again destroyed most animals of every kind. But indeed, after certain fixed cycles of time had passed, the shaking and perturbation ceased; and the world, ceasing from its turbulent crashing, ran in its accustomed progression. Having been established in due order, it took up the authority and administration of itself and of those things within it, remembering and imitating the governance of its author and father to the best of its strength. In the beginning, therefore, it executed this more perfectly; but eventually, it degenerated further from that imitation. The cause of this defect is the bodily nature, the fuel of its ancient nature. For formerly it was very deformed and void of order before it was decorated with its present ornament. From him who constructed it, it possesses all good things; but from its prior deformity, all the inconveniences and injustices that are born within the heavens arise, which the world itself sustains and inflicts upon living things. Therefore, while it nourishes its animals together with the Governor, it produces small evils and great goods; but when it is separated, in the time immediately following the departure, it conducts all things beautifully; but as time proceeds, it is seized by forgetfulness. Wherefore the passion of its prior deformity dominates more vehemently. Finally, after a long time has passed, it withers; and producing few goods, but mixing a great deal of the nature of evils with them, it undergoes the danger that both it and all things within it may be dissolved. Wherefore that God, the former author of this order, seeing the world placed in such great danger, takes pity; and lest it be tossed by such turbulent tumult and be dissolved, and sink into the infinite place of dissimilarity, he stands by it again and presides. Having resumed the rudders, he turns back all that was sick and dissolved by its ancient agitation; he adorns and corrects it, and preserves it from death and old age. This, then, is the end of the whole account. This suffices for the demonstration of the King himself, if only the things said above are held in mind. When the world was turned again to the progress of the present generation, age again ceased to proceed further, and rendered new things contrary to those that were then. Furthermore, animals that were near death because of their very frailty increased; those who had recently risen gray from the earth fell back into the earth dying. All other things were likewise transformed, following the passion of the whole world. For the imitation of generation, conception, and nourishment necessarily followed all things. For it was no longer granted for an animal to be made in the earth through other composing causes. For just as it was ordained that the world, in its motion...

# ON THE CIVIL MAN OR ON KINGSHIP.
### Book III
<meta>catchword: Book III</meta>

it was less, so by a similar process it was brought about that the parts of the world should, as far as possible, generate, give birth to, and nourish themselves. Now indeed we have arrived at the point toward which our entire discourse was looking. For concerning the remaining living creatures, many and great things could be reported: from what things each was transformed and for what reasons. But those things which happened concerning men are shorter and more relevant to the matter at hand. Since men were destitute of the providence of the Shepherd <note>original: "pastoris," referring to the Divine Shepherd in the myth of the reversal of the world's rotation</note> and of the protection of those spirits <note>original: "daemonis"</note> who watched over them, and many animals which had been wild by their own nature became fierce again, they themselves, unarmed and weak and abandoned by their guardians, were torn to pieces everywhere. Added to this was the inertia and lack of skill of former times; for they had lived ignorant of labors and cares. The earth no longer supplied food of its own accord, yet the industry of procuring it was not yet discovered, because no necessity had compelled them before. For these reasons, their affairs were reduced to the greatest danger and penury. Wherefore those gifts which are remembered as having been granted to men by the gods of old were bestowed with a certain necessary discipline and instruction: fire from Prometheus, arts from Vulcan and his consort, and seeds and the cultivation of the earth from others. In short, all the supports of human life were then provided by the work of the gods, since the providence of the gods had deserted men; and it was necessary for them to have care for their own propagation and nourishment, just like the whole world: imitating and following which through all time, we are born and live now in one way, now in another. But let the fable now have an end. It will indeed lead us to discern how much we erred above in the definition of the king and the civil man. **SOCRATES.** In what matter, and how much do you say we have erred? **GUEST.** <note>original: "HO." for Hospes, the Eleatic Stranger</note> Partly less, partly more nobly and more greatly than was then thought. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **GUEST.** Because, while seeking the king and the civil man from the present circuit and generation, we brought in the Shepherd from the contrary revolution, and instead of a mortal shepherd of the human flock, we commemorated a god; we overstepped the mark too far. While we showed that he was the prince of the entire state, we did not declare in what manner he was prince; we spoke the truth indeed, but we did not describe it fully or clearly. Wherefore we seem to have failed less in this than in that. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. **GUEST.** We ought therefore to think that we have sufficiently explained the civil man only when we have distinguished the mode of governing the city with sufficiency. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **GUEST.** For this very reason, we began that fable, so that it might be shown not only that all men claim for themselves the common nourishment of the flock against the king, but that we might more clearly behold him whom alone it is fitting to call so, since he has the care of feeding the human flock in the likeness of sheep and good shepherds. **SOCRATES.** Correct. **GUEST.** I truly think, Socrates, that the figure of the Divine Shepherd is more excellent than a king; but these civil men are more like their subjects in nature, education, and discipline. **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. **GUEST.** Nor indeed must it be scrutinized whether they were more or less, or whether they are so, or born otherwise. **SOCRATES.** Why so? **GUEST.** Let us then resume again. That art which prescribes for itself, providing for animals not privately but publicly, we immediately called above the "nourishment of the flock." Do you remember? **SOCRATES.** I remember. **GUEST.** In this we wandered. For we have neither grasped the civil man yet, nor have we named him; but his designation escaped us. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **GUEST.** To feed individual flocks belongs to all other shepherds; but we did not give a fitting name to the civil man, when it was proper to apply something common to all. **SOCRATES.** You tell the truth, if only it were permitted. **GUEST.** Indeed, it was permitted to attribute "care" <note>original: "curationem"</note> commonly, without the distinction of "nourishment" or any other business: and to bring in some other common appellation, calling it either the "leading of the flock," or "care," or "diligence"; and thus embrace the civil man together with the others, after reason had signified it ought to be so. **SOCRATES.** Very good. But in what way was it to be distinguished afterward? **GUEST.** Just as we divided the nourishment of the flock according to the species of walking and flying creatures, and the unmixed and the hornless; so it was permitted to divide the "leading of the flock" according to the same parts; and thus the kingdom of Saturn and the present age would be encompassed in the discourse. **SOCRATES.** It seems so. But what then? **GUEST.** If the name had been so imposed on that faculty that we had called it the "leading of the flock" which we called the "nourishment of the flock," it is certain that no one would have contended against us as if there were no care at all; just as it was then rightly debated that there is no art in us worthy of the name "nourishing," and if there be any, it belongs to many others before and more than to the kingly name. **SOCRATES.** Right. **GUEST.** But no other art contends about this, as if there were a greater or milder care of the whole human community than the kingly one. **SOCRATES.** You speak rightly. **GUEST.** After these things, do we not notice, Socrates, how heavily we failed toward the end? **SOCRATES.** Where do you say the fault is? **GUEST.** In this, I say: that even if we thought some art was the nourisher of the two-legged flock, we ought not immediately to have called it kingly and civil as if it were absolute. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **GUEST.** First indeed it was necessary, as we were saying, to adapt the name to "care" rather than to "nourishment"; afterward the care had to be divided. For it admits of no small divisions besides. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **GUEST.** Into the Divine Shepherd and the human caretaker. **SOCRATES.** Skillfully put. **GUEST.** Likewise, human care into two. **SOCRATES.** Which two? **GUEST.** Into that which commands the unwilling, and that which commands the willing. **SOCRATES.** What then? **GUEST.** In this we surely erred more foolishly than was fitting, for we brought the king and the tyrant into the same thing, though they are most unlike each other, and their mode of governing is far different. **SOCRATES.** You report the truth. **GUEST.** Now therefore, amending it again, as I was saying above, let us divide human care into two parts: into the violent and the voluntary. **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **GUEST.** Let us name the violent "tyrannical," but the voluntary leading of the flock of willing two-legged creatures the "civil art"; and let us call him who is endowed with this faculty the truly civil man and king. **SOCRATES.** It seems now, Guest, that the demonstrations of the civil man are at last thoroughly completed for us. **GUEST.** It would be well for us...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical dialogue, likely from a Latin translation of Plato’s *Statesman* (Politicus). The speakers are Socrates and a "Stranger" (here labeled HO for Hospes, the Guest). They are discussing the use of examples to define complex ideas like statesmanship.</meta>

# BOOK SIXTEEN.

<margin>The power of an example in demonstrating.</margin>
**SO.** Socrates has acted. But it is necessary that this appear so not only to you, but also to me along with you. And now indeed, the matter does not yet seem to me to have a perfect shape: but just as sculptors sometimes, hastening too immoderately, delay the completion of a work by interposing more and larger individual pieces than is necessary; so we too, in order that we might quickly and magnificently demonstrate the errors of the previous process regarding the King <note>The "King" or "Statesman" is the central subject of the dialogue.</note>, thinking that great examples of him should be set forth, have piled up a huge mass of myth: we were forced to use a larger part of it than was appropriate. Therefore, we introduced a more prolix demonstration, and did not entirely impose an end to the myth. But in truth, our discourse seems to me like a living creature that has a sufficient exterior outline, but is not yet decorated with the clear mixture of pigments and colors. It is more fitting to demonstrate every living creature through speech and discourse to those who can follow them, than through the works of the hands and the painter's art; but to others, it is done through the service of the hands. **SO.** Enough of this. But show me for what reason you say it has not yet been sufficiently discussed. **HO.** It is difficult, O blessed one, to sufficiently demonstrate great things without examples. For each of us seems to know all things as if through a dream, but in reality to be ignorant of them all over again. **SO.** In what way? **HO.** We have moved the affection and condition of the soul regarding knowledge quite absurdly, O Socrates. Surely we began with great and difficult things, which ought to have been started in order with the smallest and easiest things. **SO.** To what purpose is this? **HO.** An example, O happy one, requires an example in turn. **SO.** By what reasoning? Speak out, fearing nothing on my account. **HO.** I must speak, since you yourself are ready to listen. Do we notice what children do when they first learn their letters? **SO.** What is that? **HO.** They sufficiently perceive the elements in the shortest and easiest syllables, and can speak truly about them. **SO.** Why not? **HO.** Yet these same children, when doubting in other cases, are deceived in opinion and speech. **SO.** Entirely so. **HO.** Can they not thus be led most easily and best to the unknown? **SO.** In what way? **HO.** It is necessary first to lead them back to those things in which they had correctly formed an opinion: and to offer them those things which they do not yet know: and by comparing them in turn, to show that the same similarity and nature exists in both combinations; until they show the unknown things compared with all those conceived by true opinion; and once demonstrated, and having finally made examples of them, they may bring it about that from all the elements of any syllable, they call that which is different by a different name, but that which is the same, always the same according to itself. **SO.** Entirely so. **HO.** Have we not grasped this sufficiently? Namely, that the generation of an example occurs when that which is the same in either separate case, being conceived by right opinion and applied to both, produces a single common opinion of both? **SO.** So it seems. **HO.** What wonder is it, if our soul, suffering the same nature regarding the elements of all things, is sometimes established in the truth itself regarding each thing in certain cases, but at other times is carried away regarding all things in others? And in certain combinations it opines correctly in a way, but when transferred into the great and difficult syllables of things, it is ignorant of these same things again? It should certainly not seem a wonder. For by what reasoning, O friend, could anyone starting from a false opinion reach wisdom by arriving at even the smallest part of the truth? **SO.** Almost none. **HO.** If these things are so by nature, you and I would by no means go astray if we first endeavored to understand the nature of the whole example in some other small partial example; then, about to approach the greatest example of the King, bringing the same form from smaller things elsewhere, we might try again through an example to discern the care of civil affairs by art: so that the truth itself may be held as if through a dream. **SO.** Quite rightly. **HO.** Again, the previous discourse must be repeated, which inferred: since many contend with the royal race for the government of the city and usurp it for themselves, it is necessary to separate them all from him and leave him alone. And for this, we said a certain example was needed. **SO.** Greatly so. **HO.** What small example could someone bring forward that contains the same civil faculty and would sufficiently find what is being investigated? By Jove, O Socrates, unless we have something else at hand, shall we choose the art of weaving? Not the whole of it, for I think wool-working will suffice. For perhaps this chosen part will indicate what we desire. **SO.** Why not? **HO.** Why did we not do with the art of weaving as we did before, dividing each thing into parts of parts, and passing through everything as briefly as we could, choosing what leads to the purpose? **SO.** How do you mean? **HO.** I will make the discourse itself answer you. **SO.** You speak excellently. **HO.** Of the things we make and possess, some are prepared for the sake of doing something, others are defenses against sufferings. Of defenses, some are remedies, both divine and human; others are obstacles. Of obstacles, some are military armor, others are fortifications. Of fortifications, some are veils, others are protections against heat and cold. Of protections, some are coverings and restraints, others are wraps. Of wraps, some support from below, some surround. Of those that surround, some are simple, others are double and composite. Of the composite, some are perforated <note>original: "perforata", likely referring to needlework or stitching</note>, others are joined without perforation. Of these, some are made of sinews from things born of the earth; some are felted. Of the felted, some are glued together with water and earth, others are connected to each other. To these defenses and supports made from these same things bound together, we have given the name "clothes." The art which is chiefly concerned with clothes, let us call "clothes-making" from the making of clothes itself: just as we named the discipline that cares for the city "civil" <note>i.e., Statesmanship</note> from the city itself. And let us say that the faculty of weaving, insofar as it weaves clothes for the most part, differs in nothing but name from that which we called clothes-making: just as we previously distinguished the "royal" from the "civil." **SO.** Quite rightly. **HO.** After this, we shall surely conclude that someone might think the weaving of clothes has been sufficiently described, not being able to notice that it has not yet been distinguished from those things that cooperate closely, though it was separated from many other related things. **SO.** What related things? Tell me, I pray. **HO.** You seem not to have applied your mind enough to what was said above. Therefore...

<margin>The art of definition through example: which is a certain collection: and a way praised by Aristotle.</margin>

# ON CIVIL MATTERS OR THE KINGDOM. FOLIO LXXXIIII.

<note>Original Latin title: CIVILIS VEL DE REGNO. The page number is 84.</note>

...it seems we must return from the end to the beginning. For if you understand "proximity," we have distinguished each of these from the other by the composition of their divisions, supporting them and separating them by their scope. **YOUNG SOCRATES.** I understand. **THE STRANGER.** <note>The text uses "HO." for *Hospes*, the Stranger/Guest from Plato's dialogue.</note> Furthermore, we have already set aside every craft that uses flax, strings, and brushwood, and in short, those things which grow from the earth, which we recently called "sinewy." Indeed, we also separated the making of hats and that work which operates by piercing and sewing, which for the most part belongs to the leather-working faculty. **SOCRATES.** Entirely so. **THE STRANGER.** We have moreover set aside the manufacture of simple coverings which uses skins. Likewise, the mechanical devices for roofs and bindings, however many are made in building; and in all other arts used for the retention or repulsion of water; and whatever works provide restraint regarding folding, bending, and violent actions; and those that set up fences and walls, or throw up certain mounds. Likewise, the attachments of vestibules and lattices, which belong to the craft of nails. Furthermore, we have set apart armor-making, which is a portion of that great faculty which provides bulwarks and obstacles. Moreover, we separated from the beginning magic, which <margin>Magic professes to provide remedies for life.</margin> professes to provide remedies for the lives of men. What remains is a certain art which seemed to be that which we seek: the maker of woolen supports against the cold, specifically named the **art of weaving**. **SOCRATES.** So it seems. **THE STRANGER.** However, we have not yet perfectly settled the matter with these words. For he who first approaches the craft of garments seems to act in opposition to the weaver. **SOCRATES.** Why so? **THE STRANGER.** For the weaver, in a way, folds and connects. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **THE STRANGER.** But the other dissolves those things which are inserted and entangled together. **SOCRATES.** What is that? **THE STRANGER.** The work of him who cards <term>carding: the process of combing raw wool to separate fibers</term> and distinguishes. Shall we compute the work of carding and distinguishing as the same as weaving? And shall we call the carder and the distinguisher the same as the weaver? **SOCRATES.** By no means. **THE STRANGER.** If anyone should call the diligence that prepares the **warp** and the **woof** <note>original: "stamina & subtegmina"</note> "weaving," he would depart far from human opinion and the truth of that name. **SOCRATES.** Clearly. **THE STRANGER.** Furthermore, do we say that the work of fullers <term>fuller: a person who cleans and thickens cloth</term> and menders contributes nothing to the making of clothes? Or do we call all these "weaving diligences"? **SOCRATES.** Neither should be said. **THE STRANGER.** Nevertheless, all these will contend with the weaver's art regarding the care of clothes; they will grant much of this work to him, but will also claim much of the same work for themselves. **SOCRATES.** That is entirely so. **THE STRANGER.** Besides these, one must also consider the arts that produce the instruments the weaver uses, which claim a part for themselves in producing the web. **SOCRATES.** Correct. **THE STRANGER.** Will the definition of the weaving faculty, which we chose as a part, be sufficiently distinct if we call it the greatest and most beautiful of all other faculties concerned with woolen clothing? Or will it be said truly, yet by no means perfectly or clearly, until we have separated the rest from it? **SOCRATES.** Certainly so. **THE STRANGER.** Should we not proceed so that our discourse moves in a consequential order? **SOCRATES.** Nothing prevents it. **THE STRANGER.** First, let us consider the twin arts regarding all things that are made. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **THE STRANGER.** One indeed is the **co-cause** of generation, so to speak; the other is the **cause** itself. <margin>The art of the cause; the art of the co-cause.</margin> **SOCRATES.** How? **THE STRANGER.** Whatever things do not manufacture the object itself, but supply tools to the manufacturers—without which the intended work could by no means be finished—we name "co-causes." But those which principally make the object, we call "causes." **SOCRATES.** That is reasonable. **THE STRANGER.** After this, let us call all the arts that produce the distaff, the spindle, the shuttle, and the comb, and prepare other instruments for the work of clothing, "co-causes"; but those which care for and produce the garments, "causes." **SOCRATES.** Rightly. **THE STRANGER.** From the "causes," it is fitting to gather generally that part which washes and sews, and other cares of this kind where much diligence of decoration occurs, and name it the fuller's art. **SOCRATES.** Correct. **THE STRANGER.** But that part which cards, distinguishes, and spins, and all things concerning the making of clothes, one art encompasses: which is commonly named **wool-working**. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **THE STRANGER.** Furthermore, there are two divisions of wool-working, and each are parts of two arts at once. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **THE STRANGER.** That faculty which cards, and which uses a certain comb, and generally whatever things are joined it disjoins: it is called a part of wool-working. Of this, there are two greatest parts: one is **Distributive**, the other **Concretive** <note>Distributive (separating) vs. Concretive (combining/thickening)</note>. **SOCRATES.** It is entirely so. **THE STRANGER.** In that which distinguishes, there are the carding and other faculties we just mentioned. For that which divides the wool and the threads, whether with a certain comb or by hand, has obtained all the names we just mentioned in different ways. **SOCRATES.** Exactly. **THE STRANGER.** Again, let us take the part of the "concretive" and wool-working contained within it; but let us pass over whatever "distributive" elements were there, dividing all wool-working in two: into a concretive part and a distributive part. **SOCRATES.** Let us divide them. **THE STRANGER.** Therefore, O Socrates, it is fitting to divide the concretive part and wool-working together, if we wish to sufficiently grasp the art of weaving proposed to us. **SOCRATES.** It is certainly necessary. **THE STRANGER.** It is necessary without doubt. Therefore, let us say that one part of it consists in rolling and bending, and the other in intertwining. **SOCRATES.** Do I grasp this? For you seem to me to place the work of the **warp** in twisting. **THE STRANGER.** Not only of this, but also of the **woof**. Or shall we find the generation of this without twisting? **SOCRATES.** By no means. **THE STRANGER.** Describe each of these; for perhaps such a description will seem opportune. **SOCRATES.** What kind? **THE STRANGER.** Behold, the work of the carder when it is drawn out in length and breadth, we call "drawing out." **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **THE STRANGER.** When this, having been made into hanks, is twisted by the spindle and made into a solid thread, they call it the **warp** <note>Latin: stamen</note>; but the art itself which directs and draws this out, they call "warp-making." **SOCRATES.** Rightly. **THE STRANGER.** But those things which receive a soft twisting, and by the entanglement of the warp obtain a softness moderated for the pull of the reflection, those threads drawn out are called the **woof** <note>Latin: subtegmen</note>; and the art itself "woof-making." **SOCRATES.** CORRECT. **THE STRANGER.** And yet that part of weaving which we proposed is now clear to anyone. For when the part of the concretive faculty in wool-working produces the entanglement and contexture of the woof and warp by a straight drawing-through: we call the whole entanglement and contexture a "woolen garment," and the art of this kind "weaving." **SOCRATES.** Very rightly. **THE STRANGER.** But why did we not immediately answer that the art of weaving is that which entangles the woof and the warp? But instead [we went] through a long...

# BOOK SIXTEEN.

Have we wandered in vain through these long-winded circles? SO. To me at least, Guest, nothing you have said seems in vain. HO. That is no wonder now; but perhaps, O blessed one, it will seem so if you fall into this "disease" <note>original: "morbum"; referring to the habit of excessive talk</note> frequently in the future. For what a wonder! Listen to the discourse which must always be brought forward concerning all such things. SO. Just say it. HO. First, let us look at excess and deficiency in nature, so that we may praise them according to a moderate reason, and blame in each case whatever does not observe the measure of speech, whenever in such discussions we speak either more at length than is fitting or more briefly. SO. That is certainly necessary. HO. A discourse must rightly be held concerning both of these. SO. Concerning what? HO. Concerning length, I say, and brevity; and concerning every excess and deficiency. For the faculty of measurement pertains to all these things. SO. Indeed. HO. Let us therefore distinguish them into two parts. For it is conducive to what we intend. SO. Tell me how they are to be distinguished. HO. Thus: One part according to the mutual relationship of greatness and smallness; the other according to the necessary essence of generation <note>original: "gnationis" (generationis); referring to the coming-into-being of a standard or "the mean"</note>. SO. How do you mean that? HO. Does it not seem to you according to nature that what is greater must be said to be greater than nothing other than the smaller? And what is smaller is smaller only than the greater? SO. To me, indeed. HO. What then? That which exceeds the mean <note>original: "mediocritatem"; the middle point or standard of fitness</note>, and what exceeds it either in speaking or in acting—shall we not say these are the things by which good men differ from bad ones? <margin>What is greater is greater than the smaller; what is smaller is smaller only than the greater. By what good men differ from the bad.</margin> SO. It appears so. HO. It is fitting, therefore, to place these two essences as judgments of the great and the small. Nor, as we were saying a little while ago, should these be referred only to each other; rather, as has just been said, they seem to be compared partly to each other and partly to the mean. Do we wish to understand the reason for this? SO. Why would we not? HO. If someone refers the nature of the greater only to the smaller, he will not refer it to the moderate; what do you say? SO. Exactly that. HO. Would we not, by this reasoning, destroy the arts themselves and all their works? And would we not do away with the very things we seek: the civic and the weaving faculties? For all these avoid that which is greater or smaller than the moderate—not as if it does not exist, but as something difficult in action; and thus, by preserving the mean, they produce all things good and beautiful. SO. Without a doubt. HO. If we do away with civic skill, will not our search for the royal science be crippled and uncertain? SO. Greatly so. HO. Just as in the discussion about the Sophist, we compelled "non-being" to exist after the argument escaped us in that direction, so now must we compel the "more" and the "less" to be commensurable not only with each other but also toward the generation of the mean? For no one can be skilled in civic discipline or any other human faculty without this concession. SO. Must we not do the same thing most urgently in the present case? HO. This work, O Socrates, is greater than that one, even if we remember how long that one turned out to be. A certain truth must rightly be assumed concerning them. SO. What kind? HO. That someday there will be a need for what has now been said for the sake of a clear and absolute demonstration of the thing itself; but for what pertains to the present, it has been shown excellently and sufficiently. This discourse seems to me to be of great benefit, namely that it must be thought that all arts are similarly situated: that the greater and the lesser are measured not only against each other, but also toward the generation of the mean itself. For when this exists, those arts exist; and when those exist, this exists; if either of these is taken away, both are destroyed. SO. This is indeed correct; but what follows? HO. It is fitting to distinguish the art of measurement into two parts, as we said above: to place in one part all those arts which measure number, length, breadth, depth, and speed against their opposites; and in the other part those arts which look toward the moderate and the tempered, the becoming, the opportune, and the dutiful—and in short, toward all those things which, having avoided the extremes, have fled to the middle. <margin>Whatever is artistic is a participant in measure. To what extent things must be divided.</margin> SO. Both portions are indeed large, and one differs far from the other. HO. What those ornate men often say, O Socrates—those who think they speak something great and wise when they proclaim that the faculty of measurement is concerned with all things that come to be—now happens to be the case. And that is what was just said. For whatever is produced by art has appeared to be, in a certain way, a participant in measure. But because some have never been accustomed to consider the species of forms, distinguishing these things which differ so much among themselves, they immediately group them into the same category, judging them to be similar. And they do the opposite again, because other things are not distinguished by their parts. When someone first perceives the commonality of many things, he should not stop until he has inspected all the differences that are enclosed within the species; and again, whenever he perceives many dissimilarities in a multitude and is troubled by them, he cannot stop from this annoyance of sight until, concluding all things that are related within one kinship and property, he clothes them in the essence of a single genus. Concerning these things, then, and concerning excesses and deficiencies, let these words suffice; but this much must be observed: namely, that two genera were found concerning measurement itself, and those must be kept in mind. SO. We shall keep them. HO. After this discourse, let us take up another concerning the things that were just being sought, and concerning the treatment of all such discourses. SO. What is that? HO. If someone should perhaps ask us about the exercise of boys concerning letters, when they are asked what letters a certain name consists of, do we think they are then being questioned for the sake of that one name alone, or rather so that they may become more learned in all grammar? What shall we answer? SO. That it is for all grammar. HO. What then of our investigation of the statesman? Is it proposed more for his own sake than so that we may become sharper in all differences? SO. That too is clear: that it is for the sake of all things. HO. No one of sound mind would contend that he hunts for the definition of the weaving faculty for its own sake alone. But it escapes most people, I think, that for some things that are easy to know, there are certain sensible images; which are not at all difficult to declare whenever someone wants to demonstrate the reason for something to a seeker—not with the things themselves, but easily by reason alone. <margin>Here it is not true that "nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses." <note>A reference to the Aristotelian/Scholastic maxim "Nihil est in intellectu quod non prius fuerit in sensu." The author argues that the highest things have no physical image.</note></margin> However, of the greatest and most precious things, there is no image clearly fashioned for men, which, when shown, could sufficiently satisfy the sense of one who wishes to fulfill the mind of the petitioner. Therefore, we must think so that we may be able to give and receive the reason for any matter. For incorporeal things, since they are the greatest and most beautiful, are declared clearly by reason alone, and by no other way. Furthermore, all the genera of these things have just been spoken of by us. But the consideration of any matter in smaller things...

<summary>The Guest and Socrates discuss the "art of measurement," distinguishing between relative measurement (big vs. small) and the "mean" or "due measure" (the standard of fitness). They conclude that the highest, incorporeal truths have no physical images and can only be understood through reason and dialectic.</summary>

is easier than what exists in greater matters. **SOCRATES.** You speak excellently. **GUEST.** Finally, let us recall for what purpose all these things were said. **SOCRATES.** Which things? **GUEST.** Especially for the sake of that annoyance and satiety <note>original: "molestię satietatisq;" - referring to the boredom of long-windedness</note> which we felt regarding the long-winded speech about the art of weaving; also regarding the revolution of the whole world, and the Sophist’s discourse on the essence of non-being. Therefore, so that such a thing does not happen to us again in the future, consider all the things mentioned above. **SOCRATES.** Let it be so; come, say what remains. **GUEST.** I say, therefore, that both I and you must always be mindful of what we have said, whenever either brevity or length of speech falls into reproach: so that we do not judge lengths against one another, but according to the part of the faculty of measurement, which we said above must be referred to the standard of fitness <note>The "standard of fitness" refers to the Greek concept of *to prepon*, or what is appropriate to the subject at hand.</note>. **SOCRATES.** Wisely said. **GUEST.** Therefore, not all things are to be referred to this; for we shall not need a length that is not suitable for pleasure, unless it is incidental to the purpose. But so that what is sought may be found most easily and quickly, reason dictates we strive not in the first, but in the second place: but most of all, and first of all, to honor that progress by which we are able to distinguish according to species: and not to bear a long disputation with annoyance, but rather to desire it if only it contributes to discovery: and similarly for a brief one. And it commands him who blames longer words, and does not admit circuits of disputations of this kind, not to condemn length so lightly and rashly; but rather to show first that a shorter disputation would render the listeners more ready for distinguishing and more sagacious for discovering. But as for other reproaches and praises tending elsewhere, one should neither care for them nor listen to them at all. And enough of these things, if it also seems so to you. Let us return again to the civil faculty, comparing the example of the weaver which we set forth above. **SOCRATES.** You have spoken excellently; and so, as you command, let us do. **GUEST.** Has not the king already been distinguished from many offices of shepherds—indeed, from all guardians of herds? There remain the urban faculties of both contributing causes and primary causes, which we must first separate from one another. **SOCRATES.** Correct. **GUEST.** To divide these in two is difficult. The cause of this difficulty will be clear in the following discourse. **SOCRATES.** Thus it must certainly be done. **GUEST.** Let us therefore tear them apart by members like a sacrificial victim, since we are not able to cut them in two. For it is always necessary to distribute into the nearest number. **SOCRATES.** In what way? Let us try now. **GUEST.** Just as in the previous parts we placed all those who prepared the instruments of weaving as contributing causes. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **GUEST.** The same must also be done in the present case, and much more so. For whatever manufactures any large or small instrument in the city must be placed as contributing causes. For without these a city cannot exist, nor can civil discipline <note>original: "ciuilis disciplina" - the art of politics or statecraft</note> stand. Yet we shall place none of these as belonging to the royal art. **SOCRATES.** None at all. **GUEST.** And yet we would be undertaking something difficult if we were to distinguish this genus from others. He who says that a certain one of the things that exist is an instrument seems to speak something plausible; yet another of the things possessed in the city must be mentioned. **SOCRATES.** What is that? **GUEST.** That which does not have this power. For the cause of generation is not in this, as in an instrument, but it looks to the preservation of that which has been manufactured. **SOCRATES.** What kind of thing is that? **GUEST.** That varied genus produced for dry and wet things, for things heated by fire and cold things: which we name by the single term "vessel" <note>original: "vas"</note>, although the species are very many. But this is not the work of that knowledge which we seek. **SOCRATES.** Certainly not. **GUEST.** A third species of possessions appears multiform: terrestrial and aquatic, wandering and fixed, precious and cheap: signified by one name, because this whole is always made a seat for someone, for the sake of sitting, presiding, or exploring. **SOCRATES.** What is this? **GUEST.** We call it a "vehicle" <note>original: "vehiculũ"</note>, surely not much the work of civil skill, but rather the duty of the architectural, pottery, and copper-working faculties. **SOCRATES.** I understand indeed. **GUEST.** Must not a fourth be mentioned besides these, in which many of those things we referred to above are contained? Garments, many arms, walls, earth and stone enclosures, and many other things. And since all these are made for the sake of protecting and warding off, they can correctly be called "defenses" and "obstacles" in common; and they are much more the works of architects and weavers than of the civil art. **SOCRATES.** It is entirely so. **GUEST.** Now in the fifth place shall we locate the arts of decorating, painting, and singing? And whatever things use these, and the imitations made by them solely for the sake of delight, which are deservedly comprised under one name. **SOCRATES.** What name? **GUEST.** This whole is called "playful" <note>original: "iocosum" - referring to the Greek *paignion*, or diversions/toys</note>. **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **GUEST.** This one name will suit all these; for none of them is ever done for the sake of serious study, but for the sake of play. **SOCRATES.** This also I almost understand. **GUEST.** But that faculty which prepares for all these the bodies from which and in which the works of the arts we just narrated are finished—shall we not place it as a sixth species, varied and depending on many arts? **SOCRATES.** Which do you mean? **GUEST.** That which prepares gold and silver and the other metals dug from the bowels of the earth. Likewise that which cuts forests, which shears, which constructs something from these, which folds and weaves, or which trims and polishes the bark of trees or the skins of animals, and whatever arts are occupied with such things; again those from which cork, bark, paper <note>original: "codex"</note>, and bonds are prepared, so that composite species may be made from non-composite genera: we call this whole the "first-born possession" <note>original: "primogenitã possessionẽ" - raw materials</note> for men, and simple, which is by no means the work of the royal art. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **GUEST.** The possession of "nourishment" <note>original: "nutrimẽti"</note> holds the seventh place, and whatever things mixed with the body are able to nourish and care for the parts of the body with their own parts: which whole ought to be called food, unless we find something more beautiful. But this whole is more correctly attributed to agriculture, hunting, gymnastics, medicine, and cooking than to the civil art. **SOCRATES.** More correctly indeed. **GUEST.** Almost all things that are possessed, except the domestic species of animals, I think are numbered in these seven. But think of it this way. It was right to introduce the first-born species first; then the instrument...

# BOOK SIXTEEN

...then: the vessel, the vehicle, the defense, the amusement, and the animal. We certainly omit anything of no great importance that might be hidden, which could be fitted into any of these: such as the idea of the excessive, of seals, and of every mark or character. For these kinds do not have a very close kinship with those others; but they fit partly into ornament and partly into instruments, though they are thoroughly treated in a way that is consistent. Indeed, the possession of domestic animals—excluding slaves—seems to have been first distinguished by the breeding of the herd.

SO. Most certainly.

HO. There remains the class of all slaves and attendants. In this, I prophesy that those who contend with the King for the "weaving" <note>The "art of weaving" is the central metaphor for statesmanship in this dialogue.</note> will openly rise up: just as they do with the weaver who combs and spins the threads, and the others of whom we spoke. But all the rest, called "co-causes," together with the works just mentioned, are separated and distinguished from royal and civil action.

SO. That has become clear.

HO. Let us consider the remaining ones who come closest, so that we may know more certainly.

SO. We must by all means.

HO. Furthermore, we may look at the greatest attendants from here; we shall find they have an exercise and passion contrary to what we suspected.

SO. Which ones?

HO. Purchased slaves, and men forced into servitude in a certain way like sons; whom we can without controversy name as slaves.

<margin>Slaves are furthest removed from royal dignity.</margin>

SO. Why not?

HO. What shall we say of the free men, who voluntarily perform the services mentioned above? They transport the works of agriculture and other arts, and exchange them through mutual commerce, whether from market to market in the same city, or transferring them from city to city by land and sea—exchanging coins for other things, or sometimes exchanging something similar for their sons—those whom we have named money-changers, merchants, sea-carriers, and innkeepers? Will these claim for themselves the skill of the citizen <note>original: "civile peritiam" - political or statesmanlike expertise</note>?

SO. Perhaps the merchants will.

HO. Yet we shall not find those whom we see everywhere as hirelings, exposed to the service of all, usurping the royal dignity.

SO. It is as you say.

HO. But what of those who supply us with certain such things everywhere?

SO. Whom do you mean, and suppliers of what things?

HO. I mean the race of heralds, and those who wisely serve regarding public records, and certain other skillful workers who labor in the service of princes. What is to be said of these, Socrates?

SO. What you yourself said: that they are attendants, not the princes of cities.

HO. Not without reason, I think, did I say earlier that we would find by this method many vehement competitors for the care of the state: though it might seem absurd to someone to look for them in the number of attendants.

SO. Very much so.

HO. Let us, moreover, draw closer to those who have not yet been examined: these are those who possess a portion of knowledge regarding divination. For they are judged to be the interpreters of divine things to men.

SO. Certainly.

HO. Furthermore, the class of priests, as the law holds, understands and teaches in what manner gifts and sacrifices are to be offered to the gods. Likewise, by what reason one must vow, and what good is to be sought from the gods. Both of these are parts of the attendant's art.

<margin>That seers and priests are also attendants.</margin>

SO. So it seems.

HO. Now, therefore, we seem to have touched upon a certain footprint of that which we are investigating. For the figure of priests and seers abounds in magnanimity, intelligence, and clarity, because of the magnificence of the things they undertake and handle. Wherefore among the Egyptians, it is not permitted for a king to rule without the priesthood. Furthermore, if someone from another class usurps the kingdom by force, he is compelled after the assumption of the kingdom to be initiated into the sacred rites: so that he may finally be both king and priest. Moreover, in many Greek cities, especially among you, you will find the principal sacrifices are established by the highest magistrates. For even among you, the ancestral and solemn greatest sacrifices, and the purest of all others, are assigned to the chosen King <note>original: "creato regi" - referring to the Archon Basileus in Athens, a magistrate who held the title of 'king' for religious duties.</note>.

<margin>That the highest priesthood befits kings.</margin>

SO. Most certainly.

HO. We must therefore consider these chosen kings and priests, and their attendants, as well as a certain other frequent crowd that has just come to light, now that the former ones have been removed.

SO. Whom do you mean?

HO. Certain wondrous ones, I say.

SO. Why?

HO. To my thinking just now, a multiform race of these appears. Many of the men become like lions, or centaurs, and others of this kind; many also like satyrs, and weak and multiform beasts; and they quickly transform and alternate their forms and powers among themselves. Indeed, now for the first time, O Socrates, I seem to have figured out such men.

SO. Tell me, I pray, for you seem to be looking at something wondrous now.

<margin>Ignorance always causes a wonder to happen.</margin>

HO. Truly. For ignorance always causes us to experience something as a wonder. And the same has just happened to me. For suddenly, as I was doubting, it happened while I was looking at the chorus of civil affairs.

SO. Which one?

HO. The greatest juggler of all the sophists: most skilled in this art above the rest; whom it is right to discern from men who are truly royal and civil: though it be difficult, if we wish to know clearly what we seek.

SO. This must by no means be let go.

HO. Certainly not, I think. And tell me: Is not monarchy, that is, the rule of one, one of the forms of civil government?

SO. It is.

HO. After this, we can place the power of the few.

SO. Surely.

HO. And the third is the government of the multitude, which they call popular <note>Democracy</note>.

SO. Exactly.

HO. Do not these three become five in a way, since they produce two additional names from themselves?

SO. Which ones?

HO. Since many observe that one can rule over the unwilling or the willing, and it may happen that they preside by law or by whim, and those in charge may be poor or raised to power by riches, they divide the rule of one into two species: kingdom and tyranny.

SO. Both of them.

HO. And the government conducted by the few into the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note> and the power of the best <note>Aristocracy</note>.

SO. Entirely.

HO. But no one is accustomed to change the name of popular government: whether the people preside over certain rich men by will or by force, or whether they rule by law or by whim.

SO. You speak the truth.

HO. Do we think any of these civil governments is the "right" one when determined by these boundaries and distinctions: namely, by one, few, many, poverty, riches, violence, will, laws, and whim?

SO. What prevents it?

HO. Consider more diligently: and follow me this way.

SO. Which way?

HO. Shall we stand by what was said in the beginning, or not?

SO. In what?

HO. We said the royal dignity was a certain one of the sciences.

SO. We certainly said so.

# CONCERNING CIVIL MATTERS OR THE KINGDOM. FOLIO 86.

**SOCRATES.** Indeed. **STRANGER.** We previously established that this knowledge presides partly over inanimate things and partly over animate ones; dividing them in that same order, we have proceeded this far, reserving the name of "science" or "knowledge" <note>Latin: *scientia*</note> for each part. However, we have not yet been able to declare what the most essential science actually is. **SOCRATES.** You speak correctly. **STRANGER.** We have observed that the determination and description of these things ought not to be made according to violence or will, nor according to the few or the many, nor through poverty or wealth, but through a certain science, if we are to follow our previous points. **SOCRATES.** It is necessary that it be so. **STRANGER.** Necessarily, therefore, we must now consider in which of these the science of the imperial faculty <note>The art of ruling or statecraft</note> resides, which is arguably the greatest and most difficult of all to acquire. For it is necessary to inspect it, so that we may see how those who claim civil expertise for themselves—and persuade many of it, though they are far from it—are to be separated from the wise king. **SOCRATES.** We must proceed exactly as our previous reasoning advised. **STRANGER.** Does it seem to you that a multitude in a city is capable of possessing this science? **SOCRATES.** How could they? **STRANGER.** In a city of a thousand men, is it possible for a hundred, or even fifty men, to sufficiently acquire it? **SOCRATES.** This would then be the easiest of all arts; for we know that in a number of a thousand men, one could by no means find that many men who surpass the rest of the Greeks even at a game of dice, let alone kings. **STRANGER.** Certainly, one must call that man a "king" who is instructed in royal expertise, whether he rules as a master or lives as a private citizen, as our previous reasoning established. **STRANGER.** You have reminded me opportunely. I think, according to the discourse we have introduced, that right governance—if it is ever truly right—must be sought in one, or two, or a few people. **SOCRATES.** Why not? **STRANGER.** We must consider these to be the true "civil" and "royal" men, provided they rule by a certain art, whether they rule over willing or unwilling subjects; whether according to written laws or without written laws, customs, and statutes; and whether they are poor or rich. For we have likewise deemed that physicians are to be so called, whether they heal the unwilling or the willing by cutting, burning, or otherwise causing pain, and whether they cure according to written texts or not, and whether they are poor or rich—so long as they preside over the care of bodies by a certain art, by purging, or otherwise thinning, or filling and increasing them. For we name them physicians equally, provided that those who perform the cure, looking toward the good of the body, restore it from a worse condition to a better one and preserve it. In this way alone, I believe, shall we say the definition of medicine, or of any other leadership, is correct; but in no other way. **SOCRATES.** That is exactly how it must be thought. **STRANGER.** It is necessary, therefore, to consider that state to be the most—and only—correct one in which those who hold office truly know how to govern: whether they rule by laws or without laws, whether over the willing or the unwilling, or even if they are poor or rich. For none of these things matter in relation to the correct method of governing. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **STRANGER.** Furthermore, it does not matter if they purge the city for the common good through executions or banishments, or if they send out colonies like swarms of bees to reduce the population, or if they bring in men from elsewhere to be future citizens and enlarge the city. For as long as they, relying on science and justice, make the city better from a worse state to the best of their ability and preserve it: to that extent we wish the republic to be called "right," and in that alone does the definition of right governance consist. However many other forms we call "right," they are not to be thought of as being called so legitimately or truly. But we gladly praise those that imitate this one, as if they were easily tending toward better things; others, conversely, we disparage as being prone to worse things by the imitation of evils. **SOCRATES.** The rest seems well said, Stranger; but what was said—that governance can be right without laws—cannot be easily accepted. **STRANGER.** You have anticipated me slightly with your question, Socrates. For I had intended to ask you whether you admit all these things or refuse any of them. But now it is clear we wish to discuss those who rule correctly without laws. **SOCRATES.** Without a doubt. **STRANGER.** It is clear, in a way, that the making of laws belongs to the royal dignity. Yet the best thing is not for laws to hold power and be firm, but for a man with royal wisdom to do so. Do you understand the reason for this? **SOCRATES.** Explain it. **STRANGER.** Because the law cannot encompass what is best and most just for everyone at once and with total sincerity, so as to always prescribe what is worthwhile. Indeed, the differences between men and their actions, and the unstable and varied condition of human affairs, mean that no art can decree anything simple and universal for all people for all time. Do we concede this? **SOCRATES.** Clearly. **STRANGER.** Yet we see the law striving for this very thing: like some stubborn and ignorant man who permits nothing to be done contrary to his institutes, nor even allows a question to be asked, even if something new might be better or more preferable for someone than his order. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. For the law constrains men exactly as you were saying. **STRANGER.** It is impossible for a certain and simple order to be good regarding those things which are always varied and never simple. **SOCRATES.** That is apparent. **STRANGER.** Therefore, the reason must be found why the condition of laws is necessary, since the law is not itself that which is best and most right. **SOCRATES.** Who could doubt it? **STRANGER.** Are there not among us, as among others, certain common exercises for all men together, whether for running or for the sake of any other competition? **SOCRATES.** Very many. **STRANGER.** Let us recall, if you please, the precepts of those who preside over gymnasiums with a certain art. **SOCRATES.** Which ones? **STRANGER.** They believe it is impossible to prescribe for each individual specifically what is suitable for him apart from others; instead, they think a common instruction should be established: that which seems to benefit the most people the most often. **SOCRATES.** Excellent. **STRANGER.** For which reason, while they now assign equal labors to all together and drive them with equal exercises, they partly provoke them to move faster and partly weaken them, rendering bodies unfit for running, wrestling, and other contests. **SOCRATES.** So it happens. **STRANGER.** Let us also think of the lawgiver presiding over his flocks, giving laws concerning just works or mutual dealings, that he cannot—while consulting for all together—look out for the convenience or right of each individual. **SOCRATES.** That is consistent. **STRANGER.** But, as I believe, he will establish what benefits the most people the most in common; and he will leave behind written laws of this kind, and similarly the unwritten ancestral customs...

For if anyone endowed with the **royal discipline** <note>Latin: *disciplina regia*, referring to the art of statecraft or kingship</note> were able to effect this, they would never prescribe for themselves those impediments which are called laws. Or rather, would not anything of that sort occurring regarding true science and art provoke the greatest laughter in such circumstances? SO. Most certainly.
