But for that man who has established what is just and unjust, honorable and shameful, good and bad—whether by written laws or unwritten customs—for the herds of men who live in the city according to the norm of written laws, will it not be permitted to do certain other things besides those which are written, even if he himself who wrote them before should return, or if someone else like him should come? Or rather, would such a doubt not seem truly ridiculous, no less than the former one? SO. Nothing prevents it. 

HO. Do you know, then, what is commonly said about this matter? SO. Not at present. HO. Truly it is fitting. For they say: if someone finds certain laws better than the ancient ones and persuades the citizens, he ought to bring those laws forward; if he does not persuade them, it is not becoming. Is that right? SO. Perhaps. HO. But if someone introduced what is more right not by persuasion, but by force, what name would you give to this violence? Or rather, not yet to that, but to the former things first. SO. What do you mean? HO. If someone powerful in the art of medicine does not persuade, but compels the one he treats—whether a boy, a man, or a woman—to do what is better contrary to the written rules, what is the name of this violence? Is it not anything else rather than a "transgression of the art," that is, the "infliction of disease"? And must it not be said that anything else happened to the compelled person rather than a transgression of the art and a disease? SO. You speak the truth. HO. But what is an offense against the **civil art** <note>Latin: *civilis ars*, the art of politics or governing</note>? Is it not what is called shameful, evil, and unjust? SO. That very thing. 

HO. Come then, when some are compelled to do things that are more just, better, and more honorable contrary to ancestral laws and customs, will it not be the most ridiculous of all things if someone censures that force, and says that those who were compelled suffered shameful, evil, and unjust things from the caretakers who forced them? SO. You speak the absolute truth. HO. If the one who compels is rich, are the compulsions just, but if he is poor, are they unjust? Or rather, whether he has persuaded or not persuaded, whether he be poor or rich, whether according to the written rules or contrary to them, provided he introduces what is useful, must it be said that this is the true and right definition of **civil governance**? By this reasoning, a wise and good man will govern his subjects, always looking to their safety just as a pilot looks to the safety of the sailors and the ship. For as that pilot saves the sailors not by written rules, but by his art as if by a certain law, so also the truly civil man; and among those who can rule in this way, the administration of civil affairs is right,

applying the power of art as superior to laws. And in short, whatever prudent princes do, they never err, as long as they preserve this one chief thing: that by mind and art, distributing what is most just to the citizens, they are able to protect them and make them better from worse as far as possible. HO. Nor with those things besides. SO. Which things were you saying? HO. That no multitude can ever excel in that discipline by which it might rule a city according to the mind. Rather, that right administration of the city must be sought among one, or very few. 

<margin>That a multitude cannot rule. Perfect administration is with one or a few.</margin>

It is not to be made light of, if someone, having introduced this discourse, stops before he has shown the error which has now been committed regarding it. SO. What error do you mean? HO. It is necessary to seek something of such a kind that is neither customary nor easily known. Yet let us strive to comprehend it. Since this alone which we have mentioned is the right civil governance, you know that the others using its institutions must be preserved while they do what is now praised, even if it is by no means the most right? SO. What is that? HO. That no one should dare to commit anything contrary to the laws; and whoever dares, let him be punished by death and afflicted with all extreme punishments; for that is the most right and honorable in the second place, for that which was just said must be placed in the first place. But let us declare how that which we just called "second" comes about. Do you wish? SO. Very much so. 

HO. Let us come again to the images to which it is always necessary to compare royal princes. SO. Which images do you mean? HO. I mean the noble pilot of a ship, and the physician who is equivalent to many others. Let us now consider a certain figure fashioned among these. SO. Of what kind? HO. Such a kind as if we all thought we suffered certain grievances from them: as if they save those of us whom they wish to save, and conversely destroy those they wish to destroy, while they cut, burn, and demand payment as if it were a certain tribute;

and while they compel much to be spent, they pay out nothing or very little for the sick, but use the rest for themselves and their household; finally, having accepted money either from the relatives or from the enemies of the sick person himself, they force him to die. <summary>The dialogue explores the "Royal Art" of governance, arguing that a truly wise ruler's expertise is superior to fixed laws, just as a doctor's skill is superior to a written prescription. It concludes that while the rule of a wise individual is ideal, in its absence, strict adherence to law is the "second-best" way to prevent abuse of power.</summary>

# CONCERNING CIVIL MATTERS OR THE KINGDOM. FOL. 87.

I shall take away their skills: so that they may no longer rule freely over either enslaved or free men. Suppose we then formed an assembly and rushed together, either the whole people or the wealthy alone, where the advice of ignorant men and other craftsmen is heard concerning the diseases of a ship and its voyage: in what manner one ought to use the medicines and instruments of physicians toward the sick, and likewise regarding ships and their instruments for sailing, avoiding the dangers of storms and waves, and escaping the ambushes of pirates; and even if one must fight at sea with long ships <note>original: "longis nauibus" — likely referring to triremes or warships</note> against similar foes, how it is fitting to use them. Let us imagine that we then inscribed the opinions of these people—whether of certain physicians and pilots, or of some ignorant men consulting on these matters—on certain public tablets and columns, and established certain unwritten customs and rites as ancestral traditions, so that for all remaining time, navigation and healing must be conducted according to this norm.

**SOCRATES:** You have imagined something quite strange.

**STRANGER:** <note>original: "HO." for Hospes, the Eleatic Stranger in Plato's Statesman</note> Furthermore, suppose that every year the people appoint leaders, chosen either from the wealthy or by lot from the whole populace, who shall govern the ships and heal the sick according to these written institutions.

**SOCRATES:** These things seem even harsher than the previous ones.

**STRANGER:** Let us see what follows from this. When the time of each magistrate's term has expired, it will be necessary to summon those who have performed the duties of the magistracy to a court, composed either of the elected wealthy or those chosen by lot from the entire people, and to correct them. Thus, it would be permitted for anyone who wishes to challenge their past actions, as if they had governed ships or cured the sick otherwise than the laws command and ancestral custom teaches. And those found to have acted otherwise shall be condemned by the judges, with a sentence passed for either punishment or some other penalty.

**SOCRATES:** Would not anyone who voluntarily undertakes such a magistracy deserve to suffer punishment or loss?

**STRANGER:** In addition to this, it would be necessary to pass a law: if anyone introduces a method of sailing contrary to the written constitutions, or investigates the nature of health regarding winds, heat, and cold, and "philosophizes" or teaches about these things according to his own talent—first, such a person should be called neither a pilot nor a physician, but a meddling and delirious sophist <note>term: "sophistā" — here used as a derogatory term for a deceptive or useless intellectual</note>. Then, he could be dragged into court by anyone, as if he were corrupting the youth, persuading them to practice navigation and medicine contrary to the legal institutes, and to treat ships and diseases at their own discretion. And if he is found to be persuading young or old men of anything contrary to the laws, he shall be afflicted with the ultimate punishments. For nothing ought to be wiser than the laws; nor should he be ignorant of the nature of medicine and health, or the best method of governing and sailing, since it is permitted for anyone who wishes to learn the writings and customs.

If these things were to happen regarding the sciences we have described, and many others, so that actions were taken according to prescriptions rather than according to art <note>term: "artē" — from the Greek 'techne', meaning specialized skill or expertise</note>, what shall we say, O Socrates? For instance, if the same were established regarding military affairs, and all hunting, painting, and universal imitation; architecture, and the making of all instruments and furniture; agriculture and the care of all trees; and the keeping of horses and herds, prophecy, and the various services of attendants, the game of dice, pure arithmetic, or that which deals with planes, depths, speeds, or slowness?

**SOCRATES:** We would say plainly that if things were so, all arts would be utterly subverted; nor would they ever be reborn, because of this very law which forbids the investigation of new things. Wherefore life, which is now difficult, would then become altogether intolerable.

**STRANGER:** What of this? If we compelled each thing to be done according to prescribed laws, and we placed over the laws themselves a certain man, designated either by the consensus of the people or created by lot, who, despising the laws for the sake of gain or his own lust, attempts to act otherwise than these established things, though he is ignorant—is this not worse than the former evil?

**SOCRATES:** Very much so.

**STRANGER:** For if someone unskilled dares to act against those laws which were laid down with much expertise by consultants who graciously persuaded the people to accept them, he commits a crime far worse than the previous error; and much more than the written laws, he confuses and perverts the duties of life.

**SOCRATES:** Greatly so.

**STRANGER:** Therefore, in the second place, it is established that those who write laws about any matter should permit no one ever to do anything contrary to them, whether one man or the people attempt it.

**SOCRATES:** Wisely said.

**STRANGER:** Will these not be certain imitations of the truth of individual things, which were written down by those who understand, as far as possible?

**SOCRATES:** Nothing stands in the way of that.

**STRANGER:** And if we remember, we said earlier that the truly civil man <note>note: the true Statesman</note> and expert would often perform many things by his art contrary to the institutes he had written before, whenever he thought he had found something better than what he left for those who are absent.

**SOCRATES:** We certainly said that.

**STRANGER:** Does not whoever—either one man or a people—for whom laws are prescribed, attempts something else as if it were better, do the same thing to the best of his power as that true civil man?

**SOCRATES:** Most certainly.

**STRANGER:** If, therefore, the ignorant were to do this, they would indeed strive to imitate the truth itself, yet they would imitate it perversely. But if the experts were to strive for the same, this would no longer be an imitation, but that very truth itself.

**SOCRATES:** Entirely so.

**STRANGER:** But indeed, we agreed earlier that no art belongs to the many.

**SOCRATES:** We certainly agreed.

**STRANGER:** Therefore, if the royal art is a certain faculty, the crowd of the wealthy and the whole people will never attain this civil science.

**SOCRATES:** Never.

**STRANGER:** It is necessary, therefore, that if such republics are to imitate to the best of their power that true government of one man ruling by art, they must never attempt anything contrary to the written laws and ancestral customs.

**SOCRATES:** You have spoken excellently.

**STRANGER:** When the wealthy imitate that government, we call the republic an Aristocracy; but when they hold the laws as nothing, it is called an Oligarchy <note>original: "paucorum potentiam" — the power of the few</note>.

**SOCRATES:** It appears so.

**STRANGER:** Furthermore, whenever one man rules according to the laws, imitating the one who knows, we call him a King; not distinguishing by name the one who rules by science alone from him who rules by opinion according to the laws.

**SOCRATES:** So it seems.

**STRANGER:** Therefore, if one man endowed with true science rules, does he not have this same name of King, and is not signified by any other title? For out of the five names of civil governments we recounted, this was the only one.

**SOCRATES:** It seems so.

<margin>A city is robust by its very nature.</margin>
**STRANGER.** What further? Whenever someone rules neither according to law nor according to custom, and as if knowing better, pretends that it is necessary and superior to act beyond the laws—yet there is a certain lust within him, and ignorance is the leader of such imitation—must not such a man be called a tyrant? **SOCRATES.** Most certainly. **STRANGER.** By this reasoning, the king has emerged, as we said, and the tyrant; the power of the few, which is the government of the aristocracy <note>literally "of the best men"</note>, and also the administration of the people. For men bore the rule of one with difficulty, and they distrusted that such a man could ever be found worthy of such great power—one who both could and would rule with virtue and knowledge, holily and justly granting to each his own right. They feared, moreover, lest perhaps one man, having gained license, might harm, oppress, and kill anyone according to his whim. Since, if such a person as we have described were to be encountered by us, his administration would surely be loved; for it alone is the most correct of all, and leads to living well and happily. **SOCRATES.** Truly. **STRANGER.** But now, since such a king is not born in cities as he is among swarms of bees—immediately from the beginning excelling the others in the habit of both body and mind—it is necessary, having formed a gathering of counselors, to write down institutions and to follow the truest footsteps of that original republic. **SOCRATES.** So it appears. **STRANGER.** And do we wonder, O Socrates, that in governments of this kind evils happen and are destined to come, since the foundation has been laid such that we are compelled to act not by knowledge, but by certain written institutions and customs? No one surely doubts that any other government or city using these [true principles] would utterly overturn all things that are done in this way. But this rather ought to seem a wonder: how robust a city is by nature. For now some cities remain so long infected and nevertheless do not collapse; many, however, like ships, have perished submerged, are perishing, and will perish, on account of the wickedness of the governors and sailors, who are held in a certain extreme ignorance regarding the greatest matters; for since they are entirely ignorant of civil affairs, they nevertheless think themselves to be exceedingly wise in them. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. **STRANGER.** Since, therefore, all incorrect republics are difficult to live in, we must see which is lighter and which is the most burdensome of all; and even if it seems to pertain less to that which we are now discussing, nevertheless, looking perhaps at the whole, we do all things for the sake of this. **SOCRATES.** It must certainly be done so. **STRANGER.** Of the three, they say one and the same is at once the easiest and the most difficult. **SOCRATES.** How do you say that? **STRANGER.** Not otherwise than I touched upon above: namely, that there are three primary civil governments: of one, of the few, and of the many, amplifying the previous discourse. **SOCRATES.** They were there above as well. **STRANGER.** But by dividing each into two, we shall make six; and let us set apart that correct one itself as the seventh from the others. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** We distribute the sovereignty of one into kingship and tyranny. The domination which belongs to the few we divide into one species which is to be praised, namely the government of the aristocracy, and another which is to be blamed, the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>. But the administration of the many we then placed as simple, naming it popular government <note>Democracy</note>. Now again let us say that this also is twofold. **SOCRATES.** By what reasoning shall we divide this? **STRANGER.** By no other than the rest, even if the name of this one is twin. Truly, this is common to this as to the others: that they either observe the laws or transgress them. **SOCRATES.** It is so indeed. **STRANGER.** Then surely for the correct government, this partition was by no means expedient, as we showed above. But after we have set that one apart and introduced the others as if necessary, in these now the observation of the law and its transgression divide each in two. **SOCRATES.** So it seems from the discourse now spoken. **STRANGER.** Therefore, the domination of one with good written records, which we have called laws, is the best of all six; but when devoid of laws, it is harsh and the most burdensome of all for the subjects. **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **STRANGER.** But the government in which not many participate, we ought to judge as middle in respect to both; just as that which is of the few holds the middle between one and many. Furthermore, the administration of the many is weak in all respects; inasmuch as, compared to the others, it is capable of nothing great, whether good or evil, because the magistracies are reduced to small parts and divided among many. Wherefore, of all lawful republics, this is the worst; of the lawless ones, it is the best. And if all are intemperate, it is better to live in a popular one; if all are temperate, one should live in that one least of all. But it is most powerful and best to lead a life in the first <note>Kingship</note>, the seventh being excepted. For it is fitting to distinguish that one from all other governments, just as one distinguishes a god from men. **SOCRATES.** These things seem to happen and occur so; and it must be done as you say. **STRANGER.** And is it not fitting to segregate all the administrators of these republics—except for the prince of the wise republic—as those who are not truly statesmen, but rather seditious men, presiding over vast phantoms, and very like them, the greatest imitators, the greatest tricksters, and the sophists of sophists! **SOCRATES.** This nickname seems to apply by right to those who are called statesmen. **STRANGER.** Now at last we have with difficulty separated from the civil art that dance of Centaurs and Satyrs which we said above we perceived and judged should be separated from the civil [art]. **SOCRATES.** It seems so. **STRANGER.** Besides these, something remains: which is the more difficult to distinguish from the king, the more it is joined to him by nature; and therefore the same thing seems to have happened to us as to those digging for gold. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **STRANGER.** The craftsmen first separate earth, stones, and many other things from it; but after these, there remain certain things more closely related to gold and more precious mixed in: to be separated from the gold by fire alone—copper, silver, and sometimes even adamant <note>likely referring to a hard stone or diamond</note>—which at last are barely segregated when the trial by fire is made, and they allow pure and sincere gold to be discerned in itself. **SOCRATES.** So it is said of them. **STRANGER.** By the same reasoning, we now seem to have separated things quite foreign and distant from the civil science, but to have left those things which are honored and very close. From the number of which is the command of the army, the judicial office, and the dignity of oratory communicating with the royal authority, while it persuades what is just and governs public affairs with it; which, if someone easily separates them in a certain way, he will show us that naked and solitary one whom we seek. **SOCRATES.** There is no doubt this must be tried with all zeal. **STRANGER.** It will be made clear for the sake of the trial; but let us attempt to demonstrate it through music. And tell me— **SOCRATES.** What shall I say? **STRANGER.** Is there for us any discipline of music or of the arts which perform their work by the service of hands? **SOCRATES.** There is. **STRANGER.** Shall we say...

<meta>This page continues a philosophical dialogue, likely a Latin translation of Plato’s *Statesman* (Politicus), discussing the hierarchy of sciences and the definition of the "Royal" or "Civil" art.</meta>

# CIVIL OR CONCERNING THE KINGDOM. FOLIO LXXXVIII.

Regarding all these things, is there not some science that teaches which arts are to be learned and which are not? **SOCRATES.** We shall plainly say there is. **HOSPES.** <note>The "Guest" or "Stranger" in the dialogue.</note> Is this not different from the others? **SOCRATES.** That too. **HOSPES.** Shall we say that none of them rule over the others, or that they rule over this one? Or rather, shall we say that this one, as the overseer of all, presides over the others and commands them, since it judges which of the individual arts are to be learned and which are not? Do you assert then that it commands both the teacher and the learner? **SOCRATES.** Entirely. **HOSPES.** And does the art that judges whether one should use persuasion or not command the art that is able to persuade? **SOCRATES.** Why not? **HOSPES.** To which science shall we chiefly attribute that persuasion which is directed at the crowd through a kind of conversation and exhortation rather than through teaching? **SOCRATES.** It is clear it must be attributed to the oratorical art. <margin>That oratory is subject to the civil art.</margin> **HOSPES.** To which art’s duty do we say it belongs to judge whether to use force or persuasion, and in what matters, and toward whom it is fitting to use them? **SOCRATES.** To that which is the mistress of the skill of persuading and speaking. <margin>How oratory is distinguished from the civil art.</margin> **HOSPES.** And that, I believe, is none other than the faculty of the civil man <note>The statesman.</note>. **SOCRATES.** Excellently put. **HOSPES.** Thus, oratory is immediately seen to be distinct from the civil art, as a certain other species, yet nonetheless serving the civil art. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **HOSPES.** What, moreover, should be thought of this power? **SOCRATES.** Which one? **HOSPES.** That by which we fight against those upon whom we have declared war. Shall we say this is an art, or devoid of art? **SOCRATES.** Who would say that the actions of the military art and of all warfare are devoid of art? **HOSPES.** But that faculty which can deliberate prudently by consulting as to whom war should be waged with, or peace entered into—shall we think it is different from the former, or the same? **SOCRATES.** Different, if we stand by our previous points. **HOSPES.** If we follow the reasoning of the previous points, shall we not say that this one which consults about war rules over that which carries out the war? **SOCRATES.** Even so. **HOSPES.** What faculty, then, besides the royal civil discipline, shall we say commands such a vast and powerful art—namely, the whole of military affairs? <margin>That the command of the army is subject to the civil art.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Absolutely no other. **HOSPES.** Therefore, the science of those who lead armies, since it obeys and serves another, we shall by no means affirm to be the civil science itself. **SOCRATES.** It would hardly be fitting. **HOSPES.** Come now, let us consider the power of the judges who judge individual matters justly. **SOCRATES.** Let us consider it. **HOSPES.** Does the legal authority of that person extend beyond the rights of commerce, so that he considers regarding these what is just and what is not? And looking toward the standard of the laws which the king himself has established, does he judge individual cases, his own virtue always being applied: through which he may not transgress the laws because of gifts, or threats, or pity, or hatred, or love, and settle alternating causes beyond what is right? **SOCRATES.** Certainly, the duty of a judge is nothing other than what has now been said by you. **HOSPES.** It is established, therefore, that the power of judges is not the royal majesty, but rather the guardian of the laws and the king’s attendant. <margin>That the judiciary is the king's attendant.</margin> **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **HOSPES.** Whoever considers all the arts we have mentioned ought to think that none of them is the civil discipline we seek. For it is the duty of the royal majesty not to act itself, but to command those who are able to act; and it should know the beginning and the progress of the greatest things in the city: what is becoming and opportune, and what is the opposite. The other faculties, however, are to take up orders and carry out mandates. <margin>What the civil science is.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Very well. **HOSPES.** For this reason, those arts which we just recounted, since they are masters neither of themselves nor of each other, but each applies itself to certain proper works, have rightly obtained their own names from their own actions. **SOCRATES.** It appears so. **HOSPES.** But that which presides over all these, and has care of the laws and of all things in the city, and weaves everything together—rightly comprehending it by a common appellation, we shall call it the civil science. <margin>What the king's weaving is like.</margin> **SOCRATES.** Entirely. Do we wish now to run through it according to the example of the weaver’s faculty, after we have revealed all the kinds that exist in the city? **SOCRATES.** Very much so. **HOSPES.** It must be declared next, as it seems, what the royal "weaving" is: in what manner it complicates and weaves, and what kind of texture it produces for us. **SOCRATES.** It is established. **HOSPES.** The thing is indeed difficult to demonstrate; but since it has seemed necessary, it must be declared according to our strength. For how parts of virtue may disagree with the appearance of virtue can easily be proven by contentious men against the opinion of many. **SOCRATES.** I do not understand. **HOSPES.** Perhaps you will understand it this way: I think you believe Fortitude to be some part of virtue. **SOCRATES.** Entirely. **HOSPES.** And Temperance to be different from Fortitude, yet still a part of the same thing of which Fortitude is a part. **SOCRATES.** Yes. **HOSPES.** One must dare to bring forth a certain wonderful discourse about these. **SOCRATES.** What? **HOSPES.** That these two, in a certain way, are in many things very much opposed to each other. **SOCRATES.** In what way do you say that? **HOSPES.** This is unheard of; for indeed all parts of virtue are said to be bound together by mutual friendship. **SOCRATES.** Certainly. **HOSPES.** Let us therefore consider diligently whether this is so simple, or whether it has a very great difference among things that are in a way related. **SOCRATES.** Indeed. But tell me where it should be considered. **HOSPES.** In all things whatsoever we call beautiful; and we refer them to two species contrary to each other. **SOCRATES.** Say something more clearly. **HOSPES.** Have you ever praised, or heard another praising, sharpness and speed, whether of bodies or of minds or of voices? Whether of these themselves, or even in the likenesses which either music or painting produces by imitating? **SOCRATES.** Often. **HOSPES.** Do you remember how they praise those things in each of these? **SOCRATES.** Not at all. **HOSPES.** Will I be able to explain these in words as I understand them? **SOCRATES.** What prevents it? **HOSPES.** You seem to think this easy; let us consider it in contrary categories. Whenever we admire the speed, vehemence, and sharpness of many actions—whether of thought, or of body, or even of voice—we are accustomed to use one certain appellation of praise, the name of "fortitude" <note>original: "fortitudinis" - here meaning courage or strength/vigor</note> being always applied. **SOCRATES.** In what way? **HOSPES.** We say "sharp and strong," "swift and strong," "vehement and strong." And they are accustomed to praise these natures by the common name of fortitude. **SOCRATES.** Indeed. **HOSPES.** Have we not also often praised the species of quiet generation in many actions? **SOCRATES.** Greatly. **HOSPES.** Do we not use contrary terms in this praise and in those? **SOCRATES.** How so? **HOSPES.** These things are quiet, we often say, and temperate; and we love and praise these regarding thought; regarding actions, slow, etc.

SO. You speak the truth all too well. HO. But whenever these things do not observe timeliness, we conversely criticize them with changed names. SO. How so? HO. When they become sharper and faster, and harsher or harder than the occasion demands, we call them insolent, petulant, and frantic. But when they become deeper, slower, and softer, we call them timid, inept, and sluggish. And for the most part, we shall find that the nature of these temperaments, and the courage of their opposites—being, as it were, hostile <term>ideas</term><note>Platonic Forms or archetypes</note> and mutually seditious—neither mix with one another in actions concerning such matters, nor do those in whose souls these qualities reside agree with one another, but rather they disagree, if we investigate diligently. SO. Why do you say that? HO. In all those things I mentioned, and indeed in others, as is consistent for many. For since both groups, according to the suitability of their own nature, praise some things as their own and proper to them, and reject others as foreign and strange, they finally turn out to be vehement adversaries among themselves in many respects. SO. So it seems. HO. This dispute of such types is a kind of game in some matters; but in the greatest affairs, it becomes the most serious disease of all states. SO. In what kind of affairs do you mean? HO. In every constitution of living, as is consistent. For those who excel others in modesty strive for a life of tranquility, always attending to their own private affairs, eager for peace and harmony both toward strangers and toward their fellow citizens and kin. And by an excess of this love, it happens that while they

devote themselves to their private works, they themselves are secretly rendered weak and enervated; and they soften and effeminate the younger men by their example. Whence they are exposed to any invaders whatsoever; and in a short time they themselves, their children, and their entire fatherland, having lost their liberty, succumb. SO. You have described a very hard and heavy disease. HO. But those who incline more than is proper toward courage, vehemently affecting a warlike life, these men often provoke their fatherlands to war and exhort them, and thus they render many and powerful nations hostile to their citizens. For which reason they either utterly overturn their states or imprudently reduce them to the slavery of enemies. SO. That also happens. HO. Shall anyone then deny that in these matters both of these are greatly opposed to each other? SO. No one, certainly. HO. Have we not now found what we were seeking from the beginning? Namely, that certain parts of virtue, not small ones, are naturally at war with themselves, and cause those who possess them to differ greatly among themselves? SO. It appears so. HO. Let us likewise assume this.

<margin>All science rejects evils: it seeks the useful.</margin>
SO. What? HO. Does any science <note>original: "scientia" - here meaning a craft or systematic knowledge</note> whose action consists in composing, ever voluntarily construct any of its works, even the lowliest, out of both bad and good things? Or rather, does every science always reject the wicked to the best of its power, and seek out the fit and useful? And from these, partly similar and partly dissimilar, all brought together into one, does it forge a certain single power and idea? SO. The latter, rather. HO. Never, therefore, will a true

<margin>No science makes a work out of bad and good.</margin>
skill in civil affairs voluntarily constitute any state out of bad or good men. Rather, discipline will first examine each person; and having performed the examination, it will thereafter commit the task to those who are able to assist in educating them, over whom it will diligently preside and command, just as the art of weaving presides over the carders and other preparers of wool: prescribing such things to each as it judges conducive to its own texture. SO. Exactly so.

<margin>Certain duties of royal majesty.</margin>
HO. By the same reasoning, it seems to me that royal majesty, presiding over all teachers and educators who follow the law, permits them to exercise and teach only that which, pertaining to its own sequence, introduces decorous morals. But those who are unable to attain the morals of courage, moderation, and the other virtues, but are snatched away by the depravity of nature to impiety, petulance, and injustice, it casts out from the assembly of citizens, and condemns them to exile, death, and extreme disgrace. SO. So it is handed down, in a way. HO. But the ignorant and small-minded little men it subjects to servile ministry. SO. Very skillfully. HO. But the others, whose natures can be raised to a noble habit through discipline, and can receive a mutual mixing with one another by art, it preserves and protects. Of these, it judges those which incline more toward courage to hold the place of the warp <note>The longitudinal threads in a loom</note> because of their solid character; but those which incline toward modesty, being of soft and rich material, it judges to have the place of the woof <note>The crosswise threads</note>, like a thread of saffron color or a little flower. And so it strives to bind and weave together both of these, though they tend toward contrary natures. SO. In what way? HO. First, indeed, according to the nature of kinship, it binds the part of their soul which is of eternal generation with a divine bond; and after that divine part, it binds that which is of animal nature with human bonds. SO. How so? HO. Whenever a true and stable opinion about the beautiful, the just, and the good, or their opposites, arises in souls, I assert that it becomes divine in a <term>demonic</term> <note>original: "genero demonico" - referring to the 'daimon' or divine spirit, meaning a divinely inspired or fortunate nature</note> kind—that is, a wise and happy one. SO. That is indeed fitting. HO. Do we not know that it is necessary for a civil man and a good lawgiver, alone by the royal muse, to be able to instill this in those who are rightly participants in discipline as is fitting, and whom we just mentioned? SO. That too is consistent. HO. But he who cannot do that, O Socrates, ought not to be called by the names we have sought. SO. Certainly not. HO. Does not a courageous soul, if it participates in truth of this kind, become gentle; and thus it especially desires to live and act justly among others? But if it is entirely devoid of it, does it not slide down toward a wild nature? SO. Without a doubt. HO. And yet a soul modest by nature, imbued with those opinions, is rendered truly temperate and moderate, so as to be useful to the republic. But if it is empty, it carries away a shameful infamy of stupidity and sluggishness. SO. Greatly so. HO. Must it not be said that a complication and bond of this kind between the wicked and the wicked, or the good and the wicked, never remains indissoluble; and that no science ever uses this on purpose to bind such men? SO. Certainly. HO. But to those whom nature has gifted with noble morals, and has educated according to the norm of nature...

Because this is the condition of the brave nature: that if it remains devoid of temperance <term>temperantia: self-control or moderation</term> through many generations, it is robust at the start, but at last, having turned into madness, it fails. SO. It is consistent that this also happens so. HO. With these bonds, as we have said, we can easily bind both kinds of men, provided that this exists: that both have the same opinion concerning the good and the beautiful. This, moreover, is the single and complete work of the royal weaving: that it never permits moderate characters to be separate from the brave ones. Instead, by weaving both natures together through the consensus of the same opinion, through honors and reproaches, and through reciprocal marriages, it produces from these a smooth and excellently woven fabric. To these people, it should always commonly commit the civil magistracies and duties. SO. In what way? HO. Where the governance of one person suffices, it will appoint a man endowed with both characters. Where there is need for many, it will mix together some parts of each kind. For the characters of temperate leaders are very cautious, just, and salutary; but they lack a sharp readiness and a certain vehemence suitable for action. SO. So it seems regarding these as well. HO. Courage, however, yields to those others in caution and justice, but it greatly excels in the performance of deeds. Truly, all things in the city cannot be well managed, privately or publicly, unless both of these are present. SO. Certainly not. HO. Let us say then that the end of civil action, woven by a right folding together, then exists when you reconcile the natures of the brave and the temperate through concord and friendship; it makes their life common, which is surely the most noble and best of all weavings. Protecting and embracing all others in the city, both slaves and free men, it includes them in this texture and series. And so it dominates and presides over the city, so that it omits nothing of those things which, as far as possible, make a city happy. SO. Truly, Guest, you have excellently defined for us the royal and civil man himself.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument on the Protagoras.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a classical figure or scholar amidst foliage.</image-desc> There exists among the Greeks a most true saying about Plato: namely, that Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> fathered two sons especially, Aesculapius and Plato. Aesculapius was to heal bodies, but Plato was to heal souls. All the Socratics also testify that Socrates was sent by God for the sake of purging souls. Now, the disease of the soul seems to consist in false opinions and evil habits. Such a great evil is not usually inflicted upon noble souls as easily by others as it is by the Sophists. Indeed, philosophers are those who, being students of truth, seek it solely for the love of truth itself. But Sophists are those who affect opinion for the love of the "daughter of opinion" <note>meaning vanity or reputation</note>. For these men, like merchants and innkeepers of the disciplines, gather various opinions from everywhere without selection—pertaining both to thinking and to speaking however they please—which they then sell like wares to wealthy youths for the sake of riches and empty glory. Therefore, they never have any concern whether what they learn themselves or teach others is true or good, or the opposite; instead, they both confuse things and pour out many errors everywhere daily. With absolutely no regard for right choice, they heap up a mass of riches and pursue common glory. For this reason, it is necessary that youths and men—who greatly value the Sophists for their reputation for wisdom and the veneer of their eloquence—daily drink down from them the poisons of false opinions and the worst habits. Since evil habits follow false opinions, they are easily transferred into the disciples by greedy and ambitious teachers who are nonetheless highly esteemed. Plato, therefore, pitying the souls of those endangered so nearly and so gravely, very frequently—under the persona of his Socrates—detests the wicked and poisonous Sophists with all his might. He does this so that men desiring to learn might cautiously avoid the deceptive songs of the Sirens and the noxious potions of Circe. Yet he does not strike them down with manifest invectives, lest he himself seem moved by any disturbance or hatred toward them, or lest they and their followers hurl back the poisonous weapons of a most impudent tongue against him. Therefore, partly by irony, partly by laughter, often by jest and play, and more often by a certain honest refutation, he tries to strip the Sophists of their unmerited authority. This indeed, in the case of the most sharp Sophist...

<summary>This page concludes the "Statesman" with a discussion on harmonizing brave and temperate natures through statecraft and marriage, followed by Marsilio Ficino's introduction to Plato's "Protagoras," contrasting true philosophers with deceptive Sophists.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Marsilio Ficino, Protagoras, Sophists, Aesculapius, Statecraft, Kingship, Temperance, Courage</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the introductory argument or preface to Plato's dialogue *Protagoras*. It establishes the philosophical context, contrasting the vanity of the Sophists with the genuine pursuit of virtue through Socrates.</meta>

# ARGUMENT ON THE PROTAGORAS.

...finishes most excellently. He does the same in the *Gorgias* with great elegance; in the *Hippias* with much wit and urbanity; in the *Euthydemus* with skill and sharpness; and also in the *Protagoras* with great artistry—and often in a similar fashion elsewhere. Everywhere, indeed, he introduces the <term>Sophists</term><note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece who often prioritized rhetoric and winning arguments over absolute truth.</note> as boasters who profess to know everything, being glorious, reckless, and moreover, greedy. At the start of a dispute they seem capable enough, but gradually they become more foolish, and finally the most foolish of all. They understand nothing of importance—neither what a thing is, nor its magnitude, nor its quality. Although they profess all things, he proves they know nothing at all. Let it suffice to have prefaced this much regarding all of Plato's dialogues in which the Sophists are mentioned.

Let us now proceed to the *Protagoras*. Socrates learned the "art of love" from the prophetess Diotima. Through this art, he knew how to sagaciously hunt for the beauty of the soul, the angelic mind, and the beauty of God by following the tracks of physical beauty. He taught this same art everywhere. Plato treated this art of his often elsewhere, but especially in the *Symposium* and the *Phaedrus*. He signaled this same art at the beginning of this book. For that reason, he added that he <note>Socrates</note> loves a man no less than a youth; and a little later, that he loves the elders even more ardently, provided they appear wiser.

After this, while Socrates most skillfully warns the youth Hippocrates—who is most greedy for learning—not to rashly commit himself to just any teaching, he admonishes not only him but also us: that we should have far more care for the soul than for the body, and we must carefully beware lest we imbue it with harmful teachings. For I say these things hurt the soul more than poison hurts our body. Soon, like a painter, he places the pride and vanity of the Sophists before our eyes. He also demonstrates how much the credulous youth admire their pomp and are captured by their allurements.

Then he descends to those matters which pertain most to life and character, and in which the Sophists glory the most: inquiring into all <term>virtue</term><note>original: "virtute"; here referring to 'arete' or moral excellence/effectiveness.</note>, but especially the primary one, that is, **civic virtue**, through which both private and family affairs, as well as public matters, are disposed toward the **Highest Good** by right reason. Plato seeks this virtue in almost all his dialogues as being more necessary than the rest. Meanwhile, he shows that this is by no means to be sought from the Sophists, but in a certain way from the philosophers; for since they understand the truth and cultivate the good, they can surely lead one to it by a straight path with God as their guide.

But let us return now to the Sophist. That he is unable to hand down such virtue by example or teach it by dispute is clearly seen from this: that he himself is devoid of virtue and does not observe the right order of disputation. For when Protagoras is asked here by Socrates whether virtue can be taught or not, being ignorant of the true art of discourse, he immediately undertakes to show that virtue can be taught before explaining what it is or into how many parts it is divided. Socrates, however, for the sake of testing the Sophist, argues that it cannot be taught, using nearly these words: When there is a public consultation regarding some craft of an art that can be taught by certain masters, no one is admitted to the council except those who learned such an art from those masters and practiced it themselves. But when there is deliberation on public matters pertaining to civic virtue, almost everyone is admitted alike; nor is it asked of anyone whether, from whom, or when he received his civic skill—as if everyone understands that it cannot be learned in specific schools. Furthermore, if it were handed down from one to another, the most famous men in that field would often leave this precious thing to their heirs by a kind of hereditary right.

To these points, Protagoras proves with long-winded circumlocutions that virtue can be taught. In these, certain mysteries of the ancients he relates should be noted. For it is fitting that one who is a Sophist should have read some good things, and since he speaks at length in Plato, he should bring forward some useful points. The ancient theologians relate that animals once lay hidden under the earth—that is, the seeds of things existed in the primary matter of the world. Furthermore, that Jove—that is, God the creator of the world—composed animals from the elements through the succeeding gods, which is to say, through the stars. The gods, moreover, through the ministry of <term>daemons</term><note>original: "daemonum"; in the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>, armed the animals with the instruments and supports necessary for life. This was done in such a way that **Prometheus**, who signifies the order of the higher daemons, should arm humans; while **Epimetheus**, who represents the army of lower daemons, should support the brutes. And this was not done without justice, since the higher daemons favor the incorporeal and rational nature, while the lower favor the corporeal and irrational.

However much Epimetheus of the lower nature favored the brutes in those things pertaining to the body, so much does Prometheus, superior in providence, seem to have consulted for humans in those things pertaining to the soul. For when he granted the principle of art, he showed himself a skillful craftsman of all that nature had given to the beasts. He received the art itself along with fire from the workshop of **Minerva** and **Vulcan**. Minerva contains genius in art, while Vulcan contains efficacy; finally, fire is the instrument. These twin deities, Minerva and Vulcan, are first conceived in the very ideas of the arts; then in the powers of Mercury and Mars; and finally in the daemons who govern the arts. From all these, therefore, Prometheus, the governor of the rational soul, transferred the industry of art into man.

Because this gift was divine, man immediately worshipped God on account of his kinship with the beings above, even before he spoke or practiced any arts. Indeed, since a divine gift, because of its wonderful power, raises one toward divine things before it extends through human ones. That Prometheus was affected by pain because of this gift signifies that our demonic caretaker—in whom feelings can exist—is affected by a certain mercy toward us; and considering us because of the gift of reason either given or rather awakened by him, he sees that we lead a life on earth as much more miserable than the beasts as it is more anxious and inexplicable. Pythagoras, noticing this, preferred Epimetheus to Prometheus in this specific regard. This seems somewhat similar to the phrase: *It repents me that I made man* <note>A reference to Genesis 6:6</note>. Therefore, remember that man here, as in Moses, was created from the earth and created last. Likewise, in a Mosaic fashion, the world had a beginning. But of these things elsewhere. Through the same Prometheus, it is said in the *Philebus* that the art of discourse was given to us by the gods along with fire. For the art of discourse, where universals into particu-

# ARGUMENT FOR THE PROTAGORAS.
## m.ii.

...divides the particulars, it represents the process of things from higher powers; where it duly resolves particulars back into universals, it designates the return of things to higher levels; where it defines and where it demonstrates, it shows the existence of things: in the former case as they are in themselves, in the latter as they depend on others. Therefore, the faculty of discourse is a divine gift, since it reflects the divine order of the universe. It is said to be given with fire because fire similarly divides, resolves, defines, and demonstrates. Likewise, because the rational faculty, like fire, illuminates the intellect, inflames the will, and elevates both to sublime heights. 

However, regarding the claim that Prometheus could not bestow civic virtue <note>Latin: *virtus civilis*, the skill of living in a community</note>—which is utterly necessary for the safety of men—because such virtue rests with Jupiter, whom Prometheus is not permitted to approach: this must be understood to mean that the duty of civic virtue is to command not only human affairs, but also the arts; to organize each with the other; and finally to direct them all into a form common to all. Indeed, the same duty belongs to Jupiter himself in the universe as appears to be the duty of civic science in the human race. Wherefore, not without justice, it belongs to Jupiter himself to bestow this upon us from on high. For universal virtue pertains to the universal providence of Jupiter. 

The providence of demons <note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans</note> is particular and narrow; therefore, it cannot ascend to the citadel of Jupiter, since a narrower and lower providence cannot equal the most ample and eminent one. Jupiter, therefore, through Mercury—that is, the angel <note>The translator uses "angelus" to interpret Mercury as a messenger of divine will</note> and interpreter of the divine will—inscribes the laws of civic science (that is, the decrees of his will regarding the safety of human society and the race) upon our minds. He incribes them, I say, both from the beginning—which the *Timaeus* clearly teaches—and daily through the angels interpreting the divine will to us. From this, an internal judge presides within us: an inextinguishable light of reason, a right examination of truth and falsehood, of good and evil, and the unavoidable sting of conscience. Through this law infused by God into all, He directs almost everyone toward the common good, just as He raises all flames upward by their lightness. 

From this innate law, the written law then derives its origin. Plato revealed this at the very beginning of the book *The Laws*, saying that laws did not have their beginning from man, but from God himself. But to return to the present dialogue: he adds that Jupiter, through Mercury, established the law by which he commands all to be participants in citizenship; for this alone is the bond of the city. He says that he sent down from heaven the city itself, consisting of justice and shame <note>Latin: *pudor*, often translated as "a sense of respect" or "modesty"</note>; and did so with the pact that whoever hereafter is found entirely devoid of this virtue shall be afflicted with the ultimate punishment as a plague to the city. 

What he first called "shame," he later named "temperance." For innate shame is the foundation of temperance. Temperance, indeed, moderates the specific affections of each citizen and composes their gestures. Justice, however, directs the actions of each person toward what is conducive to others. Remember, however, that citizenship in a private person is content with these two; but in a public person, according to Plato’s mind, prudence must be added to these. And that would be almost enough in peace; but in war, add fortitude; and thus the description of citizenship will be absolute. 

After this, Protagoras confirms by the common opinion of men that all ought to be participants in this virtue; because if anyone were to openly confess his own injustice, he would commonly be considered insane—as if everyone thinks justice is so necessary to the common city that even if someone does not have it, they ought at least to pretend to have it. 

When he has shown thus far that civic virtue is the most necessary of all things for everyone, and that a certain affection or fuel and seed of it was infused in us by God from the beginning, he next proceeds to demonstrate that civic virtue—and indeed others (for that one encompasses the common ones)—cannot obtain a finished and firm habit by nature or by chance, but that its habit is acquired only through teaching and practice. To this end, he first brings forth a reason showing that men are not accustomed to ever approve or disapprove of anyone for those things which happen either by nature or by chance; but they always praise or blame actions of virtue or vice. 

Next, he arranges the education of childhood and youth under domestic tutors, grammarians, musicians, gymnasts, and laws in a certain long order, showing that the entire institution of life strives toward this: that vices be declined and virtues possessed—as if neither vices nor virtues arise by fortune or fate, but by will and exercise. Meanwhile, he touches upon the opinion of the ancients concerning the punishment of vices, which is worthy of consideration: namely, that no one should be punished because he has sinned, but lest he himself sin further, or another sin by his example. He then responds to those things which Socrates had objected. 

We, however, from all that has been disputed thus far, keep that golden opinion of the ancients stored deep in our minds: First, that God himself provides for and counsels our life and safety in every way and from every side. Second, that civic virtue is a divine gift, lest anyone perchance trust that he will govern the republic rightly and happily without divine grace. For Plato, confirming this in *The Laws* and elsewhere, says: just as many beasts cannot be led rightly by one of their own unless under a human shepherd, so many men cannot be ruled happily by one man unless that one is himself ruled by God. Therefore, he proves in the *Theages* and *Meno* that the faculty of ruling is obtained from nowhere else but God. As for what Protagoras the Sophist intends, let him see to it himself. 

Finally, let us remember how necessary is that inviolate justice sent from heaven, if those voices of the ancients continually ring in our ears: "Miserable mortals once, before citizenship was sent from heaven, could neither live apart without being torn to pieces everywhere by wild beasts, nor gather together without being mangled by one another." Therefore, the safety which all the arts together could not provide, justice alone finally provided for us. 

After these things, lest the Sophist be an object of admiration to the listeners on account of some good things he had narrated (which were received from others), Socrates, by a certain ironic, urbane, and skillful method of refutation, renders him a laughingstock to those present. For he asks, after Protagoras had spoken so magnificently of virtue: whether there is only one virtue or many. Furthermore, if there are many, whether they are parts of one, or not.

<summary>This page interprets the myth of Prometheus and Jupiter to argue that civic virtue (justice and temperance) is a divine gift essential for human survival and social order. It emphasizes that while the seeds of virtue are divinely infused, they must be cultivated through education and practice.</summary>

# THE SEVENTEENTH BOOK.
<meta>Catchword: yenis:SO.</meta>

Again, [it is asked] whether the parts [of virtue] are similar to one another and to the whole, or whether they are different on both sides. To these points, Protagoras knows neither how to answer correctly, nor how to define or divide the virtues, nor how to distinguish in what respect they are similar and in what respect they are different. Nor can he avoid what is most shameful in disputation: being easily led to the point where he frequently contradicts himself. At last, when Protagoras began to stall due to his ignorance of how to respond, and Socrates therefore feigned that he was about to depart, the sophist was called back to the discussion by the listeners. In this altercation, the superstitious curiosity of the sophist Prodicus regarding words is first demonstrated; then the rather swollen ostentation of the sophist Hippias in public speaking is shown. Finally, Protagoras, having been recalled to the dispute too importunately and foolishly, digresses into songs and poetry, questioning Socrates about a certain opinion of the poet Simonides. Socrates soon proves that Protagoras does not understand this at all, as Socrates explains Simonides' intent: as if he had said that it is indeed difficult for a man to *become* good, but impossible to *remain* so. Here you will hear that the wisdom of the ancients was content with as few words as possible, and that being able to embrace many things in brief is the work of an absolutely learned man. Likewise, that no one commits evil and shameful acts willingly, but rather out of ignorance. Finally, where one disputes in the dialectical manner <note>The Socratic method of logical questioning</note>, poetic matters should be rejected. After these things, the sophist stalls again and is barely recalled by those present. Then Socrates returns to the earlier dispute about virtue: whether there are many parts of one virtue, and in what relation they stand to one another. Protagoras, however, slips again, affirming that some virtues are very similar to each other—which he had not admitted previously—and likewise separating courage very far from the others, agreeing that men can be brave without prudence <note>Practical wisdom or "phronesis"</note> and the other virtues. In this matter, he is then compelled to contradict himself and to confess that not only courage, but indeed no virtues can exist without prudence. Then, truly, many things are treated concerning good and evil. Since prudence is the science of choosing the good and avoiding the evil. It is doubted, however, whether good and evil are entirely the same as pleasure and pain. This is not affirmed entirely, nor is it clearly denied; for this is discussed in the *Gorgias*, the *Philebus*, and elsewhere. It is entirely proven that prudence itself—in which consists both the knowledge of the end of life and the choice of the ways leading to it—is the prince and leader of the moral virtues. This is asserted to such an extent that the virtues seem to be certain kinds of science (that is, prudence), while vices seem to be certain kinds of ignorance (that is, imprudence). It is then added that all sins proceed from ignorance; and that a person would never choose evil unless deceived by the image of good, nor flee from good unless terrified by some image of evil. If someone should say that a man who discerns good and evil nevertheless turns away from the former and toward the latter because he is overcome by pleasure or some other sensory affection, Socrates will deny it, asserting that this very thing which is said to be "overcome by affection" is nothing other than ignorance. For the knowledge of all things that are in us and around us is most powerful, and can never be overcome by anything. Finally, it is concluded that science contributes most—indeed everything—to virtue and happiness, while ignorance contributes equally to their opposites. Again, he reproves Protagoras for having both contradicted himself and used a backwards order. For before he defines what virtue is, he attempts to divide it and disputes whether it can be taught. Socrates even pretends that he himself has been led into a contradiction, solely because he followed the wandering sophist; and he warns that we should imitate the foresight of Prometheus rather than the haste of Epimetheus <note>Prometheus means "forethought"; Epimetheus means "afterthought"</note> in all of life to the best of our ability.

From where, O Socrates? Do you come from that hunt to which the noble character of Alcibiades is accustomed to provoke you? For I saw him recently. Indeed, he seems to show a noble appearance as a man. A man, I say: for much downy beard now creeps across his cheeks. SOCRATES. So be it; what then? Do you not approve of Homer, who says that the most pleasing age is that of the first downy beard? Alcibiades is now at that age. FRIEND. Indeed. But at present, from where do you come? Was it from him? And how is the youth now disposed toward you? SOCRATES. Well indeed; he seemed so to me today especially, for he often came to my aid today in speaking; and I come from him now. And I shall tell you something wonderful: I was looking at him very little while he was present, and, intending my mind elsewhere, I hardly noticed him. FRIEND. What was of such great importance that it diverted you from him? For no one more handsome among our citizens could be present. SOCRATES. On the contrary, someone much more beautiful was present. # PROTAGORAS, OR THE SOPHISTS. PAGE 91.
## m.iii
<meta>catchword: that in</meta>

-> It seems to be Protagoras. <-

**FRIEND:** Look, what are you saying? Has Protagoras actually arrived here?
**SOCRATES:** The day before yesterday.
**FRIEND:** And were you just with him?
**SOCRATES:** Just now: and I spoke much, and heard much as well.
**FRIEND:** Why not recount those things to us? Unless something prevents you. You may sit here. This boy will certainly give up his seat for you.
**SOCRATES:** I shall certainly recount it, and I will even be grateful to you if you listen.
**FRIEND:** On the contrary, we shall be grateful to you if you speak.
**SOCRATES:** Listen then. Last night, before the rising of the sun, Hippocrates, son of Apollodorus and brother of Phason, beat violently upon my door with his staff. When someone opened the door, he entered immediately, shouting: "Are you sleeping, Socrates, or are you awake?" Recognizing his voice, I said, "This is Hippocrates. O Hippocrates, is there any news?" "Nothing," he said, "except I come to bring welcome news." "Excellent," I said. "But what is it? What cause drove you here?" "Protagoras has arrived," he said, "and is staying near me." Then I said: "He arrived some time ago. Have you only just heard?" "By the gods," he said, "only yesterday evening." Feeling for a stool, he sat at my feet and added: "Late yesterday evening, having returned from Oenoe—for my slave Satyrus had run away from me—and though I intended to tell you I was going after him, I forgot because someone else intervened. But when I had come back, and we had dined and were about to give ourselves to sleep, only then did my brother announce that Protagoras had arrived. I tried to hurry to you immediately, but the unseasonable hour of the night held me back. But having woken from sleep and being relieved of my weariness, I have hurried here to you just now."

Recognizing his courage and his excitement <note>original: "stuporeq⁹" - here implying a state of being dazed or overwhelmed by enthusiasm</note>, I said: "What is this to you? Has Protagoras done you some injury?" He, smiling, said: "By the gods, Socrates, only because he alone is wise, but he does not make me wise."
**SOCRATES:** Indeed, he will certainly make you wise if you persuade him by offering him a fee.
**HIPPOCRATES:** O Jupiter and all the other gods! I would spare neither my own nor my friends' resources, if only I could be confident of achieving that. That is why I come to you now, so that you might intercede with him on my behalf. For I am younger, and I have never seen or heard Protagoras; I was but a boy when he first came here. All men, Socrates, praise this man and say he is most wise in speaking. But why do we not hurry to him, so that we may find him at home? He is staying, as I heard, with Callias son of Hipponicus. Let us go now.
**SOCRATES:** Not yet, my good man, I said. For it is still deep night. But let us go into the courtyard, where we shall walk until dawn breaks; afterward we shall go to Protagoras himself. For Protagoras does not leave the house in the early morning. Therefore, be confident: we shall find him at home.

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue.</margin>

Having said these things, we rose and went into the courtyard. Wanting to test his resolve, I examined him carefully and questioned him thus: "Tell me, Hippocrates: you are now going to Protagoras to pay him a fee on your behalf. To what kind of man are you going? And what kind of man do you expect to become because of him? Just as if you wished to go to Hippocrates <note>The famous physician of Cos</note>, your namesake of the line of Asclepius <note>The god of medicine</note>, to pay a fee on your behalf, and someone asked: 'Tell me, Hippocrates, you are giving a fee to Hippocrates? To what kind of man, and for what reason?' What would you answer?"
**HIPPOCRATES:** As to a physician.
**SOCRATES:** And what would you yourself become—that is, for what purpose?
**HIPPOCRATES:** To become a physician.
**SOCRATES:** But if you went to either Polycletus of Argos or Phidias of Athens <note>Famous Greek sculptors</note> with a fee offered for yourself, and someone asked to what kind of men and for what reason you offer money to Polycletus and Phidias, what would you say?
**HIPPOCRATES:** As to sculptors.
**SOCRATES:** And what kind of man would you become?
**HIPPOCRATES:** A sculptor, obviously.
**SOCRATES:** Pay attention, I pray: you and I are now setting out to Protagoras, and we are prepared to give him money for your sake—if our money is sufficient to persuade him; if not, we will spend our friends' money besides. If someone, therefore, seeing us hurrying so, should ask: 'Tell me, I pray, Socrates and Hippocrates, to what kind of man and for what reason do you intend to give money to Protagoras?' what would we answer him? What famous title have we heard for Protagoras? They call Phidias a sculptor and Homer a poet. But Protagoras?"
**HIPPOCRATES:** Men call this man a Sophist <term>Sophista: a professional teacher of virtue and rhetoric in Ancient Greece</term>, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** So we are going to him as to a Sophist to persuade him with a fee?
**HIPPOCRATES:** Exactly.
**SOCRATES:** If someone further asked you with what intent and what you yourself would become by going to Protagoras, what then?
At this, Hippocrates blushed. For by now the dawn had begun to shine a little, so that his face could be seen. He then answered, as the previous points concluded, that he would go as one who would himself become a Sophist.
**SOCRATES:** Would you not be ashamed to be known as a Sophist among the Greeks?
**HIPPOCRATES:** Greatly, Socrates, if I must speak what I feel.
**SOCRATES:** But see, Hippocrates, if perhaps this study of yours in the Protagorean art tends toward something other than becoming a Sophist. Just as you attended the school of the grammarian, the lyre-player, and the gymnastics teacher—not for the sake of practicing the art itself, but rather out of a certain eagerness for learning, as befits a private and free-born man.
**HIPPOCRATES:** Such entirely seems to be the reason for my study with Protagoras.
**SOCRATES:** Do you know what you are about to do now? Or does it escape you?
**HIPPOCRATES:** Regarding what?
**SOCRATES:** You are about to commit the care of your soul to a man who is, as you say, a Sophist. But I would be greatly surprised if you knew what a Sophist is. And if you are ignorant of that, you do not know whether this thing to which you strive to apply your efforts is good or evil.
**HIPPOCRATES:** I think I know, certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Tell me then, what do you think a Sophist is?
**HIPPOCRATES:** I think he is, as the name signifies, one who understands the principles pertaining to wisdom.
**SOCRATES:** One could say the same of painters and carpenters: that they are those who understand principles pertaining to wisdom. But if someone asked about painters, "wisdom regarding what things?", we would answer "regarding the wisdom of making images," and similarly for the others. And if we were asked in the same way about the Sophist: what kind of wisdom would we say is his? What is his office?
**HIPPOCRATES:** Surely the wisdom by which men are made eloquent in speaking.
**SOCRATES:** Perhaps we might truly say that, but not sufficiently. For that answer in...

# BOOK SEVENTEEN
### Page 101

Socrates pursues the matter with another question: by what kind of speaking do the Sophists make men eloquent? Surely a lute-player makes them skilled in the same kind of speaking in which they are also learned—namely, in the playing of the lute, is it not so? HIPPOCRATES: Certainly. SOCRATES: But indeed, what faculty of speaking does the Sophist provide? On what subjects? It is clear he speaks on those things which he understands. HIPPOCRATES: That seems likely. SOCRATES: What then is this thing that the Sophist himself understands and teaches to others? HIPPOCRATES: By Jove, I do not know. SOCRATES: Do you not see how great a risk you are submitting your soul to? If you were going to put your body at such a risk, where it might turn out for better or for worse, would you not first commit yourself to someone who was going to take such a risk with you only after you had diligently considered whether you should commit yourself or not, and even consulted your friends and relatives for a long time about this very thing? Since you value your soul more than your body, and since upon its corruption or integrity depends whether all your affairs go well or ill, have you consulted no one, neither relatives nor friends, on whether your soul should be committed to this stranger? But when you heard of his arrival yesterday evening, you hurried to him at early dawn, having held no counsel on this matter of whether you ought to trust yourself to him or not. Rather, you are ready to spend all your own money and that of your friends, as if you had already decided that one must absolutely adhere to Protagoras—whom you have never seen, as you say, nor ever spoken with. You call him a "Sophist" <note>term: Sophist (Sophista). Originally meaning a "wise man" or teacher of virtue, Socrates here treats the term with suspicion, suggesting they are mere retailers of knowledge.</note>, yet you do not know what a Sophist is, to whom you are about to surrender yourself. HIPPOCRATES: You seem to speak the truth, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Is a Sophist not, O Hippocrates, a kind of merchant or a hawker of certain wares by which the soul is nourished? HIPPOCRATES: He certainly seems so to me. But by what things is the soul nourished? SOCRATES: By teachings <note>original: "disciplinis" (disciplines/learnings)</note>. But we must beware, my friend, lest the Sophist deceive us while he praises what he sells, just as those do who sell food for the body, the merchants and hawkers. They praise all their own goods, yet they do not understand whether the things they sell are healthy or harmful to the body; and those who buy are equally ignorant, unless by chance one of them is a physician or a physical trainer. In the same way, those who carry various teachings around the cities for sale, hawking them to buyers, praise them all. And perhaps some of them are often ignorant of what is useful or useless to the soul among the things they sell. Similarly, those who buy from them are also ignorant, unless one of them happens to be a physician of the soul. If, therefore, you yourself understand what among these things is beneficial and what is harmful, <margin>The danger in buying teachings is far more serious than in buying food.</margin> you can safely buy teachings from Protagoras or anyone else. Otherwise, beware, blessed youth, lest you bring what is most dear to you into the greatest risk of loss. For the danger is far more serious in buying teachings than in buying food. For he who buys meat and drink can, before he consumes them, carry them home in other vessels; and having deposited them there, he can examine them diligently and, having called in someone expert in such matters, deliberate on what should be eaten or drunk, how much, and when. Therefore, there is no great danger in the buying. But teachings cannot be carried away in another vessel. It is necessary that he who buys them receives them into his soul; and having paid the price, he departs, carrying them within himself, already either tainted or moved toward better things. Let us discuss these things with our elders, for we are younger than the judgment of such a great matter requires. Nevertheless, for the present, let us proceed where we began and hear this man. Having heard him, we will communicate with others. For Protagoras is not there alone, but also Hippias of Elis, and Prodicus of Ceos, I believe, and many other very wise men. These things pleased us, and we proceeded. And having entered the vestibule, we discussed a certain matter that we had happened upon by chance. So that it would not be left unfinished, we talked in the vestibule itself until we reached an agreement in our dispute. A certain eunuch, the doorkeeper, heard us; but because of the crowd of Sophists, he was angry with those who were coming. We knocked; he opened. When he saw us, he said, "Ha! These are also Sophists; he has no leisure." And at the same time, pushing with both hands, he shut the door. We knocked again, but he said from behind the closed doors, "O good men, do you not hear that he has no leisure?" "O good man," I said, "we have not come to see Callias, nor are we Sophists. But be confident, we are looking for Protagoras. We desire to see him." This being announced, he finally opened the doors. Having entered, we found Protagoras walking in the front part of the portico. Many followed him: here was Callias, son of Hipponicus, and his half-brother Paralus, son of Pericles, and Charmides, son of Glaucon. On the other side was the other son of Pericles, Xanthippus, and Philippides, son of Philomelus, and Antimoerus of Mende, who was considered the most distinguished among all Protagoras' pupils; he was learning that faculty with the intention of becoming a Sophist himself and teaching the same things one day. Behind them followed others listening to Protagoras, most of whom seemed to be foreigners whom he gathers from every city through which he wanders, charming them with his voice like Orpheus, and alluring them. They, enchanted, follow his voice everywhere. Some of our own countrymen were also in that chorus. When I contemplated this chorus, their order delighted me wonderfully. For with diligent caution, each one took care never to precede Protagoras in step. But when he turned back, the attendant listeners moved aside so aptly, dividing into a circle on both sides, that they were always behind him. After him I saw, to speak in the words of Homer: Hippias of Elis sitting on a throne in the opposite vestibule of the portico. Around him on some benches sat several others: Eryximachus, son of Acumenus, and Phaedrus of Myrrhinus, and Andron, son of Androtion, and several others, partly citizens and partly foreigners, who seemed to be questioning Hippias about sublime matters of nature and the movements of the stars; he, sitting on his throne, unraveled the doubts of each. Furthermore, I saw Tantalus <note>A literary reference to Prodicus, whom Socrates describes using Homeric imagery of the underworld.</note>. Moreover, Prodicus of Ceos was present, who had retired into a certain small room which Hipponicus used to use as a storehouse; but so that the whole crowd of gathering guests could be received, Callias had cleared out that corner, removing the provisions...
