**PROTAGORAS.** "Do you wish to speak with me privately from the others, or in front of everyone?"

**SOCRATES.** "It makes no difference to us. But when you have heard why we have come, you shall see for yourself."

**PROTAGORAS.** "What is it then? For what sake have you come here?"

**SOCRATES.** "This Hippocrates is a townsman of ours, the son of Apollodorus, born of a noble and prosperous family. He himself, stirred by emulation with his equals, strives for virtue <note>original: "virtute" - here meaning excellence or civic skill</note>; he desires to become an illustrious man in the republic, and he hopes that through your friendship he will achieve this. Consider whether it is proper for us to consult with you about this alone or in front of the others."

**PROTAGORAS.** "O Socrates, you seem to consult rightly for my safety. For a foreigner who travels to great cities needs prudent caution when he persuades the most famous young men everywhere to leave the company of all others—both their own kin and strangers, both old and young—and adhere to him alone, as if they were to become more excellent than others through his friendship. Envy must necessarily rise up against him, and many malicious people will plot against him. I, however, believe the **Sophistic art** to be ancient; but that the ancient men skilled in it, fearing this envy and offense, disguised it under the appearance of other arts: partly under the appearance of poetry, as **Homer** did, and **Hesiod**, and **Simonides**; partly under the name of sacred rites and oracles, as **Orpheus** and **Musaeus** and their followers did. I have heard, moreover, that some called this art gymnastics, which **Iccus of Tarentum** seems to have done, and the Sophist who still survives, inferior to none, **Herodicus of Selymbria**, who traces his origin from the Megarians. Furthermore, **Pythocleides of Chios**, a most learned Sophist, and many others hid the sophistic faculty under the veil of the musical art. All these, as has been said, in order to avoid envy, practiced great dissimulation and hid the sophistic art under the pretext of other arts.

<margin>Apparent reasons.</margin>
But I disagree with all of them in this; nor do I think those trickeries are beneficial. For I do not believe they achieve their desire. For the leading men in the city perceive all dissimulations of this kind. The common people, in a way, do not notice, but they praise whatever the leaders proclaim. When this zeal for subterfuge does not attain what it attempts, it both shows the one fleeing to be unskilled and makes those who notice more hostile. For they think, among other things, that such a man is crafty and a deceiver. I, therefore, have entered upon a contrary path. I confess that I am a **Sophist** and that I teach others; and I judge that envy is avoided more safely by this candid confession than by that dissimulation. I have provided for myself by other reasons as well, so that, with God's help, I have suffered no evil on account of the profession of a Sophist, although I have practiced this faculty for many years. Indeed, I am advanced in age, and I could be the father of any of you in years. Therefore, it will be most pleasing to me if you wish to speak of these things with me in the hearing of all who are within."

Here I, suspecting that he wished to show off his authority before Prodicus and **Hippias**—since we had set out to hear him inflamed with greed for his wisdom—said: "Why do we not call Prodicus and Hippias and those who accompany them here, so that they too may hear us?"

**PROTAGORAS.** "Let us call them."

**CALLIAS.** "Do you wish us to prepare seats here, so that you may discourse while sitting?"

We all agreed; and hurrying quite a bit in our eagerness to hear, we gathered all the seats and arranged them immediately next to Hippias, for there were many benches there. Then Callias and Alcibiades arrived, bringing Prodicus and his supporters with them. After everyone had sat down, Protagoras said: "Repeat, O Socrates, in the presence of these men, what you were asking me a moment ago on behalf of this youth."

I said: "I shall begin now from the same starting point as before. This Hippocrates vehemently desires to join you. But he would gladly hear what he is going to report back from this association. Thus far our speech extends."

**PROTAGORAS.** "Young man, you ask what you will gain with me: you will never approach me without going away more learned, and every single day you will make progress with me."

**SOCRATES.** "This is no wonder, O Protagoras, for it is fitting: since even you, at such a great age and so wise, if you were to learn something you did not know from someone, you would go away more excellent. But that is not exactly what we are inquiring. But just as if Hippocrates, having changed his mind, desired to associate with this youth who recently arrived here, **Zeuxippus** the son of Heracleotus, and having approached him as he does you, were to hear the same things from him as from you—namely, that he would daily make progress with him—and then were to ask Zeuxippus in what matter he was going to progress: he would surely answer, 'in painting.' And if he met **Orthagoras of Thebes** and heard from him that he would turn out more learned day by day through his company, but were to ask in what matter he would be more learned, Orthagoras would answer, 'in the sound of the flutes.' In the same way, you also answer this youth and me asking on his behalf. For you say that if Hippocrates adheres to Protagoras..."

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

...that he would become more learned day by day: but in what exactly? Declare it. Then Protagoras said: "You ask skillfully indeed, O Socrates, and I gladly answer those who question me so well. If Hippocrates associates with me, he will not fall into that error which he undoubtedly would have encountered had he dealt with other Sophists. For others actually harm the youth; they drag them back against their will to the very arts they had fled from, handing them over to reasoning and calculations, Astronomy, Geometry, and Music." And looking at Hippias <note>Hippias of Elis, another Sophist present, known for his wide-ranging polymathy</note> at the same time, he added: "Whoever comes to me, however, will learn only that for which he came: and this discipline is prudence in domestic affairs and wisdom in public consultation, by which one may rightly govern his home and best manage the business of the city both in speaking and in acting."

SOCRATES: Do I understand what you mean, Protagoras? For you seem to me to be describing the <term>civil art</term> <note>original: "ciuilem artem," referring to political science or the art of citizenship</note> and promising to make men the best of citizens.

PROTAGORAS: This is the very thing, O Socrates, that I proclaim everywhere.

SOCRATES: O, what a noble craft you have obtained, if indeed you have obtained it. Truly, I should offer you nothing other than what I feel. I had previously thought, O Protagoras, that this could not be taught. Yet I cannot withhold my faith from you when you assert it. However, I ought to rightly declare the reason why I judge it can neither be taught nor handed down from one man to another. Indeed, as the rest of the Greeks testify, I call the Athenians wise men. I see, therefore, when the city is gathered in assembly and wishes to deliberate on building, the advice of builders is sought; and when concerning the construction of ships, the shipwrights are summoned. They do the same in all other matters which they believe can be taught and learned. And if anyone else proceeds to give advice on the work of that art of which they think him ignorant—even if he be a most distinguished man in other things, or very rich, or of noble birth—they admit him no more for it. Instead, they hiss and mock him until either he, deterred by the tumult, ceases speaking, or the archers <note>The Scythian archers who served as the public police force in Athens</note> at the command of the magistrates either drag him out or remove him. This, therefore, they are accustomed to observe in all things pertaining to the perception of the arts.

But when there is to be consultation regarding the public administration of the city, the architect advises equally with the blacksmith; likewise the cobbler, the merchant, the sailor, the rich man, the poor, the low-born, and the noble. Nor does anyone mock any of these, as happened in the previous cases, on the grounds that he has never learned or had no teacher; yet they dare to give counsel. It is clear, then, that they do not think it can be taught. Nor is this seen only publicly, but also privately. For those who excel in civil wisdom cannot pour this virtue into another. Indeed, Pericles, the father of these youths, educated them diligently in those things learned under a master; but in those things in which he himself is wise, he neither educates them himself nor commits them to any other to be educated. Instead, they wander about everywhere like grazing animals without a shepherd, to see if by some chance they might stumble upon this virtue. Likewise, when Pericles was the guardian of Clinias, the younger brother of this Alcibiades, and feared for him because of Alcibiades—lest he be corrupted by his company—he separated them and educated Clinias at the house of Ariphron. But before six months had passed, he returned the boy to him, as he despaired of his talent. I could mention many others besides, who, though they were excellent men in the republic, taught no one, whether kinsman or stranger.

Indeed, O Protagoras, while I observe these things, I doubt that virtue can be taught. On the other hand, when I hear you asserting this, I am forced to change my mind; and I judge that what you say is by no means to be despised, considering that you are wise through the experience of many things, through learning, and through discovery. Therefore, if you can show us more clearly that virtue is acquired through some teaching, show us, I pray, and do not be begrudging.

PROTAGORAS: I shall not be begrudging, O Socrates.

<margin>The myth which strives to demonstrate that virtue is taught.</margin>

"But shall I, as an elder to younger men, tell you a story? Or shall I proceed by argument?" Then many of the listeners allowed him to speak in whichever way he preferred.

PROTAGORAS: I think a story will be more pleasing to you. Once upon a time, there were only gods; there were no races of mortals. But when the fated time for their generation came, the gods themselves fashioned them in the bowels of the earth from fire and earth, and from those things which are mixed with fire and earth. When they wished to bring them out into the light, they commanded Prometheus and Epimetheus to equip each with competent powers. Epimetheus, therefore, asked Prometheus to grant him the office of that distribution, and that Prometheus should inspect him as he distributed. Prometheus consented. He distributed: to some he gave strength without speed; some weaker ones he gifted with velocity. He armed some. For the unarmed, he devised some other mechanism for safety. For those he enclosed in a small body, he commanded that they be lifted by wings through the air or creep through the earth. But those he drew out into a large mass, he fortified by that very mass for their safety. And similarly, balancing all other things, he distributed to each, so that no race should utterly perish.

After he had so equipped them that they might avoid mutual destruction, he then began to devise a way by which they might most easily live their lives under the open sky. He clothed them with very thick hair and bristles and very hard skins, by which they might easily endure the intemperance of both winter and summer; and he prepared for them natural bedding and lairs from these same things. To their feet he added soles, claws, bristles, calluses, and likewise very hard hides. Then he supplied different foods to different creatures: to some herbs from the earth, to some fruits and berries from trees, and roots to others. Nor were there lacking those to whom he gave food from the consumption of one another. However, to the predatory animals he gave a somewhat sterile nature, but to the others he gave fertility, so that in this way the race might be preserved. But since Epimetheus was not altogether wise, he squandered all the endowments unknowingly upon the brutes; nor did he notice that nothing would be left over from such a great bestowal with which to gift our race next. Therefore, the race of men remained unprovided for, and he was at a loss which way to turn. To the one doubting...

# PROTAGORAS OR THE SOPHISTS

XCIII.

Prometheus stood by as the observer of that distribution: and he saw that the other animals were each supported by their own gifts and filled with good things; but man he saw naked, unarmed, without shoes or bedding. Now indeed the fatal day itself was imminent, on which the earth was compelled to bring man forth into the light. And since Prometheus, consulting every way for human safety, could find no other path, he stole the ingenious wisdom of Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcanus," the Roman name for Hephaestus, god of fire and craftsmanship</note> and Minerva <note>original: "Minerva," the Roman name for Athena, goddess of wisdom</note> together with fire. For it was not possible for anyone to obtain or even use that wisdom without fire. Thus Prometheus bestowed it upon the human race; and so we obtained the wisdom that provides for life's sustenance. 

Yet, human beings still lacked political wisdom <note>original: "civilis sapientia," the art of living together in a state</note>. For that resided with Jupiter <note>original: "Iuppiter," the Roman name for Zeus</note>: and it was not yet permitted for Prometheus to ascend to his citadel. Indeed, the terrifying guards of Jupiter himself standing around the citadel deterred Prometheus. However, having secretly entered the shared workshop of Vulcan and Minerva in which the arts were cultivated, he stole the fiery art of Vulcan and the other art of Minerva, and handed them over to man; by which the faculty of living was obtained. But Prometheus, as it is said, paid the penalty for the theft because of Epimetheus <note>Prometheus's brother, whose name means "afterthought"</note>. 

Since man alone of all living creatures was made a participant in a divine lot, in the beginning, he alone because of this kinship believed there were gods: and he dedicated altars and statues to them. Then, by art, he distinguished the voice into articulate words: he constructed houses, made clothes and shoes, and fashioned bedding: he gathered nourishment from the earth. Thus humans, established from the beginning, wandered and lived in a scattered fashion, for they had not yet built cities. Therefore, since they were weaker than the wild beasts, they were torn to pieces everywhere. For the faculty of the arts was sufficient for procuring food, but by no means for the fight against savage beasts. For they were unskilled in political expertise <note>original: "civilis peritia"</note>, of which military matters are a part. 

Therefore, so that they might fortify themselves against that plague, they gathered together by building cities. But once gathered, they wronged one another in turn, because they lacked the political art; for which reason, being dispersed again, they were mangled by the beasts. But Jupiter, consulting for human safety, sent Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius," the Roman name for Hermes</note> bringing shame <note>original: "pudor," translating the Greek 'aidos'—a sense of moral shame or respect</note> and justice to men: so that these two might adorn and bind the cities together, and reconcile the citizens through mutual goodwill. 

Mercury therefore asked on what condition he should deliver shame and justice to men. "Should these be distributed in the same way as the arts?" said Mercury. "For those are distributed such that one person skilled in the art of medicine is sufficient for many unskilled people, and the others similarly. Shall I give shame and justice to men in this way? Or shall I implant them in all?" Jupiter replied: "Indeed, all ought to be participants in these. For no cities would stand if only a few were participants in these, as is the case with the other arts. Furthermore, you shall establish a law in my name: that whoever is entirely without a share of justice and shame shall be put to death as a plague upon the city." 

For this reason, O Socrates, all others as well as the Athenians, whenever a discussion is to be held regarding architecture or any other craft, admit only a few to the council; but they exclude the rest who are unskilled in the arts, as you say and I approve. But whenever a council is entered regarding political administration—which consists of virtue, temperance, and justice—they rightly admit everyone. Since it is necessary for all to be participants in this virtue; otherwise, no cities could exist. This, O Socrates, is the cause of that which you were doubting. 

But lest you suspect you are being deceived, accept this further conjecture: that all men judge each individual to be possessed of this political virtue—namely temperance and justice. For truly, in other faculties, as you say, if someone boasts—suppose he claims to be the best flute-player when he is actually unskilled in it—those hearing him laugh, or most are indignant. His relatives also warn him as if he were insane, and rebuke him. But the opposite happens in political virtue. For although they may know someone is unjust, yet if he confesses this openly before those who do not know, they think him insane; they do not think iniquity should be made manifest. Rather, they think justice must always be displayed, whether it is present or not. They believe that he who does not pretend to be just is raving mad: as if it were necessary for every single person to be a participant in political virtue in some way, or else be exterminated from the gathering and life of men. 

From these things, I think it has been sufficiently shown by what merit they admit anyone as a counselor on political matters: because they judge everyone to be possessed of this virtue. But that they think virtue is neither innate nor happens by chance, but is acquired by teaching and study, I shall next endeavor to show you. No one is angry with, or rebukes, or teaches, or punishes those for those evils which they think happen by nature or by chance, lest they be such; rather, all pity them, such as the deformed, the small, or the sickly. For who is so mindless as to correct these? They surely understand, as I think, that all these evils and their opposites come to men by nature and fortune. On the contrary, when they think certain evils are present in someone from a lack of study, habit, and teaching, then they are indignant, they rebuke, and they punish. In this number are iniquity and impiety: and in short, whatever is repugnant to political virtue. Which things everyone everywhere condemns and corrects, because such contrary depravity as well as political virtue comes from industry and discipline. 

For if you wish to consider the intention of punishment, Socrates, you will understand from that also that men think virtue is acquired by study. For no one punishes for the sake of the past: nor does one afflict the unjust with penalties for the simple reason that they have committed a wrong—unless one rages without reason like a beast. But he who undertakes to punish with reason does not punish because of a past crime—for he cannot bring it about that what is done is undone—but he looks to the future: so that neither the offender himself nor anyone else might sin again, being moved by his example. Anyone who takes notice of errors with this purpose and such a judgment considers virtue to be obtainable by teaching. For he strikes for the sake of deterrence. With this mind and opinion, they approach punishing both publicly and privately, whoever takes notice of those sinning. Moreover, all others condemn and punish those whom they judge to be sinners, and especially your fellow citizens, the Athenians. Wherefore the Athenians also, by this reasoning, are among those who—

He further argues that the practice of punishment proves that virtue is something that can be taught and learned rather than being purely innate.</summary>

# BOOK SEVENTEEN
### Page 17

It is established: those who believe that virtue can be taught. From these points, it has been clearly shown, I believe, O Socrates <note>The speaker is addressing Socrates, likely in the context of Plato's dialogue *Protagoras*</note>, that your citizens are not wrong to accept the advice of a blacksmith or a tanner in matters of public administration; for they believe that virtue can be acquired through instruction, study, and practice. There remains that doubt which you yourself raised concerning men famous for their virtue: for what reason do they educate their sons in all subjects learned under a tutor, yet regarding the father’s own virtue, they make them no more distinguished than other men? To this, O Socrates, I will offer a reasoned argument rather than a myth. 

For consider it thus: is there one single thing, or not, in which it is necessary for all citizens to participate, if indeed a city is to stand? For in this way your ambiguity is resolved; otherwise, not at all. If this one thing exists—and it is not the work of architects, nor of blacksmiths, nor of potters, but is **justice**, **temperance**, and **holiness** <note>original: "iustitia, temperantia, sanctitas"</note>, and to comprehend it in a few words, the specific virtue of a man—if this is, I say, that in which everyone must share: and if it pleases one to learn and do anything else along with this, but never without it; and if the person who lacks it must be taught and corrected, whether boy, man, or woman, until through correction they are made better; and if anyone should despise this discipline, he is to be expelled from the cities as incurable or put to death—if it is so, I say, as we have said, and yet excellent citizens educate their sons in other matters but in this not at all, observe how strangely they would be turning out. 

For we have shown that they believe it can be taught both privately and publicly. Since it can be acquired through both instruction and care, do they teach their sons other things in which the penalty of death is not proposed for those who are ignorant, yet in those matters where death, exile, confiscation of property, or the overturning of homes threatens the ignorant and unrefined sons, do fathers not instruct them with all diligence? And where such threats urge them on, is instruction and care applied more lightly? 

One should believe, O Socrates, that from tender years until the end of life they are educated and admonished. For as soon as a boy understands what is being said, the nurse, the mother, the tutor <note>term: *pedagogus* — a slave or guardian who escorted children to school and supervised their behavior</note>, and the father strive with all care and zeal for this: that in every single thing, both in words and deeds, the boy may turn out as best as possible. They show him point by point what is **just** and what is **unjust**; what is **honorable** and what is **base**; what is **holy** and what is **profane**; what should be done and what should not. If the boy obeys these things, they think it goes well with him. But if he resists, then like a warped and crooked piece of wood, they straighten him with threats and blows. 

After this, he hands the boys over to schoolmasters to be cared for, and they demand from the masters a diligence for good character much more than for the instruction of letters and the lyre <note>original: "citharæ"</note>; the teachers, in turn, take care and cultivate them. And after they have learned their letters and turn to written works, they set before them the works of excellent poets to be read and learned by heart, in which many moral lessons are inserted: the deeds of ancient men outstanding in virtue are praised, so that the boy, kindled by emulation, may imitate the noble actions of his ancestors. 

The lyre-players also strive for other such things, especially **temperance**, and they take care that the youths do nothing wrong. And when they have learned to strike the lyre, they teach them the songs of other poets who excel in beautiful melody, which they sing to the lyre; and they endeavor to shape the souls of the boys with rhythms and harmonies, so that having been made milder, more modest, and more harmonious, they may be useful for acting and speaking. For the whole life of man requires a certain rhythmic harmony. 

After this, parents send their sons to the masters of the gymnasia, so that having acquired a firm and fit physical condition, they may best serve the mind, lest being hindered by the fragility of their bodies, they be deterred from military and civil actions as if they were too laborious. Surely those who are most able observe these things most; and those who are most able are the wealthiest men. Their sons are the first to enter the schools of discipline and the last to leave. 

Once they have left the schools, they are compelled by the magistrates to learn the laws and rights, and to live by their example, lest they act rashly by relying on their own wit. But just as writing masters trace a certain pattern with a pen for boys who do not yet know how to write, whose characters they learn to follow by imitating the art of writing, so the city, prescribing laws—the inventions of ancient men most wise in law-giving—compels them to rule and obey according to that norm. Those who transgress, it punishes; and a punishment of this kind, both among you and among many others, because it directs the transgressor like a judicial penalty, is called a "direction" or "correction." 

Since, therefore, there is such great care for virtue both privately and publicly, do you still doubt, O Socrates, and wonder if virtue can be taught? Indeed, no one should wonder at this; rather, it would be much more surprising if it could *not* be taught. You asked, furthermore, for what reason the sons of good fathers are often found to be bad. I proceed to teach you this again. This should not seem strange if what I have said is true: namely, that the care of virtue ought to belong not to one person alone, but to all, if the city is to stand. 

If it is as I say—or rather, since it certainly is so—choose and consider any other of the faculties and disciplines: for instance, if the city could not stand unless we were all flute-players <note>original: "tibicines"</note>, of whatever quality each might be, would not everyone, privately and publicly, teach this to everyone else? And would they not correct one who was ignorant of it without the sting of envy? Just as now everyone proclaims what is just and lawful without envy, and does not hide these things as they might others. For common justice and virtue benefit everyone. And for that reason, everyone most freely shows everyone else what is just and lawful. 

If, therefore, we were to instruct one another in flute-playing with the same fervor of mind and charity, would the sons of the best flute-players turn out more skilled in these sounds than the sons of the worse? Not at all, I think. But whoever was naturally gifted at blowing the flutes would make great progress, while the slow one would make little. And often the son of a skilled flute-player would turn out unrefined, and often the son of an unskilled one, fit. Nevertheless, all would be sufficient flute-players if they were compared with those who are unrefined and understand nothing of these matters. Similarly, when you consider—

# PROTAGORAS OR THE SOPHISTS.

But Socrates, even the man who seems most unjust to you among those living under the law would appear just and a guardian of right if he were ever compared with men who have neither education, nor courts, nor laws, nor any necessity in life to compel them to cultivate virtue. They would be savages, like those whom the poet Pherecrates brought on stage at the Lenaea <note>An Athenian festival involving dramatic competitions</note> last year. If you were to fall among such people, who are the enemies of the human race, you would think yourself well off if you met an Eurybatus or a Phrynondas <note>Notorious villains of the era</note>, and you would bewail your lot, longing for the "wickedness" of our own people. But now, Socrates, you are being fastidious because everyone is a teacher of virtue to the best of his power, yet no one appears so to you. It is as if you were to ask who is the teacher who taught us to speak Greek; no one would appear. Likewise, if you asked who taught the sons of craftsmen the very trade which their fathers and their fathers' colleagues practice, and which the sons imitate—it would not be easy, Socrates, to find a specific teacher for them. But for those who know nothing of the craft, it would be very easy. So it must be said of virtue and all such things. Indeed, we should consider ourselves satisfied if someone is even a little more capable than others at advancing youth toward virtue.

I profess to be one of these: to know more subtly than others the law and reason by which men become good and honorable, and thus to perfect the matter itself so that I am worthy of the fee I demand—indeed, even a greater fee, as my students themselves judge. This is the condition of my payment: after someone has learned from me, if he wishes, he pays the amount I demand in silver. If not, he goes into a temple and, after taking an oath, estimates how much my lessons seem worth to him, and pays that much. Therefore, Socrates, let it be proven to you by this fable and this reasoning that virtue can be taught and learned. The Athenians themselves bear witness to this. We have also shown that it should not seem strange if good fathers have bad sons, and bad fathers have good sons; for even the sons of Polycletus <note>A famous sculptor</note>, the peers of Paralus and Xanthippus here, are surpassed by a vast distance when compared to their father. Similarly with the sons of other craftsmen. Yet these youths are not yet to be rejected, for their tender age offers hope.

When Protagoras had shown these things, he made an end of speaking. But for a long time afterward, as if charmed by the preceding speech, I kept staring at Protagoras's face, inflamed by the desire for more words. But after I perceived he had truly stopped, I recovered myself and, turning to Hippocrates, I said: "O son of Apollodorus, I owe you great thanks for bringing me here today. For I value very highly having heard these things from Protagoras. Previously, I did not think it was a human concern by which men are made good; now I am persuaded that it is. But a small point remains to be cleared up, which Protagoras will surely demonstrate easily after teaching all these great things. For if one speaks of these same matters with any of the public orators, one will hear such speeches as Pericles is wont to make, or other eloquent men. But if one asks them a further question, like books they have nothing to answer or to ask themselves. And if one questions any point of what was said, they ring out like struck brass and prolong their resonance, unless one stops them immediately. Thus rhetoricians, when asked a brief question, produce a long-winded speech. But Protagoras here is able to speak copiously and ornately, as the previous speech testifies, and he is also able, when asked, to respond summarily and briefly—to endure the questioner, and to receive and give an account, which can be said of few men.

At present, therefore, Protagoras, I desire one small thing more. If you clarify this, I shall consider myself satisfied in all things. You say that virtue is obtainable through the study of teaching. And I believe you more than anyone. But I wonder at one thing you said; I pray you, open it up to me. You said that Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> bestowed justice and shame upon men. Then, as your speech proceeded, you often named justice, temperance, and holiness, as if all these were contained under one single virtue, and virtue itself were some single thing. I would like this explained clearly to me: whether virtue is one single thing, of which justice, temperance, and holiness are parts; or whether all these things I have mentioned are names of one and the same thing. This is what I require further."

PROTAGORAS: "That is an easy answer, Socrates. All the things you ask about are parts of virtue itself, which is a single whole."

SOCRATES: "Are they parts in the way that the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears are parts of a single face? Or are they like the parts of gold, which differ in no way from the whole except in size and smallness?"

PROTAGORAS: "It seems to me, Socrates, that the parts of virtue are related to the whole as the parts of the face are to the whole."

SOCRATES: "Do some men receive one part of virtue and others another? Or is it necessary that he who has one has them all?"

PROTAGORAS: "By no means; for many are brave but unjust, and others are just but not at all wise."

SOCRATES: "Are wisdom and courage parts of virtue?"

PROTAGORAS: "Entirely so; and wisdom is the most excellent part of all."

SOCRATES: "Is one of these one thing, and the other another?"

PROTAGORAS: "Yes."

SOCRATES: "And does each have its own power? Just as in the parts of the face, the eye is not like the ears, nor is their power the same; nor is any other part like another in power or otherwise. Do the parts of virtue likewise differ, so that no one is like the others, nor the same in essence or power? Is it established that it is so? For the example of the nature of virtue which we introduced agrees with this."

PROTAGORAS: "It is certainly so, Socrates."

SOCRATES: "Then no part of virtue is like knowledge, nor like justice, or courage, or temperance, or holiness."

PROTAGORAS: "Certainly not."

SOCRATES: "Come, let us consider together what sort of thing each of these is. First, like this: Is justice a certain thing, or nothing? To me it seems to be a certain thing. And to you?"

PROTAGORAS: "To me as well."

SOCRATES: "What then? If someone were to ask me and you: 'O Prota—'"

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

**Socrates:** Protagoras and Socrates—tell me, I pray, whether this thing which you just now called "justice," by the very fact that it is justice, is also "just," or is it "unjust"? For my part, I would say it is just, and you will surely agree with me; or do you think otherwise?
**Protagoras:** Plainly with you.
**Socrates:** I would therefore answer anyone asking that justice is of such a nature as to be just. And you?
**Protagoras:** I also.
**Socrates:** If he asked again, "Do we say that there is also such a thing as 'holiness'?" we would certainly agree, I think.
**Protagoras:** We would agree.
**Socrates:** "And do you not say that this thing is also something?" he would ask; and we would assent?
**Protagoras:** This too.
**Socrates:** "Do you think the nature of this thing is such that it is holy, or profane?" I would be annoyed by this question, and turning to him I would object: "Watch your words, please! For nothing else could ever be holy, unless holiness itself were holy." What about you? Would you not answer similarly?
**Protagoras:** Similarly.
**Socrates:** If he added to this: "Have I correctly understood what you said above? You seemed to me a little while ago to assert that the parts of virtue relate to one another in such a way that one part is not like another." I would reply to this that he understood the rest correctly, but that he was wrong to think I had agreed to that part. For it was Protagoras here who answered those things; I was the one asking. Therefore, if he should say, "O Protagoras, is Socrates speaking the truth? Are you the one who says that one part of virtue is not like another? Is this your speech?" What will you answer him?
**Protagoras:** It is necessary, Socrates, to assent.
**Socrates:** Having conceded these things, what shall we answer him most especially if he further objects: "Therefore holiness is not of such a nature as to be a just thing, nor is justice such as to be holy; but the former is such as to be not-just, and the latter such as to be not-holy. Thus the former is unjust, and the latter profane." What shall I say to this? For my part, I will say that justice is holy, and again that holiness is just. I think you will also permit me to answer these very things on your behalf: namely, that either justice is the same as holiness, or these two are most similar to one another; so that above all else, justice is such as holiness is, and holiness is such as justice is. See whether you forbid me to answer thus, or whether you feel the same.
**Protagoras:** That does not seem so simple to me, Socrates, that it can be granted that holiness is just, or justice holy. Rather, it seems to me that a certain difference is present. But what does that matter in the end? If you wish, let holiness be just for us, and justice holy.
**Socrates:** I do not accept these terms, Protagoras; nor do I desire it to be said to me "if you wish" or "if it pleases you," but rather let the argument be refuted. I require that you say "me" and "you." I say "me" and "you" because I believe the discourse is only then rightly discussed when that "if" condition is removed from it.
**Protagoras:** Indeed, justice has something similar to holiness. For anything has something similar to anything else, except for those things which are entirely contrary to each other, like white and black, or soft and hard. And yet even those things which we said above have different powers from one another, and where one is not such as the other—like the parts of a face—they have something similar among themselves, and in a way one is such as the other. And by this reasoning, you may refute these things if you please, on the grounds that all things are mutually similar; yet things that have some similarity are not necessarily to be called "similar," nor are things that have some dissimilarity to be called "dissimilar," if they only have a tiny bit of similarity or dissimilarity.
**Socrates:** I am amazed, Protagoras; do the just and the holy relate to each other in such a way that they have only a little similarity between them?
**Protagoras:** Not entirely so; yet not exactly as you seem to think.
**Socrates:** Since these things are troublesome to you, I will let them go; let us consider another thing from what you were saying. Do you call something "folly" <note>original: *insaniam*, literally madness or lack of health of mind</note>? And do you say that "wisdom" is its contrary?
**Protagoras:** I do.
**Socrates:** When men act rightly and usefully, do they seem to you to act "temperately" <note>original: *temperate*, acting with self-control or moderation</note> in so operating, or when they act the opposite?
**Protagoras:** It seems to me they act temperately when they act usefully and rightly.
**Socrates:** Do they not act temperately by "temperance"?
**Protagoras:** It must be so.
**Socrates:** Do not those who act wrongly act foolishly? And those who act so, do they not act intemperately?
**Protagoras:** So it seems.
**Socrates:** Therefore, to act foolishly is the contrary of what is called acting temperately.
**Protagoras:** It is indeed.
**Socrates:** Therefore, are not things done foolishly done by "folly," and things done temperately by "temperance"?
**Protagoras:** Certainly.
**Socrates:** Does not whatever is done by strength happen strongly? And whatever by weakness, weakly?
**Protagoras:** It appears so.
**Socrates:** And whatever by speed, speedily? And whatever by slowness, slowly?
**Protagoras:** This too.
**Socrates:** And that which is done in the same way entirely is produced by the same thing; but that which is done in a contrary way is produced by a contrary?
**Protagoras:** I agree.
**Socrates:** Tell me, I pray: is there such a thing as "the beautiful"?
**Protagoras:** There is indeed.
**Socrates:** Is there any contrary to this other than "the ugly"?
**Protagoras:** Nothing else.
**Socrates:** Is there also something "good"?
**Protagoras:** Also good.
**Socrates:** Is there any other contrary to it except "the evil"?
**Protagoras:** No other.
**Socrates:** Is there such a thing as "high-pitched" in the voice?
**Protagoras:** Surely.
**Socrates:** Is there any other contrary to it besides "low-pitched"?
**Protagoras:** That very thing.
**Socrates:** Does not each one of the contraries have not many, but only one contrary?
**Protagoras:** Only one.
**Socrates:** Let us now resume what has been conceded by us so far. We clearly conceded that for one thing there is only one contrary.
**Protagoras:** Indeed.
**Socrates:** Likewise, that what is done in a contrary way is produced by contraries.
**Protagoras:** This too.
**Socrates:** We admitted, moreover, that what is done foolishly and what is done temperately are done in a contrary way.
**Protagoras:** Yes.
**Socrates:** Again, that what is acted temperately proceeds from temperance; what is acted foolishly from folly.
**Protagoras:** It is agreed.
**Socrates:** If it is done in a contrary way, is it not done by a contrary?
**Protagoras:** Certainly.
**Socrates:** But this is done by temperance, and that by folly.
**Protagoras:** Surely.
**Socrates:** In a contrary way?
**Protagoras:** Contrary.
**Socrates:** Therefore, by contraries?
**Protagoras:** And by contraries.
**Socrates:** Therefore, is folly the contrary of temperance?
**Protagoras:** It appears so.
**Socrates:** Do we remember that we conceded above that folly is the contrary of wisdom?
**Protagoras:** Certainly.
**Socrates:** And that for one thing there is only one contrary?
**Protagoras:** This too.
**Socrates:** Which of the two arguments shall we reject, Protagoras? The one that says for one thing there is only one contrary? Or the one that claimed wisdom was different from temperance, and that both were parts of virtue, and moreover...

Interrogations through related and contrary terms to prove that one thing has only one contrary.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates uses a series of logical questions to lead Protagoras toward the conclusion that different virtues, such as justice and holiness or wisdom and temperance, are closely related or even identical. He specifically argues that since every quality has only one true opposite, and both wisdom and temperance are opposites of folly, they must be the same thing.</summary>

# PROTAGORAS, OR THE SOPHISTS.

...and if these two are different, are they also unlike, both in themselves and in their powers, just as the parts of a face are? Which of these shall we refute? Both of these arguments are presented in a way that is hardly musical <note>original: "haud satis musice"; meaning they lack harmony or logical consistency</note>, for they do not harmonize with one another. For how can they agree if it is necessary for one thing to have only one contrary, and not many? Yet "folly," which is a single thing, appears to be the contrary of both "wisdom" and "temperance." Is it so, or otherwise, O Protagoras?

PROTAGORAS: Let it be so, then. What now?

SOCRATES: Will not wisdom and temperance then be one according to this reasoning? And did it not stand settled above that justice and holiness are also in some way the same? Come, Protagoras, do not be reluctant; let us proceed to the rest. Does it seem to you that an unjust man, in acting unjustly, is temperately wise?

PROTAGORAS: I, for my part, Socrates, would not dare to confess this; yet many men assert it.

SOCRATES: Shall I direct my words to them, or to you?

PROTAGORAS: If it pleases you, discuss this common talk of the multitude first.

SOCRATES: It matters nothing to me, provided you yourself answer, whether these things seem so to you or not. For I am examining the argument itself first and foremost. It happens, however, that both I, the questioner, and the one responding are examined by this process.

At this, Protagoras first, wishing to distinguish himself, began to complain of the difficulty of the discourse; but afterwards he agreed to answer.

SOCRATES: Come then, answer me from the beginning. Do some people seem to you to be temperately wise while acting unjustly?

PROTAGORAS: Let it be so.

SOCRATES: And by "being temperately wise," do you mean "thinking well"?

PROTAGORAS: I do.

SOCRATES: And is "thinking well" the same as "deliberating well" in that which they do unjustly?

PROTAGORAS: Let it be so.

SOCRATES: Is this if they fare well and live well while doing injury, or if they fare badly?

PROTAGORAS: If they fare well.

SOCRATES: Do you say then that there are certain "good things"?

PROTAGORAS: I do.

SOCRATES: Are those things good which are useful to men?

PROTAGORAS: Indeed, by Jove, I call certain things good even if they are not useful to men!

SOCRATES: When I saw that Protagoras was becoming irritated and was descending to the answer unwillingly, I asked him more mildly and submissively: Do you mean, Protagoras, things which are useful to no man, or things which are useful in no way at all? Do you call such things "good"?

PROTAGORAS: Not at all. But I know many things that are useless to men—foods, drinks, medicines, and many other things— <margin>The sophist wanders.</margin> while others are useful. Some things are neutral toward men but are of some importance when applied to horses. Some are for oxen, others for dogs; some for none of these, but rather for trees. And of those things for trees, some are such that they often benefit the roots but harm the shoots. Just as manure is useful to the roots, but very harmful to the branches and stems. Oil, too, is most beneficial to all trees and plants, but it is very harmful to the hair of all animals except humans. For it benefits the hair of men and the whole body. And so "the good" exists as something varied and multiform. Hence, oil is best for the external parts of our body, but worst for the internal parts. For this reason, physicians forbid the use of oil to the sick, nor do they permit its use except in the smallest amount to offset the unpleasant smell of certain foods.

When Protagoras had said these things, those present approved his words with frequent applause and shouting.

SOCRATES: But I, O Protagoras, said: I am indeed excessively forgetful; if someone draws out a speech at length, I immediately forget what the words are about. Truly, if I were somewhat deaf and you were having a conversation with me, you would think you had to shout louder to me than to others. So now, since you are addressing a forgetful man, use more concise answers with me, if you care for me to follow you.

PROTAGORAS: What brevity do you demand? Do you bid me deal with you in fewer words than is proper?

SOCRATES: Not at all.

PROTAGORAS: Or perhaps in as many words as are necessary?

SOCRATES: Exactly so.

PROTAGORAS: Shall I impose the limit on the speech? Or will you rather establish the due boundary which I may not transgress, and which I must observe while speaking?

SOCRATES: I have heard indeed that you know how to speak so abundantly whenever it pleases you, and at such length, that speech never fails you; and also that you can touch upon the same matters in fewer words than all others. And you can teach others to do the same, as I hear. If, therefore, you are going to dispute with me, please use that brief and concise method of speaking.

PROTAGORAS: O Socrates, I have competed in speaking with many men before. And if I had acted as you advise—if, I say, I had spoken according to the rule imposed on me by the listener—I would certainly be no more distinguished than any other man, and the name of Protagoras would not resound throughout all Greece.

SOCRATES: But when I realized that the former manner of answering did not please him at all, and that he would by no means answer in that way thereafter of his own accord, I judged it was not at all expedient for me to be present at those disputes. And therefore I said: O Protagoras, I do not demand that our dispute proceed against your will. For if you are willing to discourse so that I can follow, I will stay; for you yourself, as is said of you and as you profess, are equally able to touch upon the same things both summarily and to speak of them most amply. For you are wise, but I am unsuited for a long speech; and would that I were capable of it! But it was in your interest to indulge us a little, since you are equally prepared for both, so that the dispute might be completed. But since you are not willing, and business presses me so much that I cannot stay here while you orate at length—though I would have heard those things gladly—I am leaving now for where the matter itself calls me.

Having said these things, I rose immediately to depart. But Callias grabbed my right hand with his and my cloak with his left, saying: We shall not let you go, Socrates; for if you leave, we shall no longer converse with one another in this way. Stay, I beseech you. No one's speech could happen to be more pleasing to me than your dispute with Protagoras. Therefore, comply with both me and all these people.

But I had already risen to leave, and I said to Callias: O son of Hipponicus, I have always admired your love of wisdom <note>original: "philosophiam"</note>; now I praise and love it besides. Therefore, I would vehemently desire to gratify you if you asked for possible things. But what you now ask is just as if you were praying that I should follow Crison of Himera, the runner and young man, <margin>Crison of Himera, a runner.</margin> with equal strides, or some of those who are accustomed to run the longest distance, or a day's course...

But if you wish to see me and this man, like another Crison <note>Crison of Himera was a famous Olympic runner mentioned by Plato</note>, running together, pray that he accompanies me with equal paces. You see, O Socrates, said Callias: Protagoras seems to speak justly: while he judges it permissible for him to discuss at his own will, and for you likewise at yours. Here Alcibiades said, you do not speak rightly, O Callias. For Socrates here confesses himself to be powerless at orating: and in this he yields to Protagoras. But if he should yield to anyone in disputing, in receiving and returning reasons: I shall wonder greatly. If therefore Protagoras confesses himself to be inferior to Socrates in disputing: Socrates has enough already. But if he also claims this for himself: let him discuss with Socrates questioning: and in turn in responding let him not wander around through long circuits: nor by orating let him cut off the opportunity for disputing: nor refuse to give a reason to Socrates while he speaks too profusely, until most of the listeners forget that which is being dealt with. Indeed, I give my word for Socrates: that he will by no means commit what is said to oblivion: although he jokes with us, saying that he is forgetful. To me indeed Socrates seems to ask for quite fair things. For it is fitting for each one to express his own opinion. After Alcibiades, as I think, Critias said: O Prodicus and Hippias, Callias indeed seems to favor Protagoras vehemently. But Alcibiades is too contentious and persistent, whichever way he turns. But it is not fitting for us to favor one more than the other: either Socrates or Protagoras: but commonly to ask both: lest after they have begun, they stop in the middle of the dispute. When he had said these things, Prodicus said, you speak rightly, Critias: for it is fitting that those who are present at these disputes should be common listeners of both speakers: but by no means equal. <margin>The difference between common and equal listeners.</margin> Nor indeed is this and that the same thing. For it is fitting to hear both commonly: but not to attribute equally to both. To the wiser indeed more: but to the more unskilled less. Indeed, O Protagoras and Socrates, I think you ought to concede something to each other: and about these things which shall be said, to doubt together indeed: but by no means to contend. Friends doubt with friends on account of goodwill. But adversaries and enemies contend together. And so our dispute would proceed best. For you, if you were disputing, would thus be most approved by us listeners: I would not say praised. <margin>The difference between approving and praising.</margin> Both are approved by the judgment of the listeners' mind itself without deception: they praise with words, often extolling someone with a lie contrary to their opinion. Likewise we listeners would thus be affected most by joy, not by pleasure. <margin>The difference between rejoicing and taking pleasure.</margin> He is affected by joy who is delighted by the intelligence itself in learning and contemplating. He is drenched in pleasure who, while he eats or enjoys some other delight, is delighted by the sense of the body itself. When Prodicus had said these things, most of those present agreed. Then the wise Hippias began to speak thus. I think, O men present, that you are all kinsmen, relatives, and fellow citizens to each other by nature, not by law. For like is kinsman to like by nature. But law, the tyrant of men, compels many things contrary to nature. It would be shameful therefore if we, who understand the nature of things, and are the wisest of all the Greeks, after we have come together for the purpose of disputing about this very thing in this city, the citadel of all Greek wisdom, and are gathered in these most ample and most sumptuous houses of all the Athenians, should show nothing worthy of such great amplitude: but bickering in the manner of vile little men, should disagree with each other. I indeed exhort and beseech you, O Socrates and Protagoras, that you should willingly come together under us as if under arbiters: who will lead you back to the middle. Neither should you, O Socrates, cut back the amplitude of speech to the quick: and observe that "brevity of speech" of yours, so to speak, perfectly to the fingernail <note>A Latin idiom meaning "to the highest degree of precision"</note>. Loosen the rudders for the speeches for a little while, I pray, so that they may appear more magnificent and more splendid. I pray moreover to Protagoras, that he should not, with ropes entirely taut and sails inflated, having abandoned the helm, glide straight into the deep sea of speeches, from where land is nowhere seen: but both of you together strive so that you observe moderation according to your strengths. Do, I beg, what I advise: and so that you may keep it more entirely, choose some staff-bearer as president and judge: who may set a limit to the words and observe each speaker. These things pleased those present: and all praised them. But Callias exhorted me to the same: and they asked me to choose an arbiter. But I said, it is not fitting to put a judge over this dispute. For if the judge is more unskilled than us: it will be unjust that someone inferior should preside over his betters. But if he is similar: again it will not be done rightly. For one similar to us will do similar things. Wherefore he will be superfluous. But to choose anyone superior to us is truly impossible, as I think: since another wiser than Protagoras cannot be chosen. But if you choose someone in no way more learned, yet you bring him forward, this will be given as a disgrace to Protagoras, that you have prescribed an arbiter for him as if for one ignorant and ignoble. But it makes no difference to me. However, so that we may proceed to dispute as you desire, it seems to me it should be done thus. If Protagoras does not wish to answer, let him at least question: and I will answer and will try to show him in what way one ought to answer another in my judgment. After I have given an answer to him for any of his questioning, let him in turn submit a similar speech to me. If by chance he seems to shuffle, I and you together will entreat him, just as you now entreat me, not to dissolve the assembly. Nor indeed is there need to propose one censor for the sake of this. For you all will judge together. All agreed that it should be done so. But Protagoras, having looked on, seemed to descend to these terms. At last he was compelled to concede in—

# PROTAGORAS OR THE SOPHISTS.
## FOLIO XCVI.

<margin>Protagoras begins to question Socrates about poetry.</margin>
He said he would be the one to ask questions, and after he had questioned enough, he would respond briefly. Thus, he began to question in this manner: "I believe, O Socrates, that the most important part of education consists in this: that one becomes skilled in poems. This means being able to understand the sayings of the poets—namely, which are correctly composed and which are not—and knowing how to distinguish between them, and when questioned, to give an account of them. And now, perhaps someone will ask about that which we are both investigating together: namely, about virtue. But there will be this difference: that the subject will be transferred to poems. For Simonides says to Scopas, the son of Creon the Thessalian: 'It is difficult for a man to become truly good, fashioned <term>tetragonum</term> <note>original: "tetragonum" - meaning four-square or perfectly balanced</note>—that is, rectangular—in hands, feet, and mind, without reproach.' Do you hold these poems in your memory, or do you wish for me to recite them?" 

SOCRATES: "There is no need. For I hold them in mind, and I have given diligent care to these poems." 

PROTAGORAS: "You speak well. Does it seem to you that Simonides spoke well and correctly, or not?" 

SOCRATES: "Indeed, most excellently." 

PROTAGORAS: "Does a poet seem to speak correctly if he contradicts himself?" 

SOCRATES: "Not at all." 

PROTAGORAS: "Pay attention then more diligently." 

SOCRATES: "We are paying enough attention, my good man." 

PROTAGORAS: "In the same poems he says later: that the opinion of Pittacus, though he was a wise man, seems discordant to him, where he says: 'It is difficult to *remain* good.' Do you see that this same Simonides said both this and the former?" 

SOCRATES: "I do." 

PROTAGORAS: "Does he not then put forward later the same thing he did before? The same, I say, as it seems to me." And at the same time, fearing lest he should add anything further, I asked whether it did not seem so to him as well. "Do you ask," he said, "whether I think he is consistent with himself, he who said both these things? First he proposed that it is truly difficult for a man to *become* good; but a little later, as if having forgotten himself, he rebukes Pittacus for saying the same thing as he—namely, that it is difficult for a man to *remain* good—rejecting the words of one who had said the same thing? Truly, when he accuses Pittacus, the author of the same opinion, he condemns himself. Therefore, either the former or the latter statement is not correct."

At these words, many of the listeners shouted out and praised Protagoras. But I, at first, as if struck by a robust boxer, staggered with eyes darkened by dizziness. For both his voice and the shouting of the others had utterly overwhelmed me. Then, to confess the truth to you frankly, in order to gain a delay to investigate the poet's meaning, I turned to Prodicus and said: "Simonides was your fellow citizen, O Prodicus. Therefore, it is in your interest to bring him aid. I seem to be calling upon you just as Homer says the Scamander, when beset by Achilles, called upon the Simois: 'O dear brother, let us both together restrain this force.' In no different way do I now summon you, lest Protagoras conquer our Simonides. Your <term>musical</term> <note>In this context, "musical" refers to the art of the Muses, including grammar and the precise use of language.</note> skill is surely needed for the correction of Simonides' words, by which you distinguish 'to will' and 'to desire,' and many other excellent things you were just saying. And now, see if you see the same as I; for Simonides does not seem to contradict himself in his speaking. You, O Prodicus, express your opinion first: does 'to become' and 'to be' seem the same to you, or different?" 

"Different," said Prodicus. 

"Did not Simonides first reveal his mind," I said, "that it is difficult for a man to *become* truly good?" 

"You speak the truth," said Prodicus. 

"But he disapproves of Pittacus, not as Protagoras thinks, for saying the same thing, but something else. For Pittacus did not say it is difficult for a man to *become* good, as Simonides did, but to *remain* good. Now, 'to be' and 'to become' are not the same, O Protagoras, as this Prodicus here thinks. And if 'to be' is not the same as 'to become,' Simonides by no means sets down things contrary to himself. And perhaps this Prodicus and many others would say, according to Hesiod, that it is difficult to *be made* good. For he says the gods placed sweat before virtue. But when the summit is reached, it is easy, though it was difficult to acquire." 

Prodicus, when he had heard these things, praised me. But Protagoras said, "That correction of yours, O Socrates, is more absurd than what you are correcting." 

Then I said, "O Protagoras, it has gone badly for me, it seems; I am a ridiculous doctor, who, while I strive to cure, increase the disease." 

PROTAGORAS: "Yet that is how the matter stands." 

SOCRATES: "By what reasoning?" 

PROTAGORAS: "That poet would have been too ignorant if he had valued virtue so little as to think its possession easy, when it is the most difficult of all things, as it seems to all men." 

SOCRATES: "How opportunely this Prodicus has intervened in our discourse! Truly, O Protagoras, the wisdom of Prodicus seems divine, having long ago either drawn its origin from Simonides or even arisen from those more ancient; but you, though you are skilled in many other things, appear unskilled in this. I, however, have experience of it, having been a disciple of this Prodicus. And yet at present, you do not seem to me to notice sufficiently that perhaps Simonides did not take the word 'difficult' as you yourself now take it; for Prodicus constantly warns me that it is to be understood as something 'evil' and 'grievous.' For whenever I speak as if praising another or you, saying 'Protagoras is a wise and wealthy man'—that is, powerful and 'heavy'—he immediately corrects me for saying good things are 'heavy' <note>original: "grave" - meaning heavy, serious, or grievous</note>, since 'heavy' is an evil. For no one speaks so as to say 'heavy riches,' 'heavy peace,' or 'heavy health.' Rather, 'heavy disease,' 'heavy war,' or 'heavy poverty,' as if 'heavy' were a burdensome evil. Perhaps, therefore, the Chians and Simonides take 'difficult' itself either as 'evil' or something else which you do not understand. Therefore, let us inquire of Prodicus. For it is most fitting to ask him about the writings of Simonides. What, O Prodicus, did Simonides wish to be understood by the name 'difficult' itself?" 

PRODICUS: "Evil, certainly." 

SOCRATES: "For this reason, I believe, Prodicus, he rebuked Pittacus for saying it is 'difficult' to remain good, as if he had said it is 'evil' to remain good." 

PRODICUS: "And what else do you think, O Socrates, Simonides intended but to censure Pittacus, because he did not know how to distinguish names correctly, being a Lesbian and brought up in a barbarian tongue?" 

SOCRATES: "Do you hear, O Protagoras, what Prodicus says here? What do you say to this?" 

PROTAGORAS: "It is very far from being so, Prodicus. For I certainly know that Simonides, by the name 'difficult,' intended that which others are also accustomed to signify: not 'evil.'"

For that Simonides does not want "difficult" to be understood as "evil" is proven by what follows; for he adds that only a god enjoys this privilege. Nor indeed, if he wanted it to be an evil to remain good, would he add a little later that only a god is capable of this, and attribute that gift to God alone. Prodicus would clearly be destroying the man <note>i.e., Simonides' reputation</note> and would by no means say that Simonides was a Chian <note>Prodicus was from Ceos, as was Simonides; Socrates is playfully suggesting Prodicus wouldn't disown his countryman</note>. But as for what I think Simonides finally meant in these verses, I shall reveal it to you, if you wish to make a trial of me to see how I am affected toward poetry. If, however, you prefer, I shall listen to you. When Protagoras had heard this, he said, "As you please, O Socrates." But Prodicus and Hippias and all the others urged me to act in this way. I said: I will try to explain to you what I think about these verses. The oldest and greatest study of wisdom among the Greeks exists in Crete and Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>. And more sophists <note>term: Sophist (a paid teacher of philosophy and rhetoric in Ancient Greece)</note> are found there than anywhere else; but they disguise it and pretend to be ignorant, so that they are not discovered to surpass the rest of the Greeks in wisdom—like those whom Protagoras called sophists above—but rather so that they appear to excel others in military affairs and courage. For they suspect that if their mental disposition were revealed, everyone else would pursue the same study. Therefore they hide it, and deceive the inhabitants who imitate the Lacedaemonians by the cropping of their ears, the wrapping of thongs <note>referring to athletic training gear</note>, physical exercises, and short cloaks, as if the Lacedaemonians surpassed the rest of the Greeks in such things. But the Lacedaemonians, whenever they wish to meet more freely with their sophists, are annoyed by the familiarity of foreigners and gather in secret; having excluded all strangers, they philosophize together with the sophists. Furthermore, both they and the Cretans prohibit young men from visiting other cities, lest they might unlearn elsewhere what they are taught among them. In these states there are found not only men outstanding in learning, but also women. That I speak the truth, and that the Lacedaemonians are best educated for philosophy and discourse, can be seen most clearly from this: if anyone talks with even the lowliest of the Lacedaemonians, he will find him appearing mostly crude in his words at first. Then, wherever the opportunity of the matter requires, like a powerful javelin-thrower, he hurls a short and twisted word of no small weight, so that the one speaking with him thinks himself no different from a child. That the virtue of the Lacedaemonians consists more in wisdom than in the study of exercise is understood by some men of our age, and many noticed the same long ago, knowing that to be able to utter such words is the duty of a perfectly learned man. From their number was Thales of Miletus, Pittacus of Mitylene, Bias of Priene, our Solon, Cleobulus of Lindus, and Myson of Chenae. The seventh of these was said to be Chilo the Lacedaemonian. All these were emulators and studious disciples of Lacedaemonian wisdom. We find their wisdom to be of such a kind: short words worthy of being remembered by everyone. These men, having formed a council by common consent, dedicated these first-fruits of wisdom to the temple of Delphic Apollo; which, inscribed on the temple, are celebrated by all: *Know thyself* and *Nothing in excess*. I mention these things for this reason: to make it clear that this was the form of ancient philosophy—a certain Lacedaemonian "brevity of speech," if I may call it that. And indeed, this specific saying of Pittacus was circulated and celebrated by the wise: *It is difficult to remain good*. Simonides, therefore, since he desired the glory of wisdom, knew that if he could refute and overcome that proverb as if it were a famous competitor, he himself would be held illustrious by everyone. For this reason he composed those verses, lying in wait for him to disturb his words, as I think. Let us all discuss these together to see whether I speak the truth. First, indeed, those earlier verses would indicate an insane man if, wanting to say it is difficult for a man to *become* good, he then inserted the particle "indeed." For this seems to be inserted for no reason, unless one thinks Simonides is speaking in opposition to the words of Pittacus; and when the latter says it is difficult to *remain* good, Simonides objects to this: "It is not so, O Pittacus. Rather, it is difficult *indeed* for a man to become good"—and truly, not "really" good. He does not say "really" because some are truly good and others are good indeed but not truly. This would certainly seem absurd and unworthy of Simonides. But one must place that which is said "truly" as an intensification in the words, by supplying Pittacus's words as if we were imagining Pittacus himself saying: "O men, it is difficult to remain good," and Simonides answering: "O Pittacus, you speak very little truth. For not to *be*, but to *become* a good man, square in hands and feet and mind, fashioned without any blame, is truly difficult." Thus the "indeed" seems inserted against the speech, and the "truly" placed at the end for a reason. And indeed, all that follows testifies to this, because it is said in this manner. Many things besides exist which, correctly arranged in these verses, we can show one by one. For they are skillfully and accurately composed. But the speech would be too long. Therefore, the form and plan of this poet must be explained summarily. He intends in every word to refute the words of Pittacus. For he says a little later almost in this manner: that to become a good man is truly difficult, yet possible for a time. But having become good, to persevere in that habit and to *be* good as you say, O Pittacus, is impossible and not human; but God alone enjoys this gift. For it is impossible for a man to remain so good that he does not slip again, whom unexpected chance breaks down. For what kind of unexpected accident mostly sinks the steering of a ship? Not an unskilled man, for he is always sinking, and in a way no one casts down one who is already lying on the ground; but someone sometimes fails one who is standing so as to force him to lie down, but by no means one already lying down. Thus an unexpected accident sometimes circumvented a skillful and wise man. Truly, it never happens to one who has no care. And sometimes a huge, unforeseen force of a storm overcomes a pilot; and to a farmer...

# PROTAGORAS OR THE SOPHISTS

...the intemperance of the seasons: and similar things happen to a doctor. Thus, they seem to have been improvident at that time. For a good man could become bad; as another poet testifies, saying: *A good man is at one time base, at another time good.* <note>Socrates is likely quoting or paraphrasing a lost lyric fragment to support his argument that virtue is not a permanent state.</note> But as for a bad man, it is not possible for him to *become* bad. For it is necessary that he always *be* so. Therefore, whenever an unexpected misfortune strikes a provident, wise, and good man, he is made bad. But you, O Pittacus, say that it is difficult to *remain* good. The matter, however, stands thus: to *become* good is possible, though difficult; but to *remain* good is utterly impossible. For anyone acting well is good; conversely, one acting poorly is bad. Now, what is a "good action" regarding letters? Or what action makes a man good at them? It is clear that it is the perception <note>or learning</note> of them. Likewise, what good action makes a good doctor? Clearly, the skill of curing diseases. He who cures well is a good doctor; he who cures poorly is a bad one. Who, then, ever becomes a bad doctor? Certainly he who first possesses the quality of being a doctor, and then of being a good doctor. For this man can at some point become a bad doctor. But we, being ignorant of the medical art, would never become either doctors or craftsmen by acting poorly, or anything of that sort. And he who is not a doctor cannot be one who has operated poorly, nor can he be a bad doctor. In the same way, a good man can sometimes become bad, either because of time, or labor, or disease, or some other accident. Furthermore, this is the only truly "base action": to be deprived of knowledge. A bad man, however, would never become bad: for he always is so. And if he were to become bad, it would be necessary for him to have been made good beforehand. Therefore, those verses tend toward this: to affirm that it is impossible for a man to persevere as always good; but to become good, and then to become bad again, is possible. Moreover, those whom the gods love are the best for the longest time. All these things, therefore, are brought against Pittacus, which the following lines reveal more clearly. For this reason, he says: *Never shall I, seeking what cannot be, hope in vain for some man to live perpetually without reproach among those of us who eat the fruits of the earth.* Then he says: *I proclaim to you what I have discovered,* and the rest that follows. Thus, throughout the poem, he vehemently inveighs against the words of Pittacus. *But I praise and willingly love everyone who commits nothing shameful. Against necessity, not even the gods themselves fight.* This is the same thing said again. For Simonides was not so ignorant of things as to say he praised him who commits nothing shameful *willingly*—as if there were some who act poorly willingly! I believe, indeed, that no wise man thinks there is any human being who errs of his own accord, or commits evil and shameful acts willingly. For all wise men know that those who commit evil and shameful things do so against their will. <note>This reflects the famous Socratic paradox: "No one does evil knowingly."</note> And yet Simonides by no means says he praises him who does not commit crimes willingly; rather, he predicates that word "willingly" of himself. For he thought that a noble and good man often forces himself to become the friend and praiser of someone, and continues to love and praise them. For instance, if he should happen to have peevish and unjust parents, or a country, or something of that sort. He judged that wicked men are accustomed to inveighing gladly against the errors of their parents and country, and to divulge them everywhere to everyone, so that no one might dare to rebuke them for neglecting their parents and country. Therefore, they also disparage their parents and country and agitate them with voluntary hatreds and enmities beyond necessity. But good men rather hide such things and compel themselves to praise; and if they are indignant with their parents or country for some just cause, they console themselves and reconcile themselves to their own, so that even if they do not do so with a willing mind, they nevertheless praise and love them. I believe Simonides himself often applied himself to praising and extolling some tyrant or other such person, not from the conviction of his own mind, but unwillingly. These things, therefore, he refers to Pittacus. *I, indeed, O Pittacus, do not find fault with you because I am a detractor by nature; since even he satisfies me who is not excessively bad or lazy. A healthy man who knows what is right will help a just city. Nor will I myself disparage him; for I am not fond of disparaging. For the lineage of fools is infinite.* Therefore, if anyone proceeds to disparage them, he will grow weary. *Furthermore, all things are honorable in which shameful things are not mixed.* He does not say this as if he were saying "all things are white in which no black is mixed"—for that would be ridiculous—but as if to say he will accept middle things and not disparage them. *I do not seek,* he says, *a man entirely beyond reproach among those who everywhere eat the fruits of the earth. Then I announce to you what I have discovered: namely, that for this reason I shall praise no one. But he who holds the middle ground is sufficient for me, provided he does nothing shameful. For I love and praise all such men.* Here he certainly used the tongue of the Mityleneans <note>original: "Mitylenæorum lingua," referring to the Aeolic dialect of Pittacus</note> as if speaking against Pittacus, saying: *But I praise and love everyone willingly.* Here it is necessary to take the word "willingly" separately from what follows, and then say: *whoever commits nothing shameful.* For there are some whom I do not praise and love willingly. Because if you, my Pittacus, had spoken even moderately consistent and true things, I would never have rebuked you. But now, since you bring forth false things that appear true to many, and that most greatly and in the greatest matters, I am forced to rebuke you. This, O Prodicus and Protagoras, seems to me to have been the mind of Simonides himself in these verses.

Then Hippias said, "O Socrates, you seem to have explained these verses well. I also have an account suited to them, which I will show you if you wish." "On the contrary," said Alcibiades, "but later. For now it is proper to finish what was agreed upon between Socrates and Protagoras. And if Protagoras wishes to question further, Socrates ought to respond. But if Protagoras wishes to respond, Socrates should question." "But," I said, "I concede to Protagoras whichever of these will be more pleasing to him; if it pleases him, let us pass over the verses. But those things which I first asked of you, Protagoras, I would gladly finish together with you. For it seems to me that a dispute about poetic matters is very similar to the banquets of unskillful and common men. Who, because of their ignorance, are unable to converse with one another in their own voices and their own speeches, and so, having paid a fee, they introduce flute-girls; and with an alien voice—that is, the blast of flutes—the banquet...

</margin>
