->they pass the time. But where good, distinguished, and learned men gather, you will see neither flute-girls, nor dancing-girls, nor singing-girls; instead, they celebrate the banquet with their own voices, setting aside these trifles and jests, and they converse modestly with alternating questions and answers, even if they have drunk wine in abundance. In the same way, if such men as many proclaim us to be meet for discussions of this kind, they have no need for a foreign voice or the words of poets—whom one cannot question about what they write, and when people bring their testimonies into the midst of the debate, some interpret the poet as feeling one thing and some another; they can neither prove their point nor resolve the matter they are discussing. Therefore, wise men dismiss such conversations; they speak among themselves and, in turn, put their own intellect to the test. I believe you and I ought now to imitate such debaters: setting the poets aside, we should discuss the matter itself through our own reasoning, making a trial of both our intellect and the truth.<-

<margin>Who the true debaters are.</margin>

If, therefore, you desire to inquire further, I am ready to answer you; but if you prefer otherwise, offer yourself to me and help to finish what we left interrupted. When I had brought forward these and other such points, Protagoras by no means revealed what he chose as the best course of action. Then Alcibiades, turning to Callias, said: "O Callias, does it seem to you that Protagoras is acting rightly now, since he refuses to declare whether it pleases him to give an account or not? It certainly does not seem so to me. Let him either debate now, or say he does not wish to debate, so that we may record this of him. Then Socrates may converse with anyone else, or anyone else who wishes may converse with another." Protagoras then, as it seemed to me, moved by shame because of Alcibiades' speech and the prayers of Callias and the others present, finally and with difficulty descended to the debate; he bade Socrates himself to ask the questions, promising that he would answer. "O Protagoras," I said, "do not think I am debating with you for any other reason than that I wish to discuss the things I doubt everywhere. For I believe that saying of Homer was not said without cause: *When two go together, one understands more than the other.* <note>original: "Si duo simul congrediantur..." A reference to the Iliad, Book 10, often cited to justify collaborative inquiry.</note> For we are all more sagacious at investigating any work, word, or sense. If someone thinks of something alone, he immediately searches everywhere for someone to communicate it to and approve it, until he finds them. For this reason, I now dispute more willingly with you than with anyone else, thinking that you will best judge all things: both concerning all other matters that pertain to the judgment of an honest man, and especially concerning those things which I myself was seeking—namely, virtue. For whom could I hope would do this better than you? Indeed, most others are honest themselves, but they cannot make others so. You, however, not only consider yourself endowed with virtue, but you also promise to adorn other men with the same. And you are so confident in your talent that, while all others conceal it, you alone profess this art, and you openly proclaim yourself a Sophist <term>Sophist: a professional teacher of rhetoric and virtue in Ancient Greece</term> before all the Greeks as if by a public herald: a master of doctrine and morals; and you are the first to demand a fee for that craft. What, then, prevents you from being called before others to judge these matters, to be questioned, and to have all things shared with you? Nothing at all prevents it. And yet I myself now desire that those things about which I first asked be partly brought back to my mind by you, and partly discussed by our common judgment. The question was such, I believe: whether wisdom, temperance, fortitude, justice, and holiness are five names for the same thing, or whether there underlies each of these names a certain proper essence and a thing having its own power, so that one is not like the other. You said then that these names were by no means for one thing, but that individual names were applied to individual things. Furthermore, that all these are parts of virtue, not at all like the parts of gold which are similar to each other and the whole, but like the parts of a face, which are mutually dissimilar to each other and the whole, and distinguished by their own powers. If you confirm these things again as above, express it. If you feel otherwise, distinguish this. Indeed, I will not hold anything against you in our talk if you say something different now. For I would not wonder if you said those things then for the sake of testing Socrates." PROTAGORAS: "I say that all these are parts of virtue, of which four are reasonably similar to each other. Fortitude <note>or Courage</note>, however, differs far from the others. That I speak the truth, you will know in this way: you will find some men who are most unjust, most profane, most intemperate, and most ignorant, who nevertheless excel others in fortitude." SOCRATES: "Pay attention, please; we must consider what you say. Do you call the brave 'daring,' or something else?" PROTAGORAS: "Indeed, even those who rush headlong into things from which most are deterred." SOCRATES: "Come then; do you assert that virtue is something honorable and beautiful, and do you teach it as something beautiful?" PROTAGORAS: "The most beautiful indeed, unless I am insane." SOCRATES: "Is part of it base and part beautiful? Or is it beautiful as a whole?" PROTAGORAS: "The whole is as beautiful as can be." SOCRATES: "Do you know those who boldly dive into wells?" PROTAGORAS: "Certainly. Divers." SOCRATES: "Is it because they know how to dive, or for some other reason?" PROTAGORAS: "Because they know how to dive." SOCRATES: "Who are most daring in fighting from horses? Those who carry shields, or those unskilled in equestrian industry?" PROTAGORAS: "Horsemen." SOCRATES: "Who fight boldly with shields? Shield-bearers, or others?" PROTAGORAS: "Those indeed—and in all other things if you ask this—those who know are more daring than those who do not; and the same men, after they have learned, are more daring than when they were ignorant." SOCRATES: "Have you ever seen any who are ignorant of all these things, yet daring toward them all?" PROTAGORAS: "I have indeed, and they are the most daring." SOCRATES: "Are those daring ones brave?" PROTAGORAS: "Fortitude would be something base, since those daring ones are madmen." SOCRATES: "Did you not say the brave are the daring themselves?" PROTAGORAS: "I said it indeed, and I say it." SOCRATES: "Do not those who are daring in this way appear not brave at all, but mad? And above, again, the wisest appeared to us as the most daring; and because they are the most daring, therefore also the bravest; and so, according to sound reason, would not wisdom itself be fortitude?" PROTAGORAS: "You do not well remember, O Socrates, what I said above and answered to you."

# PROTAGORAS OR THE SOPHISTS. FOLIO XCVIII.
## n.ii.

Indeed, when I asked you whether brave men were daring, I agreed. But whether daring men were brave, you did not ask. For if you had asked then, I would certainly have answered "not all." You could never have shown that I conceded that brave men are not daring, because I would not have conceded that correctly. Furthermore, you show that knowledgeable men are more daring than the ignorant, both compared to themselves and to others; and for that reason, you think that wisdom and courage are the same. Proceeding by the same logic, you would also consider strength to be wisdom. For if you had asked me in a similar way whether robust men are powerful, I would certainly have asserted it. Then, if you asked whether those skilled in wrestling are more powerful for competing than the ignorant, and whether they themselves are more powerful after they have learned than when they were ignorant, I would have admitted this again. With me confessing these things, it would have been permitted for you, using the same arguments, to say that according to my confession, strength exists as wisdom. I, however, nowhere at present confess that powerful men are robust. Yet I do say that robust men are powerful. I do not think that strength and power are the same. For power can come both from knowledge, and from madness, and from anger. Strength, however, proceeds only from nature and the proper nourishment of bodies. Similarly, in those other matters, one should by no means think that courage and daring are the same. Wherefore it happens that brave men are indeed daring, but not all daring men are brave. For daring is given to men by art <note>original: "ab arte"; here meaning skill or technical training</note>, by anger, and by madness, just as we said of power. But courage comes from nature and the proper education of souls.

**SOCRATES:** Do you say, O Protagoras, that some men live well and others live badly?
**PROTAGORAS:** I do indeed.
**SOCRATES:** Does a man seem to you to live well if he lives with distress and pain?
**PROTAGORAS:** Not at all.
**SOCRATES:** But if someone has lived pleasantly until the end of life, should he be said to have lived well?
**PROTAGORAS:** Certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, to live pleasantly is good, and to live distressfully is bad.
**PROTAGORAS:** Provided he was delighted by honorable things.
**SOCRATES:** Do you yourself, Protagoras, call certain pleasant things "evil" and certain sad things "good," as many others do? I ask it this way: insofar as they are pleasant, are they not to that extent good? (Unless something else results from them). And again, similarly, are sad things not evil simply because they are sad?
**PROTAGORAS:** I do not know, Socrates, whether it is proper for me to answer as simply as you ask—that all pleasant things are good and all sad things are evil. But it seems safer to me, not only for the present question but also for the whole reasoning of my life, to answer that there are some pleasant things that are not good, and some sad things that are not evil; and again, there are neutral things which are neither good nor evil.
**SOCRATES:** Do you call "pleasant" those things which either participate in pleasure or produce pleasure?
**PROTAGORAS:** Exactly.
**SOCRATES:** I ask this, then: whether insofar as they are pleasant, they are not good. That is, whether pleasure itself is not a good.
**PROTAGORAS:** As you yourself always say, Socrates, let us consider this; and if this consideration seems to lead to the point, and the pleasant and the good appear to be the same, we shall concede it. If not, then we shall raise our doubts.
**SOCRATES:** Do you wish to be the leader of the discussion, or do you bid me to lead?
**PROTAGORAS:** It is fair that you be the leader. For you began.
**SOCRATES:** Perhaps in this way what we seek will become clear: just as if someone, wanting to judge a man's health or some other physical condition and function, having looked at his face and the extremities of his hands, might add: "Come now, bare your chest and back for me, so that I may inspect more clearly." So now I require the same for this judgment. For since I have recognized your disposition toward the good and pleasure from your words, it is necessary for me to say something like this: Come, Protagoras, and open your mind on this: what do you think about knowledge <term>scientia: the Latin translation of the Greek 'episteme', referring to certain knowledge or science</term>? Does the same thing please you as pleases others, or something else? Most people truly judge this about knowledge: that it is neither something robust, nor does it lead, nor does it even rule. For they do not think of it as a leader or a prince; rather, they often think that when knowledge is present in a man, it does not rule him, but something else does—sometimes anger, sometimes pleasure, sometimes pain, sometimes love, and often fear. And so they think of knowledge as if it were a certain slave <note>original: "mancipio"; a piece of property or a slave</note> dragged about by all other things. Do you also feel the same? Or do you rather think knowledge is something noble and the ruler of man, so that if someone discerns good and evil, he would never be led by anything else to do other than what knowledge commands, but that prudence <term>prudentia: practical wisdom or foresight</term> is a sufficient helper and protection for a man?
**PROTAGORAS:** It seems to me as you say, O Socrates. For if it is shameful for any man to deny that wisdom and knowledge are the most powerful of all human things, it would certainly be most shameful for me.
**SOCRATES:** You speak excellently and truly. But do you know that many people do not believe you and me? They say, moreover, that many who are conscious of what is good, when it is permitted to do good things, are unwilling to do them, but do other things. And whenever I have asked what the cause of this is, they say that men do these things because they are overcome by pleasure, or pain, or some other of those things we mentioned above.
**PROTAGORAS:** There are also many other things, O Socrates, in which men err.
**SOCRATES:** Come then, try with me to persuade men and teach them what this "passion" is, which they say is being "overcome by pleasures," and for this reason they do not do the good they know. For perhaps if we told them they were erring, they would immediately object: "O Protagoras and Socrates, if this passion is not being conquered by pleasures, what else is it? What do you say it is? Explain it."
**PROTAGORAS:** Why should we care about the opinion of the many, who speak however it happens?
**SOCRATES:** I think this will help us find how courage relates to the other parts of virtue. Therefore, if you think we should stand by our previous agreement that I should lead—because I think what we seek can best be found that way—then follow. If not, and you prefer to be dismissed, I will let it go.
**PROTAGORAS:** You speak rightly; proceed then as you began.
**SOCRATES:** If they asked us again: "What is this thing you say we called 'being conquered by pleasures'?" I would say to them: Listen now; Protagoras and I will try to declare this to you. Do you not say this happens just as it often occurs that men, enticed and conquered by the pleasure of food, drink, and sex, take those things up even if they know they are evil? They would agree. Then we would say: Evil...

# BOOK SEVENTEEN

But why indeed do you say those things? Is it because they provide this present pleasure and soothe with sweetness? Or because in the future they bring about diseases, poverty, and many other things of this kind? Or even if they bring nothing of the sort in the future, are they nonetheless evil for the reason that they delight the person experiencing them? Do we think, O Protagoras, that they would answer otherwise than that they are not evil because of the present bringing of pleasure itself, but because of the diseases and other things that follow? PROTAGORAS: The common people would answer thus. SOCRATES: Is it not true that while they bring diseases, they bring pains; and while they bring poverty, they bring pain? They would agree, I think. PROTAGORAS: Certainly indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, O men, these things appear evil to you for no other reason, as I and Protagoras think, than that they end in pains and deprive one of other pleasures. They would confess it. PROTAGORAS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: If, on the other hand, I were to ask again: O men, what good things do you in turn admit to be distressing? Do you not speak of things such as physical exercises, the labors of military service, and the treatments of doctors—which are done either by cutting <note>surgery</note>, or by burning <note>cautery</note>, or by drugs, or by fasting—do you call these things good, but troublesome? They would agree. PROTAGORAS: This too. SOCRATES: Do you call these things good because they are accomplished with present pains and tortures? Or rather for the reason that in the future, health and a good condition of the body, the safety of the fatherland, power, and riches follow from them? For that very reason they would say so, I suppose. PROTAGORAS: I also judge it so. SOCRATES: Are these things good for any other reason than that they end in pleasures and drive away troubles? Can you assign any other end, looking toward which you call these things good, than pleasures and pains? We cannot, I think, they would answer. PROTAGORAS: So indeed I think. SOCRATES: Do you not follow pleasure as a good and flee pain as an evil? They would grant it. PROTAGORAS: Surely. SOCRATES: Therefore you consider this to be evil, namely pain, and pleasure to be good, since you then say that even delight itself is surely evil when it deprives one of greater pleasures than it provides, or when it brings more vehement pains than the pleasures it contains. For if you called delight itself evil for some other reason, looking toward another end, you would also be able to show it to us. But you will by no means be able to. PROTAGORAS: It does not seem possible to me either. SOCRATES: Similarly, you also say that pain itself is good only then, when it drives away greater pains than it brings, or induces pleasures more vehement than the troubles; since if you judged pain to be good looking toward another end, you would be able to reveal it to us, but you will not be able to. PROTAGORAS: You speak the truth, O Socrates. SOCRATES: If you were to ask me in return, O men: "Why do you speak so much about this everywhere?"—forgive me, I would answer first. For first, it is not easily demonstrated what this is that you say: "to be overcome by pleasures." Secondly, all demonstrations consist in this very thing. And even now it is permitted to retract, if in any way you have something else that you call good other than pleasure, and something else evil other than pain. Or is it sufficient for you to lead a life pleasantly without sadness? If it is sufficient, and you cannot say there is any other good or evil that does not tend toward these, hear what follows. I say indeed, these things being so, your speech is ridiculous when you say that a man, knowing evil things to be evil, nonetheless does them—when it is permitted not to do them—because he is drawn and struck down by pleasures. And again, when you say a man conscious of good things is unwilling to act, being held back by present pleasure. That these things are ridiculous will be clear, unless we use many names: "pleasant," "sad," "good," and "evil." But after these two have appeared to be the same, let us call them by two names: first indeed "good" and "evil," and afterward "pleasant" and "sad." These being established, let us say: a man knowing evil things to be evil, nonetheless does them. If someone then asks why, we shall answer: "Because he was overcome." By what? he will ask. It will not be permitted for us to say further "overcome by pleasure," for it has taken another name, "good," in place of pleasure. Therefore we shall answer him: "overcome by the good." Then, if he who asks us happens to be an insulting man, he will laugh at us and say: "How absurd is what you say! If someone does evil things, knowing they are evil, when he ought not to do them, because he is overcome by good things—are these good things worthy to overcome the evil, or not worthy?" We shall say: "Not worthy"; for otherwise he whom we say was overcome by pleasures would not have erred. To this he will say: "Why are the good things unworthy to overcome the evil, or the evil to overcome the good? Is it for any other reason than when these are larger and those smaller? Or these more numerous and those fewer?" We shall have no other cause besides this. He will add: "It is clear now that 'to be overcome' means this: to receive greater evils in place of small goods." Let these things be so. Let us therefore change these names and take for the same things "pleasant" and "sad," saying: we said then that a man does evil things; let us say now he does "sad" things, knowing they are sad, being overcome by "pleasant" things—such, namely, that they are unworthy of victory. What other unworthiness is there in pleasure compared to pain than the excess or defect between them? That is, when these become larger or smaller than each other, or more numerous and fewer, or more vehement and more relaxed. If someone should say: "But Socrates, present pleasure differs much from future pleasure and trouble," I would say indeed: "Does it differ by anything other than pleasure and trouble?" Surely it cannot by anything else. But it is just as if a man skilled in weights, having collected the pleasant things and collected the sad things, were to place them on the scales, both those near at hand and those far off, and say which are more. For if you weigh pleasant things against pleasant things, the larger and more numerous are always to be chosen; but if you compare sad things with sad things, the fewer and smaller; if pleasant with sad, and the sad are exceeded by the pleasant—whether near to remote or remote to near—that choice must be made in which these are present: but if the pleasant are exceeded by the sad, not at all. Or is the matter otherwise, O men? I know indeed that they can bring nothing else. PROTAGORAS: I judge the same myself. SOCRATES: Since this is so, I will ask them in this manner: Do the same masses appear larger to your eyes when near, and smaller when far off? They will answer "Yes." And thick things and many things similarly; and equal voices appear louder <note>literally: "larger"</note> near at hand, but smaller far away. They will agree. If our acting well and our happiness consisted in this—that is, in preparing and taking up great masses...

<summary>Socrates argues that "being overcome by pleasure" is a logical absurdity if pleasure is equated with the good, suggesting instead that moral failure is a failure of measurement or "hedonic calculus." He posits that people choose immediate pleasure over future good only because they lack the skill to weigh long-term consequences against short-term gratification.</summary>

and in avoiding them, what would most especially be the salvation of our life? Would it be the art of measurement <note>Latin: *ars dimetiendi*, referring to the ability to calculate long-term pleasure vs. short-term pain</note>? Or the power of appearances? Indeed, this power of appearance would deceive us, and by confounding us with error, it would often force us to judge the same things differently at different times: and thus to choose and adopt actions, whether great or small, which we would later frequently repent. But the faculty of measurement would render this appearance null and would refute it; by revealing the truth, it would give peace to the soul remaining in the truth, and thus it would save our life. Would men agree that the art of measurement saves us, or some other? PROTAGORAS: This very one. SOCRATES: What further? If the salvation of our life consisted in the very choice of the even and the odd: when it was necessary that the greater be rightly chosen, and when the lesser, whether compared to itself or perhaps one thing to another, whether near or far: what would most especially save our life? Would it not be knowledge <note>Latin: *scientia*, translating the Greek *episteme*</note>? And certainly not just any measurement: since this is the art of excess and defect. Since, however, it concerns the ratio of even and odd, it is nothing other than the science of numbering. Would men grant this? Or not? PROTAGORAS: They would agree without controversy. SOCRATES: Since, then, the salvation of life has appeared to consist in the right choice of pleasure and pain, as it pertains to the more and the fewer, the greater and the lesser, the nearer and the more remote: is not the faculty of measurement first of all a consideration of excess, defect, and mutual equality? PROTAGORAS: It must be so. SOCRATES: Since it is a faculty of measurement, it must necessarily be an art and a science. PROTAGORAS: They will admit it. SOCRATES: What this science most especially is, we shall consider at another time. It suffices for the present that it is knowledge: insofar as it pertains to that answer which I and Protagoras were going to give to your question. This, if you remember, was the question. We indeed agreed that nothing is more powerful than knowledge: rather, wherever it is present, it always dominates pleasure and all other things. Then you objected that pleasure frequently dominates a man who has knowledge. Since we by no means granted this to you, you immediately asked us: "O Protagoras and Socrates, if this is not 'being overcome by pleasures,' but something else, declare to us what that thing is." If we had replied to you then and there that it is ignorance <note>Latin: *inscitia*</note>, you would have laughed at us immediately. But now, if you mock us, you will also mock yourselves. For you yourselves confessed a little while ago that those who fail in the choice of pleasures and pains wander through a defect of knowledge. And those things are indeed good and evil. Nor did you say it was a defect of knowledge only, but you added further, namely, a defect of the science of measurement. An action that errs without knowledge, as is not hidden from you, proceeds from ignorance. Wherefore, what is commonly called "being overcome by pleasures" is the extreme of ignorance. Which Protagoras here, and Prodicus, and Hippias, profess to cure as if they were physicians. You, however, because you think this is something other than ignorance, neither hand yourselves over nor your sons to be cured by these Sophists, the teachers of these matters, as if virtue could not be taught: but because you indulge too much in money, and do not offer a fee to these teachers, you fail both privately and publicly. This is plainly what we would have answered to the common people. But now I ask you also, O Prodicus and Hippias, together with Protagoras—for this discourse is common to you all—whether I seem to you to speak truly or falsely. It seemed to everyone that the things said above were very true. You grant therefore, I said, that what is pleasant is good, and what is sad is evil. But that distinction of names, which Prodicus here is accustomed to introduce, I reject, and I ask for his judgment. For whether you call it "pleasurable," or "delightful," or "joyful," or by whatever other name you might call it, most excellent Prodicus, answer me now regarding what I wish to know. Smiling, Prodicus assented, and the others likewise agreed. Then I said: what of this, O men? Are not all actions which tend toward living pleasantly and without trouble honorable and useful? And is not an honorable work both good and useful? They nodded. If therefore the pleasant itself is good, no one—either knowing or believing other things to be better than those he does, and which he is able to do—then does these things when he is able to do better. To say one is "overcome by passions" is nothing other than ignorance, and to "dominate passions" is wisdom. This pleased everyone. What then of ignorance? Do you not say it is something such as this: when someone is deceived by a false opinion concerning things of the greatest value? This also they granted. No one indeed willingly descends toward evils, or toward those things which he believes to be evil. Nor, as it seems, is it in the nature of man to wish to decline toward those things he judges evil in place of good things. And when he is forced to choose one of two evils, no one chooses the worse when it is permitted to choose that which is the lesser evil. All these things seemed to be ratified by all of us. What, I said, do you call fear and terror? Is it not what I say to you, Prodicus? I myself call it a certain expectation of evil, whether you call it fear or terror. It seemed to Protagoras and Hippias that fear and terror were this; but to Prodicus, it seemed that fear was this, but terror was not. That matters nothing, I said, O Prodicus: but consider this, if the things said above are true. Will anyone wish to proceed toward those things which he fears, while it is permitted to go toward those which he fears least? Or is it impossible according to what we have already granted? For what one fears, it is established that he thinks those things are evil: and no one willingly descends to and accepts those things which he believes to be evil. These things also pleased everyone. These things being thus established, O Prodicus and Hippias, I said, let Protagoras defend his first answer before you as if it were true—or rather, not the first one now. For he said at first: that of the five parts of virtue, none was such as the other, and each had its own power. I do not demand this now, but what he said afterward. For he said in the following parts that four parts of virtue were sufficiently close to one another, but one of them, namely courage <note>Latin: *fortitudo*</note>, differed greatly from the rest. He said this could be inferred from the fact that many men are found to be very courageous, who are nevertheless most unholy, most unjust, most intemperate, and most ignorant. From which he wished it to be clear that courage differs most of all from all other parts of virtue. At whose answer I was immediately and vehemently astonished; and much more so after I treated these things with you. Therefore I inquired of him whether the courageous are...

...called them bold. He even added "headlong" to that. Do you remember, Protagoras, that you answered this way? PRO. I remember. SO. Tell us, I pray, for what reason do you call "bold" men brave? Is it for those things which the fearful approach? PRO. No. SO. Therefore for other things? PRO. Certainly. SO. Do the fearful approach things to be dared? And the brave things to be feared? PRO. So it is said, Socrates. SO. You speak the truth. But I do not ask this: rather, why do you call the bold "brave"? Is it because they know things to be evil and destructive, or because they are not such? PRO. It was shown by your previous arguments that this is impossible. SO. And in this too you speak truly. Therefore, if this has been rightly demonstrated, no one approaches those things which he judges to be evil and destructive; since it was established that ignorance is what is called "being overcome by the passions." <note>original: "ab affectibus superari" - a reference to the Greek concept of akrasia or lack of self-control.</note> PRO. Clearly. SO. Indeed, all men pursue those things in which they are confident, the fearful as well as the brave. And by this reasoning, both the fearful and the brave approach the same things. PRO. On the contrary, Socrates, the things toward which the brave and the fearful proceed are entirely opposite. For these are willing to go to war, while those are unwilling. SO. Is going to war honorable or base? PRO. Honorable. SO. If it is honorable, did we not agree above that it is also good? For we agreed that all honorable and beautiful actions are also good. PRO. You speak the truth; and so it always seems to me. SO. Rightly so. But who do you say are unwilling to go into battle, when that journey is beautiful and good? PRO. The fearful. SO. If it is beautiful and good, is it not also pleasant? PRO. That was granted. SO. Do the fearful then, knowing this, refuse to proceed toward what is beautiful, better, and more pleasant? PRO. But truly, if we admit this, we overturn our previous agreements. SO. What then? Does not the brave man tend toward that which is beautiful, better, and more pleasant? PRO. It is necessary to confess it. SO. Entirely, therefore, brave men do not fear basely when they fear, nor do they dare basely. PRO. That is so. SO. If not basely, then honorably and beautifully. PRO. Certainly. SO. And if honorably, then also well. PRO. Indeed. SO. Do not the fearful, the fierce, and the frantic, on the contrary, dare basely and fear basely? PRO. That also. SO. Why do they dare basely and badly, if not because of ignorance and lack of skill? <note>original: "ignorantiam & inscitiam"</note> PRO. For that very reason. SO. What do you call that by which the fearful are themselves fearful? Is it cowardice or courage? PRO. Cowardice. SO. And have the fearful not appeared to be so because of their ignorance of what is to be feared? PRO. Indeed. SO. Therefore they are fearful because of this ignorance? PRO. Certainly. SO. But you asserted that that by which they are fearful is cowardice. PRO. I did. SO. Therefore, will not the ignorance of what is to be feared and what is not to be feared be cowardice? PRO. It will. SO. But courage is the opposite of cowardice. PRO. Without a doubt. SO. Is not the wisdom <note>original: "sapientia" - translating the Greek 'sophia' or 'episteme' as knowledge/wisdom.</note> regarding what is to be feared and what is not to be feared the opposite of that ignorance? PRO. Entirely. SO. And the ignorance of these things is cowardice. PRO. Most certainly. SO. Therefore, the wisdom regarding what is to be feared and what is not to be feared is courage, being the opposite of the ignorance of those same things. Protagoras nodded no further, but remained silent. Then I said: Why are you silent, Protagoras? Why do you neither nod nor deny? He said: Finish it yourself. I said: I will conclude immediately, if I may ask just this one thing: whether it still seems to you now, as it did above, that there are some who are most ignorant and yet most brave. He said: You seem to strive too much, Socrates, that I myself should answer; therefore I will gratify you. I say it seems impossible from those things which we granted above. I said: I question you about all these things for no other reason than that I desire to know what kind of things pertain to virtue, or what virtue itself is. I know indeed that once this is declared, that matter over which you and I have spent so many words will immediately be known: while I denied that virtue could be taught, and you asserted that it could. And I think the outcome of our dispute, if it could find a human voice, would laugh at us and rebuke us with these and similar reproaches: "How absurd <margin>Conclusion</margin> you are, Socrates and Protagoras. You, Socrates, said from the beginning that virtue could not be taught, yet now you strive to contradict yourself by attempting to show that all these things—justice, temperance, and courage—are knowledge. By which reasoning it would most certainly follow that virtue can be taught. For if knowledge were something other than virtue, as Protagoras attempted to assert above, it clearly could not be taught. But now if the whole appears to be knowledge, as you yourself try to infer, Socrates, it will be a wonder if virtue cannot be acquired through teaching. Protagoras, on the other hand, at first wished virtue to be taught; now, conversely, he seems to struggle so that virtue appears to be anything rather than knowledge. In which way it would be the least teachable of all things." Indeed, Protagoras, seeing all these things so heavily disturbed and turned upside down, I am vehemently moved to bring them into the light. I would wish, after these things are narrated between us, that we might show what virtue is, and again demonstrate whether it can be taught or not; lest that Epimetheus <note>In Greek mythology, Epimetheus ("afterthought") failed to provide for humans, while Prometheus ("forethought") helped them.</note> deceive us often, failing us in consideration just as he neglected the distribution in the story you told. For Prometheus pleases me more in that fable than Epimetheus; using him and looking forward to my whole life, I treat all these matters. And if you were willing, as I said from the beginning, I would most gladly deliberate with you on these things. Then Protagoras said: I praise this zeal of yours, Socrates, and the discourse of your speech. For among other things, unless my opinion deceives me, I am free from vices, and certainly furthest from envy. And I have already said to many concerning you, that of all whom I have met, I admire you the most—certainly the most of those your own age. I add even that it would be no wonder to me if you become famous in the study of wisdom. And we shall discuss these things at another time whenever you wish. Now it is time for me to attend to other matters. I said: So it must be done, if it seems so to you: since I myself was compelled to go elsewhere long ago as I said; nevertheless, to gratify the noble youth Callias, I remained. Having said and heard these things, we departed.

<summary>Socrates concludes the argument by proving that courage is the knowledge of what is and is not to be feared, leading to the paradoxical conclusion that virtue must be teachable because it is a form of knowledge. Protagoras, exhausted by the logic, ends the conversation with mutual respect, and the dialogue concludes at the house of Callias.</summary>

# THE ARGUMENT OF MARSILIO FICINO FOR THE EUTHYDEMUS.
## FOLIO 100.
<note>original: "ARGVMENTVM IN EVTHYDEMVM. FO. C."</note>
**n.iiii.**
<meta>catchword: safely.</meta>

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino for the Euthydemus.

Plato, a man distinguished by his charity, strives in the *Euthydemus*—as he often does elsewhere—to turn souls born for serious matters away from the vain trifles of the sophists. He shows that even when they discuss the weightiest subjects, they are merely playing, and they deceive the hopes of their audience at every turn. He describes them here, as in other places, as meddlesome and vain competitors in verbal disputes, ready to refute any statement whatever, whether it be true or false.

First, he shows how greedy the character of the sophists is: for the brothers Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, being sophists, are prepared to teach for a fee the military art in which they boast—an art which no one has ever sold before. Second, how ambitious they are: for they profess judicial skill along with military skill, and both of these together with the sophistic art, though these fields are vastly different from one another. Third, how vain they are: for even as old men, they turn themselves from things to words, and from the study of truth to lies. Fourth, how contemptible they are: for in a short time—at most two years—anyone can acquire this faculty of quibbling. Fifth, how dangerous they are: for who should wonder that simple youths are easily ensnared by the cleverness of the sophists and imbued with false opinions and ruinous habits? Even Socrates himself, an old and most wise man, pretends to be caught by the same bait and hastens with feigned wonder to the gymnasia of the sophists. Furthermore, even that "spirit" of Socrates <note>The "daimon" or inner voice of Socrates</note>, which seems unable to be deceived by anyone, pretends to be deceived by the sophistic illusions of these rascals.

Meanwhile, Socrates, by frequenting the schools of boys, musical games, and the rudiments of words even in his old age, admonishes us: first, that we should not despise even the smallest thing regarding the perfection of disciplines; second, that we should not, as often happens, be kept away from the study of disciplines by a certain rustic blush of shame. Third, that we should believe, in the manner of Solon, that we must keep learning as long as we must live.

Furthermore, the fact that the sophists never notice the Socratic irony directed against them—indeed, he brings forward nothing so magnificent in their praise that they do not easily believe it and openly accept it—declares two things to us especially: first, that nothing vainer than these rascals can be found; and second, that those who study too intently to deceive others are, naturally, most easily deceived by their own fallaciousness. Moreover, the fact that these "illusionists" never provide the virtue they promise, nor do they ever exhort anyone toward it, but instead flee everywhere to their accustomed verbal quibbles—treating these as serious matters while treating other studies as mere play—signifies three things to us. First, those who are not adorned with virtue themselves can never teach it by reason or example. Second, men who are too curious about words never attain or bring about good things. Third, those who most easily promise the most things are the least likely of all to keep their promises.

To this is added that Socrates lures the sophists to teach virtue by mentioning a crowd of wealthy disciples, as they are overly ambitious and greedy. But there, under the persona of Crito, we are warned not to rashly commit the care of our soul to just anyone. Because Socrates, while the sophists promise virtue, meanwhile entreats them as if they were gods, he aptly declares that virtue must be sought from God himself, and that men endowed with virtue are to be regarded as divine. Likewise, because he considers them happier than kings due to their study of virtue, he clearly signifies that a man endowed with virtue is first a king of himself, and then a king of kings.

Socrates further teaches, in his care for Clinias, with what great charity and diligence we ought to apply ourselves to the care of youth. But soon, under the insolent promises of the sophists, "the mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse will be born" <note>A reference to Horace's *Ars Poetica*, describing grand promises that lead to nothing.</note>. One must also note there a certain hyperbolic irony of Socrates used to mock vain men. Then, there is the incomparable vanity of the rascals who offer words instead of things—and the most inept words at that—and who, having promised an exhortation to wisdom, slide back into childish follies.

Then Socrates says that the entire gymnasium of the sophists is a game of words, and that the nature of things is entirely hidden from them; he claims their artificial webs can be dissolved solely by the exposition of words and the distinction of meanings. Then, with a most witty irony, he implores the sophists to come to serious matters after their games, and he proposes a certain formula: a model of the exhortation to philosophy that he desires from them. In this formula, he first describes happiness by the common notion of "living well." Then he proves that this "living well" consists either in the attainment of things according to one's wish, or in the right use of those things. And through inductions on both sides, he concludes that wisdom alone—since it alone both attains things as wished and uses them rightly—is what makes men blessed.

In these inductions, such an order is seen: if through the individual parts of life wisdom both attains what is wished and uses it rightly, then wisdom brings about the common and highest good of life in the entirety of life, consisting in prosperous attainment and right use. During the argument, a noble sentiment shines forth as the foundation of the Stoic sect: namely, that external and corporeal things are "indifferent" <term>indifferentia: things that are neither morally good nor evil in themselves</term> and common, rather than to be called good or evil. Properly speaking, wisdom is the only good, and foolishness the only evil. Since through the former all things turn out well for us, and through the latter all things turn out badly, wisdom alone can make us blessed.

Because the power for happiness consists entirely in knowledge, the three names for happiness established by the ancient Greek authors declare this: *eudaimonia* <note>original: "eudęmonia"</note>, *eutychia*, and *eupragia*. The first signifies the knowledge of the good; the second, its attainment; the third, its use. Knowledge perfects all these for us. This knowledge of the good Plato calls, both here and elsewhere, the virtue of all things in a certain way. Wisdom is the knowledge of the absolute and divine good, while Prudence is the knowledge of goods and evils...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces Plato's Euthydemus, contrasting Socratic wisdom and irony with the greedy, vain, and deceptive practices of the sophists. He argues that true happiness (eudaimonia) is found only through the wisdom that allows for the right use of all things.</summary>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE EUTHYDEMUS

pertaining properly to man. Justice is also the science <note>original: *scientiam*; here meaning a systematic body of knowledge</note> of distributing things to the good and the evil according to their merits. Fortitude, moreover, is the science of daring and fearing regarding good and evil things. Finally, Temperance is the science of similarly choosing and fleeing good and evil things. One must remember above all else that Plato hints here, and often elsewhere, that wisdom is not so much acquired by human study as it is accustomed to be infused by divine power into purified minds. For since the soul, when joined to this body, is rendered unfit for things entirely separated from the body, it grows dim like an owl in the excessive splendor of divine things. Therefore, the Socratic exhortation to wisdom pertains not so much to speculation as to morals. By these, at last, the purified soul attains wisdom from God, as well as science and prudence. Through these means, while Socrates pretends to demand from the Sophists an exhortation to philosophy (which is the study of wisdom), he himself meanwhile, with a certain most fitting dissimulation, wonderfully exhorts one to philosophize. Nevertheless, the Sophists do not yet accept the exhortation, either for themselves or at least for others. Instead, they revolve back into their usual follies. Here it appears how persistent a character is—whether born wickedly or educated wrongly—even in trifles. Among these things, observe most diligently the divine opinion of Plato: by which we are commanded, for the sake of attaining virtue and wisdom, to endure not only inconveniences, losses, labors, and servitude, but even—if we hope to emerge better at last from the very dissolution of ourselves—to permit ourselves to be flayed, melted down, and utterly dissolved by Him who has promised this very thing. Here it appears how much the good of the soul surpasses corporeal things, and how much those most brave ancient Christian martyrs are to be approved. To this, that saying is similar: *He who loves his soul in this world shall lose it; but he who loses it here shall receive the same in eternal life.* <note>A reference to John 12:25</note> Furthermore, Socrates, by refuting the little traps of the Sophists, demonstrates that sophisms can very easily be turned back against the Sophists; especially because he forces them both to contradict themselves and to confess the most absurd things. These things having been done, by again simulating a formula similar to the previous one, he declares that listeners receive nothing of good from the Sophists, and that the Sophists themselves, being as it were most abandoned, cannot be recalled to a good harvest. Because, however, he often repeats these three names during the dispute—wisdom, science, and prudence—it must be noted that where he speaks more strictly, he defines **wisdom** as the cognition of divine things, **science** as that of natural things, and **prudence** as that of human things. Where he speaks less strictly, he is accustomed to use the name of "science" to signify these three. But where he speaks more freely, he uses each one equally for all. Furthermore, he brings forward two kinds of arts: namely, those which produce works, and those which use the things made. And since the art which uses the work of another art both prescribes the end for that manufacturing and applies the model for completing the work, we not unjustly place the "using art" above the "making art" in dignity. Note here that Plato makes so little of the making art and so much of the using art: that he most aptly wishes that if anyone could even turn all materials into gold at will—or indeed even acquire immortality itself among men—neither such a mass of gold nor immortality would profit him unless he knew how to use it. Note again that the common abuse of the oratorical art is here censured as being entirely similar to sophistry, as if it were a species of wicked fascination, everywhere striving like a sorceress to infect souls with disturbances. By a similar reasoning, he detests the common abuse of poetry elsewhere. But because here, in numbering the arts, he names **dialectic**—lest I should say *dialecticen* after the manner of some, for *dialectic* sounds more Latin to me—it must be remembered that "logic" in Plato signifies the art arranging the rules of names, speeches, and arguments; but "dialectic" signifies the sagacious investigation of the philosopher using these rules to search out the reasons of things: especially divine things, from which the highest reasons of subsequent things are also received. Therefore, dialectic in Plato most often signifies **theology** to us. In the same place, he names the "royal and civil art": namely, the prudence of happily governing the human race. Which indeed, whether it be in a private or public person, or in one or many, is equally called by him both "civil" and "royal." To this, as if to a queen, he subjects all faculties which are occupied in acting and making: to which she herself gives laws, and uses them as instruments and handmaidens. He similarly subjects to theology all sciences which are occupied in speculation: toward which these stand in the same relation as private arts do to the royal art. Wherefore Socrates, while in that same formula (continued again from the previous formula) he seeks the faculty leading most especially to happiness, deservedly dismisses the others and flees to royal theology: especially since happiness consists in the best use of things. These arts indeed strive to bring the most correct use, both of speculating and of acting and making, to all people through all things. He handed down the same in the *Philebus*; the same in the last book of the *Laws*; the same in the books of the *Republic*, where for the happiness of the human race he instructs the future governor first in theology, then in civil discipline: asserting that the divine Idea of the Good itself is at last hardly perceived except by the legitimate theologian; and unless it has been perceived, nothing can be rightly done or happily arranged, either privately or publicly. Although this may be so, Socrates nevertheless does not judge that these mysteries should be revealed here among adolescents and sophists. For the Socratic custom is to only exhort adolescents, only to confute sophists, and finally to teach legitimate men. Here, therefore, under irony and dissimulation, he touches upon mysteries of this kind, and pretends to hesitate, and as if among dizzy sophists, to suffer dizziness himself. Perhaps, indeed, he pretends to doubt whether theology and civil science provide happiness for this reason: because he often confirms that the absolute perfection of neither theology nor civil discipline can be had by any human way, but rather by divine inspiration. Wherefore, not unjustly distrusting human powers, he refers happiness to divine munificence: to which he undoubtedly referred both the wisdom of theology and the prudence of civil life. Finally, all these things are to be received by us in this way: so that human duties indeed prepare minds for happiness—

It emphasizes that wisdom is a divine gift rather than a mere human acquisition and contrasts Socratic irony with Sophistic empty reasoning.</summary>

# EUTHYDEMUS, OR THE LITIGIOUS. FOLIO 101.

would be governed most rightly, especially under theological and civil discipline: indeed, the most merciful goodness of God himself might finally bestow the highest good of man upon those who have turned toward Him through these intermediary means. I had determined to place a sufficiently honorable end to this argument—or rather, this commentary—here; but a necessary question still detains me: to what end does the frequent irony of Socrates serve? For it always disguises Socrates' own good qualities, while often feigning the good qualities of the proud. And as much as it always detracts from Socrates, it often attributes just as much to the proud. This he achieves through frequent jokes and witticisms, and often beyond belief: so that by depressing himself, he makes his listeners more modest; but by extolling the proud beyond the measure of belief, he renders their pride a thing to be derided by all. Certainly, those who are praised beyond measure by Socrates, if they are not entirely lost, amend themselves out of confusion and blushing; but if they are already utterly lost, it is no longer they, but those present who, by the example of his correction, most cautiously avoid such a ridiculous vanity of pride. Moreover, Socratic irony is a very skillful thing: sophisticated, witty, and charming. It supports the truth more safely and avoids hatred, while it aptly disguises his profession; and he clearly detracts from himself before he is caught detracting, even secretly, from another. And what is greatest in correcting vices, he escapes the mark of being a slanderer. Through this irony, certainly, near the end of this dialogue, he gathers the censure of sophistical quibbling into three heads. First, that all the most esteemed men despise trifles of this sort. Second, that sophisms confound themselves. Third, that even boys can master these very light things within two days. Presently, he descends from the sophist to the rhetorician. For each falsely professes civil virtue, as he writes in the *Gorgias*; and the sophist indeed simulates the speculation of the philosopher, while the rhetorician simulates the discipline of moral philosophy, though at a distance. He shows, moreover, that rhetoricians and orators, while they profess to be both philosophers and statesmen at the same time, are utterly useless for either. Finally, he concludes the dialogue with a twin and most excellent sentiment. One is that more care should be taken that children be good than that they merely exist; and that you should leave them good, rather than leaving them goods <note>A play on words: being "good" (virtuous) vs. having "goods" (wealth).</note>. The other is that one must philosophize altogether, since philosophy itself is a divine thing; nor should so precious a possession be abandoned either because of its false professors or because of lying detractors.

### EUTHYDEMUS, OR THE LITIGIOUS, TRANSLATED FROM THE GREEK LANGUAGE INTO LATIN BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE, TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PIERO DE' MEDICI.

->CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE.<-
->CRITO. SOCRATES. EUTHYDEMUS. DIONYSODORUS. CLINIAS. CTESIPPUS.<-

### CRITO.

WHO WAS THAT, O Socrates, with whom you were disputing yesterday in the Lyceum? <note>The Lyceum was a public gymnasium in Athens where philosophers gathered.</note> Truly, a large crowd was standing around. Therefore, although I approached quite near, eager to hear, I could perceive nothing clearly. But when I stood up on my tiptoes to look, he seemed to me to be some stranger with whom you were discoursing. Who was he? SOCRATES. About whom do you ask, Crito? For there was not just one, but two were present. CRITO. The third one was sitting on your right, whose name I greatly desire to hear. But in the middle was that youth, the son of Axiochus, who seemed to me to have made quite enough progress. He is almost the same age as our Critobulus. But that one has a leaner habit of body, while this one seems to present a grander appearance, of a truly honorable and excellent character. SOCRATES. That is Euthydemus whom you seek, O Crito. But the one sitting on the left was Dionysodorus, his brother, who likewise took part in the dispute. CRITO. I know neither of them, O Socrates. SOCRATES. I know them; they are, as it seems, sophists. <note>term: Sophist. A paid teacher of rhetoric and philosophy in Ancient Greece, often criticized by Plato for prioritizing winning arguments over finding truth.</note> CRITO. From what country are they? What is their wisdom? SOCRATES. They are from Chios, I believe, by birth; they went to the people of Thurii. Having departed from there, they have now spent many years in these parts. Their wisdom is indeed wonderful, O Crito. In all things they are certainly most wise. And until now, I did not know they were perfect athletes. For they are powerful in every kind of contest; not like the Acarnanian brothers, the athletes. For those are strong only in body; but these are able to fight primarily with the body, and in that kind of fighting by which they overcome all things. Indeed, they are very well instructed in military matters; and they can make anyone else a strenuous man in that regard, provided he pays a fee. Then, they can also handle and settle judicial combat, and instruct anyone in writing and pleading cases. Hitherto they were skilled only in these things; but now they have perfectly put the finishing touch on the faculty of athletes. For whatever kind of contesting was lacking, they have recently attained: so that no one is able to resist them; they have turned out so strong in the altercation of words, and prompt to refute any saying whatsoever, whether it be true or false. Therefore, O Crito, I am thinking of handing myself over to these men. For they promise that they will make anyone else a master of these same things in a short time. CRITO. Does not your advanced age deter you, O Socrates? SOCRATES. Not at all, Crito. For there is something that is customary for me, nor does it let me despair. Truly, even these men, being now old, so to speak, have devoted themselves to this contentious faculty which I now desire. For two years ago they did not yet know it. But I fear this one thing only: lest I be a disgrace to them, just as I am to Connus, the son of Metrobius, the lyre-player, who even now teaches me the strings. The boys, my fellow-students, therefore...

They laugh every day and call Connus himself "the old man's teacher." <note>Connus was a music teacher whom Socrates famously visited in his old age to learn the lyre, much to the amusement of the local boys.</note> Therefore, lest someone should cast this same reproach at these guests, and they, fearing this, might refuse me, I have exhorted several others of advanced age, O Crito, to go there with me for the sake of learning; and I shall likewise endeavor to persuade others here. But why do you not come as well, bringing your sons with you? Furthermore, when they see them—since they will hope for the gathering of your sons as well—they will be more willingly drawn by these enticements to accept us for instruction.

**CRITO:** Nothing prevents it, Socrates, if it seems right to you. But first, narrate what their wisdom is, so that we may know what we are about to perceive.

**SOCRATES:** I shall by no means object now, provided I can remember it well enough, as I might not have paid sufficient attention; on the contrary, I applied myself diligently and I remember it; I will endeavor to relate everything to you from the beginning. Indeed, by a certain divine fortune, I was sitting alone in the gymnasium where you saw me, and I was just then thinking of departing. But immediately as I was rising, that accustomed **daemonic sign** <note>Socrates' "daimonion" or inner voice that warned him against certain actions.</note> stopped me. I stayed, therefore, and a little while later these men entered: Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, and many others with them who appeared to me to be their disciples. Having entered, they began walking about in the covered race-course. They had not yet completed that circuit two or three times when that Clinias arrived, who you say has made such progress—and you speak truly. Following him were many friends and others, and a certain youth, Ctesippus of Paeania, a man of good and beautiful character, though somewhat headstrong due to his youth. Clinias, seeing me from the entrance sitting alone, came toward me and sat at my right hand, just as you say.

When Dionysodorus and Euthydemus saw him, they first stood near us and conversed with each other, turning their eyes toward us from one side and then the other—for I was observing them most diligently. Then, approaching closer, they sat down: Euthydemus next to the youth himself, and Dionysodorus next to me on the left; the others sat wherever they happened to find a place. I therefore congratulated them, as I had not seen them for a long time. After this, turning to Clinias, I said: "These men, O Clinias—Euthydemus and Dionysodorus—are wise not in small matters, but in the greatest. For they know everything pertaining to military affairs that anyone must know who is to be a vigorous leader of an army: concerning battle lines, ranks, the instruction of troops, and battles. They can even make anyone a skilled lawyer and a most sharp accuser of those who have committed injuries."

They looked at me with contempt as I spoke thus, and smiling at one another, Euthydemus said: "We no longer treat these matters seriously, O Socrates; rather, we use them as a way to pass the time between our studies."

Admiring this, I said: "How magnificent your studies must be, if such great matters are held by you as mere interludes and jests! Tell me, I beseech you by the gods, what is this extraordinary work of yours?"

**EUTHYDEMUS:** We believe, O Socrates, that we can teach **virtue** <note>Latin: *virtus*; Greek: *arete*—meaning excellence or moral character.</note> most easily and best of all men.

**SOCRATES:** By Jupiter, what a precious thing you promise! By what fortune did this gain chiefly fall to you? Indeed, I thought of you until now as I just said: as men outstanding in military affairs, and I proclaimed that of you. For I remember when you first came here, you professed only this; but if you have now truly attained this science, be favorable: I truly call upon you as if you were gods, praying that you now forgive my previous errors. But see, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, whether you speak the truth. Nor should it seem strange if someone, estimating the magnitude of this thing you promise, finds it difficult to believe.

**EUTHYDEMUS:** Know for certain, O Socrates, that it is so.

**SOCRATES:** I consider you more blessed for the possession of this thing than the Great King is for his kingdom. But tell me, I pray, whether you intend to demonstrate this wisdom, or if you have decided otherwise.

**EUTHYDEMUS:** We have come for this very purpose, O Socrates, to demonstrate and to teach, if anyone desires to learn.

**SOCRATES:** But all who lack it will desire it, I myself affirm to you as a sponsor: first I, then also Clinias here, and besides him Ctesippus, and the others present. For I showed them the friends of Clinias himself, who were already standing around us. Ctesippus happened to be sitting far from Clinias. But when Euthydemus, moving forward during the dispute, placed himself between us in the middle of Clinias and blocked Ctesippus's view, Ctesippus stood up and was the first to stand in our sight, so that he might both see his friend and hear the disputants. Similarly, others followed him and stood near us: both the friends of Clinias and the companions of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus. Pointing to all these with my finger, I promised Euthydemus they would be his disciples. Ctesippus then vehemently agreed, as did the others, and they ordered them to show the power of their wisdom.

Then I said: "O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus, would you please gratify these men and demonstrate for my sake? There are many such things that would be a long task to show. But tell me this: can you make a man good who is already persuaded that he ought to learn from you? Or can you also persuade him who has not yet been persuaded—either because he thinks virtue cannot be taught in any way, or perhaps because he thinks you are not its teachers? Is it the work of the same art to persuade a man so affected that virtue can be taught, and that you are the ones from whom anyone might best learn? Is it so, or otherwise?"

"It is the work of this same art, O Socrates," said Dionysodorus.

"Therefore," I said, "you would best exhort men above all others to the care of **philosophy** and virtue."

"So we believe, O Socrates."

"Show the rest later," I said, "but show this now: persuade this youth, I pray, that he must apply himself with all his strength to the study of philosophy and virtue; and do this favor for me and all these people. Furthermore, this youth is of such concern to me and all these that we desire most greatly for him to turn out to be an excellent man."

He is the son of Axiocus, born from the elder Alcibiades, and the cousin of the younger Alcibiades who is now living. His name is Clinias. Since he is of a tender age, we fear for him, as is fitting, lest someone perhaps reaching him before us might turn his mind elsewhere and corrupt it. Therefore, you have come most opportunely. And unless something prevents it, make a trial of this boy and discourse with him in our presence. When I had said these things, Euthydemus...

# EUTHYDEMUS, OR THE DISPUTATIOUS. FOLIO 102.

"With too much strength and boldness," he said, "nothing, O Socrates, prevents it, provided the youth is willing to answer us." "He is not unaccustomed to this," I said. "For these men present here frequently dispute with him and ask him many things. Therefore, it is fitting that he should now dare to answer." What follows, O Crito—would that I were able to recount it worthily! For it must not be thought a small task for anyone to be able to describe their inestimable wisdom. Wherefore it seems to me now, as it does to the poets, that there is need for the help of the Muses, and to invoke the aid of Memory before I begin the narration of so great a matter.

Euthydemus, I believe, began in this manner: "Are those who learn something, O Clinias, wise men or ignorant men?" The boy, because of the weight of that question, blushed; and hesitating, he turned his eyes toward me. But I, noticing his confusion, said: "Be of good courage, Clinias, and answer him manfully whichever way seems right to you. For perhaps it will benefit you greatly." As I was speaking, Dionysodorus leaned to my ear and said with a laugh: "I predict to you, O Socrates, that whatever the boy answers, he will be refuted." Meanwhile Clinias had answered, so I was not permitted to warn the boy. He had answered that those who learn are the wise.

To him Euthydemus said: "Do you call some people teachers, or not?" He agreed. "Are teachers not the teachers of those who learn? Just as the lyre-player <note>original: citharistę</note> and the grammarian were teachers of you and the other boys, and you were the disciples." He consented. "When you were learning, did you not yet know these same things which you were learning?" "Not yet." "Were you wise when you were ignorant of these things?" "By no means." "If not wise, then you were ignorant?" "Entirely." "Therefore, while you were learning what you did not know, you were learning as ignorant men." The youth nodded. "From this it follows, O Clinias, that the ignorant learn, not the wise, as you yourself thought."

When he had said this, as if a chorus were following the signal of a master, the followers of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus shouted and laughed with the loudest applause. And before the boy could catch his breath, Dionysodorus, taking up the discourse right well and nobly, said: "What further, O Clinias? When the grammarian recites something, which of the boys learn those things: the wise or the ignorant?" "The wise," said Clinias. "Therefore the wise learn, not the ignorant. Wherefore you did not answer Euthydemus correctly just now." At this, their supporters shouted louder and laughed, admiring the wisdom of Euthydemus and Dionysodorus. We, however, were silent as if stunned.

When Euthydemus perceived that we had been rendered stupid by these things, in order to draw even greater admiration to himself, he did not yet dismiss the boy, but questioned him further; and in the manner of those in a chorus who are most ready for dancing, he performed a double-turn around the same question, saying: "Do those who learn, learn what they know, or what they do not know?" Then Dionysodorus, whispering again in my ear, said: "This too, O Socrates, is just like what was brought up before." "By Jupiter!" I said, "how noble even the previous question seemed to us." "We always propose such inescapable questions," he said. "And therefore," I replied, "you seem to hold no small authority among your disciples."

Meanwhile Clinias answered Euthydemus that those who learn, learn thoroughly what they are ignorant of. Immediately he questioned him just as before: "Do you yourself know your letters?" "I know them." "Do you not know them all?" "Yes, all." "When someone recites, does he not recite letters?" He conceded. "Therefore he recites those things which you know, since you yourself know all the letters." He admitted this too. "Do you not learn what someone recites?" He agreed. "But do you learn letters while being ignorant of them?" "Not at all. Rather, I learn knowing them." "Therefore, do you not learn what you know, if indeed you know all the letters?" He nodded. "Therefore you did not answer correctly."

Hardly had Euthydemus said these things, when Dionysodorus, catching the discourse like a ball <note>original: sphęram</note> against the youth, brought this in: "Euthydemus deceives you, O Clinias. Tell me: is not learning the receiving of knowledge of that which one learns?" Clinias admitted it. "But is knowing anything else than already having that very knowledge?" He conceded. "To not know, therefore, is to not yet have knowledge." He granted this too. "Do those who have a thing, or those who do not have it, receive it?" "Those who do not have it." "And have you not confessed that ignorant men are among the number of those who do not have it?" He nodded. "Learners, therefore, are among the number of those who receive, not those who have." He approved. "Therefore those who do not know, O Clinias, learn; not those who know."

After this, Euthydemus was already hastening to attack the youth in a third contest. But I, pitying him as he was sinking, so that I might refresh him a little lest he perhaps become too terrified, began to console him in this manner: "Do not wonder, O Clinias, if these discourses seem unusual to you; for perhaps you do not perceive what these strangers are doing toward you. They are doing exactly what those frenzied priests called Corybantes do in the mysteries, <margin>The manner in which the Corybantes initiate anyone into the sacred rites. Prodicus.</margin> when they place the one they are about to initiate into the rites upon a throne, and applaud with various jests and lead dances. I think you understand these things if you yourself have been initiated. These men are playing similarly now, and leading dances and jumping around you, as if now purifying you, and later they will initiate you into the rites. Therefore, for the present, consider that certain first ceremonies of the sophistical rites are being celebrated. For first, as Prodicus commands, it is necessary to receive the proper meanings of names; which the strangers have shown you regarding that which is called 'to learn,' the property of which you did not know at all. For men use this word to signify that act when someone, having no knowledge of a thing from the beginning, then receives knowledge of it. They also use the same word to signify the observation of one who, having knowledge, recognizes that same thing by this very knowledge whenever it is done or said. More properly, they call this 'to think' or 'to notice' rather than 'to learn,' though sometimes they also call it 'to learn.' But that escaped you, as these men showed: namely, that the same name is attributed by men to contrary things—to the one who knows and the one who does not know. Similar to this is also that which they proposed in the second question, asking whether men learn what they know or what they do not know."

<summary>Socrates recounts how the sophists Euthydemus and Dionysodorus use semantic traps to confuse the young Clinias, alternating between arguing that only the wise learn and then only the ignorant learn. Socrates intervenes to comfort Clinias, comparing the sophists' confusing tactics to the dizzying initiation rites of the Corybantes.</summary>
