->**What are called "riddle games."**<- <margin>What are called "riddle games."</margin> All these things are a kind of game within the disciplines of learning. For this reason, I think they are playing with you. I call it a "game" for this reason: because if someone knows many or all things of this kind, they will understand the natures of things no less, yet they will be able to play against men based on the very difference of names—as if tripping them up by sticking out a leg, in the manner of those who secretly pull away benches from people wanting to sit down, and laugh immoderately when they see someone has fallen flat on their back. Therefore, receive these things from them as mere games. Next, however, they will treat serious matters with you, and I will demand from them what they promised. They promised, furthermore, that they would demonstrate the wisdom of exhortation <note>The art of encouraging someone toward virtue.</note>. But now, it seems to me they thought they should joke with you first. Enough of this playing, then, O Euthydemus and Dionysodorus! Now show what follows. It remains, surely, for you to exhort this young man toward the study of virtue and wisdom. But first, I myself will define for you a certain example and formula of that exhortation, as best as I am able. If I seem to prescribe this in a rustic or absurd way, I beg you not to mock me. For, moved by the eagerness to hear your wisdom, I dare now to show you my own silliness. Listen then, without laughter, both you and your disciples. And you, son of Axiochus <note>Clinia</note>, answer me: do we all desire to do well—that is, to live well? Or is this question perhaps, as I feared, among those that are ridiculous? For it is the mark of a demented man to bring such things into controversy. For who among men does not desire to live well? CLINIA: No one. SOCRATES: Come then, since we wish to live well, in what way can we attain this? Is it not if many good things are present to us? Or is he more foolish who doubts this? For it is agreed to be so. CLINIA: It is certainly agreed. SOCRATES: But what kind of things, from every category, are "goods"? Is it perhaps not difficult to find, nor to be doubted by an elegant mind? For anyone would say that to be rich is a good. Is it not? CLINIA: Greatly so. SOCRATES: And is it not also to be healthy and beautiful, and to enjoy the other gifts of the body? CLINIA: Certainly. SOCRATES: Furthermore, nobility of birth, power, and honors in one's own city are goods. CLINIA: Those as well. SOCRATES: What goods remain besides these? If we say that temperance, justice, and fortitude are goods, would we be right? CLINIA: Someone might perhaps doubt it. SOCRATES: But what do you say? CLINIA: They must certainly be called goods. SOCRATES: And wisdom—in what category shall we place it? Among the goods, or otherwise? CLINIA: In the category of goods. SOCRATES: See that I do not overlook anything worthy of being considered a good. CLINIA: To me, we seem to have overlooked nothing. Then, 

<margin>A certain definition of happiness.</margin> recollecting myself, I said: We seem, O Clinia, to have neglected the greatest of all goods. "What is this?" he asked. Happiness—which consists in the attainment of things according to one's wish, which even the most unlearned men call the "highest good." "You speak the truth," he said. Then I, moved again by regret, said: O Clinia, we have stirred up laughter among our guests. "Why so?" SOCRATES: Because, although we placed happiness among the things above, we were just now speaking of the same thing again. "What of that?" It is ridiculous to propose again what was placed before, and to recount the same things twice. "For what reason do you say that?" 

<margin>Wisdom is Happiness</margin> Wisdom itself, I said, is happiness; this, indeed, even any boy might understand. Yet he marveled at this because of his boyish lack of experience. But I, recognizing his state of mind, questioned him in this manner: Do you not know, O Clinia, that skilled flute-players attain best of all whatever pertains to the use of flutes? He agreed. And learned grammarians in what pertains to letters, both in writing and reading? "Entirely." Do not wise pilots also reach the desired harbor of navigation better than others? "It is so." And does not a wise leader of war dispatch what pertains to military service more securely? And will you not campaign more safely with him than with an ignorant one? "Without a doubt." And will a wise doctor not lead you to the desired health of the body better than an ignorant one? And would you not commit yourself to him more willingly? "Certainly." Is it not because you thought that things would turn out more happily and according to your wish with him, because of his wisdom? He agreed. 

<margin>Wisdom makes us happy</margin> Wisdom, therefore, in all human affairs, makes us happy—that is, masters of our wish. For wisdom never wanders nor is it ever deceived, but it performs the work rightly and attains its goal; otherwise, it would be no wisdom at all. We agreed at last, I know not how, that it should be said summarily: where wisdom is present, happiness is no longer lacking. These things having been granted, I asked him again what we thought about those things granted above. For we confessed that if we have many goods, we live well and blessedly. He admitted it. Do we live blessedly because of the presence of goods if they do us no profit, or if they do profit us? "If they profit us," he said. But do they contribute anything if we merely have them, but do not use them? For example, if we have many feasts and cups, but do not eat or drink; do they help at all? "Not at all." Furthermore, if all the tools for finishing a work were set out and prepared for craftsmen, but they did not use them, would they do well merely because of the possession of those things required for the perfection of the work? As if all the tools and sufficient wood were prepared for a carpenter, but he himself built nothing, would he be helped by the mere possession? "In no way," he said. What then? If someone 

<margin>It is necessary for a happy man not only to possess goods, but to use them.</margin> obtained riches and all the goods we mentioned, but never used them, would he be happy by the mere possession of those goods? "Not at all, Socrates." It is necessary, therefore, I said, that he who is to be happy must not only possess goods of this kind, 

<margin>Possession alone helps nothing</margin> but use them. For possession alone helps nothing. "You speak the truth." Is the possession and use of goods sufficient, O Clinia, for living blessedly? "It seems so to me." But do you say so if one uses them rightly, or even if one uses them wrongly? "If rightly." 

<margin>He who abuses goods is further from blessedness than he who lets them go.</margin> You speak well. For he who abuses things is, I think, much further from blessedness than he who lets them go. For to the former they are evils, while to the latter they are neither goods nor evils. Must it not be said so? He approved. In the working and use of wood, does anything other than the science of carpentry make one use each thing rightly? "Nothing else." Furthermore, in the making of vessels, does science provide the right use? He nodded. And regarding the use of the goods we listed above—riches, health, and beauty—was not science <note>Here meaning "knowledge" or "wisdom."</note> itself the leader, teaching how to use these things rightly...

By the gods, is there any utility in other possessions without prudence and wisdom? Which of these two brings greater utility: one who is out of his mind but abounds in many things and does much, or one who possesses little and does little, but is of sound mind? Consider it this way: Does not he who does fewer things err less often? And erring less, does he not act badly less often? And acting badly less often, is he not less miserable? Entirely so, he said. In what way does one do fewer things: if he is poor, or if he is wealthy? If he is poor. Whether if he is weak or robust? If he is weak. Whether if he is honored or cast down? If he is cast down. Does a brave and temperate man do fewer things, or a timid one? A timid one. And does not a lazy man prove better than one who is prompt to act? He admitted it. And the slow rather than the swift, or one dull of sight and hearing rather than the sharp? All these things were agreed upon between us.

Then indeed I concluded the previous discourse in this manner: None of these things which we were calling "goods," O Clinias, appear to be good in themselves. Rather, it must be stated thus: if ignorance presides over them, they are worse than their opposites, to the extent that they can more abundantly supply the tools of wickedness to an evil leader. But if prudence and wisdom preside over them, then finally they are better. In their own nature, however, they are neither good nor bad, nor worthy of any particular estimation. It seems, he said, to be as you say. What else, I said, is concluded from what has been said, than that none of the other things are good or evil; but of these two themselves, wisdom is indeed a good, and folly an evil? He approved.

<margin>He who does fewer things errs less often.</margin>
<margin>Beautifully like a ladder of reasoning <note>Referring to the "sorites" or chain of logic Socrates uses here.</note></margin>

Let us consider what follows in addition. Since we all desire to be happy, and we are made happy, as it appeared, by the fact that we use things and use them rightly—and knowledge provides the rectitude of use and the success of the outcome—everyone ought to strive with all zeal to become as wise as possible, should they not? Certainly. Everyone ought to think, therefore, that this is to be sought from parents rather than an inheritance of much money; and from tutors and friends, and from others, but especially from those who claim to be more ardent in their love, whether they be guests or citizens. These people one must humbly implore to impart their wisdom. Nor is it shameful or shrinking, O Clinias, for the sake of attaining wisdom, to serve anyone and to comply with everyone in honorable service. Do you also feel this way? Entirely the same, for you seem to speak rightly.

<margin>Everyone ought to seek wisdom more than money.</margin>

If only, I said, wisdom can be taught, and does not come to men by chance. For this remains to be investigated further, as it has not yet been established between us. Then he said: It seems to me, O Socrates, that it can be taught. Delighted by this response, I said: O how beautifully you speak, best of men! You have bestowed a very great benefit upon me, freeing my mind from a long investigation. I was indeed doubting whether wisdom could be taught or not. But now, since it seems to you that it can be acquired by teaching, and this alone of all things makes a man blessed and happy, what else would you say must be done now, other than to practice philosophy <note>original: "philosophandum"</note>? Do you not intend to do this yourself? As much as possible, O Socrates, he said.

When I had heard these things gladly, I said: O Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, the example of the exhortation which I seek is such as this, though it was barely scraped together by me in unpolished and lengthy words. Whichever of you prefers, let him show us this same thing woven together skillfully. If you do not wish this, at least demonstrate to the youth what follows from my speech: whether it is necessary to acquire all knowledge, or if there is one specific knowledge which whoever is to be a good and happy man ought to acquire, and declare what this knowledge is. For, as I said at the beginning of the discussion, we vehemently desire this youth to turn out wise and good.

I said these things then, O Crito, and I prepared myself with attention of mind for what followed, observing what kind of beginning to their speech they would make, and by what reasoning they would especially exhort Clinias to the study of wisdom and virtue. Immediately, Dionysodorus, who is the elder, began to speak first. We all turned our eyes toward him, as if we were about to hear a wonderful oration. And that is what happened to us. For he began a marvelous discourse, O Crito, which is truly worthy for you to hear, seeing how beautifully he provokes one to virtue.

Tell me, he said, O Socrates and you others, whoever of you cares for this youth to become wise: are you joking, or do you speak seriously, and truly desire this? I, therefore, thinking that they supposed we had been joking with them from the beginning when we asked them to dispute with the youth—and that they had therefore played with us until now and had not treated matters seriously—immediately said that we desired it most greatly and most studiously.

Then Dionysodorus said: See, O Socrates, that you do not later deny what you now assert. I know I shall never deny it. What do you both say? Do you want him to become wise? We do, why not? Is Clinias wise now, or not? Not yet, I said; for he is not at all boastful. And you, he said, do you want him to become wise, and not be ignorant at all? We admitted it. Therefore, you desire him to become what he is not, and what he is now, to be no longer. When I heard this, I was disturbed; and he, noticing I was disturbed, said: Since you want him who now is to be no longer, you want, it seems, for him to perish. But truly, what dear friends or lovers of this kind must be, who strive with all care to destroy those they love!

Hearing this, Ctesippus took it heavily for the sake of his beloved, and being indignant, said: O Guest from Thurii, if it were not a rustic thing to say, I would have said "on your head" <note>A common ancient curse or retort, similar to "back at you."</note> for the lie you tell against me and the others in this matter, which I consider wicked even to say: that I would wish him to perish. Here Euthydemus, turning to Ctesippus, said: Does it seem to you possible for someone to lie? By Jove, he said, unless perhaps I am insane. But he who lies, does he speak the thing itself about which the speech is, or does he not speak it? He speaks it, he said. If he speaks the thing itself, he speaks nothing else than that which he speaks. How could it be otherwise? Ctesippus said. Is there not one certain thing...

Therefore, Dionysodorus, if he says the things that are, speaks the truth; nor does he lie at all against you. So says Ctesippus. But he who speaks these things, O Euthydemus, does not say the things that are. To whom Euthydemus replied: Are non-existent things not "nothing"? He said no. Is it not true that things which are not, are nowhere existent? Nowhere. Is it possible for anyone to act concerning those things which are not: so that someone might make those things, which exist nowhere? It does not seem so to me at all, said Ctesippus. When the orators <term>rhetors</term> <note>Professional public speakers or teachers of rhetoric in ancient Greece.</note> harangue the people, do they do nothing? They do something. If they do, then they also make or produce something. It follows. Therefore, the act of speaking itself is to act and to make. He agreed. No one, therefore, says things that do not exist; for he would be making something. But you have confessed it is impossible for anyone to make non-existent things. Therefore, according to your own speech, no one speaks falsely. On the contrary, if Dionysodorus speaks, he speaks things that are true and existent. It is so, Euthydemus, said Ctesippus. For he says existent things in a certain way, yet he does not say them as they truly are. Why do you say that, Ctesippus? asked Dionysodorus. Are there those who speak of things exactly as they are? There certainly are, he replied: good, noble, and truth-telling men. What then, the other asked, do good things not fare well? And bad things, conversely, fare badly? He approved. And do you admit that good and noble men speak of things exactly as they are? I admit it. Therefore, O Ctesippus, good men speak badly of bad things, if indeed they announce them as they are. Most certainly, by Jove! And they speak badly of bad men. You will take care not to be among their number yourself, if you believe me: lest good men speak badly of you. Then Euthydemus added: Do they also speak greatly of great men, and hotly of hot men? Most definitely, replied Ctesippus: And they speak coldly of cold men, and they say they argue "coldly" <note>A pun on "cold" meaning both temperature and a dull or lifeless style of speaking.</note>. Then Dionysodorus said: You are being abusive, Ctesippus, you are being abusive. Not by Jove, Dionysodorus: for I cherish you: rather, I warn you as a friend: and I strive to persuade you never to bite me so sharply in my presence as to say that I wish those whom I hold most dear to be destroyed.

But I, when I perceived they were now becoming bitterly irritated with one another, joked with Ctesippus and said: It seems to me, Ctesippus, that we ought to accept from these guests what they give, if only they wish to impart anything, and not to quarrel over words. For if they know how to "destroy" men in such a way as to make them honest and wise instead of evil and ignorant—whether they themselves were the inventors of such a "destruction" or learned it from someone else—so that they restore a good man in place of a bad one... it is clear that they know how. For they said they have recently acquired an art by which they make good men out of bad ones. If they know this, I say, let us permit them to "destroy" the youth for us, provided they make him wise; indeed, let us even hand ourselves over to them to be cured in this way. But if you younger men are afraid, I certainly, like some little man from Caria <note>A reference to the proverb "to take the risk on a Carian," meaning to let a person of little value take a dangerous risk first.</note>, will undergo this danger; for the risk is lighter for me, being an older man. I therefore give myself up to this Dionysodorus as if to Medea of Colchis <note>In mythology, Medea restored youth by cutting people up and boiling them; Socrates uses this as a metaphor for the Sophists' "transformative" methods.</note>: let him dismantle me, and if he wishes, let him boil me, or do whatever else he prefers to me, provided he turns me into an excellent man. Ctesippus also said: I likewise, O Socrates, commit myself to the will of the guests; and even if they wish to flay me more than they do now <margin>Marsyas was flayed by Phoebus [Apollo] and turned into a river.</margin>, let them flay me, provided my skin is not turned into a wine-skin like that of Marsyas, but into virtue. And yet Dionysodorus here thinks I am angry with him. I am not angry at all; but I speak against those things which he says incorrectly about me. But you, Dionysodorus, do not call contradiction itself "abuse." For it is one thing to contradict, and quite another to abuse. To this Dionysodorus retorted: Do you speak of contradicting as if there were such a thing as contradicting? Most certainly, said Ctesippus. Do you not think there is such a thing as contradicting? You would not be able to show this, replied Dionysodorus, since you have never heard one person contradicting another. You speak the truth, he said. But let us hear it now: if I demonstrate to you Ctesippus contradicting Dionysodorus, will you promise to acknowledge his speech? Certainly, he said. Are there not descriptions and reasons <term>logoi</term> for each thing? There are. As each thing is, or as it is not? As it is. If you remember, Ctesippus, he said, a little while ago we showed that no one says what is not. For it appeared to us that no one says that which is not. What then? said Ctesippus. What prevents this, so that you and I might contradict each other? Then the other: Would we be contradicting if we both thought of the description or reason of the same thing? Or would we rather be saying the same things? He agreed. Or perhaps when neither of us brings forth the reason of the thing, do we contradict each other? Or in that case, would neither of us be making mention of the thing itself? He admitted that too. Well then, he said, when I pronounce the reason of the thing, but you pronounce that of some other thing, do we then finally contradict? Or rather, do I then speak of the thing, while you do not speak of it at all? And how could one who does not speak contradict one who does? At this, Ctesippus fell silent. But I, marvelling at what they were saying, said: In what way do you say this, Dionysodorus? Indeed, though I have heard this kind of argument many times from many people, I am always accustomed to marvel at it. For the followers of Protagoras and those even older than they used to employ it frequently. To me it has always seemed wonderful, and of such a nature as to subvert both others and itself. But I think I shall now hear the truth of it most especially from you. Does the argument mean that it is impossible to speak falsely, and that he who speaks must necessarily bring forth the truth, or not speak at all? He asserted this. Is it impossible to speak falsely, but possible to think falsely? Not even to think it, he said. Therefore, I said, there is no such thing as a false opinion. None at all. Nor is there ignorance or ignorant men. Or would it not be ignorance, if it existed, to have false feelings about things? Entirely. But that does not exist, I said. Certainly not, he replied. Do you introduce these things for the sake of conversation, O Dionysodorus, to bring in something marvelous? Or does it truly seem to you that no man is ignorant? But you yourself, he said, refute it. Can anything be refuted when no one, as you assert, lies? It cannot, said Euthydemus. You, Dionysodorus: I did not therefore order you to refute. For in what way could anyone order that which is not? O Euthydemus, I said, I do not learn these clever and noble things very well, but only touch upon them as if in passing. Perhaps, therefore, the question I ask is burdensome—

# EUTHYDEMUS, OR THE DISPUTATIOUS. FOLIO 104.

I will speak. But forgive me, I beseech you. Look, I pray: if no one can lie, nor hold false opinions, nor be ignorant, then no one can ever err while they are doing anything. For no one wanders away from that which they are doing. Is this not what you say? Plainly so. This, I said, is that burdensome question. For if we never err—neither in acting, nor in speaking, nor even in thinking—then what on earth did you come here to teach? Did you not proclaim above that you would deliver the highest virtue to anyone who wished it, more than all others? Are you so empty-headed, Socrates, said Dionysodorus, that you now remember what we said at the beginning? And if I said something last year, you are going to remember it now; yet you do not know how to deal with what has been said in the present moment. These arguments are very difficult, I said, and not without reason. For they are proclaimed by wise men, since it is most difficult to deal even with what was said most recently. For when you say, Dionysodorus, that I do not know how to deal with it, what is your primary point? Do you mean that I have no way to refute the present argument? For tell me, does that word mean something else to you—that I do not know how to "deal" with arguments? You yourself say something else, he said; is this not very difficult to deal with? Indeed, answer me. Before you answer, I said, Dionysodorus: Why do you not answer! he said. Is it fair? I asked. Fair. Then I: By what particular reason? Is it perhaps because you yourself have come to us as the wisest in disputation, and you know when one must answer and when one must not? And therefore you now answer nothing, because you recognize that nothing should be answered? To this he said: You are trifing, Socrates, and you neglect to answer. But, my good man, trust me and answer, since you confess that I am wise. I must obey entirely, for so it is fitting since you are presiding. Ask then. He said: Do all things that understand something have a soul? Or do they lack a soul? They have a soul. Do you know any word that has a soul? None indeed. Why then did you just now ask what that word "understood" to me? For no other reason, I said, than my own sluggishness, which forced me to err. Or perhaps I did not err; rather, I spoke correctly when I said that words "understand." But do you say I erred, or not? For if I did not err, you will not refute me now, wise though you may be, nor will you know how to deal with the argument. But if I did err, you are not speaking correctly even then, when you say that no one can err. And I do not bring these things up now against what you were saying last year. But it seems to me, Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, that this argument revolves back to the same point; and now, as used to happen in the past, it falls down after having thrown others down. That this should not happen to the men themselves, it seems your art—admirable as it is for its sharp diligence regarding arguments—has not yet provided a safeguard. Here Ctesippus spoke: You say marvelous things, O men of Thurii or Chios, or whatever other surname you please to claim. For you care nothing for delusions and trifles. But I, fearing it might come to insults, again calmed Ctesippus thus: O Ctesippus, I say the same things to you now that I said to Clinias: that you do not know how marvelous the wisdom of these guests is. 

<margin>Proteus the Egyptian sophist.</margin>

But they did not want to show it to us while acting seriously; instead, imitating Proteus the Egyptian sophist <note>A mythical sea-god who could change his shape to avoid answering questions; Socrates compares the sophists' slippery logic to this transformation.</note>, they deceive us with certain tricks. Let us therefore imitate Menelaus <note>In mythology, Menelaus held onto Proteus until he returned to his true form and gave answers.</note>; let us not let these men go before they reveal their true studies to us. For I think their work will appear to be something most beautiful when they begin to treat it seriously. Therefore, let us entreat them with exhortations and prayers as suppliants, that they might disclose their study to us. It seems I must again explain what sort of form of studies I require from them. I will therefore try to continue the discourse from where we left off above, if by some means I can provoke them to take pity on me as I struggle with heavy matters, and then they themselves might treat the matter earnestly. But you, Clinias, remind me where we interrupted the speech in the previous parts. For as I think, we broke off the speech here: when it had already been concluded by us that one must practice philosophy. Is it not so? CLINIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Philosophy is indeed the acquisition of knowledge. 

<margin>Philosophy is the acquisition of knowledge.</margin>

CLINIAS: Surely. SOCRATES: What knowledge, then, is it most fitting to acquire? Is it not, to speak briefly, that which profits us? CLINIAS: That very one. SOCRATES: Would that knowledge profit us most if we knew in which lands much gold is dug up? CLINIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: However, we refuted that above; because that knowledge would profit us no more even if we found all the gold without labor or digging the earth, or even if we turned stones into gold, as long as we were ignorant of how to use the gold. Do you not remember? CLINIAS: I remember, and very much so. SOCRATES: Nor is there any utility in any other knowledge, whether of money-changing, or medicine, or any other which teaches how to make something, but not at all how to use that which has been made. Is it not so? CLINIAS: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Moreover, even if there were a knowledge that made men immortal, but did not teach how to use that immortality itself, it would be entirely useless, if any faith is to be placed in our previous points. CLINIAS: All these things seemed so to us. SOCRATES: Therefore, noble boy, we need that knowledge in which both the making of the work and the use of the work coincide. CLINIAS: It appears so. SOCRATES: It is far from the case, then, that we ought to be makers of lyres and pursue such knowledge. For in these, the productive art is distinguished from the art which uses the same thing. For the art which manufactures the lyre and the one which strikes the lyre differ greatly from each other. Do they not? CLINIAS: It is so. SOCRATES: Nor again do we need the maker of flutes. For that art differs from the one that uses them. CLINIAS: Truly. SOCRATES: Is perhaps the faculty of composing speeches to be sought out, if one desires to be happy? CLINIAS: I do not think so. SOCRATES: What reason moves you? CLINIAS: I know certain authors of speeches who do not know how to use these speeches they have composed, just like the lyre-makers themselves with lyres: they constructed lyres for the use of others, which they who use them do not know how to make. It is similarly established regarding speeches that there is one art which composes and another which uses what has been composed. SOCRATES: You seem to have shown by a most evident argument that the art of those who compose speeches...

For indeed, men of this sort—the authors of Clinias’s speeches—whenever I speak to them, they seem to me wise above all other men, and their very art seems deeply divine and sublime. Nor is that surprising. For it is a small part of the art of enchantment, only slightly inferior to it. Furthermore, the power of enchantments consists in the charming and soothing of vipers, spiders, scorpions, and other wild beasts, as well as diseases. Oratory, in truth, is a certain delighting and softening of judges, assemblymen, and other crowds. Or do you feel otherwise? CLINIAS: Not otherwise; but exactly as you say. SOCRATES: Where then shall we turn? To which art, specifically? CLINIAS: I am in doubt. SOCRATES: But I think I have found it. CLINIAS: Which one? SOCRATES: The command of an army <note>Generalship</note> seems to me to be the one which, by its acquisition, makes anyone happy. CLINIAS: It does not seem so to me. SOCRATES: Why? CLINIAS: Because this seems to be a certain hunting art of men. SOCRATES: What of it? CLINIAS: Surely no work of hunting extends further than to tracking and capturing. But after the hunters have caught what they pursued, they are unable to use it. Instead, both those who hunt with dogs and those who fish present their prey to the cooks. Likewise, geometers, astronomers, and calculators are certain kinds of hunters; for they do not make figures and diagrams, but they discover these existing things. Since they themselves do not know how to use them, but are only able to hunt, whoever among them is not out of their mind hands over their discoveries to the practitioners of dialectic <note>The art of logical discussion and investigation of truth</note>, so that they may use them. SOCRATES: Ha! Most beautiful and wise Clinias, is it so? CLINIAS: Exactly so. And by the same reasoning, leaders of an army, after they have occupied either a city or an army, hand over the prey and spoils to the civil authorities. For they themselves do not know how to use those things which they have captured, just as bird-catchers, after they have caught quails, give them to the bird-keepers. If, therefore, we need that art which, once acquired, is engaged either in producing or in hunting, and also knows how to use what it has, and thereby makes its possessors happy, we must seek some other art besides the military one. CRITO: What are you saying, O Socrates! Did that mere youth say such things? SOCRATES: Do you not think so, Crito? CRITO: Not by Jove! For I believe that if he said such things, he would no longer need the instruction of Euthydemus or any other man. SOCRATES: Perhaps, indeed, Ctesippus said these things; I truly do not remember. CRITO: What Ctesippus! SOCRATES: At least I remember this: neither Euthydemus nor Dionysodorus brought these things forward. But, O blessed Crito, I suspect some more excellent man present said these things. For I do not doubt that I heard them. CRITO: By Jove, O Socrates, someone more excellent seems to have brought those things forth. But after this, what art did you examine? Did you find the art you were seeking, or not? SOCRATES: You ask if we found it? Something worthy of laughter happened to us. For in the manner of children who chase crested larks or skylarks, we were pursuing individual sciences with a certain vehement passion; and those sciences, which we always thought we were about to catch immediately, eluded us and suddenly slipped away. Why should I tell you many things? We certainly entered upon the "Kingly Art" <note>The art of ruling or statesmanship</note>; we contemplated whether this was the one that makes men happy. But as if having fallen into a labyrinth, while we were already hoping to be near the end, we were turned back again to the beginning, affected in the same way as we had been at the start of the inquiry. CRITO: How did this happen to you? SOCRATES: I will tell you. The kingly faculty seemed to us to be the same as the civil faculty. And since the military art and all other faculties seemed to yield the command of their works to the civil art—inasmuch as it alone knows how to use them—we thought nothing would hinder this from being the one we sought, and the cause of acting rightly in the city; and according to that line of Aeschylus, sitting alone at the stern of the city, ruling the rudders of the whole, it would dominate all things and render each thing useful. CRITO: Did it not seem right to you, O Socrates? SOCRATES: You yourself shall judge, Crito, if you wish to hear what happened to us next. For we searched again in this manner: "Come now, does the kingly art, presiding over all things, produce any work for us, or none?" We all agreed together that it certainly displays something. Would you not also grant this, Crito? CRITO: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: What, then, would you say its work is? Just as if I were to ask you: while Medicine rules over all things of which it is mistress, what work does it display? Would you not immediately answer "health"? CRITO: Certainly. SOCRATES: Likewise, your art of agriculture, while it rules over all things of which it is mistress, what work does it fulfill? Would you not say it provides us with nourishment from the earth? CRITO: Indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, the kingly faculty, since it rules over all things of which it is mistress, what work does it complete? Perhaps you do not have it ready at hand. CRITO: Not by Jove, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Nor did we, O Crito. But you know this at least: if this is the one we desire, it must be useful. CRITO: Greatly so. SOCRATES: Therefore, is it not necessary that it bring us some good? CRITO: Absolutely necessary. SOCRATES: But Clinias and I agreed together that "good" is nothing other than a certain knowledge. CRITO: So you were saying, certainly. SOCRATES: Anyone would say that these are the works of civil government: to make citizens wealthy, free, and harmonious. But all these things appeared to be neither good nor bad. It must, however, as was established, make them wise and bestow knowledge, if indeed it is to be the one that profits and makes them happy. CRITO: You tell the truth. For so it was established among you then, as you yourself have recounted. SOCRATES: Does the kingly discipline make men wise and good? CRITO: What prevents it, Socrates? SOCRATES: Does it provide all men, and in all things, goodness and every science? Shoemaking, carpentry, and all the rest? CRITO: I certainly do not think so, O Socrates. SOCRATES: But what knowledge? And in what matter shall we be helped? It must not be the maker of those works which are neither good nor bad. It is fitting that it provide no other knowledge than itself. Let us say, therefore, what this is, and by what we are helped. Do you wish us to say, O Crito, that it is the one by which we shall make others good? CRITO: I certainly wish it. SOCRATES: In what way will they be good to us? Or in what way useful? Or shall we say again that they will make others good? And those others again others? In which way...

# EUTHYDEMUS, OR THE DISPUTATIOUS

<margin>The proverb "Corinthus, son of Zeus."</margin>As if they were good, they appear nowhere. After we neglected those works which are proclaimed as the civil art, that which is said in the proverb happened to us: "Corinthus, son of Zeus" <note>original: "Iouis Corinthus." A Greek proverb referring to tedious repetition or someone who overrates their own importance, like the citizens of Corinth claiming divine ancestry.</note>. And, as I said above, we are at an equal distance—or even further than before—from the discovery of that art which is able to provide us with blessedness.

CRITO: By Jove, Socrates, you seem to have fallen into a great deal of ambiguity.

SOCRATES: Indeed, Crito, when I was submerged in this doubt, I immediately cried out as loudly as I could, imploring those strangers as if they were Castor and Pollux, the sons of Jove, to rescue us—namely myself and the youth—from the turbulent tossing of these arguments. I begged them to set aside their jokes and show us, through a serious method of disputation, what that most powerful knowledge is, which, once attained, allows us to spend the rest of our lives happily.

CRITO: And did Euthydemus wish to show you?

SOCRATES: Why not? With excessive magnificence, my friend, he began to speak in this manner:

EUTHYDEMUS: Shall I teach you, Socrates, this knowledge you have been seeking for so long? Or shall I show that you already possess it?

SOCRATES: O blessed man, is such authority within you?

EUTHYDEMUS: Greatly so.

SOCRATES: Show me then that I have it; for that would be easier for me than learning it anew at this age.

EUTHYDEMUS: Come then, tell me: do you know anything?

SOCRATES: I certainly know many things, but they are small.

EUTHYDEMUS: That suffices. Do you think it possible for any of the things that exist, to not be that very thing which it is?

SOCRATES: In no way.

EUTHYDEMUS: Do you assert that you know something?

SOCRATES: Certainly.

EUTHYDEMUS: Are you not then "knowing," if indeed you know?

SOCRATES: I am indeed, but only of that specific thing which I know.

EUTHYDEMUS: It makes no difference. Is it not necessary that you know all things, if you know any of the things that exist?

SOCRATES: No, by Jove! Since there are many other things I do not know at all.

EUTHYDEMUS: If there is something you do not know, are you "unknowing"?

SOCRATES: Of that specific thing, my friend, which I do not know.

EUTHYDEMUS: Nevertheless, you are "unknowing"; and a moment ago you were proclaiming yourself to be "knowing." And so it happens that you are the very one who both is and is not, at the same time, and in the same respect.

SOCRATES: Look, Euthydemus, as the proverb says, how beautifully <margin>The proverb "How beautifully you speak."</margin>you speak! By what reasoning, then, do I have that knowledge we are seeking? Because, evidently, it is impossible for a thing to be and not be at the same time. From which it follows that if I know one certain thing, I know all things; for I cannot be knowing and unknowing at the same time. And if I know all things, I also possess that knowledge. Is that not how you speak? And is this wisdom itself?

EUTHYDEMUS: You refute yourself, Socrates.

SOCRATES: But what of you, Euthydemus? Has the same not happened to you? For it does not trouble me much to suffer this alongside you and Dionysodorus, that charming head. Tell me, do you two not know some things and remain ignorant of others?

DIONYSODORUS: Not at all, Socrates.

SOCRATES: What are you saying? Do you know nothing?

DIONYSODORUS: On the contrary, we know.

SOCRATES: Then you know all things, if you know anything.

DIONYSODORUS: All things, certainly; and you too know all things, if you know any one thing.

SOCRATES: O Jupiter, what a marvelous thing to say, and what a huge benefit! Do all other men also know all things? Or nothing? For it does not seem right to say they know some things and are ignorant of others, and thus are knowing and unknowing at the same time. What shall we say then?

DIONYSODORUS: That all clearly know all things, if they know one thing.

SOCRATES: Good gods! Now at last, Dionysodorus, you seem to me to be speaking seriously. I have finally prevailed upon you to act with earnestness. Do you truly know all things? For instance, the art of the carpenter and the tanner?

DIONYSODORUS: Absolutely all.

SOCRATES: Do you also know how to stitch with sinews?

DIONYSODORUS: Certainly, and to make shoes.

SOCRATES: And the number of the stars, and of the grains of sand?

DIONYSODORUS: Those too.

SOCRATES: Do you expect us to concede these things?

CTESIPPUS: Bring us some proof by which we may be convinced you speak the truth.

DIONYSODORUS: What kind of proof?

CTESIPPUS: Do you know how many teeth Euthydemus has? And does Euthydemus know how many you have?

DIONYSODORUS: Is it not enough for you to have heard that we know all things?

CTESIPPUS: Not at all; just show us this one thing so we know you speak truly. For if you tell us how many teeth each of you has, and we count them afterward and find you were right, we will believe you in other matters as well.

But they, thinking Ctesippus was mocking them, refused to answer anything except that they knew all things, when questioned on individual points by Ctesippus. Indeed, Ctesippus asked openly about every single thing, even the smallest. They, however, answered with a brave spirit that they understood everything—like wild boars that rush together against a blow. Wherefore, Crito, I myself was finally forced by my own incredulity to ask Euthydemus if Dionysodorus also knew how to dance. He agreed. "Surely not," I said, "to leap over swords with his head bent toward the ground, or to be whirled upon a wheel?"—thinking his wisdom so great and surpassing. "There is nothing," he said, "that he does not know."

Then I asked: "Do you know all things only now? Or always?" "Always." "Did you know all things from a tender age, immediately upon being born?" "Everything," they both replied at once. To both of us, the thing seemed incredible.

Then Euthydemus said: "Do you not believe it, Socrates?" "Except for this," I said, "that it is likely you are wise men. But if you are willing to answer me," he said, "I will show that you too confess to these wonders." "This refutation will be welcome to me," I said. "For if my wisdom has been hidden from me in some matter, and you show that I know all things and have always known them, what greater gain could I find in life?"

"Answer now," he said. "Ask, as if I am ready to answer," I replied. "Are you a 'knower' of anything, Socrates, or of nothing?" "Of something." "And do you know by that same thing by which you are a knower, or by something else?" "By that which I am a knower. For I think you mean the soul. Is this what you understand?" "Are you not ashamed, Socrates," he said, "to ask a question in return when you are being questioned?" "But what shall I do?" I said. "I will do whatever you command; since I am ignorant of what you are asking. You command me to answer, and not to ask." "Do you conceive in any way," he said, "that which I am asking?" "Indeed." "Then answer according to what you conceive." "What," I said, "if you ask with one meaning and I answer with another, having conceived something different than you? Will you be satisfied if I answer nothing to the point?" "It will be enough for me," he said, "though not for you, I think."

Then I said: "By Jove, I will not answer until I understand how I must answer." "You do not answer," he said, "always according to what you conceive in your mind, because you are trifler, Socrates, and more foolish than is proper." I recognized then that he was angry with me, because I was scattering the words with which he sought to entangle me. Furthermore, Connus <note>Connus was Socrates' music teacher, often mentioned as being frustrated by Socrates' slow progress or questioning.</note> came to my mind, who is frequently indignant with me whenever I do not obey him; then me...

Wherefore I said to him: "If it seems to you, Euthydemus, that this is how we must proceed, then proceed. For you understand the method of disputation much better than I; since you possess this art, while I am but a novice. Therefore, ask again from the beginning."

"Answer again," he said. "Do you know by something that which you know, or by nothing?"

"By the soul," I said.

"Here," he said, "he anticipates the matter and answers more than was asked. I do not ask *by what* you know, but *whether* you know by something or not."

To this I replied more than was proper because of my lack of skill. "But forgive me, I pray. I will answer simply now: that I always know by something, whatever I know."

"Whether," he said, "always by this same thing, or sometimes by this and sometimes by another?"

"Always," I said, "when I know, I know by this."

At this he said, "Will you not cease to prevaricate?"

"Lest perhaps," I said, "that which is always said might deceive us, I answered thus."

"Do not say 'us,'" he said, "but 'yourself.' But answer: do you always know by this?"

"Always," I said, "after I have subtracted the 'when it is necessary' <note>Socrates is trying to qualify his answers with "when I know," but the sophists want an absolute "always."</note>."

"Do you not always know by this? And do you always know whether you know by some one thing that by which you know, or some things by one and others by another? Or do you know all things by this very same thing?"

"All things," I said, "whatever I know."

"Here again you overstep, Socrates."

"Let them except," I said, "what was said: 'whatever I know.'"

"I demand that you except nothing; rather, answer: could you know all things, unless you knew all things?"

"That would be a marvel," I said.

"Add now whatever you please," he said. "For you confess that you know all things."

"So it seems," I said, "since it is of no consequence what is said regarding 'whatever I know,' but rather that I know all things."

"And did you not always confess to know by this by which you know? Whether when you know, or in whatever way you please? For you have confessed to always know, and all things at once. It is established, therefore, that you knew as a boy: both when you were conceived, and when you were born; indeed, even before you were born; and before the origin of heaven and earth you knew all things, if indeed you always know. And by Jove <note>original: "per Iovem"</note>, you shall always know, and all things, if I so wish."

"But you will wish it," I said, "O highly honored Euthydemus, if you speak the absolute truth. But I do not have much confidence that you are able, unless your brother Dionysodorus here wishes the same thing with you; for thus perhaps you will have the power. Tell me further. How I shall not grant you the rest, I do not know—endowed as you are with such wonderful and new wisdom—so that I might know all things, since you assert it. But how shall I say that I know certain things of this sort, Euthydemus? Namely, that good men are just. Tell me, do I know that, or do I not?"

"You certainly know it."

"What? That good men are not unjust?"

"I have known that for a long time," I said. "But I am not asking that; rather, when did I learn that good men are unjust?" <note>Socrates is playing with their logic to see if they will force him to admit he knows a falsehood.</note>

"Nowhere," said Dionysodorus.

"Then I do not know this," I said.

Then Euthydemus, turning to Dionysodorus, said, "You are destroying the argument; and it will appear that this man, if he does not know, is both knowing and not knowing at the same time."

Dionysodorus indeed blushed. But I said: "What do you say, Euthydemus? Does it not seem to you that your brother speaks the truth, since he knows all things?"

"I am the brother of Euthydemus," Dionysodorus said.

"Let it be, O good man," I said, "until Euthydemus teaches me how I know that good men are unjust; and do not envy me this lesson."

"You are fleeing, O Socrates," said Dionysodorus, "and you do not wish to answer."

"I flee not without cause," I said, "for since I am weaker than either one of you, why

<margin>Hercules against the sophistical Hydra and the sophist Crab.</margin>

should I not flee from both? Indeed, I am much weaker than Hercules, who was not strong enough to fight at the same time against the sophistical Hydra—which, because of its wisdom, sprouted many heads for every one head of argument cut off—and also against a certain sophist Crab coming from the sea, and recently, as I think, brought in by ship. When Hercules was being distressed by the Crab on the left and bitten sharply with words, he implored the help of his nephew Iolaus, who greatly succored him. But if my Iolaus, Patrocles, should come, he would do far otherwise."

"Answer then," said Dionysodorus, "since you yourself proclaim these things: was Iolaus more the nephew of Hercules than yours?"

"I think it will be best that I answer you, Dionysodorus. For you would not cease questioning, and you would disturb the matter out of a certain envy, lest the wise Euthydemus teach me that thing. Answer then," he said.

"I answer," I said, "that Iolaus was the nephew of Hercules; but mine, as it seems, not at all. For his father Patrocles was not my brother; but someone named Iphicles, the brother of Hercules, was very close to him."

"And your Patrocles?" he said.

"Certainly, but from the same mother, not the same father."

"He is therefore a brother to you, and not a brother."

"Not from the same father, O best of men," I said. "For his father was Chaeredemus, but mine was Sophronicus."

"But were Sophronicus and Chaeredemus fathers?" he asked.

"Entirely; the former mine, the latter his."

"Was Chaeredemus other than a father?"

"Other than *my* father, certainly."

"Was he a father, while being other than a father? Or are you the same thing as a stone?"

"I feared," I said, "lest I should seem the same by your assertion. But to myself I do not seem so."

"Are you not, therefore, other than a stone?"

"Other, certainly."

"Because if you are other than a stone, you are not a stone. And if you are other than gold, you are not gold."

"So it is."

"By the same reasoning, since Chaeredemus is other than a father, will he not be a father?"

"It seems," I said, "that he is not a father."

To this Euthydemus added: "Chaeredemus is hardly a father; and again, since Sophronicus is other than a father, he is not a father. Therefore you are without a father, O Socrates."

But Ctesippus, taking up the discourse, broke in: "And your father, since the same thing has happened to him, is other than my father."

"Far from it," Euthydemus said.

"Is he the same?"

"The same, surely."

"I would not agree. But Euthydemus, is he my father only, or also the father of all other men?"

"Of all others as well. Do you think the same man, being a father, is not a father?"

"I had thought so," Ctesippus said.

"And gold, being gold, is not gold? And a man, being a man, is not a man?"

Then Ctesippus said, "Not as the saying goes, Euthydemus,

<margin>Proverb: To join flax to flax <note>Meaning to pile one absurdity upon another or to use circular reasoning.</note>.</margin>

you join flax to flax. You say a grave thing: if your father is the father of all."

"He is, however."

"Whether of men only, or also of horses and all other animals?"

"Of all, absolutely."

"And is your mother the mother of all?"

"The mother also."

"Therefore your mother is the mother of sea urchins."

"And yours," he said.

"And you, in turn, are the brother of gudgeons, puppies, and piglets."

"And you," he said.

"Furthermore, your father is a dog."

"And yours as well."

Here Dionysodorus said: "If you are willing to answer me, Ctesippus, I will make you concede these things. Tell me, do you have a dog?"

"And a very troublesome dog," Ctesippus said.

"Does he have puppies?"

"He has many such."

"And is the dog not the father of those?"

"Absolutely."

# EUTHYDEMUS OR THE DISPUTATIOUS ONE. FOLIO 106.

...for I have seen great signs from which I gather that he is their father. Is he not your dog? He is. Therefore, being a father, is he not yours? Wherefore your father is a dog, and you are the brother of puppies. But before Ctesippus could cut him off, Dionysodorus suddenly added: Answer a little further. Do you beat this dog? Laughing, Ctesippus said: I beat him, but I cannot beat you. Do you not then beat your own father? It would be far more just, he replied, if I beat your father, who, having acquired such "learning," fathered such wise sons. Surely, Euthydemus, your father and the father of the puppies has gained many good things from your wisdom. Neither he nor you, O Ctesippus, lack many good things. Nor do you, Euthydemus, nor any other man, he said. For tell me, Ctesippus, do you think it is a good thing for a sick man to drink a <term>drug</term><note>original: "pharmacum"</note> when he needs it, or not? Or is it good for a man about to fight to go forth armed or unarmed? I certainly think so, for I expect something extraordinary from you. You shall see for yourself best of all, he said. But answer: since you have confessed it is good to drink a drug when the situation demands, should one drink as much of this good thing as possible? And will it be best if someone grinds and pours into a cup as much <term>hellebore</term><note>A medicinal plant used in antiquity to treat madness, but poisonous in large doses.</note> as a wagon can carry? Certainly, said Ctesippus, if the one who is to drink it is as large as the Delphic statue. Is it not similar in war, he said, that if it is good to be supported by arms, one should have as many arms as possible, and a pack of javelins and shields should be carried around, since that is a good thing? Most certainly, said Ctesippus. But you, Euthydemus, do not think that only one javelin should be carried? I do indeed. Would you then arm <note>Geryon and Briareus were multi-armed/multi-headed giants of Greek mythology.</note> Geryon and Briareus in that way? I thought you were stronger, and this companion of yours likewise, being men-at-arms. Euthydemus remained silent. But Dionysodorus, in response to what Ctesippus had first answered, brought up: Does it seem good to you to have gold? Very much so, replied Ctesippus. And is it not good to have money always and everywhere? Most certainly, he said. Do you not confess that gold is good? We have already confessed it. Then one ought to have it always and everywhere, and as much as possible within oneself? And would he not be most happy who had three <term>talents</term><note>A very large unit of weight/currency.</note> of gold in his belly, one talent under his skull, and a <term>stater</term><note>original: "staterem .i. nummum quendam" - a specific gold coin.</note>—that is, a certain coin and weight of gold—in each of his eyes? They say, O Euthydemus, said Ctesippus, that among the Scythians those are the happiest and best men who contain much gold in their own skulls—just as you were saying a moment ago that the dog was a father. What is even more wonderful, they drink from their own gilded skulls and look into them, lifting their own scalps and foreheads with their hands. To this Euthydemus said: Do the Scythians and other men who can see, Ctesippus, see things that are capable of being seen, or things that are not? Things that are capable, clearly. And do you not also? I do likewise. Do you see our clothes? I see them. Therefore, these clothes can see. Ctesippus said: Marvellous! What further? he said. Nothing. But do you not think they see? You are such a pleasant man! You seem to me, Euthydemus, to have fallen asleep while wide awake, and I think you are able to speak while saying nothing. And you seem to be doing this. Is it not impossible, said Dionysodorus, to speak while being silent? Impossible, said Ctesippus. But for a speaker to be silent? Much less possible. Therefore, when you speak of a stone, do you not speak of a silent thing? And when you speak of wood and iron likewise? I will not grant you that iron things are silent, said Ctesippus. For if someone strikes them, they are said to ring and echo. Wherefore, because of your "wisdom," it escaped you that you were saying nothing in this. But show me what remains: that it is possible for a speaker to be silent. Certainly, it seemed to me then that Ctesippus was contending vehemently for the sake of his friend. When you are silent, said Euthydemus, are you not silent about all things? I am. Are you not then silent about any thing that speaks? If indeed those things that speak are counted in the number of all things. What then? asked Ctesippus, are all things not silent? No, said Euthydemus. Do all things speak, my good man? Rather, certainly, those that speak. I was not asking that, he said, but whether all things are silent or speak. Then, snatching the argument, Dionysodorus said: Neither, and both. For I know for certain that you will not know what to object to this answer. Immediately Ctesippus, as is his custom, bursting into loud laughter, cried out: O Euthydemus, this brother of yours has doubled back on his own speech and destroyed it; your logic has succumbed! Clinias also laughed, being greatly delighted. Wherefore Ctesippus, exulting, grew more than tenfold in joy. It seemed to me, however, that Ctesippus had extorted these very things from them by a certain cleverness through their own seduction. For such wisdom is not found among other men of our time. After this I said: Why do you laugh, O Clinias, at matters so serious and so beautiful? But Dionysodorus, turning to me, said: Have you ever seen a beautiful thing, Socrates? Many indeed, Dionysodorus. Are they anything other than <term>Beauty itself</term><note>A reference to the Platonic Idea or Form of Beauty.</note>? Or are they the same? I hesitated for a moment, and I thought I suffered this not without cause, since I could not remain silent any longer. At the same time, I answered that they were different from Beauty itself, yet a certain beauty was present in each. If a bull is present to you, he said, will you yourself be a bull? And because I am now present to you, are you Dionysodorus? Heaven forbid! I said. But he asked: In what way is one thing present to another, when one is one thing and the other is another? Do you doubt this? I said. For I was now striving to imitate their wisdom, being kindled by a desire for it. Why should I not doubt, he said, both I and all others, that which in no way exists? What are you saying, Dionysodorus? Is not the beautiful, beautiful? And the ugly, ugly? If it seems so to me, he said. Does it not seem so? Entirely. And is not the same, the same? And the different, likewise different? But surely that which is different is not the same! But I did not think even a child would suspect this: that what is different is anything but different. But, O Dionysodorus, you omitted that on purpose. You seem to me like craftsmen who, as is fitting for those traveling abroad, elegantly finish and hand over each point of the argument. Do you know, he said, what is fitting for each craftsman to perform? In the first place, do you know whom it becomes to forge bronze? A blacksmith, I said. And who should mold clay? A potter. Who again should slaughter and skin, and roast the meat cut into pieces, or...

Ctesippus manages to turn their own circular logic against them, leading to a moment of triumph and laughter.</summary>

...to boil? <note>The sophists are using a "reductio ad absurdum" argument here, suggesting that if it is right for a cook to do what is appropriate to his craft, then it must be right to treat the cook himself like the meat he prepares.</note> The Cook. Is it not true that whoever does what is appropriate acts rightly? Most certainly. And it is appropriate, as you say, for a cook to chop and skin. Did you grant this, or not? I granted it, I said: but please, forgive me. It stands to reason then, that if someone, by throat-cutting and carving, boils or roasts the cook, he will be doing what is appropriate. Furthermore, if someone hammers a blacksmith like bronze, or molds a potter like clay, he will similarly be performing what is fitting. O Neptune! I cried, now you have reached the very limit of wisdom. Will this wisdom ever be mine so that it becomes my own? Would you recognize it, Socrates, he asked, if it had already become your own? If you wish it so, I said: for I certainly wish it. What then: do you think you know what is yours? Indeed: unless perhaps you say otherwise. For it must begin from you, and end in this Euthydemus. Do you not think those things are yours, he asked, of which you are the master? And which you may use as you please: such as oxen and sheep? Do you consider those things yours which you can sell and give away, and vow to whichever of the gods you wish? And those which you cannot, are they not yours? Then I, thinking that some splendid question was about to arise from this, and immediately inflamed with a greed for hearing it, said: it is exactly so, for such things are indeed mine. Do you call those "animals" which have a soul? Those very ones. You confess then that of animals, only those are yours over which you can do all these things I just mentioned? I confess it. Here he drew back quite ironically, as if about to contemplate something great: then he said: Come tell me, O Socrates. Do you have a paternal Jupiter? <note>original: "Iupiter patrius." This refers to the "Ancestral Zeus." In Athenian tradition, Zeus was not usually called "Patrius" (Ancestral); that title belonged to Apollo.</note> Now I suspected the conversation would end up exactly where it did: and turning aside through a certain ambiguous detour, I wound myself up rightly and replied: He is not mine, O Dionysodorus. You are a miserable man, he said, and no Athenian: you who have neither ancestral gods, nor sacred rites, nor anything else noble and magnificent. Stop that, Dionysodorus, I said: do not speak ill omens, and do not instruct me so harshly. For I do have altars, and domestic and ancestral rites, and everything else of that kind that other Athenians have. Do the rest of the Athenians have an ancestral Jupiter? he asked. There is no such title among the Ionians, I said, nor among those who migrated from this city: nor among us, but rather an Ancestral Apollo because of the birth of Ion. <note>Ion was the mythical ancestor of the Ionian Greeks; Apollo was his father.</note> Jupiter is not called "Ancestral" by us: however, he is called the Protector of the City and the Guardian of the Tribes: and Minerva is the Guardian of the Tribes. That is enough, said Dionysodorus. For you have, it seems, Apollo, Jupiter, and Minerva. Entirely. And will these not be your gods? Namely, your progenitors and masters? Are they not yours? Did you not confess they were yours? I confessed it, what then? Are these gods not animals? You further granted that whatever has a soul is an animal: do these gods not have a soul? They certainly do. Are they therefore animals? They certainly are. And of animals, you said those were yours which you had the power to sell, give away, or dedicate to the gods at your pleasure. I cannot deny, Euthydemus, that I granted those things. Immediately he followed up: Since you confess that Jupiter is yours, and the other gods are yours, is it permitted for you to sell them, and give them away: and to treat them according to your whim like the other animals that are yours? I then, Crito, struck dumb by this wise speech, fell silent. But Ctesippus, trying to come to my aid, said: Bah! By Hercules, what a most splendid speech! To which Dionysodorus replied: Is Hercules "Bah," or is "Bah" Hercules? <note>The sophist is mocking Ctesippus's exclamation by treating the interjection as a noun.</note> Then Ctesippus said: By Neptune, what strong and hard speeches. I give up now. These men are invincible. At this point, friend Crito, no one present could contain themselves any longer from extolling their oration with the highest praise: and those guests, Dionysodorus and Euthydemus, exulting with laughter, noise, and joy, were almost undone by their own excitement. For previously, while individual points were being brought forward, only their followers would immediately applaud. But here, it seemed the very columns of the Lyceum <note>The gymnasium in Athens where Socrates often taught.</note> were shouting, applauding, and rejoicing. I myself was so affected that I asserted I had never seen any men of equal wisdom. And being utterly enslaved to their wisdom, I began to praise and celebrate them exceedingly. O men, I said, blessed by the wondrous gifts of nature: who have completed so great a task so easily and in so short a time. There are indeed many other noble things in your speeches, Euthydemus and Dionysodorus: in which this is especially magnificent: that you have no care for the many men who are considered illustrious, but only for those like yourselves. Indeed, I know for certain that very few people love speeches of this kind, and those are only people like you: the rest are so ignorant of them and despise them that I think they would feel more ashamed if they were to convict others with these arguments than if they were convicted by others themselves. Furthermore, your speeches have this popular and gentle quality: that when you say nothing is good or evil, nor white, nor anything else of the sort—nor that anything is at all different from anything else—you truly, as you claim, bruise and block the mouths of men. But because you block not only the mouths of others, but your own as well, it is a gracious thing: and you avoid the hatred and offense of the listeners. But the greatest thing is this: that these things have been so skillfully invented and established by you that you are able to pass them on to anyone in a short time. I have realized this, and I observe Ctesippus, and I consider how suddenly he began to imitate you. It is a fine thing to be able to teach the mystery of this matter as quickly as possible. However, it does not seem it would be worth the effort for you to discuss this in front of many people: rather, if you believe me: you will take care not to speak in a large gathering: lest perhaps those who first perceive these things feel no gratitude. Therefore, communicate these things only among yourselves: and let no one else hear them unless they have laid out silver. <note>A jab at the Sophists' practice of charging high fees for their lessons.</note> If you are wise, you will advise your disciples the same: never to speak of these things with anyone but themselves and you. For what is rare, Euthydemus, is to be honored. For water is bought at a very cheap price, though it is the most precious thing in nature, as Pindarus says. <note>A reference to the poet Pindar's famous line "Water is best."</note> But come, I said, take up this Clinia and me. When these and certain other brief things, O Crito...

# EUTHYDEMUS, OR THE DISPUTATIOUS. FOLIO CVII.

we followed, and then departed. Consider then whether you will come with me to these men. For they promise that they will teach anyone who is prepared to give them money; they exclude no natural talent or age. What is most profitable for you to hear: they say that the pursuit of amassing wealth does not prevent anyone from easily perceiving their wisdom. CRITO: Indeed, O Socrates, I am eager to hear them, and I would most willingly learn. Yet I seem to be one of those who are not like Euthydemus, but rather like those you mentioned a little while ago: who prefer to be refuted by others with little traps of this kind, rather than to refute others. Truly, I would be ridiculous if I proceeded to admonish you. Nevertheless, nothing prevents me from reporting to you now what I heard from those who left you when the assembly broke up. While I was walking, I met one of those who are esteemed to excel greatly in judicial cases <note>legal or courtroom oratory</note>. "O Crito," he said, "have you heard nothing from these wise men?" "Nothing, by Jove," I replied. "For the dense crowd and the tumult prevented me from attending." "Yet," he said, "it was a thing worth hearing." "Why?" "So that you might have heard those men disputing, who excel others in this kind of discourse." To him I said: "What did it seem like to you?" What else did he answer but what is always heard from such men when they are talking nonsense: that they wrangle with one another with a certain unworthy zeal over matters of no importance! He used such names with me. Then I said: "Nevertheless, philosophy is a graceful thing." "What do you mean 'graceful,' O blessed man!" he said. "Is it perhaps of no value? And yet if you had been present a little while ago, you would have blushed, I think, for the sake of your friend, who was so foolish that he wished to hand himself over to men who have no care for what they say, but catch at every single word and throw it back; even though they, as I was saying above, excel other such men of our age." "Truly, O Crito, both this study is most vile, and those who are engaged in it are ridiculous." To me indeed, O Socrates, that man—or whoever else disapproves—did not seem to disapprove of the matter itself correctly. But because someone would study to dispute with such men in a large assembly, he seems to me to have rightly censured it. SOCRATES: O Crito, these men are worthy of admiration. But I do not yet know who it is I am about to speak of. From which group was the one who met you and disparaged philosophy? Was he some orator from among those who are powerful in judicial contention? Or from those who send such men out, and compose the speeches with which the orators contend in court? CRITO: Not an orator at all; nor do I think he has ever pleaded in court; but they say he understands the judicial matter itself best, and composes elegant and eloquent speeches. SOCRATES: I understand now. And I myself was just about to say the same thing. Surely these are the ones, O Crito, whom Prodicus <note>A famous Greek sophist and contemporary of Socrates</note> placed on the borders between the philosopher and the statesman. These men think they are the wisest of all, and moreover appear so to very many; but they think that only philosophers are an impediment to them, preventing them from being equally approved by all. They believe, therefore, that if they spread this common opinion against philosophers—that they are of no value—they will without controversy carry off the highest glory of wisdom among all people. For they think they are truly the wisest, but are hindered in private conversations when the followers of Euthydemus oppose them. Because they are wise, they wish to seem consistent for this reason: that they have enough of philosophy, and enough also of political skill; and as much as is necessary, they are masters of both; and being placed outside the turbulent tumults of civil business, they enjoy the fruits of wisdom pleasantly. CRITO: Do these men seem to you to say anything of substance, O Socrates? SOCRATES: Not at all. CRITO: Nevertheless, the speech of these men has something plausible about it. SOCRATES: It has, as you say, O Crito, plausibility rather than truth. Nor can they easily be persuaded that both men and all other things which are intermediate between two certain things, and participate in both, are so constituted that if they are from a bad and a good thing, they become better than the one and worse than the other; but those which are from two good things not leading to the same end, are worse than both for performing that work toward which both those things from which the composition is made look. But those things which are constituted from two evils not tending to the same end, these alone are better than both of those in which they participate. If, therefore, philosophy is good, and civil action is good, but each contributing to a different end, and these men are masters of both and are placed in the middle of both, they conclude nothing; for they are worse than both. But if one of these is good and the other bad, they are better than the one and worse than the other. But if both are bad, only then would they speak the truth; otherwise, not at all. Nor do I think they will confess that both are bad, nor even that one is good and the other bad. But truly these masters of both are more foolish than both for that purpose to which philosophy and civil action pertain; and though they hold the third place, they do not hesitate to usurp the first. Their desire should be forgiven and not be a cause for indignation; yet they are to be judged as they are. For we ought to love everyone who says anything leading to prudence and acts manfully. CRITO: Indeed, O Socrates, as I often speak with you, I am in doubt by what means I should educate my sons. The younger one is still more tender than discipline requires; but Critobolus is now an adult and needs someone to direct him. Whenever I speak with you, I am so affected that I think it is madness to have struggled for the sake of my sons, first regarding marriage—that they might be born from the most noble mother—then that I might leave them a large inheritance, but to neglect their education. But when I look at those who profess to instruct men, I am deterred; and to me, considering it, every one of them seems far removed from the thing he preaches. And to tell you the truth, I do not know how to exhort and provoke my son toward philosophy. SOCRATES: O friend Crito, are you unaware that in every pursuit, vile and worthless men are many, but the upright are few, and those are to be held in the highest value? Does it not seem to you that gymnastics, commerce, rhetoric, and military affairs are something beautiful? CRITO: To me, certainly. SOCRATES: Do you not see that in each of these arts, many are foolish and unfit for every work?

CRITO: That would not be becoming, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Take care then, O Crito, lest you do what is unbecoming. ->The Argument <note>A summary or introduction</note> of Marsilio Ficino for the Lesser Hippias.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring a seated figure (possibly a scholar or saint) within a classical architectural frame with floral motifs.</image-desc> Since the wonderful goodness of our Socrates and Plato most diligently provides in many ways everywhere lest credulous youth be captured by the deceitful snares of the sophists <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece often criticized by Plato for prioritizing persuasion over truth</note> and, once captured, be destroyed: not without justice does he harass Hippias of Elis, the most insolent and deceitful of the sophists, in two dialogues, namely the Greater and the Lesser. In the Greater, he demonstrates that Hippias, a professor of the most beautiful things, is entirely ignorant of what beauty itself is. In the Lesser, he shows that this same man, boasting that he can discern the liar from the truthful man better than others, errs completely in the definition of both. Thus it is clear that as Hippias is the most arrogant of all, so he is also the most ignorant and appears most foolish. I pass over now how, as is the custom of sophists, he depicts him as a boastful and reckless author; and though he promises everything, in all things he gives only words, performing nothing in truth; and while he glories in the greatest things, he falters even in the smallest. But to return to the definition of the liar and the truthful man, the liar ought to be rightly described as: he who most wishes to, and in whatever way he can and knows how, tells lies. The truthful man, on the contrary, is he who most wishes to, and in whatever way he can and knows how, speaks the truth. But Hippias, the most unskilled master of all arts and the most confused distinguisher of the truthful and the liar, defines them in the opposite order. He says the liar is he who is most able and knows how to lie whenever he wishes; and the truthful man is he who, whenever he wishes, is able and knows how to speak the truth. From this he is first forced to admit that liars are powerful, knowing, prudent, and wise. Secondly, that they are good at those things in which they are powerful and wise. Thirdly, by leading him through individual arts, he is compelled to admit that in any matter or art, the same person is both truthful and a liar, which he had denied from the beginning. For indeed, in any matter, he who is best skilled is likewise best able and knows how, at his own will, to speak the truth as well as to lie. Fourthly, he is led to concede that the truthful man is no better than the liar; since as much as the truthful man is sufficient and good for speaking the truth, so much does the liar appear sufficient and good for lying. After this, Socrates brings the sophist into an ambiguity: which of the two sins more gravely—he who lies willingly, or he who lies unwillingly? The sophist does not know how to solve this, nor does Socrates wish to solve it for the sophist. But it is to be solved thus: In those things which pertain to the intellect, those who lie voluntarily err less; but in those things which regard morals, they err more. He who tells a lie unwillingly, however, has the truth against him. Then he doubts which err more: those who sin by deliberate effort, or those who sin through weakness or ignorance. It is proved by long circuits of induction that in those things pertaining to nature and art, and their instruments, a vice committed through impotence or ignorance is more grave than one perpetrated by malice. For the good of nature consists in power itself; the good of art consists in this same power and, moreover, in knowledge. Evil, therefore, is in the opposites. From these points, Socrates transfers the argument from the specific topic to morals: concluding the same in the category of morals as in the category of nature and art. Although Socrates understands that this ought not to be done, he nevertheless strives to declare that the sophist notices this not at all. Certainly, in those things which pertain to the will and morals: malice (that is, a certain will to sin) sins more gravely than if one sins through impotence or ignorance. Finally, Socrates says that justice is either power or knowledge or both. He knew to add—but did not wish to—a third thing, namely: the will. For justice consists most of all in the will. He wished to demonstrate that this was hidden from the sophist. But let us now conclude the argument with these previous precepts: One must teach without envy. One must learn without shame. Thanks must always be given to the teacher. The inventions of others must not be usurped for oneself.

->THE END OF THE ARGUMENT.<-
