# HIPPIAS MINOR, OR ON LYING

<margin>Signature: o iiii</margin>

Envy will not prevent Hippias from answering what is asked. Will you answer, Hippias, if Socrates asks something? HIPPIAS: I would not be acting rightly, Eudicus, if I were now to reject Socrates' questioning. I am a man accustomed to traveling from my homeland of Elis to the Olympic festivals—where Greeks from all sides flow together for the common celebration—and there at the temple, I offer myself to speak on whatever anyone desires to have demonstrated, and to answer every single question. SOCRATES: Oh, what a happy fortune has befallen you, Hippias, if you arrive at the sacred festival every Olympiad <note>The four-year interval between Olympic games</note> with such confidence in your mind's wisdom. I would certainly be amazed if any athlete concerned with bodily exercise went there to compete relying as much on his physical strength as you do on the subtlety of your mind. HIPPIAS: I am rightly so disposed, Socrates; for from the time I began to compete in the Olympics, I have not yet found anyone superior to me in any matter. SOCRATES: By Hercules, what you say is magnificent, Hippias! This glory of yours will be a monument of wisdom for both your country and your parents. But what, then, do you judge concerning Achilles and Ulysses <note>Odysseus</note>? Which of these do you think is the more excellent, and in what way? Furthermore, while many of us were inside and you were holding forth, some of your words escaped me; yet I hesitated to inquire because there was a great crowd, and also lest I should be a hindrance to your speech. But now, since we are fewer, and Eudicus here bids me ask, show us more clearly what you were saying about these men, and how you were judging them. HIPPIAS: I am indeed willing, Socrates, to report more openly than I did then what I think about these and others. I assert that Homer fashioned Achilles as the best man of all who besieged Troy; Nestor as the wisest; and Ulysses as the most exceptionally shrewd and "multiform" <note>original: *multiformem*, translating the Greek *polytropos*, meaning versatile, wily, or of many shifts</note>. SOCRATES: Good heavens, Hippias! Will you grant me this favor: not to laugh at me if I am slow to perceive and ask questions repeatedly? Please deign to answer me freely and easily. HIPPIAS: It would indeed be shameful, Socrates—since I teach these same things to others and demand money for them—if I did not indulge you when you ask, or answer with a cheerful mind. SOCRATES: You speak very well indeed. Truly, when you said Achilles was fashioned as the best man and Nestor as the wisest, I thought I understood what you were saying. But when you called Ulysses shrewd and multiform, to tell the truth, I did not understand what you meant to signify. And tell me—for perhaps from this I may perceive it better—was not Achilles also introduced by Homer as multiform and shrewd, or not? HIPPIAS: Not at all, Socrates; he is entirely simple. For in the "Supplications" <note>Referring to Book 9 of the Iliad, the Embassy to Achilles</note> themselves, when he introduces them debating, he makes Achilles speak thus against Ulysses:

-> "O most noble weaver of deceits, Ulysses, <-
-> It is fitting for me to repel your words without fear, <-
-> As I think ought to be done: so that you do not <-
-> Wear me down from this side and that with deceptive fictions. <-
-> For that man is more hateful to me than the gates of dark Hades, <-
-> Who hides one thing in his heart, <-
-> And then openly utters whatever else seems fit. <-
-> But I will now speak as I believe it shall be." <-

In these verses, he declares the character of each: that Achilles is truthful and simple, while Ulysses is shrewd and a liar. Indeed, in this passage, Achilles directs these words against Ulysses. SOCRATES: I think I now understand what you say, Hippias. For by "shrewd," you apparently mean "a liar." HIPPIAS: Exactly, Socrates. For Homer often fashions Ulysses as such in both the *Iliad* and the *Oldyssey*. SOCRATES: Therefore, Homer thought that the truthful man was one person, and the liar was another; and that both were not the same person. HIPPIAS: What prevents that, Socrates? SOCRATES: And do you yourself think the same, Hippias? HIPPIAS: Most of all. For I would be greatly in error if I felt otherwise. SOCRATES: Let us set Homer aside, then, since it is not possible to ask him what his meaning was in composing these verses. But since you have taken up the cause, and those things which you assert Homer said seem right to you, answer for Homer and yourself at the same time. HIPPIAS: So be it. Ask briefly whatever you please. SOCRATES: Do you call "liars" those who are unable to do anything—like the weak or the exhausted—or those who are able to do something? HIPPIAS: Those who are powerful; and especially so in many other things, but also in deceiving men. SOCRATES: They are therefore powerful according to your speech, and shrewd, are they not? HIPPIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: But are they shrewd and crafty through some sort of stupidity and imprudence? Or rather through cunning and prudence <note>original: *prudentia*, meaning practical wisdom or foresight</note>? HIPPIAS: Through cunning most of all, and prudence. SOCRATES: They are prudent, then, as it seems. HIPPIAS: Very much so. SOCRATES: And since they are prudent, are they ignorant? HIPPIAS: On the contrary, they are most knowing. For this is why they seduce others. SOCRATES: Since they are knowing in these things which they know, are they foolish, or rather wise? HIPPIAS: Wise, evidently, in these very matters of deceiving. SOCRATES: Stop, I pray; let us repeat what has been said so we may inspect what you are saying. You say that liars are powerful, and prudent, and likewise knowing and wise, regarding those things in which they are liars? HIPPIAS: I do. SOCRATES: And that others are truthful, while others are liars, and these are far contrary to one another? HIPPIAS: I say that too. SOCRATES: From this it follows, then, that liars are among the number of the powerful and the wise. HIPPIAS: Most certainly. SOCRATES: But when you say that liars are powerful and wise in these same things, do you mean they are powerful at lying if they wish, or powerless in the things they lie about? HIPPIAS: Powerful, indeed. SOCRATES: To speak summarily, then, liars are those who are powerful and wise at lying. HIPPIAS: Clearly. SOCRATES: Therefore, a man who cannot lie, and knows nothing, will not be a liar. HIPPIAS: That is so. SOCRATES: But a man is powerful who does what he wants when he wants—I mean one not hindered by disease or such things; but just as you can write my name whenever you wish, so I now ask: do you not call a man so disposed "powerful"? HIPPIAS: Truly. SOCRATES: Tell me, Hippias: are you not skilled in numbering and calculating? HIPPIAS: Most of all. SOCRATES: If someone, therefore, should ask you how much three times seven hundred is...

# BOOK NINETEEN.

<meta>Catchword: Ulysses indeed [is] deceitful</meta>

to complete the number, would you not answer most quickly and most truly of all concerning these things? HIPPIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Is it not because you are most powerful and most wise regarding these matters? HIPPIAS: Surely. SOCRATES: Are you merely the wisest and most powerful? Or are you also the best in those same things in which you excel in wisdom and power: that is, in calculating numbers? HIPPIAS: And the best as well, Socrates. SOCRATES: Therefore, you could speak the truth about these things best above all others: or not? HIPPIAS: I believe so, indeed. SOCRATES: And what about false things regarding the same? Come now, Hippias, answer as before, generously and magnificently. If someone asks how much is three times seven hundred: would you yourself lie most effectively about these things? And would you always pronounce falsehoods about them according to the same principles, if you wished to lie, and never offer the truth? Or would he who is ignorant of numbers be able to lie more than you when you wish to lie? Or rather, would the ignorant man often, while wishing to speak falsehoods, perhaps speak the truth against his own intention because he is ignorant of the matter itself? Whereas you, since you are wise, whenever you wish to lie, would you always lie consistently? HIPPIAS: It is as you say. SOCRATES: Therefore, is the liar a liar regarding other things, but not regarding numbers, nor will he lie about number? HIPPIAS: On the contrary, also regarding numbers. SOCRATES: Let us assume this then, Hippias: that regarding calculation and number, there is someone who is a liar. HIPPIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Who will this be? It is necessary that he be able to lie, as you yourself were saying, if he is to be a liar. For it was said by you, if you remember, that he who is unable to lie is not a liar. HIPPIAS: I remember indeed; and it was so said. SOCRATES: Was it not established just a moment ago that you are the most powerful at lying in calculating numbers? HIPPIAS: That was also said. SOCRATES: And are you not also most powerful at offering the truth about these same numbers? HIPPIAS: Very much so. SOCRATES: Therefore, the same person is most able to speak the truth and to lie in calculating: and that is the one who is good at numbers, namely the calculator. HIPPIAS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Who else then, Hippias, would be a liar in calculating except the one who is good at it? For this one is powerful, and this one is also truthful. HIPPIAS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Do you see that the same person is truthful in these things and a liar? And the truthful man is in no way better than the liar himself. For they are the same; nor are they greatly contrary, as you recently thought. HIPPIAS: It certainly does not appear so now in these matters. SOCRATES: Do you wish for us to consider this in other things as well? HIPPIAS: As you please. SOCRATES: Are you not also skilled in geometry? HIPPIAS: I am. SOCRATES: And does not the same thing happen in geometry? Furthermore, the same man can pronounce falsehoods most effectively about figures who can also speak the truth. And that man is the geometer. HIPPIAS: Indeed. SOCRATES: Is anyone else good at these things besides him? HIPPIAS: No one else. SOCRATES: Can the good and wise geometer not do both? And if anyone else is a liar regarding figures, it is most of all he who is good at them: for he is powerful; but the bad man is powerless at lying, nor could he ever be a liar who is powerless at lying, as was conceded. HIPPIAS: These things are true. SOCRATES: Let us look further at a third, the astronomer: which art you, Hippias, are accustomed to profess even more than the previous ones. Is it not so? HIPPIAS: Certainly so. SOCRATES: Does not the same thing happen in astronomy? HIPPIAS: It is consistent, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Therefore, in astronomy also, if anyone else is a liar: it will be most of all he who is a good astronomer. HIPPIAS: For he is able to lie to the highest degree. For he who is powerless is not [a liar]: for he is ignorant in himself. SOCRATES: Therefore, the same man will be both truthful and a liar in astronomy. HIPPIAS: It seems so. SOCRATES: Come, Hippias, think generally through all the sciences whether it is so or otherwise. For you are adorned with more arts than all others. Just as I once heard you boasting: that you abounded in much wisdom to be desired above others: and while walking and disputing in the forum among the [money-changers'] tables. You added moreover

<margin>It is related that Hippias made for himself his ring, clothes, etc.</margin>

that you once went to the Olympic contest, a sight to behold in the adornment of your body: and that you had made all the ornaments of your body with your own hands. First indeed the ring which you had, for you began from here, was your own work, as if you were skilled in engraving: furthermore, you carried a certain seal, your own work: and a strigil <note>A curved tool used by ancient Greeks to scrape oil and dirt from the skin</note> and an ointment jar likewise your own work: even shoes sewn by your own hands: a cloak and an undergarment woven by you. And what seemed even more wonderful, and a sign of singular wisdom, you said you had shown a belt, your own work, similar to Persian and precious ones. Likewise certain of your poems, songs, tragedies, dithyrambs <note>Choral hymns sung in honor of Dionysus</note>, and many varied orations composed in prose style: besides, you had made trial before all others in the arts which I mentioned above: and in rhythms and harmonies and the study of letters: and in many others of this kind, if I remember correctly. But indeed, I had overlooked the art of your memory, in which you think you excel in a wonderful way. Perhaps indeed I have forgotten many other things. But what I myself ask, observing your arts, by which you will sufficiently judge others as well, come tell me if you find anywhere from these things which were conceded between us, that the truthful man is different from the liar, and that they are not the same. Seek in whatever wisdom or cleverness or however it pleases you to call it. But you will never find it, my friend: for it is nowhere; if it is anywhere, tell me. HIPPIAS: I do not find it at present, Socrates. SOCRATES: Nor will you find it hereafter, as I think. But if I speak the truth, remember, Hippias, what follows from the previous points. HIPPIAS: I do not quite notice what you are saying, Socrates. SOCRATES: There is no need at present for the art of memory: for it is clear that you are at work, not merely opining: but I will now remind you. You remember saying that Achilles was a man who spoke the truth: but Ulysses was a liar and versatile <note>original: "versutum" - meaning clever, shifty, or many-turned</note>. HIPPIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: But now you perceive that the same man has appeared to be both truthful and a liar. Therefore, if Ulysses was a liar, he was also truthful. Likewise, if Achilles was truthful, he was also a liar. These men are neither different from each other nor contrary: rather, they turned out to be similar. HIPPIAS: You always, Socrates, weave such little traps: and you catch what is most troublesome in speech, and for this you handle these smallest points: nor do you contend against the whole matter itself about which we are speaking. For if you wish, I will now show you with more arguments and sufficient reason that Homer fashioned Achilles as better and truthful: but Ulysses indeed [is] deceitful...

<summary>Socrates uses the examples of arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy to force Hippias to admit that the person most capable of telling the truth is also the one most capable of lying. He then applies this logic to Homer's heroes, arguing that Achilles and Ulysses are not opposites but possess the same capacity for both truth and deception.</summary>

# HIPPIAS MINOR, OR ON LYING. PAGE 109.

<note>original: "HIPPIAS MINOR VEL DE MENDACIO"</note>

...and in many things measuring; and that Achilles is the inferior. But if it pleases you, answer in turn: and compare your speech with mine, by which you may show the other to be better. And so those present here will better understand which of us has spoken more correctly. 

**SOCRATES:** I do not doubt that, nor do I contend, Hippias, that you appear wiser than I. Indeed, I yield to you. But I have always been accustomed, when someone disputes about a matter, to attend diligently: especially when the one speaking seems to me to be wise. Then, truly eager to learn, I observe what is said: I inquire, I connect, and I repeat, so that I may perceive the words more clearly. But if I hold the speaker himself in small regard, I neither ask anything of him, nor do I attend to what he says. And by this very conjecture, you will understand whom I estimate as wise. For you will see me listening most accurately to their words, and questioning them, so that I may profit in life by learning something. And now indeed, when I turned my attention to your words—by which you show, through the testimony of those poems, that Achilles speaks against Ulysses as a boaster—it seemed a certain wonder to me if you spoke the truth. Since Ulysses himself is crafty, his lying can be refuted by no other; but Achilles seems to be both crafty and versatile, or at least he is so in your speech. For he lies. For when he had pronounced those verses which you have now reviewed:

> *He is more hateful to me than the gates of dark Hades,*
> *Who hides one thing in his heart, and speaks another:*
> *Then openly brings forth whatever else seems fit:*
> <note>A translation of Homer, Iliad 9.312-314</note>

shortly after he adds:

> *Ulysses the crafty shall not persuade me hereafter,*
> *But tomorrow, when I have performed sacrifices to Jove and the rest,*
> *I will draw my ships into the sea: which you shall see at first light,*
> *In which you will behold, if you only desire to see, strong men,*
> *Neptune will fill the sails with favorable winds,*

Likewise above, quarreling against Agamemnon, he says:

> *In my fatherland Phthia: for my mind does not wish that here*
> *Neither you, Agamemnon, should persist on Trojan lands.*
> *To the inhabitants of heaven, the ships gathered on the curved shore*
> *To sail through the Hellespontine sea fit for fish.*
> *And learned men leaning on their oars. For if*
> *The third light stays in the fruit-bearing shores of Phthia.*
> *Behold, I shall go home with my black ships, which is better,*
> *I shall fill them with riches, inglorious in strong arms.*

Having said these things, then before the whole army, and then to his friends, it nowhere appears that he either girds himself for the work or draws the ships, as if about to return home; rather, he cares very little whether the things he speaks are true. I asked you this, Hippias, from the beginning, when I was uncertain which of these is held more excellent by the poet, and I thought both were the best of men: and it is difficult to know which of them excels more in lying, and in truth, and in other virtue. For both are very close in this. 

**HIPPIAS:** You do not discern correctly, O Socrates. For when Achilles lies, he seems to lie not out of treachery, but unwillingly because of the misfortune of the army: forced to remain and give aid; but Ulysses lies voluntarily and by guile. 

**SOCRATES:** You deceive me, dearest Hippias, and you yourself imitate Ulysses. 

**HIPPIAS:** Not at all, Socrates. What do you say, and for what reason? 

**SOCRATES:** Because you say Achilles does not lie out of treachery: he who was so much a deceiver and a plotter beyond his own boasting, just as Homer fashions him: that he was so much more clever than Ulysses that he hid his own vanity from him, while he dared to speak things contrary to himself in his presence, and concealed it from Ulysses. Wherefore Ulysses seems to bring nothing against him, as one who did not notice the lie. 

**HIPPIAS:** What are these things you say, O Socrates! 

**SOCRATES:** Do you not know that he said to Ulysses that he would depart at first light; but to Ajax, not so, but otherwise? 

**HIPPIAS:** Where then? 

**SOCRATES:** In these verses:

> *When I shall have heard that Hector, son of Priam, has come in arms,*
> *Who may press the Greeks subdued by war:*
> *For Hector raging against my ships or camp,*
> *No care of dire war shall hold me before then,*
> *Seeking the ships and long tents of the Myrmidons,*
> *And he who would hereafter hurl fire into the ships themselves.*
> *I do not think he will dare to touch them in the doubtful war.*

Or do you think, Hippias, that the son of Thetis, educated by the most wise Chiron, was so forgetful that, although he had previously thundered against those very vain and various boasters, he himself immediately said to Ulysses—as if having forgotten his own words—that he would sail; but to Ajax that he would stay: rather than having plotted, since he knew Ulysses was older, and far more powerful than himself in fabricated machinations and guiles? 

**HIPPIAS:** It does not seem to me that Achilles said those things by guile: rather, persuaded otherwise by his very simplicity, he spoke differently with Ajax than with Ulysses. But Ulysses, whether he speaks true or false things, always stretches out snares. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, as it seems, Ulysses is better than Achilles. 

**HIPPIAS:** Not at all, O Socrates. 

**SOCRATES:** Did it not appear above that those who speak a lie voluntarily are better than those who do so involuntarily? 

**HIPPIAS:** In what way, Socrates, can those who knowingly and willingly do injustice, deceive, and harm, be better than those who do these things against their intention? Since much is forgiven to him who brings injury through ignorance: speaks a lie: or commits any other evil: and the laws look more severely upon those who do evils and lie willingly, than those who do so unwillingly. 

**SOCRATES:** You see, Hippias, that I speak the truth when I say that I am accurate in the questioning of wise men: and while I fail greatly in other things, I have only this much good. For what the nature of things itself is, I do not know: which can be conjectured most from this: because as often as I speak with any of you, who excel in the reputation of wisdom, and have all the Greeks as witnesses of your learning, I appear to know nothing. For never does the same thing seem to me, so to speak, as it does to you. And what is a more evident proof of ignorance than if someone disagrees with wise men? Yet I have this wonderful good which saves me: since without the blush of shame I prepare myself for learning. I ask and I inquire: and I have great gratitude for the one responding: nor have I ever been ungrateful to anyone: nor have I ever claimed for myself the inventions of others before listeners: but I follow the teacher with praises...

# BOOK NINETEEN.
## XIX.

I always praise him: and I grant to each man what is his own. And yet, regarding what you yourself are saying now: I by no means accept it; on the contrary, I disagree greatly, and I know for certain that this happens through my own fault. Indeed, I confess myself to be such as I am, so that I do not exalt myself. To me, Hippias, it seems entirely the opposite of how it appears to you. For I think that those who harm people, act unjustly, lie, deceive, and do wrong on purpose <note>original: "sponte" — voluntarily or by choice</note> are better than those who do so unintentionally. Sometimes, however, I judge the opposite, and I wander astray concerning these matters, as one who is ignorant of the thing itself. Behold, now a certain sickness of the mind has invaded me: and it seems to me that those who sin on purpose regarding something are better than those who err against their own intention. I consider our previous discussions to be the cause of my present passion, from which it happens that, for the moment, I think those who sin unintentionally are worse than those who do so on purpose. Therefore, be gracious to me, and let no envy hold you back from curing my soul. You will confer a much greater benefit upon me if you free my soul from ignorance than if you free my body from disease. If you wish to accomplish this with many words, I foretell to you that you will not cure me in this way, for I shall not follow. But if you are willing to answer as before, you will help me greatly. I hope, moreover, that this will not be harmful to you. Truly, I shall now rightly call upon you, son of Apemantus <note>Socrates addresses Eudicus, the son of Apemantus, who arranged the meeting</note>. For you yourself induced me to dispute with Hippias. Therefore, if Hippias is now willing to answer, ask him on my behalf.

**EUDICUS.** There is no need for my prayers to Hippias, Socrates. For he did not set out to answer as if by compulsion; rather, he promised he would answer everyone freely. Were these not the things you were saying, Hippias?

**HIPPIAS.** I was indeed saying them. But Socrates here, O Eudicus, always throws the speakers into confusion and seems to be a sort of troublemaker <note>original: "maleficus" — literally an evildoer or sorcerer, here meaning one who uses "dirty tricks" in logic</note>.

**SOCRATES.** O best of men, Hippias, I do not do these things on purpose. I would certainly be wise and clever according to your own speech! But I act against my intention. Therefore, forgive me. For you say that one who sins unintentionally ought to be forgiven.

**EUDICUS.** Do not do otherwise, Hippias; but for our sake, and because of the things said to you above, answer the things Socrates asks.

**HIPPIAS.** I shall indeed answer, since you ask it. Ask, therefore, whatever you please.

**SOCRATES.** I vehemently desire, Hippias, to consider what was just said: which ones are better,

<margin>The question of which are better: those who sin voluntarily by choice, or those who do the opposite.</margin>

those who sin voluntarily on purpose, or those who do the opposite? I hope, moreover, that it can be considered most rightly in this way. Answer now. Do you call a certain runner good?

**HIPPIAS.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** And a bad one?

**HIPPIAS.** Yes.

**SOCRATES.** Is not the one who runs well good, and the one who runs poorly bad?

**HIPPIAS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Does not he who runs slowly run poorly, and he who runs swiftly run well?

**HIPPIAS.** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES.** In running itself, therefore, speed is a good thing, and slowness is an evil.

**HIPPIAS.** What then?

**SOCRATES.** Which runner, therefore, is better: the one who runs slowly on purpose, or the one who does so otherwise?

**HIPPIAS.** The one who does so of his own will.

**SOCRATES.** Is not running a form of doing something?

**HIPPIAS.** It is doing, certainly.

**SOCRATES.** And is doing something a form of performing an action <note>original: "operari" — to work or produce an effect</note>?

**HIPPIAS.** Indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who runs poorly performs this evil and shameful thing in his running.

**HIPPIAS.** Evil, why not?

**SOCRATES.** But he runs poorly who runs slowly.

**HIPPIAS.** Truly.

**SOCRATES.** Does not, therefore, the good runner perform this evil and shameful thing by design, while the bad runner does it contrary to his purpose?

**HIPPIAS.** It seems so.

**SOCRATES.** In running, therefore, he is worse who does evil things against his will than he who does them willingly.

**HIPPIAS.** In running, clearly.

**SOCRATES.** What about in the wrestling school <term>palæstra</term>? Which wrestler is better: the one who falls by deliberate effort, or the one who falls unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS.** The one who does so by deliberate effort.

**SOCRATES.** So it seems. Is it worse and more shameful in the wrestling school to fall, or to throw someone down?

**HIPPIAS.** To fall.

**SOCRATES.** And in the wrestling school, therefore, he who does evil and shameful things by study <note>original: "studio" — with intent or zeal</note> is a better wrestler than he who does them through weakness and sluggishness.

**HIPPIAS.** It seems so.

**SOCRATES.** What about in every other use of the body? Is it not the case that he who is more robust and fit in body can do both things at his discretion: both the things of a strong man and those of a weak man, both the beautiful and the shameful? For this reason, whenever he who excels in bodily condition does evil things according to the body, he does them willingly; but the weak man does them unwillingly.

**HIPPIAS.** It seems the same thing happens regarding strength.

**SOCRATES.** What should be said about the gracefulness of the figure itself? Does it not belong to a more beautiful and better body to fashion shameful figures by great effort, while the deformed body does so by necessity? What does it seem to you?

**HIPPIAS.** The same as it seems to you.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, voluntary lack of grace in a figure pertains to the virtue of the body, while the opposite pertains to a vice.

**HIPPIAS.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** What do you say about the voice? Which do you assert is better: that which is out of tune by the will of the mind, or that which is so from sluggishness?

**HIPPIAS.** By the will of the mind.

**SOCRATES.** And the other is worse.

**HIPPIAS.** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES.** Do you wish to have good things, or bad?

**HIPPIAS.** Good things.

**SOCRATES.** Would you choose to have feet that limped by deliberate effort, or those that did so unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS.** Clearly those that did so by design.

**SOCRATES.** Is not the limping of the feet a vice and a deformity?

**HIPPIAS.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** And is not dullness of sight a vice of the eyes?

**HIPPIAS.** A vice.

**SOCRATES.** Which eyes, therefore, would you rather choose: those with which someone might see confusedly or look perversely on purpose, or those with which someone sees poorly against his will?

**HIPPIAS.** Those with which he does so willingly.

**SOCRATES.** Of those things which are your own, do you consider those which do poorly on purpose to be better than those which do so unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS.** In such matters, evidently.

**SOCRATES.** Does not one single logic encompass all the rest—ears, nose, mouth, and all the senses—which teaches that senses that sin against one's purpose are never to be chosen, as they are depraved; but those that do so by design, as if they were good, are rather to be chosen?

**HIPPIAS.** It seems so to me.

**SOCRATES.** Of which instruments is the use better? Those with which someone errs willingly, or those with which he errs unwillingly? For example, a rudder: is that one better with which someone steers poorly by design, or that with which he does so unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS.** That with which he does so by design.

**SOCRATES.** Is it not the same for the plow? And similarly for the lyre, and the flutes, and all other things?

**HIPPIAS.** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES.** Which horse's soul is better to possess: that with which someone would ride poorly on purpose, or that with which he would do so unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS.** That with which he does so on purpose.

**SOCRATES.** It is therefore better.

**HIPPIAS.** It is.

**SOCRATES.** With the better soul of a horse, therefore, someone will perform the evil works of this soul willingly; but with the opposite, unwillingly.

**HIPPIAS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** Is not the same logic true for the soul of a dog, and of all other animals?

**HIPPIAS.** The same.

**SOCRATES.** Which archer's soul would you choose as being better? That of the one who misses the mark willingly, or that of the one who misses unwillingly?

**HIPPIAS.** That of the one who does so of his own will.

**SOCRATES.** Is this not the better soul for the art of archery?

**HIPPIAS.** Better.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, the soul that misses without knowing it is worse

<summary>Socrates uses an inductive argument to convince Hippias that in physical skills and tools, voluntary error is a sign of superior ability compared to involuntary error. This leads toward the controversial suggestion that the same might apply to moral failings.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Hippias, Eudicus, voluntary vs involuntary, sin, virtue, soul, wrestling school, archery, intentionality</keywords>

# ARGUMENT OF THE CHARMIDES. FOLIO 110.

...she who errs knowingly. HIPPIAS: In the skill of archery, clearly. SOCRATES: What then in the study of medicine? Is not the one who, in healing, intentionally inserts some harm into bodies, more skilled—as far as the art of medicine is concerned—than the one who errs through ignorance? HIPPIAS: Plainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, this person is better in the art of medicine. HIPPIAS: Better. SOCRATES: And is not the soul more instructed in playing the lyre, or blowing the pipes, and in the other works of every art or science, and therefore better at these? And if it does something poorly beyond the art, it does so by design, whereas the inferior soul does so against its intention? HIPPIAS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Would we not also choose servants who err in their service knowingly rather than those who do so ignorantly, as being better for these tasks? HIPPIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: And our own soul—do we not desire to have it as the best possible? HIPPIAS: Indeed. SOCRATES: Will it not then be better if it does evil and transgresses voluntarily, rather than unknowingly? HIPPIAS: That would be a heavy thing, Socrates: if those who do injustice voluntarily were better than those who do so involuntarily. SOCRATES: Yet from what was said above, it seems to follow. HIPPIAS: Not to me, certainly. SOCRATES: I had thought, Hippias, that it seemed the same to you. Answer again, then. Is justice not either a certain power, or knowledge, or both? Is it not necessary that justice be one of these? HIPPIAS: It is necessary. SOCRATES: If justice is a certain power of the soul, will the more powerful soul be the more just? For such a soul, O best of men, appeared better to us. HIPPIAS: It certainly appeared so. SOCRATES: What if justice is knowledge? Is not the wiser soul the more just? And the more ignorant, on the contrary, the more unjust? HIPPIAS: It is so. SOCRATES: What if it is both? Will not the soul that has both—namely, knowledge and power—be more just? And the one that lacks them, more unjust? Is it not necessary that the matter stands thus? HIPPIAS: It appears so. SOCRATES: But the soul that is more powerful and wiser appeared to be better, and more ready for both beautiful and shameful things in every action it performs? HIPPIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, whenever it does shameful things, it does them willingly because of its art and power. And these—either both or one of them—pertain to justice. HIPPIAS: So it seems. SOCRATES: Truly, to do injustice is to do evil. Not to do injustice is to do good. HIPPIAS: It is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, will not the more powerful and better soul, whenever it acts unjustly, act voluntarily? And the base soul the opposite? HIPPIAS: It appears so. SOCRATES: Is not the good man he who has a good soul? And the bad man, on the contrary, he who has a bad soul? HIPPIAS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Wherefore it belongs to the good man to do injustice voluntarily, and to the bad man to do so involuntarily—if indeed the good man has a good soul. HIPPIAS: He has indeed. SOCRATES: If there is any man, therefore, who errs voluntarily and commits shameful and unjust acts, he is none other, O Hippias, than the good man. HIPPIAS: I cannot concede those things to you, Socrates. SOCRATES: Nor can I to myself, Hippias; nevertheless, from the preceding discourse, it must necessarily appear so to us for the present. But truly, as I was saying before, I am always tossed up and down regarding these matters, and I never persist in the same opinion. Nor is it a wonder that I, an unlearned man, wander about in contradictions, if even you wise men also go astray. This would be a heavy evil for us, if not even by coming to you we should cease to err.

-> THE END OF THE LESSER HIPPIAS. <-

### Argument of Marsilio Ficino <note>Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator of Plato into Latin during the Renaissance.</note> for the Charmides, or on Temperance.

The aim of Socrates in this dialogue is to exhort everyone to temperance <note>Latin: *temperantia*, often translated as "moderation" or "self-control"</note>, but three groups in particular: namely, the young, the noble, and the beautiful. The young, for this reason: because medicine must be applied quickly to diseases. *Resist the beginnings; the medicine is prepared too late when the evils have grown strong through long delays.* <note>original: "Principiis obsta: sero medicina paratur, Cum mala per longas inualuere moras." A quote from Ovid's *Remedia Amoris*.</note> The noble also, both to show that true nobility must be placed in virtue, and because the noble are often an example to others; and they are daily admitted to the republic, becoming most grave—if they be evil—to the detriment of the human race. Finally, the beautiful: for these are most especially corrupted by the company of the wicked, which results in them needing medicine all the more. Furthermore, the beautiful ought to study so that, just as nature has given a brief beauty to the body, they in turn may restore an everlasting beauty of the soul to God, the author of nature. Nor should it be permitted that while our exterior parts please many with their beauty, our interior parts meanwhile displease by their deformity. Although all things in this dialogue contain a wonderful allegory—especially the amorous parts, not unlike the Song of Solomon—I have nevertheless changed some things and omitted others. For those things which harmonized with the most refined ears of the Athenians might perhaps not harmonize at all with ruder ears. Therefore, a certain Aristarchus <note>A famous grammarian and critic of Homer; Ficino uses the name here to represent a rigorous critic.</note> of Homer, or rather of Plato, might say that the things which harmonize less are not by Plato, but by Chronus. Three things are to be noted in the very beginning: first, those things which transfer love from this form of the body to incorporeal beauty. First: because Socrates says that he discerns nothing between this beautiful person and that one, but that all beautiful people please him equally; as if to say, one must not plant one's foot in the form of a single body, but must ascend to the common beauty of the whole species itself. Since this beauty is one in many, it reflects the single Idea of beauty over many things. Just as, therefore, we transcend by thinking from the individual to the species, and from the species to the Idea, so we are admonished to proceed from the love of this form to the love of the prior common form, and then to the love of the ideal form. To these Socrates adds that the beauty of the body is not to be loved for itself, but is to be thought of by us as an image of divine beauty. Finally, he commands us to strip the soul; and having set aside the form of the body, to look upon the beauty of the soul—both the natural beauty and that which must be more diligently acquired through study. And meanwhile he rebukes Chaerephon, who had said something or other about stripping the body as if in the wrestling school. Not without reason does the exhortation to temperance begin from the beauty of the body. For this beauty is a certain temperance of lines and colors. But from this he passes immediately to the health of the body, which is also a certain temperance of the humors and...

<summary>This page concludes the *Hippias Minor* with a paradoxical argument that the good man is he who sins voluntarily, before transitioning into Marsilio Ficino's introduction to Plato's *Charmides*, focusing on temperance and the soul's beauty.</summary>

<meta>This page provides the introductory argument (argumentum) for Plato's dialogue *Charmides*, likely written by Marsilio Ficino or a similar Renaissance commentator. It establishes the philosophical framework of temperance as both a physical and spiritual harmony.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE CHARMIDES

...of the members. Third, from this to the adornment of the soul itself: for temperance exists both in emotion—that is, the very moderation of movements—and similarly in cognition, consisting of a certain harmonious congruence of the intellect with the things understood. Thus, Pythagoras did not without merit say that temperance was the most healthful of all virtues, the preserver of human society both publicly and privately. This is especially true since justice is also a kind of temperance: that is, a fitting moderation in exchanging and distributing. Indeed, although temperance is properly concerned with restraining vehement lusts and pleasures, it is nevertheless transferred by a certain similarity to the cutting away of all desires and to the moderating of any act whatsoever. Thus, the duty of fortitude is found in the moderation of boldness and fear; similarly, justice in the measure of rewards and punishments; liberality also in the manner of spending; and finally, the health of the whole life, so that there is "nothing in excess." <note>The famous Greek maxim "Mēden agan," often attributed to the Seven Sages.</note> Here applies that Pythagorean saying: *Measure is the best of all.* 

But remember that those in the *Phaedo* are denied to be temperate who abstain from pleasures for the sake of bodily pleasure. For he commands that moral actions be directed toward purifying the mind for the sake of attaining wisdom and the divine likeness. So great indeed is the excellence of temperance that all elegant craftsmen observe it in their works; and by its virtue, not only any body beneath the moon, but even the heaven itself and the universe are guided. This is confirmed in the *Gorgias* by the testimony of the wise. To this is similar that saying: *God disposes all things sweetly.* Likewise: *He disposes all things in number, weight, and measure.* <note>A reference to the Biblical Book of Wisdom 11:20.</note>

But let us now return to the dialogue. Socrates, while following the opinion of the Magi <note>The "Magi" here refers to Persian priests/philosophers often cited in Neoplatonic texts as sources of ancient wisdom.</note>, forbids the body to be cured before the soul is cured; he manifestly reproves those who, caring for the smallest things, neglect the greatest. For example, those who seek remedies for their horses and dogs when they are sick, but in the diseases of their own body and soul, they least of all consult physicians. They properly arrange the smallest pieces of furniture, yet they themselves are disordered in both soul and body. They tune the lute <note>original: "citharam"</note> while having an untempered soul. Daily they busily handle the affairs of others, but desert their own. Indeed, all things except the soul itself are foreign to us. Therefore, he called the medicine of the body a "leaf"—a light, fragile, and altogether changeable thing, and utterly to be despised. 

He also signifies that many inconveniences, both of body and fortune, frequently happen to us due to intemperance; and on the contrary, many goods arrive through temperance. Likewise, for a perfectly composed soul, whatever happens is both prudently arranged and equally endured, so that nothing at last turns into evil. But for a disordered soul, nothing can be well-composed, either in the body or outside it. In the *Cratylus*, he explains the Greek name for temperance, *sophrosyne* <term>sophrosyne: a Greek term implying "soundness of mind" or self-control</term>, as a certain health and preservation of prudence. For he thinks that the lights of all things were innate to the true soul; and therefore, if it looks entirely into itself, it will behold all true things within itself. But the cause of its not looking within is its immoderate affection toward the body and bodily things. Thus, temperance is needed above all; through it, the mist of perturbations having been expelled, the mind is made more serene and is abundantly surrounded by the light of the divine sun. From this, it first recovers wisdom and then attains prudence. 

Since, therefore, wisdom and prudence accompany temperance, Plato often elsewhere, and in this dialogue, intends that wisdom and prudence be contained under the very name of temperance. Socrates, however, warns Charmides to look into himself when he is about to speak concerning temperance; for this very turning into oneself is the duty of this virtue. Whoever has been thoroughly turned into himself will then, through the innate idea of temperance in the mind, understand human temperance; then he will recognize that very moderation by which God tempered the parts of the soul with each other from the beginning, and he will learn by what reason the affection of the soul must be tempered. 

Added to this is what he signifies in this precept: that no one, unless he is temperate, either ought to or can speak about temperance for the sake of persuasion. Furthermore, it is taught in the *Timaeus* that all prosperous things happen to us from a certain consonant modulation of the soul, both toward itself and toward the body. Whence also the Pythagoreans (whom the Roman Censorinus follows in this) promise perpetual health of both and a long life for the body if the soul prudently moderates each movement, both of itself and of the body. This has indeed been found to happen to many wise and holy men, as Censorinus and we ourselves hold. To this same or a similar cause, some would refer the long lives of the ancients. 

But something more wonderful is added to these: that the Magi promise immortality to bodies by their songs. Plato, in the *Alcibiades*, says that the Magic of Zoroaster is nothing other than divine worship. Here it is further added that the soul is tempered not only by magical songs, but also by philosophical reasons; and the body is preserved, either forever or at least for a long time, far from death. Indeed, that speech which is to be entirely persuasive of temperance to its hearers, and moreover effective, requires two things especially: a power infused by God, and reasons prepared by philosophers. And Plato calls a speech composed of these two a "magical incantation." By this, Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> first, and then the Pythagoreans, wonderfully expelled diseases from the soul and body. 

Nor should it be thought false that a body under a soul that is thoroughly tempered can be made immortal, and under an intemperate one, it falls into diseases and all evils. For that contains the Mosaic mystery concerning the state and fall of the first parent <note>Adam</note>. And Avicenna, following the Platonists and Hippocrates, proves that the soul by its very nature so exceeds all matter that when it is first restored into itself, it can move the elements of the world with a certain wonderful virtue, and have command over bodies; whence it follows that it can do so much more over its own body. This indeed Adam could experience from the beginning; and some think Enoch and Elijah, and some suspect the Evangelist <note>John the Apostle</note>, still live by some similar reason. But concerning all these things, we dispute most extensively in our *Theology*. 

Finally, to speak summarily, wonderful things regarding the virtue of temperance are declared in this: which happily restores to itself a soul that had unhappily fallen into worse things. The wonderful power of the soul is also declared: from which all things, both good and evil, flow down into the body; and by whose will the body may be able to be preserved incorrupt. This indeed harmonizes almost everywhere with the Mosaic mysteries. After these things, it is frequently asked what temperance is; which indeed neither Charmides nor Critias ever fully explains. For the former brings forward not temperance properly, but what accompanies it; while the latter brings forward things that pertain more to prudence...

<summary>This page introduces the concept of temperance (sophrosyne) as a holistic harmony of soul and body, linking Platonic philosophy with Pythagorean, Hermetic, and Biblical traditions. It argues that true health and even longevity or immortality stem from the soul's internal order and its ability to govern the physical form.</summary>

# PAGE 111.
## CHARMIDES, OR ON TEMPERANCE.
<meta>Catchword: these</meta>

...of the seven sages: namely, to declare that it is not for just anyone to discourse upon so noble a virtue. Meanwhile, note that the ancient priests were accustomed to consecrate the third bowl of libation in sacred rites especially to Jupiter the Savior: to declare that the beginning, middle, and ends of all things, as Plato reports in the *Laws*, are disposed and preserved under the providence of Jupiter. But let us return to the subtleties of Critias: who says there is a certain knowledge which knows both itself and all other knowledges, but does not know the actual things of which they are knowledges. This is indeed absurd, because truth itself and the essence of knowledge consist in a kind of contact and congruence with the very things that are known. Furthermore, a knowledge cannot be perfectly known unless it discerns what kind of knowledge it is. But that cannot be grasped unless it holds the object to which it belongs. Likewise, Critias admits that someone who knows nothing can, in turn, know that he does not know. But Socrates does not accept this, because things that are in no way known cannot, meanwhile, be known in some way. For whoever notices that he is ignorant of something, by that very fact recognizes that he lacks it. If he judges thus, he has already described a certain notion of it within himself, by which he may judge both that he lacks it and what it is he specifically lacks. Thus it happens: that whoever knows himself to be ignorant of a thing is not entirely ignorant of the thing itself; rather, he describes it by a certain general outline—general, because perfect knowledge consists in the specific distinction of things, which Plato produces in all his disputes. But where he introduces Socrates acknowledging that he knows nothing, he judges that he possesses general, if not specific, descriptions of things; otherwise, he could not acknowledge his own ignorance. Therefore, while he knew nothing, he knew all things in a certain way. Since Critias had transferred the discourse from temperance to prudence <note>Latin: *prudentia*, often used by Ficino to translate the Greek *phronesis* or practical wisdom</note>—and that by a certain Platonic license—Socrates asserts that prudence (that is, the knowledge of good and evil) holds the highest authority for achieving happiness: both because it demonstrates the good end and the good means to it, and because all things and arts, insofar as they are ruled by it, lead us toward the good; but otherwise, not at all. Finally, Socrates teaches that nothing is more difficult either to define or to compare than temperance. The difficulty of definition proceeds from the fact that it can hardly be discerned from the other virtues, of which it is a certain harmony. Add to this that it is understood and expressed in words with as much difficulty as it is possessed inwardly. Indeed, since from the very commerce of the body we are greatly inclined toward pleasure and intemperance, and are nurtured in them from infancy, we attain temperance with the greatest difficulty. Furthermore, the first affections of the senses seem sometimes to contribute something either to fortitude through anger and boldness; or to prudence through fear; or to patience through pain; or to justice and liberality through love. But every impulse is always opposed to temperance, for since it can be placed only in a certain supreme tranquility, it is hindered on all sides by any affection. It also increases the difficulty that, just as it is difficult to find a perfectly harmonious temperament of humors and limbs in the body, so it is most difficult of all to find a harmonic temperance of all its parts in the soul. Wherefore, not without reason does Socrates say, both in the epilogue and the beginning, that to attain temperance—which is like celestial harmony—there is need of celestial and divine power, using both the soul and reasons and words. Everywhere, however, he warns that we should strive rather to become temperate under lawful institutions than to dispute about temperance under dialectical reasons: since it is known only with the greatest difficulty, and once known without practice, it not only does no good but even hinders greatly; and what is more, unless it is possessed in reality, it cannot be perfectly known. For it is not permitted for the impure to touch the purest of all things.

->END OF THE ARGUMENT.<-

### PLATO’S CHARMIDES, OR ON TEMPERANCE, TRANSLATED FROM THE GREEK LANGUAGE INTO LATIN BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE, TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PIERO DE' MEDICI.

->PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.<-
->SOCRATES. CHAEREPHO. CRITIAS. CHARMIDES.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring classical figures and architectural elements.</image-desc>

YESTERDAY, when I had returned in the evening from the army at Potidaea <note>A Greek city-state; Socrates served there as a hoplite during the Peloponnesian War</note>, I immediately sought out my accustomed places of exercise, seeing as I had been away for a long time; and I entered the wrestling school <note>Latin: *palaestra*</note> of Taureas, which is opposite the temple of the Royal Majesty. There I found many people, some unknown to me, some known—and indeed a great many. When they saw me unexpectedly, they congratulated me from afar, one running up after another. Chaerepho especially, being of a more excitable nature, immediately leaped out from the middle and ran to me; and taking me by the hand, he said, "O Socrates, how did you escape unharmed? For a little before we left, a battle was fought at Potidaea, which these men have just heard about." And I, answering them, said, "Just as you see, I escaped." "It was reported to us," he said, "that the battle was most bitter, and that many known to us fell in it." "The reports you received were true," I said. "Were you present at the battle?" he asked. "I was present." "Sit here, then, and tell us; for we have not yet understood everything clearly." Having said this, he ordered me to sit near Critias, the son of Callaeschrus. Sitting down, therefore, I first greeted Critias and the others; then I recounted what had happened in the military expedition, as each one asked—for one desired to know one thing, another something else. But when we had spoken enough of these matters, I in turn asked them what the current condition of philosophy was among them, and if there were any youths distinguished either for wisdom, or for natural talent, or for both. Then Critias, looking toward the doors and seeing some youths entering and arguing with one another, and another crowd behind them, said, "Socrates, regarding the handsome ones you ask about..."

# BOOK TWENTY
### 105

...you will soon be able to judge. For those who are entering now are the precursors and lovers of one who is judged the most honorable and beautiful of all at this time. And you see, he is almost entering himself. Who is that? I asked, and whose son? You know him in a way yourself, he said, but when you left from here, he had not yet reached manhood. Did you know Charmides, the son of our uncle Glaucon, my cousin? I certainly knew him, I said; even then he was no ordinary boy. I believe he must be a grown man by now. You will immediately understand, he said, how great and of what sort he has turned out to be. While he was saying this, Charmides entered. In my view, oh friend, I have almost no faculty for weighing or discerning such things. Truly—

<margin>Proverb: A white son on a white stone. <note>original: "albū filiū ī lapide albo." A Greek/Latin idiom referring to something marked as exceptionally lucky or excellent.</note></margin>

—I would submerge the noble nature of the famous among them: a white son on a white stone. For almost all such men please me to a great degree. But especially then did he appear marvelous, both in the height of his body and his extraordinary character. All the others seemed captured by love for him, to the point that they were stunned and perturbed by his entrance. Many lovers, moreover, followed behind him. As far as the men are concerned, it is no wonder; but what is marvelous is that I also observed the boys: not one of them, even the smallest, looked at anything else; rather, they all contemplated him as if he were some image of a god. Here Chaerephon turned to me: How does the youth seem to you, Socrates? Does he not bear a beautiful face and character? Wonderfully, I said. And yet, he said, if he were willing to strip, you would think his face was nothing compared to that marvelous beauty which lies hidden within. The others also agreed with Chaerephon on this. By Hercules, I said, you describe an insuperable man, if only one small thing were added to him. What is that? Critias asked. If, I said, by choice of the soul's habit, he were beautiful by nature. Yet it is consistent, Critias, that he should be such, since he is born from your stock. Indeed, certainly as far as his intellect is concerned, he is both most beautiful and best. Why then, I said, do we not strip his soul first and contemplate his interior beauty rather than his exterior appearance? For since he is such, he will not refuse to discourse with us. He will certainly be willing, Critias replied. For he is a student of wisdom: and as he seems to you and others, he is quite poetic. By a long series, I said, you draw this nobility from the race of Solon. But why do you not show me the youth now? Summon him here. For it is not unseemly, even if he were younger, to discourse with him in the presence of you, his cousin and guardian. You speak rightly, he said. He must be called now. And having said these things, turning to the one who followed behind, he said: Call Charmides, telling him that I wish to commit him to a certain physician for the sake of his ill health, about which he complained to me. Critias then said to me: A little while ago, Charmides was complaining that he rose from sunrise with a heavy head. What prevents you, therefore, from pretending that you have some remedy against the heaviness of the head? Nothing prevents it, I said, provided he comes. And he will come. Which was done; for he came, and provoked a more unrestrained laughter in everyone: for each of us sitting together, wishing to yield a place to Charmides so that he might sit near him, pushed his neighbor sideways on purpose. The result was that of those sitting at either end, we forced one to stand up and knocked the other flat on the ground. He, however, approaching, sat down between me and Critias. When he asked me if I knew a cure for the head, I finally answered with difficulty that I did. What is it? he asked. A certain leaf, I said. But in addition, a certain incantation must be added, which if someone employs and uses the leaf, health is restored. But without the incantation, the leaf alone confers nothing. To this he said: I will certainly write down this incantation as you dictate it. Whether you persuade me, I said, or even if you do not? He, smiling, said: If I persuade you, Socrates. Ha! You clearly have my name. I have it indeed, unless I am mistaken. For frequent talk is held about you among my peers. I even remember when I was still a boy, you used to associate with Critias. You are right. I shall show you the manner of the incantation more boldly. A little while ago, I did not know how I should show its power to you.

<margin>Certain precepts of medicine: the head.</margin>

It is such, oh Charmides, that it cannot cure the head alone: just as you have often heard from skilled physicians: who, whenever someone afflicted with pain in the eyes consults them, say they cannot heal the eyes unless they first heal the head; nor can the head be cured without the medicine of the whole body. For this reason, they use certain rules beneficial to the whole; and they pass from the whole to the part to be restored. Have you not heard them speak thus, and that it is so? Entirely. Do they seem to speak rightly to you, and do you approve of this discourse? Most of all. Indeed, when I heard these things were approved by him: Such, I said, oh Charmides, is the power of this incantation also. Which I learned there in the army from a certain Thracian physician of the followers of Zamolxis, who are also said to bring immortality. That Thracian physician added, moreover, that the Greek physicians also preach what was narrated above. But Zamolxis, he said, our king and god, hands down: just as it is not fitting to cure eyes without the head, nor the head without the rest of the body, so neither the body without the soul. And that is the reason why many diseases of the body escape Greek physicians: because they are ignorant of the whole itself, which ought to be cared for first.

<margin><unclear>which is ignored by you yourselves</unclear></margin>

When the whole is in a bad state, it is impossible for any part to be well. For all things, whether good or evil, flow from the soul into the body and the whole man; and from there similarly, as from the head into the eyes. He commands, therefore, that the soul be cared for first and most of all, if the head and the entire body are to be well. He teaches that the medicines of the soul are certain incantations. That these are contained in noble reasons by which temperance is granted to the soul; which being inserted and present, it is easy to grant health to the head and the whole body. He, therefore, when he taught the medicine and the incantations, commanded that I should be moved by no prayers to apply the remedy against headache to anyone, unless he first committed his soul to be purged by the incantations themselves. He said this was surely the error of our times, that many strive to be physicians without the study of temperance and health. Thus he forewarned me in a wonderful way, and commanded me to beware lest any man, whether rich or noble or beautiful, should persuade me to do otherwise. To him, by this oath...

# CHARMIDES, OR ON TEMPERANCE. FOLIO 112.

I confirmed this with an oath and promised I would not do otherwise. Therefore, I must obey and comply with you. For if you are willing, according to the precepts of my host, to first subject your soul to all the incantations of that Thracian <note>Socrates refers to a Thracian physician of Zamolxis who taught him that the body cannot be cured without the soul.</note>, I will apply the medicine to your head. If not, I will not be able to help you, my friend Charmides. When Critias heard this, he said: "This heaviness of the head will be a profit to the youth if, for its sake, he gains health of mind. I assure you, Socrates, that this Charmides excels all his peers not only in appearance, but also in that very quality for which you said you had an incantation. Did you not mention temperance?" "Of that very thing," I replied. "Know then," he said, "that of all the youths of his age, he is seen to be the most temperate; and in all other things, according to his growth in years, he is inferior to none." "It is fitting, Charmides," I said, "that in these things Critias has spoken, you should excel others. For I do not think anyone could point to a union of two Athenian families from which a more beautiful and noble offspring would likely be born than from the union of your ancestors. For the paternal line of this Critias and Dropides has been celebrated by Anacreon, Solon, and many other poets for its excellence in beauty, virtue, and other happiness. The glory of your maternal line is the same. For no one ever seemed more beautiful or greater in stature to all on the continent than your uncle Pyrilampes, whenever he went as an ambassador to the Great King <note>The King of Persia.</note> or to anyone else on the continent. In short, this entire house is inferior to no other. Therefore, it is probable that you, born of such a lineage, should hold the first place in all things. As far as that appearance which is perceived by the eyes is concerned, O son of sweet Glaucon, you seem to me to have degenerated in no way from your superiors; and if, as Critias here testifies, you are naturally disposed toward temperance and other virtues, then your mother bore you a blessed man, dear Charmides. So the matter stands: if temperance is in you, as Critias says, and you are sufficiently temperate, you need neither the incantations of Zamolxis nor those of Abaris the Hyperborean <note>Legendary figures associated with mystical healing and wisdom.</note>; rather, the medicine for the head should be applied to you now. But if temperance is lacking in you, the incantation must precede the medicine. Answer me then: do you agree with Critias and assert that you have enough temperance, or do you recognize that something is lacking?" Then Charmides' cheeks were suffused with a blush, showing a more graceful appearance; for modesty becomes that age. Then he answered quite nobly: "It is by no means easy to either admit or deny what has been asked at present. For if I deny that I am temperate, it will first seem shameful that I disparage myself; and secondly, I shall be refuting the opinion of Critias and many others to whom I seem to be temperate, as if it were false. But if I affirm it, this boasting about myself will seem hateful. Therefore, I do not know which way to turn." "You seem to speak rightly, Charmides," I said; "therefore I think we should investigate together whether you possess what I seek or not, lest you be forced to speak otherwise than you wish, or I hastily attempt a cure. If it will be pleasing to you, I desire to investigate with you; if not, I think we should let it go." "Indeed, it is most pleasing of all," he said. "Therefore, search in whatever way you think best." "In this way," I said, "the investigation seems likely to be more convenient. It is certain that if temperance is in you, you have some opinion about what it is. For it is necessary that if it dwells within you, it provides some sense of itself, from which an opinion arises concerning what and of what sort temperance is; do you not think so?" "I certainly think so." "Do you not believe this: that since you know how to speak Greek, you could tell us both what it seems to be to you?" "Perhaps." "So that we may guess whether temperance is in you or not, come, tell me: what do you say temperance is, in your opinion?" At first he hesitated and was not willing to answer; finally, he replied: "I think temperance is doing everything decently and walking quietly along the way; speaking quietly; and in short, doing all things quietly. To embrace what you ask briefly, it seems to me to be a certain quietness." "Is that right?" I said. "They certainly say that quiet men are temperate. But let us see if they speak the truth. Tell me then, is temperance something beautiful?" CHARMIDES: "It certainly is." SOCRATES: "In the skill of a grammarian, is it more beautiful to write the same letters quickly or quietly?" CHARMIDES: "Quickly." SOCRATES: "And to read—quickly or slowly?" CHARMIDES: "Quickly." SOCRATES: "Is it more beautiful to play the lyre quickly and to compete promptly than quietly and slowly?" CHARMIDES: "It is so." SOCRATES: "What about in boxing and wrestling matches? Is not speed itself praised?" CHARMIDES: "Certainly." SOCRATES: "And running and jumping, and other bodily acts—if they are done swiftly and promptly, do they not look toward the beautiful; and if sluggishly and remissly, toward the shameful?" CHARMIDES: "It appears so." SOCRATES: "It is clear then, as far as the body is concerned, that not what is slow, but what is swiftest is most beautiful; is it not?" CHARMIDES: "Entirely." SOCRATES: "But it was agreed that temperance is something beautiful?" CHARMIDES: "It was." SOCRATES: "Therefore, regarding the body, not quietness but rather speed will pertain to temperance, provided that temperance is something beautiful." CHARMIDES: "It seems so." SOCRATES: "And is not quickness of learning <term>docilitas</term> more beautiful than dullness?" CHARMIDES: "More beautiful, certainly." SOCRATES: "And quickness of learning is to learn quickly; dullness is to learn late and slowly." CHARMIDES: "Indeed." SOCRATES: "Is it not more beautiful to teach another as swiftly as possible than slowly?" CHARMIDES: "Without a doubt." SOCRATES: "Likewise, to recollect and remember—is it more beautiful to do so late and slowly, or easily and promptly?" CHARMIDES: "Promptly." SOCRATES: "And is not shrewdness <term>solertia</term> a certain speed of the mind rather than slowness?" CHARMIDES: "It is." SOCRATES: "And to understand what is said in the schools of grammarians and lyre-players, and in all other things—is it not most beautiful to do so as swiftly as possible, rather than as slowly as possible?" CHARMIDES: "This too." SOCRATES: "Furthermore, in the very investigations and consultations of the mind, I think it is not the one who finds what is sought quietly, late, and with difficulty who is to be praised, but rather the one who does so briefly and most easily." CHARMIDES: "These things are true." SOCRATES: "From these things it is gathered, O Charmides, that both in those things which pertain to the body and those which pertain to the mind, swift and prompt things seem more beautiful than slow and quiet ones." CHARMIDES: "So it appears." SOCRATES: "Therefore, temperance will not be a certain quietness, nor will a quiet life be a temperate one, as is concluded by this reasoning; since [temperance must be beautiful...]"

# BOOK TWENTY

->**Socrates and Charmides on Temperance**<-

...it is tempered, and it ought to be beautiful. For of two things, one must be true: either never, or only very rarely, have actions performed slowly appeared more beautiful to us in life than those done with speed and intensity. But if slow actions were found to surpass fast and intense ones in beauty no less frequently, then it would not follow by this reasoning that temperance is acting slowly rather than intensely and quickly—neither in walking, nor in speech, nor in anything else. Nor would a quiet life be more becoming and temperate than a restless one; for in our previous talk, it was assumed that temperance is something beautiful, yet it has been established that fast things are no less beautiful than slow ones. 

**Charmides:** You seem to me to have spoken rightly, O Socrates.

**Socrates:** Look at yourself again then, O Charmides, more attentively; and consider what sort of person temperance makes you when it is present, and what kind of thing it is itself while it makes you such a person. Observing all these things, answer me quite manfully what it seems to you to be.

He then collected himself; and having contemplated himself more diligently, he said: "It seems to me that temperance induces a certain modesty <note>original: *verecundia*</note> or blushing, and makes a man modest; and I think that temperance is shame <note>original: *pudor*</note>."

**Socrates:** What are you saying? Did you not say a little while ago that temperance was something beautiful?

**Charmides:** I certainly did.

**Socrates:** And are not temperate men themselves good?

**Charmides:** They are.

**Socrates:** Do you think that which does not make men good can be good?

**Charmides:** Not at all.

**Socrates:** Therefore, it is not only beautiful, but also good.

**Charmides:** So it seems to me.

**Socrates:** Do you not believe Homer speaks rightly when he says, "Shame is not good for a needy man"? <note>A reference to the Odyssey, Book 17, where Homer suggests that a beggar cannot afford to be too shy or shameful if he wishes to survive.</note>

**Charmides:** I do indeed believe it.

**Socrates:** Therefore, it appears that shame is both "not good" and "good."

**Charmides:** It appears so.

**Socrates:** But temperance is only good, since it makes those to whom it is present good, and never bad.

**Charmides:** It seems to me to be exactly as you say.

**Socrates:** Therefore, temperance cannot be shame, since temperance is only good, while shame is no more good than it is evil.

**Charmides:** This seems rightly said to me, O Socrates. But please consider what you think of this other idea I am bringing forward. For I have just now remembered what I heard from someone who said that temperance is "minding one's own business" <note>original: *ut sua quisque agat* - literally "that each does his own things."</note>. Consider whether he who says this seems to speak rightly to you.

**Socrates:** O you rogue! Did you hear this from Critias here, or from some other wise man?

**Critias:** He surely seems to have heard it from someone else; for he never heard it from me.

**Charmides:** What does it matter, Socrates, from whom I heard it?

**Socrates:** Not at all. We should not consider who said it, but rather whether it is said truly or not.

**Charmides:** Now you speak well.

**Socrates:** Rightly, by Jove! Yet I shall wonder if we find how this stands, for it is very much like a riddle.

**Charmides:** Why so?

**Socrates:** Because I do not think he meant it in the way the words sound—namely, that temperance is for anyone to do just his own things. Do you think a grammarian <note>In this context, a teacher of letters or literacy.</note> does nothing when he writes or reads?

**Charmides:** I think he certainly does something.

**Socrates:** Does it seem to you that a grammarian writes and reads only his own name? Or does he also teach you boys? For you were writing the names of your enemies no less than those of yourselves and your friends.

**Charmides:** Certainly no less.

**Socrates:** And when you were doing this, were you more meddlesome than is becoming, and departing from the law of temperance?

**Charmides:** Not at all.

**Socrates:** And yet you were not doing only your own business, if writing and reading is "doing something."

**Charmides:** It certainly is.

**Socrates:** Furthermore, my friend, is healing, building, weaving, or completing the work of any art "doing something," or is it nothing?

**Charmides:** It is certainly something.

**Socrates:** Would a city seem well-ordered to you in which the laws commanded that everyone weave and wash his own cloak, make his own shoes, his own scrapers <note>term: *strigil* - a curved tool used by Greeks and Romans to scrape oil and sweat from the skin.</note>, his own oil flasks, his own perfume jars, and all his furniture? That he should never touch the things of others, but always work on his own?

**Charmides:** Not at all.

**Socrates:** Nevertheless, if a city is temperately disposed, it is well-ordered.

**Charmides:** Why not?

**Socrates:** Therefore, temperance will not be doing such things, nor doing one's own business in this manner.

**Charmides:** Not as it appears.

**Socrates:** Therefore, as I said before, he who proclaimed that temperance is "minding one's own business" was speaking in riddles. For he must not be thought so foolish that his meaning was the same as the sound of his words. Did some fool hand this down to you, Charmides?

**Charmides:** Least of all. Rather, in my judgment, he was someone very wise.

**Socrates:** Then he altogether wrapped his meaning in obscure words, so that it is difficult to know what "minding one's own business" is.

**Charmides:** Perhaps.

**Socrates:** Can you explain to us what "minding one's own business" is?

**Charmides:** I truly do not know. Perhaps even he who said these things did not sufficiently understand what he meant.

While he was saying this, Charmides smiled and looked at Critias. Critias, although he had previously been restrained despite a desire for glory to argue against Charmides and the others, could no longer contain himself. It seemed to me that my suspicion was true: namely, that Charmides had received that previous definition of temperance from Critias. Therefore, Charmides, unwilling to defend the answer himself and desiring to throw this labor onto Critias, provoked him and showed him as if he had been refuted. Critias could not tolerate this; indeed, he seemed as indignant toward him as a poet toward an actor reciting his poems badly. And so, looking at him, he said: "Do you think, Charmides, that if you do not understand the meaning of him who asserted that temperance is minding one's own business, that he himself did not understand it either?"

"O best of men," I said, "it is no wonder that this youth does not understand. But it is fitting for you to know these things, both because of your age and your studies. If, therefore, you yourself confirm that temperance is what he said, and take up this argument, I will more gladly investigate with you whether it is true or not."

**Critias:** I do indeed confirm it, and I take it up.

**Socrates:** You do well. Tell me, I pray: do you admit what I was asking a moment ago—that all craftsmen make something?

**Critias:** I do.

**Socrates:** Do they seem to you to make only their own things, or the things of others as well?

**Critias:** The things of others also.

**Socrates:** Do they act temperately, then, who do not make only their own things?

**Critias:** What prevents it?

**Socrates:** As far as I am concerned, nothing. But see if anything prevents it for him who, having assumed that temperance is minding one's own business, then says there is no obstacle to those who do the business of others being temperate.

**Critias:** I have indeed granted that those who do the business of others are temperate. But was it granted regarding those who *make*?

**Socrates:** Tell me, Critias, do you not call "acting" and "making" the same thing?

**Critias:** Certainly not.
