# CHARMIDES, OR ON TEMPERANCE.

nor are "working" and "doing" the same thing. For I learned this from Hesiod, who said: *No work is a disgrace.* <note>original: "Opus nullū turpe eē." A reference to Hesiod's *Works and Days*.</note> Do you think that if he had named such works as "working" and "acting" as those you were just describing, he would have said that no work is a disgrace to anyone—such as cutting leather, or selling seasoned meats as a tavern-keeper, or sitting in a shop? One should not think so, Socrates. Rather, in my judgment, he considered "making" to be something different from "acting" and "working." He thought that a "making" is sometimes a matter of reproach when one does something that is not honorable, but that "work" is never a disgrace to us. For those things which are done honorably and usefully, he called "works," and such "workings" and "actions" he called "makings." Furthermore, we must believe that he considered only these honorable things to be one's own, while all harmful things are utterly alien. For this reason, one must believe that Hesiod, and every other man of sound mind, calls a man "temperate" who thus does his own business.

**SOCRATES:** O Critias, as soon as you began to speak, I perceived that you were calling "one's own" and "one's business" that which is good, and that you were naming the "makings" of good things "actions." Indeed, I have often heard Prodicus <note>A Greek Sophist known for his focus on the precise meaning of words.</note> distinguish names in this manner. I grant you the right to use names however you please, provided you declare what you intend to signify by each name. Now, therefore, define it more clearly again from the beginning: do you say that temperance is the action or the making of good things, or however else you wish to name it?

**CRITIAS:** I do indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Then he who does evil does not act temperately; rather, he who does good acts temperately.

**CRITIAS:** Does it not seem so to you, my good man?

**SOCRATES:** Let that pass for the present; we are not yet considering what I think, but what you yourself are saying.

**CRITIAS:** Truly, I would never declare that he who does not do good, but evil, acts temperately. For I clearly define temperance as the very action of good things.

**SOCRATES:** Perhaps nothing prevents you from speaking the truth; yet I wonder at this: if you think that men acting temperately are ignorant that they are acting temperately.

**CRITIAS:** I do not think so at all.

**SOCRATES:** Was it not said by you a little while ago that nothing prevents craftsmen, even while they are working, from living temperately?

**CRITIAS:** It was indeed said, but what of it?

**SOCRATES:** Nothing else. But tell me, does any physician seem to you, when he effects something, to effect what is useful both for himself and for the one he cures?

**CRITIAS:** He does to me.

**SOCRATES:** Does not whoever does these things do what is fitting?

**CRITIAS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** And he who does what is fitting, does he not act temperately?

**CRITIAS:** He acts temperately.

**SOCRATES:** Is it necessary for a physician to understand when he cures usefully and when he does not? And for every craftsman to know when the work he performs will be beneficial to him, and when it will not?

**CRITIAS:** Perhaps not.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, sometimes the physician has worked usefully without knowing how he has worked; yet if he has worked usefully, as you yourself admitted, he has acted temperately. Did you not say so?

**CRITIAS:** I did.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, does it not appear that sometimes, having worked usefully, he acts temperately and is temperate, yet he himself is ignorant that he acts temperately and is temperate?

**CRITIAS:** This cannot be, Socrates. But if anything was said in our previous remarks from which this follows, I would rather retract it. For I maintain that this very thing is temperance: **to know oneself.** <note>The famous Delphic maxim "Gnothi Seauton."</note> And I agree with him who inscribed this precept on the temple of Apollo itself. Indeed, this inscription seems to be a kind of greeting from the god to the men who enter the temple, in place of the greeting "Rejoice." As if "Rejoice" were not the proper thing to say, nor should people command this of one another, but rather to live temperately. Thus the god addresses those entering the temple with a singular sentiment, greeting us differently than men do—as he who inscribed it intended, in my judgment. He commands the one entering nothing else but to live temperately. But like a prophet, he delivers this precept in obscure words. For "Know thyself" is the same as "Live temperately," as the letters testify and I interpret them. Perhaps someone will think it is something else, which I believe happened to those who added the subsequent inscriptions: **Nothing in excess** and **Pledge and ruin is near.** <note>Other famous maxims inscribed at Delphi.</note> For they thought "Know thyself" was a piece of advice, not the god's own admonition to those entering. Then, so that they might offer no less worthy counsel, they added the rest. Why do I say all this, Socrates? To concede all the previous points to you without controversy. Now, however, I wish to give you an account of this, if you will not grant that temperance is to know oneself.

Know thyself. Nothing in excess.

**CRITIAS:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** If you were to ask me: "Since medicine is the knowledge of health, what does it confer upon us? What does it produce?" I would answer that it is most beneficial. Furthermore, it produces for us a beautiful work: health. Do you accept this?

# BOOK XX.

...could he attribute it to many arts? Can you show me any such work produced by these? You certainly cannot. **SOCRATES:** You speak the truth. However, I can show you this: what the knowledge of each of these sciences is, which is something other than the science itself. Just as the skill of calculation is the science of even and odd numbers—how they relate to themselves and to each other. Is it not so? **CRITIAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** And is not the even and the odd something different from the science of calculation itself? **CRITIAS:** It is. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, the faculty of weighing is the balancing of heavier and lighter weights. But the heavy and light themselves are something other than the art of weighing itself. Do you agree? **CRITIAS:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** Tell me then, of what is <term>temperance</term><note>Latin: *temperantia*, translating the Greek *sophrosyne*, meaning moderation, self-control, or soundness of mind</note> the science, which is something other than temperance itself? **CRITIAS:** This is exactly what you are looking for; it is the very thing by which temperance differs from all other sciences. You are demanding some similarity between this and the others. But the matter stands differently. For all others are sciences of something else, and not at all of themselves. This alone is the science of other sciences and of itself. You are far from being ignorant of this; but I think you are doing what you denied a moment ago: you are trying to refute me, and you are setting aside the subject we are discussing. **SOCRATES:** What are you doing? Do you think that if I refute you, I do it for any other reason than that for which I examine myself—fearing lest I might think I know what I do not know, and my ignorance remain hidden from me? And now I assert that I am doing this very thing: discussing and examining the argument for my own sake first, and perhaps also for the sake of my friends. Or do you not think it is a common good for all men that the condition of every thing should become clear to all? **CRITIAS:** Most certainly, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Be bold then, my friend, and answering the questions according to your opinion, do not care whether it is Critias or Socrates who is being refuted; but attend to the argument itself, to see where the refutation leads. **CRITIAS:** I will do so, for you seem to speak well. **SOCRATES:** Repeat then what you say about temperance. **CRITIAS:** I say indeed that of all other sciences, this alone is the science of both itself and of the remaining sciences. **SOCRATES:** And is it not also the science of ignorance, if indeed it is the science of science? **CRITIAS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, only the temperate man will know himself, and will be able to examine what he knows and what he is ignorant of. He will also be able to judge in other men what each one knows and thinks he knows (if he knows it), and what he is ignorant of while thinking he knows it; but no one else will be able to do this. And this is what it is to be temperate, and what temperance is: to know oneself—that is, to understand what one knows and what one does not know. Are these the things you are saying? **CRITIAS:** They are. **SOCRATES:** Again then, for the third time—as they say, <margin>Proverb: Give tribute to Jupiter the Liberator.</margin> giving tribute to <term>Jupiter the Liberator</term><note>Latin: *Ioui liberatori*, a traditional Greek toast or invocation to Zeus Soter (the Savior/Liberator) at the end of a meal or a major argument</note>—let us consider these things from the beginning. First, whether this is possible or not: that one should know what he knows and what he does not know. Secondly, if it were possible, what utility it would have for those who understand it. **CRITIAS:** We must certainly proceed. **SOCRATES:** Pay attention, Critias, if you have anything certain in these matters; for I have nothing, and I will reveal where I am in doubt, if you wish. **CRITIAS:** Indeed, I do wish it. **SOCRATES:** These things follow if what you just said stands: namely, that there is one certain science which is the science of no other thing than itself and other sciences, and that same science is also the science of ignorance. **CRITIAS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** See, my friend, how absurd our discourse is. For truly, if you consider this same thing in certain other cases, I think it will seem impossible to you. **CRITIAS:** In what way? And where? **SOCRATES:** Think clearly here: whether it seems to you that there could be a certain sight which is not the sight of those things which other sights see, but is a sight of itself and of other sights, and likewise a sight of non-sight; and though it is a sight, it sees no color, but only looks upon itself and other sights. Does any such sight seem possible to you? **CRITIAS:** None. **SOCRATES:** And do you trust that you can find any power of hearing which hears no voice, but perceives itself and other hearings and non-hearings? **CRITIAS:** That is not possible either. **SOCRATES:** Run through all the senses in general: consider whether any sense can be found which perceives itself and other senses, yet feels none of those things which other senses feel. **CRITIAS:** I think this is also impossible. **SOCRATES:** Or do you perhaps think there is any desire which seeks no pleasure, but is a desire for itself and for other lusts? **CRITIAS:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Nor a will, I think, which desires no good, but seeks itself and other wills. **CRITIAS:** Not in the least. **SOCRATES:** Will you say there is any such love that is not a love of anything beautiful, but is a passion for itself and for other loves? **CRITIAS:** Not I. **SOCRATES:** Have you ever thought of a fear which is terrified of itself and other fears, but dreads nothing terrible or dangerous? **CRITIAS:** Never at all. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, an opinion such that it is an opinion of other opinions and of itself, but opines nothing of those things which other opinions consider? **CRITIAS:** In no way. **SOCRATES:** But yet we said there is a certain science of this kind, which is a science of no doctrine, but a science of itself and of other sciences. **CRITIAS:** We certainly said so. **SOCRATES:** Is it not a strange thing, if it exists? Yet we must not yet deny its existence, but consider whether it is possible. **CRITIAS:** You speak wisely. **SOCRATES:** I will explain. Is this science a science of something? And does it have a certain power of this kind, by which it belongs to something? **CRITIAS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Likewise, do we say that the "greater" has a power by which it is greater than something? **CRITIAS:** It certainly has. **SOCRATES:** Is it not greater than something smaller, if it is to be greater? **CRITIAS:** It is necessary. **SOCRATES:** If we found something "greater" which was greater than other greater things and greater than itself, but was not greater than any of those things which other things are greater than, this would altogether happen to it: that just as it is greater than itself, so it would also be smaller? **CRITIAS:** It is necessary, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, if something is double compared to other doubles and to itself, surely it will be double to itself as a half, and double to other halves. For whatever is double is double of nothing other than a half. **CRITIAS:** That is true. **SOCRATES:** Moreover, that which is "more" than itself, is it not also "less"? And what is heavier, is it not also lighter? And what is older, also younger? And in all other things in the same way, whatever has its own power directed toward itself, will it not also have that essence toward which its power is directed? I mean something like this: we say hearing is the hearing of nothing other than a voice? **CRITIAS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** If it hears itself, it will hear its own voice...

For without color, sight can perceive nothing. **CRITIAS:** Nothing indeed. **SOCRATES:** Do you see, O Critias, that the things we have described are partly impossible and partly incredible? That a faculty of sight should be directed toward itself, or that magnitude and multitude and other things of this kind should have their power directed toward themselves—is that not utterly impossible? **CRITIAS:** It is entirely so. **SOCRATES:** But that sight and hearing should perceive themselves, or that motion should move itself, or heat should warm itself, and other such things—these are not believed by some, though perhaps they seem believable to others. We have need of a great man, O friend, who can sufficiently distinguish through all these things: whether nothing at all has the power to act upon itself except for knowledge, but only upon something else; or whether some things can and others cannot. And if there are things that have power over themselves, whether this knowledge which we call temperance <note>original: *temperantia*, translating the Greek *sophrosyne*, meaning moderation or self-control</note> is among their number. And even if this were granted, I would not yet agree that such a thing is temperance until I have investigated whether such a temperance, existing in this way, profits us at all or profits us nothing. For I prophesy that temperance is something beneficial and good. You, therefore, son of Callaeschrus, since you posit that temperance is the science of science and of ignorance, show first that what I said above is possible; and afterward, beyond it being possible, show that it is also beneficial. In this way, you might perhaps satisfy me regarding the definition of temperance itself.

But Critias, when he heard this and saw me doubting, acted in the same way as those who, seeing others yawn in their presence, yawn themselves; he seemed to hesitate just as I was hesitating. But because he was a man of reputation, he was ashamed before those present; he did not want to admit that he was unable to discern the things I had put forward, yet he produced nothing clear, thus concealing his own ambiguity. But I, so that our discussion might proceed, said: "If it seems right to you, O Critias, let us grant for now that a science of science can exist. Whether it truly can or not, we will investigate another time. Nevertheless, if this is indeed possible, how is it more possible to know what someone knows and what he does not know? For we said that this—knowing oneself and being temperate—was exactly that. Is it not so?" **CRITIAS:** "Very much so," Socrates replied, "and it follows in a way. For if someone possesses that science which knows itself, he himself becomes such as that which he possesses. Just as when someone has speed, he is speedy; and when he has beauty, he is beautiful; and when he has knowledge, he is knowing. Therefore, when someone has the knowledge of himself, he is now made knowing of himself." **SOCRATES:** "I do not doubt that if someone has in himself that which knows itself, he would know himself. But what necessity compels a man so affected to know what he knows and what he does not know?" **CRITIAS:** "Because this and that are the same thing." **SOCRATES:** "Perhaps so. But I always seem to be the same: I do not understand how knowing what one knows and knowing what one does not know are the same thing." **CRITIAS:** "How can you say that?" **SOCRATES:** "In this way: if a science of science exists, will it be able to discern anything further than that, of these two, one is science and the other is ignorance?" **CRITIAS:** "No further; only to that extent." **SOCRATES:** "Is the science and ignorance of health, then, the same as the science and ignorance of justice?" **CRITIAS:** "By no means." **SOCRATES:** "But one is medicine, and the other is political skill; this is nothing other than science." **CRITIAS:** "Why not?" **SOCRATES:** "Unless someone knows health and justice in addition, but only science—having only the science of this alone—he will recognize that he knows, or that he has a certain science, both concerning himself and others. Is it not so? But what he actually knows by this science, how will he understand? For medicine knows the healthy and the wholesome, not temperance; music knows the harmonic, not temperance; architecture knows the building, not temperance; and similarly with all things. Is it not so?" **CRITIAS:** "It appears so." **SOCRATES:** "But if temperance is only the science of sciences, how will it understand what knows the healthy or what knows the building?" **CRITIAS:** "In no way." **SOCRATES:** "Therefore, he will not understand *what* he knows, being ignorant of this; but only *that* he knows." **CRITIAS:** "So it seems." **SOCRATES:** "Therefore, being temperate will not be this: nor will temperance be understanding what one knows or what one does not know; but, as it seems, only that one knows and that one does not know." **CRITIAS:** "It appears so." **SOCRATES:** "Nor will such a person be able to examine another who professes a science of something, to see whether he knows what he promises or does not know. Rather, as it seems, he will only recognize this: that the person has a certain science. But of what matter that science is, temperance will not show." **CRITIAS:** "It does not seem so." **SOCRATES:** "Therefore, he will not distinguish a pretending physician from a true one, nor any other person who knows from one who does not. But let us consider it this way: if a temperate man, or anyone else, is to judge a true and a false physician, will he not do it thus? Concerning the art of healing, he will not differ from the physician at all. For as we were saying, the physician understands nothing other than the healthy and the sick, the wholesome and the harmful. Is it not so?" **CRITIAS:** "Exactly so." **SOCRATES:** "Furthermore, he knows nothing of science. For we attributed this to temperance alone." **CRITIAS:** "So it is." **SOCRATES:** "Therefore, the physician knows nothing of medicine, since medicine is a certain science." **CRITIAS:** "You speak the truth." **SOCRATES:** "The temperate man will recognize that the physician has some science; but someone else will have to consider what kind of skill it is, or of what things. For it is clear then: when it is known of what things it is a science. Is not every science defined not just as being a science, but as being a *specific* science? And is it not known what science it is by knowing the things of which it is the science?" **CRITIAS:** "Exactly so." **SOCRATES:** "Is the science of medicine distinguished from other sciences by the fact that it is the skill of the healthy and the unhealthy?" **CRITIAS:** "Certainly." **SOCRATES:** "Must not anyone who intends to consider medicine look into those things in which it is occupied? For it would not seem right to seek it in extraneous things where it does not exist." **CRITIAS:** "Certainly not." **SOCRATES:** "Therefore, whoever examines a physician correctly will consider him in the context of healthy things and their opposites, insofar as he is a physician." **CRITIAS:** "So it seems." **SOCRATES:** "Will he not observe in these things, whether spoken or done, what is truly said and what is rightly acted?" **CRITIAS:** "It is necessary." **SOCRATES:** "But can anyone perceive these things without the skill of medicine?" **CRITIAS:** "No one." **SOCRATES:** "Nor anyone else, as it seems, except the physician. Therefore, not even the temperate man. For besides being temperate, he would also have to be a physician." **CRITIAS:** "These things are true." **SOCRATES:** "Altogether then, if temperance is the science of science or of ignorance, it will not be able to discern a physician...

CRI. So it appears. SO. What further benefit, O Critias, will come to us from temperance if it is such a thing? For if, as we supposed in the beginning, the temperate man knew what he knew and what he did not know—the former because he knows it, the latter because he is ignorant of it—and could judge another person affected in the same way: we would report a huge advantage in being endowed with temperance. For we would lead a life without error, both we ourselves who participate in temperance, and all others who were governed by our command. For we would not attempt to do those things which we are ignorant of, but having sought out men who know, we would surely yield to them: nor would we permit others subject to our governance to do anything else except what they were going to do rightly by having attempted it. That is, either that of which they had knowledge. And so, through temperance, both the affairs of the home would be rightly governed, and the established city would be best ruled: and every other thing over which temperance itself presided. For once error is removed, and rectitude acts as the guide in individual actions, it is necessary that men so instructed act honorably and well: and those acting well are blessed. Did we not speak thus, O Critias, concerning temperance: saying how great a good it is to know what someone knows and what he does not know? CRI. Entirely so. SO. But now you see that no such science has appeared to us. CRI. I see it indeed. SO. Does this good contain that which we have now found temperance to be: namely, to know both knowledge and ignorance? <note>Socrates is questioning if "knowing that you know" is the same as "knowing how to do good."</note> He who attempts to learn anything is armed by this, he will learn more easily, and all things will offer themselves more clearly to him: inasmuch as he looks upon the science itself regarding all things that are to be learned, and he will better examine others in these matters which he himself learns. But those who examine without this will do so more weakly and foolishly. Are these the sorts of things, O friend, which temperance confers upon us? Which I indeed conjecture from this: because certain absurdities often appear concerning temperance, if it be such a thing. Let us see then, if it pleases you: granting that it is possible for knowledge to be known: which we posed in the beginning, namely that temperance is to know what someone knows or does not know, let us not withdraw it: but let us rather grant it, and having granted these things, let us investigate even more diligently whether it helps us in the present if it exists as such. For those things which we were just saying: that temperance would be a certain huge good for us if it were such, ruling some disposition and the home and the city, we seem not to have rightly granted, O Critias. CRI. Why so? SO. Because we asserted too easily that it would be a huge good for men if each of us did those things which they indeed know: but left those things which they are ignorant of to certain others who know. CRI. Were these things not rightly asserted? SO. Not as it seems to me. CRI. You speak truly absurd things, Socrates. SO. By the dog! <note>A favorite oath of Socrates (original: "Per canem").</note> so it seems to me at present: and just now noticing that certain absurdities occur: and I fear lest I was considering it less than rightly. For truly, if temperance is such, I hardly see what good it brings us. CRI. By what reasoning do you say this: so that we also may know what you feel. SO. I think I am indeed talking nonsense. Yet it is necessary to consider what occurs: and not to pass it by fruitlessly and rashly: if anyone has a care for it in any way. CRI. You speak wisely. SO. Hear now my dream, whether it has emerged through the horn or through the ivory. <note>A reference to Homer’s Odyssey: true dreams come through the gate of horn, false ones through ivory.</note> For if temperance, being such as we just described, ruled us as much as possible, it would surely act according to the sciences: nor would anyone boasting that he is a pilot when he is least so, deceive us: nor would a physician, nor a leader of an army, nor any other false professor of science escape us. With things arranged in this way, something else would happen to us: for we would be in better health in our bodies than now: and we would emerge safer in maritime and military dangers. Likewise, we would possess vessels and instruments: clothes and shoes: and finally all household furniture established more conveniently and according to art: because we would employ true craftsmen. Let us also grant, if you wish, that prophecy is the science of the future, and that temperance presiding over it avoids vain boasters: but chooses true prophets for the prediction of future things. I agree that the human race, so established, would act and live wisely. For temperance, the guardian of human life, would never permit ignorance to creep in and use its own strength. But that by acting according to science, we would act well and be blessed: we cannot yet perceive, friend Critias. CRI. You will not easily find another end and perfection of acting well if you reject action according to science. SO. Explain a little further according to which science. Is it according to a contrary science? CRI. Not by Jove! SO. Or perhaps the craft of smithing? CRI. Not that one. SO. Is it according to wool-working or the craft of wood or something of this sort? CRI. Not that either. SO. It seems, therefore, that we must no longer stand by that speech in which it was asserted that he was blessed who lived according to science. For these living according to science, you by no means affirm to live blessedly. But perhaps from many living ignorantly, you determine one certain person living knowingly from a certain science to be blessed. And perhaps you mean the one I spoke of a little while ago, the prophet knowing all future things. Do you mean him, or another? CRI. Both him and another. SO. Whom? Is it that man who knows not only future things, but also past and present things, and is ignorant of nothing? Let us imagine someone of this sort. I think you would say no one else lives more out of science than he. CRI. No one at all. SO. Add this also: which of the sciences especially makes one blessed? Are they all similarly so? CRI. Not similarly. SO. But which is it most of all? That by which one knows the present, past, and future? Is it that by which one knows how to play? CRI. Why do you mention dice? SO. Or perhaps that by which one calculates? CRI. By no means. SO. Is it that by which one knows healthy things? CRI. This one more so. SO. But that one which I say most of all, what do I mean? CRI. That by which one knows good and evil. SO. O you rogue! for a long time you have been leading me around in a circle...

# ARGUMENT FOR THE LACHES. FOLIO 115.

you withdraw; and to this point: that living blessedly is not living according to all sciences, but rather according to one certain science of good and evil. Furthermore, if you wish, O Critias, to except this from the other sciences, medicine itself will effect health no less; and the shoemaker’s art will provide shoes no less; and the weaver’s art, clothes; the pilot’s art will avoid maritime dangers; and the military art will ward off the perils of war and preserve us no less. CRITIAS. Not at all less. SOCRATES. But truly, my friend Critias, if this very science of good and evil is taken away, none of these things will be done well or usefully. CRITIAS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. This, it seems, is not temperance <note>Latin: *temperantia*; the Greek *sophrosyne*, meaning moderation or self-control</note>; but that whose work it is to benefit us. For it is not the science of sciences and ignorances, but the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore, if temperance is useful to us, it contributes to something else. CRITIAS. Does this not also benefit us? Surely if temperance is the science of sciences and presides over the other sciences, it will benefit us by likewise commanding this science which discerns good and evil. SOCRATES. Will this provide good health of the body more than medicine? And will it effect the other works of the other arts, while the individual craftsmen cease from their own works? Or did we not long ago agree among ourselves that temperance is the science of science or ignorance, and not the faculty of any other? Is it not so? CRITIAS. It certainly appears so. SOCRATES. Therefore, it will not be the craftsman of health. CRITIAS. No. SOCRATES. For health is the work of another art. CRITIAS. Of another, certainly. SOCRATES. Nor of utility then, my friend. For we attributed this work to another art a little while ago, did we not? CRITIAS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. In what way then will temperance be useful to us, since it is the craftsman of no utility? CRITIAS. In no way do I see it, Socrates. SOCRATES. Do you see, Critias, that I did not fear without cause earlier, and that I blamed myself because I understood nothing great or useful concerning temperance? For never would this, which is held to be the most beautiful of all things, have appeared useless to us if I were in any way useful for searching correctly. But now we succumb on all sides, nor are we able to find for what principal significance the author of names himself established the name of temperance; although we have conceded many things that are entirely abhorrent to reason. Furthermore, we agreed that it is the science of science, though reason was reluctant and had previously refuted it. Moreover, we conceded that the works of the remaining sciences are known by this very science, with reason similarly opposing it: so that a temperate man would be such that he knows what he knows, knows himself, and again understands what he does not know. This we conceded quite magnificently and too freely, not noticing that it is impossible for someone to know in some way what he in no way knows. In this, however, we agreed: namely, that someone knows that he does not know certain things which he does not know. And yet there is nothing, as my opinion goes, that seems more absurd than this. Nevertheless, this investigation, having found us foolish rather than hard and persistent, can find the truth no more; but it has mocked itself to such an extent that what we have for a long time fashioned by common consent and posited to be temperance, has finally appeared as something useless, insolent, and quite insulting. I am distressed by this for your sake, O Charmides, rather than my own: if you, endowed with such an excellent nature and temperance of soul, are helped nothing by such great virtue, and it profits you nothing in life itself. I am also annoyed on account of the incantation <note>A reference to the Thracian "Zalmoxis" charm Socrates claims to use to cure Charmides' headache</note> which I learned from that Thracian; if I have placed so much study in perceiving a thing of no value. Therefore, that these things are so, I do not quite believe. Rather, I think myself a lazy investigator: since I deem temperance to be a certain great good, and if you possess it, you are blessed. But consider whether you possess it and do not need the incantation. For if you have it, I would advise you to think me a madman and incapable of investigating the truth; but you, the more temperate you are, the happier you are. CHARMIDES. I do not know, by Jove, O Socrates, whether I have it or not. For how should I understand that which you yourselves, as you say, cannot yet find out what it is? Indeed, I do not believe you much, Socrates. Rather, I think I need the incantation; and as far as I am concerned, nothing prevents you from healing me with incantations daily, until you think I have enough. CRITIAS. Look, Charmides, if you do this, it will be proof to me that you are temperate: because you subject yourself to the incantations of Socrates and never depart from his side. CHARMIDES. Consider that I will obey and follow him everywhere. Indeed, I would sin gravely unless I obeyed you, my guardian, and performed what you command. CRITIAS. I do command it. CHARMIDES. I will do it diligently, and I shall begin today. SOCRATES. What are these two deliberating? CHARMIDES. Nothing more. Indeed, it is decreed. SOCRATES. Will you use force? And leave me no judgment for consulting in turn? CHARMIDES. Consider that I will certainly use force, since he commands it. To this, you also consult what you are going to do. SOCRATES. No place for consultation remains. For no one will be able to resist you when you are attempting and compelling something. CHARMIDES. Then you do not resist. SOCRATES. I shall certainly not oppose you.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for the Laches, or on Fortitude.

<note>Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator of Plato into Latin during the Renaissance. His "Arguments" serve as introductory commentaries.</note>

Plato oftentimes places the best magistrates above the laws: because laws without them seem entirely useless, for no one will keep them; but the best magistrates are themselves the laws. But he says that magistrates cannot become the best unless the citizens are the best men; nor will men be such unless the youths and boys are also such. For this reason, in almost all the dialogues, he exhorts parents especially to educate their children correctly, knowing that the human race cannot live honestly or be governed happily without the best governors. Furthermore, there will never be good princes in a republic unless they are men of the highest character: specifically, cultivated diligently from a tender age. But since childhood is for the most part sufficiently ruled under domestic providence; whereas youth, having obtained a looser license, wanders everywhere without bridles; rightly our Plato [spends] much [effort]...

<summary>This page concludes the Charmides with Socrates and Charmides playfully agreeing to continue their "incantations," followed by Marsilio Ficino's introduction to the Laches, emphasizing the importance of education and character in leadership.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Critias, Charmides, Marsilio Ficino, Laches, temperance, fortitude, Plato, education, governance</keywords>

--- Page 252 ---
<meta>This page serves as the "Argument" or introductory summary for Plato's dialogue *Laches*. It establishes the pedagogical and moral framework for the discussion on courage and the education of the youth.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE LACHES.

First, it treats the correction and restraining of young men: and it heavily complains of that age which joins softness and wantonness with insolence and pride. Therefore, it is placed in the greatest danger: both because it is insufficiently observed by those at home, and because it is unhappily neglected by laws and magistrates—especially since young men infect one another just as they are infected everywhere by their elders. Therefore, in the *Laws* and the *Republic*, <note>Referring to Plato's other works, *De Legibus* and *Respublica*.</note> he appoints a specific magistrate for the youth above all others. This man, like a scout or explorer (if I may put it that way), should be sent daily, both by night and by day, throughout the entire city to observe the individual habits, words, and gestures of every young man: and to faithfully report their individual deeds and sayings to the magistrate, as if to a shepherd and father. Nor was this necessary diligence regarding youth a concern for Plato alone among all men; indeed, not even Aristotle himself could fail to highly approve of Plato in this matter.

But let us come to the dialogue. Lysimachus and Melesias are thinking about educating their sons: having complained about their own parents, whose preoccupation with public affairs led them to neglect domestic matters and their children—even though the primary care of the state consists in caring for the youth. And although they are now old men, so that they might deliberate more rightly on this matter, they likewise call together Nicias and Laches (also old men who have sons) for consultation. And lest anything be overlooked, they bring Socrates into the counsel, not only as a partner but as a judge: Socrates, I say, who in his entire life treated nothing else but the proper care of every age, and especially of youth. 

Meanwhile, you will truly consider the wonderful praises of the Socratic life: likewise, that those are true praises which proceed from a man worthy of praise. But truly, since in some states the institution of laws inclines more toward gentleness than toward boldness, and in others the opposite: Plato, judging both to be dangerous, commands in the *Statesman* <note>original: "in Politico"</note> that gentleness be mixed with boldness and, in turn, boldness with gentleness. If anyone joins the *Charmides* to the *Laches*, and couples the exhortation to temperance there with the exhortation to fortitude here, he will rightly temper the souls of the youth. I pass over how, in this present dialogue's exhortation to fortitude, both Nicias and Laches admire military fortitude more than is becoming: and Nicias, moreover, extols the games of arms beyond measure as highly necessary preludes to warfare. But Laches, not without justice, corrects him. 

After this, the opinion is transferred to Socrates. Whereupon, notice that no harmony delights more than that which occurs in a wise man from the very concord of soul and speech. And on the contrary, no dissonance offends more than where the tongue is at odds with the mind. Furthermore, a ruined man is not to be listened to even if he speaks beautifully. Nor is it permitted to speak of morals unless one is moral. Besides, Socrates was always accustomed, whatever the subject being disputed, to lead his partner in dispute to the point where he would give an account of his whole life: as if you learn the affairs of others in vain unless you know yourself. He adds that it is necessary above all to subject oneself to some examination, to which accounts of one's past life are often rendered. This indeed strongly confirms the annual confession instituted by Christians. <note>The translator is drawing a parallel between Socratic self-examination and the Catholic Sacrament of Penance.</note> He adds also that one must learn as long as one must live. 

Socrates, however, the most cautious of all, says the judgment enjoined upon him should be transferred to the elders. But meanwhile, entreated by everyone, he approaches the matter itself, before all things approving of diligence in educating sons and disapproving of negligence. He adds that it cannot happen that someone exhorts another to fortitude unless he knows how to express what fortitude itself is. Soon, when Laches is asked what fortitude is, he answers rather confidently that it is the virtue by which one, not deserting the rank, defeats the enemy. This is refuted because someone can defeat an enemy no less by fleeing than by staying, after the manner of the Scythians, and be equally brave. Therefore, Homer calls him brave who knows how to dare and to fear at the opportune time. 

A little later, the victory of fortitude is drawn toward any subject matter: as if it befits a brave man to overcome not only fears, but also pains, lusts, and pleasures. Here a common definition of fortitude for all these things is sought. To this Laches responds that it is a certain endurance of the soul. But since this is insufficiently defined, Socrates compels him to add: that endurance itself ought to be honorable and beneficial; but it will not be of such a kind unless it is done prudently. Therefore, he compels Laches to say that fortitude is properly "prudent endurance." If indeed fortitude is something beautiful and good. 

Then it is asked: what endurance, and for what is it prudent? That is, concerning what matter, or what duty? Laches slips when he is asked generally whether where there is greater boldness, there is greater fortitude: he concedes this, and again admits that boldness is necessarily greater in him who, without skill in the matter itself yet knowing the danger, approaches the task, than in him who enters it equipped with skill. For the latter acts more cautiously and safely. Laches finally accepts that where there is more boldness and less skill or prudence, fortitude is greater. In this concession, he both contradicts himself and admits a falsehood. For fortitude is indeed something beautiful and beneficial: but imprudent boldness is base and harmful. 

Among these things, note the well-worn opinion of Socrates and Plato: each man is good at those things in which he is wise, and bad at those in which he is ignorant. Surely, just as all errors—both of the hand in grasping and of the foot in walking—proceed from a defect of sight itself: so Socrates thinks all errors of men, both in choosing and in acting, proceed from a defect of intelligence. For where the leader himself is blind and striking out swiftly, all things fall headlong. 

After Laches, Nicias defines fortitude as the knowledge of things to be feared and things not to be feared: namely, by what reason and to what extent they are to be feared or attacked. He calls fortitude a certain habit established with prudence concerning things to be feared and attacked. But he calls rash boldness without prudence "ferocity." Socrates argues against Nicias thus: of whatever things there is some knowledge, there is not one knowledge of past things as they were done, another of present things as they are being done, and another of future things as they might best be done: but it belongs to the same knowledge to understand all these. If, therefore, fortitude is the knowledge of daring and fearing regarding good and evil things, namely as they are in the future: it is surely also the knowledge of the same as they are in the present and the past—of all things simply. It is, therefore, universal virtue. But we [defined] forti-

# FOLIO CXVI.
## LACHES, OR ON FORTITUDE.
### p iiii
<meta>catchword: this</meta>

...as if from the beginning we were seeking some part of virtue. This objection was made not so much to refute Nicias, as to test him. But Nicias did not know how to defend his definition. Socrates, however, being unwilling to act as a teacher among his elders out of modesty, pretends that he is similarly ignorant of the definition. He exhorts them to prepare themselves together as students of virtue before they profess the ability to educate youth, showing that in every age moral discipline is greatly necessary, and that one must always learn without the blush of shame. Indeed, the definitions which he seeks here concerning fortitude <note>original: "fortitudine"; courage</note>, or in the *Charmides* concerning temperance, are not completed here or there—where the intent is merely to exhort and advise—but in the *Republic* and the *Laws*. 

But to speak briefly of fortitude and temperance together as if they were siblings: Plato, in the *Phaedrus* and the *Symposium*, compares this life of ours to a certain journey. In directing this journey, Reason represents the charioteer; the passions, however, partly superior and partly inferior, represent twin horses, namely the white and the black. And so that we may distinguish more conveniently as pertains to the proposed question: he says that Divine Providence established modesty to call us back from shameful things and to continually provoke us toward honorable ones. Therefore, it implanted in us shame and magnanimity <note>high-mindedness or greatness of soul</note>, so that our charioteer might restrain our passions—like horses—from shameful though sweet things using shame as a bridle, but might stimulate them toward honorable though difficult things using the spurs of magnanimity. 

For a certain evil demon allures us toward shameful things with the enticements of pleasure, and frightens us away from honorable things with the bitterness of pain. Wherefore temperance, using the reins of shame, ensures that we always abstain from shameful things despite the pleasure; and fortitude, relying on the spurs of magnanimity, takes care that we strive manfully toward honorable things, having despised the fear of difficulty and pain. And by as much as it is more difficult to overcome pains than to abstain from pleasures, by so much might it perhaps seem to someone that fortitude is to be preferred over temperance. Finally, temperance ensures that we are not cast down from being men into beasts; but fortitude, beyond that, ensures that we are in a certain way transformed into God by overcoming all things. On account of this virtue especially, all antiquity placed Hercules in the number of the gods—Hercules, I say, who while a victor of the earth climbed the celestial steps, with these words crying out: *Go now, brave ones, where the high path of a great example leads; why do you, idle ones, turn your backs? The earth, once overcome, grants the stars.* <note>A quote from Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy, Book IV, Meter 7.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring a classical figure, possibly a deity or hero, seated within an architectural frame with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>
LYSIMACHUS: You have watched this man fighting in armor, O Nicias and Laches; but for what reason I and Melesias here asked you to watch this with us, we have not yet declared. Now, however, we shall open the matter, for we think we must speak freely with you. For there are some who mock these things; and if anyone consults them, they do not express their true opinion, but guessing at the matter under consultation and the mind of the consultant, they bring forth things other than what they truly feel. But since we judge you both sufficient to understand and able to explain simply what you know, we have taken you as partners in the deliberation of those things we shall relate. 

The matter about which I began is of this sort: These are our sons. This one here is the son of Melesias, named Thucydides after his grandfather; my son likewise bears the name of his grandfather, for we call him Aristides. It seems to us that the most diligent care must be taken for them; nor do we think, as many are accustomed to do, that as soon as their sons have grown up, they should be allowed to live according to their own lust; rather, then especially should diligent study be applied. Since, therefore, we see our sons are present with us, we judged that you, above all others, have considered by what method they should be educated so that they might become the best. If you have not turned much attention to it, we remind you at present that you ought not to neglect it, and we exhort you to deliberate with us on the education of our sons. 

Why this seems so to us, O Nicias and Laches, it is fitting to hear, though the things that follow are a little longer. We were reclining at a banquet together, I and Melesias here, and these youths were with us. As I indicated at the beginning of my speech, let us speak freely and boldly with you. Surely each of us can narrate to our sons many illustrious deeds of our fathers, both in peace and in war, and recount the famous things they did for the republic and its allies; but we can relate no deeds performed by ourselves. Wherefore we are ashamed of these things and we condemn them; and we often blame the negligence of our fathers, who, after we grew up, permitted us to live in a certain softness and in delights, while they performed the deeds of others. Showing these same things to these youths, we declare that if they neglect themselves and despise our precepts, they will be ignoble; but if they take care, they will perhaps turn out worthy of their ancestral names. They, for their part, reply that they will obey us. 

But while we were pleasantly consulting about this—by what discipline or custom they might best become the best—someone explained that it would be worthwhile for them to learn to fight in armor; and he praised this man whom you just now watched competing, and told us to observe him. Therefore, we thought it would be best for us to come to this spectacle and to call you together with us, both to watch and also, if you wish, to deliberate in common counsel concerning the education of the youths. These are the things we desired to confer with you about. It is now your part to advise both on this matter—whether it should be learned or not—and on any other discipline or study you think worthy of praise for a youth.

<margin>That boys ought to learn the discipline of arms.</margin>

prohibits it, Socrates. It seems to me that this skill is useful to youths everywhere; nor should they linger in those things to which youths are accustomed to give themselves when they find leisure: but it is better to acquire that faculty through which a robust habit of the body is acquired. For this exercise is inferior to no other, nor is it less laborious. Moreover, such exercise and equestrian skill especially befit a free man. For in that contest of which we are athletes, and in these things also where a contest is proposed to us, only those contend who exercise themselves in such instruments of war. Furthermore, this skill will be of use in the fight itself, as often as one must contend in the battle line and in rank. But it will be most useful then, when the lines are dissolved: and in singular combat it will be necessary either to pursue one resisting or to repel one attacking in flight. Surely he who is instructed in this faculty will never succumb to one; perhaps not even to many; rather, he will everywhere excel. Besides, this faculty brings a desire for another certain noble discipline. For anyone, when he has learned to fight in arms, will desire the discipline concerning the ordering of battle lines which follows immediately; and having attained this, and being inflamed with a desire for glory regarding these things, he will betake himself to the command of armies; and summarily he will turn himself to all noble institutions and studies which revolve around these things, worthy of knowledge and use, with that primary skill leading him. We shall also add something not to be despised: that this faculty will make everyone wonderfully bolder and stronger in battle. Nor should that be kept silent, though it might seem lighter to some, that it will make a man appear more fit there where it is most necessary to appear fit and ready. Certainly, on account of his very dexterity, he will appear more terrible to the enemies. Therefore, O Lysimachus, it seems to me desirable that youths perceive these things; and for what reason I think so, I have explained. Nevertheless, I would gladly hear if Laches wishes to bring forward anything besides these things. LA. ...to think of it as a kind of inaccessible temple, nor ever dare to ascend even with the tip of one's foot. Instead, such a man wanders around the outside, boasting to others—especially among those who themselves would confess to being inferior to many others in military matters. Furthermore, Lysimachus, I have been present with not a few men of this sort while they were fighting, and I know what they are like; one may also judge from this: as if by deliberate effort, no one who has devoted himself to these games has ever turned out distinguished in war. While in all other pursuits those who practice frequently make the most progress, these men alone, beyond all others, are unable to achieve their desire in this; they seem to be so utterly unfortunate. 

For this Stesileus, whom you and I watched showing himself off in such a great crowd and professing such wonderful things, I have also observed elsewhere more accurately, when he was showing his true self to onlookers, though not by his own choice. He once boarded a great ship to fight against another, holding in his hands a certain military instrument quite different from the others—just as he himself differed from the rest. He had a <term>Dorydrepanum</term> <note>original: "Dorydrepanum. i. telum falcatum." A spear-tipped scythe or "spear-sickle."</note>, that is, a hooked weapon. The rest of this man's deeds are hardly worth hearing, yet this must not be passed over in silence: what happened because of such wonderful caution and this man's "machine"—I mean the scythe he added to the spear. While he was fighting, the scythe became entangled in the ship's rigging. Stesileus pulled to free it, but he could not; the ship was passing the other ship, and he meanwhile followed the ship's course while holding onto the spear. But when the ship had already passed and was pulling the man holding the spear along, the weapon finally slipped from his hand. 

A great shout of laughter arose on the ship because of Stesileus's appearance, and moreover because a stone thrown at his feet from the upper deck forced him to let go of the spear. Then indeed, even those on the <term>trireme</term> <note>A standard ancient Greek warship with three banks of oars.</note> could no longer contain their laughter when they saw his weapon hanging from that scythe on the ship. Perhaps to someone else these things are as Nicias asserts; but truly, the things I witnessed are such as these. Therefore, as I said at the beginning, whether this is a discipline, it is of little use; or if it is not, but is merely a pretense of what they profess, it does not seem a matter worthy of study. Indeed, I think that if a timid man should pursue this skill, he would become bolder because of it and thus more conspicuous in his cowardice than he was before. But if a brave man should follow it, he will be watched by men, and if he errs even slightly, he will undergo great slander. For the profession of this knowledge is an envious one; therefore, unless he who claims this knowledge for himself surpasses others in virtue in a wonderful way, he cannot avoid being held as a laughingstock. Such, Lysimachus, does the study of this discipline seem to me. It is necessary, as I was saying from the start, to earnestly entreat this Socrates to give his opinion on the proposed question.

**LYSIMACHUS:** I do indeed ask you, Socrates; for this definition requires the judgment of someone to decide it. If these two had agreed with each other, there would be less need for such consultation; but since Laches and Nicias disagree, as you see, it is better to hear now which opinion you yourself would support.

**SOCRATES:** What then, Lysimachus? Will you stick with whichever side more of us praise?

**LYSIMACHUS:** What else should one do, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** And would you, Melesias, do the same? If you were consulting about the exercise of your son, would you trust the majority of us, or rather the one who had learned under a skilled master of exercise and had practiced himself?

**MELESIAS:** To that one, deservedly, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** You would therefore give greater trust to that one man than to the four of us.

**MELESIAS:** Perhaps.

**SOCRATES:** For one ought to judge by knowledge, not by multitude, that which is to be judged rightly.

**MELESIAS:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Must we not first consider this: whether any among us is an expert in the matter about which we are now deliberating, or not? And if such a person is found, he should be believed, setting aside the opinion of the others. But if no one is found, we must seek someone else! Or do you think you are undergoing a small risk now, you and Lysimachus, rather than a risk concerning the most precious of all your possessions? For if sons turn out good or bad, the entire paternal house will be governed in the same way that the sons are disposed.

**MELESIAS:** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we must watch over this matter diligently.

**MELESIAS:** Very much so.

**SOCRATES:** In what way, then, should we have considered what I was just saying, if we wanted to find which of us turned out most skillful in competing? Would we not have examined the one who both learned and practiced—the one, evidently, for whom suitable teachers of this matter existed?

**MELESIAS:** So I think, indeed.

**SOCRATES:** And should we not first determine what that thing is for which we are seeking teachers?

**MELESIAS:** How do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** Perhaps you will perceive it more clearly this way. It does not seem to have been established between us at the start what that thing is in which we are searching for who among us is most skilled, and for the sake of which one has had teachers and another has not.

**NICIAS:** Were we not asking, Socrates, whether young men ought to learn to fight in armor, or not?

**SOCRATES:** Exactly so, Nicias. But when someone asks about a remedy for the eyes, whether it should be applied or not, do you think the consultation is about the remedy or about the eyes?

**NICIAS:** About the eyes.

**SOCRATES:** And when someone asks whether a bridle should be used on a horse or not, and when, then he consults not about the bridle, but rather about the horse?

**NICIAS:** True.

**SOCRATES:** To put it briefly: whenever someone seeks something for the sake of another thing, the consultation is about that very thing for whose sake the other is sought, not about that which is sought for the sake of another.

**NICIAS:** It must be so.

**SOCRATES:** It is necessary, therefore, to examine the counselor: whether he is skilled in the care of that thing for whose sake we are presently deliberating.

**NICIAS:** Entirely.

**SOCRATES:** Has it not been said that the inquiry into the discipline is for the sake of the souls of the young men?

**NICIAS:** It has been said.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we must inquire if any of us is powerful in the art of caring for souls, and is able to cultivate them sufficiently, and has had learned teachers.

**NICIAS:** Have you never seen, Socrates, some people turn out more skilled in a certain matter without teachers than those who had them?

**SOCRATES:** I have indeed seen them, Laches; yet you yourself would not believe them if they proclaimed themselves the best craftsmen, unless they showed some work of their art rightly constructed, whether one or many.

**NICIAS:** What you say is true.

**SOCRATES:** It befits us, therefore, Laches and Nicias—since Lysimachus and Melesias have called us together to consult about their sons, desiring their souls to be made the best—if we claim to have had teachers, to show them: those who were themselves first the best...

...they have educated the minds of many young men, and afterwards taught us as well. Or if any of us denies having had a teacher, he ought to show his own works: and bring into the open which of the Athenians or strangers, whether slave or free, has indisputably turned out good through his diligence. But if we can show neither, we ought to bid them go to other counselors, lest we undergo the danger of corrupting the sons of our friends, for which we would deserve the greatest accusation from the youths' households. 

Indeed, O Lysimachus and Melesias, I say of myself first of all that no master has appeared for me in this matter, although from a tender age I have always desired this thing. Nevertheless, I am not able to pay the fee to the Sophists <note>Professional teachers in Ancient Greece who charged for lessons in virtue and rhetoric.</note>, who alone promised to make me good and distinguished. Truly, by my own talent, I am even now quite unable to discover this art. If Nicias here or Laches has discovered or learned it, I shall certainly not wonder at it. For they abound more in money, so that they might learn from others, and they are older, so that they might have already discovered it. They seem to me, moreover, to be sufficient for educating; for they would not have decided so fearlessly about the good or bad studies of the young unless they thought they sufficiently understood these things. 

In other matters I believe them; but I am amazed that they disagree. And just as Laches recently urged you not to let me go, but to question me, so now I in turn ask and command you, Lysimachus, do not let Laches and Nicias go, but inquire of them, saying to them that Socrates says he does not understand the matter himself, nor can he judge which of you speaks the truth, especially since he was neither the inventor of these things himself, nor did he learn from another teacher. 

But you, Laches and Nicias, tell us both: whom have you met who is most learned regarding the education of youth? And do you know these things from learning from someone, or are you rather the inventors yourselves? If you learned them, who was the master of each? Or who are the other professors of that same art? So that if you have little leisure for these things due to the business of the Republic, we may go to them and persuade them, either by gifts or favor or both, to undertake the care of our sons and yours, lest by becoming wicked they be a disgrace to their ancestors. But if you yourselves discovered this, bring into the open any others whom perhaps by your diligence you have rendered good and distinguished men from being depraved. 

For truly, if you are now beginning to teach for the first time, it must be observed that you are not risking some hired Carian <note>original: "Carem quendam mercede conductum" - referring to a proverb about taking risks with something of little value (a Carian slave) before risking something precious.</note>, but you are leading both your own sons and those of your friends into danger. And indeed, as the proverb has it,

you are "learning the potter's art on the great jar" <note>A Greek proverb meaning to start learning a craft on a large, expensive project rather than a small, cheap one.</note>. Tell us, therefore: what of these things do you claim to possess and be fit for, or what do you deny? Inquire these things of them, Lysimachus, and do not let them go before they answer.

**LYSIMACHUS:** Socrates speaks well, O men, or so it seems to me. If, therefore, it will be pleasing to you, O Nicias and Laches, to answer those questioning, you yourselves shall see to it; it is certainly pleasing to me and to Melesias here if you are willing to go through everything Socrates asks with reason. For I said right from the beginning that I called you together for consultation for this reason: because we thought these things were already thought out by you, as is fitting, especially since you have sons as we do, now established at almost that age in which one must think about education. **NICIAS:** You seem to me, Lysimachus, to know Socrates only from his father, and never to have had familiarity with him, unless perhaps when he was a boy, following his father, he stayed near you at some time either in a temple or another public assembly. But it appears you have not yet spoken to him now that he has become a man.

**LYSIMACHUS:** Why, O Nicias?

**NICIAS:** You seem to be ignorant that whoever approaches Socrates in speech as if by kinship, and sticks to him in dispute—even if he began to dispute about something else—is finally led by Socrates' words to give an account of his own life: what the condition of his present and past life is. And after he falls into this, Socrates does not let him go until he has sufficiently examined all these things. I, however, have experienced this familiarly, and I know from his words that it is necessary to endure this; and I am not ignorant of what I myself will now suffer. This familiarity, O Lysimachus, delights me greatly. For I do not think it is harmful to be brought to remembrance if we have done or are doing anything not rightly. Rather, it is necessary that he who does not flee these things becomes more cautious for the future, thinking according to that saying of Solon <note>Solon was an Athenian statesman and poet; the saying refers to "learning as long as one lives."</note> that one must learn as long as he lives, and not hoping that old age itself will give us wisdom. 

<margin>
Commendation of Socrates.
</margin>

<margin>
The precept of Solon.
</margin>

To me, therefore, it is neither unusual nor unpleasant to be examined by Socrates. Indeed, I knew long ago that with Socrates present, the discussion would not be about the boys, but about ourselves. Therefore, nothing prohibits me from debating with Socrates however he himself wishes. But consider how Laches is affected toward this.

**LACHES:** I am affected simply toward discussions, Nicias; or rather, if you wish, doubly. Furthermore, I might seem to anyone to be a lover of words, and at other times the opposite. For as often as I hear someone disputing about virtue or some wisdom who is truly a man and worthy of the words themselves, I am affected by a certain wonderful pleasure, contemplating the speaker and the words together, how they are congruent and harmonious with each other. And such a man truly seems to me to be a musician, having tuned a most sweet harmony—not on a lyre or some playful instruments, but truly tempering his life with the concord of words and deeds: harmonizing according to the Dorian melody <note>The Dorian mode was considered by Greeks to be the only truly brave and Greek musical scale, as opposed to the softer Ionian or Phrygian modes.</note>, not the Ionian, or Phrygian, or Lydian, but that which is the only truly Greek harmony. Such a man, therefore, delights me wonderfully with his words, and makes me seem more greedy for words, so great is the attention with which I receive his sayings. But whoever acts to the contrary offends my ears; and the more elegantly he seems to speak, the more he makes me seem to abhor discussions. I have not yet experienced Socrates' words, but his deeds have certainly proved to me at times that he is worthy of noble words and all freedom of speech. If, therefore, he possesses this also, I plainly agree with him, and most willingly...

Nicias and Laches express their willingness to be questioned, noting that Socrates' character matches his speech.</summary>

# LACHES, OR ON FORTITUDE. PAGE 118.

I shall be most excellently examined by such a man; nor will it be troublesome for me to learn anything from him. And yet I also yield to Solon <note>The Athenian lawmaker known for the saying "I grow old always learning many things."</note> with this addition: that I wish to learn many things as I grow old, but only from good men. Let this, therefore, be granted to me, that the teacher himself is good, lest by chance I seem to be an unwilling pupil. Nor do I care whether the teacher is younger, or not yet famous in the opinion of men, or possesses any other such quality. I declare to you then, Socrates, that you may teach me and refute me however you wish, and learn what I myself may know. I have certainly been so disposed toward you since that day when you underwent danger with me, and provided that mirror of your virtue—that testimony which anyone must exhibit who is to undergo a trial justly. Therefore, say what you please, having no fear of our age.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we shall not be able to excuse you as being less prepared for consulting and investigating.

**LYSIMACHUS:** But it is certainly our task, O Socrates. For I consider you one of us. Think, therefore, on my behalf for the sake of the youths, what we ought to seek from them; and consult by debating with them. For many things indeed slip from my memory due to old age, out of those things I had determined to inquire into; and again, I do not sufficiently recall those things I have heard if other conversations intervene. For this reason, you all proceed in turn with what we proposed; I indeed shall listen, and when I have heard, I will carry out whatever you and Melesias here decide.

**SOCRATES:** O Nicias and Laches, we must obey Lysimachus and Melesias. Therefore, regarding what we strove to investigate above—namely, who has stood out to us as teachers of such discipline, or what others we ourselves have made better—it would perhaps do no harm to examine ourselves. But a consideration of this sort will, I think, return to the same point and seek from a deeper source. If by chance we knew of something that, being present in someone, makes that person better, and again we were able to apply that very thing to him, it is clear that we would know that very thing about which we were then taking counsel, investigating by what means someone might attain it most easily and best. Perhaps you do not understand; but you will comprehend more easily this way. If we knew that sight, when present in eyes, makes them better, and again we were able to apply it to the eyes, it is clear that we would also know what sight itself is. Concerning this, we would then have to consult by what method someone might acquire it most easily and conveniently. For if we were ignorant of what sight itself is, or what hearing is, we would never be suitable consultants of medicine regarding the eyes or ears, investigating how someone might best recover sight and hearing.

**LACHES:** You speak the truth, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Have these men not chosen us at present, O Laches, to consult by what means virtue, applied to the souls of their sons, might make them better?

**LACHES:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not necessary, therefore, to establish this: namely, to understand what virtue itself is? For if we are entirely ignorant of what virtue is, in what way could we advise anyone, and show the best and easiest way to virtue?

**LACHES:** In no way, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Do we admit, Laches, that we understand what virtue is?

**LACHES:** We certainly admit it.

**SOCRATES:** If we understand it, we can certainly also express what it is.

**LACHES:** Nothing prevents it.

**SOCRATES:** However, let us not immediately seek what the whole of virtue is, best of men. For that is a greater task. But let us first look at some part of it, to see if it is sufficiently clear to us. And in this way, the investigation will be easier for us.

**LACHES:** Let us do as you please.

**SOCRATES:** Which part of virtue, then, shall we single out? Is it perhaps that to which the discipline of arms itself seems to look? It seems to many to look toward fortitude <note>The Latin *fortitudo* translates the Greek *andreia*, meaning courage or manliness.</note>, does it not?

**LACHES:** Very much so.

**SOCRATES:** First, therefore, let us attempt to reveal what fortitude is, O Laches; then we shall investigate in what way it may be acquired by youths, as far as can be done through exercise and instruction. Therefore, strive to explain to us what fortitude is.

<margin>Thus far the occasion of the dialogue was promised. A false definition of fortitude.</margin>

**LACHES:** That is not difficult to say, O Socrates. Know for certain that he is brave who, keeping his rank, presses on against the enemy and does not flee.

**SOCRATES:** You speak well, Laches. But perhaps because I asked you with obscure words, I gave cause for you to answer something other than what I myself intended to ask.

**LACHES:** Why do you say that, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** I will explain if I can. The brave man is he whom you yourself describe: whoever, not deserting his rank, fights against the enemy.

**LACHES:** This is the very one I mean.

**SOCRATES:** And I as well. But does not he also fight who does not remain, but flees?

**LACHES:** How "flees"?

**SOCRATES:** Just as the Scythians are said to fight no less by fleeing than by pursuing. Whence also Homer, praising the horses of Aeneas, says they follow and flee most swiftly here and there. And he similarly praised Aeneas himself for his very knowledge of fearing; and he said that he was skilled in fearing and fleeing.

**LACHES:** And rightly so, O Socrates; for he was speaking of chariots, but you are speaking of the Scythian cavalry. Their cavalry certainly fight in that way; but the experts of Greek armor fight as I myself was saying.

**SOCRATES:** Except for the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, Laches. For they say that the Lacedaemonians at Plataea, when they had approached the shield-bearers, did not withstand their first attack, nor did they stand their ground, but rather fled. But after the ranks of the Persians were broken, they turned back; and fighting in the manner of cavalry, they emerged victors in that battle.

**LACHES:** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES:** Rightly, therefore, I said that my questioning was the cause of your less-than-correct response. For I wished to ask not only about those who are brave regarding light armor, but also about the cavalry, and about all simply who are brave in any kind of war; and not only on land, but also in storms at sea; and even about those who are brave against diseases or poverty or civil affairs. Nor only about those who are steadfast against pains or fears, but also about those who can fight bravely against pleasures and desires, whether by standing firm or even by turning away. For there are some, O Laches, who are brave in these matters as well.

**LACHES:** Very much so, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Are not all these brave? Yet some possess fortitude regarding pleasures, some regarding pains, some regarding desires, and some regarding fears; and those who are timid regarding the same things are, I think, cowards.

**LACHES:** That is entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** I was asking what each of these is.

<margin>An enumeration is made so that fortitude may be sought simply.</margin>
