### PAGE XXI.

<meta>Image quality: Good, clear typography. Catchword at bottom right: "fortis" (brave).</meta>

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, try again to the best of your ability to express what courage itself is, which is found to be the same in all these instances. Do you not yet understand? **LACHES:** Not sufficiently. **SOCRATES:** I am speaking just as if I had asked what speed itself is, which is present in us when running, and in playing the lyre, and in speaking, and in learning, and in many other things; which we possess, as is worth saying, either in the movements of the hands, or the feet, or the mouth and voice, or the intellect. Do you not say the same? **LACHES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if someone were to ask me: "O Socrates, what do you say this thing is which you name 'speed' in all these activities?"

<margin>Definition of speed.</margin>
I would certainly answer that I call the power of accomplishing many things in a short time "speed," whether in regard to the voice, or running, or all other things. **LACHES:** Correct. **SOCRATES:** Try then, Laches, to similarly define courage: what power is it that is the same in pleasure and pain, and in all those things in which we were just saying it was equally present, and which is named "courage" in each instance? **LACHES:** It seems to me that courage is a certain endurance of the soul, if one must say what applies to courage across all things. **SOCRATES:** We must certainly say so, if we are to answer the questions ourselves. However, I do not think you consider every kind of endurance to be courage. I gather this from the following: I know this much, Laches, that you consider courage to be something beautiful <note>original: "pulchrum" - in this context, it implies "noble" or "morally excellent".</note>. **LACHES:** Indeed, certainly most beautiful. **SOCRATES:** Is not endurance accompanied by prudence <note>original: "prudentia" - practical wisdom or foresight.</note> both beautiful and good? **LACHES:** Absolutely. **SOCRATES:** But that which is accompanied by imprudence—is it not, on the contrary, harmful and noxious? **LACHES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Will you call something "beautiful" that is of such a kind—harmful and noxious? **LACHES:** That would be a sin, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you will not call such endurance "courage," since it is not beautiful, while courage itself is beautiful. **LACHES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** According to your argument, then, prudent endurance is courage. **LACHES:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Let us see, then, what kind of endurance it is, and in what respect it is "prudent." Is it in respect to all things, both great and small? For instance, if someone endures while prudently spending money, knowing that from this expense he will make a profit—would you perhaps call him brave? **LACHES:** By no means. **SOCRATES:** Or if a doctor, when his son or someone else is burdened by a lung ailment and begs for drink or food, endures and does not yield? **LACHES:** I would not call this endurance courage either. **SOCRATES:** But what about a man in war who is enduring and ready for battle, who prudently provides for himself by looking around at each detail, knowing that others will come to his aid, and that he is to fight against fewer and weaker men, and moreover holds more advantageous positions and defenses? Would you say a man enduring with such foresight and preparation is braver than the one in the opposing army who stands his ground and endures? **LACHES:** On the contrary, Socrates, the one in the opposing army. **SOCRATES:** Yet the endurance of this man is more "imprudent" than that of the other. **LACHES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, would you say a man gifted with equestrian skill who endures in a cavalry battle is less brave than one who endures without such skill? **LACHES:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** And furthermore, that he who knows how to use a sling, or draw a bow, or any other such thing and endures, is less brave? **LACHES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Likewise, those who, without the art of swimming, descend into a well and dare to endure and persist in that work, or in any other work without skill—would you say they are braver than those who are learned in those arts? **LACHES:** What else could one say, Socrates! **SOCRATES:** Nothing, if that is what one thinks. **LACHES:** I certainly think so. **SOCRATES:** And yet, these men undergo dangers and endure more imprudently than those who approach these things with art. **LACHES:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Did not imprudent boldness and endurance previously appear to us as shameful and harmful? **LACHES:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** And it was agreed that courage is something beautiful. **LACHES:** It was clearly agreed. **SOCRATES:** Now, on the other hand, we have conceded that that shameful and imprudent endurance is courage. **LACHES:** So it appeared. **SOCRATES:** Do we seem to you to be speaking correctly? **LACHES:** Not to me, by Jove, Socrates! **SOCRATES:** Therefore, to use your words, you and I have not just now sung in "Doric harmony" <note>A metaphor for being in tune or consistent; the Doric mode was associated with bravery and stability.</note>. For our deeds do not harmonize with our words. In actual deed, someone might say we partake in courage, but in words, I think, not at all, if he were to hear us disputing at present. **LACHES:** You tell the absolute truth. **SOCRATES:** Does it seem beautiful to you that we should be in this state? **LACHES:** By no means. **SOCRATES:** Do you wish for us to at least trust and obey the argument we have introduced? **LACHES:** What argument, and which one especially? **SOCRATES:** The argument that commands us to "endure." If it pleases you, let us also stand firm and endure in this very inquiry, lest courage itself mock us for not investigating it bravely—if indeed endurance and constancy are often courage itself. **LACHES:** I, for my part, Socrates, am ready to persevere, even though these types of arguments are unfamiliar to me. But a certain ardor incites me to strive against what was said before, and I am exceedingly annoyed if I am so inept at expressing what I feel. For I seem to myself to understand what courage is, yet I know not how it just now escaped me, so that I could not encompass in words what it is. **SOCRATES:** Does it not befit a good hunter to run about exploring in a friendly way and to follow sagaciously, and not to give up lazily? **LACHES:** It certainly befits him. **SOCRATES:** Do you wish, then, that we invite Nicias here into this hunt, in case he might be more sagacious than we are? **LACHES:** Why wouldn't I! **SOCRATES:** Come then, Nicias, come to the aid of your friends who are tossing in a sea of words; run to those who are wavering, if you have any power. You see how much we are failing and in doubt. You, therefore, explaining what you think courage is, resolve the ambiguity and confirm your opinion with reason. **NICIAS:** You seem to me, Socrates, for some time now to have not defined courage correctly. Furthermore, you make no mention of that opinion which I have heard you introduce quite rightly at times. **SOCRATES:** Which opinion is that, Nicias?

<margin>A sentiment frequently on the lips of Socrates concerning all virtue and goodness.</margin>
**NICIAS:** I have often heard from you that everyone is good in those things in which he is wise, and bad in those in which he is ignorant. **SOCRATES:** By Jove, you report the truth, Nicias. **NICIAS:** Therefore, if a brave man is good, is he not also wise? **SOCRATES:** Do you hear, Laches? **LACHES:** I hear indeed, but I do not quite understand what he is saying. **SOCRATES:** But I seem to understand. For I suspect he is calling courage a certain kind of wisdom. **LACHES:** What wisdom, Socrates? **SOCRATES:** Are you not asking him this? **LACHES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Come, Nicias, declare to him what kind of wisdom courage is according to your argument.

# LACHES, OR ON COURAGE

**SO.** <note>Socrates</note> It is not fitting for him, nor for a flute-player. **NI.** <note>Nicias</note> No. **SO.** Nor indeed for a lyre-player. **NI.** Nor those. **SO.** But truly, what kind of wisdom is it, and knowledge of what matter? **LA.** <note>Laches</note> You question him quite rightly, Socrates. Therefore, let him explain what wisdom he says it is. **NI.** It is the knowledge of fearful things and non-fearful things, both in war and in all other matters. **LA.** How absurdly he speaks, Socrates! **SO.** Why do you say that, Laches? **LA.** Because wisdom is distinct from courage. **SO.** Nicias says it is not! **LA.** No, by Hercules; and for that reason, he is raving. **SO.** Why don't we teach him, setting aside these insults? **NI.** But Laches desires me to be refuted as if I were saying nothing, Socrates, because the same thing happened to him just now. **LA.** Without a doubt, Nicias: and I shall endeavor to show that you are saying nothing. Do not doctors know the fearful things in diseases? Or do those who are courageous seem to you to know those things? Or do you call doctors courageous? **NI.** Not at all. **LA.** Nor farmers, I think, although they know what is to be feared in cultivating the fields; furthermore, other craftsmen know what they ought to dare and what to fear in their own arts, yet they are no more courageous for it. **SO.** What does Laches seem to be saying to you, Nicias? **NI.** He says something, certainly, yet it is not true. **SO.** Why? **NI.** Because he thinks doctors know anything further regarding the sick beyond what is healthy and harmful, or what is sound and wholesome. They truly understand only this much. But whether it is to be dreaded, and whether it is an evil for someone to be healthy rather than to be sick: do you think, Laches, that doctors understand this? Or do you not think it is better for some not to rise from a disease than to recover? Tell me: do you assert it is better for all to live, and that death is not beneficial to many? **LA.** I think this is so. **NI.** Do you think the same things are fearful and evil for those for whom it is better to die as for those for whom it is better to live? **LA.** By no means. **NI.** Do you grant the judgment of these things to a doctor? Or to any other craftsman except one who understands fearful and non-fearful things, whom I call courageous? **SO.** Do you notice, Laches, what he is saying? **LA.** I notice indeed that he calls seers <note>original: "vates"</note> courageous. For who else would know for whom it is better to die than to live? And so, Nicias, do you confess that you are a seer, or neither a seer nor courageous? **NI.** Do you think it is the duty of a seer to distinguish between things to be feared and things to be undertaken? **LA.** I do indeed; for whose else? **NI.** Clearly his of whom I speak, my good man, much more so. For it belongs to the seer only to foreknow the portents and signs of the future, whether death threatens someone, or disease, or loss of property, or victory, or slaughter in war, or any other contest. But which of these it is better for someone to suffer or not to suffer, why should a seer judge rather than anyone else? **LA.** I do not know what he wants for himself, Socrates. For he declares neither the seer, nor the doctor, nor any other to be the one he calls courageous—unless perhaps he says he is some god. It seems to me that Nicias is unwilling to frankly admit he is saying nothing; he is carried up and down, and hides his ignorance. Indeed, a little while ago, you and I, Socrates, could have dodged the issue in the same way if we had wished to dissemble, so that we would not seem to speak contradictions. If, therefore, we had to plead in a court of law, it would be fitting in a way to do this. But now, what need is there to vainly adorn oneself with words in this gathering? **SO.** None, as it seems to me, Laches. But let us see if perhaps Nicias thinks he is saying something, and does not say these things for the sake of wordy grace. Therefore, let us inquire more clearly from him what he feels; and if he seems to bring any truth, we shall agree; otherwise, we shall teach him. **LA.** You ask him yourself, if you wish, Socrates. For I have inquired enough. **SO.** Nothing prevents me. For the interrogation will be common to both me and you. **LA.** Entirely so. **SO.** Tell me, Nicias—or rather tell us, for this question is common to both me and Laches: do you say courage is the knowledge of fearful and non-fearful things? **NI.** I do. **SO.** And that to distinguish this is not the work of just any man, since neither the doctor nor the seer knows this, nor is he courageous unless he has attained this very knowledge—did you not say so? **NI.** Exactly so. **SO.** Therefore, as the proverb goes, "not even a pig would know this," nor would it be courageous. **NI.** Certainly not, as it seems to me. **SO.** It is certain then, <margin>Proverb: Not even a pig would know this.</margin> Nicias, that you do not believe even the Crommyonian sow was courageous. I do not say these things for the sake of joking; but I think he who speaks thus admits the courage of no brute beast, nor concedes that any beast is so wise that it knows what very few men know because of the difficulty—whether it be a lion, or a leopard, or some wild boar. But it is necessary for him who defines courage as you do to say that the lion, the deer, the bull, and the monkey are equally fashioned by nature for courage. **LA.** By the gods, you speak rightly, Socrates! And tell us truly, Nicias: do you say these wild beasts are wiser than us, all of which we confess to be courageous? Or do you dare, against the opinion of all, to deny they are courageous? **NI.** Indeed, Laches, I do not call brute beasts courageous, nor anything else that does not fear terrible things through ignorance; rather, I call them intrepid and foolish. Or do you think I call all children courageous who fear nothing because of their lack of knowledge? I think that being intrepid is not the same as being courageous. For I think courage and prudence <note>original: "pudentia," here used in the sense of foresight or wise caution</note> are found in very few; but ferocity, audacity, and intrepidity without prudence are found in many men, women, children, and beasts. Therefore, what you and many others call courageous, I name ferocious; but I call courageous those things which prudently discern what is worthy of audacity and what of fear. **LA.** Do you see, Socrates, how beautifully this man, as he thinks himself, suborns himself with words? He contends to deprive those of the gift of courage whom all others agree are courageous. **SO.** Not I, Laches; but be of good cheer. For I say that both you and Lamachus are wise if you are courageous, and many other Athenians besides. **LA.** I will bring nothing against these things even if I were able, lest you say I am truly a certain Exonean <note>A reference to the deme of Aexone, whose inhabitants were stereotyped as slanderers.</note> slanderer and detractor. **SO.** Do not say so, Laches; for you seem to me not to have noticed that he received this kind of wisdom from our friend Damon. And Damon is very much a student of Prodicus. Prodicus, indeed, is said to distinguish such things excellently above all other sophists. **NI.** Truly, Socrates, it is more fitting for a sophist to exalt himself with these studies than for a man worthily performing public duties. **SO.** It is fitting for him

# BOOK

XXI.

Laches, who performs great deeds, must also possess great wisdom. But I think we must now inquire what Nicias primarily intended to signify by the name of courage. **LACHES:** You yourself investigate these things, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** I shall do so, best of men, lest you think you are excluded from our common discussion; but you also apply your mind and consider with us what must be said. **LACHES:** Let it be so, if it seems right to you to proceed thus. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, it certainly does. Now you, Nicias, tell us again from the beginning. You know that at the start of our talk we considered courage as a certain part of virtue? **NICIAS:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And did you not also, as was brought up above, answer that it was a certain part—as if there were other parts as well—all of which are called by the name of virtue? **NICIAS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** Do you name the same parts as I do? For I, besides courage, name temperance, justice, and other such things. Do you also? **NICIAS:** I do likewise. **SOCRATES:** Pay attention now. We admit these things. Next, let us consider those things which are worthy of fear and are "terrible," and those which are worthy of "boldness" <note>Latin: *audacia*, often translated as confidence or daring</note>; lest perhaps you think they are one thing, and we think they are another.

<margin>What things are terrible. What things are worthy of boldness. Fear is the expectation of a future evil.</margin>

For we will set forth what we believe. You, if you disagree, teach us. We think that "terrible" things are those which strike fear; "bold" things are those which present no fear. But fear is not brought by past evils, nor present ones, but by those which are expected. Indeed, we call fear the expectation of a future evil. Do you not feel the same, Laches? **LACHES:** Most certainly, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** You hear, Nicias: we say that "terrible" things to be feared are future evils; but "bold" things are future goods, or at least not evils. Do you feel this way about them, or otherwise? **NICIAS:** Certainly so. **SOCRATES:** And do you call the knowledge <note>Latin: *scientia*, translating the Greek *episteme*</note> of these things "courage"? **NICIAS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Let us see further if you agree with us on this third point. **NICIAS:** What is that? **SOCRATES:** I will say it. It seems to me and to this man <note>referring to Laches</note> that wherever there is a branch of knowledge, there is not one knowledge of past things as they happened, another of present things as they happen, and another of future things as they might best happen; rather, it is the work of the same knowledge to know all these. Just as regarding health and what is wholesome throughout all time, no knowledge other than the single art of medicine looks upon what is, what has been, and what will be, and in what manner they happen. And regarding those things which grow from the earth, agriculture is the same. Furthermore, in war you yourselves will be witnesses that the military art subtly foresees both all other things and the future; for you do not wish it to be subject to prophecy, but rather to rule over it, as it foresees more sharply what is happening and what will happen in war. And the law also decrees this: not that the prophet should rule the commander of the army, but that the commander should rule the prophet. Shall we assert this, Laches? **LACHES:** We shall. **SOCRATES:** Do you agree with us, Nicias, that it belongs to the same knowledge to know the same things whether they are past, present, or future? **NICIAS:** I do; for so it seems to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Then, best of men, is courage not the knowledge of things to be feared and their opposites, as you yourself declare? **NICIAS:** It is indeed. **SOCRATES:** But it was agreed that the things we fear are future evils, and the things we dare are future goods. **NICIAS:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** And the same knowledge covers the same things in the past, present, and future. **NICIAS:** These things are true. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, courage is not only the knowledge of things to be feared and their opposites. For it does not understand only future goods or evils, but also present and past ones, and looks upon all things simply, just as other branches of knowledge do. **NICIAS:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, Nicias, you have answered us regarding only a third part of courage, even though we asked what courage is as a whole. And now, as it appears at present according to your speech, courage is not only the knowledge of things to be feared and their opposites, but the knowledge of all goods and evils, and of all things simply, however they may be. Do you judge it so now, Nicias, or otherwise? **NICIAS:** So it seems to me, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Do you think, blessed man, that such a person lacks any virtue, who knows all goods exactly as they have been done, are being done, and will be done, and evils likewise? And do you think that man is in need of temperance, justice, or holiness, to whom alone it belongs to wisely understand both goods and evils concerning gods and men, to avoid the latter and reach for the former, since he knows how to live rightly with all? **NICIAS:** You seem to speak the truth, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, Nicias, what was introduced by you is not a part of virtue, but virtue in its entirety. **NICIAS:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** Yet we said that courage was a certain part of virtue. **NICIAS:** We clearly said so. **SOCRATES:** But what is said now does not appear to be that. **NICIAS:** No. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, Nicias, we have not found what courage itself is. **NICIAS:** We do not seem to have. **LACHES:** And I thought, my friend Nicias, that you would find it, after you looked down on me while I was answering Socrates. And so I hoped you would declare this to us from the wisdom of Damon <note>A famous music theorist and advisor to Pericles, mentioned here as Nicias's teacher</note>. **NICIAS:** How nicely you act, Laches, that you think it of no importance that you were shown above to understand nothing of courage; you only care whether I also appear such. You will think it makes no difference if you yourself understand nothing of these matters which anyone who prides himself ought to know. You seem, therefore, to act in a truly human way: looking not at yourself but at others. But I think enough has been said by me on the matters above. If anything was said insufficiently, I will correct it hereafter with Damon himself—whom you, though you have never seen him, think should be mocked—and I will also amend it with others. And after I have confirmed everything, I will teach you without grudge. For you seem to be very much in need of this instruction. **LACHES:** You are indeed a wise man, Nicias. Nevertheless, I advise Lysimachus here and Melesias not to require my or your efforts regarding the education of their sons, but to earnestly summon this Socrates for this work, as I had said in the beginning. I too, if my sons were grown, would have done the same. **NICIAS:** Indeed, I also think that if only Socrates wishes to take up the care of the youths, no one else should be sought. Certainly, I would most gladly commend Niceratus <note>Nicias's son</note> to him if he would accept. But as often as I speak to him about this, he offers certain others; he himself refuses. Try then, Lysimachus, whether Socrates will obey you more. **LYSIMACHUS:** It is only fair, Nicias; since I myself would strive to do many things for this man that I would not do for many others. What do you say, Socrates? Will you comply, and take care that these youths turn out as the best of men? **SOCRATES:** It would certainly be a hard thing, Lysimachus, if anyone were to refuse such care. # FOLIO 120.
## CLITOPHO, OR THE EXHORTATORY.

...if I had obeyed, these men would be ignorant, and I myself would deservedly be called to this work above all. But since we are all in equal doubt as to which of us should be chosen: it seems to me that no one in particular ought to be selected. However, since things stand as they do, see if I advise us rightly. I think it necessary, O men—for these matters should not be kept silent—that we all commonly and in turn seek out, first for ourselves, the best teacher (for we are in need); and then for the youths, sparing neither money nor anything else. But to live as we are living now, and to care for our sons in such a manner, I do not advise. And if anyone mocks us because at such an advanced age I decide to enter a teacher’s school, that saying of Homer must be cast back at them. For he says that shame is not a good companion for a man in need. <note>original: "Homeri illud obiciendum. Ait enim viro egeno verecundiam non conferre." Referring to Odyssey 17.347.</note> Therefore, despising all <margin>Homer’s saying: Shame does not benefit a man in need.</margin> the words of detractors, let us undertake this common care for ourselves and the youths. LYSIMACHUS: What you say pleases me, Socrates; and I determine that the older I am, the more studiously I shall learn along with the youths. But keep this for me: come to my house tomorrow at first light, and do not do otherwise, so that we may take counsel on these matters. For today’s gathering must now be dismissed. SOCRATES: I will do what you command, Lysimachus. And if God wills it, I shall come to you tomorrow.

->THE END OF LACHES.<-

### THE CLITOPHO OF PLATO, OR THE EXHORTATORY, TRANSLATED BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE TO PIERO DE' MEDICI, THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN.

->PERSONS OF THE HALVED DIALOGUE.<-
->SOCRATES, CLITOPHO.<-

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue, the explanation of which has fallen away.</margin> Someone recently reported to me that Clitopho, the son of Aristonymus, while speaking with Lysias, was accustomed to find fault with the way of life of Socrates, but to greatly praise that of Thrasymachus. <note>Thrasymachus was a famous Sophist, often portrayed as Socrates' intellectual rival.</note> CLITOPHO: Whoever that was, O Socrates, he did not correctly report what I said about you with Lysias. For in some things I praised you, and in others not at all. But since I have the opportunity—even though you pretend as if you do not care—I would most gladly report those things to you myself, especially since we are alone, so that you do not think I despise you. For perhaps you have now heard incorrectly, and for that reason you are more angry with me than is proper. But if you give me leave and listen, I will most gladly tell you the matter. SOCRATES: Indeed, it would be quite shameful if I did not tolerate you when you wish to benefit me. For it is clear that once I am conscious of where I am bad and where I am good, I shall avoid the worse to the best of my strength and pursue the better. CLITOPHO: Listen then. Indeed, having often been in your company, Socrates, I have been vehemently struck with wonder while hearing you speak; and you seemed to me to speak most excellently of all men whenever you rebuke men as if from a tragic stage-machine, <note>original: "machinamentum tragicum," referring to the *deus ex machina* used in Greek theater.</note> crying out like a God: "Whither are you rushing, O men? You know not where you are being carried, nor do you do anything seasonable; you who lean with all your zeal toward amassing money, but neglect the sons to whom you will leave it. You do not commend them to teachers of justice who might teach them justice—if it can be taught—and if it must be acquired by exercise and habit, might diligently train them. Nor have you ever cared for yourselves. But when you see that you and your sons have attained a sufficiency in letters, music, and gymnastics—which you think to be a perfect discipline of virtue—and yet you are nonetheless thereafter obsessed with money, why do you not despise your present education? Why do you not seek some who might free you from this dissonance in music?" <note>Here "music" refers to the Greek *mousike*, the harmony of the soul and education.</note> For because of this fault and sluggishness, more than because of a foot moving out of tune with the lyre, brother rises against brother, and cities against other cities in immoderate and discordant sedition, and having joined in battle, they suffer and inflict the extremes. But you say: it is not because of rudeness and ignorance, but by choice that those who are unjust are unjust. And again you do not hesitate to assert that justice is a shameful thing and adverse to God. For what reason, then, does anyone choose such a great evil? You answer that a man undergoes this because he is overcome by pleasures. Is not being overcome against one's will, since to overcome is by will? Therefore, reason dictates everywhere that to act unjustly is against the will. Thus, all men privately and cities publicly ought to apply more diligent care than they are accustomed to. Whenever I hear you saying these things, Socrates, I am wonderfully delighted and I praise you; and I do the same when I listen to what follows. For you add that whoever exercises the body but neglects the soul, cherishes that which is by nature subject, but despises that which commands. Likewise, you grant to each the use of that thing which he knows how to use. But he who knows not how to use his eyes, ears, or whole body, it is better for him neither to see, nor to hear, nor otherwise to use his body, than to use it. Similarly also in the arts. For whoever knows not how to use his own lyre, it is clear, as you yourself say, that he knows not how to use another's lyre; and he who knows not how to use another's, knows not his own. And the same reasoning applies to other instruments and possessions. And finally, your discourse proceeds so excellently that you conclude: for the soul that knows not how to use itself, it is better that the soul keep holiday and not live, than that it should live and be its own master in acting. But if some necessity compels it to live, it is better for such a one to lead a life as a slave than as a free man. And this is: just as with a ship, so to commit the rudders of thought to another who has attained the discipline of governing human life—which you, Socrates, often call civil skill, and the same as judicial skill and justice. To these discourses, therefore, and many others of this kind and most noble, asserting that virtue can be taught and commanding one to take care of oneself above all, I have almost never been opposed, nor do I think I shall be opposed in the future. <meta>This page begins the introduction to Plato's Cratylus by the Renaissance Neoplatonist Marsilio Ficino. It establishes a connection between Platonic philosophy and the mystical traditions of the Hebrews and ancient Egyptians regarding the power of names.</meta>

# ARGUMENT ON THE CRATYLUS.
q
<meta>Catchword: After</meta>

->Marsilio Ficino’s Argument on the Cratylus, or on the Right Reason of Names.<-

Platonic wisdom always looks up toward the sublime, yet it never despises humble things. Since the knowledge of things through names is not a lowly matter—indeed, it is exalted, especially concerning divine things—the wise Hebrews valued it so highly that they preferred it not only to all other sciences but even to the written Law itself. They affirmed that this knowledge was granted by God to the patriarchs and to Moses. I say that it was inscribed for Moses not in letters, but in the minds of holy men—specifically, in the minds of the succeeding prophets. Thereafter, the wisdom of divine names was propagated through a long series into the minds of those who followed. By the power of these names, they say, their ancestors performed miraculous works. Furthermore, they inserted some of these names into their writings, but mostly in a scattered or veiled manner. If anyone recognizes, collects, and perfectly pronounces them with the same purity of mind with which and to whom they were granted, they will likewise perform wonders. This is especially true regarding the primary name of God <note>The Tetragrammaton, YHWH</note>, which, since it is wonderfully composed of only four letters—and these being vowels—can surely be pronounced correctly by no one unless they are divinely inspired. Hence, they are forced to admit that Jesus, whom they call the Nazarene, was divine, since they confess that he performed miracles through the true understanding and perfect pronunciation of this four-lettered name <note>original: "tetragrammaton"</note>. But enough has been said by us on these matters in our book *On Religion*.

Origen also, when he had considered the miraculous power of divine names and prayers, says in his books *Against Celsus* that a marvelous power lies hidden in certain sacred names. Therefore, these names are not to be translated from the Hebrew tongue into another, but are to be preserved in their own characters. For perhaps, just as life remains in a body composed in a certain proportion—which does not remain if it is composed differently or changed—so he thinks a certain vital power exists in divine names when they are composed in a specific, divinely ordained way. And just as Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trismegistus," the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with alchemy and magic</note> taught from the beginning, and much later Plotinus and Iamblichus, that spirits <note>original: "demones," referring to intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil demons</note> are in a way enclosed in certain statues composed in a specific order, so certain divine gifts are distributed through words tempered to a certain celestial likeness. This is done by the providence of God so that, whenever the situation requires, we may rightly invoke divine aid. This practice is said to have been observed by Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> and Pythagoras themselves, who are reported to have wonderfully cured diseases of both soul and body using only certain divine words. Indeed, we find that the entire wisdom of Zoroaster consisted in this, which Plato calls "divine" in the *Alcibiades* and the healer of diseases of soul and body in the *Charmides*.

I pass over the fact that all nations and languages pronounce the principal name of God with only four letters. We have treated this more extensively in our commentaries on the *Philebus*, where it is proved that all nations could not have agreed on this one thing unless by divine influence. Hence the Egyptians <margin>The four names of God</margin> <margin>The name of God among diverse peoples</margin> call Him whom we call God, *Theut*; the Persians, *Syre*; the Magi, *Orsi* (whence *Oromasis*); the Hebrews express that ineffable name of four vowels as best they can through *Adonai*; the Greeks, *Theos*; the Arabs, *Alla*; Muhammad, *Abgd*; and we received *Jesus* from the angel. But why did God wish to be invoked everywhere by four letters? Perhaps because He Himself disposes all things through four stages: namely, composing them by Essence, Being, Power, and Action. Likewise, He disposes celestial things by four triplicities of signs—fiery, airy, watery, and earthy—and those things under heaven by the four elements.

No one will wonder that such great power lies hidden in true names if they only consider that the natural power of a thing, which we truly perceive, comes from objects to the senses, from these to the imagination, and from there in a certain way to the mind. Then it is conceived by the mind first, and then expressed through the voice as if by a birth. And in this very voice, established by its own articulations, the very power of the thing lies hidden under the form of its meaning like a life—a life, I say, first conceived from the mind through the "womb" of things, then brought forth through voices, and finally preserved through writings. If the names of other things preserve the power of those things in some way—and therefore the things themselves are recognized through those names as if through images—how much more do divine names, handed down by God Himself, perpetually preserve their power? And not without merit: for a true name, as Plato pleases, is nothing other than <margin>Name</margin> a certain power of the thing itself, first conceived in the mind (as I said), then expressed by the voice, and finally signified by letters. Now, the power of a divine thing must be divine. For this reason, since divine power is in them, Plato commands us to venerate the names of God both here and in the *Philebus*; and, as he indicates in the *Laws*, much more so than divine shrines and statues. For a more express image of God is reserved in the craftsmanship of the mind—especially one divinely inspired—than in the works of hands.

He judges that the first and purest names of God exist among the supernal and celestial minds, by whom God Himself is more expressly conceived. The second are in the purer spirits. The third are in the souls of men, and these were brought forth through ancient men inspired by God as if they were the trumpets of God. Therefore, the names of God handed down to us through the ancients and the holy seem to be like images and rays of God Himself, penetrating through the higher powers and through the holier souls of men. Whoever admires the sun as is fitting, rightly venerates the light of the sun; so also one ought to worship God primarily, and simultaneously the rays, powers, and images of God hidden in the meaning of sacred names. Let us therefore hear Socrates crying out in the *Philebus*: "My reverence toward the names of the gods is always no mere human dread, but surpasses the greatest fear." Let us hear him again in the *Phaedrus* purifying himself because he perhaps erred in discussing the name of the god Love. Let us hear Plato himself in the eleventh book of the *Laws*, judging those who defile the names of the gods with lies and perjury to be altogether sacrilegious, and commanding that they may be killed by anyone with impunity—while rigidly condemning as a traitor to the laws anyone who, being present, does not punish them. Nor should it disturb us that he often names many gods. For he proves in the *Parmenides* and *Timaeus* that there is only one God through Himself; but when he names others as "gods," he understands them not so much as gods but as divine angelic and celestial ministers of God. After, indeed, in the *Parmenides* <margin>Note: God is to be venerated</margin>

He aligns Platonic philosophy with Hebrew mysticism, Egyptian lore, and the teachings of figures like Pythagoras and Zoroaster to emphasize the sacredness of language.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the "Argumentum" or introductory summary to Plato's dialogue *Cratylus*. It establishes the philosophical framework for the debate on the nature of names, connecting Platonic thought with Christian theology and earlier Greek philosophy.</meta>

# ARGUMENT

He has compared all things to the one God, and did not think that His names should be despised; since wonderful gifts of God lie hidden within them, that divine theologian Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian philosopher who wrote *On the Divine Names*, often conflated in the Renaissance with the convert of St. Paul.</note> not unjustly sought out all the mysteries of theology in the divine names. But why have we passed over in silence that splendor and apostle of truth, Paul, who says: "The word of God is living and effective, and piercing more sharply than any two-edged sword"? <note>Hebrews 4:12</note> Likewise, the same apostle says: "God gave him a name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth." <note>Philippians 2:9-10</note> But now let us return to the dialogue.

Hermogenes, a disciple and follower of Parmenides, and Cratylus, a follower of Heraclitus, disagree concerning the correctness of names. While the former thinks names possess their force solely by human will <note>arbitrio; i.e., by social convention</note>, the latter believes they have it by a certain natural reason; finally, they submit themselves to the judgment of Socrates. At the beginning, three of Plato's teachers fittingly meet here. For he is said to have received moral philosophy from Socrates, physics from Cratylus, and metaphysics chiefly from Hermogenes, in addition to those things which he discovered himself. Cratylus is indeed a follower of Heraclitus and other ancients who philosophized many centuries before Heraclitus; they thought that nothing was ever stable, but that all things were engaged in perpetual motion. Whence they also established names for things based largely on that very motion. Hermogenes, however, a devotee of Parmenides and the Pythagoreans, believed on the contrary that all things remain permanent.

Socrates and Plato settle this controversy between Hermogenes and Cratylus in such a way that the opinion of Heraclitus is approved in physics <note>natural philosophy</note>, but that of Parmenides in metaphysics <note>the study of being and divine things</note>; however, if anyone should transfer true stability to natural things, or motion to divine things, he should be utterly rejected. But leaving these things aside, as far as names are concerned, Socrates seems to incline more toward the opinion of Cratylus, confirming it in this way: One speech is true, another is false; and of a true speech, the parts are true; of a false speech, the parts are also false. But the parts of speech are names; thus it happens that some names are true and others are false. A speech is true which describes things as they are; a false one, the opposite. Therefore, true names are those which express things as they are, rather than as it pleases human will.

But since Protagoras thinks that things are such as they appear to each person, so much so that things have no essence of their own, but human opinion is the measure of all things; therefore Socrates argues against Protagoras: that some men are the best (namely, the most prudent) and others the worst (namely, those furthest from prudence). But if, as Protagoras thinks, those things are true for each person which he happens to believe, there will certainly be no distinction between the prudent and the imprudent. But Protagoras is most subtly refuted in the book *On Science* <note>The *Theaetetus*</note>; nevertheless, it was necessary to refute him briefly here as well, so that the opinion of Hermogenes concerning names—which is in some way similar to his—could be more easily rebuffed. Indeed, Hermogenes does not at all believe Protagoras regarding the <margin><unclear>...on in</unclear></margin> difference of things; but while he confesses that the truth of names depends on human will, he secretly declines into the Protagorean opinion regarding things. He also falls secretly into the opinion of Euthydemus, who says that all things are always present to all people similarly; which is briefly disproved by this: that some would not be good and others evil if both virtue and vice were equally present to all.

But you, meanwhile, note this most well-worn opinion of our Plato: that the entire power of virtue is placed in prudence itself, and the entire power of vice in imprudence. After the opinions of Protagoras and Euthydemus are refuted, it is concluded that things themselves exist in that order of things as such-and-such, not through our opinion, but through their own nature. For if essences exist naturally, then actions and passions are also natural. Thus, if we endeavor to divide or burn any thing, we will do it not so much according to our will as according to the nature of the thing: so that we divide it in that manner and with that instrument by which it can most aptly be divided; and similarly for burning. But speaking and naming seem to be a certain action; therefore it ought to have its own nature: so that we name things not as it pleases us, but as the mode of the thing requires. For a name is a certain instrument by which we discern and divide the named thing from others.

Such an instrument, as is evident in other cases, must be adapted to its proper duty not by chance, nor by whim, but by art: so that its form is disposed through the very "Idea" of the art, which leads as if to an end toward the most apt discerning and dividing. However, it is not for just anyone to manufacture an instrument of this kind—that is, a name—adapted both for discerning things and for teaching listeners; but for a certain craftsman, a "founder of names," who is the rarest of all. This man manufactures names according to the reasoning that the craftsman who will use the names <note>the Dialectician</note> requires and instructs. Plato wishes the Dialectician to be such a person. But he who manufactures the name composes it by looking with his mind at the "Idea" of the thing itself, in which the true reason of the name consists, endowed with a certain definite significance. And this very ideal reason and significance is the "true name"; and it remains the same regarding the same thing in whatever material of letters it may be made, among whatever nations, provided that it teaches what the thing is by discerning it.

Conclude that names, if they are to be true and correctly placed, must be established by a wise founder of names; and this indeed with the Dialectician advising that they agree with the form, by which they may imitate and explain the properties of things according to their powers. After these things, entering diligently into the source from which the correctness of names is derived—that is, the proper reason by which they were established—he mocks the Sophists; and we are led instead to the poets, not just any, but the divine ones: as if they were those who received the true names of things from the gods, among whom names are true. Among these things, he shows that Homer's poetry is allegorical, even when it seems to narrate history, as appears in names created allegorically. He relates many names of heroes in Homer composed by a certain method of allegory, then ascends to the names of the gods, the reasons for which he received from the more venerable theologians.

By the first positioning of names, **Caelus** <note>Uranus/Sky</note> signifies the soul of the star-bearing sphere; **Saturn** the soul of the following sphere; and **Jupiter** truly the third. By the second positioning, **Caelus** signifies God; **Saturn** the angelic mind; **Jupiter** the soul of the world and the celestial. By the third, **Caelus** signifies the fecundity of God himself; **Saturn** His intelligence; **Jupiter** the beneficent will providing for all. By the fourth, **Caelus** designates in any deity the looking toward higher things; **Saturn** the respect toward oneself; **Jupiter** the perspective providing for lower things. I shall be forced to be more prolix if I [treat] each of the gods here theologically...

It bridges Greek philosophy with Christian theology by citing St. Paul and Dionysius the Areopagite on the power of divine names.</summary>

# ON THE CRATYLUS. FOLIO CLXVIII.
## q.ii.

I will wish to interpret; and that which we have treated more extensively in the book *On Love* <note>original: "de Amore"</note> and in the *Theology*. Since, indeed, to treat of divine matters is not for one who always says he knows nothing: appropriately Socrates, where he acts more deeply concerning divine things, says that a wisdom has recently shone upon him from whence he knows not; signifying that there is need of divine inspiration for a true perception of divine things. This he confirms also in the *Timaeus*, the *Symposium*, and the *Phaedrus*. He proves the same also in his *Epistles*. But that he says here he received the contemplation of divine things from Euthyphro is ironic: he mocks him and similar ambitious professors of divine law. Wherefore it happens: that not undeservedly, what he feigns to have heard from him, he asserts will be dismissed a little later, warning that one must not consider the doctrines of the ambitious, especially where they judge of divine things: concerning which even the most approved man can never speak as a man: but rather sometimes as the trumpet of God. To this that which Plutarch says is in some way similar: that a law exists among the Greeks: by which it is ordered that the books of wicked men, even the good ones, be removed from the midst: so that the memory of the authors might be deleted. He signifies moreover that the ancients were accustomed even for those who were seized by a demon during sacred rites, lest they be fatigued by it any longer, to be released from the demon a little later by certain prayers and sacrifices. He teaches also that a long time should not be wasted on names. Hence he reproves those who think only the spheres and stars of the world are divine: since from these, as if closer to our sight by nature and mobile, one must ascend to higher divinities, more stable and unknown to our senses because of their greater excellence. It is narrated moreover that the names of the gods were found not by chance, but partly by human reason, partly by divine inspiration. But heroic and human names were often bestowed either from the surnames of ancestors, or from a vow: and therefore a certain reason for names is to be sought in divine names rather than in others. After these things he descends to demons: and asserts that by the opinion of Hesiod and the most approved men of old, souls ascend into aerial demons: who both prevail in the wisdom of things: and provide for the human race. But you here observe that every good man is wise: and conversely that the good man turns out wise for this reason, because God fills the purged and serene mind of the good man with the light of his wisdom. The wise man also is good for this reason: because he neither wanders from the end: nor is he deceived in choosing those things which lead to the end. Observe that heroes and demigods are considered the same: and are born from the mutual love between God and man. Hence that saying: *But they are born of God.* <note>original: "Sed ex deo nati sunt"</note> In which matter the kinship between the human and divine race is shown. Attend soon that the duty of man is not to feel, but to consider those things which he feels. Then that the state of the soul in the body is not to be contained: but to contain the nature of the body: yet the body is called the prison and tomb of the soul according to Orpheus: inasmuch as it is judged as if dead in the body. Remember also that Anaxagoras thought that one soul was in the machine of the world before others: and one mind presided. Hence that: *The spirit nourishes within: and the Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass.* <note>original: "Spūs intus alit: totāq; infusa per artus Mēs agitat mole." A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, VI.726-7.</note> Then consider the pious modesty of Plato saying: Whoever is wise acknowledges that he is ignorant of the gods and the names of the gods among themselves. He adds that one must pray to God: that he might reveal his own proper name to us: it must also be thought that the names which we attribute to God signify not the nature of God itself, but our notion and affection toward God. Therefore God must be beseeched lest we displease him in naming him. The same in the *Philebus*, and *Parmenides*, and *Phaedrus*, and *Timaeus*. He then interprets the names of the gods: narrating first the opinions of those who thought all things flow: which finally he will disapprove. But in these things truly remember that the goddess Vesta signifies the essence of separate forms, and the stable foundation of divine things: and therefore the ancients were accustomed to sacrifice to Vesta before the other gods. Likewise names which signify state in divine things are referred to their substance: but those which signify motion, to action: improperly indeed to intellectual action: but properly to the animal <note>meaning "pertaining to the soul" or *anima*</note> action. Again, masculine names of gods signify in divine things the effecting act: but feminine ones the receiving power. <margin>What masculine and feminine names signify in divine things.</margin> Moreover, that heaven by its motion generates time, consuming and continually consuming, is a certain image referring to the god Uranus <note>original: "Cęliū"</note>, and Rhea, and Saturn devouring his sons. In these, however, Uranus is the divine essence itself: Rhea is the life of the same: Saturn is the mind of the same. <margin><insert>celestial essence, Rhea life, Saturn mind, Pluto</insert></margin> The sons of Saturn are the same as the things generated within the divine intelligence: which just as they are produced by the mind, so also they are reduced into the mind, absorbing them into itself, so to speak. But the multitude of gods distributed around the various parts of the world is contained both in the ideas of those same parts: and in the angelic minds contemplating the ideas in many ways: and in the souls ruling the spheres and stars of the world. Observe above all that Pluto here signifies especially the divine providence pertaining to separate souls: which so ravishes and detains pure souls by the perpetual allurements of its goods: that they do not wish to return to us further. Which indeed does not agree with the depths of the souls of our Plotinus and Proclus. It is proved that souls are detained in the power of Pluto by a certain very tight and insoluble bond, because they are held by an amatory affection. Where that Platonic saying in the *Symposium*, and the *Laws*, and often elsewhere is confirmed: that the amatory knot is more powerful than all others. Nor indeed is that by injustice: for he who draws someone through appetite, both draws more powerfully and retains more firmly than he who tries to attract through other force: because he is not only snatched from the outside: but from the inside. Moreover, that which is so snatched, not only does not struggle to be released: but even leans upon the binder: and involves itself more tightly in the same bond. I pass over how another ravisher occurs as if superior and foreign. But the amatory ravisher insinuates himself into us both openly and secretly as an equal and a domestic. Hence Boethius proves from the mind of Plotinus, that God ravishes all things to himself most powerfully and at the same time most sweetly: namely by the love of his own good, drawing them as if with bait. <margin><insert>Philo, verses 6-7</insert></margin> Which also the Platonist Philo confirms. God from the beginning to the end has touched all things powerfully and disposes them sweetly. We will show elsewhere that this whole thing was taken from the fourth book of the *Laws*. But concerning Phoebus, who according to Orpheus signifies the vital light, there are many and excellent things in the Orphic hymn of Apollo, in the sixth book of the *Republic*, and in the oration of the Platonist Julian, and in our little work *On Light*. Here indeed the name Apollo is briefly explained. Which signifies a triple sun: divine, angelic, and celestial. In the first indeed, the light is above the intellect. In the second, the intellect...

# ARGUMENT FOR THE CRATYLUS.

<meta>Catchword: not deceived</meta>

actual light above sight. In the third, visible light. The second is called by the Platonists the son of the first; the third is said to be the image of both. But to speak briefly, Apollo signifies, first, the simplicity of the divine and angelic substance; second, the power through which God and the angel wash souls and purge them from lower affections; third, the benefit by which they are released from worse things and joined to better; fourth, the "archery" virtue, so to speak, by which they hurl their gifts from afar and pierce the unjust with their stings; fifth, the efficacy tempering all things and converting them with musical measures. In these appears the prophecy of Apollo: where he is called simple, and by purging, washing, and releasing. In the same place appear medicine, and likewise skill in archery and singing: where he powerfully extends his strengths through all things, and sweetly tempers all things together among themselves, and happily converts them to himself by tempering. Similar gifts and effects are seen in the sun and toward the third and celestial sun. Among these things, Socrates says he is joking in explaining the names of the gods: namely, knowing that he does not reach the divine substance with these names, but either narrates their effects or explains our affections toward them according to his strength. He adds that the gods sometimes joke and play. We indeed joke about divine things; the gods also joke about ours: namely, insofar as these things of ours, compared to theirs, are very small, and they govern these with no labor, but with inestimable ease. I omit for the present that Platonic saying: *Man is a joke and a plaything of the gods.* <note>original: "Homo iocus est ludusque deorum." A reference to Plato's Laws.</note> For we shall explain that where the matter requires. After these things, for the third time now, the exceedingly religious man says he fears to dispute further about the gods. Indeed, both in the very beginning of the dispute, it is to be feared lest perhaps we speak of God without God; and in the middle of the dispute again, lest we rashly measure the immeasurable; and around the end again, lest we prolong the discourse about the deities further than their will inspires us. Soon, note that the whole power of Mercury <margin>Mercury</margin> revolves around speech: so that you may understand the power of intelligence to belong rather to Saturn. Likewise, what he adds: that Pan <margin>Pan</margin> is the two-formed son of Mercury: namely, on account of twofold speech, true and false. Note where Pan is painted as a man: it signifies true speech; where indeed as a brute, false: so that warned by this, by speaking false things you may be a false man and a true brute. Furthermore, where he derides many of the ancients who, because the gods themselves appeared to be in a whirl, thought all things were turned, he warns that we should not measure eternal things by our nature, especially the temporal. Likewise, where he says that temperance is the safety and preservation of prudence: he shows that a soul drunk with the perturbations of the body cannot perceive the truth of things themselves, especially incorporeal ones. Soon, where he interprets the name of the Good, <margin>The Good, Justice</margin> he shows three things pertain to the Good itself: namely, that it is to be admired, to be loved, and to be pleasant. It is to be admired when it excites us, turns us away from other things, and converts us to itself. To be loved, when we approach it and cling to it. Pleasant, when we are filled by it. A little after, explaining the name of Justice, he teaches that divine judgment penetrates all things. Which Orpheus also sang. Then he signifies that justice, among the followers of Anaxagoras, is the divine mind, the ordainer of all things. Which indeed Socrates dares neither to affirm nor deny. He does not deny it, indeed, because justice pertains to God. He does not affirm it, because it would be more appropriately said that justice is the divine will, distributing individual things according to merits of either nature or will. Notice that the reason of the Good pertains to a certain nature diffusing itself through all things. But the reason of the Beautiful pertains to the wisdom and order flowing from it, and provoking other things to itself. Finally, the power of love looks to a certain influx penetrating from the eyes through the eyes. After these things, he brings forward many things about names which are sufficiently understood through the preceding. He touches upon a triple opinion concerning the origin of names: either that they were once received from the gods, or from barbarians, or that by the length of time they have been so changed from their original origin that the original impositions of names are least discerned. Soon he derides those who profess knowledge of subsequent things when they are ignorant of the antecedents. But you, in what follows, notice the golden sentiment: That the most grave deception of all is that by which a man deceives himself. For in that, the deceiver is never absent from the deceived. Since indeed Cratylus inclines toward the sect of Euthydemus, which thinks no one speaks false things (because whoever speaks, speaks that which is; therefore he also speaks the truth), Socrates refutes it in this way. We often say that things are present to someone which are far away, and conversely that things are absent which are present, which is nothing other than to speak false things. And similarly, we can name conveniently, expressing through the name and the sounds of the letters in a certain way the nature and action of a thing or its passion, and on the contrary, name incongruously. After these things, where he makes mention of numbers and qualities, he says that in the order of numbers, the species of the number is always changed by unity being either added or subtracted; which does not happen in quality. I think this happens for this reason: because the whole ratio of number consists in unity and its replication. In quality indeed, since besides unity and its replication, there is another nature that is made, deservedly the species of quality is not changed by one degree added or subtracted, or even by many. Similarly in an image: it is an image insofar as it represents the thing; it can, however, refer more or less. Almost the same happens with names. For some are images of the things themselves. Furthermore, since the end of a name is to refer to the thing itself, it is better to refer by a certain likeness of the thing than by the convention of men. Again, since a name consists of letters, it cannot aptly express a thing unless it is composed of syllables and letters properly expressing the thing itself. But since it is a laborious thing to accommodate letters, syllables, and names entirely to individual things—indeed, it even cannot be done in numbers—therefore, custom must be mixed with nature: so that as far as can be done, the nature of things may have the authority of names. Where indeed it can be done in no way or with great difficulty through the property of nature, let it be done through human custom and convention, whether alone or joined to nature. Notice after these things that the greatest diligence must be applied to principles, and much must be disputed in establishing them. Again, each person goes by a certain very easy way to knowledge, as Cratylus warns, hunting for the properties of things through the properties of names; since the author of names did not institute such names as the things themselves are, but such as he himself thought; [he could] not be deceived...

...could. Add that some people can interpret the same names in different ways, and apply them to opposite meanings with equal probability. Indeed, many names are established as if things are in a state of flux; many others as if they remain still. It is therefore most deceptive to judge things through names. Consider a little later: first, that the one who named things must have known them before he named them. Likewise, consider the ancient opinion which asserts that a certain divine power instructed man from the beginning and taught him the names of things. This is consistent with what is said in the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note>. For it is impossible that the human race, either from the beginning of the world or after the great floods, was instructed in any way other than divinely. However, when Socrates says he is "dreaming" about the Ideas <note>The Platonic Forms</note>, he declares both that Socrates was accustomed to being mocked for this by the common people and by comic poets, and that the knowledge of Ideas is obtained through a separation of the mind, similar to a prophetic dream. Soon he proves that Ideas exist: because above imperfect forms there must be perfect ones. Likewise, that Ideas are immutable: if indeed the species of things, their reasons, and their definitions always remain the same. He adds: if it is established that all [constancy] is taken away from things, it follows that no thing truly exists, nor can it be known as "this thing" or "such a thing"; since at any moment it would deceive the one judging it, who would necessarily be lying. He adds that there would be no knowledge: namely, the specific Idea of knowledge itself, which always remains the same. He concludes that the science of things is to be sought not from names, but from the Ideas, whose innate notions within us are the first and true names of things. Finally, he admonishes young men not to pass judgment easily on grave matters; rather, let them speak for a long time and wait for a more mature age before they judge.

### PLATO'S CRATYLUS, OR ON THE RIGHT RATIONALE OF NAMES, TRANSLATED BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE, TO PETER DE' MEDICI, A MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN.

-> HERMOGENES. CRATYLVS. SOCRATES. <-

-> HERMOGENES. <-

DO YOU WISH for us to join our conversation with Socrates here? CRATYLUS. I am willing indeed, if it seems right to you. HERMOGENES. Cratylus here, O Socrates, says that a right rationale for a name exists by nature for each individual thing; and that a name is not merely what some people call it by agreement, while pronouncing some small part of their own voice; but that there is a certain right rationale of names, the same for both Greeks and barbarians, innate in all. I ask him, therefore, whether "Cratylus" is truly his name. He admits it. "What then is the name for Socrates?" I ask. "Socrates," he says. "Is not the name for each man that which we call him?" I ask. He replies, "However, your name is not Hermogenes <note>Hermogenes means "born of Hermes," the god of profit and luck</note>, even if all men should call you so." While I beg him to reveal what he means to me as I inquire, he explains nothing at all; but using a certain irony with me, he pretends that he is turning something over in his mind, as if he understands something about this matter which, if he wished to express it, would force me to agree and say the same things he proclaims. Therefore, I would gladly hear from you if you can guess the prophecy of Cratylus by any reasoning. Yet I would more gladly hear your own opinion on the correctness of names, if it pleases you. SOCRATES. O Hermogenes, son of Hipponicus, it is said in an old proverb that "beautiful things are difficult to know." <margin>Proverb: Beautiful things are difficult to know.</margin> And yet the understanding of names is no small matter. Indeed, if I had ever heard from Prodicus <note>A Sophist famous for his lectures on the precise meaning of words</note> that fifty-drachma demonstration, in the tradition of which this perception consists (as he himself testifies), nothing would prevent you from immediately understanding the correctness of names. Furthermore, I have never heard it; I have only received the one-drachma lesson. Therefore, I do not know what the truth is in these matters. However, I am prepared to investigate what is right along with you and Cratylus. But as for his saying that your name is not truly Hermogenes—which is derived from "profit"—I suspect he is mocking you, as if you are greedy for money and failing to obtain your wish. But, as I was just saying, these things are difficult to know. It is necessary, by bringing the arguments from both sides into the open, to inquire whether it is as you say, or rather as Cratylus says. HERMOGENES. Truly, O Socrates, although I have already disputed frequently with him and many others, I cannot yet be persuaded that there is any other correctness of a name than convention and consensus. It seems to me that whatever name anyone imposes on anything, that is the right name. And if he changes it again and imposes another, the one that succeeds it is no less a right name than the first; just as we are accustomed to change the names of slaves. For no name belongs to any thing by nature, but by the law and usage of those who have become accustomed to calling it so. If this is indeed otherwise, I am ready to learn and hear it not only from Cratylus, but from anyone else. SOCRATES. Perhaps you are saying something, Hermogenes. Let us consider it then. Do you assert that whatever name anyone imposes on a thing and calls it, that is its name? HERMOGENES. It certainly seems so to me. SOCRATES. And whether a private person calls it so, or a city? HERMOGENES. I assert it. SOCRATES. What if I myself should call a thing—for instance, if I called what we now call a "man" a "horse," and what we call a "horse" a "man"—publicly its name will be "man," but privately "horse," and again privately "man," but publicly "horse." Is that how you speak? HERMOGENES. So it seems. SOCRATES. Tell me again, do you call one thing "speaking the truth" and another "speaking falsehoods"? HERMOGENES. Indeed. SOCRATES. Will not that speech be true, and this speech false? HERMOGENES. Exactly so. SOCRATES. And is that speech which describes things as they exist true, and that which describes them as they do not exist false? HERMOGENES. Certainly. SOCRATES. Is this then: in speech, those things which are and those which are not...

# CRATYLUS, OR ON THE RIGHT RATIONALE OF NAMES. FOLIO CLXXI.

he will use it rightly; rightly, I say, according to the method of weaving. And he who teaches will use the name, and rightly: rightly, clearly, according to the proper method of teaching. HERMOGENES. Certainly. SOCRATES. Whose craftsman’s work does the weaver use well when he uses the shuttle and the comb? HERMOGENES. The carpenter’s. SOCRATES. Is every man a carpenter, or rather he who possesses the art? HERMOGENES. He who possesses the art. SOCRATES. Likewise, whose work does the piercer use rightly? HERMOGENES. The coppersmith’s. SOCRATES. Is every man a coppersmith? Or rather he who possesses the art? HERMOGENES. He who has the art. SOCRATES. Come then: tell me whose work the teacher himself uses whenever he uses a name. HERMOGENES. I do not know. SOCRATES. You cannot assign this either? Who delivers to us the names which we use? HERMOGENES. I am ignorant of this as well. SOCRATES. Does it not seem to you that the law <note>Latin: *lex*, translating the Greek *nomos*, which implies both law and custom.</note> has established names for us? HERMOGENES. It seems so. SOCRATES. Therefore, the teacher will use the work of the legislator <note>The "Law-giver" or *Nomothetes*.</note> when he uses the name itself. HERMOGENES. I suppose so. SOCRATES. Does every man seem to you to be a founder of law, or only he who is endowed with the art? HERMOGENES. He who is endowed with the art. SOCRATES. Therefore, Hermogenes, it is not the role of just any man to impose a name, but of a certain author of names. This person, it seems, is the "establisher of names" <note>Latin: *nominũ institor*</note>, who is found more rarely than any other craftsman among men. HERMOGENES. So it appears. SOCRATES. Observe, I pray, what the establisher of names looks toward when he imposes names on things; rather, judge from the previous examples: what does the carpenter look toward when he makes the shuttle and the comb? Is it not toward something that is by nature fit for weaving? HERMOGENES. Entirely. SOCRATES. If the shuttle breaks while in use, will he manufacture another according to the image of the broken one, or will he rather look toward the Form <note>Latin: *speciem*, referring to the Platonic Idea or Form.</note> itself, according to whose model he had made the shuttle that broke? HERMOGENES. Toward the Form itself, I believe. SOCRATES. Should we not rightly call that Form the very rationale of the shuttle, and the "shuttle itself"? HERMOGENES. I think so. SOCRATES. If it is necessary to prepare a shuttle for a fine or thick garment, whether of linen or wool or any other kind, every single shuttle must have the Form of the shuttle itself; but such a one as is naturally most accommodated to each task must be applied, as nature demands. HERMOGENES. Quite right. SOCRATES. The same rationale applies to other instruments. For whatever nature fits for each thing is the instrument to be discovered; and that must be attributed to it: from which it follows that the maker does not produce whatever he wishes, but what nature itself requires. For one must know how to produce the drill accommodated to each task in iron. HERMOGENES. It is clear. SOCRATES. And the shuttle appropriate to each in wood. HERMOGENES. These things are true. SOCRATES. Indeed, by this very rationale, one shuttle is naturally suited to one web, and another to another; and in other things in the same way. HERMOGENES. Certainly. SOCRATES. It is also necessary, my excellent man, that the establisher of names <margin>How he who names rightly shall name.</margin> express in sounds and syllables the name naturally fit for each thing; and looking toward that which is the name itself, he should fashion and attribute individual names, if he is truly to be an author of names. And if every founder of names does not express the name in the same syllables, we must notice that not even all coppersmiths do this in the same iron, even when they manufacture the same instrument for the same purpose. But insofar as they attribute the same Idea <note>Latin: *ideam*</note>, even if in different iron, the instrument is rightly made, whether here or among the barbarians. Is it not so? HERMOGENES. Most certainly. SOCRATES. And will you not judge in the same way, that as long as the establisher of names—whether among us or among the barbarians—assigns the Form of the name appropriate to each thing in whatever syllables, one is no worse than the other in imposing names? HERMOGENES. Indeed. SOCRATES. Who is to know whether the fitting Form of the shuttle has been impressed upon any particular wood? Is it the carpenter who made it, or the weaver who will use it? HERMOGENES. It is probable, O Socrates, that he who will use it knows better. SOCRATES. Who uses the work of the lyre-maker? Is it not he who knows how to play the instrument, and can judge whether the work has been done rightly or otherwise? HERMOGENES. Entirely. SOCRATES. Who then? HERMOGENES. The lyre-player. SOCRATES. And who uses the work of the ship-builder? HERMOGENES. The pilot. SOCRATES. Who then will best preside over the work of the founder of names, and judge the result among both Greeks and barbarians? Is it not he who will use it? HERMOGENES. He, certainly. SOCRATES. And is he not the one who knows how to ask questions? HERMOGENES. That is the one. SOCRATES. And also how to answer? HERMOGENES. Indeed. SOCRATES. But do you call him who knows how to ask and answer anything other <margin>The Dialectician knows rightly how to ask and answer.</margin> than a dialectician? <note>A practitioner of *dialectic*, the Socratic method of philosophical inquiry.</note> HERMOGENES. A dialectician, certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, it is the carpenter's work to make a rudder under the pilot's direction, if the rudder is to be good. HERMOGENES. It appears so. SOCRATES. And it is the author of names' work to establish a name under the direction of the dialectician, if names are to be rightly placed. HERMOGENES. These things are true. SOCRATES. It appears then, Hermogenes, that the imposition of names is no light matter, as you yourself think, nor is it the work of unskilled or ordinary men. Indeed, Cratylus speaks the truth when he says that names belong to things by nature, and that not every man is an author of names, but only he who looks toward the name which fits each thing by nature, and can insert its Form into letters and syllables. HERMOGENES. I do not know, Socrates, by what rationale I should resist what you have said; but perhaps it is not easy to be so suddenly persuaded. I think I would rather agree with you in this way, if you would show me what you say is the naturally right rationale of a name. SOCRATES. Indeed, my blessed Hermogenes, I say none yet; for it has almost slipped my memory what I said above: namely, that I am ignorant of this, but am searching for it together with you. But now, as we investigate together, this much at least has been found beyond what was said before: that a name has some rectitude by nature, and that not every man knows how to accommodate it to things. Is it not so? HERMOGENES. Very much so. SOCRATES. It remains to be considered, if you desire to know, what the rectitude—that is, the right rationale—of the name itself is. HERMOGENES. I do desire it. SOCRATES. Observe then. HERMOGENES. By what path do you advise we investigate? SOCRATES. The most right consideration, my friend, is to seek it from those who know, by offering money and giving thanks besides; these are the Sophists, through whom your brother Callias, having spent much money, seems to have turned out wise. But since you have no right to your father's estate, it remains for you to humbly entreat your brother to teach you the rectitude of names which he learned from Protagoras. HERMOGENES. That would be an absurd request, Socrates; if I do not in any way accept that "Truth" of Protagoras, why should I value the things said based on that truth?

He concludes that names are not arbitrary but have a natural fitness, though he admits he is still searching for the specific rationale behind them.</summary>

HERMOGENES: What about names, and where does Homer teach this, O Socrates? SOCRATES: In many places throughout; but the greatest and most beautiful instances are those in which he distinguishes between the names that men use and those which the gods themselves introduce for the same things.
