HERMOGENES: I do not know. SOCRATES: Consider it thus: if someone asked you whether you think the wiser or the less wise impose names on things more correctly, you would surely answer the wiser. HERMOGENES: Certainly so. SOCRATES: Do the women in cities seem wiser to you, or the men, as far as the gender is concerned? HERMOGENES: The men. SOCRATES: Do you not know that Homer says the son of Hector was called Astyanax by the Trojans, but Scamandrius by the women? Since indeed the men were accustomed to call him Astyanax. HERMOGENES: It seems so. SOCRATES: Did not Homer consider the Trojan men to be wiser than their women? HERMOGENES: I believe so indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore he judged that he was more rightly named Astyanax than Scamandrius, for he protected the city and its wide walls for them. Wherefore it is fitting, as it seems, to name the protector's son Astyanax, that is, "king of the city" <note>original: "regem urbis"</note>; of that city, I say, which his father saved, as Homer says. HERMOGENES: The same seems true to me as well. SOCRATES: But as for why this is especially so, I myself do not yet sufficiently understand, O Hermogenes. Do you perceive it? HERMOGENES: No, by Jove. SOCRATES: And yet, my good man, Homer himself imposed the name on Hector. HERMOGENES: For what reason? SOCRATES: Because the name Hector seems to me to be very close to Astyanax. For they signify almost the same thing: he thinks that both these names are royal among the Greeks. For of whomever anyone is an *Anax* <note>original: "Anax", i.e., king</note>, of the same he is also a *Hector* <note>original: "Hector", i.e., possessor/holder</note>. For it is certain that he rules, possesses, and holds it. Or perhaps I seem to be saying nothing to you? And am I deceived by the opinion by which I trusted I was touching upon Homer's meaning regarding the rectitude of names as if by certain tracks? HERMOGENES: Not at all, as I judge. For perhaps you are touching upon something. SOCRATES: It is fitting, as it seems to me, to name the son of a lion a lion; the son of a horse a horse. I certainly do not mean if something like a monster is born from a horse, something other than a horse; but I mean that which is born according to the nature of its kind. For if, according to nature, the son of an ox begets a horse, it is not a calf that is born, but it must be called a horse-foal. And if a horse, contrary to nature, begets a calf, it must not be called a horse-foal, but a calf. Nor even if a progeny other than human is produced from a human, should that which is born be called a human. And the same is to be judged of trees and of all other things. Do you approve of these things? HERMOGENES: I certainly do. SOCRATES: Watch me, lest I deceive you in anything. For by the same reason, if someone is born of a king, he is to be named a king; but whether the same thing is signified in different syllables matters nothing; nor does it matter if some letter is added or even taken away, as long as the essence of the thing signified dominates in the name itself. HERMOGENES: Why do you say that? SOCRATES: I say nothing varied or diverse; but just as you see happening in the elements <note>letters of the alphabet</note>. For you know that we speak the names of the elements, but not the elements themselves—except for four: namely *e, y, omicron, omega* <note>original: "ε, υ, ο, ω"</note>. But for the others, both vowels and non-vowels, we constitute names by adding other letters, and so we utter them. But as long as we bring in the power of the element itself declared, it is fitting to call that name the very thing which signifies the element to us; as appears in *Beta* <note>original: "Vita" / "βῆτα"</note>: where, with *i, t, a* <note>original: "η, τ, α"</note> added, nothing prevented the nature of that element from being shown in the whole name, which the author of the name intended. To such an extent did he skillfully provide names with letters. HERMOGENES: You seem to me to speak the truth. SOCRATES: Will not the same reason apply to a king? A king will surely come from a king; a good man from a good man; a beautiful man from a beautiful man; and in all other things, the offspring of any kind will be another such thing, unless a monster is created; and the names should be called the same. But it is permitted to vary them through syllables, so that they may seem different to an unrefined man, though they are the same, just as the drugs of physicians, varied by colors and odors, often seem different to us though they are the same; but to a physician considering the power of the drugs, they are judged the same; nor do the additions disturb him. Similarly, perhaps he who is learned in names considers their power; nor is his judgment disturbed if any letter is added, or transposed, or taken away, or if the same power of the name is found in other and many letters. As those names which we mentioned above, Astyanax and Hector, have entirely different letters except for *t* alone; yet they signify the same thing. Likewise, because *Archepolis* <note>original: "ἀρχέπολις"</note> is said to be "prince of the city," what communion of letters does it have with the two above? Nevertheless, it means the same. And there are many other things which signify nothing else than a king. There are many others, moreover, which signify a leader of an army: such as *Agis, Polemarchus, Eupolemus*, and others likewise.

<summary>Socrates discusses the etymological relationship between names and the essence of things, arguing that names given by gods are more "natural" than those given by men. He uses the examples of Hector and Astyanax to show how different names can share the same underlying meaning of kingship or protection.</summary>

# FOLIO CLXXI.
## CRATYLUS, OR ON THE RIGHT RECKONING OF NAMES.
-> q.v. <-

<margin>
Iatrocles.
Acesimbrotus.
</margin>
which declare a professor of medicine: such as *Iatrocles* <note>original: "Iatrocles" - from the Greek for 'physician-glory'</note>, and *Acesimbrotus* <note>original: "Acesimbrotus" - 'healer of mortals'</note>; and many others can be found that differ in syllables and letters, but entirely harmonize in the power of their meaning. Do you think so yourself, or otherwise? HERMOGENES. Certainly so. SOCRATES. To those things which come to be according to nature, the same names ought surely to be assigned. HER. Entirely. SOC. But whenever some men are born contrary to nature in a kind of monstrous form: as when an impious man is fathered by a good and pious man: he who is born ought not to obtain the name of the father, but of the genus in which he himself exists: just as we said above, if a horse should sire the offspring of an ox, it should not be named a horse as his son, but an ox. HER. That is so. SOC. Therefore, to an impious man born of a pious one, the name not of the parent, but of the kind, should be attributed. HER. These things are true. SOC. Therefore, it is not fitting to call such a son *Theophilus* (that is, friend of God), nor *Mnesitheus* (that is, mindful of God), or any such name; but rather to call them by names signifying the opposite: if indeed names are to be rightly established. HER. It must be done exactly so, O Socrates. SOC. Truly, the name *Orestes* <note>original: "Orestis"</note> seems rightly imposed, O Hermogenes: whether some chance gave him the name, or some poet, signifying his beast-like, wild, and mountain-dwelling nature by that name. HER. So it appears, Socrates. SOC. And it seems his father has a name according to his nature. HER. It appears so. SOC. It certainly appears that *Agamemnon* is such a man: that he deems he must labor and endure; and through virtue persevere in those things he has decreed. A proof of his endurance was his long stay at Troy with so great an army. Therefore, the name *Agamemnon* signifies how wonderful a perseverance this man had: as if from *agastos* (that is, admirable) and *epimoni* (that is, perseverance). Perhaps also *Atreus* was rightly named. For the murder of Chrysippus, and his cruelty toward Thyestes, show him to be harmful and cut off from virtue. Whence the name declines a little and secretly hints at it: so that it does not declare the nature of this man to just anyone. But to those who are skilled in names, the significance of *Atreus* is sufficiently clear. For it is said according to *ateres*, *atrepton*, *ateron*: as if he were indomitable, inexorable, harmful, and insolent. It seems also the name *Pelops* was assigned not without reason. For this name fittingly signifies a man who sees only what is near. HER. Why does that suit him? SOC. Because in the murder of Myrtilus, as it is told, he could foresee nothing; nor look forward from a distance to how great a calamity hung over his entire race. For he looked only at what was before his feet and at present things: and this is to look "near" (*pelas*): which he did when he contended with all effort to enter into marriage with Hippodamia. Whence the name *Pelops* comes from *pelas* (that is, near) and *opsis* (which pertains to vision). Furthermore, the name *Tantalus* seems imposed by nature itself, if the things circulated about him are true. HER. What things are those? SOC. Because while still living, many and heavy adversities befell him; and finally his whole country was overturned. Moreover, after his death, a stone hangs over his head: a most hard fate indeed. These things entirely agree with his name: just as if one had wished to name him *talantaton* (that is, most unhappy): but speaking a little more obscurely, placed *Tantalus* for *talantato*. Such a name his adverse fortune seems to have provided by the very rumor of the nations. Furthermore, the name of his father, *Jupiter* <note>original: "Ioui" / Zeus</note>, is rightly bestowed: yet it is not easily understood. For the name of Jupiter is like a certain discourse: which we, dividing into two parts, use sometimes one part and sometimes the other. Some call him *Zina* (that is, living and life), some *Dia* (that is, "through," and the cause through which). These parts, composed into one, show the nature of the god himself, which is what a name ought most to be able to do. For there is no greater cause of living for us and all others than the prince and king of all. Wherefore this god has obtained a fitting name: through whom life is always in all living things. But the name, as I was saying, is one divided into two: namely into *Dia* and *Zina*. Hearing him called the son of *Saturn* <note>original: "Saturni" / Cronus</note>, one might suddenly think him insolent and insulting. But it is probable that Jupiter is the offspring of some great intelligence. For what he calls *coros* does not signify a boy: but the purity of his mind and sincere integrity. Moreover, he is the son of *Uranus* (that is, of heaven): as it is told. Indeed, the looking toward higher things is deservedly called *Urania*: as if from *horosa* (that is, looking) and *ano* (that is, toward higher things). Whence, Hermogenes, those who deal with sublime matters affirm that a pure mind is present: and the name was rightly imposed on *Uranus* (that is, heaven). If I held in mind the genealogy of the gods delivered by Hesiod, and remembered which progenitors he introduces, I would by no means cease to show you that names were rightly inscribed upon them: until I made a trial of this wisdom, to see if it achieves anything or if it fails; which has just now shone upon me, I know not from where. HER. Truly, Socrates, you seem to me like those who are seized by a divine spirit, pouring forth oracles. SOC. I believe indeed, O Hermogenes, that this wisdom has flowed into me from Euthyphron, the son of Pantios. For I stood by him from early morning with diligence and gave him my ears. It appears, therefore, that being full of the god, he has not only filled my ears with blessed wisdom but has also occupied my soul. Thus I think we should act: that today we use it and investigate the rest pertaining to names. But tomorrow, if we agree on this, we shall expiate it: and we shall expiate it by seeking out someone, whether a priest or a sophist, who is able to purge these things. HER. I greatly approve of these things, Socrates, for I would most gladly hear what remains concerning names. SOC. So it must first be done. From where then do you judge we should best begin: after we have prescribed a certain formula: so that we may know if the names themselves testify to us that they were not made by some chance, but contain a certain rectitude? The names of Heroes and men might perhaps deceive us. For many of these are placed according to the surnames of ancestors: and often they do not fit at all, as we said in the beginning. Many men assign names according to a wish: such as *Eutychides*, *Sosias*, *Theophilus* (that is, prosperous, savior, dear to God), and many others. Such things I think should be passed over. For it is most fitting and consistent that we find those which are in eternal things and the order of nature...

# BOOK XXIII.

...are rightly established. For in the founding of names, it is most fitting to have bestowed great care upon such matters. Perhaps, indeed, some of them were instituted by a certain divine power rather than a human one. HERMOGENES: You seem to me to speak excellently, O Socrates. SOCRATES: Is it not right to begin with the gods themselves, and to investigate the reason why the gods were called *Theoi* <note>original: "Thei"</note>? HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: I conjecture it thus. It seems to me that the ancient Greeks thought those were the only gods whom many of the barbarians also believe in at this time: the sun, the moon, the earth, the stars, and the sky. Since they saw all these things in perpetual motion, from this nature of *thein* <note>original: "thin"</note>, that is, "to run," they seem to have named them *theous*, that is, "gods." Later, noticing others, they called them all by the same name. Does what I say have some likelihood, or not? HERMOGENES: It certainly does. SOCRATES: What should be investigated after this? It is agreed that we must inquire about demons, heroes, and men. HERMOGENES: About demons first. SOCRATES: Without a doubt, Hermogenes, consider what the name of "demons" <note>term: *daemon* — in Greek thought, a supernatural being or spirit, often a mediator between gods and men</note> intends; see if I am saying anything of substance. HERMOGENES: Just speak. SOCRATES: Do you know who Hesiod says the demons are? HERMOGENES: No. SOCRATES: Nor even that he says a "golden race" of men existed in the beginning? HERMOGENES: That much I do know. SOCRATES: For he says that from this race, after the fates of the present life, they become holy demons, dwellers on earth, the best, the expellers of evils, and the guardians of men. HERMOGENES: What then? SOCRATES: Surely I think he calls them a "golden race" not because they were made of gold, but because they were good and noble. I gather this from the fact that he says our own race is "iron." HERMOGENES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Do you not think that if someone among us now is good, he would be esteemed by Hesiod as belonging to the golden race? HERMOGENES: That is consistent. SOCRATES: But are the good anything other than the wise? HERMOGENES: They are the wise. SOCRATES: Therefore, as I think, he calls them "demons" <note>original: "dęmones"</note> especially because they are wise and *daemones*, that is, "knowing ones" <note>note: Socrates is punning on the Greek *daēmōn* (knowing/wise) and *daimōn* (spirit)</note>. And that name exists from our ancient language. Wherefore both he and many other poets speak excellently whenever they say: namely, that after a good man has finished his life, he obtains the greatest dignity and reward; he becomes a demon, according to the surname of wisdom. Thus I myself assert that every man who is good is a "demon," that is, a wise man; and that he is "demonic," that is, wise and happy, both living and dead; and is rightly called a demon. HERMOGENES: It seems to me, O Socrates, that I agree with you most strongly on this. SOCRATES: But what does "hero" signify? That is by no means difficult to find. For the name of "heroes" differs only a little from its origin, indicating that their generation flowed from *Erotos*, that is, from "love." HERMOGENES: By what reason do you say that? SOCRATES: Are you unaware that heroes are demigods? HERMOGENES: What then? SOCRATES: Surely all heroes were born either from the love of gods for human women, or the love of men for goddesses. Furthermore, if you consider this according to the ancient Attic language, you will understand better. For you will find that it has been changed slightly for the sake of the name from *erotos*, that is, "love," from which the heroes were born. Either the name of heroes was derived from here, or from the fact that they were wise and rulers—eloquent, indeed, and most ready for questioning and discussing. For *erein* <note>original: "erin"</note> means "to speak." Wherefore, as I was just saying, in the Attic tongue, heroes appear to be certain rhetoricians, and disputers, and lovers. Whence the heroic offspring of rhetoricians and sophists exists.

->Truly, that is not difficult to know; rather, this is obscure: for what reason are men called *Anthropoi*? Do you have anything to assert yourself? HERMOGENES: From where would I have it, good man? Rather, if I could find it in any way, I would not strive for it, because I hope you will find it better and more easily than I. SOCRATES: You seem to me to trust in the inspiration of Euthyphro. HERMOGENES: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: And you trust rightly. For I seem to myself to have thought quite beautifully just now; and there is a danger, unless I am careful, that today I may turn out to appear wiser than is fitting. Attend to what I say. This especially should be noted regarding names: that we often add letters, and often take them away, at our pleasure while we are naming; and we very often change the accents. As when we say *Dii philos*, that is, "friend to Jove." So that this might be a name for us instead of a phrase, we took out one *iota* from it, and instead of an acute syllable in the middle, we pronounced it grave. In some others we interpose letters; others we utter more heavily. HERMOGENES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: This also happens in the name *anthropos*, as it seems to me. For the name was established from a phrase, with one 'a' excepted, and a heavier ending produced. HERMOGENES: How do you mean that? SOCRATES: Thus that name of "man" signifies this: that while other animals do not consider, nor notice, nor contemplate what they see, man both sees and at the same time contemplates and notices what he sees. Here, rightly, alone of all living things, man is called *anthropos*, as if *anathron*, that is, "contemplating" what *opope*, that is, "he has seen." What shall I seek after these? Perhaps what I would gladly learn? HERMOGENES: By all means. SOCRATES: A consideration of the soul and the body seems to me to follow immediately upon the previous points. For soul and body are the components of a man. HERMOGENES: Without controversy. SOCRATES: Let us try to distinguish these just as we did the previous ones. Do you think we should first ask about the soul, whether it was rightly named *Psyche* <note>original: "Psychi"</note>, and then about the body? HERMOGENES: Indeed. SOCRATES: To express suddenly what first offers itself to me now, I think those who so called the soul intended this most of all: that as long as it is present in the body, it is the cause of its living, providing the power of breathing and cooling; and as soon as that which cools fails, the body is dissolved and perishes. Whence they seem to have named it *psyche*, as if *anapsychon*, that is, "cooling by breathing." But indeed, if it pleases you, stop for a moment. I seem to see something more probable among those who follow Euthyphro. For they would despise that, I think, and consider it something harsh. But see if this will please you. HERMOGENES: Just say it. SOCRATES: What else than the soul do you think possesses, contains, and carries the body, so that it both lives and walks? HERMOGENES: Nothing else. SOCRATES: Do you not believe Anaxagoras, that the nature of all things is at once adorned and contained by a certain mind and soul? HERMOGENES: I do believe it. SOCRATES: It is fitting, therefore, to name that power *physeche*, because it *ochei* and *echei* the *physin*, that is, "carries and contains nature." But it is more elegantly pronounced *psyche*. HERMOGENES: It is entirely so. And that seems to me to be more ingenious. SOCRATES: It is indeed. But it would appear ridiculous if it were named exactly as it was composed. As for what follows after this, the body, do you not call it *soma*? HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And it seems to me that in this name there is a slight deviation from its origin; for indeed, this body is said to be the *sema*, that is, the "tomb" of the soul...

# CRATYLUS, OR ON THE RIGHTNESS OF NAMES. FOLIO 172.

as if it were buried in the present time; and also because the soul <gloss>original: "smegni," likely a corruption of "semainei"</gloss> signifies whatever it wants to signify through the body: therefore it is rightly called a sign <note>original: "sima," Greek *sēma* (sign/tomb)</note>. Furthermore, it seems to me that the followers of Orpheus established this name chiefly because the soul pays the penalty for its sins in this body: and it is enclosed by this boundary as if in a prison, so that it may be kept safe <note>original: "sōitṛe," Greek *sōzētai*</note>. They wish it to be as it is named: the body <note>original: "soma"</note> is an enclosure for the sake of keeping <note>original: "seruandi"</note> the soul until it has paid its debts; and they think not a single letter should be added.

**HERMOGENES.** I think enough has been said of these things, Socrates. But could we consider the names of some of the gods, just as was done with Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, to see according to what rightness the names were imposed?

**SOCRATES.** By Jove, Hermogenes, if we had any sense, we would consider it the highest form of rightness to admit that we know nothing of the gods: neither of the gods themselves, nor of the names by which they call themselves. For it is clear that they call themselves by their true names. But according to a second mode of right naming, I think—just as the law establishes in our prayers that we should entreat the gods by whatever names it pleases them to be called—so we also shall call them, as if knowing nothing else. For this seems to me a right decree. Therefore, if you wish, let us proceed with this investigation: first prefacing to the gods that we shall consider nothing regarding their actual natures—for we do not trust ourselves to be able—but rather regarding the men who, affected by their opinions about the gods, established names for them. This approach is far from divine indignation.

**HERMOGENES.** You seem to speak modestly, Socrates; and so we must proceed.

**SOCRATES.** Should we not begin with Vesta <note>Hestia</note> according to the law?

**HERMOGENES.** That is certainly fitting.

**SOCRATES.** By what reasoning shall we say this "Hestia" was named?

**HERMOGENES.** By Jove, that is not easily found.

**SOCRATES.** It seems, Hermogenes, that the first authors of names were not dull, but were acute and sublime investigators of things.

**HERMOGENES.** Why so?

**SOCRATES.** Names appear to have been imposed by the invention of such men. And if one considers foreign names, one nonetheless finds what each intends. Just as that which we call "essence" <note>original: "vsia," Greek *ousia*</note>, some call "hestia," and others "osia." First, according to the second of these names, it seems not far from reason that the essence of things be called "hestia." And because we call that which participates in essence "hestia," it could rightly be named from this. Our ancestors once called essence <note>original: "vsia"</note> "esia." If anyone observes the sacred rites, he will think that those who established them thought this way. For it is fitting for those who named the essence of all things "Vesta" to sacrifice to Vesta before all other gods. Those who likewise named it "osia" almost certainly judged, according to Heraclitus, that all things are always flowing and nothing stands still. Therefore, they lead the cause and origin of things to "that which impels" <note>original: "othun," Greek *ōthoun*</note>; wherefore it is deservedly named "Osia," the impelling cause. Let this be said of these things as if by those who understand nothing. After Vesta, it is appropriate to consider Rhea and Saturn; although we spoke of Saturn's name previously. But perhaps I am saying nothing.

**HERMOGENES.** Why so, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** O good man, I have noticed a certain swarm of wisdom.

**HERMOGENES.** What kind is that?

**SOCRATES.** Ridiculous to say, yet it has something probable about it.

**HERMOGENES.** What do you mean? And in what way is it probable?

**SOCRATES.** I seem to see that Heraclitus long ago wisely handed down certain things about Saturn and Rhea, which Homer had also said.

**HERMOGENES.** How do you mean?

**SOCRATES.** For Heraclitus says that all things flow and nothing remains; and comparing the progress of things to the flow of a river, he says it is impossible to dip yourself twice into the same water.

**HERMOGENES.** These things are true.

**SOCRATES.** Does he seem to you to differ from Heraclitus, who included Rhea and Saturn among the progenitors of the other gods? Do you think he imposed those names at random? Indeed, Homer established Oceanus as the origin of the gods and Tethys as the mother. And I think Hesiod intended the same. Furthermore, Orpheus says that Oceanus was the first to begin a marriage of beautiful flow, who mingled with his sister Tethys. See how greatly these things harmonize with one another, and all return to the opinion of Heraclitus.

**HERMOGENES.** You seem to be onto something, Socrates. But I do not quite understand what the name of Tethys means.

**SOCRATES.** This signifies almost the same thing, for it is a hidden name for a fountain. For "gushing" and "straining through" <note>original: "diattomenō & ethumenō"</note> present the image of a fountain; and from both of these names, the name of Tethys is composed.

**HERMOGENES.** This is very fine, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Why not? But what next? We have certainly spoken of Jove.

**HERMOGENES.** So it is.

**SOCRATES.** Let us then speak of his brothers, Neptune and Pluto, and the other name by which they call him.

**HERMOGENES.** By all means.

**SOCRATES.** It seems that Neptune was called "Posidon" by the one who first named him because the nature of the sea held him back as he went, and did not permit him to proceed further, but cast chains upon his feet. Therefore he called the prince of the sea "Posidona," as if he has a "fetter for the feet" <note>original: "posi... desmō"</note>. The letter "e" was perhaps added for the sake of beauty. Or perhaps it does not mean this, but a double "l" was originally placed instead of "s," as if to say "one who knows many things" <note>original: "pollā eidōs"</note>. Perhaps he was named "Sion" from the word for "to shake" <note>original: "siin"</note>, to which "p" and "a" were added. We call Pluto the giver of wealth <note>original: "plutu," Greek *ploutos*</note> because riches are dug from the bowels of the earth. "Hades" is interpreted by the multitude as "gloomy" or "dark" <note>original: "Aiden"</note>. And those who dread this name call him Pluto.

**HERMOGENES.** But what do you think, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** It seems to me that men have erred in many ways regarding the power of this god, and have always dreaded him when it is least fitting. Furthermore, everyone fears this: that no one returns here after they have died, and that the soul, stripped of the body, goes there. But all these things—the kingdom and the name of this god—seem to me to tend toward the same point.

**HERMOGENES.** In what way?

**SOCRATES.** I will say what I think. Come, tell me! Which of these is the stronger bond to keep any animal anywhere: necessity or desire?

**HERMOGENES.** Desire is far superior, Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** Would not many flee from Hades daily, unless he bound those who descend there with the strongest bond?

**HERMOGENES.** Evidently.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, it seems he holds them by a certain desire rather than by necessity...

...binds you, if only he knits you with the strongest bond. HERMOGENES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Are there not, again, many desires? HERMOGENES: Many. SOCRATES: Therefore, he binds them with the most vehement desire of all, if indeed he is to connect them with an unbreakable knot. HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Is there any desire more vehement than that by which someone is affected when he hopes to emerge as a better man through someone's company? HERMOGENES: By Hercules, none, Socrates. SOCRATES: For this reason, Hermogenes, we must say that no one wishes to return from there to here—not even the Sirens themselves—but rather that they and all others are soothed by the most sweet speeches of Pluto. And as this reasoning testifies, this god is without a doubt a most eloquent <term>sophist</term> <note>Here used in the classical sense of a "wise teacher" or "master of rhetoric."</note> for them. He bestows immense benefits upon those who dwell with him; for he abounds so greatly in riches that he supplies us with such great goods: hence he was named Pluto <note>From the Greek 'ploutos', meaning wealth.</note>. Does it not seem to you the duty of a philosopher that he should not wish to cling to men while they have bodies, but only then admit them when their soul is purged of all bodily evils and desires? Indeed, this god devised this method so as not to detain souls unless he conquered them with a greed for virtue. But those who are infected by the stupor and madness of the body, not even the father of Pluto, Saturn himself, would be able to restrain with those famous chains of his, nor keep them with him. HERMOGENES: You seem to be saying something significant, Socrates. SOCRATES: It is far from the truth, Hermogenes, that the name *Adis* <note>Hades</note> was spoken as if it were *aides*, that is, "gloomy" or "dark"; rather, it is derived from that which is *idene*, that is, "to know all beautiful things." From this, therefore, this god was named *Adis* by the founder of names. HERMOGENES: What do we say further of the names of Ceres, Juno, Apollo, Minerva, Vulcan, and Mars, and the rest of the gods? SOCRATES: Ceres <note>Demeter</note> is named from the very granting of nourishment: as if *didusa miter*, which is "the giving mother." But *Era* <note>Hera</note>, that is Juno, is as if *erate*, that is "lovely," because of the love with which Jupiter is affected toward her. Perhaps also the one who established this name, looking toward the sublime, named the air *Era* <note>An anagram of 'aer' in Greek</note>: and spoke obscurely, placing the beginning at the end. This will be clear to you if you pronounce that name frequently. Some are afraid to name *Pherephatta*, that is Proserpina, and Apollo, because the correctness of these names is unknown to them. Indeed, changing it, they consider *Persephone* herself, and that appears terrifying to them. But this indicates the wisdom of the god himself. For wisdom is that which touches and attains "flowing things." Wherefore this goddess would be rightly named *Pherepapha* because of wisdom and *epaphen*, that is "touch," of the *pheromenu*, that is "of that which is carried," or something of the sort. Therefore, the wise Pluto himself clings to her because she is such. But now they decline this name, making more of the grace of pronunciation than of the truth, so that they call her *Pherephattan*. The same also happens regarding the name of Apollo; for many dread that name as if it held something terrible. Do you know this? HERMOGENES: You speak the absolute truth. SOCRATES: But this, as I think, most fits the power of this god. HERMOGENES: In what way? SOCRATES: I will try to express my opinion. Surely no other single name could have been found more suitable for the four powers of this god: which would both encompass them all and in a way declare his music, prophecy, medicine, and skill in archery. HERMOGENES: Reveal it now. You say it is a wonderful name. SOCRATES: It is indeed harmoniously composed, and it accords with him as a musical god. In the first place, purgation and purifications, both according to medicine and according to prophecy, likewise those things which are performed by the drugs of physicians and the incantations and expiations of seers, washings and sprinklings—all these intend one thing: to render a man pure in both body and soul. HERMOGENES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Will not the god who purges be himself *Apoluon* and *apolyon*, that is, "washing away from evils" and "releasing," which Apollo himself signifies? HERMOGENES: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Insofar as he thus dilutes and releases, as a physician of such things, he is rightly called *apoluon*. But according to divination and the truth and *aplun*, that is "simple"—which is the same thing—we can rightly name him in the manner of the Thessalians; for they all call this god *Aplon*. Insofar as he is *ai vallon*, that is, "always throwing" and powerful with the bow, he can be called *aiuallon*, that is, "perpetual thrower." According to music, one must think of this as we do of what is called *acoluthos* and *achitis*, that is, "follower," "companion," and "wife." In these, as in many others, the 'a' signifies "together." In these also, the 'a' and *poleo* signify a turning which is performed together and as one: which we may call a "conversion." Through these, in the heavens, it signifies the conversion which happens through those things we call *polos* <note>poles</note>; and in song, harmony, which we call symphony. Because in these, as those skilled in music and astronomy teach, all things turn together in a certain harmony. But this god presides over harmony as *homopolon*, that is, "turning all these things together," both among gods and among men. Just as, therefore, we called *homocheleuton* and *homochitin*—that is, "traveling together" and "lying together"—*acholuton* and *achitin*, changing the 'o' into 'a': so we named him Apollo who was *homopolon*, with a second 'l' inserted: because it would have been ambiguous with a harsh name. Many in these times, suspecting this because they do not rightly perceive the force of this name, fear it as if it signified some destruction. But in truth, this name embraces all the powers of this god, as we said above. For it signifies simple, perpetual, thrower, expiator, and turner. The name of the Muses and of music is drawn from that which is called *mosthae*, that is, "to seek," and from the investigation and study of wisdom. *Leto* is named from her gentleness, because she is *ethelemon*, that is, "prompt," "exposed," and "willing" to grant what anyone seeks. Or perhaps as foreigners call her: for many name her *Litho*; which name he seems to have given because her mind is not rigid, but mild: therefore *Litho* as if *lion ethos*, that is, "a smooth and mild character," is her nickname among them. *Artemis*, that is Diana, is from the fact that she is *Artemes*, as if "complete and modest" because of her choice of virginity. Perhaps also the institutor of the name called her as if *aretis histora*, that is, "knower of virtue." Perhaps she was also called Artemis as if *Aroton misifasis*, that is, as if she who [hated] plying...

...it would be hateful for a man to be with a woman. Either because of one of these things or because of all such things, the name was established. HERMOGENES: What then of Dionysus and Aphrodite? SOCRATES: You ask great things, son of Hipponicus. Indeed, the reasoning for the names imposed on these gods is twofold: namely, serious and playful. Seek the serious from others; however, nothing prevents us from recounting the playful. For the gods are surely playful too: and Dionysus is "the giver of wine" <note>original: "didus oinon"</note>, that is, the wine-giver, nicknamed as if he were "Didinysos" in a certain joke. Wine, moreover, can deservedly be called "ionus" <note>a play on "oionous" or "thinking one has a mind"</note> because it makes most who drink it alienated in mind, so that they think they "have a mind" <note>original: "hen nunechin"</note>. Concerning Venus <note>Aphrodite</note>, it is not fitting to disagree with Hesiod, but to concede that she is called Aphrodite because of her generation from "aphros," that is, from foam. HERMOGENES: But truly, Socrates, since you are an Athenian, you will not pass over Minerva <note>Athena</note>, Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note>, and Mars <note>Ares</note> in silence. SOCRATES: That would not be fitting at all. HERMOGENES: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Why one of her names was imposed is not difficult to say. HERMOGENES: Which? SOCRATES: We call her Pallas. HERMOGENES: Clearly. SOCRATES: This name must be judged to have been derived from dancing in war; furthermore, we say "pallin" and "pallethae" for lifting oneself or another from the earth, or carrying something in the hands—that is, to vibrate, to shake, to be shaken, to leap, and to perform a dance. HERMOGENES: Without controversy. SOCRATES: We call her Pallas for this reason, and deservedly so. HERMOGENES: How do you interpret her other name? SOCRATES: You ask about Athena? HERMOGENES: That very one. SOCRATES: This is a weightier matter, friend; the ancients seem to have thought of Athena just as those who are learned in the interpretations of Homer do in these times. For most of them explain that Homer fashioned Athena as "mind" <note>nous</note> and "thought." And those who find names seem to have felt something similar about her; indeed, exalting her even higher, they introduced her as the "mind of God" <note>theou noesis</note>, as if saying "Ethenoe"—using an *alpha* instead of an *eta* in a foreign fashion—and removing the *iota* and *omicron*. Or perhaps not so, but "Theia noesis," that is, as one who knows divine things, he called her "Theonoe" above all others. Nor will it be out of place if we say he wished to call her "Ethenoe," as if she were "intelligence in character" <note>ethos</note>. Later, they named her Athena, perhaps lengthening it into something more beautiful, as it seemed to them. HERMOGENES: What of Vulcan, whom they call Hephaestus? SOCRATES: What do you say? Do you ask about the noble "phaos histora," that is, the "guardian of light"? HERMOGENES: I seem to have asked for him. SOCRATES: This one, as can be clear to anyone, is "phaestos" <note>shining</note>, and he claims the *eta* for himself. Whence he was called "Hephaestus," that is, the guardian of light. HERMOGENES: It appears so, unless it seems otherwise to you in some way. SOCRATES: Ask if it seems otherwise regarding Mars. HERMOGENES: I ask. SOCRATES: If you please, Ares is named according to "arrhen," that is, male, and "andrion," that is, brave. Furthermore, if you wish, because of a certain harsh, hard, and unconquered nature, which is called "arrhoton" <note>unbreakable</note>, he was called Ares; this also suits a thoroughly warlike god. HERMOGENES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Let us now leave the gods, by the gods I beseech you! For I fear to discourse about them. Challenge me to any other things you wish, so that you may know what kind of horses Euthyphro has <note>Socrates jokingly credits his sudden "inspiration" to the priest Euthyphro</note>. HERMOGENES: I will do as you ask; I will ask one thing of myself, since Cratylus denies that I am Hermogenes. Let us investigate what the name of Hermes signifies, so that we may see if he speaks any truth. SOCRATES: Hermes seems to pertain to speech, insofar as he is an "hermeneus," that is, an interpreter and messenger, a thief, a deceiver in speaking, and a forceful orator. All of that revolves around speech. Indeed, as we said before, "Irin" is the use of speech; and Homer often says of this, "emesato," that is, he contrived. From both, therefore, the name of this god is composed: both from "to speak" and from "to contrive and devise things to be said." It is as if the author of the name commanded us: "It is right, O men, that you call that god who 'irin emesato' (contrived to speak) 'Iremen'." But we, thinking it more elegant to speak thus, call him "Hermen." Furthermore, Iris has her name from "irin," to speak, because she is a messenger. HERMOGENES: By my faith, Cratylus seems to have correctly denied that I am Hermogenes <note>a "son of Hermes"</note>. For I am dull at the invention of speech. SOCRATES: It is also fitting, friend, that Pan, the double-formed, is the son of Hermes. HERMOGENES: By what reason? SOCRATES: Do you know that speech signifies "pan," that is, everything, and it always revolves and rolls, and is twofold—namely, true and false? HERMOGENES: Certainly. SOCRATES: Is not that which is true in speech smooth and divine, dwelling above among the gods? While the false is below among the many men, harsh and tragic? For from here the fictions of fables and many falsehoods are found around the tragic life. HERMOGENES: It is entirely so. SOCRATES: Deservedly, therefore, he who is "pan" (announcing all) and "aei polon" (always wandering) would be called "Pan aipolos" <note>a pun on "goat-herd"</note>, the double-formed son of Hermes. Smooth and delicate in his upper parts, but harsh and goat-like in his lower parts. And Pan is either speech itself, or the brother of speech, since he is the son of Hermes. And what wonder is it that a brother is like a brother? But now, O blessed man, as I was asking a little while ago, let us break off this talk of the gods. HERMOGENES: Let us leave such gods if you wish, Socrates; but what prevents us from running through things of this sort: the Sun, the Moon, the Stars, the Earth, the Ether, the Air, Fire, Water, Spring, and the Year? SOCRATES: You ask many and great things. However, if it will be pleasing to you, I will comply. HERMOGENES: Very pleasing indeed. SOCRATES: What do you ask first? Or as you were saying, first "helion," the sun? HERMOGENES: Exactly. SOCRATES: It seems it would be manifest if one used the Doric name. For the Dorians call it "halion"; and it is so called according to "halizin," from the fact that it assembles men into one when it rises. Also from the fact that it always revolves <note>original: "hilin"</note> around the earth. Furthermore, because it varies in its circuit the things that are born from the earth. To vary and "aeolin" are the same. HERMOGENES: What then should be said of "Selene," the moon? SOCRATES: This name seems to bring forth Anaxagoras. HERMOGENES: Why? SOCRATES: Because it carries something older than what he recently said: that the moon draws its light from the sun. HERMOGENES: In what way? SOCRATES: "Selas" is the same as light. HERMOGENES: The same. SOCRATES: This light is perpetually "Neon" and "Ennon" (new and old) around the moon, if the followers of Anaxagoras speak the truth. For circling it, it continually renews it, but it is old...

of the past light. **Hermogenes.** Certainly. **Socrates.** Many call the Moon *Selanea*. <note>original: "selanęā"</note> **Hermogenes.** Indeed. **Socrates.** Since it always has a light that is both new and old, it should rightly be called *Sela-en-neo-aia* <note>A composite meaning "shining-in-the-new-always."</note>. Now, however, it is called *Selanea* by a shortened name. **Hermogenes.** This is a dithyrambic name, O Socrates. But how do you interpret *mena* (month) and *astra* (stars)? **Socrates.** "Month" would be correctly named from *meiesthai* (to diminish). "Stars" <note>original: "Astra"</note> have the surname of *astrapes* (lightning). Lightning, because it *anastrephei* (turns back) the sight toward itself, ought to be called *Anastrope*, but is now named *Astrape* by a more elegant word. **Hermogenes.** From where do the names *Pyr* and *Hydor* (fire and water) draw their origin? **Socrates.** I am in doubt; it seems either the muse of Euthyphro has deserted me, or this is something very difficult. Notice, I pray, where I take refuge in all things about which I doubt. **Hermogenes.** Where? **Socrates.** I will tell you; do you yourself know by what reasoning fire is named? **Hermogenes.** By Hercules, I do not. **Socrates.** See what I suspect about this. I truly believe the Greeks had many names from the barbarians, especially those who lived under the barbarians. **Hermogenes.** To what end is this? **Socrates.** If anyone seeks the correct imposition of these according to the Greek tongue, and not according to the language in which the name was invented, he will surely be in doubt. **Hermogenes.** That is likely. **Socrates.** See then if this name *pyr* (fire) is barbarian, for it is not easy to accommodate it to the Greek language; it is well known that the Phrygians name it thus, declining it only slightly, as they do *hydor* (water) and *cynas* (dogs), and many other things. **Hermogenes.** These things are true. **Socrates.** Therefore, there is no need to pull these apart, since no one can say anything certain about them. For this reason, I reject those names of fire and water in this manner. But "Air" <note>original: "Aer"</note> is so called, Hermogenes, because it *erei* (lifts) those things which are around the earth; or because it *aei rhei* (always flows); or because by its flux the breath is stirred. Poets indeed call the gale *Aetas*. Perhaps therefore air is called as if it were *pneumatorrhun* (flowing breath), or a flowing flame. Furthermore, I think "Ether" <note>original: "Aether"</note> should be explained thus: because it *aei thei* (always runs) flowing around the air; wherefore it could be called *aeitheer*. *Ge* (earth) expresses its sense more plainly if it is called *Gea*. For *Gea* can rightly be called *gennetira* (mother/genitrix), as Homer says. For when he says *gegaasi*, he means "born in her." What remains next? **Hermogenes.** Spring and the year, O Socrates. **Socrates.** The *Horae* (Seasons/Hours) must be spoken of in the ancient Attic voice if you wish to know what is fitting. For they are called *Horae* because they *horizusi* (limit/terminate) winter and summer, and the winds and the fruits born from the earth. *Eniautos* and *Etos* (the year) seem to be the same thing. For that which in turn brings into light whatever is born and made from the earth, and examines and discerns it within itself, is the year. And as we said above that the name of Jove (Zeus) was cut in two—called *Zena* by some and *Dia* by others—so some call the year *eniauto* because it is "in itself," and others *etos* because it "examines." The whole expression is "that which examines in itself." From this one phrase, two names were selected: for what is said together as *ton en eauto etazon* (examining in itself) is said distinctly as *eniauton* and *etos* (year). **Hermogenes.** But truly, O Socrates, you are now going a long way. **Socrates.** I seem to wander quite far in philosophy. **Hermogenes.** Indeed. **Socrates.** Perhaps you will concede more. **Hermogenes.** Truly, after this kind, I would most gladly contemplate by what reasoning these noble names of the virtues were imposed: such as *Phronesis* (prudence), *Synesis* (intelligence), *Diceosyne* (justice), and all others of this sort. **Socrates.** You have raised no contemptible class of names, my friend. Nevertheless, since I have put on the lion's skin <note>A reference to Hercules; meaning he has taken on a brave or difficult task.</note>, it is not fitting to be deterred; rather, I must consider those noble names of prudence, intelligence, thought, knowledge, and others of this kind. **Hermogenes.** Indeed, we must by no means stop before then. **Socrates.** By Pollux, I think I do not guess badly about what I was just considering: namely, that those most ancient authors of names—as has happened to many of our wise men—fell into a dizziness of the brain due to the frequent revolution in investigating things. Because of this, I think things appeared to them to be carried along and wavering. They believe the cause of this opinion is not an internal dizziness, but an external circuit of the things themselves; they think nature is such that nothing in them is firm or stable, but all things flow and are carried along, and are agitated in every way, and are always being born and flowing away. This I see in these names which have now been reported. **Hermogenes.** In what way, Socrates? **Socrates.** Have you not noticed that the above names were imposed on things as if they were carried, flowing, and transferred in a perpetual generation? **Hermogenes.** I did not quite perceive it. **Socrates.** In the beginning, what we first reported pertains to something of this kind. **Hermogenes.** What is that? **Socrates.** *Phronesis* (prudence) is *phoras* and *rhu noesis* (the perception of motion and flux). It can also signify receiving *onesin phoras* (the utility of motion). Finally, it is occupied with agitation itself. Furthermore, if you wish, *Gnome* (thought/judgment) signifies *gones nomesin* (the consideration of generation), for *noman* is to consider. *Noesis* (intellection) is *neu esis* (the desire for the new). That things are "new" signifies they are always becoming; and that the soul desires and approaches this is indicated by the one who found the name *neoesin*. For in the beginning it was not called *Noesis*, but was pronounced with a 'u' and two 'e's as *Neoesis*, as if it were *neu esis* (the seeking and approaching of the new). *Sophrosyne* (temperance) is the safety and preservation of that *Phroneseos* (prudence) which we just mentioned. *Episteme* (knowledge) is drawn from that which follows and stands by; as if the skillful soul follows flowing things, stands by them, and accompanies them. It becomes neither later by delay nor earlier by running ahead. Therefore, with an 'e' inserted, it is right to call it *epistemem*. *Synesis* (understanding) seems to be like a *syllogismus* (a reasoning). When *syniene* is said, the same is understood as if one said *epistasthe* (to know). For it shows the soul coming together with things. *Sophia* (wisdom) is the touching of agitation. This is somewhat obscure and foreign to us. But it should be noted in the poets that whenever they wish to express someone arriving and rushing in, they say *esythe* (he rushed forth). Moreover, a certain illustrious man among the Lacedaemonians (Spartans) had the name *Sus*, which means "swift." For thus the Lacedaemonians indicate the force of an impulse. As if all things were being carried along, *sophia* demonstrates the *epaphen* (touching and perception) of this very agitation, which is signified by that which is called *sus*. *Agathon* (The Good)...

# CRATYLUS, OR ON THE RIGHTNESS OF NAMES. FOLIO CLXXIII.

<margin>
Goodness
Justice. *Justitia*
The Just
Understanding.
The Just.
Through-going.
The Just.
</margin>
The **good** of each nature, *agathon* <note>original: "agaston"</note>, signifies that which is admirable, lovable, and delightful. Indeed, since all things are in flux, there is in them partly speed and partly slowness. Therefore, not everything is swift, but there is something of the "admirable" (*agaston*) itself. This very quality is declared by the name of **Good** (*Agathon*). **Justice** (*Dikaiosyne*), which implies the "understanding of the just" (*dikaiou synesis*), is something we can easily conjecture. But what the **Just** (*dikaion*) itself means is difficult to know. It seems that what has been said so far is granted by many, but the rest remains doubtful. For those who believe the whole universe is in motion think that it is greatly agitated, and that there is something permeating through everything by which individual things are made; this must be the thinnest and swiftest element. For it could not run through all things unless it were so thin that nothing could resist its penetration, and so swift that it treats other things as if they were standing still. Since it governs all things by "running through" (*diaion*) and permeating them, it is rightly called the **Just** (*dikaion*), with the letter "k" <note>the Greek letter kappa</note> inserted for the sake of a more refined pronunciation. Thus far, as we have just said, it is agreed among many that this is the Just.

But I, Hermogenes, burning with the desire to learn, have scrutinized all these things; and I perceived in secret teachings that this "Just" is the cause itself—for that by which things are made is the cause—and someone handed down that it ought to be properly called by that name. But when, after hearing these things, I nevertheless diligently inquire of them what the Just itself is, since it is so, I seem already to demand more than is fitting, and to "overstep the trench and the rampart," as the saying goes. <margin>Proverb: He oversteps the trench and the rampart.</margin> For they respond that I have asked and heard enough and more; and wishing to satisfy me, they try to bring forward different explanations, nor do they agree further. One says the Just is the **Sun**. For only the Sun, by running through and heating all things, governs them. But when I eagerly report this to someone as if I had heard something excellent, he immediately laughs at me and asks whether I think no justice remains for men after the sun has set. So, when I ask what he thinks, he says that **Fire** itself is the Just, though that is not easy to know. Wherefore another says it is not fire itself, but rather the **Heat** innate in fire. Another holds all these things as nothing, saying that the Just is that **Mind** which Anaxagoras introduced. He says that Mind, being mistress by its own nature and mixed with nothing, adorns all things by penetrating through all things. Here indeed, O friend, I have fallen into greater ambiguity than before, when I was asking nothing about justice. But to return to that for the sake of which we are disputing, such a name was attributed to it for these reasons we have mentioned.

HERMOGENES: You seem, O Socrates, to have heard these things from someone, and not to have brought them forth crudely from your own workshop.
SOCRATES: What about the others?
HERMOGENES: Not so.
SOCRATES: Pay attention then, for perhaps I might deceive you in the remaining things, as if I had not heard what I shall bring forward. After justice, what remains? We have not yet finished with **Courage** (*Andria*). Injustice is surely an obstacle to that which "runs through all things"; Courage is engaged in "fight" (*pygna*). Fight in things, if indeed they are in flux, is nothing other than a "contrary flux" (*rhous*). Therefore, if one subtracts the letter "d" from this name *andria*, the remaining name *anria* <note>original: "amaria"</note> declares the work itself. It is clearly established that courage is not just any contrary flux (*rhoe*), but the one opposed to that flux which occurs contrary to justice. For otherwise, courage would not be praiseworthy. **Male** (*arrhen*) and **Man** (*aner*) derive their origin from something similar, namely from "upward flux" (*ano rhoe*). **Woman** (*gyne*) is as if it were *gone*, that is, "fruitful and generative." **Female** (*thely*) is named from *thele*, that is, "nipple." And *thele* seems to be so called, Hermogenes, because it makes things "sprout and bud" (*thelenin*), like one watering those things that are irrigated.
HERMOGENES: So it appears, O Socrates.
SOCRATES: **To flourish** (*thallin*), that is, to grow green, to mature, to bloom, represents the growth of the young; it is like something swift and sudden, which he who fashioned the name hinted at from "to run" (*thein*) and "to leap" (*hallesthai*). Do you notice me being carried as if "outside the racecourse" now that I have found smooth and passable ground? Many things also remain which seem to pertain to serious matters.
HERMOGENES: You speak the truth.
SOCRATES: One of which is that we should see what **Art** (*techne*) implies.
HERMOGENES: By all means.
SOCRATES: Does this not show a "possession of mind" (*hexin nou*), if the "t" is removed? But an "o" is inserted in the middle between the "ch" and the "n" and "y"! <note>Socrates is playing with the Greek spelling of Techne vs. Hechon-nou</note>
HERMOGENES: That is too dry and unpolished, Socrates.
SOCRATES: Do you not know, blessed man, that ancient names have by now been pulled apart and confused by those fond of tragic elegance, who add and subtract letters for the sake of beauty? They pervert them everywhere, partly through the long passage of time and partly through a desire for ornamentation—as for example in the word for **mirror** (*katoptro*), how absurd is the addition of the "r"? <margin>The length of time and ornamentation pervert ancient names.</margin> Certainly, those who value the charms of the mouth more than the truth do such things, I think. Wherefore, since they have added much to the names themselves, they have finally brought it about that no one now notices the meaning of the names. Just as when they say **Sphinx** (*sphinga*), a certain monster, when they ought to pronounce it *sphigga* <note>meaning "the throttler"</note>, and many other things. Surely, if it were given to anyone to subtract and add at his own discretion, there would be great license, and each person would attribute any name to any thing.
HERMOGENES: You tell the truth.
SOCRATES: Plainly true. But it becomes you, as a wise presiding officer, to observe a certain moderation and propriety.
HERMOGENES: O, I wish I could!
SOCRATES: And I myself wish it, O Hermogenes. But, happy man, do not require too exact a discussion, lest you utterly exhaust my strength. For I shall ascend to the peak of what was said above, after we have considered **Device** (*mechane*), that is, skillful machination and thinking out. It seems to signify the same as "to reach far" and "to ascend." It is therefore composed of these two: *mecus*, that is, "long and much," and *anein*, that is, "to ascend, penetrate, or reach." But as I was just saying, we must come to the summit of these sayings: we must ask what these names signify: **Virtue** (*arete*) and **Wickedness** (*kakia*). One I have not yet found; the other seems to be open. For it harmonizes with all the previous ones. Since all things "go," wickedness (*kakia*) will be "going badly" (*kakos ion*). Therefore, when the soul approaches things badly, it is generally called wicked; but specifically and most greatly, this difficulty of proceeding is evident in **Cowardice** (*deilia*), which we have not yet declared. For we passed it over. It was necessary to bring it in immediately after courage itself. We seem to have passed over many other things besides. **Cowardice** (*deilia*) signifies a "hard bond of the soul." For *desmos* is a bond, and *lian* signifies something very hard. Therefore, cowardice is a vehement and great...

# CRATYLUS, OR ON THE RIGHT RATIONALE OF NAMES.

## PAGE CXXIX.

<margin>ἡμέραν, ἡμέρα, ἡμέρα.</margin>
They called the day *himera*. **HERMOGENES.** That is apparent. **SOCRATES.** But now it is chanted in such a tragic fashion that you can by no means understand what *hemera* <note>original: "ἡμέραν" (day)</note> intends to mean. Although some think *himera* is so called because it makes things *hemera*, that is, "tame" or "gentle." **HERMOGENES.** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES.** Nor does it escape you that the ancients called *zygon* (a yoke) *dyogon*. **HERMOGENES.** Clearly. **SOCRATES.** It seems to be <margin>ζυγόν, δυογόν.</margin> as if it were *blaueron*, that is, something related to the harmful. **HERMOGENES.** So it most greatly appears, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But in truth, the word *zygon* <margin>ζυγόν, δυογόν, ἀνερ ἀγωγὴν.</margin> reveals nothing; yet *dyogon* demonstrates *dyin agoge*, that is, the "leading of two" for the sake of binding them together. The same must be judged concerning many other words. **HERMOGENES.** It is plain. **SOCRATES.** By the same reasoning, *Deon* <note>original: "δέον" (that which is binding/necessary)</note> is pronounced in a way that shows it to be the opposite of all names <margin>δέον δεσμός.</margin> looking toward the good. Furthermore, being a species of the good, *deon* seems to be *desmos*, that is, a certain "bond" and "impediment" to possession, <margin>βλαβεροῦ, δέον</margin> as if it were *blaueron*, that is, something related to the harmful. **HERMOGENES.** So it most greatly appears, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But it is not so in the <margin>δέον, ὠφέλιμον, λυσιτελοῦν</margin> ancient name, which is more likely to have been rightly established than our own. Indeed, you will agree with the superior "goods" if you restore the *i* for the *u*. For it is not *Deon*, but *Dion* that signifies that "good" which the inventor of names always praises. But <margin>κερδαλέον, ἀγαθὸν, συμφέρον.</margin> what I have done myself does not disagree; rather, they look toward the same thing: *Deon* as if *Dion*, *Ophelimon* (profitable), *lysiteloun* (advantageous), *cerdaleon* (gainful), *agathon* (good), <margin>εὔπορον, ζημιῶδες, δεῦντι τὸ μὴ δέον, Δημιῶδες.</margin> *sympheron* (expedient), *euporon* (easy of passage). This whole universe hints at one thing through diverse names: something penetrating through all things and <margin>ἡδονὴ, λύπη, ἐπιθυμία, ἡδονὴ</margin> adorning all things; and that is everywhere praised. But that which stands in the way and detains is disapproved. Furthermore, in this name <margin>ὁρμήσιν, ὁρμίσις, ἡδονὴ, λύπη, Διάλυσις, ἀνία.</margin> *Zemiodes* (harmful), if you place *d* for *z* according to the ancient custom, it will appear to you that this name was imposed upon that which "binds and stops" <margin>ἰέναι, ἀλγηδὼν</margin> that which proceeds. Whence it should be named *Demiodes*. **HERMOGENES.** What of *hedone*, *lype*, *epithymia*—that is, pleasure, <margin>ἀλγηδών, ὀδύνη.</margin> pain, and desire, Socrates—and the rest of this kind? **SOCRATES.** They do not seem too obscure to me, Hermogenes. *Hedone* (pleasure), if indeed it is the name of that action which tends toward *onim*, that is, "utility" and "profit"; <margin>ἐμοῦσεωσ, ἄχθος</margin> but the *l* is added, making it so that instead of *ionisis*, it is pronounced *Hedone*. *Lype* (pain) seems to be drawn from *dialyseos*, that is, the "dissolution" of the <margin>ἀὼν, Χαρά, Διάχυσις, εὐπορίασ, ῥόησ, τέρψισ</margin> body. For in such a passion the body dissolves. *Ania*, that is "sorrow," demonstrates that which impedes *ienai*, that is, "going." *Algedon*, that is "torment," seems to be a foreign name, <margin>τέρπνον, πνόη</margin> spoken from *alginu*. *Odyne*, that is "pain and affliction," is named from *endyseos*, that is, the "entry" of pain. **HERMOGENES.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** *Achthe- <margin>ἕρπνουμ, τερπνὸν, εὐφροσύνη</margin> don*, that is "grief and languor," signifies the heaviness and slowness of "bearing." For *Achthos* is a "burden," while *ion* is "going." *Chara*, that is "joy and gladness," is said from <margin>εὐ, συμφέρεσθαι</margin> *diachyseos*, that is "outpouring," and *Euporias*, that is "facility," and *Rhoes*, that is the "motion" of the soul. *Terpsis*, that is "delight," is derived from *terpnu*, <margin>εὐφεροσύνη, εὐφροσύνη, ἐπιθυμία, θυμὸν, θυμὸσ, θύσεωσ, ζέσεωσ, ἵμεροσ.</margin> that is "delectation." But *terpnon* is from *pnoi*, that is the "inspiration" of delight into the soul. Wherefore it would rightly be called *erpnon*, that is "inspiring." But with the interval of time, it arrived at *terpnon*. *Euphrosyne*, that is "cheerfulness and alacrity": there is no need to assign why it is so called. For it is plain to anyone that this name is drawn from that which is called *Eu*, that is "well," and *sympheresthe*, that is "to be carried together"; as if one said the soul "bears things well." Whence it ought to be called *euphrosyne*. Yet we call it *Euphrosyne*. <margin>ῥῶ, ἰέμενος, ῥέον, ἵμεροσ, πόθοσ, ἀπόντοσ ἵμεροσ, πόθοσ, ἔρωσ</margin> But it is not difficult to assign what *epithymia*, that is "desire," intends. For this name shows a force tending into the *thymon*, that is, the "soul" and "anger" and "fury." But *thymos* is from *thyseos* and *zeseos*, that is "burning," "fervor," and the "impetus" of the soul. Likewise, <margin>εἰσρεῖ, ῥοὴ, ἔσρετυ, ἔρωσ, ἔρασ</margin> *Himeros*, that is a "sweet and bland outpouring," is said from *Rho*, that is the "flow" vehemently alluring the soul. For from that which is *hiemenos rhi*, that is, "incited and seeking things," it flows and vehemently attracts the soul because of the impetus or incitement of the <margin>δόξα, δόξα, Δίωξισ, ζήτουσα</margin> flow. From this whole force *himeros* was named. Furthermore, he calls it *pothos*, that is "longing": which surely does not look to present sweetness, <margin>λῆ, δίωξισ οἷσι μ</margin> as *himeros* does, but burns for that which is absent. Whence *pothos* is said as if from *pontos*, that is, "concupiscence for the absent." And the same thing is the striving of the mind for that which is pleasing: when what it desires is present, it is named *himeros*; when absent, *pothos*. But *Eros*, that is "love," is because it *ifrhi*, that is, "flows in" from the outside; nor is that *Rhoe*, that is "flux," proper to the one who has it, but it is infused through the eyes. Therefore, from *efrin*, that is "to flow in," *efros*, that is "flux," love was called by our ancestors. For they used *o* instead of *o-mega*. But now it is called *eros* with the *o-mega* interposed for the *o*. But what do you bid us consider next? **HERMOGENES.** *Doxa*, that is "opinion," and such things, whence they have their name. **SOCRATES.** *Doxa* is said either from *dioxi*, that is "pursuit," by which the soul proceeds and pursues, investigating the condition of things; or from *toxu bole*, that is the "shot of a bow." It seems, however, to depend rather on this. *Oiesis*, that is "estimation," accords with this. For it shows *isin*, that is the "entry" of the soul into each thing to be considered, *oion*, that is "of what sort it is"; just as *vule*, that is "will," is said from *vole*, that is a "throw." And *vulesthae*, that is "to will," because of the very effort of reaching. It also signifies *ephiesthae*, that is "to desire," and *vuleusthae*, that is "to consult." All these things following "opinion" seem to be images of *voles* itself, that is, of "throwing" and "striving." Just as the contrary, *avulia*, that is the "privation of will," appears as a certain defect of being unable to attain: as if one does not contend; nor does he want, desire, investigate, or acquire what he intends. **HERMOGENES.** You seem to be heaping these up quite frequently, O Socrates. Therefore let there be an end now, God willing. I wish, however, for *Anancen* and *Ecusion*, that is "necessity" and "voluntary," to be declared. For these follow the previous ones. **SOCRATES.** *Ecusion* indeed is *icon*, that is "yielding" and not resisting. For by this name is declared *icon ionti*, that is "yielding to the one going," or that which is perfected out of will. But *Ananceon*, that is "necessary" and "resisting," since it is against the will, will be concerned with error and ignorance; it is described from the process according to necessity, because in a rough way they prohibit the path of progress. Whence *Ananceon* is said, as if "going through a valley" <note>original: "per Ancusioni"</note>. But as long as our strength thrives, let us not desert. Wherefore ask, I pray, and do not stop. **HERMOGENES.** Behold, I ask what are the greatest and most beautiful: *Alethia*, that is "truth," and *Pseudos*, that is "falsehood," and *on*, that is "being"; and why that which we are dealing with here is called *onoma*, that is "a name." **SOCRATES.** What do you call *maiesthae*? **HERMOGENES.** I call it "to inquire." **SOCRATES.** This word "name" <note>original: "onoma"</note> seems to be fashioned from that speech in which it is said *on*, that is "being is"; of which the "name" is the inquiry. Which you will certainly comprehend more clearly in that which we call *onomaston*, that is "to be named." For here is expressed what a name is: namely, the "inquiry into being." But *Alethia* (truth), just like the others, seems to be composed. For

# BOOK

<margin>

The divine motion of being includes this name. *Truth* <note>original: "alethia"</note> is as if it were "divine wandering" <note>original: "thia ale"</note>. *Falsehood* <note>original: "pseudos"</note>, however, is the opposite of motion. Again, here he censures the obstacle to agitation, or that which forces one to stand still. For it is derived from *to sleep* <note>original: "catheudo"</note>. The added letter "P" hides the sense of the name. *Being* <note>original: "on"</note> and *Essence* <note>original: "usia"</note> agree with *Truth* <note>original: "alethia"</note> if an "i" is added; for *going* <note>original: "ion"</note> signifies one who moves. But *not being* <note>original: "ucon"</note>: some name it *not going* <note>original: "ucion"</note>. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me, O Socrates, to have discussed these things quite vigorously. But if someone were to ask you what the correct interpretation is of those words called *going* <note>original: "ion"</note>, *flowing* <note>original: "rheon"</note>, and *binding or detaining* <note>original: "dun"</note>: what would we chiefly answer them? Do you have an answer? **SOCRATES:** I do indeed. Especially since something occurred to me recently, by which we might seem to offer a response to anything. **HERMOGENES:** What is that? **SOCRATES:** That whatever we least understand, we say is "barbaric" <note>meaning foreign or non-Greek</note>. For perhaps some are truly such; or perhaps some, especially proper names, are inscrutable due to the confusion of time. Indeed, since words are pulled apart everywhere, it would be no wonder if the ancient language, compared to ours, differed in no way from a barbaric tongue. **HERMOGENES:** What you say is not far from reason. **SOCRATES:** I offer plausible things; yet the contest does not seem to admit an excuse for that reason. But let us try to separate these things and consider them thus: if someone always generated the words by which a name is spoken, and again inquired into those words by which those words are spoken, and proceeded to search thus: would not the one who answers eventually be exhausted and forced to refuse? **HERMOGENES:** It certainly seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, when he who denies an answer deservedly stops: will it not be after he has reached those names which are the elements of other speeches and names? If these are indeed elements, they ought not to appear composed of other names. Just as we said above that *Good* <note>original: "Agathon"</note> was composed of *admirable* <note>original: "Agastu"</note> and *swift* <note>original: "Thoon"</note>. We shall say *Swift* <note>original: "Thoon"</note> again consists of others, and those of others. But after we have come to that which is no longer constituted from other names, we shall rightly say we have reached an element, and this must not be referred further into other names. **HERMOGENES:** You seem to me to speak skillfully. **SOCRATES:** Are not those names about which you were asking just now elements? And must their correct reasoning be investigated differently than the rest? **HERMOGENES:** That is probable. **SOCRATES:** Probable indeed, Hermogenes. All the previous things seem reduced to these; and if the matter stands thus, as it seems to me, come again and consider this with me, lest I perhaps rave while I attempt to explain the correct reasoning of the primary names. **HERMOGENES:** Just speak: for I will meditate with all my strength. **SOCRATES:** I think you agree with this: that there is one correct reasoning for both the first and the last name, and none of them differs from another in being a name. **HERMOGENES:** Greatly so. **SOCRATES:** For the correct reasoning of all the names we referred to above consisted in this: that the nature of each thing should be indicated. **HERMOGENES:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** This surely ought to apply no less to the prior than to the posterior names, if they are to be names. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And the posterior names could achieve this through the prior ones. **HERMOGENES:** It appears so. **SOCRATES:** But the primary ones, which no others precede, in what way will they best show us the things themselves, if they are to be names? Answer me this: if we lacked voice and tongue, and wished to declare things to one another, would we not, like the mute do now, attempt to signify with hands, head, and other members? **HERMOGENES:** Not otherwise, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, to demonstrate something high and light, we would have raised our hand toward heaven, imitating the nature of the thing itself; but for lower and heavy things, we would have pointed toward the ground with a certain cast. Moreover, to indicate a running horse or any other animal, we would have shaped the gestures and figure of our bodies as closely as possible to their likeness. **HERMOGENES:** What you say seems necessary to me. **SOCRATES:** In this manner, I think, there would be a naming by these parts of the body; the body, clearly, imitating what it wished to show. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly so. **SOCRATES:** But since we wished to declare things by voice, tongue, and mouth: will not the showing finally be done through these, if an imitation is made through them concerning anything? **HERMOGENES:** I think it necessary. **SOCRATES:** A name, therefore, as it appears, is an imitation of the voice: by which whoever imitates something, imitates and names it through the voice. **HERMOGENES:** It seems the same to me. **SOCRATES:** Yet I do not think it is yet correctly stated. **HERMOGENES:** Why? **SOCRATES:** Because we would be forced to admit that those who imitate sheep and roosters and other animals are naming the very things they imitate. **HERMOGENES:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** Do you think that is fitting? **HERMOGENES:** Not at all. But what kind of imitation, O Socrates, will a name be? **SOCRATES:** Not such an imitation as is made through music, although it is made by voice; nor even of the same things of which music is an imitation. For we do not seem to name through musical imitation. I say it thus: Voice, figure, and color belong to many things. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** It seems to me that if someone imitates these, the faculty of naming does not consist in those imitations. For these are partly music, and partly painting. Is it not so? **HERMOGENES:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** What of this: do you not think there is an essence to each thing, just as there is to color and the other things we mentioned? Is there not a certain essence in color and voice, and in all other things worthy of the name of "being"? **HERMOGENES:** It seems so to me. **SOCRATES:** If someone were able to imitate the essence of each thing with letters and syllables, would he not declare what each thing is? **HERMOGENES:** Most greatly. **SOCRATES:** What would you call such a person? You called the former ones partly musicians, partly painters; but what will you call this one? **HERMOGENES:** This seems to me, O Socrates, to be the author of naming whom we have long sought. **SOCRATES:** If this is true, we must now consider those names you required: *Flow* <note>original: "Rhoes"</note>, *Going* <note>original: "iene"</note>, *Restraint* <note>original: "scheseos"</note>: whether he truly imitates the essence with his letters and syllables, or not. **HERMOGENES:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** Come, let us see whether these alone are proper names, or if there are others besides these. **HERMOGENES:** I think there are others. **SOCRATES:** It is consistent. But what is the method of distinguishing, where does the imitator begin to imitate? Since the imitation of essence is made by letters and syllables, is it not best first to distinguish the elements? Just as those who work with rhythms first distinguish the powers of the elements; then of the syllables; and finally they approach the rhythms themselves, but never before. **HERMOGENES:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Must we not also first distinguish the vocal letters <note>vowels</note>; then the rest according to their species, the mutes and semivocals? For thus learned men speak of these, and again of the vowels: not...
