# CRATYLUS, OR ON THE CORRECTNESS OF NAMES. FOLIO 130.

...yet the semi-vowels and the types of vowels themselves differ from one another. And after we have distinguished all these things, we must in turn introduce names and consider if there are principles to which they all refer, just like the elements <note>original: "elementa," referring to the basic sounds/letters of the alphabet</note> from which one can know them; and if species are contained within them in the same way as in the elements. Having carefully thought out all these things, one must know how to apply each according to its likeness—whether one sound should be applied to one thing, or many mixed together. Just as painters, wishing to express a likeness, sometimes use only purple color, sometimes any other color, and sometimes mix many—as when they wish to fashion a most lifelike image of a man or something of that sort—insofar as each image requires certain colors. In no different way shall we also adapt elements to things, applying one to one wherever it seems most needed. And we shall fashion <term>symbols<note>original: "symbola," explained here as "conjecta" or things thrown together</note></term>, which they call syllables. When we have joined these, and from them constituted names and verbs, we shall again construct from names and verbs something large, beautiful, and whole. And just as the whole composite itself is called a "picture of a living being," so we shall call this entire fabric either "speech" <note>original: "orationem"</note> to be named by its skill, or "constructed rhetoric," or by whatever other art produces it.

Indeed, we ourselves shall not do this; for I have exceeded the proper limit in speaking. For the ancients established it so, if it was so established. But it behooves us, if we are to consider this artistically, to distinguish all these things—whether the primary names and the later ones are placed as is fitting or not. But we must see, my friend Hermogenes, whether there might be an error in connecting them otherwise.

**HERMOGENES:** Perhaps, by Jove, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Do you trust that you yourself can distinguish them so? For I distrust that I can.

**HERMOGENES:** Much more, then, do I distrust myself.

**SOCRATES:** Shall we then give it up? Or do you wish that we try as best we can? And if we are able to do but little of these things, let us attempt it; yet as we agreed before, and as we declared to them: that we, understanding nothing of the truth, merely guess at the opinions of men about them. So let us now proceed, declaring similarly to ourselves: that if these things were to be distinguished perfectly, either by someone else or by us, they certainly ought to have been distinguished thus. But now, as it goes, it will befit us to treat these things according to our strength. Do you admit this? Or what do you say?

**HERMOGENES:** I think exactly so.

**SOCRATES:** I think it will seem ridiculous, O Hermogenes, that things themselves are made manifest by imitation through letters and syllables. Yet it is necessary; for we have nothing better than this to which we may look to judge the truth of the primary names—unless perhaps, just as the Tragic poets, whenever they are in doubt, flee to the gods by means of certain invented machines. So we too might expedite the matter quickly by saying that the gods established the primary names, and therefore they were rightly instituted. Is this the best argument for us, or rather that we received them from certain barbarians? For the barbarians are more ancient than we. Or that because of their antiquity they cannot be discerned, just like barbarian words? These are evasions—and very clever ones—of those who do not wish to give an account of the correct imposition of the primary names. For whoever is ignorant of the correct reason for primary names cannot know the subsequent ones. Furthermore, these later ones must be explained from the former; but he is ignorant of those. Rather, it is necessary for one professing skill in subsequent names to have grasped the preceding ones much earlier and more perfectly, and to be able to demonstrate them. Otherwise, he should know that he will be talking nonsense in the subsequent ones. Or do you think otherwise?

**HERMOGENES:** Not otherwise, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** The things I have sensed regarding the primary names seem to me to be quite unusual and ridiculous; I will communicate them with you if you wish. If you find anything better, communicate it with me in turn.

**HERMOGENES:** I shall do so. But speak now with a brave heart.

**SOCRATES:** In the first place, the letter **r** <note>Greek: ρ (rho)</note> seems to be an instrument of all motion. But why motion is called *kinesis*, we have not said. It is clear, however, that it intends to be *iesis*, that is, "going." For we did not use the letter **eta** <note>ε</note> from a certain source, but we used **epsilon**. The beginning is from *kiein*, that is, "to go," which is a foreign word; and it signifies *ienai*, that is, "to go." Therefore, if its ancient name were found translated into our tongue, it would rightly be called *iesis*. But now, from the foreign name *kiein*, and by the change of its **eta** and the interpolation of **rho**, it is called *kinesis*. It ought to have been called *kieinesis* or *isis*. *Stasis*, that is, "standing still," intends to be the negation of *ienai* (to go), but for the sake of ornament it is named *stasis*.

The element **rho** itself seemed to the author of names to be a most suitable instrument of motion, as I was just saying, for expressing the likeness of movement; thus he uses it everywhere for the expression of motion. In the first place, in the words *rhein* and *rhoe*, that is, "to flow" and "a flow," the letter **rho** imitates the movement. Then in *tromos*, that is, "trembling," and *trachys*, "rough." Likewise in verbs of this sort: *krouein*, "to strike"; *thrauein*, "to wound"; *erykein*, "to drag"; *thryptein*, "to break or weaken"; *kermatizein*, "to cut into pieces"; *rhembein*, "to vacillate, provoke, and whirl around." In all these, he fashions the **rho** for the likeness of motion. For I omit that the tongue, in pronouncing this letter **rho**, does not linger at all, but is rather set in motion. Therefore, he seems to have used it primarily for the expression of these things.

He also used **i**, that is, *iota*, for thin things which most especially penetrate through all things. Therefore, *ienai* and *iesthai*, that is, "to go" and "to proceed," are imitated by **iota**. Just as **phi**, **psi**, **sigma**, and **zeta**, which are letters of more vehement breath, the author of names uses to express such things as: *psychron*, "cold"; *zeon*, "boiling"; *seiesthai*, "to be shaken"; and commonly *seismon*, "a concussion or quaking." Whenever the institutor of names wishes to imitate something vehement and full of breath, he employs such letters for the most part.

Furthermore, he seems to have thought the compression of **delta** and **tau**, and the retraction of the tongue as if it were sticking, to be very suitable for expressing the power of binding and of standing still. And because in pronouncing **lambda** the tongue especially slips forward, therefore because of this likeness he named *leia*, that is, "smooth things"; and *olisthanein*, "to slip"; and *kollodes*, "liquid/gluey"; *liparon*, "fat/oily"; and others of this sort. But because the **gamma** holds back the slipping tongue, by inserting it he formed *glischron*, "slippery/sticky"; *glyky*, "sweet"; *gloiodes*, "viscous/muddy." Noticing also that the sound of **nu** is held within the throat, he named *endon* and *entos*, that is, "that which is within" and "things which are internal," so that he might represent the things through the letters. He assigned **alpha** to *megalo*, that is, "to the great"; and **eta** to *mekei*, that is, "to length," because they are great letters. In the name *strongylon*, however, that is, "round," needing the letter **o**, he used **o** for the most part...

# BOOK

...first mixed. And by the same reasoning, the author of names seems to accommodate the rest according to letters and syllables to individual things, establishing a sign and a name: from these, he then establishes the remaining species through similarity. This reasoning regarding names seems correct to me, Hermogenes, unless Cratylus here brings forward something else.

**HERMOGENES.** Indeed, O Socrates, this Cratylus often disturbs me; as I said from the beginning, he asserts that there is a certain inherent correctness in the reasoning of names, but what it actually is, he does not explain; so that I cannot discern whether he is being obscure on purpose or not. Therefore, in your presence, O Cratylus, speak before Socrates: whether those things which Socrates proclaims about names please you, or whether you can bring forward something more excellent. If you can, bring it into the midst, so that you may either learn from Socrates or instruct us both.

**CRATYLUS.** Does it not seem to you, Hermogenes, to be easy to perceive and teach anything in so short a time, let alone so great a matter, which is esteemed among the greatest of the great?

**HERMOGENES.** Not to me, by Jove! On the contrary, I think Hesiod spoke wisely, that it is worth the effort to add a little to a little. <note>A reference to Hesiod's *Works and Days*: "If you add little to little and do it often, soon the little will become great."</note> Therefore, if you are able to accomplish even something small, do not be burdened; but help both Socrates here and me besides. For you ought to.

**SOCRATES.** Truly, Cratylus, I would assert none of those things which I mentioned above. To be sure, I have tracked this out with Hermogenes however it seemed fit. Therefore, if you have anything better, dare to express it, as I would gladly receive what you say. For I would not wonder if you had something more excellent than these things. Furthermore, you yourself seem to have considered such things and to have learned them from others. If, therefore, you say something superior, count me as one among your disciples concerning the correct reasoning of names.

**CRATYLUS.** Certainly, O Socrates, as you say, these things have been a care to me, and perhaps I might make you a disciple. I fear, however, lest the matter stands entirely to the contrary. It is fitting for me now to say the same to you as Achilles says to Ajax in the sacred rites <note>original: "in sacris" - likely referring to the Iliad as a venerable text</note>: "Noble Ajax, son of Telamon, prince of the people, you have spoken all things according to my own mind." <note>original: "omnia mea ex sententia protulisti" - quoting Iliad 9.644-645</note> So you too, O Socrates, seem to prophesy from our own mind; whether you have been inspired by Euthyphro, or whether some Muse long inherent in you has now suddenly stirred you.

**SOCRATES.** O good man Cratylus, I too have long wondered at my own wisdom, yet I do not trust it too much. Therefore, I think what I say must be examined. For to be deceived by oneself is the most grievous thing. It is an exceedingly dangerous matter when the seducer is never absent, but always accompanies the deceived most closely. It is necessary, therefore, to turn back frequently to what was said before and, as that poet says, to look "both before and behind." <note>A common Homeric expression for wisdom/foresight.</note> And so, let us see in the present what has been said by us. We said that the correct reasoning of a name is that which shows what the quality of each thing is. Do we assert that this has been sufficiently stated?

**CRATYLUS.** I certainly assert it.

**SOCRATES.** Names, therefore, are said for the sake of instruction?

**CRATYLUS.** Exactly.

**SOCRATES.** And do we not say that this is an art, and that there are practitioners of it?

**CRATYLUS.** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Who?

**CRATYLUS.** Those whom you called from the beginning the establishers of laws and names.

**SOCRATES.** Do we think this art exists in men similarly to other arts, or otherwise? This is what I mean: are some painters worse and some more excellent?

**CRATYLUS.** They are.

**SOCRATES.** Do not the more excellent ones make their works more beautiful—namely, the figures of animals—and the others the opposite? Builders also, similarly, make some houses more beautiful and some more ugly?

**CRATYLUS.** It is so.

**SOCRATES.** And do not the authors of laws themselves make some of their works more beautiful and some more ugly?

**CRATYLUS.** I no longer admit that.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, some laws do not seem better to you and others worse?

**CRATYLUS.** No.

**SOCRATES.** Nor, as it appears, do you think one name is better imposed and another worse?

**CRATYLUS.** Not that either.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, all names are correctly placed?

**CRATYLUS.** Whichever are indeed names.

**SOCRATES.** What about this name of Hermogenes, which was mentioned above? Should we say that this was not imposed on him, unless he happens to be of the "birth of Hermes"? <margin>Birth of Hermes.</margin> <note>original: "Hermu genesis" - Socrates is punning on the name Hermogenes, suggesting it implies being born from the god Hermes/Mercury.</note> Or was it indeed imposed, but not correctly?

**CRATYLUS.** I do not even think it was imposed, O Socrates, but only seems to be. Rather, it is the name of someone else, in whom the nature contained in the name exists.

**SOCRATES.** Does he not lie, whoever says he is Hermogenes? For it is not to be doubted that he says he is Hermogenes when he is not.

**CRATYLUS.** By what reasoning do you say that?

**SOCRATES.** Does your speech consist of and revolve around the idea that it is not possible to speak falsely? For many, O friend Cratylus, both now and in the past, have asserted this.

**CRATYLUS.** In what way, O Socrates, when someone says what he says, could he have said that which is not? Is this not speaking falsely: to say things which are not?

**SOCRATES.** This discourse is more elegant, friend, than my condition and age require. Nevertheless, tell me: does it seem to you that someone cannot speak falsely, but can utter it?

**CRATYLUS.** Not even utter it.

**SOCRATES.** And also neither say it, nor call it, nor greet it? Just as if someone meeting you by the right of hospitality, taking your hand, should say: "Greetings, Athenian guest, Hermogenes, son of Smicrion." Would he be speaking those things, or uttering them, or saying them, or greeting and calling you so—not you, but this Hermogenes, or no one?

**CRATYLUS.** It seems to me, O Socrates, that this man would be shouting these things in vain.

**SOCRATES.** I am satisfied. Does he who shouts thus shout true things or false things? Or partly true and partly false? For this also would be sufficient.

**CRATYLUS.** I would say this man makes a sound, moving himself in vain, as if someone were striking brass.

**SOCRATES.** Consider, Cratylus, whether we agree in any way. Do you not say that the name is one thing, and that which the name belongs to is another?

**CRATYLUS.** I do.

**SOCRATES.** And that a name is a certain imitation of the thing itself?

**CRATYLUS.** Most of all.

**SOCRATES.** And paintings are imitations of certain things in another way?

**CRATYLUS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Come now: perhaps I do not sufficiently understand what you say, but you perhaps speak correctly. Can we attribute both of these imitations—both paintings and names—to those things of which they are imitations, or not?

**CRATYLUS.** We can.

**SOCRATES.** Consider this first: could someone attribute the image of a man to a man, and of a woman to a woman, and in other things in the same way?

**CRATYLUS.** Certainly so.

**SOCRATES.** And what about the opposite: the image of a man to a woman, and of a woman to a man?

**CRATYLUS.** That too.

**SOCRATES.** Are both such distributions correct, or rather the one which attributes to each what is proper and similar?

**CRATYLUS.** The latter, it seems to me.

**SOCRATES.** Lest, therefore, you and I, since we are friends, in words...

# CRATYLUS, OR ON THE RIGHTNESS OF NAMES. PAGE 131.

<margin>r iii</margin>

let us struggle: pay attention to what I say. I call such a distribution in both imitations—in names as well as in paintings—"right," and in the case of names, not only right, but "true." But the other distribution, which is unlike the thing itself, I call "not right," and in the case of names, "false." 

CRATYLUS: But see, O Socrates, whether it might be that while in paintings one can distribute poorly, in names it is not possible at all; rather, it is necessary to always assign them rightly. 

SOCRATES: What are you saying? How does this differ from the other? Is it not possible that if someone meets a man, he might say, "this is your likeness," and show him perhaps the likeness of that man, or perhaps even that of a woman? By "showing," I mean offering it to the senses of the eyes. 

CRATYLUS: Certainly. 

SOCRATES: And again, if meeting the same man, could he not say, "this is your name"? For a name is a kind of imitation, just as a likeness is. I say it thus: will it not be permitted for him to say "this is your name," and then pour it into his ear, perhaps saying the imitation of him as a man, or perhaps saying the imitation of some human female, calling it a woman? Does it not seem to you that this can sometimes happen? 

CRATYLUS: I am willing to grant this to you, Socrates; let it be so. 

SOCRATES: You do well, my friend, for if this is the case, the controversy is now removed. Furthermore, if in these things a certain division occurs, we call one "speaking truly" and the other "speaking falsely." If this happens, and we are able to distribute names incorrectly—and not return to each what is its own—similarly it will be permitted to err in verbs. But if it is granted that verbs and names can be so assembled, it is necessary that sentences <note>original: "orationes"</note> be the same. For a sentence, as I think, is a composition of verbs and names. What do you say to these things, Cratylus? 

CRATYLUS: The same as you, for you seem to speak rightly. 

SOCRATES: Furthermore, if we refer the first names to the letters themselves by a certain imitation, it can happen in these just as in paintings: in which it happens that we apply all the fitting shapes and colors. And likewise, that we do not apply all of them, but add some and subtract others, and show more or fewer. Can this not happen? 

CRATYLUS: Without a doubt. 

SOCRATES: He who assigns all the fitting things renders beautiful letters and images. But he who adds or takes away also makes letters and images, but bad ones. 

CRATYLUS: Indeed. 

SOCRATES: But he who imitates the essence of things through letters and syllables: by the same reasoning, if he assigns all the competent things, does he not produce a beautiful image? And that is a name. But if he falls short or exceeds in a few things, an image will indeed be produced, but not a beautiful one. For which reason some names will be well-established, and others the opposite. 

CRATYLUS: Perhaps. 

SOCRATES: Perhaps, therefore, one will be a good craftsman of names, and another a bad one. 

CRATYLUS: Certainly. 

SOCRATES: And was not the name for this person a "setter of names"? <note>The Greek term is "nomothete" or lawgiver/name-giver.</note> 

CRATYLUS: Clearly. 

SOCRATES: Therefore, in this as in other arts, there will be one good setter of names and another not good, if only those previous points are agreed upon between us. 

CRATYLUS: These things are true. But you see, O Socrates, whenever we assign these letters alpha and beta and any of the elements to names through the art of grammar, if we take anything away, or add, or even change it: we write a name indeed, but not rightly; rather, we do not write it at all, but it immediately becomes something else as soon as it suffers any of these changes. 

SOCRATES: We must see, Cratylus, lest perhaps we consider it less rightly in this way. 

CRATYLUS: In what way? 

SOCRATES: Perhaps whatever must consist or not consist of a certain number is as you say: just as ten or any other number. For any number, if anything is added or taken away, immediately becomes another. But perhaps the logic of a quality or an image is not the same, but different. For an image ought not to have all the things that the thing of which it is an image has, if it is to be an image. Pay attention to whether I am saying anything. Would these be two things—namely, Cratylus and an image of him—if some god expressed your color and shape as painters do, but also made all the internal parts similar to yours: the same softness, color, motion, soul, and wisdom; and to embrace it briefly, fashioned all things exactly as they are in you? I ask, would one of those be Cratylus and the other an image of Cratylus? Or rather two twin Cratyluses? 

CRATYLUS: Two Cratyluses, Socrates, as I think. 

SOCRATES: Do you see, my friend, that another logic of the image must be sought than those we spoke of a little while ago? And that it should not be forced that if anything is added or taken away, it is no longer an image? Do you not perceive how much images lack, so that they do not have the same things as those of which they are images? 

CRATYLUS: I do indeed. 

SOCRATES: Something ridiculous would happen to the things of which they are names, Cratylus, if they were rendered entirely similar to them. For all things would become twins; and it could not be said which of them was which—the thing itself or the name. 

CRATYLUS: You speak the truth. 

SOCRATES: Therefore, noble man, confess frankly that one name is well-placed and another the opposite; and do not force it to contain all the letters, so that it is entirely such as that of which it is the name. But allow even a less fitting letter to be brought in sometimes; and if a letter, then a name similarly in speech; and if a name in speech, then a speech that is by no means fitting to the things may be assigned—and yet the thing itself is nonetheless named and spoken of as long as the "form" <note>original: "figura"</note> of the thing being discussed is present. Just as in the names of the elements which I and Hermogenes recounted recently, if you remember. 

CRATYLUS: I remember indeed. 

SOCRATES: By Hercules, it is well then! Whenever this is present, even if all the fitting parts are not present first, it will be said "well" when all are there, but "badly" when few are. Let us therefore stop saying this, O blessed one, lest like those who wander around Aegina at night and finish their journey late, we too seem to have arrived at the truth of things later than is proper; or at least seek some other right logic of the name, and do not confess that the declaration of a thing made by letters and syllables is a name. Furthermore, if you say both these things, you will not be able to be consistent or agree with yourself. 

CRATYLUS: You seem to me to speak rightly, Socrates, and I grant it so. 

SOCRATES: Since we agree on these things, let us discuss what remains. If a name ought to be well-placed, we said it is necessary that fitting letters be in it. 

CRATYLUS: Clearly. 

SOCRATES: And it is fitting that letters similar to the things be in it. 

CRATYLUS: Entirely. 

SOCRATES: Therefore, those which are rightly placed are placed thus. But if anything is not rightly placed...

<summary>Socrates argues against Cratylus's rigid view of names, explaining that a name is an "image" of a thing and does not need to be a perfect replica to function. He uses the analogy of a god creating a perfect double of Cratylus to show that a perfect imitation results in two identical things rather than an object and its name.</summary>

## PAGE XXIII.

It is established that a name consists mostly of appropriate and similar letters; if it is an image, it also contains something inappropriate, because of which it is not perfectly "right," nor is the name perfectly established. Do we say it is so, or otherwise? 

**CRATYLUS:** There is no need to contend, O Socrates, as I think; for it does not please me to say that a name exists, yet is not rightly assigned. 

**SOCRATES:** Does this not please you: that a name is a declaration of the thing itself? 

**CRATYLUS:** It pleases me. 

**SOCRATES:** But truly, do you not think it well said that some names are primary, and others are constituted from those primaries? 

**CRATYLUS:** Well said. 

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, if primary names must be declarations of certain things, do you have any more convenient way for that to happen than if they are made like the things we wish to declare? Or does that method please you more which Hermogenes and many others hand down: namely, that names are certain conventions <note>Latin: *conventiones*</note> among those who established them and foreknew the things themselves, referring to something; and that the right reasoning of a name consists in convention? And that it makes no difference whether someone decrees it as it is now established, or the opposite—so that, for instance, what is now called "small" <note>Latin: *parvum*</note> should be named "large" <note>Latin: *magnum*</note>, and what is now called "large" should be called "small"? Which of these two methods pleases you more?

**CRATYLUS:** It is altogether better, O Socrates, to represent by similarity what one wishes to show, than by any other way.

**SOCRATES:** You speak skillfully. If a name is similar to a thing, is it not necessary that the elements <note>The basic sounds or letters</note> from which the primary names are composed be similar by nature to the things themselves? I say it thus: could anyone have ever fashioned a painting (as we said above) similar to any object, unless the colors themselves of which the image consists were by nature similar to the thing which the painter’s study imitates? Is it not impossible?

**CRATYLUS:** Plainly impossible.

**SOCRATES:** By the same reasoning, names themselves would never become similar to anything, unless those things from which names are composed held some similarity to those things of which the names are imitations. Those things of which names consist are the elements.

**CRATYLUS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Now you be a participant in the speech which Hermogenes recently shared. Did we seem to you to speak rightly when we said that the letter *rho* [ρ] is suited to rushing, motion, and roughness?

**CRATYLUS:** Rightly to me, indeed.

**SOCRATES:** And the letter *lambda* [λ] to the smooth and soft and the others we recounted?

**CRATYLUS:** Assuredly.

**SOCRATES:** Do you know that for the same thing—that is, roughness itself—we call it *Sclerotes*, but the Eretrians call it *Scleroter*?

**CRATYLUS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Do both of these, the *rho* [ρ] and the *sigma* [σ], belong to the same family? And do they show the same thing to them by the *rho* at the end, as to us by the *sigma* at the end? Or does it make no difference to some of us?

**CRATYLUS:** They plainly demonstrate it to both.

**SOCRATES:** Is it insofar as *rho* and *sigma* are similar, or insofar as they are dissimilar?

**CRATYLUS:** Insofar as they are similar.

**SOCRATES:** Are they entirely similar for signifying motion equally? And what of the *lambda* [λ] inserted there: why does it not signify the opposite of that roughness?

**CRATYLUS:** Perhaps it was not rightly inserted, O Socrates; just as in those things you treated above with Hermogenes, when you were both taking away and adding letters where it was most appropriate. And you seemed to me to act rightly. And now perhaps *rho* [ρ] should be put in place of *lambda* [λ].

**SOCRATES:** You speak well. But what of this: as we speak now, do we perceive nothing between us when someone pronounces *Scleron* <note>Hard</note>? And do you not understand what I am saying now?

**CRATYLUS:** I understand it indeed, because of custom <note>Latin: *consuetudinem*</note>.

**SOCRATES:** O most charming man, when you say "custom," what else do you think you are saying besides "convention"? Or do you call custom something other than this: that when I pronounce this, I think of that, and you also perceive what I am thinking? Is this not what you say?

**CRATYLUS:** This very thing.

**SOCRATES:** If you recognize it when I pronounce it, a declaration is made to you by me; even though I utter it from something dissimilar to what you are thinking: since the *lambda* [λ] itself is dissimilar to that which you call *Sclerotera*—that is, roughness. If this is so, you certainly accustom yourself to it, and from this convention you propose a right reasoning of the name for yourself; since both dissimilar and similar letters represent the same thing to you because of the addition of custom and convention. But if custom and convention do not occur, it cannot yet be rightly said that similarity is the declaration; rather, one ought to say it is custom. Since custom declares from both similarity and dissimilarity. These things being granted by both, O Cratylus—for I shall take your silence as a concession—it is necessary to contribute something of custom and convention toward the exposition of what we feel and speak. For if you wish, best of men, to descend to the consideration of numbers, in what way do you hope you will find names so proper that you can attribute a similar name to every single number, if you do not permit convention and your concession to have some authority regarding the reasoning of names? To me, indeed, this also pleases: that names be as similar to things as possible. I fear, however, lest perhaps as Hermogenes said, the use of this similarity be somewhat thin; and we may be compelled to use this burdensome thing, namely convention, for the right reasoning of names. For then perhaps names would be spoken best according to our power, when we speak with entirely or mostly similar (that is, appropriate) elements; and most basely when the opposite. But after these things, tell me this in addition: what power do names have for us, and what beauty do we assert is achieved for us through them?

**CRATYLUS:** Names seem to me to teach, O Socrates; and it should be simply asserted that whoever knows the names also knows the things.

**SOCRATES:** Perhaps, O Cratylus, you are saying something like this: that when someone knows what the name is like—and it is such as the thing exists—he will also recognize the thing itself, since the thing is similar to the name. For the art of all things similar to one another is one and the same. Led by this reasoning, you seem to have said that whoever knows the names will also recognize the things themselves.

**CRATYLUS:** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES:** Come, let us see what this method of teaching things is which you now mention; and whether there is another besides it—though this one be held better—or no other besides this one. Which of these do you rather think?

**CRATYLUS:** This certainly: that there is plainly no other, but this one alone and the best.

**SOCRATES:** Do you also think that things themselves are discovered in such a way, that whoever finds the names also finds those things of which they are the names? Or should some other way rather be sought, and this other way be learned?

**CRATYLUS:** Most of all, according to those points, this very way should be both sought and found.

**SOCRATES:** Come, let us consider it thus, O Cratylus: if someone, while investigating things, follows the names themselves, and estimates what each one wants to be, do you see how great a danger of deception—

Entirely so. SOCRATES. If, therefore, he did not perceive correctly, and established them as he perceived them, do you not think that we, following in his footsteps, will be deceived? CRATYLUS. Let us see then, repeating some of those. In the beginning, this name *Episteme* <note>original: "Episteme", meaning knowledge</note>, that is, **knowledge**, is ambiguous, and seems rather to signify that it *estesi en* <note>original: "histesi en", meaning "stops in"</note>, that is, it **stops the soul** in things, rather than being carried around together with things; and it seems more correct that its beginning be as we say now, rather than through the insertion of the *e* [epsilon], and that we should rather add the *ei* [iota]. Next, *bebaion* <note>original: "bebaion"</note>, that is, **firm**, is so called because it is an imitation of *baseos* and *staseos* <note>original: "baseos & staseos"</note>, that is, of **foundation and standing**, rather than of motion. Furthermore, *historia* <note>original: "historia", inquiry/history</note> perhaps signifies that which *Histesi Rhun* <note>original: "histesi rhoun"</note>, that is, it **stops the flow**. And *Piston* <note>original: "piston"</note> itself, that is, **faithful/credible**, signifies altogether *histan* <note>original: "histan"</note>, that is, **to make firm**. Moreover, *Mneme* <note>original: "Mneme"</note>, that is, **memory**, shows clearly that there is no agitation in the soul, but *mone* <note>original: "mone"</note>, that is, **rest and stable remaining**. And if one observes the names themselves *hamartia* and *symphora* <note>original: "hamartia & symphora"</note>, that is, **error and misfortune**, they will seem to imply the same as *synesis* and *episteme* <note>original: "synesis & episteme"</note>, that is, **understanding and knowledge**, and other noble names imposed upon things. Likewise, *Hamathia* and *Acolasia* <note>original: "Hamathia & Acolasia"</note>, that is, **ignorance and intemperance**, seem close to these. *Hamathia* indeed seems to import *Hama Theo Iontos Porian* <note>original: "Hama Theo Iontos Poreian"</note>, that is, **the progress of one going together with God**. And *Acolasia* truly signifies altogether a certain *Acoluthia* <note>original: "Acolouthian"</note>, that is, **a following and meeting** of the things themselves. And so, those which we think are names of the most shameful things will seem almost identical to those names which concern the most beautiful things. I think many other things could be found, if one were to apply himself to these: from which he will again judge that the author of names did not indicate things as running and carried along, but rather as stable. CRATYLUS. Nevertheless, O Socrates, you see that he established many according to the signification of agitation. SOCRATES. What shall we do, O Cratylus? Shall we count the names themselves like the casting of votes? And shall we judge the right reason of names by this rule, so that those are finally true which the significations of the majority of names support? CRATYLUS. That would not be proper. SOCRATES. Certainly not, my friend. But leaving these things aside, let us return to where we digressed. You said recently, if you remember, that it was necessary for him who established names to have prior knowledge of those things to which he gave the names. Do you still persist in that opinion, or not? CRATYLUS. I still do. SOCRATES. Do you say that he who placed the first names also knew them while he was placing them? CRATYLUS. He knew them. SOCRATES. From what names had he either learned or discovered the things, when the first names had not yet been instituted? Since it has been said that it is impossible to find or learn things unless we have learned what the names are, or have found them ourselves. CRATYLUS. You seem to me, O Socrates, to be saying something. SOCRATES. In what way then shall we say they knew the names they placed? Or that the founders of laws and names existed before the placement of any name, and that they knew the things beforehand, if indeed things cannot be learned otherwise than from names? CRATYLUS. I think indeed, Socrates, that the truest account is that which says a certain power more excellent than the human provided the first names for things, whereby it is necessary that they were rightly distributed. SOCRATES. Do you think the author of names, if some Spirit or God existed, established things contrary to himself? Or do we seem to you to have said nothing above? CRATYLUS. Perhaps one of those sets of names were not yet names. SOCRATES. Which ones then were they, best of men? Those which tend toward stability? Or those rather toward motion? For as we just said, it will not be judged by the multitude. CRATYLUS. That is right, Socrates. SOCRATES. Since, therefore, names disagree and contend with one another concerning the truth, and both these and those assert themselves to be closer to the truth, by what rule shall we decide? Where shall we turn? For we shall not flee to other names, because there are none besides these. Truly, some other things besides names must be sought, which may show us without names which of these are true, namely by demonstrating the truth of the things themselves. CRATYLUS. So it seems to me. SOCRATES. If these things are true, Cratylus, it seems that things can be perceived without names. CRATYLUS. It appears so. SOCRATES. Through what other thing especially do you hope to perceive the things themselves? Is it not through what is consistent and proper? Through their mutual communion, namely in the way they are related to one another, and through themselves most of all. For that which is different from them signifies something else, not them. # THE ARGUMENT

to be understood, to judge this seems to be a work of a greater intellect than mine or yours. Let it suffice for now that we have agreed that things are not to be learned from their names; rather, they are to be learned and believed from the things themselves. CRA. So it appears, O Socrates. SO. Let us also consider this further: lest these many names tending toward the same point deceive us—since those who imposed them thought that all things are always running and flowing, and they established them with that consideration. Indeed, it seems to me they thought so; however, if such an opinion existed, it must be held as false. Truly, they, as if fallen into a certain vertigo, are themselves wavering and tossed about, and dragging us along, they plunge us into the same. Consider, wonderful Cratylus, what I often dream: whether we must say there is something that is "the Beautiful itself" and "the Good itself," and so for each of the things that exist, or not? CRA. To me at least, O Socrates, it seems to be so. SO. Let us therefore consider that thing itself: not if a certain face or something of such a kind is beautiful—for all these things flow—but do we say the Beautiful itself does not always remain such as it is? CRA. It is necessary. SO. Is it possible to name it correctly if it always escapes? And first to say what it is, then of what kind it is? Or is it necessary, while we are speaking, that it immediately becomes something else and constantly flees away, and is no longer such? CRA. Necessary. SO. In what way will that thing be something, which never stays in the same state? For if it ever stays in the same state, in that time it is not changed at all; but if it always stays in the same state and exists as the same, how does it pass away or move, since it does not depart from its own form <note>original: "idea"</note>? CRA. In no way. SO. Furthermore, it would be known by no one. For while the power of knowing approached it, it would become something else and foreign; wherefore what it becomes or of what kind it is could not be known. For no knowledge perceives a thing in such a way that it perceives it as being in no certain state. CRA. It is as you say. SO. But neither must it be affirmed that knowledge itself exists, O Cratylus, if all things fall away and nothing remains. For if knowledge, from the fact that it is knowledge, does not fall away, it will always remain, and there will always be knowledge; but if the very form <note>original: "species"</note> of knowledge departs, it will simultaneously fall into another form of knowledge, and it will not be knowledge. But if it perpetually migrates, there will never be knowledge. And by this reasoning, neither that which is to know nor that which is to be known will ever exist. But if there is always that which knows, and there is that which is known, and there is the Beautiful, and there is the Good, and finally there is each of the existing things which we are currently discussing, they do not seem similar to a flux or a current. Whether these things are so, or as the followers of Heraclitus <note>A Greek philosopher famous for the idea that "everything flows" (Panta Rhei).</note> and many others say, cannot easily be discerned. Nor is it the part of a man of sound mind to entrust himself and his soul to names, and to assert that the author of names is wise, and thus to think ill of himself and all things—as if he thinks nothing exists whole and firm, but all things flow and collapse like earthenware; and just as men sick with rheum <note>original: "destillationibus capitis" - a cold or catarrh</note> of the head, he judges that things themselves are similarly affected, so that all things are gripped by dripping and flux. Perhaps, O Cratylus, it is so; perhaps also it is otherwise; the matter must be investigated with a brave mind and diligent study. For one must not easily assent. You are still young, and your age is sufficient. And if you find anything by searching, you ought to share it with me as well. CRA. I will do my best, Socrates. And know for certain that even now I am not idle; rather, to me as I think and revolve many things in my mind, it seems much more as you were saying than as Heraclitus says. SO. Then, my friend, teach me after you return. But now, as you have decided, go into the field. And Hermogenes here will accompany you. CRA. It shall be as you advise, Socrates. But you also, think now on these things.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for the Gorgias.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'V' containing a scene of a figure (possibly a scholar or saint) seated at a desk or lectern within an architectural setting.</image-desc>

Since there are two most powerful things in the soul, knowledge <note>original: "cognitio"</note> and affection <note>original: "affectus" - emotion or disposition</note>: the sophists indeed twist knowledge toward falsehood under the appearance of truth, while the popular poets often plunge affection into discordant disturbances under the bait of harmonious pleasure. Finally, the popular orators both deceive knowledge with false conjectures and stir affection into various movements. Therefore, lest their works force the minds of men to be sick, both with false opinions and with ruinous affections, Plato—the physician of human souls—leads us far away from the sophists entirely, and also from the orators and poets in a certain way. Indeed, he exterminates the sophists everywhere and all of them. But the poets he does not remove entirely, but only those who either invent shameful things about the gods or who too sharply imitate and report disturbed souls. Nor does he remove them from everywhere, but from the city—that is, from the crowd of youth and the ignorant, which was very prone to disturbances and does not penetrate the allegorical sense of the poets. For which reason, in the books on the Republic, he orders the poets either to be expelled or to be forced to speak honorably of God; nor should they accustom the listeners to disturbances, but rather sing divine hymns and gravely recount the laws of the fathers and the deeds of great men. But to return to the orators, Plato does not blame all of them either, but only those who apply themselves constantly to persuading the listeners of whatever they please, by whatever means they can, without choice—whether it be evil or good, whether the reasoning be false or true, whether by pity, or incitement, or conjecture. Such had been the purpose of Lysias the Theban, and Tisias, and also Gorgias of Leontini. He prefers Pericles in the *Phaedrus* and Isocrates to others, because he joined eloquence with philosophy. And he adds that the legitimate orator ought to understand the reasons of things, the laws of morals, the powers of words, the natures of dispositions, and to compose words by a certain certain reason accommodated to the minds of the listeners as far as possible, for the sake of persuading them of the common good; nor should he apply himself so much to making what he says pleasing to men as to making it acceptable to God. But he who, in the manner of Tisias and Gorgias, follows not truth itself and justice, but only the conjecture of the crowd—what is likely and probable—he detests as a man harmful to the state above others, as if eloquence without wisdom were a sharp sword in the hands of a madman. Two, however, he attacks above others: Lysias indeed in the *Phaedrus*; here

# ON THE GORGIAS. FOLIO 133.

Indeed, concerning Gorgias: for the greater their authority was, the more dangerous they were. Here, Polus the orator, a follower of Gorgias, is brought into the midst, as well as Callicles, their supporter. Socrates, however, first acts through Chaerephon, his close friend, and does so against Polus. Then he himself, on his own behalf, acts against Gorgias. Since these men were accustomed to boast in a wonderful manner before the people when assigning reasons for other things, he shows—in order to strip them of all credibility—that they do not know how to provide the reasons for their own profession. Polus asks him what the art of Gorgias is; whereas he ought to have defined it only through necessary terms and explained what it *is*, he instead described it through superfluous terms and what *sort* of thing it is. He did this, moreover, in an excessively affected style, which Socrates confirms was his custom in the *Phaedrus* <note>A reference to Plato's dialogue *Phaedrus*, which discusses the styles of various orators.</note> where he treats the styles of orators. Then Gorgias himself is questioned as to what his art is; with a certain inept boastfulness, he replies that it is rhetoric. Next, Socrates asks him to define what rhetoric is.

We ought to remember that any given thing, in that which it is, partly agrees with other things and partly differs. That by which it agrees is called the *genus* <note>The general category or family of a concept.</note>; that by which it disagrees is called the *difference*. Thus it happens that a definition, which encompasses the very thing that a matter is, ought to be assigned through a genus of this kind and a difference. Gorgias, therefore, as one who does not know how to define his own art, puts forward its genus, and does so ineptly. As for the difference, which he ought to have brought forward immediately in the same response along with the genus, he is finally compelled to bring it into the open with difficulty after many questions, with Socrates extorting it from him.

At the beginning, he replies that rhetoric is an art concerning speeches. And since there are others that are similar, Socrates asks: concerning what or what kind of speeches? This is so that he may discern in what matter it differs from other arts. He replies: concerning speeches which provide the power of speaking. Again, this is common to other arts. Whence he is forced again to add that rhetoric is occupied mostly with speeches, even unto the point of speaking <note>original: "usque dicendi"</note>. But since that too is common to many, Socrates urges him again to add "concerning speeches," namely, "concerning the greatest matters." When even that is found to be common, he is compelled to bring forward something more distinct: namely, that through the oratory we achieve the state of serving no one, but ruling over others; and that the oratorical art is the creator of persuasion according to one's will.

Meanwhile, Socrates warns that in a dispute we should not direct our attention so much to the person with whom we dispute, but to the speech itself and the soul. Then, since every art persuades concerning some matter, it is asked concerning what matter and of what kind the rhetorician's persuasion is. Soon, persuasion is divided into two types: namely, into that which produces knowledge, and into that which produces belief. It is concluded that oratorical persuasion does not bring knowledge, but belief; not properly concerning just anything, but concerning the just and the unjust; not everywhere, but especially in a crowd, and concerning matters which chiefly pertain to the republic.

It is further added that the orator can speak more persuasively than the craftsmen themselves even about matters properly pertaining to other arts—not, indeed, among those skilled in the arts themselves, but among the unskilled. Amidst these things, we are warned never to abuse power and art. Likewise, we are warned not to be disturbed in a dispute where tranquility is necessary for perceiving the truth. Again, we should receive refutation with an even and most willing mind, especially in the correction of morals. For nothing is worse than to hold false opinions concerning morals.

After this, Gorgias concedes that it does not pertain to the orator to know the nature of things themselves, but to devise a certain machinery for persuasion so that he himself, though ignorant, may nevertheless appear to understand more among the ignorant than those who actually know. He claims it is his duty to speak strenuously about anything in a crowd, not by teaching, but by persuading. He also concedes that an orator ought to and can know what is likely <note>The "verisimile" or "probable," as opposed to the absolute truth.</note>, even if he does not know what is true. This, indeed, can in no way happen. For unless you know the thing itself, you will never recognize what is similar to it.

Accordingly, it is asked whether, just as it does not concern the orator to know other things, it also does not concern him to understand what is good, honorable, and just. Gorgias, although he had said elsewhere that the orator stands in the same relation to these things as to others, here contradicts himself and agrees that he ought at least to know these. From this, Socrates argues: if the orator knows just things, therefore he is just. He is clearly testing Gorgias to see if he grasps the force of the consequence. Gorgias admits it immediately. While in the sciences and arts pertaining to the intellect it follows that "he knows astrology or carpentry, therefore he is an astrologer or a carpenter," in those things pertaining to the will and morals it does not follow that "he knows just things, therefore he is just." For justice requires the will.

Nevertheless, if someone were to have a certain divine knowledge of justice—which Plato maintains can sometimes happen by the breathing of God—the consequence would rightly follow. For whoever knows most certainly how great a good justice is, or how great a reward awaits it, and conversely how great an evil is in injustice, or how great a punishment is owed to it, he would without doubt embrace justice while fleeing injustice. But however matters may stand, Gorgias is forced to contradict himself; for whereas in the earlier parts he conceded that an orator could sometimes be unjust, here he denies it.

After this, Socrates, using a certain irony prompted by the arrogance of Polus, both disapproves of younger men if they ever arrogantly rebuke their elders, and instructs everyone to easily allow themselves to be corrected by anyone. Furthermore, so that what follows may be clearly understood, it must be noted that oratory can be considered either in its general nature or in its specific types. In its general nature, it is defined as an industry most ready for persuading in civil matters, both by a certain faculty of proof and, most especially, by the grace of eloquence. Therefore, it is established in a certain way between the art of discourse and poetry. Thus far, oratory is a good for the intellect, but for the will it is neither good nor evil. Of this, however, there are two species: the philosophical and the popular (or flattering). The former is good, but the latter is evil. The end of the former is to lead the listeners to the common good through certain reasons of things, words, and morals. This he praises most highly in the *Phaedrus*, as being composed of philosophy and the weightier kind of poetry.

<summary>This page provides a commentary on the opening of Plato's Gorgias, detailing Socrates' interrogation of Gorgias and Polus regarding the definition of rhetoric. It explores the distinction between knowledge and belief, and the moral implications of the orator's art.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introductory argument (Argumentum) for Plato's dialogue "Gorgias," likely translated or commented upon by a Renaissance humanist such as Marsilio Ficino. It establishes the structural analogies between the health of the body and the health of the soul.</meta>

# ARGUMENT

<margin>v 2</margin>

The other end <note>referring to the goal of rhetoric</note>, however, is to obtain whatever one pleases through conjectures likely to sway the crowd and through the agitation of souls. This we place between **sophistry** and **common poetry**, as a mixture of both; it is this which is detested in this dialogue. He divides the arts that specifically care for man himself into two primary kinds. The first of these cares for the **soul**, the second for the **body**. In the soul, he says there is a **legislative faculty**, the founder of laws and moderator of morals, which forms and stabilizes the soul itself in a certain habit agreeable to nature; and the **judicial art**, which restores the soul if it should happen to fall from this state. In the body, he likewise places twin arts, similarly the caretakers of the body: **gymnastics**, which, as the mistress of exercising the body, confirms it in a good habit according to its strength; and **medicine**, which restores lost health to the body. Therefore, as the legislative is to the soul, such is gymnastics seen to be to the body. Likewise, as the judicial is to the soul, such is medicine to the body. All these he calls **arts**, because they lead to the good by a certain reason.

He adds a certain nature or skill: **flattery**, which is servile and deceitful, and which falsely emulates these four. Through **sophistry**, it simulates the legislative; through **oratory** (that is, the common kind), it feigns the judicial; through **adornment** <note>original: "fucatoria," the art of cosmetics or dyeing</note>, it puts on the appearance of gymnastics; through **cookery**, it represents the physician. He denies that this whole genus of flattery is an art, because it does not strive for the true good by certain reason, but for favor through allurements. But lest anyone think that **Plato**, the most eloquent of all by far, compares legitimate eloquence to cookery, let him read the *Phaedrus*, in which he both approves of it and most subtly hands down its end, duty, and precepts, asserting that it is similar to medicine.

Since **Polus**, extolling the power of oratory, says that orators have the greatest power because they are able, at their whim, to condemn adversaries to prison and death, or to despoil them of goods, or deprive them of their city, **Socrates** proves by two principal arguments that the unjust are not powerful. First, because the power of all things is desired by everyone as a good; it is certain that the license to do whatever one pleases is not only not good for unjust men (who are as if captured in mind), but evil and ultimately ruinous. Second, that the greatest power is to be able to effect that very thing which you wish. It is clear, however, that all people wish for the **true good**. But the wicked never act upon or attain the true good. Add to this that a wicked mind, by the very fact that it is wicked, is judged to be discordant within itself and insane, already overcome by those things which the senses bring in. Who then would say that a mind both languid and serving its own slaves like a bondman is powerful?

Meanwhile, all human things are distinguished into three: namely, into **good**, **evil**, and **intermediate**. The first of the goods is **wisdom**. The second is the desirable condition of the body. The third is the convenience of fortune. But these latter two are judged good only insofar as they provide a convenient ministry to the mind. Their opposites are called evils; but the intermediates between these are as if indifferent, which incline no more to good than to evil, such as walking, sitting, and the like. He adds that no one wants either evils or intermediates, or those things which he specifically does; rather, he wants only the goods, and those things for the sake of which he is moved and acts. Therefore, those who do injuries do not want the injuries themselves, but the good for the sake of which they do them. But they do not attain the good; therefore, they do not achieve what they want. Therefore, they are not powerful.

Next, Socrates, having found an occasion from the error of Polus (common to many), hands down holy precepts to us:
* He to whom it is permitted to sin gravely is wretched.
* He who already sins gravely is wretched.
* He who does not pay the penalty for his sin is more wretched.
* To suffer injuries is to be chosen rather than to inflict them.

The license to do whatever one pleases is not power, unless it is ultimately to our advantage. It will be to the advantage only of those using it justly. The unjust, even if they should possess the unholy power of the whole world, are unhappy—indeed, most unhappy. For the more one is permitted to sin and the less punishment is given for the sin, the more unhappy they are held to be. **Happiness** consists in wisdom and justice; **unhappiness** in their contraries.

Since Polus places the judgment of truth in a multitude of any witnesses (which ought instead to be referred to the quality of the judge rather than the number of those judging), Socrates responds that the best mode of proof is if you bring forth a single witness in the cause: namely, the adversary convicted by reason; otherwise, a multitude of witnesses heaped together from everywhere is of little moment for the truth. Furthermore, because Polus says that to do an injury is more shameful, but to suffer one is worse, Socrates argues against this, asserting that in human affairs and morals, the same thing is good and beautiful (or honorable), and likewise the same thing is evil and shameful. Then, he thinks that the "beautiful" is esteemed either because of pleasure or utility, or both; the "shameful" is the opposite. From here he argues: if doing an injury is more shameful than suffering one, it is not because it is more painful, but because it is more damaging; if so, it is therefore judged to be worse.

Soon he adds that one ought to commit oneself to reason to be cured, as if to a physician. He also affirms that the just punishment of sinners profits the one who is punished most greatly. For if this is just, it is therefore beautiful and honorable. If so, it is therefore good. If it is good, it benefits the soul: namely, as medicine to the body, and much more so, for it frees the soul from disease, which is the gravest of all diseases and evils. Among these things, note the opinion of **theologians**: that nothing is more necessary or useful for sinners than to confess sins, to be affected by penitence, to seek punishment from a judge, and to bear it with an even mind, so that the soul may be purged before its disease becomes incurable.

After these things, you will hear that it is very easy for us to signify our affection to one who labors under a similar affection. Likewise, that Socrates, captured by the love of **philosophy**, always obeys her. Furthermore, that it is to be chosen rather than that all other things should be dissonant to us, that the soul should be dissonant within itself. Accordingly, where **Callicles** reproaches Socrates as if he were too studious of subtleties, understand that under the person of Socrates, the **Sophists** are being refuted by Plato. Afterward, Callicles touches upon the profane opinion of **Thrasymachus** and many others, saying that morals and laws consist not in the order of nature, but only in the opinion or fiction of men. This is confuted in the books on the *Republic* and in those following. As for what Callicles seems to bring against the philosophers, understand these things are said not against legitimate philosophers, but partly against the most idle of the sophists, and partly against those who [study philosophy...]

<summary>This page outlines the philosophical arguments of Plato's Gorgias, specifically the analogies between the health of the body (medicine/gymnastics) and the soul (justice/legislation), while refuting the idea that unjust power leads to happiness.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Plato, Polus, Callicles, Thrasymachus, sophistry, rhetoric, justice, medicine, gymnastics, flattery, ethics, punishment, soul vs body</keywords>

--- Page 286 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato's dialogue "Gorgias," specifically focusing on the debate between Socrates and Callicles regarding the nature of justice, the definition of power, and the pursuit of pleasure versus virtue.</meta>

# ON THE GORGIAS.

## Page 134.

They abuse [philosophy]: either when they pursue logic alone in such a way that they abandon other parts of speculation, or when they embrace speculation alone so that they neglect the philosophical precepts of morals and civil institutions. Indeed, some things in the speech of Callicles are said to be false, which will be refuted in what follows. After this, however, [Socrates] teaches that all diligence must be applied in the examination and testing of our soul: and for that purpose, one judge should be chosen in whom there is wisdom regarding the matter itself being discussed, benevolence by which he may counsel you, and furthermore, boldness <note>original: "audacia"</note> through which he does not fear to express what he thinks will be beneficial. Next, Socrates warns us that since we are rational by nature, we should not live by irrational chance and fortune: but we should most diligently prescribe a certain end for our life and choose the more convenient ways toward it. Finally, while he repeatedly beseeches Callicles to refute him freely and boldly, he warns us that nothing ought to be sought more earnestly than the medicine of the soul.

These things being done, Callicles concedes that by nature the more powerful, the stronger, and the better are the same thing: and he says that natural justice wills that those who are more powerful should have more than those who are inferior, and should rule over them; and that the law of the more powerful is naturally just. To this, Socrates replies as follows: If the more powerful, the stronger, and the better are the same, and the multitude is stronger than one individual, then the multitude is also more powerful and better. Therefore, since the laws of the multitude are those of the more powerful and better, they will be naturally just. But the laws of the multitude decree that it is just for equality to be preserved among all, and that it is more shameful to inflict an injury than to suffer one. Wherefore, it is not only by law that it is more shameful to do wrong than to suffer it—and just to preserve equity, as Callicles had said earlier—but also by nature itself.

Furthermore, because Callicles had previously thought those to be more powerful who surpassed others in cunning, boldness, and violence, Socrates gradually corrects him: he forces him to admit that the more powerful person is the one who is more prudent and brave in governing the state. He also signifies during this that he always brings forward the same arguments about the same things: thereby proving constancy and disapproving of levity. Now he attempts to lead Callicles beyond prudence and fortitude to temperance <term>temperantia: self-control or moderation</term> as well. But here, just as he had previously erred regarding justice and power by imitating Thrasymachus <note>A sophist in Plato's Republic who argued "might makes right."</note>, so now he errs similarly regarding temperance by following Aristippus <note>A philosopher who taught that pleasure is the highest good.</note>: calling temperance the stupid idleness of a slavish mind, and asserting that virtue and happiness consist in fostering and satisfying the lusts of the senses.

Socrates, however, soon prepares himself to demonstrate that temperance consists not in human opinion, but in the order of nature. Indeed, natural order requires that the lower parts of the soul obey the superior parts: and the whole soul should be harmonious in every respect, healthy and beautiful; nor should it act in vain, but should attain the proposed end, which is the condition of a temperate life. On the contrary, in an intemperate man, reason—the queen of man—serves as a slave to concupiscence <note>original: "concupiscentiæ"; intense desire or lust</note>: it is also discordant and languid; it undertakes an inexhaustible task and follows fleeting pleasure with incomparable distress. Socrates explains all of this through the opinions of the Pythagoreans, especially those of Philolaus and Empedocles, chiefly in two ways: namely, through a fable and an example. In these, consider that the soul in this body is entirely dead; moreover, the intemperate soul is assigned to the underworld, miserably agitated by useless and constant labor, while it continually schemes with a certain "leaky jar" <note>A famous Platonic metaphor for the insatiable nature of desire.</note>—that is, in a depraved and deceptive judgment. The other leaky jar—namely, inexhaustible concupiscence—it tries to fill with waves of delights.

After this, because Callicles placed not only virtue but also happiness in the constant satisfaction of lusts, and affirms that pleasure is the same as the Good itself, and pain the same as Evil, Socrates refutes this with several reasons. **First:** it is established that pleasure is not the Good itself, since it is often most shameful and is present in the most shameful men. **Second:** Good and Evil, being contraries, cannot be in the same thing at the same time. But pleasure and pain are in the same person at the same time: namely, when someone who is thirsty drinks. For then the distress of thirst concurs with the pleasure of drinking. **Third:** Good and Evil, as other contraries are wont to do, do not depart from the same thing at the same time. But pleasure and pain do depart from the same thing at the same time: since at the same moment while one drinks, one ceases both to thirst and to be delighted by drinking. **Fourth:** everyone becomes good by the presence of good, and bad by the presence of evil. But men do not become good by the presence of pleasure—rather they become dissolute—nor do upright men become bad through pain. Indeed, since the good and the bad often rejoice or grieve equally—and sometimes the bad rejoice more and the good grieve more—certainly if pleasure were the Good and pain were Evil, it would follow that frequently both the good and the bad would be equally good or bad; and sometimes the good would be more "bad" than the bad themselves, and vice versa.

Among these things, note the precept of Socrates to be observed: namely, that one must not hasten to the most serious matters unless one has first attained the lighter ones. Then some points are asserted from which one could confirm that pleasure is not the Good in itself: because many pleasures are found to be bad—namely, harmful to both the soul and the body—diverting us from the best things; whereas if pleasure were the Good in itself, no pleasure would be bad. Accordingly, the faculties are distinguished again: those which, like arts, proceed toward the good and the useful by a certain reason; and those which, like flatteries, seek only pleasure without any regard for the true good—among which number he places poetry, music, and common oratory.

But you, during the discussion, note this sentiment: that the virtue and health of the body consist in a certain order and arrangement; and similarly, the virtue and health of the soul consist in its own order and arrangement. From which it follows: that just as the virtue and vice of the body are found not in opinion, but in the thing itself—either agreeable to or opposed to nature—so the virtue and vice of the soul are to be judged not by human opinion, but by the law of nature. He concludes at last: that as much as it is naturally better to have a healthy body than a sick one, it is similarly better to possess a temperate soul than an intemperate one. Furthermore, the Pythagorean sentiment is confirmed in what follows: that in all things, temperance is the best of all, which indeed is the first of all...

<summary>This page outlines Socrates' refutation of Callicles' hedonism, arguing that true power lies in self-control (temperance) rather than the pursuit of pleasure, and that the soul's health depends on natural order rather than human opinion.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Callicles, temperance, justice, nature, pleasure vs. good, Pythagorean philosophy, Philolaus, Empedocles, ethics, soul's health</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the "Argumentum" or summary introduction to a Platonic dialogue, likely the Gorgias, given the focus on rhetoric, justice, and the myth of the afterlife. It establishes the philosophical framework for the text that follows.</meta>

# ARGUMENT

<note>This section outlines the core moral philosophy of the text, focusing on self-control as the foundation of all virtue.</note>

Self-control <note>original: *temperantia*</note> must be handed down to young men, so that through it the intemperance of youth may be corrected and the entire soul tempered; for it is believed that the other virtues soon follow. Indeed, the man who is temperate toward God and men acts with propriety: he is pious, just, and brave. Next, it concludes that happiness lies in virtue alone, and misery in wickedness alone, and that all human affairs should be referred to virtue as if to a most certain target. Furthermore, just as virtue is necessary for happiness, so too the correction and punishment of vices is necessary, acting as a medicine for the diseases of the soul. Finally, the intemperate man can be a friend neither to men, nor to God, nor to himself.

To show us the natural excellence of temperance, the author adds—following the mind of the Pythagoreans and Orphics—that the universe is held together by temperance, and even by concord and justice, which are contained within temperance itself. Therefore, as Pythagoras also says, intemperance in all things must be fled with all one's might as a most ruinous thing. Since equality pertains especially to both temperance and justice, he teaches that equality should be observed above all, asserting that it has the greatest power among both gods and men.

I speak of **geometric equality**, through which an equal distribution is made to each person according to their capacity and merits. Equal, I say, meaning neither more nor less than what capacity or merit is judged to require. Geometric equality consists in a certain fitting proportion. **Arithmetic equality**, however, consists in an equal number on both sides. These two are not the same. Truly, the excess of six over four, and likewise the excess of four over two, is equal to a mathematician considering numbers, for each exceeds the other by two. But to a geometer, who judges proportion, it is unequal. For the number six exceeds four by a "sesquialter" proportion <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1</note>, in which the larger number contains the smaller once plus its half. But four exceeds two by a double proportion. He says that all things are preserved by the kind of equality that does not merely give the same weight to one as to another like a counter of numbers, but in the manner of a measurer, gives to each exactly what is fitting. In this is contained both the justice of God in His works and the justice of man toward men. In both cases, distribution is made according to the measure of each person's capacity and merit.

Having said these things, he asserts that the theological foundations of morals are confirmed by the firmest reasons: especially that it is worse to commit an injury than to suffer one; and worst of all, if you have committed an injury, not to pay the penalties, which act as medicines to free the soul from the greatest disease of all: injustice. No greater harm can be imagined than that which is brought upon the soul by vice; so much so that just as it is not profitable for a man to live with a completely diseased body, so it is not profitable to live with a soul sick with vices. Likewise, life in the body is not to be highly valued, but rather virtue; and it is worse to make oneself similar to disgraceful men because of a similarity of character than to be killed by them.

Amidst these things, he warns that we should not attempt to handle matters of which we are ignorant, especially the more serious public ones. He holds oratory in very low esteem if it can bring no health to the soul, either privately or publicly, but only looks after the body and things pertaining to it. He mocks those who, when they held the rudders of the state, always increased the city with external goods but neglected to form the souls of the citizens with temperance and justice. This alone is the duty of a legitimate governor. He concludes that governors who look to the goods of fortune rather than the goods of the soul not only do not benefit the city but harm it greatly. Furthermore, all the power and wisdom of a man consist in keeping his soul unstained by sins against God and men. For the loss of this life is the lightest thing, but the loss of eternal salvation is the gravest.

Furthermore, so that you may understand what Plato affirms regarding the future rewards of virtues or punishments of vices: know that **Saturn**, in Plato, is understood as the supreme intelligence, in which resides the universal law and providence of all things concerning the essences, lives, and order of forms. Subject to him are three principal orders of deities, in which Saturnian providence is distributed into three main offices. Those deities who specifically assist in distributing essences are called by the common name of **Jupiter**. Those who contribute to providing lives are called **Neptune**. Those who arrange the orders of forms are called **Pluto**. **Prometheus** represents a grade of deities somewhat lower than these, who distributes the formal order of nature only to rational beings, especially in this life. Finally, the three sons of Jupiter—the judges of Asia, Europe, and Africa—are to be understood as three deities serving Jupiter and Pluto, so that the formal order of justice may be fulfilled in souls separated from their bodies.

Note here that divine law washes away the erasable stains of vice by punishing them at certain times. But it afflicts the unerasable stains with everlasting punishments. This indeed seems to disapprove of the eternal transmigration of souls through bodies. As for his saying that the judges once erred in judging the living, it signifies two things to us. First, that human judgment regarding virtues and vices is deceived, while divine judgment is not. Second, that divine providence foresaw within itself that judgments would be false if the living were judged by the living in this body. Therefore, not from a certain point in time (as the words sound), but from eternity, it was decreed that judgment should take place after this life. Meanwhile, remember that the soul carries with it the dispositions and habits of men and virtues. Finally, Socrates affirms these things deeply, fearing nothing else except such damage to the soul and the sight of the divine judgment. Therefore, he concludes that we must strive more fiercely in this contest than in any other, so that we may offer a most pure soul to the judge who inspects all things. All other things that men admire are to be utterly despised; and only those things are to be honored which contribute to the eternal salvation of the soul.

<summary>This page provides a philosophical summary of the moral and metaphysical themes in a Platonic dialogue, emphasizing that self-control and justice are essential for the soul's health and eternal salvation. It explains the difference between arithmetic and geometric equality and interprets the mythological figures of Saturn, Jupiter, and Pluto as allegories for divine providence and judgment.</summary>

<keywords>temperance, justice, geometric equality, arithmetic equality, Plato, Saturn, Jupiter, Neptune, Pluto, Socrates, soul, divine judgment, virtue, vice, afterlife</keywords>
