<meta>This page begins the translation of Plato's "Gorgias," a foundational philosophical dialogue regarding the nature of rhetoric (the art of persuasion). The scene is set in Athens, where Socrates and his friend Chaerepho arrive just after the famous sophist Gorgias has finished a public demonstration.</meta>

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC.
### CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE.
### CALLICLES, SOCRATES, CHAEREPHO, GORGIAS, POLUS.

<margin>The occasion of the dialogue.</margin>
<margin>Proverb: We have come too late, after the feast.</margin>
**CALLICLES.** This, Socrates, is how they say one should come to war and battle <note>original: "Sic ad bellum & pugnam... accedendum." Callicles is joking that Socrates has arrived late for the intellectual "battle."</note>. **SOCRATES.** Have we then come "after the feast," as the saying goes, being too slow? **CALLICLES.** And a very elegant feast it was, too; for Gorgias has just now displayed many wonderful things to us. **SOCRATES.** The cause of this lateness, Callicles, was Chaerepho here, who compelled us to linger in the marketplace. **CHAEREPHO.** That shall be no hindrance, Socrates; for I will also provide the remedy. Gorgias is a friend of mine. Therefore, whether you wish it now or at another time, he will demonstrate these same things for us. **CALLICLES.** What, Chaerepho? Does Socrates desire to hear Gorgias? **CHAEREPHO.** It was for that very purpose we were present. **CALLICLES.** Whenever it pleases you to come into my house—for Gorgias is staying with me—he will reveal it to you. **SOCRATES.** You speak well, Callicles. But would he be willing to converse with us at present? For I desire to inquire of him what the power of his art is, and what it is that he professes and teaches. As for the exposition of other matters, let him bring that to us at another time, as you suggest. **CALLICLES.** The questioning will not be troublesome, Socrates; for that was also part of his demonstration. Just now he invited everyone present to ask whatever they wished, and he professed that he would answer everything. **SOCRATES.** You tell of a truly excellent thing. Therefore, Chaerepho, question him. **CHAEREPHO.** What should I ask? **SOCRATES.** Who he is. **CHAEREPHO.** How do you mean? **SOCRATES.** Just as if he were a maker of shoes, he would surely answer that he is a shoemaker. Do you not yet understand what I mean? **CHAEREPHO.** I understand indeed, and I will ask him now. Tell me, Gorgias: is it true what Callicles says, that you profess to answer all things that anyone might ask? **GORGIAS.** He speaks the truth, Chaerepho. Indeed, I was just now proclaiming that very thing; and I say that for many years no one has asked me anything new. **CHAEREPHO.** Then you answer with great ease, Gorgias. **GORGIAS.** You may make a trial of this very thing, Chaerepho. **POLUS.** By Zeus, you may! <note>original: "per Iovem"</note> But try it with me instead, if you please, Chaerepho; for Gorgias seems to me to be exhausted from speaking, having just discussed many things. **CHAEREPHO.** What, Polus? Do you think you will answer better than Gorgias? **POLUS.** What does it matter, provided it is sufficient for you? **CHAEREPHO.** Nothing; but since you wish it, answer. **POLUS.** Ask. **CHAEREPHO.** I ask then: if Gorgias possessed the art which his brother Herodicus has, what would we rightly call him? Would it not be the same as his brother? **POLUS.** Certainly. **CHAEREPHO.** Then by calling him a physician, we would call him rightly? **POLUS.** Yes. **CHAEREPHO.** But if he had knowledge of the art of Aristophon, son of Aglaophon, or his brother, what would we rightly name him? **POLUS.** Surely a painter. **CHAEREPHO.** But now, since Gorgias is skilled in some art, what should we rightly call him?

<margin>Gorgias professed that he would answer any question whatsoever.</margin>
<margin>Art follows skill; chance follows lack of skill.</margin>
**POLUS.** O Chaerepho, there are many arts among men discovered through experience. For experience causes our life to proceed by art, but lack of experience causes it to wander by chance. Of these individual arts, different men participate in different ways; the best men participate in the best arts. Gorgias is of their number, being endowed with the most beautiful art. **SOCRATES.** Truly, Gorgias, Polus seems well-prepared for making speeches <note>original: "adorandum paratus," likely a reference to Polus's flowery, rhetorical style</note>. However, he is not keeping what he promised to Chaerepho. **GORGIAS.** Why not, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** He does not seem to me to have answered the question at all. **GORGIAS.** Then you ask him again, if you wish. **SOCRATES.** If you were willing to answer me yourself, Gorgias, I would much rather ask you than Polus. For it is clear that Polus, from what he just answered, has devoted more effort to the art of rhetoric than to the art of discussion <note>original: "disserendi arti," referring to dialectic or logical inquiry</note>. **POLUS.** Why do you say that, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Because when Chaerepho asked what art Gorgias was skilled in, you praised his art, Polus, as if someone had criticized it; but you did not answer what that art actually is. **POLUS.** Did I not answer that it was the most beautiful? **SOCRATES.** Indeed you did. But no one was asking what the quality of Gorgias's art is, but rather what the art is, and what Gorgias ought to be called—just as Chaerepho was instructing you before, and you answered him briefly. Now, therefore, tell us in the same way: what is the art, and what are we to call Gorgias? Or rather, Gorgias, you show us yourself what it is right to name you, and of what art you are a master. **GORGIAS.** Rhetoric, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Then we ought to call you a rhetorician? **GORGIAS.** And a good one, too, if you wish to name me what I profess to be—as Homer says. **SOCRATES.** I do wish it. **GORGIAS.** Then name me so. **SOCRATES.** And shall we say that you are able to make others rhetoricians as well? **GORGIAS.** I profess this not only among you, but indeed among all people. **SOCRATES.** But would you be willing, Gorgias, to finish the dispute as we have begun—partly by questioning and partly by answering—and reserve that long-windedness of words which Polus started for another time? Keep your promise to me, and be willing to answer the questions as briefly as possible. **GORGIAS.** There are some answers, Socrates, which must necessarily be made with longer words. Nevertheless, I will attempt to answer as briefly as possible. For this is one of the things I profess: that no one can explain the same things in fewer words than I. **SOCRATES.** This brevity is exactly what I need, Gorgias. I pray you, demonstrate this to me; reserve the abundance of words for another time. **GORGIAS.** I shall do so, so that you will say you have never heard anyone more brief. **SOCRATES.** Come then. You say you have the knowledge of the art of rhetoric, and can make others rhetoricians. Now, rhetoric itself is concerned with something, just as weaving is concerned with the making of garments. Is it not so? **GORGIAS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** And is not music concerned with the perfection of melody? **GORGIAS.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** By Zeus, Gorgias, these answers of yours delight me, for you finish them in the briefest way. **GORGIAS.** I hope, Socrates, to satisfy your wish in this. **SOCRATES.** You speak rightly. Come then, and answer me similarly about rhetoric: of what things is it the knowledge? **GORGIAS.** Of speeches. **SOCRATES.** Of what kind of speeches, Gorgias? Is it of those which show by what rule of living the sick may recover? **GORGIAS.** No. **SOCRATES.** Then rhetoric is not concerned with all speeches. **GORGIAS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, it is concerned with those speeches which...

<margin>Music is concerned with the perfection of melody.</margin>
<margin>The first definition is bad.</margin>

GORGIAS: Because, O Socrates, the entire knowledge of the other arts is concerned with manual tasks and actions of that kind, so to speak; but of rhetoric, there is no such manual work; rather, its entire action and power consists in speaking. Furthermore, if he should ask what I call the art of calculation, I will answer that this too is numbered among those arts which fulfill everything with words. And if he should demand what it is concerned with, I will answer in the manner of those who write decrees for the people: namely, that calculation is in other respects the same as arithmetic—for both are concerned with the same thing, the even and the odd—but they differ in this: that calculation considers the even and the odd in terms of what quantity they produce in sum, both in themselves and in relation to each other. Moreover, if I were to place astronomy in that genus of arts which are completed entirely by words, and someone asked again what the words of astronomy tend toward most, I would reply: toward the motion of the stars, the sun, and the moon, and how their courses relate to one another. And if I were to ask him who he is, he would perhaps say he is a physician. "What do you say then? Is the work of your art the greatest good?" "Why not?" he would answer, "since such work is health, and nothing is happier than health." After this, perhaps the physical trainer would say he wondered greatly if you could show more good in your art than he in his. And if I asked: "And who are you? What is your work?" You certainly know that these dockyards and the walls of Athens, and the layout of the harbors, were constructed partly by the counsel of Themistocles and partly by Pericles, and not by the advice of the craftsmen. **SOCRATES:** They say these things, O Gorgias, regarding Themistocles. As for Pericles, I myself heard him when he was persuading the city concerning the construction of the middle wall. **GORGIAS:** Furthermore, whenever there is a deliberation concerning those things you just mentioned, you see that the orators themselves give counsel, and it is their opinions that prevail in these matters. **SOCRATES:** It is because I marvel at this, O Gorgias, that I have been asking you for some time now about the power of rhetoric. Indeed, to me, as I consider it, the magnitude of its power seems like something divine. **GORGIAS:** Oh, if only you knew everything, Socrates! You would see that it embraces within itself, to put it briefly, almost all powers. I will give you a great proof of this. Often I have gone with my brother <note>Gorgias' brother was Herodicus, a famous physician.</note> and other doctors to the bedside of some sick person who either refused to drink a medicine or would not permit the doctor to cut or cauterize him. When the doctor was unable to persuade him, I persuaded him by no other faculty than that of rhetoric. I assert, moreover, that if a rhetorician and a doctor were to enter any city and had to compete in words before the assembly or any other gathering as to which of them should be chosen as the doctor, the doctor would appear nowhere <note>i.e., he would be ignored</note>; instead, the man skilled in speaking would be chosen, if he so wished. In the same way, if a rhetorician were to compete against any other craftsman, he would ensure that he himself was chosen rather than any other person whatsoever. For there is nothing about which a rhetorician cannot speak before a crowd with greater persuasion than any craftsman. Such and so great is the power of this art. However, Socrates, one ought to use rhetoric in the same way as any other competitive skill. For if someone has learned to fight with fists or limbs and weapons so that he can overcome both friends and enemies, he should not, because of this, fight against everyone equally, so as to strike, pierce, or kill even his friends. Nor, by Jove, if someone who has exercised in the wrestling school as a boxer comes out with a robust body and then strikes his parents or some other relative or friend, should we for that reason hate the physical trainers and those who teach fighting with weapons and expel them from the cities. For they handed down these skills so that those learning them might use them against enemies and those committing injustice—using them for defense, clearly, not for aggression. But some people pervert these things and abuse their strength and art. Yet it is not because of this that those who taught them should be judged wicked, nor is the art to be blamed or held as evil; rather, in my judgment, it is those who use it perversely. The same logic applies to rhetoric. For an orator is able to speak against everyone and about any matter, so that he can very easily be superior in persuading a multitude about anything. But if someone, having acquired rhetoric, then uses the power of this art unjustly, it is not right to hate the one who taught him and expel him from the city. For he handed it over for a just use, but the other uses it for the opposite. Therefore, it is right to hate, exile, and put to death the one who does not use it correctly, but not the teacher.

<margin>The character of Socrates in debate.</margin>
**SOCRATES:** I believe, Gorgias, that you have been present at many debates, and you have observed this in them: that those who debate with one another cannot easily, once they have begun to discuss, depart having defined the matter itself so that they have only taught and learned from one another. Instead, if they disagree about something, and one does not concede to the other that he is speaking either truly or clearly, they become indignant and think the other speaks out of envy, striving for victory rather than seeking what was proposed for inquiry. Sometimes they finally depart so disgracefully, with mutual insults and curses, that those listening even regret that they thought such men were worth hearing. Why do I say this? Because you do not seem to me now to be saying things entirely consistent or harmonious with what you said earlier about rhetoric. Yet I fear to refute you, lest you think I am striving not to clarify the matter, but for the sake of defeating you. If, therefore, you are of the same number as I am, I will gladly inquire into the matter with you; if not, I would let it go. If you ask what sort of man I am, I will answer: one of those who gladly suffers himself to be refuted if he says anything untrue, and who gladly refutes another if they say anything untrue—and for whom it is no less pleasing to be corrected than to correct. For I consider it to be a greater good, insofar as it is a greater good to be freed from the greatest evil oneself than to free others. For I believe there is no evil so great for men as a false opinion <note>original: "opinio falsa"</note> regarding those matters which are the subject of our present discourse. If, therefore, you also say you are such a man, let us debate; but if you think we should stop, let us stop now and break up the gathering.

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC.

Is rhetoric then of such a nature that it is not the business of the rhetorician to know how things actually are, but rather to devise a certain <term>machination</term> <note>original: "machinationem"; here meaning a clever method or trick</note> for persuasion, so that among the ignorant he appears to know more than those who truly possess knowledge?

**GORGIAS.** Is this not a great convenience, Socrates? That those who have never learned other arts, but this one alone, are nevertheless in no way inferior to the others?

**SOCRATES.** Whether the orator is inferior or not inferior to others because of this single faculty, we shall inquire a little later if it seems to contribute anything to the discussion. But now, let us first consider this: regarding the just and the unjust, the honorable and the shameful, the good and the evil, does the orator stand in the same relation as he does toward health and the other matters belonging to the other arts? That is to say, is he ignorant of what is good or evil, beautiful or ugly, just or unjust, but devises a kind of persuasion about such things so that, being ignorant himself among the ignorant, he appears to know more than those who know? Or is it perhaps necessary that he knows these things? And is it required that he comes to you, the future orator, with this knowledge already acquired? And if he does not bring the knowledge of such things with him, will you, as a teacher of rhetoric, not teach him such things? For it is not your duty to teach these. Yet you will make it so that he appears to the common people to know such things when he does not, and appears to be good when he is not at all. Or will you be entirely unable to teach him rhetoric unless he has first attained the truth of these matters? Or how do these things stand, Gorgias? By Jove, I pray you, as you began a little while ago, reveal to us the power of rhetoric.

**GORGIAS.** Indeed, Socrates, I think that if someone happens to be ignorant of these things, he will also learn them from me.

**SOCRATES.** Stop there. For you speak rightly: if you are to make someone a rhetorician, he must know just and unjust things, either before he comes to you or by learning them from you afterward.

**GORGIAS.** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES.** What then? Is not he who has learned the things pertaining to building a builder?

**GORGIAS.** He is.

**SOCRATES.** And he who has learned music, a musician?

**GORGIAS.** Yes.

**SOCRATES.** And he who has learned the things pertaining to medicine, a physician? And in other matters in the same way: whoever has learned something becomes such a person as the knowledge of each subject makes him?

**GORGIAS.** Entirely.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, by this reasoning, will not he be just who has learned just things?

**GORGIAS.** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES.** And the just man does just things.

**GORGIAS.** It is so.

**SOCRATES.** Is it not therefore necessary for the rhetorician to be just? And for the just man to wish to act justly?

**GORGIAS.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, the just man will never wish to do an injury.

**GORGIAS.** Never.

**SOCRATES.** And the rhetorician must be just, according to the preceding reasoning.

**GORGIAS.** It is necessary.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, the rhetorician will never wish to do an injury.

**GORGIAS.** Never, as it appears.

**SOCRATES.** Remember that you said a little while ago that one ought not to accuse or expel the gymnastics teachers if a boxer makes bad use of his boxing skill and inflicts an injury; and in the same way, if an orator uses rhetoric unjustly, it is not the teacher who should be accused and expelled, but the one acting unjustly and not using rhetoric rightly. Were these things said, or not?

**GORGIAS.** They were said.

**SOCRATES.** But now, this same orator appears as one who would never do an injury.

**GORGIAS.** Never.

**SOCRATES.** And yet, Gorgias, it was said in the earlier parts that rhetoric is concerned with speeches, not about the even and the odd, but about the just and the unjust.

**GORGIAS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** I therefore, when you said these things, thought that rhetoric was never an unjust thing, since it always spoke about justice. But when you said a little later that if an orator used rhetoric unjustly—I was immediately astonished, and thinking that what was being said by you was not consistent, I brought forth those words: that if you thought it would be beneficial to be refuted, as I think, it would be worthwhile to discourse; otherwise, to let it go. Then, as we considered it, as is not hidden from you, it was conceded that it is impossible for a rhetorician to use rhetoric unjustly or to wish to do an injury. To discern how these things stand, Gorgias, by the dog <note>A common Socratic oath: "By the dog of Egypt"</note>, no small diligence is needed.

**POLUS.** What is this, Socrates? Do you actually hold such an opinion of rhetoric as you now say? Or do you rather think that Gorgias, led by a certain shame, conceded to you that the rhetorician knows just, honorable, and good things, and that if someone comes to him ignorant of these, he would teach them? From which concession, perhaps, something contradictory followed in the dispute. You catch at this too eagerly, Socrates, leading him to such answers by your questioning. For who do you think would have denied to you that he knows just things and will teach others? Truly, it is a great rudeness to lead one to these things by questioning.

**SOCRATES.** O most beautiful Polus, for this very reason we acquire friends and sons: so that if ever we stumble in our old age, you younger men being present may correct our lives in both words and deeds. And now, if anything has deceived me and Gorgias in our disputation, you being present, amend it. For so you ought; and I promise you: that if you think any of those things which were conceded were not rightly conceded, you may change it at your discretion, provided you avoid one thing for me.

**POLUS.** What is this, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** That prolixity <note>Long-windedness or excessive wordiness</note>, Polus, which you were beginning from the very start of the dispute.

**POLUS.** What? Shall I not be allowed to speak as much as I wish?

**SOCRATES.** You would be treated with a very heavy injury indeed, Polus, if having come to Athens, where there is the greatest freedom of speech in all of Greece, you alone in this place should not have the power of speaking according to your will. But consider the opposite: namely, if while you were speaking at length and were unwilling to answer the questions, it were not permitted for me to go away and not listen to you; would I not also suffer heavy things if I were not allowed to leave and refuse to hear you? But if you have any care for this dispute and wish to correct it: as I was just saying, retracting what seems to you to be retracted, and asking and answering in turn, as I and Gorgias did, refute me and allow yourself to be refuted. Or do you say that you also know what Gorgias professes to know?

**POLUS.** I do indeed.

**SOCRATES.** And do you bid that anyone ask of you what they wish, as from a man who knows how to answer?

**POLUS.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** Now then, do either one at your discretion: either ask or answer.

**POLUS.** I shall do so; and answer me, Socrates: since Gorgias does not satisfy you regarding rhetoric, what do you say it is?

**SOCRATES.** Do you ask what art I think it is?

**POLUS.** That very thing.

**SOCRATES.** None at all, Polus, to tell you the truth.

**POLUS.** What then does rhetoric seem to be to you?

**SOCRATES.** A thing which you say created art in that book which I recently read.

**POLUS.** What do you mean?

**SOCRATES.** A certain <term>knack</term> <note>original: "peritiam"; an experiential skill or "knack" rather than a systematic art (techne)</note>.

**POLUS.** Does rhetoric then seem to be a knack to you?

**SOCRATES.** To me, indeed; unless you say otherwise.

**POLUS.** A knack of what thing?

**SOCRATES.** Of producing a certain grace and pleasure.

<margin>
Rhetoric is no art.
Rhetoric is a knack for producing a certain grace and pleasure.
</margin>

Have you already heard what I say it is, that you next ask whether I think it is beautiful? POLUS: Did I not hear you saying it was a certain kind of skill? SOCRATES: Since you value favor so highly, are you willing to gratify me a little? POLUS: I am willing. SOCRATES: Ask me now what kind of art I consider cookery to be. POLUS: Behold, I ask: what kind of art is cookery? SOCRATES: None at all. POLUS: But what is it then? SOCRATES: I say it is a certain kind of skill. POLUS: What kind of skill? SOCRATES: Of producing gratification and pleasure. POLUS: Are cookery and rhetoric the same thing then? SOCRATES: By no means; but they are parts of the same pursuit. POLUS: Of what pursuit? SOCRATES: I fear it may be too harsh to speak the truth for Gorgias's sake, lest he think I am disparaging his own pursuit. Whether the rhetoric that Gorgias practices is this, I do not know; for from this discussion nothing has been made clear to us as to what he himself thinks. But what I call rhetoric is a part of a certain thing that is not at all honorable. GORGIAS: What is it, O Socrates? Come, speak; do not be afraid on my account. SOCRATES: It seems to me, O Gorgias, to be a certain pursuit, not scientific <note>original: "artificioſum" - Socrates distinguishes between a true 'ars' (systematic knowledge) and a mere 'peritia' (knack or experience)</note> indeed, but belonging to a shrewd mind, naturally powerful at winning over human society. I call its sum and substance flattery. Of this pursuit, many parts seem to me to exist. One indeed is cookery; which, although it seems to be an art, is in my judgment not an art, but a skill discovered by practice. Furthermore, I say that rhetoric is also a part of this same thing, as is beautification <note>original: "fucatoria" - the art of using dyes or makeup to create a false appearance of health</note>—which is called the trade of the panderer—and sophistry. These four parts, certainly, pertain to four things. If therefore Polus wishes to ask, let him ask. For he has not yet heard what part of flattery I say rhetoric is, nor has he noticed that I have not yet answered that. And so he asks whether I consider it beautiful or not. But I will not answer whether I think rhetoric is something beautiful or base until I have revealed what it is itself. For it is not fitting to answer otherwise, O Polus. Therefore, if you wish to hear, ask what part of flattery I say rhetoric is. POLUS: I ask you now, what kind of part? SOCRATES: Will you understand my answer? For rhetoric is, in my opinion, a shadow-image <note>original: "simulacrum" - a deceptive imitation or phantom</note> of a part of politics. POLUS: What then? Do you say it is something beautiful or base? SOCRATES: Base. For I call bad things base, since I must answer you as if you already knew what I am saying. GORGIAS: By Jove, O Socrates, I do not even understand what you are saying. SOCRATES: And not without reason, Gorgias, for I have not yet expressed it clearly enough. But this Polus is young. GORGIAS: But leave him aside; answer me indeed in what way you say rhetoric is a shadow-image of a part of politics. SOCRATES: I will try to express what rhetoric seems to me to be. If it is not that, Polus here will refute it. Do you call something "body" and something "soul"? GORGIAS: Why not? SOCRATES: And do you not think there is a certain good condition for each of these? GORGIAS: I certainly think so. SOCRATES: Furthermore, can a condition appear to be good when it is not at all? I mean something of this sort: many people seem to have a well-affected body, whose bad health and condition no one would easily detect except a physician or a master of gymnastics. GORGIAS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: I say there is something of such a kind in both the body and the soul, which indeed makes both the body and the soul seem to be well when they are not well. GORGIAS: It is so. SOCRATES: Come then, let me see if I can show this more clearly. Since there are two things, I think there are twin arts: and the art pertaining to the soul, I call "politics"; but that which pertains to the body, I cannot name with one name, but of this one art which cares for the body, I pose two parts: one indeed is gymnastics, the other medicine. In politics, I place "nomothetic" (that is, the legislative) corresponding to gymnastics; and "justice" (that is, the judicial) corresponding in a certain way to medicine. They communicate with each other, since they are about the same thing—medicine and gymnastics, and again the judicial and the legislative. Nevertheless, they also differ among themselves. Since these are four, and always care for what is best—these for the body, those for the soul—the faculty of flattery, sensing this (not knowing it indeed, but guessing), divides itself fourfold. It creeps under each of the parts, pretending to be that which it has gone under; and it has no care for what is best, but always catches the unwary mind with what is sweetest, as if with a hook; and it deceives to such an extent that it seems most highly esteemed. Cookery, creeping under medicine, pretends to provide the best foods for the body. Wherefore, if it were necessary for a cook and a physician to contend before children, or men as foolish as children, as to which of them understands more about good or bad foods, the physician would die of hunger. This, therefore, I call flattery; and I consider it something base, O Polus. I say the same against you. Because it hunts for pleasure without any regard for what is best. Nor do I say it is an art, but a certain skill; because it has no rational account of the things it offers, as to what their nature is; whence it follows that it can offer no reason. But I do not call that an "art" which lacks reason. But if you doubt these things, I promise to give you a reason. Thus, as I said, cookery-flattery creeps under medicine; and similarly beautification under gymnastics—a harmful, deceptive, ignoble, and illiberal thing, deceiving with shapes, colors, lines, and a certain sense, so that by following an extrinsic dye <note>original: "fucum" - also meaning a pretense or sham</note> we neglect the proper and true form which comes through gymnastics. But lest I be too long-winded, I wish to speak to you in the manner of a geometer; for thus perhaps you will follow. Surely, what beautification is to gymnastics, cookery is to medicine. Or rather thus: what beautification is to gymnastics, sophistry is to the legislative. Again, what cookery is to medicine, rhetoric is to the judicial. Nevertheless, as I was saying, they are distinguished by nature; and yet, being near, they are mixed together in the same place and about the same things—namely, sophists and rhetoricians; nor do they look to any utility which they might follow for themselves or for others. For if the soul did not rule the body but the body ruled itself, and if cookery and medicine were not perceived and discerned by the soul, but the body itself weighed these things by its own grace and pleasure, that saying of Anaxagoras would surely happen, friend Polus (for you have skill in these things): all things would be mixed together indiscriminately—both what pertains to medicine and health, and what pertains to cookery. You have heard now what I say rhetoric is: namely, a thing corresponding to cookery.

<margin>
Cookery, rhetoric, beautification, and sophistry are parts of an unscientific pursuit, the head and sum of which is flattery.
</margin>

<margin>
Rhetoric is a shadow-image of a part of politics.
</margin>

<margin>
That which lacks reason is not an art. Every art is with reason.
</margin>

<margin>
FLATTERIES CREEP UNDER THE ARTS.
Cookery [under] Medicine.
Beautification [under] Gymnastics.
Sophistry [under] Legislative.
Rhetoric [under] Judicial.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates defines rhetoric not as a true art, but as a form of flattery and a "shadow-image" of justice, comparing it to how cookery mimics medicine by offering pleasure instead of health.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Polus from the previous folio. Socrates is in the midst of dismantling Polus's admiration for the "power" of rhetoricians and tyrants.</meta>

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC

...natural [power] in the soul, just as there is in the body. But perhaps I have behaved rather rudely: while I forbid you from being long-winded, I have stretched out a long speech myself. Nevertheless, I deserve some pardon: for if I had spoken more briefly, you would not have understood at all, nor would my answer have satisfied you; instead, you would have required a further explanation. Therefore, if I am unable to follow you when you answer, you too may extend your speech. But if I can follow, then permit me to use your answer or my own at my discretion. For that is only just. And now, if you can make use of this answer in any opportune way, do so.

**POLUS:** What are you saying then? Does rhetoric seem to be flattery to you?

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, I said it was a *part* of flattery. Do you not remember this, Polus, at your age? What might you do hereafter? <note>Socrates is teasing Polus for his youthful forgetfulness or lack of focus.</note>

**POLUS:** Do good rhetoricians seem to you to be looked down upon in the city in the same way as flatterers?

**SOCRATES:** Are you asking a question, or are you starting some oration?

**POLUS:** I am asking a question.

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, O Polus, they seem to me to have no standing at all.

**POLUS:** How can you say "none"? Do they not have the greatest power in cities?

**SOCRATES:** Not at all—if you say that power is something *good* for the one who possesses it.

**POLUS:** I certainly say so.

**SOCRATES:** Then rhetoricians seem to me to have the least power of all in the state.

**POLUS:** What are you saying? Do they not, like tyrants, kill whom they wish, and strip them of their inheritance, and drive them out of the city?

**SOCRATES:** By the dog <note>original: "Per canem" - Socrates's famous idiosyncratic oath</note>, O Polus, I am in doubt regarding every single thing you say, whether you are explaining your own opinion or asking for mine.

**POLUS:** I am asking for yours.

**SOCRATES:** Very well, my friend. Then you are asking me two questions at once.

**POLUS:** How two?

**SOCRATES:** Did you not just say that rhetoricians and tyrants kill whomever they wish, and strip them of their goods, and send them into exile?

**POLUS:** Indeed I did.

**SOCRATES:** I tell you then, these are two separate questions, and I shall answer both. I assert, Polus, that both rhetoricians and tyrants have the least power in cities, just as I was saying a moment ago. For they do nothing, so to speak, of what they *will*; yet they do what seems best to them in their own opinion.

**POLUS:** Is this not great power?

**SOCRATES:** Not according to Polus.

**POLUS:** Am I not saying it is? I certainly say so.

**SOCRATES:** By Jove <note>original: "Per Iovem" - translating the Greek "By Zeus"</note>, you are not saying it; since you said that great power is a *good* for the one who has it.

**POLUS:** I do say that.

**SOCRATES:** Do you then say it is a good thing if someone does what seems best to him while he is out of his mind? And do you call that "great power"?

**POLUS:** Certainly not.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, must you not show that rhetoricians possess a mind <note>meaning "reason" or "intellect"</note>, and that rhetoric is not flattery but an art <term>art: "ars" (Greek: techne), a systematic skill based on knowledge</term>, in order to convict me? Otherwise, unless you show this, you will not have refuted me: rhetoricians and tyrants who do whatever seems best to them in the city will gain no good from it. If indeed having power is a good thing, as you say, but doing whatever one sees fit without a mind, you yourself confess to be an evil. Is it not so?

**POLUS:** It is certainly so.

**SOCRATES:** How then can rhetoricians or tyrants be powerful in the state, unless Socrates is convinced by Polus that they do what they *will*?

**POLUS:** Look at this man!

**SOCRATES:** I deny that they do what they will; you, however, must refute me.

**POLUS:** Did you not just confess a moment ago that they do what seems good to them?

**SOCRATES:** And now I confess it again.

**POLUS:** Do they not, therefore, do what they will?

**SOCRATES:** Not as I judge it.

**POLUS:** But they do what seems best to them?

**SOCRATES:** I grant that.

**POLUS:** You say troublesome and incredible things, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Do not accuse me, fair Polus—to address you in your own style <note>A pun on Polus's name, which sounds like the Greek word for "colt" or "fine".</note>. But if you have something to inquire, refute my error; if not, answer me.

**POLUS:** But I prefer to answer, so that I may understand what you are saying.

**SOCRATES:** Does it seem to you then that men will <note>i.e., "desire" or "intend"</note> the thing they do in every instance, or rather that thing for the sake of which they do what they do? For example, those who drink medicines given by doctors: does it seem to you that they will the thing they are doing—namely, drinking the medicine and suffering its bitterness—or rather the health for the sake of which they drink it?

**POLUS:** It is manifest that they will to be made healthy, for which sake they take the potion.

**SOCRATES:** And is it not the same for those who sail the seas, or engage in other business for the sake of profit? They do not will what they are doing—for who would want to sail, undergo dangers, and have troubles?—but they will that for the sake of which they sail: namely, riches. For they sail for the sake of these.

**POLUS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not the same in all things? Whenever someone does something for the sake of another thing, he does not will the thing he does, but the thing for the sake of which he does it?

**POLUS:** So it seems.

<margin>
Whoever does something for the sake of another thing: he does not will the thing he does, but that for the sake of which he does it. A negative disjunctive is placed: so that it may be asked of something that perhaps is not in the disjunctive.
</margin>

**SOCRATES:** Is there anything among all things that is not either good, or evil, or intermediate between these—that is, neither good nor evil?

**POLUS:** Nothing at all.

**SOCRATES:** Do you not call wisdom, health, riches, and other things of that kind "good"? and their opposites "evil"?

**POLUS:** Indeed.

**SOCRATES:** And those things which are neither good nor evil, do you mean things such as those which sometimes participate in the good, sometimes in the evil, and sometimes in neither? Such as sitting, walking, running, or sailing. Or again, like stones, wood, and other similar things. Do you not say there are such things, which you call neither good nor evil?

**POLUS:** Certainly such things.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, do they do these intermediate things for the sake of the good whenever they do them? Or do they do the good for the sake of the intermediate?

**POLUS:** The intermediate for the sake of the good.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, pursuing the good, we walk when we walk, thinking it is better to do so; and conversely, we rest whenever we rest for the sake of that same good. Is it not so?

**POLUS:** Exactly so.

**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, if we kill anyone, we kill for that same sake; similarly, we expel people and seize property, thinking it is better for us to do such things.

**POLUS:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, they do all these things, whatever they do, for the sake of the good.

**POLUS:** I agree.

**SOCRATES:** And did we not agree that we do not "will" the things we do for the sake of something else, but rather that thing for the sake of which we do them?

**POLUS:** Most certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we do not simply and absolutely will to slaughter, nor to expel, nor to seize money; rather, if these things are beneficial, we will to do them; if they are harmful, we do not will them. For we will good things, as you say. But those things which are neither good nor evil, we do not properly will, nor do we will the evil. Do I seem to you, Polus, to speak the truth or not? Why do you not answer?

**POLUS:** The truth.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, if we agree on these things, if someone kills another, or casts him out of the city, or deprives him of his inheritance—whether he be a tyrant or a rhetorician—thinking it will be better for him when it is actually worse, he is surely doing what seems best to him, is he not?

**POLUS:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** But is he also doing what he *wills*, if these things happen to be evil? Why do you not answer?

**POLUS:** It does not seem to me that he is doing what he wills.

**SOCRATES:** By what reasoning then does such a man have great power in the state, if indeed great power is a good thing, as you yourself confess?

**POLUS:** By no means.

**SOCRATES:** Then I was speaking the truth: that it is possible for a man to do what seems best to him in the city, and yet not have great power...

<summary>Socrates argues that tyrants and rhetoricians lack true power because they do what "seems best" rather than what they actually "will" (which is always the Good). He distinguishes between intermediate actions and the ultimate goals for which those actions are performed.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Polus, rhetoric, power, the Good, will vs. opinion, tyranny, ethics, intermediate actions</keywords>

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC.
### Folio 139.
#### Signature s iii

<margin>One who acts unjustly cannot be happy.</margin>
than Archelaus? SOCRATES: Even from the very beginning of our discussion, Polus, I praised you because you seemed well-instructed in the art of oratory, though I said you had neglected the art of dialectic <note>The art of logical investigation through dialogue.</note>. And now, is this the reasoning by which even a child, as you yourself said, could refute me? For I have been convicted by you, as you judge, in this present argument, because I said that one who acts unjustly cannot be happy? Why is that, my good man? For I do not agree with a single thing you say. POLUS: That is because you do not *wish* to agree, even though the truth is apparent to you. SOCRATES: My dear friend, you are attempting to refute me in the manner of an orator. This is what usually happens in the law courts, where people think they are refuting one another when they produce many reputable witnesses for their case; if the opponent produces only one witness, or none at all, they consider the proof settled. But this kind of proof is of no value regarding the truth. For often, false testimonies are brought forward by many people who appear to be quite respectable. And in the present case, regarding what you say, almost everyone—Athenians and foreigners alike—would agree with you if you wished to produce witnesses against me to testify that I am speaking falsely. You could call Nicias, son of Niceratus, and his brothers with him (whose tripods stand in a row in the Dionysium <note>A temple or precinct dedicated to Dionysus.</note>); or Aristocrates, son of Scellius, whose beautiful offering stands in the Pythium <note>A temple of Apollo.</note>; or the entire house of Pericles, or any other Athenian family you wish to summon as testimony. But I, standing alone, do not agree with you. For you do not compel me by logic; instead, by producing false witnesses against me, you strive to cast me out from the very substance of truth. But I believe that unless I produce *you* as the single witness agreeing with me, I have accomplished nothing worthy of consideration in the matters we are treating. I also think you will achieve nothing unless I, alone and by myself, agree with you; and that you must set aside the multitude of other witnesses to achieve this. There is, therefore, as I said, one mode of refutation which you and many others believe in, and there is another which I believe in. Let us therefore compare them and see how they differ from one another. For our discussion is not about small matters, but about those things which it is most beautiful to know and most shameful to be ignorant of. For the head and summit of our inquiry is to either know or be ignorant of who is happy and who is miserable. To begin with, in these matters we are searching out, you believe it is possible for a man who does wrong and is unjust to be happy—since you admit Archelaus is unjust, yet happy. Must we assume this is your opinion? POLUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: But I say that is impossible. This, then, is one point we disagree on. Very well: will an unjust man be happy if he pays the penalty for his injustice? POLUS: Not at all; indeed, he would be most miserable. SOCRATES: But if the unjust man escapes punishment, as you say, he will be happy? POLUS: I say so, indeed. SOCRATES: But according to my opinion, Polus, the one who acts unjustly and is unjust is altogether more miserable than others; and more miserable still if he never pays the penalty for his wrongs, but less miserable if he does pay the penalty and receives a just punishment before gods and men. POLUS: What absurdities you dare to speak, Socrates! SOCRATES: I shall try, my friend, to make you agree with me, for I consider you a friend. Now, the things we disagree on are as follows—pay attention. I said earlier that doing an injury is worse than suffering one. POLUS: You did say that. SOCRATES: But you, on the contrary, said suffering it is worse than doing it. POLUS: Without a doubt. SOCRATES: Furthermore, I called those who do injury "miserable," and I was rebuked by you. POLUS: Indeed you were. SOCRATES: At least in your opinion, Polus. POLUS: And perhaps my opinion is the true one. SOCRATES: You, however, said that those who do injury are happy when they have not paid the penalty. POLUS: Most certainly. SOCRATES: But I say those people are the most miserable, while those who are punished are less miserable. Do you wish to refute that as well? POLUS: Why, Socrates, that is even more difficult to refute than the first point! Who could possibly disprove it? SOCRATES: You should judge it not difficult, Polus, but impossible; for that which is true can never be refuted. POLUS: What are you saying? If someone is caught plotting a tyranny through injustice, and being captured, is tortured, mutilated, has his eyes burned out, and suffers many other various and heavy punishments—and sees his children and wife suffer the same, and finally is impaled on a cross or burned with pitch—will he be happy while suffering these things? Or rather, would he be happy if he escaped, became a tyrant, and lived as he pleased, so that his state of life is envied and judged happy by citizens and foreigners? Do you say these things cannot be refuted? SOCRATES: You are trying to terrify me now, noble Polus, rather than refuting me; just a moment ago you were calling witnesses. However, remind me slightly: did you say "plotting a tyranny *unjustly*"? POLUS: I did. SOCRATES: Then neither of them will ever be happier: neither the one who unjustly attained the tyranny, nor the one who was caught and punished. For of two miserable people, neither can be called happier than the other; yet the one who attained the tyranny and avoided punishment is the more miserable. Why are you laughing, Polus? Is this another species of refutation—to laugh when someone says something, rather than to argue against it? POLUS: But do you not think you are refuted, Socrates, when you say things that no human being would ever say? Ask any of these people here. SOCRATES: Polus, I am not one of those who are involved in public affairs. Last year, when my tribe held the presidency <note>The "prytany" or executive committee of the Athenian senate.</note> and it fell to me to count the votes and report to the council, I caused a great laugh because I did not know how to do it. Therefore, do not ask me to take the vote of those present. Instead, unless you have a better way of arguing, as I was just saying, yield to me in turn and try the kind of refutation I think is necessary. For I know how to produce one witness for what I say: the very person with whom I am speaking. I disregard the multitude. I know how to ask for the vote of one man, but to the multitude I have not a word to say. See then if you are willing to grant me a turn at refutation and answer what is asked. For I believe that both I and you and all other men believe that doing an injury is worse than receiving one, and escaping punishment is worse than undergoing it. POLUS: And I believe that neither I nor any other person thinks so; for you alone would prefer to suffer an injury than to inflict one. SOCRATES: On the contrary: both you and everyone else. POLUS: Far from it...

<margin>From whom false testimonies are brought.</margin>
<margin>The place of witnesses and reasons.</margin>
<margin>That it is worse to inflict an injury than to suffer one.</margin>
<margin>Socrates moved the senate to laughter because he did not know how to report the count of the votes. In disputation, the testimony of no one should be heard except the one responding.</margin>

<summary>Socrates argues with Polus that committing injustice is the greatest evil, particularly if the perpetrator escapes punishment. He rejects Polus's reliance on "witnesses" (public opinion), insisting that true dialectic requires only the agreement of the interlocutor.</summary>

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

->**Socrates**<-
<margin>He proposes a discussion to determine whether it is worse to do an injury or to suffer one.</margin>
I am not the only one who thinks so; neither you, nor any other man does. **Polus**: Will you not answer? **Socrates**: I certainly will; for I am eager to understand what it is you are finally going to say. **Socrates**: Answer me then, so that you may understand, as if I were questioning you from the beginning. Which do you think, Polus, is worse: to do an injury, or to suffer one? **Polus**: To suffer one. **Socrates**: But which is more shameful? Answer, I pray. **Polus**: To do an injury. **Socrates**: Is it not also worse if it is more shameful? **Polus**: Not at all. **Socrates**: I understand now. Clearly you do not think, as it seems, that the beautiful and the good are the same, nor that the shameful and the evil are the same. **Polus**: Certainly not. **Socrates**: What then of all beautiful things—such as bodies, colors, figures, voices, and pursuits—do you call them beautiful while looking at nothing else, or do you look toward

<margin>Beautiful things are those which bring either utility, or pleasure, or both.</margin>
something? For instance, first regarding beautiful bodies, do you not say they are beautiful either because of their utility—being beautiful for the use they serve—or because of some pleasure, namely that they delight those who look at them? Do you have anything else besides this that can be said of the beauty of the body? **Polus**: Nothing else. **Socrates**: And do you not call all other things similarly—whether figures or colors—beautiful either because of some pleasure, or utility, or both? **Polus**: Exactly so. **Socrates**: And voices too, and everything pertaining to music likewise? **Polus**: Yes. **Socrates**: Furthermore, the ordinances of laws and pursuits are beautiful for no other reason than that they either are beneficial, or they delight, or they accomplish both. **Polus**: For no other reason, certainly. **Socrates**: Finally, do we think the same regarding the beauty of the sciences <note>original: *disciplinarum*, referring to branches of learning or knowledge</note>? **Polus**: Exactly the same. And you define it beautifully now, Socrates, by defining the beautiful through delight and the contributing good. **Socrates**: And

<margin>The shameful is that which affects one with either loss, or pain, or both.</margin>
must not the shameful be defined by the opposite—namely by pain and evil, that is, by detriment? **Polus**: It must be. **Socrates**: Whenever, therefore, of two beautiful things one is more beautiful, it is more beautiful by exceeding the other in one of those two things or in both: namely, in delight, or utility, or both. **Polus**: Certainly. **Socrates**: Again, when of two shameful things one is more shameful, it is more shameful by exceeding in either pain or detriment. Is this not necessary? **Polus**: Yes. **Socrates**: Come then, what was being said a little while ago about inflicting and receiving an injury: did you not say that suffering an injury is worse, but doing it is more shameful? **Polus**: I did indeed say so. **Socrates**: If, therefore, doing an injury is more shameful than suffering it, it is either more painful—and by surpassing in pain it is more shameful—or it is so by detriment, or by both; is this not also necessary? **Polus**: Why not? **Socrates**: First, let us consider whether the pain surpasses: whether those who inflict an injury feel more pain than those who suffer it. **Polus**: Not at all, Socrates. **Socrates**: Therefore it does not exceed in pain. **Polus**: It does not appear so. **Socrates**: If not in pain, then not in both. **Polus**: It does not seem so. **Socrates**: Therefore it must be the other. **Polus**: The other. **Socrates**: By evil, then, and detriment. **Polus**: It appears so. **Socrates**: Wherefore, doing an injury, by exceeding in detriment, will be worse than suffering it. **Polus**: It is manifest. **Socrates**: Was it not conceded by many men and by yourself above that it is more shameful to inflict an injury than to receive one? **Polus**: Yes. **Socrates**: Now has it also appeared to be worse? **Polus**: It has appeared so. **Socrates**: Would you choose, my Polus, that which is worse and more shameful rather than that which is less so? Do not be reluctant to answer, Polus; for it will do no harm. Rather, commit yourself to the argument as if to a physician, and answer candidly: either concede what I say or deny it. **Polus**: I would never choose that, Socrates. **Socrates**: Would any other man accept it? **Polus**: According to this reasoning, it does not seem to me that anyone would accept it. **Socrates**: Therefore I was speaking the truth: that neither I, nor you, nor any other man would rather choose to do an injury than to suffer one, since it is worse. **Polus**: It appears so. **Socrates**: You see then, Polus, that when a comparison of the arguments is made, they differ greatly from one another. For while everyone else except me agrees with you, you alone are sufficient for me by agreeing and testifying; you are the only one whose vote and opinion I have asked for; the others I dismiss. And let that be settled. But after this, let us now consider what we

<margin>Whether it is the greatest of evils for one who inflicts injuries to pay the penalty or not to pay it.</margin>
doubted in the second place: whether for the wrongdoer to pay the penalty is the greatest of evils, as you thought, or whether it is a greater evil not to pay the penalty, as I thought. Let us consider it in this way. To pay the penalty for injuries and to be justly punished: do you not call these the same? **Polus**: The same. **Socrates**: Can you deny that all just things, insofar as they are just, are beautiful? And see that you answer carefully. **Polus**: It seems so to me, just as it does to you. **Socrates**: Observe this also: if someone does something, must there be something that suffers <note>original: *patiens*, meaning the recipient of an action</note> from that agent? **Polus**: It seems so. **Socrates**: And must it suffer that which the agent does, and moreover, in such a manner as the agent does it? As if someone strikes, is it not necessary that something is struck? **Polus**: Necessary. **Socrates**: And if he strikes vehemently or swiftly, is the thing struck not struck in the same way? **Polus**: In the same way. **Socrates**: Therefore, such a passion <note>original: *passio*, the state of being acted upon</note> exists in the thing struck as the striker produces? **Polus**: Entirely. **Socrates**: And if someone burns something, must something be burned? **Polus**: It must. **Socrates**: And if he burns it vehemently—and, so to speak, painfully—must that which is burned be burned in the same way as the burner burns it? **Polus**: Exactly. **Socrates**: Similarly, if someone cuts, something is cut. **Polus**: Yes. **Socrates**: And if the cut is wide or deep

<margin>In what manner a thing that suffers is affected by the action.</margin>
or painful, is it not necessary that the thing being cut is cut by such a cutting as the cutter himself cuts? **Polus**: It seems so. **Socrates**: Consider then, in summary, whether you confess what I was just saying in all cases: namely, that in whatever way the agent acts, the agent acts in that way; and in such a way the sufferer suffers. **Polus**: I confess it. **Socrates**: These things being granted, answer: is paying the penalty a suffering of something or a doing of something? **Polus**: A suffering. **Socrates**: And is it not from some agent? **Polus**: It is certain: namely, from the one who punishes. **Socrates**: But he who punishes rightly, does he not punish justly? **Polus**: Justly. **Socrates**: Doing just things, or not? **Polus**: Just things. **Socrates**: Therefore he who is punished, while he pays the penalty for injustice, suffers just things. **Polus**: It appears so. **Socrates**: But just things were said to be beautiful. **Polus**: Exactly. **Socrates**: Therefore, one of these does beautiful things, and the other—namely the one punished—suffers beautiful things. **Polus**: It is so. **Socrates**: And if they are beautiful, they are also good. For they are either pleasant or useful. **Polus**: It is necessary. **Socrates**: Therefore, whoever is justly punished suffers good things. **Polus**: It seems so. **Socrates**: Therefore, it profits him. **Polus**: It is beneficial. **Socrates**: Is it not—to explain how I judge it—that he carries away a better soul...

<summary>Socrates leads Polus through a dialectical argument to prove that doing an injury is worse than suffering one because it is more "shameful" (defined by detriment). They then begin to argue that being justly punished is a "good" for the soul of the wrongdoer.</summary>

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC. FOLIO 140.

...if indeed he is punished justly? PO. That is consistent. SO. Therefore, he who pays the penalty is liberated from the wickedness of the soul. PO. Certainly. SO. Thus, he is liberated from the greatest evil. Consider it in this way: regarding money, do you see any other evil for man than poverty? PO. Only that. SO. Regarding the body, would you call the evil weakness, disease, deformity, and other things of that kind? PO. Indeed. SO. And do you not believe there is also some evil in the soul? PO. Why not? SO. And do you not call this injustice, ignorance, cowardice, and other things of the same kind? PO. Very much so. SO. Since there are these three—money, body, and soul—you have said there are three evils belonging to them: poverty, disease, and injustice. PO. Certainly. SO. Of these evils, which is the most shameful? Is it not injustice? And to put it briefly: the vice of the soul? PO. Very much so. SO. But if the vice of the soul is the most shameful, then it is also the worst. PO. By what reasoning do you say this, Socrates? SO. By this: whatever is most shameful is so either because it brings the greatest pain, or the greatest harm, or both; as appears through those things granted in the previous arguments. PO. Very much so. SO. And was it not granted to us that injustice and every vice of the soul is the most shameful? PO. Certainly. SO. Therefore, it is the most shameful of these either because it is the most painful and exceeding in distress, or because it brings harm, or because of both. PO. It must be so. SO. Is it then more painful to be unjust, intemperate, cowardly, and ignorant, than to be oppressed by poverty and disease? PO. Certainly not, as far as can be gathered from these things. SO. Since, therefore, the vice of the soul surpasses other evils by some incredible and wonderful magnitude of harm and evil, it is for that reason the most shameful of all; seeing as it does not exceed them in pain, as you yourself say. PO. So it appears. SO. Now, that which exceeds in the greatest damage is the greatest of all evils. PO. It is so. SO. For which reason injustice, intemperance, and the rest of the soul's wickedness is the greatest evil of all. PO. It seems so. SO. What art, then, frees us from poverty? Is it not the art of profit-making? <note>original: "quæstuaria"</note> PO. That very one. SO. And what frees us from disease? Is it not medicine? PO. That indeed. SO. But what frees us from wickedness and injustice? If it does not occur to you, consider it this way: where, and to whom, do we primarily lead those who are sick with bodily diseases? PO. To physicians, Socrates. SO. And where do we lead the unjust and the dissolute? PO. To the judges. SO. So that they may be punished, clearly. PO. I agree. SO. And do not those who punish correctly do so by relying on a certain kind of justice? PO. Without a doubt. SO. Therefore, the art of profit-making drives out poverty; medicine drives away diseases; and finally, the judicial art <note>original: "iudiciaria"</note> removes intemperance and injustice. PO. So it appears. SO. Which of these, then, is the most beautiful? PO. Of which do you speak? SO. Of profit-making, medicine, and the judicial art. PO. The judicial art far excels, Socrates. SO. Therefore, it brings either the most pleasure, or utility, or both, if indeed it is the most beautiful. PO. It follows. SO. Is it then delightful to be treated by a physician? And do the hands of the physician provide pleasure while they treat the sick? PO. It does not seem so. SO. Yet it is beneficial, is it not? PO. It is profitable. SO. Because, clearly, they are liberated from a great evil. For which reason it is useful to endure pain so that you may emerge healthy. PO. Without a doubt. SO. Would he then be the happiest, as far as the body is concerned, who has recovered after being treated by medicine, or rather he who was not sick from the beginning? PO. Certainly he who was not sick. SO. Indeed, happiness does not seem to consist in being liberated from evils, but in being sound from the very start. PO. It is so. SO. But what if two are badly affected, either in body or soul? Which of these is more miserable: the one who is treated and liberated from the evil, or the one who is not? PO. The one who is not treated. SO. And was not being punished in court a liberation from a certain maximum evil, that is, from wickedness? PO. It certainly was. SO. Since just punishment moderates and makes one more just, like a kind of medicine for wickedness. PO. It is so. SO. He is happiest, therefore, who has no vice of the soul, since that appeared to be the greatest evil. PO. Without a doubt. SO. And in the second place is he who is liberated from an evil of this kind. PO. It appears so. SO. And this is he who, having been seized and rebuked, has paid the penalty. PO. That very man. SO. He lives worst, therefore, who is unjust and is not released from injustice. PO. It appears so. SO. Is this not the one who, having committed the greatest wrongs and relying on the greatest [lack of] justice, has brought it about that he is neither seized, nor punished, nor pays the penalty—just as you say Archelaus <note>Archelaus was the King of Macedon, whom Polus previously cited as a "happy" man despite his many crimes.</note> has done, and other tyrants, orators, and powerful men? PO. It appears so. SO. For such men, O best of men, act almost as if someone occupied by the gravest diseases should take care that he does not receive the "punishment" of his bodily vices under a physician, nor be cured; fearing, like a child, the burning and the cutting <note>Socrates compares legal punishment to the painful but necessary surgical practices of the time.</note> as a painful thing. Does it not seem so to you as well? PO. To me, indeed. SO. Because, clearly, they are ignorant of how much health and bodily virtue are worth. It seems, by those things we just granted, O Polus, that those who flee judgment do something similar: they look at the pain of it, but are blind to the utility; and they are ignorant of how much more miserable it is to live with a soul that is not healthy, but broken, unjust, and impious, than with an unhealthy body. And so they take care that they do not undergo judgment, nor be released from the greatest evil. For that reason they amass money, acquire friends, and study eloquence. But if we, O Polus, have confessed the truth, do you perceive what follows from this discussion? Or do you wish for us to arrange the points one by one in sequence? PO. As you please. SO. Is it not agreed that injustice and wrongdoing is the greatest evil? PO. It seems so. SO. Furthermore, it was established that the release from this evil is to pay the penalty? PO. It appeared so. SO. And that to escape the penalty is the persistence of the evil? PO. Certainly. SO. Therefore, among evils, doing wrong holds the second place in magnitude. But to bring it about that the penalty for wrongs is not undergone at all is, by its nature, the greatest and first of all evils.

<summary>Socrates argues that while injustice is the greatest evil of the soul, escaping punishment is even worse because it prevents the "cure" of the soul's wickedness. He compares the judicial process to medicine, suggesting that the criminal who avoids justice is like a sick man who avoids a doctor out of fear of painful surgery.</summary>

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

**POLUS.** It seems so. **SOCRATES.** This, then, my friend, is the point we were debating. You were saying that Archelaus <note>Archelaus was the King of Macedon, often cited in these dialogues as a tyrant who gained power through crime but lived in luxury.</note> was happy because, despite committing the greatest injustices, he paid no penalty. I, on the contrary, thought that whether it be Archelaus or any other man who does not pay the penalty for his injustices, he is the most miserable of all. I maintained that the one who inflicts an injury is always more miserable than the one who suffers it, and finally, that he who does not pay the penalty is more miserable than he who does. Were these not the things I said? **POLUS.** These very things. **SOCRATES.** And has it not been demonstrated that these things were spoken truly? **POLUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** Very well, Polus. If these things are true, then what is the use of rhetoric? <note>Rhetoric is the art of persuasive speaking, which Socrates argues is often used to escape justice.</note> For it follows from what we have agreed that we must most diligently guard ourselves first of all against doing injury to anyone, as we would possess a great evil by doing so—is that not right? **POLUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, if an injury is committed by us or by someone dear to us, we should go of our own accord to the judge to be punished, as if to a doctor, hurrying so that the disease of injustice does not become old and infect the soul until it is incurable. In what other way can we speak, Polus, if our previous concessions are to stand? Do not these conclusions harmonize necessarily with those, while any others would not? **POLUS.** What else can we say, Socrates? **SOCRATES.** Therefore, for the purpose of defending or excusing our own injustice, or that of our parents, friends, children, or country when they do wrong, rhetoric is of no use to us at all, Polus. Unless, perhaps, one thinks rhetoric should be used for the opposite purpose: namely, for accusing oneself first, and then one's family and friends, if any of those dear to us have committed an injury. We should not hide their crimes but bring them into the light so they may pay the penalty and become healthy again. Moreover, one should compel oneself and others not to be sluggish or fearful, but with a brave heart and as if with eyes closed, submit to the judge as to a surgeon to be cut and cauterized, seeking the good and the honorable while despising the pain. Thus, if they have committed acts worthy of stripes, they should offer themselves to be beaten; if of bonds, to be bound; if of a fine, to pay it; if of exile, to be expelled; if of death, to be killed. In this matter, each man should be the accuser of himself and his own kin, and use the faculty of oratory for this: so that by making their injustices manifest, they may be freed from the greatest evil, which is injustice. Shall we say this, Polus, or something else? **POLUS.** These things seem absurd to me, Socrates. Yet, perhaps they do harmonize with what you said before. **SOCRATES.** Must we not either refute those earlier statements or grant these consequences? **POLUS.** That is how it stands. **SOCRATES.** On the other hand, if one must do harm to someone, whether an enemy or anyone else, one must only take care that he himself does not suffer an injury from his adversary. But if an enemy does an injury to others, we must provide every effort in both word and deed to ensure he does *not* pay the penalty and is *not* brought before a judge. Or if he is brought there, we must strive so that the enemy escapes and is not punished. Indeed, if he has stolen much gold, we should strive that he does not restore it, but possesses it himself and spends it unjustly and impiously on himself and his kin. If he has committed crimes worthy of death, we should strive that he never dies if possible, but remains an immortal villain. Or if that is not possible, that he lives as long as possible in that state. For these and suchlike things, Polus, rhetoric seems useful to me. But for one who is not going to commit an injury, its utility does not seem great—if indeed there is any utility in it at all. For in the things we discussed earlier, none appeared.

**CALLICLES.** Tell me, Chaerephon, is Socrates speaking seriously here, or is he joking? **CHAEREPHON.** To me, Callicles, he seems to be speaking with extraordinary seriousness. However, there is no harm in asking him. **CALLICLES.** By the gods, tell me, Socrates, should we think you are speaking seriously now or joking? For if you are serious and what you say is true, then our life is undoubtedly turned upside down, and we are doing everything the opposite of what we should. **SOCRATES.** O Callicles, if there were not a common feeling among us—though different people have different passions—if one of us had a unique feeling unlike the rest, it would not be easy to explain to others what one feels. Why do I say this? Because I notice that you and I are now experiencing the same thing: we are both in love with two things. I love philosophy; you love the Athenian people <note>original: "populum Atheniensem," referring to the *Demos*.</note>. I notice that if the people contradict you in the assembly, you are accustomed to changing your opinion and saying whatever you understand will please them; you cannot resist their will. Therefore, if someone were amazed by the absurd things you say to please the people and objected to them, you would perhaps respond—if you wished to speak the truth—that unless the people you love change their opinion, you will never change yours either. The same would happen to you regarding a private person, if you loved one intensely. Think, then, that you are hearing such things from me, and do not be amazed that I say them; rather, see to it that philosophy, which I love, ceases to want these things. For she, my sweet friend, always says what you hear from me. And while my other acquaintances might say one thing at one time and another at another, philosophy is always the same. She says the things you now wonder at, for you were just now present to hear them. Therefore, either refute her, as I was just saying, and show that doing an injury and not paying the penalty is not the extreme of all evils; or, if you let this stand, I predict to you, Callicles, by the dog, the god of the Egyptians, <note>A favorite oath of Socrates: "By the dog."</note> that Callicles will never agree with himself, but will be at odds throughout his whole life. And yet, my best of men, I judge it better that my lyre be out of tune and dissonant, and that the choir I lead, and many other men besides, should contradict me, rather than that I, being one, should be out of harmony with and contradict myself. **CALLICLES.** O Socrates, this seems to be a kind of youthful boastfulness in your disputing; you appear to be a common rabble-rouser. And now you are haranguing us in this way because the same thing happened to Polus that happened—

<margin>Socrates wants us to accuse our friends of injustice and reveal them to the judge.</margin>

<summary>Socrates argues that rhetoric's only moral use is to accuse oneself or loved ones so they may face justice and heal their souls. Callicles interrupts, questioning if Socrates is serious, leading Socrates to contrast his devotion to unchanging philosophy with Callicles' fickle devotion to the Athenian public.</summary>
