# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC. FOLIO 141.

<note>This is a Latin translation of Plato's Greek dialogue "Gorgias." The speaker here is Callicles, a wealthy and ambitious Athenian politician who represents the "might makes right" worldview.</note>

...accused Gorgias of the same thing just a little while ago regarding you. For Polus said that in a certain place, when Gorgias was asked by you whether he would teach justice to someone who came to learn rhetoric but was ignorant of the law, Gorgias—out of a sense of shame—affirmed that he would teach him. He did this because of human customs: people would take it badly if someone did not concede such things. Then, because of this kind of concession, Gorgias was forced to contradict himself. In my judgment, Polus rightly mocked you then for following such foolishness. 

But now, the same thing has happened to Polus in turn. I certainly do not approve of Polus in this: that he conceded to you that doing an injury is more shameful than suffering one. Because of this concession, he was blocked by you and could not explain what he was thinking. Truly, Socrates, you lead your listeners into difficulties and public-speaking traps while you profess to be following the truth. You bring into the open things that are not beautiful by **nature**, but only by **law** <note>original: "lege." Callicles distinguishes between Physis (Nature) and Nomos (Man-made Law/Custom).</note>. It often happens that law and nature are contrary to one another. Therefore, if someone is ashamed and does not dare to express what they think, they are compelled to contradict themselves. 

You, noticing this craftily, lay traps in words. For if someone speaks according to the law, you then ask questions according to nature. If he speaks according to nature, you ask according to the law—just as you did just now regarding the inflicting or the enduring of an injury. For when Polus said that according to the law it is more shameful to inflict injury, you pursued the law. By **nature**, however, whatever is worse is also more shameful—such as suffering an injury. But by **law**, it is more shameful to inflict one. For it is not the part of a man to suffer injuries, but of some slave, for whom it would be better to be dead than alive. Such a person, when affected by insults and injuries, can help neither himself nor his own people. 

But, as I think, those who establish the laws are the many who are weaker. Thus, looking out for their own utility, they constitute the laws. Furthermore, they distribute praise and blame, driven by fear of the more powerful, so that the powerful cannot exceed them in any matter. And so they say it is shameful and unjust for some to have more than others; and they define "doing injury" as seeking to have more than others. For they think they have done enough for themselves if, being inferior, they have an equal portion. For this reason, therefore, it is called unjust and shameful by **law** to seek to have more than others, and the common people call this "injury." 

But **nature** itself, I think, demonstrates that the superior should have more than the inferior, and the more powerful more than the weaker. Nature shows this in many ways: in other animals, and in all states and nations, among whom it is judged to be just that the more powerful should rule the weaker and possess more. For by what right did Xerxes lead his army against the Greeks? Or his father against the Scythians, or the countless others one could mention? But these men, I think, act according to the nature of right itself—and by Jove, according to the **law of nature itself**—though perhaps not according to these laws established by us. By our laws, we take the most excellent and strongest-natured youths from the cradle, like lions, and we fascinate them with certain "magic charms" and subject them in a slavish manner, saying that equality must be preserved and that this is beautiful and just. 

But if a man of superior nature should rise up, shaking off and tearing apart all your writings, fascinations, and incantations, and overturning all laws that fall short of nature, and should rule over the rest—in him the right of nature itself would shine forth. It seems to me that Pindarus shows these same things in a certain song, where 

<margin>From Pindar: Law is the queen of all mortals and immortals.</margin> 

he says that law is the queen of all mortals and immortals, and that she leads justice with a violent and powerful hand. He says he conjectures this from the deeds of Hercules; for, although I do not remember the poem itself well enough, I remember him saying that Hercules drove away the oxen of Geryon without having bought them or received them as a gift—as if natural right itself dictated that the oxen, and all other things possessed by men, ought to belong to him who is superior and stronger. 

The truth is thus: and you would clearly recognize it if, having now dismissed your concern for philosophizing, you turned to greater things. For **philosophy**, O Socrates, is a graceful and charming thing if one touches upon it moderately in youth. But if one spends more time on it than is proper, it is the ruin of men. For even if someone is endowed by nature with the best talent, yet if he philosophizes too long into advanced age, he will necessarily turn out ignorant of all those things in which a famous, good, and excellent man ought to have skill. 

<margin>Callicles' speech concerning philosophy.</margin> 

For they become utterly ignorant of civil laws, and of the words which it is proper to use in the customs and assemblies of men, both publicly and privately, and of human pleasures and desires; and to be brief, they are ignorant of morals altogether. Therefore, whenever they apply themselves to managing any matter, whether public or private, they are held as ridiculous—just as men of the city are if they descend into your exercises and disputes. For that saying of Euripides happens: "Each man hastens to that in which he is famous, and imparts the greatest part of the day to it, so that he may surpass himself." But where he is inferior, he flees from there and disparages it, but praises the other thing, thinking out of a certain self-benevolence that he is thus praising himself. 

But I think it is better to participate in both. It is proper to touch philosophy for the sake of education, and it is not shameful for a youth to philosophize. But when one of older age still broods over philosophy, it is a very ridiculous thing, O Socrates. I am affected toward those who give their effort to philosophy in the same way as toward those who stammer and play. For whenever I see a little boy, for whom it is still becoming to stammer and play, I am delighted; it seems festive and liberal to me, and becoming of a boyish age. But whenever I hear a boy expressing words too precisely, it becomes something annoying to me and offends my ears, and seems to show something slavish. However, when one hears a man either stammering or...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "videtur" (it seems) indicates the start of the next page.</meta>

<summary>Callicles argues that "natural justice" allows the strong to dominate the weak, dismissing conventional morality as a tool of the weak to restrain the powerful. He also critiques Socrates for over-indulging in philosophy, which he views as a hobby for children that makes grown men socially incompetent.</summary>

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

He sees someone playing, it seems ridiculous, unbefitting a man, and deserving of blows. I feel the same way toward those who practice philosophy. When I see philosophy in a youth, I am delighted; I judge it appropriate and consider such a person well-bred. But one who does not philosophize I consider illiberal <note>Greek: *aneleutheron*, meaning one who lacks the qualities of a free-born citizen</note>, as one who will never provide anything noble or generous from himself. However, when I notice an older man still philosophizing and not abandoning such studies, I believe this man, O Socrates, now deserves a beating. For as I was just saying, it happens to such a man that even if he is of a noble nature, he becomes unmanly; he flees the heart of the city and the customs of the marketplace—where the poet says men become most eminent—hiding himself away with three or four boys, spending his life whispering in corners, never to utter anything liberal or magnificent. 

Now, Socrates, I have a great affection for you. Therefore, I feel toward you as Zethus felt toward Amphion in Euripides' play <note>Referring to a lost play by Euripides where two brothers debate the active vs. contemplative life</note>, whom I mentioned just now. It occurs to me to say such things to you as he said to his brother: "Truly, Socrates, you neglect those things you ought to care for, and you shape the excellence of a noble mind into a sort of boyish form; you would not know how to speak correctly in judgments or consultations, nor choose anything fitting or persuasive, nor offer prompt counsel to others." 

O friend Socrates, do not be angry with me. It is my goodwill toward you that leads me to say this. Do you not think it a disgrace to be in the state I believe you and all others who pursue philosophy too long are in? If someone were to seize you or any of your sort right now and drag you to prison, asserting that you have committed an injustice even if you have not, you certainly would not know what to do. You would stagger and gape, utterly ignorant of your defense; then, brought into court by even a base and contemptible accuser, you would be put to death if that were his pleasure. 

Now, how can this be wisdom, Socrates—if an art finds a man of noble mind and renders him worse, so that he can neither help himself nor save himself or anyone else from the gravest dangers, but leaves him exposed to the insults of enemies and plunderers, living without honor in the city? Indeed, such a man—if I may speak somewhat crudely—may be struck on the cheek with impunity. Therefore, my good man, believe me: stop dealing in vain subtleties; practice the decorous duties of business, and practice those things through which you may appear wise. Leave these subtleties—whether they should be called delusions or trifles—which will leave you living in an empty house, to others. Finally, imitate not those who hunt for these small things, but those who possess life, glory, and many other goods.

**SOCRATES:** If my soul were made of gold, O Callicles, do you not think I would gladly find one of those stones used to test gold? If I applied my soul to that stone and it approved of my soul as having been rightly educated, I would know for certain that I am in good condition and need no further testing.

**CALLICLES:** To what end is this, Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** I will tell you. I think that in finding you, I have found this precious touchstone.

**CALLICLES:** For what reason?

**SOCRATES:** Because I know for certain that whatever you agree with me on regarding the opinions of my soul will undoubtedly be true. 

<margin>One who wishes to test someone's soul must have three things: knowledge, goodwill, and boldness.</margin>

For I believe that he who is to sufficiently test a soul to see if it is rightly established or not must possess three things above all, all of which you have: first, knowledge; second, prudence or goodwill; and third, boldness. For I find many who cannot test me with a correct examination because they are not wise as you seem to be. Others are indeed wise, but they are unwilling to tell me the truth because they do not care for me as you do. These foreigners, Gorgias and Polus, are indeed wise and they love me, but they lack boldness and are more modest than they ought to be. How can there be any doubt of this? For they proceeded so far in their bashfulness that, out of that very modesty, they dared to contradict themselves on the greatest matters in the presence of many men. 

But you have all these things that others lack. First, you are abundantly learned, as many 

<margin>The opinion of Callicles and the prominent Athenians: One should not strive for an exact diligence in philosophy, but must take care lest, by becoming wise beyond what is fitting, they secretly corrupt themselves.</margin>

Athenians would confirm. And you are well-disposed toward me, which I will tell you how I know. I know, Callicles, that there are four of you who are partners in the study of wisdom: yourself, Thysandrus of Aphidnae, Andron the son of Androtion, and Nausicydes of Cholargus. I once heard you discussing how far one should study wisdom, and this opinion prevailed among you: that one should not strive for an exact diligence in philosophy, but should take care lest, by becoming wise beyond what is fitting, you might secretly corrupt yourselves. Since, therefore, I hear you giving me the same advice you gave your closest friends, it is a sufficient argument of your true love for me. Furthermore, that you have enough boldness and that shame does not hinder you, you affirm yourself, and the speech you gave just now bears witness to it. 

Since these things are so, if you grant me anything in this dispute, it will be sufficiently proven for us; there will be no need to refer it to another examination. Otherwise, you would never have granted it to me, either through a lack of wisdom or led by modesty to deceive me. For you are my friend, as you say. Truly, then, your confession and mine will reach the end of truth. The consideration of these things, for which you have reproved me, is the most beautiful of all: 

<margin>The consideration of which things is most beautiful.</margin>

what kind of man one ought to be, and what one should practice, and to what extent, both in youth and in old age. If I do anything in my life that is not right, be certain that I do not err by my own will, but rather through ignorance. Therefore, as you have begun to admonish me, please continue and show me clearly what it is I must seek and by what path I may attain it. If you find me agreeing with you now, but later failing to perform what I assented to, then consider me utterly dull and cowardly, and do not waste further effort in admonishing me as one who is completely lost. 

<meta>Catchword: "Resumme ve" (Resume then)</meta>

Socrates responds by praising Callicles as the perfect "touchstone" for truth because he possesses knowledge, goodwill, and the boldness to speak plainly.</summary>

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC. FOLIO 142.

<margin>Socrates</margin>
Repeat for me from the beginning: in what way did you and Pindar say that it is "just by nature" for the more powerful to take by force the possessions of the weaker, for the better to rule the worse, and for the superior man to have more than the lowly? Do you say justice is anything other than this, or do I remember correctly? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** I said these things then, and I say them now. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** But do you call the "better" and the "more powerful" the same thing? For I could not clearly understand what you meant then. Do you call the stronger "more powerful," and must the weaker obey the stronger? You seemed to demonstrate this earlier when you said that great cities rise up against small ones by natural right because they are more powerful and stronger—as if "more powerful," "stronger," and "better" were the same thing. Or is it possible for someone to be better, yet inferior and weaker? Similarly, can one be more powerful, yet worse? Or is the definition of "better" and "more powerful" the same? Explain this very point to me more clearly: are "more powerful," "better," and "stronger" the same or different? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** I manifesty assert to you that they are the same. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Is not a multitude <note>the masses or the majority</note> naturally more powerful than a single person? For they are the ones who establish laws over the individual, as you yourself just said. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** Why not? <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Therefore, the laws of the multitude are the laws of the "more powerful." <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** Entirely so. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Are they not also the laws of the "better"? For those who are more powerful, as you say, are surely better. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** Certainly so. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Are their decrees not "right by nature," since they are more powerful? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** I affirm it. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Does the multitude not decree—as you were just saying—that it is just for equality to be preserved among all, and that it is more shameful to inflict an injury than to suffer one? Is it so, or otherwise? And see that you are not caught here by a sense of modesty. Does the multitude decree this or not: namely, that it is just to preserve equality, and not for one to have more than another, and that it is more shameful to do wrong than to receive it? I ask you, Callicles, let no ill-will hold you back from answering me; for if you agree with me, I shall be confirmed by you as a man fully sufficient in judgment. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** The multitude certainly decrees this. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Therefore, it is not by law alone, but also by nature, that it is more shameful to do wrong than to suffer it, and just to preserve equality. Consequently, you seem to have spoken untruly in your earlier remarks, and you accused me wrongly when you said that law and nature were opposites, and that I, noticing this, used to lay traps in words—leading the conversation toward law if someone spoke according to nature, and toward nature if someone spoke according to law. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** This man will never cease dealing in trifles! Tell me, Socrates, are you not ashamed, at your great age, to be hunting after words? If someone slips up in a word, you catch it greedily as if it were a prize. Do you think I mean that "more powerful" is anything other than "better"? Have I not been telling you for a long time that "better" and "more powerful" are the same? Or do you think I am saying that if a dreg of slaves and all sorts of the vilest men flow together—who are perhaps more powerful only in bodily strength—that what they decree should be the law? <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Come now, most wise Callicles, is that what you are saying? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** Most certainly. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** But, blessed man, I have long suspected you meant something else by "more powerful," and I am questioning you because I desire to know clearly what you mean. For you do not judge two slaves to be better than one just because they are stronger, do you? Tell me again from the beginning: who do you say are the "better," if they are not the "stronger"? And please, wonderful man, teach me more gently so that I do not run away from your school. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** You are speaking with irony, Socrates. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** No, by Zethus <note>A character from a play by Euripides, used here as a mock-oath</note>, Callicles—the one you relied on to use much irony against me just now. But come, tell me: whom do you call the "better"? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** The superior ones, of course. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** You see, then, that you are merely saying words but showing nothing. You do not reveal whether you mean the "better" and "more powerful" are the "more prudent" <note>wise or practical</note> or some others. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** By Jove, I mean these, and most especially so! <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Often, then, one prudent man is more powerful than many imprudent ones according to your argument; and it is right for him to rule, and for the others to be subjects, and for him to have more than those he commands. This seems to be what you want to say—and I am not "hunting for words"—if indeed one man is more powerful than many. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** That is exactly what I am saying. For I judge this to be the right of nature: that he who is better and more prudent should rule and possess more than his inferiors. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Stay a moment. What would you think if we were gathered in this place, as we are now, many of us, and we had a great common supply of food and drink, and we were all sorts of people—some strong, some weak—but one of us was the most prudent regarding these things, perhaps a physician? He would be, as is likely, stronger than some and weaker than others. Would he not, being more prudent, be better and more powerful in this regard? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** Entirely. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Should he, as the distributor of these things, retain more for himself? Otherwise he should be punished. Or should he, in distributing, give more to some and less to others? And if he were the weakest of all, should the smallest portion be given to him, even though he is the best, Callicles? Is that not how it must be said, my good man? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** You talk of food, drink, physicians, and such trifles; I am not speaking of these. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Do you say the more prudent is the better, or not? Answer. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** I do. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** But should the better not receive more? <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** Not of food and drink. <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** I understand. Perhaps of clothes? And the one most skilled in making clothes should have the largest tunic and walk about adorned in many precious garments. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** What clothes are you talking about? <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Or perhaps in shoes, he who is more prudent and better in them should receive more; perhaps the shoemaker should have the largest and most numerous shoes and carry them about on his feet. <margin>Callicles</margin> **CAL.** What shoes are you raving about now? <margin>Socrates</margin> **SO.** Well, if not such things, at least you mean something like this: that a man prudent, honest, and good in cultivating fields should receive more...

<summary>Socrates challenges Callicles' definition of "the more powerful," forcing him to admit that he means the "more prudent" rather than just the physically strong. Socrates then uses absurd examples of shoemakers and doctors to question whether superior knowledge entitles someone to a larger share of material goods.</summary>

CALLICLES: But I have been saying it for a long time: first, indeed, who the more powerful are. For I do not mean shoemakers or cooks, but those who are prudent in administering the republic; and not only prudent, but also brave, who are most fit to accomplish those things they have devised, and do not succumb to any softness of mind. SOCRATES: Do you notice, Callicles, that I am not accused by you, and you in turn by me, of the same things? You indeed accuse me as if I were always repeating the same things; I, however, accuse you of the opposite, as if you never bring forward the same things concerning the same matters. For at one time you define the "better" and "more powerful" as the stronger, and at another time as the more prudent. Now, moreover, you bring forward something else. CALLICLES: I have already said: namely, those prudent and brave in public affairs. For it is fitting for us to rule cities; and it is just that those dominating should have more than others: namely, the subjects. SOCRATES: What then? Is it fitting for them to rule themselves in any way, or to obey themselves? CALLICLES: What do you mean? SOCRATES: I mean whether each man ought to rule himself; or is there no need for him to rule himself, but only others? CALLICLES: How do you mean "to rule oneself"? SOCRATES: I say nothing obscure: but just as many say, to be temperate <term>temperatum: self-controlled or moderate</term> and master of oneself, ruling over one's own pleasures and desires. CALLICLES: Since you are so festive, O Socrates, you call stupid men "temperate." SOCRATES: What are you saying? There is no one who does not know that I mean no such thing. CALLICLES: On the contrary, very much so, O Socrates. For how can a man be happy who serves anyone? But this is naturally just and beautiful, which I now boldly tell you: that he who is to lead a life rightly ought to permit his desires to be increased to the utmost, and not restrain them in any way; and to provide for these, as great as they may be, whatever they seek, on account of his bravery and prudence, and to utterly fulfill the craving of any of them. Because many are unable to achieve this, they blame those who do attain it, hiding their own impotence behind their shame; and they say that intemperance is shameful, just as I was saying earlier. Furthermore, they reduce men of a better nature to a servile condition; and they themselves, since they cannot fulfill their own lusts, praise temperance and justice because of their own cowardice. But if it had happened to them from the beginning that they were either sons of kings, or their own nature was sufficient to acquire for themselves a command, or a tyranny, or some power, surely it would be more shameful and worse for them to use this kind of temperance: that when it was permitted for them to enjoy good things, and they were not hindered by anyone, they themselves should set over themselves as a master the law, the talk, and the blame of the multitude. For in what way would they not be miserable? If indeed, on account of a certain justice and the "honor" of temperance, they should grant nothing more to their friends than to their enemies, even while they were dominating in their own city. But, O Socrates, the truth itself, which you claim to follow, is this: luxury, intemperance, and liberty—provided the means are available—this is power, virtue, and happiness. All these other showy things, invented contrary to nature, are the delusions of men and trifles to be utterly despised. SOCRATES: Not ungenerously, O Callicles, do you proceed in the discussion using such audacity. Certainly, those things have now been spoken openly by you which others indeed think, but are unwilling to say. Wherefore I beseech you to desist in no way, so that we may truly be made more certain of the way in which one must live. Tell me then: you say desires are not to be coerced, if anyone wishes to be such as one ought to be; rather, they are to be permitted to increase to the utmost, and their fulfillment is to be procured from elsewhere; and you say this is virtue? CALLICLES: I do say so. SOCRATES: If it were so, they would not rightly say that those are happy who need nothing. Otherwise, stones and the dead would be most happy. CALLICLES: But even that life which you describe is unpleasant. Nor would I wonder if Euripides speaks the truth in saying: <margin>Euripides on life and death</margin> *Who knows whether to live is indeed to die, and to die is to live!* And now perhaps we are truly dead. I have already heard from a certain wise man that we are now dead; and that our body is a tomb for us; and that part of the soul in which the desires are is just as if it were driven up and down by persuasion and dissuasion in turn. And so a certain elegant man, perhaps a Sicilian or an Italian, speaking figuratively of these things, called this part of the soul—on account of its persuasibility and credulity—a "jar," playing on the name <note>original: "doliũ" (dolium). Socrates is likely referencing a Greek pun between "pithanos" (persuasive) and "pithos" (jar).</note>; but the foolish he called "uninitiated" and "damned." Of these, however, he says that this part of the soul which is agitated by lusts, being leaky on account of its insatiable incontinence, is a "perforated jar." Wherefore this man, O Callicles, shows the opposite to you: that of those who are in the dark underworld, those are the most miserable who, as if altogether uninitiated, are damned; and they carry water into a perforated vessel with another vessel that is also perforated. And that this other vessel, or sieve, as he who taught me said, is the mind of the foolish, which he compared to a perforated vessel for this reason: that on account of its unfaithful disposition and forgetfulness, it cannot contain anything poured into it. These things will seem in some way strange to someone; yet they demonstrate that which I desire: if by any means I might be able to persuade you to choose, instead of an insatiable and incontinent life, one that is moderate and always content with present things. But do I persuade you of anything through these things? And having changed your opinion, do you think those who live temperately are happier than those who live intemperately? Or do I accomplish nothing? And though I may speak of many things in a similar way, will you change your opinion no more? CALLICLES: This last thing you said, Socrates, is truer. SOCRATES: Come then, I will bring forward a certain similarity to you from the same school. Consider whether you judge the same of the life of each, the temperate and the intemperate, as if two men...

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC

...two men who each had many jars: and one man's jars were intact and full, some with wine, some with honey, some with milk, and others likewise with other things. Suppose these liquids were rare and difficult to find, obtained only through many heavy labors. Now, the man whose jars are full takes no further care to pour anything in, but as far as they are concerned, he rests easy. But for the other man, though the liquids are available as they were for the first—attainable, yet with difficulty—his jars are perforated and broken. He is forced to keep filling them day and night continually, or else he suffers the most extreme miseries. Since such is the life of each, do you say that the life of the intemperate man <note>The "leaky jar" metaphor for a life of uncontrolled desire.</note> is happier than that of the temperate man? Do I persuade you with these words to concede that the moderate life is better than the immoderate one? Or do I not yet persuade you?

**CALLICLES:** Not at all, Socrates. For the man who has filled everything has no more pleasure; rather, as I was just saying, he lives like a stone once he is full, feeling neither pleasure nor pain anymore. But the sweetness of life consists in the greatest possible amount flowing in.

**SOCRATES:** If much flows in, is it not necessary that much must also flow out, and that the holes for the outflow must be large?

**CALLICLES:** Certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Then you are describing the life of a stone-curlew <note>original: "Charadrii auis." A bird known in folklore for eating and excreting simultaneously; Socrates uses it to mock the "leaky" life of constant consumption.</note>—a sort of gullet—rather than that of a corpse or a stone. But answer me: do you mean something like being hungry and eating when hungry?

**CALLICLES:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** And being thirsty and drinking when thirsty?

**CALLICLES:** I do; and likewise having all other desires and being able to fulfill them, and living happily in that fulfillment.

**SOCRATES:** Well done, best of men! Proceed as you have begun, and do not be ashamed. It seems I, too, must not be held back by shame. Tell me first: if a man has an itch and scratches it, and has plenty of opportunity to scratch, and spends his whole life scratching, is he living happily?

**CALLICLES:** How absurd you are, Socrates, and truly a common stump-speaker.

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, Callicles, I terrified Polus and Gorgias and made them blush. But you, take care not to be terrified or hindered by shame. For you are brave. Just answer me.

**CALLICLES:** I say then that the one scratching also lives pleasantly.

**SOCRATES:** And if pleasantly, then also happily?

**CALLICLES:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** What if he only scratches his head—or should I ask further? See what you will answer, Callicles, if someone asks what follows in sequence. For if these things are granted as primary points, the life of catamites <note>original: "cinædorū." Socrates uses a shocking example of base physical pleasure to challenge Callicles' claim that all pleasure is good.</note> would have to be called grave, shameful, and unhappy, would it not? Or will you dare to say they are happy if they have what they desire in abundance?

**CALLICLES:** Are you not ashamed, Socrates, to lead the conversation to such things?

**SOCRATES:** Is it I who lead it there, noble sir, or rather the one who asserts so impudently that those who enjoy themselves, in whatever way they enjoy themselves, are happy, and who does not distinguish which pleasures are good and which are evil? But tell me now: do you assert that pleasure and the good are the same thing, or is there some pleasure that is not good?

**CALLICLES:** So that my argument is not inconsistent if I say they are different, I say they are the same.

**SOCRATES:** You are overturning what was said before, Callicles, and you are no longer fit to investigate the truth with me if you answer contrary to what you really think.

**CALLICLES:** You do the same, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Then neither of us acts rightly if that is so. But, my dear man, see if the good is not something entirely different from rejoicing; otherwise, many shameful things and many other evils clearly follow if this is the case.

**CALLICLES:** So you think, Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** But do you truly affirm this, Callicles?

**CALLICLES:** I certainly do.

**SOCRATES:** Shall we then take up the dispute as if you were speaking seriously?

**CALLICLES:** I certainly wish to.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, since you hold this opinion, answer me distinctly: Do you call something "knowledge"?

**CALLICLES:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** And did you not say just now that "courage" was something distinct from knowledge?

**CALLICLES:** I did indeed.

**SOCRATES:** And did you say they were two different things, courage and knowledge?

**CALLICLES:** Very much so.

**SOCRATES:** And what of pleasure and knowledge? Are they the same or different?

**CALLICLES:** Different, O wisest man.

**SOCRATES:** And is courage different from pleasure?

**CALLICLES:** Of course.

**SOCRATES:** Let us remember this then: Callicles of Acharnae says pleasure and the good are the same, but knowledge and courage are different from each other and different from the good. But Socrates of Alopece <note>The speakers identify themselves by their Athenian demes (districts).</note> does not concede this. Do you concede it?

**CALLICLES:** Not at all.

**SOCRATES:** And I think Callicles will not concede it either when he considers it rightly. Tell me: do you not think that those who are happy and those who are unhappy are affected in opposite ways?

**CALLICLES:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** If these states are opposites, is it not necessary that they behave like health and disease? For a man is not healthy and sick at the same time, nor does he lose health and disease at the same time.

**CALLICLES:** What do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** Take any part of the body as an example. Do a man's eyes ever suffer from the disease called ophthalmia?

**CALLICLES:** They do.

**SOCRATES:** But they are not healthy at the same time?

**CALLICLES:** No.

**SOCRATES:** And when he is rid of the disease, does his health then cease? Do disease and health depart at the same moment?

**CALLICLES:** Not at all.

**SOCRATES:** For that would be wonderful and absurd, I think.

**CALLICLES:** Exceedingly so.

**SOCRATES:** But I think he acquires and loses each in turn.

**CALLICLES:** I agree.

**SOCRATES:** And does he not likewise receive and lose both good things and happiness, and their opposites, evils and misery, in turn?

**CALLICLES:** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** If, therefore, we find things which a man loses and possesses at the same time, it is clear that these things are not the "good" and the "evil." Do we agree on this? Consider your answer carefully.

**CALLICLES:** I agree without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Let us return to what we granted before. Did you say hungering was pleasant or painful? I ask about the hunger itself.

**CALLICLES:** Painful, certainly; yet for the hungry man to eat is pleasant.

**SOCRATES:** I understand. But hunger itself is painful, is it not?

**CALLICLES:** Painful.

**SOCRATES:** And thirst?

**CALLICLES:** Vehemently so.

**SOCRATES:** Shall I ask further, or do you concede that all want and desire is a participant in pain?

**CALLICLES:** I concede it...

<summary>Socrates uses the metaphors of leaky jars and the stone-curlew bird to challenge Callicles' hedonistic view that happiness is the constant fulfillment of desire. They begin a logical proof to show that pleasure and the good are not identical because pleasure and pain can coexist, whereas good and evil (like health and sickness) cannot.</summary>

seek no further. SOCRATES: So be it. But do you say that drinking when one is thirsty is pleasurable? CALLICLES: I do. SOCRATES: From this, then, as you say, to be thirsty is to be in pain. CALLICLES: It is. SOCRATES: But drinking is the filling of a deficiency and a pleasure. CALLICLES: Yes. SOCRATES: Therefore, in the very act of drinking, do you say one rejoices? CALLICLES: Most certainly. SOCRATES: But insofar as he is thirsty, he is in pain? CALLICLES: Surely. SOCRATES: Do you perceive then what follows: namely, that you admit to rejoicing and feeling pain at the same time, when you say the thirsty man drinks? Or does this not happen simultaneously in the same place and time, whether you wish it to be in the soul or in the body? It makes no difference, I think. Is it so, or otherwise? CALLICLES: It is so. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, you said it was impossible to be happy and unhappy at the same time. CALLICLES: Indeed. SOCRATES: Yet you have confessed that one can feel pain and joy simultaneously. CALLICLES: So it appears. SOCRATES: Therefore, to rejoice is not the same as to be happy, nor is to feel pain the same as to be unhappy. And thus, pleasure is something other than the Good. CALLICLES: I do not know what you are dreaming up, Socrates. SOCRATES: On the contrary, you know; but you do not wish to admit it, Callicles. But go on, I pray, by answering; for you are wandering further <note>original: "vltro em̃ deliras" - implies wandering from the point or talking nonsense</note> so that you may recognize how wise you are, you who chastise me. Does not each of us cease to be thirsty, and at the same time cease to rejoice because of the drink? CALLICLES: I do not know what you are saying. GORGIAS: Not so, Callicles! Rather, answer for our sake, so that the dispute may be concluded. CALLICLES: But Socrates is always like this, Gorgias. He searches out and refutes things that are tiny and of no importance. GORGIAS: What does it matter to you? For this is not your duty, Callicles; but permit him to argue as he sees fit. CALLICLES: Ask then, Socrates, about these narrow and worthless things, since it pleases Gorgias. SOCRATES: Are you so blessed, Callicles, as to have attained the Great Mysteries before the Lesser? <note>A reference to the Eleusinian Mysteries; Socrates is mocking Callicles for thinking he is above basic logic.</note> I did not think it was permitted. But now, resuming from where you left off, answer. Does one not cease to be thirsty and to rejoice at the same time? CALLICLES: I grant it. SOCRATES: And does he not also cease to be hungry and have other desires at the same time as the pleasures? CALLICLES: It is so. SOCRATES: Does he not therefore cease to have both pains and pleasures at the same time? CALLICLES: Yes. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, he does not cease from good things and bad things at the same time, as you just admitted. Do you not admit it now? CALLICLES: Indeed. But what of it? SOCRATES: Surely, my friend, good things and pleasurable things are not the same, nor are bad things the same as painful things. For one ceases from the latter at the same time, but from the former not at all, as they are different. By what reasoning, then, would pleasurable things be the same as good things, or painful things the same as bad? Now, if you wish, consider it in this way again. For I think that even in this manner you will not agree with yourself. Attend then: do you not call good men good by the presence of good things, just as you call those beautiful in whom beauty is present? CALLICLES: Indeed. SOCRATES: What then? Do you call foolish and cowardly men good? Certainly not a moment ago; rather, you called the brave and the wise good. Do you not call these very ones good? CALLICLES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: What then: have you ever seen a foolish child filled with pleasure? CALLICLES: I have. SOCRATES: And have you ever seen a foolish man affected by pleasure? CALLICLES: I believe I have. But to what end is this? SOCRATES: It matters not; just answer. CALLICLES: I have seen it. SOCRATES: What then? Have you seen a man of sound mind feeling pain and rejoicing? CALLICLES: Surely. SOCRATES: Which of them rejoice and feel pain more: the wise or the foolish? CALLICLES: I think there is not much difference. SOCRATES: That is enough. In war, have you ever seen a cowardly man? CALLICLES: Why not? SOCRATES: When the enemies retreated, which seemed to you to rejoice more: the cowards or the brave? CALLICLES: Both seemed to me to rejoice more, or at least nearly the same. SOCRATES: It matters not. Therefore, even cowards rejoice. CALLICLES: Greatly. SOCRATES: And the foolish, as it appears. CALLICLES: Them too. SOCRATES: But when the enemy approaches, do only the cowards feel pain, or also the brave? CALLICLES: Both. SOCRATES: Equally? CALLICLES: Perhaps the cowards more. SOCRATES: And when they depart, do they not rejoice more? CALLICLES: Perhaps. SOCRATES: Therefore, do not the foolish and the wise, and the cowards and the brave, feel pain and rejoice similarly, as you say—yet the cowards more than the brave? CALLICLES: I say so indeed. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, the wise and the brave are good, while the cowards and the foolish are bad. CALLICLES: It is so. SOCRATES: For which reason, both the good and the bad rejoice and feel pain equally. CALLICLES: I agree. SOCRATES: Are those who are good and those who are bad therefore equally good and bad? Or rather, are only the good ones good, and the bad ones bad? CALLICLES: By Jove, I do not know what you are entangling. SOCRATES: Do you not know you said that the good are good by the presence of good things, and the bad by the presence of bad things? And that pleasures are good things, and pains are bad things? CALLICLES: Indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, are not good things—namely, pleasures—present in those who are delighted, if indeed they are delighted? CALLICLES: What prevents it? SOCRATES: And are they not good when good things are present? CALLICLES: They are. SOCRATES: And bad things are present in those who feel pain, namely the pains themselves? CALLICLES: They are. SOCRATES: And you say the bad are bad by the presence of bad things. Do you not still say so? CALLICLES: Indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, those who rejoice are good, and those who feel pain are bad. CALLICLES: Most certainly. SOCRATES: And those who feel it more are surely more so; those who feel it less, less; and those who feel it equally, are equally so. CALLICLES: Yes. SOCRATES: Do you not say that the wise and the foolish, and again the cowards and the brave, rejoice and feel pain equally? Or even the cowards more? CALLICLES: I do. SOCRATES: Consider then with me what results for us from these things which have been granted. For they say it is a beautiful thing to say and consider beautiful things twice and even thrice.

We said that the wise and brave man is good, did we not? CALLICLES: We did. SOCRATES: And the foolish and cowardly man is bad? CALLICLES: Entirely. SOCRATES: And again, that he who rejoices is good? # GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC. FOLIO 144.

Are you being crafty? You play with me as if I were a child, sometimes presenting things one way, sometimes another, trying to deceive me. I did not think at the start that I would be willingly deceived by you, since you are a friend. But now you have misled me greatly; and it seems, as the old proverb goes, <margin>Proverb: I am led by necessity</margin> I am necessarily led to make the best of the current situation and accept what you give me. What you are now proposing is this: that some pleasures are good, while others are bad; is that not so?

CALLICLES. Without a doubt.

SOCRATES. And are not the good ones those that are useful? And the bad ones those that are harmful?

CALLICLES. Certainly.

SOCRATES. And the useful ones are those that bring about some good, while the harmful ones bring about some evil?

CALLICLES. I agree.

SOCRATES. Now, do you mean such pleasures as those of the body we were just speaking of—eating and drinking? Do those among them that produce health in the body, or strength, or some other bodily virtue, count as good, while those that produce the opposite are bad?

CALLICLES. Exactly.

SOCRATES. And in the same way, are some pains good and others bad?

CALLICLES. Nothing prevents it.

SOCRATES. Then we ought to choose and pursue the good pleasures and pains?

CALLICLES. Exactly.

SOCRATES. And the bad ones not at all?

CALLICLES. That is clear.

SOCRATES. For Polus and I agreed that all things should be done for the sake of what is good; do you remember? And does it seem the same to you—that the good is the end <note>The "end" or *finis* refers to the ultimate goal or purpose of an action.</note> of all actions, and for its sake all other things are to be done, but the good is not done for the sake of the rest? Do you join us as a third in this opinion?

CALLICLES. I do.

SOCRATES. Therefore, for the sake of good things, we must pursue both other things and pleasures; we must not pursue good things for the sake of pleasures.

CALLICLES. Exactly.

SOCRATES. Now, is it the task of any ordinary man to choose which of these delightful things are good and which are bad? Or does it rather require a man of skill <term>artificiosi viri</term> <note>original: *artificiosi viri*. Refers to a person possessing a technical "art" or *techne*, rather than just intuition.</note>?

CALLICLES. A man of skill.

SOCRATES. Let us then recall what I was saying to Polus and Gorgias. I said, if you remember, that there are certain preparatory faculties: some that aim only at pleasure, being ignorant of what is better or worse; and others that know what is good or bad. Among those concerned with pleasure, I placed the "knack" of cookery <note>original: *coquinariam peritiam*. Socrates argues cooking is a mere habit of pleasing the palate, not a science of health.</note> regarding the body, but not as an art; but among those that aim at the good, I placed the art of medicine. And by Jove the god of friendship, I pray you, Callicles, do not play games with me; do not answer whatever happens to occur to you, nor again take these things from me as if I were joking. For you see that our conversation is about a matter which a man of sound mind should strive to know above all else: namely, how one ought to live. Should it be the way you urge me, by doing those things you say are the duties of a man—speaking before the people, practicing oratory, and governing the state as you all do now? Or should one embrace this philosophical life, and in what way does this life differ from that one? Perhaps it is worthwhile, as I began to do a little while ago, to distinguish between them; and then, once we have agreed on the distinction, if these are indeed two different lives, to consider what the difference is and which one should be lived. Perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying.

CALLICLES. Not yet, certainly.

SOCRATES. Then I will speak more plainly to you. Since you and I have confessed that there is something called "the good" and something called "the pleasant," but that the pleasant is different from the good, and that there is a certain study and preparation for acquiring each of them—one being the hunt for the good, the other for pleasure—first, before I go further, do you agree with me on this or not?

CALLICLES. I agree.

SOCRATES. Come then, agree with me also on what I said to those men, if I seemed to you then to speak the truth. I said that cookery did not seem to me to be an art, but a certain knack. Medicine, however, is an art, because <margin>Why medicine is an art.</margin> the faculty of medicine considers the nature of that which it treats and the cause of the things it does, and can give a rational account of each of these. But the other faculty, the nurse of pleasure, proceeds toward that pleasure—upon which its whole study is focused—entirely without art, neither considering the nature of the pleasure itself nor the cause. It is entirely reckless, so to speak, having no regard for anything, but relying solely on habit and experience and the memory <margin>See what things are in a "knack."</margin> of what usually happens; it provides pleasures through study. Consider these things first: whether you think this has been sufficiently stated. Do you think there are also certain such faculties regarding the soul? Some being artistic, having a care for what is best for the soul; but others neglecting that, thinking only (as we said of the body) how they might be able to delight the soul. These do not think at all whether the pleasure is better or worse, nor do they care for anything other than how they may delight it, whether for better or for worse. To me, Callicles, there seem to be such faculties, and I call that whole service "flattery," whether it concerns the soul or the body or anything else whose pleasure one pursues without any regard for better or worse. Do you agree with us in this opinion, or do you dissent?

CALLICLES. Not at all; rather, I agree, so that your argument may reach a conclusion and to gratify Gorgias here.

SOCRATES. Does this apply only to one soul? Is it not the same for two, or many?

CALLICLES. Not so; it is the same for two and for many.

SOCRATES. Then can one not also gratify many people gathered together without any regard for what is best?

CALLICLES. So I believe.

SOCRATES. Can you say which studies these are that do this? Or rather, if you wish, as I ask about each one that seems so to you, grant that it is such. If it is not, deny it. First, let us consider flute-playing: does it not seem to you, Callicles, to be such a thing that cares for nothing other than delighting the ears?

CALLICLES. It seems so to me.

SOCRATES. And are not all others of that kind, such as the art of the lyre used in contests?

CALLICLES. Certainly.

SOCRATES. What about the teaching of choruses and the poetry of dithyrambs <note>Dithyrambs were wild, choral hymns sung in honor of Dionysus.</note>? Does it not seem to be something of that sort? Or do you think Cinesias, the son of Meles, cares to say anything that would make the listeners better? Or rather, does he care for what might please the theatrical crowd?

CALLICLES. That is certainly manifest, Socrates, regarding Cinesias.

SOCRATES. And his father Meles—did he look toward what is best?

<summary>Socrates argues that true arts (like medicine) seek the good and can explain their methods, while "knacks" (like cookery or popular music) merely aim to please the audience without regard for their well-being. Callicles reluctantly agrees that many public performances are forms of flattery rather than paths to virtue.</summary>

Which indeed we do not greatly approve of, since we have confessed it to be a form of flattery. **CAL.** So it is, indeed.

**SO.** Come then, what shall we say of that rhetoric which they use toward the Athenian people and the peoples of other cities of free men? What kind of rhetoric is this? Do the orators seem to you to always direct their words toward what is best: aiming only at this: by what means the citizens may become as good as possible through their speeches? Or do these men also hunt for the favor of the listeners, seeking only their own private grace, neglecting the public good: and treating the people like children, intent only on favor: but caring nothing whether they become better or worse because of this? **CAL.** That which you ask is not simple. For there are some who, in speaking, consult the utility of the citizens: and there are others such as you yourself describe. **SO.** That is enough. Let us see now, considering it plainly, whether any of these men existed as such. Come, tell me: a good man, speaking toward what is best, will not speak at random: but will certainly look toward something: just as all other craftsmen do: each of whom looks toward his own work: he does not choose by chance what he brings to his work: but so that the work may attain some form according to the model set before him. Just as if it pleases you to look at painters, and architects, and shipbuilders, and all other craftsmen. Any one of them disposes each thing in a certain order everywhere: and forces some things to fit and agree with others, until he constitutes a whole adorned with a certain order. Therefore, all craftsmen do this: and those whom we were calling physical trainers <term>paedotriuæ</term> <note>Teachers of gymnastics and physical discipline</note> in the previous parts: and physicians similarly do this regarding the body. For they adorn and compose it. Do we confess that it is so, or not? **CAL.** Let it be so. **SO.** Therefore, a house having attained adornment and order will be good: if less so, it will be bad. **CAL.** I agree. **SO.** And a ship in the same way. **CAL.** In the same way. **SO.** And our bodies likewise. **CAL.** Likewise. **SO.** What then of the soul? If it is devoid of order, will it be good: or rather if it is possessed of order and adornment? **CAL.** It is necessary from the previous points to confess this also. **SO.** What then is the name for that which is produced in the body from order and adornment?

<margin>Health in the ordering of the body.</margin>

**CAL.** You mean health and strength, perhaps. **SO.** I do indeed. And what is the name for that which is produced in the soul from order and adornment? Try to find and express it, just as you did for the other. **CAL.** Why do you not say it yourself, O Socrates? **SO.** But if it pleases you, I shall say it: and you, if I seem to speak the truth, grant it: if not, refute it: and do not permit it in any way. To me indeed, it seems the name for the ordering of the body is "healthy": from which health and other bodily virtues arise in it. Is it so, or otherwise? **CAL.** So.

<margin>Legitimacy and law in the ordering of the soul: which is justice and temperance.</margin>

**SO.** And for the ordering and adornment of the soul, the name is "lawful" or "law": from which men become law-abiding and orderly. These indeed are justice and temperance <term>temperantia</term> <note>Self-control or moderation</note>. Do you agree, or not? **CAL.** So be it. **SO.** Will not, therefore, that skilled and good rhetorician, looking toward these things, apply his words to the souls of men? And will he not always intend all his actions, and whatever he may at any time grant or deny, to this end: that justice indeed may be present in the souls of the citizens, and injustice be absent: again, that temperance may be present, and intemperance be cast out: and that the other virtues may be held, and wickedness expelled? Do you grant this, or not? **CAL.** I grant it indeed. **SO.** What then does it profit, O Callicles, to offer many and most sweet foods to a body that is sick and ill-affected, or drink, or anything else which will not be beneficial: that is...

And he who acts justly and piously must necessarily be just and pious. Such is the truth. Moreover, he must be brave. For it is not the part of a temperate man to pursue or flee otherwise than is fitting. Rather, he ought to flee, pursue, and also endure individual things, men, pleasures, and pains where it is necessary. Therefore, it is entirely necessary, Callicles, that the temperate man—since, as we said, he is just, brave, and pious—is perfectly good. And the good man acts well and honorably in whatever he does. And he who acts well is happy and blessed. But the wicked man who acts poorly is miserable. But if he or anyone else among his associates should need it, whether a private citizen or a city, he must be restrained by the application of punishment if he is to be happy. And those things which you thought Polus conceded out of shame were actually true: namely, that to do an injury is as much more disgraceful than to suffer one as it is worse; and that he who is to be a proper orator must be just, and must know what things are just. This is what Polus said Gorgias <note>The text reads *Georgiam*, likely an OCR error for *Gorgiam*.</note> conceded out of shame.

Since these things are so, let us consider those matters for which you reproach me: whether it is said correctly or not that I am unable to bring help either to myself or to my friends and household, nor to deliver them from the greatest dangers. You say I am in the power and whim of anyone, just as the most abject people are; whether someone wishes to strike me (as you boastfully said) upon the cheek, or seize my money, or expel me from the city, or even inflict the ultimate punishment <note>Death.</note>. You said that to be in such a state is the most disgraceful of all things.

But my opinion—already stated many times, and to be stated again despite any objection—is the opposite: namely, that it is not the most disgraceful thing, O Callicles, to be struck on the cheek unjustly, or to have one's body or purse cut; but to strike and cut me unjustly is both more disgraceful and worse for the one doing it. Likewise, to steal, to lead into slavery, to dig through walls <note>A common term for burglary in antiquity.</note>, and in short, to do any injury whatsoever, is both worse and more disgraceful for the one who does it than for the one who receives it. These things, having been conceded by us above, are held and bound—if I may use a somewhat rustic expression—with **iron and adamantine reasons**; by which I am led to feel this way. Unless you, or someone stronger than you, can break them, it is impossible for anyone speaking otherwise than I do now to speak correctly. For to me, the argument always remains the same: that I do not know how these things are, yet of all those with whom I have spoken until now (just as with you today), no one has ever been able to speak otherwise without appearing ridiculous.

Therefore, I set these things down again as being so. And if they are so, and injustice is the greatest of evils to the one who commits it, and if, being the greatest, it is judged even greater if the one who did it never pays the penalty: what help is it that a man cannot bring to himself, for which he should truly be despised? Is it not that which removes the greatest harm from us? Surely it must be most disgraceful not to be able to provide such help to oneself, one's friends, and one's kin. The second most disgraceful is not being able to help against the second evil, the third against the third, and so on, according to the magnitude of each evil. Thus, it is beautiful to be able to bring aid, and disgraceful not to be able to. Is it any other way than this, Callicles?

**CALLICLES:** Certainly not otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** Since, therefore, there are these two things—doing an injury and suffering one—we say that to inflict it is the greater evil, and to suffer it is the lesser. What help, then, should someone provide for himself to gain the advantage of neither inflicting nor receiving injury? Is it **power** or **will**? I put it this way: if someone does not wish to suffer injury, will he not suffer it? Or will he only avoid suffering it if he provides himself with power?

**CALLICLES:** It is certain he needs power.

**SOCRATES:** What about inflicting injury? If someone does not wish to do wrong, will that will be a sufficient remedy? For he will not inflict injury. Or must a certain power and art <note>original: *ars*, meaning a skill or systematic knowledge</note> be acquired for this, which unless one learns and practices it, he will do injury? Why do you not answer me at least on this, Callicles? Do Polus and I seem to you to have been correctly compelled by the previous reasons or not, when we confessed that no one does injury willingly, but that all who inflict it do so against their will?

**CALLICLES:** Let it be so for you, Socrates, so that you may conclude this discussion.

**SOCRATES:** For this purpose, then, does it seem that a certain power and art must be acquired, so that we do not do injury to anyone?

**CALLICLES:** Entirely so.

**SOCRATES:** What then is the art for acquiring the faculty by which one suffers either no injury or the very least? Consider if you see it the same way I do. To me, it seems one must either obtain the leadership in the Republic, or seize a tyranny, or have dealings with the current government.

**CALLICLES:** You see, Socrates, how ready I am to approve if you say something correctly. This seems to me to have been said by you exceedingly well.

**SOCRATES:** Consider this further, if I seem to speak rightly. It seems to me that each person is a friend to another most of all when, as the ancient and wise teach, they are most alike. Do you not agree?

**CALLICLES:** I do.

**SOCRATES:** Where a fierce and unrefined tyrant rules, if there is someone in that city much better than he, will the tyrant not fear him? And can he ever be a friend to him with his whole heart?

**CALLICLES:** So it happens.

**SOCRATES:** Nor if he were much worse; for the tyrant will despise him, and never be affected toward him as toward a friend.

**CALLICLES:** You speak the truth.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the only one who can be a friend to him, worthy of esteem in his eyes, is one who is similar in character, praising and blaming the same things, and who is willing to be subject to the master and obey him. This man will surely have great power in that state; no one will inflict injury on him with impunity. Is it not so?

**CALLICLES:** Yes.

...is able to acquire great power by this very method: so that no one can inflict injury upon him. Indeed, I think a state of life of this kind is most suited for this: so that he can do as many injuries as possible and entirely escape the punishment for those injuries. Is it not so? CALLICLES: It appears so. SOCRATES: Will he not then be occupied by the greatest evil, since he is shameful and has become corrupted through the imitation of his master and by having similar power? CALLICLES: I do not know by what speech, O Socrates, you turn things upside down. <note>original: "sursum deorsumque vertas" - a common idiom for Socrates's tendency to subvert conventional logic.</note> Do you not know that he who imitates in this way can kill the one who does not imitate, if he only wishes, and strip him of his property? SOCRATES: I know it indeed, my good Callicles, unless I am deaf; since I have heard this same thing frequently not only from you, but also from Polus recently, and from almost everyone else in the city. But listen to me: he will certainly kill him, if he wishes; but a wicked man will kill the honorable and good man. CALLICLES: But this is exactly what is so grievous. SOCRATES: Not certainly to a man who has a mind, as your own speech indicates. Or do you think a man should labor greatly for this: that he may live as long as possible, and meditate on those arts which can always save us from dangers, such as rhetoric is, which you exhort me to take up, as it often saves us in the courts? CALLICLES: By Jove, I advise you rightly! SOCRATES: What then, best of men! Does the skill of swimming seem noble to you? CALLICLES: Not by Jove. SOCRATES: And yet this saves men from death whenever they fall into a place where such knowledge is needed. But if this seems small to you, I will bring forward a greater one than this, namely the art of navigation <note>original: "gubernatoria" - the art of the pilot or steersman.</note>, which saves not only lives, but also bodies and money from extreme dangers, no differently than rhetoric. And yet this art is humble and modest; not boastful, nor bombastic, as if it had achieved something miraculous. But though it performs the same things as rhetoric, if it saves us from Aegina to here, it demands only two coins. If indeed it brings us back safe from Egypt or the Pontus <note>The Black Sea region.</note>, as I was just saying—us and our children, wives, and riches—it demands two drachmas. And the man himself, endowed with this art who has performed these things, when he descends and walks along the shore by the sea and his ship, by no means carries himself high nor is he puffed up. For he perceives, I think, that it is uncertain whether he has benefited or harmed those whom he saved from being submerged in the waves; understanding that he has brought back those who are not a bit better in body or soul than they were when they first entered the ship. He considers, therefore, that if someone suffering from great and incurable diseases of the body does not perish in the sea, this man is miserable because he did not die, and has received no utility from him. But if someone has many incurable diseases in his soul, which is more precious than the body, must this man live? And would it bring him utility if someone saves him, whether from the sea, or from the court, or from elsewhere? But surely he knows that it is not expedient for a shameful man to live. For it is necessary that he live badly. Wherefore there is no law by which a pilot, however much he saves us, can boast and be held in honor; nor, O wonderful man, the maker of machines <term>machinarum faber</term><note>An engineer or architect of war machines.</note> himself, who can sometimes save no less than a pilot, or even a leader of an army, or anyone else; since he sometimes provides safety to entire cities. So much so that you could not even compare a lawyer to him. And if he wished, Callicles, to extol his business as you do, he would surely overwhelm you with words, exhorting everyone to become makers of machines, as if all other things were of no moment. For he would not lack material. Nevertheless, you would nonetheless despise him and his art, and as if in insult you would call him a "mechanic" <note>original: "machinarium" - used here as a derogatory term for a manual laborer or technician.</note>; nor would you wish to give your daughter to his son, nor would you take his daughter for yourself. Although, from what reasons you praise your own faculty, in what way can you justly despise the mechanic or the others whom I mentioned a little while ago? I think you believe yourself to be better and born of better stock. But if "the better" is not what I say it is, but if virtue is this very thing—to save oneself and one's own, whatever sort of person one may be—then your reproach against the mechanic or the physician or other arts, as many as were invented for the sake of safety, is certainly ridiculous. But, O blessed one, see whether the generous and the good be something other than saving and being saved. For a man who is truly a man ought not to desire to live for however much time; nor is this life to be loved; but he ought to leave this care to God, and, giving faith to the women who say that no one can escape fate, <margin>The saying of women: that no one can escape fate.</margin> he should consider this above all: by what reasoning he may live as well as possible in this very time in which he spends his life. Is it by making himself very similar to the citizens with whom he lives? And must you now turn out most similar to the Athenian people if you are to be a friend to them and of great authority among the people? Consider therefore whether this is expedient for you and for me, or not; lest that happen to us, O blessed man, which they say happens to the Thessalian women who draw down the moon with their dearest ones: that the choice of this power becomes ours. <note>A reference to the belief that Thessalian witches could draw down the moon, but at the cost of their own sight or the lives of their kin.</note> But if you think any man will deliver such an art by which you may be made powerful in this city, while you are dissimilar to the public government, whether better or worse, you do not think rightly at all, as it seems to me, O Callicles. For one must not be an imitator, but by nature very similar to them, if you are to achieve anything great toward gaining the goodwill of the Athenian people; and by Jove, moreover, the son of Pyrilampes. <note>A reference to Demus, the son of Pyrilampes, whom Callicles was said to love; also a pun on "Demos," the people.</note> Whoever makes you similar to these will make you as you desire, so that you may be a statesman and a rhetorician. For all are delighted by those words which are consistent with their own character, and are disturbed by different ones. Unless you, O charming head, <margin>Charming head.</margin> <note>A Greek idiom of endearment or irony: "lepidum caput."</note> bring forward something else. Shall I say anything to these things, O Callicles? CALLICLES: I do not know how, but you seem to speak well, O Socrates. It happens to me, however, what is accustomed to happen to many others: for I do not have great faith in you. SOCRATES: The love of the people...

# TWENTY-FOURTH BOOK.

ii 2

...the people, O Callicles, implanted in you, resists me; but if we consider these same things more often and more deeply, perhaps they will seem more persuasive to you. Remember, then, that two types of preparation were described by us, pertaining both to the body and to the soul. One of these aims at pleasure; the other aims at what is best, not gratifying, but resisting. Did we not define these in the previous sections? CALLICLES. Entirely so. SOCRATES. And the one that declines toward pleasure is slavish; and it is nothing other than flattery, is it not? CALLICLES. Let it be as you please. SOCRATES. But the other strives so that whatever we care for—whether soul or body—becomes as excellent as possible. CALLICLES. Altogether. SOCRATES. Therefore, we must undertake the care of the state and the citizens in such a way that we make the citizens themselves good. Otherwise, as we remembered earlier, it is of no use to confer any other benefit unless the mind of those who are to receive either much money, or power, or any other authority, is honorable and good. Do we posit that it is so, or not? CALLICLES. Entirely, if it pleases you. SOCRATES. If, therefore, we were encouraging each other, O Callicles, while handling public civil affairs regarding the great buildings of walls, or shipyards, or temples: would it not be necessary for us to consider ourselves and recognize first whether we have the knowledge of that art or not, and from whom we learned it? And would it be necessary for that to happen or not? CALLICLES. Entirely. SOCRATES. Secondly, we should ask if we have ever constructed any building privately for ourselves or for our friends, and whether such a structure is beautiful or ugly.

<margin>Regarding the proof held by a master and the work.</margin>
For if we found that we had good and outstanding masters, and that many and noble buildings were built both together with the masters and by ourselves, then finally it would be consistent with reason to turn ourselves to public works. But if we can show neither our master nor any buildings—or none well constructed—it would certainly be foolish to attempt public works and to encourage each other toward them. Do we admit these things are said correctly, or not? CALLICLES. Entirely. SOCRATES. Is it not similarly so in all other things? And if we were encouraging each other while handling civil affairs, as if we were fit to be physicians, we ought to consider each other, I you and you me, in this manner: "Come, by the gods, how is Socrates himself disposed toward health of body? Or what other person, whether free or slave, has escaped from disease by the work of Socrates?" I also ought to consider the same regarding you; and unless we found someone who had been made healthy through us, whether of foreigners or citizens, whether man or woman, by Jove, O Callicles, it would be truly ridiculous to have proceeded to such a point of madness that, before we have attempted many things privately and perfected many things, and practiced the art abundantly—<note>original: "figulariam in ipso vase discere"</note> to begin learning the potter's craft on the large jar itself, as the saying goes—we should approach the republic ourselves and provoke others to it. Would you not think that attempting that is the mark of a foolish man? CALLICLES. Certainly. SOCRATES. But truly, O best of men, since you have recently begun to administer the republic, and you even exhort me, and reproach me for not doing so, should we not consider each other in turn? "Come now, Callicles, which of the citizens has he rendered better?" Is there anyone who, while previously being wicked and unjust and incontinent and unwise, finally became honorable and good through the work of Callicles, whether foreigner, or citizen, or slave, or free? Tell me, if someone were to demand this of you, what will you answer, O Callicles? Whom will you bring forward who was ever made better by your company? Or does it loathe you to answer if any such work of yours was done by you privately before you turned yourself to the republic? CALLICLES. You are being contentious, O Socrates. SOCRATES. But I do not ask this for the sake of contention, but truly out of a desire for learning how you think the public should be administered by us: whether we should have any other concern around the republic than that the citizens be made the best possible. Have we not already confessed many times that this is what a civil man must do? Have we confessed it? Answer, I pray. Certainly we have confessed it; let me answer for you. If, therefore, a good man ought to devote himself to this in his city, now calling it to memory, I would like you to tell me whether those whom you mentioned in the previous sections still seem to you to have been good men: Pericles, Cimon, Miltiades, Themistocles. CALLICLES. To me, indeed. SOCRATES. If they were good men, did not each one of them render the citizens better from being worse? Is it not so? CALLICLES. So it is. SOCRATES. If it is so: therefore, when Pericles first began to speak to the people, the Athenians were worse than when he held his last speech to them. CALLICLES. Perhaps. SOCRATES. It is not permitted, O best man, to say "perhaps." For it follows necessarily from those things we have granted, if only he was a good citizen. CALLICLES. What then? SOCRATES. Nothing. But tell me this: do the Athenians say they were made better by the work of Pericles, or altogether the opposite, corrupted by him? Indeed, I hear that Pericles made the Athenians lazy, cowardly, talkative, and greedy, and that he first introduced mercenary wages <note>Socrates refers to the introduction of pay for jury duty and other public services, which critics argued made the populace idle.</note>. CALLICLES. You hear these things from those who have "broken ears," O Socrates <note>A Greek idiom for those who were fans of the Spartan lifestyle (who often had cauliflower ears from wrestling) and were thus critics of Athenian democracy.</note>. SOCRATES. But I no longer just hear these things, I know them very clearly, both I and you: namely, that Pericles was held in great value from the beginning, and the Athenians did not pass any shameful sentence against him while they were "wicked"; but after they were made "honorable and good" by him, at the end of his life they condemned him for theft, and they were nearly on the verge of punishing him with the ultimate penalty as a bad man. CALLICLES. What then? Did Pericles turn out to be a bad man because of that? SOCRATES. Such a caretaker of donkeys and horses and men is seen as bad: if, when he received them, they were neither kickers, nor givers of head-butts, nor biters, yet they developed these vices out of wildness. Or does it seem to you that a caretaker of any animal is bad who, having received it tame, rendered it more wild than he received it? Does it seem so to you or not? CALLICLES. I grant it, indeed, to do you a favor. SOCRATES. Furthermore, gratify me in this by answering whether man is one of the animals or not. CALLICLES. Why do you ask? SOCRATES. Did Pericles not have the care of men? CALLICLES. He did. SOCRATES. What then? Should they not, as we just agreed, have been made more just from being less just by him, if indeed he who cared for them was skilled in civil affairs? CALLICLES. Entirely. SOCRATES. Are not the just "tame," as Homer says? But what do you say? Is it not similarly so? CALLICLES. I say so. SOCRATES. Yet he rendered them more wild than he had received them, and that against himself, which he certainly would have least desired. CALLICLES. Do you want me to agree with you? SOCRATES. If I seem to you to speak the truth. CALLICLES. Let it be.
