# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, if they made them more wild, they made them more unjust and worse. **CALLICLES.** So be it. **SOCRATES.** Then Pericles was not a good citizen in administering the state, as these facts show. **CALLICLES.** Not as you say. **SOCRATES.** By Jove, nor as you say, according to what you admit. But tell me again about Cimon: did not those very people he cared for ostracize him so they would not hear his voice for ten years? <note>Cimon was a famous Athenian statesman and general exiled by ostracism in 461 BCE.</note> Furthermore, they did the same against Themistocles and condemned him to exile besides. And Miltiades, who fought at Marathon, they decreed should be cast into the pit of the prison; and if the magistrate had not stood in the way, he would have surely fallen in. Yet truly, if these had been good men, as you say, they would never have suffered such things. For good charioteers do not fall out at the beginning; but after they have cared for the horses and have themselves become better charioteers, then they fall out? Surely it is not so, as it seems to me, in chariot-driving or in any other work. **CALLICLES.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, what was said by us earlier was true: namely, that we know of no man who has existed in this city who should be considered a good citizen in the republic. You indeed confessed that none of those who are now living are such; but of those who preceded, you said some existed, and among them you chose these men above the rest. Yet these have appeared to behave no differently in this matter than those who are now. Wherefore, if these were orators, they used neither true rhetoric—otherwise they would never have fallen—nor the flattering kind. **CALLICLES.** Yet it is a far cry, Socrates, that any of those who are now should have performed such deeds as any of those men performed. **SOCRATES.** O blessed man, I do not blame them insofar as it pertains to the administration of the city; indeed, in this matter they seem to me to have been more diligent than our contemporaries, and more fit for providing those things which the city desired. But in that which requires chastening the desires of the citizens, and not yielding to them, but rather by persuading and compelling them to lead them to that very point where the citizens will be better: in this, so to speak, there is no difference between these and those. This alone is the duty of a good citizen. And yet I confess to you that they were more fit than these men for providing ships, dockyards, walls, and many other such things for the republic. Therefore, you and I are revolving back into a ridiculous dispute: for in all this discussion we are constantly carried around the same point, being ignorant of what we are saying to one another. For I think you have often conceded and recognized that this care is twofold, concerning both the body and the soul. One part is ministerial, through which the things the body desires are provided: such as food if it hungers, drink if it thirsts, clothes, bedding, shoes, and other things required for the use of the body if it is cold. And indeed, I speak to you through these images on purpose so you may understand more easily: that the provider of these is either a shopkeeper, or a merchant, or a craftsman of some of these things; namely a baker, or a cook, or a weaver, or a shoemaker, or a tanner. And it is no wonder that one who is such appears to be a caretaker of the body, both to himself and to others who are ignorant. But there is besides a certain art of gymnastics and medicine, in which the care of the body truly consists. It is proper for these arts to command the others and to use their works, because they have knowledge of what is good and bad for the body regarding nourishment and health. This is ignored by all these others. For which reason it must be said: these others are servile, ministerial, and illiberal concerning the cultivation of the body, while gymnastics and medicine rightly rule over them. You seem to me at times to recognize that these same things apply to the soul; and you concede to me as if understanding what I say. But a little later you bring forward men who were once famous and good in this city; and when I ask who they were, you seem to me to offer men very similar in regard to the republic as if, when I asked who were or are good caretakers of the bodies in gymnastics, you answered me quite seriously: Thearion the baker, and Mithecus who wrote on the Sicilian art of cooking, and Sarabus the shopkeeper—as if these were wonderful cultivators of bodies because one prepared sweet breads, another feasts, and another wine. Perhaps, therefore, you would be indignant if I said to you: "O good man, you understand nothing of gymnastics. For you bring forward to me ministers and champions of desires, who in no way judge what is honorable or good in these things, but fulfill the bodies of men with whatever happens to fatten them." These men are even praised by the people, even though they have wasted away their old flesh through excessive filling. And later, when disease arrives, those who were so nourished accuse those who advised them later out of ignorance, but they in no way accuse those who nourished them for their lusts. When, I say, such a filling, being immoderate, finally brings on disease, then they complain and find fault with the present advisors; and they even inflict injury if they can; but those prior ones who gave cause for the disease, they extol with praises. And then, O Callicles, you do something very similar, praising men who nourished these people and filled them with those things for which a desire had come; men who they say made the city great. But they do not perceive that the city is now swollen and diseased within because of those ancient leaders. For without temperance and justice, they have filled this city with harbors, dockyards, walls, tributes, taxes, and such trifles. Therefore, when the disease breaks out, then those who currently govern the republic are blamed. But Themistocles himself, and Cimon, and Pericles, who were the cause of the evils, are praised. And you, perhaps, unless you take care, will be caught, along with my friend Alcibiades, when the old things are lost along with those that were acquired; not that you are the cause of the evils, but you are a cause along with the others. And I see a foolish thing now and hear of it regarding those ancients. For I perceive that when the city attempts to condemn any of those who are engaged in the republic for injustice, they take it heavily and suffer as if they were being afflicted by an injustice, having conferred many benefits upon the republic. Indeed, they say they are being unjustly condemned by it. This is entirely false. For a governor of a republic is never unjustly condemned by the city over which he presides. It seems the same thing happens to those engaged in the republic as to the sophists. For the sophists, though wise in other things, behave absurdly in this one: that while they affirm they teach virtues, they often accuse their disciples of being ungrateful and unjust, because having received good things from them, they return no payment or thanks.

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

...nothing is more foreign to reason: namely, that men who have been made good and just, and who have been removed from the works of injustice by the labor of a teacher, and are endowed with justice, should then inflict injuries upon those very teachers through that same injustice which they do not possess. Or does all this not seem absurd to you? In truth, Callicles, you have compelled me to play the orator <note>original: "concionari," meaning to deliver a public speech</note> because you are unwilling to respond.

**CALLICLES.** Can you not speak for yourself unless someone responds to you?

**SOCRATES.** I seem able to; at least now I am drawing out long speeches since you do not wish to answer me. But, my good man, tell me by Zeus, the god of friendship, does it not seem contrary to reason to you that someone who says he has made another person good should then complain about that same person—as if the one made good by him were actually wicked?

**CALLICLES.** It certainly seems so to me.

**SOCRATES.** Do you not hear those who profess to teach virtue <note>The Sophists</note> making such complaints?

**CALLICLES.** I do indeed; but what can you say of men of no value?

**SOCRATES.** But what would you say of those who claim to lead the state, and to think diligently on how it might become the best, yet turn around and accuse it, as happens, as if it were the worst? Do you think these men differ from the others? Truly, the Sophist and the Orator are the same thing, or something very near and similar, as I was saying to Polus. But you, through ignorance, think Rhetoric is something magnificent, while you despise Sophistry. Yet in truth, Sophistry is more beautiful than Rhetoric, just as the art of law-giving is more beautiful than the judicial art, and gymnastics more beautiful than medicine. I think that only public speakers and Sophists should be least permitted to complain about that which they themselves teach, as if it were an evil to them. Otherwise, in that very accusation, they would simultaneously incriminate themselves, as if they had benefited nothing for those to whom they claim to have brought utility. Is this not how it stands?

**CALLICLES.** Exactly so.

**SOCRATES.** And to have bestowed a benefit without a fee, as is consistent, was fitting only for these men, if indeed they spoke the truth. For when someone receives other benefits—for instance, becoming fast through a gymnastics master—he might perhaps not return the favor unless a precaution was taken that he pay the fee as soon as he became fast enough. For it is not by slowness, I think, that men do injury, but by injustice. Is it not?

**CALLICLES.** Yes.

**SOCRATES.** If someone, therefore, takes away this very thing—that is, injustice—the danger of injury would then be avoided. Truly, a benefit can be placed in safety by this alone: if one can truly make those upon whom it is conferred good. Is it not so?

**CALLICLES.** I agree.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, it seems that in other contracts it is not shameful to take precautions for oneself, such as for buildings and other crafts.

**CALLICLES.** It appears so.

**SOCRATES.** But for this faculty—namely, that one becomes good and best governs his own family and the state—it is considered shameful to be unwilling to teach anything before taking precautions regarding money. Is it not?

**CALLICLES.** Certainly.

**SOCRATES.** For this reason is clear: because this alone among other benefits received makes one desirous of returning the favor. Wherefore it seems a clear proof if he who has performed a service of this kind should himself receive it in turn; otherwise, not at all. Do these things stand thus?

**CALLICLES.** They do.

**SOCRATES.** To which care of the city, then, do you exhort me? Come, define it for me. To that by which I might struggle against the Athenians and strive so that they become the best, like a doctor? Or to that by which I might strive to serve them as a minister of their pleasure? Tell me the truth, Callicles; for it is fitting that you continue boldly as you began, by freely expressing to me what you feel. And now, therefore, answer well and nobly.

**CALLICLES.** I certainly exhort you to the ministry <note>i.e., to serve the people's desires</note>.

**SOCRATES.** Then you provoke me to flattery, O most noble man.

**CALLICLES.** If you prefer to be called a Mysian <note>A term of contempt; the Mysians were considered the lowest of people</note>, Socrates, you shall be called so, unless you believe me.

**SOCRATES.** Do not throw in my face now what you have already thrown so often: namely, "whoever wishes will kill you, Socrates"—lest I respond again: "but a wicked man kills a good one." Nor say again: "anyone will take from you, Socrates, whatever you have"—lest I also respond: "but truly, he who takes it will not know how to use those things as if they were useful to him; but just as he took them from me unjustly, so he himself will use them unjustly. And if unjustly, then also shamefully; finally, if shamefully, then badly."

**CALLICLES.** You seem to me, Socrates, to think you will suffer nothing of this kind, as if you lived far from here; nor do you think you could be led into court by even the most cowardly man of no value.

**SOCRATES.** I would certainly be mindless, Callicles, if I did not think that in this city anyone could suffer anything of this kind. Yet this I know for certain: if I come into court risking these things which you assert, it will be a wicked man

<margin>No good man accuses the innocent.</margin>

who accuses me. For no good man accuses an innocent man. Indeed, it would be no wonder if I were condemned to death. Do you want me to tell you for what reason I expect these things?

**CALLICLES.** I do indeed.

**SOCRATES.** I think that I, along with a few other Athenians—not to say alone—truly handle the civil discipline <note>The art of politics</note>; and that I alone of all who now exist practice civil affairs. Therefore, as one who does not speak for favor—which I do very frequently—but rather toward that which is best rather than what is sweetest; and since I do not undertake to do those things which you now exhort me toward as if they were something magnificent, I certainly will not have anything to say in court. And now indeed there recurs to my mind what I had said to Polus. For I would be judged just as a doctor would be judged among children if a Cook were to accuse him. For consider by what reason a doctor would defend himself, a day having been set for him among the children, if someone were to accuse him with these words: "This man, O children, has brought many evils upon you. For he twists both you and your younger ones by cutting and burning; and he afflicts you by making you thin and choking you. Furthermore, he offers the most bitter drinks and drives you to hunger and thirst. I, however, prepare many and various sweet things for you." If a cook were to bring these accusations, I say, what do you think a doctor caught in this evil would answer? Or perhaps he will confess the truth, saying: "I did these things, O children, for the sake of your health"? But how vehemently do you think judges of that kind would cry out against him?

**CALLICLES.** Very vehemently, one must suppose.

**SOCRATES.** Do you not think, therefore, that he would then be held in the greatest ambiguity and lack of defense?

**CALLICLES.** Entirely.

**SOCRATES.** I know the same would happen to me if I were dragged into court. For I would not be able to recount any pleasures invented by me for their lust <note>original: "libidinem"</note>, which they themselves consider in the place of benefit and utility; but I...

# GORGIAS, OR ON RHETORIC. FOLIO CXLVIII.
-> e iiii <-

not at all. Nor do I even approve of the ministers of those things: nor for that reason do I consider those to whom they provide them to be any happier. Furthermore, if someone should say that I either corrupt the youth by leading them into ambiguity and helplessness, or that I reproach the elders with certain biting words either privately or publicly: I will not be given the faculty of speaking the truth—namely, that I say all these things justly, and that I consult only the utility of those very people—nor will I easily be able to bring forward anything else. For which reason, perhaps there is nothing that might not be decreed against me. CALLICLES: Does it seem to you then, O Socrates, to be well with a man who is in such a state in the city that he could not even be a defense for himself? SOCRATES: Provided that this one thing be in him, O Callicles, which you have often agreed to: that he can provide that help to himself by which he has done or said nothing unjust either against men or against gods. For we have already often agreed that this kind of help to oneself is the best. If, therefore, someone should convince me that I cannot bring help of this kind to myself or to others, I would undoubtedly blush, whether I were refuted among many, or among few, or alone by one person. And so, if I were to die because of this impotence, I would take it heavily. But if I were to be afflicted with the ultimate punishment because of a defect in flattering rhetoric, I know for certain that you would see me bearing death very easily. For no one fears dying except one who is entirely devoid of reason and cowardly; but he does fear acting unjustly. For it is the extreme of all evils for a soul filled with many sins to descend to the underworld. Accordingly, if you wish it to be so, I want to give you an account of it. CALLICLES: Indeed, since you have finished the rest, finish this also. SOCRATES: Listen then, as they say, to a most beautiful discourse, which I think you will consider a fable, but I consider it not a fable, but a discourse. For I will tell you what I am about to say as if it were true. Truly, as Homer says, Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto divided among themselves the kingdom which they received from their father. <note>Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto are the Latin names for Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades.</note> Moreover, a law concerning men existed under Saturn <note>Saturn is the Latin name for Cronus.</note> and has always existed and even now exists among the gods: that whatever men had lived justly and piously, when they departed from life, having set out for the Isles of the Blessed, they should live in all happiness, far separated from evils; but those who had lived unjustly and impiously should go into the prison of punishment and just retribution, which they call Tartarus. Now, the judges of these people under Saturn, and even under Jupiter himself when his reign was recently beginning, were living men judging living men; and they judged on the same day on which someone was about to die. For which reason, judgment was not justly rendered. Therefore, Pluto and the guardians of the Isles of the Blessed, approaching Jupiter, reported that unworthy men were coming to them from both sides. To whom Jupiter spoke thus: "But I will apply a remedy. For now they judge unjustly because they judge while clothed and surrounded by things, since they judge before death. And so many who have wicked souls are surrounded by the beauty of the body, and noble birth, and riches. Furthermore, since the judgment is imminent, a multitude of witnesses stands by asserting that they have lived justly. Whereby it happens that the judges are dazed by these things. Added to this is that the judges themselves judge while clothed and surrounded, having eyes and ears and the whole body as if before a veil. For all these things are obstacles to them: namely, their own clothing as much as that of those whom they judge. First, it must be provided," he said, "that men do not foresee their death; for now they foresee it; and it has been commanded to Prometheus that he not permit them to foresee it. Then, they must be judged naked of all these things. For they are to be judged after death. It is also necessary that the judge himself be naked—that is, dead—and with his soul alone inspecting the soul of each person immediately after their unexpected death: the soul, I say, deserted by all its kin, and leaving all exterior ornament on the earth, so that the judgment may proceed justly. I, therefore, as one who foresaw these things before you, have already appointed my sons as judges: two from Asia, namely Minos and Rhadamanthus; and one from Europe, Aeacus. These, therefore, after they have died, will judge in a certain meadow, and there at the crossroads from which two ways lead: one indeed to Tartarus, the other to the Isles of the Blessed. And Rhadamanthus shall judge the Asians; but Aeacus shall judge those who come from Europe. To Minos, however, I shall enjoin the duty that he himself decide if anything should be ambiguous to the others: so that the judgment may proceed most justly, and the passage of souls may be made rightly." These are the things, O Callicles, which I have heard and believe to be true. And led by these discourses, I reflect thus with myself. Death, indeed, as it seems to me, is nothing other than the dissolution of two things—namely, the soul and the body—from each other. But when these two are separated from each other, it is not far from the case that each of them keeps the same habit which it possessed while the man was living. First, the body displays its nature as well as its cultivation and suffering. Just as if someone's body was large either by nature, or by nourishment, or by both while he lived: even when the man is dead, it will be large. And so if it had been fat, it will also be fat; and other things similarly. Furthermore, if the man had been fond of long hair, he will keep his hair. Again, if someone was a scoundrel and had many traces of blows impressed on his body either from lashes or from wounds while he lived: we see the body of this dead man also retaining the same. And if it was broken or distorted in any part, these same things appear even when he is dead; and to say it briefly, whatever the body was while living, all or most such things of the dead man appear for a time. The same also seems to me to be the case, O Callicles, concerning the soul. For all things appear in the soul when it has stripped off the body, both those which were there by nature and those which were there from affections, which the man contracted into his soul from the pursuit of each matter. When, therefore, they have come to the judge—the Asians to Rhadamanthus—Rhadamanthus, making them stand, looks into the soul of each one, not noting whose soul it then is. But for the most part, having contemplated the soul of the Great King of the Persians or some other king or potentate, he sees nothing healthy in it; but it is infected by perjuries and injustice as if by certain lashes and scars, such as each person's action has contracted and impressed upon the soul; and all things are twisted by lies and vanity, having nothing straight because it had been educated without truth; furthermore, because of the license of sinning, and petulance, and soft lewdness, and intemperance in individual actions: it is utterly disordered and foul. The soul, therefore...

<meta>This page continues the concluding moral exhortation of Socrates in Plato's Gorgias, focusing on the myth of the afterlife and the final judgment of souls.</meta>

# BOOK TWENTY-FOUR

<note>original: LIBER VIGESIMVSQVARTVS</note>

Having been contemplated in such a state of affection, he is immediately sent away in disgrace from custody to that place where it is necessary to undergo well-deserved punishments. It is fitting, moreover, that everyone who is rightly punished by another should either become better himself and receive a benefit, or serve as an example to others; so that others, witnessing his punishments, may become better through fear. Those who indeed pay such penalties before gods and men that they derive some benefit from it are those who have committed curable sins <note>original: peccata sanabilia</note>; for them, pain and torture are beneficial both among men and among those in the underworld. For in no other way can anyone be freed from injustice. 

But those who are held by extreme injustice and are incurable because of such crimes are used as examples; they themselves no longer report any benefit from it, seeing as they cannot be healed. Instead, they serve only as an example to others who behold them, tormented for all time with the greatest, most bitter, and most terrible punishments for their sins—offered as an example, a memorial, and a spectacle in the prison of the underworld to all the unjust who descend to those places. One of these, I say, will be Archelaus, if what Polus says is true, and any other such tyrant who has existed. 

I believe, however, that in the number of those who provide only examples, the majority are tyrants, kings, potentates, and governors of cities. For these, because of the very license to sin, commit the gravest and most profane crimes. Homer bears witness to us of this, for he introduces kings and potentates in the underworld tormented for all time, such as Tantalus, Sisyphus, and Tityus. But Thersites, or anyone else who was evil in a private capacity, no one ever depicted as being tortured with great punishments as if he were incurable; for he did not have the license to sin, I believe. For that reason, he was happier than those to whom the license for perpetrating wickedness was given. 

Certainly, O Callicles, among those who have power and license, there are those who have been excessively depraved. Nothing, however, prevents there being some good men even among these, and certainly, whoever is such a man is to be wonderfully admired. Indeed, it is difficult, O Callicles, and worthy of great praise, for someone placed in great license for sinning to lead a just life; and few such are found. Yet there have been, both here and elsewhere, and I believe there will be, some distinguished and good men endowed with this virtue: namely, that they would treat justly those things over which authority was granted to them. One of all the Greeks who stood out as most approved was Aristides, the son of Lysimachus. But most of those in power, O best of men, are wicked. 

Therefore, as I was saying, when Rhadamanthus <note>One of the three judges of the underworld</note> catches someone of this sort, he knows nothing else about him: neither who he is, nor from whom he is descended, but only whether he is evil. And when he discovers this, he sends him to Tartarus, marking whether he seems curable or incurable. He, having been sent there, undergoes his deserved punishments. Sometimes, however, having looked upon another soul—either of a private citizen or of someone else who lived piously and with integrity, which I believe happens most especially to a philosopher who minds his own business and does not entangle himself in many affairs—he applauds him and sends him to the Islands of the Blessed. 

Aeacus performs these same duties. Each of them holds a rod while he judges. But Minos sits alone watching, holding a golden scepter, just as Ulysses says of him in Homer: namely, that he saw him holding a golden scepter and giving laws to the dead. I, therefore, O Callicles, am moved by these discourses, and I am already considering by what reasoning I may show the healthiest soul to the judge. Therefore, scorning the honors of all the people and considering the truth, I will endeavor to live and die as truly good as I possibly can. 

I exhort all others as much as I can. You also I call back to this kind of life and this contest, which I declare is to be undergone by man above all other contests in this life. Therefore, I also rebuke you, because you will not be able to bring help to yourself when he judges you, and the sentence I just mentioned will be imminent. But when you come before the judge, the son of Aegina <note>Referring to Aeacus</note>, and he leads you away having seized you, you will gape and stagger there no less than I do here before your judges. There, perhaps, someone will strike you shamefully upon the cheek and treat you with utter contempt and injury. 

Perhaps these things seem to you like some old woman's fable, and you despise what has been said. But truly, it would be nothing wonderful to despise these things if, by searching, we could find something better and truer than them. But now you see: although you are three men who are the wisest of all the Greeks now living—you, Polus, and Gorgias—you are nevertheless unable to show that one must live by any other rule than that which seems to be of benefit there as well. 

Indeed, in so many discourses, while the others have been refuted, this one alone remains firm: namely, that one must be more careful to avoid doing injury than suffering it; and that a man must meditate on this above all else—not that he should *seem* good, but that he should *truly be* good, both publicly and privately. If anyone should be evil in some way, he must be punished; and this is the second-best thing after being just: namely, to become good through chastisement and to pay the penalty for injustice. Furthermore, all flattery—whether toward oneself or others, whether few or many—must be fled. Finally, rhetoric and every other kind of action must be used for justice alone. 

Therefore, believe me and follow me to that place where, when you arrive, you will be blessed both living and dead, just as your own discourse signifies. And permit someone to despise you as a fool and to treat you with injuries if he wishes. And by Jove, do not care if you are struck ignominiously. For you will suffer nothing grave if you are truly honorable and good and practice virtue. After we have been exercised together in this way, then, if it seems worthwhile to you, we will apply ourselves to public affairs, or to whatever then seems best to us as we deliberate—since we can never deliberate now. For it is shameful, being such as we now appear to be, to boast in words as if we were something, when we never seem to hold the same views on the same and most important matters; so far have we proceeded in ignorance. 

Let us, therefore, follow this reasoning which has now become known to us as a guide, showing us that this is the best way of living: to practice justice and the other virtues throughout our whole life. Let us obey this, and exhort others to it. Let us not obey that reasoning in which you trust and to which you exhort me. For it is of no value, Callicles.

<summary>Socrates concludes his dialogue with Callicles by describing the divine judgment of souls, where worldly power offers no protection and only a life of virtue and justice ensures a blessed afterlife. He urges Callicles to abandon the pursuit of political power and rhetoric in favor of moral integrity.</summary>

# COMMENTARY ON THE BANQUET.

### THE COMMENTARY OF MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE ON PLATO’S BANQUET CONCERNING LOVE. CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>The death of Plato.</margin>
PLATO, the Father of Philosophers, having reached eighty-one years of age, passed away on the seventh day of November—the very day of his birth—while reclining at a banquet after the tables had been cleared. This banquet, which celebrated both Plato’s birthday and his anniversary, was renewed annually by all the ancient Platonists until the times of Plotinus and Porphyry <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) and Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) were the primary founders of Neoplatonism</note>. However, after Porphyry, for one thousand two hundred years, these solemn feasts were neglected. Finally, in our own times, the most illustrious Lorenzo de' Medici, intending to renew the Platonic banquet, appointed Francesco Bandini as the Master of the Feast. Therefore, when Bandini set out to observe the seventh day of November, he received nine Platonic guests with royal preparation at the villa in Careggi: Antonio Agli, the Bishop of Fiesole; Ficino the Physician; Cristoforo Landino the poet; Bernardo Nuzzi the rhetorician; Tommaso Benci; Giovanni Cavalcanti, our close friend—whom the guests named "The Hero" because of his virtue of soul and noble character; the two Marsuppini, Cristoforo and Carlo, sons of the poet Carlo; and finally, Bandini wished me to be the ninth, so that by adding me to the others, the number of the Muses might be fulfilled.

After the tables were cleared, Bernardo Nuzzi took up Plato’s book titled *The Banquet, or Concerning Love*, and read all the speeches of this symposium. Once they were read, he asked the remaining guests to each explain one speech. Everyone agreed; and after lots were cast, that first speech of Phaedrus fell to Giovanni Cavalcanti to explain. The speech of Pausanias went to Antonio the Theologian <note>Antonio Agli</note>. That of Eryximachus the Physician went to Ficino the Physician. That of the poet Aristophanes went to Cristoforo the Poet. That of the youth Agathon went to Carlo Marsuppini. The discourse of Socrates was given to Tommaso Benci, and that of Alcibiades to Cristoforo Marsuppini. Everyone approved of this lot. However, the Bishop and the Physician—one compelled to leave for the care of souls, the other for the care of bodies—left their speaking parts to Giovanni Cavalcanti. The others turned toward him and, ready to listen, fell silent. Then that "Hero" began in this manner:

---

#### By what rule Love should be praised. What is its dignity and greatness. Chapter II.

<margin>What kind of man Phaedrus was.</margin>
This lot that fell to me today, best of guests, is most pleasing; it has brought it about that I should play the part of Phaedrus of Myrrhinus. I speak of that Phaedrus whose friendship Lysias of Thebes, the greatest orator, valued so highly that he strove to win him over with a speech composed with much midnight oil; whose character Socrates so admired that, moved by his brilliance while near the river Ilissus and lifted to a higher state, he sang of divine mysteries—he who previously had proclaimed himself ignorant not only of heavenly things, but of all lower things as well. Plato was so delighted by his talent that he dedicated the first fruits of his studies to Phaedrus. To him are addressed the epigrams and elegies of Plato; to him is dedicated his first book on Beauty, which is titled *Phaedrus*. Since, therefore, not I myself—for I do not claim so much for myself—but first the chance of the lot and then your applause has judged me similar to this Phaedrus, I will gladly interpret his speech first under these happy auspices. Then I shall carry out the parts of Antonio and Ficino to the best of my abilities.

Every philosopher who is an imitator of Plato, best of men, considers three things in every matter: what precedes, what accompanies, and what follows. If these are good, he praises the thing itself; if bad, he censures it. Therefore, a perfect praise is one which recounts the preceding origin of the thing, describes its present form, and shows the following outcomes. A thing is praised for its preceding factors as being **noble**; for its present factors as being **great**; and for its following factors as being **useful**. Therefore, from those three, these three qualities are concluded in praises: Nobility, Greatness, and Utility.

<margin>What constitutes a proper praise.</margin>
For this reason, our Phaedrus, first contemplating the present excellence of Love, called him a "Great God." He added: "To be wondered at by gods and men." And not without reason. For we properly wonder at those things which are great. He is indeed great, to whose command men and gods, as they say, are subject. For among the ancients, the gods love just as men do. This is what Orpheus and Hesiod signify when they say that the minds of mortals and immortals are tamed by love. Furthermore, he is said to be "wonderful" because everyone loves that whose beauty he wonders at. The gods—or as our people say, the Angels—wonder at and love divine beauty; men wonder at and love the appearance of bodies. And this indeed is the praise of Love derived from the present excellence that accompanies it.

<margin>Orpheus on the principle of things.</margin>
Next, Phaedrus praises him from his preceding factors when he asserts that he is the oldest of all the gods. In this, the nobility of love shines forth, as its ancient origin is recounted. He will praise him thirdly from the following factors, where his wonderful utility will appear from the outcome. But we shall treat first of his ancient and noble origin, and then of his future utility. Orpheus, in the *Argonautica*, when he sang of the principles of things in the presence of Chiron and the heroes...

->COMMENTARY<-
->Page 10<-

Following the theology of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica."</note>, he placed Chaos before the world, and before Saturn, Jupiter, and the other gods. He located Love in the very bosom of Chaos and praised it with these words:

### The Origin of Love from Chaos. Chapter III.

Love is the most ancient, perfect in itself, and most wise. Hesiod in his *Theogony*, and in the book *On Nature* the Pythagorean Parmenides and the poet Acusileus, have agreed with Orpheus and Mercury <note>Mercury here refers to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>. Plato in the *Timaeus* describes Chaos in a similar way and places Love within it. And Phaedrus recounted the same in the *Symposium*. The Platonists call an unformed world "Chaos," and a formed chaos "the World." According to them, there are three worlds, and likewise there will be three chaoses. The first of all is God, the author of the universe, whom we call the Good itself. He first creates the Angelic Mind; then the Soul of this world, as Plato wishes; and finally the body of the world. We do not call that supreme God a "world," because "world" <note>original: *mundus*</note> signifies an ornament composed of many things, whereas He must be entirely simple; but we assert Him to be the beginning and the end of all worlds.

The Angelic Mind is the first world made by God. The second is the Soul of the universal body. The third is this entire machine that we perceive. In each of these three worlds, three chaoses are considered. In the beginning, God creates the substance of that Mind, which we also call Essence. In that first moment of its creation, this essence is unformed and dark. But because it is born from God, it turns toward God, its own principle, by a certain innate appetite. Having turned toward God, it is illuminated by His ray. By the brightness of that ray, its appetite is set on fire. The ignited appetite clings entirely to God; by clinging, it is formed. For God, who can do all things, fashions the natures of things to be created within the Mind that clings to Him. In that Mind, therefore, all things that we sense in these physical bodies are painted in a certain spiritual way, so to speak. There, the spheres of the heavens and the elements, the stars, the natures of vapors, and the forms of stones, metals, plants, and animals are brought forth.

We do not doubt that these species of all things, conceived in that celestial Mind by a certain nourishment from God, are the "Ideas"; and we often call that form and idea of the heavens the god "Uranus" <note>original: *Caelum*</note>. The form of the first planet we call the god Saturn; of the second, Jupiter; and so on for the following planets. Likewise, the idea of this fire we call the god Vulcan; of the air, Jupiter and Juno; of the water, Neptune; of the earth, Pluto. Therefore, all the gods assigned to certain parts of the lower world are the Ideas of those parts collected in that celestial Mind.

But that conception of Ideas, perfected by God the Former, was preceded by that approach of the Mind toward God. This was preceded by the fire of appetite, this by the infusion of the ray, this by that first turning of the appetite, and this by the essence of the unformed Mind. Furthermore, we maintain that this essence, not yet formed, is "Chaos." Its first turning toward God is the "birth of Love"; the infusion of the ray is the "food of Love"; the following fire is the "growth of Love"; the approach is the "impulse of Love"; the formation is the "perfection of Love." The collection of all forms and Ideas we call *Mundus* in Latin, and in Greek *Kosmos*, that is, "ornament." The grace of this ornament is Beauty. Toward this Beauty, Love—immediately upon being born—drew the Mind; and it led the Mind, which was previously deformed, to that same Mind which was thereafter beautiful. Therefore, the condition of Love is such that it ravishes toward beauty and joins the deformed to the beautiful.

Who, then, will doubt that Love immediately follows Chaos and precedes the World and all the gods who are distributed among the parts of the world? Since that appetite of the Mind exists before its formation, and the gods and the world are born in the formed Mind. Rightly, therefore, did Orpheus name Love "the most ancient." Furthermore, he called it "perfect in itself," as if to say "perfecting itself." For that first instinct of the Mind seems by its own nature to draw its perfection from God and to offer it to the Mind which is formed therefrom, and to the gods who are born therefrom. Moreover, he called it "most wise," and not without reason. For all wisdom, to which counsel properly belongs, was given to the Mind for this reason: because, having turned toward God through love, it shone with His brightness. The Mind is directed toward God in the same way the eye is directed toward the light of the sun. For the eye first looks, then sees the light of the sun, and thirdly, in the light of the sun, it perceives the colors and shapes of things. Therefore the eye, which is dark at first and unformed like chaos, loves the light while it looks; it is irradiated by looking; and by receiving the ray, it is formed with the colors and shapes of things.

Just as that Mind, immediately born and unformed, is turned and formed by love toward God, so the Soul of the world reflects itself toward the Mind and God, from whom it was generated. And although it is at first unformed and a chaos, when directed toward the Mind by love, it becomes a "world" by receiving forms from it. Not otherwise did the matter of this world lie as an unformed chaos without the ornament of forms; immediately, by a love innate to itself, it directed itself toward the Soul and offered itself as obedient to it. And with love acting as the mediator, having obtained from the Soul the ornament of all forms seen in the world, it was made into a world out of chaos.

There are, therefore, three worlds and three chaoses. In all of them, finally, Love accompanies chaos, precedes the world, awakens the sluggish, illuminates the dark, gives life to the dead, forms the unformed, and perfects the imperfect. No greater praises than these can be spoken or even imagined.

### On the Utility of Love. Chapter IIII.

But enough concerning its origin and nobility. I think we must now discuss its utility. Indeed, it is superfluous to recount the individual benefits of love bestowed upon the human race, especially since they can all be understood in summary. For they all consist in this: that by avoiding evils, we follow the good—

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion of Love (Amor) as a divine and moral force, likely from Marsilio Ficino’s Commentary on Plato’s Symposium. It distinguishes between true Love and base lust.</meta>

# ON THE BANQUET

...follow. The bad and shameful things for a man are the same. Likewise, the good and the honorable are the same. Indeed, all laws and teachings strive for nothing else than to so instruct men that they turn away from shameful things and perform honorable ones. However, that which countless laws and arts barely achieve over a long period of time, **Love** alone accomplishes in a short time. For shame deters one from shameful things, while the desire for excellence provokes one toward honorable ones. Love provides these two things to men more easily and more quickly than anything else. When we speak of Love, understand it as the **desire for beauty**. This is the definition of love among all philosophers.

Beauty <margin>beauty</margin> is indeed a certain grace, which is born most of all and primarily in harmony. This is threefold: since there is a grace in souls from the harmony of many virtues; a grace is born in bodies from the concord of many colors and lines; and likewise, there is a great grace in sounds from the consonance of many voices. Therefore, beauty is threefold: of souls, of bodies, and of voices. That of souls is known by the **Mind**; that of bodies is perceived by the **Eyes**; and that of voices is perceived by the **Ears** alone. Since, therefore, the mind, sight, and hearing are the only means by which we can enjoy beauty—and since Love is the desire for enjoying beauty—Love is always content with the Mind, the Eyes, and the Ears.

What need is there for smell? What for taste? What for touch? These senses perceive odors, flavors, heat, cold, softness, and hardness, and things similar to these. None of these is human beauty, since forms are simple, whereas the beauty of the human body requires the concord of diverse parts. Love regards the enjoyment of beauty as its end; this pertains only to the mind, sight, and hearing. Love, therefore, is limited to these three. But the appetite which follows the remaining senses is called not love <margin>In which there is lust, not love.</margin> but **lust** and madness. Furthermore, if love toward a human being desires beauty itself, and the beauty of the human body consists in a certain harmony, and harmony is temperance, then love requires only those things which are temperate, modest, and decorous.

Therefore, the pleasures of taste and touch—which are so vehement and furious that they move the mind from its state and disturb the man—Love not only does not desire, but abhors and flees, as they are contrary to beauty because of their intemperance. Venereal madness drags one toward intemperance, and therefore toward disharmony; for which reason it seems likewise to allure one toward deformity. Love, however, leads to beauty. Deformity and beauty are opposites. Therefore, movements of this kind, which snatch one toward these things, are seen to be contrary to one another. For this reason, lust (intercourse) and love are shown to be not only not the same movements, but even opposites.

The ancient theologians also testify to this, for they attributed the name of **Love** to God. This the later theologians also most strongly confirmed. Indeed, no name suitable for God is common to shameful things. Therefore, every person of sound mind ought to beware lest he rashly transfer "Love," a divine name, to insane disturbances. Let Dicaearchus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle who criticized Plato.</note> blush, and anyone else who does not fear to carp at the Platonic majesty because he indulged too much in love. For we can never indulge too much, nor even enough, in decorous, honest, and divine affections.

From this it follows that all love is honorable, and every lover is just. For every lover is beautiful and decorous, and properly loves the decorous. However, that turbulent heat by which we are snatched toward lewdness, since it drags us toward deformity, is judged to be the opposite of love.

To return at last to the utility of love: <margin>The utility of love.</margin> shame, which deters us from shameful things, and the zeal which makes us burning for honorable things, proceed easily and quickly from love. First, because love, which seeks beautiful things, always desires the decorous and the magnificent; and he who hates deformed things necessarily flees shameful and obscene ones. Second, if any two people love each other mutually, they watch over one another and desire to please each other. Insofar as one is observed by the other—as one who never lacks a witness—they abstain from shameful acts. Insofar as they strive to please one another, they always undertake magnificent things with burning zeal, lest they be held in contempt by the beloved, but rather be thought worthy of a return of love.

Phaedrus explains this reasoning most copiously where he posits three examples of love. One of the love of a woman for a male, where he speaks of **Alcestis**, the wife of Admetus, who wished to die for her husband. Another of the love of a male for a female, such as **Orpheus** for Eurydice. A third of the love of a male for a male, such as **Patroclus** for Achilles; where he shows that nothing renders men braver than love. It is not my intention at present to scrutinize the allegory of either Alcestis or Orpheus. For these things express the power and empire of love more vehemently if they are narrated as historical deeds than if they are thought to be spoken through allegory.

Therefore, let us confess without controversy that Love is a great and wonderful God, noble moreover and most useful, and let us so indulge in love that we are content with its own end, which is beauty itself. But we enjoy that part which we know; we know by the Mind, by sight, and by hearing. These, therefore, we enjoy; with the other senses we do not use beauty (which love desires), but rather whatever else the body requires. Therefore, we shall hunt beauty with these three: and through that beauty which shines forth in voices and bodies, as if through certain tracks, we shall investigate the decorum of the soul. We shall indeed praise the former, but we shall approve the latter; and we shall always strive to observe this: that the love be as great as the beauty was. And where the body is indeed beautiful but the soul is not at all, let us love it only slightly and lightly, as a shadowy and fleeting image of beauty. Where the soul alone is beautiful, let us ardently love this stable decorum of the soul. But where both beauties concur, let us admire more vehemently, and so [prove] ourselves to be truly of the Platonic family...

# COMMENTARY

we shall stand firm. For that [the soul] knows nothing except what is festive, broad, celestial, and sublime. But let these remarks on the speech of Phaedrus now suffice; let us come to Pausanias.

### THE SECOND SPEECH.

#### God is goodness, beauty, justice; the beginning, the middle, and the end. CHAPTER I.

<margin>The Pythagorean Trinity.</margin>
The Pythagorean philosophers maintained that a Trinity is the measure of all things, for the reason, I believe, that God governs things by the number three, and also that things themselves are limited by the number three. Hence that saying of Maro <note>Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note>: "God delights in an uneven number." <note>original: "Numero Deus impare gaudet"</note> Indeed, that supreme Author first creates individual things; second, he draws them back; third, he perfects them. So too, individual things flow out from that perennial fountain in the beginning while they are being born; then they flow back into the same when they seek their own origin; finally, they are perfected after they have returned to their beginning. Orpheus, prophesying this, called the Light <note>or "the Smooth One"</note> the beginning, the middle, and the end of the universe. The beginning insofar as he produces; the middle insofar as he draws back the things produced to himself; the end insofar as he perfects those returning. Hence we can name that King of the universe Good, Beautiful, and Just, as is often said in Plato. Good, I say, when he creates; Beautiful when he entices; Just when he perfects according to each one's merit. Beauty, therefore—whose property it is to entice—is located between goodness and justice; it flows out from goodness and flows forth toward justice.

#### In what way divine beauty gives birth to love. Chapter II.

Truly, this divine appearance has procreated in all things love, which is the desire for itself. Since if God draws the world to himself, and the world is drawn, there is one continuous attraction beginning from God, passing into the world, and finally ending in God; which returns again, as if in a certain circle, into that same place from which it flowed. Therefore, one and the same circle from God into the world, and from the world into God, is called by three names. Insofar as it begins in God and entices, it is Beauty; insofar as passing into the world it seizes the world itself, it is Love; insofar as returning to the Author it joins his work to him, it is Pleasure. Love, therefore, starts from Beauty and ends in Pleasure. This is what that famous hymn of Hierotheus and Dionysius the Areopagite <note>Christian Neoplatonist theologians</note> meant when these theologians sang: "Love is a good circle perpetually revolved from good, through good, into good." For love is necessarily good since, being born from good, it returns to good. For it is the same God whose appearance all things desire, and in whose possession all things find rest. From there, then, our desire is kindled; there the ardor of lovers rests, not extinguished, but fulfilled. Nor does Dionysius compare God to the sun without justice; because just as the sun illuminates the body and warms it, so God provides the clarity of truth and the heat of charity to souls. We gather this comparison from the sixth book of Plato’s *Republic* in this manner: The sun certainly procreates visible bodies and seeing eyes; it infuses a lucid spirit into the eyes so they may see; it paints bodies with colors so they may be seen. Yet neither the ray proper to the eyes, nor the colors proper to the bodies, are sufficient to complete the vision unless the light itself—the one above the many, from which the many and proper lights are distributed to eyes and bodies—arrives, illustrates, excites, and strengthens. In the same way, that first act of all things, which is called God, has bestowed appearance and act upon individual things by producing them. Which act, certainly, when it is received in a created thing and in a passive subject, is weak and powerless for the execution of work. But the perpetual and invisible light of the divine sun is always present as one to all; it cherishes, vivifies, excites, completes, and strengthens. Concerning which Orpheus divinely said: "Cherishing all things and bearing himself above all." <note>original: "Cuncta fovens atque ipse ferens super omnia sese"</note> Insofar as he is the act of all and strengthens them, he is called Good. Insofar as he vivifies, softens, soothes, and excites, he is called Beautiful. Insofar as he entices those three knowing powers of the soul—Mind, Sight, and Hearing—in the objects that are to be born, he is Beauty. Insofar as he applies the knowing power to the thing known, he is Truth. Finally, as the Good, he procreates, rules, and completes; as the Beautiful, he illuminates and infuses grace.

#### Beauty is the splendor of divine goodness, and God is the center of four circles. Chapter III.

Nor was it without reason that the ancient theologians placed Goodness in the center and Beauty in the circle. Goodness, I say, in the single center; but Beauty in four circles. The one center of all is God. The four circles assiduously revolved around it are Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter. Mind is a stable circle. Soul is mobile by itself. Nature is mobile in another, not by another. Matter is mobile by another and in another. Furthermore, I shall explain why we call God the center and those four things circles. The center of a circle is a point: one, indivisible, stable. From there many divisible, mobile lines are led to their similar circumference; which circumference, being divisible, turns around the center as if on a hinge. And such is the nature of the center that, although it is one, individual, and immobile, it is nevertheless found everywhere in many—indeed in all—divisible and mobile lines. For the point is everywhere in the line. Because nothing can be touched by its dissimilar, the lines drawn from the circumference to the center are each compelled to touch such a middle point with a certain single, simple, and immobile point of their own. Who denies that God is deservedly called the center of all things, since he is inwardly one, simple, and immobile in all; while all things produced by him are many, composite, and mobile, and just as they flow from him, so they flow back into him like lines and a circumference? Thus, Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter, proceeding from God, strive to return to the same; and they revolve themselves everywhere around him according to their strength. And just as the center-point is found everywhere in the lines and in the whole circle, and through their own point the individual lines...

# ON THE BANQUET
<note>original: "IN CONVIVIVM" - This refers to Marsilio Ficino's Commentary on Plato's Symposium.</note>

<margin>God is the simplest unity.</margin> Just as the lines of a circle touch the center point, so God is the center of all things. He is the simplest unity and purest act <note>A scholastic term meaning pure existence without mere potential</note>, who inserts himself into the universe—not only because he is present to all things, but also because he has bestowed upon all things created by him a certain part, or an innermost, simplest, and most excellent power, which is called the "unity of things." From this unity, and toward it, as if from a center and toward its own center, the remaining parts and powers of each thing depend. It is clearly necessary that created things first collect themselves toward this, their own center and their own unity, before they can adhere to their Creator; so that through their own center (which we have now frequently encountered) they may adhere to the center of all. The mind of an angel rises up into its own apex and head before it ascends into God. The soul also, and the rest, function in the same way. And of those invisible circles—namely, Mind, Soul, and Nature—the circle of the visible world is the image. For bodies are the shadows and footprints of souls and minds. Indeed, a shadow and a footprint reflect the figure of that which cast the shadow and left the trace. For this reason, those four are not wrongly called the "four circles." But the Mind is an immobile circle because its operation as well as its substance always remains the same; it operates similarly, always understanding in the same way and willing similarly. On the other hand, the Mind can sometimes be called "mobile" only in the sense that, like all other things proceeding from God, it turns itself back toward Him. The Soul of the World, and any other soul, is a mobile circle. For these, by their nature, know by "discursive reasoning" <note>moving from one thought to another rather than instant intuition</note> and operate through the courses of time. Now, discourse from one thing to another and temporal operation are undoubtedly called "motion." If there is any stability in the soul's knowledge, it exists by the benefit of the Mind rather than the soul. Nature is also a mobile circuit. When we say "Soul," we understand (after the manner of the ancient theologians) the power placed in reason and sense; when we say "Nature," we mean the power of the soul located in generation <note>reproduction and biological growth</note>. That former power in us they properly called "the human"; this latter they called the "idol" and "simulacrum" of the human. This faculty of generating is called mobile because it executes its work through spaces of time. But in this it differs from that property of the soul: the soul moves by itself and in itself. By itself, I say, because it exists as the principle of motion. In itself also, because the operation of reason and sense remains within the substance of the soul itself. From these, no work necessarily results in the body. But that power of generating which we call "Nature" is indeed moved by itself (since it is a certain power of the soul moved by itself), but it is said to be "moved in another" because all its operation is terminated in the mass of the body. For it nourishes, increases, and generates the body. Matter and the mass of the body, however, is a circle moved by another and in another. By another, indeed, because it is necessarily agitated by the soul. In another, however, because the motion of the body acts within the space of a location. Now, therefore, we can clearly understand why the theologians place Goodness in the center and Beauty in the circle. For the Goodness of all things is God himself, through whom all things are good. Beauty, however, is the ray of God, implanted in those four circles revolving in a certain way around God. A ray of this kind fashions all the species of all things in those four: we are accustomed to call those species "Ideas" in the Mind, "Reasons" in the Soul, "Seeds" in Nature, and "Forms" in Matter. Therefore, in the four circles, there appear to be four splendors: the splendor of Ideas in the first, of Reasons in the second, of Seeds in the third, and of Forms in the last.

### How Plato is to be interpreted concerning divine matters. Chapter IV.

Plato signified this mystery in his letter to King Dionysius when he affirmed God to be the cause of all beautiful things, as if he were the principle and origin of all beauty. "Around the King of all," he says, "are all things; for his sake are all things; he is the cause of all beautiful things. Second things around the second; third things around the third." <note>A famous, cryptic passage from Plato's Second Letter</note> The human mind strives to understand what sort of things these are, looking upon those things which are kindred to itself, none of which are sufficient. But around the King himself and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of that sort; but the mind speaks of what comes after this. "Around the King" signifies not *inside* the King, but *outside*. For in God there is no composition. What that word "around" signifies, Plato explains when he adds: "For his sake are all things; he is the cause of all beautiful things." As if he were to say: all things are "around the King" because all things, according to their nature, revolve toward him as toward their end, just as all things were produced by him as from a principle. "Of all beautiful things"—that is, of the whole beauty which shines forth in the aforementioned circles. For the forms of bodies are led back to God through seeds; these through reasons; these through ideas; and by these same steps they are produced by God. Properly, when he says "All things," he understands the Ideas; for in these the rest are included. "Second things around the second; third things around the third." Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet, whom Renaissance Neoplatonists viewed as a source of divine wisdom</note> posited three princes of the world, lords of three orders: Oromasin, Mitrin, and Arimanin <note>Ormuzd, Mithras, and Ahriman</note>. These Plato calls God, Mind, and Soul. He placed three orders in the divine species: Ideas, Reasons, and Seeds. Therefore, the first—that is, the Ideas—are around the first, which is God, since they are granted to the Mind by God and lead the Mind to which they are given back to Him. The second things are around the second—that is, the Reasons around the Mind—since they pass through the Mind into the Soul and direct the Soul toward the Mind. The third things are around the third—that is, the Seeds of things around the Soul; for they pass through the Soul into Nature (namely, into that power of generating) and in turn couple Nature to the Soul. In the same order, Forms descend from Nature into Matter. But Plato does not count these in the established order because, having been asked by Dionysius about divine matters, he introduced the three orders pertaining to incorporeal species as being divine; he omitted the forms of bodies. He did not wish to call God the "first king," but the "King of all," lest if he called him "first," he might perhaps seem to place him together with the following leaders in some species of number or parity of condition. Nor did he say "first things around him," but "all things"...

# COMMENTARY

...lest we should believe him to be the governor of one specific rank rather than of all things. The human mind yearns to understand the nature of those things. Wisely, after those three splendors of divine beauty shining forth in three circles, he added the love of the soul toward them. For from that source, the ardor of the soul is ignited. Indeed, it is only right that divine things should desire divine things, looking upon those matters which are kindred to itself. Since human knowledge arises from the senses, we are often accustomed to judge divine things through those excellences we see in bodies: through the powers of corporeal things, we investigate the power of God; through their order, His wisdom; through their utility, His goodness. Moreover, he calls the forms of bodies "kindred" to the soul, as if they were born next to it. For the forms of bodies are arranged in the step immediately following the soul. Yet none of these is sufficient in itself. Forms of this kind are neither sufficient in their existence, nor do they sufficiently reveal divine things to us. For the true things are the <term>Ideas</term><note>The eternal, perfect archetypes in Platonic philosophy</note>, the reasons, and the seeds; the forms of bodies, however, seem to be shadows of things rather than true things. Just as the shadow of a body does not indicate the exact and distinct figure of that body, so bodies do not demonstrate the proper nature of divine things. Concerning the King himself and those things I have mentioned, there is nothing of such a [corporeal] kind. For in what way could mortal things be like immortal ones, or false things like the true? But as for what follows, the mind speaks; that is, as long as the mind judges divine things through mortal ones, it speaks falsely of the divine; it does not pronounce divine truths, but mortal ones.

### ->Divine beauty shines through all things and is loved in all things. Chapter V.<-

Furthermore, to encompass many things in a few words: the very transcending existence of God is called the Good. Beauty is a certain act or ray penetrating from there through all things: first into the **Angelic Mind**; second into the **Soul of the Universe** and other souls; third into **Nature**; fourth into the **Matter of bodies**. It graces the Mind with the order of Ideas; it fills the Soul with a series of reasons; it supports Nature with seeds; it adorns Matter with forms. Just as a single ray of the sun illuminates four bodies—fire, air, water, and earth—so a single ray of God illuminates Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter. And whoever looks upon the light in these four elements beholds a ray of the sun itself, and through it is turned toward contemplating the sublime light of the sun. So, whoever contemplates and loves the grace in these four—Mind, Soul, Nature, and Body—beholds and loves the glitter of God in them, and through such glitter, God Himself.

### ->The passions of lovers. Chapter VI.<-

From this it happens that the impulse of a lover is not extinguished by the sight or touch of any body. For he does not desire this or that body, but he admires, yearns for, and is struck amazed by the splendor of the celestial light shining through bodies. Therefore, lovers do not know what they desire or what they seek. For they are ignorant of God Himself, whose hidden flavor has instilled a certain most sweet odor of Himself in His works. By this odor, indeed, we are daily aroused. We perceive the odor, certainly; the flavor, beyond doubt, we do not know. Since, therefore, we are enticed by the manifest odor and desire the hidden flavor, we rightly do not know what we desire and what we suffer. From this it also always happens that lovers in some way fear and venerate the sight of the beloved. Even the brave—I will say it even if I fear some of you might blush hearing this—and the wise are accustomed to suffer an inequality of spirit in the presence of any inferior beloved. Truly, it is not a human thing that terrifies them, breaks them, and occupies them. For human power is always more excellent in the brave and the wise. But that glitter of divinity shining in the beautiful, like an image of God, compels lovers to be struck amazed, to tremble, and to venerate. For the same reason, because of the presence of the beloved, the lover despises riches and honors and holds them as nothing. For it is right that divine things be preferred to human ones. It also frequently happens that someone desires to transform themselves into the person of the beloved. And not without reason. For God desires and strives to become man. Who, then, would not exchange being a man for being God? It also happens that those ensnared by love sigh and rejoice by turns. They sigh because they lose themselves, because they perish, because they are destroyed. They rejoice because they transfer themselves into something better. They also grow hot and cold by turns, like those seized by a tertian fever. They are rightly cold because they are deserted by their own heat; and they are hot because they are kindled by the glitters of the celestial rays. Timidity follows the coldness; audacity follows the heat. Therefore, they appear by turns both timid and audacious. Furthermore, the dullest of men are rendered more acute by loving. For who, when inspired by a celestial ray, would not see most sharply? But concerning love itself, its beauty, its origin, and the affections of lovers, let these things suffice.

### ->Concerning the two kinds of Love, and the double Venus. Chapter VII.<-

Next, we must briefly dispute the two kinds of Love. Pausanias, in Plato's writings, asserts that Cupid is the companion of Venus. He thinks it necessary that there be as many Cupids as there are Venuses. Moreover, he commemorates two Venuses, whom likewise twin Cupids accompany. He places one Venus as **Celestial**, born of Uranus <note>original: "Cælo" (Heaven/Uranus)</note> without a mother; the other as **Vulgar**, born of Jupiter and Dione. The Platonists call the highest God "Uranus" because just as this sublime body of the heavens rules and contains all bodies, so that highest God transcends all spirits. They designate the **Mind** by many names. For sometimes they call it Saturn, sometimes Jupiter, sometimes Venus. For that Mind exists, it lives, and it understands. Its Essence they call Saturn, its Life Jupiter, and its Intelligence Venus...

# ON THE BANQUET.

<note>original: "IN CONVIVIVM"</note>

they are accustomed to call. Furthermore, we call the Soul of the World Saturn, and likewise Jupiter and Venus. Insofar as it understands celestial things, it is Saturn. Insofar as it moves the heavens, it is Jupiter. Insofar as it generates lower things, it is Venus. The **first Venus**, which is in the Mind, is said to be born of Uranus <note>the Heavens</note> without a mother; for among the natural philosophers, "mother" signifies matter. That Mind, however, is foreign to any association with corporeal matter. The **second Venus**, which is placed in the Soul of the World, was fathered by Jupiter and Dione. By Jupiter—that is, by that power of the soul itself which moves the heavens. For that power created this secondary power which generates these lower things. They also attribute a mother to her because, being infused into the matter of the world, she is thought to have commerce with matter.

Finally, to speak briefly, Venus is twofold. One is indeed that intelligence which we placed in the Angelic Mind. The other is the power of generation attributed to the Soul of the World. Each has a companion, Love, similar to itself. For the former is carried away by an innate love to contemplate the beauty of God. The latter is likewise carried by its own love to procreate that same beauty in bodies. The former first embraces the splendor of divinity within itself, then translates this into the second Venus. This second one pours the sparks of that splendor into the matter of the world. Through the presence of sparks of this kind, the individual bodies of the world appear beautiful, according to the capacity of their nature. The human soul perceives the appearance of these bodies through the eyes. 

The soul, in turn, possesses twin powers: it has the power of understanding, and it has the power of generating. These twin powers are the two Venuses within us, which are accompanied by twin Loves. As soon as the appearance of a human body offers itself to our eyes, our mind—which is the first Venus in us—venerates and loves it as an image of divine beauty; and through this, it is frequently incited toward the divine. However, the power of generation—the second Venus—desires to generate a form similar to this one. Therefore, love is present in both: in the former, there is a desire to contemplate beauty; in the latter, a desire to procreate it. Both loves are honorable and to be approved, for both follow a divine image. 

What, then, does Pausanias <note>a character in Plato's Symposium</note> disapprove of in love? I shall say: if someone, too greedy for generation, deserts contemplation, or pursues generation beyond measure with women, or against the order of nature with males, or prefers the form of the body to the beauty of the soul, he certainly abuses the dignity of love. Pausanias censures this abuse of love. He who uses it rightly praises the form of the body, but through it, he contemplates the more excellent appearance of the soul, the mind, and God, and admires and loves that more vehemently. He uses the office of generation and intercourse only so far as the natural order and the civil laws established by the prudent prescribe. Pausanias speaks of these things more diffusely.

---

-> **Chapter VIII. An Exhortation to Love. On Simple Love, and on Mutual Love.** <-

But you, O friends, I exhort and beseech to embrace love—a truly divine thing—with all your strength. Do not let that which they say Plato said of a certain lover deter you: "That lover," he says, "is a soul dead in its own body, but living in another's body." Nor should you be disturbed by what Orpheus sang concerning the bitter and wretched lot of lovers. For how these things are to be understood, and by what way they are to be remedied, I ask you then, if you please, to attend to diligently. 

Plato calls love a "bitter thing," and not without justice, because whoever loves, dies. Orpheus also names it <margin>that is, bittersweet</margin> "bitter-sweet." Since love is a voluntary death, as it is death, it is a bitter thing; as it is voluntary, it is sweet. Moreover, whoever loves, dies. For his thoughts, forgetful of himself, are always centered on the beloved. If he does not think of himself, he certainly does not think in himself. Therefore, a soul so affected does not function in itself, since the principal operation of the soul is thought itself. He who does not function in himself, is not in himself. For these two things—being and operation—are equal to one another; there is no being without operation, nor does operation exceed being itself. No one functions where he is not, and wherever he is, he functions. Therefore, the soul of the lover is not in himself, because he does not act in himself. If he is not in himself, he does not even live in himself. He who does not live is dead. Therefore, whoever loves is dead in himself. 

Does he at least live in another? Certainly. There are two species of love: one is simple love, the other is mutual. Simple love is where the beloved does not love the lover. There, the lover is entirely dead; for he neither lives in himself, as we have already sufficiently demonstrated, nor does he live in the beloved, since he is rejected by him. Where then does he live? In the air, or water, or fire, or earth, or some body of a brute beast? By no means. For the human soul does not live in any body other than a human one. Or perhaps he leads his life in some other body of a person not loved? Not even that. For if he does not live where he most vehemently desires to live, in what way shall he live in another? Therefore, he who loves another without being loved in return lives nowhere. For that reason, the unloved lover is entirely dead. Nor will he ever revive unless indignation rouses him. 

But where the beloved responds in love, the lover at least carries on his life in him. Here, certainly, is a marvelous thing: as often as two people embrace each other with mutual benevolence, this one lives in that one, and that one in this. In turn, men of this kind exchange themselves, and each gives himself to the other so that they may receive the other. How they give themselves while they forget themselves, I see. But how they receive the other, I do not understand; for he who does not possess himself will much less possess another. On the contrary, each has himself, and has the other. This one indeed has himself, but in that one. That one also possesses himself, but in this one. Indeed, while I love you who love me, I find myself in you thinking of me, and I recover myself—lost by my own negligence—in you who preserve me. You do the same in me. Again, this also appears marvelous: for after I have lost myself, if I redeem myself through you, I have myself through you. If I have myself through you, I have you first and more than myself; I am closer to you than to myself, since I am attached to myself in no other way than through you as the intermediary. In this, certainly, the power of Cupid...
