# COMMENTARY
## Page 10

The violence of tyranny differs greatly. Indeed, power and love are distinct in this way: a ruler possesses others through himself, but a lover embraces himself through another. Each lover, being further from himself, becomes closer to the other; and though dead in himself, he comes back to life in the other. In mutual love, however, there is only one death, but a twofold rebirth. For he who loves dies in himself once when he neglects himself. He is reborn in the beloved immediately when the beloved embraces him with ardent thought. He is reborn again when he finally recognizes himself in the beloved and does not doubt that he is loved. O happy death, which two lives follow! O wondrous exchange, by which one gives himself up for another, possesses the other, and yet does not cease to possess himself! O inestimable gain, when two become one in such a way that each of the two, instead of being only one, becomes two; and as if doubled, he who had one life now has two, with one death intervening. For he who dies once and is reborn twice has gained a twin life for a single one, and two selves for one. 

Certainly, there is a most just vengeance in mutual love. A homicide must be punished by death. For who would deny that a lover is a homicide, since he separates the soul from the lover? <note>The idea here is that the lover's soul "leaves" their own body to dwell in the beloved.</note> Who, again, would deny that the beloved dies in a similar way, since they love the lover in return? This is a most necessary restitution: when this one returns to that one, and that one to this, the soul which was received. Each gives up his own by loving, and by loving in return, restores the other's soul in place of his own. Therefore, by right itself, whoever loves ought to be loved. Indeed, he who does not love the lover back must be held guilty of homicide. Nay, rather, he is a thief, a homicide, and a sacrilegious man. Money is possessed by the body, and the body by the soul. Therefore, he who seizes the soul—from which both body and money are possessed—seizes the soul, body, and money all at once. Thus it happens that as a thief, homicide, and sacrilegious man, he is liable to a triple death; and as one utterly infamous and profane, he might be killed by anyone with impunity, unless he himself spontaneously fulfills that law: namely, that he loves the lover. Whereupon, as the lover dies once, he likewise dies once; and as the lover is reborn twice, he likewise is reborn twice. 

By the previous reasons it has been shown that the beloved ought to love the lover in return; but that he is not only *obliged* to, but *compelled* to, is shown thus. Likeness procreates love. Likeness is a certain nature that is the same in many. For if I am like you, you are also necessarily like me. Therefore, the same likeness which compels me to love you also forces you to love me. Furthermore, the lover takes himself away from himself and gives himself to the beloved. Therefore, the beloved cares for him as his own property; for his own things are most dear to everyone. Added to this is that the lover carves the figure of the beloved in his own soul. Thus, the soul of the lover becomes a mirror in which the image of the beloved shines back. Therefore, when the beloved recognizes himself in the lover, he is compelled to love him. 

Astrologers believe that the exchange of love is especially strong between those in whose birth charts <note>original: "genesi"</note> there was an exchange of the lights—that is, the Sun and the Moon. For instance, if at my birth the Sun was in Aries and the Moon in Libra, and at your birth the Sun was in Libra and the Moon in Aries. Or those for whom the same or a similar sign and the same or a similar planet was ascending; or if benign planets looked upon the eastern angle in a similar way; or if Venus was positioned in the same house of the nativity and in the same degree. The Platonists add: those whose life is guided by the same, or certainly a similar, *daemon* <note>A guiding spirit or inner divinity in Platonic thought.</note>. Indeed, physicians and moral philosophers maintain that a likeness of temperament <note>original: "complexionis"</note>, nourishment, education, habit, and counsel is the cause of a similar affection. Finally, where more causes concur, there a more vehement exchange is found. Where all are present, there the affections of Pythias and Damon, or Pylades and Orestes, rise again. <note>Famous pairs of devoted friends from classical antiquity.</note>

-> What lovers seek. Chapter IX. <-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a classical figure or cherub amidst foliage.</image-desc>
But what do these people seek when they love one another? They seek beauty. For love is the desire of enjoying beauty. Beauty, moreover, is a certain splendor capturing the human soul for itself. Indeed, the beauty of the body is nothing other than that very splendor in the grace of colors and lines. The beauty of the soul is also a brilliance in the harmony of learning and morals. That light of the body is perceived not by the ears, nor smell, nor taste, nor touch, but by the eye. If the eye alone recognizes it, the eye alone enjoys it. Therefore, the eye alone enjoys the beauty of the body. Since love is nothing else but the desire of enjoying beauty, and this is grasped by the eyes alone, the lover of the body is content with sight alone. The desire for touching, however, is not a part of love, nor an affection of the lover, but a species of wantonness and the disturbance of a servile man. Furthermore, we grasp that light and beauty of the soul with the mind alone. Therefore, he who seeks the beauty of the soul is content with the intuition of the mind alone. Finally, beauty is exchanged for beauty between lovers. A man enjoys the beauty of the younger beloved with his eyes; the youth attains the beauty of the man with his mind. And he who is beautiful only in body becomes, through this association, beautiful also in soul; he who is beautiful only in soul fills the eyes of the body with the beauty of the body. It is clearly a marvelous exchange, honorable, useful, and pleasant to both. Honorable, since it is equal in both, for it is equally honorable to learn and to teach. The pleasure is greater in the elder, who is delighted by sight and intelligence. But in the younger, the utility is greater; for as much as his soul is more excellent than his body, so much more precious is the attainment of the beauty of the soul than that of the body. Thus far for Pausanias; now let us interpret the speech of Eryximachus.

### THE THIRD SPEECH.

-> Love is in all things, toward all things, the creator of all, and the master of all. Chapter I. <-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within an architectural frame.</image-desc>
Three things, next, seem to us to be treated according to the mind of our Eryximachus. First, that love, implanted in all things, is extended through all things. Second, that it is the maker and preserver of all works which are according to nature. Third, that it is the master and lord of every single art. Truly, three grades of things are considered in nature: the Higher, the Lower, and the Equal. Those which are above are the causes of the lower. Those which are below are the works of the higher. Those which are equal are endowed with the same nature among themselves. Causes, indeed, [cherish] their works...

...as if they love their own parts and images. Furthermore, works seek out their causes as if they were their own preservers. Those things which are placed in the same order are affected by a mutual charity toward one another, like similar members of one and the same body. Therefore, God governs the angels, and the angels together with God govern souls, and souls together with them govern bodies with a certain benevolence. In this, the love of the superior for the inferior is clearly perceived. Conversely, bodies join themselves most greedily to their souls, and are separated from them most painfully. Our souls desire the beatitude of celestial things; the celestial beings happily venerate the majesty of the supreme divinity. And here is the affection of love from the inferior toward the superior. Likewise, all parts of fire willingly cling together. Again, the parts of earth, water, and air do the same; and in any species of animal, animals of the same species always associate with one another through mutual habit. Here, love is seen toward equals and similar things. Who then will doubt that love is innate in all things toward all things? And this is what Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> signified in his book *On the Divine Names*, following the mind of Hierotheus, with these words: Whether we speak of love as divine, or angelic, or spiritual, or animal, or natural, let us understand it as a certain joining and mixing power: which moves the superior to provide for the inferior; reconciles equals to a social communion with one another; and finally admonishes all inferior things to turn toward the better and more sublime. Thus he spoke.

### Love is the Author and Preserver of All Things. Chapter II.

Regarding the second part of our speech, in which love was called the maker and preserver of all things, it is proved thus. The desire for propagating one's own perfection is a certain kind of love. Absolute perfection is in the supreme power of God. The divine intelligence contemplates this, and likewise the divine will desires to propagate it outside of itself; from which love of propagating, all things were created by Him. Therefore our Dionysius says: Divine love did not permit the King of all things to remain within Himself without offspring. This same instinct for propagation was instilled in all things by that first author. Through this, those spirits of the holy heavens move the heavens and bestow their gifts upon all that follow. Through this, the stars diffuse their light into the elements. Through this, fire moves the air by the sharing of its heat, the air moves the water, the water the earth; and conversely, the earth draws the water to itself, the water the air, and the air the fire. Herbs also and trees, desiring to propagate their seed, beget things like themselves. Brute animals also and men are snatched away by the allurements of this same desire to procreate offspring. Because if love makes all things, it also preserves all things. For the office of making and preserving is always the same. Surely, like things are preserved by like. But love draws like to like. Individual parts of the earth, with mutual love coupling them, betake themselves to other parts of the earth similar to them. The whole earth also descends with greed for that center of the world similar to itself. Parts of water are similarly carried toward each other and toward a place suitable for them with the whole body of water. The parts of air and fire do the same; and even these two elements are drawn toward the upper region suitable and similar to them by love of that region. The heaven also, as Plato says in the book *On Kingship* <note>Likely referring to the *Statesman* (Politikos).</note>, is moved by innate love. For the soul of the heaven is entirely present at once in any points of the heaven. Therefore, the heaven, desiring to enjoy the soul, runs so that through all its parts it may everywhere enjoy the whole soul. It flies most rapidly so that, as far as possible, it may be everywhere at once, wherever the whole soul is at once. Furthermore, the concave surface of a larger sphere is the natural place of a smaller sphere; and because any particle of this sphere agrees equally with any particle of that one, any part seeks to touch all its particles. If they were at rest, individual parts would touch individual parts, not every part touching all. By running, it almost attains what it could not attain by resting. It runs most swiftly so that every part may touch all others at nearly the same time, according to its strength. Furthermore, all things are preserved by the unity of their parts; they perish by the dispersion of parts. Mutual love of those same parts first effects this unity. This may be observed in the humors of our bodies and the elements of the world, by whose concord (as Empedocles the Pythagorean says) both the world and our body consist; by discord they are dissipated. Concord, however, provides them with an exchange of peace and love.

### How Love is the Master of Arts and the Governor. Chapter III.

It remains after this that we explain in what way Love is the master of all arts and the governor. We shall understand him to be the master of arts if we only consider that no one can ever either find or learn any art unless the delight of investigation and the desire for finding incites them; and he who teaches loves his disciples, and the disciples most greedily thirst for that teaching. Furthermore, he is deservedly called the Governor. For whoever most loves the crafts themselves and the persons for whom they are made, diligently executes and exactly completes the works of art. It is added that craftsmen in individual arts bring in and care for nothing other than love. We shall briefly run through those arts at present which Eryximachus commemorates in Plato. For what else does Medicine consider, than how the four humors of the body may become and remain friends to one another? What foods and drinks, and other uses of living or healing, does nature love and require? Those two loves, the Celestial and the Common, which Pausanias had distinguished above, Eryximachus also found here through a certain similarity. For a temperate affection of the body has a moderate love, directed toward moderate and suitable things. An intemperate one contains the contrary, and is directed toward contraries. The former should be indulged; the latter should never be obeyed. In gymnastic exercise also, one must investigate what habit of body, what modes of exercising, what gestures [love] desires and requires...

# COMMENTARY

<margin>Catchword: rit</margin>

In agriculture, love determines which soil and which seeds are required, what kind of cultivation is needed, and what method of tending is preferred by individual trees. The same is observed in music: its practitioners investigate which rhythms <note>original: "numeri"</note> love which other rhythms more or less. They find the least love between one and two, or one and seven. However, between one and three, four, five, and six, they find a more vehement love. Between one and eight, the love is most vehement. They make high and low voices, which are different by nature, more friendly to one another through fixed intervals and measures. From this, the composition and sweetness of harmony is born. They also temper slower and faster movements with one another so that they become the greatest of friends, exhibiting rhythm and elegance. Two kinds of music or melody are handed down. One is solemn and constant; the other is soft and wanton. Plato judges in his books on the Republic and the Laws that the former is useful to those who use it, while the latter is harmful. At the banquet, he placed the Muse Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy, representing heavenly love</note> over the former, and Polymnia <note>The Muse of many songs, here representing varied or common love</note> over the latter. Some love the first kind, others the second. The love of the former must be complied with, and the sounds they seek must be employed. The appetite of the latter must be resisted. For the love of the former is celestial, while the love of the latter is common. There is also a certain friendship in the stars and the four elements, which astronomy considers. In these, those two kinds of love are found in a certain way. For there is a moderate love in them when they harmonize most temperately with mutual strengths. There is also an immoderate love, when one of them loves itself too much and in some way abandons the others. From the former comes the pleasing temperance of the air, the tranquility of water, the fertility of lands, and the health of animals; from the latter, the opposites proceed. Finally, the faculty of the Prophet and the Priest seems to be occupied chiefly with this: that they may teach us which duties of men are friendly to God, and by what means men may become friends to God; what measure of love and charity should be applied toward God, toward one's country, parents, and others, both living and deceased. The same may be conjectured in the remaining arts; and it may be concluded summarily that love in all things and toward all things is the author and preserver of all, and exists as the lord and master of all arts. Divine Orpheus rightly called him "twice-born," <note>original: "bigenitum"</note> holding the keys to all things. For how he is of a twin nature you have heard first from Pausanias and then from Eryximachus. By what reasoning he is said by Orpheus to hold the keys of the world, we can sufficiently understand from the above; for as we have shown, this desire for propagating one's own perfection, innate in all things, unfolds the hidden and folded fertility of each thing. It compels seeds to sprout into a bud, draws out the strengths of each thing from its bosom, conceives offspring, and, as if by certain keys, brings them into the light by opening what was conceived. Wherefore all parts of the world, because they are the works of a single artist and members of the same machine, are bound to one another in being and living by a certain mutual charity. Thus it can rightly be said that love is a perpetual knot and the bond of the world, the immovable support of its parts, and the firm foundation of the entire machine.

### No member of the world hates another member. Chapter IV.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a classical figure or deity within a circular frame, surrounded by floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

If this is so, no members of this work can be enemies to one another in any way. For fire does not flee water out of hatred for water, but out of love for itself, lest it be extinguished by the cold of the water. Nor does water extinguish fire out of hatred for fire, but it is drawn by a certain desire of amplifying its own cold to produce water similar to itself from the body of the fire. For since all natural appetite tends toward the good and none toward evil, the purpose of water is not to extinguish fire (which is an evil), but to generate water like itself (which is a good). If it could fulfill this without the destruction of the fire, it would certainly not consume the fire. The same reasoning is assigned to other things that seem contrary and inimical. Furthermore, the lamb does not hate the life and form of the wolf, but dreads its own destruction which is brought by the wolf. Nor does the wolf tear and devour the lamb out of hatred for the lamb, but out of love for itself. Nor does man dread man, but the vices of man; nor do we envy the gifts of those more powerful or acute out of hatred for them, but out of benevolence for ourselves, fearing lest we succumb entirely to them. Therefore, nothing prevents love from being in all things and penetrating through all things. This great god, therefore—because he is everywhere and sits in the innermost shrines of all things—let us undoubtedly fear him as a powerful lord whose command we cannot escape, and as a most wise judge from whom our thoughts cannot be hidden. Because he is the creator and preserver of all, let us venerate him as a father and honor him as a protector and defense. Because he teaches the individual arts, let us follow him as a teacher; by whose authorship we exist and live, by whose preservation we remain perpetually, and by whose presidency and judgment we are governed. By whose scepter we are instructed and formed to live well and blessedly.

### THE FOURTH SPEECH. Chapter I.

Aristophanes says that Love, above all other gods, is exceedingly beneficial to the human race, the curator and guardian of men, and their physician. It is necessary first to observe what the nature of men once was, and what its passions were. For it was not formerly as it is now, but far di—

...turned. In the beginning, there were three kinds of humans: not only the two that exist now, male and female, but also a third kind composed of both. Furthermore, the form of every human was complete and round, having a back and sides forming a circle; they had four hands and an equal number of legs. They also had two faces joined to a rounded neck and entirely alike. The male kind was born from the sun; the female from the earth; the mixed kind from the moon. Because of this, they were of high spirit and robust body; for which reason they attempted to fight with the gods and ascend into heaven. Therefore Jupiter cut each of them lengthwise and made two out of one, in the manner of those who cut eggs lengthwise with a hair. He also threatened that if they appeared to go mad against the gods again out of pride, he would divide them once more in the same way. After human nature was thus divided, each half desired its other half. Therefore they ran together, and throwing their arms around each other, they embraced one another, longing to be restored to their former condition. Because of this, they began to die from hunger and inactivity, unless God had imposed a limit on their meeting. From this, surely, a mutual love was born in humans, the reconciler of our ancient nature, striving to make one out of two and to heal the nature of humanity. For each of us is a half of a human, as if sliced, just as the little fish called "flatfish" <note>original: "psectae & auratae" — likely referring to soles or gilt-heads which appear as if split</note> make two out of one when cut. Each, therefore, seeks his own half. Whenever, then, his own half meets someone—of whichever sex he may be greedy for—he is most vehemently moved, clings with burning love, and does not suffer to be separated from that person for even a moment. Therefore, the desire for restoring the whole has received the name of "Love." This love helps us greatly in the present time, for it leads each person to his own half, once his dearest friend; and for the future, it inspires in us the highest hope that by piously worshipping God, He will restore us to our old form and, by healing us, make us most blessed.

### The opinion of Plato concerning the ancient form of humans is explained. Chapter II.

Aristophanes tells these and many other things, similar to monsters and portents, under which, as if under certain veils, it must be believed that divine mysteries lie hidden. For it was the custom of ancient theologians to cover their sacred secrets with the shadows of figures, so that they would not be polluted by the profane and impure. We, however, do not think that every single thing described in the figures above and others pertains exactly to the literal sense. For Aurelius Augustine says that not everything fashioned in figures should be thought to signify something. For many things are added for the sake of order and connection to those things which they do signify. The earth is cut open by the plowshare alone; but so that this can be done, the other parts of the plow are also joined to it. Therefore, this is the summary of what is proposed for us to explain: Humans once had three sexes—Male, Female, and Mixed—the children of the Sun, Earth, and Moon. They were also whole. But because of pride, when they wished to equal themselves to God, they were split in two; if they are proud again, they are to be split in two once more. Once the section is made, one half is drawn to the other half by love, so that a restoration of integrity may occur, which when completed, the human race will be blessed. The summary of our interpretation is of this sort: Humans—that is, the souls of humans—once—that is, when they are created by God—are whole. They are adorned with two lights, the innate and the infused: so that by the innate they might see equal and inferior things, and by the infused they might behold superior things. They wished to equal themselves to God, and they turned themselves back toward the single innate light. Here they were divided. They lost the infused splendor when they were turned toward the innate light alone; and immediately they fell into bodies. Having become more proud, they will be divided again: that is, if they trust too much in their natural talent, that innate and natural light which remained will be extinguished in a certain way. They had three sexes: Males born from the sun, Females from the earth, Mixed from the moon. Some received the radiance of God according to courage (which is male); others according to temperance (which is female); others according to justice (which is mixed). These three virtues in us are the daughters of the other three which God has. But in God those three are called Sun, Moon, and Earth; in us, they are called Male, Female, and Mixed. Once the section is made, one half is drawn to the other by love. The souls, now divided and immersed in bodies, as soon as they come to the years of adolescence, are excited by the natural and innate light which they preserved—as if by a certain half of themselves—toward that infused and divine light, once their other half, which they lost when falling, to be recovered by the study of truth. Once this is received, they will now be whole and blessed by the vision of God. This, therefore, shall be the compendium of our interpretation.

### Man is the soul itself, and the soul is immortal. Chapter III.

Since the body consists of matter and quantity, and it pertains to matter to receive and to quantity to be only divided and extended; and since that reception and division are passions <note>In this context, "passions" means things acted upon or suffered, rather than emotions.</note>, it follows that by its own part, nature is subject only to passion and corruption. If indeed any action seems to belong to the body, it does not act insofar as it is a body, but insofar as a certain incorporeal power and quality is in it, as heat is in the mass of fire, cold in the matter of water, and temperament <note>original: "complexio" — the balance of humors</note> in our body. From these qualities, certainly, the operations of bodies proceed. For fire does not heat because it is long, or wide, or deep, but because it is hot. Nor does a more extended fire heat more—indeed, because of dispersion, it heats less—but rather the fire which is hotter. Since, therefore, operations come forth by the benefit of powers and qualities, and the powers and qualities themselves do not consist of matter and quantity (although they are in matter and quantity), it follows that to be acted upon belongs to the body, but to act belongs to something incorporeal. Both these powers are indeed instruments for working. But they themselves are by no means sufficient for working on their own, because they are not...

Ficino argues that "Love" is the drive to recover this lost spiritual integrity and begins a new chapter on the immortality of the soul.</summary>

are sufficient for existence. For that which lies in another, and cannot sustain itself, certainly depends upon another. Thus it happens that qualities, because they are necessarily sustained by the body, are created and governed by some higher substance which is neither a body nor lies within a body. The soul is of this kind: being present in and dwelling within bodies, it sustains itself; it grants to bodies the quality and power of their physical makeup <note>original: "complexionis"</note>, through which, as if through instruments in the body and by means of the body, it carries out various operations. Hence, it is asserted that "the human" generates, nourishes, grows, runs, stands, sits, speaks, crafts works of art, perceives, and understands. Because the soul itself does these things, the soul itself must be the human. If we say a human generates, grows, and nourishes, the soul—acting as the father and architect of the body—begets, increases, and nourishes it. If a human stands, sits, or speaks, the soul sustains, bends, and moves the limbs of the body. If a human crafts or runs, the soul stretches out the hands and twists them at will, and moves the feet. If a human perceives, the soul perceives external bodies through the instruments of the senses, as if through windows and openings. If a human understands, the soul attains the truth through itself without any bodily instrument. Therefore, everything that a human is said to do, the soul <note>original: "animus"</note> itself does; the body merely undergoes it. For this reason, the human is the soul alone; the body, however, is the work and instrument of the human. This is especially true because the soul exercises its most vital operation—namely, intelligence—without any bodily instrument, since it understands incorporeal things through intelligence, whereas only corporeal things are known through the body. Therefore, if the soul acts through itself in any way, it certainly exists and lives through itself. Moreover, it lives without the body because it operates without the body. If it exists through itself, it is fitting that it has an existence proper to itself and not shared with the body; therefore, it can claim for itself the name of "human" separately from the mass of the body. Indeed, since this name is spoken of each of us throughout our entire life—for everyone at every age is called a human—it seems to signify something that remains stable. The body flows incessantly, changing by growing, shrinking, continuous dissolution, melting, and alternating heat and cold. The soul always remains the same, which the investigation of truth clearly shows us: the will for the good is always the same, as is the firm preservation of memory. Who, then, would be so insane as to attribute the name of "human," which is most firm in us, to the flowing body that is always and everywhere changing, rather than to the most stable soul? From these points, it can be clear why Aristophanes <note>A reference to the character in Plato's *Symposium*</note>, in the Platonic manner, named "humans" to signify our souls.

### That the soul is adorned with two lights: and why the creation of the soul with two lights descends into the body. Chapter IV.

Furthermore, the soul, as soon as it is born from God, is turned toward its parent by a certain natural instinct, just as fire generated on earth by the power of the upper regions is immediately directed toward the heights by the impulse of nature; having turned toward Him, it is illuminated by His rays. But this first brightness, received into the substance of the soul which was previously formless in itself, becomes darker; it becomes proper and natural to the soul according to the capacity of that space. Therefore, through this light, as if through something equal to itself, the soul indeed sees itself and the things below it (that is, all bodies), but it does not see God or other higher things. However, having been made closer to God through this first spark, it receives a second, clearer light by which it may also know the things above. Thus, it has a twin light: one Natural or innate, the other Divine and infused. Joined together like two wings, the soul may fly through the sublime region. And if it always used that divine light, it would always cling to divine things; the Earth would be empty of rational animals. But it was decreed by divine providence that the soul should be mistress of itself, able to use both lights together or one at a time. Hence it happens that, with nature as its guide, the soul turns toward its own light and, neglecting the divine, notices itself and its powers regarding the construction of the body; it desires to exercise these powers in crafting bodies. Weighted down by this desire, as they say, it descends into the body, where it exercises the powers of generating, moving, and perceiving; by its presence, it adorns the earth, the lowest seat of the world. The earth, therefore, ought not to lack reason, lest any part of the world be destitute of the presence of rational living beings, just as the Author in whose likeness the whole world was made is Himself Reason. Our soul fell into the body when, neglecting the divine light, it used only its own light and began to be content with itself. God alone, who lacks nothing and above whom there is nothing, remains content with Himself, being self-sufficient. Therefore, the soul made itself equal to God when it wished to be content with itself alone, as if it were no less self-sufficient than God.

### In how many ways the soul returns to God. Chapter V.

Aristophanes says this pride was clearly the cause for the soul, which was born whole, to be divided—that is, to use only one of the twin lights thereafter and neglect the other. Here, immersed in the abyss of the body as if in the river Lethe <note>The mythological river of forgetfulness</note>, having forgotten itself for a time, it is snatched away by the senses and lust, as if by attendants and a tyrant. But when the body is mature, the instruments of the senses purged, and learning contributes its part, the soul recovers its senses a little. Then the natural brightness shines forth, and it investigates the order of natural things; through this investigation, it perceives that there is some architect of this vast machine. It desires both to see and to possess Him, but He is seen only by divine splendor. Therefore, the mind, by the investigation of its own light, is most vehemently incited to recover the divine light. This incitement and desire...

# ON THE BANQUET.

This is the nature of true love: with it as our guide, one half of a human yearns for the other half. This is because the natural light, which is one half of the soul, strives to rekindle that divine light—the other half of the soul, once neglected—within the spirit. And this is what Plato says in his *Letter to Dionysius*: "The human soul longs to understand the nature of divine things, looking upon those things which are akin to itself." <note>Plato’s Second Letter (312e) discusses the soul's desire to know the "King of All."</note> Truly, when God poured His light into the soul, He adapted it chiefly for this purpose: to lead humanity toward the blessedness that consists in possessing Him.

We are led to this blessedness by four virtues: Prudence, Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance. <term>Prudence</term> <note>Practical wisdom or discernment.</note> first reveals this blessedness to us. The other three virtues act as three paths leading toward it. Thus, God tempers His spark in various souls toward this end in different ways: so that with Prudence as the guide, some seek their Creator through the duties of Fortitude, others through Justice, and others through Temperance.

Indeed, some, by the grace of this gift, undergo dangers and death with a brave spirit for the sake of divine worship, for honor, or for their country. Others establish their lives so justly that they neither inflict injury on anyone nor, to the best of their power, allow it to be inflicted. Others subdue their lusts through vigils, fasting, and labor. These proceed by three different paths, yet they strive to reach the same goal of blessedness, with Prudence showing them the way. Furthermore, these three virtues are also contained within the Prudence of God Himself.

Inflamed by the desire for these virtues, the souls of men wish to reach them through their duties, to cling to them, and to possess them forever. We call the **Fortitude** of men "masculine" because of its strength and boldness. We call **Temperance** "feminine" because of its somewhat relaxed and cooler habit of desire and its mild nature. **Justice** we call "promiscuous" <note>In this historical context, "promiscuous" means "shared," "mixed," or "common to both sexes."</note>: feminine insofar as its innocence harms no one, but masculine insofar as it does not allow harm to be done to others and turns a more severe judgment against wicked men.

Because it is the nature of the male to give and the female to receive, we call the **Sun** male, which receives light from no one but displays it to all. The **Moon**, which receives from the sun and gives to the elements, we call promiscuous because of its giving and receiving. The **Earth**, since it receives from all but gives to none, we call female. Therefore, the Sun, Moon, and Earth—and Fortitude, Justice, and Temperance—are rightly marked by the names of male, promiscuous, and female. And so that we may give a more excellent title to God, we call these virtues in Him "Sun, Moon, and Earth," while in us we call them "masculine, promiscuous, and feminine" sexes.

To those whom that divine light was infused from the Sun of God with the affection of Fortitude at their birth, we say a masculine light was granted. To those from the Moon of God with the affection of Justice, a promiscuous light. To those from the Earth of God with the affection of Temperance, a feminine light. We neglected that inward and divine light and immediately turned back toward the natural light. Thus, having set one aside, we preserved the other; where we hold one half of ourselves, we have let go of the other half.

At a certain time of life, led by the natural light, we all indeed affect the divine, but we proceed toward its attainment in different ways. Those who once received it from the Fortitude of God with the affection of Fortitude proceed through Fortitude; others through Justice or Temperance in like manner. Finally, each seeks his own "half" as he had received it. Some, through the masculine light of God once lost and now recovered, wish to enjoy God with masculine Fortitude; others through the promiscuous light with promiscuous virtue; others through the feminine in the same way.

Truly, those attain so great a gift who, after the natural spark has shone forth in them in their adult years, judge that it is not sufficient for judging divine things. They take care lest, by the judgment of the natural spark, they attribute the affections of souls or bodies to the Divine Majesty, or think that He is not more excellent than bodies or souls. In this, many are said to have erred: those who, trusting in their natural talent in the investigation of divine matters, either said there is no God (like **Diagoras**), or doubted (like **Protagoras**), or judged Him to be a body (like the **Epicureans, Stoics, Cyrenaics**, and many others), or some kind of soul (like **Marcus Varro, Marcus Manilius**, and several others).

These men, as if impious, not only failed to recover the divine light once neglected, but even corrupted the natural light through its abuse. That which is corrupted is rightly considered broken and torn apart. Therefore, the souls of those who, as if proud and swollen with conceit, trust in their own strengths, are "cut again" (as **Aristophanes** says) <note>A reference to the myth in Plato's *Symposium* where Zeus splits humans in half to humble them.</note> when they obscure even the natural light that remained to them with false opinions and extinguish it with wicked morals.

Therefore, those use the natural light rightly who, recognizing it to be crippled and mutilated, judge it to be sufficient in some way for judging natural things; but for those things which are above nature, thinking they need a more sublime light, they prepare themselves by a most exact purification of the soul so that the divine light may shine upon them again. By its rays, they will think rightly of God and be restored to that former integrity.

### Love leads back to heaven: it distributes the grades of blessedness: it bestows eternal joy. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring a seated figure in a landscape.</image-desc>

**V**enerable guests, now make that god—whom Aristophanes says is a benefactor to the human race above all other gods—propitious to you with every kind of sacrifice. Invoke him with pious prayers; embrace him with your whole heart. He, by his beneficence, first leads souls to the heavenly table, abounding in ambrosia and nectar; then he settles each in their own seat; finally, he sweetly detains them forever. For none return to heaven except those who have pleased the King of the heavens; and those please Him who love Him exceedingly. To know Him truly is entirely impossible at the present time. But to love Him truly as He is known is both possible and easy. He who [loves] God...

# COMMENTARY

...they know Him, yet He does not yet take pleasure in them unless they love what they have known. For those who know and love are loved by God, not because they know, but because they love. For we ourselves embrace with charity not those who merely know us, but those who have loved us. Indeed, we have many enemies who know us. Therefore, it is not the knowledge of God, but love, that restores us to heaven. Furthermore, the order of those reclining at the celestial table follows the diverse ranks of lovers. For those who loved God more excellently feast there on more excellent banquets. Truly, those who honored the strength of God through works of fortitude enjoy that very strength. Those who honored justice enjoy justice; likewise temperance, they enjoy temperance; and thus various souls enjoy various ideas and reasons of the divine mind according to the various rapture of their love. Yet all enjoy God in His entirety, because He is whole in every individual idea. But they possess the whole of God more excellently who behold Him in a more excellent idea. Each person possesses that virtue of God which they loved. Therefore, envy—as Plato says in the *Phaedrus*—is absent from the divine choir. For since it is the most pleasant thing of all to possess the beloved object, anyone lives content and full in possessing that which they love. Indeed, if two lovers should obtain their delights, each rests in the beloved possession of his own; nor will he have any care if another should possess a more beautiful beloved. Wherefore, by the benefit of love, it is brought about that in the diverse degrees of happiness, everyone is content with their portion without any envy. It also happens that the souls feast upon the same banquets eternally without any satiety. For just as guests are not satisfied by feasts or wines unless hunger and thirst entice them to eat, so the delight lasts as long as the greed <note>original: "auiditas", here meaning a spiritual craving or intense desire</note> remains. And who would deny that this greed is a certain kind of love? Therefore, the eternal love with which the soul is always moved toward God ensures that it always rejoices in God as if in a new spectacle. The same goodness of God always kindles this love in the soul, which also makes the lover blessed. Therefore, to embrace it briefly, we shall praise three benefits of love: that by restoring us—who were once divided—into a whole, it leads us back to heaven; that it places each in their proper seats and makes all peaceful in that distribution; and that, with all boredom expelled, it continually kindles a new delight in the soul by its own heat, rendering it blessed by a charming and sweet fruition.

### FIFTH SPEECH. Love is most blessed because it is beautiful and good. Chapter I.

Carolo Marsuppini <note>A 15th-century Italian humanist and chancellor of the Florentine Republic</note>, the sweet foster-child of the Muses, following Landino, approaches Agathon’s speech in this way. Our Agathon considers the god Love to be most blessed because he is most beautiful and best. He diligently enumerates what is required for him to be most beautiful, and likewise what is required for him to be best; in enumerating these, he fashions Love himself. Finally, after he has described what Love is like, he counts the benefits bestowed by him upon the human race, and this is the sum of that discussion. It is in our primary interest to inquire for what reason, in order to show him as blessed, he said he was exceedingly beautiful and good; or what the distinction is between goodness and beauty. In the *Philebus*, Plato wants the "blessed" to be that which lacks nothing; and that is what is perfect in every part. Now, there is a certain internal perfection, and an external one. The internal we call goodness; the external, beauty. Therefore, that which is inwardly good and outwardly beautiful, we call "most blessed" as being perfect from every side. We certainly observe this difference in all things. Truly, in gemstones—as the natural philosophers <note>original: "physici"</note> maintain—a certain internal, most temperate mixing of the four elements produces an external luster. Furthermore, in herbs and trees, an innate fertility in the roots and marrow clothes them with a most pleasing variety of flowers and leaves. In animals, a healthy complexion of the humors procreates a pleasant appearance of features and colors. Even the virtue of the soul is seen to display a certain most honorable decorum in words, gestures, and deeds. The heavens also, by their sublime substance, are surrounded by a most clear light. In all these things, internal perfection produces the external. We may call the former goodness, and the latter beauty. Wherefore, we hold beauty to be a certain flower of goodness; by the allurements of this flower, as if by a kind of bait, the goodness hidden within entices those who look upon it. Since the knowledge of our mind takes its origin from the senses, we would never understand nor desire the goodness itself implanted in the inner recesses of things, unless we were led to it by the manifest signs of the external appearance. In this matter, the utility of this form and its companion <note>Love</note> appears truly wonderful. By these things, I think it is sufficiently shown that there is as much difference between goodness and appearance as there is between a seed and a small flower; and just as the flowers of trees, having risen from seeds, also produce seeds themselves, so this appearance—the flower of goodness—as it sprouts from the good, so it leads lovers back to the good, which indeed our hero here has abundantly demonstrated in the preceding sections.

### How love is depicted, and by which parts of the soul beauty is known, and love is born. Chapter II.

After these things, Agathon enumerates more diffusely how many things are required for the beautiful appearance of that god. He is, he says, young, tender, agile, well-proportioned, and shining. But we must first ask what these things contribute to beauty. Then, when they are attributed to this god, in what way they ought to be understood. Humans possess reason and sense. Reason, through itself, comprehends the incorporeal natures <note>original: "rationes", the formal principles or 'reasons' of things</note> of all things. Sense, through the five instruments of its body, reaches the images and qualities of bodies: colors through the eyes, voices through the ears, smells through the nostrils, tastes through the tongue, and through the nerves the simple qualities of the elements, namely heat and cold, and the rest. Therefore...

# ON THE BANQUET
<note>original: "IN CONVIVIVM" — This refers to Plato's Symposium, a dialogue about the nature of Love.</note>

...pertaining to cognition, as far as the proposed question is concerned, they count the powers of the soul as: Reason, Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, and Touch. Reason is attributed to the supreme divinity, Sight to fire, Hearing to air, Smell to the odor of vapors, Taste to water, and Touch to earth. Reason indeed investigates celestial things and has no specific seat in any member of the body, just as divinity has no fixed seat in any part of the world. Sight is located in the highest part of the body like fire in the highest region of the world, and by its nature perceives light, which is characteristic of fire. Hearing, following sight just as pure air follows fire, draws in voices; these are both produced in broken air and glide into the ears through the interval of the air. Smell is assigned entirely to misty air and to vapors mixed from air and water; because it is positioned between the ears and the tongue—as if between air and water—it easily apprehends and delights in those vapors, especially those arising from the mixture of air and water, such as the scents of herbs, flowers, and fruits, which are most sweet to the nostrils. Who would doubt to compare taste to the liquids of water? It succeeds smell as a thicker kind of air, and being drenched in the constant liquid of saliva, it is most vehemently delighted by drink and moist flavors. Who likewise would hesitate to ascribe touch to the earth? Since it is made of all the parts of the earthly body, it is fulfilled in the nerves which are most earthly; it most easily touches those things that have solidity and weight, which earth bestows upon bodies. Here it also happens that Touch, Taste, and Smell only perceive things placed in close proximity to them, and are affected considerably in the act of sensing, although Smell seems to apprehend more remote things than taste and touch. Hearing, however, knows more distant things and is not so easily offended. Sight looks out even further and acts in a moment; for the eyes see a flash of lightning before the ears hear the thunder. Reason grasps the most remote things of all; for it perceives not only what has been in the world and what is present, like the senses, but also what is above the heavens and what has been or will be. From these things it can be clear to anyone that of those six powers of the soul, three pertain rather to the body and matter—namely Touch, Taste, and Smell—while the other three—namely Reason, Sight, and Hearing—pertain to the spirit. Therefore, those three declining toward the body agree more with the body than with the soul; and those things perceived by them, since they move the body in a way suitable to itself, hardly reach as far as the soul, and please it very little as they are least similar to it. But the three higher powers, most remote from matter, agree much more with the soul; they capture those things which move the body very little indeed, but move the soul most vehemently. For Scents, Flavors, Heat, and similar things either harm or benefit the body greatly; they contribute little to the soul in terms of wonder or judgment, and are only moderately desired by it. Reason, [the perception of] incorporeal truth, colors, figures, and voices move the body either not at all or very minimally; but they especially sharpen the edge of the soul for investigation and snatch its desire toward themselves. The food of the soul is truth. To find it, the eyes contribute greatly; to learn it, the ears. Therefore, the soul affects those things pertaining to reason, sight, and hearing for their own sake, as its own proper nourishment. But those things which move the other three senses are more necessary for the body, either for nourishing, warming, or generating. Thus the soul seeks them not for its own sake, but for the sake of another—that is, the body. We are said to "love" those things which we desire for our own sake; but those things we desire for the sake of something else, we do not love at all. Rightly, therefore, we wish love to pertain only to sciences, figures, and voices; and for that reason, that grace alone which is found in these three—in the virtue of the soul, in figure, and in voice—is called "beauty" because it most calls out to the soul. <margin>which the word signifies</margin> <margin>kalos</margin> <note>Greek: καλὸς — "beautiful" or "good." The author is linking the Greek word for beauty to the idea of "calling" (kalein).</note> indeed signifies beauty in Latin. Truly, the true and best character of the soul is pleasing to us; the figure of a handsome body is pleasing; the harmony of voices is pleasing. And since the soul—as if they were its kin and in a way incorporeal—values these three much more than the remaining three, it is consistent that it should adopt them more greedily, embrace them more ardently, and admire them more vehemently. And this very grace, whether of virtue, figure, or voices, which calls and ravishes the soul to itself through reason, sight, or hearing, is most rightly called beauty. And these are those three Graces of which Orpheus spoke:

> Splendor, youthfulness, and most abundant joy. 

He calls "Splendor" that grace and beauty of the soul which consists in the clarity of truth and virtue. "Youthfulness" <note>original: "viriditatem" — literally "greenness" or "vigor."</note> he calls the sweetness of figure and color, for this flourishes most of all in the greenness of youth. Finally, "Joy" he calls that sincere, healthy, and perpetual delight which we feel in music.

### Beauty is something incorporeal. Chapter III.

Since these things are so, it is necessary that beauty be something common to virtue, figures, and voices. For we would not call any of these three "beautiful" in a similar way unless one definition of beauty were present in all three. From this it follows that the very principle of beauty cannot be a body; since if beauty were corporeal, it would not at all suit the virtues of the soul, which are incorporeal. And yet, beauty is so far from being a body that not only that which is in the virtues of the soul, but even that which is in bodies and voices, cannot be corporeal. For although we call certain bodies "beautiful," they are not beautiful because of their very matter. Indeed, the body of a man is one and the same today when it is handsome, and tomorrow when it is deformed by some disfiguring accident; as if being a body were one thing, and being handsome were another. Nor are they beautiful because of their size; since some large things are...

# COMMENTARY

Likewise, some short things appear beautiful, and often large things are deformed, while small things are beautiful; and conversely, small things are foul, while large things are most pleasing. It also sometimes happens that beauty is similar in certain large and small bodies. If, therefore, while the quantity <note>size or physical bulk</note> remains the same, beauty is frequently changed by some chance, and if beauty remains when the quantity is changed, and appears similar in both large and small things, then certainly these two—beauty and quantity—must be entirely different. Furthermore, if the beauty of any body were in some way corporeal <note>physical</note> through the very thickness of its own body, it would not, however, please the beholder insofar as it is physical. The appearance of a person pleases the soul not as it lies in the exterior matter, but as its image is captured or conceived by the soul through sight. That image in the sight and the soul, since these are incorporeal, cannot be a body. For in what way could the small pupil of the eye capture the whole of a hundred <note>original: "centum," likely referring to a large measurement or a hundred-foot object</note>, so to speak, if it received it in a physical manner? In no way, surely. But indeed, the spirit receives the entire amplitude of the body in a point, in a spiritual manner and as an incorporeal image; thus, only that appearance which is received by the soul pleases it. Moreover, although this is a likeness of the exterior body within the soul, it is nevertheless incorporeal. Therefore, an incorporeal appearance pleases. That which pleases is pleasing to someone; that which is pleasing is, finally, beautiful. From this it follows that love is directed toward something incorporeal; and beauty itself is a certain spiritual likeness of a thing rather than a physical appearance.

There are, however, some who think that beauty is a certain position of all the members, or, to use their words, a commensuration <term>commensuratio: the proportional relationship between parts</term> and proportion along with a certain sweetness of colors. We do not admit their opinion for this reason: since this kind of arrangement of parts exists only in composite things, nothing simple would be beautiful. But now we call pure colors, lights, a single voice, the glitter of gold, the whiteness of silver, knowledge, and the soul—all of which are simple—beautiful; and these things delight us wonderfully as if they were truly beautiful. Added to this is that such proportion includes all the composite members of the body and is not in the individual parts, but in the whole. Therefore, the individual members will not be beautiful in themselves. Yet from the individual little parts, the proportion of the whole composite is born. From this follows something most absurd: that things which are not beautiful by their own nature should give birth to beauty. 

Often it also happens that while the same proportion and measure of the members remains, the body does not please as much as before. Furthermore, the figure of your body is the same today as it was last year, but the grace <note>original: "gratia," referring to a charming or divine quality beyond mere shape</note> is not the same. Nothing ages more slowly than the figure, and nothing more quickly than grace. From this it is clearly established that beauty and figure are not the same. We also often see a more correct arrangement of parts and measure of members in one person than in another; yet another person, for some unknown reason, is judged more beautiful by us and is loved more ardently. By this we seem sufficiently warned to consider beauty as something other than the arrangement of parts. The same reasoning warns us not to suspect that beauty is the sweetness of colors. For frequently color is brighter in an older person, but grace is greater in a younger one. And among equals it sometimes happens that one who surpasses the other in color is nevertheless surpassed by that person in grace and beauty. 

Nor should anyone dare to assert that beauty is a certain mixture of figure and colors. For in that case, neither knowledge nor voices, which lack color and figure, nor colors and lights, which have no certain figure, would be judged worthy of love. Furthermore, the desire of anyone is satisfied once they have what they wanted. To be sure, hunger and thirst are stilled by food and drink; but love is satisfied by no sight or embrace of the body. Therefore, it does not burn for any physical nature; it certainly pursues beauty. Thus it happens that beauty cannot be anything corporeal. From all this it is gathered that those who, inflamed by love, thirst for beauty—if only they wish to extinguish their most burning thirst by drinking this liquid—must seek the most sweet moisture of this beauty, by which their thirst is kindled, elsewhere than in the river of matter, or the streams of quantity, or figure, or any colors. Where will you turn at last, you miserable lovers? Who will kindle the fiercest flames of your heart? Who will settle such a great fire? This is the task; this is the labor. I shall speak immediately. But pay attention.

### Beauty is the Splendor of the Divine Countenance. Chapter 4.

The Divine power, surpassing all things, immediately pours that ray of its own—in which exists the secondary power of all things to be created—into the angels and souls born from it, as if into its children. This ray paints the arrangement and order of the whole world much more exactly in them, as they are closer to it, than in the matter of the world. Therefore, this entire picture of the world which we perceive shines more expressively in the angels and souls. For in them are the figure of every sphere, of the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars, and also of the elements, stones, trees, and individual animals. Such pictures are called "exemplars" and "ideas" in the angels; "reasons" and "notions" in the souls; and "forms" and "images" in the matter of the world by the Platonists. They are indeed bright in the world, brighter in the soul, and brightest in the mind of the angel. Therefore, the one countenance of God shines in three mirrors placed in order: the Angel, the Soul, and the Body of the world. In the first, as it is nearer, it shines most brightly; in the second, being more remote, more obscurely; in the third, most remote, it shines most obscurely if you compare it to the others. Hence the holy mind of the angel, hindered by no service to a body, reflects upon itself, where it looks into that countenance of God engraved in its own bosom. Having looked upon it, it immediately admires it and always clings to it most greedily. We call the grace of that divine countenance "Beauty." We call the greed of the angel, clinging deeply to the countenance of God, "Love." Oh, would that the same might happen to us! But indeed, our soul was created on the condition that it is surrounded by an earthly body...

is gladdened, it inclines toward the duty of procreation. Weighted down by this inclination, the soul neglects the treasure hidden within its own inner chambers. Then, wrapped in an earthly body, it serves the needs of the body for a very long time; to this work it applies its senses for a time, and its reason also longer than is fitting. From this it happens that the soul does not notice the brightness of that divine countenance shining perpetually within itself until the body is fully grown; then, with reason awakened, it considers through thought the face of God shining in the "machine of the world" <note>original: "dei machina" — a common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a divinely constructed mechanism</note> and manifest to the eyes. By this consideration, the soul is led forward to gaze upon that which flashes within. Truly, since the face of a parent is pleasing to the children, it is necessary that the face of God the Father be most pleasing to souls. The brilliance and grace of this face—to repeat the same point often—whether in an angel, in a soul, or in the matter of the world, must be called universal beauty; and the impulse toward it must be called universal love. We do not doubt that this beauty is everywhere incorporeal. For no one doubts that in the angel and the soul, beauty is not a physical body. We have shown above, and understand now chiefly from this, that beauty is also incorporeal in physical bodies: for the eye perceives nothing other than the light of the sun. For the shapes and colors of bodies are never perceived unless they are illuminated by light, nor do they come to the eyes along with their own matter. Yet it seems necessary that they be in the eyes in order to be seen by the eyes. Therefore, the single light of the sun, depicted with the colors and shapes of all the bodies illuminated by it, offers itself to the eyes. Thus the eyes perceive the affected light with the help of a certain ray of their own; they see the perception itself and all things that are in it. Therefore, this whole order of the world which is seen is discerned not in the way it exists in the matter of bodies, but in the way it exists in the light infused into the eyes. Since in that light it is separated from matter, it is necessarily devoid of body. This also appears clearly from the fact that light itself cannot be a body, since in a moment it fills almost the entire world from the east to the west; it penetrates the body of air and water everywhere without any hindrance; and though mixed with filth, it is never stained. These things truly do not suit the nature of bodies at all. For a body is moved not in a moment, but in time; nor does one penetrate another without hindrance to itself, or the other, or both; and two bodies mixed together stain each other by mutual contact. This we see in the mixing of water and wine, or fire and earth. Since therefore the light of the sun is incorporeal, whatever it receives, it receives according to its own nature. For that reason, it receives the colors and shapes of bodies in a spiritual <note>In this context, "spiritual" refers to a non-material, refined state of existence</note> manner; and in the same way, it is inspected by the eyes after being received. Thus it happens that this whole beauty of the world, which is the third face of God, offers itself to the eyes as something incorporeal through the incorporeal light of the sun.

### Chapter V. How Love and Hatred are born, and that beauty is incorporeal.

From all these things it follows that every grace of the divine countenance—which is called universal beauty—is incorporeal not only in the angel and the soul, but also in the sight of the eyes. Nor do we love this face only as a whole all at once, but moved by admiration, we also love its parts. Here, a particular love is born toward a particular beauty. Thus we are also attracted to some human being, a member of the world’s order, especially when a spark of divine beauty clearly shines forth in them. An affection of this kind is born from two causes: both because the image of the paternal face pleases us, and also because the appearance and shape of a well-proportioned human being fits most aptly with that "reason of the human race" <note>The "idea" or blueprint of humanity</note> which our soul receives and retains from the Author of all. Hence the image of the external man, received through the senses and passing into the soul, if it disagrees with the shape of man which the soul possesses, it immediately displeases and is held in hatred as if deformed. If it agrees, it pleases at once and is loved as if beautiful. Thus it happens that some people we meet please or displease us immediately, and we do not know the cause of such affection. Indeed, the soul, hindered by the service of the body, by no means looks back at those innermost forms of its own. But it happens by a certain natural and hidden incongruity or congruity: that the form of an external thing, striking with its image the form of that same thing painted in the soul, either disagrees or agrees; and the soul, moved by this hidden offense or charm, either hates or loves the thing itself. That divine power implanted the complete configuration for creating man in the angel and the soul; but in the matter of the world, as it is most remote from that Craftsman, the constitution of man degenerates from that complete figure of itself. Yet in matter that is better disposed, it comes out more similar; in other matter, more dissimilar. That which comes out more similar squares and agrees with the reason of the soul, just as it does with the power of God and the Ideas of the angel. The soul approves of this congruity. In that very congruity consists beauty; in that approval consists the affection of love. Truly, since the Idea and the Reason are foreign to the matter of the body, the constitution of a man is judged similar to them not because of matter or quantity, but rather because of something incorporeal. Insofar as it is similar, it agrees with them; insofar as it agrees, it is beautiful. Therefore, body and beauty are [distinct] <note>The text implies a distinction here</note>. For if anyone should ask in what way the form of a body can be similar to the form and reason of the soul and mind, let him, I pray, consider the building of an architect. In the beginning, the architect conceives the reason and, as it were, the Idea of the building in his mind. Then he builds such a house as he has thought out, according to his strength. Who would deny that the house exists as a body, and that it is most similar <note>original: "pessimā" — likely a printer's error for "simillimam" (most similar)</note> to the incorporeal Idea of the craftsman, according to whose likeness it was made? Furthermore, it must be judged similar to the architect because of its incorporeal nature and a certain order, rather than because of its matter. Come then, subtract the matter if you can—and you can subtract it in thought—but leave the order: nothing of the body will remain for you, nothing of matter. Rather, it will be the same...

# COMMENTARY

### What things are required for a thing to be beautiful; and that beauty is a spiritual gift. Chapter VI.

What, then, is the beauty of the body? It is a vivacity of action: and a certain grace shining back in the body by the influence of its own <term>Idea</term><note>In the Platonic sense, the perfect "Idea" or "Form" of a thing that exists in the divine mind.</note>. A brilliance of this kind does not descend into matter until it has been most aptly prepared. Indeed, the preparation of a living body consists of these three: **Order**, **Measure**, and **Appearance**. **Order** signifies the intervals of the parts; **Measure** signifies the quantity; **Appearance** signifies the lineaments and color. First, it is necessary that each member of the body has its natural site: that the ears are in their place, the eyes, the nostrils, and the rest; and that the eyes are nearest to the nose by equal intervals; likewise, that both ears are equally distant from the eyes. Nor is this equality of intervals pertaining to **Order** sufficient, unless **Measure** is added: which, having preserved a moderate proportion due to the whole body, grants a specific magnitude to individual members: so that three noses placed in length fulfill the length of one face; the semicircles of both ears joined together make the circle of an open mouth. Let the joining of the eyebrows effect the same. Let the length of the nose equal the length of the lip; and the ear similarly. Let the twin orbs of the eyes equal one opening of the mouth. Let eight heads encompass the height of the body. Let the extension of the arms to the side show the same, and likewise the legs and feet. Furthermore, we consider **Appearance** necessary, so that the artistic drawing of lines, the folds, and the splendor of the eyes may decorate that order and measure of the parts. And yet, although these three are in matter, they cannot be any part of the body. The **Order** of the members is no member at all. For order is in all members; but no single member is found in all members. Add to this that order is nothing other than a decent interval of parts. But an interval—what else shall we call it but the distance of parts? Finally, distance is either nothing (and a completely empty void), or it is some drawing of lines. But who would call lines "bodies," since they lack the width and depth which are necessary for a body? Likewise, **Measure** is not quantity, but the limit of quantity. But limits are surfaces, lines, and points: which, since they lack the thickness of depth, are not considered bodies. We also place **Appearance** in the pleasant concord of lights, shadows, and lines, not in the matter itself. From all this, it is clear that beauty is so foreign to the bulk of the body that it never communicates itself to matter unless it is affected by those three incorporeal preparations which we have described. The foundation of these, however, is the temperate <term>complexion</term><note>The balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) in the body.</note> of the four elements: so that our body may be most similar to heaven, whose substance is temperate; nor should it fail the formation of the soul by any excess of humors. For thus the celestial splendor will easily shine in a body very similar to heaven: and that perfect form of man which the soul possesses will result more expressively in peaceful and obedient matter. Furthermore, to receive their own beauty, voices are similarly arranged in a firm manner. For their **Order** is the ascent from a deep voice to the octave, and the descent from there; **Measure** is the due progression through thirds, fourths, fifths, and sixths, likewise tones and semitones; **Appearance** is the sonorous intensity of a clear voice. Certainly by these three, as if by certain elements, bodies composed of many members—and trees, and animals, and the congregation of many voices—are disposed to receive beauty. But simpler bodies, such as the four elements, stones, and metals, and likewise single voices, are sufficiently adapted to the same by a certain interior temperance, fecundity, and clarity of their nature. But the soul is most especially accommodated to beauty by its own nature, because it is both a spirit and like a mirror nearest to God. In which, as we said in the previous sections, the image of the divine countenance shines. Therefore, just as nothing at all needs to be added to gold for it to appear beautiful—but the filth of the earth, if any has clung to it, must be separated—so the soul needs no additions to appear beautiful: but the care and anxious solicitude for the body must be laid aside; the perturbation of desire and fear must be driven away: and immediately the natural appearance of the soul will shine forth. But lest the speech wander too far, let us briefly conclude from the above: that beauty is a certain vivid and spiritual grace, first infused into the Angel by the illuminating ray of God: then into the souls of men, the shapes of bodies, and voices; which through reason, sight, and hearing, moves and delights our souls: by delighting it ravishes: by ravishing it inflames them with burning love.

### Concerning the painting of Love. Chapter VII.

Agatho the poet, in the manner of the ancient poets, clothes this god in a human image: and he paints him beautiful like a man, young, tender, flexible or agile, aptly composed and shining. To what purpose is this? These preparations are indeed for a beautiful nature rather than beauty itself. For out of these five parts, the first three signify a temperate complexion of the body, which is the first foundation: the remaining two indicate order, measure, and appearance. Physicians demonstrate that the sign of a temperate body is the smooth and firm equality of tender flesh. Where heat exceeds too much, the body is dry and hairy; where cold, it is rigid; where dryness, it is hard and rough; where humidity, it is flowing, drooping, unequal, and twisted. Therefore, an equal and firm tenderness of the body indicates its moderated affection in the four humors. For this reason, Agatho called Love soft, delicate, and tender. Why young? Because not only by nature, but also by the benefit of age, the tenderness...
