For with the passage of a long duration of time, as the thinner parts of the humors are dissolved, the much thicker parts remain; and once the fire and air have exhaled, an excess of water and earth reigns. But why does he call Love agile and flexible? So that you may understand him to be fit for all movements and ready for action. Do not think that when he called him "soft," he meant the softness of water—which is womanish, languid, and inept. For such a quality is contrary to a moderate temperament. After these things, Agathon added that Love is "aptly composed": that is, most honorably shaped in the order and measure of his parts. He also added "shining": that is, radiant with a sweet appearance of colors. Having set forth these preparations, Agathon remained silent about what remained. For it is our task, after these things, to understand the arrival of grace. These five parts are seen in the figure of a man as we have said; however, in the power of Love, they are to be understood differently, for they show his force and quality. He is called **Young** because young people are most often ensnared by love, and being caught in his snares, they seek out those of a youthful age. He is **Soft** because gentle natures are more easily captured, and those who are captured—though they were fierce before—are rendered mild. He is **Agile** and **Flexible** because he flows in secretly and flows out in the same way. He is **Elegant and Composed** because he desires beautiful and orderly things and flees their opposites. He is **Shining** because he breathes into the character of a man in the flowery and shining season of life, and he longs for flowery things. Since Agathon pursues these points most copiously, let it suffice to have touched upon them briefly.

### On the Virtue of Love. Chapter VIII.

Those things which are said by Agathon concerning the four virtues <note>The four cardinal virtues: Justice, Temperance, Fortitude, and Wisdom.</note> to signify the goodness of Love are to be understood in this way: He is affirmed to be **Just** because where love is whole and true, there is a reciprocity of goodwill which admits no insult or injury. So great is the power of this charity that it alone can keep the human race in tranquil peace—something which neither prudence, nor fortitude, nor the force of arms, laws, or eloquence can achieve without goodwill. He calls him, furthermore, **Temperate**, because he tames shameful desires. For since Love seeks beauty, which consists in a certain order and temperance, he scorns vile and immoderate lusts; he always shrinks from shameful acts (as you heard sufficiently from the hero <note>Referring to the previous speaker in the dialogue</note> at the beginning). Where this affection reigns, all other desires are held in contempt. He is **Most Brave**. For what is stronger than boldness? Who fights more boldly than a lover for the beloved? Among the other gods—that is, the other planets—Mars excels in fortitude because he makes men stronger. Yet Venus tames him. For when Mars, positioned in the angles of the sky, or the second house of the nativity, or the eighth, portends evils to the one being born, Venus often restrains the malice of Mars (so to speak) by her conjunction, opposition, reception, or by a sextile or trine aspect. Again, when Mars rules in a man’s rising, he bestows greatness of soul and wrathfulness. If Venus approaches closely, she does not hinder that virtue of greatness of soul given by Mars, but she represses the vice of wrath; therein she is seen to make Mars more merciful and to tame him. But Mars never tames Venus. Indeed, if she is the leader of life, she provides the affection of love. If Mars leads nearby, he makes the impulse of Venus more burning with his heat; so that if, at someone's birth, Mars is in the house of Venus (Libra or Taurus), the one born then is burned by the sharpest loves because of the presence of Mars. Again, Mars follows Venus; Venus does not follow Mars. For boldness is the handmaiden of love, not love the handmaiden of boldness. Men are not ensnared by love because they are bold; rather, because they are wounded by love, they usually become most bold to undergo any dangers intrepidly for the sake of the beloved. Finally, the most evident proof of his excellence in fortitude is that all things obey Love, but he obeys none. Not only the celestial beings love, but animals and all bodies. Likewise, the brave and the wise, wealthy men and the greatest kings, submit their necks to the empire of Love. But Love is subject to none of these. For neither the gifts of the wealthy buy love, nor can the threats and violence of the powerful force us to love or to stop loving. For Love is free, and arises of its own accord in a free will, which even God will not compel, having decreed from the beginning that it should be free. Thus it happens that Love, who brings force to all, escapes the violence of all. So great is his liberty that while other affections of the soul, or arts and operations, usually desire some reward different from themselves, Love is content with himself as his own reward—as if there were no other reward besides love that is worthy of love. For he who loves, loves love chiefly. He wants this most from the beloved: that the beloved love the lover in return. He is also **Most Wise**. By what reason Love is the creator and preserver of all things, and the master and lord of individual arts, I believe was sufficiently discussed in the speech of Eryximachus. In those things, the wisdom of Love is shown. From all this, it is concluded that Love is therefore most blessed, because he is most beautiful and best. That he is most beautiful is clear from the fact that he delights in beautiful things as being like himself. He is also the best because he makes lovers the best. It is necessary that he who makes others best is himself the best.

### On the Gifts of Love. Chapter IX.

What Love is has appeared from our discourse. What he is like is clear from the words of Agathon above. What gifts he bestows is easily said from what has been mentioned. For one kind of love is simple; the other is mutual. Simple love makes whoever it seizes prudent in foresight, sharp in debating, eloquent in speaking, magnanimous in conducting affairs, witty in jokes, ready for games, and for serious...

and everything most powerful. When mutual dangers are driven away, it provides security; when dissension is removed, it provides concord; when misery is avoided, it provides happiness. For where there is mutual charity, there are no snares; there all things are held in common; there lawsuits, thefts, homicides, and wars cease. Agathon touches upon the fact that tranquility of this kind is granted by mutual love not only to living creatures, but also to the heavens and the elements—a point demonstrated more diffusely above in the speech of Eryximachus <note>Eryximachus was the physician in the dialogue who argued love is a universal physical force</note>. At the conclusion of this speech, he says that Love, by his song, soothes the minds of gods and men. Anyone will clearly understand this who remembers that it was demonstrated in the previous sections that Love is in all things and extends to all things.

### Love is both older and younger than the other gods. Chapter X.

But before I make an end, best of men, I shall resolve three questions according to the strength of my intellect which arise in Agathon’s discussion. First, it is asked why Phaedrus said Love was older than Saturn and Jupiter, while Agathon said he was younger. Second, what the "Kingdom of Necessity" signifies in Plato, and what the "wickedness" of Love <note>original: "impiu[m]" - likely referring to the lack of piety or the harshness of Necessity before Love's rule</note> means. Third, which gods discovered which arts while Love was reigning. God, the Father of all, generated those minds that are his ministers—which move Saturn, Jupiter, and the other planets—through a certain love of propagating his own seeds and through the kindness of his providence. These minds, in turn, having been born, immediately recognize and love their parent. We call that Love by which the celestial beings are created "older" than them; but that love by which they are moved toward their creator, we call "younger." Furthermore, the Angelic Mind did not receive the Ideas <note>The eternal forms or archetypes</note> of the planet Saturn and the others from its father before it turned toward His face with an innate love. Again, after it received them, it loved the gift of the parent more ardently. Thus, that angel's love for God is partly older than the Ideas (which are called gods) and partly younger. Therefore, Love is the beginning and the end, the first and the last of the gods.

### Love reigns before Necessity. Chapter XI.

Truly, so that the second question may be solved, Love must be said to reign here before Necessity because divine love gave origin to all things born from itself, in which no violence of necessity is placed. For since it has nothing above itself, it works not by compulsion, but spontaneously. However, the Mind which follows it sprouts forth necessarily as Love carries it along. Therefore, Love produces; the Mind is produced by necessity. There the dominion of Love begins, here the dominion of Necessity. Although this [Necessity] is born from the highest goodness of God and is therefore good, nevertheless, because it proceeded outside of God, it necessarily degenerates from the infinite perfection of the parent. For an effect never receives the full goodness of its cause. In this necessary procession and degeneration of the effect consists the "wickedness" of necessity. But indeed, the Mind, having been born, immediately loves its author, as we have said: where the kingdom of Love rises again. For the Mind is raised toward God by love, and God illuminates it, having turned toward Him, by love. But here again, the power of necessity creeps in. Indeed, since that light descending from God is not received with as much clarity by the Mind (which is dark by its own nature) as is granted by God. For it is compelled to receive according to the capacity of its nature. Therefore, by the violence of the receiving nature, the light becomes more obscure. To this necessity, the sovereignty of Love succeeds again. For once the Mind is kindled by this first brightness of God, it turns more ardently toward Him, and being incited by this spark of light, as it were, it seeks the full abundance of light. Hence God, by the kindness of His providence, grants a divine light beyond that first natural light; and so the power of Love and Necessity succeed each other alternately. This succession happens in divine things by the origin of nature; in others, by intervals of time; yet in such a way that Love is the first and last of all. Regarding the soul and other things made by God, one must judge similarly concerning these two empires. Therefore, if we speak absolutely, the empire of Love is older than that of Necessity, since the power of the former begins in God, and the latter in created things. If we understand it regarding things created by God, the tyranny of Necessity precedes the kingdom of Love, since things themselves first proceed by necessity and degenerate in proceeding before they turn themselves to their father by love. Orpheus sang of these two empires in two hymns. The empire of Necessity is thus in the *Hymn to Night*.
> <margin>i.e., Heavy necessity rules over all. But the kingdom of Love is thus in the *Hymn to Venus*.</margin> You command the three Fates and generate all things. Divine Orpheus established two kingdoms and compared them to each other, and he placed Love before Necessity when he said that Love commands the three Fates in whom Necessity consists.

### In what way, while Necessity reigned, Saturn castrated Uranus and Jupiter bound Saturn. Chapter XII.

In what way, while Necessity was dominant, the following gods are said by Agathon here to have either castrated or bound their parents, we easily understand from what has been said. For these things are not to be understood as if the Angelic Mind [castrated] God himself, but rather that it divides and tears apart the gift granted to it by God within itself. We showed a little while ago that the gifts of God in the receiving spirit necessarily fall away from the highest perfection of God. Whereby it happens that that fecundity of nature, which is whole in God, is diminished and in a certain way mutilated in the angel; it is deservedly said to have been "castrated." This is said to happen while Necessity reigns because it happens necessarily—not by the will of the giver or the receiver, but by that necessity in which the effect cannot be equal to its cause. For thus Saturn (that is, the Angel) seems to castrate Uranus <note>original: "Cęlium" - Heaven/Uranus</note> (that is, the supreme God); Jupiter also (that is, the Soul of the World) binds Saturn (that is, the power received from the Angel), constraining it within narrower limits in himself by the defect of his own nature. For the power of the former is greater than the latter. Therefore, the power which is unhampered and free in the former because of its amplitude, is judged to be bound and narrowed in the latter because of its limitation. I omit what the astrologers think: that the malice of the planet Saturn is very often coerced by the conjunction, reception, opposition, sextile, or trine aspect of Jupiter. But enough of these things; let us descend to the third question.

### Which gods grant which arts to men. Chapter XIII.

Agathon believes that the arts were delivered to the human race by the gods because of love. The art of ruling from Jove <note>Jupiter</note>. The arts of archery, prophecy, and healing from Apollo. The craft of metalworking from Vulcan. The art of weaving from Minerva. Finally, music from the Muses. Twelve deities preside over the twelve signs of the Zodiac. Pallas <note>Athena</note> over Aries; Venus over Taurus; Apollo over Gemini; Mercury over Cancer; Jupiter over Leo; Ceres over Virgo; Vulcan over Libra; Mars over Scorpio; Diana over Sagittarius; Vesta over Capricorn; Juno over Aquarius; and indeed Neptune over Pisces. From these, all arts are delivered to our race. Those signs pour their powers into the body, while the deities who preside over them pour their powers into the soul for each specific art. Thus, Jupiter through Leo renders a man most fit for the governance of gods and men—that is, for performing both divine and human affairs with excellence. Apollo through Gemini provides prophecy, medicine, and the skill of the bow. Pallas through Aries provides the skill of weaving. Vulcan through Libra provides metalworking; and others provide the remaining arts. Because they grant their gifts to us magnificently out of the kindness of their providence, we say they bestow them urged by love. Furthermore, we believe that musical consonance is born from that swiftest and most orderly revolution of the heavens, and eight tones from the motions of the eight circles; moreover, from all of them together, one single harmony is produced. Therefore, we name the nine sounds of the heavens the nine Muses, after musical concord. Our soul was once gifted with the principle of this music. For since its origin is celestial, it is rightly said that a celestial harmony is innate within it. This it later imitates with various instruments and songs. And this gift, likewise, was granted to us by divine providence out of love. Therefore, most distinguished men, let us love this god because he is most beautiful; let us imitate him because he is best; let us worship him because he is most blessed, so that by his mercy and bounty he may grant us the possession of his beauty, goodness, and beatitude.

### INTRODUCTION To the disputation on Love. The Sixth Speech. Chapter I.

Thus far spoke Carlo Marsuppini. But Tommaso Benci, a diligent imitator of Socrates, applied himself to the commentary on the Socratic words with a willing mind and a cheerful countenance. Our Socrates, he said, judged the wisest of all Greeks by the oracle of Apollo, used to profess the art of loving above all others, as if by the skill of this art especially both Socrates and others should be judged as to who was the wisest. He said he received this kind of art not from Anaxagoras, Damon, or Archelaus the physicists; not from Prodicus of Ceos or Aspasia the professors of rhetoric; not from Connus the musician—from whom he had learned much—but from Diotima, a prophetic woman inspired by a divine spirit. In my opinion, this was to show that only by the inspiration of divinity can men understand what true beauty is, what legitimate love is, and by what reason one should love. So great is the power of the amatory faculty; so great its sublimity. Therefore, stay far away from these celestial feasts, stay far away, I say, you profane ones, who, overwhelmed by earthly filth and utterly enslaved to Bacchus and Priapus <note>gods of wine and lust</note>, cast down love, a celestial gift, into the dirt in the manner of swine. But you, most chaste companions, and all others consecrated to Diana and Pallas, who exult in the liberty of a most pure soul and the perpetual joy of the mind, be present happily: and listen diligently to the divine mysteries revealed to Socrates by Diotima. But before you hear Diotima, a certain controversy must be resolved that has arisen between those who treated love in the preceding sections and those who are about to treat it. For the previous speakers called love beautiful, good, blessed, and a god; Socrates and Diotima deny this, and place him in the middle between the beautiful and the ugly, the good and the evil, the blessed and the miserable, and between god and man. We consider both opinions to be true, though for different reasons.

### Love is the middle between beauty and ugliness, and between god and man. Chapter II.

The magnet stone inserts its own quality into iron, so that the iron, having become very similar to the magnet, inclines toward this stone. This kind of inclination, insofar as it arises from the stone and tends toward the stone, is certainly called a "stony" inclination; insofar as it is in the iron, it is equally "iron-like" and "stony." For the material of the iron is not pure, but is already formed by the quality of the stone. Therefore, it retains the property of both. Also, to speak more aptly, fire kindles flax with its quality, that is, heat. The flax, suspended by the quality of heat, flies up to the higher region of fire. This kind of flight, insofar as it is excited by the fire and tends toward the fire, we clearly call "fiery"; insofar as it is in the flax—not pure flax, but already ignited—we call it "flaxen" as well as "fiery" from the nature of both the flax and the fire. Often, the figure of a man, on account of an interior goodness happily granted by God, is most beautiful in appearance and transmits a ray of its splendor through the eyes of those looking into the soul. By this spark, as if drawn by a certain hook, the soul hastens toward the one drawing it. This "draw," which is also love—since it depends on the beautiful, the good, and the happy and reflects back into the same—we do not hesitate to name beautiful, blessed, and a god, according to the opinion of Agathon and the others above. But because it is in the soul, which is so kindled by that ray of the presence of the beautiful, we are forced to name the affection a "middle" between the beautiful and the non-beautiful. Since the soul, which has not yet received any image of a beautiful thing, does not yet love that thing as if it were unknown; and he who possesses total beauty is not vexed by the stings of love. For who desires what he already has? It remains, then, that one burns with ardent love when, having obtained some beautiful likeness of a beautiful thing, he is urged by that foretaste toward the full possession of beauty. Since, therefore, the soul of the lover partly has the beautiful thing itself and partly does not have it, it is not wrongly called partly beautiful and partly not beautiful. And so, from this kind of mixture, we maintain that love is a certain middle affection between the beautiful and the non-beautiful, participating in both. For this very reason, to come now to her, Diotima called love a "daemon" <note>a mediating spirit, not a malevolent demon</note>; because just as daemons are middle beings between celestial and earthly things, so love holds the middle place between formlessness and form. This middle state of his...

# COMMENTARY

The region between unformed and beautiful nature John has sufficiently explained in his first and second oration. <note>Referring to Giovanni Cavalcanti, a speaker in Ficino's "De Amore."</note>

### On the Souls of the Spheres and Demons. Chapter III.

But how demons inhabit the middle region between heaven and earth, you may learn from the words of Diotima in Socrates' *Symposium*, in the *Phaedrus*, and in the *Philebus* of the Athenian guest, in the *Laws*, and the *Epinomis*. Plato considers that the entire machine of this world is ruled and moved by a certain soul. Indeed, the whole body of the world is a single body composed of all four elements, of which the bodies of all living creatures are small parts. For the little body of any animal is a particle of the world’s body. Nor is it composed of the entirety of the elements of fire, air, water, and earth, but of certain parts of these elements. Therefore, just as the whole is more perfect than the part, so the body of the world is more perfect than the body of individual living beings. It would be absurd for an imperfect body to have a soul, while a perfect one neither had a soul nor lived. For who is so out of their mind as to say the part lives, but deny it to the whole? Therefore, the whole body of the world lives, since the bodies of animals, which are its parts, live. There must be one soul for the whole, just as there is one matter and one construction.

Since, therefore, there are twelve spheres of the world (as Plato pleases): eight of heaven, and four elements below heaven; and since these twelve spheres are distinct from one another, diverse in appearance, motions, and properties, it is necessary that twelve souls be present in them, diverse in kind and power. There will be, therefore, one soul of the single primary matter. Of the twelve circles, twelve souls. Who would deny that the earth or water live, which grant life to animals born from them? For if these dregs of the world live, and the heights are full: why should not air and fire, the more excellent parts of the world, live, and similarly have living things within them, and the heavens likewise? But those celestial animals—which are the stars—and the terrestrial and aquatic ones we indeed see; but the fiery and aerial ones we do not see. Indeed, we do not even perceive the pure element of fire or air. 

But there is this difference: that on earth there are two kinds of living beings: the brute and the rational. And similarly in the water. Since water is more excellent in body than earth, it ought to be no less a possessor of reason. Truly the ten superior globes, on account of their sublimity, are adorned with rational beings alone. The Platonists name the Soul of the World (that is, of primary matter), and the souls of the twelve spheres and the stars, as "gods," as they are the handmaidens of the angelic mind and the supreme God. Those living beings which inhabit the region of ethereal fire located below the moon, or of pure air, or of misty air near the water, they call **demons** <note>In the Greek sense of *daimones*, meaning intermediary spirits or guardians, not necessarily evil spirits.</note>. Those which inhabit the earth are rational beings, **men**. The gods are also immortal and impassible <note>incapable of suffering or being changed by external force</note>; men are passible and mortal. Demons are indeed immortal, but passible. They do not attribute passions of the body to demons, but certain affections of the soul, by which they love good men in a certain way and hate the evil; and they involve themselves more closely and ardently in governing inferior things, especially human affairs. All these, by this duty, appear good. 

However, some Platonists and Christian theologians have maintained that there are certain other evil demons. But concerning evil demons, we have no dispute at present. Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 500 AD) who integrated Neoplatonism with Christianity.</note> is accustomed to call the good ones—our guardians and governors of the lower world—by the proper name of **angels**, which differs very little from the mind of Plato. Furthermore, those whom Plato calls gods and the souls of the spheres and stars, we can call the ministering angels of God in the manner of Dionysius. This also does not dissent from Plato for this reason: because he by no means binds souls of this kind to the enclosures of the spheres in the same way as the souls of earthly beings are bound to bodies, as appears in the tenth book of the *Laws*. Instead, he affirms they are gifted with such power by the supreme God that they are able to enjoy the vision of God and, without any labor or anxiety, rule and move the globes of the world according to the will of their Father, and by moving these, easily govern inferior things. Therefore, between Plato and Dionysius, the discrepancy is more in words than in sentiment.

### On the seven Gifts which are granted by God to men through intermediary spirits. Chapter IIII.

The gods who follow are said to serve the gifts of God through the ideas of all things which the divine mind contains, and the demons serve under them. For from the highest to the lowest, all things pass through intermediaries; so that those ideas, the conceptions of the divine mind, bestow their gifts upon men through the gods and demons. Of these, there are seven principal ones: 
1. Sharpness of contemplation. 
2. Power of governing. 
3. Courage <note>original: *animositas*</note>. 
4. Clarity of the senses. 
5. Ardor of love. 
6. Subtlety of interpreting. 
7. Fecundity of generating. 

God contains the force of these first in Himself. Then He grants the power of these to the seven gods who move the seven planets (and are called angels by us), so that each one receives one gift above the others. Those seven, with orders of demons serving them, exhibit each gift specifically to individuals. These they hand down to men. Truly, God infuses these into souls immediately upon their birth from Him. These souls, gliding from the Milky Way through Cancer, are wrapped in a certain celestial and shining body; surrounded by which, they are enclosed in earthly bodies. For the order of nature requires that the purest soul cannot fall into this most impure body before it has received a certain middle and pure covering. Since this is thicker than the soul, but purer and more subtle than this body, it is judged by the Platonists to be the most suitable bond for the soul with the earthly body. 

From this it happens that the souls of the planets confirm and strengthen the powers of those seven gifts given by God to our souls, and their bodies to our bodies, immediately from the beginning and continually. The same duty is overseen by as many demons of a middle nature between the celestials and men. Saturn strengthens the gift of **contemplation** through Saturnian demons. Jupiter, the power of **governing and commanding**, by the ministry of Jovial demons. Mars, **greatness of soul**, through Martial demons. The Sun, **clarity of the senses and opinion** (from which prophecy follows), with the help of solar demons. Venus inspires **love** through Venereal ones. Mercury aids the **skill of pronouncing and interpreting** with Mercurial intermediaries. Finally, the Moon, by conferring lunar demons...

Although they impart this faculty to all men, they do so especially to those in whose conception and birth they can do the most through the disposition of the heavens. Although these things, being divinely infused, are honorable, they can sometimes appear deformed in us because of abuse, which is evident in the use of governance, courage, love, and generation. We have the instinct of love—not to digress too far—from the highest God, and from Venus, who is called a goddess, and from the Venereal <term>daemons</term><note>In the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern evil sense.</note>. Since he descends from God, he is a god; since he is confirmed by daemons, he is to be called a daemon. Therefore, he was rightly called a god by Agathon, and a daemon by Diotima. A Venereal daemon, I say.

### On the order of Venereal Daemons, and how they hurl the darts of love. Chapter V.

The Venereal daemon, moreover, is a threefold love. The first is placed by the Platonists in the Celestial Venus—that is, in the intelligence of the Angelic Mind. The second is in the Common Venus: namely, in that power of generating which the Soul of the World possesses. These two are called daemons because they are intermediaries between formlessness and form, as we touched upon above and will explain more broadly a little later. The third is the order of daemons who accompany the planet Venus. Of these Venereal daemons, we also posit a threefold order. Some are assigned to the element of fire, others to the purest air, and others to the thicker and misty air; all are named "Heroes" from the Greek word *Eros*, which signifies love—that is, "the amorous ones." The first group hurl the stings of love into those men in whom bile, the choleric and fiery humor, dominates. The second into those in whom blood, the airy humor, prevails. The third into those in whom phlegm and black bile—the watery and earthy humors—rule. While all men are wounded by Cupid’s arrows, four types of people are especially affected. For Plato in the *Phaedrus* indicated that the souls who follow Jupiter, Phoebus <note>Apollo</note>, Mars, and Juno (that is, Venus) are most likely to be wounded; and that from the very beginnings of their generation they are prone to love, and they usually love most intensely those men who were born under the same stars. Hence, those of Jupiter are drawn to those of Jupiter, those of Mars to those of Mars, and others are similarly moved by their own kind.

### How we are captured by Love. Chapter VI.

What I say regarding one example, understand for the other three. Whichever soul falls into an earthly body under the empire of Jupiter, conceives for itself in that very descent a certain figure for fabricating a man that is agreeable to the star of Jupiter. This soul expresses that exact figure in its ethereal body as if in its best state. If the seed found on earth is similarly tempered, it paints in that seed a third figure very similar to the first and second. If not, it is not so similar. It often happens that two souls, though they descended at different intervals of time, did so while Jupiter was reigning; one of them found suitable seed on earth and fashioned a body most illustriously according to the prior Ideas; the other, however, because of the unsuitability of the matter, began the same work but did not execute it with such great similarity to its exemplar. The former body is more beautiful than the latter. Both please each other because of a certain similarity of nature. But the one judged more beautiful between them pleases more. Thus it happens that people do not love just anyone who is most beautiful, but "their own"—that is, those born similarly—even if they are less beautiful than many others. Therefore, those who, as we said, were born under that star, are so constituted that the image of the more beautiful one, flowing through the eyes into the soul of the other, fits and harmonizes in every way with a similar image formed from birth both in the ethereal body and in the inner recesses of the soul. The soul, thus struck, recognizes that encountered image as something familiar. This image is as powerful as that which the soul already possessed within itself and wished to fashion in its own body but could not; the soul immediately draws that image to its interior. If anything is lacking for the perfect likeness of a "Jovial" <note>Jupiter-like</note> body, the soul restores it by reforming it. Then it loves that reformed image as its own work. Hence it happens that lovers are so deceived that they think the beloved is more beautiful than they actually are. For as time goes proceed, they do not look at the beloved in the mere image received through the senses, but they behold an image already reformed by the soul into the likeness of its own Idea, which is more beautiful than the body itself. They desire, moreover, to behold daily that body from which the image first flowed. For although the soul may preserve the image of the absent body within itself—and that might almost be enough for it—nevertheless the <term>spirit</term><note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a thin vapor that connected the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note>, the instrument of the soul, and the eye are not satisfied. Three things indeed seem to be in us: Soul, Spirit, and Body. The soul and body, being very different in nature, are joined by the intermediary spirit, which is a certain very thin and mild vapor generated by the heat of the heart from the most subtle part of the blood. Thence, diffused through all the limbs, it receives the powers of the soul and transfers them into the body. It receives again through the organs of the senses the images of external bodies; these cannot be fixed in the soul because it is an incorporeal substance, which is superior to bodies and cannot be formed by them through the reception of images. But the soul, being present to the spirit, easily perceives the images of bodies shining in it as if in a mirror, through which it judges those bodies; and this cognition is called "sense" by the Platonists. While it perceives them, it conceives in itself by its own power images similar to them but much purer; we call this kind of conception "phantasy" or imagination. Here the conceived images are preserved in memory. Through these, the sharp sight of the mind is often incited to behold the universal Ideas of things which it contains within itself. Therefore, it perceives a certain individual man by sense and conceives him by imagination. By the intellect, it contemplates the reason and definition common to all men through the innate Idea of humanity; and it preserves what has been contemplated. Therefore, it would be enough for the soul to have seen the beloved once, since it preserves the image of the beautiful man once conceived and reformed within itself in memory; however, for the eye and the spi—

### On the Birth of Love. Chapter VII.

But let us now return to Diotima. Since she had referred Love to the rank of the <term>daemons</term><note>In Platonic philosophy, a 'daemon' is a mediating spirit between gods and mortals, not an evil entity.</note> for those reasons we have recounted, she demonstrated his origin to Socrates in this manner. At the birth of Venus, while the gods were feasting, Porus <note>Resource or Plenty</note>, the son of Counsel, drunk with the draught of nectar, coupled with Penia <note>Poverty</note> in the garden of Jove. From that union, Love was born. "At the birth of Venus"—that is, when the angelic mind and the soul of the world (which we have named 'Venuses' for the reason we stated elsewhere) were arising from the highest majesty of God. "The gods were feasting"—that is, Coelius, Saturn, and Jupiter were feeding upon their own goods. For when intelligence in the angel, and the power of generating in the soul of the world (which we call the proper twin Venuses), were coming forth into the light, that highest god whom they call Coelius <note>The Sky or Heavens</note> already existed; moreover, Essence and Life were in the angel, whom we call Saturn and Jupiter. And also in the soul of the world there was the knowledge of supernal things and the motion of celestial bodies, which we again call Saturn and Jupiter. Porus and Penia signify abundance and want. Porus, the son of Counsel—that is, a spark of the highest God. Indeed, God is called Counsel and the fountain of counsel, because He is the truth and goodness of all things. By His splendor, every true counsel is made effective. Toward His goodness, every counsel tends. By "the garden of Jove," he understands the fecundity of the angelic life; into which, when Porus descends—that is, that ray of God—mixed with Penia—that is, the prior lack of this [soul]—he creates Love. In the beginning, the angel exists and lives through God; in respect to these two, Essence and Life, he is named Saturn and Jupiter. He has, moreover, the power of understanding, which we judge to be Venus. A power of this kind is by its nature formless and dark unless it be illuminated by God, just as the power of the eye is before the arrival of the sun. This darkness we consider to be Penia, namely, a certain lack and defect of light. But that power of understanding, reflected toward its own parent by a certain natural instinct, receives from Him a divine ray, which is Porus and abundance. In this ray, as if in a certain seed, the reasons of all things are included. By the flames of this ray, that natural instinct is kindled; this fire, this ardor arising from the prior darkness and the approaching spark, is Love, born from want and abundance, in the garden of Jove—that is, procreated under the shadow of life. For immediately after the vigor of life, the ardor for understanding arises. But why does he introduce Porus drunk with nectar? Because he overflows with the reason of divine vivacity. Why is Love partly rich and partly poor? Because we are accustomed to burn neither for what we perfectly possess, nor for what we entirely lack. For since everyone seeks that which he lacks, what more should he seek who possesses the whole thing? Furthermore, since no one desires unknown things, it is necessary that what we love was in some way known to us before. Nor is it only known—for we are accustomed to hate many things known to us—but it must be judged as good and pleasant to us. Nor does that seem to be enough for a burning benevolence, unless we judge that we can easily attain what we have deemed pleasant. Everyone, therefore, loves something which in reality he does not yet fully possess. Yet by the thought of the mind, he knows that very thing, judges it pleasant, and trusts he can attain it. This very knowledge, judgment, and hope is like a certain present anticipation of an absent good. For he would not burn unless that thing pleased him, nor would it please him unless it had been tasted in some way beforehand. Therefore, since lovers partly have what they desire and partly do not have it, Love is not without reason mixed from a certain want and abundance. By this very logic, that supernal Venus, kindled by the first tasting of the divine ray itself, is carried by love toward the integral fullness of the whole light; by this effort, clinging more effectively to its parent, it immediately flashes with His fullest brightness. And those confused reasons of things, which had previously been folded within the ray we call Porus, are unfolded; now, with that Venus clinging to them, they shine more clearly and distinctly. Just as the angel relates to God, so the soul of the world relates to the angel and God. For she, turning herself toward supernal things, likewise receives a ray from them and is kindled, and she begets a love participating in abundance and want. Hence, adorned with the forms of all things, she moves the heavens according to their exemplar; because of the power of generating, she produces forms similar to them in the matter of the elements. Here we behold the twin Venuses again. One is surely the power of the soul for knowing supernal things. The other is the power of the same soul, the procreatress of inferior things. The former is not proper to the soul but is an imitation of angelic contemplation; the latter, however, is proper to the nature of the soul. Therefore, whenever we place one Venus in the soul, we understand its peculiar power and its own Venus. Whenever we place two, one is common with the angel, the other is proper to the soul itself. Let there be, therefore, two Venuses in the soul: the first celestial, the second common. Let both have Love. The Celestial for contemplating divine beauty; the Common for generating the same in the matter of the world. For such beauty as the former sees, the latter wishes to hand over to the machine of the world according to its strength. Indeed, both are carried toward generating beauty, but each in its own way. The Celestial Venus strives by her intelligence to fashion within herself the most exact beauty of supernal things; the Common Venus strives to give birth in the matter of the world to the beauty conceived within herself from the abundance of divine seeds. We sometimes call that [first] Love a god because it directs to divine things. For the most part, we call it a daemon because it is midway between want and plenty. We always call the other Love a daemon because it seems to have a certain affection for the body and is more inclined toward the inferior region of the world. This is indeed foreign to God, but suitable to the nature of Daemons.

<margin>Chapter VIII.</margin>
In all souls there are two loves; but in ours, there are five.
These two Venuses <note>The "Two Venuses" refer to Aphrodite Urania (Heavenly) and Aphrodite Pandemos (Common), representing spiritual and physical beauty.</note> and their twin loves exist not only in the soul of the world, but also in the souls of the spheres, the stars, demons, and men. Since all souls are traced back to that first series of the natural order, it is necessary that the loves of all be traced back to the love of that first soul, so that they depend on it in some way. For this reason, Diotima was accustomed to call these others simply "demons," but that first one the "Great Demon." <note>In this context, "demon" (daimon) refers to a mediating spirit between gods and men, not an evil entity.</note> Hovering over all things throughout the entire universe, he does not allow hearts to grow sluggish, but arouses them everywhere to love. In us, however, not only two, but five loves are found. Two are the extreme demons; the middle three are not only demons but also "affections" or states of feeling. Certainly, in the human mind, there is an eternal love for perceiving divine beauty; for the sake of this, we pursue the study of philosophy and the duties of justice and piety. There is also in the power of generation a certain hidden stimulus for procreating offspring; and this love is perpetual, by which we are constantly incited to model a likeness of that higher beauty in the form of the child we create. These two loves in us are perpetual; they are those two demons which Plato prophesies are always present in our souls: one of which raises us to the heavens, the other presses us down to the depths. One is a *calodaemon* <note>original: "calodęmon" from Greek *kalos* (good) + *daimon*</note>, that is, a good demon; the other is a *cacodaemon* <note>original: "cacodęmon" from Greek *kakos* (bad) + *daimon*</note>, that is, an evil demon. In truth, both are good, since both the procreation of offspring and the search for truth are considered necessary and honorable. But the second is called "evil" because, through our abuse of it, it often disturbs us and turns the soul away from its principal good—which consists in the contemplation of truth—and twists it toward viler mysteries. Between these, three middle loves hold sway in us. Since these are not as firmly established in the soul as the others, but rather begin, grow, decrease, and end, they are more rightly called "movements" and "affections" than "demons." One of these is equidistant from both extremes. The remaining two lean toward one side or the other. Furthermore, the shape of a body is such—due to the preparation of its matter—as the divine mind contains in its "Idea." When this shape meets the eyes, penetrating through the eyes into the spirit, it pleases the elevated soul, since it harmonizes with those internal patterns which our mind and our power of generation preserve as explanations of the thing itself, received long ago from the divine. From this, as we have said, a triple love creeps in. For we are born and educated with a leaning toward either the contemplative, the active, or the pleasurable life. If toward the contemplative: we are immediately raised from the sight of bodily form to the consideration of the spiritual and divine. If toward the pleasurable: we suddenly descend from sight to the lust of touching. If toward the active and moral: we remain only in that delight of seeing and conversing. The first are so gifted that they are carried to the highest heights; the second are so dull that they are depressed to the lowest depths; the third, as if in the middle, remain in the middle region. Therefore, all love begins with sight. But the love of the contemplative man ascends from sight into the mind. That of the pleasurable man descends from sight into touch. That of the active man remains in sight. The love of the former turns more toward the highest demon than the lowest; that of the latter deflects toward the lowest rather than the highest; that of the middle man stands at equal distances from both. These three loves are given three names: the love of the contemplative man is called **Divine**; of the active man, **Human**; and of the pleasurable man, **Bestial**.

<margin>Chapter IX.</margin>
->What passions exist in lovers because of the mother of Love.<-
We have declared so far that Love is a demon born of Plenty and Poverty, and divided into five species. Next, we shall treat, from the words of Diotima, what kind of affections are born in lovers from this nature of love. She says that because Love was fathered at the birth of Venus, he follows and worships Venus, and is captured by the desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is most beautiful. Because he is the son of Poverty, he is parched, thin, and squalid, barefoot, humble, without a home, without bedding or any covering, sleeping at doors or in the street under the open sky, and finally, always needy. Because he is the son of Plenty, he lays snares for the beautiful and the good. He is manly, bold, fierce, vehement, a clever and sagacious hunter, always weaving new devices, a student of wisdom, eloquent, philosophizing through his whole life, a powerful enchanter and sorcerer, a dealer in charms and a sophist. He is neither entirely immortal by nature, nor mortal. But sometimes on the same day he flourishes and lives whenever he abounds; sometimes he fails and then lives again because of his father’s nature. Yet what he acquires always slips away. Therefore, Love is never either destitute or wealthy. Furthermore, he is placed in the middle between wisdom and ignorance. These are the words of Diotima. We shall explain them as briefly as possible. Although these traits are in all kinds of love, they appear more clearly in the three middle ones as they are more manifest to us. Born at the birth of Venus, he follows Venus; that is, being born with those celestial spirits we called "Venuses," he leads the souls of men back to the heavens and is captured by the desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is most beautiful. That is, he inflames souls with a desire for the highest and divine beauty, since he himself arose in those spirits who, being closest to God, are greatly illuminated by God’s splendor and raise us toward those same rays. Furthermore, since the life of all living things and trees and the fertility of the earth consist in moisture and heat, Diotima hints that both moisture and heat are lacking in Love to demonstrate his poverty, when she called him "parched, thin, and squalid." For who does not know that those things which moisture has deserted are parched and dry? Who would say that paleness and squalor come from anywhere else than a lack of bloody heat? Indeed, by long-lasting love, mortals are made pale and thin. For the power of nature is hardly sufficient for two works at once. The intention of the lover's soul is focused on...

the whole soul is occupied with the thought of the beloved. There, all the force of the natural complexion is also focused. For this reason, food is not perfectly digested in the stomach. Thus it happens that the greater part is cast out as superfluous remains; a smaller portion, and a raw one at that, is drawn to the liver. There also, for the same reason, it is poorly cooked <note>The author uses "cooked" (concoquitur) in the classical medical sense of metabolic digestion.</note>. Therefore, a meager and raw blood is spread from there through the veins. For this reason, all the limbs are thinned and become pale due to the lack and rawness of nourishment. Furthermore, wherever the constant attention of the mind is carried, there also the spirits—which are either the chariots or the instruments of the soul—fly. Spirits are created in the heart from the most subtle part of the blood. The mind of the lover seizes upon the image of the beloved fixed in the imagination and upon the beloved himself. The spirits are drawn to the same place. Flying out there constantly, they are dissipated. Wherefore there is need for a very frequent fuel of pure blood to recreate the consumed spirits; when all the more subtle and lucid parts of the blood exhale daily in restoring the spirits, because the pure and clear blood is dissolved, what remains is spotted, thick, dry, and black. This dries out the body and makes it shaggy; and here lovers turn out to be <term>melancholic</term> <note>In medieval medicine, melancholy was caused by an excess of "black bile," leading to depression or madness.</note>. For from dry, thick, and black blood, melancholy—that is, black bile—is produced, which fills the head with its vapors, dries the brain, and does not cease to trouble the soul day and night with foul and horrendous images, which we read happened to the Epicurean philosopher Lucretius on account of love. He, vexed first by love and then by insanity, finally laid hands upon himself. These things are accustomed to happen to those who, having abused love, have transferred what belongs to contemplation to the desire for an embrace. For we endure the desire of seeing more easily than the lust for both seeing and touching. When the ancient physicians observed this, they said that love was a passion very close to the melancholic disease; and the physician Rasis <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD), a Persian physician influential in the West.</note> prescribed that it be cured by sexual intercourse, fasting, inebriation, and walking. Nor does love only render men such, but also whoever are such by nature exist as more prone to love. Such are those in whom bile (which they call <term>cholera</term>) or black bile (which they call <term>melancholia</term>) prevails over the other humors. Bile is hot and dry. Black bile is dry and cold. The former holds the place of fire in the bodies of living creatures; the latter, the place of earth. Therefore, the dry melancholic types are understood to be shaggy and dry in the likeness of earth; the squalid and pale choleric types in the likeness of fire. The choleric, on account of the impetus of the fiery humor, are carried headlong into love; the melancholic, because of the sluggishness of the earthy humor, love more slowly. But on account of the stability of the humor itself, after they have been ensnared, they persevere for a very long time. Justly, therefore, Love is imagined as dry and squalid, since men who are such are accustomed to indulge in love beyond others. We judge this to happen chiefly because the choleric burn with the fire of bile; the melancholic are corroded by the harshness of black bile, as Aristotle affirmed in the seventh book of the *Ethics*. Therefore, a troublesome humor always distresses both, and forces them to seek some greatest and continuous solace against the continuous trouble of the humors. Of this kind are the delights of music and love. For we can bestow our labor so constantly on no other distractions as on the charms of music and voices, and the allurements of beauty. For the other senses are quickly satiated. But the sight or the hearing is fed longer by voices and "empty painting" <note>A reference to Virgil's Aeneid: "pascit animum pictura inani."</note>. Nor are the pleasures of these senses only firmer, but also more related to the human complexion. For what is more suitable to the spirits of the human body than the voices and figures of men—especially of those who please not only by a likeness of nature, but also by the grace of beauty? Wherefore choleric and melancholic men, as if for a unique remedy and solace for their most troublesome complexion, pursue the distractions of song and form. And therefore they are more prone to the allurements of Venus. And Socrates—whom Aristotle judged to be melancholic—was, as he himself confessed, the most inclined of all toward the art of loving. And so we can judge concerning the melancholic Sappho, as she herself testifies. Likewise our Maro <note>The poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note>, whom his likeness indicates to have been choleric, although he was modest, was nevertheless more inclined to loving. **With bare feet.** For this reason Diotima depicted Love such, since the lover is so occupied in amorous affairs that in the other duties of life, both private and public, he does not walk cautiously as is fitting, but without any foresight of dangers, he is carried rashly wherever he goes. Therefore, in his progress, he runs into frequent dangers, no differently than those who do not support their feet with leather, whence they strike against frequent thorns and pebbles. **Humble.** The Greek word of Plato signifies "on the ground" and "flying through the lowest things." For he saw many times that on account of the abuse of love, lovers live without sense, and great goods perish for the sake of light cares. These indeed give themselves up to the beloved to such an extent that they strive to pass entirely into them, and they fashion the beloved in themselves as much by words as by gestures. Indeed, by the very frequent imitation of boys and girls, who would not become effeminate? Who would not turn out a boy or a woman? **Without a home.** The home of human thought is the soul itself. The home of the soul is the spirit. The home of this spirit is the body. There are three inhabitants; there are three homes. Each of these, having lost its natural home, is in exile. For all thought turns itself not to the discipline and tranquility of its own mind, but to the service of the beloved person; and the soul deserts the ministry of its own body and strives to leap across into the body of the beloved. The spirit, the chariot of the soul, while the mind hastens elsewhere, also flies out elsewhere by exhaling. Therefore, thought exits its proper house; the soul exits; and the spirit exits. The first exit is accompanied by insanity and restlessness; the second by weakness and the dread of death; the third by trembling, fear, and sighing. Wherefore love is deprived of its own hearth, its natural seat, and its desired rest. **Without bedding or any covering.** For it has nowhere to rest and nothing to be covered with. For since every thing seeks its own origin, the little fire of love, from the sight of a beautiful body in the appetite of the lover—

O life more wretched than any death, unless perhaps your soul, snatched from its own body by this violence of love, should further neglect the form of the beloved and betake itself to the house of divine splendor: where at last it shall rest, and where it shall be fulfilled. Who, likewise, would deny that love wanders naked and without cover? For who can hide love, which a fixed, bull-like gaze betrays? Which interrupted speech declares: the flushing and paling of the face, frequent sighs, the tossing of limbs, perpetual complaining, untimely praises, sudden indignation, boasting, impudence, petulance, vain suspicion, and the meanest services reveal it? Just as light and rays accompany the heat in the sun and fire, so external signs follow the internal fire of love. **He sleeps at the doors.** The doors of the soul seem to be the eyes and ears; for through these, many things are carried into the soul, and the soul's affections and character shine out most clearly through the eyes. In gazing at figures and hearing voices, lovers linger for the most part. Rarely does their mind collect itself within itself. More often it wanders through the eyes and ears. Therefore, they are said to lie before the doors. They are also said to **lie in the way.** For the beauty of the body ought to be a kind of "way" through which we begin to ascend to a higher beauty. But those who prostrate themselves in foul lusts, or even dwell upon appearances more than is fitting, are seen to remain in the way itself, and by no means proceed to its end. **Under the open sky.** Deservedly. For being entirely occupied in one thing, they consider nothing in the conduct of affairs. Thus, living their lives by chance, they lead a life under the open sky as if naked to all the perils of fortune; they are exposed to all storms. **Always needy because of his mother's nature.** Truly, since the first origin of love was from want <note>Latin: *indigentia*</note>, and that which is natural cannot be entirely uprooted, love is always needy and always thirsty. For as long as something is lacking to be attained, the fire of love burns. When it possesses everything on all sides, the ardor ceases along with the want, rather than enduring without need.

### What gifts lovers have because of Love's father. Chapter X.

These things follow Poverty, the mother of love; but the opposite qualities follow Plenty, his father. Anyone may recognize what the opposites are from the previous points. Above, he was described as simple, incautious, lowly, and unarmed. Here, their opposites are introduced. For he is called **Cunning: a keen Hunter, a Deviser, an Ensnarer, a student of wisdom, a philosopher, manly and bold: vehement: eloquent, a Magician and a sophist.** The same love, which makes a lover careless and sluggish in other business, renders him shrewd and cunning in matters of love, so that he may court the favor of the beloved in marvelous ways, whether he entangles them with snares, or captures them with services, or soothes them with eloquence, or charms them with song. The same madness that had made him mild in service—the same madness, I say, provides arms: ferocity for those indignant against the beloved, and security and invincible strength for those fighting on their behalf.

Love, as we have said, takes its origin from sight. Sight is midway between the mind and touch. Hence the soul of the lover is always distracted and tossed up and down in turn. Sometimes a desire for an embrace arises; sometimes, however, a chaste desire for celestial beauty, and now the former, now the latter prevails and leads. In those who are most honorably educated and excel in sharpness of mind, the latter more often overcomes the former. Whoever prostrates themselves in the dregs of the body are deservedly judged to be parched, naked, lowly, unarmed, and sluggish. **Parched**, because they always hunger and are never filled. **Naked**, because like reckless men they are subject to all perils, and are held infamous as if most impudent and unrefined. **Lowly**, because they think nothing high or magnificent. **Unarmed**, because they succumb shamefully to desire. **Sluggish**, because they are so dull that they do not know where love draws them, and they remain in the way, not reaching the end.

Those affected in the opposite way are seen differently, for feeding on the solid goods of the soul, they are more filled and love more tranquilly. They preserve shame, neglect the shadowy beauty of the body, and are raised higher; and as if fortified with arms, they put to flight vain lusts from themselves and subject the senses to reason. These, as the most skillful and prudent of all, practice philosophy in such a way that they walk most providently through the shapes of bodies as if by certain tracks or scents: from these, one sagaciously investigates the sacred beauty of the soul and the divinity; and thus by hunting prudently, they happily attain what they desire.

Truly, such a great gift of love proceeds from his father, Plenty, since the ray of beauty—which is both Plenty and the father of love—has this power: that it is reflected back to where it came from and draws the lover with it. It descends first from God; passing into the Angel and the Soul as if through glass-like materials, and easily flowing from the soul into a body prepared for its reception, it shines out from that very body of the younger man, especially through the eyes, the clearest windows of the soul. It flies through the air immediately and, penetrating the eyes of the older man, it pierces the soul, kindles the appetite, and leads the wounded soul and the kindled appetite toward its healing and refreshment, while it ravishes it back to the same place from which it had descended. Step by step, indeed: into the body of the beloved first, into the soul second, thirdly into the Angel, and finally into God, the first origin of this splendor. This is the useful hunt, this the happy fowling of lovers. This very "hunting" is attributed to our Socrates by a certain friend of his in Plato's *Protagoras*. "From where, O Socrates!" he says, "I believe indeed you return from that hunt to which the noble character of Alcibiades is wont to provoke you."

Furthermore, he calls Love a **Sophist and a Magician.** Plato, in the dialogue *The Sophist*, defines a sophist as an ambitious and deceitful disputant who, by captious shifts, shows us the false for the true, and forces those who dispute with him to contradict themselves in their own speech. Both lovers and the beloved sometimes suffer this. Indeed, lovers, blinded by the clouds of love, often accept false things for true, while they consider their beloved ones more beautiful, more keen...

# COMMENTARY
## PAGE 172

They consider themselves better than they are. Because of the violence of their love, they contradict themselves. For reason counsels one thing, while desire follows another. They change their own plans at the command of the beloved; they oppose themselves in order to comply with others. Often, even the beautiful are ensnared by the cunning of lovers, and those who were previously stubborn become easy to win. But why do we think Love is a magician? Because the entire power of magic consists in love. The work of magic is the attraction of one thing by another through a certain kinship of nature. Moreover, the parts of this world, like the limbs of a single animal <note>The concept of the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, where the universe is viewed as a living organism.</note>, all hanging from one author, are joined together by the communion of a single nature. Therefore, just as in us the brain, lungs, heart, liver, and the rest of the limbs draw something from each other, and help one another, and when one of them suffers, they suffer together: so the limbs of this great animal—that is, all the bodies of the world—being similarly connected, borrow and lend their natures to one another. From this common kinship, a common love is born; from love, a common attraction. This, moreover, is true magic. Thus, from the concavity of the moon's sphere, fire is drawn upward because of the harmony of nature; from the concavity of fire, air is drawn; from the center of the world, the earth is drawn to the lowest depths; and water is also snatched from its own place. Hence also the Magnet turns iron, and amber turns chaff, fire turns sulfur, and the sun turns many flowers and leaves toward itself; the moon moves the waters; Mars is accustomed to stir the winds; and various herbs also invite various kinds of living creatures to themselves. Even in human affairs, his own pleasure draws each man. Therefore, the works of magic are the works of nature; Art is truly the servant. For where something is lacking in natural kinship, Art supplies it through vapors, numbers, figures, and qualities at opportune times; just as in agriculture nature produces the crops, but art prepares them. The ancients attributed this art to demons <note>original: "daemonibus" — here referring to intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses rather than evil entities</note> because they understand what the fellowship of natural things is like: what fits with what, and how the harmony of things, if it is lacking anywhere, may be restored. Some are said to have been friends to these demons either by a certain similarity of nature, such as Zoroaster and Socrates, or beloved through worship, such as Apollonius of Tyana and Porphyry. Therefore, it is told that signs, voices, and portents happened to them while awake, or oracles and visions from demons while asleep. Those who have escaped the friendship of demons seem to be magicians, just as demons are magicians knowing the friendship of things themselves; and all nature is called a magician because of mutual love. Furthermore, every beautiful person fascinates us with their tender eyes. Men soothe them with the powers of eloquence and the measures of songs as if with certain incantations, and win them over; moreover, they are appeased and captured by attention and gifts no differently than by sorceries. Wherefore no one doubts that Love is a magician, since the entire power of magic consists in love, and the work of love is fulfilled by fascinations, incantations, and sorceries. It is neither entirely mortal, nor yet immortal. Not mortal: since two loves are in us—those two which we call demons—and they are perpetual. Not immortal: since three of these intermediate loves change daily; they grow and they decrease. Furthermore, in the appetite of men from the very beginnings of life, an inextinguishable fervor is innate, which does not permit the soul to rest, and always impels it to apply itself with zeal to a certain thing. The dispositions of men are diverse, nor do they live by one wish. Whence that continuous fervor of desire, which is natural love, impels some to the study of letters; others to music or figures; others to honesty of character or a religious life; others to honors; some to accumulating money; most to the luxury of the belly; others to other things; and even the same man to different things at different ages. Therefore, the same fervor is called both immortal and mortal. Immortal: because it is never extinguished; it changes its material rather than vanishing. Mortal: because it does not always dwell upon the same thing, but either from a change of nature or from a satiety arising from long-standing familiarity with the same thing, it seeks new delights; and that which has almost failed in one thing, in a way revives in another. It is also said to be immortal for this reason: that a figure once beloved is always loved. For as long as the same figure remains in the same person, it is loved in that very person; but when it has flowed away from them, the same figure which you loved before is no longer in them. You do not burn for this current mark, because you had not burned for it before; yet you do not cease to love that prior one. However, there is this difference: that you previously looked upon it in another; but now you look upon it only in yourself; and always fixed in the same memory, you always love it; and as often as it occurs to the eyes of the mind, so often does it burn you, the lover. Therefore, as often as we meet that person once most dear to us, so often are we moved: either the heart fails or trembles, or the liver melts, or the eyes quiver, and the face takes on various colors in their presence. For their presence suggests the hidden figure of the mind to the eyes of the soul, and as if by blowing, it rouses the fires sleeping under the ashes. For this reason, love is called immortal. But it is also held to be mortal here, because although the faces remain always fixed in the breast, they do not offer themselves equally to the eyes of the mind. Wherefore benevolence seems to burn and cool in turn. Added to this is that both wild and human love can never be without indignation. Who would not be indignant at one who has stolen their soul! For as liberty is pleasing above all things, so servitude is burdensome. Therefore, you hate and love the beautiful at the same time: you hate them as thieves and murderers; yet as mirrors gleaming with celestial brightness, you are compelled to wonder and to love. What can you do, wretch! Where you should turn, you know not, alas, lost one. Since you would not wish this to be your murderer, you also would not wish to live without the blessed spectacle. Since you cannot be with this one who destroys you, who kills you; yet without this one you cannot live, who steals you from yourself with such wondrous allurements, who claims all of you for themselves. You desire to flee this one who burns you with their flames; yet you also desire to cling to this one, so that being closest to the one possessing you, you may also cling to yourself. You seek yourself, wretch, outside of yourself, and you cling to the robber so that you might one day redeem yourself, the captive. You would indeed not wish to love, insane one: because

you would not wish to die; nor would you wish not to love, since you judge that the image of heavenly things must be served. Therefore, by this alternation, it happens that at every moment (so to speak) love withers away and then flourishes again. Diotima also places Love in the middle between wisdom and ignorance. Furthermore, Love follows those things which are beautiful. Wisdom is the most beautiful of all things. Therefore, Love desires wisdom. He who desires wisdom does not possess it entirely—for who would seek what is already present? Yet, he is not entirely without it either. For in this one respect at least he is wise: he recognizes his own lack of knowledge. But he who does not know that he is ignorant, ignores both the things themselves and his own ignorance; nor does he seek knowledge, of which he does not know himself to be void. Therefore, the love of wisdom <note>original: "Amor... sapientiæ", referring to Philosophy</note>, because it is partly deprived of wisdom and partly wise, is located between wisdom and ignorance. This, says Diotima, is the condition of Love; but the nature of the "Beautiful itself"—that is, supreme beauty—is such that it is delicate, perfect, and blessed. It is delicate, I say, because it draws every desire to itself by its own sweetness; it is perfect, insofar as it illuminates those who approach it with its rays and perfects them; it is blessed, insofar as it fills those it has illuminated with eternal goods.

### What the utility of love is, based on its definition. Chapter XI.

After Diotima explained the origin of love and what kind of thing it is, she now reveals where it tends and what benefit it brings to men. We all certainly desire to have good things; and not only to have them, but to have them always. Yet the individual goods of mortals change and fail; and all things would quickly vanish unless new things were created daily in the place of those departing. Therefore, so that good things may somehow endure for us forever, we desire to recreate what is perishing. This recreation happens through generation <note>procreation or the act of bringing forth</note>. Hence, the instinct for generation is innate in all. Since generation makes mortal things similar to divine things through continuity, it is surely a divine gift. To divine things (which are beautiful), ugly things are contrary; beautiful things are similar and friendly. Therefore, the divine work of generation is completed perfectly and easily in that which is beautiful; but in the contrary, it is the opposite. For this reason, the effort of generation seeks out beautiful things and flees from their opposites. You ask: what is the love of men? To what does it lead? It is the desire for generation in the beautiful, for the sake of preserving a perpetual life in mortal things. This is the love of men living on earth; this is the goal of our love. Indeed, in the very time in which any animal is said to live and be the same—as from childhood to old age—although it is called the same, it never contains the same things within itself. Instead, it is always making something new, as Plato says, and shedding the old: in terms of hair, flesh, bones, blood, and the entire body. And this happens not only in the body, but also in the soul. Manners, customs, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears are constantly changing; none of these remains the same or similar. The prior ones are abolished; new ones succeed them and grow. Even more wonderful, knowledge also behaves this way: some pieces of knowledge vanish while others arise. We are not always the same in respect to our knowledge; even a single branch of knowledge suffers nearly the same fate. For study and recollection are, as it were, the taking up again of a departing knowledge. Forgetting seems to be the exit of knowledge. But study, by always restoring a new memory in place of the one departing, preserves knowledge so that it seems to be the same. In this twofold way, whatever things in the soul or body are changeable are preserved: not because they are always entirely the same (for this is the property of divine things), but because that which wastes away and departs leaves behind something new and similar to itself. By this remedy, certainly, mortal things are made similar to immortal things. Therefore, in both parts of the soul—both that which looks toward cognition and that by which the body is ruled—there is an innate love of generation for the sake of preserving life perpetually. The love in the part adapted for ruling the body impels us from the very beginning to take food and drink, so that from these nourishments the humors <note>bodily fluids</note> may be generated, by which that which flows out of the body is replaced. By this generation, the body is nourished and grows. When the body is adult, the seed itself is stirred, provoking the lust for procreating offspring; so that what cannot remain forever in itself may remain eternal, reserved in an offspring very similar to itself. Also, the love of generation attributed to the cognitive part of the soul makes the soul desire truth, its own proper nourishment, through which it may be nourished and grow in its own way. And if anything has fallen from the soul through forgetfulness, or grows numb through sloth and neglect, the soul regenerates it through the zeal of recollection and study; it calls back to mind what had perished through forgetting or had grown sluggish through laziness. When the soul is adult, it is stimulated by a most burning desire for teaching and writing; so that knowledge, generated either in writings or in the souls of disciples, may allow the teacher's intelligence and truth to remain eternal among men. And so, by the benefit of love, both the body and the soul of every man seem able to survive forever in human affairs after death. Both types of love pursue beautiful things. Surely, the one who rules and governs the body desires to nourish his own body with the most delicate, pleasant, and beautiful feasts, and to generate beautiful offspring with a comely woman. And the one who pertains to the soul strives to imbue it with the most ornate and pleasing disciplines, and to bring forth a knowledge most similar to his own by writing in an ornate and beautiful style, and by teaching, to generate it in a most beautiful soul—I mean a pure, sharp, and excellent soul. We do not see the soul itself, and therefore we do not behold its beauty. But we see the body, the shadow and image of the soul. Therefore, suspecting from its image, we conjecture that in a beautiful body there is a comely soul. For this reason, we educate beautiful men more willingly.
