### On the two loves, and that the soul is born endowed with truth. Chapter XII.

<margin>Chapter XII.</margin>
We have already said enough regarding the definition of love: now, however, let us declare what distinction exists in Plato concerning love, arising from the fertility of the soul and the body. He says that the bodies of all men are pregnant and heavy with seed: and so too is the soul. The seeds of all its parts are inserted into the body from the beginning. From this, at fixed cycles of time, the teeth break through: the hair comes forth: the beard grows thick: the seeds of procreation flow down. If the body is fertile and heavy with seeds, how much more is the soul—which is more excellent than the body—most abundant, possessing the seeds of all its own qualities from the beginning. Therefore, the soul has long ago been allotted the <term>rational principles</term> <note>original: rationes; the underlying logic or blueprints of things</note> of morals, arts, and disciplines: and from there, if it is rightly cultivated, it brings forth its offspring into the light at the appointed times. Moreover, we recognize that it possesses the innate principles of all its qualities from its appetite, investigation, discovery, judgment, and comparison. Who would deny that the soul, immediately from a tender age, longs for things that are true, good, honest, and useful? Yet no one longs for the unknown. Therefore, there are certain notions of these things in the soul even before it desires them: through which, as if through their forms and principles, it judges that they are to be desired. The same is proved by investigation and discovery. If Socrates seeks Alcibiades <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and student of Socrates</note> in a crowd of men, and is eventually to find him, it is necessary that the image of Alcibiades be present in Socrates' mind, so that he knows which man he seeks above the others, and upon finding him in a gathering of many, he is able to distinguish Alcibiades from the rest. In the same way, the soul would neither track down those four things, nor ever find them, unless it held some notion of them: 1. Truth, Goodness, Honesty, and Utility, through which it might seek them with the intent to find, so that whenever it finds what it investigated, it recognizes it and distinguishes it from its opposites. We prove this not only from appetite, investigation, and discovery, but also from judgment. For whoever judges someone to be a friend or an enemy is not ignorant of what friendship or ill-will is. In what way, therefore, would we daily judge many things to be true or false, good or bad, as we are accustomed to do—and judge them correctly—unless truth and goodness were in some way known to us beforehand? Again, how would many people, even those not practiced in these arts, very often correctly approve or disapprove of works of architecture, music, painting, and the other arts, as well as the discoveries of philosophers, unless the same form and principle of those things had been granted to them by nature? Comparison also shows us the same thing. For whoever, comparing honey to wine, pronounces one sweeter than the other, recognizes what a sweet flavor is: and he who, comparing Speusippus and Xenocrates <note>Successors of Plato in the Academy</note> to Plato, deems Xenocrates more similar to Plato than Speusippus, undoubtedly knows the form of Plato. In the same way, when we rightly judge one thing better than another among many good things: and when one thing appears better or worse than another by a greater or lesser participation in goodness: it is necessary that we are not ignorant of goodness. Furthermore, since among many diverse opinions of philosophers or even others, we often judge best which is more like the truth and more probable, it is necessary that we do not lack some intuition of truth, so that we are not unaware of what things are more similar to it. For this reason, some are said to have turned out most learned in their youth, some even without a teacher, and most from the very few rudiments of doctrine demonstrated by teachers. This could never have happened unless nature, as we said, assisted them greatly. Socrates demonstrated this abundantly to the boys Phaedo, Theaetetus, and Meno: and he taught that boys can answer correctly in individual arts if someone questions them prudently: since they are by nature endowed with the principles of all arts and disciplines.

### The light of truth is in the Soul. Chapter XIII.

<margin>Chapter XIII.</margin>
In what way these principles are in the soul, however, seems ambiguous in Plato. If one follows those books which Plato wrote as a younger man—the *Phaedrus*, *Meno*, and *Phaedo*—he will perhaps think that they are painted in the substance of the soul almost like figures on a wall: a point touched upon often in the preceding sections both by me and by yourselves, for he seems to hint at it there. But in the sixth book of the *Republic*, that divine man opens up the whole matter: he says that the light of the mind for understanding all things is that same God by whom all things were made. For he compares the sun and God to each other in such a way that, just as the sun is to the eyes, so God is to minds. The sun generates the eyes and provides them with the power of seeing. This power would be in vain, and overwhelmed by eternal darkness, unless the light of the sun were present, painted with the colors and shapes of bodies: in which light the eye sees the colors and shapes of bodies. Nor does the eye behold anything other than light. Yet it seems to behold various things, because the light infused into it is adorned with various formulas of external bodies. Indeed, the eye perceives this light reflected in bodies: but it cannot endure the light itself in its own source. In the same way, God procreates the soul: and grants it a mind, a power for understanding, which would be empty and dark unless the light of God were present to it: in which it may inspect the principles of all things. Whence it understands through the light of God: and recognizes only the divine light itself. Yet it seems to recognize diverse things, because it understands that light under diverse ideas and principles of things. When someone, seeing a man with his eyes, fashions an image of the man in his imagination, and revolves longer in judging it, he raises the sharp edge of his mind to look upon the principle of man existing in the divine light: from there a spark immediately flashes in the mind: and in truth, the nature itself of man is understood: and concerning... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence</note>

-> x iiii <-

in the same way as all other things. Therefore, we understand all things through the light of God; yet we cannot see that pure light itself and its fountainhead in this life. Clearly, the entire fertility of the soul consists in this: that within its innermost chambers shines that eternal light of God, most full of the reasons and Ideas <note>original: "ideisque" - referring to the Platonic Forms</note> of all things. To these the soul turns as often as it wishes through purity of life and the highest intensity of study; having turned, it flashes forth with the sparks of the Ideas.

### Whence comes love toward males. Whence toward females. Chapter 14.

Thus the human body is pregnant, as Plato wishes, and the soul is pregnant too; both are stimulated to give birth by the incitements of love. However, some—either by nature or by education—are more fit for the offspring of the soul than those of the body; others, and indeed the majority, are the opposite. The former follow celestial love; the latter, vulgar love. The former naturally love males, and specifically those who are almost adults, rather than females or children; for in them the sharpness of the mind flourishes more fully, which is most fit for the learning they intend to procreate because of its more excellent beauty. Others, on the contrary, seek the pleasure of sexual union and the effect of bodily generation. 

Since that genital power of the soul, being devoid of cognition, makes no distinction between the sexes, yet by its own nature it incites one to procreate as often as we judge a body to be beautiful, it frequently happens that those who associate with males—in order to satisfy the stings of the genital part—mingle with them. This occurs especially in those in whose birth-chart <note>original: "genesi" - an astrological reference to the natal horoscope</note> Venus was in a masculine sign and with Saturn, or in the bounds of Saturn, or opposite Saturn. However, one ought to have noticed that the incitements of that genital part should not affect this vain work of waste, but rather the duty of bearing and procreating, and should transfer it from males to females. We believe that from an error of this kind arose that nefarious crime which Plato, in his *Laws*, detests most sharply as a species of homicide. Indeed, he who snatches away a human being about to be born is to be judged no less a murderer than he who removes a living person from our midst. Bolder indeed is he who cuts short a present life, but more cruel is he who envies the light to one about to be born, and kills his own sons not yet born.

### Above the Body is the Soul; above the Soul, the Angel; above the Angel, God. Chapter 15.

But enough concerning the twin fertility of the soul and the twin loves. Next, let us discuss by what steps Diotima <note>The priestess in Plato's Symposium who teaches Socrates about Love</note> raises Socrates from the lowest things to the highest: from the body into the soul, from the soul into the Angel, and from the Angel she leads him back to God. One may argue that these four levels of things must exist in nature in this way: Every body is moved by something else; it cannot move itself by its own nature, since it cannot perform any action by itself. But it appears to be moved by itself because of the presence of the soul, and to live because of the soul. While the soul is present, it moves itself in a certain way; but when the soul is absent, it is moved only by another, since it does not have this nature from itself. The soul, however, properly possesses the power of moving itself. For to whatever it is present, it imparts the power to move itself. That which it imparts to others by its own presence, it must itself possess much earlier and more greatly. 

Therefore, the soul is above bodies, as it is able to move itself according to its own essence; and for that reason, it must be above those things which do not move by themselves, but achieve movement through the presence of others. When we say the soul is moved by itself, we do not utter that word "transitively" (as Aristotle wished Plato to be understood), but absolutely—just as we assert that God stands by Himself, the sun shines by itself, and fire is hot by itself. For it is not that one part of the soul moves and another part is agitated; rather, the whole soul moves from itself (that is, by its own nature). This means it ranges by reason from one thing to another, and carries out the works of nutrition, growth, and generation through intervals of time. This temporal discourse belongs to the soul from itself, because that which is above it understands all things simultaneously in a single point of eternity, not at different moments. 

For this reason, the "first motion" and the "first interval of time" are rightly placed by Plato in the soul; from there, motion and time pass into bodies. Since it is necessary for rest to exist before motion (as rest is more perfect than motion), one must find above the mobile reason of the soul some stable Intelligence <note>term: Intelligence - here referring to the "Angel" or pure Mind</note> which is intelligence according to its whole self, and is always intelligence in act. For the soul does not understand with its whole self, nor always, but only from a certain part of itself and at certain times; nor does it have a certain power of understanding, but an ambiguous one. Therefore, so that what is more perfect may precede what is less perfect, above the mind of the soul—which is mobile, partial, intermittent, and doubtful—must be placed the stable, whole, continuous, and most certain Mind of the Angel. Just as the soul (moved by itself) precedes the body (agitated by another), so the stable Mind (stable by itself) precedes the soul (agitated by itself). And just as the body has the power to move itself through the soul—and thus not all bodies, but only animated ones, seem to move of their own accord—so the soul has the power to understand always through the Mind. For if intellect were in the soul by its own nature, it would also belong to the souls of beasts, just as the power of agitating itself does. Therefore, intellect does not belong to the soul by itself and primarily; wherefore it must be preceded by that which possesses mind by itself and primarily. Such a thing is the Angel, more excellent than souls. But indeed, that Principle of things and the Supreme Good, which Plato in the *Parmenides* calls "The One" itself, necessarily towers above the Mind of the Angel. For above every multitude of a composite thing, "The One" itself must be simple by nature; for from the one comes number, and from simple things the entire composition is fashioned. The Mind...

# COMMENTARY

However, although that [the angelic mind] is immobile, it does not exist as one pure, simple thing. For it understands itself in a way where these three appear distinct from one another: that which understands, that which is understood, and the act of understanding. For its rationale is one thing insofar as it understands, another insofar as it is understood, and another insofar as it is the act of understanding. Furthermore, it possesses a power of knowing that is entirely formless in itself before the act of cognition; it is formed by the act of knowing. In the process of understanding, it desires and receives the light of truth, which it seems to have lacked before it understood. It also contains within itself a multitude of Ideas <note>The Platonic "Ideas" or "Forms," the perfect blueprints of all things.</note>. You see how great and varied a multitude and composition exists within an angel. Therefore, we are compelled to place the pure One and the Simple above the angel.

But we can place nothing before the one God, because the true One is devoid of all multitude and all composition. If He had anything above Him, He would certainly be made by it; therefore, depending on it, He would degenerate from it, as an effect usually does from its cause. Thus, He would no longer be one and simple, but composed of at least two things: namely, from the gift of His cause and His own inherent lack. Therefore, the One itself, as Plato wills and Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th century who blended Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine.</note> confirms, towers above all things; and the "One itself" is judged by both to be the most excellent name of God.

Reason also shows us this sublimity: that the gift of the most eminent cause ought to be the most ample, and the excellence of its power should extend itself to all things. The gift of the One propagates itself through the universe. For not only is the mind one, and every soul one, and every body one; but even formless matter itself and the privation of things <note>The state of being without form or quality.</note> is said to be "one" in a certain way. For we speak of "one silence," "one darkness," and "one death." Yet the gifts of the Mind and the Soul do not extend that far. For the Mind bestows artistic form and order; the Soul provides life and motion; but formless and primary matter, and the privation of things, are devoid of form and life. Thus, the One itself precedes the Mind and the Soul, since its gift is more widely diffused. By the same reasoning, the Mind seems to exceed the Soul, because life—the gift of the Soul—is not given to all bodies. Yet the Mind grants form and order to all of them.

->What the comparison is between God, Angel, Soul, and Body. Chapter XVI.<-

Therefore, we ascend from the body into the soul, from the soul into the angel, and from the angel into God. God is above eternity; the Angel is entirely within eternity. Surely both its operation and its essence remain stable. Now, stability is the proper state of eternity. The Soul is partly in eternity and partly in time. For its substance endures always the same without any change of increase or decrease. But its operation, as we showed a little while ago, runs through intervals of time. The Body is entirely subject to time. For both its substance is changed, and its every operation requires a space of time. Therefore, the One itself exists above stability or motion; the Angel is in stability; the Soul is in stability and motion alike; the Body is placed in motion alone. Again, the One remains above number, motion, and place; the Angel is placed in number, but above motion and place; the Soul is in number and motion, but above place; the Body is subject to number, motion, and place. For the One itself has neither any number nor composition of parts; nor is it changed in any way from what it is; nor is it enclosed by any place. The Angel indeed has a number of parts or forms, but is free from motion and place. The Soul has a multitude of parts and affections, and is changed by the progression of reasoning and the variety of disturbances, but it is exempt from the limits of place. The Body, however, is liable to all of these.

->What the comparison is between the beauties of God, Angel, Soul, and Body. Chapter XVII.<-

There is indeed the same comparison between these four and their forms. Truly, the form of the body consists in the composition of many parts; it is constrained by place; it glides away in time. The beauty of the soul suffers the vicissitudes of time and contains a multitude of parts, but it is absolute from the boundaries of place. The beauty of the angel has number alone; it exists immune from the other two. In God, however, none of these are found. You certainly see the form of the body. Do you wish also to behold the beauty of the soul? Subtract from the bodily form the weight of the matter itself and the limits of places; leave the rest: now you have the beauty of the Soul. Do you want that of the angel too? I pray you, take away not only the spaces of place, but also the progress of time; keep the multiple composition: you obtain it immediately. Do you desire also to see the beauty of God? Take away, in addition, that multiple composition of forms; leave the form entirely simple: you will have instantly attained the beauty of God.

But what, after all, will remain for me when these things are subtracted? Do you think beauty is anything other than light? Furthermore, the beauty of all bodies is that light of the sun which you see, infected <note>original: "infectum" - here meaning "stained" or "imbued" with material qualities.</note> by those three things: by the multitude of forms (for it is depicted with many aspects, figures, and colors), by the space of place, and by temporal change. Take away its seat in matter, so that it retains the other two besides place: the beauty of the soul is exactly of this kind. Take away from here, if you please, the change of time; let the rest go: there remains a light without place, without motion, most clear, but engraved with all the rational principles of all things. That is the angel; that is the beauty of the angel. Finally, take away that number of diverse ideas; leave one simple and pure light: like the light that remains in the globe of the sun itself and is not dispersed through the air; now [you see] the beauty of God in a certain...

# ON THE BANQUET
## FOLIO 165

...you only now comprehend: which at least surpasses all other forms as much as that light of the sun, pure, single, and inviolate in itself, excels the splendor of the sun when it is scattered, divided, stained, and darkened through the cloudy air. Therefore, the fountain of all beauty is God. Therefore, the fountain of all love is God. Furthermore, the light of the sun in water is a kind of shadow compared to its clearer light in the air. The splendor in the air is likewise a shadow compared to its brilliance in fire. The brilliance in fire is a shadow compared to the light of the sun shining in the sun itself. The same comparison exists between those four beauties: of the body, of the soul, of the angel, and of God. God is never so deceived as to love the shadow of His own likeness in an angel while neglecting His own true beauty. Nor is an angel so captivated by the beauty of a soul—which is its own shadow—that it abandons its own beauty, detained by the shadow. 

However, our soul—which is most deeply to be lamented, for this is the origin of all our unhappiness—the soul, I say, alone is so charmed by the allurements of bodily form that it holds its own beauty in second place; forgetting itself, it pursues the form of the body, which is but its own shadow. Hence arises that most cruel fate of Narcissus in the Orphic <note>Referring to the Orphic mysteries or the poetic tradition associated with Orpheus</note> myths. Hence the pitiable calamity of men. For Narcissus the youth—that is, the soul of the rash and inexperienced man—does not behold his own face: he in no way perceives his own substance and virtue. Instead, he pursues its shadow in the water and tries to embrace it; that is, he admires beauty in a fragile body, flowing like water, which is the shadow of the soul itself. He deserts his own figure; he never catches the shadow, because the soul, by pursuing the body, neglects itself and is not fulfilled by the use of the body. For it does not truly desire the body itself, but rather its own beauty, enticed by the bodily form which is the image of its own beauty, just as Narcissus was affected. And since he does not notice this, while he desires one thing and follows another, he cannot satisfy his longing. Therefore, dissolved into tears, he is consumed; that is, the soul, placed thus outside itself and fallen into the body, is tortured by destructive disturbances; stained by the filth of the body, it "dies," as it were, since it now seems to be a body rather than a soul. To ensure that Socrates avoided such a death, Diotima led him back from the body to the soul, from the soul to the angel, and from the angel to God.

### How the Soul is Raised from the Beauty of the Body to the Beauty of God. Chapter XVIII.

Come now, dearest guests, imagine Diotima speaking thus to Socrates: "No body, O Socrates, is beautiful in every respect. For it is either beautiful in this part and deformed in that; or beautiful today and not at all at another time; or judged beautiful by one person and ugly by another. Therefore, the beauty of the body, defiled by the contagion of ugliness, cannot be pure, true, and primary beauty. Furthermore, no one ever suspects beauty itself of being ugly, just as no one suspects wisdom of being foolish. Yet we think the arrangement of bodies is sometimes beautiful and sometimes ugly, and at the same time, different people feel differently about it. Therefore, the primary and true beauty is not in bodies. 

Add to this that many bodies are called by the single name of 'beauty.' There is, therefore, one common nature of beauty in bodies, through which they are similarly called beautiful. But consider that a single nature of this kind, just as it exists in another thing (that is, in matter), so it depends on another. For that which cannot be sustained in itself can much less depend on itself. Will it depend on matter? Not at all. For nothing deformed and imperfect can adorn or perfect itself. But that which is one must arise from one. For this reason, the single beauty of many bodies depends on some single incorporeal artisan. The one artisan of all is God, who through angels and souls daily renders all the matter of the world beautiful. Therefore, one must believe that the true principle of beauty is found in God and His ministers <note>The "ministers" here refer to the celestial hierarchy or angels</note> rather than in the body of the world. 

To this beauty, I believe, you will easily ascend, O Socrates, by these steps. If nature had given you lynx-like eyes, my Socrates, so that you could penetrate whatever met your gaze, that most handsome body of your Alcibiades <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and student of Socrates, famous for his physical beauty</note> would appear most foul to you. How little it is that you love, my friend! Only the surface, or rather a color, ravishes you; or rather a certain reflection of lights and a very light shadow. Or a vain imagination deceives you, so that you love what you dream of rather than what you see. But lest I seem to oppose you entirely, let us grant that this Alcibiades is handsome. But in how many parts is he handsome? In all his members, surely, except for his snub nose and eyebrows higher than is fitting. Yet these features are beautiful in Phaedrus. But the thickness of Phaedrus's legs is unpleasing. These are graceful in Charmides, unless his slender neck should offend you. Thus, if you observe individual men, you will praise none in every part. You will collect whatever is right everywhere; you will fashion an entire figure within yourself from the observation of all, so that the absolute beauty of the human race, which is found scattered in many bodies, may be gathered in your soul by the thought of a single image. You will value the figure of any individual man little, O Socrates, if you compare it to that one. Indeed, you possess that image not so much by the body's gift as by the benefit of your soul. Therefore, love that image which your soul has fashioned, and the soul itself as its artisan, rather than that external beauty which is maimed and dispersed. 

But what do I command you to love in the soul? The beauty of the soul. For light is the beauty of bodies; light is also the beauty of the soul. The light of the soul is Truth, which alone your friend Plato seems to ask of God in his prayers. 'Grant me, O God,' he says, 'that my soul may be made beautiful; and that those things which pertain to the body may not hinder the beauty of the soul; may I consider only the wise man to be rich.' In these words, Plato declares that the beauty of the soul consists in truth..."

# COMMENTARY
## VI
<meta>catchword: twin</meta>

...that wisdom consists in you: and that it is granted to humans by God. Truth is one; and this same truth, granted to us by God, acquires the names of various virtues according to its different effects. As it demonstrates divine wisdom, which Plato asked of God above all else, it is called **Wisdom** <note>original: *sapientia*</note>; as it concerns natural things, **Science** <note>original: *scientia*</note>; as it concerns human affairs, **Prudence**; as it makes men just, **Justice**; as it makes them unconquerable, **Fortitude**; and as it makes them tranquil, it is called **Temperance**. From these, two kinds of virtues are numbered: the **Moral** virtues, and the **Intellectual** virtues which are superior to them. The Intellectual are Wisdom, Science, and Prudence; the Moral are Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance. The Moral virtues are better known because of their actions and civic duties; the Intellectual are more hidden because of the depth of their truths. Furthermore, he who is educated in honest morals, being purer than others, is easily raised to the intellectual virtues. Therefore, I command you to first consider the beauty of the soul which consists in morals, so that you may understand that there is one principle of morals by which men are similarly called honest. That is, the one truth of a most pure life, which through the actions of Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, leads us to true happiness. Therefore, love first this one truth of morals and this most beautiful light of the soul. Know also that you will ascend more quickly above morals to the most lucid truth of wisdom, science, and prudence if you consider that these are granted to a soul educated in the best morals, and that the most upright rule of moral life is contained within them. Although you may behold various doctrines of Wisdom, Science, and Prudence, believe nevertheless that in all of them there is a single light of truth, through which all are similarly called beautiful. I command you to love that light exceedingly, as it is the supreme beauty of the soul. But indeed, this one truth in many doctrines cannot be the first truth of all, because it exists in something else, being distributed among many doctrines. Whatever lies in another certainly depends upon another. Yet the one truth is not born from a multitude of doctrines. For that which is one must arise from one. Wherefore it is necessary that there be a certain single wisdom above the soul of man, which is not divided through diverse doctrines, but is one wisdom, from whose unique truth the manifold truth of men arises. Remember, O Socrates, that this unique light of unique wisdom is the beauty of the **Angel** <note>Ficino uses "Angel" to refer to the Platonic "Divine Mind" or *Nous*</note>, which you must worship above the beauty of the soul. As we demonstrated above, it excels the beauty of bodies because it is neither bound by place, nor divided according to the parts of matter, nor corrupted. It also excels the beauty of the soul because it is entirely eternal and is not moved by the passage of time. But since the light of the Angel shines in a series of many **Ideas** <note>The eternal archetypes of all things</note>, and since above every multitude there must be a unity which is the origin of the whole number, it is necessary that it flows from the one principle of all things, which we call **The One** itself. Therefore, the light of The One itself is a completely simple and infinite beauty; for it is neither stained by the filth of matter like the beauty of the body, nor changed by temporal progression like the form of the soul, nor dissipated by multitude like the beauty of the Angel. Moreover, every quality that is separated from any external addition is called **infinite** by the Physicists. If heat exists in itself, not hindered by cold or moisture, and not weighed down by the mass of matter, it is called infinite heat, because its power is free and not narrowed by any limits of addition. Similarly, light free from every body is infinite; for it shines without measure or end, because it shines by its own nature when it is not limited by another. Thus the light and beauty of God, which is pure and entirely absolute from all others, is without doubt called infinite beauty. Truly, infinite beauty requires an immense love. Therefore, I beseech you, Socrates, that you love other things with a certain measure and limit, but love God with an infinite love, and let no measure be present in divine love.

### How God is to be Loved. Chapter XIX.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring a classical figure or saint within a square frame.</image-desc>Thus spoke Diotima to Socrates. But we, most illustrious men, shall love God not only without measure, as Diotima feigns to command, but we shall love God alone. For the mind is related to God as the sight of the eyes is to the sun. The eye desires not only light above all else, but desires light alone. If we love bodies, if we love souls, if we love angels, we shall not love these things themselves, but God in them. In bodies, we love the shadow of God; in souls, the likeness of God; in angels, His image. Thus we shall love God in all things for the present, so that at last we may love all things in God. For living thus, we shall set out so that we may see both God and all things in God, and love both Him and all things that are in Him. And whoever devotes himself to God through charity in this time will finally recover himself in God. Indeed, he will return to his own **Idea** through which he was created; there, if anything was lacking in him, he will be reformed, and he will adhere to his Idea forever. For the true man and the Idea of man are the same. Therefore, each of us on earth, separated from God, is not a "true man," since he is disjoined from his own Idea and form. Divine love and piety will lead us back to it, though here we are torn apart and mutilated. Therefore, then, joined by loving to our Idea, we shall emerge as whole men; so that we may seem to have worshipped God first in things, in order that we may then worship things in God; and to venerate things in God so that we may embrace ourselves above all else, and in loving God, we may seem to have loved ourselves.

### Conclusion of the aforementioned things: and the opinion of Guido Cavalcanti the philosopher. Chapter I.

...divided it into two forms: namely, the heavenly and the common. Eryximachus revealed its vastness by showing how it exists in all things, distributed into twin parts. Aristophanes declared what the presence of so great a god achieves in individuals, showing that through him, broken humanity is mended. Agathon treated how great its virtue and power are, arguing that men are made blessed by him alone. Finally, Socrates, having been taught by Diotima, explained in summary what love is and of what kind, where it originates, how many parts it has, where it tends, and how much power it possesses. 

Guido Cavalcanti <note>A 13th-century Florentine poet and friend of Dante</note>, the philosopher, seems to have woven all these things most skillfully into his poems. Just as a mirror, struck in a certain way by a ray of the sun, shines again and, by that reflection of splendor, inflames a piece of wool placed near it; so he considers that part of the soul which he calls the **dark fantasy** <note>The "phantasia" or imagination, which in medieval psychology was the faculty that processed sensory images</note> and memory to be struck like a mirror by the image of beauty itself (which holds the place of the sun) as if by a ray drawn through the eyes. He believes it is struck in such a way that it fashions for itself from that first image another likeness, as if it were the splendor of the first image; by this, the power of desire is ignited and loves, not otherwise than the wool is set on fire. 

He adds that love is first created here, ignited in the sensory appetite by a bodily form seen through the eyes. But he notes that this very form is not imprinted on the imagination in the same way it exists in the matter of the body, but rather without matter—yet in such a way that it remains the image of a specific person located in a certain place and time. Again, a certain species of this image immediately shines in the mind, which no longer appears to be the likeness of one specific human body as it was in the imagination, but rather the common reason and definition of the entire human race. 

Therefore, just as from the image in the imagination taken from the body, a love inclined toward the senses arises in the appetite devoted to the body; so from this mental species and common reason—as if most remote from the body—another love is born in the will, most foreign to any commerce with the body. He placed the former in pleasure, and the latter in contemplation. He thinks the former is held by the particular form of one body, while the latter is concerned with the universal beauty of the whole human race. These two loves struggle against each other within a person: the former drives one downward toward a beast-like and voluptuous life, while the latter raises one upward toward the angelic and contemplative life. He wishes the latter to be without disturbance and found in few people; the former he sees as anxious with many passions and occupying the majority of men. Therefore, he dispatches the former in few words, being more lengthy in describing the passions of the other. 

Since he explains here most clearly the same things that you have narrated in the previous sections, I did not think it necessary to review them at present. But let it suffice to have known that this philosopher mixed in a certain "chaos of formlessness" (such as you posited above) in the procreation of love, when he said the dark fantasy is illuminated; and that from the mixture of that darkness and this light, love takes its origin. Furthermore, who would not see in his words that twin love, the heavenly and the common? He even places its first origin in the beauty of divine things, and its second in the beauty of bodies. For by the "Sun," he understands the light of God; by the "Ray," the form of bodies. Finally, he wants its end to correspond to its principles: while the instigation of love carries some as far as the form of the body, it carries others as far as the species of love itself.

### Socrates was a true lover, and like unto Cupid. Chapter II.

So much for love. Let us come to Alcibiades and Socrates. After the guests had sufficiently praised the God of lovers, it remained for the legitimate worshippers of this god to be praised. Socrates is held by all to have loved most legitimately of all. Although throughout his entire life he had campaigned openly and without any dissimulation in the camps of Cupid, he was never marked by anyone as having loved anyone in a less than honorable way. The severity of his life and his frequent correction of others' vices had made many great men hostile to him (as truth usually does)—especially Anytus, Meletus, and Lycon, most powerful citizens in the republic. He also had the orators Thrasymachus, Polus, and Callicles, and moreover the comic poet Aristophanes, as sharp persecutors. 

But neither did those citizens include "dishonorable loves" in the accusation by which they dragged Socrates to judgment; nor did his enemies the orators object to any such thing; nor did Aristophanes the Comic poet, although he collected many other absurd insults against Socrates during the Dionysia <note>The Great Dionysia, the Athenian dramatic festival</note>. Do you think that if he had stained himself with such a foul blot—indeed, unless he had been most remote from the suspicion of this crime—he would have escaped the poisonous tongues of such detractors? 

Did you not notice, best of men, in the previous sections, that while Plato fashions Love himself, he paints the entire likeness of Socrates? He describes the figure of that deity from the person of Socrates, as if true love and Socrates are most similar, and therefore he, before all others, is the true and legitimate lover. Come now, recall that picture of Love to your mind. You will see Socrates figured in it. Place the person of Socrates before your eyes. You will see a man lean, parched, and squalid; a man, as it happens, naturally melancholic and hairy. Thinned by fasting. Dirty from neglect. Furthermore, naked—that is, covered by a simple and old little cloak. Walking without shoes. Phaedrus shows in Plato that Socrates was always accustomed to walk thus. Flying very low to the ground. Socrates' gaze was always fixed on the ground, as Phaedo says. Moreover, he frequented lowly places: for he was found either in the shop of Simon the cobbler or in the workshops of sculptors. He used rustic and unpolished words, which Callicles reproaches him for in the *Gorgias*. He was, moreover, so wonderfully patient that although provoked by many injuries and often even struck, he is said not to have been moved in spirit. Without a home. When Socrates was asked from where he came, he said, "A citizen of the world." For there is one's fatherland, wherever there is good. But he had neither his own hearth, nor...

# COMMENTARY

no soft bed, nor delicate food, nor precious furniture. He would sleep at the doors in the street under the open sky. These things signify the open breast and the heart lying open to all in our Socrates. Furthermore, he was delighted by sight and hearing, which are the doors of the soul; he also walked about secure and intrepid, and would lie down anywhere wrapped in his cloak if necessary. Always needy. Who does not know that Socrates was the son of a sculptor and a midwife <note>His father was Sophroniscus and his mother Phaenarete</note>, and that even into old age he sought his living by carving stones with his own hand, and did not have the means to sufficiently feed himself and his sons? He everywhere confessed the poverty of his mind, questioning everyone and proclaiming that he knew nothing. For he was manly, of a constant soul, and of invincible opinion, so that he even looked down upon Archelaus of Macedon, Scopas of Cranon, and Eurylochus of Larissa with a high mind; for he did not accept the money sent by them, nor did he wish to travel to them. Bold and fierce. How great his fortitude was in military matters, Alcibiades explains most fully in the banquet; to whom Socrates, when he had conquered at Potidaea, says he voluntarily conceded the victory. He was vehement, for as the physiognomist Zopyrus <note>Original: "Topirus," likely a typo for Zopyrus, who famously judged Socrates' character by his face</note> had rightly judged, he was most excitable. Indeed, during a speech, driven by the vehemence of his oration, he was often accustomed to toss his fingers and pluck at his hair. Eloquent. Arguments for either side were supplied to him almost equally while he discussed. Although he used unpolished words, as Alcibiades says in the banquet, he nevertheless moved the minds of his listeners more than Themistocles, Pericles, and all other orators. He lays snares for the beautiful and the good. Alcibiades says that Socrates was always laying snares for him. For being captured by the love of those who seemed endowed with a noble disposition, Socrates captured them in turn by his reasoning for the study of philosophy. A cunning and sagacious hunter. It has been sufficiently said above that Socrates was accustomed to hunt for the divine beauty from the form of the body; and Plato testifies to this in the *Protagoras*. A deviser. In many ways, as Plato's dialogues indicate, he refuted the sophists, exhorted the youth, and instructed modest men. Zealous for prudence. For he was of such great prudence, and so clear-sighted in foreseeing, that whoever dared anything against his counsel was ruined; which is narrated by Plato in the *Theages*. Philosophizing through his whole life. In that defense of his before the judges, he declared to the judges that if they should acquit him of death on the condition that he never philosophize thereafter, he would prefer to die than to cease philosophizing. An enchanter, a fascinator, a sorcerer, and a sophist. For Alcibiades says he is soothed more by Socratic words than by the melody of Marsyas, Olympus, and excellent musicians. That a *daemon* <note>A guiding spirit or inner voice</note> was familiar to him, both his accusers and his friends testify. The comic poet Aristophanes also called Socrates a sophist, as did his accusers. Indeed, he had an equal faculty for exhorting and dehorting. A middle point between wisdom and ignorance. Since all men are ignorant, Socrates says, "I differ from the rest only in this: that I am not ignorant of my ignorance, while others are utterly ignorant." Thus he was a middle point between wisdom and ignorance; because although he did not know the things themselves, he nevertheless recognized his own ignorance. For these reasons, Alcibiades judged Socrates to be most like Love, and therefore a most true lover to be praised after Love itself, so that in his praise we may understand that all who love in a similar way are praised. What the praises of Socrates are, you have heard here, and they lie open most clearly in Plato's words through the mouth of Alcibiades; in what manner Socrates loved can be known if one remembers the teaching of Diotima. For Socrates loved just as Diotima taught above.

->On bestial love, which is a species of insanity. Chapter III.<-

But perhaps someone may ask: what does that Socratic love benefit the human race? Why should it be celebrated with such great praises, and what harm does the contrary cause? I shall speak, having begun somewhat more deeply. Our Plato defines "fury" <note>Original: *furor*, meaning a divine or manic inspiration</note> in the *Phaedrus* as an alienation of the mind. He teaches that there are two kinds of alienation. One he considers to proceed from human diseases, the other from God. The former he calls "insanity," the latter "divine fury." By the disease of insanity, a man is cast down below the species of man, and from a man is made in a certain way a brute. There are two kinds of insanity. One is born from a defect of the brain, the other from a defect of the heart. The brain is often occupied by burnt bile, often by burnt blood, and sometimes by too much black bile <note>Melancholy</note>; hence men are sometimes rendered demented. Those who are vexed by burnt bile are most vehemently angered even when provoked by no one; they shout loudly, rush at those in their way, and strike themselves and others. Those who suffer from burnt blood break out into excessive laughter; they boast beyond all custom, promise wonderful things about themselves, delight in song, and exult in dancing. Those who are pressed by black bile mourn perpetually; they fashion dreams for themselves, which they either dread in the present or fear in the future. And these three species of insanity happen by a defect of the brain. For when those humors are retained in the heart, they produce anguish and anxiety, not dementia; but they truly produce madness when they have oppressed the head. Therefore they are said to happen by a defect of the brain. However, we think that insanity is properly caused by a disease of the heart in those who are afflicted by desperate love. To these, the most sacred name of "love" is falsely attributed. But lest we seem perhaps to be too wise against the many, for the sake of disputation let us also use the name for them.

->Vulgar love is a certain fascination. Chapter IV.<-

Apply your ears and mind to the intention of my words. Blood in youth is subtle and clear, hot and sweet. As age proceeds, the more subtle parts being resolved, it becomes thicker; therefore it also becomes darker. Surely that which is thin and rare is pure and lucid; the contrary is the opposite. Why hot and sweet? Because life, and the beginning of living—namely generation itself—consists in heat and moisture, and the seed is the primary offspring of living things...

# ON THE BANQUET
### FOLIO CLXVII.

The nature of the blood is hot and moist; such a nature flourishes in childhood and youth. In the following ages, it necessarily changes little by little into the opposite qualities of dryness and coldness. Therefore, the blood in a young person is subtle, clear, hot, and sweet: it is subtle and clear because it is fresh; it is hot and moist, and because it is hot and moist, it appears to be sweet. For sweetness arises from the mixture of the hot and the moist. You should certainly understand from these things that the spirits in this age are subtle, clear, hot, and sweet. Since these are generated from the heat of the heart out of the purest blood, they are always such within us as the humor of the blood itself is. Just as the vapor of the spirits is created from the blood in this way, so too it emits rays similar to itself through the eyes as if through glass windows. And just as the sun, the heart of the world, sends down its light through its circuit, and through that light its virtues to lower things, so the heart of our body, by its own perpetual motion agitating the blood nearest to it, diffuses spirits from it into the whole body, and through those spirits, it scatters sparks of light through the limbs, but most especially through the eyes. The spirit, being very light, flies up to the highest parts of the body; and its light flashes forth more abundantly through the eyes, which are themselves transparent and the brightest of all parts. That there is indeed some light in the eyes and the brain, though small, many animals that see at night can serve as testimony, for their eyes gleam in the darkness. And also, if anyone presses the corner of the eye with a finger in a certain way and twists it, they see a certain brighter circle looking back within themselves. It is said that the Divine Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor, known for his striking gaze.</note> had eyes so clear and bright that when he looked quite sharply, he forced the other person to lower their face as if before the glare of the sun. It is also recorded that Tiberius had eyes of an extraordinary size, and what was marvelous, they could see at night and in the dark: but only for a short time, and only when they first awoke from sleep; thereafter they grew dim again.

Because the ray emitted from the eyes draws a spiritual vapor with it, and that vapor draws blood, we perceive this from the fact that those with bleary and red eyes, by the emission of their own ray, compel nearby eyes to suffer a similar disease. Here it appears both that the ray extends as far as the person it meets, and that together with the ray, a vapor of corrupted blood flows out, by whose contagion the spectator is infected. Aristotle writes that when women undergo their menstrual flow, they often foul a mirror with drops of blood by their gaze. I think this happens because the spirit, which is the vapor of the blood, appears to be a certain very thin blood, so much so that it escapes the sight of the eyes; but having become thicker on the surface of the mirror, it is clearly perceived. If this falls upon some more porous material—such as cloth or wood—it is not seen because it does not remain on the surface of that thing but penetrates it. If it falls on something dense but rough, such as stones, bricks, and the like, it is dissipated and broken by the inequality of that body. But a mirror, on account of its hardness, stops the spirit on the surface; on account of its equality and smoothness, it keeps it unbroken; on account of its brightness, it aids and increases the ray of the spirit itself; and on account of its coldness, it condenses that very thin mist into droplets. By almost the same reasoning, whenever we breathe hard with open mouths onto glass, we sprinkle its face with a certain very thin dew of saliva; for the breath flying out from the saliva, being compressed in that material, falls back into saliva.

Therefore, what wonder is it if the eye, opened and intent upon someone, hurls the stings of its rays into the eyes of the bystander? And also with those stings, which are the vehicles of the spirits, it aims that bloody vapor which we call "spirit." From this, the poisonous sting pierces through the eyes; and since it is sent from the heart of the striker, it seeks the vitals of the person struck as if seeking its own proper region; it wounds the heart, and in the harder back of the heart it grows blunt and returns into blood. This foreign blood, being somewhat alien to the nature of the person it has reached, infects their own blood; the infected blood becomes sick. From this follows a double fascination <note>In this context, "fascination" refers to a physical or magical binding or infection through the gaze.</note>. The gaze of a foul old man or a menstruating woman fascinates a child. The gaze of a youth fascinates an elder. But because the humor of the elder is cold and very slow, it hardly reaches the back of the heart in the child; and being unfit for passage, it moves the heart very little unless it be very soft due to infancy. This is therefore a light fascination; but that other is most grave, through which the younger pierces the vitals of the elder. This is that thing, best of friends, about which the Platonist Apuleius <note>Author of 'The Golden Ass'; here cited for his poetic descriptions of love's physical impact.</note> complains: "The cause," he says, "and the origin of this present pain, and even the remedy itself and my only salvation, is you yourself. For those eyes of yours, having slipped through my eyes to my innermost vitals, stir up a most sharp fire in my marrow. Therefore, have pity on one perishing for your sake."

Place before your eyes, I pray, Phaedrus of Myrrhinus and that Theban orator Lysias, captured by love for him. Lysias gapes at the face of Phaedrus; Phaedrus fixes the sparks of his own eyes into the eyes of Lysias, and together with the sparks, he transmits spirit as well. The ray of Phaedrus is easily coupled with the ray of Lysias; spirit is also easily joined to spirit. A vapor of this kind, generated from the heart of Phaedrus, immediately seeks the vitals of Lysias; by their dullness, it becomes more compact and falls back into the former blood of Phaedrus: so that, marvelously, the blood of Phaedrus is now in the heart of Lysias. From this, both immediately break out into a cry: Lysias to Phaedrus, "My heart, Phaedrus, my dearest vitals!" Phaedrus to Lysias, "O my spirit, O my blood, Lysias!" Phaedrus follows Lysias because his heart demands its humor. Lysias pursues Phaedrus because the bloody humor demands its proper vessel and requires its own seat. But Lysias pursues Phaedrus more ardently. For a heart lives more easily without a tiny particle of its humor than the humor itself lives without its own heart. The stream needs the spring more than the spring needs the stream. Therefore, just as iron, having received the quality of a magnet, is drawn to this stone, but does not attract the stone; so Lysias follows Phaedrus more than Phaedrus follows Lysias.

# COMMENTARY ON THE SYMPOSIUM
<meta>Catchword: so</meta>

### How we are easily ensnared by love. Chapter V.

Can it be, someone might ask, that a thin ray, a most light spirit, or a tiny bit of blood from Phædrus could so quickly, so vehemently, and so dangerously infect the whole of Lysias? This will certainly not seem strange if you consider other diseases that are born from contagion, such as the itch, the scab, leprosy, pleurisy, consumption, dysentery, bleary-eyedness <note>original: "lippitudinem" - an inflammatory eye condition</note>, or the plague. Indeed, the contagion of love happens easily and turns out to be the most serious pestilence of all. For that spiritual vapor and blood, cast from the youth directly into the elder, has four qualities as we said above. It is clear, subtle, hot, and sweet. Because it is clear, it matches the clarity of the eyes and spirits in the elder most perfectly; it soothes and allures, which causes it to be greedily drunk in by them. Because it is subtle, it flies very swiftly into the heart; from there it flows most easily through the veins and arteries into the entire body. Because it is hot, it acts vehemently and moves, and more strongly infects the blood of the elder, converting it into its own nature. Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus, Roman poet and philosopher</note> touched upon this thus:
->From here, first into you, the drop of Venus's sweetness<-
->Dripped into the heart: and cold care followed.<-
Furthermore, because it is sweet, it nourishes the internal organs in a certain way, feeds them, and delights them. Hence it happens that the man's entire blood, changed into the nature of the youth's blood, desires the body of that younger one, so that it may inhabit its own veins, and so that the moisture of the fresh blood may glide into veins that are also fresh and tender. It also happens that this sick person is touched by pleasure and pain at the same time. By pleasure because of the clarity and sweetness of that vapor and blood; for the former allures, and the latter delights. By pain because of its subtlety and heat; for the former divides and tears the organs, while the latter takes away from a man what is his own and changes it into the nature of another. Through this very change, it does not allow him to rest within himself, but always draws him toward the one by whom he was infected. Lucretius suggests this as follows:
->And the mind seeks that body from which it is wounded by love.<-
->The blood springs forth toward the part from where we are struck by the blow.<-
->For almost all fall toward the wound: and that<-
->Red moisture occupies the enemy, if he is at hand.<-
In these verses, Lucretius means nothing other than that the blood of a man wounded by the ray of the eyes flows toward the one who wounded him, just as the blood of a man struck by a sword flows toward the one striking him. If you seek the reason for this miracle, so to speak, I shall provide it. Hector wounds Patroclus and presses him. Patroclus looks upon the wounded Hector. From this, his thought judges that he must be avenged; immediately bile is kindled for vengeance, the blood is inflamed by it, and it hastens to the wound on the spot, both to nourish that part of the body and also for revenge. The spirits <note>term: "spiritus" - in Renaissance medicine, these were thin vapors that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the soul</note> also run to the same place; since they are light, flying all the way to Hector, they migrate into him. They are kept warm by his heat for a time, say for seven hours; in that very time, if Hector should look closely into the wound of the corpse, the wound ejects gore toward Hector. For the gore can flow out toward the enemy in a certain way, both because all the heat is not yet extinguished and the internal agitation has not yet ceased, and because a little while before it had been stirred up against him, and finally because the blood seeks its own spirits, and the spirits also attract their own blood. In a similar way, Lucretius perceived that the blood of a man wounded by love hastens toward the one who struck him, and we strongly approve of this.

### Concerning a certain miraculous effect of common love. Chapter VI.

Shall I say, most chaste men, what follows, or rather pass it over? I shall certainly say it, since the matter requires it, even if it seems absurd to say. But who would speak of shameful things in a shameful way? So great a change of the older man, urging him toward the likeness of the younger, makes him strive to transfer his whole body into the other and to pour the other's whole body into himself, so that either the fresh moisture may follow the fresh vessels, or the more tender vessels may follow the more tender moisture. Hence they are compelled to do many most shameful things among themselves. For since the genital seed flows from the whole body, they trust that by the casting or drawing of this alone they can give over their whole body and receive the whole. Lucretius, that Epicurean philosopher and most unhappy of all lovers, sensed this in himself:
->So therefore, he who receives the blows from the weapons of Venus,<-
->And they press mouth to mouth, breathing into each other with their teeth.<-
->Whether a boy hurls this at female limbs<-
->In vain: since they can scrape nothing away from there:<-
->Or a woman, casting love from her whole body,<-
->Neither can she penetrate and pass into the body with her whole body.<-
->Where one is struck, there he tends and longs to join:<-
->For they seem sometimes to want to do and to struggle,<-
->And to cast the moisture drawn from the body into the body.<-
->To such an extent do they cling greedily to the joints of Venus,<-
->They fix the body eagerly and join their salivas<-
->While the limbs of pleasure, overcome by force, melt away.<-
Thus says Lucretius the Epicurean. That lovers also desire to take the beloved entirely into themselves is shown by Artemisia, the wife of King Mausolus of Caria; she is said to have loved her husband beyond the belief of human affection, and to have reduced the body of her deceased husband to powder, put it in water, and drunk it.

### Common love is a disturbance of the blood. Chapter VII.

That this passion is indeed in the blood is proven by the fact that this kind of heat lacks any alternating rest. A continuous fever is placed by physicians in the blood; one that leaves six hours for rest is in the phlegm; one that rests for one day is in the bile; one that rests for two is in the humor of black bile. Therefore, we rightly place this in the blood. In the melancholic blood, to be sure, as you heard in the speech of Socrates. A constant attachment to this contagion of the blood always accompanies it.

### How lovers become like the beloved. Chapter VIII.

Let none of you wonder if he hears that some lover has contracted some likeness or shape of his beloved in his own body. Pregnant women often think intensely about the wine they most greedily desire; intense thought moves the internal spirits, and in these, it depicts the image of the thing thought of. These so...

...they move the blood in a similar way: and they express the image of the wine in the very soft matter of the fetus <note>A reference to the belief that a mother's cravings or sights could mark an unborn child</note>. But a lover desires his delights more ardently than pregnant women; he thinks more vehemently and firmly. What wonder is it then if the faces, so clinging and fixed in the breast, are purified from thought itself into the spirit: and from the spirit are immediately marked into the blood: especially since in the veins of Lysias the very soft blood of Phaedrus has already been fathered, so that the face of Phaedrus can most easily shine back in the receptive blood. Since indeed the individual members of the body, just as they dry up every day, so they grow green again daily by taking in the dew of nourishment: it follows that day by day the body of every man, which has gradually dried out, is little by little restored. Moreover, the members are restored by the blood flowing out from the small streams of the veins. Therefore, will you marvel if the blood, painted with a certain likeness, has impressed that same likeness upon the members: so that Lysias finally seems to have turned out similar to Phaedrus in several colors, or features, or dispositions, or gestures?

### By whom we are chiefly ensnared. Chapter IX.

Someone will perhaps ask: by whom chiefly and in what manner are we ensnared, and how are lovers released. Women certainly capture men easily: but those women more easily who display a certain masculine nature: and males capture all the more easily as they are more similar to men than to women: and they have blood and spirit that is clearer, warmer, and thinner: in which the ensnarement of love consists. Among males, moreover, those fascinate men or women most swiftly who are primarily of a sanguine <note>The "sanguine" temperament was thought to be cheerful and ruddy, dominated by blood</note> and partly of a choleric <note>The "choleric" temperament was thought to be ambitious and hot-tempered, dominated by yellow bile</note> nature, having large eyes, bluish-gray and shining: especially indeed if they live chastely, and have not defiled their serene faces by exhausting the clear juice of their humors through sexual intercourse. For these things are required for the proper emitting of those very arrows which wound the heart, as we touched upon above. Furthermore, those are quickly ensnared at whose birth Venus was in Leo, or the Moon looked upon Venus vehemently, and those who are endowed with the same complexion <note>In this context, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>. Phlegmatic people, in whom phlegm dominates, are never captured: Melancholic people, in whom black bile dominates, are captured only with difficulty: but once captured, they are never afterwards released. When a sanguine person binds a sanguine person, it is a light yoke, a sweet bond, for a similar complexion creates mutual love. Furthermore, the sweetness of this humor provides hope and confidence to the lover. When a choleric person binds a choleric person, the servitude is more intolerable. The similarity of complexion does indeed create some exchange of goodwill in these, but that fiery humor of bile disturbs them with frequent anger. When a sanguine person binds a choleric person, or vice versa, because of the mixture of sweet and sharp humor, a certain alteration arises between anger and grace, pleasure and pain. When a sanguine person binds a melancholic, the knot is perpetual but not most miserable. Indeed, the sweetness of the blood tempers the bitterness of the melancholy. But when a choleric person ensnares a melancholic, it is the most ruinous plague of all. The very sharp humor of the youth glides everywhere into the internal organs of the elder. A soft flame eats the marrow. The unhappy lover is burned. Cholera <note>Yellow bile</note> provokes to anger and slaughter. Melancholy leads to sorrow and perpetual lamentation. For these, the end of love is often the same as it was for Phyllis, Dido, and Lucretius <note>Historical and mythological figures who died of broken hearts or by suicide due to love</note>. But a phlegmatic or melancholic youth, on account of the thickness of his blood and spirits, captures no one.

### The manner of ensnarement. Chapter X.

We seem to have said enough above about the way in which lovers fascinate, if I only add this: that mortals are then most greatly fascinated when, directing the sharp edge of their sight to the sharp edge of another's in a very frequent gaze, they join lights to lights, and the wretched ones drink in a long love. Of this disease, as it pleases Musaeus <note>A legendary Greek poet</note>, the whole cause and origin is the eye. Therefore, if anyone excels in the brightness of the eyes, even if he is less well-composed in his other members, he more often compels those looking at him to go mad by that reasoning which we have stated. He who is disposed to the contrary invites a certain moderate goodwill rather than ardor. The harmony of the other members besides the eyes seems to have the force not of a cause for this kind of sickness, but of an impulsive occasion. For such a composition urges the one looking from afar to approach nearer: then it detains the one looking closely for a very long time in the consideration of itself: but the gaze alone strikes the one who lingers. But for that moderate love, the participant in divinity, about which we mostly dispute in this banquet: not the eye alone as a cause, but the concord and pleasantness of all the parts concur.

### The cure of love. Chapter XI.

Thus far we have treated how and by whom we are ensnared: it remains that we teach in a few words how we are released. The release is twofold: one indeed of nature, the other of diligence. The natural one is that which is completed at certain intervals of time. This pertains not only to this but to all diseases. Indeed, an itch remains on the skin only so long as the dregs of raging blood or the saltiness of phlegm flourishes in the members. When the blood is purified and the phlegm softened, the itch stops: and the foul spots of the skin are abolished. Nevertheless, the timely diligence of evacuation <note>Medical purging or bloodletting</note> contributes much. Sudden evacuation or anointing is judged most dangerous. The restlessness of lovers also necessarily perseveres so long as that infection of the blood, cast into the vitals through fascination, remains and burdens the body with heavy care. The wound feeds in the veins: it burns the members with hidden flames. For the transition is from the heart into the veins: from the veins into the members. Finally, when this is purged, the restlessness of lovers—or rather, of the mad—ceases. This requires a long space of time in all: but in the melancholic, the longest: especially if they were ensnared by the influence of Saturn. Add also the most bitter: if they are subject to Saturn in retrograde, or joined to Mars, or opposite to the Sun. Those also suffer for a very long time in whose nativity Venus was in the house of Saturn, or she looked vehemently upon Saturn and the Moon. To this natural purgation must be added the industry of the most diligent art. Care must be taken in the first place lest...

FOL. LXVIII.

...we should not attempt to pluck out or cut away immature things, nor should we tear them apart with the greatest danger; those things which we can more safely set aside require a cessation of habit. One must take the greatest care, however, that the eyes do not meet the eyes of the beloved <note>Ficino believed love was a physical contagion passed through the "spirit" via the eyes</note>. If there is any vice in the mind or body of the beloved, it must be diligently revolved in the mind. The mind should be applied to many, various, and serious affairs; blood must often be let, clear wine should be used, and sometimes even drunkenness, so that when the old blood is emptied, new blood may come, and a new spirit. It is better to use exercise often, even unto sweat, through which the passages of the body are opened for performing a purging. Furthermore, all those things which physicians apply for the protection against pain and the nourishment of the brain are of the greatest benefit. Lucretius also often prescribes sexual union <note>original: "coëtũ"</note>:
*But it is fitting to flee the images and scare away the food of love from oneself, and to turn the mind elsewhere, and to cast the gathered fluid into any body at hand, and not to retain the seed by being turned toward a single love.*

### That vulgar love is harmful. Chapter XII.

But lest we ourselves become insane by speaking too long of insanity, let us conclude briefly thus. That anxious solicitude by which vulgar lovers are vexed day and night is a certain species of insanity; while their love lasts, they are afflicted first by the burning of yellow bile, and then by the scorching of black bile <note>term: black bile (melancholy). In medieval medicine, excessive "burning" of humors led to madness</note>, and they rush into furies and fire; and like blind men, they know not where they are being precipitated. How ruinous this adulterous love is to both the beloved and the lovers, Lysias the Theban and Socrates demonstrate in Plato's *Phaedrus*. By this fury, therefore, man is cast down into the nature of a beast.

### That divine love is useful: and concerning its four species. Chapter XIII.

By divine fury, however, man is raised above his own nature and passes into God. Divine fury is an illumination of the rational soul, through which God draws back the soul—which has fallen from the upper regions to the lower—from the lower regions to the upper. The fall of the soul from the very One, the principle of all things, into bodies, is effected through four steps: through Mind, Reason, Opinion, and Nature. For since in the whole order of things there exist six steps—of which the highest is the One itself and the lowest is the body, while the middle four are those we have just mentioned—it is necessary that whatever falls from the first to the last must fall through the four intermediaries. The One itself is the limit and measure of all things, devoid of confusion and multiplicity. The Angelic Mind is indeed a multiplicity of Ideas, but stable and eternal. The Reason of the soul is a mobile multiplicity of notions and arguments, but ordered. Opinion, however, is a disordered and mobile multiplicity of images, yet united in substance and point, since the soul itself in which opinion resides is a single substance occupying no place. Nature—that is, the power of nourishing from the soul and the animal complexion likewise—except that it is diffused through the points of the body. The Body, however, is an indeterminate multiplicity of parts and accidents subject to motion, and a substance divided by points and moments. Our soul regards all these; through these it descends, and through these it also ascends. For as it is produced from the One itself, which is the principle of all, it has obtained a certain unity which unites its entire essence, powers, and operations; from which and toward which the other things in the soul are related, just as lines are related from and to the center of a circle. It unites not only the parts of the soul to each other and to the whole soul, but the whole soul to the One itself, the cause of all things. As it shines by the ray of the divine mind, it contemplates the Ideas of all things through the Mind in a stable act. As it regards itself, it thinks the universal reasons of things and discourses from principles to conclusions by reasoning. As it regards bodies, it revolves in Opinion the particular forms and images of mobile things received through the senses. As it touches matter, it uses Nature as an instrument by which it unites, moves, and forms matter. From this proceed generations, growth, and their opposites. You see, therefore, how from the One, which is above eternity, the soul falls into eternal multiplicity; from eternity into time; from time into place and matter. It falls, I say, when it departs further from that purity in which it was born by embracing the body.

### By which steps the divine furies extol the soul. Chapter XIIII.

Just as it descended through four steps, it must necessarily ascend through four. It is divine fury which lifts it to the upper regions, as established in its definition. There are, therefore, four species of divine fury. The first is the poetic fury. The second is the mystery-rite. The third is prophecy. The fourth is the lover's affection. Poetry is from the Muses, Mystery from Dionysus, Prophecy from Apollo, and Love from Venus. Indeed, the soul cannot return to the One unless it itself is made one. But it has been made many, because it has fallen into the body, distributed into various operations, and looks toward an infinite multiplicity of corporal things. From this, its higher parts almost fall asleep, while the lower parts dominate the others. The former are affected by torpor, the latter by perturbation. The whole soul is filled with discord and lack of harmony. Therefore, there is first a need for poetic fury, which through musical tones arouses what is torpid; through harmonic sweetness soothes what is disturbed; and finally, through the consonance of diverse things, drives out dissonant discord and tempers the various parts of the soul. Nor is this enough. For multiplicity and diversity still remain in the soul. Therefore, the mystery-rite pertaining to Dionysus approaches, which through expiations, sacrifices, and all divine worship, directs the intention of all parts toward the Mind, by which God is worshipped. Whence, since the individual parts of the soul have been reduced to one Mind, the soul has now become a certain whole "one" out of many. Yet there is still need for a third fury, which leads the Mind back to the unity itself, the head of the soul. This Apollo performs through...
