<meta>This page continues the discussion of the four divine madnesses (furores) as described by Plato, specifically focusing on how they elevate the soul toward unity and God. It transitions into a defense of "Socratic Love" as a tool for moral education.</meta>

# ON THE BANQUET.

...produces prophecy. For when the soul rises above the mind into unity, it foretells future things. Finally, when the soul has become one—one, I say, which is in its very nature and essence—it remains for it to immediately recall itself into the One which is above essence, that is, God. This the celestial Venus <note>In Platonic thought, the "Celestial Venus" represents the drive toward divine, intellectual beauty rather than physical lust.</note> fulfills through love, that is, the desire for divine beauty and the ardor for the Good. Therefore, the first madness <note>Poetic madness</note> tempers what is unharmonious and dissonant. The second <note>Mystery/Religious madness</note> makes a single whole out of the tempered parts. The third <note>Prophetic madness</note> leads to a single whole above the parts. The fourth <note>Amorous madness/Love</note> leads into the One which is above essence and above the whole. 

Plato, in the *Phaedrus*, calls the mind devoted to divine things the "charioteer" in the soul of man. He calls the unity of the soul the "head of the charioteer." Reason and opinion running through natural things he calls the "good horse." Confused imagination and the appetite of the senses he calls the "bad horse." The nature of the whole soul he calls the "chariot," because its motion is, as it were, circular, beginning from itself and finally returning to itself when it observes its own nature—where its consideration, having proceeded from the soul, returns to the same. He attributes wings to the soul through which it may be carried into the sublime. One of these we think to be that investigation by which the mind constantly strives toward truth; the other is the desire for the good, by which our will is always affected. 

These parts of the soul lose their order when they are confused by the disturbance of the body. Therefore, the first madness distinguishes the good horse (that is, reason and opinion) from the bad horse (that is, from confused imagination and the appetite of the senses). The second subjects the bad horse to the good, and the good to the Charioteer (that is, the mind). The third directs the charioteer toward his own head (that is, toward the unity of the mind's peak). The last turns the head of the charioteer toward the Head of all things. There the charioteer is blessed, and standing the horses at the manger (that is, accommodating all the parts of the soul subject to him to divine beauty), he offers them ambrosia and above that nectar to drink—that is, the vision of beauty, and joy from that vision. These are the works of the four madnesses. He disputes concerning them generally in the *Phaedrus*, but specifically concerning poetic madness in the *Ion*, and concerning amorous madness in the *Banquet* <note>The *Symposium*</note>. That Orpheus was occupied by all these madnesses can be evidenced by his books. We have heard that Sappho, Anacreon, and Socrates were especially seized by the amorous madness.

### Love is more excellent than all these madnesses. Chapter XV.

The amorous madness is the most powerful and excellent of all. Most powerful, I say, because all others necessarily stand in need of it. For we do not attain poetry, nor mysteries, nor prophecy without great zeal, flaming piety, and diligent worship of divinity. And what else do we call zeal, piety, and worship but love? Therefore, all consist by the power of love. It is also the most excellent, because the others are referred to this as to an end. This, moreover, joins us most closely to God. 

Indeed, four counterfeit affections seem falsely to imitate these four madnesses. That vulgar music which only flatters the ears imitates the poetic. The vain superstition of many men imitates the mystery-madness. The deceptive conjecture of human skill imitates the prophetic. The impulse of lust imitates the amorous. For true love is nothing other than a certain effort to fly away toward divine beauty, excited by the sight of bodily beauty. But counterfeit love is a headlong fall from sight into touch.

### How useful Socratic love is. Chapter XVI.

Do you ask what Socratic love contributes? First, indeed, to Socrates himself it contributes much toward recovering those wings by which he may fly back to his fatherland. Then, to his city, it contributes greatly toward living honorably and happily. Truly, men, not stones, make a city. Men, however, must be cared for from a tender age just as trees are, and directed toward the best fruit. Parents and tutors have the care of boys. But adolescents do not cross the boundaries of parents and tutors before they are corrupted by the wicked custom of the common people. They would surely follow the higher norm of living drunk in at home, unless they were turned aside from it by the use and custom of wicked men, especially those who flatter them. 

What then shall Socrates do? Will he permit youth, which is the seed of the future republic, to be corrupted by the contagion of the shameful? Where then is the love of country? Therefore, Socrates will succor his country and its sons, and deliver his brothers from ruin. Perhaps he will write laws by which he will segregate lustful men from the company of youth. But we cannot all be Lycurguses or Solons <note>Famous lawgivers of Sparta and Athens</note>. The authority for founding laws is given to few; very few obey the laws once they are passed. What then? Will he use force, and by laying on hands drive the elders away from the youth? But only Hercules is said to have fought with monsters; for others, violence of this kind is most dangerous. Perhaps he will warn, rebuke, and scold the wicked men. But a disturbed mind despises the words of a monitor, and what is worse, rages against the monitor. For this reason, Socrates was struck by one with a fist and by another with a heel while he attempted this. 

Only one way of safety remains for youth: the company of Socrates. Therefore, that wisest of the Greeks, overcome by charity, mixes himself everywhere: and he walks with a great crowd of adolescents accompanying him. Thus the true lover, like a shepherd of lambs, protects the flock from the abyss and plague of false lovers, who are like wolves. Since, however, like very easily gathers with like, he makes himself equal to the younger ones by the purity of his life, the simplicity of his words, games, jokes, and witticisms. He makes himself a boy out of an old man, primarily so that he may eventually make the boys "old" <note>i.e., wise and mature</note> through domestic and pleasant familiarity. Youth, prone to pleasure, is held by pleasure alone and flees rigid teachers. This tutor of our youth, having neglected the administration of his own affairs for the safety of his country, undertakes the care of the juniors, and first captures them with the sweetness of pleasant company. Thus having ensnared them, he then warns them more severely. Finally, he chastises them with a more rigid censure. In this way, he redeemed the youth Phaedo, who had been prostituted in a public brothel, from that calamity...

BOOK

and he cites the philosopher. Plato, who was devoted to poetry, he compelled to consign his tragedies to the flames and to take up more precious studies. Xenophon he led away from common luxury to the sober wisdom of the wise. Aeschines and Aristippus he turned from poor men into rich ones; Phaedrus from an orator into a philosopher; and Alcibiades from an ignorant man into one most learned. He made Charmides grave and modest, and Theages a just and brave citizen in the republic. Euthydemus and Menon he transferred from the quibbles of the sophists <note>Sophists were paid teachers in ancient Greece often criticized for using clever but fallacious arguments.</note> to true wisdom. Thus it happened that the company of Socrates was not so much pleasant as it was useful; and, as Alcibiades says, Socrates was loved by young men much more ardently than he himself loved.

### How thanks must be given to the Holy Spirit, who has illuminated and ignited us for this discussion. Chapter XVII.

<note>original: "Quomodo agendae sunt gratiae Spiritui sancto..." Ficino here blends Platonic philosophy with Christian theology, identifying the "divine madness" of love with the Holy Spirit.</note>

Now therefore, best guests, we seem to have happily discovered—first from your discussion and then from mine—what love is, who is a true lover, and what the utility of the lover may be. You should undoubtedly consider that the cause and master of this most happy discovery was that very same love which was discovered. For, ignited by the love of finding love (if I may put it that way), we sought love and found it; so that thanks must be given to him equally for the inquiry and the discovery. O wonderful magnificence of this divinity! O incomparable kindness of love! For while other divinities scarcely show themselves for a moment after you have sought them for a long time, Love even runs to meet those who are about to seek him. Therefore, men confess they owe themselves to him much more than to the others. There are those who often dare to curse the divine power, the thunderer against our crimes. Some even hate the wisdom that explores all our disgraces. But we cannot help but love Divine Love, the giver of all good things. We, however, shall worship this Love, who is so favorable to us, with the intention that we may venerate Wisdom and admire Power; so that with Love as our leader, we may have the whole of God (so to speak) favorable to us; and loving the whole with the fire of love, we may also enjoy the whole of God in perpetual love.

APOLLODORUS: I believe I am well-prepared regarding the things you ask. For yesterday, when I was returning home from Phalerum to the city, an acquaintance of mine saw me from behind and called out from a distance. While calling, he joked: "O Apollodorus of Phalerum, why don't you wait?" I waited. Then he said, "I was just looking for you, desiring to hear what speeches were held concerning love at that banquet where Agatho, Socrates, Alcibiades, and several others gathered." Indeed, someone else reported it to me, who had heard it from Phoenix, the son of Philip; and he added that you knew. But he could not bring any certainty to the matter. Therefore, you should tell me. For it is in your interest to narrate the speeches of your friend. But first tell me this: were you yourself present at that discussion, or not? "In truth," I said, "it seems he told you nothing certain if you think they met recently so that I could have been present." "I certainly thought so," he said. Then I: "From where did you hear or guess that? Don't you know, O Glaucon, that Agatho has not come here for many years? From the time I began to associate constantly with Socrates and to observe his words and deeds more diligently, not yet three years have passed. Before that, however, whenever I happened to be wandering about, thinking I was doing something, I was the most miserable of all men—just as you are now, who think anything else should be done rather than philosophizing." "Don't bite," he said, "but tell me at what time the banquet was celebrated." To this I said: "While we were still boys, Agatho won the victory in his first tragedy contest. On the following day after the prize, when the sacred rites for the victory had been celebrated and a banquet prepared, the discussion was instituted." GLAUCON: "That is certainly a long time ago. But who told you? Was it Socrates himself?" APOLLODORUS: "No, by Jove! Rather the same one who told Phoenix: a certain Aristodemus of Cydathenaeum, who was small of body and always went with bare feet. For he was present at the discussion, since he loved Socrates, it seems to me, most of all those who were there then. Moreover, I questioned Socrates himself about some of the things he had reported, and he agreed with him in the reporting." GLAUCON: "Why then do you not tell me? The road that leads to the city is certainly fit for both hearing and speaking." APOLLODORUS: "And so, while walking, we spoke of those things. Therefore, as I said from the beginning, I am well-prepared in these matters. If you want these things recounted to you again, I will recount them. For as often as I either have a conversation about philosophy myself or hear others speaking, besides thinking it benefits me, I rejoice wonderfully. you are always eager to amass money, and I am both distressed by this and pity you: because you think you are accomplishing something, when you are accomplishing nothing. Perhaps you also think me unhappy: and I believe you think the truth about me. I, however, do not merely think so regarding you, but I know it for certain. **FRIEND.** You are always disparaging yourself and others equally, Apollodorus: and you seem beyond doubt to think that you are the first among the unhappy, and then all others except for Socrates alone. Homer indeed seems not only not to observe, but even to violate the proverb. Whereby he made the inferior man come unsummoned to the table of the more excellent man. **ARISTODEMUS.** "Perhaps I too, O Socrates, am not such as you say, but as Homer depicted—a worthless little man coming of his own accord to the banquet of a wise man. Since you are leading me, see what reason you assign for my arrival. Having said these things, Aristodemus said, they began to go: and Socrates, being pensive, walked with a step far too slow; he waited often, until at last Socrates ordered him to go ahead. When he approached the house of Agathon, he found the door open, and something ridiculous happened there. For he said that on the very threshold a certain servant meeting him from within led him inside where the others were reclining. He found them already about to dine. As soon as Agathon saw him, he said: "O Aristodemus, you have come at an opportune time to dine with us. If you want anything else, defer it to another time. Indeed, I looked for you yesterday to invite you and saw you nowhere. But why do you not lead Socrates to us?" "I indeed," said Aristodemus, "having turned back, saw him nowhere: and I replied to Agathon, 'I certainly came with him, having been called here to dinner by him.'" **AGATHON.** "You have done rightly. But where is Socrates?" **ARISTODEMUS.** "He was coming just behind me a little while ago. Therefore I also wonder, and I do not know where he is." **AGATHON.** "Boy, seek Socrates and bring him in to us. You, Aristodemus, recline next to Eryximachus. Hey you, give water for his hands so that he may now sit." Then Aristodemus said a certain boy entered and announced: that Socrates himself had withdrawn into the nearest porch, and though summoned, he refused to enter. **AGATHON.** "You tell of something absurd. Call him again: and do not let him go until he comes." **ARISTODEMUS.** "Not so, O Agathon, but let him be. For that is a habit of Socrates. Sometimes he stops and is accustomed to stand still wherever it happens. He will come quickly, I think. Do not be disturbed by him, but permit him to come at his own discretion." **AGATHON.** "If it seems so to you, it must be done. For the rest, you boys, bring the feast to the others, and set out whatever pleases you. Since no one presides over you. I have never done that. Therefore, thinking now that I along with the others am received by you at a banquet, take care of everything diligently, so that we may approve of your work." After these things, Aristodemus added that they began to dine: and Socrates, though often called by Agathon’s order, did not enter until he had exercised himself for some time in his usual way, and he came in the middle of the dinner. To whom Agathon, who sat last and alone, spoke thus: "Here, Socrates, sit near me, so that by touching you I may enjoy that wise thought which you worked out in the porches. For it is certain that you found it and have it. Otherwise you would not have stood still so long." Socrates sat down and said: "Our affairs would be well, Agathon, if wisdom were such that it flowed from the fuller man into the empty one by contact itself: just as water flows from a full cup into an empty one through a piece of wool. For if wisdom is so, I value it greatly that I sit by you. For I think I am being filled by you with a most abundant and illustrious wisdom. Since mine is thin and ambiguous, like a certain dream: but yours is very bright and powerful: inasmuch as it shone and flashed so clearly in your youth yesterday in the sight of more than thirty thousand Greek men." <note>A reference to the audience at the theater where Agathon's play was performed.</note> **AGATHON.** "You are insulting, O Socrates. But we two shall judge these things about wisdom later, with Dionysus <note>The god of wine and theater</note> as judge. But now, dine." After these things, Aristodemus said, with Socrates and the others reclining together, they began to pour libations and taste the wines in the manner of those sacrificing, and to sing to the god, and doing other things as is the custom, they turned themselves to drinking. Whereupon Pausanias spoke thus: "It must be seen, O men, by what means we may drink more lightly and pleasantly. For to confess the truth about myself first, I feel myself still burdened by yesterday’s unmixed wine: and I need a certain intermission. I think also that most of you are similarly affected. For you were present yesterday. Consider therefore how we may drink more lightly and healthfully." To whom soon Aristo...

### Phaedrus’ Eulogy in Praise of Love.

Love is a great god, and wonderful among gods and men; both for many other reasons and especially for his origin. For since he is among the number of the most ancient gods, he appears worthy of honor. This is established by the fact that the parents of Love have been described by no poet or anyone else. But Hesiod asserts that in the beginning Chaos existed, in these words: *First Chaos came to be, then broad-bosomed Earth, the ever-firm seat of all, and Love.* Asserting, clearly, that after Chaos these two existed: Earth and Love. Parmenides, moreover, says of his generation: *First of all the gods, she devised Love.* Acusileus also seems to agree with Hesiod. And so it is widely conceded that Love is among the most ancient. Since he is such, he is the cause of the greatest goods for us. For I do not find what better thing could happen to a youth than a virtuous lover, or to a lover than a virtuous beloved. There are two things which, from boyhood, ought to lead him through his whole life who intends to live nobly: shame in base things, and devotion to honorable pursuits. Neither lineage, nor riches, nor honors can provide these to us more quickly or better than love. Without these two, neither a city nor a private citizen will ever be able to accomplish anything noble and magnificent. I assert indeed that a lover—if he were caught doing something base or suffering it from another through cowardice, whether by his father, or by friends, or by any other man—would not be so vehemently distressed as if he were caught by his beloved. Similarly, we see a youth blush most of all when a lover finds him committing something base. If by some means a city or an army could be made partly of those who love and partly of those who are loved, it would manage each thing more bravely than can be said, while through shame they would abstain from base things and strive for honorable ones in a kind of emulation. Such men, even if few in number, would conquer almost all men in battle, so to speak. A lover would surely blush more vehemently to desert his rank or throw away his arms in the presence of his beloved than before all other men. Indeed, he would often prefer to die than to abandon his beloved and not help him in dangers. Nor is anyone so cowardly...

# THE BANQUET, OR CONCERNING LOVE.
## y iii

whom love does not inflame and restore to divine virtue, so that he emerges as an equal to the bravest man. For indeed, what Homer says—that a force and fury is inspired by a god into certain heroes—this is what love effects in lovers. Furthermore, lovers alone choose to die for another; not only men, but even women. <margin>Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, died for her husband out of love.</margin> Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, provided a manifest testimony of this discourse to the Greeks: she alone chose to perish for her husband, even though both his father and mother were present. Because of love, she so surpassed them in affection that she showed them to be strangers and joined to their son in name only. This deed was judged so noble not only by men, but also by the gods, that while the gods have granted the gift of returning to life to only a very few and most pious among the many who performed great and distinguished deeds, they immediately raised her from the lower world, delighted by such an extraordinary act. So much do the gods value devotion and virtue regarding love. 

But they sent Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus, away from the lower world without granting his prayer. <margin>Orpheus, son of Oeagrus, is sharply criticized.</margin> For they did not restore the woman for whose sake he had descended, but showed him a phantom of her; since he did not dare to die for the sake of love as Alcestis did, but being a player of the lyre <note>Latin: citharœdus</note>, he was deterred by a certain softness. He devised a scheme by which he might descend to the underworld while still living. They decreed that he should pay the penalty for this fault and ordered that he be torn apart by women. 

However, they honored Achilles, the son of Thetis, and sent him to the Isles of the Blessed. <margin>Achilles the most beautiful.</margin> For when he had learned from his mother that if he killed Hector, he would have to die immediately, but if not, he would return to his fatherland and finally die as an old man, he boldly chose to fight for his lover Patroclus and avenge his death; not only to die for him, but to be slain after he had been killed. The gods, greatly approving of this, decorated him with signal glory because he had done so much for his lover. Aeschylus is clearly raving when he says that Patroclus was loved by Achilles; for Achilles excelled not only Patroclus but all the heroes in beauty, and was still beardless and much younger in age, as Homer says. 

In truth, the gods value this virtue in love most highly. <margin>The lover is more divine than the beloved, and is moved by a divine fury.</margin> They admire and delight more vehemently, and confer greater benefits, when the beloved protects and loves the lover than when the lover loves the beloved. For the lover is more divine than the beloved, since he is seized by a divine fury <note>Latin: furor diuinus; a state of inspired madness or poetic/romantic ecstasy</note>. For this reason, they honored Achilles more than Alcestis; indeed, they transferred him to the Isles of the Blessed. From all these things, I assert that Love is the most ancient of all the gods and most worthy of veneration, and contributes most of all to men—both living and deceased—in attaining virtue and blessedness.

->The Praise of Pausanias.<-

<margin>This discussion is more dense and ample than that of Phaedrus.</margin>
<margin>Twin Love, Twin Venus.</margin>
It seems to me, Phaedrus, that the topic has not been proposed to us quite correctly, in that we are ordered simply to praise Love. For if there were only one Love, it would have been well said. But since there is not just one, it is better to define him before he is praised. I shall therefore attempt to correct this. First, I will explain which Love it is proper to praise; then I shall strive to extol him according to the dignity of that god. 

Surely it escapes no one that without Love, Venus never exists. Therefore, if there were one Venus, there would be one Love. But since there are two Venuses, it is necessary that there be a twin Love as well. Who would deny that this goddess is twofold? Is not one older and without a mother, born of the heavens, whom we call the Celestial Venus? The other is younger, born of Jupiter and Dione, whom we call the Vulgar and Common Venus? It is necessary, then, that the Love who is the companion of the former Venus be called Celestial, and the companion of the latter be called Vulgar. 

It is proper to praise all gods. But the works of each Love must be distinguished. This is the condition of any action: that by its own nature it is neither honorable nor base—such as the things we are doing now: drinking, singing, debating. None of these is base or honorable in itself. But the manner of acting gives a certain name to the action. For that which is done well and rightly results in honor; that which is not right results in baseness. By the same reasoning, not just any love or any way of loving is honorable and praiseworthy, but only that one which exhorts us to love honorably. 

Indeed, the love of the Vulgar and Common Venus is truly vulgar itself, and it performs whatever happens to come along. This is the love by which depraved and base men love. Furthermore, they love women no less than males, and bodies more than souls; and they prefer people without minds to those who are prudent. They gape only to fulfill their desire; they do not care at all whether they fulfill it honorably or not. Thus it happens that they carry out whatever chance offers them, both good and evil alike. For an affection of this kind flows from that younger Venus, who participates in the generation of both sexes. 

But the Love that follows the Celestial Venus—who participates in generation not of the female, but of the male sex only—looks toward the male kind. Then, since he is the companion of the more ancient and modest Venus, he himself is free from all wantonness. Therefore, those who are inspired by this love prefer the male kind, which is by nature more robust, more noble, and more a participant in the mind. And those who are seized by this love sincerely and perfectly are clearly distinguished by this: they do not love boys, but youths, when they have already begun to be strong in mind. This kind of age is closer to the exercise of the mind, and a familiarity is entered into between them for the purpose of exercising it. For I believe those who begin to love in this way are prepared to live their whole lives together and in common; neither to deceive the beloved, nor to leave one beloved for another. For they do not love boys who are still without minds, whom they might later mock and abandon when they are grown. It ought to be established by laws that no one should love boys, so that such great devotion is not placed in vain upon an ambiguous matter. For it is uncertain where either the body or the soul of boys will ultimately end up, whether toward virtue or toward vice. Honorable men indeed propose this law for themselves voluntarily. It is also necessary...

# BOOK XXV.
## Page 70

I have decided to subject common lovers to the law of necessity: just as we prohibit them from loving free women to the best of our power. For these are the ones who fall into every most shameful act. From this arose the opinion of those who say it is shameful to yield to lovers. Indeed, they say these things concerning vulgar lovers, because they recognize and disapprove of their persistence and injustice. However, nothing that is done modestly and lawfully deserves to be blamed. Certainly, the law established concerning love in other cities is easy to understand, since it is handed down simply. But among us and the **Lacedæmonians** <note>The Spartans</note>, it is varied. For in **Elis** and among the **Boeotians**, and where men lack the art of speaking, it is simply established by law that one should gratify lovers; nor would anyone there, whether young or old, declare it shameful. I believe this was done by them for this reason: so that they would not have to labor in persuading the youths, seeing as they are unskilled in oratory. 

In **Ionia**, however, and among many others who are subject to the **Barbarians** <note>Non-Greeks, likely referring to the Persians</note>, this is altogether judged shameful by law. For among the Barbarians, this is considered shameful because of their tyrannies, and furthermore because of their study of wisdom and gymnastics. For those studies are not conducive to tyranny, as they render the minds of the subjects sharp and noble, and they produce indissoluble friendships and frequent associations among them. These are accustomed to be born from many things, but most especially from love. Our own tyrants learned this by the very event. For the love of **Aristogiton** and the confirmed friendship of **Harmodius** <note>Famous Athenian "tyrannicides" who overthrew the sons of Pisistratus</note> dissipated their tyranny. And so, wherever the indulgence of love has been utterly removed, it has been forbidden through the wickedness of those who founded the laws: namely, by the iniquity and violence of the princes, and the cowardice of the subjects. But where it is permitted without restriction, it is permitted because of the sluggishness and laziness of those who so established it. 

Here, however, the institution is much more upright, but, as I was saying, not easy to know. It clearly seems to be conceded, if anyone notices what is said: that it is more honorable to love openly than secretly, and especially those who are noble and best, even if they seem less beautiful than others. The common encouragement of all also greatly favors the lover, as if he were attempting nothing shameful. For commonly, if anyone captures the beloved, it is seen as something beautiful; if he does not capture him, it is shameful. And the law grants the lover wonderful devices for winning over the beloved, and permits him to be praised for things which, if anyone ever dared to attempt for the sake of anything else, he would incur the greatest reproaches among philosophers. 

For if anyone, for the sake of receiving money from someone, or for the power of a magistracy, should attempt those things which lovers do toward their beloveds—if he should run everywhere, pray as a suppliant, swear oaths, lie at the doors at night, and serve with a certain diligent observance and obey in all things—acts which even a slave would neither wish to do nor be forced to do—he would be scolded by enemies and friends alike. The former would blame his servile flatteries and fawning. The latter would rebuke him, and would be ashamed of their friend's servitude. But the lover, while doing these things, gains favor; and as if he were doing something noble, the law permits him to do these things without any 

<margin>The Gods grant more pardon to lovers alone. The oath of Venus.</margin>

mark of infamy. And what is greatest of all, it is commonly said that the gods grant pardon to the perjuries of lovers alone. For they say that an oath to **Venus** <note>original: "Venereum iusiurandum"</note> has no force. And so both gods and men have permitted every license to the lover, as our law testifies. If we look at these things that have been said, it will seem that to love someone, and for the beloved to indulge the lover, is considered something most noble in this city. 

If, on the other hand, we notice the things I shall say, we will think this is held to be most shameful among us. For parents entrust their sons to tutors <note>original: "paedagogis"</note>, who prohibit the beloveds from speaking with their lovers. Their companions and peers also, whenever they see such a thing, blame them; and the elders do not restrain those who criticize such things, nor do they rebuke them as if they were in error. Therefore, I think the matter stands thus: that the act itself, as was said from the beginning, is in itself neither honorable nor shameful. For it is not a simple thing, but if done rightly it is honorable; if otherwise, shameful. It is indeed shameful to yield to a wicked person in a shameful manner. But it is honorable to yield to a good person in an honorable manner. 

The vulgar lover is wicked: he who loves the body more than the soul. Nor is he stable, since he pursues a thing that is least stable. For as soon as the beauty of the body which he had desired fades, he departs, keeping none of the things he had promised. But the lover of good character perseveres in friendship throughout his whole life, seeing as he was seeking a stable thing. Our law commands that these be diligently examined, and that one should gratify the latter and flee the former. It bids one to follow these and flee those, judging and examining who loves whom, and in what way they love. And for this reason, it is first judged shameful to be captured easily and quickly, so that time may intervene, which is required for examining character. Secondly, it is absurd to be captured by a wealth of money or the power of a magistracy: whether he be ensnared by a certain fear rather than by will, or whether, having accepted money and acquired civil offices, he does not despise them. For nothing of these things seems to be solid and firm, besides the fact that a noble friendship cannot arise from them. 

Therefore, one way remains according to our law by which beloveds can rightly gratify their lovers. For just as that law was related among us concerning lovers, which says: no voluntary service of a lover toward the beloved is to be thought flattering or infamous; so also another certain voluntary servitude remains according to the law, which undergoes no infamy. This is the one which concerns virtue <note>original: "virtutem"</note>. For it is established by our laws: if anyone wishes to cultivate someone, thinking that through him he may profit either in a certain wisdom or in any other part of virtue, this voluntary servitude in turn shall neither be a disgrace to the one serving, nor should it be called flattery. 

It is necessary, however, for these laws to lead to the same end: namely, that law concerning lovers, and this one written concerning philosophy and other virtue, if it ought to happen by any reason that it is fitting for beloveds to yield to lovers. For whenever the lover and the beloved meet in the same purpose, both having the law—the former prepared to minister and serve the beloved justly in all things, the latter in turn ready to obey his teacher of knowledge and character justly in every detail—and the former being able to contribute to wisdom and other virtues, while the latter is in need of instruction and wisdom...

FOLIO CLXXII.

-> THE BANQUET, OR CONCERNING LOVE. <-

...needy: then surely, when these laws concur, it happens that it is honorable for the beloved to gratify their lovers; otherwise, it is in no way so. In this specific case, it is not shameful to be deceived. In all other cases, such compliance is judged shameful, whether the opinion deceives the one complying or not. For if someone gratifies a lover as if he were wealthy for the sake of riches, and is deceived and does not obtain his wish because the lover is poor, he is nonetheless blamed. For he is seen here to have revealed a servile mind in his character, because for the sake of money he would serve anyone in any matter, which is not at all honorable. By the same reasoning, if someone gratifies another as if he were a good man, hoping through this association to become better himself, and is deceived when that man is found to be wicked: this is a certain honorable deception. For he is seen to have demonstrated his affection as ready to endure all services for the sake of attaining virtue. This is indeed judged most noble; therefore, by this reasoning, to gratify and serve out of a greed for virtue is always honorable. This, moreover, is the love of the Celestial Goddess herself, and is itself celestial: which is precious both privately and publicly: and it compels both the lover and the beloved to undertake the care and study of virtue. Other loves, however, are the companions of the Common Venus. These things, O Phaedrus, I contribute to you concerning Love as if on the spur of the moment. When Pausanias had made a *pausa* <note>original: "pausam," a pun on the name Pausanias</note>—that is, an end of speaking (for the wise teach me to play with words in this way)—Aristodemus says that Aristophanes ought to have spoken, but was hindered by a hiccup, occurring either from fullness or some other cause. Wherefore, he spoke to Eryximachus <margin>Aristophanes is criticized and mocked.</margin> who sat immediately after him, saying: "O Eryximachus, it is now your concern either to suppress my hiccup or to speak for me until it ceases." To which Eryximachus replied: "I will do both. I will take your turn and speak for you: and you shall speak for me after the hiccup has gone away. Meanwhile, while I speak, if you wish to hold your breath for some time, the hiccup will cease. If that pleases you less, at least wash your throat within with much water. And if by chance it is violent, <margin>Remedies for a hiccup.</margin> stimulate your nostrils properly so that a sneezing is provoked. For if you do this once or twice, even if it is very frequent, it will be removed." "Before you make an end of speaking," said Aristophanes, "I will do what you command." Eryximachus, therefore, spoke thus:

### The praise by Eryximachus, which is more embracing than that of Pausanias.

<margin>What medicine is.</margin> It seems necessary to me: since Pausanias, having begun rightly, imposed an insufficient end, that what is missing be now filled by me. That distinction by which Love is distributed into two, I approve. But by this our art of medicine, I seem to have discovered that Love exists not only in the souls of men toward the beautiful: but also toward many other things, and in other bodies of all animals: as well as in those things which spring from the earth: and finally in all things, so to speak, which consist in the nature of things. This god is great and wonderful, extending himself most widely through all things, both human and divine. I shall first take an example from the skill of medicine, so that I may honor my art. The nature of bodies contains this twin Love. For that which is healthy in our bodies and that which is ill are admittedly different and dissimilar. That which is dissimilar desires and loves dissimilar things. Therefore, the Love in a healthy body is one thing, and that in a sick body is another. And as Pausanias asserted a little while ago that temperate men should be gratified, but the intemperate not at all: so also in the bodies themselves, the good and healthy parts must be complied with (in which the method of medicine chiefly consists), but the bad and sick parts not at all, if anyone wishes to be a skillful doctor. Medicine is, to speak summarily, the science by which the amorous affections of the body regarding fullness or evacuation are known. And whoever discerns the beautiful and deformed love in these, he is the most skilled doctor. Or he who can so commute these things that one love is born in place of another: or can instill Love where it is absent but ought to be present, and can extirpate what is implanted: he is a learned craftsman. For it is necessary to be able to reconcile those things which are most hostile in the body, and to implant a mutual love in them. Those things are most hostile which are most contrary: cold to hot, bitter to sweet, moist to dry, and others of this kind. Since our ancestor Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine</note> knew how to instill mutual love and concord in these, as these poets testify (whom I also believe), he composed our art. Therefore, all medicine is governed by this god in the manner of which I speak. Likewise also agriculture and gymnastics. That the same reasoning applies to music can be clear to anyone who has paid attention even for a little while. This is perhaps what Heraclitus <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for the doctrine of change and opposites</note> means, though he explains it poorly in words. He says that "the one, disagreeing with itself, accords: like the harmony of the bow and the lyre." It is an absurd saying that harmony "disagrees," or that it exists from disagreeing things as long as they are dissonant. But perhaps he wished to signify this: that from things which previously disagreed—namely, the low and the high pitch—harmony is fashioned when they later sound together through the musical art. For harmony is never blown together from low and high while they disagree. For harmony is a symphony. Symphony, moreover, is a certain concord, and concord cannot arise from disagreeing things as long as they disagree. That which disagrees and is not in accord cannot harmonize: just as rhythm is constituted from the fast and the slow, previously disagreeing but afterwards harmonizing. And just as medicine grants concord to the humors, so music, by attributing consonance to voices, begets mutual Love and consensus. And indeed, music is the science of judging amorous affections and powers regarding harmony and rhythm. Surely in the very composition of harmony and rhythm, the amorous power can easily be perceived: but here the twin Love is not yet distinguished: but only then, when rhythm and harmony must be used toward others, either in composing (which they call the creation of melody) or in correctly using those melodies and meters which have been made (which they call education). Here the observation is difficult, and there is need of a skilled craftsman. To this point that earlier discourse now returns: namely, that modest men, and those who are not yet modest enough so that they may become so, are to be gratified: and their Love is to be preserved. And this is the decorous Love of the Celestial Muse, Urania. But that of the Muse Polymnia is the common love, which must be indulged with the greatest caution...

I intend to speak of Love in a different way than you and Pausanias have spoken. It seems plain to me that men have hitherto been entirely ignorant of the power of Love. For if they knew it, they would have dedicated distinguished shrines, altars, and sacrifices to him. None of these things are done in these times, though it would be most fitting of all to observe them toward him. For he is, above all other gods, exceedingly beneficial to the human race: the curator and tutor of men, and a physician; if these were healed, our race would attain the highest happiness. In the beginning there were three kinds of men, not only the two we have now, male and female, but there was also a certain third kind, composed of both. Of this, only the name remains to us; the thing itself has perished. For there was then the "Androgynous" <note>From the Greek *andros* (man) and *gyne* (woman).</note> both in form and name, mixed from the male and female sex. There was one head for both faces, which were turned in opposite directions. Four ears, two sets of genitalia, and all other parts as anyone can imagine from these. He walked then both upright as now, in whichever direction he wished; and whenever he contended to go more quickly, like those who, with head down, turn their legs upward and perform a circular dance, he was then supported by eight limbs and carried in a swift circle. For this reason there were three kinds and of such a sort: because the male was born from the Sun, the female from the Earth, and the promiscuous kind from the Moon. For the moon participates in both. They were spherical in both shape and motion, because they were like their parents. Hence they were of robust body and high spirit. Wherefore they attempted to fight with the gods and to ascend into heaven, just as Homer writes of Ephialtes and Otus. Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus.</note> therefore, along with the other gods, consulted on what should be done. In this matter there was no small ambiguity. For it did not please them to destroy those men with lightning as they had the giants, for if the human race were extinct, the human cult and veneration of the gods would perish. Nor did they think they should be permitted to persevere in such insolence. At last Jupiter explained his opinion. "I have found," he said, "by what means it can be brought about that men may both exist and be more modest. And that will be if they are made weaker. I shall now divide each one into two parts. From which they will be both weaker, and it will also be more advantageous to us. For they will be more in number who worship us. They shall walk upright on two legs. # THE BANQUET, OR CONCERNING LOVE
## FOLIO CLXXIII.

...I will cut them in two, so that they shall be forced to hop on a single leg as if they were lame. Having spoken these words, he divided each person into two parts, just like those who slice fruit to preserve it with salt, or like those who cut eggs with a hair. He then commanded Apollo that, as soon as the division was made, he should turn the face and the half of the neck of each toward the side that had been cut, so that by beholding his own split, the human might become more modest; the rest he ordered to be healed. Apollo immediately turned the faces and, drawing the skin together from all sides toward what is now called the belly—like a drawstring purse—he left one opening in the middle of the belly, which connection they call the navel. He smoothed out most of the other wrinkles, shaping the breasts with a tool such as cobblers use when smoothing the wrinkles of leather over a foot-mold; however, he left a few wrinkles around the middle of the belly and the navel to be scars that would remind us of our ancient suffering. 

After the nature of humans was thus divided, since each desired his own recognized half, they would run toward one another. Throwing their arms around each other, they embraced, longing to be fused into one. Consequently, they began to perish from hunger and inactivity, because they would never do anything apart from one another. When one half died and the other remained, the survivor would seek out and embrace another half, whether it was the half of a whole woman—which we now call a woman—or the half of a man. And so the human race was dying out. 

Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus</note>, taking pity, devised another remedy: he moved their genitals. Previously, these had been on the backside, and they did not conceive through one another but by casting seed into the earth like cicadas. By moving them to the front, he enabled them to generate through one another: the male in the female. This was done so that if a man embraced a woman, they might propagate the species; but if a male embraced a male, they might reach a point of satiety and turn their attention to the affairs of life and labor. 

From that time, then, mutual love has been innate in humans, the reconciler of our ancient nature, striving to make one out of two and to heal the human condition. Each of us is, therefore, a "tally" <note>original: *symbolon*, a broken piece of a whole</note> of a human, having been cut like the small flat-fish called *Psectae* <note>likely a type of sole or flounder</note> which are made into two from one. Each seeks his own half. Therefore, those men who are a slice of the formerly "Androgynous" sex are fond of women; most adulterers come from this group. Likewise, women who are fond of men and are adulteresses come from this stock. But those women who are a slice of the female sex do not care much for men, but are more inclined toward women. Those who are a slice of the male follow the male. While they are boys, being slices of the male, they love men and enjoy the company and embrace of men; these are the most noble of boys and youths, for they are by nature the most manly. Some falsely call them shameless. For it is not through shamelessness, but through courage, fortitude, and a certain masculine nature that they do this, rejoicing in what is like themselves. A clear proof of this is that when they grow up, they are the only ones who turn to civic administration and become outstanding men. When they reach manhood, they love youths; by nature, they do not care for marriage or procreation, unless compelled by law. They prefer a life of celibacy. 

In short, such a man loves males and is devoted to his friends, always rejoicing in his own kind. Whenever he happens upon his own half—regardless of the sex he is drawn to—they are struck with a violent affection and wonder; they burn with friendship, intimacy, and love. They cannot bear to be separated for even a moment. These are the people who continue loving through their whole lives, yet they cannot even say what they want from one another. For it does not seem that sexual intimacy is the reason they delight so much in each other's company. It is clearly something else that the soul of each desires, which it cannot express, but rather divines and pursues through obscure traces. 

If, while they were lying together, Vulcan <note>The Roman name for Hephaestus, the smith-god</note> were to stand over them with his tools and ask: "What is it, O humans, that you want from one another?" and as they hesitated, he asked again: "Is this what you long for: to be merged into one and the same so completely that you are never separated day or night? If this is your desire, I will melt you down and fuse you together so that from two you become one, and as long as you live, and even among the dead, you shall remain one. See if this is what you burn for." If Vulcan asked this, it is certain no one would refuse. Each would think he had finally heard what he had always desired: to be made one out of two through union with the beloved. The cause of this is that our ancient nature was as I described: we were once whole. The desire and pursuit of this wholeness is what we call "Love." 

Once, as I said, we were one. But because of our injustice, we were split apart by God, just as the Arcadians were by the Lacedaemonians <note>A historical reference to the Spartans breaking up the people of Mantinea into villages</note>. There is reason to fear that if we are not modest toward the gods, we may be split again and become like those figures carved in relief on pillars, with our noses sliced off, looking like the thinnest animals called *lispae*. For this reason, it is right for every man to worship the gods with great piety and to exhort others to do the same, so that we may avoid these evils and attain the blessings to which our leader and commander, Love, points us. No one should act against him; for he who opposes Love opposes the gods. If we are reconciled to God and have him as our friend, we shall each find and obtain our own beloved half—which few do in these times. Let not Eryximachus mock my speech, as if I were referring only to Pausanias and Agathon; for perhaps they too are among those...

->The Eulogy of Agathon<-

<margin>The right method of praising.</margin>

<note>The decorative 'P' begins the word "Praeclare" (Excellently).</note> You speak excellently, Phaedrus. Nor does anything prohibit me from speaking. Indeed, it will be possible to dispute with Socrates often at other times. I, however, will now first show how I ought to speak; afterwards I shall speak. It seems to me that those who have spoken so far have not praised the god himself, but have recounted the benefits which are happily conferred by him upon men. But what he himself is like, who is the cause of these goods, no one has yet expressed. The only right method of praising in all things is that which first shows the nature of him who is being discussed, and afterwards declares the things of which he is the cause. Thus, in the present case, it is fitting first to show what sort of being Love himself is, and then to explain his gifts. I assert indeed, since all gods are blessed, that Love—if it is right and tolerable to say—is the most blessed of all: since he exists as the most beautiful and best of all. That he is the most beautiful is first evident from this:

<margin>Old age is swift.</margin>

that he is the youngest of all the gods. Of which he himself provides clear proof: since he flees old age—the swift kind, to be sure, which arrives sooner than it ought. Love by nature hates it and flees it; but he mingles with the young. As the old proverb skillfully says, "like always clings to like." And though I grant many things to

<margin>Proverb: Like rejoices in like.</margin>

Phaedrus, in this one thing I least agree: that Love is older than Saturn and Iapetus <note>Titans representing the oldest generation of gods.</note>. Rather, I say he is young above the other gods, and always young; the ancient deeds of the gods, which Hesiod and Parmenides describe, are to be attributed to Necessity rather than to Love, if indeed they told the truth. For neither would castrations of one another, nor bindings, nor many other violent things have happened among the gods of old, if Love had been present with them then; but benevolence and the highest peace would have reigned, just as now, since Love began to rule the gods. Therefore he is young, and moreover tender and soft. But there is need of such a poet as Homer was, to demonstrate the tender

<margin><insert>Arys den</insert> <note>This marginal insertion appears to be a fragmentary reference or name.</note></margin>

softness of Love. Homer indeed says that Ate—that is, Calamity—is a goddess and soft. And to show that her feet are tender, he says she never treads upon the pavement, but walks upon the heads of men—a clear conjecture indeed he seems to have used for how tender she is, because she does not walk on hard things, but touches soft ones. We must use the same argument to show that Love is tender. For he does not go upon the earth and rocks, which are rough, but he implants himself and remains in the softest of all things. Indeed, he places his seat in the souls of gods and men. Yet not in just any souls: for if he encounters a hard habit of soul, he flees; but if a mild and soft one, he inhabits it. Since therefore he always touches with his feet and his whole self the softest parts of the softest things, it is necessary that Love be most tender. For which reason Love is both young and tender above others. He is also fluid like water, and slippery. For he could not flow around everywhere through the whole soul, and flow in secretly, and flow out secretly, if he were hard and rigid. Of his fit, composed, and flexible form, his beauty can be the proof: that is, the harmony of his figure, with which Love is undoubtedly adorned most of all. # THE BANQUET, OR CONCERNING LOVE.

## FOLIO 174.

Whether it be the body, or the soul, or whatever else it may be, Love itself does not settle there. But wherever there is a flowery and fragrant place, there he sits most graciously. Much more could be brought forward concerning his beauty, but these things suffice. Next, we must speak of the virtue of Love. This is what must be valued most of all. Love neither inflicts injury upon a god or a man, nor does he suffer injury from a god or a man. For he does not suffer by force, if he suffers at all. For violence does not touch Love. Nor does he act by force, if he does anything. For everyone willingly obeys Love in all things. And whatever one willing party settles with another willing party, these things are considered just, as the laws of the royal city <note>Likely referring to the ideal state or the laws of Athens</note> decree. 

<margin>All pleasure is overcome by Love.</margin>

Nor is he a participant in justice alone, but also in the highest temperance <term>temperantia: self-control or moderation</term>. Indeed, it is agreed among all that temperance is the mastery over lusts and pleasures; and no pleasure is more powerful than Love. But if all pleasures are weaker than Love, they are certainly overcome by him, and he indeed masters them. Therefore, since Love masters lusts and pleasures, he is wonderfully temperate. Furthermore, as to courage, not even Mars <note>The Roman name for Ares, the god of war</note> resists Love. For Mars does not hold Love, but the love of Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> holds Mars, as the story goes. And the one who holds is more powerful than the one who is held. He who masters the most courageous of others must, without doubt, be judged the most courageous of all. 

Concerning the justice, temperance, and courage of this god, enough has been said. It remains next to speak of his wisdom, which must be carried out to the best of my ability. In the first place—so that I may honor my own art just as Eryximachus <note>The physician who spoke earlier</note> honored his—this god is a poet so wise that he can make others poets as well. For anyone, even if he were unrefined before, becomes a poet as soon as Love has breathed upon him. From this, one may clearly infer that Love is a skilled poet, and that, in short, he contains all the musical measures of poetry. For what someone does not have or does not know, he cannot give to another or show to him. 

<margin>He gave those things to us first: in spirit. What someone does not have or know, he cannot give or provide to another. Apollo is a disciple of Love. The art of weaving belongs to Minerva.</margin>

Who would doubt that all living creatures are begotten and born through the wisdom of Love? Furthermore, do we not see that the faculty of the arts is handed down by this god, and that the man who has him as a teacher excels in every art and becomes famous? Conversely, does he not leave in obscurity the one who is not touched by Love? For Apollo <note>God of music, healing, and prophecy</note> discovered the skill of archery, healing, and divination with desire and love as his guides; thus he is a disciple of Love. Similarly, the Muses discovered music, Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> the craft of bronze-working, Minerva <note>Athena</note> the art of weaving, and Jupiter <note>Zeus</note> the governance of gods and men. 

<margin><unclear>Note: concerning Love</unclear></margin>

Therefore, the affairs of the gods were arranged when Love intervened—the love, I say, of beauty. For love does not follow deformity. But before that, as I was saying above, many and cruel things happened among the gods because of the "kingdom of Necessity," as it is called. But after this god was born from the desire for beautiful things, all good things came to both gods and men. Thus it seems to me, O Phaedrus, that Love himself is first most beautiful and best, and then bestows such qualities upon others as well. 

A certain rhythmic and harmonious thought occurs to me at present: This is the god who bestows peace upon men, tranquility to the sea, rest to the winds, and a secure bed for all living things. He removes alienation from us; he unites us in intimacy, bringing together all gatherings of this kind. In solemnities and on feast days, in dances, and in sacrifices, he is our leader and presiding officer: offering gentleness, banishing wildness, the giver of benevolence, the expeller of all ill-will. He is propitious, beneficial, to be gazed upon by the wise, pleasing to the gods, longed for by those who lack him, and to be possessed and held by those who share in him. He is the father of delights, of soft allurements, of graces, of sweet infusion, and of desire. He is the studious pursuer of good things, the teacher of the wicked <note>original: "malorum praeceptor" - likely meaning he guides even the wayward</note>, a governor in labor, in fear, in desire, and in speech; a perfect helper and a chief savior. He is the glory of all gods and men, and the most beautiful and best leader. Every man ought to follow him and worship him with noble hymns, participating in that song which Love himself sings, soothing the minds of gods and men. 

This speech of mine, Phaedrus, is dedicated to the god, filled partly with jests and partly with serious matters, according to the capacity of my talent. 

When Agathon had said these things, as Aristodemus reported, all the guests approved the speech with a great applause, seeing that it was held to be worthy of both Agathon and the god. Therefore, Socrates, turning to Eryximachus, said: "Does it not seem now, O Eryximachus, son of Acumenus, that I was rightly afraid before? What I predicted has truly happened: that Agathon would speak most elegantly, and that words would fail me." 

ERYXIMACHUS: I think you predicted one thing correctly—that Agathon would speak skillfully; but that eloquence would fail you, I do not believe at all. 

SOCRATES: Why, O blessed man, should not I or anyone else be deterred from speaking, who must talk after such a brilliant and copious oration? And while the other parts were aptly composed, they did not seem so wonderful; but the elegance of the names and words which he used at the conclusion of his speech—if anyone noticed—would immediately strike them dumb. Indeed, when I realized that I could not come close to his eloquence, I was almost moved by shame to slip away and leave, if it had been permitted. For the speech of Gorgias <note>A famous Greek sophist and rhetorician known for his flowery style</note> reminded me of that Homeric occurrence. I was afraid that Agathon, putting an end to his words, would send the head of the eloquent Gorgias from his speech into mine, making me mute and turning me into a stone instead of a man. Then at last I realized that I had rashly promised to praise Love with you in my turn, and that I had foolishly professed to be an expert in love-matters, when I did not know at all the proper way to praise anything. I had thought, in my ignorance, that one ought to tell the truth about whatever is being praised by us, and that this should be the foundation; and that from these truths we should select the most beautiful things and assign them in the most becoming way. Therefore, I was elated with a great hope, as if I were going to speak well, since I held, as it seemed, the true method of praising. But in the end, this "method" of praise appeared not to be suitable at all.

-> XXV. <-

<margin>
He critiques the shared praise, noting that they bring forth false things so that all things might be seen as the greatest.
</margin>
For it seems necessary to ascribe all the greatest and most excellent things to the matter we are praising, whether these qualities are actually present or not. For it matters nothing whether they be false or true; since the purpose is not for love itself to be praised <note>original: "amor ipse laudet"</note>, but rather that everyone should seem to praise love as much as possible. Therefore, you attribute the universe to love: and you affirm him to be of such a kind, and the cause of such and so many things, so that he appears most beautiful and best—to those who are ignorant, of course. For never would such praise be judged right and pure by those who understand. Indeed, I was entirely ignorant of this method of praising. Not knowing it, I agreed with you that I too would join the others in offering praise. My tongue therefore promised, but my mind by no means did. Far be it from me, then, to give such a praise. For I could not extol him in that way. Nevertheless, if you wish, I desire to speak the truth in my own fashion: and to look to myself rather than to compare my foolish fear with your orations, lest I move you to laughter. See then, Phaedrus, whether it pleases you all to hear a speech of this kind now, which tells only the truth about love: proceeding with whatever composition of words and names happens to occur. PHAEDRUS. It certainly pleases me, and the others, that you speak according to your own judgment. SOCRATES. Grant me, O Phaedrus, that I may ask Agathon a few certain questions: so that, having been confirmed by him, I may speak. PHAEDRUS. I grant it indeed. Just ask. SOCRATES.

### The Oration of Socrates.

<margin>
<unclear>Socrates begins his interrogation</unclear>
</margin>
You seem to have laid the first foundations of your speech, my friend Agathon, when you said first that it must be shown what love is, and afterwards its works must be enumerated. This beginning I greatly approve. Come then, since you have spoken so ornately and magnificently about the other things concerning love, declare this further to me regarding his nature: whether love is of such a kind that it is the love *of something*, or of nothing? I do not ask whether it is the love of some mother or father. For it would be a ridiculous question whether the love of a father or mother is love. But if I had asked whether a father were the father of someone or not, you would have answered (if you wished to speak properly) that a father is the father of a son or a daughter. Is it not so? AGATHON. Entirely. SOCRATES. And is not a mother the mother of someone? AGATHON. That also. SOCRATES. Answer a few more things, so that you may better understand what I mean. Is a brother, by the very fact that he is a brother, the brother of someone? AGATHON. He is, certainly. SOCRATES. Is it not of a brother or a sister? AGATHON. Of those, surely. SOCRATES. Try similarly to show us concerning love, whether love is the love of something. AGATHON. Of something, certainly. SOCRATES. Keep this, then, in your memory, remembering what it is of. And answer this: does love desire that very thing of which it is the love, or not? AGATHON. Most greatly indeed. SOCRATES. Does he have this very thing with him, and yet desire and love what he already has? Or rather, does he not have what he loves and desires? AGATHON. It is likely he does not have it. SOCRATES. Consider further whether, instead of it being "likely," it is *necessary* that whatever desires, desires that which it lacks; and if it does not lack, it does not desire. To me, indeed, this is wonderfully pleasing, that it should be necessary. But how does it seem to you, Agathon? AGATHON. The same as to you. SOCRATES. You speak well. Would a man who is already great wish to be great? Or one who is robust wish to be robust? AGATHON. From those things we granted above, it seems to me this cannot happen. SOCRATES. For he would not be in need of those things which he already contained within himself. AGATHON. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. For if he who is robust wants to be robust, and he who is swift to be swift, and finally he who is healthy to be healthy: perhaps someone might believe that these, and any others, desire the things they already have. Let us not be deceived here. If you observe this diligently, Agathon, you will see it is necessary that whatever these men have in the present time, they have it in that same time whether they want to or not. Who then would desire this very thing? But when someone adds: "But I, being healthy, want to be healthy; and being rich, I want to be rich; and therefore I desire the things I have," we answer him immediately: "O good man, you who have obtained riches, health, and strength, you wish to possess these also in the future; since in the present you have them whether you want to or not." See then, when you say "I desire the things which are present to me," whether you mean anything other than this: "I desire that the things which are now present to me may also be present in the future." Do you think this man would answer this, Agathon, or something else? AGATHON. Nothing else. SOCRATES. Love, surely, is of this kind: it looks toward that which is not yet at hand nor possessed—namely, that those things be present and preserved in the time that follows. AGATHON. It is entirely so. SOCRATES. And here, therefore, he and anyone else who desires, desires what is not yet set forth or ready; or what is not present; or what he does not have; or what he himself is not; or what he lacks. Such are the things of which there is desire and love. AGATHON. Such, without a doubt. SOCRATES. Come, let us repeat what was said above. First, love was said to be the love of certain things; then, of those things especially which he lacks. AGATHON. Certainly. SOCRATES. Remember, moreover, what you asserted love was the love of. I will bring it back to your memory if you wish. Indeed, I think you said it thus: that all things were arranged by the gods because of the love of beautiful things. For of ugly things there is no love at all. Did you not say so? AGATHON. Indeed, I did. SOCRATES. You speak probably, my friend. And if it is so, love is certainly the love of beauty; but of ugliness, not at all. AGATHON. I agree. SOCRATES. Was it not granted that one loves that which he lacks and does not have? AGATHON. Plainly granted. SOCRATES. Therefore, love lacks beauty, and does not have it. AGATHON. It is necessary. SOCRATES. What then? Do you call that beautiful which is lacking in beauty and does not have it? AGATHON. By no means. SOCRATES. Do you still assert, if these things are so, that love is beautiful? AGATHON. I seem to have understood nothing of those things I said before. SOCRATES. You have spoken rightly. But answer a little further: do not good things themselves seem to be beautiful? AGATHON. To me, they do. SOCRATES. If, therefore, love lacks beautiful things, and good things are beautiful, he lacks good things also. AGATHON. I could in no way resist you, O Socrates. Let it be <note>original: "Esto"</note> then, as you say. SOCRATES. You could never, O beloved Agathon, oppose the truth; but you can oppose Socrates very easily.

# FOLIO CLXXV.
## THE BANQUET, OR CONCERNING LOVE.

<margin>Diotima the prophetess.</margin>
But I shall now dismiss Agatho, and to you, O guests, I shall recount the discourse on Love which I once received from a prophetic woman named Diotima. She was skilled in these matters and understood many other things wisely; she once even caused a ten-year delay of the plague for the Athenians by means of sacrifices. She was the one who instructed me in the art of love. Therefore, I will attempt to express to you, on my own, what she said, following the points upon which Agatho and I just agreed. First, O Agatho, as you also set forth, one must show what Love is and what he is like, and then enumerate his works. It is best, as it seems to me, to recount this to you in the same order in which that stranger examined me. For I said almost the same things to her that Agatho said to me: that Love was a great god and that he looked toward beautiful things. And she refuted me with the same arguments I used against him: that Love was neither beautiful, as I said, nor good. To which I then said: "What are you saying, O Diotima? Is Love therefore ugly and evil?" DIOTIMA: "Speak better words, I pray. Do you think it necessary that whatever is not beautiful must be ugly?" SOCRATES: "Most certainly." DIOTIMA: "And that he who is not wise is ignorant? Have you not noticed that there is something in the middle between wisdom and ignorance?" SOCRATES: "What is that?" DIOTIMA: "To hold a right opinion; that is, to participate in the truth without a certain reason <note>original: "sine certa ratione," meaning without a logical proof or formal demonstration</note>. For this is not science, since science is never without reason. Nor, on the other hand, is it ignorance. For that which attains the truth is not called ignorance. Right opinion is something of this sort, a middle ground between wisdom and ignorance." SOCRATES: "You speak the truth." DIOTIMA: "Do not, therefore, force that which is not beautiful to be ugly, or that which is not good to be evil. By the same reasoning, when you concede that Love is neither beautiful nor good, you should not think he is necessarily ugly or evil, but something in between." SOCRATES: "But truly everyone agrees on this: that Love is a great god." DIOTIMA: "Do you mean everyone who is ignorant, or those who know?" SOCRATES: "I mean everyone." DIOTIMA: "How could they ridiculously confess him to be a great god when they do not even want him to be a god at all?" SOCRATES: "Who are these people?" DIOTIMA: "You are one of them, and I am the other." SOCRATES: "How can you say I assert this?" DIOTIMA: "I will easily show you; come, speak. Do you not affirm that all gods are beautiful and blessed? Would you ever dare to say any of the gods is not beautiful or blessed?" SOCRATES: "By Jupiter, I would not." DIOTIMA: "And do you not call those blessed who possess good and beautiful things?" SOCRATES: "Them alone." DIOTIMA: "And yet you admitted earlier that Love, because of a lack of beautiful and good things, desires these very things which he lacks." SOCRATES: "I did indeed admit it." DIOTIMA: "How then is he a god, who is devoid of beautiful and good things?" SOCRATES: "In no way, it seems." DIOTIMA: "Do you see then that you yourself also do not think Love is a god?" SOCRATES: "What then? Is Love mortal?" DIOTIMA: "Not at all." SOCRATES: "What then?" DIOTIMA: "A middle between those things mentioned: the mortal and the immortal." SOCRATES: "What is he, O Diotima?" DIOTIMA: "A great <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "daemon," referring to a supernatural being intermediate between gods and men, not an evil spirit</note>, O Socrates. For the entire nature of spirits is intermediate between mortals and gods." SOCRATES: "What power does it have?" DIOTIMA: "It interprets and conveys human things to the gods and divine things to men: the prayers and sacrifices of the former, and the commands and sacred solemnities, institutions, and orders of the latter. Being stationed in the middle of both, it fills the whole, so that the universe is connected to itself by such a bond. Through this, all prophecy proceeds, as well as the diligence of priests regarding sacrifices, expiations, incantations, and all divination and magic. God does not mingle with man, but through this medium, all commerce and conversation between gods and men is conducted, both while we are awake and while we sleep. Whoever is skilled in these things is called 'daemonic'—that is, a happy and wise man; but those who are skilled in other arts and faculties performed by the hands are called 'mercenaries.' Truly, these spirits are many and various. One of these is Love." SOCRATES: "Who are the parents of Love?" DIOTIMA: "Though it is long to tell, I will explain: When Venus was born, the other gods sat down to a prepared banquet, including the son of <insert>Metis</insert> (that is, Counsel), <insert>Porus</insert> (that is, the god of Plenty or Affluence). When they had dined, <insert>Penia</insert> (that is, Poverty or Beggary) came to get food, as there was an abundance at the feast, and she lingered about the doors. Porus, drunk on nectar—for wine did not yet exist—entered the garden of Jove and, heavy with sleep, lay down. Penia, compelled by her own need, devised a plan to conceive a son from Porus by a kind of ambush. Therefore, she lay down beside him and conceived Love. Hence Love was born a follower and servant of Venus, because he was begotten on the birthday of Venus. Furthermore, by nature, he is captured by a desire for the beautiful, since Venus herself is beautiful. Because Love is the son of Porus and Penia, he has obtained a lot like this: First, he is parched and squalid, with bare feet, always flying on the ground, without a home, without bedding or any covering, sleeping at the doors or in the street under the open sky, and keeping the nature of his mother, he is always in want. But according to his father’s lineage, he plots against the beautiful and the good; he is manly, bold, vehement, and a sagacious hunter, always weaving new machinations, a student of wisdom, eloquent, philosophizing through all his life, an enchanter, a powerful fascinator, a sorcerer, and a sophist. He is neither entirely immortal by nature, nor mortal; but sometimes on the same day he flourishes and lives whenever he has abundance, and sometimes he fades away and then lives again because of his father's nature. But what he acquires continually flows away. Therefore, Love is never either destitute or wealthy. Furthermore, he is placed between wisdom and ignorance. For the matter stands thus: No god philosophizes or desires to become wise, for he already is so. Nor does any other who is wise philosophize. Neither do the ignorant philosophize at all, nor do they desire to become wise. For ignorance has this worst quality: that he who is neither beautiful, good, nor wise, thinks himself to have these things sufficiently. Does he then seek those things of which he does not perceive himself to be unworthy?" SOCRATES: "Who then, Diotima, are those who philosophize, if neither the wise nor the ignorant do so?" DIOTIMA: "Even a child would understand this: that they are those who are in the middle between these two; because..."
