...is love. For wisdom is surely a most beautiful thing, and love is directed toward the beautiful. From this it necessarily follows that Love is a philosopher <note>original: "philosophum" - literally a "lover of wisdom"</note>; and being a philosopher, he holds the middle ground between the ignorant and the wise. The cause of these traits lies in his birth. For he was fathered by one who is wise and wealthy, but his mother was not at all wise and certainly poor. Such, then, is the nature of this spirit, my friend Socrates. Nor is it a wonder that you imagined Love to be such as you did, based on the opinion you held of his nature. For, as I gather from your words, you thought Love was the one being loved, not the lover; and for that reason, I believe, Love appeared most beautiful to you. Indeed, that which is lovable is truly beautiful, delicate, perfect, and most blessed. But the lover has a different character, such as I described above.

SOCRATES: Let it be as you say, guest, for you speak excellently. But since Love is such as this, of what use is he to men?

DIOTIMA: This is what I shall try to teach you next, Socrates. Such is Love, and so was he born. He is directed toward beautiful things, as you say. But if someone were to ask: "For what purpose is the love of beautiful things, Socrates and Diotima?" Or rather, to be clearer: "He who loves beautiful things, what does he specifically seek to gain from them?" What shall we answer?

SOCRATES: That they may be present to him, clearly.

DIOTIMA: But this answer requires a further question of this sort: What will he have, to whom beautiful things are present?

SOCRATES: I have no answer ready at hand.

DIOTIMA: But if someone, changing the terms and using "the good" instead of "the beautiful," should ask: "He who loves good things, what does he desire?"

SOCRATES: That they be present to him.

DIOTIMA: And what will he have, to whom good things are present?

SOCRATES: The answer to that is easier. He will be happy.

DIOTIMA: Indeed, by the possession of good things, those who are happy are happy; nor is there any need to ask further for what purpose he wishes to be happy who desires happiness; rather, the answer seems to have reached its end.

SOCRATES: You speak the truth.

DIOTIMA: Do you think this will and this love is common to all men? And that all wish for good things to be always present to them?

SOCRATES: It is plainly common.

DIOTIMA: Why then, Socrates, do we not say that everyone loves, if indeed they all love the same things and always? Why do we say some love and others do not?

SOCRATES: I wonder at that myself.

DIOTIMA: Do not wonder. For selecting one specific kind of lovers, we give them the name "Love," attributing to them the name of the whole. In other cases, we use other names.

SOCRATES: Declare this by some example.

DIOTIMA: For instance: you know that "making" <note>original: "factionem" / "poesis"</note> is a broad thing.
<margin>poetry is making</margin>
For "making" is generally called the cause by which anything proceeds from non-being into being. Therefore, all the actions of every art are "makings," and all craftsmen are "poets" (that is, makers).

SOCRATES: You tell the truth.

DIOTIMA:
<margin>poetry, i.e., making</margin>
Yet you see they are not called poets, but are allotted other names. From the whole of "making," one selected part—specifically that which concerns music and verses—is called by the name of the whole. For this alone is called "Poetry" (which is "making"), and those who possess this part of making are called "poets."

SOCRATES: These things are true.

DIOTIMA: The same thing happens regarding love. For in sum, the desire for all good things and for happiness is the greatest and most treacherous love in everyone. But those who proceed toward the good through the pursuit of money, or gymnastics, or wisdom, are neither said to "love" nor are they named "lovers." But those who strive toward it according to one certain species take the name of the whole: namely, Love, and loving, and lovers.

SOCRATES: You seem to speak rightly.

DIOTIMA: Some say that those who seek their other half are the ones who love. But I assert that love is neither for the half nor for the whole, unless it be in some way good; since men are willing to cut off even their own hands and feet if they seem to be evil. For a person does not cherish what is his own, unless perhaps someone calls what is good "his own" and "proper" to himself, and what is evil "alien." Indeed, men love nothing other than the good. Does it not seem so to you?

SOCRATES: It does indeed.

DIOTIMA: Should we then say simply that men love the good?

SOCRATES: Without a doubt.

DIOTIMA: And should we not add that they desire the good to be present to them?

SOCRATES: It should be added.

DIOTIMA: And not only present, but always present?

SOCRATES: Always.

DIOTIMA: Love is, therefore, in sum, the desire by which one wishes the good to be his own forever.

SOCRATES: You speak the absolute truth.

DIOTIMA: Since universal love is always something of this kind, can you say what is the specific condition of this desiring, or what is the mode of pursuit, and in what action or study it is properly named "Love"?

SOCRATES: If I could have shown that, Diotima, I would never have wondered at your wisdom, nor would I have come to you for the sake of learning.

DIOTIMA: Then I shall tell you. It is, I say, a birth in beauty, according to both the soul and the body.

SOCRATES: One needs a prophecy to understand what you say; for I do not perceive this at all.

DIOTIMA: I will speak more plainly. All men, Socrates, are pregnant and their bodies are heavy with seed; their souls are pregnant too. And as soon as we reach a certain age, our nature desires to bring forth. But it cannot bring forth in the ugly; it can only do so in the beautiful. The union of man and woman is a bringing forth. This is a divine work; and in the mortal animal itself, this is the immortal element: conception and generation. These cannot be fulfilled in that which is out of proportion and discordant. But the ugly is discordant with all that is divine, while the beautiful is in harmony with the divine. Beauty, therefore, is the Fate and the Midwife <note>original: "Parca et Lucina" - Roman goddesses of birth</note> to generation. Therefore, whenever that which is pregnant draws near to the beautiful, it exults with joy; it is diffused with cheerfulness and pleasure, and it brings forth and generates. Conversely, when it approaches the ugly, it is contracted with a certain sadness and pain; it is frightened away and restrained; it does not beget, but, retaining the fetus, it suffers. For this reason, that which has conceived and is now bursting, longing to generate as it reaches maturity, hovers around the beautiful; for by this it is relieved of sharp anxiety. For Love, Socrates, is not of the beautiful, as you think.

SOCRATES: Of what then?

DIOTIMA: Of generation and birth in the beautiful.

SOCRATES: Truly?

DIOTIMA: Truly, I say.

SOCRATES: Why of generation?

DIOTIMA: Because love is something everlasting and immortal, just as generation is within the mortal itself. It is necessary to desire immortality along with the good, from those things we granted above: since love is the desire that the good be present to oneself forever...

<summary>Diotima explains to Socrates that Love is not merely the desire for beauty, but the desire to "give birth" in beauty, which is the human way of achieving immortality. She clarifies that while all people seek the good, only those pursuing it through specific creative or procreative acts are commonly called "lovers."</summary>

# THE BANQUET, OR ON LOVE

FOLIO CLXXVI.

<margin>Love is the desire for immortality.</margin>
...desires. From these points, she concludes that Love is also the desire for immortality. Diotima delivered all these teachings to me when she held a discourse on matters of love, and she questioned me thus: "What do you think, O Socrates, is the cause of this love and desire? Do you not see how deeply all living creatures are affected—those that walk and those that fly—when they are carried by a total impulse toward procreation, and are maddened by the fire of love? First, they are driven by the cause of procreation, for which they long to unite vehemently. Then, they labor immensely to provide nourishment for their offspring. For the sake of these, even weak animals demand to fight against the strongest, and are prepared to die for them and perish from hunger, provided they may nourish their children; they boldly undertake any other task. Now, someone might think that human beings do these things through the discourse of reason; but among the brutes, what is the cause of such ardent love? Can you assign a reason for this?"

**SOCRATES:** Not at all. **DIOTIMA:** "Do you believe you will ever be skilled in matters of love while you remain ignorant of these things?" **SOCRATES:** For this very reason, O Diotima, as I said before, I flee to you for refuge, because I recognize that I am in need of a teacher. Therefore, I pray you, explain the cause of these and other things pertaining to love. **DIOTIMA:** "If you believe in that which is the nature of love, of which we have already spoken often, do not wonder. For by this same principle, as with the things mentioned above, a mortal nature always strives to be immortal as far as it is able. But it achieves this only through procreation <note>original: "generatione"</note>, because it always substitutes a new young being in place of the old. Indeed, in that very time in which each of the living creatures is said to live and be the same—as from childhood to old age—although one may call it the same,

<margin>Constant change in body and soul.</margin>
it never contains the same things within itself. Instead, it is always making something new and shedding the old, in respect to hair, flesh, bones, blood, and the entire body. And this happens not only in the body, but also in the soul. Manners, customs, opinions, desires, pleasures, pains, and fears are continually changing; none of these remains the same or identical, but the prior ones are abolished while new ones succeed them. Furthermore, what is more wonderful is that with sciences <note>or "branches of knowledge"</note> also, not only do some vanish while others arise—and we are not always the same in respect to our knowledge—but even each single science suffers the same fate. For what is called 'meditation' <note>or "study/practice"</note> is spoken of as if knowledge were departing. For forgetfulness is the exit of knowledge. But meditation, by always restoring a new memory in place of that which is departing, preserves the science so that it seems to be the same. In this way, everything mortal is preserved: not by being entirely the same forever, like the divine, but because that which grows old and departs leaves behind something new and similar to itself. By this remedy, Socrates, that which is mortal—whether it be the body or anything else—becomes a participant in immortality; but that which is divine and immortal does so by another principle. Therefore, you ought not to wonder if all things by nature hold their own offspring most dear. For for the sake of immortality, this striving and love is inherent in everyone."

When I had heard these things, moved by admiration, I said: "Is it truly to be judged so, O wise Diotima?" Then she, as perfect sophists <note>wise teachers</note> are accustomed to do, said: "Know it for certain, O Socrates. For if you wish to consider the pursuit of glory that is inherent in men, you will wonder at your own simplicity in not having sufficiently grasped what I have said. You will see how vehemently they long to show themselves known to all, and to attain immortal glory for the future. For the sake of this, more than for their own children, they undergo dangers, spend their money, reject no labors, and finally expose themselves to death. Do you think Alcestis would have wished to die for Admetus, or Achilles to perish in vengeance for Patroclus, or your Codrus <note>A legendary King of Athens who sacrificed himself to save the city</note> to die for the kingdom of his sons, unless they had foreseen that they would attain an immortal memory of virtue, such as exists among us? **SOCRATES:** Far from it. On the contrary, for the sake of immortal virtue and an honorable reputation, they do all these things, as I believe. And the better men are, the more they strive for these things. For they love immortality. **DIOTIMA:** "Those, therefore, who are fertile in body turn themselves more toward women; and thus they love, and through the procreation of children, they hope to attain immortality, memory, and happiness for all time. But there are also those who have a soul more pregnant and fertile than the body. These surely conceive those things which it is fitting for the soul both to have conceived and to conceive. But what is fitting? Prudence <note>practical wisdom</note>, namely, and the other virtues, of which things all poets are the parents, as well as those craftsmen who are called inventors. But the greatest and most excellent prudence of all is that by which civil and domestic affairs are governed, the name of which is temperance and justice. Therefore, whoever is by nature full and pregnant with such virtues—and is thus divine—when the proper age approaches, he already longs to bring forth and generate, and therefore wanders everywhere seeking the beautiful in which he may generate. For in the ugly he would not generate at all. Therefore, being pregnant, he welcomes beautiful bodies more than deformed ones. But if, moreover, he finds a soul that is beautiful, noble, and well-disposed, he is wonderfully delighted by the concurrence of both beauties. In the presence of that person, he immediately abounds in discourse concerning virtue, discussing what a good man ought to be and what his duty is, and he strives to imbue him with this teaching. Indeed, by adhering to the beautiful and using it familiarly, he brings forth and begets what he had previously conceived, mindful of it both in absence and presence; and that which is born from it, he nourishes and educates in common with the other. Whence they contract a more august union and a firmer friendship with one another than the parents of mortal children, inasmuch as they communicate together in children who are more immortal and more beautiful. Indeed, anyone would choose to have such children rather than human ones; let him especially consider Homer and Hesiod, and emulate other poets, when he sees what kind of children they left behind: which, since they are immortal, have provided immortal glory and memory for their parents. Such children Lycurgus left to the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> as the saviors of Lacedaemon and almost all of Greece. Solon is also honored among you for the generation of his laws; and many others elsewhere among the Greeks and Barbarians, who have demonstrated many and noble works, begetting every virtue. To these men, many sacred temples have often been dedicated on account of such offspring, but for human children, never yet to anyone. Into these matters of love, O Socrates, you yourself might perhaps have entered by your own industry. But whether you may proceed further, even to the perfect mysteries of love, or..."

<summary>Diotima explains to Socrates that Love is the desire for immortality, achieved through procreation—either physically through children or spiritually through virtue, art, and laws. She argues that the soul's "offspring" (like the works of Homer or the laws of Solon) are superior to biological children because they grant eternal fame.</summary>

# BOOK
### PAGE XXV.

...look toward the sublime, for which this grace was intended. Take heed: whether you are able to proceed further or not, I do not know. I will tell you, however, and I will assist you with all my zeal. You, for your part, strive to follow me with all your strength. For it is necessary that he who is to proceed correctly along this path must, from his youth, contemplate beautiful bodies. And first, if he is led rightly, he should love one single body, and there generate beautiful discourses. Then he should consider that the beauty which exists in any one body is the sibling of the beauty in another body. And if it is proper to follow what is beautiful in form, it is absurd to believe that the beauty which exists in all bodies is not one and the same. And he who notices this ought to become a lover of all beautiful bodies in general, and by this reasoning, relax the intensity of his love toward one, and think little of that single form.

After this, he should consider the beauty in the soul to be more excellent than that in the body; so much so, that if someone is of a noble mind, even if the beauty of their body yields to others, he should deem it sufficient, and love, and care for them, and give birth to such discourses, and seek out all conversations which can make young men better. Thus, he is led to behold the beauty found in duties and laws <note>original: "officiis ac legibus"</note>, and he should understand that all of it is uniform and related to itself, so that he may think little of the beauty concerning the body.

After duties and laws, let him pass to the sciences, so that he may contemplate the beauty of the sciences. And while he beholds that which overflows with ample beauty, he should no longer admire the form of a single boy like a slave, nor be content with the beauty of one man or one duty. For whoever fails in this is a meager and abject servant. But let him plunge himself into the deep sea of beauty, where by that very intuition, he may abundantly give birth to many, noble, and magnificent reasonings and understandings in philosophy; until, strengthened and invigorated there, he may at last behold one such science, which is the science of such beauty.

Now, apply the sharpness of your mind with all your strength. Whoever has been led step by step through the matters of love, having beheld beautiful things in the correct order, and now reaching the end of the affective journey of love, will suddenly behold a certain nature of marvelous beauty. This is that for the sake of which we underwent all the preceding labors. In the first place, it always exists; it is neither born nor does it perish; it neither grows nor decreases. Furthermore, it is not beautiful in one part and ugly in another, nor beautiful at one time and not at another. Nor is it beautiful in relation to this thing and ugly in relation to that. Nor is it beautiful here and ugly there, as if it were beautiful to some but by no means to others. Nor again will beauty itself be imagined as a certain face, or beautiful hands, or anything else in which a body participates. Nor is it like a certain speech, or reason, or some science. Nor will he think it lies in another, such as in an animal, or the earth, or the sky, or anything else; but it exists as itself, by itself, with itself, always uniform. All other things which are beautiful are beautiful through participation in it; on this condition, that while others are born and perish, nothing is taken away from it or added to it, nor does it incur any change.

When someone, ascending from these things by loving legitimately, begins to look upon that beauty itself, he has almost reached the end. This is indeed the way to proceed correctly toward matters of love, or to be led by another: namely, when someone begins to ascend from these beautiful things for the sake of that beauty, using them as if they were steps, passing from one first to two, and from two to all bodies that are beautiful; from these to all beautiful duties; from beautiful duties to beautiful doctrines; and finally coming from many doctrines to that doctrine which is the doctrine of nothing other than that beauty itself. And so at last, he contemplates what beauty itself is.

In this state of life, O Socrates, if anywhere else, a man must live, namely, in beholding beauty itself. If you ever see it, you will judge it to be precious beyond what can be said of gold, or ornate garments, or beautiful boys and youths. When you and many others look upon these now, you are utterly stunned; and if it were possible, you would choose to be always among them, neglecting food and drink. How happy do we think that spectacle would be, if it should happen that one beholds beauty itself—sincere, whole, pure, simple, not contaminated by human flesh, colors, or other mortal trifles—but beholds the divine beauty itself, fruitful in itself. Do you think the life of a man who looks up there, who contemplates so noble a spectacle, and who clings to it, would be worthless? Do you not consider that there alone, seeing beauty with that eye by which it can be perceived, he will give birth not to images of virtue, but to virtues themselves; since he touches not a shadow, but the reality itself? And when he has given birth to and nourished true virtue, he will become a friend of God; and if any other man is, he especially shall be immortal.

These things, O Phædrus and other guests, Diotima said. I believe her, and I strive to persuade others: that human nature cannot easily find anything more conducive to the possession of blessed immortality than legitimate love. Wherefore, I judge that love ought to be honored by all men. Indeed, I cultivate matters of love, and I exercise myself in them to the highest degree, and I exhort others. And now and always, according to the faculty of my talent, I praise the power and fortitude of love. This speech, O Phædrus, if you wish, consider as a certain eulogy of love; but if it pleases you to call it otherwise, call it so.

When he had said these things, as Aristodemus reported, all the rest approved. Aristophanes alone tried to object, because Socrates had made mention of his speech earlier. But suddenly the door of the hall was struck and made a sound, and the shout of reveling youths and a flute-player was heard. Then Agatho said: "Attendants, see who has arrived; and if any of our friends are among them, invite them to us. If no one, announce that we are no longer drinking, but are already resting." But a little later they heard the voice of Alcibiades, insulting in his drunkenness, and shouting loudly in the vestibule. He demanded where Agatho was and ordered himself to be led to him. Therefore, the flute-player and others of his companions led him in; and he stood at the doors of the hall, crowned with a thick wreath of ivy and violets, and his head bound with many ribbons—

When he had sat down, he congratulated Agatho and crowned him. Agatho said, "Boys, unbind Alcibiades' sandals so that he may lie down as a third on this couch." Alcibiades agreed and asked who the third guest was; turning around, he saw Socrates. Jumping up, he cried, "By Hercules! What is this? Have you sat here to waylay me again, Socrates? When he had filled the vessel, he drank first himself; then he ordered it to be poured for Socrates, saying, "Against Socrates, O guests, this trick of mine achieves nothing. However much one orders him, he will drink it all, and you will never see him drunk." As the boy poured, Socrates drank. Then Eryximachus said, "What are we doing, Alcibiades? I shall attempt, O fellow guests, to praise Socrates through images. He will perhaps suspect that I am turning my speech toward ridicule. But the image will be used for the sake of truth, not for laughter." ALCIBIADES.

## PAGE XXV.

...often when we hear someone else recounting the words of another, even if they are a very good orator, we nevertheless feel—if I may put it this way—that those words belong to no one. But when someone hears you, or hears your words being recounted by any other person, no matter how unskilled the speaker might be, and whether the listener is a man, a woman, or a youth, we are struck with amazement and seized in our minds. Indeed, if I did not suspect that I might seem too drunk, I would affirm under oath the things I have experienced from this man's words in the past, and which I still experience even now whenever I hear him. Much more than those who dance in the manner of the **Corybantes** <note>Priests of Cybele known for wild, ecstatic dancing</note>, my heart leaps within me because of his words; I shed tears, and I see this same thing happening to many others. 

And when I used to hear **Pericles** <note>The famous Athenian statesman and orator</note> and other good orators, they seemed to me to speak excellently; but nothing of this sort happened to me, nor was my soul stirred, nor did it condemn itself as if it were living the life of a slave. But by this **Marsyas** <note>A satyr who challenged Apollo to a musical contest; here used as a metaphor for Socrates's captivating "music" or speech</note> of ours, I am often so moved that I feel I simply cannot go on living in my current state. Do not deny these things, O Socrates. For I know for certain that if I were willing to lend him my ears at this moment, I could not bear it; the same things would happen to me. For he forces me to admit that while I myself am deficient in many things, I nevertheless neglect myself and instead attend to the affairs of the Athenian people. 

By force, therefore, as if plugging my ears against the **Sirens**, I flee from him and avoid him, lest I grow old sitting by his side. I suffer a feeling toward this man alone that no one would believe: that I am held back by a sense of shame and modesty. And him alone I fear. For I am conscious that I cannot defend myself or deny that I should do the things he commands; but when I leave him, I am overcome by the ambition for popular favor. <margin>24104</margin> I flee from him, therefore, and avoid him; and whenever I look at him, I am seized by shame because I have not kept my promises, so that I often wish he would depart from this life. Yet again, if that were to happen, I know I would tolerate it with far more difficulty. Therefore, I do not know where to turn or how to deal with this man. 

And such things have happened to me and many others from the melodies of this Satyr. But hear the rest, so that you may see how like he is to those things I compared him to, and behold the wonderful power he possesses. Know that none of you truly knows Socrates. But I shall show you, since I have already begun to speak. You see how vehemently Socrates is affected toward beautiful youths: he is always among them and is struck with wonder; he pretends to be ignorant of everything and to know nothing. This outward appearance is exactly like a **Silenus** <note>A tutor of Bacchus, often depicted as a hollow statue that was ugly on the outside but contained golden images of gods inside</note>. Know then that he is clothed in this outward form like a carved Silenus. But if he were opened up inside, O fellow guests, what temperance and integrity dwell there! For he does not value the beauty of anyone's body, nor riches, nor honors, nor the other things the common people admire; but he despises all these things more than can be imagined and counts them as nothing. 

Therefore, I tell you that we are nothing to him; yet he acts the **ironist** <note>original: "ironicus" - referring to Socratic irony, where he feigns ignorance</note> and never ceases to joke openly about these matters. But when he is acting seriously and is opened up within, I do not know if any of you has ever seen the divine images that lie hidden inside. I certainly have seen them at times; and they seemed to me so divine, and golden, and beautiful, and wonderful, that I thought it in no way right to act otherwise than as Socrates commands. 

I once thought, O fellow guests, that Socrates was truly delighted by my beauty, and I thought I had found a wonderful and lucky opportunity for what I desired. Indeed, I decided to gratify Socrates so that he would share with me everything he knew. For I thought my beauty was something great and wonderful, and I trusted in it greatly. And whereas before I was never accustomed to speak with him without a companion, once, when the companion was sent away, he remained alone with me. I must reveal the whole truth to you. Pay attention, I pray. If I lie, Socrates, refute me yourself. Indeed, O fellow guests, I was alone with him; I hoped he would say the same things to me that lovers are accustomed to say to their beloveds when they are alone. I rejoiced greatly in this hope. But nothing of the sort happened: instead, as was his custom, after he had discussed things until evening, he left. 

After this, I challenged him to the wrestling grounds and exercised with him, as if I would achieve something there; so we often practiced gymnastics together alone. Why use many words? I had no success. But when I had in no way succeeded by this means, I decided to attack this man with more difficult engines of war and not to desist from my undertaking. Hear how vehemently I laid snares for him. I invited him to dinner, just as a lover lays snares for the beloved. He did not comply easily or at first; but finally, he gave in. He came, then; but having taken his food, he rose to leave immediately. Then, held back by shame, I permitted him to go. But laying other, more vehement snares, I protracted our conversation after dinner far into the night; and when he wanted to leave, I forced him to stay, citing the lateness of the hour. He rested, therefore, on the couch next to mine where he had sat for dinner, and no one else slept there that night except us. What has been said so far can be told anywhere without a blush. 

<margin>
Proverb
Wine and childhood are truthful.
How those bitten by a viper are affected.
</margin>

But what follows, you shall not hear until I have recounted that proverb: **Wine and childhood**—and even without childhood—**are truthful.** <note>A variation of "In vino veritas"</note> Indeed, it seems just that he who praises Socrates should not pass over his proud and unconquered deed in silence. Furthermore, I am affected no differently than one who is bitten by a viper. For they say such a person is unwilling to reveal his suffering except to those who have been similarly afflicted; as if only these, being not ignorant of the pain, would forgive him if, compelled by torture, he did not hesitate to say and do everything. I, therefore, being bound more than others by the more vehement bite of **philosophy**, which is the sharpest of all—and whether it be the heart, or the soul, or whatever it should be called, wounded by the desire for philosophical discourse, which bites more sharply than a viper and takes hold of a youthful soul that is not entirely cowardly, compelling it to do and say whatever it may—I decided to leave nothing untried to make Socrates most closely joined to me to satisfy this thirst. I would not say the things I am about to say, were I not speaking before these guests, whom I have always seen as if seized by a certain insane frenzy of philosophy and acting like Bacchants: the **Phaedruses, Agathons, Eryximachuses, Pausaniases, Aristodemuses, Aristophaneses**, and finally Socrates himself, and the rest. For these things should not be told by me except to those who have felt the same. Therefore, you who hear will grant me pardon for the things that were then done by me and are now spoken. But as for the servants and any other profane or rustic person who may be present...

You are trying to win the reality of beauty in exchange for the appearance of it: to receive gold for brass. But, O blessed one, look more closely, lest my condition escapes you, for I may be of no value.

Then the eye of the mind begins to see clearly only when the eye of the body begins to fade. You, however, are still far from that age." ALCI. "My feelings are exactly as I have stated. I do not have one thing on my lips and another in my heart. You must decide what you think will be best for both you and me." SO. "You speak well. Therefore, hereafter we shall consult together and do what we think most profitable for us both, in this and in all other matters." When I heard this, I thought I had struck him as if with a javelin; rising up, I allowed him to say not another word. Wrapping him in this cloak you see—for it was winter—I lay down under his old mantle and, with these arms, I embraced this happy, wise, and truly marvelous man, and so I rested the whole night. These things, O Socrates, I know you will not deny. Yet he, utterly despising the beauty in which I so greatly trusted, mocked and looked down on it with pride. I call all the gods and goddesses to witness, O Judges—for you are the judges of Socratic pride—that I rose from that bed no differently than if I had slept with my father or an older brother. What do you think my state of mind was after this? I felt myself despised, yet I admired his nature, his temperance <term>temperantia: self-control or moderation</term>, and his fortitude, having found a man such as I never believed I would find for wisdom and endurance. Therefore, I could find no reason to be angry with him or to leave him, nor any means to win him over. I knew he could no more be conquered by money than Ajax could be by steel; and the one way I hoped he might be trapped had failed me. So I wandered about, more enslaved to this man than anyone ever was to another. All these things happened then. Later, we served together in the military campaign against Potidaea <note>A Greek city-state; the siege took place c. 432–430 BCE</note>, and Socrates and I were messmates in that army. First, in enduring hardships, he surpassed not only me but everyone else. If we were cut off from supplies, as often happens in war, no one was his equal in bearing hunger and thirst. Yet, in times of plenty and at military feasts, he alone seemed able to enjoy them. Even if he did not wish to drink, if compelled, he surpassed everyone; and what is most wonderful, no one ever saw him drunk. But I think this may be proven further in the future. Against the winters and the cold, which are most bitter in those parts, he did wonders. For when there was a most intense and intolerable frost, so that no one dared leave their tents—and if they did, they went out heavily wrapped, their feet and legs bound in skins and wool—Socrates went out among the other soldiers in the same clothing he usually wore. He walked barefoot over the ice more easily than others did in shoes. The soldiers, seeing this, suspected he was looking down on them. Such was Socrates in these matters. But it is worth hearing what this most enduring man did elsewhere in the same army. For when some thought occurred to him, he stood thinking in the same spot from morning; and when he could not unravel what he was thinking, he remained standing, not giving up, and it was already noon. The soldiers noticed this and wondered, telling one another that Socrates had been standing there thinking since dawn. Finally, some Ionian soldiers, when night was falling, brought their bedding out after dinner—it was summer then—and lay under the open sky to watch if he would persist through the night. Socrates stood there until the following dawn and the rising of the sun. Then he went away, after he had offered a prayer to the sun at its rising. His conduct in battles, too, must not be passed over in silence. For in that battle where the generals gave me the prize for the best fighter, no one else saved me but Socrates. You see, though I was severely wounded, he would not desert me, but leaping in front of me, he protected both me and my armor and saved me from the enemy. And I then urged that the prize be given not to me, but to Socrates, by whom I had been saved. You cannot refute this, Socrates, nor deny it as false. But the generals, looking to my rank, preferred to give it to me, while you, O Socrates, were the first to urge that the honor be shown to me and not to yourself. It is also worth remembering how Socrates behaved during our retreat from Delium <note>A battle in 424 BCE where the Athenians were defeated by the Boeotians</note>. For I was present on horseback, while Socrates was on foot. Our forces being routed and everyone in flight, Socrates and Laches were retreating together. When I happened upon them, I told them to be of good heart and said I would not desert them. Here I could observe Socrates even better than at Potidaea, for being on horseback, I was in less danger. First, I could see how much he surpassed Laches in caution and presence of mind. Then he seemed to me, O Aristophanes, as you yourself [wrote]...

### THE SYMPOSIUM

<page-num>XXV.</page-num>

...you say, he departed there no differently than he does here: haughty, calmly surveying everything with his eyes, and cautiously examining each detail. Indeed, he looked back at enemies and citizens in turn, carrying himself with such a look and aspect that he showed even to those far off that if anyone should attack him, it would not be done with impunity. Thus, he and his companion went away safely; for almost no one attacks those who depart in such a manner, but rather those who flee in headlong flight. In many other things, Socrates can be wonderfully praised; but such things are of a kind that perhaps some others might also deserve the same praise. Truly, those qualities are chief in him by which he is found to be like no other man, neither among the ancients nor the moderns. For just as Achilles was, one might perhaps guess Brasidas <note>A famous Spartan general</note> and certain others to have been; and as Pericles was, so were Antenor and Nestor. There are others also who can be compared to one another in this way. But as to what kind of man Socrates is, and what his wonderful manner of speaking is like, no one comes near to his likeness, neither of the ancients nor of those who exist now—unless, as I have now said, I compare him to others. For he himself is like no man, but rather to the Sileni and Satyrs, as are his speeches.

For this also I had omitted before: his speeches are like the statues of Sileni made by craftsmen, which, when opened, reveal images of gods. For if anyone listens to his speeches, they seem at first glance, as they say, to be exceedingly absurd. Indeed, the names and words on the exterior surface present the character of some insulting Satyr. For he always has donkeys, blacksmiths, shoemakers, and tanners in his mouth, and he seems to always say the same things about the same subjects, so that almost all who are less experienced or skilled mock his words. But if one looks inside his speeches, he will first find that they alone of all others possess a depth of meaning; and furthermore, they are most divine, containing many most beautiful images of the virtues, and extending themselves to many things—indeed, they encompass all the precepts by which he who is to live honestly and well ought to be instructed. These are the things, O fellow guests, for which I praise Socrates; and also those of which I complain. For you have heard meanwhile what injuries he has brought upon me. Nor has he behaved this way toward me alone, but also toward Charmides, son of Glaucon, and toward Euthydemus, son of Diocles, and many others he has done the same: whom he deceived under the guise of a lover, for instead of the lover, he turned out to be the beloved. Therefore, I warn you too, Agatho: beware of his pretenses and dissimulations, and knowing him from these things I have suffered, look to your own interest; do not, according to the proverb, finally recognize your mistakes only after the punishment, like infants.

<margin>
Proverb: You recognize your faults after the punishment, like infants.
</margin>

Thus far spoke Alcibiades, whose boldness and freedom of speech provoked laughter in everyone, since he seemed to be captivated by the love of Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** You seem to me to be sober, O Alcibiades. Otherwise, you would never have so artfully made such a long circuit of words to hide that for the sake of which you said everything else—which you finally added at the tail end of your speech as if you were bringing it up by chance: as if you did not say all these things for the purpose of dividing me from Agatho. You think that I ought to love no one but you alone, and that Agatho should be loved by no one else but you. But your Satyric and Silenic fiction did not escape us. But, O friend Agatho, care must be taken so that his machinations do not profit him, and that no discord is made between me and you by any of his slanders.

**AGATHO:** You seem to speak the truth, O Socrates. For to separate us, he placed himself in the middle between you and me. But this will profit him nothing; for rising from here, I will sit near you.

**SOCRATES:** So it must be done indeed. Sit here below me.

**ALCIBIADES:** By Jupiter! What things this man compels me to endure! He wishes to surpass me in everything. At least permit Agatho to sit here in the middle.

**SOCRATES:** By no means is it fitting. For you have praised me. It is necessary, however, that I now praise this man sitting to my right. If, therefore, Agatho remains after you, he will hardly praise me again before he is praised by me. But let him be, happy man, and do not envy him my praises. Indeed, I desire to praise him vehemently.

**AGATHO:** Ha, ha, Alcibiades! Why do I stay here? I am leaving now so that Socrates may praise me.

**ALCIBIADES:** This is the custom of Socrates: that when he is present, no one else is allowed to win over the beautiful for themselves. See now, I pray, how easily and by what probable reasoning he has drawn this man to himself.

Agatho therefore rose to rest near Socrates. Then suddenly many revelers, finding the doors open (for someone had gone out just before), entered and sat down among them. By their noise, everything was thrown into confusion, and after this, no limit was observed in drinking. Aristodemus recounted that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others had left; and that he himself had slept for a long time (for the nights were long then) and rose around dawn as the cocks were already crowing. Having been awakened from sleep, he found that some of the others were sleeping, while others had departed. But Agatho, Aristophanes, and Socrates alone were still awake, drinking from a large bowl, passing it to the right in turn. Socrates, however, was arguing continuously. Aristodemus said he did not remember the rest of the discussion, for he had not been there from the beginning and was heavy with sleep. But the sum of that disputation was this: that Socrates was compelling them to admit that it is the office of the same man to compose both tragedy and comedy, and that he who is a tragic poet by art is also a comic poet. When they had conceded these things, compelled rather than persuaded, Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then Agatho as the light was already rising. But Socrates, while they were sleeping, set out for the Lyceum <note>A gymnasium and public meeting place in Athens</note>, with Aristodemus following him as he was accustomed; and having washed in his usual manner, he spent the whole day in his activities, and finally at evening rested at home.

->THE END OF THE SYMPOSIUM<-

# Argument on the *Phaedrus* by Marsilio Ficino. Folio 179.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument on the *Phaedrus*.

Our Plato, pregnant with the fury of the poetic muse—which he followed from a tender age, or rather from his Apolline birth—first gave birth to a book that is almost entirely poetic and most radiant. Concerning beauty and Love simultaneously, it is a most beautiful work, most worthy of everyone's love. Justly, he thereafter produced his other children full of loveliness and grace, having ventured a happy beginning from the Venusian muse; he alone of all men everywhere joined loveliness with dignity. Since we have explained many of the mysteries of this book in our *Theology* and our book *On Love* <note>Ficino refers to his own works, *Theologia Platonica* and *De Amore*</note>, we shall touch upon its argument very briefly. The *Symposium* treats primarily of Love, and consequently of beauty. But the *Phaedrus* disputes concerning love for the sake of Beauty. Nor is the speech of Lysias and the dispute of the orator inserted without reason. For beauty pertains to the mind, to sight, and to hearing. Thus it happens that where he treats of the beauty of souls and divinities, and likewise of the beauty of the body, he rightly disputes the beauty of speech.

Immediately in the very beginning, Socrates, while joking, hands down very serious precepts: that all things must be utterly despised for the sake of the study of wisdom; and that the most important study of wisdom is to consider oneself. Amidst these things, the most skillful description of the place allegorically signifies the Academy: the Plane tree signifies Plato; the chaste shrub signifies the chastity of Platonic and Socratic love; the fountain signifies bounty in communicating wisdom; the other ornaments signify the oratorical and poetic flowers in which Plato’s Academy abounds. Lysias is rightly criticized because he asks what the effect of love is without first defining or distinguishing love itself. Consider, amidst this, the modesty of Socratic love, for being about to pronounce things that are not at all honorable, he begins with his head covered. Soon he invokes the Muses, so that they might honor a less-than-honorable matter with at least their own splendor of eloquence.

But before he disparages the base lover, lest he fall into the same fault as Lysias, he defines base love as a certain desire or lust rebelling against reason, which snatches one away from the opinion tending toward the right and toward the pleasure of forms. But while he proceeds to the definition, he grants us two guides: one is an inborn appetite for pleasure; the other is a certain legitimate opinion acquired gradually through discipline and leading toward honorable things. Truly, two external forces move these internal guides: a certain "golden" spirit <term>Dæmon: in this context, a guiding spirit or intermediary being, not a malevolent demon</term> moves opinion, while a "watery" one moves lust. After he has defined it, he separates the youth from base loves with many reasons.

Then, meanwhile, note a wonderful mystery, similar to the Mosaic mystery <note>A reference to the secrets of Moses or the Hebrew scriptures</note>. In the very beginning of most evils, some spirit mingles pleasure. Since he acts not so much a philosophical as a poetic persona, he describes himself as being seized by a spirit because he disparaged Love, which is the name of a god. He does this so that Love may be distinguished, and he distinguishes it in a poetic rather than a dialectical manner. In this, he observes that it is a most grave sin to offend against the name of a god. Again, there is a power of presage in the soul. Then, by certain poetic windings, he separates art from fury <term>Furor: divine inspiration or "madness" that elevates the soul</term>. He divides fury into the divine and the human. The divine he divides into four: namely, prophecy, mystery <note>or ritual/priestly madness</note>, poetry, and love. He confirms providence and religion. He places wisdom infused by divine fury far before human wisdom.

Before he completes the treatment of particular souls, he brings common souls into the midst: the soul of the world, which he names Jove <note>Jupiter</note>; and under it the twelve souls of the twelve mundane spheres, to which he subjects as many orders of spirits and as many particular souls. He assigns chariots to each—that is, celestial and eternal bodies. He disputes concerning rational souls, both divine and human; concerning the circuit of both; and by what reason the souls of men both accompany the contemplation of celestial souls in heaven and follow the intuition of the angelic above heaven. What the soul is, the vehicle of the Chariot, the wings, the charioteer, the horses, Fate, and the fall into the body, and again what the great Jove is in heaven and the other following gods, we explain in our *Theology*. It will be enough for you to understand at present that the twin wings are a twin instinct inborn in the mind elevating it above the soul: in the intellect, an instinct toward divine truth; in the will, an instinct toward divine good, converting it by its powers. When these wings relax, the inclination of the vegetative nature stretches toward governing corporeal things; the Pythagoreans think that souls, with their wings now broken, descend into the elements.

After this, he distributes the soul falling from heaven into nine grades. In all these things, he uses poetic license and relates Pythagorean matters rather than his own. Amidst these, notice that a similar fall of souls is described by the Pythagoreans and the demonic prophets. Also, the number nine fits both the angelic choirs and the spirits fallen from there. I pass over now that Pherecydes the Syrian relates a similar fall happened to spirits. And he adds that *Ophioneus*—that is, the demonic serpent—was the head of the army rebelling against the divine mind. Similar to this is what is contained in the divine mysteries: namely, that Jove cast down the lower spirits to the underworld.

But let us return to the dialogue. Finally, the man with a purified mind devoted to God is filled with all good things from there, and he alone is wise; he who, as if placed outside himself, is mocked by the common people as if insane. After this, he descends to the divine, legitimate fury of love, which he thinks is kindled in the soul when, beholding a beautiful form of the body, it easily remembers the divine beauty which it had once contemplated; it is inflamed by the desire of recovering that beauty, and it rages. But he describes a fury contrary to this, as if bestial, not ascending from the form of the body to divine intuition, but basely descending to Venusian intercourse. He describes again a certain human fury between the divine and the bestial, kindled in the soul of one who, occupied by admiration of corporeal form, neither consigns the divine to oblivion entirely, nor...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces Plato's "Phaedrus," interpreting it as a poetic and divinely inspired work that explores the relationship between earthly beauty, divine love, and the soul's journey.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the summary and translation of Plato's Phaedrus, specifically focusing on the transition from the philosophical analysis of the soul to the critique of rhetoric and the beginning of the dialogue itself.</meta>

# XXVI.

remembers. From which it happens, that he is neither entirely intemperate, nor yet entirely temperate: but at one moment he seems as if incontinent, and at another continent. Wherefore, he does not later flee to the stars—of which the souls were companions from the beginning—as the causes for which some love others more or less. For he disposes as many orders of human souls in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and the soul.</note> as there are stars in the sky. Here he returns again to dividing the powers of the soul: and indeed he calls Reason the charioteer: but the twin appetites he calls twin horses: the rational appetite the good horse: the irrational appetite the bad horse. But in this class, he considers the appetite verging toward anger to be less evil: while that declining toward lust is more evil. Then he depicts, almost like a poet, the passions of lovers, both the continent and the incontinent, and their mutual love. From which it follows, that these must be indulged allegorically, no differently than the *Songs of Solomon* <note>Ficino compares Plato's erotic imagery to the biblical Song of Songs to justify its spiritual interpretation.</note>. These things being done, when he had treated of the beauty which pertains to the mind and to sight, he now proceeds to examine the speech of Lysias, and to demonstrate the duty of the orator: so that it may be clear what kind of beauty belongs to speech, which pertains to hearing. He places the beauty of a speech in its order: namely, that it should have a head differing from the end: and that it should have a middle, necessarily coupled to the head and the end and to each other. He teaches that this kind of order is to be observed by the orator above all. Moreover, he proves that no one can be a true orator unless he has knowledge of things, especially human affairs and souls. However, so that the orator may attain this, he teaches that he should learn from the dialectician the faculty of dividing and composing: whom he wishes to be the principal instrument for investigating and finding the truth: and in the *Philebus* <note>Another Platonic dialogue.</note> he calls it a gift of the gods: because just as in the world the perpetual office of God is to divide and compose, so it is also the art of the dialectician. And therefore he judges the consummate dialectician—that is, the metaphysician—to be worshiped as if he were a god. After these things, he compares orators to one another and censures those who, preferring the plausible to the true, deceive the people and themselves: and foolishly trust that what is most like the truth can be known even without knowledge of the truth itself. Soon certain excellent well-known precepts follow. Three things are first necessary for an orator: Talent, Learning, and Practice. Philosophy is needed for the very perfection of any art. From dialectical exercise and the sublime contemplation of things, a sublimity of mind is finally prepared, effective even for action. Which two things are greatly necessary in the perfection of the greatest arts. Then he compares the illegitimate orator to cooks and flatterers, just as in the *Gorgias*: but the legitimate one to a physician. Accordingly, he hands down the rule that the nature of both the soul and the body, indeed of every thing, must be known: and immediately he returns to the duty of the orator. He adds that for the sake of writing itself, letters were discovered in Egypt by a certain demon <note>In the classical sense, a 'daimon' or spirit/lesser deity.</note> named Theuth, along with the other disciplines. Furthermore, he derides the zeal for writing, namely in that he trusts to reveal the truth to posterity through letters as if it were indubitable. And in the manner of the Pythagoreans, he approves the contemplation and tradition of truth in souls, rather than in books. Which he also confirms in his letters. Finally, he praises only that orator who becomes a philosopher by talent and study. He concludes the dialogue with a prayer, seeking beauty of the soul from God. In which, consider that Socrates, all other things being utterly despised, is content with the beauty of the soul alone—that is, wisdom: yet he judges that this very thing is obtained not so much by human study as by divine gift.

### PHAEDRUS, OR ON BEAUTY, TRANSLATED BY MARSILIO FICINO TO THE MAGNANIMOUS LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

-> CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE. <-
-> SOCRATES AND PHAEDRUS. <-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a classical figure (possibly a scholar or deity) seated and holding a book or tablet, surrounded by architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>

**SOCRATES:** My friend Phaedrus, to where and from where? **PHAEDRUS:** From Lysias, O Socrates, the son of Cephalus. But I am going for a walk outside the city. For I sat with him a long time, from morning until this very hour. But having been persuaded by your and my companion Acumenus, I am exercising by walking, which kind of exercise he thinks is easier and more healthful than a running contest. **SOCRATES:** He advises well indeed, O friend. But Lysias was, as it seems, in the city. **PHAEDRUS:** He was. For he is staying with Epicrates in this house of Morychus, next to the Olympium. **SOCRATES:** What was he doing there? Did Lysias perhaps entertain you with a feast of speeches? **PHAEDRUS:** You shall know, if only you have the leisure to hear me as you walk along. **SOCRATES:** What indeed? Do you not think that I, according to Pindar, would prefer to hear your and Lysias's conversation even over business? **PHAEDRUS:** Proceed then. **SOCRATES:** Speak then. **PHAEDRUS:** And that discussion, O Socrates, is suited to your ears. For the talk that was held was, I know not how, about love. For Lysias had written an elaborate and brilliant speech, not indeed on behalf of a lover: but the speech was ingenious and elegant for this very reason, that he said one should gratify a non-lover rather than a lover. **SOCRATES:** O generous man! I wish he would write that one should gratify the poor rather than the rich, and the old rather than the young, and all others affected just as I and many of us are. For thus the speech would be sophisticated and publicly useful. Yet such a great desire for hearing has seized me, that even if you were to walk as far as Megara—and in the manner of Herodicus, when you reached the wall, you were to turn back immediately—I would not leave you. **PHAEDRUS:** What are you saying, best Socrates! Do you think that I, an unlearned man, can remember and relate as is worthy of him those things which Lysias, the most eloquent of all who now write, composed over a long time at leisure? I am certainly far from it, although I would truly rather have that ability than much gold. **SOCRATES:** O Phaedrus, if I do not know Phaedrus, I have also forgotten myself. But surely neither of these is the case. For I know for certain that he did not hear that speech of Lysias only once: but he ordered it to be repeated often...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Phaedrus as they leave the city of Athens. It follows their initial meeting where Phaedrus has just come from listening to a speech by the orator Lysias.</meta>

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON BEAUTY.

...to be discussed. Lysias, however, was willing to comply. But this was not enough for Phaedrus; instead, having finally taken up the book, he examined what he most desired. When he had done this, remaining diligent there since morning, he departed to take a walk—by the Dog <note>original: "per Canem"; a common Socratic oath, "by the dog of Egypt"</note> as I indeed believe—committing it to memory, unless perhaps the oration was too long. He was now heading outside the walls so that he might meditate on those very things. Meeting a man with an insane love for speeches <note>Socrates</note>, he was delighted by the sight, because he would have someone to share in his joy and exultation; and so he bid him to come along. Then, when he was asked to speak by that man so greedy for discourse, he pretended to be reluctant, as if he did not wish to recite it; but finally, even if no one wanted to hear it of their own accord, he was prepared to force it upon a listener. Therefore, Phaedrus, I would ask you to do for me now what you were going to do even without being asked.

**PHAEDRUS.** It is better then that I speak as best I can. For you seem as though you will not let me go until I have spoken to the best of my ability.

**SOCRATES.** You truly seem to understand me.

**PHAEDRUS.** Thus I shall do. But look, Socrates, I have not learned the actual words by heart; however, I hold the general sense of almost all the points by which he shows how a lover differs from a non-lover, and I shall proceed to relate them to you briefly in order.

**SOCRATES.** Show me first, my friend, what you have in your left hand under your cloak. For I suspect you have the book itself. If that is so, think of it this way: I hold you in high regard, but while Lysias is present, I have no intention of offering myself to you as a listener <note>Socrates prefers the written text of the master to Phaedrus's paraphrase</note>; so come, show it.

**PHAEDRUS.** Stop. You have cast me down from a great hope, Socrates, which I had in you, as if I were going to exercise my mind along with yours. But where do you wish us to sit and read?

**SOCRATES.** Let us turn aside here toward the Ilissus river; afterward, wherever it seems best, we shall sit and rest.

**PHAEDRUS.** I am very fortunately barefoot; for you, of course, always are. It will be easy for us to wade through the water itself, and not unpleasant, especially at this time of year and day.

**SOCRATES.** Lead on then, and at the same time look for where we might sit.

**PHAEDRUS.** Do you see that very tall Plane tree?

**SOCRATES.** I see it.

**PHAEDRUS.** There is shade there, a gentle breeze, and soft grass, wherever we might wish to sit or even lie down.

**SOCRATES.** Lead on then.

**PHAEDRUS.** Tell me, Socrates. Is it not said that here, once upon a time, Boreas <note>The North Wind</note> snatched Orithyia from the Ilissus?

**SOCRATES.** So it is said.

**PHAEDRUS.** And does not the water here appear pleasant, pure, and clear, and suitable for girls' play?

**SOCRATES.** Not at all; but a little further down, about two or three stadia <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet</note>, where we find the temple of Diana; and there is a certain altar of Boreas there.

**PHAEDRUS.** I did not know that. But tell me by Jove, Socrates: do you believe this fable to be true?

**SOCRATES.** If I did not believe it, like the wise men, I would not be out of place; then, interpreting the matter, I would say that the wind Boreas pushed Orithyia while she was playing with Pharmacia from the nearby rocks, and thus she died, and was imagined to have been snatched by Boreas; or from the Areopagus. For there is also another story that she was snatched not from this place, but from that one. But I, Phaedrus, think these things are pleasant; yet they belong to a man who is overly curious and anxious, and not particularly fortunate, if for no other reason than that he must then explain the form of Centaurs and the Chimera. And there also flows in a crowd of Gorgons and Pegasuses, and a multitude of other monstrous forms. So if someone does not believe these things are as they are told, but wants to bring each one down to a probable sense, being supported by a certain rustic wisdom, he will need far too much leisure. But I have no leisure for these things, for this reason, my friend: because I am not yet able, according to the Delphic precept, to know myself. <margin>It is ridiculous to want to scrutinize the affairs of others when they are ignorant of their own.</margin> Therefore I think it ridiculous, while I am ignorant of my own self, to want to scrutinize the affairs of others. Therefore, dismissing these things and accepting the common opinion about them, I consider not the myths, but myself: whether I am some beast more complex than Typhon, and more burning and furious, or a calmer and simpler animal, participating by nature in some divine and gentle lot. But my friend, was not this the tree to which you were leading us?

**PHAEDRUS.** This is certainly it.

**SOCRATES.** By Juno, a beautiful retreat. For that Plane tree is very spreading with its branches and tall; and the height of that willow which they call "chaste" <note>The Agnus Castus tree</note> provides a very beautiful and lovely shade; and it is now at the peak of its flowering, so that the whole place is filled with the sweetness of its scent. A very clear spring also flows under the Plane tree with very cold water, as can be guessed by the touch of a foot. The little statues of girls and other images here testify that it is sacred to the nymphs and Achelous. Do you not also notice how pleasant and sweet a breeze blows here; moreover, something summery and musical resounds from the choir of cicadas. But most ornate of all is to look at the grass itself, how it is suited to gently support the head of one reclining on the sweetly sloping meadow. And so you have led me here most excellently, like a guest, friend Phaedrus.

**PHAEDRUS.** O admirable man, you seem most strange; and indeed, as you say, you are like a guest being led, not a local inhabitant: so much so that you appear never to have crossed our borders, nor even to have gone outside the walls.

**SOCRATES.** Forgive me, best Phaedrus. For <margin>That one must live among men, not among trees.</margin> I am desirous of learning; the fields and trees can teach me nothing, but the men who dwell in the city can. You, however, seem to have found the incentive for me to go out. For just as they lead hungry animals by holding out leaves or fruit, so you, by holding out a book to me, could lead me through all of Attica and anywhere else you wish. Now then, since we have arrived here, it pleases me to recline. And you, in whatever posture it seems you can read most comfortably, take it up and read.

**PHAEDRUS.** Listen then. "My affairs stand thus: and I think it will be most advantageous for us, as you have heard. But I think I ought to obtain what I ask from you no less because I am not captured by love for you. For lovers, as soon as they have satisfied their lust, repent of the benefit conferred; but those who are not ensnared by love never repent. For they conferred benefits not by compulsion, but <margin>The speech of Lysias against lovers.</margin> voluntarily, as they best consulted their own affairs according to their means. Furthermore, lovers sometimes revolve in their minds how they have neglected their own business because of love, and what benefits they have conferred to their own loss, and what labors they have undergone; and therefore they think they have returned a worthy thanks to their beloveds. But those who are not deceived by love, neither neglect their domestic affairs, nor past labors, nor the discord of their kinsmen..."

# BOOK V.

remembers. From this it follows that he is neither entirely intemperate nor entirely temperate: but appears at one moment incontinent, and at another continent. Therefore, in responding to the causes for which some love others more or less, he flees to the stars, of which the souls were companions from the beginning. However, so that the orator may achieve this, he instructs him to learn from the <term>dialectician</term> <note>A philosopher skilled in logical analysis and division.</note> the faculty of dividing and composing: whom he wishes to be the chief instrument for investigating truth: and in the *Philebus* he calls it a gift of God: because just as in the world the perpetual office of God is to divide and compose, so it is for the dialectician in his art. And therefore he judges the consummate dialectician—that is, the metaphysician—to be honored as if he were a god. After this, he compares orators with one another and rebukes those who, preferring the "likely" to the "true," deceive the people and themselves; they foolishly trust that they can recognize what is most like the truth even without knowledge of the truth itself. Soon certain excellent principles are noted. Three things are primarily necessary for the orator: Talent, Learning, and Practice. Philosophy is needed for the very perfection of any art. From dialectical practice and the contemplation of sublime things, a sublimity of mind and an effective power for action are finally acquired. These two are greatly necessary for the perfection of the greatest arts. Then he compares the illegitimate orator to cooks and flatterers, just as in the *Gorgias*: but the legitimate one to a physician. Accordingly, he hands down the rule that the nature of both the soul and the body—indeed, of every thing—must be known: and immediately returns to the duty of the orator. He adds that for the sake of this, the writing of letters was invented in Egypt by a certain demon <note>In the Renaissance sense, a "daimon" or supernatural spirit.</note> named Theuth, along with the other disciplines. Furthermore, he mocks the zeal for writing, namely in that one trusts to reveal the indubitable truth to posterity through letters. And in the manner of the Pythagoreans, he approves the contemplation and tradition of truth in souls rather than in books. This he also confirms in his letters. Finally, he praises only that orator who is a philosopher by talent and study. He concludes the dialogue with a speech and prayers seeking beauty of the soul from God. In this, consider that Socrates, having utterly despised all other things, is content with the beauty of the soul alone—that is, wisdom: yet he judges that this itself is acquired not so much by human study as by divine gift.

**Socrates:** My friend Phaedrus, where to and from where? <margin>PHAEDRUS: From Lysias, O Socrates, the son of Cephalus.</margin> I am going for a walk outside the city. For I sat with him a long time, remaining there from morning until this hour. But having been persuaded by your and my companion Acumenus, I am exercising by walking, for he thinks this kind of exercise is easier and more healthful than a running contest. <margin>SOCRATES: He advises well indeed, my friend. But Lysias, it seems, was in the city. PHAEDRUS: He was. For he is staying with Epicrates in the house of Morychus, near the temple of Olympian Zeus. SOCRATES: What was he doing there? Did Lysias perhaps entertain you with a feast of speeches? PHAEDRUS: You shall know, if you have the leisure to hear it while walking with me. SOCRATES: What indeed? Do you not think that I, according to Pindar, would prefer to hear your and Lysias's conversation even over business? PHAEDRUS: Lead on then. SOCRATES: Speak then. PHAEDRUS: And that discussion, O Socrates, is suited to your ears. For the talk that was held was, I know not how, about love. For Lysias had written an elaborate and brilliant speech, not indeed on behalf of a lover: but the speech was skillful and elegant for this very reason, that he said one should gratify a non-lover rather than a lover. SOCRATES: O generous man! I wish he would write that one should gratify the poor rather than the rich, and the old rather than the young, and all others affected just as I and many of us are. For then the speech would be witty and of public use. Yet such a great desire for hearing has seized me, that even if you were to walk as far as Megara, and in the manner of Herodicus, having reached the wall, you should immediately turn back from there, I would not leave you. PHAEDRUS: What are you saying, best Socrates! Do you think that I, an unlearned man, can remember and report those things which Lysias, the most eloquent of all who now write, composed over a long time at leisure, in a way worthy of him? I am certainly far from it; yet I would rather have that ability than much gold. SOCRATES: O Phaedrus, if I do not know Phaedrus, I have also forgotten myself. But surely neither of these is true. For I know certainly that he did not hear that speech of Lysias only once: but asked him to repeat it often...</margin>

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON BEAUTY. FOLIO CLXXX.

Lysias, however, was happy to comply. But this was not enough for Phaedrus; instead, finally taking the book, he examined what he most desired. When he had done this, staying there diligently from the morning, he went out for a walk—by the Dog <note>original: "per Canem"; a common Socratic oath</note>, as I believe—having committed it to memory, unless perhaps the speech was too long. He was weary, however, of being outside the walls, so that he might meditate on that very thing. Meeting a man with an insane love for discourse, he rejoiced at seeing him, because he would have a fellow-rejoicer and one to share his exultation; and he ordered him to walk along. Then, being asked to speak by that very man who was greedy for discourse, he pretended to be reluctant, as if he did not desire to recount it; yet finally, even if no one wanted to hear it of their own accord, he was going to be compelled by force to be heard. I would ask you then, Phaedrus, to do for me now what you were going to do even without being asked.

**PHAEDRUS:** It is better, then, that I speak as best I can. For you seem as though you will not let me go until I have spoken to the best of my ability.

**SOCRATES:** You truly seem that way to me.

**PHAEDRUS:** Thus I shall do. But I have not learned the actual words by heart, O Socrates; however, I hold the sense of almost all the points by which he shows how a lover differs from a non-lover. I proceed to relate these to you briefly in order.

**SOCRATES:** Show me first, my friend, what you have in your left hand under your cloak. For I suspect you have the book itself there. If that is so, think of it this way: I hold you in high regard, but while Lysias is present, I have no intention of offering myself to you as a listener <note>Socrates prefers to hear the written text of Lysias rather than Phaedrus's summary</note>. But come, show it.

**PHAEDRUS:** Stop. You have cast me down from the great hope I had in you, O Socrates, as if I were going to exercise my wits together with you. But where do you wish us to sit and read?

**SOCRATES:** Let us turn aside here toward the Ilissus river; afterward, wherever it seems best, we shall sit and rest.

**PHAEDRUS:** Very opportunely, I am barefoot; for you always are. It will be easy for us, then, to wade through the water itself, and not unpleasant, especially at this time of year and day.

**SOCRATES:** Lead on then, and at the same time look for where we may sit.

**PHAEDRUS:** Do you see that very tall Plane tree?

**SOCRATES:** I see it.

**PHAEDRUS:** There is shade there, and a moderate breeze, and soft grass, wherever we might wish to sit or even lie down.

**SOCRATES:** Lead on then.

**PHAEDRUS:** Tell me, O Socrates, is it not said that Boreas <note>The North Wind</note> once snatched Orithyia from here by the Ilissus?

**SOCRATES:** So it is said.

**PHAEDRUS:** And does not the water here appear pleasant, pure, and clear, and suited for maidenly games?

**SOCRATES:** Not at all; but a little lower down, about two or three stadia, where we find the temple of Diana; and there is a certain altar of Boreas there.

**PHAEDRUS:** I did not know it well. But tell me by Jove, Socrates: do you believe this fable was true?

**SOCRATES:** Now, if I did not believe it, like the wise men, I would not be absurd; then, explaining the matter, I would say that the wind Boreas pushed Orithyia while she was playing with Pharmacia from the nearby rocks, and thus she died, and was imagined to have been snatched here by Boreas—or from the Areopagus. For there is also another story that she was snatched not from this place, but from that one. But I, O Phaedrus, consider these things pleasant indeed, but the work of an excessively curious and anxious man, and not a particularly fortunate one, if for no other reason than that he must then interpret the form of Centaurs and the Chimera. And there also flows in a crowd of Gorgons and Pegasuses, and a multitude of other monstrous forms. Therefore, if anyone does not believe these things are as they are told, but wants to bring each one back to a plausible sense, being supported by a certain rustic wisdom, he will need far too much leisure. But I have no leisure for these things, for this reason, O friend: because I am not yet able, according to the Delphic precept, to know myself. <margin>It is ridiculous to scrutinize the affairs of others while ignorant of one's own.</margin> It seems ridiculous to me, therefore, while I am ignorant of my own self, to want to scrutinize the things of others. Therefore, dismissing these things and giving credit to the opinion I was just now relating about them, I consider not the myths, but myself: whether I am some beast more complex and more fiery and more furious than Typhon, or a calmer and simpler animal, participating by nature in some divine and gentle lot. But, my friend, was not this the tree to which you were leading us as we talked?

**PHAEDRUS:** This is certainly it.

**SOCRATES:** By Juno, a beautiful retreat! For that Plane tree is quite spreading with its branches and very tall; and the height of that willow-tree which they call "chaste" <note>The Agnus Castus tree</note> and its shade are exceedingly beautiful and lovely; and it is now at the height of its flowering, so that the whole place is filled with the sweetness of its scent. A very clear spring also flows under the Plane tree with very cold water, as one can guess by the touch of a foot. The girls and other images carved here testify that it is sacred to the nymphs and to Achelous. Do you not also notice how pleasant and sweet a breeze breathes here? Moreover, something summery and musical resounds with the chorus of cicadas. But the most ornate thing of all is to look at the grass itself, how it is suited to softly support the head of one reclining on the gently sloping meadow. Thus you have led me here most excellently, like a guest, O friend Phaedrus.

**PHAEDRUS:** O admirable man, you seem most absurd; and truly, as you say, you are like some guest being led, not like a local inhabitant: so much so that you appear never to have crossed our borders, nor even to have gone outside the walls themselves. <margin>One must live among men, not among trees.</margin>

**SOCRATES:** Forgive me, best Phaedrus. For I am a lover of learning; the fields and trees can teach me nothing, but the men who dwell in the city can. You, however, seem to have found the incentive for my going out. For just as they lead hungry animals by holding out leaves or fruit, so you, by holding out a book to me, could lead me through all of Attica and anywhere else you wish. Now, therefore, since we have arrived here, it pleases me to recline. You, however, in whatever posture it seems you can read most comfortably, take that up and read.

**PHAEDRUS:** Listen then. <margin>The speech of Lysias against lovers.</margin> "My situation is as follows: and I think it will be most advantageous for us, as you have heard. I think, moreover, that I ought to obtain what I ask from you no less because I am not at all captured by love for you. For lovers, as soon as they have satisfied their lust, repent of the benefit conferred; but those who are not ensnared by love never repent. For not by compulsion, but of their own will, as they have best consulted their own affairs, they have conferred benefits according to the capacity of their resources. Furthermore, lovers sometimes revolve in their minds how negligently they have managed their affairs because of love, and what benefits they have conferred to their own loss, and what labors they have endured; and therefore they think they have returned sufficient gratitude to those they loved. But those who are not deceived by love [regret] neither the neglect of domestic affairs, nor past labors, nor discord with kinsmen..."
