# BOOK
## XXVI.

...they complain that they have run into difficulties for the sake of a friend. Therefore, once such evils are removed, nothing remains except that they should be ready to do all things which they believe will be pleasing to them. Many say that lovers ought to be valued more because they are overcome by the greatest affection toward those they love, and are always ready to obey their beloved in both words and deeds, even if they offend all others by doing so. We can easily gather that their opinion is not true from this: that having transferred their goodwill from some to others, they prefer their later loves to their former ones; and if the more recent ones command it, they pursue their former loves with hostility. And by what reason is it fitting to grant such a thing to one who is afflicted by such a calamity <note>The "calamity" refers to the madness of love</note> as no experienced person would ever allow? Indeed, they themselves confess that they are insane rather than wise; they know their own madness but are unable to contain themselves. But as for those who are wise, how could they approve the plans and wills of those who are so afflicted? Furthermore, if you wish to choose the best from among the lovers, your choice will be from a few; but if you seek the most suitable companion for yourself from among others, you will certainly be allowed to choose from many. There is indeed greater hope that a man worthy of your friendship will be found among many than among few.

If, therefore, you fear public infamy according to the constitution of the laws, you ought to remember that lovers—who think they should be loved just as they love others—are accustomed to boast openly that their vigilance was not in vain. But those who do not love, because they can contain themselves, are accustomed to seek what is best rather than the rumors of the multitude. Add to this that when the common people see lovers constantly following their beloveds and obeying them in all things, they suspect that a base desire has seized them, or perhaps is seizing them now. But they do not dare to disapprove of the familiarity of those who are not lovers. For they know it is necessary for men to associate often with one another for the sake of either friendship or some advantage.

Furthermore, if fear should seize you, thinking it will be difficult for friendship to remain—or rather, that if a grudge arises, a common loss for both will occur, and that you will be most harmed by granting those things you value highly—you will not be wrong to fear lovers greatly. For many things offend them, and they think everything happens to their detriment. For this reason, they prohibit their beloveds from associating with others, fearing lest wealthy men surpass them with riches, or learned men excel them in intelligence; and generally, if they see anyone have something excellent in themselves, they try to keep their beloveds far from them. Thus, by persuading them to abstain from such people, they deprive them of all friends. But if you, having taken account of your own affairs, deliberate better than they do, you will disagree with them and depart.

But those who are not captured by love for you, but perform what is proper on account of virtue, will not at all envy your familiarity with others; rather, they will hate those who do not wish to stick by you, thinking that you are despised by those people but helped by your familiars. Therefore, there is much greater hope that friendships will come from this commerce than enmities. Added to this is that most lovers desire the body before they know either the character or any other things pertaining to the person. From this it follows that it is doubtful whether they will persevere in friendship once their desire is extinguished. But for non-lovers, who were friends before and did not do everything for the sake of pleasure, it is consistent that their goodwill does not remain so burning, but that their services are received as monuments of future things.

Indeed, you will turn out better if you believe me rather than if you give your ears to a lover. For lovers extol your words and deeds with praise beyond measure: partly because they fear they might offend you, and partly because they are deceived in judging on account of the heat of desire. For love produces certain other things from itself: it compels the unfortunate to think those things are sad which provide no annoyance to others; but it forces the fortunate and those who have obtained their wish to praise as pleasant things which are not worthy of joy. Therefore, it is more fitting to pity them than to love them.

But if you believe me: first, I will use our familiarity not for present pleasure, but for future utility, not as a slave to love, but commanding myself; nor will I stir up heavy enmities for the smallest causes; rather, being moved at last only by the greatest, I will forgive involuntary errors and attempt to correct and avoid voluntary ones. These are the arguments for a friendship that will last a long time. But if it should come into your mind that a firm friendship cannot be born except from love, you ought to consider that by this reasoning we would not value our sons highly, nor would we have parents or children as friends, who were made friends not from the heat of this love, but from any other pursuits.

To this, if one must especially obey the needy, it is altogether fitting to help not the better men, but the poorest, for having been freed from the greatest evils, they will have great gratitude. In your own private expenses, too, it will not be friends who should be summoned, but the hungry and the suppliants. For these will perform the greatest benefit: they will follow you, wait at your doors, applaud, give great thanks, and pour out prayers for you. However, it is perhaps fitting to indulge not the needy most of all, but rather those who can return the favor; not lovers only, but those worthy of the benefit; not those who are delighted by your beauty, but those who will be of use to you even when you are old; not those who, having obtained their wish, will boast openly, but those who will keep silent with modesty; not those who will cherish you for a short time, but those who will love you similarly through all your life; not those who, when the heat of desire is extinguished, will seek occasions for enmities, but those who will show their virtue and constancy when your beauty fades.

You, therefore, remember what I have said; and think on this: that lovers are rebuked by their friends as if love were something shameful. But no familiar reproaches those who do not love on the grounds that they are consulting poorly for themselves in this way. Perhaps you will ask me whether I advise you to obey all non-lovers. But I think not even the lover himself would command you to have this same mind toward all lovers. For it is not worthy of equal grace to the one receiving it, nor is it similarly easy for you if you wish to remain hidden from others. It is necessary that no loss comes from this, but rather some utility to both. I think what has been said is sufficient; but if you see anything to be added, ask.

What does it seem to you, Socrates? Does it not seem that this speech is wonderfully composed both in other matters and in its words?

SOCRATES: In a wonderful way indeed, my friend, so that I was stunned; and so, O Phaedrus, on account of...

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL.

I was affected in the same way, while I watched you, because you seemed to me to be exulting in the reading of the speech. Do you think then that you know such things better than I, and that I should follow you? Together with that divine head of yours, I too have joined in the Bacchic frenzy <note>original: "bacchatus sum" - referring to a state of divinely inspired madness or enthusiasm</note>. PHAEDRUS. Does it seem to you a matter for joking? SOCRATES. Do I seem to be joking to you? Or am I not speaking seriously? PHAEDRUS. Not at all, O Socrates, but tell the truth by Jove the Friend <note>Jupiter Philios, the god of friendship</note>, do you think any of the Greeks could say more or greater things on this very subject? SOCRATES. What indeed? Should we judge a writer to be praised only because he said what was necessary? And not also because he placed each word clearly, roundly, and elegantly? For if you wish, it must be conceded for your sake; for it escaped me because of my own laziness and lack of skill. I was attending only to the eloquence of the speaker. To that end, I did not think even Lysias himself would consider himself sufficient. Truly it seemed to me, O Phaedrus, unless you say otherwise, that he repeated the same things two or three times, as if he lacked the abundance to say many things on the same subject; or as if he had no care for this. And he seemed to me to be showing off, that he could say the same thing differently and in various ways, having spoken brilliantly in both manners. PHAEDRUS. You say nothing, O Socrates: for this is exactly what the speech possessed. For of those things which were in the matter about which one could speak fittingly, nothing was omitted: so that beyond those things said by him, no one could say more or more convincingly on the same subject. SOCRATES. That I can no longer concede, for the ancient and wise men and women who have spoken and written about these things will refute me, if I grant that for your sake. PHAEDRUS. Who are they? And where have you heard better things? SOCRATES. At the moment I do not quite remember. But surely I have heard certain things somewhere, either from the beautiful Sappho <margin>Sappho</margin>, or the wise Anacreon, or other writers. From where do I conjecture this? Because, O blessed one, I feel my breast is full of the thoughts of others, and not inferior to what can be said. Since I have learned nothing of the sort from myself, I understand this, being conscious of my own ignorance. It remains, therefore, that like a vessel I have drawn these things from the fountains of others: but again, because of my rudeness, I have forgotten both how and from whom I received them. PHAEDRUS. O most noble one, you have spoken excellently. From whom you received it and how, do not say even if I command you. But say that which you profess: that you have more and better things than those written by Lysias. If you do this, abstaining from his points, I promise you a golden statue at Delphi, equal in weight to yourself, as the nine archons are accustomed to do, to set up not only my statue but yours as well. SOCRATES. You are most friendly, and truly golden, O Phaedrus, if you think I mean that Lysias has missed the mark entirely: and that other better things can be said besides all these. For I think this happens even to the worst writer. In the first place, as far as the subject of the discourse is concerned, do you think anyone wishing to prove that a non-lover should be favored more than a lover could do so, unless he proved that the non-lover is prudent, while the lover is insane, and praised the former while censuring the latter? These things are indeed necessary; what else would he have to say? But I think: such things as these are to be left to the writers and conceded to them, and not the invention of these, but the arrangement is to be praised: but in those things which are not necessary and are found with difficulty: I think not only the arrangement, but the invention also should be praised. PHAEDRUS. I concede what you say, for you seem to have spoken reasonably. I will therefore do this myself. For I will permit you to presuppose that the lover is more sick than the non-lover. But in other matters, if you say more and better things than Lysias, you shall stand in gold at Olympia next to the offerings of the Cypselids. SOCRATES. You take this seriously, O Phaedrus: because I rebuked a man most dear to you. But I was joking with you. Do you think I would truly attempt this, to say something else more ornate than his wisdom? PHAEDRUS. On this matter, O friend, you have fallen into your own trap. You must speak by all means, however you can. Beware therefore lest we be compelled to repay one another in the annoying manner of the comedians: and do not force me to say: "If I, O Socrates, do not know Socrates, I have also forgotten myself." And he desired it indeed, but pretended to be reluctant. Finally, think thus: we shall not leave here until you have said what you claimed to have in your breast. For we are alone, and indeed in a wilderness: and I am younger and stronger. From all these things understand what I mean: and do not wish to speak by force rather than of your own will. SOCRATES. But, O blessed Phaedrus, I shall be ridiculous if I, an unrefined man, contend with that excellent writer, and dispute on the same matters on the spur of the moment. PHAEDRUS. Do you know how the matter stands? Stop these excuses with me. For I have almost found the means by which I shall compel you. SOCRATES. Do not say it, I beseech you. PHAEDRUS. Not say it? Indeed, I say it now. I shall turn to an oath <margin>He threatens</margin>. For I swear to you by some god, or if you wish, by this plane tree <margin>An oath</margin>, that unless you speak in its presence, I will never hereafter show or report anyone's speech to you. SOCRATES. Oh, you rogue! How beautifully you have found the way to compel a man greedy for speeches to do whatever you wish! PHAEDRUS. Why then, since you are such a man, do you hesitate? SOCRATES. No longer, since you have sworn thus. For how could I want to be away from such a feast? PHAEDRUS. Speak then. SOCRATES. Do you know what I shall do? PHAEDRUS. About what do you speak? SOCRATES. I shall speak with my head covered: so that I may run through the discourse more quickly: and not looking at you, I may not be hindered by shame. PHAEDRUS. Just speak: as for the rest, do as you wish. SOCRATES. Come now, O Clear-toned Muses <note>original: "musae Ligiae" - likely a pun on the "Ligyans" or simply meaning "clear-voiced"</note>, whether you have this name because of the beauty of your song, or because of that musical race of the Ligyans, help my discourse, which this excellent man compels me to speak: so that his companion, who first seemed wise to him, may now seem even more so. There was a certain boy, or rather a youth endowed with an excellent nature: he had many lovers: one of whom was a truly crafty man who, although he loved him no less than the others, persuaded the boy that he did not love him. And once when he was seeking a favor from him, he argued that one should gratify a non-lover rather than a lover, and spoke thus. "In all things, O boy, the only principle for those who deliberate well is to understand what that thing is about which they deliberate: or else they must miss the mark entirely. It escapes most people that they do not know the substance of the matter. As if they knew it, they do not define it at the beginning of the discussion, and as they proceed, it follows as is natural that they agree neither with themselves nor with others. Lest this happen to you and me..."

# BOOK

<page-num>XXVI.</page-num>

->**LIBER**<-

that which we condemn in others, since there is a disagreement among us whether one should grant favors to a lover or a non-lover, let us define what love itself is and what power it possesses, based on a consensus. Looking back and referring to this definition, let us consider whether it brings benefit or harm. Now, it is manifest to all that love is a certain desire; yet we are not ignorant of the fact that even those who do not love still desire beautiful or good things. Therefore, so that we may understand how a lover is distinguished from a non-lover, it is necessary to know that there are two dominant and leading <term>Ideas</term><note>original: "Ideas" - here referring to guiding principles or forms of the mind</note> in each of us, which we follow wherever they lead. One is an innate desire for pleasures. The other is an acquired opinion that strives for the best. These sometimes agree within us, and sometimes they are in sedition and discord; now one prevails, now the other. When, therefore, opinion leads by reason toward that which is best and overcomes, this power of living is called **temperance**. But when desire, devoid of reason, drags us toward pleasures and rules over us, this rule is called **lust**.

<margin>Love</margin>
<margin>Lust</margin>

Since lust is multiform and has many parts, it certainly has many names; and whichever of these forms overflows most in someone, it gives that person its own name, nor does it grant any honorable or worthy title to its followers. For concerning food, the desire that overcomes reason and other desires is called gluttony; and it gives this very name to the one who possesses it. Again, that which exercises tyranny over drunkenness and leads the one it possesses in that direction—it is clear what name it will have. And it is manifest how other names of these kindred desires should be assigned where one dominates most. The reason why we have said all the things above is now almost clear; yet if it is spoken rather than omitted, it will be clearer. For the desire without reason which overcomes the opinion tending toward the right, and which is snatched away toward the beauty of form, and is vehemently strengthened by kindred desires toward the form of the body, prevails and overcomes; from *rhomis* (that is, strength and vehemence), it is called *eros* (that is, **love**).

<margin><unclear>indistinct</unclear></margin>
<margin>Rhomis eros <note>Greek: ῥώμη (strength) and ἔρως (love)</note></margin>

Does it not seem to you, O friend Phædrus, as it does to me, that I have experienced something divine?

PHAE. Certainly, O Socrates, a certain unusual flowing fullness has seized you.

SO. Listen to me then in silence. For in truth, this place seems divine. Therefore, if I am seized by the nymphs as the discourse proceeds, do not wonder. Certainly, those things I was just singing do not differ much from <term>dithyrambs</term><note>Wild, choral hymns usually dedicated to Dionysus</note>.

PHAE. You speak the truth.

SO. You are the cause of these things. But hear the rest, lest that which has come upon me should depart. But the god will take care of that; let us return to the boy in our discussion. Come then, O best of men, that which was to be consulted has been spoken and defined. Looking to this, let us see what remains: what benefit or harm will likely come from the lover and the non-lover to the one who complies. It is necessary that a man enslaved to lust and serving pleasures should make his beloved as joined to himself as possible. To a sick man, whatever does not resist is pleasant; but whatever is better or equal is troublesome. Therefore, a lover will never willingly endure his beloved being either superior or equal. He will always make him inferior and more needy as far as he can. The ignorant is inferior to the wise, the timid to the brave, the unpolished to the rhetorical, the dull to the sharp. When these and more evils of the soul are present by nature or arise in the beloved, the lover rejoices; and he even tries to introduce others. Otherwise, he is deprived of pleasure.

<margin><unclear>indistinct</unclear></margin>

Therefore, the lover must necessarily envy the beloved; and by removing him from every association and study from which he might emerge as an excellent man, he causes great harm. He harms him most of all by depriving him of that which makes him most prudent. Divine **philosophy** makes one most prudent, from which the lover is compelled to lead the beloved far away, fearing lest, if he becomes wiser, he might be despised by him. In short, he does everything so that the youth may turn out ignorant of all things and admire only the lover. When he is such, he will be most pleasant to the lover, but most ruinous to himself. And so, in those things pertaining to the intellect, association with a lover is harmful.

After this, we must see how he who is compelled to prefer the sweet to the good will care for the body of the one he loves, if it is committed to him. He will surely desire a body not solid, but soft and delicate; not nourished under the sun but in the shade; which has been brought up far from dangers and labors and the sweat of the gymnasium, in a womanly and delicate lifestyle; adorned with artificial colors and foreign ornaments for lack of its own; and accustomed to other things similar to these. Since it would be unworthy to recount all these things at length, we will conclude briefly for now so that we may proceed. Truly, in battles and any other great necessity, enemies boldly attack such a habit of body, while friends and the lovers themselves fear greatly for it. But this, being manifest, must be dismissed.

Next, we must say what benefit or harm the familiarity and guardianship of a lover provides us in external matters. Yet this is manifest to everyone, especially to the lover: that he desires the beloved to be bereft of his most friendly, dear, and divine possessions. For he wishes him to be deprived of parents, kinsmen, and friends, thinking they will be an impediment to his sweetest association with the beloved. Furthermore, if the boy is very rich in gold or any possession, he thinks he cannot be easily captured, nor if captured, can he be held. Wherefore the lover, as if envious, must grieve at the beloved's prosperity and rejoice in his adversity. Moreover, he wishes the youth to live for a long time without a wife, without children, without a home, desiring to enjoy his own sweetness for the longest time. There are also other evils; but to most of these, some <term>daemon</term><note>A guiding spirit or supernatural power</note> has mixed a certain pleasure at the very beginning; just as nature has inserted a not unpleasing delight into a flatterer, a most heavy beast and a great calamity. Someone will also blame a harlot as being harmful...

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL.

...and other such animals and pursuits: which are accustomed to delight us for the present. But the lover, besides being harmful, is also by his very habit the most troublesome of all. For "equals with equals" <margin>Proverb: Like associates with like.</margin> are most pleasantly joined together, according to the ancient proverb. For equality of age, because it leads to equal pleasures through similarity, gives birth to friendship. Nevertheless, even these things bring a surfeit of boredom. Therefore, necessity in all things is heavy to everyone; and this is especially true in the case of the lover toward the beloved when there is a lack of similarity. For the elder, clinging to the younger, does not willingly depart from him by day or night, but is driven by necessity and madness. He draws the youth along with the allurements of pleasures—seeing him, hearing him, touching him, and perceiving the beloved with every sense—so that he follows him constantly with great pleasure. But as for the beloved, what pleasure or what comfort will keep him for an equal time, so that he is not vexed by extreme annoyance? For he beholds a face that is aged and deformed, and other things likewise, which are unpleasant not only to experience but even to hear about. He is constantly subjected to a kind of necessity to be "captured," while being observed everywhere by diligent snares; and he hears untimely and immoderate praises as well as reproaches with which the lover pursues him. These are indeed intolerable in sobriety, but in drunkenness they are not only intolerable but even most shameful due to an excessive license for speaking openly. Furthermore, while he loves, he is ruinous and troublesome. But when he ceases to love, he is thereafter unfaithful toward the one whom he had finally induced, with many oaths, prayers, and promises, to endure his harmful company in the hope of rewards. At last, when it is time to repay, he receives within himself another principle and a different faith: a mind of temperance instead of love and madness. Having now become another person, he hides from the beloved. Then the beloved, mindful of those things which were once said and done, demands the favor of benefits, thinking he is speaking with the same man. But the other, out of shame, neither dares to confess that he has changed, nor finds a way to fulfill the oaths and promises of that former mad rule, having now become master of his mind and temperance—fearing that if he does the same things as before, he might again become similar to and the same as he was then. From this it follows: that he who loved before now flees; and having changed, he departs as if the "woven fabric has fallen the other way" <note>A Greek proverbial expression meaning a total reversal of fortune or situation.</note>. The other is forced to pursue, bearing it heavily and turning to imprecations. He was truly deceived from the beginning, since he did not know that he should never have gratified a lover who was necessarily out of his mind, but rather a man free from love and possessing his senses. Otherwise, it would be necessary to commit oneself to a man who is unfaithful, peevish, envious, troublesome, ruinous to one's possessions, ruinous to the condition of the body, and by far most ruinous to the discipline of the soul—than which nothing is, or ever will be, more venerable among gods and men. <margin>These things, O boy, must be considered: and this further must be noted: the friendship of a lover consists of no goodwill, but of a certain greed for satiation, like hunger. "As the wolf loves the lamb, so the lover burns for the boy."</margin> This is what I predicted, O Phaedrus. You shall not hear me speaking further; let the speech now have an end, although I thought half of the discussion was finished, and that an equal amount remained to be said about the non-lover—that one should rather indulge him—and to enumerate how many good things are in him.

**PHAEDRUS:** Why then do you stop, O Socrates?

**SOCRATES:** Have you not noticed, Phaedrus, that I am now singing in verses and no longer merely in dithyrambs <note>A wild, passionate choral hymn; Socrates suggests his speech has become unnaturally poetic or inspired.</note>, even though my speech is engaged in censuring? If I proceed to praise the other, what do you think I will do? Do you not perceive that I am being breathed upon by the nymphs, both through your efforts and by divine providence? Therefore, I say in summary: as many good things exist in the one as we have numbered evils in the other. But what need is there for many words? For enough has been said about both. And so the story shall rest as is fitting. I am now going away, having crossed the river, before I am compelled by you to something greater.

**PHAEDRUS:** Not yet, O Socrates, not before the heat departs. Do you not see that it is now plainly midday, the hour in which the heat is most intense? But let us stay a while and talk about what we have said, and as soon as it has cooled, then let us go.

**SOCRATES:** You are divine regarding speeches, O Phaedrus, and truly wonderful. I think indeed that of the orations delivered in your time, no one has been the author and cause of more than you—whether by speaking yourself or by compelling others in some way. I except Simmias the Theban <note>A disciple of Socrates known for his interest in Pythagorean philosophy.</note>. But you far excel the others. And now you seem to be the cause of some speech being delivered by me.

**PHAEDRUS:** You certainly do not declare war, but in what way, and what speech?

**SOCRATES:** When I was about to cross the river, the *daemonium* <note>Socrates' "divine sign" or inner voice that warned him against certain actions.</note> and the sign that usually comes to me occurred. Whenever it happens, it prohibits me from doing what I was about to do. Hence I seemed to hear a voice which forbids me to depart before I have made expiation, as if I had committed some offense against the god. I am therefore a seer—not a very good one, but like those who know letters poorly, sufficient for myself. Thus I now clearly understand my offense. For indeed, my friend, there is even something of prophecy in the soul. It moved me even before while I was speaking, whence I somehow feared lest, according to Ibycus <note>A Greek lyric poet; the reference is to a fragment about offending the gods but gaining glory among men.</note>, I might offend the gods and gain glory among men. Now I feel in what I have offended.

**PHAEDRUS:** What is it?

**SOCRATES:** A grave, O Phaedrus, a grave speech I say, you have brought forward and compelled me to speak.

**PHAEDRUS:** In what way?

**SOCRATES:** It was foolish and in a way impious. What can be graver than that?

**PHAEDRUS:** Nothing, if what you say is true.

**SOCRATES:** What then? Do you not think Love <note>original: "Amor"</note> is the son of Venus <note>original: "Veneris"</note> and some kind of god?

**PHAEDRUS:** So it is said.

**SOCRATES:** Yet not by Lysias, nor by your speech, which was uttered through my mouth after being charmed by you as if by some incantation. But if Love is, as he certainly is, a god or something divine, he could not be evil. Yet the speeches were held about him as if he were evil. In this, therefore, against Love...

# BOOK XXVI.
## Page 26

we have sinned. And yet these discussions of ours seem very foolish, even if clever; for while they contain nothing sincere or true, they nevertheless boast as if they were of great value, provided they are approved by some deceived little men. Therefore, my friend, it is necessary for me to be purified. For those who sin in speech, there is an ancient form of purification <note>original: "expiatio"</note> which Homer did not know, but Stesichorus did. For when he was deprived of his eyes for slandering Helen, he was not ignorant of the cause of his blindness as Homer was; but, being a man of the Muses <note>original: "musicus"</note>, he recognized it. And so he immediately composed these verses: *That story was not true, nor did you depart in the well-decked ships, nor did you come to the towers of Troy.* And so, having published the poem which they call a **palinodia** <margin>palinodia <note>A "recantation" or "singing back" of previous words.</note></margin>, that is, a contrary song, he immediately recovered his lost sight.

I, however, will be wiser than both of them in this: before any evil happens to me for slandering Love, I will attempt to offer him a recantation; and indeed with my head uncovered, whereas before it was veiled out of shame.

PHAEDRUS: Truly, Socrates, you could do nothing more pleasing to me than this.

SOCRATES: For you remember, O Phaedrus, how shamelessly the text from the book was read, and what was said by me as well concerning the lover. For if some noble and modest man, who loves or has loved another like himself, should hear us saying that lovers often stir up the greatest enmities for the smallest reasons, and that they are envious and harmful men to those they love, he would think he was hearing men raised on ships <note>A metaphor for unrefined or "salty" men who have never known noble, cultured love.</note> who have never seen any liberal love; nor would he agree with us in any way in the slanders we bring against love.

PHAEDRUS: Perhaps, by Jove, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Fearing this man, and fearing Love himself, I desire to wash away that foul and harmful speech from our ears with a "potable" <note>Socrates uses a metaphor of a fresh drink to wash out the salty/bitter taste of the previous speech.</note> discourse. I even advise Lysias to write as soon as possible that one should favor the lover rather than the non-lover, all else being equal.

PHAEDRUS: Know for certain it shall be so. For after you have praised the lover, it will be necessary for Lysias to be compelled by me to write the same.

SOCRATES: I believe it, as long as you remain who you are.

PHAEDRUS: Speak then, with a brave heart.

SOCRATES: Come then, where is that boy to whom I addressed my earlier speech? Let him hear this one too, lest if he fails to hear it, he rashly obeys the non-lover.

PHAEDRUS: He is always right here next to you, as long as you wish.

SOCRATES: Think then, O noble boy: the previous speech was by Phaedrus, son of Pythocles of Myrrhinus; but the following one will be by Stesichorus, son of Euphemus, a man of love. This shall be its beginning: *That story is not true which says that, when a lover is present, one should rather gratify the non-lover because the lover is mad and the non-lover is sane.* For if it were simply true <margin>On madness. The greatest goods come through madness granted by divinity. The Delphic and Dodonian prophets.</margin> that madness is an evil, we would have spoken rightly. But now, the greatest of goods come to us through madness, granted by a certain divine gift. For both the prophetess at Delphi and the priests at Dodona, while in a state of madness, have brought many and great benefits to the Greeks, both privately and publicly; but when they are sane, they bring little or none. And if we were to mention the Sibyl and others who have used divine prophecy, how many things they have predicted that benefited the future, we would extend our speech too far, bringing forth a matter manifest to everyone.

Yet this is worthy of testimony: that the ancients who gave names to things did not think madness was something foul or disgraceful. For they would not have attached this name to the most noble art by which the future is discerned, calling it *Manicē* (that is, madness); rather, as if madness were something good when it proceeds by divine chance, they gave this name to the honorable art. But now the younger generation, through ignorance, have inserted the letter 'T' and called it *Manticen* <note>Socrates is making a pun: "Manicē" (madness) vs "Manticē" (prophecy).</note>. Indeed, the investigations of the future by sane men through birds and other signs—proceeding as they do from human conjecture to intelligence—they named the "augural history of the mind." This name the later people, changing a small 'o' into a large 'o', adorned with a more honorable title. Therefore, as much as prophecy is more perfect and more excellent than augural conjecture—both in name and in work—so much do the ancients testify that madness proceeding from God is more noble than human prudence.

Furthermore, against the greatest diseases and labors that sometimes hang over mortals by divine indignation due to ancient crimes, a madness arriving from somewhere has found remedies for certain peoples, predicting what was needed and fleeing to prayers and the worship of the gods. From this, having obtained purifications and propitiations, it rendered the possessor safe for both the present and the future, having found a release from present evils for the one who is rightly mad and possessed.

<margin>Poetic madness</margin> A third kind of possession and madness comes from the Muses; taking hold of a tender and untouched soul, it awakens and inspires it. From there, adorning the infinite deeds of the ancients through songs and other poetry, it instructs posterity. But he who approaches the gates of poetry without the madness of the Muses, trusting that by some art he will turn out to be a good poet, is himself empty, and his poetry vanishes before that which proceeds from madness—just as the poetry of the prudent man fades away.

I can relate so many, and even more, noble works of divine madness. Therefore, let us not fear this, nor let any reasoning frighten us away, which tries to show that a prudent and sane friend is to be chosen rather than an inspired one. Let that man further show, if he can, and carry off the victory, that love was not granted by the gods for the benefit of the lover and the beloved. We, however, must now show the opposite: that such madness is given by the gods to men for the greatest happiness. The demonstration will be unbelievable to the litigious, but believable to the wise. First, we must know the truth about the nature of the divine and human soul by looking at its affections and works. This shall be the principle of the demonstration:

<margin>The soul is immortal</margin> Every soul is immortal. For that which is always in motion is immortal. But that which moves another and is moved by another, since it has an end to its motion, has also an end to its life. Only that which [moves] itself...

<summary>Socrates recants his previous speech against love, arguing that "divine madness" (prophecy, healing, and poetry) is superior to human reason. He begins a philosophical proof for the immortality of the soul based on its nature as a self-moving entity.</summary>

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL.

## FOLIO CLXXXIII.

It moves <note>original: *mouet*</note>, because it never deserts itself, and never ceases to be moved. Rather, for all other things that are moved, this is the fountain and principle of motion. Now, a principle is without a beginning. For it is necessary that whatever is generated must arise from a principle, but the principle itself arises from nothing. For if a principle arose from something else, it would certainly not be a principle. Since it is without beginning, it must also be without end. For if the principle were to perish, it could neither be reborn from another, nor could anything else be born from it, since it is necessary that all things arise from a principle. Thus, the principle of motion is that which moves itself. This can neither die nor be born. Otherwise, the whole heaven and all generation would necessarily collapse and cease, nor could they ever stand again, having lost the source from which they gained their motion. Since, therefore, it appears that what moves itself is immortal, one will not blush to say that this is the very substance and definition of the soul. For every body that receives motion from the outside is inanimate <note>without a soul</note>. But that which possesses motion from within itself is animate <note>souled</note>, as this is the very nature of the soul. If this is so—that there is nothing else which moves itself except the soul—then the soul is necessarily unbegotten and immortal. Regarding the immortality of the soul, enough has been said.

<margin>On the Idea of the soul <unclear>...</unclear></margin>

But concerning its **Idea** <note>its form or essential nature</note>, we must speak in this manner. To describe what it is entirely would be a task for a divine and very long narration; but to describe a certain likeness of it is a human task, and a shorter one. Let us speak, then, in this way. Let the soul be likened to the combined power of a winged chariot and a charioteer. Now, the horses and charioteers of the gods are all good and of good stock, but those of others are mixed. In the first place, our ruler <note>the intellect</note> guides a pair of horses with reins; then, of the horses, one is good and beautiful and of such stock, but the other is the opposite and of opposite stock. Thus, our charioteering is necessarily difficult and troublesome.

<margin>In what way a living being is made.</margin>

We must now attempt to say how a living being is called "mortal" and "immortal." All soul has care for all that is inanimate, and it traverses the whole heaven, appearing now in one form, now in another. While it is perfect and winged, it marches on high and governs the whole world. But the soul that has shed its wings is carried along until it catches hold of something solid; there, having found a dwelling place, it takes on an earthly body, appearing to move itself because of the soul's power. The whole is called a "living being"—soul and body joined together—and is surnamed a "mortal living being." "Immortal," however, is a term not grasped by any rational discourse, but is something we imagine; for though we have neither seen nor sufficiently understood God, we imagine Him as an immortal living being, having a soul and having a body naturally joined for all time. But let these things be as it pleases God, and be so described.

Now let us state the cause by which the wings are cast off and fall from the soul. It is something like this: the natural power of the wing is to lift what is heavy into the heights, where the race of the gods dwells. Of all things associated with the body, the mind participates most in the divine. The divine is beautiful, wise, good, and whatever else may be so called. By these, the "winging" of the soul is chiefly nourished and increased; but by what is foul, evil, and the opposite of these, it wastes away and perishes.

<margin>Jupiter</margin>

Indeed, the great leader in heaven, **Jupiter**, driving a winged chariot, goes first, adorning all things and providing for them. Him follows an army of gods and demons, ordered in eleven parts. **Vesta** alone remains in the house of the gods. But of the other gods, whoever is counted in the number of the twelve, each leads in the order to which he was assigned.

<margin>Envy</margin>

Many, therefore, are the blessed sights and paths within the heaven, which the race of the blessed gods frequents, each performing his own office. He who wills and is able follows them, for envy stands far apart from the divine choir. But when they go to the banquet and the feast, they proceed upward to the highest vault of heaven. The vehicles of the gods, being well-balanced and easy to rein, advance easily; but the others struggle. For the horse that participates in wickedness is heavy, turning toward the earth and dragging down whichever charioteer has not nourished his horse well. Here, then, the ultimate labor and contest is set before the soul.

<margin>See how Plato places some things outside of heaven. The intellect is the governor of the soul.</margin>

For those souls called immortal, when they reach the summit, go outside and stand upon the back of heaven. As they stand there, the revolution of the sphere carries them around, and they behold the things that are outside the heaven. No poet among us has yet praised this "supracelestial" place, nor will any ever praise it according to its dignity. But it is in this manner—for one must dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about Truth. Without color, without shape, without touch; the truly existing essence, visible only to the intellect, the governor of the soul; around this essence, the genus of true knowledge occupies this place. Since, therefore, the thought of God is nourished by intellect and pure knowledge, so also every soul that is about to receive its proper condition, having gazed for a time upon that which *is*, is nourished and rejoices in the contemplation of truth, until the revolution carries it back to the same place. In this circuit, it beholds **Justice** itself; it beholds **Temperance**; it beholds **Knowledge**—not the kind that is subject to change, nor that which varies in different objects which we now call "beings," but that knowledge which exists in that which is truly Being. And having likewise contemplated the other things that truly are and having been nourished by them, it sinks back inside the heaven and returns home. When it has returned, the charioteer, stopping the horses at the manger, throws them ambrosia and gives them nectar to drink. And this is the life of the gods.

Of the other souls, that which has followed God best and become most like Him raises the head of the charioteer into the supracelestial place and is carried around with the revolution; but it is troubled by the horses and hardly beholds the things that truly are. Another soul sometimes raises its head and sometimes sinks it; because of the violence of the horses, it sees some things but not others. The rest of the souls, though all desiring the higher place, follow along, but being unable to reach it, they are carried around submerged, trampling and crowding one another, each striving to precede the other.

<summary>This page contains Plato's famous proof for the immortality of the soul as a self-moving principle and begins the Allegory of the Chariot, describing the soul's journey to the supracelestial realm to behold absolute Truth, Justice, and Temperance.</summary>

<keywords>immortality of the soul, Charioteer allegory, supracelestial realm, Plato, Phaedrus, divine madness, Justice, Temperance, Jupiter, Vesta</keywords>

# BOOK
### PAGE XXVI.

<meta>Catchword: reason,</meta>

Then there arises a great tumult, a contest, and extreme toil. Here, indeed, by the fault of the charioteers, many souls are left crippled; many have many of their feathers <note>The "feathers" or "wings" of the soul represent its ability to rise toward divine truth.</note> broken. All of them, after much labor, depart without having achieved a vision of that which truly is; and after their departure, they make use of the food of mere opinion. The reason there is such great effort to see where the "Field of Truth" lies is this: from such a meadow, the best power of the soul receives its fitting nourishment, and the nature of the wings by which the soul is elevated is fed by this. And the Law of Adrastia <note>original: "Regula Adrastię deę". Adrastia is another name for Nemesis or Destiny; the "inevitable goddess."</note>—that is, of the inevitable divinity—is this:

<margin>The goddess Adrastia</margin>

that whatever soul, having followed a God, has glimpsed any of the true things, it shall be unharmed until the next circuit; and if it can always do this, it shall remain forever unhurt. But if, being unable to keep up, it does not see, and by some chance is filled with forgetfulness and vice and grows heavy, and being weighed down breaks its wings and falls to the earth, then the law forbids it to enter into any brutal <note>animal</note> nature in its first generation. Instead, it commands that the soul:

<margin>Nine conditions of souls.</margin>

which has seen the most shall enter into the birth of a man who will be a philosopher, or a seeker of beauty, or a musical and amorous person. The soul in the second place shall descend into a lawful king, or a man warlike and commanding. The third into a governor of a state, or a manager of a household or a merchant. The fourth into a hardworking gymnast, or one concerned with the healing and care of the body. The fifth into those who will be prophets or involved in certain mysteries. The sixth into a poet or any other of those who are occupied with imitation. The seventh into a craftsman or a farmer. The eighth into a sophist or a demagogue. The ninth into a tyrant. In all these, whoever lives his life justly later obtains a better lot; but he who lives unjustly, a worse one.

<margin>The soul returns to the same place after ten thousand years.</margin>

For each soul does not return to the same place from which it set out for ten thousand years. For it does not recover its wings before this space of time, except for the soul of one who has philosophized without guile, or who has loved beauty together with the study of wisdom. These indeed, in the third circuit of a thousand years, if they have chosen this same life three times in succession, thus recover their wings and fly away after the three-thousandth year. But the other souls, having reached the end of their first life, are judged. Once judged, some go to places of judgment under the earth and suffer their deserved punishments there. Others, elevated by judgment into a certain place in heaven, live in a manner worthy of the life they led in human form. In the thousandth year, both groups return and happen to choose their second life; each selects

<margin>The human soul into the life of a beast, and from a beast into a man.</margin>

the life that it wishes. Here, a human soul may pass into the life of a beast, and from a beast back into a man, provided that the soul was once formerly human. For a soul that has never glimpsed the truth will not be able to come into this human form. For it is necessary for a man to understand according to "species" <note>The Platonic "Form" or "Idea"</note>, proceeding from many sensations into a single concept by reasoning. This is the recollection of those things which our soul once saw when it was perfect with God, looking down upon those things which we now say "exist," and looking upward toward that which truly is. Therefore, the thought of the philosopher alone rightly recovers its wings. For his memory always clings, as much as possible, to those things by which a god is divine. He who uses such reminders rightly, and is always initiated into perfect mysteries, alone becomes truly perfect. Separated from human pursuits and clinging to the divine, he is rebuked by the multitude as if he were out of his mind; but he, being full of God, is unnoticed by the multitude. The whole discourse tends toward this: the fourth kind of madness <note>Plato identifies four types of divine madness: prophetic, telestic (ritual), poetic, and erotic.</note>. By this, when someone sees beauty here and remembers that true beauty, he receives his wings, and having received them, strives to fly away. But since he is unable to do so, like a bird looking upward and despising the things below, he is accused of being possessed by madness. This divine alienation is the best of all alienations, and comes from the best things for both the one who has it and the one who participates in it; and he who is held by this madness, since he loves beautiful things, is called a lover. For as has been said, every human soul has glimpsed the things that truly are; otherwise, it would not have come into this living being. But to remember those things from the things that are here is not easy for everyone—neither for those who saw them there for only a short time, nor for those who were unfortunate in descending here, so that, corrupted by certain associations, they have accepted forgetfulness of the sacred things they once beheld. Therefore, few remain who have enough memory left. These, when they see here some likeness of the things they beheld there, are struck with awe and are moved outside themselves; yet they do not know what this affection is, because they do not perceive it clearly enough. We see no splendor of justice or temperance or the other things venerable to souls in these images; rather, through certain obscure instruments, only a very few, approaching these images, hardly discern the nature of that which is being imitated. But then it was possible to see Beauty most clearly, when with that blessed choir we followed the happy vision and contemplation—we with Jupiter <note>original: "Ioue" (Jove/Zeus)</note>, and others with some other of the gods—and were initiated into the mysteries which it is right to call the most blessed of all. We performed these as whole beings, free from the evils that awaited us in the future; and as initiates, we gazed upon whole, simple, immovable, and blessed spectacles in pure light, being pure and unstained ourselves, and released from this which we now carry about and call a "body," bound to it in the manner of an oyster. Let these things be attributed to the benefit of memory, for the sake of which we now extend our discourse out of a longing for those things we once saw. Beauty, as we said, was shining then as it moved with those beings, and having come here, we have perceived it through

<margin>Sight is for us the sharpest of all senses.</margin>

the most piercing of our senses, shining most clearly. For sight is to us the sharpest of all the senses that occur through the body; yet Wisdom is not seen by it. For she would excite burning loves if any such manifest image of her were to come before our eyes. The same reason applies to the other things that are lovable.

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON BEAUTY.

<margin>Beauty alone is the most lovable of all things.</margin>But in truth, beauty alone has obtained this lot: that it is the most manifest and the most lovable of all things. Therefore, he who has not been recently initiated into the mysteries, or rather has become corrupted, is not quickly moved from this world to that world toward beauty itself, even when he beholds here a certain likeness which is named after it. For this reason, he does not feel veneration when he looks upon it; instead, following the manner of a four-footed beast, he is given over to pleasure and strives to assault and to mate. Approaching with insolence, he neither fears nor blushes to pursue pleasure against nature. But he who has been recently purified by the sacred rites, or who once contemplated many things <note>referring to the soul's pre-existence in the heavens</note>, when he sees a face of divine form or some bodily appearance that aptly imitates beauty itself, he first shudders; a certain ancient fear returns to him. Then, looking upon it, he worships it as a god; and unless he feared the charge of severe madness, he would offer sacrifices to his beloved no differently than to the statues of the gods. As he gazes, he is seized by a transformation, a sweat, and an unusual heat following that shudder. For when he receives the influx of beauty through his eyes, he grows warm; by this, the nature of his "feathers" <note>Plato uses the metaphor of the soul growing wings</note> is watered. Once he has become warm, the parts which had long been compacted by hardness and prevented the sprout from emerging begin to melt. When this nourishment flows in, the stalks of the feathers swell from their very roots and strive to burst forth through the whole form of the soul; for once, the soul was entirely supported by wings. Thus, it seethes and leaps; and just as infants are vexed by itching and pain in the gums when they are cutting teeth, so the soul of one growing feathers seethes and is affected by tingling and distress. Therefore, when it gazes at the beauty of a youth and drinks in the desire flowing from him, it is watered and warmed; it ceases from its pain and rejoices. But when it is far away, and the channels through which the wing strives to gush forth have dried up, they become parched and constricted, confining the sprout of the feathers. These sprouts, shut inside with that desire and the influx, swell and throb, and soon leaping back, each obstructs its own passages on every side and pricks the soul. Thus the whole soul, wounded on all sides, is driven by the sting and is in anguish; yet again, remembering beauty, it rejoices. From the mixture of both, it is vexed by the vehemence and novelty of such a passion; in its anxiety, it rages and goes mad. Being so affected, it can neither sleep by night nor stay still by day because of its frenzy; but it runs everywhere, struck by the longing to see the beautiful one. Seeing him, and drinking in that influx of desire, it opens and releases what was previously obstructed and closed. Once it has breathed again, it is freed from the stings and anguishes. It is so soothed by this most sweet pleasure in the present moment that it never willingly departs from these allurements; nor does it value anyone more than the beloved. It consigns parents, brothers, and all friends to oblivion; it is not moved in the least by the loss of its patrimony through neglect. It utterly despises the ancestral customs and honors in which it used to glory, and is ready to serve and lie down wherever permitted, provided it may be near its little fire <note>the object of its passion</note>. For it does not only worship and venerate the beautiful one, but has found in him the only physician for its most grievous diseases. This affection, noble youth to whom my speech is directed, men call <term>Erota</term> <margin><term>Erota</term></margin> <note>original: "Erota" (Greek: Eros), meaning Love</note> or Love. But if you hear what the gods call it, you will rightly laugh on account of your youth. For certain followers of Homer, I believe, pass down two verses on Love from hidden poems; one of which is quite insolent and not very harmonious. They say it thus: "Mortals call him <term>Erota</term>, that is, winged Love; but the immortals call him <term>Pterota</term> <note>original: "Pterota," a play on words in Greek involving 'pteron' (wing) and 'eros'</note>, that is, 'the Winged One,' because of the necessity of flying." One may believe these things in part, and in part not. Yet this is the very cause of the affection of lovers. Therefore, as many as were captured from the retinue of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> can bear the burden of "wing-growing" more heavily and constantly. But those who worshipped Mars and were driven in that celestial circuit, when ensnared by love, if they think they are being injured by the beloved, they easily fly into a slaughter and are carried headlong to kill both themselves and their beloveds. And so, according to whichever of the gods each person followed in the choir, he honors and imitates that god always in his life to the best of his power, as long as he remains uncorrupted; and in this manner, he conducts his first generation of life here, and exhibits himself such as he is to his beloveds and others. Each person, therefore, chooses a love of beautiful ones according to his own character; and as if that person were a God to him, he fashions and adorns him like a statue, as one who will honor and sacrifice to him. Thus, the followers of Jove seek for themselves a beloved whose soul is Jovial <note>possessing the qualities of Jupiter: wisdom and leadership</note>. Wherefore they consider whether his nature is fit for philosophy and command; and when they love him once found, they strive with every effort that he may become such a person. And if they have not previously entered upon what they desire, they then strive greatly in their study, learning from wherever they can, and they themselves proceed to this work. Investigating the nature of their god from within themselves, they finally become masters of their wish, because they are compelled to raise the vision of their mind toward the god with the highest attention. Then, when they touch him through memory, they are inspired by divinity; and from him, they take their customs and studies, insofar as it is permitted for a man to become a participant in God. Since they refer the causes of all these things to the beloved, they approach with more burning affection. And if they draw from Jove, in the manner of bacchic priests, they pour it into the soul of the beloved, rendering him as similar as possible to their own god. Those who followed Juno seek a royal youth; having found him, they do all the same things toward him. Furthermore, the followers of Apollo or any of the other gods, each imitating their own god, seek a youth of a similar nature; and having obtained him, both imitating the god themselves and persuading the youths, they lead them toward the study and idea of that deity according to their strength. They do not use envy or illiberal malice toward their youths, but with all zeal, they try to form them into a perfect likeness of both themselves and the god whom they worship. The care and the end of true lovers, if only they attain what they desire, is indeed such...

</margin>...of the sort we have described: and a truly remarkable and happy result comes to the beloved from a friend who is "maddened" by love, if the beloved is captured. Now, each person grasps or captures it in this way. At the beginning of this fable, we divided every soul into three parts: we established two forms of horses as two distinct species, and the Charioteer <note>Latin: *Auriga*</note> as the third species; let these remain the same for us at present. Of the horses, one is good, the other is not. We have not yet clearly stated what the virtue of the good horse is, or the depravity of the bad one, but now it must be told. The good one is of a more excellent condition: he is upright in form and well-defined in his joints, with a high neck, slightly aquiline nostrils, a bright color, and black eyes. He is a lover of honor, temperance, and modesty; a friend of true opinion, needing no whip, for he is guided by exhortation and reason alone. The other is twisted and bulky, carried along recklessly, put together in a confused and messy way; with a stiff, hard neck and a low-slung throat, a flat face, dark color, and grey eyes bloodshot with red. He is moody and insolent, with shaggy and deaf ears, scarcely obeying the lash and the spurs. Therefore, when the charioteer beholds the face of the beloved, and his whole soul is inflamed with the sensation and stirred by the stings of tickling and desire, then the horse that is obedient to the charioteer, restrained as usual by modesty, keeps himself from leaping upon the beloved. But the other can be restrained neither by spurs nor by lashes, but leaps forward; and carried away by violence, he troubles his yoke-mate and the charioteer, dragging them toward the pleasures of Venus <note>The goddess of love; here referring to physical lust.</note>. At first, they resist him, indignant that they are being pulled toward such heavy and wicked things. Finally, since the evil does not cease, they are driven along, and they now yield and consent to do what they are ordered. From here they cling to the little spark and gaze upon the flashing face of the beloved. Looking upon this, the charioteer recalls the nature of beauty itself in his memory; and he sees it again joined with Temperance, firmly placed upon a chaste pedestal. Seeing this, he fears, and out of reverence falls backward; where at the same time he is forced to pull back the reins so far that both horses sit back on their haunches or rumps on the ground: but one does so willingly, because he does not resist at all; while the wanton horse is utterly unwilling. As they move further away, one, out of shame and wonder, drenches the whole soul with sweat; but the other, freed from the pain which both the bit and the fall had inflicted, finally catches his breath. Recovering himself, moved by indignation, he rebukes the charioteer and his yoke-mate, claiming that out of fear and cowardice they deserted their appointed rank. Again, as they are unwilling to approach, he forces them, and finally yields when they beg for it to be deferred until later. When the appointed time arrives, which they pretend to have forgotten while he reminds them, he neighs and pulls them, compelling them again to address the beloved with the same words. After they have come close, he bends down, leans forward, extends his tail, bites the bit, and most impudently drags them along. But the charioteer, suffering the same thing much more intensely, and as if turning from a starting post, pulls the reins far back with great force; he checks the teeth of the wicked horse, and fixes his foul tongue and bloody jaws, as well as his legs and haunches, to the ground, compelling him to pay the penalty. When that same wicked horse, having been frequently suppressed, ceases his wantonness, he is finally tamed and obeys the charioteer's modesty; and even when he sees the beautiful one, he trembles with fear, so that it sometimes happens that the soul of the lover follows the footsteps of the youth with a certain reverence and fear. Therefore, since the youth is observed by the lover with all devotion as if he were equal to a God—not feignedly, but truly affected in this way—and especially since the youth is by nature a friend to the one who honors him, he eventually conspires with the lover. Even if he had previously been deceived by the slanders of his associates, schoolmates, and others saying it is shameful to cling to a lover, and had therefore rejected the lover, eventually, as time proceeds, his age and the natural order of things lead him into intimacy with the lover. For it was never decreed by fate that an evil man should be a friend to an evil man, or that a good man should not be a friend to a good man. Therefore, when the youth has received the lover into conversation and intimacy, then the benevolence of that lover, having become closer, compels the youth to admire the lover himself. He notices that the benevolence of all his other relatives and friends, if compared with a friend inspired by the divine, is of no weight. And if the elder man continues thus for a long time, clinging to him and touching him in the gymnasia and other such places, then the fountain of that flowing liquid which Jupiter, captured by love for Ganymede, called *himeros* <note>Greek: ἵμερος, meaning "longing" or "desire."</note> (that is, the flow of desire), which flowed abundantly into the lover, is partly poured into the youth himself, and partly overflows outside of him. And just as a breeze or an Echo is reflected back from smooth and solid bodies to the place from which they came, so that stream of beauty, flowing back into the beautiful one through the eyes where it is accustomed to penetrate the soul, so waters the passages of the wings that they are now able and begin to sprout; and thus he fills the beloved with mutual love. He loves, therefore, but he is uncertain what he loves; he neither knows his own affection nor can he speak of it. But just as if he were infected in his eyes by the ailment of someone with bleary eyes, he does not know how to assign a cause for his present malady, nor does he notice that he sees himself in the lover as if in a mirror. Thus, in the lover's presence, his pain ceases just as the lover's does; but in his absence, he longs in turn as he is longed for: possessing a mutual love as a reflection of Love. He calls it and thinks of it not as love itself, but as friendship. He desires, therefore, almost as much as the other (though more moderately), to see him and to enjoy constant intimacy; and as is natural, he does these things immediately thereafter. In the very intimacy of the lover, the intemperate horse, urging the charioteer, demands a brief pleasure in exchange for many labors; but the youth's horse does not know what to say to the same; but stirred and anxious, he follows the lover with mutual benevolence, congratulating his most loving friend: and in that very familiarity, he is prepared to obey the lover's desire to the best of his ability. But the yoke-mate horse and the charioteer, with modesty and reason, oppose him in these matters. Therefore, if according to a right way of life and the studies of philosophy, the better parts of thought...

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL.

parts hold sway, they lead a blessed and harmonious life here and now: being masters of themselves and temperate, because that part in which the soul's vice dwells has been subjected, while that part to which virtue belongs has been liberated. At the end of this life, having recovered their wings, they fly away swift-winged, having triumphed in one of the three truly Olympic contests. Indeed, neither human temperance nor divine madness can bestow a greater good upon men than this. But if they have followed a more shameless life, devoid of philosophy though otherwise ambitious—perhaps in a state of drunkenness or some other careless license—the intemperate horses of their souls invade them when they are off guard. Bringing them together, they compel them to pursue that kind of delight which the common people judge most blessed, and they occasionally persist in fulfilling that desire. Yet they indulge in this but rarely, because the whole mind does not consent to this thought. These two live as friends, though less so than the former, both while their love is burning and after it has cooled; they believe they have given and received the firmest pledges to one another, which they consider a divine law never to break, lest they should one day become enemies instead of friends. Finally, when they depart from this life, they leave without wings indeed, but having begun in a way to sprout feathers. Therefore, they carry off no small prize for their amorous madness. For the law prohibits those who have already begun their journey under the heavens from descending into darkness and the place beneath the earth; instead, it commands that they lead a bright life and become blessed while they travel together and sprout wings at the same time, and these things happen because of Love. So many and such divine things, O boy, will the friendship of a lover confer upon you. But the familiarity of the non-lover, joined with a mortal temperance and devoted to mortal and meager interests, will generate in the soul of his companion that illiberality <note>original: "illiberalitatem," referring to a narrow-minded or ungenerous spirit</note> which the common people hold to be virtue; it will cause the soul to wander mindlessly for nine thousand years above and beneath the earth. This, O beloved Love, is the most beautiful and best recantation <note>original: "palinodia," a poem retracting a previous one</note> we could offer you, sung in poetic words and figures at the urging of Phaedrus. 

<margin>Prayer to Love.</margin> Therefore, forgive what was said before and graciously accept these words from us; assist me with favor and kindness. Do not, in some fit of indignation, take away the art of love which you granted to us, nor diminish it. Furthermore, grant that I may be held in higher esteem among the honorable than I am now. If anything unworthy of your divinity was said by Phaedrus or me, blame Lysias <note>A famous speechwriter of the time</note>, the author of this discourse, and make him desist from such speeches. Turn him toward philosophy, just as his brother Polemarchus has turned, so that his lover Phaedrus here may no longer waver back and forth as he does now, but may spend his life entirely in the pursuit of Love and wisdom together.

PHAEDRUS: I also pray to the god, O Socrates, that it may be so, if this is better. Indeed, I have long admired your speech, seeing how much it excels your previous one; I am now afraid that Lysias will appear humble to me if he strives to produce another in competition with it. In fact, O wonderful man, a certain citizen recently rebuked him for this very thing, and throughout the whole accusation called him a "writer of speeches." Perhaps, therefore, out of a sense of honor, he will abstain from this kind of writing.

SOCRATES: This is a ridiculous opinion, O youth, and you wander far from your friend's mind if you think him so timid. Perhaps you truly believe his detractor spoke the truth in his reproaches?

PHAEDRUS: It certainly seemed so, Socrates. Nor is it unknown to you that the most powerful and prominent men in the republic are afraid to compose speeches and leave behind written works, lest they appear to posterity as "sophists" <note>Professional teachers of rhetoric who were often viewed with suspicion as being more interested in persuasion than truth</note>.

SOCRATES: That proverb, "Sweet Ancon" <note>original: "dulcis Ancon." A Greek proverb meaning "sweet bend" or "sweet elbow." Socrates explains its origin below.</note>, has escaped you, O Phaedrus; it is derived from the long bend of the Nile. And not only that, but it also escapes you that those citizens most excellent in wisdom strive most earnestly to compose and leave speeches for posterity. They love the praisers of their works so much that they write down at the beginning the names of those who everywhere praise their writings.

<margin>Proverb: Sweet Ancon.</margin> PHAEDRUS: How do you mean? I do not understand.

SOCRATES: Do you not know that at the beginning of a book composed by a statesman, the name of the praiser is written first?

PHAEDRUS: In what way?

SOCRATES: He says, "It seemed good to the Senate, or the people, or both," and he mentions the one who proposed it, naming him with ambition and extolling the author of the opinion. Then he continues, showing off his own wisdom to his praisers, often after delivering a very long speech. Does that seem to be anything other than a written speech?

PHAEDRUS: Certainly nothing else.

SOCRATES: And if it is approved, he leaves the theater rejoicing like a poet; but if it is rejected and he is excluded from writing down his opinion, or judged unworthy of having his opinion committed to letters, he and his friends mourn.

PHAEDRUS: Very much so.

SOCRATES: In this they clearly demonstrate that they do not despise this pursuit, but value it highly.

PHAEDRUS: Most highly.

SOCRATES: What then? If some orator or king has attained such power that, like Lycurgus, or Solon, or Darius, he can be considered an immortal writer in the city, does he not think himself equal to a god while still living? And do not posterity, looking upon his monuments, judge him similarly?

PHAEDRUS: Vehemently so.

SOCRATES: Do you then think that any such person, however malevolent toward Lysias, would rebuke him for this pursuit of writing?

PHAEDRUS: From what you say, it does not seem likely; for he would, it seems, be rebuking his own pursuit.

SOCRATES: Therefore, it can be clear to anyone that writing itself is not something to be rebuked.

PHAEDRUS: Why should it be?

SOCRATES: But this, I think, is shameful: to speak and write shamefully and badly.

PHAEDRUS: That is manifest.

SOCRATES: What then is the method of writing well and not well? Do we need, O Phaedrus, to inquire about these things from Lysias or someone else who has written or will write something—whether a public political work or a private one, whether in verse as a poet or in prose as a private citizen?

PHAEDRUS: You ask if we need to? For what else, so to speak, should a man live, if not for pleasures of this kind? Certainly not for those pleasures which pain must necessarily precede, otherwise the pleasure does not come at all—which is the case with almost all [physical pleasures].
