has almost the same pleasures as the body. For this reason, they are not unjustly called slavish. **SOCRATES:** We certainly have leisure in abundance; and it seems to me as if the cicadas, singing above our heads in the heat and disputing with one another, are looking down at us. If they were to see us, like so many others at midday, not disputing but sleeping—lulled by them into a mental sluggishness—they would deservedly laugh at us, thinking that some slaves had turned aside to them here, and in this very retreat were held by midday sleep like cattle under the shade beside a spring. But if they see us debating, and not at all captured by the allurements of those "Sirens" <note>Socrates compares the cicadas' song to the Sirens of Greek myth, whose song lured sailors to their doom.</note> so that we might sail on toward the harbor, they might perhaps most gladly grant us that prize which they are able to pass on to men by the concession of the gods. **PHAEDRUS:** What is this gift that they possess? For I do not think I have ever heard of it. **SOCRATES:** Yet it is not fitting for a man <margin>The fable of the origin and benefit of the Cicadas.</margin> who is a student of the Muses to be ignorant of such things. It is said that these cicadas were once men, before the Muses existed. Then, when the Muses were born and song was revealed, some of those men were so charmed by the pleasure of singing that they neglected food and drink while they sang, and so perished through their own imprudence. From these men the race of cicadas was subsequently born, obtaining this gift from the Muses: that they should not need nourishment, but without food or drink they should sing for as long as they live. Afterward, they go to the Muses to report which human honors which Muse here on earth. Therefore, by reporting to Terpsichore <note>The Muse of choral song and dance.</note> those who have celebrated her especially in dances and assemblies, they make her favorable to them. To Erato <note>The Muse of lyric and love poetry.</note> they report those who have honored her in matters of love, and to the others in the same way according to each one's kind of veneration. But to Calliope <note>The Muse of epic poetry and eloquence.</note>, the eldest, and to Urania <note>The Muse of astronomy.</note> who follows her, they report those who live in philosophy and honor their particular music; for these Muses, above all others, are concerned with the heavens and with discourses, both divine and human, modulating their voices most beautifully. Therefore, for many reasons we must speak of something, and not sleep at midday. **PHAEDRUS:** We must certainly speak. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, what we just now determined must now be discussed: namely, by what reasoning a person speaks and writes either rightly or not rightly. **PHAEDRUS:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Is it not necessary for one who is to speak rightly to have a true understanding of the matter about which he speaks? **PHAEDRUS:** I have heard, indeed, my dear Socrates, that it is not necessary for a future orator to learn what is truly just, but rather what seems so to the judging multitude; nor what is truly good or honorable, but what appears so. For it is from these appearances, rather than from the truth, that one is able to persuade. **SOCRATES:** The sayings of the wise, O Phaedrus, are never to be despised; rather, one must diligently consider what they mean. Therefore, I do not think we should pass over what you just said. **PHAEDRUS:** You speak rightly. **SOCRATES:** Let us then consider it in this way. **PHAEDRUS:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Plainly this: If I were to persuade you to fight off enemies with a horse, but we were both ignorant of what a horse is—yet I knew only this much about you, that Phaedrus thinks a horse is a domestic animal with large ears... **PHAEDRUS:** That would be ridiculous, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Not yet; but if I were to try earnestly to persuade you by a speech composed in praise of an ass, calling it a horse and affirming it to be a most excellent animal, useful at home and abroad, most ready for war, fit for carrying burdens, and most convenient for many other things... <margin>It is better to be a ridiculous friend than a heavy and hostile one.</margin> **PHAEDRUS:** That would be utterly absurd. **SOCRATES:** Is it not better to be a ridiculous friend than a heavy and hostile one? **PHAEDRUS:** So it seems. **SOCRATES:** When, therefore, an orator who is ignorant of good and evil persuades a city in a similar state of mind—not indeed by a speech in praise of the "shadow of an ass" as if it were a horse, but by debating about evil as if it were good—and having caught the opinions of the crowd, induces them to do evil instead of good, what kind of harvest do you think such an orator will reap from the seed he has sown? **PHAEDRUS:** A hardly good one. **SOCRATES:** Now, my good man, have we disparaged the art of speaking more rudely than is proper? She might perhaps say: "Why do you wonderful men talk nonsense? For I compel no one who is ignorant of the truth to learn to speak. But if anyone follows my advice, he will take me after having perceived the truth. This I certainly affirm to be the greatest thing: that without me, even he who knows the facts will possess the art of persuasion no more for it." **PHAEDRUS:** Would she not be right to say this? **SOCRATES:** I confess it, provided that the following arguments testify that she is an art. For I seem to hear some arguments asserting that she lies, and that she is not an art, but a certain <margin>The art of speaking rightly will not exist without truth.</margin> practice without art. "A true art of speaking without truth," says the Spartan, "neither exists nor ever will exist." **PHAEDRUS:** There is need of these arguments, Socrates. Therefore, bringing them here, discuss what they say and how. **SOCRATES:** Come here, noble creatures <note>Socrates addresses the cicadas or perhaps the arguments themselves as living things.</note>, and persuade Phaedrus, this honorable youth, that unless he philosophizes sufficiently, he will never be able to speak sufficiently about anything. Let Phaedrus answer Socrates' questioning. Will not rhetoric be entirely an art that allures the soul through speeches—not only in courts and other public assemblies, but also in private gatherings—the same regarding both great and small matters? For nothing is more honorable in great things than to conduct oneself according to the right reason of the art in small things. Have you not heard these things? <margin>Concerning what the right reason of speaking is occupied. Nestor and Ulysses used the art of speaking.</margin> **PHAEDRUS:** Not exactly, by Jove. But this art is said and written about chiefly concerning courts and also concerning public assemblies; I have not heard of it being extended further. **SOCRATES:** Have you only heard of the art of speaking which Nestor and Ulysses used at Troy? Have you never heard of that which Palamedes used? **PHAEDRUS:** By Jove, I have heard the speeches of Nestor—unless perhaps you are pretending that Gorgias is Nestor, or that Thrasymachus and Theodorus are Ulysses. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps. But let us leave them. You, however, answer: What do adversaries do in the courts? Do they not speak against one another? Or shall we say they do something else? **PHAEDRUS:** That is it. **SOCRATES:** Is it about the just and the unjust? **PHAEDRUS:** Yes. **SOCRATES:** Will not he who does this by art make the same thing appear to the same people now just, now unjust? **PHAEDRUS:** What prevents it? **SOCRATES:** And in a public assembly, so that the same things seem to the city now good, now the opposite? **PHAEDRUS:** Certainly. **SOCRATES:** Do we not hear that the Eleatic Palamedes <note>Likely referring to Zeno of Elea, known for his paradoxes.</note> was accustomed to act by his skill so that the same things appeared to his listeners both similar and dissimilar, one and many, remaining and flowing? **PHAEDRUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the faculty of contradiction...

<summary>Socrates recounts the myth of the cicadas to emphasize the importance of intellectual labor over idleness, then begins a dialectical inquiry with Phaedrus into whether rhetoric can truly be an "art" if it is divorced from the truth of its subject matter.</summary>

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON THE BEAUTIFUL.

...not only in courts of law and public assemblies, but also in all other matters, as it appears, in whatever men say; since it is a single art, it is practiced wherever one is able to make all things similar to all others—both those that can be and to those to whom they can be—and to bring those similarities into the light while another hides them. 

**PHAEDRUS.** In what way do you mean this? 

**SOCRATES.** In this way, certainly. Does deception happen in those things which differ much, or those which differ little? 

**PHAEDRUS.** In those which differ little. 

**SOCRATES.** And yet, if you transition little by little, you will remain hidden longer as you move toward the opposite than if you were to leap across suddenly. 

**PHAEDRUS.** How could it be otherwise? 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, whoever intends to deceive another without being deceived himself must exquisitely distinguish the similarity and dissimilarity of things. 

**PHAEDRUS.** That is necessary. 

**SOCRATES.** Can someone who is ignorant of the truth of individual things judge the small or great similarity of that which he does not know? 

**PHAEDRUS.** That is indeed impossible. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is clear that those who hold opinions contrary to the nature of things and are mistaken have been so affected because of certain similarities. 

**PHAEDRUS.** So it happens. 

**SOCRATES.** Can anyone, then, if he is ignorant of a thing, skillfully and gradually lead someone away from the truth to its opposite through specific similarities? Or can he avoid this error in himself? 

**PHAEDRUS.** Never. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, my friend, whoever is ignorant of the truth and is led by opinions exhibits a faculty of speaking that is, it seems, unskilled and ridiculous. 

**PHAEDRUS.** So it seems. 

**SOCRATES.** Do you wish to see in the speech of Lysias <note>A famous Athenian orator known for his clear, simple style.</note> which you have in your hands, and in our own discussion, where things are done skillfully and where they are done without art? 

**PHAEDRUS.** Most of all. For we are speaking plainly at present, since we lack clear examples. 

**SOCRATES.** But by some fortune, these speeches were spoken, as it seems, to show by example how a man who possesses the truth can, while playing with words, lead his listeners. And I, O Phaedrus, think the local gods are the causes of this. Perhaps also the interpreters of the Muses, the singers above our heads, have inspired us with this gift. For I myself possess no art of speaking. 

**PHAEDRUS.** Let it be as you say. Only show what you mean. 

**SOCRATES.** Come then; read the beginning of Lysias’s speech. 

**PHAEDRUS.** "The state of my affairs is as you have understood, and since it is so, you have heard how I think it would be to our advantage. I believe I should not fail to obtain what I ask from you for the reason that I am not captured by love for you. For lovers, as soon as they cease to love, repent of the benefits they have bestowed." 

**SOCRATES.** Stop. We must say where he fails and what he does without art. Must we not? 

**PHAEDRUS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** Is it not clear to everyone that in some things we all feel the same when we speak, but in others we do not? 

**PHAEDRUS.** I seem to understand what you say, yet I wish you would speak more plainly. 

**SOCRATES.** When someone pronounces the name of "iron" or "silver," we all immediately understand the same thing. 

**PHAEDRUS.** Exactly. 

**SOCRATES.** But what when the name of "the just" or "the good" is spoken? Is not one person carried one way and another another? And do we not disagree with others and even with ourselves? 

**PHAEDRUS.** Greatly. 

**SOCRATES.** In some things, therefore, we agree, and in others, we disagree. 

**PHAEDRUS.** That is so. 

**SOCRATES.** In which of these can we be more easily deceived? And in which of these does rhetoric have the most power? 

**PHAEDRUS.** It is clear: in those things about which we disagree. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, he who is to master rhetoric must first have distinguished these in order and perceived the form of each species: where the multitude can most easily be deceived by ambiguity, and where they cannot. 

**PHAEDRUS.** He would recognize a noble species, O Socrates, who could grasp that in thought. 

**SOCRATES.** Then I think nothing should escape him when he comes to individual cases; he must acutely perceive to which genus the thing he is about to speak of belongs. 

**PHAEDRUS.** Why not? 

**SOCRATES.** What then of Love? Do we say he is of the ambiguous genus or the other? 

**PHAEDRUS.** Of the ambiguous, certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** Or do you think he would allow you to say those things about him which you said above? Namely, that he is ruinous to the beloved and the lover alike, and again, that he is the greatest of all goods? 

**PHAEDRUS.** You speak cleverly. 

**SOCRATES.** But tell me this also—for because of that divine possession <note>Socrates refers to his "divine sign" or the inspiration of the local spirits.</note>, I do not quite remember—whether I defined Love at the beginning of the discussion. 

**PHAEDRUS.** By Jove, wonderfully so. 

**SOCRATES.** Oh, how much more skillful you show the nymphs of Achelous and Pan, the son of Mercury, to be at composing speeches than Lysias, the son of Cephalus! Or am I saying nothing? But did Lysias also, in the beginning of his amorous discourse, force us to understand Love to be some certain thing that he himself wanted? And did he complete the whole speech following that? Do you want us to read the beginning again? 

**PHAEDRUS.** As you please; though what you seek is not there. 

**SOCRATES.** Read, so that I may hear the man himself. 

**PHAEDRUS.** "The state of my affairs is as you have understood, and since it is so, you have heard how I think it would be to our advantage. I believe I should not fail to obtain what I ask from you for the reason that I am not captured by love for you. For lovers, as soon as they cease to love, repent of the benefits they have bestowed." 

**SOCRATES.** He seems to be very far from doing what we seek. Indeed, he attempts to carry through his discourse not from the beginning but from the end, in a reversed and backward manner; he begins with those things which a lover, once his love is extinguished, reproaches a youth with. Or have I said nothing, my dear Phaedrus, you charming man? 

**PHAEDRUS.** It is certainly the end of the matter of which he speaks, Socrates. 

**SOCRATES.** What of the rest? Do not the parts of the speech seem to you to be tossed about at random? Or do you think that what is placed in the second position is joined there by some necessity? Or any other of the things said? For to me, as one ignorant of all things, it seems that whatever occurred to the writer was said not ungenerously. But do you have some "necessity of writing" by which he arranged those things in such a sequence? 

**PHAEDRUS.** You are too kind, Socrates, if you think I can judge his writings with such subtlety. 

**SOCRATES.** But this I think you would say: that every speech ought to be constituted like a living creature <term>animal: a living being or organism</term>, so that it has its own body, which is neither without a head nor lacks feet; but has a middle and extremes, fitting to each other and to the whole. 

**PHAEDRUS.** How could it be otherwise? 

**SOCRATES.** Consider, I pray, whether your friend's speech is like that or otherwise. You will find it...

# BOOK
## XXVI.

...in no way differing from that epitaph which some say was inscribed for Midas the Phrygian. PHAEDRUS.
<margin>Epitaph upon the tomb of Midas.</margin>
What was that, and of what sort? SOCRATES. Listen. *I am a maiden of bronze placed upon the tomb of Midas: as long as water flows and trees grow green, remaining here I shall announce to passers-by: that Midas lies in this lamented tomb.* <note>Socrates is quoting a famous poem to illustrate a disorganized speech where the lines can be read in any order without changing the meaning.</note> But truly, it makes no difference whether you place any part of it first or last, as I believe you yourself see.
PHAEDRUS. You are mocking our speech, Socrates. SOCRATES. Let us then dismiss this one, lest you become angry with us; although many examples could be found in it which, if examined, might be useful to us in learning not to imitate such things. But let us descend to the other speeches; for they contain something, I believe, that should be observed by men studious of speaking. PHAEDRUS. What is that? SOCRATES. They were certainly contrary: for one asserted that one should yield to a lover, the other to a non-lover. PHAEDRUS. And quite strenuously, too. SOCRATES. I thought you were going to answer more truly: namely, and quite "madly" indeed. But what I was seeking is this very thing. We called Love a certain kind of madness. Did we not? PHAEDRUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Now, we posit two species of madness.
<margin>Madness divides.</margin>
One arising from human diseases. The other from a divine alienation <note>original: "alienatione diuina" — a state of being "beside oneself" or inspired by the gods</note>, by which one is snatched out of the accustomed institution of life.
<margin>FOUR DIVINE MADNESSES.
Prophecy to Apollo.
Mysteries to Dionysus.
Poetry to the Muses.
Love to Venus & Cupid.</margin>
PHAEDRUS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Moreover, there are four divine parts, just as four gods preside over them. And we attributed prophecy and inspiration to Apollo; Mysteries to Dionysus; Poetry to the Muses; and the madness of Love to Venus and Cupid <note>original: "Amori"</note>, the best of all. And I know not how, while we were sketching the affection of Love through certain images, we perhaps touched upon some truth; perhaps also we wandered elsewhere. Therefore, mixing a speech that was not entirely improbable, we composed a certain mythical hymn: and as if playing, O Phaedrus, we modestly praised my master and yours, Love, the guardian of beautiful boys. PHAEDRUS. These things are not unpleasant for me to hear. SOCRATES. Let us therefore take this from it: in what way the discussion passed from blame to praise. PHAEDRUS. How do you mean that? SOCRATES. To me indeed we seem to have played at the rest. But if someone were to grasp by art the power of the two species into which we just now fell by chance, he would have achieved a not ungrateful work. PHAEDRUS. Which species do you mean? SOCRATES. That by looking toward one Idea, he may bring together things scattered far and wide: so that by defining each thing, he makes manifest always that which is being discussed. Just as we just now defined what Love is, whether it was done well or ill. Certainly from this our discussion had clarity in itself, and a constant harmony with itself. PHAEDRUS. But what is the other species you speak of, Socrates? SOCRATES. That he may again cut it back into species, joint by joint, according to the nature of things: and not, in the manner of an unskilled cook, break any limbs; but act just as the previous discourses did: which took the agitation of the mind as one common species. Just as in one body the twin limbs are called by the same name, one right and the other left: so those discourses considered the species of agitation in us to be one by nature. And the first one indeed, dividing the left part, and again partitioning this, did not stop until it found a certain "left-handed" love; and having found it, quite rightly, it condemned it. The following one led us to the right-hand part of madness: where finding a Love similar in name to the first, but divine, and amplifying it, it praised it as the cause of our greatest goods. PHAEDRUS. You speak most truly. SOCRATES. I am a friend of these divisions and collections, O Phaedrus, so that I may be capable of both understanding and speaking. And if I think anyone else is able to look both toward the one and toward the many according to the nature of things, I follow behind him as if in the footsteps of a god. And those who can do this, whether I name them rightly or otherwise, God himself knows.
<margin>He who can divide according to the nature of things is a dialectician, i.e., a metaphysician.</margin>
But thus far I call them dialecticians. But now tell me, I pray, by what name it ought to be called according to your and Lysias's opinion. Or is this the art of speaking which Thrasymachus and others used, and were themselves wise in speaking, and make others such, who wish to offer gifts to them as if to kings? PHAEDRUS. Those men are indeed kingly: yet they are not skilled in those things about which you ask. But you seem to rightly call this species "dialectic"; however, "rhetoric" still escapes us. SOCRATES. How do you say that? Can there be anything beautiful which, though distinct from these, is yet perceived by art? It is by no means to be despised by you and me: but we must say what remains in rhetoric. PHAEDRUS. Very many things, Socrates, are handed down in the books composed on the art of speaking. SOCRATES. You have reminded me opportunely. I believe the "Introduction" <note>original: "Prooemium"</note> must be called the first part of a speech. Do you call such things those distinguished ornaments of the art? PHAEDRUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. There follows in the second place the "Narration" and the "Assertion of Witnesses." In the third, "Conjectures." In the fourth, "Probabilities." And I believe the excellent maker of speeches from Byzantium introduced "Proof" and "Confirmation." PHAEDRUS. You mean the eminent Theodorus! SOCRATES. Indeed. He also discovered how "Refutation" and "Double Refutation" can be made in accusation and defense. And why do we not bring forward the distinguished Evenus of Paros? Who first discovered "Sub-declarations" and also "Praises." And there are those who say he inserts "Reproaches" of this kind into poems for the sake of memory. For he is a wise man. But we shall let Lysias and Gorgias go: who preferred probabilities to truths; and by the power of speech make small things seem great, and great things in turn small, likewise old things new, and the newest old. They also discovered a concise brevity of speaking, and again an infinite prolixity of words. When Prodicus once heard these things from me, he laughed, and asserted that he alone had found what words that art requires. Namely, that it needs neither few nor many: but a moderate amount. PHAEDRUS. You have answered most wisely, Prodicus. SOCRATES. Hippias...

<summary>Socrates explains the method of dialectic—the ability to synthesize many things into one definition and divide them again by their natural joints—while contrasting it with the technical rules of famous rhetoricians.</summary>

# PHAEDRUS, OR ON BEAUTY.

...but we do not mention him at all. For I believe the guest from Elis <note>Referring to Hippias of Elis, a famous Sophist</note> also agrees with him. 
**PHAE.** Why not? 
**SO.** What further shall we say of musical harmony? Of him who introduced the doubling of words, notable maxims, comparisons, and likenesses—and the use of names for the splendor of speech, just as he learned from Licymnius? 
**PHAE.** But were not the writings of Protagoras of such a kind, O Socrates? 
**SO.** Indeed, the style of Protagoras was correct and proper, O youth, and there was much that was excellent in his prose. But in the art of stirring pity for old age and poverty, the orator of Chalcedon <note>Thrasymachus of Chalcedon</note> excelled; he was also powerful in provoking anger and then calming it, as if he were soothing it with an incantation, as he says; he was also supreme in concocting slanders whenever necessary. Regarding the conclusion of a speech, everyone seems to agree, though some call it a "recapitulation" and others by different names. 
**PHAE.** By "conclusion," do you mean summarizing everything said above at the heel of the speech to bring it back to the listeners' memory? 
**SO.** That is what I mean—and if you have anything else to say about this art. 
**PHAE.** I have only small things, not worth mentioning. 
**SO.** Let us set aside the small things; let us rather bring these matters into the light, so we may see what power of art they have and when they have it. 
**PHAE.** And they have the greatest power, O Socrates, in the gatherings of men. 
**SO.** They certainly do. But, O blessed one, see whether the fabric of these things appears as thin and loose to you as it does to me. 
**PHAE.** Just show me. 
**SO.** Tell me then: if someone should say to your friend Eryximachus, or to his father Acumenus, in this manner: "I know how to apply such things to the body so as to make it warm or cold as I please; I also know how to induce vomiting, or a movement of the bowels, and other purgings, and many other such things; and knowing these, I profess myself to be a physician and able to make anyone else a physician"—what do you think they would answer? 
**PHAE.** What else but to ask whether he also knows to whom, when, and to what extent each of these should be applied? 
**SO.** Therefore, if he should say he understands that in no way, but that the one who learned from him ought to be able to do such things—what will they answer? 
**PHAE.** Surely that such a man is insane; who, having heard something from a medical book and stumbled upon a few remedies, thinks he has become a physician without understanding anything of the art. 
**SO.** And what if someone said to Sophocles and Euripides that he knew how to make a long speech about a small matter, and conversely a very short one about a great matter; and whenever he wished, to move one to pity, or the opposite, to strike horror and threats, and other similar things; and by teaching these, he thought he was teaching the art of tragic poetry? 
**PHAE.** They too, O Socrates, I think, would laugh at him, thinking tragedy to be anything other than the composition of these elements, fitting both to each other and to the whole. 
**SO.** They would not, I think, rebuke him rudely, but would act just as a musician might when meeting a man who thinks himself a musician because he knows how to produce the lowest and highest notes on a string. For he would not say harshly, "You are a miserable madman," but as a musician, he would advise more gently: "O best of men, it is absolutely necessary for one who is to be a musician to hold these things. However, nothing prevents one who is in your state from understanding nothing at all of harmony. You recognize the things necessary *before* harmony, but you are utterly ignorant of harmony itself." 
**PHAE.** Most correctly. 
**SO.** So too Sophocles would say to the one meeting him that he possessed the preliminaries of tragedy rather than tragedy itself; and Acumenus would say the same of the preliminaries of medicine, not medicine. 
**PHAE.** Exactly so. 
**SO.** What then? If the honey-tongued Adrastus, or Pericles, heard of those excellent devices of words we were just relating—the brevity, the likenesses, and those other things we judged worthy of consideration—do we think they would, out of rudeness, be harshly angry with those who wrote and taught such things as the "rhetorical faculty"? Or would they, being wiser than us, rebuke us thus: "O Phaedrus and Socrates, one should not be angry, but should forgive, if some who are ignorant of the art of discourse are unable to define what rhetoric is; and being in such a state, while they possess the preliminary rudiments of the art, they boast they have discovered rhetoric, and by teaching these things, they profess to hand down the complete art of oratory. But to arrange each of these for persuasion, and to weave together the whole speech—as if a teacher were not needed for these—they say their disciples must acquire by their own industry." 
**PHAE.** Such indeed, O Socrates, that art seems to be, which those men teach and write about as rhetoric. And you seem to me to have spoken the truth. But the art of the true orator and persuader—in what way and from where can we claim it for ourselves? 
**SO.** It is consistent, O Phaedrus, and perhaps even necessary, that just as in other contests, so in this one, perfection is required. For if nature has granted you to be an orator, you will be an excellent one if doctrine and exercise are added. But if you lack any of these, you will be incomplete. As for how great such an art is, it seems to consist not in the path followed by Gorgias and Thrasymachus, but rather in another. 
**PHAE.** In which one especially? 
**SO.** It seems, O best of men, not without reason that Pericles stood out as the most perfect of all orators. 
**PHAE.** Why? 
**SO.** All great arts require dialectical exercise and the contemplation of the sublime in the nature of things. For the very sublimity of mind and effective power in accomplishing any matter seem to proceed from this in some way. This is what Pericles added to his sharpness of intellect. For relying on his familiarity with Anaxagoras, an investigator of such things, he gave himself to contemplation; he grasped that nature of mind and mindlessness about which Anaxagoras discoursed so diffusely. From there, he drew into the art of speaking what seemed useful to him. 
**PHAE.** How do you mean that? 
**SO.** The method of the art of healing and the art of speaking is almost the same. 
**PHAE.** In what way? 
**SO.** In both, it is necessary to divide nature: that of the body in one, and that of the soul in the other, if not only by exercise and use, but...

XXVI.

...also by art you will provide medicines and nourishment to the body in such a way that you make it both healthy and robust; but to the soul, you will apply persuasion and virtue in abundance through reason and lawful institutions.

PHAEDRUS: That seems likely, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Do you think, then, that the nature of the soul can be sufficiently understood without the nature of the whole <note>original: "totius natura" - referring to the macrocosm or the universe as a whole</note>?

PHAEDRUS: If Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician, often called the Father of Medicine</note>, the successor of Asclepius, is to be believed, we shall not even think the nature of the body can be understood without 

<margin>That it is necessary to seek beyond the author's opinion and reason. On the reasoning of nature.</margin>

this kind of study.

SOCRATES: He speaks wisely, my friend. But we must consider, besides Hippocrates, whether the reasoning of our discussion is in harmony.

PHAEDRUS: I agree.

SOCRATES: Attend then to what Hippocrates and true reason say about the investigation of nature. Must not the nature of anything be thought out in this way: First, whether that thing is simple or multiform, concerning which we desire to possess art ourselves and be able to give it to others; then, if it is simple, to investigate what power it has by nature for acting and upon what, and again, what power it has for being acted upon and by what. But if it has many forms, these having been enumerated, one must inquire into the natural power of acting and being acted upon in each individual part just as in the whole.

PHAEDRUS: So it appears, Socrates.

SOCRATES: Indeed, progress without these seems like the journey of a blind man. However, one who treats something by art is not to be compared to the blind or the deaf. But it is clear that whoever adapts speeches to someone by art will exquisitely demonstrate the nature of the substance of that person to whom he applies the speeches; and that is the soul.

PHAEDRUS: Without a doubt.

SOCRATES: Does not all his effort strive toward this: that he may thoroughly persuade the soul?

PHAEDRUS: Entirely.

SOCRATES: It is established, therefore, that Thrasymachus <note>A famous teacher of rhetoric (sophist) mentioned in Plato's Republic</note> and whoever else applies himself to the teaching of rhetoric must first, with the greatest diligence, describe and declare whether the soul is naturally one and uniform, or multiform according to the shape of the body; for we say that this is to show its nature.

PHAEDRUS: Absolutely.

SOCRATES: Secondly, he must show what it can do to each thing or what it can suffer from each.

PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Thirdly, having classified the types of speeches and the emotions, he must run through all the causes, adapting each to each, and teaching what kind of soul is necessarily moved by what kinds of speeches and for what cause, while another is not moved at all.

PHAEDRUS: This would be most excellent, as it seems.

SOCRATES: Therefore, my friend, neither this nor anything else, if treated otherwise, will ever be treated artistically. But our modern writers on this art, whom you yourself have heard, are clever, and while knowing the nature of the soul most beautifully, they hide it from us. Until they speak and write in this manner, we will never 

<margin>In what way one must write by art.</margin>

confess that they write by art.

PHAEDRUS: What manner do you mean?

SOCRATES: The words themselves I could not easily say. But in what manner one ought to write if we are to write by art, I will explain as far as possible.

PHAEDRUS: Speak, I pray.

SOCRATES: Since the faculty of speaking is a certain leading of the soul <note>original: "animi attractio ac perductio" - translating the Greek 'psychagogia' or soul-leading</note>, it is necessary for the future orator to know how many forms the soul has. These are so many and of such a kind; whence some people become like this, and others like that. These being thus distinguished, there are also so many and such kinds of speeches. Therefore, souls of such a kind are easily persuaded to such things by certain speeches of such a kind for a certain cause; while those affected otherwise are, for some cause, not persuaded at all. It is necessary, therefore, for a man who has contemplated such things, when he sees these happening in individuals and as they are in actual practice, to follow them quickly through his senses; otherwise, he does not yet possess anything more than the words once handed down to him by teachers. But when he can sufficiently say what kind of person is persuaded by what kinds of speeches, and acutely perceives the person present to be endowed with that character about which he previously disputed—and thus that this person must be compelled to such things by such speeches—he, being thus instructed, will then finally have perfectly attained the art, when he has added to these the knowledge of the opportunity for speaking and keeping silent, and knows the right use or abuse of brevity, of piteousness, of sharp vehemence, of amplification, and of the other parts of oratory handed down by teachers, but not before. But he who lacks any of these in speaking, teaching, or writing, and yet says he speaks by art, is overcome by the one who is not persuaded. But perhaps the writer will compel us thus: "O Phaedrus and Socrates, do you think the art of speaking should be grasped in this way or otherwise?"

PHAEDRUS: It is impossible, Socrates, to do it otherwise; although that work appears to be no small task.

SOCRATES: You speak the truth, and for the sake of these things, having turned all speeches upside down and inside out, one must inquire whether any easier and shorter way to that art occurs; lest we wander blindly through a long and rough path when we might proceed through a short and level one. Therefore, if you can bring any help from those things you received from Lysias or anyone else, recall it to memory and set it forth.

PHAEDRUS: For the sake of trying, I could indeed; but not at present.

SOCRATES: Do you want me to recount to you a discourse which I once heard concerning such matters?

PHAEDRUS: Why not?

SOCRATES: It is said to be just, O Phaedrus, to "give the Wolf his due" <note>A proverb meaning to hear the other side of the argument</note>, and so you should do. They say, at any rate, that there is no need to extol these things so much, nor to carry them to the heights by a long circuit of discussion. For, as we said at the beginning of the discussion, the future orator does not need to know the truth about what is just and good, whether in things or in men by nature or education. For in the courts, no one cares at all for the truth of these things, but only for persuasion. And that is "the probable" <note>original: "verisimile" - literally 'truth-like' or 'probable'</note>; to which he who is to speak by art must intend his mind. Sometimes even facts should not be told, unless it is probable that they happened; but both in accusation and defense, one must always introduce probabilities; and the speaker should altogether pursue the probable, but neglect the truth. For if this is observed in every speech, it exhibits the perfect art of oratory.

PHAEDRUS: You have related those things, Socrates, which they say who profess the art of rhetoric. For I remember we briefly touched on this in the earlier parts. This seems to be something great to those who are engaged in this art. But you have also heavily criticized Tisias <note>One of the legendary founders of Greek rhetoric</note> himself.

SOCRATES: Let Tisias also tell us then, whether he calls anything else "probable" and "likely" than that which...

<summary>Socrates explains to Phaedrus that true rhetoric requires a scientific understanding of the soul's nature and how different types of souls are affected by specific types of speech. He contrasts this "artistic" approach with the common practice of sophists who prioritize probability and persuasion over truth.</summary>

as is commonly thought. PHAEDRUS. What else then? SOCRATES. In addition to this, he <note>Referring to the rhetorician Tisias</note> seems to have discovered and written down a clever and artistic rule: that if a weak but bold man, having beaten a strong but cowardly man and stripped him, is brought to court, neither of them should confess the truth. Instead, the coward should say he was not beaten by the bold man alone, while the bold man should refute this by showing they were alone, and resort to a plea such as: "How could I, being so weak, have attacked this strong man?" The other will not admit his own cowardice, but by devising some other lie, will perhaps try to argue against his adversary. And in other matters too, there are such things said according to the "art." Is it not so, Phaedrus? PHAEDRUS. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Oh, how cleverly Tisias seems to have discovered this hidden art—or whoever else it was, or by whatever other name he delights to be called! But shall we say this to him, my friend, or not? PHAEDRUS. Say what? SOCRATES. "O Tisias, long before your arrival we were affirming that this 'probability' and 'verisimilitude' is produced in the minds of the masses only through a likeness to the truth. And we were asserting that likenesses of the truth can be most aptly discovered everywhere by one who actually knows the truth." Therefore, if you have anything else to say about this art, we will listen; if not, we will trust what we said a little while ago: namely, that unless <margin>A precept for speaking rightly.</margin> a speaker knows the different natures of his listeners, and can distinguish things into their specific kinds, and again encompass individuals under a single idea, he will never attain the art of speaking as far as is possible for a human. But he will never achieve these things without long study. A wise man will not labor in this for the sake of speaking and acting before men, but rather so that he may be able to speak and do what is pleasing to the gods. For those wiser than us, O Tisias, say that a man in possession of his mind ought not to meditate on how to please his fellow-slaves—except as a secondary matter—but how to obey good masters of good character. Therefore, if the circuitous path is long, do not wonder; for it must be traveled for the sake of great things, not for the reasons you think. Yet, as reason dictates, if anyone wishes, these rhetorical goals will also be most beautifully achieved as a result of those greater pursuits. PHAEDRUS. This seems to be very beautifully said, Socrates, if only one could achieve it. SOCRATES. But it is noble to always strive for noble things, and to endure whatever happens. PHAEDRUS. Truly. SOCRATES. Let this be enough said concerning the art and the lack of art in speech. PHAEDRUS. Enough indeed. SOCRATES. It remains for us to discuss the fitness and unfitness of writing, and how it comes about. PHAEDRUS. Clearly. SOCRATES. Do you know how you can best please God in the matter of words, whether speaking or acting? PHAEDRUS. Not at all. Do you? SOCRATES. <margin>On the fitness of writing.</margin> I have heard some things handed down from the ancients; whether they are true, they themselves know. But if we could find the truth ourselves, would we still care about human opinions? PHAEDRUS. A ridiculous question indeed. But relate what you say you have heard. SOCRATES. I heard that in the region of Naucratis in Egypt, there was one of the ancient gods, to whom the bird called the Ibis was sacred. The name of the divinity himself was Theuth. He was the first to discover number and calculation, geometry and astronomy, and further, the games of draughts and dice, and also letters. <margin>The Ibis bird dedicated to the spirit Theuth. Egyptian Thebes.</margin> At that time, Thamus was king of all Egypt, residing in the great city of the upper region which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and they call the god himself Ammon. Theuth went to him and showed him his arts, saying they ought to be distributed to the rest of the Egyptians. The king asked what the utility of each was; as Theuth explained them, the king praised what seemed well said and blamed what was not. Thamus is said to have shown Theuth many points for and against each art, which would take too long to recount. But when they came to letters, Theuth said: "This discipline, O King, will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memories. For it is a remedy <note>original: "remedium" - here used in the sense of a 'potion' or 'tool' (Greek: pharmakon)</note> for memory and wisdom that has been discovered." But the king replied: "O most ingenious Theuth, one man is able to give birth to an art, but another is better able to judge what measure of harm or profit it will bring to those who use it. And now you, the father of letters, out of benevolence have claimed the opposite of what they can actually do. For the use of these will create forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn them, because of the neglect of memory; since, relying on external written marks, they will not recall things from within themselves. Therefore, you have found a remedy not for memory, but for reminding. You provide your disciples with the reputation of wisdom rather than the truth. For when they have read many things without the teaching of a master, they will seem to be experts in many things while they are mostly ignorant. They will be difficult to associate with, as they are not endowed with true wisdom, but merely adorned with the reputation of it." PHAEDRUS. O Socrates, you easily make up stories from Egypt or any other nation you please. SOCRATES. But my friend, those in the temple of Zeus at Dodona say that the first prophetic utterances came from an oak tree. To those ancients, since they were not "wise" like you moderns, it was enough in their simplicity to listen to rocks and oaks, provided they spoke the truth. You, perhaps, think it matters who the speaker is and where he comes from. You do not consider only whether what is said is true or false. PHAEDRUS. You have rebuked me rightly; I think it is with letters just as the Theban king says. SOCRATES. Therefore, whoever thinks he can hand down an art in writing, or receives it as if something certain and firm will come from the writing, is quite foolish. He truly ignores the prophecy of Ammon, believing that there is something more in written words than a means of reminding one who already knows the subjects which the writing signifies. PHAEDRUS. Most right. SOCRATES. Writing has this grave drawback, O Phaedrus, and it is truly similar to painting. For the works of painting stand there as if they were alive; but if you ask them anything, they keep a very respectful silence. Think of written discourses in the same way: they might seem to speak as if they had some intelligence. But if, being eager to learn, you question them about something they have said, they always signify one and the same thing. And every discourse, once it is written, is tossed about everywhere...

When it is unjustly attacked or undeservedly insulted, it always needs its father <note>The "father" here refers to the author or creator of the text.</note> to protect it. For the writing itself can neither push back against an adversary nor bring help to itself.

**PHAEDRUS** These things also seem to have been rightly spoken by you.

**SOCRATES** What further? Shall we look at another kind of discourse, the brother of this one? Let us see how it is produced legitimately, and how much better and more powerful it is than the other when it is born.

**PHAEDRUS** Which one is that? And how do you say it comes to be?

**SOCRATES** I mean the one that is written with knowledge in the soul of the learner; because it is able to help itself, and it understands with whom it should speak and before whom it should remain silent.

**PHAEDRUS** You are speaking of the living and breathing discourse of the man who knows, of which the written word might not unfairly be called a kind of image <note>original: "simulacrum"</note>.

**SOCRATES** Entirely so. But tell me this as well. Would a farmer who has his wits about him take the seeds he cares for most, from which he expects fruit, and sow them with great zeal and diligence during the summer in the "Gardens of Adonis" <note>The Gardens of Adonis were small pots used to grow quick-fading flowers for festivals; Socrates uses them as a metaphor for superficial, rapid growth versus deep, lasting knowledge.</note>, just so he can see them become beautiful flowers in eight days? Or if he ever did such a thing, would he not do it for the sake of a festival or a game? But when he acts in earnest, applying his skill in agriculture, he will sow where it is appropriate, and he will consider himself satisfied if his sowing reaches its fruit in the interval of eight months?

**PHAEDRUS** Exactly so, Socrates; he would do the former as a joke, as you say, but the latter in earnest.

**SOCRATES** And shall we think that a man who possesses the knowledge of what is just, noble, and good is less skilled than a farmer when it comes to sowing his own seeds?

**PHAEDRUS** Not at all.

**SOCRATES** Therefore, he will not zealously "sow" them with a pen in black water <note>ink</note> through discourses that are unable to help themselves when in danger, and unable to sufficiently demonstrate the truth.

**PHAEDRUS** Certainly, that would not be reasonable.

**SOCRATES** Indeed not. Rather, he will sow and write in the "gardens of letters," as it seems, for the sake of play; and when he writes, he does so to lay up a treasure of reminders against the forgetfulness of old age, both for himself and for others who follow the same path. He will rejoice as he beholds his tender fruits growing; and while other men pursue other games, celebrating banquets and similar things, he will instead spend his life in the delights of discourse.

**PHAEDRUS** You describe a most noble game, Socrates, compared to other very cheap ones—the game of a man who can play with discourses, conversing about justice and the other things you mention.

**SOCRATES** It is so indeed, my friend Phaedrus. But in my opinion, the pursuit is much more noble when someone, using the <term>art of dialectic</term> <note>The method of seeking truth through guided questioning and logical division.</note> and finding a suitable soul, plants and sows discourses with knowledge. These are able to bring help both to themselves and to the one who sowed them; they produce fruit and yield seeds from which other discourses, planted in other characters, are able to preserve that immortal gift forever. This makes the one who possesses them as happy as it is possible for a human to be.

**PHAEDRUS** That is also much more noble.

**SOCRATES** Now then, Phaedrus, since these things are agreed upon, we can decide those other matters.

**PHAEDRUS** Which ones?

**SOCRATES** Those for the sake of which we came this far: to examine the reproach against Lysias regarding the art of writing, and to distinguish between discourses written with art and those without art. I think we have now sufficiently declared what is artistic and what is devoid of art.

**PHAEDRUS** So it appears.

**SOCRATES** Again, one must remember that no one can fully master the art of speaking for the purpose of persuasion and teaching—as our previous reasoning showed—until he knows the truth of the things he says or writes. He must know how to define the whole subject, and having set the definition, know how to divide it again according to its species until he reaches the indivisible parts. By this method, having contemplated the nature of the soul and discovered what fits each nature, he should arrange and adorn his discourse accordingly: offering complex and harmonious discourses to a complex soul, and simple discourses to a simple soul.

**PHAEDRUS** That has certainly been made clear.

**SOCRATES** But what shall we say about that question we touched on above: whether it is honorable or shameful to compose speeches, and how this pursuit can be rightly blamed or not? Have our words sufficiently declared this?

**PHAEDRUS** Which words?

**SOCRATES** Namely, that if Lysias or anyone else ever wrote or writes—whether privately or publicly as civil laws—in such a way that he thinks there is great stability and certainty in his writings, that must be considered a disgrace to the writer, whether someone says so or not. For to be ignorant of what is true and what is false concerning justice and injustice, good and evil, even if the entire crowd praises it, can never truly be anything but most shameful.

**PHAEDRUS** Most shameful indeed.

**SOCRATES** On the other hand, consider the man who thinks that written words are mostly for play and are necessarily like jokes; who believes that no discourse, whether in prose or poetry, is worth great effort in composition (like those poems recited for the sake of persuasion without judgment or instruction). Instead, he believes that the best of those discourses were composed only to serve as reminders for those who already know. He believes that only in discourses spoken for the sake of teaching and learning—those truly written in the soul about justice, nobility, and goodness—is there clarity and perfection, and that these alone are worthy of serious study. He judges that such discourses should be called his legitimate sons: first the one found within himself, and then any sons or brothers of that discourse that have grown worthily in the souls of others. He sets all other writings aside. This man, I say, Phaedrus, seems to be the kind of person we would pray to become.

**PHAEDRUS** I entirely desire and pray for what you say.

**SOCRATES** But let these things be said by us regarding the art of speaking, as if we were playing. Therefore, go and tell Lysias that we went down to the spring of the nymphs and the gathering of the Muses, and we heard discourses which commanded us to tell Lysias and the other writers of speeches—and Homer too, and whoever else composed poetry, whether plain or set to song—and finally Solon and all who committed civil institutions to writing: that if they composed such things while knowing the truth, and can defend their work when it is challenged, and can show by speaking that their writings are of less value than their spoken words, then they should be called not by names derived from what they played with using a pen, but rather from those things they seriously thought out...

<summary>Socrates argues that written text is a mere "image" of the living word and that true knowledge is planted through dialectic in the soul. He concludes that a writer is only worthy of respect if they recognize the limitations of the written word compared to the truth found in spoken discourse.</summary>

### Marsilio’s Argument for the Apology.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a classical figure or deity within an architectural frame.</image-desc> THE ancient theologians of the nations were divided into three sects. Some sacrificed only to demons <note>original: "daemonibus" - in the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil</note>, because they distrusted, I believe, that the prayers of men could reach the celestial beings. Others also worshipped the celestial beings, thinking that they not only live and understand, but also look around at all things with their rays and hear them; and therefore, that the rites of sacrifices are seen by them, and the praises and prayers of suppliants are heard. Nevertheless, they thought the prayers of souls living in these bodies could not reach those gods who have no commerce with bodies. Finally, others venerated these very gods above all, judging that all effects are perfectly contained by the highest causes of things, both in human knowledge and virtue. They called these gods sometimes "visible" (that is, the celestial bodies) and sometimes "invisible" (that is, the super-celestial, whom our people call angels and they call gods, as if they were the closest contemplators and ministers of the highest God). Furthermore, they think there is a triple providence. One is universal in God, through which He foresees and provides all things for everyone. A less universal one is in the gods, through which they indeed consult for everyone, yet do not exhibit all gifts, but only certain ones to all. Finally, a particular providence is in the demons, by which they grant certain things to certain people. And they distribute the demons into as many orders as there are stars in heaven, so that some are Saturnian, others Jovian <note>associated with Jupiter</note>, and others likewise. Moreover, they place all these orders in fire, but in a fiery manner; and in pure air, but in an airy manner; and in thick air, in a watery manner. These "watery" ones they believe preside over different species of living things and favor the sensual and vegetative nature everywhere. These are the ones Plato says mixed pleasure with many evils right from the beginning. The "airy" demons, however, favor the rational power and separate it in a way from the vegetative and sensual nature. Finally, the "fiery" ones turn the discourse of reason toward the contemplation of higher things. And in this way, the watery demons rule the voluptuous life, the airy the active life, and the fiery the contemplative life. Since they judge the gods to be immortal and impassible <note>incapable of suffering or being affected by external force</note>, but men to be mortal and passible, they hold that all demons are passible in their affections; the higher and middle ones are also immortal, but the lowest are long-lived. Furthermore, they place in all of them an affection toward corporeal things: but in the first, according to a certain manner of tranquil providence; in the second, human-like but moderate; in the third, already declining toward our disturbances. Likewise, some demons are natural, established from the beginning; others are "foreign," namely the souls of men translated into airy bodies, caring for men in the same manner they were accustomed to before. Furthermore, some demons preside over larger regions of the earth, others over narrower ones and cities. Some even govern individual men; these are the ones which souls falling into the body have obtained by lot according to their choice of life, thereafter becoming leaders, scouts, and judges of the chosen life. Accordingly, some souls of men are adapted to the natures of Saturnian demons, others to Jovian, and others to other stars and demons. The complexions of our bodies are also distinguished by a similar reasoning. Likewise, animals, plants, metals, and stones are naturally discerned among themselves according to the variety of stars and demons, so that some among these are solar, others lunar, and others likewise. In these things we have mentioned, the Platonists believe the entire power of sacrifices, oracles, and divinations consists. Indeed, he himself...

<meta>This page serves as the "Argument" or introductory summary to Plato's *Apology*. The translator/commentator (likely Marsilio Ficino) establishes the philosophical and theological framework for Socrates' defense, specifically addressing the nature of the Socratic "daemon" or divine sign.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE APOLOGY

Plato imitated the ancient theologians, and all Platonists everywhere accept the history of oracles as true and confirm them with reasons. I will pass over how much faith he places in these in the *Phaedrus*, and how much also in the *Timaeus*. In the *Phaedrus* indeed, he considers human wisdom as nothing compared to that which is held from oracles and divine furies <note>original: "furoribus," referring to divine inspiration or "poetic madness"</note>; in the *Timaeus*, however, he says that a philosopher should affirm divine matters only insofar as they are confirmed by divine oracles. I pass over many similar points in Plato; certainly, in the *Apology*, he begins the entire defense of his Socrates with oracles and prophecies. Indeed, what is most significant is that he asserts the entire life of Socrates—the wisest and most just of men—was instituted according to the oracle of Apollo and the prophecy of a certain spirit <note>original: "daemonis"</note> of his own.

If you ask what kind of spirit Socrates had, he will answer: of fire, because it raised him to the contemplation of sublime things. Likewise, it was Saturnian <note>associated with the planet/god Saturn, linked to melancholy and deep intellect</note>, because it withdrew the intention of his mind from the body in a wonderful way every day. It was also attributed to him from the beginning, not acquired; for he says it breathed upon him from childhood. It never provoked him to action, because it was not of Mars <note>the god of war/action</note>, but often recalled him from actions, because it was Saturnian. Likewise, it did not apply spurs to a man already sufficiently inclined toward honest things, but held him back with a bridle when it saw he might be deceived in choosing paths toward an end due to the fallacy of conjectures. It breathed upon his mind, suggested signs to his eyes, and voices to his ears. But to which eyes and ears? To the sight and hearing, clearly, of the ethereal body <note>a subtle, spiritual body believed to sit between the soul and the physical flesh</note> lurking beneath this manifest body. Socrates, moreover, was able to perceive beyond heroes, easily withdrawing his senses from elemental perceptions. He discerned signs through these same senses and dreams, both while sleeping and waking. Similarly, Avicenna <note>the Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note> proves that prophets both see the forms of angels and hear their voices.

But why do Socrates and a few like him notice their spirit? Because few are "daemonic" by birth or discipline; more are merely human, and most are beast-like. Why, likewise, does he call it sometimes a spirit <note>daemon</note> and sometimes a god? Because the sublime spirit breathed upon Socrates as an interpreter and messenger of God. But can we call the very intellect of Socrates a spirit? We certainly can. For in the *Timaeus*, he says God granted us the supreme part of the soul as a spirit. Again, in the *Symposium*, the very love of the mind for contemplating divine beauty is named a spirit. 

Truly, besides these, it is necessary that a substance superior to us presides as a spirit; because, as is proved in the *Symposium* and the *Laws*, the human race—being most distant from divine things—needs a certain middle nature, such as the daemonic, as a sort of conciliator. Nor did divine providence wrongly set spirits over us as closer guardians, like shepherds (as proved in the *Statesman* and *Protagoras*) or as governors (as said in the *Critias*). For man, placed in this darkness of ignorance and agitated or distracted by the innumerable allurements of fortune or evils, cannot reach the end appointed for him by God without the perpetual help of God. Hence he proves that God commended us to purer spirits as rulers, who might help through prophecies, auguries, dreams, oracles, voices, sacrifices, and inspirations. He wishes the familiar spirit of Socrates to be of this number, differing from the Socratic mind itself. For the mind often provokes Socrates, but the spirit never does. Likewise, the mind cannot teach unless it speaks or writes; but the spirit, as proved in the *Theages*, taught many even by remaining silent. Furthermore, because it corrects Socrates with both voice and signs, it signifies that this spirit is something beyond the mind. But if it pleases you less to call the familiar guide of a man a "daemon," at least call it a "good angel," as pleases our people <note>referring to Christian terminology</note>.

After this, the *Apology* compels us to treat somewhat of oracles and statues. First, if you ask for what reason spirits do not perform those accustomed miracles in our ages, the answer will be that Christ deprived the evil spirits of their empire and took away from men both the worship of spirits and the daemonic art. If you ask again by what reason the influences of spirits are drawn into statues or into men, attend diligently. Something natural is drawn daily through art: as whenever wood, which could not be ignited by a thin flame because of its dense thickness, is either smeared with oil or stained with sulfur, and catches the flame in the tinder. And something divine is also drawn daily through nature: when a tender fetus in the womb, shaped by a certain affection and manner, thus draws a human soul from God through nature, just as a statue receives a spirit from the world through magic. 

Whence the Egyptians also called nature a "magician," placing the magic power itself in a certain attraction of likes by likes, or at least of fitting things through fitting things. You emit a voice daily; you also emit the image of your face. But your voice and image are not reflected back to you everywhere. Only a wall so disposed and so positioned reflects the voice through an echo; and a mirror-like body returns your image to you. Let that wall also be mirror-like: suddenly you will be entirely, so to speak, in it. For there you will be seen, heard, and understood, almost as a spirit in a statue. If you consult Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure</note>, you will learn that a statue duly composed of the world's own materials fitting a certain spirit is immediately animated by a corresponding spirit—either by a spirit, he says, or by an angel. Understand that it is accustomed to be breathed upon either by an impure or a pure spirit. You will also hear this Mercury <note>Hermes</note> condemning many of the ancients: because, doubting either that there were divinities above the heavens or that the prayers of earthly beings reached the celestial and higher things, they fabricated statues as habitations of spirits, whom they might worship as familiar gods. He thought, surely, that although sometimes salutary spirits were called into the shrines, often noxious ones descended instead. You have heard in a few words of the drawing of spirits into the bodies of statues. Hear also in a few words of the seizure into the bodies of men. When either through black bile <note>melancholy</note> or something similar or a vice, the whole soul is turned into the imagination...

<meta>This page continues the introductory argument or commentary on Plato's Apology, likely written by Marsilio Ficino. It explores the Socratic paradox of "knowing nothing" and the nature of the "daimon" or guiding spirit.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE APOLOGY

<page-num>FOLIO 190</page-num>

...the soul easily becomes a dwelling place for lower spirits <note>original: "dæmonum"</note>: by whose presence it may become both insane and troubled in both mind and body. When it has passed entirely into the realm of reason through philosophical purification, it becomes a temple for middle spirits: from whom it frequently receives wondrous insights into human affairs, and sometimes even into natural things. Since through piety it raises itself entirely into the mind, it becomes a breathing-hole for sublime spirits, or rather angels, by whose guidance it penetrates the secrets of divine matters in a marvelous way. I see you wish to understand which oracles Plato trusts most, whether those delivered through statues or through men. Know that he trusts only those which he calculates by certain reason to have come not through deceptive spirits, but through truth-telling ones, or rather through angels. For he had also received from the mysteries of the Egyptians: that Jupiter cast down the more impure spirits to the underworld, who similarly drag men down to the depths by their power; and from Pherecydes the Syrian <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek thinker often cited as a teacher of Pythagoras</note> that many spirits rebelled against Jupiter, whose army the serpentine Ophioneus led. He judged, therefore, that one must guard most diligently against these evildoers.

Socrates, however, led by his own reasons and signs, committed himself to a certain oracle and to a certain spirit <note>The "daimonion" of Socrates</note> of his own to be guided by its judgment. Finally, however it may be, he so ordered his life toward these things that he preferred eternal things to temporal ones: he feared justice more than death; for the sake of truth, piety, and charity, he did not hesitate to undergo labors, poverty, insults, injuries, beatings, and death. Among men, truth brought forth false slanders against him; charity brought hatred; piety brought an impious accusation and death. But he weighed all these things as little, or rather as nothing, hoping to merit good things from the divine judge in exchange for his good deeds. Therefore, relying on this hope and confidence, he went willingly to the judges; he did not excuse himself, but rather accused the judges. And like a prophet—which he says happens to those who are near death—he predicted that repentance and punishment would follow them after their false judgment, while he himself meanwhile departed to the eternal judges with marvelous joy of mind and a cheerful countenance.

I had intended to put an end to this noble argument, or rather short commentary, here. But two doubts hold me back for a moment. First, that Socratic saying repeated both here and often elsewhere: *This one thing I know, that I know nothing.* Yet he affirms many things both here and elsewhere as if he knew them. But this is similar to the saying: *I said in my excess, every man is a liar.* <note>A reference to Psalm 116:11</note> Thus Socrates says: I, abstracted from the body, snatched up by a spirit, illuminated by God, certainly know this one thing in the divine light—namely, that otherwise, when joined to the body, I know nothing in the natural light. I do not know, I say, in the natural light, things as they are through the mode of affirmation. For that kind of knowledge belongs to God alone, who understands both the natures themselves and the causes of those natures, since he himself made them. Yet I know many things through a certain mode of negation. Just as I know that God is not a body, rather than knowing what He is. Likewise, that the soul is not mortal, rather than what it is. And again, that the absolute Good is not this or that specific good, rather than what it is. And in this way, Socrates both knows and teaches many things. Furthermore, there is the fact that his spirit <note>daimon</note> calls him back rather than provoking him forward; that is, it illuminates him toward denying rather than affirming. Sometimes, however, he does affirm certain things, and great ones at that, as if he were not only snatched up by a spirit but already full of God. He also affirms when he brings forward the testimonies of the ancient saints, or cites the souls of men rising from the dead as testimony.

There follows a second doubt: for what reason does Socrates, though he is never accustomed to doubt that the soul is immortal, use this disjunction at the end of the *Apology*: *Either no sensation remains after death, or some remains.* I answer first that he does not doubt all sensation—that is, all knowledge—but rather doubts our specific sensation of things or something similar to ours. This is signified by those things which are seen in the other part of the disjunction, where he says the same as in the *Republic*: namely, that separated souls recognize each other there in the same way they were accustomed to here. Here one should consider what is said against those who say that souls transmigrate from bodies into other bodies.

Secondly, answer more safely in this way: Socrates does not use this disjunction in this instance because he thinks it should be doubted—for he holds it most constantly everywhere through negative knowledge and through divine inspiration and approval—but he is looking to the persons of his adversaries in the present moment. Since they were entirely eager to harm him, they inflicted death upon him as if it were undoubtedly an evil. Socrates, therefore, counters that it is in no way an evil, whether our affairs stand this way or another. Where that which appears ambiguous concerning immortality is added for the sake of those who, like tyrants in the Epicurean fashion, might have been able to mock Socrates as if he could be easily deceived if he had affirmed that death was not an evil solely because other good things remain after this life. These eternal goods, even if they were certain to Socrates, were in no way certain to them; nor could they be demonstrated in that narrow brevity of time, though they are demonstrated in the *Phædo* and often elsewhere.

But you, note the certain confidence of our Socrates speaking to his friends near the end of the *Apology*: *You ought to hope well concerning death. For nothing evil can happen to a good man, whether living or dead.* For the affairs of a man who is in some way like God are not neglected by God. As for his crying out with his final voice to the judges: *I indeed depart from here to die, but you to live; which of us goes to the better lot is certain to God alone*—understand that he does not doubt what he affirmed shortly before, but rather says that the reason for affirmation is certain to God alone through Himself, yet it can become certain to man through God Himself and through the reason of negation. Add to this that he does not dare to affirm that he departs with a soul so purified that he can affirm his present migration will immediately return his soul to the heavenly fatherland.

<margin>I know this, that I know nothing, etc.</margin>

# THE BOOK OF THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATIS.

### THE APOLOGY OF SOCRATIS.

<margin>This is spoken on my behalf</margin> How you have been affected, Men of Athens, by my accusers, I do not know; for my part, I was almost carried away by them myself, so persuasively did they seem to speak. And yet, they have brought forward practically nothing that is true. But among the many falsehoods they told, I wondered at this most of all: their warning that you must be careful not to be deceived by me, on the grounds that I am a "clever speaker." For their lack of shame in asserting this—when I was about to disprove it immediately by my very actions, since I appear before you now as someone far removed from eloquence—this, I say, seemed to me the most impudent of all. Unless, perhaps, they call a "clever speaker" one who speaks the truth. If that is what they mean, I would certainly admit that I am an orator, though not after their fashion. For these men, as I say, have said nothing true; but from me, you shall hear the whole truth. And by Jupiter <note>original: "per Iove"; Socrates frequently swears by Zeus/Jupiter</note>, Men of Athens, you will not hear from me a flowery speech like theirs, adorned with elegant words and phrases; rather, you will hear things spoken plainly with whatever words come to hand. For I trust that what I say is just, and let none of you expect me to speak otherwise. Indeed, it would not befit a man of my age, Men of Athens, to come before you like a young lad weaving carefully crafted phrases. Furthermore, Men of Athens, I earnestly beg and entreat this of you: if you hear me defending myself with the same words I am accustomed to using in the marketplace at the tables of the money-changers—where many of you have heard me—and elsewhere, do not be surprised, and do not take offense. For the matter stands thus: I come now for the first time before a court of law, though I am more than seventy years old; consequently, I am a complete stranger to the language of this place. And just as you would surely forgive me if I were truly a stranger in Athens and spoke in the dialect and manner in which I had been raised, so now I ask this of you—and I think it is a fair request—that you disregard my manner of speaking, which might be better or worse, and instead consider only this: give your mind to whether what I say is just or unjust. For that is the duty of a judge, while the duty of an orator is to speak the truth. It is right, Men of Athens, that I first respond to the first false accusations and my first accusers, and then to the later ones. For many have accused me to you for many years now, and falsely; I fear these more than I fear Anytus and his associates, though they too are powerful in persuasion. But those others are more dangerous, Men of Athens, who took hold of most of you from childhood and persuaded you with accusations far from the truth: namely, that there is a certain Socrates, a "wise man," a searcher into the things above the air and under the earth, who is accustomed to making the weaker argument appear the stronger. These men, Men of Athens, who have spread this rumor, are my most dangerous accusers. For those who hear these things believe that researchers of such matters do not believe in the gods. Indeed, such accusers are numerous and have been accusing me for a long time; they spoke to you at an age when you were most easily convinced—when you were children or mere youths—in a case that went by default, with no one to defend me. And what is most absurd of all, I cannot even know or name them, unless one of them happens to be a comic poet <note>A reference to Aristophanes</note>. All those who, through envy or slander, persuaded you—and those who, once persuaded themselves, persuaded others—all these are very difficult to deal with. It is not possible to bring any of them here to court or to cross-examine them; instead, it is necessary to fight against them as if fighting with shadows, defending myself and refuting them with no one to answer. Consider then, as I was saying, that my accusers are of two kinds: those who have accused me recently, and those from long ago whom I just described. Judge then that I must first answer those whom you yourselves heard first and much more often. But now I must make my defense, Men of Athens, against those old charges, and attempt in this short time to erase the prejudice which you have held against me for so long. I wish to succeed in refuting my adversaries, provided that would be better for both you and me. However, I think this will be difficult. I am not unaware of how great a task it is. But let it proceed as God pleases; I must obey the law and make my defense. Let us repeat from the beginning what the accusation is, from which that slander arose that gave Meletus the confidence to bring this suit against me. What then do my accusers say? As if they were present in court, let their accusation be read, in which they swear against me (and which in turn requires an oath from me): "Socrates acts unjustly; he is overly curious, searching into things under the earth and in the heavens; he makes the weaker argument the stronger, and he teaches these same things to others." Such is the accusation. Indeed, you have seen such things in the comedy of Aristophanes <note>The play "The Clouds"</note>. For a character named Socrates is carried about there, claiming he is walking on air and talking a great deal of other nonsense. I know nothing of these matters, neither much nor little. I do not say this to disparage such knowledge, if anyone is truly wise in such things—may I not be so burdened by Meletus's charges that I would deny this—but because in reality, Men of Athens, I know nothing of them. I call most of you as witnesses to this. I ask you to tell one another: how many of you have ever heard me conversing? And many of you have. Tell each other, then, if any of you ever heard me disputing about such matters, whether much or little; and from this you will recognize that the other things people say about me are of the same sort. But none of these things are true. And if you have heard from anyone that I attempt to teach men and amass money for it, that is also false.
