# APOLOGY.

<margin>
<unclear>This is not wisdom</unclear>
</margin>
nor is it the truth. And yet, it seems to me a magnificent thing if someone is able to teach men, as do Gorgias of Leontini, Prodicus of Ceos, and Hippias of Elis. For each of these has the faculty by which, traveling to various cities, they persuade young men—who could otherwise be taught for free by their own fellow citizens at home—to leave those teachers and follow them instead; and for this, they pay money and are grateful besides. There is also another wise man here, whose arrival I was quite delighted to hear of. It happened that I met a man who has spent more money on Sophists <note>Professional teachers in ancient Greece who charged for lessons in rhetoric and virtue.</note> than all others combined: Callias, son of Hipponicus. I questioned him thus (for he has two sons): "O Callias," I said, "if your sons were colts or calves, we would have someone to hire who could make them perfect in their proper excellence; such a person would be either a horse-trainer or a farmer. But since your sons are human beings, whom do you intend to set over them to make them perfect? And who possesses the knowledge of this human and civic virtue? I assume you have thought of this, since you have sons. Is there such a person," I asked, "or not?" "There certainly is," he replied. "Who is he?" I asked, "And from where? And for what fee does he teach?" "Evanus of Paros," he said, "O Socrates; and his fee is five minae." <note>A significant sum of money in ancient Athens.</note> And I considered Evanus blessed if he truly possesses this art and teaches it so diligently. As for myself, if I knew such things, I would be quite proud and hold myself in high regard. But certainly, O men of Athens, I know nothing of these things.

But perhaps one of you will reply: "What then, O Socrates, is your business? And from where have these slanders against you arisen? For unless you were doing something out of the ordinary, such a great rumor would never have been stirred up about you. For why is there such frequent talk of you, unless you had acted differently from others? Tell us, therefore, what it is, so that we do not judge you rashly." This seems to me a fair question. And I will try to show you what it is that has harmed me and given birth to this slander. Listen now; and though I fear I may seem to some of you to be joking, rest assured that I will tell you the absolute truth.

Indeed, O men of Athens, I have acquired this name for no other reason than for a certain kind of wisdom. But what kind of wisdom? Perhaps that which is human wisdom. For in this, I truly seem to be wise. Those whom I mentioned just now might perhaps possess a wisdom greater than human, or I know not what to call it; for I certainly do not possess it. If anyone says that I do, he lies and speaks to slander me. But do not be offended, O men of Athens, if I seem to say something great about myself; for the words I speak are not my own, but I will bring you a witness worthy of belief. If I have any wisdom at all, and of what sort it is, I will offer the Delphic god <note>Apollo, whose oracle was at Delphi.</note> as my witness. You certainly knew Chaerephon. He was my companion from youth and a friend to your democratic party; he was exiled with you and returned with you. You know well what kind of man Chaerephon was, how vehement he was in whatever he turned his mind to. Once, having gone to Delphi, he dared to seek this prophecy. Do not take it ill, O men, what I am about to say. He asked if there was anyone wiser than I. The Pythia <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi who delivered the oracles.</note> answered that no one was wiser. His brother here will testify to these things for you, for Chaerephon himself has passed away.

Consider why I say these things. I must reveal to you where this slander against me originated. Indeed, when I heard this, I thought to myself: "What does the god mean? What is the riddle? For I am conscious that I am wise in nothing, neither great nor small. What then does he mean when he asserts that I am the wisest? For it is not to be believed that a god lies;
<margin>
<unclear>God does not lie</unclear>
</margin>
that is not permitted to a god." And so for a long time I remained in ambiguity, searching for what the oracle signified. At last, after great hesitation, I entered upon a path of this sort: I approached one of those who seem to be wise, as if to refute the prophecy there if anywhere, and to show the oracle: "This man is to be preferred in wisdom, not I, whom you designated." While I was examining him—it is not necessary to mention his name, but he was one of those involved in public affairs—while I was examining and conversing with him, O men of Athens, I was affected in this way: this man seemed to be wise to many others, and especially to himself, but he was not so at all. Then I tried to show him that he thought he was wise, but was not. Because of this, he became hateful toward me, and many who were present took it badly.

Therefore, returning to myself, I reasoned thus: "I am certainly wiser than this man. For it appears that neither of us knows anything beautiful or good. But there is this difference: while he knows nothing, he thinks he knows something. I, however, just as I do not know, do not think that I know. I seem, therefore, in this small matter to be wiser than this man: that what I do not know, I do not think I know." After this, I went to another of those held to be even wiser than the first, and in considering him, I judged exactly the same. And I made him and many others my enemies.

Thereafter, I proceeded to others in succession, not unaware of how much hatred I was stirring up against myself; I proceeded with a certain grief and fear. Nevertheless, it seemed necessary to me to put the divine oracle before all else, and to go everywhere searching for what the oracle meant. For this reason, I had to go to all who seemed to know something. And by the Dog, <note>A common idiosyncratic oath used by Socrates.</note> O men of Athens—for I must tell you the truth—something like this happened to me as I pursued the oracle's meaning: those who were most highly regarded in the opinion of men, I found to be almost the most lacking; while others who were considered inferior were, in respect to prudence, better off. I must recount to you my wanderings and labors which I sustained so that the oracle might be proven so thoroughly that it could not be refuted further. After the politicians, I turned to the poets of tragedies and dithyrambs and other poems...

# BOOK OF THE APOLOGY XXVII.

<margin>

</margin>
matter: as if he were to see quite clearly here that I would be found more ignorant than these men. Therefore, having taken up their books in which they seemed to have labored most, I questioned them on their meanings, so that I might learn something from them. I am ashamed, O men <note>Socrates is addressing the Athenian jury</note>, to reveal the truth to you here, but it must nevertheless be said. Almost all others present, so to speak, would have spoken better about these matters concerning which the poets themselves wrote their poems. I discovered, therefore, in a short time this regarding poets: that they do not do what they do by wisdom, but by a certain nature and by a divine agitation of the soul, just like those who prophesy being inspired by a divine frenzy. For these also say many and excellent things, but they understand nothing of what they say. The poets seem to me to have been affected in some such way; and at the same time, I noticed that because of their poetry, they judged themselves to be the wisest of all men in other matters in which they are not wise. I went away, therefore, from there with entirely the same opinion with which I had left the statesmen. But at last I betook myself to the artisans: being conscious in myself that, so to speak, I knew nothing of the crafts, but I knew that these men knew many and beautiful things; nor was I deceived in this. For they knew things which I myself did not know, and in this part they were wiser than I. But, O men of Athens, I found the skilled artisans in the same error as the poets. For because of the very fact that they performed their own craft rightly, each one of them thought himself to be the wisest in other matters as well, even the greatest. And this error obscured even that wisdom which they did possess. Therefore, I asked myself in the place of the oracle: whether I would choose to be as I am, namely neither knowing what they know nor being ignorant of my own ignorance, or having both which they have. I answered plainly to myself and to the oracle that it is better for me to be as I am.

From this inquiry of mine, O men of Athens, many enmities, most difficult and heavy, have arisen against me, from which many slanders have followed. Indeed, the name of "wise man" has arisen for me because of this, for those present think that I know most about those things in which I refute others. But it seems, O men of Athens, that in truth only God is wise; and in this oracle he means this: namely, that human wisdom is to be valued little, or rather, as nothing. And that he names Socrates as wise, he does so for this reason: using my name as a kind of example, as if he were to say: "He, O men, is the wisest, who, like Socrates, knows in truth that his wisdom is worth nothing." Therefore, I, being thus disposed, even now do not cease to go about seeking and searching out the will of God, meeting anyone, whether citizen or stranger, whom I think to be wise. And if at any time he does not seem so to me, then I, assisting the God, demonstrate that he is not wise. And because of occupations of this sort, almost no leisure is left to me either to do anything for the public or for my private affairs; but I am established in extreme poverty because of the service of God. Furthermore, the youths, especially the most wealthy who have leisure from business, following me of their own accord, take delight when they see men being refuted by us. They also sometimes, having imitated me, then strive to confute others. In which matter they find a great crowd of men who think they know something, when they either know nothing or very little. Those who are convicted by these youths are not so much angry with them as with me; and they cry out that there is a certain Socrates, a most wicked man and a corrupter of the youth. But if anyone should ask them what he does or teaches to corrupt them, they can assign nothing; indeed, they are utterly ignorant. But lest they seem to lack material, they flee to those things which are commonly and easily thrown as objections against those who practice philosophy: namely, that they study things in the heavens and things under the earth, and do not believe in the gods, and make the worse reason appear the better. For the truth, as I think, they do not wish to confess: namely, that they are indignant because, having been convicted, they pretend to know those things which they do not know. Therefore, being ambitious, and vehement, and many, and as if by a composed and persistent diligence in the zeal of persuasion, they have filled your ears with accusations against me, both for a long time and recently with slanders studiously devised against me. From among these, Melitus and Anytus and Lyco have risen up against me: Melitus indeed being hostile to me on account of the poets; Anytus on account of the artisans and the governors of the republic; and finally Lyco on account of the rhetoricians. Wherefore, as I was saying from the beginning, I would indeed wonder if I were able to remove from you in so short a time this opinion, conceived from such great slanders and so long-established. This indeed, O men of Athens, I speak truly to you; I neither hide nor subtract anything, whether great or small, although I know well that in saying these things I shall be troublesome to them. Which is indeed a proof to you that I speak the truth, and that this is the slander that has arisen against me, and its causes are of this sort. And whether you inquire into these things in the present or in the future, you will find it to be so. To those things, therefore, which the first accusers brought forward, let this be a sufficient defense for me before you.

But to Melitus, the "good man" and, as he says, the lover of his country, and the other following accusers, I shall next proceed to answer. But let us bring forward the accusation of these men in turn, as if they were another set of accusers, an accusation asserted by oath and to be asserted in turn. It holds itself roughly in this manner: "Socrates acts unjustly by depraving the youth; and not believing in the gods whom the city believes in, but in certain other new spiritual beings <term>daimonia: divine signs or spirits</term>." The accusation is indeed of this sort. Let us discuss each part of this accusation. He objects that I deprave the young, and in this I do an injury. But I, O men of Athens, say on the contrary that Melitus does an injury, because he plays at being serious, so easily dragging men into court, and pretending to apply himself to serious matters, and to have a care for those things for which he never cared. That this is so, I will try to show to you. "Ho there, Melitus, answer me: do you not care most of all that the youths turn out as well as possible?"
MELITUS: "I do indeed."
SOCRATES: "Come then, tell these men now, who is it that makes the youths better? For it is clear that you know, since it is a care to you. You have certainly found me to be their corrupter, as you say; you have accused me before these men; you have dragged me into court. Come then, and also tell these men who makes them better, and show who it is. Why are you silent, O Melitus? Do you see that you have nothing to say? And does that not seem shameful to you, and sufficient..."

# APOLOGY

<note>original: "APOLOGIA"</note>

...proof of what I am saying, that you have never cared about these matters! But tell us now, good man, who is it that makes the youth good? 

MELETUS: The laws. 

SOCRATES: But that is not what I am asking, most excellent sir, but rather what *man*—who, of course, must first know this very thing, the laws—makes them better? 

MELETUS: These men, Socrates, the judges. 

SOCRATES: What are you saying, Meletus? Can these men truly instruct the youth and make them good? 

MELETUS: Most certainly. 

SOCRATES: All of them? Or can some do it, while others cannot? 

MELETUS: All of them. 

SOCRATES: By Juno <note>A common Socratic oath; Juno is the Roman equivalent of Hera</note>, you speak well, and you provide a great abundance of benefactors for the youth. But what about these men who listen to the trial? Do they also make them better, or not? 

MELETUS: They do as well. 

SOCRATES: And what of the senators? 

MELETUS: The senators too. 

SOCRATES: But surely, Meletus, we must be careful lest the members of the assembly <note>original: "concionatores"</note> perhaps corrupt the young. Or do all of these likewise make them better? 

MELETUS: These too. 

SOCRATES: It seems then that all the Athenians make them honorable and good except for me alone. I alone am the corrupter. Is that what you are saying? 

MELETUS: That is exactly what I say, and most vehemently. 

SOCRATES: You condemn me to a great misfortune. Now answer me: do you think the same is true of horses? That is, that all men make horses good, while only one person ruins them? Or is it entirely the opposite—that there is only one, or very few, skilled in horsemanship who can make horses better, while the many, if they deal with and use horses, spoil them? Is this not the case, Meletus, regarding horses and all other living creatures? It is entirely so, whether you and Anytus <note>One of the other primary accusers of Socrates</note> admit it or not. Indeed, the youth would be very fortunate if only one person could pervert them while everyone else helped them. But, Meletus, you have shown sufficiently that you never had any care for the youth, and you clearly reveal your own negligence: that you have never reflected on the things for which you accuse me. 

Furthermore, I beseech you by Jupiter <note>original: "per Iovem"; the Roman name for Zeus</note>, Meletus, answer us: is it better for us to live among good citizens or among bad ones? Answer, please. I am asking nothing difficult. Do not the bad always do some evil to those with whom they associate, while the good do something good? 

MELETUS: Without a doubt. 

SOCRATES: Is there anyone who would rather receive harm than benefit from those he associates with? Answer, good man. For the law commands you to answer. Is there anyone who wishes to be harmed? 

MELETUS: No one. 

SOCRATES: Come then, do you call me here to judgment as a corrupter of youth, and do you say I do this willingly or unwillingly? 

MELETUS: I say you do it willingly. 

SOCRATES: How is this, Meletus? Are you, who are so much younger than I, so much wiser than I at my advanced age, that you clearly recognize that the bad harm their associates and the good benefit them? Have I fallen into such a state of childishness <note>original: "infantiam"</note> that I do not even recognize this: that if I make one of my associates wicked, I run the risk of suffering some evil from him? And yet I would bring this great evil upon myself willingly, as you say? I do not believe you in this, Meletus. And I think no one else will grant it to you. Either I do not corrupt the youth, or if I do corrupt them, I do so unwillingly. Therefore, you lie in either case. But if I corrupt them unwillingly, the law does not require one to be dragged into court for involuntary offenses, but rather to be taught and admonished privately. For it is clear that if I learn better, I will no longer do what I was doing out of ignorance. You, however, were unwilling to associate with me to correct me; instead, you hurry me into court, where the law requires those to be taken who need punishment rather than instruction. 

Now it is manifest from this, men of Athens, what I was just saying: that Meletus has never had any care, great or small, for the education of youth. Now come, tell us, Meletus, in what way do you assert that I pervert the youth? Is it, as you wrote in the indictment, because I teach them not to believe in the gods the city believes in, but in certain other new divinities <note>original: "demonia"; referring to Socrates' "daimon" or inner voice</note>? Do you not affirm that I corrupt the youth by teaching these things? 

MELETUS: I certainly and most vehemently assert this. 

SOCRATES: By those very gods, Meletus, of whom we are now speaking, explain this more clearly both to me and to these men. For I do not yet plainly understand whether you say I teach the youth to believe that *some* gods exist—and if so, then I do believe gods exist and am not an atheist <note>original: "absque deo"</note>, nor do I act unjustly in this, except that I teach they are not the ones the city holds, but others—is this what you accuse me of, that I introduce *other* gods? Or do you say that I altogether deny the gods, and that I teach others to deny them as well? 

MELETUS: I assert that you altogether deny the gods. 

SOCRATES: O wonderful Meletus, why do you say such things? Do I not even believe that the sun and the moon are gods, as other men do? 

MELETUS: By Jupiter, no, judges! For he says the sun is a stone and the moon is earth. 

SOCRATES: Do you think you are accusing Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who was also charged with impiety for his scientific views</note>, my friend Meletus? Do you hold these men in such low esteem, thinking them so ignorant of letters that they do not know the books of Anaxagoras of Clazomenae are full of such opinions? And the gymnasium is the place for this. You say the youth learn these things from me, when they could occasionally buy them from the Orchestra <note>A part of the theater or marketplace where books were sold</note> for the price of a single drachma at most, and then laugh at Socrates if he pretended these ideas were his own—especially since they are so absurd! But by God, Meletus, do you truly think I believe in no god at all? 

MELETUS: None at all, by Jupiter. 

SOCRATES: What you say is incredible, Meletus, and, it seems to me, even to yourself. For it seems to me, men of Athens, that this man is excessively insulting and reckless, and that he has written this indictment out of a certain insolence, malice, and youthful rashness. He seems to be composing a sort of riddle, testing whether "Socrates the wise" will catch him playing a game and contradicting himself, or if Socrates and the audience will be deceived. For he seems to me to contradict himself in the very words of the indictment, as if he said: "Socrates acts against the laws by not believing in the gods, but by believing in the gods." This seems like the jesting of a trifler. Pay attention, men, to how Meletus seems to me to be saying this. And you, Meletus, answer us. But you, as I requested at the beginning, do not be offended if I speak in my usual manner. Is there anyone, Meletus, who believes human things exist, but not humans? Let him answer me, men, and let him not make a disturbance first with one thing and then another. Is there anyone who does not believe horses exist, but...

<summary>Socrates cross-examines Meletus, exposing the logical inconsistencies in the charges of corrupting the youth and atheism. He argues that if he did harm anyone, it was unintentional and requires instruction rather than trial.</summary>

## PAGE XXVII.

...equestrian matters: or that there are no flute players, but only the activities of flute players? There is no one who thinks so, O best of men. For I answer for you, both to yourself and to these others, since you yourself do not wish to answer. But at least answer this, which pertains more to the matter: Is there anyone who believes that there are **divine works** <note>original: "dæmonia opa" - referring to the 'daimonion' or divine sign Socrates claimed to hear</note>, but does not believe in **divinities** <note>original: "dæmones" - in Greek thought, these were intermediate beings between gods and men</note> at all? 

**ME.** No one. 

**SO.** How slowly and reluctantly you answered, forced by these men! Do you not therefore confess that I both believe in and teach divine works, whether they be new or old? For at all events, as you confess, I assert there are divine things: and I will swear to these things in my response to the written accusation. But if I believe in divine things, it is absolutely necessary that I believe there are divinities as well. Is it not so? Certainly it is. For I assume you confess it, since you do not wish to answer. And do we not consider divinities to be either gods or the children of gods? Do you grant this, or deny it? 

**ME.** Entirely. 

**SO.** If I believe there are divinities, as you yourself concede, and if divinities are a kind of god, does it not happen as I just said: that you are proposing a riddle and playing a joke by saying that I, who do not believe in gods, nevertheless do believe in gods, since I hold that divinities exist? Again, if divinities are the children of gods—bastard children, as it were, born of nymphs or certain others, as is said—who among men would believe that there are children of gods, but deny the gods themselves? It would be just as absurd as if someone believed there were offspring of horses or donkeys—namely mules—but did not believe that horses and donkeys existed. 

But, O Melitus, you have undoubtedly brought this accusation either to test our wits, or because you had no true crime with which to charge me. By what reason could you persuade anyone with even the smallest amount of mind that it is not the mark of the same man to believe in both divine and spiritual things, and yet again for that same man to believe in neither divinities, nor gods, nor heroes? Certainly, it can be shown in no other way. 

Furthermore, O men of Athens, that I have not committed a crime as Melitus accuses, does not seem to me to require a great defense; I judge that what has been said is sufficient. But what I said from the beginning—that great ill-will has been stirred up against me among the many—is indeed very true. And this is what will destroy me, if I am destroyed: not Melitus, nor Anytus, but the slander and envy of the many. These things have destroyed many other good men before now, and I think they will continue to do so. For there is nothing grave or strange if it does not cease to be a hindrance in my case. 

Perhaps, however, someone will ask me: "Are you not ashamed, O Socrates, to have practiced such a thing from which you now run the risk of dying?" To this objection I will give this just response: You do not speak rightly, O man, if you think that a man who is of even small use should take much account of life or death; rather, he should consider only this: whenever he acts, whether he acts justly or unjustly, and whether his works are those of a good man or a bad one. Otherwise, by your reasoning, all the demigods who fell at Troy would be held in contempt, and others, and especially the son of Thetis <note>Achilles</note>; he so despised the danger of death rather than undergo shameful disgrace that when his mother, a goddess, spoke to him as he hurried to kill Hector—in these words, I believe: "O son, if you kill Hector to avenge the death of your friend Patroclus, you yourself shall perish; for," she said, "immediately after Hector, an unhappy fate awaits you." When, I say, he heard this from her, he so despised the danger and death that he feared a shameful life and leaving his friends unavenged much more than death. He answered immediately that he would rather die seeking just vengeance for his friend than live as a laughingstock and a contemptible man lingering by the ships. Who would say that he had any care for danger or death? 

And truly, O men of Athens, this is how the matter stands. In whatever place a man has stationed himself, thinking it to be best, or has been commanded to stand by a superior, there, it seems to me, he ought to remain and undergo danger, fearing neither death nor anything else more than disgrace. Indeed, O men of Athens, I would have erred gravely if, when I obeyed those leaders whom you placed over me at Potidaea, at Amphipolis, and at Delos—for then, where they ordered me to stand, I stood like any other and underwent the risk of death—if now, when God has stationed me and willed me to remain (as I have thought and believed) to live as a philosopher and to examine myself and others, I should desert my rank for fear of death or any other thing. That would indeed be a grave offense; and then truly someone might justly drag me into court as one who does not believe in the gods, since I would be disobeying the oracle, fearing death, and thinking myself wise when I am not. 

<margin>For to fear death is to think one knows what he does not know.</margin>

For to fear death, O men, is nothing other than to seem wise when one is not. For it is to seem to know what one does not know. No one knows whether death may be the greatest of all goods for a man, yet they fear it as if they knew it to be the greatest of evils. And who can doubt that this very ignorance is most blameworthy, through which someone thinks he knows what he does not know? But I, O men, perhaps differ from many men in this: and if I were to say I am wiser than someone in any matter, it would be in this: that since I do not sufficiently know the things of the underworld, I likewise recognize that I do not know them. But to do injustice, and not to obey a superior, whether God or man, I know to be an evil and a shameful thing. Therefore, these things which I do not know to be good, I will never fear or flee more than those things which I know to be evil. 

Wherefore, if you should now acquit me, not believing Anytus—who said that either I should not have been called to judgment from the beginning, or having been called, I must necessarily be condemned (for if I were acquitted by you, he said your sons, following the footsteps of Socrates, would all be entirely corrupted)—if, I say, you should say to me: "O Socrates, we do not believe Anytus, and we acquit you by our vote, but on this condition: that you never again occupy yourself in this inquiry and philosophy; and if you do..."

# APOLOGY

...to yield. If, therefore, as I was saying, you were willing to dismiss me on these conditions, I would surely answer you: O men of Athens, I cherish and love you indeed; yet I prefer to obey God rather than you. And as long as I draw breath and my strength suffices, I shall not cease to practice philosophy: exhorting and teaching whomever I happen upon, in my usual manner, in this fashion: "Why do you, O best of men, since you are a citizen of Athens—a city most great, and most outstanding in wisdom and power—not feel ashamed to bestow all your effort on this: that you may have as much money, glory, and honor as possible, while you neither think of nor care for prudence, truth, and the best possible state of your soul?" And if any of you should dispute with me, asserting that he does care for these things, I will not immediately let him go, nor depart; but I will question, examine, and refute him. And if he does not seem to me to possess virtue, yet professes to, I shall rebuke him because he values at nothing those things which are of the highest price, while he prizes most highly the vilest things. This duty I shall perform for the younger and the older, whomever I happen upon, and again for the stranger and the citizen; but more so for the citizens, by as much as you are closer to me in kin. For God himself commands this. Moreover, I believe it should not escape your notice that no greater good has yet befallen you in this city than this ministry of mine, which I perform in obedience to God. For I go about doing nothing else than persuading the younger and older among you that care should be had neither for bodies, nor for money, nor for any other things at all, before or more vehemently than for the soul, so that it may be as good as possible; teaching that virtue does not come from money, but money and all other goods, both private and public, come to men from virtue. If, therefore, by teaching these things I pervert the youth, they would certainly be harmful. But if anyone says that I teach things other than these, he says nothing. For the sake of these things, O men of Athens, I profess indeed—whether you believe Anytus <note>One of Socrates' primary accusers</note> or do not believe him, whether you dismiss me or do not dismiss me—I profess that I shall do nothing else, not even if I must die many times over. Do not be disturbed, O men of Athens. But as I asked from the beginning, hear me with an even mind; for it will be useful to you, I think, if you hear what I am now about to say. Indeed, I am going to say some things to you which, upon hearing, you might perhaps be provoked to shout out at present; but I ask for silence from you. Know that if you kill me, being such a man as I just told you, you will not harm me more than yourselves. For neither Meletus <note>The lead accuser</note> nor Anytus will ever harm me. Nor indeed could they. Since it is a divine law, I believe, that a better man cannot be harmed by a worse one. He can, however, kill, or banish, or affect one with some indignity; and these things he and perhaps some others might think to be great evils. But I do not think so; rather, I think it is a much worse thing to do what he is doing now, attempting to kill a man unjustly. Wherefore, O men of Athens, there is not so much need for me now to meditate on a defense for my own sake, as someone might think, but rather for your sake, lest by condemning me you should offend against that gift which God has granted to you. For if you kill me, you will not easily find another such as I—truly, even if perhaps it sounds ridiculous to say—attached to your city as if to a great and noble horse, but one rather sluggish because of its very size, and needing to be stirred up by some Gadfly <note>Latin: *Tabano*. Socrates famously compared himself to a gadfly stinging the "lazy horse" of the Athenian state into action.</note>; such a one as God seems to have added me to the city: who, awakening and admonishing and rebuking each one, do not cease to stand by you everywhere the whole day long. You will not easily find another such as me, O men of Athens. Therefore, if you believe me, you will acquit me by your votes. But if perhaps, like those who are drowsy, you take it ill being awakened and—as Anytus wishes—you rashly kill me, you will sleep for all the time that remains, unless perhaps God, looking out for you, should send someone else. That I am such a person as to seem to have been granted to the city by God, you can perceive from this: it certainly does not seem human that I should have utterly neglected all my own affairs, and have persevered for so many years now in this neglect of my household business, always intent upon your good, while approaching each of you like a father or an elder brother, persuading you to have a care for virtue. And if I received any reward for my service, that would have some human explanation. But now, as you yourselves clearly see, although these accusers of mine have most shamelessly heaped all other charges against me, they have not dared to attempt this one thing with their usual impudence: to produce witnesses who might prove that I ever demanded or asked for any reward for these things. Of this matter, I bring you a sufficient witness, I think: my poverty. But perhaps it may seem absurd to someone that I go about giving this advice to individuals privately with such great anxiety, yet in public assemblies I have not dared to give this same advice to the city. The cause of this is what you have often heard me saying in various places: namely, that something divine and demonic <note>Latin: *daemonium*. Socrates referred to a "daimonion" or inner voice that warned him against certain actions.</note> is present to me in a certain voice. Which thing Meletus indeed mocked in the accusation. But this has been with me since childhood: a certain voice, which, whenever it occurs, forbids me to do what I was about to do, but never provokes me to act. This is what opposes me from involving myself in public affairs. And it seems to me to oppose me quite rightly. For it is certain, O men of Athens, that if I had long ago attempted public business, I would have perished long ago; and so I would have brought no utility either to you or to myself. Do not be angry with me, I pray, for speaking the truth. For no one can remain safe for long if he legitimately opposes either you or any other populace, in order to prohibit many unjust and iniquitous things which are accustomed to happen in the city. But it is necessary for him who truly fights for justice, if he is to be safe for even a short time, to live as a private citizen and not to touch the republic. Of these things I shall bring you great arguments: not words indeed, but what you value highly—deeds. Hear now what has happened to me, so that you may more clearly perceive that I would have conceded nothing to anyone against justice for fear of death; and that by not conceding, I would have perished at once. I shall relate to you indeed some troublesome and judicial matters, yet they are true. For I, O men of Athens...

## PAGE XXVII.

<meta>Catchword: born</meta>

I have never held any public office, except that I was elected to the Council. It so happened that my tribe, <term>Antiochis</term><note>One of the ten administrative divisions of ancient Athens.</note>, was presiding at the time when you wished to judge the ten commanders of the fleet collectively—those who had failed to pick up the survivors of the naval battle. This was illegal, as all of you later realized. At that time, I was the only one of the presiding officers to oppose you, insisting that nothing be done contrary to the laws, and I voted against the proposal. Even though many orators were ready to indict me and drag me to court, and you yourselves were urging them on with great shouts, I considered it my duty to face danger on the side of law and justice rather than to join you in an unjust cause out of fear of imprisonment or death.

These things took place while the city was still governed by the people's liberty. But after the power passed to the few, the <term>Thirty</term><note>The "Thirty Tyrants," a pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens briefly after the Peloponnesian War.</note> who had seized the state summoned me and four others to the <term>Tholos</term><note>A round building in Athens used as the headquarters for the government.</note> and ordered us to bring <term>Leon of Salamis</term> from Salamis so that he might be executed. They gave many such orders to many people at that time, intending to involve as many as possible in their crimes. Then I showed again, not by words but by my actions, that I do not care a straw for death—if that is not too crude a way to put it—but that my entire concern is to do nothing unjust or impious. That terrifying power did not frighten me into doing anything wrong. When we left the Tholos, the other four went to Salamis and brought Leon back, but I simply went home. I might have been put to death for this, had their power not been dissolved shortly thereafter. There are many witnesses who can testify to these events.

Do you think I could have survived so many years if I had entered public life and, acting as a good man should, had supported justice and placed it above all else? Far from it, men of Athens! No other man could have survived so long behaving in such a way. Throughout my life, whenever I have dealt with public affairs, I have remained the same person; and in private, I have never yielded to anyone in anything contrary to justice—not even to those whom my accusers claim are my disciples.

I have never been anyone’s teacher. But if anyone, young or old, desired to hear me speaking or going about my business, I never begrudged them. Nor am I the kind of person who speaks only when paid and remains silent when not; I offer myself to be questioned by rich and poor alike, and likewise to anyone who wishes to answer me and hear what I have to say. If any of these people turns out well or poorly, I cannot justly be blamed, for I never promised or provided any formal "instruction." If anyone claims to have learned or heard anything from me in private that I did not say openly to everyone else, they are not telling the truth.

But why do some people enjoy spending so much time in my company? You have heard the reason, men of Athens; I have told you the whole truth. They enjoy hearing the cross-examination of those who think they are wise but are not. It is not an unpleasant thing to witness. To me, as I have said, this task has been commanded by God through oracles, dreams, and every other way that divine providence has ever commanded a man to do anything.

These things, men of Athens, are both true and easily proven. For if I am currently corrupting some of the youth, or have corrupted others in the past, it would be natural for those who have grown older to realize I gave them bad advice in their youth; they should now rise up against me and demand punishment. Or if they were unwilling, their relatives—fathers, brothers, or other kin—should remember the harm their family suffered and seek vengeance now. I see many of them present here: first <term>Crito</term>, my contemporary and fellow tribesman, the father of <term>Critobulus</term> here; then <term>Lysanias of Sphettus</term>, the father of <term>Aeschines</term>; also <term>Antiphon of Cephisus</term>, the father of <term>Epigenes</term>. There are others whose brothers spent time with me: <term>Nicostratus</term>, son of <term>Zotidas</term> and brother of <term>Theodotus</term> (Theodotus is dead, so he cannot influence his brother); and <term>Paralus</term>, son of <term>Demodocus</term>, whose brother was <term>Theages</term>; also <term>Adimantus</term>, son of <term>Ariston</term>, whose brother is <term>Plato</term> here; and finally <term>Eantodorus</term>, whose brother is <term>Apollodorus</term>.

I could name many others, any one of whom <term>Meletus</term><note>One of Socrates' primary accusers.</note> ought to have produced as a witness during his speech. If he forgot then, let him produce one now—I will allow it. Let him bring forward any such evidence. But the truth, men of Athens, is exactly the opposite. You will find that they are all ready to help me—the man who is accused of corrupting and harming their relatives by Meletus and <term>Anytus</term>. Now, if the corrupted youths themselves helped me, it might not be surprising; but why should their older relatives, who have never been corrupted by me, support me, unless it is for the sake of what is right and just? They know that Meletus is lying and that I am telling the truth.

These, men of Athens, are the arguments I have for my defense, along with others of the same sort. Perhaps some of you, remembering your own habits, will be annoyed with me. You might recall how, even in less serious cases, a defendant often pleads with many tears and brings his children and a crowd of relatives and friends into court to stir up pity. I will do none of these things, even though I am, as it seems, in the greatest danger. Someone might be offended by this and cast his vote in anger. If any of you feel this way, I do not think it right to beg, but rather to speak reasonably. I too, my good man, have relatives. As <margin>Homer</margin> says, I was not born "from an oak or a rock," but from human beings. Thus I have relatives, men of Athens, and three sons: one who is already a young man, and two who are still...

# APOLOGY. PAGE 194.

...are small children. Yet I will bring none of them here to plead with you for my acquittal in that manner. Why then will I do none of these things? It is not out of any stubbornness or contempt for you, men of Athens, nor is it a question of whether I am brave in the face of death or not—that is another matter. However, for the sake of my reputation, yours, and that of the entire city, I do not think it right for me to do such things at my age and with the name I have earned, whether that reputation be true or false. For it is a long-held opinion among men that Socrates excels among many in some particular way. If, therefore, those among you who are thought to surpass others in wisdom, or courage, or any other virtue, were to act as I have often seen some act when they were being judged, it would surely be a disgrace. These men, though thought to be of some value, nevertheless behaved in court with a marvelous display of misery, as if they were going to suffer something terrible if they departed from this life—as if they would be immortal if only you did not kill them. Indeed, these men seem to me to bring shame upon the city; for a foreigner might suppose that those Athenians who excel in virtue, and who are preferred for magistracies and other honors, are no different from women. These things, O men of Athens, neither you who appear to hold some authority ought to do, nor, if we should wish to do them, should you permit it. Instead, you should show that you will much more readily condemn the man who introduces such pathetic scenes and makes the city look ridiculous, than the man who awaits the judgment in silence.

Furthermore, O men of Athens, in addition to what has been said regarding the city's reputation, it does not seem just to me to entreat a judge, nor to be acquitted by entreaty, but rather to teach and persuade. For a judge does not sit for the purpose of granting favors, but to judge according to the laws. And he has promised this by oath: not to show favor to whomever he pleases, but to judge according to the laws. Therefore, we must not accustom you to perjure yourselves, nor should you become accustomed to it. For neither of us would be observing religious duty. Do not, therefore, O men of Athens, require me to act in such a way before you which I consider neither honorable, nor just, nor holy—especially, by Jove <note>original: "per Iouem" - a common Latin rendering of the Greek oath "by Zeus"</note>, when I am accused of impiety toward the god by Melitus here. For surely, if I were to try to persuade you and force you by entreaty when you are under oath, I would be teaching you not to believe that there are gods; and in truth, while preparing my defense, I would meanwhile be accusing myself of not believing in the gods at all. But that is far from the case. For I believe, O men of Athens, that there are gods more than any of my accusers do; and I leave it to you and to the god to judge concerning me in whatever way will be best for both me and for you.

As for the fact that I am not distressed, O men of Athens, that I have been condemned by you, many things contribute to this, and especially that this outcome did not happen contrary to my expectation. Indeed, I am much more surprised by the number of votes on each side. For I did not think I would miss acquittal by so small a number of votes. Now, however, as it appears, if only three votes had fallen differently, I would have escaped. I seem to have escaped Melitus, certainly; and not only escaped, but it is clear to everyone that if Anytus and Lyco had not stood up to accuse me, he would have had to pay a thousand drachmas <note>A significant fine in ancient Athens for accusers who failed to receive at least one-fifth of the jury's votes.</note>, since he would not have received a fifth part of the votes.

This man, then, proposes the penalty of death. So be it. But what penalty, O men of Athens, shall I propose for myself? Is it not clearly that which I deserve? What then? What do I deserve to suffer or pay because I did not remain silent about what I learned, but neglected the things that the crowd values—wealth, family affairs, military commands, public speeches, and other magistracies—and moreover stayed away from the conspiracies and seditions that have occurred in the republic, thinking myself truly born for more equitable duties than to think my safety depended on these things? To these things, I say, I did not apply myself, for in them I would have been of no use either to you or to myself. Instead, I devoted myself to this one duty alone: that by greeting each of you privately, I might bring the greatest benefit, as I believe—persuading each of you not to care for his possessions before he cares for himself, so that he might become as good and as wise as possible; nor to care for the affairs of the city before the city itself; and that care for other things should be held in the same manner.

What then, being such a man, do I deserve to receive from you? Something good, certainly, O men of Athens, if you truly estimate me according to my worth; and such a good as would be appropriate for me. What, then, is appropriate for a poor man who is a benefactor, who requires leisure from other occupations so that he may exhort you toward virtue? There is surely no other reward, O men of Athens, that more becomes such a man than to be nourished in the Prytaneum <note>The town hall of Athens where distinguished citizens and Olympic victors were fed at public expense.</note> at public expense—and much more so than if any of you has won at Olympia with a horse, or a pair of horses, or a four-horse chariot. For that man makes you *appear* happy, but I make you *be* happy. Furthermore, he does not need the nourishment, but I do. Therefore, if I must be estimated according to worth and justice, I judge myself worthy of this: that food be provided for me publicly in the Prytaneum.

Perhaps in saying these things to you, I seem as stubborn as I did before when I rejected pity and supplications. But it is not so, O men of Athens; it is rather like this. For I am persuaded that I have never intentionally done wrong to anyone. I cannot persuade you of this because we have had only a short time for conversation. Indeed, if there were a law among you such as exists among others, that in a trial where death is the penalty, the case is discussed not for one day but for many, I believe I would have persuaded you. But now it was not easy to dissolve great slanders in so short a time. Since, therefore, I am persuaded that I should do wrong to no one, I am far from about to do wrong to myself. What then? Should I, fearing lest I suffer that which Melitus deems me worthy of—which I say I do not know whether it be good or evil—choose instead one of those things which I know plainly to be evils, and judge myself worthy of those? Should it be chains? And why should I live my life in prison, always serving the Eleven <note>The "Eleven" were the officials in charge of the prison and executions in Athens.</note>...

<summary>Socrates argues that he will not beg for mercy as it would disgrace Athens and violate his religious principles. After being found guilty, he boldly suggests that his "punishment" should be free meals at the public's expense for his service as a benefactor.</summary>

# BOOK XXVII.
-> 27 <-

What then? Should I pay a fine and remain in chains until it is paid? But that is the same as what I said above, since I lack the means to pay. Or perhaps exile? For perhaps I might be deemed worthy of this. Yet a desperate desire for life would have to possess me, O men of Athens, if I were so mindless that I could not notice that if you, my fellow citizens, could not bear my ways and my discourses—but rather my company and speech were so heavy and hateful to you that you have now decided to free yourselves from them—how could I think others would easily tolerate me? Far from it, O men of Athens. A fine life it would be for me, at this age, living as an exile, wandering from one city to another, and living in continual rejection. For I understand clearly that wherever I go, the young men will listen to me just as they do here; and if I drive them away, they will in turn persuade their elders to drive me out. If I do not drive them away, their fathers and kinsmen will expel me on their account.

Perhaps someone will say: "Socrates, can you not live in exile in silence and quiet?" But this is the most difficult thing of all to persuade some of you of. For if I answer that this would be to disobey the God <note>original: "deo"; referring to the divine mission Socrates believed he received from Apollo at Delphi</note>, and that for this reason I cannot remain quiet, you will not believe me, thinking I am speaking in irony. If, on the other hand, I say that I do not wish to be exempt from this duty because the greatest good that can happen to a man is to speak every day about virtue and the other things about which you hear me talking daily—thus examining myself and others, and considering that the unexamined life <note>original: "vitam inconsideratam"; the famous Socratic dictum that the life without inquiry is not worth living</note> is to be rejected—you will believe me even less. These things are exactly as I say, O men of Athens, but they are not easily persuaded.

And at the same time, I have never been accustomed to deem myself worthy of any evil. If I had money, I would propose a fine of as much as I was able to pay, for it would not harm me to lose it. But now I have none, unless perhaps you wish to value the fine at what I am able to pay. I can perhaps pay one mina of silver <note>term: mina; an ancient unit of currency. One mina was roughly 100 drachmae, a significant but modest sum for a commoner</note>. I therefore propose a fine of that much. But Plato here, O men of Athens, and Crito, and Critobulus, and Apollodorus, urge me to propose thirty minae. They are ready to guarantee that much to you. I therefore propose that amount. These men will be sufficient guarantors of this silver to you.

For the sake of a short time, O men of Athens, you have provided a subject for reproach to those who wish to defame the city—namely, that you have killed Socrates, a wise man. For those who wish to defame you will say I am wise, even if I am not. If you had waited a short time, death would have come to you of its own accord. See my age, how far it is already from life and how near to death. I do not say this to all of you, but only to those who condemned me to death. I say this also to these very men: Perhaps you think, O men of Athens, that I have been convicted in court for a lack of such words as might have persuaded you, if I had thought I should do and say everything to be acquitted by you. Far from it. Certainly, I have been condemned for a poverty—not of words, but of audacity and impudence, and because I was unwilling to say such things to you as would have been most pleasing for you to hear: namely, hearing me weeping and lamenting, and doing and saying many other things unworthy of me, as I said, such as you are accustomed to hear from others. But I did not think from the beginning that I should do anything illiberal <note>meaning unbefitting a free man or noble spirit</note> to avoid danger, nor do I now repent having used this method of defense. I would much rather die having relied on such a defense than live by the opposite. For neither in court nor in war should I or anyone else do everything possible to avoid death. In battles it is often clear that death could be avoided if one threw down his arms and turned as a suppliant to his pursuers. There are other devices in every danger by which one might escape death, if one is not ashamed to do or say anything.

But consider, O men of Athens, that it is not difficult to escape death; it is much more difficult to escape wickedness. For it runs faster than death. And now I, being slow and old, have been caught by the slower runner; but my accusers, being vigorous and swift, have been caught by the swifter, which is wickedness. And now I go away, condemned by you to undergo death; but they go away condemned by Truth herself to wickedness and injustice. I accept my penalty, and they theirs. Perhaps these things had to be so, and I think they are as they should be.

After this, I desire to prophesy to you who condemned me. For I have now reached that point where men are most likely to prophesy: namely, when they are near death. I predict to you, O men of Athens, that if you kill me, a punishment will come upon you immediately after my death, and by Jove <note>original: "per Iovem"; a Latinization of "by Zeus"</note>, one much harsher than that which you have inflicted on me. For you have done this now thinking you would be freed from giving an account of your lives to a critic. But the opposite will happen to you. For I think there will be more who will rebuke you, whom I was holding back—though you did not perceive it—and they will be all the more troublesome as they are younger, and you will be more vexed by them. Truly, if you think that by killing men you can be freed from reproach, you are greatly mistaken. For this liberation is neither sufficiently effective nor honorable. But that which is both easiest and best is not to suppress others, but to prepare oneself to become as good as possible. Having prophesied these things to you who condemned me, I make an end.

But to you who acquitted me, I would gladly speak about this thing that has happened, as long as the magistrates are busy and I have not yet gone to the place where I must die. But, O men, stay with me for this time. For nothing prevents us from talking with one another while it is permitted. Indeed, I want to show you, as friends, what has just happened to me and what it might mean. To me, O judges—for I can rightly call you judges—a marvelous thing has happened. For that prophetic voice of the spirit <note>original: "vox illa daemonis vaticinatrix"; referring to Socrates' 'daimonion' or inner divine sign</note> has always been accustomed to offer itself to me frequently in former times, opposing me even in the most trivial matters if I were about to do something incorrectly. But now these things which you see have happened to me, which someone might think and consider the extreme...

He concludes by prophesying that his death will only bring more critics to Athens and begins to discuss his "divine sign" with those who voted for his acquittal.</summary>

# ARGUMENT OF THE CRITO.

<note>original: "ARGVMENTVM IN CRITONEM"</note>

...to be the greatest of evils. But for me, neither when I left home this morning did the divine sign <note>Socrates' "daimonion" or inner voice</note> oppose me, nor while I was coming to judgment, nor in any part of my speech while I was speaking—though at other times it has frequently been accustomed to restrain me in the middle of a sentence. Now, however, in this matter, it has nowhere opposed me in either action or speech. I will reveal to you what I consider to be the cause of this. For it appears to me that what has happened is a good thing. Nor is it rightly judged by any of us who suppose that death is an evil. Indeed, I have a great proof of this: that the sign would have resisted me as it usually does, unless I were about to do something good. We can also consider it in this way: there is much hope that death is a good thing. For death is one of two things: either it is as if one were nothing at all, and the departed retains no sensation of anything; or, as it is said, it is a certain change and migration of the soul from this place to another. Therefore, if no sensation remains, but it is like a sleep in which one sees no dream, death will be a wonderful gain. I truly believe that if someone had to compare that night in which he passed such quiet rest that he did not even see a dream, with all the other nights and days of his whole life, and say how many nights and days he spent better and more sweetly than that one—I believe not only a private citizen, but not even the Great King <note>The King of Persia, a standard of ultimate earthly wealth</note> could count many. If, therefore, death is such a thing, I say it is a gain. Indeed, in this way, all time seems to be nothing more than a single night. But if death is like a migration from here to another place, and what is said is true—namely, that all the dead are in another place apart from us—what could be better than this, O judges! For if one travels there, free from those who profess to be judges here, and finds the true judges who are said to judge there—Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and others of the demigods who lived justly—would <margin>Orpheus, Musaeus, Immortality of souls.</margin> such a migration be considered of little value? Again, to meet with Orpheus and Musaeus and Hesiod and Homer—how much would any of you pay for that? Truly, if these things are true, I would wish to die often. For that habitation and company would be wonderfully pleasing to me, especially when I shall be with Palamedes, and Ajax son of Telamon, and others of the ancients who died by a false judgment; to compare my misfortunes with theirs would, I think, be not unpleasant. Furthermore, the greatest thing would be to spend time there searching and examining each person, just as I have done here, to see who among them is wise, and who thinks he is wise when he is not. Therefore, how much should it be valued, O judges, to examine the leader who led such a great army to Troy, or Ulysses, or Sisyphus, and countless other men and women? To speak with them and be occupied in examining them would be an altogether inestimable happiness. For those who live there do not die anymore; they are both happier than we are in other matters, and moreover, they remain immortal for the rest of time—if indeed what is said is true. You too, O judges, ought to hope well regarding death, and consider this one thing to be true: that no evil can happen to a good man, neither living nor dead, nor are his affairs neglected by the gods. Nor have my current circumstances happened by some mere accident; rather, it is clear to me that to die now and be freed from labors was better for me, and for this reason the divine sign did not withstand me. Indeed, I am not at all angry with those who accused or condemned me, although they did not accuse or condemn me with that intention, but because they hoped to do me harm. For this, they certainly deserve blame. But now, having returned to those same men, I address them thus: I pray only this of you, O men: that when my sons have grown up, if they are troublesome to you as I have been, you punish them similarly—especially if they seem to you to care more for money or anything else than for virtue, and if they wish to seem or think themselves to be of some value when they are worth nothing. Reprove them, just as I have reproved you, because they do not apply themselves to what they ought, and they think they are something when they are of no value. If you do this, I and my sons will have suffered justice from you. But now it is the hour to depart: I to die, and you to live. Which of us goes to the better lot is hidden from everyone except God.

***

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino for the Crito, addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici, a Magnanimous Man.

Just as with the Apology, the arrangement of the *Crito* is so orderly and plain that it needs no summary. Note, however, first of all, that just as Socrates prophesied while awake in the *Apology*, so he prophesies while sleeping in the *Crito*. This is so you may know that God is always present to a wise and pious man, both waking and sleeping. From all this, gather a confirmation of the Gospel doctrine: the approval of martyrs, the exemplar of justice, incomparable fortitude, contempt for mortal things, desire for eternal things, and finally, the foundation of religion. Why should I mention that the opinion of the common people is to be despised, and only the opinion of the wise—or rather, Truth itself—is to be cherished? Or again, that it is not merely living, but living well that is to be desired? That one must never do evil to enemies, nor avenge injuries? Again, that the danger of death and destruction must be undergone rather than sinning? Why should I recount his singular observance of the laws and his inestimable love for his country? Which he undoubtedly prefers to both parents and life, for this reason (as he says): so that, having traveled into the other life, he may be able to give a just account of his past life to the Eternal Judge, and not be compelled to dread the laws that rule there, which are the sisters of human laws. Finally, he concludes the arguments...

### CRITO, OR ON WHAT IS TO BE DONE.

->PERSONS OF THE DIALOGUE.<-
->SOCRATES. CRITO.<-

<margin><unclear>Socrates in prison</unclear></margin> **SO.** Why have you come at this hour, O Crito? Or is it not still very much before light? **CRI.** It is indeed. **SO.** Approximately what time? **CRI.** Deep dawn <note>The period just before sunrise.</note>. **SO.** I wonder how the guardian of the prison himself was willing to comply with you. **CRI.** He is already familiar to me, O Socrates, because of my frequent visits here. Moreover, he has received some small benefit from me. **SO.** Have you just arrived? Or was it some time ago? **CRI.** Quite some time ago. **SO.** Then why did you not wake me immediately? Instead, you sat by in silence? **CRI.** By Jupiter <note>original: "p Iouē" (per Jovem). A common oath in Latin translations of Greek texts.</note>, O Socrates, I would never have woken you. For I myself would not wish to be awake in such great sorrow. But I have been wondering at you for a long time, seeing how sweetly you sleep. And I deliberately did not wake you, so that you might spend your time as peacefully as possible. Indeed, throughout your whole life, I have judged you blessed because of this character; but especially so in your present calamity, because you bear it so easily and calmly. **SO.** It would be quite absurd, O Crito, if someone of such a great age should bear imminent death with grievance. **CRI.** But others, O Socrates, equally old, are overwhelmed by similar calamities; yet their age does not liberate them from the affliction which their present lot brings with it. **SO.** That is true. But why then have you come so early? **CRI.** Bringing a bitter message, O Socrates—not to you indeed, as it appears to me, but rather to me and to all your friends, both bitter and heavy. Which indeed I would count among the heaviest things, as I think. **SO.** What is this then? Has the ship from Delos <note>The return of this sacred ship from the festival at Delos signaled the time for Socrates' execution.</note> already returned? Upon whose return I must die. **CRI.** It has not yet returned; but it seems it will return today, as some coming from Sunium <note>A promontory at the southern tip of Attica.</note> report, who left it there. It is certain, therefore, from these reports, that it will arrive today; and therefore it will be necessary for you, O Socrates, to depart from life tomorrow. **SO.** Good fortune, O Crito. If it pleases God <note>original: "Si ita placet" - literally "if it so pleases [them/the gods]".</note>, so be it. However, I do not think it will return today. **CRI.** From where do you conjecture that? **SO.** I will tell you: if indeed I must die on the day after the ship returns. **CRI.** So at least say those in whose power this matter lies. **SO.** Therefore I do not think it will come on this day, but on the next. I take this conjecture from a certain dream which appeared to me a little while ago in this very night; and you seem to have timely avoided disturbing my sleep. **CRI.** But what sort of dream was it? **SO.** A certain woman seemed to come to me, beautiful and pleasing in appearance, having white garments, to call me and say: "O Socrates, on the third day hence you shall reach fertile Phthia" <note>A reference to Homer's Iliad; Phthia was the home of Achilles. Here it symbolizes the journey to the afterlife.</note>. **CRI.** What a strange dream, Socrates. **SO.** Manifest, however, as it seems to me. **CRI.** Manifest indeed. But, O blessed Socrates, even now believe me, and be willing to be saved. For if you die, not only one calamity threatens me: but besides that I shall be bereaved of such a friend as I shall never find another, I shall certainly seem to many—who do not know either of us well enough—that I could have saved you if I had been less sparing of money, and that I utterly neglected you. And what greater infamy can there be than to seem to have valued money more than friends? For many will not be able to be persuaded that you were unwilling to depart from here, even though we were striving with all zeal to make it happen. **SO.** But why, O blessed Crito, do we care so much for the opinion of the multitude? For the most esteemed men, whose opinion should be held in higher regard, will think these things were done just as they were done. **CRI.** Yet you see, O Socrates, that we are compelled to care for the opinion of the crowd as well. For these present circumstances declare that the crowd can inflict not the least of evils, but rather almost the greatest, if someone is agitated by slanders among the people. **SO.** I wish, O Crito, that the crowd could inflict the greatest evils, so that in turn they could do the greatest goods, and then things would be well. But they can do neither: for they are able to make a man neither wise nor foolish. They do whatever they please, however it happens. **CRI.** Let these things be as they are. But answer me this, Socrates: perhaps respect for me and your other friends holds you back, lest if you escape from here, informers may trouble us afterward, as if we had stolen you from here; and we might be forced to lose either our whole patrimony or a great deal of money, or suffer something else besides these things. If you fear anything of the sort, put away such a care. For it is just that for the sake of your safety we undergo not only this, but even if it were necessary, some other greater danger. But comply with me; do not do otherwise. **SO.** I am considering both these things and many others, O Crito. **CRI.** Therefore do not fear these things. For the silver is not much which those demand who promise to save you and lead you out from here. You see, moreover, how insignificant your informers are, so that there is no need for a large bribe to appease them. Indeed, my money is available to you, sufficient for this as I think. Furthermore, if out of respect for me you do not think my money should be spent: there are foreign guests here ready to pay. One of whom has even brought sufficient money here prepared for this very purpose, Simmias the Theban. Ready for this very thing is also Cebes, and many others. Wherefore, as I was just saying, fear no such thing that would prevent you from saving yourself. And let not that which you said in court delay you: that if you left this city, you would not know where to turn yourself. For in many other places, wherever you go, men will cherish you; and if you wish to betake yourself to Thessaly, you will find my guests there, who will most gladly embrace you; and they will provide such a safe protection that no one in Thessaly will do you injury. Added to this, O Socrates, you seem to be attempting a thing that is not at all just: if, when you could be safe, you betray yourself, and strive to do such things against yourself as your very enemies would strive—and have striven—to do, hoping to destroy you.

<summary>Crito visits Socrates in prison at dawn to urge him to escape, reporting that the ship from Delos is near. Socrates remains calm, citing a prophetic dream, while Crito argues that staying to face execution is an act of self-betrayal and a failure of his friends.</summary>

# CRITO, OR ON WHAT IS TO BE DONE
## Folio 196
->con.iiii.<-

Therefore, you also seem to me to be betraying your own sons; though it is in your power to bring them up and educate them, you abandon them entirely and, as much as lies within you, you commit their characters to fortune. It is likely that what usually happens to orphans will happen to them. Truly, one ought either not to have fathered children at all, or not to refuse the labor of bringing them up and educating them. But you seem to me to have chosen what a sluggish and lazy man would choose, whereas it was fitting to choose as a good and brave man would, especially since you profess a devotion to virtue throughout your whole life. Thus, I cannot help but feel ashamed for your sake and for ours, your friends, fearing lest this whole affair of yours should seem to have been handled with a certain cowardice on our part. First, that the case entered the court when it was possible not to enter; then, the very conduct of the trial itself; and finally this end, which seems like a ridiculous failure due to our cowardice and sluggishness—as if we have let the opportunity slip away because we did not save you, nor did you save yourself, though it could have been done without great difficulty if there had been even a little use of industry in us. Consider these things, therefore, O Socrates, lest besides being evils, they also bring disgrace upon you and us. Take counsel for yourself. Or rather, it is no longer the time for taking counsel, but the counsel ought already to have been taken. There is but one plan: namely, that all these things must be done this coming night. But if we delay further, nothing at all can be done hereafter. Therefore, by all means, trust me, O Socrates, and do not do otherwise.

**SOCRATES:** O friend Crito, this zeal of yours would be worth much if it were undertaken with some right reason. But if not, the more vehement it is, the more troublesome. We must consider, therefore, whether these things ought to be done by us or not. For I am the sort of man—not only now but always—who obeys nothing of mine except the reason <note>original: "rationi"</note> which seems best to me upon reflection. Those reasons which I used in former times I cannot reject now, even after this fortune has befallen me; they appear almost the same to me, and I honor and profess the same ones in the present as I did before. So much so, that unless we can bring forward better ones now, you should know clearly that I will not concede to you—not even if the power of the multitude should attempt to scare us like children with even more terrors than now, threatening us with punishments, losses, chains, and death.

**CRITO:** In what way, then, shall we consider this moderately?

**SOCRATES:** In this way: if we take up again what you were saying a little while ago about opinions—whether it is always right or not to hold that one should pay attention to some opinions, but not to others. Or perhaps, before I fell into the danger of death, that was said rightly, but now it is clear it was said in vain for the sake of argument, when in truth it was brought forward as a kind of joke or nonsense. I desire, O Crito, to consider with you whether that former discourse appears different to me now, situated in this fortune, or the same as before; and whether it is to be dismissed by us, or if we should obey it. Consider, then, if it does not seem to you to be sufficiently stated that one ought not to follow all the opinions of men, but to follow some and neglect others; and not the opinions of everyone, but only of certain people. What do you say? Is this not rightly said?

**CRITO:** Rightly.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not fitting to honor the good ones, but to despise the bad ones?

**CRITO:** It is fitting.

**SOCRATES:** And are not the good ones those of the wise <note>original: "prudentum" - those possessing practical wisdom</note>? And the bad ones, on the contrary, those of the unwise?

**CRITO:** Why not?

**SOCRATES:** Come then, in what way were such things said? Does he who exercises in the gymnasiums pay attention to the praise or blame of any man, or only to that of the one who is a physician or a trainer?

**CRITO:** Of that one alone.

**SOCRATES:** Is it not fitting, then, to fear the blame and desire the praise of that one person rather than of the many?

**CRITO:** Without a doubt.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, he must act, exercise, eat, and drink in the way that seems best to that one person who presides and understands, rather than as it seems to the crowd.

**CRITO:** These things are true.

**SOCRATES:** But what if he does not obey that one person, and sets his opinion and commendations at nothing, but honors the commendations of the many who are ignorant? Will he not be safe from harm?

**CRITO:** Not at all.

**SOCRATES:** And what is that harm? Where does it lead, and upon what part of the disobedient man does it act?

**CRITO:** Upon the body, clearly, for this is what is corrupted.

**SOCRATES:** You speak rightly. Is it not the same, O Crito, regarding other things? Not to run through them all: I mean regarding things just and unjust, shameful and honorable, good and evil—about which our consultation now is—whether we ought to follow and fear the opinion of the many, or rather that of the one who understands, whom it is fitting to both revere and fear more than all others? Unless we obey him, we shall be harmed and corrupted in that which is made better by justice but is usually corrupted by injustice. Or is that nothing?

**CRITO:** I think the same, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** Come then, if that which is made better by health but corrupted by what is unhealthy is destroyed because we followed the judgments of the unskilled rather than the skilled, will life be worth living for us once it is destroyed? That is the body, is it not?

**CRITO:** The body.

**SOCRATES:** Is life then worth living for us with a depraved and destroyed body?

**CRITO:** In no way.

**SOCRATES:** But is life worth living for us with that part corrupted which is harmed by injustice but helped by justice? Do we consider that part—whatever it is of ours that is concerned with justice and injustice—to be cheaper than the body?

**CRITO:** In no way.

**SOCRATES:** But more precious?

**CRITO:** Much more.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, O best of men, we must not care very much what the many say of us, but what the one who understands the just and the unjust says, and what Truth itself says. Therefore, in the first place, you did not lead correctly when you thought the common opinion about just, honorable, and good things (and their opposites) should be considered. But someone might say, "The crowd is able to kill us."

**CRITO:** That can certainly be said, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** You speak the truth. But, O wonderful man, this reason we have run through seems to be similar to the previous one. Consider this again: whether it remains true for us or not—namely, that we should not value living most of all, but living well.

**CRITO:** It remains true.

**SOCRATES:** But does this also remain: that to live well, honorably, and justly are the same thing?

**CRITO:** It is agreed.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, from these things we have confessed, this must be considered: whether it is just for me to try to go out from here without the Athenians dismissing me, or unjust. And if it appears to be just, let us attempt it.
