# BOOK
### PAGE XXVIII.

...if not, let us dismiss it. As for the considerations you bring forward regarding the expense of money, public opinion, and the upbringing of children, we must take care, O Crito, lest these be the reflections of those many people who would lightly put men to death, and would bring them back to life if they could, and that without any reason. But for us, since reason so demands, we must attend to nothing else than what we were just saying: whether we act justly in giving money and showing gratitude to those who would lead me out of here—whether, I say, we act justly in being led out while they act justly in leading us—or whether instead we act unjustly in doing all these things. And if it appears that we are attempting something unjust, we ought not to deliberate on what that is, but rather it is fitting to submissively undergo both death and any other punishment whatsoever before we act unjustly.

**CRITO:** You seem to speak rightly, Socrates. Consider, however, what we should do.

**SOCRATES:** Let us consider it together, my good man. And if you can refute me in any part of my speech, refute me. I shall then agree. If not, I beg you, blessed man, cease repeating the same words to me so many times: namely, that I ought to depart from here against the will of the Athenians. Indeed, I place great value on acting with your persuasion and not against your will. Pay attention, then, to whether the beginning of this consideration has been sufficiently stated for you: and try to answer what you are asked in the way you think most appropriate.

**CRITO:** I shall try.

**SOCRATES:** We say, surely, that one must in no way do wrong <note>original: "iniuriandū" - to commit an injustice or injury</note> willingly. Or is it perhaps that in some way an injustice should be committed, but in another way not at all? Or rather, is doing wrong in no way either good or honorable, as we have often confessed in times past? This was indeed confirmed just recently. Or have all those former agreements of ours vanished in these few days, and for a long time now, O Crito, have we—men of such great age—been hidden from the fact that we differ not at all from children, despite our earnest discussions with one another? Or is the matter rather exactly as we used to say: whether the multitude affirms it or denies it, and whether we are forced to undergo things more severe or lighter than the present ones? Nevertheless, do we confess that to do wrong is altogether an evil and a shameful thing for the one who does it, or not?

**CRITO:** We certainly confess it.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, one must in no way do wrong.

**CRITO:** In no way indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Nor, if you have suffered a wrong, should you take revenge <margin>No revenging</margin> <note>original: "vlciscēdū" - to take vengeance or retaliate</note>, as the common people think; since one must in no way do wrong.

**CRITO:** So it seems.

**SOCRATES:** What then? Is it fitting to do evil to anyone, O Crito, or not?

**CRITO:** Certainly not, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES:** What then? When one suffers evil, ought he to return evil in turn to the one who brought it, as it seems to the common people? Would that be just or unjust?

**CRITO:** Unjust.

**SOCRATES:** For indeed, to bring evil upon men does not differ from doing wrong.

**CRITO:** You speak truly.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, one ought neither to take revenge nor to do evil to any man, whatever you yourself may have suffered from others. And see to it, O Crito, that while you concede these things, you do not agree with us against your own opinion. For I know that to very few does this seem true, or will it seem so. But for those to whom it seems so, and those for whom it seems otherwise, there is no common deliberation; instead, it is necessary that they despise one another when they look upon each other's counsels. Consider carefully, then, whether you share this opinion with me and feel the same; and whether we may deliberate starting from this principle: that it is never right either to do wrong, or to take revenge for a wrong, or to return evil to the one who brought it. Or do you depart from us here, not consenting to this principle? To me, indeed, it has seemed so for a long time and still does now. But if it appears otherwise to you, speak and teach me. But if you remain in our former views, hear now what follows.

**CRITO:** I do indeed consent and remain.

**SOCRATES:** I say then next—or rather, I ask: whether those things which someone confesses to another to be just, he ought to do, or to deceive?

**CRITO:** He ought to do them.

**SOCRATES:** From these things, then, consider this: if we depart from here without the consent of the city, shall we be doing evil to some, and to those indeed whom it is least fitting, or not? And shall we remain in those things which we agreed were unjust, or the opposite?

**CRITO:** I am unable, O Socrates, to answer these things. For I do not understand.

**SOCRATES:** Then consider it in this way: just as if, while we were intending either to run away from here or however this must be called, the Laws and the Republic of this city should come and, standing before us, say: "Tell us, O Socrates, what are you thinking of doing? Do you not understand that by this deed you are attempting, you are—as far as it lies in you—plotting the destruction of us, the Laws, and the entire fatherland? Or do you think any city can still stand and not be subverted in which public judgments have no force, but are despised and broken by private men?" What shall we say to these things, O Crito, and others of this kind? For anyone, especially an orator, could bring forward many things on behalf of a law thus dissolved—a law which commands that sentences passed by public judgment be valid. Or shall we answer them that the city brought a wrong upon us by not judging rightly? Shall we say that, or something else?

**CRITO:** That, by Jove, O Socrates!

**SOCRATES:** But the Laws themselves might respond: "O Socrates, was this not agreed between us and you, that you must stand by the judgments which the city has brought?" And if we wondered at the Laws speaking thus, they might perhaps say: "Do not wonder, Socrates, at what we have just said; rather answer, since you are accustomed to both asking and answering. Come, tell us, what grievance do you have against us and the city, that you strive to destroy us? In the first place, did we not beget you? And through us did your father not take your mother and bring you forth? Tell us then: do you find fault with those laws among us concerning marriage, as being in some part not right?" "I find no fault," I would say. "But what of those laws which provide for the upbringing and education of children, in which you yourself were educated? Did these laws, established for this duty, not dispose things rightly when they commanded your father to instruct you in music and gymnastics?" I would concede they disposed them rightly. "Come then: after you were born and brought up and educated through us, can you first of all deny that you are our offspring and servant, both yourself and your ancestors? Then, since this is so, do you think right is equal between you and us, and that whatever we attempt to do to you, the same may be done in turn to us by you..."

# CRITO, OR ON WHAT IS TO BE DONE.

## FOLIO 197.

<meta>Catchword: con.v.</meta>

Do you judge it just to be carried out? Or, since you would not have an equal right against your father, or your master if you had one—so that you could return against them what you suffered from them, nor if they provoked you with verbal abuse could you abuse them in return, nor if he struck you could you strike back, nor would it be permitted to attempt other such things against them—will it then be permitted to you against your fatherland and the laws? To such an extent that if we <note>The Laws speaking</note> judge it to be just that you should be put to death, you in turn should attempt to destroy us, the laws and the fatherland, to the best of your power, and say that in doing these things you act justly—you, who profess to truly have a care for virtue? Or are you so wise that it has escaped your notice that the fatherland is to be preferred before father and mother and all ancestors? And that the fatherland is something more venerable and more holy, and placed in a higher lot both among the gods and among men of sound mind: and that one ought to cherish it more and obey it, and bear oneself more rigidly toward it and more mildly submit to it than to a father? And if it commands anything, one must either persuade it otherwise as far as is permitted, or do it, and most patiently endure whatever it has ordered to be suffered: and whether it has commanded that you be beaten, or thrown into chains, or if it sends you into battle to receive wounds and undergo death, it must be obeyed entirely. For justice dictates thus: and one must neither shrink back, nor flee, nor desert one's rank: but both in war, and in the court of justice, and absolutely everywhere, those things which the Republic and the fatherland have commanded must be done: or certainly one may use words, insofar as it is just, to persuade it and appease it. But to use violence is a divine sin, whether against a mother or against a father, but most of all against the fatherland. What shall we say to these things, Crito? Do the laws speak the truth or the opposite?

**CRITO.** So it seems to me, indeed.

**SOCRATES.** Therefore the laws might perhaps say: observe, O Socrates, whether we speak the truth when we say that you are attempting unjust things against us. We, indeed, who gave birth to you and other citizens, educated you, nourished you, and made you participants in all the goods that were in our power: yet we permitted any of the Athenians, once they had come to know the customs of the city and the laws and the form of governing the republic, if we did not please him, to be allowed to take his belongings and go away wherever he pleased. Nor does any of us laws hinder or deny it, if any of you whom we and the city do not please at all wishes to depart hence into some colony, or desires to transfer his habitation elsewhere, from being able to do so according to his own judgment: and to carry his things with him. But truly, whoever of you, after he has known how we dispose judgments and rule the city in all other matters, has nevertheless remained, we now assert that he has agreed with us by his very deed that he will do whatever we command. And him who does not obey, we judge to be threefold injurious: both because he does not obey us who are his parents, and because he does not comply with us who are his nourishers, and because having pledged to obey us, he neither obeys nor strives to persuade us if we seem to do anything incorrectly. And although we propose our precepts freely and do not command rigidly, but permit one of two things—either that we be persuaded by words or that our commands be fulfilled—you do neither of these. We judge, therefore, O Socrates, that you will be liable to these charges if you do what you are thinking of: and not the least of the Athenians, but most of all. And if I should ask the cause why I am liable above the others, perhaps they would justly rebuke me, saying that I most of all the Athenians consented to the laws of the city. For they would infer thus: "We have great proofs of these things, O Socrates, that we and the city pleased you. For you would never have drawn out continuous stays in it more than all other Athenians unless it had pleased you wonderfully. Therefore, you never went out of the city for the sake of a spectacle, except once to the Isthmus <note>The Isthmian Games</note>, nor anywhere else except on military service: nor did you ever make any other pilgrimage, as others are accustomed to do: nor did a desire for another city or other laws take hold of you: but we and our city were enough for you: to such an extent did you vehemently approve of us: and you consented that you would live by our customs: both in other things, and because you procreated children in it, as it was pleasing to you. Furthermore, it was permitted to you in the trial itself to ask for exile if you had wished, and what you now attempt against the will of the city, you could have done then with its consent. But you then boasted in words as if you would not take it heavily if it were necessary for you to die. Rather, you chose death itself, as you said, instead of exile. But now you are neither ashamed of those words of yours, nor do you revere us, the laws: but you plot our destruction. You do what the worst slave would do, attempting to snatch a flight against the pacts and conventions in which you agreed with us that you would offer yourself to be governed by our institutions. First, answer us: do we speak this very thing truly: that you consented not in words but in the deed itself that you ought to be governed by our customs? Or are these things not true?" What shall we say to these things, Crito? Shall we not confess?

**CRITO.** It is necessary, O Socrates.

**SOCRATES.** "Do you not then," the laws will say, "transgress the conventions and pacts made with us, which you were neither forced to enter into with us, nor deceived, nor compelled to deliberate for a short time in choosing these things, but you were permitted to deliberate for seventy years? In which time it was permitted to go away, if we had not pleased you, and if the just conventions had seemed cheap to you. But you preferred neither Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> nor Crete to us—which cities you yourself continually preach are rightly governed—nor any other of the cities, whether Greek or barbarian. Indeed, you have traveled away from here more rarely than the lame and the blind and other maimed people are accustomed to do. To such an extent did the city of the Athenians please you above all other cities, and us, namely the laws. For whom can a city please whose laws do not please him? But now you do not remain in those things in which it has long been agreed between us and you. You will certainly remain if you believe us: lest by going out of the city you turn out to be a laughingstock. Consider again, if you transgress these things and perpetrate those things which you unjustly think of, to what end will it finally lead either for you or for your close associates? For it is clear to everyone that your associates will be in danger of being expelled into exile themselves and deprived of the city, and stripped of their patrimony. But you, if you betake yourself to some neighboring city, either Thebes or Megara—both of which...

# ARGUMENT ON THE PHAEDO.

<margin>What kind of person is a corrupter of laws.</margin> For if [cities] are governed rightly, you will arrive first as an enemy to that republic; and all who care for their fatherland will look down upon you and abominate you, regarding you as a corrupter of the laws. And thereby you will confirm the opinion of those who condemned you, so that they may seem to have passed their sentence against you rightly. For whoever is a corrupter of laws will most certainly be seen as a corrupter of the young and the ignorant. What then? Will you avoid those cities that are governed rightly and all the most modest men? And if you do this, will life be worth living? Or will you perhaps impudently mix with them, and not blush to discuss among them the same things you were accustomed to discuss among us? Namely, that virtue and justice, laws and institutions, are to be valued above all else! Do you not think it would appear absurd and discordant with these things for Socrates to act thus? Without a doubt, it must be thought so. But perhaps, declining these cities, you will go off to Thessaly to Crito’s guests. For there, life is lived without order or temperance. And perhaps they will listen to you gladly as you tell the story of how ridiculously you fled from prison, perhaps putting on some bundle or covering yourself with a hide, or wrapping yourself in other things as those who steal away in flight are accustomed to do, and having transformed yourself into a foreign shape, you escaped from there. But will no one say how an old man, with so little time left to live as is likely, dared to live in such filthy poverty out of a desire for life, having transgressed the greatest laws? Perhaps, if you offend no one. Otherwise, O Socrates, you will hear many things unworthy of you. You will live subject to all men and serving them. What indeed will you do in Thessaly? Will you frequent banquets? As if you had traveled to Thessaly as if to some dinner party! And those disputations concerning justice and the other virtues: where will they be for us any longer? But truly, you desire to live for the sake of your sons, so that you may nourish and educate them. Will you then lead them away into Thessaly to nourish and educate them there, making them foreigners, so that they may carry away this "benefit" from you besides? Or will you not do that, but if they are left here, will they be better nourished and educated by your kin while you are alive but absent? But if you go away to Thessaly, will your kin care for them; yet if you pass into the other life, will they not care for them? Surely, if there is any help in those who say they are your kin, it must be believed they will care for them. Therefore, O Socrates, putting your trust in us who are your nurturers <note>The "Laws" are speaking here, personified as Socrates' parents/nurturers</note>, do not value your children, or your life, or anything else more than justice; so that when you have migrated into the other life, you may be able to give an account of all these things to the rulers there. Certainly, if you do these things having transgressed the laws, it will happen neither better, nor more justly, nor more holily for you or for yours; nor will it profit you there. Rather, depart now as one who has suffered injury, if you depart, not indeed from us the Laws, but from men. But if you flee so basely, returning injuries and evils in turn, transgressing the agreements and promises made with us, and harming those whom you least ought to—namely yourself, your friends, your fatherland, and us—we shall certainly be angry with you while you live here; and in the other life, the laws which are our sisters there will by no means receive you kindly, knowing that you attempted to destroy us to the best of your power. Therefore, beware lest Crito persuade you otherwise than we do. These things indeed, O sweet friend Crito, I seem to hear, just as the Corybantes <note>Priests of Cybele who experienced ecstatic trances accompanied by the sound of flutes</note> think they hear the flutes. And the sound of such words echoes so loudly within me that I am unable to hear anything else. You see how things appear to me at present; if you attempt to contradict them, you will labor in vain. Nevertheless, if you are confident you will achieve anything, speak. CRITO: Indeed, O Socrates, I have nothing to say. SOCRATES: Let it be then, Crito; and let us proceed this way, since God himself leads us this way.

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino on the Phaedo.

<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator of Plato into Latin during the Renaissance. His "Arguments" are interpretive introductions.</note>

Our book *On Religion* proves a matter sufficiently known in itself: that the life of Christ is the idea <note>The perfect archetype or pattern</note> of all virtue. Moreover, the eighth book of our *Epistles* demonstrates that the life of Socrates is a certain image, or at least a shadow, of the Christian life; and indeed it confirms the Old Testament through Plato, and the New through Socrates. But as for what pertains to this Socratic similarity, if anyone doubts it, let him read Xenophon and Plato, and the others who wrote down the words and deeds of Socrates: especially Plato’s *Gorgias*, *Apology*, *Crito*, and *Phaedo*. We shall therefore run through the argument of this *Phaedo* with a steady, or rather a swift leap. For we seem to have sufficiently explained its mysteries in our *Theology*. This one thing we shall advise first: let no one wonder that Socrates, among the arguments pertaining to the immortality of the soul, omitted here that one in which he trusts alone in the *Phaedrus*: namely, that the soul is the principle of motion; from which it follows that it is moved by itself and perpetually, and lives forever. For this was done by Socrates because that kind of reasoning is common not only to our souls, but also to celestial and demonic <note>In the Platonic sense: "daimonic" or intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil</note> souls. In the *Phaedo*, however, reasons more proper to us are required. But let us now come to the briefest arrangement of the dialogue. First, it must be observed how wonderfully Socrates consoles his friends, who greeted him on that day especially when he was about to drink the poison in prison, as if they were the ones to console him. Second, how religiously he observes even the precepts of dreams as if they were certain oracles; and how he is especially cautious in this, lest he fail in the slightest way regarding divine mandates. Third, it must be committed to memory: that men are under the constant custody of God, and it is not permitted to depart from here unless when God wills it. Fourth, it must be carefully noted what he means when he says he hopes indeed in death to go to good men, and to other good gods,

<meta>This page continues the introductory argument (argumentum) for Plato's Phaedo, likely translated or commented upon by Marsilio Ficino. It focuses on the soul's journey toward the divine and the philosophical preparation for death.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE PHAEDO

But he asserts more strongly that one goes to good gods than to good men. First, indeed, when he speaks of "other and very good gods," he understands that besides the souls of the spheres <note>The celestial bodies in ancient cosmology</note> there are angelic minds higher than the spheres. He hopes that our souls may also one day be admitted into their intimacy. However, he does not dare to assert this absolutely, because it seemed sufficient to most wise men for the soul's destiny if it were eventually received into the company of the celestial souls. Indeed, his doubt specifically falls upon that part which calls them "good men." For he does not then dare to assert that the souls of men are good in the same sense in which he had called the gods good. After this, intending to console both himself and his friends under the persona of one practicing philosophy, he says: Since the whole study of a philosopher is a certain separation from the body, and is perfected daily through it, he certainly ought not only not to fear the separation from the body which occurs through death, but should expect it with the best hope and joy. 

Soon he shows that the philosopher separates the soul from the body in two ways. First, indeed, from disturbances through the <term>purgation</term> <note>A cleansing or purification process</note> of moral discipline; then from the senses and from imagination itself through the intensity of contemplation itself. Wise physicians use a twofold purgation: the first by soothing, the second by dissolving; knowing that it is neither enough to soothe, nor safe to dissolve before you soothe. Similarly among philosophers, moral purgation precedes as if soothing; for it does not root out the internal diseases of the imagination, that is, its deceptions. There follows the speculative purgation, which at times disperses the clouds of the imagination according to its strength. But it is not safe to approach the duty of speculation before moral purgation, lest someone infected with the diseases of vice should abuse the very sharpness of speculation to defend injustice and impiety. From these things he concludes that the philosopher, to the extent that he segregates the edge of the mind from corporeal things, to that extent joins it to incorporeal reasons and <term>Ideas</term> <note>Plato's eternal, perfect forms</note>. 

But when he had numbered many inconveniences brought upon the soul by the body, he added that the last and greatest of evils is that fallacy by which the imagination, while the mind is raising itself to incorporeal things, meanwhile very often distracts it toward certain images of bodies, and forces it to think in a certain corporeal manner. After this, and from the fact that the soul cannot attain the truth of separate things—which it naturally desires—while joined to the body, he infers by disjunction that it either never attains it, or attains it after death. But it is not consistent to say it is never attained, since it is perpetually desired by every mind. 

Furthermore, he disapproves of those who think that temperance is abstaining from smaller bodily pleasures so that they may later obtain greater bodily pleasures. Again, those who define fortitude as overcoming certain fears for the sake of those fears which have already overcome us. For he wants every duty of moral virtue to be occupied in a certain purgation of the soul for the sake of wisdom. Otherwise, there is no virtue. Indeed, he even calls human wisdom a certain purification; just as if he thinks we attain nothing else by the meditation of our wisdom than a certain purity, which divine illumination soon follows, which properly becomes wisdom. He signifies, moreover, that it is not so much a habit acquired by our labors, but the purification itself that joins us to God. 

These things being done, intending to prove the immortality of the soul, he says: a progression occurs from one kind of opposites into the other, and likewise a regression. Therefore, just as the dead are made from the living, so the living sometimes rise again from the dead. Here he seems to prophesy the <term>resurrection</term> of the dead, which he also confirms in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note>. Furthermore, he hints through long circuitous paths: just as the substance of heaven and the matter of the elements pass infinitely from one disposition to another in turn, so also the rational soul, which is the principle of motion, life, and generation, can be infinitely joined to the body and separated in turn. For indeed, many substances in nature change qualities in a long-lasting alternation, and everywhere an eternal circuit occurs by the power of the soul. In the following parts, finally, with a certain great confidence, he asserts the resurrection which he had hinted at. 

He then approaches the argument concerning <term>reminiscence</term> <note>The Platonic theory that learning is actually remembering innate knowledge</note>, proving the same thing as a little before: that the soul lives both before the body and after the body. But you should understand that such arguments are <term>Pythagorean</term> <note>Referring to the school of Pythagoras, known for belief in reincarnation</note>. And from them, choose what leads more toward the truth. He says, therefore: if learning is reminiscence, souls lived before the body. He proves that it is reminiscence chiefly in two ways. First, because to one questioning correctly, we often answer the truth about those things which we never learned. Secondly, because from the knowledge of those things which are sensed, we ascend by a certain sudden abstraction into the knowledge of the Ideas; as by knowing these "equal things," we ascend to the knowledge of Equality itself. There we recognize that these things fall short of those, and strive to become similar; again, how much they approach them, and which more or which less. And since we do this through our whole life, it is necessary that we had the Idea itself before birth. For we did not suddenly receive the perfect knowledge of a thing from imperfect things. 

He shows, moreover, that Ideas exist in two ways. First: any subject which is called "equal" can, while remaining the same in substance, both become and seem unequal. But Equality can never either become or seem inequality. Furthermore, these equal things, being imperfect, participate in inequality; but Equality itself does not. In the following parts, note with what great assurance he affirms the Ideas; and adds that the essence of the Ideas is our own. And since our soul refers individual things to the Ideas, it shows itself to be eternal along with the essence of the Ideas, and recognizes that essence as its own. Note, moreover, that one must labor in nothing more than that we may expel the fear of death, like a most grave disease, through the demonstration of immortality. Immediately he approaches another argument drawn from the proportion of the intellect to the intelligible. He calls the "intelligible" itself the incorporeal and eternal Idea itself. And since the intellect with it as its object...

<meta>This page continues the introductory argument for Plato's dialogue, the Phaedo, focusing on the metaphysical causes of the world and the nature of the soul.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE PHAEDO.

He says that the power of the good is the efficient cause. Since, however, he cannot grasp the full magnitude of the good itself, he chooses in the second place the ideal principles of divine intelligence, according to whose likeness all things are expressed in the matter of the world. Among these things, note the confirmation of the Mosaic mystery <note>original: "Moſaici myſterii"</note>, just as in the *Timaeus*. God saw that individual things were good; even that the whole was very good. Likewise, that all things are connected by the good itself. Again, that the soul, while gazing upon bodily things, is meanwhile blinded to the intuition of the incorporeal. Nor can the truth of things be possessed unless we flee to the Ideas <note>The "Ideas" or "Forms" are Plato's perfect, eternal archetypes of reality.</note>. Furthermore, the formulas of the Ideas are present in our minds; according to their agreement or disagreement, individual things are judged to be true or otherwise. Socrates was never accustomed to cease the certain contemplation of the Ideas, and used to affirm them alone. The certain cause of things is situated in the Ideas; the immortality of the soul is also most powerfully demonstrated from the Ideas. The process among the Ideas occurs from the less common through the intermediate to the most common. And there is a descent from the Ideas to their effects. Finally, he arranges the reason for immortality from the fact that the rational soul provides life to the body, not as an accidental form inherent in the body, but as a substantial form remaining in itself, living formally from itself as if it were a certain Idea of bodily life, and effectively vivifying the body through itself. Therefore, he concludes that the soul cannot receive death, since death is the opposite of life; the soul truly has its own life and remains in itself, so that it can receive death neither through itself properly, nor through another subject. After these things, because the soul is immortal, he exhorts everyone to moral and speculative discipline: so that the soul, purified and perfected through both the will and the intellect, may fly back to the heavenly fatherland on these two wings, as it were. Meanwhile, he confirms that the soul is immortal because neither should virtue ultimately be a hindrance, nor vice a benefit. The laborious path of virtue would hinder the good, and conversely, a voluptuous life would benefit the wicked, unless the soul were immortal. And lest anyone perhaps deny that after this life either vice can hinder or virtue benefit, he adds that the soul carries with it the affections and habits acquired of both the will and the intelligence, whether good or evil, which will suddenly either harm or benefit. For a guiding spirit <note>original: "Dæmonẽ," referring to a personal guardian spirit or 'daimon'</note> leads everyone suddenly to the judge of divine life into a place designated for common judgment: namely, into the air for those who are less pure, and into the ether for those who are purer; and there, having been judged, they are drawn individually by another spirit through a triple-way <note>original: "triuium," a place where three roads meet</note> to their own places—that is, to things similar to themselves. Through a triple-way, I say, because some are sent into heaven, others into Tartarus, and others into the middle regions. The spirit leads them, however: in the good, moving the intelligence; in the evil, disturbing the imagination and affection. But when he says the wicked wander without a guide, understand this as being without a *beneficent* guide. Add that they do not recognize where they are being drawn, and are snatched away by violence. Furthermore, before he distributes the lots of the souls, he describes the orb of the earth, saying there are certain regions of the earth, and those indeed most vast and so high that they are not struck by winds and rains. Where there is a most temperate air, under which all the most precious things are born: men most acute in their senses and long-lived in life. There are those who wish both the men and other things born there to be composed mostly of ether and air, and very little from the thicker elements, so that the bodies of men are as if aerial, and they are nourished by mostly aerial fruits. Lest anyone deny this as impossible, <margin>Olympiodorus on Aristotle's *On the Soul*.</margin> Olympiodorus brings forward a story of Aristotle, in which Aristotle says he saw a man who was nourished by air and sun alone. As for his dividing the face of the sublime earth into twelve regions, it arises from this: because twelve corresponds to the signs of the zodiac; it is ruled by the souls of the twelve spheres; and the twelfth is the sphere of the world; and just as the foundation of the whole, it assumes for itself that dodecahedron shape which the *Timaeus* attributes to the world. But concerning this very shape, and other questions proper to the earth, we shall speak in the *Timaeus*. You, however, remember that a habitation of the earth of this kind is similar to the terrestrial Paradise of Moses. Hence he describes rivers under the earth, by which souls are nourished. Whoever explains these according to the humors of our body and the perturbations of the soul afflicting us in this life, brings forward something not unlike the truth; nevertheless, he does not attain the whole truth. For Plato here, and in the *Republic*, signifies that the rewards of virtues and the punishments of vices pertain most especially to the other life. Acheron, therefore, a river under the earth, is a purgatorial place, and pertains to care and sorrow. It also responds to the air and the southern part of the world. Phlegethon responds to fire and the east, and contains the power of punishing through heat; it punishes the fervor of anger and desire. Styx and Cocytus respond to the earth and the west; they punish hatred through mourning and weeping. They differ between themselves only in this: that the rising one is called Styx, but the progressing one Cocytus. He wishes Tartarus to hold the lowest place of the underworld, in which the most wicked are afflicted, not for the sake of medicine but for the sake of example, just as is read here, and in the *Republic*, and the *Gorgias*. Some add to these rivers that the Ocean also pertains in some way, responding to water and the north, in which the virtue of distinguishing and defining may be understood. You, however, regarding what is said of the rivers, understand it most especially of the spirits and deities punishing the shameful in such an order. Indeed, sins are easily curable which have not yet been turned into a habit. But those which have already generated a habit are cured with difficulty. Nevertheless, they are committed together with a certain repugnance of reason, and affect those committing them with repentance. But those are altogether incurable whose habit puts both repugnance and repentance to flight. The first are purged in Acheron. The second, if they incline toward the first, are punished in Phlegethon; if toward the third, in Styx and Cocytus. The third are afflicted in Tartarus, from which, as Plato says, they never exit. In what way others explain it differently, I more willingly pass over for the present. For souls can be afflicted...

XXIX.

# BOOK

...that I am not merely unhappily disturbed by demons through the imagination, but through certain aerial bodies, which they designate by the names "vehicle" and "skiff." <note>Neoplatonic terms for the "astral body" or soul-carrier.</note> Plato distinguishes the rewards in this way: Souls that have lived justly and holily without philosophy ascend to the heights of the earth, such as we described above, and dwell there in very thin and spiritual bodies. Those, however, who practiced philosophy for the sake of social virtue dwell in heaven with splendid and celestial bodies. But those who have been perfectly purified through exacting philosophy fly away to a place above the heavens, where they live for all time entirely without bodies, as Plato says here. By what reasoning some explain this, I will deliberately not recount. Certainly, Porphyry and Iamblichus <note>Famous Neoplatonist philosophers who commented on Plato.</note> teach that souls perfectly restored to God never fall back. This indeed corresponds appropriately to the opposites: those who are judged never to emerge from Tartarus <note>The deep abyss of torment in Greek mythology.</note>. If this is so, the infinite cycles of rebirth would be abolished; temporal cycles would instead seem to be employed for the sake of a certain purification. Finally, Socrates confesses that he owes a cock to Aesculapius <note>The god of healing; Socrates' famous last words suggest that death is the "cure" for the sickness of life.</note> and orders it to be paid most diligently. The ancients used to sacrifice a cock—the messenger of day and the sun—to Aesculapius the physician, son of Phoebus [Apollo], that is, to the divine beneficence that cures all diseases, which is called the daughter of divine providence. He confessed that he owed the "day," that is, the light of life, to him. He had ordered them earlier to seek such a physician as a healer of the diseases of the soul. And as if they have now been freed from every disease of doubt and fear, he orders thanks and a victim to be returned to the god. Furthermore, the oracles of the ancients teach that souls returning to heaven sing a *paean* <note>original: "pęana" — a song of triumph or thanksgiving</note>, that is, a triumphal song, to Phoebus. He therefore returns his vow to God, so that he may return to his celestial fatherland briskly singing the Paean.

### PHAEDO, OR ON THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL, OR ON THE SOUL, TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI, A MAGNANIMOUS MAN.

-> CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE. <-
-> ECHECRATES. PHAEDO. APOLLODORUS. SOCRATES. CEBES. <-
-> SIMMIAS. CRITO. THE SERVANT OF THE ELEVEN COMMISSIONERS. <-

WERE YOU YOURSELF present, O Phaedo, on that day when Socrates drank the poison in prison? Or did you hear of it from another? PHAEDO. Indeed, O Echecrates, I was present. ECHE. What then are the things that man spoke before he died? And how did he depart from life? For I would gladly hear. For neither does any of the citizens of Phlius <note>A city in the Peloponnese.</note> travel frequently to Athens now, nor has any guest come to us from there for a long time who could report anything certain to us regarding that matter, except that he departed from life by drinking poison. Regarding the rest, they had nothing to report. PHAE. Did you not then hear how the matters pertaining to the trial were handled? ECHE. We heard those things, for someone reported them to us. And we were indeed surprised that, the trial having already been finished, he seems to have died a long time afterward. What was the cause of this, O Phaedo? PHAE. That happened to Socrates by a certain stroke of luck, O Echecrates. For on the day before he was judged, it happened that the stern of the ship was decorated—the one which the Athenians send to Delos. ECHE. What does that mean? PHAE. This is that ship, as the Athenians say, in which Theseus once carried those "twice-seven" <note>The fourteen youths sent as tribute to the Minotaur.</note> with him to Crete; he saved them, and he himself was saved. He had vowed, as it is told, to Apollo that if he were saved, he would send a certain spectacle to Delos every year. Which indeed they still send to the god every year from that time. Therefore, when the beginning of the spectacle is underway, they meanwhile purify the city by law; and they execute no one publicly during that time, until the ship reaches Delos and returns again to Athens from Delos. This is sometimes carried out over a long time when the winds hold them back. The beginning of the spectacle is after the priest of Apollo has crowned the stern of that ship. This, as I was just saying, had been done the day before he was judged. For which reason Socrates was in prison for a long time between the judgment and his death. ECHE. But concerning the death itself, O Phaedo, what was said by him, what was done, and which of his friends were present? Or did the magistrates perhaps not permit them to be present, and so he died deprived of friends? PHAE. They did permit it. And therefore some were present, and indeed many. ECHE. Prepare yourself then to report all these things to us as clearly as possible, unless some business hinders you. PHAE. I am indeed at leisure, and I will try to narrate it to you. For to remember Socrates, whether I speak myself or hear others speaking, is always the sweetest of all things to me. ECHE. Likewise, O Phaedo, you will find those who are about to hear you to be so affected. But now, according to your strength, report everything most diligently. PHAE. And yet, O Echecrates, I was affected in a certain wonderful way while present there. For pity did not possess me as one present at the death of a most intimate man. Surely that man seemed happy to me, O Echecrates, considering both the habit of his mind and his speech: so intrepidly and nobly did he depart from life, that he seemed to me to be migrating into the other life not without a divine fate, but that he would be happy there too, if anyone ever was. For which reason I was not moved much, as it would seem consistent for a man present at such a thing to be moved by mourning; nor again was I affected by joy, as I usually was at other times when we were engaged in philosophy. For the discourses were indeed of that kind, but in truth a certain strange affection and an unusual mixture of pleasure and pain had invaded me, considering that he would have to die a little later. And all of us who were present were affected almost similarly: at times laughing, at other times weeping. One, however, above the rest, was Apollodorus—for you know the man and his manner. ECHE.

# PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL.

Why not? PHAEDO. He was indeed affected in such a way, and I myself and all the others present were similarly distracted and held a troubled spirit. ECHECRATES. But who by chance was there, O Phaedo? PHAEDO. Of the citizens and locals, there were present Apollodorus, and Critobulus with his father Crito, then Hermogenes, Epigenes, Aeschines, and Antisthenes. Ctesippus of Paeania was also there, and Menexenus, and certain other locals. Plato, however, I believe was ill. ECHECRATES. But were any strangers <note>foreigners or non-Athenians</note> present? PHAEDO. Strangers were also present: Simmias the Theban, and Cebes, and Phaedondes; and from Megara, Euclides and Terpsion. ECHECRATES. Were Aristippus <margin>Euclides of Megara in the time of Socrates.</margin> and Cleombrotus present? PHAEDO. No. For they were said to be in Aegina. ECHECRATES. Were any others there besides? PHAEDO. I believe these are almost all who were present. ECHECRATES. Tell me then, what was the nature of the discourse? PHAEDO. I will endeavor to relate everything to you from the beginning. In the preceding days, I and the others were accustomed to go to Socrates, meeting in the morning at that court where the trial had been held. For it was very near the prison. While talking among ourselves, we always waited there until the prison was opened; for it was not opened very early. Once opened, we went in to Socrates and spent most of the day conversing with him. On that day, therefore, we met earlier than usual. For on the evening of the day before, when we had left the prison, we heard that the ship from Delos had returned. Therefore, we told one another to return to the accustomed place as early as possible in the morning. When we had returned, the porter who usually admitted us came out to meet us and told us to wait, and not to enter until he himself called us. "For," he said, "the Eleven <note>The Athenian officials in charge of executions</note> are releasing Socrates from his bonds, and they are announcing to him that he must meet his death today." Not long after, he returned to us and told us to enter. So, entering, we found Socrates just recently released from his shackles, and Xanthippe—you know <margin>Xanthippe</margin> the woman—sitting near him, holding his child in her arms. When she saw us, she began to wail and cry out as women are accustomed to do. "O Socrates," she said, "never again will your friends speak to you, nor you to them." But Socrates, looking at Crito, said, "O Crito, let someone take her home." And some of Crito's servants led her away as she was shouting and lamenting. Socrates, sitting up on the bed, drew up his leg and rubbed it with his hand; and while rubbing it, he said: "How strange a thing it seems, O men, this thing which humans call pleasure; and how wonderfully it is related by nature to pain itself, which seems to be its opposite. For they are unwilling to be present in a person at the same time. Yet if someone pursues and catches one, he is almost always compelled to receive the other as well, as if both were joined from a single head. I think indeed that if Aesop had noticed this, he would have made a fable of it: <margin>Aesop</margin> namely, that God himself, wishing to reconcile these things that fight against each other but being unable to do so, joined their tips into one; and for that reason, to whomever one is present, the other soon follows. This is exactly what has happened to me now. Since just now my leg was suffering pain because of the chains, pleasure now seems to follow in its place." To this Cebes said, "By Jove, O Socrates, you have opportunely brought this to my memory. For since you have composed poems by setting the stories of Aesop to verse and a hymn to Apollo, <margin>Aesop</margin> many others have asked me, and especially Evenus recently: by what intention, after you came here, did you do these things which you had never done before? If therefore you care for me to have an answer for Evenus when he asks me again—which I know for certain he will do—tell me, I pray, what should be answered." "Tell him the truth, O Cebes," he said: "that I did this not because I wished to rival him or his poems—for I knew that would not be easy—but to test certain dreams and to purify myself, in case this might be the 'music' <note>The Greek 'mousike' refers to all arts presided over by the Muses, including philosophy</note> which they have often commanded me to practice. For frequently in times past, the same dream appeared to me in various forms, always giving the same command: 'O Socrates, make music and practice it.' I therefore thought that what I was doing in the past was what was being commanded, and just as people encourage those who are running, so I thought the dream was encouraging me in what I was already doing, as if philosophy were the highest music. But after the judgment was made against me and the festival of the god <note>The festival of Apollo</note> delayed my death, I thought it necessary, if by chance the dream so many times commanded this popular music, not to neglect its precept. For I thought it would be safer, before I departed from life, to purify my soul and, as the dream warned, to make poems. Therefore, first I sang of the god himself, whose sacred rites were then being celebrated; and after the god, judging that he who would be a poet must make not mere discourses but fables—and I myself am not a maker of fables—I took some of the fables of Aesop which I knew and had at hand, and set to verse those I first happened upon. Tell these things, O Cebes, to Evenus, and bid him farewell. And advise him that if he is truly wise, he should follow me; for I depart from here today. For so the Athenians command." Then Simmias said: "What is this you say, O Socrates, that you command to Evenus? I have often been with him, and from what I perceive of him, he will by no means be willing to obey you." SOCRATES. "Why so? Is Evenus not a philosopher?" SIMMIAS. "So it seems to me." SOCRATES. "Then Evenus will be willing, as will everyone who is a worthy participant in this matter. Yet perhaps he will not lay violent hands upon himself. For they say it is not lawful." And saying this, he put his legs down from the bed to the ground. And so sitting, he discussed the rest. Cebes then asked him: "In what way do you say this, O Socrates: that it is not lawful to violate oneself, yet a philosopher should wish to follow one who is dying?" SOCRATES. "But tell me, O Cebes, have you and Simmias not heard such things from Philolaus, with whom you were intimate?" CEBES. "Nothing clearly, O Socrates." SOCRATES. "And yet I also speak of these things from hearsay. What I have happened to hear, no ill-will shall prevent me from relating to you. For perhaps it is most fitting for one about to depart there to consider and..."

...to imagine what kind of thing this very migration <note>The passage of the soul from the body</note> must be thought to be. For what else should one do until the setting of the sun? **CEBES:** For what reason, Socrates, do you say it is a sin to lay hands upon oneself? For I have already heard from Philolaus <note>A Pythagorean philosopher</note> when he was staying with us, and from several others besides, that it is not proper to do this; yet I have never heard anything clear on the matter from anyone. **SOCRATES:** But now there is need of attention. For if you listen, it might perhaps seem a wonder if this alone of all things were simple, and if it never happened to a man—as it does in all other cases—that for some it is better to die than to live. And so it will perhaps seem a wonder to you if those for whom it is better to die are not permitted to benefit themselves, but must wait for another to be their benefactor. Then Cebes, smiling in the Theban manner, said: "By Jupiter!" **SOCRATES:** And yet it might indeed seem absurd in this way. Perhaps, however, it has a certain reason. Indeed, that saying which is held concerning these things in the secret rites <note>original: "in arcanis"; likely referring to Orphic or Pythagorean mysteries</note>—that men are in a kind of custody, and that it is not proper for anyone to release himself from this nor to run away—seems to me a great saying, and not easy to understand. Nevertheless, Cebes, this appears to me to be rightly said: that the gods are those who have care for us, and that we men are one of the possessions of the gods. Or does it not seem so to you? **CEBES:** It does to me. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if one of your slaves were to kill himself when you had in no way permitted it, would you not be angry with him? And if you had the power, would you not inflict some punishment? **CEBES:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Perhaps, then, by this reasoning, it is not without reason that it is not proper to kill oneself until the god has imposed some necessity, such as he has imposed on us at present. **CEBES:** That indeed appears likely. But as for what you were saying just now—that philosophers are very willing to die—that seems absurd, Socrates, if indeed what we just said has reason: namely, that God is our caretaker and that we are placed among his things. For it has no reason that the wisest men should not be distressed to be removed from that care which the gods, the best governors of all things, provide for them. For a wise man would never think that he will care for himself better if he escapes to freedom; perhaps some foolish person might think so—that one must flee from a master—and would not consider that one must not flee from what is good, but rather remain in it as much as possible. Therefore, he would flee without reason. But he who has a mind always desires to be with him who is better. And so, Socrates, the opposite of what was said a little while ago seems to be fitting: that the wise should be distressed by death, but the foolish should rejoice.

Socrates, having heard this, seemed to be delighted by the cleverness of Cebes. Turning to us, he said: "This Cebes is always searching out certain reasons, and he is not at all willing to admit easily what anyone says." Then Simmias said: "To me also, Cebes seems to be saying something. For with what purpose would truly wise men flee those who are better than themselves, and easily endure being without them? And Cebes seems to direct his speech at you, because you leave us so easily, as well as the gods, who are—as you yourself admit—good rulers." "You speak justly," said Socrates, "for I think you are saying that I ought to clear myself as if in a court of justice." **SIMMIAS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Come then, I will now try to defend myself before you more accurately than I did recently before the Athenian judges. Indeed, Simmias and Cebes, if I did not think I was migrating, first to other gods who are wise and good, and then to deceased men better than those who are here, I would be acting unjustly in not being distressed by death. But now, be assured, I hope that I am going to good men; though I would not altogether assert this. But that I am going to gods who are very good masters, be assured that if I would affirm anything else of this kind, I would certainly affirm this. For that reason, I am not similarly distressed by death. But I am of good courage, hoping that something remains for those who have died, and as has been said for a long time, that it will be much better for the good than for the evil. **SIMMIAS:** What are you thinking, Socrates? Do you intend to depart from here with that opinion alone? Or will you leave us as sharers in it? For I think this good ought to be common to us as well. Besides, you will have cleared yourself before us only if you persuade us of what you say. **SOCRATES:** I will indeed do my best. But let us first listen to Crito. For he has seemed to me for some time to want to signify something. **CRITO:** What else do you think, Socrates, than what he who is to give you the poison has been telling me for a long time? For he bids you be warned to speak as little as possible, saying that those who dispute grow too warm, and nothing of that sort is suitable for those about to drink the poison. Otherwise, those who have done so are sometimes forced to drink the poison twice or even three times. **SOCRATES:** Let him be. Let him only prepare his duty, as if he were to provide it twice, or if necessary, three times. **CRITO:** I almost knew you would answer that, but he has been urging me for a long time. **SOCRATES:** Let him be. But to you, my judges, I now wish to render the reason why it seems to me that a man who has applied himself to philosophy throughout his whole life rightly expects approaching death with great confidence, and is in good hope that he will obtain the greatest goods there after he has migrated from here. How this is so, Simmias and Cebes, I will indeed try to reveal. Whoever has rightly touched upon philosophy seems to have remained hidden <note>original: "latuisse"</note> from other men in this: that they themselves meditate on nothing else than dying and being dead. If that is true, it would be utterly absurd if, when they have studied nothing but this through their whole life, they should be distressed when this very thing arrives which they have long been considering and practicing. At this, Simmias smiled and said: "By Jove, Socrates, you have drawn a laugh from me, though I was not at all desiring to laugh. For I think there will be many who, if they heard this, would think it most aptly said against philosophers; and our people <note>The people of Thebes</note> would agree, and very much so, that philosophers truly offer themselves to death—nor has it escaped them how much they deserve death." **SOCRATES:** Perhaps they would say so rightly, Simmias, except for the part about it not escaping them. For it has indeed escaped them...

# PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL.

<margin>
What death is:
</margin>
...by what reasoning true philosophers both strive to die and are worthy of death. But let us leave them for now and speak among ourselves. Do we think that death is something? SIMMIAS. Certainly something. SOCRATES. Is it anything other than the release of the soul from the body? And is this what it means to be dead: that the body, released from the soul, exists by itself apart? And that the soul, released from the body, exists by itself? Is death anything besides this? SIM. Nothing else. SOC. Consider, good man, if you and I see this the same way. For from these points, I think we shall more clearly find what we seek. Does it seem to you to be the duty of a philosopher to pursue those things called pleasures, such as those of feasting and drinking? SIM. Not at all, O Socrates. SOC. What about the pleasures of love <note>original: "venereorum," referring to sexual pleasures</note>? SIM. In no way. SOC. What about the rest of the care of the body? Does it seem to you that a philosopher sets great value on it? For instance, having fine clothes and shoes, and other ornaments concerning the body—does he value them, or does he think nothing of them, except insofar as great necessity forces him to use them? SIM. It seems to me that the true philosopher cares not a straw for these things. 

<margin>
Pleasures are [to be disregarded].
</margin>

<margin>
The study of the philosopher does not incline toward the body.
</margin>
SOC. Does it not seem to you that such a man’s study is directed not toward the body, but as much as possible departs from it and turns toward the soul? SIM. It does. SOC. Is it not then manifest in such things that the philosopher, more than other men, separates the soul as much as possible from its commerce with the body? SIM. It is manifest. SOC. Indeed, Simmias, most people think that a man for whom none of these things are sweet, and who does not enjoy them, is not worthy of living, but is almost dead—he who perceives no pleasures of the body. SIM. You speak the very truth. 

<margin>
The body is an impediment to the philosopher. Because the senses do not grasp anything purely.
</margin>
SOC. But what about the acquisition of wisdom itself? Is the body an impediment if one takes it along as a partner in the investigation, or not? I mean something like this: Do sight and hearing possess any truth for men? Or is it as the poets are always singing to us, that we hear nothing and see nothing accurately? And yet, if these bodily senses are not accurate and certain, neither are the others, since all the rest are somehow inferior to these. Do they not seem so to you? SIM. Entirely. SOC. When, then, does the soul touch the truth? For when it attempts to investigate anything with the body, it is clearly deceived by the body. SIM. You speak truly. SOC. Is it not in reasoning, if anywhere, that some of the things that truly exist become manifest to it? SIM. It is so. SOC. And it reasons best when none of these things disturb it—neither hearing, nor sight, nor pain, nor pleasure—but when, gathering itself as much as possible into itself, it leaves the body behind. Communicating with the body as little as possible and not touching it, the soul reaches out for that which truly is. SIM. That is so. SOC. In this, too, does not the soul of the philosopher most despise the body and flee from it, seeking to live according to itself? SIM. It appears so. 

SOC. What about these things, Simmias? Do we say that Justice itself is something, or nothing? SIM. Something, by Jove! SOC. And again, that Beauty itself and Goodness itself are something? SIM. How could they not be? SOC. Have you ever perceived any of these with your eyes? SIM. Never. SOC. Or have you touched them with any other sense of the body? I am speaking of all things: such as Magnitude itself, Health, Strength, and in short, the essence <term>essentia: the fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing</term> of all other things—that which each thing is. Is the truth of them perceived through the body? Or is it rather that whoever among us prepares himself to think most deeply and purely about the thing he intends to consider, he comes closest to the knowledge of it? SIM. Entirely. SOC. Would he not do this most purely who, with the thinking of the mind alone, approaches each thing as much as possible, neither employing sight in his thinking nor joining any other sense to his reasoning? Instead, using the pure thinking of the mind by itself, he would strive to hunt down each of the things that exist, free from eyes, ears, and—to put it briefly—from the whole body, as something that disturbs the soul and does not permit it to attain truth and wisdom whenever it is joined with it? Is it not this man, Simmias, if anyone, who will reach that which truly is? SIM. You speak wonderfully true words, Socrates. 

<margin>
The speech of one eager to learn, and of the philosopher inquiring about the body. The body <unclear>disturbs</unclear>.
</margin>
SOC. Does it not necessarily follow from all this that a certain opinion must remain with legitimate philosophers, so that they say such things to one another? "A certain path of reason leads us to this consideration: namely, that as long as we have the body and our soul is mixed with such an evil, we shall never attain what we desire—which is the truth. For the body provides almost innumerable impediments because of the necessity of its nourishment; furthermore, diseases falling upon us from this source hinder our investigation of truth. It fills us with loves, desires, fears, and many kinds of phantoms and much nonsense, so that it is truly said that it never brings us anything of the truth. For nothing else but the body and its desires incite wars, seditions, and battles. 

<margin>
<unclear>All things for the sake of money</unclear>
</margin>
All these things happen for the sake of money. And we are forced to seek money for the sake of the body, serving its needs; thus it happens that because of all these things, we are drawn away from the study of philosophy. The final blow of all is that if we do get some leisure from it and turn ourselves to considering something, it breaks in everywhere during our investigations, causing a tumult and disturbing the soul, striking us so that we are stunned and unable, because of this obstacle, to perceive the truth. But it has been truly demonstrated to us that if we ever wish to understand anything purely, we must depart from the body and consider the things themselves with the soul itself. And then, as it appears, we shall obtain that which we desire and of which we profess to be lovers—namely, wisdom—when we are dead, as the argument indicates, but by no means while we live. For if nothing can be purely discerned with the body, one of two things follows: either we can in no way attain knowledge, or we can do so after death. For then the soul will be by itself, apart from the body, but before then, not at all. And while we live, we shall, it seems, come closest to knowledge if we have as little commerce as possible with the body and do not communicate with it, except as far as the highest necessity requires; nor [shall we allow ourselves to be filled with] its [nature]...

<summary>Socrates argues that the body is a constant distraction and impediment to the soul's pursuit of truth and wisdom. He concludes that pure knowledge is only attainable after death, when the soul is finally liberated from physical needs and sensory deception.</summary>

# BOOK
<meta>Catchword: satione (conversation)</meta>

nature we shall be filled: but we shall guard ourselves against its contagion, until God himself sets us free. And being thus pure, and liberated from the insanity of the body, as is fitting, we shall be with those like ourselves; and we shall know through our own selves whatever is pure, which is perhaps the truth itself; for it is not permitted for the impure to touch the pure. Such things, O Simmias, I judge it necessary for all lovers of learning to say to one another and to believe. Does it not seem so to you? SIM. Most certainly of all, O Socrates. SO. If these things are true, then, O friend, there is great hope that he who travels to where I am now going, if anywhere, will there sufficiently become master of that thing for the sake of which we have undertaken so much labor in our former life. This migration, therefore, now enjoined upon me, I undertake with good hope; and likewise anyone else who believes his mind has been prepared as if purified. SIM. Quite so. SO. And does not purification consist in this, which we were saying just now: namely, that as much as we are able, we should separate the soul from the body? It can be released from the body as if from chains, both in the present time and in the future. SIM. Most certainly. SO. Is not this then called death—the release and separation of the soul from the body? <margin>What death is:</margin> SIM. Exactly. SO. And to release it, as we confess, is at all times the chief and sole study of those who philosophize rightly. And this very meditation of philosophers is to release and separate the soul from the body, is it not? SIM. So it seems. SO. Therefore, as I was saying at the beginning, it would be ridiculous if a man who has so prepared himself in life that he lived as close to death as possible, should then be troubled when death arrives. Would it not be ridiculous? SIM. How could it not be? SO. In truth, therefore, those who philosophize rightly practice dying; and they are the least of all men terrified by it. Consider it this way: since the body is everywhere despised, and they desire to have the soul itself by itself, would it not be the height of absurdity if they were to fear and be distressed when this happens, and not go gladly to that place where, upon arriving, there is hope of obtaining what they loved in life? And they loved wisdom <note>original: "sapientiam"</note>; and they hoped to be liberated from that whose company they found troublesome. Or indeed, have many of their own will desired to go to the underworld when their lovers, wives, and sons have died, hoping to see them there and be with those they loved? And shall a true lover of wisdom, who has been led strongly into this very hope—that he will not worthily obtain it anywhere else except by dying—be distressed at approaching death, and not go there gladly? One must believe, O friend, if he is truly a philosopher, that this opinion prevails greatly with him: that he can attain pure wisdom nowhere else but in the life after death. If this is so, would it not be, as I just said, entirely beyond reason if such a man feared death? SIM. By Jove, it would be against reason. SO. It will be a sufficient proof, then: if you see anyone distressed by death, he is not a philosopher, but a "body-lover" <note>original: "philosomanus"</note>; and the same is likely a "money-lover" <note>original: "phylosimatū"</note> and a "honor-lover" <note>original: "phylosimus"</note>, <margin>Body-lover, money-lover, honor-lover</margin> that is, greedy for riches and honors; and such a man affects either one of these, or both. SIM. It is entirely as you say. SO. Therefore, O Simmias, does not that which we call courage belong most of all to such men? SIM. Most certainly. SO. And does not temperance—which most say consists in not being cast down by lusts, but in holding them of little account and maintaining modesty—belong only to those who despise the body most and live in philosophy? <margin>To hold lusts of little account:</margin> SIM. It must be so. SO. For if you wish to consider the courage and temperance of others, it will seem quite absurd to you. SIM. In what way, O Socrates? SO. You know that all others consider death to be one of the greatest evils. SIM. Most certainly. SO. Is it not, then, through a greater fear of evils that those among them who are brave endure death when they do? SIM. That is the way of it. SO. Therefore, all except philosophers are brave through fearing and through fear; and yet it is absurd for someone to be brave through fear or cowardice. SIM. Certainly. SO. What then? Are not those among them called "moderate" affected in a similar way: namely, tempered by a kind of intemperance? Although we say that is impossible, nevertheless a state similar to this happens to them in that foolish temperance of theirs. For fearing that they may be deprived of other pleasures, and desiring them, they abstain from some because they are overcome by others; and though they call it "intemperance" to be overcome by pleasures, it nevertheless happens to them that by being overcome by some pleasures, they overcome others. Now this is similar to what was just said: that in a certain way they become temperate through intemperance. SIM. It is indeed similar. SO. It must be observed, O blessed Simmias, that this is by no means the right path to virtue: namely, to exchange pleasures for pleasures, pains for pains, and fear for fear, the greater for the lesser, as if they were coins. But that alone is the right coin for which all these things ought to be exchanged and sold: wisdom and prudence, for which and with which all things are truly bought and sold—both courage, and temperance, and justice. In short, true virtue exists with wisdom or prudence, whether pleasures and fears and other things of that kind come or go. But if they are exchanged for one another apart from wisdom, such virtue becomes a mere shadow-painting, and is in truth slavish, possessing nothing healthy or true. The truth of virtue actually consists in the purification from all these things: and temperance, and justice, and courage, and wisdom itself is a kind of purification. Wherefore those who established the mysteries for us seem not to be despised; but in truth they have long been secretly admonishing us: that whoever goes to the underworld unexpiated and uninitiated shall lie in the mud; but whoever arrives there purified and initiated shall dwell with the gods. For those who deal with the mysteries say, "The ministers of Bacchus carry the wands": <margin>Many wand-bearers; few Bacchi.</margin> there are many wand-bearers <note>original: "narthecophori"</note>, but few true Bacchi <note>The "Bacchi" are those truly inspired by the god, as opposed to those merely performing the outward ritual.</note>. These, as I believe, are none other than those who have philosophized rightly. To be in their number I have not fallen short, but have tried with all my zeal and strength. Whether I have contended rightly or achieved anything, we shall know for certain when we arrive there, if God wills, a little later, as it seems to me. This then is my excuse...

<summary>Socrates argues that true virtue is a form of purification guided by wisdom, rather than a mere trade-off between different fears or pleasures. He concludes that the soul's separation from the body at death is the ultimate goal of the philosopher, who seeks pure knowledge beyond physical distractions.</summary>
