# PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL.

## FOLIO CCII.

<margin>He proposes to discuss whether the human soul exists after death.</margin>

This is the reason, O Simmias and Cebes: why I do not take it hardly or feel disturbed that I am leaving you and those who are the masters here. For I hope that there, no less than here, I shall find good masters and friends. Many people, however, do not believe this at all. If, therefore, my defense has persuaded you more than it did the Athenian judges, it is well. When Socrates had said this, Cebes took up the discourse and said: "The rest, O Socrates, seems rightly said; but as far as the soul itself is concerned, men are in great doubt whether, once separated from the body, it might no longer exist anywhere. They fear that on the very day a man dies, the soul perishes: that as soon as it is set free from the body, it is dissolved; and exhaling like wind or smoke, it is scattered and vanishes, and is no longer anything at all. Certainly, if it were gathered into itself somewhere, and freed from those evils which you just described, there would be a great and good hope, O Socrates, that what you said would be true. But perhaps it requires no small persuasion and faith to believe that the soul survives after the death of a man, and that it possesses some power and intelligence."

SOCRATES: "You speak the truth, O Cebes. But what do you think should be done? Shall we perhaps converse about these very things, whether it is probable that it is so or otherwise?"

CEBES: "I would certainly be glad to hear what you think about these matters."

SOCRATES: "I do not think anyone hearing this—not even a comic poet <note>original: "comoedus" - likely a reference to Aristophanes, who mocked Socrates in his plays</note>—would say that I am talking nonsense now, or speaking of things that are inappropriate. If it pleases you, then, we ought to consider it in this way: whether the souls of the dead are in the underworld or not. There is an ancient tradition <note>original: "Vetus sermo" - referring to Orphic or Pythagorean beliefs in reincarnation</note> which we remember: that souls depart from here to that place, and return here again, and are born from the dead. And if this is true, that the living are born again from the dead, then our souls must be there. For they would not be born again if they were not somewhere. And this is a sufficient conjecture that it is so, if it truly stands that the living are produced from nowhere else than from the dead. But if that is not the case, we will need another argument."

CEBES: "Certainly."

<margin>Generation arises from opposites.</margin>

SOCRATES: "Now, if you wish to understand this more clearly, do not consider it only in men, but in all animals and plants; and, to put it briefly, in all things that are generated. Let us consider in all these whether everything is produced in this way: that opposites come from nowhere else than from their opposites, in whatever things such a condition occurs. Just as the beautiful is in a way the opposite of the ugly, and the just of the unjust; and many other such things we see. Therefore, is it necessary that whenever something has an opposite, it is produced from no other source than from its own opposite? For example, when something becomes greater, it must necessarily have been smaller before, and afterwards become greater."

CEBES: "It is so."

SOCRATES: "And if it becomes smaller, will it not become smaller from what was previously greater?"

CEBES: "Exactly so."

SOCRATES: "Furthermore, does the weaker come from the stronger, and the swifter from the slower?"

CEBES: "Entirely."

SOCRATES: "What then? If something becomes worse, is it not from the better? And if more just, from the more unjust?"

CEBES: "Why not?"

SOCRATES: "In all things, therefore, we have sufficiently explored this: that all things are produced in this way, namely, opposites from opposites."

CEBES: "Entirely."

SOCRATES: "What next? Is there something in the middle between two opposites? Namely, two generations or progressions between them: from one into the other, and back again from the other into the first? Between the greater and the smaller, there is 'increase' and 'decrease'; and we say that one grows and the other diminishes."

CEBES: "Yes."

SOCRATES: "And is it not the same with being separated and being mixed, cooling and heating, and all things in the same way? Even if we lack names for them in some places, it is nevertheless necessary that it happens everywhere: namely, that all things come from their opposites in turn, and there is a generation of each into the other."

CEBES: "Certainly."

SOCRATES: "What then? Is there something opposite to living? Just as sleeping is the opposite of being awake?"

CEBES: "There is indeed."

SOCRATES: "What is it?"

CEBES: "Dying."

SOCRATES: "And do these not arise from each other, since they are opposites? And since there are two, are there not also two mutual generations or progressions between them?"

CEBES: "Nothing prevents it."

<margin>An argument for the immortality of the soul taken from the mutual generation of opposites.</margin>

SOCRATES: "I will tell you one pair of those I just mentioned, both the pair itself and their generations. You, in turn, shall reveal the other to me. I say that one is sleeping and the other is waking; and from sleep comes waking, and from waking comes sleep. The generations of these are, in one case, 'falling asleep,' and in the other, 'awakening.' Have I satisfied you or not?"

CEBES: "You have certainly satisfied me."

SOCRATES: "Tell me then, in the same way, about life and death. Do you not say that living is the opposite of dying?"

CEBES: "I do."

SOCRATES: "And that they arise from each other?"

CEBES: "Yes."

SOCRATES: "Therefore, what is produced from the living?"

CEBES: "The dead."

SOCRATES: "And what from the dead?"

CEBES: "One must confess: the living."

SOCRATES: "Therefore, O Cebes, from the dead, living things and living people are produced."

CEBES: "It appears so."

SOCRATES: "Therefore, our souls are in the underworld."

CEBES: "It seems so."

SOCRATES: "And of the generations concerning these, is not one of them manifest? For dying is manifest, is it not?"

CEBES: "Yes, entirely."

SOCRATES: "What then shall we do? Shall we not grant in return the opposite generation? Shall we say that nature is lopsided in this one thing? Or is it necessary to grant some generation opposite to dying?"

CEBES: "Entirely."

SOCRATES: "What is that?"

CEBES: "Coming back to life."

SOCRATES: "Therefore, if 'coming back to life' is a certain progression, is it not from the dead to the living?"

CEBES: "It is indeed."

SOCRATES: "It is agreed between us, then, by this reasoning as well: that the living are produced from the dead no less than the dead from the living. Since this is so, it is a sufficient conjecture that the souls of the dead must necessarily be somewhere, from whence they return again."

CEBES: "It seems to me, O Socrates, that this follows necessarily from what has been conceded."

SOCRATES: "Observe then, O Cebes, that we have not conceded these things without reason, as I think. For if one did not continually return in place of the other, as if traveling in a circle, but the progression were a straight line only from one into its opposite, and they did not turn back again into the other or make a return, believe me, all things would finally have the same form and suffer the same fate: they would cease to be produced."

CEBES: "How do you mean that?"

SOCRATES: "It is not at all difficult to understand what I am saying. For example, if there were such a thing as falling asleep, but one never rose again from it into waking, you are well aware that all things would finally end up making the story of Endymion <note>A youth in Greek mythology who was cast into an eternal sleep</note> look like a joke; he would nowhere be seen, since everything else would likewise be overwhelmed by sleep. Furthermore, if all things were mixed together..."

<summary>Socrates presents the "Argument from Opposites," suggesting that just as waking comes from sleep, life must come from death, implying that souls exist in an afterlife before being reborn. He warns that without this cyclical return, the universe would eventually "run down" into a single, static state.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Cebes, immortality of the soul, opposites, reincarnation, underworld, Endymion, cyclical argument</keywords>

By the same reasoning, my dear friend Cebes, if all things that have received life should die, and once dead, they remain in that state and do not live again, is it not absolutely necessary that all things would eventually be destroyed and nothing would live? For if living things were made from other things, and then perished, what would prevent everything from being consumed by destruction? CEBES: Nothing at all, Socrates; you seem to me to speak the absolute truth. SOCRATES: It is certainly so, Cebes, above all else, as it seems to me; nor have we confessed these things as if we were deceived. In truth, there is a living again; the living are produced from the dead, and the souls of the dead survive. And indeed, it is better for the good, and worse for the evil.

On immortality

CEBES: And also according to that principle, Socrates, which you are frequently accustomed to use—if it is indeed true—that our learning is nothing other than recollection <note>original: "reminiscentia"; the Platonic theory that learning is actually the soul remembering knowledge it had before birth.</note>; and according to this, I say, it is necessary that we learned in some previous time those things which we now remember. But that would be impossible unless our soul had been somewhere before it entered into this human form. Therefore, by this reasoning also, the soul seems to be something immortal. 

<margin>
It is shown that our knowledge is recollection.
</margin>

SIMMIAS: What demonstrations of this matter do you have, Cebes? Remind us of them, for I do not sufficiently remember them at present. CEBES: One most beautiful reason is that when men are questioned, if someone questions them rightly, they themselves answer everything just as it is. And they could never do this unless knowledge and right reason were within them. Furthermore, if someone directs them to geometric figures and diagrams, or something similar, he will clearly discover there that this is the case. SOCRATES: If this reasoning does not satisfy you, Simmias, see if it appears the same to you when considering it this way. For you doubt that what they call learning can be recollection. SIMMIAS: I do not exactly doubt it. Nevertheless, it is helpful for me to learn about the very thing being discussed: namely, recollection. And indeed, from what Cebes began to say, I already remember and believe. Nonetheless, I would gladly hear from you, Socrates, by what reasoning you yourself were just now attempting to prove it. 

<margin>
What recollection is.
How recollection occurs.
</margin>

SOCRATES: By this reasoning. We surely agree in a way that if someone remembers something, he must have known it at some time before. SIMMIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: Do we also agree on this: that whenever knowledge arrives in this manner, it is recollection? I mean it in this way: if someone sees something, or hears it, or perceives it by another sense, and not only knows that thing, but also recognizes something else, of which the knowledge is not one and the same but different—should we not rightly say that he remembers that thing which came into his mind? SIMMIAS: How do you mean? SOCRATES: This: the knowledge of a man is one thing, and the knowledge of a lyre <note>A stringed musical instrument common in Ancient Greece.</note> is another. SIMMIAS: Why not? SOCRATES: Do you not know that this happens to lovers, when they see a lyre, or a garment, or anything else which their beloveds were accustomed to use? For they recognize the lyre, and at the same time, they recall in their mind the form of the girl to whom the lyre belonged. This is indeed to remember. Just as if someone sees Simmias, he often remembers Cebes; and infinite other things of the same kind. SIMMIAS: Infinite, by Jove! SOCRATES: Is not, therefore, such a thing a kind of recording? Especially if it happens to us regarding those things which, through length of time and neglect, we have already surrendered to oblivion? SIMMIAS: Certainly. SOCRATES: What then? Does it happen that he who sees a painted horse, or a painted lyre, remembers a man? And when he looks at a painting of Simmias, does Cebes come into his mind? SIMMIAS: Yes, indeed. SOCRATES: Does it not also happen that he who looks at a painting of Simmias remembers Simmias himself? SIMMIAS: It certainly happens. SOCRATES: Does it not follow from all these things that recollection arises both from similar things and from dissimilar things? SIMMIAS: It does. SOCRATES: But whenever someone remembers from similar things, is it not necessary to further understand this: whether this thing falls short in its similarity, or not, from that of which the memory was repeated? SIMMIAS: It is necessary. SOCRATES: Consider then if these things are so. We say there is something "equal." I do not mean one piece of wood equal to another piece of wood, nor stone to stone, nor anything else of that kind; but beyond all these, something else: Equality itself. Do we say it is something, or nothing? SIMMIAS: We say it is something, by Jove, and wonderfully so. SOCRATES: And do we know what Equality itself is? SIMMIAS: Entirely. SOCRATES: From where did we receive the knowledge of it? Was it not from those things we just mentioned—namely, seeing either woods, or stones, or certain other equal things—that from these we conceived that which is different from them? Does it not appear to be something else? Consider it also in this way: Do not stones or equal woods, while remaining the same, appear to us at one time equal and at another time unequal? SIMMIAS: Completely so. SOCRATES: But what about the Equals themselves? Can they ever appear unequal to you? Or can Equality appear to be Inequality? SIMMIAS: Never, Socrates. SOCRATES: Therefore, these equal things and Equality itself are not the same. SIMMIAS: They do not appear the same to me at all, Socrates. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, from these equal things, which are different from that Equality itself, you have at the same time conceived and perceived the knowledge of it. SIMMIAS: You speak the very truth. SOCRATES: Whether it be similar to them or dissimilar? SIMMIAS: Entirely. SOCRATES: It makes no difference. For as long as you see one thing and from this very sight you understand another, whether similar or dissimilar, it is necessary that recollection arises from this. SIMMIAS: Very much so. SOCRATES: What then regarding this? How do we feel about the equal things in the woods and stones we were just mentioning? Do they seem to be equal in the same way as Equality itself? Or do they rather lack something so as not to be such as Equality itself is? SIMMIAS: They certainly lack a great deal. SOCRATES: Do we not agree that when someone, looking at something, notices that this thing he sees desires to be like some other thing that exists, but falls short and cannot be such an equal as that is, but is inferior—is it not necessary that he who notices this must have previously known that which he says this thing is in some way trying to be like, but fails to reach full similarity? SIMMIAS: It is necessary. SOCRATES: What then? Does something like this happen to us or not, regarding these equal things and Equality itself? SIMMIAS: Most definitely. SOCRATES: It is necessary, therefore, that we [had] the knowledge of Equality itself...

...possessed it before that time: in which, first seeing equal things, we recognized that all such things strive to be like that which is the "Equal" itself, yet fall short of its perfection. SIMMIAS. That is so. SOCRATES. And yet we also confess that we have not recognized this from any other source—nor could we—except from sight, or touch, or some other sense. For I judge the same regarding all these things. SIMMIAS. They are indeed the same, Socrates, in respect to what must be demonstrated. SOCRATES. Not otherwise. SOCRATES. Before we began to see, or hear, or use the other senses, it was necessary for us to have possessed the knowledge of the "Equal" itself: namely, what it is; if indeed we are to refer these equal things, which are subject to the senses, to it, judging that all these strive to be such as it is, yet remain inferior. SIMMIAS. That follows necessarily from the previous points, Socrates. SOCRATES. And were we not born immediately seeing and hearing, and exercising the other senses? SIMMIAS. Entirely so. SOCRATES. But it was necessary, as we said, to have had the knowledge of the "Equal" itself before these. SIMMIAS. It was necessary. SOCRATES. Therefore, as it seems, it is necessary that we grasped it before we were born. SIMMIAS. So it appears. SOCRATES. If, having obtained it before birth, we were born already possessing it, did we not know both before birth and immediately upon being born not only the "Equal" itself, and the greater and the lesser, but also all things of the same kind? For our discussion now is no more about the "Equal" than it is about the **Beautiful** itself, the **Good** itself, the **Just**, and the **Holy**; and as I say, about all those things to which we assign this very "what it is" <note>original: "quod est" — referring to the essence or "Being" of a thing</note> both in the questions we ask and the answers we give: so that it is necessary for us to have had knowledge of all these before we were born. SIMMIAS. It is so. SOCRATES. And if, having accepted these knowledges, we did not always forget them, it would be necessary to be born with them and to always know them through our whole life. For "to know" is this: to retain a knowledge of something received and not to have lost it. Do we not say that "forgetting" is the loss of knowledge? SIMMIAS. Exactly so, Socrates. SOCRATES. But if, I suppose, having acquired knowledge before birth, we lost it at birth, and then later, relying on the senses regarding those same knowledges, we recover those which we previously held—would not that which we call "learning" be the recovery of our own knowledge? And in naming this "recollection," would we not name it correctly? SIMMIAS. Correctly. SOCRATES. For it appeared possible that when someone perceives something, either by seeing, or hearing, or some other sensation, he recognizes from this something else which he had forgotten, to which this thing was in some way related, whether it be similar or dissimilar. So, as I have been saying for a long time, one of two things must be: either we were born knowing and we all know through our whole life, or those whom we say "learn" afterwards are merely recollecting; and thus learning is recollection. SIMMIAS. That is entirely the case, Socrates. SOCRATES. Which then do you choose, Simmias: that we are born with knowledge, or that we recollect later those things of which we previously received knowledge? SIMMIAS. I am uncertain, Socrates, which to choose at present. SOCRATES. What then? Can you choose what you think about this: can a man who knows give a rational account <note>original: "rationem reddere" — to give a logical explanation or 'logos'</note> of the things he knows, or not? SIMMIAS. It is necessary, Socrates, that he be able to. SOCRATES. And does it seem to you that everyone can bring forth a rational account of these things we were just discussing? SIMMIAS. I would indeed wish so. But I fear much more that by tomorrow there will be no man here who is able to do so worthily. SOCRATES. Then you do not think, Simmias, that everyone understands these things? SIMMIAS. By no means. SOCRATES. Therefore they recollect what they once learned. SIMMIAS. It must be so. SOCRATES. But when did our souls receive this knowledge? For it was not after we were born as human beings. SIMMIAS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Therefore, before. SIMMIAS. Yes. SOCRATES. Therefore, Simmias, souls existed even before they came into human form, separate from the body, and they possessed intelligence. SIMMIAS. Unless perhaps, Socrates, we received these knowledges at the very moment we were born. For that time still remains. SOCRATES. Let it be so, my friend. But at what other time did we lose them? For we are not born possessing them now, as we just admitted. Or did we lose them in the same moment in which we received them? Or can you suggest another time? SIMMIAS. Not at all, Socrates; I did not notice that I was saying nothing. SOCRATES. Is this then how it stands for us, Simmias? If indeed those things exist which we constantly speak of—namely, a certain **Beautiful**, and **Good**, and every essence of that kind—to which we refer all things perceived by the senses, which was ours before, and which we find again as we seek our own, and refer back to its exemplar: it is necessary that just as these things exist, so also our soul must have existed even before we were born. But if these things do not exist, then this argument would have been treated in vain. Is it not so? And is there not an equal necessity both that these things exist and that our souls existed before we were born, and if the former do not exist, neither do the latter? SIMMIAS. Wonderfully, Socrates, the same necessity seems to me to exist; and the argument leads us most beautifully to this: that we confess our soul existed before we were born, just like the essence itself of which you were just speaking. For I hold nothing so certain as that all such things exist in the highest degree: namely, the **Beautiful** itself, and the **Good**, and all the other things you mentioned. And as far as I am concerned, it has been sufficiently demonstrated. SOCRATES. But what does it seem to Cebes? For it is necessary to persuade him as well. SIMMIAS. I think he too is sufficiently persuaded, even though he is the most resistant of all men and slowest to believe. Yet I think it has been sufficiently proven to him: that the soul existed before our birth. But whether it will still exist after our death does not yet seem to me, Socrates, to have been sufficiently shown. For that doubt of many which Cebes brought forward still remains: namely, that when a man dies, the soul is simultaneously scattered and thus ceases to be. For what prevents it from coming into being and being established from elsewhere, and existing even before it fell into a human body, but then, after it has departed from it, it then perishes as well? CEBES. You speak rightly, Simmias. For it seems that only half of what is necessary has been proven...

He concludes that learning is actually a process of recollection (anamnesis), proving the soul's existence prior to the body.</summary>

then: namely, that before we were born our soul existed; but it is necessary to show this also: that after we are dead it will exist no less than it did before we were born, if the demonstration is to reach its goal.
**SOCRATES.** That has indeed been demonstrated, O Simmias and O Cebes, even now: if only you are willing to connect into one both what has just been proven and that which we had previously conceded—namely, that every living thing comes from the dead. For if the soul exists beforehand, and when it enters into this life and becomes a human being, it must necessarily proceed from nowhere else than from the dead, why is it not necessary that it also remains after the death of the body, since it must return again to this life? Therefore, what is said has been demonstrated even now. Nevertheless, you and Simmias seem to desire to treat this same matter again more diligently; and perhaps in the **manner of children** you dread lest, in truth, as the soul departs the body, the wind might dissolve and scatter it—especially if it should exit during a time of more vehement gusts of wind. At this, **Cebes** said with a smile: "As if we were dreading it, O Socrates, try to persuade us to the contrary. Or rather, not as if we ourselves were dreading it, but perhaps there is a child among us who fears such things. Let us strive to persuade him, then, not to fear death as if it were **ghosts**." <note>original: "laruas" - masks or specters used to frighten children.</note> **SOCRATES.** It is certainly necessary to heal him with **charms** <note>original: "carminibus" - incantations or poetic songs used for healing.</note> every day until he is made healthy. **CEBES.** But where shall we find such a doctor, O Socrates, when you have departed? **SOCRATES.** Greece is wide, O Cebes, in which there are excellent men; and there are many **barbarian nations**; <note>To a Greek, "barbarian" simply meant anyone who did not speak Greek.</note> through all of these you must search for such a doctor, sparing neither money nor labor. For there is nothing for which one might more profitably spend everything. You must also search among yourselves; for perhaps you will not easily find those who can do it better than you. **CEBES.** That shall be done; but let us return now, if it pleases you, to where we left off. **SOCRATES.** It pleases me indeed. For what prevents it? **CEBES.** You answer rightly. **SOCRATES.** Ought we not to ask ourselves something like this: To what kind of thing does that passion belong by which it can be dissolved? And for what kind of thing should one fear lest it suffer this? And according to what part? Then we should consider what kind of thing the soul is; and finally, from these things, either have confidence or fear for the sake of our soul. **CEBES.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Is it not then suitable for that which is **composed**, and is already a composite, to suffer this by its nature: that insofar as it is composed, it may be dissolved? But if anything is not composed, does it not happen to this alone, above all, that no dissolution occurs? **CEBES.** So it appears to me. **SOCRATES.** And is it not most likely that those things which are always the same and in the same state are **simple**? While those that are sometimes one way and sometimes another, and never the same, are **composites**? **CEBES.** I think so indeed. **SOCRATES.** Let us return now to those things which we proceeded toward in the previous discussion. Does that **Essence** <note>The "Forms" or "Ideas" - the perfect, unchanging reality of things.</note> itself, to which we assigned the definition of "that which is" in our questioning and answering, always remain the same and in the same state? Or is it sometimes one way and sometimes another? Namely, **Equality** itself, **Beauty** itself, every single thing that is a **Being**—do they ever receive any mutation? Or does each of them, always being a **uniform** thing existing by itself, remain the same and in the same state, never, nowhere, and in no way undergoing any change? **CEBES.** It is necessary, O Socrates, that these always remain the same and in the same state. **SOCRATES.** But what shall we say of the many things which are called beautiful—such as men, horses, garments, or any other such things which are called either beautiful or equal, or even of all things that are **synonymous** with them? Do these always remain the same? Or rather, are they entirely the opposite of those others: namely, they are never the same as themselves, nor with each other, to speak simply, in any way? **CEBES.** These, O Socrates, are never in the same state. **SOCRATES.** And these indeed can be touched, seen, and reached by the other senses. But those which always remain the same are perceived only by the **reason of the intellect**; and those things which are such are **invisible**, and are never seen. **CEBES.** You speak the absolute truth. **SOCRATES.** Do you wish, then, that we posit two species of things: one **visible**, the other **invisible**? **CEBES.** Let us posit them. **SOCRATES.** And that the invisible is always the same, while the visible is sometimes not the same? **CEBES.** Let us posit this also. **SOCRATES.** Come now. Is there anything else in us than, on one hand, the **body**, and on the other, the **soul**? **CEBES.** Nothing else. **SOCRATES.** To which species do we say the body is more similar and akin? **CEBES.** To no one is it doubtful that it is to the visible. **SOCRATES.** But what of the soul? Is it something visible, or the opposite? **CEBES.** Not to men, at least, O Socrates. **SOCRATES.** But we were speaking only of those things which can or cannot be seen by the nature of men. Or were we treating of those which belong to another nature? **CEBES.** Only of those which belong to the human. **SOCRATES.** What then did we say of the soul? That it was visible? **CEBES.** Not visible. **SOCRATES.** Invisible, then. **CEBES.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the soul is more similar to the invisible species than the body is. And the body to the visible. **CEBES.** That is entirely necessary. **SOCRATES.** And did we not also say this in what went before? That when the soul assumes the body as a partner for considering something, either through sight, or through hearing, or through another sense—for this is what it means to consider through the body, because it is done through the senses—then indeed it is dragged by the body toward those things which are never the same; and it wanders, and is troubled, and staggers as if **drunk**, because it has touched such things. **CEBES.** Exactly. **SOCRATES.** But truly, whenever the mind itself thinks by itself, it goes thither to that which is **pure, eternal, and immortal**: always remaining the same; and as if akin to it, it always clings to it whenever it returns into itself, and as far as it is permitted, it ceases from error; and concerning those things it always remains the same and in the same state, as one who has now touched such things. And this affection of it is named **Wisdom** or **Prudence**. **CEBES.** You speak most excellently and truly, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** To which species, then, does the soul again seem to you to be more similar, from those things which were said both before and just now...

<summary>Socrates argues that the soul is akin to the invisible, unchanging, and divine realm of "Essence," while the body belongs to the visible, changing, and mortal realm. He concludes that the soul achieves wisdom when it detaches from the senses and contemplates eternal truths.</summary>

# PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL. FOLIO 204.

...more related. CEBES: I certainly think, O Socrates, that anyone, even the most unlearned and stubborn, would grant from this discussion that the soul is, in every way and entirely, more similar to that which is always the same than to its opposite. SOCRATES: But what of the body? CEBES: It belongs to the other species <note>i.e., the changeable and mortal</note>. SOCRATES: Consider it again in this way. As long as the soul and body are in the same place, 
<margin>Argument from actions.</margin>
nature commands the latter to serve and be subject, but the former to rule and dominate. According to these facts, which of the two seems to you to be like the divine, and which like the mortal? Or do you not think the divine is such by nature that it rules and leads, while the mortal is such that it is subject and serves? CEBES: I certainly think so. SOCRATES: To which of these, then, is the soul similar? CEBES: It is clear, O Socrates, that the soul is similar to the divine, and the body to the mortal. SOCRATES: Observe now, O Cebes, whether these things follow from all that has been said. 
<margin>Soul Body</margin>
Namely, that the soul is most similar to the divine, immortal, intelligible <note>understandable by the mind rather than the senses</note>, uniform, indissoluble, and that which is always the same and remains consistent with itself; whereas the body is most similar to the human, mortal, non-intelligible, multiform, dissoluble, and that which is never the same as itself. Can we, O friend Cebes, offer anything else to show this is not the case? CEBES: We cannot. SOCRATES: What then? Since these things are so, is it not fitting for the body to be quickly dissolved, but for the soul to be entirely indissoluble, or something very close to being entirely indissoluble? CEBES: Why not? SOCRATES: You see, therefore, after a man has died, that the visible part of him—the body—placed in a visible location, which we call a corpse, and which is liable to be dissolved, 
<margin>corpse:</margin>
to fall apart and flow away, suffers none of these things immediately. Instead, it remains for a long time, especially if someone dies with their body in good condition. For the body, if preserved and treated with certain things for durability, 
<margin>The Egyptians preserve corpses with medicines.</margin>
as they do in Egypt, remains almost whole for an incredible amount of time. Even if it should decay, some parts of the body—namely the bones, nerves, and similar things—remain, so to speak, immortal. Do they not? CEBES: Yes. SOCRATES: But the soul, which is something invisible, migrating to some similar and different place—excellent, pure, invisible, and truly hidden from us—to the good and wise God, where, if God wills, my own soul must also migrate shortly; I ask, shall a soul of such a nature, endowed with such qualities, be dissipated and perish as soon as it is freed from the body, as many people think? 
<margin>Immortal soul</margin>
Far from it, O dear Cebes and Simmias. Rather, the matter stands much more like this: if it departs pure, dragging nothing of the body with it—since it never willingly shared anything with the body, but always fled from it and gathered itself into itself as if always practicing for this—which is nothing other than to philosophize rightly and to truly practice dying with ease; or is this not the "meditation on death"? CEBES: It certainly is. SOCRATES: I say, then, if the soul departs in such a state, does it not go to something like itself, the divine? To the divine, immortal, and wise? Where, when it arrives, it becomes happy, freed from error, folly, fears, harsh loves, and other human evils, and as is often said of the initiated <note>those initiated into the sacred mysteries</note>, it truly spends the rest of time living with the gods? Should we say it is so, Cebes, or otherwise? CEBES: So it is, by Jove! SOCRATES: But if it departs polluted and impure, as one that always embraced the body and cared for it and loved it, and was so charmed by its pleasures and lusts—as if by sorcery—that it thought nothing was true except what is corporeal, what can be touched, seen, drunk, eaten, or used for sexual pleasure; but had grown accustomed to hate, tremble at, and flee from that which is hidden and invisible to the eyes, yet intelligible and graspable by philosophy; do you think a soul so conditioned can escape by itself in a pure state? CEBES: In no way. SOCRATES: But it is infected and wrapped up, I think, by the corporeal contagion, which the habit and association with the body has implanted as if it were natural, because of their constant intimacy and great care for it? CEBES: So we think. SOCRATES: We must think, my friend, that this is heavy, weighty, earthy, and visible, which such a soul drags with it. Therefore, it is weighed down by this and 
<margin>The souls of the wicked haunt tombs and appear as shadowy images.</margin>
is drawn back to the visible world through fear of the invisible and hidden; and as it is said, it wanders around monuments and tombs, around which certain shadowy phantasms of souls have appeared—the kind of images produced by such souls that did not depart purely from the body, but still drag something visible with them, which is why they can be seen. CEBES: That is likely, Socrates. SOCRATES: It is likely indeed, Cebes; but these are not the souls of the good, but of the wicked, who are forced to wander around such places as punishment for their badly spent lives. And they wander until, accompanied by the desire for their corporeal nature, they are again clothed in a body. And they take on, as is fitting, the kind of character they practiced in life. CEBES: What kind of character do you mean, Socrates? SOCRATES: For example, those who lived a life devoted to the belly through laziness and wantonness, 
<margin>to enter into donkeys; wolves and kites</margin>
and had no regard for shame, it is fitting that they should enter the forms of donkeys and similar animals. Don't you think so? CEBES: What you say is likely. SOCRATES: But those who preferred injustice, tyranny, and robbery above all else, it is right that they should pass into the tribes of wolves, hawks, and kites. Or should we say they migrate elsewhere? CEBES: Certainly to those. SOCRATES: Similarly, the others go into whatever kinds of animals match the habits they contracted in life. CEBES: That is indeed manifest. SOCRATES: Are not the happiest of these, who go to the best place, those who have practiced the popular and social virtues—which they call temperance and justice—acquired through habit and exercise without philosophy or the mind? CEBES: In what way are these the happiest? SOCRATES: Because it is fitting that these should pass into some such social genus...

...again to migrate into a civil and mild kind, such as bees, or wasps, or ants; and then from those to return again into the human race, and that modest men are formed from them. CEBES: That is likely. SOCRATES: But into the genus of the gods, it is permitted for none to arrive, except those who, burning with the desire for learning, have both practiced philosophy and departed entirely pure. For the sake of these things, O my friends Simmias and Cebes, those who rightly practice philosophy abstain from all bodily desires; and they persevere in this, never surrendering themselves to them. They do not fear the loss of their household or poverty, as many who are greedy for money do; nor again do they fear contempt and ignominy, as do those who seek after magistracies and honors; therefore they abstain from these things. CEBES: For it would not be fitting, O Socrates. SOCRATES: No, by Jupiter <note>original: "per Iouem" - a common oath in Latin translations of Greek texts</note>. Wherefore those who cultivate their own soul, and do not live for the sake of fashioning the body, having despised all these things, do not walk in that way by which those others we mentioned travel, because they are clearly ignorant of where they are going. But they themselves, believing that they must not resist philosophy and its liberation, follow this path wherever it leads them. CEBES: In what way, O Socrates? SOCRATES: I will tell you. Those who desire knowledge surely recognize how philosophy takes up their soul, which is in truth bound within the body and entangled, forced to consider things through the body as if through a prison; and since the soul does not do this through itself, it is wrapped in utter ignorance. They recognize, moreover, how philosophy, perceiving how cleverly the bodily bond constrains the soul—since it happens through desire itself, by which the bound soul becomes a helper in its own binding—they recognize, I say, men who desire knowledge, how philosophy, taking up their soul in such a state, gradually instructs it and attempts to release it. It shows how deceptive is the judgment of the eyes, how deceptive the ears and the other senses; it persuades the soul to withdraw from these, insofar as the greatest necessity does not compel it to cling to them, and to recall and collect itself into itself. It teaches the soul to trust nothing except itself, so that it may understand by itself whatever exists in itself. But whatever the soul considers through other things, existing in other things, it should consider nothing of that to be true; for such things are sensible and visible <note>perceivable by the senses</note>, but what the soul considers by itself is intelligible and invisible. Therefore, the soul of a true philosopher, judging that it must not resist this liberation, abstains from pleasures, pains, and fears as much as possible. It judges that when someone is vehemently delighted, or fears, or grieves, or desires, he does not suffer only such evil from these things as one might suppose—such as falling ill or wasting money because of his lusts—but he suffers that which is the greatest, extreme, and most foul of all evils, yet he does not notice it. CEBES: What is this, Socrates? SOCRATES: That the soul of every human is compelled to be delighted or to grieve vehemently about something, and at the same time to think that the thing about which it suffers most is the most manifest and the most true, when it is far otherwise. These are mostly the things that are visible, are they not? CEBES: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Is it not in this passion that the soul is most bound by the body? CEBES: In what way? SOCRATES: Because every pleasure and pain, as if holding a nail, fastens the soul to the body; it connects them and makes the soul so corporeal that it now believes those things to be true which the body suggests. Indeed, because it holds the same opinions as the body and is delighted by the same things, it is compelled, I think, to become of the same character and the same nourishment, so that it can never depart pure into the other life, but always goes out full of the stain of the body. Therefore, it quickly falls again into another body, and is sown again as if by fate; and because of this, it becomes entirely alienated from the commerce of the divine, pure, and uniform essence. CEBES: You speak most truly, O Socrates. SOCRATES: For the sake of these things, therefore, O Cebes, the just students of knowledge pursue temperance and fortitude; but not for the reasons the common people believe. Or do you think so? CEBES: Not at all. SOCRATES: Certainly not. But the soul of a true philosopher would think thus: it would not think that, once philosophy had set it free, it should again surrender itself to pleasures and pains to be bound once more, making its work in vain—like unweaving the web of Penelope <note>A reference to Odysseus' wife, who delayed suitors by weaving a shroud by day and unravelling it by night</note>. Rather, seeking tranquility from these things and following reason, and always remaining in it, the soul contemplates the true, the divine, and that which is above mere opinion. Nourished by this, it believes it must live thus as long as it lives; and it hopes that when it departs, migrating to that which is kindred and of such a nature, it will be removed from human evils. From such an education, O Simmias and Cebes, there is no reason to fear that when it recedes from the body, it will be torn apart and dissipated, and its whole life vanish into the winds.

When Socrates had said these things, a long silence followed. And Socrates himself was repeating to himself what had been said, as it seemed, and most of us were doing the same. # PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL. FOLIO CCV.

<margin>The Swans</margin>
As it appears, I seem to you to be inferior to the swans in my power of divination <note>original: "divinando"; referring to the prophetic gift of foretelling the future</note>. For when they perceive that they must shortly die, they sing much more and more sweetly than they were accustomed to do before, rejoicing that they are about to go to the god whose servants they were, being now about to depart. But men, because they themselves dread death, falsely slander the swans, saying that they sing a mournful song out of grief for their death. Indeed, they do not consider that no bird sings when it is hungry, or cold, or affected by any other distress. Not the nightingale <note>original: "philomena"</note>, nor the swallow, nor the hoopoe <note>original: "epops"</note>, which they say sing mournfully out of lamentation. But to me, neither do these birds seem to sing out of grief, nor do the swans. Rather, because they are sacred to Apollo <note>original: "Phœbo"</note>, as I believe, and are endowed with divination, they foresee the blessings of the other life; and therefore they sing more cheerfully and exult on that day than in their previous time. And I also believe myself to be a fellow-servant of the swans, and sacred to the same god; and that I have no worse a gift of prophecy from the same master than they do, nor do I depart from life more despondently. Therefore, for this reason, you may speak and ask whatever you please, as long as the Eleven men of Athens <note>The "Eleven" were the officials in charge of prisons and executions</note> permit it. 

SIMMIAS: You speak excellently. Therefore, I will open to you the matter in which I doubt, and likewise Cebes here will say what part of the previous dispute he finds less acceptable. To me indeed, O Socrates, as perhaps to you also, it seems that regarding these matters, the manifest truth in this present life can be understood either not at all, or only with the greatest difficulty. Yet, to fail to test what is said about them in every way, so that one does not stop until by examining them from every side he gives up, I judge to be the mark of a very soft man. For one must achieve one of these things regarding these matters: either learn or find out how they stand; or if these are impossible, choose the best and safest of human reasons, upon which one may be carried as if on a raft, and so pass through the storms of this life—unless one could sail through more safely and with less danger on a firmer vessel, such as some divine word <note>original: "diuino aliquo verbo"</note>. And so now I shall not be afraid to ask, especially since you yourself encourage us to do so, lest I should perhaps blame myself later for not having said now what I think. Indeed, O Socrates, when I consider your words together with Cebes, they do not seem to be sufficiently confirmed. 

SOCRATES: Perhaps, my friend, you judge truly. But say in what part you think they were spoken insufficiently. 

CEBES: In this part specifically. For someone might say the same thing about harmony, and the lyre, and its strings: namely, that harmony is something invisible, and incorporeal, and very beautiful and divine in a rightly tuned lyre. But the lyre itself and the strings are bodies, and corporeal, and composite and earthly, and kin to the mortal. When, therefore, someone has broken the lyre, or cut or snapped the strings, one could prove by the same reasoning you used that it is necessary for that harmony to survive and not be destroyed. For there would be no way for the lyre to still exist with the strings broken, and the strings themselves are of a mortal nature, while the harmony, which was kin to the divine and immortal, would have perished before that mortal thing. Rather, he would say that the harmony must still be somewhere, and that the wood and strings would rot before it suffered anything. 

I think indeed, O Socrates, that you have noticed that we most especially think the soul to be something of this sort: that there is in our body a certain tension and composition of the hot, the cold, the dry, the moist, and other such things; and that the soul is the temperament and consonance of these, resulting in the body after these things have been well and moderately tempered with one another. If, therefore, the soul is a certain harmony, whenever the nature of these things in the body is immoderately relaxed or intended <note>tightened</note> because of diseases or other evils, it is necessary for the soul, however divine it may be, to perish suddenly—just as other consonances do, whether in voices or in other works of craftsmen—while the remains of each body stay for a longer time, until they are either burned or rot. Consider, therefore, what should be answered to this reasoning, if someone should think the soul is a certain temperament of those things which are in the body, and that it perishes first in death. 

Then Socrates, looking quite sharply as he often used to do, and smiling, said: Simmias, what you say is fair. If, then, any of you is more eloquent than I, why did he not answer these things? For he seems to have touched upon the argument not at all lazily. I judge, however, that before Simmias is answered, we should hear what Cebes also finds fault with, so that in the intervening time we may have the opportunity to deliberate. Then, having heard these things, we must either concede to them, if they seem to bring forward what is consistent with the truth; or if not, the former reasoning must be defended and retained. Therefore, come, O Cebes, tell us what most disturbs you, so that you do not assent. 

CEBES: To me indeed, it seems to revolve back to the same point, and to be liable to the same charge we spoke of in the previous parts. For that the soul existed before it descended into human form, I do not retract, for it was very beautifully stated. And unless it were an invidious thing to say, I would assert it was sufficiently demonstrated. However, that it will survive after we are dead, I do not so agree. Nor yet do I concede to Simmias's objection that the soul is not stronger and more lasting than the body. For it seems to me that the soul far excels all these things. Here, then, the former reasoning, turned toward me, will say: "Why do you still doubt? Since you see that when a man is dead, that which was weaker in him survives, why do you not concede that it is necessary for that which was stronger and more lasting to also survive in this time?" But observe now how much weight there is in what I answer to that. I also need a simile, just as Simmias did. Indeed, these things seem to me to be said just as if someone were to say of an old weaver who had died, that he had not yet perished, but perhaps survived somewhere; and he would bring as a conjecture the garment which the man himself had woven and used, and would assert that it was still intact and had not perished; and if someone did not believe it, he would ask him which is more lasting, the race of man or a garment which one uses daily. And if he should answer that the human race is more lasting, then he would think it demonstrated that the man is much more safe, since that which was more fragile in him had not yet perished. But I do not think, O Simmias, that this is the case. But you also consider what...

# BOOK
### PAGE XXIX.
<meta>Catchword: SO.</meta>

Indeed, anyone would understand that such an argument is ineptly brought forward. For this weaver, who may have worn out many garments and woven many others, died after many of them, but before the last one; yet it does not follow that a man is cheaper or weaker than a garment. I believe the same analogy can be applied to the soul and the body: and if someone were to apply those same points to these two, he would seem to speak appropriately: namely, that the soul is indeed more long-lasting, while the body is weaker and less durable. But he would say that each soul wears out many bodies, especially if they live many years. For if the body flows away and dissolves even while the man is living, and the soul continually re-weaves what is consumed, it will nevertheless be necessary that when the soul perishes, it then possesses its last garment, and perishes before that one alone. But when the soul has perished, then at last the body shows the weakness of its nature, quickly rotting and vanishing; so that by this reasoning we cannot yet be confident that our soul survives even when we have departed. For if someone were to grant even more than what you say—and were to admit not only that the soul existed before our birth, but also that nothing prevents it from remaining after the death of some of us, and from being born and dying repeatedly (for the nature of the soul is so strong that it often preserves itself and the body it is placed in)—even if these things were granted, he would not yet grant you that the soul does not grow weary in many generations, but would say that it is finally destroyed entirely by some death among the many. Furthermore, he would add that no one can discern by death that dissolution of the body which also brings about the destruction of the soul, for it is impossible for any of us to perceive it. If this is the case, everyone is foolish to be confident in death, unless he can demonstrate that the soul is entirely immortal and indissoluble. Otherwise, it is necessarily consistent that he who is about to die must fear for his soul, and always be anxious lest it utterly perish in that destruction of the body which is most imminent.

When we had all heard these things, we were troubled, as we later revealed to one another: because, although we had been greatly persuaded by the previous discussion, they seemed to have disturbed us from that state at present, and to have cast us down so far that we would no longer place any faith in the reasons already brought forward, nor in those yet to be spoken; fearing that either we were by no means good judges, or that the matters themselves were unworthy of belief.

ECHE. By Jove, I certainly grant you pardon, O Phaedo. For to me, just now listening to you, something of the sort came to mind: To what reasoning shall we trust hereafter? Since that reasoning of Socrates, which was so plausible a little while ago, has now lost its credit. For it is wonderful how much that argument—which proves our soul to be a certain harmony—has power over me and always has had; and now that I have heard it, it suddenly recalled to my memory how much it had persuaded me at other times. The result is that I need some other reasoning again, as if from the very beginning, which might persuade me that the soul does not perish with the body. Tell me then, I pray by Jove, in what manner Socrates completed the discussion: and whether he himself also—just as you confess of yourselves—seemed to take it heavily, or on the contrary, kindly defended his reasoning; and furthermore, whether he protected it sufficiently or not. Report all these things to us as diligently as you can.

PHAE. Indeed, O Echecrates, though I have often admired Socrates, I never admired him with greater pleasure than when I was present then. It is perhaps not surprising that he had something to answer to the objections; but I admired this most of all in him: first, how pleasantly, kindly, and amiably he received the young men's words; then how shrewdly he sensed that we had been moved by their arguments; and finally, how opportunely he applied medicine to us, and recalled us as if we were fleeing and defeated, and turned us back to follow and consider the matter.

ECHE. In what way?

PHAE. I will tell you. I happened to be sitting to his right on a certain low stool next to the bed. Socrates himself sat much higher. Stroking my head, then, and pressing the hair down on my neck—for he was accustomed, whenever it happened, to play with my hair—he said, "Tomorrow, perhaps, O Phaedo, you will cut off these beautiful locks." <note>Cutting hair was a traditional sign of mourning.</note>

PHAE. "So I think."

SO. "Certainly not, if you will listen to me."

PHAE. "What then?"

SO. "Rather today, both I mine and you yours; if our reasoning <note>original: "ratio" - here meaning the logical argument</note> dies and we cannot revive it ourselves. And if I were you, and the argument escaped me, I would swear after the manner of the Argives not to grow my hair again until I had defeated Simias and Cebes in turn."

PHAE. "But indeed, it is said that not even Hercules was sufficient against two." <note>A Greek proverb: "Ne Hercules quidem adversus duos."</note>

SO. "Then call me as your Iolaus <note>Hercules' nephew and helper.</note> while it is still light."

PHAE. "I call you indeed, but not as Hercules called Iolaus; rather as Iolaus calls Hercules."

SO. "It makes no difference. But first of all, we must beware lest a certain thing happen to us."

PHAE. "What is that?"

SO. "Lest we become haters of reasoning <note>original: "misologi" - those who hate logic/discourse.</note>, just as some become haters of men <note>original: "misanthropi".</note>. For no greater evil than this could happen to us: namely, if we should hold reasoning in hatred. Hatred arises in the same way toward both reasoning and men. Hatred against men usually enters when we trust someone too much without skill <note>without the "art" of judging character</note>, and we think him to be entirely true, sincere, and a faithful man; then shortly after we find him wicked and unfaithful; and again another in the same way. And so, when someone is often offended and thus deceived, especially by those whom he considered his most familiar and dearest friends, he finally hates everyone intensely, and thinks that nothing at all is sincere in anyone. Has it escaped you that it usually happens this way?"

PHAE. "I have noticed it."

SO. "Is it not shameful, and without the art of human affairs, for this man to attempt to deal with men? For if he studied to deal with them by art, he would surely think that the matter itself stands as it is: namely, that very good or very bad men are very few, but those in the middle are the most numerous."

PHAE. "In what way do you say that?"

SO.

# PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL. PAGE 205.

Just as it happens in things that are either very small or very large. Do you think anything is rarer than finding a man, or a dog, or anything else, that is either very large or very small? Or again, something very fast or very slow, very beautiful or very ugly, very white or very black? Do you not know that in all these things, the extremes are rare and few, while the middle instances are frequent and many? PHAEDO. I think so. SOCRATES. Therefore, do you not think that if a contest of wickedness were proposed, very few would be found at the top of that category? PHAEDO. That is likely. SOCRATES. Likely indeed. But in this respect, arguments are not exactly like men; rather, I followed where you were leading. Instead, the similarity lies in this: when someone without the art of reasoning believes an argument to be true, but a little later it appears false—sometimes it truly is, sometimes not—and then again with another and another. This happens especially to those who spend their time on contradictory arguments. For you know that these men think they have finally become the wisest of all, and that they alone have noticed that there is nothing healthy or firm either in things or in arguments; but that all things are in truth tossed up and down as if in the <term>Euripus</term> <note>A strait in Greece famous for its violent and unpredictable currents; used here as a metaphor for unstable thinking.</note>, and never remain in any state for any time. PHAEDO. You speak the truth all too well. SOCRATES. Would it not be a miserable affliction, Phaedo, if—while there is a true and firm reason that can be understood—someone, after hearing these kinds of arguments that seem now true and now false, should not blame himself or his own lack of skill, but finally, like a sick man, gladly shift all the blame from himself onto the arguments? And for the rest of his life, he would hate and revile them, deprived of the truth and knowledge of reality itself. PHAEDO. By Jove, a miserable affliction indeed. SOCRATES. First, therefore, let us diligently beware of this: let us not persuade ourselves that there is nothing healthy in arguments; but much more that we ourselves are not yet healthy. Thus, we must strive with all our strength to become healthy: you and the others for the sake of your whole remaining life, but I for the sake of my death. For I am in danger, at this very time, of behaving not like a philosopher, but like a contentious and stubborn man, as those most alienated from learning are accustomed to do. For when there is a dispute about something, they do not care how the matter itself stands, but they strive stubbornly so that what they have proposed appears true to those present. And I seem to myself to differ from them at present only in this: that I shall not strive to prove what I say to those present—except perhaps by chance—but rather that it may appear as true as possible to myself. For I think thus, sweet friend—and see how much profit my reasoning brings. If what I say happens to be true, it is worthwhile to believe it; but if nothing remains after death, at least in this time before my passing I will be less annoying to those present, and I will mourn less. Moreover, this ignorance will not persist with me—that would be an evil—but it will be wiped away shortly. Thus prepared, O Simmias and Cebes, I return to the discussion. You, however, if you agree with me, do not yield to Socrates, but to the truth. If I seem to speak the truth to you, grant it; if not, oppose me entirely, taking diligent care lest I, in my striving, deceive both myself and you at once, and depart like a bee, leaving my sting in you.

<margin>
Proverb:
You depart like a bee, leaving your sting behind.
</margin>

But now we must proceed. First, bring back to my memory what you were saying, if I seem not to remember. Simmias, I think, is distrustful and fears lest the soul, though more divine and beautiful than the body, might nevertheless perish first, being of the nature of a <term>harmony</term> <note>The theory that the soul is merely a "tuning" or "balance" of bodily elements, which ceases when the body breaks.</note>. Cebes, however, seemed to me to grant that the soul is more lasting than the body, but he added that no one can know if, after wearing out many bodies, it finally perishes upon leaving the last body; and that death is only the destruction of the soul, while the body is accustomed to dissolve continually. Are these not the things, O Simmias and Cebes, which we ought to consider? SIMMIAS & CEBES. We certainly confess they are. SOCRATES. But do you deny all the things that were said previously? Or do you deny some and grant others? SIMMIAS & CEBES. Some, without a doubt. SOCRATES. What then of that which we said—that learning is <term>reminiscence</term> <note>The Platonic theory that "learning" is actually the soul remembering knowledge it possessed before birth.</note>? And if that is the case, it necessarily follows that the soul was somewhere before it was enclosed in the body. CEBES. To me, that was wonderfully pleasing when you said it; and now, if ever I remained firm in any opinion, I remain in this one most of all. SIMMIAS. I am affected in the same way; and I would be greatly surprised if I ever felt otherwise about this matter. SOCRATES. But it is necessary, my Theban guest, for you to feel otherwise if you persist in the opinion that harmony is a composite thing, and that the soul is a kind of harmony constituted from those things stretched through the body. For you will never admit that a composite concord exists before those things from which the concord had to be composed. Will you admit that? SIMMIAS. In no way, Socrates. SOCRATES. Do you notice, then, that you are forced to confess this when you say the soul exists before it comes into human form and the body, and yet is a concord of the body—namely, that it is constituted from things that do not yet exist? For a concord is not such a thing as you say it is like. Rather, the lyre, the strings, and the still-unharmonized sounds exist first; and finally, the concord is composed from them all, the last of all, and is the first to be destroyed. How, then, will this discourse harmonize with that one of yours? SIMMIAS. In no way. SOCRATES. And yet, if words ought to maintain harmony anywhere, it is especially fitting they be harmonious when discussing concord. SIMMIAS. It is fitting indeed. SOCRATES. Here, then, your discourse is out of tune. But see which of these two you choose: that learning is reminiscence, or rather that the soul is a concord? SIMMIAS. I choose the first, indeed. For I admitted the other without demonstration, based on a certain likely agreement, as it seems to many. But I judge those words which make demonstrations through what is merely "likely" to be always empty.

...itself: and unless one is very careful, they deceive greatly, both in geometry and in all other things. But the reasoning concerning recollection and learning <note>original: "reminiscentia atq; disciplina"</note> rests upon a foundation worthy of belief. For it has been said that our soul existed somewhere even before it fell into the body, just as that essence of the soul possesses the name of "that which is." I have accepted this, as I persuade myself, sufficiently and rightly; therefore, I cannot agree with myself or others who call the soul a harmony.

**SOCRATES:** But what of this, Simmias! Does it seem to you that either a harmony <note>original: "consonantie"</note> or any other composition should be in a different state than the elements from which it is fashioned?
**SIMMIAS:** In no way.
**SOCRATES:** Nor indeed that it should suffer or do anything other than what those elements do or suffer?
**SIMMIAS:** I agree.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, it is not fitting for a harmony to lead those things from which it is composed, but rather to follow them.
**SIMMIAS:** I think so.
**SOCRATES:** For this reason, a harmony is very far from moving in an opposite direction, or sounding, or producing anything else adverse to its own parts.
**SIMMIAS:** Very far indeed.
**SOCRATES:** But what of the attunement? Is it not an attunement according to its nature only insofar as it is tempered?
**SIMMIAS:** I do not quite understand.
**SOCRATES:** Is it not true that if it were tempered more and to a greater degree—if such a thing were possible—it would be more of an attunement? But if less and to a very small degree, would it not be less of an attunement?
**SIMMIAS:** Entirely so.
**SOCRATES:** Can this be said of the soul? That even in the smallest matter, one soul is more or to a greater degree "soul" than another, or the opposite?
**SIMMIAS:** Not at all.
**SOCRATES:** Tell me then, by Jove I pray, do we not say that one soul possesses mind and virtue and is good, while another possesses folly and wickedness and is evil? Are these things said truly?
**SIMMIAS:** Truly indeed.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, among those who assert the soul is a harmony, what will anyone say these things are in the souls? Namely, vice and virtue? Are they another kind of harmony and dissonance? And that the good soul is harmonized, and being itself a harmony, possesses another harmony within itself; while the evil soul is dissonant and is itself dissonance, having no other harmony within it?
**SIMMIAS:** I have no answer to give. It is clear, however, that one who posits the soul is a harmony would answer something of that sort.
**SOCRATES:** But it has already been granted that one soul is no more or less a soul than another. And this concession means that one harmony is no more, nor to a greater or lesser degree, nor in fewer steps, a harmony than another. Is it not so?
**SIMMIAS:** Precisely.
**SOCRATES:** And that which is neither more nor less a harmony is surely neither more nor less tempered. Is that so?
**SIMMIAS:** It is.
**SOCRATES:** But can that which is neither more nor less tempered participate in harmony in more or fewer degrees? Or rather equally?
**SIMMIAS:** Equally rather.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore the soul, if indeed one is no more or less a soul than another according to the nature of the soul, is consequently neither more nor less tempered.
**SIMMIAS:** It is as you say.
**SOCRATES:** To one so affected, it participates no more in harmony or dissonance.
**SIMMIAS:** No more at all.
**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, since it is so constituted, does one soul possess more of wickedness or virtue than another? Since wickedness is indeed dissonance, and virtue is harmony.
**SIMMIAS:** Certainly nothing more.
**SOCRATES:** Rather, according to right reason, Simmias, no soul will ever be affected by wickedness if it is a harmony. Since a true harmony, according to what a harmony is, never participates in dissonance.
**SIMMIAS:** Never, certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the soul, which is entirely a soul, will not be infected by wickedness.
**SIMMIAS:** For how, according to what has been said, could that happen?
**SOCRATES:** By this reasoning, then, the souls of all living beings will be similarly good, if they are similarly souls according to the nature of the soul itself.
**SIMMIAS:** It seems so to me, Socrates.
**SOCRATES:** Does it seem to you that this is rightly said, and that these conclusions follow, if that position were true—that the soul is a harmony?
**SIMMIAS:** In no way.
**SOCRATES:** But what of this? Of all things in a human being, do you assert that anything else rules besides the mind, especially a prudent one?
**SIMMIAS:** Nothing else.
**SOCRATES:** Does it indulge the disturbances of the body, or rather resist them? I mean something like this: as if when one is parched with thirst, the mind nevertheless opposes it and pulls back in the opposite direction so that he does not drink; and similarly if hunger presses, that he does not eat; and in many other things we see the mind resisting the affections of the body. Do we not?
**SIMMIAS:** Most certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Did we not confess in the earlier parts that the soul, if it were a harmony, would never be at odds with those things which it stretches, or relaxes, or vibrates, or whatever else those elements from which it consists might suffer; but that it would follow them, and never lead them?
**SIMMIAS:** We confessed it.
**SOCRATES:** But what now? Does it not seem to act entirely to the contrary, insofar as it leads all those things from which someone might say it is constituted? And it resists almost all of them through all of life, and rules them in many ways: sometimes punishing more rigidly with pain through gymnastics and medicine; sometimes chastising more mildly by threatening or warning against desires, and angers, and fears, as if one thing were speaking against another; just as Homer relates in the *Odyssey*:
->*Then striking his breast, Ulysses thus addressed his heart:*<-
->*Endure this too, my heart: for you have borne even heavier things.*<-
Do you think Homer said these things as if the soul were a kind of harmony, and such that it would be subject to the passions of the body? Or rather that the mind is something far more divine than a harmony?
**SIMMIAS:** By Jove, it seems to me he signified something more divine.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, my good man, we would not be right to say the soul is a harmony. For in doing so, as it appears, we would agree neither with Homer the divine poet, nor with ourselves.
**SIMMIAS:** That is so.
**SOCRATES:** Come now, we have sufficiently appeased the "Theban harmony," as it seems. But the "Cadmean reason," <note>Socrates uses "Theban harmony" to refer to Simmias's argument and "Cadmean reason" for Cebes's, referencing the founders of Thebes.</note> O Cebes, in what way and by what reasoning shall we appease it?
**CEBES:** You, Socrates, seem to me likely to find a way. Indeed, you devised this reasoning against the harmony wonderfully beyond our expectation. For when I heard Simmias doubting, I wondered greatly if anyone could resist his arguments. Therefore, it was a matter of greatest wonder to me, when the very...

# PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL.

I was not even able to withstand the force of your argument at first. Therefore, I would not be surprised if the **Cadmean argument** <note>A "Cadmean victory" or argument refers to one that involves great difficulty or a reversal; here it implies a formidable challenge that might be overturned.</note> suffered the same fate. **SOCRATES:** My dear man, speak more moderately, lest some "evil eye" <note>original: *invidia*; a reference to the Greek belief that boasting invites divine misfortune.</note> throw our coming argument into confusion. But these matters will be the care of God; let us, however, as **Homer** says, "drawing near in close combat," test whether there is any weight in what you say. The sum of the matters you require is of this sort: you judge it must be demonstrated that our soul is indissoluble and immortal, lest a philosopher, facing death with security and hoping with great confidence that he will be far more blessed in the other life because of his study of philosophy, should be foolish and trust in a vain hope. You say that to show the soul is something strong and godlike, and even that it existed before we did, does not prevent all these things from signifying, not indeed immortality, but merely that the soul is more long-lasting than the body and existed for many ages before us, knowing and doing many things; yet it is not for this reason to be thought any more immortal. Rather, its very entry into a human body was like a disease, the beginning of its destruction, so that it both lives in misery in this life and perishes in the death of the body. You think it makes no difference whether it falls into a body once or many times, as far as our fear is concerned. For it is right to be afraid, unless one is a fool, if he neither knows nor can provide a rational account of the soul's immortality. These are the sorts of things you say, O Cebes; and I repeat them deliberately so that nothing escapes us, whether you wish to add or take away anything from them. **CEBES:** I have nothing at present to take away or add; these are the things I am saying.

Then Socrates, after he had paused for a moment and turned inward, said: "You require no light matter, Cebes; for it is necessary to discuss thoroughly the cause of generation and corruption <note>The philosophical study of how things come into being and how they pass away.</note>. I will therefore, if you wish, relate to you my own experiences. Then, if you think any of what I say helps to reveal the truth of your question, make use of it." **CEBES:** "I certainly wish to hear it." **SOCRATES:** "Listen then to my story. Indeed, Cebes, when I was young, I was inflamed by a wonderful desire for that wisdom which they call **Natural History** <note>original: *naturalē historiā*; the study of the physical world and its origins.</note>. For I thought it a most noble thing to understand the causes through which each thing comes to be, why it perishes, and why it exists. I tossed myself up and down, considering such things as these: whether, after heat and cold have undergone a certain putrefaction—as some have said—then living creatures are formed? Furthermore, whether it is the blood by which we think, or air, or fire? Or is it none of these, but rather the brain that provides the senses of hearing, seeing, and smelling, and from these memory and opinion arise, and from memory and opinion reaching a state of rest, knowledge is born? Likewise, considering the corruption of these things and the changes that happen concerning the heavens and the earth, I finally seemed to myself so dull at this study that nothing could be more so. I will give you a sufficient proof of this: for by this kind of consideration I was so blinded that those things which I previously knew clearly (as it seemed to me and others), I unlearned—along with many other things I thought I knew before, such as the reason why a human grows. For I previously thought it was manifest to everyone that a human grows through eating and drinking. For when, through these, flesh is added to flesh and bone to bone, and in the same way the other parts are added to their like, then the mass which was first small becomes large, and thus the small human becomes a large one. So I thought then; do I not seem to have thought well enough?" **CEBES:** "To me, indeed." **SOCRATES:** "Consider these things further. For I thought I was right whenever I judged a large man standing near a small one to be greater by a head. And even more clearly, ten things seemed to me more than eight because ten contains two more than eight. Furthermore, a two-cubit measure seemed larger than a one-cubit measure because it exceeded it by half." **CEBES:** "And what do you judge of these things now?" **SOCRATES:** "By Jove, I seem to myself to be far from thinking I understand the cause of any of these things. I cannot even persuade myself that when someone adds one to one, either the one to which it was added becomes two, or the one added becomes two, simply because of the addition of one to the other. I wonder if, when each of these was separate, each was one and they were not then two; but after they came together, this very thing was the cause of their becoming two: namely, the meeting by which they were placed closer together. Nor, if someone divides one, can I still be persuaded that this very division is the cause of its becoming two. For then the cause of becoming two is the opposite of the previous cause. For then it was because they were joined closer together; now it is because they are removed and separated from one another. Nor do I think I know why 'one' comes to be, nor, to put it briefly, do I profess to know by this path why anything else comes to be, or perishes, or exists. Instead, I haphazardly mix together another method of my own, for I do not admit that one at all.

But having once heard someone reading from a book (by **Anaxagoras**, as he said) that it is **Mind** that orders all things and is the cause of all, I was greatly delighted by this kind of cause <margin>Mind is the cause of all</margin> thinking it somehow consistent that Mind should be the cause of all things. I thought that if this were so, and Mind ordered all things, each thing would be disposed in the way that was best. Therefore, if anyone wished to find the cause by which each thing comes to be, or perishes, or exists, he must find this: in what way it is best for that thing to exist, or to suffer, or to act. In this way, a man should consider nothing else, regarding himself or others, except what is most excellent and best. It is necessary, moreover, that he who knows the best should also know what is worse, since the science of both is the same. Reflecting on these things, I rejoiced, thinking I had found in Anaxagoras a teacher who would teach me the causes of things as I so greatly desired: first telling me whether the earth is flat or round, and having said this, would explain the cause and the necessity, by showing that it was better for it to be so. Furthermore, if he said the earth was in the center of the world...

<summary>Socrates recounts his early intellectual journey, moving from physical explanations of the world to the realization that "Mind" must be the ultimate cause of all things being ordered for the best.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, Cebes, Anaxagoras, immortality of the soul, teleology, Mind (Nous), natural philosophy, causation</keywords>
