### PAGE XXIX.

<meta>Catchword: p- (likely "particeps" or "praesentia")</meta>

to be in the middle: he would soon explain that it was better for it to be in the middle. If he could show me these things, I was prepared to ask for no further kind of cause. Furthermore, concerning the sun and the moon and the other stars, their relative speeds and revolutions and all such things, I had prepared myself to ask and listen in a similar way: namely, by what reason it is better for each of these to either act or be acted upon in whatever way they do. For I did not think that since he had said from the beginning that all things are ordered by **Mind** <note>Latin: *mente*; referring to Anaxagoras's concept of *Nous*</note>, he would later assign any other cause to things except that it is best for them to be exactly as they are. Therefore, I thought that in rendering the causes of both individual things and all things together, he would assign to each what is best for it, and to all the common good. Nor did I hold my hopes cheaply: but with the greatest zeal, I read the books I had received as quickly as I could, so that I might know as soon as possible what was best and what was its opposite.

Led by this wonderful hope, as I proceeded to read, I saw a man making no use of **Mind** at all, nor referring to any cause for the ordering of things; instead, he assigned as causes aerial, ethereal, and watery natures, and many other such incredible things. In this, he seemed to me to act exactly as if someone were to say that Socrates does whatever he does by mind, and then, wishing to explain the causes of each thing I do, should say first that I am sitting here now because my body is composed of bones and nerves: and that the bones are solid and have joints between them, while the nerves are designed so they can be extended and contracted, binding the bones together with the flesh and the skin that contains them. Therefore, when the bones are lifted in their joints, the nerves, which both stretch and relax conveniently, make it so I have the faculty of bending my limbs; and for this cause, I sit here bent over. 

And again, concerning my conversation, he might assign other such causes: voices and air and hearing and many other things of that kind, neglecting the truest causes: namely, that since it seemed better to the Athenians to condemn me, it therefore also seemed better to me to sit here, and I judged it more just to remain and undergo the punishment they commanded. For by the Dog! <note>A common Socratic oath</note> I think these nerves and bones would have been in Megara or Boeotia long ago—carried there by an opinion of what is best—had I not judged it more just and honorable to pay the penalty to the city, whatever it might demand of me, rather than to flee and live as an exile. 

But to call such things "causes" is most remote from reason. If someone were to say that without bones and nerves and such things I could not fulfill what I see fit to do, he would speak truly. But to assert that I do whatever I do *because* of these things, while I act by **Mind**, and not by the choice of what is best, would be a great and vast negligence of speech. For such a person cannot distinguish that the true cause of a thing is one thing, while that without which the cause could not be a cause is another. This is what many people, as if groping in the dark, call by a false name when they term it a "cause." 

Wherefore some, placing a vortex around the earth, make it stable beneath the heavens. Others support it like a broad kneading-trough with the air as a base. But the power itself, by which it is now so disposed as it could best be disposed, they neither seek out nor believe to have any divine <note>Latin: *demonicam*; in the sense of a spiritual or supernatural power</note> force; instead, they think they have found some Atlas more robust and immortal and more capable of holding all things together. But they believe that the **Good** and the **Fitting** truly connect and contain nothing. 

I, therefore, would most gladly have been the disciple of anyone to learn how this cause operates. But since I was deprived of this, and could neither find it myself nor learn it from another, I set out on a "second voyage" <note>A famous metaphor for Socrates's shift from natural philosophy to the study of definitions and forms</note> to investigate the cause. Do you wish, O Cebes, for this to be demonstrated to you by me? 
**CEBES:** I desire it wonderfully. 
**SOCRATES:** I decided at last, since I was weary from considering things, that I must take care lest the same thing happen to me as happens to those who fix their gaze upon a solar eclipse; for they are sometimes robbed of their sight unless they look at its image in water or something of that kind. I considered something similar, and I feared lest my soul be altogether blinded if I looked at things with my eyes and tried to grasp them with any of the senses. Therefore, I decided it would be best to take refuge in **Reason** <note>Latin: *rationes*; often translated as "definitions" or "arguments" in this context</note> and to consider the truth of things within it. 

Perhaps this likeness of ours does not fit in every part. For I do not altogether grant that he who contemplates things in reason is looking at images any more than he who looks at them in their effects. Nevertheless, I directed my path this way: always supposing the reason which I judge to be strongest, whatever things seem to harmonize with it, I set down as true—both concerning the causes of things and all else—and those which disagree, I deny to be true. I wish to explain more clearly what I am saying to you. For I think you do not yet understand. 
**CEBES:** By Jove, not much! 
**SOCRATES:** Yet I bring forward nothing new, but only what I have never ceased to say both elsewhere and in our previous discussion. I proceed now to demonstrate to you the kind of cause I have continually treated; and I return to those things so often repeated, and I begin from them, <margin>m</margin> supposing that there is something that is **Beauty** itself, and **Good**, and **Great**, and all the rest. If you grant these to me, and concede that they exist, I hope to demonstrate the cause itself to you from them, and likewise to find that the soul is immortal. 
**CEBES:** As if I had already granted it to you; you need no more zeal to reach your conclusion. 
**SOCRATES:** Consider now what follows next, whether you agree with me in these things. For I think that if there is anything else beautiful besides Beauty itself, it is beautiful for no other reason than because it participates in that Beauty. And I say the same for all things. Do you accept this as the cause? 
**CEBES:** I do indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, I do not yet perceive further, nor can I know those other "splendid" causes. If someone tells me why a thing is beautiful—namely, because it has a blooming color or a shape or any other such thing—I let those other things go. In all of them, I am usually confused. But this one thing, simply and undoubtedly, and perhaps even foolishly, I hold to myself: that nothing else makes a thing beautiful except the presence or communication of that Beauty, in whatever way and by whatever means it...

<summary>Socrates recounts his disappointment with Anaxagoras's materialist explanations and introduces his "second voyage": the theory that things possess qualities like Beauty or Goodness by participating in absolute Forms.</summary>

...might come. For I do not yet dare to affirm that, but that by Beauty all beautiful things are beautiful; this seems to me to be the safest answer to give both to myself and to others. And leaning upon this foundation, I think I shall never fall: but that it is safe for me and anyone else to answer that whatever things are beautiful, they become beautiful by Beauty itself. Do you not agree? CEBES: I certainly agree. SOCRATES: Therefore, also, those things which are great are great by Greatness itself; and those which are greater are similarly greater; and those which are smaller are smaller by Smallness. CEBES: It is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, you would not agree if someone said that one person is greater than another by a "head" <note>original: "capite"; Socrates is mocking the idea of physical or relative causes rather than absolute Forms</note>; and also that the one who is smaller is smaller by that same head. Instead, you would protest that you have nothing else to say except that every greater thing is greater than another by no other thing than Greatness, and is greater because of it—namely, because of Greatness itself. Likewise, the smaller is smaller by nothing else than Smallness, and because of this it is smaller—namely, because of Smallness itself. You would fear, I think, that if you said someone was greater or smaller by a head, someone might object to you: first, that by the same thing the greater would be greater and the smaller would be smaller; and then, that you affirm the greater is greater by a head, which is a small thing. This, he would say, is like a monster: that you should say someone is great by something small. Would you not fear these things? Then Cebes, smiling, said: I certainly would. SOCRATES: Would you not similarly fear to say that ten is more than eight by two, and exceeds for this cause, rather than by Multitude and because of Multitude? And similarly, that a two-cubit measure is greater than a one-cubit measure by a half, rather than by Greatness? For that is similarly to be feared. CEBES: Entirely. SOCRATES: What then? If one is added to one, would you not be afraid to say that the addition itself is the cause of them becoming two? Or if it is divided, that the division itself is the cause of the two? You would cry out loudly that you do not know by what other way anything comes to be, except by a certain participation in the Essence <note>original: "essentiae"; referring to the Form or Idea</note> proper to each thing in which it participates. And in these cases, you have no other cause for them becoming two except participation in Twoness itself; and it is necessary for those things to be participants in this, whatever things are to be two; and similarly in Oneness, whatever is to be one. You would let those divisions and additions and other such subtleties go, leaving them to those wiser than you to answer as they please. But you, fearing—as the saying goes—your own shadow and inexperience <margin>Proverb: You fear your own shadow.</margin>, and leaning upon that safest position, would answer thus. But if anyone should attack that position itself, you would let him be, and not answer until you had considered whether the things flowing from it agree with one another or disagree. But when it was necessary to give an account of that principle itself, you would give it in the same way: you would bring forward another position, whichever seemed the best of the higher ones, until you reached something sufficient. You would never confuse things together in the manner of contentious debaters, where you dispute both about the starting principle and the things derived from the principle—if, that is, you wished to find any of the things that truly exist. For those people perhaps have no talk or care for this matter. For they are able, by their "wisdom," to mix all things together and yet be pleased with themselves. But you, if you are of the number of philosophers, will do as I say, I believe. SIMMIAS & CEBES: You speak most truly. ECHECRATES: By Jove, O Phaedo, they rightly agreed. For it seems to me he has explained the matter wonderfully, even to the dullest person. PHAEDO: So it seemed to all who were present, Echecrates. ECHECRATES: What wonder? Since it seems so to us as well, who were not there, now hearing it similarly. But what was said after this? PHAEDO: As I recall, after they granted these things to Socrates, and agreed that each Form <note>original: "speciem"</note> is something, and that the things participating in them take their names from them, he then questioned them in this way: If these things are so, when you say that Simmias is greater than Socrates but smaller than Phaedo, do you not then affirm that in Simmias there is both Greatness and Smallness at the same time? CEBES: Certainly. SOCRATES: And yet you confess that Simmias exceeds Socrates, not truly as the words sound. For you do not think Simmias is so constituted by nature that he exceeds by the fact that he is Simmias, but by the Greatness which he has; nor again that Socrates is exceeded because he is Socrates, but because he has Smallness in comparison to the other's Greatness. CEBES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Similarly, he is not surpassed by Phaedo because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo has Greatness compared to Simmias's Smallness. CEBES: It is so. SOCRATES: Thus, then, Simmias has the name of both small and great, since being placed in the middle of both, he surpasses the smallness of one with greatness, and yields to the greatness of the other with smallness. And smiling at the same time, he said: I seem to have described this quite affectedly, but it is as I say. CEBES: So it appears. SOCRATES: I say this for this reason: because I desire that what seems so to me should seem so to you. For I think not only that Greatness itself never wants to be great and small at the same time, but also that this greatness which is in us never receives smallness nor wants to be surpassed. Instead, one of two things happens: either it flees and withdraws when its opposite, Smallness, approaches; or when it has arrived, it perishes. It does not want to wait and, in receiving smallness, become something other than what it was. Just as I, having received and sustained smallness, as long as I am who I am, I am thus small. But that Greatness which is itself never sustained being small. Similarly, the small which is in us never wants to become or be great, nor does any other of the opposites, as long as it is what it was, suffer itself to become or be its opposite at the same time; but it either goes away or perishes when the opposite approaches. CEBES: I think exactly so. PHAEDO: Then one of those present, hearing this—who it was I do not quite remember—said: "Good gods! Was not the opposite of what is now being said granted to us in the earlier part of the discussion? Namely, that the greater comes from the smaller, and the smaller from the greater, and that the generation of opposites is undoubtedly from opposites? Now, however, you seem to be saying that this cannot happen." Then Socrates, moving his head to listen, said: You have remembered that manfully. However, you do not perceive the difference between what is being said now and what was said then. For then it was said that from a contrary thing, a contrary thing comes to be; but now, that the Opposite itself can never become its own opposite, neither the opposite in us nor the opposite in nature. Then, my friend, we were speaking of those things which possess opposites, calling them by the names of those...

<summary>Socrates explains the Theory of Forms, arguing that things possess qualities like "greatness" or "smallness" through participation in absolute Forms, and that while objects can change, the Forms themselves (and the qualities within us) can never become their own opposites.</summary>

CEBES: "I am certainly not so affected; and I affirm to you that I am not much troubled." SOCRATES: "We have therefore simply agreed on this: that an opposite will never be opposite to itself." CEBES: "Entirely." SOCRATES: "Observe further whether you agree with me on this also. Do you call something heat and cold?" CEBES: "I certainly do." SOCRATES: "Is it the same as snow and fire?" CEBES: "No, by Jupiter <note>original: "per Iouem" - a common Roman oath used here to translate the Greek "by Zeus."</note>." SOCRATES: "Is heat something other than fire, and cold something other than snow?" CEBES: "Yes." SOCRATES: "But I think this also is apparent to you: that snow, as long as it is snow, will never admit heat—as we were saying before—and remain snow as it was before and be simultaneously hot. But at the approach of heat, it either retreats or perishes." CEBES: "Completely." SOCRATES: "Similarly, fire, when cold enters it, either flows away or is extinguished; nor can it ever both admit cold and simultaneously be fire as it was before, and cold." CEBES: "You speak the truth." SOCRATES: "There are, therefore, some things of such a kind that they are worthy of their own name not only for all time, but also something else, which is not that first thing, but possesses its form as long as it exists. In this again, what I want will perhaps be more manifest to you. For the 'odd' <note>The mathematical concept of odd numbers.</note> must always possess this name which we now speak of. Must it not?" CEBES: "It must indeed." SOCRATES: "Is it the only one of all things? For I ask this: whether there is also something else, which is not the 'odd' itself, yet must always be called by this name in addition to its own name, because it is so constituted by nature that it is never deserted by the 'odd'? I say this is the case, for example, with the number three <note>original: "ternarium"</note> and many others. Consider the number three. Does it not seem to you that it must always be called both by its own name and simultaneously by the name of the 'odd'? Although the 'odd' is not the same as the number three. Nevertheless, the number three, and five, and every half of the number series are so naturally composed that although they are not the same as the 'odd,' yet each of them is always odd. Furthermore, two and four, and the whole other order of number, although they are not the same as the 'even' <note>original: "par"</note>, yet each of them always exists as even. Do you concede or not?" CEBES: "How could I not?" SOCRATES: "Contemplate then what I mean. It is like this: it appears that not only do those opposites themselves not receive one another, but also whatever things are such that, although they are not opposites to each other, they always possess opposites, they never receive that form which is opposite to the form they have in themselves; but when it approaches, they either perish immediately or depart. Shall we not say that the number three will perish or suffer anything else before it sustains becoming even, insofar as it is three?" CEBES: "Exactly so." SOCRATES: "Yet the number two <note>original: "duitas"</note> is not the opposite of the number three <note>original: "trinitati"</note>." CEBES: "Certainly not." SOCRATES: "Therefore, not only do the opposite forms themselves never receive each other, but also certain other things do not admit the mutual entrance of opposites." CEBES: "You speak most truly." SOCRATES: "Do you wish, then, if we can, for us to define what kind of things these are?" CEBES: "I certainly do." SOCRATES: "Will these not be, Cebes, the things which, whatever they occupy, they make such that it is compelled not only to retain its own idea, but also the work of whatever is opposite to that?" CEBES: "How do you mean?" SOCRATES: "Just as we were saying a little while ago, for you know that those things contained by the idea of three must be not only three, but also odd." CEBES: "Certainly." SOCRATES: "To such a thing, we were saying, the idea opposite to the form that completes it never approaches." CEBES: "Never." SOCRATES: "But the idea of the 'odd' completed it." CEBES: "This very one." SOCRATES: "And the idea of the 'even' is opposite to this." CEBES: "It is so." SOCRATES: "Therefore, the idea of the 'even' will never insinuate itself into the number three." CEBES: "Never." SOCRATES: "Wherefore the number three is devoid of the 'even'." CEBES: "Devoid." SOCRATES: "The trinity <note>The number three.</note> is therefore necessarily odd." CEBES: "It is." SOCRATES: "That which I had undertaken to define—namely, what kind of things they are which, even if they are not opposites to something, yet do not admit the opposite itself—is just like the trinity: which, though it is not the opposite of the 'even,' nevertheless does not accept it, because it always brings its opposite with it. Similarly, the number two <note>original: "binarius"</note> stands toward the 'odd,' and fire toward the cold, and many others. But see now whether you think it should be defined thus: that not only does an opposite not admit an opposite, but also that which brings something opposite to that which it approaches—that very thing which brings it—never receives the opposite form of that which is brought. Again, remember, for it is not useless to be reminded often. Five will not admit the form of the 'even'; nor will ten—which is the double—admit the 'odd.' This itself is opposite to something else, yet it will never receive the form of the 'odd'; and similarly a number and a half, nor other such things which have a half, do they admit the form of the whole; and similarly a number which has a third part, and others of the same kind, if only you follow and agree." CEBES: "I entirely agree and follow." SOCRATES: "Tell me again as if from the beginning. And do not answer me through that which I now ask, but through something else, imitating me. I speak of another safe answer found through those things just said, besides that safe answer positioned from the beginning. For instance, if you ask me, O Socrates, what is in a body if the body becomes hot, I will not give you that safe and unrefined answer, namely 'if heat is in it,' but a more exquisite one from the present words, such as 'if fire is in it.' Similarly, if you ask me: what if it be in a body, it will be sick: I will not answer 'if sickness is in it,' but 'if a fever is.' Again, if you inquire what if it be in a number, it will be odd, I will not say 'if oddness,' but rather 'if unity'; and in other things in the same way. But see whether you clearly perceive what I want." CEBES: "Most clearly." SOCRATES: "Answer then: what is it that, if it be in a body, it will be alive?" CEBES: "If a soul <note>original: "anima"</note> is." SOCRATES: "Is it not always so?"

CEBES: Always. SOCRATES: Therefore, whatever the soul occupies, does it always bring life to it? CEBES: It brings it, without a doubt. SOCRATES: Is there something contrary to life, or not? CEBES: There certainly is. SOCRATES: What is it? CEBES: Death. SOCRATES: Now, the soul will never admit the opposite of that which it always brings with it, as has been granted from our previous points. CEBES: That is entirely so. SOCRATES: What then? That which does not admit the idea of the "even," what did we name it just a moment ago? CEBES: The "uneven" <note>original: "impar"; referring to odd numbers</note>. SOCRATES: And that which does not admit justice, or that which does not receive music? CEBES: We call them the unjust and the unmusical. SOCRATES: Come then: that which does not undergo death, what shall we call it? CEBES: The immortal. SOCRATES: And the soul indeed does not receive death. CEBES: Not at all. SOCRATES: Therefore, the soul is immortal. CEBES: It is indeed immortal. SOCRATES: Come now: shall we say this has been demonstrated? Or does it seem otherwise to you? CEBES: It is most sufficiently demonstrated, O Socrates. SOCRATES: What then, Cebes? If it were necessary that what is "uneven" be also imperishable, would not the number three be imperishable? SOCRATES: Furthermore, if that which is "un-heatable" <note>original: "inalcescibile"; referring to that which cannot be withered or affected by heat</note> were necessarily imperishable: when someone brought heat near to snow, the snow would escape safe and unmelted. For it would not perish, nor would it remain and admit the heat. CEBES: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: By a similar reason, I think, if that which is "un-chillable" were also imperishable: when cold approached fire, the fire would not be extinguished or vanish, but would depart unharmed. CEBES: That would be necessary. SOCRATES: In the same way, we must speak of the immortal. If that which is immortal is also imperishable, it is impossible for the soul to perish when death approaches. For it will not receive death, as is clear from the above, nor will it have died; just as the number three, as we said, will never be even; nor again will the "uneven" be "even"; nor fire be cold; nor the heat that is in the fire ever be coldness. But someone might say: what prevents the "uneven" itself from not becoming "even" when the "even" approaches—as we agreed—but instead, when that is dissolved, the "even" succeeds in its place? We would not be able to argue against one saying this, unless it were proven that the "uneven" is indestructible. Indeed, "uneven" and "indestructible" are not the same thing. Otherwise, if we had established that, we could easily maintain that when the "even" attacks, the "uneven" and the number three depart safe and sound. And we would assert the same regarding fire and heat and the rest. Is it not so? CEBES: Entirely. SOCRATES: Now then, concerning the immortal: if it is established for us that what is immortal is also imperishable, it follows that the soul, besides being immortal, is also imperishable. But if that is not granted, another argument will be needed. CEBES: But there is no need for another argument as far as that is concerned. For what else could be indestructible, if the immortal and eternal itself were to be dissolved? SOCRATES: God indeed, and the very Form of Life, and if anything else is immortal, all would confess them to be indestructible. CEBES: All men, by Jove! And much more so, I think, the gods themselves. SOCRATES: Since, therefore, that which is immortal is also incorruptible, what prevents the soul, if it be immortal, from being incorruptible as well? CEBES: It follows necessarily. SOCRATES: Therefore, when death approaches a man, that which is mortal in him perishes; but that which is immortal withdraws from death, uncorrupted and safe. CEBES: It is manifest. SOCRATES: Therefore, most of all, O Cebes, the soul is immortal and incorruptible, and our souls will exist among the spirits of the dead <note>original: "manes"; the Roman term for the souls of the deceased</note>. CEBES: I have nothing to say against these things, O Socrates, to prevent me from assenting to your reasons. But if Simmias here, or anyone else, has something to say, it would be worthwhile not to remain silent. For I do not know to what other time one should defer, if he desires to say or hear anything about such matters. SIMMIAS: And I too have nothing to prevent me from assenting to the previous reasons. Nevertheless, considering the magnitude of the subject itself and human weakness, I am forced within myself not to yet fully rest in what has been said. SOCRATES: On the contrary, Simmias, you speak well; and those first positions <note>the initial premises of the argument</note>, even if they seem worthy of your trust, must nevertheless be considered more diligently. And if you grasp them sufficiently, as I believe, you will follow this reasoning as far as is possible for a man. And if this itself becomes manifest, you will seek nothing further. SIMMIAS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES:

<margin>That which is immortal is indissoluble.</margin>
<margin>The Soul is Immortal</margin>

->But it is just, O men, to consider that if the soul is immortal, it stands in great need of care, not only for this time in which we are said to live, but also for the sake of all eternity. For it must be thought a grave danger if anyone neglects the soul. For if death were the dissolution of the whole, it would certainly be a gain for the wicked: to be liberated from the body and from their own depravity along with the soul. But now, since the soul appears to be immortal, no escape from evils remains, no salvation, except that it becomes as good and as wise as possible. For the soul, when it migrates to the spirits of the dead, carries nothing else with it except its education and upbringing. These things, indeed, are said to be of the greatest benefit or harm immediately at the beginning of that migration. For they say that each person, migrating from here to there, is led by that guardian spirit <note>original: "demone"; the *daemon* or personal spirit assigned to a person at birth</note> which had fallen to his lot while living, to a certain place where all must be gathered together to be judged, and then set out for the lower world with that leader who was commanded to translate those departing from here to those places. But having obtained there what was necessary to obtain, and having stayed the required time, they are led back here again by another leader after many and long circuits of time. But the journey is not such as Telephus says in Aeschylus. For he says that the way to the lower world is simple. But I think it is neither simple nor one. Otherwise, there would be no need for leaders. For no one can go astray on a single path. On the contrary, it has many tracks and many turnings. This indeed may be conjectured from sacrifices and rites. Therefore, the moderate and wise soul follows its leader willingly and is not ignorant of its surroundings. But the soul that is infected by the desire for the body, as I said before, is for a long time passionately attached to it, and having struggled in many ways around the visible place and suffered much, is at last led away with difficulty by the spirit to whom its care had been assigned. But when it has arrived at those places where the other souls are: whoever is found to be unfaithful and liable to such a crime, who has contaminated himself with injustices...<-

Thus, destitute of all help, he wanders about until certain cycles of time are fulfilled. When these are finally completed, he is transferred by Necessity itself into a habitation suitable for him. But he who has passed a pure and moderate life, having found gods as companions and guides, dwells there where it is fitting for each. There are indeed many and wonderful places on the earth; and the earth itself is neither of such a kind nor of such a size as those who speak of the earth suppose, as has been passed down to me by someone. SIMMIAS. By what reasoning do you say these things, O Socrates? I have indeed heard many things about the orb of the earth. However, not these things which you say you have received as true. I would therefore gladly hear them from you. SOCRATES. And yet, O Simmias, the <margin>The Art of Glaucus. <note>A Greek proverb referring to a difficult or technical skill, named after a famous metalworker.</note></margin> Art of Glaucus does not seem to me necessary to narrate what those things are; but to prove that they are true seems to me to exceed the capacity of the Art of Glaucus. Furthermore, I perhaps would not be sufficient for it. Moreover, even if I knew it, my life, O Simmias, would by no means suffice for this longer narration. However, there is nothing to prevent me from saying what I believe to be the form of the orb of the earth and its regions. SIMMIAS. That will be enough. SOCRATES. I am persuaded, first, that if the earth is round in the middle of the heavens, it has no need of either air or any other such necessity to prevent it from ever falling. But for its support, it is enough that the heaven is entirely similar to itself on all sides, and the earth is in equilibrium on all sides. For a thing in equilibrium, placed in the middle of something similar, cannot incline more or less in any direction. And since it remains in a similar state, it stays free from inclination. This is the first thing I am persuaded of. SIMMIAS. And rightly so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, that the orb of the earth is immense; and that we dwell from Phasis <note>The Rioni River in Georgia, then considered the eastern limit of the known world.</note> to the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, the western limit.</note> in a certain small portion of it, like ants and frogs around marshes and the sea; and that there are indeed others in many similar places, for there are many and various hollows everywhere throughout the earth, according to their shapes and sizes, into which water, mists, and air flow together. But the pure earth itself lies in the pure heaven in which the stars are. Which most of those who treat these matters call the Ether. These things <note>the water and mist</note> are subject to it, as if settling, and always flow into the gaps of the earth. We, therefore, dwelling in these hollows, are so deceived that we believe we dwell upon the high surface of the earth. Just as if someone dwelling in the depths of the sea should think he inhabits the upper parts of the sea; and looking at the sun and the other stars through the sea, should think the sea itself is the heaven; because, on account of his slowness and weakness, he never emerged to the top of the sea, nor raised his head above the waves, and clearly saw how much purer and more beautiful this place is than that depth; nor indeed had he heard it from another who had looked upon it. This same thing, therefore, happens to us, who, dwelling in a certain hollow of the terrestrial orb, think we inhabit the high surface; and we call the air "heaven," as if we were looking at the movements of the stars through the heaven itself. And this happens to us because, on account of our weakness and slowness, we are unable to transcend to the very top of the air. But if someone were to emerge to the summit, or fly there relying on wings, he would see what is there as he emerged, just as fishes emerging from the sea see these things of ours. And if his nature were sufficient for looking, he would immediately recognize that that is the true heaven, and the true light, and also the true earth. For this earth which is inhabited by us, and these stones, and this whole place, are eaten away and corrupted, like the things in the sea are by the saltiness; nor does anything worthy of esteem grow in the sea; and, so to speak, there is nothing perfect in it, <margin>Nothing worthy grows in the sea.</margin> but there are caverns, sand, incredible slime, and filth wherever there is also earth. These things are in no way to be compared to our beauties. But the beauty of that place appears to exceed our own by far. Therefore, if it is also necessary to tell a beautiful story, it is worth the effort, Simmias, to hear what <margin>A story of the pure earth: and my own views.</margin> those regions of the earth are like that lie beneath the heaven. SIMMIAS. Indeed, we would most gladly hear this story. SOCRATES. They say then, O friend, first of all, that the face of that earth, if one looks down from above, appears like those balls which are woven from twelve pieces of leather, distinct with various colors, of which our colors, which painters use, retain a certain likeness. But there, the entire earth is made of such colors, and even much more brilliant and purer ones: part indeed is purple, endowed with wonderful beauty; part is of a golden color; part whiter than plaster and snow. Furthermore, it is similarly adorned with other colors, and even more and more beautiful ones than have ever come to our sight. For indeed, these very hollows of it, filled with water and air, bring a certain splendid appearance of color among the variety of the other colors, so that its single appearance always seems varied. In such an earth, trees, flowers, and fruits grow in a similar, fitting proportion. Furthermore, the mountains and stones there have perfection and transparency in a similar way, and colors much more beautiful. Of which indeed certain particles are the little stones which are prized among us: Sardius, Jaspers, Emeralds, and others of that kind. But there, there is nothing that is not of such a kind, or even more beautiful. The cause of which thing is that those stones are pure, and not worn away and corrupted by rot and saltiness like ours; which, flowing together into this place, infect the stones, the earth, animals, and plants, and force them to be diseased. But the earth itself is adorned with all these things, and also with gold and silver and other similar things. These shining things grow there, both many and large, throughout the whole earth; so that to see it is a spectacle for happy spectators. Furthermore, there are many animals there and men, some inhabiting the inland region, some around the air as we are around the shores of the sea; some also inhabit islands which, placed not far from the continent, are surrounded by air. But to speak summarily, what water and the sea are to us for our use, the air is there

# PHAEDO, OR ON THE SOUL.
## A.ii.

<note>original: "qd' vero nobis aer, id illis etherē esse"</note> What the air is to us, the ether is to them. The seasons there have such a perfect balance that the inhabitants live without disease, continuously, and far longer than those of our world. Likewise, in sight, hearing, wisdom, and all such faculties, they surpass us as much as the air surpasses water and the ether surpasses air in purity. Furthermore, there are temples and groves of the gods in which the gods truly dwell in familiarity; and oracles, divinations, and perceptions of the gods, and such intimacy exists between those men and the gods. The sun, moon, and stars are seen by them as they truly are; and in all other matters, they possess a happiness consistent with these things.

Thus, they relate that the entire Earth is naturally established, along with the things around it. Moreover, within the Earth itself, there are many hollow places in a circle, some deeper and wider than the region inhabited by us; others are indeed deeper, but have a narrower opening than our region; and in some places, they are less deep but wider than ours. All these are connected to one another beneath the earth and break through in many ways from all sides, sometimes through narrower passages and sometimes through wider ones, having channels and exits through which a great abundance of waters flows from some into others as if into mixing bowls. Likewise, there are incredible magnitudes of perpetual underground rivers of water, both hot and cold; and much fire, and vast rivers of fire. There are also many rivers of muddy liquid, some purer and some more foul, like the torrents of mud in Sicily <note>A reference to volcanic mudflows, likely from Mount Etna</note>, and the muddy rivers that follow them. Each place is filled by these wherever they happen to flow. All these things are moved up and down as if by a certain swinging mechanism <note>original: "suspēdiculo," referring to the oscillation of fluids</note> placed beneath the earth, balanced in such a way that it inclines and raises each side in turn.

This swinging exists because of a certain nature of this kind. One of the openings in the earth is indeed the greatest, pierced through the entire earth and staying open; concerning which Homer says: *Far, far away is the deepest pit beneath the earth.* <margin>Homer. The Pit <note>Barathrum</note> or Tartarus</margin> Which he elsewhere, and many of the poets, have called Tartarus. Into this reservoir all rivers flow together, and from it they flow out again. Each river takes on the character of the land through which it glides. The reason why all things flow out from here and flow back again is this: because this liquid has neither bottom nor foundation. Thus it is lifted and overflows up and down. The air and spirit <note>or breath</note> that move around it do the same. For the spirit follows the liquid both when it moves toward the upper parts of the earth and when it moves toward our parts. And just as in breathing animals the breath continually exhales and respires, so there also the spirit, raised together with the liquid, stirs up certain violent and incredible winds, whether it flows in or out.

Therefore, when the water falls down into the lower place through the passages of the earth, it flows in along those streams and overflows everywhere through them, filling them like those who draw water. But when it breaks out from there to here, it fills these places again. When they are full, the water overflows through the streams and the passages of the earth. And when the individual liquids have flowed there—each to its appropriate place—they create seas, lakes, rivers, and springs. Then, gliding back from here through the earth, some through longer and more numerous windings, and others through fewer and shorter ones, they flow back again into Tartarus. Some flow in much deeper than they were drawn out, others only a little; but all flow in lower than they flowed out, and some glide out through the opposite side from where they flowed in, while others go through the same side. But some, flowing around everywhere once or several times, coiling around the globe of the earth like snakes, glide back down as far as possible and mix again. It is permitted for each to flow down as far as the center, but no further; for the slope beyond that would be an ascent from either side.

Accordingly, there are many other large and various streams. But there are four principal ones. The largest and outermost of these, surrounding the earth, is called Oceanus. <margin>Oceanus, Acheron, Acherusia</margin> From the opposite region flows the Acheron, which, flowing through other desert places and through underground regions, flows down into the Acherusian Lake. This is where the souls of most of the deceased arrive; and there, having stayed for certain fated cycles of time—some longer, some shorter—they are sent back again into the generations of living beings. A third river flows between these two. Not having progressed very far, it falls into a vast place burning with much fire, and creates a lake larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. From here it flows around, turbid and muddy, encircling the earth, and reaches the edges of the Acherusian Lake, yet it does not mix with that water; but having revolved many times under the earth, it flows down swallowed up below Tartarus. <margin>Pyriphlegethon, Styx or Stygius</margin> They name this river Pyriphlegethon <note>The "Fire-Flaming" river</note>; some of its streams break off and flow wherever they happen upon the earth. From the opposite region, a fourth river first breaks out into a wild and harsh place, as they say, and the whole place has a color like Cyaneus <note>Dark blue or lapis lazuli</note>. They name this the Stygian river, and this river, gliding along, creates the lake Styx. Falling into this place and taking on violent powers in the water, it hides itself under the earth; winding around, it glides opposite the Pyriphlegethon and meets it in the Acherusian Lake from the opposite side. Nor does its water mix with any other.

When the deceased have arrived at that place <margin>The immortal soul</margin> to which the guiding spirit <note>daemon</note> leads each one, they are first judged—both those who lived honorably and holily, and those who lived otherwise. Thus, whoever is found to have held a certain middle path in life, having set out for the Acheron on the vehicles provided for each, arrives at the Acherusian Lake; there they dwell, being purged and paying the penalties for their injuries; and when they are purified, they are absolved; and each receives rewards for their good deeds according to their merit. But those who, because of the magnitude of their crimes, seem incurable—namely those who have committed many and great sacrileges, or unjust murders, or other similar things—a fitting fate plunges these into Tartarus, from which they never emerge. But those who have committed curable but great sins, such as if they did something through violence in anger against a father or mother...

# BOOK ON THE SOLE

<page-num>XXIX.</page-num>

...they have lived, but moved by repentance have honored them for the rest of their lives; or those who in a similar way were once murderers: it is necessary for these to fall into **Tartarus** <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld used as a dungeon of torment</note>, but having stayed there for a year, they are cast out by the wave—the murderers through **Cocytus** <note>The river of lamentation</note>, and the violators of parents through **Pyriphlegethon** <note>The river of fire</note>. After they have been carried by these rivers to the **Acherusian marsh**, they call out there and summon those whom they either killed or affected with injuries; they beg as suppliants and pray that they be permitted to pass through the marsh and be absolved there. If they succeed, they enter and receive an end to their evils. If they cannot persuade them, they are carried back into Tartarus and from there again into the rivers, and they do not cease being carried through these evils until they have obtained forgiveness from those they injured. For this is the penalty imposed on them by the judges.

But those who are found to have lived piously above others, these are they who, released and freed from these earthly places as if from a prison, ascend to higher things and inhabit a pure region above the earth. Among these, whoever has been sufficiently purified through **philosophy** live entirely without bodies for all time to come, and they obtain even more beautiful habitations. The beauty of these is neither easy to describe, nor would the present time suffice for the telling.

But for the sake of these things which have been narrated, O **Simmias**, every effort must be made so that in this life we may attain virtue, prudence, and wisdom. For the reward is beautiful, and the hope is great. Now, to assert that these things are exactly as I have laid them out does not befit a man of sound mind; yet that either these or some such things exist concerning our souls and their habitations—since the soul itself appears to be immortal—seems to me to be fitting and worthy for those taking the risk to believe. For the danger is noble; and it is necessary to pour these things into our minds like the songs of the **magi** <note>original: "magorum ritu" - referring to incantations or healing songs</note>, which is why I have been drawing out this myth for so long.

But for the sake of these things, a man ought to have good hope for his soul, whoever has neglected the pleasures and ornaments of the body as being foreign and leading to the opposite, and has pursued the pleasures perceived in learning with zeal, and has decorated his soul not with a foreign ornament, but with its own: **temperance, justice, fortitude, liberty, and truth**. Thus he awaits the migration from this life, ready to migrate whenever fate shall call. You indeed, O Simmias and **Cebes**, and the others present, will each migrate at some time in the future. But me, as some tragic poet might say, fate now calls. And it is almost time for me to turn to the bath. For it is better, I think, to drink the poison after the bath, so that we do not provide the women the trouble of washing a corpse.

When he had said these things, **Crito** spoke thus: "Tell me, O Socrates, what do you charge these men or me to do, either regarding your sons or other matters? By doing what would we most please you?"

"I prescribe nothing new," he said, "but what I always tell you: namely, if you take care of yourselves, whatever you do will be pleasing to me and to yourselves, even if you do not agree to it now in words. But if you neglect yourselves and are unwilling to direct your lives according to the footsteps of what has been said from former times, you will profit nothing at all, even if you grant many things to us now in our dispute."

"These things," said Crito, "will be our care. But how do you command us to bury you?"

"However you please," he said, "if indeed you can catch me and I do not escape you." And smiling at the same time and turning to us, he said: "I cannot persuade Crito that I am this Socrates who now disputes and arranges each word. But he thinks I am that which he will see as a corpse a little later. And so he asks how he should bury me. But what I have contended for a long time with many words—that after I have drunk the poison, I shall no longer be with you, but shall depart to the felicities of the blessed—this I seem to have said to Crito in vain, consoling you and myself at the same time. Therefore, give a guarantee for me to Crito, a guarantee contrary to that which he gave to the judges. For he guaranteed that I would stand at the trial; but you, guarantee that I will not stay after I have died, but will depart; so that Crito may bear my death more easily, and not, seeing my body either burned or buried, lament for me as if I were suffering something dire. Nor should he say at the funeral that Socrates is laid out, or carried out, or placed under the earth. Know this for certain, best Crito: to speak wrongly is not only a fault in itself, but it also does some harm to souls. But one must be confident and say that my body is being buried, and buried in such a way as will please you and as you judge to be most just."

Having said these things, he rose and entered a certain chamber as if to wash. Crito followed him, but he ordered us to wait. We waited, therefore, talking among ourselves about the things that had been said and considering them again. Moreover, we lamented our fortune, that as if deprived of a parent, we were to be orphans for the remainder of our lives. When Socrates had washed, his boys were brought to him. For he had two small sons and one who was already grown. The women of his household also came. When Socrates had spoken to them in the presence of Crito and had commanded what he wished, he ordered the women and boys to depart; he himself returned to us, now near sunset; for he had stayed inside for a very long time.

When he had come to us washed, he sat down. Not much was said after this, when the officer of the **Eleven** <note>The magistrates in charge of executions in Athens</note> came. Standing by him, he said: "O Socrates, I do not think I shall find in you that novelty which I am accustomed to find in others. For they are indignant with me and curse me when I announce to them that the poison must be drunk, as the magistrates compel. But I have known you, especially in this time, to be the most noble, the gentlest, and the best man of all who have ever come to this place. And now I know for certain that you will not be angry with me, but with those whom you know are the cause of this matter. Now, therefore, you know what news I bring to you. Farewell, and strive to bear what is necessary as easily as you can." And saying this, he turned away weeping.

Socrates, looking at him, said: "And you, farewell; we shall do so." And turning to us at the same time: "How polite this man is," he said. "Not only now, but in the past time also he used to greet me and speak with me sometimes, and he was always the best of men. And now how noble..."

# ARGUMENT OF THE MENEXENUS.
A.iiii.

me to tears. But come, O Crito, let us spare him; and if the poison is already ground, let someone bring it here. If it is not yet ground, let that man grind it. But I think indeed, said Crito, O Socrates, that the sun has not yet left the mountains nor set. And I know others who, after it was announced to them, were accustomed to drink it very late, having dined and drunk abundantly; and sometimes even having enjoyed those for whose love they were affected. Therefore, do not hurry so much. For there is still time remaining. Then Socrates said: Rightly, O Crito, do those men do those things. For they think that by doing these things they gain something. But I shall rightly not do those things. For I hope to gain nothing if I drink the poison a little later, except that I might seem ridiculous to myself as if I were greedy for life, and a preserver of that thing of which nothing more is now present to me. But come now, obey me, and do not do otherwise. Crito, having heard these things, nodded to the boy who was not far away. He, having gone out and stayed a little while, returned, leading with him the one who was to give the poison; he brought it ground in a cup. Looking at him, Socrates said: Come, good man, for you have skill in these matters, what ought I to do? Nothing else, he said, than to walk about after the drink until you feel your legs grow heavy. Then indeed lie down; and so you shall do. Saying these things, he reached out the cup to Socrates. Socrates indeed received it quite cheerfully, O Echecrates, not at all disturbed, with neither his color nor his expression changed. But just as he was accustomed, looking at him like a bull <note>original: "taurine" - a reference to Socrates' characteristic steady, intense gaze</note>, he said: What do you say? Is it permitted to sacrifice from this cup by pouring a libation? We have ground only so much, O Socrates, as we thought would be enough. I understand, he said. But it is both permitted and necessary to pray to the gods that our migration <note>death/transition of the soul</note> may be happy. Which indeed I pray for; and may it be so. And as soon as he had said these things, he drank it off quite easily and readily. Most of us had been able to hold back our tears in a way until then; but after we saw him drinking, and having drunk, we could no longer; but indeed grief so overcame me that tears now flowed abundantly from me. Therefore, covering myself, I wept for myself; not for him indeed, but for my own fortune, who had been deprived of such a friend. Crito, even before this, since he could not contain his tears, had risen. But Apollodorus had never ceased to weep even in the time before. Then indeed, crying out especially, he left no one of those present whose lot he did not bewail, except for the lot of Socrates alone. He, noticing these things, said: What are you doing, O wonderful men! Indeed, I sent away the women chiefly for this reason, lest they should do such things. For I have heard that one should depart from this life in a blessing <note>in peace/silence</note>. Be quiet, therefore, and endure. We, hearing these things, felt ashamed and ceased from tears. But he, when he felt his legs grow heavy while walking about, lay down on his back; for so the one who provided the poison had ordered. He, a little later touching him, examined his feet and legs. Then, pressing his foot more heavily, he asked if he felt it. Socrates said no. He pressed the shins again; and gradually ascending with his hand, he showed us that they were becoming cold and stiff. And he touched him again; and said that when it reached the heart, then he would depart. Now therefore his vitals had grown cold, when, uncovering himself—for he was covered with a garment—he said, which was his last voice: O Crito, we owe a cock to Aesculapius <note>The god of healing; Socrates implies death is the cure for the "sickness" of life</note>; pay it, and do not neglect it. It shall be done, said Crito, as you command. But see if you wish anything else. To this question he answered nothing <margin>A cock to Aesculapius</margin> further. But a little later he was moved. And the attendant uncovered him; and his eyes were fixed. When Crito saw this, he composed his mouth and eyes. This was the end of our friend, O Echecrates: a man, in our judgment, of all those whom we have known, the best, and especially the wisest and most just.

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino on the Menexenus to Lorenzo de' Medici, a Magnanimous Man.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a classical figure or scholar seated at a desk with books.</image-desc>

The purpose of Plato in the *Menexenus* is to exhort all to the highest love of country; and he does the same elsewhere in the *Crito*, the *Laws*, and the *Republic*. Here, however, he effects this in two principal ways. First indeed, while he praises those who intrepidly undergo dangers and death for the safety of the fatherland. Then while he himself extols the antiquity and virtues of his own fatherland with wonderful praises. But you, note immediately from the beginning, that moral philosophy is indeed greatly necessary for a man about to govern a republic. Soon, that it is noble to fall in war, namely for the safety of the fatherland; and that this is confirmed by the fact that this is honored most of all among all nations. Then, taking the occasion from oratorical praises, observe how pernicious flattery is. For he judges common oratory in the *Gorgias* to be a species of flattery. In the *Phaedrus*, however, he calls a flatterer a beast pestilential to the human race. And he affirms him to be similar to an impure demon, continually polluting incautious minds with the filth of the body under the bait of harmful pleasure. Here, furthermore, he judges the flatterer, both private and public, to be very similar to sorcerers and poisoners: since he, worse and more unjust than a thief or a murderer, takes away from us not money, nor merely the life of the body itself; but rather, like a sacrilegious man, he steals and withdraws a sacred thing, namely the judgment of reason, under the appearance of good. And see how greatly he deceives. For not only in hidden matters, but—what is wonderful—he deceives most skillfully in the most manifest things. For to whom is the origin of his grandfathers and fathers not most evident? Likewise the very size and form of his own body! Nevertheless, in these things also, the poisoner-flatterers circumvent us: as much more cruel than Circe as they inflict a more grievous loss. For she, with her cups, changed the exterior of men...

# BOOK XXX.
### XXX.

<note>original: "nis fertur in bestias transformasse"</note> is said to have transformed men into beasts, these people [the orators] transform the inner man with their charms. Therefore, Socrates mocks the orators who hunt for popular favor with every possible device: they praise others beyond measure so that they themselves might be praised in return; they treat a trivial matter with heavy zeal and long-standing premeditation. He then proceeds to what he had established from the beginning, namely, to exhort everyone to defend their fatherland: specifically by praising those who fell for their country. For this was an ancient custom of the Athenians: to praise them annually in a public assembly and, moreover, to celebrate funeral rites. But lest he attribute more to the oratorical faculty than is right, he asserts that he received a speech of this kind from another, and indeed from a woman, Aspasia <note>The mistress of Pericles and a famous rhetorician</note>. This is especially because it is not in the nature of the Socratic spirit to harangue in the manner of orators. He clearly declares in what specific order praise should be given, especially in a funeral oration. 

As for his statement that in the beginning, in the region of Attica, only humans were born spontaneously from the earth, while in other regions only brutes were similarly produced from the earth, accept this however you please, whether as from a philosopher or rather an orator. Know, however, that it is a Platonic opinion: that after vast floods of the earth, from the abundant moisture and heat following the deluge, the earth is rendered so fertile that not only tiny animals, such as now exist, but even large ones, and even humans themselves, are born of their own accord. He confirms this both here and often elsewhere. Many of the Egyptians and Greeks felt this, as did many Arabs; finally, Al-Ghazali and Avicenna <note>Famous Persian philosophers</note> especially confirmed it. Aristotle used this opinion in his *Natural Questions* according to the mind of the ancients, saying: just as in small changes of time certain small animals sprout from the earth, so in greater changes greater ones, and finally in the greatest changes the largest and most perfect. Plato, however, everywhere brings forth living beings from the bowels of the earth itself, employing the "artisan gods" as ministers of the worldly architect. By "gods," I mean the Ideas and specific Reasons residing in the life of the world and the divine intelligence: through which, both immediately after deluges and daily, the species of living things are formed wherever the seed of that same species seems to be absent. We have sufficiently proved in our *Theology* that this must happen. 

But where a human is born, he does not only employ the hands of the gods as for the others, but also a certain breath of the highest God and a more express image. Then, for those just born, at least in the first ages, he appoints the gods themselves as leaders and teachers. You, however, should prudently choose from all these things those which are more in harmony with Mosaic wisdom <note>Referring to the Bible/Moses</note>. Indeed, it most agrees with Moses that here, and in the *Protagoras*, *Statesman*, and *Critias*, he maintains that man was once produced from the earth by the authorship of God in the likeness of God himself. What kind of floods these are, and when and for what cause, we shall teach in the *Timaeus*. 

After this, a man distinguished by piety pursues the praises of his fatherland with a certain wonderful charity and art: from the origin of the fatherland, from the very form of the republic, from daily discipline, and from outstanding deeds: which are most manifest both here and elsewhere from other writers. Therefore, let us conclude our argument in a few words, noting sentences of this kind: 
* Prosperity first breeds emulation, then envy, and finally dissensions and wars. 
* All possession without moral virtue is not only useless but harmful. 
* Knowledge separated from moral virtue is to be judged not wisdom, but a certain craftiness. 
* The splendor of ancestors becomes obscure in their sons unless it is passed on to posterity through their own lack of idleness. 
* It is not to be wished that everything succeeds according to one's vow. 
* The old proverb must be observed in all things: *Nothing in excess.* 
* He who has so prepared himself that everything contributing to happiness depends on himself, or comes as close as possible to this, has instituted his life best. 
* Do not exult with joy or be cast down by grief. 
* Parents ought to judge that they have begotten sons not to be immortal, but to be good. 
* The mournful lamentations of the household are troublesome to the deceased, if indeed they hear them. 
* It is fitting to pursue with a certain perpetual solemn honor those who bore themselves strenuously in war for the safety of the fatherland: their children are to be educated by public care, and their parents are to be cherished. 
* Lest circumstances themselves be unjust to us, they must be endured with an equal mind.

### THE MENEXENUS OF PLATO, OR ON ATTIC ANTIQUITY, OR THE FUNERAL ORATION, TRANSLATED BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE TO JULIAN DE' MEDICI, A MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN.

-> SOCRATES, MENEXENUS. <-

<margin>
It is noble to fall in war.
</margin>

Do you come from the Forum, Menexenus? Or from where? ME. From the forum, O Socrates, and from the senate-house. SO. What brings you to the senate? Is it perhaps because you think you have already reached the end of your discipline and philosophy and have sufficiently perfected yourself, and now study to attempt greater things hereafter, and even to command us elders, you who are so much younger: so that your family might always, as it is accustomed, provide us with a counselor? ME. If you yourself permit and advise it, O Socrates, I will give it my effort. But if not, by no means. Now, however, I went to the council for this reason: because I had heard that someone was to be chosen who should adorn the deceased with praises. For, as you know, they are about to perform funeral rites. SO. I have indeed heard; but whom did they choose especially? ME. No one. For they deferred it until tomorrow. I think, however, that Archinus or Dion will be chosen. SOCRA. It seems, Menexenus, among many nations to be a noble thing to fall in war. For he who thus departs from life is honored with a most magnificent funeral and tomb. And even if a poor man dies thus—

# MENEXENUS OR THE FUNERAL ORATION. FOLIO CCXII.
A.iiii.

<margin>That those who had fallen in war were honored with praise and a funeral</margin>
...departs, he does not lack praise: even if someone is of low station or a coward, he is nonetheless extolled by wise men. These men do not praise in vain or at random, but with a maturely composed and deliberate speech so extraordinary that while they proclaim both the qualities that are present and those that are not, they steal away and lead captive the minds of the listeners with the elegance of their words, as if by some magic or sorcery. Meanwhile, they adorn the City <note>Athens</note> as they please, and those who fell in arms. They weave again the origin of our ancestors. They even extol us who are still living. For this reason, Menexenus, being uplifted by them, I am usually affected in a very noble manner: and as I give them my ears, I am soothed by a wonderful sweetness. Immediately I consider myself greater, nobler, and more beautiful than before. Often some guests hear these things with me, and in their eyes I am rendered more excellent than before. Indeed, the same thing seems to happen to them as to me, both toward myself and the rest of the city. For they are immediately persuaded by the orator to think the city more admirable than before. And this glorious beauty remains with me for more than three days: so harmonious is the speech and the melodious voice flowing from the orator's mouth into my ears, that only on the fourth or fifth day do I remember myself and recognize where in the world I am. Only then do I realize I was deceived, having previously thought myself settled in the Islands of the Blessed <note>A mythical paradise for heroes</note>. To such an extent are the rhetoricians among us ingenious.

**MENEXENUS.** You are always joking about the rhetoricians, O Socrates. But now I suspect that the one who is chosen may lack the faculty of speaking, for the choice fell upon him suddenly. Therefore, whoever is to speak will perhaps be forced to make words unexpectedly.

**SOCRATES.** Why, my good man? Are there not speeches composed for each of these? Besides, it is not difficult to speak of these things without meditation. If indeed it were necessary for Athenians to speak in the Peloponnese, or Peloponnesians in Athens, then an eloquent orator would be needed to persuade and prove his point. But when someone exerts himself among the very people he praises, his words are easily approved.

**MENEXENUS.** Do you think that is easy, Socrates?

**SOCRATES.** I certainly do.

**MENEXENUS.** And do you hope that you could speak yourself, if it were necessary and you were chosen by the council?

**SOCRATES.** What wonder is it, Menexenus, that I am sufficient for speaking, I who have had a teacher by no means unskilled in rhetoric? She has rendered many others eloquent orators, including the one most excellent of all the Greeks, Pericles the son of Xanthippus.

**MENEXENUS.** Who is she? Do you mean Aspasia? <note>A highly influential woman in Athens, partner of Pericles, known for her intellectual and rhetorical skill.</note>

**SOCRATES.** I mean her, and also Connus the son of Metrobius. These two are my instructors: Connus in music, and Aspasia in rhetoric. Thus it is no wonder that a man so educated is eloquent in these matters. Indeed, even if someone were less learned than I—taught music by Lamprus and rhetoric by Antiphon of Rhamnus—he could still, by praising Athenians among the Athenians themselves, speak so as to have his speech approved by the listeners.

**MENEXENUS.** What then would you have to bring forward, if you had to speak?

**SOCRATES.** From myself, perhaps nothing. But yesterday I heard Aspasia herself dictating a funeral oration about these men. For she had heard what you yourself were saying, that the Athenians were going to elect someone to hold a speech over them. Then, partly from what she composed on the spot, and partly from what she had previously considered, she wove together a funeral oration, which she said Pericles composed by putting together certain remains from it.

**MENEXENUS.** Could you remember what Aspasia said?

**SOCRATES.** Certainly, unless I am mistaken; for I learned it from her, and she nearly struck me with blows because of my forgetfulness.

**MENEXENUS.** Why do you not repeat it?

**SOCRATES.** I fear my teacher might be angry with me if I publish her speech.

**MENEXENUS.** Not at all, Socrates. Rather, do me the favor: whether you wish to say the speech of Aspasia or anyone else, only speak.

**SOCRATES.** Perhaps you will laugh at me, if I, an old man, still seem to you to be joking.

**MENEXENUS.** Far be it, O Socrates. Speak, I pray you.

**SOCRATES.** I must indulge you. For indeed, if you ordered me to dance naked, since we are alone, I would obey. But listen now. For in this manner, I believe, she began to speak, taking her beginning from the deceased themselves.

<margin>Those praised give a wide-ranging speech of blessing about themselves.</margin>

<margin>The Funeral Oration.</margin>
In deed itself, fitting honors have been shown to these men among us: those who, having reached the end, now make their fatal journey, honored both publicly by the city and privately by their kin with magnificent expense and a great gathering of followers. Furthermore, the law commands that a word of praise be added; and indeed, it is fitting. For when deeds are well done, through the very adornment of words, a perennial memory and splendor reaches the listeners on behalf of those who performed them. There is a need for a speech that sufficiently praises the dead, kindly warns the survivors, exhorts their sons and brothers to the imitation of their virtue, and consoles the parents and any other ancestors who remain. What speech, then, shall we have? Or from where shall we most powerfully begin to praise these illustrious men, who while living delighted their own people wonderfully with their virtue, and did not hesitate to offer themselves to death for the safety of the living? It seems to me, therefore, that it is necessary to praise them according to their nature, just as they became good men; and they became good because they drew their origin from good stock. Therefore, let us first praise their noble lineage. Then their education and discipline. Finally, let us relate how their deeds were performed in a manner most becoming to those who were born of such ancestors and so educated. The first praise of their race is that the origin of their ancestors was not foreign; nor did they leave these successors here as if they were strangers or new men born of immigrants, but as indigenous people truly inhabiting their own fatherland, living and nourished not by a stepmother, as others are, but by their own mother—the very region they inhabited. In this land they are now buried after finishing their lives, namely in the bowels of her who bore them, nourished them, and received them. It is right, therefore, to honor the mother herself before all things, for in this way their race is most highly cultivated. This region is to be celebrated not only by us, but by all men, for many other reasons and especially because it is most dear to the gods. This is testified by the contest of the gods <note>The myth of Athena and Poseidon competing for patronage of the city</note> concerning this place. Why then should a land praised by the gods not be praised by all men—

<margin>
The Attic land produced man first.

Who would not join in praising her? Her second glory is this: that at the time when the earth was producing all kinds of living creatures, wild beasts and all grazing things, our land alone remained sterile of these and void of wild animals, but specifically chose to give birth to man from among all living beings. Man excels the rest in intelligence and alone pays heed to justice and the gods. That this region truly fathered these ancestors of ours can be most clearly recognized from this: for everything that gives birth contains the nourishment suitable for the newborn. By this, one plainly discerns the woman who has truly given birth from the one who has substituted a child by pretense; for she who gave birth abounds in milk for the nourishment of that which was begotten, while the other does not. Therefore, our land and mother provides a clear proof that she procreated men. For she was the first and only one then to offer human food: the fruits of wheat and barley, by which the human race is most conveniently nourished, as she truly produced that specific living being. Moreover, one may infer this more truly of the earth than of a woman. For the earth does not imitate a woman in conception and birth, but woman imitates the earth. Indeed, this kind of food she supplied without envy, in abundance, not only to men

but also to the cattle. After this, she supplied olive oil as a relief for the labors of her children. Once her sons were nourished and grown, she introduced gods as rulers and teachers. Their names must be passed over for now <note>The author likely refers to Athena and Hephaestus, or perhaps Demeter</note>. For it is not hidden from us who fortified our life, both by the invention of arts looking toward daily sustenance and by the tradition and skill of arms for the protection of the region itself. Thus the ancestors of these men, having been born and educated, established a Republic <note>Latin: *respublica*, here referring to the Athenian constitution or "Politeia"</note>, which it is fitting to touch upon in a few words. For a Republic is the education of men: a good one for good men, and the opposite for the contrary. It must be declared, therefore, that our ancestors were nurtured in an excellent Republic, through which both they and these men became the good men they were, including those who have now departed from life. For it was the same Republic then as it is now: namely, a government of the best <note>Aristocracy/Optimatum gubernatio</note>, under which we live in these times and have lived almost always since that time. Some call it a democracy, others by other names, however it pleases them. But in reality, it is a government of the best with a certain authority of the people. We always have leaders, sometimes created by succession of birth, sometimes by election; but the greatest authority of the city lies with the people, who always bestow the magistracies upon those judged to be the best. There, no one is rejected because of the weakness, poverty, or ignobility of their parents, nor is anyone honored for the opposite reasons, as is customary in other cities. But this is the sum of it: whoever is held to be wise or good, rules and commands. The cause of this kind of government for us is our birth from equality. For other cities are composed of various and dissimilar races. Thus it happens that their governments are also unequal: tyrannies and the powers of a few. In these, men live in such a way that they regard one another partly as masters and partly as slaves. But we and our people, all born from one mother as brothers to one another, do not think we are masters and slaves of each other; rather, the equality of our birth leads us to seek equality of law, and to yield to no thing at all except the reputation for virtue and wisdom. For this reason, both our parents and the parents of these men, being honorably born and nurtured in all liberty, performed many noble deeds well-known among all nations both privately and publicly; they believed that for the sake of liberty they must fight against Greeks for the sake of other Greeks, and against barbarians for the sake of all Greeks. Truly, how the Argives once behaved in war against the Cadmeans, and the Heraclidae against the Argives, and when Eumolpus and the Amazons and even those before them invaded the region, it would be a brief matter to relate according to their dignity; and the virtue of those poets elegantly celebrating them with music has spread their fame among all nations. Therefore, if we were to attempt to repeat the same things now in plain speech, we might perhaps seem inferior to them. I think these things should be left aside for this reason: since they seem already sufficiently celebrated according to their dignity. But those things which have not yet been sung by any poet as the dignity of the matter requires, and yet have not been deleted by oblivion, these I think must now be proclaimed by us, so that we may praise and assist them, and provoke others to adorn the same with odes and other songs as is fitting. Of the things I speak of, these are the first. When the Persians ruled Asia and were dominating Europe, the men of this region stood in their way—men born here, our ancestors, whom it is especially necessary and fitting to remember and to praise for their virtue. For one must know their virtue if one is to sufficiently praise the deeds done by them in that time when all Asia had already served a third king. The first of these, Cyrus, by a certain greatness of soul, restoring his fellow Persians to liberty, simultaneously subjected their masters the Medes and ruled all Asia as far as Egypt. His son then ruled Egypt and Libya as far as he was able to penetrate. The third, Darius, extended his empire by land-battle as far as the Scythians, and by naval power he dominated the sea and the islands. Thus it happened that no one dared to resist him. Indeed, the minds of all men were already cast down by a certain slavish dread, so many, numerous, and warlike were the nations held under the Persian empire. But Darius, accusing us and the Eretrians of plotting against Sardis, and having found this occasion for war, sent five hundred thousand men in fleets, and three hundred ships; he put Datis in charge of these and commanded him to bring the Eretrians and Athenians to him as captives, if his own head were dear to him. He, having sailed to Eretria—where there were not a few men, and who moreover were numbered among the most illustrious of the Greeks of that time in matters of war—made them captives in three days. And so that there would be no place for escape, he searched the entire region. Indeed, his soldiers, having reached the borders of Eretria and extending themselves from sea to sea, ran through the entire region with joined hands, so that they could report to the king that no one had escaped them. With the same intent, they descended from Eretria to Marathon, as it was the most suitable place for them to lead the Athenians away as captives together with the Eretrians, as if under the same yoke. While these things were partly accomplished and partly attempted, none of the Greeks except the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> came to the aid of the Eretrians or Athenians. And they arrived on the day following the battle...
