# MENEXENUS OR THE FUNERAL ORATION

...others <note>original: "rũ. Cæteri"</note> were all terrified: and thinking they were doing well if they escaped the present danger, they remained quiet. From this one may perceive how great was the valor of those who sustained the attack of the barbarians at Marathon and subdued their pride. It is fitting, therefore, to award the first prize of honor to them in our speech; and the second to those who defeated the enemy in the naval battles around Salamis and Artemisium. Indeed, we could relate many deeds performed by these men: how many dangers threatening by land and sea they endured and overcame; but I will now recount what I consider most extraordinary above all else. For they completed what remained after the Battle of Marathon. If those who fought at Marathon demonstrated only this to the Greeks: that a few Greeks could break the attack of many barbarians in a land battle, the victory at sea was still uncertain. The Persians believed themselves to be invincible in maritime battles due to their multitude, wealth, skill, and strength. Therefore, this is worthy of praise in those who then fought in the ships: that they utterly drove away the deep-seated fear instilled in the Greeks, and ensured they would no longer dread the number of ships or the prowess of the enemy. Both things were achieved twice, as much by those fighting on land at Marathon as by those later at sea around Salamis: so that the rest of the Greeks might be both taught and provoked—by the former on land, and by the latter at sea—to fearlessly engage in battles against the barbarians. I assert that the third event, which took place at Plataea, was the cause of Greek safety through both numbers and valor. That deed was common to both the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note> and the Athenians. Therefore, all these Greeks will be praised in the highest degree by us and by posterity. After these things, many Greek cities were still falling under the barbarians. Moreover, the King <note>The Persian King</note> threatened that he would invade the Greeks again. It is surely right to commemorate those who put the finishing touch on the works of their predecessors by driving every barbarian from the sea. These were the men who fought with the fleet around Eurymedon, and those who went to campaign in Cyprus, and likewise those who sailed to Egypt and traveled through many other coastal lands. It is necessary to remember these men; thanks must be given to them, for they compelled the terrified King to think of his own safety rather than to lay snares for the destruction of the Greeks. And that war was spread through all the cities, while the Greeks defended themselves and all men of the same tongue against the barbarians. But when peace was finally made and the city was honored, there happened to her what usually arises among men toward those who are successful: first indeed emulation, <margin>Emulation, Envy, war arising from prosperity.</margin> and from emulation, then envy, which dragged this city unwillingly into waging war with the Greeks. After this, the war having begun, they clashed at Tanagra, contending for the liberty of the Boeotians against the Lacedaemonians. And since the outcome of the battle was uncertain, what followed afterward revealed the matter itself. For many indeed fled, deserting the Boeotians to whom they had come to bring aid. Our men, however, gaining victory on the third day at Oenophyta, justly brought back those who had unjustly fled. These were certainly the first after the Persian war to help the Greeks for the sake of liberty against other Greeks; being noble men and authors of liberty for those to whom they brought help, they are placed first among those honored by the city in these monuments. After these things were accomplished, when the war increased in intensity and all the Greeks took up arms and devastated the region, returning an unworthy thanks to the city, our men overcame them in a naval battle and captured their leaders, the Lacedaemonians. Although it was permitted to slay them, they released them and confirmed a peace, thinking that against men of the same race one should fight only until victory, <margin>One must fight against those of the same race until victory; against barbarians until death.</margin> and that the Greek community should not be utterly dissolved because of the city's own indignation; but against barbarians, one must fight to the death. It is fitting, therefore, to praise these men who lie here after this war was finished, since they showed that the suspicion of those was vain who, distrusting the valor of the Athenians, thought that in the first war against the barbarians some others had been more outstanding than the Athenians. For when all Greece was agitated by seditions, and they themselves had captured men superior to the rest of the Greeks in war, they declared that they could conquer individually those with whom they had collectively defeated the barbarians. A third unforeseen and heavy war arose after this peace, in which many brave men fell and are buried here. Many of them gained numerous victories around Sicily for the safety of the Leontines, to whom they were bound by oath to bring aid, under which treaty they had sailed to those places. But since the voyage was long, and meanwhile the city was pressed by a crisis of affairs and poverty and could not help them, their affairs did not succeed well because supplies were denied. Their enemies and adversaries in war have a greater praise for temperance and valor than the friends of others. Furthermore, many in the naval war through the Hellespont captured all the ships of the adversaries in one day and defeated many others. I have called the war "unforeseen and hard" for this reason: because no one would have thought that all the remaining Greeks would be kindled with such bitter zeal of contention against the city that they would not hesitate to provoke that most hostile barbarian King (whom they had expelled together with us) through ambassadors to bring war upon the Greeks, and to gather everyone, both Greeks and barbarians, to besiege this city. There especially the power and valor of this city shone forth. For when it was thought she had already succumbed, and the ships were besieged around Mitylene, they themselves, going aboard sixty ships to bring aid, being men of undisputed bravery, routed the enemy and liberated their friends; but falling into a hard and unworthy fate, not being recovered from the sea, they lie here. It is fitting to remember them always with praise. For by their valor not only—

# BOOK VII.

### PAGE XXX.

...from the naval battle at that time: but we also carried away the victory in the remaining fight. Indeed, it was because of those men that our city attained such great glory, that it was believed by all men that she could never be conquered. This was certainly judged to be not far from the truth. For we were not overcome by the traps or strength of others, but by our own internal dissension. Truly, even now we remain unconquered by them; rather, we conquered ourselves: we succumbed to our own selves. After these times, when all was quiet and peace had been made with others, an internal sedition <note>civil strife or domestic uprising</note> arose among us. In this, they conducted themselves in such a way that, if it were decreed by the fates that men must be agitated by seditions, no one would wish to be "sick" for their fatherland in any other way. 

For how kindly and like members of one household did the citizens from the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens, associated with the democratic faction</note> and the City meet with one another, contrary to the expectation of the rest of the Greeks! And how moderately did they manage and settle the war stirred up against those who were at Eleusis? Truly, there is no other cause for all these things except for their true kinship: which instilled a firm and kindred friendship in these men, not in word, but in deed. 

It is necessary, moreover, to honor the memory even of those who fell by mutual wounds in this war; and as much as we are able, we must reconcile them to one another with prayers and sacrifices, performed on behalf of those who survived: since we ourselves have been reconciled. For it was not through wickedness or enmity, but through a certain misfortune that they joined hands against each other. We who are survivors are ourselves witnesses of these things. For we are joined to them by race: we mutually give and receive forgiveness, whether for what we inflicted upon another, or what we suffered from another. 

Then, when the city was resting in the greatest tranquility of affairs, she forgave the barbarians <note>Non-Greeks, specifically the Persians</note> who, having been harassed by her, had fought back bravely. But she was indignant with the Greeks, because in return for benefits received, they had at times returned injury by entering into an alliance with the barbarians; they plundered the ships by which they had been saved, and they tore down the walls which we once defended so that their own walls would not fall. Therefore, the city resolved no longer to protect the Greeks if they should ever be oppressed by either Greeks or barbarians. 

While we were settled in this opinion, the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>—thinking that we, the guardians of liberty, were cast down, and that it would be their task hereafter to subjugate others—acted in this way. What need is there for many words? For I would not speak of ancient deeds, nor the deeds of many men that followed. It does not escape us that in the past the leading Greeks—the Argives, Boeotians, and Corinthians—implored the help of this city. And what is most divine of all: the King <note>The Great King of Persia</note> himself was pressed by such great need that he trusted he could protect his safety from no other source than from this city, which he had previously attempted to destroy with all his zeal. 

Truly, if anyone wishes to accuse the character of this city, he will only be able to object to this: that she is affected too much by mercy, and too diligently lifts up those who are falling. For at that time she could not endure to keep what she had resolved. She had indeed decreed never to bring aid to any of those from whom she had received injury when they were falling. Yet she changed her purpose and provided help. Whence she liberated the Greeks from slavery, so that they lived as free men until they subjugated each other. To the King, however, she hardly dared to run to his aid. For she feared the triumphs previously reported from Marathon, Salamis, and Plataea <note>The three major Greek victories over the Persians</note>. But while she allowed exiles and voluntary helpers to favor him, she undoubtedly saved him as well. 

Having built walls and constructed ships and undertaken war when she was forced to wage it, she fought for the safety of the Parians against the Lacedaemonians. But the King, fearing the city after he had seen the Lacedaemonians refuse a naval war, and wishing for that reason to desist, sought out the Greeks who were on the mainland: whom the Lacedaemonians themselves had previously surrendered. If he were to fight against us and the rest of the allies, he thought this would be denied to him, whereby he might find an occasion for stalling. There he was deceived by the defenders and the other allies. For they were willing to surrender them; and the Corinthians, Argives, Boeotians, and the rest of the allies met and took an oath that if he gave money, they would hand over to him those Greeks who were on the mainland. 

We alone at that time dared neither to hand them over nor to swear the oath: so noble, free, constant, and upright is the custom of this city, and by nature she is hostile to barbarians. This is because these men are pure and whole Greeks without any barbarian mixture. For there are no Pelopes, or Cadmi, or Egyptians, or Danaans, or many others mixed with us, who are barbarians by nature and Greeks only by law; but we ourselves, being only Greeks and infected by no barbarian confusion at all, persevere. This purity has engendered in this city a hatred against foreign races. Again, we alone remained pure because we refused to perform a wicked and unholy deed: to hand over Greeks into the hands of barbarians. 

Descending then to these things: from which we were first overcome; with God favoring us, we ended the war more happily than then. For retaining our ships, walls, and our colonies, we were freed from war; so willingly did even the enemies themselves desist. Nevertheless, we lost brave men in this war as well: some intercepted at Corinth by the roughness and narrowness of the region, others defeated by treachery at Lechaeum. There were also distinguished men who both liberated the King and expelled the Lacedaemonians from the sea. These men I indeed bring back to your memory. It is fitting for you to praise and celebrate men of this kind. 

And indeed, these deeds of the men lying here, and of all others who died for their country, which have been related, are many and noble. But those which remain are far more numerous and more excellent. Many days and nights would scarcely suffice if one wished to embrace them all. Therefore, with these things recalled to memory, it behooves every man to constantly exhort his sons: that they should keep their rank just as in the war of their ancestors, and not flee through cowardice. Indeed, O sons of excellent men, I myself both exhort you in the present and will always admonish and encourage whichever of you I encounter in the future: that you strive to turn out as the best of men. Now also it is right to relate to you what your fathers fashioned for us, and commanded us to preach to posterity if anything should happen when there was a risk. I will therefore recount to you in the present what I heard from those very men, or what they themselves would now gladly command you, if the opportunity were given...

# MENEXENUS OR THE FUNERAL ORATION. FOLIO CCXIIII.

I conclude this from what they used to say. Imagine now that you are hearing those very men speaking the things I shall report. They began in this manner: "O children, that you are born of noble parents, the present circumstances testify to you. Indeed, when we were permitted to live basely, we preferred to die honorably rather than subject you and the rest of our descendants to infamy, or to be a disgrace to our parents and ancestors; for we believe that a man whose own people are disgraced has no reason to live. To such a man, neither in life nor after death is anyone a friend, whether among men or the gods. It is necessary, therefore, that you remain mindful of our words, and if you practice anything else, practice it with virtue <note>Latin: *virtus*—meaning moral excellence and manly courage</note>. Know that without virtue, all exercises and possessions are base and evil. For riches bring no splendor to a possessor who is cowardly; for such a man does not possess riches for himself, but for another. Nor do beauty and strength of body provide any grace when they belong to the fearful and wicked; for they misbecome him, making his cowardice more notable and exposing it. Furthermore, any knowledge removed from justice and other virtue is seen not as wisdom, but as cunning. For this cause, first and last and with all zeal and diligence, strive to surpass both us and our ancestors in the glory of virtue. Otherwise, know that if we excel you in virtue, this victory will bring us disgrace. But if we are surpassed by you, it will bring us happiness. We shall be most truly surpassed, and you shall surpass us, if you so order your life as not to abuse the glory of your ancestors, nor, so to speak, to spend and exhaust it. Know that for a man who thinks himself to be something, nothing more shameful can happen than to offer himself to be honored not for his own virtue, but because of the glory of his predecessors. For the glory of parents is a noble and magnificent treasure for their children. But to use a treasure of money and honors and not to transmit it to posterity, through a lack of one's own possession and glory, is shameful and utterly foreign to a man’s nobility. If you practice these things, then when the fates of life are finished, you shall come to us as dear children to dear parents. But if you neglect these things and turn out wicked, no one will receive you willingly." Let these things be said to our children. But our fathers and mothers, if any of ours survive and need consolation, ought to be comforted; for it is fitting to bear easily whatever happens, and their misfortune is not to be deplored along with them. For they will not need the lamentations of others; fate will bring them enough sadness. It is necessary to heal and soothe them, and especially to remind them that the gods have already granted the greatest of those things they used to pray for. For they did not pray for immortal children to be given to them, but for good and illustrious ones. They have been made masters of this gift, which must be considered the greatest good. It is not easy for all things to succeed according to the wish of a mortal man in life. And if they endure with a brave spirit, they will show themselves to be truly the parents of brave sons, and be brave themselves. But if they succumb to grief, they will cause men to suspect that they are perhaps not our parents at all, or that those who extol us with praise are lying. Neither of these should happen; rather, let those who praise us be proven right by the fact that these parents show themselves to be truly the parents of men. Indeed, that old proverb, 
<margin>Proverb: Nothing in excess</margin>
"Nothing in excess" <note>Latin: *Nihil nimis*; Greek: *Mēden agan*—one of the Delphic maxims</note>, seems wisely said. For he who has so prepared himself that all things contributing to happiness depend upon himself, or comes as close to this as possible, and does not depend on other men—whose good or bad actions might force his own state to change—this man has ordered his life best. This man is temperate; he is brave; he is prudent. Whether he gains or loses money and children, he will always obey the proverb. For he will never exult too much in joy, nor be cast down in grief, because he obeys himself. We judge that our people ought to be such, and we wish it. And in the present moment, we show ourselves to be such, certainly not disturbed or terrified by excessive fear, even if it is now necessary for us to depart from life. We also pray that our fathers and mothers lead their future lives similarly affected, knowing that they will not please us most with lamentations and wailing. Rather, if there is any sense of the living among those who are dead, they will be most troublesome to us if they destroy themselves and bear their lot poorly; but if they bear it moderately and lightly, they will obey us greatly. Furthermore, our lives will now have that end which is most beautiful for men. Therefore, they are to be praised rather than wept for. Truly, if they protect and nourish our wives and children and devote themselves to them, they will thus best consign our fall to oblivion, and lead a life more beautiful, more right, and more pleasing to us. Let it suffice to proclaim these things on our behalf to our people. To the City, we mandate that it take care of our parents and children: let it educate the children honorably and cherish the old age of the parents worthily. We know certainly that you will take the best care, even if we did not command these things. These things, then, O children and parents of the deceased, they mandated us to warn you; and I, as much as I am able, warn you most diligently. In their name, I beseech the younger: to imitate the noble deeds of their own; and the elder: to hope for the best for themselves. Indeed, we shall nourish your old age privately and publicly, and whatever offspring of theirs we find, we shall embrace with the greatest benevolence. You yourselves are not ignorant of the city's providence, which, by established laws, protects the parents and children of those who died in war, and commits the care of such to the highest magistrate above other citizens, so that the parents of these men are not affected by any injury at all. It educates the children itself and strives so that orphanhood is unknown to them. For the city itself acts in the place of a parent while they are boys; and when they have come to mature age, it sends them to their duties, supporting and adorning them with full armor. It shows and reminds them of their father's pursuits while it grants them the instruments of paternal virtue. And at the same time, for the sake of a good omen, it commands the son then for the first time to enter his paternal house as if to command, supported by arms and strength. Furthermore, it honors those who have departed from life, renewing every year the ceremonies decreed by law for all in common, which are usually performed privately for each individual. It likewise establishes gymnastic and equestrian contests, and provides various musical games...

# SUMMARY OF THE DIALOGUE: MENEXENUS

And indeed, as far as the deceased are concerned, he takes on the condition of an heir and a son; as for the children, that of a father; as for the parents and others of this kind, that of a guardian: always providing for all with every diligence. Fourthly, in your observation of events, you ought to bear what has happened with a level mind. For in this way, you will be more pleasing to both the dead and the living; you will care for them easily, and you will be easily cared for. But now, you and all the others who have collectively followed the funeral rites for those who have yielded to nature according to the law, depart. This, O Menexenus, is the discourse of Aspasia of Miletus <note>Aspasia was a highly influential woman in Periclean Athens, known for her intellect and rhetorical skill; Socrates jokingly credits her with composing the famous funeral oration.</note>.

**MENEXENUS:** By Jove, Socrates, you say Aspasia is blessed if, being a woman, she can compose such speeches.

**SOCRATES:** But if you do not believe it, follow me, and you shall hear her speak it herself.

**MENEXENUS:** I have been with Aspasia many times, Socrates, and I know what she is like.

**SOCRATES:** Why then do you not revere her? Why do you not feel gratitude toward her for this speech?

**MENEXENUS:** I do indeed feel great gratitude, Socrates, to this woman—or to the man, whoever it was who delivered this speech to you. And I am grateful for the narration above many others.

**SOCRATES:** Very well. But do not betray me, so that hereafter I may recount to you many of her excellent speeches on civil affairs.

**MENEXENUS:** Have confidence. I will not betray you. Just report them.

**SOCRATES:** It shall be done as you ask.

->THE END OF MENEXENUS.<-

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino of Florence for the First Dialogue on the Republic, or on Justice, addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici, a man of great soul.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within a circular frame surrounded by floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

By as much as the eye excels the hands, the head the feet, reason the senses, the soul the body, the end excels all things directed toward that end, stability excels motion, and eternity excels time—by so much does the contemplative life seem to excel the active life. For contemplation is both the beginning and the end of action; it leads action at its will and brings it to a halt, finally commanding lower motions and external action to cease, so that an internal and stable action may at last possess a greater freedom. Thus, indeed, from the very contemplation of God, all celestial and natural motions and actions are led as if from a beginning, and are led back as if to an end.

For this reason, our Plato is more excellent than other founders of cities and laws, in that others established the city more for action, as if for human things; but he, as if divine, leads all action of the city, both public and private, chiefly toward contemplation. He established a city that is mistress of itself before being mistress of the world, not to be feared by many, but to be revered by all nations—a sort of heavenly Jerusalem <note>original: "caelestem quasi Hierusalem"; Ficino uses Christian imagery to explain Plato's Ideal City to his Renaissance audience.</note> expressed on earth as far as possible. In this city, with contentions removed for the sake of private possession, all things are common to all by the very law of nature; there is common abundance, firm concord, a single will among all, and therefore a tranquility always ready for contemplation.

He composes the complete form of an absolute Republic in a ten-book count, the most complete of all numbers, containing numbers counted within itself and unfolding innumerable ones from itself. And as he often declares in these books, especially in the second, he prefers the whole discussion to be titled "On Justice" rather than "On the Republic," teaching, as I judge, that every thing and action, both public and private, is not for abundance, nor for power, nor for victory, but is to be referred entirely to justice itself. This justice, once perturbation is removed and the impediments of contention expelled, finally renders the citizens most ready to investigate the truth and worship God. Our Plato judges such contemplation and worship to be the chief end of the republic. So that what neither one man could achieve if he lived alone, nor many if they lived together without law, at least many citizens gathered into one assembly of a city by a common law might perfect.

Furthermore, Timaeus and Critias <note>Characters from Plato's dialogues of the same names.</note> teach us that before the great flood of the lands, other Athens existed, both among the Greeks and the Egyptians, governed by similar laws among themselves, which the goddess Pallas <note>Athena</note> founded, educated, and taught; and she handed down to them that form of the republic which Plato writes in these books. In the books *On the Laws*, however, he composes a republic from the Cretan, Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note>, and a new Attic government; and he begins that composition from God, the author of all laws.

But to return to the present matters, he begins this republic also under happy auspices from the very sacred rites of divine wisdom: from the custom and counsel of the elders, and from religious justice and sanctity. For from the fact that he had said that vows must be paid to God and to each his own, he begins now to dispute concerning a certain private justice, through which he will opportunely pass to public justice in its proper place. You, however, remember that in these things it is signified by Plato: that without divine and human justice, the counsel of elders, and the favor of divine wisdom, a city can neither be established prosperously from the beginning, nor governed happily once established.

Next, touching upon the argument of the first book, I shall extract certain necessary points from many weighty precepts. A moderate youth easily brings about an easy old age; an immoderate one, a difficult one. He who obeys the lusts of the body undoubtedly serves insane tyrants. The soul in old age, with the perturbations that youth brings with it having been calmed, and being separated from the body, inspects divine things more closely and more fitly. Innocence alone offers the best hope to the soul for the future: the sole comfort of a finished life. A man of sound mind will judge money to be useful primarily for this: so that whatever he has vowed to God, or promised to a man, or otherwise owed, he may fulfill; and that he may not be led by poverty to lie to anyone or defraud in any matter. For money is to be referred to justice, and justice to the reward of the other life. But before we pursue the discussion of justice, I advise that it be considered that individual things are arranged by Plato under a certain allegory. First indeed, Cephalus the old man, that is, the head, leads the dispute...

# ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE I ON THE REPUBLIC
## FO. CCXV.

<margin>

...and...

</margin>
...the head of the discussion. Then Polemarchus—whose name actually signifies "war-leader" <note>original: "Polemarchus, qđ & nome eius significat, princeps"</note>—begins the battle with moderation. Finally, Thrasymachus—that is, the "fierce fighter"—acts more harshly. Socrates, however—the "savior"—is able to save everyone everywhere from error and injustice. But leaving the allegory to the commentaries, let us now proceed to the definition of justice. They say that Simonides, Pittacus, and Bias <note>Three of the Seven Sages of Greece</note> said that justice is to speak the truth and to render to each person what is due. Indeed, some interpret it this way: simply to open the truth to anyone and to restore what you have received. However, Socrates rejects this because one should not disclose every truth to a madman, nor should weapons be returned to him which he had deposited with you while he was sane. Others explain it thus: to give to each what is appropriate for them, such as benefit to friends but harm to enemies; to be useful to the good, but to hurt the wicked. This he rejects again, because it is never proper to hurt anyone. For whoever hurts something makes that very thing worse and more unfit for its own work and proper virtue—just as one who hurts a dog renders it unfit for the proper virtue of a dog. Justice is truly the virtue of a human being. Therefore, whoever hurts a human being makes them worse in regard to justice. But justice never diminishes justice, just as the work of music does not destroy music. For which reason, it is not just to hurt anyone. During these things, Thrasymachus—as many others do elsewhere—reproaches Socrates because he never wishes to answer, but always to interrogate. Truly, it should not escape your notice that Socrates was accustomed to always ask rather than teach for many reasons. First, to warn the arrogant that at every age one must learn rather than teach. Second, to signify that truth is immediately poured in by divine influence <note>original: "diuinus"</note> into minds that have been separated from the body and from errors through timely inquiry. This, Avicenna <note>The Persian polymath Ibn Sina</note> also greatly approves. Third, to show that the forms of things are innate in our souls, through which the truth of things itself sometimes shines forth in minds turned toward them through questioning. Fourth, to declare that human knowledge consists in a certain negation of the false rather than in the affirmation of the truth. Then a definition of justice is brought forward by Thrasymachus, similar to the one by Callicles in the *Gorgias*: that the just is what is useful to the more powerful. For the more powerful always dominate, and they carry out laws and govern subjects for their own utility. Then the subjects act justly when they obey those laws which were established for the utility of the governors. Socrates draws him into a contradiction. Since a prince might command through ignorance things that will be a detriment to himself. If a private citizen observes these, he will be both just (because he obeys the ruler) and unjust (because he acts against the utility of the ruler). He adds that any perfected art—and therefore one least in need—in handling its materials and men, consults not its own utility, but the utility of the things commended to it: like a tutor to orphans, a doctor to the sick, a pilot to sailors; and similarly, a legitimate magistrate looks out for the utility of the subjects. If any art, like medicine, demands a fee, it does not make a profit insofar as it is medicine (whose end is the cure of disease), but insofar as it is mixed with a certain mercenary and profit-seeking trade. It is established, therefore, that the most perfect art of all—and therefore the least needy and servile—governs much less for the sake of utility. I pass over the things Thrasymachus brings forward rashly and with a certain self-contradiction against justice. But you, note that it is not fitting for anyone to seek leadership or to solicit magistracies. Likewise, if there ever existed a city of good men, they would fight no differently for the sake of *not* ruling than men now contend with a desire for ruling. Now observe three things. First: the wicked are not to be admitted to the magistracy. Second: citizens who are not wicked are to be invited so that they might willingly undergo the heavy burden of governing, with a certain reward of pay and honor imposed. Third: upright men who are moved neither by greed nor ambition ought to be provoked to the republic only by this distinction and fear: namely, lest they themselves be subjected to an unjust and inferior government. The divine Plato understands, if anyone ever did, that the duty of governing the fatherland, if it is to be just, ought to be voluntary. But by the example of the most esteemed citizen, he wishes to rebuke the wicked arrogance of those who always solicit magistracies by any path and hunt for dignities. Truly, they do not care at all by what reason they themselves might become worthy of those dignities. He wishes, therefore, that duty to be voluntary and necessary at the same time: so that the most esteemed man most willingly takes up the helm of his fatherland, but does so only when necessity demands; meanwhile, he should prefer contemplation to action. Truly, with matters sometimes pressing, he should prefer action concerning the public good for a time over his own contemplation. This whole matter can be understood most clearly from the letter of Plato to Archytas of Tarentum. Next, he refutes the tyrannical saying of Thrasymachus, which places justice in the category of foolishness and malice, and injustice in the category of wisdom and the good. He shows this to be false because any art is a certain wisdom, and concerning that which it is wise, it is also good. A man learned in any art does not seek more than another learned man in a skillful action; rather, he seeks to execute the action equally and similarly. And he who is learned only wishes to equal his peer, yet he wishes to surpass the unlearned. But the unlearned man sometimes rashly attempts to take more for himself than the learned and unlearned combined. The just man is most similar to the former, desiring to have nothing more than another just man, but yet something more (that is, virtue) than the unjust man. The unjust man, however, like the unlearned, contends to have more than both the just and the unjust. Conclude against Thrasymachus: justice is to be referred to the category of wisdom and the good, but injustice to the category of foolishness and malice. Add that injustice is the cause of weakness for all. For in any assembly, by birthing hatred and discord, it first renders the assembly very weak, and then dissolves it. An assembly can stand only insofar as it preserves some measure of just distribution. Therefore, it stands through justice, but is dissolved through injustice. Through the former, one is a friend to oneself and others; through the latter, an enemy on all sides. As for what occurs in any gathering...

It emphasizes that true leadership should be a reluctant duty performed by the wise for the benefit of the governed.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the introductory philosophical summary of Book I and begins the primary text of Plato’s Republic, translated from Greek into Latin by the Renaissance humanist Marsilio Ficino. It establishes the setting in the Piraeus and introduces the dialogue between Socrates and the elderly Cephalus regarding old age.</meta>

# BOOK
<page-num>XXXI.</page-num>

...gation: the same occurs in any soul where justice and injustice act. Justice makes a man consistent with himself, a friend to himself, to other men, and to the gods. Indeed, the gods are most just, so it is no wonder that the just man, being like them, is also their friend. The unjust man, however, is the opposite in all these things. Furthermore, every thing has its own specific function <note>original: "opus"</note>. It also requires its own specific virtue—that is, a certain faculty through which it may most aptly perform its function, and without which it cannot achieve it. Since, therefore, the soul has its own function—such as deliberating and governing, and much more importantly, living—it also requires its own specific virtue through which these tasks are performed most suitably; if this virtue is removed, the soul suffers. The virtue of the soul is justice, while injustice is its vice. Therefore, through justice, the soul deliberates and governs perfectly, and lives happily. But if justice is removed, the opposite occurs. With these things said, the first book concludes with a certain correction. Namely, since it should have been said first what justice *is* before what *kind* of thing it is, the reverse has happened so far; while Socrates partly followed those disputing, and partly disputed through better-known principles, he both indulged the character of his listeners and looked to their capacity for understanding.

### THE REPUBLIC OF PLATO, OR CONCERNING JUSTICE, TRANSLATED BY MARSILIO FICINO THE FLORENTINE, AND DEDICATED TO THE MAGNANIMOUS LORENZO DE' MEDICI. DIALOGUE ONE.

-> CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE. <-
-> SOCRATES. GLAUCON. POLEMARCHUS. ADEIMANTUS. CEPHALUS. <-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring a classical figure (possibly a philosopher or deity) seated within the letter's frame, surrounded by architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>

I HAD GONE DOWN yesterday to the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens</note> together with Glaucon, the son of Ariston, so that I might both pray to the goddess and observe the festival, to see in what manner they would celebrate the beautiful rites which were then being performed for the first time. The procession of our fellow citizens seemed beautiful to me, but no less decent, it appeared, was the one sent by the Thracians. When we had finished our prayers and witnessed the spectacle, we began to return to the city. However, Polemarchus, the son of Cephalus, saw us from a distance as we were heading home and ordered his servant to run and stop us. The servant, catching me by my cloak from behind, said: "Polemarchus bids you wait." I turned to him and asked where his master was. "He is coming behind you," he said, "just wait." "We will wait," replied Glaucon. And a little later Polemarchus arrived, and with him Adeimantus, Glaucon’s brother, and Niceratus, the son of Nicias, and several others, who appeared to be coming from the procession. Then Polemarchus said, "O Socrates, you seem to be approaching the city as if you intend to depart." "You do not guess wrongly," I said. "Do you see," he asked, "how many of us there are?" "Of course." "Then you must either be stronger than these men, or you must stay." "One option remains," I said, "namely, that we might persuade you to let us go." "Could you persuade those who will not listen?" he asked. "By no means," replied Glaucon. "Then consider it settled that we are not going to listen." Then Adeimantus said, "Do you not know that there will be a torch race on horseback this evening in honor of the goddess?" "A race on horseback?" I asked. "That is certainly a novelty. Will they carry torches and pass them to one another while competing on horses? Is that what you mean?" "Exactly," he said, "therefore you must either be more powerful or stay here." To this Polemarchus added, "Furthermore, they will perform nocturnal rites well worth seeing. For we shall rise after dinner and watch those rites, and many young men will be there with whom we shall converse. So stay, and do not do otherwise." And Glaucon said, "It seems we must stay." "If it seems so," I said, "then so we must do." We went, therefore, to the house of Polemarchus, and there we found Euthydemus and Lysias, the brothers of Polemarchus, Thrasymachus of Chalcedon, Charmantides of Paeania, and Cleitophon, the son of Aristonymus. Also inside was Cephalus, the father of Polemarchus, who seemed to me quite old, for I had not seen him for a long time. He was sitting crowned <note>Wearing a ritual garland</note> upon a cushioned seat, for he had been sacrificing in the courtyard. We sat down next to him, as many seats were arranged in a circle. As soon as Cephalus saw me, he greeted me and said: "O Socrates, you come down to the Piraeus to visit us far too seldom. You ought to come more often. For if I were still strong enough to be able to come to the city, there would be no need for you to come to us, but we would go to you. But now it is right for you to come here frequently. Truly, the more the pleasures of the body fail me, the more the desire for conversation and the pleasure I take from it increases. Do this, then: come here to us and join these young men as if you were coming to

<margin>The talk of old men should be heard gladly.</margin>
very close friends." "Indeed, Cephalus," I said, "I am greatly delighted by the conversation of old men. For it seems to me that we ought to hear from those who have already traveled a path which we perhaps must also tread: whether it be rough and difficult, or easy and passable. And I would gladly hear from you what you think about this, now that you have reached this age which the poets call 'the threshold of old age' <note>original: "in limine senectutis"</note>. Whether you call it a difficult time of life, or how you would describe it."

<margin>Concerning the complaint and the praise of old age.</margin>
"By Jove, Socrates," he said, "I will tell you what I think. Many of us who are roughly the same age often meet, keeping that ancient proverb <note>'Birds of a feather flock together'</note>. Most of us at these meetings lament, longing for the pleasures we enjoyed in youth, remembering sex, banquets, and other things of that kind. They take it heavily, as if they were deprived of the greatest things, and they say that they lived well then, but now they do not even live. Some also deplore the insults and outrages of their household members, and for this they especially blame old age, as if...

# DIALOGUE I. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

...the cause of the greatest evils for themselves. But to me, such men do not seem to blame old age rightly as the cause of these things. For if this were the cause, I would have suffered the same things on account of old age, as would all others who have reached this time of life. But I have found many who are not so affected: and notably with the poet Sophocles <note>Sophocles (c. 496–406 BCE) was a famous Greek playwright</note>, who, when asked by someone how he fared in matters of love, and whether he was still able to enjoy the company of women, rightly replied: "Peace, I pray you, my friend; most gladly have I escaped from those things, as if from some furious and savage master." It seemed to me then that he spoke very well, and it seems no less so now. For in old age, there is altogether much peace and freedom from such things. For when the desires have faded and ceased, that saying of Sophocles truly comes to pass: we are set free from many masters, and frantic ones at that. But regarding these complaints,

<margin>The very fine response of Sophocles.</margin>

O Socrates, and those complaints made against kinsmen, there is but one cause—not old age, but the character of the men. For if they are moderate and easy-tempered, old age is not excessively burdensome for them. But if otherwise, then both old age and youth, O Socrates, are difficult for them. Then I, being wonderfully delighted by what he said and wishing to hear more, provoked him further: "O Cephalus, I think that many, when you say such things, do not accept them. Rather, they think you bear old age easily because of your riches rather than your character. For they say the rich have many comforts." "You speak the truth," he said. "They do not accept it; and they say something of weight, yet not as much as might be said. But that saying of Themistocles <note>Themistocles was an Athenian statesman and general</note> is excellent: when a certain man from Seriphus <note>A small, insignificant Greek island</note> insultingly cast it in his teeth that he had achieved such glory not through himself but through his country, he replied: 'Indeed, if I were a Seriphian, I would not be in such glory; but neither would you, if you were an Athenian.' The same can be said to those who are not rich and bear old age heavily: for neither would a moderate man bear old age easily with poverty, nor would an immoderate man find it easy even with riches." "But," I said, "of the things you possess, were more left to you by your ancestors than you acquired yourself? Or was it the opposite?" "I have acquired some, O Socrates," he said. "I have stood midway in money-making between my father and grandfather. For my grandfather, Cephalus, receiving about as much as I have now, increased it greatly. But my father, Lysanias, made those riches even less than they are now. I am satisfied if I leave to these sons not less than I received, but a little more." "I asked this," I said, "because you seemed to me not to admire riches overmuch; which is usually the case with those who did not earn them. But those who have acquired them love them twice as much as others. For just as poets love their poems and fathers their sons, in the same way those who have acquired money are devoted to it as their own work, and not merely for its use and necessity as others are. Because of this, their company is difficult, since they wish to praise nothing except wealth." "You tell the truth," he said. "Very much so," I said. "But tell me this also: What do you think is the greatest good you have gained from the possession of riches?" "That," he said, "which I might not easily persuade many of if I told them. Know for certain, O Socrates, that after someone reaches the point where he thinks he is soon to die, there falls upon him a fear and a care for those things which he neglected in his former life. For the stories told about the underworld <note>original: "inferis" - referring to Hades or the afterlife</note>—how those who have acted unjustly must pay the penalty there—which were laughed at until now, then trouble the soul, suspecting they might be true. And he himself, either because of the weakness of old age or because he sees those things more sharply as he is closer to the other life, becomes full of anxiety and fear; he reckons and examines whether he has wronged anyone. He who finds many iniquities in his life is frequently startled out of sleep like a child and lives in wretched hope. But for him who is conscious of no injustice, a pleasant hope is always present, the 'excellent nurse of old age,' as Pindarus <note>Pindar (c. 518–438 BCE), a Greek lyric poet</note> says. For he sang that beautifully, O Socrates: 'Whosoever lives a just and holy life, sweet hope accompanies him, nourishing his heart and fostering his old age—hope which chiefly governs the fickle mind of mortals.' He speaks well and most admirably. Therefore, I think the possession of money is of greatest value, not to every man, but to the moderate and fair man. The possession of riches contributes much to this: that one may depart for that other world without fear, having neither deceived nor lied to anyone, nor owing sacrifices to a god or money to a man. It has other uses too, and very many indeed. But comparing one thing to another, O Socrates, I would place this as not the least, but rather the greatest benefit of money to a man of sense." "You speak excellently, Cephalus," I said. "But this very thing, namely justice—shall we say it is simply telling the truth and returning what one has received? Or is doing these same things sometimes just and sometimes unjust? For example: everyone would say that if someone received weapons from a friend of sound mind, and that friend asked for them back while insane, one ought not to return them; nor would he be just who did return them, or who insisted on telling the whole truth to a man in such a state." "You speak rightly," he said. "Therefore, this is not the definition of justice: to speak the truth and return what has been deposited." "You speak rightly indeed, O Socrates," said Polemarchus, interrupting the conversation, "if we are to believe anything of Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BCE), a Greek lyric poet</note>." At this, Cephalus said, "I hand the conversation over to you two, for I must go tend to the sacred rites." "Is Polemarchus then your heir to the argument?" I asked. And he, smiling, said, "He is indeed," and at once departed to the sacrifice. "Tell me then," I said, "heir to the argument: what do you assert was rightly said about justice by Simonides?" "That," he said, "it is just to render to each man what is his due." And in saying this, he seems to speak rightly. "Yet," I said, "it is not easy to deny credit to Simonides. For he was a wise and divine man. But what he means, you perhaps understand, O Polemarchus, but I do not. For it is clear he does not mean what we were saying just now: namely, returning a deposit to someone not of sound mind who asks for it back. And yet, a deposit is in some sense a 'due.' Is it not..."

# BOOK I.

**PO.** Certainly. **SO.** But one must not give it back, surely, not when someone who is not in their right mind asks for it. **PO.** You speak the truth. **SO.** Therefore, Simonides means something other than this when he asserts that it is just to give back what is owed. **PO.** Something else indeed, by Jove! For he thinks that friends ought to do good to their friends, and never evil. **SO.** I understand then that he who returns gold to one from whom he received it as a deposit would not be giving back what is "owed" if the returning and receiving were to prove harmful—provided the giver and receiver are friends. Is this not what you affirm Simonides means? **PO.** Exactly so. **SO.** But what must be given back to enemies? What is "owed" to them? **PO.** Entirely what is owed to them. And what is owed by an enemy to an enemy is, I suppose, what is appropriate: namely, some evil. **SO.** It seems then that Simonides, after the fashion of poets, spoke in riddles about what is just. For he judged, as it appears, that justice is to render to each what is appropriate to him; and this he called "what is owed." But what do you think he would say if someone asked him: "O Simonides, what is the art <note>original: "facultas," referring to a skill or power</note> that, by rendering what is owed and appropriate, and to whom, is called medicine?" What do you think he would answer us? **PO.** Surely that which renders medicines, food, and drinks to bodies. **SO.** And in the same way, if he were asked what art renders what is owed and appropriate, and to whom, to be called cookery, what would he answer? **PO.** That which gives seasoned flavors to cooked meats. **SO.** Come then, what art, by rendering what and to whom, shall be called Justice? **PO.** If we are to follow what was said before, justice is that which renders benefits to friends and injuries to enemies. **SO.** Does he then call it justice to treat friends well and enemies ill? **PO.** So it seems to me. **SO.** Who is best able to treat sick friends well, and enemies the opposite, in matters of health and disease? **PO.** A physician. **SO.** And who can best do so for those sailing through the perils of the sea? **PO.** A pilot. **SO.** In what action and for what work is the just man best able to benefit friends and harm enemies? **PO.** In fighting and making war, as it seems to me. **SO.** But to those who are not sick, friend Polemarchus, a physician is useless. **PO.** True. **SO.** And a pilot to those not sailing. **PO.** Certainly. **SO.** Is the just man then useless to those who are not at war? **PO.** I do not admit that at all. **SO.** Justice, then, is useful also in peace? **PO.** It is useful. **SO.** Agriculture is also useful in peace, is it not? **PO.** It is. **SO.** For the gathering of fruits. **PO.** Indeed. **SO.** And shoemaking? **PO.** Certainly. **SO.** For the making of shoes, for instance. **PO.** Plainly. **SO.** What then of justice? For what use or gain would you say it is useful in peace? **PO.** For commerce, Socrates. **SO.** By commerce do you mean partnerships <note>original: "communicationes"</note>, or something else? **PO.** That very thing. **SO.** Is the just man a good and useful partner in a game of dice? Or is the player of dice? **PO.** The player, surely. **SO.** And in the laying of bricks or stones, is the just man a better and more useful partner than the architect? **PO.** Not at all. **SO.** But in what partnership is the just man better than the lyre-player, just as the lyre-player is more useful than the just man in striking the strings? **PO.** In matters of money, as it seems to me. **SO.** But not, O Polemarchus, in the *use* of money; for when horses are to be bought or sold for money, then surely the horse-dealer <note>original: "mango"</note> would be more useful. Would he not? **PO.** It appears so. **SO.** And when it concerns a ship, the shipbuilder or the sailor? **PO.** So it seems. **SO.** For what common use of gold or silver, then, is the just man more useful than others? **PO.** When we wish to deposit it and have it kept safe, O Socrates. **SO.** Do you mean when there is no need to use it, but only to keep it? **PO.** Exactly. **SO.** Therefore, when money is useless, then justice is useful in regard to it? **PO.** It appears so. **SO.** And when a pruning-hook must be guarded, justice is useful both privately and publicly; but when it is to be used, the art of vine-culture is useful? **PO.** It is clear. **SO.** Would you also say that when a shield and a lyre must be guarded, but not used, justice is useful? But when one wishes to use them, then the art of arms and music are useful? **PO.** Necessarily. **SO.** And so it must be said of all other things: that justice is useless in the use of things, but useful when they are not being used? **PO.** It appears so. **SO.** Justice, then, my friend, is not a thing of great worth if it is only useful for useless things. But let us consider this: Is not he who is most skilled at striking in a fight, whether as a boxer or otherwise, also the best at guarding himself? **PO.** Certainly. **SO.** And is not he who is able to avoid and escape a disease also the best at inflicting it? **PO.** So it seems to me. **SO.** And he is the best guardian of an army who can also steal the plans and other actions of the enemy. **PO.** Quite so. **SO.** Therefore, of whatever thing a man is a clever guardian, of that he is also a clever thief. **PO.** It appears so. **SO.** If, then, the just man is best at keeping money safe, he is also best at stealing it. **PO.** So the argument suggests. **SO.** The just man, then, has turned out to be a kind of thief; and you seem to have learned this from Homer. For he admired Autolycus, the maternal grandfather of Ulysses, and says of him that he surpassed all men in thievery and in swearing oaths. It seems then, according to you and according to Homer and Simonides, that justice is a kind of art of stealing—for the benefit of friends, however, and the harm of enemies. Was that not what you were saying? **PO.** No, by Jove! But I no longer know what I was saying. Yet this I still believe: that justice is to benefit friends and harm enemies. **SO.** But by "friends" do you mean those who *seem* to be good and useful to a person, or those who *are* so, even if they do not seem so? And the same for enemies? **PO.** It is fitting to love those whom one thinks are good and useful, and to hate those one considers evil and useless. **SO.** Do not men err in this? So that many seem to them to be good and useful when they are actually evil and useless, and many the opposite? **PO.** They certainly err. **SO.** To such people, then, the good are enemies and the evil are friends. **PO.** Very much so. **SO.** Then it is just for these people to help the evil and harm the good. **PO.** It appears so. **SO.** But the good are just, and such as to do no injustice. **PO.** You speak the truth. **SO.** According to your argument, then, it is just to harm those who commit no injury. **PO.** Not at all, Socrates! For that is a wicked way of speaking. **SO.** It is just, then, to harm those who are unjust and to help the just. **PO.** This speech is more reasonable than the former. **SO.** It will happen then to many who have erred in judging their friends, that it is just for them to...

# DIALOGUE I. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

<margin>The work of a just man is not to harm anyone.</margin>
...harm their friends: for sometimes bad men are their friends; and likewise that they should benefit their enemies, since sometimes they are good. And so we shall say the opposite of those things which we said were brought forward by Simonides <note>A Greek lyric poet often cited in Plato's dialogues for his traditional moral maxims.</note>. POLEMARCHUS: It will happen exactly so. But let us reconsider. For we seem not to have correctly defined "friend" and "enemy." SOCRATES: What do you find fault with in this definition, Polemarchus? POLEMARCHUS: That which we said: that a friend is one who is good and useful. SOCRATES: How shall we correct this for the present? POLEMARCHUS: We shall call a friend one who both seems to be and is good and useful. But one who seems so, but is not, appears to be a friend but is not actually a friend. And the same reasoning will apply to the enemy. SOCRATES: The friend, then, as it seems by this reasoning, will be the good man; the enemy, however, will be the bad man. POLEMARCHUS: Exactly. SOCRATES: Do you bid us add something to what we were saying about the just man? We were saying further that it is just to benefit a friend and harm an enemy. Now, however, do you wish us to say it is just that we help a friend who is good, and conversely harm an enemy who is bad? POLEMARCHUS: It seems to me to be stated very beautifully in this way. SOCRATES: Is it then the part of a just man to harm any human being? POLEMARCHUS: It is certainly fitting to harm the wicked and enemies. SOCRATES: When horses are affected by harm, do they become better or worse? POLEMARCHUS: Worse. SOCRATES: Is it in the excellence <note>original: "virtutem" (virtue/excellence)</note> of dogs, or rather of horses? POLEMARCHUS: Of horses. SOCRATES: And if dogs are harmed, do they not become worse in the excellence of dogs, not of horses? POLEMARCHUS: Necessarily so. SOCRATES: Therefore, my friend, shall we not judge that men who are affected by harm become worse in human excellence? POLEMARCHUS: Entirely so. SOCRATES: But is not justice a human excellence? POLEMARCHUS: It clearly is. SOCRATES: It will therefore be necessary that harmed men become more unjust. POLEMARCHUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: Can musicians, by music itself, make anyone unmusical? POLEMARCHUS: By no means. SOCRATES: Can horsemen, by horsemanship, make men unskilled in horsemanship? POLEMARCHUS: It is not possible. SOCRATES: Or can just men, by justice itself, make men unjust? And in short, can good men make others bad by excellence itself? Certainly not. For I do not think it is the work of heat to make something cold, but of its opposite. POLEMARCHUS: So it is. SOCRATES: Nor of dryness to make something wet, but of its opposite. POLEMARCHUS: Very much so. SOCRATES: Therefore, it is not the part of the good man to harm, but of his opposite. POLEMARCHUS: It seems so. SOCRATES: But the just man is good. POLEMARCHUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: It is not, therefore, the work of the just man, O Polemarchus, to harm either a friend or anyone else, but of his opposite, the unjust man. POLEMARCHUS: You seem to speak the absolute truth, O Socrates. SOCRATES: If anyone, therefore, says that it is just for what is owed to be rendered to each, and understands by this that harm is owed to enemies by the just man, and benefit to friends, he is by no means to be judged wise. For these things are not true. For it has been established that it is in no way just to harm anyone. POLEMARCHUS: I confess it indeed. SOCRATES: We shall therefore fight together, I and you, if anyone brings forward that Simonides said this, or Bias, or Pittacus <note>Two of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note>, or any other of the wise and blessed men. POLEMARCHUS: I for my part am prepared to fight together with you against him. SOCRATES: But do you know whose opinion this seems to me to be, which asserts it is just to benefit friends and hinder enemies? POLEMARCHUS: Whose? SOCRATES: I think it belongs to Periander, or Perdiccas, or Xerxes, or Ismenias the Theban, or some other wealthy man who thinks himself capable of great power. POLEMARCHUS: You speak the truth indeed. SOCRATES: Since this appears to be neither justice nor just, what else would anyone say it is?

Now Thrasymachus <note>A Sophist who represents the view that "might makes right."</note> had often desired to interrupt us while we were disputing, but he had been restrained by those present who wished to hear us. But after we made an end of speaking, and I said these things, he could no longer contain himself; but gathering himself up like a wild beast, he made an onset upon us as if he were about to tear us to pieces. And so both I and Polemarchus were terrified. But he shouted out: "What nonsense has occupied you until now, O Socrates? Why do you act like fools together, yielding to one another? For if you truly desire to know what the just is, do not only ask questions; nor desire to conquer by refuting after an answer has been given to you, noticing that it is easier to ask than to answer. But you yourself answer what you think the just is; and do not tell me that it is the 'fitting,' nor the 'useful,' nor the 'profitable,' nor the 'expedient,' nor the 'advantageous'; but tell me plainly and clearly what you say it is. For I will not admit it if you introduce such nonsense." Hearing these things, I was terrified; and looking at him, I shuddered; and as I think, unless I had looked at him before he looked at me, I would have become utterly speechless. But now, when he began to be exasperated by the discourse itself, I looked at him first; wherefore I was able to answer him, and trembling slightly I said: "O Thrasymachus, do not be harsh with us. For if we have stumbled in the investigation of the argument, both I and this man, hold it for certain that we have erred as just men. Surely if we were searching for gold, we would never willingly yield to one another in the search so as to impede the discovery. Therefore do not think, since we are searching for justice—a thing much more precious than gold—that we would so lazily yield to one another as not to strive with all zeal to find it clearly. But as I think, we are not able to attain it. Wherefore it is much more fitting for you wise men to pity us than to be harsh." 

<margin>A Sardonic laugh.</margin>
Then he, hearing these things, laughed very sardonically <note>A bitter or cynical laugh, historically associated with a Sardinian plant that caused facial convulsions.</note> and profusely, and said: "O Hercules! This is that usual irony of Socrates. Indeed, I knew this and predicted it: that you would not be willing to answer, but would rather use irony, and finally do anything rather than answer anyone who questioned you." "You are wise, O Thrasymachus," I said, "and you know well that if you asked someone how many twelve is, and while asking you told him: 'Do not tell me, friend, that twelve is twice six, nor three times four, nor six times two, nor four times three, otherwise I will by no means admit such nonsense'—no one would answer you if you questioned him thus. But if he said to you: 'How do you mean, O Thrasymachus? Should I not answer any of those things you predicted? Even if it is one of these, O wonderful man, should I not answer that, but something foreign to the truth? Or how do you mean that?'" THRASIMACHUS: "How is this similar to that?" SOCRATES: "Nothing prevents it. For even if it is not similar, if it nevertheless seems so to the one questioned, do you think he will be any less likely to answer what appears to him, whether we forbid it or not?" THRASIMACHUS: "So you will do this too: you will answer one of those things which I had forbidden!" SOCRATES: "I would not be at all surprised if it seemed so to me upon inquiring." THRASIMACHUS: "But if I show another answer concerning justice besides all these, and better than these, what penalty will you think you deserve?" 

<margin>The penalty which is fitting for the ignorant.</margin>
SOCRATES: "What other than that which is fitting for one who is ignorant? It is fitting that he learn from one who is learned. And I therefore judge myself worthy to suffer this—"

# BOOK I.

### XXXI.

->Socrates<-

...THRA. How witty. But besides what you will learn, you shall also pay money. SO. When, clearly, I have some. GLAU. On the contrary, the money is ready. Speak now, Thrasymachus: for the silver will not be lacking. Furthermore, we all stand as sureties for Socrates here. THRA. I suppose so, provided that Socrates keeps to his usual habit—that he answers nothing himself, but taking up the speech of the one answering, he finds fault with it. SO. My best of men, how could anyone answer, first when he neither knows nor claims to know anything? Then, if he should have some opinion on these matters, has he not been forbidden to say what he thinks by a man of no small authority? But it is more proper for you to speak. For you profess to know, and it is permitted for you to discourse. Therefore, grant me this favor: and do not grudge teaching Glaucon here and the others. While I was saying these things, Glaucon and the rest were begging for this very thing. It was manifest that Thrasymachus was moved by a very great desire to speak so that he might show himself off. For he thought he had the best possible answers; but he pretended to insist that I should be the one to answer. At last, however, he gave in. And he said: "This is the wisdom of Socrates: that he himself is unwilling to teach, but learns from others, and returns no thanks for it." To which I replied: "That I learn from others is true; but that I return no thanks is far from the truth. For I pay as much as I am able. But I am only able to give praise. For I have no silver. How much indulgence I will show if someone seems to me to speak well, you will soon understand when you have answered. For I think you will speak well." "Listen then," he said. "I affirm indeed that justice is nothing other than what is useful to the stronger <note>original: "quod potentiori utile"</note>. Why do you not praise me? I know you will not." SO. If indeed I first learn what you are saying. For now I do not yet know when you say justice is what is useful to the stronger, what you mean to imply, Thrasymachus. For you do not mean something like this: if Polydamas the athlete is stronger than us, and beef is beneficial to his body, that this food is at the same time useful and just for us who are weaker than him. THRA. You are too troublesome, O Socrates; and you take my words in the way you can most distort the discourse. SO. Not at all, best of men. But explain this more clearly. THRA. Are you unaware that of cities, some are governed by tyrants, others by the people, and some by the aristocracy? SO. I know it well. THRA. Is it not true that in any city, that which commands has the most power? SO. Why not? THRA. Moreover, each government carries out laws for its own utility: a popular government makes popular laws; a tyrannical one makes tyrannical laws; and it happens similarly in the others. By establishing laws, they show that what is useful for themselves is just for those who are subjects; and they punish the one who transcends this as one acting unjustly and against the laws. This, therefore, best of men, is what I say: in all cities, justice is the same thing—that which is beneficial to the ruling power. But the ruling power everywhere dominates as the stronger. Therefore, it is established for one who reasons correctly that everywhere this same thing is just: what is conducive to the stronger. SO. Now at last I understand what you are saying. But whether it be true, I will try to learn. You have answered that the useful is just, Thrasymachus; although you had forbidden me to answer that. But there is added to it that further point: "to the stronger." THRA. Perhaps a small addition. SO. It is not yet manifest whether it be great or small. But it is clear that it must be investigated whether you speak the truth. Since I confess that justice is something beneficial, and you add "beneficial to the stronger," which I do not know, it must be considered. THRA.

<margin>XIII</margin>

Consider it then. SO. I shall do so now. And tell me: do you assert that it is just to obey those who dominate? THRA. I do indeed. SO. Are those who command in whatever cities always without error, or do they err sometimes? THRA. They can err sometimes. SO. Therefore, when they set about to make laws, do they make some correctly and some not correctly? THRA. So I think. SO. They make them correctly when they establish what is useful for themselves, and not correctly when it is the opposite. Is it so, or do you say otherwise? THRA. Exactly so. SO. But what they have established must be observed by those who are subject to them. And that is justice. THRA. Why not? SO. Therefore, according to your own speech, it is not only just to do what is conducive to the stronger, but also the opposite: what is harmful. THRA. What are you saying? SO. What you are, I think. But let us inquire more diligently. Is it not now agreed between us that the rulers sometimes command those things which wander away from their own utility; and also that whatever they themselves command, it is just for the subjects to observe? Have these things not been agreed between us? THRA. So I suppose. SO. Think then that it has been conceded by you that it is just to do what is useless to the commanders and the stronger; since the commanders, out of ignorance, command those things which are bad for themselves. But you affirm it is just to do these things which are commanded by them. Does it not then follow, O wisest Thrasymachus, that it happens to be just to do the contrary of what you were saying? For what is useless to the stronger is in a way commanded to the subjects. Here Polemarchus said, "By Jove, these things are most manifest, O Socrates." Then Clitopho said, "Exactly so, if you should act as a witness." PO. "But there is no need of witnesses," he said. "For Thrasymachus himself confesses that the rulers sometimes command things that are not conducive to themselves. Which things, indeed, it would be just for the inferiors to perform." CLI. "For Thrasymachus established that to do what is commanded by the rulers is just, O Polemarchus." PO. "And indeed he established that what is useful to the stronger is just, O Clitopho. But establishing both of these, he confessed again that sometimes the stronger command things to the inferiors that are not useful to themselves. From these concessions it follows: that what is useful to the stronger is no more just than what is useless." To these things Clitopho said, "But Thrasymachus called 'useful to the stronger' what the stronger estimated to be beneficial to himself; and that this must be done by the subjects; and that this is just." But Polemarchus said, "That is not how it was said by Thrasymachus." "It matters nothing, O Polemarchus," I said. "But if Thrasymachus says so now, let us accept it so. And tell me, O Thrasymachus, is this what you wished to call just: the 'useful to the stronger' being what seems useful to him, whether it is beneficial or not? Is it so?" THRA. "Not at all. But do you think I call him who errs 'stronger' when he is mistaken?" SO. "I thought you were saying so, when you confessed that rulers are not entirely beyond error, but also make mistakes." THRA. "You are truly a sycophant <note>original: "sycophanta" - here meaning a trickster or false accuser in argument</note> in your speeches, Socrates. If someone errs regarding the sick, do you immediately call him a doctor insofar as he errs? Or a calculator when in his reckoning..."

<summary>Socrates and Thrasymachus debate the definition of justice, with Thrasymachus famously arguing that justice is "the interest of the stronger." Socrates begins to dismantle this by pointing out that rulers often make mistakes and command things that are actually harmful to their own interests.</summary>

# DIALOGUE I. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.
## FO. CCXVIII.
### B ii
<meta>Catchword: pti</meta>
