...he errs in his calculations, then at the moment he errs, he does so according to this error. But as I believe we are accustomed to speak, we say that the physician, the accountant, and the grammarian "err." I think, however, that none of these, insofar as he is what we call him, ever errs. Therefore, according to **exact reasoning**—since you too are cutting to the quick <note>original: "ad vivum resecas," a metaphor for precise, surgical scrutiny</note>—no craftsman errs. For whoever errs, does so because his knowledge fails him, and in that moment he is certainly not a craftsman. Consequently, no craftsman, or wise man, or ruler errs at the time when he is a ruler. Yet anyone might say that the physician erred, or the ruler erred. Consider my answer to you to be of this sort.

But the matter must be stated in exact reasoning: the ruler, insofar as he is a ruler, does not err; and not erring, he commands what is best for himself. This, indeed, must be done by those who are under his command. For which reason, as I said from the beginning, I maintain that it is **just** to do what is conducive to the stronger.

**SOCRATES:** Do I seem to you, O Thrasymachus, to be playing the sycophant by misrepresenting you?
**THRASYMACHUS:** Most certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Do you think I am asking these questions by design, as if to trap you, as I was just doing?
**THRASYMACHUS:** Indeed, I know this perfectly well. But you will achieve nothing. For your snares do not escape me, nor, since they do not escape me, will you be able to use force against my words.
**SOCRATES:** I would never attempt such a thing, my blessed friend. But so that nothing of the sort happens to us again, distinguish whether you speak of the "ruler" and the "stronger" according to common opinion, or according to **exact reasoning**, as you mentioned a moment ago. Whose advantage, since he is the stronger, is it just for the subjects to serve?
**THRASYMACHUS:** I mean the ruler in the most exact sense of the word. Pervert this with your quibbles if you can! Indeed, I am surpassed by you in nothing, nor will you be able to do so.
**SOCRATES:** Do you think me so mad that I would dare to "shave a lion" <note>A Greek proverb meaning to attempt something dangerously impossible</note> and lay snares for Thrasymachus?
**THRASYMACHUS:** You have just attempted it, though you could accomplish nothing.
**SOCRATES:** Enough has been said of these things. But tell me: he who is a physician in the right sense, as you yourself were saying just now, is he a seeker of money, or a healer of the sick? Speak of him who is truly a physician.
**THRASYMACHUS:** A healer of diseases, certainly.
**SOCRATES:** And a pilot—he who is truly a pilot—is he a leader of sailors, or a sailor?
**THRASYMACHUS:** A leader of sailors.
**SOCRATES:** I think it should not be considered that he merely sails in a ship, nor should he be called a sailor. For he is not called a pilot because of the sailing, but because of the **art** <note>term: "art" (Latin: *ars*, Greek: *techne*) refers to a specialized skill or craft governed by rational principles</note> itself and his leadership over the sailors.
**THRASYMACHUS:** You speak the truth.
**SOCRATES:** Is there not something advantageous for each of these?
**THRASYMACHUS:** There certainly is.
**SOCRATES:** And does not the art aim at this: to investigate and provide what is advantageous to each?
**THRASYMACHUS:** To that very thing.
**SOCRATES:** Is there anything else advantageous to each art, other than that it be as perfect as possible?
**THRASYMACHUS:** How do you mean that question?
**SOCRATES:** Just as if you were to ask me whether it is enough for the body to be a body, or if it lacks anything else, I would answer that it lacks everything. And for this reason, the art of medicine has now been invented, because the body is weak and infirm, and does not suffice for itself. Therefore, so that it might bring advantage to the body, the art itself was discovered. But do I seem to you to speak the truth?
**THRASYMACHUS:** Entirely true.
**SOCRATES:** What then? Is the art of medicine itself, or any other art, so weak in itself that it lacks some virtue, just as eyes lack sight or ears lack hearing? Because of which, is there a need in them for some art that investigates and provides what contributes to these? Is there some defect in the art itself, and does every art need another art to consider what is advantageous for it, and that one in turn need another, and so on to infinity? Or does each art look out for its own advantage? Or does it need neither itself nor another to investigate what might counteract its defect? For no defect or error exists in any art. Nor is it fitting for an art to seek advantage for anything except that subject of which it is the art. The art itself remains whole and inviolate always, insofar as each remains entirely and immaculately what it is. Consider this with sincere and exact reasoning: is it so, or otherwise?
**THRASYMACHUS:** It is so, certainly.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, medicine does not look out for medicine, but for the body.
**THRASYMACHUS:** So it is.
**SOCRATES:** Nor does horsemanship look out for horsemanship, but for horses; nor does any other art look out for itself—for it is not in need—but for that of which it is the art.
**THRASYMACHUS:** So it appears.
**SOCRATES:** And yet, O Thrasymachus, the arts preside over and dominate that of which they are the arts.
He conceded this, though with difficulty.
**SOCRATES:** No science, then, inquires into or prescribes the advantage of the stronger, but rather that of the weaker, and of that which is commanded by it.
He did not deny this, but prepared to fight against it. Then I, adding other things to these, said:
**SOCRATES:** No physician, insofar as he is a physician, studies to benefit the physician, or prescribes anything for him, but for the sick man. For it was conceded that he who is truly a physician is the master of bodies, not a gatherer of money. Was that not conceded?
He agreed.
**SOCRATES:** And that the exact pilot of a ship is a leader of sailors, not a sailor?
This too.
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, such a pilot and leader does not inquire into and prescribe what is advantageous to the pilot himself, but what is advantageous to the sailors who are ruled by him.
This also he confessed with difficulty. And here I said:
**SOCRATES:** Nor does any other person, Thrasymachus, in any position of leadership or power, insofar as he is a ruler, think of or prescribe what is advantageous to himself, but what is conducive to the subject; and everything he says and does, he says and does for the advantage and dignity of that subject.

When we had reached this point, and it was clear to all that the definition of justice had fallen into its opposite, Thrasymachus did not respond as he ought, but said:
**THRASYMACHUS:** Tell me, Socrates, do you have a nurse?
**SOCRATES:** Why is that? I said it would be better to answer than to ask such things.
**THRASYMACHUS:** Because, he said, she neglects you; and she does not wipe your nose when it is stuffed, even though you need it; you who know neither the duty of the sheep nor of the shepherd.
**SOCRATES:** Why do you say that?
**THRASYMACHUS:** Because you think that shepherds or cowherds consider the good of the sheep or the oxen, and feed and care for them, looking to anything other than the advantage of their masters and themselves. And those who rule in cities as they ought, you think they look upon those who are under them in any other way than a shepherd looks at his sheep; and that they think of anything else night and day than where advantage might come to them. And so far are you from understanding the just and justice, and likewise the unjust and injustice, that you are ignorant that the just is actually another's good, and truly...

# BOOK I

...of the ruler and the superior, but to the detriment of the one who obeys and is subject. He claims that injustice, on the contrary, rules over those who are truly simple and just; those who obey do what is conducive to the stronger man's power and, by their service, make him happy, while they do nothing for their own benefit. You must consider it in this way, O most foolish Socrates, that a just man always has less than an unjust one. First, in private business dealings, wherever a just and an unjust man enter into a contract together, you will find that at the dissolution of the partnership, the just man always carries away less than the unjust. Furthermore, in public affairs, when taxes are to be paid, the just man contributes more from an equal estate, and the unjust man less. But when there is something to be received from the public treasury, the just man gains nothing, while the unjust man gains much. Moreover, if both should hold a public office <note>Latin: *magistratu*</note>, even if no other loss falls upon the just man, his domestic affairs at least suffer through neglect, and he gains nothing from the public store because he is just. Added to this, he makes his relatives and acquaintances his enemies because he refuses to serve them in any way beyond what is just. For the unjust man, however, all the opposite occurs. I mean, as I said before, the man who is able to get the better of everyone else. Consider him, then, if you wish to judge how much more it profits a man privately to be unjust than just. You will learn this most easily if you look at the highest form of injustice: that which makes the one who commits it most happy, and those who suffer the wrong—and who are unwilling to do wrong themselves—the most miserable. This is tyranny, which usurps the property of others not little by little, but all at once, by stealth and by force, whether it be sacred or holy, private or public. If someone commits a crime in only one of these parts and is caught, he is punished and suffers the greatest reproach. Indeed, temple-robbers, thieves, burglars, and swindlers are the names given to those who sin in these particular parts. But when a man, in addition to stealing the property of the citizens, has even reduced the citizens themselves to slavery, he is no longer called by those shameful names, but is called blessed and happy, not only by his fellow citizens but by all who hear that he has fulfilled the height of wickedness. For those who revile injustice do so not because they fear committing it, but because they fear suffering it. In this way, Socrates, injustice, when it is absolute, is something stronger, more free, and more masterly than justice; and as I said from the beginning, justice is what is conducive to the stronger, while injustice is what is useful and profitable to oneself.

When Thrasymachus had said this, he intended to depart, after having poured his speech into our ears with great force, just like a bath-attendant <note>original: *balneator*. Thrasymachus is compared to someone who dumps a bucket of water over a bather's head.</note>. However, those present would not permit this, but compelled him to remain and give an account of what he had said. I myself especially begged him: "O blessed Thrasymachus, do you hurry to leave after tossing out such a speech, before you have sufficiently taught us or learned yourself whether this is as you say or otherwise? Or do you think you have undertaken to define a small matter, and not rather the rule of life—by which, if any of us followed it, he might live the best life?"

**THRA.** Do I think it is otherwise?

**SO.** You seem to have no care for us, nor do you worry whether we live worse or better through our ignorance of what you claim to know. But, my good man, show this to us freely. It will not be a bad investment for you to bestow a benefit on so many of us. I will tell you what I think: I am not at all persuaded that injustice brings more profit than justice, even if one is given total license to do whatever he desires. Let a man be unjust, and let him be able to do wrong either by stealth or by force; nevertheless, you do not persuade me that there is more profit in injustice itself than in justice. Perhaps not only I, but someone else among us, feels this way. Persuade us, then, blessed man, that we are not right to value justice more than injustice.

**THRA.** How shall I persuade you further, if you are not persuaded by what I just said? What more shall I do? Shall I cram the argument into your soul?

**SO.** By Jupiter, no! But first, I would wish that you stand by what you have said. Or if you wish to change anything, do so openly, and do not deceive us. Now you see, Thrasymachus—to resume what was said before—that while you first defined the true physician as a healer of the sick, you later did not think it necessary to define the shepherd so strictly. You thought that insofar as he is a shepherd, he merely fattens the sheep, not for the benefit of the sheep, but for the sake of a feast, like a guest who is going to eat, or for the sake of money, like a merchant who is going to sell them. Surely the art of shepherding <note>original: *pastoralī arti*</note> cares for nothing else than that which it governs, that it may be in the best condition. For as long as it is the true faculty of shepherding, it lacks nothing to be sufficient and best. Thus I thought it necessary for us to admit that every rule <note>original: *principatum*, referring to leadership or office</note>, insofar as it is a rule, looks to the good of nothing else but that which is subject to it and cared for by it, whether it be private or public. But do you think that the rulers in cities, those who are truly rulers, hold their offices willingly?

**THRA.** I do not think it; I know it for certain.

**SO.** What about other types of rule? Do you not know that no one is willing to take them, but they demand pay, as if no benefit would come to themselves from such command, but rather to those who are subject? Tell me: do we not say that each art is different from another because it has a different power? And do not answer me contrary to your opinion, my happy man, so that we may make some progress.

**THRA.** It is different by this very power.

**SO.** And does not each art provide us with some specific benefit, and not one common to all? Just as medicine provides health, the pilot's art <note>original: *gubernatoria*</note> provides safety in navigation, and others likewise?

**THRA.** Certainly.

**SO.** And does not the art of pay <note>original: *mercenaria*</note> provide wages? For this is its power. Or do you call medicine and the pilot's art the same? Or if you wish to define and distinguish them more precisely, as you proposed, even if someone steering a ship becomes healthy because the voyage benefits him, you would not for this reason call the pilot's art "medicine"?

**THRA.** Certainly not.

**SO.** Nor, I think, would you call the art of pay "medicine" if someone earning a wage becomes healthy while serving.

**THRA.** No.

**SO.** What then? Would you call medicine the "art of pay" if a physician makes a profit while healing?

**THRA.** Not at all.

**SO.** Did we not agree that the benefit of each art is specific to it?

**THRA.** Let it be so.

**SO.** If therefore...

all craftsmen commonly obtain a benefit; it is clear that by using a certain common thing, one and the same, they obtain a benefit of this kind from it. THRA. It seems so. SO. Now, we say that craftsmen who receive a wage follow a benefit from the fact that they use the <term>mercenary art</term> <note>The "mercenary art" or "wage-earning art" (Latin: *mercenaria arte*) refers to the skill of earning pay, which Socrates distinguishes from the specific skill of a craft like medicine.</note>. THRA. What then? SO. Therefore, this benefit—namely the receiving of a reward—does not come to each person from his own specific art. But if we wish to inquire diligently: medicine indeed produces health; the mercenary art produces profit; and architecture produces a building; the profit-making art produces this secure wage; and all the rest similarly. Furthermore, each art performs its own work and contributes to that for which it was invented. But if no reward is given to the craftsman himself, does he receive any benefit from the art? THRA. None. SO. Does it then not even provide a benefit when he works for free? THRA. I certainly think so. SO. Therefore, O Thrasymachus, as is now manifest, no art and no <term>magistracy</term> <note>Latin: *magistratus*; referring to public office or leadership.</note> provides what is beneficial for itself; but as we were saying in the previous parts, it provides and commands what is advantageous for the subject, looking always to the convenience of the inferior and not the superior. For these reasons, therefore, my dear Thrasymachus, I was saying just now that no one is willing to undertake command and to approach the correction of others' evils of their own accord, but they seek a reward; because he who is to act rightly according to his art never acts for his own advantage according to the command of that art, but for the benefit of the inferior. For which reason, as it seems, a reward must be set for those who are to govern willingly: either money, or honor, or a penalty if they do not take up the command. GLAU. How do you say this, O Socrates? I know of two rewards; but the "penalty" you speak of, and how you place it in the category of a wage, I do not know. SO. Then you are ignorant of the reward of the best men, for the sake of which the best men rule whenever they accept command. Or is it hidden from you that to be ambitious and greedy is considered a reproach, and truly is so? GLAU. I know that indeed. SO. For this reason, then, good men are not willing to rule led by either money or honor. For they do not wish to be called "mercenaries" by openly receiving a wage for their office, nor "thieves" by taking it secretly. Nor again for the sake of honor, for they are not ambitious. It is necessary, therefore, that a necessity and a penalty be imposed upon them if they are to be driven to accept a magistracy. For this reason, it seems to be considered shameful for anyone to approach ruling spontaneously without waiting for necessity. But the greatest of penalties is to be subjected to the administration of evil men, unless one accepts the helm of the state himself. Fearing this very penalty, honest men seem to me to take up office if they ever do; and then they approach it not as if toward some good, nor as if taking any pleasure from it, but as a necessary thing—since they are able to commit themselves neither to better men nor to those like themselves. Indeed, if there were a city of good men, there would be a struggle *not* to rule, just as now there is a contest out of a desire for ruling; and there it would be clear: that a true and legitimate prince looks not to his own advantage, but to the advantage of the one who is under him. Therefore, anyone who is not insane would rather choose that another benefit him than to involve himself in business while he consults for others. This, therefore, I grant to Thrasymachus in no way: that justice is the "utility of the more powerful." But this must be considered next. It seems to me a much greater thing which Thrasymachus now says, when he affirms that the life of the unjust man is better than the life of the just man. You, therefore, O Glaucon, which of these do you choose as more true? GLAU. I think the life of the just man is preferable. SO. Did you hear how many goods of the unjust life Thrasymachus was numbering just a moment ago? GLAU. I heard indeed, but I do not agree. SO. Do you wish for us to show him, if we can in any way, that he is by no means speaking the truth? GLAU. Why would I not wish it? SO. If we oppose his speech with a contrary speech, as if a comparison were proposed, and we enumerate how many goods the just man obtains, and he in turn brings his own, it will be necessary for some third party to enumerate and measure the goods again—however many we have collected for both sides—and thus there will be a need for certain judges to settle this dispute. But if, as we just began, we discuss the matter itself by bringing forward mutual concessions, we ourselves will be both the orators and the judges at the same time. GLAU. It is entirely so. SO. Which way pleases you more? GLAU. That one. SO. Come then, O Thrasymachus, answer us from the beginning. Do you affirm that extreme injustice is more useful than extreme justice? THRA. I do indeed affirm it, and I have brought the reason. SO. What about this? Do you call one of these a virtue and the other a vice? THRA. Why not? SO. Is justice then a virtue, and injustice a vice? THRA. Is it fitting for me to confess that, O charming man, when I say that injustice is profitable and justice is not? SO. What then? THRA. The contrary. SO. Will you perhaps call justice a vice? THRA. No, but a very noble foolishness. SO. Then you call injustice wickedness? THRA. Not even that. But good counsel and sagacity. SO. Do unjust men, Thrasymachus, seem to you to be prudent and good? <margin>Another false definition of justice</margin> THRA. Those, clearly, who are able to inflict injury upon cities and subject nations to themselves. But you perhaps think I am speaking of those who steal purses secretly. These things are also profitable if they remain hidden, but they are not worthy of estimation. Rather, those things I was speaking of just now are to be valued most. SO. I certainly understand what you mean. <margin>Refutation of that definition.</margin> But I wonder greatly if you place injustice in the category of virtue and wisdom, and justice in their contraries. THRA. I place them exactly so. SO. This is now harder, O friend, and no longer easy to find what one might say. For if you had asserted that injustice is profitable, yet confessed it to be a vice or something shameful, as some others do, we could say something according to common opinions. But now it is clear that you will say that injustice is something both beautiful and robust, and you will give to it all the other things that we attribute to justice, since you do not hesitate to place it in both virtue and wisdom.

# BOOK XXXI.

<note>original: LIBER XXXI. Note: In this Renaissance edition, the numbering refers to a specific division of the text rather than the modern chapter 1.</note>

chaste. **THRA.** You certainly prophesy most truly. **SO.** Yet we must not stop searching through discussion until I think you are saying what you actually think. For you seem to me, Thrasymachus, to not be mocking us at present, but to be bringing forward what you see as the truth. **THRA.** What does it matter to you whether I see it that way or not, as long as you do not refute my reasoning? **SO.** Nothing, certainly. But answer me this besides: does it seem to you that a just man wants to have more than another just man? **THRA.** By no means; for then he would not be well-bred and simple <note>meaning "straightforward" or "guileless"</note> as he is now. **SO.** What then: would he want to outdo a just action? **THRA.** Not even a just action. **SO.** But would he think it worthy to have more than an unjust man, and would he consider that just, or the opposite? **THRA.** He would certainly consider it so and think it worthy, but he would not be able to achieve it. **SO.** But that is not what I am asking; rather, whether the just man thinks it unworthy and does not wish to have more than another just man, but does wish to have more than the unjust. **THRA.** That is exactly how it is. **SO.** And what of the unjust man? Does he think it right to have more than both the just man and the just action? **THRA.** Why not? Since he thinks himself worthy to have more than everyone. **SO.** Therefore, will the unjust man also have more than an unjust person and an unjust action, and will he strive to surpass everyone in possessing? **THRA.** These things are true. **SO.** Thus we say: the just man does not wish to have more than his like, but more than his unlike; whereas the unjust man wishes to take more than both. **THRA.** You have spoken correctly. **SO.** And yet the prudent and good man is the unjust one himself <note>Thrasymachus's earlier claim</note>, while the just man is neither. **THRA.** That is also correct. **SO.** Therefore the unjust man is like the prudent and the good, but the just man is not at all. **THRA.** What prevents one who is such from being like those who are also such? And he who is not such, from not being like them? **SO.** You say it beautifully. Each of them, then, is of the same sort as those they resemble. **THRA.** What else? **SO.** Let it be so, then. But tell me, Thrasymachus, would you call someone "musical" and another "unmusical"? **THRA.** I would. **SO.** Which of these is prudent <note>wise/skilled</note> and which is imprudent? **THRA.** The musical one is prudent, and the one unskilled in music is imprudent. **SO.** And is he not good in the things in which he is prudent, and bad in the things in which he is imprudent? **THRA.** Certainly. **SO.** And shall we say the same of the physician? **THRA.** The same. **SO.** Does it seem to you, most excellent man, that when a musical man tunes a lyre, he wishes to surpass another musical man in the tightening and loosening of the strings, or thinks it worthy to achieve more than him? **THRA.** Not at all. **SO.** But does he strive to surpass the man unskilled in music? **THRA.** Necessarily. **SO.** What of the physician? In the quantity of a prescription, would you say he seeks to achieve more than either another physician or what the science itself requires? **THRA.** By no means. **SO.** But more than one unskilled in the medical art? **THRA.** Without a doubt. **SO.** Finally, consider all the sciences and ignorances: does anyone who possesses a science seem to you to want to take more, either in speaking or acting, than another who knows? Or would he not rather take the same actions as the one who is like himself? **THRA.** Perhaps it must be so. **SO.** But what of the unlearned man? Would he not want to take more for himself than both the learned and the unlearned? **THRA.** Perhaps. **SO.** But is the learned man not wise? **THRA.** I grant it. **SO.** And is the wise man not good? **THRA.** That also. **SO.** Therefore, the good and wise man will not want to claim more for himself than his like, but he will want more than his unlike and opposite. **THRA.** So it seems. **SO.** But the bad and unlearned man will claim more for himself than both his like and his unlike. **THRA.** It appears so. **SO.** Does not the unjust man, Thrasymachus, strive to usurp more than both his like and unlike? Did you not say so? **THRA.** I did indeed. **SO.** But the just man will not want more than his like, but more than his unlike. **THRA.** I admit it. **SO.** Therefore, the just man is like the wise and the good, while the unjust man is like the bad and the ignorant. **THRA.** It appears so. **SO.** And yet we agreed that each is of the same sort as the one he resembles. **THRA.** We clearly agreed. **SO.** Thus the just man has appeared to us to be good and wise, while the unjust man is unlearned and bad. Thrasymachus conceded all these things, though not with the ease with which I now report them, but with difficulty and having been dragged along with much sweat—for it was then summer. And I saw then for the first time, what I had never seen before: Thrasymachus blushing. Since, therefore, it was established that justice is both virtue and wisdom, while injustice is vice and ignorance, I said: let this remain so for us. But we were saying that injustice is something strong and powerful. Do you not remember, Thrasymachus? **THRA.** I remember. But what you say now does not please me, and I have something to say against it. But if I were to bring it up, I know for certain you would say I am making a public speech. Therefore, either let me say what I wish, or if you want to ask questions, ask. I will nod and shake my head to you, just as one does for old women telling fables. **SO.** Not at all against your own opinion. **THRA.** Just to gratify you in everything, since you do not let me speak. What else do you want? **SO.** Nothing, by Jove! If you do that, then do it; and I will ask the questions. **THRA.** Ask then. **SO.** I ask this now, as I did a little while ago, so that we may consider in order in the following discourse how justice stands against injustice. For it was said that injustice is more powerful and robust than justice. **THRA.** And what new thing do you bring now? **SO.** If indeed justice is wisdom and virtue, it will easily appear, I think, to be more robust than injustice, since injustice is ignorance; no one could be unaware of this. But I do not wish to act so simply, but to consider it this way: would you say that some city is unjust, and that other cities wish to unjustly reduce it to slavery, and keep those sent under them as slaves? **THRA.** Why not? Indeed, the city that is most excellent and has reached the extreme of injustice will do this most of all. **SO.** I understand that this was your argument. But I am considering this about it: whether this city which is superior to another city will have this power without justice, or if it is necessary that it have it with justice. **THRA.** If indeed, as you were saying a little while ago, justice itself is wisdom, it must be with justice. But if as I said, then without justice. **SO.** I am greatly delighted by your answers, O Thrasymachus, because you not only nod and shake your head, but you also answer excellently. **THRA.** To make myself pleasing to you. **SO.** You do well indeed. But gratify me in this also, and tell me: do you think a city...

# DIALOGUE I. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO CCXX.

city, or an army, or robbers, or thieves, or any other group of men unjustly attacking something together, be able to achieve anything if they treat one another with injustice? THRA. Not at all. SO. But what if they abstain from injustice? Would they not achieve more? THRA. Certainly. SO. For dissensions, Thrasymachus, are produced by injustice, along with enmities and contentions; but justice produces concord and friendship. Is it not so? THRA. Let it be so, so that I do not disagree with you. SO. You do well, best of men. But tell me this also: if this is the work of injustice—to beget hatred wherever it exists—then if it exists between free men and slaves, will it not cause them to hate one another and engage in contentions? And will they not be unable to do anything together in common concord? THRA. Entirely so. SO. What then? If it exists between two people, will they not disagree with one another, and pursue each other with hatred, and be enemies both to themselves and to the just? THRA. They certainly will. SO. But if injustice exists within one person, O wonderful man, will it not destroy his power? Or will he have it any less? THRA. Let him have it no less. SO. Does it not seem to have such a power that, in whomever it exists—whether a city, a nation, an army, or any other thing—it first renders that thing in which it exists powerless to act with itself because of dissension and discord; and then it makes it an enemy both to itself and to every opponent, and to the just? Is it not so? SO. <note>The text repeats SO. here, likely a printer's error for THRA.</note> It is so. And if it exists in one person, it will do all these same things which follow from its nature. First, it will render him powerless to act, since he is at odds with himself and is not consistent with himself. Then it will make him an enemy both to himself and to the just. Will it not? THRA. Certainly. SO. But the just, O friend, are also of God. <note>original: "et dei" - Socrates argues that the just are friends of the gods.</note> THRA. Let them be. SO. Therefore the unjust man will be an enemy to the gods, Thrasymachus; but the just man will be a friend. THRA. Fill yourself up, Socrates, according to your pleasure, as if at a feast of delicacies. For I will not oppose you, lest I make these people here angry with me. SO. Come then, provide the rest of the banquet, just as you were doing a little while ago by answering. It is certainly established that the just are wiser, better, and more powerful in action; while the unjust are not even able to manage anything together. Indeed, what we say most strongly—that those who are entirely unjust are able to accomplish something together in common—is not entirely true. For they would not abstain from injuring one another if they were altogether unjust. But it is clear that there is a certain justice in them, which affects them so that they do not wish to harm each other at the same time as they harm others; through this [justice] they do whatever they do. But they are driven to act unjustly by injustice, since they were only half-evil. For those who have reached the height of wickedness and injustice are entirely unable to achieve anything. I understand these things to be so, and not as you laid them down above. But whether the just live better than the unjust, and are happier—which is what we proposed to consider later—must now be considered. And as it seems to me, this follows from what we have said. But nevertheless, it must be considered more carefully. For the discussion is not about some cheap or contemptible matter, but about the very way in which one ought to live. THRA. Consider it then. SO. Behold, I am considering. Tell me then, does it seem to you that a horse has a specific function? <note>term: "opus" - translated here as function or work; the specific purpose for which a thing exists.</note> THRA. It does to me. SO. Would you not say that the function of a horse, or of anything else, is that which one could perform only with that thing, or best with it? THRA. I do not understand. SO. Then pay attention; perhaps you will understand this way. Can you see with anything other than your eyes? THRA. Not at all. SO. What then? Could you hear with anything other than your ears? THRA. By no means. SO. Therefore we would rightly call these the functions of those organs. THRA. Rightly. SO. Could you prune the shoots of a vine with a sword, or a small knife, or many other tools? THRA. Why not? SO. But yet not so conveniently as with a pruning-hook manufactured for this use. THRA. It is as you say. SO. Therefore shall we not say that this is the function of that tool? THRA. We shall certainly say so. SO. I think you now grasp better what I was saying a moment ago: when I asked whether the function of each thing is that which it alone, or it better than others, performs. THRA. I understand now, and that does seem to me to be the function of each thing. SO. Does it not also seem to you that there is a virtue <note>term: "virtus" - in this context, 'excellence' or the quality that allows a thing to perform its function well.</note> belonging to each thing to which a function is assigned? Let us return then to the previous points. We say the eyes have a certain function? THRA. Certainly. SO. Therefore is there not also a virtue of the eyes? THRA. There is a virtue. SO. And a function of the ears? THRA. And of the ears. SO. There is therefore also a virtue. THRA. There is. SO. Must we not say the same about all other things? THRA. The same. SO. Would the eyes ever perform their function beautifully if they did not have their own proper virtue, but had a vice instead of virtue? THRA. But how? For you are perhaps speaking of blindness instead of sight. SO. Whatever their virtue may be—for I am not asking that yet—but whether they perform their function rightly by their own proper virtue, and not rightly by vice. THRA. You speak the truth. SO. And will the ears, deprived of their private virtue, perform their function badly? THRA. Badly. SO. Do we feel the same about all other things? THRA. The same. SO. Come then, and consider this besides. Is there some function of the soul which you could perform with nothing else, such as <margin>living well</margin> caring, ruling, deliberating, and other things of that kind? Could we rightly attribute these to any other thing than the soul, and say they are its own? THRA. To no other. SO. What then about living itself? Shall we not say it is the function of the soul? THRA. Most of all. SO. And do we not say there is a certain virtue of the soul? THRA. We do. SO. Will the soul ever, O Thrasymachus, perform its own functions well if it is deprived of its proper virtue? Or will it be unable in any way? THRA. It will be unable. SO. It is necessary, therefore, that a bad soul rules and cares badly, but a good soul does all these things well. THRA. Necessary. SO. Did we not agree that the virtue of the soul is justice, and its vice is injustice? THRA. We agreed. SO. Therefore the just soul and the just man will live well; but the unjust man will live badly. THRA. So it appears according to your reasoning. SO. But he who lives well is blessed and happy. He who lives badly, the opposite. THRA. Why not? SO. Therefore the just man is happy; the unjust man is miserable. THRA. Let them be. SO. But it is not profitable to be miserable; it is profitable to be happy. THRA. Without a doubt. SO. Never then, O blessed Thrasymachus, will injustice be more advantageous than justice. THRA. You have been feasted on these things at the festival of Dionysus, O Socrates. <note>original: "in Dionysiis" - Thrasymachus sarcastically refers to the festival of Dionysus, suggesting Socrates has had his fill of "food for thought."</note> SO. I have indeed eaten at your table, Thrasymachus, since you have become milder toward me and have ceased to be difficult. Yet I have not happened to eat abundantly; and that is my own fault rather than yours. For just as at a banquet...

# ARGUMENT FOR THE SECOND DIALOGUE.

Greedy and unrestrained men always snatch at whatever is served up at a banquet, tasting it before they have sufficiently eaten of the previous dishes. In the same way, I seem to have done the same: before I could find what was originally proposed—namely, what justice itself is—I set that aside and turned to consider whether it is wickedness and ignorance, or wisdom and virtue. And finally, when that speech was brought forward claiming that injustice was more profitable than justice, I could not restrain myself from descending from the former topic to this one. Therefore, it happens to me at present from this discussion that I know nothing. For since I am ignorant of what justice is, I can in no way know whether it is a virtue or the opposite, and whether he who possesses it is happy or unhappy.

->END OF THE FIRST DIALOGUE.<-

### Marsilio's Argument for the Second Dialogue on Justice.

The second dialogue begins from a threefold division of goods. A "good" is surely that which is desirable. We desire something either for its own sake alone, such as pleasures and joy; or something for the sake of another thing only, such as whatever things are laborious; or something both for its own sake and for the sake of the things that follow from it, such as knowledge and good health. Justice, indeed, is said to be desirable both for the sake of the things following from it and, most especially, for its own sake. But before anything is perfectly defined regarding justice, Glaucon takes up the points omitted by Thrasymachus in defense of injustice, pursuing them more copiously and elegantly—and also more modestly. For he says: not because he feels this way, but to provoke Socrates to a sharper defense of justice, he will praise injustice. We have similar instances in the *Gorgias* <note>Another dialogue by Plato concerning rhetoric and morality</note>. After him, Adeimantus speaks first for justice, attributing to it both human and divine opinions; here you will note certain religious mysteries of the poets. Then he brings forward some points in favor of injustice, representing the personas of both Socrates and Thrasymachus, adding also that he does not wish to disparage justice, but in a way to irritate Socrates. He wishes to hear praises of justice which are drawn not from external things, but from the intrinsic nature of justice—the kind not usually offered by others. You should notice that Plato did not randomly place many things here pertaining to poets and priests; for he shows that in these matters, the license to sin often comes from poets, and even more often from wicked priests. Here he mocks the superstitions of the nations. Furthermore, it is not without reason that in these books, which were most dear to him, he inserted the persons most dear to him: Glaucon and Adeimantus, his brothers, and his father Ariston. Again, Socrates in his whole life contemplated nothing more earnestly than—with external emotions set aside—what virtue and vice themselves are and what they do in the soul. This he will subsequently demonstrate regarding justice and injustice, both spontaneously and when provoked. But I have here unjustly passed over that wonderful reward of justice brought from the mind of Musaeus <note>A legendary polymath and philosopher of ancient Greece</note>: I mean "perpetual drunkenness." Musaeus received this from Orpheus, who signified the same through the rites of Dionysus. This is consistent with that prophetic thread: *I shall be inebriated by the abundance of your house* <note>A reference to Psalm 36:8</note>. Drunkenness, therefore, is twofold. One is beneath the moon, induced by the drink of Lethe <note>The river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note>, through which the soul, placed outside and below itself, forgets divine things while raving about earthly ones. The other is above the moon, coming from a nectarean potion; through which the soul, placed outside and above itself, forgets mortal diseases. Looking up at divine things, it is dazzled as if by their first splendor, or rather, tasting them, it is transformed from its prior state by a certain new heat. Soon, however, it clearly perceives and tastes healthfully; indeed, it is nourished. Truly, the divine Idea through which the soul was made glides into the returning soul like a flavor to the sense of taste. From this, it first sweetly washes away anything foreign; then it fills it inwardly, and in filling it, delights it more. Thirdly, it restores the soul into itself, drenching it with inestimable pleasure. Where the soul from a "soul" is first made "intellect," and from "intellect" finally "god." It no longer tastes as it did before, nor what it did before, but tastes differently and different things. And just as among us a vehement imagination moves and forms the body, so there the body subject to the soul and its senses is immediately moved and formed by the most powerful thought of the mind: so much so that by the ineffable sweetness of the mind, the senses and the body also become wonderfully sweet. But now let us return to justice. Socrates, seeking this as the goal and object of his dispute through individual cases, because he found it difficult to find in the soul, first seeks it in the city, as if it would be more manifest there; so that through this, he might finally define the justice of the soul clearly. But so that he may consider justice in the city, he establishes a city from the beginning: saying first what its origin is, namely, mutual need; then what its matter is, namely, necessary things and crafts; finally, what its form is, namely, the rule of living and legitimate governance. And see how much he praises a sober life, and how much he disparages a delicate and luxurious one. The former is healthy and sufficient; the latter is insane and in need of many things. Finally, since war is born because of this, there is a need for soldiers in such a city; therefore, descending to the diligent institution of the military art, he accurately pursues how many things are necessary for a strenuous soldier and guardian of the fatherland. In all things, remember: no one can be born most fit for diverse things. Therefore, they ought to practice different crafts. Especially since by the work of one, the work of another is hindered. It is necessary for each to practice his own craft immediately from childhood and continuously throughout his whole life. Furthermore, the soldier-guardian of the fatherland ought to be born and educated such that, like dogs, he is mild toward those known to him and fierce toward strangers, and always vigilant and sagacious. Hence Socrates asserts that the beginning of any work is a certain greatest thing, easily formable in both ways, especially at a tender age. Therefore, he rightly forms the future soldiers from their "tender fingernails" <note>An idiom meaning from earliest childhood</note>, first according to the soul through music, and then according to the body through gymnastics; including under "music" poetic fables as well. These he commands to be applied diligently to the ears of boys. But only such kinds as might both provoke and instruct them toward military study as if they were certain preludes. Similarly, he orders others to be accustomed from childhood to these fables which most contribute to their future study. Contrary ones he keeps far away. That indeed is most...

# FOLIO CCXXI.

### DIALOGUE II. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON THE JUST.
**B.v.**

...is the [first] precept. He <note>referring to Plato/Socrates</note> soon detests poetic impiety which fashions shameful things about the gods. And he forbids such fables from being heard. He joins to this two forms of theology. The first: That God is entirely good, and the cause only of good things. Truly, God is the cause of no evil. Likewise, if God punishes anyone, He punishes for the sake of the good. The second: That God is utterly immutable <note>unchanging</note>, because He is most simple, most powerful, best, and most wise. From this it follows that he denies that God ever deceives anyone, either by false visions, or by signs and words. For He does not change into various forms; nor, since He does not change, does He pretend to be transformed. He concludes the book with a certain golden sentence: A lie is the most hateful of all things to both gods and men. Because if a lie in speech is hateful—which is a mere likeness of the lie itself which is in the soul—then surely the lie which is in the soul is exceedingly hateful to both gods and men. Truly, a lie of that kind is ignorance: through which the soul itself lies to itself concerning the truth of things. Since truth looks toward that which is said to *be*, and falsehood declines toward *not being*, the liar is rightly said to wander into nothingness insofar as he falls into falsehood.

---

-> THE SECOND DIALOGUE ON THE REPUBLIC <-

**SOCRATES**
When I had said these things, I thought I was freed from the dispute; but this was only the introduction. For Glaucon, a man certainly most courageous in all things (as he is elsewhere), did not then accept the concession of Thrasymachus, who was as if exhausted; instead he said: "O Socrates, do you wish to seem to have persuaded us, or to truly persuade us, that it is in every way better to be just than unjust?" **SOCRATES** "I indeed, if it were in my choice, would prefer to truly persuade you." **GLAUCON** "You are not doing what you wish. Tell me further: does there seem to you to be some good of this kind: which we would choose, certainly not desiring what follows from it, but loving it for its own sake? Just as rejoicing and pleasures, which are without harm, and which in the future bring nothing to the possessor except the joy of having them." **SOCRATES** "To me indeed there seems to be something of that sort." **GLAUCON** "What then? Is there something which we love both for its own sake and for the sake of those things which flow from it? Such as wisdom, sight, and health. For we choose these sorts of things for both reasons." **SOCRATES** "Certainly." **GLAUCON** "But do you see a third kind of good, in which is included physical exercise, being cured when ill, medical treatment, and making money? We admit these are indeed laborious, but they benefit us. And we would never seek them for their own sake, but for the sake of profit and the other things which proceed from them." **SOCRATES** "This is clearly the third kind. What then?" **GLAUCON** "In which of these do you place justice?" **SOCRATES** "In my opinion, in the most beautiful kind, which is sought by one who is to be happy both for its own sake and for the sake of what it effects." **GLAUCON** "It does not seem so to many, but rather to be of the laborious kind: which should be sought for the sake of rewards, honors, and glory, but for its own sake should be fled as something difficult." **SOCRATES** "I know indeed that it seems so to many. Wherefore it has long been disparaged by Thrasymachus as being such a thing, while injustice is praised. But I am dull, as it seems." **GLAUCON** "Come then, hear me, to see if these things seem so to you as well. For Thrasymachus seems to me to have been charmed by you like a snake by songs sooner than he ought. But to me, the demonstration of both has not yet happened according to my satisfaction. For I desire to hear what each is, and what power each has existing by itself in the soul—to set aside the rewards and what comes from them. I will do this, then, if it pleases you. I will renew the speech of Thrasymachus: and first I will say what sort of thing they say justice is, and whence they claim it arose. In the second place, that all who practice justice do so unwillingly, as a necessary thing but not a good one. Third, that they do this with reason. For the life of the unjust man is much better than that of the just, as they teach. To me indeed, O Socrates, it does not seem so. Yet I am often in doubt, because I am dinned daily by hearing Thrasymachus and countless others. But the speech on behalf of justice itself—how it is better than injustice—I have from no one yet heard as I would wish. I would desire to hear justice itself praised according to itself. I think I shall hear this most of all from you. Therefore, I will speak at length praising the unjust life: and by speaking I will show you in what way I most want to hear you, censuring injustice and praising justice. But see if this pleases you." **SOCRATES** "Most of all. For about what subject would anyone of sound mind more gladly hear and speak?" **GLAUCON** "You speak excellently. Indeed, hear now what I first promised to speak of: what justice is and whence it arose. They say by nature to do wrong is good; but to suffer wrong is evil. But there is far more evil in suffering the wrong than there is good in doing it. Therefore, after they have both inflicted and received injury in turn, and have tasted both, those who are unable to avoid the one and attain the other think it worthwhile to make a compact with one another, so that injury can neither be inflicted nor received. And from here they claim laws and constitutions had their origin, and the precepts of the laws were named 'lawful' and 'just.' This, therefore, they claim is the origin and substance of justice, which is a sort of middle ground between the best and the worst. Since the best is to do wrong and not pay the penalty; the worst is to suffer it and be unable to take revenge. Justice, therefore, being established in the middle of these, is loved not as a good, but is honored out of the weakness for doing wrong, as an obstacle to inflicting injuries. For a man who is truly a man, and able to do this, would never covenant with another to neither inflict nor suffer injury; otherwise he would be insane. This, O Socrates, is the nature of justice and of this kind, and from such things, as they say, it is produced. But that those who keep justice do so unwillingly, because from weakness they are unable to do wrong, we would clearly see if we imagined such a thing in the mind..."

# BOOK
### PAGE XXXI.

...we would carry out: if we were to grant to both the license to do whatever they pleased, to the just and the unjust man alike; then let us follow them, observing where desire leads each one. We would surely find the just man, driven by the greed for having more <note>original: "plus habendi auiditate" - a translation of the Greek *pleonexia*, the desire to outdo others or have more than one's share</note>, turning to the same path as the unjust man. Indeed, every nature seeks this as a good, but is led by law and force to maintain equality. 

The license I speak of would be such as they say was once granted to the ancestor of Gyges the Lydian. <margin>Gyges who found the ring.</margin> For they say he was a hired shepherd to the one who then ruled the Lydians. When a great storm of rain arose and the earth was moved, they say the earth opened with a chasm in that region where he was pasturing his herds. When he saw this, marvelling, he descended into the chasm and beheld other wonderful things of which they tell fables, including a hollow bronze horse. Through a window in the horse's belly, he noticed a corpse, larger than human form, which had nothing else upon it except a golden ring on its finger. Having taken this, he departed. 

Shortly after, he came to the assembly of shepherds where a messenger was to be chosen to report to the king every month concerning the state of the flocks. He sat down among the others, and it happened that when he by chance turned the stone of the ring toward the palm of his hand—the ring he had taken from the corpse—he suddenly became invisible to everyone, and they spoke of him as if he were absent. Marvelling at this, he turned the stone outward again; when he did so, he reappeared. Noticing this, he tested the ring more carefully to see if it had this power, and so it was discovered by him: that when the stone was turned toward himself he was seen by no one, but when turned away, he became visible. 

Having proven this, he ensured he was sent as a messenger to the king with the others. Upon arrival, he seduced the king's wife, and with her help, he entered into a plot to kill the king; having slain him, he seized the kingdom. 

If, therefore, there were two such rings, and the just man possessed one and the unjust the other, no one, it seems, would be so "adamantine" <note>meaning unbreakable or of such firm character</note> that he would remain in justice itself and wish to abstain from the property of others, when it was permitted for him to fearlessly snatch whatever he wanted from the marketplace, enter other people's houses, sleep with whomever he pleased in secret, kill anyone at his whim, release people from prison, and do other things among men as if he were a god. 

If both did these things, the one would differ in no way from the other in their actions, but both would tend toward the same goal. This indeed can be the greatest proof among all that no one is just willingly, but rather by compulsion—as if justice is not a good for the individual privately. For wherever anyone trusts he can act unjustly, he does so immediately. For every man believes in his private life that injustice is much more profitable than justice. And whoever judges in this way thinks rightly, according to the authors of this discourse. 

But if someone, having obtained such a power, should wish to abstain from injustice and not touch what belongs to others, he would be thought the most miserable and foolish of all by those who observed him. Yet they would praise him openly to one another, deceiving each other because they greatly fear suffering an injustice themselves. And so these things are said.

But we shall clearly judge the life of each—namely the just and the unjust—if we distinguish the most just man and the most unjust man separately; otherwise, we cannot. Let the distinction be this: that we take nothing of injustice away from the unjust man, nor anything of justice from the just man, but let us place each perfectly in his own pursuit. 

First, then, let the unjust man act like the best of craftsmen—just as a supreme pilot or a physician perceives what can be accomplished in his art and what cannot, attempting the former and leaving the latter, and if he fails in anything, he is able to correct it. So too, the unjust man, attempting injustices rightly, should remain hidden if he is to be truly unjust. But if he is caught, he must be considered unskilled. For the extreme of injustice is to seem just when one is not. 

Therefore, the most unjust man must be given the extreme of injustice, and nothing taken away; but it must be allowed that he who has committed many unjust acts should have a reputation for justice among all. If he fails in anything, he should be able to correct it, being fit to persuade if any report of his evil deed is announced, and able to use force if necessary, through his courage, strength, and abundance of friends. 

When we have fashioned such a man, let us place the just man beside him: a simple and noble man who, according to Aeschylus <note>A famous Greek tragic poet</note>, desires not to *seem* but to *be* good. All reputation for justice must be removed from him, lest he seem just to anyone. For if he is seen to be just, honors and rewards will come to him. It would then be uncertain whether he is such for the sake of justice or for the sake of honors and gifts. He must therefore be deprived of all things except justice, and so placed that he is the opposite of the one above. Though he does nothing unjust, let him be believed to be most unjust, so that he may be tested for justice as if by a trial, in that neither infamy nor the things that follow it move him from his purpose; but let him remain immovable until death, being thought unjust throughout his whole life, though he is in fact just. 

When both have reached the extreme—the one of justice, the other of injustice—let it be judged which of them is the happier.

**SOCRATES:** My goodness! <note>original: "Papae" - an exclamation of surprise</note> How vehemently, friend Glaucon, you bring both men into clear judgment, as if they were statues.

**GLAUCON:** As much as I am able. Since both are such, it is no longer difficult, I think, to describe what kind of life awaits each. It must be said, then: if I say anything rather harsh, do not think, Socrates, that *I* say these things, but those who praise injustice over justice. For they will say that the just man so situated will be scourged, tortured, and suffer bonds. His eyes will be put out, and finally, having suffered all evils, he will be impaled <note>original: "suspendetur" - can mean hanged or impaled</note>, and he will realize that one should desire not to *be*, but to *seem* just. 

The poem of Aeschylus could be more rightly understood regarding the unjust man. For they will say the unjust man, as one following what is consistent with truth and not living according to the opinion of men, desires not to seem, but to *be* unjust: "having a mind like a deep and fruitful furrow, from which glorious counsels germinate." First, he holds offices in his city because he appears just. Then he marries whichever woman he wants, and gives his children in marriage to whomever he wants; he joins and communicates with whomever he pleases; and in all these things he gains profit and wealth, since he does not fear committing injustice. In public contests and private ones, he comes out on top and gains more advantage than his adversary...

<summary>Glaucon presents the famous "Ring of Gyges" thought experiment to Socrates, arguing that people are only just because they lack the power to be safely unjust. He challenges Socrates to prove that a truly just man who is perceived as evil is happier than a truly evil man who is perceived as saintly.</summary>

to pick out various things from there: and thus become wealthy from it; whereby he may both benefit his friends and harm his enemies. He may worship the Gods magnificently with gifts and sacrifices, and be able to win over any of men or gods much better than the just man can. From which they wish it to be agreed that he is dearer to God than the just man. For this reason they say, O Socrates, that among both gods and men, a better life is established for the unjust man than for the just. When Glauco had said these things, and I was thinking of responding something to them, his brother Adimantus said: "It has not yet been sufficiently spoken of this matter, O Socrates." SOCRATES: "Why so?" ADIMANTUS: "That which most ought to have been said, certainly was not said." SOCRATES: "As the proverb goes, 'Let a brother stand by the man.' <margin>Proverb: Let a brother assist.</margin> Therefore, if he has left anything out here, you help him. Since the things said by him are enough to overwhelm me and make me unable to defend justice." ADIMANTUS: "You say nothing. Listen also to these things besides. For it is proper to bring in the contrary arguments to those he brought forward: those by which one praises justice and conversely disparages injustice, so that what Glauco seems to me to want may become manifest. Fathers certainly instruct their sons, as do all who have care of anyone, that it is necessary to be just: praising justice not for its own sake, but for the honors that follow from it; so that he who is considered just may obtain from that reputation public offices, marriages, and whatever Glauco was saying a little while ago regarding the man who is thought to be just. Indeed, they bring in a certain reward of glory among the first things. For by introducing the approvals of the gods, they can report the greatest benefits bestowed by the gods upon holy men. To which the noble Hesiod and Homer bear witness. For the former <note>Hesiod, in Works and Days</note> claims the gods make it so for the just that oaks bear acorns on their higher branches, bees in the middle, and sheep are weighed down with wool, and many other goods of the same kind. The other <note>Homer, in the Odyssey</note> says similar things to these. For just as, he says, for a good king who is like a son of god, the black earth bears wheat and barley, the trees are heavy with fruit, the flocks bring forth young easily, and the sea provides fish. Likewise Musaeus <note>A legendary polymath and poet</note> and his son wished even more excellent goods to be granted to the just by the gods themselves. For placing them among those in the underworld, and seating them at the banquets of the holy, they make them live forever drunk and crowned in great pleasure, <margin>Musaeus</margin> considering eternal drunkenness to be the most beautiful reward of virtue. But those who wish longer rewards than these to be given by the gods say that the sons and descendants of a just and faithful man propagate his race through the ages. By these and such things they praise justice; but the profane and unjust they bury in a certain mud in the underworld, and compel them to carry water in a sieve. They also mark the living with infamy. And finally, whatever punishments Glauco related of those who are just but seen as unjust, they relate the same of the unjust; but they have no others. Thus the praise and disparagement of both stand. Besides these things, Socrates, consider another kind of speech about justice and injustice brought in both privately and by the poets. For all sing with one voice that temperance and justice are good, but difficult and laborious; while intemperance and injustice are something pleasant and easy to acquire, and only shameful by reputation. Furthermore, they commonly say that unjust things are for the most part more useful than just ones. And they easily honor wicked men who are rich and powerful, calling them happy both privately and publicly; but they despise those who are weak and poor, even though they concede they are better than the others. But of all these things, the most wonderful stories are circulated about the gods and virtue: that the gods have given an unhappy life to many good men, and the opposite to the wicked. Moreover, prophets and soothsayers, approaching the doors of the rich, persuade them that they have a power, received from the gods by sacrifices and incantations, of purging by certain ceremonies and delights if any crime has been committed by them or their ancestors; and of harming any of their enemies at little expense, whether just or unjust alike. They assert, indeed, that by certain charms and bonds they lead the gods to obey them in all these things. To all this they bring the testimony of poets: partly that we slide easily into vice. *Mortals fall headlong into every vice, since the easy path leads to it; because this clings to us even as we are born.* *The gods placed labor before virtue itself.* <margin>The gods are appeased by sacrifice</margin> *The way is difficult for all who approach it.* Partly that god is turned by our prayers and gifts. They bring Homer as a witness, who says: *The gods are also exorable and changeable; and men turn them by praying with sacrifices, vows, and libations when they have sinned.* *The high gods are easy, they are turned by prayers, and likewise* <margin>Musaeus</margin> *they are appeased by the pious scent of sacrifices, and by the very vows of men, which if anyone has erred against them, asking for pardon, he offers upon the altars.* They also circulate the books of Musaeus and Orpheus, sons of the Moon and the Muses, according to which they celebrate sacred rites, persuading not only individuals but also cities that absolutions and purifications of crimes are made through sacrifices with the delights of games for both the living and the dead; which indeed they call *Teletas* (that is, expiations), which free us from those evils that are there; but for those who neglect sacrifices, grave things await us. All these things, O Socrates, such and so great, we say concerning the rewards of virtue and vice as pertains to gods and men. What do we think the minds of those young men will do who hear these things, who are clever by nature, and being easily and quickly turned to all that is said, can deliberate for themselves what sort of person one should be and what path one should follow to lead the best life? It is likely such a young man would turn over in his mind that saying of Pindar: <margin>Pindar on the just and unjust.</margin> *Shall I climb the high walls of justice, or shall I enter the crooked paths of deceit, and thus supporting myself, lead my life?* For they say that if I am just, but do not appear so, it is of no profit to me, but the labors and penalties are certain. But for the unjust man who has attained the reputation of justice, a divine life is said to be his. Therefore, since this estimation of justice, as the wise hand down, compels and violates the truth, and is the chief thing for happiness, must one not tend toward it entirely? It is necessary, therefore, to put on the mask of justice, and to display a certain shadow of virtue; but behind one's back, to drag that cunning and versatile fox of the wise Archilochus. # BOOK II.

Someone might perhaps say that it is not easy for a wicked man to always remain hidden. To this we shall respond that nothing great is easy. Nevertheless, if we wish to be happy, we must go this way, where the tracks of the arguments lead. For in order that our wickedness may remain concealed, we will enter into conspiracies and secret societies. There are, moreover, masters of persuasion who hand down the wisdom of the public assembly and the courtroom; by these means, we will partly persuade and partly use force, so that while we claim more for ourselves, we shall pay no penalty at all. But it is impossible, they say, either to hide from the gods or to compel them. Yet, if the gods do not exist, or if they do not care for human affairs, we need not worry about hiding from them. But if they do exist and do care for human affairs, we know of it from no other source than the talk of the multitude and from the poets who write their genealogies. These very same poets declare that the gods can be moved by sacred prayers and offerings. One must either believe both of these claims or neither. If we are to believe them, then we should act unjustly and offer sacrifices to the gods from the very fruits of our plunder. For if we are just, we shall indeed be unharmed by the gods, but we shall lose the profits gained through injustice. If we are unjust, however, we shall gain riches, and after committing crimes, we shall be freed from punishment by swaying the gods with prayers. But indeed, in the underworld we shall pay the penalty for the injustices we committed here, either we ourselves or our children's children.

<margin>The poets are sons of the gods</margin> But, oh friend, one might say with some reason: the supreme expiations <note>original: "expiationes" — rituals for cleansing guilt or sin</note> for sins committed have great power, and the gods are easily moved, as the greatest cities say. And the poets, who are sons of the gods, and the prophets of the gods, testify that these things are so. Therefore, what reason will further induce us to choose justice over the greatest injustice? For if we conceal our injustice under a false appearance of respectability, everything will succeed according to our wishes with both gods and men, both while living and after death, as the speech of many excellent men testifies. From all that has been said, oh Socrates, who would believe that a man would preserve justice if he possessed any power of fortune, wealth, body, or birth—and would he not rather smile if he heard it being praised? Indeed, if anyone can show that what we have said is false, and truly knows that justice is best, he will be greatly forgiving and not angry with the unjust, understanding that unless someone hates iniquity by a divine nature, or abstains from injustice through knowledge, no one is just of his own will; rather, it is through fear, old age, or some other weakness that one disparages injustice, being unable to practice it. This is clear enough from the fact that as soon as anyone acquires power, he is the first to act unjustly to the extent of his strength. And there is no other cause for all these things than that from which this entire speech of mine, and that of Glaucon here, oh Socrates, has proceeded against you. For of all of you, oh wonderful Socrates, who profess to be praisers of justice—beginning from those ancient Heroes of whom any memory survives, down to the men of our own time—no one has ever praised justice or disparaged injustice otherwise than by looking to the reputation, honors, and rewards that come from them. But as to what each of them does by its own nature when hidden in the soul of the possessor, unseen by gods and men, no one has ever sufficiently explained, either in poetry or in prose: namely, that injustice is the greatest of all evils that the soul contains, and justice is the greatest good. For if this had been said by all of you from the beginning, and we had been persuaded of it from our very childhood, we would not be guarding one another to prevent injustice; rather, each man would be his own guardian, fearing lest by acting unjustly he should dwell with the greatest evil. These things, oh Socrates, and perhaps even more, Thrasymachus or someone else might say concerning justice and injustice, perverting the power of each—and quite burdensomely, as it seems to me. But I, wishing to hide nothing from you and desiring to hear the opposite from you, prolong the speech. Therefore, do not merely show us that justice is superior to injustice, but show what each of them does by itself to the soul of the possessor, the one being an evil and the other a good. Remove the reputations, as Glaucon also commanded. For if you do not take away the true reputations from both sides and add false ones, we shall say you are not praising justice, but that which *seems* just; nor disparaging injustice, but that which *seems* unjust; and that you are commanding the unjust man to hide his injustice, agreeing with Thrasymachus that justice is another's good, serving the more powerful, while injustice is useful to oneself but disadvantageous to the weaker. Since, therefore, you have agreed that justice is among those goods which are to be sought both for their consequences and much more for their own sake—such as sight, hearing, wisdom, health, and whatever other goods are fruitful by their own nature and precious, not consisting merely in opinion—praise this very quality in justice: how it helps the one who possesses it by itself, while injustice harms him. Leave the reputations and rewards for others to praise. For I could endure others when they praise justice or disparage injustice in such a way, praising or disparaging the reputations and rewards. But you I can least of all endure, unless perhaps you command it, since you have spent your whole life in no other thing than this very speculation. Therefore, do not only show us by your speech that justice is superior to injustice, but in what way each of them affects its participant—whether it be hidden or not hidden from gods and men—the one being a good and the other an evil. When I had heard these things—though I had always loved the character of Glaucon and Adeimantus—I was then greatly astonished and said: Not badly did the lover of Glaucon write the beginning of those elegiac poems to you, oh sons of that man, when you had fought bravely in the battle of Megara: "Oh sons of Aristo, divine offspring of a renowned man." This seems to be well said, my friends. For you are affected in a divine way if you are not persuaded that injustice is better than justice, seeing as you speak so abundantly on its behalf. You seem to me, however, not to be truly persuaded. I gather this from your characters; for according to the speech itself, I would have believed you least of all. But the more I believe you, the more I am in doubt as to where I should turn. For I do not know how I may help. Indeed, I seem unable. The proof of this is that you did not accept those arguments by which I thought I had sufficiently shown against Thrasymachus that justice is better than injustice. Nor, on the other hand, do I find how I may now come to the rescue, fearing lest perhaps...
