# DIALOGUE II. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

<page-num>FOLIO CCXXIII.</page-num>

it happens that one who hears justice being disparaged in his presence may shrink away, failing to speak in its defense as long as he is permitted to breathe and speak. It is better, therefore, to support it with all one's strength. Then Glaucon and all the others asked that I help with every resource and not abandon the discussion, but rather investigate what each <note>justice and injustice</note> was, and what the true utility of each might be. I said then, as was my opinion, that this question we are undertaking is not to be despised, but is the work of a man of sharp vision, as it seems to me. And since we are otherwise not strong enough, justice must be investigated just as if someone had ordered people who do not see sharply to read small letters placed far away; then someone noticed that those same letters were elsewhere in a larger place and larger in size; and from there, those possessing them decided that they should read those first, so that they might finally consider the smaller ones to see if they are the same. Adimantus said, "Exactly so. But what similarity do you see in this question of justice, O Socrates?" 

**SOCRATES:** I will tell you. Do we not say that justice belongs to a single man? We also say it belongs to a whole city! 
**ADIMANTUS:** Clearly. 
**SOCRATES:** And is a city not larger than one man? 
**ADIMANTUS:** Larger! 
**SOCRATES:** Perhaps, therefore, justice exists more amply in the larger thing, and is easier to recognize. Therefore, if you wish, we shall first seek what it is in cities. Then we shall consider it in individuals, contemplating the likeness of the larger in the form of the smaller. 
**ADIMANTUS:** You seem to speak skillfully. 
**SOCRATES:** If we were to inspect a city established in speech, we would also see its justice and injustice. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Perhaps. 
**SOCRATES:** Once this is done, there will be hope of more easily recognizing what we seek. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Greatly so. 
**SOCRATES:** It is necessary, therefore, to accomplish this. For it is no small matter, as I think. Consider it, then. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Behold, we are considering it. But do not do otherwise. 

**SOCRATES:** A city comes into being, as I think, since none of us is sufficient unto himself, but stands in need of many things. Or do you think there was any other beginning for establishing cities? 
**ADIMANTUS:** No other. 
**SOCRATES:** Thus, men take one another in turn, and summon one for one use and another for another, since they need many things; and they gather many partners and helpers into one habitation. This assembly we call a city, do we not? 
**ADIMANTUS:** Entirely. 
**SOCRATES:** They share their own things in turn, and receive the things of others in turn, thinking this exchange to be to their advantage. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Exactly so. 
**SOCRATES:** Come now, let us establish a city in our speech from the beginning. Our need, as it seems, will create it. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Why not? 
**SOCRATES:** The first and greatest of all needs is the preparation of food, so that we may exist and live. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** The second is habitation. The third is clothing and such things. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It is as you say. 
**SOCRATES:** Come then. But in what way will the city be sufficient for this preparation? Will there not be one farmer, another a builder, and another a weaver? Shall we also count a shoemaker there, or some other caretaker of things pertaining to the body's use? 
**ADIMANTUS:** Greatly so. 
**SOCRATES:** The city itself will therefore consist of at least four or five men. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It appears so. 

**SOCRATES:** What then? Must each of these communicate his work to the others: for instance, must one farmer prepare food for four, and consume four times the time and labor in agriculture to share with the others? Or rather, neglecting the care of others, should he prepare a fourth part for himself alone—namely, the preparation of food—in a fourth part of the time? And spend the remaining parts, one in building a house, another in clothing, another in making shoes, and not trouble to share his things with others, but provide for himself without the help of another? 
**ADIMANTUS:** Perhaps in this way, O Socrates, it would be easier than in that. 
**SOCRATES:** Not at all, by Jove! For it is absurd. For as you speak, I consider that we are born not altogether alike, but differing from one another, and each is produced by nature ready for specific tasks. Does it not seem so to you? 
**ADIMANTUS:** To me, indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** What then? Would one man do better performing all the arts at once, or individuals performing individual arts? 
**ADIMANTUS:** Individuals performing individual arts. 
**SOCRATES:** And I think this is also manifest: that if an opportunity for some work passes us by while we are occupied in some other business, the action itself perishes. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It is clear. 
**SOCRATES:** For the thing to be done does not wish to wait for the leisure of the doer; but necessity compels the doer to follow the work itself, always observing the opportunity. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It is necessary. 
**SOCRATES:** From these things it is clear that individual things are done both in greater number and better and more easily when individuals perform individual tasks according to nature, with the opportunity preserved, ceasing from other things. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It is entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** More citizens are needed, therefore, O Adimantus, than four, to provide those things we mentioned. For the farmer, as it seems, will not make his own plow if it is to be suitable for the work; nor hoes and rakes, nor other instruments which agriculture needs. Nor again the builder. For he also needs many things. And the same must be said of the weaver and the shoemaker. 
**ADIMANTUS:** The same. 
**SOCRATES:** Therefore, carpenters and blacksmiths, and many other such craftsmen, having become our fellow citizens in that town, will make it more crowded. 
**ADIMANTUS:** You speak the truth. 
**SOCRATES:** But this would not yet be large enough, unless we added to them ox-herds and shepherds and other herdsmen; so that the farmers might have oxen for plowing, and the architects might use beasts of burden for transporting materials, and the weavers and shoemakers might have hides and wool. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Surely it would be no small city that had all these things. 
**SOCRATES:** And to establish a city in a place where it does not need imports is almost impossible. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Impossible, certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** It will therefore need others as well, who may import from another city those things which this one lacks. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It will. 
**SOCRATES:** But a servant would be useless bringing nothing of those things needed by those from whom he brings what his own city needs. For he would return empty-handed. Would he not? 
**ADIMANTUS:** It seems so. 
**SOCRATES:** It is necessary, therefore, not only to make those things which suffice for that city, but such and as many as are needed by those from whom they require things. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It is necessary indeed. 
**SOCRATES:** We need more farmers, then, and other craftsmen in the city. 
**ADIMANTUS:** More, certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** And other servants besides, who both import and export individual items. These, moreover, are merchants. Are they not? 
**ADIMANTUS:** They are. 
**SOCRATES:** We shall therefore need merchants. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Certainly. 
**SOCRATES:** And if indeed there is maritime trade, many will also be needed who are skilled in maritime trade. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Many, clearly. 
**SOCRATES:**

# BOOK
### PAGE XXXI.

What then of the city itself? How will they share with one another the things that each person produces? It was for the sake of this sharing, after all, that we established a partnership and founded the city. **ADEIMANTUS.** It is clear that they will do so by buying and selling. **SOCRATES.** A marketplace, therefore, and a currency for the sake of exchange will be established for us for this commerce. **ADEIMANTUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Now, if a farmer or any other craftsman brings something he has made to the market, but does not arrive at the same time as those who wish to trade with him, will he sit idle in the marketplace, away from his work? **ADEIMANTUS.** Not at all. There are those who, noticing this, prepare themselves for this service. In well-ordered cities, this is done by men who are weakest in body and useless for other work. Stationed there in the market, they exchange money for goods with those who wish to sell, and give goods for money to those who wish to buy. **SOCRATES.** This necessity, then, creates the class of shopkeepers <note>original: "cauponum" - refers to local retailers or petty traders</note> in our city. Do we not call those who station themselves in the market for buying and selling "shopkeepers," while those who travel between different cities are called "merchants"? **ADEIMANTUS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** There are also others, I believe, who serve: those who can contribute little in terms of mental ability to this society, but who possess sufficient bodily strength for labor. These men, selling the use of their strength and calling the price of it "wages," are named "mercenaries" <note>original: "mercenarii" - here meaning wage-laborers or hired hands, not necessarily soldiers</note>. Is it not so? **ADEIMANTUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** Thus, the city is filled out by wage-laborers as well. **ADEIMANTUS.** So it seems. **SOCRATES.** Has our city now grown so much, O Adeimantus, that it is complete? **ADEIMANTUS.** Perhaps. **SOCRATES.** Where then, within it, will justice and injustice be found? And with which of the things we have discussed did they arise? **ADEIMANTUS.** I do not know, O Socrates, unless perhaps it exists in some mutual use of the things we have mentioned. **SOCRATES.** Perhaps you speak well; however, we must consider it and not give up. First, let us see how those so established will live. Will they not produce food, wine, clothes, shoes, and houses? In summer, for the most part, they will work without clothes or shoes. In winter, however, they will be sufficiently provided with garments and footwear. They will nourish themselves by making flour from barley and wheat, partly by kneading it and partly by cooking cakes and loaves, placing them upon reeds or clean leaves. Reclining on beds made of yew-leaf and myrtle, they and their children will feast together, drinking wine with garlands on their heads and singing the praises of the gods. They will live pleasantly together, and they will not beget children beyond their means, guarding against both poverty and war. **GLAUCON.** You have made these men feast without any relish <note>original: "obsonio" - side dishes or savory additions to bread</note>, it seems. **SOCRATES.** You speak the truth. I had forgotten that they would have relishes: salt, of course, and olives, cheese, and leeks. Furthermore, they will have vegetables, the "pottage" of the fields. And we shall add desserts for them: figs, chickpeas, and beans; they will toast myrtle berries and beech-nuts by the fire, drinking in moderation. Thus, living peacefully and healthily to old age, they will leave a similar life to their descendants. **GLAUCON.** If you were founding a city of pigs, O Socrates, what other fodder would you provide for them? **SOCRATES.** What then should we do, O Glaucon? **GLAUCON.** What is customary: they should recline on couches unless we want them to live miserably, and eat from tables, with the relishes and desserts that people use nowadays. **SOCRATES.** Very well, Glaucon. I understand. We are considering at present not just how a city is made, but how a *luxurious* city is made. Perhaps that is not a bad idea. For by looking at such a city, we might discover where justice and injustice take root in states. The true city, in my view, is the one we have described—the healthy one. But if you wish, let us also consider the "feverish" city. Nothing prevents it. For some, it seems, the simple life will not suffice; they will want couches, tables, and other furniture, as well as delicacies, perfumes, incense, prostitutes, sweets—and all these in abundance. We must no longer limit ourselves to the necessities we first mentioned—houses, clothes, and shoes—but we must set to work with painting and embroidery, and procure gold, ivory, and all such things. Is it not so? **GLAUCON.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Must the city not, therefore, be made larger? For that healthy one is no longer sufficient; it must be filled with a multitude of people who are no longer in cities for the sake of necessity. Such are hunters, actors, and imitators—some dealing with shapes and colors, others with music—poets and their assistants, rhapsodes, reciters of poems, actors, singers, dancers, contractors, and makers of all sorts of luxury items, including those for women's adornment. Furthermore, we shall need more servants. Do you not think we will need tutors, nurses, governesses, barbers, and other such attendants? Moreover, we will need those who prepare relishes and cookery; we will also need swineherds, for these were not in our earlier city. There was no need for them. But in this one, we will need them, and many other kinds of meat from animals, will we not? **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** And shall we not need doctors much more, living in this way, than we did before? **GLAUCON.** Much more. **SOCRATES.** And the land, which then was sufficient to feed those men, will now be too small. Or what do we say? **GLAUCON.** It is as you say. **SOCRATES.** Must we not then seize a portion of our neighbors' land, so that we have enough for pasture and plowing? And will they not do the same to ours, if they also give themselves up to the limitless accumulation of wealth, exceeding the boundaries of necessity? **GLAUCON.** It will be quite necessary, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Shall we then go to war? Or what shall we do? **GLAUCON.** We shall go to war. **SOCRATES.** We are not yet saying whether war brings evil or good; only this: we have found the origin of war, from which, when it occurs, great calamities fall upon cities both publicly and privately. **GLAUCON.** That is exactly what happens. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the city must be even larger to accommodate a great army, which can go out and fight those who invade, to defend all the things we have mentioned. **GLAUCON.** Are those men we described not sufficient? **SOCRATES.** Not if you and we were right in what we agreed upon earlier: when we were founding the city, we agreed it was impossible for one man to practice many arts well...

<summary>Socrates and his companions discuss the transition from a simple, "healthy" city based on necessity to a "luxurious" city. This expansion leads to the need for specialized professions, more land, and eventually the inevitability of war.</summary>

# DIALOGUE II. CONCERNING THE REPUBLIC, OR CONCERNING JUSTICE.

**FOLIO CCXXIIII.**

**GLAUCON.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Is military combat not a skill requiring specialized training? **GLAUCON.** It is, and very much so. **SOCRATES.** Should we then take more care for the craft of leather-working than for the craft of war? **GLAUCON.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** Yet we forbade the leather-worker from attempting the work of the farmer, the weaver, or the architect at the same time; we commanded him to be occupied only in his own art, so that his work might be finished as well as possible for us. We assigned to each of the others a single task according to each man's natural talent, so that each might undertake the one thing to which nature leads him. By remaining free from other tasks and observing the right opportunity of time, he may perform it excellently. Or is it of little importance whether military matters are conducted rightly or not? Is this study perhaps so easy that a man can be a warrior and at the same time a farmer, or a leather-worker, or any other craftsman? Yet no one would be a fit player of dice or gaming-tables unless he had applied himself to that art from childhood and had bent over it diligently. And will a man, by merely taking up a shield or other military arms and instruments, become a fit soldier in any kind of combat in a single day? No other instrument will make a man a craftsman or an athlete, nor will it be useful to him who has not been skilled in that study and sufficiently exercised. **GLAUCON.** Such instruments would be precious indeed <note>Glaucon is being sarcastic here, implying that if tools alone made the master, they would be of impossible value</note>. **SOCRATES.** Then, the greater the work of the guardianship is, does it not require more leisure, and greater art and exercise? **GLAUCON.** I think so. **SOCRATES.** And does it not also require a nature suited to the study itself? **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** It will be our duty then, it seems, to choose as far as possible which and what kind of natures are fit for guarding the city. **GLAUCON.** Clearly it is our duty. **SOCRATES.** By Jove, we have taken up no humble business; however, we must not be afraid, as long as our strength holds out. **GLAUCON.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Do you think the nature of a well-bred dog and a well-bred youth differ at all in regards to acting as a guard? **GLAUCON.** What do you mean by this? **SOCRATES.** Each of them must be keen-sighted to perceive, swift to pursue, and finally robust to fight and capture once they have caught up. **GLAUCON.** There is certainly a need for all these things. **SOCRATES.** And he must be bold and brave if he is to fight well. **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** But will he be brave and bold who is not spirited <note>original: "iracundus" - here meaning "full of thumos" or high-spirited/spirited, rather than simply "angry"</note>, whether it be a horse, a dog, or any other animal? Have you not noticed that spirit is something unconquerable and invincible, in the presence of which every soul is fearless and indomitable against all things? **GLAUCON.** I have noticed it. **SOCRATES.** It is manifest then what the guardian ought to be in body. **GLAUCON.** Manifest. **SOCRATES.** And also what he should be in soul: namely, spirited. **GLAUCON.** That too. **SOCRATES.** How then, O Glaucon, will they not be harsh toward one another and the other citizens, since they are endowed with such a nature? **GLAUCON.** By Jove, that will not be easy. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, they must be gentle toward their own people, but fierce toward their enemies; otherwise, they will not wait for others to destroy them, but will destroy themselves first. **GLAUCON.** So it will happen. **SOCRATES.** What then shall we do? Where shall we find a character that is at once gentle and high-spirited? For a mild nature is the opposite of a spirited one. Yet he who lacks either of these will not be a good guardian. These things seem impossible to bring together in one. And so it follows that a good guardian cannot be found. **GLAUCON.** It seems as you say. **SOCRATES.** Then I was truly in doubt, and revolving the previous points in my mind, I said: "We are rightly in doubt, my friend. For we have departed from the comparison we introduced above." **GLAUCON.** How do you mean? **SOCRATES.** Have we not found that there are indeed such natures, which we least expected, having these contrary qualities within them? **GLAUCON.** Where? **SOCRATES.** One may see this in other animals, and not least in that guardian with whom we compared our own guardian. For you know that this is the natural character of a well-bred dog: to be most gentle toward familiars and acquaintances, but the opposite toward those he does not know. **GLAUCON.** I know it certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, what we seek is neither impossible nor contrary to nature: namely, that the guardian be such a person. **GLAUCON.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** Does it seem to you, moreover, that the future guardian needs to add this to his ferocity: that he be a philosopher by nature? **GLAUCON.** How do you mean? For I do not understand. **SOCRATES.** And yet you may observe this in dogs; which is indeed a thing worthy of admiration in a beast. **GLAUCON.** What sort of thing? **SOCRATES.** Because when he sees someone unknown, he is angry, even if he has suffered no evil from him. But he fawns upon an acquaintance, even if he has received no good from him. Have you not wondered at this yet? **GLAUCON.** I have not noticed it much until now; but it is manifest that he does this. **SOCRATES.** But this seems to be an innate affection of his nature, and truly philosophical. **GLAUCON.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** Because he distinguishes a friendly appearance from an enemy by no other means than that he knows the one and is ignorant of the other. Must he not then be called a lover of learning <note>original: "discendi cupidum" - Socrates is playfully linking the dog's reliance on "knowing" to the philosopher's love of knowledge</note>, since he distinguishes the domestic from the stranger by knowledge and ignorance? **GLAUCON.** He must. Why not? **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, the lover of learning and the philosopher are the same. **GLAUCON.** The same. **SOCRATES.** Why then should we not boldly posit in the case of a man too, that if he is to be gentle toward his familiars and acquaintances, he must be a philosopher and a lover of learning. **GLAUCON.** Let us posit it. **SOCRATES.** He then who is to be the best guardian of the city will be by nature a philosopher, high-spirited, swift, and robust. **GLAUCON.** He will be so entirely. **SOCRATES.** Let the guardian be such, then. But in what way shall these guardians be nourished and educated by you? And will this consideration help us toward that for the sake of which we consider all things: namely, to understand how justice and injustice arise in a city? We must certainly think on this, lest we either omit what is necessary or pursue what is superfluous. **ADIMANTUS.** I think indeed that this discussion contributes greatly to what has been proposed to us. **SOCRATES.** So I also think, by Jove, O friend Adimantus. Therefore we must not desist, even if the discussion should be somewhat long. **ADIMANTUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Come then, as if we were telling stories in our leisure, let us instruct these men in our discourse. **ADIMANTUS.** Indeed, that is proper. **SOCRATES.** What then will be the discipline? Will it be difficult to find a better one than that which has been found over a long time? This is, for the body, gymnastics; for the soul, music <note>In the Greek sense, "music" (musica) included poetry, literature, and all the arts overseen by the Muses</note>.

<margin>
The nature of the dog partakes in contraries.
What sort of person the guardian ought to be.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates and his interlocutors determine that the ideal "Guardian" of the city must possess a paradoxical nature—both high-spirited and gentle—likening them to well-bred dogs who are friendly to those they know and fierce to strangers. They conclude that the education of these guardians must consist of gymnastics for the body and "music" (the arts) for the soul.</summary>

# BOOK
### PAGE XXXI.

**ADIMANTUS.** It is plainly so. **SOCRATES.** Should not this education begin with music <note>original: "musica" — in the Greek sense, this refers to all the arts of the Muses, including poetry and literature, not just melody</note> before gymnastics? **ADIMANTUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** When you say music, do you also include speeches <note>or "stories/discourses"</note> or not? **ADIMANTUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Now, there are two kinds of speech: the true and the false. **ADIMANTUS.** That is so. **SOCRATES.** Must the future guardian be educated in both, but in the false first? **ADIMANTUS.** I do not understand what you mean. **SOCRATES.** Do you not know that we first tell fables to children? These, to speak simply, are false, though they contain some truths. We use fables with children before we use the gymnasiums. **ADIMANTUS.** It is as you say. **SOCRATES.** This, then, is what I meant when I said that music must be touched upon before gymnastics. **ADIMANTUS.** Rightly so. **SOCRATES.** Do you not know that the beginning is the most important part of every work, <margin>The beginning of every work is the most important.</margin> especially for the young and tender? For it is then that the form is most easily molded and the character is taken on which one wishes to impress upon each individual. **ADIMANTUS.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Shall we then so easily permit children to hear just any fables composed by just anyone, and to drink into their minds opinions that are for the most part contrary to those we think they should have when they grow up? **ADIMANTUS.** We shall by no means permit it. **SOCRATES.** First, then, it seems we must oversee the makers of fables; and if they compose a good fable, it should be selected, but the others rejected. Those we select we shall persuade nurses and mothers to tell to the children, so that their minds may be shaped by fables far more than their bodies are shaped by hands. But of those fables they now recount, many must be cast out. **ADIMANTUS.** Which ones? **SOCRATES.** In the greater ones we shall see the lesser. For the same pattern and the same power must belong to both the greater and the lesser. Do you not think so? **ADIMANTUS.** I do indeed. But I do not at all understand which ones you call "greater." **SOCRATES.** Those which Hesiod and Homer and the rest of the poets wrote. For these men composed false fables for mankind, which are still circulated every day. **ADIMANTUS.** Which fables do you mean? And what do you condemn in them? **SOCRATES.** That which ought first and most of all to be condemned: especially when someone does not lie well. <margin>The worst lie is to tell things about the gods that are not fitting.</margin> **ADIMANTUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** When someone poorly portrays in words the nature of gods and heroes—like a painter who draws something that bears no resemblance to the objects he is trying to imitate. **ADIMANTUS.** Such things are rightly censured. But how do we say this, and what examples of such things do we find in them? **SOCRATES.** First and greatest is the lie about the greatest matters, which Hesiod did not tell well when he imagined the deeds of Uranus <note>original: "Cęlio" — referring to the sky-god Caelus/Uranus</note>, and added how Saturn <note>Cronus</note> punished him, and recounted what Saturn did and what he suffered from his son <note>Zeus/Jupiter</note>. Even if these things were true, I should not think they ought to be so openly presented to the simple-minded and the young; they should rather be passed over in silence. But if there were a necessity to speak of them, they should be heard in secret by a few who have sacrificed not a pig, but some great and rare victim, so that it happens that as few as possible hear them. **ADIMANTUS.** Truly, these are difficult stories. **SOCRATES.** Nor are they to be told, O Adimantus, in our city. Nor should it be said to a young listener that in committing the most wicked crimes he does nothing strange; or that in punishing a father who has done wrong, he does nothing extreme, but rather does what the first and greatest of the gods did. **ADIMANTUS.** By no means. For to me also, these things do not seem worthy of being told. **SOCRATES.** Nor should it be told at all that gods wage war against gods, plot against one another, and fight. For these things are not true, if indeed it is necessary for the future guardians of our city to think it a disgrace to be at odds with one another. Therefore, the battle of the giants must not be narrated to them in any way, nor the many battles of gods and heroes against their own kin and neighbors. But if we are to persuade them by any means that no citizen has ever been an adversary to another, and that this is not holy, such things should rather be told to children immediately, and to adolescents by the elders and old women; and the poets must be compelled to direct their fables toward these ends. But the chains put on Juno <note>Hera</note> by her son, and the throwing out of Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note> by his father when he wanted to help his beaten mother, or the battles of the gods—as many as Homer wrote—we must by no means receive into the city, whether they were spoken as allegory or without allegory. For the adolescent is not able to distinguish what is allegory and what is not; but whatever opinions are taken in at that age tend to stick deep and are usually very difficult to eradicate. For the sake of these things, perhaps every effort must be made that these first stories they hear are best fashioned toward the goal of virtue. **ADIMANTUS.** What you say is not far from reason. But if someone asks what these are, and what kind of fables, what shall we say? **SOCRATES.** O Adimantus, you and I are not poets at this present time, but founders of a city. It is necessary for founders to know the patterns <note>original: "figuras" — the models or types</note> according to which the poets must fashion their fables; if they exceed these, such fables are not to be admitted. But it does not belong to the founders of the city to invent the fables themselves. **ADIMANTUS.** You speak rightly. But declare this to me: what are these patterns concerning theology? **SOCRATES.** They are such as this: God must always be described as He truly is, whether He is described in epic verse, or in songs, or even in tragedy. **ADIMANTUS.** So it is fitting. **SOCRATES.** Is not God good in Himself, and must He not be called so? **ADIMANTUS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** And nothing good is harmful. **ADIMANTUS.** None, I think. **SOCRATES.** Does that which is not harmful ever do harm? **ADIMANTUS.** By no means. **SOCRATES.** Does that which does no harm ever do evil? **ADIMANTUS.** Not even that. **SOCRATES.** But that which does no evil is the cause of no evil. **ADIMANTUS.** Of none. **SOCRATES.** Likewise, is not the good beneficial? **ADIMANTUS.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it is the cause of acting well and happily. **ADIMANTUS.** It is. **SOCRATES.** The good, therefore, is not the cause of all things, but the cause of those things that are well; but of those things that are ill, it is by no means the cause. <margin>God is the cause of good, not of evil.</margin> **ADIMANTUS.** That is absolutely so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore God, since He is good, is not the cause of all things, as many say; but He is the cause of a few things for men, while of many things He is not the cause. For our goods are much fewer than our evils. And of the goods, God alone must be called the cause. But for evils, one must seek any cause other than God. **ADIMANTUS.** You seem to me to speak very truly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must not accept the error of Homer or any other poet who speaks foolishly about the gods, saying that "two jars lie on the threshold of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> full of fates: one of Good, the other of Evil." <margin>Two jars</margin> And that to whomsoever Jove gives a mixture of these, he is sometimes well and sometimes ill. But to whom he gives from the other jar alone, "him a ravenous hunger drives over the earth." Nor must we admit that Jove is for us the dispenser of both goods and evils. Confusion...

<meta>Catchword: Confusionem (Confusion)</meta>

<summary>Socrates argues that the education of the guardians must begin with carefully censored fables, asserting that God is only the source of good and never the cause of evil or strife.</summary>

# SECOND DIALOGUE ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO 225.

Indeed, if anyone says that the breaking of the oaths and truces was brought about by Pandarus <note>In the *Iliad*, Pandarus breaks a truce by wounding Menelaus, prompted by the gods</note> through the agency of Jupiter and Minerva, we shall by no means praise it; nor the strife and dissension of the gods, and the judgment through Themis and Jupiter. Nor should the young hear what Aeschylus says: that God provides a cause for mortals when he wishes to utterly subvert a house. But if someone introduces iambic verses in which the sufferings of Niobe are related, or those of the Pelopidae, or the Trojans, or anything of this sort, either he must not be allowed to say these are the works of a god, or if they are of a god, the explanation we are now seeking must be brought out: it must be said that God did what was good and just, and helped them by punishing them. But that those who pay the penalty are "miserable," and that it is a god who thus afflicts them—the poet must not be permitted to say this. 

However, if he were to say that wicked men, being miserable, were in need of punishment, and that by paying it they were helped by God, it should be permitted. But the claim that God, who is good, is the cause of evil to anyone must be utterly refuted. No one should be allowed to say this in his city, if the city is to be established with good laws; nor should anyone hear it, whether young or old, whether woven into songs or told in prose. Such things are neither holy to say, nor useful to us, nor consistent with themselves.

**ADEIMANTUS:** I am your fellow-voter in passing this law; these things certainly please me.

**SOCRATES:** Let this, then, be one law and pattern among those concerning the gods: that everyone is compelled both to say and to represent God not as the cause of all things, but only of the good. <margin>God: the cause of good things</margin>

**ADEIMANTUS:** That is sufficient.

**SOCRATES:** But what of this second point? Do you think God is a sorcerer, appearing by design now in one form, now in another? Does he change his own appearance into many shapes and effects, or deceive us by offering vain images of himself? Or is he rather simple, and least of all likely to depart from his own form?

**ADEIMANTUS:** I do not know what to say to this at present.

**SOCRATES:** What about this? Is it not necessary that if anything departs from its own form, it must be changed either by itself or by another?

**ADEIMANTUS:** It is necessary.

**SOCRATES:** Things that are in the best condition are least of all changed or moved by another; just as the body is affected by food, drink, and labor, and all plants by heat and windstorms—where that which is most healthy and robust is changed the least. <margin>That which is most whole and robust is least changed</margin>

**ADEIMANTUS:** Certainly so.

**SOCRATES:** And would not the strongest and wisest soul be least changed by external disturbance?

**ADEIMANTUS:** Yes.

**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, all composite things—vessels, buildings, garments—by the same reasoning, if well-constructed and in good condition, are least changed by time or other external influences.

**ADEIMANTUS:** It is as you say.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, whatever is in a good state, whether by nature, by art, or by both, admits the least change from another.

**ADEIMANTUS:** So it seems.

**SOCRATES:** But truly God, and the things of God, are in every way in the best possible state.

**ADEIMANTUS:** Of course!

**SOCRATES:** By this reasoning, then, God would least of all assume many forms.

**ADEIMANTUS:** Least of all.

**SOCRATES:** But would God transform and change himself?

**ADEIMANTUS:** Clearly he would, if he were to change at all.

**SOCRATES:** Would he then change himself into something better and more beautiful, or into something worse and uglier?

**ADEIMANTUS:** It must be into something worse, if he is changed at all. For we surely do not say that God is lacking in beauty or virtue.

**SOCRATES:** You speak most correctly. But this being so, do you believe that anyone, whether god or man, would willingly make himself worse?

**ADEIMANTUS:** That is certainly impossible.

**SOCRATES:** It is impossible, then, for a god to wish to change himself. But as it seems, since each of the gods is as beautiful and excellent as possible, they all remain forever and simply in their own form.

**ADEIMANTUS:** I think this is entirely necessary.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, O best of men, let none of the poets tell us that "gods, like strangers, visit cities in various forms." <note>A reference to Homer's *Odyssey*</note> Nor let anyone tell lies about Proteus and Thetis. Nor in tragedies or other poems let them introduce Juno transformed into the likeness of a priestess, collecting gifts for the "life-giving sons of Inachus, the Argive river." <note>A lost line from an Aeschylus play</note> Let no one dare to feign such things. Nor should mothers terrify their children with these vain fables, saying that certain gods wander at night in various strange forms—lest they both speak ill of the gods and make their children more cowardly.

**ADEIMANTUS:** By no means.

**SOCRATES:** But is it that the gods themselves are immutable, yet by some sorcery they appear to us changed into various forms to deceive us?

**ADEIMANTUS:** Perhaps so.

**SOCRATES:** What! Would a god wish to lie, either in words or by presenting a false image?

**ADEIMANTUS:** I do not know.

**SOCRATES:** Do you not know that the "true lie"—if it can be called that—is hated by all gods and men? <margin>Lying</margin>

**ADEIMANTUS:** How do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** Thus: No one willingly wishes to lie in the most vital part of himself about the most vital things; rather, he fears a lie there above all.

**ADEIMANTUS:** I still do not understand.

**SOCRATES:** You think I am saying something profound. But I am saying that to lie in the soul itself regarding reality—to have been deceived, to be ignorant, and to hold a lie there—is what no one would ever choose. Everyone hates having a lie in their soul above all else.

**ADEIMANTUS:** Above all else.

**SOCRATES:** And yet what I just said is correct: this would be called a "true lie"—ignorance in the soul of the one who is deceived. For a lie in words is a kind of imitation of the state in the soul, an image that arises later, and not a purely unmixed lie. Is it not so?

**ADEIMANTUS:** Exactly so.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, the "true lie" is hateful not only to gods but also to men.

**ADEIMANTUS:** So it seems to me.

**SOCRATES:** But what about the lie in words? When and for whom is it so useful as not to be worthy of hatred?

**ADEIMANTUS:** Is it not against enemies, or those called friends, when out of madness or some ignorance they attempt to do something evil? Then it is useful as a kind of medicine to turn them away. And in those fables we were just discussing, because we do not know the truth of ancient things, we make the lie as much like the truth as possible; in this way we make it most useful.

**ADEIMANTUS:** That is exactly how it is.

**SOCRATES:** According to which of these, then, is a lie useful to God?

<summary>Socrates argues that God is perfectly good and immutable, meaning poets must not depict gods as changing shape or causing evil. He distinguishes between the "true lie" in the soul, which is universally hated, and the "lie in words," which can be a useful medicine for humans but is unnecessary for God.</summary>

# BOOK II.

### PAGE XXXI.

Is it because he does not know ancient things that he lies under the guise of truth? ADIMANTUS: That would be ridiculous indeed. SOCRATES: A poet, therefore, is not a liar in the person of a god. ADIMANTUS: It does not seem so to me. SOCRATES: Or would he lie for fear of enemies? ADIMANTUS: Far from it. SOCRATES: Or perhaps because of the madness and insanity of his friends? ADIMANTUS: But no one who is foolish or insane is a friend to God. SOCRATES: There is, therefore, no reason why God should lie? ADIMANTUS: None. SOCRATES: Therefore, the nature of gods and spirits <note>original: "demonumque," referring here to intermediary spirits or divine beings, not necessarily evil demons</note> is entirely without falsehood. ADIMANTUS: Entirely. SOCRATES: Wherefore God is altogether simple and true in both words and deeds; <margin>God: one</margin> neither does he change himself, nor does he deceive others, neither through visions, nor through speeches, nor through signs; neither while we are sleeping, nor while we are awake. ADIMANTUS: It seems so to me as well, as you say this. SOCRATES: Do you grant then that this is the second figure <note>or "pattern/rule" for speaking about the divine</note> in which it is necessary to speak and hear concerning the gods: that they are neither sorcerers who change themselves, nor do they seduce us with lies, whether in words or in deeds? ADIMANTUS: I grant it. SOCRATES: Therefore, while we praise many things said by Homer, we shall by no means praise the dream sent by Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> to Agamemnon. Nor shall we praise Aeschylus when Thetis says that Apollo killed her son—the same Apollo who, reclining at her wedding feast, had sung that the offspring of Thetis would be long-lived and untouched by disease. Apollo sang many things indeed, she says: he predicted that my fortunes would be dear to God, and he filled me with joy by his praises. And I hoped the mouth of Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> was divine, truthful, and prophetic. But he himself who was praising, he who was reclining at the table, he who spoke these things, he himself has killed my son. Whenever such things are said about the gods, we shall immediately protest and hiss them off; nor shall we permit teachers of games to use them for the discipline of youth, if our guardians are to be pious and divine, as far as is possible for a human being. ADIMANTUS: I certainly accept these figures, and I shall use them everywhere as laws.

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino on the Third Dialogue, concerning Justice.

<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the scholar who translated Plato's works into Latin; this is his summary of the upcoming section.</note>

The THIRD DIALOGUE pursues the education of the guardians begun in the second. And just as in the second he forbade them to hear false and shameful things about the gods, so here he forbids hearing tragic things about the underworld, which might make them more fearful. Likewise, he forbids comic things, because an effusion of laughter excites the mind. For one who daily dissolves into profuse laughter turns out just as soft as one whose tears are compelled by grief. Since, however, the guardians must be kept not only from fearfulness, but also from intemperance, greed, and injustice, he again forbids the hearing of the poems of poets in which the lusts, robberies, and iniquities of the gods, heroes, or great men are fashioned. This military education is common to almost all citizens. Among these things, pay attention to what he says about lying. A lie is the calamity of a city: namely, when private citizens lie among themselves, but especially if they lie to the magistrates. It is just as if the sick were to lie to a doctor, or sailors to a pilot. It is permitted, however, for the governors sometimes to use a lie for the sake of public safety—and for a private person sometimes toward another private person—only for the sake of avoiding some most grave evil. It is also permitted to tell stories moderately about ancient things whose truth is unknown, and to fashion those things of which we hardly have a certain form as if through certain images. Furthermore, he distinguishes speech into three species. For it is either simple narration, or simple imitation, or a mixture of both. He rejects all speech that relates the most vile things without selection and acts out a disturbed man. For whoever studiously imitates something for a long time passes into its nature. Therefore, he commands the poet who sharply imitates disturbed minds—as being harmful to youth—either to imitate a constant character by changing his style, or to depart far from the city. He also says that he who handles many things, either by imitating or by doing, eventually fails in each one so that he turns out excellent in none. He proceeds then from the first music (that is, poetry) to the following, and divides it into three species: Speech, harmony, and rhythm. In the beginning, musicians call a "phthongus" a harmonic voice, that is, one fit for consonance, which is neither so deep that it cannot be made deeper by the same singer, nor so sharp <note>high-pitched</note> that a sharper one cannot be produced. Then he constitutes harmony from these sounds: namely, by a congruent measure in the excess and defect of deep, sharp, and middle voices. There are four voices here: deep, sharp, rising toward sharp, and declining toward deep. Likewise, there are four primary proportions: double (between two and one); sesquialter (between three and two); sesquitertial (between four and three); and sesquioctave (between nine and eight). The double proportion is followed by the consonance of the octave; the sesquialter by the fifth; the sesquitertial by the fourth; and finally the sesquioctave by the tone. But concerning these things, more diligently elsewhere. In the third place comes rhythm, that is, a certain order of motion and time, as is perceived from the second book of the *Laws*. For after you have reconciled the voices by a certain harmonic measure of excess and defect through tension and relaxation, there is need of rhythm, through which you may measure the motions and times of the sharp, deep, and middle voices, and between each one. By motions, I mean the more gentle, the more severe, and the middle. By times, I mean the longer, shorter, and equal, through long, short, and middle accents. In these, note that the word "base" is diverse; for as the matter requires, it signifies a foundation, a seat, a weight, a progress, <unclear>and</unclear> a limit. Besides these, nine degrees of the most common consonances and dissonances must be considered. The first is in reason: that is, an opinion consenting with the truth of the thing itself. The contrary of which is an opinion...

# DIALOGUE III. ON THE REPUBLIC
## C ii
<meta>Catchword: firm</meta>

...falsehood, you will disagree with the truth. The second is in the imagination, whose harmony is the following of reason, while its dissonance is the pursuit of external things. The third is in the effect, either temperately following reason or intemperately following the imagination. The fourth is in speech, whether decorous or indecorous, insofar as it follows either right reason or a tumultuous imagination. The fifth is in song; its harmony is to imitate decorous speech, its dissonance is in the indecorous. The sixth is in sound, imitating the song in one way or another. The seventh is in graceful or ungraceful dancing pertaining to the choral dance. The eighth is in a certain composition of the limbs and the whole body, as pleasing to the sight as it is ready for gymnastic exercise. The ninth is in the skillful works of any art, composed with a certain musical proportion. From here, these nine steps represent the Muses to you. <note>The author links the nine Muses to nine levels of harmony ranging from internal thought to physical art.</note> Remember, however, that the best harmony of all is the temperance of the soul. The others that follow imitate this, and in turn, when they are practiced, they increase it. For this reason, he commands that only those harmonies be practiced, heard, and watched which reflect a constant state of mind—not one elated by pride, nor made wild by anger, nor softened and dissolved by pleasure; not broken by grief, nor complaining through misery or want. He therefore approves of a grave and constant harmony, but disapproves of the extremes—that is, the agitated and the soft. He also condemns the complex <note>original: "multiplicem," referring to overly ornate or polyphonic music</note> and praises the simple above all others. He judges that harmony has the greatest power over the soul. Indeed, the soul is a certain divine harmony and was once accustomed, if I may speak in a Platonic way, to celestial harmony. Furthermore, the body consists of a certain harmony, as does the spirit. Moreover, the harmony of voices, being airy, penetrates the airy spirit through motion; it carries with it the emotion of the singer and the soul, moving the emotion of the listener by emotion, affecting the soul by the soul, and gradually instilling character. In all things, notice that Plato governs his city with not only civil but also quite religious observance; and always, as he also prescribes in the *Statesman* <note>original: "Politico"</note>, he mixes temperance with fortitude. Finally, consider how foul and dissonant he judges sexual pleasure to be; therefore, he separates it far from legitimate love, which always desires only the beautiful and the harmonious. He treats many things concerning music and gymnastics, for they were of the greatest importance; indeed, everyone used to apply themselves to these, and ought to do so. For the former wonderfully forms and composes the soul and spirit, while the latter does so for the body for the sake of the soul. He adds: a good soul does not come from a good body, but a good body is made from a good soul. He subjoins that simple music for the soul and a simple diet for the body benefit health, while complexity harms both; and that as long as men lived soberly, they did not need the help of physical doctors. He condemns superstitious observations of the body regarding diet and medicines. He says a chief sign of a badly instituted city is if it requires the diligent work and judgment of doctors. He describes the duty of the doctor and the judge: he chooses a judge who is good in character, prudent, and old, having experienced many men, both good and bad. He asserts that wickedness is like a certain privation; it knows neither itself nor virtue. But virtue, being like a habit, knows itself through itself alone; and through itself, with the addition of experience, it judges vices. One must always remember that Plato confirms—not only here but also in the *Laws*, the *Statesman*, and the *Protagoras*—that nothing is more necessary for every civic and philosophical man than a bond forged equally from fortitude and temperance. Through the former, they may seek high things; through the latter, they may not despise humble things; and from both, you may never dare or fear anything too much. Through the former, again, you may repel private and public injuries; through the latter, you may abstain from injury. Through the former, you may be called to honorable things; through the latter, you may be restrained from base things. Thus it happens that he refers both gymnastics and music to these two ends: that through the former, fortitude (not so much of the body as of the soul) is acquired, and through the latter, temperance. He commands, however, that both be rightly mixed together. For gymnastics alone produces ferocity, and music alone produces softness; but both together produce fortitude and temperance. Finally, from the number of those who have been so educated, he chooses both the guardians (that is, the magistrates) and the defenders (that is, the soldiers). He wants prudent, brave, old men who are lovers of the public good and proven in this very thing through experience to be taken into the magistracy. He likewise prescribes that young men be tested in the midst of pleasures and pains, so it may be discerned whether they are temperate and brave, or the opposite; and whether they might easily change their opinion about preserving the public good because of deceits, threats, or allurements. Finally, he says the natures of men are similar to metals: one fit for governing is like gold; one fit for military service is like silver; and one fit for craftsmanship and agriculture is like iron and bronze. He commands that individual natures be directed to those things for which they are fit; thus, the sons of governors are sometimes moved to lower tasks according to their nature, and conversely, the sons of inferiors are moved to nobler duties. He also forbids soldiers from possessing anything of their own, lest through avarice they turn from dogs into wolves.

# DIALOGUE III. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

### Folio 227.

as far as subjects are concerned, the greatest virtues are these: namely, that they obey their magistrates; and as for the leaders themselves, that they be temperate in the use of pleasures, feasts, and drinking? SOCRATES: We shall therefore assert that such things as these are well said, like those words Diomedes speaks in Homer: *“Come now, sit in silence, and obey my words,”* <note>original: "Eia age silẽtio cõside: ac meis verbis obtempera." SOCRATES: But wherever the deeds or words of excellent men are narrated with modesty and constancy, these are the things to be noticed and heard. SOCRATES: Nor should we permit the citizens themselves to be corrupted by gifts, nor to be greedy for money. ADIMANTUS: By no means. SOCRATES: Therefore, they should not sing: *“Gifts, believe me, win over both men and gods.”* <note>A common Greek proverb attributed to Hesiod or Ovid.</note> <margin>On gifts and corruption.</margin> Nor should Phoenix, the teacher of Achilles, be praised as if he spoke rightly when he advised him to bring help to the Achaeans if he received gifts, but if he did not receive them, by no means to set aside his anger. Nor again shall we think Achilles himself worthy, nor shall we agree that he ought to have been so greedy for money that he would accept gifts from Agamemnon, or that he would refuse to return the corpse of Hector without a price. ADIMANTUS: Certainly, it is not becoming to praise such things. SOCRATES: Indeed, I fear to say it, for it is not right to believe that Homer preached these things about Achilles, or to believe others who say them. Or when he says he will give the hair consecrated to the river Sperchius to the dead hero Patroclus—it should by no means be believed that he did this. The dragging of Hector around the tomb of Patroclus, and the slaughter of the captives upon the pyre, and all such things—we shall neither affirm that they are true, nor allow our people to be persuaded that Achilles—the son of a goddess and of Peleus (the most temperate of men and the grandson of Jupiter), educated by the most wise Chiron—was agitated by such great disturbance that his soul suffered from two contrary diseases: illiberality combined with greed, and likewise contempt for both gods and men. Rather, let us compel the poets either to deny that these were their works, or not to affirm that they were the sons of gods. But by no means let them assert both at once. Nor let them labor to persuade our youths that any evils arise from the gods, or that heroes are in no way better than men. Since, as has already been said, these things are neither holy nor true. For we have shown that it is impossible for any evils to proceed from the gods. ADIMANTUS: We have clearly shown it. SOCRATES: Furthermore, these things are harmful to those who hear them. For everyone will forgive their own wickedness, being persuaded that such things are done and have been done even by those who are born closest to the race of the gods—of whom it is said: *“Born closest to the gods, near to Jupiter, for whom an altar to Father Jupiter exists in the high ether on the Idean peak, and the blood of the gods has not yet vanished from them.”* Therefore, fables of this kind are not to be received, lest they provide an easy opportunity for vice to our adolescents. ADIMANTUS: It must be done exactly so. SOCRATES: What remaining species of discourse is left for us to distinguish, regarding what should or should not be narrated? For it has been stated how it is becoming to speak about the gods. And likewise about the spirits <term>daemones: intermediary spirits between gods and men</term>, and heroes, and those things which are in the underworld. ADIMANTUS: Sufficiently and abundantly. SOCRATES: Would it perhaps remain for us to speak about men? ADIMANTUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: It is impossible, my friend, to settle that at present. ADIMANTUS: Why so? SOCRATES: Because I think we shall say that poets and orators speak badly about men regarding matters of the greatest importance when they write: that many unjust men are happy, while the just are unhappy; and that it is profitable to act unjustly if it remains hidden; and that justice itself is another's good but one's own loss; and other such damnable things. We shall forbid them to say these things, and command them to sing and insert into fables the contrary of these. Do you not think so? ADIMANTUS: I know it for certain. SOCRATES: Therefore, if you confess that I speak rightly, shall I say that you have granted the very thing we have been seeking for a long time? ADIMANTUS: You have understood me quite correctly. SOCRATES: Shall we not then agree that such discourses should be held about men only when [we have discovered] what...

And I believe you know this: that up to these verses where he prays, the poet himself speaks as the poet, and does not attempt to turn our minds elsewhere, as if someone other than himself were speaking. But thereafter, he speaks as if he were Chryses himself; he strives to show us not Homer, but that old priest. And in the rest of the work, he always explains things in this way, both in the deeds done at Ilium and those sung in the *Odyssey* at Ithaca. ADEIMANTUS. It is entirely so. SOCRATES. Is it not therefore a narration, both when he delivers continuous speeches and when he describes what happens between them? ADEIMANTUS. Why not! SOCRATES. But when he delivers a speech as if he were someone else, shall we not then say that he makes his own speech as similar as possible to the one he introduced as speaking? ADEIMANTUS. Why should we not say so! SOCRATES. And is not making oneself similar to another, either in form or voice, the act of imitating the one to whom he makes himself similar? ADEIMANTUS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. In this, therefore, as it seems, both he and the rest of the poets narrate through imitation. ADEIMANTUS. I agree. SOCRATES. But where the poet does not hide himself, that entire poetry and narration is without imitation. Lest you say you do not understand how this happens, I will tell you. For if Homer, after saying that Chryses had come to redeem his daughter and had supplicated the Achaeans and especially the kings, had thereafter spoken not as if he were Chryses, but as if he were Homer, you know surely that there would have been no imitation, but simple narration. It would have been like this—I shall speak it without verse, since I am not poetic: "The priest, having set out, prayed to the gods that they might grant them to capture Troy safely and, having accepted the gifts, restore his daughter to him, out of reverence for the god Apollo. When he had said these things, the rest approved the priest's words. But Agamemnon, greatly disturbed, ordered him to depart at once, so that he should not return again; for neither the god's crown nor the scepter would profit him; and he asserted that before he would return the daughter to him, she would grow old with him in the fields. Therefore he should depart, and not provoke him, so that he might depart safe." When the old man heard these things, he was afraid and departed in silence. But having left the camp, he prayed as a suppliant to Apollo, calling upon his many names: that if he had ever done anything pleasing to him in building temples or sacrificing victims, he should punish the Achaeans and avenge his tears with his arrows. In this manner, O friend, simple narration proceeds without imitation. ADEIMANTUS. I understand now. SOCRATES. And know this besides: the opposite of this is when, the words of the poet which usually intervene between speeches being removed, the speeches themselves are left alternating in turn. ADEIMANTUS. I understand that too. For tragedy and comedy are of this sort. SOCRATES. You have understood quite rightly. I think I can now reveal to you what you were unable to perceive before: that poetry and the fictions of fables are either entirely through imitation, as you yourself said of tragedy and comedy; or are delivered through the announcement of the poet, which is seen mostly in <term>dithyrambs</term> <note>Hymns sung by a chorus, usually to Dionysus, where the poet speaks in his own voice.</note>; or are composed of both, as appears in heroic verse and many others, if you understand. ADEIMANTUS. I understand now what you wished to imply then. SOCRATES. And remember also that before this we said that *what* should be said had already been explained, but *how* it should be said must be explained next. ADEIMANTUS. I remember indeed. SOCRATES. This, then, was it: that I said we must agree between us whether we allow the poets to use perpetual imitation, or to imitate in part and not at all in part (and what kind each should be), or to imitate nothing at all. ADEIMANTUS. I divine indeed that you will consider whether

<margin>

comedy and tragedy are to be received into the city or not. SOCRATES. Perhaps even more than these. For I do not yet know; but wherever the reason, like a wind, carries us, there we must go. ADEIMANTUS. You speak excellently. SOCRATES. Consider this then, O Adeimantus: whether it is necessary for our guardians to be imitators or not. Or does this depend on what was said before: that individuals can do one thing rightly, but many things not at all? So that if anyone attempts to handle many things, he will fail in each so much that he turns out excellent in none. ADEIMANTUS. It would happen exactly so. SOCRATES. Does not the same reason apply to imitation, that someone cannot imitate many things as well as he can one? ADEIMANTUS. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Never, therefore, will anyone apply himself to any pursuit worthy of esteem and at the same time imitate many things and be a fit imitator; since the same men cannot even handle well two imitations at once which seem to differ little from each other, such as comedy and tragedy together. Did you not just now say these were certain imitations? ADEIMANTUS. Indeed; and you say the truth, that the same men cannot. SOCRATES. Nor can <term>rhapsodes</term> <note>original: "rhaphodi" — professional performers of epic poetry.</note> (that is, singers of heroic songs) and actors be the same. ADEIMANTUS. True. SOCRATES. But neither are the same men tragic and comic actors. All these are certain imitations, are they not? ADEIMANTUS. Imitations. SOCRATES. Furthermore...

# DIALOGUE III. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE. PAGE 228.

### Ciiii

It seems to me, O Adeimantus, that human nature is divided into such small parts that it is impossible for a man to imitate many things well, or even to perform those very actions of which the imitations are themselves mere likenesses. **ADEIMANTUS.** It is as you say. **SOCRATES.** If, therefore, we wish our previous reasoning to hold firm, our guardians—who are to be the craftsmen of the fatherland's liberty—must be estranged from all other crafts and be exceedingly skillful in this one. They must care for nothing else that does not tend toward this goal. They should neither perform nor imitate anything else; or, if they do imitate, they should imitate from childhood only what is consistent with their profession: namely, men who are brave, temperate, holy, and generous, and other such qualities. They must neither perform nor be capable of imitating illiberal <note>meaning unfree or ignoble</note> acts, nor anything else shameful, lest from the imitation itself they become in reality the kind of things they mimic. Have you not noticed that imitations, if they begin from tender years and persist, turn into habits and nature, affecting the body, the voice, and even the very mind? **ADEIMANTUS.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** We shall not permit those for whom we claim to care, and whom we desire to be excellent men, to imitate—while they are men—a woman, whether young or old, or one who rails against her husband, or contends against the gods and boasts because she thinks herself happy, or one overwhelmed by calamities, weeping and wailing; nor one who is laboring, or inflamed by love, or oppressed by the pains of childbirth. **ADEIMANTUS.** By no means. **SOCRATES.** Nor should they imitate male or female slaves performing the duties of slaves. **ADEIMANTUS.** Not even that. **SOCRATES.** Nor, it seems, should they imitate wicked men who are cowardly and do the opposite of what we have described: men who revile and mock one another, speaking shameful things whether drunk or sober, or any other sins such men commit in words or deeds against themselves and others. I also think they should not, through imitation, make themselves like those who are insane in word or action. For while one must recognize the insane and the wicked, whether men or women, nothing of their words or deeds is to be performed or imitated. **ADEIMANTUS.** You speak the absolute truth. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, is it fitting for them to imitate craftsmen—those working in bronze or other trades—or rowers of ships, or those who command them, or anything else related to these? **ADEIMANTUS.** How could they, since they are not permitted to apply their minds to any such things? **SOCRATES.** Will they then imitate neighing horses, or lowing bulls, or the roar and murmur of rivers, or the crashing of the sea, or thunder, or other things of that kind? **ADEIMANTUS.** Indeed, they are forbidden both to be insane and to make themselves like the insane. **SOCRATES.** If I understand what you are saying, there is a certain style of speech and narration in which the truly good man speaks when he has something to say, and another style, quite unlike it, which is kept by one who is born and raised in the opposite way. **ADEIMANTUS.** What styles are these? **SOCRATES.** It seems to me that when a moderate man comes across the speech or action of a good man in his narration, he will report it as if he were that person himself, and will undertake such an imitation without any shame or disgrace. He will primarily and mostly imitate the good man acting prudently and without error; but he will do so more rarely and less often when that man is failing due to illness, or love, or drunkenness, or some other misfortune. But when he comes to someone unworthy of himself, he will be unwilling, I think, to seriously liken himself to an inferior person, except perhaps briefly when that person does something good. He will feel ashamed, being unpracticed in imitating such people, and will find it distasteful to take on the forms of his inferiors, scorning such images unless perhaps he does it for the sake of a joke or amusement. **ADEIMANTUS.** Not without reason. **SOCRATES.** Will he not then use a style of narration such as I mentioned a little while ago regarding the words of Homer? <note>referring to the mix of direct speech and third-person description</note> His speech will participate in both: namely, imitation and the other form of narration. But the part of imitation in his long speech will be very small. Am I saying something or nothing at all? **ADEIMANTUS.** You are certainly describing the form that such a speaker must take. **SOCRATES.** On the other hand, will not the man who is not of this character—the more foolish and unlearned he is—narrate more things and imitate everything? Will he not think nothing is beneath him? Therefore, he will attempt to imitate everything, and in the sight of many: especially those things I mentioned just now—thunder, the murmuring of winds and hail, the creaking of axles and wheels, trumpets, flutes, pipes, and the sounds of all instruments; furthermore, the cries of dogs, sheep, and birds. His entire speech will consist almost entirely of imitation in voice and gesture, with only a small bit of narration. **ADEIMANTUS.** That is also necessary. **SOCRATES.** And these are the two styles of speech I was mentioning above. **ADEIMANTUS.** They clearly are. **SOCRATES.** Does not one of these styles have very little variation? And if one gives the speech a fitting harmony and rhythm, the person speaking correctly will always speak in nearly the same form of speech, and moreover in a single harmony—for the changes are small—and in a nearly similar rhythm? **ADEIMANTUS.** That is exactly how it is. **SOCRATES.** What about the other style? Does it not require the opposite: namely, all harmonies and all rhythms, if it is to be spoken properly, since it has many and varied forms of change? **ADEIMANTUS.** It is entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Do not all poets and others who speak use either one of these styles of speaking, or the other, or a mixture of both? **ADEIMANTUS.** They must. **SOCRATES.** What then shall we do? Shall we admit all of these into our city, or only one of the simple styles, or the mixed one? **ADEIMANTUS.** If the choice were mine, I would choose the simple style that imitates the decent man. **SOCRATES.** And yet, O Adeimantus, the mixed style is pleasant; but it is much more pleasant to children and their tutors than the one you choose, and to the great majority of the crowd. **ADEIMANTUS.** It is indeed most pleasant. **SOCRATES.** But perhaps you will not think it fits our republic, because with us a man is not double or manifold, since each person does only one thing. **ADEIMANTUS.** It certainly does not fit. **SOCRATES.** Shall we not then find that in such a city, a shoemaker is only a shoemaker, and not a pilot as well; and a farmer is only a farmer, and not a judge besides? A soldier is a soldier, and not a money-changer too, and so on for the rest? **ADEIMANTUS.** These things are true. **SOCRATES.** If, therefore, a man should come to our city who, through his wisdom, is able to turn himself into all forms and imitate all things...

<summary>Socrates and Adeimantus discuss the psychological dangers of "mimesis" (imitation), arguing that guardians should only imitate virtuous behavior to avoid internalizing bad habits. They conclude that the ideal state should only permit simple, virtuous narration rather than the complex, multi-voiced style of poets like Homer.</summary>

# BOOK VI
### PAGE XXXI.

If a man should come to us who is able by his wisdom to take on any shape and imitate all things, and should wish to show us his poems, we would worship him as a sacred, admirable, and pleasant being. But we would say that there is no such man in our republic, nor is it lawful for there to be one. We would send him away to another city, pouring ointment upon his head and crowning him with wool <note>A ritual gesture of honor before dismissal</note>. We, however, for the sake of utility, shall employ a more austere and less pleasant poet and storyteller, who may express for us the style of a virtuous man, and who says what is said in those forms which we established as laws from the beginning, when we undertook to educate the soldiers. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Exactly so; if it were up to us, that is what we would do. 

**SOCRATES:** It seems now, my friend, that we have said enough about that part of music which concerns speech and stories. For both what must be said and how it must be said have been explained. 

**ADIMANTUS:** It seems the same to me. 

**SOCRATES:** It remains to discuss the nature of song and melody. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** Could not everyone now find what we ought to say about these things—what kind they ought to be—if indeed they must harmonize with what was said before? 

Then **GLAUCON**, smiling, said: I seem to be outside the group. For I cannot sufficiently grasp at present what kind of things ought to be said. 

**SOCRATES:** At least we can surely say this first: that melody consists of three things: the words, the harmony <note>In this context, 'harmony' refers to musical modes or scales</note>, and the rhythm. 

**GLAUCON:** That much I can do. 

**SOCRATES:** And does not the word-part of the melody differ not at all from the speech that is without song, insofar as it must be expressed in the same forms we were speaking of a little while ago, and in the same manner? 

**GLAUCON:** You speak the truth. 

**SOCRATES:** And yet the harmony and rhythm ought to follow the words. 

**GLAUCON:** Why not? 

**SOCRATES:** Moreover, we said that we have no need for lamentations and wailing in our speech. 

**GLAUCON:** Certainly not. 

**SOCRATES:** Which, then, are the mournful harmonies? Tell me, for you are a musician. 

**GLAUCON:** The Mixed Lydian, the "Sharp" Lydian, and others of this sort. 

**SOCRATES:** Must these not be removed? For they are useless even for women—who ought to be decent—let alone for men. 

**GLAUCON:** Very much so. 

**SOCRATES:** Furthermore, drunkenness, softness, and laziness are least becoming for guardians. 

**GLAUCON:** Least of all. 

**SOCRATES:** Which then are the soft and drunken harmonies? 

**GLAUCON:** The Ionian and the Lydian, as many as are called "slack" <gloss>that is, relaxed, remiss, and loosened</gloss>. 

**SOCRATES:** Will you then, my friend, use these in any way for the benefit of soldiers? 

**GLAUCON:** In no way. But it seems to you that the remaining ones are the Dorian and Phrygian harmonies. 

**SOCRATES:** I do not know the harmonies myself, but leave me that harmony which appropriately imitates the voices and accents of a man going bravely into battle, or behaving manfully in any violent work; and of one who is in danger, or rushing into wounds or death, or falling into some other heavy fortune, and in all these things repelling fortune constantly and manfully. And leave another harmony which imitates the voices and accents of a man engaged in a peaceful and non-violent action, either persuading someone of something, or praying, or by his prayers to God, or by his teaching and admonition to a man; or on the contrary, showing himself yielding to another who prays, teaches, or dissuades him; and who, though he has achieved his wish, is not puffed up with pride, but behaves temperately and modestly in all these things and bears both fortunes rightly. Let him follow these two harmonies: the violent and the voluntary; of the fortunate and the unfortunate; of the temperate and the brave; and whichever most beautifully imitates their accents—leave all these harmonies. 

**GLAUCON:** But truly, you ask for no others to be chosen than those I mentioned just now. 

**SOCRATES:** We shall not, therefore, have need in our songs and melodies for a harmony that consists of many strings and all types of chords. 

**GLAUCON:** Not as it seems to me. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we shall not support the makers of triangles, harps <note>original: "pactidarū"</note>, and whatever instruments consist of many strings and many consonances. 

**GLAUCON:** It seems we will not. 

**SOCRATES:** What then? Will you receive flute-makers and flute-players into the city? Do not the instruments of many strings and all harmonies imitate the flute? 

**GLAUCON:** It is clear. 

**SOCRATES:** The lyre, then, remains, and the cithara is useful in the city; and the pipe <note>original: "fistula"</note> is convenient for shepherds in the fields. 

**GLAUCON:** So the argument shows us. 

**SOCRATES:** We are introducing nothing strange, my friend, when we prefer Apollo and Apollo's instruments to Marsyas himself and the organs that belong to Marsyas <note>Apollo played the lyre; Marsyas played the flute and was punished for his hubris</note>. 

**GLAUCON:** Not by Jove, as it seems to me. 

**SOCRATES:** By the Dog <note>A favorite oath of Socrates</note>, we have begun to purge the city little by little and secretly, which we said above was given over to too many luxuries. 

**GLAUCON:** We are indeed acting temperately. 

**SOCRATES:** Come then, let us purge the rest. It follows from what has been said about harmonies that we should pursue rhythms in such a way that we do not wander through too many varieties, nor through all kinds of bases; but let us distinguish what are the rhythms of a brave and temperate life. Having recognized these, we shall compel the foot and the song to follow the speech of such a man, not the speech to follow the foot and the song. Which rhythms these are, it is your business to declare, just as you explained the harmonies. 

**GLAUCON:** By Jove, I do not know what to say. For that there are three species from which the bases are woven and bent, just as in voices there are four from which all harmonies are composed, I have observed and could say. But what kind of imitations of what kind of life they are, I cannot open up. 

**SOCRATES:** But concerning these things we shall deliberate with Damon: which progressions of feet are proper to illiberality, insolence, madness, and other wickedness; and which rhythms agree with their opposites. I think I have heard him, though not clearly enough, when he named a certain warlike base of feet a "composite dactyl," and also the "heroic," which he arranged I know not how, equal above and below in short and long effect; and as I think, he called one an "iamb" and another a "trochee." He applied lengths and brevities. And in some of these, I think he blamed or praised the movements of the foot no less than the rhythms themselves, or something mixed from both. For I cannot declare these things sufficiently. But these, as I was saying, let them be referred and deferred to Damon himself. For a long speech would be needed to distinguish these things. Don't you think? 

**GLAUCON:** A long one, by Jove. 

**SOCRATES:** But this you can discern: that gracefulness and unseemliness follow the congruence and incongruence of the rhythm. 

**GLAUCON:** Why not? 

**SOCRATES:** And indeed congruence follows beautiful speech...
