...follows: and it imitates that which is similar to it, while it imitates the incongruous as the opposite. Furthermore, the consonant and the dissonant follow in the same way; since rhythm and harmony, as was said a little while ago, follow the speech, and the speech itself does not follow rhythm and harmony. **GLAUCON.** Certainly, these things ought to follow the speech. **SOCRATES.** But what of the manner of speaking and the speech itself? Does it not follow the disposition of the soul? **GLAUCON.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** And do the other things also follow the speech? **GLAUCON.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, beauty of language, consonance, grace, and the congruence of rhythm follow a moderate disposition of the soul, which they call *euethia* <note>original: "euethiã" (εὐήθεια). Socrates distinguishes here between its literal meaning of "goodness of character" and its common derogatory use meaning "simplicity" or "naivety".</note>. I do not mean that which, when it is often accompanied by ignorance, we call "goodness" with a certain flattering derision, signifying a kind of foolishness under the name of good character; but rather that *euethia* in which the thought is truly endowed with the best character. **GLAUCON.** It is entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Must not our young men follow these things everywhere if they wish to do their duty? **GLAUCON.** They certainly must. **SOCRATES.** Now, the whole art of painting is full of these things, as is every such craftsmanship: the skill of weaving is full of it, as is the ingenuity of various works, the study of building, and moreover the production of all other furniture and instruments; and even the nature of bodies and plants. Furthermore, in all these things, there is either a certain decency or indecency. And indeed, indecency and lack of rhythm and dissonance are sisters of foul speech and wicked character; while their opposites are the sisters and imitations of the opposite: the temperate and the best character. **GLAUCON.** It is as you say. **SOCRATES.** Must we then supervise only the poets, and compel them to express the image of good character in their poems, or else not write among us? Or must we also take care that other craftsmen do not create an image of evil character—a work not well-disciplined, illiberal, deformed, and indecent—whether in the figures of living beings, or in buildings, or in any other craftsmanship? Or if someone cannot provide this, must he be prohibited from working among us, lest our guardians, being nourished on images of depravity as if on poisonous grass, and daily plucking and grazing on many things little by little from many sources, unknowingly contract one single great evil in their souls? For this reason, we must seek out those craftsmen who, by a certain natural industry, are able to track down and express the nature of the beautiful and the decent itself, so that the youth, dwelling as if in a healthy place, may be helped on all sides: whenever something of the noble reaches their eyes or ears from beautiful and honorable works, like a sweet breeze bringing health from healthy places. This breeze, beginning to blow immediately from their earliest years, gradually leads the souls of men into a likeness, friendship, and harmony with noble speech and reason. **GLAUCON.** They would be nourished in an exceedingly excellent way by that method. **SOCRATES.** For this reason then, Glaucon, because of this primary nourishment according to music <note>In the Greek sense, "music" (mousike) refers to all the arts of the Muses, including poetry, literature, and music.</note>, rhythm and harmony penetrate the inner parts of the soul and strike the soul most vehemently, bringing a certain graceful form through which a person is made graceful and beautiful, if he is rightly educated in music; but the opposite if he has been educated otherwise. And because he will most sharply perceive things that are deficient, or not rightly crafted, or not well-born, he who has been nourished there as is proper will rightly be troubled by these things, but will praise beautiful things and, loving them and greedily seizing them, will be nourished by them and become both good and beautiful. Foul things he will rightly censure and hate, even at that age when he has not yet received reason. Finally, when reason arrives, he who has been so nourished will gladly embrace it, recognizing it because of its affinity and familiarity. **GLAUCON.** It seems to me also that they should be nourished in music for the sake of these things. **SOCRATES.** Just as we are sufficiently skilled in letters when the elements do not escape us—the few elements that exist in all things—and we do not despise them in small things or in great, as if it were not necessary to understand them, but we set out to discern them everywhere, since we would not be future grammarians until we had so prepared ourselves. **GLAUCON.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, we will not recognize the images of letters, if they appear anywhere in water or in mirrors, until we know the letters themselves. For this belongs to the same art and practice. **GLAUCON.** It is entirely as you say. **SOCRATES.** To what end do I say this? Surely by the same reasoning we shall not be musicians—neither ourselves nor those whom we educate for the guardianship of the city—until we recognize the forms of temperance, and of fortitude, liberality, and magnificence, and whatever are the sisters of these, and their opposites, wherever they may be; so that we perceive both these and their images in whatever they are found, and do not despise them in small things or in great, but consider them to belong to the same art and study. **GLAUCON.** It is absolutely necessary. **SOCRATES.** If these things should concur in any man—that beautiful characters exist in his soul, and that in the appearance of his body individual things correspond and harmonize with them, receiving the same principle—this will be the most beautiful sight for him who is able to behold it. **GLAUCON.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** And yet, what is most beautiful is also most lovable. **GLAUCON.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** A musical man would love such people most of all; but if he noticed something dissonant, he would not. **GLAUCON.** Not certainly if it were dissonant by a defect of the soul; but if something were merely lacking in the body, he would endure it so far as to be willing to love and cherish it. **SOCRATES.** I understand indeed, because such people are either loved by you or have already been loved; and I agree. But tell me this: Is there any commerce between temperance and unrestrained pleasure? **GLAUCON.** In what way? For pleasure of this kind moves the mind from its state no less than pain does. **SOCRATES.** But with other virtues? **GLAUCON.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** What then: do petulance and intemperance have communion with excessive pleasure? **GLAUCON.** Most of all. **SOCRATES.** Do you know of any greater and more vehement pleasure than that which concerns sexual matters? **GLAUCON.** Nor more vehe-

# BOOK III.

I make no mention of it, nor of anything more frantic. **SOCRATES:** But right love is by its very nature temperate and musical in its love of the beautiful and the decorous. **GLAUCON:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, nothing frantic or characteristic of intemperance should be brought near to right love. **GLAUCON:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Neither, then, should sexual pleasure itself be joined to it; nor should lovers and their beloved youths share in it if they love legitimately. **GLAUCON:** By Jupiter, in no way, Socrates. **SOCRATES:** Thus, as it seems, you will establish a law in the city you are founding: that a lover may love, be with, and touch his beloved—if he persuades him—as if he were a son, for the sake of honorable things; and in all matters he should so conduct himself with the one he loves that he never appears to require anything from the youth beyond what is honorable. If he acts otherwise, he should undergo reproach as one who knows nothing of the musical arts <note>original: "musicum" - here referring to the harmony of the soul</note> or the beautiful. **GLAUCON:** Exactly so. **SOCRATES:** Does it not seem to you that the discourse on music has now reached its end? For where it ought to end, it has now arrived. For music ought to end in the love of the beautiful. **GLAUCON:** I certainly agree.

**SOCRATES:** After music, the young men must be trained in gymnastics <note>technical term for physical education and athletics</note>. **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** It is necessary that they be educated diligently in this from childhood throughout their whole life. The matter stands somewhat like this, I think—see what you think as well. To me, it does not seem that a well-conditioned body makes the soul good by its own excellence; but on the contrary, a well-conditioned soul, by its own excellence, renders the body as good as it can be. What does it seem to you? **GLAUCON:** The same as to you. **SOCRATES:** If, after we have sufficiently instructed the mind, we hand over to it the task of diligently and exactly looking after the things pertaining to the body—while we merely propose certain outlines so as not to be too long-winded—would we be doing rightly? **GLAUCON:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** We said, then, that they must abstain from drunkenness. For it is more permissible for anyone else than for a guardian to be so weighed down by drunkenness that he does not know where on earth he is. **GLAUCON:** Indeed, it would be ridiculous for a guardian to need a guardian. **SOCRATES:** But what shall we say of food? For these men are athletes of the greatest contest. Are they not? **GLAUCON:** Plainly the greatest. **SOCRATES:** Would the habit of other athletes be suitable for our guardians? **GLAUCON:** Perhaps. **SOCRATES:** But this habit is a sleepy one and precarious for health. Do you not see that they sleep their lives away? And if they depart even a little from their prescribed diet, such trainees become gravely ill. **GLAUCON:** I see it indeed. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, a more elegant kind of exercise is needed for our warlike athletes, who ought to be like sleepless dogs: to see and hear most acutely, and to endure many changes in the field—of water, food, heat, and cold—so that they may defend themselves from disease. **GLAUCON:** So it seems to me. **SOCRATES:** The best gymnastics, then, would be the sister of the simple music we discussed a little while ago. **GLAUCON:** How so? **SOCRATES:** A simple and suitable gymnastics, namely, the training of soldiers. **GLAUCON:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** We can learn this from Homer. For you know how, in the expeditions of war at the tables of the heroes, he provides them neither with fish—even though they were by the Hellespont sea—nor with boiled meats, but only roasted ones, which are easier for soldiers to prepare. For everywhere it is easier, so to speak, to use fire itself than to carry vessels around. Nor does Homer ever mention varied seasonings, I believe. But this is known by others who exercise: that he who would have a robust body must abstain from all such things. **GLAUCON:** They know it rightly, and they abstain. **SOCRATES:** Then, my friend, you do not praise Syracusan tables and Sicilian varieties of side-dishes, as it seems, if these things seem right to you. **GLAUCON:** Certainly not, I think. **SOCRATES:** You also find fault with the Corinthian luxury of seductive girls for those who are to be in the best physical condition. **GLAUCON:** Most greatly. **SOCRATES:** And also Attic desserts and seasonings, which seem pleasant and delicate to many. **GLAUCON:** Necessarily. **SOCRATES:** For if we say all such diet is similar to the melody and song composed in every kind of harmony and rhythm, we would compare it rightly. **GLAUCON:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** There [in music], variety breeds intemperance; here [in diet], it breeds disease. But simplicity in music produces temperance in souls, and in gymnastics, health in bodies. **GLAUCON:** You speak most truly. **SOCRATES:** But when intemperance and diseases multiply in a city, we have great need of courtrooms and the help of doctors. Hence, the legal and medical arts are held in high esteem, especially when many free men study them with great zeal. **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you can take no greater proof of bad and shameful discipline in a city than the need for supreme judges and doctors—not only for lowly and mechanical men, but even for those who boast of having been educated in liberal discipline. Does it not seem shameful, and a great sign of bad education, to be compelled to use an external justice because of a lack of one's own virtue, being forced to act justly by others as if they were masters and judges? **GLAUCON:** Of all things, surely the most shameful. **SOCRATES:** Or do you not think this is even more shameful: when someone not only spends his whole life in courts, accusing and defending, but, elated by a certain crude boastfulness, even glories in these very affairs? As if he were powerful at inflicting injury and able to dodge through his cleverness so as to pay no penalty for his wrongs—he who often undergoes such anxious business for the sake of the smallest and most worthless things, ignorant of how much more noble and better it would be to so prepare himself that he would have no need of a sleepy judge? **GLAUCON:** Certainly, this is more shameful than the other. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, it must be considered absurd that men need doctors not only to heal wounds and cure diseases occurring from the weather or accidents, but mostly for "catarrhs" <note>original: "destillationes" - a buildup of bodily fluids</note> and the rush of swelling internal vapors caused by softness and laziness, and the luxury we condemned in their diet. The result of which is that men [become like] pools...

<summary>Socrates argues that physical training (gymnastics) should mirror the simplicity of musical education to foster health and temperance, noting that a reliance on doctors and lawyers is a sign of a decaying, undisciplined society.</summary>

# DIALOGUE III. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO 230.

...just like water and air overflowing, it has forced the successors of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing</note> to call certain diseases by new names, such as "distillations" <note>catarrh or runny nose</note>, "inflations" <note>bloating</note>, and "creaking of the bowels," because they are so over-filled. GLAUCON: These are certainly new names for diseases, and quite absurd. SOCRATES: These, I believe, did not exist in the time of Aesculapius. I gather this clearly from the fact that his sons at Troy did not condemn the cup offered to the wounded Eurypilus at Patroclus's command, even though it contained a mixture of meal, wine, and grated cheese—all of which increase phlegm. GLAUCON: Truly that was an absurd drink, and not at all suitable for someone in that condition. SOCRATES: Not if you notice that before the time of Herodicus, the followers of Aesculapius did not use this modern medical faculty which acts as a "pedissequa" <note>a handmaid or constant follower</note> of diseases. But Herodicus, being a master of gymnastic exercises for youth and having become sickly himself, mixed gymnastics with medicine; first he tormented himself, and then his successors, with much long-lasting weariness. GLAUCON: In what way? SOCRATES: He provided himself with a long death. For while he followed his disease toward its terminal end, he could not, I think, cure himself; yet, occupied with the study of healing and neglecting all other actions, he wasted his life in this indulgence of the body. He fared poorly if he departed even a little from his accustomed diet; yet, not easily yielding to nature, he lived to old age through this "wisdom" and then departed from life. GLAUCON: He won a grand prize from his art! SOCRATES: Indeed, the prize he deserved; for he did not know that Aesculapius did not fail to show this type of healing to his descendants out of ignorance or lack of skill, but because he knew that in a well-governed city, everyone has a task assigned to them which they must perform, and no one has the leisure to spend their whole life being a "valitudinarian" <note>a person chronically preoccupied with their health</note> in the care of the body. We notice this in a ridiculous way among craftsmen, but not at all among those who are considered wealthy and happy. GLAUCON: How so? SOCRATES: If a blacksmith falls ill, he demands a quick cure from the doctor: either through vomiting, or a purging of the bowels, or cautery, or incision. But if someone prescribes for him a long observation of diet, or wrapping his head in bandages and such things, he immediately objects that he has no leisure to be sick; nor is it worth it to him to drag out his life lying there with constant bandages while neglecting his craft. Therefore, dismissing the doctor and returning to his usual diet, if he recovers, he performs his work; but if his body cannot sustain the disease, he dies and is freed from his troubles. GLAUCON: It certainly seems proper for a craftsman to use medicine in that way. SOCRATES: And for that reason I said his work is set before him, which if he does not perform, it is not worth it for him to live. GLAUCON: That is clear. SOCRATES: But the rich man, as we said, is pressed by no work, which if he were forced to stop, he would no longer have to live. GLAUCON: None at all, so they say. SOCRATES: Perhaps you have not heard Phocylides <note>An ancient Greek gnomic poet</note> saying that one ought to practice virtue as soon as one has the means to live. GLAUCON: I think even before then. SOCRATES: Let us not argue with him on this, but let us teach ourselves whether the rich man ought to meditate on this in such a way: otherwise, if he wastes his time in "nurturing" his diseases, he should not live. For this is an impediment to the craft of the blacksmith and others, as it turns the mind away from work. But the precept of Phocylides is no impediment. GLAUCON: By Jove, it occupies us most of all if this superfluous care of the body is extended beyond all gymnastics. SOCRATES: Indeed, it is a great hindrance to household affairs, military service, and all urban magistracies; and what is worst, it hinders the desire for learning and all diligence in understanding and meditating, while one always suspects headaches and dizziness, blaming the study of wisdom as if these things were born from it. Therefore, it is an absolute hindrance to the exercise and testing of virtue. It makes us think we are always sick and never stop complaining about the condition of the body. GLAUCON: That is consistent. SOCRATES: We say that Aesculapius, knowing these things, showed medicine to men who were healthy by nature and upbringing, but who were suddenly sickened by some external cause or wound. He removed the infirmity with drugs and incisions, but then prescribed a customary diet so as not to disturb their civic duties. But for bodies thoroughly diseased with internal corruption, he by no means attempted to prolong life through a diligent diet and long observation, so that men would live poorly and, as a consequence, father sickly children. Nor did he think a man should be cured who could not live within the established and usual diet and rule, as if it would benefit neither the man himself nor the city. GLAUCON: You are saying Aesculapius was a statesman-like man. SOCRATES: It is quite clear; and his sons testify that he was such. Or are you unaware that they were famous in warfare at Troy, even though they also practiced the study of medicine, as I was saying? Do you not remember that when Menelaus was wounded by the hands of Pandarus, they wiped the blood from the wound and applied soothing ointments? But they prescribed a certain law regarding food and drink no more for him than for Eurypilus, as if drugs were sufficient to cure men who, before receiving wounds, had been of firm body and moderate diet—even if they had immediately drunk that aforementioned cup. But they thought that men who were sickly by nature and incontinence should not live, as it benefited neither themselves nor others; they believed their art should not be practiced on them, nor should they be cured even if they were wealthier than Midas. GLAUCON: You represent the sons of Aesculapius as very clever men. SOCRATES: It is fitting, although the Tragedians and Pindar do not testify with us, for they say Aesculapius was the son of Apollo and was induced by gold to restore a wealthy man to life when he was being overwhelmed by extreme sickness leading to death. For which reason he was struck by a lightning bolt. But we, because of what we said above, do not concede both of these things to them. Rather, if he was the son of a god, we shall deny that he was greedy for shameful gain...

<meta>Catchword: ...ing (mus)</meta>

<summary>Socrates argues that medicine should only be used to quickly return productive citizens to their duties, rather than to prolong the lives of the chronically ill or the idle rich. He uses the examples of Aesculapius and his sons to show that ancient medicine prioritized civic function over the mere preservation of life.</summary>

# BOOK III.

...we [must reject these stories]: but if he is base and greedy for gain, we shall reject the claim that he was a son of a god. <note>Socrates is discussing the need to censor myths that portray gods or their children as having human vices.</note> **GLAUCON:** Those things are indeed rightly said. But what do you say about this, Socrates? Is it not necessary to have good physicians in the city? And would those not be the best who had conversed with the greatest number of healthy people, and the greatest number of the sick? Likewise, would not the best judges be those who had experienced the various characters of men? **SOCRATES:** I certainly say we need very good ones. But do you understand whom I consider to be such? **GLAUCON:** I will if you tell me. **SOCRATES:** I will try. However, you were not asking about a similar thing in the same way. **GLAUCON:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Physicians would indeed become most skilled if, from an early age, beyond the study of their art, they conversed among many people with diseased bodies; and if they themselves suffered from every kind of disease and were of a weak constitution. For they do not, I think, cure the body with the body. For it would be impossible for the physicians themselves to have been or to be ill; rather, they cure the body with the soul. Or is it not possible that a soul which is or has been evil could cure anything well? **GLAUCON:** Quite right. **SOCRATES:** But the judge, my friend, rules the soul with his own soul. Is it not possible for a soul that has conversed with evil souls from childhood, and has performed every kind of unjust deed, to sharply infer the crimes of others from itself, just as one infers diseases from one's own body? Must he not rather have been innocent himself and inexperienced in evil character while he was young, if he, being good and honorable, is to judge just things sincerely? Therefore, modest men, while they are young, appear to be simpletons; and they are easily deceived by the unjust, as they do not have within themselves the same examples of evil passions that the wicked possess. **GLAUCON:** They certainly suffer that very thing. **SOCRATES:** But indeed, <margin>The Old Man</margin> a good judge ought to be not a young man, but an old one: one who has learned late in life what sort of thing injustice is; as one who has not sensed it as a property in his own soul, but has known it as a foreign thing in the souls of others over a long time; and therefore discerns what kind of evil it is, judging by knowledge rather than by his own experience. **GLAUCON:** Such a man seems to be a most noble judge. **SOCRATES:** And a good one besides, which is what you were asking. For he who has a good soul is good. But that crafty man who suspects evil—he who commits many injustices—is thought to be shrewd and wise when he deals with his own kind; he appears cautious and clever because he looks to the patterns within himself to guard himself. But when he associates with good and older men, he appears a fool, since he is distrustful beyond what is proper and is ignorant of healthy and sincere character, for he has no examples of it. But because he associates more frequently with the wicked than the good, he often seems wiser than foolish to himself and others. **GLAUCON:** You speak the truth beyond doubt. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, one ought not to seek such a judge as being good and wise, but rather the kind I described just now. For vice could never know itself or virtue. But virtue, with the addition of discipline over time, will understand both itself and vice. Thus, it is not the wicked man, in my opinion, but this virtuous man who becomes wise. **GLAUCON:** It seems so to me as well. **SOCRATES:** Will you not then establish in the city a law for medicine such as we have described, along with this kind of judicial equity, which will care for those citizens who are well-constituted in both soul and body? But as for those who are not so, they shall let those who are deficient in body die; and those who are born with an evil and incurable nature, they shall put to death? **GLAUCON:** This is perhaps conducive both to those who suffer such things and to the city. **SOCRATES:** It is also clear that the young men will take care not to fall into the need for the judicial art, by using that simple music <note>original: "musica"; in the Greek sense, this refers to all the arts of the Muses, including poetry and literature, not just melody.</note> which we said produces temperance. **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** And will not the musician, following these same tracks into gymnastics <note>original: "gymnastica"; physical training and athletics.</note>, if he wishes, achieve a state where he has no need of medicine, unless necessity compels him? **GLAUCON:** I certainly agree. **SOCRATES:** He will exercise his body in the gymnasiums, looking more to the spiritedness of his nature and exciting it, rather than to mere strength; unlike other athletes, he will not arrange his diet and labors for the sake of bodily power. **GLAUCON:** Quite right. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, Glaucon, those who establish education in music and gymnastics do not do so for the reason many think—to care for the body with one and the soul with the other. **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** They seem to practice both chiefly for the sake of the soul. **GLAUCON:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Do you not see how those are affected in their soul who practice gymnastics throughout their whole life but do not touch music? Or those who do the opposite? **GLAUCON:** Of which are you speaking? **SOCRATES:** Of rustic harshness and ferocity on the one hand, and of softness and gentleness on the other. **GLAUCON:** I know indeed that those who use pure gymnastics become more savage than is proper. Those who use only music become softer than is decent for them. **SOCRATES:** And that savage force belongs to the spiritedness of a passionate nature; which, if rightly nourished, becomes brave; but if it grows beyond what is proper, it becomes fierce and harsh, as is likely. **GLAUCON:** I agree. **SOCRATES:** What about the mild and gentle force? Does not the philosopher possess this by nature? If it is allowed to grow too much, it becomes softer than is proper, but if well-nourished, it becomes sweet and modest. **GLAUCON:** It is as you say. **SOCRATES:** But we were saying that the guardians themselves ought to have both natures. **GLAUCON:** They certainly should. **SOCRATES:** Must they not then be harmonized and in accord with each other? **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** And the soul in which these things are in harmony is temperate and brave? **GLAUCON:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** But the soul in which they are discordant is timid and savage? **GLAUCON:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Whoever allows music to occupy and soothe his soul, surrounding it with sound, and pours into his ears—as if through a funnel—the harmonies we mentioned before (sweet, charming, soft, and mournful), and spends his life in melodies that delight the soul: such a man at first, if he had any spiritedness, softens it like iron, making it useful from what was useless and hard. But when he persists too long and is soothed further, he then begins to melt and dissolve the soul, until he drains away all spiritedness and cuts away, as it were, the nerves from the soul, from which the soul [becomes] as if...

<summary>Socrates argues that judges must be old and virtuous to recognize evil without being tainted by it, and that education must balance music and gymnastics to prevent the soul from becoming either too savage or too soft.</summary>

# DIALOGUE III. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

...makes a soldier lazy. **GLAUCON.** That is entirely so. **SOCRATES.** And if nature has provided a person with a spirited character from the beginning, if it lacks the strength of the soul <note>original: "fine animi robore"</note>, it quickly casts this away. But if one is high-spirited, it breaks the strengths of the soul and turns them toward headlong anger: so that they are irritated by the smallest slights and easily boil over again. Thus, from being high-spirited, they become quick-tempered and morose, full of trouble and annoyance. **GLAUCON.** That is exactly what happens. **SOCRATES.** But if someone gives himself over to the lifestyle and exercise of gymnastics, while neglecting music <note>In this context, "music" refers to all the arts presided over by the Muses, including literature and philosophy.</note> and philosophy, at first he achieves a firm physical condition and is filled with the strength and greatness of the soul; he becomes braver than he was. **GLAUCON.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** Then, if he perseveres in this so that he does nothing else, and never touches the Muse at all: surely if there was any spark of a desire for learning in his soul, it becomes weak, deaf, and blind; since he has neither tasted any doctrine, nor any investigation of things, nor any reason at all, nor any other music from which his senses could be awakened, united, and made pure. **GLAUCON.** Clearly so. **SOCRATES.** Such a man, I believe, becomes an enemy to reason and a stranger to the Muses; he uses no persuasion of reason to lead others, but carries everything out with force and wild cruelty like a beast; he lives in ignorance and rudeness, without rhythm, grace, or refinement. **GLAUCON.** The matter stands exactly as you say. **SOCRATES.** Since these two exist, it appears I would assert that some god has given two arts to men—music and gymnastics—for the spirited and the philosophical natures: not for the soul and body specifically, except by accident, but for those two natures, so that they might harmonize with each other, being stretched and relaxed to the proper degree. **GLAUCON.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the one who most beautifully blends gymnastics with music, and applies these to the soul with the greatest moderation, we would rightly call the most perfect musician and composed of the highest harmony, much more than the one who merely tunes strings together. **GLAUCON.** And rightly so, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Will we not, therefore, always need such a presiding officer in our city, Glaucon, if the Republic is to be safe? **GLAUCON.** We will certainly need one most greatly. **SOCRATES.** These, then, would be the methods of discipline and education. Indeed, who would place dances in this category, along with hunting and the chasing of dogs, as well as gymnastic and equestrian contests? For it is generally agreed that these ought to follow, and they will not be difficult to find. **GLAUCON.** Perhaps they are not difficult. **SOCRATES.** What must we distinguish next? Is it not which of all these should command, and which should obey? **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** It is agreed that the elders ought to command, and the younger should be subject to them. **GLAUCON.** It is certainly agreed. **SOCRATES.** And it is clear from these that the best must be chosen. **GLAUCON.** That is also clear. **SOCRATES.** Are not the best of farmers those who have the greatest skill in cultivating the fields? **GLAUCON.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Now, since the best must be chosen from the guardians, must they not be those who have the greatest skill in guarding the city? **GLAUCON.** Clearly them. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, they must be prudent for this task, and powerful, and those who have a care for the Republic. **GLAUCON.** Just so. **SOCRATES.** But everyone cares most for that which he most loves. **GLAUCON.** That is necessary. **SOCRATES.** And he loves that most which he considers to have the same interests as himself, and upon whose happiness or unhappiness he believes his own happiness or unhappiness depends. **GLAUCON.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we must choose from all the guardians those who, upon our observation, seem to do with the greatest zeal throughout their whole lives what they judge to be in the interest of the Republic, and to avoid what is contrary to it. **GLAUCON.** These are certainly the most suitable. **SOCRATES.** They must be observed, I think, at every age, to see whether they keep this precept, and whether—neither deceived by certain tricks <note>original: "praestigiis," referring to illusions or deceptions</note> nor compelled by any force—they forget themselves and cast out the opinion that they should only do what is best for the Republic. **GLAUCON.** What "casting out" do you mean? **SOCRATES.** I will tell you. It seems to me an opinion leaves the mind either voluntarily or involuntarily. A false opinion leaves voluntarily when one unlearns what is false and learns what is true. But every true opinion leaves involuntarily. **GLAUCON.** I understand what you say about the voluntary exit, but I desire to learn about the involuntary. **SOCRATES.** Do you not think men are deprived of good things against their will, but of bad things by their own will? Is it not a bad thing to be deceived and to be ignorant of the truth, but a good thing to judge truly? Does it not seem to you that to hold an opinion of things as they are is to think truly? **GLAUCON.** You speak rightly; it seems to me men are deprived of a true opinion against their will. **SOCRATES.** Do they not suffer this either by theft, or by deception, or by force? **GLAUCON.** I do not understand that either. **SOCRATES.** I seem to be speaking like a tragic poet. I say opinions are "stolen" from those who change their minds, either because the opinion is erased by time or secretly taken away by a contrary argument. Now do you understand? **GLAUCON.** I do indeed. **SOCRATES.** And "force" is brought upon those whom pain or torture compels to think differently. **GLAUCON.** I understand that, and you speak correctly. **SOCRATES.** And you would also say, I think, that those are led away as if by "tricks" who abandon their former opinion because they are either charmed by pleasure or terrified by fear. **GLAUCON.** It seems that everything which deceives us seduces us by tricks. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, as I was saying just now, we must seek out who are the constant preservers of the conviction they hold: namely, that they must always do what they judge to be conducive to the Republic. They must be observed right from childhood, and tasks must be set for them in which one might most easily forget that precept or be deceived. And he who remembers it and is not led away is to be chosen; the one who is not is to be rejected. Is it not so? **GLAUCON.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, labors, pains, and contests must be set before them, and in these, the same things must be observed. **GLAUCON.** Wisely said. **SOCRATES.** Must we not also contend against that third type—that is, a kind of hallucination of tricks? Just as those who wish to see if young colts are skittish lead them into noise and tumult, so the young men must be pushed into certain terrors and then into pleasures; in these, they must be tested much more than gold is tested by fire, so that we may discover if there is anyone among them who is not easily provoked and who remains composed...

<summary>Socrates discusses the necessity of balancing physical and intellectual education to create guardians who are neither too aggressive nor too soft. He outlines a testing process to select leaders who will remain loyal to the State's interests despite pain, fear, or deception.</summary>
<keywords>guardians, education, gymnastics, music, soul, Republic, Socrates, Glaucon, testing, truth, deception</keywords>

# BOOK III

...placed in all things as the best guardian of himself and of the music he has learned, he should show himself to be balanced and harmonious in all these matters. Such a man is most useful both to himself and to his country. And he who, through every stage of life—childhood, youth, and adulthood—has been tested and remains unblemished, should be appointed as the guardian and prince of the city. Honors must be granted to him both in life and in death, and he shall receive the greatest rewards of tombs and other monuments. But he who is not of such a character must be rejected. Therefore, O Glaucon, it seems to me that the selection and education of princes and guardians ought to be of this sort, stated summarily rather than in exact detail.

**GLAUCON:** It seems the same to me.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, they will most truly be called guardians in every respect, both against external enemies and internal friends: so that the latter will not wish to, and the former will not be able to, devise any evil. The young men whom we were calling guardians a little while ago shall rightly be called "auxiliaries" <note>Latin: *auxiliarii*, the warrior class supporting the rulers</note> and defenders of the decrees of the princes themselves.

**GLAUCON:** I agree.

**SOCRATES:** What way is there, then, that by those lies which are sometimes necessary—just as we introduced a "noble" sort of lie in the previous sections—we might persuade first the princes themselves, or if not them, at least the rest of the citizens?

**GLAUCON:** What sort of thing do you mean?

**SOCRATES:** Nothing new, but a certain "Phoenician" story <note>A reference to the myth of Cadmus and the dragon's teeth; Socrates is introducing the "Myth of the Metals"</note>: something that happened among many people long ago, as the poets have said and persuaded others to believe, but not at all in our times; nor do I know if it ever will happen again. To persuade others of it is certainly difficult.

**GLAUCON:** You seem to approach the telling of it with great hesitation.

**SOCRATES:** You will see that I hesitate with good reason once I have told it.

**GLAUCON:** Speak then, and do not fear.

**SOCRATES:** Behold, I speak now, though I know not with what audacity or with what words I shall rely upon as I begin to persuade first the princes and the soldiers, and then the rest of the citizens: that all those things in which we nurtured and educated them were like dreams they seemed to have about themselves. In reality, they were then under the earth, being formed and nurtured within, they and their weapons and all their equipment. But after they were entirely finished, the earth, as their mother, brought them forth. And now, as if to a mother and nurse, they ought to look after and succor this region in which they are, if anyone should invade it; and they should think of the other citizens as brothers born of the same earth.

**GLAUCON:** It was not for nothing that you were blushing to tell this lie.

**SOCRATES:** Quite appropriately; but hear now the rest of the fable. "You are all indeed brothers in the city," as we shall say to them, "but when God was forming you, he mixed gold into the generation of those among you who are fit to rule, for which reason they are the most honored. Into those who are to be auxiliaries, he put silver. Finally, he put iron and bronze into the farmers and other craftsmen." Since you are all of the same stock, you will mostly produce children like yourselves. However, it sometimes happens that a silver child is born from a golden parent, and a golden one from a silver parent, and so on interchangeably. Therefore, God commands the princes first and foremost that they should exercise no greater care or guardianship over anything than over the children: to discern which of these four metals is mixed in their souls. And if a bronze or iron child is born to them, they must show no mercy, but assigning the honor appropriate to that nature, they should send him among the craftsmen or farmers. Conversely, if one of those classes produces a golden or silver child, they should honor them and promote them, some to be guardians and others to be auxiliaries. For there is an oracle that the Republic will perish when a bronze or iron guardian governs it. Do you have any way to make them believe this fable?

**GLAUCON:** Not these men themselves, in no way; but I see how their sons and subsequent descendants might believe it.

**SOCRATES:** Even that would be good for the greater care of themselves and the city.

**GLAUCON:** I understand roughly what you are saying.

**SOCRATES:** And this indeed leads to where the oracle points. But let us lead these "earth-born" men out, armed, with the princes as their leaders. Once they have gone forth, let them scout where it is best to place a camp in the city: from which they might best restrain those within, should anyone refuse to obey the laws, and repel those from without, if an enemy should come like a wolf to the sheepfold. When they have placed the camp and sacrificed to the proper gods, let them build their dwellings. Is it so, or otherwise?

**GLAUCON:** So, certainly.

**SOCRATES:** Should these be of a sort that suffice against winter and heat?

**GLAUCON:** Why not? You seem to be describing houses.

**SOCRATES:** Yes, but military ones, not opulent or mercantile ones.

**GLAUCON:** How do you say this differs from that?

**SOCRATES:** I will try to explain. It would be the most serious and shameful thing of all for shepherds to nurture dogs as guardians of the flock in such a way that, through lack of discipline or hunger or some other bad habit, the dogs themselves begin to harm the sheep and become like wolves instead of dogs.

**GLAUCON:** Very serious indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, we must take every precaution that those who are employed as defenders do not do such a thing against the citizens, since they are stronger than them; lest instead of benevolent allies, they show themselves to be like savage masters.

**GLAUCON:** We must indeed take care.

**SOCRATES:** Would not the greatest caution be applied if they were truly educated in a noble way?

**GLAUCON:** They are.

**SOCRATES:** It is not right to assert this, my friend Glaucon, as we were just saying: but it is right that they must obtain the correct discipline, whatever it may be, if they are to be gentle both to one another and to those they guard.

**GLAUCON:** And rightly so.

**SOCRATES:** Regarding this discipline, any sane person would say that their housing and other property should be arranged so as not to prevent them from being the best men, nor to induce them to harm the other citizens.

**GLAUCON:** Truly indeed.

**SOCRATES:** Consider then whether they ought to live and dwell in such a manner, if they are to be such men. First, let no one possess any private property, except what is strictly necessary. Then, let them have neither a house nor a storeroom that is not open to everyone. As for their food, let it be as much as is needed by military athletes who are temperate and brave; let them receive it as a fixed wage from the other citizens for the sake of their guardianship, so that at the end of the year nothing is lacking and nothing remains. Living together in common messes as if in a camp, let them eat together. And it must be told to them: "The gold and silver of the divine is from the gods in the soul..."

He also outlines the communal, non-materialistic lifestyle required for the guardians to prevent them from becoming tyrants over the citizens.</summary>

...that they possess these [divine qualities]; and that they have no need of human gold; nor is it holy to pollute the possession of that divine metal by mixing it with mortal touch. For indeed, many impious things have arisen from the money of the common people, but that which is within them <note>referring to the souls of the guardians</note> is gold entirely immaculate. Truly, to them alone of all who are in the city, it is a divine law <note>original: "nefas" - a violation of religious law</note> not to touch gold or silver: nor to receive it under their roof: nor to carry it about, nor even to drink from vessels made of that material. In this way, they would ensure safety both for themselves and for the city. But if ever they should possess a house or land or money for themselves, they will become household managers and farmers instead of guardians; and instead of being helpers to the citizens, they will become their hateful masters. And they themselves, being hated and hating others, plotting and being plotted against, will spend their entire lives in this manner. Then they will fear their fellow citizens much more than external enemies; and both they and the rest of the city will then be very close to destruction. For the sake of all these things, therefore, let us say that the guardians themselves ought to be so instructed concerning their home and all other matters. Shall this law be enacted, or not? GLAUCON: Let it be so.

->Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for the Fourth Dialogue on Justice.<-

IN THE FOURTH BOOK is delivered the manner of possession and of the city: so that the citizens are neither too rich nor too poor. For he thinks that seditions arise and the city is scattered as much from excessive abundance as from poverty. He judges, moreover, that such a city is not one, but many: if some are indeed poor and others rich; and as usually happens, the rich despise the poor, while the poor are affected by both envy and hatred toward them. From there, he gradually descends to his mystery <note>Ficino often uses "mystery" to describe Plato's deeper philosophical truths</note>: namely, that all things should be common, lest some have less and others more; for from that spring envy, lies, and thefts; and from this, luxury, pride, and laziness are born. Add to this that the possession of things, whether exceeding or lacking, hinders not only morals and concord, but even intellect and the arts. He teaches that the city is preserved and great things are achieved not by riches but by virtue. Likewise, any part of the city should not be so arranged that it seems to fare as well as possible for itself alone, but so that it contributes to all and serves the common good of the entire city. Otherwise, neither the city itself nor any of its parts can stand. He adds, furthermore, the method of increasing the city, specifically as long as the city remains one. But as soon as it appears that unity might be lost, it must not be increased further. He commands, therefore, that the city be neither tiny nor vast, but moderate, equal, and harmonious, whereby its unity may be preserved. Since, however, he who was negligent in sowing hopes for a harvest in vain, he judges that all zeal must be applied to childhood and youth, as if to the sowing of the city's harvest, so much so that a diligent account is kept of every word, game, and gesture among children and adolescents. Otherwise, if this age is neglected, laboring over daily laws will be as useless as if someone tried to cure a man daily with medicines who refused to observe any measure of temperance in his diet. Among these things, consider how games gradually turn into studies and habits. Likewise, just as a man who is naturally robust and prudent and temperate in diet needs almost no medicines, so a city that is excellently constituted from the beginning and perseveres in that form needs neither many laws at the start nor daily new regulations thereafter. For bad republics are occupied with daily cures through new laws, but never truly thrive. Wherefore, in this Republic, as the best possible, Plato applied no zeal toward laws, hoping that prudent and good men would be "living laws." Regarding sacred laws: he certainly thought one should labor much less on these. For no one ever understands by what reasoning God is to be worshipped unless he first understands God. We cannot see the divine sun unless that divine sun shows itself. He judges, therefore, that the laws of religion must be sought from Apollo—that is, from the divine light; sought, I say, not with the tongue, but with a purified and serene mind. I pass over what he touches upon here regarding the history of oracles, for these things are very well known. Allegorically, however, he signifies that Apollo—that is, the divine light—"sits," meaning he is firmly present in the "middle of the earth," which is to say everywhere in the innermost parts of all things. He "rests in the navel," that is, in the mind segregated from the senses, and reflected into itself like a spherical figure and motion. Furthermore, Apollo is "ancestral" to all: that is, a present, familiar, and propitious father to those being born, and finally a fatherland to those returning. Once the Republic is established, he then recognizes four virtues in it: **Prudence** in the rulers, which is the science of rightly guarding and consulting; **Fortitude** in the soldiers, which is a firm resolve to dare for the fatherland in dangers despite both allurements and threats, as far as the laws and magistrates command; **Temperance** in the rulers, soldiers, and craftsmen alike, which is a certain agreement by which all willingly agree that some should command and others obey—and among those who obey, some in war and others in craftsmanship—nor should such agreement be hindered by any pleasures; rather, the desires of the lower should obey the command and counsel of the higher. Also **Justice** in all, through which each person performs his own work and duty—that is, that for which he is most fit by nature and study—both publicly and privately for the sake of the common good; nor does anyone claim for himself what belongs to another. As for his calling Temperance a "diapason harmony" <note>term: diapason - the musical interval of an octave</note>, understand the diapason consonance resulting from a double proportion of tension, speed, and vehemence to that which is twice as relaxed, slower, and softer. From which double proportion indeed arises the excess of the high—that is, the eighth voice <note>the octave</note>—to the low, and not without merit. For the first double proportion is between two and one. In which proportion the number two, while it seems to surpass...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato’s Republic, specifically focusing on the relationship between musical harmony (the octave), the number eight, and the nature of justice in both the state and the soul. It transitions into the beginning of Book IV of the Republic.</meta>

# BOOK

...one refreshes, and doubles the one. Then, when the number two <note>the dyad</note> moves and revolves into itself, it produces the number eight, a solid number. For twice two, twice over, makes eight. Now, he calls this the *diapason* <note>original: "diapason," the Greek term for an octave</note>, which means "through all." For a consonance of this kind both contains all things within itself and repeats them in all things. It is not without reason that Plato says temperance is extended like a *diapason* through the highest, lowest, and middle citizens. For in the octave there is the deep voice, the highest voice, and those in the middle. 

But to return to justice: just as in the *diapason* consonance the eighth voice accords so perfectly with the deep voice that the double voice appears as one, so in a well-ordered city the gravity of temperance agrees so aptly with the strength of justice that these two virtues can scarcely be distinguished from one another. And see how opportunely Socrates moves from the *diapason* consonance of the eighth voice to justice, which among the Pythagoreans is designated by the number eight. For since justice is an entirely equal distribution according to each person's merits, and the solid foundation of the city, it is justly described by the number eight. For this number is the first of the solids: and it is the first of all to be resolved into "even-even" numbers, that is, into twice four; so that the division itself is resolved no less into numbers equally "even-even," that is, into twice two. Again, by whatever equality it is resolved, by that same equality it is woven back together. For twice two, twice over, constitutes the number eight—as I said, a likeness of just equality. 

For this reason, Orpheus, whenever he wished to call upon divine justice, swore by eight deities: fire, water, earth, heaven, moon, sun, the planets, and night. Also, on an Egyptian column placed as a sign of justice, eight deities were noted in the inscription, as Evander testifies: Saturn, Rhea, Osiris, Spirit, Heaven, Earth, Night, and Day. Finally, all antiquity believed that the order of celestial justice was arranged in eight spheres. 

After this, Socrates shows that injustice is the sudden ruin of a city, when individuals, usurping what belongs to others, disturb and confound everything. Justice, however, is the order and salvation of the city. Accordingly, from this more manifest justice of the city, he passes to the more hidden justice latent, as it were, in the soul. He divides the powers of the soul into three parts: reason in the place of the prince; the power of anger <note>the spirited part</note> in the place of the soldiers; and the nature of desire <note>the appetitive part</note> similar to the craftsmen. He proves that there is one soul in us, in which these three powers exist, distinct not by location within themselves, but by their specific properties. This indeed refutes certain Peripatetic "barkers" <note>likely a jab at contemporary Aristotelian critics</note> and can be made manifest to anyone reading diligently. 

He introduces this distinction so that it may be clear how the soul and the city, and the justice of the former and the latter, are very similar. He says, therefore: since the soul cannot, through the same power of itself, do opposite things toward the same object at the same time, it must have at least three powers. For at the same time it may be snatched toward pleasure through lust, and meanwhile called back through reason. Likewise, through lust it may be drawn back from battle, while through anger it is provoked to fight. From these things it is clear that reason is different from lust, and the vigor of anger also differs from it. It is also clear that this [anger] differs from reason: both in children who do not yet use reason but are very hot with anger, and in others who do many things through anger against the law of reason. He proves that the vigor of anger is closer to reason because indignation often helps reason against lust. 

He concludes next that justice, together with temperance, is a certain lawful agreement, both in the soul of anyone regarding the three parts we mentioned, and in the city regarding the three parts similar to these. An agreement, I say, in governing, executing, and obeying; and in performing one's own duties and not usurping those of others. Not without merit does he here call justice the sibling of temperance, a "harmony" consisting of high, low, and middle voices—voices, I say, representing the leaders, the spirited soldiers, and those in the middle. 

Then, to respond to the question raised long ago—what exactly produces justice and injustice in the soul—he says that virtue is the health, beauty, and strength of the soul, while vice is disease, ugliness, and weakness. For virtue disposes and preserves all parts of the soul as nature ordained. Vice, however, confounds and disturbs them against the order of nature. Since, indeed, when the nature of the body is entirely depraved, it is better to die than to live (even if external goods are supplied to us in abundance), he therefore concludes that a life in which the soul—through which we live—is depraved by vice is miserable and to be fled by all. Finally, at the very heel <note>the end</note> of this book, he asserts that the kind of soul and city he has described is the best and happiest. A royal soul and city, I say, arranged by the queen of man: reason. He adds that such a government is called "Kingship" when one person, clearly the most excellent of all, excels among many good men; and an "Aristocracy" <note>original: "Remp. optimatū"</note> when several appear to excel equally. Truly, it should be considered the same form of government. He also agrees that in the following book he will distinguish in order the four remaining dispositions of both souls and republics.

# DIALOGUE IV: ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. PAGE 233.

Certainly, you were putting forward many other such things in your reproach. **ADEIMANTUS.** And yet, let those things also be included in the accusation. **SOCRATES.** Do you ask, then, by what reasoning I may defend our previous statements? **ADEIMANTUS.** Indeed, that is what I ask. **SOCRATES.** By entering upon the same path, we shall find, I think, what ought to be said. We shall say, furthermore, that it would be no wonder if these men were most happy in this way. Nevertheless, we did not establish the city looking toward this—that one particular class among us should be especially happy—but so that the entire city should be as happy as possible. For we thought that in such a city we would most likely find justice, and again, in one that was worst established, injustice. Having inspected these, we thought we would easily judge what we have been seeking for so long. Now, indeed, as we intended, we are shaping a "blessed" city, not so that a few certain people in it should be blessed, but so that the whole city is. Next, we shall contemplate the opposite. 

If someone were to blame us while we were painting the figure of a human being, saying that we did not apply the most beautiful colors to the most beautiful parts of the animal—for the eyes, the most beautiful member, were painted not with purple but with black—we would seem to answer him fittingly by saying: "You ought not to think that we must paint eyes so beautiful that they do not even look like eyes, and the other members similarly; but you should consider whether, by attributing to each part its own proper grace, we make the whole beautiful." Therefore, do not now force us, we would say, to bestow such happiness upon the guardians that it makes them anything other than guardians. For we know how to command farmers to till the earth for their own pleasure, dressed in the most precious finery and adorned with gold; and potters to recline at their ease from right to left, celebrating a banquet by the hearth, having cast aside the wheel as much as they desire to practice pottery; and to make all others "blessed" in this manner, so that the entire city is happy. 

But do not advise us so. Furthermore, if we obey you, the farmer will not be a farmer, nor the potter a potter, nor will anyone else hold the form of those from whom a city is made. But for the others, the reasoning is of less weight; for if shoemakers become inferior and corrupted, and pretend to be what they are not, they bring nothing grave upon the city. But if the guardians of the laws and the city are not truly so, but only appear to be, do you see how they utterly destroy the entire city at once? Conversely, the guardians themselves, by being well-established, have the sole opportunity to make the city blessed. Wherefore, if we seek true guardians of the city, we must by no means choose those who would harm the city. But those who say such things—making the farmers happy not as if in a city, but as if at some festive celebration—are certainly considering something other than the good of the city. 

It must be seen, therefore, whether we establish guardians looking to this: that they abound in the greatest happiness; or whether we should rather take account of the whole city so that it is happy as a whole. It is fitting to compel and persuade these assistants <note>original: "auxiliarios" - referring to the warrior class</note> and guardians to do those things by which they may be the best craftsmen of their own work, and all others similarly. And so, with the entire city increased and rightly established, it must be allowed that individuals participate in blessedness insofar as the nature of each is capable. **ADEIMANTUS.** You seem to me to speak rightly. **SOCRATES.** And will I seem to you to speak fittingly regarding what is closest to this? **ADEIMANTUS.** What in particular? **SOCRATES.** Consider whether these things also corrupt the other craftsmen so that they become wicked. **ADEIMANTUS.** What things are those? **SOCRATES.** Riches, clearly, and poverty. **ADEIMANTUS.** By what reasoning? **SOCRATES.** In this way: does a potter who has become rich seem to you to have any further care for his art? **ADEIMANTUS.** Not at all. **SOCRATES.** He will certainly be rendered lazier and more negligent. **ADEIMANTUS.** Greatly so. **SOCRATES.** Wherefore he becomes a worse potter. **ADEIMANTUS.** That too. **SOCRATES.** Again, if because of want he lacks the tools and other things which the art requires, he will both make the works themselves inferior, and he will make his sons and the others whom he teaches into inferior craftsmen. **ADEIMANTUS.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** From both, therefore—as much from wealth as from poverty—both the works of the craftsmen become wicked, and the craftsmen themselves become wicked. **ADEIMANTUS.** So it appears. **SOCRATES.** We have found, then, other things for our guardians to watch over, lest they creep into the city without them noticing. **ADEIMANTUS.** What are those? **SOCRATES.** Wealth, I say, and want. For the former produces luxury, idleness, sedition, and a desire for revolution. The latter, along with revolution, gives birth to meanness and wrongdoing. 

<margin>
What evils arise from wealth and poverty
</margin>

**ADEIMANTUS.** It is exactly so. But nevertheless, Socrates, take heed, I pray: in what way will this city of ours be able to wage war since it lacks money, especially if it is ever forced to take up arms against a large and wealthy city? **SOCRATES.** It is certain that against one such city it is difficult, but against two such, it is certainly easier. **ADEIMANTUS.** How do you say that? **SOCRATES.** I say what is fair. First, if a fight must be joined, will not these men, exercised in warlike matters, fight against rich men? **ADEIMANTUS.** I confess that. **SOCRATES.** What then, Adeimantus? Does it not seem to you that one boxer, most perfectly trained for this, could easily fight against two who are ignorant of this skill, and who are moreover rich and fat? **ADEIMANTUS.** Perhaps not both at once. **SOCRATES.** Not even if it were permitted to avoid the blows of the one who attacks first by fleeing, and then to strike him by a sudden turning? Indeed, if he did this often under the sun and heat, such a man would subdue many men of that sort. **ADEIMANTUS.** Certainly, it is no wonder. **SOCRATES.** Do you not think the rich participate more in the science and experience of the boxer's skill than in the military skill? **ADEIMANTUS.** I do. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, our athletes will easily, as is consistent, contend with double and triple their number. **ADEIMANTUS.** I will admit that too. For you seem to speak rightly. **SOCRATES.** What if, having sent another embassy, they told the truth: "We indeed do not use gold or silver, nor is it lawful for us; you, therefore, who are waging war with us, take what others possess"? Do you think that anyone, having heard this, would choose to fight against hard dogs and boars rather than with the dogs against fat and soft sheep? **ADEIMANTUS.** Not at all, it seems to me. But if the money of the others is piled up in one city, beware lest it bring danger to the less wealthy. **SOCRATES.** You are blessed, since you think it is fitting to call any other a "city" except such a one as we have established. **ADEIMANTUS.** What forbids it? **SOCRATES.** Others require a broader title.

<summary>Socrates argues that the goal of the Republic is the happiness of the whole state rather than any single class, and explains how both wealth and poverty corrupt craftsmen and citizens. He further contends that a disciplined, lean city of "warrior-athletes" could easily defeat larger, wealthier, but softer cities.</summary>

For each of those is many cities, not one city—to speak in a most joking manner. Each is surely at least two, at odds with one another: one of the poor, the other of the rich. And again, in each of these there are many; if you treat them as one, you will miss the mark entirely. But if you treat them as many, handing over the things of some to others—both money and power or even the people themselves—you will always have many allies and helpers, but few enemies. And as long as the city remains tempered as it was just now ordered, it will be the greatest. I do not mean in reputation, but it will truly be the greatest, even if it consists of only a thousand defenders. For you will not easily find one such great city either among the Greeks or among the Barbarians <note>The term "Barbarians" refers to non-Greek speakers, not necessarily "uncivilized" people</note>; yet you will find many that seem many times larger than this kind of city. Or do you think otherwise? ADIMANTUS: Not otherwise, by Jove! SOCRATES: Will this not then be the most beautiful limit for our princes for increasing the city: to grant it as much territory as is appropriate for its size, but to let the rest go? ADIMANTUS: What limit is that? SOCRATES: I think, indeed, that the city should be increased only so long as it remains one; it should be increased to that point, and no further. ADIMANTUS: Excellent. SOCRATES: Furthermore, we shall command the guardians to observe this precept: that the city should seem to be neither small nor large, but one and sufficient. ADIMANTUS: And perhaps that is a light thing we are commanding them. SOCRATES: And this is even lighter, which we mentioned earlier: saying that if an inferior child is born to the guardians, he must be sent away to the others; or if a noble child is born among the others, he should be transferred to the guardians themselves. In this, we clearly wished to show that each of the other citizens should be led to that one task for which he is naturally fit, so that each person, practicing his own single task, becomes not many, but one; and thus the whole city may become one, not many. ADIMANTUS: This is even less than the other. SOCRATES: Not at all, my good man Adimantus; we are not commanding them many and great things, as someone might think, but all light and small things, if they observe the "one great thing," as the saying goes—or rather, instead of "great," the "sufficient" thing. ADIMANTUS:

<margin>On education.</margin>
What is that? SOCRATES: Education, I say, and instruction. For if they are well educated and turn out to be moderate men, they will easily discern all these things: both the other matters we are omitting for the present, and the unions of women and men, and

<margin>The proverb: all things are common among friends.</margin>
the procreation of children; for it is clear that all these things ought to be as common as possible, according to the proverb "friends have all things in common." ADIMANTUS: That would certainly be most right. SOCRATES: Indeed, if a republic once begins well, it proceeds like a circle, always improving itself. For good education and instruction, when preserved, produce good natures. And again, good natures, having obtained this kind of education, turn out even better than before, both for other things and for generating children, just as in other animals. ADIMANTUS: That is consistent. SOCRATES: Finally, to speak briefly, this must be diligently observed by the tutors of the city: that it does not secretly become corrupted without them knowing. Rather, let them care for this above all: that nothing be innovated against the order given by us regarding gymnastics and music; but let everyone follow it as much as possible. And when someone says that poetic line—namely, that men are most delighted by new songs—the guardians themselves ought to fear lest someone thinks the poet is speaking not of new songs, but of new *modes* of singing, and praises them. But one ought neither to praise such a thing nor accept it. One must surely beware of introducing a new kind of music, as if it were a total shipwreck. For the modes of music are never changed without the changing of the greatest civil laws, as Damon says:

<margin>With the change of musical modes, the greatest civil laws are changed.</margin>
and I myself agree with him. ADIMANTUS: Know that I also agree, Socrates. SOCRATES: Therefore, the guardians must build a kind of citadel for the sake of protection here in music. ADIMANTUS: Indeed, such a transgression creeps in secretly and easily. SOCRATES: Certainly, in the manner of a joke, and as if it seemed to harm nothing. ADIMANTUS: And yet, having gradually become familiar to us, it slowly creeps into morals and pursuits; from these it then emerges more fully into commerce; finally, from commerce it breaks out into laws and republics with great insolence and wantonness, O Socrates, until it finally perverts everything, privately and publicly. SOCRATES: Is this so? ADIMANTUS: So it seems to me. SOCRATES: Therefore, as we said from the beginning, children must be accustomed to honorable play immediately from their first years.

<margin>The instruction of children in honorable play.</margin>
For if they become accustomed to less decent play, they can never turn out to be law-abiding and good men. ADIMANTUS: Why not? SOCRATES: Therefore, when children, beginning well, play and sport and drink in the law-abiding custom through music, music tends toward the opposite of those things mentioned before; and it proceeds to set upright whatever was previously lying low in the city. ADIMANTUS: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: These men, then, will discover those institutions of the city which seem small, as I said, which the previous generation used to disturb. ADIMANTUS: What kind of things? SOCRATES: These, for instance: how the younger should be silent before the elders, give place to them, and rise; to honor parents; what style of hair-cutting is to be observed by each; what clothes or shoes are to be used; and in general, what bodily ornament is appropriate; and other things of that kind. Do you not think so? ADIMANTUS: Indeed. SOCRATES: But to prescribe these things by laws would, I think, seem foolish. For it is never done, nor would these things remain if committed to words and letters. ADIMANTUS: Why so? SOCRATES: It appears then, O Adimantus, that whatever the beginning of a child's education was, such will be the things that follow. Does not like always call forth like? ADIMANTUS: Why not? SOCRATES: And finally, it must be said that it ends in one thing that is supreme and powerful, whether good or evil. ADIMANTUS: What prevents it? SOCRATES: For this reason, I would never strive to establish these things by laws. ADIMANTUS: And rightly so. SOCRATES: Tell me, by the gods, shall we attempt to mark out by laws the business of the marketplace, mutual commerce, and contracts in the mechanical arts, the laws of quarreling and striking, the summons to court, the appointment of judges, and whatever taxes must be either imposed or collected in the market or the ports? Or in general, any laws of the market, the city, or the navy, and others of that kind? ADIMANTUS: It is not at all fitting to command good and noble men. For most of these things...
