# DIALOGUE IV. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE. PAGE 234.

<margin>To pass and change laws is to cut off the heads of a Hydra.</margin>

...and how they should be established, they themselves will easily discover. **SOCRATES:** Certainly, my friend, if God grants them the preservation of those laws which we set down above. **ADIMANTUS:** But if not, they will spend their lives enacting many such laws, always correcting and renewing them, thinking they will thus achieve what is best. **SOCRATES:** You mean that such people will live just like those who, being sick, refuse to change their unhealthy way of life due to intemperance. **ADIMANTUS:** Exactly so. **SOCRATES:** Truly, those people seem to persist in their diseases in a ridiculous manner; by their cures they achieve nothing except making their diseases more numerous and severe, yet they always hope that if someone suggests a medicine, they will soon be well. **ADIMANTUS:** The diseases of those suffering in this way are entirely of that sort. **SOCRATES:** What then? Is this not a charming trait in them? That they consider the person who tells them the truth to be their greatest enemy—the one who says that neither medicines, nor cauterizations, nor incisions, nor incantations <note>original: "incantationes," referring to magical charms or spells used in ancient medicine</note>, nor things applied from the outside, nor anything of the sort will do any good until one stops indulging in drunkenness, gluttony, lust, and idleness? **ADIMANTUS:** That is not very charming at all. For there is no grace in being angry at someone who offers useful advice. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, you do not approve of such men, as it seems. **ADIMANTUS:** Not in the least, by Jove! **SOCRATES:** Nor will you praise a whole city if it acts as we were just saying. Or do you not think that ill-governed cities do the same as these men? They forbid the citizens from moving the entire state of the republic, under penalty of death for anyone who innovates. On the other hand, whoever approves and confirms the present government, catering to the will of the rulers, flattering them and complying with them—is he not the one considered a good man, wise in the greatest matters, and worthy of honor? **ADIMANTUS:** They seem to me to do exactly that, and I do not praise such republics in any way. **SOCRATES:** But what of those who strive to cure these cities? Do you not admire their courage and readiness? **ADIMANTUS:** I admire them indeed, except for those who are deceived by themselves and think they are truly statesmen because they are praised by the crowd. **SOCRATES:** What are you saying? Do you not forgive them? Do you think a man ignorant of measurement could escape believing he is four cubits tall <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches; four cubits would be about 6 feet</note> if many others like him told him he was? **ADIMANTUS:** Not that, certainly. **SOCRATES:** Then do not be annoyed. For these are the most charming of all in a ridiculous way: they pass laws on the matters we mentioned and are always amending them, confident they will find some end to the injustices committed in commerce and those things I spoke of a moment ago, not knowing that they are truly cutting off the heads of a Hydra <note>The Hydra was a mythological serpent that grew two heads for every one cut off; Socrates uses it as a metaphor for endless, ineffective legislation</note>. **ADIMANTUS:** Certainly, they do nothing else. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, I think the true founder of laws should not bother with this kind of institution regarding laws and the republic, neither in an ill-disposed city nor in a well-constituted one: in the former, because such institutions are useless and change nothing; in the latter, because some things anyone can find, and others follow naturally from their previous studies. **ADIMANTUS:** What then remains for us to prescribe by law? **SOCRATES:** For us, nothing. But for the Delphic Apollo <note>The god of the oracle at Delphi, traditionally consulted for religious and foundational laws</note>, the greatest, most noble, and primary institutions. **ADIMANTUS:** Which are those? **SOCRATES:** The establishment of temples and sacrifices, and other worship of gods, spirits, and heroes; furthermore, the graves and funerals of the deceased, and whatever services must be undertaken to appease them. Such things we certainly do not know ourselves; and in organizing the city, we will trust no one else if we are wise, nor will we use any other interpreter than the ancestral god. For this god is the ancestral interpreter for all men in such matters, sitting in the center of the earth upon the navel <note>original: "umbilicum," referring to the Omphalos at Delphi, believed to be the center of the world</note> and explaining them. **ADIMANTUS:** You speak wisely; and so it must be done. **SOCRATES:** Now, O son of Ariston <note>Referring to Glaucon or Adimantus, the brothers of Plato</note>, let your city be established. Next, look into it yourself, providing sufficient light from somewhere; and call your brother, and Polemarchus, and the others besides, so that we may see if we can somehow perceive where justice is, and where injustice is, and how they differ from each other, and which of these he must possess who is to live happily, whether it be hidden or not hidden from all gods and men. **GLAUCON:** You say nothing, Socrates. For you promised to investigate it yourself, as if it would be a crime if you did not support justice with all your might. **SOCRATES:** You remind me truly, and so it must be done. However, it is necessary for you all to be present with me. **GLAUCON:** We will do so. **SOCRATES:** I hope, therefore, to find it in this way. I think the city, if it has been rightly established by us, exists as absolutely good. **GLAUCON:** It must be so. **SOCRATES:** It is certain, then, that it is wise, brave, temperate, and just. **GLAUCON:** It is certain. **SOCRATES:** Whichever of these we find in the city, the remainder will be what has not yet been found. **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** If we were looking for any one of four things in some subject, and that one was first apparent, our task would be done; but if we first recognized the other three, by this very fact the thing sought would be known, for it would be certain that it was nothing else than what remained. **GLAUCON:** You speak well. **SOCRATES:** Should we not seek in the same way concerning these, since they are only four? **GLAUCON:** Plainly. **SOCRATES:** And of all these, wisdom seems to shine forth first in the city; and something wonderful appears regarding it. **GLAUCON:** What is that? **SOCRATES:** The city we described seems to me to be truly wise. For it is well-advised. Is it not? **GLAUCON:** It is indeed. **SOCRATES:** And this very foresight in counsel is a certain kind of knowledge. For it is not through ignorance, but rather through knowledge, that men take good counsel. **GLAUCON:** That is clear. **SOCRATES:** But there are many and various kinds of knowledge in the city. **GLAUCON:** There are. **SOCRATES:** Should the city be called wise and well-advised because of the knowledge of smiths? **GLAUCON:** By no means because of that; it would be called "skilled in smithing." **SOCRATES:** Therefore, the city is not to be called wise because it takes good counsel regarding wooden works and how they are made through the knowledge of carpentry. **GLAUCON:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Or perhaps for the knowledge that fashions bronze works, or any other such thing? **GLAUCON:** Certainly not for any of those. **SOCRATES:** Nor is it called wise and well-advised for the knowledge of counsel regarding the production and gathering of fruits from the earth, but rather "agricultural." **GLAUCON:** So I think. **SOCRATES:** What then? Is there any knowledge in the city recently founded by us, among any citizens, by which one deliberates not about some private thing in the city, but rather about the whole city, and how it may best conduct itself toward itself and toward other cities? **GLAUCON:** There is indeed. **SOCRATES:** What is this, and in whom is it found? **GLAUCON:** It is the guardianship...

...diligence in listening: and among these leaders whom we just now called perfect guardians. **SOCRATES:** Because of this knowledge, then, what name do you give to the city? **GLAUCON:** Prudent in counsel, and truly wise. **SOCRATES:** Do you think there are more blacksmiths in the city than these true guardians? And this class is by nature the fewest and rarest: to whom it belongs to be the leader of this knowledge, which alone among all others deserves to be called wisdom. **GLAUCON:** What you say is very true. **SOCRATES:** So, do you see how we have found this one of the four [virtues]? **GLAUCON:** I do. **SOCRATES:** And in what part of the city it is located? **GLAUCON:** It seems to me to be sufficiently discovered.

<margin>What courage is: and how a city is brave.</margin>
**SOCRATES:** Now indeed it is not difficult to find what courage is, and in what part of the city it is located, because of which the city is called brave. **GLAUCON:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Who, looking to anything else, would call a city either cowardly or brave, except to that part which fights and campaigns on its behalf? **GLAUCON:** Certainly no one would look to anything else. **SOCRATES:** For the others in the city, being either cowardly or brave, do not have the authority to make it cowardly or brave. **GLAUCON:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** A city, then, will be brave because of a certain part of itself, because it possesses in that part a certain power which preserves a constant opinion about all things: namely, that those things are to be feared—and are of such a kind—which the legislator proclaimed in their education. Do you not call this courage? **GLAUCON:** I did not quite grasp what you said; say it again. **SOCRATES:** I say that courage is a kind of preservation.

<margin>Definition of courage.</margin>
**GLAUCON:** What kind of preservation? **SOCRATES:** Of the opinion, clearly, conceived through education under the law: which judges what things are fearful and of what sort. And I said this preservation exists in all things, that is, so that it is kept constant always and everywhere, whether one is affected by pains, or pleasures, or desires, or fears; and that one is not moved away from it by any of these. I will show you what I think this is like, if you wish. **GLAUCON:** I certainly desire it. **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that dyers, whenever they wish to dye wool a purple color, first choose the white from among all colors, then prepare it with no small effort so that it may best receive the "bloom" <note>The "bloom" or *flos* refers to the most vibrant intensity of the dye.</note>; and only then do they steep it in the purple dye? Whatever is dyed in this way remains indelible: the color cannot be washed out by water alone, nor even by adding those cleansers used for scouring. But those not prepared this way—you know how they turn out, whether one dyes them with other colors or these, when they have been less refined beforehand? **GLAUCON:** Certainly they are ugly, and their colors are easily washed away. **SOCRATES:** Think of us as having studied to do something similar to the best of our ability when we were choosing the soldiers themselves and educating them in music and gymnastics: and believe that we devised nothing else than that they should, being best persuaded, soak up the laws like a kind of dye; so that their opinion about fearful things and all other things remains immovable, because they were born with the best nature and nourished with a fitting education. Nor can those cleansers, however powerful for washing away, delete their "coloration": namely Pleasure, sharper than any stinging soap, alum, or lime for scouring; likewise Pain, fear, and desire, more powerful than any other cleanser for wiping away. This power, which everywhere preserves the right and lawful opinion concerning fearful things and their opposites, I call and assert to be courage, unless you perhaps say otherwise. **GLAUCON:** But I say nothing else. For you seem to think that the same opinion about these things, if conceived without discipline—namely a wild and slavish one—is not lawful at all, but something other than courage. **SOCRATES:** You speak most truly. **GLAUCON:** I admit, then, that this is courage. **SOCRATES:** Understand it further to be "civic" courage, and you will accept it correctly. Later, if you wish, we will treat this more diligently. For the present, however, we were seeking not this, but justice. For the investigation of that, enough has been said of this, I think. **GLAUCON:** You speak excellently. **SOCRATES:**

<margin>See how everything here is done to track down justice.</margin>
Two things remain to be considered in the city: namely temperance <note>Also translated as self-control or moderation.</note>, and that for the sake of which we investigate everything: justice. **GLAUCON:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** Is there any way we can find justice now, so that we do not linger again in investigating temperance? **GLAUCON:** I do not see how that could be done; nor would I want justice to become known to us before we have considered temperance. Therefore, if you wish to gratify me, investigate the latter before the former. **SOCRATES:** I certainly wish to, unless it would be a wrong to you. **GLAUCON:** Proceed then. **SOCRATES:** Behold, I search: and as it may be seen from here, it is more like a consonance and harmony than the previous virtues. **GLAUCON:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Temperance is a certain order; and, as they say, an abstinence from certain pleasures and desires. Indeed, they say a temperate man is "master of himself" and a "victor over himself" in some way; and they mark other similar things as traces of temperance. Do they not? **GLAUCON:** Most of all. **SOCRATES:** Does not the term "master of himself" appear somewhat ridiculous? For whoever is master of himself will also be weaker than himself; and again, he who is weaker will be the master. For the same person is referred to in all these things. **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** Yet this speech seems to me to mean that in a man's soul there are two parts. One is better, the other worse. And when that which is better by nature rules the worse, then someone is said to be "master of himself"; and he is praised by this speech. But whenever, because of bad upbringing or some habit, that which is better—being the smaller part—is overcome by the multitude of the worse, this is called "weaker than himself" as a reproach: and he who is so affected is called intemperate. **GLAUCON:** So it appears. **SOCRATES:** Contemplate this city recently founded by us; you will find one of these two present in it. Master...

# DIALOGUE IIII. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO 235.
## D iii
<meta>Catchword: tent</meta>

Indeed, you will admit that the city rightly calls itself "master of itself." For if the better part in it rules over the inferior part, it must be called temperate and better than itself. GLAUCON: I am considering it; and you speak the truth. SOCRATES: Furthermore, one will be able to find many and various desires, pleasures, and pains in people, especially in women and servants; and among those who are said to be free, they are found in the common and lowly people. GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: But simple and moderate desires, which are led by the mind and right opinion through actual reasoning, you will find in only a few: namely those born with the best nature and the best education. GLAUCON: These things are true. SOCRATES: Do you not see these things existing in this city: that here the desires of the crowd and of base persons are overcome by the desires and the temperance of the few and modest men? GLAUCON: I certainly perceive it. SOCRATES: If, therefore, any city is to be called "more powerful than its own desires and pleasures" and thus "master of itself," this one especially must be so named. GLAUCON: Absolutely. SOCRATES: And so, are not all these things just and temperate? GLAUCON: Most especially. SOCRATES: And if in any city the same opinion exists in both the subjects and the rulers as to who should govern the state, must it not be in this one? Or do you not think so? GLAUCON: Very much so. SOCRATES: In which citizens, then, will you say temperance resides when they are so disposed: in the leaders or in the subjects? GLAUCON: In both, in a certain way. SOCRATES: Do you see how aptly we prophesied a little while ago that temperance is similar to a certain harmony? <margin>What temperance is.</margin> GLAUCON: Why so? SOCRATES: Because it does not act like wisdom and courage, which, residing in certain parts, make the city wise or brave; it does not act that way. Instead, like the harmony called the *diapason* <note>original: "diapason" — the musical interval of an octave, representing perfect consonance</note>, it is diffused through the whole city, making the weaker, the stronger, and those in the middle all sing in the same accord, whether in prudence, power, numbers, wealth, or any other such thing. Therefore, we can most rightly call this temperance "concord," namely the agreement of the naturally inferior and superior parts as to which should rule in the city or in each individual. GLAUCON: I certainly agree. SOCRATES: Since this is so, three virtues have now been found in our city, as appears from these things. But what is the remaining species, on account of which the city would further excel in virtue? It is established that this is justice. <margin>The investigation of justice.</margin> GLAUCON: It is clearly established. SOCRATES: Is it not now necessary, O Glaucon, like hunters, for us to surround this thicket, looking about lest justice escape in some direction and, vanishing from our eyes, hide itself? For it is clear that it is here. Fix your gaze everywhere, then, and strive if in any way you can see it before me and show it to me. GLAUCON: I wish I could. But use me rather as a follower who can perceive what is pointed out. SOCRATES: Follow then, having first prayed to God with me. GLAUCON: I will do as you advise. Only lead on. SOCRATES: This place seems inaccessible and shadowy; it is certainly a hidden and inscrutable lair. Nevertheless, we must proceed. GLAUCON: We must clearly proceed. SOCRATES: Ho, ho, Glaucon! We seem to have found certain tracks of what we seek; it appears it will not escape us for long. GLAUCON: Truly joyful news. SOCRATES: O, how soft and dull we have been, O Glaucon! GLAUCON: Why is that? SOCRATES: For a long time now, from the very beginning, O blessed man, what we seek has been rolling at our feet, yet we did not look at it. Instead, we were as ridiculous as those who often search for what they have in their hands. We too were looking far off at what was near us; or perhaps it was hidden from us. GLAUCON: How do you mean? SOCRATES: In this way: we seem to have been speaking and hearing this for a long time without realizing that we were saying it in some way. GLAUCON: A long prologue indeed for one desiring to hear the point. SOCRATES: Attend to what I say. That which we established from the beginning as necessary to do when we founded the city is, I think, either justice itself or some species of it. <margin>Justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in others' affairs.</margin> For we said many times, if you remember, that each person ought to practice one thing of those which contribute to the city, for which his own nature is best suited. GLAUCON: We said that without a doubt. SOCRATES: Indeed, that justice is "doing one's own business and not meddling curiously in the affairs of others" is something we have heard from many others and have often said ourselves. GLAUCON: We clearly said it. SOCRATES: This, then, my friend, seems to be justice in a certain way: doing one's own work. Do you know from where I infer this? GLAUCON: Not at all, but tell me. SOCRATES: It seems to me that what remains for us in the city, besides those things we have considered—temperance, courage, and prudence—is this very thing which provided the power for all of them to be born and, once born, to be preserved as long as it is present. And yet we said justice would be what remained if the other three were found. <margin>Which of the four things mentioned most makes a city good.</margin> GLAUCON: That is necessary. SOCRATES: Nevertheless, if one had to judge which of these, when present, most makes the city good, it would be ambiguous: whether it is the agreement of the rulers and the subjects, or the preservation of lawful opinion among the soldiers (judging according to the law what things are to be feared and what are not), or the prudence and guardianship in the leaders themselves. Or rather, does this make the city good above all else: when it is present in children, women, servants, free men, craftsmen, magistrates, and private citizens—namely, that each one does his own single task and does not wander into the business of others? GLAUCON: It is certainly ambiguous. Why not! SOCRATES: Therefore, the very power by which each person does his own work in the city competes equally for the virtue of the city with its wisdom, its temperance, and its courage. GLAUCON: Very much so. SOCRATES: Will you not, therefore, define justice as that which competes equally with those others for the virtue of the city? GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Consider it further by this reasoning, to see if it seems so to you. Will you mandate that the leaders in the city deliver judgments justly? GLAUCON: Why not? SOCRATES: And will they judge with any other aim than this: that individuals neither usurp what belongs to others nor be deprived of their own? GLAUCON: Certainly for no other aim than that. SOCRATES: As if that were just? GLAUCON: Exactly. SOCRATES: And by this reasoning also, it is asserted that the possession and the practice of what is one's own and proper to oneself is justice. GLAUCON: It is so. SOCRATES: See if the same thing seems to you as to me. If a carpenter should attempt the work of a cobbler, or a cobbler the work of a carpenter, or if they should exchange tools or rewards, or if the same man should strive to practice both, and all such things were exchanged in turn, would such an exchange...

...do you think this change causes a great loss to the city? GLAUCON: Not much, certainly. SOCRATES: Whenever a craftsman or someone else who is by nature a <term>money-maker</term><note>Latin: quaestuarius; referring to the third class of the state focused on commerce</note>, puffed up by wealth, or by a great following and abundance, or by strength, or some other such thing, attempts to pass into the rank of the military; or when a soldier, though unworthy, strives to ascend to the dignity of the <term>counselor</term><note>Latin: consularis; the ruling or guardian class</note> and guardian, and they exchange their tools and rewards with one another; or when one person attempts to do all these things at once: then I think you would see such confusion and wandering as the destruction of the entire city. GLAUCON: Most certainly. SOCRATES: Since there are three classes in the city, the mutual exchange and wandering between them across these extremes is the city's calamity and greatest corruption. GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And would you not say that the corruption of your city is injustice? GLAUCON: Why not? SOCRATES: This, then, is injustice. Or let us say it again this way: the proper action of the money-making, the <term>auxiliary</term><note>Latin: auxiliarii; the military/warrior class</note>, and the counselor classes, with each performing its own work in the city—contrary to that confusion mentioned above—will be justice, and will make the city just. GLAUCON: It seems to be no other way than this. SOCRATES: We ought not yet to assert this absolutely. But if, when we consider it, these same forms are affirmed to be justice in the soul of each individual man, then at last we shall agree. For what else could I say? Otherwise, we will think of something else. But now let us bring this discussion to an end: following what we thought, if we first contemplated justice in something larger that possesses it, we might then easily inspect what it is like in a single man. And it seemed to us that the city was the larger thing; and so we founded it as best we could, knowing that justice exists in a good republic. Therefore, let us refer what appeared to us there to the individual: and if the same holds true there, we shall be satisfied. But if something else appears in the individual, we shall return again to the city and examine these things; and perhaps by comparing them and rubbing them together like fire-sticks, we will strike out the spark of justice from them; and once it shines clearly, we will establish it firmly within ourselves. GLAUCON: You speak wisely; and so it must be done. SOCRATES: Is that which we call by the same name, whether larger or smaller, dissimilar in so far as it is the same, or is it similar? GLAUCON: Similar, certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, a just man will not differ at all from a just city in regard to the form of justice, but will be similar. GLAUCON: Similar. SOCRATES: And the city seemed to be just when the three classes of men within it were established according to the nature of each, so that each performed its own work; and it was again temperate and brave and wise because of certain other dispositions and habits of these same classes. GLAUCON: These things are true. SOCRATES: And so, my friend, we shall judge that the individual who has these same forms in his soul, because of the same dispositions, deserves to receive the same names as the city. GLAUCON: It is entirely necessary. SOCRATES: Have we fallen again, my friend, into a slight thought about the soul—whether it has these three forms in itself or not? GLAUCON: It does not seem to me that we have fallen into a slight discussion. For perhaps what is said is true, O Socrates: that "beautiful things are difficult." SOCRATES:

A proverb:

SOCRATES: It will be quite sufficient for me as well. GLAUCON: Then do not grow weary, but consider it. The question of the soul: whether it has three forms or is one.

to know. GLAUCON: Certainly not difficult. SOCRATES: But this is difficult: whether we do each of these things with one and the same part of ourselves, or rather have three parts in us, by each of which we perform individual tasks: learning with one, being angry with another, and with a third desiring those pleasures pertaining to nutrition and generation and such things; or whether we perform each with the whole soul when we set about a task. These things are not easy to distinguish according to the dignity of the matter. GLAUCON: It seems the same to me. SOCRATES: Let us attempt to distinguish them in this way: whether they are the same as one another or different. GLAUCON: In what way? SOCRATES: It is clearly established that the same thing cannot do or suffer opposites according to the same part and in relation to the same thing at the same time. Therefore, if we ever find these things happening in them, we will know they are not one and the same, but many. GLAUCON: So be it. SOCRATES: Pay attention to what I say. GLAUCON: Speak. SOCRATES: Can the same thing stand still and move at the same time according to the same part? GLAUCON: In no way. SOCRATES: Furthermore, let us confirm this more diligently, lest an ambiguity arise as we proceed. For if someone says that a man who is standing still, but moving his hands and head, is the same man standing and moving at the same time, we should not think it ought to be said that way, but rather that one part of him remains still and another part moves. Is it not so? GLAUCON: Exactly so. SOCRATES: And if a disputant should play a more clever and sharp trick, asserting that a spinning top moves and stands still as a whole when it revolves with its center and point fixed in the same spot—or anything else saying the same thing, that it moves in a circle while fixed to a hinge—we shall by no means agree; because it is not according to the same parts of itself that it then moves and remains still. We should say that such things have in them a straight line and a circumference: and according to the straight line they stand still, since they do not lean in any direction; but according to the circumference, they move in a circle. But whenever, while revolving, it also moves in a straight line, either to the right or the left, forward or backward, then it in no way remains still. GLAUCON: Quite right. SOCRATES: Therefore, none of these objections will disturb us or persuade us that the same thing at any time, simultaneously, according to the same part and in relation to the same thing, becomes or acts in opposite ways.

<margin>
He explains the circumstances which are placed in the definition of opposites.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates and Glaucon discuss how justice in the state (the harmony of three classes) mirrors justice in the individual soul. They begin to analyze whether the soul has three distinct parts by applying the principle of non-contradiction regarding motion and rest.</summary>

# DIALOGUE IV. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

## D iiii

or suffer. GLAUCON. Those things will certainly not move me. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, lest we be forced to dwell too long on explaining and refuting these little objections as if they were false, let us proceed further, assuming for now that this is so, having mutually agreed that if these things should ever appear otherwise than they do now, all the conclusions drawn from them will be dissolved. GLAUCON. That is certainly fitting. SOCRATES. Are not nodding "yes" and nodding "no," <note>original: "annuere & renuere"</note> striving after and turning away, accepting and rejecting—would you not place these as opposites to one another, whether they are actions or passions? It makes no difference. GLAUCON. They are opposites. SOCRATES. What then of these: hungering, thirsting, and generally desiring, willing, choosing—would you not refer them to the same categories we just mentioned? For instance, would you not say that the soul of one who desires is either striving after that which it appetites, or you would say it accepts that which it chooses to have present? Or insofar as it wants something to be offered to it, it nods "yes" and draws it to itself, like a lover seeking the fulfillment of his desire? GLAUCON. Indeed. SOCRATES. But what of not willing, spurning, neglecting, and not desiring—shall we not refer these to the category of rejecting and repelling, and to all things contrary to the former? GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. Since these things are so, shall we say there is a certain category of desires, and that the most manifest of all other desires are thirst and hunger? GLAUCON. We shall say so of both. SOCRATES. And this one indeed is for drink, and that one for food? GLAUCON. It is so. SOCRATES. Now, insofar as it is thirst, is it a desire for anything more than that which we say it is: namely, drink and thirst? GLAUCON. Only for this thirst. SOCRATES. Is it for a hot drink, or a cold one, or much, or little? Or even, in a small way, for a certain kind of cup? Or rather, if heat is present in the thirsting, does it induce a longing for the cold; but if cold, for the hot? And if because of the presence of a great amount, the thirst becomes great, does it bring a greed for much; but if little, for little? But thirsting itself is never a longing for anything else than that which is its own nature—namely, drink itself; and likewise hungering, for eating? GLAUCON. Certainly, each desire itself is only for that thing which is its own nature. But it is called "such or such" a kind because of certain additions. SOCRATES. We must be careful lest, being improvident, we are disturbed by someone suggesting that no one desires drink, but *good* drink; or food, but *good* food. For surely everyone seeks good things. Therefore, if thirst is a longing, it is for the good, whether it be for drink or any other greed. And similarly for the rest. GLAUCON. Perhaps one who says such things might seem to achieve something. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, however many things are of such a kind as to belong to something, they are "such a kind" of "such a thing," as I think. But the things themselves are only of the thing itself. GLAUCON. I do not quite understand. SOCRATES. Do you not understand that the "greater" itself is of such a kind that it always exists as greater than something? GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. Is it not greater than the lesser? GLAUCON. The lesser. SOCRATES. And the much greater than the much lesser, is it not? GLAUCON. It is so. SOCRATES. And the once greater than the once lesser, and the future greater than the future lesser? GLAUCON. Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES. And also the more to the fewer, the double to the half, and all such things; likewise the heavier to the lighter, and the faster to the slower; and the hot likewise to the cold, and all things similar to these—are they not referred to one another in the same way? GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. And is not the same reasoning true of those things which pertain to the sciences? <note>The Latin "scientia" here refers to "knowledge" or "disciplines of study."</note> Science itself is the science of the thing itself which is known, or of whatever else it must be called the science. But a certain science, and a science of such a thing, is said to be of a certain kind and of such a thing. I mean something like this: after the science of building houses arose, it was distinguished from other sciences, so that it was called "architecture." GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. Was it not because it became such a kind as no other science is? GLAUCON. Surely. SOCRATES. Therefore, because it was of a certain kind of thing, it was made into a certain kind of science. And in the same way, all other arts and sciences. GLAUCON. It is so. SOCRATES. Say then that I wanted to infer this—if you have now understood—that whatever things are of such a kind as to belong to something, they themselves are only of those things themselves; but "certain kinds" of things are of "certain kinds." I do not say that they are of the same quality as the things they are of; for example, that the science of the sick and the healthy itself becomes healthy or sick; or that of good and evil, it becomes good and evil; but because it did not turn out to be a science only of that thing of which it is absolutely a science, but rather of a certain kind—namely, the healthy and the unhealthy—it was itself made into a certain kind. From which it happened that it is no longer called "science" simply, but with a certain quality added, "medical science." GLAUCON. I grasp it now, and it seems to me to be so. SOCRATES. And will you not number thirst among those things which are what they are in relation to something? For thirst is— GLAUCON. I do number it, and I say thirst is for drink. SOCRATES. And is not a certain kind of thirst for a certain kind of drink? And therefore thirst itself is neither for much, nor for little, nor for good, nor for bad, nor—to embrace it in one word—for any "certain kind," but the nature of thirst itself is for drink alone? GLAUCON. It is entirely so. SOCRATES. Therefore, the soul of the thirsty person, insofar as it thirsts, desires nothing else than to drink; and it longs for this, and is carried toward it. GLAUCON. It is agreed. SOCRATES. If, therefore, something sometimes pulls back the thirsty soul, it will be something else in it, different from that part which thirsts and drives it like a beast to drink. For we say it is not possible for the same thing to act in contrary ways with the same part of itself toward the same thing at the same time. GLAUCON. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Just as it is absurd to say that the same hand of an archer at the same time pushes the bow away and pulls it back. Rather, it must be said that there is one hand that pushes and another that pulls. GLAUCON. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Do we admit that there are some who, though they thirst, are sometimes unwilling to drink? GLAUCON. Many, and often. SOCRATES. What shall one say of these: is there not something in their soul that allures them to drink, and something else that restrains them, which is different and dominates the part that allures? GLAUCON. So it seems to me. SOCRATES. Is it not, therefore, that which prohibits these things arises from reason, whenever it operates? But those things which incite and draw them arise from affections and disturbances? GLAUCON. It appears so. SOCRATES. We shall rightly, therefore, deem these two to be different from each other. And that part by which the soul reasons, we shall name the **rational** part of it. But that by which it loves, hungers, thirsts, and falls more prone to other lusts, we shall call the **irrational** and the greedy for fulfillments.

<margin>
That in the soul there are two contrary species: the rational and the irrational.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates argues that the soul contains distinct parts—the rational and the irrational—by demonstrating that a person can simultaneously desire something (like drink) and restrain themselves from it. He uses the analogy of an archer's hands to show that contrary impulses must come from different parts of the same entity.</summary>

But what of that which pertains to the <term>irascible</term><note>The "spirited" or "angry" part of the soul (thymos), distinct from reason and desire.</note> part, by which we feel anger? Is it a third thing? Or is it related to one of the others? GLAUCON: Perhaps it is related to that which desires pleasures. SOCRATES: Yet I believe this instead, based on what I once heard: namely, that when Leontius, son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus under the North Wall toward the city, he perceived dead bodies lying near the shore. At once he desired to look, yet he was also horrified and turned away, covering his face while struggling with himself. Finally, overcome by desire, he ran toward the corpses with eyes wide open, saying: "Look now, you wretches, satiate yourselves with this beautiful sight!" GLAUCON: I have heard this myself. SOCRATES: Thus the story testifies that anger often fights against concupiscence <note>Physical desire or appetite.</note>, as if these are different things from one another. GLAUCON: It certainly signifies that. SOCRATES: And do we not frequently notice elsewhere, when desires pull someone contrary to reason, that he reproaches himself and is indignant against that part of himself which is being pulled? And as if two were in disagreement, anger runs to the aid of reason? But I do not think you have ever sensed—either in yourself or another—that anger joins with the desires to oppose reason when reason commands it must not be contradicted. GLAUCON: Never, by Jove! SOCRATES: What further? When someone thinks he is committing an injustice, is it not true that the more noble he is, the less he is able to feel anger even while he hungers or freezes or suffers any such thing from the one he deems to be acting justly? And as I said, his anger is not provoked against that person? GLAUCON: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: But what when a man thinks he is suffering an injustice? Does he not then boil and chafe, and offer aid to what seems just, enduring hunger, cold, and other such things? And he strives for victory, nor does he cease from his noble work until he has either succeeded or died, or—like a dog by a shepherd—is finally called back by the reason within him and becomes mild? GLAUCON: This power is entirely similar to the one you compare it to. For in our city we placed the <term>auxiliaries</term><note>The warrior or guardian class.</note> like dogs, obedient to the princes as if to the shepherds of the city. SOCRATES: You have understood perfectly what I wished to say. But do you also notice this besides? GLAUCON: What is that? SOCRATES: That our present judgment of anger is the opposite of what it was above. Then, we were referring the power of anger to the nature of desire. But now we say there is a great difference, and we assert much more that anger takes up arms for the sake of reason when the parts of the soul are at odds. GLAUCON: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Is the power of anger then different from reason, or is it a species of reason, so that there are not three <margin>Three classes in the city: the money-makers, the auxiliaries, the consulship <note>The ruling class.</note>.</margin> but only two species in the soul: the rational and the desiring? Or rather, just as three classes appeared in the city which contain it—the money-makers, the auxiliaries, and the consulship—is there also a third power in the soul, anger, which by its nature protects the parts of reason, unless it has been corrupted by bad education? GLAUCON: It must be a third. SOCRATES: Certainly, if it appears to be something other than reason, just as it was seen above to differ from desire. GLAUCON: But that can easily be shown. For anyone may see it in small children, who are full of anger as soon as they are born. Yet some seem to me never to become partakers of reason, and many only late in life. SOCRATES: By Jove, you speak excellently! Furthermore, one may find it to be so in beasts, as you say. And that line of Homer which we introduced above also testifies to this: *Striking his breast, he rebuked his heart with bitter words: "Endure, O heart, for you have borne far worse than this."* <note>original: "Pectora castigans monitis affatur acerbis. Perpetere o cor: nã tu lõge alias grauiora tulisti." A quote from the Odyssey.</note> In these lines, Homer makes one part reproach the other as if they were different: namely, reason itself, consulting about better and worse, restraining the irrational impulse of anger. GLAUCON: You speak very rightly. SOCRATES: In these things, then, we have finally agreed; and it is sufficiently established between us that the same classes exist in the city and in the soul of each person, and they are equal in number. GLAUCON: Certainly so. SOCRATES: And is this not also necessary: that in the same way and by the same means that a city was wise, so too is the private individual wise? GLAUCON: Clearly. SOCRATES: Likewise, in the way and manner a private individual is brave, in that same way the city is brave; and in all other things pertaining to virtue, both stand similarly. GLAUCON: It is necessary. SOCRATES: And so, O Glaucon, we shall call a man just by the same rule by which we call a city just. GLAUCON: That is altogether necessary. SOCRATES: But we have not yet forgotten that the city appeared just because each of the three classes of men within it fulfills its own office. GLAUCON: We have certainly not forgotten. SOCRATES: We must remember then, that each of us, in whom the individual parts of the soul do what is their own, will be both just and a performer of his own duties. GLAUCON: We must indeed remember. SOCRATES: Does it not then befit the rational power to command, since it is wise and exercises providence for the whole soul? And for the nature of anger to be obedient to reason and fight for it? GLAUCON: Entirely. SOCRATES: And as we discussed above, does not the mixture and tempering of music and gymnastics produce this concord? Stretching, nourishing, and increasing one of these with noble discourse and disciplines, while relaxing, soothing, and softening the other through harmony and rhythm? GLAUCON: Most certainly. SOCRATES: And when these have been so nourished, and have truly learned their own duties and been best educated, they will preside over the heat of desire—which is the greatest part in every soul and can never be filled by the possession of money. They will take care lest, increased by the satiation of bodily pleasures, it becomes larger and stronger and refuses to perform its own office, but instead strives to subject to itself those things which by nature it ought not to rule, and so overturns the entire life of all. GLAUCON: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Who also...

this soul guards the entire body from external enemies: while the former provides foresight through counsel, the latter fights in its defense; it obeys the prince and carries out through courage what has been decided. GLAUCON. These things are true. SOCRATES. We certainly call a man brave in this respect, because the vigor of his anger <note>original: "iracundiae vigor," referring to the 'spirited' part of the soul (thumos)</note> is so established within him that, in the midst of pleasures and pains, he persists in his opinion, judging what is to be feared and what is not to be feared exactly as reason itself has dictated. GLAUCON. Correct. SOCRATES. And we call him wise by that small part which commanded within him and dictated those things, possessing in itself the knowledge which discerns what is most useful for each individual part as well as for the whole community constituted of these three parts. GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. Again, we call someone temperate because of the friendship and concord of these very parts, when both that which presides and that which is subject agree in the same opinion: namely, that it is fitting for reason to command, and that one must not revolt against it. GLAUCON. Temperance is surely nothing else, both privately and publicly. SOCRATES. Finally, a person will be just because of that and in the same way as we have already said many times and as we have explained. GLAUCON. That is altogether necessary. SOCRATES. What then? Is there anything that so disturbs our opinion as to make justice seem to us to be something other than what it appeared to be in the city? GLAUCON. It does not seem so to me. SOCRATES. On the contrary, if anything still remains in controversy between us, we will thoroughly confirm the previous points again by applying absurd cases to this definition. GLAUCON. Of what kind? SOCRATES. For instance, if we had to deliberate concerning that city, and similarly concerning a man born and nurtured like it: whether such a man, when he has received a deposit of gold or silver, would ever be seen devising a fraud. Do you think anyone would judge such a man more likely to commit a fraud than men differently disposed? GLAUCON. No one at all. SOCRATES. And will he not be innocent of sacrileges, thefts, and betrayals, both privately against his companions and publicly against the republic? GLAUCON. Innocent. SOCRATES. Moreover, he will not be unfaithful in oaths or in any kind of dealings. GLAUCON. By no means. SOCRATES. Adultery, contempt for parents, and impiety toward the gods fit anyone else rather than him. GLAUCON. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Is not the cause of all these things this: because whatever is within him performs its own work, both in commanding and in obeying? GLAUCON. Certainly no other. SOCRATES. What? Do you seek justice to be anything other than this very power which makes such men and such cities? GLAUCON. I certainly do not. SOCRATES. At last, that dream which we said we suspected has been fulfilled for us: that soon after beginning to found the city, by some divine favor, we seem to have stumbled upon a certain principle and image of justice. GLAUCON. Entirely so. SOCRATES. This, O Glaucon, was why a certain likeness of justice was useful. Namely, that he who is a shoemaker by nature ought to practice this art and attempt nothing else; and he who is a smith should do smithing. And similarly in other matters. GLAUCON. It is apparent. SOCRATES. In truth, justice is such a thing, but not concerning outward action, rather concerning the inward action of its parts truly toward the soul itself and its own affairs: while it permits nothing of its own to attempt what belongs to another; nor does it allow the types of the soul, by confusing their works, to wander through many things; but in truth it rightly arranges its own affairs; it is master of itself, it adorns itself, having become a friend to itself, tempering those three parts within itself just like the three terms of a harmony—the high, the low, and the middle <note>original: "neates, hypates, & mediae," referring to the strings of a lyre</note>, that is, the octave, the bass, and the fifth—or whatever other middle there may be. And so, binding all these together, and having become one from many, tempered and harmonious, he only then acts if he does anything, whether concerning the acquisition of money, or the care of the body, or even concerning civil or private dealings: in all these things considering that action to be just and noble which achieves and preserves this habit; and calling the Wisdom presiding over this operation "knowledge"; but an unjust operation which dissolves this, "ignorance"; and finally, the leader of this operation, "opinion." GLAUCON. You speak the absolute truth, O Socrates. SOCRATES. If, therefore, we should say we have found the just man and the just city, and what justice is in both: I think we shall not be seen to be lying much. GLAUCON. Not by Jove! SOCRATES. It must be asserted then. GLAUCON. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. So be it. Indeed, it seems we must next consider injustice. GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. When is it proper to call the injustice of these three a "sedition"? A meddlesome and varied usurpation of another's work, and an insolent transgression of a certain part rebelling against the whole soul, and rising <margin>On injustice.</margin> up to command the royal kind of the soul, which nature commands it to serve. Such things, I think, and the disturbance and error of these, we shall call injustice, and intemperance, cowardice, ignorance, and finally, universal depravity. GLAUCON. These things are exactly so. SOCRATES. Is it not now clear enough what it is to do unjust things and to commit injury, and again what it is to do just things, since justice and injustice are evident? GLAUCON. In what way? SOCRATES. Because they differ in no way from healthy and unhealthy things. For as these are to the body, so are those to the soul. GLAUCON. By what reason? SOCRATES. Healthy things induce health; unhealthy things induce disease. GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. Similarly, doing just things begets justice in the soul; doing unjust things begets injustice. GLAUCON. It is necessary. SOCRATES. But to bring health is to arrange the things in the body so that they dominate and are dominated by one another according to the order of nature itself. To induce disease, however, is to affect the parts of the body to such an extent that they dominate and are subjected to one another contrary to the law of nature. GLAUCON. It is so. SOCRATES. By the same reasoning, to provide justice to anyone is nothing else than to arrange the parts of the soul in their own order, so that they obey and command according to the norm of nature. Injustice, however, is that they should exceed and succumb to one another contrary to nature. GLAUCON. Exactly. SOCRATES. Virtue, therefore, as it appears, is a certain health, and beauty, and robust vigor of the soul. Depravity, <margin>Virtue is health. Depravity is disease.</margin> on the contrary, is disease, ugliness, and weakness. GLAUCON. It is as you say. SOCRATES. Do not honorable exercises, therefore, lead to the acquisition of virtue, while shameful ones lead to depravity? GLAUCON. It is necessary. SOCRATES. It remains, as it seems, to be discussed: whether it is better to do just things, to cultivate honorable things, and to be just, whether this be hidden from anyone or not; or to do injury...

<summary>Socrates and Glaucon define justice as the internal harmony of the soul's three parts (reason, spirit, and appetite) and injustice as a "sedition" or rebellion of these parts against their natural order. They conclude that virtue is the health of the soul, while vice is its disease.</summary>

and that it is unjust, provided he is not punished and does not become better through that punishment. GLAUCON: To me indeed, O Socrates, that discussion seems ridiculous. For if the nature of the body is corrupted, it seems that life is not worth living, even amidst the greatest abundance of all feasts and drinks, all riches, and the empire of the whole world. But if the nature of that by which we live <note>The soul</note> is polluted and corrupted, will life be worth living if someone does whatever he pleases, doing anything other than this one thing: by which he may be freed from wickedness and iniquity, and may attain justice and probity—especially after both these things have appeared to be such as we have described? SOCRATES: Truly, as many modes of things as there are, having their own forms, just as many appear to be of the soul itself. GLAUCON: How many? SOCRATES: Five of commonwealths; and again, five of the soul. GLAUCON: Tell me what kind. SOCRATES: I assert that one mode of the republic is this one which we have set forth. It can, however, be declared by two names. For if among the leaders of the city one should be the most outstanding of all, it will be called a Kingdom. But if more than one, it will be called the government of the Best <note>Aristocracy</note>. GLAUCON: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: I say this is one form for this reason: because whether many govern or one, no one who has been educated and instructed in the way we have said will change anything worthy of esteem in the laws of the republic. GLAUCON: For that would not be reasonable.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for the Fifth Dialogue
### Concerning Justice.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a classical figure or deity amidst foliage.</image-desc> I am not unaware that there will be some who expect an Apology <note>A formal defense</note> from us, by which we might defend this fifth dialogue—which proposes the community of all things in the city—against the slanders of both the malicious and the ignorant. But let them read Plato himself, I pray, let them read diligently, and let them judge without envy; they will (I know what I am saying) desire no apology. Plato, therefore, the Phoebian <note>Apollo-like</note> physician of the human race, when he noticed that both individual men and families and cities were always and everywhere gravely ill—and that they were not freed from the disease by any medicines of the civil physicians who had been treating them in vain for so many centuries, nor even relieved a little or recovered in the slightest—he turned himself as prudently as he did piously to that principal law among physicians which the authors of medicine sanction: if anyone does not recover at all with such medicines (say, cold ones) applied for a long time, one must finally duly cross over to hot ones. Knowing, therefore, that the human race achieved nothing through laws distributing private property for so many centuries, but rather slipped daily into worse conditions, he not unjustly transferred himself to the laws of friendship, which command that "all things shall be common among friends": so that, the cause of division and misery being removed, we might attain concord, union, and happiness. But let us begin again in another way. Socrates, at the beginning of the fourth book, placing the discipline of educating youth above all laws, touched upon it hastily, saying it seemed the best discipline would be if a community of wives, children, and things were established. But because the matter is both new to very many and unheard of by most, he is called back to it immediately at the beginning of the fifth to declare it more openly and confirm it more firmly. Now, even if you have learned from Critias and Timaeus that a similar discipline once existed in the Greek and Egyptian Athens, you will neither wonder at it too much as something new, nor listen with distrust as if it were utterly difficult, nor admit it unwillingly as if it were not good. I pass over what many report, that in Bohemia the city of Prague was once governed similarly. Moreover, Diodorus describes an island in the southern ocean in which, besides other things, wives are also common, and the men are very studious of philosophy and astrology. Pomponius Mela is also a witness that the Garamantes in the furthest parts of Africa have all things in common in their republic. Furthermore, we have found that there was a similar communion of goods among the Brahman philosophers, the Gymnosophists, the Essenes, the Pythagoreans, and finally among the holy founders of the Christian republic. We also see in our own times that only those religious orders approach virtue and happiness among whom nothing is private property. But if the community of wives disturbs you, first consider that in Plato this is done duly according to law, whereas among adulterous priests it is done in common through sacrilege. Then, hear Plato himself before you judge, declaiming more deeply in his own cause. In what follows, note first indeed the Socratic providence, which deems it a greater error to err in establishing laws than to kill a man. For an error of that kind kills many souls and bodies at once through many centuries. Then, note his modesty in approaching difficult things with distrust, and as if unwilling and compelled. Third, his piety in invoking divine aid, according to his custom, in grave matters. And lest he err in founding laws, he seeks help from the goddess Adrastia, whom he also mentioned in the *Phaedrus*. This Adrastia, among the ancient theologians, is the most powerful queen of inevitable laws: laws, I say, both Saturnian, pertaining to minds, and Jovian, pertaining to natures. I call Adrastia divine providence, insofar as nothing can either escape her eyes or flee her hands. Nor is it without reason that he wishes firmly—

# ARGUMENT OF THE FIFTH DIALOGUE. PAGE 238.

...to establish the most excellent laws: which neither oblivion may erase, nor craftiness defraud, nor violence break, and which absolutely no one may avoid, since **Adrastia** <note>original: "Adrastia"; a Greek name for Nemesis or Fate, representing inescapable destiny</note> prays for the sanctioning of the inevitable, which no one can escape. Next, he proceeds gradually to a common discipline: namely, from the instruction of men to a similar instruction of women, mandating that all private and public pursuits, both of peace and of war, be made common to women along with men. This is so that the human race is not "maimed" <note>i.e., rendered incomplete or lopsided by only utilizing half the population</note>; yet it is done on the condition that in individual tasks, the heavier burdens attend the men and the lighter ones the women. Similarly, he teaches elsewhere that the arms must be so trained that individuals are right-handed on both sides—those whom he calls **Amphidexterous** <note>original: "Amphidexteros"; ambidextrous</note>. He shows that this will be useful and possible, and in what manner it ought to be done.

Then he introduces another community: namely, that of wives and children. And here, observe with what great prudence of order he establishes the magistrates: the overseers of marriages, the sacred rites, the times, and the ages, taking care lest anything be done intemperately or uselessly for the city. And after the generation, how diligently he thinks about the nursing of those born: yet in such a way that neither man nor woman recognizes their own child, nor the child their own parents, nor some recognize others. Instead, the elders are compelled to believe that almost all the younger ones are their children or grandchildren; the younger ones, in turn, suspect all the elders to be their progenitors, and those of equal age to be their brothers and sisters.

Among these things, where he disregards the nursing of one who is born either against the law, or from useless stock, or is himself useless, understand that he is not to be destroyed: but is to be nursed in a more hidden place or in the suburbs more cheaply, outside that most exact rule by which those are nursed who are judged fit to be taken into the guardianship. But that one is to be raised by an inferior rule and transmitted in his own time to the smaller services of the city or field; or perhaps transferred to other cities immediately upon birth.

Soon, recognize the invention of "common charity": where he so disposes individual things that individuals judge the same things—whether a thing or a person shown to their eyes—equally, and say, "this is mine." Since his own things are most dear to each person, individuals will care for the whole; especially when they are led to such care by the laws and the magistrates. Hence, he will remove our carelessness and negligence, which exists in all of us regarding many things as if they were alien to us. He will also remove the daily fallacy by which our judgment is foolishly deceived in cherishing that which we perceive to be our own. Finally, he will remove the extreme perturbation, anxiety, and misery which torments us out of an insane love for our own things. I pass over the fact that, with the cause of discord removed, charity will be both common and whole.

Furthermore, attend to how diligent, how just, and how mild he makes the laws of war: what rewards await the victors—namely, a certain divinity. For he says these are transferred into the "blessed demons" <note>original: "beatos demones"; in the Platonic sense, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not evil entities</note>, the caretakers of men, to be rightly worshipped as dear gods. As for what he says about the eyes of children <note>referring to taking children to watch battles from a distance</note>, it is a certain jest of Glaucon's, spoken for the sake of relieving boredom. Add also something triumphant and festive.

It remained to be proven that this community could be realized, after it had been affirmed that it would be the best. First, therefore, even if it cannot be done, he shows that he has not brought this into the midst in vain: namely, as a model to be imitated according to one's strength in forming cities. Then he demonstrates that it can finally be done when **philosophers govern**, and that there will be no rest from evils before then. For which reason, he opportunely descends to the forming of philosophers as future governors of the city: teaching what the nature of a civil philosopher is, and what their affection and discipline are.

In the beginning, just as the common people are greedy and curious regarding the perception of these lower sensible things, so the philosophical nature is greedy and prone to finding the **Ideal** <note>original: "ideales"; relating to Plato's Theory of Forms</note> reasons of all these things, and is a sagacious hunter of the truth itself. Since those things which are perceived are either natural forms or images of the Ideas, he says not without reason that people "dream," thinking that the things which are images are true things. But the philosophers alone among others are "awake."

And since he places a middle ground between **being** and **non-being**, remember that all things are thought of in five grades:
1. **Pure non-being** is said to be whatever is imagined below matter.
2. **Pure being** exists in the pure mind and the Idea.
3. The **Soul** and the **Heaven** are called being and non-being simultaneously, namely on account of motion: yet they are more "being" than "non-being."
4. **Matter**, on the contrary, is in a certain way more "non-being" than "being."
5. But those things which are composed by nature under the moon are equally being and non-being.

Knowledge itself is concerned with those things which truly *are*. Ignorance is concerned with those things which truly *are not*. Opinion revolves around those things which equally *are* and *are not*. He attributes ignorance and opinion both to the common people and to the sophists. But knowledge—that is, science—he attributes only to philosophers. When he calls science and opinion a certain "power," understand it not as an unformed power, but one endowed partly by natural form and partly by habit.

Furthermore, where he treats the Ideas, to which the science of philosophers is referred, he says in his usual manner: **the Good, the Beautiful, the Just**. This triad is explained in three ways:
* **First:** The Good becomes God; the Beautiful, the multiform angelic mind; the Just, the celestial mundane soul distributing justly.
* **Second:** The Good is the form and act of the divine nature; the Beautiful is its intelligence; the Just is its will.
* **Third:** Among the Ideas, the Good is the model of the form and act of every nature; the Beautiful is the model of the order which results from any form within itself; the Just is the model of the order which is referred from any form to others.

When, however, he subjects the Evil to the Good, the Ugly to the Beautiful, and the Unjust to the Just, beware of placing these three opposites among the Ideas. Rather, place these both in the informity and deformity of matter (which in the book *On Science* he calls a model devoid of divinity) and in the "place of dissimilarity" <note>a reference to the *Statesman* (Politicus)</note>, and also in the soul already depraved and turned entirely toward matter.

Finally, as for the "childish riddle of the eunuch" he touches upon, it is of this sort: *A man and not a man, seeing and not seeing, struck and did not strike, with a stone and not a stone, a bird and not a bird, upon a tree and not a tree.* That is: a one-eyed eunuch struck the wing of a bat with a pumice stone upon an elder tree. But you will laugh at this, I know. It was added for the sake of the ridiculous.

<margin>The riddle of the man and not a man.</margin>

# BOOK V.

### FIFTH DIALOGUE CONCERNING THE JUST.

**SOCRATES.** Indeed, I call a city of this kind good and a Republic right; and I say such a man is good. And if this republic is right, I call the others depraved, insofar as they wander astray regarding the government of the city itself and the discipline of private individuals; these are indeed found in four species of depravity. **GLAUCON.** Which are those? Then I was proceeding to narrate in what manner each seemed to me to depend on the other in turn. But Polemarchus, who was a little further away from me than Adimantus, sitting behind Adimantus’s back, extended his hand; and catching Adimantus’s cloak from above around the shoulders, he drew him a little toward himself, and moved his mouth to his ear, whispering in a low voice. Of the things he said, we perceived nothing except this one thing: he said, "Shall we let it pass? Or what shall we do?" To which Adimantus, responding more loudly, said, "Not at all." At this I said, "What is it that you do not wish to let pass?" **ADIMANTUS.** You. **SOCRATES.** Why me especially? **ADIMANTUS.** Because you seem to us to be turning aside, and to be withdrawing and stealing away a whole section of this discussion—and no small one at that—so that you do not have to explain it to us. Thinking you could remain hidden from us, you said quite carelessly that regarding wives and children, it will be clear to everyone that all things ought to be common among friends. <note>original: "omnia sicut inter amicos communia esse debere." This refers to the famous Platonic idea of communal property and family.</note> **SOCRATES.** Was I not right to say so, Adimantus? **ADIMANTUS.** Right, certainly; but just as in other matters, so in this it is necessary to explain by what reason it is right, and what the manner of this community is. For there can be many ways. Therefore, do not omit it, lest you fail to reveal to us which way you specifically mean. Indeed, we have been waiting for a long time now, hoping that you would explain both the condition of generation regarding the procreation of children, and what the method of their nutrition and education will be: and what this whole community of women and children you speak of ought to be. For we consider this to be of great importance—indeed, everything—to the republic, whether it acts rightly or not. But now, since you are moving on to another form of republic before you have sufficiently treated these matters, it seemed best to us (as you yourself heard) not to permit you to move on to anything else until you have explained all these things just as you did the others. **GLAUCON.** Consider me to be of the same mind as them. **THRASYMACHUS.** You may assume, Socrates, that we all agree on this without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** What are you doing, I pray, by calling me back in this way? What a heavy discussion you are stirring up again, as if from the beginning, concerning the Republic! Indeed, I was already congratulating myself as if I had finished it, thinking it was enough for me if someone let these things go now, having accepted them as I said above. By demanding these things now, you do not know what a swarm of disputes you are inciting. Foreseeing this then, I gladly yielded and passed over it, lest it disturb us with frequent tumult. **THRASYMACHUS.** Do you think these men have come here, Socrates, to smelt gold, rather than to listen to discourses? <note>A Greek proverb meaning "to waste time on a fruitless search for wealth" instead of seeking wisdom.</note> **SOCRATES.** To listen to discourses, certainly, but moderate ones. **GLAUCON.** Surely the measure and limit of hearing such discourses, Socrates, is the whole of life for men of mind. But never mind us. Do not be burdened if it seems right to you to declare what we seek: what the community of women and children will be for our guardians; and what method of nourishing children should be applied in that very time which falls between birth and education, which certainly seems most laborious. Try, we beg you, to open these things to us. **SOCRATES.** It is not easy, O blessed man, to explain these things. For there are more ambiguities in these than in the previous matters. First, one might doubt whether these things are possible. Furthermore, even if they are possible, one will doubt whether they are the best, and how. Therefore, this difficulty discourages me, fearing, O sweet friend, lest this speech of mine should seem like a mere wish or a fiction. **GLAUCON.** Do not be reluctant, I pray. For you do not have ungrateful, or incredulous, or malevolent listeners. **SOCRATES.** O best of men, do you bring this to encourage me? **GLAUCON.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** You do quite the opposite. For if I were confident in myself regarding the things I say I know, this consolation would be right. Indeed, it is safe and bold to announce the truths one knows about the greatest and most precious things among friends and prudent men. But to speak with distrust and ambiguity as I am doing is fearful and deceptive. I do not mean I fear moving the listeners to laughter—for that would be childish—but rather lest, wandering far from the truth, I myself succumb to falsehood and drag my friends down into ruin with me, and we be deceived together in those things where it is least fitting of all to err. Therefore, I humbly adore Adrastia <note>Adrastia was a goddess of divine retribution, often identified with Nemesis; Socrates invokes her to avoid the "hubris" of speaking falsely on sacred matters.</note> regarding the things I am about to say, Glaucon. For I believe it is a lesser offense to kill someone unintentionally than to deceive someone regarding the institutions of honest, good, and just things. It is better to undergo this risk among enemies than among friends. Therefore, you console me better, O Glaucon. **GLAUCON.** But Socrates, if by some chance we happen to err because of this discussion, we will absolve you as if from a homicide, and pronounce you innocent in this deception. Therefore, enter the discussion boldly. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, he who is absolved there is innocent, as the laws teach. Therefore, he who is absolved here is also innocent. **GLAUCON.** Speak, then, for this reason. **SOCRATES.** Now I must speak again of things that perhaps ought to have been said in sequence. But perhaps it is worthwhile: after we have expressed the complete work of the men, to report next what pertains to the women, especially since you yourself exhort me to this. For men born and educated as we have narrated above, in my opinion, there is no other right acquisition and use of children and women than by walking that path which we entered from the beginning. For we have tried, as guardians of a flock, to set the men over the women. **GLAUCON.** Indeed. **SOCRATES.** Let us follow the generation, then, applying a very similar nutrition: and let us consider whether in this way...
