# DIALOGUE V. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO CCXXXIX.

<note>This is a Latin translation of Plato’s *Republic*, Book V. The speakers are Socrates (SO.) and Glauco (GLAV.).</note>

whether it is fitting or not. GLAUCO: In what way? SOCRATES: In this way: regarding the dogs that guard the flock, do we think that the females themselves ought to perform the same guarding duties as the males? And should they hunt together and do all other things in common? Or should the females be kept inside as if for domestic service—as if they were incapable of outdoor work because of the birth and nursing of puppies—while the males undergo the labors and take all care of the herd? GLAUCO: We assign all these things to them in common; except that we use the females as the weaker and the males as the stronger. SOCRATES: Is it possible to use any animal for the same tasks unless you have nourished and educated it in the same manner? GLAUCO: In no way. SOCRATES: If, therefore, we are to use the women for the same tasks as the men, it is fitting to educate them in the same things. GLAUCO: Certainly. SOCRATES: Now, we educated the men in the previous sections in music <note>In the classical sense, "music" included poetry, literature, and the arts of the Muses.</note> and gymnastics. GLAUCO: Indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, these arts and the matters of war must be assigned to the women similarly; and it is fitting to use them for these same things. GLAUCO: That follows logically from what you say. SOCRATES: Perhaps many of the things now introduced will seem ridiculous and contrary to custom if they are done or spoken of. GLAUCO: Very much so. SOCRATES: What do you see as most ridiculous in these things? Is it because you would see naked women in the wrestling schools contending with men—not only the young, but even the old women, just as old men are seen in the gymnasiums when they exercise together, even though they are already wrinkled and withered? GLAUCO: Yes, by Jove! For that would indeed seem laughable as things now stand. SOCRATES: Therefore, since we have begun to speak, we must by no means fear the wit of clever men, however many and of whatever kind they may be, directed against such a change which we are introducing regarding music and gymnastics—and no less regarding armor and the skill of horsemanship. GLAUCO: You speak rightly. SOCRATES: Therefore, since we have begun to speak, let us proceed to the severity of the law, asking those men not to jest in their usual way, but to think seriously, and reminding them that not much time has passed since it seemed shameful and ridiculous to the Greeks—as it still seems today to many of the Barbarians—to see naked men. And when they first attempted exercises of this kind, first the Cretans and then also the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, it was certainly permitted for the witty men of that time to mock all these things. Do you not think so? GLAUCO: I do. SOCRATES: But after, as I believe, it appeared more advantageous to those practicing to exercise with the body naked rather than covered, it happened that because it had been judged best by reason, it ceased to look ridiculous to the eyes. From this it is clear that he is a vain man who considers anything laughable except what is evil; and who attempts to mock things themselves, proposing some other cause for derision than that which is foolish and evil, or who values anything as honorable and worthy of study by looking to any standard other than the Good. GLAUCO: That is absolutely so. SOCRATES: Must we not first agree on this: whether these things are possible or not? And should we not grant to anyone to doubt these things according to their judgment, whether they wish to doubt in jest or in earnest: whether in human nature the female is able to share with the male in all works, or in none, or whether she is capable in some but by no means in others; and in which of these categories does military service fall? Will not whoever begins correctly in this way, as is fitting, also finish correctly? GLAUCO: Most certainly. SOCRATES: Do you wish, then, that for the sake of others, we oppose ourselves with these doubts, so that the arguments of the other side are not attacked without a defense? GLAUCO: Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES: I shall speak, therefore, in their persona in this manner: "There is no need, O Socrates and Glauco, for others to fight you. For among yourselves, from the very beginning of founding the city, it was agreed that it is necessary for each one to perform the one thing that is his own according to nature." SOCRATES: It was agreed. Why not! OPPONENT <insert>ADVER.</insert>: "Do you doubt, then, that the woman differs greatly in her very nature from the man?" SOCRATES: Why would she not differ? OPPONENT: "Therefore, must not a different work be assigned to each according to the nature of each?" SOCRATES: Without a doubt. OPPONENT: "What remains then, but that you are now in error and contradict yourselves! Since you assert that men and women ought to perform the same works, even though they differ greatly in nature." SOCRATES: Will you have anything, O wonderful man, to answer to these things for our defense? GLAUCO: At the present moment, it is not easy enough; but I beg you and pray: that you explain what can best be brought forward in defense of our discourse. SOCRATES: These things, O Glauco, and many others of the same kind, I foresaw long ago, and I was fearful and unwilling to descend to this law concerning the possession and nourishment of women and children. GLAUCO: Indeed, that does not appear to be a light matter. SOCRATES: Certainly not, but this is how it is: whether someone has fallen into a small pond or into the deep sea, he must nonetheless swim in the middle of the water. GLAUCO: Entirely so. SOCRATES: And must we not also swim and try to escape safely from the waves of this dispute, hoping that either some dolphin will pick us up and lift us, or that there will be some other hidden cause of safety for us? GLAUCO: So it seems. SOCRATES: Look around, I pray, if we may find an exit. Pay attention, then. We agreed indeed that a different nature ought to handle a different work; but that the nature of a woman and a man is different. Now we are commanding different natures to pursue the same studies. In this, they accuse us. GLAUCO: Greatly. SOCRATES: How noble, O Glauco, is the power of the art of contradiction! GLAUCO: Why? SOCRATES: Because many seem to me to fall into it even unwillingly; and they think they are not quarreling, but debating, because they are unable to contemplate what is proposed to them by dividing it according to its species; rather, they pursue the contradiction of the proposal according to the name itself: contending with one another rather than disputing. GLAUCO: This does indeed happen to many. But does the same thing now happen to us? SOCRATES: Very much so. We seem indeed to touch upon contradiction unwillingly. GLAUCO: In what way? SOCRATES: That the same nature should not handle the same works, bravely...

# BOOK

...at length and contentiously, we have begun to pursue the matter according to the name. We have considered, however, in no way what the species of the "other" and the "same" nature is, and toward what we were looking when we then defined them, when we attributed different pursuits to a different nature, but the same pursuits to the same nature. GLAUCON. Certainly we did not think that through. SOCRATES. But it is permitted to us, as it seems, to ask of ourselves: whether the nature of bald men and hairy men is the same, or rather the opposite? And after we have conceded that it is opposite, if bald men should cut leather and make shoes, we should by no means allow hairy men to do the same; but if the hairy do so, we should by no means permit the bald. GLAUCON. But that would be worthy of laughter. SOCRATES. And is it laughable for any other reason than that we did not then establish "same" and "different" nature in an absolute sense, but only observed that species of similarity and dissimilarity which pertained to those very pursuits? Just as we said a physician and a man having a mind suited to the study of medicine have the same nature; or do you not think so? GLAUCON. Indeed I do. SOCRATES. But one suited to medicine has one nature, and a man ready for carpentry has another. GLAUCON. Entirely. SOCRATES. Therefore, if the race of men and the race of women differ between themselves in respect to some art or other pursuit, shall we not say this must be assigned to each? But if they seem to differ in this alone—that the female conceives and the male begets—we shall not admit any more that it has been shown that a woman differs from a man in respect to that of which we are now speaking; but we shall still judge that both our guardians and their wives ought to engage in the same exercises. GLAUCON. Rightly, indeed. SOCRATES. Shall we not next bid him who says the opposite to show us this very thing: for which art or which duty among those which contribute to the instruction of the city is the nature of a man and a woman not the same, but different? GLAUCON. That is certainly fitting. SOCRATES. Perhaps what you were saying a little while ago, another might also say: that it is not easy to speak sufficiently on the spot, but if it be considered, it is not very difficult. GLAUCON. He would say so. SOCRATES. Do you wish, then, that we pray him who opposes these things to us to lend us his ears and attend, if by any means we can show him that there is no pursuit in the administration of the city's affairs that is proper to a woman? GLAUCON. Entirely. SOCRATES. Come then, we shall say to him, answer: did you not say that one person was endowed by nature with a good disposition for some work, and another the opposite, because the former perceives anything easily, the latter with difficulty? And the former, if he learns something brief from anyone, discovers much more from it himself; but the latter, though he has learned and meditated on many things, forgets them a little later? And for the former, the members of the body sufficiently serve the mind, but for the latter they are resistant? Are there any other things besides these by which you distinguish a man well-disposed by nature for something from one who is affected to the contrary? GLAUCON. No one will say anything else. SOCRATES. Do you know of anything practiced by humans in which the race of men does not have all the same things and more excellently than the race of women? Or shall we wander far in words, mentioning the craft of weaving, and the preparation of cakes and side-dishes? In which things something seems to belong to women—where it appears truly ridiculous when they are beaten? GLAUCON. You speak the truth, because in all things, so to speak, one race is far surpassed by the other. Yet many women are superior to many men in many things. But the whole matter is as you say. SOCRATES. There is, therefore, no duty among those who govern the city that is proper to a woman insofar as she is a woman, or proper to a man insofar as he is a

<margin>
Woman and man are capable of all things, but the woman is weaker.
</margin>

man; but the natures are equally dispersed in the living beings of both kinds: and the woman is capable of all works by nature, and the man is capable of all. But in all things, the woman is weaker. GLAUCON. It is exactly so. SOCRATES. Shall we then assign everything to men and nothing to a woman? GLAUCON. But how? SOCRATES. It is certainly as we assert: among women also, one is fit for medicine, another not; one is musical, another by nature a stranger to music. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. And one indeed is ready for gymnastic exercises and military matters, but another is unfit for these. GLAUCON. So I think. SOCRATES. And is not one a lover of wisdom <note>original: "sapientiae studiosa" (philosopher)</note>, while another despises wisdom? And one is high-spirited, another low-spirited? GLAUCON. This also I assert. SOCRATES. There is, therefore, among women one suitable for guarding, and another not. Did we not choose a certain nature of this kind for the men who guard the city? GLAUCON. Certainly of that kind. SOCRATES. Therefore, the nature of the woman and the man is the same for guarding the city, except that women are to be treated as the weaker and men as the stronger. GLAUCON. It appears so. SOCRATES. Such women, therefore, are to be chosen to dwell with and guard the city together with the men, since they are fit and their natures are akin to them. GLAUCON. Entirely. SOCRATES. And must not the same pursuits be attributed to the same natures? GLAUCON. The same. SOCRATES. At last, by a long circuit, we have returned to those prior things; and we have conceded that it is not against nature for the wives of the guardians to be exercised in music and gymnastics. GLAUCON. Most certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, we have not established by law things that are impossible or merely wishful thinking, since we have brought forth the law according to nature. Rather, the things done in these times against these principles are much more "contrary to nature," as it seems. GLAUCON. It seems so. SOCRATES. Were we not to discuss whether we were saying things possible and best, or not? GLAUCON. We were. SOCRATES. That they are possible is established. GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. That they are best must be asserted after this. GLAUCON. It is evident. SOCRATES. To this end, that women may turn out sufficient for guarding, there is no need for any other discipline than that by which we instruct men for the same, especially since the same nature is found in both. GLAUCON. No other. SOCRATES. Furthermore, what do you think of this? GLAUCON. What do you ask? SOCRATES. I ask whether you think some men are better and others worse, or are all similar? GLAUCON. By no means similar. SOCRATES. In the city which we have founded, do you think the men are made better guardians by having obtained the discipline we gave them, or are the cobblers better by being imbued with the skill of leather-working? GLAUCON.

<summary>Socrates argues that men and women possess the same fundamental natures and capacities, concluding that women should be educated in music and gymnastics to serve as guardians of the state alongside men.</summary>

# DIALOGUE V: ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE

What you ask is ridiculous. **SOCRATES:** I understand indeed. But what of this: are these not the best among the rest of their kind? **GLAUCON:** They are. **SOCRATES:** And will such women not also be the best of women? **GLAUCON:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Is there anything better for a city than to produce the best possible men and the best possible women? **GLAUCON:** There is not. **SOCRATES:** And this, as we discussed above, can be achieved through music and gymnastics <note>The traditional Greek curriculum of arts/intellect and physical training</note>. **GLAUCON:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, we have established by law something that is not only possible but also the best thing for the city. **GLAUCON:** That is so. **SOCRATES:** The bodies of the female guardians must therefore be stripped, since they will clothe themselves in virtue instead of garments. They must share in war and all other guardianship and protection of the city; they shall do nothing else. However, the lighter of these duties are to be assigned to the women because of the weakness of their sex.

<margin>That women must be stripped.</margin>

But the man who laughs at naked women, who are stripped for the sake of what is best, plucks the fruit of wisdom in the form of empty and ridiculous trifles; he understands neither what he laughs at nor what he does. For this saying is and remains well-stated: that what is useful is honorable, but what is harmful is shameful. **GLAUCON:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Let us say then that we have escaped this one wave, as it were, by swimming through the discussion of the law concerning women, so that we were not entirely submerged while asserting that our guardians, both men and women, ought to perform all exercises in common. Indeed, our argument was consistent with itself, showing that these things were both possible and useful. **GLAUCON:** You have certainly escaped a deep sea. **SOCRATES:** You will not say it was so great a wave when you see what follows next. **GLAUCON:** Speak now, so that I may see. **SOCRATES:** This law follows the previous ones, as I think, and all those before it. **GLAUCON:** Which one? **SOCRATES:** That these women shall all be common to all these men; that no woman shall live privately with any man, and furthermore, that the children shall be common; so that no father shall know his own son, nor any son recognize his father. **GLAUCON:** This will certainly be much harder to believe, whether it is possible or even useful. **SOCRATES:** I do not think anyone would doubt that it would be useful and the greatest good for women and children to be held in common, if only it were possible. But I think the greatest controversy will surround whether it can be done or not. **GLAUCON:** Both points will certainly be disputed. **SOCRATES:** You speak of a conspiracy of arguments. I thought I would be freed from one of them if you agreed it was useful. Then it would only remain for me to investigate whether it is possible or not. **GLAUCON:** But you could not remain hidden while you fled. Give an account of both. **SOCRATES:** I must certainly endure the penalty; but indulge me in this. Let me feast my mind for a little while at my own whim, just as those who are lazy in mind are accustomed to feast themselves whenever they walk alone. For such men, before they have discovered how what they desire might happen, set aside that concern so they are not burdened by too much labor while deliberating on the possible and impossible; they assume that what they desire already exists, and then they arrange the rest. They delight themselves by imagining what they will do when that thing is present, and thus they make a sluggish mind even more faint. I myself am becoming lazy in the same way, and I wish to defer that debate—whether these things are possible or not—to another time. For the present, assuming they are possible, I will investigate, if you permit, how the rulers themselves will arrange these matters, and how they will be the most useful of all things if they happen, both for the guardians and the city. I will try to consider these things with you first, and the others later, if you allow it. **GLAUCON:** I do allow it; consider it now. **SOCRATES:** I think, then, if the rulers are worthy of the name, and likewise their assistants, that the latter will be willing to carry out what is commanded, and the former will give the orders: partly obeying the laws themselves, and partly imitating them in those matters we have entrusted to them. **GLAUCON:** That is probable. **SOCRATES:** You, therefore, as the lawgiver, just as you chose the men, so also by choosing the women, you will provide those who are as similar in nature as possible. And these people, since they have common dwellings and common meals, and possess nothing of the sort privately, will live together. And by associating with one another in the gymnasiums and in the rest of their daily life, they will be drawn to mutual union by an innate necessity, I believe. Does it not seem to you that I speak of a necessity? **GLAUCON:** Not a geometric necessity, but an amorous one, which is much sharper than the other for persuading and drawing the common people. **SOCRATES:** Very much so. But after this, O Glaucon, to be stripped among one another without order, or to do anything else of that kind, is neither holy in a city of blessed men, nor will the overseers permit it. **GLAUCON:** For it would not be right. **SOCRATES:** It is certain, then, that we shall next establish marriages as sacred as possible. And those that are most useful would be sacred. **GLAUCON:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** In what way will they be most useful? Tell me this, O Glaucon. I see in your house many hunting dogs and noble birds. Have you ever applied your mind to their mating and breeding? **GLAUCON:** To what end? **SOCRATES:** Among these themselves, even though they are noble, are there not some who are the best? **GLAUCON:** There are. **SOCRATES:** Do you permit breeding from any of them indifferently? Or do you take care that it is from the best? **GLAUCON:** From the best. **SOCRATES:** And from the youngest? Or those worn out by age? Or rather those in the flower of their youth? **GLAUCON:** From those in their prime. **SOCRATES:** And unless the breeding is conducted in this way, do you think the breed of dogs and birds would become much worse? **GLAUCON:** I do. **SOCRATES:** Do you think it happens differently with horses and other animals? **GLAUCON:** That would be absurd. **SOCRATES:** Good heavens, my dear friend, what remarkably keen and excellent rulers we need, if the same holds true for the human race! **GLAUCON:** It certainly does; what then? **SOCRATES:** Because it is necessary for them to use many medicines. For when bodies do not need medicines but only require a regulated diet, we think a weaker doctor suffices. But when medicines must be used, we know a stronger doctor is needed. **GLAUCON:** You speak the truth. But to what end is this? **SOCRATES:** It seems it will be necessary for the rulers to use frequent lies and deception for the benefit of their subjects. We said above that all such things are like drugs <note>original: "pharmaci" - referring to the 'Noble Lie' or medicinal deception used by the state</note>.

<margin>That women and children are to be held in common.</margin>

# BOOK V.

...and that it is necessary in the place of medicine. <note>original: "medicínęq; loco neceſſaria eſſe." Socrates is arguing that "noble lies" or deceptions are sometimes necessary tools for rulers, like medicine.</note> GLAUCON. And rightly so. SOCRATES. It seems, then, that this must be done in no small measure regarding marriages and the procreation of children. GLAUCON. In what way? SOCRATES. It is certainly necessary, according to what we granted above, that the best men should have intercourse with the best women as often as possible; and the worst, on the contrary, with the worst. And the offspring of the former should be reared, but those of the latter not at all, if the flock is to be of the highest excellence. And all these things should be done in such a way that they remain unknown to everyone except the rulers, if the flock of guardians is to remain free from internal strife. GLAUCON.

<margin>Concerning weddings and marriages.</margin>
Quite right. SOCRATES. Therefore, certain festivals will be designated by law, in which we will bring together the brides and bridegrooms; there shall be sacrifices, and hymns composed by our poets, suitable for the marriages being celebrated. But the number of marriages we shall leave to the discretion of the rulers, so that, looking toward diseases and other such factors, they may maintain the same maximum number of citizens; so that, as far as possible, the city does not become too populous nor too empty. GLAUCON. You speak rightly. SOCRATES. Therefore, certain lots must be instituted with such craftiness that the inferior man, in any coupling, blames his fortune and not the rulers. GLAUCON. Most certainly. SOCRATES. Indeed, to those who are more outstanding among the youths, whether in military matters or in other things, rewards and prizes must be given, and among many other things, a more frequent license to sleep with women; so that by this occasion, more children may be fathered by them than by others. GLAUCON. Excellent. SOCRATES. Thus, the children who are born from these will be taken up by those magistrates appointed for such duties, whether men or women, or both; for the magistracies are common to both men and women. GLAUCON. It is so. SOCRATES. Taking the offspring of the excellent men, they will carry them to the fold <note>original: "ouile" - a metaphor for a nursery or rearing center.</note>, to certain nurses dwelling apart in some part of the city. But those born of the inferior parents, or even any others who are born with some defect of limb, they will hide in secret and obscure places, as is fitting; for the race of guardians must remain pure. Furthermore, these nurses will take care of the nursing. The mothers will be brought to the fold when their breasts are full of milk, taking care that none can recognize her own child. And if the mothers' milk is insufficient, they will bring in other women who are full of milk. They will also provide that a moderate time be observed for suckling. Likewise, they will impose the night-watches and other labors upon the nurses. GLAUCON. You grant much ease to the women of the guardians for the procreation of children. SOCRATES. So it is fitting. But come, let us proceed with what we especially intended. We said clearly that children ought to be procreated from the most robust parents. GLAUCON. We said so. SOCRATES. Does it not also seem to you that the moderate time of adult strength

<margin>At what age women are fit for generating offspring.</margin>
is twenty years for a woman, and thirty for a man? GLAUCON. What is the measure of these? SOCRATES. Namely, that a woman, beginning from her twentieth year of age, should bear children until her fortieth; but a man, after he has passed the sharpest vigor of his course—that is, thirty years—should procreate from then until his fifty-fifth year. GLAUCON. Truly, in these ages the vigor of mind and body consists. SOCRATES. If, therefore, anyone older or younger than these touches upon procreation for the community, we shall deem this a profane and unjust crime; as if a child is being brought into the city who, if it remains hidden, will be born not under sacrifices and prayers—which all the priests, both men and women, and the whole city will perform at each wedding, praying that from the good, better children may be born, and from the useful, more useful ones—but rather, born in darkness out of a certain sharp incontinence. GLAUCON. You speak rightly. SOCRATES. The same reasoning must also be held concerning that man who, while still in the age for generating, touches a woman of adult age when the ruler has not joined them. For we shall assert that he generates a child who is a bastard, incestuous, and profane. GLAUCON. Very 

<margin>What kinship is to be observed of the man toward women and the woman toward men.</margin>
skillfully put. SOCRATES. When, therefore, the women and men have passed the age fit for generation, we shall say it is permitted for the men to associate with whomever they wish, except for a daughter or mother, or the children of daughters, or the ancestors of a mother; and it is permitted for women to be joined to anyone, except for a son or father, and their superiors and inferiors. But when we have commanded all these things, we shall forbid such an offspring, if it should happen, to be brought into the light. If anything should force it, we will command that it be placed in such a way as if there were no nourishment for it. <note>A reference to the practice of exposure or infanticide for unauthorized births.</note> GLAUCON. These things also are rightly said. But the fathers and mothers and the other kinsmen you mentioned, how will they be distinguished from one another? SOCRATES. In no way; but all those born in the tenth month, or the seventh, from the day on which someone devoted himself to procreation, the males shall be called sons and the females daughters. And those born shall call him father; likewise, he will call that generation sons and grandsons; and these in turn will name the superiors grandfathers and grandmothers. But those who were born at the time when their fathers and mothers were generating with one another, they shall call brothers and sisters. And thus, as I was just saying, they should in no way touch one another. But the law will permit cohabitation to brothers and sisters if chance grants it, and if the Pythia <note>The priestess of the Oracle at Delphi.</note> confirms it through her responses. GLAUCON. Quite right. SOCRATES. Such, then, O Glaucon, will be the community of women and children among the guardians of the city. That this is consistent with the rest of the city's order, and is by far the best, must next be asserted by reason. Or what shall we do? GLAUCON. This, by all means. SOCRATES. Is not the beginning of this agreement to ask ourselves what we find to be the greatest good in the constitution of a city—toward which the legislator ought to look when making laws—and what is the greatest evil? Let us then consider whether those things we just described

<margin>Nothing is more ruinous to a city than division: as nothing is better than union.</margin>
agree with the footprint of that good, or differ from the footprint of evil. GLAUCON. Most of all. SOCRATES. Do we have any evil more ruinous to a city than that which divides it and makes many out of one? Or anything better than that which binds it together and makes it one? GLAUCON. We do not. SOCRATES. Does not the community of pleasure and pain unite them, when all citizens rejoice and grieve equally at the gain or loss of the same things? GLAUCON. Most certainly. SOCRATES. But the diversity of these things dissolves it, when some grieve vehemently and others exult over the same events of the city and those who are in it. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. From this, then, such a thing happens, when they do not...

# DIALOGUE V. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE.

...at the same time in the city these words are spread: "Mine," and "not mine"; and in the same way regarding what belongs to another. GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES.
<margin>What power these words, "mine" and "not mine," have in the city.</margin>
In whichever city, therefore, the greatest number of people say this same thing about the same thing—"Mine" and "not mine"—that city is best governed. GLAUCON. Entirely. SOCRATES. And whichever is affected most nearly like a single human being. Furthermore, whenever the finger of one of us is struck, the entire communion of the body, reaching to the soul and into a single coordination of that which rules in the soul itself, feels it immediately, and the whole suffers together with the afflicted part. And for that reason, we say the *man* has a hurting finger. The same logic applies to any other part or passion of a man: namely, concerning pain, when some part hurts; and concerning pleasure, when some part of himself is refreshed. GLAUCON. The logic is certainly the same: and as you ask, the city which is best governed comes closest to this. SOCRATES. Whenever, I believe, any good or evil happens to any of the citizens, such a city will surely cry out that the one so affected is its own, and therefore the whole will either rejoice together or grieve together. GLAUCON. It must necessarily happen so in a city governed by the best laws. SOCRATES. But it is now time for us to return to our city: and let us examine those things which have now been agreed upon between us, whether they suit this city best, or rather another. GLAUCON. By all means. SOCRATES. Are there not both rulers and the people in other cities, and similarly in this one? GLAUCON. There are. SOCRATES. And yet will all these citizens call one another by the same name? GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. But besides the name of "citizen," what does the people call the rulers in other cities? GLAUCON. In most, indeed, "masters"; but in a popular government <note>original: "populari gubernatione," referring to a democracy</note>, "rulers." SOCRATES. But the people of our city, what will they name the rulers beyond the name of "citizen"? GLAUCON. "Saviors" and "helpers." SOCRATES. And in what way will these [rulers] call the people? GLAUCON. "Payers of wages" and "providers of nourishment." SOCRATES. But those who are in charge in other places, what do they call the people? GLAUCON. "Slaves." SOCRATES. And the rulers themselves, what do they call each other? GLAUCON. "Co-rulers." SOCRATES. And ours? GLAUCON. "Co-guardians." SOCRATES. Do you think there is anyone among the rulers of other cities who calls one of his colleagues a "relative" and another a "stranger"? GLAUCON. Indeed, many. SOCRATES. He therefore thinks of and speaks of the relative as "his own," but the stranger as "not his own." GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. But among our guardians, is there any who would consider or call any of his colleagues a "stranger"? GLAUCON. None. For whomever he meets, he will think he meets either a brother, or a sister, or a father, or a mother, or a son, or a daughter, or the children or ancestors of these. SOCRATES. You speak excellently. But answer this as well. Will you establish by law only these names of kinship and family among your citizens? Or also the duties of kinship: namely, that they behave as the dignity of the name itself demands; and that they observe toward parents whatever the law commands to be shown to them—reverence, care, and obedience? Otherwise, they may have both gods and men against them, as people who act neither holily nor justly if they do the opposite. Will any other words than these, from all the citizens, ring in the ears of children from the start—both toward parents, whomever anyone points out to them, and toward others close in kin? GLAUCON. These very ones. For it would be absurd if they only uttered domestic names with the mouth without the duty. SOCRATES. In this city, therefore, most of all, when one person is affected well or ill, all will cry out with one voice: "My own is doing well," or "My own is doing poorly." GLAUCON. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. We said that with this opinion and such words, it follows that both pleasures and pains are held in common. GLAUCON. And rightly so. SOCRATES. In this, therefore, our citizens will especially communicate with one another, because they will say "mine"; from which communion it follows that they have pleasures and pains in common. GLAUCON. Entirely. SOCRATES. And the single cause of these things, along with the rest of the city's constitution, is the communion itself of the guardians regarding wives and children. GLAUCON. It is altogether so. SOCRATES.
<margin>When the city is in its best state.</margin>
Indeed, we confessed this to be the highest good for the city: when we said that a rightly governed city is like a body, communicating in every way with its individual parts regarding pleasure and pain. GLAUCON. And we rightly conceded it. SOCRATES. Therefore, the cause of the greatest good for the city appeared to us to be this very communion of wives and children among the helpers <note>original: "auxiliarios," the warrior class of the Republic</note>. GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. And yet these things harmonize with what was said before. For we said that they ought to have neither their own houses, nor fields, nor any possession: but should receive nourishment from others as a wage for their guardianship: and all consume it in common, if they are to be true guardians. GLAUCON. Correct. SOCRATES. Do not the things I say—both what was said before and what is now introduced—especially ensure that these become true guardians? So that they do not divide the city by saying "mine" not of the same thing for all, but one thing for some and another for others; and one drags into his own house whatever he can seize for himself apart from the others, and another into his own different house; and because of their own wives and children, different people rejoice and grieve at different things. Rather, from one single opinion of what is "their own," all tending toward the same goal as far as possible, they are affected by similar pleasures and pains in the same circumstances. GLAUCON. Most certainly. SOCRATES. What then? Will not all controversies of judgments and mutual accusations cease, since no one will possess anything of his own except his body, while the rest is common? From which it follows that they will be without sedition, as far as those lawsuits are concerned which usually arise because of money, or children, or relatives. GLAUCON. It is entirely necessary that these be absent. SOCRATES. Furthermore, there will be no contention regarding violence inflicted. For we shall assert that it is honorable and just for equals to help equals, imposing a necessity for protecting their bodies. GLAUCON. Correct. SOCRATES. And this law contains this right: that if anyone is angry with someone, and strives to satisfy his anger, he will be less likely to pass into greater seditions against his elders. GLAUCON. It is exactly so. SOCRATES. For our law has appointed the elder to be in charge of all the younger, and to correct them. GLAUCON. That is clear. SOCRATES.
<margin>Fear and shame are the guardians of the ranks.</margin>
It is established, moreover, that a younger person will never use violence against an elder unless by command of the rulers; nor will he dare to strike him, as is fitting; nor to inflict any ignominy. For fear and shame are guardians sufficient to prohibit these things...

<summary>Socrates explains that the ideal city functions like a single biological body, where the shared use of the terms "mine" and "not mine" creates total social unity. By holding wives, children, and property in common, the guardians avoid the private interests and legal disputes that cause sedition in typical cities.</summary>

# BOOK V.

Shame, indeed, will not allow them to violate those whom they suspect to be their parents. Furthermore, fear will deter each man from causing injury, as he dreads that all the others—some acting as sons, some as brothers, and some as fathers—will rush to the aid of the one suffering. GLAUCON. That is exactly how it would happen. SOCRATES. It is certain, then, that because of these laws, the citizens will live their lives in peace with one another. GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. And since they have no reason to distrust one another, there is no fear that the city will ever be at war against itself, or that they will stir up seditions among themselves. GLAUCON. Certainly not. SOCRATES. I am almost ashamed to mention—as it is somewhat beneath our dignity—all the minor evils from which these free citizens will be liberated. Flattery will surely be absent: the kind that the poor are often forced to use toward the wealthy. Likewise, the anxieties and sorrows of the needy will vanish: those burdens they face in nourishing children and seeking money, being vexed by the necessary support of households and servants; while they also busy themselves with high-interest loans, or deny what they have received, and strive for profit from any source. They also set aside many things with women and servants <note>original: "ministrosque"</note> to store away for a time. Indeed, how many and what kind of things men suffer in these matters, O friend; they are obvious to everyone, and they are both illiberal and unworthy of being told. GLAUCON. They are plain even to a blind man. SOCRATES. Furthermore, they will be free from all these things; and they will lead a happier life than that most blessed life of those who have won at the Olympic games <note>original: "olympia"</note>. GLAUCON. For what reason? SOCRATES. Surely those victors are considered blessed for only a small portion of what these citizens possess. For the victory of our guardians is more noble, and their public maintenance more complete; the victory of these men is the safety of the entire state. Moreover, they and their children receive food and whatever else is necessary for life as a reward, in place of a crown. In addition, they receive honors and prizes from the Republic itself while living; and when they have finished their lives, they receive monuments for their tombs worthy of their virtues. GLAUCON. These things are certainly quite remarkable. SOCRATES. Do you remember that in the earlier part of our discussion, someone's argument <note>A reference to Adeimantus's objection at the start of Book IV</note> objected to us, claiming that we were making the guardians <term>custodes</term> <note>The "Guardians" or "Watchmen" of the ideal city</note> not at all happy, since they would possess nothing, even though it was permitted for them to possess all the goods of the citizens? We responded then that we would consider this later if the occasion arose. For at present, we were making the guardians truly guardians, and seeking to make the city as happy as possible—not looking to any one part, but to the whole happiness. GLAUCON. I remember indeed. SOCRATES. Now, certainly, the life of the auxiliaries <note>The warrior class</note> appears far more noble and better than that of those who win at the Olympics; it does not seem at all similar to the lives of cobblers, or other craftsmen, or farmers. GLAUCON. Certainly not, as I also judge. SOCRATES. Nevertheless, what I said above, it is right that I repeat here: that if the guardian should strive to become happy in such a way that he is no longer a guardian, and if a life so moderate and stable—and as we assert, the best—is not enough for him, but instead an insane and childish opinion of happiness seizes him because of his power <margin>Hesiod said that the half is more than the whole.</margin> to claim for himself everything in the city, he will learn that Hesiod spoke wisely when he said "the half is more than the whole." GLAUCON. If he takes me as his advisor, he will remain in this life. SOCRATES. Do you then approve of the community <term>communionem</term> <note>The sharing of property and family</note> which we assign to women along with men, regarding education, the raising of children, and the guarding of citizens: so that they may govern in peace together with the men, serve in war, and guard and hunt together like dogs; and be participants in all duties in every way as far as possible? And while they do these things, do you concede that they are doing what is best, and nothing contrary to the nature of the female, by which she was designed to share with the male? GLAUCON. I do indeed approve. SOCRATES. Does it not remain, then, for us to declare whether this community can exist among men just as it does among other animals, and in what manner it is possible? GLAUCON. You have anticipated what I was going to ask. SOCRATES. Regarding the matter of war, I think it is clear how they will handle it. GLAUCON. In what way? SOCRATES. They will surely go to war in common, both males and females; and they will take their adult children with them to battle, so that just as the children of other craftsmen, these too may observe the works of their fathers, which they themselves will perform when they reach a mature age; and furthermore, so that they may be a help to their parents, and provide all things that pertain to war, and care for their fathers and mothers. Have you not noticed what happens in the arts? For instance, how for a long time the sons of potters watch their fathers molding, and assist them, before they themselves mold anything? GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. Should those who are guardians not educate their children with even greater care through experience and the inspection of works suitable to each? GLAUCON. That would indeed be ridiculous. SOCRATES. Moreover, every kind of living creature fights more ardently when its offspring are present. GLAUCON. That is so. But there is a very great danger, O Socrates, lest if by chance—as happens in war—an adverse fortune occurs, they might lose their children along with themselves; from which the city, deprived of too many people, might not be able to rise again to its value. SOCRATES. You speak the truth. But do you think the first thing to be provided for is that they never face danger? GLAUCON. By no means. SOCRATES. What then? Must they not come into danger at the time when, if they conduct themselves nobly, they will turn out better? GLAUCON. That is clear. SOCRATES. Do you think it makes little difference—or is not worth the risk—whether the boys who are to be soldiers observe or do not observe the affairs of war? GLAUCON. On the contrary, it matters for the reason you say. SOCRATES. Effort must be made, therefore, so that the boys observe war only, and a way must be devised so that they are safe; and thus it will be done rightly. GLAUCON. Surely. SOCRATES. In the first place, their parents will not be ignorant, but as far as is granted to men, they will be perceptive in discerning which camps have danger in them and which do not. GLAUCON. That is likely. SOCRATES. Therefore, they will lead them to the safer ones, and to the others not at all. GLAUCON. Rightly so. SOCRATES. Then they will appoint leaders over them, not the most cowardly, but men who are suitable by both experience and age to be guides and tutors <term>pædagogos</term>. GLAUCON. So it is fitting. SOCRATES. But we shall say that many things have happened to men contrary to expectation. GLAUCON. And very much so. SOCRATES. For this reason, O friend, right from their tender years, certain wings should be applied to the children, so that if there is ever a need, they may fly away and escape immediately. GLAUCON. How do you mean that? SOCRATES. The boys will become accustomed to riding from their first years; and when they have learned this, [they will go] on horses to the sights... <margin>Women and adult children serve in the military.</margin>

<summary>Socrates discusses the communal life of the guardians, arguing that shared responsibilities and the absence of private property lead to a peaceful, blessed state. He also proposes that children should observe warfare from horseback to learn their future duties safely.</summary>

# DIALOGUE V. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

<margin>Children should be led to watch battles.</margin>
...they will lead them into the outskirts of war: not indeed on fierce or overly warlike horses, but on those that are very swift and easily obedient to the reins. In this way, they will most conveniently observe their own work and escape most safely if any adversity should happen, following the senior leaders. 

**GLAUCON:** You seem to me to speak quite wisely. 

**SOCRATES:** What must be said concerning those things that pertain to war? What rules should be observed by soldiers both toward one another and against enemies? Do I perceive rightly, or not? 

**GLAUCON:** In what way? 

**SOCRATES:** I think that whoever deserts his rank in the battle line, or throws away his weapons, or commits any such act because of cowardice, should be demoted to the rank of craftsmen or farmers. 

**GLAUCON:** That is fitting. 

**SOCRATES:** But he who is captured alive by the enemy should be left to them, even if they wish to return him for free, so that they may use their prey however they please. 

**GLAUCON:** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** But as for the one who excels by behaving remarkably, first indeed during the expedition itself, do you not think he should be crowned individually by each of the youths and boys who serve with him? 

**GLAUCON:** I certainly do. 

**SOCRATES:** What? Should they not also join right hands with him? 

**GLAUCON:** That also. 

**SOCRATES:** But perhaps this further point does not occur to you. 

**GLAUCON:** What is it? 

**SOCRATES:** That he ought to receive and give a kiss to everyone. 

**GLAUCON:** Nay, most of all. And I think this should be added to the law: that as long as he is on that expedition, no one is allowed to refuse him, whomever he desires to kiss; so that if anyone is captured by love for another, whether male or female, he may be sharper in pursuing victory. 

**SOCRATES:** Excellent. For it has already been said that marriages are more easily prepared for strenuous men than for others, and their choices in these matters will be more frequent, so that as many children as possible may be born from them. 

**GLAUCON:** We certainly said that. 

**SOCRATES:** For indeed, according to Homer <note>referring to the Iliad</note>, it is just to honor such youths especially. For he said that Ajax, excelling in war, was honored with "continuous cuts of meat from the chine" <note>original: "continuis ab humeris honoratum"</note>; as if this were a fitting honor for a young and brave man, from which honor both his strength and his status might increase at the same time. 

**GLAUCON:** Quite right. 

**SOCRATES:** In these matters, therefore, we shall obey Homer. For in our sacrifices and other such things, the more good men excel, the more we shall honor them both with hymns and those things we just mentioned: with seats of honor, meats, and full cups; so that we may simultaneously honor and train these outstanding men and women. 

**GLAUCON:** You speak most beautifully. 

**SOCRATES:** But as for him who dies in military service after behaving strenuously, we shall say first that he belongs to the "Golden Race." <note>A reference to Hesiod's ages of man; the Golden Race was the most noble.</note> 

**GLAUCON:** Most of all. 

**SOCRATES:** Then, placing faith in Hesiod, we shall assert that whoever of this race departs from life becomes "holy earthly spirits <note>original: "dæmones"</note>, the best warders-off of evils, and guardians of mortals." 

**GLAUCON:** So indeed we shall believe. 

**SOCRATES:** We shall therefore consult the oracle as to how it is fitting to bury blessed and divine men, and with what special insignia to decorate them; and so we shall bury them as the oracle commands. 

**GLAUCON:** Without a doubt. 

**SOCRATES:** And for the rest of time, we shall tend and adore their sepulchers as those of divine spirits. We shall also observe the same toward those who are judged to have excelled in exceptional integrity during life, whether they ceased from life through old age or in some other way. 

**GLAUCON:** It is surely fitting. 

**SOCRATES:** But how shall our soldiers behave toward enemies? 

**GLAUCON:** In what regard? 

**SOCRATES:** First indeed, I ask about slavery: whether you think it just that Greeks should reduce Greek cities to slavery; or rather, that they should not permit this to be done by others, and should resist with all their might, and accustom themselves to sparing the Greek race, taking care lest they themselves be forced to serve the barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speakers.</note>. 

**GLAUCON:** It is entirely and in all ways important to spare the Greeks. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, our armies ought to make no Greek a slave, but rather advise other Greeks to beware of this themselves? 

**GLAUCON:** Precisely. For thus they will rise up more easily and strongly against the barbarians and abstain from one another. 

**SOCRATES:** What then: is it honorable to despoil the dead of anything besides their weapons after they have conquered, or not? Does this not offer an excuse to cowards not to advance against the enemy, as if they were doing something magnificent while they wallow among corpses? Indeed, many armies have already perished through the greed for plundering. 

**GLAUCON:** Very much so. 

**SOCRATES:** Does it not seem a somewhat illiberal thing, of a greedy, womanish, and vile mind, to despoil a corpse—to think the body of the dead is the enemy when the adversary himself has flown away, leaving behind the instrument with which he fought? Do you think those who do this differ at all from dogs who grow angry at the stones thrown at them, letting go of the one who threw them? 

**GLAUCON:** I think they differ not at all. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, one must abstain from such plunder, for it hinders victory. 

**GLAUCON:** One must abstain entirely. 

**SOCRATES:** Nor shall we carry weapons into the temple to consecrate them to God, especially the weapons of Greeks, if we care at all for goodwill with other Greeks. Rather, we shall greatly fear lest it be an impious crime to bring such things from our own people into sacred places, unless God says otherwise. 

**GLAUCON:** Quite right. 

**SOCRATES:** And will your soldiers depopulate the fields and burn the houses of the Greeks with whom they fight? 

**GLAUCON:** I would gladly hear what you think about this. 

**SOCRATES:** To me, it seems no such thing should be done; only the annual harvest should be taken away. Shall I tell you the reason? 

**GLAUCON:** Please do. 

**SOCRATES:** It seems to me that just as these two names exist, "war" and "sedition" <note>civil strife</note>, so also two distinct things underlie them. I say these two are: one being private and kindred, the other foreign and external. Enmities among kindred they call "sedition"; among foreigners, they call it "war." 

<margin>Greeks are kindred by race, and different from barbarians. What is war. What is sedition.</margin>

**GLAUCON:** What you say is not beside the point. 

**SOCRATES:** Observe whether I also say this to the point. I assert indeed that all Greeks are related and kindred by race, but different and foreign from barbarians. 

**GLAUCON:** You speak excellently. 

**SOCRATES:** Whenever, therefore, Greeks fight against barbarians or barbarians against Greeks, we shall assert they are waging war and are enemies by nature; and we shall call these enmities "war." But when Greeks rise up against Greeks, we shall say they are friends by nature, but that Greece is laboring under a disease; and that this is a sedition, and we shall call these enmities "sedition." 

**GLAUCON:** I certainly agree. 

**SOCRATES:** If in a seditious city the men of both factions were to ravage the fields of their adversaries and set fire to their houses, you see how ruinous that sedition would be, and that neither of them are lovers of their fatherland. For if they loved it, they would certainly never dare to [harm] their nurse and mother...

To devastate: but they would think it sufficient if the victors seized the crops of the others, believing that they would not always be at war with one another, but would eventually be reconciled. 

**GLAUCON:** This is certainly a milder opinion for men to hold. 

**SOCRATES:** This city which we are founding, is it not Greek? 

**GLAUCON:** It ought to be. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore the citizens in it will be both good and mild. 

**GLAUCON:** Very much so. 

**SOCRATES:** Consequently, they will be friends of the Greeks. They will surely consider all of Greece as their own kin, and they will hold the sacred rites in common with others. 

**GLAUCON:** Most definitely. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, they will consider a contention arising against other Greeks to be like a quarrel with their own people; they will call it "discord" <note>original: *seditionem*; referring to internal strife rather than foreign war</note>, not "war." 

**GLAUCON:** They will act exactly so. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, they will argue as those who must one day be reconciled. 

**GLAUCON:** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** They will act with a pious opinion and a temperate mind, not looking toward slavery or death, as those who are by no means enemies. 

**GLAUCON:** In that way, indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** Since they are Greeks, they will not destroy Greece, nor burn houses; nor will they think that in individual cities everyone—men, women, and children—is their enemy, but only the very few who were the cause of the discord. For this reason, they will not devastate the land, as it belongs mostly to friends, nor will they overturn the houses; they will carry the fight only so far as to compel those who caused the discord to pay the penalty to the innocent. 

**GLAUCON:** I agree that this is how Greeks should fight against one another; but against barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to any non-Greeks</note>, they ought to be disposed as Greeks are currently disposed toward other Greeks. 

**SOCRATES:** Let us then establish this law for the guardians: that they neither ravage the fields nor consume the dwellings with fire. 

**GLAUCON:** Let us establish it; and let us affirm that this, along with the previous rules, is right. But you seem to me, O Socrates—if one allows you to speak of such things—that you will never remember that which you set aside in the earlier parts to bring all these things into the open: namely, whether it is possible for this republic to exist, and in what way it can be done. For if it were to exist, I do not doubt that all good things would come to the city itself, including those things you omitted: namely, that those citizens will fight strenuously against enemies because they will never desert one another, recognizing each other as kin and calling one another by these names: brothers, fathers, sons. And if the women should also serve in the military, whether in the same rank or in the rear guard, both to terrify the enemy and to bring aid to the men when necessity demands, I know for certain they would be invincible. And I understand how many good things would follow them at home, even if all have not been mentioned. But since I concede that all these things and many others would happen if this republic were to exist, do not go on further about it; rather, let us now try to persuade ourselves of this very thing: that it is possible, and by what reasoning it is possible for this republic to exist. Let us set the other matters aside. 

**SOCRATES:** You have made a sudden assault upon my discourse again! You neither forgive me for being exhausted from the labors of the argument, nor do you perhaps notice that I have barely emerged from two waves, and now you push me back into a third, most profound sea. When you have seen and heard it, you will surely grant me pardon, recognizing that I was not wrong to fear entering upon a discourse so far removed from the common opinion of men. 

**GLAUCON:** The more you pile up such excuses, the less we will let you off until you show by what means this republic can be realized. Therefore, speak now, and delay no further. 

**SOCRATES:** First, it is necessary to remember that we arrived at this point in the discussion by inquiring into what kind of thing justice is. 

**GLAUCON:** It is necessary indeed; but to what end? 

**SOCRATES:** Surely, if we perceive what justice is, shall we judge that the just man ought to differ in no way from it, but be entirely such as justice itself is? Or shall we think it sufficient if he approaches it as closely as possible and participates in it more than all others? 

**GLAUCON:** We shall think that is sufficient. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, for the sake of an example, we sought what justice is and what a perfectly just man would be like if he existed; and likewise, what injustice is and the most unjust man. We did this so that, seeing how they appeared to us regarding happiness and misery, we would be forced to confess concerning ourselves that each of us would have a lot similar to theirs, whoever among us showed himself most like them. But we did not scrutinize these things for the purpose of demonstrating that they *could* happen. 

**GLAUCON:** That is true. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you think someone would be a less good painter because, after he had produced a perfect model of human beauty and omitted nothing from the appearance, he could not demonstrate that such a man could actually be found? 

**GLAUCON:** Not at all. 

**SOCRATES:** And did we not also fashion a model of a most excellent city in our discourse? 

**GLAUCON:** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you think, then, that we speak any less correctly if we cannot show that such a city can exist as we have depicted in our speech? 

**GLAUCON:** Not in the least. 

**SOCRATES:** Such is the truth of the matter. But if, for your sake, I must also demonstrate how and by what means it might most likely be achieved, confirm these same points for me again. 

**GLAUCON:** Which ones? 

**SOCRATES:** Can anything be carried out exactly as it is described? Or is it the nature of things that action attains the truth less than speech does, even if it does not seem so to some? Do you grant this or not? 

**GLAUCON:** I do grant it. 

**SOCRATES:** Then do not force me to point out with my finger that everything we have shaped in words must exist exactly so in reality. But if we are able to find how a city's institution might most closely approach these things, it must be confessed that we have discovered how the things you require can be achieved. Would you not be satisfied if you achieved this much? For I would be satisfied. 

**GLAUCON:** I would be too. 

**SOCRATES:** Let us then try to declare hereafter what is now done badly in cities, because of which they are not so governed; and whether by the change of one small thing a city might be brought to this order; and what that thing might be; and whether it happens by the change of one thing, or at least two, or as few as possible and of the least power. 

**GLAUCON:** Exactly so. 

**SOCRATES:** We can show that by changing one thing, it is possible, though not a small or easy change. 

**GLAUCON:** What is it? 

**SOCRATES:** I am now descending to that which we compared to a giant wave. It shall be said, then, though I suspect it may be overwhelmed by a flood of laughter and disbelief. Consider what I am about to say.

# DIALOGUE V. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.
## E iii
<meta>Catchword: ritate</meta>

<margin>Either philosophers must rule or kings must philosophize if a city is to be happy.</margin>GLAUCON. Speak now. SOCRATES. Unless philosophers rule over cities, or those who are now called kings and potentates philosophize legitimately and sufficiently, and civil power and philosophy concur in the same person—and not as it is now, where these two are handled by different natures—there will be no end to evils for cities, or, as is my opinion, for the human race; nor will this republic, which we have set forth in words, ever arise according to its strength and behold the light of the sun. This is what I have long feared to say: as if it were incredible to speak. For it is not easily persuaded that no other governance, privately or publicly, will be happy. GLAUCON. From this speech of yours, O Socrates, consider that many people, and not insignificant men at that, will cast off their cloaks and, seizing whatever weapons happen to be at hand, make an attack upon you: as if they were about to achieve some wonder against you. Unless you repel them with speech and escape them, you will be torn apart by many insults and pay the penalty. SOCRATES. Are you not the cause of this for me? GLAUCON. And rightly so. But I shall not betray you; indeed, I will certainly defend you by whatever means I can. I can certainly do so with goodwill and exhortations: and perhaps I will respond to you more diligently than anyone else. Therefore, aided by such a defender, try to demonstrate to these skeptics that it is as you say. SOCRATES. I must certainly strive, since you also seem ready to fight fiercely. It seems necessary to me, if we wish to escape them, to declare to them first of all what kind of men we consider philosophers to be when we offer them command: so that once these things are revealed, someone might be able to bring help, showing that it is fitting by nature for some to touch upon both the study of philosophy and the administration of the republic, while others should not touch them at all, but obey those who lead. GLAUCON. Declare it now. SOCRATES. Come, follow me this way, if in some manner we are able to explain this sufficiently. GLAUCON. Lead on. SOCRATES. Do you need to be reminded? Or do you remember well enough yourself that when we say someone loves something, it must be seen, if it is truly said, that he does not love one part and not another, but is affected toward the whole? GLAUCON. I indeed need a reminder. For I do not quite grasp it. SOCRATES. It would be more fitting for anyone else, O Glaucon, to speak thus. But it does not befit a man who indulges much in love to be ignorant that all those in the flower of youth stimulate and excite a lover of boys in some way, since they seem worthy of care and affection. Are you not so affected toward beautiful youths? One, because he is snub-nosed <note>original: "simus"</note>, is judged graceful by you and praised. Another, with a hooked nose, you call "royal" <note>original: "aquilinum... regium"</note>. Another, who is between these, seems to you to be very well-proportioned. Dark ones you call manly. Fair ones, children of the gods. And who called a youth "pale" <note>original: "pallidum"</note> except a flattering lover who, in a way, easily bears paleness in youths by giving it a name? And to speak briefly, you catch whatever small occasions you can so that you reject no youth at all who is in the flower of his age. GLAUCON. If you wish to show in me how lovers are affected, I accept this for the sake of the discussion. SOCRATES. What about those greedy for wine? Do you not see them similarly affected? That they vehemently seek out any wine whatever, seizing any occasion? GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, I think you observe that ambitious men, if they cannot achieve the command of an army, at least wish to be made tribunes: and unless they are honored by great and venerable men, they demand honor from the ignoble: as those who utterly crave honor. GLAUCON. Greatly. SOCRATES. Will you admit this or not? Shall we say that he whom we say loves something burns for the whole of it, or shall we admit he desires one part and not another? GLAUCON. The whole. SOCRATES. Shall we not then say the philosopher is a student of wisdom—not greedy for this part and not that, but rather for all wisdom? GLAUCON. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Therefore, he who scorns any learning, especially while he is young and does not yet have the reason to discern what is useful and what is not, we shall by no means assert to be a seeker of learning or a lover of wisdom: just as we say that he who loathes feasts is neither hungry nor desires feasts, and we call him not a lover of food, but a scorner. GLAUCON. And rightly so. SOCRATES. But the man who is inclined to taste any learning whatever, and is most prompt to learn, and gapes for it insatiably, we shall rightly name a philosopher. Shall we not? GLAUCON. But indeed, many and absurd men will be found to be such. For those who are greedy for spectacles all seem to be seekers of learning: and it is absurd to call those who are curious to hear things philosophers, for they do not willingly approach the reason of speaking and debating: but they attend all the choruses to listen as if their ears were hired for a fee at the festivals of Bacchus <note>The Dionysia, where plays and music were performed</note>, and they desire to hear all songs, whether they are performed in the city or in the suburbs. Shall we name all these, and others greedy for perceiving such things and devoted to the cheapest arts, philosophers? SOCRATES. By no means: but similar to philosophers. GLAUCON. But whom do you call true philosophers? SOCRATES. Those greedy for beholding the truth. GLAUCON. That is indeed right: but how do you mean that? SOCRATES. It is not easy to say this to others. But I think you will grant me this. GLAUCON. What especially? SOCRATES. Since the beautiful is the opposite of the ugly, these are two things. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. And since these are two, each will be one. GLAUCON. That too. SOCRATES. Regarding the just and the unjust, the good and the evil, and all species, the reason is the same. For each of these is one in itself, but because of the communion of bodies, actions, and each other appearing everywhere, they each seem to be many. GLAUCON. You speak skillfully. SOCRATES. By this reasoning I distinguish, on one side, those you just called curious to see, to hear, and to handle the arts, and on the other side, those of whom we speak, whom alone one might rightly call philosophers. GLAUCON. How do you say that? SOCRATES. Men devoted to eyes and ears are greatly delighted by beautiful voices, colors, and shapes, and all things that consist of such; but their thought cannot reach the nature of the beautiful itself. GLAUCON. It is so. SOCRATES. But are they not rare who are able to ascend to the beautiful itself, and behold it according to itself? GLAUCON. Very rare indeed. SOCRATES. He who considers these beautiful things, but [does not consider] the...

# BOOK V.

<margin>He who dreams.</margin> ...to beauty, he neither thinks it exists, nor if someone should lead him to it, is he able to reach the perception of it. Does he seem to you to live truly, or to be played with by dreams? Consider therefore: is not dreaming this—whether one is asleep or awake—when one considers that which is similar to something to be not merely similar, but the very thing itself which it resembles? GLAUCON. I would say such a man is seeing dreams. SOCRATES. What then? He who is affected in the opposite way, who understands the beautiful itself, and is able to discern both it and those things which participate in it: so that he thinks neither that those things are it, nor that it is those things; does he live awake, or drowsing? GLAUCON. Certainly, wide awake. SOCRATES. Therefore, we shall rightly call the thought of this man "knowledge," as he is one who knows; but the thought of the other "opinion," as he is one who opines. GLAUCON. Entirely so. SOCRATES. If he whom we say opines but does not know should be angry with us, and deny that we speak the truth, by what reasoning shall we soothe him, and slowly and gently persuade him that he is not of sound mind? GLAUCON. It is certainly necessary. SOCRATES. Pay attention to what we shall say to him. If you wish, we shall inquire of him in this manner, saying that if he <margin>Concerning knowledge and the knowable.</margin> knows anything, there is no envy: rather, it will be pleasing to us both that he knows something, and to have known what he knows. But tell me this: whoever knows, does he know something, or nothing? You answer in his place. GLAUCON. Something, certainly. SOCRATES. Is it something that *is* <note>Latin: *ens* (being/existing thing)</note>, or something that *is not*? GLAUCON. That which *is*. For how could that which is not be known? SOCRATES. This will be sufficiently established if he investigates it under various reasons: namely, that what entirely *is*, can be entirely known; but what in no way *is*, can in no way be known. GLAUCON. Most sufficiently. SOCRATES. But if something is so constituted that it both *is* and *is not*, will it not be a medium between that which entirely is, and that which in no way is? GLAUCON. A medium. SOCRATES. Knowledge itself is concerned with that which *is*. Ignorance, by necessity, is concerned with that which *is not*. Concerning the medium between these: some medium must be investigated between knowledge and ignorance, if any such thing is found. GLAUCON. Exactly. SOCRATES. Do we say that opinion is something? GLAUCON. <margin>Knowledge is about one thing; opinion about another.</margin> Why not? SOCRATES. Is it the same power as knowledge, or a different one? GLAUCON. A different one. SOCRATES. Therefore, opinion is concerned with one thing, and knowledge with another: either according to a different power, or according to the same power of each itself. GLAUCON. It is so. SOCRATES. Does not knowledge indeed know that which *is*, by that reason in which it is a being? Rather, I think it is necessary that I first distinguish these things. GLAUCON. How? SOCRATES. We shall say that powers are a certain genus of things that exist: by which we are able to do whatever we are able, and anything else is able to do whatever it does. For example, I call sight and hearing certain "powers"—if you understand what I am saying. GLAUCON. I do understand. SOCRATES. Hear what seems to me regarding these. For I do not see any color of the power itself, nor any shape, nor any such thing as I do in many other things; looking at which, I distinguish some things among themselves, that these are one thing and those are another. But in a power, I look only to that toward which it is directed, or what it performs: and by this reason, I have named each of them a power. That which tends toward the same thing and performs the same thing, I call the same; but that which looks toward another thing and works another thing, I call another. What do you do in these matters? GLAUCON. <margin>Knowledge is a type of power.</margin> The same as you. SOCRATES. Come then, turn back to these things, O best of men. Do you say that knowledge is a certain power? Or do you refer it to another genus? GLAUCON. A power, and indeed the most powerful of all. SOCRATES. And opinion: shall we say it is a power, or something else? GLAUCON. A power, certainly. For that by which we are able to opine is nothing other than opinion. SOCRATES. But a little while ago you confessed that knowledge and opinion are not the same. GLAUCON. How could anyone with a mind assert that what can be deceived is the same as what cannot? SOCRATES. Very well. It is established, therefore, that knowledge is something different for us than opinion. GLAUCON. Plainly different. SOCRATES. Each, therefore, by its own nature, is able to work toward a different thing. GLAUCON. It is necessary. SOCRATES. Knowledge, indeed, is to know that which *is*, the being itself as it is. GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. But opinion is to opine. GLAUCON. That too. SOCRATES. Will it know the same thing that knowledge knows? And will that which is perceived by opinion be the same as that which is perceived by knowledge? Or is it rather impossible? GLAUCON. Impossible, certainly, from what we have conceded; if indeed a different power by its very nature is concerned with a different thing; and both are powers—namely, knowledge and opinion—and each is different, as was said. From these things it cannot happen that what knowledge comprehends is the same as what opinion conceives. SOCRATES. Therefore, if being itself is perceived by knowledge, must we not say that what is conceived by opinion is something other than being itself? GLAUCON. Something else. SOCRATES. Does one opine that which *is not*? Or is it impossible to opine that which is not? Think of it this way: does not whoever opines direct his opinion toward something? Or is it possible to opine, but to opine nothing? GLAUCON. Impossible. SOCRATES. But whoever opines, opines some one thing. GLAUCON. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. But that which is not, is not "some one thing"; <margin>That which is not: this is nothing.</margin> rather, it should be called "nothing." GLAUCON. Exactly. SOCRATES. We have assigned ignorance to non-being by necessity; but to being, we assigned knowledge. GLAUCON. Very rightly. SOCRATES. Therefore, one opines neither being nor non-being. <margin>Because opinion is neither ignorance nor knowledge.</margin> GLAUCON. So it seems. SOCRATES. Wherefore opinion will be neither ignorance nor knowledge. GLAUCON. No, as it seems. SOCRATES. Does it exist outside of these, surpassing knowledge in clarity, or ignorance in obscurity? GLAUCON. Neither of those. SOCRATES. Or does opinion perhaps seem to you more obscure than knowledge, but clearer than ignorance? GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. And it lies between both? GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, opinion will be the medium of these? GLAUCON. The medium. SOCRATES. Did we not say above, that if anything appeared such that it simultaneously *was* and *was not*, it should be placed between that which truly is and that which entirely is not? And that neither knowledge nor ignorance pertains to it, but that which appears as a medium between ignorance and knowledge? GLAUCON. Wisely said. SOCRATES. But now it has appeared that the medium of these is what we call opinion. GLAUCON. Plainly. SOCRATES. That, therefore, remains for us to find, I think: that which participates in both—namely, in being and non-being—and which should be called neither of them purely; so that if it is revealed to us, we may deservedly call it the "opinable": attributing extremes to extremes, and means to means. Is it not so? GLAUCON. Exactly so. SOCRATES. These things being so supposed, I shall question him: he who denies that the beautiful itself and the one idea of beauty exist—always being in the same way according to the same things—but says there are many beautiful things...

<summary>Socrates leads Glaucon through a logical proof to define "opinion" as a middle state between knowledge (which concerns what exists) and ignorance (which concerns what does not exist). They conclude that opinion deals with things that both "are" and "are not," such as the many beautiful things that are not Beauty itself.</summary>
