# ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE VI. FOLIO 243.
## E iiii

<margin>Observe how the "one" and the "many" are understood: for the "one" is the Idea and Form, while the "many" are those things participating in the Form.</margin>
...and devoted to seeing beautiful things, in no way admits that the Beautiful is one, or the Just is one, and similarly regarding the rest. I will question him in this manner: "Is there any of these many beautiful things, my good man, which might not also appear ugly? And likewise of the just things, any that might not appear unjust? Or of holy things, any that might not appear profane?" GLAUCON: "No; it is necessary that these beautiful things, and ugly things, and whatever else you ask about, appear as such <note>i.e., they appear to shift between opposites</note>." SOCRATES: "What about many double things? Do they appear any less half than double?" GLAUCON: "Not at all." SOCRATES: "And things called large and small, or light and heavy—will they be called these things any more than their opposites?" GLAUCON: "No; but each will always participate in both." SOCRATES: "Is each of these many things, then, more truly that which one says it is, or is it not?" GLAUCON: "This is like those puns told at banquets, or the children’s riddle about the eunuch hitting the bat—how and on what they say he struck that bird <note>A famous Greek riddle: A man who is not a man (eunuch) threw a stone that was not a stone (pumice) at a bird that was not a bird (bat) perched on a branch that was not a branch (a reed).</note>. These things are ambiguous: one cannot firmly answer that any of them *is*, or *is not*, or both, or neither." SOCRATES: "Do you know how to treat them? Can you find a more suitable place for them than the middle ground between Essence <note>Being</note> and Non-Being? For they will not appear more obscure than non-being (so as to exist less), nor clearer than being (so as to exist more)." GLAUCON: "You speak the truth." SOCRATES: "We have found then, it seems, that the many things which the multitude considers beautiful or otherwise, wander in the middle between that which entirely *is* and that which entirely *is not*." GLAUCON: "We have found it plainly." SOCRATES: "But we agreed previously that if any such thing appeared, it must be said to be perceived by opinion, not by knowledge; for that which wanders in the middle is grasped by the intermediate power." GLAUCON: "It was agreed." SOCRATES: "Therefore, those who look upon these many beautiful things, but do not see the Beautiful itself, nor can follow one who leads them to it—and who behold many just things, but the Just itself not at all—we shall say that they *opine* all things, but *know* nothing of what they opine." GLAUCON: "It must be so." SOCRATES: "What of those who contemplate the things themselves, which are always the same and in the same state? Do they not know rather than opine?" GLAUCON: "This too is necessary." SOCRATES: "Shall we not say that these men love and admire the things which knowledge concerns, while the others love those which opinion concerns? Do we not remember that we said these latter people love and look upon certain voices and colors and such things, but do not admit that the Beautiful itself is a reality?" GLAUCON: "We remember." SOCRATES: "Therefore we shall not err if we call them *philodoxers* <note>original: "philodoxos"</note>—that is, lovers of opinion—rather than philosophers. Though they will be bitterly angry with us if we say so." GLAUCON: "Not if they listen to me. For it is wrong to be angry with the truth." SOCRATES: "Thus, those who admire and love that which *is* in itself, each thing as one, we shall call philosophers, not philodoxers." GLAUCON: "That is fitting."

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for the Sixth Dialogue, On Justice.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "C" featuring a classical figure or scholar amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

SINCE all laws, even the best, are dead without the most proven magistrates, and the best magistrates are themselves living laws even without written laws, our Plato—as we have explained elsewhere—rightly labors with all diligence in his excellent Republic not merely in establishing laws, but in forming magistrates. He strives for this not only from a tender age, but even from the very conception of the offspring, so that from chosen seeds and continuous cultivation, the best fruit may be produced. Because he calls these men "guardians," and the most specific duty of guardians is to look forward and look around, he chooses the philosophical intellect—without controversy the most sharp-sighted of all—to guard the human flock. For to the eye of this man alone lies open the pattern of the Good itself and of Justice, according to whose image the city must be painted as good, just, and blessed. Furthermore, it pertains to a guardian to be truthful, generous, temperate, brave, just, high-minded, and gentle. He will prove these same qualities to be proper to the philosopher, so that finally it is concluded that the office of guarding must be committed to the philosopher above all others. For this reason, he will first prove that the nature of the philosopher is of this kind; then, because a noble nature without right cultivation is both useless and often harmful, he will hand down the discipline for cultivating this intellect. Meanwhile, he treats the "spurious" and "adulterous" philosopher who mimics the legitimate one. Likewise, he discusses a certain abuse of philosophizing. Again, he treats the form of philosophizing belonging to him who is one day to rule the state. He teaches that the most proper trait of the philosopher is a perpetual love of Truth itself regarding eternal things. Therefore, both the love of temporary things and lying are more alien to the philosopher than to anyone else. He shows, moreover, that the mind of the philosopher, in the very investigation of truth, is separated from the body and joined to the Divine Mind through a certain kinship; and through the "formulas of the Ideas" <note>innate concepts</note> implanted in it from the beginning, it reaches the Ideas themselves. From these, by that very contact, it strikes a light, so that having been made more fertile, it conceives—or rather, having been made stronger, it gives birth to truth; that is, through its own conceptions, it harmonizes with the Ideas in every way. Note here that the act of understanding is called "generation" and "birth," just as in the *Symposium*. This indeed agrees with Christian theology, showing that there is in the mind not only an imaginary form, but a certain natural form and truth. Furthermore, he believes such an intellect is born very rarely and in few people, and even then it requires many conditions and is hindered by many obstacles. It is especially corrupted by the speech and opinion of the common people, and much more by the works of that same crowd. Again, it is corrupted by common teachers, who themselves accommodate their life and speech to the crowd like flatterers, and hand down a similar discipline to their listeners. And see how fittingly Plato compares the crowd to a vast beast. Likewise, he compares all cities to ships...

<summary>This page concludes the distinction between philosophers, who grasp eternal Forms, and "philodoxers," who only perceive the shifting world of opinion. Marsilio Ficino then introduces Book VI, arguing that philosophers are the only fit guardians for a state because they alone perceive the divine pattern of Justice.</summary>

<meta>This page provides the introductory argument or summary for the sixth dialogue of Plato’s Republic. It establishes the central metaphors of the navigator and the sun, while attempting to reconcile Platonic thought with Christian theology and Aristotelian ethics.</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE SIXTH DIALOGUE

In which a comparison is made to a ship governed by sailors entirely ignorant of the art of steering, who mock the man endowed with navigational skill. Note that even the best gifts, whether of nature or fortune, if neglected or poorly cultivated, eventually turn into evils, or if badly cultivated, into the very worst things. Furthermore, that sometimes—though very rarely—a great and most proven man may appear in a poorly ordered state (such as he judges all to be); this is attributed not to art or nature, but solely to divinity. Where he mentions **Momus** <note>The Greek god of satire and mockery</note>, the god of reproach, understand Momus to be the divine care which foresees what could have been reproached in individual things if they had been made differently than they are: and therefore he disposes each thing so that they cannot rightly be reproached. 

He then assigns the causes for the slanders arising against philosophers: as if they are either evil or useless to the republic. First, indeed, many who are most unfit for the study of philosophy—possessing as much a perverse nature as a small judgment, yet with no small ambition or greed—invade and seize upon philosophy. From this association, they procreate adulterated and ridiculous opinions; moreover, they disgrace the philosophical faculty with their evil morals. Next, if any are born for that study, they are either immediately corrupted by a wicked education and habit; or, if they persevere with integrity of character, they are nonetheless not instructed in the appropriate grades of discipline; or, if indeed instructed, they are not admitted to the republic; or rather, they themselves are unwilling to immerse themselves in the public waves, fearing certain dangers and despairing that they can benefit the city with sound counsel among men who are everywhere corrupt. 

Amidst these things, he touches upon the storms of the active life and the tranquility of the contemplative life, the sublime mind of the philosopher, the contempt for mortal things, the study of divine matters, and a certain formula for the doctrines according to the stages of age. He educates the philosopher and the citizen by an entirely similar reason, and not without justice. For he asserts in the *Statesman* and the *Sophist* that the royal man, the citizen, and the philosopher are the same. He proves it necessary that two types of nature, which very rarely coincide in men, must meet here: namely, a nature sharp in intellect, fit for contemplation, and burning with a greed for truth, together with a nature that is grave, strenuous in action, and foresighted for the public good. 

He leads such a genius through all the grades of discipline (as will be clear in the seventh book); he also wishes him to be exercised in civil actions: and among pleasures, pains, labors, and dangers, to be diligently examined and proven like gold in the fire, before the rudders of the city are entrusted to him. Above all, however, he judges the **science of the Good itself** <note>The "Idea of the Good," Plato's highest form of knowledge</note> to be the most excellent of all and necessary for this man, affirming that just as all things are possessed uselessly without the possession of the good, so also the knowledge of all things and arts is utterly useless without the understanding of the good itself. Nor can a citizen rightly direct either private or public affairs toward the good unless he has known by reason what the good is. 

And if this science of the divine good might seem superfluous to an **Aristotelian** for governing a republic according to human morals, it is nonetheless necessary for this very governance: through which Plato says in the preceding parts one must strive to render the citizens like unto God and his friends. He added, moreover, that a governor is both blind and carried by a certain chance regarding individual goods to be disposed toward the good itself, unless he has first looked upon the very form of the good, the exemplar and cause of all good things. 

But so that you may notice that **Aristotle** in his *Ethics* plays against **Plato** regarding the idea of the good: read Plato’s words most diligently, and you will clearly perceive that the idea of the good is not this or that species, here or there: but the most eminent fecundity of the divinity itself, propagating itself powerfully, sweetly, and healthfully through all things. He wishes the visible sun in the visible world to be a certain image of this, diffusing its powers similarly through all things. 

Truly, before this sun which we see, Plato conceives of another in the invisible world: the primary image of God the Father, and the true Son. Therefore he called them "sons of the good": so that above this visible and imaginary son, you might contemplate the invisible and archetypal one. We read of this Father and Son in the *Letter to Hermias*. Regarding this, the Platonist **Philo** <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who harmonized scripture with Plato</note> says in his book *On Causes*: "One must strive first of all to ascend to Being itself (that is, of which it is said, *I am who I am* <note>Exodus 3:14</note>). Or at least to its image and most sacred reason and first-born Word." Through such reason and Word all things are made according to **Heraclitus** and Plato, as **Amelius the Platonist** asserts; and he uses the testimony of **John the Evangelist** <note>Referring to the Gospel of John: "In the beginning was the Word"</note>. Plato testifies to the same in the *Epinomis*. 

And although some of the Platonists distinguish the Son of God from the Father by substance, after the manner of the **Arians** <note>Followers of Arius, who believed the Son was distinct from and subordinate to the Father</note>—especially **Julian** in his book *On the Sun*—nevertheless Julian’s teacher, **Iamblichus**, brings forward the Egyptian mysteries: in which there is indeed a different reason for the Father and the Son, but the substance is seen to be the same. But hear the mystery: 

-> The first God and the One is the Father of the first God, whom he begets while remaining in the solitary unity of himself. He is the exemplar of the Son, who is named his own son, his own father, and the single-father, God truly good. For he is the fountain of ideas: from which one, indeed, God, sufficient through himself, unfolded himself into the light. Therefore he is named sufficient through himself and his own father. For he is the principle, the God of gods, one from one, above all essence, and the principle of essence. <-

Iamblichus testifies that this is the mystery of **Mercury** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>. 

How the good itself is above pleasure, and morals, and wisdom, Plato signifies here briefly. Above pleasure, indeed, because if pleasure itself were the good itself, no pleasure would be evil and harmful. Likewise above morals, since many think they have enough regarding morals if they seem to have honest morals. But that which they judge to be the true good, they do not seek by opinion, but to have it in the thing itself. Furthermore, above knowledge, because you do not chiefly desire to know in just any way, nor just any things: but rather to know well and to know good things. Otherwise, you either reject or neglect knowledge. Nor should you say that the good itself is the knowledge of the good, lest you foolishly define the same thing by the same thing. Again, it is above the intellect, for the intellect assiduously seeks the good. But the good itself does not seek the good. Add also that it is above truth. Which...

# DIALOGUE VI. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO CCXLV.

For you judge a thing to be good more strongly, the more you choose it. Indeed, you choose a disease or a loss less truly than you choose what is more true. Finally, you choose what is above mere being. For in order to be well, you desire to exist. But concerning these matters—and how the intellect understands all truths by the light of the Good itself—we dispute more extensively in our Theology. There follows a distinction of things into two genera: the visible and the invisible; and each of these into two parts, namely, the antecedent and the subsequent; and a similar distinction of human perception. ### THE SIXTH DIALOGUE ON JUSTICE.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within a rectangular frame with floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>WHAT SORT OF PEOPLE PHILOSOPHERS are, and how different they are from those who are strangers to philosophy, O Glaucon, has at last been established through a long discourse. GLAUCON: Perhaps it was not easy to explain this in fewer words. SOCRATES: No, so it appears. But it would shine forth more clearly, I think, if I were only to narrate this one point, and not wander through many other things, to see how the just life differs from the unjust. GLAUCON: What remains for us to do after this? SOCRATES: What else but what follows in order? Since philosophers are those who are able to grasp that which always remains the same in the same way <note>referring to the eternal Forms or Truths</note>, while those who cannot do so, but wander through many changeable things, are not philosophers—which of these ought to be the leaders of the city? GLAUCON: How can we answer this correctly? SOCRATES: Whosoever are able to guard the laws and the duties of the city, to these the rudders of the Republic must be committed. GLAUCON: Rightly so. SOCRATES: Is this not clear then: whether a blind man or one who sees sharply ought to guard anything? GLAUCON: How could it not be clear? SOCRATES: Do they seem to you to differ from the blind, who lack the knowledge of what each thing truly is, and have no clear pattern in their soul? Nor can they, like painters looking toward a most true model and referring back to it, and beholding it most purely, finally establish laws here concerning the beautiful, the just, and the good, if necessary, and guard and preserve the laws once they are established? GLAUCON: Truly, they do not differ much. SOCRATES: Shall we choose these as guardians rather than those who know what each thing truly is, and who are in no way inferior in experience or any other part of virtue? GLAUCON: It would be absurd to choose any others, especially if they are not lacking in other respects. This quality certainly excels above all. SOCRATES: Shall we now say this: in what way will the same men be able to have both those qualities and these? GLAUCON: By all means. SOCRATES: Therefore, as we said at the beginning of this dispute, it is necessary first of all to learn their nature; and I think if we agree on those points sufficiently, we will further grant that it is possible for the same men to attain these things, and that no others besides these ought to be the leaders of the city. GLAUCON: In what way? SOCRATES: Let this first be agreed between us concerning the natures of philosophers: that they always love that learning by which that nature which always exists, and is not changed by generation and corruption, becomes known to them. <margin>Qualities proper to the natures of Philosophers.</margin> GLAUCON: Let it be agreed. SOCRATES: Furthermore, that they strive for the whole of it, and do not willingly despise any part of it, neither small nor large, neither the honored nor the base, just as we said before concerning the ambitious and those captured by love. <margin>The philosopher loves to contemplate even the parts of lowly being.</margin> GLAUCON: Correct. SOCRATES: Besides this, consider whether it is necessary for this to be in the nature of those who are to be such as we have described. GLAUCON: What sort of thing? SOCRATES: That they be entirely free from the nature of falsehood, and never willingly lie, but hate all falsehood and love the truth. GLAUCON: That is probable. SOCRATES: Not only is it probable, my friend, but entirely necessary; for one who is inclined by nature toward something with love must love everything that is kindred and familiar to the beloved. <margin>A lover loves not only the beloved, but also everything familiar to them.</margin> GLAUCON: Wisely said. SOCRATES: Is anything found more familiar to wisdom than truth? GLAUCON: Nothing. SOCRATES: Is it then possible for the same nature to be both philosophical and deceitful? GLAUCON: In no way. SOCRATES: Therefore, it is necessary for the lover of learning to strive greatly for all truth immediately from boyhood. GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: But when desires carry someone toward a certain thing ardently, his desires for other things are weaker, as if the streams were diverted elsewhere. GLAUCON: No doubt. SOCRATES: Whoever, therefore, burns with all desire for learning and such things, seeks the pure pleasure of the soul itself, and despises the delights of the body—unless he be a false philosopher rather than a true one. GLAUCON: That is most necessary. SOCRATES: Such a man will therefore be temperate and not a lover of money. For it belongs to anyone else rather than to him to gape after the accumulation of money, for the sake of which others pour themselves into seeking wealth with the greatest loss. GLAUCON: So it is. SOCRATES: Furthermore, this must be considered whenever you wish to discern the nature of him who is a philosopher and him who is not. GLAUCON: What is that? SOCRATES: Lest perhaps some hidden illiberality <note>meaning narrow-mindedness or lack of generosity</note> dwells within. For smallness of mind is entirely opposed to a soul that is always to investigate the whole of the divine and the human. <margin><insert>a modest man</insert></margin> GLAUCON: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: Indeed, for one who possesses magnificence of thought and the contemplation of all time and all substance, human life cannot seem to be anything great. GLAUCON: Certainly not. SOCRATES: Will such a man then think death to be a terrible thing? GLAUCON: Not at all. SOCRATES: Therefore, true philosophy does not suit a timid and illiberal nature. GLAUCON: Not as it seems to me. SOCRATES: But will a modest man, not given to gain, not small-minded, not proud, not timid, ever be difficult in his dealings or unjust? GLAUCON: In no way. SOCRATES: Furthermore, when you wish to discern which soul is philosophical and which is not, you will observe this immediately from its tender years: whether it is just and mild, or unfair and savage. GLAUCON: Especially so. SOCRATES: Nor, I think, will you overlook this. GLAUCON: What? SOCRATES: Whether he is quick or slow to perceive; for do you think anyone will ever love that which he does with the greatest difficulty when he attempts it, and at last accomplishes barely a little? GLAUCON: Never, surely. SOCRATES: What if he preserves nothing of the things he learns, forget— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "oblivioni" or "obliviscitur" (forgetting).</note>

# BOOK VI.

...and of all things: will he not be void of knowledge? GLAUCON. Void indeed. SOCRATES. Since, then, all his labor is undertaken in vain, will he not finally be compelled to hate both himself and such activity? GLAUCON. Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES. We should therefore by no means think that a forgetful soul is suited to the natures of true philosophers; rather, it must be very mindful. GLAUCON. Quite so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, a discordant <margin>An unharmonious nature is always drawn toward excess.</margin> and unharmonious nature always draws one toward excess <note>Latin: *intemperiem*, referring to a lack of moderation or balance</note>. GLAUCON. Always. SOCRATES. But do you think truth is compatible with excess, or rather with moderation? GLAUCON. With moderation. SOCRATES. Therefore, let us grant a balanced and graceful mind, among other qualities, to this nature, which we wish to be naturally inclined toward contemplating the Idea of each thing as it truly is. GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. Does it not seem to you that we have run through each quality that must follow in a continuous series for a soul that is to perfectly attain the truth of things? GLAUCON. Quite so. SOCRATES. Can you then in any way condemn this pursuit, which no one can sufficiently carry out unless he is by nature quick-witted, mindful, <margin>Proverbial: Not even Momus could find fault.</margin> magnificent, graceful, and a friend and kinsman to truth, justice, courage, and moderation? GLAUCON. Not even Momus <note>The Greek god of mockery and harsh criticism</note> could find fault with it. SOCRATES. Will you not entrust the State to be administered by these alone, when they have finally been perfected by education and age? ADEIMANTUS. No one, O Socrates, could contradict you on these points. But truly, those who hear what you narrate are affected in this way: they think that because of their inexperience in questioning and answering, they are led astray little by little by each small point in the argument, until at the end of the discussion, all those small points are collected, and a great error appears that contradicts their original positions. Just as those who do not know how to play a game of draughts <note>A board game similar to checkers</note> are eventually cornered by those who are skilled in the game until they have nowhere to move, so they feel themselves cornered and find nothing to say, blocked by words as if by game-pieces—though the truth is not changed by this. I say this looking at the present situation. For now, someone might say to you that while they cannot oppose you in words, they see in reality that whoever applies themselves to the study of philosophy—not just tasting it in youth for the sake of education and then leaving it, but staying with it too long—most of them turn out quite absurd, not to say wicked, and alienated from human affairs. Even those who seem the most excellent are so tainted by this pursuit you praise that they become useless for governing the State. SOCRATES. Do you think those who say these things are lying? ADEIMANTUS. I do not know, but I would gladly hear what you think. SOCRATES. You shall certainly hear, if you ask, that they seem to me to speak the truth. ADEIMANTUS. How then is it right to say that there will be no rest from evils for cities until philosophers rule in them, whom we admit are useless to the State? SOCRATES. That question requires an answer through an image. ADEIMANTUS. But you, I believe, are not accustomed to speaking in metaphors! SOCRATES. Are you mocking me, after pushing me into a discussion so difficult to demonstrate? Hear then the comparison, so you may better know how poorly I compare them. The treatment that the most excellent men of philosophy suffer in governing the State is so harsh that there is nothing else like it. Therefore, one must collect this from <margin><image-desc>Marginal sketch of a face or mask.</image-desc> Goat-stags</margin> mixed parts, and compare it with these things, explaining the reason for each. Just as painters depict "Goat-stags" <note>Latin: *Tragelaphos*, a mythical creature like a chimera</note> and other such manifold fictions. Imagine in your mind a certain pilot of a ship or a fleet, who exceeds the rest of the sailors in size and bodily strength, but is somewhat deaf, dim-sighted, and ignorant of navigation. Imagine the sailors quarreling with one another over the steering, each thinking he is worthy to rule, though he has never learned the art, nor can he show any teacher of his, nor assign a time when he learned it. They even deny that the art can be taught, and are ready to strike anyone who asserts it can. Think of them crowding around that pilot, begging and striving with all their might for him to hand over the helm to them. Sometimes, <margin>Mandrake</margin> if they do not persuade him but others do instead, they either kill the others or cast them out of the ship. Then they bind that noble master of the ship with Mandrake <note>A plant used as a sedative or anesthetic</note> or wine, and so seize control of the ship, indulging in the ship's stores, drinking and feasting, and conducting the voyage as such men are likely to do. Furthermore, they praise and call anyone a "navigator" and "pilot" who is clever at helping them usurp the leadership of the ship, whether by persuasion or force. But they despise the man who refuses this as useless. They do not understand that the true pilot must pay attention to the year, the seasons, the sky, the stars, the winds, and all that belongs to the art, if he is to be a true leader of a ship. As for how he might govern—whether some want him to or not—they think it impossible to acquire the skill and practice of navigation along with the art of the pilot. With these things happening on the ships, do you not think the true pilot would be called a "star-gazer," a "babbler," and "useless" to the ship by those who sail in such vessels? ADEIMANTUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. I do not think it necessary to explain further how the citizens in states are disposed toward true philosophers, just as the sailors in such ships are toward the true pilot; I believe you understand. ADEIMANTUS. Entirely. SOCRATES. First, then, to the man who wonders why philosophers are not honored in cities, explain this image, and try to persuade him that it would be much more wonderful if they were honored. ADEIMANTUS. I shall do so. SOCRATES. And add this as well: that those who say the most skilled in philosophy are useless to the multitude speak the truth. But tell him that for this uselessness, he should not blame the philosophers, but rather those who do not make use of them. For it is not natural for a pilot to beg sailors to allow him to govern them, nor for the wise to go to the doors of the rich. Whoever first joked about that was lying. The truth of nature is this: whether a man be rich or poor, if he is sick, he must go to the doors of physicians; and all who need to be governed must go to the houses of men capable of governing. It is not for the governors, if they are of any worth, to beg the inferiors to be governed by them. Indeed, if you compare those who currently administer the State with these...

# DIALOGUE VI. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

If you compare them to the sailors I was just mentioning, you will not go astray; and if you compare those whom they call vain and superstitious seekers of hidden things to the true navigators, you will indeed act rightly. ADIMANTUS: Quite rightly. SOCRATES: For these reasons, therefore, it is not easy for an honorable pursuit to be approved by those who are accustomed to contrary ways of life. But the greatest and most vehement slander of philosophy arises because of the character of those who profess the study of philosophy. Indeed, those who find fault with philosophy say—as you yourself mention—that most of those who apply themselves to philosophy are quite wicked, and that those who excel among them are useless. And I conceded these things to you, did I not? ADIMANTUS: Certainly. SOCRATES: And did we not explain the cause of why legitimate philosophers seem useless? ADIMANTUS: We did. SOCRATES: Do you wish for us to next reveal why most are wicked, and declare to the best of our ability that this is not the fault of philosophy? ADIMANTUS: I certainly do. SOCRATES: Let us proceed to this, repeating what we introduced above: what the nature of one who is to be honorable and good must be. Its leader, first of all, if you recall, was Truth, which he must follow entirely and everywhere; for if he be a pretender, he can have no part in true philosophy. ADIMANTUS: So it was said. SOCRATES: This one point, then, is entirely foreign to the current opinions held about him. ADIMANTUS: Most foreign. SOCRATES: Shall we not defend his cause in this manner: saying that a man desirous of knowledge is so constituted by nature that he always strives toward that which truly *is*? He does not linger among those many individual things about which opinion hovers, but pressing onward, he does not rest until he touches the proper nature of each thing with that power of the soul which is fit to apprehend it. Now, it is fit to do so by a certain kindred power. When he has clung to this, and mixed himself with that which truly *is*, and has thereby generated intelligence and truth, he will truly know; he will live and grow truly. Finally, from this birth, all his labor will cease, but not before. ADIMANTUS: That is very well said. SOCRATES: Will such a man in any way love a lie, or will he rather hate it entirely? ADIMANTUS: He will certainly hate it. SOCRATES: Surely, where Truth is the leader, we shall not say, I think, that a chorus of evils follows. ADIMANTUS: How could it? SOCRATES: Rather, a sincere and just character follows; and we shall say that Temperance also follows this. ADIMANTUS: Cleverly put. SOCRATES: Furthermore, what need is there to recount the rest of the chorus of the philosophical nature from the beginning? For you remember that courage, magnificence, quickness of wit, and memory are consistent with these, as we were saying. But when you objected—though anyone would be forced to admit what we were saying—that, setting aside our words and turning to those of whom we spoke, you saw them to be partly useless and partly corrupted by every wickedness, we then began to investigate the cause of this slander, and why many of them are bad. For this reason, we have returned to the nature of legitimate philosophers and have necessarily defined it. ADIMANTUS: That is so. SOCRATES: We must next inquire in what way the nature of the philosopher is corrupted in many people. A small point escaped us. Namely, this must be noticed: those whom they call not wicked, but useless. Then also, what kind of talents those men have who imitate this nature and usurp its work; and by undertaking a study unworthy of them and beyond their strength, they often fail, and everywhere bring about that reputation of philosophy which you were describing. ADIMANTUS: But what corruptions do you mean? SOCRATES: I will show you if I can. I think anyone will grant us this: that a talent such as we described, endowed with all these qualities which a future perfect philosopher requires, arises rarely and among few. Do you not think so? ADIMANTUS: Very much so. SOCRATES: And see how many great causes of destruction there are for these few. ADIMANTUS: Which ones? SOCRATES: For what is most wonderful to hear is that each of the qualities we just approved in the philosophical talent actually destroys the soul and drags it away from philosophy—I mean courage, temperance, and all the others we recounted. ADIMANTUS: That is absurd to hear. SOCRATES: Moreover, all those things commonly called "goods" corrupt the soul and impede it: beauty, riches, strength of body, a powerful family in the city, and other things of that kind. You have the general formula of what I am saying. ADIMANTUS: I have it indeed, and I would gladly hear more exactly what you mean. SOCRATES: Grasp the whole concept correctly, and it will appear clear to you; the things said about them will not seem absurd. ADIMANTUS: How do you perceive this? SOCRATES: For we know that every seed and plant and animal, if it does not obtain the nourishment proper to it, nor the right time or place, the more vigorous and powerful it is, the more it lacks suitable conditions. <margin>Evil is more contrary to the good than to the non-good.</margin> For evil is more contrary to the good than to the non-good. ADIMANTUS: Why not? SOCRATES: It is therefore, I think, reasonable that the best nature, if nourished under adverse conditions, turns out worse than a weak nature. ADIMANTUS: It is so. SOCRATES: By this reasoning, then, Adimantus, we say that souls endowed with the most excellent talent, if they are badly educated, become the worst. Or do you think that unspeakable crimes and extreme wickedness proceed from a weak talent rather than from a noble one corrupted by education? Will a feeble nature ever be the cause of great things, either good or evil? ADIMANTUS: Certainly not. SOCRATES: If, therefore, this philosophical nature obtains the appropriate discipline, it must necessarily reach every virtue by always improving. But if it is sown and born and thus nourished in a different way, it falls back into all the opposites, unless perhaps some god helps it. Or do you also think, as many do, that it is true that certain youths are corrupted by sophists? <note>Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece often criticized by Plato for prioritizing rhetoric over truth.</note> And that the corrupters are certain private sophists, and not rather those very people who speak this way, who are the greatest sophists? Do they not teach thoroughly and make both young and old, men and women, exactly as they desire? ADIMANTUS: When does that happen most? SOCRATES: When many are gathered together in assemblies, or courts, or theaters, or camps, or any other public gathering of men, with a great noise they blame some of the things said or done and praise others. They boil over fiercely at both, while they hiss and applaud with the greatest din and shouting. Even the walls and the places around them echo loudly, and by their sound, they vehemently increase the tumult of praise and blame. At such a time, what do you think is the state of the youth's soul in such a crowd? Or what private discipline do you think can resist these rumors, so as not to be washed away and dispersed by such blame and praise, and carried wherever this current leads? So that he will approve the same things as they do as honorable, and...

He argues that the most gifted natures become the most wicked when misdirected.</summary>

# BOOK VI.

### PAGE XXXI.

...he will also reject those things as shameful. Furthermore, he will devote himself to those same pursuits as they do, and he will turn out just like them. ADEIMANTUS. That is absolutely necessary, Socrates. SOCRATES. And yet we have not yet introduced the most powerful necessity. ADEIMANTUS. Which one? SOCRATES. The one which those teachers and <term>Sophists</term><note>Professional teachers in Ancient Greece who were often criticized by Plato for prioritizing persuasion over truth.</note> impose through actions when they cannot persuade with words. Do you not see that they mark the man who does not obey them with infamy? They condemn him to the loss of his property and even to the penalty of death. ADEIMANTUS. Most certainly. SOCRATES. What other Sophist, then, or what other private discourses do you think could oppose these and resist them? ADEIMANTUS. None, surely. SOCRATES. None indeed. In fact, to resist them is the height of folly. For there never was, nor is, nor shall there ever be a different character trained toward virtue apart from the discipline of these men—a human character, I mean, my friend.

<margin>Proverb. We except the divine.</margin>

For as the proverb goes, we must except the divine. For know this for certain: whoever emerges immaculate and intact from this constitution of Republics, has emerged so by divine help. ADEIMANTUS. It seems no different to me. SOCRATES. Furthermore, this ought to seem true to you as well. ADEIMANTUS. What is that? SOCRATES. Each of those who, for a fee, privately educate men—whom they call Sophists and rivals in the arts—thinks nothing else should be taught except the opinions of the many, which they agree upon whenever they gather; and this they call wisdom. It is as if someone were keeping a vast, brute, and very powerful animal, nourished by man, and had observed its various angers and desires: in what way it is proper to approach it, how to touch it, and when it is most fierce or most gentle, and from what causes it becomes so. Likewise, the sounds it is accustomed to make in each situation, and by what sounds of others the animal is irritated or calmed. After he has learned these things one by one through long habit, he calls this experience "wisdom," and as if it were an art he had collected, he applies himself to teaching it. In truth, he is ignorant of which of these opinions and desires is noble or shameful, good or evil, just or unjust. He names each thing according to the opinion of that great beast: calling "good" the things it delights in, and "evil" the things that offend it. He offers no other reason for these things at all, but calls the things that are necessary "just" and "noble." Yet, how the nature of the good itself differs from the necessary, he has never seen himself, nor can he show it to others. If someone were so disposed, I ask you, by Jove, would he not seem to you an absurd teacher? ADEIMANTUS. To me, indeed. SOCRATES. And does he seem to you any different from the man who thinks it is wisdom to have mastered the anger and pleasures of many various men gathered together—whether in painting, music, or in the administration of the Republic? For it is clear that if someone associates with these people and presents to them a work of poetry or some other art, or a service pertaining to the Republic, and gives the crowd the authority to judge the work, he will be compelled—beyond what is necessary—by a <term>Diomedean necessity</term><note>original: "Diomedea neceſſitate"; a Greek proverb referring to an absolute or unavoidable compulsion.</note>, as they say, to do those things which they approve.

<margin>Proverb. Compelled by Diomedean necessity.</margin>

But as for whether these things are truly good and noble, have you ever heard any of them assign a plausible reason? ADEIMANTUS. I have never heard one, nor do I think I shall. SOCRATES. Having looked at all this, remember this as well: Can the crowd ever admit or grasp the "Beautiful itself" <note>Plato's concept of the ideal Form of Beauty, as opposed to many beautiful things.</note> as explained by another? Or can they grasp the essence of each thing, rather than the many particular things? ADEIMANTUS. Not at all. SOCRATES. Therefore, it is impossible for the crowd to be a philosopher. ADEIMANTUS. No. SOCRATES. Moreover, it is necessary that those who practice philosophy be disparaged by them. ADEIMANTUS. Necessary. SOCRATES. And by all those who wish to please the people. ADEIMANTUS. That is clear. SOCRATES. From this, then, what way do you see of preserving a philosophical nature, so that by persevering in its study it may reach the end of philosophizing? Consider it from what has been said. It was granted that sharpness in learning, memory, courage, and magnificence belong to this nature. ADEIMANTUS. Clearly. SOCRATES. Will not such a person immediately be first among all in everything, especially if he has obtained a body by nature that matches his mind? ADEIMANTUS. Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES. Therefore, all his relatives and citizens will want to use him for their own business when he grows up. ADEIMANTUS. Certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore, they will preoccupy his future virtue and power with prayers, supplications, honors, and flatteries. ADEIMANTUS. That is what usually happens. SOCRATES. What do you think such a man will do then, especially if he is born in a great city, and is distinguished there by wealth and lineage, and is moreover of a noble disposition and tall? Do you not think he will be elated by immense hope, thinking himself sufficient to manage the affairs of both Greeks and Barbarians? From this, he will exalt himself, wanton with a fastidious manner, and inflated with empty conceit and insane pride. ADEIMANTUS. Vehemently so. SOCRATES. If someone should kindly warn a man so affected, saying that he has no mind at all, though he needs one, and that it cannot be acquired by anyone unless he subjects himself to its attainment—do you think it will be easy for him, occupied by such great evils, to lend an ear to the one warning him? ADEIMANTUS. Far from it. SOCRATES. But if, by goodness of nature and a certain innate affection for reason, someone should listen and be turned and drawn toward philosophy, what do we think those will do who believe they are losing the youth's use and companionship to that advisor? Will they not strive with all zeal, both in speaking and acting, so that the youth does not obey the warnings, and that the exhorter cannot persuade him of anything—pursuing him with both private snares and public accusations? ADEIMANTUS. That is very much inevitable. SOCRATES. Will there then remain for him any faculty for philosophizing? ADEIMANTUS. Very little indeed. SOCRATES. Do you see that we were not wrong to say above that the very parts of the philosophical nature, if a perverse education is applied, are in a way the causes of one turning away from that study? Furthermore, even those things which are commonly thought to be "goods"—namely wealth and all such equipment—act as impediments? ADEIMANTUS. It was indeed rightly said. SOCRATES. This, O wonderful man, is the destruction and corruption of such a great nature, which is best suited for the most excellent duty, and which is found only rarely, as we said. And from this nature come those men who perpetrate heinous crimes, both privately and publicly, and also those who are the authors of great goods for individuals and cities.

<margin>A meager nature never achieves anything great.</margin>

But a meager nature never achieves anything great, either privately or publicly. ADEIMANTUS. Truly...

# DIALOGUE VI. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE.

...you speak. **SOCRATES:** Since many who are naturally fit for philosophy are turned away from this study, they leave philosophy incomplete and desolate. They lead a life that is neither becoming nor true. But others, certainly unworthy of her, approach philosophy as if she were a bereaved kinswoman and utterly disgrace her; they bring upon her that infamy which you mentioned was noted by her detractors—those who object that some who devote themselves to philosophy are of little account, and many are most wicked. **ADIMANTUS:** These things were certainly said. **SOCRATES:** And rightly said. For many other little men <note>Latin: *homunculi* - a diminutive, suggesting men of small spirit or stature</note>, seeing this seat vacant—though it is illustrious with noble titles and dignity—leap gladly from the crafts into philosophy, just like those who flee from a prison to take sanctuary in temples, especially those who excel in their own little trade. For although philosophy is in such a state, she still surpasses the other arts in dignity and magnificence. Many desire her whose natures are imperfect, and whose souls are as cramped and broken by their mechanical tasks and services as their bodies are marred by their crafts and trades. Is this not inevitable? **ADIMANTUS:** Most certainly. **SOCRATES:** Do you think they look any different from a little bald copper-smith who, having recently come into money, has been released from his chains, washed himself in the baths, dressed himself in a new garment like a bridegroom, and married his master’s daughter because the father is pressed by poverty and has no one else to give her to? **ADIMANTUS:** I think there is not much difference. **SOCRATES:** What kind of offspring must we think will be born from such as these? Will they not be bastards <note>original: *notha*</note> and base? **ADIMANTUS:** It is entirely necessary. **SOCRATES:** And when men unworthy of education attach themselves to it beyond their merit, what kind of thoughts and opinions do we say they produce? Are they not what should rightly be called sophisms—nothing legitimate, nothing worthy, nothing consistent with true wisdom? **ADIMANTUS:** That is exactly what must be said. **SOCRATES:** And so, Adimantus, very few men remain who associate worthily with philosophy. These are those born with a good disposition and well-nurtured, who find leisure for philosophy through exile. Thus, being free from other occupations, they persevere in their studies under the guidance of nature. Or perhaps a magnificent soul born in a small city, despising the offices of the State itself, and much more scorning the trades of the other arts, betakes himself to philosophy because of his natural gifts. There might also be the "bridle" of our friend Theages <note>Theages was a contemporary of Socrates known for his poor health, which Socrates argues kept him focused on philosophy rather than politics.</note>, which is strong enough to restrain him. For in our friend Theages' case, everything was such that he might have fallen away from philosophy, but the weakness of his body prohibits him from civil affairs. As for the sign of my "Daemon" <note>Socrates' *daimonion*, an inner voice or divine sign that warned him against certain actions.</note>, it is not fitting to mention it now, for it has happened to perhaps only one other, or to no one among those who came before. Now, those few who taste how sweet and blessed this possession is, and see the madness of the many—because, to put it briefly and simply, no one acts rightly in the affairs of Republics, nor is any ally or helper found with whom one might escape safely while taking up the care of defending justice—instead, like a man who falls among wild beasts, being neither willing to join in injustice nor able by himself to resist all the fierce creatures, he would perish before he could help either the city or his friends, and thus be useless to himself and others. Whoever diligently observes all these things remains quiet and minds his own business. As if in a storm, while the whirlwind rages and the winds blow and the sky is poured out with dust, he remains safe within his walls. Seeing others overwhelmed by wickedness, he considers himself satisfied if he can live his life pure from injustice and wicked deeds, and when his life's course is run, depart with good hope, cheerful and pious. **ADIMANTUS:** Certainly, he will have achieved no small thing who passes his life in such a way. **SOCRATES:** Yet not the greatest thing either, if he has not found a Republic suitable for him. For in such a state he himself will flourish and shine more, and he will preserve both private and public interests. Thus far, I think enough has been said regarding why philosophy has suffered calumny, and how unjust that calumny is, unless you perhaps have something else to add. **ADIMANTUS:** I have nothing further to say to this. But of the Republics that now exist, which do you think most suits philosophers? **SOCRATES:** None at all. And for that reason I complain: because I see no institution in any of the Republics now existing that is worthy of a philosophical mind. Therefore, this nature must be changed and turned. Just as a foreign seed cast into alien soil is weakened and, degenerating, turns toward the nature of the local soil and seed, so this type of man now loses his own virtue and is transformed into an alien species. But if he should find the best Republic, just as he himself is the best, then at last he will declare himself to be truly divine, while all other things—both temperaments and studies—are merely human. But you seem to me to be about to ask immediately what that Republic is. **ADIMANTUS:** You have not guessed correctly. For I did not desire this from you, but rather whether this is the very one we introduced in founding our city, or another. **SOCRATES:** As for other things, it is this very one. But this was also said then: that there must always be something in the city that holds the same rationale for the Republic as you, the legislator, held while you were establishing the laws. **ADIMANTUS:** That was clearly said. **SOCRATES:** However, it was not sufficiently explained. Indeed, your speech deterred us, objecting that this would be a long and arduous demonstration. For what follows is not easy to say at all. **ADIMANTUS:** What is that? **SOCRATES:** In what way especially the city ought to take up philosophy so that it is not destroyed. For all great things are prone to failure, and as the proverb truly goes: "Fine things are difficult." <margin>Proverb.</margin> **ADIMANTUS:** Nevertheless, since this is agreed between us, let the demonstration now reach its end. **SOCRATES:** Power may perhaps fail me, but will certainly never. You will understand my present zeal. Come now, observe how promptly and fearlessly I am about to say that the city ought to handle this study in a way contrary to how it is done now. **ADIMANTUS:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, now when youths, immediately from their tender years, between household matters and money-making business, approach the most difficult part of this study, they depart a little later—even those who are thought to be especially studious of wisdom. I call the most difficult part the skill of debating. Then, if they are invited by others engaged in it to listen...

<summary>Socrates explains why philosophy is often disparaged, blaming the "little men" who pursue it for status, and argues that a philosopher can only truly thrive in a Republic that matches their divine nature. He begins to describe how a city should properly integrate philosophical study to avoid corruption.</summary>

# BOOK SIX.

...allow things to happen, they are contemplating something great; nor do they think they should apply themselves diligently to these matters. In old age, however—with a few exceptions—they are extinguished much more than the sun of Heraclitus <note>The philosopher Heraclitus famously said the sun is new every day; Socrates suggests these men burn out and never reignite.</note>, since they are never lit again. 

**ADIMANTUS:** What then should be done? 

**SOCRATES:** Entirely the opposite. For it is fitting for young boys and youths to handle youthful discipline and philosophy, and to take care of their bodies as they grow and strengthen, as a service to philosophy. But as age proceeds, in which the soul now reaches maturity, they should increase its exercises. Then, when their strength fails due to old age, they should live according to their will, free and exempt from civil and military labors like retired veterans, and be bound by no fixed duty—those, at least, who are to live happily, and who after the migration of the soul <note>A reference to the afterlife or reincarnation.</note> will perhaps receive a life suitable to the one they led before. 

**ADIMANTUS:** You truly seem to me to speak very readily, O Socrates. However, I think most people, when they hear these things, will resist even more readily, being not at all persuaded by you. And I think Thrasymachus <note>The sophist who argued "might makes right" in Book I.</note> will be the first to do so. 

**SOCRATES:** Do not sow distrust in the mutual goodwill between me and Thrasymachus. For we have recently become friends, nor were we enemies before. Indeed, we shall not stop until we persuade him and the others, or at least do something beneficial for that life in which, when they arrive, they will find these words again. 

**ADIMANTUS:** You speak of a short time. 

**SOCRATES:** On the contrary, it is nothing compared to eternity. But that many do not give credit to what has been said is no wonder. For they have never seen what has just been described actually happen; rather, they have seen such words intentionally composed into a certain likeness <note>original: "in similitudinem quandam composita" — referring to artificial or poetic rhetoric.</note>, not occurring by chance as they do now. But a man who is as perfect in virtue as possible, and most powerful in deeds and words in such a city—they have never seen even one, let alone many. Or do you think they have? 

**ADIMANTUS:** Not at all. 

**SOCRATES:** Nor, O blessed one, have they ever given their ears to noble and free discourses, in which the truth is sought with great effort and every zeal for the sake of knowing. Instead, they encounter those full of trickery and the adorned machinery of litigation, seeking nothing other than opinion, vain glory, and contention, both in the courts and in private conversations. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Certainly not. 

**SOCRATES:** For this reason, since we foresaw and feared these things, we were compelled by the truth to say: neither a city, nor a state, nor a perfect man will exist until some necessity happens by chance to these few philosophers—who are not evil, but are considered useless by the common people—so that, whether they want to or not, they take up the care of the city, or are listened to by the citizens; or at least until a true love of true philosophy, by some divine inspiration, takes hold of those who rule, or their sons. I think it cannot be demonstrated that either or both of these things are impossible. Otherwise, we would rightly be laughed at, as if we were fashioning things according to our own desires. Is it not so? 

**ADIMANTUS:** Exactly so. 

**SOCRATES:** If, therefore, at some time in the infinite past, men outstanding in philosophy were driven by necessity to govern the Republic; or if they rule in these times in some barbarian region inaccessible to us; or if they shall govern in the future: in this state of affairs, we certainly assert without doubt that the Republic described above has existed, exists, and will exist. Whenever this Muse <note>The "Muse" of philosophy and political harmony.</note> presides over a city, it can certainly happen. Nor are we imagining impossible things. However, we have also conceded that these things are difficult. 

**ADIMANTUS:** It seems so to me as well. 

**SOCRATES:** You will perhaps add that the common people do not think so. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Perhaps. 

**SOCRATES:** Do not blame the common people so much, O blessed man. But what do you think they would feel if, not out of a desire for contention but with friendly warnings, you showed them—having dissolved the slander against philosophy—what kind of men you call philosophers? And if you distinguished, as we did recently, both their nature and their study, so they do not suspect you are talking about the people they have in mind? Or if they understood it this way, would you say they are mistaken in their opinion and do not respond to the proposal? Or do you think anyone is so harsh as to be provoked against a mild man, or that a man without envy and malice would envy a man who is not envious? I answer for you: such a harsh nature exists not in the multitude of men, but in very few. 

**ADIMANTUS:** I think the same. 

**SOCRATES:** And do you also think this? The reason why the multitude bears philosophy with an ill will is because of those who, being unfit for philosophy, have professed it and everywhere provoke men with insults; and as if they delighted in enmities, they are always speaking ill of people, doing something least suitable to philosophy. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** For indeed, O Adimantus, for that man who has directed the whole sharpness of his mind toward those things which truly exist, there is no leisure left to look down at the inferior affairs of men, and by fighting with them, to stir up envy and malevolence for himself. Instead, he contemplates those things which always keep the same order: which neither inflict nor suffer injury upon one another, but are all arranged elegantly and according to reason. And these he imitates, and makes himself as similar to them as possible. Or do you think it possible that someone would not imitate that which he clings to with admiring love? 

**ADIMANTUS:** In no way. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, since the philosopher frequently clings to what is divine and orderly, he himself becomes divine and orderly as far as is possible for a human. Yet slander is abundant in all things. 

**ADIMANTUS:** That is absolutely true. 

**SOCRATES:** If, then, he were led by some necessity to transfer those things which he beholds there <note>In the realm of eternal truths.</note> into the morals of men, both privately and publicly, and to shape not only himself but others as well, do you think he would be an unskilled craftsman of temperance, justice, and all popular virtue? 

**ADIMANTUS:** Not at all. 

**SOCRATES:** If the common people perceive that we are telling the truth about this, will they be angry with the philosopher? And will they not believe us when we say that a city will not otherwise be happy unless painters who use a divine model shape it? 

**ADIMANTUS:** They will not be angry at all, if they perceive it. But what manner of painting do you mean? 

**SOCRATES:** When these painters receive the city and the morals of men like a tablet, they will first clean it—which is not at all easy. Or do you not know that philosophers differ from others especially in this: that they do not intend to touch either a private person or a city, nor to establish laws...

He compares the philosopher-ruler to a painter who uses divine patterns to shape human society.</summary>

# DIALOGUE VI. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

state, before they have either received it already purified, or have purified it themselves. ADI. And rightly so. SO. Do you not think that after this they will sketch out the form of the Republic? ADI. Why should they not? SO. Then, in doing this, I think they will frequently look in both directions: first, toward that which is by nature just, honorable, and temperate, and other things of this sort; and again toward the human realm, and they will arrange human affairs according to the model of that higher reality, blending human nature from the duties of men, according to the figure of that which Homer, when it exists in men, called the "form and image of God." <note>original: "dei speciem & imaginem". Socrates refers to the process of the philosopher-artist molding society to reflect divine virtues.</note> ADI. Skillfully put. SO. Therefore, the philosophers will partly erase and partly color in, until they have joined human customs as much as possible to God in love. ADI. This is certainly a most beautiful painting. SO. Shall we now persuade those who you said were attacking us, that such a man is the painter of republics—the man whom we praised above before them, and at whom they were indignant because we entrusted the governing of the city to him? Do they hear this now with a more equitable mind? ADI. Most certainly, if they are wise. SO. In what part will they now oppose us? Will they assert that philosophers are not lovers of those things which truly exist, and of truth itself? ADI. That would be absurd. SO. Or will they perhaps deny that the nature of philosophers, which we have described, is intimately familiar with the best? ADI. Not even that. SO. What then? Will they refuse to believe that this nature, instructed in suitable duties, will be absolutely good and, above all others, closest to wisdom? Or will they prefer those whom we ourselves set aside? ADI. Not at all. SO. Will they still be angry with us when we say that unless the race of philosophers takes up the rudders of the city, there will be no rest from troubles for the city or the citizens, nor will the Republic which we are describing in speech ever emerge into the light? ADI. Perhaps less so. SO. Do you wish for us to say that they have been not just a little, but entirely softened and persuaded, lest perhaps out of shame they confess something else? ADI. Without a doubt. SO. Let them, therefore, be persuaded of this. But who would doubt this: that sons of kings and powerful men might be born as philosophers? ADI. No one. SO. But someone might add that even if such are born, it is necessary that they be corrupted. For we also concede that it is difficult to be kept pure from stains. But who will further add this: that in all time, out of all men, not even one could ever emerge whole and immaculate? ADI. No one would say that. SO. But truly, one man so constituted by nature, having found an obedient city, is sufficient to accomplish all these things which are now rejected as impossible. ADI. Sufficient indeed. SO. I suppose if some prince commands the laws and duties which we have described, it is not impossible that the citizens would be willing to obey them. ADI. Certainly not. SO. And is it a wonder, or impossible, that we should feel this, and others should feel the same as we do? ADI. No, I think not. SO. And that these things are best, if indeed they are possible, has been sufficiently disputed above, I believe. ADI. Sufficiently. SO. Therefore, from what has been said, it follows that the things we predicted about the making of laws will be best if they are carried out; they are difficult to do, yet not impossible. ADI. It follows clearly. SO. Since we have finally reached an end to these matters, we must now proceed to the rest: in what manner, namely, and by what disciplines and studies the guardians of this our Republic shall be instructed, and at what age each shall practice each thing. ADI. We must certainly speak of these things now. SO. I did not act very wisely when I left out the difficulty and trouble of marriages, the procreation of children, and the appointment of princes in the earlier parts. For I knew how envious a matter it would be and how difficult to do, even if entirely true. But now, nonetheless, we are compelled to go through these things; and those which pertain to women and children we have already finished; but those which pertain to princes seem to need to be run through again from the beginning. We said, if you remember, that they ought to be lovers of the city, tested in pleasures and pains, and that they should not be moved from this purpose by labors, nor by fear of dangers, nor by any other change. But he who is unable to do this must be rejected; while he who emerges everywhere sincere and incorrupt, like gold tested in the trial of fire, should be placed in charge of governing the city, and should be honored with gifts both while living and after death. Let the rewards be such as were commonly stated briefly in this running and, as it were, evasive discourse; for we were afraid to move things as they now are. ADI. You speak the truth. I remember it well. SO. For I feared, O friend, what I have dared to say. But let us now dare to assert this: that the most diligent guardians and the best must be philosophers. ADI. Let that be settled. SO. Notice how few such men there will be. For the parts of that nature which we said they must possess rarely concur in one person; for the most part, they are born separate. ADI. In what way do you say that? SO. Are you unaware that the same men are not usually teachable, mindful, ingenious, and sharp, and also brave and high-minded, so as to live moderately, tranquilly, and constantly? For such men are carried away by the fervor of their own sharpness wherever it happens; they are devoid of all stability and gravity. ADI. You speak the truth. SO. On the other hand, those stable dispositions of mind, entirely foreign to levity, in whose gravity one must especially trust—inasmuch as they are intrepid in war—are just as immobile when it comes to learning, and are dull. For they grow numb and yawn whenever they must be vigilant in contemplation. ADI. It is as you say. SO. But we said in the earlier parts that a prince ought to participate in the best of both natures. Otherwise, the supreme discipline should not be shown to him, nor should honors and magistracies be imparted. ADI. Rightly so. SO. Do you not think this will happen rarely? ADI. Very rarely indeed. SO. Therefore, the nature of the future prince must be examined in those things we mentioned above: in labors, fears, and pleasures. We add, moreover, what we omitted above: that it is necessary to exercise him in many disciplines, so that it may be clear whether he is capable of perceiving the greatest learning, or whether he fails, just as some tremble and fail in other works. ADI. It is indeed proper to investigate thus. But what do you call the "greatest learning"? SO. Do you remember in a way, when we had placed three parts in the soul, how we defined what justice, temperance, fortitude, and wisdom were by comparing them to one another? ADI.

# BOOK XXXI.

If I did not remember, I would hardly be worthy to hear the rest from you. **SOCRATES:** Do you also hold this in your memory: what was said before these things? **ADIMANTUS:** What indeed? **SOCRATES:** We certainly said, in a somewhat more extensive circuit of speech, that these things could be understood 
<margin>With a heavy Minerva <note>original: "Pingui Minerva" — a Latin idiom meaning "plainly" or "without subtlety," referring to common sense rather than refined intellect.</note></margin>
more precisely. But it would be more convenient to introduce demonstrations more consistent with the preceding ones. To which you replied that it was sufficient. And so then these things were treated "with a heavy Minerva," as it seemed to me. But if it pleases you, say so yourself. **ADIMANTUS:** It seemed moderately stated both to me and to the others. **SOCRATES:** But, O friend, a measure of such things that omits any part of the truth becomes immeasurable. For nothing that is deficient is the measure of anything. Although it sometimes seems to some that a matter has been treated sufficiently at once, and that there is no need for a longer inquiry. **ADIMANTUS:** This happens to very many because of laziness. **SOCRATES:** This vice ought to be most foreign to a guardian of the city and the laws. **ADIMANTUS:** That is consistent. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, my friend, a longer circuit must be traveled by him: and no less effort must be spent in learning than in exercising: otherwise, as we said a little while ago, he will never arrive at the end of the highest and most deeply necessary learning. **ADIMANTUS:** Are these not the greatest things? Is there something else besides justice and the others we have recounted that is more excellent? **SOCRATES:** Certainly more outstanding. And indeed, it is not fitting to look at a mere sketch of these things, such as we see now: but to comprehend their absolute reason. Is it not ridiculous to place all one's zeal in the smallest matters, and to strive obstinately so that they are arranged as diligently and purely as possible, but in the greatest matters to think a light effort is enough? **ADIMANTUS:** Entirely ridiculous. But do you think anyone will be content without inquiring from you now: what is that discipline which you call the greatest, and what is it concerned with? **SOCRATES:** Not at all. But ask it yourself: although I think you have heard it many times. Now, however, either you do not notice, or rather you intend to trouble 
<margin>On the excellence and utility of the Idea in knowing things.</margin>
me with your objections. Which is what I rather think. For you have often heard that the **Idea of the Good** is the greatest discipline. By this, indeed, both just things and other virtues, when they have been used, become useful and conducive. And know that I want to say almost this: and this besides: that we do not know the Idea itself sufficiently. But if we are truly ignorant of it: even if we knew other things as much as possible without it, know that there will be no utility for us from the others: just as nothing would profit us which we possessed without the good. Or do you think it is a great thing to possess all other things without the possession of the good, rather than to understand all other things without the understanding of the good itself and the beautiful? **ADIMANTUS:** Certainly not. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, to many, the good 
<margin>The opinion that pleasure is the highest good is an ancient one, from the position of Epicurus.</margin>
seems to be pleasure; to the more refined, it seems to be wisdom. **ADIMANTUS:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Furthermore, you also know this, that those who think wisdom is the good, if they are asked: "What wisdom specifically?" they are unable to declare it: but are finally forced to say it is the "wisdom of the good." **ADIMANTUS:** What a ridiculous response. **SOCRATES:** Why should it not seem ridiculous: if, while they reproach us for being ignorant of the good, they speak of the good to us again as if we understood it! For they say the good is the "wisdom of the good": as if we knew what they were saying when they pronounce the name of the good. **ADIMANTUS:** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES:** But those who define the good as pleasure, do they err any less than the others? Are they not also forced to admit that there are bad pleasures? **ADIMANTUS:** Greatly so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, they are forced to admit that the same things are both good and bad. Are they not? **ADIMANTUS:** Clearly. **SOCRATES:** Is it not clear that many and very great ambiguities arise concerning this? **ADIMANTUS:** It is clear. **SOCRATES:** And is this not also evident: that many would choose to do, possess, and seem to men to have those things which seem just and honorable, even if they are not: but no one thinks it is enough for himself to possess things that only *seem* good; rather, everyone seeks those things which are truly good: and in these matters, everyone despises mere opinion? **ADIMANTUS:** Most especially. **SOCRATES:** Every soul indeed seeks the good: and for its sake does all things, divining that it is something: yet it doubts: it can neither sufficiently comprehend what it is, nor cling to a stable faith, such as it uses concerning other things; and therefore, it fails in other things as well when it proceeds to judge what is useful. Should we say that those most excellent men in the city, to whom we commit everything, ought to be similarly blind concerning a matter of such a nature and such magnitude? **ADIMANTUS:** Least of all. **SOCRATES:** I think, indeed, that he who does not know—as now almost happens—in what way just and honorable things are good, can hardly present himself as a guardian worthy of much. But I prophesy that no one will know those things before he knows the good sufficiently. **ADIMANTUS:** You prophesy skillfully. **SOCRATES:** Our Republic will therefore be perfectly disposed if a guardian skilled in these things rules it. **ADIMANTUS:** It must be so. But you, O Socrates, do you say the good itself is knowledge, or pleasure, or something else besides these? **SOCRATES:** I have long since discovered, Adimantus, that it would not be enough for you if I reported the opinions of others. **ADIMANTUS:** It does not seem fitting to me, O Socrates, to be able to report the opinions of others, but not one's own: especially for a man who has spent so much time in these matters. **SOCRATES:** Do you think it is fitting that one should speak of those things which he does not know as if he were knowing? **ADIMANTUS:** In no way as if knowing: but as if bringing forth what he feels from opinion. **SOCRATES:** Do you not know that all opinions 
<margin>On right opinion, which is also blind.</margin>
without knowledge are base: of which the best are blind? Or do you think those who, without understanding, have a right opinion about something, differ from those who, although they are blind, nevertheless walk on the right path? **ADIMANTUS:** Not at all. **SOCRATES:** Do you wish, then, to contemplate base, blind, and crooked things, when it is permitted to hear clear and beautiful things from others? **GLAUCON:** Come, by Jove, Socrates, do not stop when you have almost reached the goal. For it will suffice for us if, in the same way you treated justice and temperance and the others, you also treat the good. **SOCRATES:** To me also, 
<margin>The question of the good is most difficult // The son of the good, that is, the sun.</margin>
O friend, it will greatly suffice. But I fear lest my strength fail: and I, having dared beyond my strength, appear more inept and move the listeners to laughter. But, O happy men: let us dismiss for the present what the good itself is. For it seems to me to be beyond our present contemplation. But what appears to be the son of the good itself, and most like it: if it pleases you, I will say: if not, I will dismiss it. **GLAUCON:** Come, speak; but declare the father afterward...

He distinguishes between mere opinion and actual knowledge, eventually proposing to describe the "son of the good" (the sun) as an analogy.</summary>
