# DIALOGUE VI. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

[Signature: F]

...you will [continue]. SOCRATES: I truly wish that I were able to explain, and you to perceive, not only the "offspring" of the good as we do now, but the Good itself. For the present, then, receive this "offspring" and child of the Good itself. Take care, however, that I do not unintentionally deceive you by giving a false account of this child. GLAUCON: We shall take care as best we can. Just speak. SOCRATES: I shall speak, indeed, if we first recap and confirm among ourselves what was mentioned above and has been said many times elsewhere. GLAUCON: What things? SOCRATES: We say that there are many beautiful things, and many good things, and we distinguish each of them in our speech. GLAUCON: We certainly do. SOCRATES: And yet we also posit a "Beauty itself" and a "Good itself"; and similarly, for all those things which we previously set down as many, we now posit a single "Idea" <note>original: "ideā"; referring to Plato's Theory of Forms</note> for each, as if there were only one, and we call it that which each thing truly "is." GLAUCON: These things are true. SOCRATES: And we say that the many things are seen, but not known by the intellect; whereas the Ideas are known by the intellect, but not seen. GLAUCON: That is entirely so. SOCRATES: By what power among the many we possess do we perceive the things that are visible to the eyes? GLAUCON: By sight. SOCRATES: And do we not perceive what is heard by hearing, and all sensible things by the other senses? GLAUCON: Why not? SOCRATES: Have you ever noticed how the Creator <note>original: "auctor"; the Demiurge or craftsman of the senses</note> of the senses fashioned a power of the highest perfection for the purpose of seeing and being seen? GLAUCON: Not sufficiently. SOCRATES: Consider it this way. Do hearing and voice require another kind <margin>Concerning the medium between the sense and the sensible</margin> of thing in order for the one to hear and the other to be heard? If this third thing were absent, would the one not hear and the other not be heard? GLAUCON: Not at all. SOCRATES: I think, indeed, that many other senses—not to say all—require no such thing. Or can you find any such power? GLAUCON: Not at all. SOCRATES: But do you not notice that sight itself, and that which is subject to sight, require such a thing? GLAUCON: In what way? SOCRATES: Even if sight is present in the eyes and they are directed toward looking, and even if color is present, unless a third kind of thing is also present, which is naturally suited for this purpose, the sight will see nothing and the colors will be unable to be seen. GLAUCON: What is this thing you speak of? SOCRATES: That which you call light. GLAUCON: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: <margin>Light is the medium between sight and color.</margin> Truly, the power of the visible itself and the potential of the seer are joined together by a bond far more honorable than all other pairings—provided that light is not to be held in low esteem. GLAUCON: It is far from being held in low esteem. SOCRATES: Which of the celestial gods do you think is the cause of this? Whose light makes our sight see so perfectly and makes the objects seen by our eyes? GLAUCON: The same one you and others think of. Surely you are asking about the Sun. <margin>The Sun as the intermediary between sight and the visible.</margin> SOCRATES: Indeed, sight stands in relation to this god in a certain way. GLAUCON: How? SOCRATES: Sight is not the sun; nor is the eye, in which sight resides, the sun. GLAUCON: Certainly not. SOCRATES: But of all the organs of the senses, it is the one most like the sun. GLAUCON: Very much so. SOCRATES: And does it not preserve the power it has as something infused from the sun? GLAUCON: Entirely. SOCRATES: Therefore, the sun is not sight, but it is the cause of sight, and it is seen by sight. GLAUCON: Quite clearly. SOCRATES: You may say that this is what I call the "child of the Good," <margin>How the Good begot a son similar to itself.</margin> which the Good itself begot as an analogue to itself: so that what the Good is in the intelligible realm <note>the world of thought and Ideas</note> in relation to the intellect and the things understood, the sun is in the visible realm in relation to sight and the things seen. GLAUCON: In what way? Explain more broadly. SOCRATES: Furthermore, when the eyes are not turned toward things whose colors are illuminated and shown by the glow of day, but toward things touched by the rays of night, they grow dim and seem almost blind, as if pure sight were not in them. GLAUCON: So it happens. SOCRATES: But whenever they look at things the sun illustrates, they see clearly; and sight appears to be in those same eyes. GLAUCON: It is so. SOCRATES: Think of the soul in the same way. When it clings to that in which truth and Being itself shine forth, it understands and knows it, and appears to possess intellect. But when it turns toward that which is mixed with darkness—that which is born and perishes—its edge is blunted; it wanders among various opinions and seems to be devoid of mind. GLAUCON: So it appears. SOCRATES: That, therefore, which provides truth to the things understood and gives the power of understanding to the one who understands, you must say is the "Idea of the Good," the cause of the knowledge and truth perceived through the intellect. Since these two things, knowledge and truth, are so beautiful, if you judge the Good itself to be something else and even more beautiful than these, you will judge rightly. And just as it is proper to think of light and sight as having a certain "sun-like" quality <margin>As sight is to the sun, so the soul and intellect are to the Good and the intelligible.</margin> but not to think they are the sun itself, so it is right to think that knowledge and truth have a certain "Good-like" quality, but not that they are the Good itself. For the majesty of the Good itself is even more venerable. GLAUCON: You speak of an inestimable beauty, if it provides knowledge and truth but surpasses them in its own grace. For surely you do not say that pleasure is the Good. SOCRATES: Hush, please! <note>original: "Bona verba"; a formula to avoid ill-omened speech</note> Rather, contemplate its image more clearly in this way. GLAUCON: How? SOCRATES: You will say, I think, that the sun provides to visible things not only the power of being seen, but also their generation, growth, and nourishment—though the sun itself is not "generation." GLAUCON: How could it be? SOCRATES: In the same way, you may say that the Good gives to the things known not only the fact that they are known, but also their very being and essence—though the Good itself is not "essence," but beyond essence, surpassing it in dignity and power. GLAUCON: By Apollo! <note>original: "Aedepol"; a Latin oath</note> This is a marvelous transcendence. SOCRATES: You are certainly the cause of this, for you compelled me to reveal what I thought about these things. GLAUCON: Do not stop yet; finish the comparison with the sun, if anything has been left out. SOCRATES: Indeed, many things are being left out. GLAUCON: Do not omit even the smallest thing. SOCRATES: I suspect many things will remain; nevertheless, as many as can be related at present, I shall not willingly leave behind. GLAUCON: Please do so. SOCRATES: Think of these as being two: one reigning over the intelligible class and realm, the other over the visible—I will not say "the heavens" lest I seem to play on words. You have, then, these two species: the visible and the intelligible. GLAUCON: I have them. SOCRATES: It is as if you took a line cut into two unequal portions, and divided each part again in the same ratio, so that now you have the visible genus...

# ARGUMENT OF THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE

...visible, and the other intelligible; now divide each again into two parts according to their clarity and obscurity. In the visible category, one portion will contain images. By images, I mean first shadows, then reflections appearing in water, and those in dense, smooth, polished, and bright bodies, and everything of that kind, if you follow me.
GLAUCON: I follow.
SOCRATES: The other portion comprises those things of which these are the likenesses: namely, the animals around us, plants, and the entire world of manufactured objects.
GLAUCON: I accept that.
SOCRATES: Would you also say that this category is divided according to truth and lack of truth? Just as the world of opinion <note>original: "opinione"</note> relates to the world of knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note>, so does the likeness relate to the object it resembles?
GLAUCON: Most certainly.
SOCRATES: Now consider the division of the intelligible.
GLAUCON: In what way?
SOCRATES: In one part, the soul is forced to investigate by using those things previously divided as images, proceeding from hypotheses not toward a first principle, but toward a conclusion. In the other part, the soul moves from a hypothesis toward an unhypothesized first principle; it does not use the images used in the other part, but moves through the forms <note>Platonic Ideas</note> themselves and by means of them.
GLAUCON: I do not quite understand what you are saying.
SOCRATES: You will understand more easily through this: I think you are aware that those who deal with geometry, arithmetic, and similar arts, hypothesize the even and the odd, figures, three types of angles, and the like in each of their arguments. Having laid these down as if they were obvious to everyone, they think no further account of them is required. Starting from here, they descend through the rest and finally reach the goal they were seeking.
GLAUCON: I know that well.
SOCRATES: Then you also know that they use these visible forms and speak about them, though they are not thinking of these, but rather of the things they resemble—the "Square Itself" or the "Diameter Itself"—not the ones they draw. In other cases, they use these shapes they describe and mold (which have their own shadows and reflections in water) as images, seeking to behold those things which can only be perceived by thought <note>original: "cogitatione"</note>.
GLAUCON: You speak the truth.
SOCRATES: This was the type of the intelligible category I was speaking of, where the soul is forced to use hypotheses in its investigation, not going to the first principle because it is unable to rise above hypotheses. It uses as images those very things which were imitated by the lower levels; these are esteemed and distinguished by opinion as if they were clear representations of the higher truths.
GLAUCON: I understand you are speaking of what happens in geometry and its sister arts.
SOCRATES: Now understand that by the second part of the intelligible, I mean that which reason itself attains by the power of dialectic <note>original: "demonstrandi facultatem"</note>. It does not treat hypotheses as first principles, but truly as hypotheses—as steps and starting points—until it reaches that which is unhypothesized, the first principle of the universe. Having touched that, it turns back to cling to those things which depend on that principle, and so descends to a conclusion, using nothing sensible at all, but moving from forms, through forms, and toward forms.
GLAUCON: I understand at last, though not as fully as I would wish. You seem to be proposing a great task: you intend to distinguish that part of true existence and the intelligible world, which we contemplate through the science of dialectic, as being clearer than that which we investigate through the "arts." In those arts, hypotheses are taken as principles, and those who study them are forced to look with the mind rather than the senses. However, because they do not ascend to a first principle but search from hypotheses, they do not seem to you to possess true intellect <note>original: "intellectum"</note> regarding these things, even though they are intelligible when joined to a first principle. You seem to call the habit of geometricians and the like "thought" <note>original: "cogitationem"</note> rather than "intellect," as if thought held a middle place between opinion and intellect.
SOCRATES: You have understood perfectly. Now, apply four states of the soul to these four divisions: **Intelligence** <note>original: "Intelligentiam" / Noesis</note> for the highest; **Thought** <note>original: "cogitationem" / Dianoia</note> for the second; **Faith** <note>original: "fidem" / Pistis</note> for the third; and **Likeness** or **Imagination** <note>original: "imaginationē" / Eikasia</note> for the last. Arrange them in a ratio, so that they participate in clarity just as their objects participate in truth.
GLAUCON: I understand, I agree, and I arrange them as you command.

***

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for the Seventh Dialogue: On Justice.

WISE MEN endowed with divine genius have turned all the soul's devotion away from earthly things toward the celestial, from the movable to the immovable, and from those things which are sensed to those which surpass the senses, as much as they were able. Considering the machine of the world to be both one and marvelously ordered—yet unable to exist by itself since it is composed of diverse parts and is subject to change—they rightly recognized that it depends on another. It depends, I say, on one most wise Being, who makes one work out of many, wisely orders that unity everywhere, and rules it powerfully. This work is vast and manifold, moving in a perpetual and most rapid—yet never wandering—revolution. He leads each thing most kindly toward the Good, running with both wonderful convenience and ease. For this reason, by a certain common conception, they have agreed that God exists, the One...

# PREFACE TO THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE.
## FO. CCL.

of the universe, a powerful, wise, and merciful King. Him, earthly kings and governors of republics ought to imitate to the best of their powers. After this common conception of God, they began to proceed more clearly and closely toward God by a twofold path: one by way of negation, the other by way of reference. For by the former, they proved by arguing what the Good itself—that is, what God—is *not*, namely that He is nothing of those things perceived by the senses, nor of those things comprehended by the mind. In the latter path, however, by referring creatures to the Creator and, conversely, the Creator to His creatures, they devised the means by which the Creator makes and perfects each thing, and how creatures may either relate to Him, imitate Him, or attain Him. Our Plato shows that the intellect of the philosopher proceeds this far both in the *Parmenides* and confirms it in the preceding book. Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 5th–6th century) who merged Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine; Ficino heavily synchronized his work with Plato's.</note> also greatly approves of this. I say it proceeds this far, partly by a certain ray infused into the mind from the beginning, and partly by the approaching light of divinity constantly illuminating the mind.

But as for what the Good itself is in its own essence—that is, the divine substance—as he shows both in the *Parmenides* and here, no one can attain it through such paths. It is only through these paths that one finally arrives where the Divine Good, out of its sole benevolence, shapes its approaching lover with its own light, warms them with its heat, and transforms the mind with its power; then at last the mind knows God when it has itself already been made god <note>original: "facta sit deus" - referring to the concept of 'theosis' or deification through divine union.</note>. This is indeed signified in his Epistles as well.

Only after the philosopher has contemplated God governing the heavens will he, and he alone, be able to govern earthly things by divine guidance. In this matter, Plato praises Minos for seeking laws from Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> through contemplation before promulgating them to men. I pass over how much many praise Scipio, who approached the republic with Jove as his teacher. What shall I say of Numa Pompilius, who governed the city with religious laws? Did not the Mosaic laws, by which the people of God were divinely governed, come to men through the teaching of God Himself? Here Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle.</note> relates that the Indian philosophers held that mysteries, in which truth is contained, cannot be rightly or happily administered either privately or publicly without a divine rule, and one demonstrated by God. Because the Egyptians also discovered this same truth, they granted the rudders of the kingdom only to philosophers, and specifically to those who were perfected and moreover initiated into sacred rites. And they thought to such an extent that nothing could be done happily without divine aid, that they inaugurated all public affairs with sacred vows. Furthermore, they asserted that nothing could be understood without a certain divine inspiration, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who emphasized theurgy and ritual.</note> reports: so much so that among them, all books of philosophy were ascribed to the name of the god Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, as if they were not the inventions of men, but of God. Timaeus also signifies this, saying that philosophy is a divine gift. In the *Protagoras* and the *Statesman*, he teaches that civil skill is also a divine gift.

And to return to this seventh book, no one is admitted to the governing of this republic of his unless it is established that they have received both gifts divinely, as much by a certain divine nature as by education. Such a person alone he calls everywhere a legitimate citizen and a philosopher. But why does he say there is need for a divine gift for this? I pass over other reasons. It is clearly because, since it is most difficult for anyone to govern himself happily, it is certainly impossible to happily organize a city—composed of so many and diverse elements, and which daily faces innumerable and uncertain accidents—without God, the author of happiness. Hence it happened that various cities recognized a certain specific deity as a patron. Plato wishes the governor of the city to be the vicar and interpreter of this deity, who, like a deity, contemplates divine things and provides for human things from that source. Therefore, he utterly expels evil men from the republic as being entirely devoid of the divine gift. He accepts only the good. Yet not even all of them. For he calls those ignorant of theology "blind" and "dreamers," inasmuch as they take the images of things for the things themselves; and he deems it foolish to entrust the guardianship of the city to the blind and the dreaming.

However, theologians who as yet possess no experience in human affairs are not admitted to conducting public business until he has accustomed them to handling private and lighter matters. Meanwhile, he concludes that no magistracy should be given to anyone unless his life is better than the magistracy itself, and he neither seeks nor even desires the office.

But where Plato, in educating the civil philosopher, sets forth the image of the cave, and of chains, and of a certain light, and of shadows and water: understand the **Cave** to be this world which we see, if compared to the invisible world. The **Chain** is the human body, or rather the perturbation of the soul binding it to the body. The **Shadows** are all things that move the senses. For these are the shadows of true things, that is, of the **Ideas**. When he says that the soul does not descend from the invisible world to the visible, nor conversely ascend, without sudden offense <note>A sense of shock or disorientation.</note>, you can take this in two ways according to the Platonic manner: either in this life, when one passes without a middle stage from this human study to the supreme study of divine things and back; or between this life and the next. That is, when an impure soul migrates from the darkness of the body to the divine light, under which it first grows dim and is tormented, or when descending from the divine light into an elemental body, it is long blinded and troubled.

Remember that it is the property of light to create and demonstrate all things. And this light is threefold: divine, intellectual, and visible. The **Divine** is called the Sun of both suns. The **Intellectual** is named the Angelic Sun, the Sun of the mundane sun. Finally, the **Visible** light is the celestial sun and its splendor. Just as the splendor spreading itself from the celestial sun through all things is the image and act of the sun, so also the light within the sun is the image and act of the angelic mind. Then, light in the angel is the act and image of the divine light. And just as visible light is received only in a transparent nature, so the invisible is received in a perceptive nature. <meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the nature of light and its relationship to the divine, likely serving as a commentary or introduction to Book VII of Plato's Republic (the Allegory of the Cave).</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE VII

The act of divine and angelic intelligence shines perpetually through the solar window to our eyes, and from there it is diffused through transparent materials that are, so to speak, compatible with it. However, do not doubt that this light appears: know that it is an image of the non-apparent light, and that this light is not a body <note>i.e., not a physical substance</note>. For it penetrates bodies without causing harm or being divided. Likewise, it does not become a specific quality of a composite body. Otherwise, it would require the specific quality of the elements—either hot or cold—in the body it enters; and when the sun withdrew, it would remain in the transparent object for a time. Furthermore, it is not bound by physical dimensions. For it does not arrive over time, nor does it illuminate one part now and another part later. Add to this that it fills a wide space without dissipating itself, and conversely, in a moment, it collects itself into a narrow space without any constriction of itself or its container. It is not properly corporeal, but a medium between the incorporeal and the corporeal, and truly a specific quality of the heavens. Its nature is very close to incorporeal things, yet it is shared with the elements, provided they are transparent—resembling the heavens in this very transparency. I say that light comes first to transparent things, then heat; but to solid things, heat comes first, while light does not appear until they are reduced to a transparent nature through heat. However, it does not pour into opaque bodies where an earthy nature dominates. This is not because it cannot penetrate them—since it penetrates crystal, which is more solid than many opaque things—but because an earthy nature, being most foreign to a heavenly nature, cannot be capable of a heavenly quality. Nevertheless, it communicates heat to opaque things, as I said, though heat is not as specific to the heavens as light is. For because the heavens shine, they are therefore hot. 

Now, why the light diffused from the heavens into our transparent world should be called an "image of the sun" appears from this: it is the common and specific origin of all images. For the images of things spring forth under its brightness; it is itself an image so powerful that it appears not only when it bounces off a mirroring body, but even when it leaps forth from the sun—which is not at all the case with other images. Yet all images are incorporeal, since they pour themselves through the whole in a moment, and many can exist in the same point without mutual confusion. Therefore, light is also incorporeal, and it is by its power that this is achieved. Consequently, in a moment, it carries with it the ray of the sun, the act of light, and the force of heat. Through light, it reflects the clarity of divine and angelic intelligence; through heat, it reflects the affection of the will and of charity <note>Latin: *charitas*, meaning divine love</note> in both. Since the higher beings, like craftsmen, perform their works through will rather than through intelligence, this visible ray—flowing from their invisible ray—rightly acts upon the individual things they beget through heat rather than through light. Or rather, it acts through light upon the spiritual images of things, but through heat upon corporeal qualities. And this heat depends on light just as in divine matters all things are represented ideally through the intellect, but all things are generated through the affection rising therefrom. 

We, therefore, being warned by this, should expel earthy affections far from us if our earthy nature does not receive heavenly light, so that we may be filled with divine light. And if the lowest body does not receive the first light unless it first grows hot and is rendered similar to it: behold, let us also, the lowest of minds, first burn with love for the First Mind, so that being purified by love and made similar, we may then shine divinely and rejoice in the full light. 

But let us now touch upon the rest of this seventh book. Since there is a triple light, as we said—namely, the visible, the intellectual above sight, and the divine above intellect—Plato therefore mentions light here in three stages: in the cave, in the night, and in the day, signifying those three lights. Three times also he mentions water: in the cave, in the night, and in the day. For just as light both creates and demonstrates all things, so water washes all things and represents them. The first signifies morals, the second contemplation. And he carries out both through three stages. Indeed, through the moral stage, he washes and purifies three times: first by cutting away the fertile impulses through the "civil virtues"; second by uprooting them through the "purgatory virtues"; third by most absolutely moderating the first impulses through the virtues of a soul already purified—whence it may now reach the "exemplary virtues" which are in God, especially through contemplation. Of this contemplation there are three stages, which the water named three times refers to, insofar as it represents intelligence by reflecting images. 

For divine things are seen to be represented in three "waters," so to speak. First, though more confusedly, in physical reasons; second, more distinctly in mathematical ones; third, most clearly in the entirely absolute metaphysical ones. Plato calls physical forms "entirely material" because they require both common and specific matter and cannot be thought of without it. But he calls mathematical forms "not so material" because they do not need specific matter, but either common matter only (like dimensions) or none at all (like numbers); and these can be thought of without matter. Finally, he considers divine forms to be "entirely immaterial" and the "true things"—of which mathematical forms are images, and natural things are shadows. This is a Pythagorean mystery. 

Therefore, when he noticed that Thales, Democritus, and Anaxagoras were as negligent in divine matters as they were diligent in natural ones—while on the contrary Pherecydes, Pythagoras, and all the Pythagoreans, the princes of mathematicians, stood out as the highest theologians and were divine in their character—he rightly concluded, partly by reason and partly by experience, that a curious study of natural things very often turns the soul away from divine things. For this reason, Solomon also judged this a "most evil occupation" and called those miserable who occupied themselves too much in it. Socrates detests the same people in the *Phaedo*—those, I say, who curiously refer the causes of natural effects only to certain elemental qualities and rest in such a beginning and end, seeking neither the highest beginning nor the end of the universe. Wherefore, this Seventh Book, where it leads the soul to the Highest Good and the Sun (that is, God) and the divine ideas (like stars) by appropriate steps, makes no mention of natural skill in the ascent itself. Instead, it brings into the midst certain mathematical steps that lead more conveniently to divine things, among which two are pure: for Arithmetic deals with pure numbers, and Geome... <note>The text cuts off mid-word: *Geometria* (Geometry)</note>

# ARGUMENT FOR THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE.
## FO. CCLI.
### F ii

...three concerning pure dimensions. There are, however, three mixed levels. For **Music** adds voices and movements to numbers, pertaining chiefly to the sense of hearing. **Stereometry** <note>The measurement of solid figures or three-dimensional space.</note> adds weights to dimensions. **Astronomy** measures the celestial spheres and their movements through numbers and dimensions. 

Plato uses natural expertise in descent rather than ascent, as he teaches in the *Timaeus*, the *Philebus*, the *Parmenides*, and often elsewhere. For in the descent, he wishes natural principles to be demonstrated through the divine causes of natural things. But in the ascent, he thinks that through an anxious care for natural things—as if they were far removed from the divine—the soul is diverted from them rather than converted toward them. 

Altogether, he counts all actions as nothing, even if they seem most honorable, unless they lead to the imitation and attainment of the **Divine Good**. Similarly, he either neglects all speculations unless they contribute to finding the Divine Good, or he even detests them if they divert us from it in any way. Accordingly, he wants the whole study of philosophy to be a conversion from sensible things <note>Things perceived by the senses.</note> to intelligible things <note>Things understood by the intellect.</note>, and an ascent to the supreme light of the intelligibles themselves. 

He says that just as the sight stands in relation to the highest of visible things—that is, the **Sun**—so the intellect stands in relation to the highest light of the intelligibles—namely, **God**. Therefore, just as the sun generates the eye and, in generating it, bestows the power of seeing, and continually provides the act of seeing to that which is generated; so God both creates the intellect and, in creating it, provides the power of understanding, and continually provides the act of understanding to that which is created. 

Again, just as there is no need for anything to be done by art regarding the eye except to purge it and turn it; so philosophy provides only two things regarding the intellect: **purging** it (both from disturbances and from false opinions) and **turning** it (through prayers and exhortation) from sensible forms to the intellectual forms innate within us, and through these to the intelligible forms—that is, the **Ideas**. Again, through the Ideas to the Divine Mind, by which the Ideas are comprehended; and finally from this to the **Divine Good**, the principle and light of the Ideas. 

When, therefore, he says the soul is raised from the lamp to the moon, and from the moon to the sun, he means it is elevated from natural forms to mathematical ones, and finally from these to divine ones: not indeed by teaching—for divine things, as is handed down in the *Epistles*, cannot be taught—but rather by purging and converting. For in these ways, just as the sun, which is the light of visible things, shows visible things to the eye; so the **Good** itself, which is the light of intelligible things, opens up the things to be understood to the intellect. But concerning these matters, we have written most extensively in our *Theology*. 

Therefore, no one should wonder that Plato rarely uses the order of writing for instruction, but always for purging and exhortation—that is, for conversion. After this, note that from the number of things that are sensed, those especially excite the intelligence which are not clearly discerned from their opposites by the sense; therefore, they need a discerning intelligence. 

Likewise, **Numbers** are not corporeal. Indeed, number is nothing other than unity repeated. But **Unity** is not a body. For it is not divided into parts; and if it is imagined to be divided, it is not cut, but rather multiplied. It is multiplied, I say, into itself, not into any parts. For any part is usually smaller than the whole. But no unity is either greater or smaller than another unity. And this very unity and number raise us to an incorporeal essence; similarly also **Figures**, the true reason for which is found in the mind rather than in the body. 

Similarly, **Astronomy** seems to investigate the reason of the Mover from the order of heaven. Plato denies that he is an astronomer who looks up at the heights but does not look through the heaven itself to what is above the heaven; especially because celestial things, since they do not fulfill a complete order, undoubtedly depend on some higher and complete order. He also mocks the **Musician** unless he withdraws from the consonance of the voice to the intellectual reason of consonance. 

Finally, he places **Dialectic** (that is, Metaphysics or Theology) before all faculties, as it leads all others and uses the ministry of each for its own duty. Its duty is to progress through the whole breadth of what is called **Being**, and to betake itself to the **Good** itself, the cause of all being: and in that very order of beings to define what each thing is, assigning the reason of each essence, and demonstrating what follows from any essence. 

He judges the other faculties to be servile in comparison to the nobility of this one. For they either decline toward the opinions of men, or toward the generations and compositions of inferior things, or toward the cultivation of those things which are produced; or at least, even if they raise themselves toward incorporeal things as far as they are able, they nevertheless dream about them in a certain way. Such, he says, are the mathematical disciplines. 

But soon he joins two kinds: **Essence** and **Generation**. He considers that **Intelligence** pertains to the former, and **Opinion** to the latter. Again, within intelligence, he says **Science** follows essence and pertains to the Dialectician; while **Thought** follows essence and belongs to the Mathematician. In opinion, he similarly counts **Faith** <note>In the sense of "conviction" or "belief" regarding the physical world.</note> and **Imagination**; and through the former, bodies are perceived, while through the latter, the images and shadows of bodies are perceived. 

Then he concludes that the other faculties are blind without Dialectic. And that they, together with Dialectic, are moreover vain unless one clearly knows the **Idea of the Good** itself; and through it, one knows how to discern true goods from false ones in individual cases. But he who is ignorant of the reason of the Good is both mocked and disturbed here in dreams, and descending to the underworld, is mocked and vexed even more. 

He adds that the man is "lame" who is unfit and unskilled for either action or speculation. For this reason, he chooses those for governing who are both fit by nature for both and sufficiently instructed by discipline. Meanwhile, note that the **Liar** is to be excluded from the Republic as if he were maimed and mutilated. He calls him a liar both who lies to others by deliberate effort, and who lies to himself through ignorance. 

Remember also that the labors of the soul are heavier than those of the body; therefore, one must learn in youth, and the liberal disciplines must be taught far from servitude. Yet **Dialectic** is not to be handed over to youths. The *Philebus* also teaches us this. For as is distinguished in the *Phaedrus* as well, two leaders are within us all: namely, an innate desire for pleasures, and a certain opinion acquired through education, dictating that honorable and just things defined for us by the laws must be preserved in all things. These two leaders very often pull us in opposite directions. Since, however, the faculty of disputing...

# BOOK VII.

should be handed down to young men, it weakens their sense of honor, from which they turn out intemperate, and indeed both proud and impious; as one reads also in the *Philebus* and the *Laws*. <note>Plato’s dialogues *Philebus* and *Laws* discuss the dangers of misapplied dialectic or logic.</note> Therefore, before the thirtieth year of their age, they are to be instructed in the mathematical arts: and likewise exercised in public affairs at intervals. But when they have reached thirty, they are to be admitted to dialectic <note>The art of logical discussion and investigation of truth.</note>, yet in such a way that they are again recalled to public actions at intervals. You should know that he names the industry of discoursing "dialectic" from its form; "logic" from its beginning; and "metaphysics" and "theology" from its end. Know also that men are called to such a divine end of dialectic in the fiftieth year of their age: because there is need of a purified and serene mind for the intuition of divine things. Meanwhile, take note here of what we frequently use both here and in theology, that three things are noted by Plato: the ray, the stream, and the light. The ray indeed is proper and naturally implanted in individual minds just as in the eyes. But the light is common to all eyes. Finally, the divine light presides over the common light of all minds, just as the light in the sun presides over the equally common light of the eyes. He concludes that after the citizen has contemplated the light of the Good itself, both through the ray naturally implanted in him and through the light of the same further illustrated, he ought to govern the city according to the exemplar of the Good itself to the best of his strength.

### SEVENTH DIALOGUE ON JUSTICE.

->SOCRATES<-

<margin>He devises the cave so that we may contemplate beings compared to it.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'P' containing a scene of a man sitting at a desk or table, possibly a scholar or scribe.</image-desc>AFTER THESE THINGS, contemplate our nature in respect to its enlightenment and ignorance by a certain image. Imagine a subterranean cave, whose entrance lies open toward the light through the whole length of the cavern. In it are men nurtured from childhood, their necks and legs so bound that they are forced to remain immobile, and to look only toward the front: for they are unable to turn their heads around, being restricted by the bonds. But behind their backs, a light of fire is suspended above and far off: and between the fire and the bound men, a path lies above: along which a small wall is constructed, much like the screens placed before performers of wonders who devise miracles, over which they show their marvels before the eyes of the spectators. GLAUCON. So be it. SOCRATES. Imagine again men carrying various vessels and artifacts behind the wall, projecting above the wall: and stone statues of men and other animals, and wooden images, fashioned in various ways. And as is natural, some of those carrying these things are silent, others are speaking. GLAUCON. What portentous fictions these are. SOCRATES. But they are similar to us. For first of all, do you think those men see anything else, either of themselves or of the men next to them, besides the shadows which fall from the fire onto the opposite part of the cave? GLAUCON. Nothing else: if they have never been able to move their heads in their lives. SOCRATES. What about the things being carried past, do they not see only the shadows? GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. If therefore they were allowed to speak to one another, would they not think they were naming these things which they saw before them? GLAUCON. It must be so. SOCRATES. And if an echo resonated from the opposite side of the prison, as often as any of the passers-by spoke, do you think they would believe anything else was speaking except the shadows passing by? GLAUCON. Not by Jove <note>original: "per Iovem" - a common oath to Jupiter/Zeus.</note>. SOCRATES. Altogether then, such people would judge nothing to be true except the shadows of fabricated things. GLAUCON. It is absolutely necessary. SOCRATES. On the contrary, now observe what the release from their bonds and the cure of their ignorance would be like. Surely if someone were released, and forced suddenly to rise, to turn his neck, to walk, to look at the light itself: he would feel pain immediately: nor because of the brightness would he be able to look upon those things whose shadows he saw before. Then if someone said to him, that he had seen trifles before: but that now he is closer to real things and looks toward more true things: and pointing out each of the passers-by, asked what it was, do you not think he would be at a loss, and would believe that the things he saw before were truer than those now being shown? GLAUCON. Much more so. SOCRATES. And if he forced him to look at the light: do you not think his eyes would be afflicted with pain: and he would turn his eyes back to those things which he had easily seen before, thinking them more certain than those suddenly offered? GLAUCON. Truly so. SOCRATES. But if someone dragged him by force up the steep and arduous path, and did not let go until he had dragged him to the light of the sun, do you not think he would feel pain and take it badly while being snatched away? And when he has been brought out to the light, his eyes being filled with brightness, he would be dazed: and able to see nothing of these things which are now considered true by men? GLAUCON. Certainly nothing suddenly. SOCRATES. There is need of habituation first, if he is to look at things above. And first he will more easily look at shadows. After these, the images of men and other things in the waters. Then later he will more easily contemplate the things that are in heaven and heaven itself by night, while he looks at the light of the stars and the moon, than if he were to look at the sun itself by day and the glare of the sun. GLAUCON. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. And so at last he will look up at the sun itself: no longer in the waters and in a foreign region will he see its likeness: but he will behold it as it is in itself in its own place: and he will be able to know what sort of thing it is. GLAUCON. It is necessary. SOCRATES. He will finally realize that it is the sun: which tempers the seasons and years: which rules all things under the heavens: and which is in a certain way the author of all those things which were seen by them before. GLAUCON. It is certain he would ascend to this by these steps. SOCRATES. What if he recalled to memory his first habitation, and the wisdom of those men, and the bonds: do you not think he would judge himself happy for the change of place, and pity them? GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, if they used to bestow honors and praises on one another there, and prizes were given to him who most sharply saw whatever passed by, and remembered best which of them used to go before, which after, and which used to proceed together, and from these things predicted the future best, do you think he would desire these things: and judge those happy who are honored and hold power among them? Or would he desire for himself what Homer says, to be in another's field, namely the countryside, as the servant of some poor man...

### DIALOGUE VII. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.
F iiii
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the famous "Allegory of the Cave" from Plato's Republic, Book VII. Socrates is describing the difficult transition of a prisoner returning from the light of truth back into the darkness of the cave.</meta>

...to be made more so, and to suffer anything else rather than be mocked by those opinions and live in such misery. GLAUCON: I believe he would choose anything rather than a life of that sort. SOCRATES: If this man should go down again and take the same seat he had before, would he not, having suddenly departed from the sun, be overwhelmed by darkness? GLAUCON: Vehemently so. SOCRATES: And if it were necessary to discern those shadows again, and to dispute about them with those who have been pressed by perpetual chains—and his opinion must be delivered in that very time while his eyes are hallucinating, before his sight is cleared (which will not happen in a short time)—will he not provoke laughter? And will it not be said to his disgrace by everyone that after he ascended upward, he returned with corrupted eyes? And will it not be said that one must never strive for the heights, and that if anyone tries to release them and lead them upward, if they should catch him, he must be killed immediately? This whole image, O friend Glaucon, must be applied to those things said above.
<margin>Declaration of the likeness of the cave and of beings.</margin>
The prison, indeed, is this world-machine which is perceived by the eyes; the light of the fire in the cave corresponds to the power of the sun. Finally, if you relate the ascent to the heights and the sight of them to that ascent which tends toward the intelligible region <note>The realm of pure thought and forms, rather than physical objects.</note>, you will not wander from the truth, as I hope—since you desire to hear my opinion. But God knows whether it be true. These things, then, which appear to me, I think exist in this way: in the intelligible order itself, the **Idea of the Good** is the supreme thing and is seen only with difficulty. But if it has been seen, it must be asserted that she <note>The Idea of the Good is often treated as a feminine principle in Latin (Idea/Forma).</note> is the ruler of all things and the cause of all good; since she created light and the author of light in the visible place, while in the intelligible realm she reigns herself, producing truth and mind. It is necessary for anyone who is to act with a sane mind, whether privately or publicly, to know her. GLAUCON: I also think so, as far as I am able. SOCRATES: Come then, and consider this: do not wonder that those who descend here are unwilling to deal with human affairs, but the sharpness of their minds is always directed toward the heights. For that is probable, if indeed it follows the superior image. GLAUCON: Probable indeed. SOCRATES: But what of this? Do you think it a wonder if someone, falling from divine spectacles to these human evils, is somewhat inept in action and is laughed at—especially if, before he becomes accustomed to the present darkness, while he still stumbles, he is forced in courts or elsewhere to contend concerning the **shadows of justice** or those statues of which these are shadows, and to dispute concerning the judgments of those who have never seen Justice itself? GLAUCON: In no way is it a wonder. SOCRATES: But if anyone has a mind, he will remember that the eyes are accustomed to be disturbed in two ways and for two causes: both when we descend from light into shadow, and when we go forth from darkness into light. He will believe the soul is affected in the same way whenever he sees it disturbed and somewhat dull for discerning something. Therefore, he will not break out into laughter thoughtlessly, but will diligently inquire whether, descending from a more lucid life, it is overwhelmed by new darkness, or rising from much ignorance to a shining spectacle, it fails under too much flashing splendor. And he will approve the condition of the one and judge his life to be blessed. He will pity the other; and if by chance he begins to laugh, he will not laugh at him so ineptly as at the one who has fallen from the light above. GLAUCON: That is reasonable. SOCRATES: If these things are true, then we must think of them thus: that education is not such as some proclaim it to be. For they promise that they will hand over knowledge to a soul entirely devoid of it, as if putting sight into blind eyes. GLAUCON: They certainly profess that. SOCRATES: But the present argument signifies to us that the power which is in the soul of everyone, and the instrument by which each can learn things—just as if it were impossible to turn the eye toward a clear object from a dark one except together with the whole body—so it is necessary to turn the whole soul away from the world of "becoming" <note>The physical world where things change and decay.</note> until it can endure contemplating that which is called "being" <note>The eternal, unchanging reality.</note>, and the clearest part of it. And this very thing, we say, is the **Good**. GLAUCON: Certainly. SOCRATES: Therefore, a fitting education for this will be a certain faculty of directing the soul: so that its eye may turn as easily and effectively as possible. It will not give sight to this eye, but rather, since it already has sight but is not rightly turned nor looking where it ought, it will strive by every device to turn it. GLAUCON: So it seems. SOCRATES: Therefore, the other things which are called virtues of the soul seem in this to be similar to the virtues of the body. For since they are not present by
<margin>Virtues are acquired by custom and exercise.</margin>
nature, they seem to be acquired little by little through custom and exercise. But **Wisdom**, most of all, exists as a virtue of something more divine; it never loses its power, but by the very act of "turning," it becomes either useful and beneficial, or again useless and harmful. Have you not yet noticed how sharply the little soul of those who, though they are evil, are yet considered "wise," sees and quickly discerns those things to which it is turned? As if it had a sight that was by no
<margin>He who is evil and considered wise performs more evils the more sharply he looks.</margin>
means dull, but was forced to serve wickedness? And therefore, the more sharply it looks, the more evils it performs. GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: If from this nature, immediately from childhood, those things which are related to "becoming" were pruned away—like leaden weights which, clinging to gluttony and such pleasures and lusts and delights, twist the sight of the mind toward inferior things—if it were freed from these, its intuition, turned toward those things which are true, would discern them just as sharply in those same men as it does these things upon which it is presently intent. GLAUCON: It is probable. SOCRATES: What then? Is it not probable and necessary from what has been said: that neither unlearned men and those ignorant of the truth can sufficiently administer the republic, nor those who have always been occupied in the study of letters? Because the former have no certain goal proposed for themselves in life, looking toward which they ought to do whatever they do, both privately and publicly. The latter, however, will not touch civil affairs of their own will, thinking that they already dwell in the "Isles of the Blessed," far removed from human business even in this life. GLAUCON: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: It will be our duty, then, as founders of the city, to compel the best natures of men toward that which we called above the greatest discipline: to know the Good, so that they may ascend upward; and after they have ascended and looked enough, we must not permit them what is now allowed. GLAUCON: What is that? SOCRATES: Namely, that they remain in that contemplation, and not...

...they would be unwilling to descend again to those men imprisoned in the cave, or to share in their labors and honors, whether those be of little or great value. GLAUCON: Shall we then do them an injustice, and force them to lead a worse life when they are capable of enjoying a better one? SOCRATES: You have forgotten, my friend, that the law is not concerned with making any one single class in the city especially happy, but rather the whole city. Indeed, it draws the citizens together by persuasion and compulsion, making them help one another and cultivate a common utility according to their strengths. For the law gathers men into a civil assembly not to allow each to go wherever he pleases, but to use them as a bond for the city. GLAUCON: You speak the truth. That had escaped me. SOCRATES: Consider then, Glaucon, that we will do no injustice to the philosophers who are found among us. Rather, when we compel them to take care of others, we shall say to them with justice: that while philosophers in other cities rightly avoid the labors of administering the state—because they spring up on their own in any city without the state's help—it is only fair that what grows by itself, owing nothing to anyone for its nourishment, should not have to pay for its food. But we have bred you, both for yourselves and for the rest of the citizens, like leaders and kings in a hive of bees, educated better and more perfectly than the others, and more capable of undertaking both duties <note>The "both duties" refers to the life of contemplation and the life of action/governance.</note>. You must therefore descend in turn, each of you, into the assembly of other men, and become accustomed to looking at obscure things. For once you are accustomed, you will see those things much more sharply than those who observe them daily, and you will recognize what the various images are and what they represent, because you have truly known what is honorable, just, and good. And so, the city will be governed by us and by you as if by those who are awake and thinking rightly, not as if by those dreaming—which is how most cities are inhabited now, namely by those who fight amongst themselves over shadows and contend for leadership as if it were the greatest good. But the truth is this: the city in which the citizens are least ambitious to seek magistracies <note>term: magistracy (magistratus) — a high-ranking public office or civil governorship.</note> remains the best and furthest from sedition; but the city that has citizens of a different disposition is the opposite. GLAUCON: It is so. SOCRATES: Will our pupils refuse our warnings when they hear this? Will they be unwilling to take their turn in the administration of the city, preferring to linger longer in the leisure of contemplation? GLAUCON: Not at all. For we shall be giving just orders to just men. Each of them will approach the magistracy as a necessary thing—quite the opposite of those who now rule in individual cities. SOCRATES: Indeed, that is how it stands, my friend. If you find a life for those who are to rule that is better than the ruling itself, then for the first time a well-ordered city will shine forth for you. For in that city alone will the truly rich rule—not rich in gold, I say, but in what a happy man ought to be rich in: a life of integrity and wisdom. But if those who are poor and lacking in their own goods come to public affairs, desiring to snatch goods from there, that city cannot be happy. For where there is a struggle for leadership, since this is a personal and internal war, it destroys both those who fight and the rest of the city. GLAUCON: You tell the truth. SOCRATES: Do you know of any who despise civil honors, besides true philosophers? GLAUCON: No, by Jove! SOCRATES: But surely magistracies must be given to men who are least desirous of power; otherwise, a grudge will arise between rivals. GLAUCON: Certainly. SOCRATES: Whom else then will you bring to the guardianship of the city, besides those who best understand these things by which a city is rightly cultivated, and who possess other honors and a life superior to that of a citizen? GLAUCON: None other, indeed. SOCRATES: Do you wish then that we now inquire how such men may be produced in the city, and by what means one might lead them out into the light—just as some are said to have ascended from the underworld to the gods? GLAUCON: How could I not wish it? SOCRATES: This, it seems, will not be the "turning of a shell" <note>original: "testae revolutio" — an ancient game of chance; here meaning a trivial flip, as opposed to a serious soul-turning.</note>, but the turning around of a soul from a sort of nocturnal day toward the contemplation of that which truly exists. This ascent we shall call true philosophy. GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Must we not investigate which discipline possesses this power most of all? GLAUCON: Why not? SOCRATES: What then, O Glaucon, will be the discipline by which the soul is led back from things that flow <note>referring to the changing, physical world</note> to those things that truly exist? But as I speak, I am thinking: did we not say it is necessary for these young men to be athletes of war? GLAUCON: We did indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, we must add to the previous discipline this one which we seek. GLAUCON: Which one in particular? SOCRATES: That which is not useless to warlike men. GLAUCON: It must be so, if it is possible. SOCRATES: Now, gymnastics and music were the subjects in which they were previously educated by us.

<margin>
Gymnastics considers the growth and decay of the body.
</margin>
GLAUCON: That is exactly how it was done. SOCRATES: Gymnastics, indeed, seems to be concerned with that which increases and declines. For it considers the growth and decay of the body. GLAUCON: That is apparent. SOCRATES: This, then, will not be the discipline we are seeking. GLAUCON: No. SOCRATES: Then perhaps that kind of music which we described above? GLAUCON: But that was, if you remember, a sort of counterpart to gymnastics; it educated the guardians through habits and morals, providing through harmony a certain composition and grace rather than science, and through rhythm a certain modulation and numerical propriety. Furthermore, it contains other things of the same kind in speech, both in fictional stories and in true ones. But a knowledge of the kind of "good" you are now investigating does not exist in it at all. SOCRATES: You have reminded me quite accurately. For in truth, it is found to have nothing of the sort. is to be learned. **GLAUCON.** What sort of thing is that? **SOCRATES.** This simple and childish thing: to recognize one, two, and three. I call this, in short, number and calculation. Is it not so arranged by nature that every art and science is forced to participate in this? **GLAUCON.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Does it not also apply to the business of war? **GLAUCON.** It is entirely necessary. **SOCRATES.** Palamedes <note>A Greek hero of the Trojan War credited with inventing counting and the alphabet.</note> shows Agamemnon to have been a ridiculous general throughout the tragedies. Or are you unaware that he claims to be the inventor of number, and asserts that he marshaled the battle lines at Troy and numbered the ships and all other things? It is as if their number had been unknown before, and Agamemnon, as it seems, did not even know how many feet he had, since he was ignorant of calculation. What sort of general do you think he was then? **GLAUCON.** An absurd one indeed, if these things were true. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, we shall say that the knowledge of numbers is necessary for a soldier, so that he is able both to number and to calculate.

<margin>Arithmetic and calculation are necessary for the soldier.</margin>

**GLAUCON.** Most of all, if he is not to be entirely unskilled in marshaling battle lines. Or rather, if he is to be a man at all. **SOCRATES.** Do you perceive in this discipline what has come into my mind? **GLAUCON.** What is it? **SOCRATES.** It seems by nature to be among those things that elevate men toward understanding, which are the things we are seeking. And since it is of such a nature that it can altogether lift the mind toward essence <note>original: "essentiam" — the true reality or being of a thing.</note>, no one seems to use this knowledge as is fitting. **GLAUCON.** In what way do you say this? **SOCRATES.** I will try to express my meaning. Observe, I pray, how I distinguish classes of things in my own mind: some lead toward understanding (the kind we are discussing), and some do not. Confirm or deny what I say, so that I may more clearly discern whether this is as I divine it to be. **GLAUCON.** Show me now. **SOCRATES.** Behold, I show you: if you see that the things which move the senses are first of all such that they do not provoke the understanding to consideration, because they are sufficiently judged by the senses; and partly such that they do provoke it, because the sense judges nothing clearly in them. **GLAUCON.** You mean those things seen from a great distance, or those that are somehow shadowed. **SOCRATES.** You have not quite grasped what I meant. **GLAUCON.** What then? **SOCRATES.** I say that those things do not provoke the mind which do not fall into the sense simultaneously with their opposite. But those which fall under the sense together with their opposite, I say do provoke it, since the sense shows this no more than its opposite, whether it is seen from afar or near at hand. What I am saying will be more open to you in this way: we say these are three fingers—the thumb, the index, and the middle. **GLAUCON.** Clearly. **SOCRATES.** Think of me as speaking as if they are seen from close by. And consider this in them. **GLAUCON.** What? **SOCRATES.** Each of them appears equally to be a finger, and in this it makes no difference whether it is the middle one or the last, white or black, thick or thin, and whatever is of that kind. For in all these things, the soul is not forced to provoke the understanding to debate, as happens with many fingers. For the sense has not signified to it at the same time that a finger is the opposite of a finger. **GLAUCON.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** Rightly, therefore, such a thing will neither move nor excite the mind. **GLAUCON.** Rightly. **SOCRATES.** But does the sight sufficiently discern their greatness and smallness? And does it matter to the sight whether one of them lies in the middle or at the ends? And in the same way, does touch discern thickness, thinness, or softness and hardness? And do not other senses declare such things imperfectly? Or does each of them act thus? For first, the sense that pertains to the hard is forced also to touch upon the soft; and it reports to the soul as if it has sensed the same thing to be both soft and hard. **GLAUCON.** Certainly so. **SOCRATES.** Is it not necessary in such things for the soul to doubt what this sense signifies by "hard," if indeed it asserts the same thing to be "soft"? Likewise, the sense of the heavy and light—what is heavy and light, if it signifies that the light is heavy and the heavy is light? **GLAUCON.** Truly, these interpretations reach the soul in an absurd way and require consideration. **SOCRATES.** Rightly, therefore, in these matters the soul first strives with reason and, provoking the understanding, considers whether each of the things reported is one or two. **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** If two appear, does not each appear as one and distinct? **GLAUCON.** Yes. **SOCRATES.** If therefore each is one, and both together are two, the soul will understand two separate things. For if it perceived them as indistinct, it would understand not two, but one. **GLAUCON.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** We say the sight sees "great" and "small," not as something discrete, but confused. Is it not so? **GLAUCON.** Clearly. **SOCRATES.** For the sake of clarifying this, the understanding is forced to look again at "great" and "small," not as confused, but as distinct, contrary to the sense. **GLAUCON.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** From this we are immediately incited to inquire: what is "great" and what is "small"? **GLAUCON.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** And so we have called one "intelligible" and the other "visible." **GLAUCON.** Very skillfully put. **SOCRATES.** These are the things I just began to discuss: namely, that some things raise the soul toward understanding, and some do not. Those that fall into the senses together with their contraries raise it; those that do not, do not stir the mind. **GLAUCON.** I understand now, and it seems so to me. **SOCRATES.** What then of number and the "one"? In which class do they seem to be? **GLAUCON.** I do not understand. **SOCRATES.** But consider it from what was said above. For if the "one" is sufficiently inspected by itself, or is grasped by some other sense, it by no means leads the mind toward essence—just as we said of the finger. But if something contrary to it always arises at the same time, so that it seems no more "one" than its opposite, then it requires the discretion of a judge; and the soul is forced to doubt and inquire within it, and stirring the understanding within itself, to ask what the "one" itself is. And in this way, the consideration of the "one" will be among those things that lift the soul and turn it toward the contemplation of that which truly is. **GLAUCON.** But the inspection of the "one" has something of this sort. For we see the same thing at once as one and as an infinite multitude. **SOCRATES.** If the "one" experiences this, every number will experience the same. **GLAUCON.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, all the science of calculation and numbering is about number. **GLAUCON.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** And these things seem to lead toward the truth. **GLAUCON.** In a wonderful way. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, this discipline will be of the kind we seek: most necessary for the soldier to know for marshaling battle lines, and for the philosopher...

He argues that because the senses often perceive contradictory qualities (like a finger being both large and small), the soul must use reason to distinguish these concepts, leading it toward the contemplation of true reality.</summary>

...so that he may emerge from the waves of becoming and reach toward true essence; without which discipline, he will be unable to calculate or reason. **GLAUCON.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** Our guardian is both a soldier and a philosopher. **GLAUCON.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** It would be a fitting education then, O Glaucon, to persuade those who are to perform the duties of the state to apply themselves to the science of calculation—not as amateurs, but to pursue it until they reach the contemplation of the nature of numbers by the mind itself. What do you think, Glaucon, they would answer to this? **GLAUCON.** I suppose they would answer that they are speaking of those numbers which can only be grasped by thought, and cannot be handled in any other way. **SOCRATES.** Do you see then, my friend, that this skill in this discipline is truly necessary for us? even if those who are slower in intellect devote themselves to this study, even if they receive no other benefit, they at least achieve this: they become sharper than they were before. **GLAUCON.** That is true. **SOCRATES.** But indeed, I think you will not easily find many things that are learned with greater difficulty than this. **GLAUCON.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** For all the reasons we have brought forward, this must not be neglected, but those with the best natures must be educated in these things. **GLAUCON.** I agree. **SOCRATES.** Let this then be established for us. Next, let us consider the subject that follows this, to see if it is of use to us. **GLAUCON.** What is that? Do you mean Geometry? **SOCRATES.** That very one. **GLAUCON.** Insofar as it pertains to military matters, it is certainly suitable for us. For in pitching camp, occupying a region, drawing up troops or even scattering them, and for all other maneuvers which they are accustomed to use in battle or in a siege, it makes a great difference whether a man is a geometrician or not. **SOCRATES.** For these things, a very small portion of Geometry and Arithmetic suffices. But we must inquire whether a more prolonged study and a fuller understanding contributes to making the "Idea of the Good" easier to discern. All things contribute to this which turn the soul toward that place where the most blessed essence exists, which the soul must know fully. **GLAUCON.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, if the study of Geometry compels one to contemplate essence, it is suitable; if it forces one to look at "becoming," it is not. **GLAUCON.** So we say. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, no one who has even a small taste of Geometry will deny that this science is entirely the opposite of how those who practice it speak of it. **GLAUCON.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** They often speak in a quite ridiculous and forced manner. For they speak as if they were "doing" something and for the sake of action, saying they "square" and "extend" and "add," and other such terms. But in truth, this entire discipline is sought for the sake of knowledge. **GLAUCON.** That is entirely true. **SOCRATES.** And must we not also concede this? **GLAUCON.** What? **SOCRATES.** That it is sought for the sake of 

<margin>On whether Geometry is useful.</margin>
<margin>In what way Geometry helps in philosophizing.</margin>
knowing that which always *is*, not that which at some time arises and then perishes. **GLAUCON.** It must plainly be conceded, for Geometry is the knowledge of that which always exists. **SOCRATES.** It will therefore, O noble man, uplift the soul toward truth, and will so prepare the thought for philosophizing that we may turn upward those things which we now, contrary to what is proper, cast downward. **GLAUCON.** As much as is possible. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, it must be commanded as much as possible that those who inhabit this most excellent city should in no way despise Geometry. For even its "by-products," so to speak, are not small. **GLAUCON.** Of what kind? **SOCRATES.** Those you mentioned regarding military matters. We also know that for learning all disciplines more easily, it makes an entire difference whether someone has touched upon Geometry or not. **GLAUCON.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Let us then establish this as the second discipline to be learned by the youth. **GLAUCON.** Let us establish it. **SOCRATES.** Shall we put Astronomy in the third place? What do you think? **GLAUCON.** It should certainly be placed there. For perceiving the changes and opportunities of the seasons is no less suitable for military affairs than for agriculture and navigation. **SOCRATES.** What a pleasant man you are! You seem to fear lest the many think you are introducing useless disciplines. But it is no light thing, but rather very difficult, to persuade people that by such disciplines an instrument of the soul is purified and rekindled—an instrument which had previously been fouled and blinded by other studies—and which is more worth saving than ten thousand bodily eyes. For by this alone is the truth beheld. To those who feel this way, you will seem to speak wonderfully well. But those who have never reflected on this will rightly think you are saying nothing; for they see no other value in it worthy of esteem. Consider then with which group you are discussing. Or perhaps with neither, but you speak chiefly for your own sake—though you would not begrudge anyone else if they should receive some benefit from these things. **GLAUCON.** I choose the latter: to discuss primarily for my own sake by asking and answering. **SOCRATES.**

# DIALOGUE VII. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO 254.

Go back a bit. We did not correctly accept what follows Geometry just now. GLAUCON: Why? SOCRATES: Because after the plane, we immediately accepted that solid which revolves <note>original: "solidum illud quod circumfertur" – referring to astronomy/spheres</note> before we had grasped the solid in itself. It is proper to take the third increase immediately after the second: and this concerns the increase of cubes and that which partakes of depth. GLAUCON: It is certainly so. But these things, O Socrates, do not yet seem to have been discovered. SOCRATES: Of this <margin>Note how in the time of Socrates there was no part of mathematics dealing with [solid] bodies.</margin> there are two causes: namely, that no city honors these things, and since they are difficult to discover, they are not sought after ardently; and those who do investigate them need a leader, without whom they would hardly find anything. To find such a leader is first of all difficult, and then even if he existed, those who now investigate these things are so puffed up with pride that they would by no means obey him. But if the whole city should preside over this work, holding it in honor, these leaders would be obeyed; and these matters, pursued with diligent study and discussed, would shine forth more clearly. For even now, although the common people despise and hinder these things, and those who study them are ignorant of how they are useful, nevertheless they flourish by a certain natural vigor. Nor is it a wonder if they appear so. GLAUCON: Indeed, what is pleasing is foremost. But explain to me more clearly what you were just saying. You called the study that deals with the plane Geometry. SOCRATES: I did. GLAUCON: After Geometry, you immediately placed Astronomy. But a little later you stepped back. SOCRATES: Truly, the more I hurry, the later I arrive. For while that faculty which deals with the increase in depth <note>Stereometry or solid geometry</note> should have followed, because its investigation is considered ridiculous, I passed over it and, after Geometry, I immediately touched upon Astronomy, which consists of the motion of depth itself. GLAUCON: You speak rightly. SOCRATES: Therefore, let us place Astronomy in the fourth place: as if that faculty which had just been omitted were present, <margin>Astronomy consists in the motion of depth, that is, of a body.</margin> if only it were taken up by the city. GLAUCON: So it should be. And that praise of Astronomy, O Socrates, for which you rebuked me as if I were extolling it too unseasonably, I now follow according to your progress. For I think it is clear to everyone that this study directs the eyes of the soul to higher things, and leads it from here to there. SOCRATES: Perhaps this is clear to everyone except me. Since to me, at least, it does not seem so. GLAUCON: But in what way? SOCRATES: Furthermore, as those who now join it to philosophy treat it, it seems to me to cast the eyes of the soul downward to lower things. GLAUCON: Why do you say that? SOCRATES: You seem to me to define the understanding of "higher things" in no small way within yourself. For it is evident that if someone, looking up at a ceiling painted with various colors, perceives anything, you think he is not looking with his eyes but understanding with his mind. And perhaps you feel rightly, and I foolishly. I, for my part, believe that no other discipline excites the soul to the inspection of higher things except that which deals with essence and that which cannot be seen. But if someone, gaping upward and never turning downward, strives to perceive something sensible, I by no means assert that he is learning, for I deny that he is acquiring knowledge: and I judge his soul to be looking not upward but downward; even if he were lying on his back on the shore of the earth or the surface of the sea, whatever he perceived. GLAUCON: You have corrected me not without justice. But what is the right method of learning Astronomy <margin>Astronomical contemplations which contribute to philosophy are not about sensible things.</margin> besides the one they follow, if this perception is to be useful to us for what we are saying? SOCRATES: This way. It must be considered that these varieties which are in the heavens, since they are in a visible place, if compared to other things of that kind, are arranged most excellently and perfectly; but if compared to the true ones, they fall far short. I mean the true varieties and motions, by which true velocity itself and true slowness itself are carried in true number and in all true figures, both in relation to each other and carrying what is within them. All of which can be grasped by reason and thought, but by sight not at all. What do you think? GLAUCON: Exactly the same. SOCRATES: Therefore, must we not use the variety of the heavens as a sort of example for the contemplation of higher things? Just as if someone were to see figures especially composed and elaborated by Daedalus or some other craftsman or painter. Surely, if someone skilled in Geometry saw them, he would praise the craftsmanship itself; yet he would think it ridiculous if anyone considered such things too attentively, as if he were going to find in them the truth of equals, or doubles, or of any other proportion. GLAUCON: Why would that not seem absurd? SOCRATES: We must think that the true Astronomer will do the same when he looks at the movements of the stars: he will think, namely, that the heaven itself and the things in it were fabricated as beautifully as possible by the creator of heaven himself; yet he will consider it absurd if someone thinks that the comparison of night to day, and of these to the month, and of the month to the year, and of the other stars to each other and to these things, always happens in the same way; or that they never change their course in any way since they have a body and are seen; and that he seeks the truth in these things with all his zeal. GLAUCON: To me, certainly, hearing you at present, it seems the same. SOCRATES: Therefore, we shall use propositions as in Geometry, so also in Astronomy itself; and we shall let the things in the heavens go, if we are to perceive Astronomy in such a way that we make the nature of wisdom within us useful instead of useless. GLAUCON: How much more work you prescribe than what is now given to Astronomy! SOCRATES: I think, moreover, that we ought to perceive other things in the same way, if any utility is to come from us as lawmakers. But what other suitable disciplines will you mention now? GLAUCON: I have none to mention at present. SOCRATES: And yet motion provides not just one, but several species. Anyone who is wise will be able to bring them all forth. But those which occur to us are two. GLAUCON: Which ones? SOCRATES: One is somewhat similar to Astronomy, placed alongside it by comparison and conversion. GLAUCON: Which one, I ask? SOCRATES: Just as the eyes are made for Astronomy, so the ears seem to be made for harmonic motion. Whence these are sister sciences to each other: as both the Pythagoreans think, and we, O Glaucon, agree. Or what shall we do? GLAUCON: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Since this is a great work, shall we not ask them how...

<summary>Socrates explains to Glaucon that true Astronomy should not focus on visible celestial movements but on the mathematical and rational principles behind them, treating the physical sky only as a geometric diagram.</summary>
