SOCRATES. That they should never take pains to teach our pupils anything from these subjects that is less than perfect, or that does not always tend toward that place where all things ought to arrive, just as we recently discussed concerning Astronomy. Or are you unaware that they do something similar regarding harmony? For while they measure and compare the concerts and tones <note>original: "concentus & tonos," referring to musical intervals and pitches</note> which they perceive with their ears, they waste their labor to no effect, just as the Astronomers waste their time. GLAUCO. By the gods, it is quite ridiculous how they introduce certain "crowdings" of notes, and apply their ears and compare them, as if they were hunting for a sound from a neighboring place. And some of them say they can still hear a certain sound in the middle, and that this is the smallest interval by which one ought to measure. Others, however, disagree, as if the sound already heard were similar. And both prefer their ears to their minds. SOCRATES. But do you call those musicians useful who continually vex and examine the strings, and twist the beats by tightening and loosening the pegs? But lest this comparison proceed too far regarding the accusation of the plectrum <note>the tool used to pluck strings</note> and the denial and elevation of the chords, I now put an end to this image. But they do not pass from there to the investigation of which numbers are consonant and which are not, and for what reason each is so. GLAUCO. You describe a magnificent thing. SOCRATES. Add also that it is useful for the investigation of the Good and the Beautiful itself; if it is sought otherwise, it becomes utterly useless. GLAUCO. That is indeed probable. SOCRATES. I think, moreover, that the treatment of all the aforementioned subjects, if it touches upon their mutual communion and kinship, and investigates in what way they cohere with one another, will lead toward those things we seek, and men will not labor in them in vain, but very usefully; but futilely, if it is done otherwise. GLAUCO. I too prophesy thus: but it is a great task you command, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Do you speak of the prelude, or of something else? Or are we ignorant that all these things are the preludes to the law itself, which one must learn? For men skilled in these matters do not yet seem to you to be dialecticians—that is, fit for discourse. GLAUCO. No, by Jupiter, except for a very few of all those I have ever known. SOCRATES. But unless someone is able both to receive and to give a reason <note>original: "rationem," meaning a rational account or logical justification</note>, he will never know anything of those things which we say must be known. GLAUCO. Never, indeed. SOCRATES. Is this not now the law, O Glauco, which the art of discourse <note>Dialectic</note> reveals? Which, in turn, the power of sight imitates, which we said above turns itself toward living things, and toward the stars, and finally toward the sun itself? Not otherwise when someone betakes himself to the dialectic art—that is, of discourse—without the senses, striving by reason alone toward that which each thing is in itself. And if he does not desist until he has grasped the understanding of the Good itself, then at last he arrives at the end of the intelligible world, just as that other man ascended to the end of the visible world. GLAUCO. It happens exactly so. SOCRATES. Do you not call this progress "Dialectic"? GLAUCO. What forbids it? SOCRATES. And just as that release from chains, and the turning away from shadows toward the images and the light, and the exit from the cave to the light of the sun, and there the inspection of animals and plants, and the looking at the sun and stars in water because of the weakness of the eyes, turns that which is clearest in bodies toward that which is the most radiant of all in the corporeal and visible region: so the study of all the aforementioned arts leads the soul through shadows—not of images, but rather of those things which truly are—and enables it to judge appearances by another light as if by the sun, and has a certain power of raising that which is most excellent in the soul to the contemplation of that which is best in the order of things. GLAUCO. I accept this; although such things seem to me to be of a kind that they can neither be easily admitted nor easily rejected. Nevertheless, since they must be heard not only at present but often repeated hereafter, these things being settled as they have now been handed down, let us come to the law itself and run through it just as we finished the prelude. Therefore, tell me, I pray: what is the mode of the power of discourse? Into what species is it distributed? And what are the paths? For these are, it seems, what lead there; where whoever arrives, will at last rest as if at the end of a journey. SOCRATES. You will not yet be able to follow, O friend Glauco, though certainly as far as is in me, no zeal shall be lacking for you to obtain your wish. You would no longer see an image of that which we are discussing, but the true thing itself as it appears to me. Whether it is truly so or not, it is by no means proper to affirm. But this much must be asserted: that there is some such thing to be known. Is it not so? GLAUCO. Nothing forbids it. SOCRATES. Furthermore, 

<margin>On the method of discourse.</margin>

this also: that only the faculty of discourse will show this to a man educated in those things we have mentioned. Otherwise, it is entirely impossible to know it. GLAUCO. This too must be asserted. SOCRATES. No one will oppose us when we say that the faculty of discourse alone attempts by a certain order to find out what each thing itself is. 

<margin>To which art it belongs to define.</margin>

Since the other arts look either to the opinions and desires of men, or to generations and compositions, or to the cultivation of those things which are generated and composed. The remaining arts, which we said participate in some way in true things—namely Geometry and its companions—dream in a way about essence itself; but it is impossible to see anything clearly from them as long as they cling to suppositions <note>axioms or unproven assumptions</note>, and keep them so fixed and immovable that they cannot give an account of them. For where the beginning is something unknown, and the end and the middle are connected from that unknown thing, by what agreement shall we call the resulting assertion "science"? GLAUCO. By none. SOCRATES. But Dialectic alone, having removed all suppositions, proceeds to the principle itself to confirm it; and truly it draws and leads the eye of the soul, buried in barbaric mud, gradually upward, using as certain helpers and ministers those arts we have described. These we have often called "sciences" because of custom. But they require another, clearer name...

<summary>Socrates explains that while mathematics and music are useful preludes, only the art of Dialectic can lead the soul out of the "cave" of shadows to grasp the true essence of the Good. He distinguishes Dialectic from other sciences because it does not rely on unproven assumptions but seeks the ultimate principle of reality.</summary>

# DIALOGUE VII. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO 255.

...lower indeed than opinion, but more obscure than science. We certainly named "thought" <note>original: *cogitationem*; referring to *dianoia* or mathematical reasoning</note> in the previous sections regarding the cognition of these things. Yet there is no controversy over the name among those who are debating matters as great as those before us now. GLAUCON. Certainly not; for they only require the expression of internal concepts for the understanding of things. SOCRATES. It is pleasing then, as before, to call the first portion **science** <note>original: *scientia*; *episteme*</note>; the second **thought**; the third **faith** <note>original: *fides*; *pistis* or conviction</note>; and the last **imagination** or **assimilation**. And both of those former together as **intelligence**; but these latter two together as **opinion**. And opinion indeed is concerned with *generation* <note>the world of becoming/change</note>; but intelligence is concerned with *essence* <note>the world of true being</note>. Moreover, as essence is to generation, so is intelligence to opinion. And as intelligence is to opinion, so is science to faith, and finally, thought to imagination. But let us omit, O Glaucon, the comparison of those things in which these are engaged, and the twin division of each—namely, the opinable and the intelligible—lest a longer speech be held concerning these than the previous ones. GLAUCON. Indeed, I agree with the others as much as my mind can grasp. SOCRATES. Do you not call him a **dialectician** who grasps the reason of any essence? But as for him who does not have this reason, insofar as he can render a reason neither to himself nor to another, will you deny that he has intelligence regarding this? GLAUCON. Certainly, it cannot be said otherwise. SOCRATES. One must judge similarly regarding **the Good**. Unless one can define the idea of the Good by reason, distinguishing it from all others, and as if in a battle penetrating through all things, rejecting all else—arguing and refuting not according to opinion, but according to substance—and unless he passes through all these with a stable and unshaken reason, you will say that such a man in this state knows neither the Good itself, nor any other good. Rather, if he happens to touch upon some phantom, he touches it by opinion rather than by science; and in this life he is mocked while slumbering in dreams; and before he wakes up, descending to the underworld, he is finally occupied by the ultimate sleep. GLAUCON. By Jove, I shall assert all these things entirely. SOCRATES. Furthermore, as for your children, whom you are now instructing in speech, if you were ever to educate them in reality, I think you would not permit them to hold the greatest power in the city while they were like "lines" <note>meaning irrational or without foundation</note> unable to render a reason for anything. GLAUCON. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Therefore, you will establish a law by which they are commanded to take up that discipline especially, from which they may be rendered most fit and most skillful at questioning and answering. GLAUCON. I shall prescribe that along with you. SOCRATES. Does it then seem to you that **dialectic** is placed like a summit <margin>See the excellence of the science of dialectic.</margin> atop the doctrines? And that no further or more eminent doctrine can be found, but that this is now the end of all doctrines? GLAUCON. It seems so to me. SOCRATES. It remains, therefore, to reveal to whom these disciplines are to be distributed, and in what manner. GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. Do you remember in that first choice what kind of leaders we selected? GLAUCON. Why should I not remember? SOCRATES. As for other things, consider that those natures ought to be chosen. For it is fitting to choose the most serious and the strongest men, and as far as possible, the most handsome. Not only are noble and formidable men to be sought, but those who additionally possess those natural gifts which this discipline requires. GLAUCON. Which ones? SOCRATES. I say that sharpness and facility of wit must be present for the perception of doctrines. For the mind is more deterred by the difficulty of disciplines than by the exercises of the body. Since that labor is more its own, belonging to it alone, whereas bodily labor is shared with the body. GLAUCON. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Therefore, a man must be sought who is mindful, most upright, and most enduring. For whom else do you think will willingly undergo the labors of the body, and follow the arduous study of doctrine and meditation to the very end? GLAUCON. No one at all, unless he be endowed with the best nature. SOCRATES. From that very error, as I was saying above, infamy has arisen against philosophy, because men do not touch it according to its dignity. For it is not to be handled by the "spurious" <note>those unfit or illegitimate</note> but by the "legitimate." GLAUCON. In what way? SOCRATES. In the first place, anyone who is to be initiated into the sacred rites of philosophy must not be "lame" in undertaking labors, such that he approaches some and refuses others. This happens whenever someone is devoted to gymnasiums and hunting and other bodily exercises, but flees from the study of disciplines, neither delighting in hearing nor in inquiring, but hating all such care. Moreover, he is also "lame" who delights in the exercises of the mind but despises the others. GLAUCON. You tell the truth. SOCRATES. And regarding truth, shall we not similarly consider that mind "maimed" which hates a voluntary lie and bears it poorly in itself, and is indignant at others lying, but easily tolerates an involuntary lie? And if it is caught being ignorant of something, it does not take it heavily, but willingly wallows in the filth of ignorance like a pig? GLAUCON. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, regarding temperance and fortitude and magnificence and the other parts of virtue, it must be no less observed who is legitimate and who is spurious. For when these things are less considered, both private citizens and the city, being ignorant, use the maimed and the spurious for whatever of these tasks happens to arise: private citizens for friends, and the Republic for its leaders. GLAUCON. It happens exactly so. SOCRATES. We must take precaution against all these things. For if we lead and educate men who are most upright in the habit of body and mind to such great doctrine and exercise, Justice itself will not be angry with us, and we shall preserve the city and the Republic. But if we lead men affected otherwise to these things, we shall do all the opposite, and we shall disgrace philosophy even much more. GLAUCON. That would indeed be shameful. SOCRATES. In a wondrous way. But something worthy of laughter seems to have happened to me at present. GLAUCON. What is that? SOCRATES. It escaped me, no doubt, that we were joking; therefore I acted more sharply than was becoming. For while speaking, having turned toward philosophy itself, I saw her affected by disgrace. Because of this, I seem to have been heavily oppressed, and as if indignant at those who are at fault, I said these things too severely. GLAUCON. Not by Jove, as it seems to me while listening. SOCRATES. To me <margin>Which ages are fit for learning.</margin> however, as I speak, it appears so. But let this not escape us: that in the previous election we chose old men; but in this one...

<summary>Socrates defines the four levels of knowledge (science, thought, faith, and imagination) and argues that only those with "legitimate" and un-maimed natures—possessing both physical and mental endurance—should be trained in dialectic to lead the Republic.</summary>

...it will by no means be permitted. <margin>In what manner boys are to be taught.</margin>

and sleep are enemies to learning. And at the same time, this trial seems not the least among others: namely, how each one will appear in the gymnasiums themselves. GLAUCON: Why not? For whoever is perceptive in discerning this is a Dialectician; but he who is dull is by no means so. GLAUCON: I understand indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, having observed these things, it will be necessary to take those who are found to be most excellent—stable in their studies, constant in war, and persevering in other lawful duties—and after they have passed their thirtieth year, to appoint them from the chosen to be the pre-elected for greater honors. Then, you must examine them diligently by the faculty of disputation: to see which of them can, without the help of the eyes or other senses, transcend to that which truly exists with truth. In this, my friend, there is need of the greatest caution. GLAUCON: Why so? SOCRATES: Do you not notice how much evil grows around the skill of disputation? GLAUCON: What sort of evil? SOCRATES: 

<margin>What things are to be observed in educating boys.</margin>
It is utterly full of lawlessness. GLAUCON: Very much so. SOCRATES: Do you think they have suffered something strange, and do you not forgive them? GLAUCON: For what reason especially? SOCRATES: Suppose a child were raised in great luxury by a noble family, among many flatterers, but as an adult he sensed that he was not born from those he thought were his parents, yet could nowhere find his true progenitors. Can you predict what his feelings would be toward the flatterers and toward those who took him in, both in the time when he suspected nothing of the substitution, and after he knew the truth? Or do you wish to hear my prediction? GLAUCON: I do indeed. SOCRATES: I predict, therefore, that while he is ignorant of the substitution, he will honor those he thinks are his parents and relatives more than the sycophants; he will be less likely to neglect them in their need, less prone to do them injury or speak insults, and more likely to obey them in serious matters than the flatterers. GLAUCON: That is likely. SOCRATES: But if he perceives the truth, he will certainly honor and care for them less; he will cherish the sycophants more than before, obey them more readily, and model his life after theirs, conversing with them openly and freely. But for those he had thought were his parents and relatives, unless he is by nature exceptionally just, he will care nothing at all. GLAUCON: Everything would happen exactly as you describe. But how does this comparison apply to those who pursue disputations? SOCRATES: You shall hear. We have from childhood opinions about honorable and just duties, under which we were educated as if by parents; we obey these and honor them above all else. GLAUCON: We do indeed. SOCRATES: But pleasures also offer themselves to us, which entice us to the opposite, and while they flatter the soul, they twist it toward themselves. Yet those who are even a little more moderate than the rest are not turned by these, but cherish those paternal values and obey them. GLAUCON: So it happens. SOCRATES: If the art of Dialectic approaches someone so disposed and asks him what is "honorable," and when he answers what he learned from the lawmaker, Reason refutes him, and by frequent and various rebukes leads him to think that the thing is no more honorable than it is base; and if it argues similarly about the just and the good, and about the other things he previously held in highest honor, do you think he will pursue them with the same honor and observance hereafter? GLAUCON: I think with much less. SOCRATES: When, therefore, he no longer considers those traditional values to be honored as before, nor finds the true ones, he slides—as is natural—into a life of pleasure rather than any other. GLAUCON: That is likely. SOCRATES: Thus, from a just man, he becomes unjust. GLAUCON: It is necessary. SOCRATES: Is it not right, as I was just saying, that the condition of those who approach disputation in this way deserves much forgiveness? GLAUCON: And mercy besides. SOCRATES: 

<margin>Dialectic is to be tasted at the thirtieth year.</margin>
Therefore, so that this miserable outcome may be avoided, let those who are thirty years old taste dialectical arguments only with great caution. GLAUCON: Exactly so. SOCRATES: Is this not a prudent caution: that younger men should not touch them? For it does not escape you, I think, that as soon as youths taste the art of disputation, they immediately use it as a kind of game for refuting others; and zealously imitating those who confute others, they themselves also rebuke others, and like puppies they delight in pulling apart and tearing at those nearby...

# ARGUMENT FOR THE EIGHTH DIALOGUE. FOLIO 256.

...delight them constantly. GLAUCON: In a wonderful way. SOCRATES: But when they have refuted many, and have themselves been refuted by many, they quickly fall into a state where they hold nothing as certain from their former opinions. And because of this, both they themselves and the whole of philosophy fall into slander among others. GLAUCON: You speak the truth. SOCRATES: But a man of more mature age will carefully avoid this madness; he will instead imitate one who disputes for the sake of investigating the truth, rather than one who, for the sake of amusement, devotes himself to trickery and deceptive catch-questions. Indeed, he will conduct himself with more modesty, and will turn the pursuit of disputation from something infamous into something illustrious. GLAUCON: Wisely said. SOCRATES: Furthermore, all the things said previously were for the sake of such caution. Namely, that those who are admitted to the study of disputation <note>original: "disputationis studium," referring here to Dialectic</note> must be moderate and grave; and that it must not be shared with unfit men, nor, as is currently done, with anyone whom chance happens to bring along. GLAUCON: Most certainly. SOCRATES: If someone should give his labor to the study of disputation diligently and constantly, doing nothing else except perhaps exercising his body in the gymnasiums in turn, five years <note>original: "anni duplices superiorum" (double the previous years) followed by the correction to five</note> will be sufficient for him to perceive these things. GLAUCON: Do you say six? Or four? SOCRATES: You should apply five. Then they must be led down again into that cave, and compelled to take up those leadership roles that pertain to war, and whatever leadership roles belong to the youth: lest they be surpassed by others in experience. And in these matters they must also be examined, to see whether they remain constant while being pulled from every side, or if they waver. GLAUCON: And how many years do you assign to these tasks? SOCRATES: Fifteen years. But when they have reached their fiftieth year, whoever among them has appeared sound and excelling in both deeds and sciences must finally be led to the end: they must be compelled to direct the ray of their mind toward the things above, and to look upon that which provides light to all things; and when they have known the Good itself, they shall use it as a pattern to adorn the city, private individuals, and themselves through all the rest of their lives, each taking their turn. They shall spend most of their time in philosophy; but when they are called to the magistracies, they shall keep watch over civil affairs and govern each thing for the sake of the Republic: so that they seem to perform this not as something good or a desirable service, but rather as a necessity. And so, when they have similarly instructed others, they will leave them behind as guardians of the Republic in their turn; they themselves shall then pass over to the Isles of the Blessed. Monuments and sacrifices shall be dedicated to them publicly as if to semi-divine spirits <note>original: "daemonibus"</note> if the Pythian oracle confirms it; if not, then at least as to blessed and divine men. GLAUCON: O Socrates, like a sculptor you seem to have shaped wonderful leaders. SOCRATES: What I have said of men must be understood the same for women. Do not think, Glaucon, that I have spoken more of men than of women; namely, those who are by nature fit for these duties. GLAUCON: That is correct, since they will share in all things equally with the men, as we have described. SOCRATES: Do you grant, then, that we have not merely fashioned these things about the Republic as a wish, but have spoken the truth? Difficult things to do, certainly, but possible; at least in the way we have said: namely, when men who are truly philosophers—either one or many—having obtained power in the city, will despise present honors, thinking them illiberal and of no value; but they will value most highly that which is right and the honors that proceed from it; and they will consider Justice the greatest and most necessary thing: and by serving it and increasing it, they will duly arrange their city. GLAUCON: In what way? SOCRATES: All those in the city who have completed ten years of age, they will send into the fields; they will take their children, far away from those customs which their parents use today, and educate them in their own customs and laws, the nature of which we have described. And thus, most quickly and easily, that city and Republic will arise which we said would be blessed if it ever existed, and would most greatly benefit the race of men in which it was founded. GLAUCON: Most certainly. And it seems to me, Socrates, you have found how such a city can be established, if it ever were to be. SOCRATES: Is enough not now said, both about this city and about the man most like it? For it is clear what sort of man we shall say is like it. GLAUCON: It is clearly established: and what you seek seems to me now to have its end.

### Argument of Marsilio Ficino for the Eighth Dialogue, on Justice.

<margin>
<unclear>illegible marginalia</unclear>
</margin>

SOCRATES has now completed the perfect form of the Republic in seven Dialogues, consecrated to the septenary number of Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva, goddess of wisdom</note>. He calls this government both "Royal" and "Aristocratic" <note>original: "optimatum," government by the best</note>. Aristocratic indeed, because in it many men distinguished by virtue perform public duties and constitute the Senate. Royal, however, because there is one will of all toward the public good: one mind, as it were, acting as queen; and if anyone among them is singular in probity, he is singularly honored. Yet not so much is granted to him that he can change public affairs without the Senate—that is, the number of all approved men. It remained, after the best and blessed form of the Republic, to bring the inferior forms into the midst. He counts four of these. The first he wishes to be that into which the best soon degenerates, which he names the "Ambitious" <note>Timocracy</note>. The second is the "Power of the Few" <note>Oligarchy</note> born from the ambitious. The third is the "Popular" <note>Democracy</note> proceeding from this. The fourth and last is "Tyranny," sprouting especially from the popular. Since the forms of republics come from the forms of souls, he describes with a certain wonderful art five successive affections and habits of souls, and as many similar and similarly named cities. In summary, he concludes that the soul ruled by reason is the best and most blessed, and the city like it is the same. The tyrannical soul is the worst and most miserable. Cities also...

oppressed by tyrants, which are likewise the worst and most miserable. He concludes that middle-ground souls and middle-ground governments hold a certain middle position. From all these things, it appears how ruinous injustice is both in the city and in the soul, and how salutary justice is in both. Everywhere, he explains with wonderful diligence the mutations of both souls and cities from some forms into others. But he especially explains the mutation of the blessed Republic—and, if I may say so, the golden one—into the ambitious, or the silver, or the iron, starting from a higher origin; and he feigns that the Muses pour this out like an oracle, or rather, confound it. Certainly, if the blessed Republic cannot fall into decay by its own defect, and yet it sometimes falls, it falls by some common defect and cause. In this matter, one may laugh at the calumnies of Aristotle. For Aristotle ought not, in the fifth book of his *Politics*, to have demanded from his Plato—or rather, never truly his—a specific cause for the changing of the blessed Republic, since there is no specific one; rather, he ought to have been content with a common one. For just as a man who is both very strong and very temperate suffers from disease not so much from a specific cause as from a common one—that is, by a certain fatal order, so revolving perpetually through the celestial circuits which are below the moon—so that those things which are composed by certain configurations of the spheres and cycles of time are sometimes dissolved by adverse ones. Since, however, the assignment of such a cause far exceeds the limits of the present civil faculty, Socrates employs the prophecy of the Muses. And indeed, he uses it in such a way that we also need the prophecy of Apollo to interpret these things. Not without merit did Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note>—when he wished to briefly express that a matter was most obscure—say that it was "more obscure than the number of Plato." Nor am I surprised that Theon of Smyrna, a mathematician and foremost professor of Platonic doctrine, shrewdly bypassed such a mystery as if it were inexplicable. Which indeed Iamblichus of Chalcis, while he wished to explain it, seems to have entangled. But what if there is more difficulty than weight in such words! Especially since he himself feigns the Muses babbling with a certain tragic swelling, terrifying the childish and simple soul and bringing on stupor. Finally, whatever that may be, you will receive it more opportunely from our commentaries on the exposition of the *Timaeus*. For the rest, consider these moral precepts: It is impossible for wealth and virtue to be honored in a city at the same time. Likewise, to hand over the rudders of the Republic to the wealthier is just as if a ship were handed over to be steered not by the one more skilled in navigation, but by the more affluent. Surely both this and that will be endangered. Again, the safest guardian against all vices is knowledge. Furthermore, the extreme of one thing is the beginning of its opposite; thus, the extreme license of liberty is the beginning of extreme servitude. Just as in any quality of things and times, every excess is accustomed to be turned immediately into its opposite. He says the same in his letters, approving above all things a moderated liberty.

### EIGHTH DIALOGUE ON THE JUST.

<margin>Commonality of women</margin>

IT HAS NOW BEEN AGREED BETWEEN US, O Glauco, that in a city best instituted, women and children ought to be common. All education should likewise be common. Similarly, all duties, both of war and of peace, should be common. Moreover, their kings should be men most excellent in the study of philosophy and military affairs. GLAU. It has clearly been agreed. SO. Furthermore, we also conceded these things: that when such princes have already been established, they, going out on an expedition, will assign to the soldiers dwellings such as we described before: common, namely, to all, in which nothing belongs to anyone as their own. And not only concerning the dwelling, but also concerning the furniture and possessions, if you remember what kind they ought to be, we came to an agreement. GLAU. I indeed remember that we judged that none of those things which others now possess should be possessed by anyone; but like athletes of war and guardians, receiving annual nourishment from others as a reward for their guardianship, they ought to protect themselves and the city. SO. You speak rightly. But after we have finished these things, let us now repeat from where we digressed to here, so that we may proceed again through the same points. GLAU. That is not at all difficult. For almost just as now, as if you had treated the city sufficiently, you added that you called such a city "good" as you had described, and the man "good" whoever was very similar to it; although you could still, as it appeared, report a better city and man. You said besides that if this Republic be right, the others err. Of the remaining Republics, as I remember, there are four species, concerning which it was necessary to speak, and to inspect their defects, and to declare the men similar to them. So that having looked at them all and declaring who is the best man and who is the worst, we might consider whether the best man is the happiest, and the worst the most miserable, or if the matter stands otherwise. But when I asked you which four Republics you especially meant, then indeed Polemarchus and Adeimantus intercepted my speech; from which you, taking up the discourse, have finally arrived here. SO. You remember quite rightly. GLAU. Therefore, like a wrestler, offer the same grip again; and with me asking the same thing, try now to say those things which you were then about to declare. SO. If indeed I am able. GLAU. I truly desire to hear which four Republics you were speaking of above. SO. You shall hear that without difficulty. For those which I mean are those which also have names: namely, that which is praised by many, the Cretan and Laconian <note>Spartan</note>. Second, and praised in the second place, that which is named by the power of the few <term>Oligarchy: rule by a small group of wealthy individuals</term>, a Republic full of many evils. Likewise, that which differs most from this and follows it, the popular government <note>Democracy</note>. Furthermore, the noble tyranny, differing from all these, the fourth and final disease of the city. Or do you have another form of Republic, which exists in some clear and distinct

# DIALOGUE VIII. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

## FOLIO CCLVII. [257]

...in what form does it lie? For there are certain lesser princedoms, and kingdoms for sale, and various such civil powers that hold a middle ground between these. Of these, no fewer are found among the Barbarians <note>In the Greek context, "Barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples.</note> than among the Greeks. GLAUCON: Many certainly, and strange ones, are mentioned. SOCRATES: There are also just as many species <margin>As many characters of men, so many Republics.</margin> and characters of men. Or do you perhaps think that a republic is made from an oak or a rock, rather than from the characters of the citizens? For whichever way these characters flow, they drag the rest of the state along with them. GLAUCON: From the characters, without a doubt. SOCRATES: Therefore, if there are five species of government, there will also be five dispositions of private souls. GLAUCON: Nothing stands in the way of that. SOCRATES: We have certainly described the man who is like the government of the best (Aristocracy), whom we rightly asserted to be good and just. GLAUCON: We have described him. SOCRATES: Next, it is proper to describe the inferior types: the contentious and ambitious man, fashioned according to the Spartan republic; furthermore, the man greedy for the power of the few (Oligarchy); and the man of the people (Democrat), and the tyrannical man. Thus, by discerning the most unjust man and comparing him with the most just, we may perfectly distinguish how supreme and pure justice stands in relation to supreme and pure injustice—regarding the happiness or misery of the just or unjust man. We shall see whether we should follow injustice, obeying Thrasymachus, or justice, persuaded by the present arguments. GLAUCON: That is exactly how we must proceed. SOCRATES: Now, just as we began before to observe characters in the republic rather than in private persons because they are more evident there, so now we must first consider the ambitious republic. I have no name for it other than "ambitious power" <margin>The ambitious Republic (Timocracy).</margin> or "rule of honor" <note>Original: "ambitiosam potentiam." This refers to Timocracy, where honor and ambition are the primary drivers.</note>. After that, we shall devise such a man; then the power of the few, and such a man; then the government of the multitude and the man of the people; and finally, considering tyranny itself and the tyrannical soul, we will attempt to sufficiently judge the matters we proposed. GLAUCON: The inspection and judgment will proceed correctly in this manner. SOCRATES: Come then, let us try to explain in what way the ambitious and impious man is born from the government of the best. Is this not simply true: that every republic is changed by that part which rules <margin>The ambitious and impious arises from the government of the best.</margin> when sedition arises within it? But as long as it is in agreement with itself, even if it be very small, it is impossible for it to be changed. GLAUCON: It is so. SOCRATES: But in what way, O Glaucon, will this city of ours be moved from its state? How will the leaders and defenders disagree with one another? Or do you wish that, imitating Homer, we pray to the Muses to explain to us how sedition first falls upon us? Shall we say that they speak to us in the manner of tragic poets—as if playing and trifling with us like children—yet while they trifle, they speak as if in earnest and with high eloquence? GLAUCON: In what way? SOCRATES: Roughly thus. It is indeed difficult for a city so constituted to be moved from its state. But since everything that is born is subject to corruption, even such a constitution cannot remain forever, but will be dissolved. This is the dissolution: not only for plants, but also for earthly animals, there occurs a fertility and sterility of soul and body whenever the revolutions join the circuits of their individual spheres—shorter circuits for those of short life, and the opposite for the opposite. But those whom you have educated for the government of the city, though they be wise, will not by reason combined with sense-perception comprehend the fertile or sterile generation of your race; the opportunity for breeding will escape them, and they will often labor at begetting children when it is not the opportune time. For that which is divinely generated, there is a cycle contained by a perfect number. But for human generation, there is a number <note>This refers to the famous and notoriously difficult "Platonic Number," a mathematical allegory for the timing of births to maintain the quality of the ruling class.</note> in which first augmentations, surpassing and surpassed, taking three distances and four terms... <note>Socrates proceeds into a complex geometric and harmonic explanation of the "nuptial number."</note> ...all things were made corresponding and comparable to one another. When the sesquitertian root (4:3) is joined to the number five, it provides two harmonies when tripled... This entire geometric number, having such authority, has power over better and worse generation. If the guardians of your city are ignorant of this and join brides to grooms at an inopportune time, the children born will be neither gifted nor fortunate. And although their elders may appoint them as leaders because they seem superior, yet because they will be unworthy of their parents' succession, they will neglect their subjects while in office. They will not care for music as is proper, nor for gymnastics; hence the youth will become too alienated from music. From these, leaders will be appointed who are more negligent than is proper in examining those races which Hesiod mentions, and which are mentioned among you: namely, the golden race, the silver, the bronze, and the iron. When iron is mixed with silver <margin>Hesiod's Golden, Silver, Bronze, and Iron races.</margin> and bronze with gold, discord, dissimilarity, and inequality will arise. Wherever these are born, they always give birth to war and enmities. Wherever such a race of men is present, it is always agitated by seditions. GLAUCON: We shall say the Muses answer quite correctly. SOCRATES: It is necessary, for they are Muses. GLAUCON: What then will the Muses say after this? SOCRATES: After sedition has arisen, both races will be carried away: the iron and bronze toward profit and the possession of fields and houses, and an abundance of gold and silver. But the golden and silver races, as they possess a nature not poor but wealthy in virtue, will strive for the ancient state. Struggling and pulling against one another, they will finally meet in the middle and agree to divide the fields and houses to be possessed privately. Those who were previously guarded by them as free men, friends, and providers, they will now reduce to servitude and hold as subjects and slaves, compelling them to take care of war and their own protection. GLAUCON: It certainly seems to me that the change happens this way. SOCRATES: This government, then, will be a middle point between the best (Aristocracy) and the power of the few (Oligarchy). GLAUCON: It certainly will. SOCRATES: It will be changed in this way. But when it has been so changed, what kind of government...

# BOOK VIII. PLATO’S REPUBLIC.
### PAGE XXXI.

<meta>Catchword: con-</meta>

...will he keep the measure! Or it is certain that he will partly imitate the former republic, and partly the power of the few <note>original: "paucorum potentia," referring to oligarchy</note>, inasmuch as it is situated in the middle: and it will also obtain something of its own! GLAUCON. Exactly so. SOCRATES. And it will indeed imitate the former in this: that the leaders will be honored, and the soldiers will abstain from agriculture, mechanical arts, and other money-making pursuits; and there will be communal meals: they will frequent gymnastic games and contests of war! GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. But it will have certain characteristics of its own: such as being afraid to admit wise men to leadership, because it possesses men of this kind who are not simple and pure-hearted, but of a mixed nature; and it will rather choose more high-spirited and simpler men for governing, who seem born for war rather than for peace. Furthermore, it will highly value the deceits and engines of war, and will always be at war! GLAUCON. Surely. SOCRATES. And yet these men will be greedy for money, just as those who live under the power of the few: and in the dark they will greedily honor gold and silver, inasmuch as they have private treasuries and storehouses in which to hide them: and also walled houses like private nests, in which they will spend much on women and others for their pleasure. GLAUCON. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. And will they not be more stingy in their own affairs than is proper? Since they value money so highly and do not acquire it openly: but in the affairs of others they will be more profuse for the sake of pleasure, and will indulge in secret delights, fleeing the law everywhere just like children fleeing the sight of a father: educated not by persuasion but by force: because they have neglected the true Muse which is joined with discourse and philosophy, and have honored gymnastics much more than music! <note>In this context, "Music" refers to all the arts of the Muses, including literature and philosophy, while "Gymnastics" refers to physical training.</note> GLAUCON. You describe a Republic mixed of bad and good. SOCRATES. It is indeed mixed: but above all others, because of the rule of high spirit and anger, the pursuits of contention and ambition prevail in it. GLAUCON. Vehemently so. SOCRATES. Will not this republic grow together in this way, and be such as can be described in speech as a sketch of a republic, without too much exact diligence of work? For it suffices from the summary of the description itself to discern the most just or most unjust man; and it would be an almost inextricable task if one were to attempt to narrate all republics and all characters without omitting anything at all! GLAUCON. Rightly so. SOCRATES. Who then is the man according to this republic, how is he made, and what is he like? ADIMANTUS. I think indeed he is similar to Glaucon here, for the sake of contention. SOCRATES. Perhaps in this he is similar. But in these things his nature does not seem to be similar. ADIMANTUS. In what things? SOCRATES. He must certainly be more stubborn, and somewhat more a stranger to music, yet a lover of music, and indeed fond of listening, but by no means a rhetorician. And such a man will be harsh toward slaves: not despising slaves as a man educated to sufficiency would; but toward free men he will be mild: toward leaders indeed most obedient: but also more greedy for leadership and honors: thinking that one ought to be able to lead not by the art of speaking or any other similar faculty, but by warlike deeds and the like: since he is very fond of both gymnastics and hunting. ADIMANTUS. This is certainly the character of that republic. SOCRATES. And will he not despise money in his youth? But the more he ages, the more he will love money, because he shares in a greedy nature and is not pure toward virtue, because he lacks the best guardian! ADIMANTUS. From whom? SOCRATES. From reason and discourse, I say, mixed with music: which alone, when it is present, preserves virtue throughout all life in him whom it protects. ADIMANTUS. You speak excellently. SOCRATES. Such a youth is indeed greedy for ambitious command, similar to such a city. ADIMANTUS. Entirely. SOCRATES.

<margin>
How youths become most ambitious.
</margin>

But he becomes such a person in this way sometimes: namely, when a certain young man is the son of a good father living in a city not well governed, fleeing honors, leadership, and lawsuits, and other care of such business: and willingly lowering himself to avoid labors. ADIMANTUS. In what way does he become so? SOCRATES. When, for instance, he hears his mother taking it badly that her husband does not hold magistracies, and hears among other women that for this reason he is held in contempt; and she suffers grievously whenever she sees her husband not indulging in piling up money, nor fighting or litigating for it privately in judgments or publicly: but being rather negligent toward all these things, and such that he lives mostly with himself: and neither despises his wife nor honors her very much. From which things the mother often tells the son that his father is cowardly and too remiss, and whatever else women are accustomed to chatter about such men. ADIMANTUS. Indeed, women are accustomed to say many such things suitable to themselves. SOCRATES. And it does not escape you that even servants and domestics, especially those who seem most benevolent, often whisper such things into the ears of boys. And if they see someone either owing money to the father, whom he does not confront, or acting unjustly in some other way: they tell the boy that when he is a man he ought to avenge all these things, and will be more of a man than his father was. Furthermore, having gone out of the house, he hears and sees other things similar to these: namely, that men who keep their own duties in the city, not curious about the affairs of others, are called fools and utterly despised: but those unlike them are honored and praised. When the youth hears and sees these things, and again hears his father's words, and observes his duties closely beyond the pursuits of others: he is pulled apart by both: by the father indeed his rational power is nourished and increased: but by others the nature of desiring and of anger. Therefore, since he is not born with a bad disposition, but has used the bad custom of others: being drawn into the middle by these, he descends: and subjects himself to a certain middle power, contentious and angry: and becomes a man of lofty mind and greedy for glory. ADIMANTUS.

<margin>
Another man to suit another city.
</margin>

You seem to me to have narrated his nature sufficiently. SOCRATES. We have therefore the second republic and the second man. ADIMANTUS. We have indeed. SOCRATES. Shall we not after this say that word of Aeschylus: "Another man suited to another city"? <note>original: "Alterum hominem alteri civitati convenientem," a reference to Aeschylus' play 'Seven Against Thebes'.</note> Nay, rather according to that former supposition, another city to another...

# DIALOGUE VIII. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

## G ii

...fitting! **ADEIMANTUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** Now, the type of republic that follows this one is, I believe, the "Power of the Few" <note>original: *paucorum potentia*, referring to Oligarchy</note>. **ADEIMANTUS.** What sort of constitution do you specifically call the power of the few? **SOCRATES.** That in which magistrates are chosen based on a census evaluation of the citizens; where the rich rule, and the poor have no share in the government. **ADEIMANTUS.** I understand. **SOCRATES.** Must we not describe how the transition occurs from an ambitious government <note>Timocracy</note> to this one? **ADEIMANTUS.** Certainly. **SOCRATES.** Even to a blind man it is clear how the transition happens. **ADEIMANTUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** That treasury of theirs, full of gold: that is what destroys such a republic. For first, they invent new ways to spend; for this purpose they twist the laws, which neither they nor their wives obey. **ADEIMANTUS.** That is likely. **SOCRATES.** Then, as one person follows the example and rivalry of another, the majority eventually become like this. **ADEIMANTUS.** It is probable. **SOCRATES.** From there, they slide further into the accumulation of money; the more they value wealth, the cheaper they consider virtue. Does virtue not differ from riches in this way: as if both were placed on the scales of a balance, <margin>On riches and virtue.</margin> they always tip in opposite directions? **ADEIMANTUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, when wealth and the wealthy are honored in a city, virtue and good men are despised. **ADEIMANTUS.** That is established. **SOCRATES.** And everyone is inflamed toward those pursuits which are held in honor, and they frequent them; but those things held in no honor are neglected by everyone. And so, from being lovers of victory and honor, they finally become greedy for gain and money. They praise and admire the rich men and elevate them to magistracies, but they despise the poor. **ADEIMANTUS.** It happens exactly like that. **SOCRATES.** And do they not establish the limits of sovereignty by law? They decree that where there is a greater abundance of money, there the sovereignty is greater; where there is less, it is smaller. They forbid anyone to rule who has not reached a certain census level! They achieve this either by force of arms or by establishing such a republic after striking fear into the people. Is it not so? **ADEIMANTUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** This is the constitution, so to speak. **ADEIMANTUS.** It is indeed. But what is the character of this republic? And what are the defects we said it possessed? **SOCRATES.** First, look at the nature of the limit prescribed here. If someone, in the steering of a ship, were to choose captains based on a census evaluation, but would by no means admit a poor man even if he were more skilled at steering—what do you think would follow? **ADEIMANTUS.** That they would steer the ship badly. **SOCRATES.** Is it not the same in any other office of leadership? **ADEIMANTUS.** I think so. **SOCRATES.** Is it so in all things except a city? Or in a city as well? **ADEIMANTUS.** Much more so in a city, since this is the most difficult and greatest form of steering. **SOCRATES.** This, then, is one great defect that the power of the few suffers from. **ADEIMANTUS.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** But what about this? Is it any less serious? **ADEIMANTUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** That it is necessary for this to be not one republic, but two: one of the poor, the other of the rich; and though they inhabit the same walls, they are always plotting against one another. **ADEIMANTUS.** Certainly that is no light matter. **SOCRATES.** But neither is this honorable: that they are unable to wage war. This is because they are forced either to use an armed populace—whom they fear more than the enemy—or, if they do not use them, they appear truly as "the few" in the heat of battle. Furthermore, they are unwilling to spend money because they are greedy men; this is hardly becoming. **ADEIMANTUS.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** And do you think it is right—that which we criticized above—that in such a city the same men are occupied with various duties: farming the land, accumulating money, and serving as soldiers? **ADEIMANTUS.** In no way is it right. **SOCRATES.** See then if this is the greatest of all these evils. **ADEIMANTUS.** What is that? **SOCRATES.** That it is permitted for anyone to sell all his possessions, and for another to possess them; and for the one who sold them to live in the city while being no part of the city—neither a money-changer, nor a craftsman, nor a knight, nor a soldier, but simply called "poor" and "destitute." **ADEIMANTUS.** This is certainly the first such evil. **SOCRATES.** In cities subject to the rule of the few, this is by no means prohibited; otherwise, some would not be more wealthy than is fitting, while others are utterly beggars. **ADEIMANTUS.** You speak rightly. **SOCRATES.** But consider this: when such a rich man was spending his money, was he of any greater utility to the city in those roles we mentioned? Or did he merely seem to be among the number of the rulers, while in truth he was neither a ruler nor a servant, but a consumer of his own resources? **ADEIMANTUS.** So it seems. He was nothing other than a consumer. **SOCRATES.** Shall we say that, just as a drone <note>A male bee that does no work</note> born in a honeycomb is a disease to the swarm of bees, so also a man of this sort born in a home is a plague to the republic? **ADEIMANTUS.** Entirely so, Socrates. **SOCRATES.** Has God not made all winged drones without stings? But these land-drones we see are partly without stings and <margin>Two kinds of drones: winged and land-based. Where doctors see them, they are thieves and robbers and authors of all crimes.</margin> partly armed with dreadful stings. Those without stings end up as paupers in their old age; but those equipped with stings are those called criminals. **ADEIMANTUS.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** It is certain, then, that in a city where you see beggars, there are hidden thieves, robbers, sacrilegious men, and authors of all these crimes. **ADEIMANTUS.** It is certainly certain. **SOCRATES.** Do you not see that in cities ruled by the few, there are destitute people? **ADEIMANTUS.** Almost everyone, except the rulers. **SOCRATES.** Do we not then believe that there are many criminals there, armed with stings, whom the rulers restrain by diligence and force? **ADEIMANTUS.** We clearly believe so. **SOCRATES.** Shall we assert that men become like this there because of bad education, a lack of discipline, and an unfair disposition of the republic? **ADEIMANTUS.** We shall. **SOCRATES.** Such then will be the city subject to a few rulers; it is pressed by so many evils, and perhaps even more. **ADEIMANTUS.** Almost so. **SOCRATES.** Let this republic now be established for us, which they call the "Power of the Few," choosing rulers by a census evaluation. After this, let us investigate how a man becomes like this system, and once he has become so, what he is like. **ADEIMANTUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** Does he not transition from an ambitious man to one greedy for the rule of the few in this way? **ADEIMANTUS.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** When a certain youth there first sees his father...

# BOOK VIII.

He imitates his father and follows in his footsteps; then he observes him, as one who has struck against a reef in the city as if against a rock, suddenly falling from the height of dignity, ruining himself and all his possessions—whether after a military expedition or some other high magisterial office—dragged into court by informers, surrounded by slanderers, cast out, degraded, and stripped of his inheritance. ADI. That is certainly consistent. SO. Then, my friend, this man, having suffered these things and being crushed, having lost his patrimony, immediately out of fear casts down that ambition and high-spiritedness from the throne of his soul; and having become humbled by poverty, he turns himself to profit-making. With a very narrow mind, living excessively meagerly and sparingly, and by vexing himself, he gathers money through labor. Do you not think that such a man then installs the greedy and profit-seeking affection in that seat of the soul? And makes it a great king within himself? Adorning it with royal ornaments, crowns, belts, brooches, fringes, and a Persian sword? <note>The "Persian sword" (acinaces) symbolizes the absolute, despotic rule of greed over the other faculties of the soul.</note> ADI. I do indeed. SO. And here, indeed, he tramples the rational power and the heat of high-spiritedness on the ground on this side and that, reducing them to slavery; he permits the former to investigate and consider nothing else except how more money may be gathered from less, and the latter to admire and worship nothing else but riches and the wealthy, nor to seek dignity from any other thing than money and whatever else contributes to it. ADI. Certainly no other change is so swift and vehement as that from an ambitious youth to a lover of money. SO. Is not this man, then, a seeker of the rule of the few <note>term: "rule of the few" (oligarchy)</note>? His change from such a man is similar to that of the republic from which the power of the few emerged. Let us consider whether he is similar. ADI. Let us consider it. SO. In the first place, he will be similar in that he values money highly. ADI. Why not? SO. Furthermore, also in that he is more sparing and greedier for profit; he satisfies only his necessary desires, but by no means indulges in other expenses; rather, he restrains other appetites as if they were superfluous. ADI. Greatly so. SO. Therefore he lives more meagerly and squalidly, increasing his family estate from all sides with the greatest parsimony, and by storing it up in an inward treasury; such men the common people approve. Will not this man be like such a republic? ADI. It seems so to me. Money is therefore most honored both by him and by every such city. SO. For he has not, I think, applied his mind to education. ADI. I think not. For he would not have appointed a blind leader for himself. <note>Plato often refers to Wealth as a "blind god."</note> SO. Very well; but notice this: do we not learn that desires similar to the nature of drones <note>term: "drones" (fucorum) - Plato's metaphor for the unproductive, parasitic class in a city or the lawless desires in a soul.</note> exist in him due to a lack of education—some like beggars, others like villains—restrained by force through other diligence? ADI. And most especially. SO. Do you know where you should look to see their villainies? ADI. Where? SO. To the guardianships of orphans, and if any such thing happens to them where they obtain the greatest license for wrongdoing. ADI. You speak the truth. SO. Is it not clear that in other dealings, where such a man is held to be honest because he seems to be just, he restrains the other wicked desires within him by a certain competent force? Not by persuading them that it is not better, nor by taming them with reason, but by necessity and fear, trembling for the rest of his substance? ADI. Most certainly. SO. Indeed, my friend, you will find in many of them, when it is necessary to spend the money of others, desires very much like drones. ADI. Very much so. SO. Therefore, such a man will not be free from internal sedition; nor will he be one person, but double; he will have within himself desires that for the most part dominate other desires—the better ones dominating the worse. ADI. It is so. SO. Wherefore this man will be more modest than many others. However, the true virtue of a consenting and composed mind will fly far from him. ADI. It seems so to me. SO. Furthermore, the sparing man will be slower toward a contest whenever there is a private competition in the city for some honorable victory and magnificence; since he is unwilling to spend money for the sake of such decorum and struggles, fearing to arouse prodigal lusts and to provoke them to fight and struggle. Therefore, fighting with only a few of the things that are around him, in the manner of the few who rule, he is for the most part defeated—and his riches increase. ADI. Most certainly. SO. Do we any longer doubt that the sparing and greedy man is established according to the example of the city which is governed by the few? ADI. In no way. SO. After this, it seems we must investigate in what manner a popular government <note>term: "popular government" (democracy)</note> is constituted, and what its condition is; so that recognizing the same condition in such a man, we may bring him to judgment. ADI. Thus indeed we shall proceed with the journey we have begun. SO. Does not a city change from the power of the few into a popular government in this way: because the leading citizens have proposed to be the best, so that they may be the richest? ADI. In what way? SO. Because the rulers dominate in it on account of riches, they neglect to prohibit the prodigality of dissolute youths by laws, so that by buying up and lending on interest they may usurp their goods, and become even wealthier and more honored. ADI. Most of all. SO. It is clear, then, that it is impossible in a city to honor riches and at the same time possess temperance; but it is necessary that one of these is always neglected for the estimation of the other. ADI. It is quite clear. SO. While, therefore, in the power of the few they neglect the education of youth and permit them to live according to lust, they frequently compel men who are not ungenerous to become poor. ADI. Most certainly. SO. These men sit, I think, in the city armed with stings—some burdened by debt, some afflicted by ignominy, some oppressed by both evils—plotting against those whom they know have possessed their property, and against others, and for that reason they stir up revolution daily. ADI. It is so. SO. But the greedy men, while they lean upon profit and do not seem to notice them, and always wounding with their money anyone of the rest who yields, and bringing back many "sons" of the father and "interest" <note>note: original: "foenora" - a pun on the Greek word 'tokos' which means both 'offspring' and 'interest on a loan.'</note>, they thus fill the city with drones and needy men. ADI. Most certainly. SO. Nor do they wish to extinguish the fire of such an evil, so as not to permit each person to manage his own affairs at his own discretion. Nor, again, are such things prohibited according to a second law. ADI. According to which one especially? SO. According to—

# DIALOGUE VIII. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE. PAGE 259.

...that which follows immediately after those things, and compels the citizens to take care for virtue. For if someone were to command that many of the voluntary contracts be handled at the person's own risk <note>Socrates suggests that if lenders weren't legally guaranteed repayment, they would be more cautious, reducing the greed that destabilizes cities</note>, they would not gather money so shamelessly; and fewer such evils as we have described would be born in the city. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** Now, however, for these reasons, the rulers dispose their subjects in the city in this way: they render themselves, and their own, and the younger men, delicate, soft, and sluggish, tolerating no labor of mind or body, and succumbing to pleasures and pains. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Precisely. 

**SOCRATES:** And they themselves indeed become such that they value nothing other than profit; nor do they have any greater care for virtue than do beggars. 

**ADIMANTUS:** So it is, certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** Thus, therefore, having been so trained, whenever the rulers and the subjects meet one another, whether on journeys or in some other common business and work, or at public spectacles, or in the army—either sailing together or serving as soldiers—or even observing one another in the midst of dangers, in no way are the poor despised by the rich in these moments. Instead, frequently a poor man, lean and hardened by the sun <note>original: "cutimque sole obduratus"</note>, when he is placed in the battle line next to a wealthy man who has been softly nourished in the shade and is burdened by an obese body, and sees him panting and in distress—will he not judge that it is through their own cowardice that such men are rich? And whenever they meet in private, will they not tell one another that their "superiors" are worth nothing? 

**ADIMANTUS:** I know for certain that they do so. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, just as a weak and sickly body falls into disease at the slightest external change—and often even when no external thing is harming it, it rebels within itself—so also a city disposed in the same way falls ill and disagrees with itself upon a small occasion, whether others from outside provide aid to the city subjected to the power of the few, or others provide aid to the popular side. Often, even without external help, it is shaken by seditions. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** A popular government <note>term: "gubernatio popularis" - Democracy</note> comes about, I think, when the poor, being victorious, kill some of the rich, drive others into exile, and bestow equal shares of the republic's honors and offices upon the rest; and for the most part, the magistrates in it are chosen by lot. 

**ADIMANTUS:** This is certainly the constitution of a popular city, whether it is brought about by arms or by fear when others depart. 

**SOCRATES:** What then will be the life of these citizens? What kind of government? For it is clear that a man of this popular sort will appear. 

**ADIMANTUS:** That is evident. 

**SOCRATES:** Will they not first of all be free, and the city full of liberty, and will they not all dare to do all things with the greatest license according to their own lust? 

**ADIMANTUS:** So it is said. 

**SOCRATES:** And where there is license, there each man will arrange his life according to his own judgment. 

**ADIMANTUS:** It is clear. 

**SOCRATES:** All sorts of men are born in this city. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Very much so. 

**SOCRATES:** This seems, at any rate, to be the most beautiful of all republics; just as a cloak embroidered with various colors appears most beautiful, so this city, varied with diverse characters, appears altogether most beautiful. And just as children and women are delighted by works and spectacles distinguished by variety, so many judge this republic the most beautiful because of its variety. 

**ADIMANTUS:** And most especially so. 

**SOCRATES:** And yet, O blessed one, it is easy to seek a republic in this city. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Why so? 

**SOCRATES:** Because it contains all types of republics on account of its license; and it seems necessary for one who desires to establish a republic—as we have just done—to enter a popular city and choose that constitution of a republic which pleases him most, as if he were going to a marketplace <note>original: "nundinas" - a fair or market</note> of republics, and having so chosen, to establish the character of his city. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Perhaps examples for this will by no means be lacking. 

**SOCRATES:** What then? Does not this life seem sweet at first glance, and even divine? That you are not compelled to hold office in this city, even if you are fit for it; nor to obey if you do not wish; nor to wage war when others are waging war; nor to keep peace when others are keeping it, unless it pleases you? Or even if some law forbids you to rule or to pass judgment, you may nevertheless both rule and pass judgment in court, provided it seems good to you? 

**ADIMANTUS:** Perhaps it seems so at first. 

**SOCRATES:** And what of the mildness toward certain condemned men? Is it not graceful? Or have you not yet seen in this city men condemned to death or exile who nevertheless remain in the city and walk about in public? And often, as if no one saw or cared, they walk through the city like certain heroes? 

**ADIMANTUS:** I have indeed seen many. 

**SOCRATES:** Then there is its excessive indulgence, and its disregard for all those things we were saying were honorable when we were founding the city: namely, that unless someone is endowed with an excellent nature, he will never become an outstanding man unless from his earliest childhood he is involved in honorable pursuits and frequently practices all such things. This government, with a high mind, tramples all these things underfoot; it has no concern for what studies a person comes from to enter civil life, but honors him if only he is loved by the common people. 

**ADIMANTUS:** A very generous government indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** These and similar things a popular government will have; and it will be, as it appears, a sweet republic, without a leader, and varied, distributing a certain equality to equals and unequals alike. 

**ADIMANTUS:** You tell of things that are very manifest. 

**SOCRATES:** Consider now what sort of man such a person is in private. Or perhaps we should first investigate, as we did with the republic, in what manner such a man is produced? 

**ADIMANTUS:** Entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** Does it not mostly happen that a son of a greedy father who desires the power of the few is brought up under his parent's character? 

**ADIMANTUS:** Why not? 

**SOCRATES:** This son forcibly restrains his pleasures—those which entice one to spending and not to profit. These pleasures are called "unnecessary." 

**ADIMANTUS:** That is clear. 

**SOCRATES:** Do you wish, lest we wander in ambiguity, that we first discern which desires are necessary and which are not necessary? 

**ADIMANTUS:** I certainly do. 

**SOCRATES:** Those would rightly be called necessary which we cannot remove, and which, when <margin>Which pleasures are necessary, and which are not necessary.</margin> they are perceived, help us. For it is necessary for our nature to seek both of these. Is it not? 

**ADIMANTUS:** Most certainly. 

**SOCRATES:** Rightly, therefore, we shall call them necessary. 

**ADIMANTUS:** Rightly. 

**SOCRATES:** And shall we not correctly deny those are necessary which can be removed if one is accustomed to it from youth, and which, when they are present, bring no good—or rather...

<summary>Socrates describes the transition from oligarchy to democracy, characterizing the latter as a "sweet" but chaotic system of total liberty and variety. He begins to define the "democratic man" by distinguishing between necessary and unnecessary desires.</summary>

# BOOK VIII.

...often they are harmful. **ADIMANTUS:** Quite right. **SOCRATES:** Let us take an example of them, so that we may recognize what both kinds are and look upon them in a certain mental image. **ADIMANTUS:** That is how it should be done. **SOCRATES:** The desire for eating, for example—for food and nourishment only as far as health and a good bodily condition are concerned—is necessary. **ADIMANTUS:** I believe so. **SOCRATES:** Certainly the use of food is necessary for two reasons: both because life cannot be sustained without it, and because it is beneficial. <note>Socrates is defining "necessary desires" as those we cannot avoid or those that benefit us.</note> **ADIMANTUS:** It is so. **SOCRATES:** And the same for other seasonings, insofar as they contribute to a good habit of the body. **ADIMANTUS:** Exactly. **SOCRATES:** But if a desire contributes nothing to this, and is a superfluous craving that can be restrained from youth through temperance <note>original: *temperantia*</note>, and is harmful to the body and harmful to the mind’s pursuit of wisdom and moderation, it will rightly be called "unnecessary." **ADIMANTUS:** Rightly so. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, we shall call these "sumptuous" or "expensive" desires, while the others we call "profitable" because they assist us in our actions. **ADIMANTUS:** Why not! **SOCRATES:** And we shall say the same regarding sexual matters and others. **ADIMANTUS:** The same. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, the man we named a "drone" just a moment ago was the one we said is full of such pleasures and lusts, and is enslaved to unnecessary desires; but the one ruled by necessary desires we call "frugal" and a seeker of the "power of the few" <note>original: *paucorum potentiae*, referring to the oligarchic character.</note>. **ADIMANTUS:** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES:** Now let us say again how the "man of the people" <note>The democratic man.</note> is created from the seeker of the power of the few. It seems to me to happen mostly in this way. **ADIMANTUS:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** When a young man, as we just said, is raised crudely and too parsimoniously, and tastes the honey of the "drones," and keeps company with burning, vehement, and clever creatures who are able to provide all-various and diverse pleasures from every side—from this, you must believe, arises that transformation by which the "rule of the few" within him passes into the "rule of the people." **ADIMANTUS:** It is inevitable. **SOCRATES:** Just as the city changed when an external alliance provided aid to one side—like helping like—does the character of the youth change when a kindred and similar species of external desires supports the species of desires already within him? **ADIMANTUS:** Entirely so. **SOCRATES:** But if some counter-favor is shown to the nature of his "oligarchic" side, whether by his father or other household members who advise and rebuke him, then sedition, resistance, and a battle within himself against himself is born. **ADIMANTUS:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** And sometimes, I think, the "popular" condition yields to the "oligarchic" state; and some desires perish while others are cast out, as a certain sense of shame arises in the young man's soul, by which he is refined again. **ADIMANTUS:** That happens sometimes. **SOCRATES:** Then again, besides those desires that were cast out, other kindred ones secretly grow because of the ignorance of the father’s education, becoming many and vehement. **ADIMANTUS:** That is certainly how it usually happens. **SOCRATES:** They draw him back to his old habits, and while they creep in secretly, they grow into a great number. **ADIMANTUS:** What is to stop them? **SOCRATES:** At last, they occupy the citadel of the young man's soul, sensing it to be empty of learning, honorable duties, and true reasonings—which are surely the best guardians and preservers in the minds of men beloved by the gods. **ADIMANTUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** Then false, arrogant, and insolent reasons and opinions rush in to take their place, occupying the position of such a man. **ADIMANTUS:** Greatly so. **SOCRATES:** Does he not then return to those "lotus-eaters" <note>original: *delicatos illos*, a reference to the Homeric Lotus-eaters, symbolizing those lost in pleasure.</note> and live openly among them? And if any help is offered by his family to the more frugal part of his soul, those arrogant and insolent arguments close the royal gates of the wall within him; they neither admit the aid itself nor receive the embassies of the advice of elder private citizens. Instead, they win the battle: calling shame "silliness," they shamefully drive it into exile; calling temperance "cowardice," they reject and cast it out; and they detest modesty in behavior and moderation in spending as if they were "rusticity" and "meanness," chasing them away with the help of many futile desires. **ADIMANTUS:** Very much so. **SOCRATES:** When they have emptied and purged the soul of the one they have occupied—performing great "initiation rites" upon it—they then lead in Insolence, Anarchy, Prodigality, and Impudence, in a great procession, crowned and accompanied by a choir. They praise and flatter them, calling Insolence "good breeding," Anarchy "liberty," Prodigality "magnificence," and Impudence "courage." Is it not in this way that a young man passes from a childhood of necessary desires into the unrestrained license of unnecessary and futile pleasures? **ADIMANTUS:** That is clearly established. **SOCRATES:** Thereafter, such a man lives, I think, spending his money, labor, and study no more on necessary pleasures than on superfluous ones. But if he is fortunate enough not to be driven into total madness—and as he grows older, the great turmoil having passed, he admits some parts of the excluded virtues and does not commit himself entirely to the intruders—he brings his pleasures to a sort of equality. He lives by handing over the rule of himself to whatever desire happens to fall to him, as if by lot, until it is satisfied; then to another, scorning none but nourishing all equally. **ADIMANTUS:** So it happens. **SOCRATES:** Such a man does not accept true reason, nor does he admit it into the citadel of his guard. If someone says that some pleasures belong to honorable and good desires, but others to evil ones, and that the former should be practiced and honored while the latter should be restrained and suppressed, he shakes his head at all this and asserts that they are all alike and to be honored equally. **ADIMANTUS:** Indeed, anyone so disposed acts in that way. **SOCRATES:** Does he not live day by day in this manner, yielding to whatever desire is present? At one time he indulges in drunkenness and music; then he is content with water and fasting; sometimes he exercises in the gymnasium; other times he is idle and sluggish; sometimes he dabbles in philosophy; often he turns to politics, jumping up and saying or doing whatever happens to occur to him. If he admires soldiers, he is carried that way; if merchants, he turns to them. There is no order or necessity directing his life; but calling this life pleasant, free, and blessed, he follows it constantly. **ADIMANTUS:** You have skillfully described the life of a "man of the people" who has no fixed order of living. **SOCRATES:** I believe this man is full of the greatest variety of characters; he is beautiful and many-colored, just like that city...

He illustrates how the soul's "citadel" is captured by insolence and anarchy when it lacks the protection of true education and reason.</summary>
