Indeed, many men and women would judge themselves to live happily there, since it contains within itself many examples of both constitutions and morals. ADIMANTUS. That is certainly so. SOCRATES. Let such a man stand for us as the likeness of the democratic republic, seeing as he is rightly named "democratic." ADIMANTUS. Let him be so. SOCRATES. It remains for us to speak of that most famous republic and that most famous man: tyranny and the tyrant. ADIMANTUS. <margin>On tyranny and the tyrant.</margin> By all means. SOCRATES. Come then, let us see, my dear friend, what the manner of tyranny’s birth is. That it arises from democracy is almost self-evident. ADIMANTUS. It is manifest. SOCRATES. Does tyranny then arise from democracy in the same way that democracy arises from oligarchy <note>original: "paucorum potentia" - the power of the few</note>? ADIMANTUS. In what way? SOCRATES. That which the citizens proposed to themselves as the "good" in an oligarchy—and by which oligarchy grew—was the abundance of wealth. Was it not? ADIMANTUS. That very thing. SOCRATES. Thus, an insatiable thirst for riches, and the neglect of other duties for the sake of making money, destroys it. ADIMANTUS. What you say is true. SOCRATES. Furthermore, does not an insatiable desire for that which is considered the "good" in a democracy also subvert it? ADIMANTUS. What do you say is considered the chief good in it? SOCRATES. Liberty. For you will hear that in a democratic city, this is considered the most excellent thing. Therefore, in this city alone is it fit for a man to live who is free by nature. ADIMANTUS. Certainly, the name of "liberty" is frequently proclaimed in this city. SOCRATES. Is it not as I was about to say: the insatiable desire for this very thing, and the neglect of all else, changes this republic and compels it to stand in need of tyranny? ADIMANTUS. In what manner? SOCRATES. When, clearly, a democratic city thirsting for liberty happens upon bad cupbearers <note>A metaphor for leaders who provide "intoxicating" amounts of freedom</note> who serve it, and it becomes drunk by gorging itself more profusely than is proper; it then punishes its leaders as if they were rigid and tyrannical unless they are very mild and grant a great deal of license. ADIMANTUS. That is exactly what happens. SOCRATES. And it reproaches those who are obedient to the leaders as being slave-like and men of no value; but it praises and honors, both privately and publicly, leaders who are like subjects, and subjects who are like leaders. Is it not necessary that in such a city, men reach the height of liberty? ADIMANTUS. Without a doubt. SOCRATES. And this innate impatience with obedience, my friend, creeps into private homes and eventually spreads even to the brute beasts! ADIMANTUS. How do we mean this? SOCRATES. For example: if a father becomes like his son and fears his sons, and the son is equal to the father, neither respecting nor fearing his parents so that he may be "most free"; and moreover, the resident alien is made equal to the citizen, and the citizen to the resident alien, and the foreigner likewise. ADIMANTUS. So it happens. SOCRATES. These and other similar minor things occur. Surely in such a city the teacher fears his students and flatters them; the students despise the teachers and likewise their tutors. To put it briefly, the young act as if they are equal to the seniors, opposing them in words and deeds. The seniors, in turn, take the place of the young, and like jesters they delight them with wit, lest they appear too severe or imperious. ADIMANTUS. Very much so. SOCRATES. And how great, my friend, is the extreme liberty of the common people in such a city! For even the purchased slaves are no less free than those who bought them; and we almost forgot to mention how much equality and liberty there is for women toward men, and men toward women. ADIMANTUS. Shall we not say, according to Aeschylus, "what now comes into our mouths"? <note>A Greek idiom meaning "to speak what is on one's mind."</note> SOCRATES. Exactly so. And I say this: truly, no one would believe unless they experienced it how much freer the beasts who are nourished under men are in this city than elsewhere. For even the little dogs, as the <margin>Proverb: Little dogs are just like their mistresses.</margin> proverb goes, are just like their mistresses. And the horses and donkeys are accustomed to walk through the streets with such liberty that they charge at anyone they meet unless he gives way. All other things are conducted with the highest license. ADIMANTUS. You are certainly describing my own dream to me. For these things frequently happen to me when I am traveling to the countryside. SOCRATES. Do you see where the sum of all these things mentioned above finally leads? It renders the souls of the citizens so delicate that if anyone suggests even a little bit of servitude, they are annoyed and will not tolerate it. Finally, they despise all laws, both written and unwritten, so that no master may rule over them. ADIMANTUS. What you say is manifest. SOCRATES. This, my friend, is that "excellent" and "elegant" republic from which, as it seems to me, tyranny is born. ADIMANTUS. Elegant indeed. But to what end is this? SOCRATES. Furthermore, the same disease that crept into the oligarchy and undermined it, now budding and increasing in this state out of excessive license, brings the democratic city under the yoke of slavery. In short, every excess is usually turned into its opposite: in the weather, in trees, in animals, and especially in republics. ADIMANTUS. Not without reason. For excessive liberty seems to turn into nothing other than excessive slavery, both privately and publicly. SOCRATES. Certainly, that is consistent. Therefore, I was not wrong to say that tyranny arises from no other republic than the democratic one: from extreme liberty comes the gravest and harshest slavery. ADIMANTUS. So reason shows. SOCRATES. But this, I think, was not what you were asking; rather, you asked what that same disease is which, being innate in both oligarchy and democratic government, reduces it to slavery. ADIMANTUS. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. I was speaking of the class of idle and extravagant men: part of them are stronger and more manly, part are more cowardly; the former lead, while the latter follow. We compared these men to drones in our previous discussion—the former to drones with stings, the latter to drones without stings. ADIMANTUS. And rightly so. SOCRATES. These men disturb whatever city they are in, just as phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note> and bile disturb the body. A good physician and law-founder, no less than a skillful bee-keeper, must take precautions from afar: first, that they do not arise in the city, and if they do arise, that they are cut out immediately along with the honeycombs. ADIMANTUS. That is exactly how one must act. SOCRATES. Let us then take it this way, so that we may more clearly recognize what we seek. ADIMANTUS. In what way? SOCRATES. Let us divide the democratic city into three parts, as it is in reality. One part is this class [of drones] which is born in it because of license, no less than in an oligarchy. ADIMANTUS. It is so. SOCRATES. But it is far more fierce in this state than in that one. ADIMANTUS. For what reason? SOCRATES. There, because it is held in contempt and lives privately, it becomes weak through idleness. In a democracy, however, this whole class (with few exceptions) presides; and the fiercest part of it speaks and acts, while the rest huddle around the tribunals whispering, and will not tolerate anyone saying anything else. Wherefore...

<summary>Socrates explains to Adimantus how the transition from democracy to tyranny occurs, arguing that extreme liberty inevitably leads to extreme slavery. He uses the metaphor of "drones" (idle, ambitious men) to describe the class that destabilizes the state.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book VIII of Plato’s Republic, specifically focusing on the transition from a democracy to a tyranny. The speakers are Socrates (SO.) and Adimantus (ADI.).</meta>

# BOOK VIII.

Everything of this kind, with a few exceptions, is managed in a city of this sort. ADI. Most certainly. SO. Is not another such group always separated from the multitude? ADI. Which one? SO. From all those engaged in trade, those who are by nature the most orderly usually become the wealthiest. ADI. That is likely. SO. From these, a more abundant and easier supply of honey is squeezed out for the drones <note>In Plato's allegory, "drones" refers to the idle, predatory class of people in a city who consume without producing.</note>. ADI. Indeed, for how could honey be squeezed from those who possess little? SO. The wealthy, I believe, are called the "drones' herb" <note>original: "fucorum herba"; implying they are the feeding ground for the idle class.</note>. ADI. Almost so. SO. The people, however, will be the third class: as many as mind only their own business and do not involve themselves in the affairs of others, having little property. This class is both the most numerous and the most powerful in a popular state whenever it assembles. ADI. It is indeed. But it is not often willing to do so unless it is made a sharer of the honey. SO. Does it not always share, insofar as those in power—having despoiled the wealthy and distributed the spoils to the people—are able to keep the greatest portion for themselves? ADI. Truly, in that way, it becomes a sharer. SO. Those who have been despoiled are forced to resist, speaking and acting before the people as best they can. ADI. Why wouldn't they? SO. They are then accused by others—even if they themselves had no desire for revolution—of plotting against the people and setting their minds toward an oligarchy <note>The rule of the few.</note>. ADI. Why not? SO. Finally, when they see the people—not by choice, but through ignorance and being misled by slanderers—attempting to do them wrong, then indeed, whether they wish it or not, they truly become supporters of oligarchy. This is not of their own will, but that evil "drone" goads them by stinging them. ADI. Very much so. SO. Therefore, accusations, lawsuits, and mutual contentions arise. ADI. Most certainly. SO. And so the people are accustomed to set up one particular man as their champion, to nourish him, and to cherish him so that he becomes great. ADI. They are indeed accustomed to do so. SO. From this, it is clear that a tyrant sprouts from a "protectorate" root. <margin>The tyrant [comes] from the root of a protector.</margin> ADI. That is certain. SO. What then is the origin of the change from a protector into a tyrant? Is it not clearly after he begins to do what the fable tells regarding the temple of Lycean Jove in Arcadia? <margin>How a man becomes a wolf.</margin> ADI. What is that? SO. That whoever tastes human entrails mixed with the entrails of other victims is forced to become a wolf. Have you not heard the fable? ADI. I have. SO. In the same way, this man, whom the crowd obeys implicitly, does not abstain from the blood of his own kin. Instead, bringing them into court with false accusations, as is their custom, he drags those he fears into judgment and stains himself with unjust slaughter, extinguishing a man's life. With an impure tongue and profane mouth, he tastes the blood of his closest relatives; he expels some and kills others, using the pretext of the cancellation of debts and the redistribution of lands. Therefore, it is necessary for such a man either to be killed by his enemies or to exercise a tyranny and become a wolf instead of a man. ADI. It is absolutely necessary. SO. This man, then, becomes seditious against the wealthy. ADI. Certainly. SO. Does not danger loom over him from the power of his enemies? If he is expelled and returns against the will of his enemies, does he not return as a perfected tyrant? ADI. It is well known. SO. And if they cannot expel him or kill him through public slanders, they plot a violent death for him and ambush him in secret. ADI. That is certainly how it usually happens. SO. Hence arises that well-known tyrannical request for a guard. Namely, all who have reached this point ask the people for some bodyguards, so that the "helper of the people" may be safe. ADI. Most especially. SO. The people then give them, fearing for him but being too confident in themselves. ADI. Greatly so. SO. When a man of wealth notices this—one who is an enemy to the people because of his riches—then indeed, according to the oracle given to Croesus <note>Croesus was the King of Lydia; the oracle warned him that if he crossed the river Halys, he would destroy a great empire (it turned out to be his own).</note>, he flees to the stony river Hermus; he does not delay, nor is he ashamed to be called a coward. ADI. He certainly would not fear it a second time. SO. Truly, anyone who is caught is usually put to death. ADI. Necessarily. SO. But that great champion of the people does not behave magnificently at all; instead, he strikes down many others and sits in the chariot of the state, a tyrant transformed from a protector. ADI. What prevents it? SO. Shall we then describe the happiness of this man and of the city in which such a man is born? ADI. By all means. SO. In the beginning, he greets everyone with a smile wherever he meets them, and he refuses the name of "tyrant." He promises many things both privately and publicly; he releases people from debt and distributes land to the people and to his followers. Finally, he pretends to be mild and gentle to everyone. ADI. It must be so. SO. But as soon as he has reconciled with some foreign enemies and destroyed others, and matters are at peace, he immediately strives to stir up some war so that the people may always be in need of a leader. ADI. That is consistent. SO. In doing so, he also ensures that his subjects, exhausted by heavy expenses, are forced to turn to their daily survival and thus meditate less on plots against the tyrant. ADI. It is clear. SO. Furthermore, if he recognizes any who are of a free spirit and seem likely to refuse his rule, he exposes them to the enemy so that he may have an occasion to destroy them. For these reasons, it is necessary for a tyrant to always stir up new wars. ADI. Necessary. SO. Because of this, he makes the citizens hateful toward him. ADI. To the highest degree. SO. It is likely, then, that some of those who helped him to power and who hold great influence with the tyrant will boldly criticize what is being done, both among themselves and to him—especially those of a higher spirit. ADI. It is likely. SO. It follows that the tyrant must remove all of these from the midst if he is to remain ruler, until he leaves no one among his friends or enemies who is of any consequence. ADI. That is indeed manifest. SO. He must, therefore, keenly observe who is brave, who is high-minded, who is prudent, or who is wealthy. He is not so "blessed" that, whether he wishes it or not, he must be an enemy to these and plot against them until he has "purged" the city. ADI. You describe a remarkable purging indeed. SO. Quite the opposite of the purging done by physicians. For physicians remove what is worst from the body and leave what is best. The tyrant does the opposite. ADI. He is indeed forced to do so if he is to remain ruler. SO.

<summary>This page describes the psychological and political evolution of a democratic leader into a tyrant, using the metaphor of a man turning into a wolf after tasting human blood. It details how the tyrant uses war and "purges" of virtuous citizens to maintain absolute control.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Adeimantus regarding the transition from democracy to tyranny, specifically focusing on the tyrant's reliance on mercenaries and the eventual oppression of the people who empowered him.</meta>

He is bound, of course, by a blessed necessity <note>original: "Beata nimirū necessitate"</note> which commands him either to live with a great many wicked men—by whom he is also hated—or not to live at all. ADI. That is certainly his condition. SO. Now, as he makes his citizens more hostile while doing these things, does he not require more numerous and more faithful bodyguards? ADI. What prevents it? SO. Who then are most faithful to him? From where will he summon them? ADI. Many will fly to him of their own accord from all sides, lured by pay. SO. You seem to be speaking again of drones <note>Socrates uses "drones" as a metaphor for idle, predatory people who consume the resources of the state</note> from abroad, a diverse lot flowing in from various nations. ADI. You see it correctly. SO. But what of the natives? Would there not be some if he wished? ADI. In what way? SO. That is, if he were to take away the slaves of the citizens, set them free, and enroll them among his bodyguards. ADI. Most certainly, since these are the most faithful to him. SO. What a splendid possession you describe for a tyrant, if indeed he uses such friends and faithful men after having destroyed those former ones. ADI. Yet he does use such as these. SO. And so these friends admire him, and these new citizens associate with him, while the more upright men hate and flee from him. ADI. Why not? SO. It is not without reason, then, that tragedy seems to be a wise art, and in it Euripides is particularly clear. ADI. Why so? SO. Because he sang this from a profound mind: "Tyrants are wise by the company of the wise," <note>original: "Sapientes tyrannos esse sapientū cōsuetudine"</note> and he said those are wise who associate with them. ADI. Furthermore, he extols tyranny as something divine, as do many other poets. SO. Indeed, the tragic poets, being wise, will forgive us and those who govern the republic as we do, for not admitting them into our state, since they are praisers of tyranny. ADI. They will forgive us, I think, at least those among them who are more eloquent. SO. But they go around to other cities, gathering crowds, and with fine, loud, and persuasive voices—which do not lack a price—they drag republics toward tyrannies and democracies. ADI. Very much so. SO. Do they not receive pay for this and are they not honored, first, as is likely, by tyrants, and then also by the democratic state? But truly, the higher they climb toward the steep summit of republics, the more their honor fails, as if exhausted by frequent panting, it were unable to proceed further. ADI. Exactly so. SO. But lest we wander further, having digressed this far, let us say how the tyrant nourishes that splendid, varied, and ever-changing army of his. ADI. It is clear, first of all, that if there are any sacred riches in the city, he will seize them; and he will consume them as long as the things for sale suffice, while he exacts lighter tributes from the common people. SO. What if these riches fail? ADI. It is obvious that he, his colleagues, his companions, and his mistresses will be fed from his father's estate. SO. I understand then that the people who fathered the tyrant will nourish him and his friends. ADI. They are forced to. SO. But what if the people become angry and say it is not fair for a grown son to be nourished by his father any longer, but rather the father by the son? And that they did not create him for this—so that after he grew up, they themselves should serve his slaves and nourish him, his slaves, and all the others flowing in from everywhere—but rather so that they might be liberated from those who are considered rich and good in the city under his leadership? And what if the people then order him and his friends to leave the city, just as a father drives a son from the house along with a crowd of revelers? ADI. Then, by Zeus, the people will finally realize what sort of beast they have delighted in, fathering and educating it, and that they, being the weaker, are attempting to cast out the stronger. SO. What do you say? Will the tyrant dare to use force against his father, and if he does not obey, to strike him? ADI. Yes indeed, for he will take away his weapons. SO. You are saying then that the tyrant is a parricide <note>A killer of his own father/parents</note> and a harsh nourisher of old age. And as it seems, this is truly tyranny: as the saying goes, the people, fleeing the smoke of the slavery of free men, have fallen into the fire of the mastery of slaves; in place of that great and unseasonable liberty, they undergo the harshest and most bitter slavery to servants. ADI. That is exactly what happens. SO. Shall we not then have rightly said, if we have narrated it sufficiently, how tyranny is born from democratic government, and what it is like once born? ADI. Very sufficiently indeed.

### Summary of Marsilio Ficino on the Ninth Dialogue concerning Justice.

Socrates, having treated at length the royal life of the best men, also disputes much concerning its opposite, tyranny, so that we may approve the former as most blessed and reject the latter as most miserable. Therefore, not only in the eighth but also in the ninth book, tyranny is discussed: by what means it chiefly arises from democracy, what it is like, how harmful, and how unhappy. This is so that we may avoid with all our strength the primary tyranny that occurs in the soul, and in turn embrace the kingship established in the soul. Through these things, the dispute will immediately return to its first purpose: to demonstrate that justice is not only praiseworthy by human opinion, but also by its own nature, wonderfully honorable, and above all to be revered as salutary. Likewise, that injustice is to be condemned not only for fear of laws or infamy, but also to be fled far away because of the poison of its own malevolent nature. When he names justice, he sometimes designates legal and common justice—that is, universal virtue established under the providence of laws; at other times, a more specific or distributive justice, through which honors, rewards, and punishments are distributed in the city according to merit, and actions and duties are assigned in the parts of the soul according to the dignity of nature; or commutative justice, through which things are exchanged in the city for a fair and legal price, and in the soul, duties are exchanged in a similar way, so that as much as reason consults the lower parts, so much do the lower powers necessarily obey the command of reason...

It then introduces Marsilio Ficino's commentary on the Ninth Dialogue, focusing on the internal tyranny of the soul versus the virtue of justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato’s Republic, specifically focusing on the transition from the analysis of the tyrant to the nature of pleasure and the tripartite soul. # BOOK

...provides support. Meanwhile, note that the **tyrannical mind** is so disturbed that it is properly judged to be ruined by lust, drunken, furious, and monstrous. Indeed, it is carried away by these monstrous lusts like a wild beast—the kind of ferocity that others only occasionally experience while dreaming. As for what pertains here to the falsehood, truth, and prophecy of dreams, we have treated that abundantly in our *Theology* <note>Likely referring to the author's "Platonic Theology" regarding the soul's immortality.</note>. Consider how diligently he enumerates all the evils by which a city oppressed by tyranny is weighed down; or how aptly he counts just as many evils, and even more, in the soul of the tyrant, so that nothing more miserable could be imagined. 

Soon, he reduces the entire dispute—which tends toward showing that a wise and just life is preferred to its opposite—into three main heads. 

**The first** is intended to be what has been treated up to this point: namely, the comparison of the foolish and unjust man to a city governed by no wisdom or justice. There, it certainly appears that both that city and that man are, by equal measure, in the worst and most unhappy state. 

**The second head** he now approaches by repeating that distinction of the parts of the soul into the natures of **reasoning**, **anger**, and **desire** <note>The tripartite soul: Logistikon (reason), Thymoeides (spirit/anger), and Epithymetikon (appetite/desire).</note>; to which he also accommodates three lives: the philosophical, the ambitious, and the covetous. I call it "covetous" for the sake of money and pleasures, and therefore he also names it "avaricious." He similarly arranges three parts in the city: magistrates, soldiers, and profit-makers. He then proves that a life endowed with virtue is more to be chosen than a vicious one, especially because it is truly sweeter. Surely, since each of those three prefers the pleasure of his own life to the others, only the **philosopher** can rightly judge this. For judgment requires experience, prudence, and reason. 

In the first place, as far as experience is concerned, the philosopher has experienced both his own pleasures and those of others; thus he can easily know which is to be preferred. The others, however, have never tasted the joys of the one who practices philosophy, and therefore they cannot compare their own pleasures with the joy of the philosopher. Furthermore, only the philosopher excels in prudence and the industry of assigning reasons—two things which are necessary for judgment. Since, therefore, the philosopher prefers the joys of a wise and just life over the delights of an ambitious and lustful life, we ought—by the sentence of the true judge himself—rightly to prefer a life directed by virtue over a life dissolved in vice. 

**The third head**, finally, begins chiefly from this: that **true pleasure** can be found only in the wise and just man. In others, however, it is established that pleasure is false and shadowy. This is proved as follows: pleasures that are for the most part vehement are certain "fillings" of a deficiency. And where both that which is filled and that which fills are truer and more perfect, and the mode of filling is purer and more effective, there the pleasure is truer, more perfect, and greater. Since, therefore, the intellect and the truth to be understood have a truer and more perfect nature than the senses and the sensible—and truth penetrates the intellect more deeply than the sensible penetrates the sense, and it approaches without the mixture of pain—it follows that the pleasure of the intelligence is truer and more perfect. 

Among these things, by some chance, something mathematical intervenes; you will receive the explanation of this more opportunely from the commentaries on the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's dialogue on the physical world and mathematics.</note>. 

Pay attention next to that figure of the soul's nature. In it, understand the nature of **desire** under the name of a "manifold beast"; the vigor of **anger** under the figure of a "lion"; and **reason** under the form of a "man." See how expressly he depicts the life of the ambitious, unjust, and lustful man—or rather, his miserable servitude. Likewise, accept there the formula by which you can interpret the "migration of souls into beasts" <note>Metempsychosis or reincarnation.</note> in such a way that they are said to migrate into the *dispositions and habits* of beasts rather than into their physical bodies. 

Furthermore, remember that just as in the body the sharpness of sense, health, strength, and beauty are goods not by opinion but by nature (and their opposites are similarly evils), so in the soul **prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice** are naturally good, and their opposites naturally evil. Finally, accept the form of the whole life, through which you may so arrange all bodily things that they harmonize with the temperance of the soul. Choose individual things only insofar as they contribute to the health of the soul; and conversely, flee far from those things that hinder it. Dwell always in the "citadel of the mind," and allow yourself to be cast down from it by no allurements or services. When you wish to form both yourself and others in this way, look up at the clear **model of this Republic in heaven**—in heaven, I say, in the order of the celestial motions, and higher still in the Divine Mind; so that from there, at last, you may compose first yourself, then your family, and thirdly your city, justly and happily according to His image.

### THE NINTH DIALOGUE ON THE JUST.

<margin>Concerning pleasures more distinctly.</note>
Next, it remains to be considered: by what means the tyrannical man is made from the democratic man, what he is like, and whether he leads a miserable or a blessed life. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Certainly, that is what remains. 
**SOCRATES:** Do you know what I still desire? 
**ADIMANTUS:** What? 
**SOCRATES:** We do not yet seem to have sufficiently distinguished how many and of what sort the desires are. And unless that is clear, the investigation of what we seek will be more obscure. 
**ADIMANTUS:** It will still be an opportune time. 
**SOCRATES:** Entirely so. And notice what I wish to know in them. It is this: of those pleasures and desires that are not necessary, some seem to me to be repugnant to the laws. These are present in everyone; but when they are restrained by the laws and by better desires along with reason, in some men they either fade away entirely or are so repressed that they are rendered very rare and weak; in others, however, they turn out more vehement and frequent. 
**ADIMANTUS:** Which ones do you especially call these? 
**SOCRATES:** Those which are often excited in **dreams**, when that part of the soul sleeps which is a participant in reason and is mild and holds dominion; but the other part, in which there is ferocity and wild monstrosity, since it is filled with immoderate drink and food, leaps up...

It introduces the famous tripartite image of the soul as a man, a lion, and a multi-headed beast, concluding with the soul's alignment with a heavenly model of justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Socrates and Adimantus from Plato's Republic, Book IX. The previous discussion likely established the transition from a democratic man to a tyrannical one.</meta>

# DIALOGUE IX. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE, FOLIO 262.

...and he attempts to shake off sleep: and to indulge in his accustomed lusts. Then indeed there is nothing that he does not dare: as if released and free from all the precepts of shame and prudence: so that he seems either to join his body with his mother, or with any other man or god, often even a beast; and even to slaughter someone, and be stained with blood himself: and to abstain from no abyss whatsoever: nor, to embrace it briefly, to temper himself from any insanity or impudence. 

**ADIMANTUS.** You speak all too truly. 

**SOCRATES.** But when someone who has given himself over to a healthy and moderate cultivation and way of life—with that part of the soul in which reason dwells <note>The "rational" part of the soul (logistikon)</note> awakened and upright, and sated with the feasts of good thoughts, and turned toward contemplating itself—and with that part of the soul which is nourished by pleasure <note>The "appetitive" part (epithymetikon)</note> neither oppressed by want nor overflowing with satiety, so that it may rest most deeply, and not disturb that best part either by rejoicing or by grieving, but allows it to consider by itself, alone and pure, to track down and perceive whatever was hitherto unknown, whether of the present, the past, or the future; and with that third part of the soul in which the heat of anger seethes <note>The "spirited" part (thymoeides)</note> calmed and extinguished, so far that it rests hostile to no one; and thus, with these two parts pacified and the mind indeed uplifted, he prepares himself for sleep, then at last the pure mind touches the truth: and the wicked visions of dreams do not present themselves. 

**ADIMANTUS.** I think exactly so. 

**SOCRATES.** What more? We wish for this in summary: that there is in everyone a certain dire, wild, and lawless species of desires: even in those who seem most moderate among men. This becomes manifest in dreams. If I seem to say anything of substance, and you agree, take note. 

**ADIMANTUS.** I certainly agree. 

**SOCRATES.** Remember what kind of man we said the "popular" <note>The democratic man</note> man was. He was one who, from his early years, was nourished under a frugal father: who indulged only the desire for profit; but the other desires, which are not necessary but are companions of play and finery, he despised. Was it not so? 

**ADIMANTUS.** Exactly so. 

**SOCRATES.** Then, having associated with more haughty men, and those full of these lusts which we just described, he began to decline toward every insolence and their habits, out of hatred for his father's parsimony. Since he was of a better nature than his corrupters, being pulled from both sides, he hit upon a middle state between both habits: following both moderately, as he himself thinks, leading a life neither illiberal nor dissolved: changed from a lover of the power of the few <note>The oligarchic man</note> into a popular one. 

**ADIMANTUS.** This was and is the opinion regarding such a man. 

**SOCRATES.** Suppose again that this man, having grown older, has a son, nourished from his first years under his parent's habits. 

**ADIMANTUS.** I suppose it. 

**SOCRATES.** Suppose again that the same things happen to him as happened to his father: that he is drawn toward every disgrace and the license of a wanton life—which those who draw him, however, call "pure liberty"—while the father and other household members support these middle desires. But those who offer him help: when indeed those vehement enchanters and nourishers of tyranny have hoped that they cannot hold the youth in any other way, they excite in him a certain love <note>original: "amorem"</note> by certain machinations, as a protector and tutor of his idle desires and those ministering to his lust—a winged and surely huge drone <note>original: "fucum" - referring to the drone bee, a metaphor for the parasitic consumer</note>. Do you think the love of such things is anything else? 

**ADIMANTUS.** Nothing else. 

**SOCRATES.** When indeed other desires, full of the smell of incense, ointments, crowns, and unmixed wine, whispering around him and relaxed by the pleasures of such customs, altogether increase and nourish that longing, and thus add a sting to the drone: then at last this protector of the soul rages entirely, and glows with madness itself; and then, surrounded by henchmen and driven by a sting, if he finds any frugal and modest opinions or desires within himself, he immediately uproots and expels them: until he casts out all temperance and fills himself with a foreign and external insanity. 

**ADIMANTUS.** You describe the origin of the tyrannical man excellently. 

**SOCRATES.** And was it not for this reason that of old, Love was called a tyrant? 

**ADIMANTUS.** It plainly seems so. 

**SOCRATES.** And a drunken man, O friend, does he not carry a tyrannical soul? 

**ADIMANTUS.** Certainly. 

**SOCRATES.** Moreover, the man who is furious and out of his mind strives to command not only men, but even the gods, and hopes that he will achieve it. 

**ADIMANTUS.** Vehemently so. 

**SOCRATES.** A tyrannical man, O blessed one, truly becomes such when, either by nature or by habit or both, he becomes intoxicated, subject to love, and furious. 

**ADIMANTUS.** That is exactly how the matter stands. 

**SOCRATES.** Thus, then, such a man is made, as it appears. But in what way does he live? 

**ADIMANTUS.** That indeed, as they say in a joke, you shall tell me. 

**SOCRATES.** I shall tell you. After these things, as I think, they indulge in festive revelries, banquets, harlots, and all other things of this kind: those in whom tyrant love, dwelling within the inner chambers of the soul, rules everything. 

**ADIMANTUS.** It must be so. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, many vehement desires, in need of many things, sprout forth by day and night. 

**ADIMANTUS.** Many indeed. 

**SOCRATES.** Therefore, whatever revenues there are, they are quickly consumed. 

**ADIMANTUS.** Why not? 

**SOCRATES.** After this, surely, come high-interest loans and the dissipation of the patrimony. 

**ADIMANTUS.** Without a doubt. 

**SOCRATES.** When indeed everything fails, it is necessary to cry out and complain: for many and burning desires lurk in the nest of the soul; and these, as if struck by certain stings—namely, by other lusts—and especially with love as the leader of all the others as if they were its henchmen, are tossed about and carried away to explore if anyone possesses anything that can be snatched by fraud or taken by force. 

**ADIMANTUS.** Very much so. 

**SOCRATES.** Wherefore they are compelled either to usurp from everywhere or to be tortured by huge stings and pains. 

**ADIMANTUS.** They are plainly compelled. 

**SOCRATES.** Just as his new and grown desires surpassed the old ones and usurped what was theirs, will he not also judge it to be just that he, being younger, should have more than his parents? And if he has consumed his own portion, will he not spend his father's as well? 

**ADIMANTUS.** Why not? 

**SOCRATES.** And if those parents should by no means permit it, will he not first attempt to steal from them and deceive them? 

**ADIMANTUS.** Entirely. 

**SOCRATES.** But if he cannot do that, he will then seize it and bring force upon his parents. 

**ADIMANTUS.** So I think. 

**SOCRATES.** And if the father and mother, being old, O wonderful man, should resist and fight back, will he then stand in awe of them?

<summary>This page describes the psychological descent of a man into tyranny, driven by lawless desires that manifest in dreams and eventually consume his waking life. Socrates explains how "Love" acts as a tyrant within the soul, leading the individual to exhaust his wealth and eventually turn violently against his own parents.</summary>

# BOOK NINE. XXXI.

And so he will restrain himself so that he does nothing tyrannical! **ADIMANTUS.** Indeed, you have described how he would treat his father and mother. **SOCRATES.** By Jove, O Adimantus, do you not think that for the sake of some newly beloved and unnecessary mistress, he would strike his mother—an old and necessary friend—or for the sake of some beautiful, newly beloved and unnecessary youth, he would strike his father—a deformed and necessary old man, the oldest of all his friends? Do you think he would subject his parents to these newcomers if he brought them into the same house? **ADIMANTUS.** By Jove, absolutely. **SOCRATES.** How "blessed" you see it is to have fathered a tyrannical son. **ADIMANTUS.** Not very. **SOCRATES.** What then? When his parents' wealth is no longer sufficient, and there is already within him a thick swarm of pleasures, will he not first break through the wall of someone's house or snatch the cloak of a traveler? **SOCRATES.** <note>The OCR repeats Socrates here; he continues the thought.</note> Will he not snatch such things? Then he will plunder even more from elsewhere. And in all these things, those opinions which he held since childhood regarding the honorable and the base—the "laws" by which he used to judge—will now be overcome by those desires recently released from slavery. These desires, acting like bodyguards surrounding Love <note>original: "amorem," referring to Eros as a driving tyrannical force</note>, will triumph along with him. These are the desires that used to be released only during sleep in dreams, while he was still under the laws and his father’s instructions within a democratic self-governance. But finally, ensnared by the tyranny of Love, he becomes while awake the sort of man he rarely was even in his dreams! For he will abstain from no slaughter, no gluttony, and no crime; but he will live tyrannically within that love with all license and transgression. Since Love is his sole master, he will shamelessly plunder the man subjected to him as if he were a city, so that he may feed himself and the crowd of followers—partly those who entered from the outside through wicked habits, and partly those from within who were released and freed by his own character. Is this not the life of such a man? **ADIMANTUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** And if there are only a few such men in the city, while all others are modest, they might serve as bodyguards to some other tyrant; and if war threatens anywhere, they fight as mercenaries. But if there is peace in the city, they commit many "minor" evils. **ADIMANTUS.** What kind? **SOCRATES.** They will steal; they will dig through walls; they will cut purses; they will plunder and pillage; they will snatch sacred objects and force captured men into slavery. They will also bring false accusations if they are eloquent in speech, deceive men with perjuries, and corrupt judges with bribes. **ADIMANTUS.** You call these "minor" evils, if there are only a few such men! **SOCRATES.** These are indeed called small when compared to greater ones. But all these things do not even come close, as the proverb says, to the wickedness and misery of a city under a tyrant. For whenever many such men are found in a city, and many others follow them, and they realize their own great number, they create a tyrant through the ignorance of the people—specifically that man among them who has the most powerful tyrant within his own soul. **ADIMANTUS.** That is consistent; he would indeed be the most powerful tyrant. **SOCRATES.** Does this not happen easily if everyone yields? But if the city resists this tyrant, then just as he previously subdued his father and mother, he will again subdue his fatherland <note>original: "patriam"</note> with all his might. He will bring in other youths and force his once-dear fatherland and "mother"—to use the Cretan expression—to serve them. This will be the end of that man's desire. **ADIMANTUS.** Precisely. **SOCRATES.** Do such men not behave this way in private before they take power? At first, they associate mostly with those who flatter them and agree with them in everything. And if they need anything, they do the same: they submit themselves and play whatever part is needed as if they were household intimates. But once they have gained what they wanted, they show themselves to be strangers. **ADIMANTUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** Thus they spend their whole lives. They are never a friend to anyone; they are always either mastering someone or serving someone. A tyrannical nature never tastes true liberty or friendship. **ADIMANTUS.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Shall we not rightly call such men faithless? **ADIMANTUS.** Rightly. **SOCRATES.** And also as unjust as possible, if we correctly agreed earlier on what justice is. **ADIMANTUS.** Correct indeed. **SOCRATES.** Let us conclude then, who the worst man is. He is the one who, while awake, is exactly like the one we described earlier in his dreams. **ADIMANTUS.** Absolutely. **SOCRATES.** Such a man is created when one who is tyrannical by nature gains absolute power; and the longer he lives in tyranny, the more he becomes this way. **GLAUCON.** It must be so. **SOCRATES.** Whoever appears most wicked will also appear most miserable; and he who holds tyranny the longest and most firmly is in truth the most wicked and miserable for the longest time. Though many people will see many different things. **GLAUCON.** This must be the case. **SOCRATES.** The tyrannical man is most like a city oppressed by tyranny. The democratic man is like the democratic city, and so on. **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** As city stands to city in virtue and happiness, so does man stand to man. **GLAUCON.** Nothing prevents that. **SOCRATES.** How does a city subjected to a tyrant compare to one ruled by a king, such as we first described? **GLAUCON.** They are complete opposites. For one is the best, the other the worst. **SOCRATES.** I will not ask which you mean, for it is obvious. But do you judge their happiness and misery in the same way? Let us not be dazzled by the outward appearance of the tyrannical city, looking only at the tyrant or the few who hold power; but as is proper, let us enter into the whole city, examine every part, and give our verdict after turning our eyes to everything. **GLAUCON.** You advise well. It is clear to anyone that no city is more miserable than one pressed by tyranny, and none happier than one governed by a king. **SOCRATES.** If I ordered the same to be observed regarding men, would I be right? That is, if the judgment were left to one who could in thought creep into a man's mind and look deeply into his character—not like a child who, looking at the outside, is stunned by the tyrannical display shown to those watching from afar—but judges with insight. If, I say, we should listen to one who is able to discern, who has lived with the man and been present during his domestic actions...

# DIALOGUE IX. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE.

<page-num>FOLIO CCLXIII. [262]</page-num>

...he will have seen: when he has learned in what manner he is affected toward each of his household: in whom it most clearly appears what sort of man he is: having stripped off all the tragic apparatus <note>original: "tragicum apparatum" - referring to the outward pomp and theatrical display of a ruler</note>, and again in the face of public dangers: and I would bid one who discerns all these things to declare in what way the tyrant holds himself toward others, and toward happiness and misery: would I not be bidding rightly? GLAUCON. You would be bidding quite rightly. SOCRATES. Do you wish then that we should pretend that we are of the number of those who are able to judge: and who have stayed close to them: so that we may have someone to answer those things which we ask? GLAUCON. I certainly do. SOCRATES. Come then, consider the similarity in this way, calling to memory the city and the man: and so, point by point and in turn, observe the affections of both. GLAUCON. Tell me what kind. SOCRATES. In the first place, will you call a tyrannical city free, or enslaved? GLAUCON. Most of all, enslaved. SOCRATES. And yet in it you see masters and free men. GLAUCON. Clearly: but that part is small indeed: the whole, however, so to speak, and the most excellent part in it, is shamefully and miserably enslaved. SOCRATES. If therefore the man is similar to the city, it is necessary that the same order exists in him: and that his soul be oppressed by much illiberality and servitude: and that those parts of the soul serve which are most excellent: while a small part, the most worthless and most sunken, plays the master. GLAUCON. It is necessary. SOCRATES. What further? Will you call such a soul enslaved or free? GLAUCON. Enslaved. SOCRATES. And yet a city that is enslaved and subjected to a tyrant does the least of what it wishes. GLAUCON. Undoubtedly. SOCRATES. Therefore a tyrannical soul will do the least of what it wishes: to speak thus of the whole soul: but always spurred by a violent sting, it will be filled with perturbation and repentance. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. Is it necessary for a tyrannical city to be wealthy or poor? GLAUCON. Poor. SOCRATES. Is it also necessary for a tyrannical soul to be always beggarly and insatiable? GLAUCON. It is as you say. SOCRATES. Is it not necessary for such a city and such a man to be troubled by fear? GLAUCON. Greatly. SOCRATES. Furthermore, do you think you will find lamentations, sighs, weeping, and distresses more frequent in any other city? GLAUCON. In no way. SOCRATES. Moreover, do you think such things exist more in any other man than in this tyrannical one: who is maddened by desires and loves? GLAUCON. How could it be otherwise? SOCRATES. Surely, looking at all these things and others of the same kind, you have judged the tyrannical city to be the most miserable of all cities. GLAUCON. Is it not rightly so? SOCRATES. Most certainly. But what do you say again of the tyrannical man, whenever you observe these same things? GLAUCON. I say he is by far the most miserable of all. SOCRATES. You do not say this rightly. GLAUCON. Why? SOCRATES. This one is not yet, as I think, the most miserable. GLAUCON. Who then? SOCRATES. This one perhaps will seem to you more miserable than him. GLAUCON. Who, I ask? SOCRATES. He who, being tyrannical by nature, does not lead a private life, but is unhappy, and by some chance is led to obtain a tyranny <note>i.e., becomes an actual political dictator rather than just a private individual with a tyrannical temperament</note>. GLAUCON. From these things which have been said, I guess you speak the truth. SOCRATES. It is so. But one ought not merely to opine such things: rather, one must investigate them most diligently by such reasoning. For our dispute is concerning the greatest matter, namely, the good life and the bad. GLAUCON. Wisely said. SOCRATES. Attend then to what I say. For it seems to me that this must be considered from these points. GLAUCON. From which? SOCRATES. From each of the private citizens, as many as abound in riches so that they have many slaves. For these are similar to tyrants in that they rule over many. There is a difference, however: that the tyrant rules over more. GLAUCON. There is indeed a difference. SOCRATES. Do you know that these live securely with their household, nor do they fear their servants? GLAUCON. Certainly. For why should they fear? SOCRATES. Nothing. But do you grasp the reason? GLAUCON. Indeed: because clearly the whole city comes to the aid of each of the private citizens. SOCRATES. You speak excellently. What if some god should lead one man, who has fifty or more slaves, out of the city together with his wife and children, and should place him in a solitude with all his things and slaves, where no free man could bring him help; with what and how great a dread do you think he would be vexed: lest perhaps the slaves should kill him and his children and his wife? GLAUCON. The greatest, I think. SOCRATES. Would he not be compelled to flatter certain slaves: and to promise many things: and to set them free, when he has no need to do so? Whence he himself would be a flatterer to his own servants. GLAUCON. He would be compelled entirely either to do so or to perish. SOCRATES. What if the god should place many others around him in a circle: who would by no means endure that one should rule over another: and if they should catch anyone claiming lordship for himself, they would afflict him with extreme punishments? GLAUCON. I think his condition would be much worse, if he were enclosed by a wall of enemies. SOCRATES. Is not the tyrant shut up in such a prison, being by nature such as we have explained in the previous parts, agitated by many and diverse fears and loves? Since he is by nature exceedingly greedy, he alone is neither allowed to go out anywhere, nor to look at what other free men desire: but within the walls of his house he remains fearful like a woman, envying other citizens if anyone walks outside the walls: and sees anything of good. GLAUCON. Exactly so. SOCRATES. Does not that man incur even more evils of this kind, who, governing himself badly—whom you just now judged most miserable, the tyrannical man—by no means lives as a private person: but by some force of fortune, is compelled to exercise a tyranny: even though he cannot command himself, he strives to command others! Just as if someone with a weak body: and not sustaining himself by his own strength, were compelled not to live quietly by himself, but to strive and fight against other bodies. GLAUCON. You bring forward very similar and very true things, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Is not then, O friend Glaucon, this condition altogether miserable, and the life of a man who has obtained a tyranny harder than that life which you above judged to be the hardest? GLAUCON. Greatly. SOCRATES. But in reality, though he may not seem so to some, the true tyrant is a true slave bound to extreme flattery and servitude: a flatterer of the most wicked men: who never fills his appetites: but is always in need of most things: and appears to be truly destitute, if one looks into the inner chambers of his soul. Terrified also by perpetual dread: and by anxiety and distress...

disturbed: provided that he is like the state of the city over which he presides. And he does indeed emerge as such. Is it not so? GLAUCON. Most certainly. SOCRATES. In addition to these things, we shall also attribute to this man those qualities we mentioned before: which he must necessarily possess first, and much more so afterward once he has attained the tyranny; being envious, unjust, lacking in benevolence, impious, the sink and fuel of every wickedness: and because of all these things, he is the most miserable of all: and he renders those who cling to him similar to himself. GLAUCON. No one of sound mind would contradict these things. SOCRATES. Come then, just as a judge who looks around at everything gives judgment on individual cases, so you should now declare who in your judgment is first in happiness, who is second, and describe the others in order, as they are in number: the Royal, the ambitious <note>original: "honorificum," referring to the timocratic or honor-loving man</note>, the seeker of few men's power <note>the oligarch</note>, the popular <note>the democrat</note>, and the tyrannical. GLAUCON. But that judgment is easy. For just as I have entered, I compare them among themselves like choruses in virtue, depravity, and happiness: and its opposite: and so I judge. SOCRATES. Shall we hire a herald? Or shall I rather announce these things! That the son of Ariston <note>Plato's father; Socrates is referring to Plato/Glaucon's lineage</note> has judged the best and most just man to be the happiest: and has said that he is the man who is most kingly and rules himself. But the worst and most unjust man is the most miserable: and such a one is he who is most a tyrant: and who most oppresses himself and his city with tyranny? GLAUCON. Let it be so proclaimed. SOCRATES. Shall I add whether such men remain hidden, or whether they do not remain hidden from men and gods alike? GLAUCON. Add it. SOCRATES. Let it be so then. And let this be one demonstration; but if it seems right, it is fitting to look at a second one. GLAUCON. Which one is that? SOCRATES. Since the city is divided into three parts, so also the soul of each person is divided into three ways, as I think; and from this a second demonstration will be born. GLAUCON. Which one? SOCRATES. This one. Since there are three parts of the soul, there also appear to be three pleasures: each part having its own. There are also as many desires and types of rule. GLAUCON. In what way?

<margin>The three parts of the soul, three pleasures, and desires.</margin>

SOCRATES. One part, we say, is that by which a man learns. The second, that which feels anger. The third, however, because of its variety, we could not name with a single proper word of its own: but we have called it "the concupiscible" <note>the desiring or appetitive part</note> after that which it contains as its greatest and most vehement element: because of the vehemence of those desires which snatch one toward feasts and drinks and sexual matters: and toward those things which follow them: and we have also named it the "money-loving" part, because such desires are mostly satisfied by means of money. GLAUCON. Correct. SOCRATES. And if we say its pleasure and affection is for gain, we shall reduce it to one greatest summary in our speech so that we may signify something certain to ourselves whenever we speak of this part of the soul. And if we name this whole part the "desirer of money and gain," we shall name it quite correctly. GLAUCON. So it seems to me. SOCRATES. What then? Do we not assert that the nature of anger draws the whole person toward power, victory, and glory? GLAUCON. Greatly so. SOCRATES. If therefore we call it "contentious" and "ambitious," would we be right? GLAUCON. Most rightly. SOCRATES. But indeed, that part by which we learn: it is certain that it always strives to investigate the truth, and has the least care for money and glory. GLAUCON. Entirely so. SOCRATES. If we name this third part "desirous of learning" and "philosophical," the name will not be ill-imposed. GLAUCON. It is as you say. SOCRATES. Do we not say that in the souls of some, one of these parts dominates: and in others, another, whichever it happens to be? GLAUCON. We do. SOCRATES. For this reason we say there are three primary kinds of men: the philosopher, the contentious, and the money-lover. GLAUCON. Exactly. SOCRATES. And also three species of pleasure: subject to these, each its own. GLAUCON. Entirely. SOCRATES. If you were to ask each of these men separately which of these lives is the sweetest: each will prefer his own to the others. The money-lover, in comparison to gain itself, will think the delights of honors or learning are worth nothing, unless perhaps they contribute something to silver. GLAUCON. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. But the ambitious man thinks the pleasure of gain is troublesome: and again, that which is perceived by learning he thinks is empty and a mere shadow, unless the teaching produces glory among men. GLAUCON. That is how it stands. SOCRATES. Let us suppose the philosopher also values the other pleasures at a straw <note>original: "floccipendentem," to care not a fig/straw</note>: while he compares them to the continuous joy of learning in which he is occupied in investigating the truth: and calls the others "necessary": because he would not pursue them unless necessity compelled him. GLAUCON. This is well known. SOCRATES. When, therefore, the pleasures of each life and the life itself come into competition—not concerning which is more honorable or shameful, or better or worse, but concerning the sweeter and more peaceful state of life—by what reason shall we discern whose opinion is truer? GLAUCON. I do not quite know how to answer. SOCRATES. Consider it this way. By what thing ought one to judge whatever things are to be rightly decided? Is it not by experience, prudence, and reason? Or does anyone have other things by which he might judge better? GLAUCON. In no way. SOCRATES. Pay attention then. Since there are three: who is most experienced in all the pleasures we have described? Does the money-lover, by learning what the truth is, seem to you more experienced in the pleasantness of learning than the philosopher is in gain? Or rather the opposite? GLAUCON. There is a great difference. For it is necessary for the philosopher to have tasted the pleasure of the other from childhood. But it is by no means necessary for the money-lover to have perceived how much delight there is in the investigation of truth, and to have been experienced in it. Indeed, even if he strives, he does not easily achieve that. SOCRATES. Therefore the philosopher far surpasses the money-lover in the experience of both pleasures. GLAUCON. By far. SOCRATES. But has the ambitious man tasted the delights of wisdom more than the philosopher has tasted honor? GLAUCON. Honor indeed follows all of them, if they perform the duty set before them. For the rich man is honored by the multitude, as is the brave man and the wise man. Therefore all understand by use itself how much pleasure comes from honor. But how great the sweetness is in the contemplation of truth, only the philosopher feels. SOCRATES. Therefore, as far as experience is concerned, he judges best above the others. GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. Furthermore, he alone will be experienced together with prudence. GLAUCON. Nothing prevents it. SOCRATES. Moreover, that organ through which judgment must be made is not the instrument of the money-lover or the ambitious man, but of the philosopher. GLAUCON. What is that? SOCRATES. Through...

They conclude that the philosopher is the best judge of pleasure because he alone has experienced the joys of all three parts.</summary>

# DIALOGUE IX. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

...we said that these reasons must be judged. GLAUCON. We said so. SOCRATES. Moreover, reasons are especially the instruments of the philosopher. GLAUCON. It appears so. SOCRATES. If individual things were best judged by riches and profit, what the man devoted to gain praised or disapproved of would necessarily be the truest. GLAUCON. Entirely. SOCRATES. But if they were judged by honor, victory, and courage, then what the ambitious man, most burning for victory, judged would be truest. GLAUCON. That is established. SOCRATES. But since they are judged by experience, prudence, and reason, it is necessary that what the philosopher and the man studious of reason praises must be the truest. Therefore, since there are three pleasures, the pleasure of that part by which we learn will certainly be the most pleasant, and the life in which this part rules will be the sweetest. GLAUCON. Nothing stands in the way of that. SOCRATES. Surely he who possesses the authority of judging truly praises his own life most. But which life does the judge deem to be second, or which pleasure second? It is established: that of the warlike and ambitious man. For these are closer to him than those of the greedy man. Therefore, he seems to place the life of the one desirous of profit last. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. These two thus follow one another in turn: and twice now justice <note>original: "iustusia," likely a typo for "iustitia"</note> has conquered the unjust. But for the third, in the manner of the Olympic games, dedicating it to the Savior and Olympian Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, consider that no pleasure exists as entirely true except that of the prudent man; nor is it pure, but rather a shadow and empty: as I seem to have heard from some wise man: and this will be the heaviest fall and ruin of the [un]just. GLAUCON. Wonderfully so. But in what way do you say this? SOCRATES. I shall certainly find out, if you search with me by responding. GLAUCON. Ask. SOCRATES. Tell me, I pray: do we not say that pleasure is the contrary of pain? GLAUCON. We do. SOCRATES. And do we not also place a certain middle state, which is neither to rejoice nor to grieve? <margin>Concerning the middle between pleasure and pain.</margin> GLAUCON. We do. SOCRATES. And since it is a middle, is it a rest and a vacation of the soul from both? Is this not how you say it? GLAUCON. Plainly so. SOCRATES. Do you remember what the words of the sick are like while they labor under disease? GLAUCON. What do you mean? SOCRATES. That nothing is sweeter than health: but they say it escaped them how sweet it was before they were sick. GLAUCON. I remember indeed. SOCRATES. And do you not hear men vexed by the sharpest pains exclaiming that nothing is sweeter than to be free from that affliction? GLAUCON. I hear them. SOCRATES. Furthermore, you hear men tormented by many other such afflictions, while they are tortured, shouting and asserting that it is sweetest to be affected by no pain, and to be free from present trouble: but they do not say it is sweetest to rejoice. GLAUCON. Surely that rest is then perhaps most pleasing to them. SOCRATES. But indeed, when someone stops rejoicing, will he think that cessation of pleasure is troublesome? GLAUCON. Perhaps. SOCRATES. Therefore, that rest which we said a little while ago was the middle of both, will sometimes be both: namely, both pain and pleasure. GLAUCON. It seems so. SOCRATES. Can it be that what is neither becomes both? GLAUCON. No, I think. SOCRATES. And when pleasure or pain is in the soul, are they both certain motions? GLAUCON. Both are. SOCRATES. But that third thing which is neither pain nor pleasure: did it not just now appear to be a certain rest and a middle of those? GLAUCON. Plainly. SOCRATES. In what way, therefore, is it right to think that not grieving is pleasant, or that not rejoicing is troublesome? GLAUCON. In no way. SOCRATES. Therefore it is not so: but that which is the middle and rest appears pleasant compared to the troublesome, and troublesome compared to the pleasant. These visions offer us nothing of the truth concerning pleasure: but they come from a certain deception. GLAUCON. So reason shows. SOCRATES. Look then at pleasures which follow no pain: lest you think too often in the present dispute that it is so arranged by nature that pleasure is the privation of pain, and pain the privation of pleasure. GLAUCON. Where should I look? Where are such pleasures? SOCRATES. There are many others, but especially, if you wish to notice, the pleasures concerning smell. For these, with no prior pain preceding, suddenly come forth in great strength: and when they cease, no pain follows them. GLAUCON. You speak most truly. SOCRATES. Let us not believe, therefore, that the cessation of pain is pure pleasure: nor that pain is the absence of pleasure. GLAUCON. No. SOCRATES. But indeed, of those pleasures which enter the soul through the body, almost all the greatest and most numerous are of such a kind: that they are liberations from pains. GLAUCON. They are indeed. SOCRATES. And those which arise from the expectation of these things in the future, certain foretastes of pleasure, behave in the same way. GLAUCON. In the same way. SOCRATES. Do you know what these pleasures are like, and to what they are most similar? GLAUCON. To what? SOCRATES. Do you think there is anything in nature that is highest, lowest, and middle? GLAUCON. I do. SOCRATES. Do you think someone, when he is carried from the lowest to the middle, thinks anything else than that he is ascending to the highest? And while he stands in the middle, and turns his eyes back to where he came from, does he think he is anywhere else than in the highest, since he does not look upon that which is truly the highest? GLAUCON. By Jove, I do not think such a man would think otherwise. SOCRATES. If he were brought down again, he would think he was being brought downward: and would he think truly? GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. Do not all these things happen to him for this reason: because he has not yet experienced what is truly highest, what is middle, and what is lowest? GLAUCON. That is indeed manifest. SOCRATES. Will you then wonder if men unskilled in the truth not only think incorrectly about many other things, but are also so affected regarding pleasure and pain and the middle of these, that as often as they are brought into pain, they judge truly and truly grieve: but as often as they rise from pain into the middle, they think they have attained both fullness and pleasure? And just as those who look only at the dark gray next to black, because they do not see white, think it is most bright, so also those who compare the absence of pain with pain, but have not experienced true pleasure, are deceived in judging? GLAUCON. By Jove, I will not wonder at that. Indeed, if the opposite happened, I would wonder more. SOCRATES. Consider it also thus. Are not hunger and thirst and other things of that kind certain "emptinesses" of the body's condition? GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. And ignorance and imprudence are a certain emptiness of the soul's condition. GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. <margin>Which is greater and lesser, the pleasure of the soul or of the body.</margin> Moreover, the former is filled when it takes nourishment: and the latter when it receives intelligence. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. Which filling is truer? That which happens through things that are more truly real, or through others? GLAUCON. Those which [are]...

<summary>Socrates argues that the philosopher's pleasure is superior because it is based on reason and truth, whereas most physical pleasures are merely the temporary cessation of pain. He uses the analogy of spatial height to show how people mistake a neutral state for "high" pleasure because they have never experienced the truly "highest" intellectual joys.</summary>

# BOOK NINE.

...those things which possess more "being." SOCRATES: Which kinds do you judge to be of a purer substance? Those of food, drink, delicacies, and all types of nourishment? Or the species of true opinion, knowledge, and mind—and in short, of all virtue? Judge it in this way: that which is always attached to the similar, the immortal, and the truth—and is itself of such a nature and exists in such a medium—does it seem to you to possess more "being" than that which is never constant or mortal, and is of such a nature and produced in such a medium? GLAUCON: That which is related to the always-similar is far superior. SOCRATES: Does the essence <note>original: *essentia*</note> of the always-similar possess more "being" than it does knowledge? GLAUCON: Not at all. SOCRATES: Or more than truth? GLAUCON: Nor that. SOCRATES: But if it has less of truth, does it not also have less of essence? GLAUCON: Necessarily so. SOCRATES: In general, do not all the classes of things concerning the care of the body participate less in truth and essence than those things which concern the care of the soul? GLAUCON: Much less. SOCRATES: And does the body itself not possess less "being" than the soul? GLAUCON: The body as well. SOCRATES: Therefore, is not that which is filled with things that exist more truly, and which itself exists more truly, more "filled" than that which is filled with things that exist less, and is itself less? GLAUCON: How could it be otherwise? SOCRATES: If, therefore, to be filled with things agreeable to nature is pleasant, then that which is truly filled with more real things is affected by a more natural and true pleasure. But that which receives things that are both "less" and less true is filled less truly and firmly, and participates in a more deceptive and false pleasure. GLAUCON: That is absolutely necessary. SOCRATES: Therefore, those men who are inexperienced in wisdom and virtue, and are enslaved to feasts and similar things, are carried downward and then back again to the middle; they wander in this way throughout their whole lives. They never emerge above this, nor do they ever look up toward what is truly highest, nor are they raised to the heights, nor do they ever enjoy any true thing, nor do they taste stable and pure pleasure. Instead, like cattle, they look downward toward the ground; obeying their bellies, they spend their lives grazing and mating. To get a larger share of these things, they kick and butt one another with iron horns and hooves, killing each other because of their insatiable lust, inasmuch as they are not filling the true and firm part of themselves, nor filling it with true fodder. GLAUCON: You describe the life of the common people, Socrates, like some sort of oracle.

<margin>The life of the common people.</margin>
SOCRATES: It is necessary, then, that they pursue pleasures mixed with pains, which are mere images <note>original: *simulacra*</note> and shadows of true pleasure, so stained by mutual comparison with pain that both the pleasures and the pains appear more intense by the contrast. Such pleasures breed a mad love in the foolish and inflame them to fight. 

<margin>On the nature of transcendent desire and pleasure.</margin>
Just as Stesichorus <note>A Greek lyric poet who famously claimed that the Greeks fought over a phantom of Helen in Troy, while the real Helen was in Egypt.</note> says the Trojans, ignorant of the truth, fought over the image of Helen. GLAUCON: It is absolutely necessary that it be so. SOCRATES: And what about the spirited part of the soul? Must not similar things happen when someone pursues the satisfaction of honor, victory, or anger without reason or mind—whether through envy because of ambition, or violence because of a love of contention, or anger because of a difficult temperament? GLAUCON: Such things must also happen regarding that part. SOCRATES: May we therefore boldly assert that regarding both the part greedy for gain and the part fond of victory, whatever desires follow knowledge and reason—and pursue and capture those pleasures which reason itself permits—will attain the truest pleasures possible for their nature, because they follow truth? Moreover, they will perceive the pleasures proper to themselves. 

<margin>That which is best for each is most truly its own.</margin>
Since what is best for each is also most truly its own. GLAUCON: Most truly indeed. SOCRATES: When, therefore, the whole soul follows the part in which philosophy resides, far from all sedition, then it happens that each part performs its own office and is just; and each part reaps its own pleasures, which are the best and, as far as possible, the truest. GLAUCON: Very much so. SOCRATES: But when one of the other parts dominates, it happens that it neither finds its own proper pleasure nor allows the other parts to follow their own true pleasure. GLAUCON: That is what happens. SOCRATES: And do not those things which are furthest from philosophy and reason produce such effects? GLAUCON: Certainly. SOCRATES: And that which is furthest from law and order is furthest from reason. GLAUCON: Obviously. SOCRATES: And those desires burning with love and tyranny were seen to be at the greatest distance. GLAUCON: Entirely. SOCRATES: While the kingly and moderate desires appeared to deviate the least. GLAUCON: Yes. SOCRATES: The tyrant, therefore, will be very far from true and proper pleasure, while the King is closest to it. GLAUCON: Necessarily. SOCRATES: The tyrant, then, will lead the most bitter life, and the King the sweetest. GLAUCON: That is absolutely necessary. SOCRATES: Do you know how much more sadly the tyrant lives than the king? GLAUCON: I shall know if you tell me. SOCRATES: Since there are three desires—one legitimate and two illegitimate—the tyrant, in fleeing law and reason, crosses beyond the illegitimate ones and surrounds himself with certain slave-like and bodyguard pleasures. How far he is separated from legitimate pleasure is not easily expressed, except perhaps in this way. GLAUCON: In what way? SOCRATES: The tyrant appeared third from the man of the few <note>The "man of the few" refers to the Oligarch.</note>. For the man of the people <note>The Democrat.</note> stands in the middle between them. GLAUCON: That is so. SOCRATES: Therefore, he meets with an image of pleasure that is third in truth after that man, if what we said before is true. GLAUCON: So it must be said. SOCRATES: Furthermore, the man devoted to the power of the few is third from the king, if we place the aristocrat and the king in the same category. GLAUCON: Third indeed. SOCRATES: Therefore, the tyrant is distant from true pleasure by a number that is three times three. GLAUCON: It appears so. SOCRATES: Thus the image of tyrannical pleasure is a plane figure according to the number of its length. GLAUCON: Certainly. SOCRATES: But according to its power and the third increase <note>Socrates is moving from a linear distance to a squared number (3x3=9) and then to a cubed number (9x9x9=729) to mathematically illustrate the gap between the King's happiness and the Tyrant's misery.</note>, it is manifest how great the interval is. GLAUCON: Manifest indeed to a calculator. SOCRATES: If one conversely calculates how much the king exceeds in the truth of pleasure...

<summary>Socrates argues that the soul's pleasures are more real than the body's because they participate in eternal truth. He concludes by beginning a mathematical calculation to prove the King is 729 times happier than the Tyrant.</summary>
