# DIALOGUE IX. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

<margin>The number of degrees by which the life of a king excels the life of a tyrant.</margin>
...the king of tyrants, whoever he was, once the multiplication is completed, will be found to surpass the tyrant in the sweetness of life, and the tyrant to [be surpassed by] the king in the bitterness of life, by seven hundred and twenty-nine degrees. <note>original: "gradibus vigintinouē &amp; septingētis" — Socrates uses a complex geometric calculation (3 to the 6th power) to quantify the difference in happiness.</note> **GLAUCON:** You have piled up a truly marvelous interval between the just and the unjust man regarding the life of pleasure and pain. **SOCRATES:** Indeed, this is a true and fitting number for the lives of men, since days, nights, months, and years are fitting to them. **GLAUCON:** They are indeed. **SOCRATES:** And if the good and just man so greatly exceeds the evil and [un]just man in pleasure, it is surely a wonder by how much more he will exceed him in elegance, beauty, and the virtue of life. **GLAUCON:** A wonder indeed. **SOCRATES:** But since we have arrived here in our dispute, let us repeat what was said at the beginning, from which we were led to these points. It was said at one time that acting unjustly was profitable for him who, though entirely unjust, is nevertheless thought to be just. Was it not said so? **GLAUCON:** It was. **SOCRATES:** To these things, therefore, let us now argue: since we have agreed on one thing, what power both just and unjust action possesses. **GLAUCON:** In what way? **SOCRATES:** Let us fashion an image of the soul, so that he who said those things may recognize what sort of things he said. **GLAUCON:** What sort of image? **SOCRATES:** Something like this: such as the natures of the Chimera, Scylla, and Cerberus are remembered to have been of old, and many others in which various forms are said to have grown together into one. **GLAUCON:** They are so described. **SOCRATES:** Fashion, therefore, one figure of a very varied beast, having many heads all around: some heads of domestic animals, some of wild ones, which it can change and produce from itself. <margin>Speech is easier than wax for fashioning.</margin> **GLAUCON:** You describe the skill of a strange craftsman; yet, since speech is easier for fashioning than wax, let it be fashioned. **SOCRATES:** Join to these, moreover, from above, one form of a lion. To this, add one of a man. And let the first be the largest, the second smaller, and the third the smallest. **GLAUCON:** These are easy things; they are thus formed. **SOCRATES:** Join these three together, therefore, so that they may cohere with one another to form a single being. **GLAUCON:** They are joined. **SOCRATES:** Place around them externally the image of a single man, so that to those who cannot look inside, but see only the outer covering, it appears to be one animal—namely, a man. **GLAUCON:** I have placed it around. **SOCRATES:** Let us say, then, to him who asserts that it is profitable for this man to act unjustly, but that living justly is by no means profitable, that he asserts nothing else than that it is profitable for him to feed that manifold beast and the lion, and to make the lion stronger; but to allow the man to perish from hunger and to be weakened, so much so that he is dragged wherever those others pull him because of his feebleness; nor should he tame one with the other, or reconcile them, but rather let them tear each other apart with their habits and devour one another in their fighting. **GLAUCON:** Anyone who praised injustice would certainly be saying these things. **SOCRATES:** Therefore, if someone says that just duties are profitable, he will advise that these things be done and said by which that man—the inner part of such a creature—may obtain the greatest power, and take care of that many-headed beast like a farmer: fostering, watering, and nourishing the domestic heads, while immediately cutting off the wild ones; while he accepts the nature of the lion as a helper for this; and he cares for all things in common, and reconciles them to one another and to himself with mutual goodwill. **GLAUCON:** Certainly, he who praises the just says these things. **SOCRATES:** In every way, therefore, he who praises justice speaks the truth; but he who praises injustice lies. For both in regard to pleasure, and in regard to beauty, and in regard to profit, the praiser of the just pronounces true things. But the censurer brings nothing of truth, nor does he know what he disapproves of. **GLAUCON:** In no way, as it seems to me at least. **SOCRATES:** Let us therefore persuade him with mild words, for he does not err willingly. Let us ask him thus: "O blessed man, do we not say that the honorable and the shameful institutions of life exist for such reasons? The honorable: those which subject the beast-like part of nature to the man, or rather perhaps to the divine. The shameful: those which subject the gentle part to the wild master." Will he agree, or not? **GLAUCON:** He will agree, if he believes me. **SOCRATES:** Is there anyone for whom it is profitable by this reasoning to take gold unjustly, if it happens that while he takes the gold, he compels the most excellent part of himself to serve the most ignoble? For if, in taking gold, he made his son or daughter a slave to wild and wicked men, that taking would by no means profit him, even if he took much. But if he forces the most divine part of himself to serve the most profane and wicked part, and is not touched by mercy, will he not be wretched? And corrupted by gifts of gold with a much more heavy destruction of himself than Eriphyle, who received that necklace against the life of her husband? <note>Eriphyle was a figure in Greek mythology who was bribed with a necklace to betray her husband, Amphiaraus.</note> **GLAUCON:** Very much so, as I answer for him. **SOCRATES:** And do you not think that intemperance was of old called so for some such reason: because in it, that dire, huge, and manifold beast is relaxed more than is fitting? **GLAUCON:** It is clear. **SOCRATES:** But are not stubbornness and insolence disapproved of when that lion-like and snake-like nature increases, so that it grows strong beyond all modesty? **GLAUCON:** Entirely. **SOCRATES:** And is not luxurious softness blamed for the excessive loosening and remission of this same part, when it creates cowardice and laziness in him? **GLAUCON:** Why not? **SOCRATES:** Moreover, flattery and illiberality: when someone subjects this very vigor of spirit to the turbulent and manifold beast, and for the sake of gain and its insatiable desire, casts it down, and so accustoms it from its first years that the lion is turned into an ape? **GLAUCON:** Greatly so. **SOCRATES:** But why is the mechanical and mercenary disposition held in infamy? Surely this infamy is in us when someone has been allotted a weak nature of the best part, so that he cannot dominate the beasts that are in him, but can only serve them and study only to know their flatteries. **GLAUCON:** It seems so. **SOCRATES:** In order that such a man may be ruled by a leader such as the best man is ruled by, do we not say that he ought to be the servant of the best man, who has the divine commander within himself? We do not think he should obey the superior to the loss of the subject, as Thrasymachus thought about all subjects; but because it is better for everyone to be subjected to a divine and wise ruler—especially if he has such a ruler in himself; if not, then at least to this external ruler—so that we may all be, as far as possible, similar and friends, governed by the same ruler? **GLAUCON:** Most rightly. **SOCRATES:**

<summary>Socrates uses the allegory of a tripartite creature (a multi-headed beast, a lion, and a man) hidden inside a human shell to illustrate the soul's internal struggle between desire, spirit, and reason. He concludes that justice is profitable because it allows the "inner man" to govern the other parts, whereas injustice enslaves the divine part of the soul to the bestial.</summary>

# ARGUMENT OF DIALOGUE X.

It is indeed clear from the law that such is its purpose: to look out for all citizens equally. That same authority over children demonstrates this: they are forbidden to be their own masters until we have established a "republic" within them, just as we have in the city. By cultivating the best part of them, we create a certain guardian and ruler within them to take the place of our own external rule. Only then do we permit them to be free. GLAUCON: That is clearly established. SOCRATES: By what reason then, O Glaucon, shall we assert that it profits anyone to act unjustly, or intemperately, or basely—works by which he will become worse—even if he acquires more money or any other power? GLAUCON: By none. SOCRATES: In what way shall we say it profits the wrongdoer to escape notice and avoid punishment? Does not he who remains hidden become even worse? In the man who is caught and chastised, however, the beast-like part is quieted and tamed, while the domestic part is liberated. The whole soul, restored to its best nature, takes on a habit so much more precious—attaining temperance and justice along with wisdom—than the body does when it acquires strength and beauty along with health, insofar as the soul is more precious than the body. GLAUCON: That is entirely so. SOCRATES: Therefore, whoever is of sound mind will direct his whole life toward this. Indeed, he will value above all those disciplines which make his soul such as this, while scorning others. GLAUCON: Manifestly. SOCRATES: And yet he will not cultivate and nourish his body to indulge in beastly and irrational pleasure; nor will he refer health to that end; nor will he zealously seek to be strong, healthy, or beautiful, unless these things also cultivate temperance: so that he may temper the harmony of the body for the sake of the soul’s consonance. GLAUCON: Exactly so, if indeed he is truly to be a musician <note>original: "musicus" — here meaning one attuned to the harmony of the arts and the soul</note>. SOCRATES: But neither will he be moved by the estimation of the common people to admire the accumulation of money, or its order and concord; nor will he increase his wealth infinitely, becoming subject to infinite evils. GLAUCON: Certainly not, I think. SOCRATES: Rather, always looking toward the republic within himself, he will take care that nothing is moved from its state because of a lack or an abundance of money. And so, he will always govern his getting and spending of money to the best of his power. GLAUCON: Most certainly. SOCRATES: Furthermore, he will refer honors to the same end. For he will taste only those from which he hopes to emerge a better man; but he will flee those, both privately and publicly, by which he fears the present state of his soul might one day be disturbed. GLAUCON: He will not, then, wish to administer civil affairs, if that is his care. SOCRATES: Yes, by the dog! <note>A common Socratic oath</note> but in the city of his own self. And most greatly indeed. Yet perhaps not in his fatherland, unless some divine fortune should occur. GLAUCON: I understand; you speak of that city which we have just now founded: which exists only in words, but nowhere on earth, I believe. SOCRATES: But perhaps a model of it exists in heaven, visible to him who wishes to see it, and who, having seen it, establishes himself according to it. It matters nothing whether it exists anywhere or ever will. For he will perform the duties of that city alone, and those of another, not at all. GLAUCON: That is reasonable.

### Argument by Marsilio Ficino for the Tenth Dialogue concerning Justice.

<margin>
Justice requires only the care of the soul.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' featuring a classical figure or scholar amidst foliage.</image-desc>

Hitherto, Socrates, that most diligent teacher of the human race, has provoked mankind toward legal justice—and toward universal virtue through the beauty of justice itself; similarly, he has called them back from injustice through the foulness of injustice. Next, however, he will exhort them toward justice for the sake of its eternal fruit and reward, and deter them from injustice because of its eternal loss and punishment; and this is the primary duty of this tenth book. But before he performs this principal duty, he employs a certain preface, in which he diligently completes what he had touched upon in previous dialogues and left at the end of the ninth, which is greatly necessary for public safety. Truly, this physician of ours for human diseases is more diligent in curing that species of disease which others not only treat with neglect, but do not treat at all; or rather, what is worse, they love it as a most healthy thing and embrace it with all zeal: I mean poetic imitation <note>original: "imitationem poeticam" — the concept of Mimesis</note>, by which ingenious poets, while they more sharply express disturbed minds, meanwhile more vehemently and deeply imprint similar disturbances upon the minds of those listening and reading. And they infect everyone all the more, the more they are praised and please. Such a preface follows the end of the ninth book fittingly, for there the soul is divided into reason and into lower parts agitated by disturbances, the rule of which he calls "tyrannical," first in the soul and then in the city. And since poetic imitation arouses, fosters, and increases such parts—irritating anger, tickling lust, loosening laughter, and pouring out tears and complaints—it therefore seems to undermine the kingdom of reason and bring in the tyranny of disturbance. Wherefore Socrates destroys such a plague, otherwise pleasant but most poisonous, lest it destroy us. And see with what great charity our Plato everywhere consults for the human race, searching out and looking around for those dangers which no one else would suspect; add to this that he strongly opposes his own nature and education (that is, the poetic), provided he may fight strenuously for the public safety. Wherefore it should seem a wonder to no one that Plato here, for the love of truth, does not even spare his own Homer: since for the sake of cultivating justice, he does not even indulge his own genius. He disparages Homer especially so that, through the prince of imitators himself, we may consider the others much more condemned. And when he says that neither divine nor human things are taught by Homer, understand the praises attributed to Homer in Plato's *Philebus* as being drawn from common opinion, not from Plato's own judgment. He proves, moreover, that the skill of imitating is, as we have narrated, very dangerous; furthermore, it is slavish and most base. For imitators neither understand the things themselves, nor do they make them; but following the forms of things appearing to the senses, and common...

# ARGUMENT FOR THE DIALOGUE X. FOLIO CCLXVI.

<margin>H ii</margin>
<meta>catchword: therefore, that</meta>

...having hunted after these opinions, they report certain images and obey the senses and disturbances, having no regard for reason. However, as much as he <note>Plato</note> disapproves of poets when they cause disturbance, he approves of them just as much if they exhort toward virtue and piety through the honorable praises of heroes and divine hymns. But in order to express how base all imitation is, he divides the genus of arts into three species: the user, the maker, and the imitator. And indeed, he says the one who uses the lyre—that is, Music—surpasses the art of the lyre-maker, because with a certain prescribed end in mind, the user proposes to the maker the form of the work to be fabricated. The maker, in turn, surpasses the painter, who imitates the lyre only with colors. He judges the poet to be of such a kind, bringing images of things to the ears just as the painter brings them to the eyes. 

But among these matters, certain theological mysteries concerning the <term>Ideas</term> <note>The eternal, perfect archetypes of all things in Platonic philosophy</note> are introduced. Since we have opened these more extensively in our *Theology* <note>Likely referring to Ficino's "Platonic Theology"</note>, we will touch upon them briefly for the present. Come now, Platonic contemplator, ascend from these forms which you perceive in the matter of the world to the nature that is the mother of such forms. Even if you do not perceive her, think of her as infused into the matter of the world like a vital spirit, full of seeds, and skillfully disposing each thing through those seeds. Know that this Nature in the world is such as you know the vegetative power to be in yourself. Therefore, just as you understand the power of sensing to be above the vegetative nature in yourself, so also in the world, reduce a similar but most universal nature into a royal fountain of sensing that is similar but most universal. Then, in yourself, reduce sense into reason, and reason into intellect; and similarly in the world, reduce the genus of sensing into a rational nature, and this into an intellectual genus. 

Furthermore, since you perceive in yourself that the intellect desires that which is <term>intelligible</term> <note>That which can be understood by the mind, as opposed to the senses</note> as something more perfect, and is formed by it as by something more powerful, propose an intelligible nature for the intellectual nature both in the world and in yourself. Call this "the Intelligible" entirely the same as "Being itself." Finally, to this which you have called both the Intelligible and Being, propose the Good itself. For you desire to be so that you may be well, and you desire the Intelligible for the sake of the Good itself. After you have ascended to this point, you will perceive the universe designated by a certain sacred <term>septenary</term> <note>A group of seven</note>, rising from the lowest matter through sensible qualities, through nature, through sense, reason, intellect, the intelligible, unto the Good itself. 

Furthermore, the Good Spirit perfected all things under the number six, as if on the sixth day, and rested in the seventh degree, as if on the seventh day—that is, in Himself. For the end of all other things is the Good itself. Of the Good, therefore, no end outside of Himself can either exist or be imagined. If all things desire the Good toward which they tend, conclude that all things are produced by the Good. Likewise, if He makes all things by an intrinsic and proper power, understand that He embraces the entire universe in Himself. But since His is the first and therefore simplest nature, remember that the forms of all things in Him are one single form of His own, which Plato calls the <term>Idea of the Good</term>. In this, Timaeus said that God, the craftsman of the world, rested when he had created the world, saying that the craftsman of the world withdrew into his own vantage point. 

Accordingly, the Idea of the Good itself generates <term>Ideas</term>—that is, the specific forms of all things, distinct among themselves only by species—within the intelligible nature; by which it comprehends the universal Being in a certain intelligible way, and also every intelligence by a certain wonderful reason above intelligence. All intellects look up toward this intelligible nature, and from it they receive the stable formulas of the Ideas. Rational souls also look up to it, whence they have received formulas, though in a certain way they are changeable. After these formulas of rational beings, the images of the Ideas descend into the sensual power. Next, the seeds descend into the vegetative nature, and finally, through qualities, into matter. 

Therefore, when Plato says God makes the Ideas in nature, understand this to be in the nature and the intelligible world at the head of angelic minds. But because he spoke of a "bed" and a "table," let this be said for the sake of example, so that through these man-made things you may understand natural things—that is, through the bed and the table, understand the man who uses them. Furthermore, the example in art seemed suited to the question proposed. But perhaps he does not think that the forms necessary for the rules of the arts are absent from the Ideas. Nor should it seem strange that man possesses the forms of the arts by divine gift, since the imaginations of the arts are not lacking even in beasts. And if forms of this kind are produced divinely in the soul, they shall be said to be produced "in nature" for the reason that they are naturally implanted. But if anyone seems poorly suited to certain crafts, the Platonists will say he has either been distracted by various things or has turned himself entirely toward opposites. 

Note the words of Plato saying that God not only understands but also wills; signifying that God conceives within Himself by understanding, and fabricates outside Himself by willing. Note again that God has expressed only one Idea for one natural species in the intelligible world itself—for instance, one "Ideal Humanity" for the human species. For if in matter, where there is innumerable and shifting variety, a certain common union of nature is preserved in individual men, much more so in a simple and stable nature is a single Idea sufficient for one natural species. Indeed, these diverse and unstable things cannot have a single communion of nature from anywhere else than from the unity of that sublime nature itself. 

Again, if two "Humanities" were posited, certainly in the respect that both are Humanity, they would not differ from each other; rather, they are one. Therefore, if they were to differ, they would surely be distinguished from each other by certain additions joined to both. Thus, neither would be the absolute Humanity itself, but a "certain" humanity of such a kind, and a "certain human thing" rather than Humanity. And both, as if participating in the same Humanity, would similarly be called human; and besides these, there would be a Humanity in itself, which is one before it is received by many subjects. Rightly, since God is simply the Cause, He is not to be called the author of "a certain man" or "a certain horse," but the author of Man and Horse. Therefore, He created one absolute Idea for any species of things. But since among us here, "this man" generates "that one," this man is by no means to be called the author of Man simply, but the author of "a certain man." For he is not the sole cause, but is among the causes—namely, in the number of causes—nor does he make the whole. For he does not make the prime matter, or the soul, nor does he give the beginning to man himself. For before this man, "Man" existed everywhere, and surely by his work, "Man" exists and will exist everywhere. But where Plato says God brought forth one Idea because, namely, He either did not wish there to be more, or some other necessity was present that there should not be more, understand that in God, necessity is so turned with will, therefore, that...

# ARGUMENT OF THE TENTH DIALOGUE

It is necessary for things to be as they are, because God wills them to be so. Indeed, in the supreme simplicity of the Divinity, necessity is nothing other than will. Therefore, if you say it is necessary for God to so will or act, I will conversely say that God wills it to be so necessary. Justly, where supreme goodness concurs with supreme power, there supreme liberty breathes together with supreme necessity. Among these things, certain separate points must be considered, which are nevertheless very useful. Such as this: Reading or doctrine is futile unless it leads to the best <term>reason of life</term><note>The Latin "ratio vitae" refers to a guided way of living or a moral system.</note>. In this matter, the life and discipline of Pythagoras was admirable; and by right, it held the greatest authority among all, even in the time of Plato. Likewise, poems, if the harmonic composition of words is taken away, turn out to be of no moment. Furthermore, the virtue of either a human or a thing consists in a certain faculty contributing chiefly to that end for whose sake the thing itself was made and the human was born. Meanwhile, a certain distinction between sense and reason appears: for the senses frequently deceive regarding magnitude, figure, number, and weight; yet meanwhile, reason, through the faculty of measuring, numbering, and weighing, corrects the judgment of the sense. It is established, moreover, that the soul cannot at the same time, through the same power of itself, judge the same thing in a contrary manner. It also appears that our powers of desiring are diverse. For indeed, we may desire and reject the same thing at the same time. It should be noted that it is required of an upright citizen not to grieve at all, but to console the rising grief with such reasons. Whereby it appears that one part of the soul, like a sick person, needs medicine, while another part, being healthy, acts as the healer. These reasons against grief are chiefly four. First, because it is uncertain whether what has happened is a good or an evil. Second, because whatever it may be, it is certainly to be esteemed of little value. For nothing among human dreams is to be greatly valued. Third, because we accomplish nothing at all by grieving. Fourth, because grief always impedes that which could suddenly be of help to us. This is confirmed by the fact that it is most shameful to be overcome, and most beautiful to overcome. He who is pressed by grief or any other perturbation is already most shamefully overcome. Therefore, he prescribes that in adversities and perturbations, we should use only the office of a physician, who does not grieve with the grieving, but heals them. He compares the lots of daily life to the throws of dice: which he wants to be corrected by reasons, just as the throws of dice are seen to be corrected by a certain skill of the game. But the above precepts are, as it were, certain preludes to those which follow. Indeed, the greatest contest of all is proposed to us in life: by which we may overcome vice and follow virtue, so that we may hold as nothing all things which are considered good among humans, in order that we ourselves may be good. Indeed, the reward of one's own justice is greater than all the rewards that can be carried away among humans. For the splendor of justice itself surpasses all these things beyond measure; and in movable and shadowy things, a reward fitting for immovable, eternal, and truest justice cannot be found. From these things, it is concluded that for the immovable habit of justice, an immovable reward ought to be desired. Which indeed remains after the course of the present life for the labors of justice. Otherwise, justice itself, which is judged the most excellent good, would be an evil for just men who continually labor for the love of justice, and are often affected by injury, neither avenging the injury; add also that they despise present goods out of a desire for eternal ones; nor do they receive a reward among humans for their justice, but rather often report an unjust punishment for their justice. Wherefore, lest the good should harm, and justice lack a reward, and God either provide too little or not repay according to merits, it must be judged that souls will be immortal. Especially so that the unjust, who while living did not pay the penalties for their injustice, may at least pay them when deceased; and that the just, who were altogether despised among mortals, may be crowned among those above. Hence a noble precept is handed down: The immortal soul ought not to be solicitous for this brief time, but for all time. Plato shows the immortality of the soul in the *Phaedrus* and *Phaedo*, and elsewhere. And he shows that there are certain demonstrations of this kind of reason in the book *On Science* <note>Likely referring to the *Theaetetus*</note>, saying: the words of those who feel the contrary, upon examination, finally turn out to be ridiculous. Likewise in the *Gorgias*, affirming that these mysteries are proved by "Adamantine reasons" <note>Unbreakable or diamond-like arguments</note>. Furthermore, in this tenth book, where after the argumentation it is added, that both by such argumentation and by many others we are compelled to confess it. I think indeed that in Plato's words there lies a certain wonderful power understood by very few: so that it is no wonder if, through Platonic argumentations, some indeed think it demonstrated, while others think it not yet demonstrated. Certainly Demosthenes, a listener of Plato, was persuaded with such efficacy by the living voice that he said he would rather die honorably than live shamefully, after he had heard Plato and Xenocrates discoursing on the immortality of souls. Cleombrotus also perceived the same power in the Platonic writings, as did many listeners of Hegesias at Cyrene, who freed themselves from the prison of the body out of a desire for the other life. The Platonist Boethius perceived the same, granting, with Philosophy as his witness, that this was demonstrated to him by certain reasons. Aurelius Augustine seems to have felt the same, where he says he never doubted this matter. These things are confirmed by Avicenna, saying that there are certain reasons that are demonstrations for these things. And Plato says here not only that it can be demonstrated, but even that it is easily demonstrated, among those, as I think: who, since they themselves have a mind purged and segregated from the body, rightly do not doubt that the soul can live segregated from the body. Since they themselves experience that their mind lives better when separated from the senses than when joined to them. It is also found that the souls of others, immersed in bodies and therefore vicious, are nevertheless not destroyed by their own vice and disease; and therefore, much less can they be corrupted by a foreign, that is, a bodily disease. For even the body itself is not pressed by an external evil until an intrinsic evil is brought in from there, by which it is next destroyed. Furthermore, lest one doubt the divinity of one's soul, he commands to thoroughly purge it from the filth contracted from bodily love, and when purged, to perceive how pure, how simple, how greedy for divine things it is, as if kindred to divinity, and how quickly and fully it is capable of divine light. When, however, he says that souls do not become more numerous daily, understand it to mean they do not become so as to arise and be composed from bodies. Which indeed the following reason...

# ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X

<note>This is a summary or "argument" for the tenth book of Plato's Republic, likely written by Marsilio Ficino or a contemporary Renaissance commentator.</note>

->Hiii<-

...it manifests, saying: if divine things were composed of bodies, they would eventually be resolved back into bodies as they divine, with the result that nothing of the nature of bodies would remain. Again, notice what he adds: that the soul is not composite; otherwise, it could not be indissoluble. And understand that for an essence to be unable to be dissolved, it must either be composed of nothing, or if it is composed, it must not be composed of any matter, and thus be so fused together that in its composition multitude does not overcome unity; indeed, rather, unity overcomes multitude through a harmonic union, and stability overcomes motion. Conclude the mystery, pertaining partly to providence and partly to immortality and the reward of justice. The just man turns out to be like God; the unjust, however, unlike Him. Since it is not hidden from God that this one is like Him and that one is unlike, it is consistent with reason that the just man is dear and a friend to God, and the unjust the opposite. Therefore, God by no means neglects the just as His friends: but always looks out for them so that those things which seem adverse to them eventually turn out prosperous, whether they are living or dead. 

But why did he assert the mystery of immortality here by a certain historical example rather than by the diligence of arguments? Because citizens are to be provoked to justice not so much by the artifice of words as by example and aid. Furthermore, why does he bring forward a man rising from the dead to confirm this? Because even if immortality is established by reasons, and a certain common execution of justice, nevertheless one must receive the location, form, and disposition of either reward or punishment from one who has been present there. This is what he signifies to us near the end of the *Phaedo*. Nor is it without reason that he testifies that Herus the Pamphylian <note>original: "Herum Pamphylii"; referring to Er, son of Armenius, from Plato's Republic</note> rose again, having died in battle for the safety of his fatherland: to signify that those who die for the public good will rise again to true life; although out of many, only one rose again for our sake. 

But is this a history or a fable? Justin the Platonist and Christian martyr <note>Justin Martyr, an early Christian apologist who saw parallels between Plato and Christianity</note> wishes it to be history. Which I, for my part, will not refute. But where Plato names it an "apologue" or "fable," it can be explained that a history can be called a fable whenever it has a more august allegory beyond the deeds performed. For this reason, Olympiodorus <note>A Neoplatonist commentator</note> also says that Plato often called histories and reasons "fables." And since he figures the spirits of the dead and the places of justice differently in the *Phaedrus*, differently in the *Gorgias*, differently in the *Phaedo*, and disposes them here and elsewhere, it is clearly evident that these contain an allegoric sense beyond the form of the place. 

As for the fact that he moves here around the resurrection in the number twelve: which among the ancients is the number of the mundane spheres, thinking there to be eight heavens above the four elements. It is as if he says there is need of divine power, the mistress of the universe, to rouse the dead; and that this is done sometimes by divine providence for the instruction of men. There are also those who say that the "Great Year," in which everything completes its circuit through which it returns to the same point, is comprised of twelve thousand years; and by three such years, the Great Year of the world is made equal: in which the soul of the world, through the motion of the firmament, completes its circuit, to be performed in thirty-six thousand years. They wish the circuit of our soul to be through twelve thousand years for the same reason, because it must run through all the spheres, and the choirs of demons and gods: which in the *Phaedrus* are distributed through twelve orders. 

But what do the two openings in the earth and the two in heaven mean? So that you may understand that souls descend to earthly things by one way—namely, by a certain corporeal habit—but ascend from the lands by another—namely, by the purging of that habit. Similarly, they slip from heaven into the elements of the body out of love for the elemental; and conversely, they rise again into celestial things when this love is extinguished and celestial love is kindled. Here Orpheus says that Love has the keys to all things both above and below. He places the judges of souls in the air and the ether as angels, ministers of divine providence. After the sentence, the just seek heaven, carrying their works and judgments before them: because they clearly knew themselves and shine both to themselves and to others. The unjust, on the contrary, descend carrying theirs on their backs. For they neither knew themselves nor were they of use to themselves, but are examples to others rather than a help to themselves. 

The meadow in which both those ascending and descending rest for a time is a certain middle region between the lower and celestial realms, and a disposition between a good habit and a bad one: and a state between blessedness and misery, designated like a "limbo" in the air. Here notice that souls which had mutual knowledge in the previous life recognize each other in the other. Likewise, according to the Platonists, the souls of those who died in infancy reside in such a meadow for a very long time; concerning whom Herus recounted certain things little worthy of memory. Because since they declined toward neither side by choosing, nor contracted a habit, the Platonists leave them only in natural light. But they think the blessed are placed above natural light, and the miserable below it. 

He treats here, moreover, of purgatorial punishments. But why is guilt abolished by pains? Because it clearly grew through pleasures. Do not doctors also cure diseases mostly by their contrary? Notice that Plato does not use the number ten, and a hundred besides, and a thousand, rashly for the erasing of guilt. Indeed, for any degree of pleasure, he applies ten degrees of punishment. First, it is asked why more degrees of punishment are paid than were perceived of pleasure. He responds that it is so owed on account of the crime of injured divine majesty. Furthermore, just as the joys of blessedness exceed the pains of human justice, so the tortures of misery exceed the pleasures of injustice. Finally, marks are not as easily erased as they are easily imprinted; nor would he have confirmed the habit of sin if he had ceased to transgress by living longer. 

He asks next why there are ten degrees. What if Plato imitated the Mosaic Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments</note>? Since he thought that a man acts in some way against the precepts of divine law by ten, because he altogether neglected some out of the ten, he is rightly judged to be tortured ten times over. Hence the number ten is called "universal." For it either enfolds all numbers within itself, or explains and unfolds them through itself and its own by repeating. Moreover, the universal number is opportunely accommodated to purging souls, so that through this it may signify that the entire stain of the body must be laid down before you reach the Prince of the Universe, with whom nothing corporeal can exist. He asks after this, why besides the ten degrees of punishment, the unjust are afflicted for a hundred years. I respond, because if they had lived up to a hundred years, which term the life of men in some way...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument regarding the destiny of the soul and the significance of numbers in the afterlife, likely following a discussion of Plato’s Republic (Book X, the Myth of Er).</meta>

# ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X.

designates, they would have sinned continually. However, he attributes the number one hundred to each of the ten steps, from which the number one thousand is composed. Hence that saying: *They wander for a hundred years.* <note>Original: "Centum errant annos." A reference to Virgil's Aeneid regarding souls waiting to cross the Styx.</note> Also that: *They rolled the wheel through a thousand years.* <note>Original: "Mille rotam voluere per annos." Another Virgilian reference to the cycle of reincarnation.</note> Furthermore, you shall receive a hundred for one. For Plato uses these numbers not only in punishment, but also in certain rewards. Indeed, if the number ten is led into itself by multiplying ten times ten, the hundred is born from it. Then if it is led back into itself, by calculating ten times ten times ten, the thousand is created. Therefore, both ten is a universal number, and a hundred and a thousand are universal numbers. Likewise, if you proceed from one to ten, a linear number is born. If from ten to a hundred, it becomes a surface number. If from ten to a thousand, it becomes a solid. 

To explain allegorically, the soul of a just man departed from itself into the body and was infected by corporeal stain. Through the number ten, which is universal, it will purge this entire stain. Because it is necessary for ten to be led into itself to create a hundred, it signifies that the soul must emerge from the body toward itself. Then, because there is a need to lead the number ten back into itself to generate a thousand, it teaches allegorically that the soul ought not only to be turned toward itself through reason, but also to be converted into itself through intelligence: and thus be led back into its own unity; so that finally it may enjoy God, the highest unity of all. 

The linear, surface, and solid numbers mystically teach that to purify the mind, one must diligently search not only the outer surface of works, words, and thoughts, but also the deepest inner recesses. After the <term>limbo</term> <note>A place of waiting or transition.</note> and <term>purgatory</term>, he descends to the lower world. But know that the Platonists wish there to be not only temporal punishments in purgatory, but also temporal joys in a certain celestial region: so that on both sides like responds to like. For it is distinguished thus: either the senses in life entirely obeyed reason, or reason entirely obeyed the senses, or they always fought each other. And in that fight, either the senses or reason mostly prevailed. Therefore, souls in which the senses entirely obeyed reason through a confirmed habit obtain an eternal reward. On the contrary, those affected otherwise are condemned to eternal punishments. But the middle ones—if reason prevailed, they are transferred to temporal rewards; but if the senses prevailed, to temporal punishments. 

For those to whom no time for deliberation was given, a place of choosing is reserved among the Platonists called <term>limbo</term>, designated here under the name of a "meadow." And even if the Platonists sometimes suspect these meadows to be celestial, here the meadows signify an aerial region. For how could a meadow signify the sublime heaven here, when he says that some souls descend to these from the heavens, while others arrive suddenly from the bowels of the earth? Let such meadows therefore be certain sublime tracts of air, contiguous to those sublime tracts of earth which he describes in the *Phaedo* in the form of an earthly paradise, having happy inhabitants under a perpetual spring. In the same place, he also places the Elysian fields—earthly ones, I mean. For the eighth heaven holds the celestial Elysian fields. Hence that saying: *The stars hold the celestial floor, and the forms of the gods.* <note>Original: "Astra tenent caeleste solum, formaeque deorum." From Ovid's Metamorphoses.</note> 

I pass over for now Proclus and Plotinus, who, where Plato says "eternal," explain it as the entire time of a "Great Year," in which the circuits of individual times are completed. I approve more of Porphyry and Iamblichus in this part: that eternal things should be understood from this. For where Plato calls a soul "incurable" and such that it can never be purged, he sufficiently indicates eternal punishments, and likewise infinite joys. How certain others explain these things, I did not judge worthy of memory. 

Furthermore, if you consider Plato's words, you will recognize that Gospel saying: *Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness.* <note>Matthew 22:13.</note> But he adds here "with the head bound." The binding of the head signifies the impediment of reason and the loss of light. The knot of the hands signifies the privation of action and progress. Finally, the bound feet do not lead, do not proceed, do not arrive, but are dragged by force. You will also recognize under the figure of "fiery men" the avenging demons and corporeal punishments; you will perceive the same from many conjectures. You will note the specific word "outer." Furthermore, the darkness, where the chasms are closed. Also under the name of "bellowing," the gnashing of teeth and weeping. 

After he has arranged the places and punishments, and signified the joys through the opposite form, and touched upon the middle states, he now returns to those souls which flowed together into the meadow, partly from heaven after a temporal reward, and partly from the earth after a temporal punishment. He says it is necessary for these to return again into elemental generation: and to progress through it until each deserves a firmer or firmest state. He says these souls rested in the meadow for seven days. If you interpret this sevenfold number through the seven planets; likewise through the seven weeks of days in which the fetus rests in the womb before movement; and also through every seven days in which the forms are changed step by step in the uterus: perhaps you will seem to contribute something. But what is that to souls who are no longer in the planets (for they have descended) and are not yet enclosed in a womb? For they are about to descend into the womb after they have come to the three Fates. Meanwhile, with an aerial body, they inhabit an aerial region. 

But let it be so, if you please. Perhaps also because in the meantime they live in a way sterile, they are assigned to a sterile number: and since the number seven is neither born from any number multiplied, nor generates any number within ten, it most aptly fits souls still vacant from generation on both sides. The Pythagoreans attribute this same number to <term>Pallas</term> <note>Athena/Minerva, the goddess of wisdom.</note> because she was not born from a mother, nor has she given birth. They want it to suit souls still removed from an earthly mother, and contemplating the universe under the wisdom of Pallas. But as soon as they rise from such a vacation, they undergo the number eight, which is both generated and is the first among solid numbers. Therefore, it fits when the soul is almost about to approach a solid body. We call eight a "solid" number because it is created from two repeated three times by itself and returning into itself, signifying a triple dimension. For from twice two, twice, eight is completed. Add, if you cultivate music, that the seventh voice is utterly dissonant, but the eighth is the most consonant of all. Moreover, the body must harmonize with the soul, and both with fate, so that the celestial soul may enter into commerce with the earthly body. Of which harmony...

# ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X. PAGE 268.

finally, when the numbers are fulfilled, the soul itself now dissonates with the earth and consonates with heaven, if it is to be happy in the future. Furthermore, regarding the four days for the progress of generation, to which Plato added eight days: understand that in the <term>vegetative nature of the soul</term> <note>the lowest part of the soul responsible for growth and biological life</note> a certain power and affection already reigns, in a way, to form the body constituted from the four elements. Likewise, under the eighth consonance, it is necessary for the fourth to approach the consonance in some way, and now the fifth is a true consonance. Five indeed become subsequent when you wish to compute the four with the preceding one. Moreover, you will see here the <term>number twelve</term> <note>Latin: duodenarius</note> assigned, by which the soul approaches the beginnings of generation. For there is need for the assistance of the twelve spheres and the divine and demonic orders for that work. Furthermore, the voice and the twelfth consonance is most perfect, resulting from the <term>diapason and diapente</term> <note>the octave and the fifth</note>, arising from the eighth and the fifth, fitting earthly matters with its own grace: and also suitable for marriages. Indeed, souls of this kind, with a certain love—Venereal love, so to speak—as their leader, are to be reconciled to earthly marriages. 

But why, when Plato was about to compute the twelve, and after the seven was to add the remainder, did he not suddenly say five? Namely, so that he might hint at the mysteries of the 8 and the 8 and the 4 which you have heard: and again, through the addition of one day's journey to complete the twelve, you might notice that the body composed of four elements cannot be prepared for the soul before it has been tempered into a single and fifth form, as if similar to heaven: and the soul easily imprints one vital act from itself upon the figured body. Since, however, souls declining toward composite bodies are for the most part subjected to the laws of fate, and in turn glide toward them with fate as their leader, he says for this reason that these souls proceed into the sight of fate. 

In the beginning, therefore, he depicts nature itself under a columnar light, which becomes the bond of the universe. Understand "Nature" as the vital and seminal power infused into the matter of the world by the World Soul itself. It is called "light" for this reason, because it is penetrating and vital. Likewise, it is called a "straight column" because it penetrates the whole of matter everywhere as if through a long path, and produces many successive grades of forms differing in species and genus. It is also said to be extended through the whole, and to bind the heaven on all sides, because it is present everywhere in its entirety and contains it, and propagates many things as if through certain equal and similar sides. Yet in such a way that they arrive from length to breadth. Since by penetrating it diffuses: and insofar as it diffuses, it fills and rules the things to be filled. Here is that saying: *The Spirit fills all.* <note>A reference to Wisdom 1:7, "The Spirit of the Lord hath filled the whole world."</note> 

The variety of colors declares the variety of seminal powers. In this nature, surely, the fatal spindle lies hidden: according to the imagination, it is the axis of the spheres itself, adorned with twin poles and a center; but according to reason, it is a certain image of the World Soul, and its vegetative power presiding over that nature, moving it like an instrument to manufacture natural things not only skillfully but also inevitably. So that there is not only an order from nature in the world, but also a more inevitable order from fate. Here is that saying in the *Statesman*: *The world is led by natural desire and fate.* But so great is the kinship of nature with fate that they are scarcely distinguished from one another by physicists. 

However, to express the immutable nature of fate, he said its spindle is made of adamant. The whorl in the heaven is again of adamant, and of other materials, namely the stars, not only fixed but also mobile and common: with a manifold variety of forms. Clearly, he then depicts eight spheres, which are indeed agitated by nature, but are immutably agitated by fate presiding over nature: and they are said to be the instruments of fate. Among these things, many points are emphasized pertaining to the measurements, depths, intervals, motions, harmonies, forms, and powers of the celestial spheres, which we shall explain more opportunely in the commentaries on the *Timaeus*. 

In summary, however, from the swiftest and most orderly motion of the heavens, and their most powerful contact, imagine a melody both varied and most sweet to be created: deeper voices from slower motions, sharper <note>higher pitched</note> voices from swifter ones, and middle voices from the middle ones. But since elemental hearing <note>human hearing made of the four elements</note> lacks proportion to the celestial melody, a sound of this kind is not heard. Here we imagine there are nine Muses and Sirens, the tones of the eight spheres, and the harmonic concert resulting from the tones. 

Furthermore, he says the fatal spindle is turned in the lap between the knees of the goddess Necessity. To whom there are three daughters: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos: who, together with their mother, turn the celestial things. I pass over what Proclus thinks of these, placing not only one universal Jupiter as the maker of the whole world, but three particular Jupiters as makers under him. Next, with equal proportion, one goddess Necessity in that order guarding all things, in which the common Jupiter composed all things. Furthermore, three Fates: that is, three goddesses, daughters of this Necessity: of whom some, under the mother's command, preserve others from transgression. And he places the goddess Necessity entirely above the world: but the daughters first as remote from the world, and partly also declining toward the world. 

To me, however, as to most other Platonists, it is more pleasing that Necessity is the Soul of the World. The three daughters, moreover, are the three powers of this soul pertaining to fatal matters. He calls her "Necessity," not because she brings violence either to nature or to reason: but because she preserves all things in their certain order instituted by the Maker of things: nor does she permit anything to transgress his laws to such an extent that it does not soon return into the laws. He wished the heavens to be [turned] by her knees, that is, by the lowest part of herself, with such great ease that she meanwhile enjoys the joy of contemplation most expeditiously. 

But he calls this vegetative part of her by three names. Lachesis indeed, because she is pregnant with the seeds of things, and with the lots and forms of lives: which she inserts into the souls about to descend. Clotho next, because she unfolds the indwelling lots of life in their order into the act of living, and explains them into effect. Finally Atropos, because she preserves and guards the lives already unfolded into act by a certain indeclinable progress, even to the inevitable end. Some name the first Vesta; the second Minerva; the third indeed Mars or Martia. 

Then, as to what he says about the Fates singing to the harmonic motions of the Sirens, understand that the fatal powers proceed to their effect through the celestial motions and influences. The seats of Necessity and her daughters show the firmness of the fatal order: as if it were necessary for the progression of mobile things to be ruled and ordered by the immobility of the mover itself. The equal intervals of the seats [show] that a just distribution is made both among the fates and through the fates...

# ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X.
## PAGE CXVIII

clearly demonstrates. The white robes show both the inviolate nature of the fates and their innocence. For the leader of the universe, who is the best, does not act as the cause of universal evil. The crown describes their imperial power. To sing is to arrange individual things through intervals of time with that harmony by which the divine mind, beholding everything in a single moment, prescribes the things to be arranged in their proper times. Hence it happens that all the Fates sing of temporal things. But why does Lachesis sing of the past, Clotho of the present, and Atropos of the future? Let Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 412–485 AD) whose commentaries on Plato are heavily used here.</note> respond: in the past, three times are thought of. For it is already called the past; it was once the present; and before it was present, it was the future. In the present, the present itself is thought of, which was previously future. Finally, in the future, only the future is recognized. Through these things, it is declared that Lachesis is the chief, Clotho holds the second place of dignity, and Atropos the third.

But why do the Fates handle the spheres with their hands, while their mother <note>Necessity (Ananke).</note> does not? Because the powers of that lowest soul are more closely related to the spheres than the substance of the soul itself. Why also does Lachesis touch them with both hands? Because she contains the beginning, the middle, and the end. Why then does Clotho touch the larger and outer circumference with her right hand, while Atropos touches the narrower and inner one with her left? Because the evolution of life through the middle and from the outer cause is the beginning, and is more ample, and also touches upon the superior. But the inevitable end proceeds from an inner property already conceived, and defines itself in a narrow space. Add to this that it creeps up secretly, and for the most part against one's wish. 

When he says that the Fates touch the heavens with a certain intermission of time, do not think that the fatal powers of the world-soul govern worldly things at one moment and not at another. For if mutability exists in Fate, whose proper characteristic is immutability itself, nothing can be imagined that is not mutable. Plato, therefore, painting divine offices in a human manner and speech, wishes to imply that the fates partly handle the things themselves and partly do not: both because the virtue of the world-soul, consisting in the dignity of its own integrity, accommodates its action to governing things, and in turn while it accommodates it does not mix with them; and because they exhibit a temporal succession in their works. The "intermission" they are said to have in their operation is demonstrated not in themselves, but in the effect; also because they handle natural things but do not touch supernatural things. For those things which pertain either to pure and free reason, or to the divine intelligence superior to Fate, they do not touch at all. Such things are reduced by a wonderful order to the sublime providence of God, which is superior to celestial Fate. 

Similarly, in the *Statesman*, he writes that some worldly things are governed by Fate, others by Providence: not because such a change happens by an intermittent succession of times, but because daily certain things happen under Fate, while others are disposed through the laws of Providence above the fatal series. Added to this is that our souls are sometimes entirely in Providence, sometimes entirely in Fate, and sometimes in both at once. For when they live with a ready, contemplative mind, they live in Providence alone and are thoroughly free. But when the inclination toward this body grows strong in the vegetative part, and such an inclination propagates as far as the imagination, they—now declining toward Fate—likewise degenerate from freedom. But while they are joined to the composite body, they now merge themselves into the fate of their own body, and retain less of their former liberty. Finally, after they have contracted bodily affections into a habit, they are now utterly overwhelmed by Fate, deprived of all liberty. 

It is asked for what reason the souls here seem to approach Lachesis by a certain natural instinct. Certainly, in general corporeal nature, the seeds of all species are the "machines" destined to sprout not only in certain forms and modes, but also at certain times. Furthermore, in the specific nature of any species, there is a similar seminal order, but pertaining to the propagation and preservation of that specific species. There is also in any individual under a species a particular fuel <note>original: "fomes," meaning a spark or incentive.</note> for producing things in their own proper modes and times. These three natures are arranged in succession so that the individual follows the specific, and the specific follows the general; so much so that for the most part, what is from the nature of one is likewise from the others, and the particular nature agrees with the universal. 

Fate holds almost the same rationale: that is, a certain prefiguration of things to be unfolded, both in the soul of the world itself, and in the souls of the twelve spheres and stars, and also in the souls that are now, as it were, particular, among which are human souls. In the vegetative power of our soul, therefore, there is a certain proper fate and an involved series of future things, consenting in form, mode, and time together with the fates of the celestial souls and the world-soul. Just as you see the sprout of any plant, budding with its own figures and in its own time, spontaneously concur with the universal nature of springtime calling it to the same, so also souls by their own nature and their own fate opportunely bring forth certain lives when the universal fate calls them to the same. Thus the choir of souls, with their own figures of dancing and the simultaneous diversity of various dancers, imitates the fatal song and sound. I would prefer "song" to be understood in the celestial souls, "sound" in the spheres, and finally "dance" <note>original: "saltum," referring to the rhythmic movement or leap of the soul.</note> in us. 

By such an instinct, souls at the beginning of life come to Lachesis to have their lots confirmed by the lots of Lachesis. They are confirmed, therefore, through a certain prophet. The "prophet" here signifies two things: both the universal and primary influx of providence into the soul, and the opportunity under which such a concurrence happens, so that souls are carried to that toward which universal fate also carries them. When the prophet is said to dispose the souls in order and transfer the lots from Lachesis to them, it signifies that all these things are confirmed both by the favor of divine providence and by the opportunity of that concurrence. Nor is it said without reason that the Fates govern the universe with their hands, but the lots of souls are taken from the knees of Lachesis. For since the government of the universe is more excellent than the disposition of souls, the former is rightly judged to be performed by the hands, the latter by the knees. Sitting on a tribunal expresses authority and judgment. Among the lots of lives and their "examples" <note>The patterns or models of lives souls choose from.</note>, there seems to be such a distinction: that the lots pertain to the vegetative powers, while the examples pertain to the imaginations—superior indeed to the vegetative power, but near—

# ARGUMENT FOR THE TENTH DIALOGUE

### H v
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

...which. For indeed, when certain seeds of the future life first grow strong in this power <note>the soul's imaginative faculty</note> above others, there simultaneously arise figures and machinations in the imagination of a similar life, and the passions grow hot. Just as among us a cheerful imagination follows a sanguine bodily temperament, an angry one follows the choleric, a sad one follows the melancholic, and a lustful one follows the fertile <note>phlegmatic/procreative</note>. Thus far does fatal necessity proceed. But reason is superior to imagination; to reason belongs ratiocination, counsel, and choice, and therefore its movement is free toward either side. Perceiving the figures and passions of the imagination, reason can equally approve or reject such a description of life. For this reason, he <note>Plato</note> says that virtue is free from fate, and the blame for choosing a worse life belongs to the chooser, not to fate. For even if it is from fate—both in a general and specific sense—that a soul chooses a new life now, or chose one before, it is nevertheless from counsel <note>deliberate choice</note> that it specifically chooses this or that kind. Indeed, if reason, by examining it, rejects the first form of living offered to the eyes by the imagination, another better one will immediately appear, and then another. Hence that inspiration of providence is called a "prophet." For it pre-demonstrates to the reason, by a certain light of judgment, that it possesses a free faculty for consulting and choosing, and shows what follows especially from a rash choice. The prophet is also said to cast lots and propose examples of living, not only because the influx of divine providence in some way sanctions fated things, but because he brings fatal lots and fatal examples into the examination and judgment of reason. Because he announces in the proclamation that souls are "diurnal" <note>creatures of a day</note>, he expresses that they are also there in perpetual day, and the life they lead is but a single day and night. He adds that there will be the beginning of another circuit, to open the mystery of souls returning from heaven to earth and back again. He calls the human race not only "mortal," but—so that souls may lament their own evils—he adds "death-bringing," as if to say the life of the body is the death of the soul. He then foretells that although reason is free at the beginning in choosing a life, after it has chosen, it will no longer be free to reject this thing, although each will be free within that life, whatever it may be, to compose or temper it in various ways. If you ask why some souls of men choose some lives and others choose others, some will answer that there are certain species of differences in the natures of souls; others that they are individual and personal; and they will add many differences deduced from the diversity of a previous life. This Plotinus <note>Neoplatonist philosopher, 204–270 AD</note> strongly confirms, and it agrees most closely with what follows. Furthermore, souls choosing a life simultaneously receive by lot a *daemon* <note>a guardian spirit or guiding divinity</note> as the leader of the chosen life. We have spoken much of this elsewhere. Here, distinguish it thus: The Platonists think of some Gods as outside the world—namely, minds separated from the body, inhabiting intellectual spheres, worshipping the one God as the firmest and most stable center and unity of themselves. Others they call "worldly" Gods, namely those accommodated to the revolving spheres of the world beyond divine worship. To these they subject *daemones*, as ministers for arranging and composing those things which happen either in species, or in the spheres, or from the spheres. They therefore count as many genera of *daemones* as there are powers found in the worldly Gods who lead them. But truly, in any worldly God, the unity itself is the highest part of its substance, by which it reflects the divine unity. After this is the intellect, beholding all things at once, through which it represents the angelic minds. Likewise, there is reason, running through forms in a certain progression, which is proper to such souls. Furthermore, there is a certain imagination, proceeding through particular forms to the extent that reason itself proceeds through universals. Next follows the "vegetal" nature of the sphere, which is both life-giving and a mover. According to these five powers, five genera of *daemones* are reckoned. From this number, the **celestial** *daemones* follow the unity of the worldly gods in an accommodated way; the **ethereal** (that is, fiery) *daemones* follow the intelligence of those same gods; the **aerial** *daemones* follow reason; the **aqueous** follow imagination; and the **terrestrial** follow the nature which we called "vegetal" in the gods. Beneath these, the Orphics <note>followers of the mystical teachings attributed to Orpheus</note> place **subterranean** *daemones*, reflecting the bodies of the worldly gods in a certain lowest order, and these are the avengers of crimes. Plato seems to have made mention of these here. If you ask what kind of *daemones* are primarily the leaders of souls descending into bodies, he will answer: not the celestial, nor the fiery. For these, being more sublime, lead souls back <note>to heaven</note>, they do not lead them down. Likewise, neither the aqueous nor the terrestrial. For these, being the artisans of the lowest generation, do not so much lead the soul on its fatal journey as plunge it into the ignorance of fate. Therefore, the **aerial** *daemones* remain—middle leaders through middle things—who, as companions of divine reason, lead human reason on this journey. From this genus of *daemones*, some lead some souls and others lead others: Saturnian spirits lead Saturnian souls, Martian lead Martian, and others similarly lead others, each being most accommodated to each, both from the soul's own disposition and from common providence and fate, but especially according to the form of the chosen life. Under this leader of life, the souls are now subject to the three Fates <note>the Parcae: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos</note>, which they had only looked upon before; namely, with the *daemon* (the executor of the whole order) so decreeing, and with the bodily affection now gradually outweighing. Finally, after the three Fates, they pass to the mother of the Fates, **Necessity** herself, whose impulses they now experience. Then, that souls go under a vehement heat of anger can signify three things: namely, that the ardor of bodily love increases, and simultaneously care and anxiety are augmented. Likewise, that they descend from heaven through the sphere of fire. Furthermore, the ministry of natural heat for the sake of vivifying the terrestrial body. But because through excessive care for terrestrial things, celestial things are consigned to oblivion, and through oblivion sterility happens instead of fertility, they soon descend into the "Lethean" (that is, oblivious) plain, which is utterly sterile. And because, due to diligent care for mortal things, eternal things are neglected—whence both oblivion and loss are born, as well as the difficulty of remembrance—he says the souls descend in the plain of Lethe to the river **Amelita** (that is, the depth of negligence), and there they lie down under the night (that is, they are prostrated under the privation of divine light). But what does it signify that the water of Amelita can never be contained in any vessel? This is a poetic metaphor, signifying that the lower matter, which is called a river, flows away through forms and fluctuates fleetingly. Likewise, the vice of oblivion, which is [unable] to retain...

# BOOK

...nothing, but immediately pour it out. Add to this that no external support preserves a soul that is perishing through its own negligence. Furthermore, it is clear that it is necessary to drink from the river of forgetfulness <note>The river Lethe</note>, since it is so ordained by its own nature, by common fate, and by providence. However, to drink either more or less water arises from an inclination toward the body, being more or less prone to it; and this same thing is the cause of greater or lesser forgetfulness, or rather a greater or lesser faculty for remembrance. Certainly, the soul experiences these passions in a certain way while in a body composed of thicker air in the upper field, before it is enclosed in the womb of an earthly mother. For the descent from celestial bodies to earthly ones occurs not only through the elements, but through an airy body. It is said that souls in this airy body sleep until midnight, showing that soon, under the earthly body, there will be not just a half-night, but a full night of ignorance. Sleep bears witness to both the hindrance of reason and the falsity of judgment. Finally, he says that souls are introduced into the earthly fetus amid a certain thunder and earthquake, for two reasons as I think: both indicating that they enter this prison under unhappy auspices, and showing that both celestial and earthly motion—and indeed a violent one—must concur to restrain the divine soul in such a foul prison. That souls leap forth toward generation like stars <note>original: "stellarum instar"</note> further suggests, beyond the poetic figure, that souls are in some way stellar and will finally return to the stars. 

As for what Plato brings forward regarding the migration of souls into the bodies of beasts—such a ridiculous tale, differing not at all from old wives' fables—it surely warns us that the whole thing must be explained allegorically; namely, that rational souls migrate not into the life of a brute, but into a "brutish" life, that is, one similar to a brute. This was especially pleasing to almost all Platonists except Plotinus. And Origen, in his books *Against Celsus*, seems to confirm the same. But you, do not neglect the moral precept: that the skill of right choice is to be preferred above all things and arts. Furthermore, so many things have been brought forward here concerning the beauty and power of the spheres so that we might reflect that justice will attain a great reward in heaven, and will greatly lead toward the best choice of living. But you will say now, high-minded Lawrence <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron</note>, that you have received a commentary here from Marsilio Ficino rather than a mere summary. So be it: I think it was snatched away, and will be, that I promised a summary but provided a commentary.

### TENTH DIALOGUE ON JUSTICE.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a classical figure (possibly a philosopher or deity) seated within the letter's curve, surrounded by ornate floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

**SOCRATES.** When I think about this city which we have recently established in words, among many other things that we seem to have established quite rightly, I am especially pleased with what we decreed concerning poetry. **GLAUCON.** What things are those? **SOCRATES.** That is, that no part of poetry which consists in imitation should be admitted. For it is now most clear, as it seems to me, that nothing of that sort should be taken up by us, now that the individual species of the soul have been separately distinguished. **GLAUCON.** How do you mean that? **SOCRATES.** So that I may communicate these things with you; for you will not accuse me before the tragic poets and other imitators. Everything of that sort seems to be a certain corruption of the minds of those who, when they hear these imitations, do not possess that medicine of the mind by which they might discern what kind of stories these are. **GLAUCON.** To what purpose is this? **SOCRATES.** It must be said: even if a certain friendship and reverence for Homer, contracted from my boyhood, holds me back. For he seems to have been the first leader and teacher of all those distinguished tragedians. But I do not think a man should be preferred to the truth. Therefore, what I have set out to do must be said. **GLAUCON.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Listen then. Or rather, answer. **GLAUCON.** Ask. **SOCRATES.** Can you explain to me at all what imitation <term>mimesis</term> is? For I do not sufficiently understand what it is. **GLAUCON.** Will I then understand it? **SOCRATES.** That would be no wonder. For it often happens that those who have a duller vision see some things sooner than those who see more sharply. **GLAUCON.** It is as you say. But in your presence, I would never dare to express what I think. But see to it yourself. **SOCRATES.** Shall we begin from here, considering it by our usual method? We are accustomed to posit a single Form <term>Idea</term> for each group of many things to which we give the same name. Do you not understand? **GLAUCON.** I do indeed. **SOCRATES.** Let us posit now any one of the many. For example, there are many beds and tables. **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** Yet there are two Ideas of these things. One of the bed; the other of the table. **GLAUCON.** So it is. **SOCRATES.** And we are accustomed to say that the craftsman of both pieces of furniture, looking toward the Idea, produces his work: one makes the beds, the other the tables, which we ourselves use; and other things similarly. For no craftsman makes the Idea itself. For how could he? **GLAUCON.** In no way. **SOCRATES.** See further if you would call someone such a craftsman? **GLAUCON.** What kind? **SOCRATES.** One who makes all things whatsoever that every single craftsman works with his hands. **GLAUCON.** You speak of a powerful and wonderful man. **SOCRATES.** I have not yet expressed his full power. Perhaps you will wonder much more if I do. For this same craftsman is not only able to make all furniture, but he also makes everything that grows from the earth; and he produces all animals and himself. He also fashions the earth, the sky, and the gods, and everything in heaven and under the earth among those in the underworld. **GLAUCON.** You speak of a wonderful Sophist. **SOCRATES.** Do you doubt it? Tell me, I pray, does it seem to you that such a craftsman exists in no way? Or that in one way he is the maker of all these things, but in another way he is not? Do you not notice that you could produce all these things in a certain way? **GLAUCON.** What way is this? **SOCRATES.** It is not difficult: for you can make all things everywhere and quickly. Take a mirror and carry it around everywhere. You will immediately make the sun and the things in the sky, the earth at once, and most swiftly yourself, and likewise other animals, furniture, plants, and all the things we just mentioned. **GLAUCON.** The images of these things, certainly; but the things themselves, not at all.
