# DIALOGUE X. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE. FOLIO CCLXX.

SOCRATES. You have answered quite opportunely. Such a craftsman, then, is the painter himself. Is he not? GLAUCON. He is. SOCRATES. But you will say that he does not at all make the true things that he makes; although in some way the painter also makes a bed. Does he not? GLAUCON. He does indeed make one, but an appearing one <note>original: "apparentem"; meaning a representation or semblance rather than a physical object</note>. SOCRATES. Did you not say that the maker of the bed <note>the carpenter</note> does not make the "form" itself, which we say is that which a bed truly is, but only a particular bed? GLAUCON. I did indeed say that. SOCRATES. If he does not make that which *is* <note>the ideal Form</note>, he certainly does not make that which is truly real; but something of such a kind as that which is truly real, yet not the very thing which is real. If anyone should say that the work of the carpenter, or of any other craftsman, exists perfectly, would he be wandering from the truth? GLAUCON. No, so it seems to those who are occupied in these disputes. SOCRATES. It is no wonder then, if this too is thin and frivolous compared to the truth. GLAUCON. Certainly not. SOCRATES. Do you wish for us to investigate who this "imitator" is in these matters as well? GLAUCON. If you please. SOCRATES. Are there not these three beds? One existing in nature itself, which we would say God produced, I suppose. <margin>Three beds by three makers.</margin> Or did anyone else? GLAUCON. No one. SOCRATES. The second, which the carpenter makes. GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. And the third, which the painter makes. Is it not so? GLAUCON. It is. SOCRATES. Thus the painter, the bed-maker, and God are three, presiding over three species of beds. GLAUCON. Three indeed. SOCRATES. God, therefore, whether because he did not wish to, or because some necessity was present, did not make more beds, but only that one bed in nature was made by him; thus he made only that one bed, which truly is that which a bed is. But two such beds, or more, have neither been brought forth by God, nor will they ever be. GLAUCON. For what reason? SOCRATES. Because if he made only two, one would appear again whose form both would have; and that one would be that which a bed is, but those two would not be it. GLAUCON. Cleverly said. SOCRATES. Since God understood these things, and wished to be the true author of a true bed, and not just a certain author of a certain bed, he brought forth only one by nature. GLAUCON. So it seems. <margin>See how nature wants one to be made.</margin> SOCRATES. Do you wish, then, for us to call him the planter of this, or something of that sort? GLAUCON. That is fair, since by nature he made both this and all other things. SOCRATES. And the carpenter, is he not the worker of the bed? GLAUCON. He is that too. SOCRATES. But is the painter also a maker and worker of this work? GLAUCON. By no means. SOCRATES. Then how will you say he relates to the bed? GLAUCON. It seems to me he can most aptly be called the imitator of that which those others are the workers of. SOCRATES. Therefore, you call him an imitator who makes something three steps removed from nature? GLAUCON. Very much so. SOCRATES. Such a person, then, will also be the tragic poet, if indeed he is an imitator: someone third from the king <note>the "king" here represents Truth or the Divine Creator</note> and the truth; and likewise all other imitators. GLAUCON. <margin>An imitator is one who makes something third from nature.</margin> It appears so. SOCRATES. We have agreed then about the imitator. But I would like you to tell me about the painter: whether he strives to imitate each thing as it is in nature, or the works of craftsmen. GLAUCON. The works of craftsmen. SOCRATES. As they are, or as they appear to us? Distinguish this for me further. GLAUCON. How do you mean? SOCRATES. Thus: if a bed is seen from the side, or from the front, or in any other way, does it differ from itself? Or does it differ not at all, but only appears different to those looking at it, and other things likewise? GLAUCON. It appears so indeed, but it differs not at all. SOCRATES. Consider this too: what does the painter's industry aim at in each case? To imitate each thing as it is? Or rather that which appears, as it appears? Is it an imitation of an appearing image, or rather of the truth? GLAUCON. Of an appearing image. SOCRATES. The imitator, therefore, is far from the truth; and <margin>The imitator is far from the truth.</margin> as it seems, he can make all things for this reason: because he touches only a certain small phantom of each thing. Just as a painter will paint for us a cobbler, a carpenter, and other craftsmen, though he understands nothing of these arts; nevertheless, if he were a skilled painter and displayed a painted image of a carpenter from a distance, he would deceive children and foolish men into thinking he was a true carpenter. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. But, my friend, this must be considered in all such cases. Whenever someone tells us of this very thing—that he has met a man learned in all arts, and understanding everything more perfectly than anyone else—we must <margin>No one can understand all things exactly.</margin> immediately reply to him that he is a fool, and has fallen in with a certain sorcerer and imitator by whose imitations he was deceived; so that he seemed to himself to be the wisest in all things, because he himself was unable to discern knowledge from ignorance and imitation from reality. GLAUCON. You speak most truly. SOCRATES. Is it not fitting after this to discuss tragedy, and its leader Homer? Since we have heard from some that tragic poets understand all arts, and all human things pertaining to both virtue and vice, and even divine things; and further, that a good poet must have knowledge of the things he composes if he is to handle them rightly, or else he cannot compose. Therefore we ought to discern whether those who praise them have been deceived by the imitative industry of poets, and when they look at their works, do not clearly perceive that they are three degrees distant from the truth; and that they are easy to make even for a man ignorant of the truth. For they make shadows, not true things. Or perhaps they say something of substance, and good poets really do understand those things about which they seem to the common people to speak well. GLAUCON. We must certainly discern this. SOCRATES. If someone were able to produce both—the thing that falls under imitation and the image of it—do you think he would linger in the fashioning of images? And set that work before himself as the best thing in life? GLAUCON. Not at all. SOCRATES. Surely if he had true skill in those things which he imitates, he would apply himself much more to the works themselves than to their imitations, as I think; and he would strive to leave many and noble works as monuments of himself to posterity; and he would judge it better to be praised by others than to always be the praiser of other men's works. GLAUCON. I think so indeed; for the honor is not equal, nor is the profit. SOCRATES. However, let us not demand an account of other things, but let us ask Homer or <margin>Homer is sharply criticized.</margin> any other of the poets: if any of them was truly a physician, and not just an imitator of words looking toward a physician, which people has the poet restored to health, either of the men of old or of recent times, as Aesculapius did? Or what disciples of the medical art did he leave behind, as he left his sons? But neither...

<summary>Socrates and Glaucon discuss the nature of art as a "third-hand" imitation of reality, using the example of a bed created by God (the Form), a carpenter (the object), and a painter (the image). They conclude that artists and poets like Homer deal in appearances rather than true knowledge or utility.</summary>

let us inquire of them concerning other arts. For let us set aside the rest. But truly, concerning those greatest and most illustrious things which Homer attempts—wars, military commands, the administration of republics, and the education of men—it is fair to question him thus: "O sweet Homer, if you are not third from the truth, or if you do not merely fashion an image of virtue (which we defined above as the role of the imitator), but if you are second <note>original: "secundus" - meaning one step closer to the truth/reality than a mere imitator</note>, and are able to discern which pursuits make men either better or worse in private and public life, tell us, I pray, which city was better governed because of you? Just as Lacedaemonia <note>Sparta</note> was by Lycurgus, and many other cities, both small and large, were by others. Which city's men proclaim you the best founder of laws and commemorate your benefits to them? Italy and Sicily celebrate Charondas. We celebrate Solon. But who will proclaim you, and in what capacity?" GLAUCON. None, I think, commemorate such benefits from him. Indeed, not even <margin>Supporters of Homer</margin> the supporters of Homer themselves dare to testify to this. SOCRATES. What particular war in Homer's time is remembered as having been successfully managed with him as counselor or leader? GLAUCON. None. SOCRATES. Furthermore, what inventions of this man, as one wise in such matters, are recorded as being most fit for the duties of life and art, such as those of Thales of Miletus and Anacharsis the Scythian? GLAUCON. Nothing of the sort. SOCRATES. If not publicly, then at least privately: for whom was Homer himself, while he lived, said to have been a leader in education? Who delighted in his company and handed down to posterity a certain Homeric way of life? Just as Pythagoras lived with the greatest authority in this regard, and his successors even in these times, celebrating the Pythagorean life, are held as illustrious among others. GLAUCON. Again, no such thing is told of Homer. For Creophilus, Socrates, perhaps the companion of Homer, will appear even <margin>Creophilus, disciple of Homer</margin> more ridiculous in his education than in his name <note>The name "Creophilus" suggests "flesh-lover" or "tribe-lover," which Socrates plays upon</note>, if the things told about Homer are true. For it is said he was quite negligent toward his education while he lived under him. SOCRATES. So it is said. But truly, O Glaucon, if Homer were really able to instruct men and make them better—inasmuch as he would be a master of understanding and not merely of imitation—why did he not claim many friends for himself? Why was he not honored while living? Why not loved? Surely Protagoras of Abdera, and Prodicus of Chios, and many others are able to persuade the men of their time, approaching individuals privately, that they will never govern their domestic or public affairs rightly unless they themselves educate them; and for this wisdom they are so ardently loved that their followers can hardly restrain themselves from carrying them about on their shoulders. But as for Homer or Hesiod, if those poets could have helped the men of those times toward virtue, they would never have permitted them to wander about for so long chanting their poems everywhere. Rather, they would have embraced them more than gold and would have induced them to live familiarly with them at home. And if they had not persuaded them, they would have followed them themselves wherever they went, until they were sufficiently instructed in their studies. GLAUCON. You seem to me to speak the truth entirely, O Socrates. SOCRATES. Let us suppose, then, that all the poetic men, beginning with Homer, are imitators of the images of virtue and of the other things they sing about, but never touch the truth. But as we said a little while ago, the painter will paint a likeness of a cobbler, though he himself <margin>Aristotle in the Poetics</margin> understands nothing of cobbling; and that image appears to be a cobbler to those who likewise understand nothing of the craft itself, and who judge by colors and shapes. GLAUCON. Exactly. SOCRATES. In the same way, we shall say the poet expresses certain colors of the individual arts with names and words, though he himself understands nothing of them, but only imitates; so that to those who consider these things from words, he seems to speak well—whether he speaks of cobbling in verse, rhythm, and harmony, or of military matters, or of anything else. To such an extent do these poetic devices naturally soothe the ears. But I think you know what these works of the poets look like when they are stripped of the colors of music and considered on their own. Have you ever noticed? GLAUCON. I have. SOCRATES. Do they not look like the faces of those who, because of youth, are "fair" rather than truly beautiful, as they appear when the bloom of youth has left them? GLAUCON. Entirely so. SOCRATES. Come then, and observe this. The imitator, the author of the representation, understands nothing of the thing itself, but only the appearing image of the thing. GLAUCON. So it is. SOCRATES. Let us not leave this incomplete, but contemplate it sufficiently. GLAUCON. Speak on. SOCRATES. A painter will paint reins and a bridle. GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. But the cobbler and the blacksmith will make them. GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. Does the painter understand how the reins and the bridle ought to be? Or does even the maker—the blacksmith or the cobbler—not know? Is it only the one who knows how to use them, the horseman? GLAUCON. You speak the truth. SOCRATES. Shall we not say it is thus concerning everything? GLAUCON. How so? SOCRATES. That concerning everything there are these three arts: the user's, the maker's, and the imitator's? GLAUCON. Certainly. SOCRATES. Therefore the virtue, beauty, and correctness of every instrument, animal, and action is referred to nothing else than the use for which each was made or born. GLAUCON. So it is. SOCRATES. It is necessary, therefore, that he who uses a thing be the most skilled, and that he report to the maker what good or bad effects it has in the use of it. Just as the flute-player reports to the flute-maker which flutes are most fit for use; and he prescribes what kind he ought to make, and the other serves him. GLAUCON. Why not? SOCRATES. Does not the one who understands pronounce concerning fit and unfit flutes to the other, and the other makes them, believing him? GLAUCON. Clearly. SOCRATES. Concerning the same instrument, therefore, the maker has a correct "faith" <note>original: "fidem" - here meaning a correct belief or opinion</note> regarding beauty and defect, by being in contact with the one who understands and being compelled to listen to the one who knows. But the user has the "science" <note>original: "scientiam" - certain knowledge</note>. GLAUCON. Exactly. SOCRATES. But will the imitator have science from the use of the things he paints, as to whether they are beautiful and correct or the opposite? Or will he have correct opinion, from the fact that he must necessarily be in contact with the one who understands and be instructed by him as to how things should be painted? GLAUCON. Neither. SOCRATES. Therefore the imitator will neither understand nor have a correct opinion concerning those things which...

<summary>Socrates argues that poets like Homer are mere imitators who lack practical knowledge of the subjects they describe, such as law, war, or crafts. He establishes a hierarchy of knowledge where the user of an object has true science, the maker has correct belief, and the poet/imitator has neither.</summary>

# DIALOGUE X. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.

## FOLIO CCLXXI.

...imitates, in beauty: or the contrary? **GLAUCON.** It does not seem so. **SOCRATES.** Will the imitator be graceful in his execution regarding wisdom in the things he creates? **GLAUCON.** Not much. **SOCRATES.** Nevertheless, he will imitate; hardly understanding in what way each thing is well-off or poorly-off. But as it appears: whatever seems beautiful to the many and the ignorant, this he will imitate. **GLAUCON.** What else indeed? **SOCRATES.** These things seem sufficiently asserted by us: namely, that imitators 
<margin>Imitation is a kind of play.</margin>
<margin>Tragic poetry is the greatest imitator.</margin>
understand nothing worthy of esteem regarding these things which they imitate; but that imitation is a kind of play rather than a serious matter: and that all those who handle tragic poetry in iambic and heroic verses are imitators above all others. **GLAUCON.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** By Jove! This imitation, however, is concerned with something three steps removed from the truth. Is it not? **GLAUCON.** It is as you say. **SOCRATES.** To which part of those things that are in man, then, does it belong, insofar as it has power of that kind? **GLAUCON.** About what sort of thing do you ask? **SOCRATES.** About something like this. The same magnitude does not appear equal through sight from a distance and from close up. **GLAUCON.** No. **SOCRATES.** The same things also appear crooked and straight to us when looking at them in water and out of water: and again concave and convex because of the error of sight regarding colors. 
<margin>Error of sight regarding colors and magnitudes.</margin>
And every such disturbance is found to be present in our soul. Indeed, the faculty of shadow-painting <note>original: "adumbrationis" - referring to *skiagraphia*, a technique using light and shadow to create illusion</note> itself, having attacked this passion of our nature, and the ingenuity of magic tricks <note>original: "prestigiarum"</note>, and other such devices, leave nothing unattempted in the way of seduction. **GLAUCON.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Are not the skills of measuring, counting, and weighing opportune helps for men against these things: so that what appears larger or smaller, or more, or heavier, does not prevail in us: but rather that which measures, computes, and weighs? **GLAUCON.** Why not? **SOCRATES.** And yet this is the duty of the rational part of the soul. **GLAUCON.** Of this very part. **SOCRATES.** But while this part is frequently measuring and judging some things to be larger or smaller than others, or equal, contrary appearances appear to us at the same time regarding these same things. **GLAUCON.** So it happens. **SOCRATES.** Did we not say elsewhere that it is impossible for the same power of the soul to hold contrary opinions at the same time about the same things? **GLAUCON.** And we said so rightly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the power of the soul which opines contrary to measurement will not be the same as that which opines with measurement. **GLAUCON.** Certainly not. **SOCRATES.** But indeed, that part of the soul which trusts in measurement, reasoning, and computation is the best part. **GLAUCON.** Nothing stands in the way. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, that which opposes it will be some ignoble part of us. **GLAUCON.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** It was to assert this that I said above that painting and the whole faculty of imitation perform their work far from the truth: and again, it joins with some part of us that is entirely devoid of wisdom, and contracts a friendship; leading to nothing sincere or true. **GLAUCON.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, the base faculty of imitation, mixing itself with something base, procreates base things. **GLAUCON.** It appears so. **SOCRATES.** Is it such only in that which pertains to sight? Or also in that which pertains to hearing? Which we call poetry. **GLAUCON.** It is probable that this is also such. **SOCRATES.** Let us not, therefore, trust only in what appears likely to us from painting: but let us come to that very nature of thought to which poetic imitation accommodates itself: and let us see whether it be something base or precious. **GLAUCON.** So it must be. **SOCRATES.** Let us propose it in this way. Poetry indeed imitates men acting either by force or voluntarily, and thinking that from their actions either something good or evil comes to them: and therefore being affected either by pain or by pleasure. Is it anything else? **GLAUCON.** Nothing else. **SOCRATES.** In all these things, is a man at one with himself? Or rather, just as he is at odds regarding sight, as we recounted, and has contrary opinions in himself at the same time about the same things, so also in acting is he at odds and at war with himself? But now it comes to my mind that we need not discuss this at present. For in the previous dispute we sufficiently agreed on these things: namely, confessing that our soul is agitated by many and various contentions of this kind, opposing itself at the same time. **GLAUCON.** Correct. **SOCRATES.** That is correct indeed. But what was then omitted by us, it seems to me should now be explained. **GLAUCON.** What sort of thing is that? **SOCRATES.** A good man, when he has such a soul, if he loses a son or anything else most dear to him, will bear it more easily than others, as we said. **GLAUCON.** Clearly. **SOCRATES.** But now let us also consider this: whether he will not grieve at all. Or is this indeed impossible: but he will moderate his grief in some way. **GLAUCON.** This certainly is truer. **SOCRATES.** Tell me this about him now: whether you think this man will resist grief more when he is seen by men like himself, or when he is alone, destitute of the company of others. **GLAUCON.** It makes a great difference if he is in the sight of others. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, when he is alone, he will utter many things out of sorrow which he 
<margin>Concerning the good man, that he may endure pain.</margin>
would be ashamed to let out in front of others. He will do many things which he would never wish to be seen by others. **GLAUCON.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** That which commands him to resist is reason and law. That which drags him toward grief is the disturbance <note>original: "perturbatio" - referring to the irrational emotions or passions</note>. **GLAUCON.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** When a man is agitated by contrary motions regarding the same thing at the same time, we say those must necessarily be two distinct things. **GLAUCON.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** One part indeed is ready to obey the law, however it may command. **GLAUCON.** In what way? **SOCRATES.** The law dictates to each that it is best in adversities, as much as can be, to keep quiet and not to complain: as if it were uncertain whether what happened be good or evil: and that we accomplish nothing by grief, nor is any of human affairs to be highly valued: and that grief hinders that which can be of immediate help. **GLAUCON.** What do you mean by this? **SOCRATES.** I mean that one ought especially to deliberate about those things which have happened, and as if in a throw of the dice, according to the throw, in whatever way reason says the matter is best, to arrange one's affairs. Nor indeed, if any adversity falls upon us, ought we to prostrate ourselves: and as children are accustomed to do when they stumble on a stone, falling down around that which hurt them, to waste time in wailing. But to accustom the soul to be present and ready to heal: and whatever is sick, to correct it, having dismissed lamentations. **GLAUCON.** This is indeed an opportune remedy against the blows of fortune. **SOCRATES.** That which is truly best, willingly obeys this reason. **GLAUCON.** It is agreed. **SOCRATES.** But that which drags one toward the memory of the disturbance and toward mourning...

<summary>Socrates argues that artistic imitation is far removed from truth and appeals to the lower, irrational parts of the soul. He contrasts this with the rational man who uses reason and law to moderate his grief in the face of misfortune.</summary>

# BOOK X.
### PAGE XXXI.
<meta>Catchword: fi (referring to the start of the next page's first word, likely "fides" or "finis")</meta>

...and detains them in these [emotions] for a long time, is irrational, sluggish, and fearful. 

**GLAUCON:** It must be said so. 

**SOCRATES:** That which is prone to lamentation admits of a great and varied range of imitation. But the prudent and calm character, being always consistent with itself, is neither easy to imitate, nor, if imitated, is it easily understood by a crowd flowing into a theater from various nations. For the imitation becomes something foreign to their own experiences. 

**GLAUCON:** That is entirely so. 

**SOCRATES:** Indeed, the imitation of the poet does not aim at this: that his wisdom should please this [rational] nature of the soul—if he intends to please the common people—but rather he observes the complaining soul and the fickle character, because it can be easily portrayed through imitation. 

**GLAUCON:** It is clear. 

**SOCRATES:** Justly, therefore, we shall find fault with poetic imitation, and we shall say it corresponds alternately to the imitation of the painter. First, they are similar in this: that both produce works that are of little value in relation to the truth. Next, they likewise support the part of the soul that lacks reason and abandon the best part. And for that reason, we shall by no means accept it into a city that is to be governed by law; since it arouses and nourishes this [emotional] part of the soul, and while it strengthens this, it destroys the power that possesses reason. Just as if someone, by making the wicked powerful in a city, should betray the city and destroy the virtuous; so also the imitative poet introduces a perverse <term>republic</term><note>original: "rempublicam" - here referring to the internal governance or constitution of the individual soul</note> into the soul of each person, while he flatters that part of the soul which is without mind, and which discerns neither greater nor lesser things, but thinks the same things are now small and now great; and for this part, he fashions phantoms, being far removed from the truth. 

**GLAUCON:** Far indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** We have not yet recounted the greatest evil that comes from it. For this must be considered the most vehement harm: that it can corrupt even virtuous men, with very few exceptions. 

**GLAUCON:** Why should it not be able to do so, if indeed it effects that very thing? 

**SOCRATES:** Listen and consider. Do not even the best of us, when we hear Homer, or any other tragic poet imitating some hero afflicted with grief, crying out and bewailing his fortune with mournful melodies, and beating his breast with his fists—do we not delight in it in a way, and gaping at those things, do we not follow them and are affected along with them? And do we not seriously and studiously praise him as a good poet who moves us most in this way? 

**GLAUCON:** I have noticed it. 

**SOCRATES:** However, whenever a private sorrow invades one of us, we strive on the contrary to behave honorably, if by any means we are able to keep quiet and endure it; as if this indeed were the part of a man, while that which we praised before belonged to a woman. 

**GLAUCON:** Clearly. 

**SOCRATES:** What a fine praise this is! Indeed, it is absurd that one who watches such a man—the kind of man he would least want to be himself, and of whom he would be most ashamed—should not nevertheless loathe him, but should delight in and praise him. 

**GLAUCON:** That is altogether contrary to reason. 

**SOCRATES:** Certainly, if you also observe it in this way. 

**GLAUCON:** In what way? 

**SOCRATES:** Namely, that the very thing which is forcibly restrained in our own calamities, and is prohibited from breaking out into tears and weeping, and from indulging its nature which is greedy for tears—that is the very thing which the poets satisfy and which they thoroughly flatter. Then, certainly, that which is best in our nature—as it is sufficiently instructed neither by reason nor by habit—ceases to guard that complaining part, as if it were watching the disturbances of another, and as if it were no disgrace to itself if, while another man who claims to excel in virtue weeps immoderately, it should itself praise and pity him. Indeed, it thinks it gains that pleasure; nor would it wish to be deprived of it by any contempt for poetry. Few indeed realize, I think, that it is necessary for something to be transferred from the affairs of others into one's own. For when you have nourished that tearful disposition in the miseries of others and made it more vehement, you will not easily restrain it in your own. 

**GLAUCON:** You speak the truth only too well. 

**SOCRATES:** Is not the same reasoning true regarding laughter? That when you would be ashamed to imitate with excessive laughter yourself, yet when you hear it in a comedy or in private imitation as something ridiculous, you listen most willingly and imitate it; and you do the same thing here that we said happens in mournful imitation. For that disposition of yours which is more prone to laughter, which you yourself would have restrained from laughing in your own person, fearing the crime of buffoonery, you now release into jokes here, and gradually you make the affection of laughter itself more vehement: so that even in your own gestures you begin to be carried away into laughter beyond what is fitting, and you turn out to be a ridiculous buffoon, imbued with the jokes of comedy. 

**GLAUCON:** Vehemently indeed. 

**SOCRATES:** We say the same also concerning lusts and anger; and concerning all the desires and affections of the soul, concerning the sad and the pleasant: all of which actions we said we follow in the things above; and that poetic imitation fashions such things in us. For it nourishes these things while it cherishes and waters them, when they ought rather to be thinned out by dryness; and it causes these to rule in us, when it would be more fitting for them to be subject: so that we might turn out better and happier instead of worse and more miserable. 

**GLAUCON:** I cannot say otherwise. 

**SOCRATES:** Therefore, Glaucon, whenever you encounter the praisers of Homer, and hear them saying that Homer has educated all of Greece, and advising that this poet should be observed for the governance and discipline of human affairs, and that one should arrange one's whole life according to his institutes: remember to congratulate these men as being the best men according to their capacity; and it must be granted that Homer is the chief of poets and the leader of tragic writers. But know that only hymns to the gods and praises of good men ought to be admitted from poetry into the city. For if you accept the pleasurable Muse in songs and poems, pleasure and pain will rule in the city instead of law and that which has always seemed best, namely, reason. 

**GLAUCON:** You speak the truth. 

**SOCRATES:** Let these things, therefore, be said by us in that opinion: that we have deservedly expelled poetry from the city, since it is such as it is. 

**GLAUCON:** For so reason compelled us. 

**SOCRATES:** Let us also add this, lest she accuse us of rigidity and rusticity: that there exists an ancient disagreement between poetry and philosophy. Certainly, these things which I shall subjoin, and many others, can be used as an argument for this contention. Namely, "that yelping dog barking at the ears of her mistress" signifies that. And "that great one in the vain talk of fools." And "the crowd of superstitious wise men excelling." Likewise, that which was said: "Those who meditate on minute and thin things are common in poverty." And innumerable other signs of this contrariety appear. Nevertheless, let it also be said, that if...

# DIALOGUE X. ON THE REPUBLIC OR ON JUSTICE.

If poetry, the handmaid of pleasure, and imitation can bring forward any reason why she should be received into a well-ordered city, we will gladly receive her, so that we may enjoy her delights. For we are indeed conscious of her charm. But truly, it is a sin to betray what seems to be the truth. For are you not also, my friend, soothed by her? Especially by the poetry of Homer? GLAUCON: Very much so. SOCRATES: Is it not then fair that she should come forward into the midst to defend herself, either in song or in any other meter? GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Let us certainly grant to her defenders—those who are not poets themselves but friends of poets—the chance to defend her without verse, asserting that she is not only pleasant but also useful to the republic and for the ordering of human life. We shall listen to such a defense with a favorable mind, for we consider it to be to our profit if she appears to us not only sweet but also useful. GLAUCON: What stands in the way of it being to our profit? SOCRATES: Otherwise, my dear friend: just as those who have at some time loved something, if they later judge that love to be useless to them, they cease to love, even if they do so with difficulty; so too we, because of the innate love of such poetry bred in us by a noble education, will kindly wait for her to appear as the best and truest thing. Yet as long as she cannot bring forward a reason for herself, we shall listen to her in this way: so that by the discourse set forth by us above, we may fortify ourselves as if by a certain incantation against imminent dangers, taking care lest we be ensnared again by the amorous delights and loves of the common people. We shall also feel this: that one must not study this kind of poetry as if it were true or serious. Rather, anyone listening to it must take care, fearing for the "republic" within his own soul <note>original: "interiorique animi sui reip." - referring to the internal self-governance of the soul</note>. And what we have related concerning poetry must be thought of in this way. GLAUCON: I certainly agree. SOCRATES: Furthermore, my friend Glaucon, the struggle to become good or evil is a great one—greater than it seems. Therefore, it is not right to neglect justice and the other virtues for the sake of money, or honor, or power, or any poetic delight. GLAUCON: I certainly assent based on these reasons we have discussed. Moreover, I think anyone else would confess the same. SOCRATES: And yet, we have by no means related the great rewards and prizes of virtue proposed for her. GLAUCON: You speak of immense rewards, if there are any greater than those we have recounted. SOCRATES: What can be great in a short time? For this whole time from childhood to the end of old age is but a tiny thing compared to the whole of eternity. GLAUCON: Indeed, it is nothing. SOCRATES: Do you then think that an immortal thing should be concerned with this short time, and not rather with the whole of eternity? GLAUCON: Certainly for the whole. But to what end is this? SOCRATES: Are you unaware that the soul of man is immortal and free from destruction? Then Glaucon, suddenly turning toward me and wondering, said: By Jove <note>original: "Per Iovem" - a common oath to Zeus/Jupiter</note>, I for my part do not know it. Can you actually demonstrate it? SOCRATES: Certainly, unless I wish to be unjust. I think you can do it too. It is not difficult. GLAUCON: It seems difficult to me. But I would gladly hear you declaring that which you say is not difficult. SOCRATES: You shall hear it now. GLAUCON: Speak. SOCRATES: Do you call something "Good"? And something "Evil"? GLAUCON: I do. SOCRATES: Does the same view of these things seem right to you as to me? GLAUCON: What is it? SOCRATES: I think everything that dissolves and corrupts is Evil. But that which preserves and helps is Good. GLAUCON: I agree. SOCRATES: And do you say there is a specific Good and a specific Evil for each thing? Just as bleary-eyedness is for the eyes, and disease for the whole body; blight for grain and food; rot and decay for wood; rust for bronze and iron; and, as I say, almost in all things there is a specific evil and disease according to their nature? GLAUCON: I do. SOCRATES: Whenever any such thing happens to something, it makes it worse, and finally dissolves and destroys the whole. GLAUCON: Why not? SOCRATES: Therefore, the specific evil of each thing, and its own depravity, corrupts it. And unless that corrupts it, nothing else will ever corrupt it. For that which is good destroys nothing, nor again does that which is neither good nor evil. GLAUCON: How could it? SOCRATES: If, therefore, there is something of such a nature that it has a certain evil which makes it worse, yet is not able to dissolve it, then certainly there can be no destruction for a thing so naturally constituted. GLAUCON: That is consistent. SOCRATES: Is there not something that makes the soul depraved? GLAUCON: Most certainly those things we mentioned: injustice, intemperance, cowardice, and ignorance. SOCRATES: Does any of these destroy the soul? And take heed, lest we be deceived, thinking that when an unjust and foolish man is caught in a crime, he is then corrupted by injustice, which is the vice of the soul. Tell me: does not the specific vice of the body, which is disease, liquefy and dissolve it, and lead it to the point where it is no longer a body? And all the things we spoke of a moment ago, do they not cease to be because of their own evil, insofar as it adheres and is within them, defiling them? Do they not? GLAUCON: Entirely so. SOCRATES: Does not injustice and the rest of depravity, when it is within the soul, likewise destroy and waste it away by its very presence, until, dragging it toward death, it separates it from the body? GLAUCON: Not at all. SOCRATES: But truly it is absurd that a foreign vice should kill something, when its own specific vice does not provide its destruction. GLAUCON: That is indeed beyond reason. SOCRATES: Pay attention, Glaucon. We do not think the body can perish from the specific depravity of food—whether it be spoiled, or rotten, or affected in any other way. But if the defect of the food brings upon the body its own specific defect, we shall say that through the food the body is destroyed by its own vice, namely disease. But we shall never think that the body itself, since it is one thing, can be dissipated by the foreign defect of food, which is of another nature, unless it induces its own specific defect. GLAUCON: You speak very rightly. SOCRATES: By the same reasoning, unless the detriment of the body brings upon the soul the soul's own specific detriment, we should by no means think that the soul perishes from a foreign evil without its own depravity; nor does one thing dissipate by the evil of another. GLAUCON: So reason advises. SOCRATES: Either, then, let us refute these things as not being said correctly, or, as long as they remain intact, let us not grant that the soul is dissipated by fever or any other disease, nor by the cutting of the throat, nor even if someone should chop the body into the smallest pieces—until someone demonstrates that because of these sufferings of the body, the soul itself becomes more unjust...

<margin>
Demonstration of the immortality of the soul.
</margin>

<margin>
Injustice and the vice of the soul.
</margin>

<summary>Socrates argues that while poetry is charming, it must be excluded from the state unless it can be proven useful to virtue. He then begins a logical proof for the immortality of the soul, arguing that things are only destroyed by their own specific internal vices, and since the soul's vices (like injustice) do not kill it, the soul must be immortal.</summary>

# BOOK X. ON THE REPUBLIC.

<margin>
The Immortal Soul
</margin>

...that the matter becomes more profane. Insofar as an external evil is present to another, and no internal evil adheres to it, let us by no means concede that anything is corrupted. **GLAUCON.** But surely no one will ever show that the souls of the dying become more unjust because of death. **SOCRATES.** If anyone should dare to object to us that he who dies becomes worse and more unjust—lest he be forced to confess that souls are immortal—we shall say that if he speaks the truth, then injustice is lethal to the unjust man, just like a disease; and by this very thing which kills by its own nature, those who receive it are destroyed: those more so more quickly, and those less so more slowly. It would not happen as it does now, where the unjust only die because of their injustice when others inflict punishments upon them. **GLAUCON.** By Jove, injustice will not seem to be such a very heavy evil if it is lethal to the wicked man. For it would be a liberation from evils. But I think, on the contrary, it is entirely otherwise: that it kills others to the best of its power, but makes the man who possesses it very much alive, and especially wakeful; so far is it from being lethal. **SOCRATES.** You speak skillfully. For when its own particular depravity and its own evil cannot destroy the soul, an evil arising from the destruction of another and directed toward something else will never dissolve either the soul or anything else beyond that to which it specifically happens. **GLAUCON.** Never, as is probable. **SOCRATES.** Since it is destroyed by no evil at all, whether its own or another's, it is clear that it must necessarily always exist. And if it always exists, it exists as immortal. **GLAUCON.** Necessarily. **SOCRATES.** Let this, therefore, be so. And if it is so, you will observe that these same souls will always exist. For they will never become fewer, since none at all perish. Nor, again, will they become more. For if anything among the immortals were to increase, it would be from the mortal, and eventually all things would be immortal. **GLAUCON.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** But indeed we do not think this at all, for reason forbids it. Nor, again, do we believe the soul in its truest nature to be such that it is varied, dissimilar, and differing within itself. **GLAUCON.** How do you mean? **SOCRATES.** It is not easy for that which is composed of many parts to be eternal, unless it has obtained the finest composition, as the soul has now appeared to us. **GLAUCON.** That is consistent. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, both the present reasoning and others can compel the conclusion that the soul is immortal. But if one truly desires to see what it is like in reality, one must not look at it polluted by its association with the body and other evils, as we see it now; but one must diligently discern with reason what it is like when it is pure. Then it will certainly appear much more beautiful; and when it is such, it will judge more clearly what is just and what is not, and the other things we have spoken of above. Now, indeed, we have spoken the truth about it as it appears in the present. But we have looked at it no differently than those who look upon the marine Glaucus <note>A mythological fisherman who became a sea-god; his body was encrusted with shells and seaweed, hiding his true form.</note>. For they cannot easily contemplate the ancient nature of Glaucus, because the ancient parts of his body are partly broken, partly worn away, and utterly scattered by the waves; and other things have grown onto him—shells, seaweed, and stones—so that he bears the image of a beast more than his original nature. So too do we always see the soul polluted by innumerable evils. But indeed, Glaucon, one must turn one's eyes there. **GLAUCON.** To where? **SOCRATES.** To its philosophy, I say; and one must observe what things the soul touches, and with what things it seeks to enter into fellowship and strives for, inasmuch as it is kindred to the divine, the immortal, and the eternal. And what it would become if it followed such a nature entirely, being led by this affection and effort out of the sea in which it is presently submerged; emerging naked and shaking off the rocks and oysters which now, as if from earthly nourishment, cling to it in great number—earthy, stony, and wild—because of that "sustenance" which many think blessed. Then at last we shall contemplate the true nature of the soul itself, and we shall recognize whether it is multiform or simple, or what its whole condition is. But now, I think, we have sufficiently declared the affections and forms of the soul in human life. **GLAUCON.** Entirely so. **SOCRATES.** Have we not set aside the other things we explained in this discussion? We have by no means brought in its rewards and honors, as you said Homer and Hesiod did, but we have found that justice itself is the best reward for the soul itself; and we have shown that one must act justly, whether one has the Ring of Gyges <note>A mythical ring that granted invisibility, used as a thought experiment regarding whether a person would stay just if they could never be caught.</note> or even the Helmet of Pluto <note>Also known as the Cap of Invisibility.</note>. **GLAUCON.** You speak the truth. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, now besides these things, no ill-will prevents us from attributing to justice and all virtue those rewards which are provided for the soul by both men and gods, both while the man is living and when he is dead. **GLAUCON.** Greatly so. **SOCRATES.** Will you therefore restore to me what you borrowed in the conversation? **GLAUCON.** What in particular? **SOCRATES.** I granted to you that the just man might seem unjust, and the unjust man just. For you had asked that, even if it were impossible for these things to be hidden from men and gods, it should nevertheless be conceded for the sake of the discussion, so that justice itself might be judged compared to injustice itself. Do you not remember? **GLAUCON.** How could I not remember? **SOCRATES.** Since they have been judged, I demand from you in turn that it be explained what reward justice receives from gods and men: so that it may also carry off the palm <note>The prize of victory.</note> from reputation and manifest esteem, with which justice honors those who participate in it; since it has clearly been seen to confer benefits by its very presence, and not to deceive those who truly possess it. **GLAUCON.** You demand what is owed. **SOCRATES.** First, then, you will grant me this: that it is not hidden from the gods what sort of person each of them is—namely, the just and the unjust. **GLAUCON.** We shall grant it. **SOCRATES.** If it is not hidden from the gods, one will be loved by God, and the other hated, as we confessed in the beginning. **GLAUCON.** It is so. **SOCRATES.** To the friend of the gods, all things are granted by the gods as best as can be, unless some evil from a prior fault necessarily hangs over him. **GLAUCON.** Entirely. **SOCRATES.** Thus it must be thought of the just man: whether he be in poverty, or diseases, or any other of those things that seem to be evils, these things will eventually lead to some good for him, either while living or dead. For he is never neglected by the gods, whoever wishes to strive to become just...

<summary>Socrates argues for the immortality of the soul by demonstrating that if its own internal vice (injustice) cannot destroy it, then no external force can. He concludes by shifting the discussion toward the actual rewards and reputation that justice earns from both gods and men.</summary>

# DIALOGUE 10. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.
## I

and through the duties of virtue, as far as is divinely permitted, to become like God. **GLAUCON.** It is fitting that such a man should not be looked down upon by his Like <note>i.e., by the Divine</note>. **SOCRATES.** But regarding the unjust man, must we not think the exact opposite? **GLAUCON.** Most certainly. **SOCRATES.** Therefore, in the eyes of the gods, this prize shall be given to the just man. **GLAUCON.** So I believe. **SOCRATES.** But among men, does it not happen thus, if we must speak the truth? Clever but wicked men act just like those runners who run well from the starting line but poorly at the finish. For at first they leap out quickly, but in the end they are mocked; they depart with their ears hanging low and without a crown. But the true runners reach the finish, receive the prize, and are crowned. The same thing, for the most part, happens to just men. Indeed, at the end of every action, social interaction, and life itself, they are esteemed and receive rewards from men. **GLAUCON.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** Will you tolerate it if I apply to these men what you said of the unjust? I shall speak indeed. For when the just reach a mature age, they hold offices in the city <margin>On the end of just and unjust men</margin> at their own choice; they enter into marriages with whomever they wish, both giving and receiving in turn. In short, whatever you affirmed of the unjust, I now affirm of the just. Conversely, I assert this of unjust men: even if most of them hide their vices for a time, they are caught at the end of the race and shown for what they are. They become utterly ridiculous, and in their old age, they are wretchedly rebuked by both foreigners and citizens. They are beaten and suffer all those things which you truly said were harsh—for they shall be racked and burned. Imagine you are hearing from me everything you yourself recounted. But as I was saying, see if you can tolerate these things. **GLAUCON.** I shall certainly endure it, for you speak what is proper. **SOCRATES.** These, then, are the prizes, wages, and gifts which are granted to the just man by gods and men, in addition to those goods which justice itself contains within. **GLAUCON.** These are truly excellent and enduring. **SOCRATES.** Yet these are nothing in number or magnitude if compared to those things which await both after death. These things must also be heard, so that everything that pertains to both may be fully understood. **GLAUCON.** Speak then—not as if you have already said too much, but as to one who will listen most gladly. **SOCRATES.** I shall relate to you not a "Tale of Alcinous" <note>original: "Alcyni apologum"; a reference to a long-winded story from the Odyssey</note>, but the account of a most excellent man, Er, the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth. He died in battle, and when the bodies were taken up ten days later, already decayed, he was found whole with an uncorrupted body and carried home for the funeral rites. There, on the twelfth day after his death, while he was placed upon the pyre, he revived and recounted what he had seen in the meantime. He said that after his soul had been separated from his body, it traveled with many others to a certain demonic place. There he saw two openings in the earth, and two others opposite them above in the region of heaven. Between these openings sat judges. After they judged the souls, they commanded the just to ascend to the right, upward through heaven, hanging signs upon their fronts of the judgments passed. The unjust, conversely, they ordered to the left and downward, bearing behind their backs the signs of everything they had done in life. When he himself approached the judges, they told him that he must be a messenger to men concerning the things he saw there, and they commanded him to listen and observe diligently whatever happened in those places. He saw there, through each gate of heaven and earth, souls departing; through the other two, he saw souls ascending from the earth, covered in dust, filth, and leanness, while other bright souls descended from heaven. He said the souls arriving from every side seemed as if exhausted by a long journey; they lay down gladly in the meadow there as if in a great assembly. Those who were known to one another greeted each other, and all of them—both those from the earth and those from heaven—questioned one another about what they had seen in their respective places. They answered each other in turn: some grieving and weeping at the memory of the evils they had endured and seen on their journey under the earth (which he said was a journey of a thousand years), while those who descended from heaven told of delights and sights of immense beauty. To recount all these things, Glaucon, would take a very long narrative. But he said the sum of it was this: for whatever wrongs anyone had committed, they paid the penalty ten times over for each—that is, once for every hundred years (this being the span of a human life), so that the soul might pay a tenfold restitution for its injustices. Thus, if any were responsible for many deaths, or betrayed cities and armies, or cast men into slavery, or were accomplices in any other atrocity or crime, they paid tenfold penalties for each deed. Likewise, if any had bestowed benefits and practiced justice and piety, they received rewards in the same proportion. Regarding those who died immediately after birth or lived only a short time, he recounted things hardly worth remembering. But concerning piety or impiety toward gods and parents, and concerning murderers who polluted their hands with slaughter, he said they were affected by even greater rewards and punishments. For he said he was present when someone asked another where "Ardiaeus the Great" was. This man had been a tyrant in a certain city of Pamphylia a thousand years before; he had killed his aged father and elder brother and committed many other impious crimes. He said the one questioned replied: "Ardiaeus has not come, nor will he come." O, what a terrible sight! For as we were about to exit through the opening, having endured all else, we suddenly saw him and others with him, almost all of them tyrants (though there were also some private individuals who had committed great crimes). When they were confident they were about to ascend, the opening would not permit them, but gave a horrific roar whenever anyone attempted to exit who was either incurable or not yet purified. There were fierce men there, fiery in appearance, who, when they heard the roar, seized them—Ardiaeus and those like him—and binding their hands, feet, and necks, they threw them down...

<summary>Socrates concludes the argument for justice by describing the earthly rewards of the just and begins the "Myth of Er," a vision of the afterlife where souls are judged and punished or rewarded tenfold for their deeds.</summary>

# BOOK TEN.
### PAGE XXXI.

...and he tormented them, and having dragged them aside toward an outer path, he mangled them upon thorns: indicating to those passing by the reason why they suffered such things: that they were being carried away to be cast into Tartarus <note>The deepest abyss of the underworld in Greek mythology</note>. Where, although many and various things terrified them, this fear vexed them most vehemently: when a bellowing sound arose during the ascent; but when it was silent, each soul ascended most gladly. And indeed, he recounted punishments and penalties of this kind, and conversely, benefits of the same sort. 

But when those souls mentioned above had rested seven days in the meadow, he said it was necessary for them to rise on the eighth day and depart from there; and finally on the fourth day to arrive at a certain place from where a light is seen extended from above through the whole of heaven and earth like a standing column, most similar to a rainbow, yet clearer and purer. Into this they proceeded after a day's journey; and they saw there in the middle of the light the extremities of the celestial bonds extended from heaven. For that light is the bond of heaven: just as the under-girding of triremes <note>Ancient warships; the "under-girding" refers to ropes used to reinforce the hull</note>, and thus the entire circumference is held together. 

From the extremities, however, is suspended the Spindle of Necessity <note>A cosmic model representing the rotation of the celestial spheres</note>, through which all the circuits are completed. Its shaft and point are of adamant <note>An unbreakable, diamond-like legendary metal</note>; but the whorl is mixed from this and other kinds. Its nature is of such a kind in its shape as is seen among us. It must be understood from his speech, however, as if in one large and hollow whorl, carved throughout, another smaller and similar one lies inserted: fitting together just like jars that are inserted into one another; and thus a third and a fourth, and four others. For there are eight whorls in total, circles inserted into one another, showing their rims at the top, but forming the continuous back of a single whorl around the shaft. 

That shaft is driven through the middle of the eighth and through the whole. The first and outermost whorl has the widest circle of the rim. The sixth is second. The third is fourth. The fourth is eighth. The fifth is seventh. The fifth is sixth. The third is seventh. The eighth is second. <note>This describes the relative widths of the planetary spheres' rims</note>. Likewise, the circle of the first and greatest is variegated. The seventh is the brightest. The circle of the eighth whorl receives its color from the seventh shining upon it. The second and fifth are similar to each other, somewhat yellower than those. The third possesses the whitest color. The fourth is reddish. The second surpasses the sixth in whiteness. 

And the whole spindle is turned by the rotation of the thread; but while the whole revolves, the seven interior circles are turned more slowly by a motion contrary to the whole. Of these, clearly the eighth is driven with the swiftest motion. The second ones follow one another: the seventh, the sixth, and the fifth. The third is carried with such a motion that it seems to revolve with the fourth. The fourth with the third, and the fifth with the second. The spindle is turned in the lap of Necessity. 

Above each circle sits a Siren, carried along with the sphere, emitting a single voice, namely a single tone. Yet one harmony <note>The "Music of the Spheres"</note> sounds forth from all eight. Furthermore, the three daughters of Necessity sit on thrones at equal intervals from one another, the Fates in white robes with crowned heads: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos. They sing to the harmony: Lachesis of the past, Clotho of the present, and Atropos of the future. And Clotho, together with her mother, with a certain intermission of time, turns the outermost circumference of the spindle, touching it with her right hand. Atropos with her left hand turns the inner ones similarly. Finally, Lachesis touches both from either side with each hand. 

<margin>
Concerning the three daughters of Necessity: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos.
</margin>

Therefore, when the souls arrived there, it was necessary to approach Lachesis immediately. There, a certain prophet first arranges them each in order; afterward, when he has taken the lots and the models of lives from the knees of Lachesis, ascending a high platform, he speaks thus: "The word of the virgin Lachesis, daughter of Necessity: O souls of a day, this is the beginning of another circuit of a mortal and death-bringing race; a divinity <note>original: "daemon" — a guiding spirit or destiny</note> will not choose you by lot, but you shall rather choose your divinity. Let him who draws the first lot first choose a life, to which he shall be bound by necessity. But virtue is inviolable and free. As each honors or neglects her, so shall he possess more or less of her. All blame belongs to the chooser; God is without blame." 

<margin>
God is without blame.
</margin>

Having spoken these things, he pours the lots over them, from which each snatches up that which falls near him. Nor is it permitted for anyone to know what his place in the order is until he has taken it. For only then does he understand what number he has drawn. After this, he likewise displays the models of lives before them on the floor: many more than are present here. He asserted that the lives of men and of all animals were of every form. For tyrannies existed among them: some perpetual, some for a time, which collapsed in the middle of their span, falling into poverty, exile, and want. There existed also the lives of famous men, some outstanding in appearance, beauty, strength, and contests; others for the nobility of their ancestors; and likewise for the ignoble. And for women in the same way. 

But the character and condition of the soul was not included, because it is necessary that by choosing another life, it becomes of another condition. But other things were mixed with one another: some with riches and poverty, some with disease or health, and some held a middle ground between these. Here indeed, O Glaucon, lies the whole danger for man. Wherefore every effort must be given to this study: that each of us, omitting other disciplines, may seek and pursue this discipline according to his strength: through which he may be both able and know how to discern a good life from a bad one, and to choose the better from all as far as possible; observing all that we have now said, what things joined together or disjoined lead to a virtuous life. 

Furthermore, let him understand what beauty joined with poverty or riches—and with what habit of the soul—works evil or good; what nobility or ignobility, private life and power, strength and weakness, a quick wit and a slow one, and other such things which are by nature around the soul, or which are acquired, do when coupled together. So that from all these he may be able to consider the nature of each thing with respect to the nature of the soul, and discern the better life from the worse: calling that the worse which makes the soul more unjust, and the better that which makes it more just. But the rest...

# DIALOGUE X. ON THE REPUBLIC, OR ON JUSTICE.
-> I ii <-

<note>original: "contemnat"</note> ...should despise. For we have seen that both for the living and the dead, this choice is the best. Therefore, with this opinion, firm and fixed like a diamond, one must depart to the underworld, so that there he is not dazzled by riches and such evils; nor, by falling into tyrannies and other such actions, should he perpetrate many and incurable crimes, and in turn suffer even worse himself. Rather, let him know how to always choose the middle life among all these, leaving behind the extremes, both in this life and in the future. In this way, each man becomes most blessed. Indeed, the messenger who returned from there reported that the Prophet <note>The "Prophet" or spokesman of Lachesis</note> said: that even for the one who comes last, if he chooses with wisdom, there lies a desirable life, not an evil one, for him who lives with diligence. Let not the first choose carelessly, nor the last despair because of his place. When he had said this, he said that the one who by chance had received the first lot immediately ran and chose the greatest tyranny; and because of ignorance and greed, he had not sufficiently examined the details beforehand. Thus it escaped his notice that it was decreed by fate in that life that he would devour his own children and endure many other evils. But after he had considered the chosen life at leisure, he wailed and lamented the harmful choice, not observing what the Prophet had foretold; nor did he blame himself as the cause of his misfortunes, but rather fortune, the demons, and everything else rather than himself. He was one of those who had descended from heaven; he had lived his previous life in a well-ordered city and had practiced virtue by habit, without the study of philosophy. No fewer of those who fall from above are deceived in their choosing than others, being, as it were, unacquainted with hardships. But of those who came from the earth, many, because they themselves had labored through calamities and had seen others laboring, did not choose their lives rashly. For this reason, and also because of the luck of the lot, a change of good and evil happens to many souls. Furthermore, if anyone, whenever he comes into this life, philosophizes sincerely, and the lot of choice does not fall to him last, it appears from what is reported from there that he will not only be happy here, but his passage from here to there, and his return back here again, will not be earthly and rough, but smooth and heavenly. He said this was a spectacle worthy of consideration: how the individual souls chose their individual lives. For it was piteous, ridiculous, and wonderful to see. The choice was made, for the most part, according to the habit of the former life. For he said he saw the soul which had once been that of Orpheus choosing the life of a Swan out of hatred for the female sex; for he was unwilling to be born of women, by whom he had been killed. He saw the soul of Thamyris <note>A legendary Thracian singer</note> choosing the life of a nightingale; he also saw a Swan turned to the choice of a human life, and other musical animals likewise, as is fitting. One of the brave souls chose the life of a lion; this, he said, was Ajax the son of Telamon, who avoided becoming a man because he remembered the judgment of the arms <note>The contest for Achilles' armor, which Ajax lost</note> once given. After him, the soul of Agamemnon, because of his sufferings and out of hatred for the human race, took up the life of an eagle. The soul of Atalanta, to whom a middle lot had fallen, seeing the great honors a male athlete receives, said she could not restrain herself from choosing the life of an athlete. Then the soul of Epeus the Panopean <note>The builder of the Trojan Horse</note> passed into the nature of a craftswoman. Far among the last, the soul of the ridiculous Thersites <note>A low-ranking, ugly soldier in the Iliad</note> put on the form of an ape. By chance, the soul of Ulysses happened to have the very last lot. Therefore, he said, he came forward to choose last. Remembering his past labors and ceasing from ambition, he went around for a long time before choosing, seeking the life of a private man who minds his own business. He found it at last lying somewhere, neglected by the others; and he said he would not have chosen any other life even if he had received the first lot. Therefore, he embraced that life gladly. He asserted that souls also pass from other wild beasts into men, and change into one another: the unjust into savage beasts, and the just into the lives of gentle animals; and all are mixed in this manner. When all the souls had chosen their lives in order, as the lot had given, he saw them approach Lachesis in a long line. To each, Lachesis assigned the demon <note>A guardian spirit or 'daimon'</note> they had received as the guardian of their life and the executor of the chosen works. This demon first leads the soul to Clotho, and under her hand and the revolution of the whirling spindle, he ratifies the fate the soul had chosen by lot. When he has touched her, he immediately leads the soul to the spinning of Atropos, making the threads unalterable. From there, they quickly go to the throne of Necessity; and when all have passed through it, they proceed under a vehement heat and scorching glow to the Plain of Lethe <note>The Plain of Forgetfulness</note>, which is utterly destitute of trees and everything that grows from the earth. They camped, therefore, as night approached, by the River Amelita <margin>The River Amelita</margin>, whose water no vessel can hold. It is necessary for everyone to drink a certain amount of this water. But those who are not guided by wisdom drink more than is proper. And he who drinks always forgets all things. When they had slept until midnight, suddenly there was thunder and an earthquake, and they were suddenly driven upward, one this way and another that, to their birth, springing up like stars. He himself, however, said he was forbidden to drink from the river. How he returned to his body, he did not know; but suddenly, looking around at dawn, he said he saw himself lying upon the funeral pyre. And so, O Glaucon, the story was saved and did not perish; and it will save us likewise, if we obey it: and we shall cross the Lethe, that is, the river of forgetfulness, well, and we shall not infect our soul with any stain. Wherefore, if we listen to my words, believing the soul to be immortal and capable of enduring all evils and all goods, we shall always follow the road leading upward, and we shall practice justice with wisdom by every means. Thus we shall be dear to ourselves and to the gods, while we lead this life; and after we have carried off the prizes of virtue, as if having achieved victory and triumphs, both here and in the thousand-year journey which we have described, we may fare happily.

It ends with a moral exhortation to Glaucon to pursue justice and wisdom to ensure a favorable journey in both this life and the afterlife.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the "Compendium on the Timaeus" by Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century scholar who revived Platonic philosophy. It serves as an introduction to Plato's dialogue on the origin of the universe.</meta>

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS.

### COMPENDIUM BY MARSILIO FICINO ON THE TIMAEUS, CONCERNING THE SUBJECT OF THE BOOK. CHAPTER I.

JUST AS in the *Parmenides* <note>Plato's dialogue on the "One" and the nature of being.</note> he encompasses all the divine kinds by his powers of invention, so in the *Timaeus* he embraces natural things. In both, he is profoundly Pythagorean, disputing under a Pythagorean persona. In the *Parmenides*, indeed, he imitates Parmenides and Zeno the Eleatics, who were Pythagoreans and wrote on divine matters. In the *Timaeus*, however, he follows Timaeus of Locri, a Pythagorean who composed a book on the nature of the universe. Yet he does this in such a way that he adds not only eloquence to these men, but mysteries. Since divine things are the principles and models of natural things, while natural things are the effects and images of the divine, for that reason, even in the *Parmenides* while he deals with divine matters, he occasionally descends to the natural; and in the *Timaeus*, while treating nature, he rises more often into the divine. Nor does he wrongly couple divinity and nature together. For nature is the instrument of divinity. And so he either treats natural things divinely, as Aristotle does, or he treats divine things naturally. He also intersperses mathematics as a middle ground between both—that is, between the divine and the natural. For these signify divine things through numbers, but natural things through measures. Let the subject of this book, therefore, be the very nature of the universe: that is, a certain seminal and life-giving power infused into the whole world, subject indeed to the World Soul, but presiding over matter, bringing forth individual things in the same order in which the Soul itself conceived them, looking up to the divine mind as much as it desires the Good.

### On the Order of the Book and its Parts. Chapter II.

It will be clear, moreover, that the nature of the universe and the universe itself do not consist of themselves, but depend on a superior and divine cause. It will be clear, furthermore, into how many grades nature is distributed: celestial, elemental, simple, composite, rational, and those lacking reason. It will be clear that the entire generation beneath the moon is referred to the rational animal <note>i.e., Mankind.</note> as if to its end and home. Many things, besides, will be treated concerning this very animal, looking both to the soul and to the body. Many things also concerning those matters which are composed by nature below the rational animal. And to speak briefly, he will treat of a triple world: namely, the divine, the celestial, and the human. He will also show that of all things composed in the world, and of the world itself, there are two principal intrinsic elements: namely, matter and form; but there are three extrinsic principles: namely, the efficient cause of the world, the exemplary cause, and the final cause. The efficient cause is divine power, intelligence, and will; the Exemplary cause is the Ideas conceived by the divine intelligence; and finally, the Final cause is the Good.

### On the Introduction to the Dialogue. Chapter III.

But to come to the very arrangement of the dialogue, Plato had destined five continuous days for discussions. On the first day, Socrates disputed in the Piraeus <note>The port of Athens.</note> with Polemarchus, Glaucon, Adeimantus, and Thrasymachus the Sophist concerning the Republic. On the second day, in the city, he recounted the same to Timaeus, Critias, and Hermocrates, and to a certain fourth unnamed stranger, perhaps a companion of Timaeus. On the third day, they make an epilogue of these things. With this introduction having been made, Timaeus immediately disputed concerning nature, in the presence of the three: Socrates, Critias, and Hermocrates. For the fourth person, who was present for the second narration without a name, is now absent from the third; for it is not for just anyone to be present at more secret matters. On the fourth day, Critias held his discourse. Finally, the fifth day has not yet dawned. Quite fittingly, after both the arrangement and the epilogue of the divine republic among men, he approached the celestial republic in the *Timaeus*—the model of this one—composed by God himself; then he moved to the antiquity of the world and the human race, and the wondrous deeds strenuously performed by the ancients.

### Allegory of the history which is narrated in the prologue. Chapter IIII.

He narrates, moreover, among the beginnings of this dialogue, a history of a war once waged between the Athenians and the Atlanteans. Crantor, the first interpreter of Plato, takes this as a bare history without allegory. Certain others, on the contrary, take it as only an allegory. But the most esteemed of the Platonists refute these; they affirm it is a history because Plato said: "The speech to come is very wonderful, but entirely true." Furthermore, they think an allegorical sense should be applied to Plato, who never does anything at random. They think that war between the Athenians and the Atlanteans presents an image of all the oppositions that exist in the universe. For war—that is, opposition—is the father of all things according to Heraclitus. Amelius brings forward the opposition between the firmament and the planets, especially since in the *Critias* it is said the Atlantic island was divided into seven circles. Origen, however, sees the opposition of the superior demons to the inferior ones, and the victory; the former exceeding in power, the latter in number. Numenius sees the tension of excellent souls following Pallas <note>Athena.</note> against other souls following generation under Neptune. Porphyry sees the fight between demons leading souls into generation, and souls striving for the things above. He distinguishes demons in a threefold way: some are divine; others are according to a certain disposition, whose number particular souls fill when they happen upon a demonic state; others are evil and harmful to souls. These lowest demons always conflict with souls in their ascent and descent; especially the western demons, for that region is assigned by the Egyptians to harmful demons. Hence Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus add to these the opposition itself flourishing perpetually in all things, between the One and the Multitude; Limit and Infinity; the Same and the Other; Rest and Motion; from which all things are composed under the former. Likewise, Being, either through itself or not through itself. Again, essence either incorporeal or corporeal, and the incorporeal indeed either not of...
