...inclines toward bodies, or declines. Indeed, bodies are either non-perishing like the celestial, or perishing like the elemental. Finally, in the heavens there are motions opposite to one another and diverse powers. But beneath the heavens, there are qualities repugnant to one another. In short, the discrepancy of these things is signified by that ancient war <note>A reference to the war between Atlantis and Athens mentioned in the Timaeus</note>: and everywhere the superior things are signified by the Athenians, and the inferior things by the Westerners. Indeed, an allegory of this kind is not moderately suited to the discussion of the Timaeus. It is also confirmed by those things which we comment upon in the *Critias*.

### Cap. V.
->The Fall of Phaethon. Floods. Conflagrations. A Description of Minerva.<-

Here again I admonish you to remember that the nine thousand years are computed by Eudoxus <note>Eudoxus of Cnidus, an ancient Greek astronomer</note> as nine thousand months. Likewise, that Phaethon, the son of the Sun, having been struck by lightning, burned the earth, signifies among some that a vast comet of a solar nature, finally dissolved, stirred up intolerable heats. Perhaps also the conflagrations which Moses <note>original: "Moyses"</note> narrates were sent by divinity. But when he comes to the floods, remember that fire is indeed the most effective of all things: but water is more effective than earth, and less passive than air. Likewise, fire divides powerfully and penetrates: water strikes violently from every side. Therefore, through these two elements, vaster calamities happen. Add also the final cause: because namely through the exit made by these two, a greater good follows, that is, a more fruitful reign of things, than through the pests of the air or the openings of the earth. Therefore, providence uses these two especially for the most ample destruction. To which the celestial wheels rightly obey from there: so that at whatever intervals of time God ordained there would be destruction, or rather reformation, at those same times all the planets rightly concur toward stars either fiery or watery, with the fixed stars also contributing to the same. Remember furthermore that Neptune signifies natural providence, but Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva</note> signifies intellectual providence: and this same Pallas is described by the Platonists as the divinity who wisely and powerfully both adorns celestial things and builds those things which happen beneath the heavens: presiding among the stars especially over Aries: and the leader of the equinoctial circle: where they think the moving power of the universe flourishes most. You shall commit to memory the golden epigram which Proclus read in the histories of the Egyptians inscribed in the temples of Minerva: "I am what is, what will be, and what has been. No one has revealed my veil. The fruit which I have brought forth is the born sun."

### Cap. VI.
->Most select precepts concerning Vows and prayers.<-

<margin>Porphyry</margin>
But where Plato comes to the point of suppliantly adoring God: hear Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher and student of Plotinus</note> thus approving divine supplications. Since God provides for us, and our affairs could be otherwise, certainly we adore usefully for the benefit of our affairs: namely if we are good. For thus, having been made like unto God, we shall be joined more closely. In which conjunction, indeed, the whole force of adoration consists. For since we are children of God: but separated from him as if in exile and prison: it is fitting to adore suppliantly, so that having been liberated from here we may return to the Father. Otherwise, we shall be like those who are deprived of the protection of parents. Certainly, since we are parts of the universe, we undoubtedly need the universe. For the conversion itself toward the whole provides safety to the parts. Therefore, whether you follow virtue, you must adore Him who contains all virtue. For to love the Good itself will be the cause for you of that good which is expedient for you. Or if you desire a bodily good, there exists in the universe a power containing all bodies. From there, therefore, it is necessary that safety comes to whatever parts. Indeed, we have found that all the most excellent men of wisdom among all nations have brooded especially over divine vows: particularly the Brahmans <note>original: "Brachmanas"</note> of the Indians: the Magi of the Persians: the theologians of the Greeks: but the Chaldeans adored something else. For calling the very power of the superiors "God," they venerated it by this one name. These are the words of Porphyry. After him, let us hear his disciple, the divine Iamblichus, approved in this matter especially by Proclus. All things are from God in such a way that nowhere are even the smallest things deserted by God. For everywhere divine unity flourishes: through which each thing consists: and by a certain perpetual and intimate circle they revolve wonderfully back to God himself from whom and in whom they are. Otherwise, they would suddenly fall into nothingness. From divine unity all things proceed: and they retain a certain unity impressed upon them as they proceed, an image of the divine unity: which both recalls them into it, and perfects them once recalled. This very thing snatches souls toward vows, by which union with God may be fully accomplished in us. Because if nature, flowing from God, inserted certain properties into certain things corresponding with the superiors, through which they turn themselves in a certain way toward the superiors, as the sunflower <note>original: "heliotropium" implied by "solaria"</note> to the sun, and lunar things to the moon, much more did the Father of souls impress upon them powers snatching them toward himself. Which indeed seem situated primarily in a certain divine unity in the superior intellect, as well as in the intellectual reflection itself. But may suppliant adoration, having arisen here, absolutely consume our restitution into God: drawing divine beneficence into us by a natural congruity: coupling the adorers with the adored: fitting the prayers of those vowing to the intelligence of the superiors: moving the will of those who embrace all goods in themselves, to impart goods to us according to our vow, the effecter of divine persuasion, stabilizing all our things in the firm stability of the superiors. Indeed, five principal things pertain to the perfection of a vow. The first is a certain notion of that which is to be adored, and by what reason it is to be worshipped. The second is a certain assimilation of our life to the divine life proceeding by purity, chastity, holiness, discipline, and order, and catching divine benevolence: and subjecting souls to divine bounty. The third is some contact: through which we almost now touch the divine essence: and we incline toward it with a certain summit of the soul. The fourth is a certain entrance into the vestibule of divine light. The fifth, finally, is union, intimately insinuating and connecting the soul's own unity to the divine unity: and now fusing one and the same action of the soul and of God: so much so that we are no longer of our own right: but are of God: overwhelmed and surrounded by divine splendor. Of this adoration, which must be done without intermission, the supreme end is this: namely, that it may join the conversion of the soul with its very remaining: and whatever proceeded from the divine unity, it may firmly restore again to the same unity.

## PAGE 275.

And may our light be surrounded by the light from above. Therefore, adoration alone restores souls to their rightful, blessed fatherland. Holiness alone is full virtue. Only the good man, as Plato writes in the *Laws*, prays to God properly and successfully. Only intimacy with the beings above makes men blessed. From this, the wicked are entirely alienated; like profane people, they are to be separated from vows and sacrifices. But the pure approach to prayer properly, leading with them three principal companions: **faith, truth, and love**, <note>Latin: *fidem veritatem, & charitatem*</note> hemmed in by which they may conceive a firm hope of good things, and being placed outside all other things and their very selves, they may plunge themselves entirely into the divine light. For he seeks God in vain who does not apply himself "alone to the alone," <note>A famous Neoplatonic formula for mystical union.</note> the immobile to the stable, and the simple to the most simple. For just as we cannot be joined to being through non-being, so we cannot be joined to unity through multitude, nor to stability through motion, nor to simplicity through mixture; rather, we fall back into the opposite. These are the views of Iamblichus and Proclus. To these, the great Theodore adds: if anyone explores the natures of things more diligently, he will find that not only souls and minds, but in a certain way all things—except the First—adore and offer vows.

### That the world has three causes above itself: and depends on an incorporeal cause. Chapter VII.

<margin>Chapter VII.</margin>
After these prayers have been performed, Timaeus, because he considers the world to be created, and therefore created by another, examines its triple cause. First, the efficient cause: that is, the divine mind; second, the exemplary cause: that is, the series of Ideas conceived in the divine mind; third, the final cause: that is, the Good. He judges that the world is from another because, even if it is most perfect according to its corporeal nature, it is nonetheless not entirely perfect according to absolute nature. Since, on account of matter, it suffers formlessness and deformity; on account of dimension, it undergoes a defect of power and awaits division if a divider approaches; on account of its composition, it is liable to dissolution; because of the repugnance of its parts, they contrive evil; because of motion, it displays indigence and suffers an admixture of privation; finally, because of its very assembly from diverse things, it requires a certain higher connector. He who is most perfect exists from himself; just as the world, because it is not most perfect, is known not to be from itself. Generally, all kinds of composite things are reduced to something that is not composite in that kind: just as dimensions are reduced to the point <note>Latin: *signum*</note>, which is not composed of dimensions; numbers to unity, which is not made of numbers; elements to that which is not mixed from elements; therefore, the entire order of beings is reduced to Being, which does not consist of beings. That, moreover, will be substance with no accidents mixed in. Therefore, it will be neither "how much" (quantity) nor "of what kind" (quality), but a total and impartible substance. Nor, because it is the only and most simple thing, will it have less than those things which undergo accidents beyond substance. For those things which are accidents in subsequent things must be substance in the highest; and indeed, the best substance. Truly, the more things you add to the "best," the further you force it to depart from "best-ness" itself. For if a quality is rejected there by a new admixture, you degenerate. Not only, therefore, does this world depend on a higher simplicity because it is entirely composite, but even if there is something higher that is still in some way composite, it depends on a higher simplicity. This simplicity stands even above eternity, from which an integral eternity is made in divine minds; a mixed eternity of time in rational souls; and a temporal everlastingness in the spheres of the world. In those things, however, which are made by the motion and power of the spheres, there is a certain portion of time. Therefore, those things which are thought of above the soul always *are*, and never *become*. The soul itself both *is* and *becomes* always. The world is indeed never, but *becomes* always. Those things which are generated in the world are also never, but *become* at some time. We say "to become" is to be carried through time. Since the world is driven by perpetual motion and time, it is judged to "become" always. Insofar as it "becomes," it is not yet; therefore it is said to "be" never, just as if an image of a mountain were continually made and restored in a torrent, always being drawn in the act of becoming, never consisting in being. The Platonists think this is the difference between the soul and the world: that the heaven "becomes" continuously not only by action, but also by essence. But the soul "becomes" by action, while by essence it rather *is* from God than *becomes* from God; and since its essence is impartible, it has a certain power of its own that is in a way self-productive, through which it brings forth its own life and motion within itself. The heaven, however, hangs from elsewhere on all sides. In short, just as from the same rock over a pond and a torrent, that which is in the pond *is* steadily, but in the torrent an image *becomes*; so the soul is continually recreated; thus both always depend on God, but in different ways. For from Him the soul always *is*, but the world always *becomes*. But let us begin again from another principle.

### The Good itself is the cause of all things more than the subsequent causes: nor has it any proportion with the rest. Chapter VIII.

<margin>Chapter VIII.</margin>
All Platonists confess without controversy that this universe has everything from the supreme God: action, power, and essence alike. For they receive this from Plato out of all his books. They also hear him confirming the same in his *Epistles*. Where indeed, with a great mystery, he referred third effects to a third cause, and second effects to a second; but all things to the one cause of all. Nor did he say that only the first effects are to be reduced to the first cause, lest by pronouncing only the first, we might suspect that they alone depend on God; nor, by naming Him the "first cause," might we suspect that He meets with other causes in a certain genus, or agrees with effects in some property of ordination. Therefore, he showed that all things proceed from Him; and that He, meanwhile, is entirely absolved from any communion with those things proceeding. And because of His absolute simplicity, he names Him "the One"; but because of His exuberant beneficence, through which He both acts as a principle by producing all things and as an end by perfecting and reducing them, he names Him "the Good." He thinks, moreover, that whatever things are made depend more on Him than on other causes. For He acts in any work both earlier, and longer, and more vehemently than the remaining causes; and the remaining causes, whatever they are, exist because He makes them; and whatever they do, they do under His guidance. To show that individual things emanate from Him more than from other causes, he repeated three times that He is the principle of all. He said: "All things are around the King of all." Likewise: "All things are for His sake." Again: "He is the cause of all," so that we might understand both that all things arise from there most of all, and that God is the maker, the exemplar, and the end of all. Hence He is the One, and—

<meta>This page continues the philosophical commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, specifically discussing the hierarchy of being and the relationship between the One (the Good) and the material world.</meta>

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS. 276.
<sig>I iiii</sig>

In the sixth book of the *Republic*, as well as in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*, Plato clearly demonstrates that the **Good** is above all essence and intellect, and is the cause of both. It is established, moreover, that the **One** and the **Good** are the same; otherwise, if they were different, we would be forced to admit two supreme principles. A principle must certainly be both most simple and most excellent. Nothing is simpler than simple Unity, nor better than Goodness. Neither is Unity better than Goodness, nor Goodness simpler than Unity. Therefore, both are one and the same supreme God. We have sufficiently confirmed in our *Theology* and elsewhere that this totality exists above essence and mind.

->**Chapter IX. On the dependence of Matter upon the Good itself; and on the action of the mind and soul upon matter; and on the intelligible world.**<-

From this very One-Good, which towers above all essence, Plato in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist* derives all the levels of things that have been brought forth: both those which truly exist (that is, the **separated forms** <note>The Platonic Ideas or Archetypes</note>) and those which do not truly exist (that is, the **forms inherent in matter**), and finally the lowest level of **matter**. This matter "truly exists" so little that it is closest to that which is imagined to "truly not be." This very matter, which in the *Parmenides* is derived from the Good itself at the final level of things, is treated in the *Timaeus* as if it were already brought into being and subjected to the Architect of the world for the completion of the worldly work. 

But is the God who is the author of the world the same as the one who effects matter? **Ammonius** <note>Ammonius Saccas, teacher of Plotinus</note> and the school of **Origen** would answer that they are the same. They argue that in the *Parmenides* it is discussed how matter receives its *being* from God, while in the *Timaeus* it is discussed by what reason it receives its *well-being* <note>original: "bene esse" - meaning its ordered, formed state</note>; for in a certain way, "being" is conceived of before "well-being." 

The common school of Platonists will answer differently: that the God who makes matter is not the same as the one who immediately forms it. Rather, matter exists from the **Supreme Good**; it is formed by the **Intellect**; and finally, it is moved by the **Soul**. Yet, in truth, all these things come from the First Principle: but *being* comes from the First alone. *Being formed* comes from the First through the Intellect; *being moved* (and being formed through motion) comes from the First through the Intellect and the Soul simultaneously. 

It is just as if we imagine a certain potter who makes the clay with his own hand, then forms the made clay by means of a wheel, and while forming it, distinguishes and shapes it with a certain wooden comb. No one would say the vessel was made by the comb and the wheel more than by the potter, even though it was made by the potter *through* the wheel and the comb. Similarly, they judge that this universe proceeds from the Good itself through a certain Divine Intellect and the Soul of the universe. Justly, the world is made most "one" by the One itself, and most "good" by the Good itself. 

But since this visible world—due to the manifold distance of its parts, the repugnance of its qualities, the diversity of its effects, and the deformity of its materials—is neither "most one" nor "most good," it is thought that before this world, another world emanates directly from the Divine Unity and Goodness. This world is most similar to its parent by nature: not visible, but **intelligible** and **intellectual**, containing the patterns <note>exemplaria</note> of all things that are produced in this world. This Divine Intellect he names not the Good itself, but the "most excellent son of the Good." If we understand this son to be of one substance with the Father, we shall better reconcile Plato with **Christian Theology**. But the other interpreters of Plato will protest.

->**Chapter X. Sun, light, radiance, brightness, heat, generation; similarly unity, goodness, intellect, soul, nature, the body of the world, the image of the higher worlds.**<-

Therefore, let the Christian and Mosaic truth remain. Meanwhile, if it pleases many of the interpreters, perhaps this was the opinion of either Plato or Pythagoras: that the **Intelligible World** is a medium between the visible world and the Good itself. It is an image of the Good, but a pattern for the corporeal world. It hangs from the Good just as light outside the sun hangs from the light within the sun. Furthermore, it produces from itself the **Soul of the World**, just as light pours forth brightness; through this Soul, individual things are generated daily, just as brightness produces corporeal things through heat. 

Therefore, just as these six levels are arranged in order: 
1. First, the substance of the sun itself. 
2. Second, the substantial and inward light. 
3. Third, the light emanating from there. 
4. Fourth, the brightness resulting from that light. 
5. Fifth, the heat kindled by the brightness. 
6. Sixth, the generation coalescing from the glow of the heat. 

So let the other six be arranged: 
1. First, **Unity**. 
2. Second, **Goodness**. These two are not different in reality, but are distinguished in a certain way by reason. For it is the same Divinity: it is called Unity because it towers above all things, and Goodness because it overflows through all things. Plato calls this power of overflowing the **Idea of the Good** in the sixth book of the *Republic*. 
3. In the third level is placed a certain **Divine Mind**, like light emanating from light, multiform and—so to speak—conceiving Ideas within itself by the nourishment of the simple supreme light and the Idea of the Divine One; not otherwise than how many rays are derived from a single ray of light. In this Mind, Ideas are not only contained as if in a fountain, but many "armies of minds" <note>angelic or intellectual hierarchies</note> are led back to it as their leader. This whole class is called the **Superior World**: regarding the minds that follow, it is the **Intellectual World**; regarding the leader, it is the **Intelligible World**. 
4. After this archetypal world, the fourth level follows: the **Soul of the Corporeal World**. This is the **Rational World**, begotten from the Intellectual World like brightness from light. And just as brightness is mixed with motion, so the Soul reaches and runs through the reasons of the immobile Ideas in a certain mobile fashion. 
5. The fifth level follows this: the **Nature of things**, the **Seminal World**, resulting from the Rational World of the soul like heat from brightness. 
6. Finally, in the sixth level, this **Corporeal World** is placed, led forth from the Seminal World just as the generation of things comes from heat. But if to the others...

It uses the analogy of the sun and its light to illustrate how different levels of reality (Intelligible, Intellectual, Rational, and Corporeal) relate to their divine source.</summary>

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS.

If you wish to more aptly compare the things omitted, you will imagine in a certain most wise architect a natural power and goodness. Second, a geometric and contemplative intellect, possessing the common ratios of measurements. Third, a reason—as they say—that is practical, already consulting the actual proportions of the craftsmanship. Fourth, the imagination, fashioning the figures and modes conducive to the work. Fifth, the affection <note>or disposition/desire</note>. Sixth, the power of movement. In such comparisons, you will see that effects are produced much more by the preceding factors than by the following ones.

Individual orders are reduced to individual heads; the universal order to a universal head, by whom all things are composed out of act and potency.

### Chapter XI.

Nor should it escape us that specific kinds of things must be referred to specific heads, and the universal genus to the universal head. For all the bodies of the world refer to one Body; all Natures to one Nature; Souls to a Soul; Minds to a Mind; and finally, good things to the Good. And because they are good, therefore they are all things. Thus, indeed, all things by a certain natural conversion desire the Good as their end, since they proceeded from the Good itself by a common procession as if from a principle; and to such an extent do all things desire it, that even the lowest matter desires it with a desire that is not the lowest. For in all things to be generated, it perpetually tends toward the likeness of the Good itself, so that it appears this matter depends upon the Good. I say it depends upon the Good rather than upon the Mind. For while the action of the Mind, which occurs through ideal forms, terminates at forms, the action of the Good—being the most ample—descends beyond forms even into matter, making it greedy for and capable of the Good. 

But what I now call "matter," Plato in the *Philebus* calls by the broader name of "infinity" <note>original: *infinitudinem*</note>, saying that the Good itself first gave birth to infinity and the limit <note>original: *terminum*</note>; and immediately mixed them in turn, and from this mixture composed all things: that is, from a certain formable potency and an approaching form. For he calls the formable potency "infinity," as if it were not yet defined or perfected by itself. But the form applied to this he names the "limit," which clearly, as a finite idea, defines the potency and perfects it into the desired species. From these two, therefore, they wish the intelligible world to be first forged by God, and the sensible world then constituted from the intelligible out of the same or similar elements. 

Thus, that proximate intellect, the architect of the visible world, received from the Good itself a matter that was in a sense spiritual, but already degenerating beneath it into the dimension of mass, formless and void; and if perhaps it moved by itself, it would waver without order. But through the order of ideas received from the same Good, he formed it and reduced it to order before it could wander out of order. Especially since he first infused into it a rational soul, the mistress of most orderly motion. He says not only that matter would be formless by itself, but that the soul also would be formless unless God formed both. What the corporeal species is in matter, reason and intelligence are in the soul; if the soul lacks these, it will move matter inordinately. To express this, he considered matter without form and an irrational soul, and saw that motion would proceed from there without order. Matter was not inordinate before the world in terms of time, but by a certain logic of order.

### Chapter XII.

From all this we can gather that matter is not equal to the maker of the world; it does not exist before the world by any interval of time, though it does by a certain origin and order. It was not tossed about inordinately before order, but would have wandered far from order, as far as is in itself, unless it had been immediately ordered from above. 

But lest anyone should disapprove of this mode of speaking in Plato—imagining matter tossed about inordinately before the world—let him hear Moses also, who, before the distinction of the world, says that the earth was empty and composite <note>original: *inane & incomposita*, referring to Genesis 1:2</note>, and that darkness existed over the face of the abyss. I pass over the poetic "Chaos" for the present. It is helpful to bring forward Philo the Jew, who explains the Genesis of Moses in similar words: "If anyone wishes to seek the cause why this universe was created, he will not err, in my judgment, if he thinks what one of the ancients offered: that the creator himself is good, both the parent and author of the universe; and by grace of his goodness he envied no substance, which by its own nature had nothing of good, yet could become all things." For its own nature was inordinate, formless, inanimate, entirely varied, incongruous, unrefined, inconstant; fit to be changed into opposites, and to receive the logic of the best things—namely of form, animation, likeness, congruity, and refinement; finally, of the better idea of all things. 

Likewise in the second volume of the same book: "When," he says, "the creator began to form the inordinate substance, confused by its own nature, into order from inordination, and into distinction from confusion, he fixed the earth and water in the middle place." Thus says Philo. Therefore, if you consider the six grades of things brought forward above, you will perhaps see how similar Plato is to Moses, who completed the genesis of the world in six days; and how similar to Pythagoras, who through the number six <note>the senary number</note> showed it to be entirely suited to genesis and "marriages." Whence he also calls it *Gamon* <note>Greek: *Gamos*, marriage</note>, because its parts placed together beget it and render the offspring similar to the parent.

### Chapter XII.
-> Twofold opinion on the origin of the world. <-

If anyone asks whether the world was eternal according to Plato: I respond, according to the interpreters Severus, Atticus, Plutarch, and many others as Proclus relates, that it was not always. But according to the interpreters Crantor, Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, Proclus, and most others: it has indeed always been, and has always been from God—or rather, flowed from Him. For they say God always is, but the world is always being made and flowing. And if you consider it as lacking a beginning in time, the World is said to be unbegotten; but if you consider its perpetual efflux from God, it is continually begotten.

and that it depends no less upon God if it has always depended and continues to depend, than if it began to depend at some point or were to cease. Just as light derives its origin no less from the sun, and serves the sun no less, if it has always flowed forth and continues to flow from the sun, than if it had only begun at some point.

### A triple conjecture of the Platonic opinion concerning the world: and what the certainty of the Platonic judgment is concerning the world. Chapter XIV.

Furthermore, in Platonic matters, we proceed either by conjecture or by knowledge. As far as conjecture is concerned, he speaks thus and his followers dispute in such a way that his opinion on the origin of the world can be gathered into three heads. For either he thought that **matter** was at some time created from nothing by God and simultaneously formed in time. Because in this work which is composed of matter, according to a certain order of production, matter itself would be thought of as being made before being formed: and that being matter comes before being formed: and before a work is made from matter, the matter from which the work was to be finished is usually sought. Or, that God did not produce a new matter at some time, but from eternity, and similarly adorned it: although it is imagined as unadorned before being adorned. Since by its own nature it lacks order, which it expects from another. And since any thing is first thought of according to what it is, rather than according to what it receives, it can rightly be thought of by itself, apart from order, as being in itself devoid of order. Or, as I said, that matter has always been from God: and continuously: but not continuously ordered, rather through intervals of time: so that it belongs to God to order stably, but to matter to be ordered moveably: and it receives the temporal tempering of its order no differently than a clock <note>original: "horologium"</note> receives it from a craftsman: and by certain intervals of time fixed by its nature, it loses its order gradually and finally entirely: and returns into **Chaos**: but God, suddenly unable to tolerate the extreme confusion, retempers it into its prior disposition with a single nod: and this happens infinitely in turn: God never being changed, while matter is infinitely reformed. Thus far has human conjecture proceeded in Platonic matters. 

But as far as we have knowledge, we affirm that our Plato affirmed that the **World** does not exist from itself: but from a cause: not from a fortuitous cause: but from a certain one: not from a natural cause alone: but an intellectual one: not from an intellect determined by the mode of nature: but rather a voluntary one: not by a will compelled by some natural instinct: but a free one. For nothing is more free than that which is through itself: and acts entirely through itself: nor yet by any contingent will. For nothing is contingent where will and necessity are the same. Again, nothing is violent where necessity and will are in turn the same. But so that he might disclose this, he repeated the name of divine **will** no less than that of **intelligence** in the fabrication of the world. And he added that the will of the good itself is the highest cause: and the most certain of causes. Which he shows to be free from the fact that he often says God, in the manner of an architect, consulted and deliberated concerning the work to be constructed. By which words he does not want God to be understood as wavering, but as freely choosing. Hence he says the mundane work did not proceed from God only once, but proceeds and is preserved continually. Furthermore, the supreme deities of the world, together with the world, would be dissoluble of themselves, unless they were ruled by the divine will. It shall be enough, therefore, and indeed the greatest thing, to have affirmed such things about the affirming philosopher. For these being granted, you will easily be able to say that when God provides and effects with a free will, He composed a world that is new without any novelty in Himself. And if you hear that it is not "at some time new," but rather produced from eternity: you will be able to preserve simultaneously the majesty of God, on whose will—and a free one at that—the world no less needs and depends if it needs and depends always, than if it had proceeded at some point. Since, however, Plato often says that one should assert concerning divine matters only so far as they are confirmed by divine oracles: we also ought to assent to the Sacred Scriptures rather than to our own conjectures.

### The World procreated for the sake of the Good according to the likeness of the divine Reason and the divine Word. Chapter XV.

He made the world, therefore, by His will, that is, by His goodness, as much voluntarily as naturally, overflowing on account of His immense fecundity. Which first indeed rejoices in itself: and because of that, it is then delighted by this image of itself: yet in such a way that it establishes the end of this delight not in this image, but in the exemplar itself, and the principle. Since, therefore, He made the world by goodness: for that reason He made it for the sake of the good. For He did not procreate it simply so that it might be, live, and understand: but so that it might both be well: and live well: and understand and acquire the good. This is very much in harmony with that Mosaic saying: *God saw this and that, that it was good: and all things were very good.* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:31</note> And because beauty is the splendor of goodness, he therefore adds that the most beautiful world was procreated by the best God: temporal indeed, but according to the image of the eternal exemplar. He will also say often, that as many intelligible and imitable species as there are in the **archetype**—that is, the principal world—so many forms of things has He disposed in this world: and thus made it similar to Himself: namely, because he understands that the **Ideas** of things do not consist among the clouds (as certain slanderers falsely claim) but in the mind of the mundane architect. But where he says that the Ideas are in life itself, he seems to prophesy that Gospel saying: *That which was made, in Him was life.* <note>John 1:3-4</note> And where he says and often finds the world established by divine providence: he confirms the whole of religion. Which indeed, when **Theophrastus** <note>A student of Aristotle and successor at the Lyceum</note> had observed it as something wonderful in a philosopher, he said: "Plato alone, or certainly the most of all, assigned the causes of things to divine providence." But O Theophrastus, with whatever mind you say that of Plato: without doubt you will confess that Plato alone, or most of all, is provident and divine.

### Why the World is one, and spherical: and moved in a sphere. Chapter XVI.

He shows next that the divine exemplar of the world itself—which the Evangelist, but with a more divine sense, calls the **Word** <note>original: "verbum"</note>—is unique: because since it contains all things, it leaves nothing outside...

## PAGE 377

himself: and therefore he is necessarily unique. But concerning this very matter, I have written more diffusely in the *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's *Platonic Theology*</note>. Since this world reflects the intelligible and divine world in other respects as far as possible—so much so that he who perceives the forms in this matter looks upon them as if beholding the divine countenance in a mirror—certainly it represents him in that very unity which effects and preserves all things, so that there is one work of one architect. Therefore, there is one world of one God. Indeed, if a human architect were able to dominate his material, after he had made several buildings (each of which was one in itself), he would eventually surround them all with one single enclosure. God, however, is entirely able to do this, since he is the master of matter. Nor is it permitted to dream of many worlds like balls, one outside the other. For in that way the divine work would be scattered, and there would be empty spaces between the worlds. You will think it more probable that if you imagine many orbs scattered through a vacuum, you should instead conceive of spheres within spheres, so that any given sphere is a world within a world. Thus the entire work becomes one and is mutually ordered; nothing is found to be either empty or devoid of order and union.

Let the shape of the world be spherical. For in this way it is most uniform, capacious, indestructible, and agile; and thus, and not otherwise, can mass be placed within mass without a vacuum, and be moved without collision—that is, if not squares are inserted into squares or circles, but orbs into orbs. Finally, the principal cause of this worldly sphere is that the nature of the divine world is also orbicular, reflecting back into itself by understanding and loving. The reason for the spherical motion is both the figure itself which receives the motion, and the internal revolution of the world-soul itself which moves through intellectual <term>species</term> <note>The formal patterns or "ideas" through which the soul perceives and acts.</note>.

### Why the world is divided either into five or six regions; and how the number seven and the circular number apply to it; and how it is distributed according to the likeness of the intelligible world. Chapter XVII.

For which reason, numbers are not unjustly applied to the worldly division, in which the primary roots of circular numbers are found: namely, five from the odd numbers, and six from the even. Let us say that the number twenty-five is multiplied from five in the manner of a circle, because in a certain way it returns from the same to the same, since five times five is computed as twenty-five. Likewise, by a similar circle, the number one hundred twenty-five; for five times twenty-five makes that total. The same logic of the circular six applies to thirty-six, and likewise to two hundred sixteen. For six times six fills out thirty-six. Likewise, six times thirty-six fills out two hundred sixteen. And if they call the higher numbers "square" or "oblong" by reason of their origin, they nevertheless call them "circular" by reason of their falling back and their end.

Therefore, by five and six, the primary roots of circular numbers, we divide the circular body of the world. First, indeed, into five parts: Celestial Fire, Ethereal Fire below the moon, Air, Water, and Earth. This division is indeed approved in the *Epinomis* <note>A dialogue attributed to Plato or his circle, acting as an appendix to the *Laws*.</note>. Next, we distribute it by six, where we divide the celestial fire into the non-wandering <note>The fixed stars</note> and the wandering <note>The planets</note>. This partition is used more frequently by Plato.

But we shall derive the distribution of the sensible world from the distribution of its own exemplar more conveniently in this Platonic manner. God indeed conceives in the world existing within his own intelligible self one power that is "formable" and another that is "form-giving." The former, as I have said, the Pythagoreans and Platonists call "Infinity"; the latter they call "Limit." He also conceives a mutual mixture of these powers, and understands that a certain third form immediately coalesces from this mixture. But he also notices this very form as if it were triple: for it has something of infinity, something of limit, and something of its own. Thus it happens that after the number two (of infinity and limit), the number three rises up immediately, the third form having been added. Let the number five also rise, with a form of this kind distributed in a threefold way. Finally, the number six is born when the office of that world is extended to produce lower things. The number seven is also born when that world, like an image, is referred back to the Father. In which seventh degree, as if on the seventh day, it may rest.

If indeed you render each thing to its counterpart, you will notice that this corporeal world has Fire as its form from the very "Limit" of the supernal world; but from "Infinity" it has Earth as its matter. From the middle form of that world, it has the "Moisture" <note>The fluid or connecting element</note> that reconciles fire and earth: which both glues together the earth (which is by its own nature dissipatable) and nourishes the fire (which is resolvable from its surface). This middle element possesses three things in itself: on one side something fiery, on the other something earthy, but in the middle something of its own, pure Air; since on one side it tends toward fire through the heights, and on the other it tends toward earth through the depths. After this "five-fold" of the world comes the "six-fold," if you conceive of the common form of all things. Again, the "seven-fold" occurs if you reform this very shape of the world according to the exemplar; in which seventh day it may rest.

### Why there are distinct parts in the world; and why they are contrary; and concerning the four elements. Chapter XVIII.

We see in the world not only a distinction of forms but also a repugnance <note>Opposition or conflict</note>. For it proceeds from the First, and in proceeding, it degenerates. The procession indeed creates distinction; the degeneration creates repugnance. Rather, the origin of the division itself is the fecundity of the Cause overflowing outward and propagating itself into the vastness. As the division proceeds through many steps, it finally arrives at repugnance—especially since the matter of the world, on account of its weakness, cannot reconcile forms to one another in the way that the higher world reconciles them within itself. Thus it happened that God extended matter by dimension, so that he might receive forms that would otherwise fight amongst themselves into different lodgings. Finally, since we say those things are "contrary" which are most distant within the same genus, and those things are "diverse" which are separated by their genera: from the fact that there are contraries in the world, it appears that every genus has species which...

very many: from the fact that they are diverse, it is established that the universe possesses very many kinds. Since indeed all species are reduced to genera, and genera to the universe and finally to its common form, he concludes that just as the higher world <note>The intelligible or divine realm</note> is uniform and all-forming, so this world is all-forming and uniform. Furthermore, the contrary quality and shape of the elements and the heavens contribute to the daily generation of new forms, with motion clearly assisting. For if there were only a single element, it would certainly generate nothing—which **Hippocrates** also asserts. Or if there were many elements similar to one another, it would produce nothing known—which **Heraclitus** proves. It is necessary, however, for this world to imitate the eternal action of the superior all-forming world to the best of its ability through the perpetual generation of new forms. Let there be, therefore, as the poetry of **Empedocles** sings, elements contrary to one another. Let there also be a medium between the contraries, since contraries are both most distant and, without a medium, least compatible. But this medium cannot be indivisible; otherwise, the contraries would not be distant through it. It therefore has dimension. But in the part where it touches one, it does not touch the other. And it must moreover have a middle part, through which it is equally distant from the extremes. For this reason, **Plato** always inserts at least two media between contraries, as appears evidently from his words. He even inserts a third where he says the medium has a power through which it preserves not only the union of the extremes but also its own. But let him clearly set down two—for we do not contend that now—as between fire and earth, there are two certain things: namely, Air and Water. That there must be at least two media between entirely contrary bodies, he shows from numbers and dimensions, which in a certain way precede natural bodies.

### Linear, Plane, and Solid Numbers. And why one medium suffices between planes, but does not satisfy between solids. And how Mathematical ratios are referred to Physical ones. Chapter XIX.

We have declared elsewhere that there are three types of numbers among the **Pythagoreans**: Linear, Plane, and Solid. Linear numbers are those which unity alone measures like a point: such as Two, Three, Five, Seven, and the like. Plane numbers, however, are those multiplied from numbers as if from sides. For example, six is made from twice three or thrice two. And from the number of planes, we call those "quadrangular" and "equilateral" <note>Square numbers</note> which are produced from the drawing of some number into itself. Such as four from twice two, and nine from thrice three, and sixteen from four times four. "Inequilateral" <note>Rectangular numbers</note> are those from the drawing of a smaller number into a larger one, such as six from the leading of two into three. We also call them "oblong" when they are produced from the drawing of a much smaller number into a much larger one, such as ten resulting from the leading of two into five. Indeed, from twice five comes ten. If we called this "linear" in a certain way in the tenth book of the *Republic*, we wished it to be understood as oblong. Besides these, we called those "solid" which, from the leading and reducing of some number into itself, produce the likeness of a solid mass in a triple dimension, as it were: such as twice two twice is eight; thrice three thrice is twenty-seven; four times four four times is sixty-four. Take the first two of the planes, namely those created from the first linear numbers: for instance, four created from two on one side, and nine created from three on the other. You will be able to bind these two planes—nine and four—together with a single fitting medium: that is, six. For whatever proportion nine has to six, the same six will have to four. In both cases, it is a *sesquialter* ratio <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2</note>. For nine contains six and one part of it besides, i.e., three. Similarly, six comprises four and two besides, which is the other half-part of four. That six is the fitting medium is evident from the fact that it is composed of both. For the side of four is two, and the side of nine is three. From the multiplication of two into three comes six. Similarly, if you take another square beyond nine, namely sixteen, the medium will be twelve, which is born from their sides. For the side of nine is three, and of sixteen is four. But if you lead three into four, you will bring back twelve, which connects these as a medium by an equal ratio for both, namely a *sesquitertia* ratio <note>A ratio of 1.33 to 1, or 4:3</note>. For sixteen encompasses twelve and a third part of it besides. Similarly, twelve includes a third portion of nine beyond nine. You see, therefore, what Plato says: that plane numbers can be bound by a single medium. Take furthermore the first of the solid numbers: those, I say, which are first produced from the first linear numbers led and reduced into themselves: eight from two on this side, and twenty-seven from three on that. You will certainly not be able to couple these together with a single medium, but you will be forced to take at least two media: namely twelve and eighteen. For you will take twelve from twice two thrice, and eighteen from thrice three twice; and through these numbers, you will reconcile the extremes in a *sesquialter* ratio. For the number twenty-seven embraces eighteen and again another part of it, that is, nine. Similarly, eighteen exceeds twelve. Likewise, twelve equally exceeds eight. Through these things, it is clear: solid numbers always require more media by which they may be congruously coupled. What we have explained in numbers, we can demonstrate the same in dimensions, both plane and solid: showing that between comparable planes, one medium often suffices; but between comparable solids, several true media must be placed. This would indeed be too long, and has been sufficiently shown by **Iamblichus**, **Proclus**, and **Chalcidius**. Since, however, Plato accepted these Mathematical things here not for their own sake, but for the sake of natural things, let us set these aside and consider what mysteries of nature he chiefly understands through mathematical images. In the beginning, what is read in Holy Scripture: that God perfected all things in number, measure, and weight—Plato clearly touches upon numbers, measures,

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Plato's Timaeus, specifically focusing on the mathematical and metaphysical structure of the universe. The catchword "vtrinq; par" (equal on both sides) links to the start of the next page.</meta>

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS.

By bringing in **solids** as the medium, he <note>Plato</note> encompasses both volumes and weights; he also signifies this later when, after dimensions, he mentions the "powers of inclinations" as the causes of weights. By **numbers**, he wishes to be understood the very species and substantial forms of natural things, which Aristotle also compared to numbers. By **measures**, he means certain instrumental figures or magnitudes adapted to specific species. Finally, by **solids and powers**, he signifies qualities, which extend thoroughly through the masses and provide momentum to motions and actions. He judges that all things in the universe—the species of things, the shapes and magnitudes of those species, and the qualities—are composed according to **geometric** and **musical proportion**, so that the lowest are exceeded by the middle in the same ratio as the middle are exceeded by the higher. Likewise, through numbers he designates the **arithmetic mean**, which consists in the equality of numbers. Through dimensions and measures, he designates the **geometric mean**, which is located in the identity of ratio and proportion. Through weights and powers, he designates the **musical mean**: which is situated in the equality or likeness of portion, and is understood by the power of the speed and slowness of motions, and the sharpness <note>high pitch</note> and gravity <note>low pitch</note> of voices.

->First discourse: why the fourfold number of elements is appropriate for the world. Chapter 20.<-

But of these things elsewhere at greater length. Now let us return to the division of the world’s parts, so that we may behold their harmonic composition. In the preceding sections, we said that the numbers five and six were suitable to the circular figure of the world. Now, moreover, we say that the **quaternary** <note>the number four</note> is appropriate for its fullness. Indeed, the quaternary is the first to fulfill every difference of numbers: embracing within itself the first even and the first odd. It also fulfills the simple progression of numbers: for in four terms it completes the **denary** <note>the number ten</note>, perfectly finishing the ten by one, two, three, and four. It also fulfills the process of dimensions, attaining them in four terms: the point, length, width, and depth. It fulfills musical consonance. For within the limits of the quaternary are restrained the double, triple, quadruple, sesquialter <note>3:2 ratio</note>, and sesquitertial <note>4:3 ratio</note>, as well as the octave, double octave, fifth, and fourth. It fulfills nature, proceeding as far as four terms: substance, quantity, quality, and motion. Finally, it fulfills the universe, whether in nature or above nature: by essence, being, power, and action. Justly, therefore, did the **Pythagoreans** designate the fullness of the worldly body and soul by the "quaternity"; and they swore by it as the fourfold fountain of perpetually flowing nature. From this fountain, surely, flows the fourfold number of the elements. Hence the fourfold nature in the heavens. Hence, below the heavens, the four seasons. Hence, under time, the four humors, complexions, and affections. Hence, above time, the four virtues arise. Hence, in eternity, the four archetypes of the virtues.

->Second discourse to prove the same. Chapter 21.<-

Furthermore, if I did not fear partly prolixity and partly novelty, I would recount certain wonderful inventions of **Iamblichus, Syrianus, and Proclus**, who establish four grades above the celestial world: namely, the One, Limit, Infinity, and Mixture. Then the celestial world, that is, the first and intelligible Mind; after that, they place the Mind of the world, which is partly intelligible and partly intellectual; after this, the purely intellectual Mind and world; and in the fourth place, the Mind which is already the Soul of the world and the leader of the sensible world. Likewise, they say the supreme Mind looks up to those four—the One, Limit, Infinity, and Mixture—and possesses four by its own nature: namely, unity on one hand, and essence on the other. Again, essential unity and uniform essence; and all the Ideas of things are similarly participants in a fourfold nature. Likewise, the intellectual and "Jovial" <note>pertaining to Jupiter/Zeus</note> Mind, the craftsman of the world, in fabricating the world, looks up to the intelligible and supreme Mind as a model, and to the Good as an end. And by the same reason that in the intelligible world (which they call "Being itself" and "Living itself") it beholds the principles and Ideas of a fourfold nature, it distributes the world into four similar regions. The first of these extends from the first heaven, through the spheres of the heavens down to the sphere of fire and the beginning of the air; the second from there to the middle of the air; the third from there to the earth; and the fourth is the earth itself. To this division, four armies of rational inhabitants correspond in each region: namely, the worldly gods, then the angels, then the demons, and finally the particular souls. But leaving these aside, let us return to our purpose.

->Third discourse to confirm the same. Chapter 22.<-

There are four elements according to the **metaphysician**: essence, being, power, and action. Four according to the **mathematician**: the point, the line, the plane, and the depth. Four according to the **physicist**: the seed-power of nature, the natural sprouting, the adult form, and the composite. Assign each to each: to essence belong the point and the seed; to being itself, the line and the sprouting; to power, the plane and the form; to action, the depth and the composite. Everywhere, the extremes are reconciled by two means, just as solids are. Clearly, what is the **point** in mathematics, Plato considers in physics to be the **seed-power**, indivisible and stable. What is the linear extension in length in mathematics, he considers in physics to be the "sprouting" (so to speak) of the germinating form. Likewise, what is the **plane** there, is properly the **form** here; for as the plane terminates a body, so form terminates matter. Finally, what is **depth** there, is the **composite** here—a double composite, I say: both formal (that is, a certain complexion of several forms similar to a solid sphere) and material (that is, consisting of form and matter, more similar to a cube). Therefore, when he says that one medium suffices between two planes, understand that a single medium satisfies between two forms: namely, the formal medium. For when forms follow one another where they touch at their extremes, they agree by a certain single formal medium, equal on both sides...

## FO. CCLXXIX.

partly agreeing and partly differing. But indeed, when he says that solids are coupled to solids by a double mean <note>original: "medio duplici." Plato argues that while one mean term suffices to link two plane numbers, two mean terms are required to link two solid (three-dimensional) numbers.</note>, it signifies that between natural compounds, two twin means of a different nature are interposed. One of these is formal, while the other is material. For in any compound, one considers on one hand the principal form, and on the other, the subject <note>The "subject" here refers to the underlying matter or substance that receives the form.</note> accommodated to that form. From this it follows that a double discrepancy arises between different compounds: one more by reason of form, the other more by reason of the subject.

### Fourth discussion on the same; and concerning the powers and proportions of the elements. Chapter XXIII.

These same points are corroborated by another reason: if you descend from the "four-fold groups" just described to the four-fold nature of the sphere. In this, one certainly considers the nature of the center; one also considers the nature of the circumference, which are most distant from each other both in property and in position. One further considers, on one hand, the space as far as the proper power of the center extends; and on the other, the space as far as the proper power of the circumference is stretched out. From this, the four quarters of the world are reckoned, and similarly the four elements.

->By substance. By power. By action.<- ->Another arrangement of the same.<-

| | | | | | | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fire: | subtle: | sharp: | mobile. | Fire: | sharp: | subtle: | mobile. |
| Air: | subtle: | blunt: | mobile. | Air: | blunt: | subtle: | mobile. |
| Water: | thick: | blunt: | mobile. | Water: | blunt: | thick: | mobile. |
| Earth: | thick: | blunt: | immobile. | Earth: | blunt: | thick: | immobile. |

That which is placed in the circumference, following its nature, is the most ample, and therefore the most subtle of all by **substance**; by **power** it is the sharpest and most fit for penetration; and finally, by **action** it is the most prompt for motion. But that which is situated in the middle <note>The center of the sphere, representing Earth.</note>, following the nature of the center, is the most narrow and dense by substance; by power it is blunt; and finally, by action it is most unsuited for motion. The two means <note>Air and Water.</note> hold themselves in a middle fashion between these. Therefore, just as the perimeter and the center are most distant in a sphere, so fire and earth differ most by position and nature. For the former so seeks the perimeter that it is never naturally in the middle; the latter so seeks the center that it is never naturally at the perimeter. Air, however, sometimes descends, namely if it is placed in the high region of fire. Water also ascends, if it is confined beneath the earth. Just as in fire and earth three things are considered—namely substance, power, and action—so also there are three principal properties: in fire, **subtlety** by substance, **sharpness** by power, and **mobility** by action. In earth, the opposites: **thickness** by substance, **bluntness** by power, and **immobility** by action.

Now, these natures are called "solid" in Plato's writing because, like a triple dimension, they possess triple qualities; for if they only had them like planes, one mean would suffice, which would agree with the extremes in one quality but differ in another. But since they have three mutually opposite qualities, two means are needed to bind them. Each of these means agrees with its neighbor (whether extreme or mean) in two qualities and differs in one; but with the remote extreme, it agrees in one and differs in two. Thus, air follows fire, being very similar to fire in subtlety and mobility, but dissimilar in a certain bluntness of power—in which single quality it somehow agrees with earth. With water, however, it agrees in two: namely bluntness and mobility. Water follows air, similar to air in these two, but similar to fire in only one: namely mobility alone; yet it is dissimilar to fire in two: thickness and bluntness together. It is dissimilar to earth in mobility, but similar in thickness and bluntness.

Indeed, it appears that fire is comparable to earth by a certain analogy—that is, a similarity of ratio and proportion. For as the subtlety of fire is to the thickness of earth, so is the sharpness of fire to the bluntness of earth; and so again is the mobility of fire to the immobility of earth. That fire is also comparable, but by some more potent ratio, to air—air to water, and water to earth—is manifest from the agreement of their qualities. It seems, moreover, that the agreement of a proximate element to its neighbor is double its discrepancy; but toward a remote element, the discrepancy is double the agreement. Fire seems twice as subtle as air, three times as mobile, and four times as sharp. Likewise, air is twice as sharp as water, three times as mobile, and four times as subtle. Again, water is twice as sharp as earth, three times as subtle, and four times more ready for motion. <margin>I would have said: air is twice as mobile as water, and three times as sharp. For water agrees more with fire in mobility, but more with earth in bluntness.</margin> To proceed among related things only as far as a quadruple proportion is permitted among musicians; for the ears are offended by a longer progression. Furthermore, the perfect ratios of music are contained in these. In these, certainly, through three qualities as if through three dimensions and certain solids, we proceed three times and through solids unto solids. For through the double ratio, at the fourth step, we reach eight, which is the first solid number <note>2 x 2 x 2 = 8.</note>. Likewise, through triple ratios, at the fourth step, we reach twenty-seven, which is the second solid <note>3 x 3 x 3 = 27.</note>. Again, through quadruple ratios, in the fourth place, we reach sixty-four, which holds the third place among solid numbers; for eight is created from two taken solidly (that is, three times or led into itself); twenty-seven from three led three times; and sixty-four from four similarly multiplied into itself three times. But so that it may be better known how much congruence there is in Plato between mathematics and physics, those two means of the first solids must be repeated. For we placed between eight and twenty-seven two fitting means, namely twelve and eighteen. The number twelve is born both from eight and from twenty-seven. Since the "side" from which eight is multiplied is two...

But from the number two and the number three, the number twelve is produced in this way: if you multiply two by two, then by three. Here, the emerging twelve receives two sides from the number eight, but one from twenty-seven. Likewise, from two and three, eighteen is produced if you multiply three by three, then by two. Here, the resulting number eighteen receives one side from the distant eight (where it is said "twice"), but two sides from the number twenty-seven (where it is said "thrice"). Similarly, the two elements <note>Air and Water</note> are in the middle between fire and earth: while they are tempered from the extremes, they carry back twin natures from the neighbor, but borrow a single nature from the distant one. By this, the whole world is composed of four elements: and how these are in one way in heaven, and in another way below the moon.

### Chapter XXIV.

From these four elements, joined to one another by geometric and musical proportion <note>term: "ratio" - here meaning both mathematical ratio and rational structure</note>, all Pythagoreans and Platonists believe the entire world to be composed. However, it is in such a way that the consonance of these in heaven never suffers any dissonance; below heaven, however, a certain dissonance may seem to arise somewhere at times, but it is immediately reduced into a consonant form in a wonderful way by the superior harmony. That these elements are below the moon, no one will deny. But that they are in heaven, some natural philosophers <note>original: "physici"</note> will deny. But let those men, I pray, listen to the metaphysicians proving that the elements exist through their **Ideas** in the very Craftsman of the world; that they are from there in the **Soul of the World** through their rational principles; and that they are in **Nature** through their seeds. Therefore, they are also in heaven through their powers <note>original: "virtutes"</note>, and below heaven through their forms. For in what way do the natures of the elements pass from causes superior to heaven to below heaven—where they are indeed more unstable—unless their moderating powers are meanwhile infused into heaven? Furthermore, just as a farmer does not rule an architect, because he contains no principles of architecture, but the geometer, possessing these, does rule him; so also heaven, unless it grasped the forces of the elements and elemental things, would never govern them. But in governing, it embraces them; indeed, by embracing, it governs. Let them also listen to the astronomers designating the natures of the elements both in the signs and in the planets, and proving it by the effect. Finally, let them listen to the Sacred Scriptures, which often place "waters" in the heavens, and also place a "land of the living." If these two things, which are most dissimilar among celestial things, are placed there, much more are fire and air, which are more similar to celestial things, placed there by the Sacred Scriptures.

Some will respond, I think, that the most excellent powers of the elements are to be placed there in the manner of a cause; but in the spheres of the elements below the moon, their natures are according to form; and finally in composite things by a certain participation. But they will deny that the natures of the elements themselves are in heaven. To this, the Platonists will argue that specific powers are everywhere founded in a specific nature. Therefore, if the powers of these things are in heaven, their natures are also there; but just as the powers there consist in a genus far more excellent than these, so the natures consist in a more excellent—indeed, to speak more correctly, the most excellent—genus. And that most eminent nature of fire provides the heaven with sensible light, life-giving heat, and the readiest motion. The nature of earth grants solid and firm stability. Likewise, it gives to the stars the density by which they can be seen, and to the moon the density by which it reflects solar rays. The nature of air provides the transparent quality, which they call "translucent." The nature of water brings a most delicate and most even smoothness. And what is greatest, it implants in the very "lips" of the spheres where they touch each other that power of cold and moisture, through which it happens that although they touch each other most rapidly and vehemently from the swiftest motion, yet no burning heat or dissolution occurs there. The Hebrews will strongly approve of these "waters" in the heavens. They will also approve, I think, if they hear that through the nature of "earth" there, the "land of the living" is created, so that materials which are otherwise very thin do not dissipate from such great motion.

One must remember, however, that there is such great power in the celestial substance, and so effective for reconciliation, that qualities and motions which among us are repugnant to each other, do not fight there. Likewise, the remaining elements there, immediately from the first birth of the world, were reduced into the most excellent form—that is, of fire—just as through celestial motion the four elements among us are reduced in any birth to a single form of a mixture. Nor will you wonder that the elements are fused into one there, if you consider that even below the moon they are compacted into one mass: and that fire is a participant in earthly solidity, lest it continually disperse on account of its very thin and mobile nature; and that the earth, sluggish by itself, obtains action and life through the partnership of fire. If the extremes are mixed, then surely the middle things are mixed with the middle and the extremes. Likewise, if there is such great union below the moon, it is much greater above the moon; but the solidity or stability of the earth reigns there without thickness, in a vapor-like form. Again, the evenness and smoothness of water is far from falling; the agility of air is separate from flowing out; the efficacy of fire dominates in light and a healthy heat similar to intelligence and life, separate from that combustion which light reflected between hollows and fiery heat enclosed in a certain rough and biting matter forces us to experience here. Certainly, to the extent that it is freed from earthly thickness, to that extent it shines more purely and warms more healthily. Therefore, together with Heraclitus and Empedocles, we shall say that the intellectual light of fire itself, which is in the **Idea**, flashes as visible light to the eyes in heaven; but below heaven in the ether, its pure and harmless flame flourishes; but on earth, it is a coal burning in rough matter. We shall say finally with Orpheus that there are moreover four elements among those in the underworld: Pyriphlegethon, Acheron, Oceanus, and Cocytus <note>The four rivers of the Greek underworld, here mapped to the four elements</note>. We shall say with Plato: just as in the archetypal world all things are in all things, so in this image-world all things are in all things; but they are received everywhere according to the nature of the recipients. Thus, celestial things in the elements are elemental; elements in the heaven are celestial. And so great is the excellence of the celestial region over the others, that celestial fire, besides the elemental fire and the three remaining elements, may be called a "fifth element" <note>original: "quintum... elementum"</note> in terms of its power. Hence, he says five worlds can be named. Since all genera of things...

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS. FOLIO 280.

in whichever of these five <note>referring to the five Platonic solids or elements</note> they may be, according to the nature of each. Finally, we shall conclude with the harmony between Moses and Plato—whom Numenius <note>A second-century philosopher who sought to link Plato with ancient Near Eastern wisdom</note> calls "the other Moses." For what Moses says: *In the beginning God made heaven and earth*, Plato says: *God first made fire and earth*, understanding "fire" primarily as the heavens. For in the beginning, he considered the center and the circumference in the sphere of the world. He interposed the rest for the sake of these. Circular motion is proper to every sphere that is always in motion. Likewise, light is most proper to fire.

### Chapter XXV.

But let it not disturb us that some distrust that the heavens are fiery because the motion of the heavens is circular, while the motion of fire is straight. For even any portion of the heavens, if by chance it were placed in the middle, would suddenly ascend in a straight line, seeking its homeland by a shorter path; and yet the proper motion of the heavens is a circuit. And the earth, if it were separated from the center, would descend; and yet its proper state is to be at rest. Indeed, any mobile sphere, whether elemental or celestial, is naturally moved in a circle according to its shape, so that it may more fully enjoy its own place. However, straight motion, wherever it exists, is not so much natural as it is a return to nature. Just as a circuit is suited to a body, it is most suited to fire. For since it is most distant from the earth even by nature—just as the earth is always immobile—so fire is always mobile. If it is always mobile, then it moves in a circle. For that which moves in a straight line, once the space (which is finite) is finished, also finishes its motion. That both fire and air move in a circle is shown by the circuit of comets. The perpetual inflow and outflow also testify to the circuit of water. It was necessary for the earth to remain still, so that it might be more like an indivisible and stable center, and thereby more conveniently enjoyed. But it was necessary for the higher things to move, so that they might always produce various things according to the variety of their motion. Nor should anyone deny that the heaven is hot; rather, let them deny that it is scorching. Nor should they say that the light of the sun heats only by reflection, but rather that it burns only by reflection. For the reflected rays of the moon do not heat at all, since a watery power dominates in her. But the rays of the sun heat healthfully according to the fiery, life-giving nature of the sun. Nor should they object that it happens because of the slower motion of the moon that her rays do not heat. For even if it is granted to be slower, it is still so much closer to men than the sun that it ought to heat somewhat, if not as much, if heating were to come solely from reflection. Nor should they argue that heat is the property of fire. Indeed, the less it is mixed with foreign matter, the less it burns. But let them say that light is the property of fire. For the purer it is, the more lucid it is, though it may not be manifest to certain eyes; and it shines further than it heats; and it illuminates first, and in a moment; and it bestows warmth upon the heated object, which preserves the heat for a time after the fire is gone; but it bestows light on nothing <note>meaning light is not "stored" in the object</note>, as light is its own property. Indeed, when the fire departs, the light departs at the same time.

### On the spirit of the world: that is, on the intellect, the soul, the intelligence, and nature. Chapter XXVI.

After he has treated how God constructed the mundane body, he next proceeds to dispute how He tempered the mundane soul. He shows meanwhile that he placed before our eyes the unformed mass before the formed one, and soon the formed one in a certain way before the animated one—not because unformedness existed before formation, or bodily formation before the soul, but so that we might recognize that a nature so capable of form was divinely instituted for the sake of bodily formation, and bodily formation for the sake of the soul as its end. Therefore, God, wishing to make a perfect work, made the world living and intellectual; and so that He might more conveniently connect one animal <note>term: animal - here meaning a "living being" or "animated entity"</note> from that very spirit out of the matter of the world, He distinguished the matter into four elements, as we have said, like the humors of this living being; for He had willed its spirit also to be distinguished into four. For four things pertain to the spirit of the world. First, indeed, is the **Intellect**, remaining immobile in itself, the mover or ruler of the sphere; thus instituted by the author of all things for ruling the spheres. Second is the **Soul** of the sphere, a mobile mover indeed, but mobile through itself. Third is a certain **Intelligence**, divinely implanted in this soul by God and the higher intellect. Fourth is **Nature**, that is, the seminal and vital power infused everywhere into matter by the soul. Intellect and Soul are substances; but Intelligence and Nature are qualities—the former of the soul, the latter of matter. The four elements are images of these four. For fire refers to Intellect. Earth to Nature. Air to Intelligence. Water, finally, to the Soul. And just as three properties belong to fire, and three opposites to earth, and the middle elements agree in a certain middle reason; so three properties belong to the Intellect, and their opposites are proper to Nature, with the middle things also in the middle. For the Intellect is indivisible, uniform, and eternal. Nature is divisible, multiform, and temporal. But the Soul is in the middle between these: through Intelligence, it becomes more a participant in the Intellect itself than in Nature; but through its animal power, it agrees more with Nature than with the Intellect. Wherefore it is called partly indivisible and partly divisible. Likewise uniform and multiform. Again, partly eternal and partly temporal. Accordingly, four lives are numbered according to the fourfold spirit of the world: The **Saturnian** life in the intellect looking up to its father, Heaven (that is, God the maker of heaven). The **Jovial** life in the intelligence declining toward action, now mobile. The **Venereal** life in the animal power now loving matter. The **Dionysian** life in nature, as if drunk (that is, immersed in matter). Furthermore, four senses are counted in the universe by a similar reasoning. The first sense is in the soul of the world: I mean the common sense, and it is one. A certain imaginary power thus accompanying its intelligence and reaching the particular forms of things, just as the intelligence reaches the universal ones—reaching them, I say, intrinsically; and therefore it needs no instruments, nor does it proceed outward, nor does it suffer. The second sense is in the souls of the spheres and the stars: certainly common and similarly impassible, but proceeding outward. The third is in particular souls, distributed beyond the common power now through individual instruments, and extending itself outside, and arising from passion <note>meaning "being acted upon" by external stimuli</note>, but ending in judgment. Finally, the Pythagoreans grant a fourth sense to plants;
