The first sense represents the Intellect <note>original: "intellectum"</note>. The second, Intelligence. The third, the animal power. The fourth, finally, the natural power. One must remember that the matter of the world itself receives the soul only through nature; nor intelligence except through the soul; nor intellect except through intelligence. Just as through the earth it receives water; through water, air; and through air, fire. Furthermore, pay attention to what follows similar to these things. For God, he says, placed the soul in the middle: and from there extended it through the whole: and finally protected the outside of the world through it. First, this signifies that the soul both fills the entire mass of the world, governing other parts of the world by its high powers, and that by its highest power—that is, intellectual providence—it surpasses the world. Because the power of the soul is stretched from the center itself through the universe, he explains this twice through four steps. First, from the middle of the earth, it extends the power of connecting everywhere; from the middle of the water, it diffuses the vital power; from the air, likewise, the sensory power; from the fire, the rational power. Then, from the middle sphere of the world, the power of connecting, as we said; from the sphere of the moon (the middle between things that can be generated and those that cannot), the vital power; from the sun, the heart of the world, the sensory power; from the middle zodiac of the firmament, the rational power. Since there is a double order of things toward God: one by which they proceed from Him, the other by which those proceeding return to Him, Plato followed the order of procession where he says: God placed the intellect in the soul, and the soul in the body. Thinking also of the order of return <note>original: "conversionis"</note>, he says: God, having placed the soul in the middle, extends it from there through the whole: and meanwhile led something of it outside the world: by which, clearly, while it provides for the world, it might turn back toward God.

### On the Composition of the Soul: and how he appropriately proceeds through the number five in composing it. Chapter XXVII.

Since many things pertaining to the souls of the spheres, minds, motions, and the composition of the soul have been explained more clearly by us in the *Theology* <note>Referring to Ficino's "Platonic Theology"</note>, we have been and will be briefer here in explaining those matters. For we are now hastening toward certain more specific points. In the beginning, we judge that the <term>quinarius</term> <note>the number five</note> is suitable for the composition and partition of the soul for three reasons. First: because just as the five consists of the first even and the first odd number <note>2 + 3 = 5</note>, so the soul consists of a divisible and indivisible nature. You know, moreover, that the even number is called divisible, while the odd is called indivisible, because it cannot be divided into equal [integer] parts. Second: because the <term>genera</term> <note>categories of being</note> from which all things are composed by God are distributed into five. They are: Essence, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion. They judge the soul, as the middle of all things, to be composed by a certain principal ratio from these five genera of all things. Third: because since the soul is the middle of the universe, it naturally receives the five, the middle of the universal number <note>the number ten</note>. For five is the middle of the perfect ten. For when we rightly divide the ten five times, the five is the equally distant middle in any division. First, if you divide ten into nine and one, you will see the five is the middle between one and nine, equally distant from both. If secondly you wish to part it into eight and two, again you will find the five as the equal middle between these. If thirdly into seven and three, or fourthly into six and four, again you will receive the five as the true middle between the extremes. We call this the arithmetic middle everywhere. That you have the five as the middle when ten is divided a fifth time into five and five is superfluous to say. For these reasons, Plato, in the distribution of the universe—both of the "soul-able" body, so to speak, and of the soul—brings five main heads into the center. For in both cases, he first treats the subsistence and foundation of the thing itself, whether of the body or the soul. Second, the harmony of the parts of both. Third, the species <note>form or appearance</note> resulting from the harmony of the parts. Fourth, the virtues <note>powers</note> of the species. Fifth, the actions which arise from the virtues. The Platonists wish those three—subsistence, harmony, and species—to pertain to the essence of the soul; through these follow virtue and action. I say harmony, that is, a fitting tempering: and this is fivefold: of genera, parts, ratios, powers, and actions. For the soul consists of those five genera of things, through which its own parts are assigned. It receives again from God the ratios of all things. From this, it has many and specific powers through which it also produces actions. But where he calls the soul a harmony or a concord, remember that Plato in the *Phaedo* denies that the soul is a harmony—that is, of the corporal parts, made from them and lying within them. But in the *Timaeus*, he affirms the soul is a harmony—that is, of its own parts, remaining in itself and tempering the body from itself. Furthermore, where he says: God composed from the indivisible essence that is always the same, and from that which becomes divisible around bodies, a middle kind of essence—that is, the soul: explain these through what he says elsewhere: God made the world living, animated, and intellectual. For where he says "living," he designates a certain natural life scattered through the bodies of the world, extended together with the body of the world and acting with motion. But where he says "intellectual," he understands the angelic intellects which, properly set over the governing of the spheres, are both indivisible according to place and immutable according to time.

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS
### FOLIO 281.
### K

...having them in an opposite manner: and the natural life and bodily form is divisible and changeable. But when he speaks of the "animated" <note>Latin: *animatum*; referring to the world as a living being</note>, he signifies the very substance of the world soul, whose essence is indeed both indivisible and unchangeable, like the intellect. It can, however, be called in a certain way divisible and mobile: because it is the proper source of certain powers declining toward divisible and mobile things. Its virtue and action are partly individual and immobile, insofar as it agrees with divine things and acts stably; but partly it is also divisible in a way, both because it is manifold and because it declines toward the manifold and divided body; and it is mobile because it operates within time. Therefore, he calls this soul a "third species of essence," a medium between the individual and eternal things on one hand, and the divided and temporal things on the other. 

Furthermore, since the world prepares its life according to the intellect, it follows that as it relates to life, it relates similarly to the intellect. Therefore, just as it possesses not only a natural life lying within the matter of the world, but also an animal life—that is, a soul existing in itself—so it possesses not only an intellectual quality infused into the soul, but also an intellectual substance remaining within itself. For everywhere certain qualities are reduced to certain substances, so that just as a vital quality is referred to a vital substance, so an intellectual quality is also referred to an intellectual substance. 

He composes the soul in five principal ways. First, from the five genera of things themselves. Second, from numbers. Third, from numerous harmonies <note>Latin: *concentibus*; musical or mathematical proportions</note>. Fourth, from the beginnings of figures. Fifth, from the principles of motions: namely, so that possessing the reasons <note>Latin: *rationes*; can mean ratios, principles, or logic</note> of metaphysics and mathematics, it may thus know all things: namely essences, numbers, harmonies, figures, and motions. Likewise, insofar as the soul is kindred to divine things, it is said to be composed of the genera of things that are primarily in the divine. Insofar as it is kindred to natural things, he mixes it with figures and motions. But insofar as it holds the middle ground between both, he contemplates it through numerous harmonies and ratios. 

Indeed, he names those five—essence, the same, the other, rest <note>Latin: *status*; stability or standing still</note>, and motion—as the "genera of things" <note>These are the "Great Kinds" from Plato's Sophist</note>, because from these, except for the first, all things are composed. Essence clearly signifies the formal reason of each thing; it also hints at "being" as the proper act of essence. "The Same" is so called because anything agrees primarily with itself and with others. Again, "the Other" is added because it has a certain difference, both within itself and toward other things. Furthermore, "Rest," since it retains its own unity for some time. Finally, "Motion" in this place signifies a certain exit from potentiality into act, whether by being or by acting in any way internally or externally. 

But above these five genera are placed three: Limit, Infinity, and Mixture. Above these three is placed the One itself. Essence follows the divine One itself. "The Same" and "Rest" follow Limit. But "the Other" and "Motion" accompany Infinity. Finally, just as we have placed the four elements of the world in the highest degree in the heavens, in the middle degree below the moon, and in the lowest degree beneath the earth; so we place the five genera by a certain highest reason in divine things, in the middle in the soul, and at the lowest below the soul. For in divine things, unity overcomes multitude, limit overcomes infinity, "the same" exceeds "the other," and rest prevails over motion. In lower things, however, the opposite occurs; and those things which surpassed there are now surpassed here in turn. In the soul especially, an equal tempering of each to each emerges; so that they rightly wish this to be especially the medium of things, tempered by musical ratios. 

Mathematical things are congruent with the soul, for both are judged to be media between the divine and the natural. Musical numbers are most congruent with the soul. For they are mobile; and for that reason, they rightly signify the soul, which is the principle of motion. The soul is described not only through numbers but also through figures: so that through numbers it may be thought of as incorporeal, but through figures it may be known to decline naturally toward bodies. 

The triangle is suited to the soul. Because just as a triangle is extended from one angle into two, so the soul, flowing from an indivisible and divine substance, falls into the nature of the body which is utterly divisible; and if it is compared with divine things, it appears divided. For those divine things act through a single and stable power, and suddenly; but the soul performs through many and changeable powers and actions, and through intervals of time. If it is compared with natural things, it is judged indivisible. For it does not have different parts bound to different places like they do, but is whole in any part of the whole; nor does it pursue all things movably and in time like they do, but also attains some things suddenly and possesses them eternally. 

Furthermore, one may compare the soul with a triangle in this: that the triangle is the first of those figures which, consisting of several lines, are produced in a straight line. Similarly, the soul is the first of all to be distributed into several powers, which are brought under intelligence within it; and it seems to be produced in a straight line while it falls from divinity into nature. In which descent from the highest intelligence, it flows into three lower powers: namely, into a certain rational discourse, into sense, and into the power of growth <note>Latin: *vegetandi*; the vegetative or nutritive soul</note>. Just as a triangle, produced from a point, is led into three angles. 

I say the soul is the first of every kind and is mixed in a way from several powers, and "falls" in a straight line, so to speak. For the angelic mind above the soul needs no lower powers within itself; but it is pure mind, a whole and sufficient mind, and it does not turn toward lower things, but like a circle, it is turned back toward the divinity alone from whence it came. Therefore, its action is compared to a circle. For its action is one and equal, just as a circle is from one and equal line; and there is a certain wonderful capacity in both. Furthermore, the circle is the first and the last of figures. First, because it is contained by one line. Last, because figures constituted of several lines, the more faces they take on, the more they seem to approach the form of a circle as their end. Similarly, the intellect is created first of all by God, and the intellectual countenance—that is, the absolute order of things—is the last of all in species...

shines in the mirror of nature: toward which natural forms approach more and more by degrees, as if toward an end. But concerning the intellect, we shall speak elsewhere. Now let us return to the soul.

### Why the Soul is compared to a composite thing. Why to musical harmonies. Chapter XXVIII.

We seek three things especially concerning the soul at present. First, why Plato fashions the soul to be like a composite thing. Second, for what reason it is like a thing composed of a certain concord. Third, why it is like musical harmonies. In the first place, although the soul is indissolubly composed, it is nevertheless composed of such great multiplicity that by a certain natural inclination it leans toward those things which are entirely composite. Therefore, it is fashioned in a way similar to composite things, with which it agrees by a certain natural—I do not say consanguinity, but affinity. Next, because it is the middle of all things, it is rightly both composed of all things and binds all things together concordantly: therefore it is compared to a certain concord, or to something concordantly composed: especially since the soul reconciles those things which in nature fight among themselves, connects them once reconciled, and preserves them once connected. And so, not without justice, the soul is judged to be a certain substantial concord, or a substance that is most concordant and indissoluble. But since those things which are apprehended by the other senses are also very often concordantly composed, he asked thirdly why Plato expressed the soul as being especially like *musical* concord. He responds to this: that musical harmony occurs in the middle element of all <note>The air</note>; and through motion, and indeed a circular motion, it reaches the ears: so that it is no wonder that it suits the soul, which is both the middle of things and the principle of motion in a revolving circuit. Add to this that harmony, most of all among those things which are sensed, as if it were animate, brings the affection of the senses and the thought of the soul—whether of the singer or the player—into the souls of the listeners. And therefore, it agrees primarily with the soul. Furthermore, those things which pertain to sight, even if they are in a way pure, yet they are often apprehended without the efficacy of motion and through an image alone without the nature of the thing: they move the souls of those willing only slightly. But those things pertaining to smell, taste, and touch, being as it were very material, tickle the instruments of the senses rather than penetrating the depths of the soul. Harmony, however, through its airy nature set in motion, moves the body: through purified air it excites the "airy spirit," the knot of the soul and body <note>The "spiritus" was thought to be a subtle vapor connecting the physical body to the immaterial soul</note>: through affection, it affects the sense and the soul simultaneously: through meaning, it acts upon the mind: finally, through the motion of the subtle air itself, it penetrates vehemently: through its tempering, it licks sweetly: through its conforming quality, it pours in a certain wonderful pleasure: through its nature, both spiritual and material, it seizes the whole man at once and claims him for itself. And indeed, if someone offered harmonies to the hearing with as much art and diligence of the Muses as nature or art offers flavors to the taste or soft things to the touch, we would undoubtedly recognize that Apollo <note>God of music and light</note> seizes the soul much more with melody than Bacchus <note>God of wine</note> is accustomed to occupy the taste with wine, or Venus <note>Goddess of love</note> the touch with itching desire. Added to this: that where Plato introduces the Maker of the world speaking, both reasoning with himself and commanding the rest: he thinks that eloquence itself, like an Apollonian song and primarily musical, is the origin of both the mundane soul and body: and that the soul born from there strikes the celestial lyre in a similarly musical way. And indeed, what exists in celestial melody—both the low tone from slower motion and the high tone from faster motion—the same exists beneath the heavens as heaviness and lightness: likewise cold and heat: again the moisture and dryness of the elements. The same in the generation of things is matter and form. The same in human characters is gentleness and magnanimity: temperance and fortitude. And just as from a low and high voice, so from all the twin natures we have described, a unity is made everywhere. Since therefore musical harmony is as if living, and rational, and effective: likewise, as it is most similar to the soul, it is most pleasing to it: again, it claims the whole man for itself: and what is greater, the soul was made through it: all things were made: through it they are preserved: through it they also move: not without reason did our Plato describe the soul—the maker, preserver, and mover of all natural things—especially by musical numbers and ratios: by numbers, I say, not mathematical accidents, as some falsely claim, but established by the ideal and metaphysical ratios of numbers.

### Propositions and proportions pertaining to Pythagorean and Platonic Music. Chapter XXIX.

They call a *phthongos* <note>Greek: φθόγγος</note>, that is, a sound suited for melodies: which anyone can easily produce both lower and higher: so that it is neither so deep and relaxed that it becomes silence, nor so high and intense that it makes a noise. They think a low sound is created by a relaxed and slow motion: a high sound by an intense and fast one. Just as a very relaxed and slowest motion seems to approach rest: so the lowest sound approaches silence. Again, just as a most vehement and fastest motion approaches violence: so the highest sound approaches offense. They call the intervals of sounds certain mutual excesses between them in highness and lowness. Compositions or the congruence of sounds from appropriate proportions of harmonies, joinings, and also the fittings of strings in musical instruments: whether in a single four-stringed instrument <term>tetrachord: a scale of four notes</term>: such as Mercury found and Orpheus confirmed: or in two tetrachords joined by seven strings: such as Terpander is said to have made: or in twin tetrachords arranged and disjoined by eight strings: of which they assert Lycaon of Samos was the author: or in four joined tetrachords: and consisting of fifteen strings finally by the approval of all the Greeks: in all these tetrachords the harmony of the *diatessaron* <note>The interval of a fourth</note> resounds step by step. Now indeed, after the mention of sounds, intervals, and compositions, let us proceed to the proportions from which harmonies are made. They name the proportion of equality: which occurs between terms entirely equal to each other: as between this one and that one: and a cubit and a cubit. But of inequality: which [occurs] between... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence</note>

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS. FOLIO 282.

equal, or unequal: as between one and two, or a cubit <note>a unit of length</note> and a two-cubit measure. And one of these is of greater inequality, such as the double; the other of lesser, such as the half <note>original: "subdupla"</note>. Furthermore, we must consider a threefold proportion of inequality in this context. The first indeed, which they call **multiple**, such as double, triple, quadruple: which does not divide the smaller number by the larger, but takes up and multiplies the whole, whether twice or thrice; and thus it proceeds infinitely by way of infinitely multipliable number. The second, however, they call **superparticular**: in which the larger number, besides containing the smaller once in its entirety, then divides it; and it places the divided part above the whole; but a part which we call an **aliquot** <note>a part that contained an exact number of times in the whole</note>, i.e., from which, when replicated a certain number of times, the whole is made. The first of these is the **sesquialter** <note>the ratio 3:2</note>: between two and three. For three, containing two, adds one besides; which, taken twice, makes two. The second is the **sesquitertial** <note>the ratio 4:3</note>, between four and three; and thus it proceeds infinitely by way of the infinitely divisible continuous. The third is the **superpartient** <note>a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part, e.g., 5:3</note>: which adds a part to the whole that, even if taken several times, cannot properly create the whole. Such is the case between five and three. For five, beyond three, adds two; which, taken once, does not fill three, and taken twice, exceeds it. This proportion, which divides the whole into a part unfit for the restoration of the whole, seems unfit for **consonance** <note>musical harmony</note>; in which every division must necessarily restore the whole, and every multiplication must restore the one. But the second type is judged fit: for even if it divides, it nevertheless does not stray from the ease of restoration; and in it, the terms are judged to be mutually **commensurable**. For the difference between two and three is one; and this is the common measure of both. For taken twice, it measures two; taken thrice, it measures three. But between five and three the difference is two; and this, taken any number of times, cannot by any means measure either three or five. 

The first proportion, however, is most suited to harmonies. For it does not divide, but restores by multiplying, and multiplies by restoring. Nor does it seek a measure from elsewhere, like the superparticular; but the smaller term measures the larger, being replicated twice in the double, and thrice in the triple. It falls away neither from integrity nor from simplicity. The superparticular, however, does divide from integrity, but it preserves simplicity; for it divides by one certain part. But the superpartient not only loses integrity, but also simplicity; where it mixes several parts into a certain unity unfit for the restoration of the whole. Therefore, this one is dissonant from harmony; but the two higher ones are consonant; the multiple more so, and the double most of all. Indeed, in this one, one thing does not properly seem to exceed another, but anything is exceeded by itself. For in the double, two exceeds one by one; four exceeds two by two; and so on. Add to this that it is the first generated between the first numbers as terms, namely unity and two. Generated, I say, alone, without the commerce of others, as if free and absolute from all. But the triple, while it arises between one and three, has as a companion the sesquialter, its daughter born between two and three. The quadruple also is seen to mix with the sesquitertial. For as soon as the quadruple is born between four and one, there arises as a daughter the sesquitertial between four and three. Likewise, the double arises most closely from the proportion of equality itself; from this, the triple and sesquialter. Likewise, the triple, quadruple, and sesquitertial are born; and others similarly. Which indeed, if I did not fear prolixity, I would demonstrate clearly. To the double, therefore, as if to the beginning and the end, all others are reduced; and they either divide it or multiply it. For the double is first, whole, simple, absolute, and most equal: so it is no wonder that the consonance born from it is the most perfect of all, and is called the **diapason** <note>the octave</note>: because it extends through all things, and all proportions are reduced to it. 

But before I pursue the consonances, we must be reminded that what the Greeks call *logos*, we name **reason** and **proportion**; and what they call *analogia*, we call the comparison of reason, or the similarity of reason, and again **proportionality**; a name truly as elegant as it is proper. And a proportion indeed is made between two terms; and when it is rightly made, namely leading to melodies, it is defined as the mutual habit of two quantities commensurable between themselves, like the double between one and two, and the sesquialter between two and three, and similar ones thereafter. But proportionality is defined as the mutual comparison of two proportions. As when we say: as two is to four, so four is to eight; namely by the double reason in both cases. Which comparison, because it happens between three terms, is called **continuous**. But it is **discrete** whenever it is made between more; as when we compare thus: as two is to four, so eight is to sixteen. Likewise, such comparison is threefold: namely **arithmetic**, **geometric**, and **harmonic**. The arithmetic consists in the parity of number. Thus between three and seven, five is the middle; exceeding one term by the same number, namely two, and being exceeded by the other; by a proportion divided in two for both. But the geometric is situated in the equality of the reason: in which are the multiple and the superparticular; when, for example, we compare thus: as three is to nine, so nine is to twenty-seven; for in both it is triple. Likewise, what nine is next to six, the same is six next to four. For both here and there is the sesquialter proportion. Finally, they place the harmonic proportion in a certain similarity, through which, with three terms placed in order, as the greatest term looks upon the smallest, so the difference between the terms looks from the greater to the smaller difference. For if you place: three, four, six: the difference between six and four is two; the difference between four and three is one. But just as between six and three there is a double reason, so between two and one there is a double reason. Another similarity also flourishes here: namely of portions. For the middle term exceeds and is exceeded by a similar portion of the extremes. For four is exceeded by six by a third part of six; it also exceeds three by a third part of three. In this certainly the harmonic art is occupied: which [treats] superpartient proportions as if they were scattered and dissonant...

...reflects: it admits multiple and <term>superparticular</term><note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus one part of it, like 3:2 or 4:3.</note> ratios, composing double ratios out of the <term>sesquialtera</term><note>The ratio 3:2, a perfect fifth.</note> and <term>sesquitertia</term><note>The ratio 4:3, a perfect fourth.</note>: through a harmonic principle which, as we have said, delights in a concordant variety. Indeed, as we were saying, it loves multiple comparisons as well as superparticular ones, for this reason: there is such a facility in these for restoring identity that when several of the same ratio are composed together, the middle term multiplied by itself produces as much as the extremes multiplied by each other. Set down two, four, eight: just as twice eight is sixteen, so four times four creates sixteen. Likewise, set down four, six, nine: just as four times nine is thirty-six, so six times six multiplies to thirty-six. Similarly, if you place two means between the extremes: for instance, if between two and sixteen you place four and eight. All these numbers in succession are seen to be in a double ratio to their neighbor. Therefore, if you multiply two by sixteen, you will report the same amount as if you multiplied four by eight. The same happens in other ratios, both superparticular and multiple. 

However, in <term>superpartient</term><note>A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part of it, like 5:3.</note> ratios, the same does not occur. Arrange three, five, seven. The relationship from seven to five is superpartient: so too from five to three. For in both cases, two certain parts are added on top of the whole. If you multiply three by seven, you will not produce the same number as if you multiplied five by itself. Thus, in the first rank are the multiples, because besides what we just said: through them all numbers regard unity even while they look at other numbers. In the second rank are the superparticulars: for even if they do not look at unity itself, they always look at one certain part fitted to the whole. In the third rank are the superpartients: because they seem to look at neither of these. For this reason, the harmonic faculty avoids this relationship as if it were resistant to concord. For it desires either to create a univocal and unison sound from the proportion of equality itself, or to forge an equivocal and equisonant sound from the rational proportion of inequality in the multiple and superparticular. It is established that such an equal sound comes from the double ratio, which is closest to a unison: because in the double ratio, the smaller term measures the larger, and by measuring it, equals it; and where the larger exceeds the smaller, it seems to surpass it by no other number than the smaller one itself, so to speak.

### That in musical consonances one is made from many: by which consonance is defined. Chapter XXX.

**Q**ust as the most skilled physicians mix certain juices together by a certain ratio, through which many diverse materials may unite into one new form—and beyond their elemental power, they wonderfully acquire a celestial virtue, which is manifest in the concoction of <term>Mithridates</term><note>A famous complex herbal remedy used as an antidote to poison.</note> and the <term>theriac of Andromachus</term><note>A celebrated ancient medicinal paste.</note>—similarly, the most artistic musicians temper the deepest voices like cold materials, and the highest voices like hot ones; again, the moderately deep as moderately moist, and the high as dry, with such reason that one single form is made from many, which beyond the power of the voice, attains a celestial power as well. 

This is clearly apparent from what Democritus and Theophrastus say, and what Pythagoras proved by effect. For by certain harmonies, certain diseases of both body and soul are said to be miraculously cured; so it is no wonder that the ancient sages traced the origin of both medicine and music to the same thing, namely, the <term>Apollonian number</term><note>Referring to Apollo as the god of both healing and music.</note>. For both are medicine. But one cures the soul through the body, while the other cures the body through the soul. Most appropriately, they also attributed prophecy to Apollo, the fountain of melody. For melody alone, drawing the soul back from all things that distract it, contracts it into itself, into a certain internal hearing, so to speak, by which not only voices but the ratios of voices are perceived; and with perturbations calmed, it tempers the soul to celestial harmony and pours forth divine oracles from heaven. 

But perhaps one should not deny that a third and common vocal form is made from a high and low voice; it must be considered that deep voices can be mixed with high ones more perfectly than juices are said to be mixed with juices. First, because vocal materials, on account of their subtlety, continuous motion, and uniform quality in all parts of the airy body, are more easily brought to completion than juices, which are thick, less suited for motion, and differ greatly in qualities when forged into one. If they are forged into one, they are therefore more aptly prepared to conceive a new form. Secondly, because the natural instrument of the voice is intrinsic, and being closest and most obedient to the vital, animal, and rational power, it more easily and perfectly obeys the musical art to create that one thing it aims for, more so than the external instruments of physicians. Even if a <term>cithara</term><note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre.</note> is plucked with fingers, the strings obey the musician's wish more faithfully than herbs obey physicians. And if nature acts upon the heaped mass of herbs beyond the industry and labor of physicians—and indeed at a certain time—much more does nature act suddenly upon vocal material, which is very manageable and formable. Nature, I say, living everywhere and fortified by celestial powers, acts upon a material more similar to heaven and as if alive, to which it suddenly applies a new, living, and wonderful form, through which it may test its powers upon the body and soul by a hidden virtue. 

Therefore, just as in a body naturally constituted of four elements, the qualities of the four elements create one—and as some name it, a fifth—complexion, subject to a special virtue coming from heaven in hidden ways: so also many voices rightly mixed resound together into one certain foundation of a new and wonderful virtue. For if from a sounding cithara, a resonance suddenly sounds in another similarly tuned cithara, and from a vibrated string, a similar vibration immediately passes into an equally stretched string, who then can doubt that from many voices forged by one certain ratio, a single common form is suddenly born, through which many are one? Therefore, they are perceived as one by the sense and meet in one certain effect. The same is established from the pleasure of the sense: in which, since there is one form from many, full delight comes from a single form that is congruously made from many. Hence it happens that to hear a unison for a long time...

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS. FOLIO 283.

return: in which equality may perceive without any inequality. Let it be, moreover, that a dissonant sound offends: in which the difference does not breathe together into one. Therefore, many things are clearly discerned by the sense: and are, as it were, tasted by it as many. I say "tasted" as if speech were to voices what taste is to flavor when it is affected by a mixture. Hence that prophetic saying: *How sweet are thy words unto my taste, O Lord, sweeter than honey to my mouth.* <note>Psalm 119:103</note> Finally, whether deep sounds absorb high ones, or high ones occupy deep ones: delight does not result: and yet a certain union is required everywhere. But since union—whether from the absorbing or the occupying sound—does not please, it remains that only that union pleases which results as something new and effective from a certain moderate blending. Here, therefore, **consonance** <note>original: *consonantia*; a harmonious sounding together</note> is defined: a mixture of deep and high sound approaching the ears uniformly and sweetly. Moreover, this mixture is similar to that which satisfies the taste in flavors: in which a sweet and very rich flavor is judged similar to a quite deep and relaxed voice: while a very sharp flavor is like a very high voice. But a sweet flavor mixed with sharpness refers to a moderately deep voice. Mixed indeed with saltiness or pungency, it seems to represent a moderately high voice. And then at last a manifold mixing fills the sense, when it is not discerned as multiform: but insinuates itself as uniform. Physicists teach that sound reaches the ears in a circular shape, amplified step by step by many circles, not otherwise than when circles multiply toward the shore in a pond from the throw of a stone from on high. But we believe that a concert <note>original: *concentum*; a harmony of voices</note> composed of deep and very high sounds glides into the ears like a single form: and this one is indeed round, but oval. In this, the eighth voice <note>the octave</note> as if through a sharper peak, continuing the breadth of the first voice to itself: from itself and the first it now composes one voice: and just as the eye sees an oval roundness as one figure, although here it is wider and there less so: so the hearing drinks in the voice resulting from the deep and the octave as one, raising itself gradually and sweetly from a certain ample depth into a sharp height like an egg. Here we believe it happens that nature has granted such a shape to the instrument of hearing: and a similar one to the instrument of speaking: and art, moreover, has granted a similar one as far as possible to musical instruments. Certainly, those are more consonant which are closer to the oval shape.

### From which proportions which consonances arise. Chapter XXXI.

They say that **Pythagoras**, when he had noted among the bronze-smiths that consonance arises from the blows of hammers by the law of weights: collected the numbers in which the diversity of weights agreeing with itself was contained. Then he stretched strings with various weights tied to them, just as he had learned they were varied in the hammers: and here he clearly considered: that from a string which was stretched above another in a **sesquioctave** <note>a 9:8 ratio</note> ratio, a **tone** was discerned against the other—that is, a full and whole sound: such as was the proportion of nine to eight. Nor could he distribute the tone into two equal half-tones <note>semitones</note> between themselves, because the number nine cannot be cut into two equal parts: but he found that one half-tone was a little larger than a half: while the other was a little less than a half, which he called a **diesis**, and Plato called a **limma**. But by how much the smaller half-tone falls short of a whole tone: and <gloss>for</gloss> a true half-tone, Plato indicates the numbers in the interval of these: namely, between two hundred forty-three and two hundred fifty-six. For since the eighth part of that smaller number is thirty and nearly a half: while this larger number adds only thirteen over that smaller one: it neither returns a tone, nor a whole half-tone. Pythagoras then noticed that the whole and full breadth of a tone, so to speak, consists of two sounds and one interval: and thus he obtained the first elements of consonance. The first of these stood out as the **diapason** <note>the octave</note>: resulting from the first proportion, namely the **double** <note>2:1 ratio</note>: where, for instance, this string over that one from double weight, stretched twice as much, while both were struck, returning to its straightness twice as forcefully and quickly, rendered a voice far higher than the far deeper one in turn: yet so friendly that it appeared as if a single sound, narrower here, wider there. This sound, where the higher one occurred: he measured by modulating it at the eighth degree of height from the deep one—counting the deep one—to be located: likewise to consist of eight sounds, and seven intervals, but nearly six tones. Furthermore, where between the strings the ratio of tension and relaxation was **sesquitertia** <note>a 4:3 ratio</note>, he found the consonance **diatessaron** <note>the perfect fourth</note>: containing two tones and a smaller half-tone: but four sounds and three intervals. In the **sesquialtera** <note>a 3:2 ratio</note> indeed he found the **diapente** <note>the perfect fifth</note>: and in this he perceived three tones and a smaller half-tone: but five sounds and four intervals. He then noticed that the diapason is composed of the diatessaron and the diapente: because the double ratio which begets the diapason, where it has a middle, is constituted from the sesquitertia and the sesquialtera, from which those are made. For the first double having a middle is two to four: composed of the sesquialtera, between three and two: and of the sesquitertia, between four and three. But in a **triple** relationship he considered the **diapason-diapente** <note>an octave plus a fifth</note>: having twelve sounds: but eleven intervals. For the diapason has its seat in the double, but the diapente in the sesquialtera. But a sesquialtera continued from a double makes a triple. For six against three is double. Add nine, from which to six is born a sesquialtera: immediately you will have a triple from nine to three; yet a triple is not made if you add a sesquitertia to a double: as if you added an eight to that six. For the sesquioctave is missing, namely nine to eight. And since a sesquitertia added to a double becomes a **superpartient** <note>a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part</note>: as eight to three: for this relationship is a double super-bipartient through a double sesquitertia: therefore Pythagoras forbade continuing beyond the double—that is, the diapason—repeatedly through the sesquitertia diatessaron: although Ptolemy somewhere admits this subjunction. But the sesquitertia is conveniently joined to the triple, for here a **quadruple** proportion is made: and through the quadruple consonance the **disdiapason** <note>a double octave</note>: having fifteen sounds and fourteen intervals: for instance if, having placed a triple between nine and three, you subjoin twelve, which against nine is sesquitertia, you suddenly acquire the quadruple born from twelve to three. But the grace of melody forbids proceeding beyond the quadruple: not only because violence reaches the sense from more vehement motion and breaking: but also because as soon as beyond the first quadruple a quintuple is born between five and four: there arises at the same time a super-bipartient between...

## FOLIO LXXXII.

But to return to the quadruple ratio: for the sake of avoiding sluggishness, it also forbids descending frequently below the *sesquitertia* <note>original: "sesquitertia"; the ratio 4:3, known as a perfect fourth</note>. It forbids continuing two *sesquitertias* often, both because they are otherwise displeasing and because they do not complete the double and the *diapason* <note>original: "diapason"; the octave</note>. If you arrange nine, twelve, and sixteen, you indeed have two *sesquitertias*: but by no means a double: for the *sesquioctava* <note>original: "sesquioctava"; the ratio 9:8, a whole tone</note> is missing—namely, eighteen to sixteen—so that the double might be born from eighteen to nine. Nor does it willingly continue paired *sesquialteras* <note>original: "sesquialteras"; the ratio 3:2, a perfect fifth</note>. For these continuous ratios exceed the double by a *sesquioctava*. You can discover this if you write down four, six, and nine. For here there are two proximate *sesquialteras* from four up to nine. But the number nine exceeds eight (which is the double of four) by a *sesquioctava* portion. From this it appears that the power of the *sesquialtera* is greater than half of the double. From which it is also clear that the power of the *sesquitertia* is just as much less than half: since the double is created from both. Indeed, the *sesquialtera* exceeds the *sesquitertia* by a single eighth portion. For from eight to six you have a *sesquitertia*: but from nine to six you have a *sesquialtera*. Yet from nine to eight you have a *sesquioctava*: and by this very *sesquioctava* part you understand that the *sesquitertia* is surpassed by the *sesquialtera*. One ought to remember that the *diatessaron* <note>original: "diatessaron"; the interval of a fourth</note>—that is, the comparison of four sounds ascending to a fourth height—is not approved by the hearing on its own; yet it is willingly received because, with a tone easily added, it becomes the *diapente* <note>original: "diapente"; the interval of a fifth</note>, the most pleasing concord of the fifth voice. Likewise, if it is connected with the *diapente*, it completes the *diapason*, the most excellent of all. Nor should it disturb anyone that although we have said the *diatessaron* has four sounds and the *diapente* five: yet we say the *diapason* composed of both has no more than eight sounds. For where we deal with composite consonances, we arrange the strings themselves in joined tetrachords and continue the sounds in such a way that the last sound of the first consonance becomes the first of the second in that following composition. Hence the matter reminds us to return to the seven-stringed lyre of Terpander <note>A 7th-century BCE Greek poet and musician credited with adding strings to the lyre</note>: in which the fourth string is struck twice, so that in a certain way it turns out to be an eight-stringed lyre. Terpander followed this conjugation, as I judge, because the multiplication of voices clearly differing among themselves is increased up to the seventh sound. But the eighth now returns to the first with a certain wonderful similarity: just as the double ratio through which it is created restores the smaller number which it surpasses, while it exceeds the same by the same amount. The ninth returns to the second: and is dissonant like the second. The tenth to the third: and is consonant like the third. The eleventh to the fourth. The twelfth to the fifth. The thirteenth to the sixth. But the fourteenth returns to the seventh. Finally, the fifteenth to the eighth: and together with the eighth to the first. They name the first and lowest sound *hypate*. The following *parhypate*. The third *lichanos*. The fourth *mese*. The fifth *paramese* or *trite*. The sixth *paranete*. The seventh *nete*. Furthermore, if a comparison is made in quality and daily motion: we shall compare *hypate* with Saturn and the following with the following planets in order. But if in daily motion and its speed or slowness, we will conversely compare *hypate* with the moon: and the following thereafter with the superior planets. And we shall find deep sounds in heaven mixed with high ones: and that the spheres by one motion produce a high tone, but by another a deep one. Likewise, from vast globes come vast sounds: from divine ones, divine; from manifold revolutions, by equal reason, manifold sounds. And just as beyond the seventh sound a revolution occurs back into the same: so above the seven distinct spheres of the planets, all things revolve into one sphere: wonderfully embracing such a heptad within itself. But of these things elsewhere. Let us return to the consonances: and let us now conclude them with a certain proper end. These three are numbered among the ancients. First, the diatonic: in which any tetrachord proceeds by a minor semitone, and a tone, and a tone: which both other wise men and Plato especially approve before others, as the most natural of all, since it proceeds from the minor semitone as if from soft matter in the manner of nature toward the stronger matter of the tone: and it has a simple form: both gentle and robust at the same time. Add that it most especially suits the tetrachord: in which the *diatessaron* is created from two tones and a semitone. The second consonance is called chromatic: which is accustomed to run through a minor semitone, a major semitone, and a *triemitone* <note>a minor third</note>. But the philosophers reject this as being too soft. The third is named harmonic <note>enharmonic</note>, proceeding by roughly a quarter part of a tone, and again by a similar quarter and a *ditone* <note>a major third</note>. This also they do not approve because of the superstitious difficulty of perception and use. Many things which we omit at present regarding these matters, we treat more diligently in the eighth book of our letters.

->On the Harmonic Composition of the Soul.<-
->Chapter XXXII.<-

<margin>God, about to create the soul of the world, forged it from indivisible and divisible essence. This first division in Plato into essence—namely, the indivisible property and the divisible—is most common. For what he calls indivisible contains in itself that which is neither cut into part beyond part according to place, nor flows from the prior into the posterior according to time. By the first it is called "the Same": by the second "State" and "Stable." Similarly, what is called divisible embraces in itself both what is spread out by place and what glides by time. By the first it is called "the Other": by the second "Motion" and "Mobile"—motion, I say, in natural things. Wherefore under that division which said the soul was gathered from indivisible and divisible essence, five genera of things are in a certain way contained: Essence, Same, Other, State, Motion. But Plato, for the sake of brevity, does not repeat five but three. For he repeats Essence, Same, Other: as if they suffice. For to the Same follows State: but to the Other follows Motion. And conversely to State follows the Same: to Motion likewise the Other. He says, moreover, that God forged one nature out of Essence, and the Same, and the Other.</margin>

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS
## FOLIO 284.
### K iiii

...with such an exact mixing, that within its essence, Sameness and Difference were present everywhere; and conversely, within its Sameness, both Difference and Essence were present; and again, within its Difference, both Essence and Sameness lay hidden. For Essence, through Sameness, has the quality of agreeing with itself and others; through Difference, it is in a certain way distinguished within itself, and much more so from all other things. Indeed, Sameness and Difference both obtain their existence from Essence. But Sameness possesses harmony from itself, and differentiation from Difference. Difference, however, possesses differentiation from itself, but from Sameness it receives both harmony and order. Plato believes that the gathering of these kinds <note>The "Great Kinds" from the Sophist: Being, Sameness, Difference, Rest, and Motion.</note> leads the soul toward all things, both for judging them and for carrying them out. Surely, since it consists of Essence, it defines what each thing is; because it consists of Sameness, it recognizes what is simple—and if composite, by what union it is joined—and how it agrees with itself and others; because it consists of Difference, it recognizes what diversity exists in anything and by what condition it is either distributed within itself or separated from others; since it consists of Rest <note>original: "statu"</note>, it recognizes what sort of thing remains constant in itself and in what manner; because it consists of Motion, it is recognized from what source each thing depends and when it depends on reason, as well as what things it does and how. Furthermore, through Essence, it gives being to things; through Sameness, it joins things to itself and to others; through Difference, it separates them; through Rest, it confirms them in their own nature and order; through Motion, it moves them, and causes them to be moved and to act.

For this reason, Plato not without merit mixes the kinds of all things according to a certain ratio in the fabrication of the soul. He says these are mixed with one another by a harmonic ratio, not an arithmetic one—otherwise the distribution would be unjust in some places—nor by a geometric proportion alone—otherwise there would be such equality in the mixture that it could not closely harmonize with the extreme diversity of bodies. But a harmonic ratio, consisting of a similarity of various things, makes even dissimilar things "daughters" <note>A metaphor for harmonious results or offspring of the proportions.</note> and connects unequal things by a certain common equality. Such is the quality and office of the soul, both toward itself and toward bodies. For whether it acts within itself, it mixes a certain Alterity <note>Difference</note> with the Identity <note>Sameness</note> of intelligence, so to speak, and a certain Identity with the Alterity of reason. It does similarly in imagination and sense. Whether it acts upon the body, it produces the Alterity of motion in a certain stable order, as if by Identity; this is apparent in the heavens. Likewise, below the heavens, in the very Alterity of generation <note>The world of change and birth</note>, it preserves Identity through a continuous order; and in both places, it preserves and restores Essence.

Therefore, God, in composing the Soul of the World, uses a harmonic ratio: both in mixing the kinds of things with one another, and in the very portions which He took from them to compose the soul, and in the powers of the soul accompanying its birth from the start, and in the spheres of the world agreeing with the soul. That such a mixture befits the soul, Plato did not only investigate by reasons, but also carefully prophesied by taking conjectures from the world. For when he contemplated the body of the world—placed under the soul, made for its sake, and ruled, moved, and reformed by it—he judged it agreeable to nature that we might conjecture a certain form of that soul as a model from the figure of the world as an image. Therefore, by those same proportions by which he saw the spheres of the world composed, arranged, and driven—that is, by harmonic ratios—he divined that its soul was tempered. Just as among musicians, harmony in the voice flows from the harmony of the skillful mind, so from the harmony of the celestial soul, harmony passes into the world.

But let us now hear Plato himself. "In the beginning, he took one portion from the whole. Then a second, double the first part. Then a third, which was one-and-a-half times <term>sesquialtera: a ratio of 3:2</term> the second, but triple the first. After that a fourth, double the second. Then a fifth, triple the third. A sixth, eight times the first. Finally a seventh, which exceeded the first by twenty-six parts." These are his words. Let us therefore establish a triangle at whose apex unity <note>The number 1</note> is located, from which three numbers flow out on each side: here the even, there similarly the odd. Namely, in this fashion: on one side after unity, first two, then four, finally eight; on the other side under unity, similarly first three, then nine, and lastly twenty-seven.

The first portion which God takes from the very "leaven" of the kinds, so to speak, to fashion the soul, is Unity. The second is the number two, double the first. The third is the number three, whose ratio is triple the first (that is, of unity) but one-and-a-half times the second (that is, of two). The fourth portion is the number four, double the second (that is, of two). The fifth is nine, whose ratio is triple the third (that is, of three). The sixth is eight, whose proportion is eightfold to the first (that is, unity). The seventh is twenty-seven, a ratio triple to nine, but exceeding unity by twenty-six parts. In these numbers on both sides, he encompasses all harmonic ratios.

For in the <term>sesquioctave: a ratio of 9:8</term> proportion between nine and eight, he brought forth the **Tone** <note>The whole step in music</note> obeying the nine Muses. In the <term>sesquialtera: 3:2</term> between three and two, he created the **Fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note>, the Venus-like grace of the voice. In the <term>sesquitertia: 4:3</term> between four and three, he created the **Fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>, the Mercurial nature of the voice, adapting itself to consonances. In the double ratio between two and one, and likewise between four and two, and again between eight and four, he gave birth to the **Octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note>, that is, the universal and absolute melody of the eighth voice dedicated to Apollo. In the triple ratio between three and one, and nine and three, and again twenty-seven and nine, he composed the **Twelfth** <note>original: "diapafon diapente"</note>, that is, the Jovial symphony of the octave and fifth combined. In the quadruple ratio between four and one, and eight and two, he wove the symphony of the **Double Octave** <note>original: "disdiapafon"</note>, again sounding to Apollo through fifteen sounds. He inserted beauty into the beginnings of the third voice through the Fourth, and then subjoined the Fifth to the ends of the sixth voice, so that with the more delicate softness of each voice, the harshness of the second voice on one side and the seventh on the other...

For in this way the third and sixth intervals are similar in their softness, just as the second falling from the first, and likewise the seventh deviating from the eighth, are similar in their harshness. In the beginning, where he says God took seven portions, he touched upon a mystery, both in music and also in nature. In music indeed: because the entire divergence of voices proceeds up to the seventh degree, after which a return to the same occurs. In nature truly, both because many things in natural affairs are completed through the septenary <note>The number seven</note>—about which the other Platonists have said quite enough—and because the septenary possesses unity as a bond of a double trinity; and from these twins, it unfolds the trinity again from itself. Such indeed is the likeness of the universe. Which indeed is distributed into three at the beginning; wherefore Plato here commended the ternary <note>The number three</note>. It is distributed, I say, into the eternal, the temporal, and the media between these. Eternal things possess, under the property of trinity: in essence, simplicity; in power, stability; in action, reflection. Temporal things, in turn, have composition in their essence in a triple dimension; again, mobility of power; and finally, transition of action. Between these trinities of eternal and temporal things, the Soul, holding the middle, effects the seventh degree. It also effects the ninth, which is also praised here by Plato. The ninth, I say, because the Soul itself has three faces. For it turns toward itself, toward higher things, and toward lower things. It is helpful here, before I return to the septenary, to commend the ternary together with the nonary <note>The number nine</note> for a little while longer. The trinity of numbers, being the first, seems to contain the beginning, the middle, and the end of things; and alone among numbers to contain them by a certain indivisible reason. Inasmuch as each of these signifies individual unities. Furthermore, if one wishes to run through the causes of things, you will find a triple property in causes. For causes are in themselves; they produce effects; and they perfect those things made by leading them back. Or if you descend to consider effects, you will likewise discover a trinity. For effects are in their causes; they proceed from them; and they are converted back to them. Or if you turn yourself to the Soul, which connects sublime causes with the lowest effects, you will see it remaining in itself, declining toward effects, and ascending toward causes. And this Soul rules the world by a triple septenary. First, indeed, by certain hidden seven powers of the planets ruling through causes in the firmament. Second, by the seven forms of the planets in the seven spheres subject to the firmament. Third, by the seven gifts of the planets ruling generation beneath the moon. For indeed, beneath the moon, in fire, the life-giving light is subject to the Sun, but burning heat to Mars; on the earth, the varied surface to Mercury, but the entire mass to Saturn. But in the middle regions, moisture reigns: the airy moisture obeys Jupiter; the watery obeys the Moon; and finally, the mixed obeys Venus. Likewise, acting causes follow the Sun; matters follow the Moon. The fecundity of acting causes follows Jupiter; the fecundity of matters follows Venus. Swift dispatch toward an effect follows Mars and Mercury—the former indeed on account of vehemence, the latter on account of dexterity itself and multiform virtue. The lasting continuation of all things is dedicated chiefly to Saturn. Moreover, here the order proceeds by three septenaries from the septenaries which are distributed according to the three powers of the world-soul. For in this soul, the circle of intelligence is stable. A circle indeed: because it reflects back to that place from whence it is. Stable: because it does so suddenly. Beneath intelligence, as if beneath the firmament, there are three powers: namely, universal reason, imagination, and vegetation <note>The basic life-force or growth principle</note>. In reason there are three circles, in a way mobile and temporal. The first from the soul to the cause to be loved, and vice versa, a certain natural instinct secretly carrying it so. The second from the causes of things to the consideration of effects, and conversely. The third from forms and ideas that are more universal to those less universal, a descent and vice versa an ascent. In the remaining two powers of the soul, there are altogether four circles, similarly temporal: two in each. The first is a natural reflection toward its cause. The second is a certain and perpetual revolution from those same forms to the same at certain intervals; through which, both in heaven a temporal and certain revolution of configurations occurs, and beneath heaven, of transformations. Therefore, the circuit of generation necessarily follows the circuit of heaven; and this indeed follows the circuit of the soul. The revolution of the soul accompanies the orb of intelligence. Indeed, the motion of the soul, if it were utterly deserted by intelligence, would immediately pass only into a straight line, both in perceiving and in acting. But because it repeats itself and gathers similar gyrations through others, it is strengthened by a certain superior intellect; which, both remaining in itself and suddenly turned toward its cause, bestows intelligence upon the soul. Through this, as if by an outstretched hand, it halts the soul which is by its own nature wandering; and its restless motion, naturally prone to a straight line outside itself, it twists back into an orb, midway between straight motion and rest. Hence the soul, about to return into itself, travels; it circles the profound mind; and is turned by a similar image of heaven. But concerning these things, more diffusely in the *Theology*. Let us return to numbers.

### The sum of harmonic numbers conducive to the composition of the soul. Chapter XXXIII.

Unity in the figure above signifies the unity and sublime simplicity of the soul itself: both the proper image of divine unity, and remaining within it. Duality signifies the process of the soul into its own property by a lower unity, and now manifold by a certain reason. Trinity signifies its return to unity, both its own and the divine. Quaternary <note>The number four</note> signifies the progression of the soul from itself into matter, to be arranged by the degrees of the four elements. The septenary signifies its power about to rule the elements through the seven spheres of the planets. The octonary <note>The number eight</note> signifies the force about to govern the planets through the eighth sphere. The nonary signifies the office of the soul about to reconcile the eight spheres into one form. The sum of the number twenty-seven signifies its fullness about to collect all things in all. For the sum of twenty-seven contains the above-mentioned numbers; and from those placed in order thereafter, as is evident to one calculating, it fills them up. Nor are the even and odd numbers described in the figure without reason: whereby through the even numbers the divisible nature of the soul may be thought of, and through the odd, the indivisible; and simultaneously the feminine and masculine virtue. Linear, superficial, and solid numbers are also collected, so that we may know the soul penetrates through all things, is amplified everywhere, and fills them inwardly. Let us imagine that the soul, as both solids <note>i.e., the cubic numbers 8 and 27</note>, completely fills both compositions. As for the double and triple intervals of the numbers and the rest which we spoke of before, and what they specifically signify in the soul: even if this is still unknown among the Platonists, it is nevertheless permitted for us at present perhaps to prophesy in this manner, so to speak. Therefore, let a triangle be described again: at its summit let there be **Essence**. On the side where the odd numbers were described, let **Infinity** be designated, and thereafter **Otherness** and **Motion**. But on the side where the even numbers were arranged, let there be **Limit**; then let **Sameness** and **Rest** follow in order. Here we will likewise have seven boundaries: of which the soul can perhaps be imagined to participate under the same ratio to one another under which the boundaries of the numbers described from the beginning regard each other: so that the soul, by a proportion of this kind, participates in the five genera of things as well as the two elements of the genera, that is, Limit and Infinity.

Let there be, for the sake of example, a comparison of Essence to all things joined together, in a sesquioctave ratio <note>A 9:8 ratio, corresponding to a whole tone in music</note>. For the common form of the whole exceeds the proper qualities of the parts by at least one degree, as if by a tone. Let Infinity, that is, formable aptitude, be under Essence. Let Limit accompany this, as if its form. And let the proportion of Limit to Infinity be double. For it is necessary that the power of acting surpasses the potential for being acted upon. Let Otherness follow Infinity. But let Sameness accompany Limit. And let this Sameness surpass Otherness by a sesquialter ratio <note>A 3:2 ratio, a musical fifth</note>. After these, let Motion follow Otherness, and Rest follow Sameness. And Rest surpasses Motion by a sesquitertial proportion <note>A 4:3 ratio, a musical fourth</note>. This is what Plato signified when he said these are scarcely surpassed by those. Because if you consider the proportions explained here, you will find Essence to be triple; but Rest to the same to be quadruple.

Furthermore, so that we may be able to devise the harmonic proportion to be participated in the soul, not only according to the five genera of things and the two elements, but also according to its own powers distributed into seven grades, let us now assign the individual powers of the soul to the individual genera or elements. These powers are: **Unity, Intelligence, Will, Reason, Imagination, the Power of Connecting, and the Power of Generating.** These last two powers we often embrace under the single name of either "Nature" or "Vegetation." Let us therefore compare them in this way: the Unity of the soul to Essence; Will to Infinity; Intelligence to Limit; Imagination to Otherness; Reason to Sameness; the Power of Generating to Motion; and the Virtue of Connecting to Rest. And let us devise similar proportions among these powers to those above. But if we have said elsewhere that there are equal proportions of things in the soul, we did not wish arithmetic parity to be understood, but harmonic equality.

### By the intervals of the spheres, Plato hunts for the intervals of the reasons between the parts of the soul. Chapter XXXIV.

<margin>6 8 9 12 18 27 36 54 81 108 162</margin>
Just as we often infer the features of a living form from the features of an image, so from this imaginary face of the celestial soul, which we behold in the reflecting matter of the world, we infer its true face according to our abilities. Therefore, the double and triple and other intervals described in the primary figure of numbers, which Plato judged to be found in the spheres, he referred back to the parts and powers of the soul, from whence they were transferred into the spheres. For he thought that as much space as exists from the Earth to the Moon, double that extends from the Earth to the Sun; and as much as from the Earth to the Sun, triple that from the same to Venus. Again, as much as from the Earth to Venus, four times as much from the same to Mercury. Likewise, as much as to the star of Mercury from the Earth itself, nine times as much from the Earth to Mars. And as much as from the Earth to Mars, eight times as much from the Earth to Jupiter. And as much as it is from the Earth to Jupiter, twenty-seven times as much from the Earth to the circuit of Saturn. Here among the rest you see the heavier planets, Jupiter and Saturn, designated on both sides by solid numbers <note>8 and 27</note>. And if elsewhere I have reviewed other measures of intervals according to the opinion of some Pythagoreans, I nevertheless consider the Platonic ones more probable. Through these, however, those things which are more obscurely involved concerning the spheres in the tenth book of the *Republic* can perhaps be understood. Likewise, through those things which we have treated concerning the virtue of numbers and proportions, those things which are implied in the eighth book of the *Republic* concerning the celestial circuit and numbers and proportions can be conjectured.

### How the intervals of the double and triple numbers are filled. Chapter XXXV.

After Plato devised the first figure containing seven boundaries, in which the double and triple ratios are comprehended, he then orders a second figure to be formed, containing larger numbers to such an extent: that where the doubles are filled by sesquitertials and sesquialters, these means are also filled by sesquioctaves in such a way that the spaces of the sesquitertials contain a tone. Let us therefore describe a figure similar to the first: but let us place a six at the apex; after which, at a long interval, let us place its double, that is, twelve; and let us occupy that space with both an eight and a nine. for in the same order between twenty-four and forty-eight, we insert the means <note>mathematical averages or middle terms</note> thirty-two and thirty-six. Thus far we have completed the side of the doubles <note>the series 1, 2, 4, 8, etc.</note>. Next, let us finish the spaces of the triples <note>the series 1, 3, 9, 27, etc.</note>, making eighteen the triple of six; and between them let us designate nine and twelve. Similarly, between eighteen and fifty-four (its triple), let us place twenty-seven and thirty-six. Finally, from fifty-four to its triple, one hundred sixty-two: let us proceed through the twin means, namely eighty-one and one hundred and eight. 

So that we may return to the first figure of this double relationship: let us consider between six and twelve the two means, namely eight and nine. And indeed, the number eight stands in a <term>harmonic ratio</term> <note>A ratio where the middle term exceeds the first by the same fraction of the first as it is exceeded by the third of the third</note> between six and twelve. For it exceeds six by a third part of six (two), and is exceeded by twelve by a third part of twelve (four). Likewise, it is <term>sesquitertial</term> <note>original: "sesquitertius"; a ratio of 4:3</note> to six: but twelve is <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialter"; a ratio of 3:2</note> to it. Furthermore, the difference between twelve and eight is four. But the difference between eight and six is two. Thus, four is to two as twelve is to six, containing a double ratio. 

In these things we have described, the harmonic art is employed. Let us also compare nine to six by a sesquialter quality (3:2); and to twelve by a sesquitertial quality (4:3); and to eight by a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "sesquioctaua"; a ratio of 9:8</note> property, by which a whole tone resounds. We shall surely understand that by this very sesquioctave, two sesquitertials are bound together: i.e., eight to six, and nine to twelve. Nor is an <term>arithmetic mean</term> lacking to these numbers: since nine exceeds six by three, and is likewise surpassed by twelve by three. 

Similarly, we shall proceed through the same ratios in the following doubles, binding the doubles through sesquitertials and sesquialters: likewise connecting the twin sesquitertials by a sesquioctave proportion. In almost the same way, except for the tone, one may run through the triples. Since, however, sesquitertial ratios are made not only from two tones, but also from a <term>hemitone</term> <note>a half-step or semitone</note>—and a minor one at that, which lacks a certain small portion of being a full semitone—therefore Plato says that in the sesquitertials, a "certain portion was left over" <note>referring to the Pythagorean comma or leimma</note>. 

But what this figure, explained through larger numbers, signifies in the soul, does not yet seem sufficiently explained by the Platonists. Nor shall we explain it at present, unless perhaps—while he places several or at least two means between the extreme terms—he wishes it to be understood that the genera of things and the elements in the soul, which regard each other in an opposite way, return two qualities to one another. As if, where a limit touches infinity, it brings back the quality of the limit to the infinite; and conversely, where infinity touches a limit, it undergoes the affection of the determined infinity. Furthermore, let there be in the limit a certain "terminal infinity," and conversely in infinity itself, a limit proceeding indefinitely. Added to this is that between the very powers of the soul, such means can be imagined: and the soul, according to its own exemplar in the world, is accustomed to insert at least two means between those things which are far apart. 

A full **tone** signifies the motion and pulse of the soul both in itself and in the heavens. But the **hemitone** signifies a more relaxed motion in the elements, failing from its own nature to such an extent that it receives a portion smaller than half of its perfection. Finally, the whole preceding treatise on harmony seems to signify a triple concord: namely, between the soul and the body; between the parts of the soul with each other; and between the parts of the body with each other.

### The Division of the Soul, Motion, and Time. Chapter XXXVI.

**W**hen he says that the very mixture of the genera was consumed in the completion of the soul, he means that the soul has reached such perfection that it has almost filled its own Idea. Furthermore, the division lengthwise shows that the soul's own natural motion is straight—namely, toward the senses, and the nature of moving the seat of growth <note>the vegetative power</note>. Therefore, he cuts it into two for this reason: to show both that there is a double straight motion in the soul (for sensing and for moving), and that there is a twin motion from the soul in the body (uniform and multiform). 

He intersects two lines to figure the soul, then bends them into a circle: indicating that the nature of the soul, though more inclined by itself toward straight motion, is entirely adapted to circular motion by God through the gift of intelligence. I mean in twin circles: the firmament of the fixed stars, and after the firmament, the orbits of the wandering planets. The circuit of the firmament properly reflects the nature of Sameness and intelligence. The multiple windings of the planets properly represent the nature of Otherness and the lower parts of the soul. But from the internal motion of the soul and time together, time in the world follows along with motion. 

Among these things he touches on a few common points pertaining to Astronomy; but anyone even moderately learned easily understands these, and certain Platonists, both Greek and Latin, treat them at excessive length. Soon a question arises concerning the Ideas and the genera of worldly living beings, which we have treated very extensively in our *Theology* <note>referring to Ficino's *Platonic Theology*</note>. Furthermore, what he recounts concerning the genealogy of certain gods and demons—what likelihood it may have—is similarly declared in the *Theology* and elsewhere.

### Things made directly by God, and things made through intermediaries. Chapter XXXVII.

**H**itherto it can be clear to everyone: that from the Divine Intellect, the Maker of the world, the souls, the worldly gods, the demons, all the spheres of the world, and the very species of things have proceeded without intermediate causes. However, concerning the ambiguity among Platonists regarding prime matter, we have spoken from the beginning. 

Thereafter, the Architect of the world commands his sons—that is, the souls of the spheres and stars and the demons, or even the lower angels—that in imitation of him, they should undertake the mixing of things beneath the moon. He also subjects all things to man: the rational soul, received from God himself, he reconciles to the decaying body through a certain irrational life <note>the "spirit" or lower soul</note> which suffers from them, previously depending on the soul of the man. 

You will note, moreover, in the very words of God: that whatever is made directly by God is eternal. And that whatever is composed by any reasoning, insofar as it is composed, is also dissoluble. But insofar as certain composed things stand firm through the divine will, such that in them unity overcomes multiplicity, they are preserved undissolved. You will note further: when he says God "remains in his own habit" while he commands, but the ministers follow, that there is no mutability in God while he rules and moves mobile things; but in the ministers—
