# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS. FOLIO 286.

### On man as pertains to the soul and the body. Chapter XXXVIII.

He states that the rational soul of man was fashioned by God from the same kinds of things and mixed in the same mixing bowl as the soul of the world. The "mixing bowl" <note>Latin: *crater*</note> signifies the very Idea of rational life. But he adds that it was composed from the remnants of the previous mixture, signifying that particular lives are inferior to the universal life. Then indeed, God assigns the souls to their individual ranks, matching them to individual stars. He also provides vehicles—that is, ethereal bodies. He teaches them the laws of fate while infusing the souls with the formulas of the Ideas, through which the souls, when turned toward themselves, can recognize the reasons of things. What he says elsewhere regarding the fated descent and circuit of the soul has been explained in another place. After these things, the ministers of God <note>The lesser gods or celestial powers</note> pursue the fabrication of the human body, connecting it with hidden bonds. By these hidden bonds, understand that the temperament of man is so balanced and similar to heaven that the excess of elemental qualities scarcely appears in it.

He adds thereafter that the circuits of the soul are impeded by the mass of the body. Here, remember above all else that our soul was woven with a logic similar to that of the world soul and possesses similar circuits. Therefore, he says the circuit of the intelligence is impeded, and the circuit of reason is distracted, for two chief reasons: first, because before the body is adult, the whole soul is occupied in the fabrication of the body; and second, because those things which move the external senses strike more vehemently in a tender age, and because of the novelty of things, they make the soul full of wonder regarding bodily matters. For these reasons, the divine and the intelligence are vacant from their divine office, and the rational discourse itself, distracted toward inferior things, is troubled and deceived as if insane. Thus the whole mind takes on a childish character and leads a laborious life while reason yields to the senses—just as if someone were to fix their head to the ground in place of their feet and lift their feet high in the air in place of their head.

Now, those things which he brings forward concerning the disposition of the limbs of the body are treated sufficiently by physicians. Among these, you will observe this most of all: the head is said to be not only the principal part, but indeed the "whole" in the body, for the remaining parts were added only to serve the head. From this, you may gather that man was born for the sake of contemplation. There follows a discussion on the instruments of the senses. What is said among these regarding sight is sufficiently explained by Calcidius <note>A 4th-century commentator on the Timaeus</note>, and what is said regarding dreams is sufficiently explained by us elsewhere.

You will soon consider the firm opinion of our Plato regarding causes: that bodily things and qualities—which do not move of themselves but are moved by a certain incorporeal cause and directed to an end—should not truly be called "causes," but rather instruments of a hidden cause. They hold that the principal cause is the will of Providence, disposing all things according to its own exemplar, as it judges and decrees to be best. Thus, Plato asserts that the final cause prescribed in Providence is the highest of causes. Then he confirms again that man was born to contemplate celestial things; indeed, to imitate the mover of heaven itself according to his powers. And just as he had spoken of sight, so too he says hearing was granted to us for the sake of contemplation and learning; likewise, so that through sensible harmony, we may also compose the movements of the soul harmoniously. Other senses besides sight and hearing he holds of no account, as they contribute less to speculation.

### How the World is composed of Mind and Necessity. Chapter XXXIX.

After he treated the formal order of the world—which he calls "Intellect" because it is the image of divine intelligence—he now treats the matter of the world, which he names "Necessity." He does so not for its own sake, but because it was introduced as necessary for the ultimate forms. Likewise, because the world, on account of the admixture of matter, necessarily suffers something of deformity. Hence the saying: "The world is composed of intellect and necessity"—that is, from the order of forms and from matter. We can even understand under the name of "necessity" not only matter, but also its soul, considered in the first sign of its procession as unformed, like matter. For both soul and matter are indeed unformed in the first sign of their origin, but are easily formed through the gift of intelligence; whence the reasons and seeds of natural forms are infused into the soul itself, and qualities and forms into matter.

As for his saying that the elements existed in some way before the arrangement of the world, understand this as certain powers of the elements: both formative in the soul and formable in matter. Likewise, where he says that matter before the world was tossed about without order, explain it thus: the moving power of the soul, even before the gifts of intelligence, could agitate matter, but far from any order. Furthermore, where he says the world was adorned by God, having first "persuaded" necessity, take it this way: although that primary nature of matter and soul is thought of as unformed, it nevertheless received from the beginning a preparation from God toward forms, being so formable that it could not be more passive.

Meanwhile, this distinction must be observed: whereas the universe was divided into two at the beginning of the book—that is, the exemplar and the image—now it must be distinguished into three: the exemplar, the image, and matter. Here it may first seem that the exemplar of the world, its efficient cause, and its final cause are the same thing. Next, that the whole order of the world is not so much a substantial thing as it is an image of the invisible world. Furthermore, because he separated matter from the mind above, and here separates it from the image of the mind, we can conjecture that matter proceeds from God not so much through its own Idea as through the Idea of form; not by a preceding purpose but by a certain consequent one, "invented" as it were by intelligence. Then he diligently shows both that matter exists and what it is and how it behaves, based on the perpetual transmutation of forms; from which he also argues that material forms are in some way false. Then through them, he ascends to the true and ideal forms, all of which are declared more plainly in [our] Theology. He brings forward many names for matter: namely, the invisible species; the unformed bosom capable of all forms; Nature; Power; Mother of the world; Nurse of forms; Subject; Receptacle; Place. But from this name of "place," it is [permitted to laugh...] <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence: "ridere libet" or similar</note>

# COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS.

<note>The author is likely Marsilio Ficino, addressing Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>

...that the Peripatetic <note>A follower of Aristotle</note> is so foolish, or rather malevolent, as to falsely accuse Plato of madness, as if he intended for matter to be a strictly mathematical place. This is most evidently refuted by the other names given to matter. Finally, from the fact that matter claims informity <note>lack of form</note> for itself, one may argue that it likewise claims unity. For if it is without form, it is therefore indistinct. If so, it is also one. Yet from that same informity it does not claim "being" for itself; rather, through informity, it falls away from being. Since, therefore, "one" and "being" do not apply equally to matter, they cannot be the same thing. However, the "one" is superior to "being" because it spreads itself more widely; especially since "one" applies even to privation <note>the absence of a quality</note>, to which "being" does not apply. From this we argue again that matter can be produced only by the highest principle of all things.

### How Physics Consists of Mathematics, and Concerning the Elements and Mixtures. Chapter XL.

Next, intending to prove physical things through mathematics, he first praises the doctrine of mathematicians as the path to all noble learning. It would be long, Lorenzo, to recount at present how many in our times, having entered the mathematical path, have reached their desired goal. We know that Pierleone of Spoleto, chiefly by the benefit of mathematics, has penetrated not only Aristotelian but also Platonic meanings. Indeed, in Florence, Leon Battista Alberti, beginning from these same disciplines, produced a most beautiful work on architecture. What shall I say of our Francesco Berlinghieri, son of Niccolò? Did he not, relying on the benefit of mathematics, write excellently in verse about cosmography? Let no one be disturbed that Plato, after the manner of the Pythagoreans, seems to compose physical things out of mathematical ones. For he does not wish it to be understood that natural bodies are composed of shapes and numbers as if from elements and parts, but rather as if from limits, by a certain resolution; namely, that natural things are resolved into those as if into prior things and limits. Are not the limits of bodies dimensions and shapes? And are not numbers the limits of shapes? Furthermore, natural species require not only a common subject but a specific one. Shapes are satisfied by a common subject. But numbers require neither a specific, nor a common, nor any bodily foundation at all. From this it is clear that shapes are prior to natural species, and numbers are prior to shapes. Therefore, Pythagoras and Plato conceived a triple order in things: of species, of shapes, and of numbers. Similarly, a triple order among the Ideas: so that both in things and in Ideas, species are resolved into shapes, and shapes into numbers; and certain species correspond to certain shapes, and certain shapes to certain numbers in a certain way, the order of things so requiring. Therefore, when they say the species of fire is constituted from a pyramidal shape, and the solid pyramid from four triangles, and these from the numbers four or three, they wish to signify that a certain property is similarly present in all these commonly: and these things are to be compared among themselves rather than literally composed. By this reasoning, he assigned the pyramidal shape to fire. To air, a shape having eight faces, which he calls the octahedron. To water, one having twenty faces, which he calls the Icosahedron. To earth, one having six faces, by the name of cube or die. Finally, to the universe, one possessing twelve faces. And he wishes the pyramidal shape to suit fire because it is thin, and more apt for cutting than the others, and constituted from fewer triangles, and therefore the lightest of all shapes. But the cubic shape suits earth because it is most solid and stable. The other shapes suit the middle elements, since they behave in a middle way between fire and earth regarding motion and rest. The dodecahedron, which has twelve faces, he thinks suits the world because of the twelve spheres and the twelve signs in the zodiac. He resolves solids into planes, and planes into triangles: especially into those called right-angled. Of which one is scalene (that is, "ladder-like"), possessing all unequal sides. The other is Isosceles (that is, "equal-legged"), having two equal sides. For he considers the equilateral triangle, in which there is neither a right angle nor a straight perpendicular line, to be less fit for composing planes.

He constitutes the pyramidal, octahedron, and icosahedron mass from scalenes: since a pyramid is constituted from four equilateral triangles, each of which is divided into six scalene triangles. An octahedron shape is from eight similar ones, each of which is similarly distributed into six scalene triangles. An icosahedron shape is from twenty similar ones, each of which similarly results in six scalenes. However, the isosceles triangle is called the element of the cubic shape. For four isosceles triangles meeting together complete a quadrangle. From six such quadrangles, a cube is made. Finally, he accommodated the dodecahedron shape to the world, as I was saying, because twelve forms of stars are observed in the zodiac, each of which is cut into thirty parts. Similarly, in the dodecahedron shape, one may see twelve pentagons, individually divided into five equilateral triangles: so that each one is again made of six scalene triangles; and in the whole dodecahedron mass, three hundred and sixty triangles are found, just as many portions as exist in the zodiac. Next, he treats the motions and passions of the elements. Likewise, in what way they are distinguished into parts and mixed together, and what effects he produces by the mixture. Furthermore, what the mutual commutation is of both the elements and the mixtures. Among these, he deals with observed mixtures and perfect ones: with liquids, stones, and metals. But almost all these things are wrapped in obscure metaphors after the Pythagorean fashion. We believe that Plato handed these down to his listeners in clearer words, and that Aristotle, above all others, committed the same to writing more manifesty. Of these, therefore...

FOLIO CCLXXXVII.

-> COMPENDIUM ON THE TIMAEUS <-

...requires interpretation from Aristotle’s books *On Generation and Corruption* and the *Meteorology*. He treats, moreover, of the passions <note>original: "passionibus"; here meaning physical sensations or "affections" of the body</note> which are brought upon the senses of animals by the elements. I speak of passions both hidden and manifest; of the types of pleasure and pain, which are clearly declared in the *Philebus* and in our own book *On Pleasure*. He treats furthermore of the senses themselves and their objects. He distinguishes tastes, smells, sounds, and colors.

### Again on man, as far as pertains to the soul and the body. Chapter XLI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within a classical architectural frame.</image-desc> It is worthy of consideration how much our Plato admonishes us that effort must be given so that we may know ourselves according to our strength; and that we should remember that all things beneath the moon were subjected to us by God: nor should we, contrary to our dignity, in turn subject ourselves to inferior things. For in the very beginning of the whole dispute, it was decreed that the universe be treated right up to the very birth of man. Again, in the middle of the course of the dispute, the Father <note>referring to the Demiurge or Creator</note> commands the gods to adorn man, the master of animals, whom He wishes to be according to His image and likeness and to be in command. Then, after a few things are interposed, he returns to man. Finally, near the end, he resumes what had first been instituted: namely, that the universe was to be treated right up to the birth of man. And in all things, in the Mosaic fashion <note>referring to the similarity between Plato's account and the Book of Genesis</note>, he proves that man is proposed first in this divine workmanship, and made last as if he were the end <note>the goal or purpose</note>. Therefore, now omitting other things, he repeats the divine mandate in generating man, and the obedience of the divine ministers in accomplishing this, and indeed not without justice. For he had predicted that man alone on earth would worship justice and the gods above; so that it is most agreeable to reason that the gods diligently cultivated the birth of man. 

But leaving these things aside, I will explain what follows. Again he treats of the irrational soul, established not by the primary God, but through subsequent and mobile causes; which is subject to the rational soul, sent down from heaven by God. The Platonists think the irrational soul is not so much a substantial thing as an accidental thing, like a vestige of the rational souls: in which there are indeed senses, but divided through the diverse instruments of the body, and capable of suffering <note>original: "patibiles"; meaning subject to external impressions</note>. But they place the "common sense" <term>common sense: the internal faculty that unifies data from the five individual senses</term> in the very substance of the rational soul—simple and impassible—which does not properly receive the passions inflicted by bodies, as the other sense does, but perceives, or rather judges, the passions of the other sense. 

Hence he proves the substance of the rational soul to be undivided and consisting in itself; not entrusted to the head as if to a support, but as if accommodated to it as its instrument, or compared to something similar in its own kind. But the irrational soul resides in the members in a certain way: he entrusts the part of it capable of boldness and anger to the heart, and the part devoted to concupiscence <note>desire</note> to the liver. Indeed, concerning this very liver, you will note a wonderful opinion of the Pythagoreans: namely, that this member is so tempered from a certain solidity and an equally clear smoothness that, in the manner of a mirror, it receives images of things quite easily and reflects them. Truly, just as the vehement imagination of a pregnant woman often expresses the marks of a desired thing on the most tender fetus, so a vehement notion of the mind or imagination of the sense very easily forms the mirror-like nature of the liver. In this very mirror, demons and those above fashion images of future things, as often as other images are not painted there by a completely peaceful mind. And so the marks of future things result in this mirror-like island in the mind rather than the imagination; but there they are often so confounded by other images that they cannot portend the future. This happens when either the mind is occupied with the duties of prudence distracted by governing, or the imagination is occupied with similar business. But where the prudent, continuous, and laborious discourse of reason and imagination is vacant, the images of future things leaping from the heavens into our mirror often result clearly in judgment. 

Truly, to discern what they portend is the duty of one who is accustomed to discourse prudently and sagaciously from antecedents to consequences. But such discourse hinders prophecy; so that by merit some are those who foresee, and others are those who interpret and explain the things foreseen. After these things, he pursues matter explained most widely by physicians concerning the humors and complexions and the wonderful artifice of the human body. And our Bartholomaeus Fontius <note>a famous Renaissance humanist and orator</note>, an excellent rhetorician, so admired the elegance of Plato in describing the human body that he proved in a noble oration that neither Lactantius, nor Cornelius Celsus, nor Cicero himself could approach the wonderful eloquence of Plato in describing the same thing. 

Among these things, we shall consider a religious precept: that nothing further should be affirmed concerning divine matters than what a divine oracle confirms. Likewise, that providence in composing man had no other reason at all except that he might be most fit for contemplation. Again, that natural things are not properly the causes in producing effects, but instruments of divine providence. For the principal cause of each thing is situated in that intelligence which, having a regard for the good, fabricates each thing for the sake of future convenience. Next, he defines what health of the body is, and what disease is. He distinguishes also the types of diseases, both others and fevers, and assigns the reasons for each. I have long thought that these reasons are primarily those which I read in Galen the Platonist, and I was recently confirmed in this opinion by Georgius Cyprius, a distinguished physician. For in these days, when he frequently came to me for the sake of curing my mother, and found me reading these very things, he joined the mind of Galen with the Platonic mind in a certain wonderful order. After these things, he defines the perfect health of man as the common concord of body and soul. Which he thinks is only then possessed when both the body and the soul are well-disposed in themselves, and then best composed together. "Best," I say, in a certain equal measure: so that neither the strength of the soul exceeds the measure of the body, nor the strength of the body exceeds the measure of the soul. But before he defines this perfect health, he distinguishes the disease of the soul into two: namely, ignorance and insanity. He says insanity is twofold: one kind is hidden, which...

# BOOK

...consists in a continuous and prone affection toward insanity: consider it a certain habit most inclined toward some disturbance. The other type is manifest, where by some force a disturbance is detected having increased beyond measure, as in the highest degree of desire, pleasure, fear, pain, and anger; or when vapors of the fluids <note>humors</note> enclosed in the limbs cause it, such as black bile arising from the scorching of blood, or bile, or false phlegm. Meanwhile, where he says that **no one is evil by choice** <note>original: "neminem sponte esse malum"</note> but rather on account of a depraved nature and habit: understand that a natural proclivity could have been restrained from the beginning in no small way by an opposing habit; but that a proclivity confirmed by long-standing habit can by no means be entirely uprooted, though it may nonetheless be pruned away by precise doctrine and exhortations. After this, he teaches to cultivate the body and the soul together by a certain perpetual motion of exercise. I mean moderate exercise; I mean a motion that is proper and rightly directed toward its own good, by which both, being exercised and nourished, may attain such strength that one does not succumb to the other. Plato indeed wishes the body to yield to the soul, but not to succumb in such a way that it cannot sustain the movements of the soul. He wishes for a strong and firm body, but under a far stronger soul. Next, pay attention to how much he praises exercise and how much he censures the rash use of drugs <note>pharmaceuticals</note>. Furthermore, just as he had commanded to exercise and confirm both the body and the soul by their own motions, so he commands to preserve the three powers of the soul—that is, the **rational**, the **spirited**, and the **appetitive**—each by its own motions. Nevertheless, he advises nourishing the rational power with more frequent food <note>intellectual nourishment</note>, lest it be compelled to succumb to the others. He says the **intellect** is given to man as a **daemon** <note>a guiding spirit or inner divinity</note>, specifically an internal one. For he has another, external daemon. Likewise, he describes the right habit of the body as if granted by heaven. Again, he says that he who nourishes the irrational powers beyond measure turns out **mortal**; as if teaching how it should be understood when he says a man becomes a **brute** <note>an animal</note>, that is, very similar to a brute. He adds that he who especially nourishes the mind becomes **immortal** in such a way that no part of immortality is lacking. For that immortality is imperfect which acts in perpetual motion; but perfect immortality is that which remains still, such as exists in him who now lives by intelligence alone; and he emerges from a man into a daemon. From this he also understands that when he says a man is made a brute, it is not said properly but by a certain similarity. Furthermore, from what he adds—that women arose from males—if it pleases you, he may be obscurely reporting to us that Mosaic account, that **Eve was produced from man**. But as for all the grades of brutes being multiplied little by little from a more serious fall of the rational soul: understand that our soul, on account of a certain infinity of free motion, can both rush headlong within itself into the affections and habits of all brutes, and outside itself be transferred by a certain divine judgment into similar brutes or the places of brutes as a punishment. Likewise, all the endowments of lower living things are contained in the human soul as the most perfect; and the souls of brutes are referred to ours in the very order of things and generation, as if to an end. If you accept the progression of the rational soul into others in this manner, and conversely the regression of others into this one, perhaps you will not wander from the Platonic sense. For he himself, speaking here under a **Pythagorean persona**, opportunely devises a fable similar to Pythagorean fables. And lest we should perhaps admit these things as if under historical truth, he introduces the transformations of animals no differently than poets are accustomed to do. Moreover, **Timaeus of Locri**, in his book *On the World*, confesses these things to be fabulous. Therefore, take these things in this way, and conclude the book of Timaeus with this end: which teaches us to worship God above all things, who procreated all good things by the sole benevolence of His providence. I had decided, high-minded **Lorenzo** <note>Lorenzo de' Medici</note>, to bring forth shorter points here as seemed to befit an argument, and to reserve many things for the more ample commentaries which we have already designated for the *Timaeus*. But **Filippo Valori**, a most devoted student of Platonic matters, in whose presence I put the finishing touch to the entire Platonic work in the Maian field, compelled me to pour out more here. Filippo Valori, the most noble heir of the Valori virtue; to whom I confess I owe very much, both because he greatly cultivates all excellent Platonic things, and because he is moved by a singular love toward you and all your people.

# TIMAEUS, OR ON NATURE

### FOLIO 288.

<meta>Digitized by Google. Catchword: to be narrated</meta>

...we assigned their duties. To those who, above all others, ought to wage war, we enjoined this one task: to be the protectors of the city, both against external enemies and against citizens who might subvert the republic. Thus, they should be gentle toward subjects as if they were friends by nature, but most fierce against enemies in battle. **TIMAEUS.** Exactly so. **SOCRATES.** Indeed, we discussed how a dual nature ought to exist in the souls of the guardians: both high-spirited <note>original: "iracundam," referring to the 'thumos' or spirited part of the soul</note> and particularly suited to a philosophical disposition, so that they are rightly mild toward their own people but fierce toward strangers. **TIMAEUS.** Without a doubt. **SOCRATES.** But what shall we say of their education? Were they not trained by us in gymnastic exercises, music, and other fitting disciplines? **TIMAEUS.** Very much so. **SOCRATES.** We determined that men so educated should neither possess nor consider as their own any gold, silver, or anything else; but rather, as public helpers and ministers, they should be content with only a reward—as much as those they protect provide, which seems sufficient for those living moderately. Furthermore, we wished them to use a public stipend in common and to spend it on a communal life together, so that, setting aside all other things, they might care only for virtue and guardianship. **TIMAEUS.** These things were also spoken by you in this way. **SOCRATES.** Moreover, we commanded that the nature of women be fashioned no differently than that of men, and that all pursuits, both of war and of peace, should be common to women and men alike. **TIMAEUS.** That also was said. **SOCRATES.** And do you remember what we said about the procreation of children? Perhaps, because of the novelty of the matter, you have held it firmly in mind: for we established communal marriages and children, so that no one might distinguish his own offspring, but all should consider everyone their kin—while those of roughly the same age judge themselves to be brothers and sisters in turn, they show the reverence of fathers or grandfathers to their elders, and feel toward the younger ones as if they were children and grandchildren. **TIMAEUS.** These things are also easy to remember. **SOCRATES.** Furthermore, so that the best possible offspring might be born from the very beginning, we placed magistrates of both sexes in charge of marriages. These would secretly arrange for the brave to be paired with the brave, and the base with the base, so that good women are mixed with good men; and no discord would arise from this, since in a less successful union, each would blame fortune rather than the plan of the leaders. **TIMAEUS.** We remember. **SOCRATES.** Moreover, we ordained that the offspring of the good should be nourished in the fatherland, but the others should be sent elsewhere secretly. Finally, as adults, both groups should be carefully considered: so that if any among the exiled are of good character, they may be recalled to the fatherland; and if any among the locals are seen to be affected otherwise, they should likewise be exiled. **TIMAEUS.** So it was established. **SOCRATES.** Have we now sufficiently recounted yesterday's discussion as briefly as possible? Or do you desire anything omitted by me, friend Timaeus, to be reviewed? **TIMAEUS.** Nothing at all; for these are essentially the things you had treated. **SOCRATES.** Hear next how I feel toward this republic which we have described. I will explain it to you by a comparison. Just as if someone, having looked upon animals of extraordinary beauty—whether painted or alive but standing still—should desire to see them in motion, in action, and in some contest; so I would now gladly hear someone narrating how the city described above would contend with neighboring cities: what it would demonstrate, worthy of such education and discipline, in war or peace, both in speaking and in acting toward individual states. Indeed, O Critias and Hermocrates, I am conscious that I cannot praise that city and its men according to their dignity. That I cannot is no wonder; but I think the same of the poets, both ancient and of this age—not that I despise the poetic race, but because it is evident to everyone that those devoted to imitation easily and best imitate those things in which they were educated; but things foreign and far removed from their education are difficult to emulate in deeds, and even more difficult in words. As for the Sophists <note>itinerant teachers in Ancient Greece</note>, I judge them to be skilled in speaking and in almost all other most noble arts; but because they wander daily through many cities and have no fixed homes of their own, I fear they cannot grasp, even by conjecture, how many and what kind of things men who are both philosophers and statesmen do in war and peace toward individuals in word and deed. There remains, therefore, only your profession, which excels both by nature and by the discipline of philosophy and the study of conducting affairs. Timaeus here, from Locri <note>a city in Italy governed by excellent laws</note>, is most outstanding in nobility and wealth, has performed the highest magistracies and honors, and has ascended, as I believe, to the highest peaks of all philosophy. We know Critias also has attained both of these. And that the nature and education of Hermocrates are suited to treating all these things we have mentioned, we are warned by many testimonies and cannot doubt. Therefore, when you asked yesterday for a discussion on the republic, I most willingly obeyed; for I thought that what remained of the work could be treated by no one more conveniently than by you, if you were willing. For when you have established a city fit for war, you alone of all people will in turn provide all the things that befit it. When I had finished the tasks enjoined upon me, I committed the matters to be treated to you; and you, by common consent, have now undertaken to return to me the duty of providing a banquet of discourse. I am therefore present, most ready for the promised feast. **HERMOCRATES.** We also, Socrates, as Timaeus just promised, will execute what you command to the best of our power; especially since there is no reason for excuse why we should not do so. For yesterday, when we returned from the agreed discussion to the lodging where we were received at Critias's house, we spoke of these things both on the way and again at home. He then narrated an ancient history to us, which I wish you, Critias, would now recount to Socrates, so that when he has heard it, he may judge whether it seems to contribute to the matter he ordered us to execute. **CRITIAS.** It must be done, if it so seems to Timaeus, the participant in this discussion. **TIMAEUS.** It certainly does. **CRITIAS.** Hear, Socrates, a story that is indeed strange, but full of truth, which Solon, the wisest of the Seven Sages, used to recount. He was a very close friend of Dropides, our great-grandfather, as he himself often testifies in his poems. To our grandfather Critias, as the old man himself later related to us, he once narrated the memorable deeds of this city, forgotten by the length of time and the death of men. One noble deed above the rest he recounted, which must now be told to you...

### PAGE XXXII.

I propose that we comply with your wishes and honor the goddess to whom today’s procession is dedicated with this narrative, as if with a song of hymns, as is fitting. **SOCRATES:** You speak rightly. But what is this story that Critias disclosed to you from the account of Solon <note>Solon (c. 630 – 560 BCE) was a famous Athenian lawmaker and poet</note>—not as a fictional description, but as something once actually performed by this city? **CRITIAS:** I will relate an ancient history handed down to me as a boy by my grandfather. When Critias <note>The speaker's grandfather</note> was, as he himself said, about ninety years old, and I was ten, that solemn day was being celebrated <note>The Apaturia festival</note> on which boys are called together for the singing of poems. We gathered together with other prominent and well-known boys, and a contest for singing poems was established for us by our parents. Many poems by various poets were recited from memory, and the verses of Solon were sung by many of the boys, who admired them for the novelty of the poetry. Then a certain member of our tribe—whether he truly judged it so or wished to flatter Critias—said that it seemed to him that while Solon had been the wisest in other matters, he was also the greatest poet in his songs.

<margin>See how Solon is the most noble of all. At these words, as I rightly remember, the old man was greatly delighted and said with a laugh: "If Solon..."</margin>
<margin>Solon the poet</margin>
"If Solon, O Amynander, had followed poetry not merely for the sake of relaxing his mind, but with dedicated effort and seriousness like others, and had finished the history which he began after returning from Egypt—from which he was deterred midway by seditions and other turmoils of the city—he would have been inferior, I think, neither to Homer nor Hesiod, nor any other poet." To this the other replied: "What was the subject, O Critias, that Solon intended to treat?" "Concerning the greatest deeds," he said, "once performed by this city, the memory of which has been extinguished among us by the length of time and the passing of men." "Tell me, I pray," he said, "O Critias: what was that work, and how was it done, and from whom did Solon hear it as a true account?" He said: "There is a region of Egypt called the Delta, from the vertex of which the streams of the Nile divide. Its head is called the Saitic district. In it is a very great city called Sais, from which King Amasis <note>Amasis II, a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty</note> came. The foundress of that city was a goddess whom the Egyptians call Neith, and the Greeks call Athena. Furthermore, the people themselves are friends of the Athenians and claim to be joined to them by a certain kinship. Solon related that when he traveled there, he was received with great honor. And when he inquired about the memory of antiquity from those priests who were most experienced in this matter, he said he discovered that neither he himself nor any other Greek had any real knowledge of antiquity. Once, indeed, before the priests—in order to provoke them into telling their own stories—he began to speak of the most ancient histories of Athens: of Phoroneus the first and Niobe, and after the flood of the world, of Pyrrha and Deucalion <note>The Greek 'Noah' figure</note> and their posterity, and of the times in which each event occurred. Then one of the priests, a man of great age, said: 'O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old man from Greece.' When Solon asked why he said this, the priest replied: 'Because your minds are always young; in them there is no ancient opinion derived from the commemoration of antiquity, no gray-haired knowledge. This happens to you because there have been, and will be, many and varied destructions of men. The greatest must necessarily occur either by a conflagration of fire or by floods of water; the lesser ones by various other calamities. For what is told among you—that Phaëton, son of the Sun, once ascended his father's chariot and, not keeping to his father's path, burned the earth and was himself consumed by celestial flames—though it looks like a fable, is actually true in a certain way. For at long intervals of time, there occurs a certain shift in the celestial circuits, which is necessarily followed by a vast devastation by fire. Then those who inhabit high and arid places perish more than those near the sea and rivers. Furthermore, the Nile, which is our savior in many things, protects us from such destruction. But when the gods wash away the filth of the earth with a deluge of waters, the shepherds of sheep and the ox-herds who dwell on the mountain ridges escape that danger; but your cities situated in the plains are swept to the sea by the force of the rivers. But in this region of ours, neither then nor at any other time does water descend from above onto the fields; on the contrary, it gushes upward from the bowels of the earth. For this reason, the monuments of the most ancient things are preserved among us. Therefore, wherever there is neither excessive storm of rain nor immense fire, there are always men, though sometimes fewer, sometimes more. Whatever has been done, whether by our people or yours or other nations, that is worthy of remembrance—if it has reached our ears—is preserved, inscribed in our temples. Among you and other nations, deeds are only recently being handed down in writing and monuments; but at certain cycles of time, a deluge sent from heaven devastates everything. Therefore, those who succeed are left destitute of both letters and the Muses <note>Meaning they lose their literacy and their culture/arts</note>. Thus it happens that you are like youths again and unrefined, entirely ignorant of all past things. For even those things you just recounted from your histories, O Solon, differ little from children's fables. First, because you remember only one flood, though many preceded it. Second, because you are ignorant of the most noble and excellent race of your ancestors in your region, from whom you and the rest of the Athenians are born, from a certain small seed that survived the public disaster. This remained hidden from you because those survivors and their descendants lacked the use of writing for many centuries. For before that fatal deluge of the earth, O Solon, the city of the Athenians was most excellent in the duties of both war and peace; its works and laws excelled all those whose memory has reached us.' Then he says that Solon, in admiration, earnestly besought the priests to reveal all the deeds of the ancient citizens. And one of the priests replied: 'No envy prevents this, Solon. I will speak gladly for your sake and that of your city. But most of all for the sake of the goddess who founded, nurtured, and instructed both that city of yours and this one of ours: yours first by a thousand years, receiving the seeds from the Earth and Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note>; but the deeds of this city of ours for eight thousand years are contained in our sacred writings. Therefore, of those citizens who existed in this time of nine thousand years before us, I will briefly touch upon their institutions and famous deeds for you at present.'"

# TIMAEUS OR ON NATURE

### FOLIO 289

<margin>The deeds of the Athenians</margin>
Later, when more leisure is granted, we shall explain more broadly once the book of histories has been received. But first, consider how those laws agree with these of ours. For you will find many things here similar to those. In the beginning, the priests live a life separated from the whole crowd. Then, the various kinds of craftsmen are so distinguished among themselves that each performs his own task, and no one works indiscriminately. Similarly, the works of shepherds, hunters, and farmers are distinct from one another. The soldiers also here, as you know, are segregated from all others, commanded by law to handle only matters of war. Their armor too, such as the use of shields and spears, is similar among both; we in Asia <note>The speaker is an Egyptian priest referring to the region of the Near East/Egypt</note> used these first, and the goddess <note>Athena/Neith</note> delivered these to you first, just as she did in those places. Great care for wisdom and moderation, as you see, has been in our laws from the beginning; furthermore, divination and medicine, and health, have been procured for us by divine providence. Finally, whatever disciplines pertain to these are found to be diligently established by law. With this kind of institution and order, the goddess adorned your city first from its origins, since in founding the city she chose that region which, because of the temperament of the air, would produce the most prudent minds. For as a warlike and wise goddess, she judged that a region should be chosen such as would bring forth men similar to herself. Formed by these laws or even more honorable institutions, the ancient Athenians excelled all others in every kind of virtue, as was fitting for those who were begotten and brought forth by gods. Many and wonderful deeds of your city are read in our monuments, but one exploit is preeminent in magnitude and virtue. For it is handed down that your city once resisted innumerable forces of enemies, who, having set out from the Atlantic Sea, had occupied nearly all of Europe and Asia. For then that strait was navigable, having in its mouth and, as it were, its vestibule, an island which you call the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note>; and it is said that island was larger than Libya and Asia <note>referring to North Africa and Asia Minor</note> combined. Through it, an approach lay open to other nearby islands, and from the islands to the entire continent lying in sight truly near the sea. But within the mouth itself, it is handed down that there was a harbor with a narrow bay. That open sea was a true sea, and that land was truly a continent. In this island of Atlantis, there existed a great and admirable power of kings, who ruled over that whole island and many others, and a great part of the continent; furthermore, they ruled over these parts which are near us. Indeed, they governed a third part of the world which is called Libya, as far as Egypt, and Europe as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea <note>The sea off the west coast of Italy</note>. All their force, collected into one, invaded our region, O Solon, and yours, and whatever was contained within the Pillars of Hercules. Then the virtue of your city shone forth among all nations. Since it excelled all in greatness of soul and warlike arts, partly together with other Greeks, and partly alone when others fell away, it underwent extreme dangers; it conquered the enemies, and liberty was preserved or restored to its friends. After these things, by a huge earthquake and a continuous flood of one day and night, it happened that the earth gaping open swallowed all those warlike men of yours together, and the island of Atlantis sank beneath the vast abyss. For which reason that sea remained unnavigable because of the mud of the swallowed island. This, O Socrates, is the sum of those things which the elder Critias related, having received them from Solon. But while you were discoursing yesterday about the Republic and its citizens, a certain wonder came upon me from the recollection, thinking namely that it happened by some divine chance that you related certain things very similar, and not far off, from the history of Solon. For that reason I brought forth nothing then, since from long-standing negligence I did not sufficiently remember. Therefore, I judged it better that I should repeat it to myself before I began to relate it to you. For that reason I immediately consented to your command, because I was confident that, as is most fitting in matters of this kind, I would find something that would agree with the proposed subject. So yesterday, as he says, immediately after our departure, I was fresh in these things as I then remembered them. Then from nightly vigils I recovered almost everything. Certainly, those things which we learn in childhood we are accustomed to remember longer and more firmly, as it is said. And I do not know whether I could now relate from memory all the things I heard yesterday; but as for the things I received as a boy, I would indeed wonder if any of them escaped my memory. For I heard those things with pleasure and jest, since that old man taught me willingly, and I inquired of him zealously. Wherefore, like certain marks of letters burned in indelibly, all those things remained fixed in my memory. And I narrated these things even before the rising of the sun, so that they might be more prepared for this speech along with me. But to bring myself to that at which all these things aim: I am ready, O Socrates, to relate everything not only in summary but in detail just as I heard it. We shall set down that both the city and the citizens which you fashioned as if through a fable in yesterday's dispute are a true thing. We shall judge that city to be this city of Athens, and the citizens whom you yourself devised to have been those ancestors of ours narrated by the priest. Surely these things will agree entirely, nor will it be out of place if we say your citizens were truly those ancient ones. Wherefore, sharing the matter itself among us in common, we shall all endeavor to satisfy the task imposed on us by you according to our strength. But I see, Socrates, whether I should approve this discourse, or whether we should require another? SOCRATES: But indeed, O Critias, what discourse shall we approve more than this one? Which, because of a certain proximity, wonderfully agrees with the present sacrifices of the goddess. This is the greatest thing: that not a fashioned fable, but a true history is being recounted. In what way then and from where, if this is rejected, shall we begin another dispute? Certainly it is not permitted. Therefore, with good auspices of fortune, it is necessary that you now discourse, and that I, in return for yesterday's narration, hear you today in silence. CRITIAS: Consider, Socrates, whether I may conveniently arrange a mutual banquet for you...

# BOOK
### XXXII.

...we were. It has seemed best to us that Timaeus, being the most skilled of us all in astronomy and having devoted himself most deeply to the knowledge of the nature of things, should speak first. He shall begin from the generation of the world and proceed down to the nature of the human race. Then I, taking up the human beings who were brought into existence by Timaeus and educated for the most part by Critias, shall bring them before your judgment according to the speech and law of Solon. I will make those ancient Athenians the citizens of this state—those whom the sacred writings of the Egyptians have rescued from darkness into the light, so that we may henceforth speak of them as the ancient Athenians. **SO.** <note>Socrates</note> You seem to have prepared a rich and splendid table of discussion for me. It is now up to you, Timaeus, to begin the discourse, having called upon the gods according to the law. **TI.** <note>Timaeus</note> You advise well, Socrates. For since all who are in any way possessed of a sound mind are accustomed to invoke God at the beginning of any task, whether great or small, how much more right is it for us—who are about to dispute concerning the universe, whether it was created or uncreated—unless we are utterly foolish, to invoke divine help? Therefore, we pray to all the gods and goddesses, first that what we say may be pleasing to them, and second, that we may be consistent with ourselves. So much for our prayer to the gods. But as for ourselves, we must ask that you may easily follow and that I may complete the matter at hand according to the purpose of my mind.

<margin>
At the beginning of all works, a start must be taken from God.
</margin>

At the start, it seems to me that a distinction must be made: what is that which always is, lacking any beginning <note>original: "generatione"</note>, and what is that which is indeed born but never truly "is"? The former can be grasped by the intellect through the investigation of reason, since it is always the same. The latter is reached by opinion through irrational sense, since it is born and dies and never truly exists. Furthermore, whatever is born is necessarily born from some cause. It is impossible for anything to arise without a cause. Whenever the Craftsman <note>original: "opifex"</note>, in the construction of some work, looks toward that which is always the same, and using such a model <note>original: "exemplo"</note> draws out its idea and power into the work, then that entire work must necessarily be beautiful. But whenever he looks toward that which has been created <note>a changing model</note>, the result is not beautiful at all. 

<margin>
The name of the thing about which one must dispute should be held.
</margin>

Now, as for this whole universe—let us call it the Heaven, or the World <note>original: "mundum"</note>, or whatever other name it enjoys—let us consider first what must be investigated above all in any question about the universe: whether it has always existed without any beginning of generation, or whether it was created, taking its start from some beginning. It is certainly seen and touched, and it possesses a body. All such things move the senses. Things that move the senses are perceived by opinion through the senses. It is established that such things are of the kind that are born and have been created. We have asserted that whatever is born must necessarily be born from some cause. It is difficult to find the Maker and Father of the world, and even when you have found him, it is impossible to speak of him to the common people.

<margin>
Concerning the nature of accounts.
</margin>

Again, we must consider which model the architect of the world imitated: that which is always the same and similar, or that which was created? If this world is beautiful and its Craftsman is good, he surely preferred to imitate the eternal model. If it were otherwise—which is a sin even to say—he followed a created model instead of the eternal. But since the world is the most beautiful of all created things and its author the best of all causes, there is no doubt that he followed the eternal model. Being created in this way, it was made according to that which can be grasped by reason and wisdom alone and which remains immutable. From this it follows that this world must be an image <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> of something. 

Now, to explain the reason of its origin naturally is very difficult. Therefore, let us distinguish between the image and the model in this way: accounts <note>original: "rationes" – logical explanations</note> seem to have a certain kinship with the things they express. Therefore, when one discusses a firm and stable thing that is grasped by the mind, the accounts should likewise be stable, immutable, and as far as possible, invincible. But when one disputes concerning the image of that firm and stable thing, likely <note>original: "verisimiles" – truth-like or probable</note> accounts are sufficient. These stand in the same relation to the higher accounts as the image stands to the model. For as being is to becoming, so truth is to belief. Therefore, Socrates, if many things have been said by many people concerning the gods and the generation of the world, do not be surprised, I beg you, if I cannot provide the most certain and exact accounts of them. You should consider it enough if I bring forward accounts no less probable than anyone else’s. It is fair to remember that both I who speak and you who judge are but men; if probable things are said, you should require nothing further. **SO.** You speak wisely, Timaeus. We must act as you command. We wonderfully approve of this beginning of your speech. But come, continue with the discussion.

**TI.** Let us say, then, for what cause the Author of things established generation and this universe. He was good. And a good being is never touched by envy regarding anything. Therefore, since jealousy was most foreign to him, he willed that all things should become as like himself as possible. If anyone receives this as the principal cause for the creation of the world from wise men, he receives it most correctly. 

<margin>
Order is better than disorder. Order and beauty come from the intellect.
</margin>

And so, since God wanted all things to be good and nothing to be evil as far as nature would allow, he took everything that could fall under the sense of sight—which was not calm and quiet, but moving recklessly and fluctuating—and reduced it from disordered tossing into order. For he judged this to be better. It was not and is not permitted for him who is best to make anything except that which is most beautiful. When he had thought it over, he found that among those things which are by nature subject to sight, if they lack intelligence, nothing whole would be more beautiful [than a whole that possesses intelligence]...

# TIMAEUS, OR ON NATURE
### FO. 290
L ii
<meta>catchword: stantius.</meta>

<margin>Definition of the world. The world is a living being.</margin>
...ever to be more beautiful; however, intellect cannot be granted to anything without a soul. For this reason, he <note>the Creator, often called the Demiurge</note> gave intellect to the soul, and the soul to the body; and thus he fashioned the whole world, so that it might be the most beautiful and best work of nature. Therefore, as this probable reasoning persuades us, we must say that this world is a living being, and an intelligent one, truly constituted by divine providence. This being established, let us see according to the likeness of which living being God fashioned the world. We should not think he made it like any single or specific species of animal. For if it were made like an imperfect animal, it certainly would not be beautiful. Rather, let us consider it most like that living being of which all other living beings, both individually and by kind, are parts. For that [ideal] being encompasses within itself all living things which are perceived by the mind alone, just as this world contains us and all other visible animals. Therefore, wishing to make this world most like the most beautiful and absolutely perfect of all things that can be understood, God made it one single living being, subject to sight, containing within its own limits all living beings suited to its nature. Have we then correctly said there is one world, or would it have been more correct to say there are many or countless ones?

<margin>Question concerning the formal or exemplary cause. Concerning the unity of the intelligible world.</margin>
<margin>Question: whether there is one world or many. Solution to the question.</margin>
One indeed, if it was formed according to the likeness of one. For that which contains all living things that are understood cannot have a second companion. Otherwise, there would have to be another living being which contained these two, and these two would be parts of it; and this world would be called a likeness not of those two, but more correctly of this third one. Therefore, so that this world might be most similar to the absolute living being, by being unique and one, for that reason neither two nor innumerable worlds were created; but one world was made, and it is and shall be uniquely born <note>original: "vnigenitus" — a term often used in theology to mean "only-begotten," here applied to the unique creation of the universe</note>. Since it is bodily, visible, and tangible, and since nothing can be seen without fire, and nothing can be touched without something solid, and nothing is solid without earth, God first created fire and earth in the beginning of this work. But two things alone cannot fit together well without a third; they require some middle bond between them both. Of bonds, that is the most fitting and beautiful which makes itself and the things it binds most truly one. This is achieved most of all by proportion <term>proportion: "proportio ratioque," the mathematical relationship where the parts relate to each other in a balanced way</term> and the ratio of alternating comparison. For when, among three numbers or masses or forces, the middle relates to the last as the first relates to the middle, and conversely, as the last is to the middle, so the middle is to the first, then that which is the middle becomes both first and last; and the last and first likewise become middle. Thus necessity compels that all things so bound together are the same among themselves. And when they have become the same, it results that all are one. Now, if the body of the universe were required to have only width and no depth, one middle term would have sufficed to bind itself and the extremes. But since the world required solidity, and solid things are always joined not by one but by two middle terms, God placed air and water between fire and earth, and compared them to one another as far as possible: so that as fire is to air, so air is to water; and as air is to water, so water is to earth. From this conjunction, the world was so established that it can be seen and touched. Therefore, the body of the world was forged from these four things, four in number, connected by the comparison I have described. From this, it embraces itself in harmonious friendship <note>the author uses "amicitia" (friendship) to describe the physical bonding or attraction between the elements</note>; and thus it hangs together so aptly that it cannot be dissolved in any way, except by the one who bound it.

<margin>The power of earth and fire.</margin>
<margin>Concerning the middle and the proportion of the first, the middle, and the extreme.</margin>
<margin><image-desc>A small hand-drawn pointing finger (manicule) in the margin.</image-desc></margin>
Therefore, the world received each of these four things in its entirety. From all the fire, air, water, and earth, its craftsman composed it so that he left no part or power of any of them outside. He did this for this reason: first, so that this whole living being might be as perfect as possible, made from perfect parts. Secondly, so that it might be one, since nothing was left outside from which another could be generated. Finally, so that no disease or old age might touch it. For he saw that it is the nature of a body to be harmed by the untimely arrival of heat or cold and other very violent things, and to fail when driven into disease and old age. For this cause and reason, God established the world as one whole made of all wholes: perfect from perfect parts, and free from disease and old age. To it, he gave the most suitable and becoming shape. For this living being, which was to contain all living beings within its circuit, required above all that shape in which all other shapes are contained. Therefore, he made it spherical, in which every extremity is reached by equal rays from the center. This shape is judged the most perfect of all and most similar to itself. For he thought that the similar is much more beautiful than the dissimilar. Furthermore, he polished this globe smoothly all around on the outside. Not without reason did he turn it with the greatest equality. For it did not need eyes, because nothing was left outside that could be seen. Nor did it need ears, since there was nothing outside to be heard. Nor was the world surrounded by external air so as to require breathing. Nor was there need of such members through which it might take in new nourishment or expel the waste of digested food; no loss could occur, and no addition. For there was neither a place for such things to go, nor a place from which they could come. For it nourishes itself by the consumption and aging of itself. Indeed, the world was manufactured by divine art so that it experiences and does all things within itself and by itself. For that author judged that if the world were self-sufficient, it would be more stable than if it required the assistance of others. Nor did he think hands were necessary to it, because there was nothing to be grasped nor anything to be repelled. Nor did it need feet or other members for the progress of its frame. Mo-

<margin>The world consists of all matter. To take everything so that nothing remains outside. Old age and disease come from external causes; from which see that the world is eternal due to the lack of external matter.</margin>

The world rolled in a circle.
Parts of the substance of the soul.

...motion <note>original: "motum"</note> he assigned to it, which of the seven motions is most fitting for its body and especially pertains to the mind and intelligence. Therefore, when he had led it through the same [path], in the same [way], and within itself, he caused it to be moved in a circular rotation. He separated the other six motions from it and completely freed it from their wandering and straying. For this rotation, which did not require feet, he gave it neither legs nor feet. While that God who always exists was thinking about this god who was to be <note>meaning the created universe</note>, he made it smooth, even, and equal in every direction from the center to the summit. He made a body, whole and perfect, out of bodies that were themselves whole and perfect. He placed the Soul in its center and stretched it through the whole; he even covered the body itself from the outside. He established this world as one, alone, solitary, and circular, revolving in a circle; because of its virtue, it is easily able to sustain itself, needing no other, and is sufficiently known and friendly to itself. For all these reasons, its Creator made the world a blessed god. 

However, he did not create the soul only after he had fashioned the body, as we are beginning to say now; for he who joined these would not have permitted the older to obey the younger. But we, as participants in many chance things, often speak inconsiderately and rashly. He, however, established the soul as prior to and older than the body, both in its birth and in its virtue, as that which was to rule over an obedient body. He made it from these elements and in this manner: from that substance which is indivisible and always the same, and from that which is divided among bodies, he mixed a third middle species of substance. This was to participate in the nature of the "Same" and the nature of the "Other" <note>Platonic terms for the principle of stability and the principle of change</note>. He placed this middle substance between the indivisible substance and that which is divided among bodies. Having taken these three, he tempered them all into one form. There, he used force to harmonize the nature of the "Other" (which we call diverse and which resisted mixing) with the "Same."

After he had mixed those two with the substance and made one out of three, he divided the whole again into appropriate members, each of which consisted of the three: the Same, the Other, and Substance. The division was as follows: First, he took one portion from the whole. Second, a portion double the first. Third, a portion that was one-and-a-half times <note>term: <term>sesquialtera</term> (the ratio 3:2, a musical fifth)</note> the second and triple the first. Fourth, a portion double the second. Fifth, a portion triple the third. Sixth, eight times the first. Finally, the seventh, which exceeded the first by twenty-six parts. After this, he filled the double and triple intervals, cutting off parts from the whole and placing them in the intervals so that there were two means in each—or as I might say, "mediations." One of these exceeds one extreme by the same proportion that it is exceeded by the other extreme. The other mediation exceeds one extreme by the same number that it is exceeded by the other. 

When he had taken the intervals of one-and-a-half <note>3:2 ratio</note>, one-and-one-third <note>term: <term>sesquitertia</term> (the ratio 4:3, a musical fourth)</note>, and one-and-one-eighth <note>term: <term>sesquioctaua</term> (the ratio 9:8, a whole tone)</note>, he filled all the 4:3 intervals with the 9:8 intervals in these first spaces, leaving a small fraction of each. The ratio of the number to number in this remaining fraction was that which exists between 256 and 243 <note>This is the musical "leimma" or semitone</note>. Now, the entire mixture from which he was cutting these parts was consumed by this sectioning. Then, he cut this whole strip lengthwise and made two out of one; he joined them in the middle in the shape of the Greek letter X <note>Chi</note>. He then bent them into a circle until the ends met, so that the lines were joined both with themselves and with each other at the point of intersection. He encompassed them with that motion which always revolves in the same way and in the same place. He made one circle the outer and the other the inner. He named the outer motion the nature of the "Same" and the inner motion the nature of the "Other." He turned the circle of the "Same" to the right, and the circle of the "Other" diagonally to the left. But he gave dominion to the motion of the "Same" and the similar. For he left that one alone undivided. But the inner circle he divided six times, creating seven unequal circles by double and triple intervals <note>representing the orbits of the seven known planets</note>. Since there are three of each, he commanded the circles to move in opposite directions to one another. Of the seven inner circles, he made three move at an equal speed, and the other four to move at a speed unequal to themselves and to the first three, yet according to a proper ratio. 

After the entire constitution of the soul was finished according to the mind of its Creator, he then fashioned all that is bodily within it. Matching center to center, he joined them in a fitting harmony. The soul, stretching from the middle through everything to the extremes of heaven, and poured around the outside, turning within itself, gave a divine beginning to a life of perpetual and wise existence for all time. -># TIMAEVS OR ON NATURE<-

[Page 291]
L iii

...it escapes the gaze of the eyes: possessed of reason and harmony, it was produced by the best of all things that ever are and that pertain to the intellect, being itself the most excellent of all things that have been created. Therefore, since it was composed of three parts—namely, the Same, the Other, and Essence—distinguished and compacted by the law of proportion, and because it reflects back upon itself in a circle, whenever it touches anything that has either a divisible or an indivisible essence, it turns entirely within itself to discern what that thing is. It determines to what something is the same, from what it is other or different, and in what way, where, and when it happens that such a thing exists or is acted upon, both in those things that are generated and in those that are forever the same. Furthermore, that reason which turns toward that which is the Same is truthful, whether it deals with the Other or the Same. It revolves without sound or any noise within that which moves itself. When it turns toward something sensible, and the circle of the other and different nature <note>The "Circle of the Other" refers to the movement of the planets/zodiac, while the "Circle of the Same" refers to the fixed stars.</note> correctly announces the matter throughout its whole soul, it produces firm opinions and true convictions of faith. When, on the other hand, it deals with the rational, and the circle of that which is the Same revolves fittingly and announces the matter, intellect and knowledge are necessarily perfected. If anyone says that these things occur in anything other than the soul, they will wander far from the truth.

When the father who begat the world perceived that this most beautiful image of the eternal gods <note>original: "sempiternorum deorum pulcherrimum simulacrum." Plato often refers to the cosmos or the stars as "gods."</note> which he had made was moving and alive, he was delighted with his work. Driven by this joy, he thought to make his work even more similar to that first exemplar. Therefore, just as that exemplar is an eternal living being, so he determined to make this universe such a being to the best of his power. Now, the nature of that living being is eternal, which cannot be entirely granted to a created work. Therefore, he decided to fashion a <margin>On the birth of time.</margin> moving image of eternity. While he was adorning the heavens, he made an eternal image, staying in unity but flowing according to number, which we call time. Furthermore, he commanded that days, nights, months, and years—which did not exist before the heavens—should be born at the same time the world was born; all of these are parts of time. Moreover, "was" and "will be" are species of time that has been born, which we incorrectly assign to the eternal substance. For we say of the eternal that it *is*, *was*, and *will be*. But in truth, only *is* belongs to it. *To have been* and *to be about to be* ought to be referred to the generation that proceeds through time. For those two are certain motions. But the eternal substance, since it perseveres as always the same and immobile, becomes neither older nor younger than itself through time; it never was, nor will it be in the future, nor does it receive any of those things which corporeal and mobile things are subject to by the condition of generation. Clearly, all these are species of time which imitates eternity and revolves according to number. Often we also say that what has been done *is* done; that what is being generated *is*; that what will be *is* to be done; and that what is not *is* not. None of these do we say correctly or with exact reason. But the present discussion does not require a refined debate on these matters.

Time was made together with the heavens, so that having begun together, they might also be dissolved together, if ever any dissolution should happen to them. It was made according to the exemplar of the eternal nature, so that this world might be as similar to that more excellent one as possible. For that world is the exemplar for all eternity. This world, however, has been, is, and will be through all time. By this reasoning and the counsel of God wanting to create time, the sun, the moon, and five other stars which are called "erratic" <note>The planets, from the Greek "planētēs" meaning wanderer.</note> were made, by which the number of time might be distinguished and observed. When <margin>The 7 wandering stars.</margin> God had made seven such bodies of stars, he placed them in the seven orbits which revolve in the circuit of the "other and different" nature. He placed the Moon in the first circuit above the earth. In the second, the Sun. Then he fixed the globe of Lucifer <note>The planet Venus.</note> and the sacred orb of Mercury, as it is called, in circles equal in speed to the Sun, but contrary to it in power. Thus it happens that these stars—the Sun, Lucifer, and Mercury—overtake one another and are in turn overtaken by one another. If anyone wished to run through the orders, progresses, and reasons of the other stars, it would be more work than the purpose of the work requires. Perhaps these things will be treated by us elsewhere according to the dignity of the matter, if leisure is granted.

After each of the things pertaining to the sequence of time had obtained its proper progress, and living beings—their bodies joined by vital bonds—emerged, they held to their prescribed tenor and established order. Namely, according to the oblique motion of the "other and different" nature, which is subject to the motion of the "same," those orbits perform partly a larger and partly a smaller circle; those with the smaller circle revolve more swiftly, and those with the larger, more slowly. According to the reason of the nature of the "same," those which run through most swiftly, though they overtake, seem to be overtaken by the slower ones. Indeed, that celestial whirling, revolving all their circles with a varying rotation—because they are driven by two contrary motions at once—showed that which recedes most slowly from the swiftest to be the nearest to it. Moreover, so that there might be a certain measurement of their speed and slowness, and so that the dance of all eight motions might come to light, God kindled a most brilliant light in the second circle from the earth, which we now call the Sun. By its splendor, the whole heaven might be illuminated, and all living things, whatever their nature, that are capable of number might become participants in it, learning the use of counting from the circuit of that same and similar nature. From this also the variety of night and day arose. Because of these things, there is the revolution of the one and most wise circuit. The month occurs when the moon, having traversed its circle, catches up to the sun. The year occurs when the sun has traveled through its own orb. But of the wandering of the other stars, men are ignorant...
