# BOOK XXXII
iii I

Men, except for a very few, neither call these stars by a certain name, nor measure them against one another with distinct numbers. Thus, so to speak, they do not know that the wanderings of these stars—endowed as they are with infinite number and wonderful variety—are precisely what is rightly called "time." However, it is easy to understand that the "perfect number of time" <note>This refers to the "Great Year," a cycle where all celestial bodies return to their original relative positions.</note> completes a "perfect year" only when the eight orbits—having finished their courses as measured by that same, unchanging circle—return to their original starting point. For these reasons, those stars were born which, moving through the heavens, have their own revolutions. This was done so that this entire visible living world might be as perfect as possible, in imitation of that perfect Living Being which is perceived by the mind.

<margin>The types of living beings.</margin>
Now, the Creator had fashioned all other things up to the birth of time in the image of the proposed model. But because this world did not yet contain all living beings within its embrace, the likeness of this image fell short of its model in that respect. Therefore, God filled what was lacking according to the example of that higher model. 

<margin>The four ideas of living beings.</margin>
Just as the Mind perceives how many and what kind of "Ideas" <note>In Platonic philosophy, these are the eternal, perfect "Forms" or blueprints of which physical things are mere copies.</note> are contained in the intelligible Living Being, so the Creator thought that this world should contain just as many and of the same kind. There are four such types: first is the race of celestial gods; second is the winged and air-wandering type; third is the type adapted to the waters; and fourth is the type of land-dwelling animals. The form of the divine beings <note>The stars and planets.</note> He composed mostly of fire, so that it might be the most brilliant and beautiful to behold. And because He wished it to be similar to the figure of the universe, He made it round; He placed it in the wisdom of the Best, and commanded it to follow that path. He distributed these beings throughout the whole heaven, so that a true adornment <note>original: "ornatus", a play on the Greek word "kosmos" which means both "order/world" and "ornament."</note> might be added to it everywhere from this variety. He gave the divine beings two kinds of motion: one by which they would always turn in the same place and in the same way, thinking always the same things about the same matters; and another by which they would be led forward by the rotation of the Same and the Similar. But He willed the other five motions to be foreign to them, so that each of them might be as excellent as possible. For this reason, those stars were made which do not stray <note>The "fixed stars."</note>, being divine living beings that persist forever in the same circuit. But those which "wander" <note>The planets; "planet" comes from the Greek word for "wanderer."</note> and glide with a changing logic were arranged as we said above. 

<margin>Earth, the oldest of the gods within the heavens.</margin>
Furthermore, He willed that the Earth, our nurturer, which is bound around the axis extended through the universe, should be the maker and guardian of day and night, and the first and oldest of all the gods born within the heavens. To explain the dances of these gods, their crossings, the varied revolutions and approaches of their circles—which of them are in conjunction or opposition to each other, which move forward or backward, what signs they bring to us, and at what times and in what way they are hidden or emerge, striking fear into those unskilled in such things when they rise—to try to explain all this without a diligent inspection of their models would be a vain labor. But enough of this; let the discussion of the nature of those gods who are born to be seen <note>The visible celestial bodies.</note> come to an end.

As for the other spirits who are called "daemons," <note>original: "daemones". In this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or minor traditional deities.</note> to know and declare their origin is a task greater than our genius can bear. We must therefore believe those ancient men who, as they themselves said, were the descendants of gods and knew their own parents best. It is impossible, of course, to disbelieve the children of gods, even if their speech is not confirmed by necessary or probable reasons. But because they affirmed they were speaking of their own family matters, we shall follow the law and grant them our faith. Thus, let the generation of these gods be held and described as it was handed down by them: Oceanus and Tethys are said to have been the children of Earth and Heaven. From them were born Phorcys, Saturn, and Rhea, and the rest of their siblings. From Saturn and Rhea were born Jupiter and Juno, and all the others whom we daily hear mentioned as their brothers. From these, in turn, others were born as it is handed down.

After all these were born—both the gods who revolve in the heaven manifest to our eyes, and those who become visible to us only as far as they themselves wish—the Creator of the world spoke to them thus: "Gods of gods, of whom I am the maker and father, attend to this. The things made by me are, by my will, indissoluble. For indeed, anything that is bound together can be dissolved; but it is the mark of an evil will to wish to dissolve that which is beautifully composed and well-ordered. Therefore, because you have been generated, you are not entirely immortal or indissoluble. Yet you shall never be dissolved, nor shall you undergo the fate of death. For my will is a greater and more powerful bond for your preservation than those links by which you were bound when you were being born. But now, learn what I command. Three types of mortals still remain for us to generate; without their birth, the heaven will be incomplete. For it will not contain all types of living beings within its scope. Yet it must contain them if the world is to be entirely perfect. If these were created by me alone and granted life, they would be equal to gods. Therefore, turn yourselves according to your nature to the generation of living beings, so that you may imitate my power which I used in your own birth. And as for that part of the animal which is to be such that it is fit to share a name with the immortals—that which is called divine and shall hold sovereignty and cultivate justice together with you—I shall deliver the seed and beginning to you. It is right for you to execute the rest: weaving the mortal onto the immortal nature, you shall make and generate living beings; you shall provide them with food to make them grow, and receive them back again when they are consumed."

Having spoken thus, He poured the remains of the previous mixing into the same bowl <note>original: "cratere", referring to the metaphorical vessel used to mix the World-Soul.</note> in which He had tempered and mixed the soul of the entire universe. He mixed them in somewhat the same way, though not...

...yet similarly perfect: but falling short of the first in the second and third degrees. Finally, when he had established the whole universe, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars, assigning one to each. <margin>One star is assigned to each kind of soul.</margin> And placing them upon these stars as if on a chariot, he showed them the nature of the universe and declared the laws of fate. He showed them that the first birth would be one and the same for all in a certain order, so that no one might receive less than another. After the souls were sown, as if like seeds, into the various instruments of time <note>The "instruments of time" refers to the planets and stars whose movements create the measurement of time.</note> suited to each, he declared that a living being would be born which, of all animals, would be most devoted to divine worship. He stated that human nature would be twofold, of which the superior kind would be that which is called by the name of "man." But when souls were implanted into bodies by a certain necessity, and as something was added to their bodies and something in turn departed <note>A reference to the processes of nutrition, growth, and decay.</note>, he declared that first, of necessity, a single internal sense, common to all and joined to their nature, would be stirred there by violent passions. Secondly, he said there would be love mixed with pleasure and pain, and after these, fear and anger, <margin>Love mixed with pleasure and pain.</margin> and whatever follows from these or stands apart as their opposites. Those who overcome these passions will live justly; but those who are overcome by them will live unjustly. And he who rightly completes the course of living given by nature shall return to that star to which he was assigned and lead a blessed life. But he who acts otherwise shall be forced at his second birth to be changed in sex and become a woman. And if even then he does not cease from sinning, he shall be transformed into the nature of beasts, similar to his own character in proportion to his depravity. Nor shall he cease from these changes and labors until he follows that innate revolution of the "same and similar" nature within himself, and, subduing the turbulent and manifold disturbances later contracted from fire, water, air, and earth, he calms them by reason and returns to his first and best state. When he had decreed these things to them—so that he himself might not be the cause of any future wickedness—he sowed some into the earth, some into the moon, and others into other instruments of time, as if scattering seed. After this sowing, he commanded the younger gods <note>The "younger gods" are the created deities (like the planets or traditional Greek gods) who perform the work of creating mortal bodies, as the supreme Demiurge creates only the immortal parts.</note> to perform the remaining task: to fashion mortal bodies and to add whatever else was required for the human soul, to govern it, and to guide the nature of the mortal animal as excellently and beautifully as possible, unless the creature should become the cause of its own evils. And he who arranged all these things remained duly in his own state. While he remained so, his children, having learned their father's order, followed it immediately. And so, having received from him the immortal principle of the mortal creature, they imitated their creator and borrowed particles of fire, air, water, and earth from the world—which they would eventually return—and they joined these together. They did not use those same indissoluble bonds by which they themselves were bound, but joined them with bonds that could not be seen due to their smallness, making one body out of all by joining them with many such "bolts." And into this body, which was subject to constant inflow and outflow, they bound the revolutions of the divine soul. Thus these revolutions, immersed in a deep river, neither held nor were held, but were carried along by force and themselves carried things along. From this it happened that the whole animal moved, but without order and with a certain haphazard tossing. It happened to wander through six motions, progressing everywhere through the six differences of place: namely, forward and backward, to the right and left, upward and downward. But while the flood of nutrition flowed in and out, a much greater disturbance followed from passions brought in from the outside, whenever a body encountered the shock of external fire, or was harmed by the hardness of earth, or the moisture of water, or the blast of air. Furthermore, the motions from all these things pass through the body to the soul; for this reason, both in the beginning and now, they are called "senses." <note>Latin: *sensus* (perceptions).</note> From the start, these sensations stir many great motions, and with that river constantly flowing, these waves violently shake the revolutions of the soul. They completely block the revolution of the "Same" <note>The "Circle of the Same" represents rational, consistent thought; the "Circle of the Other" represents shifting opinion and sensory data.</note> and similar nature in its course, and they pull apart the revolution of the "Other," to such an extent that those three intervals of double and triple ratios, and the means and connections of the 4/3, 3/2, and 9/8 ratios <note>These are the musical and mathematical ratios used to construct the soul's harmony, which are disrupted by the chaos of physical birth.</note>—which can be dissolved by no one except the one who joined them—are twisted in every kind of revolution. They induce all sorts of bends and variations of the spheres, so that the orbits themselves, barely connected to each other, are carried along, but carried along without reason, now in opposition, now at an angle, now in a sort of upside-down arrangement. It is as if someone were to plant his head on the ground and raise his feet high; then I think, both for him who is so affected and for those looking on, right parts seem left and left parts seem right. And so, when the orbits of the soul suffer this and other such things, if they encounter something external of the same or another kind, they judge falsely what is the "same" as something else and what is "different." Therefore they are then lying and mindless, and there is no ruling or leading revolution in them then. And when sensations from the outside strike the soul more violently and take possession of it entirely, then those revolutions which are in truth enslaved and serving seem to dominate. For these reasons, in the beginning, when the soul is enclosed in the bonds of a mortal body, it is made mindless. But after the stream of nutrition and growth flows more gently and less forcefully, <margin>Why the elderly are wise.</margin> and the revolutions of the soul complete their journey with a calmer motion, and in the process of time...

...they become stronger and are restored to a form consistent with their nature. Then, the direct revolutions of each circle <note>In Platonic cosmology, the soul is composed of the "Circle of the Same" (rationality) and the "Circle of the Different" (opinion/sensation). In a healthy person, these circles rotate correctly.</note> properly discern the nature of both the "Same" and the "Other," making the person so constituted prudent. If someone adds appropriate discipline and learning to a right education and nourishment, they will escape the most grievous disease <note>original: "morbo grauissimo" — here referring to ignorance or folly</note> and emerge entirely healthy and whole. But if they neglect this, they enter upon a "lame" path of life, becoming like a maimed person, and entirely useless, they fall back down to the underworld.

These things, however, happen after birth. Now we must discuss the first composition of man more precisely, and show by probable reasoning the cause and providence of the gods by which each member of the body was adapted to the specific duties of the soul.

In the beginning, the gods shaped the form of the head into the roundness of the universe, and within it, they established those two divine circuits of the soul. <margin>The head is the most divine member.</margin> The head is the most divine member of the body and the ruler of all the rest; the gods commanded the whole connected body to be subject to it and obey it. They devised that it should be the master of all possible motions. However, because the earth is uneven and rough—partly sloping up and partly down—the head would not be able to pass through these obstacles without injury if it crawled upon the ground or rolled along the surface. To avoid this evil, the gods provided this tall, upright habit of the body <margin>Uprightness.</margin> as a vehicle for the head to progress more easily. Furthermore, they attached four long and flexible limbs to the body, which, by divine providence, could move easily to grasp objects, stand, stay, and walk through all places, while the head remained on top as the dwelling place of the most divine and sacred part. For this reason, they gave us legs and hands.

Believing the front parts to be more excellent than the back and more fit for commanding, they willed that we should move primarily in a forward direction. It was also necessary that the front be distinct and different. Therefore, they first added the face to the globe of the head and assigned to the face the instruments that would assist the soul's foresight; they decreed that the natural command of man should consist in this front part.

Of all parts of the face, the "light-bearing" <term>luciferi: light-bringing or light-bearing orbits</term> orbs of the eyes shine forth first. <margin>Many things concerning the eyes.</margin> The gods made the eyes participants in that specific fire which does not burn but provides a gentle light for the day. They willed that the internal fire of our body—a pure kinsman of the external fire—should flow out through the eyes. This gentle fire is collected throughout the eye, but its purest part flies out through the solid and narrow center, while the coarser fire is filtered out. Therefore, when the light of day meets the ray of vision, these two similar fires—the internal and external—meet and mix, forming a single "domestic body" of light wherever the eyes are directed. Because this body of light is uniform, whatever it touches (or whatever touches it) transmits that motion through the body and into the soul, creating the sensation we call <term>visus: vision</term>.

But when the kindred fire of the day departs into night, the ray of vision vanishes. For as it breaks out into air that is unlike itself, it is changed and extinguished, having no common nature with the dark air. Therefore, it ceases to see and brings on sleep. Indeed, the gods engineered the healthy protection of the eyelids for the eyes. When these are closed, the power of the internal fire is restrained, and its compression soothes the internal motions, bringing about rest. If deep sleep occupies us because the motions are very quiet, few dreams occur. But if some more violent motions remain from our waking hours, they create dream-images according to their nature and origin, and the memory of these remains when we wake.

Regarding the images that appear in mirrors <note>Plato explains reflections as the meeting of the internal eye-fire and the external fire of the object on the smooth surface of the mirror.</note> or in transparent and smooth surfaces, they are easy to understand. They arise necessarily from the communion and meeting of both fires—the internal and the external—on a polished surface. In a flat mirror, we see the right side as the left because we are touching the opposite parts of the eye in an unusual way. However, right corresponds to right and left to left when the light "leaps across" after being mixed. This occurs when the mirror has a curved or concave surface that twists the right part of the eye's ray to the left of the mirror and vice versa. If the mirror is turned vertically, it makes the face appear upside down, as the upper part of the light is turned to the bottom.

All these things belong to the class of <term>adiuuant causas: auxiliary causes</term>, which God uses as ministers to achieve the idea of the "Best" as far as possible. <margin>The philosopher must seek the principal causes of nature.</margin> But most people think these are not merely helpers but the primary causes of everything—attributing everything to heat, cold, density, and rarity. Such things, however, lack reason and mind. It is proper that Mind is possessed by nothing except the Soul, and Soul is invisible. But fire, water, air, and earth are visible bodies. # TIMAEUS OR NATURE

### LEAF CCXCIII.

...principal causes of a wise nature; and to consider those causes which are moved by others by necessity, but which in turn move other things, as secondary causes. <note>Plato distinguishes between "Primary Causes"—the intelligent intentions of the gods—and "Secondary Causes"—the physical mechanisms (like light or heat) that the gods use to achieve their goals.</note> Therefore, I believe we must proceed in this way: we should distinguish between both kinds of causes, treating separately those which, with intelligence, are the creators of beautiful and good things, and those which, being devoid of wisdom, produce random effects without order. I believe enough has been said regarding the secondary causes of the eyes and the power they possess. Now, I believe we must explain the greatest work for which the gods profitably granted them to us. For I believe the eyes have brought us the knowledge of the best things. Indeed, these very discussions about the world would never have been discovered if neither the stars, nor the sun, nor the heavens could have been seen. <margin>Philosophy is the greatest gift of the gods. Why eyes were given to humans.</margin> The knowledge of day and night, arising from the eyes, has allowed us to measure the cycles of months and years through counting, to know time, and to investigate the order of the whole of nature. From these things, we have attained **Philosophy**, a good so great that no gift from the gods more significant has ever been given, nor ever shall be given, to the mortal race. This, I say, is the greatest benefit of the eyes. I pass over other minor benefits. Those who are strangers to philosophy, if they were deprived of sight and complained, would complain in vain. For us, however, it must be asserted that God generated eyes for this primary reason: so that, having observed the circuits of the mind that are carried out in the heavens, we might apply them to the use of our own mind; and that we might call back the wanderings of our own thought—which are related to those celestial circuits, yet troubled in some way—to the calm temperament of the heavens. Once we have recognized them and perceived the order of each according to right reason and nature, we should imitate the revolutions of God, <note>original: "conuersiones dei" — referring to the perfectly circular and predictable movements of the stars and planets, which Plato considers divine.</note> which are performed without any error, and by their example, we should steady the wandering and erratic movements of our own thoughts.

<margin>Concerning voice and hearing.</margin> I also believe the gods gave us voice and hearing for the same purpose. For speech pertains to these very things and is of the greatest use. Every use of the musical voice is granted for the sake of harmony. And harmony, which possesses motions congruent and related to the wanderings of our soul, is useful to a person who uses the Muses with wisdom—not for irrational pleasure, as it seems to be used now, but it was given by the Muses so that through it we might compose the discordant circuit of the soul and bring it back into a concordant harmony with itself. Rhythm was also granted for this purpose: so that we might most fittingly temper that state within us which is immoderate and lacking in grace.

Thus far, with few exceptions, we have treated the works of the mind. However, we must also speak of those things which **Necessity** <term>Necessity (Ananke): In Plato's thought, this represents the "brute facts" of matter and physics that the divine Mind must persuade or work with to create the world.</term> introduces. For the generation of this world is a mixture resulting from the union of necessity and mind. <margin>The generation of the world mixed from necessity and mind.</margin> Since mind ruled over necessity by persuading it to lead most things toward the best possible outcomes, and necessity itself yielded to wise persuasion in this way, the foundations of this world were established. Therefore, he who intends to truly narrate the constitution of the world must also mix in the species of the "erratic cause," according to the instinct of nature itself. This will be done conveniently if, having taken a suitable principle for these very things, we discuss them from their origin, just as we did with the superior things. Let us, then, consider the nature and the passions of **fire, water, air, and earth** prior to the generation of the heavens. <margin>See the question whether the universe is one principle or many.</margin> To this point, no one has truly shown their generation; instead, we speak of them as if it were already known what fire and the rest are, and we establish them as the "elements" <note>original: "elementorum" — the Latin translates the Greek *stoicheia*, which means both "letters of the alphabet" and "fundamental principles." Plato argues these four things are too complex to even be called "letters."</note> of the world, when they ought not to be held as even the equivalent of syllables, let alone elements, among men who are in any way composed in mind.

For the present, we believe nothing should be said regarding the first principle of all things—whether it be one or many, or whatever else it may be called. Nothing hinders this discussion except the difficulty of expressing our views on these matters in our current mode of inquiry. You should not expect it of me, nor could I persuade myself that I could rightly undertake so great a task. However, as I said from the beginning, we shall preserve the force of **probability**, and we will strive to yield to no one in assigning probable reasons regarding these matters. Thus, we shall explain both the parts and the whole from the beginning. Let us now pray to God, the preserver of this discussion, that He may lead us out of this strange and unusual exposition toward a probable teaching; and thus, having been instructed, let us begin the discourse.

<margin>He repeats the discussion about the same things as before, concerning matter and necessity.</margin> But let us draw this discussion of the universe from a broader division than before. Previously, the division was made into two species. Now, a **third genus** must be added. For two were sufficient in the previous sections: one serving as the **Model**, which is always the same and understood by intelligence alone; the other being the **Image** derived from this model, subject to generation and sight. Though we thought these two were enough, we did not add a third. But now, reason seems to compel us to try to declare a difficult and obscure species. What power, then, or what nature should it be thought to have? This especially: that it is the **receptacle** <note>Also called the "Chora," this is the space or "matrix" in which physical things take shape.</note> of all these things that are generated, and, as it were, their **nurse**. Although this is truly said, it must be stated somewhat more clearly. That is indeed an arduous task, especially because to demonstrate this thing, it is first necessary to doubt and inquire concerning fire and the rest of the things called "elements": which of these should be called "water" rather than "fire," or "air" rather than "earth," or why any one thing should be called by one name rather than by all. It is difficult to assert anything certain and firm about these. In what way, then, and by what reason, and what probable thing shall we say in an inquiry of this kind? In the first place, that body which we just now named water...

# BOOK

### PAGE XXXII.

...when it solidifies into a solid mass, it appears to become stone and earth; but when it melts and flows away, it becomes spirit and air. Likewise, air that is burnt becomes fire. Fire, when extinguished and made more "thick" or corporeal, creates air. In turn, when air is thickened further, it condenses into mists and clouds. When these are compressed even more, rain flows down. From water, again, earth and stones are born. And so we see that all these things, in a certain circuit, <margin>Because fire and other elements are not truly "this certain thing" but rather "a thing of such a kind."</margin> grant to each other in turn the powers and nourishment of creation. Since these things never appear to remain the same, who could—without blushing or fearing they might be proven wrong—firmly call any one of them "this" rather than "that"? Surely no one. Therefore, the safest way of speaking about these things is as follows: That which we see always being formed in different ways at different times (often resembling the shape of fire) is not actually <term>fire as a "this"</term> <note>original: "hoc aliquid"; a philosophical term meaning a distinct, stable substance</note>, but rather "such a thing"—that is, something "fiery." Nor is water a "this," but rather something "watery." Nor should anything else be spoken of as having any stability. Finally, these things should not even be designated by pronouns, <margin>See how the things they call elements cannot even be pointed to by pronouns.</margin> which we usually use when pointing something out and saying "this" or "that." For they flee; they do not wait for the demonstration that designates them as "this" or "belonging to this" or "to this," nor do they wait for any name that treats them as existing and stable things. Therefore, we ought not to call all such things "this" or "that," but rather "of such a kind," or "such" because of some similarity. We should call fire "such" everywhere, and do the same for all other things that are created. But that in which each of these appears to come into being and then dissolve—that alone, I believe, should be called by the pronouns by which we signify "this" or "that." However, that underlying thing should by no means be called "of such a kind" (meaning hot or white, or any such quality or its opposite).

But let us explain what we mean more clearly. <margin>See how matter is demonstrated through an analogy.</margin> Suppose someone were to constantly reshape all kinds of figures out of one and the same material of gold, turning them into one thing after another. If someone were to point to one of those figures and ask what it is, we could most truly and safely answer that "it is gold." But to say that it is a triangle or any of the other shapes being impressed upon it—which are constantly changing—as if they were real, would not be right. Indeed, we ought to be content with that one safest answer. The same reasoning applies to that nature which receives all bodies. <margin>Matter never recedes from its potentiality.</margin> It must always be called the same. Indeed, it never recedes from its own potential power. For it always receives all things, and it never takes on any form similar to those things in any way. It is, in truth, the subject for the shaping of every nature. <margin>Those things that occur in matter are images of true things.</margin> Being stirred and given shape by the things that enter it, it appears different at different times. But the things that enter and exit are <term>images</term> <note>original: "simulacra"</note> of things that truly and always exist, shaped by those very things that truly exist in a marvelous and scarcely explainable way, as we shall describe hereafter. For the present, three "kinds" must be assumed. One is that which is generated. Another is that in which it is generated. The third is that from which the thing being born draws its likeness. Therefore, it is fitting to compare them like this: That which receives is like a **mother**. That from which it receives is like a **father**. And the nature between them is like the **offspring**. But it must be understood that since there must be an <margin>See how matter is formless: and how, being about to receive, it lacks what it receives.</margin> image of things distinguished by every variety of form, that very "womb" of formation will never be well-prepared unless it is formless, and by its own nature lacks all the forms it is intended to receive. For if it were similar to any of those things it receives, then when it tried to take on a nature contrary to its own or something entirely different, it could not express that likeness and image at all, because it would be showing its own form. Thus, it happens that that which is to receive all kinds of things must have no form of its own. Just as those who intend to create sweet-smelling ointments first prepare the liquid material (which they want to season with a certain scent) so that it has no scent of its own; and those who wish to impress figures into soft materials that yield to the touch do not allow any prior shape to appear in them, but polish them with an exact smoothness: so too, that which is to be correctly shaped into images of all the eternal things must, by its own nature, lack all those forms. For this reason, let us not say that the "mother" and receptacle of the universe—which is both created and visible to all the senses—is earth, or air, or fire, or water, nor anything constituted from these, nor anything from which these themselves subsist. Let us rather call it a certain invisible and formless species, capable of containing all things, which in a certain ambiguous and scarcely explainable way participates in the divine and intelligible nature. In itself, it cannot be grasped at all. But as far as we can reach its nature from what has been said, we can rightly say this: fire appears to be the "ignited" part of it; water, the "moistened" part; and similarly for earth and air, insofar as it receives their images.

But we must consider these things by distinguishing them through reason: is there such a thing as a "fire" existing by itself, separate from matter and remaining in itself? And do the other things we often say "exist by themselves" truly do so? Or are these things only what we perceive with the senses of the body, and truth is contained only in them? Is it the case that there is nothing else besides these anywhere, and that we are speaking in vain when we suggest there is an "intelligible species" for each thing—that these are nothing but words? <margin>He briefly proves that Ideas (Forms) exist.</margin> This is not something to be asserted rashly or without examination, nor should we add long arguments to our present discussion (which is already long by nature) if they do not pertain to the matter. However, a definition that captures great things in a few words would be very timely. Thus, I shall give my own opinion on this matter. If **intellect** and **true opinion** are two different things...

# TIMAEUS, OR ON NATURE

### PAGE CCXCIIII

...there are two kinds, it is necessary that there are species of this sort which exist by themselves and are understood by the intellect rather than the senses. But if, as it seems to some, true opinion differs not at all from the intellect, then all things which the bodily senses touch must be considered certain. Yet I believe we must say there are two: because they are created separately and are unlike each other. Indeed, instruction <note>original: "doctrina"</note> introduces us to the one, while persuasion introduces us to the other. The former is always accompanied by true reason, but the latter is without reason. The former cannot be changed by any persuasion, while the latter is subject to change. Every man participates in true opinion, but indeed all the gods and <margin>Few men are participants in the intellect.</margin> only a very few men participate in the intellect. Since these things are so, we must confess that there is a species that is always the same, without beginning or destruction, which neither receives anything else into itself from elsewhere, nor itself proceeds into anything else; it is perceived by no sense of the body. This is what pertains to the intellect alone, and is the proper object of its attention. 

But there is something else after this which shares the name of the first thing but not the reason; it carries a likeness to it, is created, and is manifest to the senses. It is always carried and sustained by another, born in some place, and then departs from it; it is to be grasped by opinion through the senses. 

The third kind is "Place," <margin>That matter is "place."</margin> which never perishes, but provides a seat for all things that are born. It is grasped without the sense of touch, by a certain <term>bastard reason</term> <note>original: "adulterina quadam ratione"; Plato uses this phrase to describe how we "know" space—not by the senses and not by pure logic, but by a strange, indirect intuition</note> and is scarcely believable. Finally, when we look toward this place with our minds, we dream in a certain way, and we think it necessary that whatever exists must be positioned in some place and occupy some region. We believe that what is neither on earth nor in heaven simply does not exist. Because we are occupied by these and similar "dreams," we are unable to distinguish these things from the truly existing nature that belongs to a wide-awake state. 

Therefore, we cannot even discern that an image—since it does not even own that in which it is created, but is always the phantom of something else—rightly belongs in something else; in this way, it participates in essence in some manner, for otherwise it could not exist at all. But for that which truly exists, this true and exquisite reason supports it, teaching that as long as one thing is different from another, neither can ever exist within the other so as to become one and two at the same time. 

This, finally, is the summary of my mind's judgment: that there are, and were even before the birth of the heavens, these three things in a triple order: Being, Place, and Generation. 

The "Nurse of Generation" <note>This refers to the "Receptacle" or Space, which "nurses" the physical elements into being</note> is fiery and moist, receiving the forms of earth and air, and suffering the experiences that follow these; she appears to the sight in every possible form. But because she is filled with forces that are neither similar nor balanced, she is in no part in equilibrium. Instead, swaying and tilting unequally in every direction, she is shaken by those things we have mentioned, and being moved, she in turn shakes them. By this impulse, they are tossed and separated in different directions, just as we see in the <term>cleansing of grain</term> <note>original: "frumenti purgatione"; referring to the use of a winnowing fan or sieve to separate wheat from chaff</note> when the heavy and solid pieces are carried one way, and the rare and light pieces another. So then, those four kinds <note>The four elements: fire, earth, air, and water</note> were moved by their own receptacle, which acted like a tumultuous winnowing tool, separating the most dissimilar things far from each other and bringing the most similar together. Thus, even before the world was ordered, they were divided into their own places; but in them, there was neither reason nor measure. 

But when it pleased God that all things should be reduced to measure, He first took fire, earth, air, and water—which indeed bore some traces of their elements, but were in such a state as things are when God is absent—and He adorned them with distinct figures, species, and numbers. Let this judgment always be held as certain and beyond doubt above all others: that God ordered these things, when they were not yet so, as beautifully and excellently as they could possibly be made. 

Now, the arrangement and birth of these elements must be demonstrated one by one, using a new and unusual kind of demonstration; but it will be plain and clear to you, who have traveled all the paths of noble learning. 

In the beginning, no one will doubt that fire, earth, water, and air are bodies. <margin>The arrangements and births of the elements.</margin> Every kind of body has depth. It is necessary that depth consists of planes. Furthermore, the straightness of a plane base is constituted of triangles. All triangles have their beginning from two types, each having one right angle and two acute angles. In one type, the acute angles are equal (the sides being equal); in the other, they are unequal (the sides being distributed unequally). Therefore, proceeding by probable reasons joined to necessity, let us lay down the origin of fire and the other bodies. Their higher principles are known only to God and to whoever is a friend of God. 

Let us see, then, by what best reason these four most beautiful bodies are made—dissimilar to one another, but able to be dissolved into one another and generated from one another. If we grasp this, we shall hold the truth about the generation of fire and earth and those things which, by a preserved ratio, become the intermediates between them. Then we shall yield to no one who says there are bodies more beautiful to the eyes than these. We must try, therefore, to constitute the four kinds of bodies, excelling in beauty, and thus assert that we have sufficiently understood their nature. 

Of the two <margin>Isosceles</margin> triangles, the Isosceles (that which consists of equal "legs") has only one nature; but the one that is longer on one side <note>The scalene triangle</note> has infinite natures. Therefore, if we wish to begin correctly, we must choose the most beautiful among the infinite. And if someone wishes to bring a more beautiful choice for the constitution of these things, his opinion shall prevail not as an adversary's, but as a friend's. Thus, setting the others aside, we posit one as the most beautiful of many triangles: the one from which an equilateral triangle is formed as a third. The reason...

# BOOK
### PAGE XXXII.

The reason why this is so would be a long story to tell. But for him who discovers it to be so through diligent investigation, a sweet reward of victory awaits. Let us take two triangles from among the many: from which the bodies of the others are composed. Let one of these be the **Isosceles** <note>A triangle with two equal sides.</note>, consisting of equal legs. But let the other be that which always has its longer side three times greater in power <note>original: "potentia triplo maius"; this refers to the 30-60-90 triangle, where the square of the long leg is three times the square of the short leg (1² vs (√3)²).</note> than the shorter side. What these triangles have done, we have discussed at length above; now we must distinguish them more clearly. It seemed to us—though perhaps not entirely correctly—that all four types of elements were generated from one another. In truth, the four types are generated from the triangles we have chosen. Three indeed come from one type (the triangle with unequal sides). But the fourth is uniquely composed from the isosceles triangle. Therefore, not all elements can be broken down and changed into one another in a way where many small things become a few large ones, or the reverse. Certainly, three of them can. Since these were all made from one source, when larger ones are dissolved, they constitute many small ones from the same parts, having obtained small shapes suited to themselves. Conversely, when many small ones are dispersed through the triangles and expanded, they make a single number of one mass, and complete another single, large species. Let these things suffice for what has been said so far regarding their mutual generation. It remains for me to say what sort of species each of them became, and from what concurring numbers they were heaped together.

The first species will be that which is composed of the fewest parts: its element is that which has a longer side twice the size of the shorter side <note>original: "duplo maius"; referring to the ratio of the hypotenuse to the shortest side in a 30-60-90 triangle.</note>. When two of this kind are composed along the diagonal, and this is done three times, and the shorter sides are led to the same center, one equilateral triangle is made out of six triangles.

<margin>
<image-desc>A diagram of an equilateral triangle divided into six smaller right-angled triangles by lines from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.</image-desc>
</margin>

When four of these equilateral triangles are composed so that three plane angles meet, they make one solid angle: which follows next in birth as the most obtuse of all plane angles. And with four such solid angles being born, the **first solid species** <note>The Tetrahedron (Pyramid), which Plato identifies as Fire.</note> arises, which divides the entire circumference into equal and similar parts. 

The **second species** <note>The Octahedron, identified as Air.</note> is made from the same triangles, but constituted of eight equilateral triangles making one solid angle from four planes. With six such angles made, it completes the second body. 

The **third species** <note>The Icosahedron, identified as Water.</note> is born from one hundred and twenty elements joined together, and twelve solid angles; any one of these is contained by five plane equilateral triangles, having twenty equilateral bases. Thus, that other element [the scalene triangle] has generated these things so far. 

Truly, the **Isosceles triangle** generated the nature of the **fourth kind** <note>The Cube, identified as Earth.</note>, being constituted according to four triangles, gathering right angles at the center and making one equilateral quadrilateral [a square]. Six of these squares joined together produced eight solid angles, each of which is fitted together by three plane right angles. The figure of the body thus constituted is made cubic, having obtained six plane equilateral quadrilateral bases. 

There is also a **fifth composition** <note>The Dodecahedron, which has 12 pentagonal faces.</note> which God used for the constitution of the universe: he described and figured it. Contemplating this, one might not absurdly doubt whether we should consider the worlds to be infinite or finite. To say they are infinite will be thought the mark of one who has no skill in the knowledge of things worthy of being known. But to inquire whether one world or five have truly been born, he will think at least less absurd. Our reason indeed asserts that this one world was born by likely proof. Another person, looking at other things, will think otherwise. But these matters must be set aside. 

And now let us distribute the four kinds we digested a little while ago into **fire, earth, water, and air**. Let us assign the **cubic** species to Earth. For of all four, Earth is the most immobile, and the most compact of all bodily things. It is necessary that such a thing be made especially of that which possesses the firmest and safest bases. Furthermore, among the triangles positioned from the beginning, those which are equilateral possess a firmer and safer base than those with unequal sides. And the equilateral quadrilateral [the square] composed of both necessarily results in something more stable than the triangle, both as a whole and in its parts. Wherefore, if we wish to follow convenient and probable reason, let us attribute this to Earth. 

Then to **Water**, let us give that which is the most immobile of the remaining three; to **Fire** that which is most mobile; and to **Air** the middle. And the smallest body to fire: the largest to water: the middle to air. Also the sharpest to fire: the second from this to air: the third to water. Of all these, that which has the fewest bases must necessarily be the fastest. For it is the most ready to penetrate, being indeed the sharpest of all. It is also the lightest, since it consists of the fewest of those same parts. That which is second should have these qualities in the second place. The third in the third. Therefore, according to right and probable reason, let the solid species of the **Pyramid** be the element and seed of Fire. Let us attribute the second species in generation to Air, and the third to Water. 

Regarding all these things, which are so small, it must be thought that if individual units of each kind are taken, none of them can be seen by us because of their smallness; but if many are gathered together, their masses and magnitudes are seen. Furthermore, all these things are connected and proportioned in their multitudes, motions, and powers, as exactly as the nature of Necessity, being willing and persuaded, was able to receive. From all these things whose kinds we have narrated above, the matter seems to hold itself reasonably. When Earth falls into Fire, being dissolved by its sharpness, it is carried along, having been resolved into fire, or air, or water; until its parts meet again, and being joined to each other, they remake Earth. For it would never migrate into another species. Furthermore, water, [when broken] by fire or air...

# TIMAEUS, OR ON NATURE, FOLIO 295.

...divided into parts, one [part of water], once its parts are reconciled, makes one body of fire and two of air: <note>This refers to the face-count of the Platonic solids: Water (an icosahedron with 20 faces) can break down and reform into two parts of Air (octahedrons with 8 faces each) and one part of Fire (a tetrahedron with 4 faces). 20 = 8 + 8 + 4.</note> while two portions of air from one dissolved part make two bodies of fire. Again, whenever fire is occupied by air or water or some earth—and being few among many, it moves and fights within those agitated things—it is tossed about and torn apart; two bodies of fire then grow together into one form of air. Then, when the air is overcome and dispersed, from two whole parts and a half, one whole form of water coalesces. 

Finally, let us consider them again in this way: whenever some other kind of element is seized by fire and cut by the sharpness of its angles and sides, it only stops being torn apart when it has passed entirely into the nature of fire. For any genus that is similar and the same suffers the least from what is similar and the same; but as long as it is changing into something else, and a weaker thing struggles with a stronger one, it does not cease to be dissolved. Again, when smaller things are surrounded by many larger ones, and a few are torn apart and extinguished, they cease to be extinguished only when they are willing to be shaped into the form of the victors: and so air is made from fire, and water from air. 

But if these are undergoing transition and some other kind attacks them, they do not cease to be dissolved while agitated, until either they are completely driven away to their own kin—since they are dissolvable—or, being conquered, they finally emerge as a single thing from many, similar to the victor, and remain familiarly with that conqueror. Indeed, through these experiences, all things change their seats in turn. For the multitudes of any genus are distinguished by their own proper place due to the agitation of the seat itself. But those things which have become unlike each other are carried, because of the surge and concussion, toward the place of those things which they have become like. 

Therefore, the unmixed and primary bodies were fabricated from causes of this sort. As for the other genera that are innate within their specific forms, the cause is the constitution of each of the two elements: which from the beginning produced not only one triangle with a certain magnitude, but also larger and smaller ones, as many in number as there are genera in the species. For this reason, these things mixed within themselves and with each other possess an infinite variety. It is necessary for those who intend to give a probable account of nature to be skilled in this. Therefore, unless one understands with certainty in what way and with what things motion and constitution occur together, many things will seem to be an impediment to the discussion that remains behind. Some of these have been discussed, while others remain to be said. 

In a nature that is smooth and level, motion is never accustomed to exist. For it is difficult, or rather impossible, to find a thing to be agitated without an agitator, or an agitator without something to be agitated. But without these, there is no motion at all. These things, however, can never be smooth and level. Thus, we shall place stability in flatness and smoothness, but motion always in the opposite nature. Furthermore, inequality is the cause of this nature, which is the opposite of smooth and flat. We have already treated the generation of inequality. 

But in what way individual things, according to their genera, do not cease to be moved and carried toward one another, we have by no means explained. We shall therefore explain it next in this way. The circuit of the whole of nature, since it has embraced the genera in its circular extent and strives to come together with itself, constricts all things and suffers no empty space to be left anywhere. <note>This describes the "horror vacui" or the idea that the universe is a plenum where every gap is filled by the compression of the outer sphere.</note> Because of this, fire has penetrated through all things most of all; then air, as it is closest to fire in its thinness; and others in a similar ratio thereafter. For those things composed of the largest parts have also left the largest vacuum in their constitution, while the smallest leave the smallest. But the narrowness of the constriction itself thrusts small things into the empty spaces of large ones. Therefore, when small things are introduced into large ones, and the small things themselves discern the large ones while the larger ones coerce the smaller, all things are carried upward or downward into their own places. For whatever changes its magnitude changes its seat. Thus, and for these reasons, the generation of the nature opposite to smoothness is always preserved, exhibiting the perpetual motion of these things both in the present and in the future. 

After this, it should be known that there are many kinds of fire: namely, flame; and that which is kindled by it (which burns indeed, but brings no light to the eyes); and that which remains within those things that had been kindled after the flame is extinguished. 

<margin>
Many kinds of fire.
</margin>

Similarly, there is another kind of air, the purest and most agile, which they call **Ether**; another most turbulent kind, dark with gloom and clouds; and it must be thought that there are other nameless species because of the inequality of the triangles themselves. 

<margin>
Many kinds of air.
</margin>

There are two primary kinds of water. One is liquid; the other is fusible. <note>original: "fusile"; referring to metals which can be melted.</note> The liquid kind, because it consists of small and unequal parts of water, is accustomed to be moved easily by itself and by others due to the condition of its inequality and the form of its shape. But that which is composed of larger, equal, and smooth parts is more stable than the former. And being heavy, it is compacted because of its smooth equality; but because of the onset of fire penetrating and dissolving it, it becomes a participant in motion once its equality is lost. Having become agile and mobile, pushed by the neighboring air and spread through the earth, it undergoes two things: for it both liquefies and falls into the earth. The first is called the "purification of movement," and the second is called "flow." 

<margin>
Two kinds of water.
</margin>

Again, as fire flies out from here—since there is no exit into a vacuum—the neighboring air, being pushed, impels the still-mobile liquid mass into the seats of the fire and mixes it with itself. Finally, the mass, being driven together and having again attained smooth equality—since fire, the craftsman of inequality, has now departed—piles itself up into the same state. We call the departure of fire "cooling," but the joining and meeting made when fire departs we call "conglutination" and "frozen rigidity."

Among these waters which we have called "fusible," that which is made most dense, uniform, splendid, and yellow from the thinnest and smoothest parts is a most precious thing: flourishing gold, compacted through rock. But the branch of gold, which is hardest because of its density and is moreover suffused with a black color, is called **Adamant**. <note>In ancient texts, "Adamant" often refers to the hardest known substance, sometimes identified as diamond or a particularly hard steel alloy.</note> But that which has parts closest to gold, and which contains more than one species, is denser than gold and a participant in a few thin parts of earth, so that it is rougher and harder, but...

Because it has large spaces within it, it is very light: this is one kind of shining and solidified water, and it is called **copper**. <note>In the Platonic system, metals are considered "fusible water" because they melt like ice when heated.</note> But when the earthy part mixed within it is separated from the other parts due to age, and is pushed to the outer surface and becomes visible, **rust** is then born. It is not at all difficult to follow the rest of this kind by similar reasoning. For if anyone, for the sake of relaxation, sets aside the study of eternal things and considers likely proofs regarding the generation [of matter], and finds delight in such a pursuit without regret, he will achieve a moderate and wise recreation in his life. 

With these things now granted, the probable things that follow concerning these matters must be run through in this way. A thin part of water is often mixed with fire; it is moist and fluid, and is so named because it flows around the slippery earth. It is also soft for this reason: because its bases are less firm and stable than those of earth, they easily yield and slide. When this [mixture] is abandoned by fire and deserted by air, it becomes smoother, and when the foreign elements are squeezed out, it is compressed into itself. If this compaction happens above the earth, it becomes **hail**; if on the earth, it becomes **ice**. These things happen when the frost is most rigid and cohesive; but when it is less frozen, if it happens above the earth, it is **snow**; if on the earth, having become thicker from dew, it is **hoar-frost**. 

<margin>On hail, ice, snow, and frost.</margin>

But when many types of water are mixed together, the whole genus that drips from the earth through trees is called **liquors** or **moisture**. These individual liquors have acquired many names because of the diversity of their mixtures, forming many classes without names; however, four species containing fire are most evident and clear, and have received names: **wine, oils, honey,** and **sap**.

<margin>Four named fiery liquors: wine, oils, honey, sap.</margin>

<margin>Wine warms the body and soul.</margin>

That which warms the soul along with the body is called **wine**. That which is smooth and divides the vision—and is therefore brilliant to the sight, shining, and appears fatty to us—is the oily species, such as **pitch, gum, oil,** and others of that kind. But that which floods the narrow passages of the mouth even to the inner parts of our nature, applying sweetness by this power, is commonly called **honey**. Finally, that which dissolves and burns the flesh and is foamy, secreted from all other liquors, is called **sap** <note>original: "succus"; likely referring to acidic juices or verjuice</note>. 

The species of earth emerging through water becomes **stone** in this manner. For when the frozen water fails in the mixture, it passes into the form of air; this air runs back to its own place. But since there is no vacuum among them, it strikes the nearest air. If this blow is heavy and is poured around the earthy mass, it strikes it violently and drives itself into those seats from which the new air had ascended. Finally, the earth, being indissolubly forced together by the air with the water, creates stones. The more beautiful stones are those which shine clearly from equal and flat parts; the uglier ones are the opposite. 

But where all moisture is dissolved by the sharpness of fire, and the body is rendered drier by it, that species remains which is called **solid** and **fusible earth**. Sometimes, when the moisture is left behind and the earth is made fusible by fire, and then frost is added, it becomes **black stone**. But when that same substance is similarly deprived of much moisture by mixing, but consists of thinner parts of earth, and is salty and half-frozen, and emerges through the water, one part is **nitre** <note>original: "nitrum"; a cleansing soda or saltpeter</note>, a genus for purging oil and earth; the other part, most convenient for daily sustenance by law, is **salt**, a body dear to God. <note>Plato famously called salt "a body dear to the gods" because of its preservative properties and use in sacrifices.</note>

<margin>On stone, nitre, salt, glass, and others.</margin>

<margin>Salt, a body dear to God.</margin>

Indeed, there are compounds made of both [earth and water] that are not soluble by water. But by fire, they are joined together for such a reason. Fire and air do not liquefy the masses of earth themselves. For since these two are the thinnest and smaller than the voids of the earth, they pass through its widest channels without any violence, so that they neither dissolve nor liquefy it. But because the parts of water are larger, they liquefy it by their violent flow. Thus, water alone dissolves loosely compacted earth by force; but only fire dissolves that which is firmly compacted. For nothing except fire penetrates this. Again, only fire can dissolve the most violent solidification of water; but both fire and air can diffuse a weaker one—air through the voids, and fire even through the triangles. <note>This refers to the "atomic" shapes of the elements; fire's tetrahedrons are sharper and can cut through other shapes.</note> Nothing dissolves air when it is forcibly constricted except through the elements; when it coheres without force, fire alone dissolves it. 

Bodies composed of water and earth in such a way that the water obstructs the voids of the earth by force are such that exterior water cannot flow through them, and therefore does not liquefy them. But fire, penetrating the passages of water just as water does the voids of earth, and affecting the water as fire does the air, provides the cause of liquefaction for the common body. Some of these have less water than earth, such as the genus of **glass** and those stones called **fusible**; others, on the contrary, have more water, such as all those things that are glued together, turn out like wax, and emit vapors. 

Thus far, we have almost demonstrated those species which vary by their shapes, communities, and mutual changes; next, we shall try to show the causes for which their passions <note>original: "passiones"; here meaning sensory perceptions or properties</note> are born. In the first place, sensation must always be present in those things that have been said. But we have not yet declared the generation of the flesh and those things pertaining to the flesh, nor the mortal part of the soul. For these are not at all separated from the passions associated with sensation, and the latter cannot be sufficiently explained without the former; yet they can hardly be completed at the same time. First, therefore, other things must be set down; then the things that follow must be explained. So that the passions themselves may follow the genera in the discussion, let those things which pertain to the body and soul stand first. 

First, let us see by what reasoning fire is called **hot**, which we shall finally perceive if we consider the separation and division made by it in our body. For it is manifest to all that this passion is a certain sharpness. Because of the thinness of its angles, the subtlety of its sides, the smallness of its particles, and the speed of its motion—by all of which it is vehement and penetrating, and always quickly divides whatever it meets—

and dissipates, we must consider by recalling the memory of the generation of its very shape. Indeed, that nature and no other, by dividing our bodies and portioning them into tiny parts, deservedly induces that experience which is legitimately named **heat**. The experience contrary to this, although manifest to anyone, should not lack its own explanation. For when the humid parts of bodies, which are larger than our own humid parts, flow into our body, they push out the smaller parts, but they cannot force themselves into those spaces. Instead, they coagulate our internal moisture; they make it immobile through equality and coagulation where it was once unequal and agitated, forcing it into a narrow space. But that which is forced contrary to nature resists according to nature, and pulls itself back in the opposite direction. In this struggle and shaking, **shivering** and **rigor** <note>original: *tremor rigorq;*</note> consist; every experience of this kind is named **cold**, and that which brings it about is called **chilled**. 

<margin>On cold.</margin>

Furthermore, we call **hard** that to which our flesh yields, and **soft** that which yields to our flesh; and by the same reasoning, we call things hard and soft in relation to one another. Whatever rests upon a small base yields. But that which is built from triangular bases is firm, as it rests forcefully on a flat plane; it resists and withstands most greatly. That which is extremely dense also beats back forcefully against anything coming toward it.

<margin>On hard and soft.</margin>

<margin>Dense and rare are the causes of hard and soft.</margin>

Furthermore, **heavy** and **light** will be most conveniently explained along with that nature which is called "up" and "down." For it is absurd to say that there are two places in nature distinguished by a long distance from one another: one called "down," to which all things having a certain bodily mass are carried, and the other called "up," toward which all things are moved by force. Since the entire heaven is round, all extremes that are made equidistant from the middle must be extremes in a similar way. The middle also, being at an equal distance from the extremes on all sides, regards everything equally from its opposite position. Since the world is disposed in this way, if someone says any of these parts is "up" or "down," he will rightfully be seen to be in error. For the middle place in it ought to be called neither up nor down, but simply the middle. That which circles around on all sides is neither the middle, nor does it have one part differing from another in relation to the middle. To that which is completely uniform, no one can rightly attribute contrary names. For if there were something solid and equilibrated in the middle of the universe, it would not incline toward any part of the extremes because of their perfect similarity; but if someone were to walk around it, he would often stand with his feet opposite to himself, and would call the same part of it now "up" and now "down." Therefore, as we said a little while ago, since the universe is round, a wise man will by no means affirm that it has an upper or lower place. 

<margin>
Heavy.
Light.
On that which is called up and down, as they are and are not.
That there is a middle place in the world: not one that is down nor up.
</margin>

But let us investigate where these names come from and in what context we observed them so as to transfer them to the whole world. If someone were to sit in that region of the world which fire has obtained as its lot, and to which fire is carried from all sides, and he gained some power by which he could seize parts of fire and weigh them, or place them in the scales of a balance to drag them by force into the "unlike" air below, it is clear that a smaller portion of fire would be forced more easily than a larger one. For when two things are suspended at once by one force, the smaller yields more, and the larger yields less to the force pulling it. And the one is said to be "heavy" and carried "down," while the other is "up" and "light." The same happens to us who inhabit the earth. For standing upon the earth and walking through it, we separate and distinguish types of earth from one another; and often we throw earth violently into the "unlike" air, contrary to nature. Here, the smaller portion, being thrown more easily into the unlike place than the larger portion, yields first to the violence; we have named it **light**, and the place toward which we compel it **up**. The contrary affection we call **heavy** and **down**. 

<margin>From where the names "up" and "down" were attributed to the world.</margin>

These things must necessarily differ from one another because the multitudes of kinds occupy places contrary to others. For what is light in one place is contrary to the light in the opposite place; and heavy is similar to heavy, and what is called down is contrary to down, and up to up. For all these things will be found to be transverse, contrary, and utterly different from one another. Yet one thing must be considered concerning all of them: that the path and movement of each toward its like and kin makes the thing being carried "heavy," and the place into which such a thing is carried "down." Things that behave otherwise produce the opposite effect. Let these be said as the causes of these experiences. 

<margin>On smooth and rough.</margin>

Any observer will be able to reveal the cause of the **smooth** and **rough** experience to others. For hardness mixed with inequality produces the latter, while equality combined with density exhibits the former. But of those experiences which happen commonly to the whole body, the greatest remains: that which is the cause of **pleasure** and **pain** in the things we have mentioned. Similarly, whatever is manifest to the senses through the parts of the body triggers pains and pleasures. Thus, let us grasp the causes of every experience, whether sensible or insensible, first recalling to memory what we distinguished above concerning that nature which is easily moved and that which is moved with difficulty. For in this way we must pursue everything we desire to comprehend. When some experience, even a brief one, falls upon that which is easily moved, its parts transmit that very experience to the following parts on all sides, until it reaches the **seat of prudence** <note>Plato’s term for the mind or the brain's rational faculty.</note>; there, through these messengers as it were, the power of that which brought the experience is known. But that which is affected in the opposite way, and remains in some way immobile, does not have that circular transmission, and only the part that suffers is affected, while it does not move the neighboring parts at all. Therefore, since the parts do not impart the first experience to one another, the whole...

an animal is least agitated by this, and that which it experiences remains devoid of sensation. This certainly happens regarding the bones, the hair, and the other parts within us that are mostly composed of earth. However, the instruments of sight and hearing function quite differently, because within them the power of fire and air is greatest. Furthermore, regarding pleasure and pain, let it be considered in this way: an experience <note>original: "passio"</note> forced upon us violently and contrary to our nature, if it is sudden and abundant, is painful. Conversely, an experience that returns us to our natural state suddenly and abundantly is sweet; those that happen gradually or in the opposite manner produce the opposite effect. 

An experience that is brought about with great ease is indeed strongly perceived, but it shares very little in pleasure or pain; such are the sensations arising from sight. We have already discussed how our body becomes akin to the light of day. To this light, burns, cuts, and similar experiences do not bring pain; nor does the restoration to its natural form bring pleasure. Nevertheless, very powerful and clear sensations belong to sight itself, insofar as it experiences something, encounters something, and touches it. For there is absolutely no violence in this process of sight dispersing or gathering. 

However, bodies composed of larger parts, which yield only with difficulty to an active force, contain pleasures and pains when they transmit the motions they receive to the whole body. Specifically, when they are moved out of their natural state, there is pain; when they return, there is pleasure. Those parts which suffer gradual emptyings or losses, but experience sudden and abundant refills, feel no sensation of the emptying but do feel the refilling; because of the mortality <note>meaning the lack of sensitivity in the fading state</note> of that power, they bring no pain, but do bring the greatest pleasures. This is recognized in the perception of sweet odors. But when parts are suddenly and abundantly driven out of their nature, and only gradually and with difficulty restored to it, the opposite of the above occurs; this is clearly seen in the cutting and burning of limbs. Now we have treated the experiences common to the whole body and the names of those things that cause them. Now, therefore, let us explain to the best of our ability those experiences that occur in specific parts of our body, where they come from, and by what causes they are brought about.

<margin>Experiences of the tongue.</margin>
First, let us declare, if we can, those things which we left out earlier when we were dealing with humors <note>bodily fluids</note>, as these are the experiences of the tongue. These seem to occur, like many other things, through certain contractions and relaxations; and furthermore, they involve smoothness and roughness more than other senses do. 

<margin>Observe that the judgment of flavor is in the heart. Flavors.</margin>
Veins extend from the tongue to the seat of the heart as messengers of flavors. If anything falls into these veins such that it penetrates the moist softness of the flesh and, being slightly liquefied by its earthy nature, causes the veins themselves to contract and dry out, it produces these kinds of flavors. Specifically, if they are quite rough, they produce harsh and pungent flavors; if they are less rough, they produce tart and astringent flavors. Things that purge these veins and wash away whatever sticks to the tongue—if they do this excessively and liquefy some of the tongue’s own nature, such as the power found in nitre <note>original: "nitro"; a naturally occurring mineral like lye or soda</note>—are all named **bitter**. 

<margin>Which things are bitter, which are salty.</margin>
But if they have a power more tempered than nitre and wipe the tongue more gently, they appear **salty** <note>original: "falsa"; likely a transcription error for "salsa"</note> without the roughness of bitterness, and are more friendly to us. Things which, when applied to the heat of the mouth, are softened and heated by it, and in turn heat the mouth itself,

<margin>Things sharp in flavor.</margin>
and by their lightness rise up to the senses of the head, dividing individual parts by their touch, are called **sharp** <note>original: "acuta"; pungent or spicy</note> because of these powers. Sometimes, however, these same things, thinned out by putrefaction, enter the narrow veins and force the interior parts—both the earthy ones and the somewhat airy ones—to be tossed about and mixed together. Being mixed, they circulate into one another, and by their entry they cause the penetrated areas to become hollow and stretched. Here, a hollow and blistered moisture surrounds the air. This moisture is sometimes earthy, and sometimes pure; thus, a moist and clear vessel of air is formed from the hollow water. That which is born from pure water is transparent on all sides and is called a **bubble** <note>original: "ampulla"</note>. But that which is formed from a more muddy moisture, being simultaneously agitated, lifted, and stretched around, is called an ebullition, a bubble, or a fermentation. 

<margin>Acid quality.</margin>
The cause of all these experiences is called the **Acid** quality. From all these things, the opposite experience proceeds from a contrary cause. When the quality of the ingredients is moist and naturally in harmony and agreement with the quality of the tongue, it smooths and softens it, soothes the contracted roughness, and relaxes or collects what had been unnaturally contracted or scattered in us; in short, it restores 

<margin>On sweetness. On odor.</margin>
the natural state to each part. Everything of this kind is sweet and friendly to all; it is a medicine and remedy for violent experiences, and is called **sweet**. Regarding the power of the nostrils, there are no specific types. For the nature of odors is half-formed. 

<margin>How the elements do not smell.</margin>
It is not within the capacity of any single element to have any odor. Rather, our veins in this area are too narrow for types of earth and water, but too wide for types of fire and air. Because of this, no one ever smells any of those elements themselves. Instead, odors are generated in the moistening, rotting, liquefying, or evaporating of certain things. For when water passes into air, or air into water, odors are created in the middle of these states. 

<margin>Odor is either smoke or mist.</margin>
Every odor is either smoke or mist. That which is changed from air into water is mist; that which is changed from water into air is smoke. Hence it happens that odors are thinner than water but thicker than air. This becomes most evident when, meeting a certain thing with the nostrils, someone draws a breath into themselves violently. 

<margin>Types of odor.</margin>
In that case, no odor flows in at the same time; rather, the breath follows alone, stripped of the odor. Therefore, these two varieties among odors are without specific names, being neither of many types nor of simple types. Only two names are clearly used there: namely, **pleasant** and **unpleasant**. The latter disturbs and violates that entire cavity which extends from the top of the head to the navel. The former soothes the same and, by a friendly entry, preserves its natural state.
