# TIMAEUS OR ON NATURE. FOLIO 297.
### M
<meta>Digitized by Google. Catchword: M</meta>

...we ought to consider: so that we may explain from what causes its passions <note>original: "passiones," referring here to sensory experiences or "affections" of the body</note> arise. Generally, then, let us define sound as a certain striking of the air, penetrating through the ears, the brain, and the blood all the way to the soul. We shall call the motion born from it, which begins from the head and ends in the seat of the liver, hearing. A swift motion produces a high-pitched <note>original: "acuta," literally sharp</note> sound, while a slow one produces a low-pitched <note>original: "gravis," literally heavy</note> one. A uniform motion is equal and smooth; the opposite is harsh. A large motion produces a loud sound; a small one, a quiet one. We shall declare the harmony and consonance of these sounds in what follows. 

The fourth kind of sensation follows to be explained, which contains within itself the greatest variety: all the things under it are called colors. Color is a kind of flame and glow <note>original: "flammula quedam fulgorque"</note> emanating from individual bodies, having parts adapted for the sight to perceive. We have treated the causes from which sight is born above. Now, it seems that probable things must be said about colors in this way. Those things which are carried from other parts and fall into our view are partly smaller, partly larger, and partly equal to the parts of the sight itself. Those that are equal cannot be felt; these are called transparent <note>original: "diaphana," meaning through-shining</note>. However, we say that those that are smaller or larger partly "discern" <note>original: "discernere," in the sense of dilating or spreading</note> and partly "contract" the sight, much like those things which by heat or cold affect the flesh, or those things which by bitterness or sharpness and heat contract or discern the tongue. 

And those things which affect the sight in this way we call white or black: these are indeed the passions of those things I was just describing—related to them and in a certain way the same, but in another genus—yet they seem different because of these causes. Thus they must be named: that which spreads the sight is **white**, and that which gathers it is **black**. We call a sharper motion of another kind of fire, which falls upon and disperses the sight all the way to the eyes, violently striking the orbits and passages of the eyes and melting them, a fire meeting it from the opposite side; by this encounter, a tear, a body mixed of fire and water, is poured out. And when one fire leaps out as if from a certain flash of lightning, while the other penetrates and is extinguished by the moisture, various colors are created from this kind of mixture. We call this passion itself "glare" or "flashing," and that which causes it, "shining" or "glittering." 

A middle kind of fire reaching the moisture of the eyes and mixing with it—hardly glittering, but from the mixing of the fire's rays with the moisture creating a blood-like color—we have named **red**. **Yellow** is produced when the shining and the white are mixed with red. However, in what measure or proportion each of these are mixed with one another, even if someone knew, it would not be the mark of a wise man to tell: especially since he could not in any way bring forth a necessary or even a plausible reason for them. **Red** with white and black produces **purple**. A color becomes **mulberry** <note>original: "moreus"</note> and somewhat **yellowish** when blackness is more closely joined to these after they have been blended and burnt. **Tawny** is produced by the tempering of yellow and dark brown <note>original: "fusci"</note>. **Dark brown** itself comes from the confusion of white and black. The coupling of white and yellow generates **pallor**. **Blue** <note>original: "ceruleum"</note> is created by joining the shining to white and blurring it with much blackness. Blue with white creates **greenish-grey** <note>original: "glaucum"</note>. From the tempering of tawny and black, the color **green** is born. Almost all other colors become manifest from these. For if anyone, imitating the previous mixtures, follows out the remaining colors, he will dispute with probable reasons. 

But if anyone attempts the discussion and proof of these things by the work itself <note>i.e., by physical experimentation</note>, he will seem to be ignorant of the difference between human and divine nature. For God is sufficient and knows how to collect many things into one, and again to lead one out into many; He knows and is able to do both at once. But no man exists now, nor ever will be, who is capable of either. 

Surely all these things, then naturally affected by necessity, that Fabricator of the most beautiful and best work assumed in those things being born, when He generated a God sufficient in Himself and most perfect. He used causes as ministers for these things, but He Himself acted in each part so that it might be well. For it is fitting to distinguish two species of causes. One is **necessary**, and the other is **divine**. We should seek the divine in all things, so that we may attain a blessed life as far as is possible for our nature. We should also investigate the necessary cause for the sake of the divine. For we must realize that without these necessary things, those others on which we place our study cannot be understood, grasped, or perceived in any other way. 

Since, however, the material lies before us now like workers—namely, the types of causes, holding the place of raw materials out of which the following discussion must be woven—let us return briefly to the beginning. Let us go back quickly to where we have proceeded so far; and thus at last let us place a conclusion and a peak upon the discussion, such as the previous parts require. 

As we said from the beginning, since these things lacked order, God bestowed a measure and a rule of proportion upon each thing, both toward itself and toward others, insofar as each was able to receive it. At that time, truly, there was no order unless perhaps by some chance; nor was anything then rightly to be called water or fire or any of those things now named among us. But He first adorned all these; then from them He constituted this universe, a single living being containing within itself all mortal and immortal animals. And of the divine things, He Himself is the author. But He handed over the generation of mortal things to His offspring <note>the lesser gods</note> to be completed. They, therefore, imitating their parent and receiving the immortal principle of the soul, enclosed that soul within a mortal body; and they gave the whole body to the soul as a vehicle. And in it they fabricated another kind of soul, which is mortal: which would be affected by heavy and necessary perturbations. 

The first of these would be **pleasure**, the greatest bait of evil; then **pain**, the flight and hindrance of goods; furthermore, **audacity** and **fear**, those foolish counselors; and there would be added implacable **anger**, and **hope**, that seductive conciliator; together with irrational sense and an all-invading love. Mixing these, they necessarily composed the mortal race. But lest they should pollute the divine part with any mortal contagion, except as much as supreme necessity compelled, they placed the mortal part separately from the divine in another seat of the body, and separated the head from the chest by the neck and neck-joint placed between them. In the chest, therefore, and...

PAGE XXXII.

#### BOOK
### M

Within the thorax, they placed the mortal kind of soul. Because it was by nature partly better and partly worse, they arranged the capacity of the thorax accordingly, distinguishing the seats of the soul as if they were separate quarters for men and women. Between these, they inserted a certain cartilage called the diaphragm <margin>The diaphragm cartilage.</margin>—which they also call the *phrenes* <note>original: "phrenas," a Greek term for the midriff or the seat of the mind</note>—to act as a middle boundary. Therefore, they placed the part of the soul that partakes in courage and anger, and is prone to contention, closer to the head, between the diaphragm and the neck. This was done so that, being obedient to reason, it might join with reason to forcefully restrain the desires whenever the appetite refuses to obey the commands issued from the citadel of the head where reason dwells. They chose to suspend the heart—which is the origin of the veins and the fount of blood <margin>The heart is the origin of the veins and the fount of blood.</margin> flowing through the whole body with a certain force—within the region of the guards. This was so that when the force of anger blazes up because reason announces that some injustice is being done from without, or some internal concupiscence is causing a disturbance, every sensing part of the body might quickly perceive the commands and threats through all the narrow passages. Thus, the body might obey and follow entirely, enduring in all things the command of that most excellent part. However, because they knew the heart would tremble at the sight of terrifying things and would often burn with anger—and that all such work would involve heat <note>original: "ignem," literally fire</note>—they provided the lungs as a covering for the heart to temper this heat. The lungs are first of all soft and bloodless, and secondly, they are divided into internal hollow tubes like a sponge. Thus, by drawing in breath and drink, the lungs might cool and refresh the heart's heat through respiration. For this reason, they diverted the arteries like aqueducts through the substance of the lungs, surrounding the heart with them like a soft cushion. In this way, when anger boils over, the heart may be tempered and subside into easier obedience, and once the tumult is calmed, it may more easily serve and obey the care of reason.

Finally, that part of the soul which desires food and drink, and all other things the body requires, they applied to the middle region between the diaphragm and the navel. There, they intended a sort of manger to exist for the nourishment of the whole body, and they tied that power of the soul there like a wild animal. Here, it is certainly necessary for it to nourish its body if the mortal race is ever to survive. So that it might always feed at its manger and live far away from the "consultant" <note>Referring to reason</note>, and thus disturb the chief leader of our being as little as possible with its noise and clamor—allowing reason to consult in tranquil leisure for the common utility of all—the gods seem to have given it this lower region to inhabit. 

Furthermore, because God saw that this part of the soul would be of such a nature that it would not listen to reason, and even if it were struck by some sensation, it would in no way obey rational arguments but would instead be snatched away by images and visions both night and day, He therefore created the nature of the liver and placed it in that soul's habitation. He made the liver a dense, thick, smooth, bright, and sweet nature, though not without bitterness. His purpose was that the power of thoughts descending from the mind might be received in the liver as if in a mirror, which catches the figures and reflects the images back to the sight. Sometimes, this power might terrify the liver when it receives these images; at other times, by using its innate bitterness and intending threats, it might spread throughout the liver, showing gall-like and terrible colors. This would cause the liver to contract and become wrinkled and rough, and would affect its lobes <note>original: "fibras"</note>, its bile-ducts, its gallbladder <note>original: "ventriculum"</note>, and the veins called the "portal veins," causing pain and distress by twisting them out of their proper shape or by obstructing and closing them. 

And again, when the inspiration of gentleness from the mind reflects contrary visions, it calms the bitterness—since it neither wishes to stir up nor touch a nature adverse to itself—and by using the sweetness natural to the liver, it renders everything straight, smooth, and free. Then, it makes the peaceful and gentle part of the soul dwelling in the liver behave moderately even in sleep, and allows it to use divination <note>original: "vaticinio," the power of prophecy</note>, since that part of the soul is devoid of reason and prudence. For those who fashioned us, mindful of the Father's command that the mortal race should be made as good as possible, instituted even our baser part <margin>The gift of divination was given to human madness. The work of the prudent man.</margin> so that it might also be, in some way, a participant in truth. Indeed, they established that divination should be fulfilled in it. 

That God gave the power of divining to human "madness" <note>original: "dementiæ," referring here to a state of being outside of oneself or irrationality</note> can be proven by this: that no one in their right mind attains any true and divine prophecy. Instead, divination usually occurs either when the power of prudence is hampered by sleep, or oppressed by disease, or moved from its state by some divine possession. However, it is the duty of the prudent man alone to understand what has been pronounced by the frenzied and prophetic nature, whether waking or sleeping. He must discern through reasoning whatever visions have shone forth, so that he may explain what they portend, for whom they are intended, and whether they signify some future, past, or present good or evil. It is not the duty of one who was and remains in a state of frenzy <note>original: "furore," a state of divine madness</note> to judge what he has seen or uttered. Truly, that ancient saying is wise: "To do one's own business and to know oneself belongs to the prudent man alone." <margin>Who are the prophets; who are the seers in the Timaeus. The liver for the sake of divining.</margin> Hence, the law ordains that "prophets" preside as judges over divine prophecies. Some call these men "seers" <note>original: "vates"</note>, being entirely ignorant that they are the interpreters of the oracles and visions wrapped in obscure veils, and are not the seers themselves. Therefore, those who judge the prophecies should not be called seers, but "prophets"—that is, interpreters and proclaimers of prophecies. 

The nature of the liver was made such, and placed in the seat we have described, for this very reason: for the sake of divination. While a person is alive, the signs of such things are expressed more clearly; but once deprived of life, the liver becomes blind, and no sign of prophecy remains evident. # TIMAEUS, OR ON NATURE. LEAF 298.
### M,ii,

<margin>The Spleen.</margin>
When the liver becomes filled with impurities due to bodily disease, the porous nature of the spleen cleanses it by soaking up those dregs, as this organ is hollow and bloodless. Thus, when filled with these waste products, it grows large and swells with foul fluid. Conversely, when the body is cleansed, the spleen contracts and settles back into itself. We have now explained what parts of the soul are mortal and what part is divine, as well as where they are located, with what they are associated, and why they are separated from one another. Whether what we have said is the absolute truth, we could only assert for certain if a divine oracle confirmed it. However, that it is likely to be so, we do not hesitate to affirm now and in our future investigations. Let this, then, be our current assertion. What follows must be treated in a similar fashion: it remains to explain how the other members of the body were arranged. It is most fitting that they consist of the following logic. The creators of our race certainly knew that we would be immoderate in eating and drinking, and that out of gluttony we would consume more than measure or necessity required. Therefore, lest a sudden death from disease occur and the mortal race come to an early and imperfect end, they crafted the lower belly <margin>Concerning the intestines and their coils.</margin> to receive the surplus of food and drink. Furthermore, they wound the intestines in coils so that the food we consume would not pass through too quickly, which would immediately force a new necessity for nourishment upon us. For if we suffered from such an insatiable and perpetual void, our race would have been left without philosophy or music, and devoid of all moderation, being entirely disobedient to that part within us which is most divine.

The nature of the bones, flesh, and other such things was composed in this way. Indeed, the generation of the marrow <margin>Concerning bones and flesh. See how the marrow is the foundation and beginning for the limbs. In the marrow, the soul is first implanted.</margin> provided the beginning for all of them. For the bonds of life—by which the soul is joined to the body—are attached to the marrow; branching out from it through every part, they bind and support the construction of our body. The marrow itself was generated from other elements. There are certain primary triangles, unbent and smooth, most perfectly suited for the generation of fire, air, water, and earth. Selecting specific types from each of these, and mixing them in balanced proportion, God established the seed and fuel for the entire generation of mortals by creating the substance of the marrow from them. Afterward, sowing within it the various kinds of souls, he bound them there. Furthermore, he distinguished right at that first distribution as many and as varied shapes as the marrow required for each species. That part of the marrow which was to be like a field for the divine seed <note>The "divine seed" refers to the rational part of the soul, which Plato believes resides in the brain.</note> to be cast into, he fashioned into a spherical and rounded shape on all sides, and willed it to be named the *encephalon* <margin>Concerning the brain; encephalon.</margin> <note>original: "encephalum .i. cerebrum"; from the Greek *en-kephalos*, meaning "in the head"</note>, that is, the brain. This was because, once each animal was fully formed, the vessel containing the brain was to be called the *cephalum* <note>original: "cephalum .i. caput"; from the Greek *kephalē* for head</note>, or the head. However, the part that was to contain the remaining mortal powers of the soul, he fashioned into shapes that were both round and oblong. He willed the whole to be called "marrow," and, casting the bonds of the entire soul from these as if from anchors, he then completed our entire body around them, supporting it from the outside with a structure of bones.

The bone itself he composed in this manner: sifting pure and smooth earth, he mixed and moistened it with marrow. He then cast it into fire, then submerged it in water, then back into fire, and again into water. By transferring it often between the two, he rendered it such that it could be melted by neither. Using this, he fashioned a bony sphere as if on a lathe and surrounded the brain with it. He left narrow passages in it, and around the marrow of the neck and back, he shaped "little wheels" or vertebrae out of the bone, placing them like hinges so that they extended from the head through the whole trunk. Thus, he preserved the seed <note>The marrow was seen as the vital "seed" of life and the soul's anchor.</note> by walling it in with a stony enclosure. He added joints as well, using the nature of the "other" <note>A reference to the Platonic concept of the "Same" and the "Other," here applied to the mechanics of motion.</note> within them to act as a mediating power for the sake of movement and bending.

But considering that the nature of bone would be drier and more rigid than it ought to be, and that if it became overheated or chilled it would quickly decay and corrupt the internal seed, he fashioned the genus of nerves <margin>Concerning the nerves.</margin> <note>In ancient anatomy, "nerui" (nerves) often referred to tendons and ligaments which bind the joints.</note> and flesh. Thus, with the nerves binding the other limbs—tightening and relaxing around the hinges—he rendered the body agile and ready for all bending and tension. The flesh, meanwhile, would be a covering against cold and heat, and a protection against various falls, much like external paddings, especially since it was designed to yield softly and gently to the body. He endowed it with a warm moisture so that in summer, being dewy and moist on the outside, it might provide a natural cooling for the whole body; conversely, in winter, it might moderately repel the external ice with its own internal fire. Thinking of these things, the Creator of our body fashioned full-edged and soft flesh by blending a mixture of water, fire, and earth, and adding a sharp and salty ferment to them. He tempered the nature of the nerves as a single medium between the power of bone and unfermented flesh, and dyed them with a yellow color. Hence, the substance of the nerves is tighter and drier than flesh, but more agile and softer than bone. With these, God bound together the marrow and the bones, and covered them all with flesh. Those bones that were the most "animated" <note>Meaning those containing the most marrow and thus most closely connected to the soul's functions.</note> he covered with the least flesh; those that were the least so, he covered with the most and thickest flesh. Furthermore, at the joints of the bones—except where necessity demanded otherwise—he added little flesh, lest it hinder the bending of the body or make the limbs slow to move, or lest its solid thickness dull the clarity of the senses, impede memory, or blunt the sharpness of the intellect. For this reason, the bones of the groin, the shins, the hips, the arms, the forearms, and all others that lack joints or are hidden deep within...

...bones, because they have a scarcity of soul within their marrow, are void of wisdom and are covered with much flesh. However, those parts which possess wisdom have less flesh—unless perhaps a certain fleshy mass was created specifically to serve a sense, 

<margin>Because a head stripped of flesh is sharper for sensing.</margin>

as is the case with the tongue. In all other parts, it is as we have described. For Nature, born and nourished of necessity, in no way allows dense bone and thick flesh to exist alongside sharp sensation. This combination would have been most prominent in the construction of the head if they could have occurred together; then the human race, possessing a fleshy, sinewy, and robust head, would have enjoyed a life twice as long—or even much longer—and one more powerful and peaceful than the one we possess. However, those creators <note>original: "fabricatoribus"; referring to the lesser gods or "demiurges" who, in Plato's Timaeus, fashioned the human body</note> of our race, when deliberating whether they should make us longer-lived but of a lower quality, or of a shorter life but a better one, decided that a short and better life was entirely preferable to a long and inferior one. Therefore, they wove the head with thin bone, and they did not bolster it with flesh or sinews, since it was not intended to have many joints. For all these reasons, the head was made more acute for sensing and wiser than all other members, but also more fragile. 

For this reason and in this manner, God placed the sinews <note>The term "nervos" in this period often conflated what we now distinguish as nerves, tendons, and ligaments.</note> around the base of the head, winding them around the spine in a similar fashion, and bound the jaws beneath the face with them; the rest he distributed through all the limbs, connecting joint to joint. Furthermore, those designers of ours adorned the nature of the mouth with teeth, a tongue, and lips—just as we see now—for the sake of both necessity and the highest purposes. For they devised the entrance for the sake of things necessary, but the exit for the sake of the best things. Indeed, whatever is admitted into the body for nourishment is necessary. But the outpouring of words, which serves wisdom, 

<margin>The outpouring of words is the servant of wisdom.</margin>

is the best and most beautiful of all outpourings. Furthermore, the head could not be left as bare bone, destitute of any other covering, due to the extremes of heat and cold; yet it could not be made dull and void of sense by being weighed down with the mass of flesh. Therefore, from the flesh that was not entirely dried out, a larger remaining portion was separated: and the skin itself, joined to itself around the moisture of the brain and germinating there, clothed the head. This moisture irrigated the joints under the crown and bound the skin together at the top. The variety of these joints was made due to the power of the soul's circuits and nourishment; where these forces struggle more against each other, there are more joints; where less, there are fewer. 

God then pricked and struck this skin all over with fire. Through the tiny rifts in the skin, the moisture flowed out; that which was pure moisture and heat escaped, but that which was mixed with the same elements as the skin was pushed out by the force of the emanations and stretched into length, having a thinness equal to the puncture that it penetrated. But because of its slowness, it was beaten back by the surrounding air and rolled back under the skin, where it took root. For these reasons, hair grows in the skin, being similar in nature to the skin or leather, but harder and denser due to the tightening caused by the cold. Indeed, the hair becomes rigid from the cold once it is pushed outside the skin. In this way, God established for us a shaggy and bristly head, using those causes we have mentioned; he intended the covering itself to protect the brain, not being heavy with flesh, but light, so that it might suffice to ward off the intemperance of cold or heat without hindering the sharpness of the senses. 

Furthermore, that complex of sinew, skin, and bone at the fingertips, having become drier, was covered with a single common covering of harder skin <note>Referring here to the fingernails.</note>. The secondary and serving cause of this was what we have described, but the principal cause was that Intelligence which fashioned it for the sake of future utility. For those craftsmen of ours were not ignorant that from men would eventually come women and other living creatures; they also understood that many beasts would have use for nails and claws for many tasks. For this reason, they armed humans with nails at their very birth. It was for this reason and these causes that they covered the extremities of the limbs with skin, hair, and nails. 

Since all the parts and limbs of a mortal living being had been created in a mutual kinship, and they necessarily possessed life through fire and spirit, the gods took care with this plan so that the animal itself would not quickly fail, dissolved and exhausted by these elements. Mixing a nature akin to the human race with other forms and senses, they planted, as it were, another kind of living thing. These are the domestic trees, plants, and seeds, which, having been sown and cultivated by art, are now mild to us, though they were once wild and without cultivation. For whatever participates in life may rightly be called a living creature. That which we speak of now participates in the third species of soul, which we placed between the diaphragm and the navel <note>The vegetative or "appetitive" soul in Platonic philosophy.</note>. In this soul, there is no opinion, reason, or intellect at all. However, it experiences the sensations of pleasure and pain along with desires. It suffers all things continuously. But because it is turned toward itself and rejects external movement, using its own internal motion, nature did not grant it the ability to consider its own condition through reason. Therefore, it lives and is no different from an animal; but because it was deprived of that power by which a creature moves itself, it remains rigid and fixed, clinging by its roots. 

When those superior ones had supplied all these things to us, the inferior ones, for our nourishment, they drew various channels through our body, like aqueducts in a garden, so that it might be irrigated by the derivation of fluid. First, they divided two veins in the back, hidden beneath the joining of the skin and flesh, according to the twofold shape of the body itself, to the right and to the left. These they sent down toward the spine, with the marrow created between them...

...to encompass such a thing: so that this system might especially flourish and sprout, and from here a more abundant overflow, as if running downhill, might provide an even irrigation. After this, they divided the veins around the head, intertwining them in turn from opposite sides—partly from the right to the left, and partly from the left to the right of the body—so that the head would have a connection to the rest of the body through the skin. This was done because the head was not bound or distinguished by nerves in a circular fashion around the crown. Furthermore, this was designed so that the power of sensation <note>original: "sentiendi vis"</note> might flow from both sides throughout the entire body from every direction. From here, they led this "aqueduct" in the following order, which we shall clearly perceive if we first agree upon this principle: whatever things are composed of smaller parts can hold larger ones, but those made of larger parts cannot contain smaller ones.

Now, Fire, above all other elements, consists of the smallest particles. Therefore, it penetrates and passes through water, air, earth, and everything composed of them, to such an extent that nothing is strong enough to contain it. The same must be thought regarding our belly <note>original: "vtero"; here referring to the abdominal cavity or stomach</note>. Indeed, it retains food and drink that have been ingested, but it cannot hold back breath <note>original: "spiritum"</note> and fire, because they are finer than the belly's own composition. Therefore, God used these elements to achieve irrigation from the belly into the veins.

For He wove a certain net <note>This is Plato's famous "leaping net" metaphor for the respiratory and circulatory systems</note> out of air and fire, like a bulging drag-net <note>original: "sagenae"</note>. At the entrance of this net, there are two convex bulges: one of these He split into two parts with a double pulse, and from these convex bulges He stretched what might be called ropes throughout the entire body to the very edges of the weaving. The interior parts of this "snare" <note>original: "tricae"</note> He composed entirely of fire, while the bulges and the container itself He made of air. Finally, taking these components, He arranged them in the formed living creature in this way: He lowered the convex parts into the mouth. Since the bulging convexity is double, He passed one part through the arteries into the lungs, and the other along the arteries into the belly. The other part He divided and led both its branches to the channels of the nostrils, so that when one part does not reach the mouth, all its flows and passages may be filled from this source.

He willed the other capacity of the bulge and the net to be around all the hollow parts of the body. He made all of this flow together gently at times—as if air were there—and at other times flow back. Since the net is a porous body, the air penetrates through it and emerges again, while the interior rays of fire follow in continuous succession, with air passing to either side. This never ceases to happen as long as the mortal creature exists. This kind of agitation we judge to be rightly named expiration and respiration.

All this work and all this process in our body occurs through a kind of irrigation and cooling for the sake of life and nourishment. For when the fire within follows the exhaling and inhaling breath, and being diffused through the belly, encounters food and drink, it immediately liquefies them. It breaks them into the smallest parts and leads them out as if from a fountain through the exits where the path lies open. It transfers whatever it has drawn out into the passages of the veins and distributes the fluids through the body as if through a valley of veins.

But let us look again at the causes for which respiration was established in the manner we now see. The consideration of the matter is as follows: since there is no vacuum <note>Plato’s physics rejected the possibility of a void; everything must be filled with matter</note> anywhere into which any moving thing can enter, and yet breath flies out from us, it is evident to anyone that this breath does not fly into a vacuum. Rather, it displaces the air next to it from its seat; that displaced air always pushes the next, and by necessity, whatever is struck back in this way is driven into the place from which the breath was excluded. It enters there, fills it, and follows the breath itself. All this happens simultaneously in a kind of revolution because no vacuum is created.

Therefore, when the chest and lungs blow out breath, they are immediately filled again by the air surrounding the body, which penetrates the passages of the body. Conversely, when the air flies out from the body and the emitted breath is released, it forces the inspiration to be drawn back in through the passages of the mouth and nostrils. We posit the cause that gives beginning to these things as follows: every living creature in this universe possesses heat in its veins and blood, like a certain fountain of fire. We have compared this to a net or drag-net stretched through the middle and woven entirely of fire, while all the exterior parts are of air.

One must certainly think that heat, by its own nature, flows outward toward its own kind in the region beyond. Since there are two paths—one through the body to the outside and the other back through the mouth and nostrils—when the breath rushes toward one and pushes it, it conversely pulls and strikes back the other. That which is pulled back, encountering the fire, grows hot; that which has breathed out grows cold. While the heat is thus exchanged, those things using the other passage grow warm, and that which is boiling migrates back to its nature; by this migration, it strikes one thing into the path of another. These things continually suffer and perform the same actions. Certainly, this breath, fluctuating back and forth in a certain circle, contains both expiration and inspiration.

Furthermore, the causes of the effects produced by physicians using cupping glasses <note>original: "ampullarum"; medical instruments used for bloodletting or creating suction</note> on the body, as well as the act of drinking, and moreover the behavior of things that are thrown—whether they are cast high or fall to the ground—should be treated according to this same principle. Additionally, voices—whether they are fast or slow, high or low—are usually heard, sometimes as dissonant because of the inequality of the motion they produce in us, and sometimes as consonant because of their similarity. For the slower voices that follow catch up to the earlier and faster motions which are already fading, occupying and overcoming them by matching their motion. In catching them, they do not...

XXXII.

...indeed, they disturb by instilling motion, but they introduce the beginning of a slower movement according to the principle of a faster one. While they adapt a certain similarity to the fading motion, they blend a single harmony <note>original: "concentum"; a musical concord</note> from high and low pitches. Thus, it provides pleasure to the unlearned, but joy to the wise, because of the imitation of divine harmony found in mortal movements. The same reasoning applies to the flow of waters, the strike of lightning, and that wonderful attraction of amber, or of that stone which is called the **Heraclian stone** <margin>the Heraclian stone</margin> <note>This refers to the loadstone or magnet, named after the city of Heraclea</note>. In truth, no "attraction" occurs in any of these. Rather, since there is no vacuum anywhere, and these things push and repel one another, and each requires its own place whether joined or separated, these wonderful events will seem to happen from these mutual interactions to a diligent investigator of such matters.

But respiration, from which we digressed to this point, arises from these causes and in the manner we described above. Namely, while fire divides the food and the internal spirit is raised, it fills the veins from the common belly with this kind of elevation: drawing from there the ground-up nutrients. For this reason, the liquids of the nutrients are spread deep through the entire body of all animals. Immediately, the nutrients—having been ground down and taken from their "kin," such as the fruits and grains which God produced for the nourishment of our body—take on various colors because of the mixing. However, a red color prevails most in these, whose nature comes from a portion of fire and a cleansing made in the moisture. Therefore, the color of that which flows through the entire body has the appearance we have described. We have named this **blood**, the food of the flesh and of the entire body. From here, the distributed irrigation fills everything that is exhausted everywhere. 

The method of filling or emptying is the same as the movement of anything in the universe: through which every kin is drawn to itself. For the things that surround us externally are constantly dissolving us and sending out individual portions of ourselves to their own kinds. However, the bloody forces within us, ground down and enclosed in the viscera—as is natural for any animal living under the heavens—are forced to imitate the movement of the whole. Therefore, when any ground-up parts within us seek their kin, they fill whatever has been exhausted. Furthermore, when more leaves than enters, the animal decreases; when the opposite happens, it grows. 

A new composition of any animal, having new **triangles** <note>Plato’s theory that matter is composed of geometric triangles; new triangles are sharp and strong</note> like a wooden framework, possesses a strong structure. Its entire mass has grown together tenderly, as it has recently solidified from fresh marrow and been nourished on milk. Therefore, it overcomes and grinds down those external triangles—from which food and drink are composed—which are older and weaker than its own young triangles, and thus makes the animal itself large, nourishing it from many similar parts. 

But when the root and binding of its own triangles relax—because they have been exhausted and tamed by great labors over a long time while struggling against many things—then it truly cannot reduce the consumed nutrients into its own likeness by grinding them down. Instead, its own members are easily dissipated by those things entering. From here, every animal begins to decrease and fail when it is overcome; and this loss is called **Old Age**. <margin>Old Age</margin>

The end <margin>Nature</margin> comes when the bonds of those triangles from which the marrow is made, once fitted together, no longer bind anything; but, now relaxed by exhaustion, they abandon the connections of the soul. The soul then, according to nature, immediately flies away with pleasure. For whatever happens against nature is painful, but what happens according to the nature of the thing is pleasant. Similarly, death caused by diseases and wounds is violent and painful; but that which creeps up naturally, with old age leading gradually to the end, is the lightest among all kinds of death, and happens with pleasure rather than pain. <margin>Natural or senile death</margin>

But as for where diseases arise, who could doubt? For there are those four elements from which the body is joined: **Earth, Fire, Water, and Air**. The unnatural excess or deficiency of these, and their relocation from their own place to a foreign one (where they do not hold what is suitable for them), brings about a certain internal sedition and diseases. For when each thing is made or moved against nature, those things which were cold before become hot, the dry become wet, the light become heavy, and all other things are similarly changed. Only when the same thing approaches or departs from itself according to the same principle, and in a similar way, and with the proper proportion maintained, will it permit itself to remain safe and whole. But whatever wanders, whether by approaching or departing, brings about various changes, diseases, and infinite corruptions. 

From the secondary compositions established according to nature, a secondary guess of good or bad health will be given to anyone seeking it. For since the marrow, bone, flesh, and nerves are composed of those elements, and blood is furthermore formed from them (albeit in a different way), many other events happen just as the ones above. But the greatest and most serious diseases arise in this way: namely, when these things are made from one another in a reversed order, they undoubtedly corrupt the body. Indeed, according to nature, flesh and nerves are generated from blood: nerves from the fibers and ligaments because of their kinship, and flesh from a certain coagulation of that which was separated and hardened from the fibers and ligaments. That which in turn flows from the nerves and flesh, being gluey and fatty, both nourishes the flesh to the nature of the bones and increases the bone itself surrounding the marrow. Furthermore, that which drips through the thickness of the bones—the purest kind of triangles, the smoothest and most abundant in fatness—as it flows down from the bones and...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of bodily health and corruption from Plato's Timaeus. Following the previous page’s description of how the body is nourished through a system of "canals" and "fire," this section shifts to the pathology of disease. It explains how the breakdown of tissues like flesh, bone, and marrow leads to the creation of toxic substances—bile and phlegm—which disrupt the body's natural order.</meta>

-># TIMAEUS, OR ON NATURE FOLIO 300.<-

<sig>M.iiii.</sig>

...flows, it irrigates the **marrow** <note>original: "medullam"; the substance Plato considers the "root" of life where the soul is anchored</note>. As long as individual things occur in this manner, good health is preserved. But bad health follows when the process is reversed. For whenever liquefied flesh sends its decay back into the veins, the blood—along with the breath—becomes abundant and varied in the veins with different colors, infected by bitter, acid, and salty tastes; it produces **bile**, **gore** <note>original: "cruorem"</note>, and much **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitam"</note>. All these things, thus generated and corrupted, primarily infect the blood itself. Providing no nourishment to the body, they are carried everywhere through the veins without observing any order of the natural circuit. These substances are truly hostile to one another because they provide no mutual benefit. Furthermore, they greatly oppose the natural condition of the body by dissolving and liquefying its stable state. 

For when the oldest portion of the flesh liquefies, it is most unsuitable for digestion; it turns black because of "old burning" <note>This refers to the ancient medical idea that humors could be "scorched" by internal heat, becoming "adust" or charred</note>. Because it has wasted away and been thoroughly eaten away, it acquires a bitterness that is hostile to all other parts of the body not yet contaminated. At that stage, instead of mere bitterness, the black color itself takes on a sourness and acrimony, as that which had been bitter is thinned out further. But then, if that bitterness is again tinged with blood, it has a red color; but when mixed with this black, it becomes "felleous" <note>yellow-green like gall</note>. Furthermore, a yellow color joins with the bitterness when new flesh liquefies due to the heat of internal fire. 

Either some physician, or certainly someone gifted with the intellect to distinguish many dissimilar things and see a single genus worthy of one name among many, gave the common name **bile** <note>original: "bilem"</note> to all these substances. The specific types of bile are named according to their variety of colors. Furthermore, **gore** <note>original: "cruor"</note>, which is the residue and discharge of blood, is smooth and mild; but the discharge of black and sharp bile is wild when, because of heat, it is mixed with a salty taste: this sort of thing is called **acid phlegm**. 

Often, a portion of younger and fresh flesh liquefies along with air; then it is inflated by trapped wind and immediately surrounded by moisture. From this, **blisters** <note>original: "ampullae"</note> are formed, which cannot be seen individually because of their smallness; but when joined together and swollen into a larger mass, they are visible and have a white color because of the generation of froth. All this liquefaction of younger flesh occurring with the spirit, which swells from moisture surrounded by wind, we call **white phlegm**. Likewise, the residue and discharge of recent phlegm is called tears and sweat, and whatever other substances into which the body dissolves daily. 

And all these are the instruments of diseases: namely, when blood increases not from food and drink according to nature, but from opposites against the laws of nature. Therefore, when any flesh is cut away but its root remains, the power of the calamity is halved, for it is easily restored. But when that which binds the flesh to the bones becomes diseased, and the blood flowing from those parts and the nerves no longer nourishes the bones or binds the flesh, but has become harsh, salty, dry, and scaly from a bad diet, then certainly everything that is sought is shaken, and it stiffens under the flesh and nerves, cut off from the bones. Flesh also falling from its roots leaves the nerves bare and covered with false humor; flowing into the streams of blood, it makes the diseases we mentioned above even more numerous. 

These are indeed heavy sufferings for bodies; but those that precede these are even heavier: namely, when the bone does not have sufficient respiration because of the thickness of the flesh. Therefore, troubled and restricted by the heat of rot, it does not receive nourishment, and it falls back into that state, having been chilled. That bone-decay falls back into the flesh, and the flesh into the blood, whence diseases sharper than the former ones are born. But the extreme of all is when the nature of the **marrow** <note>original: "medullae"</note> becomes diseased due to some defect or excess. For from this arise the most vehement and dangerous diseases leading to death, for then the entire framework of the body is necessarily dissolved. 

After these, we divide a third species of diseases into three parts: one is created by **breath** <note>original: "spiritu"</note>, another by **phlegm**, and another by **bile**. For when the lung—the guardian and, as it were, the storehouse of the breath itself—is closed off by a discharge and does not provide us with free and clear breathing passages, no breath is sent out from one part while more than is proper is taken in from another; then those parts that lack respiration and cooling waste away. But that breath which is taken in excessively, being carried through the veins, twists them and liquefies the body, occupying the **diaphragm** <note>original: "diaphragma"</note> in the center. From this, countless and extremely troublesome diseases arise with much sweat. 

Often also, breath is born within the body in separated and thinned-out flesh; since it cannot escape, it causes the same pains as those from the breath that entered. But it afflicts with huge pains when, surrounded by the nerves and nearby small veins, it inflates them and stretches and twists the ligaments and continuous nerves from the back. These diseases are indeed named **tensions** and **back-contortions** <note>original: "tensiones & a tergo contortiones"; likely referring to tetanus or opisthotonos</note> from the very passion that stretches and inflates them; the remedy for these is difficult. For fevers arising specifically resolve these. 

White phlegm, trapped inside because of the air in the blisters, is difficult; when it descends to the outer skin, it is milder, but it sprinkles the body with various eruptions and infects it with white spots, and generates other diseases of this kind. But when mixed with black bile, when it glides into the most divine passages of the head, it is accustomed to dissipate and disturb them. If this happens to those sleeping, it is milder; but if to those awake, it is more difficult to expel. Since this is a sickness of a **sacred nature** <note>original: "sacrae naturae languor"; the "sacred disease" was the ancient name for epilepsy</note>, it is hardly...

<margin><term>Catarrh</term> <note>original: "Catarrhus"; literally "a flowing down," commonly used for respiratory or mucus-related illness</note></margin> It is not without reason that catarrh is called a disease. Indeed, acidic and salty phlegm is the origin of all ailments that arise from "dripping" <note>the literal meaning of "distillatione," referring to the flow of excess humors</note>; because it slides into many places, it gives rise to many various maladies. Whatever parts of the body are said to swell are tormented by the fire and burning of bile. When this bile breathes outward, it produces various tumors by its heat; however, when it is trapped inside, it creates many burning and devouring diseases. It is at its worst when it mixes with pure blood and displaces the threads of the fibers and ligaments from their proper order. These fibers are distributed and scattered in the blood so that the blood may maintain a moderate state of thinness and thickness. This ensures that the blood does not flow out of the body too easily because of its heat and fluidity, nor become too sluggish for movement—struggling to flow and ebb through the veins—if it were thicker. Regarding this convenience of nature, these ligaments are very useful; for if anyone were to draw together and contract these fibers even in a dead person when the blood is stiff from cold, the remaining blood would be dispersed. But when they are released, the blood is immediately restricted along with the preceding cold. Because these fibers have such power over the blood, when true blood becomes bile by nature, and is again dissolved from the flesh into the blood—being hot and moist—it is gradually compressed and restricted by the force of those fibers it encounters. But when it is violently compressed and extinguished, it stirs up a storm and trembling within. Furthermore, when it flows more abundantly, overcoming the ligaments by its own heat and boiling over beyond measure, it holds its ground. And if it continues to be victorious until the end, it penetrates into the **marrow**; by burning the roots there, it loosens and cuts the bonds of the soul—like the ropes of a ship—and lets it go free. But when the heat is lesser and the liquefying body resists it, the heat itself is overcome and either falls out through the whole body or is driven through the veins into the lower or upper belly like a deserter from a rebellious city, thus escaping the body. It then induces those diseases which

<margin><term>Diarrhea</term> & <term>dysentery</term>. On fevers. <unclear>and others</unclear></margin> they call diarrheas and dysenteries—that is, slippery flows of the belly and biting flows—and it brings many other troubles of the same kind. Therefore, when the body suffers most from an excess of **fire**, it labors with a continuous fever; when from **air**, it suffers a daily <note>quotidian</note> fever; from **water**, a tertian fever <note>occurring every third day</note>, because water is more sluggish than fire and air. Finally, from an excess of **earth**, it suffers a quartan fever <note>occurring every fourth day</note>. Since earth is the slowest of all, being at the fourth degree,

<margin>Diseases of the mind</margin> it seethes and subsides in a fourfold circuit of time; hence it brings on quartan fevers, which are cured only with difficulty and after a long time. And in this manner do diseases of the body occur. But the diseases of the soul arise from the condition of the body in this way: We consider the disease of the soul to be **dementia** <note>original: "dementiam"; here meaning a lack of reason or mind</note>. We posit two kinds of it: **insanity** and **ignorance**.

<margin>Violent pleasures and pains are the most serious diseases of the soul</margin> Therefore, whatever passion brings about either one of these is to be called a sickness of the mind. For this reason, very vehement pleasures and pains must be judged the most serious of all diseases of the soul. For whoever exults in excessive joy or is depressed by excessive pain, while he tries eagerly and importunately to embrace the one and strenuously to avoid the other, he can neither see nor hear anything correctly; he rages with fury and, established in that state, is least capable of reason. He who possesses an abundance of fluid and dull seed around his marrow—like a tree heavy with more fruit than is proper, luxuriating in too much fertility—is indeed affected by many pains and many pleasures in those very lusts and their offspring and fruits. Throughout almost his whole life, he is insane on account of these great pleasures and pains. Although his mind is sick and foolish because of his body, he is commonly thought not to be sick, but rather to be acting falsely according to his own will as he pleases. But the truth is this: Intemperance in sexual matters is, for the most part,

<margin><unclear>unsound mind</unclear></margin> an infirmity of the soul, caused by the condition of a single type of substance—namely, the fluid and moist nature in the body due to the porousness of the bones. And almost every incontinence of pleasure, which is usually blamed

<margin>No one is evil by choice: but becomes evil from evil.</margin> as if we were wicked by choice, is not rightly blamed in that way. For no one is evil by choice; but because of a certain depraved habit of the body and an unrefined education, every evil man becomes evil. These things are adverse and hostile to everyone, and evil and harmful things happen because of them. Again, a soul afflicted by pain similarly falls into great depravity because of the body. For acidic and hostile phlegm, as well as bitter and bilious humors—when they do not exhale because they wander through the body, but instead are rolled back through the internal organs and pour their vapor into the secret chambers of the soul itself—produce various maladies of the soul, some greater and some lesser, sometimes many and sometimes few. These humors and vapors are carried to the three seats of the soul <note>Plato divided the soul into the rational (head), the spirited (chest), and the appetitive (belly)</note>; according to the diversity of the place, each generates various types of difficulty and trouble: audacity on the one hand, and fear on the other; furthermore, forgetfulness and dullness. Often, to this depraved condition of the body and disposition, there are added the unjust customs of a city, and private and public speeches that are not a little harmful; nor are any doctrines learned from a tender age as remedies for such great evils. And so, whichever of us are wicked, we become wicked for two reasons that happen mostly against our will. Indeed, the causes of such evils should be attributed to those who "sow" them <note>parents/ancestors</note> rather than the seed, and to those who educate rather than those who are educated. Nevertheless, one must strive with all one’s strength, through the diligence of education, studies, and learning, to reject wickedness and attain goodness. But the treatment of these matters belongs to another mode of discourse. Now, turning around, it is fitting to explain by what cultivation or by what causes we may obtain the health of the body and the soul. For it is more just to speak of good things than of evil things. Every good thing is beautiful. But the beautiful cannot exist without measure and moderation. Therefore, the living being that is to be such must be moderated by a suitable measure...

M.v.

...it ought to be. Of that number which is called proportionate and moderated, we perceive and judge only a few small instances; however, we ignore the most important and greatest of them. Furthermore, for good and bad health, and for virtues and vices, no proportion or lack thereof seems to be of greater importance than that of the soul to the body itself. We consider none of these things; nor do we notice that when a robust and great soul carries a weaker and inferior appearance <note>original: "species"; here referring to the physical form or body</note>, or when these are joined in the opposite way, the whole living being cannot be beautiful. For it lacks the greatest measure and moderation.

But that which is in the opposite state <note>where body and soul are in balance</note> appears most beautiful and lovely to everyone who has the strength to look upon it. A body that disagrees with itself—perhaps because of legs that are too large or uneven, or any other member exceeding its proper measure—is both deformed and is twisted in performing its labors; it wavers, grows weary, and collapses, providing for itself a cause of innumerable evils. The same must also be judged concerning that creature composed of soul and body, which we call a "living being." For when the soul is much more powerful than the body, it exults within it and is carried away, shaking the whole creature from within and filling it with ailments. When the soul applies itself vehemently to learning and investigating with its forces collected into one, it immediately melts and weakens the body. Finally, when it strives with an ambitious competition to teach and discuss in private and public, it inflames and dissolves the body. Sometimes, by stirring up "distillations" <note>the flow of excess fluids or humors, like catarrh</note> and flows, it even deceives many doctors, forcing them to judge contrary causes.

Conversely, when a large body of a sluggish mass exceeds and is coupled with a small and meager mind—since there are two natural desires in man, one for food through the body, and the other for wisdom <note>original: "prudentiæ"</note> through that which is most divine in us—then the prevailing agitations of that more powerful part <note>the body</note> increase what belongs to itself. However, they render the soul's part dull, unteachable, and forgetful; and thus they generate the greatest infirmity, which is ignorance.

<margin>Remedy: Neither the soul without the body, nor the body without the soul, should be moved.</margin> There is, finally, one way to health and preservation for both: that we move neither the soul without the body, nor the body without the soul; so that in mutual effort, with their forces balanced against each other, they may protect the good health of the whole. Therefore, whoever applies himself to mathematical doctrines, or studies any investigation of the mind more vehemently, must also employ the motion of the body and engage in gymnastic exercise. And again, he who strengthens and firms the body with the greatest diligence must in turn join to it the motions of the soul, using music <note>In the Greek sense, "music" includes all the arts and sciences overseen by the Muses, including literature and history</note> and all the studies of philosophy, if indeed one is to be rightly called both "good and beautiful."

Similarly, we ought to care for the individual parts of the body by imitating the form of the whole universe. For when the body is burned within by what enters it, or becomes cold, and again is made dry or wet from the outside, and suffers those things which follow, if someone leads a life of leisure and commits the body to these external motions, he is overcome by them and the body is dissolved. But if someone, in caring for the body, imitates that nature which we have called the "nurse of the universe": so that he never permits the body to be sluggish, but moves it always and everywhere resists internal and external motions according to nature with constant agitation—and with a certain moderate motion brings back the wandering passions and parts of the body into order, preserving their natural kinship according to that previous discourse we had concerning the universe—he will by no means permit enemies placed near enemies to stir up battles and diseases in the body. Instead, he will ensure that friend clinging to friend protects the health of the body.

<margin>Which is the best of motions.</margin> Of all motions, however, the best is that which occurs within oneself and from oneself. For it is most akin to the motion of the mind and of the universe itself. That motion which is caused by another is worse. <margin>Concerning purgations.</margin> But the worst motion is when the body, lying down and at rest, is moved by others in its individual parts. Therefore, the best establishment of "purgings" <note>the cleansing of the body's systems</note> for the whole body is that which is done through gymnastic exercise. Closely following this is an "easy conveyance," whether it be performed by ship or any other vehicle. The third kind of motion is useful only when extreme necessity forces it; otherwise, it is in no way to be undertaken by a man of sound mind. That is the "purgation of physicians," which is usually done with drugs <note>original: "pharmacis"; meaning medicines that purge or induce bowel movements</note>, that is, laxative remedies.

<margin>The constitution of diseases is in some way similar to the nature of living beings.</margin> For diseases, unless they are very dangerous, are not to be provoked by drugs. For every constitution of diseases is in some way similar to the nature of living beings. Indeed, the composition of living beings from the very beginning of their birth is bounded by certain cycles of time; and both the whole species suffers this, and each individual animal contains within itself from birth a fated span of living, except for necessary accidents. <insert>pharmaceuticals [affect] life</insert> For the triangles <note>Plato’s Timaeus posits that the four elements are made of geometric triangles; when these triangles wear out, the body can no longer sustain itself</note> possessing power from the very beginning of each individual cling together sufficiently for the use of life until a certain time; beyond that, life is prolonged for no one. The same mode of constitution applies to ailments. If anyone strives to cut these off with drugs before the fated course of time, they are accustomed to turn from small into great, and from few into many. <margin>Diseases are to be corrected by diligence of diet.</margin> Therefore, diseases are to be corrected and governed by diligence of diet and lifestyle, as far as leisure is given to each; and a difficult and hostile evil must not be provoked by drugs.

And regarding the common living being and its corporeal part, enough has been said about the diligence with which they are to be ruled and governed so that the proper way of living may be preserved. But the soul itself, which is to govern the body, must be instructed much more and prior to this, so that it may be prepared as best and most beautifully as possible for ruling. An exact discussion of this matter would require its own separate and complete discourse. But as far as it perhaps pertains to our current subject, if someone walks in the footsteps of what has already been said, he will arrive at a suitable end most reasonably by proceeding thus. We have often said in the preceding parts that there are three species of the soul distributed in us in three ways, and each has its own motions.

...to have. So now let us conclude in few words: whichever of those parts <note>original: "species"; referring to the three parts of the soul: reason, spirit, and appetite</note> remains idle and rests from its own movements must necessarily become very weak, whereas that which acts constantly becomes very strong. For this reason, care must be taken that the individual parts preserve their movements, balanced among themselves in a suitable harmony. Regarding the most excellent part of our soul, we should think of it in this way: namely, that God gave this to each person as our guiding spirit <note>original: "daemonem"</note>. We say that this resides in the highest citadel of the body <note>the head</note> and raises us from the earth toward our kinship in heaven, for we are creatures born of heavenly rather than earthly seed. This is indeed quite rightly said. For from that place where the first birth of the soul was given, the divine power suspends our head—the root and origin of our being—and directs the entire body. Therefore, in a person who is occupied with satisfying the passions of lust and ambitious anger, it is necessary that all their thoughts become mortal, and that they become as mortal as is possible, since they have nourished their mortal nature with all their strength. But for one who has been entirely inflamed with the desire for learning the truth, and has spent all their effort chiefly on this one thing, it is necessary—provided they touch upon the truth—that they comprehend immortal and divine things. And as far as human nature can attain immortality, they will become entirely immortal, with no part of immortality left behind. Indeed, since such a person always honors the divine and keeps that familiar guiding spirit <note>the "daemon"</note> within them in perfect order, they will be especially blessed. Now, the cultivation of every part is essentially one thing: to give to each its own proper food and movement. To that divine part within us, the movements that are kindred to it are the thoughts and revolutions of the entire universe. Therefore, it is necessary for each of us to follow these, and to correct those circuits in our head—which were once corrupted at our first birth—through the understanding of the harmony and revolution of the world. By doing so, one makes the power of the intellect similar to the thing it understands, according to its original nature. Through this similarity, we may achieve the goal of the life proposed to us by the best God, both for the present time and the future. But now, that discussion concerning the universe, which we proposed to carry through to the generation of mankind, seems to have almost reached its end. We shall briefly touch upon the generation of the other living creatures only as far as necessity demands. In this way, each person will feel they have maintained a proper measure in this discussion. Truly, let us now speak of these things as follows:

On the generation of women.

Whichever men lived unjustly and timidly, as probable reasoning shows us, were turned into women in their second birth. At that time, for this reason, the gods devised the love of sexual union. The very path of drink—which flows through the lungs, under the kidneys, into the bladder, and is discharged mixed with the breath—the gods diverted like a pipe into the compacted marrow that runs from the head through the neck and the spine.

This marrow is what we called the "seed" <note>original: "sperma"</note> in the previous sections. Because it is animated and breathing, at the part where it breathes out, it creates a vital desire to flow forth, and thus it implanted in us the love of procreation.

Wherefore the natural force of the private parts in men is innate, disobedient, and imperious—like an animal that does not listen to reason—trying to subject all things to itself through the violence of furious lusts.

In women, the womb <note>original: "vulua matrixq;"</note> and the matrix are for the same reason like an animal greedy for procreating. When it is kept for a long time without bearing fruit beyond the flower of youth, it bears the delay with difficulty and is greatly indignant. Wandering everywhere through the body, it shuts off the passages of the breath, does not allow for respiration, afflicts the person with extreme distress, and finally weighs them down with all kinds of diseases—until the desire and love of both sexes produce a child or fruit, as if from trees. They سپس <note>then</note> pluck it and scatter it into the matrix as if into a field. From this, they conceive living creatures that are at first so small they cannot be seen and are not yet formed; soon, they develop those parts that had flowed together, nourish the great things within, and finally bring them forth into the light, completing the generation of living beings. In this manner, women and all females were created.

<margin>
On the generation of birds.
</margin>
The race of birds was fashioned from our own type, but in such a way that it received feathers instead of hair. Into this form those men pass who, although they are simple and innocent, are nonetheless light-minded and vainly curious about things in the heavens; or those who are so foolish as to believe, trusting only in the judgment of their eyes, that the highest things can be firmly demonstrated by sight.

<margin>
On the generation of wild beasts.
</margin>
The race of land-walking wild beasts was born from those men who, being entirely alienated from philosophy, never lifted their eyes to the heavens. This occurred because they never used those revolutions that take place in the head, but followed those parts of the soul that dominate in the belly and the chest. Because of these pursuits, they fixed their front limbs and their heads entirely on the ground due to their lack of thought; they possessed a long and varied crown of the body because their intellectual circuits were crushed and broken there due to their sloth. For this reason, the form of four feet and even more was established: so that for the more foolish, God might provide a greater occasion for being drawn toward the earth through many feet and their way of walking.

Those who were the most foolish of these, and who prostrated their bodies entirely upon the earth as if they had no further need for feet, were changed into bodies lacking feet that crawl upon the ground.

<margin>
On the generation of aquatic creatures.
</margin>
The fourth kind is the aquatic, born from those who were the most dull-witted and ignorant. Our "transformers" <note>the lesser gods who shaped humanity</note> did not judge them worthy of pure respiration because, due to the wickedness of their extreme transgression, they possessed an utterly impure soul. Therefore, instead of that thin and pure respiration of the air, they plunged them into the deep and murky respiration of the water. From this arose the multitude of fish, oysters, and finally all aquatic creatures.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Introduction to the Critias, or the Atlantic Story.

Our Plato, a most dutiful son of his fatherland, praised it in the *Menexenus* for its brave deeds against the peoples of the East, and he praises it again in the *Critias* for its deeds performed against the peoples of the West. In both works, he commends the city for many things, including the gifts of God, nature, and art. At the same time, he reminds everyone not to be ungrateful to their country. While he commemorates how Attic virtue overcame both the rising and the setting regions <note>the East and West</note>, he teaches that everything is conquered by virtue, and that men endowed with virtue conduct themselves rightly and happily both in "western" affairs (that is, in adversity) and in "eastern" affairs (that is, in prosperity). Nor is it without reason that he wishes the *Critias*, which concerns the antiquity of the world, to be read after the *Timaeus*, which concerns the generation of the world. It appears, however, that he neither finished this history nor composed the subsequent history promised under the title of *Hermocrates*. 

That this was not a fictional tale, but a true history, is well-established. First, because whenever Plato invents something, he is accustomed to call it a myth <note>original: "fabulam"</note>; here, however, he dares to assert it as a history. Furthermore, he asserts the same thing in the *Timaeus*, calling it a wondrous thing but entirely true. He carefully recounts from whom it was received in both places: namely, from his ancestors and kinsmen. <margin>Critias</margin> For the Critias here heard it from his grandfather Critias, who heard it from his uncle Solon, who even committed it to writing; Solon, in turn, heard it from the Egyptian priests. Furthermore, Proclus cites the histories of a certain Marcellus concerning Ethiopian affairs, in which these events are most clearly confirmed, being inserted among the deeds of the Ethiopians. While none of the Platonists deny the history, Porphyry, Proclus, and before them Origen, believe it also contains a physical allegory. I fear that if they try to fit every detail perfectly to an allegory, they might be mocked by Plato himself, who, in the person of Socrates at the start of the *Phaedrus*, ridicules those who are too curious about such allegorical interpretations. 

However, lest we seem to entirely neglect the "anagogical" sense <note>the spiritual or "upward-leading" meaning</note>—without which no one can truly be a Platonist—let Pallas <note>Athena</note> be the divinity presiding over the intellectual life, while Neptune is the divinity who nourishes and governs generation <note>the physical process of birth and becoming</note>. <margin>Athena and Neptune</margin> Let the Athenians represent the souls of those living by the intellect alone, and of similar divine spirits. The Atlanteans, then, represent the types of spirits favoring generation, and of souls joined to bodies for the duty of generation and the ordering of the whole world. It is most fitting that the West, the fighting, the islands, and the various divisions of locations signify the very matter of generation and its diverse mobility. Furthermore, let the war be a diligent struggle through which the higher divinities continually turn the lower ones toward themselves, and separate souls from matter and movement as if by fire and sword. 

Accordingly, when Neptune is said to have fathered sons by a woman, understand this to mean he either generated them from the earth or, by a certain inspiration, regenerated them from an earlier form of living into another. As for the five births: these are the five forms of bodies which he composes in this "sea" of matter through perpetual agitation—namely stones, metals, plants, irrational animals, and those endowed with reason. There are ten sons because in each birth twins are created together. <margin><unclear>five spheres</unclear></margin> Truly, in any composite thing, an elemental power grows together with a certain celestial power, which physicians call a "specific virtue." From the five twin births, ten sons are counted. But the five zones or spirals surrounding the citadel of Neptune are the natures of the five spheres: celestial, fiery, airy, watery, and earthy. He says they are partly earthy and partly watery to signify stability and movement in things. The common passage through all the channels signifies the mutual generation of things among themselves. He also mentions metals, so that through the seven metals we may understand the influences of the seven planets governing the generation of all things. <margin>Metals dedicated to the planets: ☉ Sun, ☽ Moon, ♄ Saturn, ♃ Jupiter, ♂ Mars, ♀ Venus, ☿ Mercury</margin> The Platonists attribute Gold to the Sun, Silver to the Moon, Lead to Saturn, Electrum <note>an alloy of gold and silver</note> to Jupiter, Iron and Bronze to Mars, Orichalcum <note>a legendary golden-colored herb or metal, often associated with mountain copper</note> to Venus, and Tin to Mercury. 

The measures and their numbers may be drawn partly from history and partly from the logic of architecture. Something must also be attributed to the grace and beauty of both the craftsmanship and the eloquence. But enough has been said of the allegory for now. Now let us confirm the mysteries of this book in this way: the Platonists believe some gods are "super-celestial" (to use their words), others are "celestial," and others are "sub-celestial." They call the first ones the sons of God, and all the following ones the sons of gods. Again, they place the most ample providence in the first, less ample in the second, and in the third a providence reduced to narrower limits, since these already preside over specific regions of the earth and kinds of things by divine distribution—just as some celestial gods are placed over certain parts of the heaven and certain stars. These sub-celestial gods, at a certain...
