# INTRODUCTION TO THE CRITIAS.

...ern order, others have from the beginning undertaken the governance of different nations. From the beginning, I say, of either the created world or the reborn human race. For after the great floods of the terrestrial globe, Plato thinks that men are divinely generated from the earth itself, as if from a mother, by the work of the gods. For they are able to beget through the human **Idea** <note>Ficino refers to the Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas"—the eternal, perfect blueprints of things</note>, acting as a seed. The earth is also able to give birth, being soaked with an abundant moisture and made fertile by approaching heat—whether warm suns follow the deluges of water, or rains flow more abundantly after vast conflagrations. Those men born from the gods out of the earth are called **heroes**; from the beginning, they were persuaded of what is right by their parents through a certain hidden communication of mind to mind for many ages. 

However, because over a long stretch of time both the divine virtue implanted in their natures and the fertility of the earth gradually diminish—whereby souls would become entirely devoid of divinity and bodies completely empty of their ancient fertility—God either washes the earth again or burns it, and restores our race to its ancient dignity. This occurs because the celestial motions are so tempered by the **Mover** <note>The "Prime Mover" or God who sets the heavens in motion</note> that celestial fate always runs together with divine providence. 

Indeed, just as doctors judge any individual human body, so the Platonists judge the whole human race. For doctors say that life consists in a certain **natural humor** <note>original: "humore"; in ancient medicine, the "humors" were bodily fluids that determined health and temperament</note>, of such a quantity and such a quality. They say life could be extended indefinitely if only that humor were restored in the same quantity and quality; but it is not extended when the fluid that flows back in is not the same quality as that which flowed out, even if the quantity remains the same. It is just as if someone were to fill a bowl every day from a full jar of wine, and immediately pour an equal amount of water into the jar. In this way, there would always be an equal amount of liquid in the jar, but it would not be the same liquid, and it would become more dissimilar every day, until at last, from what was once pure wine, it becomes not just watery wine, but entirely water. 

Similarly, the Platonists think that the divine and fertile quality once infused into the human character by the gods, and into the body by the heavens, is gradually turned into a merely human quality, as this human subject naturally draws it down, until it slowly degenerates even into a beast-like state. But such great degeneration cannot be perpetually tolerated by God, the Orderer of things. For this reason, Plato says here and often elsewhere that the gods obtained different "lots" or provinces; understand that they obey the one Supreme God who distributes these lots, and they govern the province necessarily assigned to them. 

But **necessity** in divine matters is entirely voluntary. For among the gods, there is but one will of the Supreme Father and his children. Just as parts of the elements are carried by necessity to their proper places—which would also be their will, if only they had the power of knowing—so among the higher beings, the very necessity of the assigned and naturally effected governance is the same as their will. 

Furthermore, one must remember that here, as in the *Timaeus* and *Menexenus*, the **Attic region** <note>the area around Athens</note> is described as being especially suited for genius. In assigning reasons for this, the Platonists disagree among themselves. **Panaetius** <note>A Stoic philosopher who influenced later Platonists</note> thinks the cause is the temperate air between heat and frost. He proves this from Plato's own words in the fifth book of the *Laws* and the *Epinomis*. **Longinus** <note>A famous literary critic and philosopher</note> argues against Panaetius, because that region is often struck by frost and heat; he assigns the cause to a quality of the place that is a hidden mixture of many things. **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist</note> rejects him, as he thinks the proper cause of genius is physical. **Origen** <note>Referring here to Origen the Platonist, not the Church Father</note>, in his commentaries on the *Timaeus*, assigns the cause to celestial aspects and influences, asserting this from the eighth book of the *Republic*, where it is said that certain celestial circuits are the causes of fertility and sterility, both of bodies and of souls. 

But **Proclus** <note>One of the last major Greek philosophers of antiquity</note> says in the same place that Origen assigned a true cause in part, but had not yet perfected it. Proclus himself, together with Porphyry, seeking the matter more deeply, says: The Intellect that is the Maker of the world is an **Intellectual World**, and therefore, as it were, manifold. The **World-Soul**, however, is an animal and rational world, and even more manifold. Closely accompanying the entire space of the world, it is completely continuous and immovable, consisting of prime matter and constant dimension. Again, in space itself, before all forms that are to be generated, the Soul—following the **Ideas** according to its own reasons—imprints different powers in different places, like traces of a mind full of soul; these act as peculiar receptacles that will familiarly receive different forms in different places. 

Then the various gods, having been allotted various provinces, illuminate and form these "lodgings," some gods affecting some places, and others affecting others. Therefore, rational souls, after they have chosen an elemental life and their own character, if by chance they are directed by the celestial revolution to those places that most suit the chosen form of living, they fully fulfill the duty of that life. Thus, when those turning toward a Martian or Apolline life <note>lives influenced by Mars (war) or Apollo (prophecy/arts)</note> happen upon a region illuminated by **Mars** or **Apollo**, they perfectly complete the work of either courage or prophecy. Those who have chosen a philosophical life, if they find a region inspired by **Pallas** <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom</note>, excel in both wisdom and magnanimity at once. 

Therefore, here and in the *Timaeus*, Plato says the Attic region, ruled by Pallas, is suitable for wisdom and military service; and in the fifth book of the *Laws*, he says the inspiration of local gods and spirits <note>original: "daemonum"</note> regarding places is of the greatest importance for genius and character. This requires a certain temperance of the air, not as the primary cause, but so that the work of the cause itself is not hindered. For this reason, the diversity of a place does not so much *create* a diversity of genius among the Platonists as it *receives* and *reveals* it. For they think three things are more powerful for this than the elemental location: namely, the disposition of the soul itself (whether natural or chosen), the inspiration of its own particular deities, and celestial influences. This can be hindered, however, by an elemental mixture, or a new conjunction of planets, or by a calamity brought on by men themselves; thus the good things poured down from above are rendered "not good" by the obstacle of lower things. We have discussed this matter in the *Laws*. But enough of these things for now. From all the mysteries of this book, gather as one...

FO. CCCIII.
->CRITIAS OR THE ATLANTIC.<-

<meta>Ink smudge on right side of page; catchword "ea" at bottom right.</meta>

that human free will concurs with divine providence. Note also a concept similar to the **Mosaic mystery** <note>original: "mosaico mysterio"; Ficino refers to the biblical account in Genesis regarding the Garden of Eden</note>: that men once lived in a certain, as they say, **paradise of delights**, so long as a certain divine grace and justice flourished within them. But after that grace vanished through intemperance and pride, they fell simultaneously into crimes and the gravest calamities. Furthermore, they say that God washed away the sins of men with a deluge of waters. What is missing from this history can be repaired in summary from the prologue of the *Timaeus*. This is a history of events before the flood. After the flood, as I believe, **Hermocrates** was intended to be the narrator. Nor should those nine thousand years trouble you, if you listen to **Eudoxus** <note>A Greek astronomer and mathematician</note> saying that those years of the Egyptians were not solar, but lunar <note>i.e., months rather than years</note>. Finally, the last sentence of this book teaches that **Jupiter**—that is, the god who is the architect of the world—looks forth from his seat (which is to say, from his own self-contemplation) upon all things, even the most remote and smallest. He turns all the gods subject to him toward that same seat, which is divine contemplation, so that, having been thus instructed, they may govern lower things. Nor do they do these two things in turns; rather, by constantly contemplating divine things, they simultaneously dispense temporal affairs through them. For this reason, he calls this seat the **throne at the center of the world**, because from there all things flow out as if from a center, and thither they flow back; and from there, all things are easily surveyed and governed.

### THE CRITIAS OF PLATO, OR THE ATLANTIC.

### TIMAEUS. CRITIAS. SOCRATES. HERMOCRATES.

->TIMAEUS.<-

<margin>punishment of the ignorant</margin>
**HOW** pleasant rest is to one weary after a long journey, O Socrates; so too is sweet silence to me after the long windings of our discussion. As for this world—which is in reality ancient, but was only recently "created a god" by our discourse—I pray that if anything has been spoken fittingly, he himself may preserve and guard it for us. If, however, we have brought forth anything unseemly in the preceding parts against our will, may he exact the deserved penalties from us. Now, the proper penalty for one who has strayed through ignorance or negligence is that he be made knowledgeable and diligent. Therefore, so that we may speak more correctly hereafter about the generation of the gods, we pray that the most perfect and healthful medicine of all—**knowledge**—be given to us by God. Having finished these prayers, I now yield the following discourse to **Critias**, as was agreed among us.

**CRITIAS.** I accept it indeed, O Timaeus. And just as you previously asked for indulgence as one about to dispute great matters, I now ask the same. Indeed, I believe even greater indulgence should be granted for the things that remain, even though I know this request of mine might seem somewhat bold and unrefined. Nevertheless, I must speak. No one of sound mind would object that the things previously spoken by you were not spoken rightly; however, I will try to show that the remaining things to be said require greater leniency, inasmuch as they are more difficult. For it is easier for one who discourses on the gods to seem to satisfy men than for one who unfolds the history of mortals. For the lack of skill and the ignorance of the listeners grants a great deal of license to those speaking to invent things that are unknown. We are not ignorant of how we are affected regarding the gods; but to open my meaning more plainly to you, attend to this: Whatever is said by us, we ought to consider as a kind of imitation and expression of likeness. Let us not overlook the ease or difficulty found in a painter’s rendering of divine or human bodies, so that they might seem to the spectators to have represented them sufficiently. Surely when they paint the earth, mountains, rivers, woods, and the whole sky—and those things which exist around the sky or wander through it—we think it enough if someone can render even a small image of them. Then, being entirely ignorant of such things, we neither examine the painter’s works nor argue against them, but we make do with a certain confused sketch and deceptive shading. But when someone attempts to fashion a likeness of our own bodies, then, because of our familiar observation of our own affairs, we perceive errors more sharply; we are severe and sharp judges and taskmasters against him who has not expressed every feature and color. One may observe the same in speeches. For we think we have done enough if anything, even a small amount of what is fitting, is brought forth concerning celestial and divine things. But we are accustomed to examine mortal and human works far too exactly. For this reason, if we treat the things that are to be said presently with less than their proper dignity, it is right to forgive us. For it must be thought that mortal things are not easily—indeed, they are certainly difficult—to express through imitation to the point of belief. I have said all these things, O Socrates, desiring both to remind you and to seek greater indulgence from you for the things that remain. If I seem to ask for what is just, grant this indulgence of your own accord.

**SOCRATES.** Nothing stands in the way, O Critias, of granting you what you ask. Furthermore, let this same thing be granted by us to **Hermocrates** as a third. For it is clear that when he is about to speak a little while from now, he will pray for the same things. Therefore, so that he may begin differently, and not [repeat these...]

...should he be forced to repeat himself, let him know that pardon has been granted to him: and as if that were certain, let him immediately prepare to speak. I foretell to you, friend Critias, the opinion of this theater <note>original: "theatri"; here referring to the audience or assembly of listeners</note>, for the previous speaker was wonderfully approved by it. Therefore, you will need much indulgence if you are to grasp these matters sufficiently. 

**HERMOCRATES:** The same message applies to me, Socrates, as what you announce to him. However, the sluggish and faint-hearted have never won the palm of victory, Critias. It is fitting, therefore, to approach the discourse with a brave heart: and having called upon Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of light and music</note> and the Muses, you should illustrate the ancient citizens, those excellent men, with the highest praises. 

**CRITIAS:** O friend Hermocrates, since tomorrow's day has been assigned to you, you will follow another speaker: and therefore you are confident. But what that experience is really like, it will perhaps reveal to you soon enough. I must obey you who are exhorting me and setting me on fire for the task. And beyond the gods you mentioned, it is fitting to invoke others besides: and especially **Mnemosyne** <margin>Mnemosyne [means] Memory</margin>—that is, Memory. For almost all the most important parts of our discourses depend upon this goddess. Truly, if we remember and recount to you now what was once handed down by the priests and brought here by Solon <note>The famous Greek lawmaker who allegedly brought the story of Atlantis from Egypt</note>, we shall seem to this assembly, as I think, to have sufficiently performed what is appropriate. This must now be done, and there must be no further delay. 

First, let us commemorate that the total sum of years was nine thousand since the war was said to have broken out between all those who lived beyond and those who lived within the **Pillars of Hercules** <note>original: "colunas Herculis"; the Strait of Gibraltar</note>, which we are now about to narrate. This city [Athens] was the leader of the former, and as it is said, carried through the whole war; of the latter, the leaders were the kings of the **Atlantic Island** [Atlantis], which we have previously stated was once larger than Libya and Asia combined. But later, an unsightly mud was left there after the island was submerged by a concussion of the earth, which indeed prevents those sailing from here into the deep sea from navigating further. 

The progress of the speech itself will narrate the barbarian nations that existed then, and the Greek ones generally, here and there as the occasion is given. But it is fitting first to set forth the strengths, the governments, the order of war, and the success of the Athenians of that time and their adversaries. Of these, we will first tell of our own city. 

The gods once divided the entire circle of the earth by lot, distributed into individual regions. Nor did contention make this partition. For it would be far from reason to suggest that the gods should be ignorant of what is suitable for each of them, or that knowing what belongs rather to others, they should contend to usurp each other's rights in turn. Rather, each receiving their own by the lots of judgment and law according to their wish, and caring for each individual among their charges, they arranged the regions to be inhabited. They nourished these as their own flocks, possessions, and herds; with this exception, however: they did not wish to compel bodies with physical force, as shepherds do with blows to cattle and beasts of burden. But rather, directing them like a docile and obedient animal as if from the stern of an agile ship, they used persuasion as a rudder, and touched them in their souls: and thus leading all the mortal race according to their own mind, they governed them. 

And while other gods were allotted the government of other places and established them, **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus</note> and **Minerva** <note>Athena</note> shared a common nature—both because they are from the same father, and because they tend toward the same goal through the study of wisdom and the diligence of arts. Thus they obtained this common lot in this region [Attica], as being naturally proper and suitable for virtue and prudence. And procreating in it men who were truly noble natives, they infused the order of the republic into their minds. 

Only their names remained. But their works, because of the death of those who received them and the long intervals of time, have been carried away from the memory of men. For the survivors of the human race, as we said above, were always mountain-roaming and unrefined people, who had only heard the names of the powerful men in the region. But besides these names, there were only some small signs of their deeds. Therefore, the descendants gave the names of the ancients to their own sons out of a certain affection, while remaining ignorant of the virtues and laws of their predecessors. For they had nothing of these except hearsay, and that not certain enough. Since for many ages they lacked the necessities of life, and they and their children applied their minds to those things whose scarcity pressed upon them, they neglected the memory of ancient things. For storytelling and the investigation of ancient things usually arise in cities only when leisure exists and the necessities of life are already prepared, but not before. And so the names of the ancients have been preserved without their works. 

I say these things guessing thus, because Solon says that those Egyptian priests inserted many names very similar to the later Greeks in the narration of the ancient war, such as **Cecrops**, **Erectheus**, **Erichthonius**, **Erisichthon**, and others from those which are remembered before **Theseus**. Similarly the names of the women, and the same works: and the figure and statue of the goddess **Pallas** <note>Athena</note>, so that the studies of war were then common to men and women. Truly, at that time the armed goddess was openly displayed to give an example to all, that in every herd of animals, the brave male and female of each kind are so instituted by nature that they are able to approach all things in common. 

There lived then in this region other classes of citizens who were engaged in crafts and agriculture. But the soldiers, separated from the beginning by divine men, lived apart, having everything contributing both to food and education. None of them possessed anything of his own, for they thought all things were common among them. Beyond the sufficiency of their own food, they required nothing from the other citizens; and they practiced all those things which were explained yesterday concerning the **Guardians** whom we described <note>Critias refers back to the social structure of the ideal state discussed in Plato’s *Republic*</note>. Indeed, that was truly and probably said of our region: first, that in those times it had its boundaries distinct toward the Isthmus, and that it sloped on the other side...

# CRITIAS, OR THE ATLANTIC STORY

<meta>Catchword: Divided; handwritten folio number 302 in top right corner; Google digitization watermark bottom right.</meta>

...the land of the continent as far as the heights of Cithaeron and Parnes <note>original: "Citheronem atq; Parnaethem"; mountain ranges forming the natural borders of Attica</note>. These boundaries held Oropia on the right descent, and towards the sea on the left, they were divided by the Asopus river. It is recorded that in virtue, this entire land surpassed all others. For this reason, the region was able at that time to support the vast army gathered around it. A clearly evident proof of its excellence is this: that what remains of the land now can compete with any other in the variety of its produce, the excellence of its fruits, and the abundance of pastures suited to every kind of animal. But in those days, the land produced all these things not only in beautiful form, but in the greatest abundance. By what reasoning is this probable? Or by what evidence can one conjecture that these are the remnants of that former land? Since the whole region extends far into the sea from the rest of the continent, it lies like a promontory. The nearby depth of the sea surrounds it on all sides. Since many great floods occurred during the interval of nine thousand years—for that many years have flowed from that time to the present—the earth falling away from the heights during these times and washouts does not, as is usual elsewhere, pile up into mounds, but is always falling away and vanishing into the deep. Therefore, what remains today, compared to what it once was, is like the bones of a body wasted away by disease: the soft and rich earth has been washed away, and only the thin and arid frame of the land remains. 

Once, the intact land had very high hills and mountains. And the fields which are now called Phelleus <note>meaning "stony" or "rocky" ground</note> were fertile with rich soil. Forest growth was frequent on the mountain peaks. Even now, certain traces of this remain. For there are some mountains which now feed only bees; but once, and not so long ago, huge trees were cut there, perfectly suited for making roofs and beams, the structures of which still survive in the largest buildings. There were also many other cultivated trees, mild and tall. Furthermore, the pastures for cattle were most abundant. Moreover, every year this region drank the fruit-bearing rain from Jupiter <note>referring to Zeus/the heavens</note>. It did not, as it does now, pour the water from the bare earth into the sea through steep gullies; instead, it absorbed the water from the heights in abundance, storing it in a certain tenacious cavity, drinking it down into its depths. From there, flowing streams of rivers and springs gushed out everywhere; even now, certain sacred signs remain at the ancient springs to prove these accounts. Therefore, what is told of these matters today is true. 

And such was the condition of this region. Furthermore, it was cultivated at that time by farmers, as is fitting—men who were true to their craft and intent upon it, naturally gifted and great lovers of honor. They possessed a fertile soil, most copious water, and a climate most healthy throughout every season of the year. The city at that time was arranged in this way: First, the disposition of the citadel was then different from what it is now. For the soil of the citadel was washed away and stripped bare by the flood of a single night, and shattered by an earthquake; and it is said that a similar destruction occurred before that, during the time of Deucalion <note>The "Greek Noah" who survived a great flood</note>, after the third inundation. In the former time, however, its magnitude extended as far as the Eridanus and Ilissus <note>rivers of Athens</note>, encompassing the Pnyx within and Lycabettus as the boundary opposite the Pnyx. It was all covered in earth and, with few exceptions, flat on top. 

Its outer parts, beneath its transverse sections, were inhabited by craftsmen and farmers who worked the nearby fields. But the upper parts were inhabited by the soldiers alone, near the temple of Minerva <note>Athena</note> and Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note>, enclosed in a single circuit like the garden of a single house. They lived on the northern side, having communal houses and dining halls where they prepared communal banquets in winter. Everything that suited a communal civic life was maintained through the arrangement of their houses, both in these and in the sacred spaces, without gold or silver. Indeed, they never used these metals for any purpose. Instead, following a middle path between pride and meanness, they built honest dwellings in which they grew old, leaving them to the children of their children—descendants like themselves. They used the gardens, gymnasiums, and dining halls facing the south during the summer. There was once a single spring where the site of the citadel now is. After it was exhausted by the earthquake, only small trickles remain around it. But then, it provided an abundant irrigation for all, with a temperature that was healthful for both summer and winter. In this manner they inhabited these places: as guardians of their own citizens and leaders of the other Greeks who followed them by choice, observing above all that their number should always remain the same—specifically, twenty thousand men and women already strong in the art of war. 

Since they were such a people, always justly governing their own homeland and all of Greece in this manner, they were held to be the most esteemed and famous of all who then lived, across all of Europe and Asia, as much for the excellence of their bodies as for the innumerable gifts of their minds. Next, we shall communicate to you, as friends, what the affairs of their adversaries were like from the beginning, unless perhaps they have slipped from memory since the time we heard them as children. But before I relate this, you must be warned not to wonder if you now hear many barbarian names in Greek. This happened because Solon <margin>Solon</margin>, when he intended to insert them into his poems, investigated the actual meaning of the names. He found that those first Egyptian writers of these matters had translated those names into their own tongue. Therefore, he himself, receiving the sense of each name, converted it back into our own language. These writings were in the possession of my grandfather, and are now with me; I have meditated upon them since my childhood. Therefore, if you hear names such as those we have among us, do not be surprised, for you understand the reason for this. The beginning of that long discourse was the same as that introduced previously regarding the portions of the gods. They divided the whole earth: some into larger portions, some into smaller; and the temples...

# THE ATLANTIC STORY

<warning>Bleed-through from the reverse side of the page makes some text slightly difficult to read; marginalia is in a different hand.</warning>

...and established sacred rites for themselves. Then indeed, Neptune <note>The Roman name for Poseidon, the god of the sea.</note>, having been allotted the Atlantic island, fathered sons by a mortal woman in a certain place on the island. Near the sea, there was a level plain, but in the middle of the island was a flatland which is said to have been the most beautiful and fertile of all. Near this plain, again in the center, was a low mountain, fifty stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet or 185 meters.</note> away. Here lived one of those men who, from the beginning, were born from the earth, named Evenor. He, with his wife Leucippe, fathered an only daughter, Clito. When her parents died and the girl was of age for a husband, Neptune, captured by desire for her, united with her. He enclosed the hill where she lived with concentric rings of sea and land; these zones alternated, some wider and some narrower. Two of these circles were of land and three were of water, which, as if turned on a lathe, were at an equal distance from the center of the island on all sides. They made the hill itself inaccessible to men, for at that time there were no ships nor any skill in sailing. He himself, being a god, easily adorned the central island, and caused two types of water to burst forth from the hidden depths of the earth through springs: one hot and the other cold. He also caused various and abundant foods to sprout from the earth. 

Furthermore, he fathered and raised five pairs of male twins. He divided the entire Atlantic island into ten regions. To the firstborn, he gave the mother's dwelling and the surrounding region, which was the largest and most powerful lot. He appointed him king over the others, and the others as princes of many peoples and regions. He gave names to each. The firstborn he called 

<margin>The Atlantic Sea:</margin>

Atlas, the king of the whole island. From him, the sea is also named Atlantic. The one born immediately after him in the first twin birth, he called Gadirum in the native tongue, which in Greek we call Eumelus. He was allotted the furthest parts of the island toward the Pillars of Hercules <note>original: "columnas Herculis"; the Strait of Gibraltar, marking the edge of the known Mediterranean world.</note> and named the place Gadiric after himself. Of the second birth, he named one Ampheres, the other Evaemon. Of the third, the firstborn Mneseus, the second Autochthon. Of the fourth, Elasippus first, then Mestor. Finally, of the fifth, Azaes first, and Diaprepes second. All these and their descendants lived there for many ages, ruling over many other islands in the sea, and even as far as Egypt and Tyrrhenia <note>The land of the Etruscans in central Italy.</note> among those living on this side of the sea, as we said before. 

Certainly, the entire lineage of Atlas was held in the highest veneration; the older king always left the kingdom to his firstborn, an empire they preserved for many ages. Indeed, they had such an abundance of wealth as no previous kings ever had, nor would any of their successors easily match. Everything was built and organized in the city and throughout the kingdom for whatever use was required. Much came to them from outside because of their empire, but the island itself produced most things necessary for life. First, all things that are dug from the bowels of the earth—both those that remain solid and those that are melted. And what is now called "mined" <note>original: "fossile"</note>, then certainly orichalcum <note>original: "orichalcum"; a legendary reddish, gold-like metal, second only to gold in value to the Atlanteans.</note> was mined in many places on the island as a distinguished metal, then considered the most precious among them except for gold. And whatever the forest produces for the craft of carpenters, it bore in abundance. It also provided pasture for animals, both wild and domestic. 

<margin>There were elephants on the island which was beyond the Pillars of Hercules.</margin>

Furthermore, there was a huge abundance of elephants there. For the land provided enough for all those that feed in marshes, lakes, and rivers, or on mountains or fields. It also fed a vast and most voracious kind of animal. The earth also bore whatever it now nourishes that is fragrant: roots, grasses, woods, liquid juices, flowers, and fruits. Furthermore, it produced the sweet juice of the vine and solid nourishment <note>referring to grain or corn</note> by which we are fed. Also those things we use for food and for the sake of seasoning, which we call legumes. Likewise, oils from trees, and foods to quench thirst and hunger. Nor were ointments lacking. And for the sake of delight, the most copious fruits of various trees were added. There were also the comforts of satiety, desserts sought out by those who are weary of eating. All these things the island, which once existed—sacred, beautiful, wondrous, and most fertile—produced. 

And collecting these materials from the earth, they built temples, royal palaces, harbors, shipyards, and the entire region. Indeed, in this way, they arranged those rings of sea which surrounded the ancient metropolis, that is, the ancestral seat of their mother. First, by constructing bridges, they provided a passage to the exterior and to the royal seat. There, at the seats of the god himself and his ancestors, they built royal palaces right from the beginning. One after another, receiving the adorned buildings in continuous succession, they surpassed their predecessors in decorating them according to their strength, until they built structures wondrous in magnitude and beauty. Furthermore, they led a trench from the sea to the outermost circle, which extended three iugera <note>A measurement of width; approximately 300 feet.</note> in width, one hundred feet in depth, and fifty stadia in length. And so that ships could reach that circle from the sea as if entering a harbor, they opened its mouth so that it could receive the largest ships. 

Likewise, they cut through the zones of land that separated the rings of sea with bridges, so that one trireme <note>An ancient warship with three banks of oars.</note> could sail between them at a time; but they covered them above so that they could sail underneath. For the high banks of the land zones rose above the sea. The largest circle through which the sea flowed was three stadia in width; the next ring of land was exactly equal to it. Of the following two, the watery one was two stadia, while the dry one was again equal to the preceding watery one. Finally, there was one stadium of water which surrounded the island itself positioned in the middle. The diameter of the island in which the palace stood was five stadia. And they enclosed this, the circles, and the bridge (which was a plethrum <note>roughly 100 feet</note> in width) on both sides with a stone wall, building towers and gates at each point where the bridges crossed the sea. They quarried the stone that lay beneath the island in the middle, and under the circles, both inside and out: some white, some black, some red. They constructed two hollow ship-receptacles, doubled within, whose arches were carved from this very rock.

# FOLIO 305
## CRITIAS OR THE ATLANTIC STORY

->**N**<-

The buildings they constructed were sometimes simple, and at other times varied by mixing different types of stones, seeking a sense of play and delight through the variety itself. Furthermore, they coated the entire surface of the wall that enclosed the outermost circle with a thin layer of bronze; the inner wall they coated with tin; and finally, the wall surrounding the citadel itself was covered in <term>orichalcum <note>original: "orichalco"; a legendary reddish gold-colored metal, second only to gold in value among the Atlanteans.</note></term> which shimmered with a fiery glow. The royal palace within the citadel was constructed in the following manner. In the center stood the sacred and inaccessible temple of Clito and Neptune, surrounded by a golden enclosure. It was there that, in the beginning, the ten kings were conceived and born; and there, gathered every year from the ten regions, they performed solemn sacrifices to each of them. The temple of Neptune was one stadium <note>About 600 feet.</note> in length, three <term>iugera <note>original: "iugera"; here used as a measure of width, roughly 300 feet.</note></term> in width, and reached a height that seemed appropriate to its length and breadth. Its shape and appearance were <term>barbaric <note>original: "barbarica"; in this context, meaning "foreign" or "exotic" rather than "savage."</note></term>. They adorned the entire exterior face with silver, except for the topmost pinnacles; the peaks and gables themselves were covered in gold. Inside, however, the entire vaulted ceiling was made of ivory, intricately carved with gold, silver, and orichalcum. Furthermore, they decorated the walls, columns, and floors with orichalcum. They also erected statues made of gold. There was a statue of the god himself standing in a chariot, holding the reins of winged horses, <margin>The horses pulling Neptune’s chariot were winged.</margin> his head touching the high ceiling. Around him were a hundred Nereids <note>Sea nymphs of Greek mythology.</note> riding on dolphins, for they believed at that time that there were that many of them. There were also many other statues and offerings dedicated by private citizens. Outside, there stood golden images of all the royal women and the men who were descended from the ten kings, along with many other massive statues and offerings from both the city and the other lands subject to their empire. There was also an altar that, in its size and craftsmanship, was perfectly suited to the rest of the display. In the same way, the palace was appropriate both to the greatness of the kingdom and the splendor of the sacred ornaments.

They made use of springs of both hot and cold water, which flowed with constant moisture; these possessed a wonderful healthfulness and pleasantness for both uses. Houses were built around the springs, and water-loving trees were planted there. Water reservoirs were also placed around them, some open to the sky, others covered for hot baths suited to the winter time—separate baths for the royalty, separate ones for private citizens, and others for women, as well as for horses and other beasts of burden. Each was kept in a manner that was decent and fitting. They channeled the overflowing water into the grove of Neptune, which was filled with many kinds of trees of marvelous height and beauty due to the fertility of the soil. From there, they diverted it through aqueducts near the bridges into the outer circles. In those areas, there were many temples and shrines to the gods, gardens, and gymnasiums—some for men and others for horses—located separately on each of the two circular islands. In the middle of the largest island, there was a primary <term>hippodrome <note>original: "hippodromus"; a stadium designed for horse and chariot racing.</note></term>, <margin>hippodrome</margin> which was one stadium in width, and its length stretched around the entire circle for equestrian competition. On both sides of the hippodrome were the houses of the attendants and guards. The custody of the city was entrusted to the most faithful soldiers within the narrower circle closest to the citadel, while those who excelled all others in loyalty were granted dwellings within the citadel itself, near the kings. Furthermore, the shipyards were filled with <term>triremes <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars.</note></term> and all the equipment belonging to them, all sufficiently prepared. This was the arrangement of the royal dwellings.

As one passed through the three outer harbors, a wall appeared, starting from the sea like a rampart, standing fifty stadia from the largest circle and harbor on all sides; it closed back upon itself at the mouth of the channel facing the sea. This entire area was densely inhabited. The remaining space was filled with many frequent buildings, and the bay and largest harbor were full of ships and merchants flocking from all directions. Because of the great crowd, a continuous clamor and huge noise was heard day and night.

Thus we have now reported on the layout of the city and the ancient seat of power as it was once handed down. Next, we shall attempt to recount the nature and cultivation of the rest of the region. At the beginning, the entire location was said to be very high and sheer above the sea. The region around the city was entirely a plain, surrounding the city and enclosed by the outer perimeter. Mountains hemmed it in along the sea, but the plain itself was level and flat. On one side, it stretched for three thousand stadia; but across the middle, from the sea upwards, it was two thousand stadia. The position of the island faced South, but was sheltered from the North by the mountains. Its mountains surpassed all those that exist now in their number, height, and beauty. In them were many wealthy villages of the inhabitants, as well as rivers, lakes, and meadows, which provided abundant nourishment for all animals, both wild and domestic. There was also a vast and varied forest that supplied ample timber for every kind of work; thus the place was well-disposed by nature and had been cultivated over a long time by the diligence and wealth of many kings. The region was mostly a rectangular shape, stretching straight and long, but it had lost its perfect form because of a trench dug around it. Its depth, length, and breadth are incredible to describe. Indeed, it seems impossible that such a vast work, compared to other works, could have been made by human hands. However, we must say what we have heard: the depth was one <term>iugera <note>Approximately 100 feet deep.</note></term>, the width was one stadium everywhere, and since it was dug around the entire field, its length was ten thousand stadia. This trench received the streams flowing down from the mountains, and winding through the fields, it reached the city from both sides and finally emptied into the sea. From above the city itself, straight channels one hundred feet wide were cut through the fields and emptied back into the trench near the sea. One channel was separated from the next by one hundred stadia. They brought timber from the forests to the city, and other seasonal produce, by using boats through the cross-channels, for the paths of the trenches intersected each other obliquely as far as the city. They gathered twin harvests from the earth each year; in winter, the earth was soaked by the rains through the blessing of Jupiter <note>The Roman name for Zeus, god of the sky and rain.</note>, and in summer, it was irrigated by the streams from the aqueducts.

...was irrigated. Regarding the number of men in the plain region fit for military service, the order was as follows: each lot chose and provided its own leader. The size of a lot was ten <term>stadia <note>original: "stadia"; a Greek unit of length, approximately 600 feet.</note></term> by ten. Of all the lots, there were sixty thousand. However, of those who inhabited the mountains and other places, the number was infinite; yet they were all distributed through the regions and villages into these lots according to their leaders. It was thus established that a leader should bring to war a tenth part of a war chariot, totaling ten thousand chariots; two horses and two riders, and again yoked horses without a <term>biga <note>original: "bigis"; a two-horse chariot. The text describes a complex division of chariot equipment and personnel.</note></term>. There would also be one who would dismount armed with a small shield, and one who would steer both horses in turn with reins. Likewise, two men-at-arms; two archers and two slingers; soldiers of light armor; three stone-throwers and three javelin-throwers. Finally, four sailors to complete the complement of two hundred thousand ships. In this manner were the military affairs prepared in the royal city. However, the apparatus of the other nine cities was different in different places; a longer narrative would be required to explain them. 

The magistrates and honors were established from the beginning in this way. Each of the ten kings, in his own jurisdiction and in his own city, held power over the men and most of the laws; he punished according to his judgment and condemned any to death. Indeed, the authority and communal interaction among them were directed according to the mandates of <term>Neptune <note>original: "Neptuni"; the Roman name for the Greek god Poseidon, the legendary father of the Atlantean kings.</note></term>, just as the laws and writings from their ancestors announced on a certain column of <term>orichalcum <note>original: "orichalco"; a legendary reddish-gold metal.</note></term> near the center of the island, in the temple of Neptune himself. They gathered there every fifth year, and sometimes every sixth, alternating between even and odd years to distribute power equally. Having gathered, they deliberated on public affairs; and judging with a diligent examination, they condemned anyone who had transgressed in any matter. When, therefore, a judgment was to be entered, they bound themselves to one another with such a pledge: 

For when the bulls had been released and set loose in the temple of Neptune, the ten kings themselves—apart from all others—vowed to the god that they would capture a victim pleasing to him without the use of iron. Thus, they hunted with wooden clubs and nooses. And whichever bull they caught, they dragged it to the column and slaughtered it directly over the top of the column where the mandate had been written. There stood out on the column, besides the laws, an oath and terrible curses <note>original: "execratioq; terribilia"; an imprecation or ritual curse.</note> calling down evil upon those who did not obey. 

When, therefore, the sacrifices were prepared according to custom, and they were about to purify and burn each of the bull's limbs, they poured a drop of blood from a filled mixing-bowl over each king. The rest they gave to the fire, purifying the column. Finally, having done these things, they drew from the bowl with golden vials and, pouring a libation over the fire, they promised by oath that they would judge according to the laws inscribed on the column, and would punish those who had previously offended. Furthermore, they swore they would never willingly transgress the rule of those writings. They added that they would never command, nor obey any commander, except according to the laws of their father himself. Each of them, having prayed for these things for himself and his descendants, and having drunk and offered the vial to the god, turned himself to dinner and necessary things. 

And as night approached and the fire of the victims was nearly extinguished, each of them put on a robe of most beautiful azure <note>original: "celeste colore"; literally "heavenly color," likely a deep blue like the night sky.</note> color, and sitting on the ground near the embers of the burnt offerings, and extinguishing every fire lit during the sacred rites throughout the night, they judged and were judged together, if any of them had accused another as a transgressor of the laws. After they had judged and day had dawned, they inscribed the sentences on a golden tablet and hung them up with their robes as monuments for future generations. 

There were many other laws concerning sacred matters peculiar to each of the kings, but these were the principal ones: that they should never bring war upon one another; rather, they should all come to the aid if anyone in any of their cities attempted to extirpate the royal race. Then at last, they would deliberate in common, as their ancestors had done, concerning war and other actions, attributing the right of command to the race of <term>Atlas <note>original: "Athlāntico generi"; the lineage of the first king, Atlas.</note></term>. However, they did not grant the king the authority of death over any of his kinsmen, unless more than five out of the ten kings had agreed on the same sentence. 

Such and so great a power as existed in those places at that time, the god brought back to these places in a certain order, by such an occasion as follows. For many ages, as long as the divine nature persevered in them, they were obedient to the laws and were kindly disposed toward the divine race related to them. For magnificent and true thoughts dwelt in their minds. Whence they practiced moderation and prudence, both toward whatever happened and toward one another. Therefore, despising all things except virtue, they made little of present possessions; nor were they carried away, but rather they considered the abundance of gold and other things as a kind of burden. Nor, like men drunk from a double source of nourishment, did they wander into any error through lack of self-control; on the contrary, being sober, they clearly saw that all these things received growth from common friendship together with virtue; but by the pursuit and admiration of these material things, virtue and friendship were destroyed. 

As long as such a mind and divine nature flourished in them, all those things we have described above grew; but after the divine portion in them vanished, tainted by long misuse and frequent human passions, and human customs prevailed, then for the first time, because they could not bear their present prosperity, they succumbed to disgrace. For in the eyes of those who were able to see, they were thought to be basely affected, since they had lost the most beautiful of their most precious things. But those who were unable to see a life truly lived toward happiness then thought them to be most illustrious and blessed, even while they were being filled with an most unjust greed for having more, and with violence. 

Then indeed, <term>Jupiter <note>original: "Iupiter"; King of the Gods (Zeus).</note></term>, the god of gods, who rules all things by laws and who is able to see such things—when he noticed that the noble race was being corrupted and wished to punish those men, so that having attained temperance they might become more moderate and more harmonious—called all the gods to their most honored seat, whence, as if from a throne in the center of the world, all things that are subject to generation are beheld. # FOLIO CCCCVI.
## ARGUMENT FOR THE DIALOGUE I. ON THE LAWS.
<sig>N ii</sig>
<meta>Catchword: suddenly perishing [original: "topiturę", likely a contraction or error for "periturę"].</meta>

### Marsilio Ficino’s Introduction to the First Dialogue on the Laws, or on Legislation, addressed to Lorenzo de' Medici.

In the ancient age, great-hearted Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino’s patron.</note>, there were three primary lights of wisdom: Pythagoras, Socrates, and Plato. We hold that the wisdom of Pythagoras consisted more in contemplation, that of Socrates more in action, and finally that of Plato equally in both contemplation and action. Furthermore, the speculative discipline of Pythagoras seems more remote from the common customs of men. But the speculative and moral doctrine of Plato everywhere so tempers the divine with the human that it can easily be accommodated to the common customs of men, while simultaneously turning men toward divine and eternal things. 

Nor should it be thought that Plato is different from Pythagoras and Socrates, whom he worships like deities; rather, he is a mixture of both. He is, so to speak, a divine moderator of both geniuses for the sake of humanity. Thus, it can be said that in those others the genius was merely divine, and in Aristotle and the other philosophers after Plato it was merely human; but in Plato, it was equally divine and human. Why say this? So that we may remember that the present arrangement of laws—since it is handed down to us by Plato himself, not through a Pythagorean persona or the usual Socratic one, but rather through Plato’s own person—rightly occupies a middle path between the divine and the human. It does not drag us through hidden and impassable ways, nor does it lead us down to inferior things. Therefore, those ten books of the *Republic* are more Pythagorean and Socratic; but the present *Laws* should be judged as more Platonic. That *Republic* was for those wishing and hoping for the ideal; the present arrangement is for those choosing the practical. Those who cannot ascend that steep mountain should not disdain to approach these gentler hills. 

Consider with what great diligence our Plato looks out for human salvation: he does not only wish to be admired by men for steep heights, but also to be easy, favorable, and healthy for all through these gentler slopes. Here, therefore, he will not force men to make everything communal if they do not wish it; he permits individuals to possess property, as is customary. Yet, our most cautious charioteer will not let go of the reins entirely. For besides the great care given to other laws, he most prudently ordains that no one may increase their wealth beyond a certain moderate limit, so that some are not hindered by too much abundance while others suffer from poverty, and so that many are not forced—a thing he considers miserable—to be beggars in the arms of their own fatherland. 

Furthermore, the persona of Plato is hidden here under the name of the "Athenian Guest" <note>Atheniensis hospes; the unnamed lead character of the *Laws*.</note> for the sake of modesty, as will appear clearly to the reader in many places hereafter—especially when he affirms that he has dealt with two types of republics. Since he is about to establish laws for the Greeks, he rightly receives laws from the three best Greek lawgivers: <term>Minos <note>The legendary king and lawgiver of Crete.</note></term>, <term>Lycurgus <note>The traditional founder of the Spartan legal system.</note></term>, and <term>Solon <note>The famous lawmaker of Athens.</note></term>. He takes from them, adds, changes, and invents, and thus composes the best form from them all. And although he establishes the city and the rule of governing from the beginning, he names the work "On the Laws" rather than "The Republic." This is because in a city where possessions are private to each person, many laws are needed due to various controversies, lawsuits, and injuries. In establishing these, you will note the simultaneously admirable and most merciful genius of the divine Plato. For this man of remarkable kindness devises for each law certain "exhortatory rewards" <note>Preambles intended to persuade citizens of the law's merit rather than just threatening punishment.</note>, by which the citizens, led most humanely, might want to obey willingly. Like children of the laws, they should obey them spontaneously, whereas others are usually forced to obey them unwillingly as if they were tyrants, and try to escape their command through fraud or violence. However, after many things, he also adds threats and punishments for those who judge their fatherland not to be a mother, but a stepmother.

We shall now descend to the specific argument of the first dialogue of the *Laws*, but first we advise everyone to read the dialogue *Minos* and its argument before they approach these *Laws*. Let them approach, I say, as people who will observe them diligently in their reading and preserve them entirely in their actions. Otherwise, unless they obey these, they should understand that after such an exact knowledge of justice and injustice, they will sin with less excuse and greater crime. 

The Athenian Guest (that is, Plato), having traveled to Crete, encounters Megillus the Lacedaemonian <note>A Spartan.</note> and Clinias the Cretan near <term>Cnossus <note>The ancient capital of Crete.</note></term>. The people of Cnossus had summoned Clinias along with nine others to lead a colony from there, found a city, and give it laws. These two, therefore, were going to the sacred cave of <term>Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis"; refers to Zeus, who was said to have been born in a cave on Crete and to have instructed Minos in lawmaking.</note></term> to consult about this. Having met them, the Athenian Guest asked what they were going to do. They replied they were going to devise laws. But when they were asked many things about laws by the Guest and could not fully resolve the questions, and since the Guest seemed most fit for lawgiving, they besought him to join them as an assistant in instituting the laws for the city. 

The Guest complies, and before all things, he explains the principle from which and through which laws come to men: namely, God and the philosopher. Then he investigates the goal of laws: he teaches that such a goal will be the tranquil purity of civil souls, sufficient for the contemplation of truth as far as is possible. Third, he descends to the form and matter of the laws themselves. That laws are inspired into men by God is testified to by all antiquity, by many of Plato’s books, by our own reasons brought forth in the arguments of many dialogues, and confirmed in our *Theology* where religion is discussed. Truly, if nature—which is nothing other than the lowest instrument of divine providence—does not lead itself wherever it is seen to proceed providently, but is led by providence itself (which prescribes the ends and orders of all things in itself and inscribes them upon nature as it wills); if, I say, such nature neither abounds in superfluities nor fails in necessary things, certainly divine providence never fails in necessary things. Now, mutual congregation is necessary for the human race, which cannot live otherwise. Law is also necessary for a congregation, which would otherwise be <note>original: "subitopiture"; likely "subito peritura", meaning "about to suddenly perish".</note> suddenly perishing without law. Again, divine authority is necessary for laws, lest they either fall into disuse through negligence, or through fraud and...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino introduces Plato’s *Laws* as a practical middle ground between divine ideals and human reality, contrasting it with the more utopian *Republic*. He outlines the dialogue's setting in Crete and argues that just laws must be rooted in divine providence and persuaded through reason rather than just force.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's "Argument" or introductory essay to Plato's *Laws*. The previous page ended with Ficino discussing how Plato's doctrine balances the divine and the human, unlike the purely divine genius of Pythagoras or the purely human genius of Aristotle. ...lest they break things with violence. Finally, to match divine authority, there is a need for both holiness of life and a punishment for the wicked that is admirable to all beyond human strength. Therefore, God's providence, which looks out for the needs of every species of elements, plants, beasts, and limbs, must not be lacking in the enactment of laws—which are especially necessary for the salvation of the most perfect species of living beings, who worship the divine. Add to this that no prince can guide the vast ship of the city, tossed at every moment by countless storms and dangers, to port without a heavenly breeze. Therefore, God, both through hidden inspirations of souls and through manifest miracles whenever necessity demands, both reveals the mysteries of laws and publicly sanctions and promulgates them. 

For this reason, Plato begins his treatise on the laws with such just and happy omens, naming God immediately at the start. Three founders of laws are disputing here, and each needs divine patronage. They also imitate three authors of laws: Minos, Lycurgus, and Solon <note>Minos was the legendary king of Crete, Lycurgus the lawgiver of Sparta, and Solon the lawgiver of Athens. Plato’s dialogue features characters from these three regions.</note>. These men attributed their laws to three deities: Jupiter, Apollo, and Minerva. And not without reason. For the Sun [Apollo], lord of the planets, contains power; Jupiter contains clemency; Minerva contains wisdom. These three things complete the entire nature and perfection of law. For what else do we call law besides a certain rational rule leading subjects to the good in a certain order? For reason, rule, and order to be present, wisdom is absolutely necessary. Furthermore, so that it may lead to the end and preserve it, power primarily achieves this. Finally, so that it leads to the good—that is, to everyone’s benefit—and leads conveniently and benignly, clemency provides greatly. Thus, among the ancients, three deities representing the divine trinity necessarily consult for the laws. 

And for that reason, three similar gifts are judged necessary in a prince for the bearing of laws. But because it is necessary for these gifts to meet perfectly in turn to establish perfect laws—and human faculty cannot truly provide this—it is no wonder that there is a need for divine help for the most exact sanctioning of laws. Because Plato often repeats the number of nine years, both in the *Minos* and here, as if it were necessary for learning laws from Jupiter himself and handing them to men, he perhaps signifies the nine orders of angelic minds <note>Ficino, a Christian priest, here blends Platonic philosophy with the Christian "Celestial Hierarchy" of nine choirs of angels (Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.).</note>, through whom the very reason for enacting the law is transferred down to men as if by interpreters. In the *Protagoras*, he signifies all these orders as interpreters of laws under the single name of Mercury <note>The messenger god.</note>. Do not let it escape you that not only Christians use this ninefold number in the angels, but also the Platonists—especially Proclus and Syrianus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) and Syrianus were major Neoplatonic philosophers who influenced Ficino’s attempts to harmonize Plato with Christianity.</note>—as we have shown sufficiently in our theology. 

What if the ninefold number here signifies a threefold use of power, a threefold use of wisdom, and a triple clemency? Namely, so that each of the three exists in the law itself, in the judgment of the magistrate, and in the ministers and the very execution of the judgment? Furthermore, in the actions themselves—the beginnings, middles, and ends? Three things repeated three times clearly complete a ninefold. 

But why does the discussion in the *Republic* start with the rites of Minerva, while here it starts with the rites of Jupiter? Perhaps because that discussion took place in Athens and treats the ancient city of Athens dedicated to Minerva; but here, in Crete, he consults about building a Cretan city near the temple of Jupiter himself, and in the beginning, words are spoken about the laws of Minos, the son of Jupiter. Or rather, that form of the republic <note>Referring to the ideal city in Plato's *Republic*.</note> was earlier, more chaste, and more severe, most suitable for Pallas [Minerva]; but this one is a little more indulgent and, by its own humanity, suitable for Jupiter. In short, both here and there, we portend the happiness of a nascent city from prayers and sacrifices. 

I pass over the description of this long journey, the sacred groves, and trees dedicated to the temple, and many other things that would require a commentary rather than a summary. But after certain points that allegorically teach that human affairs—especially public ones—cannot be rightly settled without divine patronage, and that therefore the beginning of laws must be made from God himself (who is both the beginning and end of laws), he now begins gradually to inquire about the goal of laws. He signifies that their goal is divine worship, since this discussion of laws proceeds toward the temple of Jupiter. Since the ultimate goal of laws is the worship of that Jupiter who made the world and gave laws both to the world and to us, he rightly denies immediately that the goal of laws is the worship of Mars [war]. Meanwhile, he modestly corrects the laws of Minos and Lycurgus, which did not look so much toward virtue itself simply, but rather declined toward warfare. 

<margin>
The end of war ought to be peace.
The end of peace is the worship of God and truth.
Divine and human goods.
Human goods:
Health.
Beauty.
Strength.
Wealth.
Divine goods:
Prudence.
Temperance.
Justice.
Fortitude.
</margin>

Truly, laws ought to have that most powerful thing as their goal in the city, toward which everything is directed as if toward a target, which must be sought by all citizens above all else. Since battle and victory are full of labors and evils, they are not to be desired for their own sake, but should rather be chosen for the sake of peace and a safe tranquility of life. Just as no one desires to live so as to be constantly engaged in a struggle and victory against diseases. Finally, he concludes that it is not fitting to refer the studies of peace to those of war; but on the contrary, one should rather refer war to the studies and duties of peace, and peace to the ready and free truth and worship of God. 

In proving these things, he distributes the kind of goods themselves into many species, saying that some are human, while others are divine—and that human goods depend on divine ones. Among human goods, which he judges to be far inferior to divine ones, the first is health, the second beauty, the third strength, the fourth wealth. He wants prudence to be the leader of these goods, and also the leader of the divine ones. After prudence, he thinks temperance follows; after this, justice; after justice, fortitude [courage]. 

Indeed, he signifies both here and explains in the fourth book of the *Republic* the three parts of the soul: namely, the rational, the irascible, and the concupiscible <note>The "irascible" part deals with anger and spiritedness; the "concupiscible" part deals with desires and appetites.</note>. And prudence is in the rational part alone, and fortitude in the irascible alone. You may also place continence [self-control] in the concupiscible alone. But he places temperance and justice in all parts; and he calls both the "consonance" [harmony] of the whole soul. But temperance is consonance in the affections, and justice is consonance in the actions. The former becomes the health of the soul, the latter the beauty of the soul. But prudence is the eye; fortitude is the hand. If you look at the substance of the soul and the purity necessary for contemplation, place temperance before justice; if you look at human custom, put justice first. In all cases, place prudence before all, like an eye for the feet and a leader. And put fortitude before continence. For fortitude is also concerned with what is more difficult, namely pain...

<summary>Ficino explains the divine origin and goal of laws, arguing that legislation must be rooted in God rather than war. He categorizes goods into human (health, wealth) and divine (virtues), establishing prudence as the leader of all.</summary>

->### SUMMARY OF THE FIRST DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS. PAGE 307.<-

[Fortitude] <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix "-ris," completing "fortitudinis" from the previous page.</note>, namely through endurance; and the duty of restraint, which is to conquer pleasures, is contained within itself. However, it judges both temperance and justice as more significant than the lower virtues. For these two possess the entire order of the whole soul more fully, established under the leadership of prudence. From these points, it is concluded that it is necessary for the lawgiver both to refer himself, and to command that others be referred—human things indeed to divine things, and divine things (that is, the virtues) to the mind devoted to truth and divinity. While he disputes concerning the goal of laws, he also explains the duty of their founder: he wants this, in short, to be that with the greatest diligence he should cultivate the whole city like a field, so that he may have a refined plan for choosing and sowing seeds. Then, he must attend to the timely cultivation of each plant. Likewise, he must focus on rooting out harmful weeds and thorns immediately from the beginning. Finally, he must lead all things to maturity in their proper order. You, however, should take note among these things: it is considered more shameful to yield to pleasures than to succumb to pains. Likewise, it is the duty of a brave man not only to overcome fears and dangers, but also to restrain desires. Furthermore, no one can be securely judged brave unless he has been strenuously engaged for a long time among labors and dangers; add to this, unless he has also been proven in the very license and allurements of pleasures, in which the self-controlled are properly tested. Note that it is not safe to educate either a man who is to be brave far away from fears, or one who is to be temperate apart from all the allurements of pleasures. Furthermore, the whole study of the law-maker must be occupied with pleasures and pains, so that these two, like brute animals, may not lack a bridle. For if they are restrained by a bridle, the path of life turns out easy and happy. If they are restrained by no bridle, it turns out extremely difficult and unhappy. You will also note that which was said of the Athenians: that the "good Athenians" are especially good; because they alone are good by their own nature and by a certain divine lot, with no one forcing or terrifying them. In these words, Plato signifies that in a poorly instituted city, good citizens will indeed be rare; but those will be the most outstanding of all. Since they became such through no training, they were surely made so by a certain divine lot and a perfect nature, and their excellence is so great that they are not stained by the common contagion. 

After this, you will consider that unique precept of every art and of the whole of life: it is necessary that those who are to turn out as outstanding men in any study must, immediately from their tender years, practice that very thing through both play and study in every detail conducive to it. Thus, the most suitable preludes of manly studies should be proposed to boys; and so the minds of those playing may be led most of all into the love of that which they are to do seriously in manhood. Among these things, discipline <note>original: *disciplina*, referring to education or formative training</note> is defined thus:

<margin>What discipline is.</margin>
Discipline is that institution of life, starting immediately from childhood, which leads the youthful soul little by little into the love of virtue. I mean especially that virtue through which, having become a man, he may know how both to rule and to obey. That a man must, and moreover can, have a discipline of this kind from his tender years, he aptly confirms through the description of human nature which follows. For he says: although a man is a single being, he nevertheless has many and diverse things within himself; among which are two "tyrants," loving indeed but contrary to one another, pulling the soul apart: pain and pleasure. Besides these, there are opinions of future goods and evils; from these, appetite

<margin>Pain and pleasure drive the soul toward disturbances.</margin>
and confidence regarding good things arise in us, but fear regarding evil things; and similar disturbances of the mind. In addition to these, the judgment of reason is present, dictating which of these is better and which is worse. Such a judgment in each individual is "private law," and in the city, it is "public law." Since he had said that a single living being was composed of such diverse things, he adds, not without reason, that man is a divine miracle among living beings; imitating Mercury [Trismegistus], who said that man is a "great miracle." There are three kinds of souls. For they are either immortal in both body and soul; or mortal in both; or immortal in soul but decaying in body. In the first kind are the celestial, ethereal, and aerial beings, whether they be called gods or daemons <note>Ficino uses "daemons" in the Platonic sense of intermediary spirits, not modern "demons."</note>. In the last kind are the brutes. But in the middle are men and the spirits of water and earth. For since the bodies of these spirits, like human bodies, are composed of opposites, they can sometimes be dissolved and bring about certain disturbances. But leaving other things aside, why is man a miracle? Because, though he is divine, it is a marvel that he is infected by mortal things; and though he is mortal, it is also a marvel that he is moved toward divine things. But why does he call him a "divine miracle"? Because he was so instituted by divine providence: and as Timaeus teaches, we received from God the Craftsman of the world the very 

<margin>The substance of the rational soul is received from God. Vital nature from the other gods. The body from the spirits.</margin>
substance of the rational soul; but from the other gods, a certain vital nature inferior to reason; and finally, from the spirits <note>original: *daemonibus*</note>, our bodies. As for what he adds, that man was made by the gods either for "play" or for "serious study," understand it thus: that he was made for play if the soul, always transmigrating from celestial to terrestrial things and back again as if playing, never rests in an immutable seat with God. But he was made for "study" <note>or serious purpose</note> if, once in the power of the divine makers, the soul of the maker is at some point to remain immobile with God. Which side of this distinction we ought to choose, Plato does not dare to affirm here. Yet he holds it probable, as he signifies elsewhere, that man was divinely established for a serious purpose rather than for play. But if anyone wishes to read this ambiguous text of Plato in such a way that it signifies either that man was established by divine living beings (meaning the stars), or that he is composed of many living beings, let him understand that the parts and affects of the soul are named "living beings" poetically by Plato. This indeed appears in the ninth book of the *Republic* and in the beginning of the *Phaedrus*. But you shall see to those matters. After this, he descends to certain things which, even if they seem lighter, are nevertheless necessary for the perfect tradition of discipline and the testing of morals. Such are the studies of music and similar customs. Music, in a very general sense, encompasses the order of any proportion: not only in speech, song, sound, and dance, but also in gymnastic play and the grace of banquets. All these things indeed must be so arranged in the city that, with the incitement of all disturbances and vices removed, they may temper the body, the spirit, and the soul. He begins the discussion, by a certain opportunity, with banquets and wine; saying first that care must be taken lest "living" <note>The Latin catchword "uiuus" (living) transitions to the next page.</note>...

Here, however, he judges it to contribute most especially to this: that from the occasionally freer use of wine, the characters of men may be uncovered during banquets, for it is accustomed to make them more impudent and bold.
