Truly, how great a thing shame is—that is, the fear of disgrace and infamy—is evident from the fact that, because of such fear, the young both dread shameful things above all and boldly undertake honorable things, however difficult. These two things indeed are judged the most necessary of all for the republic, both in peace and in war. Therefore, the lawgiver ought to strive with diligent study to pour these qualities into the souls of the citizens.

### PLATO’S [DIALOGUE] ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE ENACTMENT OF LAWS, AS OF ONE BOOK, FIRST DIALOGUE.

-> CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE. <-
-> THE ATHENIAN STRANGER, CLINIAS THE CRETAN, MEGILLUS THE LACEDAEMONIAN. <-

-> THE ATHENIAN STRANGER. <-

<margin>Observe how the laws are attributed to God as their author.</margin>
Do you, O strangers, consider a God or some man to be the cause of the laws to be established? CLINIAS. A God, O stranger, a God, I say, as it is proper to assert. Among us, indeed, Jupiter <note>original: "Iouem"</note>. Among the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, from where this man [Megillus] comes, I believe they would say Apollo. Is it not so? MEGILLUS. Certainly. ATHENIAN. Do you say this following Homer, as if Minos <note>The legendary king of Crete</note> always sought the conversation of his father every ninth year, and by his instructions established laws for your cities? CLINIAS. So our people say. You have also heard that his brother Rhadamanthus was most just. And we Cretans judge that he achieved this praise because he then rightly distributed justice to each person. ATHENIAN. Excellent praise indeed, and most fitting for a son of Jupiter. But since you were both educated in such customs and laws—you, indeed, and he—I hope it will not be unpleasant for us if we discourse while walking <note>original: "iter esidū," likely "iter residuum" or "sedendo" implying a long journey with rests</note> about the founding of cities and laws. But the road from Knossos to the cave and temple of Jupiter is, as we have heard, long enough; and there are resting places along it under tall trees, as is fitting in the heat, providing shade. It will therefore be suitable for our age to rest frequently in these; and by the mutual comfort of speech, to complete this whole journey without weariness. CLINIAS. And yet, as we proceed, stranger, we shall come upon cypresses in the groves of wonderful height and beauty, and also pleasant meadows, in which we will gladly linger while resting. ATHENIAN. You speak very rightly. But we shall confirm these things more once we have seen them. But let us go now, with good fortune as our companion. CLINIAS. Let it be so. ATHENIAN. But tell me, I pray: for what reason did the law institute for you the practice of communal meals <note>original: "conuiuia," referring to the Spartan/Cretan *syssitia*</note> and the art of arms? CLINIAS. I think, O stranger, that these things of ours are very easy to understand. For you see the whole nature of this region is not like that of Thessaly, flat. Therefore, they <note>The Thessalians</note> use horses for racing more than we do. This inequality of places is more suited to foot-exercise and running. Therefore, it is necessary for the armor also to be lighter, lest its weight hinder the running. The lightness of bows and arrows, therefore, is most suitable. All these things, then, are adapted for war for us; and looking toward this, the legislator, as it seems to me, instituted everything. Indeed, for this sake he also seems to have sanctioned the law of communal dining; since he saw that all in military service, forced by the reality of the situation for the sake of their own protection, have common meals. In this, I surely think he condemned the others for the crime of folly: because they do not understand that war is always present in all cities against all others, continually and perpetually. For if it is necessary to celebrate communal meals for the sake of protection while there is war, and for some armed commanders to protect the cities along with their subjects, that same thing must be done even in time of peace. For what many call "peace," they should consider to be a name only. In truth, by the very nature of things, there is war for all cities against all others—even if it is not declared. You will find, if you consider it so: the lawgiver of the Cretans wrote almost all laws for us, both privately and publicly, as if he were looking toward war; and he ordered us to obey them in such a way, as if there were no utility in other things—not in possessions, nor in arts—unless one overcomes in war; since all the goods of those who are defeated pass immediately to the victors. ATHENIAN. You seem to me, O stranger, to be well-trained in the performance of Cretan laws. But say it more clearly. You seemed to say that a city is rightly ordered only when it is so established that it can conquer others in war. Is it not so? CLINIAS. Exactly so. I think this man [Megillus] will also agree. MEGILLUS. Not otherwise, O divine man, would any of the Lacedaemonians answer. ATHENIAN. Does a city stand toward a city in this way, but a village toward a village differently? CLINIAS. No differently. ATHENIAN. Therefore they stand similarly? CLINIAS. Similarly. ATHENIAN. And even house to house, which are in the same village: and individual men toward individuals? CLINIAS. Those also similarly. ATHENIAN. What then is to be said of any man toward himself? Shall we say that anyone is disposed toward himself as an enemy toward an enemy? Or otherwise? CLINIAS. O Athenian stranger. For I do not wish to call you "Attic" in name only. For you seem worthier of the surname of the goddess herself, Athens—that is, Pallas. Indeed, you have made this whole reasoning so clear by reducing it to its principle: that it may more easily be found that what was said was right—namely, that all are enemies to all, both publicly and privately: and individuals to themselves. ATHENIAN.

### ON THE LAWS OR ON LEGISLATION. FIRST DIALOGUE.

**Folio 308**

N iiii

<meta>catchword: N iiii</meta>

**ATHENIAN STRANGER.** How do you say that, O marvelous man? **CLINIAS.** I say, O guest, that the first and best victory is for a man to conquer himself. To be conquered by oneself, however, is the most shameful and worst of things. All these things signify that there is a war within each individual against themselves. **ATHENIAN.** Let us resume that line of reasoning. For since each of us is either superior to himself or inferior, should we not say the same of a city? Or is it different? **CLINIAS.** Do you mean whether a city might be superior to itself or inferior? **ATHENIAN.** Exactly that. **CLINIAS.** You have asked correctly. Indeed, this occurs no less in cities; in fact, it is most evident in them. For where the better people put the wicked multitude to flight, that city is rightly called superior to itself, and this victory is deservedly praised. Conversely, the opposite occurs. **ATHENIAN.** But let us set aside for the moment whether the worse part might ever be superior and more powerful than the better; that would require a longer discussion. But I understand what you have said to mean this: that sometimes citizens who are kin and of the same city—many and wicked—will conspire against the just, who are few, and will use force to subject them. And if they prevail, that city is called inferior to itself and depraved; but if they are defeated, it is called superior and virtuous. **CLINIAS.** What you say, guest, is strange, but it must be admitted as fact. **ATHENIAN.** Come now, let us consider this again. Many brothers can be born from the same father and mother. It is no wonder if many of them are unjust, while only a few are just. **CLINIAS.** Not a wonder at all. **ATHENIAN.** It is not fitting for me or for you to hunt for words <note>original: "verba aucupari" – a metaphor for focusing on rhetorical style rather than substance</note> in saying that a household or an entire kinship appears inferior to itself if the wicked prevail, and superior if they are defeated. For we are not disputing these things to observe the elegance or rudeness of words, as many are accustomed to do, but to investigate what the right reason is according to nature regarding laws, and what the error might be. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth, guest. **MEGILLUS.** Indeed, what has been said so far seems right to me as well. **ATHENIAN.** Let us consider this further: Could a judge decide between the aforementioned brothers? **CLINIAS.** Undoubtedly. **ATHENIAN.** Which judge, then, will be better? The one who destroys the wicked and makes it so the virtuous rule themselves? Or the one who makes the virtuous rule but allows the wicked to live, having persuaded them to submit to authority voluntarily? Let us add a third judge in virtue to these, if such a one can be found: one who manages the disagreeing family so well that he destroys no one, but writes laws for those he has reconciled, by which they will be friends to each other forever. **CLINIAS.** Such a judge and lawgiver would be far better. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, he would write laws for them looking toward the opposite of war. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** What then? He who constitutes a city looking toward war—will he look toward external wars and direct the life of the citizens toward those? Or toward internal wars, which are called seditions <note>original: "seditiones" – internal civil strife or factional conflict</note>, which no one would choose to have in his own city, and if they happen, he would wish them to be settled as quickly as possible? **CLINIAS.** Clearly toward these. **ATHENIAN.** Would anyone prefer to achieve peace from sedition by destroying one part of the citizens when the other part has gained victory, or rather that, through reconciliation, peace be made and friendship established, so that the mind of the whole city might be turned toward external wars? **CLINIAS.** Everyone would surely hope for the latter rather than the former for his city. **ATHENIAN.** And would not the lawgiver do the same? **CLINIAS.** Likewise. **ATHENIAN.** Should not all laws be made for the sake of the best thing? **CLINIAS.** Indeed. **ATHENIAN.** And the best thing is neither war nor sedition—for everyone prays that these might not be necessary—but peace and mutual benevolence. Moreover, that victory by which a city puts its own self to flight is not the best thing, but rather a necessary one. To think that the best state of a city consists in fighting and winning is like someone thinking a sick person is at his best while being treated, rather than thinking of the one who was never sick at all. If someone thinks similarly about the happiness of a city or a private man, he will never truly be a statesman—if he looks only and primarily to external wars—nor will he be an exquisite lawgiver, unless he writes laws for the sake of peace rather than for the sake of war. **CLINIAS.** These things seem rightly said, guest. Yet I would wonder if someone should contend that our laws, and those of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>, were not diligently established for the sake of war. **ATHENIAN.** Perhaps it is so. But we must inquire into the matter not contentiously but quietly, with as much zeal as possible applied to these things by both you and them. Attend, therefore, I pray. Let us begin with Tyrtaeus <note>A Greek lyric poet of the 7th century BCE, famous for his verses exhorting the Spartans to bravery in war</note>, an Athenian by birth but later a citizen of the Lacedaemonians, who devoted himself to these matters more than other men. "I make no mention," he says, "nor do I think him of any value at all, even if he were the richest of all, even if he possessed many goods," and after listing almost everything, he concludes that such a man is nothing if he does not always conduct himself excellently in war. You also have perhaps heard these poems, for I think you have been sated with hearing them by now. **MEGILLUS.** These are very common among us. **CLINIAS.** These have reached us as well, brought from Lacedaemon. **ATHENIAN.** Let us therefore question this poet together in this way: "O divine poet Tyrtaeus, you certainly seem wise and good to us, because you have extolled with excellent praise those who have excelled in war." On this point, both I and Clinias of Knossos seem to agree with you strongly. But we would like to know clearly whether we are speaking about the same men or not. Therefore, explain to us: do you also, just as we do, believe there are two kinds of war? Or otherwise? To this, I think not only Tyrtaeus, but any man far less skilled than he, would immediately respond: "Two." One which we call sedition, which we just admitted is the most serious of all. And another kind of war, which we all consider much milder than that: the one we use against foreigners and aliens. **CLINIAS.** Who could doubt it? **ATHENIAN.** Tell us then: which men in which kind of war did you praise so greatly, and which did you blame so much? For you seem to have praised those who wage external wars with great spirit. For you said in your poems: "I utterly despise those who do not dare to look upon bloody slaughter and fight hand to hand with the enemy." From this, O Tyrtaeus, we gather that you praise those who shine above others in waging external wars. Would Tyrtaeus concede these things? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** We, however, although these men are illustrious, consider those to be far more illustrious who, with the greatest—

### BOOK I

...they excel in war. We also have the poet Theognis as a witness, a citizen of Megara in Sicily, who says that a faithful man in a time of civil strife is better than all the silver and gold. <note>Theognis of Megara was a 6th-century BCE Greek poet known for his gnomic (proverbial) poetry.</note> Therefore, we say that in the most grievous kind of war, such a man is better than the other, just as justice, temperance, and wisdom joined with courage are better than courage alone. For no one can be found truly whole and faithful in civil strife without the full count of all the virtues. Yet many mercenaries can be found—as Tyrtaeus <note>Tyrtaeus was a Spartan poet who wrote elegies praising military valor.</note> would not deny—who fight intrepidly in external war, most of whom are nevertheless fierce, unjust, insolent, and, with very few exceptions, the most senseless of men. To what end is all this?

<margin>Legislators should look toward nothing other than the fullness of virtue.</margin>
What is to be declared from these things? It is that the God who gave the laws here, as well as any other lawgiver who intends to be of any use, will establish laws by looking toward nothing else than the greatest virtue at all times. This virtue is, as Theognis says, that "faithfulness" which shines most in times of danger. This we might call "perfect justice." That virtue which Tyrtaeus praised so highly, though it is beautiful and seasonably praised by the poet, is nevertheless rightly honored in the fourth and lowest place in terms of its rank of virtue. CLINIAS. Therefore, O guest, shall we cast the law-

<margin>THEOGNIS. Faithfulness shines most in dangers.</margin>
giver of our laws among the very lowest of legislators? ATHENIAN. Not him, O best of men, but rather ourselves, if we should think that Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> and Minos <note>The legendary king and lawgiver of Crete.</note> established their laws looking only toward war. CLINIAS. How then ought we to speak of this? ATHENIAN. As truth and justice demand of those who discuss a divine republic: we must believe they looked not to a mere fragment of virtue—and a lowly one at that—but to virtue as a whole. We must believe they sought out laws according to each of its forms, and did not investigate only those forms which many people today propose and seek. For every man usually seeks

<margin>A man seeks most that which he most lacks.</margin>
that which he lacks most: one seeks laws concerning inheritance, another concerning injury, and another concerning many other such things. But we believe that the search for laws is only well-conducted when it proceeds as we have just begun. I greatly approve of your starting point for explaining the laws. For by beginning with virtue, and saying that laws were established for the sake of virtue, you seem to have approached the matter correctly. However, when you affirmed that the lawgiver looked only to a fragment of virtue—and the smallest one at that—you did not seem to me to speak rightly; and for that reason, I have spoken at greater length. If you wish, I will tell you how I would have wanted you to distinguish these things for us. CLINIAS. I certainly wish it. ATHENIAN. You ought to have spoken in this manner, O guest: "The laws of the Cretans are not without reason praised among all the Greeks. For they are rightly established, since they make those who use them happy. For they provide all good things. Now, goods are of two kinds: some are human, others are

->THE ORDER OF GOODS<-

| GOODS | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Divine** | **Human** |
| Prudence <note>Also translated as Wisdom.</note> | Health |
| Temperance | Beauty |
| Justice | Strength |
| Fortitude <note>Also translated as Courage.</note> | Riches |

divine; and the human goods depend upon the divine. If a city receives the greater goods, it possesses the lesser as well; but if it lacks the former, it is deprived of both. Of the lesser goods, the first is health; beauty is second; the third is strength for running and other bodily movements; the fourth is riches, which are not 'blind' <note>A reference to Plutus, the blind god of wealth; here, wealth is only "seeing" if guided by wisdom.</note> but see clearly, if they follow prudence. This prudence stands as the primary leader of the divine goods. Next, after the mind, comes the temperate habit of the soul. From these two, mixed with fortitude, justice emerges in the third place. Fortitude holds the fourth place. All of these are by nature placed before those human goods. Therefore, it is necessary that the lawgiver also follow this same order, and command all citizens to always work toward these things specifically. For human things are to be referred to the divine, and divine things are to be referred to the leading Mind. Furthermore, the lawgiver must care for the marriages between citizens, and for the birth and education of children, both male and female, both the young and those advanced in years. He should honor those who behave rightly in these matters as is fitting, but conversely, he should blame pains, pleasures, and desires in all social interactions. He shall also diligently consider which studies each person’s love is drawn to, and through laws he shall praise right duties and blame the opposite. He shall likewise teach and define what is honorable and what is shameful in every emotion—namely regarding anger and fear, and whatever other disturbances occur in adversity, or delights in prosperity—and finally regarding all the movements that vex men arising from disease, war, poverty, or their opposites. After these things, it is necessary that the legislator diligently observe the gains and expenses of the citizens and recognize how they occur: likewise the commerce in all these things and the settlements they make, whether voluntarily or by compulsion. He should notice wherever justice is present or absent in their contracts with one another, and he should establish honors for parents and the deserved punishments for those who are not dutiful to parents. Finally, having treated all things pertaining to the end of the republic, he must notice and establish how monuments should be built for the dead, and what honors ought to be paid to each of the deceased. Once these things have been declared, the legislator shall appoint guardians over all of them, some acting with prudence and others with true opinion, so that the mind, collecting all these things into one, may lead them to this goal: that they follow temperance and justice rather than riches or ambition. This, guests, is how I would have wished—and still wish—for it to be explained by you: how all these things are present in the laws of Jupiter and Pythian Apollo, which Minos and Lycurgus wrote, and in what order they are made manifest to one who has skill in laws through art or experience, though to us others they are in no way apparent." CLINIAS. How then, guest, should the things that follow be treated? ATHENIAN. From the beginning again, as above...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger explains that laws must aim at "total virtue" rather than just military courage, introducing a hierarchy where human goods like health and wealth must be guided by divine goods like wisdom and justice.</summary>

FOLIO CCCIX.
### ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, BOOK I.
<sig>N v</sig>
<meta>Catchword: riæ</meta>

...we have begun, it seems to me that those things which pertain to fortitude <note>The Latin *fortitudo* encompasses both physical courage and moral strength.</note> must be treated first. Then we shall pass through one type of virtue after another, if that pleases you. But let us first deal with this one: and using it as a model for the others, let our conversation bring us some relief on our journey. Finally, when we have treated virtue in its entirety, we shall show, if God wills, that those things we have just mentioned point toward that goal. CLINIAS. You speak rightly; try first to prove this praise of yours to us. ATHENIAN. I shall try, both for your sake and my own. For this discourse is common to us both. Tell me, then: did we not say that common meals and gymnastics were invented by the lawgiver for the sake of war? CLINIAS. Certainly. ATHENIAN. And should a third or fourth invention be named for the same purpose? For perhaps it is necessary to enumerate them in this way, whether in this class of virtue or in any other part of the virtues, or however else it may be appropriate to name them for the sake of clarity. MEGILLUS. I would say the third is hunting, and no Spartan would deny that it was devised for this. Let us try to find a fourth and fifth. I place a fourth among my own people as the "secret service" <note>The original OCR reads *scipulū*, likely a corruption of *cryptia* or *krypteia*, a Spartan tradition where youths lived in the wild to develop stealth and endurance.</note>, namely, the endurance of pain: which is practiced daily through fighting amongst themselves and certain thefts, involving many wounds. To these is added a certain wonderful "concealment," effective for building endurance: it is told of those who wander day and night through the whole region with bare feet in winter, and often with the rest of the body naked, without any servants. Furthermore, in the exercises of our naked youths, there is a wonderful endurance among us, when the power of intense heat must be resisted. There are many other such things among us, which one could not easily enumerate. ATHENIAN. You speak well, Spartan guest. But is the battle for fortitude only against fears and pains, or also against desires and pleasures, and those potent flatteries which bend the minds even of those who seem honorable, making them like wax? MEGILLUS. It is against all these things. ATHENIAN. If we remember what was said correctly, our friend here was saying that a city can be inferior to itself, and a man inferior to himself. Is that not so, Cretan guest? CLINIAS. Quite so. ATHENIAN. Which, therefore, should we call "worse": the one who is broken by pain, or the one who is overcome by pleasure? CLINIAS. I judge him who is overcome by pleasure to be worse; and everyone thinks a man ensnared by pleasure is more inferior to himself, and indeed with greater disgrace, than one weakened by pain. ATHENIAN. Why then did the lawgivers of Jupiter and Apollo <note>Referring to the divine origins of the Cretan and Spartan laws respectively.</note> not establish a "lame" fortitude, which can resist adversity on the left, as it were, but on the right succumbs to prosperity, joy, and flattery? Should it not rather be sufficient for both? CLINIAS. For both, I believe. ATHENIAN. Let us therefore explain what duties exist in your cities that give a taste of pleasures, rather than fleeing them entirely, just as they do not flee pains. Instead, just as they deal with pains, let them lead the citizens into the midst of pleasures, compelling them to overcome them and persuading them with honors. Where in your laws is it seen that men are made strong against pleasures just as they are against pains, showing them to be victors over those things they ought to be, and in no way allowing them to be overcome by the closest and gravest enemies within themselves? Tell me, I pray: what is such a thing among you? MEGILLUS. It is not so easy, guest, to produce laws opposed to pleasure as I could for pain; I do not have great and clear sections of the law against pleasures, though perhaps I might find small ones. CLINIAS. Nor could I similarly show such a thing in the laws of the Cretans. ATHENIAN. And that is no wonder, most excellent guests. But if someone among us, as a diligent investigator of the true and the best, finds something to criticize in the ancestral laws of each of us, we ought to bear it in turn, not with a heavy heart but with a fair mind. CLINIAS. You speak well, Athenian guest. Therefore, I judge that we should comply with you. ATHENIAN. Truly, it befits men of Clinias's age and condition to do no differently. CLINIAS. Certainly not. ATHENIAN. Whether one can rightly criticize the Spartan and Cretan Republics is another question. But as for what is said by many, perhaps I can report it better than you. For you, if the laws are rightly established, one law will be the most noble of all: that which forbids any of the youth to dare to ask whether the laws are well-made or otherwise; but with one mouth and one voice, it should command that they be conceded as being rightly established by the gods. It should not allow any other thought from the young. But an old man, if he has thought of something, may report it to the leaders and his peers, provided no youth is listening. CLINIAS. You speak rightly, guest. And although you were not present at the mind of the founder, yet like a seer you seem to have guessed these things skillfully now, and to speak the complete truth. ATHENIAN. Therefore, no young people are present with us now. And we ourselves, because of our old age, are permitted by the lawgiver to discuss these things among ourselves alone without sin. CLINIAS. It is as you say. Therefore, do not spare us, but freely criticize our laws. For it is not shameful to learn if something is not handled well, in which a fault is committed. For from this, if things are received not with envy but with goodwill, a remedy is found. ATHENIAN. You speak excellently. However, I shall not speak by criticizing before I have considered it diligently with all my strength, but rather by raising doubts. For to you alone of all the Greeks and barbarians we know of, the lawgiver commanded to beware of the greatest pleasures and the most delightful games, and not to taste any of them. But concerning pains and fears, he judged as we have just discussed: that if someone is accustomed from his earliest years to decline them, then whenever he must undergo necessary pains, fears, and labors, he will flee from those who are practiced in them and become their slave. This very thing, as I judge, he ought to have considered regarding pleasure also, saying to himself: that if from their youth the citizens are devoid of the greatest pleasures, and are not practiced in restraining themselves in pleasures, doing nothing shameful for the sake of delightful enjoyment, they will succumb just as those who are conquered by fear, and in a certain other and more shameful way...

### BOOK I.
<sig>V i</sig>

...they will be slaves to those who have become accustomed to containing themselves in the midst of pleasures, and to those who, while living among pleasures, can provide themselves with amusements—who are perhaps the worst of men. And thus, they will have a soul that is partly slave and partly free, and they should by no means be called brave and free. Consider therefore if anything from what has been said seems to you to be spoken correctly. CLINIAS. So it seems, indeed. ATHENIAN. But it would be the mark of the young, or rather of the completely foolish, to assent immediately and easily to such great matters. Yet if we proceed now as we proposed, O Clinias and Lacedaemonian guest <note>Megillus the Spartan.</note>, for we were placing moderation <note>Latin: *moderationem*, translating the Greek *sophrosyne*, meaning temperance or self-control.</note> after fortitude, what difference shall we find between these and the other Republics, which seem to be governed by chance rather than law, just as is now seen in war? MEGILLUS. That is not an easy thing to say. CLINIAS. Yet it seems that common meals and gymnastic contests have been suitably joined to both. ATHENIAN. It seems, however, O guests, that it is a difficult thing in Republics, as much in words as in reality, to introduce anything safe and certain from every side. For just as it cannot happen in bodies that one single pursuit is adapted to one body which does not seem to profit some parts while harming others in that same body, so it is in the city. Indeed, these exercises and revelries contribute to other things for cities, but they are altogether harmful regarding seditions. Of which thing the Milesians, Boeotians, and Thurians are examples for us. And these ancient pursuits are customary to you by law; and the natural pleasures of love <note>Latin: *venereorum*, referring to Venus, goddess of love.</note> seem to have been used in youth, not only in men but in beasts. In which matter your own cities could be accused, and all others which have the greatest care for gymnastic exercises. And whether one should understand this in jest or in earnest, it must be understood that when a female and a male come together for procreation, the pleasure of such a meeting seems to be granted to them according to nature. Whenever, however, males are mixed with males or females with females, that pleasure is contrary to nature. And those who first dared such a deed did so through the incontinence of pleasure. Furthermore, we all strongly blame the Cretan myth about Ganymede, because it was fashioned against Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus. The myth suggests Zeus kidnapped Ganymede for his beauty.</note> 
<margin>The myth of Ganymede belongs to the Cretans.</margin>
so that, since their laws are believed to have had their origin from him, they might also enjoy this pleasure by imitating the god who delivered the laws. But let the myth be dismissed. For those who consider the laws, almost their entire thought 
<margin>Two springs, pain and pleasure: from which the happy and the miserable draw.</margin>
should be about pleasures and pains, both concerning public and private morals. For nature causes these two springs to flow, from which he who draws from where, when, and as much as is appropriate is happy—meaning the individual, the city, and every animal. But he who lives foolishly and contrary to the opportune time, on the other hand, is unhappy. MEGILLUS. These things are rightly said, O guest; nor do we see what could be said against them. It seems to me, however, that the lawgiver of the Lacedaemonians rightly commanded that pleasures be fled. Clinias here, if he wishes, will help the Gnosian <note>Cretan</note> laws. For among the Spartans, I believe those things pertaining to pleasures are best arranged of all. For that into which all men fall most greatly—violent pleasures, petulance, and insanity—our law has banished from the whole region. You will see no drinking parties either in the fields or in the cities which the Spartans govern, nor the things joined to drinking parties, by which we are moved to all pleasures. Nor is there anyone who, having met someone acting wantonly in drunkenness, would not immediately inflict the greatest punishment upon him. Nor would the occasion of the Bacchanalia <note>The festival of Bacchus/Dionysus, known for wine and revelry.</note> free him. Just as I have seen among you in your chariots, and among the Tarentines <note>People of Taras/Tarentum in Southern Italy.</note> who are our colonists, the entire city drunk during the Bacchanalia. 
<margin>Athens and Tarentum are criticized for drunkenness in the Bacchanalia; the Tarentines are colonists of the Spartans.</margin>
But among us, no such thing is seen. ATHENIAN. All these things are to be praised, O Lacedaemonian guest, where there is a certain restraint; but where they are entirely permitted, they soften men. For quickly someone defending our ways will rebuke you if the license of the women among you is revealed. Certainly, in all these cases, one laugh frees both the Tarentines and us, and indeed even you: that these things are held to be proper and not improper. For each man, answering a person surprised at what he sees as unusual, will be able to say: "Do not wonder, O guest, this law exists among us; among you, perhaps, there is another law concerning these same matters." But for us at present, O most dear men, the talk is not of other men, but of the virtue and vice of the lawgivers themselves. Truly, let us speak more broadly of the whole of drunkenness. For it is no small matter, nor does its judgment belong to any lowly person. I do not say whether wine should be drunk or not, but I say we must inquire about drunkenness: whether it should be used in the manner that the Scythians and Persians use it—and furthermore the Carthaginians, Celtiberians, and Thracians—who are all most warlike nations; or in the manner that you do, who, as you say, abstain entirely. The Scythians and Thracians use unmixed wine <note>Original: *mero*, wine not diluted with water, which Greeks considered barbaric.</note> entirely, both men and women, and they pour it over their clothes, thinking this a noble and blessed way of life. The Persians also use other delights which you despise, though they do so more moderately than those others. MEGILLUS. But all those people we rout and put to flight when we have taken up arms. ATHENIAN. Do not say these things, O best of men. For many have put others to flight and been put to flight by others, for which a certain cause of this kind cannot be rendered; and it will happen often. Therefore, we shall not take a certain but an ambiguous argument and sign concerning honorable duties and their opposites in life if we look only to victory or flight in war. Especially since younger cities are reduced to slavery by greater ones in fighting, as the Locrians were by the Syracusans—who used the best laws among those nations—and the Ceans by the Athenians. One may see many similar things of this kind. Therefore, letting victory and the offense of war pass by, let us try to persuade ourselves by considering each duty in itself, as to what is true in each. Let us say, however, how this thing is good, but that thing is not good. But first, listen to me: how good and evil should be considered in matters of this kind. MEGILLUS. In what way do you say that? ATHENIAN. Whoever immediately blames or praises any matter proposed in a dispute seems to me to have failed. They do the same as if someone were to immediately criticize a grain-based food <note>Latin: *cereale cibum*, likely bread or porridge.</note> praised by another as good, before perceiving its effects: and in what manner, for whom, with whom, how it was prepared, and how...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book I of Plato’s Laws. The Athenian Stranger is leading Clinias the Cretan and Megillus the Spartan through an inquiry into the nature of "drinking parties" (symposia) as a means of moral education. Having just established that true courage involves facing both pain and pleasure, the Athenian now begins an analogy regarding the necessity of a "sober leader" for any social gathering, comparing a drinking party to an army or a ship.</meta>

FOLIO 310.
### ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS OF THE LATINS, DIALOGUE I.

...should be offered to affected bodies. This is what we seem to do in our discussion. For as soon as mention is made of drunkenness <note>Latin: *ebrietas*; the Athenian is referring to the Greek custom of the *symposium* or drinking party.</note>, some of us immediately condemn it, while others praise it—and both do so quite absurdly. We do this by relying on witnesses and advocates. Some of us think that because we have many people asserting a thing, it is worthy of belief. Others point to those who, by abstaining from wine, are victorious in battle; yet this point is ambiguous to us. If, therefore, we proceed in this same manner regarding other matters, we shall, in my opinion, achieve nothing. 

However, I will attempt to show, by the example of drunkenness itself, how a path may open to us—according to our strength and reason—even in matters of this kind. This is especially important since countless nations, being in doubt about these same things, contend with your two cities. 

MEGILLUS. We must certainly listen if a right consideration has found anything regarding these things. 

ATHENIAN. Let us therefore consider it thus: suppose someone should approve of the tending of goats and the keeping of that kind of animal, while another should condemn it because he saw them grazing in pastures without a shepherd and acting like dogs—or indeed, if he saw any flock whatsoever governed either without a shepherd or by bad shepherds. Would we judge his condemnation to be just? 

MEGILLUS. By no means. 

ATHENIAN. Now, as for a pilot: will the leader of a ship be considered upright in governing if he possesses only the art of navigation, whether he is tormented by seasickness or not? Or how else do we speak of it? 

MEGILLUS. Not at all, if this physical disturbance is added to his art. 

ATHENIAN. And what of a leader of an army? If he should rightly hold the art of warfare, should he be considered a sufficient leader because of this, even if he is a coward, and in times of danger "nauseated" by a certain drunkenness of fear? 

MEGILLUS. How could he be? 

ATHENIAN. Furthermore: what if he lacks the art and is also a coward? 

MEGILLUS. You describe an entirely base and useless man—not a leader of men, but of some vile women. 

ATHENIAN. But what of one who praises or condemns some society <note>Latin: *societatem*, referring here to a social gathering or "company".</note> that might have a leader—a society that would be useful whenever it finds its proper governor—and yet that person has never seen it rightly governed, but always either without leaders or with wicked ones? Can such a person ever rightly condemn or praise it? 

MEGILLUS. In what way could he do so, having never seen a society that was rightly governed? 

ATHENIAN. Come now, pay attention. Shall we not place drinkers and drinking parties among the many types of social gatherings? 

MEGILLUS. Most certainly. 

ATHENIAN. Now, has anyone ever seen this kind of gathering rightly governed? It is very easy for you to answer that you have never seen it, for this is not customary according to your ancestral laws. But I have been present at many in various places, and to put it briefly, I have diligently inquired into all of them: I have almost never seen or heard of one being entirely and rightly administered—save perhaps for a few small and rare instances. Most of them, I have found, go completely astray. 

CLINIAS. For what reason do you say this, O guest? Explain it more clearly. For as you said, since we have no experience in this matter, we cannot immediately recognize what is done rightly or wrongly in it. 

ATHENIAN. That is quite reasonable; but try to learn as I speak. In every assembly and community, for whatever business is to be conducted, you admit there ought to be a leader? 

CLINIAS. Without a doubt. 

ATHENIAN. And just a moment ago, we were saying that a leader in battle ought to be brave. 

CLINIAS. We were. 

ATHENIAN. A brave man is less disturbed by fear than a coward. 

CLINIAS. That is so. 

ATHENIAN. If some way could be found to put an entirely fearless leader in charge of an army, would we not strive for that with all our zeal? 

CLINIAS. Very much so. 

ATHENIAN. But now we are not speaking of an army nor of a commander against enemies in war, but of a governor in peace over the pleasant social interaction of friends <note>The Latin OCR says *inimicorum* (enemies), but the context of "pleasant interaction" and the underlying Greek text indicates this is an error for *amicorum* (friends).</note> with one another. 

CLINIAS. That is correct. 

ATHENIAN. In such a society, if drunkenness is present, will there not also be disorder? 

CLINIAS. There certainly will. 

ATHENIAN. First, therefore, even these gatherings have need of a leader. 

CLINIAS. Most of all. 

ATHENIAN. Should we then choose a leader who, if possible, is not himself disturbed? 

CLINIAS. We certainly should. 

ATHENIAN. This leader ought to be skilled in fostering social harmony. For it must be his duty both to preserve the existing friendship among them and to ensure that a greater friendship arises from that companionship. 

CLINIAS. You speak the truth. 

ATHENIAN. Therefore, should not a sober and wise leader be appointed over the drinkers, and not the opposite? For if the leader is young, unwise, and himself drunk, he would be lucky indeed if he did not overturn everything by his rashness. 

CLINIAS. Most lucky indeed. 

ATHENIAN. If someone, therefore, were to accuse drinking parties—assuming they were as well-ordered in a city as possible—they might perhaps be right in accusing the practice itself. But if a person looks upon a drinking party governed with no order, and for that reason condemns all drinking parties, it is clear first of all that he is ignorant that it is not being rightly conducted; and secondly, it is well known that everything will appear wicked when done without a sober master and leader. Do you not notice that a drunken pilot of a ship, or of any other thing, overturns everything—whether ships, or chariots, or an army, or whatever else is ruled by him? 

CLINIAS. You have spoken quite truly, guest; but explain this to us as well. What will these drinking parties confer upon us if they are conducted rightly? For as we were saying, a rightly led army brings victory in war—surely no small good. The same is to be judged of the others. But what great thing will come to either a city or to individuals from a rightly governed drinking party? 

ATHENIAN. What great thing does a city gain from one boy, or one single group, being rightly educated? If asked this, we would answer that the benefit to the city from the education of just one person is small. But if you ask universally what the education of well-instructed youths contributes most to the Republic, it will not be difficult to say. For those who are well-educated will turn out to be good men. And having become good, they will perform all other things well, and they will even conquer their enemies in battle. Education <note>Latin: *Disciplina*.</note> certainly provides victory; though victory sometimes gives birth to negligence and lack of refinement. For many, puffed up by victory, have contracted other vices through insolence. And indeed, no education was ever a "Cadmean" victory <note>A "Cadmean victory" (Latin: *Cadmea victoria*) is one where the victors suffer as much as the defeated, or where the success leads to the winner's ruin. The Athenian argues that education, unlike military victory, never produces such a negative result.</note>. But many victories of this kind have been and will be. 

CLINIAS. You seem, O friend...

<margin>Education provides victory; victory sometimes leads to negligence and lack of refinement.</margin>

<summary>The Athenian Stranger uses analogies of shepherds, ship pilots, and generals to argue that a drinking party (symposium) requires a sober and wise leader to be beneficial. He concludes that while military victory can lead to ruinous pride, proper education (fostered through such social institutions) always produces good men and lasting benefit to the state.</summary>

...as a great part of education, the common custom of drinking wine, if done rightly, should be praised. ATHENIAN: Indeed. CLINIAS: Can you then show this to be true? ATHENIAN: To prove that these things are true, O Stranger, when many are in doubt about them, belongs to God alone. Yet if I am to say what I feel, no envy shall stand in the way, since we have decided at present to speak of laws and the Republic. CLINIAS: Come, let us try to learn what you think of these ambiguities. ATHENIAN: It is necessary, however, since both you desire to learn and I to explain, to prolong the speech somewhat. 

<margin>Athens is eloquent and talkative.
Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> is brief of speech.
Crete is a student of understanding.</margin>

But first hear this: all Greeks judge our city to be both a lover of eloquence and talkative; but Lacedaemon and Crete—one brief-speaking <note>original: *breuiloqua*, referring to the "laconic" style of the Spartans</note>, the other studying understanding more than wordiness. I fear, therefore, that I may seem to you to be like a talkative man speaking of small matters, while I use too long a speech concerning drunkenness, which is a small thing. But the right constitution of the drinking party itself according to nature can never be treated clearly and sufficiently in speech without the right rule of music; nor music without universal education. These all certainly require many words. See, therefore, what should be done. Should we pass these over for now and move on to some other question of laws? 

MEGILLUS: Perhaps you are unaware, Athenian stranger, that our house is a common guest-friend <note>Latin: *hospitem*; referring to the Greek concept of *proxeny*, a formal bond of hospitality between families and foreign cities</note> of your city. For it happens to all boys that when they hear their elders have been guest-friends of some city, a certain benevolence toward that city—as if toward a second fatherland—instantly glides into their minds from their tenderest years. This very thing happened to me. I heard from childhood the Lacedaemonians say, whenever they were either angry with the Athenians or praised them: "Your city, Megillus, has brought us this evil or this good." And hearing these things, I fought against those who disparaged you, feeling great benevolence toward you. And to me now your voice is very pleasant; and what is commonly said—that good Athenians are exceptionally good—seems to me to be spoken truly. For they alone are good by nature, by a certain divine fate, not coerced nor faked, but truly good. Therefore, as far as I am concerned, speak freely whatever you wish. 

CLINIAS: If you will also listen to me, stranger, you will put forth whatever comes to your mind with the greatest confidence. For perhaps you have heard that Epimenides <note>A semi-mythical Cretan seer and philosopher said to have purified Athens</note> was a divine man. He was from our family; and ten years before the Persian war, warned by an oracle of God, he came to you and performed certain sacrifices dictated by the oracle. To the Athenians who were dreading the Persian fleet, he predicted that the Persians would not come for ten years. And even after they arrived, they would depart with their business unfinished, having suffered more evils than they inflicted. Then some of our ancestors embraced yours with the affection of hospitality, and from that time my parents and I have been benevolent toward you. 

ATHENIAN: You are ready to listen, then, as it seems. And I am ready to speak, more out of a prompt will than a ready faculty. I will try, however, as best I can. But first, let us define what education <note>Latin: *disciplina*; in this context, it translates the Greek *paideia*, meaning the total upbringing and cultural training of a person</note> is and what power it has. For our current discussion must proceed through this, until it reaches God himself. CLINIAS: That is certainly what should be done, if it pleases you. ATHENIAN: While I say what education is, consider whether my opinion pleases you. CLINIAS: Speak. 

ATHENIAN: I assert indeed that those who are to turn out to be excellent men in any pursuit must practice that very thing from early childhood, both in play and in study, in each thing that is suitable to them. For instance, if someone is to be a skilled farmer or builder, he ought to play from his first age at tilling the earth or building certain childish houses; and he who educates them should prepare small tools for both, which are images of the true tools. They ought also to learn from these teachings those things that pertain to their work. Thus, a future carpenter should learn to measure and use a rule; a future horseman should play at riding; or do something else of this kind. For in all things we ought to try through play to turn the pleasures and desires of children toward that place where we desire them to finally arrive. 

We say the head of education is right training, which leads the mind of the one playing toward a love of that thing which he will do as a man when he has perfectly acquired virtue. But consider now, as I was saying, if what has been said so far is approved by you. CLINIAS: What is to prevent it? 

ATHENIAN: Yet it must not be left undetermined what we especially call education. For when we blame or praise the upbringings of individuals, we are accustomed to say that this man is educated, and that man is uneducated, even if he is very skilled in the trade of a shopkeeper or the art of navigation and other such things. Indeed, we do not think this is "education," but rather that which from childhood makes one desire and love virtue—and specifically that virtue by which someone, having been made a perfect citizen, knows how to rule and be ruled with justice. This discourse determines that this training alone is to be called "education." But that which tends toward collecting money, or increasing bodily strength, or seeking some other skill without mind and justice, it considers mechanical <note>Latin: *mechanicam*; often used to describe manual labor or trades that were thought to distract the soul from civic virtue</note> and illiberal <note>Latin: *illiberalem*; meaning "not fit for a free man"</note>, and unworthy of the name of education. But let us not contend over the word. Let this, however, which was recently asserted, be agreed between us: that those who have obtained right education nearly all turn out to be good; those who have the contrary, turn out bad. Therefore, education is in no way to be neglected, for it is the first of the most noble things present to excellent men. And if someone fails in any way, and can be corrected, he should amend himself, and do so through his whole life to the best of his ability. CLINIAS: You speak rightly. Therefore, what you say must be granted. ATHENIAN: And yet we have already granted that those who are able to rule themselves are good, but those who cannot are bad. CLINIAS: Very wisely. ATHENIAN: Let us then take up that very thing again, so that what we say may become clearer. And may you receive it through an image so that it may be plain, if in any way I can open this matter to you. CLINIAS: Speak now. ATHENIAN: Do we not think each of us is one? CLINIAS: One. ATHENIAN: Having, namely...

->ON THE LAWS, OR THE LATIN DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, BOOK I.<-

...within himself two counselors, contrary and foolish: whom we call pleasure and pain. 

CLINIAS: This is so. 

ATHENIAN: To these are added opinions of future things, whose common name is "expectation." Specifically, the expectation before pain is "fear," while the expectation before its contrary is "confidence." To all these, the judgment of reason is added, dictating which of them is better and which is worse. When this judgment becomes the common decree of the city, it is named "law." 

CLINIAS: I am barely following you. Nevertheless, speak what remains as if I were following. 

MEGILLUS: The same has happened to me as well. 

<margin>
Man as a miracle among the living.
</margin>
ATHENIAN: Let us think of it this way: let us suppose each of us is a kind of divine miracle <note>original: *miraculum*, often translated as "puppet" or "marionette" in this famous Platonic metaphor</note> among the genus of living things, whether we were created as a game or for some serious purpose, for we do not know the intent of the gods. But we do know this: that these internal states in us are like nerves or ropes that pull us, tugging against one another toward contrary actions, where virtue and vice reside separately. 

<margin>
Reason aims at one thing.
</margin>
For reason dictates that one pull should always be followed and never abandoned, while the other nerves must be pulled back toward it. 

<margin>
The golden and sacred pulling.
</margin>
This leading of the rational judgment is golden and sacred, and it is what is called the common law of the city. While the other pulls are hard and made of iron, this one is soft because it is golden; it is uniform, while the others take many forms. Therefore, one must always follow the most beautiful leading of the law and support it. Since the judgment of reason is a noble thing—gentle rather than violent—its leadership requires assistants so that the golden element in us might overcome the other types. In this way, the story that tells how man is a wonderful thing will be preserved through virtue, and one will more clearly understand in what sense a person is said to be "superior to himself" or "inferior to himself." <note>This refers to the concept of self-mastery: being "superior to oneself" means the rational soul controls the passions.</note> Every private individual should grasp the truth of these internal pulls through reason and direct his life accordingly. The city, likewise, receiving this reason either from a god or from one who has understood it, should hold it as law, and by its standard, arrange its own duties and its relations with other cities. Thus, virtue and vice will be more clearly distinguished for us. Once these are clearly understood, education and other studies will perhaps become clearer. Furthermore, there is the custom concerning wine; to have a long speech about it might perhaps be thought trivial. 

CLINIAS: Perhaps it will not seem unworthy of a long speech. 

ATHENIAN: You speak well. Let us say, then, what is worthy in it. 

CLINIAS: Proceed now. 

ATHENIAN: If we bring drunkenness to this wonderful thing <note>referring back to the human "miracle" or puppet</note>, what will we make of it? 

CLINIAS: To what end do you ask this? 

ATHENIAN: I do not yet say to what end. But if this wonderful thing is mixed with wine, what does it become? I will try to say what I mean more clearly. I am asking something like this: Does the use of wine excite pleasures, pains, angers, and loves more vehemently? 

CLINIAS: Most certainly. 

ATHENIAN: And does it similarly make the senses, memory, opinion, and intelligence more vehement? Or are they entirely extinguished if someone is overtaken by drunkenness? 

CLINIAS: They are certainly extinguished entirely. 

<margin>
Lessons from wine.
</margin>
ATHENIAN: Therefore, the soul returns to the habit it had as a child in its first years. 

CLINIAS: Indeed. 

ATHENIAN: Therefore, he will be least in control of himself. 

CLINIAS: Least of all. 

ATHENIAN: And so he will be at his worst? 

CLINIAS: Very much so. 

<margin>
The drunkard is also twice a child.
</margin>
ATHENIAN: It seems, then, that not only is the old man "twice a child," but the drunken man is as well. 

CLINIAS: That is very well said, Stranger. 

ATHENIAN: Is there any reasoning that can persuade us that this thing <note>drinking</note> should be tasted in any way, rather than being fled with all our strength? 

CLINIAS: There might be, as you say; you were just now showing yourself ready to speak of it. 

ATHENIAN: You remember well. Indeed, I am ready now, since you both promised you would listen willingly. 

CLINIAS: Why should we not listen? If for no other reason, then because it seems strange and absurd that a man should ever willingly throw himself into such depravity. 

ATHENIAN: Do you mean depravity of the soul? 

CLINIAS: Of the soul. 

ATHENIAN: And would we not wonder, my friend, if someone willingly fell into depravity of the body—I mean thinness, deformity, or weakness? 

CLINIAS: Of course we would. 

ATHENIAN: Do we think that those who voluntarily take the medicines of physicians are unaware that shortly afterward their bodies will be so affected for several days that, if they were to remain that way forever, they would not wish to live? Or are we unaware that those who undergo the gymnasium and hard labor become immediately weak from exhaustion? 

CLINIAS: We know all these things. 

ATHENIAN: And yet, everyone proceeds to these things voluntarily for the sake of future utility. 

CLINIAS: Excellent. 

ATHENIAN: Should we not think the same way about other things? 

CLINIAS: Exactly the same. 

ATHENIAN: We must think no differently about the drinking of wine, if it is granted that this can be considered rightly among those things. 

CLINIAS: Certainly so. 

ATHENIAN: If it is seen to have some utility no less than that which exists in physical exercise, that is well. However, in principle, it surpasses the exercise of the body in this: the latter involves pain, while the former does not. 

CLINIAS: That is true. But I would wonder if we could perceive any such utility in it. 

ATHENIAN: That is precisely what I must now try to explain. Tell me: Can we think of two types of fear that are almost contrary to one another? 

CLINIAS: Which ones do you mean? 

ATHENIAN: These: We certainly fear evils when we expect them in the future. 

CLINIAS: We fear them. 

ATHENIAN: We also frequently fear reputation <note>original: *existimationem*, referring to how one is perceived by others</note>, when we dread that by saying or doing something less than honorable, we might appear wicked. This fear we—indeed all of us, I believe—call shame [pudor]. 

CLINIAS: Who could doubt it? 

ATHENIAN: I was speaking of these two fears. One of them is contrary to pains and other fears, and it is also contrary to many great pleasures. 

CLINIAS: Quite right. 

ATHENIAN: Should not the legislator, and anyone else who can benefit men in any way, hold this fear in the highest honor and call it "shame"? And should he not name the confidence that is its opposite "impudence," and judge it to be the greatest evil for men, both privately and publicly? 

CLINIAS: Well said. 

ATHENIAN: This fear <note>shame</note> preserves us most in many other great matters; and in war, if one thing is compared to another, this certainly grants us victory and safety more than anything else.

He begins to argue that controlled drunkenness can serve as a "test of character" by temporarily stripping away shame, similar to how medicine or exercise causes temporary bodily weakness for long-term health.</summary>

...for these are the things that bring about victory: against enemies, boldness; but against friends, the fear of shameful disgrace <note>original: *infamia*; here referring to "shame" or "modesty," the social glue that prevents wrongdoing</note>.

CLINIAS: It is so.

ATHENIAN: Therefore, it is necessary for each of us to become both fearless and fearful. We have already distinguished the reasons why both are necessary.

CLINIAS: Entirely.

ATHENIAN: And whenever we wish to make someone fearless—impelled by the law into a terror of many fears—we make them such.

CLINIAS: So it seems.

ATHENIAN: But when we wish to make someone fearful with right judgment in the face of many dangers, we must surely test him against things that incline toward impudence. We must exercise him in the struggle against his own pleasures or the habits of his past life, encouraging him toward victory. In this way, by being a victor, he is rendered perfect in fortitude. But he who has never made trial of himself, nor been exercised in these contests, will not possess even half of his own strength toward virtue. For how will someone be perfectly temperate if they have not bravely resisted the many pleasures and desires that compel one toward impudence and injustice? How can they be a victor through reason, action, and skill, in both jesting and serious matters, unless they have conquered these? Or will one be temperate if they have never experienced anything of the kind?

CLINIAS: That is not at all likely.

ATHENIAN: But tell me, I pray: has some god given men a potion to induce fear? So that the more one drinks of it, the more miserable he thinks himself to be with every draught? So that he fears all things, both present and future? And so that even the bravest of all men finally descends into total dread? Then, when he has slept and been freed from such a potion, the same thing happens to him again every day?

CLINIAS: And what potion of this kind, O friend, could we ever say has existed in the life of men?

ATHENIAN: None, certainly. Nevertheless, if this potion were to be found, would it be useful to a lawmaker for the cultivation of fortitude? Could we say something like this to the author of the laws: "Come now, first tell us, O lawmaker—whether you are a Cretan or writing laws for any others—would you wish to be able to test the fortitude and cowardice of your citizens?"

CLINIAS: Anyone would surely answer that they would wish to.

ATHENIAN: And then, would you wish to do so safely and without great imminent danger, or the opposite?

CLINIAS: Anyone would confess they would prefer it safely and securely.

ATHENIAN: Would you then use this potion, compelling them toward such terrors and proving them in those very disturbances by your admonition and command, so that you might make your citizens unafraid? Would you honor some and reproach others if they did not obey your warnings? And would you leave those who conducted themselves vigorously in the exercise unpunished, while affecting those who did the opposite with a penalty? Or would you not use it at all, since you have nothing else to accuse it of?

CLINIAS: Why would he not use it, stranger?

ATHENIAN: Such an exercise, O friend, beyond its usual benefits, is of a wonderful ease, by which one person, or a few, or as many as you wish, can be exercised. And whether someone exercises himself alone in a desert—valuing shame most highly and not wishing to be seen by others until he is stronger—he will surely achieve something good by using this potion alone, prepared above many other things. Or, if someone is confident in his nature and sufficiently instructed by practice, he might not fear to exercise with many drinking companions, showing his power in the necessary struggle against the potion—prevailing and surpassing to such an extent that he errs in no great matter through impudence, and does not move from his state of virtue. He might depart after the final drink before drunkenness sets in, being especially wary of the violence of unmixed wine <note>original: *meri*; pure, undiluted wine was considered dangerous and a cause of madness by the Greeks</note> upon all men.

CLINIAS: Certainly, O stranger, such a man acting in this way would turn out moderate.

ATHENIAN: Let us speak again to the lawmaker: "O lawmaker, no god has yet given such a potion of fear to men, nor have we ourselves devised one." For I am certainly not speaking of sorcerers at a banquet. But for the sake of being very confident, and daring more than is appropriate in any circumstances—is there a certain potion for this, or none at all?

CLINIAS: He will say it is wine.

<margin>
The degrees of drunkenness.
</margin>
ATHENIAN: Furthermore, it acts in the opposite way to the potion we just mentioned. For when someone has drunk, he first becomes more cheerful than he was before. Then, the more he drinks, the more he is filled with greater and better hope and even power in his own opinion. Finally, as if he were a wise man, the human is filled with such confidence, liberty, and audacity that he fearlessly says and does whatever pleases him.

CLINIAS: I think indeed everyone would concede that.

MEGILLUS: Certainly everyone.

ATHENIAN: Let us remember, then, that there are two things in our souls that we said above must be cared for. One is that we should be as confident as possible; the other is that we should be as fearful as possible.

CLINIAS: We believe these things were said concerning shame <note>original: *pudore*; the Greek concept of *aidos*, a mix of shame, modesty, and respect for social norms</note>.

ATHENIAN: You hold it correctly. But since the habit of a brave and unafraid soul must be practiced in the midst of fears, we must consider whether the contrary habit must be practiced in contrary circumstances.

CLINIAS: That follows.

ATHENIAN: In those things where we are naturally accustomed to becoming most confident and audacious, we must think of how we might be the least impudent and audacious. Instead, we should be fearful of saying, suffering, or doing anything shameful.

CLINIAS: So it seems.

ATHENIAN: Are these not the things in which we are like this: anger, love, insolence, ignorance, avarice, and sloth? And to these we add wealth, beauty, strength, and whatever else makes men mindless with a certain intoxication of pleasure? For the sake of making an easy and harmless trial of all these, and for introducing exercise, we have no pleasure more convenient than that which examines character in the play of wine—provided that a certain prudent caution is applied. Let us consider: should we test a difficult and rustic soul, from which many injuries are perpetrated, in actual business dealings with the highest risk, or rather in the festival of Dionysus <note>original: *Dionysii spectaculo*; referring to the symposium or wine-drinking celebrations</note>? Or should we consider the affection of a soul prone to lust by committing to him those most dear to us—namely, daughters and sons—at the highest risk? One could bring forward countless examples, but words cannot express how much better it is to search out human character simply with a joke, without harm. Concerning this, we think neither the Cretans nor any other men would ever doubt that this examination of character is appropriate—and above all others, easy, safe, and brief.

CLINIAS: That is true indeed.

ATHENIAN: This, therefore, will be something most useful: to know the natures and habits of souls by that art by which they are to be cured.

The controlled environment of a drinking party (symposium) is presented as a safe and efficient laboratory for lawmakers to observe and train the character of citizens.</summary>

### SUMMARY FOR THE SECOND DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS.

->**The Summary of Marsilio Ficino for the Second Dialogue on the Laws.**<-

Our Plato, possessing a wonderful love for the human race, leaves nothing untried in his discussions that he sees might lead to human salvation by any means. While he strives for this goal with great zeal, he prefers to face the charge of being either overly wordy or even excessively meticulous rather than negligent. Therefore, in this second book, he continues to investigate the discipline of the "tender age" <note>childhood</note>. He notices that children are almost like beasts, having no sense of responsibility; they rush headlong wherever pleasure pulls them, and flee immediately from wherever pain withdraws them. Lest a harmful inclination toward seeking or fleeing things should grow into a fixed habit before reason matures, he places a charioteer over the horses of youth—one who holds the reins of pleasure and pain.

He names this charioteer "discipline." This is the virtue that first persuades us. Through it, pleasure and love, pain and hatred, flow correctly into the soul via another's reason <note>the guidance of a teacher or parent</note> before they are moved by one's own reason. Then, when reason is eventually present, these feelings agree with one's own reason because of that earlier habit of good morals. He wishes this very agreement to be the "universal virtue." He defines "discipline" as that proper habituation regarding pleasures and pains, through which men—from the beginning to the end of life—hate what ought to be hated and love what is to be loved, so long as it is governed by another's reason. Later, when it agrees with one's own awakened reason, he calls it by the name of "virtue." Aristotle himself greatly approves in his *Ethics* that this foundation of moral life is of the greatest importance.

Since the nature of children is restless and eager for amusements of all kinds, and therefore does not easily take to stern discipline, Plato rightly orders that children be educated under the "honest pleasure" of that most common music which carries the traces of virtue. Indeed, he even includes the elders at times, to whom certain honest amusements must be granted as a solace for a life of labor. For this reason, he says the gods, having pitied the laborious life of men, established solemn sacred festivals for them as a release from labor. He says they provided the Muses, Apollo, and Bacchus <note>Dionysus</note> as leaders for these celebrations to correct the wildness of behavior. Through music, they might moderate the nature that is greedy for motion, ordering those motions by reason and delighting them in an honest way.

These words not only praise the use of music as something divinely commended and granted, but also teach allegorically that man would be more miserable than the beasts for many reasons, unless he took up divine worship and religion through divine providence and kinship. In this allegory, the Muses signify the divine discovery of truth granted to God’s followers; Apollo signifies the graceful expression and prophecy of that discovery; and Bacchus signifies both the abstraction of the mind <note>the "divine madness" or inspiration</note> and the admirable works of religious men. Take note that the principle of harmony was granted to us chiefly by divine providence so that we might harmonize all the restless motions of our nature which, by their own nature, would be discordant. From the Muses, we receive the consonance of the soul's motion; from Apollo, we receive concord in speech and song; and from Bacchus, we receive a festive grace in the movement of our limbs.

While he discusses this discipline through music most diligently—pertaining both to the young and even the old—he repeats the same institutions he established in the *Republic*. By these rules, poets, musicians, and painters are never granted the license to imitate whatever they wish; instead, they must imitate only what is honest and serious for the health of those watching and listening. He wants the judges of this "imitation" <note>artistic representation</note> to be expert and most serious men. He commands that through honest imitation practiced daily, the youth should become accustomed in all their games and studies to the same things in which the laws and the elders find joy or sorrow. He judges that this habituation contains the entire foundation of virtue.

Among these points, he commends several things to memory that greatly contribute to moral precepts: The unjust man, even if he possesses all the goods known to men, is unhappy; and as long as he lives in this way, it must be said that it is better for him to die than to live. Likewise, whoever distinguishes between the "honest," the "useful," and the "pleasant" when speaking to one another is not to be heard. And though a life of honesty and justice might sometimes seem laborious, this must never be told to children; on the contrary, one should say that the most just life will be the most pleasant of all. Plato asserts that this will ultimately be seen as a necessity, even if it seems otherwise to those with whom he disputes. He orders that such doubts be kept silent. Nevertheless, Truth is a beautiful and stable thing.

After this, he descends to the use of wine, which he wants to be entirely unknown to youths before their eighteenth year. Otherwise, he says, "fire is poured upon fire" both in the soul and the body. After this age, he permits wine to be drunk moderately. After the fortieth year, however, he allows wine to be drunk more freely at banquets among hymns to the gods—treating it as a remedy against the hardness of old age. Through it, we seem to grow young again, and a forgetfulness of sadness takes hold of us. The very affection of the soul, like iron in the fire, is brought from hardness into softness and becomes more flexible. By this, he intends that elders, who might otherwise be unwilling to sing, become more cheerful at banquets and willing to sing for the ears of the younger; and thus, so to speak, "enchant" the souls of the youth. By this enchantment, through a melody of grave concord, the souls of the younger generation are tempered.

In reading these things, you will note that "grace" <note>Latin: *gratia*</note> is called "beauty" in physical things, but "pleasure" in the act of knowing. You will note that no animal except man has a sense of rhythm and harmony. Note also that rhythm is "order in time and motion," while harmony is "order in the voices themselves through the blending of high and low pitches." What we often call "harmony" in a general sense, we more properly call "concord" <note>original: *concentus*</note> in Latin. What we call "rhythm," we can conveniently call "number" <note>original: *numerus*</note>.

<vocab>Marsilius Ficino, Plato, Laws, discipline, virtue, music, Apollo, Bacchus, harmony, rhythm</vocab>

He explores the allegorical roles of the Muses, Apollo, and Bacchus in creating social harmony and discusses the moderate use of wine as a "medicine" for the elderly.</summary>
