->DIALOGUE II. CONCERNING THE LAWS OR CONCERNING LEGISLATION.<-
->ATHENIAN STRANGER.<-

<margin>The first sense of children is pleasure and pain</margin>
Next, however, we must consider whether they have this good alone, so that we may see how our natures are disposed: or whether there is also great utility worthy of much study in the drinking of wine, if it is rightly governed. What then do we say? It is surely present: as the discourse seems to indicate. But where: and how? I pray we listen attentively, lest we be hindered by it. CLINIAS: Speak then. ATHENIAN: I desire, therefore, to recall to memory what we call "right discipline." For of this, as I gather at present, there is safety in this duty when it is rightly instituted. CLINIAS: You say a great thing. ATHENIAN: I say indeed that the first sense of children is of pleasure and pain: and these two are those in which virtue and vice first arise in the soul. If however wisdom <note>original: "prudentia"</note> and true and stable opinion are present even in old age, such a man is happy. Furthermore, he is a perfect man who possesses these and all the goods that are in them. I call "discipline" <note>term: "disciplina" (education/training)</note> the virtue which first comes to children. If pleasure and love and pain and hatred flow rightly into their souls before they are moved by reason, and then, when reason is present, they agree with reason because of the prior habit of good morals, this very universal agreement is indeed virtue. If you should call "discipline" that proper habituation regarding pleasures and pains, through which men—from the beginning until the end of life—hate what ought to be hated and love what is to be loved, considering it apart by itself through reason, you will call it rightly, as I think. CLINIAS: Indeed, O Guest <note>The Athenian is often addressed as "Guest" or "Stranger"</note>, both what you said before and what you say now concerning discipline seem well-spoken. ATHENIAN: It is well, then. However, men in life transgress and often pervert this kind of right education of pleasures and pains, which is called discipline. But the gods, pitying the race of men naturally weighed down by labors, established for them remissions from labors: namely, the solemn feasts instituted in turn in honor of the gods themselves, providing the Muses, and Apollo the leader of the Muses, and Bacchus as fellow-celebrants; and by the counsel of the gods they applied reformers of morals during the solemnities. We must consider, therefore, whether this discourse is natural and true for us, which says: that all those of a tender age, to embrace it in a word, are unable to keep still in either body or voice: but are always being moved and wanting to speak: some leaping and jumping, and as if dancing and playing with pleasure, others shouting with various voices. Other animals indeed do not at all perceive order or the lack of order—which order is indeed observed in movements and is called rhythm and harmony. 

<margin>All those of a tender age are unable to keep still.</margin>
<margin>In us, and not in other animals, is the sense of rhythm and harmony.</margin>
<margin>What rhythm and harmony [are].</margin>
<margin>Chorus from "chara" [joy]</margin>
<margin>What the chorus [is].</margin>

We, however, have been granted by these gods whom we said were given to us as fellow-celebrants, a sense participant in rhythm and harmony: and they move us with pleasure and lead the "chorus" <note>term: "chorea" (a combined song and dance)</note> for us, joining us to one another with songs and dances. Which chorus indeed they named from "chara"—that is, joy <note>original: "chara" (Greek: χαρά); the Athenian suggests the word "chorus" comes from the word for "joy"</note>. But first we must consider: shall we concede that the first discipline is through the Muses and Apollo? Or how? CLINIAS: Entirely so. ATHENIAN: Therefore, he who has never used the chorus must be called unskilled in discipline. But he who has done so sufficiently is, on the contrary, possessed of discipline. CLINIAS: So we propose. ATHENIAN: Does he think he can sufficiently perform that chorus everywhere, yet neither rejoices in honorable things nor hates shameful things? Or rather is it he who, although he cannot follow with voice and body as is becoming, yet follows with pleasure and pain, so that he rejoices in good things but hates depraved ones? CLINIAS: You describe a great distinction in discipline, O Guest. ATHENIAN: If therefore we three are not ignorant of what a good song and dance <note>original: "tripudium" (a rhythmic dance)</note> are, we surely recognize both who has rightly attained discipline and who has not. But if we are ignorant of this, we shall never be able to know if there is any preservation of discipline, or where it is. Is it not so? CLINIAS: Entirely so. ATHENIAN: Next, therefore, let us track down the becoming figure, melody, song, and dance, just as dogs follow a scent. For if these escape us, we shall dispute in vain about right discipline, whether Greek or barbarian. CLINIAS: I think so. ATHENIAN: What figure and melody, then, is it becoming to call good? Are the figures and voices of a brave soul and a timid soul similar in the same or equal labors? CLINIAS: How could they be similar, when not even their colors are? ATHENIAN: Well said, my friend. But in music there are both figures and harmonies, since it is concerned with rhythm and harmony. Wherefore it is permitted to speak of the figure and song of good rhythm and harmony: but we cannot rightly speak of "good color" in the same way, imagining it as masters of the chorus are accustomed to do. However, there is a certain figure and song of a cowardly man and of a brave man: and these are rightly named "honorable" in brave men and "shameful" in cowards. But lest I be too long in these matters, simply all things pertaining to the virtue of the soul or body, or of virtue...

figures and harmonies that adhere to a good image are honorable, while the contrary are shameful. CLINIAS: You are quite right; we judge these things to be so for the present. ATHENIAN: Furthermore, let us observe this: whether we are all similarly delighted by all choral dances <note>original: "choreis"; referring to the combined art of dance, song, and music</note>, or is there a great difference? CLINIAS: A very great difference indeed. ATHENIAN: What then shall we say has driven us into error? Is it not that the same things are honorable and good to all of us? Or is it that while they are the same, they do not appear the same? For no one would dare to say that a vicious dance is better than one that partakes of virtue. Nor will anyone ever admit that he is delighted by depraved figures while others are delighted by a contrary muse. Although many proclaim that the right standard of music consists in a power to bring pleasure to the soul, this is neither to be tolerated nor spoken of at all. For it is a sacrilege <note>original: "nefas"</note>. Rather, this is the cause of the error. CLINIAS: What is it? ATHENIAN: Because in the choral dance, imitations are made of various characters and various things performed in various fortunes and habits; those who approve of these things—whether by nature, habit, or both—and whose souls find them fitting, must necessarily rejoice in them, praise them, and call them honorable. But those for whom these things are contrary to their nature, character, or some habit, can neither rejoice in them nor praise them; indeed, they must call them shameful. But truly, for those who possess a right nature but have been habituated to the contrary, or who have a right habit but a contrary nature, their praises are at odds with their pleasures. For they assert that each of these things is pleasant, yet they concede they are depraved. And therefore, in the presence of others whom they consider wise, they are ashamed to move their bodies in such a way, and they are ashamed to sing such things or to assert they are honorable and worthy of study. Yet in private, they are delighted by all of them. CLINIAS: You speak most truly. ATHENIAN: Is any harm brought upon those who are delighted by depraved figures or songs? Or is there any utility for those who take pleasure in the opposite? CLINIAS: That seems likely. ATHENIAN: Is it merely likely, or is it even necessary that it be so? Just as when someone associates with wicked men: he does not hate their manners, but rather is delighted by them and indulges them. And yet, he disparages them in jest, as if perceiving their depravity within himself as though in a dream. Then it is surely necessary that he becomes like those in whom he rejoices, even if he is ashamed to praise them. Indeed, what greater good or evil do we think could necessarily happen to us than this? CLINIAS: None, I think. ATHENIAN: Do we think that where laws are well-established, or will be so in the future, there will be such poetic license in the disciplines and games of the Muses <note>the "games of the Muses" refers to poetry, music, and the arts</note> that a poet may teach whatever delights him in rhythm, song, or poetic word? And that he may turn the children and youths of well-instituted citizens in the choral dances toward either virtue or vice, as it happens? CLINIAS: That would be against all reason. MEGILLUS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: To put it briefly, that license is permitted everywhere except in Egypt. CLINIAS: In what way do you say this law was sanctioned in Egypt? ATHENIAN: It is a wonderful thing to hear. For long ago, as it seems to me, they recognized what we have just said: that the youth in a city must be accustomed to good figures and good songs. What these are and of what kind, was established by them in their sacred rites. Beyond these, it was not permitted for painters or other makers of figures or any craftsmen to introduce anything new, nor even to devise anything other than the traditional <note>original: "patria"; literally "of the fathers"</note>; nor is it permitted today, either in these arts or in music as a whole. And so, if you search carefully, you will find there works depicted or otherwise figured ten thousand years ago—not just "old," so to speak, but neither more beautiful nor more shameful than those produced today by the same art. CLINIAS: What you say is marvelous to hear. ATHENIAN: Rather, it is profoundly statesmanlike, and most fitting for the positioning of laws. You will find other trivial things there, but this regarding music is true and worthy of notice: namely, that it was possible to provide for such things by a certain and stable law. It was permitted to conduct such gatherings with the highest confidence, which would exhibit a natural rectitude. This is surely the work of a god, or of some divine man. Just as they say there that those most ancient songs among them are the poems of Isis. Therefore, as I was saying, if anyone can understand the rectitude of these things in any way, he ought to reduce them to order and law with good hope. For the constant new affection of the appetite for pleasure and pain—which tries to make us always seek to use new music—perhaps does not have great power to corrupt those ancient choral dances with the accusation of being "old-fashioned" once they have been established by sacred laws. Certainly, it seems that it has by no means been possible to corrupt the Egyptian dances over so much time; on the contrary, quite the opposite. CLINIAS: The matter stands just as it is gathered from your words. ATHENIAN: Let us say confidently, then, that the use of games and music with choral dance is right in this way. We rejoice whenever we think we are living happily, and whenever we rejoice, we again consider ourselves to be living happily; is it not so? CLINIAS: Exactly so. ATHENIAN: And also, while we are so rejoicing, we are unable to remain still. CLINIAS: It is as you say. ATHENIAN: Are not our young men, therefore, ready to celebrate in choral dances? But we elders think it fitting to be occupied in watching them; while we enjoy their games and celebration, since the lightness of body has left us. Longing for that lightness, we set up contests for those who are most able to call it back with the help of memory. CLINIAS: You tell the truth. ATHENIAN: Do we think then that the saying so common among many regarding those who celebrate is said in vain: that he ought to be judged the wisest and the winner of the victory who makes us rejoice and be glad the most? For since playing is permitted in these things, it seems fitting that we should especially honor the one who provokes the most people to the greatest joy, and, as I was just saying, call him the victor. Is that said correctly? And would it be done correctly if it were done so? CLINIAS: Perhaps. ATHENIAN: But, oh blessed one, let us not bring forth a judgment so quickly; rather, let us consider this very thing by distinguishing it into parts in this way. If someone should incite many to a contest, and did not specify whether it was gymnastic, or musical, or equestrian, but om—

### BOOK II.

If all the citizens were gathered together for the sake of pleasure, and a certain competition were established, with a prize offered to the one who most delights the spectators—and if it were judged that he had performed best of all, with no mode of delighting being passed over <gloss>passed over</gloss>—what do we think would result from such an announcement? CLINIAS: What are you talking about? ATHENIAN: It is likely that one person, like Homer, would show a rhapsody <note>A performance of epic poetry</note>; another, a performance on the cithara <note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre</note>; another, a Tragedy; and another, a Comedy. Nor would someone be lacking who thought he might achieve victory by showing a marvel <note>Original: "miraculo"; likely referring to puppet shows or magic tricks</note>. Since many such competitors, and others of that same kind, would flock together, can we say who would emerge as the victor without being unfair? CLINIAS: You ask an absurd thing. For who could answer that skillfully before he himself, being present there, had heard each of the competitors? ATHENIAN: Do you wish, then, for me to answer this "absurd" question myself? CLINIAS: Why not? ATHENIAN: If very small boys were to give their opinion, they would judge the one who shows marvels to have defeated the others. Would they not? CLINIAS: What would stop them? ATHENIAN: But the older boys would prefer Comedy to the others. Educated women, however, along with young men and perhaps the majority of the crowd, would likely praise Tragedy. CLINIAS: Perhaps it would happen so. ATHENIAN: But we elders would perhaps listen with the greatest pleasure to a rhapsode who sang well some Homeric passage from the *Iliad* or the *Odyssey*, or something of Hesiod, and we would proclaim him the victor over all. Does it not remain, then, to declare who would be the victor by right? CLINIAS: Indeed. ATHENIAN: It is clear, as it seems to me, and you must necessarily concede, that the true victor is the one judged to have won by our equals <note>Meaning those of similar age, experience, and status to the elderly speakers</note>. For the experience of things which we have from age is everywhere a great and best thing in all civic matters. CLINIAS: Without a doubt. ATHENIAN: I myself, therefore, grant this to the many: that music should be judged by pleasure. However, not by the pleasure of just any person; rather, I say that the most beautiful "Muse" <note>Referring to art, music, and poetry collectively</note> is that which delights the best and sufficiently educated people, but especially that which delights a man outstanding in virtue and learning. For this reason, we affirm that the judges of these things must possess virtue. For they ought to participate in both prudence and fortitude. In prudence: because a true judge ought not to learn from another those things which must be determined by judgment, nor should he deliver his sentence as if stunned by the shouting of the crowd or his own ignorance. In fortitude: because even if he understands the truth for himself, he must not, out of cowardice or fear, lazily pronounce an unjust judgment from the same mouth with which he invoked the gods when he was about to judge. For the judge sits on the tribunal not as a disciple, but as a master over the spectators—as is fitting—to oppose the unseemly pleasures of the audience. The ancient Greek law permitted this, just as the Sicilian and Italian laws do now, which, by committing the matter to the multitude of spectators and declaring the victor by a show of hands, have corrupted the poets themselves. The poets now compose everything to suit the depraved pleasure of the common judges, so that the spectators themselves "educate" the poets and themselves. This has also corrupted the pleasures of the performance itself. For while it is necessary for those present to always hear things better than their own habits, and thus attain a better pleasure, now the opposite happens to them in the theater. What, then, is the meaning of these words? Observe if this is what they mean. CLINIAS: What is it? ATHENIAN: It seems to me the discourse has circled back to the same point three or four times: that education is the training of children which leads to that way of living which the law declares to be right, and which men of outstanding equity and elders have truly approved through experience. Therefore, so that the mind of the child may follow the law in this way—so that he does not feel pain or joy at things contrary to the law, but at those things which the law and the elder approve—the good lawgiver will persuade him. And if necessary, he will compel the poetic man to describe the deeds of honorable, temperate, brave, and generally good men in noble words. He shall fashion their figures in rhythms and their accents in harmonies as is fitting, through those songs which we call odes, but which are truly incantations <note>Original: "epodae"; chants or spells</note> for the soul, deliberately composed for this purpose: so that the souls of men may obey the laws in their grieving and rejoicing. Because tender souls cannot endure serious studies, these things should be said and done in the form of play and song. The same effect is achieved here as that which those who care for people with sick bodies are accustomed to do: for they smear appropriate nourishment with sweet seasonings, but taint harmful things with bitterness, so that the patients become accustomed to accepting the former and rejecting the latter. CLINIAS: Do you think, stranger, that these things are now observed in other cities? For as far as I know, the things you prescribe are done nowhere except among us and the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans</note>. For they are always inventing new things in dances and other music, changed not by laws but by certain wandering pleasures, which are by no means always the same or remain in the same manner, but are always varied, contrary to those customs of the Egyptians which you described. ATHENIAN: You speak well, Clinias. If, however, I seemed to you to say just now that the things you mention were done everywhere, I would not wonder if I explained myself less clearly than I feel. I spoke of what I wished to happen in music, and I seemed to you to speak as if they were already happening. For to rebuke a thing that is incurable and far gone in error is in no way pleasant, though sometimes it is necessary. But since we agree on these points, do you not assert that among you and those people <note>The Spartans</note> these things happen more than among others? CLINIAS: Why should we not assert it? ATHENIAN: If they were done similarly among the others, would they not act better than they do now? CLINIAS: Much more excellently, certainly, if they were arranged just as they are among those people and us, and as you prescribed a little while ago. ATHENIAN: Come then, let us see if these are the things which are proclaimed among you in all education and music. You compel the poets to say in their poems that a good man, because he is temperate and just, is happy and blessed—whether he be great and robust, or small and weak, whether he be poor or rich. But an unjust man, even if he be richer than Cinyras or Midas <note>Kings famous in mythology for their immense wealth</note>, is miserable and lives his life in sorrow. Therefore, our poet, if he speaks rightly, will say: "I shall never make mention of that man, nor call him a man, who does not possess and dispose of all things called 'good' with justice." Therefore, let that man adorned with justice delight in fighting the enemy hand-to-hand. But let the unjust man not dare to look upon bloody slaughter, nor be able to surpass the Thracian Boreas <note>The North Wind, symbolizing great speed</note> in running, nor let any of those things which are called good ever be present for him. For those things which are commonly called

He proposes that music and poetry should serve as "incantations" to train children's souls to love what is right and reject what is wrong.</summary>

PAGE 314.

# ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS OF THE LACEDAEMONIANS. DIALOGUE II.

O.ii.

<margin>Because health without virtue is not good.</margin> They call things "good," but they do not speak correctly. For they say that health is the best; beauty is the next best good; strength is the third; and wealth is the fourth. They list almost innumerable other such "goods." For keen sight and hearing, and the healthy use of the other senses, seem to be goods—and in addition to all these, the ability to do whatever you desire with **tyrannical license** <note>Absolute power used without moral restraint</note>. They claim the height of all happiness is this: if, while possessing all these things, you could become immortal as quickly as possible.

But I and you agree that for just and holy men, the possession of all these things is best; but for the unjust, it is the worst of all, starting with health itself. For to be healthy, to see, to hear, and to perceive everything easily—and indeed to live at all, or even to be immortal—is the worst thing if you live forever possessing all these things while lacking justice and the rest of the virtues. It is a lesser evil if a person so affected should end their life in the shortest possible time.

These are the things which you yourselves will invite and compel your poets to say: and by these means, you will educate the youth through appropriate rhythms and harmonies. Do you yourselves not notice this? For I assert that what the common people call "evils" are actually goods to the unjust, but evils to the just. Whereas the things they call "goods" are truly good for the good, but evil for the evil. Do we agree so far, or not? 

CLINIAS: We seem to agree in part, but in part not at all. 

ATHENIAN: Perhaps I do not persuade you that the man who is unjust and insolent is not blessed, but miserable—even if he possesses health, riches, and perpetual tyranny, and possesses moreover invincible bodily strength, high spirits, and immortality, and suffers none of those things that the common people call "evils." 

CLINIAS: You speak the truth <note>Clinias is likely agreeing that the Athenian hasn't persuaded him yet, or is acknowledging the Athenian's description of common opinion</note>. 

ATHENIAN: So be it, but what must be said next? Even if a man is powerful in strength, beautiful, and rich, and does everything throughout his whole life that he desires—does it not seem to you that if he is unjust and insolent, he must of necessity live **shamefully**? Do you at least grant that he lives shamefully? 

CLINIAS: Entirely. 

ATHENIAN: What then? Does he not also live badly? 

CLINIAS: Not in the same way. 

ATHENIAN: And do you not grant that he lives unpleasantly and to his own disadvantage? 

CLINIAS: How can we grant that? 

ATHENIAN: Would that some god, O friends, would grant us agreement of mind, for we almost disagree among ourselves. For these things seem more necessary to me, O friend Clinias, than the fact that Crete is an island. If I were the lawgiver for the Cretans, I would compel the poets and all other citizens to speak this way; and I would threaten almost the greatest of all punishments if anyone in the region asserted that there are sometimes wicked men who live pleasantly, or that some things are useful and fitting while others are more just. I would persuade my citizens to say many things contrary to what now seems to be said by the Cretans and Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>—indeed, contrary to what is said by all other men.

Come then, by Jove and Apollo, most excellent men! If we were to ask these very gods who gave us our laws: "Is the most just life the most pleasant, or are there two lives, one the most pleasant and the other the most just?"—and if they were to answer that there are two, we might perhaps ask them again (if we wished to inquire correctly): "Which of the two should be called the more blessed: those living most justly, or those living most pleasantly?" If they were to answer "those living most pleasantly," their response would be disgraceful. I would prefer such a thing to be said by mortal fathers and lawgivers rather than by the gods. Therefore, consider that I have asked my questions of a father and a lawgiver, and that he has answered me that he who lives most pleasantly is the most blessed. 

I would then oppose him thus: "O father, did you not want me to live as blessedly as possible?" "Certainly," he would say. "But you never ceased commanding me to live as justly as possible." Whoever grants both these things—whether he be a lawgiver or a father—speaks absurdly and is inconsistent with himself. 

<margin>Because he answers that the most just way is the most blessed, whoever hears this will ask, I think, what good or beauty is in that life that the law itself praises as better than pleasure? For what good can be present for the just man that is separated from pleasure? Tell me, I pray, whether praise and glory among men and gods are good and honorable, but unpleasant? And infamy the opposite? We shall say not at all, O legislator. But is neither committing nor suffering injury actually pleasant (though it is good and honorable), while other things are pleasant but shameful and evil? How could that be? The reasoning, therefore, which separates neither the pleasant from the just, nor the good from the honorable, is persuasive. Even if it served no other purpose, it is still very conducive to making someone willing to live a holy and just life. Therefore, for a legislator, it is a most shameful and contrary speech if he denies that these things are so. For no one will willingly do that which does not contain more joy than pain. That which is seen from a distance brings a dark dizziness to everyone, so to speak, even to children. Therefore, the legislator will lead the opinions of the citizens in the opposite direction, having removed the dizziness and darkness. He will persuade them—partly through praise, partly through habit, and partly through reasoning—that both just and unjust things are shaded: and that unjust things appear the opposite of just things. Indeed, to the unjust and the wicked, things seem pleasant, and just things seem most unpleasant. But to the just man, both appear entirely the opposite.</margin>

CLINIAS: So it appears. 

ATHENIAN: But in truth, which judgment shall we consider superior? That of the better soul, or the worse? 

CLINIAS: Necessarily that of the better soul. 

ATHENIAN: It is necessary, therefore, that the unjust life is not only more shameful and worse than the just and holy life, but also more unpleasant. 

CLINIAS: So it certainly seems from this reasoning, my friend. 

ATHENIAN: Therefore, even if this were not as we have just said, a lawgiver—from whom only a small benefit would come—would not think it beneath his gravity to tell a "noble lie" for the benefit of the youth (if ever any lie should be told). For he could devise no lie more useful than this falsehood: namely, that which can draw listeners in such a way that they choose to embrace justice not by force, but of their own accord. 

CLINIAS: Truth is certainly a beautiful and stable thing, O guest. But it seems it is often not easy to persuade people of it. 

ATHENIAN: So be it. But that **Sidonian fable** <note>The myth of Cadmus of Sidon, who sowed dragon's teeth from which armed soldiers grew</note>, even if it had no likeness to truth, was nevertheless easily believed, as were many others like it. 

CLINIAS: Which one? 

ATHENIAN: That armed soldiers were once born from teeth that were sown. This is a great example for the lawgiver that he can persuade the minds of the young of whatever he wishes. Therefore, he ought to investigate nothing else except by what means, once persuasion is accepted, he might confer the greatest good upon the city. Toward this, he should apply all his zeal: so that the entire city, concerning these matters, may speak with one and the same voice, as much as possible, always in their songs, their fables, and...

<margin>Because the pleasant is not separated from the just, nor the just from the pleasant.</margin>

<margin>The Sidonian fable.</margin>

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian argues that "goods" like health and wealth are only beneficial to the just, and that a legislator must use persuasion—even "noble lies" like the Sidonian fable—to convince citizens that the most just life is also the most pleasant.</summary>

...sing it in every speech. Indeed, I feel this way. If you feel otherwise, let there be no ill will in contradicting me. CLINIAS: It should not seem that any of us three could ever doubt these things. ATHENIAN: I shall proceed then, asserting that all the choruses—which are three—should instill in the still tender and soft minds of children both the other good things we have mentioned and whatever else we might describe, as if by a kind of incantation. But let this be the main point: we shall speak the truth by asserting that the gods have judged this same life to be both the best and the most pleasant. Thus, we will persuade those whom we must more effectively than if we were to speak otherwise. CLINIAS: What you say must be granted. ATHENIAN: Therefore, let the first chorus, the **childish chorus of the Muses**, enter first to eagerly sing these things to the entire city. Let the second chorus be of those who have reached up to thirty years of age; let them invoke the **Paean** <note>original: "pęana" — a song of healing or triumph, usually dedicated to Apollo</note> as a witness to the truth of what is said, and let them suppliantly pray that he be favorable to the younger ones. The third chorus shall be of those between thirty and sixty years of age. As for those older than this, because they can no longer sing stories about these same morals, we think they should be dismissed by divine oracle. CLINIAS: Stranger, who are these third choruses you speak of? For we do not clearly understand what you wish to say about them. ATHENIAN: These are the very ones for whose sake most of the previous points were introduced. CLINIAS: We do not yet understand. Speak more plainly. ATHENIAN: It was said at the beginning of the discussion, if we remember, that the nature of all youth is so burning that it can rest neither in body nor in voice, but always shouts and leaps without order; and that no other animal except the human nature has a sense of the order of both these things. The name of the order seen in motion is **rhythm** <note>original: "rhythmus", meaning number or measured flow</note>. But the order in the voice, when high and low are tempered together, is called **harmony**—that is, a concert of sound. Both together were named **chorea** <note>The combined art of dance and song</note>. We also said that the gods, taking pity on us, gave us Apollo and the Muses as fellow-celebrants and leaders of the dance. And if we remember, we counted Dionysus as the third. CLINIAS: Why should we not remember? ATHENIAN: Indeed, the choruses of Apollo and the Muses have already been mentioned. But the third, which remains, must necessarily be attributed to Dionysus. CLINIAS: In what way? Explain more fully. For at first hearing, a **Dionysian chorus of elders** <note>Dionysus is usually associated with youthful ecstasy, making a chorus of men aged 30 to 60 seem contradictory to the speakers</note> seems very absurd, if those already advanced beyond their thirtieth year to their fiftieth and even their sixtieth are to make use of it. ATHENIAN: You speak the truth. But I think reason is needed for this, so it may appear how this can be done opportunely. CLINIAS: Why not? ATHENIAN: Are those previous points agreed upon between us? CLINIAS: Which ones? ATHENIAN: That all men and boys, free and slaves, males and females, and the whole city should daily sing to the whole city what we have said, in various modes and songs, so that from an innumerable variety of hymns, they may be affected by a certain inexhaustible pleasure while singing together. CLINIAS: Nothing prevents us from granting that it should be so. ATHENIAN: But how will this best part of the city—which, due to age and prudence, possesses the highest authority for persuasion—be the cause of the greatest goods by singing the best songs? Or shall we so foolishly omit that in which the chief power of the best and most useful songs resides? CLINIAS: It is not permitted to omit it, as it now appears. ATHENIAN: How then will it be done decently? See if perhaps it is like this. CLINIAS: In what way? ATHENIAN: Every older man, already affected by a satiety of singing, takes very little delight in these things; and when the situation requires him to sing, the older and more modest he is, the more he fears to sing. Is it not so? CLINIAS: Exactly so. ATHENIAN: But he will much less tolerate singing correctly in a theater before a multitude because of shame. Especially if the choruses of elders were forced to sing like those who contend for victory, who become thin and weak for the sake of clarifying their voices. For in that way, they will sing not without annoyance and shame, and will approach these tasks more slowly. CLINIAS: What you describe is necessary. ATHENIAN: By what means, then, shall we make them ready to sing?

<margin>
Wine is forbidden to children.
</margin>
In the first place, we shall decree by law that children should entirely ignore the use of wine until their eighteenth year. For we shall warn them that one must not add fire to fire in the body and soul, before they begin to undergo the labors of becoming a man. For one must beware of the frenzied habit of youth. Then, let them use wine moderately until the thirtieth year of age. But let the youth abstain entirely from drunkenness and an excess of wine. But when they have reached the fortieth year, then reclining more freely at banquets, let them invoke the other gods and especially Dionysus for the sacred feast and games: for he granted wine to humans as a **remedy against the hardness of old age** <note>Plato views wine as a way to soften the rigidness of the elderly, allowing them to participate in the musical education of the city</note>, so that we may seem to grow young again, and that an oblivion of sadness may take hold of us. The very disposition of the soul, like iron in the fire, is led from hardness into softness and becomes more flexible. First, indeed, anyone so affected, having taken up confidence, will be less afraid to sing among others and his own friends—though not many or strangers—and to perform what we have now repeated so often: the incantation. CLINIAS: And most especially indeed. ATHENIAN: Therefore, for the purpose of inducing them to be willing to participate in songs, this method will not be unseemly. CLINIAS: Certainly not. ATHENIAN: But with what voice and what **Muse** <note>Meaning what style of music or poetic inspiration</note> will these men sing? Surely that which is suitable for them? CLINIAS: That only. ATHENIAN: What then will be suitable for divine men? Is it not that which the choruses sing? CLINIAS: We and they, stranger, cannot sing anything other than what we learned in the chorus; for we are accustomed to this kind of singing. ATHENIAN: That is likely. For you have not learned the best song, because you have a Republic like a military camp rather than a city. For this reason, you keep your youth like colts grazing in a herd. Thus, none of you takes his own and commits him to a kind of master of horses to restrain his ferocity, who might educate him by handling him gently and taming him, and performing the other things that suit education. From this, he would be made not only a good soldier, but also a fit governor of the city and towns—one who, as we said at the beginning, would be more warlike than the soldiers of **Tyrtaeus** <note>A famous Spartan poet known for his war songs</note>, and who would cultivate the duties of fortitude in the fourth place of virtue, not always and everywhere as the first, both privately and publicly. CLINIAS: I do not know why, stranger, you are again disparaging our lawgivers. ATHENIAN: I do not do it from my heart, good man, if indeed I do it; but let us proceed where reason leads, if you wish. For if we have a Muse superior to that of the choruses and the common Muse of the theater...

FOLIO CCCXV.

### ON THE LAWS, DIALOGUE II.
O.iiii.
<meta>Catchword: ctore</meta>

...teacher, let us strive to show this to those who, as we said, revere those things and seek other better ones. CLINIAS: By all means. ATHENIAN: Therefore, whatever grace follows upon a thing, it must be that either this grace alone attracts us and is its chief quality, or it is its **correctness**, or its **utility**. Let me explain what I mean by an example. Food and drink and all nourishment have a grace which we call pleasure; <margin>Every pleasing thing attracts either by grace, correctness, or utility.</margin> but they have correctness and utility if they contribute to health. CLINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: In the same way, there is a grace in learning which is called pleasure; but there is also correctness and utility, as well as a good and beautiful habit, which are produced by the truth itself. CLINIAS: That is so. ATHENIAN: Furthermore, in the arts that create likenesses, do we not look for this same thing? Surely pleasure comes from them—which it is right to call grace. CLINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: But it is the **equality** <note>original: "equalitas" — referring to the proportion or "fittingness" of an imitation to its original</note> of such things, rather than the pleasure, that makes them correct, to speak generally. CLINIAS: Excellently put. ATHENIAN: Therefore, that which produces neither utility, nor truth, nor likeness, nor harm, but is done solely for the sake of that grace which accompanies other things—which we can rightly call pleasure—should be judged by pleasure alone, provided that none of those other qualities follow it. CLINIAS: You mean pleasure alone which does no harm? ATHENIAN: Precisely. And I also call this same thing "play" or "jest," when it brings nothing worthy of estimation in terms of harm or utility. CLINIAS: You speak the truth. ATHENIAN: It follows from what we have said that no **imitation** <term>imitation: "mimesis," the Greek concept that art mirrors reality or moral truths</term> should be judged by pleasure or by false opinion. The same is true of equality. For a thing is not equal, nor is a proportioned thing proportioned, simply because it seems so to someone or because someone enjoys it; it is so by nothing other than the truth itself. CLINIAS: That is absolutely true. ATHENIAN: And do we not say that all music is imitative and a creator of likenesses? CLINIAS: Who could doubt it? ATHENIAN: Therefore, when someone asserts that music is judged by pleasure alone, they should not be listened to at all. Such music, if it is practiced anywhere, should not be sought after; rather, we should seek that music which possesses a likeness through the imitation of the good. CLINIAS: These things are true. ATHENIAN: Therefore, those who seek the best form of song and music should not seek that which is pleasant, but that which is correct. For the correctness of imitation consists in this: as we were saying, if the thing produced by imitation is as great and of such a kind as the original is in itself. CLINIAS: Who could doubt it? ATHENIAN: And yet, everyone would grant this about music: that all its poems are imitations and representations. All poets, listeners, and actors would agree on this. CLINIAS: Greatly so. ATHENIAN: It is necessary, therefore, regarding every poem and creation, that the person who is not going to make a mistake must recognize what the thing being depicted actually is. For he who knows neither what its essence is, nor of what it is an image, will never understand its correctness or its error. CLINIAS: Never, certainly. ATHENIAN: But will he who does not understand the correctness of the work know whether it is well or poorly made? I am speaking somewhat obscurely; perhaps I can say it more clearly this way. CLINIAS: In what way? ATHENIAN: Many likenesses exist that pertain to sight. CLINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: If someone does not know the proportions of a painted body, will he ever know whether it is correctly painted? For instance, whether it has the joints of the body and each individual part, and the proper number, quality, and location of each as is fitting, and moreover the colors and shapes, or whether all these things are painted in a confused way? Do you think anyone could know these things if they did not know at all what animal was being painted? CLINIAS: In no way. ATHENIAN: But if someone knows that the thing painted or shaped in any way is a human being, and that all its parts and shapes and colors have been received from art, must he not also immediately recognize if there is any defect of beauty in it? CLINIAS: Nearly everyone, Stranger, would recognize those things which are beautifully proportioned in living beings. ATHENIAN: You speak rightly. Therefore, in every image—whether it be through painting or music or in any other way—must a prudent judge not have these three things? First, that he knows <margin>The qualities that belong to a prudent judge.</margin> what it is that is being imitated; second, that it is imitated correctly; and third, that any likeness has been well-crafted with words, harmonies, and rhythms. CLINIAS: It seems so. ATHENIAN: Let us not be reluctant, then, to explain the difficulty that exists in music. Furthermore, since these likenesses are celebrated more than others, there is a need for greater diligence than in the rest. For he who wanders into error in this is harmed the most, as he drinks in bad morals under the guise of sweetness. This is difficult to recognize, because poets do not possess the poetic art in the same way as the Muses. For the Muses would never err so much as to give the colors and harmonies of women to the words of men, or to give the rhythms of slaves and the illiberal to the forms and harmonies of free men, or to give a harmony or speech contrary to the rhythms of free forms. Furthermore, they would never confound the voices of wild beasts and men, the sounds of instruments, and all sorts of noises as if they were imitating one single thing. But human poets mix many such things in a confused and irrational way, provoking laughter in men who, as Orpheus says, followed for the sake of delight. For the poets see everything in a confused way and they themselves pull it apart: separating the rhythm and gestures from the harmony, composing bare speeches in meter without harmony; and also setting harmonies and rhythms without the playing of the **cithara** <note>original: "citharę" — an ancient Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre</note> or the sound of the **tibia** <note>original: "tibię" — an ancient flute or reed pipe</note>. In this matter, it is very difficult to know what rhythm and harmony made without words mean, or what worthy imitation they resemble. But it must be understood that whatever follows closely the speed or slowness and the voices of wild beasts is full of great crudeness, such as using the pipe and lyre in a way other than what is needed for the dance and song. To use either instrument alone is an abuse, like a showy display of wonders, and is quite alien to the Muses. But this is the reason for these things. We, however, are not considering this so that those of us aged thirty or fifty and older should not use our music, but so that we may see how they *ought* to use it. From these things, this discourse seems to signify to us that those who have reached their fiftieth year and must sing, ought to possess the music of the chorus better than others. For it is necessary that they be keenly...

...perceive and understand harmonies and rhythms. For how else will anyone recognize the **correctness** of a song <note>original: "cantus" — refers to both the melody and the poetic meter</note>, seeing whether it fits or not with the **Dorian mode** <note>The Dorian mode was considered by Greeks like Plato to be the most masculine, stable, and educationally sound musical scale</note> and the rhythm the poet assigned it? Has he joined them correctly or not? 

CLINIAS: Certainly in no way at all. 

ATHENIAN: The common people, however, are quite laughable when they think they are capable of knowing what is a good harmony or rhythm and what is not. They are merely forced to follow the song and the rhythm; but since they are ignorant of what is actually happening in each of these parts, they do not know how they are made correctly. For any song, if it contains all the elements that fit it, is correct; if it does not, it is the opposite. 

CLINIAS: This is necessarily so. 

ATHENIAN: What then? If someone does not understand the reason for a thing or what it contains, will he ever recognize in what way it is "correct," as we said? 

CLINIAS: How could that be possible? 

ATHENIAN: We seem to have discovered this now: that those senior singers whom we earlier provoked—somewhat against their will—to sing gladly, must have learned these things to such a degree that each of them can follow the movements and weights of rhythms as well as the harmonic sounds of the lyre. This is so that, by understanding harmonies and rhythms, they may be able to choose those songs which are fitting for men of such age and character to sing. In doing so, they themselves may immediately perceive innocent pleasures and lead the youth toward **upright morals** by means of these songs and delights. Having been taught to this extent, they will possess a discipline more refined than that of the common people and even the poets themselves. 

The third thing—whether an imitation is good or bad—is not something the poet *must* know; however, it is necessary for him to know harmony and rhythm. But these [the senior singers] must know all three, so they can choose the best and the second best. Otherwise, they will never be able to sufficiently entice the souls of the youth toward virtue, as if by certain incantations. Indeed, what we intended from the beginning—to offer our discourse as an aid to the "Chorus of Dionysus"—has been said to the best of our ability. But let us consider if this has truly been done. Such a gathering of men necessarily becomes more turbulent as the drinking progresses. We assumed from the start that this necessarily happens in the practices of today. 

CLINIAS: It is necessary. 

ATHENIAN: Where certainly everyone, becoming lighter in spirit than himself, is uplifted and exults; he is filled with audacity and does not listen to his neighbor, but considers himself a sufficient leader of both himself and all others. 

CLINIAS: Without a doubt. 

ATHENIAN: Did we not say that whenever these things happen, the souls of the drinkers—

<margin>Just as iron is softened by fire, so the bodies of the elderly are softened by wine.</margin>

—become like iron in the fire? They become warmer, softer, and more youthful; and therefore they are more easily led, just as they were when they were young, if someone is both able and knows how to instruct and mold them. The "molder" would be that same man who was then called the **upright legislator**. Laws must prescribe the manner of the drinking party so that they can restrain the man who has become bold and more impudent than is fitting—who does not want to observe the order of silence, speech, drinking, and music in his turn. The laws should instruct him to act contrary to his current impulses, applying the "best fear" along with justice against his rising and shameful confidence. This "divine fear" we have named **shame and modesty** <note>original: "pudorem & verecundiam"</note>. 

CLINIAS: It is as you say. 

ATHENIAN: The authors and guardians of these laws must be removed from disturbance and drunkenness; they are the leaders of the wine-drinkers. Without them, it is as hard to fight against drunkenness as it is to fight against enemies without sober leaders. If anyone refuses to obey these men, or the leaders of Dionysus who are over sixty years old, he should suffer a disgrace equal to or even greater than one who does not obey the generals of Mars [War]. 

CLINIAS: Correct. 

ATHENIAN: If such drunkenness and such play were employed, would not the drinkers gain great utility from it? Would they not depart joined in greater mutual benevolence than before—not as enemies as they do now—since they had conversed legitimately and, though intoxicated, had obeyed the laws under sober leaders? 

CLINIAS: Certainly so, if the drunkenness were such as you have just described. 

ATHENIAN: Therefore, let us not simply disparage this present gift of **Liber** <note>Liber is the Roman name for the Greek god Dionysus</note> as if it were an evil thing, or unworthy to be received into the city. Indeed, many more things could be said in favor of this view; yet I fear to bring up the greatest good that Dionysus bestows before the many, for when men hear it, they may not receive it correctly or understand it. 

CLINIAS: What is that? 

ATHENIAN: A certain rumor and report has flowed down to us that this god was once driven out of his mind by his stepmother Hera, and that out of a desire for revenge he introduced the **Bacchic dance** <note>original: "bacchationis choream" — referring to the ecstatic, often wild dancing associated with Dionysus</note> and all madness, and gave wine for this very purpose. For my part, I leave these stories to those who think it safe to say such things about the gods. This much I do know: no animal is born with as much intelligence as it is fitting for it to have when it reaches maturity. During that time in which it does not yet possess its wisdom, it rages entirely; it cries out without order and, elate with pride, it leaps about wantonly. Let us remember that we said these were the principles of **Music and Gymnastics**. 

CLINIAS: We remember. 

ATHENIAN: Did we not also say that the sense of rhythm and harmony was given to us alone? And that **Apollo**, the **Muses**, and **Dionysus** were granted to us as leaders for these things? 

CLINIAS: Truly. 

ATHENIAN: 

<margin>Why wine was given to men.</margin>

Wine, as many say, was given to men for revenge, so that they might go mad. But as our discourse has it, it is a **remedy and medicine** for the opposite: so that the soul may gain modesty, and the body may gain health and strength. 

CLINIAS: You have excellently recalled your previous argument, guest. 

ATHENIAN: But now half of what pertains to the **chorea** <note>The "chorea" or dance/chorus refers to the combined education of song and movement</note> has been said. Shall we complete the remaining part, or let it pass? 

CLINIAS: What parts—

<margin>The whole dance/chorus and its parts.</margin>

—do you mean, and how do you divide them? 

ATHENIAN: Indeed, the whole *chorea* has been described by us as the entirety of education. One part of the *chorea* is in the **voice**, through rhythms and harmonies. 

CLINIAS: That is so. 

ATHENIAN: The other part is in the **movement of the body**, through rhythm and figure. Rhythm is common to both the movement of the voice and the body, but "figure" <note>original: "figura" — the specific poses or gestures in dance</note> is proper to the body. In that first part, the song itself is the movement of the voice. 

CLINIAS: You speak the truth. 

ATHENIAN: But the training of the voice, which leads to the virtue of the soul, we have somehow named **Music**. 

CLINIAS: Quite correctly. 

ATHENIAN: If, however, the movement of the body in play—which we have called **Dance**—leads to the virtue of the body...

### ARGUMENT OF DIALOGUE III ON THE LAWS.
O.iiii.

<meta>catchword: Inestimable</meta>

touches upon it, let me call this skillful leading of the soul toward that end "gymnastics" <note>In the Platonic sense, gymnastics refers not just to athletics, but to the disciplined training of the body to serve the soul.</note>. CLINIAS: Most correctly. ATHENIAN: Regarding music indeed, which we said was the middle part of the chorus, let us consider it sufficiently dealt with, and so let it be spoken of. Therefore, let us now speak of the remainder, or what must be done. CLINIAS: O best of men, you who converse with Cretans and Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, since music has now been sufficiently treated but gymnastics hardly at all, what do you think either of us would answer to such a question? ATHENIAN: I would affirm that you, by asking this, have already answered clearly. For I understand that your question is a kind of answer, as I said, and at the same time a command to finish those matters pertaining to gymnastics. CLINIAS: You have understood perfectly; so please do so. ATHENIAN: It must be done. Nor is it difficult to finish things that are very well known to both of you. Truly, you are both much more skilled in this art than in the former one. CLINIAS: You speak almost the truth. ATHENIAN: Is not the beginning of this play <note>original: "ludi" — referring to the "play" or "game" of the dialogue and cultural education</note> also this: that every animal is accustomed by nature to leap? But man, as we touched upon, when he received a sense of rhythm, gave birth to dancing. Song, likewise, awakens rhythm. Both of these joined together gave birth to the chorus and the play. CLINIAS: It is so. ATHENIAN: One part of this we have already completed; the other we shall next approach. CLINIAS: By all means. ATHENIAN: Let us therefore first conclude the discussion on the "chorus of drunkenness" <note>The Athenian refers to regulated drinking parties as a form of social "choreography" or training</note> with this opinion, if you please. CLINIAS: In what way? ATHENIAN: If a city uses drinking parties as a serious matter and according to the order of laws, for the sake of a certain exercise in temperance, and does not flee other pleasures but exercises in the same way to overcome them, then they should be used in this manner by all. But if a city uses drinking parties as mere play, and anyone is allowed to drink whenever they want and with whomever they want, and to practice any other lust, I would not be of the opinion that it is becoming for that city or this man to ever indulge in drunkenness. Rather, I would much more approve of the Carthaginian law over the custom of the Cretans and Spartans. <margin>The custom of the Carthaginians regarding wine.</margin> This law states that no one should ever dare to taste wine in a military camp, but should drink water during that whole time; and in the city, I would never grant the use of wine to a male or female slave. Nor to magistrates during the whole time they are performing their office. I would also entirely prohibit pilots and judges who are about to perform their duties from wine. Also those about to deliberate on matters that are not entirely negligible. And I would grant wine to no one at all during the day, unless it were necessary to drink for the sake of physical exercise or illnesses; nor even at night to a man or woman when they intend to apply themselves to procreating children. Many other instances could be cited in which men who possess a right law and mind would abstain from wine. Therefore, according to this reasoning, a city would not need many vineyards. Furthermore, other agriculture and the whole standard of living would keep its own order; and the use of wine would be almost the most moderate and sparing of all. Here then, guests, if it seems right to you as well, let the crown be placed upon our discourse concerning wine. CLINIAS: Well said. Therefore, it seems so to us as well.

->**The Argument of Marsilio Ficino for the Third Dialogue on the Laws.**<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a classical figure (possibly a scholar or deity) seated within the letter's frame, surrounded by architectural and floral motifs.</image-desc>

**Just** as a doctor looks to the health of the body, so the author of laws looks to the health of the soul. Since it is more desirable for everyone to retain prosperous health so that it is not lost, than to recover it when it is perishing, therefore the principal aim of both the statesman and the doctor is to preserve the health of the body or the soul. The secondary aim of both seems to be best if they restore the condition to the body or soul if it has ever been lost. For which reason, both in Plato and in truth, those writers of laws are judged to be held in contempt who suddenly decree by what census <note>original: "censura" — here meaning judgment or punishment</note> crimes already committed are to be punished. They do not provide for the method by which men might be so born, nourished, and educated that they would not wish to commit crimes. Therefore, let no one wonder that our Plato, being studious of the firmest health of the soul, dwells so accurately through many things that seem light—and which pertain to the education of boys and youths—both in the books of the *Laws* and the *Republic*. For thus it befits the most diligent doctor of souls to act: to so compose them immediately at birth that they may seem either to have been born together with firm health, or at least that as they grow up, the health of the soul may grow together with them. Hence comes that preceding diligence of the first and second books of the *Laws* regarding every kind of music and play, as well as banquets. For while he disputes concerning the duty of the author of laws, he judges that his principal study—namely, regarding boys and youths—must be declared before all else. Here I want you to remember with what great caution he judged the drinking of wine must be approached: that it is not permitted to drink daily, nor to just anyone, nor according to anyone's lust; but only in solemn banquets, and then indeed for men and moderately, and rarely pure wine <note>Ancient Greeks typically diluted wine with water; "pure" wine was considered dangerous</note>, yet under an arbiter and judge. Otherwise, remember also how much it is forbidden, so that it is not permitted for soldiers in camps to taste wine; nor for slaves in the city, nor for magistrates, nor for pilots and judges at the time of judgment itself; nor for men soon to deliberate on great matters; finally, neither for a man nor a woman at that hour in which they decide to apply themselves to procreating children. It will be worth the effort to have diligently commemorated these things. Let us proceed now to the proper argument of the Third Book. Since therefore the law itself is the form of "civility"—that is, of civil discipline—and civility is the form of the city, he, being about to treat of laws, not without reason disputes much concerning the beginning of the city and civility. He is uncertain, however, whether the human race has existed from eternity or not; and similarly regarding the world. And because in some places he names "infinite time," he does not properly mean without a beginning and without an end, but rather "infinite" according to our calculations; therefore he often calls time "inestimable" rather than "immense." And so in the sixth book, similarly doubting, he divides his opinion: either generation never began for man, or it began an inestimable length of time before us. Inestimable...

<meta>This page transitions from the end of the commentary on Book II into Marsilio Ficino's detailed "Argument" or summary for Book III of Plato’s Laws. It explores the origins of civilization after a great cataclysm and the central role of "Prudence" (wisdom) in governing both the individual soul and the state.</meta>

### ARGUMENT FOR THE THIRD DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS.

He speaks perhaps of something truly remarkable if someone should strive to count not only solar years, but also lunar years, and days, and hours. It should be enough for a Christian that the philosopher <note>Plato</note> did not affirm the eternity of the world. But what indeed will they say about these thousands of years mentioned by Moses? Perhaps that Plato, in the Egyptian manner, computed rather short years. But truly, both these matters and the deluges of the world <note>cataclysmic floods that periodically reset civilization</note> are more opportunely discussed in the *Timaeus* <note>Another of Plato's dialogues focused on the creation of the universe</note>. Now, however, let us return to the actual matter of the laws—that is, the city and citizenship. Four stages <note>original: "figurae"</note> of the city are often counted.

The first stage arose immediately after the calamity of the human race, in some surviving seed of it, preserved either by the benefit of the highest mountains or rather by divine providence. For then it is probable that sons and grandsons obeyed the command of the patriarch <note>original: "patrifamilias"</note>. This command indeed consists of the law of nature alone.

The second stage occurred among several families already gathered together either in a town or behind a similar rampart. I say they gathered both due to mutual need and for fear of wild beasts. But from the very beginning of this assembly, it is likely that there were as many forms of governing as there were households, differing widely among themselves in opinions and customs. Because of this diversity, and the mutual injuries that arose, they were compelled to establish certain common arbiters, judges, and rulers.

From this, the third stage of civil discipline arose, taking its origin from the preceding injustice. It is probable that such rulers of the city prescribed common laws for the state after they had considered the most honorable laws of the various households; through these, they transferred the discipline of domestic affairs to the discipline of the republic.

Finally, the fourth stage is found in a certain kingdom of nations. Here, several cities agree upon the same will and common law, just as several families did in one city.

The first stage is outside the city, consisting of individual laws, nature, reason, and will. The second is already in a city, but still through the individual laws of households, gathered by a certain need and fear. The third is in a state with common laws, cultivating justice on the occasion of injustice. The fourth is gathered from many cities through the same will and a similar law.

Amidst these things, the poets are reminded to sing of divine matters: where it is said that the race of poets is divine and is moved by God. The authors of laws are also advised: that they should not bring forth laws that are either arduous or violent, but light and, as far as possible, sweet. Furthermore, by a certain historical example, the principal purpose of this disputation is pursued: concerning the chief and best method of establishing laws. This indeed takes its beginning most strongly from this: if the author, in bringing these laws forth, looks toward the universal virtue of the citizens, but especially toward the greatest virtue of all and the leader. Truly, no one doubts that other virtues are led by Prudence <note>original: "prudentia" — practical wisdom or moral insight</note> as inferior limbs are led by the head.

He confirms that this is as necessary to us as it is noble from the fact that all men, by common wish, desire above all that all human things should succeed and be carried out according to their desire; even for him whose every wish succeeds, they judge him to be the happiest of all. Plato, however, infers the opposite: that he would be most miserable whose events daily follow his desires, unless he is endowed with such great prudence, and rules his soul with such moderation through prudence, that he discerns true goods; and having set aside other things, he seeks those which he has distinguished by reason.

In these matters, he warns that we should not wish or pray that all things follow our desire, but rather that our desire follows reason. He also touches upon the fitting comparison of a son to a father, and a father to God. Certainly, a boy wishes and prays that as many things as possible happen to him as if they were good, which the father meanwhile prays against as if they were evils. Similarly, the Heavenly Father daily detests the vain and harmful vows of men. Nor is there any refuge for us to avoid deceptive vows, except for prudence. Therefore, the lawgiver, studying public happiness, will labor primarily to propagate this prudence through the minds of the citizens. For so great is the perfection of prudence that it both teaches one to desire and acquire things worth wishing for, and to use those things acquired by that reason through which they may be beneficial. In these things, the entire happiness of the city consists.

Just as prudence preserves the city, so does imprudence—which he calls ignorance—destroy it. I do not mean ignorance of letters specifically, or of some art, or of certain external things foreign to us; but ignorance of the Good, as he often says elsewhere and signifies here. But he adds that this is the most ruinous ignorance both privately and publicly, through which one does not know how to temper his own soul so that the senses, like a lawfully educated people, obey the laws of his reason as if she were a queen; so much so that he does not pursue or flee other things, nor rejoice or grieve in others or otherwise, than the institutions of reason prescribe. Whoever is blinded by such ignorance, even if they are most gifted and most learned, are judged by Plato to be ignorant. But those who are temperate are judged by him to be prudent and knowing, even if they do not know their letters.

He then forbids that the government be granted to one who, on account of incontinence <note>lack of self-control</note>, does not know how to govern himself. Nor does he trust that a city can be correctly and happily composed under him in whose soul there is a certain city that is both disordered and miserable. Although he subsequently counts seven reasons which are judged by most to lead to the dignity of commanding—namely: Paternity, Nobility, Domination, Power, Old Age, Prudence, and Lot <note>choosing by random draw</note>—he himself chooses one above the rest: namely, Prudence. He says this is the proper reason for imperial dignity: namely, that the more prudent should everywhere command, and the less prudent should obey. Just as it is the office of the eyes to lead, and the service of the feet to proceed. Likewise, just as in any art—especially navigation, military affairs, and medicine—it is for him who understands more to command, and for him who knows less in that matter to execute; so also in the civil art, in every part, partly of the family, partly of the governing of the city, all ought especially to obey him who understands before others what most leads to human safety. The law, therefore, desiring common prudence, will provide that besides childish education contributing to prudence, the grades of public offices also follow the grades of prudence itself...

<summary>Marsilio Ficino outlines the four stages of societal development and argues that true governance must be rooted in "Prudence" (wisdom), defining ignorance not as a lack of education, but as a lack of internal harmony between reason and desire.</summary>

FO. CCCXVII.
->ON THE LAWS OR ON LEGISLATION, DIALOGUE III.<-
O.v.
<meta>catchword: THESE</meta>

distributing [power] everywhere. And lest they imprudently commit the rudders of governance to these men, he shall decree that pure and immense authority to command should not be granted. Instead, he will subject all to the laws, joining the kings with the senate, and the senate with the popular council. He will take care, above all, that a ruler—desiring to have more power than the laws allow—never brings about dissension and ruin through such excess. He will strive so that the entire body of the city may be as free, prudent, and friendly as possible. Free, so that any citizen may consult for the good of his fatherland; prudent, so that he knows how; and friendly, so that he wishes to do so. He should remember that these three things easily come together in a city that holds the middle ground between the power of a single ruler and that of the people: so that it neither subjects itself entirely to the will of one commander or the power of a few, nor receives just any consultant without choice. Instead, the government should consist mostly of the rule of the best men <note>the "optimates" or aristocracy</note>, though it should also have something of the kingly and something of the popular. 

He will examine the customs and fortunes of the leaders, by which he may foresee that the destruction of cities and kingdoms proceeds most of all from the delicate and luxurious lifestyle of young men and adults. Indeed, since no one can emerge as excellent in virtue from such a life, he necessarily becomes sickly, fragile, swollen, and blind. He shall therefore command that temperance <note>self-control or moderation</note> be most greatly cherished by all, ensuring those who are judged most temperate receive the highest honors. Nor will he allow fortitude <note>courage</note> to be possessed by anyone without temperance, as it is a thing very dangerous to the city. Furthermore, he will not allow the skill of many things to exist without justice, as it would be gravely harmful. In short, in the first grade of honor, he will place the gifts of the soul if they are mixed with temperance; beneath these, he will place the goods of the body; and he will command that external goods serve both the goods of the body and the soul. 

He will also prohibit excessive liberty and forbid excessive servitude. For excessive servitude removes friendship—that is, the goodwill of the people toward the prince and love toward the fatherland—to such an extent that for a slight cause, either the prince or the fatherland may perish. Excessive liberty, however, first produces lawlessness, then contempt for the laws, followed by frequent seditions, and finally, extreme servitude. No one should wonder that Plato here, and often elsewhere, makes much of "games," or rather the study of music; it is as if these studies are able to change character both publicly and privately for better or worse. For in that age, such study was familiar to all and practiced openly by many; and that which is done by everyone and continually has almost no less force upon the soul than the air has upon the body. Furthermore, things that are considered light by less careful physicians are judged not to be despised by Plato, the most observant physician of the human race. After this, he descends to the summary of the preceding points. In this summary, someone might perhaps read that concluding clause: *If indeed anything* <note>original: "Si vero quicq̄"</note> and what follows, in this way: "Have we contributed anything or not? Who will judge! Since all things have been said between us." But you shall see to those matters.

### THIRD DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS OR ON LEGISLATION.

<margin>On the beginning of civil discipline.</margin>
<margin>The infinite generation and corruption of cities.</margin>
<insert>THESE</insert> things indeed being so. What shall we say was the beginning of civil discipline <note>statecraft or political science</note>? Or can one not most easily look upon it from this point? CLINIAS. From where? ATHENIAN. From where the growth of cities toward both virtue and vice may also be observed. CLINIAS. Where do you mean? ATHENIAN. I believe it is from the length and infinity of time, and the mutations of things within it. CLINIAS. In what way do you say this? ATHENIAN. Come, tell me if you can grasp how great a multitude of time has passed since cities and the civil institutions of men first began. CLINIAS. That is by no means easy. ATHENIAN. It is certainly unsearchable and impossible to think. CLINIAS. It is entirely so. ATHENIAN. Have not innumerable cities been built in this time, and just as many destroyed? Have they not everywhere experienced every condition of civil life: being made sometimes smaller from larger ones, and sometimes larger from smaller ones; worse from better, and conversely, better from worse? CLINIAS. That is indeed necessary. ATHENIAN. Let us therefore think out the cause of this mutation if we can. For perhaps it will show us the first cause and change of civil life. CLINIAS. You speak well. Therefore, it is necessary for you to explain diligently what you feel about this matter, and for us to listen attentively. 

ATHENIAN. Do the ancient stories then seem to have some truth? CLINIAS. Which ones? ATHENIAN. Namely, that many destructions of men have occurred in the past from floods, diseases, and other plagues, from which only a few men remained as survivors. CLINIAS. That seems very likely to anyone. ATHENIAN. Come now, let us look at one of these many destructions—the one caused by the flood <note>original: "illuuione"</note>. CLINIAS. What do you wish us to think about this? ATHENIAN. Surely those who escaped the slaughter then were certain mountain-dwellers and shepherds: a few small seeds of humanity preserved on the peaks of mountains to propagate the human race. CLINIAS. That is evident. ATHENIAN. And yet it is necessary that they were both unskilled in other arts and ignorant of the pursuits of greed and contention among citizens, and other such craftiness against others. CLINIAS. That is indeed consistent. ATHENIAN. Let us also assume that the cities of the plains and the coast perished in that sudden time. CLINIAS. I will assume it. ATHENIAN. Therefore, we shall assert that all instruments and whatever arts belonged either to civil discipline or to any other faculty that had been discovered, fell away in those times. For, O best of men, if these things had remained forever as they are now, how would anything new ever have been invented by anyone? CLINIAS. Surely because an incalculable multitude of years was unknown to them. However, one thousand or two thousand years from the time anything was said to be invented were revealed partly by Daedalus <note>legendary inventor</note>, partly by Orpheus <note>mythical musician</note>, and partly by Palamedes. Just as those things pertaining to music are attributed to Marsyas and Olympus; those pertaining to the lyre to Amphion; and many other things to others, so to speak.

BOOK III. ON LAWS.
