**ATHENIAN.** Do you see, Clinias, that you have overlooked a friend of yours who was truly a man of "yesterday"? 
**CLINIAS.** Do you mean Epimenides? <note>Epimenides was a legendary Cretan seer and philosopher who supposedly slept for 57 years; he was considered a contemporary "wonder-worker" compared to the ancient figures they are discussing.</note> 
**ATHENIAN.** Him indeed. For he, my friend, far excelled everyone among you in the invention of new things. What Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet.</note> once divined in words long ago, Epimenides actually brought to fulfillment in reality, as you Cretans claim. 
**CLINIAS.** We certainly do claim that. 
**ATHENIAN.** We believe, then, that a great and terrible desolation of human affairs occurred at the time of that ancient devastation <note>Referring to the Great Flood (the Deluge), which Plato suggests wiped out previous civilizations.</note>. The vast fertility of the fields was left abandoned; and since most other animals perished, barely any genus of oxen or goats remained—and those were rare—upon which men then lived as they led their lives as shepherds. 
**CLINIAS.** Who could doubt it? 
**ATHENIAN.** Indeed, do we suppose that any memory at all remained of the city, of civil discipline, or of the laws about which our current conversation is held? 
**CLINIAS.** None at all. 
**ATHENIAN.** And is it not from those people, so disposed, that all these things have come to us: cities, civil disciplines, arts, laws, and a great abundance of both vice and virtue? 
**CLINIAS.** How do you mean? 
**ATHENIAN.** Do we imagine, O wonderful man, that those people—who were ignorant of the many things, both honorable and shameful, that exist among citizens—could have reached the heights of either virtue or vice? 
**CLINIAS.** You have spoken well; we understand what you mean. 
**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, as time progressed and the human race multiplied, all things were brought to the state we see now. 
**CLINIAS.** Quite right. 
**ATHENIAN.** Yet, this likely did not happen suddenly, but gradually over a long period of time. 
**CLINIAS.** That is very fitting. 
**ATHENIAN.** For a fresh dread prevented them from descending from the mountain peaks into the plains. 
**CLINIAS.** Certainly. 
**ATHENIAN.** And because they were so few in those times, were they not delighted to see one another? Especially since travel to others, whether by land or sea, was not easy, as almost all tools for transport had been destroyed along with the arts? Consequently, they could not easily meet one another. For iron, bronze, and all metals had perished in the confusion, so that they could not be found or extracted into the light. Thus, there were no woodworkers. For even if some tool had been left behind on the mountains, it soon wore out and vanished, and no others could be made until the art of metalworking was discovered by men again. 
**CLINIAS.** How indeed could it have been otherwise? 
**ATHENIAN.** And after how many generations do we think that occurred? 
**CLINIAS.** Surely after many. 
**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, all the arts that use iron and bronze and other such things were unknown for the same period—or rather, for an even longer time—shrouded in the darkness of ignorance. 
**CLINIAS.** That is certain. 
**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, in that time, there was neither sedition <note>Internal civil conflict or rebellion.</note> nor war. 
**CLINIAS.** For what reason? 
**ATHENIAN.** First, because of their isolation, they embraced one another with ardent goodwill. Second, food did not provoke war. For there was no shortage of pastures, except perhaps for a few at the beginning. In those times, they lived mostly on the products of their pastures. Likewise, there was no lack of milk and meat. Moreover, hunting provided them with food—and not of a bad sort. Furthermore, they had an abundance of clothing, bedding, dwellings, and vessels, both those made with fire and those without. For the arts of pottery and weaving do not require iron; by God’s will, we possess these so that if humans ever fall into such a calamity, <margin>They also could not become wealthy.</margin> they might be able to propagate the human race. For this reason, they were not very poor, nor did poverty drive them to war. They could by no means become wealthy either, since they had neither gold nor silver. In whatever assembly of men there is neither poverty nor riches, there the most just customs will be found. For there, neither insolence nor injury has a place; rivalry and envy are also far away. For these reasons, they were good men—and especially because of their simplicity. For whatever they heard was honorable or shameful, they believed to be true because of their simplicity and obeyed those warnings. No one suspected a lie because of a "reputation for wisdom," as is common now; rather, believing the things said about gods and men to be true, they ordered their lives in tranquility according to them. Therefore, they were entirely such as we described just a moment ago. 
**CLINIAS.** Both I and my companion here <note>Megillus the Spartan.</note> agree with you on these points. 
**ATHENIAN.** We have said, then, that many generations living in this way had less skill—both compared to those who lived before the deluge and to men today—not only in other arts but also in the arts of war, which are practiced today by land or sea. They also lacked the skill in legal judgments and seditions, which men now diligently pursue in cities with both words and deeds to inflict injury on others. Yet they were simpler and braver, and at the same time more modest and more just in all things. We have already stated the cause of these things. 
**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly. 
**ATHENIAN.** Let these things be settled for us then; and let everything that follows be set forth so that we may understand why they had need of laws, and who established laws for them. 
**CLINIAS.** You have spoken well. 
**ATHENIAN.** Did they then have no need of lawgivers, nor had it yet become customary in those times for such to exist? For the men of that time did not yet have writing, but lived following the customs and manners of their ancestors. 
**CLINIAS.** That is likely. 
**ATHENIAN.** But what was the mode of their civil discipline? 
**CLINIAS.** Which mode? 
**ATHENIAN.** It seems to me that everyone calls the civil discipline of that time "authority" <note>Specifically *dynasteia*, or a system of hereditary power within a family group.</note>; it still flourishes in many places today among both Greeks and barbarians, and Homer testifies that it existed in the habitation of the Cyclopes, saying:
*They have no deliberative assemblies,*
*nor our customs of legal judgments.*
*But they inhabit hollow caves on high mountains;*
*Despising public affairs, each one gives laws*
*privately to his wives and children.*
**CLINIAS.** This poet seems to have been pleasant to you. We too have run through some of his other works, which are very refined; however, not many. For we Cretans do not use foreign poetry much. 
**MEGILLUS.** But we Spartans do use him. And it seems to us that he surpassed other poets of this kind, for he teaches the Ionian life almost everywhere rather than the Laconian <note>Spartan.</note>. Yet he seems to testify well to your words just now, since he reduced the antiquity of men through fables to a rustic way of living. 
**ATHENIAN.** He certainly testifies to it. Therefore, led by his testimony, let us believe that such forms of government once existed. 
**MEGILLUS.** Rightly so. 
**ATHENIAN.** Do not these governments arise from those very men who live scattered through individual dwellings and individual families because of the poverty caused by the devastations? Among them, the eldest always rules, because the principle of authority comes from one’s...

## ON LAWS, OR ON THE GREEK LAWS, DIALOGUE III.

...taken from father and mother: whom they followed like birds, forming one flock, using the will of the father as law, and governed most justly by the kingship of all. **MEGILLUS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** Afterward, many flowing together in common established larger cities: and turning first to agriculture at the foothills of the mountains, they built stone enclosures like city walls for protection against wild beasts, establishing one large and common house. **MEGILLUS.** That seems very likely. **ATHENIAN.** And what of this? For the sacred walls had not yet been erected in the plains to stand as a city of many peoples. But they dwelt at the foot of Mount Ida, near its springs." Indeed, these songs and those earlier ones about the Cyclopes were written by divine inspiration and according to nature itself. For the race of poets is divine: they are moved by the gods and sing sacred hymns. <margin>Poets are commended.</margin> Whence, with the Muses and the Graces, they often touch upon the truth. **MEGILLUS.** Very much so. **ATHENIAN.** Let us therefore follow this excellent story. For perhaps something from it will reveal what we desire. Or should we not do so? **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** We learn then that Ilium <note>Another name for Troy.</note> was founded, coming down from the higher places into a large and beautiful plain, on a certain hill that was not high: where many rivers flowed down from Ida above. **MEGILLUS.** So it is handed down. **ATHENIAN.** Do we not think this happened a long time after the flood? **MEGILLUS.** Who would not think so? **ATHENIAN.** A great forgetfulness of that devastation seems to have seized them, when they built a city near many rivers flowing from the higher places, and trusted themselves to small hills. From this, it is clear that they lived many centuries after the vastness of the flood. Furthermore, many other cities were already inhabited then, as the race of men had spread further. **MEGILLUS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Which cities also fought against Ilium. And perhaps by sea: as if everyone now used the sea without fear. **MEGILLUS.** It appears so. **ATHENIAN.** Moreover, after ten years, the Achaeans <note>The Greeks who fought in the Trojan War.</note> overthrew Troy. **MEGILLUS.** Plainly. **ATHENIAN.** In that decade during which Troy was besieged, many evils happened at home to the besieging Achaeans because of the seditions of the youth; they did not receive the returning soldiers honorably or justly, but in such a way that many were killed and many were sent into exile. Those who were driven out returned later, led back and called "Dorians" instead of Achaeans: named after a certain Dorus, by whom the exiles were gathered and restored. <margin>The origin of the Dorians.</margin> And all these things, O Megillus, you Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans.</note> relate from your own history. **MEGILLUS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** Although our conversation was intended to be about laws, we digressed into a discussion of music and drunkenness. Now at last, as if by divine providence, the discourse has returned to the same point and has, in a way, provided us with handles. For it has drifted down to that civil discipline which you claim was rightly established by brotherly laws in both Lacedaemon and Crete. We have gained so much from this digression that, while we were being carried through civil disciplines and the habitations of cities, we have observed the first, second, and third city, each depending on the other over a very long span of time, as our opinion holds. Now, this fourth city comes to us—or if you prefer, this fourth race of men—which once lived somewhere and lives now. If from all these we can understand what was established well or poorly in their habitation, and what laws preserve what they preserve, and what things corrupted destroy them, and what change of civil institutions makes a city happy, O Megillus and Clinias, we shall consider ourselves satisfied. All these things, I say, must be treated by us again as if from the beginning, unless perhaps we reject what has been said in some way. **MEGILLUS.** If some god were to promise us, stranger, that if we undertook the discussion of the laying down of laws again, we would hear things neither fewer nor worse than what has been said, I would myself make a long journey for this reason; and this day would seem short to me, even though it now turns from the summer solstice toward the winter days. **ATHENIAN.** It seems these things must be considered then? **MEGILLUS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us finally grasp in our thought those times in which Lacedaemon, Argos, and Messene, and all things connected to them, were subject to your ancestors, Megillus. For then it pleased them, as the story goes, to divide the army into three parts and inhabit three cities: Argos, Messene, and Lacedaemon. **MEGILLUS.** So it was done. **ATHENIAN.** And indeed Temenus was made king of Argos; Cresphontes of Messene; and Eurysthenes and Patrocles together of Lacedaemon. **MEGILLUS.** So it was. **ATHENIAN.** They all likewise swore that they would resist anyone who attempted to devastate the kingdom of another. **MEGILLUS.** Plainly. **ATHENIAN.** Tell me then, by Jove, is any kingdom or sovereignty ever put down, or has it ever been put down by others than themselves? ->LIBER<-
<meta>Catchword: remus</meta>

...remember <note>original: "meminerimus," the first syllable of which appeared on the previous page</note>, we thought it was so; now we have forgotten entirely. **MEGILLUS.** Not at all. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we not now confirm the same even more from the history of deeds we have come upon? For we are prompted to affirm this by the history of the things done. Therefore, we shall not let our discourse revolve around something vain, since we are speaking of a true and historical event. These are the facts: Three kingdoms and three cities governed by kings swore mutual oaths under laws established for both ruling and obeying. The kings swore that they would not rule more violently as their lineage and time progressed; the people swore that if the kings kept their commands, the people would never depose them from the throne; indeed, they would defend them if anyone ever attacked. The kings also swore to other kings and peoples, and likewise the peoples to other peoples and kings, that they would mutually repel any injuries inflicted upon them. Is it not so? **MEGILLUS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Now, regarding what is most important in establishing civil discipline: whether kings or others brought the laws, that principle was present in those three cities. **MEGILLUS.** What was that? **ATHENIAN.** That two cities together would rise against any one city that transgressed the established laws. **MEGILLUS.** That is certainly clear. **ATHENIAN.** Many people also instruct lawmakers to bring forth laws of such a kind that the multitude and the people will willingly accept them—just as if one were to instruct gymnastic masters or doctors to care for bodies with pleasure and to heal them agreeably. **MEGILLUS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** However, it is often sufficient if someone restores a good condition and health to bodies with only a little discomfort. **MEGILLUS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, they had this advantage, which was of no small help in making the bringing of laws easy. **MEGILLUS.** What was that? **ATHENIAN.** Those lawmakers, in creating an equality of goods, did not face that greatest difficulty which usually happens to many cities when they come together under one law: if they seek to disturb the possession of lands and introduce the <term>cancellation of debts</term> <note>original: "novas tabulas," literally 'new tablets,' a Roman term for debt cancellation</note>, because they see that equality cannot be sufficiently achieved without these things. For against anyone who attempts to move any of these things, everyone cries out that one should not move what ought not to be moved. Indeed, they openly curse anyone dividing lands and introducing the cancellation of debts, so that a person does not know which way to turn. But for the <term>Dorians</term> <note>The group of Greeks who traditionally conquered the Peloponnese, including the ancestors of the Spartans</note>, this difficulty and disturbance did not exist. For they possessed lands in abundance without controversy, and their ancient and large debts of money were not great. **MEGILLUS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Why then, best of men, did that constitution and legislation turn out so badly for them? **MEGILLUS.** In what way? What do you find fault with? **ATHENIAN.** Because out of the three city constitutions, two quickly betrayed both their civil discipline and their laws, and only your city [Sparta] was left as one. **MEGILLUS.** What you ask is not easy to answer. **ATHENIAN.** And yet it is necessary that we consider this now, and—treating the laws with a certain modest, old-man’s playfulness—complete this journey without trouble, just as we said from the beginning. **MEGILLUS.** Without a doubt, it must be done as you say. **ATHENIAN.** Can we have a more beautiful consideration of laws than concerning those laws which adorned cities such as these? Or can we think of any cities or institutions more honorable and greater than these? **MEGILLUS.** It would not be easy for anyone to prefer others to these. **ATHENIAN.** No one will doubt that those people, being so joined together, believed they could defend not only the Peloponnese but all of Greece, if any barbarian intended an injury. They were warned by the example of the Trojans, who, relying on the power of the <term>Assyrians</term> <note>In Plato's view, Troy was part of the Assyrian Empire founded by the legendary King Ninus</note> which took its origin from Ninus, had stirred up war against them. For the power of that empire was still not to be looked down upon. Therefore, just as we now dread the Great King [of Persia], so everyone then was terrified of the power of those nations conspiring together as one. The second destruction of Troy provided a great accusation against them. For the power of Troy was a certain small part of the Assyrian empire. Against that power, therefore, the army divided into three cities—led by the brothers who were the sons of Hercules <note>The <term>Heraclidae</term>, or descendants of Hercules, who led the Dorian invasion</note>, then reigning—seemed best and most excellently formed, and much better equipped than the army that besieged Troy. For first, they judged they had more excellent leaders in the Heraclidae than in the <term>Pelopidae</term> <note>The house of Pelops, including Agamemnon and Menelaus, who led the Greeks at Troy</note>. Second, they believed this army excelled in virtue over the one that sought Troy. For these men were the victors, and those [the Achaeans] had been overcome by these men, the Dorians. Do we not believe they thought this way, and for that reason prepared themselves so? **MEGILLUS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** It is likely, therefore, they thought this constitution of theirs would be firm and endure for a long time, especially because they underwent many dangers and labors together, and were governed by brothers who were kings. Moreover, they had consulted many prophets, both others and the Delphic Apollo. **MEGILLUS.** Very likely. **ATHENIAN.** But these things, which they thought would be greatest, vanished in a short time, as it seems—except for that small part, as we just said, which inhabits your region [Sparta]. This part has never ceased from war against the other two parts even to this day. For if the constitution made then had remained in harmony, it would surely have been invincible in war. **MEGILLUS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** How then, and by what reason, was it dissolved? Is it not worth considering what kind of fortune overthrew such a great constitution? **MEGILLUS.** Surely, if someone ignores these things, they will never be able to understand other laws or republics by which great and beautiful things are preserved or, conversely, destroyed. **ATHENIAN.** We seem, then, to have fortunately stumbled upon this sufficient consideration. **MEGILLUS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Does not our error then escape us all, and especially at present, while we think we perceive a singular thing from which wonderful events will follow, if only someone knows how to use it in the proper way? But perhaps we do not feel correctly or according to nature about this very thing; and all others err in everything about which they think similarly. **MEGILLUS.** What are you saying? And about what matter do you say this especially? **ATHENIAN.** I was certainly mocking myself just now, my good man. For when I considered that army of which we just spoke, it seemed to me truly excellent and wonderful, and destined to perform noble deeds for the Greeks if someone had then used it well. **MEGILLUS.** Did you not speak prudently, and did we not praise you well? **ATHENIAN.**

FO. CCCXIX.

### ON THE LAWS, OR THE DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, BOOK III.

**ATHENIAN.** Perhaps I think that everyone who sees something great and endowed with immense power immediately feels that if the possessor knew how to use such a great thing, they would be happy through many famous deeds achieved by it. **MEGILLUS.** Is this not right? Or how do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Consider now toward what such a person is looking when they praise each thing correctly. First, regarding what I was saying: if those who were then in charge had known correctly how to organize the army, would they not have used the opportunity successfully? If they had established it more securely at that time, would they not have preserved it forever? Thus, they themselves would be free, and they would have subjugated others as they wished; and altogether, they and their descendants would have obtained whatever they desired among both Greeks and barbarians. Did they not desire everything for the sake of this? **MEGILLUS.** Indeed, very much so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, whoever looks upon immense wealth, or the excellent honors of noble birth, or anything of that kind, says the same things, looking toward this: as if through this, all the things he desires, or at least the most important ones, will come to pass for him. **MEGILLUS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** There is certainly one common desire of all men, which the present discourse has signified. **MEGILLUS.** Which is that? **ATHENIAN.** That all things, or at least human affairs, be conducted according to the desire of one's own soul. **MEGILLUS.** Who could doubt it? **ATHENIAN.** Since we all always want this, in childhood, adulthood, and old age, we undoubtedly pray diligently to have it. **MEGILLUS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** We also pray for these things for our friends, which they would also pray for themselves. **MEGILLUS.** This too. **ATHENIAN.** And a son is a friend to his father—a boy to a man. **MEGILLUS.** Assuredly. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, the father prays that many of those things which the boy prays might happen to him, should instead *not* happen. <margin>One should not pray that all things follow our will, but that our will follows our wisdom.</margin> **MEGILLUS.** Do you mean that this happens when the son who prays is young and foolish? **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, even when the father—whether old or quite young—knows nothing of what is honorable or just, and is affected as Theseus was toward the unfortunate Hippolytus <note>In Greek mythology, Theseus used a divine curse against his son Hippolytus based on a false accusation; the Athenian is warning that unguided desires, even those of a parent, can be destructive.</note>, he prays too vehemently, while the son, on the other hand, knows better. Do you think then that the son will pray for the same things as the father? **MEGILLUS.** I understand what you are saying. For you seem to me to be saying that we should not pray or strive for all things to follow our will, but rather that our will should follow our wisdom. And that this must be sought through prayers and studied by both the city and individuals: that they possess a mind. <margin>Wisdom is the leader of the rest.</margin> **ATHENIAN.** That is exactly it, I say. Furthermore, that a statesman and a lawmaker must always look to these things when bringing forth laws—I have remembered this myself, and now I want you to remember it. For at the beginning of the discussion, you were saying that a good lawmaker ought to refer all things to war. I, however, said that he should look toward only one virtue—though there are four—and that he should look not to one alone, but to all, and especially to the first, which is the leader of all the others. This is wisdom <term>prudentia: often translated as practical wisdom or foresight</term>, and intellect, and right opinion, together with the love and desire that follow them. Our discourse now returns to the same point. And I, who said those things then, say the same things now, whether you wish to take them in jest or in earnest. I assert, indeed, that it is not safe to use a prayer and to obtain what you pray for if you do not have a mind; rather, it is better that the opposite of what you ask for should happen. If you wish to consider these words spoken in earnest, then do so. For I hope now to persuade you of what we proposed a little while ago: that the cause of the ruin of the kings and the dissolution of that entire constitution was not cowardice, nor ignorance of military matters by either the leaders or the subjects, but general wickedness, and especially the greatest ignorance regarding the most important human affairs. I will try, as the reasoning hereafter will show, to discover how these things happened then, and if they happen anywhere now or will happen in the future, they would not occur differently; and I will explain it to you as friends, to the best of my ability. **CLINIAS.** To praise you with words, stranger, is troublesome; but we shall praise you greatly in deed. For we will gladly receive your words, because in this matter, there is a certain liberal praise that is not widely recognized. **ATHENIAN.** You speak excellently, Clinias. Therefore, let us do what you say. **CLINIAS.** It shall be so, if God wills. Just speak. <margin>If the gods <note>original: "d[e]i"</note> will it.</margin> **ATHENIAN.** We think then, proceeding through the following path of this discussion, that that great power was ruined by the greatest ignorance, and that similar outcomes of events proceed even now from the same cause. For this reason, if this is the case, the legislator ought to try, as far as possible, to give wisdom to the citizens and to take away ignorance as much as he can. **CLINIAS.** That is certainly manifest. **ATHENIAN.** What then may rightly be called the "greatest ignorance"? <margin>What is the greatest ignorance of citizens?</margin> Consider if you agree with me. For I judge it to be this. **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** When someone does not love, but hates, what seems honorable or good to him; and when he loves and embraces what is evil and unjust. I assert that this discord of pleasure and pain against the opinion that follows reason is the extreme ignorance. I also call it the greatest because it resides in the multitude of the soul. For that part of the soul which is enslaved to pains and pleasures is like the common people and the multitude of a city. Therefore, when the soul opposes knowledge, or opinion, or reason—which by nature should rule—I call this ignorance: both of the city, when the multitude does not obey the leaders and the laws, and of a single man, when, although there are good reasons in the soul, nothing is done according to them, but everything is performed to the contrary. I assert that these kinds of ignorance are the most destructive for a city and for any citizen; but I do not mean the ignorance of craftsmen—if you understand what I am saying, strangers. **CLINIAS.** We understand these things, O friend, and we grant them. **ATHENIAN.** Let it be held as settled, then, that nothing pertaining to leadership should be entrusted to citizens who are ignorant in this way; rather, they must be reproved as ignorant even if they are the sharpest and most eloquent, and have mastered everything pertaining to the ornament and sharpness of genius. But those who are affected in the opposite way should be considered wise, even if they (as the saying goes) neither know their letters nor how to swim. <margin>Proverb: Neither knows letters nor how to swim.</margin> Magistracies should be entrusted to these men as to the wise. For how, O friends, could even the smallest appearance of wisdom exist without harmony? **CLINIAS.** In no way. **ATHENIAN.** But truly, the most beautiful and greatest of all harmonies may rightly be called the greatest wisdom. He who would live according to reason must necessarily participate in this. But whoever is devoid of it is both a destroyer of his own house and never a preserver of the city, but instead is always entirely ignorant regarding these matters...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that the collapse of states is caused by "the greatest ignorance"—a discord where a person's desires and pleasures override their rational judgment—and insists that only those with internal harmony between reason and will should hold office.</summary>

...he will see it to be so. Therefore, as we said a little while ago, let these things be as they are. **CLINIAS.** Exactly. **ATHENIAN.** Now, there must be rulers and subjects in cities. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Very well. But what are the claims to the right of ruling and obeying, and how many are there, alike in large and small cities as well as in private households? Is not the first right and claim that of fathers and mothers, and simply of parents everywhere to rule over their offspring? **CLINIAS.** Very much so. **ATHENIAN.** The second: that the noble-born rule over the low-born? The third: that the older rule over the younger? **CLINIAS.** That too. **ATHENIAN.** The fourth: that masters rule over slaves? **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** The fifth: that the stronger rule, and the weaker serve? **CLINIAS.** You have just described a very necessary form of rule. **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, it is the most prevalent, and is found among all animals "according to nature," as <note>Pindar was a famous Greek lyric poet who argued that "Law is the king of all," often interpreted as the right of the stronger.</note> Pindar of Thebes says. But the sixth claim, and the greatest, is that which commands the ignorant to follow and the wise to lead and rule. And this, O most wise Pindar, I would affirm is not against nature, but is the very "natural law" itself—willingly accepted and not achieved by violence. **CLINIAS.** Well said. **ATHENIAN.** Let us bring forward a seventh kind of rule, which is decided by the lot <note>Choosing leaders by "the lot" (random draw) was considered a way of letting the gods or "Divine Chance" decide, a common practice in Athenian democracy.</note>, asserting that it happens by some grace of God and good fortune: and we deem it most just that he whom the lot selects should rule, and he whom it rejects should obey. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth.

<margin>
The seven claims to the right of ruling.
</margin>

**ATHENIAN.** We shall say then, as a sort of joke, to one of those who easily take up the task of making laws: "Do you see, O lawmaker, how many claims to authority there are concerning rulers? And how they are opposed to one another? Truly, we have now found a fountain of seditions <note>A "fountain of seditions" refers to the civil unrest that occurs when different groups claim the right to rule based on conflicting principles (e.g., birth vs. strength vs. wisdom).</note> against which you must guard." First, therefore, consider carefully with us what went wrong: how the kings of the Peloponnese, by acting poorly in these matters, destroyed their own harvest of the fields and, at the same time, their own power and the power of the Greeks, which was then wonderful. Did they not ignore that most correct saying of <note>Hesiod was an early Greek poet. The "half is more than the whole" is a famous proverb about moderation.</note> Hesiod, that "the half is sometimes more than the whole"? When, evidently, grasping the whole is harmful, but the half is a moderate portion, then surely the moderate is "more" than the immoderate, insofar as the better is more than the worse. **CLINIAS.** Most correctly.

<margin>
How it is to be understood that the half is more than the whole.
</margin>

**ATHENIAN.** Do we believe this destructive tendency began in the kings first, or in the common people? **CLINIAS.** It is probable that this disease belongs mostly to kings, who live proudly because of their luxuries. **ATHENIAN.** It is clear, then, that those kings first possessed this: they wanted to have more power than the established laws allowed, and they did not remain in harmony with what they had praised in words and oaths. But this discord—which, though it is the greatest ignorance, yet appears to be wisdom—overturned everything because of error and bitter lack of proportion. **CLINIAS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** What then? Should the lawmaker have been cautious about this disease? By the gods, the recognition of this now requires no great praise for wisdom, nor is it difficult to say! But if someone had foreseen it then, he certainly would have appeared wiser to us. **MEGILLUS.** What do you mean by that? **ATHENIAN.** One may now observe, Megillus, what was done by your people <note>The Athenian is addressing Megillus, who is a Spartan (Lacedaemonian).</note> long ago, and from there understand the matter itself, and thus more easily say what ought to have been done then. **MEGILLUS.** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** It will be best done in this way. **MEGILLUS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** If someone gives a greater power to lesser things, neglecting moderation—sails to ships, food to bodies, authority to souls—all things are subverted. For things raised beyond measure become insolent; some fall into diseases, others into the "daughter of insolence," which is injustice. What then do we say? Is it not this: that there is no human soul, O dear friends, which, if it be young and subject to no law of accountability, can bear the greatest authority among men without being occupied by the extreme disease of ignorance, and incurring the hatred of its closest friends? This quickly corrupts the man himself and destroys all his strength. To guard against this, by observing moderation itself, is the work of excellent lawmakers. What was done then is easily seen now: it seems to be this. **MEGILLUS.** What exactly? **ATHENIAN.** A god, I believe, took care of you. Foreseeing the future, he established a twin generation of kings for you from a single one, and thus contracted the power more toward moderation. Furthermore, a certain human nature joined with divine powers <note>Refers to Lycurgus, the legendary Spartan lawgiver, often seen as semi-divine.</note>, seeing your authority swelling with pride, joined the moderate strength of those who are in the judicial forum with the power of the proud nobility, making the vote of the twenty-eight <note>The *Gerousia*, or Council of Elders, consisting of 28 men over the age of 60 plus the two kings.</note> equal to the power of the kings in the greatest matters. To these, a third savior appeared: who, seeing the authority still luxuriating and raging, threw a bridle upon it—the authority of the <term>Ephors</term> <note>The Ephors were five annually elected magistrates in Sparta who held power even over the kings, acting as a final check on their authority.</note>, chosen by lot. By this reasoning, your kingdom, composed of the proper elements and moderately established, was itself preserved and became the cause of safety for others. Otherwise, under <note>Temenus, Cresphontes, and the sons of Aristodemus were the original Heraclid leaders who divided the Peloponnese into Argos, Messene, and Sparta.</note> Temenus and Cresphontes and the others who made laws for them, whoever they were, not even the faction of Aristodemus would have been preserved. For they were not sufficiently skilled in making laws. If they had been, they would never have thought that a youthful soul, having received an authority from which a tyranny could arise, would moderate itself merely by an oath. Now, however, God has shown what kind of authority ought to have been, and must be, primarily established. That we should understand this after it has happened, as I said before, is no wonder. For it is not hard to see if you are moved by an example. But if someone had foreseen it then, and could have moderated the authorities and made one out of three, he would have preserved all their magnificent plans; and neither the Persian fleet, nor any other, would have ever sailed against Greece, treating us with contempt as if we were worth nothing. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** They resisted them shamefully then, O Clinias. I say shamefully, not because those who then conquered by land and sea behaved with less courage in fighting than was fitting, but I call it shameful because only one of those three cities fought for Greece. The other two were so depraved that one of them [Messene] even prevented Lacedaemon from helping, bringing a great war upon it; and the other, the city of the Argives, though it held the first place in Greece during those times of the distribution, yet when called upon to repel the barbarian, would not listen to those pleading, nor did it defend them. Many things I could recount that were done in Greece at that time which could be accused as shameful. Nor do those who say they defended Greece...

He praises the Spartan constitution for balancing power between twin kings, a council of elders, and the Ephors, contrasting this stability with the failure of Argos and Messene.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the third book of Plato’s Laws. Having established the seven claims to authority, the Athenian Stranger now applies these principles to history, specifically examining the rise and fall of the Persian Empire. He argues that the success of a state depends on balancing monarchical authority with liberty, a balance Cyrus achieved in war but failed to instill in the education of his successors.</meta>

->### ON LAWS, DIALOGUE III. FOLIO 320.<-

...they say. For unless the common counsel and power of the Athenians and Lacedaemonians <note>The Lacedaemonians are the Spartans.</note> had repelled the looming servitude, almost everything would now be in confusion: Greeks with Greeks, and likewise barbarians with Greeks, and Greeks with barbarians. Just as those Greeks who are now subjected to the tyranny of the Persians are confused among themselves without any order, and even badly scattered. These are the things, O Clinias and Megillus, which we may set before both the ancient statesmen and lawmakers and the younger ones: so that by examining their causes, we may find what else should have been done besides these things. Such is what we have now set forth: namely, that one ought not to establish great and unmixed <note>original: "meros," meaning pure or absolute</note> sovereignties, always keeping in mind that a city ought to be free, and prudent, and a friend to itself. <margin>A city ought to be free, prudent, and a friend to itself.</margin> These are the things to which he who is to give laws must look. Do not wonder, however, if we have already proposed certain other things to which the lawmaker should look, which indeed may appear not to be the same as these. But it is necessary to remember, when we say that one must look to temperance, or prudence, or friendship, that our intention is not different, but the same; and if we use many other words of this sort, do not be disturbed. **CLINIAS.** We shall try to do so, repeating your words in order. But now explain what you were going to say: when you said the lawmaker ought to look toward friendship, liberty, and prudence.

**ATHENIAN.** Only listen. There are two "mothers," as it were, of civil governments <margin>Two mothers of civil governments.</margin> from which, if someone says the others derive their origin, he will certainly speak correctly. The one it is proper to call the rule of one <note>Monarchy</note>, and the other the rule of the people <note>Democracy</note>. We should consider the Persian race to hold the highest form of the one, and ourselves <note>The Athenians</note> to hold the other. Almost all the others, as I said, are composed of these in various ways. It is necessary, however, for a city to participate in both of these if there is to be liberty, friendship, and prudence within it. This indeed is what reason wishes to teach us when it says that a city can never be well governed if it is devoid of these things. **CLINIAS.** How so? **ATHENIAN.** Since one side embraced monarchy—that is, the rule of one—and the other side embraced liberty more than was proper, neither maintained the middle ground <note>original: "mediocritatem," the "Golden Mean" or balance</note> of servitude and liberty. Yours, however—I mean the Laconian <note>Spartan</note> and Cretan systems—did so more. But the Athenians and Persians did so formerly in this way, but now less so. Shall we also state the causes, or not? **CLINIAS.** By all means, if we wish to complete what has been proposed.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us listen then. The Persians indeed, when in the time of Cyrus they held more of a balance between servitude and liberty, were first free themselves, and then they subjected many others. For when the rulers themselves imparted liberty to their subjects and brought matters more toward equality, the soldiers were greater friends to their leaders and showed themselves ready in dangers. And if there was anyone among them who was more prudent and strong in counsel, since the ruler was not envious of such things but gave the faculty of free speech to all and honored those capable of counsel, he brought the power of prudence into the common midst. Everything, therefore, at that time was easily rendered to them through liberty, friendship, and the communion of the mind. **CLINIAS.** These things seem to have happened just as they are told. **ATHENIAN.** In what way, then, did that kingdom almost fall in the time of Cambyses, and was restored again in the time of Darius? Do you wish for us to speak as if using divination? **CLINIAS.** Why should we not? For this contributes to the goal toward which we are tending.

**ATHENIAN.** Thus, then, I prophesy concerning Cyrus: that in other respects he was both a good leader and a friend to civil life, but that he never touched upon right discipline at all, nor ever applied his mind to the administration of a household. **CLINIAS.** Why so? **ATHENIAN.** Occupied from his youth through his whole military career, he handed over his sons to women to be educated; these women raised them as if they were already "happy" and "blessed" boys, lacking nothing, and they prevented anyone from opposing them in anything because they were "blessed." They compelled everyone to praise whatever they said or did. Thus they educated them into such men. **CLINIAS.** You seem to have described a fine education! **ATHENIAN.** A feminine one, certainly, which the royal women introduced, being puffed up by new riches and left alone by the men who were occupied with war and dangers. **CLINIAS.** That is consistent. **ATHENIAN.** Their father, indeed, possessed many flocks of sheep, men, and many other things whose possession belonged to them; but he was ignorant that his sons, to whom he was to leave these things, were not being taught the paternal and Persian art. For the Persians were shepherds born in a harsh region, and the Persian art itself was hard, sufficient to make them robust shepherds who could both keep watch and stay awake, and serve as soldiers if the situation required. But he permitted women and eunuchs to nourish his sons in the Median fashion, whose education was corrupted by that which is commonly thought to be "happiness." Whence they turned out as it was fitting for those to become who had been nourished in the greatest license of things. When, therefore, upon the death of Cyrus, they took power, being nourished in unrestrained delights, first one, not bearing equality, killed the other; then he himself, through ignorance and drunkenness, lost the sovereignty. For the Medes and a certain Eunuch then called <note>The "False Smerdis," a magus who usurped the throne.</note> despised him as if he were out of his mind. **CLINIAS.** So it is said, and so it seems to have happened. **ATHENIAN.** And yet this is also said: that through Darius and those seven men, the sovereignty returned again to the Persians. **CLINIAS.** Clearly.

**ATHENIAN.** Let us then look at the matter following reason. Darius was not the son of a king, nor was he nourished in delights. When he came to the sovereignty and received it as the seventh, he divided it into seven parts, of which today some small dreams still remain. He judged that they should live under laws that bring about a certain common equality, and he ordained it so. He encompassed in law that distribution which Cyrus had promised the Persians, offering friendship and community to all Persians, and attracting the Persian people with money and gifts. Thus, being loved by the soldiers, he himself subjugated no fewer regions than Cyrus had left. After Darius came Xerxes, who was indeed educated in royal delights. But I rightly call upon you now, O Darius, you who were not warned by the evil of Cyrus, but educated Xerxes in the same habits in which Cyrus had nourished Cambyses. He himself, therefore, being imbued with such nourishment, suffered similar things. From that time, almost no king of the Persians has ever been great except in name. <margin>Much concerning the government of Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius.</margin>

### BOOK III.

I do not believe it was by chance, but rather by a wicked way of life, in which the sons of very wealthy men and tyrants usually live. For neither a boy, a man, nor an old man will ever be able to emerge outstanding in virtue from such a life. These are matters which we think the lawmaker must consider, and which we ourselves must notice in the present. And indeed, it is right for you, O Lacedaemonians <note>The Lacedaemonians are the Spartans.</note>, to grant this: that you offer no excellent honors or rewards to poverty, wealth, or private kingship, unless they were spoken to you from the beginning by the oracle of some god. Nor is it proper in a city to confer excellent honors upon anyone because they excel in wealth, or because they are swift, or handsome, or robust, if they lack virtue. But neither even if they possess some other virtue, yet do not possess temperance <note>original: "temperantia," referring to self-control or moderation</note>. **MEGILLUS.** In what way do you say this, Stranger? **ATHENIAN.** Is not courage one certain part of virtue? **ME.** It is. **ATHE.** You yourself, therefore, when you have heard this, judge. Would you wish to have a neighbor or some domestic servant who is indeed very brave, but not at all temperate—nay, even shameless? **ME.** May the gods forbid it! **ATHE.** Or truly one skilled in many arts, and wise in them, but unjust? **ME.** In no way. **ATHE.** Yet truly, justice can have no origin without temperance. **ME.** For how could it be otherwise? **ATHE.** But neither can that man whom we just now called wise—he who holds his pleasures and pains in harmony and obedience to right reason. **ME.** Certainly not. **ATHE.** Let us furthermore consider this, so that we may inspect how honors are rightly or wrongly distributed among citizens. **ME.** What do you mean? **ATHE.** If temperance were destitute of every other kind of virtue in someone’s soul, is it rightly to be honored, or the opposite? **ME.** I do not know how to answer. **ATHE.** You have answered modestly and sufficiently. For if you had granted either of those options, you would have responded, I think, quite awkwardly. **ME.** It is well done then. **ATHE.** So be it. Indeed, that addition of honors and reproaches will be worthy not of speech, but rather of an irrational silence. **ME.** You seem to me to be speaking of temperance. **ATHE.** I speak of this very thing. Therefore, that which profits us most among other things, if it be most honored with an addition, will be most rightly honored; and that which profits in the second place, should be honored second. And thus according to the logic of succession, if each thing attains the honors that follow in order, it will certainly attain them rightly. **ME.** It is so. **ATHE.** What further? Shall we say these things are also to be distributed by the lawmaker? **ME.** Most especially. **ATHE.** Do you wish that we leave the partitioning of every single and smallest task to him? But since we ourselves are in a way students of laws, we hold to a tripartite division: distinguishing the greatest, the middle, and the smallest in turn. **ME.** By all means. **ATHE.** We say, therefore, that a city which is to be safe and happy as far as human power allows, must rightly distribute honors and reproaches. Now, a right distribution is this: that the goods of the soul be considered first and most honorable, provided that temperance is joined to them. <margin>A modest response to two difficult questions.</margin> <margin>The right distribution of honors and reproaches.</margin> In the second degree of dignity, let the goods of the body be placed. In the third, external possessions and money. If any lawmaker or city transgresses these, either by honoring money above the rest, or by placing something later in honor before what is prior, they shall act neither holily nor as a citizen. Shall we hold these things as settled, or how? **ME.** Entirely so. **ATHE.** Consideration of the Persian government has led us to speak of these things more broadly. We found, however, that they have become worse than before. And we consider the cause to be this: because by taking away the liberty of the people too much, and increasing the power of lordship more than was proper, they destroyed society and friendship in the city. When these are corrupted, the princes no longer consult the subjects and the people, but their own empire. Indeed, often for the sake of their own small advantage, they utterly overturn cities, and do not care if friendly nations are consumed by fire. Thus they hate with hostility and without mercy, and are held in hatred similarly. And if ever there is a need for the people to fight for them, they find no common consent among them to be willing to undergo dangers from the heart and to fight for their princes. But though they rule over almost innumerable men, they find them all useless for war; and as if in need of men, they hire others for pay, thinking they will be safe through mercenary and foreign soldiers. Furthermore, they are compelled to act like madmen, since by their very deeds they proclaim that those things which are said to be honorable and honored in the city are trifles if compared to silver and gold. **ME.** So it is. **ATHE.** But let enough have been said of the affairs of the Persians, which are not currently in a good state because of excessive domination and servitude. **ME.** Entirely. **ATHE.** It is fitting next to run through the Attic <note>Attica is the region surrounding Athens.</note> government in a similar way: so that it may be clear how liberty subject to no magistrate is not a little worse than that which follows a middle path under the rule of magistrates. For at the time when the Persians were attacking Greece, and indeed almost the whole of Europe, we had a certain ancient republic, and magistrates chosen from a fourfold division of wealth; and there was a sense of shame within us, acting like a master, for whose sake we wished to live subject to the laws. Furthermore, the greatness of the land and sea forces terrified us to such an extent that it compelled us to comply and obey the laws and magistrates more observantly. For these reasons, a greater benevolence arose among us. For almost ten years before the naval battle was fought at Salamis, Datis himself was sent by Darius leading a Persian fleet against the Athenians and Eretrians. Death was decreed for Datis by Darius unless he brought these nations under his jurisdiction. Datis, therefore, in a short time utterly conquered the Eretrians with an innumerable multitude of soldiers; and a terrible rumor then reached our city: that no one of the Eretrians had escaped; but that the soldiers, with hands joined to each other, had thus surrounded the entire region of the Eretrians and captured everyone completely. This rumor, whether true or not, terrified the other Greeks, but especially the Athenians. Though they sent embassies everywhere to all of Greece urging them to bring help, no one except the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> was willing to help. And they, whether hindered by the war they were waging against Messene, or for some other cause—for we do not know—arrived to bring aid on the day following the Battle of Marathon. After this, great things were prepared daily, and threats of war... <margin>Concerning the Attic popular government.</margin>

FOLIO 321.

### ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS OF THE LATINS, DIALOGUE III.

He spoke of these matters. Meanwhile, it was announced that Darius had passed away <note>original: "naturæ cessisse," literally "yielded to nature"</note> and that his son, a fierce young man, had taken up the empire and intended to continue his father’s undertakings. The Athenians believed all these preparations were aimed at them because of the slaughter at Marathon. Furthermore, hearing that Mount Athos was being dug through, the Hellespont joined by a bridge, and an immense multitude of ships gathered, they thought there would be no safety for them by sea or by land, especially since they trusted in no one's protection. For they remembered that when the Persians first entered, the Eretrians had been captured, and no one had brought them help or wished to undergo danger for their safety. They expected the same outcome for themselves on land. By sea, they found no safety at all, as more than a thousand ships were being brought against them.

They saw only one safety, however thin and doubtful: looking back at what had been done before, and how they had triumphed even when safety seemed desperate, they were carried away by this hope and found refuge only in themselves and the gods. All these things, therefore, bound them together with greater goodwill toward one another—I mean the present fear, and that fear which had long been present through the laws, which they attained by serving the laws. We have often named this "shame" <note>original: "pudor," referring to "aidos" or a sense of reverent awe/respect</note> in the preceding pages, and we said that those who are to be good must serve it. Whoever is moved by this is free and unafraid. And unless that present fear had been joined to this shame, they would never have been provoked by such an onslaught to come together to defend the temples of the gods, the tombs of their ancestors, their very fatherland, and their other family and friends as they are said to have done; rather, they would have scattered, one going one way and another another.

**MEGILLUS.** You have spoken well, Stranger, and as befits yourself and your fatherland.

**ATHENIAN.** These things are true, O Megillus. For it is right to refer the things done then to you, who preserve the nature of your ancestors. But both you and Clinias consider attentively whether what we are saying pertains to the making of laws. For I do not relate these things for the sake of storytelling. Look into the reason why I say these things: namely, so that we may see that the same thing happened to us as to the Persians, though in a different way—while they dragged the common people into total slavery, we, on the contrary, dragged them into pure liberty. How we should speak and what comes next, the words already held and appropriately spoken demonstrate in some way.

**ME.** You speak well. But try to express more clearly what you were just saying.

**ATHENIAN.** I will do so. Friends, under our ancient laws, the common people were not the masters of anything; rather, they were in a way voluntary servants to the laws.

**ME.** Which laws?

**ATHENIAN.** Those, I say, which were established concerning music, so that we may trace the growth of an excessively free life from the beginning. For our music was then divided into species and forms. One species was a song for appeasing the gods with prayers, which they called **hymns** <margin>hymns to appease the gods</margin>. Another distinct species of song followed this; one might best call these "querulous" songs <note>original: "querulos hos cātus," referring to "threnoi" or laments</note>. Another species was the **Paean**. Another was the "generation of Dionysus," which I think was called the **Dithyramb**. There was also another species of song which they named "citharoedic laws" <note>original: "leges citharœdicas," traditional melodies for the lyre</note>. Therefore, it was not permitted to misuse one kind of song for another among these and certain others established by law.

The authority to know, judge, and condemn if anyone did otherwise was not granted to the whistling or the unrefined shouts of the multitude as it is now, nor to the license of the crowd praising with clapping and noise. Instead, it was granted to men outstanding in learning, and they were allowed to listen in great silence until the end. Youths, tutors <note>original: "pædagogi"</note>, and the entire populace were kept in order by the warning of the rod. Since these things were done in such order, the multitude of citizens obeyed willingly and did not dare to judge anything in a tumultuous way.

Then, as time went on, the poets themselves became the leaders of transgression, departing from the proper music. They were indeed poetic by nature, but they did not sufficiently understand what was just and lawful in the Muse; they acted like revelers, indulging in pleasure more than was proper. These poets joined laments to hymns and paeans to dithyrambs; they imitated the sounds and songs of flutes with those of the lyre, mixing all things with all things. Thus, unintentionally and through ignorance, they bore false witness against music, asserting that it has no right standard in itself, but is most correctly judged by the pleasure of the listener, whether that man be virtuous or the opposite.

By composing such poems and saying such things to the common people, they made the multitude so lawless and bold regarding music that they believed themselves sufficient to pronounce judgment on it. Hence, the audiences in the theaters began to shout out, whereas before they were accustomed to be silent, as if they keenly perceived what was beautiful in the muses and what was not. And so, the matter flowed down from the power of the best men <note>original: "optimatū potestate," referring to aristocracy</note> into the wicked power of the theater <note>original: "theatri potētiā," or "theatrocracy"</note>.

If indeed a "popular power" of free men alone had emerged, it would not have been a great evil. But now, from music began the general opinion of wisdom in all things, followed by transgression and license. For they became intrepid, as if they knew everything; this license gave birth to impudence. For if the opinion of a better person is not feared because of audacity, that is itself a most ruinous impudence, which proceeds from a certain reckless liberty.

**ME.** You speak most truly.

**ATHENIAN.** Following this liberty comes that license which makes us unwilling to be subject to magistrates. From this also originates the contempt for the servitude and precepts of father, mother, and elders. And as we reach the end of this transgression, we also refuse to obey the laws. At the very end, we neglect oaths, faith, and altogether the gods. From there, having revolved back to that ancient and "titanic" nature, we will suffer those same things again and live through hard ages once more, finding no end to our evils.

But it seems to me I must repeat why these things were said: so that the discourse may be pulled back like a horse, lest if it has an unbridled mouth, the force of the speech might, as the proverb says, "throw the rider off the ass" <margin>proverb</margin>. We must ask, therefore, for what cause these things were said.

**ME.** Indeed we must.

**ATHENIAN.** We said these things for their sake.

**ME.** For whose sake?

**ATHENIAN.** We said that the lawgiver must look toward three things: that the city which is established by laws should be free, friendly to itself, and possess a mind <note>intelligence or reason</note>. Was this said, or not?

**ME.** It was certainly said.

**ATHENIAN.** For this reason, we brought forward two types of governance: one in which there is the strictest servitude, the other in which there is loose liberty. We considered which of the two was governed correctly. We perceived, however, a moderate path in each...

...of [governing], while to the other liberty was added, and both fared very happily. But they fared unhappily when slavery in the one and liberty in the other reached the ultimate extreme. 

**MEGILLUS:** You speak the truth. 

**ATHENIAN:** And yet it was for the sake of this very point that we considered the constitution of the Dorian army, and the roots of the Dardanian mountains <note>original: "radices montium Dardani," referring to the foothills of Mount Ida where Troy was founded after the Great Flood</note>, and the maritime habitation; and also those first people who were left behind from the devastation of the deluge. It was for their sake that our discourse was held regarding music, and drunkenness, and the topics preceding them. All these things were said so that we might understand how a city can best be governed, and in what way an individual might best arrange his own life. But if we have contributed anything, what refutation will we have against ourselves, O Megillus and Cleinias? 

**CLEINIAS:** Stranger, I seem to perceive something. Indeed, all our previous words seem to have been spoken by a favorable second fortune. For I was, in a way, in need of these very things. Therefore, both of you—you and Megillus here—have found me at an opportune moment. I will not hide from you what has happened to me. For I have been confirmed by these discourses as if by an omen. The greater part of the Cretans are planning to send out a certain colony, and they have entrusted the care of this matter to the Gnosians <note>original: "Gnosiis," the people of Knossos, the leading city of Crete</note>. The city of the Gnosians has mandated me and nine other men to take care of this. It orders us to establish laws, both from those Cretan laws that please us and those that can be collected from elsewhere. It commands us not to fear foreign laws, provided they are better. Now, therefore, let us grant this favor both to me and to yourselves. With the laws collected from everywhere, let us build a city from the beginning in our discourse. In this way, we will more diligently consider that which we are seeking, and perhaps this discussion will contribute to the constitution of my future city. 

**ATHENIAN:** You do not declare war, O Cleinias <note>original: "Non bellum indicis," a metaphor meaning "you are not bringing bad news" or "this is a welcome challenge"</note>. Therefore, unless it is inconvenient for Megillus, my efforts are ready for you to the best of my strength. 

**MEGILLUS:** You speak well; I also am ready. 

**CLEINIAS:** You have both spoken excellently. Therefore, we must first attempt to found a city through our speech.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Introduction to the Fourth Dialogue on the Laws.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a classical figure or deity within a circular frame, surrounded by floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

This fourth dialogue, just like the three preceding ones and also the first part of the fifth, is concerned with the counsel and duty of the founder of laws. His counsel concerns the "matter" and the "form" of the city. By "matter," I mean the site, composition, and layout of the city. By "form," I mean the mode of public governance and order. But since this form can never be beautiful <note>original: "formosa," a play on words between 'form' and 'beauty'</note> unless the souls of the citizens are beautiful, the lawgiver is commanded to be vigilant in forming the souls of his citizens from a tender age and throughout their whole lives. 

He dispatches the "matter" of the city in few words, but treats its "form" and the formation of those souls with the utmost accuracy; for he regards all exterior things, however grand they may seem, as nothing compared to the dignity of the soul. Indeed, if our Plato were a doctor of bodies, he would labor more diligently in choosing the healthiest air to contribute to a firm and strong habit of the body. But since, in choosing the Academy <note>The site of Plato's school in Athens, which was notoriously damp and unhealthy</note>, he consulted the soul and morals rather than the body by picking an unhealthy place, he naturally appears less concerned with the physical city; but in shaping morals alongside age, he is, so to speak, the most meticulous physician of souls. 

Furthermore, if he valued the goods of fortune as much as others do, he would certainly seek out a field, a site, and a method most convenient for accumulating wealth and amplifying the empire. But he does the exact opposite. Therefore, let the city be far from the sea and the harbor; let it not be devoted to trade, especially the business of innkeeping <note>original: "cauponariæ," referring to retail trade and tavern-keeping, which Plato felt corrupted the soul</note>; let it not be luxurious; let it not be wealthy. Let the city be temperate, sober, and modest—and above all, pious. What else do you think a holy high priest of a religious life would command in building temples and the dwellings of the saints, other than what our Plato commands in the founding of a city? 

And because he speaks few words here regarding the "body" of the city, he similarly said nothing about building a physical city in that blessed Republic described in ten dialogues—and not without reason. For he left that city to heaven; this one he builds on earth, as an image of that ideal pattern, as far as it can be achieved. The purpose of the lawgiver will therefore be: to value those things which are outside the soul as little compared to the goods of the soul; and in his entire institution, to aim toward universal virtue as if at a target. Therefore, he will permit nothing in or around the city from which citizens might eventually become accustomed to bad morals, even if the victory over many nations, the greatest power, and the most abundant supply of all things should follow from it. 

For the law does not direct its edge outside the soul, but into the soul itself, to be perfected in every part. Thus, he will command that citizens do not hold the safety of this false life in the highest price. Nor should they take care merely so that they *exist* and are *safe*, but rather that as long as they *exist*, they are as *good* as possible. To fulfill the entire institution of the lawgiver, he judges three things to be primarily conducive: namely God, fortune, and art <note>original: "ars," meaning skill, craft, or human ingenuity</note>. These three are said to govern all human affairs. And the more difficult the things the author of laws attempts compared to others, the more he needs the patronage of these three. 

As for what Plato says—that God, fortune, and art together with God govern all human affairs—explain it briefly thus: God moves all things in all things through all things. He moves the spheres of the world. Their concurrence is called "fate" in some places, but here he more freely calls it "fortune." From this, various chances arise concerning external things and bodies. He also moves souls by inspiring light into minds, from which the "art" is kindled, not only for contemplating but for acting. Finally, from art proceeds the arrangement of external things and the body. Therefore, all things depend on God; who, as Paul says <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:6, "it is the same God who works all things in all men"</note>, works all in all. But from God Himself, some things proceed through fortune, and others through art. Thus it happens that neither fortune nor art can ever prevail against God, since both are always moved by Him. Between themselves, however, these two relate in this way: they either agree with each other or, perhaps, they disagree. If they disagree, either fortune overcomes art, or art overcomes fortune. Take this example: while God moves the spheres, sometimes through fortune He stirs up a storm at sea. The storm shakes the ship. Meanwhile, the same God moves the same...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s "Argument" or introductory commentary on Plato’s *Laws*. Although the header in the source text reads "III," the content focuses on Book IV, specifically discussing the relationship between divine providence, human skill (art), and the historical context of Plato’s travels to Sicily.</meta>

### PAGE 422.
### THE ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE IV ON THE LAWS.

...the ship through the mind of the pilot as well—that is, the part of him that depends continually upon God. Therefore, when Art directs a ship toward a certain port, and a storm also carries it to that same place, then Art and Fortune are in agreement. But when the wind drives it one way, while Art strives to lead it another, then Art and Fortune disagree; and finally, either Art yields to Fortune, or Fortune to Art. Meanwhile, the providence of God acts in both cases toward an end known only to Himself, with which nothing is ever out of harmony, as He tempers all things in various hidden ways into the universal harmony of His work. 

Furthermore, that very meeting of celestial dispositions, when it occurs in such a way that it must necessarily overcome Art, is called "Fate" <note>original: "Fatum"</note> rather than Fortune. But when it is such that it can overcome the lazy but be overcome by Art, it is more properly named "Fortune." Do not doubt that Art can sometimes conquer Fortune. For just as Fortune proceeds from God, so does Art. 

Observe, however, where Plato discusses "opportunity" <note>original: "occasio," referring to the specific historical moment required for political change</note>, which a great man desires when he is about to establish new laws. Under the name of a "tyrant," Plato signifies the younger Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the ruler of Syracuse whom Plato attempted to tutor in philosophy</note>, while under the title of "lawgiver," he signifies himself. He indicates that the full favor of Fortune was lacking for him. Likewise, it appears from his letters that Plato began some of the prefaces to these laws in Sicily at the court of Dionysius, but that he completed the work of the laws through the help of Ops <note>likely referring to the Roman goddess of plenty or the successful expulsion of the tyrant</note> after Dionysius was expelled. Finally, through these writings, he cleared his return to Sicily from any infamy. Know, then, that on that journey and return, Plato strove for nothing else than to transform a violent tyranny into a moderate kingdom, while keeping the prosperity of Dionysius intact. 

Meanwhile, when he speaks of the temperance and prudence of a prince, remember that Plato clearly distinguishes "moderate temperance" from "prudence." In a similar way, he discerns "moderate prudence" from "wisdom" <note>original: "sapientia"</note>. Yet, he often calls "perfected temperance" by the name of "prudence," and sometimes names "absolute prudence" as "wisdom." This is evident in the *Phaedo*, the third book of the *Laws*, here, and often elsewhere. 

He introduces, moreover, certain natural gifts of character that are similar to virtues; however, these only lead to the duties of virtue when they have been rightly cultivated. He discusses this matter more extensively in the *Republic*. You should, in the meantime, commit this to memory: that as the morals of the princes are, such also become the morals of the rest of the citizens. Nor can the morals of citizens be changed more easily or more quickly for any other reason than this. Likewise, blessed is the prudent and temperate teacher of the people; and blessed also is the people who hear words flowing from the mouth of such a teacher. Furthermore, neither will a republic be happy, nor will good laws arise, until power concurs with wisdom and temperance in the governor. Therefore, divine help must be invoked for the constitution of a city. 

Thus far, this fourth book has treated the duty of the lawgiver regarding the material and general form of the city. Next, it proceeds to a more distinct description of this duty, asking whether the form of the city ought to be a kingdom, or a senate of the best men <note>an aristocracy</note>, or the power of the few <note>an oligarchy</note>, or a popular state <note>a democracy</note>. Since nothing among men can truly be called "good" unless it imitates the Divine Good, he rightly explains the form of divine governance before he places some human governments above others. He intends, without controversy, to prefer the one most similar to the divine over the rest. 

He proves that divine government is a kingdom, and a senate of the best men joined to that kingdom. He judges that those from among all the citizens who so far excel the others in prudence and temperance—as much as men usually excel children—should be chosen to govern. And if someone among the number of those elected surpasses the others by a similar distance, he should be established as King. This can be seen both from the present "Mystery of Saturn" <note>a mythological allegory for the Golden Age</note> and from a similar passage in the *Politicus* <note>Plato’s dialogue "The Statesman"</note>, as well as from his *Letters* and the *Republic*. 

Furthermore, so that the present Mystery of Saturn may be more aptly understood, one must remember that the Platonists conjecture that the world is contained and led by a certain life and soul, based chiefly on three arguments: from the firm binding of the diverse parts of the world; from the wonderful motion of the heavens; and from the perpetual generation of things beneath the heavens. They conjecture again that the world is ruled by a Mind according to a threefold order—namely, the order seen in the connection of the world's parts, in the motion of the spheres, and in the generation of things. Our Platonist <note>referring to Virgil</note> briefly encompasses both—namely, soul and mind—when he says: 

*A spirit within nourishes, and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the mass.* <note>original: "Spiritus intus alit, totamque infusa per artus Mens agitat molem" — Virgil, Aeneid VI.726-727</note> 

Finally, they conjecture that both soul and mind are directed by the Good itself and the One, especially because the connection of parts, motion, generation, and the entire order of these three tend toward a single end and are directed toward the Good. For this reason, a twin kingdom is contained under the Good itself: namely, that of the Intellect and that of the Soul. Ancient tradition calls the former the Kingdom of Saturn, and the latter the Kingdom of Jupiter. 

They imagine that Jupiter occupied the Kingdom of Saturn for this reason: since both call souls to their own respective kingdoms—the one to the Intelligible Good and the other to the Sensible Good—only a very few souls betake themselves to the Intelligible Good of Saturn through contemplation. But the great majority flow daily toward the Sensible Good of Jupiter and toward action. The ancients hand down that souls were once blessed and lived under the reign of Saturn. They understand this in two ways: first, when souls lived among divine and angelic minds before they fell into bodies. Second, whenever and as many as neglect a life of pleasure and, while greatly loving the active part, give themselves over with the most burning love to the contemplative life. In the intellectual life, they are accepted as blessed; in the animal life, they are miserable. 

It happens that under this misery they are so deceived that, although there are two planets in the sky—the first being the messenger of the higher Saturn, the second the messenger of the higher Jupiter—men praise the star of Jupiter but disparage the star of Saturn. They do this even though Jupiter provokes them more toward temporary goods, while Saturn calls them back to eternal things. But because man is a social animal, once he is segregated from the common commerce of men, he cannot maintain a moderate habit of living. He is forced, so to speak, either to descend below humanity or to ascend above it. Thus it has happened that Saturn, as the "segregator" of men, has brought back a reputation for crime and infamy among the ignorant—namely, through the fault of those who either...
