### THE ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE IV ON THE LAWS.

...through a somewhat foolish mixture or a perverse education, some turn out such that when they are called out of their human state by Saturn <note>In Ficino’s Neoplatonic astrology, Saturn represents the highest intellectual and contemplative power</note>, they descend from being human rather than ascending. But concerning these matters, we shall speak more diligently elsewhere; let us return to the argument. Plato adds that Saturn once committed humans, who were distributed into flocks, to the guardianship of daemons <note>original: "daemonum." In the Platonic tradition, these are intermediary spirits or guardian angels, not "demons" in the modern sense</note>. He explains this in several ways. 

First, as the *Timaeus* says, the divine mind divided the souls of humans from the beginning into various orders of stars, following the number of those souls. Regarding the difference between our souls, some among the Platonists think it is only numerical, while others think it is also specific—meaning there is one genus of our souls, but within it are many species of souls, and many individuals under the same species. However they are distributed, they say they are assigned not only to different stars but also to different daemons. 

There is another way to explain this mystery: namely, that either from the beginning of the world, or immediately after the Great Flood, divine providence ruled the ruder humans through the ministry of angels or better daemons, until they gradually became more skilled and could rule themselves. It is indeed consistent with reason that humans are governed more rightly and happily by higher beings than by themselves. 

He explains it, moreover, in a third way: that every day, whoever chooses a way of life somewhat segregated from others and has been rightly educated, is said to immediately migrate into the contemplative and blessed kingdom of Saturn. But insofar as they are distinguished into various rites under the duty of contemplation, to that extent they also seem to be separated into many "flocks" and to be inspired and ruled by different deities according to the similarity of their lives. I will omit for now the many schools of excellent philosophers, which are like flocks gathered in a wonderful way under the shepherd Saturn. 

Under Saturn, I say, in three primary ways: first, under the divine and angelic mind; second, under the soul of the first planet and its sphere; third, under the body of the planet itself. But the Mind itself acts; the Soul completes; the Planet portends. It "portends," I say, when in the great conjunctions of Saturn with Jupiter, Saturn himself rejoices either in his exaltation or his domicile; and as the lord of the conjunction, he is fostered kindly by Jupiter, and by the benefit of both the Sun, Mercury, and Venus. In this way, he produced—or rather portended—the magical discipline of Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet associated by Ficino with the origins of wisdom</note> and his followers; also the theology of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical Egyptian author of the Hermetic corpus</note>; the mysteries of Orpheus; the secrets of Pythagoras; the Socratic sanctity; and the Platonic majesty. We have found this to be manifest through certain arguments. 

Hence, Plato affirms in the present book that Saturn is the lord of those who possess mind <note>original: "mentem," referring to the higher intellect</note>. He demonstrates that governance of this kind under Saturn was royal and aristocratic. Indeed, he asserts that the human race was governed by God Himself as king through chosen and excellent daemons. Many would call these "angels"; and Plato in the *Critias* calls them "gods." He indicates the ease of this governance both here and in the *Critias*, saying that humans were governed by a certain hidden inspiration of persuasion; and they are to be governed similarly whenever, being free from lower movements, they subject themselves to be led by the higher. 

In these matters, Plato advises: 
1. First, that divine providence is never lacking to humans, provided they are not lacking to themselves. 
2. Second, that the human character, in a state of total license and power, turns out to be wanton and proud. 
3. Third, just as beasts cannot be governed by beasts without some human shepherd, so neither can humans be governed by humans without God as leader; and as long as any mortal rules without God, life will be laborious and miserable—as if any guardian of a city were to watch in vain unless God Himself guarded the city. 
4. Fourth, that the distribution of the mind itself is the Law; and this must always be obeyed in every private and public governance, so that we may be happily led by our own mind toward the Divine Mind. 
5. Fifth, that no constitutions should be called "laws" unless they procure the common good of the entire city. 
6. Sixth, that the offices of the magistracy and divine worship ought to be committed most especially to those who more observantly obey the laws. 
7. Seventh, that destruction is prepared for the city in which the laws do not rule the magistrates, but the magistrates rule the laws. 
8. Eighth, that young men for the most part see these things bluntly, but old men perceive them acutely—unless perhaps God sometimes grants piety to the young or reproves impiety in the old. 

Plato now uses many words to instruct the legislator himself for his duty. He then says a few things to the people who are to receive such laws, so that they may both receive them more willingly and keep them more diligently. He exhorts them toward sacred laws first of all, and through those, to human laws discovered and confirmed by divine ones. But along with the exhortation, he mixes veneration and terror: saying that God, the craftsman of the whole world, encompasses everything within Himself. Therefore, He inspects every single thing, so that no one may trust that they can hide by transgressing; and He revolves through all things, so that no one may hope to escape His hands after a crime. 

He shows this God to be the founder of all laws where he says: *He defines and accomplishes the straight* <note>original: "Recta definit & pagit"</note>—that is, He determines every single thing by a certain straight rule of law. He determines, I say, first for each thing the measure of its nature: what sort, how many, and how great they are, and where and when and how they move. Then, He determines for souls what must be done and what must be avoided. It is established that a determination of this kind is the Law of all things in the hands of God the author; and that it is sanctioned by God Himself in the same act by which all things are understood and made by Him—namely, by a circular act, which the *Timaeus* says is natural to divine intelligence, looking from itself into itself, and by looking at itself, always seeing all things. 

But perhaps, beyond the circular motion (so to speak) inward to God, he also insinuates a straight motion: that is, the procession of things from God and the influx of God through all things. Therefore he said "straight" and "accomplishes." And he signified that the straight motion depends on the circular. Likewise, where he says that God contains the beginnings, ends, and middles of things, understand that God is the efficient and final cause of things; He preserves all things and is present to all. And lest anyone think the law is in vain, he adds that this Law is always accompanied by Judgment, by which both the keepers of the law and the transgressors are discernibly distinguished, and what is most fitting for each is effectively decided. Because this judgment both powerfully discerns and decides, an inevitable vengeance follows for sinners, and a reward for the observant. He says the divine law is kept most of all by those who [humbly submit] their necks...

<meta>Catchword: submittunt (they submit)</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains Plato’s "Age of Saturn" as an allegory for divine governance, arguing that true law must be rooted in divine intelligence and that humans require divine guidance—much like sheep require a shepherd—to avoid the arrogance of power. He lists several principles for a just state, emphasizing that laws must serve the common good and that magistrates must be servants to the law, not its masters.</summary>

### THE ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE IV ON THE LAWS.
### (Continued)

...they submit themselves to the yoke of the divine law: the reward for which is judged to be future blessedness. Truly, this law is rejected most of all by the proud, who, just as they have abandoned the law of God, are likewise abandoned by God. Once deserted, they both sin more atrociously and are tortured more miserably. But you shall keep these <term>evangelical and golden precepts</term> <note>Ficino often uses "evangelical" (gospel-like) to describe Platonic teachings that he believes align with Christian truth</note> stored deep within your mind. Since he says these mysteries consist of ancient speech, we can understand this as the <term>Mosaic</term> <note>referring to Moses</note> tradition. We can also understand it as <term>Mercurial</term> <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> and <term>Orphic</term>; among these writers, we read many such things, and indeed the most evident ones, which the length of this argument now forbids us from reviewing. 

But if you read the Orphic hymns concerning Jupiter, the law, judgment, justice, and <term>Nemesis</term> <note>the goddess of retribution</note>, you will find all these things word for word. After this, Plato exhorts the people so that each person may greatly strive to be in the number of those who follow God, contending in all things to please God; and so that they may achieve this, rendering themselves similar to God—similar, I say, through temperance and purity, by which they may measure all their own things exactly, as if by a rule. 

For indeed, <term>measure</term>—which Pythagoras also says is the best of all things—judges and makes the soul most similar to God. Since God is the measure of all things, especially for us, we must clearly follow or flee from individual things only insofar as they are judged to either harmonize or clash with the divine mind and will. Hence that saying in Plato's epistle: "To a wise man, God is the law; to a fool, it is his own lust." 

Truly, this text is read ambiguously. In one place, it is read as I have translated it. With these words, Plato seems to refute <term>Protagoras</term> <note>a Sophist philosopher</note> who said that "man is the measure of all things." His error is subtly refuted in the book on knowledge <note>Plato’s *Theaetetus*</note>. But in another place, it is read not as "what man" but "if some man," in this manner: "God is the measure of all things for us, and much more so if some man is, as they say." You can explain this part—"if some man is, as they say"—as: if any man is a measure, God is much more a measure. For we ought to live not for ourselves, but for God, through whom we live. Perhaps you could explain it as "if God is some man," that is, if he should ever become man, as they say—meaning the oracles of the prophets. Would that this exposition, as pious as it is among many, were as accepted among the Platonists. 

But so that it may appear how much fruit there is in the observation of the laws, he adds that only the observers of these laws are allowed and find it profitable to make vows and sacrifices to the gods. Truly, the prayers and gifts of the others are rejected by God. He says that this very thing, which is to please God, is the target at which we ought to aim the individual actions of our lives like arrows. But the arrows for reaching this grace of God, he says, are the diligent practice of religion. In this, he arranges the same steps which we also read in the <term>Pythagorean verses</term>. For he commands here, just as Pythagoras does, that we first worship all the celestial gods; especially those to whom the fatherland is dedicated as if to patrons. Then, following them, the gods under heaven, all of whom he calls "terrestrial." 

For it is Plato’s custom that, even if he places all elements under heaven, and all things in heaven in a celestial way, he nevertheless encompasses all things under heaven by the name of "earth," and all things in heaven by the name of "fiery heaven." By "celestial gods," he understands both the higher angels and the souls of the celestial spheres and stars. By "terrestrial gods," he understands both the lower angels and the souls of the four elements. 

Thirdly, he commands that <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "demones"; intermediary spirits</note> be worshiped, namely the purer ones, who act as interpreters from the gods to us. Fourthly, <term>heroes</term>: that is, the souls of men accepted by God and separated from the body. In all these, he commands the worship to be distributed so that greater gifts are conferred to greater powers, lesser to lesser, and equal to equal. 

Fifthly, he commands not so much that the statues of the ancestral gods be worshiped and adored, but rather that they be adorned and in some way honored, as they are consecrated by the laws. Since he began the whole exhortation to divine worship from the one God, he evidently shows that the other powers are called gods neither through themselves, but by participation in the first, nor are they to be worshiped for their own sake, but for His sake; especially since he says the entire worship of this kind is to be undertaken only that you may please that Unique One. 

Sixthly, he commands that parents be venerated as the vicars of God. Seventhly, he commands that relatives by birth, those joined by familiarity, and guests and strangers be loved with unfeigned charity according to divine command. Among these, he inserts an <term>evangelical precept</term>: namely, that an exact account of vain words must be rendered to the divine judge, over whom an angel presides for us as the vicar and minister of the superior judge, so that he may recall us from base things and provoke us toward honest ones. To those who consent, he nourishes and delights them with tranquility of conscience; but those who dissent, he vexes with the perturbation of conscience. 

Where he delights, he is named "Grace" by the ancients; where he vexes, "Fury." And Grace is indeed threefold, since he delights the good with past, present, and future grace. Fury is also threefold, because he likewise tortures the wicked. And in both cases, it is called <term>Fate</term> and the threefold <term>Parcae</term> <note>The Fates: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos</note>. It is also called Nemesis, especially by Orpheus, where she turns against the proud. Certainly, the ancients, to indicate that pride clashes most of all with God, who demands the most humble obedience, said that the proud are punished not only by divine judgment, as other vices are, but also by indignation; and they introduced a specific deity for this kind of punishment, called by the name of Nemesis, who "shows strength with his arm and scatters the proud in the imagination of their hearts" <note>original: "facit potentiam in brachio suo, dispergitq; supbos mēte cordis sui." This is a direct quote from the Magnificat, Luke 1:51</note>. 

Collect these things under many names, but especially four: law, judgment, justice, and Nemesis. Take the example of these in yourself. You have the **law** in your mind, dictating what must be done and what must not by a common rule: and that the honest must be followed, while the base must be avoided. You also have **judgment** in your reason, discerning through a more distinct discourse of arguments that which is placed in this or that action, whether it be honest or base. You have **justice** in your will, choosing to follow or flee in the way that reason, through the laws of the mind, has judged it should be followed or fled. You have **Nemesis** in your imagination and its affect, being angered by base actions and words and being legitimately indignant. Similarly, in God there is law, judgment, justice, and Nemesis, but in a divine manner. More distinctly, however: in God, there is the law and the higher angels. In the reason of the world-soul, there is judgment. In its will, justice. In the lower angels or middle daemons, Nemesis. However you distribute them, all these things serve the divine law in a certain wonderful connection for the reward of virtues and the punishment of sins.

<summary>Ficino explains the Platonic hierarchy of worship and the ethical necessity of "measure," aligning Plato's "God as the measure" against Protagoras's human-centered view. He integrates Greek mythology (Nemesis, Fates) with Christian concepts like the "evangelical" account of words and the scattering of the proud.</summary>

### THE FOURTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS OR ON LEGISLATION.

<margin>By what names the new city ought to be called:</margin> **Athenian:** Come now, what sort of city should we imagine it to be? I am not asking now about its name—either what it is called at present or what it will be called in the future. For that will perhaps be given to it by the founder of the colony, or by the location itself, or perhaps a river, a spring, or one of the local gods of that region will bestow their own name upon the new city. Rather, I am asking this: whether it will be by the sea or situated inland.

**Clinias:** This city of which we speak, **Stranger**, <note>original: "hospes"; Clinias and Megillus address the Athenian as "Guest" or "Stranger"</note> is distant from the sea by about eighty <term>stadia</term>. <note>A Greek unit of distance; 80 stadia is roughly 9 to 10 miles.</note>

**Athenian:** Are there harbors nearby, or is that coast entirely without ports?

**Clinias:** That region, **Stranger**, is as well-supplied with harbors as can possibly be.

**Athenian:** Alas, what are you saying! And does that land produce everything? Or is it in need of certain things?

**Clinias:** It produces almost everything.

**Athenian:** And is there any city close to it?

**Clinias:** Not very close. And for that reason, we are thinking of bringing inhabitants there; for since the former inhabitants were driven out long ago, the region has lain desolate for a great span of time.

**Athenian:** As for the plains, mountains, and forests, how is it laid out?

**Clinias:** It is similar to the nature of the rest of Crete.

**Athenian:** You say, then, that it is rugged and wooded rather than a level plain?

**Clinias:** Indeed I do.

**Athenian:** It is not, therefore, ill-suited for the acquisition of **virtue**. For if it were close to the sea and full of harbors, and if it did not produce everything but was in need of many things, it would require a great savior and divine lawmakers to prevent its character from becoming tainted by the many varied and wicked customs that the nature of such a region attracts. But as it is, it is fortunate that it is eighty stadia from the sea—certainly closer to the sea than it ought to be, especially since you say it is so well-supplied with harbors. Nevertheless, even this seems sufficient. Truly, the sea being close to a city provides a certain daily pleasure. <margin>The sea close to a city brings a certain pleasure.</margin> However, that proximity is in truth a very false and bitter thing. For when a city is filled with the <term>huckstering</term> <note>original: "cauponando"; referring to retail trade and middle-man commerce</note> of merchandise and money, it gives birth to deceitful souls and unstable, untrustworthy characters. Consequently, the city loses faith and friendship both with itself and with other nations. To counter these things, however, it has the remedy of producing all its own goods. And although it is forested and rugged, even if it produces all things, it does not produce them in such abundance or fertility that it would gather a great amount of gold and silver from exporting goods. In short, nothing is more ruinous than this—if one compares one thing to another—for the development of noble and just character, as was also said in our earlier discussions, if we remember correctly.

**Clinias:** We do indeed remember, and we concede that those things were said rightly then and are said rightly now.

**Athenian:** What about timber for building ships? Is it abundant there?

**Clinias:** There is no fir tree there worth mentioning, nor any pitch-pine. Likewise, there is a small supply of cypress, and you will find the pine and the plane tree only rarely. Shipbuilders must necessarily use these for the interior parts of ships.

**Athenian:** In this too, the nature of the region is not badly situated.

**Clinias:** Why is that?

**Athenian:** Because it is worthwhile that a city should not be able to easily imitate its enemies in wicked ways.

**Clinias:** For which of the things I just mentioned do you say this?

**Athenian:** Observe me, noble man. I say this for the sake of what was said at the beginning regarding the laws of the Cretans: which you were saying were directed toward one thing only—that is, war. But I added that they were well-placed insofar as they referred in some way to virtue; however, because they did not refer to virtue as a whole, but only to a part of virtue, I did not praise them highly. Now, therefore, you both must observe me carefully in this present legislation: if I should decree anything in the laws that either does not pertain to virtue, or pertains only to a part of it. For I believe those laws alone are rightly made which, like an archer, always aim the mind toward that place from which some good thing continually follows; as for other things—whether wealth or anything else of that sort—the law leaves them behind if they are separated from the virtues. 

I was saying then that the "wicked imitation of enemies" occurs when someone living near the sea is harmed by enemies. I will explain how this was—though not out of a desire to recount past injuries. <margin>Minos forced Attica to hand over seven boys.</margin> **Minos** once, relying on his naval strength, imposed a cruel tribute upon **Attica**. <note>The myth of the Minotaur, where Athens had to send seven youths and seven maidens to Crete every nine years.</note> But the **Athenians** did not yet have ships prepared for war as they do now; nor was there such a great supply of timber in that region from which ships could be easily built. Therefore, they could not, by imitating naval matters and becoming sailors themselves, immediately take revenge on their enemies. And it would have been better for them to have lost seven youths many times over than to have suffered what happened to them. For instead of remaining steady land-forces, soldiers accustomed to the sea often jump onto ships and quickly retreat, thinking they do nothing shameful when they do not dare to await the enemy's attack and die; instead, they have excuses ready so that, having thrown away their weapons, they may flee in a way that is—as they say—not at all "disgraceful." Indeed, such words are often heard in naval warfare—words worthy not of any praise, but of the highest reproach. For one should never accustom people, especially the best part of the citizens, to bad habits. 

In **Homer** too, this refuge of ships seems to be condemned. <margin>Ulysses's rebuke of Agamemnon</margin> For **Ulysses** rebukes **Agamemnon**, who, while the Greeks were occupied in battle against the Trojans, ordered them to draw the ships down into the sea. Ulysses, taking this badly, says: *"Do you order us, while the storm of war is pressing, to draw the well-decked ships into the deep, so that all things may succeed according to the Trojans' prayers, while ruinous slaughter and destruction follow us? For the men will not commit themselves to the heavy fight when they see the ships ready for flight on the sea; but, neglecting the battle, they will withdraw and fly from there."* From this, it is clear what sort of counsel that was. It is evident, therefore, that Homer also felt that triremes <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars.</note> kept ready for the flight of the combatants are a hindrance. Indeed, even lions, if they adopted such habits, would become accustomed to fleeing like deer. Furthermore, the powers of cities that rely on naval forces for their safety do not distribute honors to the best part of the military. For when the art of the pilot, and the fifty...

# FOLIO 324.

## ON THE LAWS OR ON LEGISLATION. DIALOGUE IV.

P iiii

...when the leadership and the rowing is provided by men, and a naval matter is carried out by the labor of both [virtuous] men and low-born men, one cannot rightly bestow honors upon individuals. How, indeed, can a city be rightly constituted if it is deprived of this very thing?

**Clinias:** It is almost impossible. And yet, **Stranger**, <note>original: "hospes"; Guest or Stranger</note> we Cretans believe that the naval battle of the Greeks against the barbarians at Salamis saved all of Greece.

**Athenian:** And yet many of the Greeks and barbarians assert that very thing. But I, my friend, and Megillus here, say that the infantry battles at Marathon and at Plataea were, the one the beginning of salvation, and the other its completion. And we say that the Greeks were made better by these battles, but not better by the others—if we may speak thus of the battles by which we were then saved. For to the war waged at Salamis, I add that maritime battle which was joined at Artemisium. But we are now looking at the virtue of civil discipline, the nature of the region, and the order of laws. For we do not think that merely being saved and existing is to be held in the highest value by men, as the common crowd thinks, but that as long as they exist, they should be the best. This was also said by us in our previous discussions, I believe.

**Clinias:** It was clearly said.

**Athenian:** Let us therefore attend only to this: if we are traveling that same path which is best for cities in establishing a settlement and in bringing forth laws.

**Clinias:** Most certainly.

**Athenian:** Tell me then what follows: what multitude will inhabit the colony? Will it be whoever wishes from all of Crete—as if a great, overflowing crowd exists in individual cities? Or are they chosen for the strength of the land itself? For you are not gathering all who wish from the Greeks. Although I see some from Argos and Aegina and other parts of Greece inhabiting this region. But for the present, tell me: from where will the multitude of these current citizens come to you?

**Clinias:** I think they will come from all of Crete; and among other Greeks, those who come from the Peloponnese will, I believe, be especially welcomed. And what you were just saying is true—they are from Argos. Those are the ones. For the stock that is most praised here now is the Gortynian, which migrated here from Gortyn in the Peloponnese itself. But the settling of cities does not usually happen with equal ease when it does not act in the manner of a swarm <note>Comparing colonists to a swarm of bees (examina) migrating from one hive to another</note>—where one friendly race, coming from friends out of a single region, either pressed by the narrowness of the land or forced by some other such necessity, migrates to a foreign place. Sometimes it happens that when a city is shaken by seditions, one part of the citizens secedes. An entire city, conquered in war, is also sometimes found to have fled together. All these things are partly easy, in that they may be arranged in a new settlement and governed by newly established laws, and partly difficult. For a race that is of one language and the same laws, since it has a communion of sacred rites and all such things, is joined together by some friendship; but it does not easily accept other laws and a mode of government differing from the old. However, that which was stirred by sedition because of the wickedness of laws, while it longs for those first customs by which its character was corrupted, shows itself hard and disobedient to the one governing and making laws. That which flows together from various races will perhaps more willingly hear new laws, but it is entirely difficult and needs a long time so that it can breathe together—as if horses under one yoke—into one and the same thing, as they say. But the sanction of laws and the constitution of a city is for the most perfect virtue of all men.

**Clinias:** That is probable; but explain more clearly, good man, where you are going with this.

**Athenian:** O Gods, while wanting to consider and praise legislators, I seem to have slipped into a common saying. Yet if it is said opportunely, it will cause no trouble. What then disturbs me? It seems that almost all human affairs are thus.

**Clinias:** About what are you speaking?

**Athenian:** I was about to say that no mortal ever ordains anything by law; but fortunes and various incidents of chance bring all laws to us. For either the violence of an imminent war <margin>What things they are that produce laws</margin> perverts the former republic and changes the laws, or some extreme poverty. Diseases also compel many innovations. A long-lasting plague also, and the inconveniences of many years, and unseasonable weather. If anyone observes these things, he will not fear to cry out as I do now: that no mortal establishes laws, but all human affairs are driven by fortunes. If someone affirms this regarding navigation, pilotage, medicine, or military command, he will be seen to speak rightly. But again, this is also well said in the same way about these very things.

**Clinias:** What exactly?

**Athenian:** That God, indeed, governs all things; and fortune and opportunity <margin>God and fortune and opportunity govern all things together.</margin> together with God govern all human affairs. Yet it must be granted more mildly that a third follows the former: namely, art. <note>original: "arte"; skill, craft, or technical knowledge</note> For when a storm is imminent, I think it makes a great difference whether you have the art of pilotage or not. Or how should it be said?

**Clinias:** Exactly so.

**Athenian:** Is it not the same reason in other things? And yet the same must be attributed to the making of laws: so that when other things coincide that lead to the happy habitation of a region, a legislator who is a master of truth should not be lacking to the city itself.

**Clinias:** You speak the truth.

**Athenian:** Will not he who has the art in each of those things be able to pray that something may be fortunately present for him from fortune, so that there is need for nothing other than his skill?

**Clinias:** Very much so.

**Athenian:** All the others also, whom we just mentioned—if anyone asks them, they will reveal their prayers and vows. Will they not?

**Clinias:** Clearly.

**Athenian:** The legislator, I believe, will do the same.

**Clinias:** I think so.

**Athenian:** Come then, let us ask him thus: "O legislator, what sort of city do you wish to be handed over to you, so that you yourself may afterwards be able to sufficiently arrange it from the rest?" What will be rightly said next? Or should the legislator's response be brought forward?

**Clinias:** By all means.

**Athenian:** "Hand over to me a city subject to a tyranny," <note>In the Greek sense, "tyranny" refers to a city with a single absolute ruler, which Plato suggests is the fastest way to implement radical legal changes.</note> he will say. "And let the tyrant be young, mindful, sharp, brave, and by nature magnificent." <margin>A city subject to a tyranny is to be handed over</margin> And that which we said in previous parts ought to follow all parts of virtue, let that also be in the tyrannical soul—if the other things are to be of use.

**Clinias:** It seems to me, **Stranger**, that Megillus says temperance <note>original: "temperantia"; also translated as moderation or self-control</note> ought to be in the tyrant’s soul. Is it not so?

**Athenian:** I mean popular temperance, O Clinias—not that which someone, extolling it, would show should be called prudence—but that very affection which appears immediately innate in beasts and children, so that some are born more prone to pleasure and others more continent. By which continence...

<summary>The Athenian discusses how a city's population—whether homogeneous or mixed—affects its laws, and argues that while God and Fortune govern human affairs, the "Art" of a legislator is crucial. He concludes that the ideal starting point for a new legal system is a city ruled by a young, virtuous tyrant who can quickly implement changes.</summary>

...separated from other good things, we have considered it of little value. Do you hold what I say?

**Clinias:** Most certainly.

**Athenian:** Let a tyrant <note>In this context, a "tyrant" is not necessarily a cruel villain, but an absolute ruler with the power to change laws instantly.</note> have this nature in addition to those higher qualities of nature: if a city is to achieve that governance by which it may live most happily as quickly and as well as possible. For no disposition of a city is, or can be, faster or better.

**Clinias:** How and by what reasoning, **Stranger**, <note>original: "hospes"; Guest or Stranger</note> will someone be persuaded that what you say is correct?

**Athenian:** It is easy to understand, Clinias, that this is the nature of things.

**Clinias:** What do you say? Do you assert it to be so if the tyrant is young, temperate, strong in wit and memory, brave, magnificent, and fortunate?

**Athenian:** Add nothing else, except that in his time a legislator worthy of praise be found: and that a certain fortune brings them together. If this happens, God will have given almost everything he is accustomed to give whenever he wants a city to be most happy. Next, if there are two such princes. Third, if there are three. And by the same reason of succession, the more there are, the more difficult; and conversely, the fewer, the easier.

**Clinias:** You seem to affirm that the best republic is formed from a tyranny—that with a supreme legislator and a modest tyrant, the change from the current state into the best one happens most easily and quickly. Second from the power of the few <note>Oligarchy</note>. Third from the popular power <note>Democracy</note>. Is it not so?

**Athenian:** Not at all. Rather, from tyranny first. Then from royal governance. Third from a certain popular power. Finally, the power of the few accepts the generation of an optimal republic with the greatest difficulty, for very many are powerful in it. But we say these things happen when a true founder of laws is found by nature, and a certain common power falls to him alongside those who are most powerful in the city. Where there are very few in number, but supreme in power—as happens in a tyranny—there a quick and easy change is customary.

**Clinias:** In what way? For we do not understand.

**Athenian:** But indeed, not just once, but more often, I think, has this been said by us. But perhaps you have never seen a city weighed down by tyranny.

**Clinias:** I certainly have no desire to see it.

**Athenian:** And yet what we just said, you will observe in it.

**Clinias:** What then?

**Athenian:** That it does not require much labor nor a long time for a tyrant wishing to change the morals of a city. For whether he wants to lead the citizens toward the duties of virtue or against them, he himself must first enter the path which the others follow. He must prescribe everything first by expressing it in himself through action: praising and honoring some things, while blaming others, and always shaming those who do not obey in individual actions.

**Clinias:** How indeed shall we think it anything but a great or arduous thing everywhere, that citizens should follow him immediately when he so persuades and compels them?

**Athenian:** Let no one persuade you, O friends, that laws in a city are changed in any other way more quickly and easily than by the example of princes. Nor should you think it happens faster now, or will in the future. Indeed, this is neither impossible for us, nor difficult to do. But that which is difficult to do, and rarely done in a long time, is this: which if it should ever happen, it will produce innumerable and immense goods for the city to which it occurs.

**Clinias:** What is that?

**Athenian:** If ever a divine love of acting temperately and justly is born in a great power—which is either in the power of one man, or in the leadership of many who excel in wealth or nobility of birth. Or if ever someone brings back the nature of Nestor, whom they say excelled all others far more in eloquence of speech and temperance of life—a man of such a kind as is said to have existed in the times of Troy, but not at all in ours. If, I say, such a man ever was, or will be, or is now among us, he himself lives happily; and those also are happy who hear the words flowing from a modest mouth. The same reasoning applies to all power: namely, when in the same man supreme power meets together with prudence and temperance, then finally the origin of the best governance and the best laws will shine forth; but otherwise never. But let these things be said like a kind of story in the manner of oracles, and let it be shown, partly that it is difficult for a city to be founded on good laws, but partly that if what we said happens, it is by far the easiest and shortest work of time of all.

**Clinias:** In what way?

<margin>
It is difficult to found a city with good laws.
</margin>

**Athenian:** But let us now attempt, adapting the whole matter to your city like elders telling stories to children, to fashion laws in our speech.

**Clinias:** Let us approach it now without delay.

**Athenian:** Let us first of all invoke God for the constitution of the city. May He hear us; and hearing, may He come to us favorable and kind, to adorn the city and its laws together with us.

**Clinias:** I pray He comes.

**Athenian:** But what kind of discipline do we wish to hand over to the city?

**Clinias:** Declare if you please what you wish to say: whether by the power of the people, or of the few, or of the best, or a kingdom. For we do not think you mean a tyranny.

**Athenian:** Come now, which of you wishes to answer me first: which of these is the republic of your fatherland?

**Megillus:** Is it not right, since I am older, that I myself should answer first?

**Clinias:** Perhaps.

**Megillus:** When I revolve the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> republic in my mind, **Stranger**, I cannot easily tell you what it should be called. For it seems similar to a tyranny, for the power of the Ephors <note>The five elected leaders of Sparta who oversaw the kings.</note> there is wonderfully tyrannical. Yet sometimes, above other cities, it appears most similar to a popular governance. But to deny that it is a republic of the best <note>Aristocracy</note> is altogether absurd. There is also a perpetual kingdom in it, which is said by others and by ourselves to be the most ancient of all. Therefore, having been asked so suddenly, in truth, as I was saying, I cannot at present answer you distinctly which of those it is.

**Clinias:** It seems to me also, Megillus, just as it happened to you. For I do not know which of those I should affirm the Gnosian <note>Cretan</note> republic to be most of all.

**Athenian:** For you, O best of men, are participants in true republics. But those just named are not republics, but certain dwellings of cities in which one part serves another dominant part; and from the power of the dominant part, the whole...

<margin>
God must be invoked before all works are begun.
</margin>

# FOLIO CCCXV.

## ON THE LAWS, OR THE LATIN DIALOGUE IIII.

<margin>
Note on Saturn.

...yet governance receives these things. However, if a city is to be named in this way, it ought to be called after the name of God himself, who is the true master of those who possess reason.

**CLINIAS:** But who is this God?

**ATHENIAN:** Should we use a myth for a short while, if we wish to properly explain what has just been asked? Or should we not do so?

**CLINIAS:** We should certainly do so.

**ATHENIAN:** Long before the settlements of cities, of which we made mention above, a certain leadership and governance under Saturn <note>original: "Saturno"; refers to the Golden Age of the god Cronus in Greek mythology.</note> is said to have been exceedingly happy. The government that is now ruled by the best people <note>The aristocracy.</note> bears a certain imitation of it.

**CLINIAS:** It seems we must listen more attentively to this.

**ATHENIAN:** So it seems to me as well; that is why I have brought it forward now.

**MEGILLUS:** You are quite right; and you will do well if you explain the following myth as far as it is fitting.

**ATHENIAN:** I shall do as you say. Indeed, the fame of that blessed life has reached us: it is said to have had all things in abundance and prepared of their own accord. The cause of this is handed down as follows. Saturn understood—just as we have related—that no human nature is capable of governing human affairs with absolute power without being filled with insolence, pride, and injustice. Knowing this, he did not appoint men, but rather **daemons** <note>original: "demones"; in the Platonic sense, these are divine or semi-divine spirits acting as intermediaries between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> of a more divine and excellent kind, as kings and princes for our cities. 

<margin>
Daemons and how [he] understands.
</margin>

We do the same now with flocks of sheep and herds of tame cattle. For we do not appoint oxen over oxen, nor goats over goats; instead, we, a better species, rule over them. In the same way, God, loving humanity, appointed the more excellent race of daemons over our race. With great ease, both for themselves and for us, they took care of our affairs, providing peace, modesty, liberty, and an abundance of justice; they made the human race free from discord and happy. 

This account, using the truth, asserts that for all cities where a mortal, rather than a god, rules, there will never be any rest from evils and labors. Instead, it commands us to imitate with all our zeal the life that existed under Saturn. Insofar as there is immortality within us, we should obey it and govern our homes and cities, both privately and publicly, calling this "distribution of the mind" the **law**. <note>original: "mentis distributionem, legem nuncupantes"; Plato here makes a pun in Greek between "nous" (mind/reason) and "nomos" (law).</note>

For if one man, or a small group, or even the power of the people, has a soul devoted to pleasure and desire and seeks to be filled with these things—and since this can never be satisfied, he is vexed by an unquenchable fire and an incurable disease—if such a power rules over a city or individuals, having immediately trampled the laws, there is no hope of safety, as I was just saying. We must consider, O Clinias, whether we should believe this reasoning, or do otherwise.

**CLINIAS:** It is necessary that we believe it.

**ATHENIAN:** Do you perceive that some think there are as many types of laws as there are types of government? We recently recounted how many types of government most people identify. Do not think we are discussing a trivial matter now; it is of the greatest importance. For we have fallen back into ambiguity regarding what "just" and "unjust" should look toward. For they say that laws should not refer to war, nor to all virtue, but rather to whatever benefits the established republic, whatever kind it may be, so that it always dominates and does not perish. They contend that the definition of justice is best understood in this way.

**CLINIAS:** In what way?

**ATHENIAN:** That which benefits the more powerful. <note>This echoes the argument made by Thrasymachus in Plato's *Republic*.</note>

**CLINIAS:** Speak more clearly.

**ATHENIAN:** Understand it thus: they say that the ruling power in a city always establishes the laws. Is it not so?

**CLINIAS:** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN:** "Do you think," he says, "that either a victorious people, or any other republic, or a tyrant, would voluntarily enact laws for any other purpose than their own benefit—that is, the stability of their own rule?"

**CLINIAS:** For no other purpose.

**ATHENIAN:** And if anyone should transgress these laws once they are established, he will be punished as an unjust person by the one who introduced these institutions and calls them "just."

**CLINIAS:** So it appears.

**ATHENIAN:** And so, justice will always maintain itself in this way.

**CLINIAS:** Indeed, this reasoning asserts that.

**ATHENIAN:** Truly, this is one of those injustices regarding leadership.

**CLINIAS:** From which ones?

**ATHENIAN:** From those I mentioned above, when we were explaining who ought to command whom. We said that parents should rule over children and grandchildren; the elders over the juniors; the noble over the ignoble. There were others, if you remember, some of which are obstacles to others. Among them was this one: we added that Pindar <note>An ancient Greek lyric poet.</note> considered it to be according to nature and a just command that the more powerful should rule over the weaker.

<margin>
Pindar.
</margin>

**CLINIAS:** These things were certainly said then.

**ATHENIAN:** Consider now to whom our city should be committed. For this has happened a thousand times in various cities.

**CLINIAS:** What exactly?

**ATHENIAN:** When there has been a struggle for leadership, those who won seized control so entirely for themselves that they granted no magistracy to the defeated or their descendants. They are always on guard lest someone from the defeated, having gained power, should rise up mindful of past evils. We deny that these are true republics; nor do we judge those laws to be right which were not established for the sake of the whole city in common. Those who establish laws for the sake of some faction we consider not citizens, but rebels; and we judge that they call their "rights" such in vain. 

We say these things for this reason: in your city, we will not give a magistracy to someone because he is wealthy, or possesses anything of that kind, such as strength, size, or nobility of birth. Rather, to him who most obeys the established laws, and in this excels others in the city, we shall give the highest service and ministry of the gods—first to the one who excels most, and second to the one in the second place. In the same way, we shall distribute individual offices according to worthiness to those who follow. I have called the magistrates "servants of the laws," not because I wish to innovate the vocabulary, but because I believe that the safety of the city depends mostly on this, and the opposite follows from the contrary.

[Catchword: ...of things]

<summary>The Athenian explains the myth of the Golden Age of Saturn, arguing that human nature is too flawed for absolute rule, and therefore law—as an expression of divine reason—must be the supreme authority. He rejects the idea that justice is merely the "interest of the stronger" and asserts that true laws must serve the common good rather than a ruling faction.</summary>

# BOOK IIII.

Truly, there is safety for that city where the law rules over the magistrates who serve it. I see that all the good things that the gods provide to cities will be present there. **CLINIAS:** By Jove, stranger, you see acutely, as your age requires. For a young man perceives these things quite bluntly, but an old man sees them most sharply. **MEGILLUS:** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN:** What then follows? Must we not consider that the colonists have now arrived and are present, and so address the remainder of our discourse to them? **CLINIAS:** What is to stop us? **ATHENIAN:** Let us therefore speak to them thus: "O men, God—as the ancient saying also testifies—containing the beginning,

<margin>God is the beginning, middle, and end of all things.</margin>

the end, and the middle of all things, proceeds straight ahead according to nature in his circuit. Judgment <note>original: "iudicium"; referring to the Greek "Dike," or Divine Justice.</note> always accompanies Him, punishing those who have fallen away from the divine law. Whoever intends to be happy adheres to this judgment and follows along in a humble and composed manner. But he who is lifted up by pride, because he excels in money or honors, or is powerful in the beauty of his body—with which a youthful mind burns together with madness and insolence—as if he needed neither ruler nor leader, but were a sufficient leader for others himself, he is utterly deserted by God. Having been deserted and having found others of this sort, he exults, throwing everything into confusion at once. To many, he seems least of all to be despised; however, shortly thereafter, punished by the blameless judgment of God, he overthrows himself, his house, and his entire city together." Since these things are thus arranged, what ought a prudent man to do and think, or what should he avoid? There is no doubt to anyone that each person ought to consider by what means he might be among those who follow God. What action, then, is loved by God and follows God? Truly one, having one ancient and principal reason: that like is friend to like, when it is moderate <note>original: "moderatum"; implying self-restraint or being "measured."</note>. But immoderate things are friends neither to each other nor to those that are moderate. God should indeed be for us the greatest measure of all things; and much more so than any man, as they say. <note>A direct rebuttal to the Sophist Protagoras, who famously claimed "Man is the measure of all things."</note> He, therefore, who is eager to be a friend to such a one, must necessarily strive as much as possible to become like Him according to his strength. And so, according to this reasoning, whoever among men is temperate <note>original: "temperatus"; meaning self-controlled.</note> is a friend to God, for he is like Him. But the intemperate man is unlike Him, differing and unjust; and other things follow similarly. But let us understand that this reasoning follows from all reason—the most beautiful and true, I believe—that it befits a good man to sacrifice to the gods and to take part in divine matters. Indeed, to pursue them with prayers, gifts, and other divine worship is the most beautiful, best, and most profitable way toward a blessed life; and it is fitting above all else. But for the wicked man, the opposite of all things happens. For the soul of the wicked is impure, while that of the good is pure. But it befits neither a good man nor God to receive gifts from the impure. Thus, the profane labor in vain concerning the gods, while all the holy do so seasonably. And this is the target, indeed, at which we ought to aim our sight. But what are the arrows intended for it? And what would be the proper impulse of those arrows, most rightly spoken? In the beginning, after the honors of the celestial gods and the gods who protect the city, if one pays the terrestrial gods their due, second and principal gifts, he will most rightly hit the mark of piety. To those gods mentioned above, there are unequal and alternating voices that correspond to what was said; after these gods, a man of sound mind will sacrifice to **daemons** <note>original: "demonibus"; intermediary spirits between gods and humans.</note>, and to heroes after the daemons. There follow the statues of the ancestral gods, properly consecrated according to the law. Finally, there is the worship of living parents, to whom it is right to pay the first and greatest debts of all the most ancient debts; for one ought to think that all he possesses belongs to those who fathered and raised him, so that he ought to provide all these things to them according to his strength: first, external goods, then also those of the body, and lastly those pertaining to the soul—paying back all these things as if they were given on loan. And for the ancient cares and pains of the parents, he should return fresh ones in their old age, when they are most in need. Furthermore, throughout one’s whole life, it is most fitting to venerate parents in words. For a most heavy punishment looms over light and fleeting words. For Nemesis <note>The goddess of divine retribution, here described as an "angel" or messenger of judgment.</note>, the messenger of judgment and observer of all such things, is set over them all. Therefore, it is necessary to yield to angry parents as they vent their spirits, whether they do so in words or in deeds, not ignoring that a father has a very great right to be angry with his son if he thinks he is being wronged by him. When parents are dead, the most fitting monuments are those constructed most moderately. One should not exceed the customary magnitude, nor make them smaller than those that the ancestors built for their own parents. It is also fitting to renew the annual cares for the deceased which bring honor, and with a fresh memory repeated daily, to always honor parents most highly, using a moderate expense according to one's fortune. If we observe these things and always lead our lives in this way, we shall each receive worthy rewards from the gods and others superior to our nature, living with great good hope. But as for what each person ought to do regarding children and grandchildren, kinsmen, friends, citizens, and strangers, while always worshipping the gods in the meeting of all these—and thus illustrating his life according to the law—the handling of the laws themselves will demonstrate this, partly by persuading and partly by compelling harsher characters through force and punishment; and thus, with the gods favoring us, it will make our city happy and blessed. But those things which it is again necessary for a legislator—who ponders the same things as I—to set forth, yet which do not seem able to be spoken conveniently under the form of law itself, I think an example of these should first be brought forward both for the lawgiver himself and for those to be instructed by the law; then the positioning of the laws should be begun, discussing all the rest according to one's strength. Such things, however, take a form that cannot easily be encompassed by a single formula. But let us take some measure of them in this way, if we can assert anything about them. **CLINIAS:** Come, tell us: what measure? **ATHENIAN:** I would certainly wish them to be most persuaded and obedient to the duties of virtue; and the legislator will strive to do this everywhere. **CLINIAS:** Why not? **ATHENIAN:** Those things which have been said seem to me to lead somewhat toward that, so that if the mind of the listener is not altogether raw...

FO. CCCXXVI.

# ON LAWS, OR THE FOURTH DIALOGUE ON LAWS

...makes the listener milder and more well-disposed toward hearing the precepts; and having become more well-disposed, he may learn more easily. Even if the law does not achieve its goal entirely, it should be considered sufficient if it succeeds in some small way. For there is no great abundance of people who strive to become the best as greatly and as quickly as possible. Many proclaim Hesiod <note>Hesiod was an early Greek poet, active around the same time as Homer.</note> to be wise when he says that the path to

<margin>Hesiod’s opinion on the path of virtue and vice.</margin>

vice is level and traveled without sweat, since it is very short. But before virtue, he says, the immortal gods placed sweat. And the path leading to it is long, steep, and rough at first; but after the summit is reached, the path that was so difficult becomes an easy track.

**CLINIAS:** He seems to speak well.

**ATHENIAN:** So it certainly is. But I wish to set before you the progress of our discourse.

**CLINIAS:** Set it forth.

**ATHENIAN:** Let us turn our speech to the legislator thus: "Tell us, O legislator: if you knew what we must do and say, would you not say it?"

**CLINIAS:** Necessarily.

**ATHENIAN:** And did we not hear him saying a little while ago that the legislator ought not to permit poets to fashion whatever they please? For they do not understand what sayings, when spoken against the laws, might harm the city.

**CLINIAS:** You speak truly.

**ATHENIAN:** If we say these things to him regarding the poets, will they be spoken modestly on our part?

**CLINIAS:** Which things?

**ATHENIAN:** An old tale, O legislator, is commonly told by us and confirmed by everyone else: that a poet, when he sits on the tripod of the Muse, <note>Original: "musæ tripode." This refers to the three-legged stool used by the Pythia at Delphi, symbolizing divine inspiration where the poet becomes a vessel for the gods.</note> is not in control of his mind, but flows like a fountain; and whatever flows in, he simply pours out.

<margin>In what manner poets behave when they are moved by the Muses.</margin>

And since his art is a kind of imitation, and expresses the contrary feelings of men, the poet is often forced to say things that contradict himself, not knowing whether these or those are true. But it is not permitted for a legislator to speak two different ways about one matter in a law; he must always declare one thing about one thing. You will notice this from what you were just saying. Since some tombs exceed the limit, others fall short, and others hold the middle, you simply praised the moderate ones and ordered only those to be made. But if I had a very wealthy wife who ordered me to bury her magnificently, I, exceeding in a poem, would praise a grand tomb; whereas a poor and stingy man would praise a small one. But he who possesses moderate wealth, if he himself is also moderate, will praise the middle path. But you should not speak as you were just speaking—namely, to say "moderate" alone—but you must explain what "moderate" is and how much. Otherwise, do not think such a speech is a law.

**CLINIAS:** You speak truly.

**ATHENIAN:** Will he who applies himself to making laws say nothing of the sort in the preamble of the laws? Will he immediately set forth what must be done and what must not, and, having imposed many penalties, turn to another law, bringing no reason to exhort or persuade?

<margin>Two ways of healing.</margin>

Let us bring forward two ways of healing, by which different doctors are accustomed to treat their patients differently; just as children beg a doctor to treat them in the easiest way, so let us ask the lawgiver. To make this comparison more fitting, do we not say there are some doctors and some assistants to doctors, whom we also call doctors?

**CLINIAS:** Entirely so.

**ATHENIAN:** Whether they be free men or slaves, who possess the art by the command of their masters, through observation, use, and experience, but not according to nature <note>The Athenian distinguishes between "empirical" doctors who learn by rote/experience and "scientific" doctors who understand the biological "nature" of the body.</note>—unlike the free doctors, who have learned the art in that way and instruct their sons: do you posit these two kinds of doctors?

**CLINIAS:** What forbids it?

**ATHENIAN:** Do you understand then, since both slaves and free people fall ill in the city, that slaves are mostly treated by slaves? These "doctors" hang around the surgeries and go around everywhere; they neither give nor receive any reason for the individual diseases of the slaves. Instead, they command proudly and stubbornly like tyrants, as if they possessed exact knowledge of what seems useful from experience; and thus they fly from one slave to another. In this way, they provide ease for the master in caring for the sick. But the free doctor mostly treats and considers the diseases of free men, so that from the beginning he inquires into the nature of the disease; he interacts with the sick man and his friends, both learning from them and teaching them as much as possible. He does not command anything until he has persuaded the patient, and thus by persuasion, he always tries to lead the sick back to health gently. Which is the better doctor and trainer: he who treats in this twofold way, or he who treats in the other way? Namely, he who accomplishes his goal by doubling his efforts, or he who does it simply and chooses the harsher and more cruel method?

**CLINIAS:** The one who acts in this twofold way, stranger, is much better.

**ATHENIAN:** Do you wish, then, for us to consider how this "twofold" and "simple" approach may be applied to making laws?

**CLINIAS:** I certainly do.

**ATHENIAN:** Tell me then, by the gods, what is the first law the lawmaker will write? Will he not, according to nature, first adorn the principle of generation <note>That is, the starting point of a new generation: marriage and birth.</note> in the city before all other laws?

**CLINIAS:** Clearly.

**ATHENIAN:** And the principle of generation in all cities is the meeting and communion of marriages.

**CLINIAS:** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN:** Therefore, if marriage laws are established first, they will be well-placed for the correct constitution of the whole city.

**CLINIAS:** That is entirely so.

**ATHENIAN:** Let us first state the "simple" law, which might go like this: "Every man shall marry between his thirtieth year and his thirty-fifth. If he does not marry, let him be fined in money and in disgrace: the money being such and such an amount, and the disgrace being of this or that kind." This is the simple law regarding marriage. But the "double" law is as follows:

<margin>Let him take a wife: He becomes eternal by procreation.</margin>

"Each man ought to marry from his thirtieth year to his thirty-fifth, considering that human nature somehow attains immortality, a thing for which everyone is by nature most eager. For there is no one who does not desire to have a perpetual name among posterity. Thus the human race lasts forever in this way: by leaving children’s children, it always attains immortality as one and the same through generation. It is a sin to deprive oneself of immortality by choice. He truly deprives himself from the heart who neglects children and a wife. Whoever obeys this law, let him be free from penalty. But he who does not obey, and reaches thirty-five years of age without marrying—let him not think a solitary life is a gain or a pleasure to him—let him be fined a certain sum of money every year, and let him not share in those honors which the younger men daily show to the elders in the city." Having compared these two laws, one can judge whether laws should be written "double," including both persuasion and threats, or if they should be made "simple" in length, using threats alone.

**MEGILLUS:** It is the Spartan custom, stranger, to always choose the shorter...

<summary>The Athenian argues that laws should include a persuasive "preamble" (the double method) rather than just a command and a penalty (the simple method), using an analogy of doctors who treat slaves versus those who treat free men. He illustrates this with a sample law on marriage, emphasizing the human desire for immortality through procreation.</summary>

<meta>The text continues the discussion from Book IV of Plato’s Laws, where the Athenian Stranger, Megillus the Spartan, and Clinias the Cretan discuss the nature of legislation. They are specifically debating whether laws should be concise or explanatory. This page transitions from the end of Book IV into the "Argument" (introduction) for Book V.</meta>

to act. If anyone were to make me a judge in these matters, so that I were allowed to choose which of these two types of law I would prefer in a city, I would choose the longer one; and in all other laws, if these two models were proposed, I would do the same. Nevertheless, the present laws must also be approved by Clinias here; for this is his city, for whose use these laws are being established.

**CLINIAS:** You speak well, Megillus.

**ATHENIAN:** To care overmuch about the length or brevity of writing is quite foolish. For it is not the shortest or the longest that should be chosen, I believe, but the best. And yet, in the laws proposed just a moment ago, it is not only that one version contributes more to virtue than the other because of its double nature, but what was said about the two types of doctors is also most correctly applied.

<margin>Note that in writing, it is not brevity or length, but what is best that should be chosen.</margin>

Indeed, it seems that no legislator has ever considered this. For while they have two means at their disposal for making laws—persuasion and force—to deal with a crowd unskilled in discipline, they use only one as far as they are able. For they do not join persuasion with threats, but only apply pure force. I, however, O blessed men, see a third thing that ought to be done in laws, which we never see happening.

**CLINIAS:** What is that?

**ATHENIAN:** Something that has been achieved by us through some divine inspiration regarding the matters we have discussed. For we began to dispute about the laws in the morning, and now it is noon; and we are resting most comfortably in this lovely place, doing nothing but debating the laws. And now, for the first time, we seem to be making a beginning of the laws to be treated. Everything before this was actually a preamble to the laws.

Why do I say this? Because I wanted to say that for all speeches and other things involving vocal imitation, there are preambles and a kind of prelude; these possess a skillful and useful treatment for the matter to be spoken. Surely, those songs called the "laws" of the kithara-player <note>The Greek word *nomos* meant both "law" and "musical melody." The Athenian is making a pun on this double meaning.</note>, and the other Muses, set forth wonderfully invented introductions. But of the true laws, which we call civil laws, no one has ever pronounced a preamble, nor brought one into the light in writing, as if none existed by nature.

To us, however, this delay and our current discussion seem to signify that such a thing exists. For the laws which were just now called "double" are not simply double; rather, they are two distinct things: the law itself, and the preamble to the law. And that which we compared to the tyrannical command of the doctors of slaves is the "pure law." But that which was stated before this, called persuasive by him, truly looks toward persuasion; yet it has the power of a preamble. For that whole speech was introduced for the sake of persuasion, so that the citizen might hear the legislator’s command (which is the law) more benevolently and, because of this, might accept it more easily. Therefore, in my opinion, this whole section should rightly be called the preamble, not the reasoning of the law.

After this, what more do I desire to be added? Simply this: that the legislator ought always to place a preamble before every law, and in each one, they should differ from one another just as those two we just mentioned differed.

**CLINIAS:** I would never desire a man skilled in these matters to carry out the laws in any other way.

<margin>Concerning preambles.</margin>

**ATHENIAN:** You seem to me to have spoken well, Clinias, because a certain preamble belongs to all laws; and it is necessary that at the beginning of every legal composition, an introduction for all the discourse be adapted to the individual laws. For what is said afterward is no small matter, nor does it matter little whether such things are recounted clearly or obscurely. But if we were to order that the preambles of great and small laws be composed in the same way, we would not be ordering correctly. For one should not do that in song nor in every speech. For even if an introduction can be found for everything, it need not be used for everything. This choice must always be granted to the orator, the singer, and the maker of laws himself.

**CLINIAS:** You speak the truth, Stranger. But let us not linger any further; instead, let us return to the proposed discourse, and let us begin, if it pleases you, from those things you said above, which you spoke without using a preamble. Therefore, as they say in games, "let us resume the better second parts from the beginning," as a definite preamble, not just a casual conversation as we were recently handling. Let us begin, then, and let us profess our starting point. Enough has been said regarding the honor of the gods and the care of our ancestors; let us strive to finish the rest, until you feel you have sufficiently completed the entire preamble. Finally, after the preamble, you shall approach the laws.

**ATHENIAN:** Since we have said enough in the preamble about the gods and those who follow the gods, and about parents, whether living or deceased, we must now bring into the light what remains, as you seem to command.

**CLINIAS:** Precisely so.

**ATHENIAN:** After those things, we must determine through common discussion how one should cultivate the things pertaining to souls, bodies, and external matters, so that both the speakers and the listeners may attain discipline according to our strength. Therefore, these things must truly be said and heard by us after the former ones.

**CLINIAS:** You speak quite rightly.

Every day we see wonders performed: by the magnet upon iron; by amber upon straws; by lightning upon solid objects; by ignited sulfur in a cannon; and by all of nature, whether in the movement of the heavens or in the skillful formation of the things that are born. We are indeed ignorant of the causes; yet we do not deny that the effects happen, which we see. Again, that wonders are sometimes performed by our souls in oracles and other portents is witnessed not only by all history, but also by the authority of Hermes <note>Original: *Mercurialis*, referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with ancient wisdom.</note>, Pythagoras, and Plato. And if we cannot all easily assign a certain reason for the amazing works of our mind, we nevertheless ought not to deny that the works have been done, or can be done. We see that fire, which is more similar to heaven than the other elements, acts more wonderfully: so that in a brief time it draws into its own form things which the other elements hardly draw in the longest time; nor does it endure mixing; and when it seems to be divided, it divides; and it extends its effect much further than the others, and acts most distantly through light and in a moment. Truly it has this from heaven, and it acts by the image of heaven—that is, light—which fire hardly accomplishes by its natural quality. Who...
