<meta>This page continues the introductory commentary (Argumentum) by Marsilio Ficino for Book V of Plato’s Laws. The previous page concluded the dialogue of Book IV, where the characters discussed the importance of "preambles" or explanations to laws. Here, Ficino transitions into the philosophical and symbolic foundations of Book V, emphasizing the soul’s role as a divine mirror and the structural alignment of the state with the cosmos.</meta>

FO. CCCXXVII.

### ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE V ON THE LAWS

...for who would doubt that celestial things, through their rays—which are as hidden to us as they are manifest to themselves—constantly move and shape lower things like images flowing from themselves? It is almost no different than how a face moves in a mirror, or how a concave mirror affects dry material placed within its view. But come now, let us look at the higher beings within the soul as if in this mirror. Just as fire is more effective than the other elements, and the heavens more effective than fire, so the spirits who either give life to or move the heavens (or are companions to those who do) are more effective than the heavens themselves. Therefore, these superior spirits work upon our own spirits—as if upon companions—only through the influence of their images, just as a face works upon a mirror. By acting upon our spirits, they shape them and make them most similar to themselves, to the point that souls often tend to work almost as miraculously as the celestial beings.

However, just as a mirror is specially prepared in five ways to receive images from a face: first, by its **glassy nature**; second, by its **transparency**; third, by its **smoothness**; fourth, by its **resistance** <note>Ficino refers to the "backing" of a mirror that reflects light rather than letting it pass through.</note>; and fifth, by its **position**; so too are our souls prepared for the influence of the divine powers. First, because they are intellectual natures just like those powers. Second, because through the intellect, an undoubting faith clings to them. Third, through the will, they transfer themselves into those powers with the most burning love. Fourth, they hope firmly with their entire memory in them. Fifth, if they possess a body that is both suited to them by nature and prepared by diligence, then divine inspirations glide into our minds from above, just as a sound moves from the strings of a lyre into other strings tuned in the same way. Then come portents, dreams, prophecies, and oracles.

I omit what Iamblichus and Porphyry <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote extensively on theurgy and the supernatural.</note> relate: that certain oracles were customary through water, some through air, and some through fire—perhaps because they are sent by demons of the water, air, or fire. Perhaps also because at different times and places, through hidden causes, it happened that the affections of human minds were turned toward higher things and, having been turned, were shaped from there. To be sure, our minds are distracted by too many things. But if ever they use their power in its integrity for a certain work—just as fire burns with the full intention of its nature and the heavens act with their full influence—then Plato does not doubt that more miraculous things will most easily come from our minds than from fire or the heavens. Avicenna and Al-Ghazali <note>Influential Islamic philosophers whose works were integrated into Western Scholasticism and Renaissance thought.</note> do not doubt this either, perhaps following the Platonists in many things.

But we dispute these matters more broadly in our *Theology*. This is greatly confirmed by that Gospel saying about **faith that will move mountains** <note>original: "evangelicum illud de fide montes permutatura"; see Matthew 17:20</note>. It is also confirmed by many things that Plato asserts about oracles in the previous book and this fifth one—indeed, in all the following ones—to the point that the arrangement of a city, the form of a republic, or the sanctioning of laws is handled no differently than if confirmed by oracles. Truly, though he mentions three oracles, he clearly grants his authority to other prophecies besides, which perhaps can be found to be even truer.

But let us now come to the specific argument of the Fifth Book. Since our soul is a mirror of divine things, Plato rightly commands that the soul itself be honored at the very start of the fifth book, right after the worship of divine things described in the fourth; he treats it as a sacred thing. In this, as he imitated the Pythagorean verses in the previous parts, he also willingly follows Pythagoras in the present cultivation of the soul, who teaches: **"After the gods, respect yourself above all"** <note>original: "Post deos maxime omnium revere teipsum"</note>. I could not explain how much weight such reverence carries for the observation of laws. But this practice ensures, to speak briefly, that whoever respects the constant sight of their own soul as if it were a divinity has a judge within themselves. By the law of this judge, they may direct their life most perfectly even without written laws, and finally, out of love for natural law, they will easily do what others barely do out of fear of written laws.

Consequently, while he disputes the honoring of the soul, he hands down all the precepts regarding duties, pertaining both to oneself and to others, and to all virtues both private and public, which everyone ought to learn and memorize. After this, he places an end to the "preamble" of the laws. Here it appears that the entire disputation on laws is divided into three main parts:
1.  **The Prologue (Prooemium)**, which extends from the beginning of the first book to this part of the fifth.
2.  **The Arrangement of the Laws themselves**, specifically those pertaining to the republic and the magistrates.
3.  **Laws regarding the individual actions of citizens.**

I believe you remember, moreover, that each individual law has its own individual preamble. At the beginning of the laws, let him choose the purest colonists according to their strength; and in the manner of a shepherd, let him separate the pure from the impure. Let him also purify the city; and unless the greatest necessity compels it, let him not introduce violence. Let him equalize wealth according to ability, so that some are not extremely rich while others are beggars. Let him beware lest anyone accumulate wealth unjustly. Nor should he strive to make the city the most opulent, but the most just. Let him preach that **Truth** is to be honored above all things, both among men and among gods. Likewise, hospitality toward strangers and indulgence toward suppliants. Let him warn that every soul is prone to be deceived and perverted by self-love. Let him command that no one who is himself in abundance should allow his neighbor to go hungry. Let him place the city, if possible, in a central region with every convenience considered.

Let him divide the city into twelve parts, and the entire surrounding region as well. But why into twelve parts? So that you may understand that such a great and laborious mass requires the help of the universe itself, which is distributed into twelve spheres. Likewise, the city is to be ruled according to the image of the heavenly kingdom. The heavenly city is distributed into twelve signs, like twelve tribes. Not without reason does he commend his city to the twelve gods, since the twelve gods are said to preside over the twelve signs of heaven. Indeed, there are six gods and six goddesses: Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, and Venus; and Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, and Apollo.

Assign each sign to each of our limbs:
*   To **Aries** and our head, assign **Pallas** (Minerva).
*   To **Taurus** and our neck, **Venus**.
*   To **Gemini** and the human arms, **Apollo**.
*   To **Cancer** and the chest, **Mercury**.
*   To **Leo** and the shoulders, **Jupiter**.
*   To **Virgo** and the belly, **Ceres**.
*   To **Libra** and the buttocks <note>original: "natibus," followed by "quod honeste dictum sit" — "to speak decently"</note>, **Vulcan**.
*   To **Scorpio** and the private parts, **Mars**.
*   To **Sagittarius** and the thigh, **Diana**.
*   To **Capricorn** and the knees, **Vesta**.
*   To **Aquarius** and the legs, **Juno**.
*   To **Pisces** and the feet, **Neptune**.

Understand through these things that the whole city ought to be no different—one made of many citizens—than one body made of many members. Some deities are called masculine and others feminine for this reason: so that you may know which pertain to matter and passions, and which pertain to forms and actions...

PAGE XXXIIII.
LIBER

...to be governed by those above. But why does Plato consecrate the chief citadel of the city to Vesta, Jupiter, and Pallas? Understand that in divine matters there exist three fountains of all things: Vesta as the fountain of **being**, Jupiter as the fountain of **living**, and Minerva <note>original: "Palladi/Minerva"; Ficino uses the names interchangeably for the goddess of wisdom.</note> as the fountain of **understanding**. And in all these, help is to be implored from the higher powers. 

Where indeed Plato commends the division of homes and fields into five thousand and forty, he shows that such a number contains within itself the most convenient and numerous subsequent distributions of parts. <note>The number 5,040 is a "highly composite number" with 60 divisors, including every number from 1 to 10, making it ideal for a legislator to divide a population for administrative or military purposes.</note> This indeed he will gradually reveal in the following sections, and it can be clear even to an average arithmetician. You will note, where he discusses the common life of citizens, a wonderful precept concerning evangelical love and charity. <note>Ficino, a priest as well as a philosopher, often highlights parallels between Plato’s ethics and Christian "charity" (caritas).</note> Likewise, he notes that the fatherland is to be honored more than one's mother. Or where he says the fatherland is an "immortal goddess": think of it as being said either about the divine soul of the terrestrial world, or about the deity who is the patron of the fatherland, or about the heavenly homeland.

### FIFTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, OR ON LEGISLATION.

<margin>
The soul of each person is the most divine thing after all the gods.
</margin>

<margin>
After the gods, our soul is to be cultivated.
Honor is a divine good. Nothing among evil things is to be honored.
</margin>

ATHENIAN: Let whoever was listening a little while ago about the gods and their most dear parents now hear the rest. For each person's soul, being the most one’s own of all his possessions after the gods, is the most divine. Those things which are one's own are divided in two. The more powerful and better things rule, while the weaker and worse things serve. Surely that which rules should always be honored above those things which serve. Wherefore I rightly command that our soul be cultivated after the ruling gods—and those who follow them—and be held in the second place. 

But no one, to speak briefly, rightly honors his soul as it should be seen. For honor is a *divine good*. But nothing among evil things is to be honored. Therefore, whoever thinks he can extol his soul by certain speeches, gifts, or submissions, yet does not make it better instead of worse, may *seem* to honor it, but he does not actually do so. For immediately from childhood everyone thinks himself sufficient to know all things, and thinks he honors his own soul by praising it and allowing himself to do whatever he pleases. But we say that he who does these things does not honor the soul, but harms it; yet we say the soul is to be honored in the second place after the gods. 

Neither does he honor it who, regarding his own sins and his many great crimes, considers others to be the cause and not himself. Such a person, while excusing himself, seems to honor his soul, yet he is far from it, since he harms it. Nor does he honor his soul when he indulges in pleasures against the reason and praise of the legislator; rather, he casts it down, for he fills it with evils and repentance. Nor does he honor it when he fails to undertake the labors praised by the law, or the fears and pains that must be borne, but instead yields and succumbs. For in doing all these things he <unclear>disgraces</unclear> his soul. 

Nor does he honor it when he considers this life to be the highest good; indeed, then he also disgraces it. For he assents to the soul's notion that all things among the spirits of the dead are evil, and he does not resist it, though he should teach and refute it, as if he were ignorant whether the things among the gods below might actually be the greatest of all goods for us. Furthermore, he who prefers the beauty of the body to virtue truly and deeply disgraces the soul. Nor should the body be thought more venerable than the soul. In this he certainly errs greatly. For nothing of the earth is more venerable than celestial things. And he who thinks otherwise of the soul is utterly ignorant of how he neglects a miraculous thing. 

Again, he who desires money unjustly, or does not grieve while possessing it unjustly, does not adorn his soul with gifts; he is very far from it. For what is venerable and beautiful in the soul, he betrays for a little gold; when all the gold that is upon the earth or beneath the earth cannot worthily be compared to virtue. 

<margin>
All gold cannot be weighed against virtue.
</margin>

Finally, to speak summarily: whoever flees with all his zeal those things the legislator considers foul and evil, and follows with all his strength those things he has established as good and beautiful, does not see that in all these things he affects his most divine soul in a foul and absurd way. For no one, to say it in one word, notices the greatest vengeance for acting badly according to justice. The greatest vengeance is this: that one becomes similar to evil men. Having become like them, he flees good men and their words, and separates himself from them; instead, he clings to the wicked and embraces their company. It is necessary for him who mixes with such people to suffer and do the same things that such people are accustomed to do and say among themselves. 

<margin>
Justice [as] vengeance.
</margin>

And such a suffering is not "justice," for justice and what is just are honorable. Rather, it is vengeance, a suffering that follows injustice. Both he who does not fall into it and he who does fall into it are evil and miserable: the former because he is not healed, the latter because he perishes so that many others may be saved. Honor, however—to embrace the whole concept at once—is to follow better things, and to lead whatever is worse back to the best possible state. For surely nothing is more suited or more keen for a man’s soul than to flee evil and to investigate and choose what is best of all, and to adhere firmly to it throughout his whole life. 

Therefore, honor is established for the soul in the second place. One will then understand that the third honor, according to nature, belongs to the body. One must consider which are true honors and which are counterfeit; the difference between them, it seems to me, must be declared by the legislator. For example, a body is not worthy of honor because it is beautiful or robust or fast or large or healthy (though many might see it so), nor because it is affected in contrary ways. Surely those bodies that touch the middle state of all these habits are to be judged far more moderate and safe. For some states make souls inflated and bold, while others make them cast down and illiberal. 

<margin>
The third honor is to be held for the body.
An excessive possession of riches breeds enmities and seditions; a deficient one breeds slavery.
</margin>

Similarly it is with the possession of money, estates, and wealth. For an excess of these breeds enmities and seditions both privately and in cities. A deficiency, however, for the most part breeds slavery. Let no one, therefore, for the sake of his children, labor to accumulate money so as to leave them very rich. For this is conducive neither to them nor to the city. Rather, let wealth be free from flattery, yet not lacking in necessary things...

# ON THE LAWS, OR THE LATIN DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, BOOK V. FOLIO 328.

<margin>Not gold, but a sense of shame should be left to children.</margin>
...is the most decent and best of all who are in need. For this man, being in harmony with us and adapted to all things, removes life from pains. Therefore, one ought to leave to children not a wealth of gold, but a great store of reverence <note>original: "pudoris"; in this context, it refers to a moral sense of shame or respect that prevents wrong-doing.</note>. We think we shall accomplish this by chastising the shamelessness of the youth with words. But this does not happen through that kind of chastisement in which people strike at the young, saying that an adolescent ought to be modest in all things. Instead, a wise lawmaker will command the elders to behave with reverence before the younger ones, and to take the greatest care that no youth sees or hears them doing or saying anything base. For where the old are less modest, it is inevitable that the young there will be most shameless. For the excellent discipline of both the young and the old is not the rebuking of words, but rather that a man is seen doing those very things in his own life which he would say while rebuking or advising. Moreover, whoever honors and cherishes his kinship and the entire community of his race under the same household gods, will rightly find these gods favorable in the procreation of his own children. He will also obtain the greatest goodwill from his friends and companions in the habit of life, if he considers their services to him to be greater and more excellent than they do, while he considers his own benefits toward them to be smaller than they themselves judge them to be.

<margin>On the estimation of service toward others.</margin>
Furthermore, he will conduct himself best toward the state and the citizens who prefers the glory he gains by serving the laws of his fatherland over every victory achieved in the Olympics or other contests of war or peace; and in this service, he shall strive to excel all others throughout his whole life. Regarding foreigners, let each man consider their treaties to be most sacred. For nearly all sins of foreigners and against foreigners, compared to those committed among citizens, are the concern of a vengeful God. For since a foreigner lacks friends and kinsmen, he earns greater mercy from both gods and men. Therefore, he who is more able to take revenge is more ready to bring help: and the spirit <note>original: "demon"; referring to a protective guardian spirit.</note> and god of each guest, following Jupiter the Protector of Guests <note>original: "Iouem hospitalem"; Jupiter in his role as the divine enforcer of hospitality (Xenia).</note>, is most powerful in this. Therefore, everyone who has any wisdom must consider with diligent caution that he always lives innocent of injury toward foreigners. But of all sins, whether against foreigners or citizens, the greatest is that which is committed against suppliants <note>term: "supplices" — individuals, often fleeing danger, who formally beg for protection or mercy, usually at a religious altar.</note>. For the God through whom the suppliant has obtained his treaty is his most diligent guardian. Therefore, no one who is wicked toward suppliants will go unpunished. Thus far, we have set forth nearly all the duties of each person toward parents, oneself, one's possessions, the fatherland, friends, kinsmen, foreigners, and settlers. Now, let us explain what sort of person each one ought to be regarding himself if he wishes to live as well as possible; so that not only the law, but praise and blame, teaching each individual, may restrain them more and make them more obedient to the laws that are to be passed. And these things are what we must say next. Truth is surely the leader of all goods for both gods and men. He who is to be happy and blessed must be a partaker of it from the very beginning, so that he may live his life in truth for as much time as possible. Such a man is certainly faithful; but he who lies voluntarily is unfaithful; and he who lies involuntarily is foolish. Neither of these is desirable. For both the unfaithful and the foolish man are quite estranged from friendship; and as time passes and they are found out, they fall into such great solitude in hateful old age at the end of life that, whether their friends and children are living or dead, they lead a wretched and nearly orphaned life. Certainly, he who does no injury is to be honored.

<margin>Duties toward the fatherland.</margin>
<margin>Duties toward foreigners.</margin>
<margin>Toward suppliants.</margin>
<margin>Truth is the leader of all goods. Who is faithful, unfaithful, and a liar.</margin>

<margin>Who is to be honored with single and double honor.</margin>
But he who does not even allow others to do so is to be honored with double honor, or rather, even more. For the former is compared to one man, but this latter man is compared to many, since he reports the injuries of others to the rulers. He who, together with the magistrates, takes revenge for an injury as far as he can, shall be proclaimed a great and perfect man in the city. For he excels all in virtue. There is also the same praise for temperance and wisdom. And he who abounds in other goods which can be poured out into others, if he makes the rest participants, is to be honored as a most supreme man. But he who would wish to do so but cannot, is to be held in the second place. We ought to rebuke the envious man who voluntarily confers nothing good on others; yet we should not rebuke the thing itself because of the man who possesses it badly, but rather strive for it with all our might. Furthermore, let each of us compete for virtue without envy. For he who acts thus amplifies his city; while he himself contends, he does not hold others back with slanders. But the envious man, while he thinks to excel by detracting from others, moves less rightly toward true virtue himself, and makes his fellow-competitors slower by his unjust rebukes. Therefore, by removing the vehement desire for acquiring virtue from the city, he deprives it, for his own part, of the fullness of glory. Moreover, it is necessary for everyone to be both spirited <note>original: "animosum"; having "thymos" or high-spirited courage.</note> and exceedingly mild. For we cannot escape the injuries of others, which are either difficult or impossible to cure, in any other way than by battle, defense, victory, and the remission of no sin; which no one can do without spiritedness. But in those injuries which are such that they can be cured, one must first know that no unjust man is unjust voluntarily. For no one would ever want to have any of the greatest evils anywhere; and much less in those things which are most excellent to himself. But the soul, as we have said, is truly the most excellent of all things in everyone. Therefore, since it is to be honored most of all, no one will voluntarily accept the greatest evil and wish to possess it through his whole life. Furthermore, every unjust man is entirely miserable, as is anyone who has anything of evil. It is fitting to pity those who are curable and to restrain one's anger, lest the mind be carried away by a womanly heat of wrath against them and persist too harshly. But for those who are so shameful as to be incurable, anger must be let loose more vehemently. For this reason, we said that a good man ought always to be spirited (that is, not lacking in noble wrath) and at the same time mild. But a certain greatest evil of all is innate in the souls of many men. Because they easily forgive themselves for this, they devise no remedy. It is this which people are accustomed to say: that by nature everyone is a friend to himself, and it is right that it be so. But in truth, excessive love for oneself is always the cause of all sins for all men. For the lover is blinded concerning the thing loved. Therefore, he who loves himself, since he thinks himself more worthy of honor than the truth, judges poorly what is just, good, and beautiful. It is surely fitting for him who is to be a great man to love neither himself nor his own things, but rather just things...

<margin>Good things are not to be rebuked because of a bad possessor.</margin>
<margin>No unjust person is unjust voluntarily.</margin>
<margin>The evil implanted in souls, the greatest of all, is excessive love for oneself. He who is to be great ought to love neither his own nor himself.</margin>

### BOOK V. PAGE 34.

<margin>Why it happens that while we know nothing, we think we know everything.</margin>...always, whether they are carried out by oneself or by anyone else. From this very fault, it happens to everyone that they mistake their own ignorance for wisdom. Hence it follows that, while we know nothing (so to speak), we nevertheless believe we know everything. Since we do not entrust the power of acting to others when we ourselves do not know how to do those things, we are forced to fall into error while doing them ourselves. Therefore, everyone ought to flee excessive love of oneself and instead follow those who are better, hindered by no blush of shame. There are also several other matters, smaller than these and often mentioned; but since they are no less useful, they must also be spoken of. For there is a need for constant reminding. For always, as if something flows out, something else ought to flow in to replace it. Recollection <note>original: "recordatio"</note> is, in fact, the remedy for a failing influx of wisdom. Truly, one must abstain from excessive laughter and tears; and it must be understood by everyone that excessive joy and compressed sadness should be held within a decent manner. This holds true whether a divine spirit <note>original: "daemon"; here referring to a guiding spirit or a person's allotted fate</note> establishes someone in happiness, or whether, through the accidents of fortune, opposing spirits rise up against certain actions as people strive toward steep and difficult things. Good men ought always to hope that the gifts God is accustomed to give to such men will not be lacking for them. And if any heavy labors should occur, that He will make them lighter and change present circumstances for the better; while on the contrary, good things along with good fortune will be present for them against all evils. In this hope individuals should live, and both in jest and in earnest they should diligently exhort both themselves and others to frequent remembrance of these things. 

But now, what each person ought to do and what sort of person he should be regarding divine duties has been said. Human matters, however, we have not yet explained. But they must be spoken of. For we are teaching humans, not gods. Furthermore, pleasures, pains, and desires are, by nature, most human. From these it is necessary that every mortal animal hang, as it were, and indeed with the greatest zeal. Certainly, the most honorable life is to be praised, not only because it excels in its state of glory, but also because if anyone wishes to taste it—and not immediately flee from it from youth—it also excels in that which we all seek: that throughout our whole life we may rejoice more than we grieve. That this will truly be the case if anyone tastes it rightly will be very easily and clearly evident. But in what way it may rightly be done must now be considered by reason, whether it is naturally in us in this way, or otherwise against nature. 

<margin>Concerning the choice of life regarding pleasures and pain.</margin>Therefore, one ought to compare one life to another—the more pleasant to the more troublesome—in this way. We wish pleasure to be present for us. We neither choose nor wish for pain. We by no means wish for a neutral state in place of pleasure, yet we accept it in place of pain. We also wish for a lesser pain accompanied by a greater pleasure. We by no means wish for a lesser pleasure accompanied by a greater pain. In like manner, we can declare that we do not want to have an equal amount of both. All these things differ or do not differ in the choice and will of individuals based on their number, magnitude, intensity, equality, and their opposites. Since these things are necessarily so, we want that life in which both pleasure and pain are many, great, and intense, provided that pleasures exceed. But we do not want that life in which the opposite is true. And again, we do not want that life in which, although both are small and relaxed, the troublesome things nevertheless overcome; but we want that in which the opposite is true. But if they are equal, we must think of an equal life as we said. For we want the things that exceed in that which we love, and we do not want those that are overcome by the opposite. 

It is necessary to consider how all our lives are naturally connected in these things, and which ones we would naturally want. If we say we want something else besides these, we say it through a certain ignorance and lack of experience of lives. Which, therefore, and how many are the lives in which it is necessary to know what should be avoided and what should be wanted—what is usually done voluntarily and what is contrary—and, having known these things, to prescribe a law for oneself? And from there, to choose what is friendly to oneself and simultaneously pleasant, best, and most beautiful, so that one may live as happily as is possible for a human. 

<margin>Concerning the temperate and intemperate life.</margin>Shall I say the temperate life is one? The prudent another; the brave a third; the healthy a fourth. And let us establish four others contrary to these: the imprudent, the cowardly, the intemperate, and the sickly. Whoever knows the temperate life will find it mild and moderate in all things; it has quiet pains, relaxed pleasures, soft desires, and loves that are not at all furious. But the intemperate life is sharp in all things: it is agitated by vehement pains and vehement pleasures, by burning desires, and by furious and insane loves in a wonderful way. 

<margin>The whole human crowd lives devoid of temperance. Which kind of life is chosen.</margin>But in the temperate life, pleasures exceed, while pains are exceeded. In the intemperate life, on the contrary, pleasures are exceeded by pains in magnitude, number, and frequency. Whence it happens that necessarily one life is more pleasant for us according to nature, the other more sorrowful; and it does not permit one who wishes to live pleasantly to live voluntarily and intemperately. For it is established, if what has just been said was said correctly, that every intemperate person is necessarily such against his own judgment. Indeed, either through ignorance or lack of self-control <note>original: "incontinentia"; the inability to resist impulses even when knowing they are wrong</note>, or both, the whole human crowd lives devoid of temperance. Similarly one must think about the healthy and the sickly life: both have pains and pleasures, but in health, pleasures exceed; in sickness, pains. Our will in choosing a kind of life is not that pain should exceed. But where pleasure exceeds, we have judged that life to be more pleasant. Therefore, the temperate person over the intemperate, the prudent over the imprudent, the brave over the cowardly, has both [pains and pleasures] in fewer, smaller, and rarer amounts; and one life exceeds in pleasures, the other in pains; so that the brave man exceeds the coward, the prudent the fool, the temperate the wanton, and the healthy the sick in pleasure. To summarize, whichever life partakes of virtue in body or soul is more pleasant than its opposite, and excels in beauty, correctness, power, and glory, so that he who is established in it lives more happily than his opposite in all things.

But now let the prelude <note>original: "exordium"; Plato argues that laws should have a persuasive introduction to win the citizens' consent</note> of the laws come to an end. After the prelude, it is necessary for the law to follow. Indeed, the laws of the republic must truly be written hereafter. Therefore, just as whatever things are woven are not woven entirely from similar materials in the warp and the woof <term>warp and woof (stamine et trama): The "warp" are the strong vertical threads on a loom; the "woof" are the softer horizontal threads woven through them. Plato uses this as a metaphor for social roles.</term>, but the type of warp is more robust and firmer, while the woof is softer so that it yields more easily: in the same way, the men who are to hold magistracies in the city must always be distinguished...

<summary>This page concludes the philosophical introduction (prelude) to the Laws, using a "hedonic calculus" to argue that a life of virtue and temperance is naturally more pleasant than a life of vice. It ends by transitioning into the actual drafting of laws, using the metaphor of weaving to explain the different characters required for citizens and rulers.</summary>

FOLIO 329.
### OF THE LAWS, OR THE LATIN DIALOGUES ON THE LAWS. BOOK V.
Q

...and those who prove themselves in the lighter stages of education. Truly, there are two forms in a republic: one is the appointment of magistrates, and the other is the constitution of the laws. But before all these things, one must consider this: when a shepherd, an ox-herd, a horse-groom, or others of this kind take charge of flocks and herds, they do not care for them until they first apply a suitable cleansing <note>original: "purgationem"; Plato compares social engineering to animal husbandry</note> to each. Furthermore, after separating the healthy from the sick and the well-bred from the lazy, they will send some into other flocks and tend to the others; they know that otherwise they would labor in vain for both body and soul. Indeed, the depravity of nature and education corrupts so much that unless one separates the healthy—keeping integrity from death and the various types of bodies—they will eventually be destroyed by contagion.

But there is less concern for other animals, and mention of them is made only for the sake of example. The legislator will have the greatest zeal for human beings and will diligently examine everything so that he can write what is appropriate for each, both concerning ritual purification <note>original: "lustratione"</note> and all other actions. Thus do the purifications of a city stand: they are many, some lighter and others more severe. If any tyrant should also be a law-giver, he could use the most difficult and best purifications. However, for a law-giver without a tyrant's power, who founds new laws and a republic, it will be sufficient if he applies the mildest cleansing. For the most exact purification—just as a medicine that is applied more strongly to bodies—is full of pain; it brings punishment with just vengeance, condemning the sinner to death or exile. For it is customary to entirely remove those who have committed the greatest sins, if they are incurable, since they harm the city most of all.

But we have a milder purification of this kind: those who, because of a lack of food, are ready to follow leaders in an uprising of the needy against those who possess plenty—these the law-giver expels kindly under the honorable name of a "colony," <note>In the ancient world, sending citizens to a colony was a common way to relieve "stasis" or civil unrest caused by poverty and debt.</note> as if removing a disease that is weakening the city. All these things must be done by a law-giver from the beginning, as we have said. But for us, certain more difficult things have occurred at present. For we ought not to devise either a colony or any selection for the sake of purging at this moment; but just as water flows from mild springs and torrents into the same pools, we must observe that the liquid which flows together from all sides is as clean as possible, partly by draining and pouring it out, and partly by diverting and turning it aside.

Labor, as it seems, and danger exist in every civil constitution. But since we are dealing now not with deeds but with words, let our selection be perfected and let the purification be done as we desire. For we shall prohibit the wicked—who strive to approach and govern this city—from entering by any means after we have examined them for a long enough time; but the upright, making them as benevolent and favorable as possible according to our strength, we shall entice.

But it should not escape us how fortunately we have acted. Indeed, just as we said the colony of the Heraclidae <note>The descendants of Hercules, whose return to the Peloponnese was a foundational myth of Greek history</note> was fortunate because it escaped the dangerous contention over the division of lands and the canceling of debts—a matter which a city of old, forced to carry laws, can neither omit entirely nor move in any way—so it seems to have happened to us as well. Therefore, only a "prayer," so to speak, remains: a small and cautious change, achieved by those changing it over a short time.

This change is that, in making these transformations, the citizens should possess lands mixed together with many debtors, and they should be willing to share humanely with the needy, partly by giving and partly by receiving; they should honor the "middle way" <note>original: "mediocritatem"; the Aristotelian and Platonic ideal of the Golden Mean</note> and believe that poverty consists not in the decrease of money but in the insatiable desire for acquiring more. For this is the greatest beginning of safety for a city; upon this, as if on a stable foundation, anyone will later be able to easily build whatever is fitting and congruent for a beautiful city and this constitution. But if this foundation is weak and ruinous, no civil work will succeed prosperously thereafter.

Therefore, fleeing that, or rather showing in words how it must be fled, we say there is no other way to escape, whether wide or narrow, except that we cultivate justice and do not follow the desire for acquiring. And let this already be for us a certain established support and protection of the city. For the wealth <note>original: "census"</note> which citizens have prepared for themselves ought to be somewhat free from crime; or they should voluntarily stop proceeding further in acquiring, if they have old crimes against one another, provided they are in possession of even a little bit of their minds. But those to whom God has given the constitution of a new city, as he has to us, in which there are no enmities—if they give themselves causes for enmity because of the distribution of houses and lands, they will be marked with the crime not of some human ignorance, but of the worst kind.

What, then, will be the method of right distribution? First, I think it must be established how great the number [of citizens] ought to be. <margin>On the division of fields and the number of parts.</margin> Then one must affirm into how many and what kind of parts the distribution must be made for the citizens; finally, the lands and the houses themselves must be divided as equally as possible. How great a multitude is sufficient cannot be correctly stated except by a comparison of the lands and the neighboring cities. Let the land be large enough to suffice for so many moderate men, and no larger than necessary. There ought to be as many people as are able to repel neighbors who do wrong and to help those who suffer wrong. Having inspected these things, we shall define both the land and the neighbors by deed and word.

But now, for the sake of example and description, so that the matter itself may be perfected, let the discourse descend to the making of the law. Let there be five thousand and forty <note>5,040 is the ideal number of citizens in Plato's "Laws" because it has 59 divisors (including 1 through 10), making it highly practical for administrative division.</note> participants in the distribution and defenders of the fields for the sake of a certain convenient number. Let them distribute the land and the houses into the same number of parts, so that the man and his portion agree with the distribution. And first, let a partition of the total number be made into two parts; then into three; it is also possible into four, and into five, and so on up to ten. Certainly every legislator ought to understand enough about numbers so that he is not ignorant of which number and what kind is most convenient for individual cities. <margin>On the number suited to many distributions, which is five thousand and forty.</margin> Let us speak of that number which receives within itself the most distributions, and especially those arranged in order. Furthermore, the whole number has all partitions into all things. But the number of five thousand and forty, for both war and peace, and for all contrary things—associations, taxes, distributions—can be divided into no more than sixty parts minus one. <note>In other words, it has 59 divisors.</note> Another reading: in sixty parts, only one [is missing?].

<summary>Plato discusses the "purification" of the state through the removal of disruptive elements (like the poor and debt-ridden) via colonization and establishes 5,040 as the ideal number of citizens due to its mathematical flexibility for administrative divisions.</summary>

### BOOK V.
**Page 34**

...can be inscribed as indigenous. One might continue from one up to ten. Truly, in their leisure, these things must be firmly grasped by those to whom this matter is committed by law. And these things are exactly as they are. These things must be said for the sake of the man who founds the city. Whether he founds a new one from the beginning or restores an old and dissipated one, concerning the gods and sacred rites—what is fitting for individuals in the city, and which gods or spirits <note>original: "demonibus"; in the Platonic sense, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans</note> they should be named after—no one of sound mind will attempt to innovate those things which have been received from Delphi, Dodona, or Hammon <note>sites of famous ancient oracles</note>, or which have been asserted through visions and inspirations of the gods by some ancient tradition. Once these were approved, the ancients established sacred rites mixed with solemnities, whether they are said to have originated from indigenous people, or from Tyrrhenia, or Cyprus, or wherever you wish. Through these stories, they consecrated the traditional fame and the images, as well as the altars and temples, and they established sacred fields for each of them. In all these things, the lawmaker will not innovate even the smallest detail; rather, he will assign to each part a god, a spirit, or some hero. And in the distribution of the fields, he will first dedicate groves and choice lands and all appropriate things, so that the gatherings of the individual parts at fixed times may more easily provide the opportunity for any necessary uses, and that in sacrificing, they may receive one another kindly. From this, they may become mutually familiar and know one another. Indeed, nothing is better for a city than that the citizens know each other. For where there is no light among the citizens in their customs, but rather darkness, there neither honors according to merit nor magistrates will be rightly given, nor can his own right be rendered to each. There is nothing, however—if you compare one thing to another—in which everyone in all cities ought to place greater zeal than in this: that he himself should never appear to be counterfeit, but always simple and true, and that no other such person should deceive him.

Truly, the "toss" <note>a metaphor for a roll of the dice in law-giving</note> which now follows in the very positioning of the laws—as the proverb says of the "sacred toss" in dice—since it is unusual, will perhaps at first make the listener wonder. Yet to one who reflects and experiments, it will be seen that the city is being established in the second place as to the best state. Perhaps someone will not accept it because he has not been accustomed to a lawmaker who does not use a tyrannical manner in bringing forth laws. He will act rightly, indeed, if he proposes the best republic, and the second, and the third, and if the choice is given to anyone to select whichever he wishes according to his own judgment. We shall now do the same. And when we have explained the first virtuous republic, and the second, and the third, let us give the choice to Cleinias—and to anyone who wishes to choose these according to his own manner—to assign to his own portion what pleases him. The first city, then, and the best republic and laws,

<margin>
The first city and republic.
Proverb: All things are common among friends.
</margin>

is where that ancient proverb holds sway as much as possible throughout the entire city: "All things of friends are truly common." Certainly, this will be the limit of virtue, than which none more correct can be set: if somewhere this either happens or ever will happen—that wives are common, children are common, and all money is also common, and that with every zeal what is called "private" is removed from life on all sides. It should be so to the extent that even those things which are private by nature to individuals become in a way common—so that the eyes, ears, and hands seem to see, hear, and act for common use. All people should likewise praise and blame the same things, rejoicing in the same things and grieving at the same things. Finally, they should live according to these laws as much as possible, which make the city one. Such a city, whether gods or more than one son of the gods inhabit it anywhere, living in this way and preserving it, they certainly live filled with all joy. Therefore, one ought not to look elsewhere for the exemplar of a republic; but having inspected this one, one should seek such a thing as much as possible. This one which we have undertaken here, if it should come to be, would approach immortality in a certain way. And if not in the first place, it will at least be one in the second place. But concerning the third, we shall determine later, if God wills. Now, however, let us consider what this one is and in what manner it becomes such. First, then, let them allot the houses and fields, but let them not cultivate the fields in common. For this is greater than

<margin>
The second unity and republic.
That the fatherland is to be venerated.
</margin>

this generation, nurturing, and education can bear. But let them distribute it with this mind: that individuals think their own lot is common to the whole city. Since that region is the fatherland, they ought to cultivate it more than sons cultivate a mother. For since she is a goddess, she is the mistress of mortals. The same must also be thought concerning the indigenous beings, both gods and spirits. But so that these things may last for all time, effort must be given so that however many hearths are now distributed in number, there will always be just as many in the future—neither more nor less. This will be firmly achieved in every city if each person who has obtained a lot always leaves only one of his sons, whichever he prefers, as the heir and successor of that house, a worshiper of the gods, the city, and the race, both of the living and the dead. From the remaining sons, if more than one are born to him, he should settle the females according to the law that shall be enacted; the males, however, he should commit by adoption to those citizens who have no sons, especially as a matter of grace. But if some should fail in their lineage, or if more males or females are born to individuals—or on the contrary, if fewer, because the women were perhaps not fertile—the greatest and most excellent magistrate should diligently consider what ought to be done about all these things. They should find a way altogether, whether the offspring of children is abundant or deficient, so that the five thousand and forty dwellings alone always remain. There are many ways. For the lineage can be restrained when it flows too much. Conversely, when there is need for it to increase, it can be cared for, and people may be exhorted toward it either by honor or disgrace and by the admonitions of the elderly to the young. Finally, all deficiency and want arises from here, when the number of five thousand and forty houses is not preserved. But if, on account of too much zeal in procreating children, the city is so increased that it exceeds the limit of the number and thus the lack of things presses, let it repeat that old counsel, which has often been said: that it should send out a colony, sent from dear friends to dear friends, where it seems it can be managed more conveniently. If, on the contrary, a plague of diseases or the calamity of wars should devastate the city like a flood, so that far fewer survive than the established number, citizens educated in a "counterfeit" <note>original: "adulterina"; referring to those not raised within the city's specific moral discipline</note> discipline are not to be taken in voluntarily. For as they say, not even God will violate necessity. Let us therefore think that the present speech sounds in our ears in this manner: "O best of all men, honor likeness and equality—or what is the same and consistent—according to nature; nor..."

<margin>
Citizens of counterfeit discipline are not to be admitted.
Proverb: Not even God violates necessity.

# ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS OF THE LATINS, DIALOGUE V.
### Q ii
<note>original: "Q ii" is a signature mark used by printers to keep the pages in the correct order.</note>

...ever overstep the limit: whether according to the number or according to the power of things good and beautiful. And now indeed, first of all, preserve throughout your whole life the number [of households] which we have mentioned before <note>Plato established the ideal number of citizen households at 5,040.</note>. Then, do not neglect the census <note>The property assessment or allotment</note> which you were allotted from the beginning as a moderate amount, by buying or selling to one another. Otherwise, neither the distributing god nor the lawgiver will favor you. For now, the law first commands those who might resist what has been said, that in these matters they shall take their lots whether they wish to or not: just as if the region itself, above all, were sacred to all the gods. Then, all the priests, both women and men, shall pray in the first, second, and third sacrifices, that both the buyer and the seller of the homes and lands they have been allotted should suffer what is appropriate for them to suffer in these matters. 

Furthermore, they shall write on cypress-wood monuments <note>original: "cupressea monimenta"; cypress wood was chosen for its durability and resistance to decay.</note> and place them in the temples for the instruction of posterity. Moreover, so that these things are preserved, they shall commit their custody to that magistrate who appears most sharp-sighted, so that it does not escape them if any commerce happens to occur against this reason [of the law]; but whoever does not obey the law and the god shall be punished. And how much good there is in what is now commanded when prepared in its proper order, and how much it profits the cities that obey it, no wicked man will ever understand, according to the ancient proverb; it can only be understood by one who is experienced and educated in fair morals. 

<margin>Proverb: No wicked man will understand. On profit. On holding gold and coins.</margin>

Profit in this city should not be great; indeed, it is neither necessary nor permitted for anyone to apply themselves to illiberal profit <note>Profit considered "unworthy of a free man," such as petty trade or manual labor for hire.</note>. Neither should one seek that mechanical and infamous gain which stains noble character, nor should one think in any way that money is to be accumulated from low and shameful things. To these is added another law: which commands that no private citizen shall have either gold or silver. But as much as is needed for the sake of daily exchange—which is almost necessary among craftsmen and for paying wages to mercenaries, slaves, and farmers—we grant them the right to have such coins as are valued among themselves but held in contempt by other nations. 

<margin>On dowries. On deposits and interest.</margin>

But since wars must often be waged and travel abroad is necessary (whenever ambassadors or messengers are sent to foreign nations), it is necessary that the city always possess common Greek currency <note>original: "communem graeciae monetam"; referring to currency widely accepted across the Greek world, such as the Athenian Owl or the Aeginetan Stater.</note>. If any necessity compels a private citizen to travel abroad, let him go with the permission of the magistrates. Having returned, however, if he has an abundance of foreign coins, let him exchange them for the city’s coins and restore them to the city. If anyone is caught hiding them and converting them to private use, let what he was hiding become public property. Those who are aware of this but did not report it shall be subject to curses and disgrace along with him, and they shall also be punished with a fine no less than the amount of foreign currency brought in. 

Furthermore, let it be permitted to no one to either give or receive dowries, nor to deposit money with someone you do not trust, nor to lend at interest. If anyone accepts a loan at interest, let it be permitted that he returns neither the interest nor the principal <note>original: "nec usuram nec sortem"; Plato’s radical proposal effectively bans usury by making such debts legally unenforceable.</note>. 

<margin>That the very rich are not good men.</margin>

A person will rightly judge these things to be best for the city if he always refers them to the primary intention of a righteous lawgiver. For the will of a man possessing a statesman's mind is not what many affirm it should be—that he wants the city to be as large and as wealthy as possible, filled with gold and silver, and ruling over many by land and sea. To these they add that he should want the city to be the best and happiest possible, if he is to make laws rightly. Some of these things are possible, others not at all. Therefore, the founder of laws will want what is possible; he will not want the impossible, for such a desire would be vain, and he will not attempt it. He will certainly want the citizens to be happy and virtuous, which are things that usually happen together. 

But it is impossible for men to be very rich and virtuous at the same time. I mean "rich" as many think of it: claiming those are rich who, as a few among many, possess the most money, which even any wicked person could possess. If this is so, I will never grant to them that a rich man is truly happy unless he is also good. But it is impossible for someone to excel in wealth and virtue at the same time. Why is this so? someone might ask. Because, we shall say, acquisition made both unjustly and justly is more than double that which is made only justly. And expenses that are spent neither honorably nor shamefully are half as much as those that are honorable and honorably spent. Therefore, the one who acquires twice as much and spends half as much will never be richer than the one who does the opposite <note>Plato argues that the virtuous man earns less because he won't cheat, and spends more because he fulfills his social/religious duties.</note>. One of these is virtuous; the other is not exactly wicked but merely stingy; sometimes, however, he is altogether wicked. But the good man, as we have just said, is never [the very rich one]. For he who accumulates money both justly and unjustly, and spends it neither justly nor unjustly, becomes rich when he is stingy. But the one who is altogether wicked, since he is for the most part a spendthrift and a prodigal, becomes very poor. But he who spends honorably and acquires only justly will never easily excel in riches, nor will he be oppressed by poverty. 

<margin>There are three things in which men place their pursuit: goods of the soul, goods of the body, and money.</margin>

Therefore, our discourse rightly asserts: the very rich are not good men, and if they are not good, they will not be happy either. Now, the purpose of our sanction of the laws is this: that the citizens be as happy as possible and as friendly as possible toward one another. They will never be friends if they are troubled by many mutual injuries and forced to use lawsuits and judgments; rather, these should be as minimal and as few as possible. For this reason, we say there should be neither gold nor silver in the city, nor much profit from mechanical works, inn-keeping, or interest, nor from livestock shamefully; but only from those things which agriculture offers and provides. And this should be so that profit does not compel one to neglect those things for whose sake money is sought. These things are the soul and the body: which without gymnastics and other discipline will never be of any value. 

Therefore, let the care for money—as has already been said many times—hold the very last place of honor. Indeed, since there are three things in total in which men place their pursuit, if held rightly, the pursuit of money is the third and last; that of the body is the middle; and that of the soul is the first. And yet this republic which we are now founding is rightly disposed if it distributes honors in this way. If any law or temperance prefers the health of the body, or health and temperance, to wealth, it seems to be rightly placed <note>original: "non recte posita esse videtur" in the text, but the context of the argument suggests Ficino is critiquing laws that put wealth above the soul or body.</note>. Thus the legislator often declares: if he must, what he himself wants; and if it happens, it will succeed well. If not, the hope of his institution will fail him in vain. And so perhaps he himself and others will judge from the laws he brings; otherwise, in no way.

# BOOK V.

...has drawn his own portion by lot, he should possess it under the condition we stated. It would indeed be best if all other things that come into a colony were also possessed equally. However, since this is not possible—as one person arriving will have more money and another less—it is necessary, for many reasons and for the sake of equality in the city’s various times and opportunities, to establish unequal **censuses** <note>term: census; here referring to property assessments or wealth classes used to determine a citizen's duties and rights.</note> within it. This ensures that magistrates, taxes, and distributions are granted to individuals according to their worth, not only based on their own virtue or that of their ancestors, or their physical beauty and strength, but also according to their use of wealth and poverty. This should be done as equally as possible—receiving, to be sure, an unequal portion, but one that is easily made proportional—so that they do not fall into strife. For these reasons, four levels of census should be established based on the size of one’s goods: **First, Second, Third, and Fourth**, or by whatever other names they may be called. Thus, some may remain in the same census, while others, having become richer or poorer, may move to the census that fits them.

<margin>Neither extreme poverty nor vast wealth should exist among the citizens.</margin>

To this, I shall apply the following form of the law: We say that in a city which is to be free from that greatest of diseases—which we more rightly call discord or sedition—there must be neither extreme poverty among any of the citizens nor great wealth. For both of these produce both [discord and sedition]. Therefore, the legislator must set a limit for both. Let the limit of poverty be the value of the original lot, which must remain stable; no magistrate, nor anyone else who cares for virtue, shall allow it to be less for anyone. Since the legislator has prescribed this as the measure, he shall allow one to possess double this amount, then triple, and up to quadruple. 

If anyone should possess more than this—whether found, received as a gift, earned through profit, or acquired by any other such stroke of fortune—if he gives all that remains above the limit to the city and the city's guardian gods, he shall remain unpunished and be held in high esteem. But if he does not obey the law, anyone who reports him shall receive half the surplus, and the other half shall be consecrated to the gods. The offender shall also be fined an amount equal to his own goods. Furthermore, all possessions beyond the lot must be openly recorded with the magistrate appointed by law as their guardian, so that all judgments concerning money are easy and perfectly clear.

<margin>On the site of the city.</margin>

After this, the city should first be founded in the middle of the territory as much as possible, in a place that has all the other conveniences for a city, which are not difficult to understand or describe. Next, it shall be divided into twelve parts. First, a central area shall be consecrated to **Vesta**, **Jupiter**, and **Athena** <note>original: "Vestæ... Iouis... & Palladi"; Ficino uses the Latin names for the Greek Hestia, Zeus, and Athena.</note>, and this shall be the citadel, surrounded by a circle from which the twelve parts of both the region and the city shall be partitioned. 

<margin>Division of the lands.</margin>

These parts should be made equal in such a way that the fertile lands are smaller and the unfertile lands are larger. The lots should be cut into five thousand and forty <note>The number 5,040 was chosen by Plato because it has 59 divisors, including every number from 1 to 10, making it ideal for administrative and military divisions.</note>, and each of these shall be divided in two. It is also necessary to pair two portions together to form one lot, so that each consists of one part near the city and one part far away. Thus, the part closest to the city is joined with the part furthest away to make one lot; the second closest with the second furthest, and so on for all the others. Care must also be taken in these dual partitions to address what we just said about the fertility and infertility of the region: namely, that the distribution should be equalized by the size and smallness of the plots. 

Furthermore, the villages must be divided into twelve parts, just as the other goods were, preserving an overall equality in all things. Then, the twelve lots should be assigned to twelve gods, and each part of the lot should be consecrated to its own god and called a "tribe." Also, the twelve sections of the city must be divided into two dwellings each, just as was done in the rest of the region: one near the center and the other near the edge. And the arrangement of the dwellings shall conclude in this way.

But we must altogether consider that all these things we have said will perhaps never find such an opportunity that they occur exactly as described; perhaps men will not tolerate such a dwelling-place, but would bear it with an uneasy mind. They might not wish to hold a moderate amount of money throughout their whole lives as we have established, or to have a limited number of children for each family as we said, or to be deprived of gold and silver and all the other things the legislator seems likely to command based on the above. Furthermore, they may object to having dwellings in the center and at the extremes of the region and city as we have ordered. Indeed, all these things are spoken of as if they were a kind of dream, or as if a city and its citizens were being molded out of wax. 

These objections are raised in a certain way that is not bad, but the legislator must also be allowed to speak in response. Do not think me, my friends, to be unaware that what has just been said is, in a way, true. But I believe it is right in every instance that he who presents a model, in whose likeness a work must be made, should omit nothing at all that pertains to its truest beauty. If anyone is unable to achieve some of these things in imitation, he may pass over those which are beyond his strength. But whatever is closest to these and most akin to what is fitting to be done, he should pursue with all his zeal. He should allow the legislator to bring his will to a conclusion. Once that is done, he can consider together with the legislator what parts of the speech are useful and what parts are contrary to the making of laws. For an artist should always act so that his work is entirely consistent with itself, even in the smallest detail, if he is to achieve praise.

Now, after the distribution of the twelve parts, it must be observed that since these twelve parts contain many portions within themselves, and connections arise from those connections up to five thousand and forty—from which tribes and villages are formed, and military ranks and divisions, and furthermore coins and measures for dry and liquid goods and weights—all these must be ordered by the legislator to be commensurate and harmonious with one another. 

<margin>On the measurement of furniture.</margin>

Moreover, one should not fear the reputation of being "small-minded," as if considering things too trivial, if one commands that all the vessels and furniture of the citizens should have their own measure, and that no one should possess anything without a certain measure. According to a common logic, the various divisions of numbers are useful for all things, both in length and depth, and in sounds, and in movements—whether in a straight line ascending or descending, or in a circle. The legislator must look toward all these things so that he may command all citizens not to depart from this order of numbers as far as they are able. For no other single subject in childhood...

-># ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE VI. ON THE LAWS. FOLIO 331.<-
<sig>Q iiii</sig>
<meta>catchword: sci (likely the start of "scilicet" or "scit")</meta>

<margin>Praise of arithmetic and how necessary it is for boys.</margin>
This discipline, for the management of the household, for the republic, and finally for all arts, has as much power as the knowledge of numbers of this kind. What is most important is that it even awakens those who are sleepy and naturally unrefined, making them teachable, mindful, and clever, advancing through a divine art beyond their own natural capacity. All these things are indeed good and useful foundations, provided that by other laws and duties, ungenerousness and greed are rooted out from the souls of those who are to receive this education sufficiently and profitably. Otherwise, malice rather than wisdom will secretly take root from this source—which we now see happening to the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and many other nations, on account of their lack of cultivation in other arts and abilities, whether a crude lawmaker caused this, or hostile fortune, or some other such natural cause. For indeed, O Clinias and Megillus, let it not escape us that there is a great difference in places for producing better or worse men, and laws must be made for them differently as it is expedient. 
<margin>There is great power in places for producing better and worse men.</margin>
Indeed, some places are difficult and perverse due to the variety and turbulence of the winds; others because of the waters; others because of the food produced from the earth, which brings about advantages or disadvantages not only to bodies, but no less to souls as well. But places of a region differ most of all where there is a certain divine inspiration, and which **demons** <note>term: demons; in the Neoplatonic sense, these are "daimones," intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil beings.</note> have obtained by lot, who receive those dwelling there either favorably or unfavorably. Once these things have been considered according to human capacity, the lawmaker, being of sound mind, will turn himself to the making of laws. This is what you must do, O Clinias. For you must first observe these things before you cause the region to be inhabited. **CLINIAS:** These things have been excellently spoken by you, O Athenian guest. Therefore, I must act accordingly.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument for Dialogue VI. On the Laws.

There are three types of causes by which different human characters are formed in different places. Plato briefly included these three types at the end of the previous book. I truly think it will be worthwhile to bind the sixth book to the fifth with this very material, as if with a certain knot. Let there be, therefore, a great deal of distinction in a place for generating better or worse men. Let the cause be either human, natural, or divine. The **human** cause is law, education, and differing customs. The **natural** cause is the diversity of the elements and nourishments. The **divine** cause—to the extent that I may also call the heavens divine—is the power of the stars and the divine beings. Indeed, Plato judges that just as some regions of the sky are ruled by different stars and different gods (that is, higher angels), so other regions of the earth are governed by different demons and lower angels. To this is added the opinion of astronomers, matching regions of the earth to regions of the heaven, and cities to the ascending signs. I pass over for the present how much difference of character the variety of the **familiar demon** <note>term: familiar demon; a personal guardian spirit believed to accompany an individual from birth.</note> of each man brings. But that the powers of higher spirits flow into our spirits, in whatever way that may happen, we cannot deny; for we clearly see our bodies moved by higher bodies, and continually changed in one way or another by the air. But if those spirits act upon our spirits, they act moreover upon our bodies. Indeed, the passion of human bodies, whether it is brought in by those spirits or by higher bodies, overflows into the soul to the extent that the soul, by both an acquired and a natural affection, merges itself into the body. But there is this difference: those bodies move souls through our bodies, while spirits move souls sometimes through bodies, sometimes through the soul itself, and sometimes through that **spirit** <note>term: spirit; here referring to the "pneuma," a subtle substance Ficino believed connected the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> which physicians often call the **knot of the soul and the body.** Remember, however, that all power and motion descending from higher things into us always leads to good by its own nature, since even celestial influences are always toward the good. But do not here cast either the more rigid sadness and stinginess of men upon **Saturn**, or rashness and ferocity upon **Mars**, or fraudulent malice upon **Mercury**, or lascivious loves upon **Venus**. What if the weight of Saturn in us—by the fault of temperament, nature, nutrition, and education—is converted into a vice similar to that weight? Similarly, Martian high-mindedness into a boldness somewhat similar to high-mindedness; Mercurial industry into malice; and Venereal affection into lust! Does it not happen daily under the rays of the sun—which by their nature are for seeing, preserving, and living—that some lose their sight and others their life? And those rays which warm healthfully in the open air, burn in hollow places! Just as a localized evil results for someone under the influence of beneficial rays because of an inferior nature (but not for the whole universe), so under the powers of stars that are good by nature, and under the best gifts of the divine beings, a vice of either body or soul can sometimes arise by the fault of an inferior nature or custom. But there is no vice or evil for the universe as a whole; just as in a harmony the second or seventh voice, which sounds dissonant when heard alone, meanwhile matches the others in the consonance of the whole. The Platonists are accustomed to sometimes call the lowest demons "evil," because they allure us to the lowest and sensible good of generation by a certain duty of their own, as they say. But to turn away from the highest good toward the minimal good is rightly called "evil" in comparison to the highest. I pass over for now that they say the highest demons lead to the good of contemplation, the middle to the good of action, and the lowest to the good of desire; we can both use and abuse all of these, and good things happen to those who use them, while evil things happen to those who abuse them. Plato calls the demons and gods "natives of the fatherland," not because they were born there, but because they guard the citizens born there with a certain peculiar care. He says, moreover, that the **blessed city** is inhabited by gods and the sons of gods, understanding this partly as the **celestial Jerusalem** <note>original: "caelestem Hierusalem"; Ficino is blending Plato's ideal city with the Christian concept of the New Jerusalem.</note> inhabited by angels and pure souls, and partly also as the happy life of those who, he says in the *Phaedo*, inhabit the highest parts of the earth, blessed by the familiarity of the divine beings. After this, he descends in the sixth book to the establishing of magistrates...

Ficino’s commentary defends astrology and the role of "demons" as intermediary spirits, arguing that celestial influences are inherently good but can be distorted by human vice or physical disposition.</summary>
