<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s introduction to Book VI of Plato’s Laws. It transitions from the general influence of geography and mathematics into the specific requirements for city officials and the mathematical/cosmic harmony that should underpin a well-ordered state.</meta>

-># ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE VI OF THE LAWS.<-

<meta>The catchword "ligit" from the previous page likely refers to the "diligētiā" (diligence) mentioned in the opening paragraph here, or perhaps "colligit" (collects/gathers) from the bottom of a previous missing leaf.</meta>

Namely, how many magistrates there ought to be, in what manner they should be created, and what the duty of each official should be. He [Plato] asserts, moreover, that **diligence** in establishing these offices is of such great importance that even the constitution of good laws without good magistrates would not only fail to benefit the city but would even be highly detrimental. He says it is necessary that both those who are to elect the magistrates and those who are to be elected must be of the highest character from their youth, born of the most honorable ancestors, and must be perfectly acquainted with the customs of their fellow citizens. 

In these matters, you will notice Plato's wonderful prudence regarding the hierarchy of magistrates and their duties in both human and sacred affairs, in war and in peace, and in both the city and the countryside. You will recognize and approve of a government of the "best men" <note>Aristocracy, in the Greek sense of 'rule by the best'.</note>, which contains something of the royal and something of the popular, and is established as a middle ground between the rule of a single person and the rule of the people. 

You should observe that in distributing civil offices, **equality** must always be preserved. However, this is not **arithmetic equality**, through which equal portions are given to individuals by number, measure, or weight—which is often the most unjust method—but rather **geometric equality**. <note>Geometric equality is proportional; it gives more to those who contribute more or possess more virtue, rather than giving everyone the same amount regardless of merit.</note> By this method, the merits of individuals are considered, and distribution is made according to that logic: so that just as the proportion of merit is to merit, the proportion of office is to office. Thus, the offices are not equal to other offices, but rather the offices are equal to the merits. 

Therefore, you will consider a double equality: both of office to office, and of the office itself to the merit of the person. The former [arithmetic] is often harmful and rarely useful (and then only if it happens by chance), but the latter [geometric] is necessary every day. In this proportional equality, the whole reasoning of **justice** consists. Indeed, this very principle is placed in the judgment of **Jove** <note>Jupiter/God. Ficino often identifies the Platonic "highest god" with Jove to bridge Greek philosophy and his own theology.</note>; the understanding of it is granted to few men, but by this principle alone all things are preserved, however much of it may be present among us. 

And not without cause is the duty of this equality ascribed to the judgment of the Supreme Judge. He alone penetrates the secrets of all hearts; therefore, he alone perfectly knows their merits and can perfectly render what is equal to those merits. This he does first in heaven, then in the universe, so that by this distribution alone—according to the capacity of each nature—all things are created and preserved. This was approved by the ancients and confirmed in the *Gorgias*. 

But amidst these things, Plato—following his most frequent custom—devotes himself to the **education of children**. He creates a specific magistrate for this purpose, whom he wishes to be held as the supreme official in the city and the most excellent of all magistrates. He believes that without foresight regarding the "planting of the seeds" of childhood, the entire cultivation of the city would be in vain. You will notice here that the human intellect, if well cultivated, eventually becomes most gentle and divine; but if the opposite occurs, it turns out quite differently. 

But why is it said that the human intellect can become more ferocious than the beasts? Because that which has the greatest power for good also has the greatest power for evil. Likewise, when the best thing turns toward its opposite through its own depravity, it becomes the worst. This is debated in the *Republic*. Furthermore, the cleverness of a highly perceptive mind increases the ferocity in a depraved man toward evil. Add to this that the refinement of human spirits, when in anger, turns into fury. There is also the irritation caused by certain **daemons** <note>In the Platonic sense, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense of pure evil.</note>, which Plato mentions in his *Letter to the Syracusans*. Homer also frequently employs this view regarding the Egyptians, introducing heroes who are incited to anger and blood by the gods (that is, by daemons).

He recommends again that number **five thousand and forty** <note>5040 is the ideal number of citizens/lots in Plato's Laws because it has 60 divisors, making it perfect for administrative division.</note> as the most convenient for the partitioning of magistrates, dwellings, and lands, as it can be divided into many successive whole portions. Indeed, if you divide this whole number into two parts, a half will contain 2,520. If into three, a third part is 1,680. If into four, a fourth is 1,260. If into five, a fifth part will contain 1,008. If into six, a sixth is 840. If into seven, a seventh is 720. If into eight, an eighth is 630. If into nine, a ninth is 560. If into ten, a tenth is 504. Up to this point, all parts are whole numbers. But if you divide by eleven, the eleventh part is 458 plus two-elevenths of a portion. But if by twelve, a twelfth is 420. 

Stop your foot here. Since he mentions **sixty** to us: if you divide that whole number into sixty parts, the sixtieth part will comprise 84; and if by a certain conversion you cut it into 84 parts, each part will hold 60. It seems, moreover, that Plato makes much of the fact that this number [5040] is divided by twelve into 420, which here is again divided by twelve into 35. This 35, however, divided by twelve is 2 plus eleven-twelfths of a part. And the number 420 itself is multiplied from the number twenty times twenty-one. For the number 20, replicated twenty-one times, completes 420. 

He praises the **number twelve**, and that whole number [5040] which is adapted to the duodecimal system, because in his view there are twelve spheres of the world, twelve signs in the **Zodiac**, and twelve parts in the elements. For each of the four elements is divided into three regions: the highest, the lowest, and the middle, differing not only in position but also in power. Add another "twelve" of the elements, by which the substance of the four elements and the eight qualities are comprised. Of the qualities, four are **masculine**: namely, heat, cold, lightness, and gravity. For the first two are the principles of alteration; the following two are the principles of motion toward a place. Four, however, are **feminine**, which are more subject to passion [being acted upon]: namely, moisture, dryness, rarity, and density. Iamblichus asserts that these are contained in the mysteries of the Egyptians. 

Furthermore, the Sun, the lord of the planets, completes its own course in the twelve-month number and produces various effects. Finally, he wishes each part of the city to be considered consecrated to a god—specifically to the **twelve gods**, that is, the twelve souls of the spheres. Likewise, to the twelve gods ruling the signs of the Zodiac. Again, to the twelve orders of daemons following the celestial signs. When he says the twelve parts of the city follow the circuit of the universe, perhaps he also understands the whole circuit of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note> to be completed in thirty-six thousand years. Which number, surely...

...perfectly completes this in three twelve-hundred-year periods. Thus, you may understand from the opinion of the ancients that in the first twelve-hundred years, the whole world is in its youthful state; in the second, its manly state; and in the third, its senile state. But we shall speak of these things more opportunely in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the cosmos.</note>. This agrees with what he says in the *Phaedrus*: that the army of gods and daemons <note>In this context, "daemons" are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> under the leadership of Jove is arranged into twelve orders. He concludes here that the parts of the city—partly through the twelve-fold number of tribes and temples, and partly through divine worship solemnly renewed twice in each of the twelve months—are thus prepared for the gifts of God, so that they are governed by the gods themselves as if they were presiding over them. Moreover, he wishes the principal public solemnities to be renewed twice, so that both the twelve-fold order of the tribes and the twelve-fold division of the rest of the city and country are satisfied. 

Because he commands that sacrifices be made to the gods or the sons of gods, he wishes "gods" to be understood as the souls of the celestial spheres <note>The planets and stars were thought to have guiding souls.</note>, and "sons" to be understood as the purer daemons. Indeed, he commands all these things to be done for the sake of Jove alone, the prince of all. Nor should it be passed over in silence that the twelve-fold divisions which we mentioned as pertaining to the universe are, as it were, represented by a twelve-fold division proper to every human being. This is seen to consist of the four humors of the body, the four disturbances of the senses, and an equal number of virtues. 

After the sacred rites of the gods, he descends to the sacred rites of marriage. There, you will consider the laws and rituals of marriage: the exhortation to matrimony, the duties of husband and wife toward each other, and toward the children to be begotten and educated. You will note above all: it is not fitting to apply oneself to the procreation of children while in a state of drunkenness or any other disturbance of the mind. Because of such a fault, children are born daily who are sick in both soul and body. He also commits this mystery to memory: where he says that a "Principle" and a "Spirit" <note>original: "numen"</note> are implanted in men, and if they are treated with the honor befitting them by those who use their gifts, they preserve all things. What, then, is this "Principle," and what is this "Spirit" that is implanted or presiding? The "Principle" is the Idea <note>The Platonic "Form" or blueprint.</note> of the human formation. The "Spirit" is the familiar daemon, the prince of generation, often signified by the name of Lucina <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth.</note>. Why is it called "implanted," "presiding," or "brooding"? So that you may understand that the spirit is not merely present, but is within us constantly, cherishing us. It especially favors and, by favoring, preserves us if it is worshipped with gratitude by those who enjoy its gift. 

After the mutual duties of husband and wife, he subsequently descends to the mutual duties of masters and servants. After these, with a certain accustomed skill, he returns to the walls, temples, and palaces, which he says ought to have been treated before marriage. Here, you will note first that the courts of judges and the palaces of magistrates are placed very near the temples, so that human judges, while judging men, may always remember that they themselves are being judged by God. Let the guardians of the city also remember that they cannot guard it unless God is the guardian. Likewise, nothing in the city, even the smallest thing, ought to be without a certain fixed order. For that which lacks order throws other ordered things into confusion. Most especially, however, the affairs of women require order and continuous care. Otherwise, if women's affairs are neglected, twice as much—or even more than twice—the harm comes to the city than if the affairs of men had been neglected. 

Among these things, where the antiquity of the world is recounted—when he says that the very principle of generation preceded us by an inestimable magnitude of time—understand "Moses," <note>Ficino often sought to synchronize Plato with the Bible, suggesting "inestimable time" refers to the Biblical creation timeline.</note> by an inestimable number of days and hours. Conclude the book with this sentiment: that we should not be cast headlong by the triple impulse (namely, for food, drink, and sex), but should restrain them with a triple bridle: fear, law, and true reason. Furthermore, by the moderate and honorable use of games from childhood, so that through honorable pastimes we may be called back from shameful ones and gradually provoked toward serious studies.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial "P" featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within an architectural frame with floral motifs.</image-desc> **P**OST After all the things we have said up to this point, it seems it is almost time to establish magistrates in the city. **CLINIAS.** Certainly so. **ATHENIAN.** Truly, these two categories exist in the nature of the matter. But for a little while before we elect the magistrates, let us pause and declare some things pertaining to their election. **CLINIAS.** Which things are these? **ATHENIAN.** Hear them now. No one doubts that since the making of laws is a great matter, if someone establishes unfit magistrates in a city well-governed by laws, then even if the laws are well-placed, it will not only be of no use and provoke laughter, but it will even give birth to the greatest calamities for cities. **CLINIAS.** Clearly. **ATHENIAN.** This, therefore, must be considered, my friend: how it happens in this your city and republic. For you see that those who are to rightly receive magistracies must have been sufficiently tested from their youth, both themselves and their families, up until the election itself. Then, those who cast their votes must also have been educated in lawful customs, so that they can easily recognize who should be admitted and who rejected, and bear themselves toward both according to their dignity. This must be done by me now and by you: since you have also taken up the duty of establishing a city for the Cretans with a willing mind, and you are the tenth in this work (as you say), and I have promised to bring you aid in our present conversation. Therefore, I will not suffer this discourse of ours to remain without a head. For if it were to wander, it would appear deformed to everyone. **CLINIAS.** You have spoken very well, Guest. **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, I will do so according to my strength. **CLINIAS.** Let us do exactly as we say. **ATHENIAN.** We shall do so, certainly, if God wills; so that we may even overcome our old age in this part. **CLINIAS.** But it is to be believed that God so wills. **ATHENIAN.** It is to be believed indeed. Therefore, following Him, let us say this also. **CLINIAS.** Say what? **ATHENIAN.** That the habitation of the city is now being established by us both boldly and perilously. **CLINIAS.** Whither...

# ON THE LAWS, OR DIALOGUE VI ON THE LAWS.
### Q v

...if anyone considers another person to be more outstanding <note>original: "praestantiorem"</note>, he may nominate someone else in that person’s place, provided that before he judges in this way, he confirms it by a **formal oath**. The person nominated by the greater number of votes shall then be chosen. Furthermore, let three men who are most favored be approved as **leaders of the army** and caretakers of war matters, in the same way that the Guardians of the Laws are approved. These leaders shall nominate twelve **prefects of ranks**, one for each of the twelve tribes. The announcement, the voting, the designation, and the judgment in these matters shall be carried out in the same way as it was for the army leaders.

Meetings of the assembly <term>comitia; the public gathering for voting</term> shall be held in a most sacred and suitable place before the Council is created and before the prefects of the Council are chosen. At these meetings, the Guardians of the Laws shall preside. The infantry and cavalry shall sit separately; in the third place, all others who are currently serving in arms shall sit. In electing the generals and the masters of the horse, all shall cast a vote. For the prefects of the ranks, only those who carry shields shall vote. For the military tribunes, all the cavalry shall vote. However, the army leaders themselves shall appoint for themselves the prefects of the light-armed troops, the archers, and other such units. 

There remains the designation of the **masters of the horse**. These shall be nominated by the same people who nominated the army leaders, and the voting shall be conducted in the same manner. Likewise, the comparison of candidates shall be done by public announcement. The cavalry shall cast their votes in the presence of the infantry. The two who are chosen by the greater number of votes shall preside over all the cavalry. The announcement may be made twice. If there is a doubt on the third time, the votes shall decide, as the rules of the assembly determine for each individual.

The **Council** <note>Plato’s "Boule" or Senate</note> shall consist of thirty sets of twelve <note>totaling 360 members</note>. For this distribution is suitable for a group of sixty and three hundred men. It shall be distributed into four parts of ninety men each, so that ninety councilors are selected from each of the wealth classes <term>census; wealth rankings used to determine political participation</term>. 

First, all those of the highest wealth class must necessarily cast their votes; anyone who fails to vote shall be fined according to the ruling. Once they have been nominated, they shall be recorded. On the following day, votes shall be cast for the second wealth class in the same manner. On the third day, anyone who wishes may vote for the third class. However, voting is mandatory for men of the first three wealth classes. Those of the fourth and smallest wealth class shall be free from penalty if any of them do not wish to vote. On the fourth day, everyone shall vote for the fourth and smallest class; under this condition, if anyone from the third or fourth class does not wish to vote, they shall not be punished. But if anyone of the first or second wealth class neglects to vote, they shall be fined: a member of the second class shall be fined three times the original amount, and a member of the first class four times. 

On the fifth day, the magistrates shall publish the list of names for all citizens to see, and everyone shall vote upon them. Anyone who refuses shall be fined the first penalty. Of those elected from all the wealth classes, half—that is, one hundred and eighty—shall be confirmed by lot to serve in the annual order of the Senate.

In this way, the creation of the magistrates will be a middle ground between the power of a single ruler <note>monarchy</note> and the power of the people <note>democracy</note>. It is always necessary for a Republic to hold this middle ground. For slaves and masters will never be friends, nor will the good and the wicked be friends if they are treated with equal honors. For when equal things are given to unequal people, they become unequal, unless a proper measure is applied. Indeed, it is because of these two extremes that Republics are filled with sedition <note>civil unrest</note>. 

That ancient saying—that **"friendship is created by equality"**—is spoken very rightly and gracefully. However, because it is not entirely clear what kind of equality produces this, we are often greatly troubled. Indeed, there are two equalities called by the same name, but in practice they are almost opposites in many ways. Any city or lawmaker can use the first kind by using the **lot** <note>random drawing</note> to distribute honors: this is the equality of number, weight, and measure. 

But the truest and best equality is not easily seen by everyone. This is the **judgment of Jove** <note>Jupiter/God</note>, and he grants it only sparingly to men. Yet, as far as it is granted, it brings all good things to both individuals and cities. This equality grants more to the greater and less to the smaller, giving to each according to their nature. It always grants greater honors to those who are greater in virtue, and smaller honors to those who are lesser in virtue and discipline. It imparts to each what is fitting according to reason. This is surely what we call **civil justice**. 

This is the equality we must strive for, O Clinias; we must look toward this very equality as we establish and organize this new city. Anyone else who founds a city must look to this same standard when bringing forth laws. One must not look to a few tyrants, or to one, or to the power of the people, but always toward justice. That justice is what we have just described: the distribution of equality according to the nature of those who are themselves unequal. 

Nevertheless, it is necessary for the whole city to use both of these equalities (which share the same name) if the whole city wishes to remain far from all sedition. For that praiseworthy fairness and the equal judgment of the perfect and exact is violated and broken when it departs from right judgment. Therefore, it is also necessary to use the **equality of the lot** <note>randomness</note> to completely avoid the indignation of the many. In this matter, one must invoke God and Good Fortune in prayer, so that the lot might be directed toward what is most just. 

Thus, we must necessarily use both equalities, but we should use the equality that relies on fortune <note>the lot</note> in only a very few cases. This must be observed, my friends, for this reason: so that the city may obtain safety. Just as a ship in the middle of the sea requires guards by day and night, so too a city placed in the middle of the waves of other cities—subject to various seditions and always close to the danger of captivity—needs perpetual guarding. 

Therefore, magistrates and guards must succeed one another from day into night and from night into day, so that the succession of those handing over and receiving the guard never ceases. A large multitude cannot do any of this quickly. It is therefore necessary that the greater part of the Council be allowed to spend most of their time attending to their own private affairs. But a **twelfth part** of it, distributed over twelve months, shall keep watch one after the other in sequence. 

<margin>
<image-desc>A small hand with a pointing finger (manicule) directed towards the text regarding the "twelfth part".</image-desc>
</margin>

This part shall be ready for anyone, whether from the city itself or coming from elsewhere, who wishes to report anything or ask questions about matters on which the city must either respond to other cities or receive answers to their own questions. This is also for the sake of the new upheavals that often occur: primarily so they do not happen, but if they do, so the city may perceive them as quickly as possible and apply a remedy. This should always be done by the assembly of those presiding over the city, so that both the difficulties arising from the laws and those suddenly affecting the city may be resolved. All these things shall be the care of the twelfth part...

# BOOK VI.
### LIBER VI.

...part of the council <note>original: "consilii pars"</note>, which will remain at rest for eleven months. During this period of duty, this part of the council should always act in the city together with the other magistrates. In this way, urban matters will be well ordered. But what about the care and order of the rest of the entire region? Since the whole city and the entire region is divided into twelve parts, should curators not be appointed in the city itself for the roads, dwellings, buildings, harbors, the marketplace, springs, sacred sites, temples, and all other things of this kind? 

Cleinias: Why not? 

Athenian: Shall I say, then, that temple keepers <term>aeditui; those who look after the temple buildings</term> and priests, both men and women, should be appointed? For the care of decorating roads and buildings—so that neither men commit injuries nor wild animals do harm, and so that everything appropriate for cities is carried out both within the city limits and in the suburbs—three types of magistrates should be chosen. And let the curators of the things just mentioned be called **aediles** <term>aediles; officials in charge of public buildings and infrastructure</term>. Those who have care of the marketplace and sales shall be **market curators**. Of sacred things, there shall be **priests**. And indeed, those priesthoods which have been handed down from parents by succession, whether to men or women, are by no means to be moved. But if there are no such traditions, or only a few—as is likely to happen for those coming together to inhabit a new city where these are lacking—priests and priestesses and temple keepers must be established.

<margin>On the priests</margin>
All these things should be done partly by election and partly by lot. And in every region and city, the common people <term>plebs; the general citizenry</term> should be joined in friendship with those outside the common people, so that there is the greatest agreement among all of them. And as for the creation of priests, these matters should be entrusted to God, so that as it pleases Him, divine fortune—to whom this is granted—may bring forth the lots. In the examination of those who have obtained the lot, he is to be approved who is upright and legitimate: then from a house that is most pure, free from bloodshed and all such things committed against divine law, and whose father and mother have lived in a similar way. They should seek laws about divine matters from **Delphi** <note>the famous oracle of Apollo in Greece, the ultimate authority on religious law</note>; they should appoint **interpreters** <term>interpretes; officials who explain and apply sacred laws</term> of those laws, and follow them. A priesthood should last no longer than one year. And no one should be less than sixty years old who is to sufficiently handle divine matters according to the sacred laws. Let the same statutes be understood regarding sacred women as regarding men. 

As for the interpreters: let the twelve tribes bring forward four, each tribe three from their order; and from the three approved, who were chosen by the greater vote, let them send the remaining nine to Delphi, so that from each set of three, one may be chosen by the oracle. Their approval and age shall be the same as stated for the priests. These shall have the power of interpreting and explaining for their whole life. When one dies, the four tribes shall choose another from where the previous one was lost. **Treasurers** <term>quaestores; financial officers</term> and keepers of the sacred money in each temple, who shall be the masters of the groves, lands, fruits, leases, and rentals dedicated to them: let three be chosen from the highest wealth classes for the largest temples, two for the smaller, and one for the medium and most fitting ones. They should be chosen and approved in the same way as army leaders. And these things are handled in sacred matters, as we have said. 

Care must be taken that, as far as possible, nothing is without a guard. The city indeed should be cared for by the army leaders, commanders of ranks, masters of the horse, tribunes, council leaders, aediles, and censors, after they have been elected in their order. Let the rest of the region be guarded in this way: the entire region was divided into twelve equal parts according to its strength. One tribe being given to each part by lot, let them choose each year those who are, as it were, **curators of the fields** and leaders of the tribes. Each of these should have twelve young men from his tribe, not less than twenty-one years of age nor more than thirty. To each of these, individual parts of the region shall be assigned by lot for a monthly period, so that all may have experience of the entire region. The leaders and guards shall have the care of commanding and guarding for two years. 

As soon as they have been assigned parts to guard by lot, they should change locations every month, each to the next location, and the leaders of the guards should lead them in a circle to the right first. (I call the "right" side that which faces the rising sun). Then, in the second year, they should change to the left, so that they are not only experienced in the region for one time of year, but also recognize what happens at any time in every part of the region. In the third year, let other curators—the twelve—be chosen as field and guard leaders from the tribal elders. 

The care and work in each place shall be such: first, that the region be fortified as much as possible against the attack of enemies. By digging trenches wherever necessary and surrounding with towers and barriers as strength allows, they should ward off those wishing to do harm. To do both these things, they may use beasts of burden and indigenous slaves when they are least occupied with their own work. Appointing some over them, they should arrange all locations so that it is difficult for enemies to pass through them, but easy for friends—people, cattle, and beasts of burden—for whom the region should be made most accessible. 

They should diligently ensure that rainwater not only does no harm, but is also collected as it flows from high mountains into hollow valleys; there they should force the water to pool with trenches and walls, so that the rainwater absorbed in those channels creates springs and fountains of water for all lower places and fields, and in this way irrigates the driest places with much healthy moisture. They should decorate springs and rivers with trees and buildings. Furthermore, they should take care to enrich the groves and lands dedicated to the gods with constant irrigation and the introduction of water, and apply moisture and springs to the mines <note>original: "metallis"; likely referring to channels or excavations</note>. And so they may make everything abundant and the temples of the gods more ornate. 

Everywhere in these places, the young men should prepare **gymnasiums** <note>places for physical exercise and education</note> as convenient for themselves as for the elderly, with hot baths established; and with plenty of dry wood provided, so that a remedy for the sick and a relief for those exhausted by labor may be kindly offered. This treatment is surely much better than the medicine of an unskilled physician. All these and other such things are for the ornament and utility of these places, along with a certain pleasant recreation. In summary, let this be the effort concerning these things: sixty men shall each guard the place assigned to him, not only because of enemies, but also because of those who call themselves friends.

->ON THE LAWS, DIALOGUE VI, FOLIO 333<-

And if anyone among neighbors and citizens, whether slave or free, should inflict an injury upon another, the five leaders <note>original: "principes"</note> themselves shall judge in small matters. In larger matters, however, seventeen men along with twelve others shall judge, up to the value of three minas <term>mina; an ancient unit of currency equal to 100 drachmas</term>, concerning whatever complaint one may have against another. Furthermore, let no one be a judge or magistrate who does not render an account of his conduct in office—except for those who, like kings, put a final end to affairs.

As for the **Rural Curators** <note>original: "agrorum curatores"; also known as the "Secret Police" or "Kryptoi" in Greek</note>, if they should act insultingly against those in their care, imposing burdens unequally, or taking anything by force from the farmers, or if they are swayed by flattering bribes to corrupt judgment: having been captured by such gifts and flatteries, let them be held in disgrace throughout the entire city. In other injuries, they shall voluntarily pay a fine to the neighbors and local farmers of up to one mina. 

But if they refuse to pay what they owe for larger or smaller injuries, hoping to escape judgment and punishment because they move from place to place every month, they shall be accused in a public court. Whoever is convicted shall pay double to the person he oppressed by his injury.

Both the leaders and the other Rural Curators shall live for two years in this manner: First, let there be communal meals <note>original: "convivia"</note> for all in each location. If anyone is absent—even if he keeps watch for only one day or one night—when neither the leader has ordered it nor any necessity has compelled it, if the five men also condemn him, let it be written in the forum that he deserted his guard duty. Let him be treated with great disgrace, as one who, as far as he was able, betrayed the Republic. And if anyone meets him and wishes to strike him, he may be beaten with impunity. 

All sixty men <note>The total number of rural guards</note> shall watch that none of the leaders commit such an offense. Whoever notices or hears of it and does not accuse them shall be subject to the same law as the offender, and shall be punished by a sharper censure of the youth and excluded from all youthful magistracies.

<margin>
He who has not served cannot be a praised master.
</margin>

The **Guardians of the Laws** shall diligently oversee all these things: first, that they do not happen; second, that once they have happened, they are punished as justice demands. Every man ought to consider this concerning all people: he who has never served can never be a master worthy of praise. Therefore, one ought to boast more of having served well than of having ruled well: first serving the laws—for he who serves them serves the gods—and then serving the elders who have lived honorably. 

Finally, for this entire two-year period, the Rural Curators shall lead a most humble and meager life. Therefore, the twelve men, when gathered with the five, shall consult among themselves as if they will have no other servants. For they shall use farmers and local inhabitants not for their own private service, but only for public works. In other matters, they should think of themselves as living as if they were serving themselves. Furthermore, in summer and winter, they must always be armed to patrol the entire region, so that they may guard it more diligently while becoming familiar with every place. Indeed, no knowledge seems less than this: that the entire region be known exquisitely by everyone. 

<margin>
Hunting
</margin>

For this reason, no less than for pleasure and other utility, young men ought to devote effort to breeding dogs and the rest of hunting. They themselves ought to employ that specific study which some call "hiding" <note>original: "occultando"; a reference to the Greek term *kryptia*, meaning secret service or patrolling</note>. But whether it is called "hiding," or the guarding of the fields, or whatever else anyone wishes, it is necessary that those who desire the safety of their city diligently exercise themselves in it to the best of their strength.

<margin>
Concerning Censors and Aediles.
</margin>

It follows that I speak of the election of **Censors** <term>censores; here referring to market officials or *agoranomoi*</term> and **Aediles**. Following those sixty Rural Curators are three Aediles, who embrace the twelve parts of the city in three divisions. They certainly imitate the others: they have care of the city streets, the common roads leading from the countryside into the city, and also buildings, ensuring that they are all constructed according to the laws. Furthermore, they care for the waters which the guardians manage to lead into the city, so that they are brought into the fountains as clear and sufficient as possible, to both assist and adorn the city. 

These men must be of such a character that, having set aside care for their own affairs, they have leisure to manage public business. Therefore, let everyone name from the highest census class <term>census; a division of citizens based on wealth</term> whom they wish to be a future Aedile. From the six who surpass the others in votes, three shall be chosen by lot to have these cares. Finally, once approved, they shall perform their magistracy according to the laws prescribed for them.

Next, the Censors—the curators of things for sale—shall be chosen as five men from the first and second census classes. Their election shall be carried out in nearly the same way as that of the Aediles. Indeed, from the ten who surpass the others in votes, five shall be designated by lot, and once approved, they shall be declared magistrates. Everyone shall nominate whomever he chooses. 

Whoever is accused of refusing to participate shall be fined fifty drachmas and be considered unjust. Anyone who wishes may enter the assemblies and the common gathering. To this end, all members of the first and second census classes are compelled to attend. Furthermore, whoever is absent from these shall be fined ten drachmas. Men of the third and fourth census classes, however, are not compelled; therefore, whoever does not attend shall be unpunished—unless the leaders, urged by some necessity, proclaim that everyone must be present. 

It is the duty of the Censors to maintain the order of the marketplace as established by the laws. They shall also have care of the fountains and temples in that location, so that no one acts injuriously there. If anyone does so, if he is a slave or a foreigner, he shall suffer punishment by lashes and chains. If he is a citizen, he shall be condemned by the Censors to a fine of one hundred drachmas by censorial right. However, they may not condemn him to a greater fine, up to double this amount, unless the Aediles are also present. 

The same condition of fining and punishing shall apply to the Aediles in their own magistracy. For they themselves shall have the power to condemn up to one mina. For a double fine, however, the authority of the Censors shall be required.

After this, dual magistrates of **Music** and **Gymnastics** shall be established for both faculties: some for instruction, others for exercise. Those in charge of instruction shall care for the equipment of the gymnasia and schools and the order of learning; they shall see to it that both males and females in their youth proceed to these things honorably and remain there honorably. 

The masters of the games <term>athlothetæ; those who preside over contests and award prizes</term> shall have care of exercise in gymnastics and music, and they impose duties upon and announce the athletes—namely, the competitors themselves. These likewise ought to be dual: some for music, others for gymnastics. In gymnastics, the same men shall oversee both human and horse races. In music, however, some shall oversee monody <note>original: "monodia"; solo singing or recitation</note>—that is, song and funeral orations—and imitation itself, such as that of rhapsodes <term>rhapsodes; performers who recited epic poetry</term>, namely those who compose choral songs, and of citharists <term>citharists; players of the lyre-like cithara</term>, flute-players, and others of that kind. Others shall oversee choral singing. First, therefore, in the choral play, where men, boys, and girls are exercised in dancing <note>original: "tripudio"</note> and other modes of music...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the administrative and judicial structure of the ideal city from Book VI of Plato's Laws. ### PAGE XXXVIII.

### BOOK VI.

The leaders are to be chosen. One leader is sufficient for them, who must be no younger than forty years of age. We also judge one leader to be sufficient for monody <note>original: "monodia"; solo musical performance</note>, provided they have completed thirty years of age: this person shall both introduce the performers into the contest and possess sufficient knowledge to judge them. Furthermore, the leader and organizer of the choir should be chosen in this manner: those who are devoted to this matter <note>the musical arts</note> shall go to the assembly, with a fine imposed if they do not attend. The Guardians of the Laws <note>original: "legum custodes"; the high-ranking officials of the state</note> shall be the judges of this matter; as for the others, if they do not wish to attend, no one shall compel them. Those present shall nominate candidates, and in the vetting process, this one standard of approval or rejection shall be held: whether the designated person is present or absent. Whoever among the ten designated candidates surpasses the others in votes, and is then approved, shall preside over the choir for a period of one year according to the law. Similarly, in the case of monody and flute-playing, the designation shall be made, along with the election and approval; and whoever succeeds, being confirmed by the judges in the same manner, shall preside for the year. Next, the sponsors and directors of the games in gymnastic exercise, for both horses and men, should be appointed from the second and third property classes. Members of the first three classes are compelled to enter the assembly, but the lowest class shall be free from this duty. From the twenty candidates designated by the majority vote, three shall be chosen by lot to be declared leaders, whom the vote of those approving shall confirm. If anyone is rejected or turned away in the lot or judgment of any magistracy, another shall be designated and approved from the same rank in his place.

<margin>
See how man is a gentle animal, and yet most savage.
</margin>

There remains the leader who shall have care of the entire education of both females and males in the matters we have narrated. We wish this person to be a leader according to the laws: not less than fifty years of age, and one who has legitimate children—preferably of both sexes, but if not, at least one of either sex. Both the one who chooses and the one who is chosen must consider that this magistracy is by far the most excellent of all the high offices in the state. For in all living things, the first sprouts themselves, if they begin aptly toward the virtue of their nature, have the greatest power toward achieving their proper end. This happens in plants, in beasts both wild and tame, and in humans. We say that man is a gentle animal. Furthermore, if he achieves a right education alongside a happy nature, he is accustomed to turning out as the most divine and gentle animal; but if he is not sufficiently or not well educated, he is rendered the most savage animal of all those born on the earth. Therefore, the lawgiver must not postpone the education of children, which is a most necessary thing; but he must give his effort first and foremost, if he is to care for this matter diligently: that from all the citizens, the best man be chosen for each duty, and especially that he be placed in charge of the education of children to the best of his ability. All magistrates, therefore, except the Senate and the Quastors <note>original: "quaestores"; financial officials</note>, shall go to the Temple of Apollo and cast a secret ballot before the Guardians of the Laws, each selecting the one they judge best suited for the education of children. Whoever prevails in the vote, after being approved by the magistrates who selected him (excluding the Guardians of the Laws), shall preside for five years. And in the sixth year, another leader shall be firmly established. If anyone appointed to a public magistracy departs from life more than thirty days before completing his term, those responsible for such matters shall choose another in a similar way. If a guardian of orphans dies, the relatives and kin from both parents, up to the cousins and paternal uncles who are present, shall appoint another within ten days; otherwise, each shall be fined a drachma daily until they appoint a guardian for the orphans.

<margin>
Time, delay, and frequent inquiry contribute to uncovering a controversy.
</margin>

But no city will truly be a city unless the courts are established in the proper order. A mute judge, who, in discussing cases, inquires no more than what the litigants have said (like a mere arbiter), will never be sufficient for declaring the law. For this reason, if there are many judges, they will never judge well easily; nor if they are few and lazy. It is always necessary that what is sought by both sides be declared. Time, delay, and frequent inquiry contribute to uncovering a controversy. Therefore, let those who are in litigation turn first to neighbors and friends, and especially to those who are aware of the matter in question. If it is not sufficiently judged by them, let them go to another court. If they are not reconciled by the two superior courts, let a third court impose an end. Indeed, the constitutions of the courts are in a way the elections of the magistrates.

<margin>
Every magistrate is a judge of some; not every judge is a magistrate.
</margin>

For it is necessary that every magistrate be a judge of certain things. However, not every judge is necessarily a magistrate or a leader, although on the day he performs a judgment, he is in a way a magistrate of no small importance. Therefore, as some magistrates are judges themselves, let us now discuss which and how many judges there should be in each matter. Let the most venerable judgment be that which certain parties have set over themselves, choosing a judge by common consent. Let there be two other types of courts: one when a private citizen complains of suffering from another private citizen and drags him into court; the other when someone, thinking an injury is being done to the Republic by one of the citizens, tries to help the common wealth. We must say, therefore, who and what kind of judges there should be. Let the first court, common to all private citizens who litigate among themselves for the third time, be conducted as follows: All magistrates, both annual and those of longer terms, shall assemble in one temple on the day before the Calends of that month in which the new year begins after the summer solstice.

<margin>
Note that the beginning of the year is taken from the summer solstice.
</margin>

There, with an oath taken by each magistrate as if offering first-fruits to the god, they shall select one judge who seems to them to be the best, and who will render judgments to the citizens in that year in the best and most holy manner. After the judges are designated, they shall each be approved by those who designated them. If anyone is rejected, another shall be chosen similarly. Those who are approved shall render judgments for those who were not reconciled in the preceding courts, and they shall cast their votes openly, with the counselors who chose them and the other magistrates who declared them necessarily listening and watching. As for others, anyone may attend as they please. If anyone accuses a judge of having voluntarily delivered an unjust sentence, he shall do this before the Guardians of the Laws. And whoever is condemned shall pay half of the damages to the person who suffered the injury.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book VI of Plato's Laws, transitioning from the specific appointment of officials to the broader philosophy of judicial systems and the long-term maintenance of the law by the "Guardians."</meta>

-># ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS IN LATIN, DIALOGUE VI. FOLIO 335.<-

If someone should seem worthy of a much greater fine, the judges who condemned him should decide what he must suffer or pay, either to the Republic or to the party who suffered the injury. In public accusations, however, it is necessary first of all to make the multitude <note>the general body of citizens</note> a participant in the judgment. For when a sin is committed against the city, the injury is inflicted upon everyone. Therefore, they are rightly aggrieved unless they themselves are also admitted to judge. But both the beginning and the end of such a trial ought to be referred to the people; however, the examination and the approval should be delegated to three high magistrates, upon whom the litigants agree. But if they cannot agree, the council itself shall take notice of the selection of both parties and judge.

Furthermore, it is necessary for all people to be participants in private judgments to the best of their ability. For he who is entirely repelled from the power of judging considers himself a complete stranger to the city. For these reasons, it is necessary for judgments to be made even by the tribes themselves; and let the judges, chosen by lot, judge immediately while they are incorruptible by pleas. And finally, that court shall define everything—which we have said ought to be entirely undefiled, as far as is possible in human affairs—to determine those disputes which could be settled neither by neighbors nor by fellow tribesmen.

Indeed, concerning the courts—which some might easily neither affirm nor deny to be magistrates without controversy—this description, like a rough sketch drawn from the outside, has encompassed some things, but seems to have left others out. For the exact placement and division of the judicial laws will be positioned much more rightly at the very end of the laws to be enacted. Therefore, let us defer these until that time. As for the other magistrates, they have already been mostly arranged. But the total and perfect management of civil affairs, whether it pertains to one or to all, cannot be clearly declared until the treatment itself—having embraced the beginnings, the subsequent middle parts, and all its members—reaches its conclusion. Which, having progressed at present as far as the creation of magistrates, is a sufficient end for what preceded it, and a beginning for the laws to be enacted; it no longer suffers any delay or sluggishness.

**CLINIAS.** Although you have spoken everything from my own heart, Stranger, this has happened much more graciously to me in the present: that you have joined the end of what has been spoken with the beginning of what is yet to be said.

**ATHENIAN.** Then this wise game of old men <note>original: "prudens seniorum ludus"; referring to the dialogue as a serious intellectual exercise</note> has been played well by us thus far.

**CLINIAS.** You seem to signify a truly beautiful pursuit of men.

**ATHENIAN.** It is consistent. But let us take notice if this seems so to you as it does to me.

**CLINIAS.** What is it? And regarding what things?

**ATHENIAN.** Do you not know that the same thing happens in this matter as in the skill of painters? For that skill seems to have no limit in painting animals; but by always shading and highlighting, or whatever else it is called by painters, it strives to adorn them and never ceases. For it cannot be that there is no increase toward more beautiful and more expressive results.

**CLINIAS.** I almost understand what you are saying as I listen. For I have no experience in this art.

**ATHENIAN.** That has been no hindrance to you. But let us use this analogy brought before us in this way. If someone wished to paint a most beautiful animal <note>The "animal" here represents the living State or the Body of Laws</note>, which should always progress toward the better and not the worse in future time, do you not see that since he is mortal, unless he leaves some successor in the art—who can restore whatever part of the animal might be abolished by time, or add what was omitted by the artist through weakness of skill, and thus make the animal more radiant day by day—that laborious work would last only a short time?

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** And does it not seem to you that this is the will of the legislator? First, that laws should be written for themselves sufficiently and exquisitely to the best of their power. Then, as time proceeds and the trial of things is made, do you think there is any legislator so foolish as to be ignorant that it is necessary to leave behind many such things that require the amendment of some successor, so that the Republic may never become worse, but always more decorated and better?

**CLINIAS.** It is probable. For how could he not wish that?

**ATHENIAN.** By whatever way he can, therefore, he will teach another—whether greater or lesser—both by deeds and words, how the laws are to be preserved and corrected; and he will never tire of speaking these things until he has brought them to an end.

**CLINIAS.** So it is, certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** Must not I and you do this at present?

**CLINIAS.** What are you saying?

**ATHENIAN.** Since we are about to enact laws, and guardians of the laws have been created, but we are approaching the sunset of life, and these guardians are younger than we are, we must, as we said, enact the laws and at the same time make these men both law-givers and guardians as much as we are able.

**CLINIAS.** Why not? Provided that it can be sufficiently done.

**ATHENIAN.** Nevertheless, let us strive more earnestly.

**CLINIAS.** Nothing prohibits it.

**ATHENIAN.** Thus, then, let us say to them: O friends, preservers of the laws, we will necessarily leave behind many things in each case where we establish laws; yet these will not be small things. Rather, we will signify the whole matter to the best of our power by a certain exterior outline, which it will be your duty to fill up. To what you must look while doing this, listen. Megillus and I and Clinias have spoken of these things among ourselves many times, and we agree that we have spoken rightly. And we ask you that you be willing both to indulge us and to imitate us, as disciples do their teachers, looking to those very things to which we harmoniously agreed a guardian and maker of laws must look. Of this agreement there is one head <note>main point</note>: that a man be made good, possessing the <term>virtus</term> <note>virtue or excellence</note> proper to the soul of a man, acquired by some study, or by use, or by a certain attainment, or desire, or opinion, or some kind of doctrine, whether he be male or female, young or old. And toward this very thing of which we speak, let everyone direct themselves with all zeal through their whole life, neglecting other things which are an impediment to this matter. For the fatherland, moreover, if it be necessary, let him be ready to die before he would see the city either overturned or subjected to the yoke of slavery and governed by worse men, or desert it by flight. Indeed, all extremes must be undergone rather than the city be changed into that form of government which is accustomed to make men worse. In these things we have long since agreed; and now you, looking to both of these, praise the laws and blame them. Blame those, I say, which are least able to effect these things; but love those which can, and having freely embraced them, live your life in them. But despise other pursuits which tend elsewhere and look toward common goods. But let this be the beginning of our subsequent laws, starting from sacred matters. First, it is necessary to repeat how many convenient partitions the number five thousand and forty has had, and...

...has, you yourself are the whole number: you who extend them for three; which we have established as the twelfth part of the whole: most rightly born twenty times twenty-one. And just as the whole number consists of twelve parts, so it is split by three into twelve. Therefore, we ought to consider each individual part to be a sacred gift of God, since they follow both the months and the circuit of the universe. For this reason, it leads the entire city to consecrate them, as is innate to them. Some perhaps have divided more rightly than others, and have more happily dedicated their partitions to the gods: but we now believe it most correct to have chosen the number five thousand and forty <note>original: "quinq; miliū & quadraginta"; 5,040 is Plato's "ideal" number of citizens because it has many divisors</note>: which has all the divisions from one to twelve, the eleventh number alone excepted: which is restored by a very small remedy. For it is restored if two are added to another part of the house. A discourse by no means long would demonstrate in leisure that these things are true. 

Therefore, believing the present discourse and reason, let us distribute: and invoking a god or a son of the gods for each part, with altars and other such things dedicated, let us make two gatherings for sacrifices in each month: so that twelve may be accommodated to the distribution of each of the twelve tribes and twelve to the city. Let these things be done first for the sake of the gods and the worship of divine things: then also for the sake of friendship and mutual acquaintance: and finally for the sake of common habit: which is exceedingly necessary for concluding marriages: so that, with ignorance removed, no one is deceived in these matters as far as can be: but each may know to whom he gives [a daughter], and whom and from whom he takes [a wife]. 

Indeed, for the sake of this very series, games and choruses of boys and girls together ought to be held, with their bodies naked as far as modest shame permits <note>Plato suggests this "inspection" so that spouses know the physical health of their partners before marriage</note>: so that with reason, at a suitable age, they may see one another and be seen. Let the leaders of the choruses, and the founders together with the Guardians of the Laws, take care of and adorn all these things, so that they may supply what we have left behind. For it is necessary, as we have said, especially in these matters which are many and small, that some things be overlooked in the first positioning of the laws; which the succeeding magistrates, warned by the use of things, will move and correct, until that time arrives in which these institutes seem to have been sufficiently discussed and approved. 

The time for making this trial, however, shall be a moderate and sufficient decade <note>ten years</note>, both regarding the sacred rites and dances: and finally regarding each and every thing. Indeed, let this amendment through experience be made in common with the lawmaker while he is living. If he should depart: let the individual magistrates report the defect of their magistracy to the Guardians of the Laws: and let them amend it, until each thing seems to have reached its end of approval. Then finally let them hold these laws as ratified: and let them use them together with the others which the legislator wrote from the beginning. In which they shall never move anything of their own will. But if some necessity should ever seem to urge, all the magistrates and the entire people shall consult together on this: and let all the oracles of the gods be sought. If there is one consensus of all these, let them move it: otherwise, never: but let the one who prohibits it prevail according to the law. 

Whoever, therefore, having already reached twenty-five years of age, looking upon others and being looked upon by others, believes he has found for himself a society suitable to his soul and decent for the communion and generation of children, let him take a wife within thirty-five years of age. But in what way that which is decorous and fit ought to be sought, let him first hear. For it is necessary, as Clinias says, to place a proper prologue for each person before the laws. 

**CLINIAS.** You have remembered opportunely, Guest, and you have taken a convenient time for the speech.

<margin>Which marriages ought to be contracted.</margin> 

is born from good parents, he ought to pursue those marriages which prudent men consider honest. They would surely warn that it is especially necessary neither to flee the affinity of the poor, nor to seek the affinity of the rich: but other things being equal, always to honor the poorer person, and to enter into society with him. For it is conducive both to the city and to the families who are joined. Indeed, that which is moderate and middling is wonderfully superior for virtue over that which is immoderate and exceeding. Therefore, whoever is conscious in himself of a soul more ferocious or swifter than is proper for action, he ought to take care that he marries the daughter of the quietest possible parents: and he who is affected by a contrary nature should adopt a contrary affinity for himself. 

But let there finally be one common reason for marriages: that each enters into a marriage not most pleasant to himself, but useful to the city. For individuals are always carried by nature toward what is most similar to themselves. From which the whole city is rendered as equal as possible in both wealth and character: from which those things which we would least wish to happen to us, happen most to many cities. But if we were to sanction these things by law through reason—that the rich should not admit the society of the wealthy, nor the powerful of the powerful—and if we forced the swifter in soul to be coupled with the slower, and the slower conversely with the swifter: not only would our laws seem altogether ridiculous, but they would stir up the anger of the multitude. 

For it is not easy to understand by the intellect how a city ought to be like a mixing bowl: in which the pure wine <note>original: "merum"</note> poured in boils, but is immediately corrected by the sobriety of another god <note>the "other god" here is water, which tempers the wine; Plato uses this as a metaphor for balancing social classes</note> and, being excellently tempered, becomes a good and moderate drink. In what way, however, that is done in the mixed procreation of children: no one, to speak briefly, can see. Wherefore, citizens are not to be forced by law, but induced by persuasion: so that they value the equal and tempered generation of their children more than the equality of the wealthiest affinity. And him who gasps for money in marriage: we ought not to restrain him by written law, but deter him with reproaches and rebukes. 

Therefore, both these things exhort toward celebrating marriages as is fitting, and those things which we said in previous parts: asserting that it is necessary, by leaving behind children of children—our successors, namely, in divine ministry—to attain eternal nature. All these things and even more, someone would rightly say by way of a prologue about entering into marriages. If anyone, however, does not obey of his own will, and lives in the city as a stranger to this fellowship, and passes

Then, if he should dare to strike anyone, let anyone who is present rise up against him and bring aid to the one who received the injury. He who obeys the law shall be praised by all. But he who does not comply, let the guardians of the laws condemn him as one foreign to decorum and utterly ignorant of the songs <note>original: "musarum"; literally "of the Muses," implying the cultural and harmonious education a citizen should have.</note> of the marriage-vow. Truly, drinking to the point of drunkenness is never fitting anywhere, except during the festivals of the god who gave wine <note>Dionysus.</note>, nor is it safe. Most especially, the bridegroom and bride joined in marriage ought then to be of sound mind, since they are entering no small change of life; and especially so that procreation may always occur from those who are most moderate. For it is almost uncertain which night or day carries it out with a god. Therefore, so that a solid, stable, and quiet conception may occur, it is not right to attend to the procreation of children with bodies dissolved by drunkenness. For he who is filled with wine <margin>See that the drunk should not attend to the procreation of children.</margin> is stirred by a madness of both soul and body, and is both pulled and pulls toward anything. Therefore, a drunk man, as if captured in mind, is useless for sowing. Indeed, it is likely that he will procreate offspring that are unequal, unstable, and crooked in both limbs and character. Wherefore, throughout their whole life, and especially while occupied with procreation, let each abstain and take care lest they do those things which by their own nature and will induce diseases, or which decline toward petulance and injury. For these things are necessarily transferred and imprinted upon the souls and bodies of those being born, and worse children are born from them. But especially on that day and night, one must abstain from such things. For the principle and divinity implanted in men, if it is treated with honor by those using its gift in a manner suitable to it, preserves all things. Moreover, it is necessary to receive the bride into one of the two houses, separated from the parents, as if for the procreation and education of chicks; and there to celebrate the marriage where he is to live with his children. For if a certain desire exists in friendships, it connects and binds all manners together as if with a kind of glue. But future habit, having no desire through the intermission of time, separates one from the other <margin>What future habit does.</margin> through satiety. Therefore, leaving both parents and relatives, let them set out separately as if to a colony, and live looking back at one another in turn, procreating and educating children; and the life which they received from others, let them hand it down to others like burning torches, <note>Plato uses the metaphor of the torch race (lampadedromia) to describe the passing of life and traditions from one generation to the next.</note> always worshipping the gods according to the laws. After this, it must be considered: of which things is possession most honorable? In most things, whether in learning of them or in acquiring and possessing them, there is no difficulty. But in the matter of slaves, it is altogether difficult. The cause, truly, is that we speak of them in a way that is both right and, again, not right. For words are spoken against the use of slaves and again in favor of their use. ME. In what way do we say this? For we do not understand, Guest, what you wish to say just now. ATHE. Not without reason, O Megillus. For almost that servitude of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans.</note>, which you call Helotry, <note>The Helots were a subjugated population in Sparta who worked the land for the citizen-warriors.</note> causes the greatest doubt and contention among the rest of the Greeks; since to some it seems well-instituted, and to others contrary. Truly, that of the Mariandynians is less than the Heracleidae; finally, the crowd of servants among the Thessalians. Looking at all these and things of this sort, what must be done concerning the possession of slaves? This certainly escaped me just now, and you rightly asked me what I was saying. But it is of this sort. We know perfectly well that we would all confess that slaves ought to be held who are as benevolent and good as possible. For already many slaves have been better toward all virtue than brothers and sons to some, and have preserved the homes, the entire property of their masters, and the masters themselves. We are not ignorant that these things are preached concerning slaves. ME. Certainly. ATHE. On the contrary, it is also said that nothing sound exists in a serving soul, and that nothing is to be credited to the race of slaves. Which the wisest of poets <note>Homer, in the Odyssey.</note> testifies to us, when he speaks of Jupiter thus: Jupiter takes away half the mind from those who are subjected to the lot of servitude. Therefore, men thinking such diverse things about slaves, some trust nothing of the race of slaves; but with prods and whips, as if against the nature of wild beasts, they make the souls of their ministers <term>ministers</term> <note>In this context, household servants or attendants.</note> servile not three times over, but more often. Others do the opposite. CLI. It is so. But since men feel such diverse things about slaves, what must we do, Guest, in this region of ours regarding the possession and chastisement of slaves? ATHE. It seems clear to me, O Clinias: since man is a difficult animal to tame, and he suffers with difficulty being led in actual fact to the necessary distinction of slave from freeman and master, possession of him is difficult. <margin>On slaves. ...that he is a human being. This was made clear by the example of the frequent rebellions of the Messenians. <note>The Messenians were frequently enslaved by the Spartans (as Helots) and led several famous revolts, which Plato uses here as a cautionary tale about the dangers of keeping large numbers of slaves from the same ethnic group.</note> Furthermore, cities that have many slaves speaking the same language have demonstrated how many and how great are the evils that follow from this. The thefts and robberies of pirates, which used to be most frequent around Italy, also arise from this. If anyone considers all these things, he will be in doubt as to what should be done about them. There remain, therefore, only two ways: that those who are to serve easily should not be from the same country, and as much as possible, they should speak different languages. They should be educated correctly, not only for their own sake, but much more for the sake of their masters. Now, the correct education of these people is that no insult should be offered to them; and far less injury should be done to them than to one’s equals. For it is by his treatment of those whom he can easily injure that a man shows he truly and naturally honors justice and sincerely hates iniquity. Therefore, he who never acts impiously or unjustly regarding the character and actions of his slaves, and thus keeps himself unstained in these matters, will be most fit to produce the fruits of virtue. The same can also be said of a master, a tyrant, and every person in power toward those who are weaker. Slaves should always be chastised and beaten by right, and not merely warned like free men, lest they become too soft. All speech addressed to slaves should be in the form of a command; no joke should be shared with them, whether they be female or male. Many act foolishly in this regard, and by nurturing them too delicately, they make life more difficult for themselves in commanding, and for the slaves in obeying.

**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly.

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, in this way, let each man have slaves appropriate in number and ability for the various services of life. But after this, we must describe the dwellings in our discourse.

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** For a new city, and one previously inhabited by no men, buildings must be provided first, and a plan for the temples and walls must be held. These things, O Clinias, ought to have preceded the marriages. But since we are now dealing with words, it is permissible to set them down in this way. When we truly undertake the matter itself, we shall place these things before the marriages, if God wills, and then perform all the rest in order. For now, we shall run through these things briefly as if in a sketch.

**CLINIAS.** Let it be so.

**ATHENIAN.** Let the whole city be lead in a circle on high ground, so that it may be both more fortified and cleaner. Let temples be built around the forum. Near these, the palaces of the magistrates and the courts, in which, as if in the most sacred places, they shall both receive and deliver just sentences—partly because they will be judging sacred matters, and partly because the shrines of the judging gods are there. There also shall be the judicial residences, in which they judge cases of homicide and other capital injuries. But regarding walls, O Megillus, I agree with the Spartans: I would easily allow the walls to lie on the ground. For that poetic saying is rightly praised, which advises us to build walls of bronze and iron rather than of earth. <note>This refers to the Spartan ideal that a city's "walls" should be the brave bodies of its citizens (iron and bronze armor/weapons) rather than stone fortifications, which might encourage cowardice.</note> Among us, however, it is moreover very ridiculous that every year young men are sent out into the fields—who, having prepared cages, pits, and buildings, keep the enemy far from the borders—and yet we build walls around the city. Firstly, this contributes nothing to the health of cities; secondly, it is accustomed to soften and weaken the spirits of the citizens. For walls cause them to think that they can easily retreat inside them and not put the enemy to flight, and they believe they will be safe not by being vigilant with day and night guards, but by sleeping behind the enclosure and rampart of walls—as if they were born for sloth, surely ignorant that rest draws its origin from labor, and that labor is usually born from shameful leisure and negligence. But if men must be fortified by some walls, let the private houses be built from the beginning in such a way that the whole city, by its equality and similarity, becomes a single wall, and let all the houses have a safe entrance to the streets. Surely this arrangement will be pleasing to those who look upon it, since the whole city will have the appearance of a single house; and for ease of guarding, it will be by far the most convenient of all. The citizens who are to inhabit the city should take the greatest care that these are so constructed from the beginning. Let the city supervisors <term>aediles</term> <note>The translator uses the Roman term "aedile" to describe the Greek *astynomoi*, officials responsible for urban maintenance and public order.</note> also look to this and compel those who are negligent with many fines. Let them also take care that the city is as clean as possible, and never allow anything public to be occupied by private individuals, whether by building or digging. They should also take care of the rainwater, so that it flows away abundantly and easily; likewise for all things that must be inhabited either inside or outside the city. But all these things and others which have been omitted by the laws shall be ordered by the guardians of the laws, taught by experience. But after these things—the buildings around the forum, the gymnasia, the theaters for spectators, and the dwellings for teachers and learners—have been arranged, let us proceed to the laws concerning what follows marriage.

**CLINIAS.** It must be done so.

**ATHENIAN.** Regarding marriage, therefore, O Clinias, let the matter be as we have said. After which follows the rule of living that precedes the procreation of children, which is not shorter than a year's time. But in what manner the groom and bride should live together in a most excellent city is not easy to say. Indeed, although many things in the preceding sections were difficult, those things which must be said about these matters will be accepted by the common people as the most difficult of all. Yet what appears true and right must be said, O Clinias.

**CLINIAS.** It must be said by all means.

**ATHENIAN.** Whoever thinks that only public and common matters should be ordered by laws, but does not care for private matters—even those which are necessary—and gives license to each person to live every day as he wishes, and does not think all things should be done according to a certain order, but neglects private life... <note>The text transitions into the discussion of "common meals" or *syssitia*, a practice where citizens ate together in public halls to ensure discipline and equality.</note> we shall assert that among us, the bride and groom live in communal dining no less and no differently than at other times before the marriage. **CLINIAS.** It seems so.
