# ON THE LAWS OR ON THE LATIN LAWS, DIALOGUE VI.
### R

...you fear! ATHENIAN: Listen now: let me not detain you longer in vain delay. For whatever in the city participates in law and order, all things proceed well from it. But those things that lack order, or are poorly ordered, confound even those things that are well-ordered. This is exactly what has happened in this matter. For to you, O Megillus and Clinias, the <term>common meals</term><note>original: "commessatio" (referring to the Greek *syssitia*). These were mandatory public meals for male citizens in Sparta and Crete, intended to foster military camaraderie and discipline.</note> for men have been excellently and, as I said, wonderfully established by a certain divine necessity. However, the common meals for women have been improperly neglected and lie in the shadows. This is a different kind of human being, distinct from us; their nature is more hidden and craftier because of their weakness, and thus they are less easily brought under order.

<margin>
On the Character and nature of women.
</margin>

Therefore, the legislator yielded, which was an oversight. Because this was omitted, many things are being corrupted for us, which would be in far better condition than they are now if this very thing had been regulated by laws. For the female element is not merely half of human affairs (as it might seem if left to lie disordered), but insofar as its nature is less inclined toward virtue than the male nature, it exceeds it in influence, so that it seems to be more than double. This must, therefore, be revisited and corrected; all pursuits must be established as common to women and men for the happiness of the city. But now, this gender is led so unhappily toward this gap that it would not be prudent for a man to mention this matter in other regions and cities where public meals have never been seen. From where, then, could anyone without being ridiculed force women to take their food and drink openly? There is surely nothing that this gender would seem to bear more restively. For since they have been accustomed to living timidly and in obscurity, they will resist with all their might any legislator attempting to lead them into the light. This gender, as I said, would not even listen to the speech of one speaking correctly elsewhere without a great outcry; but here, perhaps, they will endure it. Therefore, if it also seems right to you, for the sake of our conversation and so that the discussion on the republic is not left incomplete, I wish to say why this is a good and decent thing. If it pleases you, I shall speak; otherwise, I shall let it pass.

CLINIAS: Stranger, we desire to hear this in a wonderful way.

ATHENIAN: Let us listen then. But do not be surprised if I seem to trace the matter from a deeper origin. For we have an abundance of leisure, and nothing else presses us to prevent us from considering everything from all sides that pertains to the laws.

CLINIAS: You speak rightly.

ATHENIAN: Let us, therefore, return to first principles. Everyone ought to know that the generation of men either had no beginning at all and will have no end—but has always been and always will be—or if it did begin, it began an inestimable length of time ago.

CLINIAS: Clearly.

ATHENIAN: Do we not believe that across the whole earth, many cities have been built and destroyed, and that diverse human pursuits have proceeded, partly with order and partly without order? Likewise, there have been many uses of food and drink, and various ways of eating and seasoning, and various changes of seasons, in which it must be believed that animals were transformed in different ways?

CLINIAS: Nothing prevents it.

ATHENIAN: What further? Do we think that vines began at a time when they did not exist? And similarly olives, and the gifts of <note>Ceres and Proserpina are the Latin names for Demeter and Persephone, the goddesses of grain and the harvest.</note> Ceres and Proserpina, which some <note>In Greek mythology, Triptolemus was the hero who presided over the sowing of grain and the spread of agriculture.</note> Triptolemus provided? And as for animals, in the time when these things did not exist, did they not devour one another just as they do now?

CLINIAS: Without a doubt.

<margin>
Ages and customs of the past.
</margin>

ATHENIAN: But regarding sacrifices: we still see human beings sacrificed by men among many peoples; and we hear the opposite of others, as when we did not even dare to taste the flesh of cattle, nor did we immolate animals to the gods. Instead, cakes and fruits soaked in honey and other pure sacrifices of this kind were offered to the gods. They abstained from meat. For to eat flesh and to pollute the altars of the gods with blood was seen as impious. Thus, a certain <term>Orphic life</term><note>A lifestyle based on the teachings attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus, characterized by strict vegetarianism and ritual purity.</note> flourished then. Indeed, they ate only inanimate things and abstained from all animals.

<margin>
The Orphic life.
</margin>

CLINIAS: These things are widely reported, as you say, and are very credible.

ATHENIAN: But perhaps someone will ask: to what purpose have all these things been said by us now?

CLINIAS: You have guessed correctly, O stranger.

ATHENIAN: Therefore, if I am able, Clinias, I will try to declare what follows next.

CLINIAS: Speak now.

ATHENIAN: I perceive that all things for men depend on a threefold need and desire; in which, if they are led rightly, virtue is born; but if otherwise, vice. Two of these are the desires for food and drink, which animals have as soon as they are born. Since every animal has an innate appetite for these, it is carried away by impulse, and does not listen to the words of one who warns that something else should be done, other than that these desires and pleasures should be satisfied and the contrary pains avoided. The third great need and most acute desire in us, which is for the propagation of the species, arises later; but it burns men with the most ardent madness and the greatest insolence. These three diseases, which carry us away toward what is called the most pleasant, must be turned from that toward what is best by three great means: Fear, Law, and True Reason.

<margin>
Virtue and vice arise from the triple desire: food, drink, and sex.
</margin>

When the Muses and the gods of contests are employed alongside these, the excess and abundance of desire may be extinguished in this way. We ought to place the procreation of children after marriage. After procreation itself, we place education and discipline. For perhaps as the speech proceeds, each law, having progressed through the prior stages, will finally lead to the common meals. When we arrive at gatherings and communions of this kind, we shall then see more clearly whether these common rules should be commanded for men alone or also for women, once we have approached more closely and have set in their own digested order those things which ought to precede them but are not yet arranged. Thus, just as I was saying, we shall inspect the common meals more sharply and we shall hand down more suitable laws concerning them.

CLINIAS: You speak skillfully.

ATHENIAN: Let us, therefore, hold in memory the things that have just been said. For perhaps they will be of use to us at some point.

CLINIAS: Which things do you command us to hold?

ATHENIAN: Those things which we called by the names of food, drink, and <note>original: "veneris" (Venus), referring to sexual desire or procreation.</note> sex.

CLINIAS: It shall be done entirely as you command, stranger.

ATHENIAN: Excellently indeed. But let us come to the matter of the betrothal: and let us teach the groom and the bride how children are to be procreated; and unless we persuade them, let us threaten them with the positioning of certain laws.

CLINIAS: In what way?

ATHENIAN: Both the groom and the bride ought to consider how they can procreate the most beautiful and best children for the city. All men who perform something in common, whoever they are, toward each other and toward the work itself...

# THE ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE VII ON THE LAWS

...they demonstrate a mind, they do all things well and beautifully. If, however, they either do not have a mind or do not apply it, the opposite occurs. Therefore, let the groom turn his mind toward the bride and the procreation of children; and let the bride similarly turn hers toward the groom and toward this work, especially during that time when they have not yet produced offspring. A group of women—either many or few, as the elected leaders see fit—shall have care over these matters. These women shall gather daily in the temple of <term>Lucina</term><note>original: "Lucinę". In Roman mythology, Lucina was the goddess of childbirth. Ficino uses this name to translate the Greek goddess Eileithyia.</note> for a third part of an hour; and there they shall report to one another if they see any man or woman among those bound by the bond of marriage for the purpose of procreation turning their mind elsewhere than to those things commanded in the marriage sacrifices. 

The procreation of children, and the oversight of those dedicated to it, shall not exceed a period of ten years, provided that fertility for generating offspring is present. If they remain infertile until that time, they shall separate after a consultation with their relatives and the women who are caretakers of these matters, as is beneficial to both parties. If any dispute arises regarding the benefits of either party, ten of the <term>guardians of the laws</term><note>original: "legum custodibus". These were high-ranking magistrates in Plato's ideal city responsible for maintaining the integrity of the legal system.</note> chosen by the parties themselves shall judge the matter. 

Furthermore, the women overseers themselves may enter the homes of young people and, partly by warnings and partly by threats, drive them away from their ignorance and wrongdoing. If they are unable to do so, they shall report the matter to the guardians of the laws, who shall then take care of it. If those guardians cannot prevent it, they shall bring the matter before the people; having written down the names of the offenders, they shall affirm under oath that they were unable to make them better. The person whose name is thus recorded, unless he convicts his accusers of falsehood, shall be held in <term>infamy</term><note>A loss of legal standing and social reputation.</note>; he shall no longer apply himself to marriage or the procreation of children. If he attempts to do so, anyone who wishes may strike him with impunity. The same penalties apply to a woman. For such women shall live excluded from female honors; they shall not be received at weddings or celebrations of childbirth if they have been summoned to judgment and condemned. 

If, after they have procreated children according to the laws, a man joins himself to another’s wife, or a woman to another’s husband—namely while those others are still in their childbearing years—they shall be subject to the same penalties as those applied during their own childbearing period. But men and women who live chastely after the procreation of children shall be honored in all these things; those who do otherwise shall be censured. If it happens that many behave moderately in such matters, these things may be held and done by custom without written laws; but if the majority do not restrain themselves, they should be declared in the written laws, and judgment and action should be taken regarding each case according to that standard. 

The first year is the beginning of the whole life for everyone; it is necessary that it be recorded in the ancestral shrines as the beginning of life for both boy and girl. Let it be inscribed on a whitened wall in every tribe so that it is clear from the number of years who is fit for the magistracy; let the living men of each tribe always be written nearby, and let those departing this life similarly be deleted.

<margin>The age of the girl and the male who ought to be married.</margin>

The time for marriage for a girl is from sixteen to twenty years; and let that be the longest time established for this purpose. For a male, from thirty to thirty-five. The time for holding a magistracy for women shall be after the fortieth year; for men, after the thirtieth. The time for war is from age twenty to sixty for men; for women, after they have borne children, up to the fiftieth year of their age. In these matters, it must be observed that they are accepted for that military service which is both possible for them and decent.

### The Argument of Marsilio Ficino for Dialogue VII on the Laws.

**P**lato moves forward in the seventh book again with incomparable diligence to the first rudiments of a tender age; indeed, he progresses further. For he never, so to speak, departs from this very point, judging that the entire good or evil of a republic consists in the good or evil morals of private individuals; and these, moreover, all consist in the good or evil education of the earliest age. He achieves this especially in the first books immediately, and again here in the seventh; in both places, he is a most diligent painter. But there he was, as it were, sketching; here, however, I might say he is coloring. 

Again, in the earlier books, he wishes such diligence to be held as the reward of the laws; but here he considers the character of the citizens to be the substance that precedes the laws. For he says that written laws will be useless unless such diligence in upbringing has preceded them. Furthermore, there and here he progresses from the child’s discipline to that of the youth, and then to the man’s. Not without reason, after some sacred laws in the previous sections, did he proceed directly to the marriage laws as if they were sacred, so that he might begin the birth of a "divine animal" <note>Ficino's term for a human being, who possesses a soul.</note> from sacred things. 

Soon after marriage, he girds himself to the shaping of children—not only those already born, but those being born, and even those yet to be born. In this "cultivation" of human beings, he is no less wise, provident, and accurate than a farmer is with the seeds of crops. For what purpose do you think he says there is much more at stake in female matters than in male? Likewise, that women ought to abstain from wine on the night children are to be conceived, and even in the time immediately preceding, and throughout the entire year of conception, from all things that disturb the mind? These things undoubtedly aim at omitting nothing of the most exact care regarding human cultivation. 

You will notice from these points that Plato believed not only the man but also the woman holds the role of an active cause in generating children. Though <term>Aristotle</term><note>Aristotle famously argued in *Generation of Animals* that the father provides the "form" (active principle) while the mother provides only the "matter" (passive principle).</note> disagreed with this in some way, many of the most approved physicians have agreed with Plato. Certainly, if everyone loves their own work—because a father loves a son more than he is loved by the son, and a mother loves the child more ardently than the father—one may conjecture that she is a co-creator of this work together with the man. This can also be confirmed by the fact that children are no less, and often even more, similar to their mothers than to their fathers. Such a specific and frequent similarity indicates that the fetus receives its substance not only from the father’s influence but also from the mother’s. For nearly every effort of a cause is toward producing something similar to itself. Finally, since the male and female are of the same species, they have powers of the same nature. Therefore, both are effective in perfecting a form of the same nature, even if not in an equal, at least in a similar way. But these points pertain very little to the laws. Moreover, he touches here on a significant question regarding <term>black bile</term><note>original: "atra bile". In ancient and Renaissance medicine, an excess of black bile was thought to cause "melancholy," which could lead to either depression or inspired genius.</note>, by the fault of which...

### ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE VII ON THE LAWS

Infants are fearful, difficult, and morose. Regarding this very <term>humor</term><note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were thought to determine a person's temperament and health.</note> and its care, we have spoken more diligently in our book *On Caring for the Health of Men of Letters*. However, as far as the present subject is concerned, you should know that the <term>melancholic humor</term><note>original: "humorē ... melācholicū". Melancholy was associated with the element of earth and a cold, dry temperament, often linked to fear and sadness.</note> in children does not arise from its own specific compression—which is actually sanguine and mostly airy—but from certain remains of the mother’s menstrual blood which have putrefied in the child, and through a certain scorching, have then been converted into black bile. 

Added to the causes of childhood fears is the novelty of things, which indeed causes heard voices to terrify them like thunder, and seen shapes to frighten them like ghosts and lightning bolts. Meanwhile, because the <term>reason</term> has not yet been awakened, it by no means distinguishes images from the things themselves, leaving the soul to be stirred by the <term>imagination</term> at its whim. From this very fear, infants continually suffer and complain, especially since they are very easily offended by touch, and are harmed by the air, and are themselves agitated and vexed by the movement of nature, which labors greatly in its beginning. 

For this reason, Plato orders the use of a nearly perpetual and rhythmic motion in caring for infants and youths. 
**First**, because they were brought forth by motion, they are preserved by motion. 
**Second**, because by a moderate motion of life of this kind, we resist the immoderate agitation caused both internally by nature and externally by the air. 
**Third**, because motion excites natural heat and gives life to the whole body equally. 
**Fourth**, it concocts and digests nourishment throughout the limbs. 
**Fifth**, it separates superfluous waste. 
**Sixth**, it opens obstructions and balances the humors. 
**Seventh**, it contributes to growth. 
**Eighth**, it renders the limbs both fit and solid at the same time. 

Not only through a certain moderation of equality, but also by a proportion of a certain <term>number</term><note>original: "numeri". In this context, "number" refers to rhythm and mathematical proportion in music and movement.</note>, our motion ought to be harmonious. Concerning the power of music, we have discussed much in many letters. For now, let it be enough to understand that if the soul is often distracted by music in opposite directions—namely, at one time toward pleasure and at another toward pain—it can certainly be led back from both to a certain middle state of each. And if the soul is called back from the motion of the body into rest, and conversely from rest into motion, surely it can be led back by certain musical modes from a motion lacking order to one that is ordered, and from there eventually to a stable state. 

He says both here and in the *Second Letter to Dionysius* that this state is both characteristic of God and safest for human life. Whether pleasure and pain consist in a certain motion, and in what way they are defined, we dispute more extensively in the book *On Pleasure* and in the commentaries on the *Philebus*. It will be sufficient for the present if we conclude in this manner: 

The pleasures of taste and touch seem to be born in a certain restitution into the body’s <term>natural habit</term><note>original: "habitū naturalē". This refers to the healthy, balanced state of the body.</note>. Pains, on the contrary, are born in a certain fall from that natural state, whether either occurs through evacuation, or repletion, or motion, or rest, or some alteration of qualities. Furthermore, the pleasures of smell, hearing, and sight consist in a certain return to a <term>sensual order</term> from which we are daily disturbed by many accidents. 

Next, the pleasure of imagining is likewise in a regression to an <term>imaginable order</term>, from which disturbance casts us down. Indeed, both the imaginal and sensual order are founded in a certain temperament of the <term>spirits</term><note>original: "spirituū". In Ficino’s philosophy, "spirits" are a thin, vaporous substance that connects the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note>; whenever things of a similar nature are applied to this temperament, pleasure arises, resulting from a certain mutual congruence of sense and imagination with the things that influence them. After these, the joy of reason is born in a certain reformation, through which the reason—which had become formless or deformed by bodily disturbance—is formed according to its own nature and is reformed. Finally, the joy of the mind is perfected by a reformation through which, by a certain intellectual intuition, it is reformed at last into the <term>Idea</term>, from which it had fallen due to the tumult of a busy life. 

If you consider this induction correctly, you will see that human pleasure is essentially a return to a natural state; and that it is not so much the return itself, but the state [it achieves] that is produced and desired. Therefore, if such a state could be made perpetually firm, it would be the most desirable of all. But why does it seem to any thinker that delight in perpetual motion is more desirable than that perpetual status? Because imagination and opinion deceive us, being joined to a soul in a mobile body, and through such a union, the soul hungers for mobile pleasure. It would rightly neglect this for the sake of the firmness of the natural state, if ever it were placed above motion. 

For if we truly tasted the flavor of the natural state itself—outside of which we are placed here on earth—just as we taste the flavor of the motion tending toward it, we would undoubtedly prefer the state to the return by a wide margin. Surely, just as all degrees of goods are better in the stable reason of the Good than in mobile matter, so the reasons for all things to be desired are located in the reason of such a state rather than in mobile matter. Through these things, the specific joy of God and divine beings is proven to exist in a certain state incomparably more pleasant than all motions. The prudent ought to choose this for themselves and apply it to others, especially the younger. 

Furthermore, they must persuade the young that pleasure arising from motion is not only brief, light, and mixed with trouble, but also slides continuously into many long-lasting and immense pains. He distinguishes rhythmic motion, by which we moderate the awkward movements of tender age, into two kinds: namely, **music** and **gymnastics**. For through the first, we compose the spirit and the soul; through the second, the humors and the limbs. 

Under the name of **music**, he includes not only singing and sounds, but also poetry and those things pertaining to the order of figures. Under the name of **gymnastics**, he includes all motions of the body in rehearsals and games of contests and battles. You should understand <term>choral dance</term><note>original: "choreā saltationēq;".</note> and dancing as being in some way a mixture of both. Then, through all these as if they were studies, he diligently educates infants, boys, and youths—females as well as males—for the duties of both war and peace. 

Indeed, he calls such rudiments the **ancestral laws** and the **bonds of the republic**. If these were withdrawn, as if they were columns, the roofs of the republic would collapse. He orders that every single thing in these matters be done no differently than they are established by public rules, judging that from such small offenses, all crimes eventually arrive in the republic; and that from the changeability of games, jokes, and ornaments, the change of laws and the republic also proceeds. You will note that change...

<summary>Ficino explains the physiological and psychological basis for educating children through music and gymnastics, arguing that rhythmic motion restores the soul and body to their natural, healthy state. He emphasizes that the stability of a state depends on maintaining traditional games and artistic forms among the youth.</summary>

->### ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE VII ON THE LAWS<-

...change <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the thought that changing established customs—even bad ones—is risky.</note> among evils is the most dangerous of all things; so much so that even if you change for the better, you will at least undergo danger for a time. Among these matters, he <note>Plato</note> says that sacrifices should be made during the games to the gods, the sons of gods, and the <term>demons</term><note>In the Platonic tradition, "demons" (daimones) are not evil spirits, but intermediary beings who bridge the gap between the divine and the human.</note>. To the pure demons, I say, so that they might reconcile us to the sons of gods; to the sons of gods, so that they might make the gods favorable to us; and finally to the gods, so that they might make us more prepared for the gifts of the supreme God. 

Thus, indeed, ancient religion was accustomed to act: just as one passes through the celestial spheres step by step in body and sight, so too should one proceed from nearby divinities to the more remote ones in their own order. In all things, one should especially venerate that which reflects the splendor of the Supreme Being. Nor am I speaking now of civil—or rather common—superstition, nor of poetic—or rather insane—superstition, but of the philosophical worship of divine things established by the ancient sages as the order of the universe dictated. Plato commends this worship alone everywhere, truly deriding the other two. When he mentions only two classes—the gods and the sons of gods—he understands "sons" to include demons and <term>heroes</term><note>Semi-divine figures or exceptionally noble souls.</note>. But when he enumerates the gods, the sons of gods, and the demons, he understands the "Gods" to be the powers above the spheres, the "Sons" to be the powers within the spheres, and the "Demons" to be the powers below the spheres.

After this, when he commends the discipline of the lawful games, he says the games should be established for the sake of serious study rather than against it. He adds that human affairs, if compared to divine ones, are worthy of no serious study, no esteem, and no love; they should be considered not as holidays, but as trifles. Yet, he agrees they should be magnified in relation to natural things. Then he says the best thing to happen to a man is to be strongly suited for and devoted to these "games" from birth. This serves both as a solace for a laborious life and as a means to acquire discipline gradually through appropriate games. Because the soul performs a circuit through various forms of living, like a dancing choir, they think this is the best thing for the universe. Likewise, it is the same for the souls of all nature: namely, that whatever lies hidden in its power, it brings forth into the light through a certain succession. 

But why does he not say that other animals are also the "playthings" of the gods? Because they are not so familiar to the gods that the gods would play with them. Nor are they compared to the gods, as they do not compare themselves to God, nor do they ever measure divine things, which would force them to be measured against them as we are. And surely, if there is to be laughter, human "play" should laugh at the attempt to measure the immeasurable. 

Consider here Plato’s words of this kind: *“Those things which we have related from dawn until this hour, not without a certain inspiration from the gods, seem to me to be like a daughter of poetry.”* <note>original: "Ea quæ ab aurora... poesi quodammodo filia mihi videntur."</note> In this, he signifies that all his writings up to that day—that is, in his old age—were in a certain way divinely inspired and arranged in a poetic figure, so that they are mostly to be explained allegorically. He intends the same thing immediately after the beginning of the *Phaedrus*, so that we may know that both what he composed in his youth and what he wrote in his extreme old age savor greatly of poetry. For this reason, he says in his letters <note>Specifically the Second and Seventh Letters attributed to Plato.</note> that his mind can be grasped by no one, or by very few, and only then with difficulty and through a certain prophetic sagacity.

Furthermore, contemplate here how diligently Plato restrains unbridled youth, how much he detests sleepiness, and how he commends wakefulness. How opportunely he disposes the duties of each age, ordering that during play, first, literature should be taught. Second, music. Third, gymnastics. Fourth, arithmetic. Fifth, geometry. Sixth, astronomy. In the seventh place, he locates <term>dialectic</term>—that is, metaphysics—at the end of the *Laws* and the *Republic*. 

Because he says that God never fights with divine necessity, but does fight with human necessity, you must distinguish that one necessity is in the natural order of things itself as it is divinely established: that things are of such a kind, so many, and so great; that they act thus and move thus; that some precede, some accompany, and others follow; some are together, while others are separate; and as they are, so they must be judged. The other necessity is found in a certain chance departure from the natural order, where something appears deformed, monstrous, discordant, or dissolved. God does not fight with the first necessity, for such necessity consists of His own primary will. But does He fight with the other? Certainly, God never "fights"—for what could resist the Omnipotent? Nevertheless, He is imagined to fight because these things, having fallen further from the divine likeness, fall into a deformity most unlike God, as if already rebelling. But meanwhile, they are reduced to order in wondrous ways by God, as if He were resisting and conquering them.

Notice after this a saying of no small importance: *“Ignorance is not the worst of all things. Rather, the worst is the skillful knowledge of many things acquired badly.”* <note>original: "Non est pessimum rerum omnium imperitia. Immo vero pessimum est multarum rerum peritia acquisita male."</note> And if you also notice the preceding sentiment, that he labels man as "god," "demon," and "hero," you will recognize by what reasoning Plato can be explained when he says the human soul passes through various species; but this is discussed more broadly in theology. 

Furthermore, where he exhorts the youth to mathematical doctrines, he rebukes the Greeks because they have all erred in geometry and astronomy. In geometry, indeed, because they thought that any dimension was <term>commensurable</term> with any other <note>A reference to the discovery of irrational numbers, which cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of integers.</note>. That this cannot be so was first discovered among the "barbarians" <note>Ficino likely refers to the Egyptians or Pythagoreans.</note>. In astronomy, too, they erred because they said the planets "wander"—whereas in divine things there is no error. Likewise, they named the motion of the swiftest things as the slowest, and the slowest as the swiftest. He judges that to measure against the dignity of the gods through ignorance born of negligence is not only foolish, but profane. 

He greatly condemns the error of the Greeks against the will of divine providence—those who say that one should not investigate God the author of the world, nor the origin of the world itself, nor the cause of those things that are in the world—as if this investigation did not pertain to piety. Yet it is the most pious of all things, as it especially agrees with the divine will, which both placed the universe in that same order to always allure one to such investigation, and created the mind itself most greedy for this investigation. We have proved elsewhere that Plato himself thought true piety lies chiefly in the worship of the one God, and we confirm it at present through his words above. For even if he often says in the plural that the "gods" are to be worshipped, he concludes at last in the singular number and with singular worship that God Himself is worthy of all blessed study. Furthermore, in the preceding parts, being about to create judges, he gathered all the magistrates...

FO. CCCXXXIX.
DE LEG. VEL DE LEG. LAT. DIAL. VII.
R iii

in the temple, and at the very beginning of the year. He made the beginning from the summer solstice. Do not let it disturb you that he says [the beginning is] on the <term>Kalends</term><note>The first day of the month in the Roman calendar.</note> following the solstice. Consider that this was said for the sake of the people, to provide a more certain starting point; however, he believes the true beginning properly occurs at the solstice itself. This may be explained allegorically: when the light of the sun—that is, the light of God—is received by us more directly and abundantly, then truly is the beginning of living, thinking, and judging. For the sake of this one light, all people should worship whatever they worship together in one temple—that is, in one religion. He says in the books of the *Republic* that the light of the sun is the image of the presence of the One over all things, placed by the Father of all in this mundane temple as if it were His own statue. What more is there to say? He teaches elsewhere often that the one God is to be adored above all, and for His sake, other divinities are to be worshipped. He demonstrates this clearly in the letter to <term>Dionysius</term><note>Plato’s Second and Thirteenth Letters are addressed to Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse.</note>, again to <term>Hermias</term><note>The OCR reads 'Herminiam', but this refers to Hermias of Atarneus, mentioned in Plato’s Sixth Letter.</note>, in the *Parmenides* (which deals entirely with the One), in the *Timaeus* (which derives all things from the One), in the *Philebus* (which measures all things by the One), and in the *Epinomis* (which reduces all things back to the One).

### DIALOGUE VII. ON LAWS OR ON THE MAKING OF LAWS.

<margin>ATHENIAN. On the education of children.</margin>
**Athenian:** Now that we have discussed these matters, we must next speak of the education and discipline of children, both male and female. It is impossible to pass over this in total silence; even if it seems more like a mention of certain teachings rather than something suitable for laws. For the small and hidden things that happen daily in private and within individual homes—since people easily act according to their own pleasure, pain, and desire, contrary to the lawgiver's counsel—produce various and dissimilar characters in the citizens, a thing which harms the state. Because these behaviors are small and frequent, it would not be sufficiently honorable or decorous to forbid them by a formal position of law or by imposing fines on each instance. Furthermore, it would undermine the written laws if men became accustomed to despising the law in many small matters. Therefore, it is difficult to write laws about these things, yet impossible to remain silent. But I will try to bring what I mean to light, as if <margin><unclear>pointing with a finger</unclear></margin> pointing it out with a finger; for now, my words seem obscure. **Clinias:** You speak the truth. **Athenian:** Now, it has been rightly said elsewhere that we must consider that correct education can render both the body and the soul most beautiful and excellent. **Clinias:** That is so. **Athenian:** I believe that the most beautiful bodies, simply put, will be those that grew most straight during their tender age. **Clinias:** Certainly. **Athenian:** What of this? Do we not understand that the greatest and most abundant increase of growth in all living creatures occurs in their first stages? So much so, that many have argued that human bodies do not grow as much in the remaining twenty years as they do in the first five. **Clinias:** You tell the truth. **Athenian:** When so much growth flows in without much moderate labor, do not many evils naturally arise in the bodies? **Clinias:** Entirely so. **Athenian:** Therefore, there is need for more labor at that time when nourishment flows in most abundantly. **Clinias:** What are you saying, stranger? Shall we impose many labors upon newborns and most tender infants? **Athenian:** Not upon these first, but even earlier—upon those who are still nourished in the mother’s womb. **Clinias:** How do you command this to be done, best of men? Will those who are still carried in the parent's womb perform labor? **Athenian:** Certainly. It is not surprising if you are ignorant of the exercise of such a tiny age; although it may seem absurd to you, I desire to reveal it. **Clinias:** By all means. **Athenian:** Among us, this sort of thing can be better understood because some there involve themselves in certain games more than is proper. For among us, not only boys but even older men raise <term>chicks</term><note>This refers to the Greek practice of raising quails or roosters for fighting.</note> and train them for mutual combat against one another. They are far from thinking that the labors in which they drive these birds are moderate; rather, they take the smaller ones in their hands and the larger ones under their arms, and walk for many <term>stadia</term><note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note>, not for their own health, but for the sake of the good condition of these birds. In this, they certainly signify to a man of understanding that movement and agitation—as long as it is not laborious—benefits all bodies, whether they move by themselves or are moved in vehicles, or a ship, or on horses, or in any other way. Because of this, [movement] can grant us health, beauty, and strength, overcoming the excess of food and drink. Since these things are so, what do we think should be done hereafter? Do we wish to make ourselves a laughingstock by establishing laws that a pregnant woman must walk, and that a newborn must be molded like wax while it is tender, and bound in bandages for up to two years? Should we furthermore compel nurses by laws, under threat of fine, to carry the children to the fields, or the temples, or to their relatives, until they can stand on their own? And even when they begin to stand, lest their limbs be distorted by the violence of their weight due to their softness, should they still be carried until the infants have completed three years? Let the nurses be as robust as possible, and not just one, but several. And shall we impose a penalty in the written laws for each of these if they are not done? Or shall we by no means act this way? For what we just said would happen to us in abundance. **Clinias:** What is that? **Athenian:** We would surely provoke great laughter against ourselves. For the feminine and servile manners of the nurses would not be willing to obey us. **Clinias:** For what reason, then, did we think these things should be said? **Athenian:** Because the masters and the free spirits of the citizens, perhaps when they hear this, will rightly understand that unless private affairs are correctly administered in the city, it is in vain for anyone to hope that public matters will have any stability other than what is in the laws. And understanding this, they will use what we have just said as if they were laws; by the use of which, the family and the republic, being well governed, will live happily. **Clinias:** What you have said is very reasonable. **Athenian:** Let us not, therefore, cease from this kind of lawmaking before we describe the studies of the soul which pertain to very tender children; and so, in a similar way as we began with the bodies, let us complete the discourse. **Clinias:** Quite right. **Athenian:** This, therefore, as if an element...

# BOOK XXVIII. #
43
<meta>Catchword: or</meta>

<margin>
The physical training of infants contributes no small amount toward the virtue of purity.
</margin>

...then we should accept that for the cultivation of both the mind and the body of infants, constant nourishment and movement should be applied day and night; this is beneficial for all, but especially for the youngest. If it were possible, they should live as if they were constantly at sea. Since that is not possible, we must approach this as closely as we can in the care of infants. That this ought to be done can be inferred from the fact that both the nurses of children and those who perform the <term>Corybantic</term><note>original: "Coribantiū". The Corybantes were inspired priests of the goddess Cybele, famous for ecstatic drumming and dancing used to heal mental "madness" or terrors.</note> remedies have recognized it as useful. For whenever mothers wish to lull children to sleep who are slow to rest, they do not do so with quiet or silence, but rather the opposite. They carry them in their arms and keep them in constant motion, soothing them with a modulated voice as if playing a pipe. Just as in the remedies for those suffering from frenzied Bacchic possession, they make use of this kind of rhythmic motion and music.

CLI. <note>Clinias, a Cretan politician and one of the three speakers in the dialogue.</note> What is the primary reason for these things, O Stranger?

ATHE. <note>The Athenian Stranger, the lead philosopher of the dialogue.</note> It is not very difficult to understand.

CLI. In what way?

ATHE. Both of these passions consist of fear; they are certain terrors arising from an unhealthy state of the soul. Therefore, when someone applies an external motion to these internal affects, the external movement overcomes that internal, terrifying, and furious motion. When it has conquered it, it provides a tranquil peace to the soul, the racing of the heart having been somewhat calmed. Thus, in some it induces sleep; others, who are awake, it recalls from a frenzied state to a healthy habit of mind by means of the pipe and the dance, with the help of the gods to whom they were offering supplications. These matters, though briefly stated, possess a certain probable reason.

CLI. Entirely so.

ATHE. If these things have such power, we must further consider that a soul nourished in fear from infancy will be more accustomed to being carried away by dread than any other. No one can doubt that such training leads to timidity rather than to courage.

CLI. Quite so.

ATHE. On the contrary, we shall say that he is trained for courage who from a tender age becomes accustomed to conquering all fears and terrors.

CLI. Wisely said.

ATHE. Therefore, we shall say that this one thing contributes greatly to the virtue of the soul: namely, the physical training of infants through movement.

CLI. Most certainly.

ATHE. Furthermore, a disposition toward ease or moodiness has no small momentum toward the goodness or wickedness of the soul.

CLI. That is true.

ATHE. We must now speak, as best we can, about how each of these dispositions is born in the souls of infants.

CLI. Clearly.

ATHE. It seems to us that <term>luxury</term><note>original: "delitiæ". This implies pampering, over-indulgence, or "softness."</note> makes the character of the young difficult, morose, irascible, and easily provoked by slight causes. Conversely, excessive and harsh servitude makes them abject, illiberal, and misanthropic, rendering them most unfit for human society.

CLI. But how can the entire city educate infants who do not yet understand speech and cannot yet taste any other discipline, as you command?

ATHE. In this way: every animal, as soon as it is born, is accustomed to using its voice and crying out. The human race is no different; indeed, it adds wailing to its cries more than any other.

CLI. That is so.

ATHE. Nurses, therefore, wishing to know what infants desire, offer what they believe they crave. If the child is silent, it is right; if they cry and weep, they conclude from these signs that they have not offered the right thing. Crying and weeping are certainly proofs in infants of what they love and what they hate—signs that are hardly fortunate. This period lasts no less than three years, a span which is no small portion of life to be led rightly or wrongly, depending on whether the child is guided rightly or wrongly.

CLI. Correct.

ATHE. Does it not seem to you that a difficult man—never peaceful, but rather complaining and groaning more than becomes a good man—is a burden?

CLI. To me, indeed.

ATHE. If someone strives by every means and power to ensure that in these three years a boy is affected as little as possible by pain, fear, and sadness, will he not make the boy’s soul more peaceful and tranquil?

CLI. It is clear, Stranger; and much more so if one were to educate him in many pleasures.

ATHE. I will not grant you that, O wonderful Clinias! For such an education, when applied right from the beginning, is the greatest ruin of all. Let us see, then, if what I say is true.

CLI. Speak, what do you mean?

ATHE. I assert that we are now dealing with no small matter. Attend to this, you also, Megillus, and judge between our opinions. My reasoning holds that a right life should neither pursue pleasures entirely nor flee pains entirely, but rather follow that middle habit which I just now called tranquility. We all confess, correctly following a certain divine oracle, that this state is proper to God. Whoever wishes to be a godly man must follow this habit: he should not be entirely inclined toward pleasures—otherwise he will not be far from pain—nor should he allow any other person, whether old or young, male or female, to indulge in pleasures, and least of all newly born infants. For it is then that all characters are most firmly rooted through habit. Indeed, if I did not fear that I might seem to be joking, I would say that pregnant women, most of all in that year, should be so governed that they are neither carried away by many and furious pleasures, nor agitated by pains, but rather lead a tranquil, peaceful, and gentle life.

CLI. There is no need, Stranger, to ask Megillus which of us has spoken more correctly. For I agree with you that a life of pure pleasure or pure pain must be fled by all, and a middle course must always be held. Therefore, you have spoken rightly and have been heard rightly.

ATHE. Quite rightly, Clinias. But let us all three consider this together.

CLI. What is it?

ATHE. That the things we are now discussing are called "unwritten laws" by many; they are nothing other than what are named "ancestral laws." And what we touched upon a little while ago—that these should not be called laws, yet not passed over in silence—was well said. For these are the bonds of the entire republic, holding the middle ground between written laws and those yet to be written; they are, as it were, the first and most ancient of all institutions. If these are well established and men have correctly accustomed themselves to them, they protect the written laws with stable safety. But if the opposite occurs, the result is the opposite—just as happens in buildings: if the supports of the house are removed from the middle, they force everything to collapse, one thing falling upon another; and those things which were well built above fall down when the foundations are ruined. Thinking on these things, O Clinias, we must bind this new city of yours from every side, leaving nothing undone as far as possible...

<margin>
See what the pampering of children produces. What excessive servitude [produces].
</margin>

->### CONCERNING THE LAWS, OR THE SEVENTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS ###<-

...whether it pertains to laws, customs, or studies. For by all these things a city is bound together. Truly, one of these cannot remain without the other. Therefore, it is no wonder if many things seem to us to be established legally all at once and gradually, just as long-standing customs effectively become laws.

CLI. You speak rightly indeed, and we shall think similarly.

ATHE. If someone, therefore, diligently applies these things to a child of three years, whether male or female, and zealously uses the methods mentioned above, they will bring no small benefit to the newly nurtured. And this will be suitable for the disposition of those who are three, four, five, and six years old. From these children, luxuries must be removed, and <term>discipline</term><note>original: "castigatio". In this context, it refers to corrective training or mild punishment intended to build character.</note> must be applied without contempt. Moreover, just as we said that slaves ought to be disciplined without insult so they are not driven to rage—yet disciplined nonetheless so they do not become overly pampered—so we wish it for free children as well. These children have certain games that are, in a way, natural to them, which they take up spontaneously when they meet. These children are to be gathered from the age of three until six, each in the solemn assembly of their own <term>tribes</term><note>original: "tribus". The Athenian "phylai" or tribes were the primary social and political divisions of the citizenry.</note>. The nurses should observe the modesty or lack of restraint of these little ones; and over each assembly and the nurses, one woman shall preside from among the twelve women appointed for a one-year term, as the guardians of the laws shall ordain. Let these women be chosen by the overseers of marriages, one from each tribe, equal to them in age. She who is appointed to this office shall conduct herself so that she visits the sanctuary every day, and she shall always punish the wrongdoer. She may punish a male or female slave, or a male or female foreigner, through certain city attendants; but a citizen, whose punishment might be a matter of legal dispute, she shall bring to the judgment of the <term>aediles</term><note>original: "aediliũ". These were Roman-style magistrates responsible for public order and buildings, used here by Ficino to translate the Greek "astynomoi" or city-stewards.</note>. However, where there is no dispute, she shall punish the person herself.

After the age of six, females shall be separated from males; thereafter, boys shall associate with boys of their own age, and girls with girls of their own age. Both shall turn themselves toward the sciences. The males, indeed, shall go to masters of horses, bows, weapons, and slings; the females also to the same, if they agree—at least as far as the knowledge of them is concerned, and especially the use of arms. How matters stand now in these affairs is ignored by almost everyone.

CLI. What are you saying?

ATHE. That clearly, the right hand is now seen to differ from the left hand in nature as far as operations are concerned. The feet and the lower parts, however, seem to differ in no way for work. But by the ignorance of mothers and nurses together, we have become almost lame in our hands. For though nature behaves almost equally toward both sides, we ourselves have made the difference by not using them correctly through custom. Certainly, in some things this matters little. For it makes no difference to life if the lyra is in the left hand and the <term>plectrum</term><note>A small flat tool used to pluck or strum a stringed instrument.</note> in the right, and similarly in other things of this kind. But <margin>See how the right hand is not more capable by nature, but by use.</margin> to do the same in all other matters following that example is madness. The law of the **Scythians** <note>A nomadic people of ancient Central Eurasia, famous for their skills as horse-archers.</note> shows this to be so. For they do not hold the bow in the left hand and the arrow in the right only, but they use both hands for both tasks similarly. Many examples of this kind are found in the work of charioteers and others. From which it may be understood that those who make the left hands weaker than the right do so against nature. This matter, as we said, is not an impediment in horn plectrums and such instruments. But it matters a great deal when, in battle, it is necessary to use iron, the bow, the spear, and other such things—and most of all when arms are repelled by arms. There is a great difference between one who has learned and one who has not, and between one who is exercised and one who is not exercised at all. For just as one who has perfectly exercised himself in a boxing match or wrestling, or both at once, is able to engage from the left and adapts himself readily when he is forced to move to the other side, I think the very same is most correct in arms and other things. Therefore, if someone possesses two things with which he may defend himself and strike others, he ought not to leave any of these idle or unexercised, as far as his strength allows. And if anyone should have the nature of **Geryon** or **Briareus** <note>Mythological giants; Geryon had three bodies and Briareus had a hundred hands.</note>, being hundred-handed, he ought to be able to throw a hundred javelins. The leaders, both men and women, should have care for all these things: the women indeed should consider the games and nourishment, but the men the disciplines, so that all, being made equally powerful in both feet and hands, do not harm nature through custom.

Truly, it is fitting to use a double discipline: that of the body, called **gymnastics**, and that of the soul, called **music**. But gymnastics again is twofold: **dance** and **wrestling**. One kind of dance imitates the words of the Muse, observing its magnificence and freedom. Another kind is for good condition, lightness, and beauty, both of the body itself and of its parts and members, for the sake of which each part is aptly bent and stretched; so that harmonic motion is sufficiently spread abroad and follows the whole order of the dance. As for those types of wrestling which **Antaeus** and **Cercyon** <note>Mythological wrestlers known for their cruelty; Antaeus was killed by Hercules and Cercyon by Theseus.</note> brought into the art of useless contention, or those of **Epeius** or **Amycus** in boxing matches—since they contribute nothing to battle, they are not worthy of mention. But those things which are applied in "upright" wrestling, involving movements of the neck, hands, and sides, with a desire for victory and an honorable bearing, and which contribute to health and strength—since they are useful for all things, they must not be passed over. Rather, it must be commanded to both students and teachers alike: that when we come to this in the founding of laws, the former should grant these things benevolently, and the latter receive them graciously. 

Nor indeed are all imitations which are in dances to be taken up: but here indeed are the games of armed men, such as those of **Castor and Pollux** <note>The Dioscuri, twin deities and heroes often associated with athletic and martial excellence.</note> in Lacedaemon [Sparta]. Among us [Athenians] also, it must not be neglected that **Minerva** <note>The Roman name for Athena, the patron goddess of Athens, often depicted in full armor.</note>, delighting in the games of the dance, did not think one should play with bare hands, but performed the duty of dancing fully adorned with arms. These are to be imitated by young men and women, honoring the gift of the goddess for use in war and the ornament of solemnities. Indeed, before they can go forth into war, it is necessary for boys, adorned with arms and horses in the processions of all the gods, moving now faster and now slower in the dance and on the march, to pour out supplications to the gods and the sons of the gods. Furthermore, games and preludes, if they are performed for the sake of any things, they should certainly be applied for none but these. For these are useful in peace and war, both privately and publicly. Other exercises of the body, whether done in play or in earnest, O Clinias and Megillus, are not worthy of free men. That now [the study of] gymn...

...[gymnas]tics, which I said should be treated in the first discourses, I have almost completed, and this is now whole and complete. But you, if you have something better, bring it forward. CLI. It is not easy, stranger, having neglected these things, to tell of other better things regarding gymnastics and competition. ATHE. It remains that we discuss the gifts of the Muses and Apollo; concerning which we thought enough had been said, so that it seemed only gymnastics remained. But now it is clear that some things were left out, which must be spoken of first; therefore we shall speak of them next. CLI. Let them certainly be spoken. ATHE. Listen then. For you heard them also in the previous parts; although in speaking and hearing—which is very wonderful and unusual—one ought to take care. Indeed, for the present, I am about to say something that one ought rightly to fear saying; yet I shall say it. CLI. What is that, stranger? ATHE. I assert that it is nowhere recognized how much power the nature of games has over the stability or change of established laws. For if it were so ordained that the same men always use and delight in the same games, according to the same rules and in the same manner, it allows laws seriously established to remain stable as well. But if that kind of thing is changed, and new games are introduced daily, and the youth are always delighted by new things—whether in bodily figures and gestures, or in other equipment and furnishings—and they judge the decent and indecent in these matters differently from day to day, and always honor the inventors of new things, namely of colors and shapes and other such things, we judge that no plague could be greater for a city, judging quite rightly. For it changes the character of youth secretly; and it makes ancient things seem cheap, while new things seem worthy of honor. By this speech and opinion, I assert again that nothing is more ruinous to cities. But hear how great an evil I judge it to be. CLI. Do you say it is an evil for ancient things to be disparaged in cities? ATHE. I say so indeed, very much. CLI. You will not find us to be bad listeners to this speech, but as well-disposed as possible. ATHE. That is fitting. CLI. Speak now. ATHE. Come, let us listen to these things most diligently; and thus let us discuss among ourselves. I say that change in all things—except in evil ones—is most dangerous: in all seasons discovered, in the diet of the body, in the habits of souls; in all things simply, except in evils, as I was just saying. Bodies indeed, when they first use certain foods and drinks and labors, are disturbed in a certain way; then from the long-term use of these things they grow firm and are rendered robust; and they are greatly delighted by this kind of living, being now accustomed, familiar, and friendly to it; and they are in the best health. But if they are forced to pass from a proven diet to another, they fall into diseases, being disturbed at the start, before they become accustomed to the new way of life. One must think that the same also happens in the thoughts of men and the natures of souls. For all men revere those laws, and dread to innovate them, in which they were educated: if those laws, by some divine fortune, have been stabilized over long periods of time; so much so that no one either remembers or has heard that they were ever otherwise. Therefore the legislator ought to devise by what way this might somehow happen in a city. I myself have therefore devised this method: everyone thinks that the games of youth, varied daily as we said above, are nothing other than <term>trifles</term><note>original: "nugas". Usually meaning nonsense or trivial play; the Athenian argues they are actually foundational to civic stability.</note>; and that they have no weight regarding the duties of life. Therefore they yield, and easily allow this change and innovation to occur. Nor do they understand that it is necessary that boys who delight in games different from their predecessors become men different and distinct from their predecessors; and having become different, they will also seek a different life; and hence they will desire new pursuits and laws. Hence no one fears the plague which I said would be the greatest for the city. But other things indeed, especially changes regarding shapes, do less harm. Yet frequent innovation in praising and blaming habits is most serious, as I judge, and most to be dreaded. CLI. Why not! ATHE. Or do we not believe the previous discourses, in which we said that rhythms and other kinds of music are certain imitations of character, both of good men and of bad? Or what shall we say? CLI. We shall by no means think otherwise. ATHE. By every means, therefore, one must strive so that childhood never dares to imitate new things in songs and dances; nor let anyone entice children toward novelty by the allurements of pleasures. CLI. You speak excellently. ATHE. Does any of us have a better art for these things than the <term>Egyptian</term><note>Plato often points to ancient Egypt as a model of cultural stability, where artistic forms remained unchanged for millennia to preserve social order.</note> one? CLI. Which one do you mean? ATHE. That dancing and all kinds of songs be consecrated to the gods: and first, indeed, let individual feast days at certain times of the year be established for individual gods, and the sons of gods, and <term>daemons</term><note>original: "daemonibus". In Greek thought, these are intermediate spirits or divine beings, not necessarily evil "demons."</note>. Then let it be ordered which sacrifices are to be offered to which gods. Or let it be distinguished which songs and choral dances suit which sacrifices. After these have been distinguished, let all citizens sacrifice with a common libation, both to the <term>Fates</term><note>original: "Parcis". The Roman name for the Moirai, the three goddesses who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note> and to the other gods; and let them dedicate certain songs and choral dances to certain gods, or their sons, and daemons. And if anyone uses hymns or choral dances in the rites of the gods otherwise than has been established, let the priests—both men and women—together with the Guardians of the Laws, solemnly and legally exclude him; and he who has been rejected, unless he willingly obeys, shall for his whole life pay the penalties of impiety to anyone who wishes to prosecute. CLI. Rightly so. ATHENIAN. But since we have come to this point in our speech, let us be affected as is fitting for us. CLI. To what end is this? ATHENIAN. Not only every old man, but also a young man, as often as he sees or hears something wonderful and unusual, should not immediately run to it and grant what is doubtful; but as if he had come to a <term>crossroad</term><note>original: "trivium". A place where three roads meet; metaphorically, a point of decision or uncertainty.</note> either alone or with others, and were ignorant of the way, he should indeed investigate and not proceed further until he is more certain where the path leads. We must do similarly at present. For when we have fallen into a wonderful and unusual discourse about laws, we ought to consider it most diligently. For it is not fitting for such great men to suddenly pass judgment on such a great matter; and as if [clapping...]

<margin>
New allurements and new modulations of song are not to be heard by boys.
</margin>

He proposes an Egyptian-style system where all songs and dances are consecrated to specific gods and strictly regulated to prevent cultural decay.</summary>

### ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LATIN TRANSLATION OF THE LAWS, DIALOGUE VII.

...cannot affirm it immediately. CLINIAS: You speak the truth. ATHENIAN: Therefore, I will take time for this; we shall finally affirm it when it has been sufficiently considered. But so that I do not leave the subsequent order of laws in vain, let us hasten toward the proposed end. For perhaps, if God wills it, once the end of this treatise is reached, it will clearly reveal what is now doubted. CLINIAS: You speak excellently, guest. Therefore, let us do so. ATHENIAN: Let it be decreed, therefore—and let him affirm this strange and unusual thing, as we say—that our odes and songs appear to us to consist of laws <note>The Athenian is making a play on the Greek word "nomos," which means both "law" and a "musical mode" or "strain."</note>: just as the ancients used to say concerning songs played on the lyre. Thus, they too are not far from our purpose, but as if in sleep, or even while awake, they either dreamed or prophesied this. Let it therefore be decreed thus: No one shall dare to sing anything besides the public and sacred songs, nor move in a **ritual dance** <note>original: "tripudio," a rhythmic three-step dance</note> outside the established choreography of the youth, just as it is not permitted to do anything against other laws. He who obeys shall go unpunished. But he who does not comply, as was said a little while ago, the guardians of the laws and the priests—both women and men—shall punish him. But let these things be so. CLINIAS: Entirely so. ATHENIAN: But how shall someone establish these laws so that he does not appear ridiculous? Let us consider it this way. The safest method for this seems to me to be that we fashion certain images in speech. One of these, I say, is this: When sacrifices have been made and the victims burned according to custom, if someone—a son or a brother—should privately approach the altar and the sacred rites and pour forth an entirely miserable and harmful speech, would we not say that he has been an ill omen to his father and his kin? CLINIAS: We would certainly say so. ATHENIAN: In almost all of our cities, to speak briefly, this is what happens. For after some magistrate has performed the sacred rites publicly, not one, but many choruses are accustomed to gather. When they stand near the altars, they defile the sacred rite with pitiable voices. Indeed, with words, rhythms, and mournful harmonies, they infect the souls of the listeners; and whoever moves the crowd most vehemently to tears, he carries away the prizes of victory. Shall we not abolish this law? And if a plaintive speech must ever be heard by the citizens, shall we not say it is better to gather on ill-omened days rather than on the auspicious days of divine solemnities? Then, if it pleases, let choruses hired for a prize and foreign singers go forth: just as we see happening at funerals, where certain people hired for pay, after the fashion of the **Carian race** <note>The Carians were often hired as professional mourners in antiquity.</note>, wretchedly lament the deceased. This certainly seems to suit songs of this kind; and since they are pitiable and sad, a mournful garment—to speak briefly—is appropriate for them, not crowns nor golden ornaments. Therefore, I ask this of ourselves again: does it please us that this first image be applied to songs? CLINIAS: Which one? ATHENIAN: A **good omen**, I say. And let the genus of songs itself always be engaged in speaking well and prophesying happily. Or perhaps nothing should be asked, but rather it should be sprinkled and done? CLINIAS: On the contrary, it should certainly be done. For this law is worthy of all votes. ATHENIAN: What then, after the blessing, praises, and good omen, shall be the second law of music? Shall they not pour out prayers to the gods to whom we offer libations? CLINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: The third law, I believe, will be this: since poets are not ignorant that prayers themselves are the petitions of men to the gods, they should take diligent care lest they ask for evils as if they were goods. The condition of one who prays in such a way is too ridiculous. CLINIAS: Without a doubt. ATHENIAN: Did we not grant above that there ought not to be gold and silver wealth in the city? CLINIAS: Entirely. ATHENIAN: Of what, then, shall we say this discourse is an example? Is it not of this? Namely, that the whole race of poets cannot sufficiently know what things are good and what are not. Therefore, if any poet, in words or song, should hand down to us prayers that are not right and beyond reason itself, he will make the citizens seek the opposite in the greatest matters. In which error, as we have said, we shall find not many of our ancestors. Let us therefore place this one law and form in music as well. CLINIAS: Which one? Speak more clearly. ATHENIAN: Let no poet dare to fashion anything contrary to the laws of the city, and what is just, or honorable, or good. Nor shall it be permitted to show what he has composed to any private citizen before the 

<margin>Law concerning the reviewing of poems before they are published.</margin>

judges appointed for this matter and the guardians of the laws have both seen and approved them. Who should preside over music and discipline has already been mostly shown. Shall this law, form, and third image therefore be established for us, as I often ask? Or otherwise? CLINIAS: Let it be established entirely. ATHENIAN: After these things, it will be most right that hymns and praises of the gods be sung mixed with prayers; then, similarly, those of **daemons** <note>In the Greek sense: presiding spirits or lesser deities, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and heroes, with suitable prayers and praises. CLINIAS: Nothing prevents it. ATHENIAN: To these, this law follows immediately without envy: It is fitting 

<margin>Which dead are to be praised.</margin>

to adorn those citizens with praises who have departed from life, if they have performed arduous and famous deeds by the strength of body or soul, and have willingly obeyed the laws. CLINIAS: Why not? ATHENIAN: However, it is not safe to honor those 

<margin>The living are not to be praised.</margin>

still living with praises and hymns, until someone, having finished his life, has made a noble end of living. Let all these things be common to men and women distinguished by virtue. But let the songs and dances be so established. There are many ancient poems of the ancestors concerning music, and types of dancing, from which it is no cause for envy to select what is fitting and advantageous for the established city. Let the electors of these, who are not younger than fifty years of age, choose those which seem to be sufficiently spoken; but those which are wickedly spoken, let them reject entirely; and those which are less than sufficient, let them correct and complete by calling upon poets and musical men. And let them use the poetic virtue of these poets, not their pleasures or desires, except in a few instances; so that, having set forth the will of the legislator, they may prudently direct the dance, the song, and the entire chorus toward it. Truly, every ordered muse <note>Here "muse" refers to the art of music and poetry collectively.</note>, to which a sweet muse is not joined, is far better than when it is without order. But sweetness and pleasantness are common to all muses. For in whatever...
