<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's discourse on the regulation of education and social customs in Plato’s Laws, Book VII. The previous page discussed the necessity of establishing fixed laws for music and dance to prevent moral decay through constant innovation.</meta>

34.
### BOOK [VII]

...from one's earliest years until mature age, a person considers those things they were raised with to be pleasant. Indeed, if one has been educated in **moderate and orderly music** <note>original: "musa temperata," referring to the Muses' arts—music, poetry, and dance—that are balanced and disciplined.</note>, they hate the opposite when they hear it, calling it illiberal. But if one has become accustomed to hearing only the vulgar and the "pleasant," they consider the opposite to be cold and harsh. Therefore, as I was just saying, our sense of what is pleasant or troublesome in both cases depends on custom; however, the ratio of benefit and harm is unequal. For the one makes virtues better, while the other makes them worse. 

CLINIAS: Excellently said. 

ATHENIAN: Furthermore, we must distinguish by a certain form which rhythms are fitting for men and which for women, and adapt them to harmonies and numbers. For it is absurd for an entire harmony or rhythm to be discordant, or to provide things that are unsuitable for these individuals. Therefore, the forms of these must necessarily be established by laws and assigned appropriately to both. We must declare what is becoming for a man or a woman based on the very difference of their natures. Furthermore, that which is magnificent and tends toward **fortitude** <note>original: "fortitudinem," or courage/strength of character</note> should be called masculine. But that which is more graceful and modest is better suited to women; this must be established in our discussion and sanctioned by our laws. 

And let this be the order. Next, let us declare how these things are to be handed down, to whom they are to be taught, and how they are to be performed. Just as a shipbuilder first lays down the small keels according to the form of the ship, so I seem to be doing. For while I attempt to distinguish the figures of life, I am laying down certain formulas—like little keels—according to the natures of their souls, so that we may rightly see by what path and reason we might steer the ship of this life through these seas. 

<margin>
Man is a plaything of the gods
</margin>

Human affairs are indeed not worthy of great earnestness <note>This is a famous and controversial Platonic sentiment: that human life is a tragedy or a comedy, but not "serious" compared to the divine.</note>. Yet it is necessary to be earnest; this I would call a misfortune. But since we are here, if we do this in a fitting way, perhaps it will be enough for us. But someone might rightly ask what I mean by this. 

CLINIAS: Quite rightly. 

ATHENIAN: I say, therefore, that what is worthy of earnestness should be pursued earnestly, but what is not worthy, not at all. Now, God is worthy of every blessed earnestness; but man, as we said above, has been fashioned to be a **plaything of God** <note>original: "dei ludo." Plato suggests humans are like puppets or "toys" moved by divine strings.</note>, and that truly is the best thing about him. Therefore, men and women, being so disposed, ought to spend their lives in the most beautiful play, contrary to what they now think. 

CLINIAS: In what way? 

ATHENIAN: Now they think that serious pursuits must be followed for the sake of play. For they think that warfare—which is worthy of earnestness—must be well-disposed for the sake of peace; yet in war there is usually neither play nor any discipline worthy of reason, nor is there now, nor will there be. But we consider that discipline most worthy of earnestness which allows people, once instructed, to lead their lives in peace as long and as well as possible. 

What then is the right way of "playing" in life? What kind of play should be used in sacrifices, in singing, and in dancing, so that the gods may be rendered propitious to us, and our enemies may be scattered in battle? By certain formulas, as it were, it has been pre-signified which things we can achieve by imitating these in song and dance, and the paths through which we must walk have been paved. In this matter, it must be believed that the poet sang well when he said: *Telemachus, some things you will turn over in your own mind; others a divinity will suggest to you. For I do not think you were born and nurtured without the favor of the gods.* <note>Quoting Homer, Odyssey 3.26-27. The Athenian uses this to show that divine inspiration helps where human reason falls short.</note> 

Our citizens must think this same thing: that what has been said is sufficient, and if anything is missing, they should hope that a **spirit or a god** <note>original: "dæmonem deumque," referring to a tutelary spirit and the higher deity.</note> will suggest to them by which sacrifices and choral dances, and by what kind of play, they ought to appease the divine powers, living according to the manner of nature; for they themselves are wonderful things, participating for the most part in the truth. 

MEGILLUS: Guest, you truly make the race of men of very little account. 

ATHENIAN: Do not be surprised, but forgive me, O Megillus. For when I looked toward God and was moved, I said these things. Let our race, then, if it pleases you, not be vile, but worthy of some earnestness. 

After this, public buildings for gymnastics and education are to be located in three places in the middle of the city. Outside, there shall also be gymnastics for horses in the suburbs, likewise in three places. Furthermore, large organized areas shall be set aside where the youth may be instructed and exercised in archery and the throwing of weapons. If not enough was said about these in the previous sections, let it be spoken of now and sanctioned by law: foreign masters of these skills are to be hired for a price, who, living there, shall instruct those who come in both military matters and music. 

<margin>
Near the Black Sea, women go to war, whom they call Sauromatides
</margin>

And it is not only those whom the parents wish who ought to learn, while those they do not wish may let the disciplines go; but as it is said, all men, as far as possible, and boys—inasmuch as they belong more to the state than to their parents—must necessarily learn. My law shall also sanction the same things for women as for males; for we want the same exercises to be practiced by both. And I will not fear to say that equestrian skills and gymnastics are as honorable for women as for men. For I have heard this from ancient tales, and I give it credit. Even in our own times, I am not unaware that around the **Black Sea** <note>original: "Pontum"</note> there are countless thousands of women called **Sauromatides** <note>The Sarmatians, an Iranian people whose women were famous for riding and fighting alongside men, often linked to the Amazon myths.</note>, for whom there is established an equal care and exercise with men, not only in horsemanship but also in the bow and other arms. 

But I also have this reason for these things: I say indeed that if these things can be done, it is most foolish in our regions that women and men do not work together with all effort and consensus in the same studies. For nearly every state, in this way, becomes half instead of double, despite having the same labors and taxes. This is surely a very great error of the legislator. 

CLINIAS: So it appears. But guest, many things have been said by us that are contrary to the custom of Republics. 

ATHENIAN: It is fitting first to run through the whole dispute; then to choose what seems best. 

CLINIAS: You have spoken very skillfully just now, and you have made me reproach myself for what I said. Therefore, speak further as you please. 

ATHENIAN: This very thing pleases me, Clinias, which I was just saying. For if it were not sufficiently clear from the facts themselves that these things can be done, perhaps something could be said against it. But now, if anyone rejects this law, they must certainly seek another. Our precept, however, will not cease to assert that women ought to participate as much as possible with men in education and other things. For one must consider them in this way: Tell me, if women do not participate with men in all of life, will it not be necessary to assign them some other order of living? 

CLINIAS: Necessary. 

ATHENIAN: What other order could we assign them that is better than those which exist now, other than our order of communal living? Should they be like the women of the Thracians, who...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues for the equal education of men and women in music, gymnastics, and warfare, citing the Sarmatian women as proof of possibility. He famously characterizes humanity as a "plaything of God," suggesting that ritual, song, and dance are the highest forms of human activity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Stranger's argument from the previous page concerning the education of women and the division of labor in the ideal city. Having established that music and gymnastics should be regulated for both sexes, he now examines the domestic and civic duties of women compared to the customs of other nations.</meta>

### ON THE LAWS, OR THE LATIN DIALOGUE ON LAWS, BOOK VII, FOLIO 342.

...and will we, like other nations, assign to women the tasks of agriculture, the duties of ox-herds and shepherds, and other works no different from the service of slaves? Or will we follow the example of our neighbors and ourselves, where all possessions are gathered into one house, as the saying goes, and we entrust to the women the storehouse, the guarding of the home, the shuttles, the spinning of wool, and the management of the household? Or shall we choose a middle path, O Megillus, like the Laconian <note>original: "Laconicum," referring to the Spartans</note> way? In that system, the young girls attend to gymnastics and music, while the married women, though free from the labor of wool-spinning, lead a life that is not abject or meager, but rather one of greater skill. Furthermore, they undertake a moderate care for domestic management, guarding the storehouse and educating the children. Yet they do not take part in wars; so that if it were necessary to defend their fatherland and children, they would not know how to shoot arrows like the **Amazons** <note>A mythical race of warrior women often contrasted with "civilized" Greek women.</note>, nor take up other weapons with skill. They could not even take up a shield and spear to imitate the Goddess <note>Refers to Athena, often depicted in full armor.</note> and nobly resist when their homeland is besieged—if nothing else, they might at least strike a base terror into the enemy by their appearance in the battle line. For if they live in this [sheltered] manner, they will never dare to imitate the **Sarmatians** <note>original: "Sauromatas," a nomadic people where women famously rode to war alongside men.</note>; instead, compared to such women, our men would seem like women. 

In these matters, let your legislators provide what they will. For my part, I shall never say otherwise: I require a perfect duty from the legislator, not a halfway measure that allows women to be dissolved in delicacies, attending only to the males. Otherwise, instead of a city with double the happiness, he makes it only half as happy as it could be.

MEGILLUS: What shall we do here, O Clinias? Shall we allow him to attack Sparta in this way?

CLINIAS: Certainly. For since the freedom of speech has been granted to him, he must not be interrupted until the discussion of the laws has been sufficiently handled.

MEGILLUS: You speak rightly.

ATHENIAN: It is my task, then, to explain what follows.

CLINIAS: Without a doubt.

ATHENIAN: What, then, will be the mode of life for those who have the necessities provided for them in a moderate degree? The arts are left to others, and agriculture is entrusted to slaves who return the fruits of the fields—enough for men living modestly. For these people, moreover, public banquets <note>original: "conuiuia publica," referring to the *syssitia* or common mess halls typical of Sparta and Crete.</note> have been instituted: the men separately, and nearby, their families and daughters with their mothers. Over all of these, certain leaders, both men and women, are appointed to observe and watch over every detail daily. Then, they dissolve the assemblies themselves, and after both the leaders and the others have offered a libation to the gods—to whom that day and night is dedicated—they go home. For people thus established, will there be no remaining work that is necessary and fitting for them? Will they live devoted to their bellies, after the manner of cattle? 

Indeed, we consider that neither just nor honorable. Nor is it possible for a person to live in that way without eventually falling into what is fitting for him: for it is fitting that a lazy and fat animal, through its own inertia, should be torn apart by another that is exercised by labor, lean, and strong. These things would perhaps never happen if we searched sufficiently and exactly, as we now seem to do—at least until women, children, houses, and the rest are held in common as private property. However, if we follow the secondary path which we are now treating, it will certainly be done moderately well. We say, therefore, that no small or base work remains for those living thus; rather, it is the greatest work of all, mandated by a just law. 

For while individual modes of living are distracted by all other works—as when someone strives to win at the **Pythian** or **Olympic games** <note>The most prestigious athletic and musical festivals in ancient Greece.</note> and cannot find time for other things—the life of the person who devotes himself to the virtue of the soul and body is full of a double, or rather a manifold, care. For no physical exercise and no mental studies are to be neglected because of other business. Indeed, almost the entire day and the entire night are not sufficient for the one who cares for these things to reach their sufficiency and perfection. 

Since these things are so, a perpetual order for all time must be held by free men from the rising of the sun until the next sunrise. It would perhaps seem ridiculous if one were to recount many frequent and tiny details concerning domestic administration—among other things, the **nightly vigil** <note>original: "nocturna vigilia," or staying awake at night.</note> which those who intend to preserve the city must exhibit. Whether this should be called a law or a duty, it ought to appear base and illiberal to everyone if any citizen sleeps through the entire night, or is not the first to be awakened and rise, so that this is apparent to the whole household. Furthermore, it should be called shameful if the mistress is first awakened by her handmaidens, and not the handmaidens by her—this applies to slaves, handmaidens, boys, and finally, if possible, the entire house.

<margin>A few things on domestic administration.</margin>
<margin>On much sleep and vigils.</margin>

Therefore, let them rise in the night: the magistrates to attend to public business, and the fathers and mothers of the family to care for their own affairs in their private homes. For much sleep is naturally conducive neither to bodies, nor to souls, nor to the conduct of business. No one, while they sleep, is of any value, any more than if they were not alive. Therefore, whoever desires most to live and be wise should stay awake for as long as possible, provided health is maintained with moderation. For this task, much sleep is not required once you have become well-accustomed to [shorter] sleep. 

Truly, magistrates who keep watch at night in cities are a terror to evil men—both enemies and citizens—but they are loved and honored by the just and temperate; they are useful to themselves and the entire city. Moreover, a night spent in this way creates **fortitude** in the souls of the citizens regarding the things we have mentioned. 

When the sun rises, let the boys go to their teachers. Since neither flocks nor any other creatures can live without a shepherd, neither should boys be without **pedagogues** <note>original: "pędagogis." In antiquity, a pedagogue was a slave who supervised a child's behavior, escorted them to school, and enforced discipline, distinct from the *teacher* who provided academic instruction.</note>, nor slaves without masters. 

<margin>A boy is more unmanageable than any beast.</margin>

Indeed, a boy is more unmanageable than any beast. Since he does not yet possess a perfected fountain of prudence, he is the most insidious, sharp, and petulant of all animals. Therefore, he must be bound, as it were, with many bridles. As soon as he is separated from his mothers and nurses, he must be entrusted to pedagogues to rule his childish playfulness; then, as a free person, to teachers, especially for the sake of his studies. Furthermore, as if he were a slave, let any free person who happens to catch him punish the boy himself, his pedagogue, or his teacher, if he sees them failing in any matter. If the person present does not punish him as is right, let him be subjected to the greatest disgrace. Let the man who has been elected from the guardians of the laws to lead the children take note of this: whether the one who caught them failed to punish them when he should have, or did not punish them in the proper manner. This man must look upon these matters sharply and care for the education of the boys most diligently, always directing and converting their natures toward the Good itself according to the laws. 

But how shall the law sufficiently instruct this man himself? For this has not yet been spoken clearly or sufficiently; some things have been touched upon, others omitted. It is necessary...

### BOOK VII.

...to leave nothing undone according to one’s strength, but to set forth every reason, so that the interpreter here may be both a guide and an educator to others. Regarding dance, song, and the forms of jumping, it has already been stated which should be chosen, corrected, and dedicated. However, concerning writings in prose <note>original: "oratione soluta," literally 'loosened speech,' referring to non-metrical prose.</note>, we have not yet spoken: namely, which of these and in what order you, O best cultivator of youth, should hand down to your pupils. You already know what they must learn and practice in military matters. For the lawgiver has already stated what must be grasped first regarding literacy, and then regarding the lyre. Furthermore, there are things pertaining to the computation of numbers, which we said were necessary, and generally whatever conduces to war, household management, and public affairs. Likewise, there is the investigation of the orbits of the divine stars, the sun, and the moon, so that the whole city may not be ignorant of the order of days into the month, and months into the year; and thus the times, solemnities, and sacrifices, being arranged as is fitting by a certain natural guidance, may render the city living and vigilant, pay honor to the gods, and make men more prudent in these matters. These things, O friend, have been sufficiently distinguished for you by the lawgiver, but pay attention to what follows. For we said that literacy had not yet been sufficiently distinguished: since it has not been declared to what extent one should be occupied with it—namely, whether those who are to be ordinary citizens ought to comprehend it exactly, or not at all. Similarly regarding the lyre. Therefore, let boys go to their letters at ten years of age, and let them persist for three years. And when a boy has reached thirteen years, let him similarly apply himself to the lyre for three years. It shall not be permitted for a father to keep his children in these studies for more or less time, nor for the children—whether affected by boredom or compelled by desire—to spend time on these things beyond the law’s limit. If anyone does not obey, he shall not receive the honors given to those who complete their training, which we shall describe later. But hear what the teachers ought to teach and the youths learn in these years. Let them learn letters until they are able to read and write. But whether they do so quickly or very beautifully, unless nature assists within this span of time, is not to be a concern. As for the works of poets where they do not use the lyre—partly written in meter, partly without meter—which, lacking rhythm and harmony, are deceptive writings handed down to us by certain men of this kind: by what reason will you, O best guardians of the law, put them to use? I think even the lawgiver will doubt what kind of use of these he should rightly hand down to you.

**CLINIAS.** Why, Stranger, have you doubted thus with yourself?

**ATHENIAN.** You are right to ask, Clinias. But to you, who have thought with me in common about the laws, it is necessary that I open up what seems certain to me and what seems doubtful.

**CLINIAS.** What then do you say of these things now? What moves you?

**ATHENIAN.** I will tell you. Indeed, it is not easy to contradict countless men.

**CLINIAS.** Do you think that the small and few things already said about the laws are contrary to the views of many?

**ATHENIAN.** You speak the truth indeed. For you seem to command that, although this path is arduous and hateful to many, I should nevertheless proceed confidently. Along this path of laws, opened by our present discourse, I shall proceed, omitting nothing; for such a journey perhaps pleases not a few, and if they be fewer, they are not the worse for it.

**CLINIAS.** Certainly.

**ATHENIAN.** I shall omit nothing then. I say indeed that many poets have written in hexameter verse, many in trimeter <note>Terms for ancient poetic meters; hexameter was used for epics like the *Iliad*, while trimeter was common in drama.</note>, and in other kinds of meters; some have embraced serious things, others humorous. All of these, many professors of this faculty assert, should be learned by heart for the right education of youth, so that they may become "polymaths" <note>original: "factidi," likely a corruption of "polymaths" or "well-informed," referring to someone of wide-ranging but perhaps superficial learning.</note> through experience of various poets. Others contend that certain chapters selected from all and brought together should be committed to memory, if indeed any of us is to become a good and wise man from the experience and knowledge of many. But do you now command me to explain freely what is said rightly by these men and what is said to the contrary?

**CLINIAS.** Why not?

**ATHENIAN.** I will therefore say in one word what I think most powerfully about all these things: I believe this, which everyone will grant me. Many things are spoken well by the poets, but many also the opposite. If this is so, I assert that the pursuit of learning many things is dangerous for youth.

**CLINIAS.** How then, and what do you prescribe to the guardian of the laws?

**ATHENIAN.** About what matter do you speak?

**CLINIAS.** To what should he look as a kind of model <note>original: "exemplar."</note>, so that he may command some things to be learned by youth and others not even to be touched? I pray you, do not be burdened to say it.

**ATHENIAN.** O good Clinias, I seem in some way fortunate.

**CLINIAS.** In what way especially?

**ATHENIAN.** Because I am not entirely without an example. For when I consider those things which we have narrated from dawn until this hour—not, as it seems to me, without a certain inspiration from the gods—they seem to me to be in some way like poetry. Nor is it a wonder if, looking back at our own discourses as if they were all collected together, I am so affected that I am greatly pleased. For of all the things I have learned and heard, whether spoken poetically or in prose, these seem to me the most moderate and most suitable for instructing youth. Therefore, I have no better model to set before the guardian and teacher of the law than that he should compel the masters to explain these things to the children; and whatever else is similar to these, whether written poetically or in prose, or simply spoken and in agreement with this disputation—which ought by no means to be omitted. Rather, he should take care that they be written down, and first compel the instructors themselves to learn and approve of these things. Those who do not approve, he should reject; but to those who do approve, he should commit the adolescents to be erudite and instructed. But concerning literacy and its teachers, enough has been said.

**CLINIAS.** We have not, Stranger, wandered from the purpose, as it seems to me; but whether we act rightly in the whole matter or the contrary, is perhaps difficult to say.

**ATHENIAN.** Then at last, Clinias, that also will be clear, as is fitting, when (as we have said many times) the treatment of the laws receives its end.

**CLINIAS.** Correct.

**ATHENIAN.** But after the teacher of literacy, must we not speak of the cithara-player <note>A player of the cithara, an ancient Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre.</note>?

**CLINIAS.** Why not?

**ATHENIAN.** If we are mindful of our previous words, we shall give to the cithara-players what is fitting to be taught and educated, as I think, regarding their duty.

**CLINIAS.** Of what things do you speak?

**ATHENIAN.** We said it was necessary for the Dionysiac singers, sixty years of age, to perceive acutely the natures of rhythms and the constitutions of harmonies, so that in songs imitating the affections of the soul, they might distinguish the imitations of a good soul from the imitations of a wicked soul; and these they should reject, while those...

# OF THE LAWS, OR OF THE LATIN LAWS, DIALOGUE VII.

...brought into the midst, should harmonize for the ears of the youth, and draw their souls, led by a certain imitation, toward the possession of virtue itself.

**CLINIAS:** You speak the truth.

**ATHENIAN:** Therefore, the lyre-player and his pupil must use the sounds of the lyre for the sake of that expression which comes from the melodious strings, and return voices that are in harmony with the voices of the singer. But as for diversity and variety of the lyre—where the strings might produce different melodies than those the poet-composer intended, or where they might provide density against sparsity, speed against slowness, or high pitch against low, or any combination of concord and discord—and where all the variety of rhythms is adapted to the voices of the lyre: it is not permitted to introduce such complexities to those who are to grasp the utility of music within only three years. For when contrary things are confused with one another, they are difficult to learn. Moreover, it is necessary that youth learn easily. For the things we command them to learn of necessity are neither small nor few. This discourse, as it proceeds with time, will demonstrate these things. Let the teachers of music take care of these matters. 

As for which words or songs the masters of the choral dances <note>The "chorearum magistri" were leaders of the rhythmic, group dances central to Greek civic life.</note> ought to teach, these have been distinguished by us in the preceding sections, where we said they must be appropriately dedicated to solemnities, so that they may provide both happy delight and utility to the cities.

**CLINIAS:** You have spoken truly.

**ATHENIAN:** Therefore, let the magistrate elected to oversee music <note>The "electus ad musam magistratus" is the Minister of Education.</note> take up these properly distinguished matters and care for them successfully. But just as we added the method for teaching music which remained, let us now likewise add the same for dancing and for the whole of bodily gymnastics, since that is what remains. For it is necessary that both boys and girls learn choral dancing and gymnastics. Is it not so?

**CLINIAS:** So it must be.

**ATHENIAN:** Therefore, let masters of dancing be given to the boys, and mistresses to the girls, so that they may be suitably exercised by them.

**CLINIAS:** Let them be given by all means.

**ATHENIAN:** Again, let us call upon that man who is to undergo many duties: the curator of youth. Since he will have the care of both music and gymnastics, he will never have an abundance of leisure.

**CLINIAS:** But in what way can he sustain such great care, being an elder?

**ATHENIAN:** Easily, O friend. For the law has granted him, and will grant him, that he may take as associates in this care whichever citizens, both men and women, he wishes. He will know who ought to be chosen, and he will wish to choose upright associates, since he wisely recognizes and reveres the greatness of his own magistracy. Nor is he ignorant that if youth is correctly educated and brought up, the whole voyage of life is straight; but if the contrary occurs, what follows is not even worthy of mention. We shall not speak of it, fleeing such a ruinous omen for our new city. 

We have already said much about dancing and every gymnastic movement. For we call all these "gymnasia"—that is, military exercises: such as archery, javelin-throwing, the art of the light-shield soldier <note>original: "peltasticē," referring to the *peltast*, a type of Greek infantryman.</note>, and all combat of armed men, the ordering of battle lines, the leading of an army, the positioning of camps, and whatever pertains to equestrian discipline. For all these things, there ought to be public masters hired by the city, who shall teach boys and girls, and men and women, so that everyone in the city knows these things. And the girls indeed should be accustomed to dance and fight with arms. <margin>Why women ought to learn to handle arms and camps.</margin> The women, moreover, should know how to move camps, arrange ranks, and take up and lay down arms; if for no other reason, then at least so that if necessity forces all the men to go out on campaign, they themselves might meanwhile defend the city if any adversity happens, or if so great a multitude of enemies invades the fields that it is necessary for the women also to take up arms for the city—none of which is impossible to happen. Certainly, it must be considered a great vice of the Republic if women are educated so poorly that they do not even dare to fight for their little ones against fierce beasts as birds do, and would not rather choose to die and undergo all dangers than to flee immediately to altars and temples, giving the opinion that the race of humans is the most cowardly of all animals.

**CLINIAS:** By Jove, Stranger, this is both a disgrace and a detriment to the city.

**ATHENIAN:** Let us therefore make this law: that women shall not neglect military matters, but all citizens, women as well as men, shall apply themselves to it.

**CLINIAS:** Let us enact it.

**ATHENIAN:** Regarding wrestling, we have already spoken in part. But that which I think is greatest, we have not said, nor is it easy to say, unless one adds bodily gestures to the declaration of words. This, therefore, we shall judge then, when words joined to actions will more clearly signify something about the rest, and that wrestling is, most of all movements, akin to battle; and that one should apply effort to wrestling not for its own sake, but for the sake of battle.

**CLINIAS:** That is indeed proper.

**ATHENIAN:** But let this be enough for now regarding the faculty of wrestling. The other movements of the whole body, most of which can rightly be called by the name of dancing, we distribute into two species. For one movement, with more decent gestures of the body, imitates something honorable and worthy; the other, conversely, with more indecent gestures, is led toward imitating something base. And of each of these, again, there are two species. For one honorable and worthy movement is when we are engaged in war and violent labors with an excellent and strong body. The other is when the soul is moderately joyful in prosperous affairs. If anyone calls this latter a "peaceful" movement, he will seem to name it according to nature. But that former one, different from the peaceful, anyone will rightly call the *Pyrrhichē* <note>The Pyrrhic dance was a traditional Greek war dance in armor, imitating the movements of combat.</note>, which imitates the bending of bodies by which weapons and blows are avoided—by dodging, yielding, leaping into the air, and crouching on the ground—likewise the contrary gestures by which things are directed against others, such as shooting arrows, throwing javelins, and striking. In all these, one must consider that when an intrepid and constant habit is applied in the rectitude of the limbs and the fortitude of the soul, it is done correctly; but when the contrary, it is not correct. 

But let us also consider peaceful dancing in this way in each case: whether one who is educated by the best law of learned men conducts himself decently in the choral dances according to the nature of honorable dancing. First, however, the "ambiguous" dancing, which falls into controversy, must be distinguished from the "unambiguous." What then is this? And in what way are both to be distinguished? We consider "ambiguous" that which is Bacchic <note>Related to the cult of Bacchus/Dionysus, often involving wild or ecstatic movement.</note>, and belongs to those following Bacchus, whom they call Nymphs, Pans, Sileni, and Satyrs. This kind, as they say, imitates drunken people performing purifications and sacred rites. This whole genus of dancing is neither suitable for war nor for peace, nor can its purpose be easily determined. It seems most correct to me, therefore, to distinguish it so that we place it apart from the dancing of war and apart from the dancing of peace, denying that this is civic, and thus the remaining...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues for a structured education in music and gymnastics for both sexes, emphasizing that women must be trained in military arts to defend the city. He distinguishes between war-dances (the Pyrrhichic), peaceful dances, and excluded Bacchic ecstatic dances.</summary>

# BOOK VII. ON THE LAWS

...Having finished with the matters of war and peace, which are beyond controversy, let us now return to the **dance** that pertains to us. Among this nation, the play of the Muses, which we use in times of peace and the expectation of prosperity, is divided into two parts as we honor the gods and the sons of the gods. One part is employed when we have escaped dangers and labors and have obtained good things; this contains greater pleasures. The other is usually performed when previous goods are preserved and increased, in which the pleasure is more relaxed. In such matters, every person moves more excitedly out of greater pleasure, and more relaxedly out of lesser pleasure. Furthermore, anyone who is more moderate and better practiced in fortitude moves more peacefully. The lazy man, on the contrary, and one least practiced in temperance, performs greater and more violent changes in movement. Generally, whether someone speaks through song or otherwise, they cannot keep their body still. Therefore, the imitation of words expressed through the figures of the body has given birth to the whole art of dancing, in which some move gracefully and others ungracefully. 

And as antiquity is to be praised in many other names <note>original: "nominibus"; here referring to the "terms" or "categories" established by the ancients</note> positioned well and according to nature, it is also to be approved in this: that the moderator of men rightly and musically named all the dances of those rejoicing temperately in favorable circumstances, according to the harmony of reason. He established two types of honorable dance: that of war, which he called the **Pyrrhic**, and that of peace, which he called the **Emmeleia** <note>original: "concinne" / "commoda concinnitas"; the text refers to the graceful dance of peace known in Greek as the Emmeleia</note>. The legislator ought to explain these with certain figures, and the guardian must preserve them, joining them with other invented music. These should be distributed among the solemn sacrifices, dedicating each to its own, and stabilizing them as ordered, so that none of them may later be changed in dance or song. Thus, the same city persevering in the same pleasures, and the same citizens remaining always similar as far as possible, may live well and happily. 

But we have already spoken of the honorable dances of beautiful bodies and noble souls. Now it is necessary to consider and know the movements of deformed bodies and thoughts, which look toward laughter and **Comedy**, in words, song, dance, and all such imitations. For it is impossible to know serious things without the ridiculous, or generally to know opposites without their opposites, if anyone is to be wise. However, it is impossible for a citizen to perform both if we are to escape with any share of virtue. But these things must be known for this reason: so that one does not do or say something ridiculous through ignorance when it is least appropriate. Therefore, let slaves and foreigners hired for pay imitate such things; let no serious study be applied to them. Nor should any free citizen, whether man or woman, be seen learning these things, but let the imitation of them always appear as something new. And so, the games looking toward laughter, called by the name of **Comedy**, should be disposed by reason and law. 

<margin>
Things that are necessary: it is shameful not to know. 

God will never fight against necessity.
</margin>

But what of the **Tragic** poets, who relate serious matters, as they say? If they should ask us: "O friends, is it permitted for us to come into your region and city, and to bring our poems to you? Or have you decided otherwise regarding the tragic art?" What would we rightly answer to these divine men? For so it seems to me: "O best of men, we ourselves are poets of a tragedy that is the most beautiful and best possible. For our whole Republic is an imitation of the most beautiful and best life, which we certainly judge to be the truest tragedy. Therefore, you are poets, and we ourselves are poets of the same poem, and we contend as rivals for the most beautiful work of tragedy, which only true law, as we hope, can perfect. Truly, do not believe that you will be easily admitted by us to set up your stages in the forum and bring in loud-voiced actors who cry out louder than we do; and thus harangue our children, our wives, and the whole crowd of the city about the same matters, often saying the opposite of what we say. For we and the whole city would be entirely insane if we admitted you before the magistrates have seen what you have composed and judged whether it should be spoken to the people. Now therefore, O best of men, nurslings of the soft Muses, we will compare your songs with ours before the leaders; and if what you say appears to be the same or better than ours, we will give you a chorus <note>Granting a "chorus" was the official Athenian way of licensing a play for public performance</note>. But if otherwise, O friends, we can never give it." 

Let these things be established concerning all dance and its teaching, laws, and customs, with the duties of slaves separated from those of masters, if you agree. 

**CLINIAS:** It certainly seems so. 

**ATHENIAN:** But for free men, three studies still remain. One is the calculation of numbers. The second is the measure of length, width, and depth. The third is the knowledge of the circuit of the stars. Not many will learn all these things exactly, but only a few, whom we shall designate as we reach the end. For so it is fitting. But for the multitude, it is shameful not to know what is necessary and most rightly spoken. Yet to search out everything exquisitely is neither easy nor entirely possible. What is necessary among these things cannot be rejected. Indeed, he who first spoke thus of God in a proverb seems to have looked to this: "Not even God will ever fight against necessity" <note>An ancient Greek proverb often attributed to Simonides or Pittacus</note>. I think this should be understood regarding divine necessities. For if this were said of human necessities, to which many look, such a speech would be by far the most foolish of all. 

**CLINIAS:** What then, Guest, are the necessities of learning that are not human, but divine? 

**ATHENIAN:** I think they are those which, if someone does not learn or experience them in any way, he can never become a god to men, nor a demon <note>original: "daemon"; in the Greek sense of a tutelary spirit or lesser deity</note>, nor a hero, such that he can zealously take care of men. He will be far from becoming a divine man if he cannot know one, or two, or three, or even-numbered and odd-numbered things at all; if he does not know how to count, nor to number days and nights, and has not grasped the rotations of the sun and moon and the other stars. If anyone denies that these things are necessary for a man who is to perceive any of the most beautiful teachings, he thinks most foolishly. But what kind each of these is, and how many, and when they are to be learned; and what with another, and what alone without others; and what the whole mixture of them is—this must be learned correctly before all else. Then, with these teachings as guides, one must proceed to the others. For so nature and necessity itself have obtained, with which we say no god either fights now or will ever fight. 

**CLINIAS:** Guest, what you say seems rightly spoken and according to nature. 

**ATHENIAN:** Such is the case, O Clinias. But it is difficult to propose these things in this order...

It then introduces the essential curriculum of mathematics and astronomy, framing these sciences as "divine necessities" for anyone seeking to lead or achieve a god-like understanding of the world.</summary>

### ON THE LAWS OR ON THE LATIN LAWS, DIALOGUE VII. FOLIO 344.

...to bring forth laws. For this reason, let us delay these matters to another time, if it seems right, and we shall sanction them more diligently with laws. **CLINIAS:** You seem, Guest, to fear our lack of skill in these matters. And not without reason. However, you should try to explain them; do not fear anything on this account. **ATHENIAN:** I do indeed fear what you say, but I dread even more those who have tasted these doctrines, but have tasted them badly. For ignorance of things is not entirely a heavy or hard burden, nor is it the greatest evil; rather, the "knowledge" and notice of many things, when poorly acquired, is much more ruinous. **CLINIAS:** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN:** Therefore, free men <note>original: "liberos homines"; referring to citizens of the state who are not enslaved</note> ought to learn those things which a great crowd of children in Egypt learn alongside their basic literacy. First, the science of calculation was devised for children, learned with play and pleasure. Distributions of crowns <note>prizes or garlands</note> and apples are made among more or fewer people using the same fitting numbers. The seating of boxers and wrestlers, and the alternating of partners and the following order, is arranged as is usually done. Moreover, mixing golden, bronze, and silver bowls and other similar objects while playing, or passing them entirely from one to another, they adapt the necessary numbers to the games, as I said. In this way, they provide usefulness to the students for leading armies, for the arrangements of camps, for managing the Republic, and for all other things, and they make the students themselves more vigilant. Then, since a shameful and laughable ignorance of nature regarding the measurement of length, width, and depth holds all men, they lead them far away from this. **CLINIAS:** What sort of ignorance do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** O friend Clinias, when I eventually heard of it, I wondered at this ignorance of ours; it seemed to me to be a consideration not of men, but of pigs and cattle. And therefore I blushed vehemently, not only for myself, but for all Greeks. **CLINIAS:** Speak more plainly, Guest, what is this? **ATHENIAN:** I will speak. Indeed, I will reveal it by asking again. Answer me, please: do you know what length is? **CLINIAS:** Why not? **ATHENIAN:** And what of width? **CLINIAS:** Certainly. **ATHENIAN:** And that these are two things, and depth is the third? **CLINIAS:** That too. **ATHENIAN:** Do all these seem to you to be able to be measured against one another? **CLINIAS:** Surely. **ATHENIAN:** I mean length to length, width to width, and depth similarly—that they can be measured by nature. **CLINIAS:** Vehemently so. **ATHENIAN:** But if some things can do this neither vehemently nor weakly, but some things can be measured while others cannot at all, yet you think they all can, how do you feel about this? **CLINIAS:** Badly. **ATHENIAN:** Again, what about length and width compared to depth, or width and length to each other? Do not all Greeks think they can be measured in some way? **CLINIAS:** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN:** But if they cannot be measured by any means, yet all Greeks, as I was saying, think they can, is it not right that we, moved by shame for everyone, should say to them: "O best of Greeks, this is one of those things which we said was shameful to be ignorant of, but to know is necessary, though not particularly glorious"? **CLINIAS:** Why not? **ATHENIAN:** Furthermore, there are other things related to these in which we similarly err. **CLINIAS:** What are they? **ATHENIAN:** The way nature has made it so that some things can be measured against each other, while others cannot. <note>The Athenian is referring to irrational numbers and incommensurable lines, such as the relationship between the side and the diagonal of a square.</note> It is certainly necessary to know these, or else the man who is ignorant is entirely useless. One must spend time drawing the mind toward these things. For this "old man’s game" will be much more pleasant than dice or checkers, and more worthy of a free man. **CLINIAS:** Why not? For dice and these teachings seem to differ greatly from each other. **ATHENIAN:** I judge, O Clinias, that these things must be learned by the younger ones. For they are neither harmful nor difficult; and being learned through play, they will benefit the city and never hinder it. But we must pay attention if anyone says otherwise. **CLINIAS:** Why not? **ATHENIAN:** If these things seem to be so, we shall approve them. If otherwise, we shall reject them. **CLINIAS:** Certainly. Should we not then, Guest, make these teachings necessary for us now, so that our treatment of the laws is not in vain? **ATHENIAN:** I would sanction them, but on the condition that they can be separated from the rest of the order of civil discipline if perhaps they do not prove acceptable to us who propose them, or to you for whom they were proposed. **CLINIAS:** This is a fair condition. **ATHENIAN:** But let us now consider whether the teaching of the stars pleases us. **CLINIAS:** Just say it. **ATHENIAN:** A strange thing happens in these matters, which can least be tolerated. **CLINIAS:** What is that? **ATHENIAN:** We say that the greatest god and the whole world <note>original: "mundum"; the cosmos or universe</note> ought not to be investigated, nor the causes of things tracked down with much study; nor do we consider it pious, even though it seems the opposite can rightly be done. **CLINIAS:** In what way do you mean? **ATHENIAN:** To be sure, this teaching will seem foreign to the elders; but since I think it is good, true, useful to the city, and pleasing to God himself, I cannot remain silent. **CLINIAS:** You speak reasonably. But shall we find such a doctrine regarding the stars? **ATHENIAN:** At present, O good men, we—all Greeks, to put it briefly—lie about the great gods, I mean the Sun and the Moon. **CLINIAS:** In what way do we lie? **ATHENIAN:** We believe the Sun and the Moon never travel the same path, and we say certain other stars along with these "err" <note>original: "errare"; to wander</note>, which we call planets. <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek "planētēs," meaning wanderer. The Athenian argues they actually follow a precise, single path.</note> **CLINIAS:** By Jove, Guest, what you say is true. For I have often seen with my own eyes the Morning Star and the Evening Star and certain others never making the same course, but wandering everywhere. And we all know the Sun and the Moon always wander. **ATHENIAN:** These, O Megillus and Clinias, are the things I judge our younger citizens must learn about the celestial gods, to the point that they speak nothing profane about them, but always honor them with sacrifices and pious vows and praises. **CLINIAS:** This is indeed right, provided first that it is possible to perceive what you say, and then even if we now speak less than correctly about these things, we will speak correctly after we have learned. If it is so, I also concede that such a doctrine ought to be learned. Try then to explain these things diligently; we shall listen and learn. **ATHENIAN:** It is not easy to grasp what I say, nor again is it entirely difficult; nor does it require a long time to be discussed. A sign of this is that I myself heard it neither recently nor very long ago, and now in a short time I can make it known to you. If these things were deeply difficult, neither could I declare them, nor could you grasp them at this age. **CLINIAS:** You speak the truth, but what is this doctrine which you say is wonderful and necessary for the youth, and unknown to us?

# SUMMARY OF THE EIGHTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS

<margin>
That planets do not wander; nor is the fastest thing actually the slowest.
</margin>
Try to show that very clearly. **ATHENIAN:** I will certainly try. O best of men, this common opinion about the sun, the moon, and the other stars—that they ever "wander" <note>The word "planet" comes from the Greek *planetes*, meaning "wanderer." The Athenian is arguing that their motion is actually regular and purposeful, not random.</note>—is not true; the reality is quite the opposite. For each of them performs its journey in a single circle, not many, even though it may appear to be carried through many. Furthermore, we incorrectly judge that which is fastest among them to be the slowest, and the slowest to be the fastest. It is clear that those who think this way are in error. For if we were watching contestants in a race at the Olympic games, and we proclaimed that the fastest runner was running the slowest, and the slowest was running the fastest, and we sang praises to the loser as if he had won: I do not think our praises would please the runners. But now, when we make the same error regarding the gods <note>In Plato's time, the sun, moon, and planets were often associated with divine beings.</note>, are we not ridiculous, and do we not similarly stray from the right path? **CLINIAS:** It is indeed ridiculous, and certainly not acceptable to God, when we sing false things about them. **CLINIAS:** If these things are as you say, you speak the truth. **ATHENIAN:** And if we show them to be so, all these things shall be learned to that extent. If not, they shall be dismissed; and let us agree on this for now. **CLINIAS:** Entirely. **ATHENIAN:** But let the established rules regarding the discipline of learning now come to an end. Concerning hunting, however, a similar judgment must be made, as with all matters of this kind. For it seems that the office of the lawgiver is not only to write laws, but also to use that middle ground which lies between admonition <note>Advice or moral encouragement</note> and the laws themselves; a method we have used quite often, especially when we were speaking of the education of infants. For in that matter, we said there are many things that cannot be stated as formal laws, and that it would be the mark of a madman to try to set laws for them. Thus, once the laws are written and the Republic is established, the perfect praise of a citizen of outstanding virtue is not merely that he is a "good citizen" because he served the laws as well as possible and obeyed them most strictly; rather, the more perfect praise is that he lived his whole life in total obedience to the lawgiver's intent—to his writings, his praises, and his censures. This is the highest praise of a citizen. It is not enough for the founder of laws to simply write the laws; he must also add a certain declaration to them, indicating what appears to him to be honorable or shameful. The highest citizen ought to observe these things no less than the mandates enforced by legal penalties. To illustrate this, we bring forward the matter currently being discussed as a witness. For it clarifies what we want more effectively. Hunting is a broad subject, encompassed by a single name. There is hunting of water creatures, of birds, and of land animals; and not of wild beasts only, but also the "hunting" of men—not just in war, but also through friendship, one of which brings praise and the other blame. The robberies of bandits and the raiding of camps are also types of hunting. Therefore, he who is to establish laws about hunting cannot pass these over, nor can he impose menacing laws on each one in a fixed order with penalties. What, then, should be done about these? The legislator ought to praise what is praiseworthy in hunting and disparage the opposite, for the sake of the exercise of youth. When the young hear this, they ought to obey so that neither labor nor pleasure calls them to act otherwise than the legislator advised. Indeed, they should honor those things said with praise and proposed as exhortations more than those reinforced by threatening and vengeful laws. These things having been proposed, a fitting praise and disparagement of hunting can then be written: so that what makes the souls of the youth better is praised, and the opposite is disparaged. Let us say to them, then, after mentioning fish: "O dear friends, may the desire for sea-hunting and hooks never seize you; nor the idle hunting of aquatic animals by day or night with nets; nor may the love of piracy make you unjust and cruel hunters of men across the seas. Let the desire to commit theft or robbery in the city or the countryside never even enter your minds; nor the hunting of birds, which is more slavish than free. Only the hunting of land animals is left to you. But even among these, that which is done while they sleep—which happens at certain intervals and is called nocturnal hunting—is the work of idle men and is not worthy of praise; nor is that which is done as a relaxation from labor, which masters the ferocity of beasts with nets and snares rather than the steady strength of the soul. Therefore, only that hunting of four-footed animals remains best of all: that which is driven by horses, dogs, and the strength of the body. For those who care for divine fortitude <note>courage</note> ought to overcome all four-footed beasts by running, by wounding them, and with weapons by their own hand." But let the praise and blame of hunting be thus distinguished. Let this be the law: No one shall prohibit these sacred hunters from hunting wherever they wish to hunt. But no one shall ever allow a nocturnal hunter, trusting in nets and his own dogs, to hunt anywhere. A fowler shall be permitted to wander through uncultivated fields and mountains. But he shall be driven away from cultivated places and sacred uncultivated lands by anyone. A fisherman shall not hunt in ports, nor in sacred rivers, marshes, or ponds; in other places it shall be allowed, provided he does not use mixtures of juices <note>referring to the practice of poisoning water to stun fish</note>. But now, let the instructions on discipline reach their end. **CLINIAS:** You speak excellently.

### Argument of Marsilio Ficino <note>Ficino (1433–1499) was the primary translator of Plato into Latin during the Renaissance.</note> for the Eighth Dialogue on the Laws.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a classical figure or deity within a circular frame, surrounded by floral and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

THE THINGS WE JUST asserted regarding the chief and singular worship of the one God, based on many testimonies of our Plato, we can furthermore confirm without controversy through the *Phaedrus*, *Gorgias*, *Protagoras*, *The Statesman*, *Critias*, and the fourth book of the *Laws*. For in these, he subjects the entire assembly <note>original: "synagogam"</note> of the gods, so to speak, to a single King, just as he wishes individuals to be commanded: justly distributing different duties to different ones, and arranging human affairs through them; not as if He were absent from here, but rather, as appears in the fourth book of the *Laws*, because He wills it so. Therefore, Plato commands first that God be adored for His own sake. Then, those who are called "leading gods" under Him should be loved as being most like Him. They should also be honored as His deputies, and even called upon as mediators. They should be heard as interpreters of the divine mind. Finally, they should be listened to as heralds of the divine majesty. He also commands that temples be built in the city; and he divides the city itself into twelve parts, like a sacred house. In the same way, God Himself constructed a temple for Himself, the world, adorned with the choirs of the twelve spheres: and fortified with priests, that is, spirits endowed with reason, who praise God everywhere...

### SUMMARY OF THE EIGHTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS

->S<-

Plato, imitating this divine temple <note>Ficino often compares the universe to a "temple" created by God.</note> to the best of his ability, admits many gods into his own temples, just as God himself admits many into his own: and he arranges various images, just as God placed the stars in the heavens as if they were statues of his own angels. Furthermore, among many altars of many beings, he consecrates the first altar to the First Being; just as God chose the Sun as a statue uniquely suited to Himself among the stars, as Plato says in the *Republic*. Regarding this, it might perhaps be said: <note>original: "In Sole posuit tabernaculũ suũ."</note> *He has set his tabernacle in the sun.* <note>This is a reference to Psalm 19:4, which Ficino uses to bridge Platonic philosophy and Christian scripture.</note> He will treat sacrifices and statues more carefully elsewhere; but to speak briefly for the present, he wishes the First God—since He possesses nothing of matter or a similar nature—to be worshipped by the mind alone. 

However, he allows offerings and sacrifices to be brought to the subordinate deities in the manner prescribed by the laws of the fatherland. Hence, the theologians of the nations, in the rites of the celestial and fiery deities, introduced many figures and lights pertaining to the sense of sight. In the rites of the aerial spirits, they also added musical harmonies, scents, and vapors. But in the sacrifices to the aquatic and terrestrial spirits, they further employed those things that pertain to taste and solid matter. 

For this reason, it should seem a wonder to no one that Plato, a philosopher of such gravity, should promulgate all his laws, especially the sacred ones, only after consulting the oracles. At the start, he saw that one must yield to the times. It was necessary to strengthen human affairs with a certain divine counsel and authority. It was truly impossible in those times for men born and educated in such a way to be kept in divine reverence by any reason that was utterly foreign to their customs. Furthermore, the most prudent Plato judged that even if impure spirits could deceive men through oracles, nevertheless, minds withdrawn from the body for the sake of divine reverence—as if already purified—could be suddenly seized by pure deities. Just as wood, which the wind has dried by chance, is often soon ignited by the nature of fire; similarly, souls that have performed a religious rite (even one less approved among the wise) can be seized in hidden ways by a better deity. Thus, those who unknowingly ascended into the mind itself, apart from the senses, may now happily approach from on high. 

Plato does not wish us to attend so much to the ritual by which you worship the divine, but rather for whose sake you worship. For if you do this for the sake of the King of all and from a desire for eternal goods, it is probable that from wherever and however you begin, you—approaching nearer to the Highest through such veneration—will eventually either be surrounded by His immense light or at least be preserved by His overflowing goodness. 

Relying on this kind of confidence, Plato consults the oracles regarding the establishment of laws and sacrifices. He commands that the magistrates perform some public sacred rite daily: first for the safety of the fatherland, and then for their own and their families'. Following a certain order, after the basics of the youthful age were handed down in the seventh book, he soon descends to sacred matters in the eighth; as he wishes it to be understood that men are rightly instructed from their early years for this very reason: so that they may both wish and be able to participate properly in the sacred rites. 

If, however, any carping or fearful person dreads participating with so many gods and daemons <note>term: "daemons" - in Platonism, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil "demons" in the modern sense.</note> in Plato’s city, he is equally free to go to the Peripatetic city <note>term: "Peripatetic city" - a jab at the followers of Aristotle, whom Ficino sometimes viewed as too focused on the material world and lacking in spiritual devotion.</note>, which is empty not only of daemons and gods, but even of God himself. But truly, it is worth the effort—once superstitious pride and resentment are set aside—to choose the better parts from all things and to approve of Platonic piety. One should not demand that he was a Christian, for only the interval of time prevented him from being one. 

Indeed, there are first twelve sacred rites, held on the New Moons of the months. There are also a second twelve, in the middle of the months. The third are three hundred and sixty-five, namely, the daily ones. The primary ones are for the celestial gods; the middle ones for the terrestrial, namely, those gods ruling beneath the moon (for he calls everything beneath heaven "terrestrial"). The lower rites are for the daemons, and the lowest for the heroes. He thinks it necessary that the sacred rites be distinguished by these twelve types. For indeed, according to the twelve-fold system of the spheres and signs, even in any given sphere, the daemons and heroes are distinguished by a twelve-fold division. He commands that the commemoration of the festivals and their distinction be declared to the people every year in the last month—which we commonly accept as February. But especially in the Platonic manner, the month before the summer solstice. 

He rightly dedicates the last month to Pluto. For Pluto is properly "Providence," both separating souls and judging them once they are separated. He says, moreover, that the union of the soul with the body is not better than its separation. Understand this as referring to the decaying body, and insofar as it is decaying—not regarding the celestial body, or one similar to heaven, to which it is better for the soul to be joined. To this body, however, insofar as it is decaying, it is not better. It is as if he says it is worth the effort to be joined to this one as well, not for its own sake properly, but for the sake of another end. But regarding these matters, I have written more diffusely in the *Theology* <note>Ficino refers to his own major work, the *Platonic Theology*.</note>. 

But do the Platonists also offer sacrifices to the more impure daemons? Some do, partly because they oversee natural duties, and partly so they do not cause harm out of envy. Plato, however, would by no means concede this. Indeed, since he commands that sacred rites be performed for the sake of purifying the mind and for the veneration of the First God alone. He affirms that a city using divine counsel for its laws will be happy. He adds that it pertains most to the happy life of both the citizen and the city that one neither inflicts injury on others nor is affected by injury oneself. Both can be achieved through virtue. 

And lest the city be affected by injuries, he established sacrifices in which divine help might be sought, and certain solemn and festive games might be frequented, imitating military battles as much as possible. In these, he wants both females and males to be trained for battle; and in each person, both the left hand and the right, so that the city may be whole and equally useful from both sexes, and each individual, being equally useful from each hand, may be most complete. 

Among these things, you will note how much he detests avarice, as it is especially harmful to a city; it twists minds occupied with private and base gains away from the care for public safety. You will note again with what great caution he admits music, dancing, and poetry into the sacred and military games. Then, that only that command is legitimate as well as safe in which one rules over those who are willing. But since shameful loves—indeed most disgraceful ones—often occur in the gatherings of youthful games, he therefore most diligently commands that these must be countered. Indeed, they have already been partially countered where he removed gold and silver from the citizens, educated them in constant labors, and constantly subjected everyone—especially the youth—to the eyes of judges observing their conduct everywhere.

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino's commentary on Book VIII of Plato's Laws. The previous page discussed the hierarchy of gods and the use of the sun as a divine symbol. ### BOOK VIII

He considers that there are three remedies against the disease of wantonness and petulance which are quite beneficial. He also encounters a fourth present remedy: namely, that a reputation should be spread daily by the listeners of the laws and the magistrates, through which everyone might grow accustomed by common consent to think that intercourse against nature is no less shameful, and held in no less hatred by God, than intercourse between children and parents. Indeed, Plato thinks that the consensus of common reputation has a marvelous power over morals. In these matters, those who overcome pleasure live happily; those whom pleasure overcomes live unhappily. 

You will also hear a precept for abstinence that is most beneficial, highly approved by Paul the Apostle <note>Ficino frequently draws parallels between Plato and St. Paul to harmonize classical philosophy with Christian theology.</note>: just as athletes abstain from pleasures out of a desire for physical victory, much more ought everyone to abstain in the same way for the sake of the victory pertaining to the soul. 

Furthermore, he teaches that benevolence is twofold: one created by a similarity of character, the other from a certain state of need. When either of these becomes more vehement, it is called "love." Love, as far as this purpose is concerned, is threefold: for either the beauty of the soul is loved, or that of the body alone, or both together. In these matters, consider how cautiously he proceeds in establishing laws: although he may have sometimes indulged a noble lover of physical beauty in his dialogues, here he grants nothing. Indeed, he evidently banishes the accustomed love of the body. As for the moderate love of both combined, he does not dare to admit it into the laws. Finally, he seems clearly to approve only the love directed toward the soul. 

Then he denies that men of depraved nature are masters of themselves. For whoever departs from reason abandons the rational nature of man, and surely loses at the same time the liberty that is the gift of reason; yet he does not lose his guilt even when he commits a fault as if driven by impulse, since he himself provided the cause for such necessity. 

However, people contrary to these he calls those of "unimpaired nature": who worship God and, among human things, fear infamy above all else. They do not love the beauty of any body—whether their own or another's—but rather the beauty of the soul and its character. 

Regarding what he said earlier—that it is the duty of God to resist such crimes if these things could be ordered by Him—understand it this way: it is the property of God, the ordainer of natures, to restore to order those things which have fallen away from the order of nature. This is especially true since many believe that the soul fell into such crimes not so much because of the senses, but because of the instigation of certain demons from the very beginning. 

But where he says, "if they could be ordered by God," he does not doubt divine power, but rather human resistance. God can indeed order things as far as it depends on Him, but man cannot be ordered so easily. God could also compel man, if He wished to drag him by necessity, but He wishes to lead him by a certain free way. 

Next, he mentions the banquets celebrated during solemn rites and games. Likewise, from the banquets, he speaks of the diet and the laws pertaining to it. Opportunely, after the education of the soul and the laws pertaining to it, he now descends to the nourishment of the body and laws of that sort. Then he hands down laws concerning fields, boundaries, waters, fruits, cattle, pastures, and similar things. 

When speaking of boundaries, he says that the transgressor of boundaries is punished by "Jupiter of the Tribe" and "Jupiter of Hospitality." <note>original: "Ioue conatribuli atque hospitali"</note> Understand this as one Jupiter who is the guardian of both the kinsman and the guest. And since it is a trait of pride to overstep the boundaries established by law and to usurp another's domain, he says that Jupiter is stirred up to avenge this injury and rises up with the most hostile battles—as if to say that God rises against the proud not so much as a judge, but as an enemy and an avenger. 

After many constitutions, he concludes that it does not pertain to an elder of the people to describe every tiny law with precision, especially those pertaining to lawsuits and controversies over things. Instead, he should bring forward a few common laws concerning external matters, which interpreters may derive into every tiny legal detail. But regarding morals and the <term>discipline of the soul</term> <note>original: "animi disciplina"</note>, he should treat these most diligently "to the fingernail." <note>original: "ad unguem." A Latin idiom meaning to do something with perfect precision, like a sculptor checking the smoothness of a joint with their nail.</note> 

While he speaks of various artisans, he hands down three precepts that are very much worth remembering. First: no citizen—that is, one who may at some time perform public duties—ought to be occupied in any craft, nor even his servant. For the art of governing the republic, which requires much practice and many teachings, claims the whole man for itself. Second: no one should, or even can, practice two arts or studies. Third and finally: it is not fitting for a craftsman to preside over the craft of another. He also wisely forbids citizens from exporting necessities and importing luxuries, and especially from <term>inn-keeping</term> <note>original: "cauponari." In the ancient world, retail trade and inn-keeping were often viewed as socially degrading and prone to greed.</note>, especially for the sake of profit. Then he arranges the city into twelve parts, with neighborhoods, temples, and marketplaces, and he imposes laws upon the markets that are as sober as they are diligent.

## THE EIGHTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, OR ON LEGISLATION.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring intricate floral and foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

ATHENIAN.
It follows next that we should establish laws concerning festivities through the Delphic oracles: which sacrifices the city ought to offer to which gods for its success. But as to when and how many sacrifices should be made, it is perhaps our task to establish somewhat by law. 

CLINIAS.
Perhaps the number? 

ATHENIAN.
Regarding the number, then, let us speak first. I judge that there ought to be three hundred and sixty-five: so that one of the magistrates may always be sacrificing to some one of the gods or spirits, on behalf of the city, on behalf of themselves, and on behalf of their possessions. 

The interpreters and priests—both men and women—and the prophets, gathered together with the Guardians of the Laws, shall arrange those things which the legislator necessarily left out in these matters. For these people ought to be the judges of what was omitted. The law, therefore, will see to it that the citizens celebrate twelve festivals for the twelve gods after whom each tribe is named: and they shall perform sacrifices to those gods every month; furthermore, there shall be choruses, musical games, and gymnastic contests, as is fitting for each god and season. There shall be distinct festivities, so that it is clear which ones should be conducted without men, and which should not. The festivities of the terrestrial and celestial gods, and of the others who follow them, are not to be mixed, but kept separate...
