# ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LATIN TRANSLATION OF THE LAWS, DIALOGUE VIII.

**S.ii.**

...to be honored in the twelfth month, which is dedicated to Pluto, so that it may be legitimately celebrated. For this god is not to be cast aside by warlike men, but rather worshipped, as he is always the best for the human race. For the joining of the soul and the body is in no way better than their separation, as I affirm in all seriousness. Furthermore, whoever intends to distinguish these matters sufficiently must entirely consider this: that our city is of such a kind that it could not be found elsewhere, given its leisure time, its abundance of necessities, and its liberty. 

Indeed, it is necessary for the city itself to live well, just as a single man does. For those living happily, it is primarily necessary that they neither inflict injury on others, nor have others inflict injury upon them. One of these is not very difficult. But the other—to be able to be harmed by no injury—is most difficult; and no one can perfectly achieve it otherwise than by becoming perfectly good. The same is true for the city: for if it is good, it will lead its life in peace; but if it is wicked, it will be assiduously infested by both internal seditions and external wars. 

Since these things are generally so, one should not wait for a time of war, but in peace itself the citizens must be trained in military matters. Therefore, unless the city is captured by madness, it will test its military strength every month, for no less than one day—but even for several, as it seems fit to the magistrates themselves—men, women, and children alike, avoiding neither winter nor heat. This is so that all may be prepared whenever it seems right to the magistrates to lead out the entire population in some manner. For this purpose, suitable games should also be devised along with sacrifices, so that certain solemn and festive battles may take place, imitating warlike struggles as closely as possible. Rewards and praises should be given to the victors, and conversely, reproaches to the defeated, according to how each has behaved in the contests and in all of life. Thus, let every best person be raised up with praises, and the contrary be depressed by reproach. 

Not everyone shall be poets of these things: but first, one who is no less than fifty years old. Second, one who not only possesses the poetic muse sufficiently, but has also performed some noble and distinguished deed. Therefore, let the poems of those who are good men—worthy of honor in the city and who have performed noble deeds—be sung, even if they are less musical. The judgment of this matter shall be held by the one appointed over the education of the youth <note>Referring to the "Praefectus Iuventutis" or Supervisor of Education, a key role in Plato's Republic and Laws.</note> and the other guardians of the laws. They shall grant this honor to honest men: that they alone afford liberty in the muses, while they prohibit others. Let no one, therefore, dare to sing a muse not approved by the judgment of these men, even if it be sweeter than the hymns of **Thamyras** or **Orpheus**. <note>Thamyras and Orpheus were legendary Greek musicians; Thamyras was said to have challenged the Muses, while Orpheus could move stones with his song.</note> But let them sing sacred poems that have been approved by judgment and dedicated to the gods, as well as the poems of good men in which certain people are praised or blamed, and which are judged to do so with moderation. 

I judge that these same things regarding military service and poetic liberty must be done similarly for women and men. But it is necessary for the legislator to speak often in this way: "Tell me, in establishing a city, what kind of citizens do I strive to educate? Is it not athletes of the greatest contests, who have innumerable adversaries?" "Precisely," anyone would rightly answer. If, therefore, we were educating boxers, or <term>pancratiasts</term> <note>Athletes of the pancratium, an ancient Greek sport combining boxing and wrestling.</note>, or others of that kind, would we lead them into the contest itself without them having ever fought anyone before? Or if we were boxers, would we not have learned to fight many days before, doing all things which ought to be used in a true contest where one strives for victory? Approaching as closely as possible to that which is similar, would we not bind on <term>spheres and pads</term> <note>Original: "sphaeras & pilas." These were padded gloves or soft balls used to prevent serious injury during training sessions.</note> according to the precepts, so that we might learn by premeditation both to inflict and avoid wounds? Because if no companions were given to us with whom we could be exercised, would we, fearing the laughter of fools, restrain ourselves from hanging up an inanimate image against which exercise might be made? And if we had no supply of either an animate or inanimate adversary, would we not ourselves fight alone against our own shadow? Or for what else has the flexing of hands here and there and such prepared preparation been devised? 

**CLINIAS.** For almost nothing else than this very thing. 

**ATHENIAN.** Why, then, does the city study anything other than military service? Shall it dare to come to the greatest contest—to fight for life, for children, for its affairs, and for the fatherland—prepared worse than such contestants? Therefore, the legislator will not fear lest these gymnasiums seem ridiculous to some; but he shall ordain by law that military matters be conducted most vigorously. Indeed, daily with minor exercise without arms, introducing and inciting dances and all gymnastics for these things; but with major exercise no less than once a month, so that individuals may compete to capture or hold places and ambushes, and imitate every kind of warfare. They shall exercise themselves with missiles, turning themselves in every direction, and use weapons that approach as closely as possible to real and dangerous weapons, so that such play among citizens is not conducted entirely without fear, but brings dread. Thus, it may show in some way those who are of great spirit and those who are cowardly, so that honors may be granted to the former and reproaches to the latter, as is fitting. By this reasoning, the whole city may be usefully prepared for the true contest throughout its whole life. 

But if someone should die by involuntary slaughter in these contests, let the one who killed him be purified by law and be clean hereafter. For the legislator ought to think that with a few men dying in this way, the rest will not be worse. But with fear extinguished in all these things, he will find nothing further by which he may discern the better from the worse; if this is not done, it is a much greater evil to the city than that death. 

**CLINIAS.** We concede, Guest, that these things should be sanctioned by law and performed by the entire city. 

**ATHENIAN.** Do we all now know the cause why such dancing and contests are now performed almost nowhere in cities, except perhaps very little? Shall we affirm it happens because of the ignorance of the multitude and the legislators? 

**CLINIAS.** Perhaps. 

**ATHENIAN.** By no means, O blessed Clinias. But there are two sufficient causes for this matter. 

**CLINIAS.** What are they? 

**ATHENIAN.** One, indeed, is that by the desire for riches, all other things being neglected, we care only for private business; the minds of citizens, leaning toward this, can give effort to nothing else except daily accumulating money. For all most willingly embrace the arts and studies that lead to profit; they scorn the rest. This, therefore, is one cause why citizens do not care for that or any other honest and good duty; but with an insatiable desire for gold and silver, they embrace both honest and dishonest crafts alike, and do whatever they can—be it right or wrong—so long as they accumulate money. With these things supplying them, they serve the belly and lust just like cattle. 

**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly. 

**ATHENIAN.** Let this, I say, be one cause: by which it happens that citizens neither exercise anything else nobly, nor military matters sufficiently...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Latin translation and interpretation of Plato’s *Laws*, specifically the transition from the philosophical causes of civic decay to the practical legislation of military and athletic games. The Athenian Stranger is explaining why most cities fail to train their citizens for war: greed and bad government.</meta>

### BOOK VIII. DIALOGUE VIII.

...but those who are modest by nature turn to commerce, navigation, and base services; while those who are manly and noble turn to theft, robbery, sacrilege, ambushes, and tyrannical crimes. Although they were well-constituted by nature, they nonetheless became wretched through this habit. 

**CLINIAS.** Why do you say that? 

**ATHENIAN.** Indeed, why should I not call them entirely wretched, those who are compelled by hunger to torment their souls throughout their entire lives? 

**CLINIAS.** This is certainly one cause; but what is the second cause you speak of, Stranger? 

**ATHENIAN.** You have reminded me rightly. 

**CLINIAS.** Therefore, as you say, this is one: the perpetual and insatiable greed for wealth, by which individuals are so occupied that they are prohibited from caring for military matters as they should. But now explain the second. 

**ATHENIAN.** Do I seem to you to be lingering too long on this one because I lack the ability to explain the other? 

**CLINIAS.** Not at all; but you seem, stirred by hatred, to be attacking these habits of men more than is becoming for this conversation. 

**ATHENIAN.** You rebuke me most excellently, my dear friends. Therefore, listen to what follows. 

**CLINIAS.** Speak then. 

**ATHENIAN.** I assert the cause to be those types of governments which we have often mentioned: the popular government <note>democracy</note>, the power of the few <note>oligarchy</note>, and tyranny. None of these is truly a republic <note>original: *respublica*, referring to a stable, lawful state</note>; instead, they can all most rightly be called "seditions." For in none of them does a willing ruler govern willing subjects; rather, a willing ruler always dominates unwilling subjects by some force. In these systems, since the prince fears his subjects, he will never willingly allow them to become good, or rich, or robust, or brave, or in any way warlike. These two are, in a sense, the primary causes of all these things. 

However, this republic for which we are now making laws seems to have escaped both. For it enjoys the greatest leisure and is deeply free; and from these laws, men will become least greedy for money. Therefore, it is likely that this alone of all existing republics can take up military discipline and play <note>the Greek concept of *paidia*, or structured play/education</note> together, which we have rightly discussed. 

**CLINIAS.** Well said. 

**ATHENIAN.** Next, we can speak of all the gymnastic contests: that prizes be established for those that contribute to war, and the rest be dismissed. But these must be recounted from the beginning and established by laws. And first, regarding what pertains to running and speed. Is that not so? 

**CLINIAS.** It must certainly be done. 

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, above all, agility of the body—one of the feet, the other of the hands—contributes to war: agility of the feet for fleeing and pursuing, while in fighting and wrestling, one requires the strength of the hands. 

**CLINIAS.** Certainly. 

**ATHENIAN.** Yet neither is of great use without arms. 

**CLINIAS.** True. 

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, let the herald first call the one who will run the *stadium* <note>a sprint of roughly 200 yards</note>, just as is done now in contests. But let him enter with arms. For we shall by no means set prizes for a naked competitor without arms. First, then, let the one who will run the *stadium* enter armed. Then the one for the *diaulos* <note>the "double-pipe" race, down and back the track</note>. Third, the horse-race. Fourth, the *dolichos* <note>a long-distance race</note>. Fifth, we shall send out one adorned in lighter armor who will be the first to reach some Temple of Mars at a distance of sixty *stadia* <note>approx. 7 miles</note>. Another, also armed in heavier armor, to run a shorter and flatter distance. Another, an archer equipped with all the finery of bows, should travel a hundred *stadia* through mountains and various terrains to reach the Temple of Apollo and Diana. Once the contest is established, we shall wait for them to arrive and give prizes to the individual victors. 

**CLINIAS.** Rightly so. 

**ATHENIAN.** We shall distinguish these contests into three parts. One for boys. The second for the beardless <note>adolescents/youths</note>. The third for men. And for the beardless, we shall set two parts of the race out of three; for the boys, half of these. Let them compete with archers and other armed men. For females, we shall set the *stadium* for girls not yet of puberty, to run unclothed, as well as the *diaulos*, the horse-race, and the *dolichos*, that they may compete in the race itself. But beyond the thirteenth year of age, until they are married—not longer than the twentieth year nor shorter than the eighteenth—let them descend to the running contest, provided they use suitable clothing. Let these things be said concerning the running of both men and women. 

But to increase strength, in place of the wrestling and similar things held now, let more serious ones be taken up. And let there be a fight with arms: one against one, two against two, and up to ten against ten. What the victor ought to do or not suffer <note>rules of engagement</note>, just as is now determined in the wrestling school by the masters of wrestling regarding what is a well or poorly done work of a wrestler, so also in these contests of arms, experts must be brought in. They shall ordain by law what a person wins by not suffering or by doing, and similarly, what order shall discern who is defeated. These same things should be understood as ordained by law for females as well, up to a marriageable age. 

Furthermore, all light infantry fighting <note>original: *peltastica*, referring to the *pelta* shield</note> should be set against the *pancratiac* <note>a "no-holds-barred" style of combat</note> fight; and let them compete with the bow, the light shield, spears, and the throwing of stones by hand and sling. And whoever bears himself best in these things shall have the honors of victory granted to him by law. 

Now let us look at the contests of horses. The use of horses is not great in Crete. For this reason, it is necessary that the zeal for breeding horses and competing with them be of less concern to the Cretans. For none of you keeps a chariot, nor do you think it is noble to put effort into this. Since it is not customary, it seems foolish to establish such competitors by law. But for horses alone—colts before they have reached maturity, and those of middle and full age—one may grant equestrian games according to the nature of the region. Let such a contest be made according to the law: and in it, let the judgment be granted collectively to the masters of the horse and the tribunes, both concerning the entire course of the horses and concerning those who descend into it with arms. 

We do not, however, impose a contest or a prize for those without arms, neither in the gymnastic games nor here. But he who shoots an arrow or a javelin from a horse is not useless to Crete. Therefore, there should also be play, contention, and competition in this. Women, however, are not to be compelled to these things by laws. But if previous discipline and habit, or their nature, incites the girls to this and makes them not abhor it, they should be admitted. 

But we have now said enough about exercise and gymnastic discipline, whether those we perform in contests or those we practice daily under masters. Also regarding music for the most part. But regarding the rhapsodes <note>original: *rhapsodis*, i.e., singers of poems</note>, and those who follow them, and concerning the competition of choruses, as many as are established for the necessary solemnities to the gods and *daemons* <note>divine spirits or lesser deities</note> on set days, months, and years—all these things, how they are to be arranged, and whether they should happen every three or even five years, shall be understood and carried out by the counsel of the gods. Then, in turn, the contests of music will be held, just as the athletes themselves are the declarers of prizes; and the teacher of the youths, and of the laws...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger describes the transition from explaining why greed and bad government ruin a city's defenses to establishing specific military-focused athletic competitions. He details armed races, combat simulations, and the inclusion of women in physical training to ensure the city remains warlike even in times of peace.</summary>

Here, the conversation shifts to the regulation of festivals, athletic contests, and the much more difficult task of legislating human desire and sexual ethics.</meta>

# FOLIO CCCXLVII.
## ON LAWS, OR THE DIALOGUE ON LAWS, BOOK VIII.

The guardians, who have the authority for passing these laws, having gathered together, shall ordain these things. For they shall arrange when, how, and with whom individual contests should be held in all choral groups and dances. What kind each of these should be—regarding speech, song, or harmonies mixed with rhythms and dances—was often stated by the first lawgiver. Those who follow him, adhering to these sacred rhythms and times, will distribute the contests accordingly and establish festival days for the city. These and other such matters are not difficult to understand in terms of how they should be ordered by laws; nor, if they are changed in one way or another, do they greatly help or harm the city. However, there are some matters of the highest importance that are so difficult to persuade people of that they seem to be the work of God himself, if they could only be established by Him. 

But as it stands, they require the efforts of some bold man who, relying especially on freedom of speech, decrees what he judges best for the city and the citizens. He must act to recall the corrupt souls of the citizens to a decent habit and observance of the laws, even while opposing their most burning desires; and, lacking any other help, he must follow reason alone without fear.

**CLINIAS.** What are you saying, Stranger? For we do not understand this.

**ATHENIAN.** It is likely you don’t. But I will try to speak more clearly. When I was observing the discipline of life and saw young men and young women conversing humanely with one another, I feared—as is right—considering how someone might use that city where young women and youths are delicate; where they have not been subdued by great and hard labors (by which lust and insolence are extinguished), but rather where everyone spends most of their time on festival days, sacrifices, and dances. How, then, in this city, will they abstain from those desires that have led many to the extreme, so that the reason which commands them to abstain becomes law? 

Certainly, if the previous laws drive out many desires, it is no wonder. For that institution which prohibits excessive wealth <note>Plato argues that extreme wealth leads to luxury and vice</note> contributes not a little to temperance, and all the discipline we have set forth above has laws suited to this. Furthermore, the eyes of the leaders are compelled to look at nothing else but to always watch the youth, setting a limit on other human desires. But how will anyone avoid the loves of young men and women that are contrary to nature—both the abuse of men for women and women for men—from which innumerable evils have followed for people both privately and publicly? And what remedy will be found for the dangers facing individuals? 

This is altogether difficult, O Clinias. For in many other matters, all of Crete and Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> provide us great help in establishing laws that are foreign to the customs of many; but as far as morals are concerned, they oppose us and disagree entirely. If someone, following nature, were to establish that law before Laius <note>original: *ante Laium*. In Greek mythology, Laius, the father of Oedipus, was said to have introduced pederasty, which Plato's Athenian Stranger here classifies as "contrary to nature"</note>, forbidding the abuse of males instead of females, and cited the nature of beasts as a witness—among whom males do not have sexual relations with one another because it is not according to nature—he would perhaps be using a plausible reason, but it would not harmonize with your cities. 

Furthermore, he would hardly achieve what a legislator must always observe. For one must always observe what leads to virtue and what is sanctioned by law. Come now: if we agree by law that this is honorable or at least not shameful, what will it contribute to virtue? Will it generate a habit of courage in those who are unpersuaded, or a form of temperance in those who are persuaded? No one would ever believe this, but rather the opposite. For everyone will reproach the softness of one who serves pleasures and does not resist them. In the case of one who imitates women, would not anyone disapprove of that very feminine image? Who among men, then, since it is such a thing, would sanction this by law? Almost no one who has the true law in his mind. 

How then do we say this is true? It is necessary to consider the nature of friendship, of desire, and of loves, if one is to inspect these things correctly. For since there are two kinds, and a third species arising from both, all encompassed by one name, they cause all doubt and darkness.

**CLINIAS.** How so?

**ATHENIAN.** For we call a "friend" one who is like another in virtue, and an equal to an equal. Again, we call a "friend" a poor man to a rich man, even if they are opposite in kind. But when either of these becomes more vehement, we call it "love."

**CLINIAS.** Correct.

<margin>Friendship</margin>

**ATHENIAN.** Friendship that proceeds from opposites is hard and rough, and often lacks reciprocity in us. But that which comes from likes is peaceful and shared throughout life. Where it is composed of both, it is benevolence. At first, it is not easy to know what a person wants who loves with this third type of love. Then, being pulled in opposite directions by the two types, he himself doubts what he should do: as he is commanded by one to enjoy the flower of youth, and forbidden by the other. 

For he who loves the body, and hungrily seeks its form like a kind of fruit, seeks only to be satisfied and shows no honor to the soul of the beloved. But he who cares less for the body and considers rather the soul that he desires—since he loves the soul itself as is proper—regards the use of the body as insolence and insult. Because he fears and honors temperance, courage, magnificence, and wisdom, he will want to live chastely with a chaste friend. 

The love composed of both of these is the one we just placed in the third position. Since, therefore, there are three loves, are they all to be driven out by law? Or shall we clearly accept that one in the city which looks toward virtue and desires the youth to become as good as possible, while repelling the other two if possible? Does it seem otherwise to you, my friend Megillus?

**MEGILLUS.** You have spoken very well about these things just now, Stranger.

**ATHENIAN.** I was not guessing in vain, my friend, that I would have your agreement. It is not necessary for me now to inquire what your law feels about these things, but to accept what you admit. I will try to persuade Clinias of it later. For now, let what you have given be accepted, and let us diligently consider the laws.

**MEGILLUS.** You speak most rightly.

**ATHENIAN.** I have a certain art in passing this law—partly easy, and partly altogether difficult.

**MEGILLUS.** How is that?

**ATHENIAN.** It is established even now that many men, even those who are wicked, well and diligently and of their own accord abstain from union with beautiful people.

**MEGILLUS.** When does that happen?

**ATHENIAN.** Whenever a brother or sister is of exceptional beauty to someone. The same law, even if unwritten, sufficiently repels the son and daughter, and prohibits both manifest and secret intercourse between them. Nay, rather...

<sig>S.iiii.</sig>

<meta>Catchword: Nay, rather (Immo vero)</meta>

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian Stranger discusses the difficulty of legislating human desire, distinguishing between three types of love—of the body, of the soul, and a mixture of both—and argues that the law should only encourage the love of the soul to foster virtue. He cites the universal taboo against incest as proof that even strong desires can be successfully regulated by social and legal "unwritten" laws.</summary>

# PAGE XXXIIII.
## BOOK EIGHT
<meta>Catchword: latura.</meta>

...it ensures that not even any desire for this thing <note>referring to prohibited sexual acts or incest</note> approaches the common people. 

**MEGILLUS.** You speak the truth. 

**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, a single and very brief word has extinguished all pleasures of this kind. 

**MEGILLUS.** What word is that? 

**ATHENIAN.** That it is said these things are by no means lawful <term>fas</term><note>Fas refers to divine law or what is religiously permitted, as opposed to "lex," which is human law.</note>, but are held in hatred by God, and are the most shameful of all shameful things. And is this not the cause? Because no one speaks otherwise; rather, from the very earliest infancy, it is spoken of in both jest and in seriousness. In tragedies, they often hear these same things when they tell of Thyestes, or Oedipus, or Macareus <note>These are figures from Greek mythology famous for committing incest: Thyestes with his daughter-in-law, Oedipus with his mother, and Macareus with his sister.</note>, who inflicted upon themselves the death they owed as punishment for their crimes because of such sexual unions. 

**MEGILLUS.** That is rightly said. For we know the wonderful power of reputation, since no one dares to breathe otherwise than as the law commands. 

**ATHENIAN.** Was it not rightly said by us, then, that for a legislator who wishes to subject to reason any of those desires that violently subdue men, the method is easy to understand? For if he dedicates this reputation as a kind of sacred thing among all—slaves and free, males and females, and the entire city—he will make this law most firm. 

**MEGILLUS.** Exactly so. But by what reasoning will he be able to achieve this, so that everyone says the same thing willingly? 

**ATHENIAN.** You have made a good objection. For this reason, I said that I have a method <term>artem</term> for this law: that men should use sexual love according to nature for procreation. I command them, therefore, to abstain from males. For those who use such practices deliberately destroy the human race, sowing "upon stone" where what is sown can never take root. One must also abstain from that "female field" where the seed would not wish to produce sprouts <note>This likely refers to non-procreative sex or perhaps sex during pregnancy or with sterile partners, which the Athenian views as a waste of vital energy.</note>. If this law is perpetually preserved in other matters, just as it is in the case of paternal kinship, it will be the cause of innumerable goods. For first, it will be established according to nature. Then, it will repel all the madness and fury of lusts, adulteries, and the excessive luxury of food and drink. It will also reconcile husbands to their wives, and many other goods will be born, if it is established among everyone. 

But perhaps if some vigorous young man, full of much seed, hears this law being proposed, he will immediately mock it; and with a loud voice, he will cry out that we are decreeing impossible and foolish things by law. When I considered this, I said I had a method that was in one way very easy, and in another way very difficult, for observing this law. For it is easy to understand how it is possible. Since when this lawful opinion has been dedicated among all, it will tame all souls and ensure that they obey the established laws through fear. 

But matters have now reached a point where it seems it can never be achieved, just as it was not believed that the discipline of communal meals could be perpetually observed by an entire city. And yet, among us <note>The Spartans and Cretans</note>, it is seen to happen in reality, though it is thought impossible to happen among women, or even in your cities. For this reason, because of the force of this disbelief, I said it was most difficult for both of these laws to be observed. 

**MEGILLUS.** And you were right to say so. 

**ATHENIAN.** Since they are not beyond human strength, but can indeed happen, do you wish for me to explain a certain plausible reasoning to you? 

**CLINIAS.** Why not? 

**ATHENIAN.** Will someone more easily abstain from these sexual matters—and wish to moderately keep the order imposed upon them—when the body has been well-affected by some prudent diligence, or when it is the opposite? 

**CLINIAS.** Much more so when it is done well and according to skill. 

**ATHENIAN.** Have we not, then, heard of Iccus of Taras? 

<margin>Iccus of Taras, the athlete.</margin>

He was an athlete who, for the sake of the Olympic and other contests, attained both temperance and fortitude of soul through a skillful dedication to these matters; and throughout the entire time of his training, he never knew sexual love. The same is also told of Chryson, Astylus, Diopompus, and many others. And yet, O Clinias, they had cultivated their souls with good arts much worse than your citizens and mine, though they were certainly much more vigorous in their bodies. 

**CLINIAS.** You speak the truth, for it is told by the ancients that these things were done by the athletes. 

**ATHENIAN.** If they, therefore, wished to abstain from that pleasure which the common people think is "blessed" in order to conquer others in wrestling and running and other such things, will our young men not be able to do so for the sake of a far more excellent victory? This is the victory we shall proclaim to be the best, speaking into the ears of boys through songs, stories, prose, and chants, and—as is likely—we shall persuade them by delighting them. 

**CLINIAS.** Which victory do you mean? 

**ATHENIAN.** That they may live happily by conquering pleasure, whereas they live the opposite by being conquered. Furthermore, will not that fear of committing what is by no means lawful contribute most to this end: namely, that they overcome those things which others, who are inferior, are said to have overcome? 

**CLINIAS.** That is certainly reasonable. 

**ATHENIAN.** Since we have come this far in proposing this law, and have fallen into doubt because of the depravity of many, let us now boldly and clearly say that our citizens ought not to be worse than birds and many wild beasts. For we see very many flocks of them living blamelessly and chastely until the time for procreation arrives; but when they reach this age, male joined to female and female to male, they live out the rest of their lives justly and holily, persevering in their first friendship. It is necessary, therefore, that men be better than beasts. 

But if they are corrupted by many other Greeks and barbarians, and cannot contain themselves when they see and hear that disordered sexual love has great power among them, then the guardians of the laws, having obtained the authority to pass laws, should devise another second law. 

**CLINIAS.** What law do you advise passing now, if they do not accept the first one? 

**ATHENIAN.** The one that follows this, O Clinias. 

**CLINIAS.** Which one is that? 

**ATHENIAN.** That they should break the strength of sexual desire as much as possible through physical labor, and turn their energies elsewhere. This will happen if they do not use it shamelessly. For if it happens more rarely because of shame, the mistress <note>referring to Desire or Lust</note> will be weaker. Therefore, let secret custom and unwritten law persuade them that these things be done; and conversely, let it dissuade them from doing otherwise as if it were shameful—so that it is not considered shameful to refrain entirely. In this way, we shall preserve what is honorable in the second place; and one class of men, containing three types—those of a depraved nature, whom we say are not masters of themselves—will be forced not to despise the laws. 

**CLINIAS.** Which three types? 

**ATHENIAN.** Those who are worshipers of the gods, those who are lovers of honor, and those who love the beauty of the soul’s character rather than bodies. These things, spoken as if through a story or a wish, 

<margin>If God: wishes</margin>

will bring <note>original: "latura"</note> much to all cities if they are able to keep them. Perhaps, if God wills it, we shall achieve one of two things in matters of love. Either that no one of noble...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that sexual desire can be regulated through public opinion, religious taboo, and physical labor. He uses the historical example of athletes like Iccus of Taras, who remained celibate during training, to prove that self-control is possible for a higher purpose.</summary>

### ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS OF THE LATINS, DIALOGUE VIII.
#### Signature: S.iiii.

...and let no one dare to touch free women except his own wife; nor let anyone father illegitimate children from a concubine; nor let him sow the sterile fields of males against nature <note>A reference to the prohibition of homosexual acts, which Plato’s Athenian Stranger views as "contrary to nature" because they do not lead to procreation</note>. Or at the very least, let us completely abolish the latter: that no one should unite with males. If anyone should consort with other women besides those who came into the house through the sacred rites of marriage—whether they were purchased or acquired in any other way—unless it remains hidden from all men and women alike, let him be infamous by law and deprived of all city honors, like a foreigner. This law, whether it be considered simple or double, shall be enacted concerning all venereal and amorous matters, through which we act rightly or wrongly among ourselves because of such passions.

**MEGILLUS:** I certainly strongly approve of this law. But let **Clinias** here reveal what he thinks.

**CLINIAS:** I will do so, Megillus, when the opportunity arises. But for now, let us allow our guest <note>The "Athenian Stranger," the primary speaker in the dialogue</note> to proceed further in proposing the laws.

**MEGILLUS:** Very well.

**ATHENIAN:** But we have already progressed so far that we have come to the matter of common meals. We say that such a thing is difficult elsewhere, but in Crete, no one will think it happens in vain. As for the method: whether it should be as it is here, or as it is among the Spartans, or if a third way better than both can be found—it does not seem difficult to me to find, nor will it be anything but highly profitable once found. Indeed, these things seem appropriately established for now. It follows now that we should speak of the means of life <term>victus</term><note>victus: referring to the physical necessities of life, primarily food and the economy of the land</note>, and how it may be obtained.

The means of life in other cities is multifaceted and comes from various places; in most other cities, it is obtained from two main sources. For it is brought to most Greek cities by both sea and land, whereas for these people it is brought by land alone. This circumstance makes the task of the lawmaker easier. For more than half of the usual laws will suffice. Furthermore, laws will be established that are more suitable for free men. For the legislator is not much compelled to pass laws concerning naval matters, merchants, innkeepers, lodging-house keepers, tax collectors, money exchanges, mining, or high-interest loans and a thousand such things.

Therefore, in this city of ours, the lawmaker will omit those things and give laws only to farmers, shepherds, beekeepers, and the guardians and servants of such things—once he has dealt for the most part with marriage and the procreation, education, and discipline of children, and the designation of magistrates. Now, therefore, it is necessary to come to the laws concerning the means of life and those who provide it by their labor.

Let the laws of agriculture be established first; and the first of these is the law of **Jupiter of the Boundaries** <note>original: "Iouis terminalis"; Jupiter was the protector of landmarks and property lines</note>. Let no one move the markers and boundaries of the land—neither those of a fellow citizen nor those of a neighboring foreigner who possesses the edges of a field. But let each one think that what is said is true: "He who moves these moves the immovable." Let each man prefer to move a huge boulder rather than a small stone fixed by an oath from the gods, by which friendships and enmities are defined. For of the one, Jupiter of the Tribe is witness; of the other, Jupiter of Hospitality; and they always rise up against hostile conflict. He who obeys the law shall be free from penalty. He who despises it shall pay a double penalty: first, with God as the avenger, and second, by the law. The law commands that no one shall willfully move the boundaries of a neighbor's field. If someone does move them, let anyone who wishes report him to the farmers <note>referring to the rural magistrates or "agronomoi"</note>; the farmers shall lead him to judgment, and if he is convicted as a disturber of boundaries by stealth or force, he shall pay and suffer whatever the judges decide.

Furthermore, many small damages often committed in a neighborhood give birth to great enmities and make neighborliness difficult and bitter. Therefore, let a neighbor beware lest he harm his neighbor, both in other things and most especially in the cultivation of fields. For to do harm is not difficult, but is within any man's power; yet to do good is not in everyone's power. Whoever crosses the boundaries and cultivates a neighbor's fields shall restore the damage and pay the penalty for his impudence and illiberality, depositing double the amount of the fine for the one whose field he cultivated. The investigators, judges, and assessors of this matter shall be the rural stewards. In major cases, as said before, the entire order of the twelfth part shall judge; in minor cases, those who are in charge of the guards.

If anyone harms pastures, they shall judge and condemn him after considering the damages. If someone pursues another’s swarm of bees and draws the bees to himself by clashing bronze for pleasure <note>An ancient method of gathering or attracting bees using noise</note>, he shall restore the damage. If someone sets fire to timber in such a way that he does not take care for his neighbor, he shall be condemned as the magistrates see fit. Likewise, he who does not leave the proper measure of a neighbor's field when planting shall be punished as has been sufficiently stated by many legislators. We ought to use their laws and not think that many tiny matters, which are the business of any legislator, must be handled by the great founder of a city.

For the ancient laws concerning waters are also good. These certainly do not need to be diverted by a new reading. But he who wishes to lead water to his own land shall draw it from public fountains in such a way that he does not disturb the visible spring of any private person. He may lead it wherever he wishes, except through houses, tombs, or places sacred to the gods; nor shall he bring any other damage except that which is caused by the channel itself.

If, because of a natural scarcity of water in some places, the land does not retain the waters coming from Jupiter <note>referring to rainwater</note>, and if someone is oppressed by necessity, let him dig on his own land as far down as the clay <term>creta</term><note>creta: literally "chalk" or "clay," the waterproof layer where groundwater is often found</note>. If he finds no water at this depth, let him take as much water from his neighbors as necessity requires. But if the neighbors also have little, the rural stewards shall establish the limit of water he may use daily. If rainwater is abundant, and those who inhabit or cultivate the lower parts prohibit the flow so as to harm those above; or conversely, if the person above inconsiderately allows the waters to flow and harms the person below, and they cannot agree among themselves: in the city, the **aedile** <note>a Roman term Ficino uses for the Greek 'astynomos' or city official</note> shall impose a limit, and in the fields, the rural overseer. If anyone does not observe this limit, he shall pay the penalty for his envy and stubbornness and restore double the damage to his neighbor.

As for fruits, let there be a common sharing of this kind. The goddess <note>Ceres/Demeter</note> grants us two types of gifts. One is Dionysian <note>grapes/wine</note>, which cannot be stored away. The other is that which is suited for storage <note>grains/figs</note>. Let this law, therefore, be enacted concerning fruits: Whoever tastes grapes or figs from the country crops before the time of the vintage—which coincides with the rising of **Arcturus** <note>The star Arcturus rises in mid-September, signaling the harvest</note>—if he gathers them from his own field, let him pay fifty drachmas to be dedicated to **Dionysus**; if he takes them from a neighbor’s, a mina; but if from...

# BOOK VIII. ON THE LAWS.
## XXXIII.

...others, two parts of a <term>mina</term> <note>original: "minae"—a Greek unit of currency worth 100 drachmas</note>. But as for grapes and figs, which we call "noble" <note>original: "generosos"—referring to cultivated, high-quality varieties as opposed to wild fruit</note>, since they cannot be easily stored, let a man harvest them when and how he wishes if they are his own. But if they belong to another, since the law is that no one should move what he did not set down, let him be fined unless he has obtained permission. If a slave takes them without the consent of the master of the field, let him suffer a number of lashes equal to the number of figs or grapes he took. A tenant may eat purchased fruits that are unfit for storage if he desires; but if a foreigner is traveling alone or with only one companion, let him taste the fruit that cannot be stored, if he wishes, with the indulgence of hospitality. However, let the law prohibit foreigners from tasting other fruits which we call "rustic." If anyone touches fruits fit for storage out of ignorance, if he is a slave, let him be whipped; but if he is a free man, let him be dismissed with a warning that it is permitted to taste only those figs and grapes unfit for storage, but not those from which raisins, wine, and dried figs are made.

Pears, apples, pomegranates, and others of this kind shall not be considered a disgrace to take secretly. But if anyone under thirty years of age is caught, let him be beaten without wounding and punished; let no legal infamy attach to a free man on account of such a beating. A resident alien may also pick these fruits just as he may pick those unfit for storage mentioned above. If an elder eats them but does not carry them away, as is permitted to the alien, let him also share in all such fruit; but if he does not obey the law, let him be held unfit for the contest of virtue, provided this is reported to the judges presiding over such matters.

Water is the greatest benefit for nourishing gardens, but it is easily corrupted. For earth, sun, and air—which, along with water, nourish those things that grow from the earth—cannot be easily corrupted by poison, diversion, or theft. But water can easily suffer damage in these ways; therefore, it requires the aid of the law. Let this law be enacted concerning it: If anyone deliberately corrupts another’s water—whether it be spring water or collected water—by poison, digging, or theft, let him be reported to the <term>Aediles</term> <note>original: "aediles"—market overseers and public works officials</note>. If he is convicted of the offense, let him restore the damage and clean the springs or water vessel in whatever way the interpreters of the law judge the purification should be performed.

Regarding the transport of all things collected from the fields: let it be permitted for anyone to transport his property however he wishes, provided it causes no damage to anyone, or that he gains three times the profit of the damage caused to his neighbor. The judges of these matters shall be the magistrates, as they are for all other things which someone does intentionally by injury, force, or secrecy—whether by himself or by his property—against a person or a thing. I say let all these matters be brought to the magistrates if the damage does not exceed three minas. If it is greater, let the case be brought to the publicly established courts and let the one who caused the injury be punished. If any magistrate gives an unjust sentence regarding someone’s damage, he shall owe double to the person who suffered the injury. And generally, if a magistrate does anything through injury, the case may be argued in a public court by anyone who wishes.

There remain nearly infinite and small regulations regarding the correction of errors in legal procedures, citations, and summons—whether the citation is between two or many—and other such things which cannot be ignored by the laws, yet do not seem worthy of an elder lawgiver. Therefore, let younger men—imitating the ancient laws and understanding small things from great ones, and knowing through experience the necessary use of these things—arrange them by law until they are sufficient. Once they are sufficiently established, let them use them without change.

Regarding other craftsmen <note>original: "opificibus"</note>, let the laws be established as follows. First, let no citizen be occupied in any craft; nor indeed a slave of any citizen. For a citizen is occupied with a great art which requires long practice and much learning: namely, providing for the common adornment of the state—a task that is not satisfied by light labor but 

<margin>
Human nature is not able to diligently practice two arts.
</margin>

requires primary devotion. Human nature cannot diligently practice two arts or two studies. No one can sufficiently devote himself to one art while also overseeing a craftsman of another art. Therefore, let this be decreed in the city: that no one shall be both a blacksmith and a carpenter at the same time; nor shall a carpenter oversee blacksmiths more than his own craft, perhaps having found an opportunity here so that while he manages many assistants who do the work for him, he gains an advantage for his own art and manages his art better through them. Instead, let individual craftsmen focus on individual arts and earn their living from them. Let the Aediles see that this law is observed: if any citizen turns toward any craft more than toward the care of virtue, let them bring him back to his own course, marked by reproach and infamy. But if any foreigner practices two arts, let him be forced by chains, fines, and expulsion to embrace only one.

As for the wages of craftsmen, the approval or rejection of their work, and the injuries they either suffer or inflict, let the Aediles take notice up to fifty drachmas. Greater matters brought to the public courts shall be judged according to the law. Furthermore, let there be absolutely no tax on imports or exports. Regarding incense and other such things burned for the gods that are foreign, and likewise purple dye and other colors not produced in the region—in short, all foreign things—let no one bring them in unless they are necessary; nor again shall anyone export anything that is necessary. Let the twelve guardians of the laws who remain (excepting the five elders) oversee and take notice of all these things.

However, let arms and instruments of war be imported if there is need of foreign craft. Likewise, those things fit for these purposes—plants, bronze instruments, ropes, and animals that contribute to war—should be brought in. Let the masters of the horse and the leaders of the army have care of these things, so that the city is not deprived of the ability to import or export them when there is a need. Concerning these matters, the guardians of the laws shall bring forth sufficient and proper laws. But in no case shall there be any retail trade <note>original: "cauponatio"—small-scale buying and selling for profit</note> for the sake of gathering money, either in the city or in the entire region. Regarding the grain that is gathered from the fields, the distribution shall be correctly established according to the Cretan law. For what is from the region...

### FOLIO 349
### SUMMARY OF THE NINTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS

...produced [from the land] must be distributed by everyone into twelve parts, and consumed in a similar fashion. Indeed, each twelfth part—such as of wheat, barley, and all other crops and fruits, as well as all animals for sale—should be distributed in a three-fold and appropriate ratio: one part for the free citizens, a second for the servants, and a third for the artisans and all foreigners <note>The original uses "aduenis," referring to "metics" or resident aliens who provide necessary labor but lack citizenship.</note>. This applies whether they have come from elsewhere to live in the city for a time and are in need of necessities, or whether they have arrived for the public or private benefit of some citizen. This third part of all necessities shall always be for sale, and only this part is necessarily so. Of the other two parts, nothing shall be sold by necessity. 

How, then, are these things rightly distributed? It is clear, first of all, that this can be done correctly if the distribution is made partly equally and partly unequally. 

**Cleinias:** In what way? 

**Athenian:** It is necessary that the earth produce and grow each of these things, whether of better or worse quality. 

**Cleinias:** Why not? 

**Athenian:** Since there are three parts, no one—neither master, nor servant, nor foreigner—should have more in this regard; rather, the distribution should be made equally and similarly for all. Each citizen, however, after receiving two parts, may distribute them to his servants and the free members of his household in whatever quantity and quality he wishes, according to his own judgment. Whatever remains beyond these must be dispersed by measure and number in this way: once the number of all animals that are fed by the earth is determined, the partition should then be made. 

Habitations must afterwards be arranged separately. Such an order is most fitting: there should be twelve villages, one in each of the twelve parts [of the territory], located in the center. In each, there should be marketplaces, temples for the gods, and shrines for the <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "demontī" — refers to tutelary spirits or lesser deities who follow the gods</note> who follow the gods, whether they be the local <term>Magnesian</term> gods <note>The "Magnesians" refers to the specific historical/mythological group the colony identifies with.</note> or others whose statues have been consecrated by ancient memory. To these, the honors of the men of old must be rendered. Temples must also be constructed for Vesta <note>original: "Veste" — Hestia, goddess of the hearth</note>, Jupiter <note>Zeus</note>, and Minerva <note>Athena</note>, and for the other gods who preside over each of the twelve individual parts. 

First, near the temples in the highest places, let there be the most fortified dwellings for the guards. Then, the rest of the region shall be distributed among the artisans in thirteen parts. One part shall live in the city, divided among the twelve parts of the city; the others shall occupy the outer areas all around. In each village, the artisans suitable for the convenience of agriculture shall be compelled to live. The <term>magistrates who oversee the fields</term> <note>original: "magistratus qui agris pręsunt" — known in Greek as the agronomoi</note> shall have care of all these things; they shall foresee how many and which artisans each place needs, and ensure that their dwellings do not hinder the farmers, but rather bring great utility to them. Similarly, the <term>aediles</term> <note>original: "ędiles" — city officials responsible for public buildings and streets</note> shall have care of the urban artisans. 

The things for sale shall be the concern of the <term>censors</term> <note>original: "censoribus" — market overseers</note>. They should first care for sacred matters, and then watch strictly so that no one causes injury in buying or selling, and they should restrain all who are immoderate or insolent. They shall consider whether the citizens sell individual items to foreigners appropriately and as the law provides. On the first day of each month, the citizens and their ministers shall put forth a twelfth part of the wheat for sale to the foreigners; the foreigners shall buy wheat and similar goods for the duration of the entire month at this first market. On the tenth day, a sale and purchase sufficient for the month shall be established. On the twenty-third day, the sale of animals that men need, and of furniture—such as leather, clothing, and similar items—shall take place. 

It is necessary for foreigners to buy everything from the owners, so that no <term>huckstering</term> <note>original: "cauponatio" — retail trade or middleman reselling, which Plato viewed as socially corrupting</note> occurs regarding wheat, barley, flour, or other food. Neither citizens nor their servants shall be allowed to engage in huckstering at all. In the foreigners' market, however, a foreigner may exchange and sell wine and food to artisans and their servants, and similarly cooked meats; this business is called "huckstering" by many. As for firewood, a foreigner may buy it daily from those in the fields who manage it, and he may resell it to other foreigners however and whenever he wishes. 

The sale of all other things and furniture that we use shall take place in the common market, in determined locations where the guardians of the laws and the censors, along with the aediles, have designated the place and set the prices for the goods. Here, they shall exchange money for things, and things for money. Each person shall make the exchange for himself, committing it to no one else. If anyone does commit a sale to another [on credit], whether he receives payment or not, he must remain quiet; for there is no legal judgment for such exchanges. If anything is sold or bought for more or less than the law has commanded—by which the measures and prices of goods are established—the excess shall be recorded with the guardians of the laws, and the contrary [the previous record] shall be deleted. 

The same shall be done regarding the registration of the property possessed by inhabitants and foreigners. It shall be permitted for anyone to migrate to the city under a certain condition: that he practices some craft, and that he remains for no more than twenty years from the day of his registration. During this time, he shall not be compelled to pay any residency tax, except for an example of <term>frugality</term> <note>Ficino translates this as a tax of "virtue" or "moderation" rather than a monetary one.</note>; nor shall he owe anything to the treasury for the sake of buying or selling. When twenty years have passed, he shall take his property and depart. But if he has conferred some great benefit upon the city within those twenty years, and wishes to stay for a longer time or even for life, his request shall be granted if he persuades the council and the assembly. As for the children of residents, if they are also artisans, their period of residency shall begin after their fifteenth year of age, so that they may remain for twenty years thereafter. Then they may go where they wish, or if they wish to remain, they may do so after similarly persuading the authorities. He who departs having forgotten the description [of his property] that was written with the magistrates, shall be treated accordingly.

**C**ontinuing the dialogue after the general discipline of morals and the tradition of many laws, we now approach the subject of judgments. This is indeed very timely. For those who are learned in morals and instructed in the laws are now able to judge; and those who have not obeyed the preceding education and instruction must now be judged. This physician of our souls <note>Referring to Plato</note> has up to now prudently striven to preserve the complete health of the soul through salutary warnings; but now he moves to repair that which is lost by every means possible. Truly, such is the Platonic charity...

<meta>This page transitions from the specific regulations of Book VIII of Plato's Laws to Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical introduction (the "Argumentum") to Book IX. # SUMMARY OF DIALOGUE IX ON THE LAWS

Merciful and grieving, the legislator is drawn to cut and sear as if by necessity. He does this with such kind caution that he consoles the gravely ill with the sweetest words; he strives to make the healthy remain so through words that act like magic charms <note>original: "magicis carminibus," referring to the persuasive "preambles" Plato suggests should accompany every law</note>, before he even applies his medical hand. Even when he finally moves his hand to act, he does so in such a way that the suffering person hardly feels it, conceiving more hope than pain, and bringing away health from the pain rather than destruction. A man of remarkable mercy, he punishes no one without offering consolation; he abandons no one who has been punished; he saves everyone to the best of his ability. Even those he punishes with death, he claims to free from the sickness of the soul; by the minor evil of death, he halts the soul’s evil, which is otherwise vast and growing day by day. Indeed, he asserts that it is better to depart from here than to live in an incurable sickness of either the soul or the body. 

Yet he does not deprive anyone of this life unless he has recognized them to be incurable; nor does he wish any punishment inflicted by a law—which is good—to lead toward evil. On the contrary, he believes punishment itself is good for many reasons: first, because it is just, and justice is a good; second, because it either purges a present evil or prevents a future one; third, because by punishing one person, it benefits many through the example provided and purges the city of evils. To speak briefly, he mixes justice with mercy in a marvelous way everywhere, neither twisting with harsh rigidity nor leaving anything unpunished through softness.

Just as in the previous books he placed divine duties before human ones, so in the present book he prudently turns his attention to sacrilege before other crimes. While he shows how grave the crime of injured divine majesty is, he signifies—under God’s inspiration—that no such thing was ever committed by men as long as a certain divine grace flourished within them. But after that grace was lost because of other sins, men, now acting as if they were strangers to God, began to sin against God himself through sacrilege. Thus, sacrilege itself is not only a sin but also the punishment for sin—a punishment, I say, that does not purge a person but destroys them. For such a punishment is not brought about by the law, but by the transgression of the law. 

As for his statement that the ancient lawmakers were "sons of gods" and handed down laws to "heroes" who were also born of the gods: this must be explained through those matters discussed in the *Critias*, the *Statesman*, and often elsewhere. By "sons of gods," he understands the gods beneath the Moon, who were assigned to govern various regions of the earth. We can also name these "angels" in the Platonic manner. In the *Protagoras*, he teaches that the human race received laws through these beings under the name of Mercury. In the *Critias*, he also says the first men born from the earth received rights through them; and here he calls those men "heroes born from the gods"—that is, those generated from the earth by the work of the gods. But he says in the *Critias* that those laws were not written for the ears, but were infused by a kind of inspiration from divine minds into human minds; and as long as men obeyed them, they lived happily. He adds that because of the transgression of such laws, men lost divine grace; once this was lost, they also lost their happiness. Once unhappy, they rushed headlong into sacrilege, and through sacrilege, they finally turned out the worst and most miserable of all. 

In these accounts, one may recognize the mystery of the earthly paradise and the expulsion from it. Consider, indeed, where he investigates the causes of sacrilege: three causes are assigned for grave crimes. The first is the common fragility of men, strengthened by habit. The second is demonic persuasion or suggestion. Finally, the third is a ruinous guilt branded into the soul from ancient and unpurified sins, which stimulates one toward the gravest crimes. This indeed seems very similar to "original sin" <note>original: "originali culpę"</note>, about which many theologians dispute. 

Therefore, where the divine Plato, addressing the sacrilegious person, says: "It was not a human evil that drove you to sacrilege, nor a divine one," understand "human evil" as human fragility inclined toward lower things, and "divine evil" as the fraud of the devil, as he investigates it. He denies these two, not because they are not involved in the cause of sacrilege, but because they are not the *only* causes. For a third and proper cause of sacrilege is added to these, which he joins by saying: "But it is a certain deadly sting <note>original: "stimulus"</note> born within from ancient and unexpiated sins." Through this, clearly, the soul is no longer human but beast-like, and thus sins against God through sacrilege, having no further regard for God once it has lost human reason, which is the image of divine reason.

Soon after, Plato meets the first instigation toward sacrilege—as if it were a budding disease—with three remedies, just as this disease arises from three causes. First, so that the monstrous impulse may be suppressed, he sends the person to sacred expiations, which we might name in the Christian fashion as penance, confession, almsgiving, and fasting. Next, so that one may resist demonic snares, he sends them to prayers and supplications, through which protection may be obtained from the higher and liberating spirits against the lower ones. Finally, so that he may restrain human weakness, he mandates that one avoid the familiarity of evil men and adopt the company of the good.

Furthermore, since he had ordered the fatherland to be honored after God in the Pythagorean manner, he rightly proceeds after sacrileges (which are committed against persons or things consecrated to God) to the punishment of crimes and offenses committed specifically against the fatherland. These he judges not only to be close to sacrileges, but he counts them among them and punishes them similarly. He judges these to be crimes against the fatherland: for instance, one sins against the fatherland—and must be considered an enemy of the fatherland—who, having cast aside the laws, reduces the government to human will and lusts; or who, though he is able, does not come to the aid of the fatherland when it is in danger; or who, whether out of greed or some other cause, turns out to be a traitor to the fatherland on behalf of his own son. 

Among these points, he repeats the duty of the lawgiver. He wants it to be this: that the lawgiver writes laws not as a master to slaves, but as a father to sons—no less persuading than threatening, no less teaching than commanding, and no less alluring than terrifying. Thus, the work of the legislator is not so much the prescription of mandates as it is the discipline of character. For his end is to make the citizens good and happy by whatever rational means possible; punishing the wicked is a matter of necessity for him rather than of will. And because the Platonic laws alone among human laws embrace all these things, they are the most perfect of all human laws, and should almost be numbered among the divine rather than the human. Nor is it without reason that the first beginning of this disputation...

FO. CCCL.

### SUMMARY OF DIALOGUE IX ON THE LAWS

...is made by God; then it is added by Plato that all these things seem divinely inspired. Finally, from this very discussion, one arrives by a straight path at the blessed temple of highest Jove—that is, heaven. But since there are different degrees of guilt, not only in sacrilege and parricide but also in other crimes, other degrees of punishment must also be described by the lawmaker and judged by the magistrate. To distinguish these degrees, he introduces a very practical distinction. Every habit of the soul is either one of virtue or of vice. If it is of virtue, it is entirely voluntary, because it is acquired through free counsel, unhindered choice, and the soul’s own actions. But if it is a habit of vice, it is judged entirely involuntary. This is because it is a sickness of the soul, just as an imbalance of the humors is a sickness of the body. No one would call a sickness voluntary, even if someone might in some way call "voluntary" the things that unexpectedly bring on a disease. Furthermore, a habit of this kind grows from obstructed counsel, distracted choice, and through passions rather than through active deeds. From these points, that most famous and frequently repeated Platonic saying is established: *The habits of vices are involuntary, and no one becomes evil by their own will* <note>original: "Vitiorum habitus involuntarios esse: neminemque fieri sponte malum." This is the core Platonic doctrine that all wrongdoing is the result of ignorance or spiritual sickness.</note>, just as no one becomes sick, deformed, or impoverished by their own choice.

After this distinction of habits follows the distinction of actions. These actions tend specifically toward creating either a habit of virtue or of vice. If they tend toward virtue, they are voluntary in the same way the habit was said to be voluntary. But if they tend toward vice, they are called partly voluntary—because they happen with the soul’s consent in a way, and they could have been avoided before they happened—and partly involuntary. They are involuntary partly because they lead secretly toward harm, deformity, and sickness (which no one would want), and partly because they arise from a certain ignorance of the goal and the outcome. To the extent that they happen through ignorance, they are judged to happen against the very will of reason.

Distinguish them again in this way. Human actions, as far as they pertain to the matter of laws and judgments, are reduced to five categories. They either:
1. Sprout from the affections of **desire** <note>original: "concupiscentia," the part of the soul driven by physical appetites</note>;
2. Burst forth from the impulse of an **irascible nature** <note>original: "irascibilis," the part of the soul driven by anger or the desire for honor</note>;
3. Come from a certain **simple ignorance**, through which someone is ignorant of the facts but does not realize they are ignorant;
4. Happen through **double ignorance**, through which someone both does not know the facts and simultaneously does not know that they do not know—believing, in fact, that they do know;
5. Or finally, they proceed from a certain **rational opinion**—an opinion, I say, regarding what is just and unjust, held by someone who trusts in reason and the laws.

After this kind of distinction, the rules of judgment are also distinguished. Through these rules, one may look differently upon those who sin out of desire than those who sin out of anger; and among these, one may discern whether they sinned deliberately or impulsively. Furthermore, whether it was done by force and openly, or rather secretly and through fraud. Then, one must ask whether the error happened through ignorance, and whether it was simple or double ignorance.

Where he deals with the judgments of homicides, he introduces an ancient mystery concerning the slain taking vengeance on their slayers. Take note that, in Plato’s opinion, the disturbances belonging to the senses can remain in the soul even when it is separated from this body. Indeed, according to his view, there remains a certain primary "sensing nature," the substantial origin of the other senses. Through this nature, the soul—while in this body—extends its powers of sensing into these physical instruments; and when departing from the body, it somehow folds those powers back into itself. Or, to speak more in the Platonic fashion, it exercises them in an **aerial body** <term>aerial body: In Neoplatonic thought, a subtle "vehicle" or spirit-body that the soul inhabits after leaving the physical body but before ascending to higher realms.</term>. Enveloped in this, it enters this world and departs from it. Regarding these, the Platonists distinguish them thus: the soul dwells in this thicker physical body for a short time; in the aerial body for many ages; and in the celestial body for all eternity.

What is the point of this? Do not wonder that disturbances survive in the soul of the deceased if the sense and memory of these things survive. The ancient theologians thought it probable that the souls of men who were suddenly killed, being as yet "unexpiated," are agitated by disturbances. Indeed, they even harass their enemies; this is brought about not only by human indignation but also by divine **Nemesis** <note>the goddess of retribution</note> and a providing spirit <note>original: "daemone providente"</note>. That a vengeful sense and disturbance survive in the soul according to the opinion of the ancients, and that the soul uses an aerial body, our Platonic Maro <note>The poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note> stands as a witness. For what else does he mean when he says: *And now a great image of me shall go beneath the earth* <note>original: "Et nunc magna mei sub terras ibit imago," from the Aeneid IV, 654</note>? In a very Platonic way, he calls the soul's "primary sensing nature" an "image" of the rational soul. But why "great"? Because it is both the source of the other senses (the "common sense") and because after this body, it uses a large body—namely, the aerial one. While it is somehow tucked into this physical body, it is cramped; once stripped of this, it expands into a large space, as the nature of the aerial element requires. Furthermore, he writes: *I shall be present as a ghost in all places; you, wicked one, shall pay the penalty.* <note>original: "Omnibus umbra locis adero, dabis improbe poenas," from Aeneid IV, 385-386</note> He distinguishes between the "image" and the "shadow." He wants the "image" to be the soul’s sense in the aerial body, and the aerial body itself to be the "shadow" of the soul. But he calls the earthly body a "blind prison."

What he says in the judgments concerning homicide—especially regarding parricide—about the return of the human soul back into human bodies (where it often pays penalties exactly equal to the crimes committed in a previous life) is an ancient opinion of the Magi and Egyptian priests. For they judged that there was no more suitable **purgatory** for human crimes than to eventually suffer the same things in human bodies that one has done to others. Plotinus the Egyptian uses this very reasoning in his books on Providence to solve the doubts that daily arise against divine justice. For he says: those things which are not repaid by divine providence in the present life are repaid in another—and indeed a human one—by exactly the same measure. He adds that they are even repaid in the bodies of beasts, where the soul of a former man may become the soul of a brute animal. But in this last opinion, he seems to have stood alone. For it displeases the other Platonists that a soul specifically human should ever become specifically that of a brute. They do agree, however, that souls migrate back and forth into other human beings; though Plato does not hold this as certain, he holds it as highly probable. As for the soul migrating into beasts, he mentions it often, but he tells it with such a ridiculous tone—contrary to his usual gravity—that he clearly demonstrates the thing itself should be denied, and an **allegory** should be sought instead. That is, you should understand "passing into a brute" in two ways:
1. In affection, imagination, and a habit suitable to a brute.
2. In the dwelling and company among wild beasts for a time, for the sake of punishment.
For the ancients think that having a brutish habit and disposition is the punishment itself; but the return into a human being, where one undergoes equal and very similar sufferings, is not only a punishment but a purgatory.

After these things, you will come opportunely to the mention of the necessity of law:

Ficino has been discussing the psychological motivations behind crime and the necessity of legal structures. This page transitions from his philosophical commentary into the actual translated text of the Ninth Dialogue, specifically addressing the grave crime of sacrilege and the nature of punishment as a medicinal tool for the soul.</meta>

PAGE XXXIV.

### BOOK

He asserts that laws are necessary for the human race. For without laws, humanity would differ in no way from the most savage of beasts. Asserting the cause of this, he says that no man’s intellect is so naturally fashioned that he sufficiently understands everything that must necessarily be known for the public good; and even if by chance he does know it, he may not always be able or willing to act upon the best of what he knows. But if, by some divine grace, a mind were to arise among men that entirely understood the public good and always and generously aimed toward it, there would be no need for laws for that person or for their country at that time. For a true and free mind is superior to every law, and by its own right, it would rule over all things. But since such a capacity is granted to no one's intellect, he concludes that we must necessarily live under laws.

He also says that the pursuit of one's own private good utterly dissipates a city, while the pursuit of the public good connects it. Likewise, he warns that a ruinous plague dominates that city where judgment is either conducted in secret among magistrates or through clamorous outbursts. And where he mentions a "personal demon" <note>original: "familiarem demonem." In the Platonic tradition, a *daemon* is a guardian spirit or a higher level of the soul that guides an individual.</note> often resisting many evils—if you shudder at the name of a "demon," call it an "angel," as Plato also allows. And remember that our demon, as it is born with us, is not only our intellect (as some think), but a divinity.

He soon commands that elders be cherished with such paternal reverence that even if you are beaten by them, you ought not to become angry, but to endure it patiently. However, regarding the "birth gods" he mentions here, we should not take them in the astronomical fashion as ascending signs or the planetary lords of the signs, but as the "Idea" of the human race, the principle and guardian demon of our life. Finally, he warns that the indignation of those above <note>the gods</note> and the punishment of those below <note>in the underworld</note> must be feared. He warns that death is not the end, but that beyond it lie the punishments of the lower world, and that these things are told with absolute truth.
