## THE NINTH DIALOGUE: ON LAWS OR ON LEGISLATION.

<margin>
Death is the least of evils.
</margin>

->THE ATHENIAN STRANGER<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a classical figure standing within an architectural frame.</image-desc> If judgments are rendered after this in a manner consistent with the actions described previously, the natural order of establishing laws will indeed be preserved. We have already spoken of judgments regarding agriculture and similar matters; but we have not yet spoken specifically about the greatest judgments and judges. Therefore, we shall speak of these next.

CLEINIAS: Very well.

ATHENIAN: In a way, it might seem shameful to assign laws concerning the types of things we are about to discuss to that city which we say is to be entirely well-disposed toward the possession of virtue. For who would not find it absurd if someone in a city so established thought that a most wicked man would be born—as happens in other cities—so that there was a need for legal threats to prevent him from becoming such, or to prevent such things from being committed, and to punish them with established laws once committed, as if most flagitious men could be found in this republic as well? 

But since we do not act like the ancient lawgivers who, being sons of gods, brought laws to heroes (who were themselves said to be born of gods), but are instead men establishing these things for men, it is right to fear lest some citizen be born with a nature so untamable and raw that—like legumes made stubbornly hard by a lightning strike—he cannot be softened even by the fire of the strongest laws. Therefore, if someone should dare to commit sacrilege, we shall establish a law concerning this, however burdensome and unpleasant it may be to us. Indeed, we neither wish nor greatly fear that a properly educated citizen will suffer from so grave a disease. But perhaps the servants of these men, or foreigners, or the servants of foreigners, will attempt many such things. For their sake especially—and because the entire nature of man is weak—I shall write laws both concerning sacrilege and other crimes that can scarcely, or not at all, be healed. 

But first, preludes <note>original: "prooemia." Plato argued that laws should have persuasive introductions to explain their purpose to citizens before the threat of punishment.</note> must be placed before all these, as briefly as possible, according to the order established in previous sections. Therefore, to the man who is dragged by a wicked desire by day and roused by night to seek out temples to rob them, one might say these words by way of instruction and warning: 

"O wondrous man, it is no human evil, nor a divine one, that turns you toward sacrilege; rather, it is a certain deadly sting <note>original: "asilus" (gadfly/sting). A metaphor for a maddening, compulsive urge.</note> born in men from ancient and unexpiated crimes, driving you about. You must flee this with all your strength. Listen to how you may flee: when such a thought arises in your soul, flee, I pray, to the rites of expiation. Flee as a suppliant to the sacrifices of the gods who deliver us. Flee to the company of good men, where you may partly hear and partly say yourself that justice and honor must be cherished by all. Above all, flee the company of the wicked. If you do these things, and the disease ceases, it will be well with you. But otherwise, considering it better to die, depart from life."

When we have sung these preludes to those in whose minds an impious and pestilential thought toward the city has fallen, we shall dismiss those who obey as free from the law. But for those men not persuaded by the prelude, we shall thunder more loudly, establishing the law after this: 

Whoever is caught in sacrilege, if he is a slave or a foreigner, let him have the brand of his calamity burned into his face and hands, and after being beaten as seems fit to the judges, let him be driven naked beyond the borders. For perhaps, having been made more restrained by this punishment, he might finally emerge better. Indeed, no punishment established by law aims at evil. Rather, it almost always achieves one of two things: for the person who has paid the penalty usually becomes either better or certainly less wicked. 

But if any citizen is caught perpetrating such a thing against the gods, or parents, or the fatherland, and is found to have set his mind toward the greatest injury—because he did not abstain from the greatest crime despite having been well-taught and educated from boyhood—the judge should consider that he cannot be healed. For such a man, death is the least of evils. <note>Death is considered the "least of evils" here because it prevents the criminal from doing further harm to his soul and the state.</note> Having been rebuked so that he may help others by his example, let him be cast beyond the borders. His sons and his entire kin, however, if they flee their father's ways, should be shown honor and praise, because they have bravely followed virtue though born from evil. But let none of their money be confiscated into the treasury in that republic, where the allotments of land must always remain the same and equal. But since the one who committed those acts must pay fines in money, let him spend what he possesses above his allotment...

The previous page discussed the philosophical necessity of law for human society, given the limitations of human intellect. This page moves into specific legal procedures for capital crimes, treason, and theft, and introduces the famous "medical metaphor" regarding the purpose of legislation.</meta>

FOLIO 351.

-> ON LAWS, OR THE NINTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS <-

...remain intact. Regarding the exact truth of this matter, the Guardians of the Laws <term>nomophylakes; the high-ranking officials responsible for overseeing the legal system</term> shall always report to the judges from the written census, so that no one might ever be deprived of his own property by chance because of a lack of money. But if anyone is seen to be worthy of a greater penalty, and neither the bail of a <margin>kinsman</margin> nor the generosity of friends sets him free, let him be punished with conspicuous and long-lasting chains and other marks of disgrace. Let no sin go unpunished, and let no fugitive escape without a penalty; instead, let him be punished by death, or chains, or lashes, or by sitting or standing ignobly in sacred places at the borders of the region, or by fines, according to the reasoning we have stated; let him pay the penalty by being fined.

Moreover, let the Guardians of the Laws be the judges of capital crimes, and let the best among them be chosen from their number: specifically those who served in magistracies in the year immediately preceding. In what manner accusations, citations, and similar things ought to be done, the later legislators shall determine. But it is the duty of our office to prescribe by law the manner of voting and passing sentence. Therefore, let these matters be clearly set forth. But before these proceedings, the judges shall sit with the dignity most closely preserved, in the presence of the accuser and the defender. All citizens who have leisure should be present, and they should listen diligently to such judgments. In these cases, when the first speech has been delivered by the accuser, the defender shall deliver the second. Then the senior among the judges shall sufficiently examine what has been said with all diligence applied; afterward, all the others shall consider whatever each thinks should be investigated that was said or not said by the adversaries. However, whoever deems nothing worthy of his own discussion shall leave the examination itself to another.

And finally, the writings that were then concluded, with the seals of all the judges inserted, shall be deposited in the sanctuary of Vesta <note>Vesta (Hestia) was the goddess of the hearth and the state's center; placing legal documents in her temple signified their sanctity and permanence.</note>. Again, on the following day, <margin>the integrity of the seals</margin> having been gathered in the same place, they shall examine and judge in the same manner: and with the seals applied, let all the things that were said be deposited. And when they have done this similarly a third time, with seals and witnesses sufficiently provided, each judge, carrying his sacred vote, shall affirm by an oath to Vesta that he will judge truly and justly to the best of his strength; and thus they shall put an end to this judgment.

After sins committed against the gods, let us speak of those committed to the destruction of the Republic. He who reduces the leadership to the whim of a man and subjects the laws to him—and thus subjects the city to factions and fills it with sedition by using force against the laws—this man is to be judged the greatest enemy of all to the entire city. The second enemy is he who, though he may not be a participant in this crime, nevertheless, while performing the most ample magistracies in that republic, does not notice these conspiracies, or if he does notice them, does not come to the aid of his fatherland out of a certain timidity. Therefore, every man, who strives to be a citizen of any value, should report these things to the judges and drag into judgment him who, having plotted against the fatherland, tries to turn it toward unjust governance by force.

Let the judges of this crime be the same as those for sacrilege, and let the whole judgment be conducted similarly; and those votes which win by a majority shall condemn him to death. And to speak briefly, let the sons not pay for the sins of the father, unless the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather have successively owed the penalty of death. These sons, however, with their goods (always excepting the ancestral lot), the city shall send back to their ancient fatherland. And from the sons of the citizens who have more than one child not less than ten years old, let them choose by lot those whom the fathers, or paternal or maternal grandfathers have named, no fewer than they send to Delphi <note>A reference to the practice of dedicating children to Apollo at Delphi or resettling them to preserve the number of households in the city.</note>; and to him who shall be approved by the oracle of Apollo, the lot and the destitute house shall be returned with a happier fortune.

**CLINIAS.** That is certainly correct.

**ATHENIAN.** There is, furthermore, a third common law concerning judges and the manner of judgment against those who are accused of treason. And concerning the staying of sons and grandsons or their departure from the fatherland, let there be one law against three similar offenders: the traitor, the sacrilegious man, and the violent subverter of civil laws. Concerning theft, however, whether someone has stolen something large or small, let there be one law and a similar penalty for all. For anyone condemned of theft, if his goods suffice beyond his ancestral lot, let him pay double; otherwise, let him be bound until he has either persuaded the one to whom he owes it or has paid it back. But if it was a public theft, only then let him be freed from prison when he has persuaded the city or paid double.

**CLINIAS.** In what way, Guest, do we say it makes no difference whether a theft is large or small, or whether it was taken from a sacred or non-sacred place, or however else it might happen? Since theft can be committed in many ways, the legislator ought to consider the variety and dissimilarity of the crime and not punish with similar penalties those things which are not similar.

**ATHENIAN.** O Clinias, you have opportunely pulled me back in my running rush and brought back to my memory what I had once thought: that until this day, laws have in no way been correctly established, as it occurs to us to say while considering the present matters.

**CLINIAS.** How so do we say that again?

**ATHENIAN.** We have certainly used a fitting image, when we compared all who hitherto receive laws to those slaves who are cared for by other slaves. It certainly is not right to be ignorant of this: if any physician among those who heal by a certain practice without reason <note>Meaning an empirical doctor who works by habit rather than scientific principle.</note> should hear a free physician, a student of philosophy, talking with a free patient while he investigates the beginnings of the disease with reasons and speaks more diligently about the nature of bodies, he will immediately laugh. And against him, he will say those things which are always ready for most physicians in this matter. "You are not healing the sick man, O fool," he will say, "but as if he needed instruction rather than health, you are teaching him." Will he not seem to speak rightly in this way? And will he not deservedly object to the same thing in us: that whoever discourses about laws as we are doing now, does not establish laws, but educates the citizens?

**CLINIAS.** Perhaps.

**ATHENIAN.** But it has happened happily for us at present.

**CLINIAS.** Why so?

**ATHENIAN.** Because nothing urges us to pass laws; rather, having undertaken this consideration of our own accord, we strive to perceive what may be best and necessary for the whole discipline of the republic, and how it may be carried out. Since, therefore, it is permitted if we wish to consider what is best or what is most necessary in laws, which do you think we should choose to treat at present?

**CLINIAS.** This choice, Guest, is ridiculous; and it clearly makes us similar to those who are so compelled by a huge necessity to pass laws in the present that it does not seem permitted to wait until tomorrow. But to us, by the help of God, just as it is for those who construct something from stones or any other material, it is permitted to collect extensively those things from which future benefits may be chosen for the work without any haste. As if we were builders not at all in a hurry, let us lay some foundations in one way and take up other things here for building.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book IX of Plato’s Laws, translated by Marsilio Ficino. The Athenian Stranger and Clinias are discussing the philosophical foundations of criminal law, specifically the distinction between voluntary and involuntary actions.</meta>

### BOOK XI <note>While the header identifies this as Book XI, the text corresponds to the famous philosophical debate in Book IX of Plato's *Laws* regarding the nature of justice and injury.</note>

So much so that in proposing laws: some are laid down as if for the first time; others are added as if to laws already established. **ATHENIAN.** In this way, according to nature, Clinias, our overview of the laws will become more concise. But let us consider that matter of the legislators, by the gods. **CLINIAS.** What then? **ATHENIAN.** The writings and words of many are found recorded in cities; but the legislator also writes the words and letters of the law. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Shall we then apply our minds to the works of poets and other writers composed about the way of living, but not at all to those of the legislators? Or should we attend to these most of all? **CLINIAS.** To these altogether. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, it is the legislator alone among writers who ought to consult and teach about the honorable, the good, and the just—what these are, and how those who are to be happy must act. For it is a disgrace, when Homer, Tyrtaeus <note>Tyrtaeus was a Greek poet whose verses inspired the Spartans to courage</note>, and other poets have written well about the life and pursuits of men, it is a disgrace, I say, for Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta</note> and Solon <note>The famous Athenian lawgiver</note> and other legislators to do less. Rightly, therefore, laws should display this excellence remarkably above all other writings; other writings should be approved if they agree with the laws, but if they are discordant, they should be mocked. Thus, let laws be written for cities so that the lawgiver fully assumes the role of a father and mother. These writings should possess the virtue of charity and wisdom rather than the command of a lord and tyrant who only threatens and describes but assigns no reason at all. Let us consider, then, whether we should proceed by this path, whether we can or not. But let us gird ourselves now: and proceeding along this path with all our strength, let us endure even if it is necessary to suffer anything. May it be fortunate, and it surely will be if God wills it. **CLINIAS.** You have spoken rightly; therefore, let us do so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, we must first consider carefully, as we began: concerning sacrilege, theft, and all other injuries. Nor should we be distressed if, in that very description of the laws, we have already established some things while we are still debating others. For we are not yet legislators; we are only becoming so, and perhaps we will be soon. But if it seems right to discuss those things I proposed, just as I said, let us do so. **CLINIAS.** Absolutely. **ATHENIAN.** Regarding all honorable and just things, let us strive to look into that which we agree upon and that which we disagree upon—we who profess to study this most of all, so that we may differ from the many, as others also disagree with themselves. **CLINIAS.** What differences do you speak of between us, I ask? **ATHENIAN.** I will try to explain. Regarding justice in general, and just men, things, and actions, we all somehow agree: namely, that all these things are honorable and beautiful. So much so that if someone asserts that just men, even if they are physically deformed, are most beautiful according to the very habit of justice, no one would reject his judgment. **CLINIAS.** Hardly anyone who speaks thus would seem to speak incorrectly. **ATHENIAN.** Rightly then. Perhaps. **ATHENIAN.** But come, let us see: if all things that are done justly are honorable and beautiful. For almost all our experiences <note>original: "passiones"; referring to things undergone or suffered as a result of an action, such as receiving a punishment</note> are similar to our actions. **CLINIAS.** What of this? **ATHENIAN.** Certainly any action that is just, insofar as it partakes of justice, so far does it also partake of the honorable. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Wherefore if a just experience is said to partake equally of the honorable and of justice, our speech will not be discordant. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** But if we affirm that some experience is indeed just, but deny it is honorable, then the 'just' and the 'honorable' will be discordant with one another. For just things will be said to be most shameful. **CLINIAS.** How did you say that? **ATHENIAN.** It is nothing difficult to understand. For the laws we previously established will seem to command things entirely contrary to these words. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** We judged that the sacrilegious man would justly die; and likewise the enemy of well-established laws. And when we were about to write many laws of this kind, we held back—considering these experiences to be infinite in both number and magnitude: most just indeed of all experiences, but also the most shameful of all. Will not the honorable and the just appear now as the same, now as contrary? **CLINIAS.** It seems so. **ATHENIAN.** Many, therefore, discordantly call the honorable and the just different, as if they were in conflict. **CLINIAS.** It certainly appears so. **ATHENIAN.** But let us look at that again, Clinias, how we agree on these things. **CLINIAS.** What agreement do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** I think it was clearly stated by me in the previous sections. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** If it was not said above, at least consider me to be saying it now. **CLINIAS.** What then? **ATHENIAN.** That all bad men are bad entirely against their will <note>This is the famous Socratic paradox: no one does evil knowingly or voluntarily, but rather out of ignorance of the good.</note>. If this is so, this other point must also follow. **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** That injustice is an evil, and an evil person is such against his will. But what is voluntary can never, by any reasoning, happen against one's will. Therefore, he who thinks that injustice is involuntary will think that a man acting unjustly does so against his will. Now I must agree with myself: since I admit that everyone commits injury against their will, how could someone—for the sake of ambition or contention—object to us, saying: 'The unjust are indeed unjust against their will, yet many of them commit injury voluntarily'? This is not my opinion, but that. How then shall I agree with my own words if you, Clinias and Megillus, ask me this: 'If these things are so, Stranger, what do you advise us regarding the city of the Magnesians? Should we give them laws or not?' I would indeed advise giving laws. Then you would say: 'Will you therefore distinguish for them between injuries done voluntarily and those done involuntarily? And will you prescribe greater penalties for the former and lesser for the latter? Or equal penalties for all, since no injuries at all are done voluntarily?' **CLINIAS.** You speak rightly, Stranger. But what shall we use these things for that were just said? **ATHENIAN.** You have asked well. For we shall use them first of all for this. **CLINIAS.** For what then? **ATHENIAN.** Let us recall clearly that we said in the previous parts that there is much confusion and disagreement among us regarding the matter of justice. Resuming that, let us ask ourselves: is it fitting, when we have in no way declared the difference between these—which in any city are established by all ancient legislators as two species of injury, namely voluntary and involuntary, and are thus punished differently—to bring forward this opinion of ours as if it were divinely spoken, without confirming in any way how it is correct? It is not fitting at all. Rather, it is necessary before we establish laws to signify how these two are and what difference they have, so that when we impose punishment on either, everyone may understand and be able to judge...

<summary>This page explores the philosophical tension between the "Socratic paradox" (that no one does evil willingly) and the practical legal necessity of distinguishing between voluntary and involuntary crimes. The Athenian Stranger argues that a legislator should act like a nurturing parent, providing reasons for laws rather than just tyrannical commands.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Book IX of Plato’s Laws, where the Athenian Stranger and Clinias distinguish between "injury" and "damage" to refine the legal code. They are moving from a general discussion of law to the specific psychological motivations behind criminal acts.</meta>

FOLIO 352.

### ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS IN LATIN, DIALOGUE IX.

...in some way appropriately, or whether it was imposed contrary [to nature]. **CLINIAS.** You seem to us to speak rightly, guest. For we must do one of two things: either not say that no injuries are done willingly, or, before we proceed to other matters, explain how that is rightly said. **ATHENIAN.** I will by no means allow either of these—namely, to deny what I think to be the case. Nor would it be consistent with my duty, nor pious. But let us try to open up how these two things differ—that which is done willingly and that which is done unwillingly—and in what other way they might differ. **CLINIAS.** Certainly, guest, we cannot understand these things in any other way. **ATHENIAN.** It shall be done. Come then, do not many damages and inconveniences occur among citizens in their dealings and customs, in which the "voluntary" and "involuntary" seem to abound? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** But let no one, though he considers inconveniences and harms to be injuries, believe that there is a double injury within them: one committed involuntarily, the other voluntarily. For damages of all kinds done involuntarily are not fewer, in number or magnitude, than those done voluntarily. But consider, I pray, whether I shall next bring forward something true, or nothing at all. For I, O Clinias and Megillus, if someone harms another unwillingly, I will call him an "unwilling harmer," but I will not, for that reason, place this in the laws as if it were an "involuntary injury"; <note>The Athenian is making a technical distinction between *damnum* (harm/loss) and *iniuria* (legal/moral injustice). A person can cause loss without being "unjust."</note> rather, I will say it is no injury at all, whether it be greater or smaller. Often, too, we say that he who has conferred a benefit incorrectly is committing an injustice, if this is not done rightly. For almost always, my friends, whether someone gives something or takes something away, it is not right that he be called "just" or "unjust" so simply. Therefore, the legislator must not look at that alone, but at whether someone benefits or hinders another with a virtuous character and a just manner: the legislator must look at these two things, I say—at the injury and the harm. Thus, he should lead each person back to an unharmed and whole state as much as possible: restoring what was lost, raising up again what has fallen, and repairing what was killed or wounded. He must always strive so that discords stirred up by harms are reduced to friendship through the laws. **CLINIAS.** Those things are spoken excellently. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, unjust damages and gains—if by chance any profit follows from an injury—must be cured like diseases of the soul, provided they are curable. Let the cure for injustice lead to this point. **CLINIAS.** To what point? **ATHENIAN.** So that whoever has committed injuries, whether great or small, may be corrected through doctrine and law; and let him be compelled altogether so that either he never again dares to commit such a thing willingly, or does so much more rarely, having been deterred by the imposition of a penalty. Indeed, we say it is the duty of the best laws to so instruct the souls of men that they hate injustice and either love the nature of justice or, at least, do not hate it—whether the legislator achieves this through deeds or words, through pleasure or pain, through honor or infamy, or by fining money, or by gifts, or by any other way. But those whom the legislator perceives to be incurable, <margin>Those who are incurable: for these it is better to die than to live.</margin> he shall affect with the ultimate punishment <note>Original: *vltimo supplicio*—referring to the death penalty.</note>, knowing well that it would be better for those who are incurable to die than to live; and if they are deprived of life, they benefit others in two ways. For by their example, others are deterred from sin, and the city itself is cleansed of wicked men. For this reason, the maker of the law will punish incurable men with death, but others not at all. **CLINIAS.** These things seem to be spoken by you quite moderately. But we would gladly hear you speak more clearly again on the difference between "injury" and "damage," and how they occur willingly and unwillingly. **ATHENIAN.** I will try both to do and to say as you command. It is indeed agreed: as you often say when discussing the soul among yourselves, that one affection or part exists in it by nature, which we call anger <note>Original: *iracundia*—the spirited part of the soul (thumos).</note>, a contentious and difficult thing, which overthrows many things by inconsiderate force. **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** Moreover, we do not say pleasure is the same as anger, but that it rules from a contrary power; it compels through both persuasion and a certain violent deception, so that you do whatever it wishes. **CLINIAS.** Very much so. **ATHENIAN.** Whoever places ignorance as a third cause of sinning will not err. But the legislator will be better if he distinguishes this into two parts: he will set one as simple ignorance, and the other as double. He will judge simple ignorance to be the cause of light sins; but he will call it "double" when someone is held not only by ignorance, but also inflated by an opinion of wisdom—thinking he knows perfectly those things which he is entirely ignorant of. If this [double ignorance] achieves strength and vigor, he will judge it to be the cause of immense and most shameful crimes; but if it is weighed down by weakness, he will think the sins proceeding from it—such as those of children or the elderly—are indeed sins, and he will prescribe laws for them as sins, but the mildest of all, full of much mercy and indulgence. **CLINIAS.** That is fair. **ATHENIAN.** Concerning pleasure and anger, we almost all agree that some men conquer them and others are conquered by them. And so it is altogether. **CLINIAS.** Precisely so. **ATHENIAN.** But we have never heard that some surpass ignorance and others are surpassed by it. **CLINIAS.** You tell the truth. **ATHENIAN.** We say that each of these things seizes a man for itself, often pulled toward contrary things at once. **CLINIAS.** Indeed, very often. **ATHENIAN.** Now I will explain to you clearly and without any ambiguity what I call "just" and what I call "unjust." For the tyranny of anger and fear, of pleasure and pain, and of envy and desire in the soul—whether it causes harm or not—I call injustice altogether. But the opinion of the best, by which reason a city or individuals think something [to be good]—if it dominates the soul and adorns every man, even if something succeeds less rightly for him—I call justice. And whatever is done from there, I call just; and those who willingly obey this kind of leadership, I judge to live best. Many people think that kind of damage is an "involuntary injury." But we do not contend over vocabulary. However, since three types of sins have been mentioned, these must first be repeated more diligently in memory. We judge one type to be of pain, which we call anger and fear. **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** Again, another of pleasure and desires. And the third type is the longing and desire for hope and true opinion about the best. When these are divided again into two parts, they make five types; the laws, differing among themselves, must be placed in five types within two categories. **CLINIAS.** What are those categories? **ATHENIAN.** One which is committed by force and openly; the other which is committed secretly and with deception in the shadows. And sometimes it is done in both ways. Because if by right... <note>The text ends mid-sentence with the catchword "Qz si iure rra" (Because if by right...).</note>

**Vocabulary:** 
- **Injustice** (*iniuria*): Moral or legal wrongdoing.
- **Harm/Damage** (*damnum*): Physical or financial loss, distinguished here from moral intent.
- **Legislator** (*legislator*): The maker of laws who acts as a "physician of the soul."
- **Justice** (*iustitia*): The internal rule of reason and "the best opinion."
- **Anger** (*ira*): A spirited, often violent, impulse of the soul.
- **Pleasure** (*voluptas*): A seductive force that leads the soul toward its desires.
- **Ignorance** (*ignorantia*): A lack of knowledge, divided here into "simple" (not knowing) and "double" (thinking one knows when one does not).
- **Sin/Fault** (*peccatum*): An error or crime arising from psychological causes.
- **Soul** (*anima*): The seat of human character and the target of legal correction.

<summary>This page explores the philosophical causes of crime, distinguishing between mere "harm" (accidental loss) and "injustice" (intentional wrongdoing). The Athenian Stranger argues that the law should act as a medicine to heal the soul from the "tyranny" of anger, pleasure, and ignorance.</summary>
<keywords>justice vs. injustice, harm vs. injury, voluntary action, involuntary action, psychology of crime, anger, pleasure, double ignorance, capital punishment, Marsilio Ficino, Plato's Laws</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Book IX of Plato’s Laws. The previous page established a philosophical distinction between "harm" (the physical damage done) and "injury" (the legal and moral injustice intended). Here, the Athenian Stranger begins to apply these principles to specific criminal cases, moving from crimes of madness to various forms of homicide.</meta>

PAGE XXXIII.

# BOOK NINE.

...will be handled, and constrained by the harshest laws. **CLINIAS.** That is fair. **ATHENIAN.** But let us return now to where we digressed: let us apply ourselves to defining the laws. Our purpose was to discuss those guilty of sacrilege, traitors, and those who corrupt the laws by changing the state. Perhaps someone will commit one of these acts due to madness, or because they are weighed down by illness or old age, or because they are in the age of childhood, so that they differ in no way from the aforementioned. If it is declared to the chosen judges that such a person has done this, and if the judge, based on the report of the defender, decides the person was so affected when they committed the act, let the perpetrator restore the simple damage they caused <note>original: "damnum... simplex"; in legal terms, this means the person pays back only the exact value of what was lost, without additional punitive fines.</note>; let the other penalties be remitted, unless a person has been killed and the world is not yet cleansed from the slaughter <note>The Greeks believed that a killing created a "miasma" or spiritual pollution that had to be ritually purified, regardless of the killer's intent or mental state.</note>. For in such a case, the person must go elsewhere and live as an exile for a year. And if he returns before the time established by law has passed, or is caught within the borders, let him be kept in public prison for two years by the guardians of the laws; after this, let him be free from chains.

But as we began, let us write the laws regarding every kind of slaughter more absolutely. And first, let us speak of those things done by force and not of one's own will. If someone in a public contest or in the gymnasiums unintentionally kills a friend—whether death follows immediately or later from the wounds—or similarly in war, or in military exercises established by the magistrates (whether with naked bodies or armed in imitation of true war), let him be ritually clean <note>original: "mundus"; meaning free from the religious "stain" of blood-guilt.</note> according to the law brought from Delphic Apollo. Likewise, all doctors who unintentionally kill those they are treating are clean. 

But if anyone kills someone with his own hand unintentionally—whether with his bare body, or a tool, or a weapon, or by food or drink, or by the application of fire or cold, or by the waves of the sea, or by deprivation of breath, whether he does this with his own body or by some other thing—let him be considered the killer with his own hand in every way, and let him be punished as I shall say. If he kills another's slave, thinking him to be his own, let him restore the damage to the master or pay double the price. The judges shall determine how much the slave was worth. Let him use more and greater purifications than the one who killed someone in a contest. The suitable interpreters for these rites shall be those whom the oracle of the god has approved. If, however, he kills his own slave, let him be acquitted after being purified according to the law. 

But if someone kills a free man unintentionally, let him use the same purifications as the one who killed a slave. And let him not despise the ancient mystery. For it is said <note>Plato is referencing traditional Greek religious beliefs about the "Erinyes" or vengeful spirits of the dead.</note> that a man who lived freely and was killed by violence is angry at the killer in the time immediately following death; being full of terror and confusion because of his violent end, he is said to terrify and disturb the killer and his actions with all his might, especially if he sees the killer living in his usual way among his own people, memory supplying the force for this. Therefore, it is necessary for the homicide, for the sake of the killed man, to be an exile from his fatherland for a full year, and to lead his life far from every part of that region. If the one who died was a foreigner, let the homicide be expelled from the foreigner's homeland as well for the period of a year. 

If the killer obeys this law, let the next of kin to the deceased, who shall watch whether he obeys, grant him pardon; that relative shall then be reconciled and entirely fair toward him. But if the killer does not obey, and while he is still impure dares to visit the temples of the gods and offer sacrifice, or if he will not go into exile for the entire established time, let the next of kin to the deceased report this to the judges, accuse him of the slaughter, and take double all the punishments from him. If that kinsman neglects to do this, it is as if the crime has recoiled upon him—the deceased, of course, turning his suffering upon the kinsman—and let him be accused by anyone who wishes and be forced to be absent from his fatherland for five years. 

If a foreigner unintentionally kills a foreigner in the city, let anyone who wishes report it to the judges under the same law, and let it be judged similarly. But if a resident alien <term>incola: a non-citizen living in the city, often called a "metic"</term> does this, let him be in exile for one year. But if a foreigner kills another foreigner, or a resident, or a citizen, let him be an exile for his entire life from the whole region in which these laws hold power, in addition to the purification. And if he returns contrary to the laws, let him be punished with death by the guardians of the laws, and if he possesses any goods, let them be handed over to the next of kin of the deceased. But if someone is carried into that region unintentionally—perhaps driven by the force of a storm and the waves of the sea—let him wait until the opportunity for sailing arises while keeping his feet in the sea <note>This is a legal loophole: by standing in the surf, he is technically not "on the land" from which he is exiled.</note>; or if he is brought by land by others, he must be released by the magistrate to whom the matter was first reported and sent back into exile untouched. 

If someone kills a free man with his own hand, stirred by anger <note>original: "ira"; this marks the transition from purely accidental death to "crimes of passion."</note>, it is necessary first to distinguish anger into two parts. For he acts through anger who kills suddenly without the will to kill, through blows or in any other way, so that repentance follows immediately after the impulse; and he also acts through anger who, provoked by insult or injury, persists in the desire for revenge and later kills willingly, and does not repent of having done so. It pleases us, therefore, to establish a double form of slaughter, both done in anger. I would rightly place these as midway between voluntary and involuntary actions. For neither is truly voluntary or truly involuntary, but each is an image of the other. For he who preserves his anger and takes revenge later with treachery is very similar to a voluntary homicide. But he who does not preserve it but is carried away by the first impulse of anger and kills without premeditation is judged similar to an involuntary homicide. However, he is not entirely involuntary, but is said to have the likeness of the involuntary. 

Wherefore, slaughters committed through anger are difficult to define: whether they should be placed among the voluntary or the contrary. The best and truest opinion, therefore, is to call both of them "images" and to distinguish them separately, so that one is said to be committed with deliberation and the other without deliberation. It is fitting to impose greater punishments on those who killed through anger with deliberation; and for those, on the contrary, who did so suddenly and without deliberation, lighter ones. Truly, that which is similar to a heavier evil must be punished more harshly, and that which is similar to a lighter evil, more mildly. Certainly, our laws must act in this way. **CLINIAS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** But repeating again regarding anger, let us say this: If someone kills a free man with his own hand, stirred by anger without deliberation, he ought to suffer the other evils that a homicide who did not kill through anger suffers, but he shall be an exile for two full years to restrain his anger. But he who kills a free man through anger but with treachery, let him be forced to do all other things similarly to the first. However, let him be in exile not for only two years like the other, but for three, so that his anger, being more lasting, may be punished longer. Let this be the general arrangement of these matters. For it is difficult to set laws for these things individually and exactly. For sometimes a slaughter that is established by law as more savage seems lighter; and sometimes, on the contrary, that which is lighter seems more savage, being either more atrocious or...

<summary>This page outlines the legal and ritual consequences for various forms of homicide, distinguishing between accidental death, deaths in sport or war, and killings motivated by different types of anger. Plato emphasizes the need for ritual purification and varying terms of exile to appease the spirit of the deceased and the community's sense of justice.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the legal discussion from Book IX of Plato's Laws. Having previously discussed crimes committed in madness, the Athenian Stranger now transitions to specific regulations regarding homicide—distinguishing between killings motivated by sudden anger, those committed in self-defense, and those committed through premeditated greed.</meta>

DE LEGIBUS, OR THE DIALOGUES ON THE LAWS. BOOK IX. FOLIO 353.
T
<meta>catchword: by his own hand</meta>

...was carried out more mildly. But for the most part, these things happen as we just said. However, the guardians of the laws will recognize all these things. When the time for the restoration of exiles arrives, let them send twelve men to the borders of the region: who, having diligently considered all the actions of the exiles during that time, shall become the judges of their sense of shame and their worthiness for reception. These exiles shall then submit to the judgment of these magistrates. If, after restoration, either of these individuals, moved by anger, commits a crime against a family member, let him be exiled forever. And if he returns again, let him be punished in no other way than as a returning traveler who has violated his banishment.

If anyone kills his own slave in this manner <note>Plato distinguishes between the property loss of a slave and the spiritual pollution caused by the act of killing itself.</note>, let him undergo ritual purification. If he kills another person's slave, let him restore the damage twofold to the owner. If any murderer does not obey the laws, but, not yet purified, contaminates the forum, the gymnasia, and other sacred places by his entry, let whoever wishes summon both this man and the relative of the slain who is negligent in pursuing the case to court; let the court compel him to pay twofold in both money and other penalties; and let the person who brought the suit receive the payment according to the law.

If a slave, moved by anger, kills his own master, let the relatives of the deceased kill the slave in whatever way they wish, and they shall be clear of the crime, provided they do not keep him alive. But if a slave kills not his own master but another free man in a fit of anger, let him be handed over by his owner to the relatives of the deceased, who may kill him in any way they wish.

If a father or mother—which happens rarely—kills a son or daughter in anger, whether by striking them or in any other way, let them be purified just as other murderers are, and let them be exiled for three years. After the restoration itself, let the husband and wife be separated from one another. They shall no longer work together to procreate children, nor shall either of them live in the same house as the person whose child or brother they killed, nor shall they share in the sacred rites with them. He who, through an impious spirit, does not obey these laws may be accused of impiety by anyone who wishes. 

If a husband kills his wife, or a wife her husband, in a fit of anger, let them be purified in a similar manner and be exiled for three full years. When such a person returns, they shall not share in the sacred rites with their children, nor shall they eat at the same table. If the parent or child does not observe this, they may be accused of impiety by anyone who wishes. If a brother kills a brother or sister, or a sister kills a sister or brother in anger, let them undergo purification and exile in no other way than the parents who killed their children; nor, after their return, shall they share in the sacred rites or the table with those whom they have deprived of brothers, sisters, or children. Whoever transgresses this law shall be rightfully condemned as impious.

But if someone is so overcome by anger that he kills a parent in an insane fury of wrath—if the parent, before dying, voluntarily freed his killer from the slaughter <note>original: "a caede liberavit"; this refers to a dying person's legal right to forgive their attacker, which waived the state's requirement for a murder trial, though ritual purification was still required.</note>, let the killer be clean once he has been purified like those who commit involuntary homicide. But if the parent did not free him, the one who killed is guilty under many laws. For he shall be subject to the ultimate punishments for murder, impiety, and sacrilege, because he has stolen the soul of the one who gave him life. Therefore, if it were possible for a man to die multiple times, it would be most just for a parricide to be killed multiple times. For if no law allows a man to kill the parents who brought him into the light even in his own self-defense if they should attack him, but instead commands him to endure all things rather than do such a deed, how else should such a man be justly punished? Therefore, let death be the sanctioned penalty for one who kills a parent in anger.

If an uprising occurs, or if in any way a brother kills a brother who is attacking him in self-defense, let him be pure as if he had killed an enemy. Likewise, if a citizen kills a citizen, or a stranger a stranger, or a citizen a stranger (or vice versa) while defending himself, let him be similarly clean. The same applies if a slave kills a slave. But if a slave kills a free man in self-defense, let him be subject to the same laws as a parricide. 

Furthermore, let what we said about being freed from the slaughter of a parent be understood as applying to all others as well. If anyone, therefore, voluntarily forgives any of the others, let the one who killed be purified as if the slaughter were committed involuntarily, and let him be exiled for one year. 

We have now moderately set forth the matters regarding violent, involuntary, and anger-motivated slaughter. Next, let us speak of those murders committed voluntarily out of total injustice, through treachery, because of the tyranny of pleasures, desires, and envy.

**CLINIAS.** You speak rightly.

**ATHENIAN.** First, therefore, let us declare as far as we can how many causes of voluntary murder there are. The greatest cause is cupidity <note>original: "cupiditas"; here meaning an uncontrolled desire for material wealth or pleasure.</note>, which dominates a soul agitated by lusts; this is most present in that heat which violently inflames many minds. This is truly the force which, due to nature and an ignorance of riches, begets an insatiable greed. The cause of this ignorance is that riches are not correctly praised. Indeed, both Greeks and barbarians place riches in the first rank of goods, when they actually hold the third place <note>Plato’s hierarchy of goods: 1. Virtues of the Soul, 2. Health and Beauty of the Body, 3. External goods/Wealth.</note>; by this opinion, they betray both themselves and their descendants. We would live most excellently and beautifully if the true opinion about wealth were preached everywhere: which is, that wealth is for the sake of the body, and the body for the sake of the soul. Therefore, since those goods for whose sake wealth is possessed are superior, wealth will hold the third rank after the virtue of the soul and the body. 

This reasoning, therefore, will teach us as a mistress that a man who is to be happy must not seek riches by any means whatsoever, but only with justice and temperance. In this way, no murders would be committed in cities that require further murders as punishment. But as we said at the beginning of this discussion, this is one, and the greatest, cause that leads to the heaviest punishments for voluntary slaughter. The second cause is the habit of an ambitious soul, from which envies are born—firstly, a grim envy within the envious person themselves, and then against the leading citizens of the state. The third place is held by great and unjust fears: which give birth to many murders, when someone has done things, or is currently doing things, of which they would want no one to be aware. Therefore, they remove from the midst by death those who seem likely to reveal such things.

Let all these things we have said serve as preambles; and furthermore, let us consider the discourse which many of those who study sacred rites hear and believe: that murderers are punished in the underworld, and returning here, they necessarily pay the penalties owed by nature. Indeed, they are forced to endure a similar fate in this life from others, just as they did to others. If someone is persuaded by this and, warned by such a preamble, fears such punishments, there is no need to set a law for him; but for the man of the opposite disposition, let this law be written: Whoever by design kills his fellow citizen with his own hand...

<summary>This page details the legal penalties for various forms of homicide in Plato's ideal state, categorizing them by the relationship between the parties and the motivation (anger vs. premeditation). It establishes a hierarchy of goods, placing the soul above wealth, to explain why greed leads to the most punishable forms of murder.</summary>

# BOOK IX.
### PAGE 34.
<meta>catchword: comes, p</meta>

...if anyone should kill another with their own hand <note>original: "propria manu"; this refers to direct, physical homicide as opposed to instigating a murder</note> through injustice, first, let him be kept far away from temples, the marketplace, the ports, and every common gathering, lest his presence pollute these places. This applies whether someone has formally banned him or if no such order has been given. For the Law itself forbids him, and by this prohibition, it is seen to forbid him forever on behalf of the entire state. Furthermore, if the relatives of the deceased—from cousins down to first cousins—do not pursue the case as is proper, or do not bar him from these places, let the first crime and the hatred of the gods turn upon them, just as the common curse and malediction of the law dictates. Then, the culprit shall be liable to anyone who wishes to avenge the slain. 

Whoever wishes to prosecute, once he has performed all the duties established by God regarding the observance of cleansing the crime or any other necessary acts—and once he has made the required proclamations—let him proceed and compel the murderer to pay the penalty according to the law. The legislator can easily persuade the citizens that these things must be done through prayers and sacrifices to the gods who ensure that killings do not occur in cities. But as to who the masters of these rites are, and how these judgments may best be carried out according to the mind of God, let the **guardians of the laws** declare this along with the interpreters and soothsayers <note>original: "aruspicibus"; these were religious officials who interpreted the will of the gods through omens</note>, and so arrange the judgments and penalties. Indeed, let those who have been given authority to punish sacrilege be the judges of these matters. 

Whoever is condemned shall pay the penalty with death. And because he has sinned not only impiously but also shamelessly, he must not be buried in the region of the person he killed. If he flees and does not stand trial, let him be an exile forever. And if he is ever caught within the borders, the first relative of the slain or citizen who encounters him may kill him with impunity, or deliver him bound to the magistrates to be executed by the judges of this matter. If anyone comes forward to defend him, he must provide bail for the one he protects; let him provide three such sureties as the judges themselves deem sufficient, who promise to present him for trial. If anyone is unwilling or unable to do this, let him be held bound by the magistrates to be reserved for judgment. 

However, if someone kills a person not by their own hand but by their will, counsel, and treachery <note>original: "consilio, insidiisque"; this distinguishes the mastermind or "accessory before the fact" from the physical killer</note>—and though he is the cause of the slaughter and is impure in spirit, he lives in the city—let him be punished similarly when condemned. However, he shall not be required to provide sureties, and though condemned, he shall not be deprived of his own burial. Other matters regarding him should be handled as we said of the previous case. These same rules were established for foreigners against foreigners, and for citizens and foreigners against each other, and for slaves against slaves, regarding murder committed by one's own hand or by counsel and treachery—except that we judge these individuals must provide bail just like those who kill with their own hand. 

If a slave voluntarily kills a freedman, whether by his own hand or by counsel, and is condemned, let him be dragged by the public officer and avenger to the tomb of the slain man, or to a place from which it can be seen. There, let him be beaten as the judge who convicted him commands; if he survives this, let him be beaten until he dies. If anyone, fearing a slave might reveal some shameful deed he has done, or induced by some other such cause, puts that slave to death, let him be punished as if he had killed a citizen. 

Sometimes things happen for which it is difficult and troublesome to establish laws, yet impossible not to. Of this sort are the voluntary and unjust killings of relatives, whether by one's own hand or by counsel and treachery, which occur most often in ill-governed cities, but sometimes even where you would not believe it. To avoid these crimes, the previous discourse should be repeated. For perhaps, having heard these things, someone will abstain from the most wicked slaughter. 

For the **fable**—or speech, or whatever name the discourse should be called—was clearly spoken by the priests of old: that Justice is a watcher and avenger of all things, using the law we just mentioned to avenge kindred blood. Namely, she has established that whoever commits such a deed must necessarily suffer the same. Thus, if someone has put his father to death, he himself must later, at certain times, be violently killed by his own children. If he has killed his mother, he himself must later participate in the female nature <note>A reference to the Platonic/Pythagorean concept of reincarnation, where the soul is reborn in a body that allows for the repayment of cosmic debts</note> and necessarily be slain at last by his own children. For when common blood is stained, there is no other purification, nor can the stain be wiped away in any other way, unless the wicked soul cleanses the slaughter with a similar slaughter, and thus satisfies the wrath of the entire kin group. 

Therefore, men must be restrained from these crimes by the fear of such punishments inflicted by the gods. If any, however, should fall into such miserable calamity as to dare to deprive a father, mother, brother, or child of life voluntarily and with intent: the mortal legislator shall act regarding such a crime in this way. Let them be barred from public sacrificial places as was said above, and let them similarly require sureties. And he who is condemned for such a killing shall be put to death by the ministers of the judges and the magistrates. Let him be dragged outside the city to a designated three-way crossroad <note>original: "triuiū"; crossroads were often associated with Hecate and the disposal of polluted objects</note> naked; there, let each of the magistrates, on behalf of the entire city, cast a stone at the head of the dead man, and thus let them purify the whole city. Finally, having been carried beyond the borders of the region, let them cast him out unburied according to the laws. 

But what should be judged of him who betrays his closest and dearest friend with slaughter? I speak of him who deprives himself of life and the lot of the fates by a wicked force—not by the judgment of the state, nor compelled by a sad and inevitable accident of fortune, nor forced by some extreme shame, but through the cowardice and weakness of a fearful soul, unjustly bringing death upon himself? What purifications and what burial are appropriate for such a man by law, God himself knows. Nevertheless, let his closest kin inquire about these things from the interpreters and the laws of these matters, and let them do as has been established by them. Let a solitary burial be made for these men, where no one else is buried. Then, let them be buried in those places which are the most remote, deserted, and nameless among the twelve parts of the region; let them be so obscure that the graves are marked by neither a statue nor an inscribed name. 

If a beast of burden or another animal kills a man, unless it did so in a public contest, let the relatives of the slain man bring it before the judges. Let the wardens of the fields, to whom the relative has entrusted the matter, judge it, and let them kill the condemned animal outside the borders of the region. If an inanimate object—excluding a lightning bolt or another weapon sent from heaven—should deprive a person of life by falling upon them or they upon it, let the relative of the slain man appoint the nearest neighbor as a judge for this purpose. Let him perform these and other things as is appropriate toward the dead man himself, for the expiation of himself and his entire kin. As for what has been condemned, as was said of the animals...

# ON THE LAWS, OR THE DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS. DIALOGUE IX. FOLIO 354.

<sig>T ii</sig>

...is, let him be cast out. If anyone is found deprived of life and the murderer is unknown, and cannot be found despite a diligent search, let the same proclamations be made as in other cases: and let it be proclaimed publicly in the square <note>original: "scōnio," likely referring to a public platform or gathering place</note> that whoever killed this or 그 person is guilty of slaughter and must not enter sacred places, and must leave the entire region. For if he is caught, he shall be put to death and cast out unburied beyond the borders of the country. Therefore, let this be our primary law established concerning slaughter. 

And enough on these matters. Now let us speak of those cases in which the one who kills is considered "clean" <note>original: "mundus," meaning ritually and legally pure or guiltless</note>. He who kills a thief entering his house at night shall be clean. Likewise, he who kills a plunderer in his own defense. And he who kills one who has by force subjected a free woman or a boy to sexual acts <note>original: "rem veneream," literally "the matter of Venus"</note> shall go unpunished; such a predator may be deprived of life not only by the victim of the violence, but also by the victim's father, brothers, or sons. Also, if a husband kills a man committing violence against his wife, he shall be clean by law. Furthermore, if anyone kills someone while bringing aid to a father (who is by no means committing a crime), or to a mother, or to children, brothers, or a spouse, he shall be clean. 

Thus far we have written laws concerning the education and discipline of the living soul—which, if it follows what was said before, it may live; but if otherwise, it should not live. Moreover, we have spoken of violent slaughters and how they are to be punished. Also, enough was said previously concerning the nutrition and discipline of the body. Next, let us determine to the best of our ability what the violent actions are, both voluntary and involuntary, how many there are, and by what punishments they may be suitably restrained. For these are rightly treated after the previous matters. For a humble lawmaker will place laws regarding wounds and mutilations after those regarding slaughter. These are distinguished just as slaughters are. For some occur unwillingly, some through anger, some through fear, and some voluntarily and by design. 

Let the beginning of all such things be as follows. It is necessary to establish laws for men so that they may live according to those laws. For if they lived without them, they would differ in no way from the most savage beasts. The cause of this is that no man’s nature is so naturally constituted that he can sufficiently know what is beneficial for the public good of human life, and even if he knows what is best, that he is always able and willing to act upon it. 

<margin>The public good connects cities, while private interest destroys them.</margin>

For first, it is difficult to know that the civil and true art must necessarily care not for the private, but for the public interest. For the public good connects and joins cities together, while private interest dissipates them. It is better for both the public and the private if the common good is well-disposed rather than the private. Secondly, even if someone should perhaps know through art that this is so, if he should hold the power of the city with such license that he is subject to no account of reason, he could never remain in that mindset throughout his whole life—to increase the public good in the city as the chief good, and to place the private after the public. Instead, his mortal nature will always drive him toward his own utility and private convenience, for without reason it flees pain as much as it pursues pleasure. It will prefer both of these to what is more just and better, and being shrouded in darkness, it will eventually fill itself and the entire city with all manner of evils. 

To be sure, if any man were endowed by the favor of a divine lot with such a nature that he recognized the public good and generously and always intended toward it, he would need no laws to rule him. For no law and no order is better or more excellent than knowledge; nor is it right for the mind to be subjected to or serve anyone. Rather, if it is truly free, it should rule over all things. But now, such a nature is found nowhere, or at least only a tiny trace of it appears. For this reason, it is proper to choose the second-best thing: order and law, which look upon the majority of cases, though they cannot see everything. 

But with these principles proposed, let us now establish what he who has wounded another or harmed them in some other way ought to suffer or pay. For it is easy for anyone to correctly understand the details of such things: whether someone has wounded another, or not; whom; in what part; and in what manner. For these details are almost innumerable and differ greatly from one another. To commit all these to a court's judgment, or to commit none of them, is impossible. Indeed, one thing must be committed to the court in all cases: whether each of these acts was done or not. Furthermore, it is impossible to commit nothing regarding the fine for the injury to the law, but rather it is impossible to determine every large and small fine by law alone. 

How, therefore, should we speak after this? 

**The Athenian:** Thus: that a legislator ought to concede some things to the judgment of the court, but other things he ought not; he himself must determine them. However, so that he may understand which things are to be left to the judgment and prudence of the judges, and which are to be determined by the law-giver himself, we shall explain it thus. A grave plague, common to the entire city, is born there where the courts are lazy and silent, where the opinions of the judges remain hidden, and they deliver their sentences in secret. But it is even harsher when the proceedings are not done in silence, but like theaters they ring with shouting, and orators now praise, now blame, and thus decide by turns. If anyone is forced by some necessity to give laws to such courts, we consider him unfortunate. But he who is compelled to give them should commit only the smallest fines to such judges, and should himself declare the most and greatest matters in the laws he brings. 

But where the courts are correctly constituted according to one's strength, and the judges are well-educated and approved with all diligence, many things concerning the punishment and the condition of the condemned can most rightly be committed to the judges. Therefore, let no one accuse us if we do not now ordain the greatest and most numerous things by laws—things which even less-educated judges could see—and assign a fine and punishment worthy of each crime. Since we hope that those for whom we write these laws will not be unrefined judges of these matters, we believe many things should be committed to them. But what we have often said and done in previous sections—thinking that by the description and form of the punishments mentioned, examples should be given to the judges which they should never transgress—that was rightly done then, and we wish to observe it now as well, returning again to the bringing of laws. 

Regarding wounds, therefore, let us decree thus: If anyone should will and plan to kill a friendly man from among those whom the law protects, but should only wound him and not be able to kill him, we would compel him to undergo the punishment for slaughter with all mercy removed, just as if he had deprived him of life—unless we were to respect his fortune and his not-entirely wicked guiding spirit <note>original: "demonē," referring to a *daemon* or protective spirit</note>. This spirit, following both the wounded and the wounder with mercy, stood in the way of the misfortune of both, and prevented a lethal wound for the one, and an execrable calamity of fortune for the other. To this spirit, therefore, we shall be grateful; and by its benefit, we shall...

# BOOK IX. PAGE 34.
<header>THE BOOK</header>

...from him who committed the wounding, we shall withhold the punishment of death. Instead, we shall decree that he be exiled for the duration of his life to a neighboring city. He shall not be deprived of the use of any of his goods; however, the damage must first be restored to the wounded party, provided the injury caused a loss, as determined by the court in this matter. Moreover, the judges shall be the same ones who would have presided over a case of slaughter <note>original: "caedis," referring to homicide</note> if the wounded person had died. If a son should intentionally wound his parents, or a slave his master, and is convicted of having done so, let him pay for the crime with death. Furthermore, if a brother wounds a brother or sister in a similar way, or a sister a sister or brother, or if a wife wounds her husband with the intent to kill, or a husband his wife, let that person be exiled forever. If they have sons or daughters who are still children, let guardians administer the family property of the exile so that they may protect the orphans. But if they are adults, let them be permitted to possess the property themselves, though they shall not be compelled to support the exile.

If, however, someone without children should fall into such a calamity, let his kinsmen—even unto second cousins <note>original: "sobrinos cosobrinosque," referring to the extended family circle</note> on both the male and female sides—meet together. In consultation with the Guardians of the Laws <term>Guardians of the Laws: "Legum custodes," high-ranking magistrates in Plato's ideal city responsible for maintaining the legal code</term> and the priests, they shall establish an heir for this house of the exile from among the five thousand and forty households of the city. In this matter, they must surely consider this: that no house among the five thousand and forty belongs more to the inhabitant himself or his lineage than it belongs to the city, both privately and publicly. It is necessary, above all, that the city possess houses that are as holy and happy as possible. 

Therefore, whenever a house is defiled by some misfortune or impiety—either because the one who possessed it died without children, or was convicted of voluntary slaughter or any crime against the gods or citizens for which the penalty is death or eternal exile—first, let the house itself be purified according to the law. Then, let the relatives, as we said, meeting with the Guardians of the Laws, seek out some most excellent and fortunate family in the city in which there are many young men. They shall adopt one of these as a son for the father of that failing house and for his ancestors. Finally, they shall pray that this heir will be a propagator of offspring under happier auspices for the father of the family, a successor to the house, and a caretaker of the sacred rites and all other things. Thus, they shall finally establish him as the heir according to the law. As for the one who sinned, let him lie without a name, without children, and without any portion of the inheritance, seeing that he is oppressed by such calamities. 

However, a boundary is not always joined directly to another boundary in all things. For where there is some common border, there is a middle ground between the boundaries of things. And indeed, between those sins which are committed voluntarily and those committed involuntarily, we have said that what is done through anger <note>original: "per iram," suggesting a crime of passion rather than cold premeditation</note> is such a thing. Therefore, for the one convicted of a wound made in anger: if the outcome shows the wound was curable, he shall restore double the damage. But if it is incurable, he shall restore fourfold. If it is curable but brings great shame and disfigurement upon the wounded person, he shall pay fourfold. 

But if someone not only harmed the wounded person but also injured the fatherland—by depriving it of a soldier <note>original: "milite," a citizen-soldier</note> to face the enemy—let him be punished similarly. Moreover, let him restore the loss to the city: in addition to the military service he himself owes, he shall perform military service for the wounded man, doing whatever that man was supposed to do in war. If he does not do this, let him be guilty according to the law to anyone who wishes to accuse him of neglecting military duty; and let him restore double, triple, or quadruple the damage, as it shall seem fit to the judges. 

If a full brother wounds a full brother in like manner, let the tribesmen and kinsmen, even unto second cousins from both the male and female sides, both men and women, meet to judge him. They shall hand him over to his parents so that they may punish him according to nature. But if the punishment is disputed, let the relatives on the father's side decide. If they themselves cannot, let them finally bring the case to the Guardians of the Laws. If children or grandchildren have done such a thing to their parents, let only those who have passed their sixtieth year judge—those who have biological, not adopted, children. And let the convicted person be punished either by death or by some greater, or not much lesser, punishment; and let no one of his own lineage judge him, even if they have reached the age prescribed by law. 

But if a slave, moved by anger, wounds a free man, let him be handed over by his master to the wounded man so that he may avenge the injury at his own discretion; unless the master wishes to recover the loss himself. But if anyone suspects that the slave's act and the wounding were done through a malicious conspiracy, let him bring it to the judges. If he does not prove it to be so, he shall restore triple the damage; but if he does prove it, he shall hold the one who acted deceitfully with the slave guilty of enslavement. He who wounds someone involuntarily shall simply pay the damage. Indeed, no lawgiver can hope to control fortune. However, let there be judges who—just as with children and grandchildren toward parents—shall declare how much the damage was. 

All the passions we have spoken of are violent. Every kind of striking is also violent. It is necessary, therefore, for all people—women and men alike, young and old—to always think of these things in this way: that an elder is to be preferred to younger people by a significant interval, both before the gods and before men who intend to live happily. Therefore, for an elder to be struck by a younger person is both shameful and hated by the gods. It is proper for a youth struck by an elder to bear it patiently out of reverence for old age. Let us do so, therefore. Let anyone honor an elder both in deed and in word. And if someone is twenty years older, let him revere him as a father if he is a man, or as a mother if she is a woman. And thus, let him always abstain from striking all who are of an age that they could have fathered or birthed him, fearing the gods of birth. I say he should abstain not only from a citizen but even from an elder foreigner. 

As for a foreigner who dares to strike a citizen: if anyone thinks he should be punished for being struck, let him lead him to the tribunes of the people <note>original: "tribunos plebis," here referring to city magistrates</note>; but he must not strike him himself, so that he may all the more abstain from striking his own citizens when he restrains himself even from foreigners. Likewise for a foreigner or a traveler: let him not dare to strike him with blows, neither in attacking nor in defending himself. In this case, let the magistrate, fearing the God of Hospitality <note>original: "hospitalem deum," referring to Zeus Xenios</note>, inquire diligently into the matter. If a foreigner has unjustly struck a citizen, let him be given just as many lashes with a public whip, so that he may not dare such a thing again with such impudence. But if the foreigner appears innocent, they shall dismiss both, having chastised with threats the one who brought him there. 

Equals may strike equals—or those slightly older but not yet fathers, or old man against old man, or youth against youth—in striking them with blows, let them defend themselves with naked hands according to nature. But if anyone over forty years of age dares to strike anyone, whether while attacking another or defending himself, he shall be considered of a slave-like and boorish character... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

->### ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X ON THE LAWS. FOLIO 355.<-
