...he shall seem sufficiently punished by disgrace. Whoever obeys these warnings shall be considered modest and mild. But whoever spurns these introductory words shall be restrained by this law: If anyone strikes someone twenty years older than himself or more: first, any bystander, provided they are not younger or of the same age, shall intervene; and if they do not intervene, let them be held as a wicked person according to the laws. If, however, the bystander is of the same age or younger than the one being beaten, he should defend the elder as if he were a brother, a father, or a superior. Furthermore, the one who is older and struck the other, as we said, shall be subject to trial; if convicted, let him be imprisoned for no less than a year. Indeed, even longer, if it so pleases the judges. If a foreigner or a resident alien strikes an elder of twenty years or more, those present should offer aid according to the law we stated. If the one condemned is a foreigner, but not a resident of the city, let him be imprisoned for two years; but if he is a resident alien who does not obey the laws, let it be three years, unless the judges decree he should be held longer. If anyone is present and does not offer aid according to the law, if they are of the first and highest wealth class <term>census: a classification of citizens based on property and wealth</term>, let them be fined a mina <note>original: "mina," a Greek unit of currency equal to 100 drachmas</note>. If they are of the second class, fifty drachmas. Of the third, thirty. Of the fourth, twenty. The judges of these matters shall be the army leaders, the officers of the ranks, the tribunes, and the masters of the horse. 

Now, some laws, it seems, are established for the instruction of good men: so that through them they may understand how to live among one another in a friendly manner. Other laws are for suppressing the stubbornness of those who are untamed by nature and, having spurned all discipline, are moved by no reason, but rather rush toward every wickedness. These people are the reason for the following words: the legislator, compelled by necessity, imposes laws upon them. For he himself would wish there were never any use or necessity for laws. 

Whoever, therefore, dares to lay hands upon parents or grandparents, fearing neither the indignation of the gods above nor the punishments of those below—but acting as if he knows what he does not know, despising the sayings of all the ancients—he wanders from the path and requires the ultimate remedy to be turned back. Now, death is not the ultimate end; <margin>Death is not the ultimate end; rather, the extreme punishments are those of the underworld.</margin> rather, the extreme punishments are those of the underworld. Although these things are told most truly, they cannot turn such minds away. For if they did turn them away, no one would ever be found who would wickedly strike their parents. Therefore, it is necessary to set the punishments for these outrages in this life not lower than those in the underworld, but equal to them as far as is possible. 

Let us do it thus: if anyone who is not insane dares to strike a father or mother, or their ancestors, first, as stated above, those present shall bring aid. And if a resident alien or a foreigner offers aid, let him be given precedence over others in public contests as a presiding official; if he does not, let him be forever banished from the entire region. If he is not a resident, let him be praised if he helps, and let him face disgrace if he does not. If a slave offers aid, let him be set free; if he does not, let him be beaten a hundred times with a public whip. And if this happens in the marketplace, let him be punished there by the curators of trade <note>original: "venalium rerum curatoribus," likely referring to the market overseers or Agoranomoi</note>. In other parts of the city, let him be punished similarly by the city wardens <note>original: "aedilibus," Roman term for city officials</note> who are present. In the same way, outside the city in the fields, by those who then preside over the care of the fields. 

But if any citizen—man or woman, youth or elder—is present when parents are beaten by a son, let them be the first to defend them, crying out against the crime. Whoever is unwilling to help shall be burdened by the curse of Jupiter, the father and protector of the race. Finally, whoever is convicted of having struck <margin><unclear>by what penalty those who strike parents shall perish</unclear></margin> their parents: first, let them be in perpetual exile; next, let them be barred from all sacred rites. If they do not abstain from these, they shall be punished by the local authorities with beatings or any other way they wish. And if they return from exile, let them pay for their sins with death. Any free person who eats or drinks with such a man, or conducts any business with him in any way, or touches him, or speaks to him willingly, may not enter a temple, nor the marketplace, nor go anywhere in the city until they are purified. For they must consider themselves contaminated by the wicked association. If they do not obey, but wickedly defile the city and the temples, any magistrate who notices this and does not immediately punish it shall be held guilty of the greatest injuries. 

If a slave strikes a free man, whether a citizen or a foreigner, let any bystander bring help. If not, let them be punished with the aforementioned fine according to their wealth class. Those present shall help the one struck and bind the striker, and they shall hand the bound man over to the one he injured. Let the victim hold him in shackles and strike him with beatings as he wishes, provided he does no damage to the master's property. Then let him return the slave to the master to be held according to the law, which is this: If a slave strikes a free man without the orders of the magistrates, the master shall receive the bound slave from the victim on this condition: that he does not release him until the slave himself has persuaded the victim that he is worthy of being set free. These same laws should be common to all these situations: for women toward men, and men toward women.

### Argument of Marsilio Ficino for Dialogue X of the Laws.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a classical figure or saint within a square frame.</image-desc> The beginning of this tenth summary completes the ninth: it warns that judgments regarding violence against property must be handled, following the judgments regarding violence against persons arranged in the ninth book. Since no violence is harsher or more intolerable than that which is brought about by a certain contempt, he decrees that insults and injuries—properly born of contempt against either a person or a thing—must be punished upon the heads of the perpetrators. He categorizes these under five chapters: they are committed either against public sacred things, or private sacred things, or against the reverence due to parents, or against the excellence of magistrates, or against the civil dignity of some citizen. These matters, therefore, he leaves to be judged most exactly by the authors of the laws as well as by the magistrates and judges. 

After this, he distinguishes from the rest those crimes committed in contempt of the gods, as being the most serious of all beyond what can be said; in these, the focus of this tenth book is centered. But first, he hints at the difference between sacrilege and impiety. He calls sacrilege specifically "robbery," whether a thing or a person consecrated to the gods is snatched away. And that is contained as a certain species under the genus of impiety itself. For beyond sacrilege, many other things are included under impiety: whether thought, spoken, or done in contempt of the gods, and equally things committed, permitted, and even omitted. And lest anything be hidden from us, familiarity and communion also pertain to impiety...

<meta>This page transitions from the specific legal penalties for assault in Book IX to Marsilio Ficino’s introductory commentary (Argumentum) for Book X of Plato’s Laws. Book X is famous for its theological defense of the existence of the gods and its arguments against atheism and impiety.</meta>

-># ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X ON THE LAWS.<-

All [intercourse], whether in food or in speech, entered into with those who, on account of their heinous crimes, are barred from the sacred rites <note>original: "sacris," referring to both ancient Greek rituals and, in Ficino’s mind, Christian sacraments</note>; for these contaminated people also contaminate others by their very proximity. Indeed, regarding this matter, he [Plato] treats it at the end of the ninth book in such a way that he seems to have prophesied the excommunications <note>original: "execrationes," literally cursings or bans</note> made daily by our own people when they expel the profane from the communion of the church. Therefore, our physician [Plato], intending to most diligently cleanse souls languishing with the disease of impiety, first searches for the causes of this disease. And while he searches, he delivers a gospel-like sentiment: Whoever, he says, believes in God according to the laws will be religious, and will never at any time either do or say anything profane. How rightly he has given the starting point here to faith—and to the faith that must be applied to the laws!

But let not the number of gods disturb anyone, just as the number of angels does not disturb us. For many gods can do no more in Plato’s view than many angels and many blessed spirits can do among us. Furthermore, what do the sacred and most ancient laws say about the gods—that is, about God and the angels who serve God? Surely three things: First, that these gods exist. Second, that they provide for all things. Third, that they justly repay rewards and punishments according to merit. In the faith and observation of this very sentiment, all piety consists. Who, then, is the impious man? He, clearly, who will either deny that gods of this kind exist, or if they exist, deny that they provide, or even if they provide, deny that they repay justly. This last error is to think that the judgment of the higher powers <term>superos: the celestial or divine beings</term> can be easily appeased in the manner of human judges by gifts alone, even those offered by the unjust.

Plato, therefore, intending to expel the three causes of the disease of impiety, will prove that gods exist: both those who are the governors of the world’s spheres within the universe, and those who are the contemplators of the supreme God above the world. He will prove that the gods provide for all things, even the smallest. He will prove that with the steady scale and balance of upright justice, they weigh not the external gifts of the hands, but the innermost merits of souls. Finally, with this doctrine as a sort of preamble to the law, he will discourage all from the contempt of divine things and exhort them to piety. Furthermore, he will terrify and torment the impious with the threats and lashes of the laws.

In the beginning, he indicates that the gods exist through two common arguments. The first is deduced from the whole genus of things; the second from the human species. The first is of this sort: We have found that order everywhere proceeds from reason; and an order that is nowhere and never interrupted proceeds from a powerful reason; likewise, the most beneficial order proceeds from the best reason. Since, therefore, both the arrangement and the progression of the universe are most orderly, and are always and everywhere so—and this not without a certain wonderful benefit—it is necessary that the world be arranged and moved by the best and most powerful reason. And since the universe is one, and a single thing is not made from diverse parts except by one [agent], it follows that there is one supreme reason of this kind. Furthermore, there are many divine reasons under the supreme divine reason; just as in a single worldly work rationally ordered, there are many globes distinct from one another in species and virtue, yet all rationally ordered—so much so that in a certain way many worlds seem to be contained within the most ample circumference of the one world. And so, similarly, many governors of these narrower worlds are arranged in order, and are encompassed under the one governor of the most ample world. He, truly, is not only the ordainer, but is himself, so to speak, immense Order; he rejoices much more in the ordainer than in the thing ordered. Wherefore, if he is undoubtedly delighted by the many ordered things in the universe, he is also delighted by the many ordainers. For the most excellent greatness of the highest King consists in this: that he has beneath him not only humble servants, but also many great kings.

The second argument for the same conclusion, deduced from the human species, is of this sort: The natural instinct of any species cannot be in vain. Likewise, the natural judgment of the most perfect species of animals ought not to be entirely false. Since the human species, the most perfect of animals, is moved toward religion everywhere and always by a natural instinct and immutable judgment, it is necessary that there be higher powers who are worshipped through religion, and that souls survive their bodies—which indeed is the most important foundation of religion.

Take note of Plato’s saying: that reasons concerning divine things, even if at times they are not overly clever, are nevertheless true. Likewise, note the two occasions for impiety: First, intemperance—that is, the lust for bodily pleasures; and second, ignorance arising from the absurd opinions of certain poets and physicists <term>physicorum: natural philosophers or scientists</term>. He says the poets erred in three ways concerning the gods: First, that they sang of the gods breaking forth from the confusion they call Chaos. Second, that they asserted some were born from others without right reason, as if through human cohabitation. Third, that they transferred all human disturbances, errors, and outrages onto the gods with wicked impiety. Those physicists also sinned in religion who either, with Democritus, dream that the universe—arranged with such wonderful reason—is composed by some reckless chance rather than divine reason; or who, with Anaxagoras and Archelaus, believe that the celestial bodies have nothing more divine in them than the elements. Furthermore, they say that the forms of those things which are born, which are clearly directed everywhere toward an end, come from elemental impulse rather than from the art of a Mind directing individual things to a certain end.

But because we have been more extensive in the books of our own theology <note>Ficino refers here to his major work, *Theologia Platonica* (Platonic Theology)</note> in refuting these views and in confirming those things which we have just proved—and which we will subsequently bring forth from the mind of Plato in this compendium—we will run through them briefly for the present. Consider how great is our Plato’s religion, and how certain he is that God exists; for when disputing against those who deny God, he can scarcely contain himself from anger—a man who is otherwise, beyond all measure, most mild in both life and disputation. In these matters, he certainly warns: that those who deny God are not to be tolerated. Note that Plato approves of those who, at the rising and setting of the sun and moon, adore not only the sun and moon specifically, but rather the divine beneficence; for which he commands that thanks be given daily for such a great gift of light. He judges that man to be like a monster among men who, against both natural instinct and education, as well as common custom, denies that the higher powers exist. Soon, however, he warns young men, who by chance have been invaded by certain absurd opinions heard against God, that as long as they are young, they should abstain from judgment on divine matters, and should trust their elders and the laws.

-># ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X ON THE LAWS. FOLIO 356.<-
->T iiii<-

...until age, experience, and reason teach them. He furthermore brings into the discussion the opinions of certain men who were considered wise, which easily incline people toward impiety and injustice. I speak of those opinions asserting that the natures of the four elements <note>original: "quatuor elementorum," referring to earth, air, fire, and water</note>, flowing together by a kind of accidental motion, heaped all things together. Furthermore, they claim that religion and justice exist not by any truth, but by human opinion alone. Therefore, he [Plato] concludes that these views, being the most ruinous of all to both private and public life, must be refuted with reasons. Men should not be forced into obedience and observance of the laws merely by threats and torments, but additionally by persuasions and reasons. Otherwise, since man is a rational animal, and therefore free, if you do not bind him with the bond of reason, he neither ought to be, nor can be, bound in any other way.

Therefore, reason must be awakened by the laws; its power for finding God is so great that, after a rational investigation, it becomes more certain to the reason that [God] exists in nature than in the reason itself—and it is more certain to the extent that it perceives natural effects to be more orderly than human ones. From this, it also notices that art <note>original: "artem," here meaning craftsmanship or intelligent design</note> is more perfect in nature than in man. Hence, it again notices that an art presides over natural works to which human art is inferior; and that this art not only exists, but is also a participant in life and intelligence. Indeed, it is living and intelligent; or rather, it is life and intellect itself. Add to this "will" as well. For since it clearly directs individual things toward their proper ends, it is certain that it foresaw the end and willed it; or rather, that it always provides and wills, just as order is always preserved whole in individual things—or where it seems to be interrupted, it is restored faster than can be said. 

We have no doubt that this is <term>Divine Providence</term> <note>the belief that God actively guides and cares for the universe</note>. I speak of a Providence that does not neglect even the smallest things; for these are no less ordered than the greatest, nor does it labor over the greatest. For the things nearest to the Ordainer do not resist His ordering; they are continually ordered by the same nod of his will by which they are made, and they are kept far from all transgression. Hence the saying: *He dwells on high and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth* <note>original: "In altis habitat: & humilia respicit in cælo & in terra," a reference to Psalm 113:5-6</note>. Just as the heaven itself, while it completes its course without labor, meanwhile pours the most fertile gift of its rays around the earth without negligence. 

Among these things, he says that law and art consist of nature—or no less than nature—because they possess more of the mind; he says that true forms of nature exist less than those of intelligence, and are born from the divine intellect as from a father, and from the human mind as from a mother. And observe the usual piety of our Plato, invoking God to confirm the gods. One God, I say, so that he may teach that all the gods are to be referred back to the One. He says, moreover, that relying on the help of the supreme God, he will dispute most safely about divine matters. 

In the beginning, he certainly disapproves of those <term>physicists</term> <note>early materialist philosophers like Democritus or Epicurus</note> who placed the highest principles of things in bodies, from which life and intelligence would then proceed; whereas they should have said instead that corporeal things depend on intellectual life. He professes that he will prove this to be so, not by a new opinion, I say, but by reason. For an opinion of this sort belonged to the ancient theologians before Plato. But the argumentation that will be made here from <term>motion</term> <note>Plato’s famous argument that every movement must have a first cause that moves itself</note> is peculiar to Plato. He distinguishes the genus of motion itself into ten species:
1. Circular motion <note>original: "In circuitu"</note>
2. Local transition
3. Condensation
4. Rarefaction
5. Increase
6. Decrease
7. Generation
8. Corruption
9. Change or alteration made in one thing by another
10. Change made from itself, whether in itself or in another.

He admires circular motion. For in it, the indivisible center stands still while the rest are moved. Likewise, in a deep sphere, many circles are designated, some wider than others in succession. And what is wonderful is that at the same moment the narrowest circle and the widest complete their circuit: so that both the slowness of the one in a continuous body and the velocity of the other are equally to be admired. Those in the middle, regarding both dimension and motion, hold a middle way according to certain proportions. We have treated much of these things in our expositions of theology. 

He says of that motion which changes place: it changes its center (that is, the center of its place) to which the circumference of the moving body is compared; but sometimes, besides changing its center, it also in a way preserves the same center—namely when it is not fixed, but is moved through space along a kind of equal circumference. Furthermore, where he speaks of generation, he speaks of the principle (that is, the motive and seminal nature) when alteration is perfected through three steps: length, width, and depth. Likewise, it reaches even to quantity and quality, and to substantial forms manifested to the senses through their effects; and again, it arrives at formal, vital, and sensual being. He thinks that in these motions the corporeal mass is moved but does not move; whereas corporeal forms both move the masses and are moved by the soul. And the Soul moves both these things; but it is not moved by another, but rather is moved by itself. Yet it moves in such a way that, together with the things changed, it is meanwhile changed in its own way. 

Therefore, he considers divine and angelic minds to be more excellent than souls; these move lower things while they themselves are not changed at all. Finally, he judges the <term>Good</term> itself to be more eminent than minds. For all things desire truth for the sake of the Good. In these passages, he touches on many things pertaining to the nature that is "mobile of itself" <note>self-moving</note>, as if to the proper principle of motion and generation. In this, a certain formal motion and spiritual generation flourishes by its own nature as the pattern for all motions and generations. 

Above all, he confirms that whatever is moved by another requires a nature that is mobile of itself, lest there be an infinite regress <note>original: "ne procedat in infinitum," the logical problem of a chain of causes that never ends</note>. Indeed, just as one goes beyond those things that shine or are heated by another to reach something that is luminous or hot of itself, so beyond things moved by another, we must come to a thing that is mobile of itself. For if all things were now at rest, and a little later something had to be moved before the rest: what, then, will move first? Certainly not the divine substance, which is altogether immobile. Nor any corporeal thing, which borrows motion from another. Therefore, only that which is mobile of itself will move first; and exercising its motion in itself, it will transmit it to other things. For this is so established in bodies that they are moved, just as the immobile principle of things grants to things that they be moved. That the Soul is a nature mobile of itself is clear both internally (when by its own nature it freely ranges and deliberates by reasoning) and externally (when by its presence it grants to the body that it be moved, in a sense, by itself). But concerning all these things, and moreover concerning the minds that guide the spheres...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s introduction to Book X of Plato’s Laws. In the preceding section, he argued that human reason is naturally equipped to find God. Here, he begins a technical metaphysical defense of the soul's priority over the body and the nature of divine providence.</meta>

-># ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE X ON THE LAWS<-

That there must be angels and God, we have treated abundantly in our *Theology* <note>original: "theologia," referring to Ficino’s own massive work, *Platonic Theology*</note>. However, where Plato calls the soul "motion" and "generation," understand this in the sense of a cause: that is, the soul is the proper principle <note>original: "principium," the starting point or source</note> of motion and generation. And where he says that "to be moved by itself" is the definition of the soul, note that in the same place it is said that the definition of the soul is that which *can* move itself; you should not understand the soul to be the act of motion itself, but rather the power—and I do not mean an accidental power, for he also calls the soul a "substance" in that passage. Thus, you should define it as follows: The soul is a substance possessing its own power, by which it moves both itself and other things.

Just as a thing that is movable by itself precedes a thing that must be moved by another, so he [Plato] thinks the rational soul precedes the entire bodily machine, since no body is capable of moving itself. The Platonists say the soul "precedes" the body both in dignity and in time. If anyone wishes Plato to disagree less with Christians <note>Ficino often tried to harmonize Plato with Christian doctrine, though the idea of the soul existing before the body was controversial</note>, let him explain that our soul precedes the body either by a certain moment of time, or at least in the dignity and intention of the Creator. 

Furthermore, from the fact that the substance of the soul is prior to the substance of the body, he concludes that the affects, motions, and familiar gifts of the soul are prior to the passions of the body. When he lists the properties of the soul, remember that those signifying "action" are common to our soul and the higher beings [angels]. Those that signify "passion" <note>original: "passionem," meaning being acted upon or suffering an emotion</note> are proper to us, or shared only with the lowest demons. Nevertheless, a natural motion which is a "passion" in the body is an "action" in the soul. And what in the body is length, breadth, depth, quality, and motion, in the soul is sharpness, judgment, memory, habit, and affect. You can find other matters of this kind more distinctly in my *Theology*. 

He also says that the soul is the cause of evils—namely, "by accident," and because our soul possesses free will. Be careful when he says the world is governed by a soul: he adds that the soul is "twin," one being beneficial and the other contrary. Do not take this to mean a twin "substance," but rather a twin "power." Indeed, in the soul of the world and of the heavens, there is a power: one is the mover of bodies, and the other is intellectual. The intellectual power is certainly beneficial, disposing all things in order. The motive power is beneficial (that is, an orderer) only insofar as it is subject to the other. If it were not subject to the intellect, then the more effective it was at causing motion, the more it would—lacking art <note>original: "carens arte," lacking skill or intelligent design</note>—topple and confound the universe.

He proves that the celestial soul possesses a mind <note>original: "mentem"</note> from the order it always observes in every motion and generation. Truly, we see that those who are "out of their minds" are, to that same extent, "out of order." In this context, we define "order" as the mutual connection of things and actions among themselves, arranged in a fitting succession, directed toward a certain end by a specific reasoning, and preserving—as much as possible—the similar, the equal, and the same in all things. We see such order preserved only by those who are masters of their minds; and it is perfectly fulfilled in the very progression of the universe. It is fulfilled, I say, both most suitably and most beautifully. From this it appears that the universe is governed by a soul that possesses a mind both most skillful and most good.

Not without reason did he say that "circularity" is the proper characteristic of the Mind. For in a circuit, the indivisible center remains fixed while the circumference returns to the same point, and equality is preserved in both shape and motion. Similarly, in the Mind, a simple and fixed gaze directed toward the Truth itself remains, while causes are unfolded into effects through intermediary steps; and in turn, those effects are folded back into their causes. Meanwhile, the attention of the mind returns to the consideration of itself; it proceeds by understanding, willing, and acting with a similar, equal, and identical intention, rule, and progression.

After he proved that the celestial spheres are endowed with souls and the souls with excellent minds, and signified that the universe is driven by one soul and the many spheres by many souls, he now briefly distinguishes three ways in which souls might be joined to the heavenly bodies. He says the soul is either:
1. Inside the globe just as our soul is in our body, so that one "animal" <note>original: "animal," a living being</note> is made from them; 
2. Or it is present such that it does not give life to the globe, but only moves and rules it; 
3. Or it does so by a certain miraculous power of moving alone, or through some further medium. 

And although he does not clearly choose one of these three over the others here, all the Platonists choose the first without controversy; they believe that Aristotle and Theophrastus felt the same way. For they think Plato held that one to be more probable. Indeed, the very argument by which he here makes the heavens "animated" <note>original: "animatum," possessing a soul</note> implies that the soul itself moves along with the moved heaven. Unless one living being were made from the soul and the globe, the mover would certainly not be a "movable mover," but an "immobile mover." He confirms this same thing in the *Phaedrus*. He also confirms it in the *Timaeus*, saying that when the Architect of the world <note>original: "mundi architectus," the Demiurge</note> wished to make the world an intellectual living being, and since the intellect could not be present to a body without a medium, he joined the intellect to a soul, and the soul to the body; and thus he infused it into the middle of the world and diffused it through all things.

But why does Plato here only clearly confirm the "celestial gods"? Because the contemplation of higher things is quite foreign to the subject matter of laws. Furthermore, through these celestial gods who move and are bound to their own duties, he sufficiently warns that a "Higher One" must be sought, who, being himself unmoved, moves all others—a common leader who assigns specific duties to each. What more? He clearly demonstrated that above the celestial souls there is a Divine Mind and angelic minds when he says: the celestial soul—since it does not have it from itself—always brings all things to a right conclusion if it has received a "divine intellect"; just as among the gods things are held to be right and happy; otherwise, it would wander completely. Therefore, where Plato proceeds from the soul to the mind, he is like one who ascends from the eye to a higher light, and he greatly fears lest he be forced into darkness.

After he has shown that the gods exist, he demonstrates that they provide [Providence], beginning from a certain singular opinion: A certain nature akin to divinity leads men (who have not entirely degenerated from the human species) to affirm that God exists, even though sometimes the apparent prosperity of the wicked—which is a false prosperity and will pay the penalty at the appointed time—forces us to doubt the providence of God. Surely, if God acts by understanding, he consequently understands what he acts; and if he makes the whole, he also understands the whole. If he knows the whole, he also knows the parts from which the whole necessarily consists; if the parts, then the tiny particles from which the parts are necessarily made. He is therefore able to...

He defines the relationship between the World Soul, the Divine Mind, and the celestial spheres, asserting that the orderly motion of the heavens proves they are governed by an intelligent Providence.</summary>

--- Page 734 ---
<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s introduction to Book X of Plato’s *Laws*. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing how the soul precedes the body in the intention of the Creator. Here, Ficino transitions from the soul's nature to a defense of Divine Providence—the idea that God actively manages the universe down to the smallest detail.</meta>

He knows how to rule the universe: he who is able and knows how to provide. He also wishes to govern his entire work usefully. But a whole can never be well governed if its parts are not governed. Thus, neither a doctor nor an architect cares for a whole work perfectly without the parts that necessarily contribute to it. God does not neglect to govern the smallest things, since he did not neglect to create the smallest things. Nor is governing difficult for God, for whom creation is easy. Nor is he too slow or weak to care, for he is the strongest of all, governing all things more accurately than either art or nature governs the things they produce. For just as the works of God depend more on God than the works of art or nature depend on art or nature, so much more diligently does God provide for his works—by whose providence all other things also have the capacity to provide for their own. Since art is more perfect the more easily it handles small and large things at the same time, and in God art is immeasurable, he surely governs the smallest and greatest things together with the highest ease. In dispensing both, he does not arrange the whole for the sake of the parts, but the parts for the sake of the whole; and he relates the specific good of each thing to the good of the universe. Among all things under the moon, however, he has the greatest diligence concerning the human species: both because it is the most perfect, and because it worships God, as if it alone were specifically cultivated by God.

In these matters, you will note that the highest God has distributed divine rulers <note>Ficino is referring to "daemons" or planetary intelligences that act as intermediaries</note> across every single genus and species of things, who are the caretakers of even the smallest actions and experiences. Just as these rulers can do whatever they do through His power, so they take care of every tiny detail through His providence, which looks after even the smallest things. You will note that there are senses in the stars; and as Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism</note> and Hermias <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist commentator from Alexandria</note> argue, there is properly sight and hearing in them, but of a different kind and far more excellent than the senses of earthly animals. You will also note that the human soul is always joined to a body—continually to an **ethereal body** <note>Also called the "astral body" or "spirit-vehicle," believed to be a subtle, immortal casing for the soul</note>, but through a succession of time, now to an earthly body, now to an aerial one.

Likewise, the movement of the soul—because it is primary and comes from itself, and is therefore free—can be diverted into various forms: to such an extent that the soul is converted sometimes into a condition lower than man, and sometimes into one higher than man. By the former, it descends to lower places as if by a certain weight; by the latter, however, it seeks the heights as if by lightness. From this, it appears that the habits conceived from one's own movements run together with the law of the divine will. For just as that law dictates that celestial things befit good souls and earthly things befit evil souls, so—with no outside force pushing them, but by a certain natural instinct—the habits of the good spontaneously seek higher things, while those of the evil slip toward the lower.

Truly, if I were allowed to comment at greater length here, I would explain that most obscurely stated point: where he introduces a soul attempting to transmute fire into "animated water" <note>original: "aquam animatam," likely referring to the transformation of elements or the descent of the soul into a moist, generative state</note>, as if attempting the most difficult of tasks. For since water is the opposite of fire, and a soul cannot be created out of fire, surely he who strives to transmute fire into animated water attempts the impossible. Nor is that which must be explained regarding **dialectical resolution and division** <note>The logical method of breaking a concept down into its parts (division) and building it back up (resolution)</note> stated any less obscurely. Indeed, if anyone proceeds by dividing through three steps—namely, from a most general genus to intermediate species, and from those to the most specific—he then divides the species easily. It follows that if he resolves by the same steps—from the most specific species to the intermediate genus, and from there to the most general—he also resolves easily. But truly, he who wishes to wander through every single thing, infinite in number, will undertake a useless task. But regarding these, see the commentaries on the *Philebus* <note>Another of Plato's dialogues for which Ficino wrote a famous commentary</note>.

Among these things, you will note that Plato’s words are very similar to the oracle of David the Prophet <note>Ficino is referencing Psalm 139:7-8: "Whither shall I go from thy spirit?... If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there."</note>: that divine judgment cannot be avoided either by an ascent into heaven or a descent into hell. After this, he shows that God cannot be unjustly appeased by the gifts of the wicked. Here you will consider that God is a more diligent caretaker of the human race than shepherds are of sheep, pilots of ships, generals of armies, farmers of fields, charioteers of horses, or doctors of the sick. Furthermore, all things under heaven are full of evils, and there is a perpetual war surrounding souls. In this war, vices pull downward, while the gods and **daemons** <note>In the Platonic sense, these are guardian spirits or intermediaries, not "demons" in the modern sense</note> pull upward. You will consider that there are living virtues in God—or rather, lives—from whose sparks the soul is ignited and raised to the heights.

After these introductions, he turns his attention with a more severe judgment toward the impious. He diligently investigates not only wicked actions but also the impudence of words, and even the very thoughts against divine dignity. He breaks down the three types of impiety mentioned earlier into six, by dividing each part into two. For those three consist of false opinions against God. However, along with a false opinion, a wickedness of character can also occur; or a more tolerable poverty of mind. You will learn here also of the punishments for evildoers, heretics, and the superstitious, and furthermore for those who are called **False Prophets**. Again, note how much he condemns common superstition. He also condemned poetic superstition above, from which common superstition is strengthened. Everywhere, Plato disapproves of both poetic and common superstition; and above all human duties, he venerates **philosophical piety**.

Post the laws concerning murder, wounds, and blows, let that common law concerning all force be enacted: that no one shall carry away or take another's property, nor use any of his neighbor's things, unless he has first persuaded the owner. In the second place are those committed against private rites and tombs. In the third are those against parents, separate from what we have already recounted. ...uses it, before he has persuaded them. Fifth, when the civil dignity of any citizen is harmed or offended: a category that entirely demands vengeance, and the law ought to provide for each of these matters commonly. Concerning sacrilege, indeed, it has been stated summarily what ought to be done, whether it is carried out by force or in secret. But concerning those things which are done by word or deed in contempt of the gods, it seems that we must next speak on how they are to be punished, once a certain preamble <note>original: "prooemium" — an introductory statement intended to explain the reason for a law and persuade the citizens to follow it willingly.</note> has been set forth. Indeed, let the preamble be of this kind: "He who believes the gods exist according to the laws never voluntarily commits any impious act, nor speaks one." But people do or say something impious against the gods for one of three reasons: either because they deny the gods exist; or because, even if they think they exist, they judge that they do not care at all for human affairs; or thirdly, although they believe the gods both exist and have care for men, they nevertheless believe the gods are easily appeased by prayers and sacrifices. 

CLINIAS. What shall we do then? What shall we say to them? 

ATHENIAN. Let us first listen, my good man, to what I suspect they might say in a sort of joking mockery of us. 

CLINIAS. What indeed will they say? 

ATHENIAN. They will trifle with us roughly in this way: "O Athenian guest, and you Lacedaemonian <note>A citizen of Sparta.</note>, and you Gnossian <note>A citizen of Crete.</note>, you speak the truth: some of us think there are no gods at all, others that they care nothing for our affairs, and others that they are easily appeased by gifts. Therefore, what you have thought should be done in the making of all your laws, we wish you to do for us now: namely, that before the threats of the laws, you persuade us by sufficient signs that gods exist, and that they cannot be moved by any gifts beyond what is right. For now, hearing these and similar things preached daily by those who are thought to be excellent—poets, orators, prophets, priests, and many others—we are not deterred from committing injury; but when we have done it, we try to appease the gods. From you, however, who boast that you are not cruel but mild lawmakers, we demand that you first use persuasion to teach us that gods exist, so that even if you do not speak much more sublimely than others, you at least speak more truly. For perhaps we might believe you. Therefore, if we demand what is fair, comply with our request."

CLINIAS. But surely, my friend, it is easy to show this truth: that there are gods. 

ATHENIAN. In what 

<margin>and there is a God</margin> way? 

CLINIAS. First, indeed, the earth, the sun, the stars, and the universe itself, and the most ornate variety of the seasons, distinguished by years and months, show it; and furthermore, the consensus of all Greeks and barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speaking peoples.</note> who confess that there are gods. 

ATHENIAN. I fear, O blessed man, wicked men. I fear, I say—I do not blush nor am I afraid to say it—lest they perhaps despise you. For you are ignorant of the cause of their disagreement: you think that their minds fall into an impious life only because of the lack of restraint regarding pleasures and desires. 

CLINIAS. But what other cause is there for them besides these things, guest? 

ATHENIAN. Something which, because you have no share in it, completely escapes you. 

CLINIAS. What is this? 

ATHENIAN. A certain most grave ignorance, which is seen by them to be the greatest wisdom. 

CLINIAS. In what way do you mean? 

ATHENIAN. There are reports circulating among us, some written in meter and some in prose, which, as I hear, are not found among you because of the excellence of your civil discipline. The most ancient of these affirm that the first nature of the heavens and of the other gods was created; and moving not much further, they tell of the generation and conduct of the gods among themselves. Since these things are ancient, it is not easy to criticize whether they are right or not regarding other matters; yet for the worship and honor of parents, I will confess that they are neither useful nor true. Let us therefore dismiss the ancient things; and let us speak of them as it pleases the gods. But let us accuse the words of the younger "wise men" <note>This refers to the pre-Socratic natural philosophers, such as Anaxagoras, who sought material rather than divine explanations for the cosmos.</note> wherever they bring evil to men. For indeed, this is the result of their words: that when you and I bring forward these very signs to show that gods exist—producing the sun and moon, the stars and the earth, as if they were gods and divine things—then the young people, persuaded otherwise by these "wise men," say that these things are merely earth and stones, and that they can have no care for human affairs; but that the discourse about them has been composed only with ornate words to seem plausible. 

CLINIAS. That is certainly a grave matter, guest, even if only one person had said it. But now it is even more grave and troublesome because there are many who say it. 

ATHENIAN. What then ought we to do or say? Should we prepare ourselves for a defense as if we had been accused before impious men, because we affirm by laws that gods exist? Or should we set these things aside and return again to the treatment of the laws, lest this preamble to the laws grow too long for us? For the speech will not be brief if we wish to show sufficiently what those people who are prone to impiety require, and also to move them from their crime through terror, and finally, as is fitting, to pass the laws. 

CLINIAS. Frequently in this short time, guest, it has been said by us that brevity is not to be preferred to length. For nothing, as they say, urges us on. Therefore, it would be both ridiculous and wicked if we preferred shorter things to better ones. For it will contribute much if our discourse shows by plausible reason that gods exist and are good, and that they honor justice much more than men do. This will be almost the best and most beautiful beginning of all the laws. For which reason, without any trouble or haste, let us omit nothing within our power that pertains to persuading them of this matter. 

ATHENIAN. This speech of yours shows you so prepared and ready that it seems to call for prayers and vows, and admits no further delay. But how can someone discuss the gods without anger? For it is necessary to take it heavily and hate those who have provided the cause for these words of ours. These people, certainly, from childhood could have been led to affirm the gods, especially since, while they were nourished on milk by nurses and mothers, they heard many things said and sung about them in stories both joking and serious; and in the sacrifices, they saw things done in agreement with them, which children most sweetly see and hear; while they see <note>original catchword: "vident" — the text ends here and will continue with "they see" on the next page.</note> their parents sacrificing with the greatest zeal for themselves and their children, and praying as suppliants to the gods, as if they were most truly gods...

<vocab>Plato, Laws, Atheists, Preamble, Justice, Sacrilege, Prudence</vocab>

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian guest argues that laws against impiety should begin with a persuasive preamble rather than just punishments. He critiques both ancient myths and contemporary natural philosophers who claim the heavenly bodies are merely "stones" rather than divine beings, asserting that the education of the young is the best defense against atheism.</summary>

### ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE GREEK LAWS. DIALOGUE X. FOLIO 358.
<page-num>356</page-num>

...they saw <note>original: "conspicerent" — this continues the thought from the previous page about how young people observed the universal devotion of all nations</note>; furthermore, every day at the rising and setting of the sun and moon, they observed all Greeks and barbarians, in both adversity and prosperity, prostrating themselves in supplication. From this, they did not bring forth a suspicion that the gods do not exist, but rather provided testimony that they do exist without controversy. But indeed, those who—moved by no reason that any person of sound mind would speak—despise all these things, and for that reason compel us to say these things: in what way can we now correct them with gentle words and first teach them that the gods exist? Let us dare, nonetheless. For it is not fitting that while they are lost to pleasure, we also should be corrupted by anger against them.

Therefore, with all agitation of the soul extinguished, let us approach the **preamble** to those whose minds are thus corrupted; and as if to one of them, let us turn our speech gently: "O son, you are still young; and I do not doubt that the progression of time will cause you to feel differently about many things than you do now. Wait, therefore, I pray, so that you may then judge concerning the greatest matters. But the greatest matter—which you now think is nothing—is that by thinking rightly about the gods, we may live well. Truly, if I state solemnly <note>original: "sacrificauero" — likely used here in the sense of making a solemn declaration or vow</note> that this is a very great point in these matters, I shall not lie. Not you alone, nor your friends first, have held this opinion about the gods; rather, some people are always suffering from this disease, now more, now fewer. 

I will tell you what has happened to most of them. Surely none of them has ever persevered in this opinion—that the gods do not exist—from youth until old age. The other two diseases <note>The "diseases" of the soul refer to the three types of atheism: 1. Denying gods exist; 2. Denying they care for us; 3. Thinking they can be bribed.</note>, although they do not remain with many, have nevertheless persisted with some: that the gods do indeed exist, but care nothing for human affairs; or that they do care, but are easily appeased by prayers and sacrifices. You, therefore, if you believe me, will wait until it is plainly clear to you, according to your strength, what is to be judged concerning these things. And so that you may attain this, you will diligently consider whether the matter stands thus or otherwise; and you will inquire of all others, and especially of the lawmaker. Meanwhile, do not be so reckless as to think impiously of the gods. For he who sets the laws for you will attempt to teach you, both now and later, how these things stand."

**CLINIAS.** Thus far, Guest, it has been very well said by us.

**ATHENIAN.** It is exactly so, O Megillus and Clinias. But we have fallen, without knowing it, into a certain strange discourse.

**CLINIAS.** What sort?

**ATHENIAN.** One which is thought by many to be the wisest.

**CLINIAS.** Speak more clearly.

**ATHENIAN.** Some say that all things that come to be, that will be, and that have been made, are made either by **nature**, or by **fortune**, or by **art**.

**CLINIAS.** And rightly so.

**ATHENIAN.** Certainly, it is not absurd that wise men have spoken rightly. Therefore, let us follow them and inquire what they understood.

**CLINIAS.** By all means.

**ATHENIAN.** They say the greatest and most beautiful things are made by **nature** and **fortune**, but smaller things by **art**; and they say that art, having received from nature the generation of the great and primary works, fashions and fabricates all the smaller things, which are called "artificial" by everyone.

<margin>
All things are made either by nature, or by fortune, or by art.
The most beautiful things are made by nature and fortune; smaller things, however, by art.
</margin>

**CLINIAS.** How do you say that?

**ATHENIAN.** I will say it more plainly. Fire, water, earth, air: they say all these exist not by art but by nature and fortune. They also say that the bodies which follow these—of earthly things, of the sun, the moon, and all the stars—were made out of those things which are entirely lacking a soul; and that by the fortune of their powers, each has happened to coincide with others by chance: thus the cold with the hot, the dry with the moist, the soft with the hard; and altogether contraries with contraries, with fortune leading, they were necessarily mixed together. 

In this way, the whole heaven and all things in it, and animals also, and plants, and the seasons of the year were produced: not through intellect, nor through some god, but by nature, as we said, and by fortune. From these, they say that **art** was later made mortal by mortals, and generated certain later things, not fully participating in truth, but certain images akin to themselves: such as painting, music, and the other arts similar to these generate. 

If indeed some arts do something serious, they are those which communicate their power with nature: such as medicine, agriculture, and gymnastics. Furthermore, they say that civil skill concurs in some small part with nature, but in a large part with art; and thus the entire positioning of laws agrees not with nature, but with art, whose positions are not true.

<margin>
See how medicine inclines toward nature, while civil skill inclines more toward art, according to the ancient wise men.
</margin>

**CLINIAS.** In what way?

**ATHENIAN.** They want the gods, O blessed man, to exist not by nature but by art and certain laws; and they believe them to be different for different people, just as each group has established by law through mutual agreement. They say that things beautiful or honorable exist partly by nature and partly by law. But they say that **just things** do not exist by nature at all; rather, men always dispute with one another about these things and establish new ones every day; and what they have recently established is just only so far as it pleases them, not by nature, but established by art and laws. 

These are the things, O friends, which wise men—both poets and other writers—have handed down to younger people, saying that just possession is that which is acquired by force and victory. From this, impiety is born in the younger generation, leading them to believe that gods do not exist such as the laws command them to believe. From this also, seditions arise, through which men are drawn toward that life which is supposedly "right according to nature"—a life in which they live so as to conquer others, rather than serving others according to the laws.

**CLINIAS.** O Guest, what a thing you have described! And what a plague brought upon the youth, both publicly to cities and privately to their own homes.

**ATHENIAN.** You speak the truth, O Clinias. But since the matter stands thus, what do you think the lawmaker should do? Should he only threaten all men, saying they will certainly pay the penalty unless they believe gods exist—and believe them to be such as are handed down by the laws—and that concerning things honorable, just, and greatest, and concerning virtue and depravity, they should think and act entirely as the lawmaker has prescribed? If they do not obey, some are to be punished by the death penalty, others by lashes and chains, others by disgrace, others by exile and poverty. Will the lawmaker only threaten in this way? Will he care nothing for adding persuasion to the laws with threats, by which he might mitigate the severity?

**CLINIAS.** Not at all, Guest; but if any persuasion, however slight, can be found in matters of this kind, the lawmaker who is of any worth should not be deterred from the labor; but with the greatest "shout," as they say, he should bring help to the ancient law: and show by reasons that the gods exist: and whatever you yourself were saying just now: and to the law itself and...

<summary>The Athenian Guest explains a materialistic philosophy where the universe is created by nature and chance rather than divine intellect, arguing that this view leads youth to believe that justice is merely the "right of the stronger." He proposes that the legislator must use persuasive arguments (preambles) rather than just threats of punishment to combat this impiety.</summary>

Having established that some young people are led astray by materialist philosophies, the Athenian now begins the formal philosophical "preamble" to prove that the soul is prior to the body, and therefore the gods exist and govern the universe.</meta>

### BOOK X.
<page-num>XXXIIII.</page-num>

...to support art in such a way: that it affirms it exists either by nature, or no less than nature; since they are the offspring of the mind itself, as right reason shows—which you seem to me to have just said, and which I believe. **ATHENIAN.** O Clinias, you have a most ready mind. But is it not difficult to follow those matters with logic which have been so widely spread among everyone, and which are themselves so long-winded that they do not allow for brevity? **CLINIAS.** Why, Guest? When so much was said about drunkenness and music, we bore that length with a calm mind; shall we not listen to one speaking at greater length about the gods and such matters? Indeed, this will be a great defense for the prudent arrangement of the laws: since the mandates of the laws, having been committed to writing—which are usually subject to refutation for all future time—may rest thus proven. Therefore, we ought not to be afraid if things that are difficult to hear at the beginning are often repeated, so that even men of slow wit may be able to perceive them. These things, therefore, although long-winded, if only they are useful, do not seem to be things that should be cast aside. Nor is it fair not to defend these discourses to the best of our ability. **MEGILLUS.** It seems to me, Guest, that Clinias speaks very well. **ATHENIAN.** And most certainly, O Megillus; therefore we must do as he says. Surely, unless those discourses were common—so to speak—among all men, there would be no need to demonstrate by reason that the gods exist. But now it is necessary. Since, therefore, the laws are being corrupted especially by wicked men, whose duty is it more than the lawmaker's to bring help? **MEGILLUS.** Certainly no one else's. **ATHENIAN.** But tell me, Clinias—for you must be a participant in this reasoning—does not the person who says these things seem to think that fire, earth, water, and air are the first of all things? And do they not call these very things "nature," and judge the soul to be something posterior <note>Coming after or secondary to the physical elements.</note> to these? Rather, it does not only seem so; but he truly signifies those things to us by his speech. **CLINIAS.** Quite so. **ATHENIAN.** Have we then, by Jove, found as it were a certain fountain of the foolish opinion of those who have ever touched upon questions of natural things? Consider, I pray, and examine every reason. For it is of no small importance if we show that those who rely on impious reasons, and draw others into impiety, do not argue rightly but perversely. This, then, is how it seems to me. **CLINIAS.** You speak well; but try to show those things. **ATHENIAN.** But I will seem to use reasons that are not customary. **CLINIAS.** Do not fear, friend. For I understand that you will think you are going far away from the purpose of making laws if we enter into this disputation. But if we cannot otherwise convince people that what is now said about the gods according to the law is correct, it must be spoken entirely. **ATHENIAN.** I shall now speak this new and almost unheard-of reasoning. These discourses, which have made minds impious, have affirmed that that which is the first cause of the generation and corruption of all things is not the first, but a later thing. But that which is later, they claim is first. Therefore, they have been ignorant of the true substance of the gods. **CLINIAS.** I do not yet understand. **ATHENIAN.** It seems that almost everyone has been ignorant of what kind of thing the soul is, and what power it has; both in regard to other things and in regard to its generation: that it was born before all bodies, and that it is the chief ruler of all the transformation and order of bodies. If these things are so, will not those things which are proper to the soul itself necessarily be prior to those things which pertain to the body, since the soul itself is older than the body? **CLINIAS.** It must be so. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore opinion, care, intellect, art, and law are prior to hard and soft, heavy and light things. For this reason, the great and first works and operations of art itself will be among the first things; but those things which are "by nature," and nature itself (which they do not correctly call by that name), are later, and they follow art and intellect. **CLINIAS.** Why not correctly? **ATHENIAN.** Because they want to say "nature" is the generation concerning the first things; and they place bodies as the first things. But if it will appear that not fire, nor air, but the soul exists first, the soul itself will most rightly be affirmed to be older than the body; and that nature itself consists in this way: if it is established that the soul is older than bodies; but otherwise not at all. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we then prepare ourselves for these things? **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Let us flee from sophistical and deceptive reasoning; lest perhaps, being youthful itself, it deceives us old men and makes us look ridiculous; and we seem to have attempted great things but achieved not even small ones. If the three of us wished to cross a deep and rapid river, and I, being younger than you and more experienced in the waves, should say that I ought to make the trial first—leaving you in safety—to see whether the river can be crossed by you elders or not; and after the trial is made, either to encourage you to cross or, if it cannot be crossed, that I alone underwent the danger: I would seem to speak modestly. Not otherwise now, when a deeper reasoning is to be entered upon, and one almost inaccessible to your strengths; lest it should cause you dizziness and darkness, leading you into those questions to which you are not accustomed, and in this way affect you with disgrace and sadness: I think the trial should be made by me first in this way: that I both interrogate myself and respond to myself; and in this way, while you listen in safety, I may go through this whole disputation concerning the soul, by which it may be shown to be prior to the body. **CLINIAS.** You seem to speak excellently, Guest; do as you say. **ATHENIAN.** Come then, let us now more than ever invoke God with all zeal; since we are attempting to demonstrate diligently that the gods exist, let us enter upon the reasoning, with the ropes most safely stretched <note>A nautical metaphor for a ship's rigging, suggesting the argument is being carefully secured.</note>. In this disputation, I seem to respond most securely to interrogations of this kind: if someone should ask, "O friend, do all things stand still and nothing moves, or on the contrary, does nothing stand still and all things move? Or do some things move and some remain?" To this I will certainly respond that some things remain, and others move. Do they not stand and move in some place? Why not? Some do this in one seat <note>A fixed position or axis.</note>, some in many. Do you say that those things which take their power from those standing in the middle move in one place; just as circles are said to stand still, although their circumference is turned? Precisely so. We understand, however, that in this circulation, since a motion of this kind brings around the largest and smallest circle at the same time, according to proportion, it distributes itself to the larger and smaller parts; and it too, with the proportion preserved, is larger and smaller. Because of this, it has become for all...

<margin>The opinion that the principles of all things are bodies is abandoned.</margin>

<margin>He proceeds to demonstrate that the gods exist.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the Athenian Guest’s dialogue with Clinias from Plato’s *Laws*, Book X. Having previously discussed the physical nature of the universe, the Athenian is now leading Clinias through a classification of different types of motion to prove that the "soul" is the primary source of all activity in the world.</meta>

### ON THE LAWS, DIALOGUE X.
#### FOLIO 359.

...source of wonders. For one <note>referring to the motion of a sphere</note>, together with large and small circles, manages matching speeds and slownesses in such a way that it seems to perform something incredible. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** But you seem to me to be saying that movement occurs in many things—those that always pass from one place to another. Sometimes they revolve around a single center, and sometimes around many, because they are spun around. And when individual things encounter each other here and there, if they meet things that are standing still or resisting, they are split apart; but if they meet things moving toward them, they become one, and both these things and the things between them are joined and thickened. **CLINIAS.** I certainly admit these things are as you say. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, things that are joined and thickened grow larger, while things separated and thinned become smaller, as long as the previous state of each remains; but when that state does not remain, destruction follows for both. Therefore, the "generation" <note>The process of coming-into-being</note> of all things happens when a certain experience occurs: namely, when a starting principle, having taken on an increase, reaches a second transition, and from this to the next, and when it has reached as far as three <note>likely referring to the three dimensions of physical space</note>, it possesses a quality perceivable by those who have senses. By this change and transition, therefore, anything is born. It truly "is" when it remains stable. But if it is changed into another state, it is then utterly destroyed. We have now mentioned all the species of motion except two. **CLINIAS.** Which ones are those? **ATHENIAN.** O good man, we have not yet mentioned those movements for the sake of which this entire investigation exists. **CLINIAS.** Speak more clearly. **ATHENIAN.** We have undertaken this discussion for the sake of the soul. **CLINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let there be, then, one motion by which a thing can always move other things, but cannot move itself. And another by which a thing can always move both itself and others, by joining, separating, increasing, and the opposite: and furthermore by generating and destroying. This motion is distinct from all the others. **CLINIAS.** Let it be as you wish. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we not place that motion as the ninth: that by which something is moved by another and moves other things? And we shall place that one as the tenth, by which a thing moves both itself and others; which certainly adapts itself to all actions and experiences, and is truly called the "motion and transformation of all things that exist"? **CLINIAS.** Exactly so. **ATHENIAN.** Which of these ten motions should we prefer above all others as the most robust and effective? It is necessary that the one by which a thing can move both itself and others should stand apart by a very long distance, and that all the others should follow far behind. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** But one or two things were not rightly placed and must be positioned differently. **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** What we said about the tenth motion was not correctly stated. **CLINIAS.** Why? **ATHENIAN.** Because that which was numbered as the tenth is, according to reason, the first in both birth and power. And the second is that which we absurdly numbered in the ninth place. **CLINIAS.** How do you say this? **ATHENIAN.** Like this. When one thing is moved by another, and that again always by another: will there be anything in such things that is moved first? But how can that which is moved by something else be the first of those things that are moved? Certainly, that is impossible. But when something moving itself also moves another, and that another, and so on many things are moved: will there be any other beginning of the whole movement than the change of that which moved itself? **CLINIAS.** That is excellently said, and must be granted. **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, let us ask ourselves this, and answer it ourselves. If by some means all things were to stand still together, as most people of this sort dare to say, which motion among all of them would we assert happens first within them? Surely that by which a thing moves itself. For a movement depending on another will not fall upon them until some other change has first fallen upon them. Therefore, one must confess that the beginning of all motions and the first motion—which exists both in things standing still and is now present in those that move—is that by which a thing moves itself. This is the most ancient and powerful change of all; and the second is that by which something is changed by another and moves other things. **CLINIAS.** You speak most truly. **ATHENIAN.** Since we have come this far in the discussion, let us also answer this. **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** If we see this "first motion" in a body of earth, water, or fire, whether simple or mixed, what "state" shall we say is within it? **CLINIAS.** Are you asking if we should say that a thing is "alive" if it is moved by itself? **ATHENIAN.** That is it exactly. **CLINIAS.** It is alive, certainly. **ATHENIAN.** But when we see that a "soul" is in something, shall we think it is alive for any other reason than for this? **CLINIAS.** For this very reason. **ATHENIAN.** Pay attention, I pray by Jupiter, whether you wish to understand three things in any matter. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** One is the substance itself. One is the definition <note>original: *rationem*</note> of the substance. And one is the name itself. Also, there are two questions about every thing. **CLINIAS.** How two? **ATHENIAN.** Because sometimes, when a name is proposed to us, we seek the definition itself; and sometimes, having grasped the definition, we then investigate the name. But do we want to say this again? **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** A two-fold distinction is found both in other things and in numbers. And in a number thus divided, the name is "even"; but the definition is "a number divisible into two equal parts." **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** I mean something like that. Do we not signify the same thing in both cases, whether we give the definition when asked the name, or give the name when asked the definition? **CLINIAS.** Entirely the same. **ATHENIAN.** Now, for that thing whose name is "soul," what is the definition? Do we have any other definition than the one we just said: that it is able to move itself? **CLINIAS.** You assert that "being moved by itself" is the definition of that substance which we all call by the name "soul"? **ATHENIAN.** I do indeed assert it. If this is so, do we still require it to be sufficiently demonstrated that the soul is the same thing as the "first generation and motion" of things that are, that were, and that will be—and again of all their opposites—since it has appeared to be the cause of all transformation and motion in all things? **CLINIAS.** Not at all. For it has been most sufficiently shown that the soul is older than all things, since it is the principle of motion. **ATHENIAN.** Is it not true, then, that the motion which happens from one thing to another, or by which nothing ever moves itself, is second—and should be placed after the superior motion by whatever interval of numbers one wishes—since indeed...

<margin>
Which is the most ancient and powerful change.
</margin>

<margin>
The definition <note>original: *ratio*</note> of the soul: that it can move itself.
</margin>

<summary>In this passage, the Athenian Guest argues that "self-motion" is the primary cause of all activity in the universe. He concludes that the definition of the "soul" is precisely this power of self-movement, proving the soul is older and more fundamental than physical matter.</summary>
