<meta>This page continues the dialogue from Plato’s Laws, Book X, where the Athenian Guest is proving to Clinias that the soul is the primary cause of all motion and existence, predating physical matter.</meta>

# BOOK X.
## PAGE 34.

...is the change of a truly inanimate body. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** Rightly, then, and properly, and truly and absolutely, we said earlier that the soul was created before the body; whereas the body is posterior and secondary, being subject to the soul, which rules according to nature. **CLINIAS.** These things are most true. **ATHENIAN.** Do we remember that we agreed in the earlier parts of our discussion that if the soul is shown to be older than the body, then those things which belong to the soul are also shown to be prior to those which belong to the body? **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, affections, character, wills, thoughts, true opinions, cares, and memory—all these were created before the length, width, depth, and strength of bodies, just as the soul was before the body. **CLINIAS.** It must be so. **ATHENIAN.** Are we not also forced to concede that the soul is the cause of all things good and evil, honorable and base, just and unjust, and all other contraries, since we assert that it is the cause of all things? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Since the soul governs all things and dwells in everything that moves, must we not necessarily confess that it also governs the heavens? **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** One soul, then, or many? Many, certainly—let me answer for you. We must posit no fewer than two: one beneficent, and the other its opposite <note>Plato here introduces the concept of a "bad soul" or a disorderly principle to explain the existence of evil and chaos in the universe</note>. **CLINIAS.** Very rightly said.

<margin>Everything in the heaven, earth, and sea is led by the soul. What the names of the soul's motions are. The soul joined to the intellect produces all things rightly; separated, it effects the opposite.</margin>
**ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the soul leads all things in heaven, on earth, and in the sea by its own motions. The names of these motions are: willing, considering, caring, deliberating, forming right and wrong opinions, rejoicing, grieving, daring, fearing, hating, and loving. These are the primary motions. They take up the secondary motions of bodies and lead all things to growth and decay, to "concretion" (thickening) or "condensation," and to "discretion" (separation) or "rarefaction." From these follow heat, cold, weight, lightness, hardness, softness, whiteness, blackness, bitterness, sweetness, and sourness. Using all these, if the soul always takes to itself the divine Intellect <note>original: "intellectum... divinum"</note>, it rightly leads all things toward the right path and toward happiness; but if it is joined to madness <note>original: "amentia"</note>, it produces the exact opposite. Do we grant that these things are so, or are we still in doubt? **CLINIAS.** We have no doubts at all. **ATHENIAN.** Which kind of soul, then, do we believe rules the heaven, the earth, and the whole world? That which is full of mind and virtue, or that which lacks both? Shall we answer it this way? **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** Let us say this, O wonderful man: if the whole circuit of heaven and all that is in it—its progression—has a nature similar to the motion and circulation and reason of the Mind, and acts in a similar way, it is clear we must grant that the "Best Soul" takes care of the whole world and revolves it in such a manner. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** But if it moves furiously and without order, then it is the "Bad Soul" that rules. **CLINIAS.** This also is correct. **ATHENIAN.** What, then, is the nature of the motion of the Mind? This question, my friends, is difficult to answer prudently. Therefore, it is right that I answer along with you. **CLINIAS.** You speak well.

<margin>How reverently and modestly one should judge concerning God and other high things.</margin>
**ATHENIAN.** We must take care, lest—as if looking directly at the sun and experiencing night at noon—we answer as if the Mind could be sufficiently seen and known by mortal eyes. It will be safer if we look instead at an "image" of it. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Let us see which of those ten types of motion the Intellect is most similar to, so that we may use it as an image. I will bring it to your memory and answer for all. **CLINIAS.** Excellent. **ATHENIAN.** We must remember what was said by us earlier: of all things that exist, some stand still and others move. **CLINIAS.** It was said so.

<margin>A shift in the dispute: so that a higher matter may be judged through an easier one.</margin>
**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, of those that move, some move in one place, and some in many places. **CLINIAS.** This too. **ATHENIAN.** Now, the motion that always happens in one place necessarily acts around a center, similar to a sphere fashioned on a lathe <note>original: "circuli torno confecti"</note>. Therefore, it imitates the circuit of the Mind as much as possible. **CLINIAS.** Why do you say that? **ATHENIAN.** I assert that both move through the same things, in the same way, in the same place, around the same things, toward the same things, according to a single logic and a single order. If I say that the Mind and the motion that stays in one place are similar to the rotations of a sphere made on a lathe, we will never be considered unskilled makers of good images. **CLINIAS.** Very rightly so. **ATHENIAN.** On the contrary, the motion that never moves similarly, nor through the same things, nor in the same place, nor around the same things, nor with any order or reason, is surely related to total madness. **CLINIAS.** Without a doubt. **ATHENIAN.** Now we can openly proclaim that, since all things are led around by the soul, the circuit of heaven is necessarily led around by a presiding and adorning soul—either that "Best Soul" or its opposite. **CLINIAS.** But Guest, from what has been said, it now appears a sacrilege to say otherwise: that all these things are moved by anything other than the soul, filled with all virtue, whether one soul or many. **ATHENIAN.** You have understood these things very well, Clinias. But add this. **CLINIAS.** What? **ATHENIAN.** If the soul leads the sun, the moon, and the other stars, does it not lead each one individually? **CLINIAS.** Of course. **ATHENIAN.** Let us speak of one, then, in a way that can be applied to all the stars. **CLINIAS.** Which one?

<margin>The soul moves the Sun.</margin>
**ATHENIAN.** All men see the body of the Sun, but no one sees its soul—just as no one sees the soul of any other animal’s body, whether living or dead. Because this kind [of soul] is perceived by no bodily sense, it is grasped by the mind alone. Therefore, let us grasp this about the sun through intelligence alone. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** If the sun is moved by a soul, we will perhaps not be mistaken if we assert that it happens in one of three ways. **CLINIAS.** Which ways do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Either the soul is inside this round body and carries it wherever it likes—just as our soul leads us—or the soul is outside and, having found some body of fire or air (as some say), it pushes the Sun's body along by force. Or thirdly, the soul itself is naked of any body, but because it possesses other "miraculous powers" <note>original: "vires supra modum mirabiles"</note>, it guides the Sun easily. **CLINIAS.** Certainly, it is necessary that all things are moved by the soul in one of these ways. **ATHENIAN.** It is better, then—whether the soul holds that body from within like a chariot and pours light upon all, or is outside, or in whatever way one might imagine—that we all believe it to be a God. Or is it otherwise? **CLINIAS.** Truly so, unless one is possessed by extreme madness. **ATHENIAN.**

<summary>In this passage from Plato's Laws, the Athenian Guest argues that the soul is the primary mover of the universe, predating the physical body and governing all motions, including the celestial bodies like the Sun. He concludes that because the heavens move with such order, they must be guided by a "Best Soul" or divine intelligence, effectively arguing for the existence of gods.</summary>

# ON THE LAWS, DIALOGUE X.

Regarding all the stars and the moon, the years, the months, and all the seasons, what else shall we say than this very thing? Since a soul or souls, endowed with every virtue, have been demonstrated to be the causes of all these things, we shall affirm them to be gods: whether they are within bodies and, like living beings, adorn the whole heaven, or in whatever other way they are said to act. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** Thus, since these things are granted, could anyone deny that all things are full of gods? <note>This is a famous phrase often attributed to the early philosopher Thales, which Plato uses here to conclude that divinity permeates the entire cosmos.</note> **CLINIAS.** No one is so out of his mind, guest. **ATHENIAN.** To him, therefore, who denies that the gods exist, let us leave the conversation, having set the boundaries, O Clinias and Megillus. **CLINIAS.** What boundaries shall we impose? **ATHENIAN.** Either he must teach us that we do not think correctly when we say the soul is the first generation of all things; and that the other things said by us consequently are not true. Or, if he can say nothing better than we, let him believe us, and so live for the future that he does not doubt the gods. But let us now consider whether we have sufficiently shown that the gods exist against those who deny them, or not. **CLINIAS.** It has been sufficiently said, guest. **ATHENIAN.** Let the dispute against those men, then, have an end. But that man who already
<margin>That the gods have care for human affairs.</margin>
says the gods exist, yet denies they have care for human affairs, must be persuaded by us thus. "O excellent man," let us say, "a certain nature kindred to divinity leads you to affirm and honor that which is joined to you, since you assert the gods exist. But the successes of wicked and unjust men, both public and private—which, though they are not truly happy, the common people hold as happy and frequently extol in songs and other speeches—rashly drive you headlong toward impiety. Or perhaps when you see wicked men reaching old age, leaving children and grandchildren in the greatest honors, you are greatly troubled. You have heard, perhaps, or even seen for yourself some who, though they have performed many unjust and impious deeds, have nevertheless risen from a small thing to a great one through those very crimes, and from the lowest rank have arrived at tyranny. For this reason, since you are unwilling to accuse the gods of being the authors of these things because of your very connection with them, yet being led by some absurdity and unable to be angry with the gods themselves, you have at last fallen into this: that although you think the gods exist, you believe human affairs are neglected by them." Therefore, lest this opinion push you toward a more grievous disease of impiety, let us apply a remedy according to our strength by refuting this opinion. Wherefore, we shall join the following dispute with the preceding reasoning, which we used against those who denied that gods exist. You, Clinias and Megillus, answer for the young man <note>The Athenian is addressing an imaginary young skeptic who believes the gods are indifferent</note>, as you have done until now. And if any difficult point arises, I will take it up for you and lead you across the river as I just did. **CLINIAS.** You speak rightly; so do it, and we also will do our part according to our strength. **ATHENIAN.** It will perhaps not be difficult to demonstrate that the gods have no less care for the smallest things than for the greatest;
<margin>The gods have care for both the greatest things, which is the virtue of the gods by which they are good.</margin>
especially since it was said a little while ago that they, being filled with every virtue, claim the providence of all things as their own. **CLINIAS.** Most certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us investigate together what follows: what is their virtue by which they are conceded to be good? Come, do they not grant that being temperate and having a mind belong to the virtues, and their contraries to vice? **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** What further? Does not courage also belong to virtue, and cowardice to vice? **CLINIAS.** Greatly so. **ATHENIAN.** And of these, some they call base, others honorable? **CLINIAS.** It must be so. **ATHENIAN.** And those vices which are among these, we might say exist in us: but shall we in no way say the gods are participants in them? **CLINIAS.** Who would even grant this? **ATHENIAN.** Shall we think negligence,
luxury, and idleness are virtues of the soul? Or otherwise? **CLINIAS.** How could it be otherwise? **ATHENIAN.** Are they not the opposite? **CLINIAS.** Yes, indeed. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, the contraries of these belong to the opposite. **CLINIAS.** So it is. **ATHENIAN.** He who is given to luxury, negligence, and idleness, whom
Hesiod says is most like the shiftless drones <note>A reference to Hesiod's *Works and Days*, comparing lazy men to drones in a beehive</note>, is he not hateful to us? **CLINIAS.** Most rightly indeed did that poet
<margin>Hesiod</margin>
sing. **ATHENIAN.** It must not be said, then, that a god has those manners which he hates; nor must anyone be permitted to say so. **CLINIAS.** By no means. **ATHENIAN.** Can he, to whom the execution and care of some work chiefly belongs, care for the great in that work but despise the small? If we praised this opinion, would we not err? But let us consider it thus. Does not either a man or a god neglect things for two reasons? **CLINIAS.** For which? **ATHENIAN.** Either because he thinks it makes no difference to the whole if small things are neglected, or because, although he thinks it does matter, he neglects them through laziness and softness. For otherwise negligence does not happen. For when someone cannot carry out the care of all things great and small, and thus hindered by weakness does not care for them, negligence is not then said to be in him, whether it be a man who is powerless or if a god were imagined to be unable. **CLINIAS.** Certainly not. **ATHENIAN.** But now let those two men answer the three of us—one who concedes gods exist but thinks they are easily appeased, the other who thinks they are negligent in small matters. First, let them be asked thus: "You both affirm that the gods know, see, and hear all things; and that nothing can escape them of those things which are perceived either by sense or by intellect. Do you say these things are so? Or otherwise?" "So." "Next, that they can do all things which mortals or immortals can?" **CLINIAS.** Without doubt they will concede it is so. **ATHENIAN.** "And that they are good, even the best, we have all confessed." **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** "It is therefore impossible for them to be seized by any laziness or softness, since they are such as we have agreed they are." For from cowardice in us
<margin>idleness laziness</margin>
idleness is born; and laziness from idleness and softness. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, none of the gods, corrupted by idleness and laziness, neglects anything. For a god is a participant in no cowardice. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** It remains then, if they neglect small and few things in the universe, that they either neglect them because they know those things are to be despised, or some other reason remains, which is the contrary of this. **CLINIAS.** Nothing else at all. **ATHENIAN.** Which, then, O excellent man, shall we affirm you are saying? Is it because of ignorance that they do not provide, when they ought to provide? Or like we say of wicked men, that they see the better things but, broken by pleasure or pain, follow the worse; do the gods, though they know they must provide, similarly not provide? **CLINIAS.** How could that happen? **ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, human affairs participate in a living nature; and man himself, before all other animals, is a most diligent worshiper of god. **CLINIAS.** It appears so.

<summary>The Athenian Guest argues that since the gods possess perfect virtue—including wisdom, courage, and temperance—they cannot be guilty of the human vices of laziness or negligence. Therefore, it is impossible for the gods to ignore even the smallest details of human life or the universe.</summary>

# BOOK X.

**ATHENIAN.** Furthermore, we say that all mortal living things are made and possessed by the gods, just as the entire heaven is. **CLINIAS.** Undoubtedly. **ATHENIAN.** Now, whether one says these things are small or great to the gods, in no way—since they are most provident and best—should they neglect their own possession. But let us consider this further. **CLINIAS.** What is that? **ATHENIAN.** Whether the senses and powers naturally stand in a contrary relationship to one another regarding ease and difficulty. **CLINIAS.** What do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** Indeed, small things are seen and heard with more difficulty than large ones. But small and few things are held, carried, and governed by providence more easily than their opposites <note>The Athenian is arguing that while it is harder for *us* to see small things, it is actually *easier* for a manager to control small things than large ones.</note>. **CLINIAS.** Certainly much more easily. **ATHENIAN.** What then: when a doctor wishes and is able to cure the whole body, if he provides for the large parts but neglects the small, will the whole ever be well for him? **CLINIAS.** Never. **ATHENIAN.** But neither pilots, nor generals, nor heads of households, nor governors of cities, nor any such people at all, will rightly govern many and great things if the few and small are neglected. For architects also say that large stones are not well laid without small ones. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** Let us take care, however, lest we think God more worthless than mortal craftsmen. For the more skilled they are, the more exquisitely and perfectly they complete both small and large things simultaneously in their own works with a single art. But will God, who is most wise and both can and wants to care, provide only for great things? And will he neglect the small, which are easier to govern, due to laziness and sloth? **CLINIAS.** By no means, guest, do we think this opinion of the gods should be admitted. For this thought is wicked and entirely false. **ATHENIAN.** We seem now to have disputed enough against him who accuses the gods of the crime of negligence. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** But so far, we have in a way compelled him by reason to confess that his opinion is false. I think he also needs persuasion, which might captivate him like a kind of song. **CLINIAS.** What is this persuasion? **ATHENIAN.** Let us persuade this youth: that he who provides for the whole organizes everything toward the virtue and salvation of the whole. Each part of this whole acts and suffers what is fitting for it according to its strength. And there are rulers set over each of these parts, who have care even for the smallest actions and passions, arranged through every single and extreme particle of the universe to the very end. One of these is your own little part, O wretched man, which always looks toward the whole, though it is very small. But you are ignorant that every generation of individual things happens for the sake of the whole, so that the life of the universe itself may be blessed. Its existence is not for your sake; but you were made for its sake. For every doctor and skilled craftsman does individual things for the sake of the whole, and directs all things toward common perfection; he does not refer the whole to a part, but refers individual parts to the whole. But you are troubled because you do not know how that which is best for you is simultaneously fitting for the universe and for you, through the power of a common origin. Since the soul is always joined with a body, now with one, then with another, and changes through various mutations, either because of itself or because of another soul, nothing else remains for the ordainer of these things—like one throwing dice—than to change them as if by rearranging: placing better characters into a better place, and worse into a worse place, as fits each one, so that each may obtain the fate suitable to itself. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean that? **ATHENIAN.** I seem to speak of that method by which the gods most easily provide for all things. For if someone, always looking to the whole, fashions each thing and transforms all things toward it—as if making an animated water out of fire, and not many things at once from one, or one from many, participating in the first, second, or third generation—the arrangements of this rearrangement will be infinite in number. But now, there is a wonderful ease in his work who provides for the whole. **CLINIAS.** In what way do you say that again? **ATHENIAN.** Thus: Since the King saw that all human actions are animated, and that they have much virtue in them and also much depravity; and that what has been made—soul and body—does not suffer destruction, yet is not eternal, as the gods are (for if either of these were destroyed, all generation of living things would cease); furthermore, that what is good for the soul helps, and what is evil harms it; since he saw all these things, I say, he therefore devised where each part might be located most effectively and easily to provide victory for virtue and an impediment for vice throughout the universe. He therefore invented for this universe what sort of thing each action should become, and what sort of quality it should have, and which and what kind of places it ought to receive by lot. But he left the causes of becoming such or such to our own wills. For wherever someone desires, and of whatever sort the mind is, there it almost always dwells; and it becomes such, for the most part. **CLINIAS.** Fittingly. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, all things that have a soul change, since they have the cause of change within themselves. Once changed, they are moved according to the order and law of fate. And those that have sinned less wander less deeply and on the surface of the region; those that sin more and more atrociously fall into the depths and sink into the lower region. <margin>Names for souls:</margin> calling that lower region by the name and terms [of the underworld], which both the living and those released from bodies dream of and dread. But the soul that possesses greater virtue or vice, when it has changed more vehemently by its own will and constant habit and has adhered to divine virtue, becomes especially such: it is transferred to a place altogether much better and holy. But the one affected in the opposite way spends its life having been transferred to the opposite. This, O boy and youth who think you are neglected by the gods, is the judgment of the gods who inhabit heaven: that as you become worse, you go to worse souls; as you become better, to better souls; both in life and in every death you shall proceed, and you shall suffer and do what is fitting for like to be done by like. Therefore, neither you nor any other should hope or trust that you will be so fortunate as to escape and surpass this judgment of the gods. For those who ordained this established it more firmly than all other things; so it must be completely guarded against. For you will never be neglected by him—neither if you are so small that you enter into the depths of the earth, nor if you become so sublime that you fly into heaven raised on wings; but you will pay the fitting penalties, whether remaining here, or having gone to the underworld, or having been transferred to some more remote and inaccessible place. The same reasoning applies to those whom you observed to have escaped from being small men into great ones through wicked crimes, and whom you thought had attained happiness from misery. In whose actions, as if in a mirror, you thought you saw the gods' negligence toward all things, because you were ignorant of how their progress benefits the universe. It is not fitting, O most excellent man, to be ignorant of this; for he who does not know it can never perceive the form of living...

<summary>In this passage, Plato argues that the gods exercise providence over every detail of the universe, no matter how small, and that they have established a system of divine justice where souls are redistributed to better or worse states based on their moral choices.</summary>

-> **ON THE LAWS, BOOK X. FOLIO 361.** <-

...will not be able to speak of the happiness or misery of life. Therefore, here, this entire assembly of elders has persuaded you that you are entirely ignorant of what you say about the gods. God will have favored you enough if you accept this; but if you still desire some reason, listen to what we shall say to that third group. If you are a participant in reason at all, I think it has been sufficiently demonstrated that the gods exist and provide for humans. But we must by no means allow it to be said that they can be corrupted by the gifts of wicked men; and if it is said, it must be refuted with all our strength. **CLINIAS.** Excellently said; and so we shall do. **ATHENIAN.** Come then, by the gods themselves, in what way do they become appeasable—if indeed they do? And what kind of beings are they if they are appeased? For they must be princes, since they are to govern the entire heaven perpetually. **CLINIAS.** Certainly. **ATHENIAN.** But to what kind of princes are they similar? Or what princes are similar to them, so that it is possible for us to compare the lesser to the greater? Are they like the drivers of competing chariots? Or the pilots of ships? Perhaps they can be compared to the leaders of armies, or to doctors who ward off and repel the wars of diseases from human bodies? Or to farmers who watch for and guard against storms hostile to rising crops? Or even to the shepherds of flocks and herds? For since we have agreed among ourselves that the heaven is full of many good things and many evils—and indeed more of the former—this is a kind of immortal war and requires a wonderful guardianship, but both the gods and spirits <note>original: "dęmones"; in Plato's thought, these are intermediary beings between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> help us. We are the possession of the gods and spirits. Indeed, injustice and intemperance along with imprudence <term>imprudentia: a lack of foresight or wisdom</term> corrupt us. But justice and temperance along with prudence, which dwell in the living powers of the gods, bring us safety. It is clearly possible to see a small portion of these qualities dwelling here in us. For certain unjust souls dwelling on earth, fierce like wild beasts, rise up against the souls of the guardians—such as dogs or shepherds, or even the highest masters—and by the allurements of words and the prayers of certain chants, they persuade them (as the rumor of the wicked goes) that by acting wickedly they may seize much for themselves among men and pay no penalty for it. This fault, which gasps for the seizing of more, we call "disease" in the bodies of animals, "pestilence" in the seasons of the year, and in cities and republics, with a changed name, we call it "injustice." **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** It is necessary, therefore, for him who believes the gods grant forgiveness to unjust men (if one gives them a portion of the loot) to say that they are like dogs to whom wolves grant a small part of the prey, and they, appeased by these gifts, allow the flocks to be torn apart. Is this not the talk of those who preach that the gods are appeasable? **CLINIAS.** It certainly is. **ATHENIAN.** But to which of the aforementioned guardians could one compare the gods without being the most ridiculous of all men? To pilots who, diverted by the pouring of wine and the smell of roasting meat, overturn both ship and sailors? **CLINIAS.** Not at all. **ATHENIAN.** Nor to chariot drivers who, while competing, are corrupted by gifts and concede the victory itself to the chariots of their adversaries. **CLINIAS.** Certainly not. For this comparison is a shameful thing to say of the gods. **ATHENIAN.** Yet they are not similar to commanders, nor doctors, nor farmers, nor shepherds similarly persuaded, nor even to dogs lured away by the cunning of wolves. **CLINIAS.** Speak better words, I pray! <note>original: "Bona verba quęso"; a standard Roman formula used to ward off bad omens or blasphemy.</note> These things are not to be heard. **ATHENIAN.** Are not all the gods the greatest of all guardians, over the greatest of things? **CLINIAS.** Indeed they are. **ATHENIAN.** Shall we say then that the guardians of the best things, who are exceedingly excellent in the virtue of guardianship, are worse than dogs or mediocre men, who would never betray justice for gifts impiously accepted from unjust men? **CLINIAS.** By no means is this talk to be endured; and he who suffers from this opinion will be judged by right as the worst and most profane of all the impious. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, those three things we proposed—namely, that the gods exist, that they have care for all things, and that they cannot be turned from justice by any prayers—we seem to have sufficiently shown. **CLINIAS.** Certainly; and we agree with these reasons. **ATHENIAN.** We have spoken somewhat more vehemently because of the controversies of wicked men. But for this reason, O friend Clinias, we have used a contentious speech, lest the base, thinking they have won in the speaking, believe they have been given license to do whatever they wish, and whatever they think should be done against the gods. For this reason, I say, we wished to use a new and more vehement way of speaking. Because if we have brought anything toward persuasion, so that they might now be willing to hate their own habits and embrace the opposite, then the preamble of the laws concerning impiety has been well spoken by us. **CLINIAS.** We hope it will be so; but if not, at least the style of the speech will not be a disgrace to the lawmaker. **ATHENIAN.** After the preamble, the speech of the interpreter of laws follows correctly, which preaches to all the impious that they should turn themselves from their habits toward piety. But against those who do not obey, let this law concerning impiety be placed. If anyone acts or speaks impiously in any way, let whoever happens to be present defend the gods and signify it to the magistrates. Let the first of the magistrates who hears it bring them to the judgment of these matters according to the laws. But if any magistrate hears it and does not report it, let him be held guilty of impiety himself; and let anyone who wishes prosecute him for the vengeance of the laws. And if anyone is condemned, let the judges affect him with punishments for each impious act committed. Let all be restrained by prisons. There are, indeed, three prisons in the city. One is common to most in the marketplace of things for sale, where many are guarded so they do not flee. The second is where the assembly of those who congregate at night takes place, called by the name of "Correction" <note>This refers to the *Sophronisterion*, a house of reformation for those who are not beyond hope.</note>. The third is in the middle region, where the place is most deserted and wild, marked by the name of "Punishment" <note>This refers to the *Timoria*, a place of severe punishment or execution for the incorrigible.</note>. There are also three causes of impiety, as we narrated above. And since two types proceed from each individual cause of this kind, there will be six types of sins against the gods, which are worthy to be judged; nor do they require an equal and similar penalty. For some, although they do not believe the gods exist, yet because of a certain just disposition of nature, they hate the wicked; and moved by a certain hatred against injustice, they abstain from injuries, flee from the unjust, and love just men. But others, in addition to this opinion—that all things are destitute of the presence of the gods—are also more prone to pleasures and pains, and they excel in sharpness of mind and memory. To both of these, it is common that they deny the gods exist. But in this they differ: that one is less [harmful] to other men, while this one is more...

# THE ARGUMENT TO DIALOGUE XI ON THE LAWS

...is harmful. That man indeed speaks freely against the gods, sacrifices, and oaths; and thus, by mocking others, unless he is punished, he will perhaps make many people like himself. But this other man holds the same opinion, yet is thought by the common people to be endowed with a sharper wit; he is full of craft and deceit. From such men many sorcerers are made, and they are prone to every kind of poisoning and sorcery. Furthermore, from these men sometimes come tyrants, leaders of armies, public speakers, those who plot against private ceremonies, and those who deceive men with the little traps of the <term>sophists</term> <note>Sophists were professional teachers in ancient Greece often accused of using clever but fallacious reasoning for profit.</note>. Indeed, there are many types of these men, but two are worthy of the establishment of laws. One of these, which is full of hypocrisy, gives birth to crimes worthy not just of one death or two, but many. The other requires both chastisement and chains. Similarly, the opinion that the gods are negligent gives rise to two types; and that they are easily appeased by prayers and gifts gives rise to two more. Since the impious are thus distinguished, the judge shall cast those who became so not from evil character but from a certain madness into a prison of correction for no less than five years. During this time, no citizen shall speak with them, except for those who are members of the **Nocturnal Council** <note>The "Nocturnal Council" was Plato's proposed supreme judicial and religious oversight body, meeting before dawn to discuss the preservation of the laws.</note>; these men, however, shall speak with them to offer warnings for the salvation of the soul. But when the time of imprisonment has expired, if the man has become more moderate, let him live among the moderate; but if he is condemned again on a charge of impiety, let him be punished with death. But there are some who, in addition to the opinion that the gods either do not exist, or are negligent, or are easily appeased, also become monstrous; they despise men, and while living they allure and attract many to themselves, and they even claim to draw and console the dead; they profess that they soothe the gods themselves with chants, sacrifices, and prayers. By this seduction, they attempt to ruin entire houses and cities for the sake of money. Whoever among them is condemned shall be bound in prisons in the interior of the country, and no free person shall ever approach him; but a slave shall bring him the food decreed for him by the guardians of the laws. Finally, when he has finished his life, let him be cast out beyond the borders of the region without burial. If any free person buries him, let him be accused of the crime of impiety by anyone who wishes. But if he leaves behind children sufficient for the city, let the guardians of orphans take care of them no less than the others from the day he was condemned. But let this general law be established for all these cases: it will ensure that many sin less against the gods in word and deed, and that they are recalled from their madness by the fact that it will not be permitted to fashion gods and sacred rites for oneself contrary to the laws. Let a law of this kind be simply set before all: **No one may have shrines in a private house.** <margin>No one may have shrines in a private house.</margin> When someone is moved in his soul to sacrifice, let him go to public places to sacrifice, and let him offer the victims to the priests, who handle the care of these matters with the utmost purity. Let him pray with them, along with whoever else wishes to pray with him. This is done because it is not easy to establish shrines and gods. Indeed, it requires great talent to do this thing correctly. But it is the custom, especially for women and the weak, and those placed in danger or in need—whenever anyone is in want, or conversely when an abundance of something flows in—to always consecrate whatever seems to be present, to vow victims, and to promise statues to gods, spirits, and the sons of gods. Moved by apparitions while awake, and similarly remembering many things seen in dreams out of fear, they try to bring remedies to each thing and fill all houses and villages with altars and shrines. For the sake of all these, this law must be established; and furthermore, because of the impious: lest by usurping these practices for their own works, they should set up shrines and altars in their own houses, thinking they can secretly appease the gods with prayers and sacrifices; and thus they would increase their injustice infinitely, whereby they would provoke the indignation of the gods against both themselves and those who allow them these things, thinking they are better. In this way, the whole city might be held, in a sense, by the crime of impiety. The Law will certainly not be angry. For let the Law be: **No one shall possess shrines of the gods in private houses.** If someone is found to have had them or to have sacrificed elsewhere than in public, let whoever perceives it report it to the guardians of the laws. If no great crime has been committed by the woman or man, let them be ordered to move the private sacred objects to the public temples; and if they are not moved immediately, let them be fined until they are moved. But if anyone has committed not a childish but a nefarious impiety, whether he has offended in his own private place or in public by sacrificing in the worship of the gods, let him be condemned to death as one sacrificing impiously. Whether the act is childish or not, the guardians of the laws shall judge; and having thus dragged the impious into judgment, let them declare them guilty of impiety.

### Marsilio Ficino’s Argument on the Eleventh Dialogue of the Laws.

<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was the scholar who translated Plato's works into Latin, making them accessible to Renaissance Europe. His "arguments" serve as introductory commentaries.</note>

Our Plato, just as he is the wisest of all philosophers and the most eloquent of orators, so he is the most prudent of all legal experts. In order that he might not be forced, as others usually are, to produce a vast work of laws and interpretations in vain regarding contracts, he rightly strove—before descending to contracts and forensic commerce—to make the citizens good through disciplines, laws, judgments, and religion. He hoped that just men, even without laws, would spontaneously provide faith and truth in every business deal. And indeed, quite opportunely after the laws concerning judgments pertaining to persons, he brings into the open the laws of judgments regarding property. By these, both foreigners and citizens may learn to deposit things justly, to keep what has been deposited, and to honor agreements; not to move the property of others, to return to each his own, how to treat children, freedmen, and slaves; how to sell, buy, return, lead, serve in the military, protect orphans, make a will, preserve testaments, administer inheritances, arrange marriages, conduct a divorce, and govern a family. Above all others, they should religiously revere their parents; they should adulterate nothing, hate sorcery, avoid anger and childishness, flee quarrels, insults, and slanders, restore damages, and keep the truth in testimonies and oaths. And this is essentially the material of this eleventh book. After these things, however, as we are accustomed to do, we think certain more obscure points should be briefly explained. First, know that the goddess of the journey is twofold: the one who points the way and the one who preserves. And the former indeed is the light under the name of the Moon; the latter, however, is faith under the name of **Diana**. <note>original: "sub Dianę noīe fidē"</note> And whatever is found by chance on the road belonging to another must be dedicated to the god; as if...

# THE ARGUMENT FOR DIALOGUE XI ON THE LAWS
360 [handwritten], FO. CCCLXII.

V ii

Whatever prosperity you experience should be referred to the providence of God. Contemplate the Platonic goodness: he forbids, in both buying and selling, not only the adulteration of goods, false measures, and false weights, but even the taking of oaths. Indeed, he forbids praising a thing for sale or changing the price on the same day. Learn this well: <note>original: "Nemo diis invocatis mendacium dicat, aut decipiat, aut adulterare verbo vel re quicquam audeat, nisi deo velit odio esse."</note> "Let no one speak a lie while calling upon the gods, nor let anyone dare to deceive or falsify in word or deed, unless he wishes to be hated by God." For first, he who swears falsely and holds the gods in low regard is hated by Him; and next, he who lies in the presence of his elders. See again and again how free and upright Plato wishes the characters of the citizens to be, from whom he drives far away all license for <term>haggling</term> <note>cauponandi: the business of innkeeping or small-scale retail trade, often associated with dishonesty in the ancient world</note>. He adds also that both great wealth and extreme poverty are diseases of character. For from the former comes inflation <note>or pride/arrogance</note>, and from the latter, men become weaker and more abject.

But where he says that Pallas, Vulcan, and Mars preside over the arts, gather this from the many Platonic mysteries passed down here and there: that a certain <term>trinity</term> <note>Ficino often maps Christian concepts like the Trinity onto Plato’s polytheistic framework to make them compatible with Renaissance theology.</note> of divine beings, whom we call the "Craftsmen" in the Platonic style, always stands by Jupiter, the supreme architect of the world. In this trinity, Pallas is first, Vulcan is second, and Mars is third. But just as the whole trinity refers back to Jupiter himself from whom it originates, so Vulcan and Mars generally refer back to Pallas. I will pass over for now that he seems to have dreamed of Power in Mars, Wisdom in Pallas, and a Fiery Spirit in Vulcan. 

Certainly, three things are required for the art of Jupiter himself, by which he perfects the universe. First, the plan through which individual things are to be made. Second, the effective execution of those things conceived by reason. Third, the safety and defense of those things which must be carried out in effect. He names the first "Idea" as Pallas; the second as Vulcan; the third as Mars. And because both—namely conservation or defense, as well as the execution or exposition of things—require reason and wisdom, Pallas rules over both Vulcan and Mars. Whatever is either fabricated by Vulcan, or defended by Mars after it is fabricated and preserved in its own form, is done under the leadership of Pallas. 

We see three traces of these three ruling powers in divine art also in nature: through Pallas, **order**, by which individuals are arranged; through Vulcan, **effective progress** and a prompt "birth," so to speak, toward which all things hasten; and finally through Mars, the **most fortified structure** applied by the generators to the generated, and the various natural defenses protecting them from their opposites. These three children exist in human art, which ought to be civil above all: that they might first devise individual things wisely before they are made; then execute them maturely and vigorously; and finally preserve and bravely defend the forms that have been devised and produced. And so that we may know that human art depends no less than nature upon God himself and the Ideas in completing all these things, he says those three gods preside over human arts. 

But lest we think we have received only the arts from the gods, he added that the gods, as the givers of life, ought to be revered above all else—to the extent that even their names should not be uttered shamelessly or rashly. Instead, all things, even the smallest pertaining to them, should be handled purely, reverently, and chastely. Nothing holier than these precepts could be imagined, if only he had named God, rather than gods. But behold, he introduced the one substance of the highest Jupiter; nor did he multiply substances while he multiplied Ideas. What more do we desire in him? Furthermore, where he names gods, he feels no differently than what was said: "Thousands of thousands ministered to Him." <note>A reference to Daniel 7:10, equating Plato's many gods with Christian angels.</note>

Nor should we pass over in silence what he says about receiving the soul from God. This must be understood as the **middle life** between that which remains in eternity (which is the angelic nature, all at once) and that which is bounded by a certain time. This middle life is composed of eternity and time; in it, like the substance of the heavens, it always remains, yet its action and affection always flow. Therefore, in the previous book, he said the soul both *is* and *becomes* at the same time, and is indissoluble—yet not "eternal" in the way the gods are by law (that is, not entirely unchanging). He said the gods (meaning the angels) remain, not of themselves, but by divine law, which establishes them as eternally stable despite being mobile in their own nature. He says the body too is indissoluble—certainly the celestial body. Perhaps also the elemental body, insofar as the mass of the elements and primary matter do not perish; of which he says in the *Statesman* that the body is sometimes divinely recreated.

You will note where he speaks of wills and testaments: that the person and property of any citizen do not belong to himself, but to the fatherland. Likewise, where he treats the care of orphans: that the souls of the deceased sense our affairs and care for them. I say they "sense" through the celestial and airy body, and they "care" through various things to which they are more inclined by nature, habit, or divine providence. Especially those souls which, having held a "middle life," also occupy a "middle region." I say "middle" both in location and quality. In location, it is between heaven and earth; in quality, it is between supreme happiness and extreme misery. 

For it must be remembered that in the previous book it was said: just as nature assigns appropriate places to matching natures, so when souls become such-and-such by their own actions, they consequently migrate through the nature of similarity to degrees and seats that are like them. Thus, those made heavenly seek heavenly things; those made earthly seek earthly things; and those made of air seek the air. Indeed, while Plato may not dare to affirm certain other things about souls, he asserts this much most clearly both here and in the book on knowledge <note>referring to the *Meno* or *Theaetetus*</note>, and signifies it often elsewhere. Whence he says we must be careful not to harm orphans, lest the souls of their parents be justly angered with us. Therefore, in the ninth book, while dealing with homicides, he says souls are indignant at their killers. Similar to this is the idea that the souls of Marius’s followers troubled Sulla; hence also the tragedies depict the Furies driving Orestes mad. 

Pay attention after this where he treats the worship of parents: he says the sacred statues of the gods should be honored, not for themselves, but because they signify the gods to us. But parents are even more to be honored, as if they were the **living images of the gods**. He adds that the curses of parents against children are heard by God, and that nothing but pestilence happens to such children. You will hear again after many things what is truly Platonic: the wicked are troubled by punishments, not because of what they have done (for what is done cannot be undone), but so that no such thing may happen hereafter, and so that they may pursue injustice with the same hatred as those who punish them, or at least sin less in a similar vice. Furthermore, a judge is the interpreter of the legislator and a minister of justice. He then punishes whisperers and detractors, those who rebuke and rail in anger, those who offend serious persons with biting jokes, and those who grow too sharply angry while joking. You will hear that divine vengeance is most to be feared...

# BOOK XI. ON THE LAWS.

...is mentioned, where someone lies in testimonies and oaths. You will hear, finally, that in testimony and under oath, the truth itself must be confirmed by Themis, Jupiter, and Apollo. By **Themis**, indeed, he signifies law and divine right <note>original: "ius fasque"</note>, both civil and sacred: both among men and before God. This is so that anyone testifying understands that by lying under oath, they sin gravely against human and divine law, against men, and against God. By **Jupiter**, truly, who shakes all things with a nod, let him recognize: if he sins, he will by no means escape divine vengeance. By **Phoebus** <note>Apollo</note>, however, let him not trust that his crimes, whether present or past, can remain hidden from the one who foretells all future things through prophecy.

### DIALOGUE XI. ON THE LAWS OR ON THE GIVING OF LAWS.

->ATHE.<- <note>The "Athenian Stranger," the primary speaker in Plato's Laws.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a classical figure or deity amidst foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>It is right that we speak of contracts; and let us assign a fitting order to them. Let this be the simple rule: let no one touch my things by force, nor move even the smallest of my belongings, unless he has persuaded me. And I, being likewise of sound mind, shall act in the same way regarding the things of others. In the first place, when we speak of a **treasure** which someone has deposited for himself and his heirs, which was not belonging to my parents—I should never wish to find it, nor if I found it, should I move it. Nor should I believe the soothsayers <note>original: "Ariolis"</note> advising me to take what was deposited. For money will never profit me as much, if I take it, as I shall excel in virtue of soul and justice if I do not take it. Therefore, for the possession of money, the better possession for me will be justice of the soul, if I prefer virtue to riches. Indeed, since he speaks well of many things: that what is "immovable" should not be moved, he speaks quite beautifully regarding this one thing. But the common report regarding these matters must also be believed: that these things do not benefit the lineage of one's children. 

If anyone, however, cares nothing for his children and neglects the lawgiver—and thus takes what neither he nor any of his people deposited, against the will of him who deposited it—let him look upon that most excellent and simple law, which a noble man promulgated, who said: **"What you did not lay down, do not take up."** 

What, therefore, ought this man to suffer, who has despised these two lawgivers, and has taken what he himself did not deposit—not some small thing that he carried off, but a great treasure? What penalty for this is owed by the gods, God himself knows. But what is owed by men, we shall declare. He who first sees it should inform the judges. If the crime is in the city, inform the **Aediles** <note>city officials in charge of public order</note>; if in the fields, the curators of the fields and their leaders; or in the marketplace, let him signify it to the curators of sales. Once the matter is revealed, let the city send word to **Delphi**, and whatever is said by the oracle of the god, both concerning the money and the one who moved the money, let the city confirm that, following the god. And he who gave the information, if he is a free man, let him gain a reputation for virtue, and conversely for vice if he knowingly concealed it. But if he is a slave, he is to be set free, with the city paying the price to his master. A slave, however, who concealed it, is to be punished with death. 

This law is followed by a similar one regarding both small and large things. If someone leaves his property somewhere, whether willingly or otherwise, let the one who happens to find it not touch it, but think that the **Goddess of the Road** <note>original: "deam itineris," likely referring to Hecate or Enodia, protectors of travelers and crossroads</note> preserves these things as consecrated for him by law. Whoever, despising this law, carries these things to his home—if he is a slave and the item is of small value, let him be struck with many lashes by anyone who meets him and is over thirty years of age. But if he is a free man, let him first be considered illiberal and a transgressor; then, let him also pay back ten times the value of the thing he moved to the one who left it. 

When someone complains that something of theirs, great or small, is held by another—and that person admits to having it but denies it belongs to the one seeking it—if the item is registered with the magistrates according to the law, let the seeker call the holder before the magistrate. Once the matter is revealed, if it is registered that the thing belongs to the adversary, let him have it. But if it is found to belong to neither, but to some absent person, and if the holder does not give sufficient **surety** <note>original: "fideiussionem," a legal guarantee or bail</note> that he will return the thing to the absent owner, let him be forced to deposit an equal amount. Truly, if the thing in question is not registered with the magistrates, then let it be deposited with three of the senior magistrates until a sentence is passed. And if it is an animal about which there is a dispute, once the sentence is passed, the one who lost the case must repay the cost of its feed to the magistrates. Let that judgment be finished within three days. 

Any person of sound mind may lead his slave where he wishes, intending to use him honorably; he may also lead the slave of friends or relatives to restore a fugitive to favor. But if someone claims a person being led as a slave is actually free, let the one who took him release him. If the one thus led provides three worthy sureties, let him be rescued by right. Otherwise, if the captor takes him away by force, let him be seen as having committed violence; once condemned, let him restore double the damage to the one from whom he took him. 

Each person may also bring back his **freedman** <note>a formerly enslaved person</note> if he is not being honored by him, or if he is not honored sufficiently. "Honor," however, is first: that he comes to the master’s house three times every month and shows himself ready to do whatever is honorable and possible for him; next, that regarding marriage, he does whatever seems best to the master. Nor is it permitted for him to acquire greater riches for himself than those possessed by the one who freed him; rather, whatever excess he has shall be given to the master. 

A freedman, like other **foreigners** <note>original: "peregrini"</note>, shall not remain in the city beyond twenty years; but after that time, having taken his goods, let him depart, unless he has persuaded his former master and the magistrates otherwise. If the wealth of a freedman or any foreigner exceeds the **third census** <note>a specific high tier of taxable property</note>, on the thirtieth day after this is discovered, let him depart with his belongings, nor shall any further opportunity to stay be granted by the magistrates. If anyone is condemned for not obeying this law, let him be punished with death, and his goods shall be confiscated to the public treasury. Let the judges of the tribes take notice of these things, unless the litigants have first been reconciled by neighbors and arbitrators. 

If someone says an animal or some other thing is theirs, let the one who has it refer to the one who sold it, or who legitimately and sufficiently gave it, or however else it was validly and firmly handed over. And if the truth is referred to a citizen or a resident of the city, let it be found within thirty days; but if it is referred to outsiders, within five months—of which the middle month is that in which the sun turns from the summer circle to the winter...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of civil regulations in Plato’s ideal state, specifically moving from the general principles of contracts and property into the granular laws of the marketplace (the *agora*). It establishes rules for the sale of slaves with hidden defects, the prohibition of price-haggling, and the regulation of trade and innkeeping.</meta>

# ON THE LAWS OR ON THE LATIN LAWS DIALOGUE XI. FOLIO 363.
V iii

...returns poorly. Whatever things are exchanged by buying and selling must be exchanged in the designated place of the marketplace, by giving and receiving the item and the price of the item on the spot, and nowhere else. No buying or selling should be done on credit <note>original: "ad terminum," meaning a deferred payment or deadline</note>. If an exchange is made otherwise or in other places, let there be no legal judgment regarding it according to the law. Nor should a judgment be granted regarding a contribution, when several people pool money or anything else together to conduct some business between themselves.

A seller who has received no less than thirty **drachmas** <note>A silver coin of ancient Greece; thirty drachmas was a significant sum, roughly a month's wages for a skilled worker</note> as the price for a sold item must necessarily wait ten days in the city; the buyer must not be ignorant of his lodging. We wish this to be done for the sake of the returns and legitimate complaints that are customary in these matters.

A legitimate return is distinguished from an illegitimate one as follows: when someone has sold a slave suffering from **phrenesy** <note>delirium or brain fever</note>, or from **calculus** <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, or from **strangury** <note>painful or restricted urination</note>, or from that disease which they call **sacred** <note>epilepsy</note>, or from any other hidden, long-lasting, and difficult-to-cure sickness of body or mind, if a doctor or a physical trainer <note>original: "gymnasticus"</note> buys the slave, it is not permitted to return him. Nor is it permitted when the seller has foretold the truth to any buyer. But if some craftsman skilled in such things has sold such a slave to an ignorant and unskilled person, the one who bought him may return the slave within six months for other ailments, but in the case of the **sacred disease**, he may return him up to a full year.

The judgment of these matters shall be conducted before doctors whom the litigants have chosen by common consent. And whoever is condemned shall pay double the price to the buyer who bought from him. If an unskilled person has sold to an unskilled person, just as was said regarding the things above, a return and judgment shall take place, and whoever is convicted shall return the simple price. When someone has sold a murderer: if he did so knowingly to one who also knew, he shall not take the slave back; if to one who did not know, then let him take him back when the buyer realizes the truth. Five of the younger **Guardians of the Laws** shall investigate this. And if they find that the seller was not ignorant, he must first purify the buyer's house from the pollutions <note>original: "piaculis," referring to the spiritual stain or "miasma" associated with a killer</note> according to the law of the interpreters; then he must pay triple the price to the buyer.

Whoever exchanges small things for small things, or whoever wishes to exchange animals and anything else, let him neither bring nor receive anything **adulterated** <note>falsified, diluted, or counterfeit</note>, and let him observe this law diligently. But let a preface be placed before this law just as with the other laws. One ought to consider adulteration, lying, and deception as a single genus. In this matter, the speech of many is certainly to be condemned, who affirm that they use this very thing rightly whenever it is done opportunely. Since they do not determine the occasion itself—where and when—they greatly harm both themselves and others with this word. The Lawgiver, however, will not leave this undetermined, but will declare it diligently in more or fewer terms.

And yet even now, let it be determined thus: Let no one speak a lie with the gods invoked, nor deceive, nor dare to adulterate anything in word or deed, unless he wishes to be an object of hatred to God. To whom he is first an object of hatred who, swearing falsely, thinks little of the gods. Next, he who lies in the presence of his elders. We call **elders** <note>original: "maiores"</note> those who stand above others: such as seniors generally to juniors; parents to children; men to women and boys; rulers to subjects. It is right to revere these, both in every form of rule and especially in civil rule, for the sake of which we have entered into this discourse.

<margin>
<unclear>Do not name the names of the gods rashly</unclear>
</margin>

For whoever adulterates anything in the marketplace certainly lies and deceives; and by invoking the gods, he swears falsely against the **curators** <note>market inspectors</note> of the vendible goods and their laws, in which matter he certainly neither fears men nor worships the gods. It is surely equitable not to easily defile the names of the gods, nor to toss them back and forth; but to keep all things pertaining to the gods pure and chaste. He who is not persuaded by these reasons shall be compelled by this law:

Whoever sells anything in the marketplace, let him never state two prices for his saleable item. But when he has set a simple price, if he does not sell it, let him bring it back again, and on the same day let him ask for neither a greater nor a lesser price. Moreover, let praise of the saleable item and an oath be far away. Whoever transgresses this law: any citizen not less than thirty years old, when he hears him swearing, may beat him with lashes with impunity. If he does not do so, let him be held as a traitor to the laws.

Whoever does not obey the law and sells an adulterated item: whoever notices and is able, let him be accused. And if he is refuted before the magistrates, a slave or a resident alien may carry away the adulterated item for himself. A citizen, however, if he neglects to accuse, shall be held as wicked, as if he had stolen from the gods; but if he accuses and convicts the seller, let him dedicate the item to the gods who preside over the marketplace. The seller who is clearly caught in this matter shall not only be deprived of the item itself but shall also be beaten publicly with as many lashes as the number of drachmas for which he was selling it, with the voice of the criers declaring the reason why he is being beaten.

But for the seller's every malice and adulteration, the curators of the market goods and the Guardians of the Laws themselves shall diligently inquire from men expert in these matters; and they shall post them written on a **column** in the marketplace, so that it may be clearly evident from these what sellers ought and ought not to do. Regarding the laws of the **aediles** <note>officials in charge of public buildings and markets</note>, we have said enough above. And if anything is lacking, let them write down subsequent instructions.

After adulteration, it follows that we speak of **innkeeping** <note>original: "cauponatione," referring to retail trade, tavern-keeping, or small-scale commerce</note>; concerning which we will first give advice and a reason, and then we will set down the law. Every form of innkeeping in the city was invented not for the sake of harming, but entirely according to nature. For how does he not profit, who reduces an immoderate and unequal monetary matter to equality and measure? This is what the money-changer, the merchant, the hireling, and the master of a hospitable lodging house do; for these strive to supply the needs of others in these sorts of things, whether more honorable or more base, and to provide equality to things. But let us consider what the cause of slander is for this matter, and why it does not seem honorable, so that we may ordain it by laws, if not in whole, then at least in part.

CLINIA. This matter, as it seems, is neither small, nor does it require small virtue.

ATHENIAN. How do you say, Clinia? Very few men are by nature, and those indeed endowed with the best education, such that when they are affected by poverty and the desire for certain things, they can so contain themselves as to behave moderately. When they might take much money, they are content with a little, and prefer mediocrity to excess. The common crowd, however, does the opposite entirely. For it desires immoderate things, and when it is possible to profit moderately, it is vexed by an insatiable <note>The catchword *explebili* completes the word *inexplebili* on the next page</note> desire for gain. Wherefore all types of men who are in innkeeping, trade, or lodging...

It also begins a philosophical defense and critique of retail trade and innkeeping as necessary but prone to greed.</summary>

# BOOK IX.
XXXXIIII.
V.

...they frequent the marketplace, they are subject to slander and reproach. For if someone—may it never happen and far be it from us—were forced (I shall say it even if it sounds ridiculous), if someone, I say, were to force the best men everywhere to oversee inns for a time, or to be tavern-keepers, or to do anything of this sort; and if the most holy women were similarly driven by some necessity of fate to these tasks: we would clearly recognize that all these things are honorable and acceptable. Indeed, if they were not conducted corruptly, those who do these things would be thought, not without justice, to perform the role of a mother or a nurse. 

But as it is, they build houses for the sake of innkeeping in deserted places where many long roads lead; they receive those driven by storms into a desired lodging and refresh those oppressed by the heat; then, they do not send them away as friends gifted with the rites of hospitality, but like enemies and captives, they cruelly force them to ransom themselves and strip them of all their possessions. These and other shameful acts committed in all these matters cause such pursuits, which ought to bring aid to the needy, to be subject to slander. A remedy for this must be devised by the lawgiver. 

<margin>
Proverb.
It is difficult to fight against two contrary things.
</margin>

Rightly, therefore, it was said long ago in a well-worn proverb: *It is hard to fight against two contrary things.* As happens in many other diseases, so it occurs in this one. A fight now looms before us against two things: wealth and poverty. One of these corrupts the human soul with delights and softness; the other pushes it toward impudence through suffering. What remedy, therefore, shall we devise in a prudently established city to drive out this disease? First, care must be taken that we employ as few people as possible in the business of innkeeping in the city. Second, these arts of innkeeping must be entrusted to those people whose corruption would not cause great loss to the city. Third, a way and a method must be found so that the souls of those men are not easily filled with impudence and ungenerous behavior. 

With these things said, let this law regarding such matters be brought with good fortune to the Magnesians <note>The citizens of the hypothetical colony 'Magnesia' discussed in Plato’s *Laws*</note>, whose city God is raising up and causing to be inhabited again. None of those who belong to the **five thousand and forty** <note>original: "quadraginta & quinque milibus," a common humanist rendering for Plato's ideal number of citizens, 5,040</note> households shall become an innkeeper or a merchant, whether willingly or unwillingly; nor shall any become the servant of a private person who does not respond to you as an equal in the same lot, except for those of one's father’s or mother’s line, or other elder relatives who are free and live freely. 

Indeed, the distinction between a free person and one who is not free cannot easily be defined exquisitely by laws. Let it nevertheless be discerned by the leading citizens, and let it be judged by their hatred or love. If, however, anyone among the leading citizens or those first in virtue should give his effort to the ungenerous trade of innkeeping in any craft, let him be accused as a disgrace to his kin. And if he is found to have stained his paternal house with an unworthy pursuit, let him be restrained from this work by year-long chains. If he should slip again, let him be imprisoned for two years. And thereafter, as often as he is found to have sinned, let him always be detained for double the time. 

A second law commands that only foreigners and sojourners may follow the arts of innkeeping. A third law warns that caution must be taken: that the foreigner or inhabitant be either the best possible, or at least the least wicked. Nor should the guardians of the laws be ignorant that they are observers not only of those whom it is not difficult to keep from iniquity and depravity—namely, those who are well-born and well-educated—but much more so of those who are not, and who are engaged in these arts by which they are more easily impelled toward wickedness. 

Since innkeeping is manifold and varied, whenever the guardians of the law meet regarding the present types of it, they should first establish what seems necessary for the city, just as we were saying a little while ago regarding the related matter of adulteration <note>This likely refers to the adulteration or "watering down" of goods or wine</note>. Then, having diligently examined the expense and the profit, they should see what constitutes a moderate gain for the innkeeper, and they should write down both the expense and the profit. Some things should be observed by the **aediles** <note>officials in charge of public buildings and markets</note>, others by the curators of saleable goods, and others by the magistrates of the fields. In this way, the arts of innkeeping will profit individuals and cause the least harm. 

If anyone is seen not to have kept his agreements—unless a law or decree prohibits it, or necessity and force have compelled it, or an unexpected accident has detained him against his will—the tribal judges shall take cognizance of the unkept agreement, unless neighbors or arbitrators have reconciled them first. 

The class of craftsmen, who have furnished our life with their arts, is consecrated to **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus, the god of fire and blacksmiths</note> and **Pallas** <note>Athena, the goddess of wisdom and weaving</note>. But the class of those who preserve the works of craftsmen for others, prepared for protection and aid, is consecrated to **Mars** <note>Ares, the god of war</note> and Pallas. Not without reason is their kind consecrated to these gods. For all these care for the region and the people. Some, indeed, preside over warlike contests. Others produce the mercenary works and instruments. These, surely fearing the gods who are their authors, ought to deceive no one with a lie. 

If, however, any artisan does not finish a work in the appointed time through malice, and—thinking the god who is the giver of life would forgive him as if he were one of his own household, through a certain blindness of soul—does not fear him: first, he shall pay the penalty to the god himself; then, having been made a defendant by this law, let him pay the price of the work which he did not do on time, and let him perform the work again from the beginning for free within the same space of time. But what the law provided for the seller regarding the price of saleable goods, it also provides for the craftsman. Let him beware, therefore, lest he himself value his work at more than is fair; but let the bidding be done most simply and as is worthy. For the craftsman is not ignorant of what price his work is worth. Nor ought an artisan in a free city to deceive the unskilled by the very art which is a fitting thing and far removed from lying. 

In these matters, therefore, let judgment be rendered for the one suffering the injury against the one doing it. If anyone does not give the craftsman his wage according to the agreements, but neglects **Jupiter** <note>Zeus, specifically as 'Zeus Polieus,' the protector of the city</note> the guardian of the city and **Minerva** <note>Athena</note> who shares in this republic, and—moved by a small gain—dissolves a great society of men to the extent of his power, let this one law, with the help of the gods, protect the union of the city. He who does not offer the wage for the work received at the time he agreed, let him pay double; and if a year has passed, although money received as a loan ought to be returned without interest, yet let this man give one **sixth of a drachma** <note>an obol</note> for every drachma for each month. The tribal judges shall take cognizance of the causes of these matters. 

But since we have made mention of craftsmen, and since commanders and other artisans of war are, in a certain way, craftsmen, it is not out of place that we speak of these also. If, therefore, any of these should undertake some public work, whether voluntarily or by command, and should rightly finish what he began, the law shall justly [award] him honors...

It establishes strict penalties for artisans who fail to fulfill contracts or overcharge, placing their work under the divine protection of Vulcan, Pallas, and Mars.</summary>
