# OF THE LAWS OR OF THE LAWS IN LATIN DIALOGUE XI. FOLIO 364.
V iiii

...regarding what rewards should be given to warlike men, he should render them such that he never ceases to praise them. But if he gives nothing to the one who has conducted military affairs well, that man will justly complain. Therefore, a certain law concerning these men should be established, mixed with praise, which does not indeed compel, but advises the multitude of citizens. Let the good man be honored, who by either courage or some military skill has saved the entire city; and let the greatest honors be attributed first to those who have especially cherished the laws of the founders of good laws. Now, therefore, concerning the pacts <note>original: "pactis", referring to legal contracts or agreements</note> which men conduct among themselves, besides those concerning orphans and guardians, we have almost finished speaking; but of these we must now necessarily speak. The beginning of all these matters is, on the one hand, the desire of those who have died to make a will as they pleased, and on the other, the fortune of those who have made no will. For this reason, Clinias, I said it was necessary to speak, because I was considering the difficulty of this matter. For it is not possible to leave this without order. For many individuals will hastily testify to many diverse things, contrary to each other, to the laws, to the customs of the living, and to their ancestors, if anyone establishes that whatever testament was made at the end of life shall be entirely inviolable. For almost all men are oppressed by a certain foolish and dejected peevishness when they judge they are about to die. 

CLINIAS: How do you say that, Stranger? 

ATHENIAN: A man about to die, Clinias, is a certain difficult thing, and he very frequently uses these words which terrify and exhaust the lawmakers. 

CLINIAS: How so? 

ATHENIAN: Since he wishes to be the master of all his possessions, he is accustomed to say these things, and indeed with anger. 

CLINIAS: What things?

<margin>The complaint of those who make wills when about to die.</margin>
ATHENIAN: "It is too grievous, O gods," he says, "if it will not be permitted for me to leave my things to whomever I wish: more to some, fewer to others, according as they have been clearly found good or bad toward me, whether in sickness, in old age, or in my other fortunes, having been sufficiently tested." 

CLINIAS: Do they not seem to you to speak rightly, Stranger? 

ATHENIAN: The ancient lawgivers, O Clinias, seem to me to have been soft, and to have looked at very little of human affairs in making laws. 

CLINIAS: 

<margin>The ancient lawgivers are criticized.</margin>
In what way? 

ATHENIAN: Moved by those words of a dying man, O best of men, they wrote that law by which it is permitted to each person to dispose of his property simply as he wishes. But I and you, in your city, will respond more appropriately to those about to die. 

CLINIAS: How? 

ATHENIAN: "O friends," we shall say, "who are undoubtedly about to die in a short time, it is difficult for you to know your own affairs and even yourselves according to the Delphic inscription <note>The famous Greek maxim 'Gnothi Seauton' or 'Know Thyself'</note>. I, who establish the laws, judge that neither you are your own masters, nor is all this family property yours; rather, it belongs to your whole lineage, past and future, and much more so do the whole lineage and the wealth belong to the entire state." 

<margin>Nothing is anyone's certain possession, but belongs to the whole state.</margin>
"Since these things are so, if anyone, having approached you with little flatteries in sickness and old age, should persuade you to make a will contrary to what is honorable, I will never concede that this happened of your own will. Rather, considering what is beneficial to the entire state and the lineage, I will so write the laws that I may value the advantage of individuals as less than that of the whole, as is right. Therefore, go you now, mild and benevolent toward us, where the necessity of human nature calls you. Your remains shall be our care, for we do not study some things more than others, but we take care for all equally according to our strength." Let these be the consolations, O Clinias, in the preamble for both the living and the dying. 

But let the law be this: He who has children and writes a will shall first constitute one of his sons as heir, whomever he judges worthy. Then, let him write down whomever of the others he has given to others to be adopted. And if any of the sons survives who is not provided for by any inheritance, and whom he hopes will go out to a colony according to the law, let it be permitted to the father to legacy to this son as much as he wishes from other money, the paternal lot <note>term: 'paterna forte' – refers to the original allotment of land granted to a family which must remain intact to preserve the number of households in the city</note> always excepted, and all things that pertain to it. But if there are more children, let the father distribute to them whatever exists beyond the lot as he wishes. And if any of them already has a house, let him not give money to him; nor to a daughter who is betrothed to a husband; but if she has not been betrothed, let him give to her. And if some lot in the region should come to any of the sons or daughters after the will has been made, let it be left to the heir of the testator himself. 

But if he has not sons but daughters, let the one who makes the will write down which daughter's husband he wishes to be the heir for himself and for his children. And if any son, whether natural or adopted, should die before he assumes the toga of manhood <note>original: "togam virilem", the Roman garment signaling adulthood, here used for the age of majority</note>, let the testator indicate these fortunes of his also, and declare whom he wishes to be a son to him in that one's place under better auspices. If anyone entirely without children makes a will, let him legacy a tenth part of the land acquired beyond the lot to whichever citizen he wishes. All other things let him grant to the son to be acquired through adoption, kindly, without complaint, and according to the law. 

If anyone's children need guardians, and that same man, dying, has by will established whatever and however many guardians he wished who are willing to undertake the office of guardianship, let it be done as he had described. But if he has yielded to nature <note>i.e., died</note> intestate, or has not written down guardians, let those who are first in lineage—two on the father's side, two on the mother's side, and one from the friends of the deceased—undertake the guardianship. These the Guardians of the Laws <note>term: 'legum custodes' – the high magistrates of Plato's city</note> ought to establish for the needy orphans. For we wish fifteen of the seniors among them to have care of all orphans for a five-year period, such that three of them, according to their dignity, take care each year; and when the five years are finished, fifteen others similarly. And let this never fail according to their strength. 

If anyone should die having made no will, leaving children who need guardianship, let it be provided for his children by these same laws. But he who dies by unexpected fortune, leaving daughters, let him grant indulgence to the lawmaker if, looking to two out of three things, he settles his daughters: namely, to the closeness of lineage and the preservation of the lot. But the third thing, which is the father's duty—that having diligently considered the character of the citizens, he should choose a suitable son for himself and a spouse for his daughter—since that is impossible to consider, let it be omitted. 

Therefore, let the law concerning this matter, according to our strength, be of this sort: If someone dies intestate and leaves daughters, his brother from the father or from the mother, if he is without a lot, shall take the daughter and the lot of the deceased. But if no brother exists, let his son take them, unless age prevents it. Third is the sister's son, if none of those exist. Fourth, the father's brother. Fifth, his son. Sixth, the son of the paternal sister. And similarly through brothers and cousins, the proximity of lineage always being preserved: if he leaves daughters, let it proceed so that in the same degree of lineage, males are preferred to females. The judge shall judge the suitability of age for marriage and otherwise, inspecting the males entirely naked and the females also naked up to the age of puberty. But if up to the brothers...

Since these things are so by nature, first let them fear the gods, especially those above, who take care of the desolation of children; then also the spirits of the dead [manes], to whom it is natural that a special care for those born of them is held, so much so that they are propitious to those honoring them, and hostile to those despising them. These hear these things keenly and perceive them keenly: and they are benevolent to those who treat orphans justly. Warned by all these things, the guardian and magistrate, if he has any mind, will apply it to this matter; and will provide for the discipline and education of orphans with his strength: as if he seemed to provide for himself and his own.

Therefore, the law seeks the care of orphans by consoling and threatening. Nor would it be out of place if we threatened in this way. He who protects a female or male, and he who of the guardians of the laws is appointed to observe the guardian, let him love the orphans no less than if he had begotten them: nor let him govern their affairs worse than his own: rather even better with the affection of the mind. # BOOK
### XXXIIII.

...and the sons of ancestors, if there is a shortage of kinsmen, whatever citizen the girl chooses of her own will with the counsel of the guardians—if he is willing—let him take her as his wife and receive the inheritance as well. But if there is a great shortage among those who live in the city: if the girl desires to make someone sent to a colony the heir of her father, and if he is of the same kin, let him enter the inheritance according to the law. But if he is a citizen indeed, but not of the kin, let him marry her if he wishes, according to the choice of the guardians and the girl, and having returned home, let him enter the inheritance. If anyone dies intestate <note>Dying "intestate" means passing away without having made a valid legal will.</note> without any children at all, male or female, let the other matters be handled according to the aforementioned law. But let a male and a female from the same kin, as partners, enter the deserted house to whom the lot properly belongs. First the sister; then the brother’s daughter. Third, the sister’s daughter. Fourth, the paternal sister. Fifth, the daughter of the paternal father <note>original: "Paterni patris filia," referring to an aunt on the father's side.</note>. Sixth, the daughter of the paternal sister. These shall live with those who are closest in kin, as is right, just as we established in the previous sections. 

But let it not escape us how heavy the command of these laws is, by which we command one to marry a close relative. Indeed, he who brings such a law seems to consider very little how many impediments might be found that make it so no one wants to obey these precepts. For many would rather suffer anything than marry or be wedded to someone whose body is sick or crippled, or whose mind is insane. In these matters, the lawmaker might seem to have had no consideration. And indeed, in many cases, it will rightly seem so. Therefore, let there be a common introduction for both the founder of laws and the subjects. Those for whom the laws are set ought to grant pardon to the lawmaker, since, while intent on governing public affairs, he can never simultaneously provide for every private calamity. The subjects, moreover, should be forgiven if they sometimes cannot embrace the precepts of the legislator, which he wrote being ignorant of individual calamities.

**CLI.** What then, O Guest, is it fitting to do in this matter? 

**ATHE.** Arbitrators, O Clinias, must be chosen who may reconcile these laws with the act of choosing. 

**CLI.** How do you say that? 

**ATHE.** Sometimes a certain rich young man, given to delights and gasping for a grander marriage, spurns the daughter of his uncle. Sometimes, forced by the greatest calamity of the girl, whether of body or mind, he does not obey that law by which he is drawn against his will into an "insane" marriage in which he would not wish to live entangled. Therefore, let this law decree for us concerning these matters: If any complain of the laws for the sake of a testament or marriages or other things, and allege that the lawmaker, if he were alive, would by no means drive him to marry this woman or her to marry this man; and if some relative or guardian affirms that for the purpose of protecting orphans and reconciling them, fifteen of the **Guardians of the Laws** <term>nomophylakes: high-ranking officials in Plato's ideal city responsible for maintaining the legal code</term> have been religiously chosen as arbitrators and parents: let the litigants flee to these very people and obey their judgments. 

But if the Guardians of the Laws seem to urge greater things on anyone, let him bring the matter to the most elite judgment and seek a sentence; and he who is condemned shall be marked with infamy, which in the eyes of a wise man is a far greater punishment than a fine of much money.

Following this is what is, as it were, a second "procreation" of orphans. For after the first procreation comes education and discipline, of which we have spoken; but after the second, we ought to take care that those deprived of parents remain in the least miserable state of calamity. Therefore, we constitute the Guardians of the Laws as second parents to them, no worse than the first, and we command them to provide for them every year as if they were their own. 

But first, concerning the education of orphans, let us begin this way for both the Guardians of the Laws and the legal guardians. It seems we appropriately narrated in previous sections that the souls of the deceased have a certain power by which they care for human affairs. This is true, though <margin>700 B <unclear>p. y. a.</unclear></margin> it is proved by a long discourse. Therefore, one ought to believe both other ancient accounts of this matter and lawmakers who decree that these things are so—unless they are entirely insane. Since these things are so by nature, first let them fear the gods, especially those above, who watch over the desolation of children; then also the **manes** <note>original: "manes," the spirits of the dead in Roman/Latin thought, here used to translate the Greek idea of ancestral spirits.</note> of the dead, to whom it is natural that a special care for those born of them is held, so much so that they are favorable to those honoring them and hostile to those despising them. Furthermore, let them fear the minds of the living elders, who perform the greatest honors in a happy city. While children and grandchildren honor them, they live most pleasantly. These elders hear these things keenly and perceive them keenly, and they are benevolent toward those who treat orphans justly. But they are most indignant at those who afflict those bereaved of parents with insults. Indeed, they consider orphans the greatest and most sacred deposit. Warned by all these things, the guardian and magistrate, if he has any mind, will apply it to this matter and will provide for the discipline and education of orphans with all his strength, as if he seemed to provide for himself and his own. 

Whoever, persuaded by this introduction before the law, restrains himself from all insult toward orphans, will escape the wrath of the laws. But he who, despising this preface, afflicts anyone deprived of father or mother with injuries, let him restore double the damage, just as if he had harmed one who still had both parents. 

But the laws which follow we write for guardians, regarding how they should behave toward orphans, and for magistrates, regarding how they should inquire into the care provided by guardians. If the education of children had its own distinct and separate examples, and if those educating them provided for their affairs differently, we would publish separate laws for guardians. But as it stands, for all these matters, orphancy and its care do not differ much (as far as the laws are concerned) from paternal governance; yet in honor, contempt, and care, they are by no means usually equal. Therefore, the law seeks the care of orphans by both consoling and threatening. Nor would it be out of place if we threatened in this way: He who protects a girl or a boy, and he among the Guardians of the Laws who is appointed to observe the guardian, let him love the orphans no less than if he had begotten them; nor let him govern their affairs worse than his own—indeed, let him do so even better with an affection of the mind. Keeping this one law always in mind, let them perform their guardianship. If anyone derogates from this law...

<page-num>FOLIO 365</page-num>
<header>ON THE LAWS, OR ON THE LAWS OF THE LATINS. DIALOGUE XI.</header>
<sig>V v</sig>

...if it should happen, let the guardian whom the magistrate condemns pay. If a magistrate is called to the judgment of the chosen men by a guardian, let him be punished with double the loss. Let that loss be contained in the judges' sentence. But if a guardian seems to any relative or other citizens to act negligently or maliciously, and is brought into the same judgment, let him restore fourfold the damage; one part of which is given to the boy, and the other to the accuser. After the orphan has reached **adulthood**, if he believes the guardian managed his affairs poorly, he may bring a case against the guardian for up to five years after the guardianship ended. And if any guardian is condemned, the judges shall decree what he must suffer or pay. If any of the magistrates is seen to have harmed an orphan through negligence, the judges shall determine what he must restore. But if he did so through actual injustice, not only shall he restore the damage, but he shall also be deprived of his office as a <term>Guardian of the Laws</term> <note>original: "nomophylax", a high-ranking official in Plato's ideal city responsible for overseeing the legal system</note>; and another shall be immediately created by the people for the city and the region in his place.

Complaints by fathers against sons, and also of sons against parents, often occur more than is fitting. Perhaps legislators might think that fathers should be permitted to write down their reasons and, if they wish, <term>disinherit</term> <note>original: "abdicare", the formal legal process of severing a son from the family line</note> a son by public proclamation, so that he is no longer a son according to the law; and that sons should be allowed to accuse parents of <term>dementia</term> <note>original: "amentia", referring to cognitive decline or insanity that makes one unfit to manage property</note> when they are shamefully affected by disease or old age. All these things usually happen where the customs of men are altogether at their worst. For if only half were evil—for instance, if only the parents were bad or only the sons—the calamities of such grave enmities would not occur. Indeed, in any other republic, a disinherited son is not necessarily deprived of his citizenship. But in this city, which shall be governed by these laws, it is necessary for one deprived of his father to go elsewhere. For indeed, no one can be added to the five thousand and forty households <note>Plato’s ideal city, Magnesia, consists of exactly 5,040 fixed land allotments</note>. Therefore, it is necessary that a son be cast out, not by the father alone, but by the whole kindred. Therefore, in matters of this kind, the following law should be applied:

When someone, moved by unhappy indignation—whether he is angry justly or unjustly—wishes to reject from his kinship the one he begot and raised, he shall not be allowed to do this lightly or suddenly. First, he must call together his relatives up to the level of first cousins, and likewise the relatives of the son on the mother's side. Before them, he shall accuse the son and show that he is worthy of being expelled by all his relatives. Then, the son shall also be granted the power to speak his cause, to show that he is not the sort of person who ought to be rejected. Finally, all the relatives, both men and women (unless age is an impediment), shall cast their votes, except for the parents and the son himself. And if more than half of the votes support the father, he may disinherit the son; otherwise, he may not. If any citizen wishes to adopt the disinherited son, no law shall forbid it; for the character of youths often changes variously from day to day. But if no one wishes to join the rejected son to themselves by adoption within ten years, the <term>curators of offspring</term> <note>officials who manage the population levels</note>—who provide for the removal of excess population via colonies—shall also provide for these sons, so that they may be appropriately made leaders of the same colony.

<margin>
When and how a son shall accuse his father.
</margin>

If anyone, through disease, old age, or bitterness of character—or being more troubled by all these than others—should fall into **dementia**, and this is hidden from everyone except his household; and if he, as the master, dissipates the family property, and the son is afraid to accuse his father of dementia, let the law command this: first, the son shall go to the elder Guardians of the Laws and tell of his father's calamity. Having inspected the matter sufficiently, they shall consult on whether the father should be accused or not. Then, if they decree he should be accused, they shall be both witnesses and listeners for the accuser. And if the father is condemned, he shall not be able to dispose of even the smallest part of his property in the future; nor shall he live in the house as the head of the family anymore, but like a son or a child.

<margin>
On divorce.
</margin>

If a husband and wife do not agree with each other because of bitterness of character, ten men from the Guardians of the Laws (who shall act as mediators) and ten women from the <term>overseers of marriage</term> shall provide counsel. If they can be reconciled by the judgment of these people, the marriage shall be held valid and stable. But if their minds fluctuate even more vehemently with anger, then, after a **divorce** is made, let others be sought for them who are compatible. It seems that a more bitter nature exists in such people; therefore, more mature and gentler dispositions should be matched with them. Those who are without children or have fathered few, and who disagree, should be compelled to seek marriage again for the sake of procreating children. But if they have many children and disagree, they should enter another marriage after the divorce for the sake of mutually caring for each other in old age. 

If a woman dies leaving behind male and female children, the law shall not compel the man, but it shall persuade him, to raise his children without bringing in a stepmother. But if the deceased wife left no children, he shall be compelled to take another, from whom he may procreate enough offspring for both his family and the city. If a man leaves sufficient children, let the widowed mother raise them. But if she seems too young to live sanely without a husband, her relatives, having held counsel with the women who oversee marriages, shall execute what seems best to them and her. If they lack children, they shall marry for the sake of children. A sufficient number of children is one male and one female, according to the law. 

Whenever it is granted by both sides that the children born are the offspring of those who claim them, the matter still needs judgment as to which parent the child should follow. If a female slave gives birth after being joined to a slave, a free man, or a freedman, let the child be given to the master of the female slave. But if a free woman gives birth by a slave, let the master of the slave likewise be the master of the child. But if any man has a child by his own slave, or any woman gives birth by her own slave, and it is revealed, the women shall send the child born of the slave and the free man into another region along with the father. But the child born of the free woman and the slave, the Guardians of the Laws shall expel outside the borders along with the mother.

Neither a god nor a man of sound mind will ever advise anyone to neglect their parents. But that which one must not be ignorant of regarding the <term>worship of the gods</term> will be a fitting preamble to the honoring of parents. The ancient laws concerning the gods are established in two ways among all people. For some of the gods we see clearly, and we worship those very ones we see. Others, however, we do not see, but we fashion images of them; and these, though they are lifeless, when we honor...

<page-num>XXXIII</page-num>
<header>BOOK</header>

...we consider that the living gods themselves will be most grateful and well-disposed toward us for this reason. Therefore, if someone has a father, or a mother, or their grandparents, worn out by old age, lying at home like a precious treasure, let them realize that no other image <note>original: "simulacrum". Plato argues that elderly parents are "living statues" of the gods, more powerful than any man-made idol.</note> in their home could ever be as effective or powerful, provided it is honored correctly as is fitting.

**CLI.** What is the correct way of honoring them?

**ATHE.** I shall tell you. For these matters are worthy for friends to hear.

**CLI.** Come then, speak.

**ATHE.** It is said by everyone that **Oedipus**, when he was despised by his sons, called down curses upon them which the gods heard and carried out. They say also that **Amyntor** in his anger cursed his son **Phoenix**, and **Theseus** cursed **Hippolytus**, and many others have cursed others. From this, it is most clearly established that the prayers of parents against their children are heard by the gods. For nothing is more destructive to a son than a parent’s curse when he has been wronged. Indeed, let no one think that if a mother or father is despised by a child, the gods only hear their prayers according to nature at that time; rather, when they are also honored and thus, being more joyful, ask for good things for their children from the gods, we must believe the children are heard, and therefore that fair things are distributed to us. Otherwise, there would be no justice in the distribution of good things, which must be far removed from the gods.

**CLI.** Certainly.

**ATHE.** Therefore, we must consider, as we said a little while ago, that we can have no image <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> more worthy of honor among the gods than parents and grandparents worn out by old age, and the mothers of our children. When these are honored, God rejoices; otherwise, he would not listen to them. For the living image of our parents should seem more wonderful to us than even lifeless statues. For those that have a soul, because they are honored by us, pray for us and favor us daily; but when they are despised, they do the opposite. Lifeless things, however, do neither of these. Therefore, he who conducts himself rightly toward his parents, grandparents, and others of this kind, possesses the best of all images for winning the favor of the gods.

**CLI.** You have spoken excellently.

**ATHE.** All men who are not insane, therefore, revere and honor the prayers of their parents, knowing well that they have often helped or hindered many. Since these things are so established by nature, to upright men, elderly parents are held as a great treasure if they live to old age; but if they die younger, they are greatly missed. To the wicked, however, they are very terrifying. Therefore, let everyone, led by these reasons, honor his parents according to the law. But if anyone is deaf to these introductions, let him hear this law rightly established:

If anyone in this city honors his parents less than is fitting, and does not love them more than his sons, grandsons, and himself, but instead obeys the will of others in everything while neglecting them, let whoever notices this report the matter, either personally or through another, to the three eldest <term>Guardians of the Laws</term> <note>original: "nomophylax", high-ranking officials responsible for legal oversight</note> and to three women who are supervisors of marriages. These people, having investigated the matter, shall punish those who committed the wrong. Men who have not exceeded their thirtieth year, and women if they have not exceeded their fortieth, shall be punished with bonds and beatings. If, however, they are of a greater age than we have stated, and they do not cease to neglect their parents—or even worse, if they afflict them—let them be compelled to go to judgment. Let the citizens who most exceed all others in age act as judges. Let the condemned person pay or suffer what is determined by the judgment, so that nothing is omitted that might cause a man to suffer or pay.

If anyone who has been afflicted is unable to report it, any free person who hears of it shall announce it to the magistrates or be considered wicked; and he may be accused of the damage caused by anyone who wishes. If a slave reports it, let him be free. If he is the slave of the one causing the affliction or the one afflicted, let him be granted freedom by the magistrates; if he was the slave of some other citizen, let the public pay the price to his master. Let the magistrates take care that no one harms the person who reported it.

<margin>
The prayers of parents against children made to God are often heard.
</margin>

Regarding things done to others by poison, those that are lethal have already been categorized. We have not yet distinguished other types, whether they are administered through drink, food, or ointments, by intent and design. For poisons harm the human race in two ways. First, as we just said, by bodies naturally harming bodies. Second, by magical sorceries, incantations, and bindings <note>original: "nodis", referring to knot-magic or binding spells</note> by which people believe they can cause harm, and that they themselves can be easily harmed by those practicing such magic.

It is not easy to know the nature of these things and others like them, nor if someone knew could they persuade others. But as for the souls of men who are uneasy and suspicious of one another regarding these things, it is not worth trying to persuade them—as if, when they see other images whether at their doors, at a crossroads, or at the monuments of their parents, they should utterly despise them when they have no certain opinion about them. Therefore, dividing the law on poisoning into two parts, we first exhort, warn, and advise that they do not do such things, so as not to terrify many like children, nor to force the legislator and the judge to heal the fears of such men.

Indeed, he who strives to harm by poison, if he intends to inflict it on bodies, does not know what he is doing unless he is skilled in medicine. Similarly, he who attempts this through magical incantations, unless he is a soothsayer <note>original: "aruspex", a diviner or interpreter of omens</note> and an interpreter of wonders. But now let this law regarding poisons be sanctioned: Whoever uses poison, not for the death of a man but for livestock or swarms of bees, or even to harm beasts in a way other than death—if he is a physician and is judged guilty of poisoning, let him suffer the penalty of death. But if he is ignorant of medicine, let the court determine what he ought to suffer or pay.

Since someone is caught prepared to do harm through bindings, incantations, charms, and similar sorceries: if he is a soothsayer or interpreter of wonders, let him be put to death. If he is not, let the judgment similarly determine what he should pay or suffer. He who has harmed by stealth or by force shall restore much if he harmed in great matters, and less if in minor ones; and in all things he shall be punished with a fine. These are lighter if he was driven by another’s malice due to the imprudence of youth; but heavier if it was by his own madness, or by immoderate pleasures and pains, or by fear, or envy, or incurable anger.

<margin>
See something regarding the magic art and its works.
</margin>

Indeed, the wicked are troubled with punishments, not simply because they have sinned—for what is done cannot be undone—but so that in the future both the sinners themselves and those who witnessed the punishment of their iniquities may hate injustice, or at least sin less in a similar vice. For the sake of all these things, it is necessary that the laws look toward this, and like good archers, they should aim at this mark: the magnitude of punishment in each case, and what is worthy...

<margin>
Why the wicked are troubled by punishments.
</margin>

# FOLIO 366
## ON THE LAWS, DIALOGUE XI

It is fitting for a judge to act as the minister of the lawgiver: especially when the law commits to him the task of determining what a person, once condemned, ought to pay or suffer. He should execute what remains by imitating the higher principles, just as a painter paints by diligently following his models. This, O **Clinias** and **Megillus**, I believe we must do as beautifully and excellently as possible: we must state what the punishments ought to be for those who act by theft and secrecy, and for those who act by force, insofar as the gods and the sons of gods permit us to establish laws.

Let no **insane person** <note>original: "furiosus". In Roman and Platonic law, this referred to those lacking reason, requiring a legal guardian.</note> be seen openly in the city; rather, the relatives of the insane person shall guard them at home by whatever means they can. If they fail to do this, they shall be fined: those of the highest wealth class, one hundred drachmas; whether they guard a slave or a free person with insufficient diligence. Those of the second class shall pay four-fifths of a mina; the third, three; and the fourth, two. <note>original: "minae". A mina was a unit of currency worth 100 drachmas. Plato’s system uses a four-tiered social hierarchy based on property value.</note>

Men are driven by madness in many ways. Some by disease, such as those we have just mentioned. Others by the **wrath** of a corrupted nature and a vicious education: who, moved by slight enmities, shout loudly and shamefully insult one another. Truly, nothing of this sort should happen in a city established by good laws. Regarding insults, therefore, let this one law be established for all: **Let no one insult another.**

Instead, whoever has a dispute with another concerning any matter should learn and teach, both the disputant and those present, in such a way that they entirely abstain from all insulting language. For when people curse each other with foul words, they act like women; and from words, which are certainly the lightest of things, the gravest hatreds and enmities are often born. Indeed, he who indulges in such an ungrateful habit and fills himself, as if with toxic food, becomes as embittered in the angry part of his soul as he was previously cultivated by discipline. By becoming wild, he makes his life difficult through a lack of reason, receiving only a bitter "favor" from his anger. Almost all people of this sort tend to say something ridiculous about their adversary; in doing so, whoever habituates himself to this either entirely loses his good character or loses the greatest part of his magnanimity.

Therefore, let no one ever use these reproaches in a temple, nor where public sacrifices or contests are performed, nor in the marketplace of goods for sale, nor in a court of law, nor in any other common assembly. Let the presiding magistrate of these affairs freely punish anyone who offends in this. If he does not, he shall be treated as a traitor to the laws and a despiser of the legislator’s precepts, and he shall never ascend to compete for any public office as if he were to compete for virtue.

Furthermore, if anyone in other places uses insults, whether by provoking or responding, any elder present shall strike him in defense of the laws, and restrain those who have been incited by anger at another's ill. Otherwise, as we said before, let him be punished. Moreover, we believe that no one engages in these insults and witticisms without often speaking something ridiculously offensive. And this is exactly what we condemn: when it is done with **anger**.

What then? Shall we admit the wit and ridiculous insults of comic poets and satirists which they use against citizens, if they "bite" in this way without anger? Or shall we distinguish it twofold, into jesting and serious speech? Let it be permitted to use a jest so long as one speaks ridiculously without anger; but to no one, as we said before, shall it be permitted to say such things with a soul incited by anger! This, therefore, must by no means be allowed.

To whom it is permitted, and to whom it is not, must now be declared by law. To a comic poet, or a writer of iambic or musical melody, it shall not be permitted to disparage any of the citizens, either by word or by image or by person, whether he does so with anger or without anger. And whoever acts against this, let those presiding over the awarding of prizes expel him on the same day; otherwise, let them be fined three minas, to be consecrated to the god in whose honor the contest was held.

To others, however, of whom we spoke above, it shall be permitted to say something ridiculous without anger and with a jest; but seriously and with anger, by no means. The judgment of this matter shall be committed to the general curator of the education of the youth. Whatever he approves, it is permitted to bring into the open; but whatever he disapproves, let him never show it to anyone, nor teach it to another, whether slave or free. If anyone acts against this, he shall be held as wicked and a contemner of the laws.

A **miserable** person—that is, one worthy of pity—is to be so judged not because he is pressed by hunger or some other such thing, but because, while he is temperate and endowed with some other virtue or part of virtue, he is nevertheless perhaps vexed by some calamity. Therefore, it will be a wonder indeed if such a man is so neglected that, whether free or slave, he falls into extreme poverty in a moderately governed city. Therefore, the legislator may safely and not unjustly establish such a law on this matter:

**Let there be no beggar in our city.**

Whoever attempts it, and begins to gather a living by insatiable prayers, let him be driven from the market by the curators of sales; let him be ejected from the city by the magistrate of buildings (the aedile); and finally, let him be exterminated from the entire region by the magistrate of the fields, so that the entire region may be completely clean of such an "animal."

If a male or female slave damages another's property, whether by ignorance or some immoderate use, and the one who suffered the loss did not provide the cause, the master shall either provide satisfaction or hand over the slave to the one who suffered the loss. But if the master contends that the deed was a common trick between the perpetrator and the victim so that the slave might be taken away, let him bring a charge of malice against the one complaining about the slave. If he convicts him, he shall receive double the price of the slave as determined by the court. But if he himself is convicted, he shall both restore the damage and hand over the slave besides.

If a beast of burden, or a horse, or a dog, or any other domestic animal grinds down the property of a neighbor, the owner of the animal shall similarly restore the damage.

If anyone wishes to bear testimony voluntarily, let him be summoned by the one in need; and being summoned, let him be present at the proper time and bring testimony as he knows it. If he says he does not know, let him affirm he does not know by an oath naming three gods—**Jupiter, Apollo, and Themis** <note>original: "Ioue, Apolline, Themide". These three represent the highest authority, light/truth, and divine justice/order respectively.</note>—and then depart. He who is summoned to bear witness and does not come, shall pay the damage to the one who summoned him according to the law. If any judge is summoned as a witness, after the testimony is given, he shall not cast a vote in that same case. A free woman, if she has exceeded forty years of age, may be present in court both to bear witness and to speak; indeed, she may even bring an action if she is not under a husband's authority. But while her husband is living, she may only bear testimony. To a slave, however...

# THE ARGUMENT OF DIALOGUE XI ON THE LAWS

...it is permitted for female slaves and boys to testify only in cases of homicide, provided they give a suitable guarantor <note>original: "fideiussorem"; a person who takes legal responsibility for another's appearance in court</note> that they will remain until the sentence is delivered, in case they are accused of **false testimony**. If anyone wishes to bring a charge of false testimony—which is permitted for both parties regarding the whole or a part of the testimony—they must object that the witnesses were false before the judges deliver their sentence. The magistrates themselves shall keep the written accusations of false testimony brought by either side and later refer them to a trial for perjury. If anyone is found to have given false testimony twice, they shall not be compelled by any law to testify a third time. If they do so a third time, they shall by no means be permitted to testify thereafter. But if, having been caught in falsehood three times, they dare to testify further, they may be brought before a magistrate by anyone who wishes and handed over for trial; if convicted, they shall **be put to death**.

When false testimonies have intervened in a lawsuit, by which one party might seem to have overcome the opponent: if more than half of the witnesses are condemned, the judgment based on those testimonies shall not proceed. It is then proper to debate whether anything was judged according to those testimonies or not; and however it is judged, the lawsuit shall reach a just end by this agreement. 

Truly, though many things in the lives of men are good, many of them are beset by certain dire calamities that stain and defile them. Why is judicial debate and judgment not a good for man, since it has tamed all human affairs? And yet, since such debate is a good, why is it not also a good to assist someone in a lawsuit and to favor a just cause? These things being so, a **wicked slander** <note>original: "puerfa calumnia"; likely a transcription error for "perfida calumnia" (treacherous slander)</note> assumes the name of a "good art"—one which claims to have discovered a craft in lawsuits for doing and saying things such that, whether the cause be honorable or foul, one might easily prevail. This "art" promises to make victors of those it favors with its reasoning, provided money is given for the benefit of the art itself. 

Whether this be an art or an experience devoid of art, effort must be made so that it finds no entry into our city. Let the founder of the truth of the laws bring nothing against the laws, but let this "art" show its strength elsewhere. If anyone does not obey, let them be deterred by this law: If anyone attempts to turn the power of justice in the minds of the judges toward the contrary, or moves many litigations out of season, or assists those who do, anyone who wishes may bring a charge against them for malicious conduct or for defending such things. A trial of this kind shall be conducted before chosen judges. If convicted, it shall be discussed whether they did it out of **greed** or out of a certain **ambitious contention**. If it was out of contention, the judges shall prescribe a fixed time during which they may not plead or speak in any cause for themselves or another. But if it was out of greed, if they are a foreigner, let them depart the region never to return; if they return, they shall die. If a citizen is found to have done this out of greed, because they valued money so highly, they shall surely be put to death. If they are judged to have done such a thing twice out of ambitious contention, they shall undergo that same penalty.

-> Argument of Marsilio Ficino on the Twelfth Dialogue on the Laws. <-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring a classical figure or saint within a square frame.</image-desc> **P**lato the divine, in all his dialogues on the laws, delighted in the likeness of divine work and therefore in the **number twelve**. Doubtless, he wished the twelfth dialogue to be the common chest of the laws, just as the twelfth circle of the world is the common firmament of the stars. And just as if one penetrates beyond the twelfth circle, they will immediately find and even attain the perfection and happiness of the soul, so Plato, about to progress beyond the twelfth book, will demonstrate in the *Epinomis* <note>The *Epinomis* is a dialogue attributed to Plato that serves as an appendix to the *Laws*, focusing on astronomy and the soul’s ultimate wisdom.</note> not so much the laws as the blessed perfection of the soul acquired through the laws.

In the previous books, the laws pertained partly to public duties, partly to private business, partly to urban matters, and partly to external affairs, whether in peace or in war. In the twelfth, however, all are in a way gathered together as they pertain to everything—not every individual law, I mean, but several from every class of individual things. To the laws is added that which is greatest: namely, the **reason** <note>original: "ratio"</note> that is both the preserver and the corrector of the laws. To the magistrates is added that which is also greatest: namely, the system for the recovery of funds and the rendering of accounts <note>original: "repetundarum referendarumque rationum"; referring to the legal process for holding officials accountable for corruption or extortion.</note>. This is set over the public offices of magistrates no differently than the examination of conscience itself is set over the private actions of souls. By this double examination—both the private one of souls and the public one of the state—all health and universal safety consist. This is the summary argument of the twelfth book. 

But since, shortly in the beginning, in the following parts, and often in the preceding ones, he commemorates the **sons of the gods**—calling sometimes certain gods the sons of other gods, and sometimes men the sons of gods—it is necessary to remember that in Plato there are two ways for gods to be sons of gods, and two ways for men to be sons of gods. 

First, as the *Timaeus* teaches, all the rulers of the spheres of the world—whether the souls of the spheres themselves, or the demons within the spheres, or the angelic intellects beyond the spheres—are sons of the **Almighty God**, created as if by His beneficent will. Secondly, in any of these three kinds, the lower are called sons of the higher because, continually receiving rays and forms from the higher, they are in a way formed from them and seem to obey them as fathers. 

Similarly, men are said to be begotten by the gods above: either because from the beginning of things they were brought into the light from the bowels of the earth by the nourishment of the gods, or because some, being vehemently inspired daily by the breath of the gods, soon passed from their usual human affection into a certain divine state of life, as if divinely reborn. In this grade, Plato frequently places both pious philosophers and philosophical princes. 

Moreover, because right at the beginning of the book he places **Jupiter** and **Mercury** over legates and messengers, it must be understood first that by Jupiter is meant the God who is the architect of the world, and by Mercury, the whole number of angels. Secondly, by Jupiter is meant the planet that signifies emperors and laws; by Mercury, the other planet of interpretation and dispatch...

<meta>This page continues the "Arguments" or summaries of Plato’s Laws. This specific page provides Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical and practical commentary on Book XII, the final book of the Laws, which deals with planetary signs, military discipline, the integrity of judges, and the symbolic nature of religious offerings.</meta>

# ARGUMENT OF THE TWELFTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS. FOLIO 377.

->Every signifier.<- I call the planets "signifiers." As Timaeus <note>A character in Plato’s dialogues and an astronomer</note> testifies and Plotinus <note>The primary philosopher of Neoplatonism</note> discusses, the planets and all celestial things signify and announce in whatever way they can: things that are just about to happen from above, or things we are about to do on our journey, or often things we are about to suffer. Soon he expresses detestation for the poets, who, by transferring the crimes of men onto the gods, have impiously sinned against divinity; and by the bad example of the gods, they have gravely harmed men. Furthermore, he believes that thefts and other crimes should be considered based on the intention of the sin and whether the habit is curable or incurable, rather than from mere emotion. He prescribes laws for military service; this he considers the best of all things in every part of life: that no one should learn to live for himself alone or do anything apart from others, but rather at the nod of a prudent superior, and that individuals should direct their specific actions toward common use. He teaches judges that they should not deliver a sentence against the law, whether of their own accord or even under compulsion. For Judgment itself, according to the opinion of the ancients—especially Orpheus and Hesiod—is a certain chaste virgin. Truly, falsehood is especially hateful to Shame <note>original: "Pudori"</note> and Judgment. They believe that the goddess presiding over judgment is divine Providence, who must be venerated by human judges. After this, he condemns those who have shamefully thrown away their weapons; and also those military leaders who receive them back to serve under their standards again. Here, we have translated the number of minae <note>An ancient unit of currency</note> as "denarius," though the laws elsewhere use "millenarium." A little later, he asserts that the "knot" <note>The binding force or essential bond</note> of the republic is the audit of accounts <note>original: "repetundarum iudicium rationum"</note>; so that no judge in the republic shall be without a judge over them. Otherwise, through the unchecked license of judging, justice would first perish; then the city, having lost justice, would die like a body losing its soul. Truly, regarding the Temple of the Sun and Apollo, he understands it as a house dedicated not only to the planet and the solar soul, but much more to the light of the Highest Good, of which the sun is the image. You will hear that sins are committed in trials due to the absence of religion. But the worst of all the impious are those who trust that they can appease God with prayers and sacrifices <note>original: "hostili"</note> so that, because of this confidence, they may extort large sums of money with impunity. After this, he passes down very cautious laws regarding the receiving of foreigners and the travels of citizens, lest the customs of the citizens be confused by foreign and ill-considered habits, or 

<margin>
<unclear>foreign</unclear>
<unclear>vices</unclear>
</margin>

the vices of foreigners infect the republic. You will note here that even in some wicked people, there is a certain divine power through which they discern the grasp of natural talents. This shows that a certain divinity is not only acquired by us but, so to speak, is innate. He teaches that it should not be made a small matter whether you appear honest or wicked. But a reputation for virtue must also be sought, provided it is sought for the sake of virtue itself. He mentions that divine men sometimes exist even among the common people and in badly governed cities. After this, he treats many things regarding the conduct of legal cases, accusation, defense, appeal, acting as a guarantor, prescription <note>A legal time limit</note>, and other matters of this kind. He also mixes into these, at a certain opportune moment, which gifts or images should be dedicated to the divinities. This tradition is symbolic, following the Pythagorean rite. He says that the Earth and Vesta <note>Goddess of the hearth and home</note> are the sacred dwelling of all the gods. Because he added "Vesta," he signaled that under the name of this "earth," something deeper ought to be understood: both this elemental earth, the lunar earth, and finally the stellar earth <note>The firmament</note>. Likewise, he means the three souls of these three earths, and three angels. Remember, indeed, that among the ancients, whatever in the universe is effective for forming and moving is metaphorically called "fire." Likewise, whatever is most easily formed is called "air." That which is purgative <note>Cleansing</note> is called "water"; and that which is solid or stable and consistent is named "earth." Such a nature, because of its dense or consistent quality, is called "earth" by the Platonists both here, and in the moon, and in the firmament. To whom, then, should it seem strange that the Earth is the sacred dwelling of all the gods, if he encompasses the universe within the three boundaries of these three earths? And since he said it was consecrated to the gods from the beginning, he forbids it to be consecrated again, warning that you should not trust that you can offer anything to God that was not already God's own. He also forbids statues to be made of gold or silver, lest we trust that we might purge great crimes by the high price of these materials. Again, he prohibits ivory, since it has been abandoned by the sensual soul; lest we perform sacred rites without "sense," that is, without vigilance and attention. He also rejects bronze and iron, blaming them as instruments of war. For when the mind is distrustful within itself and toward others, we perform sacrifices in vain. Finally, he accepts wood and stone from which the images of the gods may be made. In stone, he commends the stability of the mind in sacred matters. In wood, he commends the "fuel for fire," that is, the burning of the soul, which is easily ignited in divine things. He commands that whole images be fashioned from a single piece of stone or wood, commending simplicity and integrity above all. Nor should it be passed over in silence that messengers were sent to four oracles in the preceding sections, so that we might know that God, the author of all things, provides equally for all parts of the world. These are designated by the four "corners": the names of East, West, North, and South. By whatever rite God is worshipped, provided He is worshipped with a pure mind and for His own sake <note>original: "gratiaque sui"</note>, it is in some way acceptable to God. But concerning these things, we speak more diligently elsewhere. Among these matters, he forbids those who serve the fatherland in any capacity to accept gifts. He also deals with taxes. He says that nothing better can be learned by anyone than that by which he himself becomes better. He says that Law <note>original: "lex"</note> is a wonderful and divine thing, and its name among the Greeks <note>The Greek word *nomos* (law) is related to *nous* (mind)</note> is derived from Mind itself—from the Mind, I say, which is both divine, like a father, and human, like a mother. Indeed, he wishes Judgment to follow Law. These two are the greatest of human goods. But here it comes to mind, as he says at the end of the eleventh book, that our goods are often defiled by certain calamities of their own. He says elsewhere that the "calamity" of Law is the wickedness of the magistrate himself. Truly, the "calamity" of judgment and judicial debate he called a certain legalistic cleverness <note>original: "peritiam quandam causidicam"</note> which, having no regard for the law, but through a zeal for greed and ambition, takes up any case to be defended without distinction. This he detests above all others as a plague upon the republic. After these things, where regarding funerals...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s philosophical commentary and summary of the twelfth and final book of Plato’s Laws. Having discussed social and military regulations, Ficino now pivots to the "Nocturnal Council"—the highest body of the state—and the metaphysical foundations of law, including the nature of the soul and its relationship to Fate.</meta>

# ARGUMENT ON THE TWELFTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS.

<margin>
Fate
</margin>

He imposes laws. Above all, he wishes that man himself be understood as the very substance of the rational soul; whereas the human body is merely a likeness of this man, and as he names it elsewhere, a shadow. What "man" truly is within us, and what the "animal" is, may be known from the *Timaeus*, the *Alcibiades*, and from Plotinus <note>Plotinus was the 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino heavily synchronized Plato's works with Plotinian thought</note>, especially where we dispute these matters in Theology. There, he concludes that the "man" is the substance of the rational soul, which, beyond reason, also possesses a certain inner sense that is impassive and common to all. The "animal," however, is a certain composite of the shaped body and a certain "trace of life" impressed upon it by the soul. Within this trace of life, a second sense is also impressed, derived from the first sense; this one is distributed through various instruments <note>the sense organs</note> and is capable of being affected by external things. This indeed seems to resonate greatly with certain sayings of the Apostle Paul <note>Ficino often sought to harmonize Plato with St. Paul, particularly the distinction between spirit, soul, and body</note>. When he says that the soul departs to "other gods" to give an account of its works, he uses the name "other gods" to mean angelic minds <note>original: "mentes angelicas"</note> existing outside of bodies, which others call the gods beyond the souls of the celestial spheres. For since our souls are joined to these bodies, they are certainly placed under the reign of the higher souls; but once separated, they are brought to the judgment of the separated beings.

Up to this point, he has established laws; but he says that laws are established in vain unless one thinks of the safety and stability of those laws. Therefore, to ensure this stability, he will devise a certain wonderful assembly of magistrates <note>Known in Plato's text as the "Nocturnal Council"</note>. But before the creation of such an assembly, he touches upon the power of the Fates <note>original: "fatorum"</note>, as he understands that human prudence alone is not sufficient for the safety of so great a work if the force of fate is utterly opposed. In this, he certainly seems to approve of those who, in building cities, establishing laws, creating magistrates, and even in the "planting" of men <note>likely referring to the timing of procreation or education</note>, diligently avoid an overly adverse disposition of the stars. 

Regarding Fate, much is said elsewhere; the points brought forward here so opportunely and briefly are consistent with those. Fate is a certain immobile disposition of mobile things within the Soul of the World <note>The "Anima Mundi," a cosmic force that mediates between the divine Mind and the physical universe</note>. The instrument of Fate, however, is the celestial nature. But the matter in which it acts through that instrument is the mass of the elements. He adopts three names—Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos—which pertain both to the instrument and to the matter. For we can name the **Firmament** <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note> Lachesis, in whose stars the powers and lots of all lower things are contained. **Clotho** we name the assembly of the planets, which unfolds the lots of things supplied by the Firmament. Finally, we name **Atropos** especially as Saturn, who by his stability inevitably confirms the lots that have been unfolded into effect. We also count the three Fates within the matter of fate, because the fatal power infused into the elements through the celestial instrument acts upon matter, form, and the composite thing. Likewise, it acts upon essence, virtue, and action. Likewise, upon the beginning, the middle, and the end. 

Because Fate acts not only upon bodies, but also upon minds—to the extent that they are affected by or use bodies—Plato says here that the Fates are able to preserve the prosperity of both bodies and minds, as well as the laws. And because the mind <note>original: "mens"</note>, by its own nature—relying as it does on the providence of the divine mind—either overcomes fate or uses fate happily, he substitutes for the safety of both public and private life the idea that the sense must be joined with the mind, so that the sense obeys and serves the mind. Similar to this union, which is composed of the mind and the senses of sight and hearing, he creates a certain assembly of magistrates in the republic to look out for the stability of the laws. This assembly should first look to the goal <note>original: "finem"</note> of the republic itself, and then determine which ways lead most powerfully to that goal. It should strive entirely so that every single thing in the city, whether private or public, is conducted by one certain reason toward the One: directing all things toward virtue, and the other virtues toward **Prudence**, and Prudence toward **Wisdom** <note>original: "sapientiam"</note>, which he often signifies under the name of "Mind." By the reason of this Mind, all virtues are judged to be approved, namely insofar as they lead to Wisdom; which he also approves for the reason that it is a participant in the one Divine Good. 

He asserts that there is a most exquisite consideration of things: one that sees not only the "many" insofar as they are many, but also the one common nature that exists in all things. Likewise, it sees from which "One Principle" they have this nature, and again, to which "One End" they can be led through it. Without this kind of contemplation, no one can perfectly govern either a private or a public life. Since this speculation belongs to the philosopher—and especially the divine philosopher—it is not without reason that, among the citizens gathered in that most select assembly, he judges the highest authority of affairs should be referred to **divine philosophers**. By "divine," I mean the observers and worshippers of divine things. Therefore, those who are dull in perceiving divine things, or lazy in worshipping them, or unsuited for teaching them, he keeps far away from the most ample offices of the republic. 

Soon after, he proves that two things are primarily necessary for a firm and supreme faith in divinity:
1. First, that we know that the genus of rational souls is itself divine and older than bodies, and that it is by souls that the spheres of the world are moved and all things within the spheres are generated.
2. Second, that we consider the genus of minds—namely, the **angelic** minds—to be superior to the genus of souls. 

And he argues that souls move the spheres in an orderly way precisely because of their participation in the Mind. For if anyone knows these two things, he will easily recognize that just as the mind is the form and order of the soul, so the Divine Good is the life and light of both the mind and the soul. These three—namely the Divine Good, the Mind, and the Soul—Plato undoubtedly either demonstrates or hints at as being the principles of all things in almost all his writings. He wrapped this in rather obscure words in his *Letter to Dionysius*. 

As for our soul being older than the body: if you do not wish to say it is older in *time*, say at least that it is more excellent in *dignity*. It is "prior" because it has its origin from a principle superior to bodies; therefore, he placed movement in the soul as coming from itself, but in the body as coming from the soul. And because mutability increases in the body, he says the body depends upon the mutable part of the soul, not only in action but even in mutable substance. 

He also reproaches Anaxagoras <note>A Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed "Mind" (Nous) as the cosmic cause but was criticized by Socrates for falling back on physical explanations</note> because, since he did not place the Soul between the Mind and bodies, he was compelled to describe natural effects as happening by elemental nature rather than being disposed by Intelligence through the Soul, as is proper. He asserts here—just as in the *Timaeus* and the *Phaedo*—that whether things are said to be done through angelic minds, through souls, or through bodies, they are done primarily by the **Divine Will** for the sake of the **Good**.

<margin>
Lachesis
Clotho
Atropos
</margin>

FO. CCCLXVIII.

DE LEG. VEL DE LEG. LAT. DIAL. XII.

<meta>image quality: good; catchword: lex</meta>

### DIALOGUE XII. ON LAWS OR ON THE PASSING OF LAWS. THE ATHENIAN.

If an ambassador or a <term>fetial priest</term> <note>original Latin: "feco," likely a corruption of *fetialis*, a Roman priest responsible for the rituals of international law and declarations of war</note> should falsely report what was entrusted to him, or remain silent when he ought to speak, or if, upon returning from enemies or friends, he is found to have reported something different than what he received from them: let him be brought to judgment for having treated the mandates and embassies of Mercury and Jupiter <note>Mercury was the patron of messengers/ambassadors; Jupiter was the god of oaths and international boundaries</note> with contempt, against the law. And let the judges decide, according to the gravity of the matter, what he must suffer or pay if he is convicted.

The theft of money is certainly illiberal, but robbery is most disgraceful. No son of Jupiter ever delighted in such things by force or by deceit, nor did they ever commit any such act. Therefore, let no one be so deceived by poets or other storytellers into believing that if they have used theft or force, they have committed nothing shameful, but rather something that the gods also have done. For that is neither true nor likely. And he who acts dishonorably against the law is neither a god nor a son of the gods. These things must be known by the lawgiver more than by all the poets. Therefore, whoever obeys this discourse of ours is happy, and always shall be in the future. He who does the opposite shall be restrained by this law:

If anyone steals anything public, whether it be small or great, let him be punished with an equal penalty. For he who takes a small thing, even if he did so with less force than the one who snatched a great thing, has nonetheless stolen with an equal desire. And he who removed something great from a place where he himself had not deposited it, is entirely unjust. The law, therefore, does not deem that one should be punished less than the other because of the smallness of the theft, but perhaps considers that it matters whether one is curable and the other incurable. If a slave or a foreigner is accused and convicted of public theft, let it be decided by judgment what he ought to suffer or pay, as if he might be cured in some way. But if any citizen, educated as we have instituted, is convicted of having stolen or violated something public—whether he is caught in the theft and crime itself or discovered in any other way—we condemn him to the penalty of death as one who is incurable.

Regarding the matter of military service, great deliberations are deservedly held, and many laws are gathered. But this is the greatest of all: that neither man nor woman should ever act without a master and a leader; nor should any citizen habituate themselves to doing anything alone or by their own judgment, whether in jest or in earnest. Rather, in war as in peace, they should always look toward the leader and magistrate, following him at all times. Let them so order their lives according to his nod that they perform even the smallest tasks under his guidance: standing when ordered, and again setting out when commanded; exercising, washing, eating, rising at night, and keeping guard. Finally, let them take their turns, and in the heat of battle, let them neither pursue nor retreat unless the leader and master have signaled it. And to speak briefly: let no one learn at all what it is to act separately from others, but let life always be as communal and shared as possible for everyone. For nothing better, nothing more excellent, and nothing more skillful will ever exist for the sake of safety and achieving victory in war. This very thing must be practiced even in peace from childhood; let them grow accustomed to leading others and being led by others. Let loose license be entirely expelled from life—not only that of humans, but also of the beasts that are under human care.

All dances must also be celebrated in such a way that war may be waged well, and all dexterity, ease, and readiness must be acquired for this same cause. For the same reason, we must accustom ourselves to abstain from food and drink, to endure cold and heat and the hardness of a bed, and especially not to ruin the strength of the head and feet with artificial coverings, nor to lose the nature given from birth by wearing hats and shoes. For these extremities, when they preserve their own nature, provide the greatest strength to the whole body; but the opposite is true if they are weakened. One part <note>the feet</note> serves the whole body most of all; the other <note>the head</note> leads the whole, since it possesses all the primary senses of nature.

But let young men hear these praises of the warlike life—and these laws. Let whoever is conscripted or assigned to any part serve in the military. But if anyone, through cowardice, is absent without the commander's leave, let him be accused before the military leaders when they return. Let all those who served as soldiers act as judges: the infantry separately, the cavalry separately, and others likewise. Indeed, the infantry must be brought before the infantry, and the cavalry likewise before the cavalry, and each to the leaders of the same rank. Whoever is convicted there shall be prohibited from entering any competition afterward and from accusing another of neglected military service. Furthermore, the judges shall determine what he must pay or suffer. But after the judgment of deserted service is settled, assemblies of the infantry and cavalry and others should be held by the leaders so that military rewards may be given to those who conducted themselves strenuously. Let whoever wishes among the leaders of his rank judge concerning victory, provided that he does not use conjectures or witnesses from past battles, but considers only that fight which was recently fought. Then, let those who seem to have fought excellently be presented with a crown woven from the branches of an evergreen tree. Let those who have obtained this hang it afterward in the temples of the warlike gods, however they please, with an inscription and a title, so that it may be a lasting testimony of their virtue. Let those declared in the second and third place do the same.

If anyone has set out for military service and leaves the army before the leaders have dismissed him, let him be accused before the same judges of the rank he abandoned, before whom the previous person accused of neglected service was tried; and if convicted, let him be punished similarly.

However, anyone who is about to judge another must take care with all his might that he does not, whether willingly or unwillingly, impose a punishment or fine falsely and undeservedly. 

<margin>No son of Jupiter is found to have committed either theft or robbery, or to have delighted in force or deceit.</margin>

For Judgment is truly said to be a certain chaste virgin. 

<margin>Judgment is a certain chaste virgin.</margin>

Lying is an abomination to shame and judgment according to nature. For this reason, in all other things, but especially in the casting away of military arms, we must take care not to offend the faithful goddess of judgment. Let no one, through ignorance, think that the abandonment of necessary arms is disgraceful and thus punish someone who does not deserve the penalty. It is indeed difficult to distinguish these things. Nevertheless, it is necessary that the law...
