<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s translation of Plato’s Laws, Book XII. The text transitions from the duties of ambassadors to military discipline and the rigorous process for auditing public officials. It specifically addresses the distinction between cowardice and misfortune in battle.</meta>

# XXXIIII.
## BOOK XII.

...to distinguish between the individual parts. Therefore, let a story be used to illustrate this. If Patroclus <note>The close companion of Achilles in Homer’s *Iliad*.</note> had been carried half-dead to the tents without his weapons—as happens to many—and the armor which, as the poet says, was given to Thetis as a dowry by the gods had been snatched away by Hector, would the son of Menoetius <note>original: "Menoetiades," a patronymic for Patroclus, son of Menoetius.</note> deserve to be blamed by detractors as if he had thrown his weapons away? Furthermore, if anyone should lose their weapons because they were forced—having been thrown from a height, or in the sea, or in a clash of storm and water, or in many other such cases which can be brought forward to clear away the suspicion of cowardice—shall they be blamed? Indeed, care must be taken that we distinguish, as far as possible, a greater and more serious evil from its opposite. In the very act of blaming, the pronunciation of the words themselves shows a distinct difference. For just as the term "thrower-away" <note>original: "abiector," specifically one who casts away weapons in cowardice.</note> is not rightly applied to everyone, whereas "loser of armor" applies to all, one who lost them should not be judged in the same way as one who threw them away voluntarily. For they differ entirely in every respect. Thus, therefore, let us act: If anyone, surrounded by enemies while armed, did not defend himself but voluntarily let go of his weapons or threw them away, preferring to obtain a shameful life through speed rather than an honorable and happy death through bravery, let a judgment be held regarding such a casting away of weapons; but for the former case, let there be none.

<margin>The evil and cowardly are to be punished: not the unfortunate.</margin>
For the evil and cowardly must always be punished so that they may become better and stronger; but the unfortunate, not at all. For punishment there accomplishes nothing. But what punishment will be fitting for one condemned for throwing away weapons and degenerating from manly courage? Especially since it is impossible for a human being to be changed into the opposite, as they say the Thessalian Caeneus <note>A mythological figure born as a woman (Caenis) who was transformed by Poseidon into an invulnerable man.</note> was changed from a woman into the nature of a man by a certain divine power. For the opposite would most fittingly suit the "thrower-away" of weapons: that he be punished by being transformed from a man into a woman. But since that cannot happen, let us devise something close to it, so that since he is so desirous of living, he should henceforth undergo no danger, but live out the rest of his life in disgrace as a most notorious coward. Let this, therefore, be the law: because he has been condemned for shamefully casting away his weapons, let no commander or official ever use him as a soldier, nor let him be received into the battle line. If he acts contrary to this, let the <term>judge of the accounts</term> <note>original: "rationum referendarum iudex," the official responsible for the *euthynai*, or the examination of a magistrate's conduct at the end of their term.</note> take notice; and if the man is of the highest property class, let him be fined ten minae; if of the second, five; if the third, three; if the fourth, one. Furthermore, let the man condemned for throwing away weapons be kept away from manly dangers not only because of his natural cowardice, but also let him be fined similarly: ten minae if he is of the highest class; five if of the second; three if of the third; and one if of the fourth. 

Now, what shall we say about the <term>auditing of accounts</term> <note>original: "repetundis," referring to the legal process for investigating official corruption or misconduct.</note>, which the annual magistrates or those chosen for a council of several years must report? For who will be a sufficient judge if some magistrate, weighed down by the burden of affairs, says or does something unworthy of his high office? This is difficult to find. For since the chosen magistrates excel others in virtue, how shall we find someone more excellent than they? And yet, some divine men must be sought by us as the examiners and judges of these reports. For the matter stands thus: there are many occasions for the dissolution of a state, just as they are seen to be for a ship or a living animal. Although their nature is one, spread everywhere, we nevertheless call them tensions, supports, sinews, extensions, and by many other names. But this occasion is not the least for either the safety or the destruction of the state. For if the judges who demand an account of the magistrate's actions excel the magistrates in virtue, and it is done in such a way that no one can rightly complain, the entire region will thus flourish happily. But if the judgment of accounts proceeds otherwise, then that judgment—by which all civil matters are bound into one—is dissolved, and all magistrates are dragged away from each other; and having now become many out of one, they turn one city into many. From this, all things are quickly overturned by sedition. Therefore, the examiners of accounts must excel all others in every kind of virtue. Let us, therefore, devise their creation in this manner.

<margin>To the Sun and Apollo</margin>
Each year after the summer solstice, let the entire city assemble at a place commonly dedicated to the Sun and to Apollo, to elect three men: each person judging the one he considers better than himself (excepting only himself), who is no less than fifty years of age. Then, of those elected, let them put forward the half who received the most votes; if they are equal, let them be put forward; but if they are unequal, excepting the one who received fewer votes, let them likewise take the remaining half, judging by the number of votes. If many have an equal number of votes and exceed the half-number, let the younger be set aside. After the others are accepted, let votes be cast again until three unequal candidates prevail. But if all these, or two of them, have equal votes, let the matter be committed to good fortune: let them be distinguished by lot. Let a crown woven from the foliage of an evergreen tree crown the one who surpasses in votes and those declared in the second and third place. When the prizes have been given, let them declare by herald that, just as the city of the Magnesians <note>The fictional Cretan colony Plato uses as a model for his laws.</note> has once again found safety under God's guidance, it consecrates its three best citizens as common first-fruits to the Sun and Apollo, according to the ancient law, insofar as they are to follow the judgment.

<margin>To the Sun and Apollo</margin>
In the first year, let twelve examiners of the accounts be appointed. And let them do this until each one has completed his seventy-fifth year; thereafter, let three always be added each year. Let these magistrates, distributed into twelve parts, judge with every free examination and observe diligently. Let them reside, during the time when the accounts are rendered to them, in the place where they were elected, dedicated to the Sun and Apollo. And then, both individually and collectively, after all things have been diligently investigated, let them write down publicly concerning each magistrate what they ought to suffer or pay according to the sentence of the judgment. And if any magistrate complains that he has been wrongly condemned by their judgment, let him bring the case to the chosen judges; and if he escapes, let him accuse the examiners if he wishes. But if he is condemned there also, and had previously been condemned to death by the examiners themselves, let him die as necessity requires. But if he was condemned by them to that fine which can be paid double by him, let him pay double. But now we must hear what [sort of] life...

FO. CCCLXIX.
## ON THE LAWS, OR THE LATIN DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS, BOOK XII.
X

...the sentence concerning the recovery of things, and how they are to be carried out. Therefore, for those who have been set over all others by the consensus of the whole city: as long as they live, let them always be granted the first seats in all solemnities. And whenever it is necessary for judges or presidents to be sent from the city to the common Greek spectacles <note>Specifically the Panhellenic games like the Olympics or Pythian games.</note> and sacrifices, let them be sent from among these men. They alone in the city shall be crowned with a laurel crown; they shall be the priests of the Sun and of Apollo. Also, the High Priest <note>original: "Pontifex summ⁹," referring here to the leader of this college of auditors.</note> shall be chosen from them each year: he who is judged to have excelled the other priests in the previous year. The years shall be distinguished by their names for as long as the city is inhabited. Furthermore, when they die, let there be funerals and tombs of such excellence as are performed for no other citizens. Their garments shall be entirely white. Let mourning and lamentation be absent. Also, let two choirs—one of fifteen girls, the other of as many boys—surround the bier on all sides and take turns praising the priests with songs, chanting his happiness throughout the entire day. In the morning, let the younger men who devote their labor to the gymnasia carry the bier to the monument; these should be chosen by the relatives of the deceased. The first group of unmarried men shall proceed as if armed for battle: some on horseback, some as infantry with light arms, and others similarly. Boys shall sing the ancestral song before the bier, and girls shall follow after them, with the grown women following last. Finally, although the priests of either gender are barred from other monuments, if the Pythian oracle <note>original: "Pythius," referring to the priestess of Apollo at Delphi.</note> also confirms it, nothing prohibits them from approaching this tomb, as if it were something pure. Let the monument for him be a certain long vault under the earth made of the hardest and most beautiful stones, where there are stone beds on either side; here they shall bury that blessed man. They shall plant trees in a circle around it, except for one part alone, so that this tomb may be enlarged if needed. Then, each year, they shall honor these men with musical, gymnastic, and equestrian contests. Let these rewards be given to those whose accounts, having been reported, were not condemned by the judgments.

<margin>The High Priest of the Sun and Apollo.</margin>
<margin>The order of the funeral processions.</margin>
<margin>The condition and excavation of the tomb.</margin>

But if any of these men, relying on the judgment by which he was preferred, should reveal the fragile condition of human nature—that is, if he should fall into error after having been held in high regard—let it be sanctioned by law that he may be accused by anyone who wishes. Let the judgment concerning him be conducted thus: First, the Guardians of the Laws <note>The highest administrative body in Plato's "Magnesia."</note> shall be present; then the colleagues of the accused man himself; and furthermore, the judges of the selected court. Let the accuser allege that the one who is accused is unworthy of both the office and the rewards of the office. If he is convicted, let him be deprived of the office, the tomb, and the other rewards belonging to that office. But if the accuser does not obtain a certain portion of the votes, let him pay a fine: if he is of the first property class, twelve minae; if the second, eight; if the third, six; if the fourth, two. 

I see that Rhadamanthus <note>A mythical king and son of Zeus, famous for his inflexible integrity and judgment in the underworld.</note> was worthy of great admiration in his judging. For he perceived that in those times, all men confessed with one voice that there were gods. And this was not without reason, since many in those times were descended from the gods, among whose number he himself was held. Thus, he seems to have thought that judgments should be committed to gods, not to men. Therefore, he conducted trials simply and swiftly. For by requiring an oath from the litigants in each case, he used to judge both quickly and safely. But now, some deny that gods exist; others do not think they care for human affairs; and many of the worst sort think the gods are so easily won over by cheap sacrifices and many flatteries that they might be allowed to extort great sums of money with impunity. Therefore, that method of judging used by Rhadamanthus is not at all suitable for these men. 

<margin>See how the oath must be prohibited.</margin>

For since the opinions of men concerning the gods have changed, the laws must also be changed. Therefore, a prudent legislator will prohibit the swearing of oaths by litigants in the execution of judgments; let the intent of the accuser and the plea of the defendant be written down in the trials without an oath. For if the license to swear is given to everyone in a city where many cases are brought before the judges daily, almost everyone would be perjured—especially since they are joined by frequent banquets and other customs and private necessities. Therefore, let it be established by law: that the judge who is to judge shall swear, and also those who appoint the magistrates of the republic by their votes; likewise the judge of the dance <note>original: "Choream," referring to the leader of a chorus in a competition.</note>, and the presidents and givers of all musical, gymnastic, and equestrian duties in the contests; and in short, in whatever cases, according to human opinion, no personal profit is to be served. But in those matters where someone might follow an advantage from perjury, let them be judged without an oath. And those who are to judge shall in no way permit the litigants to swear for the sake of persuasion, or to call down curses upon themselves and their kin, or to supplicate basely, or to use womanly commiseration; but let them teach what they think is just in a mild manner, and let the one teaching be heard. If anyone wanders from these rules, let him be brought back to the matter by the magistrate. However, for foreigners litigating among themselves, let them be allowed to swear if they wish, just as they do now. For since they ought not to grow old in the city, there is no fear that they might corrupt others. 

In the same way, let the execution of judgment be carried out among free men: if any free man does not obey the city in those matters which are punished neither by lashes, nor bonds, nor death. And if anyone does not come to celebrate a dance or a procession, or any other such common thing—such as not contributing a tax for the service of sacrifice and peace-rites, or for war—in all these things, let him first restore the loss, or let him hand over a pledge to whomever the city and law have committed it. Once the time has passed and the pledge is sold, let the money be brought into the treasury. But if a greater fine is needed, the individual magistrates shall call the principal men into judgment and compel them to obey the laws by imposing the debt-fine. 

But for a city that does not devote labor to collecting money, and has wealth only from agriculture—since it is occupied neither with commerce nor travels, nor receives foreigners from elsewhere—it is necessary to deliberate what must be done. Therefore, the legislator, by first persuading, should consult for it according to his strength. The mixing of different nations usually confuses various customs, and the habit of foreigners with foreigners introduces many innovations. This harms a city established with good and right laws most of all. But in cities poorly established, it matters nothing if both old and young travel abroad at will, and receive foreigners from elsewhere. On the other hand, to never receive any strangers, nor to allow the citizens themselves to go elsewhere, is both impossible and cruel...

PAGE XXXIIII.
### BOOK XII.

...and it must necessarily seem haughty to other men: that they brand a city with a shameful name, calling it a foe to strangers, difficult, and inhumane. One ought never to make light of whether one appears good or wicked to others. For many, even if they are devoid of virtue, are nevertheless able to judge who is good and who is wicked. Indeed, even in depraved men, there is a certain divine power of intuition <note>original: "divina quādam coniciendi vis," referring to the innate human ability to recognize truth or virtue even when one does not possess it.</note> by which many, even the worst of men, distinguish the better from the worse, both in opinion and in words. Wherefore, it is usefully commanded to cities that they should not place little value on having a good reputation among the masses. Truly, the greatest and most correct path is this: that while you are virtuous, you should seek glory in that way—otherwise not at all, if you wish to be a man of perfect virtue.

For this reason, this Cretan city also ought to strive to obtain the best reputation for virtue among other men. The greatest appearance of virtue is to live by that reason which will deservedly see the Sun and the other gods, along with a few other well-governed cities and regions. Thus, therefore, must one act regarding the travel of citizens abroad and the reception of strangers.

First, let it not be permitted for anyone who is less than forty years old to travel abroad in any way. Furthermore, let no one be permitted to travel for private reasons; but let it be permitted publicly for heralds, ambassadors, and scouts. Indeed, travel outside the region for the sake of waging war must not be considered "civilian travel."

However, some men should be sent to the Pythian Apollo, to the Olympic Jupiter, and also to Nemea and the Isthmus <note>These are the four Great Panhellenic Games: the Pythian, Olympic, Nemean, and Isthmian games.</note>, through whom our city may collectively contribute sacrifices and games to these gods. Let as many as possible be sent, the most beautiful and the best, who in the sacred assemblies pertaining to peace may acquire for their city a honor and glory that corresponds to its military glory. And when they return, let them teach the younger men that the civil institutions of others are far inferior to their own.

As for other "Spectators" <note>term: "Spectatores" (Greek: *theōroi*). These were official observers sent to study the laws and customs of other nations to see if anything could be improved at home.</note> who, having leisure from business, desire to consider the affairs of other men: let no law prohibit them, according to the institution of the Guardians of the Laws. For a city ignorant of good or wicked men, and lacking experience with foreign customs, can never be sufficiently humane and perfect; nor can it preserve its laws by habit and custom alone, unless it also becomes more prudent through the knowledge of laws. There exist even among the common people and the multitude certain divine men—few, to be sure, but nonetheless worthy of your association. These arise no more in well-governed cities than in others. Therefore, whoever in a well-governed city remains incorrupt shall follow the footsteps of these men, setting out from his fatherland by land and sea, so that having finally returned, he may approve some of the laws of his fatherland and correct others if they are deficient. Indeed, without this inspection and investigation, a city will never remain in the best state; nor will it if the investigation is done poorly.

**CLI.** <note>Chapter or section marker 151.</note> How shall both of these things be done?

**ATHENIAN.** In this way, certainly. First, such a spectator should be more than fifty years old. Second, he must be well-approved both in other matters and especially in war, if he is to leave behind an example for the Guardians of the Laws in other cities. He shall not wander beyond his sixtieth year. But within ten years, whenever he wishes, having returned home, let him go to the assembly of those who examine the laws.

This assembly shall consist of both younger and older men, and it shall meet daily in the morning until the sun rises <note>This is the famous "Nocturnal Council," meeting in the quiet hours before dawn to discuss the philosophical foundations of law.</note>. It consists first of the priests who have been granted honors as being more excellent than the others; then of the senior Guardians of the Laws; and finally of the Director of all education <note>original: "disciplinē vniuersę cēsor," likely the supervisor of the *paideia* or educational system.</note>, both the one currently holding office and those who have already completed it. And none of these should come alone, but each with a younger companion whom he has chosen, aged between thirty and forty years. These men shall always discourse on the laws and the republic, and they shall confer with one another if they have heard anything excellent regarding these matters. They shall also speak of the disciplines conducive to this end; those who know these will more easily understand the intent of the laws, while those who do not will find it more difficult.

Whatever the elders approve among these things, let the younger men learn with great zeal. But if any younger man who is brought in appears unworthy, let the whole assembly reproach the one who brought him. However, the youth who conduct themselves rightly in these matters should be honored and preserved by the whole city. But if they turn out worse than others, let them be affected by greater disgrace than others.

To this assembly, he who has inspected the laws and customs of others should immediately proceed upon his return; if he has found anything among others that should be added to the laws, discipline, or education, let him explain it. If he himself has discovered anything, let him declare it to the entire assembly. If he is seen to have returned neither worse nor better, let him be praised, because he willingly did what he could. If he returns much better, let him be affected by great honors while alive, and let the whole assembly decorate him when he is deceased. But if he is seen to have returned corrupted, while he pretends to be wise, let him not dare to mingle with any younger or older person. If he obeys the magistrates, let him live as a private citizen. But if, against the will of the magistrates, he is convicted in court of disputing about the discipline and civil laws, let him die. And if he ought rightly to be brought into court, and no magistrate brings him, let this matter be a reproach to the magistrates when rewards and duties are later decided.

Thus, one who is to set out abroad should be of this sort and travel in this way.

But guests <note>original: "aduenæ," meaning foreigners or visitors.</note> must also be kindly received. There are four kinds of strangers of whom mention must be made.

First are those who are always "summer visitors": like birds across the sea, they fly to other cities during the summer time, mostly for the sake of acquiring money. These the magistrates appointed to those places should receive in the marketplaces, ports, and public houses outside the city in the suburbs, taking care that none of them does anything new or revolutionary. Let justice be rendered to them there fairly, but only as much as necessity compels; let no great familiarity be had with them.

The second kind consists of those who come to see the sights and to hear the muses of the city <note>original: "musas illic auditurī," referring to those visiting for cultural festivals, music, or drama.</note>. All of these should have lodgings near the temples, which are most convenient for receiving guests. Let the priests and temple-wardens have care of them, so that they may remain pleasantly for a sufficient time, and see and hear those things for the sake of which they came, and finally depart without harm to themselves or others. If any of them brings injury to anyone or is affected by an injury, the priests shall judge the matter up to fifty drachmas. Greater crimes should be referred to the overseers of the market.

The third kind of strangers must be received publicly: when someone arrives from elsewhere, sent for a public cause. These the generals, masters of the horse, and military tribunes alone shall receive. And he...

### BOOK XII.

...at the house of the person with whom he stays, while the leaders of the council take care of him. The fourth type of visitor is very rare. This occurs when one of our "spectators" <note>The *Theoros*, or official observer, who travels to study the laws of other nations.</note> returns the favor; he shall be received in this way: first, if he has completed fifty years of age; second, if he has come with the intention of either considering the excellent things others possess or teaching his own. Such a man, being of this character, should freely visit the doors of the wise and the divine; as a guest of learning, he should rightly seek the house of the prefect of education, not doubting that he will find hospitality there because of their shared virtue. And when he has learned from others and taught what he deemed worthy of learning and teaching, he should depart as a friend among friends, affected by fitting honors and gifts. By these laws we shall receive male and female foreigners, and send out our own sons, fearing Jupiter, the God of Hospitality <note>original: "hospitale veriti Iovem." Referring to Zeus Xenios, the protector of travelers.</note>. For foreigners are not to be driven away with snacks and sacrifices, as is done at the Nile, nor are they to be barred from our borders by harsh edicts.

Whoever acts as a surety <note>original: "fideiussor," a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt or appearance in court.</note> should do so openly; let him declare the whole business in writing before no fewer than three witnesses if the surety is for less than a thousand drachmas; if it is for more than a thousand, at least five witnesses must be present. The surety should be the one who previously sold the item, if there is doubt about the person’s right to sell it, or someone who seems sufficient to fulfill the promises. Both the son and the one who sells shall be subject to judgment as liable parties.

If anyone wishes to search for something in another’s house as if it were his own, he must first affirm by oath that he hopes to find what he seeks there; then let him enter naked, or dressed only in an undergarment and ungirt <note>original: "nudus aut interula indutus ingrediatur praecinctus." This was a ritual search intended to prevent the searcher from smuggling a stolen object into the house to "plant" it as evidence.</note>; and the house shall offer itself to him, along with furniture, both sealed and unsealed. But if anyone refuses to permit the one wishing to search, the person who was prohibited shall accuse the one who repelled him, and if the latter is convicted, he shall restore double the value of the missing item. If the master of the house is absent, the those present should only offer what is unsealed; as for the sealed items, the searcher himself should also seal them and leave a guard for five days. If the owner has not come in that time, the searcher, taking the city officials <note>original: "aedilibus," the Roman term Ficino uses for the Greek *astynomoi* or city-wardens.</note> with him, may unseal and search the items, and then seal them again.

In disputed matters, a space of time must be determined for prescription <note>original: "praescriptionem," the legal principle where ownership is gained or lost through the passage of time; a statute of limitations.</note>. Regarding houses and lands, there shall be no dispute by this reasoning. However, for other things, if someone possesses something in the city, the forum, or the temples, and has used that thing openly for an entire year without concealing it, and if no one has claimed it in the meantime, no one shall thereafter be allowed to reclaim that thing as his own. But if he uses it openly in the fields, and the owner is not found within five years, it cannot be reclaimed after the five years have passed. If he uses it at home in the city, the one who lost it may reclaim it for up to three years. In the fields, if he holds it secretly, for up to ten years. If he is outside the region, he may reclaim it whenever he finds it.

Whenever someone by force prevents a litigant or witnesses from coming to court—if that person is a slave, whether his own or another's, the judgment rendered shall be of no effect. If he is a free man, the sentence shall be void, and the one who repelled them shall be imprisoned for a year; and if anyone wishes to accuse him of robbery, let it be lawful. If anyone by force prevents someone from entering a competition to contend in music, gymnastics, or any other skill, whoever wishes may signify this to the officials of the games, who shall ensure that any free man can compete freely. If they cannot do so, the prizes of victory shall be given to the one who was prohibited; and even if the prohibitor wins, the name of the one prohibited as the victor shall be inscribed in whatever temples he wishes. The prohibitor shall not be allowed to inscribe his name or offer the insignia of victory, and whether he wins by competing or not, he shall be guilty of the crime of damages caused.

If anyone knowingly receives a thing taken by theft, he shall be in the same guilt as the one who stole it. Whoever receives an exile or anyone fleeing in this manner shall die. For as the state has decreed someone to be a friend or an enemy, each person ought to regard the same person similarly. If anyone, by his own counsel and without public authority, enters into peace or stirs up war, let him be condemned to the ultimate punishment. But if some part of the city attempted this, the authors of this matter, dragged to judgment by the military commanders and convicted, shall be punished with death. Those who serve the fatherland in any capacity <note>original: "reministrant," serving as officials or ministers.</note> should in no way receive gifts; let us not persuade ourselves under any pretext or reason that gifts ought to be accepted for good deeds, and not at all for others. For it is not easy to know, nor once known, to restrain oneself. Therefore, it is safer to obey the laws which say that no gifts are to be accepted for service to the fatherland. If anyone is convicted of having failed to obey this, let him die.

Taxes shall be publicly arranged thus: first, for the sake of many things, a census of all the property of every citizen shall be held. Then, the tribes shall bring the written annual produce to the magistrates of the fields, so that since there are two taxes, the republic can use either one, as it sees fit each year: namely, a part of either the total census or the annual produce. From these, what is granted for maintenance shall always be excepted.

Moderate offerings shall be offered to the gods by moderate men. The Earth and Vesta <note>original: "Terra quidem & Vesta." Vesta is the goddess of the hearth.</note> are the sacred habitation of all the gods. Therefore, let no one again establish statues for the gods from this material. Gold and silver, both in temples and in other cities, are an envious possession. Ivory, since it was once abandoned by a living soul, is unsuitable for the statues of the gods. Bronze and iron are instruments of war. Therefore, let the images of the gods be established in temples in their entirety from a single piece of wood or any single stone. Work of weaving should also be offered, but no greater than what could be made by one woman in one month. White colors, both in other things and in the craft of textiles, are fitting for the gods. Dyes of other colors should be exhibited only for military insignia. The most divine offerings are birds and paintings which a single painter has painted in a single day. Let all other things be similar to these.

After the parts of the city—what and how many they ought to be—have been distinguished, and the laws regarding the greatest contracts and commerce have been set down according to our strength, it remains for us to speak now of the courts. First, therefore, let the arbitrators whom the litigants have chosen as judges have their place; these can more conveniently be called "reconcilers" than judges. Next, the neighbors and tribesmen distributed according to the twelfth part. If the parties are not reconciled by the first judges, let them litigate with greater penalty before these.

### BOOK XII.

...if the debtor is condemned again, he shall pay as much as the debt was, plus an additional half. Whoever appeals even from this judgment and wishes to contend a third time shall seek out chosen judges. And if he is condemned by these as well, he shall bring both the debt itself and a half-part in addition to the debt. If the accuser, having been rejected in the first judgment, does not remain quiet but wishes to contend again in a second judgment, he shall receive a portion if he wins; but if he loses, he shall lose an equal amount. Since they seek a third set of judges because they were not reconciled by the first and second, the defeated debtor shall, as we have said, deposit for the victor the debt plus an additional half-part; however, the defeated accuser shall deposit a half-part.

But regarding the creation and declaration of judges, the administration of all these matters, the times in which each thing must be done, the casting of votes, the delay and postponement of judgment, the term, the citation, the rejection, and all other things necessary for trials: some we have

<margin>Proverb: Beautiful things are worth repeating twice and even thrice.</margin>

touched upon in the previous sections; but as the proverb says, "beautiful things are worth repeating twice and even thrice." Any small matters that are easy to find, if an older legislator has omitted them, let a younger one fill them in. 

Concerning private judgments, enough has now been said. Public and common judgments, which magistrates use to carry out matters pertaining to them, are found to be correctly established by wise men in many cities. From these, the Guardians of the Laws <note>The *Nomophylakes*, high-ranking officials in Plato’s ideal city responsible for overseeing the legal system.</note> ought to select what is appropriate for this new republic, so that they may diligently examine, correct, and approve each item through trial until they consider them sufficient. Then, finally, having placed an end to the discussion, let these be used throughout their whole lives as if they were unchangeable. 

Regarding silence, praise and blame, and what is just, good, and honorable—which differ in other cities—we have spoken and shall speak again at the end. A future judge must look toward all these things with equity and take care to learn these constitutional laws above all else, holding them firmly in his mind. For to make the man who has learned them good, the writings of the laws, if they are correctly established, contribute more than all other teachings. Otherwise, the divine and wonderful law would possess a name that is nearly a lie. For *Nous* <note>original: "Nus."</note> signifies Mind, while *Nomos* <note>original: "nomos."</note> signifies Law. 

Since many discourses concerning the praise and blame of some people are circulated—partly in poems and partly in prose, sometimes written and sometimes held daily in public gatherings, whether in competition or in false agreement—the writings of the legislator are our clear standard for examining all of these. A good judge will always keep these with him as a remedy and medicine against the poisons of other discourses; by these, he will reform himself and the city; he will confirm and extol the good; and he will recall the wicked from their ignorance, lack of restraint, cowardice, and, to speak briefly, from all injustice to the best of his ability, if they are curable. For if they cannot be cured, those judges and chief judges who put them to death may be seen to be rightly and frequently praised by all. 

But after the annual judgments are completed, let these laws be used: First, let the magistrate who is already exercising judgment hand over all the money of the condemned debtor to the petitioner, leaving only what is necessary for his use. And let this be done immediately after the votes are cast, with the herald announcing it and the judges listening. Then, if a second month passes from the time the sentence was passed and the defeated party has not paid the victor voluntarily and justly, the judges who passed the sentence shall hand over all the debtor's money to the victor. But if his current assets are insufficient, even if only one drachma <note>A unit of silver currency.</note> is lacking, it shall not be permitted for the debtor to drag anyone else into court until he restores the entire debt to the creditor. However, he may still be sued by others. 

If anyone condemned in court harms the judges themselves or unjustly takes anything from them, let those same judges report him to the Guardians of the Laws. If he is condemned for this crime by them, as if he had overturned the entire city and its laws, let him be put to death.

Those who, born and educated under these laws, have fathered and raised children, sons, and sons-in-law, and have lived with others in such a way that their commerce was moderate—having paid the penalties for injuries inflicted and demanded them for those received—just as they lived justly under these laws until old age, so they depart from life according to nature. For the dead, both men and women, let the funeral rites and those things pertaining to the gods—whether of the underworld or the upper world—be performed according to the responses of the interpreters.

<margin>Location of graves.</margin>

No grave shall be made in a fertile place or in a field suitable for cultivation. But let that place receive the bodies of the deceased which is useless for other things and convenient only for this, so that it harms the living as little as possible. For the fertility of Mother Earth must not be hindered by either the living or the dead. Therefore, let no one, living or dead, deprive any living person of nourishment. Let no mound be higher than what five men could construct in five days. Also, let no stones be built upon it larger than can contain the praises of the deceased set forth in only four heroic verses <note>A poetic meter, typically dactylic hexameter, used for epitaphs.</note>. Let the carrying out of the body be done in no shorter or longer time than is necessary for it to be truly recognized and known that the person is dead. 

<margin>Concerning the body and the soul.</margin>

As human affairs go, a funeral procession to the grave on the third day seems moderate. Furthermore, regarding other things, one must believe the legislator and believe concerning the soul: since he says it differs entirely from the body, and that there is nothing else besides the soul itself which, in this life, makes each of us to be this very thing that we are. The body, however, follows us like a sort of shadowy image of a man. It is also fitting that the likenesses of the dead are called "bodies." But in truth, each of us—

<margin><insert>The soul is immortal and will give an account of its deeds.</insert></margin>

the soul itself—is immortal. It proceeds to other gods to give an account of its deeds, as the law of our fathers contains. In this, certainly, the good should be confident, but the wicked should be afraid, seeing that after death they lack all help. While they were living, all their relatives should have consulted with them so that they might live as justly and holily as possible, lest the greatest punishments for their crimes await them after death. Since these things are so, we ought by no means to waste the family estate, as if we thought that this mass of flesh which is buried is our true self; for that son or brother or whoever else we long for, whom we think is being buried, has departed from here to another place once his fates were completed. It will be well done, therefore, to use moderate expense for what is essentially an empty altar lacking a soul. Just how much is moderate shall be rightly established by the legislator. Let this, then, be the law: he who is of the highest property class shall spend no more than five minae <term>minae: an ancient unit of currency; one mina was equal to 100 drachmae.</term> on the funeral and burial; he of the second class...

It emphasizes that the soul is the true, immortal self that must give an account to the gods, while the body is merely a shadow.</summary>

<page-num>FOLIO 371.</page-num>
<header>ON THE LAWS, OR THE TWELFTH DIALOGUE ON THE LAWS</header>
<sig>X iii</sig>

three <note original: "tres">Three minae for the first property class.</note>; for the third class, two; for the fourth, one; and thus the expense for each shall be moderated. Furthermore, the guardians of the laws, among many other duties, must take the greatest care that boys and men, and to speak briefly, people of every sex or age, live well under their constant observation. And at the death of any person, one of the law guardians, chosen by the relatives of the deceased, shall oversee the entire funeral and provide that everything is done well and moderately, not contrary to the laws; let this be an honor to him, and the opposite a disgrace. Assuredly, the lying-in-state and the carrying out of the body and all other matters should be done according to the laws written concerning this. However, let them grant these things to the civil legislator. It is disgraceful for a lawgiver to compel people to decorate the dead with tears or not; but wailing and loud crying outside the house must be prohibited. It shall not be permitted to carry the corpse openly through the more frequented streets of the city, nor to wail publicly, or to afflict oneself outside the city before daybreak. Let these statutes regarding these matters remain fixed. Whoever obeys them shall be free from penalty; but whoever does not obey one of the guardians of the laws shall be punished by all of them as shall be seen fit in common. Other matters pertaining to the monuments of the dead, or to those who are unworthy of burial because of parricide, are to be included in the expenditures and the laws. Therefore, the positioning of the laws has almost reached its end. Truly, the end <note original: "finis">The Greek *telos*, meaning goal or purpose.</note> of all things is not in the fact that they have been made or possessed or inhabited, but rather in the fact that, just as they are rightly made, so they are also firmly established. In such preservation, one must think that as much as was necessary has been done; otherwise, not at all.

**CLI.** You speak rightly, guest; but tell us more clearly what those things are.

**ATHE.** Many things of the ancients are praised for being excellently said, O Clinias; not least the names of the Fates <note original: "Parcarum">The Moirai: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos.</note>.

**CLI.** Which ones?

**ATHE.** That Lachesis is the first, Clotho the second, and Atropos the third, who brings safety to the things previously mentioned. These have been compared to things twisted by fire because they contain an irreversible power. Indeed, in a city and republic, it is necessary to establish stability not only in the health of bodies, but also in the character of the soul through the cultivation of laws; or rather, to bring about the safety of the laws. But it seems to me that the business of laws still lacks a discussion of how that irreversible power can be inherent in them according to nature.

**CLI.** What you say is no small matter; if it is possible to find how this might occur in every single thing.

**ATHE.** It is certainly possible, as it seems to me at present.

**CLI.** Let us not depart from here, I beseech you, before we grant this to ourselves and to the laws.

<margin>It is ridiculous to have taken up labor in any matter in vain, and to have founded nothing stable.</margin>

For it is ridiculous to have taken up labor in any matter in vain, and not to have founded something stable.

**ME.** You advise rightly; you shall have me with you as well.

**CLI.** You speak well. What then is this safety? And by what reasoning shall it be present in our Republic and our laws?

**ATHE.** Did we not say that an assembly of this kind must be established in the city? Where ten of the guardians of the laws, always the seniors, should meet. To these should be added all those who have been honored with the first rewards and honors. Furthermore, also those who have traveled through many cities to find something contributing to the preservation of the laws of their fathers. But these shall not be received into an assembly of this kind unless they are proven to have returned from that pilgrimage uncorrupted and upright, and worthy of the assembly. And each of these shall take to himself one younger man, not fewer than thirty years of age, who by nature and education appears worthy of being chosen, first to the individual and then to the whole assembly. But if anyone unworthy is admitted, the opinion of that person shall be of no weight. We said it is necessary for this assembly to meet before dawn, when one is free from other business, both private and public. Did we not say something of this sort in the preceding parts?

**CLI.** Certainly.

**ATHE.** Regarding this assembly, I will say it again. For I say that if anyone casts this as a kind of anchor for the whole city, containing within itself everything required for this purpose, it will preserve everything we wish.

**CLI.** In what way?

**ATHE.** We shall speak of it opportunely now, and we shall apply ourselves with all our strength.

**CLI.** You have spoken well; and do as you intend.

**ATHE.** It is surely necessary, O Clinias, to devise a suitable savior for each individual work. Just as the soul and the head seem to hold the chief place in animals.

**CLI.** For what reason do you say that again?

**ATHE.** Surely the virtue <note original: "virtus">In this context, functional excellence or power.</note> of these provides safety to every animal.

**CLI.** In what way, I ask?

**ATHE.** For the soul, to which mind is infused, is for other things; and to the head, sight and hearing are inserted. And so, in short, the mind joined with the most beautiful senses and reduced into one, becomes the safety of each individual.

**CLI.** So it seems.

**ATHE.** Certainly. For the mind joined with the senses is also accustomed to bring safety to ships in storm and tranquility. Do you not see that the pilot and the sailors, by joining their senses with the governing mind, protect themselves and the ship?

**CLI.** Why not?

**ATHE.** There is no need for many examples. But let us consider in an army and in medicine: at what sign looking toward do generals and physicians most rightly attain safety? Do not the former look to the flight of the enemy and their own victory, and the latter to the health of the body?

**CLI.** Without a doubt.

**ATHE.** If a physician were ignorant of the body's health, or a general of victory, and the other things we were mentioning, would they seem to have a mind or to know anything in these matters?

**CLI.** Not at all.

**ATHE.** What then in a city? If someone appears to be ignorant of the end <note original: "finem">The ultimate goal or purpose of the state.</note> at which a statesman ought to look, can he first of all be rightly called a prince? Secondly, can he preserve that whose end he is entirely ignorant of?

**CLI.** Not in the least.

**ATHE.** It is necessary therefore, as it seems, if the construction of this new city is to have a good outcome, that there be something in it which knows first what the civil end is; second, how we may attain it; and finally, which law first, and then which of men has consulted rightly toward that end, or not rightly. Indeed, the city which lacks these things will not be surprising if, being seized in mind and sense, it does everything by chance and accident.

**CLI.** You speak the truth.

**ATHE.** Can we say in what part of our city especially, or by what study, some such safeguard for safety has been sufficiently established?

**CLI.** I would not dare to assert that clearly in any way, guest, but I suspect that this discourse of yours is tending toward that nocturnal assembly <note original: "nocturnum illum cœtum">The "Nocturnal Council," intended to be the intellectual and moral heart of Plato's Magnesia.</note> which you just mentioned.

**ATHE.** You have guessed correctly, O Clinias. And it is necessary, as the present matter signifies, that it be endowed with every virtue. Its first and chief virtue is that it should not wander through many and various things, but should always look toward one.

<margin>Why the laws of cities wander far astray.</margin>...to which all things, like arrows, must always be directed. **CLINIAS.** Quite so. **ATHENIAN.** Now, therefore, we understand that it is no wonder if the laws of cities wander far astray. For in any given city, one set of laws looks toward one thing, and another toward something else. To some, the goal of justice is that certain people—whether they be better or worse—should rule in the Republic <note>original: "Repub." / "Respublica"</note>. To others, the goal is to become wealthy, whether they are enslaved or not. The interest of others turns toward liberty. Others establish laws for two purposes: so that they themselves may be free, and so they may subdue other cities. **CLINIAS.** We, then, O Stranger, were correct a long while ago when we thought our laws should look toward one single thing, to which all other matters should be directed. **CLINIAS.** <note>The text repeats the speaker tag CLI. here, likely an error in the original printing or transcription</note> We, then, O Stranger, were correct a long while ago when we thought our laws should look toward one single thing; and we agreed that this should be called virtue. **ATHENIAN.** That is so. **CLINIAS.** And we established that there are four parts of virtue. **ATHENIAN.** Certainly. **CLINIAS.** And that Mind <note>original: "Mentem"</note> is the leader of all these, toward which both all other things and those three virtues must look. **ATHENIAN.** You follow most beautifully, O Clinias. And in other matters, follow in a similar way. We said that the mind of a pilot, a doctor, and a general must look toward a certain specific goal. Redefining the statesman <note>original: "Ciuilē" / "Civilem," referring to a political leader or citizen-statesman</note>, we have proceeded to this point: and now, as if he were a man, let us question this "statesmanlike mind." O wonderful man, where are you aiming? What is that one thing which the doctor can clearly assign in his own art? And can you, who say you excel other prudent men, not do the same in your own faculty? Or can you, Clinias and Megillus, answer on his behalf what this thing is, just as I have often done for you on behalf of others? **CLINIAS.** Not at all, Stranger. **ATHENIAN.** Do you not think it should be asked what that thing is, and in what people it resides? **CLINIAS.** Speak plainly. **ATHENIAN.** Since we have established four species of virtue, it is clear that each of them is one thing, if they together make up four. **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** We also call all these "one." For we say that courage <note>original: "fortitudinē" / "fortitudo"</note> is a virtue, and prudence <note>original: "prudētiā" / "prudentia"</note> is a virtue, and the other two similarly, as if they were not really many, but only that one thing which is virtue. **CLINIAS.** Entirely so. **ATHENIAN.** It is not difficult to say how these two differ from each other and received two names, and the other two likewise. But it is not so easy to say why we have placed "one" in both, and called it virtue, and did the same with the remaining two. **CLINIAS.** How do you mean? **ATHENIAN.** It is not hard to explain what I am saying. Come then, let us divide between us the duty of questioning and answering. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** You ask me why, when we call virtue "one," we then spoke of two parts: one being courage and the other prudence. I will provide the reason to you: because one of them is concerned with fears. For this reason, even beasts participate in courage, as do the souls of infants. For a soul is made courageous by nature, in a certain way, and without reason; but a soul has never been, is not, and will never be prudent <note>original: "prudens"</note> or possessing a mind without reason. Therefore, this is one thing and that is another. **CLINIAS.** You speak the truth. **ATHENIAN.** You have heard from me how these two are different in their reasoning <note>original: "rōne" / "ratione"</note>. Now, in turn, you must teach me how they are one and the same; so that you may think of how to say that although they are four, they are again one. And afterward, I will declare to you how they are four. Next, let us consider whether someone who is to sufficiently understand any matters that have both a name and a definition <note>original: "rōnē" / "rationem"</note> ought to know the name only and not the definition. Or rather, if a matter is of some value, is it not shameful for him to be ignorant of both the names and the definitions of things that excel in magnitude and beauty? **CLINIAS.** So it seems. **ATHENIAN.** For the maker and guardian of the laws, and for him who is thought to excel others in virtue and has received rewards for these things, is there anything greater than courage, temperance, justice, and prudence? **CLINIAS.** How could there be anything else? **ATHENIAN.** Regarding these things, then—interpreters, teachers, lawgivers, and guardians of others—ought they not to teach everyone else who desires to know, or who stands in need of punishment and rebuke, what power virtue has and what power vice has, and excel others in explaining these things? Or shall some poet or teacher of youth, having just entered the city, be judged more excellent than he who professes to excel in all virtue? And then, will it seem strange if that city, where the guardians do not hold the name and the definition of virtue, suffers the same things as many other cities suffer today, as if it were deserted by its protector? **CLINIAS.** It would certainly not be strange. **ATHENIAN.** Therefore, let us apply ourselves to this. How then shall we make the guardians more exquisite than others in virtue, both in deed and in word? Or in what way shall our city become like the head and senses of the prudent because of this kind of guardianship? **CLINIAS.** How, Stranger, shall we make this comparison? **ATHENIAN.** It is clear that the city will be a sort of container for the "head": and the younger guardians, being shrewd and skillful, will be placed at the very summit. From there, they will look around the whole city; and by guarding what they perceive, they will commit it to memory and announce everything to the elders. The elders, who are very like a "mind" because of their knowledge of many things, will consult for the city, using the service of the youth. And thus both together will preserve the whole city in common. Do we think they should be prepared in this way? Or do we think they should all be held as equals? And do we not want some to be educated and instructed by a more exquisite reasoning and placed above the others? **CLINIAS.** Indeed, O wonderful man, that would be impossible <note>meaning: it is impossible to have a state without this hierarchy of wisdom</note>. **ATHENIAN.** Let us come, then, to a more exquisite discipline than that which came before. **CLINIAS.** Let us do so. **ATHENIAN.** And yet, that which we just touched upon is perhaps this very thing we seek. **CLINIAS.** Entirely. **ATHENIAN.** We were saying that it is necessary for the chief craftsman and guardian in each thing not only to be able to see many things, but to tend toward one thing, and to know it; and when he has known it, to direct all things which he perceives toward it. **CLINIAS.** Correct. **ATHENIAN.** Is there, then, any more exquisite consideration of things than to be able to look toward one "Idea" <note>original: "ideam"</note> from many and dissimilar things? **CLINIAS.** Perhaps. **ATHENIAN.** Do not say "perhaps," but in truth, O blessed man, no one will ever have a more certain way and method <note>original: "rōnē" / "rationem"</note> than this. **CLINIAS.** Persuaded by your arguments, Stranger, I agree; therefore, let us proceed. **ATHENIAN.** We must, therefore, compel the guardians of our divine republic to inspect exactly, first, what is the "same" in all four [virtues]: what is in courage, temperance,

# ON LAWS, OR ON THE LATIN LAWS. DIALOGUE XII. FOLIO 372.

X iiii
<meta>catchword: ATHE.</meta>

...where justice and prudence dwell, we rightly wish them to be called by the single name of virtue. Therefore, friends, if you are willing, let us hold fast to this: let us not let go until it is sufficiently clear what that thing is—whether it be as a unity, or as a whole, or as both, or however it may be—to which we must look. Or do we think that if this escapes us, it will be clear enough to us what pertains to virtue, when we cannot explain whether it is many, or four, or just one? If you trust my counsel, we will strive to find a way for this knowledge to be present in our city; otherwise, if it seems best, we shall let it go. **CLINIAS.** By the God of Hospitality, O Stranger, this must not be let go. You seem to speak most rightly. But by what means shall one find this? **ATHENIAN.** We are not yet saying *how* it is to be done; first, let us agree among ourselves whether it *must* be done or not. **CLINIAS.** It certainly must, if it is possible. **ATHENIAN.** What then of the honorable and the good? Shall our guardians only know that they are "many" things, or shall they also know how they are "one"? **CLINIAS.** It seems necessary that they understand how they are one. **ATHENIAN.** What then? Should they only understand it, or should they be unable to declare in speech <note>original: "oratione"</note> what they understand? **CLINIAS.** How could that be? For that would be the condition of a slave. **ATHENIAN.** Is it not the same for all things worthy of study? That those who are to be the true guardians must know the truth of the laws most perfectly, and be able to explain them sufficiently in speech, and follow them in their deeds, judging according to nature what is done rightly and what is not? **CLINIAS.** Why not? **ATHENIAN.** Is not one of the best things that which we discussed seriously above? Where we demonstrated that the gods exist, and what great powers they have? We said this must be achieved by a man to the best of his ability, so that while we might forgive the many if they only follow the letter of the laws, we must commit the guardianship to someone who has achieved, with no small labor and firm faith, all things pertaining to the gods. Thus, we should never choose anyone to be a guardian of the laws, or prefer them over others in virtue, unless he is divine <note>original: "divinus"; meaning god-like in wisdom</note> and has devoted himself to divine studies. **CLINIAS.** It is fair then, as you say, that if someone is slow and unfit in divine matters, he should be kept far away from these most beautiful things. **ATHENIAN.** Do we know then that there are two things which cause those arguments we set forth about the gods to be believed? **CLINIAS.** Which ones? **ATHENIAN.** One is that point mentioned above regarding the soul: that it is the oldest and most divine of all things, whose motion allotted to it the generation of substance and produced it as an ever-flowing stream. The other is regarding the order by which the stars and all other things are moved: that an intellect <note>original: "intellectus"</note> acting as a leader has adorned all things. For no one who has diligently considered and perceived these things was ever so much an atheist <note>original: "ipsius unquam fuit" - likely a corruption of "atheos"</note> that he was not affected in a way contrary to what many suspect. For most people think that those who handle these matters—being devoted to astronomy and other necessary arts—are alienated from religion. Indeed, because they look at the "necessity" by which things happen to the best of their power, people think they do not believe all things are born by divine will for the sake of the good. **CLINIAS.** How then does the matter stand? **ATHENIAN.** It stands entirely the opposite now compared to when these things were thought to be without a soul. Even then, whoever scrutinized those things more diligently than others touched the truth in a marvelous way; for they saw that if the stars lacked a soul, they would never follow such exquisite reason, being void of mind. Some even dared to affirm that Mind adorned all the celestial things. But these same men, not knowing that the nature of the soul is older than bodies, overturned everything again—or rather, overturned themselves—when they thought the soul was younger. For they believed that what they saw before their eyes also existed in heaven. Thus, believing the heavens were filled with earth, stones, and other inanimate bodies, they assigned the causes of the whole world to these. Because of this, it happened that the philosophers who handled these things were regarded by the common people as atheists, and were compared by poets to "dogs barking in vain," and other things full of foolishness were said against them. But now, as we have said, the matter stands quite the opposite. **CLINIAS.** In what way? **ATHENIAN.** No mortal will ever be able to worship God firmly who has not first accepted these two things: First, that among all things that participate in generation, the soul is the oldest and also immortal; and since it is such, it rules over all. Second, <margin>The way of science</margin> as we have often said, he must not be ignorant that there is a true Mind in the stars, and the disciplines that lead to these things must not be hidden from him. Not being ignorant of the Muses <note>The Athenian refers to "Muses" here as the arts and musical education required for a refined soul</note> that harmonize with these, let him use them to compose his character and preserve the laws; and let him be able to give a rational account of those things that possess reason. But he who, in addition to the public virtues, does not possess these things, will almost never be a sufficient prince of the whole city, but rather a servant of others. We must now consider, O Clinias and Megillus, whether we ought to place this "apex" and guardian over the aforementioned laws, so that for the sake of safety, a Nocturnal Council <note>original: "nocturnus principum coetus"</note> of leaders may be present, endowed with the discipline we have described. What then shall we do? **CLINIAS.** What prevents us, best of men, from establishing it as much as we are able? **ATHENIAN.** Certainly, we must all strive for this. I will gladly help you. Perhaps, through my experience in these matters, I will find many other helpers as well. **CLINIAS.** Let us set out upon this way, O Stranger, where God himself seems to lead. But now, let us devise the manner in which this may be done rightly. **ATHENIAN.** Laws regarding these things, O Clinias and Megillus, cannot be written before the entire city has been adorned. For then they may be established with due authority. But it will be proven in no other way than through much teaching and a long examination of discussion. **CLINIAS.** What does this mean again? **ATHENIAN.** First, let a council be established of those men who, by age, learning, character, and habit, are fit for guardianship. Then, as for the things to be learned, it is not easy to find them, nor is it easy to become a student of the discoverer. Furthermore, it is in vain to write down the times in which individual things should be perceived. For the students themselves cannot know when something is learned opportunely until the knowledge of the thing itself is in their soul. Therefore, those things in this matter which cannot be spoken of openly are not rightly attempted—I mean they cannot be spoken of because if they are said, they explain nothing clearly. **CLINIAS.** Since these things are so, Stranger, what do you think we must do?

# ARGUMENT ON THE EPINOMIS, OR THE PHILOSOPHER.

**ATHENIAN.** As the old proverb goes, my friends, we are now all in this together: if we wish to risk everything for the sake of the entire republic, we must act as if we are **throwing three sixes or three ones** <note>original: "ter sex: vel tres talos iaciamus." This is a gambling metaphor for taking a great risk; three sixes was the best throw, and three ones (aces) the worst.</note>. I will certainly take that risk with you by speaking and explaining my thoughts on this discipline and education we have touched upon. This is no small danger, nor is it like any other. Therefore, Clinias, I charge you to take care. For you will win the greatest glory in the city of the Magnesians <note>The hypothetical "Colony of the Magnesians" being planned in the *Laws*.</note>, or in whatever city the god names after himself, if you establish it rightly. Surely you will not escape being seen as the bravest of all who come after you. Therefore, if this **divine assembly** <note>The "Nocturnal Council," a group of elder guardians who oversee the city’s spiritual and legal health.</note> of ours is established, friends, the state must be handed over to it. The remaining lawmakers will not oppose them as being insufficient. Indeed, what we touched upon a moment ago in our words as if dreaming—when we used an image to describe the union of the head and the mind—we shall nearly achieve while fully awake, if these exquisitely learned men are gathered together. If they live in the **citadel** of the region as appointed guardians of the city, they will be such as we have never known in our past lives for the keeping of the watch. **MEGILLUS.** From everything we have said, Clinias, it is clear: either this constitution of the city must be abandoned, or this guest <note>The Athenian Stranger.</note> must not be allowed to leave; rather, we must use every prayer and means to accept him as a companion in organizing the city. **CLINIAS.** You speak well, Megillus. I shall certainly do so, but you must also offer your help. **MEGILLUS.** I will indeed.

-> THE END OF THE DIALOGUES ON THE LAWS. <-

### Introduction by Marsilio Ficino to the Epinomis, that is, the Appendix to the Laws, or The Philosopher.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut letter 'T' showing a scholar-like figure seated among classical architectural ruins and vines.</image-desc>

None of the followers of Plato <note>original: "Platonicorum"</note> doubt, O high-minded Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Ficino's patron.</note>, that a treasure of the divine Plato lies hidden in this *Epinomis*—which is also titled *The Philosopher*. But to bring this treasure fully into the light, many tools are needed. It is not permitted for your Marsilio <note>Ficino refers to himself in the third person.</note>, in providing these introductions, to be too long-winded. This is especially true since the couriers of the printers and engravers are constantly pressing the work forward, greedily snatching the arguments from my hands; they scarcely allow me to reach the very heights of the subject matter in each volume. 

The purpose of the preceding *Laws* was this: to shape the souls of the citizens with all their might so that, having attained a ready tranquility, they might examine the reasons and causes of divine works. In these works, as if in mirrors, they might contemplate and worship God their author. In this contemplation consists **wisdom**, and in worship consists **religion**; in both together lies the whole of human happiness and the goal of the laws. The previous *Laws* promised such a goal, but the *Epinomis* provides it, by God's gift. Therefore, having prophesied this perfect state of mind in the opening, the author then seeks it from God through a certain prayer of supplication. 

Some have judged that happiness can be had in this life; others in the next; and others, nowhere at all. Certainly, whoever thinks it can be acquired by human strength in this life is clearly deceived, as the testimony of all life cries out against them. But those who say "nowhere" are vain, wishing the instinct of all nature to be vain as well. Our Plato very wisely hopes for happiness in the next life, to be obtained both through the virtues of the present life and by the gift of God. Yet he does not despair that a very few people might taste happiness even in this life. In the *Phaedrus*, the *Phaedo*, and the *Republic*, he describes such people as those who live outside the body rather than in it, and live for God rather than for themselves. Thus, by God's breathing upon them, even among the waves of the **River Lethe** <note>The mythological river of forgetfulness.</note>, they seem to sip a bit of **heavenly nectar**. 

Nor is it without reason that he titled this *Epinomis* as *The Philosopher*. For as is clear in the sixth and seventh books of the *Republic* and in the present book, the duty of the philosopher is to investigate the reasons for all things, so that he may find the very **Divine Reason** by which they were made; once found, he may worship it, and once worshipped, he may enjoy it. In this book, while he strives to lead us to happiness (which is undoubtedly placed in religious wisdom), he depicts the character of the true philosopher and educates and forms him through the appropriate levels of the disciplines. Everywhere he seems to demand from the philosopher more virtue and piety than mere knowledge; and whatever knowledge he does demand, he requires it so that the philosopher may venerate the true God above all others—the Master of knowledge and the Author of the things known. 

First, he proves that the power for divine happiness is naturally planted in us because, in all our actions, we both prophesy and seek it, and we are satisfied by nothing else. Then, listing each faculty in order, he shows that this happiness is not gained through natural skills, nor through necessary crafts, nor through playful and joking arts, nor through auxiliary talents. Third, he demonstrates that **wisdom** and **piety**—the foundations of blessedness—are acquired through both moral and contemplative virtues. 

Where he lists the contemplative sciences, he first not only praises **arithmetic**, but actually marvels at it. He says in earlier books that, more than all others, it sharpens the mind, strengthens memory, and makes the soul most fit and ready for every contemplation and action. Here he adds that **number** was handed down to men by God himself as a necessary instrument for reason and discourse. If it were removed, the mind would appear senseless, and the sciences and arts would utterly vanish. He further praises **geometry**, which looks at measurements; **stereometry** <note>The study of three-dimensional layers or volumes.</note>, which weighs loads; **astronomy**, which observes the heavens; and **music**, which studies harmony...
