X v

...imitating celestial things. He also commends physics, where he treats the types of bodies, their compositions, animals, motions, and the principle of generation: but he does so in such a way that he leaves the most minute details of natural things to physicians, considering them too foreign for one who devotes himself to divine matters. Finally, he places Dialectic—that is, **metaphysics** <note>Ficino identifies Plato’s "Dialectic" with the study of ultimate reality or metaphysics.</note>—and its pinnacle, **Theology**, before all others as a queen; namely, using each discipline as steps toward finding and adoring God. He proves there are three duties of this queen regarding the other faculties. First, that she surveys the multitude of all these. Second, that she observes what single communion and connection exists among them all. Third, that she clearly perceives by what reason both this multitude and its union contribute to that one and divine Good itself. He adds, moreover, that unless such a union of doctrines leading to the divine One is grasped, they all turn out entirely vain: nor can what is "one" in them be perceived unless they are compared to the One, from which they receive their very union. But the mind that has pursued all these things, and is thus united to itself, and again through itself united to God: he says that here it is blessed according to its strength, and in the other life entirely blessed. And this is the argument of the whole book.

Shortly after the beginning, where we translated these words: <note>original: "f. Breue aūt tēpus"</note> "**A brief time**," what follows thereafter is read elsewhere as, <note>original: "Ad rationis difcurfum idoneū"</note> "**Fit for the discourse of reason**." And this indeed seems to be left not only in depraved men, but also in moderate ones. Where he praises heaven as the cause of both wisdom and all goods, he wishes such praises to be transferred from the bodily heaven to the **incorporeal heaven**—that is, the **Idea** of heaven. He commands it to be adored there through the visible heaven as if through a signified image. You, however, take note here that men are judged to be in the genus of **terrestrial demons** <note>term: "demons" (dæmones) — In Platonic thought, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or beings between gods and humans.</note>, where he says, "**All other demons together**," and what follows. 

After this he says, if anyone knows what is divine in generation, he will know the true number and piety. "**Divine in generation**" signifies two things: first, a certain spiritual motion which is in the soul, or the moving force, which is the origin of bodily motion and generation; second, the natural **species** <note>The stable, formal patterns or blueprints of things that remain even as individuals are born and die.</note> which is preserved in the perpetual succession of generation. In the motion of the soul, the "true number" is **music**, as Timaeus says, sounding with proportion and harmony. In the species also there is true number. For the species of things are arranged by a certain number and order. Through these, religion is certainly confirmed. For from the free motion of the soul, we prophesy a divine substance existing through itself: and from the perpetual perseverance of ideas in species, we augur eternity. 

You will hear a sentiment similar to the **Mosaic mystery** <note>Ficino often sought to prove that Plato's philosophy was consistent with the revelations of Moses.</note>. For he says, if any evil is brought upon us by the quality of the air or plants or animals, the divine nature is not to be blamed: but the human nature, which distributes its life unjustly. In what follows, you will clearly recognize the **end of the laws** by these words: "**This end of the laws is proposed to you, that through the worship of God and purity of life you may attain the best and most beautiful exit.**" Soon he repeats the three heads of piety. First, that you believe God exists. Second, that you confess He has care for the greatest and smallest things alike. Third, that you think He is turned by no prayers or gifts to act unjustly. 

He also confirms again the faith in divinity from a certain excellent divinity of the soul itself. He thinks that whatever is thus better than the body, so as to be more divine—that is, more like divine things than bodily things—is more ancient than all bodies: because in any genus or order of things, that which is more perfect also possesses being to a greater degree: and therefore it provides the cause of existing to the imperfections. That which provides being to another is undoubtedly also more ancient. He adds that since from the meeting of soul with body a living creature is made, one certain form results there in the body—that is, a bodily life proceeding in the subject from the approach of an incorporeal life. 

He also posits two kinds of things. One indeed bodily, the other incorporeal. To the latter he attributes action, but to the former **passion** <note>term: "passion" — In this philosophical context, it means being the recipient of an action, or "being acted upon."</note>. Likewise, he says there is one form of this incorporeal kind, especially for this reason: that it is simple, and the form of substance always remains in it. But where it reads, <note>original: "Nō em̄ eft aliud"</note> "**For it is not another**," etc.: elsewhere it reads thus: "**For that which is transmuted into another is not incorporeal, and entirely devoid of color, except for the truly most divine genus of the soul.**" 

In the genus of bodies, however, he places five bodies. These he calls "**solids**" <note>The "Platonic Solids" which correspond to the elements of Fire, Air, Water, Earth, and Ether.</note> because, having been increased in depth, they are discerned from planes: and in every body, even the most liquid, there is something solid, both through the consistency of its own nature and, according to the Platonic view, through a certain similarity to the earthly nature diffused as far as heaven. He names heaven "**fire**" because it has its own light, which is the chief quality of fire. It also has perennial motion, such as we see in fire: and like fire, it does not suffer mixing: and because it is not yet driven from its natural place, it is not forced to return by ascent, but revolves. And it shines by act, but is warm by power. It is entirely of a different genus from our fire. 

After celestial fire, he places another species of fire, now more warming than shining, called by the name of the **ether** below the moon. Our fire is a certain trace of this, now not only warming but burning; burning, I say, on account of the excessive roughness of its earthly mixture. But that which flourishes in thin matter shines more purely and warms more sweetly: especially where it ranges into the wide open, restricted by nothing. Below this he places air, water, and earth. He thinks, moreover, that any sphere of the world is composed of these five: so that it is the most perfect among all, as much in the connection of substance as in the communion of power and action. But in any sphere, one is primary: and according to its nature, the others are contained therein. Thus ether in the earth is earthy; and earth in the ether turns out ethereal, and similarly in heaven. But concerning these things, there is something in the *Theology* <note>Ficino's own major work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>: and something in the commentaries on the *Timaeus* treated more diligently. 

Accordingly, he places rational animals in heaven, ether, air, water, and earth. These, he says, are made by the soul; by a triple soul, I say. For he wishes that beyond the one soul of the whole world, there be twelve souls of the twelve spheres: then in any sphere, twelve orders of souls. These orders in heaven are the constellations and stars; on earth, men; in ether, air, and water (namely, the higher part), they are demons. In each of these animated things, the rational soul [is joined] to the body...

->### ARGUMENT ON THE EPINOMIS, OR THE PHILOSOPHER.<-

<meta>catchword: Which</meta>

...joined with its own <note>The soul</note> to procreate an animal—that is, a certain composite of its own body and a life utterly infused into that body. This life, once it has become corporeal, depends on a threefold soul: namely, from its own individual soul, from the soul of its celestial sphere, and from the soul of the entire world <note>The *Anima Mundi*, a vital force that Plato believes animates the entire universe.</note>. Moreover, Plato argues that the celestial bodies possess souls based on the divinity of their celestial substance, the vastness of their size, their life-giving power over all things, and the speed and efficacy of their motion. Furthermore, that these celestial souls possess a mind is inferred from the orderly and persistent nature of their course. He adds that the "necessity" of a soul possessing a mind is of the highest degree, which you should understand in two ways. First, because natural necessity—such as the way a specific part of fire is driven from elsewhere to burn and ascend—acts by external force. However, the nature of an intellectual soul, insofar as it participates in the intellect, is the mistress of its own action. Second, because the movement of the soul, being free by nature, could easily go astray or wander back and forth, unless it were guided by a mind like a charioteer; by a perfect mind, I say, which foresees from the beginning both the best end for an action and the most choice path. When this best mind is present in the best soul—as is the case in the stars—it necessarily achieves its prescribed work. For the best souls (that is, the most powerful) do not resist their bodies, and the best mind does not change its counsel. 

From this, he says that the three **Fates** <note>original: "parcas"; the *Parcae* or Fates (Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos) who in mythology spin the thread of life.</note> preserve in perfection whatever the celestial gods have deliberated with certain counsel. He mentions three Fates, meaning a single destiny disposing three principles according to the nod of the divine minds: namely, the beginnings, the middles, and the ends of things. In the previous book, he said that the things established by fate are similar to materials worked by fire—whether they are straight or twisted. For just as these materials cannot be bent back in the opposite direction, neither can the things of fate. Nor did he mention things "twisted by fire" without reason, for the fiery spheres of the heavens are the instruments of fate. 

Furthermore, where he says the stars are either eternal or long-lived, he sufficiently touches upon the **Orphic** and perhaps the **Hermetic** <note>original: "Mercurialē"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with secret wisdom.</note> opinion: namely, that after many ages, the world is destined to be resolved into fire. For that which is composed must eventually be dissoluble; and fire, as the greatest and most powerful of all things, will eventually and wonderfully assume all things into itself. Yet the divine Mind, the craftsman of this work, will again reform a similar work from that fire with a similar fate and a most easy nod of will. This opinion was confirmed by **Anaxagoras, Empedocles, Heraclitus**, and most of the **Stoics**, who confessed that God is omnipotent and able to preserve His work forever in the same order as it was handed down; but the work itself, because it is of a finite nature and internally conflicting, cannot be preserved on its own. Thus, what is lacking in the formation, God repays through reformation. 

But let those thinkers see to that. You, however, will note here that Plato refutes those who deny that the celestial bodies are alive simply because they always move in the same way. This constancy ought to be an argument to everyone not of an absent life, but of a present sufficiency and wisdom. Remember, moreover, that the soul is considered so different from the body that they have nothing in common—that is, no common matter—likewise because the soul does not depend on matter. Again, because corporeal nature is judged to be neither true substance nor true essence, he calls the souls of the stars "gods," but their bodies he calls "statues of the gods." 

Accordingly, among the celestial gods, he gives the name **Jupiter** to the office of providence, and **Juno** to the vital power subject to that providence. He also says that the stars perceive individual things acutely, through a sense obviously far different from our own. He also describes the nature of **demons** <note>term: <term>daemones</term>; in the Platonic sense, these are not "demons" as evil spirits, but intermediary guiding spirits or "daemons" who bridge the gap between gods and humans.</note> as powerful in prudence, sensation, memory, and motion: a middle nature between gods and men, to be honored for the sake of intercession and interpretation. They know our thoughts—specifically from our expressions, movements, and affections—loving the good and hostile to the wicked. Here he seems to consider all demons to be good, specifically those who are fit to be worshiped. Elsewhere, however, he indicates that some are evil. He says the ethereal and aerial ones are invisible, but the watery ones, whom he calls "demigods," are sometimes seen, though barely, and through an internal rather than external sight. He adds that souls are warned by demons through dreams, voices, prophecies, and omens: especially at the time when the soul migrates from the body. He says many things have been added to religion because of these warnings. 

He says, furthermore, that it is not permitted for a mortal nature to change those things which have been established by laws in religion. "Mortal," he says; for it is permitted to a divine nature. Learn this divine saying: The most divine Reason of all things established the visible world; the happy man, admiring this world, is kindled with a love for finding divinity, whence he escapes as happy both here and in the next life. Through wisdom, he becomes truly one and truly at peace, translated to places congruent with virtue, destined to contemplate divine things for all remaining time. 

Soon, where it is translated, *For divine matters...* and what follows, it is read elsewhere: *For it is not the part of a prudent man to honor some divine things while neglecting others.* Amidst this, he narrates certain very well-known astronomical facts. He praises a temperate quality of air as beneficial to character and virtue. Then, where he says that motions tending toward the good proceed from a good soul, but those ending in evil are of a contrary mode, do not think that there is one "good" world soul and another "evil" one; rather, good things proceed from the soul of the world insofar as it participates in the mind. Otherwise, evil things would arrive from it—that is, things entirely lacking in order and number. For he named things "evil" in the higher realms that lack harmonious number and beauty; but "good" things are those adapted with consenting numbers. He adds that evil (that is, the privation of order) was conquered by good things from the beginning of things by the very ideas of the divine mind. Likewise, it must be conquered while the world perseveres. These things were said according to the judgment that punishes the impious: for clearly, the divine judgment punishing the wicked conquers the evil of injustice with the good of justice. 

You will note that the greatest virtue is religion, and that negligence of religion has been the cause of unhappy ignorance for men. Likewise, the best character is that which is mixed from temperance and fortitude—docile, mindful, and inclined toward divine things. When such characters are rightly educated, the truest worship of religion proceeds from them to others, which is most useful to the city. He adds that wisdom cannot be learned without God's help; and from one who does not observe a proper method in teaching, it would be better not to learn at all. Likewise, that all things are full of gods: so much so that the higher beings neither forget our affairs nor desert us. As for those things concerning numbers...

It also details the role of "daemones" as intermediaries between humans and the divine, and emphasizes that true wisdom and happiness come from studying the orderly, numerical beauty of the heavens.</summary>

# EPINOMIS OR THE PHILOSOPHER. FOLIO 374.
<meta>Catchword: Which</meta>

...he touches upon numbers briefly; where it may be more opportune, we shall explain at greater length. For now, understand it in this way. Numbers in themselves are indeed incorporeal, since they are nothing other than repeated unity, and unity is indivisible. But when they are thought to take on a position, they can be imagined as being converted into points. Likewise, from a certain drawing from point to point, a line is born; from the drawing of a line, a surface <note>The Latin *superficiem* refers to a two-dimensional plane or surface.</note> is seen; and from its descent, depth is born. Some numbers are linear, others are superficial, and others are cubes or solids. The first are like the number two, which is closest to unity. The second are like the number four, proceeding from unity by way of two. The third are like the number eight, perfected from two having been returned into itself <note>i.e., 2x2x2=8, forming a three-dimensional cube.</note>. 

Likewise, the "double" proportion <note>term: *Dupla* / Double proportion; the ratio of 2:1.</note> is considered perfect. First, because it is the primary one, generated between one and two. Second, because while it seems to have departed from the "one," by doubling it restores the "one" <note>This likely refers to the mathematical harmony where the octave returns to the same note at a higher frequency.</note>. Third, because it contains all other proportions within itself. For both the *sesquialtera* <note>term: *Sesquialtera*; a ratio of 1.5 or 3:2, which in music forms a perfect fifth.</note> and the *sesquitertia* <note>term: *Sesquitertia*; a ratio of 1.33 or 4:3, which in music forms a perfect fourth.</note> and similar ones are like parts within the double. Nature observes this in the heavens; and for its sake, it also preserves the *sesquialtera* and *sesquitertia*, from which the double is composed. 

For the Pythagoreans, when they measure the intervals of the spheres, they compare the Earth to the firmament <note>The outermost sphere of the fixed stars.</note>; likewise to the Moon and the Sun; and also the Sun to the firmament. In these comparisons, the interval from the Earth to the Sun compared to the interval from the Sun to the firmament produces a *sesquialtera* (3:2) ratio between Earth and Sun, and a *sesquitertia* (4:3) between the Sun and the firmament. In that first proportion, the *diapente* <note>original: *diapente*; the musical interval of a fifth.</note> harmony is born; from the latter, the *diatessaron* <note>original: *diatessaron*; the musical interval of a fourth.</note>. From both of these together, the double proportion and the *diapason* <note>original: *diapason*; the musical interval of an octave.</note> harmony is completed. They also maintain that from the Earth to the Moon a *diatessaron* is made, just as to the Sun a *diapente* is made, and from the Sun to the firmament a *diatessaron* again. 

Just as nature observes such proportions in the spheres, so it does in the actions and passions of the elements. For a perfect action to occur, it is necessary for the acting agent to be twice as powerful as the subject. But why? Because since it intends in its acting to double itself, it certainly requires a doubling proportion. Otherwise, if it surpasses it by a smaller space, the resisting subject will impede the perfect action. Just as the double ratio leads to the generation of a substantial form, so the *sesquialtera* leads to the familiar affection and shape of the form, and the *sesquitertia* to certain more common accidents. 

Furthermore, the measure of this same proportion is preserved in our humors. <margin>The proportion of the humors of our body.</margin> For they hold that blood should be double to the phlegm; and this double to the bile; and this likewise double to the black bile. Because if they have double proportions, they consequently contain the *sesquialtera* and *sesquitertia* which are within the double. Similar things consist in the sense of hearing. Within it, there are four degrees of Air; three of Fire; two of Water; and one of Earth. You know, however, that between four and three, a *sesquitertia* proportion is made. For the number four contains three, and additionally one unit, which is the third part of three. You also know that the *sesquialtera* is placed between three and two, since three contains two, and additionally one unit—that is, the half-portion of two. Therefore, in the very affection of hearing, all proportions are more manifest than in the others. And so also are the harmonies: the *diapason* (the eighth voice) in the double; the *diapente* (the fifth) in the *sesquialtera*; and the *diatessaron* (the fourth voice) in the *sesquitertia*. I omit how similar proportions can be imagined in the four elements. But of these, another time. 

Physicians also agree with these things in those matters pertaining to touch and, in a way, to taste, counting four degrees. First, that which is scarcely perceived by the sense. Second, that which is clearly perceived but does not offend. Third, that which is already offending and then hurting. Fourth, that which kills in a short time. In these degrees, the double, the *sesquialtera*, and the *sesquitertia* are found. But let the physicians see to these. 

Plato introduces here one, two, four, six, eight, twelve. From four to two, the ratio is double; from eight to four is also double. These excesses are equal in proportion—for each is made through the double—but they are not equal in number: for eight surpasses four by four, but four exceeds two by two. Compare again the number six, first to four and then to eight. From the first, a *sesquialtera* (3:2) is made; from the second, a *sesquitertia* (4:3) is made. These excesses are therefore unequal in proportion, but equal in number. For in both cases, the excess is by two. Again, compare six to twelve in a double proportion; and between these, compare eight to both. Certainly, from twelve to eight, a *sesquialtera* is born. From eight to six, a *sesquitertia* arises. From these two, the double ratio between six and twelve is composed, in which those two excesses appear evidently unequal both in proportion and in number. All these things are more conveniently treated in the commentaries on the *Timaeus*.

### PLATO’S EPINOMIS OR THE PHILOSOPHER. CHARACTERS OF THE DIALOGUE.
### CLINIAS. THE ATHENIAN GUEST. MEGILLUS.

<margin>CLINIAS</margin>
As we had jointly decided, all three of us have finally arrived here correctly, O Guest—I and you, and Megillus here—to inquire about prudence <note>The Greek term *phronesis*, often translated as practical wisdom or prudence.</note>, and by what reasoning we may be able to reach it. For once this is understood, the human condition holds itself best—as far as nature allows—toward prudence. For we have already treated the other matters pertaining to the making of laws. But that which is greatest both to find and to say—namely, by what knowledge a man may become wise—we have neither found nor stated. Yet I think it should by no means be omitted, lest we leave that work nearly imperfect, for the sake of opening which we have traveled this far. 

ATHENIAN GUEST: You speak skillfully, O friend Clinias. You are now about to hear a certain discourse that is at once wonderful, and yet in another way not wonderful at all...

->...I think you know.<- For many, tossed by the waves of this life, proclaim this: that the human race cannot be happy and blessed. Pay attention, therefore, and consider whether I too seem to speak correctly on this matter. I judge it impossible for men in this life—except for a very few—to attain happiness and blessedness. There is, however, good hope that after death one may obtain all those things, for the desire of which, enflamed, he lived and completed his life according to his best strength. Nor do I bring forward something unheard of and new, but something that we all, both Barbarians <note>In the Greek context, "Barbarians" refers to any non-Greek speakers, often including Persians or Egyptians.</note> and Greeks, know in a certain way. For no one is ignorant of how great the difficulty is in the first generation of animals: first in conception and the womb; then in birth and delivery; afterwards in nutrition and education. For we are not ignorant that these things happen through a thousand labors. Moreover, the time of life is brief, not only in respect to the long duration of evils, but also in whatever way one considers it: that which makes us breathe a little bit, as it were, around the middle of human life. 

<margin>Sad old age</margin>

But soon **sad old age** coming upon us makes no one wish to return to life again, when he considers past troubles—unless he be carried away by a childish opinion. That all these things are so, this is my argument, which is now being examined. For we ask in what way we can become wise: as if some power of this kind were present in individuals. Which indeed then escapes us, when one has proceeded to any of those faculties which are commonly called by the name of <term>art</term> <note>original: *ars*; refers to a technical skill or craft.</note> or prudence or science; as if none of those in these kinds of human affairs were worthy to be called by the name of wisdom. Yet the soul strongly trusts and prophesies that some power of this kind is in it according to nature; but what it is, and when and in what way it is present, it cannot easily find. Does not this doubt and inquiry of ours concerning wisdom look mostly to this? It is full of hope, no doubt, in individuals: whoever seeks to examine both themselves and others prudently and harmoniously in every kind of speech and disputation. Shall we say these things are so, or otherwise? 

**CLINIAS:** We indeed, Guest, concede those things: hoping, namely, together with you that we shall thereafter reach the truest opinion concerning these matters. 

**ATHENIAN:** Let us therefore first run through the other arts, which although they are called sciences, do not make a man wise: so that with those removed, we may bring forward and compare those which we need, and having made the comparison, let us learn. And let us see those in the first place: which the human race needs most. For truly these are the first, and most necessary of all. The practitioners of which might have seemed wise from the beginning, but now they are not held as wise; and because of those arts, they are disparaged. It must be said, therefore, what these are: and that whoever the best men wish to appear to be, they should flee the studies of such arts. 

The first indeed is that which commanded one to abstain from the eating of human flesh—which had grown among men in the manner of wild beasts, as stories tell—and called us back to a more modest diet. In which indeed the ancient men who kindly and humanely consulted for us; let them be valued nevertheless: but let them not usurp the name of wisdom. Next, the skill of cereal food <note>Refers to the cultivation and processing of grain, the "Art of Ceres."</note> is useful indeed and beautiful: but it will never make a man absolutely wise. For it brings difficulty and trouble rather than wisdom. Nor will agriculture do it. For we seem to have approached the cultivation of the earth not by art: but by nature and a certain favor of God. 

<margin>Fashioning</margin>

But neither the construction of houses, and all other building; or the **making** of furniture; nor copper-working, or wood-working, or pottery, or weaving; nor the crafts of all instruments: which, adapted to the common people, bring nothing to virtue. Even the whole art of hunting, although it is varied and ingenious, nevertheless does not bestow magnificence and wisdom. But neither does divination or any interpretation. For even if the diviner knows what they say, he does not understand whether the things are true or not. 

After it is established for us that none of those arts by which they prepare necessary things make a man wise: there remains a certain imitative faculty, least serious. For often imitation is made with instruments: mostly with deformed gestures and figures of bodies. Even in eloquence and the muses <note>Refers to poetry, music, and the liberal arts governed by the Muses.</note> there is imitation: and in modeling and painting: where they express many and varied things in bodies both hard and soft. None of these makes a man devoted to imitation wise. 

But with imitation removed, those arts remain which are seen to be occupied in bringing help. These indeed are many and varied: but among them all the warlike one, which they call generalship, excels. This is highly approved because of its use: but it is most in need of luck; and it progresses more by natural fortitude than by wisdom. Medicine also helps us against the force of immoderate cold and heat, and other things of this kind by which the nature of animals is harmed. But none of these leads to true wisdom. For they proceed by uncertain conjectures and opinions. We will not deny that sailors and pilots also bring help. But nevertheless we will not permit any of them to be called wise by anyone. For none of them knows the anger or friendship of the winds: which is both the best thing and most required in the art of piloting. Nor do we want those to be called wise who assist litigants with the power of speaking. Since indeed they adapt themselves to manners by memory and the use of opinion: and they wander far from the understanding of true justice. 

<margin>Concerning the natural power of talent.</margin>

There remains a certain wonderful power which similarly claims for itself the reputation of wisdom, which many would call nature rather than wisdom. This consists in this: that someone easily learns what he wants; and remembers many things for a long time and firmly; and returns what is suitable to each person when it is necessary, quickly and conveniently. For some will call all these things nature, others wisdom, others the cleverness of nature. But no one composed of mind will concede that anyone is truly wise because of these things. 

Nevertheless, it is necessary that some science be found which whoever has may not only seem, but in truth be wise. There is need of attention. For we have undertaken an altogether arduous thing: searching for another science beyond the said arts which may rightly be called true wisdom. He who has attained it will neither be abject nor foolish: but a wise and good citizen because of it, in manner...

# FOLIO 375.

## EPINOMIS, OR THE PHILOSOPHER.
<meta>Catchword: [we] must</meta>

...and a modest prince and subject of the city. Let us therefore inspect this first art: which is so situated among all human arts that if this one alone were removed, human nature would be rendered most ignorant and senseless. It is not difficult to find. For if you compare one to another, that art which gave the concept of number to the mortal race will surely achieve this. I believe a God, rather than mere fortune, bestowed this gift upon us for our salvation. Which God I think it is, I will tell you—even if I seem absurd, and yet in another way not absurd at all. For why should we not consider the author of all good things to be also the cause of the greatest good, I mean prudence? <note>original: "prudētię" (prudentia). In a Platonic context, this refers to practical wisdom or the ability to govern oneself and others rightly.</note> Which God, O Megillus and Clinias, do I extol with praises? The Heaven itself, almost; which it is right that we—just as all the other spirits and the rest of the gods do—should worship with honors and especially adore. All would confess that the Heaven has been the cause of all other good things for us. We affirm that it has given us number, and will continue to give it to anyone who wishes to observe. This will be attained by the one who ascends to a right contemplation of it—whether one pleases to call it the World, or Olympus, or the Heaven—provided one considers its variety, and how it effects different seasons by the winding and circuit of the stars, and grants nourishment to animals, and bestows wisdom upon humans along with number and other goods. This indeed is the greatest thing: if anyone, receiving the gift of numbers from it, traverses its whole circuit. But let us recall what was said, and most rightly so, in our earlier discussion: that if anyone takes away number from human nature, we shall never be prudent. For the soul of this living being [man] will almost never perceive the whole of virtue if you take away reason; nor can an animal that is utterly ignorant of two and three, and even and odd, ever give an account of the things which it perceives only by sense and memory. Nothing prevents it from having the other virtues, I mean courage and temperance. 

<margin>The importance of number in knowing things.</margin>

But how shall he who is devoid of true reason ever turn out wise? And he who lacks wisdom, the greatest part of all virtue—since he cannot be absolutely good—will never attain happiness. Thus it is altogether necessary to presuppose number. That this is necessary can be shown by many reasons. But it is rightly shown now by this reason: that the other arts which we enumerated a little while ago will vanish entirely if number is removed. Perhaps one thinking about the arts will think there are only a few things in which the human race needs number—though even this would be a great matter. But if one looks at what is divine in generation and what is mortal—in which matter piety toward the gods and true number will be recognized—he will surely find that no prophet, however great, can comprehend how much of a cause of virtue number is for us, provided the whole of it is present. For even all music needs the number of movements and voices. And what is greatest, we can easily know from this that number is the cause of all good things, but of no evil; because irrational, disordered, deformed, inept, and discordant movement—in short, everything in which there is some evil—lacks all number. Surely he who is finally to be happy ought not to be ignorant of this. And he who is ignorant of the just, the good, the honorable, and other such things, and has not received a true opinion about them, will not be able to use the power of number and reason to persuade himself and others. 

<margin>From where we learned number.</margin>

But let us now consider how we learned to use number. Come, from where did we perceive "one" and "two"? To notice that, we received the power and force from the nature of the whole universe. Indeed, while nature has denied many animals the ability to learn the use of number from a father, God first implanted this in us, so that we might understand number in that which He shows us. Then He showed it more aptly, and He does so continually. In this explanation of things, if you compare one thing to another, you could see nothing more beautiful than the light of day. Then you might consider the night by the service of the eyes in turn, where the greatest diversity appears. For if you do not cease to revolve these, you will see many nights and many days, by which the heaven never stops teaching men "one" and "two," so that even he who is slowest may learn from this to use number. For thus by seeing three, and four, and as many as you like, he will understand these things. Concerning these, God formed one Moon; which, appearing now smaller and now larger, is seen varying daily for up to fifteen days and nights. This is a circuit, if one wishes to bring the whole circle into one. Therefore, so to speak, even the slowest animals to whom God gave a nature capable of learning would perceive number. In these things, therefore, every animal that has the power of learning can, by considering each thing for itself, become most fit for counting. But to compare every number to number <note>This likely refers to the study of ratios and proportions.</note> is a greater task; and therefore He made the moon, as we said, now waxing and now waning. From this He established months for the year, and taught every number to be compared to number by a certain happy fortune. Hence the earth, made more fertile, conceives and brings forth fruits for the nourishment of all animals, while the winds blow sweetly and the rains flow healthfully into the lap of the earth. And if any evil happens in these, divine nature is not to be blamed, but human nature, which distributes its life unjustly. To us, now writing about laws, the other things which are best for men seem easy to know; and anyone can sufficiently understand what is said about them, and moreover do them, after seeing what is beneficial and what is not. The other things, I say, seemed to us and now seem not too difficult; but in what way men may be made good is utterly most difficult. Again, it is possible, as they say, and not arduous to possess other goods: riches to the extent that is proper or not; and a body such as is becoming or not. Everyone confesses that it is also necessary to have a good soul. Asked how one is to become good, anyone would respond thus: if he is just, moderate, and brave, and other things of this kind. Who would deny that the soul ought also to be wise? But what wisdom is to be acquired, as we recently discussed, we found that none of the many agree among themselves. Now, therefore, beyond all the wisdoms we described above, we have found one not insignificant for this very purpose: so that he who has learned what has been said may appear wise.

<summary>The author argues that the study of number, derived from observing the cycles of the heavens and the moon, is the foundation of reason, virtue, and true wisdom. Without the mathematical order provided by the cosmos, humans could not achieve prudence or happiness.</summary>

Whether the man who has learned these things is truly wise and good must be investigated by reason. CLINIAS: I remember that most especially. ATHENIAN: For that which is better, older, and more divine is prior to that which is inferior and viler. Similarly, the leader is prior by nature to the led, and the prince to the subject. Let us therefore admit this: that the soul is older than the body. If this is the case, it will surely be believed that the first thing in generation is the beginning and the lordship. Therefore, let us establish that the lordship and the principle of the principle <note>original: "principiūq; principiī" (principiumque principii). CLINIAS: Let that remain affirmed according to human strength. CLINIAS: Correct. ATHENIAN: Therefore, such a thing is rightly called a living being. CLINIAS: Certainly. ATHENIAN: We can conveniently say there are five solid bodies from which the most beautiful and best things are fashioned. <note>These are the five elements: fire, water, air, earth, and ether.</note> But the other whole genus possesses a single form. For there is nothing else that can be incorporeal and entirely devoid of color, except that most divine genus in which the soul resides. To this genus alone it belongs to fashion and manufacture; but to the body, it belongs to be fashioned, to be born, and to be seen by the eyes. But to the genus of the soul, to repeat again, it belongs to be invisible, to possess knowledge, to be intelligible, and to be a sharer of memory and reason in both the odd and even transformations. <note>The "odd and even" refers to the mathematical and harmonic laws that Platonists believed governed the movements of the soul and the cosmos.</note> 

Since there are five bodies—fire, water, thirdly air, fourthly earth, and fifthly ether—many and various individual living beings are produced by their predominances. <margin>providence prevails</margin> <margin>fire or bodies</margin> <margin>What proceeds from that which possesses a mind.</margin> This we can state in one way: let us first establish that the earthly genus of living beings includes humans, many-footed animals, and those lacking feet—both those that move and those that are stable, connected by roots. But one thing must be understood everywhere: that although all things are made from all genera of bodies, yet the nature of the solid earth is most prevalent in this earthly genus. We must also establish another genus of living beings, which can also be born and seen, and which possesses mostly fire; it also has tiny particles of earth, air, and all the rest. Therefore, we must say that various and visible living beings are born from this. These we think are the celestial living beings—the divine genus of the stars—constituted with the most beautiful bodies and the most blessed and best souls. To these living beings, we think one of two lots must be attributed: for either they are each necessarily and entirely immortal and divine without destruction, or they lead a long-lived life, sufficient for each so that they require no longer. Let us consider, I say, these two genera of living beings. And again, let us say that both are visible: one of which seems to be made entirely of fire, the other of earth. But the earthly thing moves without order, while the fiery moves by every reason of order. That which is carried without order must be thought insane—which is mostly what the living beings among us do. But that which proceeds in order in the heaven demonstrates sufficiently by that very track that it possesses a mind, because it always travels through the same paths, acting and suffering the same things. The necessity of the soul having intellect is the greatest of all necessities; for it governs as a leader and is not led. When the soul, which is the best thing, conducts itself by counsel according to the best intellect, then that which is truly perfected according to intellect will necessarily happen without perversion; nor could adamant be more solid or immovable. <note>original: "adamas." A legendary stone or metal of impenetrable hardness, used here as a metaphor for the unchangeable laws of logic and nature.</note> But the three Fates, indeed, preserve what each of the gods has deliberated with the best counsel. It was necessary, therefore, to serve as an argument to men: that the stars and that whole circuit possess a mind, because they always do the same things. For in a vast and wonderful span of time, they have already deliberated what they must do. They do not approve now this counsel and now that, shifting up and down. Therefore, they neither err nor revolve outside the ancient order. But to many of us, the opposite has seemed true: because they always act the same and in a similar way, people think they have no soul. Following this insane opinion, the common people have thought that the human race has life and mind because it is erratic, but the Divine, because it remains in the same paths, lacks a mind. <margin>The size of the stars</margin>...perfected, they always act the same. This nature of the stars is most beautiful to behold; as they perform their progression and dance—the best and most magnificent of all dances—they provide benefits to all living things. That we rightly call these beings animated <note>Latin: animata, meaning "having a soul" or "living"</note> is also proven by their size. For they are not merely as large as they appear to our eyes, but each one is of incredible magnitude. This must be believed because it is demonstrated by sufficient proofs: we understand that the whole Sun is larger than the entire Earth, and all the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> possess a marvelous magnitude.

Let us consider, then, how it could be possible for such greatness to be carried around by some nature for such a long time. I assert, therefore, that God is the cause, and it could not happen otherwise. For as we have declared, no living thing could exist except because of God. Since, therefore, God can do this, it was easy for Him first to grant life to every body and magnitude, and then to lead them in the way that is thought to be best.

Finally, we wish this true opinion to be held concerning all these things: it is impossible for the earth, heaven, all the stars, and the massive bodies composed of them to revolve with such exquisite reason through years, months, and days, and to do all good things for us, unless a soul either attends to or dwells within each of them. It becomes a man, the more lowly he is, to trifle less with these things, and to try instead to say something certain. If anyone says that either the impulses of bodies, or their natures, or anything of this kind is the cause of this order and motion, he will bring forward nothing clear. 

But let us consider again what we have said, so that it may be clear whether that speech is probable or entirely futile: in which it was first said that there are two things, soul and body; and that the many things belonging to each genus differ from others in their own kind, and both genera are diverse from one another, so that there is no third thing common to both. The soul differs from the body in that the former possesses mind <note>Latin: mentem, referring to intellect or reason</note> and the latter does not. The former rules, while the latter is subject. The soul is the cause of all passions in bodies; the body is the cause of none. 

Therefore, if anyone contends that the celestial bodies were made by something else, and do not consist of soul and body as we have said, he must be considered entirely foolish and ignorant. If, then, the reasons brought forward in all these matters have any weight, and all these things are to be judged as entirely divine, one of two things must be thought: for we shall think either that these stars are gods, and most rightly so; or we shall believe them to be images of the gods, like statues fashioned by the wise and most worthy craftsmen—the gods themselves. Let us decide one of these, I say, and hold firmly to what we have decided; let us venerate these much more than any other images. For never will more beautiful or more common images be found for all men; nor those placed in more excellent locations, or excelling in purity, majesty, and perpetual life, than these which are constructed similarly on all sides. 

But now let us also assert this concerning the gods. Since we have recognized two visible living beings—one of which is immortal, while the other is earthly and entirely mortal—let us now try to declare by probable reason the three beings out of the five that have obtained the middle place. Let us place Aether <note>The "fifth element," thought to be the substance of the highest heavens</note> after fire: from which we think the soul generates living beings. These, as in other kinds, would have much of their own nature and very little of other kinds for the sake of the bond. After aether, let us place another kind of living being from air, and a third formed by the soul from water. 

When the soul had formed all these, it filled the whole heaven with living beings, using all the kinds as far as was possible, all of which are principles of life. The second, third, fourth, and fifth kinds, beginning from the generation of the manifest gods, are led down at last to us humans. Therefore, let one place the gods—Jupiter and Juno and all the others—however one wishes, provided one keeps the same law and holds this stable reason. One must confess that the stars and those things we perceive made with the stars are the greatest visible gods, to be honored most highly, seeing all things most sharply from every side. 

Next, beneath these, we ought to worship with prayers the "demons" <note>The Greek term "daimon" refers to a guiding spirit or intermediary, not an evil entity</note> of the airy race, placed in the third and middle region for the sake of interpretation; we owe them honor for their laudable intercession and interpretation. Of these two living beings, one is from aether and the other from air. Neither can be seen entirely; but although these demons are near us, they never appear clearly to us. They share in wonderful prudence; having a sharp genius and a tenacious memory, they know all our thoughts. They love honest and good men marvelously, and they vehemently hate the wicked, as beings who share in feelings of pain. 

But God, who possesses the divine lot perfectly, is free from pains and pleasures, and enjoys wisdom and knowledge thoroughly. Since the heaven is filled with living beings, the highest gods and the demons interpret for one another. For the middle living beings are carried with light motion both to the earth and to the heaven. The fifth kind, which is from water, we shall rightly call a "semigod" <note>Often translated as "hero" in Greek mythology</note>. This is sometimes seen and sometimes withdraws from our sight; and when it is seen, perceived by a faint vision, it brings admiration. 

Since, therefore, there are these five kinds of living beings—which move our souls by appearing to us either in dreams, or by prophecy and voices heard by the healthy or the sick, or even at the departure from life—whence many sacred rites, both private and public, have been established and will be established in the future; a legislator with even a little mind will never innovate anything concerning these. For he will beware of turning his city toward a new, less certain religious cult. Nor will he dare to move those things which have been confirmed by ancestral law or custom regarding sacrifice. For he ought to know that it is not possible for mortal nature to know anything certain about these matters. 

By the same reasoning, those are to be held as the worst who do not preach that the gods are truly manifest to the eyes, and allow men to leave them without sacrifices and due honors. For they act just as if someone saw the Sun and the Moon illuminating all things and yet, seeing them held in no honor, was unwilling to do his part to make these clear to men—so that solemn days and sacrifices might be performed for them, and certain times of the years, both greater and smaller, might be distributed. Would he not rightly be called evil, both to himself and to the one who knows him? 

CLINIAS: Indeed, the very worst. 

ATHENIAN: Know, O Clinias, that this same thing has now happened to me. 

CLINIAS: In what way? 

ATHENIAN: Know that there are eight powers <note>Latin: virtutes, likely referring to the eight celestial spheres: the fixed stars, and the seven "planets" (including Sun and Moon)</note> in heaven, sisters to one another, which I...

<summary>The Athenian Stranger argues that the stars are divine, animated by souls, and far larger than they appear. He describes a hierarchy of five types of beings—gods, ethereal beings, demons, semigods, and humans—and emphasizes the importance of maintaining traditional religious honors for the visible celestial gods.</summary>

### THE PHILOSOPHER'S BOOK

<margin>All stars have one power.</margin>
...I have observed, nor did I consider it a great feat, for this is easy. Of these, there are three: one of the sun, one of the moon, and one of all the fixed stars of which we spoke before; and then there are five others. As for all these and those within them—whether they move by themselves or are carried in vehicles <note>The "vehicles" or "chariots" refer to the celestial spheres or orbits that transport the planets through the heavens</note>—let no one think that some of them are gods and others are not, or that some are legitimate and others are of a sort that is a sin to even mention. Rather, let us say they are all brothers; let us say they live in brotherly lots, and let us give them honors. We should not give one a year, another a month, and another no portion or time at all in which it runs its circuit, for together they complete the world and its adornment <note>original: "mundum ornatumque," a translation of the Greek "kosmos," which implies both order and beauty</note>, which Reason, the most divine power of all, has established as visible. This world the happy man first admires; then he burns with a desire to learn all that can be perceived by a mortal nature, believing that in this way he will live best and most happily, and when he dies, he will go to places suited to his virtue. Thus truly initiated, and having attained the one true wisdom, he spends the remainder of his time in the contemplation of all the most beautiful things.

<margin>What is the one true wisdom.</margin>
After this, we must say what they are and how many. Indeed, I dare to affirm that we shall never be found liars in this matter. Again, we say there are eight. Three of these have been mentioned; five remain. The fourth and fifth movements and orbits <note>original: "latio et anfractus"</note> are carried with almost equal speed as the sun, so they are neither slower nor faster. In these three, the intellect is always a sufficient leader—I mean the Sun, the Light-bringer <note>original: "Lucifer," the Morning Star or Venus</note>, and that third one which, because it is unknown, cannot be named. This came about because the first spectator of these things was a Barbarian <note>The term "Barbarian" in this Greek context refers to non-Greeks, specifically those from older civilizations like the Egyptians or Syrians</note>. For an ancient region nurtured those who first inspected these things because of the serenity of the summer season. Such were Egypt and Syria, where all the stars are always clearly seen, so to speak, because clouds and rain do not impede the view of the heavens. From there, these proven observations flowed here and everywhere else over an infinite time. Therefore, these things should be sanctioned by laws with great confidence. For to think that divine things are not to be venerated, or that these are not divine at all, would be the height of madness. The reason they lacked names has been stated, yet they hold the titles of gods. For the Light-bringer, which is also the Evening Star, is said to be the star of Aphrodite, that is, Venus. This title is very fitting for the Syrian author of the names. The star that runs with almost the same speed as the sun is the star of Mercury. There remain three more movements of those that move to the right with the sun and moon. Furthermore, one must speak of the eighth motion around the one, which someone might rightly call the upper world, which moves contrary to the others and draws the others with it—at least as it appears to men who know little of these things. But it is necessary to say those things which we know sufficiently. For true wisdom appears in a certain way to him who has attained even a small measure of right and divine intelligence. The remaining stars are three: one of which is slower than the rest, which is named by some after Saturn; the one placed after this in position and slowness is said to be of Jupiter; then comes the star of Mars, which is the reddest of all. These things are not difficult if someone explains them to the intellect; but once you have understood them, you must think of the gods as we have said.

Every Greek should also know this: that we inhabit a region almost the best suited for all virtue. The praise of this region consists mostly in this: it is midway between a wintry and a summery nature. Since we are further from the summer serenity than the Barbarians, as we said, we understood the order of these gods more slowly. But whatever the Greeks received from the Barbarians, they returned in a better form. We ought to think this even in the matters we are now treating: although these discoveries are difficult, there is great hope for us that the Greeks will honor all these gods with a more excellent cult than they received from the Barbarians, following all legitimate observation diligently, prompted both by their education and the Delphic oracles. Nor should any Greek think that mortals ought not to deal with divine matters; on the contrary, he should think entirely otherwise: that God is not without mind, nor is He ignorant of the nature of the human race. For He knows that He teaches men so that they might thoroughly learn what is taught. He is not ignorant that He teaches us number and how to count, nor that we are learning that very thing. For if He were ignorant of that, He would be the most senseless of all—certainly what would happen if He did not even know Himself. He would be ignorant of Himself if He envied those capable of learning rather than rejoicing that they are made good through God. Truly, it is likely that when men first began to think about the gods—who they were, of what sort, and what they did—they did not judge as wise men, nor fruitfully. They thought that fire, water, and other bodies were the most ancient things, and the marvelous soul <note>original: "animam"</note> came later. Hence, they considered the motion of the body to be more powerful and more honorable—namely, that the body moved itself by heat and cold and other such things, while the soul was neither body nor moved itself. But now, when we say that if a soul is present in a body, it is no wonder that it moves itself and carries the body around, we have no doubt that a weight can be carried around by it. Since the soul is the cause of the universe, and some things are good and others evil, it must be said that the soul is the cause of all passage and motion; but the passage and motion toward the good proceeds from the best soul, while motion toward the contrary is the opposite. It is necessary for evil things to have been conquered and to be conquered by the good. All these things have been said by us according to the judgment that punishes the impious. As far as it pertains to what is now being proven: there is no doubt that a good man should be called wise. But let us see if we might attain this wisdom, which we have sought for so long, through some discipline or art; for if we are ignorant of it, we shall be devoid and unaware of justice. So it seems to me; therefore, it must be said. What I have learned by investigating upward and downward, I will endeavor to reveal to you in speech. For the greatest virtue was neglected because of ignorance, as the things said before seem to signify to us. No one should persuade himself that a greater virtue can be found in the human race than religion and piety toward God. This failure did not happen in the best natures out of the greatest ignorance. The best natures are those which are most rarely found, and if they are found, they are of the greatest benefit. That path is certainly easy for souls which possess a nature that is not slow or contrary, but mild and moderate; such a soul admires fortitude, loves temperance, and—what is most important in these natures—is prompt to learn and has a good memory; and...

<margin>
Praise of the province of Greece.
The Greeks perceived many things later than the Barbarians, but whatever they received from them, they returned in a better form.

# EPINOMIS OR THE PHILOSOPHER. FOLIO CCCLXXVII.

one who delights most in such things and is devoted to the study of learning. These qualities certainly do not arise easily; and if they have arisen, provided they receive suitable education and discipline, they can so moderate and restrain many inferior people that—by thinking, speaking, and acting in every detail toward the gods as is fitting and when it is fitting, in sacrifices and purifications of those things done toward gods and men—they may cultivate virtue most greatly, not in pretense, but in truth. This is most useful for any state. Therefore, we assert that this part of nature is the most primary; and it can learn as much and as well as possible, if someone teaches it. However, no one will teach it unless God helps. Indeed, it is better not to learn from one who does not observe the proper method in teaching. Nevertheless, from what has just been said, it seems necessary to learn these things, and this nature is called the best by us. Therefore, let us endeavor to explain what and of what sort these things are, and how they must be learned; and let this be done according to my strength as the speaker, and for those who are able to hear, so that some aspects of divine worship may be learned. You will perhaps hear something unexpected; yet let us state the name of the thing, which no one should judge as trivial because of ignorance of the matter. Do not be unaware that **Astronomy** is something most wise. Certainly, it is necessary to be a true astronomer—not one who, according to Hesiod and all such types, merely considers the setting and rising of stars—but rather one who understands the eight circuits,

<margin>Astronomy is something most wise.</margin>

and how the seven are moved beneath the first, and in what order each completes its own circles. This is something that no nature, unless it be wonderful, will ever easily perceive, as we have just said; and we shall say it again, declaring what is necessary and how it is necessary to learn. First, therefore, let this be said: <term>φ</term> <note>The Greek letter Phi (φ) often marks a section on philosophy or "physis" (nature) in these manuscripts.</note> the Moon revolves through its circle most swiftly, and thus completes the first full moon and month. Then the Sun must be considered, which effects the solstices and the turnings of the seasons by its circuit. Moreover, those which run together with the Sun must also be considered. Finally, lest we discuss the same things too often, we ought to contemplate all the courses which we touched upon a little while ago, and which are not easily understood. This must be done so that natures are first prepared for these doctrines through long use and labor from youth—indeed, even from childhood. Wherefore, there is need of the doctrines which are called **mathematical**. First and foremost is the study of **numbers**—I do not mean those numbers that have a physical body, but rather the whole generation and power of the even and the odd, and the contribution they make to the perfecting and knowing of the nature of things. Once these have been grasped, that which they ridiculously call **Geometry** must be learned next.

<margin>See how poorly Geometry is named.</margin>

Indeed, the similarity of numbers that are naturally dissimilar to one another becomes clear when related to the study of planes <note>The author argues "Geometry" (literally "earth-measurement") is a poor name because the science is actually about the divine miracle of mathematical proportions, not just measuring dirt.</note>. This is a miracle, not human but divine, which must be seen if anyone is to understand it clearly. After this, numbers which are increased to three dimensions—similar to the nature of a solid, and again dissimilar—must be considered by another art, namely **Stereometry** <note>Stereometry is the study of three-dimensional shapes or solid geometry.</note>, which is similar to the former. But those who are engaged in it have also named this "Geometry." That which is wonderful and divine to those who understand it is this: that while the power of things always revolves in the double and its opposite, the whole of nature is formed in individual proportions according to genera and species. Therefore, the first power of the double proceeds according to number from one to two in proportion, possessing the power of the double. But toward the solid and tangible, the ratio of the double proceeds again from one to eight; another double, however, reaches the middle, perhaps the greater exceeding the lesser and the lesser exceeding the greater equally. But another exceeds the extremes by the same part, and is exceeded by them. In the middle of the number six and the number twelve, the **sesquialter** and **sesquitertia** proportions emerge <note>original: "sesquialtera" (3:2 ratio) and "sesquitertia" (4:3 ratio), which are fundamental to musical harmony and Pythagorean cosmology</note>. The power of these in the middle, turned toward both, has bestowed upon men a harmonious and convenient use, for the sake of play and temporal number and concord, attributed to the happy dance of the Muses. Therefore, let these things be done thus, and let them be so. The end of these things is that we may betake ourselves to the divine generation and to the contemplation of the most beautiful and divine nature of those things which are seen with the eyes, insofar as God has granted this to be inspected by men; which we shall never attain without the aforementioned arts. Each of these must be referred to its own species, and finally all things must be referred to the **One** in discussions, by questioning and arguing if anything is said incorrectly. For rightly, such an examination is the most beautiful and primary of all human tasks. But where the inquiry is not truly such, but merely simulated, the struggle is in vain. Furthermore, the order of the times must be considered, which perfectly completes all celestial things; so that whoever believes it was truly said that the soul is older and more divine than the body, may think it was also excellently and sufficiently said that **"all things are full of gods"** <note>A famous maxim attributed to Thales of Miletus, often cited by Plato to suggest that the divine presence is woven into the fabric of the cosmos</note>, so much so that the higher beings neither forget our affairs nor desert us. But this must be observed in all these things: it will be most profitable to the one who has perceived correctly;

<margin>All things are full of gods.</margin>

but to the one who has not, God must be invoked. This is the method. For it is necessary to touch upon this also. Every description of lines, the constitution of number, the ratio of concord, and the agreement of the circuits of the stars—the conspiracy of all these together—must be perceived by the one who learns in a fitting manner. He will perceive it, however, if he learns by looking rightly toward the One. For a single bond of intelligence will appear for all these things.

<margin><insert>God is mind and <unclear>ratio</unclear></insert></margin>

But he who strives to attain these things otherwise, let him invoke "Fortune," as we say. For never without these will any nature in cities be made happy. For this is the way; this is the education; these are the disciplines. Therefore, through these—whether they be easy or difficult—one must go. It is a sin to neglect the gods when the happy doctrine of all those things has been opened to everyone by right reason. We shall truly call him the wisest who has perceived all these things thus. I affirm, both in jest and in earnest, that when he has met his day [died], he will no longer participate in many senses as he does now, but will be a sharer in a single lot; having become one out of many, happy, most wise, and blessed. Whether one lives on the mainland or on the islands, whether publicly or privately, provided he conducts himself in this way, he will obtain the same lot from God. But what we said in the beginning now also appears true to us: that men cannot, except for a very few, perfectly attain blessedness.

<margin><insert>few emerge blessed in life</insert></margin>

This has been rightly asserted by us. For those who are at once divine and modest, and endowed by nature with other virtues, and who have furthermore attained the happy disciplines of which we spoke—to those alone does it seem that all things, by the fates, lead to happiness. Therefore, to those who have labored thus both privately and publicly, when they come to old age...

# ARGUMENTS ON THE EPISTLES OF PLATO, FOLIO 379.
Y.iiii.

### Argument for the Third Epistle.

This letter of Plato is written to Dionysius the Younger <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse in Sicily</note> after Plato’s second departure from him. First, it responds to certain questions from Dionysius; then, it dissolves the slander that Dionysius had concocted against him. In the response to the questions, therefore, he teaches that pleasure is not in God—specifically that pleasure which has pain as its opposite and consists in a certain movement or the filling of a lack. However, he does not deny that in God is all that good for the sake of which pleasure *appears* to be good. He adds that pleasure (the kind that is changeable) is a cause of harm, specifically regarding money and honor, as well as pain in the body. Furthermore, it takes away sharpness of mind, memory, judgment, and dignity. After this, against the accusations of Dionysius, he proves that he traveled to Sicily for the most just causes: to give advice openly regarding the restoration of cities formerly destroyed and concerning a fair form of governance.

### Argument for the Fourth Epistle.

After Dionysius was expelled from his tyranny, Plato writes to Dion <note>Plato’s close friend and political ally in Syracuse</note> who had now returned to his homeland, advising him as well as Heraclides, Theodotus, and the other friends who held power to live far from tyranny. He advises them to maintain a form of government drawn mostly from the rule of the best <term>aristocracy: from the Greek 'aristos' (best) and 'kratos' (power)</term> and tempered in some way by a popular element. Here are certain precepts to be committed to memory. First: it properly belongs to princes to excel everyone in truth, justice, magnificence, and temperance. In short, they should surpass others in prudence as much as men surpass boys in prudence. Second: they must present themselves to be such as they wish to be seen. Third: they must look around and see that the eyes of all are turned toward them; let them remember that their vices cannot remain hidden, nor will they satisfy the highest expectations with only mediocre virtue. Fourth: they should imitate timely lawmakers and avoid discord among colleagues like a plague. Fifth: they must remember that common goodwill is exceedingly necessary for conducting affairs. This, however, can be acquired and preserved only through <term>humanity: here meaning kindness and civil refinement</term>.

### Argument for the Fifth Epistle.

Although a certain custom attributes this fifth letter to Plato, it seems rather to be by someone modeling themselves entirely on Dion as he was influenced by Plato. It instructs Perdiccas <note>Perdiccas III, King of Macedonia</note>, who had been established in a monarchy, to remember that he is young and therefore in need of the counsel and service of elders. Not all elders, however, but the most proven ones; and not in just any matter, but in the form of government. These should be men who understand what is most characteristic of each type of governance, whether one, few, or many rule. He wishes the "voice" of the government to be its spirit and life—that is, the law—which ought to establish and carry out duties toward both God and men. Otherwise, the state cannot be safe. But since he indicates that he and Euphraeus <note>A student of Plato who became an advisor to Perdiccas</note> were imbued with Plato’s discipline and understand what pertains to civil science, he adds—lest Perdiccas lose confidence in this because Plato himself never benefited his own people in civil science—that Plato recognized his own people <note>The citizens of Athens</note> were suffering from an incurable disease. Therefore, in the manner of wise physicians, he was unwilling to undertake the cure of an incurable beast in vain and at his own risk.

### Argument for the Sixth Epistle.

The divine Plato exhorts Hermias, Herascus, and Coriscus <note>Rulers of cities in Asia Minor and students of Plato</note>, who were neighboring princes, toward the truest harmony. He prophesies that by this alone will they be safe, and through this—with the favor of God, who delights in union—they will attain all good things. Furthermore, they will finally reach a point where, with affairs rightly settled, they may be able to pursue divine wisdom with more intense zeal than human wisdom, as is fitting. He teaches that a stable harmony can be firmed between them only by a compact and a law: by a legitimate compact, I say, established between them with sacred rites properly performed and an oath interposed. This is done by calling God himself to witness and praying to Him as the author and preserver of all union. By witnessing, I say, and praying under the <term>odd number: in Pythagorean thought, odd numbers were considered divine and indivisible</term>, in which God is said to delight. For he brings forward here the three highest principles of things, which he also touched upon in the first letter <note>Original: "prima... epistola"; though the famous passage is usually cited from the Second Epistle</note>. Where he says "the leader of all things present and future," he wish the Soul of the World to be understood, which, as the principle of motion, leads all things from the future into the present and from the present into the past by a temporal logic. But where he speaks of the "Father and Lord," he signifies the Supreme God and the Good itself. But he seems to insert a certain divine Mind between these two; for when he repeats "leader," he adds "and cause." For in Plato, "King" often signifies the Good itself, "Cause" signifies the Mind, and "Leader" signifies the Soul. And since he refers the "Cause" to the Mind, the Platonists in the *Timaeus* argue that the Intellect is the son of the Good itself and was the immediate Architect of the world. Concerning this, it is written in the *Epinomis*: "The most divine Reason, or the most divine Word <note>original: "verbum" (Logos)</note>, adorned the visible world." He calls the Good itself here both Father and Lord: to designate through the first the father of the Mind, and through the second the lord of the Soul. Thus perhaps the Platonic number might be explained. So too might a "Platonic Christian" explain it, though perhaps an Arian <note>Referring to Arius, a priest whose views on the subordination of the Son to the Father were declared heretical; the translator notes that Plato's hierarchy resembles this</note>. Someone might also understand the "Leader" as the Holy Spirit and the "Mind" as the Son. For where Plato says "Father," he likewise implies "Son." And if someone posits one essence of the three, he will seem to oppose many Platonists, yet he will not manifestly contradict Plato. He exhorts them at the same time to the more serious studies of doctrines and to certain more pleasant disciplines related to these: namely eloquence, poetry, and music. By all which...
