# ARGUMENTS FOR THE EPISTLES OF PLATO.

...he commands us to apply ourselves with this intent: that by investigating these things as if they were footprints, we might track the divine scent and love Him alone, and through that love, attain a taste for the divine. He says, therefore: "if we philosophize about God truly," or "in such a way"—that is, either we investigate by loving, or we love by investigating—then we shall all undoubtedly come to know Him at last. Indeed, even if the name of *philosophy* <note>The word "philosophy" literally means "love of wisdom."</note> seems to imply a certain searching or investigation, it properly carries with it love and a loving inquiry. 

Pythagoras knew this, and Plato knew it too: that we relate to finite goods in one way, and to the infinite Good in another. Finite goods are known by us before they are loved, and they must be loved in order to be known; but the Infinite must be loved before it can be known. Nor should it be investigated so much so that it may be known, as so that it may be loved. But why must it be loved before it is understood? Because love, by transferring the lover into the beloved, supplies through a transforming affection what was lacking in proportion. Is not God often called "fire" in the sacred scriptures? By the same metaphorical license, let an angel be called a "transparent body," and the Soul an "opaque body," so long as it is shut up in this blind prison. 

Therefore, just as a transparent body—that is, a clear one like air or water—immediately admits light both outside and inside when placed under fire, but earthly bodies must first be heated intensely and thinned out by heat into the likeness of the transparent before they can receive the light of the fire; so spirits separated from the body immediately catch the divine light. However, spirits joined to earthly bodies need the fire of transforming love. Once purified by this and translated into the divine likeness, they are finally illuminated by the divine splendor of knowledge. Hence Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note> says: "Inquiry indeed purifies the divine soul, but love makes it like God" <note>original: "Inqsitio qdem diuinos purificat animū, amor vero deificat."</note>. For he expresses the matter with a very precise word. And not without reason, for no material becomes fire simply because it receives light, but because it receives the heat of the fire. 

It is therefore a Platonic sentiment that divine things must be investigated: namely, that they exist, and what sort of things they are, through a certain common perception. But meanwhile, they must be loved with a singular and incomparable charity, not a common one. For it is only in this way that we can somewhere clearly understand what they are and thus become blessed. How much these ideas harmonize with the Sacred Scriptures <note>Referring to the Christian Bible.</note>, no one except the uninitiated is ignorant.

### Argument for the Seventh Epistle.

Plato’s Seventh Epistle was written to the relatives and friends of Dion, now that their homeland had been liberated by Dion, and Dion himself had been unjustly killed. But so that the many historical details in this letter and others may be clearly understood, we must look back a little further. 

Plato traveled to Syracuse three times. Once during the time of the elder Dionysius <note>Dionysius I, the tyrant of Syracuse.</note> when he was forty years old. Twice afterward, while the younger Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the son of the former.</note> held the tyranny. What he did in each journey, or the reason he set out, appears partly in the *Life of Plato* we have written and partly in these letters. 

Dion appears to have been from the same family as Dionysius, and was further connected to him by various ties of kinship. The elder Dionysius had married Dion’s sister, Aristomache. Dion himself had Dionysius’s daughter, named Arete, as his wife. However, the younger Dionysius was not born of Dion’s sister, but of another wife named Doris. On the first journey, Dion became a student of Plato, turned his life toward virtue, and began to desire the public good of his country. 

Therefore, when the elder Dionysius died and the younger succeeded to the tyranny, and while he was still a boy governed largely by Dion’s counsel, Dion—hoping to turn him toward a desire for the philosophical life—called Plato to Syracuse with many prayers and persuaded Dionysius to summon him. Plato obeyed, led primarily by the hope that through his counsel, the state there might be changed from a tyranny into either a republic <term>commonwealth: a state governed for the common good</term> or a kingdom. 

But barely four months after Plato’s arrival, Dionysius, led by false slanders, expelled Dion on the grounds that he was plotting against the tyranny. Nevertheless, he welcomed Plato gladly. But Plato, indignant that the business was unfinished, returned to his homeland. He went a third time to reconcile Dion with Dionysius, having been entreated again and again by both, and also requested by Archytas and Archedemus the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosophy of Pythagoras.</note> and many other noblemen. At that time, Dionysius promised both the recall of Dion and that he would maintain the best form of government. 

But he fulfilled none of his promises. When Plato openly rebuked Dionysius for breaking his word—both concerning the recall of Dion and regarding the safety of Heraclides, as promised to Theodotus—Dionysius became hostile toward him. Consequently, Plato lived in great danger of being killed by the soldiers. But Archytas of Tarentum sent the orator Salmiscus to Dionysius, asking him to release Plato. He released him and provided supplies for the journey. Plato returned safely to his homeland. 

A little later, Dion, having secretly gathered troops, marched to Syracuse and expelled Dionysius, restoring liberty to the Syracusans. However, he himself was killed shortly afterward by the treachery and envy of his own people. After this, Hipparinus (Dion’s son) and another Hipparinus (Dionysius’s brother and Dion’s nephew by his sister), holding Syracuse and relying on the counsel of the nobles, deliberated on a more honorable form of government. Meanwhile, Dionysius, having joined with enemies, was attempting to return to power. Plato, therefore, writes to these men, encouraging them and instructing them in the best form of governing: that is, a kingdom obedient to laws and supported by the authority of the best men. 

Precepts of this kind are gathered sporadically from this letter: It is not foreign to a good character to desire the helm of the state, especially when necessity demands it. It is foreign to a good citizen to desire to obtain this with total license. It is not the mark of a prudent man to involve himself rashly in public affairs, especially where he undergoes danger without hope for the public safety. Only philosophy in a matter so...

### ARGUMENTS FOR THE EPISTLES OF PLATO. FOLIO 380.
Y.iiii.

...both public and private, can discern what is good and just, and what is not. The human race shall not cease to be involved in evils until either philosophers rule, or those who rule, by God's illumination, philosophize. <note>This is a restatement of Plato's famous "Philosopher King" doctrine from the *Republic*, applied here to his advice to the rulers of Syracuse.</note> A delicate and luxurious education depraves even divine talents. No one who is intemperate can be prudent. A city in which the citizens are lack self-control cannot be restrained by any power of laws; rather, it suffers frequent changes and always for the worse. Violence must be brought neither against one’s fatherland nor one’s parents. Instead, one must provide counsel to both, far removed from violence. The authority of ancient and sacred discourses is to be preferred above all other opinions. No evil can happen to a good man. The soul, once separated from this body, pays the penalties for its crimes under the sentence of a divine judge. It is better to suffer the most heavy injuries than to inflict them. The greedy and the intemperate are blind and deaf to divine matters; so much so that they neither see them for themselves, nor can they endure to hear of them from others, or perceive them even when heard. Impiety is mixed into all sins, and vice versa. Impiety itself, mixed with sins, is the stimulus by which sinners are especially troubled in this life and tortured in the next.

After these things, where he writes of his habit of life with Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse, whom Plato attempted to mentor.</note> and of the study of philosophy, he proves that no one will make progress in philosophy unless, kindled by the love of wisdom, he sustains all its labors for its sake and despises pleasures. Then indeed, since it is the part of a wise man to contemplate divine things, he opportunely shows that divine things can never be expressed to the common crowd by letters, nor even by words; indeed, they ought not to be. They cannot be expressed because, since they are greater than we are, people do not even entirely comprehend them with the mind. They ought not to be expressed because those who are the lowest among the common people would laugh at them as if they were monstrous fictions; and those who are a little higher among the people, having heard these things, would either fall into false heresy or, on account of a slight opinion of higher things, would become vain and excessively contentious. 

Plato does not say that nothing of the truth can ever be understood concerning certain divine matters, but rather that what is understood of them cannot be expressed, nor can their proper truth be understood by the same reasoning as other things. Certain <term>Forms</term> <note>original: "Formae"; in Platonic thought, these are the perfect, eternal patterns of which all earthly things are mere shadows.</note> are entirely joined to bodies, while others are thoroughly segregated. The former are called "natural," the latter "divine." There are also middle forms joined in a certain way and in a certain way separable: these are the rational souls, the middle point between the divine and the natural. Insofar as they are joined to bodies, they are necessarily disjoined from divine things. For they cannot be joined to forms separated from matter except by separation. 

One is separated from matter in two primary ways: first by moral purgation, and second by contemplative resolution. The study of philosophy achieves both. Just as one who dries damp wood first in the sun and then moves it near the fire provides the occasion for the wood to be kindled—yet he himself does not kindle the wood, but the fire does—so the study of philosophy prepares the soul for divine things through moral discipline and purification. Then, through contemplative resolution, it moves the mind toward divine things and joins them. Yet philosophy itself does not form the mind with divine truth; rather, God himself, like a fire, illuminates the mind (which is like matter prepared by the benefit of philosophy and drawing near) with the light of His own truth. 

Therefore, when Plato said that divine things can be expressed neither by letters nor by words, he meant furthermore that they cannot be taught or found by the same reasoning as other things. For in perceiving other things, our inquiry both prepares and forms the understanding; yet in perceiving divine things, even the most purified and eminent inquiry prepares the mind, but does not "form" it. For this reason, he says there is need for long-lasting "familiarity" with divine things, meaning the constancy of speculation; likewise a "conjunction" or communion of life, meaning purification perfected by moral discipline. 

He adds that into a mind thus affected, the light of truth is kindled—not gradually in a human fashion, but suddenly. But from where? From the fire, which is God, shining forth or sparking. By "sparks" he designates the <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "ideas"; the divine archetypes or blueprints of all reality existing in the mind of God.</note>—the examples of things in the divine mind. He also designates the <term>formulae</term> <note>original: "formulas"; these are the innate concepts or "inner blueprints" within the human soul that mirror the divine Ideas.</note> of the Ideas innate within us. These, though once lulled to sleep through sloth, are awakened by the "fanning" of teaching; and like rays flashing from the eyes, they are illuminated by the Ideas as if by the rays of stars. 

He adds that such light is not only kindled but "becomes" in the soul, to show both that the formulae are innate to the soul and that such splendor becomes familiar to it. And lest you think the mind in that state is ambiguous or anxious, he added: *It now nourishes itself.* That is, this light, first kindled divinely in the mind, thereafter by its own power draws an abundance of divine rays and fills the mind with nourishing joy. Here the soul feeds itself; that is, seeking nothing from the outside, it lives content with itself. And how blessedly it is affected within, it cannot—and if it wished, it would not know how to—express. 

Plato meditates on five stages in this contemplation, which you may read more diligently explained by us in the *Theology* <note>A reference to Ficino's own work, *Platonic Theology*.</note>. For he commands the one desirous of truth to proceed first through hearing from the **Name** of the thing itself; then through sight and other senses from the **Accidents** (the physical traits) of the thing itself to the **Definition** of the thing; through this to the **Formula** of the thing innate in the mind; and finally through the Formula to the **Idea**, the creator of both the formulae and the things themselves. He teaches, moreover, that the Idea differs far from the rest in four primary ways: because the Idea is a substance, simple, immobile, and not mixed with its contrary. The other four—the name, the accidental image, the definition, and our formulae—degenerate from the substance, simplicity, stability, and purity of the Idea. Therefore, they do not sufficiently impress the Idea upon us, but they accommodate us as best they can to the divine impression. Finally, the mind divinely impressed, if it should ever strive to express the characters of the Ideas in words or letters, will render deformed images of the most beautiful things. Truly, if one believes the **Pythagoreans**, he will not strive so much to "paint" the Ideas as to cultivate the souls of those listening, and to polish them like writing tablets upon which, at last, the divine forms may be painted by the divine finger.

It outlines the necessity of moral purification and the five steps of knowledge leading from a simple name to the divine Idea.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page concludes the summary of the Seventh Epistle—specifically the section on the "Seventh Way" of knowledge which cannot be written down—and provides the introductory "Arguments" (summaries) for Plato's Eighth through Twelfth Epistles. The translator, likely Marsilio Ficino or a contemporary, continues to frame Plato’s letters as practical guides for both personal virtue and political stability.</meta>

Truly, the soul, looking up at the celestial rays herself, will not try in vain to describe the shapes of those rays to the blind; rather, if they are incurable, she will leave them be. If they are curable, she will instead attempt only to purge their vision and lift it upward, as she understands that otherwise she would labor in vain. <note>This concludes the "digression" of the Seventh Letter, where Plato explains that the highest truths (the "rays") cannot be explained to those whose minds are not prepared or purified by philosophy.</note>

### Argument for the Eighth Epistle.

In the previous letter, when instructing the princes of Syracuse, Plato dwelt more extensively on marriages, precepts, and the deeds performed by himself and Dion. In this letter, however, he summarizes his specific instructions more briefly. He always maintains a middle ground between the rule of a single man and the rule of the people. Most of all, he strives to reconcile the citizens rather than expel them, so that the state of the republic may be properly stabilized as much as possible without injury to others.

Right at the beginning, he asserts that men polluted by impious crimes are incurable, and no counsel will benefit them. Likewise, in all things—both in speaking and in thinking—one must begin with God. Throughout the entire letter, you will observe what a cautious and merciful governor Plato is, and how diligent a reconciler of souls. He approves, as is his custom, a government similar to the Lacedaemonian <note>Lacedaemonian: referring to the Spartan system of government, which Plato admired for its stability.</note> model. In such a system, there is a large role for the aristocracy, yet there is also a certain royal form, and something of the popular element as well. He condemns extreme servitude, through which all things are subjected to human lust <note>original: "libidini" — here meaning unrestrained whim or passion</note>. He also disapproves of extreme liberty, or rather license, in which almost anyone is chosen by lot to steer the republic without any selection. Instead, he approves of the middle path. Note this golden saying: **Moderate servitude is that which serves God; immoderate servitude is that which serves men.** For temperate men, the law is God; for the intemperate, their law is lust.

### Argument for the Ninth Epistle.

In this letter to Archytas the philosopher <note>Archytas of Tarentum: a mathematician and statesman who was a close friend of Plato.</note>, who was very busy with public affairs, Plato gives counsel to the contemplative man that he should not abandon action that is both honorable and necessary. He calls "honorable and necessary action" that which benefits men both publicly and privately. It is honorable because, just as any member of the body does not exist for itself alone but for others—and especially for the whole—so men exist for one another, and most especially for their species. It is necessary because, unless you live for others, you cannot live for yourself; and unless you help your household and your fatherland, private and public affairs, destitute of a governor, will either totter or, governed by worse men, will be endangered and finally suffer shipwreck.

### Argument for the Tenth Epistle.

He confirms Aristodemus, a friend of Dion who practiced philosophy primarily through the elegance of his character, in his opinion and way of life. He asserts that the substance of philosophy is moral virtue. This is declared by the name itself, defined by a certain love and cultivation. He suggests that human speculations are either external ornaments of philosophy or ways to achieve that firm purity of mind which pertains to character. Once this purity is compared to things divine rather than human, and things infused from above rather than acquired, contemplation follows. When compared to that higher contemplation, Plato calls earlier speculation a kind of "play" or "game." <note>This reflects the Platonic idea that logic and dialectic are "serious play" compared to the direct experience of Truth.</note> This is the greatest precept of Pythagoras and Socrates. 

Where we translate "ornaments," the Greek word signifies an "ornament" mixed with a certain clever vanity and pride. It is as if he were saying: *Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up.* <note>original: "Scientia inflat: charitas ædificat" — a quote from 1 Corinthians 8:1.</note> Likewise, *Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul.* <note>original: "In maleuolam animam ſapientia non intrabit" — from the Book of Wisdom 1:4.</note> He places sincerity or health in a simple and tranquil soul, faith in words, and finally firmness in gestures and actions.

### Argument for the Eleventh Epistle.

To Prince Laodamas, who was consulting him on the best form of government, Plato gives his customary advice: all laws will be in vain unless, in addition, men of proven character—through whom the laws live—hold great power in the republic. Furthermore, a magistrate must be established in the city with the greatest authority to act as a censor of morals; he should diligently observe the actions of individuals through "explorers," always intent on ensuring that the daily life of the citizens leads their souls toward fortitude and temperance.

### Argument for the Twelfth Epistle.

The twelfth letter serves as evidence for us of how liberal and simple Plato was, seeing as he entrusted certain of his more secret commentaries, not yet finished, to Archytas. It is also evidence that Archytas, practicing philosophy no less in his character than in his words, was worthy of having such dear things entrusted to him. Perhaps these commentaries pertained to the completion of the *Critias* (which was not finished) or the writing of the *Hermocrates* (which was never composed). 

As for the letter to Dionysius, which is added to these by those who are ignorant, we have not translated it because both the letter itself and all learned men deny that it belongs to Plato. However, it is worthwhile in these letters to notice with what a great and constant soul our Plato acted, especially in the affairs of his friends, and what heavy risks he often underwent for a friend's safety. Furthermore, notice how freely and kindly he often corrected the tyrant, being more removed from flattery than anyone, yet yielding to no one in charity and duty. Thus, he can lead us to live well and happily no less through his life and character than through his disputations.

# LETTERS. BOOK XXXVI. OF THE TWELVE EPISTLES OF PLATO. EPISTLE I.

### Dio to Dionysius: Greetings.
<note>original: "bene agere" — a standard Greek greeting formula translated here into Latin, literally "to act well" or "farewell."</note>

WHILE I spent a long time with you, so that your empire might be administered by my efforts, I subjected myself to heavy slanders, [acting] with a loyalty and dignity that surpassed others who were merely seeking their own advantage from you. For I knew that while I was helping you manage your affairs, you would never be seen to have committed any act of cruelty. All those who were involved in that same administration can bear witness to me. By my efforts, I freed them from no small amount of harm. Serving in a quiet capacity in your empire, I frequently protected your city. Yet in the end, I have been expelled by you more ignominiously than is fitting for even the most worthless person to be cast out. I myself was ordered by you to depart—I, who devoted such long service to your benefit. Therefore, hereafter I shall look out for myself in a somewhat less humane manner. You, however, as such a tyrant, shall govern alone. As for that "splendid" sum of money you sent as a <term>viaticum</term> <note>viaticum: money or provisions provided for a journey.</note> through this man, Bachius, I am sending it back to you along with this letter. For it is neither sufficient for travel expenses, nor is it enough to be useful for the rest of one’s life; it would bring the greatest disgrace upon you for giving it, and no less upon me for accepting it. Therefore, I refused to receive it. It matters nothing to you whether you give or receive such an amount; but if you take it back, you may honor another of your followers in the same way you "honored" me. For I have already been sufficiently honored by you. And now that line from Euripides <note>Euripides: A famous Athenian playwright (c. 480–406 BC) known for his tragedies.</note> opportunely comes to my mind: that when you are pressed by circumstances, you will wish for such a man to stand by you. Moreover, I want you to remember—as many other tragic poets do—that when they bring on a dying tyrant, they attribute voices of this kind to him: "Alas, wretch! I perish, supported by no friends." Yet no poet has ever yet depicted anyone perishing for a lack of gold. That other poetic sentiment is also highly approved by those of sound mind: It is not the glitter of gold, so rare in the wretched life of mortals, nor diamonds, nor silver tables held in such price among men, that so flash before the eyes; nor do wide or fertile cultivated lands avail so much for life, as the harmonious mind of good men. Farewell; and consider how much you have erred toward us, so that you may behave more creditably toward others.

### Plato to Dionysius: Greetings. Epistle II.

I heard from Archedemus that you believe not only I, but also my associates—with the sole exception of Dion—ought to neither say nor do anything evil against you. However, this exception you make for Dion shows that I have no power over my associates. For if I held power over Dion and you, as I do over others, then I believe many great benefits would come to you and the rest of the Greeks. But as it stands, I am only "great" in this: that I present myself as obedient to my own reason. I say these things because Cratistolus and Polyxenus have reported nothing of sincerity to you. One of them is said to have claimed that at the Olympic Games he heard many of those who were with me speaking ill of you. Perhaps he hears more acutely than I do, for I heard no such thing. See to it hereafter, however, that whenever something of this kind is reported to you, you should act by writing a letter to me and inquiring into the matter itself. For I will neither fear nor blush to confess the truth. Between me and you, the situation stands thus: we are not unknown to any of the Greeks, so to speak, nor do the men of this age keep silent about our friendship; and be certain of this: posterity will not be silent either. For those who have heard of it are such that it is neither a small nor an obscure matter. To what end is this? I shall reveal it immediately, beginning from a bit further back.

By the law of nature, wisdom and power, both being excellent, tend toward the same goal. These two always affect one another, pursue one another, and come together. Furthermore, men take great delight in these things; whenever, whether in the poems of poets or in private conversations, they hear or relate such things—as when men speak of Hiero and Pausanias the Lacedaemonian <note>Hiero (Tyrant of Syracuse) and Pausanias (Spartan general) were famous rulers associated with wise men.</note>, they rejoice to commemorate the friendship of Simonides <note>Simonides: A celebrated Greek lyric poet.</note> that existed with them, and to relate what he said and did for them. Similarly, they are accustomed to celebrate Periander of Corinth and Thales of Miletus together; Pericles and Anaxagoras; Croesus and Solon (as the wise); and Cyrus (as the powerful). <note>These pairings represent the historical ideal of the "Philosopher-King" or the ruler guided by a sage.</note> Indeed, imitating these, the poets bring on Creon and Tiresias together, Polydus and Minos, Agamemnon and Nestor, Ulysses and Palamedes; and as it seems to me, by the same reasoning, the men of old joined Prometheus to Jove. Some of these they depict as being in agreement, others sometimes in harmony and sometimes in discord. They sing of both their dissensions and their agreements.

<margin>
Note how care must be taken for future times.
The best souls divine (the future).
A conjecture that there is some sense of our affairs among those who are dead.
</margin>

I have said all these things for this reason: to show that even when we are dead, men will not be silent about us. Therefore, we must not be negligent, but must take care for the time that follows. For it happens by a certain nature that the most cowardly men care nothing for what the future opinion of them will be, but the most excellent men do everything so that in future ages they may hear men speaking well of them. I make this conjecture: that there is some perception of our affairs in those who have died. For the best souls perhaps divine this, while the worst do not at all. Truly, the premonitions of divine men are stronger than those of others. I think that if it were permitted for those deceased men of whom I speak to amend their own associations, they would apply the greatest effort to spread better opinions of themselves than they do now. This is something that is permitted for us to do even now, God willing; and if anything was not done rightly in our past friendship, we can amend and correct it through both deeds and words. Thus, a true and excellent opinion of us may remain—especially regarding philosophy—and the fame of our affairs, if it is good, may become better; if bad, it may be made good. While caring for these things, we could do nothing more religious; and by neglecting them, nothing more profane. As to how this might be done fittingly and justly, I will now say,

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the Second Epistle of Plato to Dionysius II. Having established the terms of their previous interactions, Plato now addresses the public perception of their relationship and moves into the "riddles" of his deeper philosophy.</meta>

XXXVI
BOOK

When I arrived in Sicily, it was rumored that I excelled greatly among those who were then practicing philosophy. I desired, when I had come to Syracuse, that you should be a witness to this opinion, so that philosophy might be honored through me even among the multitude. However, that matter did not succeed quite as favorably as I hoped. I say that the cause of this was not what most people thought, but I assert that the cause was this: you did not seem to trust me enough, but in a way you wished to dismiss me and call others instead, asking what business I had there with a certain distrust, as it appeared to me. And those who spoke of these things were very many, affirming that you indeed held me in contempt and had turned your mind to other things. This rumor, therefore, increased at that time. Now, hear what ought to be done after this, so that I may respond to what you asked regarding how we should conduct ourselves toward each other. If you indeed utterly despise philosophy, we shall let it be. But if you have either heard from another, or have discovered for yourself, better things than those which are handed down by me, then embrace those. For if our teachings please you, you ought to honor us most highly. 

<margin>See how honor ought to begin from the superior.</margin>

But now, as if from the beginning, you should lead and I shall follow. For if I am honored by you, I will honor you; but if I am not honored, I will remain quiet. Furthermore, if you begin to honor me first, you will appear to honor philosophy; and that, among the multitude, will bring you glory as a lover of wisdom, which you especially desired. But if I should honor you when I am not honored myself, I will seem to admire and pursue riches; and we are not ignorant of how shameful this is judged by everyone. To speak briefly, if you honor me, there will be honor for both; but if I honor you [unreciprocated], there will be infamy for both. And regarding these matters, enough has been said. 

The main point itself, however, is not properly understood. Archedemus <note>Archedemus was a student of Archytas and a messenger between Plato and Dionysius.</note> himself will tell you when he returns to you. That which is more precious and more divine, about which you ask me through him, must be shown to him completely. For you say, as he reports, that the demonstration of the primary nature was not sufficiently explained to you by me. I must, therefore, speak to you 

<margin>riddles</margin>

now in certain riddles <note>original: "aenigmata" — Plato famously uses "riddles" or "enigmas" here to protect his most profound doctrines from being misunderstood by the uninitiated.</note>, so that if anything happens to this tablet either by sea or by land, he who reads it may not be able to understand it. It is thus: Around the King of all, all things exist; all things are for his sake; he is the cause of all beautiful things. Around the second are the second things; around the third are the third things. The human soul longs to understand what sort of things those are, looking into those things which are kindred to itself. None of these is sufficient. But in the King himself and in those things I mentioned, there is nothing of that sort. What comes after this, the soul asks. But this question of yours, son of Dionysius and Doris, is what is the cause of all evils. Or rather, it is more like a certain sting implanted in our soul. Unless someone plucks this out, he will certainly never attain the truth. You said to me in the gardens, when we were under the laurels, that you had thought this out and that it was your own invention. And I said that if it seemed to you to be so, you would have freed me from many disputes. I said I had never found any other inventor of this, and that most of my investigation was occupied with it. You perhaps, having heard it from someone, proceeded from there by some divine chance. However, you produced demonstrations of it that were never firm, but some at one time and some at another, according to how you were guessing by your imagination. But there is nothing of that sort here. And this happened not to you alone. But know for certain that no one, when they first hear me, is affected otherwise. One is exhausted more, another less; they only barely cease from their labor at last. Almost all, however, labor not a little. 

Since these things are and have been so, we have almost found, I believe, what you asked for through your letter: how we ought to regard one another. After you have discussed these things by yourself and compared them with the opinions of others, if you continue with a correct examination, you will prove yourself to be in agreement with us and our teachings. By what means, then, shall these and the other things we have spoken of be done? You did rightly, for that reason, in sending Archedemus to us. And after he has returned to you and reported my opinion to you, other doubts will perhaps seize you. If you consult your own interests rightly, you will send Archedemus back to me again. He, in turn, like a merchant, will return not without profit. If you do this twice or thrice, and diligently examine those things which we send, I shall indeed be surprised if you do not find yourself much better off than you are now regarding those things about which you doubt. Act boldly, therefore. For neither you nor Archedemus can undertake any business that is either more honorable or more acceptable to God. 

Take care, however, that these things never fall into the ears of men unpracticed in discipline and instruction. For in my opinion, there are no things which, when spoken to the common people, seem more ridiculous; nor any which, when brought before noble men, seem more wonderful and divine. Often spoken and always heard over many years, they are at last purified with great labor, like gold. For hear what usually happens in this matter that is so wonderful. There are many men who have already heard these things—men powerful in sharpness of mind, powerful in memory, skillful in examining and judging—who are now advanced in age and have heard these things for no less than thirty years. Yet these men affirm that what once seemed most incredible to hear, now seems to them most credible and clear; and what then seemed most probable, now seems to them the opposite. Looking at these things, therefore, take care 

<margin>See the modesty of Plato.</margin>

lest you ever regret those things which have now escaped you unworthily. The greatest safeguard of this matter is to write nothing, but to learn by heart. For what is written cannot be kept secret. For this reason, I have never written anything about these things; there is no written work of Plato’s, nor will there be. Those things which are now said belong to Socrates, who, even when he was a young man, was famous for his virtue. Farewell, and believe us. And as for this letter, when you have read it several times, burn it immediately. 

And regarding these matters, enough. You wonder why I do not send Polyxenus to you. But concerning Lycophron and the others who are with you, I affirm now exactly what I did long ago: that you far excel them both in natural talent and in the art of discourse. None of them, as some suspect, yield to you in dispute voluntarily, but only unwillingly. And yet you seem to have treated them quite modestly and provided them with honorable gifts. But regarding such men, many such things may be said. If it happens that you can use Philistio, use him as much as possible. And if it can be done, use the services of Speusippus <note>Speusippus was Plato's nephew and eventual successor as head of the Academy.</note>, and then send him back. Speusippus also has need of you. Philistio, however, promised me that if he were dismissed by you, he would seek Athens immediately. [At] Lithotoniēn...

Indeed, it was laudable to have dismissed him. However, the petition was light, both regarding his necessities and concerning Hegesippus, the son of Aristo. For you also wrote to me: if anyone should wish to bring injury to him or those men, and you should perceive it, you would by no means permit it. Regarding Lysiclides, moreover, it is right to speak the truth. Surely he alone of those who set out from Sicily to Athens changed nothing in our shared custom. ->Plato to Dionysius. Third Letter.<-

<margin>The divine nature is far from distress and pleasure.</margin>
**I** am uncertain whether it is more correct to place "Rejoice" in salutations, or, as I have been accustomed to write to friends, "Do well." <note>Plato is contrasting the common Greek greeting 'chairein' (rejoice/greetings) with his preferred 'eu prattein' (do well/fare well), which carries a more ethical weight.</note> You indeed, as those who were with you in Delphi say, were accustomed to address the god himself in this flattering way, and to write similarly. "Rejoice," you say: "and keep the life of a tyrant pleasant." I, however, would salute neither a god nor a man in this manner. Not a god, because I would be speaking contrary to his nature. For the divine nature is far from distress and pleasure. Not a man, because pleasure too often brings detriment and pain to himself, producing dullness in the soul, forgetfulness, foolishness, and insolence. And let these things be said by me concerning the salutation. Which, after you have read it, you may take however you wish. Not a few people report that you were accustomed to say to certain ambassadors, while they were visiting you, that you intended in your mind to restore the Greek cities in Sicily and to relieve the Syracusans, and to introduce a royal government to them instead of a tyranny. You claim that when I heard these things, I prevented you from doing them, even though you greatly desired it. But now, you say that Dion is teaching you to do those very things, and that your own plans are being undermined by us who are unskilled. Whether such talk brings you any utility, you yourself know; but you certainly do me an injury, since you say things contrary to the truth. And indeed, enough and more than enough envy has been stirred up against me until now by Philistides <note>Philistides was an advisor and historian loyal to the tyrant's family who opposed Plato's influence.</note> and many others, both among the soldiers and among the Syracusans. For while I was living in the citadel with you, all misdeeds were turned against me, as those who were outside asserted that you did every single thing by my counsel. But you know clearly that I dealt with you very little concerning civil governance of my own accord, and that was only from the beginning, when I thought I might be able to achieve something, and certain other small matters, while applying myself moderately to the **preambles of the Laws**. <note>original: "Legum prooemiis." This refers to Plato's philosophical work 'The Laws,' where he argues that laws should have persuasive introductions.</note> I hear, however, that later either you or someone else inserted things into them contrary to my intention. Those who are able to discern the character of my genius will easily distinguish these. But as I was saying just now, I do not seek to bring a calumny against the Syracusans and others with whom you accuse me by saying these things, but much more to provide a defense against the first calumny, and against the new one recently arisen, which is indeed greater and more vehement. Therefore, against two calumnies, it is necessary for me to undertake a double excuse. First, indeed, that I rightly did not wish to deal with you concerning the governance of the state; second, that my counsel was not that fear which you claim, as if I were persuading you not to restore the Greek cities. And first, concerning the former, hear this. I came to Syracuse called by you and by Dion; since Dion himself was of great dignity with you, and had long been my guest-friend, and was of a middle and mature age, which anyone even moderately prudent would think necessary for conducting affairs such as yours were. But you were quite young, and ignorant of all things of which you ought to have had experience. You were also very unknown to me. After this, whether some man, or a god, or some fortune was with you, it drove Dion out. You were left alone. Do you think, then, that any communion of civil affairs was left to me with you then? When I saw a prudent counselor driven away by you, and you, being imprudent, left with many shameful men, so that you did not rule, although you thought you ruled, but in truth were serving men of this sort? What, then, was it necessary for me to do? Was it not what I did? To abstain, namely, from all governance, lest I be called into calumnies by the envy of the malevolent. And to strive entirely for this: that I might restore you, who were mutually distrustful and widely divided, into your former friendship and grace. You can be a witness for me with what great effort this business was undertaken by me, and never abandoned. Finally, we barely agreed that I should return home, and that when the war which was then ongoing had ended, I and Dion would return to Syracuse, and you would call us back. These things were done in that first journey of mine to you, and in my return to my homeland. Then, when peace was made, you called me again: not, however, as we had mutually agreed, together with Dion, but alone. For you wrote that I should come then; but that Dion would be called by you later. For that reason, I did not come then; which indeed displeased Dion, who thought it better that I should obey you and come. After a year had passed, a trireme <note>A standard ancient Greek warship with three banks of oars.</note> was sent by you, and your letters with it. The head of these was that if I came, Dion’s affairs would be as I especially desired; but contrary if I did not come. I am ashamed to recount how many letters were then written, as much by you as by others on your account, from Italy and Sicily to me and to many of my relatives and familiars; all of which exhorted and prayed that I should comply and come to you. It seemed best to everyone, therefore, and especially to Dion, that I should go without delay, although I excused myself on account of age and said that I distrusted your constancy, as if I could not resist the detractors and malevolent people who were seeking to create distrust between us. For I had seen long ago, and even now I perceive, that the greater the wealth of private citizens and princes, the more they nourish plotters and designers of base and harmful pleasures, than which nothing more destructive is produced by opulence and power. Nevertheless, having dismissed all these concerns, I decided to come, lest I should leave material for complaint to any of my familiars, that when their affairs could have been safe, they had perished through my negligence. But what followed after my arrival, you know best. I certainly thought that, according to the promises of your letters, you would recall Dion as soon as possible and receive him into your former familiarity. I thought his account ought to be considered. In which if you had obeyed me, perhaps your affairs and those of the Syracusans and the rest of the Greeks would have been better, as...

# LETTERS. FOLIO 384.

Afterward, however, Dio perceived that the conviction he had embraced through right reason existed not only in himself, but also in certain others (though not many), among whose number he hoped—the gods helping—the younger Dionysius would be. If that should happen, both Dionysius himself and the rest of the Syracusans would obtain a marvelous happiness. For this reason, I judged that I ought to go to Syracuse as quickly as possible to be a partner and helper in these things. I kept in mind how easily my previous acquaintance with the man had lead him toward the desire for a most beautiful and excellent life. If he could perfect this desire in Dionysius as he had begun, he held great hope that he could establish a true and blessed way of living throughout that entire region without slaughter and blood, and without those evils which have now come to pass. 

Dio, rightly considering these things, persuaded Dionysius to call for me; and he himself also asked that I should hurry to arrive, setting all other things aside, before any others clinging to Dionysius might turn him toward other paths, neglecting the best institutions of life. To these prayers he added a long exhortation. "What other time," he said, "do we now expect more opportune for action than that which is now granted to us by a certain divine fortune?" He spoke, furthermore, of the greatness of Dionysius's empire throughout Italy and Sicily, and of his power in these very places, as well as his intense passion and desire for the study of philosophy and learning. Moreover, he noted how ready his relatives and household would be to receive the discipline of life that I would advise, and that Dionysius himself was fit to be provoked to this. Therefore, if ever there was hope, it was surely greatest now that the same men might be both philosophers and the princes of great states. <note>This is a reference to Plato's famous "Philosopher-King" ideal from the *Republic*.</note>

He, therefore, exhorted me with these reasons and many others of the same kind. I, however, feared how the passions of a youth might eventually turn out. For the desires of such people are both swift and often carry themselves in contrary directions. Yet I knew Dio to be grave by nature and now of a sufficiently mature age. Thus, as I was thinking and wavering as to whether I should go and obey him or not, it finally occurred to me that I must go and obey. If ever anyone wished to attempt to perfect those things he had thought concerning <term>laws and the republic</term><note>Plato refers here to his political theories and perhaps his work, the *Republic*.</note>, now would be the time to try. Indeed, I judged that if I could persuade only one man, I would sufficiently achieve all good things. 

For this reason, and with this conviction and confidence, I departed from home—not for the reasons some supposed, but led primarily by a certain shame of conscience: lest I should ever seem to myself to possess only words, but to perform no effect or duty by my own will; and lest I should first betray the hospitality and friendship of Dio, which was subject to no small dangers. If any adversity should happen to him, or if he were driven out by Dionysius and his other enemies and fled to us as a fugitive, he might say these words: "O Plato, I come to you driven from my fatherland; though I lacked neither soldiers nor horsemen with whose strength I might resist my enemies, I lacked words and persuasion, by which I knew you were most able—by exhorting youths toward probity and justice—to bind them in friendship and necessity. Through the defect of these things, caused by you, it has come to pass that I, expelled from Syracuse, have arrived here. My own fortune, deserted by you, brings less reproach to you. But what of philosophy itself, which you always praise, and whose lack of honor among others you complain of? Has it not now been betrayed by you along with me?" If I had been at <term>Megara</term><note>A city near Athens, used here to suggest that Plato would travel a short distance to help, so he should be willing to travel a long one.</note>, you certainly would have come as a helper to me when I called you; otherwise, you would have judged yourself the most cowardly of all men. But now, excusing yourself because of the length of the journey, the danger of the voyage, and the labors, you think you avoid infamy? It will certainly be far from it. If, I say, he had said these things, what probable response would I have? Certainly none. 

For these reasons, led by the most probable arguments possible and by right itself, I arrived—leaving behind my own customs, which were honorable enough, to live under a <term>tyranny</term><note>The rule of Dionysius II, which was an autocracy inconsistent with Plato's philosophical life.</note> that suited neither my speech nor myself. But by coming, I freed myself so that neither <term>Hospital Jupiter</term><note>Original Latin: *hospitalis Iupiter*. This refers to Zeus Xenios, the protector of guests and the laws of hospitality.</note> nor the fate of philosophy could accuse me. Certainly, I would have been a disgrace to philosophy if I could have been reproached for softness and timidity. 

However, when I had come there—for there is no need to wander too long—I found everything at Dionysius’s court full of sedition and slanders against Dio, alleging that he was aiming for the tyranny. I defended him, therefore, as much as I was able, but I could do little. For about the fourth month after my arrival, Dionysius, accusing Dio of plotting against the tyranny, cast him into a small boat and shamefully expelled him. All of us who were friends of Dio were terrified, lest by chance Dionysius should punish one of us as an accomplice in that crime. A rumor even arose in Syracuse that I had been killed by Dionysius as the author of all those things that had then happened. 

But he, perceiving that we were all affected in this way, and fearing lest something more serious might happen from our fear, received us all quite kindly. He certainly consoled me and told me to have good hope, and he asked me by all means to remain. For my flight would bring him no honor, but my staying would. And for that reason, he especially feigned to pray to me. <margin>The prayers of tyrants are mixed with necessity.</margin> But we are not ignorant that the prayers of tyrants are mixed with necessity. When he was plotting so that I would not leave, he settled me in the citadel and wished me to inhabit those places from which no sailor would hereafter take me away—not only if he prohibited it, but unless he ordered and sent it. Nor would any merchant or magistrate of any province have seen me exiting alone without suddenly bringing me back, as a captive, to Dionysius; especially since it was now spread about, contrary to what was previously rumored, that Dionysius was again embracing Plato vehemently. 

And in a certain way, it was so. For the truth must not be kept silent. Indeed, he embraced me more and more day by day, and rejoiced in our character and company. He desired to be praised by me more than Dio was, and to be considered a far greater friend. To that end, he strove greatly. But he neglected the method by which that would have been best achieved, if indeed it could have been. For this would have been for him to cling more freely to me in hearing and learning the reasons of philosophy and to agree with me. But he was too distrustful for this, fearing—as the slanderers suggested—that if he involved himself in those reasons, Dio would have achieved all that he desired. I, however, endured all things, persevering in the same conviction with which I had first set out, trying if by any means...

Upon arrival, he finds the court rife with suspicion, leading to Dio's exile and Plato's own virtual imprisonment in the citadel.</summary>

# BOOK OF LETTERS. PAGE 36.

->BOOK OF LETTERS<-

...it might be possible that he would arrive at a desire for the philosophical life. But he, struggling against me, won me over. And indeed, the first period of my journey was spent in Sicily, and my actions there were led through all these things. In later times, however, I returned again to Sicily, where Dionysius recalled me with all his zeal. For what cause I went back, and what I did there—not indeed without reason—I will finally report to you, when I have first advised you on what ought best to be done given how things currently stand. I will report these things, I say, for the sake of those who ask with what purpose I returned a second time. But lest the incidental matters be placed before the principal ones, I now come to the advice itself. I truly believe that a man advising a sick person who is intemperate in his lifestyle ought, in the first place, to persuade him to change his way of living; and if the sick man obeys in this, then he should offer him other remedies for healing. But if he refuses to obey, I will consider that man a true advisor and a physician if he abandons him; but if he persists further in advising, I will consider him the opposite: namely, a coward and unskilled in his art. I think the same also regarding a city, whether one man governs it or many. For if a people proceeding by some probable reason and a right path asks for useful advice, I judge it the duty of a wise man to provide it. But if they depart entirely from civil reason and do not wish to follow even its tracks, and say to the advisor: "It is better to leave the Republic alone and stir nothing within it—for if you stir it, you shall perish—and instead indulge our pleasures and lusts," and they seek advice on how their pleasures might always and most quickly be satisfied: I would by no means consider a man who persists in such governance to be a man; rather, he should have abandoned the task entirely.

Being established in this opinion, whenever someone consults me on weightier matters, whether they pertain to riches, or to the purging of the body or soul, if his daily life seems to maintain some measure, or at least if he seems likely to obey my counsel, I advise him freely, and I do not cease until I have led the beginning to its end with all my strength. But if he either does not seek advice from me at all, or if he who seeks it appears clearly to be in no way willing to obey my counsel, I do not approach him of my own accord to advise him—not even by force, not even if he were my own son. However, I would advise even an unwilling slave, and compel him by force <note>Plato distinguishes between the moral obligation to persuade free citizens and the legal/social right to compel those in a lower status for their own good.</note>. But to compel a father or mother by force I judge to be a sin <note>original: "nefas"</note>, unless they are alienated from their minds because of a disease. If they live according to their own custom, which I in no way approve, I would neither oppose them senselessly by fruitlessly warning them, nor again would I assent to their desires by flattering them or offering things which, if I myself were to indulge in them, I would not wish to live.

A prudent man ought to be of this same mind toward his fatherland: he should rebuke the errors of the city in such a way that his rebuke is neither in vain, nor that he might perish for his zeal in rebuking. He will never bring force to bear for a change in the Republic <note>Plato's famous "Republic" (Politeia) is the Greek term for the state or constitution.</note> when it cannot be amended without the expulsion and slaughter of citizens. Instead, he will act quietly, and pray for the best things for himself and his fatherland.

It was in this manner, therefore, that I advised you. I likewise advised Dionysius together with Dio: namely, that he should live his daily life in such a way that he might especially be made master of himself, and have faithful friends and companions, lest the same thing happen to him that happened to his father. For though his father <note>Dionysius I, the Elder.</note> had taken many great cities in Sicily that had once been devastated by barbarians and had restored them, he could not establish faithful governors of those republics in each of them—not from his own household, nor from others acquired from elsewhere, nor even from his younger brothers whom he himself had raised. Instead, he made faithful men out of private citizens, and very rich men out of the poor. Yet he could not find any of these to be a faithful partner in governance, whether by persuading, teaching, giving gifts, or receiving them into his kinship. He was seven times worse than Darius <note>Darius I, King of the Persian Empire, known for his administrative organization.</note>, who, trusting neither his brothers nor those raised under him, but only his companions, divided the parts of the empire of Midas and the eunuchs into seven provinces—each one larger than all of Sicily—and assigned them to each. And he found them to be faithful partners of his kingdom, neither plotting against him nor against each other. Furthermore, he gave an example of what a good lawmaker and king ought to be, since he brought forth laws by which the Empire of the Persians is still preserved today.

To this, add that the Athenians, though they had received many Greek cities into their power (not established by themselves, but by others, and then occupied by barbarians), held their empire over them for seventy years, because they had acquired friends for themselves in each city. But Dionysius, although he had gathered all of Sicily into one city, trusting no one because of his "wisdom," was preserved with difficulty. For he lacked friends and faithful men, than which there is no greater proof: either of wickedness if they are absent, or of goodness if they are present. These, then, were the things that I and Dio advised Dionysius: after his father’s affairs had been left in such a state that he had neither the companionship of learned men nor decent habits. We admonished him that, intending his mind toward these things, he should first acquire other friends for himself from his household and his equals who were in accord with virtue. But above all, that he should make himself consistent and constant with himself. We showed him that there was a very great lack of this quality in him—not indeed in open words (for that would not have been safe), but by a certain hidden reasoning, yet signifying the same thing: teaching him that only in this way can any man save both himself and those whom he rules, if he observes these things; but if he acts otherwise, the opposite will surely happen.

For if he proceeded as we said, and made himself prudent and temperate; and if he again restored the devastated cities of Sicily and fortified them with laws and institutions pertaining to the republic, so that they might be benevolent toward him and toward each other in helping against the force of the barbarians, he would not only double his father’s kingdom but truly multiply it. It would indeed be so if he bore himself in this way: that the Carthaginians <note>The North African power that frequently warred with the Greeks in Sicily.</note> would be subjected to his power much more easily than they had been subjected to Gelon <note>Gelon was a 5th-century BC tyrant of Syracuse who famously defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of Himera.</note>. On the contrary, look at what happened to his father: he had been forced to pay tribute to the barbarians. These were the things we said and instructed to Dionysius, even though we were supposedly "plotting" against him, as many spread abroad. These people, when they had overcome us in Dionysius's favor, drove out Dio and threw us into fear. But, to compress many things into a few words: Dio, having set out from the Peloponnese and Athens, now corrected Dionysius by his deeds...

# LETTERS. FOLIO 385.

->LETTERS<-

Z

...he warned. When, therefore, Dion had liberated the city and restored it twice to its citizens, the Syracusans were affected toward Dion in the same way as Dionysius had been before. For long ago, Dion had contended to educate and instruct Dionysius so that he might make him a king worthy of his realm, and he had determined to offer himself as such a guide throughout his life. But detractors and slanderers persuaded Dionysius that Dion was plotting against his tyranny, machining all these things at that time so that Dionysius’s mind, entangled in the study of disciplines, might neglect his rule and leave it entirely to Dion, so that Dion might then usurp the government by craft and expel him. Just as these things prevailed then with Dionysius, so later among the Syracusans these same things were said and tossed about, resulting in a victory that was utterly infamous and shameful for those who overcame him. But you who call upon me now to settle your affairs ought to hear what sort of victory that was.

I, an Athenian man and a friend and helper of Dion, came to him against the tyrant so that I might turn war into friendship; but fighting against the slanderers, I was defeated. When Dionysius tried to win me over and keep me with him, not only with words but also with money and honors, so that my familiarity with him might serve as testimony that Dion had not been unjustly expelled, he could achieve nothing with me in this great effort of his. 

In later times, when Dion was returning home, he brought two Athenian brothers with him—friends not from philosophy, but from that common and vulgar familiarity which usually contracts friendship through hospitality and frequent companionship during sacred rites and spectacles. They had established a friendship with Dion both from these things I have mentioned and from the service they provided upon his return. When these men had arrived in Sicily and realized that slanders were being cast against Dion by the very people he had liberated—claiming he was aiming for tyranny—they did not merely betray their friend and host, but were themselves the assassins, as if with their own hands. For holding arms, they openly assisted the killers. 

The foulness and impiety of that deed I will neither pass over nor fully describe, for many have narrated these things diligently and will continue to do so. But I speak in response to the infamy brought upon our city. For if those who betrayed him were Athenians, he who could never be led to betray him by promises of money or honors was also an Athenian <note>Plato is referring to himself here, defending the reputation of Athens by contrasting his own loyalty with the treachery of Dion's assassins, Callippus and his brother.</note>. For he had become a friend not through a vulgar or mercenary benevolence, but through the communion of a liberal education. Certainly, anyone who is wise places more trust in this alone than in any connection of ancestors or blood relationship. Therefore, those traitors are not to be esteemed so highly that they could bring disgrace upon the city for the murder of Dion, as if they were ever of any value. 

All these things have been said so that I might provide counsel to the friends and kin of Dion. Furthermore, I advise you now for the third time, with the same reasoning: let neither Sicily nor any city be subject to men, but only to the laws <note>A central theme in Plato's political philosophy: the rule of law is superior to the rule of any individual man.</note>, as our reasoning holds. For this is useful neither for those who rule, nor for those who serve, nor for their children or their children's children; rather, to attempt such a thing is altogether ruinous for men. It is the mark of a narrow and illiberal soul to seize such gains, understanding nothing of what is good and just, whether divine or human, either for the present or the future. 

I first tried to persuade Dion of these things, then Dionysius, and now thirdly, you. Therefore, obey me for the sake of Jupiter the Third Savior <note>original: "Iouis tertii seruatoris"; a reference to the Greek custom of offering the third libation to Zeus the Savior, signifying a final, completing act.</note>. Consider also the end of Dionysius and Dion. Dionysius, not obeying my counsels, lives even now in a manner that is not honorable. But Dion, having obeyed them, died honorably. For to that man who aims for the most noble things for himself and his country, nothing can ever happen except what is right and beautiful. 

None of us was born immortal, nor if that should happen to someone, would he therefore be happy, as the common crowd believes. For in things lacking a soul, there is nothing worthy of being called either good or evil; but these things happen to each soul, either while it is with the body or when it is separated from the body. One must always truly believe the ancient and sacred words which announce to us that the soul is immortal, that it has judges, and that it suffers the greatest punishments after it has been separated from the body. For this reason, it should be considered a lesser evil to suffer the gravest injuries brought by wrongdoers than to inflict them. 

A man dedicated to amassing money and established in a poverty of soul does not hear these things; or if he does hear them, he treats them with contempt as if they were ridiculous, following his own judgment. He impudently snatches from everywhere whatever he thinks will supply him, like a beast, with the pleasures of the belly and the delights of Venus—pleasures that are certainly servile, ungrateful, and absurd, and not worthy of the name of true pleasure. And as if blind, he does not see that he struggles in vain to satisfy an insatiable lust. Nor again does he see how great an evil impiety is, and how justice is always mixed with these things. It is necessary for the soul that has perpetrated injustices to follow this path: both while it revolves upon the earth among men, and while it is carried about everywhere beneath the earth in an utterly shameful and miserable state. 

Therefore, when I said these and other things of the same kind to Dion, I persuaded him. I would most justly be angry with his killers in the same way I am with Dionysius. For both have brought the gravest losses upon me and upon all others, if I may say so: the former by killing him who wished to practice justice, and the latter by refusing in any way to practice justice, though he held the greatest power in the entire kingdom. If, in that kingdom, philosophy and power had truly met in the same dwelling, it would have shown all men, both Greeks and Barbarians, a shining and true opinion: that neither a city nor a man will ever be happy unless they live with prudence and under justice, whether they possess these virtues in themselves or are rightly brought up and instructed under the customs of holy princes. In these things, Dionysius did harm. Other losses, if compared to these, seem very small to me. But he who killed Dion did not understand that he did the same thing as Dionysius. For I know certainly, as far as one man may affirm of another, that if Dion had held the rudders of the kingdom longer, he would never have turned to any other form of rule than that which, from the beginning, he had intended for his fatherland, Syra...

XXXVI.

### BOOK

<margin>Hiero.</margin>[Syracu]se, having expelled slavery, he established freedom in its own right with the most splendid joy; then, with all his zeal, he would have adorned the citizens with the best and most suitable laws. Furthermore, he would have applied every diligence to ensure that all of Sicily was inhabited and liberated from the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbaris" — in this context, Plato refers to the Carthaginians who frequently threatened Greek Sicily</note>, some being expelled and others being subdued more easily than Hiero had done. If these things had been carried out by a man who was just, brave, temperate, or a philosopher, the same reputation for virtue would have flourished among many; it would have remained healthy and vigorous among all men, so to speak, if Dionysius had obeyed us from the beginning. 

But now, whether some divine spirit <note>original: "dæmon"</note> or some destructive entity threw itself against these plans with iniquity and impiety—and what is worst of all, <margin>All evils stem from ignorant audacity.</margin> ignorant audacity, from which all evils for everyone take root, sprout, and produce the most bitter fruit for posterity—it has overturned and destroyed all these things again. 

But now, for the sake of a third happy omen, let us speak only of good things. I therefore advise you, his friends, to imitate Dion, embracing more and more his love for his country and his temperance in life. Under what auspices you should attempt to carry out his plans, and what sort of plans they were, you have heard clearly from me. But if there is any among you who refuses to live in the Dorian manner <note>The "Dorian" lifestyle was associated with ancient tradition, austerity, and discipline, as opposed to "Sicilian" luxury.</note> according to the institutions of the fatherland, and follows the Sicilian way of life and the way of those who killed Dion, do not receive him, nor consider him faithful or sincere in any matter. 

Rather, you ought to exhort the rest to the resettlement of all Sicily and to the equality of laws, drawing people both from Sicily itself and from the whole Peloponnesus. Do not be afraid of Athens; for there, too, are men of the most outstanding virtue, who hold in hatred the cruelty of those who pollute themselves with the murder of their guests. 

But if these measures are too slow, and daily and manifold seditions and discords urge you on, every person to whom a divine lot has granted even a small portion of right opinion must understand: there will be no end to seditions, nor to the evils born from sedition, until those who have conquered cease from the slaughter and expulsion of citizens, and even from the memory of injuries and the desire for vengeance. Let them be reconciled with their enemies and become masters of themselves. Furthermore, they must establish common laws designed no more for their own pleasure than for the pleasure of those they have conquered. They must compel them to use these laws—compel them, I say, by a twin path of necessity: namely, through fear and through shame. Through fear, because they are the more powerful, demonstrating their force; and through shame, because they again appear more capable and ready both in overcoming pleasures and in observing the laws. 

Otherwise, there is absolutely no way of ending the evils of a city laboring under internal seditions; rather, seditions, enmities, hatreds, and betrayals in the republic—as is accustomed to happen within and among cities in such a state—will always be arising. Therefore, those who hold the republic as the more powerful, if they desire safety, must choose from among themselves and prefer in honor those whom they have heard are the best: first of all, the elderly who have children, wives, and a home, and whose ancestors were numerous, approved, and distinguished, all possessing sufficient inheritance. For a city of ten thousand men, fifty such men will suffice. These, then, they should call from their homes with prayers and the greatest honors. Once called, they should be entreated and bound by an oath to establish laws that grant no more to the victors than to the vanquished, but rather provide equal and common justice to the entire city. 

Finally, once the laws are established, everything depends on this: if the victors are willing to be subject to the laws even more than those who were conquered, then everything will be full of safety and happiness, and all evils will be far away. If not, then neither I nor anyone else should be called to a common counsel for such a person who will not acquiesce to these precepts. These are essentially the same goals that Dion and I long ago attempted to achieve in Syracuse with right judgment, though these are the later steps. For the first steps would have been those which we tried to do first with Dionysius himself, for the common good of all. But a certain fortune, more powerful than men, dissolved those plans. Now, however, may you attempt these things more fortunately, by some good luck and divine fortune.

And here ends the part of the letter concerning my advice and my first voyage to Sicily. But as for my subsequent departure and voyage—that it was undertaken neither without reason nor rashly—if anyone cares to know, he may now listen. 

First, the time of my residence in Sicily had passed, as I said above, before I gave counsel to the friends and relatives of Dion. Afterward, I persuaded Dionysius as much as I could to permit me to leave. It had been agreed between us that when peace was made after the war then occurring in Sicily, and his status was more securely confirmed, Dion should be recalled, and I should return at the same time. He wanted Dion to understand and believe that he was not in exile, but rather in a sort of retirement, certain to return at a fixed time. I, agreeing, took it upon myself that I would act accordingly. 

But when peace followed, Dionysius summoned me; however, he urged Dion to tolerate his absence for another year. He asked me, however, to hurry to him by all means. Dion therefore both ordered and entreated me to go there. For a rumor had spread from Sicily that Dionysius was again possessed by a wonderful desire for philosophy. For this reason, Dion, deeply moved, demanded that I not miss the opportunity. I, however, although I knew that young men are often moved toward philosophy in such a way, nevertheless thought it would be safer to let the whole matter go, and obey neither Dionysius nor Dion. So I replied with a refusal that was hateful to both: namely, that I would not go because I was already an old man, and because nothing of what was currently happening was being done as had been agreed. 

In the meantime, I heard that Archytas of Tarentum <note>A famous Pythagorean philosopher and statesman, and a friend of Plato.</note> had come to Dionysius. Before my departure, I had introduced him and several other Tarentines into Dionysius’s circle. There were also certain others in Syracuse who had occasionally been Dion’s auditors, and among these were some who had heard many other things in philosophy. These men seemed to me to have vied with one another to dispute such matters with Dionysius, as if he had heard everything I had ever thought of. Now, Dionysius is not slow at learning, and he is vehemently inflamed by a desire for honor. Therefore, the things they said perhaps pleased him, and he was clearly ashamed that he had heard nothing from me when I had been with him. Therefore, part...
