partly the love of hearing more clearly had urged him, and partly the desire for glory spurred him on. Why indeed he did not listen during that first journey of mine, I have related in the previous parts. Therefore, when I had returned home as a guest, and when he called me back a second time and I refused, as I have said, it seemed to me that Dionysius was altogether burning with care for his own honor. He feared lest men might interpret my refusal as if I utterly despised him, having become acquainted with his character, his habits, and his way of life through actual experience. It is only just that I confess the truth: and I should bear it with an even mind if someone, hearing what happened, should despise my philosophy but think the tyrant possessed a great mind. Dionysius sent a trireme <note>A fast ancient Greek warship with three banks of oars.</note> to me for the third time, so that I might sail easily. He also sent Archidemus, whom he believed I valued most among all the associates of Archytas <note>Archytas was a famous Pythagorean philosopher and statesman from Tarentum, a close friend of Plato.</note> in Sicily; and together with him other Sicilian nobles. All affirmed with the same words that Dionysius was wonderfully devoted to philosophy. He sent, moreover, a very long letter, since he knew how I felt toward Dion, and that Dion's own desire was for me to travel to Syracuse. To all these things, therefore, the letter had been composed, with a beginning such as this: *Dionysius to Plato.* Having prefaced this with the customary and lawful greetings, he says nothing before this: "that you should come to Sicily with a willing heart. First, regarding Dion, things will be done exactly as you wish. And you will wish, I believe, for moderate things, and I shall concede them. But if you do not come, you will obtain none of those things which you desire for Dion, neither in other matters nor in those concerning his own person, which are now your primary concern." Thus he wrote. The rest would be tedious to tell and not seasonable for the narrative. Other letters also came from Archytas and other Italians and Tarentines, praising Dionysius's zeal for wisdom; moreover, they added this: that unless I set out, I would cause that friendship which I had established between them and Dionysius—which was of no small importance for their political affairs—to utterly fail. When, therefore, I was being summoned at that time, with some drawing me from Sicily and Italy, and others at Athens urging me with prayers, as it were, and when reason dictated to me that I ought not to betray Dion and my Tarentine hosts and friends—and it occurred to me that it was not surprising if a talented young man, though he previously refused to hear discourses on great matters, might now, having changed his mind, be kindled with a certain ardor for the best life—I felt I ought to test clearly which way he inclined. I did not want to betray him, nor give him cause to blame me so greatly, if his affairs truly stood as they were reported. Protected by the defense of these reasons, I began the journey, fearing many things and divining many things that did not seem right. I set out, finally, for the third time under the protection of the Savior <note>original: "sub servatore" — likely referring to Zeus Soter, the Savior, a traditional invocation for a safe voyage.</note>. For indeed I attained that end, for once again I was successfully saved. And for these things, after God, I owe thanks to Dionysius, because when many desired to kill me, he himself resisted, and showed some regard for his own honor in my affairs. When I had come to him, I judged that this must be opened first: to examine this very thing, whether Dionysius was truly kindled with a love for philosophy as if by fire, or whether the rumor that had spread all the way to Athens was empty. There is a certain way of conducting an experiment regarding these things: not an ignoble one, but truly suited to tyrants, especially those who have already heard many things—which indeed I perceived immediately upon coming had happened to Dionysius. One must show such people how great a thing philosophy is, how much zeal it requires, and with what great labors it is acquired. He who hears this, if he truly loves wisdom and is akin to it by nature and worthy of its possession, thinks a wonderful path has been shown to him, as if it were a divine way, and he believes he must walk it with every effort, and that he must not live in any other way. Therefore he exhorts himself <margin>Signs of a future philosopher.</margin> and even the leader of this path most earnestly; nor does he cease until he has either achieved the end of all things, or at least has acquired that faculty through which he can lead himself to the goal without a guide. Considering these and similar reasons, such a man, throughout his whole life, whatever he may do, is always intent upon philosophy above all things. He uses a daily diet that best allows him to preserve his intellect, memory, and judgment: showing himself sober, and always hating the diet contrary to this. But those who are not truly lovers of wisdom, but are only externally colored by opinions—like those who are tanned and colored by the sun—when they hear how many things must be learned, with how much labor, and with what temperance of daily living the study of philosophy is necessary, they immediately think the matter is hard and impossible for them, and they cannot be led to give it their effort. Many indeed persuade themselves that they have already heard everything sufficiently, and no longer need any further zeal. This test is clear and least deceptive against those who, while pretending to love philosophy, are proven incompetent. I used this method of examination with Dionysius then. I did not run through everything, nor did Dionysius require it. For there were very many and great things in which he studied to be thought sufficiently learned because of what he had heard from others. I hear, however, that he wrote afterward about the things he heard then, as if composing his own system; yet none of these things were truly his own, as I hear. Of these things I know nothing for certain. I know that certain others have written about these same things, whoever they may be, not even knowing themselves. I will say this much about all who have written or will write, claiming they know those things which I study so seriously—whether they heard them from me or from others, or whether they were the inventors themselves—it is impossible for them to perceive anything of my judgment. For I have never written about these things, nor shall I write. For it can in no way be expressed in words like other disciplines; but from long familiarity with the subject itself, and from a life joined to it, suddenly at last, as if from a leaping spark <note>original: "ignis scintillanti" — one of Plato's most famous descriptions of philosophical insight.</note>, a light shining forth in the soul now nourishes itself. But this much at least I know: namely, that the things written or said by me would be best said...

### BOOK XXXVI.

->**THE LETTERS**<-

...certainly, poorly written things would bring me no small trouble. If it seemed to me that these matters ought to be set forth to the common people in writing or by voice, what finer thing could we do in this life than to bring something so greatly useful to mankind, and to bring the very nature of all things into the light! But indeed, I do not think the effort of publishing these things is useful for men, except for a very few who are able to find the truth for themselves once a few small tracks have been pointed out. As for others, it would fill some with an unholy contempt, and others with a high and empty hope, as if they had already learned something magnificent. Therefore, I have decided to speak at greater length about these things. For perhaps if these things are said, something of what I am saying will appear more clearly. For there is a true argument that stands against anyone who dares to write anything at all about such matters—an argument often stated by me elsewhere, and now, it seems, needing to be said again.

For every existing thing, there are three components through which knowledge of it must necessarily be formed. The fourth is the knowledge itself. And as a fifth, one must place the object itself, which is knowable—that is, which can be perceived and truly exists. 
1. The first of these is the **name**. 
2. The second is the **definition** <note>original: *oratio sive ratio*; referring to the logical statement or formula of a thing's essence.</note>. 
3. The third is the **image** <note>original: *simulacrum*; a physical representation like a drawing or a model.</note>. 
4. The fourth is **knowledge** <note>original: *scientia*; including intellect and true opinion.</note>.

Take any single thing as an example if you wish to learn what has just been said, and think similarly of all things. Something is called a "circle," the name of which is exactly what we just pronounced. Next follows its **definition**, composed of nouns and verbs. For "that which is everywhere equidistant from its extremities to its center" is the definition of that which we designate by the names "round," "circumference," and "circle." The third is the **image**: for a circle may be painted or erased, or turned on a lathe or destroyed. None of these things happen to the "circle itself" <note>The abstract, perfect Form of a circle.</note> to which all these individual instances relate, for it exists as something else entirely. The fourth is **knowledge**, **intellect**, and **true opinion** regarding these things. This whole category must be placed as one, for it exists neither in sounds nor in the shapes of bodies, but in the soul. Therefore, it is manifest that the actual nature of the circle is one thing, and the three things we mentioned above are something else. Of these, **intellect** <note>original: *intellectus*</note> clings most closely by kinship and likeness to the fifth, while the others are more remote.

The same may be said of straight and curved figures, and of color; of the good, the beautiful, and the just. Again, this applies to every body, whether handmade or natural—whether fire or water and other such things—and similarly of every living creature, the character of souls, and all actions and passions. Unless one somehow grasps those four, they will never perfectly participate in the knowledge of the **fifth** <term>The Fifth (Quintum): Plato’s term for the true essence or "Form" of a thing, which exists independently of our words or physical examples.</term>.

Furthermore, these four attempt to show the *quality* of each thing no less than its *essence* <note>original: *quod sit* (what it is/essence) vs *quale sit* (of what sort/quality)</note>, because of the weakness of language. For this reason, no one of sound mind will ever dare to commit to it—that is, to an unchangeable medium—the things they have understood, especially those four forms of expression. This is particularly true of things designated by physical shapes. 

Consider again what we are now saying. Every circle that is drawn or turned by a lathe by human hands is full of the opposite of that **fifth** thing. For it participates in the "straight" everywhere <note>Meaning a physical line, no matter how curved it looks, is imperfect and composed of points that conflict with the perfect curve of the ideal Circle.</note>. But we affirm that the "circle itself" has neither more nor less of anything; that is, it has nothing of a contrary nature within it. Moreover, we say that none of these names have any inherent stability. For nothing would prevent the things we now call "round" from being called "straight," and the "straight" from being called "round"; the names would have no less stability if they were changed to their opposites. The same reasoning applies to the **definition**, since it is composed of names and verbs that possess no absolute stability. 

It can be proven in many ways that none of these four is certain or firm. But the greatest point of all is what I said a moment ago: that since there are two things—**essence** and **quality**—and the soul seeks not the "of what sort" but the "what it is," the soul will be filled with ambiguity and obscurity unless each of these four is first well-discussed by the soul through both reason and affection, and finally by the senses. 

In matters where we are not accustomed to seeking the truth because of a poor education, but think ourselves satisfied if we have touched upon the presented **images**, we do not make ourselves objects of ridicule to one another when questioned by those capable of discussing and refuting those four. However, where necessity compels us to show the **fifth**, anyone who is able to subvert and pull back the argument can "prick" the speaker. He makes the person explaining through speech, writing, or dispute appear to many listeners as if he understands nothing of what he attempts to say or write. In this, the listener often fails to realize that it is not the soul of the writer or speaker that is being refuted, but rather the flawed nature of those four tools. 

Only a journey through all of them, running up and down through each one, barely and at last gives birth to knowledge within—knowledge, I say, of that which is well-disposed by nature in a soul that is also naturally well-disposed toward it. But if someone is poorly disposed by nature—as is the natural state of the soul in many people regarding both learning and morals—not even Lynceus <note>A mythological Argonaut renowned for his keen sight, said to be able to see through trees and stone.</note> could make such a soul see. 

To put it briefly, neither quickness of mind nor memory will ever make one see a thing to which they are not kindred. For truth does not take root in alien habits. Therefore, whoever is not naturally inclined toward and kindred to justice and the other beautiful things, even if they are clever and have a good memory for other things—or again, whoever is kindred but dull and weak of memory—will never reach the highest truth of virtue or vice. For it is necessary to learn these things together: both the false and the true of the whole of reality, with total exercise and a long passage of time, as I said from the beginning. 

Only after the names, definitions, sights, and sensations of each have been rubbed together and worn down against one another—refuted through kindly testing and discussed through questioning and answering without envy—does the light of wisdom <note>original: *prudentia*</note> and intelligence finally shine forth regarding each thing, striving to the utmost of human capacity. Therefore, a serious man is very far from writing about things that are truly worthy of study, lest he expose himself and his works to the envy and ambiguity of men. From this one argument, it can be understood that whenever [someone sees] a...

### LETTERS, FOLIO 387.

Z iii
<meta>catchword: estate</meta>

You will see writings, whether of a lawmaker in the laws or of any others on any subject whatever; if the author is truly a man of study, he will realize that these writings were not his most serious or most carefully treated works. Instead, those highest truths lie within him in their own most beautiful region. But if he truly committed these things to writing as his most serious studies, then it was not the gods, but men, who surely "robbed him of his wits" <note>A reference to Homer's *Iliad*, suggesting the author has lost his mind or judgment.</note>. 

Whoever follows this story and this digression will clearly understand that whether Dionysius wrote anything about the highest and first principles of nature, or whether anyone else did, whether lesser or greater, it is my opinion that he has heard or learned nothing of the truth of what he wrote. Otherwise, he would have held these matters in the same reverence as I do, and would never have dared to expose them to the absurdity and unseemliness of a public edition. Nor did he write those things as a mere aid to memory. For there is no need to distrust memory in this matter, once the mind has grasped it. For the whole subject is gathered into the shortest of all summaries. 

Perhaps, however, he did it out of some shameful ambition—either to pass these ideas off as his own, or to appear to be a participant in a discipline of which he was unworthy, seeking the glory that comes from such participation. Now, if this had happened to Dionysius after only a single meeting, perhaps it could be excused. But what was that meeting like? "By Jupiter!" <note>original: *Proh Iupiter*; a common oath of astonishment.</note>, as the Theban said. I indeed ran through these matters for him, in the manner I described, only once; but after that, never again. 

After this, one must consider—just as we care to find the cause of what happened to us regarding those things—why we did not treat them a second, or a third, or more frequent time. Did Dionysius think he knew them well enough after hearing them only once? Did he think he had found them out himself or learned them from others? Or did he think the things I said were trivial? Or perhaps a third thing occurred: namely, that he judged these matters to be beyond his own strength, and realized he was not at all fit to live a life under the diligent care of wisdom and virtue. 

For if he is said to have judged them trivial, he will be opposed by many witnesses whose authority in judging such matters is far greater than his own. But if he found or learned them, and they seemed worthy to be admitted into a liberal mind as a discipline, who would not find it strange that Dionysius, being so disposed, so easily held in contempt the leader and author of these things? In what way he held me in contempt, I shall now say.

Indeed, not long after this time, he forbade Dion's **estate** <note>original: *patrimonium*; the inherited property and wealth of Dion.</note>—which he had previously allowed Dion to possess freely and receive the fruits thereof—from being touched by his agents. He also stopped the money from being sent to Dion in the Peloponnese as was the custom, acting as if he had entirely forgotten the letter he had written to me. For he asserted that those goods were not Dion's, but his son's; and since the boy was his nephew (being his sister's son), he claimed the boy was legally under his own guardianship. 

These things, then, were done up to that time. When I considered this, I saw clearly what Dionysius's disposition toward philosophy really was, and I was rightly disturbed, whether I wished to be or not. It was already summer, and ships were sailing frequently. It seemed to me that I should be less concerned about Dionysius than about myself and those who had pushed me to come a third time into the "straits of Scylla" and to measure again that "deadly Charybdis" <note>Scylla and Charybdis are mythological sea monsters representing a choice between two equally dangerous options. Plato refers here to his third, perilous journey to Syracuse.</note>. 

I was therefore compelled to tell Dionysius that I could not possibly stay with him while Dion was being so ignominiously held in contempt. But he tried to console me and asked me to stay, thinking it would not be honorable for himself if I were to go so quickly as the messenger of these actions he had taken. When he could not persuade me to stay, he said he himself would prepare the means and the way to send me home. I, however, had decided to cross in the merchant vessels, thinking that everything must be endured if he should try to prevent me from leaving—since I myself had clearly done Dionysius no wrong, yet I had been wronged by him. 

But when he realized I would by no means stay, he devised the following scheme to hinder my sailing. The next day, he spoke to me in a gracious and plausible manner: "Let us," he said, "remove from between us the affairs of Dion and Dionysius, so far as they provide a cause for our discord. For your sake, I will do this for Dion. I decree that Dion, receiving his property, shall live in the Peloponnese, not as an exile, but as one who is permitted to come here whenever it seems good to him, to me, and to you friends in common—provided he does me no injury. You and your friends here, as well as Dion's friends, shall be the guarantors of this for me. Dion himself must sufficiently confirm to you that he will observe this. All the money he has received shall be deposited in the Peloponnese and Athens with whomsoever you see fit. Dion may receive the income from this money, but he cannot take the capital itself without your consent. For I do not trust that if he receives all the money, he will keep faith with me—for it will be no small sum. But I have greater faith in you and your friends. Consider, then, if these things please you; stay here a year for the sake of these matters, and when they are finished, you shall depart with this money. I know Dion will be very grateful to you when you have accomplished this for him." 

When I heard this, although I took it very ill, I nevertheless replied that I would deliberate on the matter and took until the next day to respond. And so, agreeing on this, we then departed. Afterward, I deliberated with myself, being very much in doubt. But the first reason that occurred to me as a guide for my counsel was this: "Suppose Dionysius intends to keep none of his promises; nevertheless, if I leave, he could write plausible letters to Dion through himself and his friends saying that he had offered these terms of his own accord, but that I had refused them and entirely neglected Dion's affairs." 

Furthermore, I added this: if Dionysius did not want to let me go and therefore provided no ship or sailors—indeed, if he easily made it known to everyone that I wished to depart against his will—who would dare to take me in a ship from the very palace of Dionysius? For I was living, lest any inconvenience be lacking, in the gardens surrounding the palace <term>hortis</term> <note>These were the royal gardens of the Ortygia fortress, which functioned as a gilded cage for Plato.</note>. From there, not even a gatekeeper would have permitted me to leave unless Dionysius ordered it. But if I stay for a year, I will have a way to signal Dion and make known the situation I am in and what I am doing. And if Dionysius keeps any part of his promises, this work and endurance of mine will not seem entirely ridiculous. For Dion's **estate** <note>original: *patrimonium*</note> will be valued at no less than a hundred **talents** <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight/currency; a hundred talents was an enormous fortune, enough to fund a private army.</note> if someone were to estimate it correctly.

<meta>This page continues Plato’s Seventh Letter, moving from a philosophical critique of the tyrant Dionysius II to a detailed historical account of the political tensions in Syracuse. Plato describes the breakdown of his relationship with the tyrant and the betrayal regarding Dion’s property.</meta>

# BOOK XXXVI.

But if things should fall out as it is likely they will, I do not know where I should turn. Nevertheless, it is perhaps necessary that I still endure the schemes of Dionysius and refute them in actual deed according to my strength. After I had consulted with myself in this way, I reported to Dionysius the very next day that it seemed to me I should stay. But I added: he should not think that I could manage everything with Dion as if I were his master <note>original: "quasi dñm" (quasi dominum)</note>. Therefore, it was necessary that he also write to him along with me, explaining these plans of ours and asking whether these things satisfied him or not, and whether he required anything else besides them. I said this should be written as soon as possible. In the meantime, however, nothing new should be attempted by him regarding Dion’s property. These things were said between us. We agreed on nearly everything as I now describe.

But after this, when the ships had already departed and I therefore had no further opportunity to sail away, Dionysius—as if remembering something he had overlooked—said: "Half of Dion’s property ought to remain by right for his son, and the other half should be sent to Dion. I will therefore take care to sell this. When it is sold, I will hand over half the money to you to bring to Dion; the remaining part will be reserved with us for the son. For that is what justice itself requires." Struck by these words of his, I thought it ridiculous to speak further on the matter. I said, however, that we ought to wait for a response from Dion, and then write these very things back to him. But he, after this, very boldly sold all of Dion’s inheritance for whatever price and in whatever manner he pleased, to whomever he chose. He said absolutely nothing more to me about the matter; and I, likewise, spoke nothing further about Dion’s affairs from then on, since I judged that I would achieve nothing more. Thus far, in this way, I provided aid to philosophy and my friends.

After this, Dionysius and I lived in such a way that I was always looking toward the outside, like a bird desiring to fly away from somewhere <note>This famous metaphor illustrates Plato’s feeling of being a prisoner in the Syracusan court.</note>; while he, for his part, was constantly scheming how he might restrain me, granting nothing regarding Dion’s affairs. In other matters, however, throughout all of Sicily, we were acknowledged to be friends. At that time, Dionysius attempted to reduce the pay of the veteran soldiers, contrary to his father’s custom. The soldiers, being angry, gathered together and threatened that they would not tolerate it. Thus, he attempted to shut them out by closing the gates of the citadel. But they suddenly rushed to the walls, raising a certain barbaric and warlike shout. Terrified by this fear, Dionysius conceded everything customary to them and even more as they swarmed in. 

There was a rumor that Heraclides <note>Heraclides was a Syracusan politician and general who eventually helped Dion overthrow Dionysius.</note> was the cause of all the tumult. When Heraclides sensed this, he secretly fled. Dionysius, desiring to capture him but not finding him, summoned Theodotus to him in the gardens. I happened to be walking in the gardens myself at that time. As for the rest of what was discussed between them, I neither know nor heard while they were talking; but what Theodotus said to Dionysius while I was present, I both know and remember. 

"Plato," he said, "I am persuading Dionysius here that if I can bring Heraclides here to answer the charges brought against him, and if Dionysius does not wish him to remain in Sicily, he should at least permit him to take his wife and son and depart for the Peloponnese <note>The southern peninsula of Greece.</note>; and to live there, doing nothing against Dionysius, and receiving the fruits of the property he possesses here. Having this trust, I have already called for Heraclides, and I will call him again. If he comes here, whether from the first summons or the second, I have arranged with Dionysius and asked that no harm befall Heraclides, either outside the city or within it. If it seems best, he should only be sent beyond the borders until Dionysius decides otherwise. Do you concede these things, O Dionysius?" 

"I concede them," he replied, "and even if he should appear in your house, he shall suffer no harm."

The following day, at the very break of dawn, Eurybius and Theodotus flew to me, terrified in a strange way. Immediately Theodotus said, "Plato, you were present yesterday at the conditions upon which Dionysius agreed with me and you concerning Heraclides." 

"I was present," I said. 

But he said: "Now the guards are running about to seize Heraclides, and there is a danger that he is somewhere nearby. Follow us, therefore, with all haste to Dionysius." 

We went accordingly, and entering to him, they stood in silence, weeping; but I said: "These men are afraid, Dionysius, lest you do something new against Heraclides contrary to what was agreed yesterday. For it seems to me he has turned aside somewhere nearby, and it is manifest that he is present." 

Dionysius, hearing these things, flared up in anger and changed into various colors, such as anger is accustomed to bring. Theodotus, falling at his feet and taking his hand, pleaded with many tears that he should do no such thing. Then I, taking up the speech to comfort him, said: "Be of good heart, Theodotus. For Dionysius does not dare to do otherwise than what he promised yesterday." 

But Dionysius, looking at me with an excessively tyrannical expression, said: "I promised you nothing, whether great or small." 

"By the gods," I said, "you did promise not to do these very things which he is now pleading for you not to do." Having said these things, I walked out. 

After this, Dionysius continued trying to capture Heraclides. Theodotus, however, signaling this to him through messengers, warned him to take flight. Dionysius had sent a certain Tisias with guards, ordering them to pursue Heraclides everywhere. But he, as it is said, anticipating them and avoiding the guards by a small space of the day, withdrew himself into the borders of the Carthaginians. 

Now, Dionysius seems to have obtained a plausible occasion for the enmity that had arisen against me, which he had long sought through snares—namely, that money should not be sent to Dion. First, he dismissed me from the citadel, offering the excuse that the women were to perform ten days of sacrifices in the gardens where I lived. Therefore, he ordered me to stay outside the citadel with Archedemus <note>A follower of Archytas of Tarentum and a friend of Plato.</note> during those days. Meanwhile, Theodotus, calling me to him, complained much about Dionysius regarding what had then been done. When Dionysius heard that I had gone to Theodotus, finding in this again an occasion for hatred against me similar to the previous one, he sent to me a man to inquire whether, having been called to Theodotus's house, I had [spoken] anything...

where I had been. And I freely confessed that I had been present. Then he said, "Dionysius has ordered me to tell you that you are not acting rightly; for you always value Dion and Dion's friends more than him himself." These things were said. Nor after this did he ever call me into his house, as if I were clearly a friend of Theodotus and Heraclides <note>Heraclides was a Syracusan admiral and political rival to Dionysius who eventually helped Dion overthrow the tyrant.</note>, but an enemy to him. And for that reason, he was hostile because Dion's affairs had now entirely perished. I lived thereafter outside the citadel among the hired mercenary soldiers. But some people coming to me, including certain Athenian servants who were my fellow-citizens, indicated that slanders against me had been spread among the soldiers. Furthermore, they said that some had threatened that if they caught me anywhere, they would kill me.

I therefore devised an escape of this kind: I sent word to Tarentum <note>A Greek city-state in southern Italy</note> to Archytas and my other friends, indicating in what danger I was placed. They, devising a certain embassy in the name of their home country, sent Salmiscus, one of their own, together with a ship of the thirty-oared class. He, coming to Dionysius, requested that he permit me to depart safely entirely according to my will. Dionysius, having agreed, dismissed me and provided provisions for the journey. But as for Dion’s money, I did not ask for it, nor did anyone give it.

After this, when I had arrived in the Peloponnese and found Dion there watching the Olympic games, I recounted what had been done. He, calling Jupiter <note>original: "iouẽ" (Iovem). In a Greek context, this refers to Zeus, the god of oaths.</note> to witness, immediately declared to me and my relatives and friends that he would exact punishment from Dionysius—both because he had deceived me, his guest, there (for so he both said and felt), and because he had expelled Dion himself so unjustly. Hearing this, I advised him that he should call other friends for this purpose if he saw fit. As for me, however—since both his efforts and the efforts of others had, by a kind of violence, pushed me into the familiarity of Dionysius, and since I was bound by the sharing of a home, food, and religious rites—they should consider me as a kind of middle ground, and that I ought to be impartial to both sides. I added that for a long time, while many were slandering me to Dionysius as if I were plotting against him and his tyranny with you, he did not indeed kill me, but held me in respect. To this I added that my age was unfit for warlike affairs, and at the same time, I would be a kind of mediator between them, if ever there should be a need for a reconciler who could repair their friendship for those desiring it. But as long as you contend with hatreds, you will call upon others as defenders for these things. I said these things, because of the error and the fortune in Sicily that was utterly adverse to me. 

Since, however, they did not obey my reasons, they themselves provided the cause for all the evils that followed. Surely, if Dionysius had restored Dion’s property to him, or rather if he had been entirely reconciled, nothing adverse would have happened, as far as the human condition allows. For I would have easily restrained Dion by my will, counsel, and authority. But now, on the contrary, rushing against each other, they have filled everything with calamities. Dion certainly had the same will that I would say ought to be held both by me and others, whoever is moderate. Namely, that power—whether one's own, or of friends, or of the city—is to be desired so that anyone established in honors and powers, especially the greatest, may affect himself, his kin, and his country with just benefits. 

Nor does that happen if someone applies himself only to this: that he may fill himself and his friends with riches, and fill the treasury as he pleases through snares and cruel conspiracies—himself being poor, namely, powerless to restrain himself, but succumbing to pleasures through narrowness of mind. Furthermore, if he decides to slaughter wealthy men as enemies and seize their money, and meanwhile declares to his associates and family that they should not be angry with him for this since he is needy. In the same way, if someone similarly affecting his city with benefits is honored by it, while he distributes the property of a few citizens to the many through his decrees; or if someone presiding over a great city distributes the money of smaller cities unjustly to his own, while ruling over many greater and smaller cities. 

For in this way, neither Dion nor anyone else ever proceeds of his own will to a power that will be ruinous perpetually to both himself and his descendants. But a prudent man proceeds to the establishing of a republic and the founding of the most just and best laws, and that indeed without slaughters and civil expulsions. While Dion was acting in this manner—choosing to suffer unholy things rather than do them, though taking care lest he himself should suffer—he nevertheless fell when he had already reached the height of overcoming his enemies. Nor ought what happened to Dion seem a wonder to anyone. For impious men never entirely deceive a pious, temperate, and prudent man in matters of this kind. But it is not to be wondered at if the same thing happens to him which might perhaps happen to a good pilot: to whom a future storm is not entirely hidden, but the unusual and therefore unforeseen magnitude of the storms can be hidden, and by being hidden, may submerge him by force. In this way, chance seems to have deceived Dion to some extent. For it was not hidden from him that they were evil, but how deep the ignorance, iniquity, and greed was in them, remained hidden. Being deceived in this matter, he fell, subjecting Sicily to incredible grief. Therefore, what I counsel you after these things which have been narrated, let it be said thus far. But for what reasons I myself returned to Sicily as if compelled, I thought it necessary to show, lest my return should seem absurd and undertaken without reason. Wherefore, if these things I have now said seem more probable to anyone, and the occasions why it was done so seem to have been sufficient, we shall think enough and sufficiently has already been said.

### BOOK XXXVI.

<margin>Those who inflict many injuries on others suffer many things from others in return.</margin>
To tell the truth regarding what I say at present, all your counsel and zeal regarding all of Sicily—now that the tyranny is dissolved—is occupied with these matters. Indeed, some affect to raise the tyranny again; others seek to extinguish all memory of the tyranny entirely. In such matters, "right counsel" usually seems to many to be whatever results in the greatest harm to enemies and the greatest benefit to friends. Yet it is by no means easy for those who inflict many damages on others not to suffer many in turn. Nor is there any need to search far for examples of this; indeed, the things that recently happened in Sicily might be a sufficient example for us. For all things seem to have happened while some were attempting to inflict evils, and others to repel and avenge them. You can everywhere be suitable teachers of others in recounting these events. In understanding these things, there is almost no difficulty. But those things which are useful to all—to enemies and friends alike—or at least those which do the minimum of harm to them: these are certainly not easy to perceive, nor, after you have perceived them, to bring to fruition according to your wish. This consultation and inquiry, therefore, seems very much like a prayer. Therefore, let this be to us entirely like a prayer and a certain looking-forward <note>Original: "desperatio" – likely used here in an archaic or specific sense of a fixed expectation or a looking away from common outcomes.</note>.

<margin>In all things to be said and thought, the beginning ought to be from the gods.</margin>
For in all things, both in speaking and thinking, the beginning must always be made from the gods. A prayer of this kind will signify to us a perfect reason which may be profitable for you and your enemies alike. From the beginning of the time when war was waged in Sicily, one family has continuously dominated, whom your ancestors placed in charge of public affairs when they were situated in the greatest danger—at a time when they were being oppressed by the Carthaginians <note>The North African power that frequently battled Greek Sicilians for control of the island.</note> and the situation had come to an extreme crisis, lest Sicily, which was cultivated by the Greeks, should be thrown into confusion and devastated by the barbarians. At that time, they chose Dionysius <note>Dionysius I, the "Elder," who ruled Syracuse for nearly forty years.</note> as a young man vigorous in war to preside over the necessary military matters; but they wished Hipparinus <note>Dion’s father and a senior statesman who partnered with the elder Dionysius.</note>, as the elder, to moderate affairs with his counsel. And for the sake of the safety of all Sicily, granting them absolute authority, they called them "tyrants" <note>In the Greek context, "tyrant" often meant an extra-constitutional ruler, not necessarily a cruel one, though the word evolved toward its modern negative meaning.</note>, as it is said. Therefore, whether one judges a certain divine fortune and a god, or the virtue of those to whom the matter was committed, or both together with the citizens of that time, to have been the cause of that safety: let it be as each man thinks. Certainly, safety was obtained for them by this pact at that time. Wherefore, since they had conducted themselves in this way, it was just that gratitude be returned by those who had been saved. But if afterward the tyranny itself, abusing the gift of the state, committed any evil, it has judges for its crimes, from whom it may pay the penalty. But what penalties can necessarily and rightly be applied to them for those things which were done? For if either you could easily repel their force without great dangers and labors, or they thought they would easily regain their domination, we could by no means counsel you with those things we are now about to say.

But now, both sides ought to consider and remember how many times each of you has already come close to a certain hope of obtaining what you desired, thinking that only a little was lacking to achieve everything at your whim. Yet that very "little" has everywhere been the cause of huge and numerous evils; nor has it yet reached its end. Instead, in a certain continued succession, an old evil is renewed, and a new beginning arises where the end seemed to be. A circuit of this kind seems likely to destroy both the tyrannical and the popular factions; and, so far as can be feared by likely reason, all of Sicily seems destined to fall into an oblivion of the Greek language, transferred to the power and domination of the Phoenicians <note>The Carthaginians.</note> and the Opici <note>A group of ancient Italic peoples, often associated with the Oscan language.</note>. Wherefore, against these things, all Greeks ought to bring a remedy with all foresight. If anyone, therefore, brings forward a truer and better counsel than what I shall say, he will rightly be nicknamed "the Lover of Greeks." But what my opinion is, I shall now attempt to set forth quite freely, relying on common reason and law. I, therefore, assuming for myself the persona of an arbitrator—as I have long been accustomed to do—shall give counsel commonly to both the one exercising and the one suffering the tyranny. And first, to every tyrant: that he should flee this name and the thing itself, and transfer himself, if it can be done, into a kingship. That it can be done, Lycurgus <note>The legendary semi-mythical lawgiver of Sparta.</note>, a good and wise man, demonstrated in actual fact. For when he saw that his own kin were in Argos <note>A powerful Greek city-state in the Peloponnese.</note>, and had already transitioned from kingship into tyranny—and for that reason both these peoples were destroying themselves as well as each of their cities—fearing for both his country and his kin, he applied a remedy by creating a Senate and the magistracy of the Ephors <note>Five senior Spartan magistrates who served as a check on the power of the kings.</note> for the safety of the kingship. Because of this, it has been preserved with glory for so many centuries, for law, full of authority, became the queen of men, and not men the tyrants over the laws.

To this very thing, my reason at present exhorts all men, persuading those who affect tyranny to decline and flee—with a certain untiring zeal for fleeing—from the "happiness" of such starving and foolish men, and to transfer themselves as much as possible to a royal form of government, obeying royal laws, in order to eventually receive the greatest honors from men and from the laws which they follow willingly. Those, however, who prefer liberty above all ways of living, and flee the servile yoke as an evil, I warn them to beware: lest by an insatiable greed for immoderate liberty they fall into the sickness of their ancestors. Which indeed they suffered because, wishing to obey no one, they immoderately abused their love of liberty. For those who governed in Sicily before Dionysius and Hipparinus seemed to themselves to live happily, dissolved in their lusts and possessing authority. Furthermore, before Dionysius, they deposed and drove out ten prefects, judging no one according to the law, so that they might be subject to no man who judged justly, nor to any ruling law, but might be entirely free in every individual matter. For this reason, tyrannies arose among them.

<margin>Slavery and liberty, if they exceed measure, are both bad.</margin>
For both slavery and liberty, if they exceed measure, are bad. If they observe measure, both are good. Moderate servitude is that which is shown to God; immoderate is that shown to men. God indeed is to men the tempe... <note>The text breaks off here, likely intended to read "temperamentum" or "temperator," meaning "moderator" or "measure."</note>

<summary>Plato advises the factions of Sicily to abandon the cycle of vengeance and tyranny, warning that continued infighting will lead to the island being conquered by non-Greek powers. He proposes a transition from tyranny to a constitutional monarchy governed by laws, citing the Spartan lawgiver Lycurgus as a model.</summary>

## LETTERS.

...for the temperate, the law is the rule; but for the intemperate, it is pleasure. Since these things are so by nature, I advise and command the friends of Dion to proclaim to all Syracusans these points, which represent the common opinion of both Dion and myself. Indeed, I will explain to you what he, while still breathing, spoke. Someone might ask: what counsel does Dion bring to us regarding our present circumstances? Receive now this first point of all. In the beginning, let the laws be such that they do not turn minds toward the acquisition of wealth or toward lusts. Rather, since there are three things—the soul, the body, and money—let the laws place the virtue of the soul foremost. Second, let them place the virtue of the body as a servant to the virtue of the soul. Third and last, let them place the value of money, as it serves both the soul and the body. Any law that accomplishes this is correct, truly bringing happiness to those who use it. But to call the wealthy "blessed" is a mindless and unhappy way of speaking, suited only for women and children <note>Plato often uses "women and children" as a rhetorical shorthand for the unphilosophical or those easily swayed by appearances.</note>, and it makes those who believe it just like them. That I am now exhorting you toward true goods, you will understand by the work itself if you only taste what I have said regarding the laws. This examination seems to be the truest in all matters.

Once such laws are received—since Sicily is now placed in a state of crisis—you should neither seek to totally overcome others, nor should you be totally overcome yourselves. It will perhaps be just and useful for you all to strike a middle path, both for you who are fleeing the bitterness of absolute rule, and for others who desire to obtain that rule. Their ancestors once did what must be considered most important: they saved the Greeks from the Barbarians <note>Original: "Barbaris" — referring here to the Carthaginians, who frequently campaigned to conquer Sicily.</note>, so that it is even possible at present to consult about the republic. Otherwise, if affairs had been lost then, it would not be permitted to speak of these things now, nor would any hope remain. 

Now, therefore, let there be liberty for some with a royal power; for others, let there be a power subject to a kingdom, with the laws ruling over not only the other citizens, but even the kings themselves, should they act against the laws. In all these things, with a mind free from deceit and healthy, create your kings with the help of the gods. First, create my son <note>This refers to Hipparinus, the son of Dion.</note> for a double reason: for my sake and for his grandfather’s. For the grandfather in his time liberated the fatherland from the barbarians, and I have now twice liberated it from tyrants—of which you yourselves are my witnesses. Second, create as king the one who has the same name as my father: I mean the son of Dionysius <note>This refers to the son of the tyrant Dionysius the Elder, likely Dionysius II or another relative.</note>. Do this mindful of his present service to the fatherland and his previous character; though born of a tyrant father, he voluntarily attempts to liberate the fatherland, securing for himself and his lineage eternal glory in exchange for a brief and unjust tyranny. Third and finally, it is necessary to invite to the Syracusan throne—if he is willing and the city is willing—Dionysius the son of Dionysius, who is now the leader of the enemy’s army. Do this, I say, if he is willing to live content with a form of royal dignity, fearing the turns of fortune and pitying his fatherland and the sacred things and tombs of his ancestors, lest through his contention he loses everything entirely, gratifying the Barbarians through the fatherland’s unhappiness. 

Whether you give these three kings the same authority that the Lacedaemonian <note>Original: "Lacedæmonii" — the Spartans, who famously had two kings reigning simultaneously with limited powers.</note> kings have, or whether you take something away, you shall establish it by common consent through a certain pact. As was said before, hear it now again: if the family of Dionysius and Hipparinus wish to put an end to these pressing calamities for the safety of Sicily, securing honors for themselves and their whole family not only for the present but for the future, then call them to the kingdom under this condition. And choose whatever ambassadors they wish for the sake of harmony, with public authority—whether from your own citizens, from foreigners, or from both—in the number they allow. Let these men establish laws by common opinion and constitute the republic so that it is fitting for kings to be masters of the sacred rites and such other things as are proper for those whose benefits to the fatherland remain. 

Furthermore, let thirty-five men, created as <term>Guardians of the Laws</term> <note>Original: "custodes legum" — translating the Greek "nomophylakes," a common term in Plato's political theory for high-ranking magistrates who protected the constitution.</note>, have the judgment of war and peace together with the people and the senate. Let the courts be distinct, some for one thing and some for another. The authority over death and exile should rest with the thirty-five men; and besides them, with certain other judges elected from those who have most recently completed their magistracies, so that one is chosen from each magistracy who appears the best and most just. These men shall deliver sentences regarding death, imprisonment, and exile throughout the year. The king, however, shall not be permitted to take part in these trials, seeing as he is a priest; it would be a divine violation <note>Original: "nefas" — a crime against divine law or religious purity.</note> for him to be contaminated by a sentence of death, prison, or exile. 

These things I thought of while I was alive, and I still think they should be done now. And then, when I had overcome our enemies together with you, I would have established them as I had decreed, had not foreigners and Furies stood in the way. If things had proceeded according to my vow, I would have filled the rest of Sicily with colonists, after the Barbarians had been expelled from the places they now occupy—except for those who fought against tyranny for the common liberty. I would have restored the former Greek colonists to their ancient, ancestral seats. These same things, therefore, I advise everyone to deliberate upon and act on in the present by common counsel; and I exhort everyone to do these things, and if any disagree, to consider them enemies by common opinion. Nor are these things such that they cannot happen. For those things which are established in the minds of two people, and which soon and easily occur to those who seek out the best through consultation—whoever judges them impossible does not think correctly. By "two people," I mean the minds of Hipparinus (the son of Dionysius) and moreover my own son. For I believe if these two agree, the other Syracusans and all who care for the fatherland will also agree. But offer honors to all the gods with prayers, and to whatever others it is proper to vow alongside the gods. Furthermore, exhorting and inviting friends and enemies alike, do not stop until those things we have spoken of—which are like divine dreams appearing to those who are awake—are made clear...

### XXXVI.
### BOOK

->Plato to Archytas of Tarentum <note>Archytas was a celebrated Pythagorean philosopher, mathematician, and statesman who ruled Tarentum (in modern-day Italy).</note>, fare well. Letter IX.<-

<margin>No one is born for himself alone. <insert>to him</insert></margin> The associates of Archippus and Philonides have come to us, bringing the letter you gave them and reporting what was necessary regarding your affairs. They completed the public business of the city without difficulty, as it was not particularly laborious. However, they reported that you are very troubled because you are unable to free yourself from public civic duties. Now, it is clear to almost everyone that the sweetest way of life is to attend to one's own affairs—especially if one chooses to do the kind of things you do. But you ought also to consider this: that none of us is born for himself alone. Our country claims a part of our birth for itself; our parents claim a part; and our friends claim a part. Furthermore, many things happen to us through the various shifts of time that occupy our lives. Therefore, when your country itself calls you to govern the republic, it would perhaps be absurd not to obey—especially since it might otherwise happen that the way is left open for wicked men, who approach public life with no regard for what is best. Enough regarding these matters for now. As for Echecrates, we are taking care of him presently and will do so in the future, both for your sake and for that of his father Phrynion, and for the sake of the young man himself.

->Plato to Aristodorus, fare well. Letter X.<-

<margin>What true philosophy is: and the ornaments of the mind.</margin> I hear that you are now, more than others, an intimate friend of Dion, and that you have at all times practiced that wisdom of character which looks toward philosophy above all else. For I consider steadfastness, faith, and sincerity to be true philosophy. If anyone calls those other sciences and skills—which lean in different directions—"ornaments," I believe they would be naming them correctly. But fare well for now, and persevere in these present habits.

->Plato to Laodamas, fare well. Letter XI.<-

We wrote to you before that it would matter a great deal for all the things you mention if you were to come to Athens yourself. But since you say you cannot come, the second best thing would be if either I or Socrates <note>This likely refers to "Socrates the Younger," a member of the Academy, as the famous Socrates had been dead for many years by the time these letters were supposedly written.</note> could travel to you, as you indicated in your letter. Truly, however, Socrates is at this time hindered by the disease of strangury <note>A painful condition involving a blockage or difficulty in urination.</note>. As for me, it would be a disgrace for me to travel there if those goals for which you summon me could in no way be accomplished—and I have very little hope that they can be accomplished. If anyone were to attempt to recount all the reasons why I am so doubtful, it would require a very long letter. Furthermore, due to my age, my body is not healthy enough for completing the journey and facing the dangers encountered by sea and land—the kind of things a journey usually presents—especially at this time, when everything is full of danger for travelers. Nevertheless, I can offer advice to you and the colonists, though as Hesiod says (whom I now cite), to think is a deceptive thing, but to understand is difficult. For if some people think a city can ever be well-established by the mere setting down of any laws whatsoever, without there being someone presiding over the city with authority and moderating the daily life of all—so that life is temperate and brave for both the enslaved and the free—they think wrongly. Accordingly, if there are men among you worthy of this power, it might be done. But if there is a need for someone to provide instruction, I believe there are neither those among you who can teach nor those who can be taught; the remaining option is to pray to the gods. For almost as many cities as have existed up to this time were established in this way from the beginning, and were later well-refined through the coincidence of great events, whether in war or in peace, when in such times a famous and upright man attained great power. First, however, it is necessary and right to attend to these things most promptly; yet consider them as I say: do not approach them rashly as if they could be easily finished, but think of what can be conveniently achieved. Fare well and be happy.

<margin>To think is deceptive; to understand is difficult.</margin>

->Plato to Archytas of Tarentum, fare well. Letter XII.<-

<note>original: "M" - Large decorative initial M with floral and architectural motifs.</note> It is marvelous with what a glad heart we received the commentaries sent by you, and how we were delighted by the genius of their author. Indeed, the man himself seemed to us worthy of those great ancients. It is said that there were ten thousand such men among all the Trojans who rose up under Laomedon <note>The legendary king of Troy and father of Priam; the "ten thousand" refers to a lost tradition of Trojan excellence.</note>, as the legend goes. As for the commentaries which you requested from me by letter, they are not yet finished. However, I send them to you anyway, as it seems no encouragement is needed.

---

->THE END OF THE BOOK OF PLATO’S LETTERS.<-

->The remaining pieces added by the translator, since they are not by Plato, we have deliberately omitted.<-
->These, however, were printed with diligent care in the house of Ascensius <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius was a famous scholar-printer in Paris during the early 16th century.</note><-
->In the year of our Lord 1518. On the fifth day before the Kalends of June <note>May 28th, 1518.</note>.<-
->THANKS BE TO GOD.<-
